001-247556:
In *Editorial Board of the Newspaper and Internet Portal Magyar Hang and Alhambra Press Bt v. Hungary* (Application no. 52586/22), the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) examined a complaint under Article 10 of the Convention. The first applicant was the editorial board of the newspaper and internet portal *Magyar Hang*; the second applicant, Alhambra Press Bt, was its publisher.

On 17 August 2020, *Magyar Hang* published an online article entitled “Párbeszéd lodges criminal complaint in the Visegrád luxury hotel affair.” The article reported on a press conference held that day by B.T., a member of the opposition party Párbeszéd Magyarországért, concerning the allegedly fraudulent sale of a hotel in Visegrád. I.T., a businessperson and the Prime Minister’s son-in-law, was one of the shareholders of the company that sold the property.

According to the article, B.T. filed a criminal complaint suspecting misappropriation of funds causing particularly significant financial disadvantage. B.T. relied on press reports, stating that I.T.’s company, Hotel VSGRD Kft, had bought a hotel for around 1.6 billion Hungarian forints, planned to turn it into a luxury hotel, but left it half-finished. It was then allegedly sold to the business circle of X for 3.65 billion forints. B.T. claimed that I.T.’s business circle did not make value-increasing investments justifying the difference between purchase and sale prices, which exceeded two billion forints. The article also stated that Hotel VSGRD Kft had achieved a net profit of 1.21 billion forints, of which 1.075 billion was taken out as dividends.

I.T. asked the first applicant to publish a retraction, denying that he had acquired the hotel for around 1.6 billion forints through Hotel VSGRD Kft or sold it to the business circle of X for 3.65 billion. He said he had personally nothing to do with the price difference and briefly described investments on the property. When *Magyar Hang* refused, I.T. brought a civil action before the Budapest High Court, alleging dissemination of false statements.

On 13 November 2020, the High Court dismissed the action. It held that the article was based on B.T.’s press release and criminal complaint, that I.T. was a “special public figure” due to his real-estate, property-development and tourism activities and media appearances, and that he could rebut the statements himself. The court found that the article had faithfully reported statements by public figures, clearly indicated their source, and contained no further journalist discussion.

On 18 March 2021, the Budapest Court of Appeal upheld the decision for different reasons. It found the purchase-price statement true, held that I.T. lacked standing regarding the resale statement, and treated the statements about investments and value increase as value judgments.

On 13 October 2021, the Kúria reversed. It held that although the article recapitulated statements by a public figure, B.T., partly on a matter of public interest, the lower courts wrongly compared the case to public-funds cases. The hotel transactions did not involve public expenditure. I.T. could be a “public figure” only in relation to his economic role, wealth, and interest in public funds or procurement, but not here. The Kúria stated that the article factually reported the press conference, but regarding the estimated sales price, the applicants should have given I.T. an opportunity to refute the statements before publication, relying on Constitutional Court decision no. 34/2017. Public balance sheets did not prove the purchase and resale amounts. It ordered the first applicant to publish a retraction concerning the purchase and resale and the second applicant to pay I.T.’s legal costs and court fees of 322,200 forints.

On 28 June 2022, the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicants’ constitutional complaint. It held that I.T. was not a public figure, as he did not discuss politics or matters of general interest publicly and could not be considered a public figure solely because of his business interests or family ties. He could not be expected to respond by his own means, and the failure to give him an opportunity to publish a refutation was unacceptable. The applicants complained that the retraction order and costs award violated their Article 10 right to freedom of expression.

In *Editorial Board of the Newspaper and Internet Portal Magyar Hang and Alhambra Press Bt v. Hungary* (no. 52586/22), the applicants—Magyar Hang’s editorial board and its publisher Alhambra Press Bt—complained under Article 10 about a court order requiring Magyar Hang to publish a retraction of an online article and Alhambra Press to pay litigation costs, including the plaintiff’s legal fees and court fees.

On 17 August 2020, Magyar Hang published “Párbeszéd lodges criminal complaint in the Visegrád luxury hotel affair.” It reported a press conference by B.T., an opposition MP from Párbeszéd Magyarországért, about the allegedly fraudulent sale of a hotel. I.T., a businessperson and the Prime Minister’s son-in-law, was a shareholder in the selling company. The article said B.T. had filed a criminal complaint alleging misappropriation causing significant financial disadvantage. Relying on press reports, B.T. claimed that I.T.’s company, Hotel VSGRD Kft, had bought a hotel for about 1.6 billion forints, planned a luxury hotel but left it half-finished, then sold it to the business circle of X for 3.65 billion forints. He also claimed the property’s value had not significantly changed according to the property register; it was transferred to Minerva Investment Fund Management Zrt. at a much higher price; Hotel VSGRD made a net profit of 1.21 billion forints, with 1.075 billion taken as dividends; and no value-increasing investment justified the more than two-billion-forint difference. The article noted the allegations were based on media sources and prices were estimates.

I.T. requested a retraction, denying he had acquired the hotel for about 1.6 billion through Hotel VSGRD or sold it to X’s circle for 3.65 billion. He said he personally had nothing to do with the price difference and described certain investments. Magyar Hang refused, and I.T. sued for dissemination of false statements.

On 13 November 2020, the Budapest High Court dismissed the action. It found the article was based on B.T.’s press release and criminal complaint. It treated I.T. as a “special public figure” due to his business achievements in real estate, property development and tourism and his media appearances discussing his portfolio. He could rebut the statements himself, and Magyar Hang had faithfully reported public figures’ statements with clear sources and no further journalistic comment.

On 18 March 2021, the Budapest Court of Appeal upheld the dismissal for different reasons: the purchase statement was true; I.T. lacked standing on the resale statement; and the investment/value-increase issue was a value judgment. On 13 October 2021, the Kúria reversed. It held the report recapitulated B.T.’s statements partly on a matter of public interest, but the hotel transactions did not involve public funds. I.T. was not a public figure in this context, so his required tolerance was limited. Although the report factually recounted the press conference, the Kúria found that, as to the estimated sales price, the applicants should have given I.T. an opportunity to refute before publication, relying on Constitutional Court decision no. 34/2017. It ordered a retraction concerning the purchase and resale and ordered Alhambra Press to pay I.T.’s legal costs and court fees totaling 322,200 Hungarian forints.

On 28 June 2022, the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicants’ complaint. It found the article truthfully recounted B.T.’s statements. I.T. was a businessperson who did not publicly discuss politics or general-interest matters and was not a public figure merely because of his business interests or family ties. He could not be expected to reply by his own means, and the failure to give him an opportunity to publish a refutation was unacceptable. The applicants complain that the retraction order and cost liability violated Article 10.

Hungary* (Application no. 52586/22), concerns an alleged violation of Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights, namely the applicants’ right to freedom of expression. The first applicant is the editorial board of the Hungarian newspaper and internet portal *Magyar Hang*; the second applicant is its publisher, Alhambra Press Bt. They complained about a Hungarian court decision ordering the first applicant to publish a retraction concerning an online news article and ordering the second applicant to pay litigation costs, including the plaintiff’s legal expenses and court fees.

The dispute arose from an article published by *Magyar Hang* on 17 August 2020, entitled “Párbeszéd lodges criminal complaint in the Visegrád luxury hotel affair.” The article reported on a press conference held that day by B.T., a member of the opposition party Párbeszéd Magyarországért. B.T. had filed a criminal complaint regarding the allegedly fraudulent sale of a luxury hotel in Visegrád. The article stated that I.T., a businessperson and the Prime Minister’s son-in-law, was one of the shareholders of the company that sold the property. According to the article, B.T. suspected misappropriation of funds causing particularly significant financial disadvantage. Relying on press reports, B.T. alleged that I.T.’s company, Hotel VSGRD Kft, had bought a hotel for around 1.6 billion forints, planned to convert it into a luxury hotel, but left it half-finished, and then sold it to the business circle of X for 3.65 billion forints. B.T. further claimed that no value-increasing investments justified the more than two-billion-forint difference between purchase and sale prices. The article noted that B.T.’s allegations were based on media sources and that the prices were estimates.

I.T. asked *Magyar Hang* to publish a retraction, claiming the statements were false. He denied acquiring or selling the hotel for those amounts and said he personally had nothing to do with the price difference. When the applicants refused, I.T. brought a civil action, alleging dissemination of false statements.

On 13 November 2020, the Budapest High Court dismissed the action. It found that the article was based on B.T.’s press release and criminal complaint, that I.T. was a “special public figure” due to his business achievements and media appearances, and that he could rebut the statements himself. The court also found the article faithfully reported sourced statements by public figures without journalist commentary. On 18 March 2021, the Budapest Court of Appeal upheld the dismissal on different grounds: it found the purchase-price statement true, held that I.T. lacked standing regarding the resale statement, and classified the investment/value statements as value judgments.

On 13 October 2021, the Kúria reversed. It held that the article recapitulated statements by a public figure, B.T., partly on matters of public interest, but that the hotel transactions had no connection to public funds. Therefore, I.T. was not even a “public figure” in this context, and his required tolerance was limited. The Kúria found that the article gave a factually correct account of the press conference, but that the applicants should have given I.T. an opportunity to refute the statements before publication, relying on Constitutional Court decision no. 34/2017. It ordered a retraction concerning the purchase and resale of the hotel and costs of 322,200 Hungarian forints.

On 28 June 2022, the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicants’ constitutional complaint. It held that the article truthfully reported B.T.’s statements, but that I.T. was not a public figure: he was a businessperson who did not publicly discuss politics or matters of general interest, and he could not be expected to rebut press reports by his own means. The failure to offer him a prior opportunity to publish a refutation was unacceptable. The applicants therefore complained under Article 10 that the retraction order and costs award violated their freedom of expression.
001-245690:
In *Minasyan v. Armenia* (Application no. 54620/16), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 6 November 2025. The applicant, Zhorzh Minasyan, an Iranian national born in 1941 who lives in Yerevan, was represented by lawyer L. Manaseryan. The Armenian Government was represented by Y. Kirakosyan. The application was lodged under Article 34 of the Convention on 1 September 2016. The Court gave notice only of the complaint concerning the right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1 and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The case concerns the applicant’s allegation that he was denied access to the Court of Cassation in breach of Article 6 § 1.

The underlying dispute arose in 2014, when the applicant lodged civil claims with the Armavir Regional Court against a private company. He sought certain payments and annulment of a contract. On 29 April 2015, the Armavir Regional Court dismissed his claims. The applicant appealed. On 25 December 2015, the Civil Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and upheld the lower court’s judgment. The applicant received the Civil Court of Appeal’s decision on 8 January 2016.

On 28 January 2016, the applicant appealed on points of law to the Court of Cassation. In his appeal, he mentioned the date on which the Civil Court of Appeal’s decision had been served on him and provided evidence of that service. The key procedural dispute concerned the one-month time-limit for lodging an appeal on points of law.

On 9 March 2016, the Court of Cassation declared the applicant’s appeal inadmissible. It found that the appeal had been lodged outside the one-month time-limit, which it counted from the date of the Civil Court of Appeal’s decision rather than from the date of service. It further noted that no request to restore the time-limit had been submitted. In doing so, it relied on Article 233.1 § 1 (1) of the Armenian Code of Civil Procedure, under which an out-of-time appeal lodged without a request to restore the time-limit must be declared inadmissible.

The applicant complained before the European Court that this decision denied him access to the Court of Cassation, contrary to Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore narrow: the applicant filed his cassation appeal on 28 January 2016, within one month of receiving the appellate decision on 8 January 2016; he expressly referred to and evidenced the service date; nevertheless, the Court of Cassation treated the deadline as running from the date of the appellate decision, 25 December 2015, and refused to examine the appeal because it was out of time and no restoration request had been made. The case thus focuses on whether that procedural approach improperly restricted his right of access to the highest Armenian civil court. The Court adopted the judgment on 9 October 2025, and it was delivered on 6 November 2025.

**Minasyan v. Armenia** (Application no. 54620/16) is a case before the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section. The applicant, Mr Zhorzh Minasyan, an Iranian national born in 1941 who lives in Yerevan, lodged the application against Armenia on 1 September 2016 under Article 34 of the Convention. He was represented by Ms L. Manaseryan. The Armenian Government was represented by Mr Y. Kirakosyan. The Court, sitting as a Committee composed of Judges Andreas Zünd, Mykola Gnatovskyy and Vahe Grigoryan, with Martina Keller as Deputy Section Registrar, deliberated in private on 9 October 2025. Judgment was delivered on 6 November 2025.

The only complaint communicated to the Government concerned the applicant’s alleged denial of access to the Court of Cassation, in breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The underlying dispute was civil. In 2014, the applicant lodged civil claims with the Armavir Regional Court against a private company. He sought certain payments and the annulment of a contract. On 29 April 2015, the Armavir Regional Court dismissed his claims. The applicant appealed against that judgment.

On 25 December 2015, the Civil Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and upheld the lower court’s judgment. The applicant received the Civil Court of Appeal’s decision on 8 January 2016. On 28 January 2016, he lodged an appeal on points of law with the Court of Cassation. In his cassation appeal, the applicant mentioned the date on which the Civil Court of Appeal’s decision had been served on him and provided evidence of that service date.

On 9 March 2016, the Court of Cassation declared the applicant’s appeal inadmissible. It found that the appeal had been lodged outside the one-month time-limit for appeal, which it counted from the date of the Civil Court of Appeal’s decision—25 December 2015—rather than from the date of service. The Court of Cassation also noted that no request to restore the time-limit had been submitted. It relied on Article 233.1 § 1 (1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, under which an out-of-time appeal lodged without a request to restore the time-limit is to be declared inadmissible.

The applicant alleged that this refusal to examine his cassation appeal denied him access to the Court of Cassation, contrary to Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore the chronology of the domestic proceedings: the Civil Court of Appeal’s decision of 25 December 2015; the applicant’s receipt of that decision on 8 January 2016; his cassation appeal of 28 January 2016, in which he referred to and evidenced the service date; and the Court of Cassation’s decision of 9 March 2016 rejecting the appeal as time-barred without a restoration request. The central issue was whether the domestic courts’ application of the one-month time-limit, calculated from the date of the appellate decision rather than from service, and their refusal to restore the time-limit, unjustifiably restricted the applicant’s right of access to a court. The Court gave notice of this complaint to the Armenian Government and declared the rest of the application inadmissible.

CASE OF MINASYAN v. ARMENIA (Application no. 54620/16) is a European Court of Human Rights case brought against the Republic of Armenia by Mr Zhorzh Minasyan, an Iranian national born in 1941 who lives in Yerevan. The applicant was represented by L. Manaseryan. The Armenian Government was represented by Y. Kirakosyan. The Fifth Section Committee consisted of Andreas Zünd (President), Mykola Gnatovskyy, and Vahe Grigoryan, with Martina Keller as Deputy Section Registrar. The application was lodged on 1 September 2016, and the judgment was delivered on 6 November 2025. It is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The central complaint concerned the applicant’s allegation that he was denied access to the Court of Cassation, in breach of Article 6 §1 of the Convention. The Court gave notice of this access-to-court complaint to the Armenian Government and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

The underlying facts began in 2014, when the applicant filed civil claims in the Armavir Regional Court against a private company. He sought payment and annulment of a contract. On 29 April 2015, the Armavir Regional Court dismissed his claims. The applicant appealed.

On 25 December 2015, the Civil Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and upheld the lower court’s judgment. The applicant received that appellate decision on 8 January 2016. On 28 January 2016, he lodged an appeal on points of law with the Court of Cassation. In his cassation appeal, he mentioned the date on which the Civil Court of Appeal’s decision had been served on him and provided evidence of that service date.

On 9 March 2016, the Court of Cassation declared the applicant’s appeal inadmissible. It found that the appeal had been lodged outside the one-month time-limit for appeal, which it counted from the date of the Civil Court of Appeal’s decision rather than from the date of service. The Court of Cassation also noted that no request to restore the time-limit had been submitted. It relied on Article 233.1 §1(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, under which an out-of-time appeal lodged without a request to restore the time-limit must be declared inadmissible.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore: the applicant received the appellate decision on 8 January 2016; he filed his cassation appeal on 28 January 2016, which was within one month of service; he informed the Court of Cassation of the service date and provided evidence; the Court of Cassation nevertheless treated the appeal as out of time because it calculated the one-month period from 25 December 2015, the date of the appellate decision; and the applicant had not filed a separate request to restore the time-limit.

The applicant complained that this rejection barred his access to the highest domestic court, contrary to Article 6 §1. The case thus concerns whether the cassation court’s strict application of the time-limit, based on the date of the appellate decision rather than the date of service, and its refusal to examine the appeal absent a restoration request, unjustifiably restricted his right of access to a court.

The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment in *Yıldırım v. Türkiye* (Application no. 24775/19) on 10 July 2025. The application was lodged on 26 April 2019 under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicant, a Turkish national, was represented by Mr M. Çam, a lawyer practising in Çorum. The Turkish Government was given notice of the application. The judgment states that the applicant’s details and information relevant to the application appear in an appended table, but the supplied text does not reproduce that table. Consequently, the underlying domestic facts and the exact procedural failings are only referred to generally.

The applicant’s principal complaint was under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention: that domestic court decisions lacked reasoning or contained inadequate reasoning. He also raised a separate complaint under Article 8. The case therefore centred on the right to a fair hearing, specifically the right to a reasoned court decision.

The Court reiterated its established case-law that judgments of courts and tribunals should adequately state the reasons on which they are based, a principle linked to the proper administration of justice. The extent of this duty varies according to the nature of the decision and the circumstances. While courts are not required to give a detailed answer to every argument, parties to judicial proceedings can expect a specific and explicit reply to arguments decisive for the outcome. In cases concerning interference with Convention rights, the Court also examines whether the reasons given by domestic courts are automatic or stereotypical. The Court noted that these principles have been applied in a number of Turkish cases, including *Emel Boyraz*, *Deryan*, *Cihangir Yıldız*, *Hülya Ebru Demirel*, *Murat Akın*, *Pişkin*, and *Korkut and Amnesty International Türkiye*.

Applying those principles, the Court found that the domestic courts failed in their duty to provide reasons and did not address pertinent and important arguments raised by the applicant. The specific procedural failings were set out in the appended table. On that basis, the Court concluded that the applicant’s right to a reasoned court decision was not secured, and it found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The judgment therefore does not determine the merits of the underlying domestic dispute; the violation arises from the insufficiency of the reasoning and the failure to respond to the applicant’s key arguments.

As to the applicant’s remaining complaint under Article 8, the Court examined the application and considered that, in light of all the material in its possession and insofar as the matters complained of were within its competence, the complaint either did not meet the admissibility criteria in Articles 34 and 35 or did not disclose any appearance of a violation of Convention rights or Protocols. It therefore rejected that part of the application under Article 35 § 4.

In summary, *Yıldırım v. Türkiye* concerned an alleged breach of the fair-trial guarantee under Article 6 § 1 due to domestic courts’ failure to give adequate reasons and to address decisive arguments. The Court upheld that complaint, finding a violation, while rejecting the separate Article 8 complaint as inadmissible or manifestly unfounded. The key facts relevant to the violation are the domestic courts’ alleged lack of reasoning and their failure to engage with the applicant’s pertinent arguments; the precise factual details are contained in the appended table, which is not included in the supplied text.

While courts are not required to provide a detailed answer to every argument advanced by a complainant, parties to judicial proceedings can expect a specific and explicit reply to the arguments that are decisive for the outcome. In cases involving interference with Convention rights, the Court also examines whether the reasons given by domestic courts are automatic or stereotypical. The Court cited several prior Turkish cases applying these principles.

Reviewing the facts in light of those principles, the Court found that the domestic courts had failed in their duty to provide reasons for their decisions and had not addressed pertinent and important arguments raised by the applicant. On that basis, the Court concluded that the applicant’s right to a reasoned court decision under Article 6 § 1 had not been secured. It therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1.

001-243363:
**Case summary: Selimi and Krasnići v. Serbia (Apps. 20641/20 and 20644/20, ECtHR, 3 June 2025)**

The case concerned two Serbian nationals, Abdurahim Selimi and Bahrije Krasnići, whose pensions had been granted and paid by the Kosovo branch office of the Serbian Pensions and Disability Insurance Fund (SPDIF) before Kosovo came under international administration in June 1999. After that point, the SPDIF suspended payments. The Serbian authorities took the position that Serbia could no longer collect pension contributions in Kosovo and that Kosovo had established a separate pension system. The applicants complained under Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the non-payment of their pensions since 1999 and the length of the related administrative and judicial review proceedings.

The first applicant was granted an old-age SPDIF pension in December 1991, backdated to July 1990, and received monthly instalments until March 1999. In April 2013 he requested resumption of payments and arrears. The SPDIF refused in December 2013, saying he was already receiving a basic Kosovan pension and could not receive two pensions simultaneously. An appeal was dismissed in February 2014. The case was then repeatedly remitted—five times—in administrative and judicial review proceedings. In October 2021 the Administrative Court again remitted the case, finding that the SPDIF had failed to give adequate reasons and had not proved that the applicant had chosen a Kosovan pension over an SPDIF pension. In July 2022 the SPDIF again refused, citing the Kosovan pension, loss of documentation after the conflict, and the applicant’s failure to report the Kosovan pension. His appeal was dismissed in February 2024; the higher authority said he had to choose one pension, renounce the Kosovan pension, and reapply. The Administrative Court also repeatedly demanded a notarised authorisation form, although the applicant’s lawyer argued that no Serbian-recognised notaries existed in Kosovo. In December 2021 the Constitutional Court found a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time and awarded €900, but dismissed the property and pension complaints as premature because the administrative proceedings were ongoing. The first applicant died in March 2024; his widow sought to continue the case, but formal succession had not been established.

The second applicant was granted a survivor’s pension with a protective allowance in May 1986, backdated to September 1985, and received payments until February 1999. In March 2017 she requested resumption and arrears. The SPDIF refused in June 2017, citing insufficient evidence and the double-pension prohibition; the appeal was dismissed in September 2017. After four remittals, the SPDIF again ruled against her in November 2021, referring to Kosovan basic and contributory pensions and her failure to choose or provide documents. She died around 2020/2021. Her son sought to continue the proceedings, but the SPDIF and Administrative Court required a Serbian-certified authorisation from him. He lacked a Serbian ID card, and the lawyer argued that Serbian law did not require certification where the representative was a practising lawyer. The appeal was dismissed in August 2022 as brought by an unauthorised person. Further remittals followed; the SPDIF again refused in October 2023, and the appeal was dismissed in December 2023. Judicial review remained pending. The Constitutional Court in May 2021 found excessive length and awarded €500, but payment was blocked by succession and document-recognition issues. A civil claim partly succeeded in 2020 for arrears from March 2016 to December 2018, with appeals still ongoing.

The Court found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Although the suspension may have had a legal basis, the applicants were not afforded a reasonable opportunity to effectively challenge the continuing interference with their pension rights, particularly the failure to resume payments *pro futuro*. The lengthy proceedings, repeated remittals, and procedural obstacles were central to that finding.

In *Selimi and Krasnići v. Serbia* (Apps. nos. 20641/20 and 20644/20), two Serbian nationals complained under Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the prolonged administrative and judicial review proceedings and Serbia’s failure to pay their Serbian Pensions and Disability Insurance Fund (SPDIF) pensions after payments were suspended in 1999. Both pensions had originally been granted and paid by SPDIF’s Kosovo branch before Kosovo came under international administration in June 1999.

The first applicant, Mr Abdurahim Selimi, was granted an old-age pension on 5 December 1991, backdated to 1 July 1990. He received monthly payments until 1 March 1999, when they stopped. He complained repeatedly but received no answer. In 2013 he requested resumption of payments and arrears. SPDIF refused on 6 December 2013, saying he already received a basic Kosovo pension and could not receive two pensions simultaneously. After appeals and repeated remittals, the Administrative Court in 2021 criticised SPDIF for failing to give reasons and for assuming without evidence that he had not opted for the SPDIF pension. In July 2022 SPDIF again rejected his request, citing his Kosovo pension since 2004, loss of documentation after the conflict, and late reporting. He appealed in 2023. The Administrative Court repeatedly demanded a notarised authority form, although his lawyer argued that no such requirement applied to a practising lawyer and that no Serbian-recognised notaries existed in Kosovo. In 2021 the Constitutional Court found excessive length and awarded EUR 900, but dismissed his property complaints as premature. He died in March 2024, and his wife sought to continue the case.

The second applicant, Ms Bahrije Krasnići, received a survivor’s pension with a protective allowance from May 1986 until 15 February 1999. She requested resumption in 2017. SPDIF rejected her request, saying she had not proved whether she received a basic Kosovo pension and could not receive two pensions. After remittals, SPDIF in November 2021 found she received Kosovo basic and contributory pensions and asked her to choose; it also noted missing or invalid documentation. She died in 2021, and her son sought to continue. SPDIF dismissed an appeal as brought by an unauthorised person because the son had not provided an authority certified by Serbian authorities. The lawyer argued that Kosovan notary and UNMIK-certified documents, plus a lawyer’s authority, should suffice, and that obtaining Serbian ID or succession documents was impracticable. Further remittals and rejections followed. The Constitutional Court in 2021 found a length violation and awarded EUR 500, but payment was refused because the son lacked a Serbian ID and Serbian succession decision. Her civil claim for arrears partly succeeded in 2020, but appeal proceedings remained ongoing.

The central interference was the suspension of already-recognised SPDIF pensions and Serbia’s refusal to resume payment *pro futuro*. SPDIF relied on the prohibition of simultaneous pensions and on the inability to collect contributions in Kosovo since 1999. However, the applicants faced lengthy, repeatedly remitted proceedings and procedural demands for Serbian-certified authorisation or succession documents that were difficult or impossible for Kosovo residents to satisfy. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, holding that the applicants had not been afforded a reasonable opportunity to effectively challenge the interference with their property rights.

In *Selimi and Krasnići v. Serbia*, two Serbian nationals complained under Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the suspension of pensions paid by the Serbian Pensions and Disability Insurance Fund (SPDIF) through its Kosovo branch before Kosovo came under international administration in 1999, and about the length of related administrative and judicial proceedings.

After NATO intervention, Kosovo was placed under international administration in June 1999. The Serbian authorities explained that the pension system was based on ongoing financing and that, because no pension contributions had been collected in Kosovo since 1999, SPDIF pensions granted in Kosovo could not continue. Kosovo meanwhile operated a separate pension system. In 2013 Serbia invited eligible persons to seek resumption of their SPDIF pensions, requiring evidence such as identity documents, proof of life, and confirmation that they were not receiving Kosovo or UNMIK pensions, all in accordance with Serbian legislation.

The first applicant, Abdurahim Selimi, was granted an old-age pension in December 1991 by an SPDIF Kosovo branch, backdated to July 1990, and received payments until 1 March 1999. After the payments stopped, he complained repeatedly without response. In April 2013 he requested resumption and arrears. The SPDIF dismissed his request in December 2013, saying he was already receiving a basic Kosovan pension and could not receive two pensions simultaneously. The higher SPDIF authority upheld that decision in February 2014. Following five remittals, the Administrative Court in October 2021 again remitted the case, noting that the SPDIF had failed to give adequate reasons or evidence as to whether Selimi had opted for an SPDIF rather than Kosovan pension. In July 2022 the SPDIF again rejected him, citing his Kosovan pension since 2004, lost documentation, and his failure to report the Kosovan pension. He appealed in October 2023; the higher authority dismissed the appeal in February 2024, telling him to renounce his Kosovan pension and reapply. The Administrative Court repeatedly required a notarised authorisation form, although his lawyer argued this was unnecessary and that no Kosovo notaries were recognised. In December 2021 the Constitutional Court found excessive length, awarded €900, and dismissed his property and pecuniary claims as premature. Selimi died in March 2024; his wife sought to continue.

The second applicant, Bahrije Krasnići, was granted a survivor’s pension with a protective allowance in May 1986 by an SPDIF Kosovo branch, backdated to September 1985, and received payments until 15 February 1999. She also complained without response. In March 2017 she requested resumption and arrears. The SPDIF dismissed her request in June 2017, citing insufficient evidence about a Kosovan pension and the prohibition on double pensions; the higher authority upheld that in September 2017. After four remittals, the SPDIF again ruled against her in November 2021, citing Kosovan basic and contributory pensions and asking her to choose between them and her SPDIF pension. She had died, and her son sought to continue the proceedings. The SPDIF dismissed an appeal as unauthorised because no Serbian-certified authorisation from the successor was provided. Further remittals followed. In October 2023 the SPDIF again rejected the claim, saying she had received a basic Kosovan pension until death and could not receive two pensions. The higher authority upheld that decision in December 2023. The Administrative Court also demanded a Serbian-certified authorisation; the lawyer explained the son lacked a Serbian ID and that Kosovo notary and UNMIK documents were not accepted. The Constitutional Court in May 2021 found excessive length, awarded €500, but payment remained blocked over successor documentation. A civil claim for arrears partly succeeded in 2020, but appeals continued.

The Court found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning the failure to resume payments pro futuro, because the applicants had not been afforded a reasonable opportunity to effectively challenge the interference with their pension rights.

In *Zakaidze v. Georgia* (Application no. 42199/22), the applicant, Besik Zakaidze, complained that Georgia failed to conduct an effective criminal investigation into a physical assault by private individuals, that the offence was classified too leniently, that the sentence imposed was inadequate, and that he was prevented from participating effectively as a victim. The European Court of Human Rights examined the complaints under the procedural limb of Article 3.

On 9 February 2021, an altercation arose between the applicant and three neighbours after he asked one of them to repay money. All three neighbours beat him. Emergency services recorded that he had difficulty speaking and swallowing, pain and deformation in his lower jaw, and nausea. Hospital diagnosis included fractures to his lower jaw, excoriations on his nose, intracranial trauma and concussion. He underwent two jaw surgeries and was discharged in a stable condition on 16 February 2021.

A criminal investigation was opened the same day under Article 126 § 11 (b) of the Criminal Code, covering violence committed by a group. The applicant was promptly interviewed in hospital. The three neighbours were questioned and all admitted verbally and physically assaulting him. None was remanded in custody. Investigators inspected the scene, took photographs and questioned witnesses, including the emergency doctor.

The applicant complained about delay and requested information about charges. A forensic examination was ordered on 10 March 2021. The report of 1 July 2021 concluded that the abrasions were minor, while the jaw fractures and concussion were less severe bodily injuries causing long-term harm and were consistent with the date of the incident. On 8 July 2021, the prosecution reclassified the offence as intentionally causing less serious harm to health under Article 118 § 3.

The applicant had been granted victim status on 21 April 2021, but signed a document containing a pre-typed statement that he did not wish to review the case file or receive information about the case’s progress. He later alleged that he had been misled and pressured, and that his complaints went unanswered. On 22 July 2021, the Mtskheta District Court held a hearing; the applicant was not informed and was absent. The defendants pleaded guilty, and the court used simplified proceedings, convicting them and imposing suspended three-year sentences plus a non-contact order. The applicant complained that he had not been heard and that the sentence was disproportionate. He also sought access to the case file, but the court refused because he should have requested it earlier. On appeal, the Tbilisi Court of Appeal increased the suspended sentences to four years and added 200 hours of community service. The applicant attended and his written submissions were read. The Supreme Court rejected the prosecution’s cassation appeal in May 2022. A later civil compensation claim was dismissed for non-payment of court fees.

Before the Court, the Government argued non-exhaustion, time-bar and manifest ill-foundedness. The Court declared the application admissible. On the merits, it found the assault serious enough to trigger Article 3’s procedural obligation. It assessed promptness, adequacy, victim involvement and independence. The investigation was prompt and completed within about eighteen months. The forensic examination was not flawed, and the applicant had not sought additional medical evidence or investigative steps. Although his absence from the first-instance trial was regrettable, he participated at the appeal stage. The sentence was not manifestly disproportionate, and a civil compensation remedy had existed. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 3.

**Case: Zakaidze v. Georgia (Application no. 42199/22)**

The applicant, Besik Zakaidze, a Georgian national born in 1973 and living in Tvalivi, complained that Georgian authorities failed to conduct an effective criminal investigation into a violent assault by three private individuals. He originally relied on Articles 2, 6 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, but the European Court of Human Rights examined the complaints under the procedural limb of Article 3.

On 9 February 2021, an altercation arose between the applicant and three neighbours after the applicant asked one of them to repay borrowed money. The dispute ended with all three neighbours beating the applicant. Emergency services reported difficulties speaking and swallowing, pain and deformation of the lower jaw, and nausea. At hospital, he was diagnosed with fractures to his lower jaw, abrasions on his nose, intracranial trauma and concussion. He underwent two jaw surgeries and was discharged on 16 February 2021 in a stable condition.

A criminal investigation was opened the same day under Article 126 § 11(b) of the Criminal Code, concerning violence committed by a group. The applicant was interviewed in hospital, and the three neighbours were questioned shortly afterwards. All three admitted verbally and physically assaulting him. None was remanded in custody. Investigators conducted an on-site inspection, photographed the scene, questioned witnesses including the emergency doctor, and ordered a forensic medical examination of the applicant’s medical file. The forensic report of 1 July 2021 concluded that the abrasions and scratches were minor injuries, while the jaw fractures and concussion amounted to less severe bodily injuries causing long-term harm to health, consistent with the date of the incident.

The applicant repeatedly complained about delay, the allegedly inadequate and lenient legal classification, and his inability to access the case file or receive information. He was granted victim status on 21 April 2021, but signed a document containing a pre-typed statement that he did not wish to review the case file or receive information on progress. He later claimed he had been misled into signing it and that the investigator had pressured him. On 8 July 2021, the charges were reclassified from group violence to intentionally causing less serious harm to health under Article 118 § 3, and he was again granted victim status.

At trial on 22 July 2021 before the Mtskheta District Court, the applicant was not informed and did not attend. The three defendants pleaded guilty, the parties did not contest the evidence, and the court proceeded by simplified proceedings. All three were convicted and given suspended three-year prison sentences, with an order not to approach or communicate with the applicant. The applicant complained that he had not been heard and that the sentences were disproportionate. On appeal by the prosecution, the Tbilisi Court of Appeal on 3 November 2021 increased the suspended sentences to four years and added 200 hours of community service. The applicant was present and his written submissions were read, but no evidence was examined because the appeal concerned only sentencing. The Supreme Court rejected the prosecution’s cassation appeal on 30 May 2022. A later civil compensation claim by the applicant was dismissed for non-payment of court fees.

The alleged violations concerned the effectiveness of the investigation, the adequacy of the legal classification, the leniency of the sanction, and the applicant’s limited participation as a victim. The Court declared the complaint admissible but ultimately found no violation of Article 3, holding that the investigation was prompt, the forensic examination was adequate, the applicant’s participation was not so restricted as to breach the minimum standard, and the sentencing was not manifestly disproportionate.

In *Zakaidze v. Georgia* (Application no. 42199/22, judgment 4 November 2025), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Georgia had complied with its procedural obligation under Article 3 of the Convention to conduct an effective criminal investigation into an assault by private individuals. The applicant, Besik Zakaidze, originally complained under Articles 2, 6 and 8, but the Court examined the case under Article 3.

On 9 February 2021, an altercation arose between Zakaidze and three neighbours after he asked one of them to repay a loan. The three neighbours verbally and physically assaulted him. Emergency services reported difficulty speaking and swallowing, jaw deformation and nausea. At hospital he was diagnosed with bilateral lower-jaw fractures, nose abrasions, intracranial trauma and concussion. He underwent two jaw surgeries and was discharged on 16 February 2021.

A criminal investigation for group violence under Article 126 § 11(b) of the Criminal Code began the same day. The applicant was interviewed in hospital, and the three neighbours were questioned and admitted the assault. None was remanded in custody. Investigators inspected the scene, took photographs and questioned witnesses. A forensic medical examination was ordered on 10 March 2021. The applicant complained about delays and what he considered an overly lenient legal classification. On 21 April 2021 he was granted victim status, but signed a document containing a pre-typed statement that he did not wish to review the case file or receive information about the proceedings. He later alleged that the investigator had misled him and pressured him to give a less severe account; his complaints received no response.

On 1 July 2021, the forensic report concluded that the abrasions and scratches were minor, while the jaw fractures and concussion amounted to less severe bodily injuries causing long-term harm, consistent with the date of the assault. On 8 July 2021, the charges were reclassified from group violence to intentionally causing less serious harm to health under Article 118 § 3. The applicant was again granted victim status.

On 22 July 2021, the first-instance court held a hearing without informing the applicant. The three defendants pleaded guilty, did not contest the evidence, and were convicted in simplified proceedings. Each received a three-year suspended sentence and a no-contact order. The applicant complained that he had not been heard and that the sentences were inadequate. The prosecution appealed for a stricter penalty. On 3 November 2021, the Court of Appeal increased the suspended sentences to four years and imposed 200 hours of community service. The applicant attended; his written submissions were read, but no evidence was examined. The Supreme Court rejected the prosecution’s cassation appeal on 30 May 2022. A later civil compensation claim by the applicant was dismissed for non-payment of court fees, a decision upheld on appeal in June 2023.

Before the ECtHR, the Government argued non-exhaustion and time-bar. The Court declared the complaint admissible, finding that the criminal remedy was central and that the applicant had already pursued a civil claim against the assailants. On the merits, it found the assault serious enough to trigger Article 3’s procedural duty. It assessed promptness, adequacy, victim involvement and independence. The investigation was prompt; the case was finalised within about eighteen months. The forensic examination was not flawed, and the applicant did not challenge it or provide additional medical evidence. Although he was not informed of the first-instance trial, he was granted victim status twice, had opportunities to present his account, and participated at appeal. The sentencing was not manifestly disproportionate: the appeal court cited youth, no prior convictions, guilty pleas and cooperation, and imposed community service alongside suspended sentences. The civil compensation dismissal on formal grounds was not arbitrary. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 3.

In *Gullotti v. Italy* (App. no. 64753/14), the applicant, Giuseppe Gullotti, was convicted of mafia-type offences, including participation in Cosa Nostra, murder, extortion and weapons offences. Arrested in 1998, he was detained under the special prison regime of section 41 bis of the Prison Administration Act. That regime imposed severe restrictions: limited family visits, no non-family visits, no telephone use, limits on money and parcels, no participation in prison elections, reduced outdoor time, and monitoring of correspondence by judicial order under section 18 ter.

Since at least 4 December 2012, the Reggio Emilia sentence supervision judge had limited the applicant’s correspondence to relatives approved for family visits. The central challenged measure was an order of 8 January 2013, issued at the prison governor’s request, which renewed that limitation for three months, until 7 April 2013. The judge justified it by the applicant’s continued prominent role in Cosa Nostra despite his long detention, relying on investigative sources and statements by cooperating prisoners, and referring to a favourable opinion from the anti-mafia prosecution office.

The applicant appealed under sections 14 ter and 18 ter(6) of the Prison Administration Act. On 12 March 2013, the Bologna sentence supervision court upheld the order, reiterating that the applicant remained a member of the criminal organisation and had not distanced himself from it. On 21 March 2014, the Court of Cassation declared his further appeal on points of law inadmissible, finding the limitation justified.

While those appeal proceedings were pending, the Reggio Emilia judge renewed the correspondence limitation three more times, on 8 April, 9 July and 7 October 2013, each for three months. The April and October orders relied on essentially the same reasoning as the January order. On 30 October 2013, the Minister of Justice extended the section 41 bis regime for two years, citing anti-mafia information that the applicant was a mafia-clan leader in the Barcellona Pozzo di Gotto area and 2003 wiretaps referring to the impossibility of contacting him in person or by mail.

However, on 21 November 2013, the Bologna sentence supervision court allowed an appeal against the 8 April 2013 order, finding it inadequately reasoned. It noted that the order broadly referred to investigative sources without detailing their content and ignored favourable material, including a 2009 Turin decision granting early release and 2013 prison reports on good conduct and training. The applicant then asked that the 9 July and 7 October orders be declared unlawful on the same basis, but on 22 January 2014 the Bologna court found that request inadmissible under the Prison Administration Act. On 31 December 2013, the Reggio Emilia judge refused a further renewal request by the prison governor.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 8 that the limitation on his correspondence was not “necessary in a democratic society” because the 8 January 2013 order and subsequent domestic decisions were inadequately reasoned and based on stereotyped, insufficient grounds. The Government argued that the order was adequately reasoned and relied on the ministerial renewal, investigative material, wiretaps, the governor’s request, and a stopped 2012 letter allegedly containing an attempt to leak information from prison. The applicant also complained under Article 13 about the effectiveness of appeal remedies. The Court declared the Article 8 complaint admissible and ultimately found a violation, emphasising the lack of any explicit reference to specific circumstances justifying the additional correspondence limitation and insufficient evidence that a genuine assessment had been made.

Giuseppe Gullotti, an Italian national born in 1960 and detained in Parma Prison, was convicted of mafia-type offences, including participation in Cosa Nostra, murder, extortion, weapons offences and breach of preventive measures. That regime imposed restrictions on visits, telephone use, parcels, prison elections and outdoor time, and allowed monitoring of correspondence; concrete limitations on correspondence required a judicial order under section 18 ter.

Gullotti appealed under sections 14 ter and 18 ter(6). The main common issue is the Albanian Constitutional Court’s refusal to examine constitutional complaints against Supreme Court decisions because they were lodged outside the four-month time-limit. The key dispute is how that time-limit was calculated: the Constitutional Court counted it from the date the contested Supreme Court decision was adopted, not from the date it was served on or effectively communicated to the applicant. The applicants alleged that this practice breached their right of access to the Constitutional Court. In the first case, the applicant also complained about criminal proceedings; in the company’s case, it complained about inability to participate in proceedings before the Tirana District Court.

The facts follow a similar pattern. In **Ibrahimi**, the applicant was convicted of murder and sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment. The Supreme Court adopted its decision on 25 June 2015. A letter notifying him of the decision was served by prison authorities only on 12 May 2017. He lodged a constitutional complaint on 5 June 2017, alleging that he had not been informed of the Supreme Court hearing and had been unable to participate in person or defend himself through legal assistance of his own choosing. On 16 June 2017, the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible as out of time, counted from 25 June 2015.

In **Selimi**, a property dispute, the Supreme Court adopted its decision on 25 June 2015. It was served on the applicants on 18 October 2017, and they lodged a constitutional complaint on 13 February 2018. On 30 May 2018, the Constitutional Court declared it inadmissible as time-barred from the date of the Supreme Court’s adoption.

In **Nika**, concerning the applicant’s dismissal as a forestry inspector in Shkodër, the Supreme Court adopted its decision on 27 May 2020. It was served on her on 14 January 2021, and she filed a constitutional complaint on 18 January 2021. On 26 February 2021, the Constitutional Court rejected it as out of time from 27 May 2020.

In **Dedaj**, another dismissal case, the Supreme Court decided on 27 July 2020. The decision was served on the applicant on 1 April 2021, and he lodged a constitutional complaint on 9 June 2021. On 26 July 2021, the Constitutional Court declared it inadmissible as time-barred from the adoption date.

In **Industri Ndërtim (IN) SH.P.K.**, concerning civil contractual obligations, the Supreme Court adopted its decision on 17 February 2021. It was served on the company on 4 June 2021. The company lodged a constitutional complaint on 29 September 2021. On 29 October 2021, the Constitutional Court declared it inadmissible as out of time from the adoption date.

The applicants therefore alleged that the Constitutional Court’s rigid approach obstructed their access to constitutional justice. The Court gave notice of the complaints concerning access to the Constitutional Court and, in Ibrahimi, the fair-trial complaints about participation and legal assistance, and in the company’s case, participation before the Tirana District Court.
