In *Constantinou and Others v. Cyprus* (Apps nos. 77396/14, 45039/20, 45089/20, 45101/20 and 45899/20), 450 Cypriot nationals complained about Cypriot austerity laws reducing public-sector salaries and pensions during the financial crisis. The ECtHR examined alleged breaches of Article 6 §1 (fair hearing), Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (property), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 (discrimination).

The key facts concerned two laws. Law no. 112(I)/2011 imposed an extraordinary monthly contribution on gross salaries and pensions of officials, employees and pensioners in the civil service and wider public sector. Deductions were tiered: 0% below €1,500; 1.5% for €1,501–2,500; 2.5% for €2,501–3,500; 3% for €3,501–4,500; and 3.5% above €4,500. It took effect on 1 September 2011 for 24 months, but was extended to 31 December 2016. Later, Law no. 168(I)/2012 introduced reductions in emoluments and pensions from December 2012. Deductions initially ranged from 0% to 12.5%, later adjusted to rates as high as 17.5% for higher income brackets. These reductions had no fixed expiry, were amended several times, and were discontinued for all by 1 January 2023. The State deducted the relevant percentages from the applicants’ gross income or pensions.

The applicants challenged the measures domestically, arguing that their salaries and pensions were possessions and that the deductions violated Article 23 of the Cypriot Constitution (property), Articles 24 and 28 (taxation/equality), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. In *Charalambous and Others* (2014), the Supreme Court upheld Law no. 112(I)/2011 by 9–3. It accepted that salary was a proprietary right but held that the right did not extend to a particular salary amount. The small deductions did not affect the core of the right and were justified under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 24 of the Constitution in the public interest. Dissenting judges considered that Article 23 of the Constitution did not permit public-interest restrictions except for expressly listed grounds, and that compensation was required for material reductions.

As regards Law no. 168(I)/2012, the Administrative Court initially found the reductions unconstitutional under Article 23 because public interest was not one of its permitted grounds. However, in *Avgousti and Others* (2020), the Supreme Court reversed by 9–4. It held that salaries and pensions were property, but the reductions did not affect their core, were proportionate, income-related, temporary and ended in 2023. It distinguished *Koutselini-Ioannidou*, which concerned permanent deprivation. Dissents maintained that Article 23 provided stricter protection and did not allow public-interest reductions without compensation.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants alleged that the Supreme Court’s shifting case-law breached their right to a fair hearing under Article 6 §1 and violated legal certainty. They also alleged unjustified interference with possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and discriminatory targeting of public-sector workers under Article 1 of Protocol No. 12.

The Government argued that the measures were necessary to address an excessive budget deficit and financial crisis, stabilise public finances and avoid economic collapse. The ECtHR found no violation: there was no relevant divergence in the Supreme Court’s case-law, and reasonable explanations existed for its approaches. The reductions were temporary *de facto* reductions, reasonable and justified in response to the financial crisis, and struck a fair balance, within Cyprus’s wide margin of appreciation.

**Constantinou and Others v. Cyprus** concerned five applications by 450 Cypriot nationals challenging laws that reduced public-sector salaries and pensions during Cyprus’s financial crisis. Two legislative schemes were central.

**Law no. 112(I)/2011** imposed an “extraordinary contribution” on officials, employees and pensioners of the civil service and wider public sector from 1 September 2011. Deductions were tiered from gross salary/pension: 0% below €1,500, 1.5% on €1,501–2,500, 2.5% on €2,501–3,500, 3% on €3,501–4,500 and 3.5% above €4,500. Initially due to last 24 months, it was extended to 31 December 2016. A similar contribution was later imposed on the private sector.

**Law no. 168(I)/2012** imposed further monthly reductions on public-sector emoluments and pensions from December 2012. These were initially 0–12.5%, later rising to 17.5%, had no expiry date, and ended for everyone on 1 January 2023.

The applicants alleged violations of **Article 1 of Protocol No. 1** (property), **Article 6 § 1** (fair hearing/legal certainty), and, in one application, **Article 1 of Protocol No. 12** (discrimination). They argued that salaries and pensions were possessions; that the deductions were unlawful restrictions or deprivations without compensation; that fiscal consolidation was not a permissible ground under Article 23 of the Cypriot Constitution; that the measures unfairly targeted the public sector; and that there had been no individualised inquiry into their means.

Domestically, in **Charalambous (Supreme Court, 11 June 2014)**, the plenary upheld Law no. 112(I)/2011 by 9–3. The majority found that salary was a proprietary right, but that the right did not guarantee a particular amount. The small 1.5–3.5% deductions left the core of the right intact and were proportionate and justified under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The dissenters considered Article 23 of the Constitution stricter, with no public-interest exception, and found the deductions unconstitutional.

As to Law no. 168(I)/2012, the Administrative Court initially held the reductions unconstitutional. But in **Avgousti (Supreme Court, 10 April 2020)**, the Supreme Court reversed by 9–4. The majority held that the reductions were constitutional because they were temporary, tapered, income-related, rationally connected to the crisis, and did not affect the core of salary or pension rights or living standards. Dissenters said the reductions were indefinite, uncompensated, and contrary to Article 23.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants complained especially that the Supreme Court’s later case-law diverged from earlier decisions, violating fair-hearing and legal-certainty guarantees. The ECtHR found **no violation**. It concluded there was no genuine divergence in the Supreme Court’s case-law; the later decisions reasonably distinguished permanent-deprivation cases. On property, the reductions were temporary de facto measures responding to an excessive budget deficit and financial crisis. They pursued the public interest, were progressive, preserved the core of the rights, and struck a fair balance. Cyprus therefore did not exceed its wide margin of appreciation.

**Summary**

The case of *Constantinou and Others v. Cyprus* (Applications nos. 77396/14, 45039/20, 45089/20, 45101/20 and 45899/20) concerns challenges by 450 Cypriot nationals—public officials, civil servants, and pensioners—to State measures reducing their salaries and pensions during Cyprus's severe financial crisis. The applicants alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (fair hearing), Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property), and, in one application, Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 (non-discrimination).

The alleged violations arose from two pieces of legislation. First, Law no. 112(I)/2011, enacted on 31 August 2011, imposed an "extraordinary contribution" deducted monthly from the gross income and pensions of public sector officials and employees. Deductions were tiered, ranging from 0% for salaries below EUR 1,500 to 3.5% for salaries above EUR 4,501. The law was initially valid for twenty-four months but was extended to 31 December 2016, with minor amendments to the applicable percentages. The preamble cited an adverse financial period and the need to limit public expenditure, referencing the 11 July 2011 Mari naval base explosion as exacerbating the budget situation.

Second, Law no. 168(I)/2012, passed on 6 December 2012, provided for more substantial reductions in emoluments and pensions of public and broader public sector personnel. Deductions were tiered, ranging from 0% for low incomes to 12.5% initially, later adjusted to as high as 17.5% for salaries over EUR 4,000. The reductions applied from 1 December 2012 and were eventually discontinued on 1 January 2023. Amounts deducted were deposited into the State's fixed fund, calculated after income tax, and did not affect pension benefit calculations.

The applicants argued before domestic courts that the deductions were unconstitutional and violated their property rights under Article 23 of the Cypriot Constitution and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. They contended that salaries and pensions constituted proprietary rights, and that the interference did not fall within the permissible exceptions of Article 23 § 3, which permits restrictions only for specific grounds such as public safety, health, morals, town planning, or development and use of property for public benefit—grounds the applicants asserted did not cover consolidation of public finances.

In *Charalambous and Others* (11 June 2014), the Supreme Court plenary, by a 9-3 majority, upheld Law no. 112(I)/2011, finding the deductions relatively small (1.5%–3.5%) and that they did not affect the core of the applicants' property rights. The majority held that the right to a salary did not extend to a right to receive a salary of a particular amount. In *Avgousti and Others* (10 April 2020), concerning Law no. 168(I)/2012, the Supreme Court, by a 9-4 majority, reversed the Administrative Court's finding of unconstitutionality, holding that the reductions—though more substantial—did not affect the core of the right, did not endanger living standards, diminished from 2019, and ended in 2023, thus striking a fair balance.

Before the European Court, the applicants principally alleged a divergence in the Supreme Court's case-law concerning State interference with salaries and pensions, and violations of their property rights.

**K.V. Mediterranean Tours Limited v. Türkiye** (Application no. 41120/17, ECtHR Second Section, judgment 10 June 2025) concerns a Cypriot company’s property in the fenced-up area of Famagusta, northern Cyprus. The applicant company, whose shareholders and directors are Greek Cypriot, owned a building complex there but abandoned it after the 1974 Turkish military operation. In July 2010 it applied to the Immovable Property Commission (“IPC”), seeking restitution of the property, compensation for loss of use, non-pecuniary damages, statutory interest and legal costs.

After the “TRNC” authorities failed to reply, the company applied for a default judgment. Between December 2010 and June 2012, the IPC held ten hearings on that application. At each hearing, the “TRNC” Office of the Attorney General requested adjournments because a Land Registry report had not been provided. Those requests were granted. In October 2012 the applicant complained about delays. The authorities then indicated that the property appeared to be registered in the name of the Abdullah Paşa Foundation, managed by the Evkaf Administration.

In November 2012 the IPC admitted the Evkaf Administration as a third party, finding it might be affected by the claim. The applicant challenged that decision and the delays before the “TRNC” Administrative Court. In 2015 the Administrative Court held that Evkaf could not be a third party because this would make restitution impossible, and it said it lacked jurisdiction over the delay complaint. On appeal, in November 2016 the High Administrative Court held that it had exclusive jurisdiction over IPC matters but that adjournments and delays were not subject to judicial review. Relying on a 2005 Famagusta District Court judgment, it found Evkaf was the registered owner and should be admitted as a party.

In December 2019 the “TRNC” authorities filed submissions with the IPC. From January 2020 the applicant and its representative refused to attend IPC hearings, and further hearings were missed. In February 2024 the representative attended and discussed possible compensation proposals, but indicated settlement could be reached before the European Court. The IPC proceedings remain pending. The Government’s 2020 unilateral declaration was rejected by the Court in 2021.

The applicant alleged that the IPC proceedings were protracted and ineffective, contrary to Articles 6, 13 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It also complained that the admission of Evkaf as a third party and the High Administrative Court’s role undermined fairness and impartiality. The Government argued the application was premature and that domestic remedies remained available. The Republic of Cyprus alleged systemic flaws in the IPC, including excessive length, enforcement problems and independence concerns.

The Court examined the core complaint solely under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It found no violation of Article 6 § 1 concerning Evkaf’s participation as a third party: that participation was necessary to comply with fair-trial principles, and there was no arbitrariness or overall unfairness. However, it found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 because the IPC had failed to act with coherence, diligence and appropriate expedition in examining the applicant’s claim. Under Article 46, Türkiye was required to continue efforts to accelerate IPC proceedings and create an effective remedy providing genuine redress for delays.

**Case: K.V. Mediterranean Tours Limited v. Türkiye (App no. 41120/17), ECtHR Second Section, judgment 10 June 2025 (final 10 September 2025).**

The applicant is a Cypriot company established in 1967 and operating in Nicosia. It owned a building complex in the fenced-up area of Famagusta, northern Cyprus. Its shareholders and directors were Greek Cypriot. The company abandoned the property after the 1974 Turkish military operation.

On 23 July 2010 the applicant applied to the Immovable Property Commission (IPC), seeking compensation for loss of use, statutory interest, restitution of the property, non-pecuniary damages and costs. Because the TRNC authorities did not reply, the company applied for a default judgment on 1 November 2010. Between 7 December 2010 and 25 June 2012, ten hearings took place. At each hearing, the TRNC Office of the Attorney General requested an adjournment because a report on the property had not been provided, and each request was granted. On 23 October 2012 the applicant complained about these delays. At the same hearing, the authorities said the Land Registry and Surveys Department had not prepared the necessary report. A preliminary assessment suggested the property was registered in the name of a religious organisation, the Abdullah Paşa Foundation, managed by the Evkaf Administration.

On 23 November 2012 the IPC found that the Evkaf Administration might be affected and admitted it as a third party. The applicant challenged both the delays/adjournments and Evkaf’s participation before the TRNC Administrative Court. On 6 November 2015, that court held Evkaf could not be a third party because this would make restitution impossible, but it said it lacked jurisdiction over complaints about adjournments and delays. It ruled that adjournments and delays were not subject to judicial review. Relying on a 2005 Famagusta District Court judgment finding Evkaf to be registered owner, it held that Evkaf should be admitted as a party. The TRNC authorities filed their submissions only on 11 December 2019. From January 2020, the applicant and its representative refused to attend IPC hearings. A representative attended in February 2024 and agreed to forward any compensation proposals, but no settlement was reached. The IPC proceedings remained pending.

The applicant argued that the IPC had all relevant information but failed to decide, that the property’s location and registration to an Islamic foundation made restitution impossible, and that delays were caused by TRNC authorities. The Cypriot Government submitted that the IPC suffered systemic flaws, including unreasonably long procedures and enforcement problems.

The applicant alleged that the IPC procedure was protracted and ineffective and violated Articles 6, 13 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It also alleged unfairness and lack of impartiality because of Evkaf’s intervention. The Court examined the core complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It found no violation of Article 6 § 1 regarding Evkaf’s participation, holding that participation was a fair balance and necessary for the proper administration of justice, with no arbitrariness or overall unfairness. However, it found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 because the IPC failed to act with coherence, diligence and appropriate expedition in examining the applicant’s claim. Under Article 46, Türkiye was required to continue efforts to accelerate IPC proceedings and create an effective remedy providing genuine redress for delays.

In *Georgios Papadopoulos v. Cyprus* (Application no. 21454/21), the European Court of Human Rights examined the repeated annulment of the applicant’s election as a Member of Parliament, raising issues under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 concerning the right to free elections and choice of the legislature.

The key facts began with Cyprus’s May 2016 parliamentary elections. The applicant and Ms E.T. were candidates for the Solidarity Movement in Limassol. Ms E.T. was declared elected on 23 May 2016, but on 27 May 2016 she informed the Chief Returning Officer that she would not take the seat because she wished to remain a Member of the European Parliament. Domestic law at the time only provided for filling a parliamentary seat that became vacant *after* the parliamentary term had begun. It did not regulate a seat that was renounced or “not taken” before the term started.

The Chief Returning Officer, relying on an advisory opinion from the Attorney General, applied section 35(1) of the Elections Law by analogy and declared the applicant, as the first runner-up for Solidarity in Limassol, an elected MP. The applicant made the required affirmation in Parliament on 2 June 2016.

An electoral petition was filed. On 31 May 2017, the Electoral Court unanimously annulled the applicant’s election and declaration. It held that Ms E.T. had never acquired parliamentary status because she never made the affirmation required by Article 69 of the Constitution. Therefore, her seat had never been “vacated” during the parliamentary term. Section 35(1) only applied to seats vacated after the term began, and the Chief Returning Officer had impermissibly applied it by analogy.

Parliament then amended section 35(1) in June 2017 to include “not taken” seats. On 5 July 2017, the applicant was again declared an MP and took up duties. A second petition followed. On 30 April 2018, the Electoral Court, by six votes to five, annulled his election again and declared the 2017 amendment unconstitutional. The majority held that the Constitution recognised only “vacated” seats, not “not taken” seats; that the seat had never lawfully belonged to Solidarity; and that retroactively conferring the seat on the runner-up violated non-retroactivity and popular sovereignty. The minority considered that Parliament had validly filled a legislative gap.

In 2019, Parliament amended the Constitution and the Elections Law to cover renounced, not taken, and vacated seats. On 29 October 2019, the Returning Officer declared the applicant an MP for a third time. He affirmed on 1 November 2019. A third petition led to another annulment on 29 October 2020, by ten votes to one. The Electoral Court held the 2019 amendments unconstitutional and unlawful, finding retroactive interference with final judicial decisions, breach of non-retroactivity, finality, popular sovereignty, separation of powers, and equality. It applied the basic structure doctrine, reasoning that Parliament could not amend the Constitution so as to undermine fundamental democratic principles. The targeted legislation effectively appointed the applicant, deprived other candidates of a by-election, and deprived voters of an effective choice. The dissenting judge found the amendments compatible with the electoral system.

Before the ECtHR, the central alleged violation was that the applicant’s mandate was repeatedly annulled despite his status as first runner-up to a seat renounced before the parliamentary term. The Court found that the interference was not “lawful” because domestic law lacked a clear legal or constitutional framework for filling such a seat. The authorities and courts failed to resolve the issue, and repeated legislative attempts were invalidated, leaving the parliamentary seat vacant for significant periods. The annulments therefore violated Article 3 of Protocol No. 1.

Cyprus* (Application no. 21454/21, judgment 9 October 2025, final 9 January 2026), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section) found a violation of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 (right to free elections). The case concerned the repeated annulment of the applicant’s declaration as an elected member of the Cypriot Parliament.

On 31 May 2016, the CRO applied section 35(1) of the Elections Law by analogy and declared the applicant, the first runner-up, elected. The applicant affirmed his duties in Parliament on 2 June 2016. However, an electoral petition was filed. On 31 May 2017, the Electoral Court unanimously annulled his election and declaration. It held that Ms E.T. had never acquired parliamentary status because she had not made the Article 69 affirmation; the seat had never been “vacated” during the term; and the CRO could not apply section 35(1) by analogy in the absence of clear legislation.

Parliament then amended section 35 in June 2017 to include “not taken” seats. On 5 July 2017, the CRO again declared the applicant elected, and he affirmed on 7 July. A new petition followed. On 30 April 2018, the Electoral Court, by majority, annulled his election a second time and declared the 2017 amendment unconstitutional. It reasoned that the Constitution only addressed “vacated” seats, not “not taken” seats; the seat had never lawfully belonged to Solidarity; and retroactive legislation violated non-retroactivity and popular sovereignty.

On 29 October 2019, the Returning Officer declared the applicant elected a third time, and he affirmed on 1 November. A third petition was filed. On 29 October 2020, the Electoral Court, by majority, voided the applicant’s election again. It held that the 2019 constitutional and legal amendments were unconstitutional and unlawful because they retroactively affected an already decided electoral dispute, breached non-retroactivity, finality, separation of powers, equality, and the principle of popular sovereignty. The court applied the “basic structure” doctrine, saying Parliament could not amend the Constitution to undermine core democratic principles.

The Strasbourg Court found that the interference with the applicant’s right to free elections was not “lawful.” The central problem was the absence of a legal or permissible constitutional framework governing the filling of a seat that became vacant or was renounced before the start of the parliamentary term. The CRO initially acted by analogy, while later legislative attempts were struck down as unconstitutional or retroactive. Neither legislative nor judicial intervention resolved the issue, leaving the parliamentary seat vacant for significant periods and the applicant’s mandate annulled three times.

On 5 July 2017, the CRO again declared the applicant elected; he affirmed and took up duties on 7 July 2017. A new electoral petition followed. On 30 April 2018, the Electoral Court, by six votes to five, annulled the applicant’s election for a second time and declared the 2017 amendment unconstitutional. The majority found that the Constitution only addressed “vacated” seats, not “not taken” seats; the seat had never lawfully belonged to Solidarity; filling it with the runner-up required an election; and the retroactive amendment violated the principle of non-retroactivity and popular sovereignty.

In October 2019, Parliament amended Articles 66 and 71 of the Constitution and section 35 of the Elections Law to include “renounced,” “not taken,” and “vacated” seats. On 29 October 2019, the Returning Officer declared the applicant an MP for a third time, and he affirmed on 1 November 2019. Yet another petition was filed. On 29 October 2020, the Electoral Court, by ten votes to one, again annulled the applicant’s election and declaration. It held that the 2019 constitutional and legislative amendments could not be applied retroactively to the 2016 election; they violated the finality of earlier Electoral Court decisions, the principle of non-retroactivity, popular sovereignty, separation of powers, and equality. The court invoked the “basic structure” doctrine, reasoning that even constitutional amendments could not undermine fundamental democratic principles or decide an already-adjudicated electoral dispute.

The case therefore concerned the Electoral Court’s repeated annulment of the applicant’s declaration as an elected MP. The key alleged violation under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 was that there was no legal or permissible constitutional framework regulating the filling of a seat renounced before the parliamentary term began; that the applicant’s mandate was annulled three times; and that the failure of legislative or judicial intervention left the parliamentary seat vacant for significant periods. The Court found the interference was not “lawful” for Convention purposes.

In *Mediakompaniya Slovo, TOV and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 22347/14, judgment of 10 July 2025), three applicants—Mediakompaniya Slovo, its director and editor-in-chief Mr Vasylenko, and editorial director Ms Vasylenko—complained under Article 10 of the Convention that Ukrainian courts had ordered them to retract statements published in the newspaper *Subbota Plus*.

On 21 March 2013, Mr Vasylenko published an article entitled “Drained profitability of [V.]” concerning V., a large municipal water-supply company. The article alleged serious corruption and financial misconduct. It claimed that V.’s problems looked like embezzlement; that tens of millions of State funds had been squandered; that contracts were awarded through intermediary companies at inflated prices; that private enterprises had pocketed State money; that V. had given an interest-free loan of 16 million hryvnias to a private person; that renovation works involved fraud, second-hand parts and unlawful sale of pipes; that equipment was bought improperly; and that V. was near bankruptcy because of corruption, irresponsibility and poor management. The article relied partly on statements from employees and documents.

In April 2013, V. sued all three applicants, seeking retraction of the statements and compensation for non-pecuniary damage. The applicants argued that the statements were value judgments not susceptible of proof, that the information was not negative, and that it was unclear that the article referred to V. On 17 June 2013, the Zhovtnevyi District Court of Zaporizhzhya found against them. It examined each disputed statement, classified them as statements of fact, and held that the applicants had failed to prove their truth. The court ordered the applicants to retract the information, publish the operative part of the judgment in *Subbota Plus*, and refrain from disseminating the disputed information “by any possible means,” including television, print media, radio, the internet, interviews or conversations. It also ordered payment of 1 Ukrainian hryvnia in non-pecuniary damages and UAH 458 in court fees. Appeals were rejected, with a final decision by the Higher Specialized Court on 9 September 2013. According to the Government, the writs of execution were never submitted to the Bailiffs Service.

Ms Vasylenko died in 2020, and Mediakompaniya Slovo later stated that it did not wish to pursue the application. The Court struck out their complaints. The remaining applicant, Mr Vasylenko, maintained his Article 10 complaint.

The Government argued that the domestic decisions were lawful, pursued the legitimate aim of protecting V.’s reputation, and were necessary in a democratic society. Mr Vasylenko argued that Ukrainian law did not permit a court to prohibit dissemination of information “by any possible means”; Article 278 of the Civil Code allegedly allowed only prohibition of future publications or seizure of already-published copies.

The European Court of Human Rights declared the complaint admissible. It found that the judicial decisions interfered with Mr Vasylenko’s freedom of expression. The Court accepted that the interference had a legal basis in Article 278 of the Civil Code and pursued the legitimate aim of protecting V.’s reputation. It noted that a State-owned company may have an interest in protecting its business reputation and that public confidence in vital public services was important. The Court agreed with the domestic courts that the disputed statements were statements of fact, not value judgments, and that the public interest in corruption did not relieve the applicant of the duty to prove them. The penalties were modest, and the retraction order, publication of the judgment and ban on further dissemination were not unreasonable or unduly restrictive. The Court concluded that the interference was supported by relevant and sufficient reasons and struck a fair balance, so there was no violation of Article 10.

He argued that domestic law did not permit a court to ban dissemination “by any possible means”; Article 278 allegedly allowed only prohibition of future publications or seizure of already published copies. The Government argued the decisions were lawful, pursued protection of V.’s reputation, and were necessary in a democratic society.

The ECtHR declared the complaint admissible. It found the court decisions interfered with Article 10 but accepted that Article 278 provided a legal basis and that the aim—protecting V.’s reputation as a State-owned provider of a vital public service—was legitimate. The Court saw no reason to depart from the domestic courts’ finding that the statements were factual and unsupported by evidence. The public interest in exposing corruption did not relieve the applicant of proving serious factual allegations. On proportionality, the damages and fees were modest, and the retraction, publication, and non-dissemination orders were not unreasonable or unduly restrictive. The Court therefore concluded that the interference was supported by relevant and sufficient reasons and struck a fair balance, finding the measures compatible with Article 10.

Mediakompaniya Slovo, TOV and Others v. Ukraine (Application no. 22347/14) is a European Court of Human Rights Fifth Section judgment delivered on 10 July 2025. The applicants were Mediacompaniya Slovo, the publisher of the Subbota Plus newspaper; Mr Vasylenko, its director and editor-in-chief; and Ms Vasylenko, its editorial director.

On 21 March 2013, Subbota Plus published an article by Mr Vasylenko entitled “Drained profitability of [V.]”. V. was a large municipal water-supply company. The article alleged corrupt practices, embezzlement, and squandering of tens of millions of hryvnias in State funds. It claimed that funds were withdrawn through inflated contracts, intermediary suppliers, kickbacks, and fraudulent renovation works, and that public money flowed into private pockets. It also suggested that V. was near bankruptcy because of corruption, irresponsibility, and poor management.

In April 2013, V. sued all three applicants, seeking retraction of the statements and compensation for non-pecuniary damage. The applicants argued that the statements were value judgments, not facts; that the information was not negative; and that it was unclear that the article referred to V. On 17 June 2013, the Zhovtnevyi District Court of Zaporizhzhya found against them. It examined each disputed statement, classified them as statements of fact, and held that the applicants had not proved their truth. It ordered them to retract the information, publish the operative part of the judgment in the next issue of Subbota Plus, and refrain from disseminating the information “by any possible means” — including television, print media, radio, the internet, interviews, conversations, or any other means. The court also ordered payment of UAH 1 in non-pecuniary damages and UAH 458 in court fees, relying on Article 278 of the Civil Code. Appeals were rejected, with a final decision by the Higher Specialized Court on 9 September 2013.

The Government later stated that the execution writs were never submitted to the Bailiffs Service. Ms Vasylenko died in 2020, and in 2023 Mediacompaniya Slovo informed the Court that it did not wish to pursue the application. The Court struck out their complaints. Mr Vasylenko remained as the applicant.

Before the ECtHR, Mr Vasylenko complained under Article 10 that the domestic court orders violated his right to freedom of expression. The Government argued that the decisions were lawful, pursued the legitimate aim of protecting V.’s reputation, and were necessary in a democratic society. The applicant argued that Ukrainian law did not permit a court to prohibit dissemination “by any possible means”; Article 278 allegedly allowed only future publication bans or seizure of copies.

The Court declared the complaint admissible. It found that the judicial decisions interfered with Article 10. It accepted that the interference had a legal basis in Article 278 and pursued the legitimate aim of protecting V.’s reputation or rights. It saw no reason to depart from the domestic courts’ finding that the disputed statements were statements of fact rather than value judgments. Although corruption in a large municipal enterprise was a matter of serious public concern, that did not relieve the applicant of the duty to prove factual allegations. The domestic courts had found a lack of evidence. On proportionality, the penalties were modest, and the retraction order, publication of the judgment, and ban on further dissemination were not unreasonable or unduly restrictive. The Court concluded that the interference was supported by relevant and sufficient reasons and that a fair balance had been struck between free speech and V.’s reputation. Accordingly, no violation of Article 10 was found as regards Mr Vasylenko.

A.J. and L.E. v. Spain (Apps. 40312/23 and 40388/23) concerns two Spanish women who alleged that Spain failed to conduct an effective criminal investigation into their complaints of sexual assault by chemical submission, and that police lost or manipulated crucial evidence.

On the night of 7–8 December 2016, the applicants went to a bar in Pamplona and met D.C.M. and R.G.S. They drank alcohol and alleged that they had no memory of events until waking the next morning in one man’s residence, undressed and with the physical sensation of having had sexual intercourse. They claimed they had been drugged and rendered unable to consent. A.J. attended a health centre on 11 December 2016; the chemical-submission protocol was activated and police were notified. L.E. did not seek immediate medical attention.

The National Police UFAM unit investigated. On 27 December 2016, D.C.M. and R.G.S. were arrested and later questioned; both admitted sexual intercourse but said it was consensual. Restraining orders were imposed. The case was transferred to Investigating Court No. 1 of Pamplona.

A key conflict of interest emerged: R.G.S. was the brother-in-law of a UFAM police officer involved in the investigation. Several crucial evidence items also disappeared or were compromised while in police custody. The full forensic report on R.G.S.’s mobile telephone, sent from Madrid to Pamplona on 11 April 2017, vanished entirely. Bar CCTV footage was partially lost or altered. A hard drive containing forensic data from the suspects’ phones was wiped and overwritten, including backup copies.

On 20 November 2018, the investigating court declined to prosecute. Although it found the applicants credible, it held there was insufficient evidence of non-consensual acts or chemical submission. No timely toxicological evidence supported drugging. Later hair analysis found no date-rape substances, but showed prescription medication that could increase alcohol effects. Taxi drivers, bar staff and a friend observed no clear signs of incapacitation. The court acknowledged the investigation was “notably affected” by irregularities and missing digital evidence, but concluded this did not compensate for the lack of substantive evidence. Closure was upheld by the Navarra Audiencia Provincial on 23 June 2022; provisional dismissal followed on 9 July 2022, with appeals dismissed. The Constitutional Court declared the amparo appeal inadmissible on 6 July 2023, finding that fundamental-rights claims had not been sufficiently raised earlier.

Separate investigations examined the loss and manipulation of evidence. They looked at deletion of forensic data, the missing mobile report, altered bar footage, and the wiped hard drive. Officers, including R.G.S.’s relative, were investigated or questioned. Most proceedings were closed for insufficient evidence of intentional misconduct; disciplinary proceedings were suspended pending criminal outcomes.

The applicants complained under Articles 3 and 8 that Spain failed to conduct an effective investigation, failed to preserve evidence, lacked independence, and delayed excessively. The Government argued non-exhaustion. The European Court of Human Rights found violations of the procedural positive obligations under Articles 3 and 8: the systematic loss and destruction of potentially crucial evidence in police custody was not counterbalanced by other investigative measures, independence guarantees were insufficient, and the domestic response to the investigative failures was manifestly inadequate.

It held that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation: systematic loss and destruction of potentially crucial evidence in police custody was not counter-balanced by other investigative measures; there were insufficient guarantees of independence; and the domestic response to investigative failures was manifestly inadequate.

Spain* (Applications nos. 40312/23 and 40388/23), two Spanish women alleged that the authorities failed to effectively investigate their complaints of sexual assault by chemical submission. On the night of 7–8 December 2016, they met D.C.M. and R.G.S. in a Pamplona bar. They claimed they drank alcohol and later had no memory until waking undressed in one man’s residence with the physical sensation of intercourse, alleging they had been drugged and rendered unable to consent. A.J. underwent a medical examination on 11 December, triggering police notification; L.E. did not seek immediate medical attention. Police arrested the men on 27 December. Both admitted intercourse but claimed it was consensual. Restraining orders were imposed.

The investigation was marked by serious irregularities and evidence loss, central to the alleged breaches. R.G.S. was the brother-in-law of a UFAM police officer assigned to the case. A full forensic report on R.G.S.’s mobile phone, sent from Madrid to Pamplona, disappeared. CCTV footage from the bar was partially lost or altered. A hard drive containing forensic data from the suspects’ phones was wiped and overwritten, destroying all contents and backups. These materials were potentially crucial to proving chemical submission, lack of consciousness, and non-consent.

Domestically, Investigating Court No. 1 declined to prosecute in 2018, finding the applicants credible but insufficient evidence of non-consensual acts or drugging. In 2021 it concluded the summary without charges; in 2022 it provisionally dismissed the case. The Navarra Audiencia Provincial upheld closure, accepting that evidence had disappeared and that separate proceedings into those irregularities existed, but finding the remaining evidence insufficient. Hair analysis found no submission drugs, though prescription medication could have increased alcohol effects. Witnesses, taxi drivers and bar staff, saw no obvious incapacitation. Suspects’ vulgar messages were not probative. Three separate investigations into the lost digital evidence, altered video footage, and erased hard drive ended without charges, often because intent or responsibility could not be established. A police disciplinary inquiry remained suspended.

The applicants appealed, filed an *incidente de nulidad*, and sought *amparo*, arguing violations of dignity, integrity, effective remedy, equality, and fair proceedings, and relying on the Istanbul Convention. The Government argued before the ECtHR that the application was inadmissible for non-exhaustion: failure to invoke equivalent Article 3/8 rights domestically, failure to appeal the 23 June 2022 order, and failure to sue the State civilly. The ECtHR examined complaints under Articles 3 and 8 (procedural) of the Convention. It found that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into the chemical-submission sexual-assault allegations. The systematic loss and destruction of potentially crucial evidence in police custody was not counterbalanced by other investigative measures. There were insufficient guarantees of independence—especially given the family link between a suspect and a UFAM officer—and the domestic response to the investigative failures was manifestly inadequate. The Court therefore found violations of the procedural positive obligations under Articles 3 and 8.

**A.R.E. v. Greece (Application no. 15783/21), Third Section, judgment of 7 January 2025, final 30 June 2025.**

The case concerned the alleged “pushback” of a Turkish national from Greece to Türkiye. The applicant, born in 1992, had been accused in Türkiye of membership of FETÖ/PDY, detained for 28 months, and sentenced in March 2019 to six years and three months’ imprisonment. Released pending appeal, she was barred from leaving Türkiye. On 4 May 2019, she crossed the Evros River into Greece with two other Turkish nationals to seek international protection.

From early that morning, the applicant used WhatsApp “live location,” photographs and videos to communicate with her brother in Greece. She and her brother also emailed UNHCR, saying the group feared unlawful removal and that their lives would be in danger if returned to Türkiye. A lawyer, N.O., later saw the three Turkish nationals in Nea Vyssa and took a photograph. Police arrived and arrested them. At the police station, the applicant requested asylum for the first time. She was then taken to a border guard station in Neo Cheimonio, where she repeated her asylum request. She alleged she was held informally and unlawfully there until around 7 p.m., without information about the reasons for her detention.

According to her account, she was then transferred to a larger station, where belongings including phones, money and shoes were confiscated. She and others—31 people in total—were placed in a lorry and driven toward the Evros River. Masked or camouflage-uniformed officers forced them out. When some refused to disembark, officers beat them. The applicant shouted “asylum”; an officer replied in Turkish, “you will see where we will take you.” The group was put into a small inflatable boat and returned to Türkiye in several crossings. Turkish gendarmerie arrested them; the applicant was detained in Edirne and later Gebze Prison. Her brother lost her WhatsApp location later that day and was told at the border guard station that she was not there.

In June 2019, the Greek Council for Refugees filed a criminal complaint alleging abuse of power, unlawful detention, life endangerment, bodily harm and other offences. The Orestiada prosecutor dismissed it in December 2019 for lack of evidence, relying on police statements and finding no proof of pushback. An appeal led to further investigation, including testimony from lawyer N.O. and journalist Z.K., but the prosecutor dismissed the case again in September 2020. The Government denied all allegations, disputed the authenticity and probative value of the audiovisual material, and argued there were inconsistencies and no proof that the applicant had entered Greece or been pushed back.

The European Court of Human Rights found that a systematic practice of pushbacks from the Evros region to Türkiye was established. The applicant’s sufficiently convincing allegations of pushback were established beyond reasonable doubt. Her removal without any examination of her alleged risk of ill-treatment or her application for international protection violated Article 3. There was also no effective remedy under Article 13. The Court further found violations of Article 5 § 1, § 2 and § 4: her informal detention before pushback had no legal basis, she was not informed of reasons for arrest, and had no remedy to challenge the lawfulness of her detention. However, the alleged substantive Article 3 ill-treatment and Article 2 life-risk during the pushback were not proven beyond reasonable doubt for lack of clear and concordant evidence. The Court awarded just satisfaction for non-pecuniary damage given the seriousness of the violations and the lack of reparation at domestic level.

In *A.R.E. v. Greece* (ECtHR, Third Section, 7 January 2025), the applicant was a Turkish national who alleged she had been unlawfully “pushed back” from Greece to Türkiye. In Türkiye, she had been convicted of membership of FETÖ/PDY, sentenced to six years and three months, and released pending appeal with a ban on leaving the country. On 4 May 2019, she crossed the Evros River into Greece with two other Turkish nationals to seek international protection. Using WhatsApp, she shared live location, photographs, and videos with her brother in Greece, repeatedly expressing fear of being pushed back. She also emailed UNHCR and contacted a lawyer.

Greek police arrested the three in Nea Vyssa. At the police station they requested asylum for the first time. They were then taken to the Orestiada border guard station in Neo Cheimonio, where the applicant alleged they were informally and unlawfully held until 7 p.m., without information about their situation. She said they were later transferred by van and lorry with 31 other migrants, their belongings—including phones, shoes, and money—were confiscated, and she was forced to walk barefoot despite an injury. Near the Evros River, masked officers allegedly forced them onto a small inflatable boat and returned them to Türkiye in several crossings. Turkish gendarmerie arrested her; she was detained in Edirne Prison and later Gebze Prison.

The Greek Council for Refugees filed a criminal complaint alleging abuse of power, unlawful detention, life-endangerment, torture, and related offences. The Orestiada prosecutor dismissed it for lack of evidence, relying heavily on police statements. On appeal, the Thrace prosecutor ordered further investigation. Witnesses included lawyer N.O., who testified that he saw the applicant and her companions in Nea Vyssa and witnessed their arrest by an unmarked van, and journalist Z.K., who described communications and live-location tracking. The prosecutor again dismissed the case, finding no proof that Greek police carried out pushbacks. The Government denied all allegations, challenged the authenticity of the photos and videos, and questioned witness reliability.

The Court found a systematic practice of pushbacks to Türkiye from the Evros region. It held that the applicant’s allegations of pushback were sufficiently convincing and established beyond reasonable doubt, consistent with reports by national and international bodies. Her removal without any examination of her alleged risk of ill-treatment or her asylum application violated Article 3. The absence of an effective remedy violated Article 13 in conjunction with Article 3. The informal detention prior to pushback lacked any legal basis, violating Article 5 §1; she received no information on the reasons for her arrest, violating Article 5 §2; and there was no remedy to review the lawfulness of her detention, violating Article 5 §4. The Court further considered her specific allegations of ill-treatment during the pushback and risk to life, but found those alleged violations not proven beyond reasonable doubt for lack of clear and concordant evidence, so no separate violation of Article 2 or Article 3 was found on that basis. Given the seriousness of the violations and the lack of domestic reparation, the Court awarded just satisfaction.

Case A.R.E. v. Greece (Application no. 15783/21) concerns the alleged “pushback” of a Turkish national from Greece to Türkiye on 4 May 2019. The applicant, A.R.E., had been detained in Türkiye in 2016 on suspicion of membership of FETÖ/PDY, remained in pre-trial detention for 28 months, and in March 2019 was sentenced to six years and three months’ imprisonment. She was released pending appeal but prohibited from leaving the country. On 4 May 2019 she crossed the Evros River into Greece with two other Turkish nationals to seek international protection. Near Nea Vyssa, she contacted her brother via WhatsApp, used live location, sent photos and videos, and emailed UNHCR, stating that she feared being unlawfully returned and that her life would be in danger in Türkiye. A lawyer, N.O., and a Turkish journalist, Z.K., later testified that they were in contact with her and tracked her movements.

Police arrived in Nea Vyssa and arrested the three Turkish nationals. At the police station they requested asylum. The applicant alleged they were then taken to the Orestiada border guard station in Neo Cheimonio, held informally until 7 p.m., and given no information. They were transferred by van and then by lorry with 31 migrants to the Evros River. Her belongings, including phones, shoes and money, were confiscated; she was barefoot and suffering from a leg injury. At the river, masked men in camouflage uniforms forced them out. When she shouted “asylum,” an officer allegedly replied in Turkish, “you will see where we will take you.” Around 11 p.m. they were placed in a small inflatable boat and returned to Türkiye. Turkish gendarmerie arrested them; the applicant was held in Edirne and later Gebze Prison until October 2021.

A criminal complaint filed by the Greek Council for Refugees alleged abuse of power, unlawful detention, life-endangerment, torture and other offences. Greek prosecutors dismissed it in December 2019 and September 2020 for lack of evidence, relying on police statements and stating that no pushbacks had occurred. Witnesses N.O. and Z.K. were examined, but the applicant’s brother, then in Sweden, was not heard despite requests for mutual legal assistance. The Government denied all allegations, challenged the evidence’s authenticity and credibility, and relied on domestic findings that no pushbacks had been established. The applicant relied on witness testimony, WhatsApp material, a Turkish court decision confirming her return to Türkiye, and reports of systematic pushbacks in the Evros region.

The European Court of Human Rights found a systematic practice of pushbacks from the Evros region established. It held that the applicant’s allegations of pushback were sufficiently convincing and established beyond reasonable doubt. Greece violated Article 3 by removing her without examining her alleged risk of ill-treatment or her asylum application, and Article 13 read with Article 3 because no effective remedy existed. Under Article 5, her informal detention before pushback had no legal basis, she was not informed of the reasons for arrest, and had no remedy to challenge the lawfulness of detention. The Court found her account largely consistent with the reported modus operandi. However, the alleged substantive Article 2 and Article 3 violations concerning life or inhuman treatment during the pushback were not proved beyond reasonable doubt for lack of clear and concordant evidence; nevertheless, there was no effective remedy for those complaints. Just satisfaction was awarded given the seriousness of the violations and the absence of domestic reparation.

**Case: Lubarda and Milanov v. Serbia**  
**Applications nos. 6570/19 and 43604/19**  
**European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, Judgment of 29 April 2025**

The case concerned two applicants convicted in Serbian minor-offence proceedings for road-traffic offences. Their central complaint was under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights: they alleged that the proceedings were unfair because they had no opportunity to cross-examine the police officers whose reports and testimony were used to convict them.

The first applicant was convicted in 2017 of failing to comply with a traffic-light signal. He was fined EUR 120, banned from driving for three months, and received penalty points. The second applicant was convicted in 2015 of driving while intoxicated, described as being “in a state of complete intoxication.” He was fined EUR 850, banned from driving for eight months, and received penalty points. Although these were minor-offence proceedings, both offences were potentially punishable by imprisonment. Under the Minor Offences Act, if the fines were not paid, they could be converted into effective prison sentences of up to 15 days for the first applicant and up to 60 days for the second.

At the scene, both applicants signed reports drawn up by police officers. Later, however, they disputed the contents of those reports in court. Their convictions were based on the police reports and on evidence given by police officers. Critically, that officer evidence was taken in court but not during the main hearings in their cases. Neither the applicants nor their lawyers were summoned to the examination of the witnesses, even though they had explicitly requested to be present. The first applicant’s request was refused on grounds of efficiency and economy of proceedings. In the second applicant’s case, the court held that cross-examination would not have led to a different determination of facts because the officer’s evidence was consistent with the report the second applicant had signed.

Both applicants appealed their convictions. The Appeals Court upheld the convictions, and the Constitutional Court subsequently upheld them as well. The final domestic decisions were notified to the applicants on 1 August 2018 in the first applicant’s case and 26 February 2019 in the second applicant’s case.

Before the European Court, the Government objected to the applications being examined by a Committee, but that objection was rejected. The Court considered the applicants’ Article 6 complaints. The applicants did not argue that the underlying traffic offences were false; rather, they complained about the procedure by which they were convicted. Specifically, they claimed that the proceedings were not fair because the domestic courts relied on statements by police witnesses whom the applicants had not been given any opportunity to cross-examine. Although the applicants had signed the officers’ reports, they later contested those reports, and the courts’ reliance on the officers’ evidence without allowing confrontation formed the core of the alleged violation.

The case therefore concerned whether minor-offence proceedings complied with Article 6 fair-trial guarantees, particularly the right to examine witnesses whose statements are used as a basis for conviction. The Court’s judgment addressed these complaints.

Serbia* (Applications nos. 6570/19 and 43604/19), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered a judgment on 29 April 2025 concerning two applicants convicted in Serbian minor-offence proceedings for road-traffic offences. Under the Minor Offences Act, if the fines were not paid, they could be converted into effective prison sentences of up to 15 days for the first applicant and up to 60 days for the second applicant. This potential deprivation of liberty was relevant to the fairness complaint.

Both applicants appealed their convictions, but the Appeals Court upheld them. The Constitutional Court subsequently also upheld the convictions. The final domestic decisions were notified to the applicants on 1 August 2018 in the first applicant’s case and on 26 February 2019 in the second applicant’s case.

Later, however, they disputed the contents of those reports in court. The Court considered the applications together, having rejected the Government’s objection to examination by a Committee.

In *A.R. v. the United Kingdom*, the European Court of Human Rights examined the police disclosure, through enhanced criminal record certificates (“ECRCs”), of information that the applicant had been charged with rape and acquitted. A.R., born in 1978, was a qualified teacher working as a taxi driver. In March 2010 he was charged with raping a 17-year-old intoxicated passenger. He denied any sexual contact, and no forensic evidence linked him to the alleged victim. He was acquitted on 21 January 2011.

In March 2011, an ECRC was issued for A.R.’s application for a college lecturer post. Although he had no convictions or cautions, the ECRC included “other relevant information” disclosed at the chief police officer’s discretion. It stated that a 17-year-old female alleged that, while intoxicated in a taxi, the driver took her to a secluded location and forcibly had sex with her without consent. It recorded that A.R. was identified, arrested, denied sex and said she made advances he rejected; that the CPS charged him with rape; and that he was found not guilty and the case discharged.

A.R. objected, arguing that there was no conviction, the jury had rejected the complainant’s evidence, and disclosure was prejudicial and incomplete. The police upheld the disclosure. On administrative appeal, a reviewing officer concluded the information was relevant and sufficiently credible, partly reasoning that the CPS charge indicated the allegation was more likely true than false and that acquittal did not prove innocence. She found disclosure reasonable and proportionate because the allegation was recent, serious, relevant to working with vulnerable people, and the risk outweighed the impact on A.R.

In March 2012, a second ECRC for a private hire driver’s licence contained the same disclosure. The same reviewer and a senior officer again authorised it, considering relevance, gravity, reliability, elapsed time and impact. A.R. objected again, citing lifelong employment consequences, but the CRB confirmed the disclosure in August 2012.

Domestic judicial review failed. The High Court found Article 8 engaged but held the disclosure reasonable, proportionate and no more than necessary. The Court of Appeal dismissed his Article 6 § 2 and Article 8 claims. The Supreme Court dismissed the Article 8 appeal in July 2018. Lord Carnwath noted that, at the relevant time, there was no statutory guidance on the ECRC regime, no specific guidance on disclosing allegations after acquittal, and little guidance for employers. Although Article 8 was interfered with, he found no error in the proportionality assessment and said police should not conduct a “mini-trial.” In a postscript, he expressed concern about how employers use ECRCs and the danger they might infer guilt.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 8. The key facts relevant to that violation were that there was no statutory guidance to assist chief police officers in exercising their disclosure discretion; A.R. could not reasonably foresee the measure; the sensitive nature of the disclosure required comprehensive general guidance on the scope of discretion and its exercise; and there was no guidance for employers on handling such information. A.R. was not afforded an opportunity to make representations before the disclosure and had no possibility of independent review. The statutory scheme therefore gave the authorities excessively broad discretion and lacked sufficient safeguards against arbitrary exercise. The disclosure was accordingly not “in accordance with the law” for Article 8 purposes.

**Case: A.R. v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 6033/19)**

The applicant, A.R., a British national born in 1978, held a teaching qualification but worked as a taxi driver. In March 2010, he was charged with raping a 17-year-old female passenger. He denied any sexual contact, and there was no forensic evidence linking him to the alleged victim. On 21 January 2011, he was acquitted at trial.

The case concerns two police disclosures made through enhanced criminal record certificates (“ECRCs”) in 2011 and 2012. ECRCs, issued under section 113B of the Police Act 1997, contained convictions and cautions as well as “other relevant information” disclosed at a chief police officer’s discretion—sometimes called “soft intelligence.” The applicant had no convictions or cautions. Nevertheless, an ECRC issued in March 2011 for a college lecturer job included details of the rape charge, the alleged circumstances, his arrest and interview, and his subsequent acquittal. A second ECRC in March 2012, for a private hire driver’s licence, contained the same information.

The applicant objected, arguing that the disclosure was grossly prejudicial, that the jury had rejected the complainant’s evidence, and that he should not have to defend himself repeatedly after acquittal. His objections and administrative appeal were rejected. The reviewing officer reasoned that the Crown Prosecution Service’s decision to charge indicated the allegation was more likely than not true; that acquittal did not prove innocence because the criminal standard was higher than that for disclosure; and that disclosure was relevant because the applicant might encounter vulnerable females or children in the roles sought. The officer concluded that the potential risk to vulnerable people outweighed the impact on the applicant’s Article 8 rights.

The applicant sought judicial review. The High Court rejected his claim, finding the disclosure reasonable and proportionate. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal in 2016. In 2018, the Supreme Court also dismissed his Article 8 appeal. Lord Carnwath noted that at the relevant time there was no statutory guidance for chief officers on the ECRC regime and no specific guidance on disclosures following acquittal. He also observed that there was no clear evidence on how employers used ECRCs and expressed concern that employers might infer guilt from the mere fact of disclosure. Nevertheless, the Supreme Court found no error in the proportionality assessment.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged a violation of Article 8 of the Convention. The Court found that the disclosure interfered with his private life. The key issue was whether that interference was “in accordance with the law.” The Court held that it was not. At the relevant time, there was no statutory guidance to assist chief police officers in exercising their discretion, so the applicant could not reasonably foresee the impugned measure. The sensitivity of disclosing an acquitted rape charge required comprehensive general guidance indicating the scope of discretion and how it should be exercised. There was also no guidance for employers on handling such information, no opportunity for the applicant to make representations before the disclosure, and no possibility of independent review. The authorities therefore enjoyed excessively broad discretion, with insufficient safeguards against arbitrary exercise. The Court concluded that the disclosure was not in accordance with the law, violating Article 8.

In *A.R. v. the United Kingdom* (Application no. 6033/19), the European Court of Human Rights examined the police disclosure, through enhanced criminal record certificates (“ECRCs”), of information that the applicant had been charged with rape but acquitted. A.R., a qualified teacher working as a taxi driver, was charged in March 2010 with raping a 17-year-old female passenger. He denied any sexual contact. There was no forensic evidence linking him to the complainant, and on 21 January 2011 he was acquitted after trial.

In March 2011, an ECRC was issued for his application for a college lecturer post. Although he had no convictions or cautions, the certificate disclosed under “other relevant information” that he had been charged with rape, described the alleged circumstances, and noted his acquittal. A.R. objected, arguing that the disclosure was prejudicial, incomplete, and would prevent fair consideration for employment. The police upheld the disclosure. His administrative appeal was rejected. In the review, an officer relied on the CPS decision to charge as suggesting the allegation was more likely true than false, and reasoned that acquittal did not prove innocence because the criminal standard was higher than that for disclosure. The officer concluded disclosure was relevant and proportionate because the alleged offence was serious, recent, and relevant to protecting vulnerable people.

In March 2012, a further ECRC for a private hire driver licence contained the same information. A.R. again objected, saying it would affect his future and employment prospects. The disclosure was confirmed in August 2012.

A.R. sought judicial review, relying on Articles 6 § 2 and 8 ECHR. The High Court rejected his claim in 2013, finding the disclosure reasonable and proportionate and no more than necessary to protect vulnerable persons. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal in 2016, finding no breach of Article 8 and no undermining of the acquittal under Article 6 § 2. The Supreme Court dismissed his Article 8 appeal in 2018. It accepted that the reviewing officer had erred in assessing whether the allegation was more likely true than false, but found the first-instance judge had not made the same error and that disclosure was not disproportionate.

Before the ECtHR, the central issue was whether the disclosure violated Article 8. The Court found that the disclosure of the charge, acquittal, and alleged circumstances interfered with A.R.’s private life. The key violation was that the interference was not “in accordance with the law.” At the relevant time, there was no statutory guidance to assist chief police officers in exercising their discretion to disclose such sensitive non-conviction information. The applicant could not reasonably foresee the impugned measure. There was also no guidance for employers on handling such disclosed information. A.R. was not given an opportunity to make representations before the disclosure, and there was no possibility of independent review. The authorities therefore had excessively broad discretion, and the statutory disclosure provisions lacked sufficient safeguards against arbitrary exercise. The ECtHR concluded that the disclosure was not in accordance with the law and violated Article 8.

**Case: Radchenko v. Ukraine (Application no. 21217/17), ECtHR Fifth Section, judgment 11 September 2025.**

The applicant, a Ukrainian national, complained under Articles 10 and 13 of the Convention about the prolonged non-enforcement of a final domestic court judgment ordering the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources of Ukraine to provide him with public environmental information.

On 17 June 2015, prompted by environmental incidents in the Kyiv Region—a fire at a petroleum storage depot on 8 June, a fire at a plastic goods warehouse on 12 June, and peat burning from 9 June—the applicant asked the Ministry for information: (i) air-pollution levels by district and dangerous gases present; (ii) measures being taken to combat pollution and improve air quality; (iii) measures by the Ministry itself against technogenic catastrophes; and (iv) names and addresses of the owners of the depot and warehouse, their responsibility for the incidents, and how they were compensating damage. He relied on the Law on Access to Public Information and the Law on Protection of the Environment.

The Ministry’s reply allegedly did not contain the requested information. The Kyiv Circuit Administrative Court, by judgment of 17 September 2015, granted the applicant’s claim. It found that the Ministry’s reply contained none of the requested information and that other information provided was unrelated. No explanation was given as to why the information could not be supplied. The court noted that the Ministry was a central environmental authority responsible for monitoring, prevention, and informing the public; that the requested information was “public”; and that information about environmental protection and potential dangers had to be communicated within 48 hours. It ordered a full reply within that time-limit.

A further Ministry reply of 26 October 2015 provided information about air-quality monitoring bodies, links to online data, and a 2015–16 plan concerning the petroleum depot fire. The applicant again complained. On 25 November 2015, the court acknowledged the Ministry’s omissions and found the reply still incomplete. More broadly, it found that air-quality measurements were scattered and irregular, and that environmental information was not systematically gathered or published, causing a “systemic violation” of citizens’ right to environmental information, partly due to inconsistent legislation. The Ministry therefore did not possess some of the requested information. The court issued a separate ruling to several State authorities.

Enforcement proceedings followed. The Ministry sent more replies. A letter of 21 September 2018 stated that a governmental commission had been created, tests and daily air monitoring had been conducted, measures had been taken, and no excess air pollution had been found, but that the Ministry did not possess some requested air-pollution data. Enforcement was repeatedly terminated and reopened, then definitively terminated in October 2019 because enforcement was impossible “without the debtor’s participation.” A bailiff complained to the police about wilful non-enforcement, but no criminal proceedings were instituted. The applicant also complained to the Ombudsman, who stated that the Ministry lacked comparative air-pollution data and that only “existing” information was public.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant initially relied on Articles 10 and 13. He later raised Article 8, but the Court declined to examine it as a new, unsupported complaint. The Court considered the complaints under Article 10 only. The Government objected for non-exhaustion and inadmissibility under *Magyar Helsinki Bizottság*. The Court dismissed these objections: a person with a final judgment against the State need not bring separate enforcement proceedings; compensatory remedies were inadequate for non-substitutable obligations; and a criminal complaint would not secure enforcement. Article 10 was applicable because disclosure was imposed by an enforceable court order. The application was admissible. On the merits, the failure to provide the information despite the final judgment constituted an interference with Article 10; the Court examined legality, legitimate aim, and necessity together.

In Radchenko v. Ukraine (Application no. 21217/17), the applicant, a Ukrainian national, complained under Articles 10 and 13 of the Convention about Ukraine’s failure to enforce a final domestic judgment requiring the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources to provide him with public environmental information. The facts arose after several potentially harmful incidents in the Kyiv Region in June 2015: fires at a petroleum storage depot and a plastic goods warehouse, and peat burning. On 17 June 2015, the applicant asked the Ministry for information on air-pollution levels by district and dangerous gases; measures to combat pollution and improve air quality; the Ministry’s own measures against technogenic catastrophes; and the names and addresses of the entities owning the affected sites, their responsibility, and compensation. He relied on the Law on Access to Public Information and the Law on Protection of the Environment.

The Ministry’s reply, prepared with the State Ecological Inspectorate, did not supply the requested information. It referred to a ban on inspections, a request for an exceptional inspection of the company owning the depot, soil and water tests, and crisis monitoring. The applicant sued. On 17 September 2015, the Kyiv Circuit Administrative Court granted his claim, finding that the reply contained none of the requested information, gave no explanation for its absence, and that the information was public environmental information required to be disclosed within forty-eight hours. It ordered the Ministry to provide a full reply within that time.

A later Ministry reply of 26 October 2015 described monitoring bodies, provided links to public air-quality data, and attached a plan concerning the petroleum depot fire, but the applicant considered it incomplete. On 25 November 2015, the same court acknowledged the Ministry’s omissions and found that air-quality measurements were scattered and irregular and that environmental information was not systematically collected or published, causing a systemic violation of citizens’ right to environmental information. It also found that the Ministry did not possess the requested information and that the systemic deficiencies could not be resolved by enforcing the individual judgment. It issued a separate ruling addressed to several State authorities.

Enforcement proceedings were repeatedly opened and closed. A 21 September 2018 Ministry letter stated that a governmental commission had been created, tests had been conducted, information had been disseminated daily, and no excess pollution had been established; it admitted lacking some requested information. In October 2019, enforcement proceedings were definitively terminated as impossible without the debtor’s participation. A bailiff’s police complaint about wilful non-enforcement led to no criminal proceedings. The Parliamentary Ombudsman also informed the applicant that only “existing” information was public and that the Ministry did not possess comparative air-pollution data.

Before the European Court, the Government argued that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies by not claiming damages or seeking criminal proceedings, and that Article 10 did not apply because the information was not “ready and available” or instrumental to his expression. The Court dismissed these objections. It held that a final judgment against the State must be executed without separate enforcement proceedings, that damages were inadequate where the obligation was non-substitutable, and that criminal complaints were not effective. Article 10 applied because disclosure had been imposed by an enforceable court judgment. On the merits, the Court found that the Ministry’s failure to provide the information despite the final judgment interfered with the applicant’s Article 10 rights, and it examined whether that interference was lawful, legitimate, and necessary in a democratic society.

In *Radchenko v. Ukraine* (Application no. 21217/17), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) delivered judgment on 11 September 2025. The applicant, a Ukrainian national, complained under Articles 10 and 13 of the Convention about the prolonged non-enforcement of a domestic court judgment ordering the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources of Ukraine (“the Ministry”) to provide him with public environmental information.

The facts arose after several incidents in the Kyiv Region in June 2015: massive fires at a petroleum storage depot and a plastic goods warehouse, and the burning of peat. On 17 June 2015 the applicant requested information from the Ministry concerning: (i) air pollution levels in affected districts, organised by district and dangerous gases; (ii) measures being taken to combat pollution and improve air quality; (iii) measures by the Ministry to combat technogenic catastrophes; and (iv) the names and addresses of the legal entities owning the depot and warehouse, their responsibility, and compensation for damage. He relied on the Law on Access to Public Information and the Law on Protection of the Environment.

The Ministry’s reply, prepared through the State Ecologic Inspectorate, did not contain the requested information. It referred instead to a ban on inspections, a request for an exceptional inspection, and soil and water tests. The applicant sued. On 17 September 2015 the Kyiv Circuit Administrative Court granted his claim, finding that the reply contained none of the requested information and that no explanation had been given for its absence. The court ordered a full reply within 48 hours. A further Ministry letter of 26 October 2015 still did not satisfy the applicant, and on 25 November 2015 the court found continued omissions. It noted systemic deficiencies: air quality measurements were scattered and irregular, environmental information was not systematically gathered or published, and this amounted to a systemic violation of citizens’ right to environmental information. The Ministry did not possess part of the requested data. The court issued a separate ruling to several State authorities.

The applicant then initiated enforcement proceedings. The Ministry sent further replies, including a 21 September 2018 letter stating that a governmental commission had been created, monitoring had been disseminated, and pollution limits had not been exceeded, but admitting that the Ministry lacked part of the requested information on air pollution levels. Enforcement proceedings were repeatedly terminated and reopened, and in October 2019 were definitively terminated as impossible to enforce without the debtor’s participation. A police complaint about wilful non-enforcement led to no criminal proceedings. In 2016 the Ombudsman also confirmed that the Ministry did not possess comparative air pollution data and that only “existing” information was considered public.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant relied on Articles 10 and 13. He later raised Article 8, claiming health effects and personal impact, but the Court declined to examine it because it was raised late, unsupported, and not previously advanced domestically. The Court examined the case under Article 10 only. The Government objected that the applicant had not exhausted domestic remedies, namely a civil damages claim and his own criminal complaint. The Court dismissed those objections, holding that a final judgment against a State authority must be enforced without requiring separate enforcement proceedings, and that damages were inadequate where non-substitutable action was required. Article 10 was applicable because the disclosure had been imposed by an enforceable court order. The failure to provide the information despite that final judgment constituted an interference with the applicant’s Article 10 rights. The application was declared admissible and examined on the merits.
