In *Andersen v. Poland* (Application no. 53662/20), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section) examined an application lodged on 18 November 2020 by Mr Bartholomew Kyle Andersen, a Polish national born in 1988 who lives in Colwyn Bay, United Kingdom. The applicant complained under Article 8 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, which protects the right to respect for private and family life. His complaint concerned Poland’s refusal to recognise his same-sex marriage contracted abroad and the absence of any other form of legal recognition or protection for his relationship.

The key facts are these. On 7 May 2016, the applicant married his same-sex partner in Conwy, United Kingdom. In February 2017, he requested the Goszczyn Civil Status Office to register his marriage contracted abroad in the Polish civil registry. The Civil Status Office refused. It reasoned that entering a same-sex marriage in the Polish Registry would be contrary to the “basic principles of the Polish law.” The applicant appealed. The Mazowiecki Governor upheld the refusal. The Warsaw Regional Administrative Court also upheld the decision. The applicant then brought a cassation appeal. On 25 February 2020, the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed his cassation appeal. The judgment was notified to the applicant on 21 May 2020.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged that there was a total lack of recognition of his relationship in Poland. He complained that his marriage contracted abroad was not recognised by the Polish authorities in any way. He further complained that it was impossible for him to enter into any type of legally recognised union with his same-sex partner in Poland. According to the application, there was no other form of legal recognition and protection available for his relationship. The alleged violation under Article 8 therefore concerned the combined effect of the refusal to register his foreign same-sex marriage and the absence of any alternative legal framework recognising or protecting same-sex relationships in Poland. The case thus raised issues about the legal recognition of same-sex couples, the effect of such non-recognition on private and family life, and the State’s positive obligations under Article 8.

The Polish Government was given notice of the application and was represented by its Agent, Mr J. Sobczak of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The parties submitted observations. The Ordo Iuris Institute for Legal Culture was granted leave to intervene by the President of the Section and submitted third-party comments. The case was decided by a Committee of the First Section composed of Judges Erik Wennerström (President), Raffaele Sabato, and Artūrs Kučs, with Liv Tigerstedt as Deputy Section Registrar.

The judgment was delivered on 24 April 2025. It is final but may be subject to editorial revision. The central facts relevant to the alleged violation are that the applicant had a validly contracted same-sex marriage abroad, sought its registration in Poland, was refused at every domestic level on the ground that same-sex marriage conflicts with basic principles of Polish law, and had no alternative form of legally recognised union or protection available to him in Poland. The applicant’s Article 8 complaint therefore focused on the total non-recognition of his same-sex relationship and its consequences for his private and family life.

The case of *Andersen v. Poland* (Application no. 53662/20) is an Article 8 complaint before the European Court of Human Rights, First Section. The applicant, Bartholomew Kyle Andersen, is a Polish national born in 1988 who lives in Colwyn Bay, United Kingdom. He was represented by P. Knut. The Polish Government was represented by J. Sobczak. Ordo Iuris Institute for Legal Culture was granted leave to intervene and submitted comments. The application was lodged under Article 34 of the Convention on 18 November 2020. The First Section Committee, composed of Erik Wennerström, Raffaele Sabato and Artūrs Kučs, with Liv Tigerstedt as Deputy Section Registrar, deliberated on 20 March 2025 and adopted the judgment on that date; it was delivered at Strasbourg on 24 April 2025.

The factual background concerns the applicant’s same-sex relationship and his inability to obtain any legal recognition of it in Poland. Its stated reason was that entering a same-sex marriage in the Polish Registry would be contrary to the “basic principles of the Polish law.” This refusal was the first domestic decision directly affecting the applicant’s alleged right to respect for family life.

The applicant challenged the refusal. On appeal, the Mazowiecki Governor upheld the Civil Status Office’s decision. The Warsaw Regional Administrative Court also upheld the refusal. The applicant then brought a cassation appeal to the Supreme Administrative Court. On 25 February 2020 that court dismissed his cassation appeal. The judgment was notified to the applicant on 21 May 2020. The domestic proceedings thus ended with a final confirmation that the Polish authorities would not register or recognise the applicant’s same-sex marriage contracted abroad.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained under Article 8 of the Convention that his marriage with his same-sex partner, contracted abroad, had not been registered in Poland. He further alleged that there was no other form of legal recognition or protection for his relationship in Poland. In particular, he complained of a total lack of recognition of his relationship: it was impossible for him to enter into any type of legally recognised union with his same-sex partner, and his marriage contracted abroad was not recognised by the Polish authorities in any way. The alleged violation therefore centres on the cumulative effect of the refusal to register the foreign same-sex marriage and the absence of any alternative legal status or protection for same-sex couples in Poland. The Court gave notice of the application to the Government and received the parties’ observations as well as third-party comments from Ordo Iuris.

In **B.A. v. Iceland** (Application no. 17006/20), the applicant, an Icelandic national, complained that Iceland failed to protect her from domestic and sexual violence and to conduct an effective investigation into her allegations. She invoked Articles 3 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alleging ineffective investigation and inadequate protection, and Article 14, alleging gender-based discrimination in the handling of domestic violence cases.

In December 2017, B.A. lodged a police complaint against her former cohabitant, F.Þ., concerning physical, psychological, and sexual violence between 2011 and 2014. She alleged that F.Þ. humiliated and criticized her, isolated her from family, and controlled her life, with abuse escalating after she became pregnant. She described four sexual-violence incidents: being coerced into sexually stimulating F.Þ while hospitalized during pregnancy; rape at a rehabilitation clinic; rape in the hallway of their home; and rape while she was sleeping, which allegedly caused bruising. She also alleged a chokehold and a “headbutt.” She had not sought immediate medical attention after the incidents.

F.Þ. was first questioned in September 2018. He denied all wrongdoing, attributed relationship difficulties to B.A.’s alcohol consumption, admitted sexual intercourse at the rehabilitation clinic but denied rape, and admitted being controlling about her drinking and work. Eleven witnesses were questioned between eleven and thirteen months after the complaint. Several described B.A.’s isolation and changes after cohabitation began; some recounted humiliation or anger by F.Þ.; one said he heard B.A. scream and found her trembling and scared after the alleged chokehold. No witness directly observed the alleged physical or sexual violence; most accounts were based on disclosures after the relationship ended. The file included a Stígamót certificate stating B.A. had reported severe violence since 2015, psychiatric records from 2012 and 2017, and a February 2019 psychologist’s diagnosis of PTSD following an alleged sexual offence.

In June 2019, police discontinued the investigation. As to sexual violence, they found insufficient evidence and considered further investigation unlikely to improve the evidentiary position. As to physical violence, Article 218b of the General Penal Code had not entered into force until 2016, so the conduct could only be assessed under Article 217; the two-year limitation period had expired. The State Prosecutor upheld this in September 2019, concluding that Article 218b could not apply retroactively, the Article 217 limitation had expired, and the sexual-violence evidence was not sufficient or likely to secure conviction. The prosecutor also stated that further investigation would not change the position.

The applicant alleged that the legal framework before 2016 was inadequate, that psychological abuse was not criminalized, that consent was insufficiently investigated, and that the police delayed and improperly discounted corroborating evidence while giving undue weight to F.Þ.’s denials. She also alleged systemic gender bias. The Government maintained that such cases were prioritized, the investigation was comprehensive, and any delay did not prejudice the outcome.

The European Court of Human Rights declared the complaints admissible but found no violation of Articles 3 or 8: Icelandic criminal law provided adequate protective mechanisms, and the investigation as a whole met the required effectiveness threshold. It also found no violation of Article 14, as there was insufficient prima facie evidence of structural bias or disproportionate effect shifting the burden of proof to the State.

In *B.A. v. Iceland*, the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Articles 3 and 8, alone and with Article 14, that Iceland failed to protect the applicant from domestic and sexual violence, failed to conduct an effective investigation, and discriminated against her as a woman.

The applicant, born in 1975, alleged that between 2011 and 2014 her former cohabitant, F.Þ., subjected her to psychological, physical and sexual violence. She described humiliation, criticism, isolation and control, intensifying during pregnancy. She alleged four sexual-violence incidents: coerced sexual stimulation while hospitalised during pregnancy; rape at a rehabilitation clinic; rape in their home hallway; and rape while sleeping, causing bruising. She also alleged a chokehold and a headbutt. She did not seek immediate medical attention. In December 2017 she reported the conduct to police.

Police first questioned F.Þ. in September 2018, over nine months after her complaint. He denied all violence, blamed the applicant’s alcohol use, admitted controlling behaviour regarding her drinking and work, and admitted sexual intercourse at the rehabilitation clinic but denied rape. Eleven witnesses were later questioned, mostly 11–13 months after the complaint. Several described the applicant’s reduced contact with others, humiliation, F.Þ.’s anger, and one heard her scream and saw her trembling after the alleged chokehold. No witness directly observed physical or sexual violence; most accounts were based on her later disclosures. Evidence included a Stígamót certificate, psychiatric records from 2012 and 2017 noting depression and anxiety, and a 2019 psychologist statement diagnosing PTSD after the alleged sexual offence.

In June 2019 police discontinued the investigation. They found insufficient evidence on the sexual-violence allegations given F.Þ.’s denial and little prospect that further investigation would help. Regarding physical violence, Article 218b of the General Penal Code, on domestic violence, entered into force only in 2016 and could not apply retroactively; the alleged conduct fell under Article 217, but the two-year limitation period had expired. In September 2019 the State Prosecutor upheld this decision. It found Article 218b inapplicable retroactively, the sexual-violence evidence not sufficient or likely to secure conviction, and further measures unlikely to change the evidentiary position. Later, when asked whether Article 233b on gross defamation of a closely related person applied, the prosecutor said its review had not been confined to the police classification.

The applicant argued that the pre-2016 legal framework inadequately protected domestic-violence victims; that treating domestic violence like isolated assault, with a two-year limitation, was incompatible with Articles 3 and 8; and that psychological abuse and consent-based rape definitions were insufficient. She alleged investigative delays, systematic discounting of victim evidence and corroboration, over-reliance on F.Þ.’s denial, failure to investigate consent despite his admission of intercourse at the clinic, and failure to consider Article 233b. The Government maintained that sexual and domestic violence had long been prioritised; pre-2016 protection existed under Articles 217, 218 and aggravating factors; the investigation was comprehensive; delays resulted from the late complaint and resource pressures; and the evidence did not support prosecution.

The Court declared the complaints admissible but found no violation of Articles 3 or 8: Icelandic criminal law provided adequate protection mechanisms, and the investigation as a whole met the required threshold of effectiveness. On Article 14, it found insufficient prima facie evidence of structural gender bias or disproportionate effect to shift the burden of proof to the State, so no discrimination violation was established.

In *B.A. v. Iceland* (ECtHR, Second Section, 26 August 2025), the applicant, an Icelandic woman born in 1975, alleged that the Icelandic authorities failed to effectively investigate her complaints of domestic violence and sexual assault and discriminated against her on grounds of gender. She lived with her former cohabitant, F.Þ., from 2011 to 2014. She claimed he humiliated and controlled her, isolated her from family, and escalated to physical and sexual violence after she became pregnant. She described four sexual incidents: coerced sexual stimulation while hospitalised during pregnancy; rape at a rehabilitation clinic; rape in their home hallway; and rape while sleeping, causing bruising. She also alleged a chokehold and a headbutt. She did not seek immediate medical attention after the incidents.

In December 2017, she reported F.Þ. to the police. F.Þ. was first questioned in September 2018. He denied all wrongdoing, attributed relationship difficulties to the applicant’s alcohol use, admitted sexual intercourse at the rehabilitation clinic but denied rape, and admitted controlling behaviour concerning her drinking and work. Eleven witnesses were questioned 11–13 months after the complaint. None directly witnessed physical or sexual violence; several described the applicant’s isolation, changes in her behaviour, humiliation, and F.Þ.’s anger. One witness heard her scream and saw her trembling after an alleged chokehold. Evidence included a Stígamót certificate, psychiatric records, and a psychologist’s PTSD diagnosis linked to an alleged sexual offence.

In June 2019, police discontinued the investigation. As to sexual violence, they found insufficient evidence and no likely benefit from further investigation. As to physical violence, because Article 218b of the General Penal Code entered into force only in 2016, the conduct could be considered only under Article 217, for which the two-year limitation period had expired. In September 2019, the State Prosecutor upheld the decision: Article 218b could not apply retroactively; the Article 217 limitation had expired; and the sexual-violence evidence was not sufficient or likely to secure a conviction. Later, the applicant asked whether Article 233b on gross defamation of a closely related person applied; the prosecutor replied that the review had not been limited to the police’s classification.

The applicant complained under Articles 3 and 8, alone and in conjunction with Article 14, that the State failed to protect her and to conduct an effective investigation, and that the handling reflected gender-based discrimination in domestic violence cases. The Court declared the complaints admissible. On the merits, it found no violation of Articles 3 or 8: Icelandic criminal law provided adequate mechanisms for protection, and the investigation as a whole met the required threshold of effectiveness. It also found no violation of Article 14, as there was insufficient prima facie evidence of structural bias or disproportionate effect capable of shifting the burden of proof to the State. Thus, despite serious allegations and acknowledged delays, the ECtHR held that the authorities had not breached the Convention.

In *Zafferani and Others v. San Marino*, seven San Marino nationals who served as officers in the Uniformed Unit of the Fortress Guard complained about a legislative intervention that affected pending proceedings concerning their military career reconstruction. They were originally employed on a temporary basis between 2006 and 2008. They argued that under Law no. 132/1987, as amended by Law no. 99/1997, their enrolment should have become permanent after a successful one-year probation and that they were entitled to career advancement and related pay. Instead, their employment was periodically extended until 18 January 2016, when Parliament acknowledged their permanent recruitment under Article 63(1) of Law no. 189/2015 and placed them in Scale 5.

Between 28 January and 2 February 2016, the applicants asked the Public Administration Personnel Management Office (PAPMO) to reconstruct their careers, which would affect salary and entitlements. The acknowledgment receipts indicated the date from which the deadline for concluding the proceedings ran and referred to remedies under Law no. 68/1989. No immediate reply followed. On 25 July 2016, while those requests were pending, San Marino enacted Delegated Decree no. 88/2016. **Case: Panopoulou and Others v. Greece (Application no. 28983/20), European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, Committee Judgment, 23 October 2025.**

The case originated in an application lodged against Greece under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights on 6 July 2020. The applicants were represented by Mr A. Papakonstantinou, a lawyer practising in Athens. The Greek Government were given notice of the application. Following communication of the case, the parties attempted but failed to reach a friendly settlement.

The applicants’ personal details and further information relevant to the application are set out in an appended table to the judgment, which is not reproduced in the provided text. The central facts relevant to the alleged violations concern the non-enforcement of a domestic judgment given in the applicants’ favour. Specifically, the judgment at issue was no. 14300/2005 of the Athens Administrative Court of First Instance. Despite that judgment being in the applicants’ favour, the Greek authorities allegedly did not enforce it fully or in due time. The applicants therefore complained that the non-enforcement of the domestic judgment breached their rights under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and that they lacked any effective remedy in domestic law in that regard, contrary to Article 13.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants relied on Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention. Article 6 § 1 guarantees the right to a fair hearing, including the right of access to a court and the right to have final judicial decisions executed. Article 13 guarantees an effective remedy before a national authority for violations of Convention rights.

In its legal assessment, the Court reiterated its established case-law that the execution of a judgment given by any court must be regarded as an integral part of a “hearing” for the purposes of Article 6. It referred in particular to Hornsby v. Greece (no. 18357/91, § 40, Reports of Judgments and Decisions 1997-II). The Court also noted that it had already found violations in similar cases, including Kanellopoulos v. Greece (no. 11325/06, 21 February 2008) and Bousiou v. Greece (no. 21455/10, 24 October 2013).

Having examined all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on the admissibility and merits of the complaints. It considered that, in the instant case, the Greek authorities did not deploy all necessary efforts to enforce fully and in due time judgment no. 14300/2005 of the Athens Administrative Court of First Instance in the applicants’ favour. Consequently, the Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

The Court further noted that the applicants did not have at their disposal an effective remedy in respect of these complaints. It therefore also found a violation of Article 13 of the Convention.

In substance, the case concerns the failure of the Greek State to execute a final domestic judgment in the applicants’ favour within a reasonable time and the absence of an effective domestic mechanism to challenge that non-enforcement. The Court upheld the applicants’ complaints and found violations of both Article 6 § 1 and Article 13. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision. The excerpt does not provide details on just satisfaction, costs, or the specific underlying subject matter of the 2005 domestic judgment.

Chonin and Others v. Bulgaria (Application no. 30116/23) is a European Court of Human Rights case, Third Section, judgment dated 30 September 2025, concerning the length of restitution proceedings under Bulgaria’s Restitution of Title to Forests and Forestry Land Act.

The applicants are ten Bulgarian nationals, two of whom also hold Belgian and German nationality. They are heirs of Ms F., collectively inheriting about four-fifths of her estate. Ms F. had owned an afforested island in the Danube and mainland forests, all nationalised in 1948. After the Forests Restitution Act was adopted in 1997, the applicants initiated restitution proceedings. The earlier stages were described in Popov and Chonin v. Bulgaria (no. 36094/08, 17 February 2015), brought by one of the current applicants.

In a decision of 12 December 2000, the competent land commission, later renamed the Agriculture Department, recognised the heirs’ right to compensation in lieu of restitution for 93.38 hectares of forestry land. Restitution in kind was impossible because the land once owned by Ms F. was located in a frontier zone and classified as exclusive State property. Since the Forests Restitution Act only allows compensation through equivalent State-owned land, the authorities spent years attempting to identify suitable substitute plots. A 2007 court judgment identified one such plot and ordered its transfer to the applicants, but the judgment was ultimately unenforceable because the land formed part of a national park.

After the Popov and Chonin judgment, further developments occurred. In decisions issued in 2013 and 2018, the Agriculture Departments in Montana and Berkovitsa allocated forestry land totalling about 59 hectares to the applicants. These decisions were served on Mr Chonin, who acted as representative for all applicants, in 2018. He challenged the decisions, arguing that the quality of the forests was inferior to that of Ms F.’s original forests. Nevertheless, the decisions were upheld in final court judgments given in 2023 and 2024. An additional plot of about 5.3 hectares has been identified, but the process of officially allocating it to the applicants remains ongoing. The competent authorities are still working to locate further plots to compensate the applicants for the remaining approximately 29 hectares of forestry land.

The Court gave notice to the Bulgarian Government only of the complaints concerning the lengthy duration of the restitution procedure and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. Belgium and Germany, whose nationalities two applicants also hold, did not exercise their right to intervene. The central alleged violation is therefore the excessive length of the restitution process. Although the applicants have received partial substitute land, the procedure has continued for many years—initiated after the 1997 Act and still unresolved for a significant portion of the claimed 93.38 hectares. The key facts relevant to the length complaint are the prolonged efforts to find equivalent State land, the failed 2007 transfer due to the national park designation, the partial allocations in 2013 and 2018, their final validation in 2023 and 2024, and the continuing outstanding allocation of about 5.3 hectares plus the search for about 29 more hectares. The case thus focuses on whether Bulgaria violated the Convention’s reasonable-time requirement in a restitution procedure that remains partly pending.

Lasku and Others v. Albania (Application no. 6045/14) is a case brought by 13 Albanian nationals against Albania, lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 31 December 2013. The Court gave notice of complaints concerning legal certainty, property rights, and length of proceedings; the remainder was declared inadmissible. The principal complaint is under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention: that domestic authorities annulled three final property commission decisions, breaching legal certainty. Related property and length issues arise from intertwined civil and administrative proceedings over the same land.

In 1996–97, the Tirana Commission on Property Restitution and Compensation recognised the applicants’ inherited property rights over three plots totaling 1,070 sq. m and ordered their restitution. The Immovable Property Registration Office (IPRO) registered their title. In 1996, the Tirana Municipality issued a building permit for a gas station on 700 sq. m of that land. The applicants built it with M. company; in 1998 the IPRO registered their title to the gas station. The applicants then transferred administration and possession to M. company under a cooperation agreement to share profits equally.

In 2000, M. company sued the applicants for ownership of the building and land; the applicants counterclaimed for possession. In 2004, both claims were dismissed because the cooperation agreement prevented awarding possession to either party. In 2003, the applicants sued M. company for their profit share. The Tirana Court of Appeal allowed the claim in 2013, and the Supreme Court upheld that judgment in 2022. In 2021 the applicants complained about the length of these proceedings; in 2023 the Supreme Court dismissed the complaint, saying the case had already been adjudicated and the delay was attributable to Albania’s judicial reform.

The central alleged violation concerns a 2007 amendment to the Property Act that empowered the director of the Agency for the Restitution and Compensation of Property—successor to the Commission—to review and annul former commission decisions ex officio, with no time limit. On 27 November 2007, the Agency annulled the three Commission decisions restoring the 1,070 sq. m plots. It reasoned that the original commission lacked jurisdiction: the 1993 Property Act allowed it to recognise property rights and decide on restitution, but not to order actual restitution. It also said the land could not be restituted despite being registered as state property. The decision recognising the applicants’ inherited rights remained in force.

The applicants challenged that annulment. The District Court allowed their claim, but the Court of Appeal quashed that judgment in 2010 and the Supreme Court upheld it in 2012. In 2013 the Constitutional Court found violations of the applicants’ fair-trial rights by the Supreme Court and remitted the case. On retrial, in 2014 the Supreme Court again dismissed the applicants’ appeal. In 2015 the Constitutional Court dismissed their constitutional complaint, finding that the Agency’s review power was still in force when the Court of Appeal adjudicated and that its own judgments did not have retroactive effect. However, in 2010 and 2011, the Constitutional Court had annulled such amendments as unconstitutional, finding violations of legal certainty and property rights.

Separately, in 2008 the applicants brought another claim against M. company. The District Court terminated their agreement but dismissed their restitution claim; the Court of Appeal and Supreme Court upheld that outcome in 2011 and 2022. In 2023 the Constitutional Court dismissed their complaint, although it found the second set of proceedings before the Supreme Court excessively lengthy, holding it lacked jurisdiction to award compensation. In legalisation proceedings, M. company built an unauthorised construction, legalised in 2013; in 2014 the State sold M. company a 595.8 sq. m plot that formed part of the applicants’ claimed land. The applicants did not challenge the legalisation or sale. In 2016 the IPRO removed their names from the building’s owners and registered it to M. company; an administrative appeal was submitted, but no court proceedings were instituted.

The key alleged violations are therefore: annulment of final decisions undermining legal certainty; interference with property rights; and excessive length of proceedings without effective compensation.

The Tirana Court of Appeal allowed the claim in 2013, and the Supreme Court upheld that judgment in 2022. A length complaint was dismissed in 2023 on the grounds that the case had already been adjudicated and delays were attributable to Albania’s judicial reform.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations arise from the third set of proceedings. After a 2007 amendment to the Property Act, the director of the Agency for the Restitution and Compensation of Property was empowered to review and annul, ex officio and without any time limit, decisions of former commissions. On 27 November 2007, the Agency annulled the three Commission decisions concerning the applicants’ 1,070 sq. m plots. It found that the Commission had lacked jurisdiction and that only a special commission could order actual restitution; it also claimed the land could not be restituted. The recognition of the applicants’ inherited rights remained in force.

The applicants challenged the annulment. The District Court allowed their claim, but the Court of Appeal quashed that judgment in 2010, and the Supreme Court upheld the dismissal in 2012. In 2013, the Constitutional Court found a fair-trial violation by the Supreme Court and remitted the case. On retrial, the Supreme Court again dismissed the applicants’ appeal in 2014. In 2015, the Constitutional Court dismissed their complaint, finding that the Agency’s review power had still been in force when the Court of Appeal adjudicated and that its later case-law was not retroactive. However, in 2010 and 2011 the Constitutional Court had annulled the amendments granting the Agency such review powers, holding that they violated legal certainty and property rights.

Other relevant facts include a fourth set of proceedings, begun in 2008, which terminated the cooperation agreement but denied restitution of the property; this was upheld up to 2022. A 2023 constitutional complaint was dismissed, though the Constitutional Court found the profit-sharing proceedings excessively lengthy but lacked jurisdiction to award compensation. In addition, M. company built an unauthorised structure, legalised in 2013, and in 2014 the State sold it a 595.8 sq. m plot forming part of the claimed land. The applicants did not challenge the legalisation or sale. In 2016, the registration office removed the applicants as owners of the existing building and registered it to M. company; an administrative appeal was filed but no court proceedings followed.

The alleged violations therefore centre on the Agency’s annulment of final property decisions, the lack of legal certainty, interference with property rights, and the excessive length of related proceedings.
001-238658:
In *Petrosyan v. Armenia*, the applicant, mother of H. Movsisyan, complained about her son’s death in custody and the ensuing investigation. Movsisyan was conscripted in 2011 and assigned to a military unit in the unrecognised “Nagorno-Karabakh Republic.” He had difficulty adapting, left his unit, and during a conversation with an officer cut his forearm. He was diagnosed with an organic psychopathic-like disorder with non-adaptive decompensation and attempted suicide, found unfit for peacetime military service, and discharged in September 2011. Despite this, Armenian military investigators prosecuted him for evasion of military service/self-mutilation. He was arrested in July 2012, convicted in November 2012, sentenced to three years, and held in Shushi Detention Centre.

On 28 November 2012 he was found hanging by a bedsheet from his cell window bars. Autopsies concluded mechanical asphyxiation by hanging, with no significant injuries apart from a ligature mark and a scratch. The authorities treated it as suicide. The NKR prosecutor’s office opened a case concerning alleged incitement to suicide, questioned guards and cellmates, and in March 2013 terminated the proceedings, finding no threats, ill-treatment or pressure. Armenia’s Special Investigative Service then opened an official-negligence case, combined it with the earlier case, and in December 2013 terminated it, finding no official negligence by investigators, prosecutors, judges or medical commissions involved in the son’s prosecution.

The applicant was denied victim status and access to the case file. Her appeals were dismissed, and courts refused to order production of the full material underlying the termination. Meanwhile, after the General Prosecutor appealed the conviction, the Court of Appeal acquitted her son in April 2013, stating that the prosecution had ignored his discharge and mental disorder. The Court of Cassation later terminated proceedings because of his death.

These facts were central to the alleged violations. Under Article 2 (procedural), the investigation into a death in State custody was allegedly insufficient and inadequate: it failed to give a satisfactory and convincing explanation for the death, to examine whether authorities knew or should have known of the suicide risk given the diagnosed psychiatric disorder and prior suicide attempt, to assess failure to monitor or provide psychological care, and to establish responsibility. It was inaccessible to the family and ended without prosecution. Under Article 2 (substantive), the complaint concerned the State’s positive obligation to protect the life of a vulnerable detainee and to account for a death under State control. Under Article 13, there was allegedly no effective remedy to establish institutional liability for an Article 2 breach where domestic proceedings ended without prosecution or conviction; even if one existed, the statutory ceiling on non-pecuniary damages for a right-to-life breach was insufficient. Finally, the Government’s attempt to strike out the case by unilateral declaration failed because it lacked an undertaking to reopen the investigation and proposed compensation inconsistent with the Court’s awards in similar cases.

**Petrosyan v. Armenia** (Application no. 51448/15, Fifth Section, judgment 9 January 2025) concerned the death in detention of the applicant’s son, H. Movsisyan, and the adequacy of the domestic investigation. The applicant alleged violations of Articles 2 and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

H. Movsisyan was conscripted into the Armenian army in June 2011 and assigned to a military unit in the unrecognised “Nagorno-Karabakh Republic”. He quickly showed difficulty adapting to military service. On 27 June 2011, after leaving his unit without permission, he was returned and had a conversation with Lieutenant Colonel H.S.; during that conversation he cut his own left forearm with a razor blade. He was diagnosed with “an organic psychopathic-like disorder [and] non-adaptive decompensation with attempted suicide”. In August 2011 he was found unfit for military service in peacetime, and in September 2011 he was discharged on health grounds.

Despite this, criminal proceedings against him continued. He was initially charged with evasion of military service; those charges were dropped, but new charges were brought for self-mutilation to evade service. In November 2012 the Syunik Regional Court convicted him and sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment. He was transferred to Shushi Detention Centre in Nagorno-Karabakh in September 2012.

On 28 November 2012, H. Movsisyan was found dead in cell no. 8, hanging by a bedsheet from the window bars. The official account was suicide. The “NKR” authorities opened criminal proceedings concerning alleged incitement to suicide, but in March 2013 terminated them for lack of evidence of a crime. Armenia’s Special Investigative Service then opened a case concerning official negligence, combined it with the earlier investigation, and in December 2013 also terminated it, finding no criminal conduct by investigators, prosecutors, judges, or medical experts.

The applicant was refused victim status, denied access to the case file, and unable to participate effectively in the proceedings. Domestic courts dismissed her appeals, in one instance without having the full case material before them. Separately, after the son’s death, the General Prosecutor appealed the conviction. In April 2013 the Criminal Court of Appeal acquitted H. Movsisyan on the basis that he had already been unfit for service and should not have been prosecuted. In October 2013, however, the Court of Cassation overturned that acquittal and terminated the proceedings because of his death.

Before the European Court, the key issues were whether Armenia provided a satisfactory and convincing explanation for the death of a detainee known to have mental health problems, and whether the investigation was effective and accessible to the family. The Court found the investigation insufficient and inadequate: it failed to clarify the circumstances of the death, possible responsibility of officials or medical personnel, the appropriateness of psychological and medical care, the first aid provided, the mechanics and timing of the hanging, and other relevant questions. There was therefore a violation of Article 2, both substantive and procedural.

Under Article 13, the Court found a lack of an effective remedy. It could not conclusively establish that domestic law provided a mechanism to determine institutional liability where criminal proceedings ended without prosecution or conviction; even if such a mechanism existed, the domestic cap on non-pecuniary damages for right-to-life breaches would be insufficient redress.

The Government’s unilateral declaration was not accepted because it did not include an undertaking to reopen the investigation and proposed compensation inconsistent with the Court’s usual awards. The Court therefore declined to strike the application out and continued its examination.

In **Petrosyan v. Armenia** (Application no. 51448/15), judgment of 9 January 2025, the European Court of Human Rights examined the death in custody of the applicant’s son, H. Movsisyan, and the adequacy of the ensuing investigations. The applicant, Ms Heghine Petrosyan, alleged violations of Articles 2 and 13 of the Convention.

H. Movsisyan was conscripted into the Armenian army in June 2011. He had health issues and quickly showed inability to adapt to military service. In June 2011 he left his unit and, during a conversation with a battalion commander after being returned, cut his left forearm with a razor blade. He was later diagnosed with “an organic psychopathic-like disorder [and] non-adaptive decompensation with attempted suicide.” In August 2011 a military commission found him unfit for military service in peacetime, and he was discharged in September 2011.

Despite this, criminal proceedings had been initiated against him in July 2011 for evasion of military service. Charges were later changed to self-mutilation to evade service. In November 2012 the Syunik Regional Court convicted him and sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment. Seven days later, on 28 November 2012, he was found dead in cell no. 8 of Shushi Detention Centre, in the unrecognised “Nagorno-Karabakh Republic.” The official account was that he had hanged himself with a bedsheet from the window bars.

The death triggered two sets of proceedings. The “NKR” authorities investigated alleged incitement to suicide. An autopsy concluded that death was caused by mechanical asphyxiation due to hanging, with a ligature mark and a scratch on his right forearm; no alcohol or drugs were detected. In March 2013 the “NKR” prosecutor terminated the case, finding no evidence that staff or detainees had threatened, ill-treated, pressured or incited H. Movsisyan. The decision attributed his suicide to his psychiatric disorder and recent conviction. Armenia’s Special Investigative Service then opened a case concerning official negligence, combined it with the earlier investigation, but terminated it in December 2013, finding no crime by investigators, prosecutors, judges, medical commission members or forensic experts.

The applicant was not granted victim status and was denied access to the case file. Her attempts to challenge the termination were dismissed; domestic courts reviewed the decision without the full investigative material. Meanwhile, the General Prosecutor appealed H. Movsisyan’s conviction. The Court of Appeal acquitted him in April 2013, but the Court of Cassation later terminated proceedings because of his death.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged that the investigation into her son’s death was ineffective and inaccessible, failed to provide a satisfactory explanation for a death occurring under State control, and did not examine potential responsibility of officials or experts. She raised unresolved issues, including whether hanging could occur within the short interval claimed, whether proper first aid and psychological assistance were provided, and the origin of the forearm injury. She also complained of no effective remedy for the Article 2 breach.

The Government sought to strike the case out through a unilateral declaration. The Court refused, because the declaration contained no undertaking to reopen the investigation and proposed compensation below what it would award in a similar case. It found violations of Article 2, both substantive and procedural, due to the insufficient investigation and failure to give a convincing explanation for the death, and of Article 13 because no effective remedy existed, including for institutional liability, and domestic compensation limits were inadequate.
001-242757:
In *Sadigov v. Azerbaijan* (Application no. 48665/13), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) examined an application by Ildirim Sadigov, an Azerbaijani national born in 1949. The case concerns the alleged unlawful demolition of his property and the domestic courts’ alleged failure to award adequate compensation, contrary to Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention.

The building was constructed in 1955 and used as a State-owned canteen. In 2004, the applicant’s mother, who managed the canteen, purchased it under preferential privatisation conditions. The privatisation documents stated that the building had an area of 120 square metres and that she paid 3,300,000 old Azerbaijani manats (AZN 600). A technical passport was issued the same year. After the mother’s death in 2005, the applicant inherited the building. In November 2007, the Barda District Territorial Department of the State Agency on Registration of Immovable Property Rights issued a title deed confirming his ownership. The title deed and accompanying technical passport stated that the building’s area was actually 210.1 square metres and that its depreciation rate was 30%. The building housed a State-run college until January 2008.

On 3 March 2008, the Tartar District Executive Authority (“TDEA”) ordered demolition. It stated that the building, located within a public park, had been unused for several years, had deteriorated, was unusable, and did not meet modern architectural standards. The TDEA ordered demolition in the public interest without compensation. The applicant was offered five nearby plots of land as in-kind compensation but declined. The building was demolished on 13 March 2008.

The applicant sued the TDEA for AZN 117,000 in pecuniary damage for the building, AZN 60,000 in non-pecuniary damage, and AZN 25,000 for medical expenses. He claimed that although the building had been unusable at the time of privatisation, he had later fully renovated it. In August 2008, the Tartar District Court awarded him AZN 660 in pecuniary damage. On appeal, the Ganja Court of Appeal quashed that judgment and directed that the claim be examined in commercial proceedings.

In December 2008, the Ganja Local Economic Court ordered an expert valuation based on the 2004 and 2007 technical passports. The expert found the parameters essentially identical, set the price at AZN 520 per square metre, and valued the building at AZN 109,200 (about EUR 104,600 at the time). In January 2010, however, the Ganja Local Economic Court found the demolition unlawful but awarded only AZN 660 in pecuniary damages and AZN 200 in non-pecuniary damages. It rejected the expert valuation as unrealistic, found the 1955 building dilapidated and unfit for use, and dismissed the repair documents as unsigned or unapproved. It treated the AZN 660 privatisation price as adequate compensation and noted that the five-plot offer remained valid.

The Supreme Court intervened twice. In October 2010, it quashed an appellate judgment because market value could not be determined on the basis of privatisation documents and because the lower courts had not compared the expert data with the real estate register. In May 2011, the Ganja Court of Appeal awarded AZN 109,200 based on the expert report. In September 2011, the Supreme Court quashed that award because depreciation had not been considered for the old, long-used building. On re-examination, a fresh BDTD valuation in May 2012 estimated the building at AZN 16,808 (about EUR 16,253). The Ganja Court of Appeal awarded that sum, finding the building completely unusable, as the applicant himself had stated. The Supreme Court upheld this on 11 February 2013. The applicant complained to the ECtHR that the domestic courts had failed to afford him adequate redress for the unlawful demolition of his property.

Case Sadigov v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 48665/13) concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the domestic authorities failed to provide adequate redress for the unlawful demolition of his property.

The property was a building constructed in 1955 and originally used as a State-owned canteen. In 2004, the applicant’s mother, then manager of the canteen, purchased it under preferential privatisation conditions. The privatisation records referred to a surface area of 120 square metres and a payment of 3,300,000 old Azerbaijani manats (600 new manats, AZN). A technical passport was issued the same year. After his mother died in 2005, the applicant inherited the building. In November 2007, the Barda District Territorial Department of the State Agency on Registration of Immovable Property Rights issued a title deed confirming his ownership. The title deed and accompanying technical passport stated the area as 210.1 square metres and a depreciation rate of 30%. The building had housed a State-run college until January 2008.

On 3 March 2008, the Tartar District Executive Authority (TDEA) ordered the building’s demolition. The order said the building, located within a public park, had been unused for several years, had deteriorated, was unusable and did not meet modern architectural standards. It ordered demolition in the public interest without compensation. The applicant was offered five nearby plots as compensation in kind but declined. On 13 March 2008, the building was demolished pursuant to the TDEA order.

The applicant sued the TDEA, seeking AZN 117,000 in pecuniary damages, AZN 60,000 in non-pecuniary damages and AZN 25,000 for medical expenses. He claimed that although the building had been unusable at the time of privatisation, he had later fully renovated it. In August 2008, the Tartar District Court awarded him only AZN 660 in pecuniary damages. On appeal, the Ganja Court of Appeal quashed the judgment and directed that the claim be examined in commercial proceedings.

In December 2008, the Ganja Local Economic Court commissioned an expert examination. Using the 2004 and 2007 technical passports, the expert found their parameters essentially identical and estimated the market value at AZN 109,200 (about EUR 104,600), based on AZN 520 per square metre and comparable local prices. Nevertheless, in January 2010, the Ganja Local Economic Court found the demolition unlawful but awarded only AZN 660 in pecuniary damages and AZN 200 in non-pecuniary damages. It held that the expert valuation did not reflect reality because the 1955 building had not been renovated and was dilapidated and unfit for use. It rejected the applicant’s repair documents as unsigned or unapproved and treated the original privatisation payment as adequate compensation, noting the five plots offered remained available.

After further appeals, the Supreme Court twice quashed decisions. In October 2010, it held that market value could not be based on privatisation documents and criticised the lack of comparative analysis. In May 2011, the Ganja Court of Appeal awarded AZN 109,200 based on the earlier expert report. In September 2011, the Supreme Court again quashed that award because depreciation had not been considered. On re-examination, a new BDTD valuation in May 2012 estimated the building at AZN 16,808 (about EUR 16,253). The Ganja Court of Appeal then awarded that amount, finding the latest valuation convincing and the building completely unusable, as the applicant himself had indicated. On 11 February 2013, the Supreme Court upheld that judgment.

The applicant therefore complained to the European Court that the domestic courts had failed to afford him adequate redress for the unlawful demolition of his property, contrary to Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The case *Sadigov v. Azerbaijan* (Application no. 48665/13) concerns an Azerbaijani national’s complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights that the domestic authorities unlawfully demolished his property and that the domestic courts failed to afford him adequate redress.

The applicant, Ildirim Sadigov, born in 1949 and living in Tartar, inherited a building from his mother, N.A. The building had been constructed in 1955 and had been used as a State-owned canteen. In 2004, N.A., then manager of the canteen, purchased it under preferential privatisation conditions. The privatisation documents stated that the building had a total surface area of 120 square metres and that N.A. paid 3,300,000 old Azerbaijani manats (600 new Azerbaijani manats, AZN). A technical passport was issued the same year. After N.A. died in 2005, the applicant inherited the building.

On 15 November 2007, the Barda District Territorial Department of the State Agency on Registration of Immovable Property Rights issued a title deed confirming the applicant’s ownership. According to the title deed and the technical passport issued with it, the building’s surface area was in fact 210.1 square metres, with a depreciation rate of 30%. The building housed a State-run college until January 2008, when the college moved elsewhere.

On 3 March 2008, the Tartar District Executive Authority (“the TDEA”) issued a written order for demolition. The order stated that the building, located within the grounds of a public park, had been unused for several years, had deteriorated, was unfit for use, and did not meet modern architectural standards. The TDEA ordered demolition in the public interest without compensation. The applicant was offered five plots of land nearby as compensation in kind, but he declined. The building was demolished on 13 March 2008 pursuant to the TDEA order.

The applicant sued the TDEA, seeking AZN 117,000 for pecuniary damage, AZN 60,000 for non-pecuniary damage, and AZN 25,000 for medical expenses. He argued that although the building had been unusable at privatisation, he had subsequently carried out full renovation work. On 11 August 2008, the Tartar District Court awarded him AZN 660 in pecuniary damages. The Ganja Court of Appeal quashed that judgment and directed that the claim be examined in commercial proceedings.

In December 2008, the Ganja Local Economic Court ordered an expert examination to determine the market value of the demolished property based on the 2004 and 2007 technical passports. The expert found the technical parameters essentially identical, set the price at AZN 520 per square metre, and estimated the market value at AZN 109,200 (approximately EUR 104,600 at the time). On 28 January 2010, the Ganja Local Economic Court found the demolition unlawful but awarded only AZN 660 in pecuniary damages and AZN 200 in non-pecuniary damages. It held that the expert valuation did not reflect reality because the 1955 building was dilapidated and unfit for use, and it dismissed the applicant’s repair documents as unsigned or unapproved. It considered AZN 660, the privatisation price, adequate, also noting the five plots offered. The appellate court dismissed the applicant’s appeal.

On cassation, the Supreme Court quashed the appellate judgment on 14 October 2010, stating that market value could not be based on privatisation documents and that the lower courts had failed to compare the expert report with the real estate register. In May 2011, the Ganja Court of Appeal awarded AZN 109,200 based on the expert report. The Supreme Court quashed that judgment on 27 September 2011, noting that depreciation had not been considered given the building’s age and long use.

On re-examination, the Ganja Court of Appeal ordered a fresh valuation by the BDTD. A May 2012 report estimated the building’s value at AZN 16,808 (approximately EUR 16,253). The appellate court then awarded the applicant AZN 16,808, finding the latest valuation convincing and noting that the building was completely unusable, as the applicant himself had indicated. On 11 February 2013, the Supreme Court upheld that judgment. The applicant complained to the European Court that the domestic courts had failed to provide adequate redress for the unlawful demolition of his property.
001-245701:
Kyrian v. Czech Republic (no. 15956/23) concerned a Czech man’s complaint under Article 8 that the courts refused him contact with his biological son and refused to order the child’s legal parents to provide information about him. The applicant had the child in December 2013 with a married woman; her husband was the legal father by presumption. A 2015 DNA test confirmed the applicant’s biological paternity. He saw the child two to four times monthly until February 2016.

In April 2016 he sought contact under Article 927 of the Civil Code. In May 2016 the District Court granted Wednesday afternoon and summer Sunday visits, upheld in November 2016. The courts noted an emotional bond and the child’s right to know his biological father. Contact later deteriorated amid conflicts between the applicant and the legal parents. Supervised visits and mediation followed. A July 2018 agreement maintained similar contact, but visits often failed because the child refused, and an incident led to police involvement. An October 2018 psychologist report said the child was strongly attached to his mother and legal father, stressed by unfamiliar people, and that imposed contact might be causing his difficulties.

In December 2018 the legal parents sought to prohibit contact. In 2020 the courts ruled no contact regime should be set. Under Article 927, there was no indication of a positive emotional bond with the applicant or that lack of contact would harm the child. An expert found the child, who had developmental delays, was caught in a relationship triangle, mirrored the legal parents’ attitude, and was attached to his legal father. The expert advised no contact until the legal parents’ marital crisis resolved. The courts found the applicant’s pressure had worsened conflict. A constitutional appeal was dismissed in October 2022, though the decision could be revised if the situation improved.

In April 2021 the applicant renewed his contact request. At an August 2021 hearing, the legal parents said the child was anxious, and the guardian ad litem advised dismissal. A March 2022 expert report found previous visits traumatic and the child negative toward the applicant; no contact was recommended, though future contact remained possible. The child’s psychologist confirmed anxiety. At a March 2022 hearing, the applicant alternatively sought written communication through the guardian and regular information about the child’s development. The legal parents refused; the guardian advised dismissing all requests. On 24 March 2022 the District Court dismissed the claim, warning the legal parents to respect the applicant’s biological parenthood. It found contact contrary to the child’s best interests. As to information, it was a parental responsibility issue, the legal parents opposed it, and providing it was not in the child’s best interests. The Regional Court upheld this on 12 September 2022, holding information rights could only arise within contact

In *Kyrian v. the Czech Republic* (App. no. 15956/23, ECtHR, 6 November 2025), the applicant, David Kyrian, is the biological father of a child born in December 2013 from an extramarital relationship with the child’s mother. Because the mother was married, her husband became the child’s legal father, and the child lived with his legal parents. The applicant established his biological paternity through a DNA test in 2015. Until February 2016, he saw the child two to four times per month when the mother visited him.

In April 2016, the applicant sought contact rights under Article 927 of the Czech Civil Code. A District Court granted provisional contact in May 2016, upheld on appeal in November 2016. However, visits became conflictual, and supervised visits were arranged. From September 2016 to November 2017, contact mostly occurred, but the child’s psychological condition worsened. In September 2017, the applicant sought more contact, while the mother sought a prohibition, citing verbal abuse, the child’s refusal, anxiety, and psychological treatment. The legal father alleged physical assault by the applicant. After a quashed judgment and mediation in April 2018, contact improved briefly, and an agreement was approved in July 2018. Later visits failed due to the child’s refusal, an incident led to police involvement, and supervised visits in October 2018 produced further conflict. A psychologist reported that the child was strongly attached to his mother and legal father, stressed by unfamiliar people, and that imposed contact might harm him.

In December 2018, the legal parents sought to prohibit contact. In 2020, the District and Regional Courts ruled that no contact regime should be set because there was no positive emotional bond and no harm from lack of contact under Article 927. An expert clinical psychologist found the child had developmental delays, was caught in a relationship triangle, mirrored the legal parents’ attitude, and was emotionally attached to his legal father. The expert advised no contact until the legal parents’ marital crisis resolved. The courts also found the applicant had pressured the child and legal parents, exacerbating conflict. The Constitutional Court dismissed his appeal in 2022.

In April 2021, the applicant again sought contact every Wednesday. At an August 2021 hearing, the legal parents reported the child’s anxiety, and the guardian *ad litem* advised dismissal. A March 2022 expert report described previous visits as traumatic and the child’s attitude as negative, recommending no contact, though future contact was possible if the applicant became more respectful. The child’s psychologist confirmed anxiety attacks. At a March 2022 hearing, the applicant requested at least written communication via the guardian and an order that the legal parents provide information about the child’s development. The legal parents refused, saying any contact would distress the child, and noted the applicant lingered near the kindergarten and their home, bordering on stalking. The guardian said all requests were contrary to the child’s best interests.

The District Court dismissed the claim in March 2022, warning the legal parents to cooperate and respect the applicant’s biological parenthood, but holding contact was not in the child’s best interests. It found the right to information was a matter of parental responsibility, the legal parents opposed it, and no best-interests reason justified it. The Regional Court upheld this in September 2022, holding information could only be granted within contact determination and noting no positive bond existed. The Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal in January 2023.

The applicant alleged a violation of Article 8, complaining about the refusal of contact and information. The Government conceded interference with private life but argued it was justified by the child’s best interests, psychological vulnerability, expert advice, and ongoing conflict. The ECtHR found no violation, holding that the domestic courts took adequate measures, gave sufficient reasons, balanced competing interests, and protected the applicant’s Article 8 rights.

**Summary of *Kyrian v. the Czech Republic* (Application no. 15956/23)**

The case of *Kyrian v. the Czech Republic* concerns a complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights regarding the refusal of Czech courts to grant a biological father contact rights with his son and to order the child’s legal parents to provide him with information about the child.

The applicant, David Kyrian, is the biological father of a child born in December 2013 from an extramarital relationship. Due to the legal presumption of paternity, the mother’s husband became the child’s legal father, and the child lived with his legal parents. The applicant’s biological paternity was confirmed by a DNA test in 2015.

Initially, the applicant saw his son two to four times per month until February 2016. In April 2016, he sought contact rights under Article 927 of the Czech Civil Code. A provisionally enforceable judgment in May 2016 granted him regular visits, which was upheld on appeal. However, conflicts between the applicant and the child’s mother and legal father escalated, and the child’s psychological condition deteriorated. The child began refusing visits and exhibited anxiety.

In 2017, the mother sought to prohibit contact, citing the applicant’s verbal abuse and the child’s distress. Despite mediation in 2018 and an agreement for continued contact, visits again failed due to the child’s refusal and a police incident. A psychologist reported that the child was strongly attached to his legal parents and that imposed contact was harmful.

In 2020, following a request by the legal parents, the District Court and Regional Court ruled that no contact regime should be set, finding no evidence of a positive emotional bond between the child and the applicant or that lack of contact would harm the child. They relied on expert opinion that the child suffered developmental delays and was caught in a conflictual relationship triangle, mirroring his legal parents’ negative attitude toward the applicant. The courts emphasized the applicant’s pressure and the need to stabilize the child’s mental state.

In 2021, the applicant lodged a new application for contact. At hearings in 2022, the child’s legal parents and a guardian ad litem opposed any contact, citing the child’s anxiety and the applicant’s behavior, which bordered on stalking. An expert psychologist recommended against contact, noting the child’s traumatic experiences and negative attitude. The District Court dismissed the applicant’s claim, including his request for information about the child, and the Regional Court upheld this, stating that the right to information could only be granted within the framework of contact rights and that the child’s best interests did not support it. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeals as manifestly ill-founded.

The applicant complained that the refusal violated his right to respect for private and family life under Article 8. He argued that the courts failed to balance interests fairly, did not adequately consider the child’s right to know his biological father, and did not separately assess his right to information. The Government contended that the interference was justified by the child’s best interests, given the conflictual situation, the child’s psychological vulnerability, and expert recommendations against contact.

The European Court of Human Rights found no violation of Article 8. It held that the domestic courts had taken adequate measures, including mediation and supervised visits, and had adduced sufficient reasons for refusing contact and information. The decision-making process had safeguarded the applicant’s interests, and the right to information could be granted independently under domestic law but was rightly refused here based on the child’s best interests. The Court concluded that the authorities had fairly balanced competing interests and pursued the child’s well-being.
001-241986:
I.C. v. the Republic of Moldova (ECtHR, 27 February 2025) concerns an intellectually disabled Moldovan woman who was allegedly trafficked, held in servitude, and sexually abused after being placed with a family farm following “deinstitutionalisation” from State care.

The applicant was born in 1974, abandoned at birth, and had no known relatives. She spent her entire life in State institutions, including 24 years in a neuropsychiatric asylum. In 2011 a court deprived her of legal capacity, but no guardian was appointed. In 2013 a couple, L.P. and I.P., approached the asylum asking for a woman to be a “bride” for G.B., an employee on their farm. After an initial one-month stay, they sought the applicant’s permanent placement. The Ministry approved her integration into their family, and the asylum terminated her placement. At the material time, Moldova lacked an effective legal and administrative framework for deinstitutionalising persons with intellectual disabilities deprived of legal capacity. There was no guardian, no adequate monitoring, and little post-placement support. A social worker later admitted she visited the applicant only once, kept no personal file, and was unaware of abuse.

The applicant lived on the farm from January 2013 to October 2018. She alleged she worked from 4 a.m. until dark, feeding livestock, cleaning stalls, carrying milk, and disposing of rubbish, without pay except a few payments of about EUR 5–15. She alleged that I.P. raped and sexually abused her over years. She stated she could not refuse because of her intellectual disability, dependency, threats to kill her dogs, and fear of police, since I.P.’s son was in the police. She escaped several times but had nowhere to go and was returned or returned herself. L.P. allegedly verbally and physically abused and threatened her. G.B. initially corroborated witnessing abuse and unpaid work, but later retracted.

In October 2018 the applicant called a disability hotline; an NGO contacted police. She lodged a complaint alleging sexual abuse. A criminal investigation began for rape and sexual violence, and later human-trafficking charges were added against I.P. and L.P. However, the prosecutor essentially dropped separate rape and sexual abuse charges, reclassifying them as “non-commercial sexual exploitation” within trafficking. The applicant’s appeals were rejected, and domestic courts declined to review. The Labour Inspectorate could not establish an employment relationship. Medical and psychological reports described moderate/mild intellectual disability, IQ 50, high suggestibility, limited capacity, and dependency. An independent psychologist found trauma and PTSD from exploitation, abuse, and rape. Authorities knew of her vulnerability.

The ECtHR found violations of Article 4: the State failed its substantive and procedural positive obligations to protect her from trafficking and servitude. Her arguable claim and prima facie evidence triggered protective duties. Deficiencies in placement and support created a credible suspicion of a real and immediate risk of trafficking or exploitation. The State failed to take protective measures, conduct an effective investigation, and implement criminal-law mechanisms properly.

The Court also found violations of Articles 3 and 8: failure to effectively investigate rape, sexual violence, and abuse; lack of procedural accommodation for a vulnerable applicant; deficient court assessment exposing her to secondary victimisation; and failure to punish all forms of rape and sexual abuse.

Finally, Article 14, read with Articles 3, 4, and 8, was violated: she suffered discriminatory treatment as a woman with intellectual disabilities, reflecting institutional passivity and lack of awareness of violence against women with disabilities in Moldova, and no reasonable procedural accommodation.

In *I.C. v. the Republic of Moldova* (ECtHR, 27 February 2025), the applicant was a Moldovan woman with moderate intellectual disability. Abandoned at birth and in State care her whole life, she was deprived of legal capacity in 2011 and had lived for 24 years in a neuropsychiatric asylum. In 2013, a couple, L.P. and I.P., approached the asylum seeking a woman to be a “bride” for G.B., a farm worker. I.C. first went for a month, then the Ministry approved her permanent placement; the asylum terminated her institutional placement. No guardian was appointed. She lived on the couple’s farm from January 2013 to October 2018. She alleged she worked from 4 a.m. until dark, feeding livestock, cleaning stalls, carrying milk and disposing of rubbish, with little or no pay—only occasional 5–15 EUR. I.P. allegedly raped and sexually abused her over years, using psychological control, threats to kill her dogs, and telling her the police would not help. She escaped several times but had nowhere to go and was returned. In October 2018 she fled and called a disability hotline; an NGO contacted the police. She filed a criminal complaint concerning sexual abuse.

The authorities opened a criminal investigation into rape and sexual violence, later adding human-trafficking charges against I.P. and L.P. in 2019. However, the prosecutor effectively dropped separate rape and sexual-abuse charges, reclassifying the sexual relations as non-commercial sexual exploitation within the trafficking case. The applicant’s challenges were rejected. Psychiatric and psychological reports described moderate intellectual disability, IQ 50, high suggestibility, limited capacity to understand or resist, and dependency on carers. An independent forensic psychologist found trauma/PTSD resulting from exploitation, abuse and rape, and recommended a specialised shelter and long-term psychological support. A local social worker knew I.C. lived on the farm but had no personal file, visited only once and did not report abuse. The Labour Inspectorate found no formal labour relations. The placement process lacked a legal and administrative framework for deinstitutionalisation of persons with intellectual disabilities deprived of legal capacity, and post-placement monitoring and support were ineffective.

The Court found that the arguable claim and prima facie evidence of trafficking/servitude triggered protective duties. Moldova failed substantively and procedurally: it did not protect I.C. from a real and immediate risk after removal from State care; the placement and support system was deficient; protective measures were not taken; and the investigation and criminal-law mechanisms were ineffective. It also found failures to investigate rape, sexual violence and abuse, and a lack of procedural accommodation for a vulnerable applicant, exposing her to secondary victimisation. Finally, it found discriminatory treatment of I.C. as a woman with intellectual disabilities, reflecting institutional passivity and lack of awareness of violence against women with disabilities.

Case I.C. v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 36436/22) concerned a Moldovan woman with moderate intellectual disability who was abandoned at birth, deprived of legal capacity in 2011, and had lived in a State neuropsychiatric asylum for about twenty-four years. In 2013, a couple, L.P. and I.P., sought to take her into their family, allegedly as a “bride” for G.B., a farm worker. After a one-month “holiday” and Ministry approval, the asylum discharged her into the couple’s family and farm under a deinstitutionalisation procedure. No formal guardianship was apparently established, and no effective post-placement monitoring occurred.

From January 2013 to October 2018, the applicant lived and worked on the farm. She alleged that she worked from 4 a.m. until dark, feeding livestock, cleaning stalls and premises, carrying milk, and disposing of rubbish, while receiving almost no pay—only occasional small sums of 100–300 Moldovan lei. She alleged that I.P. repeatedly raped and sexually abused her, using psychological control, threats to kill her dogs, and exploitation of her intellectual disability and lack of alternatives. She also alleged physical and psychological abuse by L.P., including slapping, hair-pulling, insults, threats, and being chased away. She escaped several times but returned because she had nowhere else to go and became attached to G.B. and her dogs.

In October 2018, the applicant ran away and called a hotline run by a disability NGO, complaining of unpaid work, sexual abuse by I.P., and abuse by L.P. She then filed a criminal complaint. A criminal investigation began for rape and sexual violence. In her statements, she described repeated non-consensual oral and vaginal sex, fear of I.P., shame, and dependency. A medical examination found a sexually transmitted disease but no visible signs of violence. Psychiatric and psychological reports described moderate intellectual disability, high suggestibility, limited capacity to resist or understand relationships, dependency on the perpetrator, and trauma-related symptoms. A farm worker, G.B., initially corroborated seeing sexual acts and being told of rape, but later recanted. The Labour Inspectorate found no formal employment relationship.

Prosecutors initially charged I.P. with rape and sexual abuse, but later charged I.P. and L.P. with human trafficking and reclassified the sexual allegations as “non-commercial sexual exploitation,” effectively dropping separate rape and sexual abuse charges. The applicant’s challenges to this reclassification were rejected, and after the case was sent to trial, the courts declined jurisdiction over her appeal.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 4 because Moldova failed both substantively and procedurally to protect an intellectually disabled woman from trafficking and servitude after deinstitutionalisation. There was no adequate legal and administrative framework for deinstitutionalising persons deprived of legal capacity, and the placement process and support were deficient, creating a credible suspicion of a real and immediate risk of trafficking or exploitation. Authorities failed to take protective measures and to conduct an effective investigation. Under Articles 3 and 8, the State also failed to effectively investigate the rape and sexual violence allegations and to provide procedural accommodation for her vulnerability, exposing her to secondary victimisation and failing to apply adequate criminal-law mechanisms. Under Article 14, read with Articles 3, 4, and 8, the Court found discriminatory treatment of the applicant as a woman with intellectual disabilities, reflecting institutional passivity and lack of awareness of violence against women with disabilities.
