In *Hora v. the United Kingdom* (Application no. 1048/20), the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) examined a complaint under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 (right to free elections) brought by Michael Christopher Hora, a British national born in 1966 and detained at HMP Bure.

**Key facts:** In October 2007, Hora was convicted of two counts of rape and one count of sexual assault committed in the victim’s home. His defence that the sexual relations were consensual was rejected by the jury. He had previously been convicted of rape in similar circumstances in 2000 and was sentenced in 2001 to seven years’ imprisonment, later reduced on appeal. Following the 2007 conviction, the court imposed an indeterminate sentence of imprisonment for public protection, with a minimum term of four years, less 296 days spent on remand. The minimum term expired in 2011, but Hora remained in detention because the Parole Board had not recommended his release.

On 12 December 2019, a UK general election took place. Under section 3 of the Representation of the People Act 1983, a convicted person detained in a penal institution pursuant to his sentence is legally incapable of voting in any parliamentary or local election. Limited exceptions apply, such as imprisonment for contempt, default, or remand. Hora was therefore ineligible to vote. He complained that this disenfranchisement violated Article 3 of Protocol No. 1.

**Domestic and political background:** Hora did not bring domestic proceedings. UK courts can declare primary legislation incompatible with Convention rights but cannot disapply it. A domestic court had already made a declaration of incompatibility in *Smith v. Scott* (2007). After *Hirst v. the United Kingdom (No. 2)*, UK governments consulted on prisoner voting, but Parliament repeatedly opposed change. In 2011, the House of Commons passed a non-binding motion supporting the existing ban. A 2012 draft bill and a 2013 Joint Committee report recommended allowing prisoners serving 12 months or less to vote and pre-release registration, but no legislation followed. In 2017, the government made administrative changes: clarifying at sentencing that prisoners lose the vote and allowing prisoners on temporary licence or home detention curfew to vote. Otherwise, the blanket ban remained. Scotland later allowed prisoners serving 12 months or less to vote in Scottish Parliament and local elections; a Welsh proposal was not pursued.

**Court’s assessment:** The Court considered whether the applicant’s ineligibility, as a prisoner serving an indeterminate sentence for serious sexual offences, breached Article 3 of Protocol No. 1. It noted clear guidance in its case-law and no general domestic support for enfranchising prisoners convicted of serious offences or serving lengthy or indeterminate sentences. It declined to examine the provision in the abstract or to identify categories of prisoners whose disenfranchisement might be incompatible. Considering the seriousness of Hora’s offending, his prior conduct, the risk he posed to the public, and the harsh indeterminate sentence imposed, the Court found that his disenfranchisement was not disproportionate. His continued exclusion after expiry of the minimum term remained proportionate because he was still lawfully detained and had not been deemed safe for release. Consequently, there was no violation of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1.

In *Tsatani v. Greece*, the applicant was a Greek prosecutor at the Athens Court of Appeal. In March 2016, V.T., then President of the Court of Cassation, opened a preliminary disciplinary investigation against her after receiving letters from the Cypriot Minister of Justice and Attorney-General. Those officials were concerned about the applicant’s decision to close criminal investigations into a high-profile fraud case involving Greek and Cypriot individuals. V.T. collected evidence and asked the applicant to submit a written defence.

The applicant complained that the charges were vague, that she had not been allowed an oral defence, and that the pending confidential disciplinary proceedings had been mentioned in Parliament by Deputy Justice Minister D.P. On 4 April 2016, while submitting her defence, she also filed a recusal request against V.T. She alleged bias because V.T., a former interim prime minister, had special official relations with D.P. and with the Cypriot officials; had questioned witnesses and the applicant in a prejudicial manner; had provided an incomplete copy of the file; and had allegedly leaked confidential information. V.T. treated the recusal request as unfounded and an abuse of process, but referred further investigation to a Vice-President of the Court of Cassation to protect institutional credibility. The Vice-President completed the investigation and proposed disciplinary action, and V.T. then brought disciplinary proceedings against the applicant.

A key fact was that, on 18 April 2016, during the confidential preliminary investigation, V.T. issued an official press release as President of the Court of Cassation. The release named the applicant, referred to the pending disciplinary case, analysed her recusal grounds, described them as ill-founded and an abuse of process, denied bias, and explained why the investigation had been delegated. The press reported the statement.

The disciplinary councils found the applicant guilty of serious negligence damaging the prestige of the judiciary, imposed sixty days’ salary deprivation, and rejected her recusal complaints as inadmissible and/or unfounded. Her appeals failed.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged under Article 6 § 1 that she had not been heard by an independent and impartial tribunal. She relied on the fact that V.T. had conducted the preliminary disciplinary investigation, dealt with the recusal request directed against herself, and then initiated the disciplinary action. The Court focused on objective impartiality. It noted V.T.’s position as the highest authority in the civil and criminal courts and her public profile as a former interim prime minister. In that singular context, she should have exercised caution not to create the impression of influencing the proceedings, especially while investigating a fellow member of the judiciary. Her official press release during the confidential preliminary investigation, referring to the applicant and assessing the merits of the recusal request, was ipso facto incompatible with the notion of an “independent and impartial” tribunal. The disciplinary council’s failure to address the press release’s impact on fairness reinforced the problem. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1 due to lack of objective impartiality.

**Case Name:** *Tsatani v. Greece* (Application no. 42514/16), European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, judgment of 14 October 2025.

The applicant, Georgia Tsatani, was a Greek prosecutor at the Athens Court of Appeal. In March 2016, V.T., then President of the Court of Cassation, opened a preliminary disciplinary investigation against her. The investigation was prompted by letters dated 24 February 2016 from the Cypriot Minister of Justice and Attorney-General, who expressed concern over the applicant’s decision to close criminal investigations into a high-profile fraud case involving Greek and Cypriot individuals. V.T. collected evidence, sent it to the applicant, and invited her to submit a written defence.

The applicant objected that the Prosecutor of the Court of Cassation had exclusive competence in the matter and complained that D.P., Deputy Minister of Justice, had referred to the confidential disciplinary proceedings in Parliament on 29 March 2016. On 4 April 2016, she submitted a written defence and a recusal request against V.T. She alleged bias because V.T. had previously served as interim prime minister, had ongoing official relations with D.P. and the Cypriot officials, had asked prejudicial questions, and had provided an incomplete case file.

On 12 April 2016, V.T. referred the preliminary investigation to a Vice-President of the Court of Cassation, but stated that the recusal request was unfounded and an abuse of process. On 18 April 2016, V.T. issued an official press release as President of the Court of Cassation. The press release named the applicant, referred to the pending disciplinary proceedings, analysed the recusal grounds, and called the applicant’s request unfounded and an abuse of process. It was reported in the press.

The Vice-President concluded the preliminary investigation and proposed that disciplinary action be brought. On 24 June 2016, V.T. brought disciplinary proceedings against the applicant before the seven-member disciplinary council of the Court of Cassation. In October 2016, that council found the applicant had committed serious negligence damaging the prestige of the judiciary and imposed a sanction of sixty days’ salary deprivation. It also held that her recusal request was inadmissible and that V.T. had lawfully delegated the investigation. The nine-member disciplinary council dismissed the applicant’s appeal in March 2017.

The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that she had not been heard by an independent and impartial tribunal. She argued that V.T. had conducted the preliminary disciplinary investigation, herself examined the recusal request against her, issued a press release during the confidential investigation, and then brought disciplinary proceedings against the applicant.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 6 § 1. It accepted that the disciplinary councils themselves satisfied the requirements of a “tribunal.” However, it criticised the failure of the disciplinary council to address the impact of V.T.’s press release on the fairness of the proceedings. V.T.’s statements during the confidential preliminary investigation were incompatible with the notion of an independent and impartial tribunal. As the highest authority within the civil and criminal courts, and as a well-known former interim prime minister, V.T. should have exercised caution not to create the impression of influencing the proceedings, especially when investigating a fellow member of the judiciary. In the singular context of the case, the Court found a lack of objective impartiality.

In *Ayala Flores v. Italy* (Application no. 16803/21), the applicant, a Peruvian national living in Procida, complained under Article 8 of the Convention that enforcement of a demolition order against her home was disproportionate and that Italian courts had failed to conduct an adequate proportionality review of its impact on her right to respect for her home.

The key facts concerned a small dwelling built in the early 1990s by the applicant and her husband on land owned by him. They made it their home. The construction had no building permit or authorisation. It was located in a highly seismic zone and in an area subject to landscape protection and a “specific environmental interest,” which imposed an absolute ban on construction. In 1996 the municipality ordered restoration of the site. In 1998 it issued a demolition order. In 1999 the applicant and her husband were charged with unauthorised construction and with breaking seals placed by the police after they modified the building. In 2002 the Naples District Court convicted them, imposed a suspended five-month sentence and a fine, and ordered demolition. On appeal in 2003, some offences were time-barred, but the convictions for unauthorised construction and violation of seals were upheld; the demolition order became final in October 2003. A 2004 building-amnesty application was never answered. The applicant’s husband died in 2009, and she continued living in the dwelling.

Enforcement resumed in 2016. The public prosecutor asked the municipality whether demolition had occurred or whether public-interest reasons prevented it. The municipality served an eviction notice, and the prosecutor ordered the applicant to demolish within ninety days. The applicant asked the municipality to recognise a public interest in keeping the structure. She then sought review of the enforcement order before the Naples Court of Appeal (*incidente di esecuzione*). Her initial appeal did not raise Article 8. Only in additional written submissions did she claim that the dwelling was her only home, that she had lived there for over fifteen years after conviction, and that she faced financial difficulties; she relied on Article 8 and *Ivanova and Cherkezov v. Bulgaria*. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal in 2018/2019, treating demolition as a mandatory restorative measure and not addressing those submissions. The Court of Cassation rejected her further appeal as inadmissible for failure to satisfy the self-sufficiency requirement, as she had not attached the additional submissions. It nevertheless reasoned that her Article 8 complaint was generic, that she had not shown individual circumstances outweighing the public interest, that she could have no legitimate expectation to keep an unauthorised building, and that demolition was necessary to restore the site.

The Government later submitted inspection reports from 2020, 2022 and 2024 indicating the construction was not inhabited, appeared unfit for use or used for storage, and had unauthorised additions. The applicant submitted evidence of residence since 2001, a small pension, low income, and poor living conditions; by April 2025 the house had not been demolished. The Court found that the domestic courts had carried out the required proportionality assessment and that any lack of fuller examination was attributable to the applicant’s vague and unsubstantiated submissions. It concluded that Italy had not overstepped its margin of appreciation, balancing environmental protection and seismic safety against the applicant’s conscious defiance of building restrictions.

In *Ayala Flores v. Italy*, the applicant, a Peruvian national living in Procida, and her husband built a roughly 30 sq. m dwelling in the early 1990s without a building permit. The site was in a highly seismic zone and subject to landscape constraints and an absolute building ban because it was classified as an area of “specific environmental interest.” In 1996 the municipality found the construction unauthorised and ordered restoration; in 1998 it issued a demolition order. In 1999 the applicant and her husband were charged with unauthorised construction under Law no. 47 of 1985 and with breaking police seals after further modifying the property. In 2002 they were convicted, given a suspended five-month sentence and a fine, and the criminal court ordered demolition. The Naples Court of Appeal upheld the convictions in 2003, reduced the sentence, and lifted seizure only to allow demolition. The judgment became final in October 2003. A 2004 building-amnesty application went unanswered, but such amnesties could not generally cover landscape/environmental constraints. Her husband died in 2009, and she continued living in the dwelling.

Enforcement began in 2016. The public prosecutor asked the municipality whether demolition had occurred; the municipality served an eviction notice, and the prosecutor ordered the applicant to demolish within 90 days or have it done at her expense. She asked the municipality to recognise a public interest in keeping the structure, then filed an *incidente di esecuzione* before the Naples Court of Appeal seeking annulment or stay. Her initial appeal did not invoke Article 8. In later additional submissions, she claimed the dwelling was her only home, that she had lived there for over 15 years after conviction, that she had financial difficulties, and that demolition would be disproportionate under Article 8, citing *Ivanova and Cherkezov v. Bulgaria*. The Government disputed that these submissions had been properly filed.

The Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal in 2018/2019, treating the demolition order as a mainly restorative and mandatory response to unauthorised construction. It did not address her Article 8 submissions. The Court of Cassation rejected her further appeal as inadmissible because she failed to satisfy the self-sufficiency requirement—she did not attach the additional submissions or prove they had been filed. Nevertheless, it reasoned that Article 8 requires proportionality, but her complaint was generic; she did not identify personal circumstances outweighing the public interest. The fifteen-year delay did not create a legitimate expectation because she always knew the building was unauthorised. Demolition was necessary to restore the site, and no state of necessity was shown.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that enforcement of the demolition order would disproportionately affect her home and that domestic courts had failed to carry out a proportionality assessment under Article 8. Later evidence showed she sought public housing in 2021; municipal inspections in 2020, 2022 and 2024 reported the dwelling not inhabited, overgrown, with unauthorised fence and shutters and an interior unfit for use. She submitted statements and a surveyor’s opinion showing residence since 2001, a pension of about €551 per month, annual income of €4,943 and water damage. The house had not been demolished by April 2025.

The ECtHR (First Section, 23 October 2025; final 23 January 2026) found no violation of Article 8. Although the demolition interfered with her home, domestic law and Cassation case-law allowed proportionality review where personal circumstances were specifically raised. Her submissions were vague and unsubstantiated, while the environmental and seismic-protection interests and her conscious defiance of building restrictions justified the measure. Italy did not overstep its margin of appreciation.

**Ayala Flores v. Italy** concerned an Article 8 complaint by a Peruvian national living in Procida, Italy, that enforcement of a demolition order against her home was disproportionate and that the domestic courts had failed to conduct an adequate proportionality review.

In the early 1990s, the applicant and her husband built a small 30 sq. m dwelling on land owned by her husband. The construction lacked a building permit or authorization, and was located in a highly seismic zone subject to landscape constraints and an absolute building ban because the area had been designated as one of “specific environmental interest.” The couple made the dwelling their home.

In 1996, the municipality of Procida found that the premises had been built without permission and ordered restoration of the site. In 1998, it issued a demolition order. In 1999, the applicant and her husband were prosecuted for unauthorized construction and for breaking police seals after further modifying the building. In 2002, the Naples District Court convicted them, imposed a suspended five-month prison sentence and a fine, and ordered demolition of the construction. In 2003, the Naples Court of Appeal upheld the convictions, reduced the sentence, and lifted the seizure only to allow the applicant to demolish the building. In **Federici v. France** (Application no. 52302/19), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether requiring the applicant to answer questions from a glass dock during his criminal appeal breached Article 6 §§ 1, 2 and 3(b) of the Convention—the rights to a fair trial, presumption of innocence, and adequate facilities for the defence.

The applicant, Jean-François Federici, was charged with murder committed as part of an organised group and conspiracy to commit a crime. After failing to comply with court supervision in 2011, he absconded. In 2014 he was tried in absentia and sentenced to thirty years’ imprisonment. Arrested in 2016, he was retried in 2017 and again sentenced to thirty years. He appealed.

The appeal hearings took place in April 2018 in the standard courtroom of the Aix-en-Provence Assize Court of Appeal. Federici appeared in an open-roofed glass dock, a permanent fixture, assisted by two lawyers. According to undisputed Government descriptions, the dock measured 3.68m by 2.47m and had perforations (hygiaphones) at human height for confidential communication with defence counsel seated directly adjacent. It also had document slots, microphones, and a loudspeaker so the accused could hear and be heard. He remained free inside the dock, with guards only to prevent escape.

On 6 April 2018, he was questioned about his personality from the dock and did not complain of hearing difficulties or request removal. On 10 April, before his substantive questioning, his lawyer requested that he appear outside the dock, relying on Article 6 and Directive (EU) 2016/343. The lawyer cited security checks already undergone by the public and alleged hearing impairment that made questions harder to hear. On 11 April, the president questioned him while he remained in the dock.

On 13 April, the Assize Court dismissed the request. It relied on Articles 318 and D.294 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which require security measures for an accused’s appearance given danger and escape risk. It noted that Directive Article 5 does not prevent physical restraints necessary for case-specific security or to prevent absconding. The court found the applicant faced life imprisonment, was charged with murder by an organised group, and had previously absconded for over four years. It observed that, despite hearing problems, he could answer questions and communicate confidentially with his lawyers, and was free to move in the dock. The measure was therefore lawful, proportionate, and necessary, and did not infringe the presumption of innocence, dignity, or defence rights. That same day, he was convicted of double murder and sentenced to thirty years. The Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal in April 2019, finding no indication that he had been prevented from communicating with counsel.

Before the ECtHR, Federici alleged that his appearance in the glass dock and the refusal to let him be questioned outside it unjustifiably restricted his effective participation, defence rights, and presumption of innocence. The Court noted that he did not dispute his first-instance appearance, did not claim degrading treatment, and did not argue that exchanges with his lawyers were impaired. The Government argued the request was late and the hearing impairment unsubstantiated, while maximum security was justified by the violent organised-crime charges and his prior escape.

The ECtHR found the complaint under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(b) unsubstantiated and manifestly ill-founded. On the presumption of innocence, there were no objective reasons to fear negative presentation: the dock was sufficiently spacious and equipped, the applicant could move freely and communicate confidentially with his lawyers, and security risks justified the arrangement. No breach of Article 6 was found.

France* (Application no. 52302/19), the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, examined whether requiring an accused to answer questions from a glass dock during criminal appeal proceedings violated Article 6 §§1, 2 and 3(b) of the Convention—fair trial, presumption of innocence, and rights of the defence. The judgment was delivered on 3 April 2025 and became final on 3 July 2025.

The applicant, Jean-François Federici, a French national born in 1957, was indicted before the Bouches-du-Rhône Assize Court on charges of murder committed as a member of an organised group and conspiracy to commit a crime. After failing to comply with court supervision in 2011, he absconded and was sentenced in absentia in 2014 to thirty years’ imprisonment. Arrested in 2016, he was retried and again sentenced to thirty years in January 2017. He appealed.

The appeal hearings took place in April 2018 in Aix-en-Provence in a standard courtroom. Federici appeared in an open-roofed glass dock, a permanent fixture measuring 3.68 metres by 2.47 metres. The dock had perforations at human height for communication with his lawyers, document slots, microphones, and a loudspeaker allowing him to hear proceedings. He was not physically restrained and could move freely inside it. On 6 April 2018, he was questioned about his personality from the dock and did not mention hearing difficulties or ask to be removed. On 10 April, his lawyer requested that he be questioned outside the dock, relying on Article 6 ECHR, the presumption of innocence, and EU Directive 2016/343. Counsel cited prior security checks on the public and alleged hearing impairment that sometimes made it difficult to hear questions. On 11 April, the President questioned Federici while he remained in the dock.

On 13 April 2018, the Assize Court dismissed the request. It found the glass dock lawful, proportionate, and necessary. It noted the gravity of the charges, the possible life sentence, and that Federici had absconded for more than four years before being detained. Although he had hearing problems, the court observed that he could answer questions and communicate confidentially with his lawyers. The dock permitted free movement and confidential exchanges with counsel. The court concluded there was no infringement of dignity, the presumption of innocence, or defence rights. That same day, Federici was convicted of double murder as part of an organised group and sentenced to thirty years. The Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal on points of law in April 2019, finding no indication that he had been prevented from communicating with his lawyers.

Before the ECtHR, Federici alleged violations of Article 6 §§1, 2 and 3(b), arguing that his appearance in the glass dock restricted his right to appear freely, participate effectively, and be presumed innocent. The ECtHR focused on the refusal to question him outside the dock on 11 April 2018. It noted that he did not contest his first-instance appearance, nor claim degrading treatment under Article 3 or poor communication with counsel under Article 6 §3(c).

The Court declared the complaint unsubstantiated and manifestly ill-founded. Key factors were that the dock was sufficiently spacious and equipped; it was a permanent courtroom fixture; the applicant requested removal only near the close of the appeal proceedings; no objective reasons suggested he was presented in a negative light; his hearing impairment was unsubstantiated; and real security risks existed because of the violent organised-crime charges and his prior flight. He could move freely and communicate confidentially with his lawyers. The Court therefore found no breach of fair trial rights or the presumption of innocence.

In *Federici v. France* (Application no. 52302/19, ECtHR, 2025), the applicant, Jean-François Federici, complained that his appearance in a glass dock during his criminal appeal violated Article 6 §§ 1, 2 and 3(b) of the Convention—namely his right to a fair trial, the rights of the defence, and the presumption of innocence. The key facts concerned his questioning by an assize court of appeal while he remained inside a secure glass enclosure.

Federici had been charged with murder committed as a member of an organised group and with conspiracy to commit a crime. In 2011, while under court supervision, he absconded. In 2014 he was convicted in absentia and sentenced to thirty years’ imprisonment. After his arrest in 2016, he was placed in pre-trial detention and retried. In January 2017 the Assize Court again sentenced him to thirty years. He appealed.

The appeal hearings took place in April 2018 in the standard courtroom of the Aix-en-Provence Law Courts. Federici appeared in a permanent open-roofed glass dock measuring 3.68 metres by 2.47 metres. The dock had hygiaphones—perforations at human height—allowing communication with his lawyers, document slots, fixed microphones so he could be heard, and a loudspeaker so he could hear the courtroom. It also had a glass door and a secure access door. The Government described the dock as spacious and equipped; Federici did not dispute that description.

On 6 April 2018, Federici was heard on his personality while in the dock. He did not mention hearing difficulties or ask to be questioned outside it. On 10 April, his lawyer requested that he appear in the courtroom itself rather than the glass dock, relying on Article 6 and EU Directive 2016/343. The request cited security checks undergone by the public and an alleged hearing impairment that sometimes made it harder to hear questions. On 11 April, the president questioned Federici while he remained in the dock.

In an interlocutory judgment of 13 April 2018, the Assize Court dismissed the request. It held that Articles 318 and D.294 of the Code of Criminal Procedure required courts to take necessary security measures. Article 5 of Directive 2016/343 did not prevent physical restraint where required for case-specific security or absconding risks. The court noted that Federici faced organised-group murder charges, possible life imprisonment, and was in pre-trial detention after absconding for over four years. It observed that despite his hearing problems he could answer questions and communicate confidentially with his lawyers. The dock allowed free movement and confidential communication, so his placement was lawful, proportionate and necessary, breaching neither the presumption of innocence, dignity nor defence rights. The same day he was convicted of double murder and sentenced to thirty years. The Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal in 2019, finding no indication that he had been prevented from communicating with his lawyers.

Before the ECtHR, the Government argued that the request was late, vague, and unsubstantiated as to hearing loss, and that security required maximum measures given the violent organised-crime context and prior absconding. The National Bar Council criticised glass docks generally, but the Court focused on the specific facts. It noted Federici did not dispute his first-instance appearance or claim degrading treatment or a breach of lawyer communication under Article 6 § 3(c). The relevant facts showed a sufficiently spacious, equipped dock; free movement and confidential communication; no objective reason to fear negative presentation; unsupported hearing allegations; and substantial security and absconding risks. The Court therefore found the complaints unsubstantiated and manifestly ill-founded, with no violation of Article 6 §§ 1, 2 or 3(b).

In *Ftiti v. Greece* (Application no. 37957/14), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether the applicant’s right to appeal his criminal conviction, guaranteed by Article 2 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention, was effective. The applicant, a Tunisian national who had resided in Greece since 1996 and lived in Crete, was arrested on 29 December 2009 in Rethymno on suspicion of aggravated livestock theft committed jointly. He was detained pending trial. On 17 February 2010, the Chania Mixed Jury Court sentenced him to seventeen years’ imprisonment and a €1,000 fine. The first-instance court ruled that any appeal would not have suspensive effect and ordered his deportation after completion of his sentence. It did not give reasons for refusing to suspend execution of the sentence.

The applicant appealed. On 30 January 2014, he attended a hearing before the Crete Criminal Court of Appeal, but the case was adjourned to 13 November 2014 because key prosecution witnesses were absent. While in Kassandra Prison, the applicant informed the prosecutor that he did not wish to be transferred to court for the November hearing because his lawyer would represent him. On the day of the hearing, he requested an adjournment, claiming he could not contact his lawyer. On 20 January 2015, still detained, he was notified that the appeal hearing had been rescheduled for 1 November 2015.

On 25 February 2015, the Chalkidiki Criminal Court of First Instance granted him conditional release under Article 105 of the Criminal Code, as he had served three-fifths of his sentence after deductions for work and had shown good behaviour. He was formally released on 6 March 2015, but was transferred to a migrant detention facility in Triglia. On 22 April 2015, he was deported to Tunisia and banned from entering the Schengen area. As a result, when the Crete Mixed Jury Court of Appeal sought to secure his attendance for the 1 November 2015 hearing, the request could not reach him: he had not appointed a new representative and had provided an incomplete address in Tunisia. On 1 November 2015, the appeal court rejected his appeal as unfounded owing to his absence from the hearing.

Before the Strasbourg Court, the applicant complained that his right of appeal had been violated. The Government argued that he had failed to exhaust domestic remedies because he could have requested a stay of execution under Article 497 § 7 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Government also contended that he had lost victim status by failing to attend or appoint a representative for appeal hearings. The Court rejected the non-exhaustion objection, finding that Greece had not demonstrated that a stay request would have been an accessible and effective remedy for his complaint. It joined the victim-status objection to the merits and declared the application admissible.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation were that the appeal had no suspensive effect, the applicant was conditionally released and then immediately expelled from Greece before his appeal could be heard, and the appeal was ultimately dismissed solely because he was absent. The Court found that the delayed examination of the appeal, combined with the immediate expulsion and the non-suspensive nature of the sentence, meant that the appellate review could not effectively address any deficiencies in the lower court’s decision. The judgment therefore found a violation of Article 2 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention.

In *Ftiti v. Greece* (Application no. 37957/14), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether the applicant’s right to have his criminal conviction reviewed by a higher tribunal under Article 2 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention was effective.

The applicant, Cherif Ftiti, a Tunisian national who had a Greek residence permit and lived in Crete, was arrested in Rethymno in December 2009 on suspicion of aggravated livestock theft and detained pending trial. On 17 February 2010, the Chania Mixed Jury Court convicted him and sentenced him to seventeen years’ imprisonment and a fine of 1,000 euros. The first-instance court ruled that any appeal would not have suspensive effect and ordered his deportation upon completion of his sentence. It did not provide reasons for refusing to suspend execution of the sentence. The applicant appealed.

The appeal proceedings were delayed. A hearing took place on 30 January 2014, but the case was adjourned to 13 November 2014 because key prosecution witnesses were absent. In October 2014, the prison director informed the prosecutor that the applicant did not wish to be transferred to court for the November hearing because his lawyer would represent him. On the day of that hearing, the applicant requested an adjournment, claiming he could not contact his lawyer. The appeal hearing was then rescheduled for 1 November 2015.

In the meantime, on 25 February 2015, the Chalkidiki Criminal Court of First Instance granted the applicant conditional release under Article 105 of the Criminal Code, as he had served three-fifths of his sentence after deductions for work and had shown good behaviour. He was released on 6 March 2015, but was transferred to a migrant detention facility and deported to Tunisia on 22 April 2015. He was also banned from entering the Schengen area.

Before the rescheduled appeal hearing, the Crete Mixed Jury Court of Appeal asked the prosecutor to secure the applicant’s attendance. However, the request could not be served on him because he had not appointed a new representative and had provided an incomplete residential address in Tunisia. On 1 November 2015, the appeal court rejected his appeal because he failed to appear.

The applicant complained that his right of appeal under Article 2 of Protocol No. 7 had been violated. The key issue was that his appeal had no suspensive effect on the prison sentence, meaning he served the sentence and was released and expelled before his appeal was decided. By the time the appeal was heard, he was no longer in Greece and could not attend, leading to dismissal of the appeal for absence. The higher court therefore never effectively reviewed his conviction or sentence.

The Greek Government argued that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies because he could have requested a stay of execution under Article 497 § 7 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Court rejected this objection, finding that the Government had not shown that such a request would have been an accessible and effective remedy capable of addressing his complaint. The Government also argued that the applicant had lost victim status by failing to attend or appoint a representative. The Court joined that objection to the merits.

The Court declared the application admissible and ultimately found that the delayed examination of the appeal, after the applicant’s conditional release and expulsion, together with the non-suspensive nature of the appeal, meant that the review could not effectively address the deficiencies in the lower court’s decision. There was therefore a violation of Article 2 of Protocol No. 7.

**Ftiti v. Greece** (Application no. 37957/14) concerned a Tunisian national, Cherif Ftiti, who had lived in Crete since 1996 and held a Greek residence permit. On 29 December 2009 he was arrested in Rethymno on suspicion of aggravated joint theft of livestock and detained pending trial. On 17 February 2010 the Chania Mixed Jury Court convicted him and imposed a seventeen-year prison sentence and a €1,000 fine. The first-instance court ruled that any appeal would not have suspensive effect and ordered his deportation after completion of sentence. It did not give reasons for refusing to suspend execution.

Ftiti appealed. On 30 January 2014 he attended a hearing before the Crete Criminal Court of Appeal, but the case was adjourned to 13 November 2014 because key prosecution witnesses were absent. On 27 October 2014 the prison director informed the prosecutor that Ftiti did not wish to be transferred to court for the November hearing because his lawyer would represent him. On the day of the hearing, Ftiti requested an adjournment because he could not contact his lawyer. On 20 January 2015, while still detained, he was notified that the appeal hearing had been rescheduled for 1 November 2015.

On 25 February 2015 the Chalkidiki Criminal Court of First Instance granted Ftiti conditional release under Article 105 of the Criminal Code. He had served three-fifths of his sentence after deductions for work and had demonstrated good behaviour. He was formally released on 6 March 2015, but was transferred to a migrant detention facility in Triglia. On 22 April 2015 he was deported to Tunisia and banned from entering the Schengen area.

In October 2015 the Crete Mixed Jury Court of Appeal asked the prosecutor in Chania to secure Ftiti’s attendance at the forthcoming appeal hearing. The request could not be forwarded because Ftiti had not appointed a new representative and had provided an incomplete residential address in Tunisia. On 1 November 2015 the appeal court rejected his appeal owing to his failure to appear, dismissing it as unfounded.

The alleged violation concerned Article 2 of Protocol No. 7 to the European Convention on Human Rights, which guarantees the right to have a criminal conviction or sentence reviewed by a higher tribunal. Ftiti complained that his appeal was ineffective in practice. Because the appeal had no suspensive effect, he served the minimum required period, was granted conditional release and was expelled from Greece before the appeal hearing. By the time the appeal was heard, he was outside the country, unable to attend or easily instruct counsel, and the appeal was dismissed in his absence. The higher court therefore could not effectively address any deficiencies in the first-instance decision. The judgment’s headnote records that the delayed examination and immediate expulsion meant the review was unable to address the lower court’s decision in an effective manner.

Under Greek law, Article 497 of the Code of Criminal Procedure governed suspensive effect and allowed a convicted person to request a stay of execution. The Government argued that Ftiti had failed to exhaust domestic remedies by not seeking such a stay, and that he had lost victim status by failing to attend or appoint a representative for two appeal hearings. The European Court of Human Rights found that the Government had not demonstrated that the stay procedure was accessible and effective for his complaint, and dismissed the non-exhaustion objection. It joined the victim-status objection to the merits and declared the application admissible. The case is significant for assessing when a right of appeal becomes illusory because the appellant has already served the relevant part of the sentence and been expelled before the appeal is examined.

In *Ships Waste Oil Collector B.V. and Others v. the Netherlands* (ECtHR Grand Chamber, 1 April 2025, nos. 2799/16 and others), the applicants were several Dutch companies, including port waste-oil collection and holding/investment companies, that had been fined by the Netherlands Authority for Consumers and Markets (NMA) for competition-law infringements. The fines were based partly on data obtained by criminal authorities through telephone tapping during criminal investigations. After the Public Prosecution Service lawfully intercepted communications, it transmitted the intercept material to the NMA for use in competition-law enforcement. The NMA used that material in administrative proceedings, leading to fines. The applicants challenged the fines in Dutch administrative courts and ultimately complained to the European Court of Human Rights.

The applicants alleged violations of Article 8 (right to respect for private life and correspondence) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy). They argued that the transmission and use of intercepted data by the NMA was an unjustified interference with their Article 8 rights. In particular, they questioned the legal basis and foreseeability of Dutch law, the safeguards against arbitrariness and abuse, the lack of prior judicial authorisation, the absence of prior notice, and the proportionality of using criminal intercept data in competition proceedings. They also said they had no effective remedy to challenge the transmission and use of the data.

The Grand Chamber treated the transmission of intercept data to another law-enforcement authority as a separate interference with Article 8, distinct from the original interception. It held that such transmission requires a legal basis, foreseeability, and minimum safeguards to prevent arbitrariness and abuse. Transmission must be limited to material collected in a Convention-compliant manner. The Court also held that the margin of appreciation depends on the content and nature of the data, not on whether the applicant is a natural or legal person; minimum Article 8 safeguards apply in principle equally to legal persons.

Applying these principles, the Court found that the Dutch legal framework provided an adequate legal basis and met foreseeability requirements. Authorisation by a non-judicial authority was compatible with Article 8. Article 8 did not require prior notification of the transmission or participation in pre-transmission review. Although the transmission authorisations lacked written reasoning and the applicants were not notified in advance, those shortcomings were compensated by effective ex post facto judicial review. The administrative courts conducted a de novo assessment and could afford appropriate redress. The Court said redress did not necessarily require destruction of the transmitted data or monetary compensation; restrictions on use could suffice. The safeguards were adequate, and the applicants had an opportunity to contest the transmissions effectively. The interference pursued the legitimate aim of enforcing competition law, and the balancing exercise was adequate; the reasons were relevant and sufficient to show necessity and proportionality. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 8. It also found no violation of Article 13, as an effective remedy existed.

In *Ships Waste Oil Collector B.V. and Others v. the Netherlands* (Application no. 2799/16 and 3 others, Grand Chamber, 1 April 2025), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by several Dutch companies involved in waste-oil collection, port services, and related activities. The applicants had been subject to criminal investigations in which Dutch authorities lawfully intercepted telephone communications. Later, the Public Prosecution Service transmitted that intercept material to the Netherlands Competition Authority (NMA) for use in competition-law proceedings. The NMA relied on the data, among other evidence, to impose fines for infringements of Dutch competition law.

The applicants alleged violations of Article 8 (right to respect for private life, home, and correspondence) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy). They argued that transmitting and using the intercept data in competition proceedings constituted a separate interference with their Article 8 rights, distinct from the original interception. They complained that Dutch law did not provide a sufficiently foreseeable legal basis, that safeguards against arbitrariness and abuse were inadequate, and that the transmission was authorized by a non-judicial authority—the prosecutor—without prior judicial approval. They also objected that they were not notified in advance of the transmission, had no opportunity to participate in any pre-transmission review, and could not effectively challenge the use of the data before the NMA imposed fines.

The domestic legal framework included the Judicial and Criminal Data Act, the WJSG Instructions, and an agreement between the Public Prosecution Service and the NMA. After the NMA imposed fines, the applicants challenged the decisions in administrative proceedings. The Rotterdam Regional Court and the Supreme Administrative Court for Trade and Industry reviewed the case, including the lawfulness of the data transmission.

The ECtHR held that the transmission of intercept data to another law-enforcement authority was a separate interference with Article 8, distinct from the original interception. However, the interference had a legal basis in Dutch law that satisfied foreseeability requirements. The Court found that authorizations by a non-judicial authority were compatible with Article 8, and that Article 8 does not guarantee prior notification of the transmission or a right to participate in any review before it occurs. The absence of written reasoning in the transmission authorizations and the lack of prior notice were compensated by effective ex post facto judicial review. The domestic courts conducted a de novo assessment and could afford appropriate redress. Redress did not necessarily require destruction of the transmitted data or monetary compensation; restrictions on use could suffice.

The Court also held that the margin of appreciation depended on the content and nature of the data, not on whether the applicant was a natural or legal person, and that minimum safeguards were in principle the same for companies. Adequate safeguards against arbitrariness and abuse existed, and the applicants had an opportunity to contest the transmissions effectively. Balancing the interests at stake, the interference pursued the legitimate aim of enforcing competition law and was necessary and proportionate. Accordingly, there was no violation of Article 8. The Court further found no violation of Article 13, because the applicants had an effective remedy through the administrative courts.

**Ships Waste Oil Collector B.V. and Others v. the Netherlands** (ECtHR Grand Chamber, 1 April 2025) concerned Dutch competition-law fines imposed on companies in the port waste-oil collection sector using evidence originally obtained through telephone tapping in criminal investigations.

The applicants were several companies, including Ships Waste Oil Collector B.V., Burando Holding B.V., Port Invest B.V. and Janssen de Jong Groep B.V. and Others. During criminal investigations, Dutch authorities lawfully intercepted telephone communications under the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Public Prosecution Service then transmitted intercepted data to the Netherlands Competition Authority (NMA) for use in competition-law proceedings. The NMA used that material to impose fines for competition infringements. The applicants were not notified before the transmissions, and the transmission authorisations were issued by a non-judicial authority and did not contain written reasoning.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged violations of Article 8 (right to respect for private life and correspondence) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy). They argued that the transmission and subsequent use of intercepted communications by the NMA amounted to an unjustified interference. In particular, they complained that Dutch law lacked a sufficiently foreseeable legal basis, that the safeguards against arbitrariness and abuse were inadequate, that prior judicial authorisation and prior notification should have been required, and that they had no effective opportunity to contest the transmissions. They sought, among other things, destruction of the transmitted data or compensation.

The Grand Chamber held that transmitting intercept data from one law-enforcement authority to another constituted a separate interference with Article 8 rights, distinct from the original interception. However, such interference could be justified if accompanied by minimum safeguards. The Court required that transmissions be limited to material collected in a Convention-compliant manner and be subject to accessible and foreseeable domestic law with safeguards against arbitrariness and abuse. It also held that the breadth of the State’s margin of appreciation depended on the content and nature of the data, not on whether the applicant was a natural or legal person; legal persons were in principle entitled to the same safeguards.

The Court found that the Dutch legal framework provided a sufficient legal basis and was foreseeable. Transmission authorisations by a non-judicial authority were compatible with Article 8. Article 8 did not guarantee prior notification of the transmission or participation in pre-transmission review. In the applicants’ circumstances, the absence of written reasoning in the authorisations and of prior notice was compensated by effective ex post facto judicial review. The Supreme Administrative Court for Trade and Industry had conducted a de novo assessment and could afford appropriate redress. The Court added that redress need not necessarily require destruction of the data or monetary compensation; restrictions on use could suffice. The applicants had been able to contest the transmissions effectively, and the interference pursued the legitimate aim of enforcing competition law. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 8.

As the applicants had an effective remedy before the domestic courts, the Court also found no violation of Article 13.

In **Malgazhdarov and Others v. Russia** (Applications nos. 4562/23 and 7 others), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 16 January 2025. The case concerned multiple applications lodged against Russia under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates. The applicants were participants or organisers of solo demonstrations in Russia. The Court noted that the facts giving rise to the alleged violations occurred before 16 September 2022, when Russia ceased to be a party to the Convention. It nevertheless held that it had jurisdiction, relying on *Fedotova and Others v. Russia* and *Pivkina and Others v. Russia*. Because the applications shared a similar subject matter, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment.

The applicants complained principally that the measures against them as solo demonstrators violated their rights. They relied, expressly or in substance, on Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention. The Court examined the complaints under Article 10 § 1, taking into account its general principles developed under Article 11 concerning freedom of peaceful assembly. It referred to the leading case *Novikova and Others v. Russia*, where it had already found violations concerning similar issues. After examining all material, the Court found no fact or argument capable of leading to a different conclusion. It held that the interferences with the applicants’ freedom of expression were not “necessary in a democratic society.” Accordingly, it found a violation of Article 10 § 1.

Russia*; the absence of a prosecuting party in proceedings under the Code of Administrative Offences, contrary to *Karelin v. **Case Summary: Malgazhdarov and Others v. Russia**

The case of *Malgazhdarov and Others v. Russia* (Applications nos. 4562/23 and 7 others) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) in a judgment dated 16 January 2025. The case originated in applications lodged against Russia under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Russian Government were given notice of the applications. Because the applications raised similar subject matter, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment.

The key facts concern the applicants’ participation in or organisation of solo demonstrations in Russia. The applicants complained principally of disproportionate measures taken against them by the authorities. These measures included the termination of their demonstrations, their arrest, and their conviction for administrative offences. Some applicants also raised additional complaints under other Convention provisions. The underlying facts giving rise to the alleged violations occurred before 16 September 2022, the date on which the Russian Federation ceased to be a party to the Convention. The Court nevertheless found that it had jurisdiction to examine the applications, relying on its earlier case-law in *Fedotova and Others v. Russia* and *Pivkina and Others v. Russia*.

On the main complaint, the applicants relied expressly or in substance on Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention, alleging violations of their freedom of expression and freedom of assembly. The Court examined the complaints under Article 10 § 1, taking into account the general principles it had established under Article 11 in the context of public assemblies. It referred particularly to the leading case of *Novikova and Others v. Russia*, where it had already found violations in respect of similar issues involving solo demonstrators. After examining all the material, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion. It held that the interferences with the applicants’ freedom of expression were not “necessary in a democratic society.” Accordingly, the Court found a violation of Article 10 § 1 of the Convention.

Some applicants also submitted other complaints which raised issues already well established in the Court’s case-law. These included unlawful deprivation of liberty of organisers or participants of public assemblies, as found in *Butkevich v. Russia*, *Tsvetkova and Others v. Russia*, and *Korneyeva v. Russia*. They also included the absence of a prosecuting party in proceedings under the Code of Administrative Offences, following *Karelin v. Russia*, and disproportionate measures taken by the authorities against organisers and participants of public assemblies, following *Navalnyy and Yashin v. Russia* and *Kasparov and Others v. Russia*. The Court declared these complaints admissible and found that they disclosed violations of the Convention in light of that established case-law.

The applicant in application no. 4562/23 also raised an additional complaint under Article 6 of the Convention concerning the first set of proceedings, which ended with a final judgment on 15 September 2022. In view of the Court’s findings of violations under Articles 10 and other provisions, it considered that there was no need to deal separately with that remaining complaint.

Finally, under Article 41 of the Convention, the Court awarded the applicants the sums indicated in the appended table. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision. In essence, the case is a repetitive solo-demonstration case: the Russian authorities’ termination of demonstrations, arrest of demonstrators, and administrative convictions amounted to unjustified interferences with freedom of expression and assembly, and related detention and procedural issues also violated the Convention.

001-243782:
M.L. v. North Macedonia concerns an Article 8 family-life complaint by a Macedonian father who was barred from approaching his nine-year-old daughter during criminal proceedings. The applicant married the child’s mother in 2013, and their daughter was born in December 2013. After the applicant filed for divorce and custody in December 2021, he moved out in June 2022. From June to October 2022 the daughter apparently stayed with him every other week. On 25 October 2022 he told the Social Care Centre that the mother had begun criminal proceedings against him and that he had not seen his daughter since 2 October 2022. In January 2023 the Centre established contact rights—alternate weekends and Wednesdays—but the applicant repeatedly complained that the mother did not comply and that the daughter refused contact, allegedly because of the mother’s and her family’s influence.

The criminal proceedings involved complaints from both sides. On 20 October 2022 the mother reported that the applicant had sent threatening messages; police later filed a criminal complaint for threatening her. On 1 March 2023 the mother reported that the applicant had physically and psychologically abused their daughter between October 2022 and March 2023. That same day the daughter was interviewed. She stated that she had not seen the applicant since October 2022 because she did not want to, alleged that he had hit, threatened and insulted her, and said she did not wish to see him. A teacher, school psychologist, pedagogical expert and maternal grandmother were also interviewed. Medical notes described the daughter as upset, angry and afraid and recommended psychological support. On 6 March 2023 the applicant was detained and interviewed; he denied the allegations and said he had not seen his daughter since 2 October 2022. Police filed a criminal complaint for bodily injury through domestic violence and violence against a child.

On the same day, the public prosecutor requested protective measures. A pre-trial judge issued a barring order prohibiting the applicant from approaching the daughter and mother within 100 metres and from visiting the daughter’s school or home. The order was to last as long as necessary, up to a final criminal judgment, and was to be reassessed every two months. The judge reasoned that the seriousness of the offences, the prescribed sentence, the manner of commission and consequences justified a risk that the applicant might influence the victims. The applicant’s personal, family and material circumstances did not, in the judge’s view, sufficiently rebut that expectation. The order also referred to the daughter’s psychological and physical health and the need for unhindered criminal proceedings.

The applicant appealed on 9 March 2023, arguing that he could not have abused the daughter between October 2022 and March 2023 because he had barely seen her since 2 October 2022. He submitted Centre documents, the contact-rights decision and complaints about non-enforcement, and an expert report denying that threatening messages had been sent from his phone. He argued that the barring order would further alienate his daughter. On 15 March 2023 a three-judge panel dismissed the appeal, finding the order justified and substantiated by sufficient facts and evidence, particularly at the investigation stage.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 8. Although the initial precautionary barring order was not unreasonable, the three-judge panel failed to give sufficient reasoning or conduct an autonomous and comprehensive risk assessment. More critically, despite the mandatory two-month reassessment requirement, the pre-trial judge issued no reasoned reassessment decisions. There was no meaningful scrutiny based on updated information, no involvement of the applicant, and no procedural guarantees allowing him to protect his interest in being reunited with his daughter. The prolonged barring order therefore violated his right to respect for family life.

The ECtHR case *M.L. v. North Macedonia* (Application no. 30206/23) concerns an Article 8 complaint by a Macedonian father against a criminal barring order preventing him from approaching his nine-year-old daughter. M.L. married D.B.L. in 2013; their daughter D. was born in December 2013. After separation, custody and contact proceedings began. The Social Care Centre initially recommended custody to M.L. and in January 2023 set contact rights, including alternate weekends and Wednesdays. M.L. complained that the mother obstructed contact and that he had barely seen D. since 2 October 2022.

In parallel criminal proceedings, the mother reported in October 2022 that M.L. had sent threatening messages to her. In March 2023 she further alleged that M.L. had physically and psychologically abused D. between October 2022 and March 2023—insulting, threatening, shouting at, hitting and kicking her. When interviewed by police, D. said she had not seen her father since October 2022 because she did not want to, alleged hitting and threats, and stated she did not wish to see him. A teacher, school psychologist, pedagogical expert and maternal grandmother gave supporting accounts; psychiatric notes described D. as upset, anxious and afraid. M.L. denied the allegations, noting he had almost no contact with D. after 2 October 2022, and said he had filed counter-complaints against the mother.

On 6 March 2023, at the prosecutor’s request, a pre-trial judge issued a barring order under the Criminal Proceedings Act. It prohibited M.L. from approaching D. and the mother within 100 metres and from visiting D.’s home or school until final judgment, subject to reassessment every two months. The judge reasoned that the seriousness of the charges, the prescribed sentence, the manner and consequences of the alleged offences, and D.’s psychological and physical health justified measures to prevent influence over victims and ensure unhindered proceedings. M.L.’s personal, family and employment circumstances did not sufficiently rebut that risk. M.L. appealed, arguing that abuse during the alleged period was impossible because he had no contact with D.; he submitted contact-rights decisions, complaints about obstruction, and an expert report disputing the threatening messages. On 15 March 2023 a three-judge panel dismissed the appeal, confirming the order based on reasonable suspicion and the investigation stage, without detailed response to his updated evidence.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 8. Although the initial precautionary order was not unreasonable, the appeal panel’s reasoning and risk assessment were insufficient. More critically, the pre-trial judge failed to give reasoned decisions in the mandatory periodic reassessments, did not meaningfully scrutinise updated information, did not involve M.L. in reassessment, and provided no procedural guarantees enabling him to protect his family-life interest in being reunited with his daughter. The case therefore concerned the continuing proportionality and procedural fairness of the barring order.

**Summary of the Case M.L. v. North Macedonia**

The case of *M.L. v. North Macedonia* (Application no. 30206/23) concerns a violation of Article 8 (right to respect for family life) of the European Convention on Human Rights, stemming from a barring order that prohibited a father from approaching his nine-year-old daughter.

The applicant, M.L., married D.B.L. in 2013, and their daughter, D., was born in December 2013. Following marital difficulties, the applicant filed for divorce in December 2021 and sought custody. The Social Care Centre initially recommended in his favour in March 2022. However, the situation escalated in late 2022. The applicant notified the Centre that his wife had initiated criminal proceedings against him and that he had not seen his daughter since early October 2022. In January 2023, the Centre established his contact rights, but by late January, the applicant began complaining that the mother was not complying; he had only seen his daughter twice, and she appeared visibly upset.

The core of the case lies in concurrent criminal proceedings. On 20 October 2022, the mother reported that the applicant had sent her threatening messages. Subsequently, on 1 March 2023, she reported that the applicant had physically and psychologically abused their daughter between October 2022 and March 2023. The daughter was interviewed by police and stated that the applicant had hit, insulted, and threatened her, and that she did not wish to see him. Other witnesses, including a teacher and the maternal grandmother, provided statements corroborating behavioural changes in the child. Medical reports also noted the child’s fear and anxiety.

On 6 March 2023, based on these allegations and evidence, the public prosecutor requested that a pre-trial judge issue protective measures against the applicant. The same day, the judge issued a barring order under the Criminal Proceedings Act, prohibiting the applicant from approaching his daughter and her mother within 100 metres, and from visiting the daughter's school or home. The order was to remain in effect until a final judgment in the criminal proceedings. The judge’s reasoning cited the seriousness of the charges and a risk that the applicant might influence the victims, noting that his personal circumstances did not sufficiently justify an expectation that he would not do so.

The applicant appealed on 9 March 2023, arguing that he could not have been violent towards his daughter between October 2022 and March 2023 as he had barely seen her since October 2022. He submitted evidence of his complaints to the Social Care Centre regarding the non-enforcement of his contact rights. He also challenged the threats against the mother, providing an expert report suggesting no messages were sent from his phone on the alleged date. However, on 15 March 2023, a three-judge panel dismissed his appeal, finding the order justified and substantiated by reasonable suspicion, without addressing the applicant's specific arguments or the evidence he had submitted.

The European Court of Human Rights found that while the initial barring order was not unreasonable as a precautionary measure, the subsequent proceedings violated the applicant's rights. The key failures were: the three-judge panel's insufficient reasoning and lack of an autonomous risk assessment; the absence of reasoned decisions by the pre-trial judge concerning the mandatory periodic reassessment of the order every two months; a lack of meaningful scrutiny based on updated information; the failure to involve the applicant in the reassessment process; and the overall lack of procedural guarantees to protect his interest in being reunited with his daughter.

In the case of *Kashbullina and Others v. Russia* (Applications nos. 1964/22 and four others), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 13 November 2025. The applications were lodged against Russia under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates and were joined because they raised similar issues. The Russian Government was given notice. The Court noted that the underlying facts occurred before 16 September 2022, when Russia ceased to be a party to the Convention, but found it still had jurisdiction, relying on *Fedotova and Others v. Russia*.

The applicants were organisers or participants in public assemblies in St Petersburg. They complained of disproportionate measures taken against them in connection with their participation in various public events allegedly held in breach of regional COVID-19-related restrictions. The measures included arrest in relation to the dispersal of these assemblies and conviction for administrative offences. The applicants relied, expressly or in substance, on Article 11 of the Convention, which protects freedom of assembly.

The Court examined the Article 11 complaints under its established case-law on freedom of assembly, referring to *Kudrevičius and Others v. Lithuania*, *Oya Ataman v. Turkey*, and *Hyde Park and Others v. Moldova*. It also referred to the leading case *Nemytov and Others v. Russia*, which found a violation of Article 11 in respect of similar issues, as well as *Frumkin v. Russia*, *Navalnyy and Yashin v. Russia*, and *Kasparov and Others v. Russia*. Having examined the material, the Court found no fact or argument capable of leading to a different conclusion. It held that the interferences with the applicants’ freedom of assembly were not “necessary in a democratic society” and therefore violated Article 11.

The applicants also raised other complaints under the Convention and its Protocols. The Court found these admissible and concluded that they disclosed violations in light of well-established case-law. These included unlawful deprivation of liberty of organisers or participants of public assemblies, as addressed in *Butkevich v. Russia*, *Tsvetkova and Others v. Russia*, and *Korneyeva v. Russia*; the absence of a prosecuting party in proceedings under the Code of Administrative Offences, as addressed in *Karelin v. Russia*; and the lack of suspensive effect of an appeal against a sentence of administrative detention, as addressed in *Martynyuk v. Russia*. The applicants further raised Article 6 complaints concerning other aspects of the fairness of the administrative-offence proceedings. In view of its findings on the other violations, the Court considered there was no need to deal separately with those remaining complaints.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore that the applicants organised or took part in public assemblies in St Petersburg during regional COVID-19 restrictions; authorities dispersed the assemblies, arrested the applicants, and convicted them of administrative offences; and the applicants alleged that these actions disproportionately restricted their assembly rights and related liberty and procedural rights. The Court agreed with the core Article 11 complaint and found additional violations under its settled case-law.

001-238843:
In the European Court of Human Rights case of *Abbate and Others v. Italy* (Application no. 27814/23 and four others), the First Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 16 January 2025. The case concerned five applications lodged against Italy under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates. The Italian Government were given notice. Because the applications raised similar subject matter, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment.

The core facts, as set out in the appended table (not reproduced in the judgment text), are that each applicant had obtained a domestic decision in his or her favour. Those decisions became final and enforceable. However, the Italian authorities either did not enforce them at all or enforced them only after significant delay. The applicants therefore complained principally that the non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of final domestic decisions violated their right to a fair hearing under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. They also raised other complaints under the Convention, which the Court considered under its well-established case-law.

The Court reiterated that the execution of a judgment given by any court must be regarded as an integral part of a “hearing” for the purposes of Article 6 § 1. It recalled *Hornsby v. Greece*, where it held that the right of access to a court would be illusory if a Contracting State could leave final, binding judicial decisions unenforced to the detriment of one party. It also referred to its earlier leading cases against Italy concerning similar non-enforcement or delayed enforcement issues: *Ventorino v. Italy*, *De Trana v. Italy*, *Nicola Silvestri v. Italy*, *Antonetto v. Italy*, and *De Luca v. Italy*. In those cases, the Court had already found violations of the Convention on comparable facts.

After examining all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of leading to a different conclusion on admissibility or merits. It considered that the Italian authorities had not deployed all necessary efforts to enforce fully and in due time the decisions in the applicants’ favour. Accordingly, it found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The Court also examined the applicants’ other complaints. It held that those complaints were not manifestly ill-founded, were admissible, and disclosed violations of the Convention in the light of its findings in *Ventorino* and related case-law.

Under Article 41 of the Convention, the Court considered it reasonable to award the applicants the sums indicated in the appended table, having regard to the documents in its possession and its case-law. Finally, the Court noted that the respondent State has an outstanding obligation to enforce the judgments which remain enforceable. The judgment was final, though subject to editorial revision. In essence, the case is a repetitive non-enforcement/delayed enforcement case against Italy, where final domestic decisions in the applicants’ favour were not executed promptly, leading to a violation of Article 6 § 1 and other well-established Convention violations, with just satisfaction awarded and continuing enforcement obligations.
