001-243562:
In *Á.F.L. v. Iceland* (no. 35789/22; judgment 10 June 2025), the applicant, an Icelandic man diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder, ADHD and mild intellectual disability, complained under Articles 8 and 14 that Iceland discriminated against him by failing to provide reasonable accommodation—child-rearing support required by his disability—leading to deprivation of custody of his daughter, V.F.

V.F. was born in February 2019. Child Protection Services (CPS) became involved due parental conflict, the mother’s mental-health problems and domestic violence. After the parents separated and the mother’s care arrangements broke down, the applicant took over care in September 2019. CPS placed V.F. with him at Mánaberg, a residential diagnostic and guidance facility. Staff knew of his impairment and gave intensive, individualized guidance. Reports noted his affection, cooperation and progress, but found he needed extensive help, struggled to recognize V.F.’s needs, transfer skills and cope with changing circumstances; independent care was not recommended.

After Mánaberg, CPS implemented a detailed support plan: the applicant and child lived with the paternal grandmother; Mánaberg staff made follow-up visits four times weekly; a YLFA counsellor—a psychologist and developmental therapist with disability expertise—visited twice weekly; a support family helped; and counselling, daycare and therapy cooperation continued. The Mánaberg stay had been exceptionally long and had gradually moved him from continuous supervision to a supported “apartment.” Reports from March–June 2020 found V.F. lacked stimulation, showed poor emotional control, self-stimulation and possible attachment difficulties; she was calmer with the support family. Support was increased, but concerns persisted. In July 2020 V.F. was temporarily removed and placed in foster care.

Reassessment reports by B.E. and a court-appointed expert, R.H.A., confirmed that, despite goodwill, the applicant lacked basic parenting skills and could not sufficiently benefit from further support. The expert considered the CRPD and support available under Act no. 38/2018 on services for disabled people, consulting a disability expert, but concluded that returning V.F. would risk her development. V.F. thrived in foster care. In September 2021 the District Court, with a psychologist lay judge and after hearing about twenty witnesses, deprived the applicant of custody. It found extensive, individualized measures had been tried but V.F.’s needs remained unmet. The Court of Appeal upheld, stating disability alone could not justify deprivation, but the decision rested on the child’s best interests and practical experience of support measures. The Supreme Court denied leave.

The applicant alleged that Iceland had denied reasonable accommodation and discriminated against him because of disability. The European Court of Human Rights found no violation of Article 14 read with Article 8. Domestic authorities had implemented multiple individualized, flexible support measures tailored to correct the factual inequality created by the applicant’s disability. His parental capacity was assessed with reference to those measures, and the evidence contained a comprehensive, detailed analysis. The custody deprivation was not based on his disability but on V.F.’s best interests after all available support measures had been exhausted without acceptable results. The decision was therefore non-discriminatory and reasonable.

In **Á.F.L. v. Iceland** (ECtHR, Third Section, 10 June 2025), the applicant, born in 1990, was diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder, ADHD and a mild intellectual disability. He had a history of alcohol and drug abuse but had been sober since 2012. In February 2019 his daughter, V.F., was born. Child protection services became involved because of instability and conflict in the home, including domestic violence concerns. After the parents separated, the child lived mainly with her mother and maternal grandmother. In September 2019 the applicant assumed care of V.F. with support from his mother.

The alleged violation concerned Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention. The applicant claimed that the Icelandic authorities failed to provide reasonable accommodation—child-rearing support necessitated by his disability—and that this failure led to his being deprived of custody of his daughter in a discriminatory manner.

The key facts centred on the extensive support measures tried by the child protection authorities. In September 2019 both parents consented to V.F.’s placement at Mánaberg, a residential CPS facility for diagnosis and guidance. The applicant stayed there with his daughter. Staff knew of his disability and provided continuous, detailed guidance on parenting, routines, hygiene, feeding and household tasks. He was gradually moved to a supported “apartment” within the facility. A December 2019 parenting assessment found that, although he was not testing at the level of intellectual disability, his cognitive difficulties and autism affected his parenting. He needed extensive assistance and could not care for V.F. alone. A January 2020 Mánaberg report noted progress but concluded he still needed targeted support, supervision two to three times per week, a support family and counselling.

After discharge, the applicant and V.F. moved to the paternal grandmother’s home. The CPS plan included follow-up visits four times per week, a YLFA counsellor twice weekly for six weeks, a support family four days per month, counselling at the Centre for Parents and Children, and later increased support, including YLFA visits three times per week, support family assistance seven days per month and continued psychological counselling. COVID-19 disrupted some services.

Reports from YLFA in March–June 2020 found the applicant affectionate but lacking insight into V.F.’s physical, social and emotional needs. The child showed motor delays, self-stimulation and possible attachment problems, while improving when cared for by the support family. In July 2020 V.F. was removed for two months and placed in temporary foster care. An August 2020 parenting assessment concluded that the applicant’s autism and intellectual challenges restricted his basic parenting capacity and ability to benefit from support, while V.F. progressed significantly in foster care.

In September 2020 the CPC decided on permanent foster care and initiated custody deprivation. A court-appointed expert in 2021 considered the CRPD and Icelandic disability-support legislation, but concluded the applicant lacked basic parenting skills and could not sufficiently benefit from further support; returning V.F. would be contrary to her best interests. The District Court deprived him of custody in September 2021 under Article 29(1)(a) and (d) of the Child Protection Act. The Court of Appeal upheld this in February 2022, and the Supreme Court denied leave to appeal.

The ECtHR found **no violation of Article 14 read with Article 8**. It held that the custody decision was not based on the applicant’s disability as such, but on the child’s best interests after all available support measures had been exhausted. The domestic authorities had implemented multiple individualised and flexible measures tailored to correct the factual inequality created by his disability, and his parental capacity had been assessed with reference to those measures. The Court found the domestic analysis comprehensive and the conclusions well-reasoned.

In Á.F.L. v. Iceland, the applicant, an Icelandic man diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder, ADHD and mild intellectual disability, complained under Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention that the Icelandic authorities failed to provide reasonable accommodation—support measures needed because of his disability—and that this failure led to his being deprived of custody of his daughter, V.F., born in February 2019.

CPS became involved after reports of parental conflict, domestic violence by the applicant, the mother’s mental-health problems and concerns for the child. The parents separated, and the mother initially had most care of V.F. In September 2019, after further incidents, the applicant assumed care with his mother’s support. Soon afterwards, both parents consented to V.F.’s placement in Mánaberg, a residential CPS diagnosis and guidance facility. After the mother left, the applicant and V.F. stayed there together. Staff knew of his impairments and provided intensive guidance on virtually all aspects of parenting, gradually moving him to a supported “apartment” and encouraging independent care. Reports in December 2019 found he was affectionate and had made progress but needed extensive assistance and could not care for V.F. alone. A January 2020 report concluded he could care for her only with targeted support, including a support family, autism/anxiety counselling and regular CPS visits.

A home-based plan followed. The applicant and V.F. moved to the paternal grandmother’s home, with Mánaberg follow-up visits four times per week, YLFA support from a psychologist/developmental therapist two to three times per week, a support family for up to seven days per month, and continued counselling. Reports through 2020 showed persistent difficulties: the applicant struggled to recognise V.F.’s needs, stimulate her development, take initiative and respond to changing circumstances. V.F. showed signs of possible attachment disorder and self-stimulation. Some support was disrupted by COVID-19 and the grandmother’s absence abroad.

In June 2020 the CPS recommended temporary foster care pending reassessment. In July 2020 the Child Protection Committee ruled that V.F. be removed for two months; she was placed with a foster family. An August 2020 psychologist’s report found the applicant attached and cooperative but that his autism and intellectual challenges severely restricted his parenting capacity; V.F. improved significantly in foster care. In September 2020 the CPC concluded that all available support measures had been exhausted and initiated custody-deprivation proceedings.

A court-appointed expert in April 2021 reviewed the case, consulted a disability expert, and considered the CRPD and Icelandic disability-support legislation. He concluded the applicant lacked basic parenting skills, benefited only slowly from support, would need daily guidance initially, and that returning V.F. to the previous situation would be contrary to her interests. The District Court, sitting with a psychologist lay judge, heard nearly twenty witnesses and deprived the applicant of custody, finding extensive support had been tried without acceptable results and no realistic additional measures were proposed. The Court of Appeal upheld that decision, stating that disability alone could not justify deprivation but that the decision rested on the applicant’s demonstrated parenting incapacity despite support. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal.

The European Court of Human Rights found no violation: the custody decision was not based on the applicant’s disability as such but on the child’s best interests once support measures were exhausted. The authorities had implemented multiple individualised and flexible measures tailored to his disability, assessed his parental capacity in light of that support, and reached well-reasoned conclusions.
001-243887:
**Case:** *Arvanitis and Phileleftheros Public Company Limited v. Cyprus* (Application no. 49917/22, European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, judgment 3 July 2025, final 3 October 2025).  
**Alleged violation:** Article 10 (freedom of expression) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicants were Christos Arvanitis, a journalist and columnist, and Phileleftheros Public Company Limited, publisher of the Cypriot daily *Phileleftheros*. They complained that Cyprus violated their Article 10 rights by holding them civilly liable for defamation and ordering damages over a published article.

The underlying facts concerned C.K., a well-known Cypriot lawyer. In June 2007, C.K. published an article in the Greek newspaper *To Vima* describing how he had recovered two family paintings left in the occupied areas of Cyprus after the 1974 Turkish invasion. He said he recovered one painting after paying a sum to unknown persons and, after failing to recover the second in exchange for money, replaced it with a forgery, inspired by the film *The Thomas Crown Affair*.

On 1 July 2007, Arvanitis published an article in *Phileleftheros* entitled “Property-Dignity, One-Nil.” It commented on C.K.’s account within the wider public debate about Greek-Cypriot property in the occupied areas. The article questioned paying a “ransom” for art, compared stolen houses with stolen paintings, asked whether C.K. advised his clients in the same way, and criticised him for allegedly bargaining with thieves, selling his dignity and harming compatriots. The edition sold 24,482 copies.

C.K. brought civil defamation proceedings, claiming the article damaged his personal and professional reputation. He argued it falsely portrayed him as prioritising property over national interests, negotiating with thieves and undermining compatriots. The applicants relied on truth and fair comment on a matter of public interest, arguing good faith and that C.K.’s own article was publicly accessible online. They said no prior consultation with C.K. was required.

In 2014, the Nicosia District Court found for C.K. and awarded €12,000 in damages plus statutory interest. It held the article defamatory, personally attacking C.K. and harming his professional standing. It found the article lacked a basis in truth: C.K. had said he “recovered” paintings, not that he “bought” them, and had not stated that he negotiated with the Turkish tavern owner. The court found the applicants distorted C.K.’s article, acted without good faith, and failed to contact him beforehand. It also concluded C.K. was not a public figure. The Supreme Court upheld those findings in 2022.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 10. It emphasised that the article concerned a matter of public interest—the restitution of looted art and property in occupied Cyprus. C.K. was a well-known lawyer involved in significant property litigation and had himself publicly described his actions, inviting public reaction. The applicants’ article was a reaction containing exaggerated value judgments, but it did not overstep the wide limits permitted to a free press. The domestic courts’ approach was overly restrictive and inconsistent with Article 10 principles. The civil award imposed a significant pecuniary burden and risked a chilling effect on open discussion of matters of public concern. The domestic reasons were not relevant and sufficient; the interference was disproportionate and not “necessary in a democratic society.”

**Summary of *Arvanitis and Phileleftheros Public Company Limited v. Cyprus* (Application no. 49917/22)**

The case concerns an alleged violation of Article 10 (freedom of expression) of the European Convention on Human Rights, brought by Christos Arvanitis, a journalist, and Phileleftheros Public Company Limited, the publisher of the Cypriot daily newspaper *Phileleftheros*.

The facts stem from a public dispute over the recovery of Greek-Cypriot property from the occupied areas of Cyprus. In June 2007, a well-known lawyer, referred to as C.K., published an article in the Greek newspaper *To Vima*. He described how he had recovered two family paintings left in occupied Cyprus after the 1974 Turkish invasion. He stated he recovered the first painting "after paying a sum of over thirty silver coins" to unknown persons and the second by replacing it with a forgery, inspired by the film *The Thomas Crown Affair*.

On 1 July 2007, the first applicant, Arvanitis, published a column in *Phileleftheros* entitled "Property-Dignity, One-Nil," responding to C.K.'s article. The article criticised C.K.'s methods, questioning the morality of paying a "ransom" for stolen property and suggesting that such actions, especially by a lawyer involved in an important property case at the European level, had wider consequences. It implied C.K. had "sold his dignity" and "bargained with thieves," asking if this was how he advised his clients.

In 2008, C.K. lodged a civil defamation claim against the applicants, arguing the article damaged his personal and professional reputation. He contended it falsely portrayed him as prioritising material goods over national interest and as negotiating with thieves.

The applicants defended the article as truthful and fair comment on a matter of public interest. Arvanitis argued he commented on C.K.'s already public article, engaging in a wider debate about Greek-Cypriot movable property. He asserted the article expressed honest opinion based on C.K.'s own statements about recovering paintings by paying money and using a forgery.

In 2014, the Nicosia District Court ruled in favour of C.K., finding the publication defamatory. The court held the article exceeded fair comment, containing personal attacks that harmed C.K.'s professional standing by characterising him as having given up his dignity and sold out compatriots. It found the article lacked factual basis, as C.K. never said he "bought" the paintings; using "recovered" did not equate to a purchase, and paying a sum did not mean bargaining with thieves. The court criticised Arvanitis for failing to contact C.K. for comment before publication. It rejected the truth and fair comment defences, ordering the applicants to pay €12,000 in damages plus interest.

In 2022, the Supreme Court upheld the District Court's findings. It agreed C.K. was a private individual, not a public figure. It confirmed the article was not based on truth, as C.K. had not claimed to have purchased the paintings or negotiated with their new "owner," and thus the accusations of "bargaining with thieves" were unfounded. The Supreme Court also found the article did not constitute fair comment.

The applicants then brought the case to the European Court of Human Rights, complaining that the civil defamation judgment against them violated their right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention.

In *Arvanitis and Phileleftheros Public Company Limited v. Cyprus* (Application no. 49917/22), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) found a violation of Article 10 (freedom of expression). The judgment was delivered on 3 July 2025 and became final on 3 October 2025. The applicants were Christos Arvanitis, a journalist and columnist, and Phileleftheros Public Company Limited, the publisher of the Cypriot daily newspaper *Phileleftheros*.

The case arose from a civil defamation judgment against the applicants in Cyprus. In June 2007, a well-known Cypriot lawyer, C.K., published an article in the Greek newspaper *To Vima*. He described how he had recovered two family paintings left in the occupied areas of Cyprus after the 1974 Turkish invasion. He said he had recovered the first painting after paying “a sum of over thirty silver coins” to unknown persons, and the second by replacing it with a forgery, inspired by the film *The Thomas Crown Affair*.

On 1 July 2007, Arvanitis published an article in *Phileleftheros* entitled “Property-Dignity, One-Nil.” It commented on C.K.’s account and the wider issue of Greek Cypriots recovering property from the occupied north. The article questioned how a lawyer involved in important property litigation could pay a ransom or recover art in that manner, asked whether that was how he advised clients, and used strongly critical phrases such as “pay a ransom, sell your dignity, suck up to your rapists, ‘hang’ your compatriots.” It also referred to a “Thomas Crown affair alla turca.” The issue sold 24,482 copies.

C.K. sued the applicants for defamation in 2008. He claimed the article damaged his personal and professional reputation, falsely portraying him as advising clients against the national interest, prioritising material goods, negotiating with thieves, and harming compatriots. The applicants relied on defences of truth, fair comment on a matter of public interest, and good faith. They argued that C.K.’s own article was public and available online, and that Arvanitis had commented on an ongoing public debate about Greek-Cypriot property in the occupied areas.

In 2014, the Nicosia District Court found for C.K., awarding €12,000 plus interest. It held the article was defamatory, attacking C.K.’s dignity and patriotism and harming his professional standing while he was representing clients before the English Court of Appeal. It rejected truth because C.K. had never said he had “bought” the painting, only “recovered” it; the amount paid (CYP 1,000) was far below the painting’s value (over CYP 50,000) and did not equate to a ransom. It also found that the applicants had failed to contact C.K. or verify the facts. The court rejected fair comment, describing the article as a vulgar and bad-faith personal attack. It further held that C.K. was not a public figure. In 2022, the Supreme Court upheld those findings.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants alleged that the civil defamation judgment breached Article 10. The Court found that the article concerned a matter of public interest—the restitution of looted art and property in occupied Cyprus—and was published in reaction to C.K.’s own public article. Although the expressions were exaggerated, they did not overstep the boundaries permissible to a free press. The domestic courts’ approach was overly restrictive and inconsistent with Article 10 principles. The civil sanction imposed a significant pecuniary burden and had a chilling effect on open discussion of matters of public concern. The reasons given by the domestic courts were not relevant and sufficient, and the interference was disproportionate, not “necessary in a democratic society.” The Court therefore found a violation of Article 10.

**Case: Hagyó v. Hungary (Application no. 52624/10, ECtHR, 23 April 2013)**

The applicant, Miklós Hagyó, a Hungarian national, former Vice-Mayor of Budapest and former Member of Parliament, was arrested on 14 May 2010, shortly after losing parliamentary immunity following the 2010 general elections. He was charged with aggravated fraudulent breach of trust involving the misuse of funds at the Budapest Transport Company. Criminal proceedings had previously been opened against senior transport officials and a close colleague in the same context.

On 17 May 2010, the Buda Central District Court ordered his pre-trial detention. The prosecution alleged risks of absconding and collusion. The court relied on the seriousness of the charges, the fact that the applicant had sold properties, and an unspecified “element” suggesting he might leave the country. It also found a real risk of collusion because his immunity had only recently been removed and further investigative steps remained. The applicant’s appeal was rejected on 26 May 2010.

The defence repeatedly sought release or less coercive measures, including house arrest. It argued that the applicant had known for months that indictment was likely but had not fled; that the case had attracted intense publicity; that he had denied rumours of leaving and had offered cooperation; that he had paid off a 16 million HUF debt; and that he had not concealed evidence or influenced witnesses. The courts nonetheless prolonged detention at statutory intervals, often using stereotyped reasoning, mainly citing the prospect of a severe sentence, without an individualised assessment of his personal circumstances.

A key Article 5 complaint concerned equality of arms. The defence’s requests to consult the case file and evidence underlying the absconding allegation were disregarded. The prosecutor’s office refused access, and a complaint to the Chief Public Prosecutor remained unanswered. The evidence of his alleged intention to abscond was never disclosed, making it difficult effectively to challenge the detention.

As to Article 3, the applicant suffered from asthma, chronic sinusitis, gluten and dairy allergies, and chronic left-ear inflammation. On admission he weighed 130 kg. He was held at Budapest Penitentiary for over four months in cells of 3.52 m² per person, and another four months in cells of 4.7 m² including fixtures. From November 2010 he was permanently placed in a 4.7 m² cell. He was allowed only one hour outside per day. He received medication, a special diet, baths, and medical examinations; an expert confirmed serious health problems but considered them treatable in prison. He lost 37 kg, suffered an asthma attack, and refused some medication and one hospital transfer because it coincided with a family visit. Requests for larger cell space, less humidity, more fresh air, and better nutrition were largely unsuccessful. An extra daily outdoor hour was refused in November 2010 but granted in December.

Under Articles 8 and 13, the applicant complained about restricted family contact. From 9 November 2010, all meetings and phone calls with his common-law wife were banned due to an alleged collusion risk, the authorities claiming the couple intended to circumvent controlled family visits. His complaint to the Chief Prosecutor was unanswered. Related criminal proceedings against him for giving his wife a false retainer ended in acquittal, and wardens stated all visits had been supervised. His 11-year-old daughter never visited because of her own health, though extra phone time was granted in September 2010 and January 2011 in addition to regular calls.

Pre-trial detention lasted until 23 February 2011, when it was replaced by house arrest because his serious health problems reduced the absconding risk. House arrest continued until 10 June 2011. The applicant alleged violations of Article 5, Article 3, and Article 8 alone and with Article 13.

**Summary of *Hagyó v. Hungary* (Application no. 52624/10)**

The case of *Hagyó v. Hungary* concerns an application brought by Miklós Hagyó, a Hungarian national and former Vice-Mayor of Budapest, against the Republic of Hungary. The applicant alleged violations of Articles 3, 5, 8, and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights, primarily challenging the lawfulness and conditions of his pre-trial detention.

**Key Facts:**

On 14 May 2010, the applicant was arrested on charges of aggravated fraudulent breach of trust related to the misuse of funds at the Budapest Transport Company. His arrest occurred shortly after he lost his parliamentary immunity following the 2010 general elections. On 17 May 2010, the Buda Central District Court ordered his detention on remand, citing risks of absconding and collusion. The court noted an unspecified "element" suggesting he might flee and referenced outstanding investigative steps. His appeal was rejected on 26 May 2010.

A central issue was the violation of the "equality of arms" principle. The defence's repeated requests to consult the case file, specifically to examine the evidence purportedly justifying the detention, were consistently denied by the courts and the prosecution. The evidence of his alleged intention to abscond was never disclosed to the applicant or his lawyer.

His pre-trial detention was repeatedly prolonged. The defence argued that the applicant, knowing of his likely indictment, had not fled, had cooperated with authorities, and had paid off a significant debt. They also highlighted his deteriorating health. However, the courts rejected these arguments in stereotyped decisions, mainly citing the impending severe sentence, without conducting an individualised assessment of his personal circumstances or the defence's fresh arguments against the risk of collusion.

Regarding his health (Article 3), the applicant suffered from asthma, chronic sinusitis, allergies, and other conditions. He was initially held in overcrowded cells of 3.52 m² and later 4.7 m². He lost 37 kilograms during detention. While he received some medical treatment and dietary accommodations, he persistently complained of inadequate conditions, including humidity and lack of fresh air. His requests for improved conditions and examination by a medical expert were delayed, though he was eventually granted extended outdoor time in December 2010 based on an expert opinion.

Concerning family contact (Article 8), from 9 November 2010, all meetings and phone calls with his common-law wife were prohibited due to a perceived risk of collusion. The authorities claimed they intended to circumvent controlled visits, relying on domestic law. The defence argued this was unjustified and that any lack of supervision was the prison's fault. This complaint to the Chief Prosecutor remained unanswered. Additional criminal proceedings against the applicant for providing a false retainer to his wife were initiated but resulted in acquittal, with wardens confirming all visits were supervised. The applicant also could not receive visits from his 11-year-old daughter due to her health, though he was granted extra phone time with her.

On 23 February 2011, the Regional Court replaced his pre-trial detention with house arrest, acknowledging that the risk of absconding had lessened due to his serious health problems. This measure lasted until 10 June 2011.

**Hagyó v. Hungary** (Application no. 52624/10, ECtHR 2013) concerned Miklós Hagyó, a Hungarian former Vice-Mayor of Budapest and former Member of Parliament. On 14 May 2010, shortly after losing parliamentary immunity, he was arrested and charged with aggravated fraudulent breach of trust involving alleged misuse of funds at the Budapest Transport Company. The prosecution sought pre-trial detention, citing risks of absconding and collusion. The defence argued that Hagyó had known for months that indictment was likely, had not left the country, had denied press rumours about fleeing, and had offered cooperation. Nevertheless, on 17 May 2010 the Buda Central District Court ordered remand detention, rejecting house arrest. It relied on the serious charges, the fact that he had sold properties, an unspecified “element” suggesting possible flight, and the risk of collusion because investigation was ongoing. His appeal was rejected on 26 May 2010.

A key complaint concerned the procedure for prolonging detention. The defence repeatedly asked to inspect the case file and the evidence supposedly justifying detention, especially the alleged flight risk. These requests were refused, the evidence was never disclosed, and a complaint to the Chief Public Prosecutor went unanswered. Detention was repeatedly extended. The defence argued there were no concrete grounds, that collusion fears were unfounded, and that Hagyó’s health had deteriorated. The courts allegedly responded with stereotyped decisions, mainly stressing that a severe sentence was likely, without individualised assessment of his circumstances.

As to Article 3, Hagyó was held at Budapest Penitentiary for over four months in cells of 3.52 m² and another four months in cells of 4.7 m² per person, including fixtures. From 21 November 2010 he was permanently placed in a 4.7 m² cell. He was allowed only one hour outdoors daily. On admission he reported asthma, chronic sinusitis, gluten and dairy allergies, and chronic left-ear inflammation. He received medication, immune-strengthening products, a special diet, daily baths due to being overweight (130 kg), and later a stimulation belt. Medical examinations took place in June 2010; after continued complaints and a 37 kg weight loss, further examinations occurred in September 2010, followed by hospital treatment from 17 September to 6 October 2010. His lung condition initially worsened but later improved. A medical expert, appointed only in September 2010, confirmed serious health problems but considered them treatable in prison. He repeatedly requested larger, less humid cells, more fresh air, and better nutrition. An extra outdoor hour was refused in November 2010 but granted in December.

Regarding Article 8 and Article 13, Hagyó’s common-law wife received extra visits in August 2010 as his civil-law representative. However, from 9 November 2010 all meetings and phone calls with her were banned due to an alleged collusion risk and suspected attempt to circumvent controlled family contact under Law-Decree No. 11 of 1979, section 118(2). His complaint to the Chief Prosecutor was unanswered. Additional criminal proceedings accusing him of giving her a false retainer to circumvent visit rules ended in acquittal; wardens confirmed all visits had been supervised. His 11-year-old daughter did not visit because of her own health. Requests for a less coercive measure or unlimited phone contact with her were denied, though extra phone time was granted in September 2010 and January 2011. Pre-trial detention ended on 23 February 2011, replaced by house arrest until 10 June 2011, because his serious health problems lessened the absconding risk.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 5 (unduly protracted detention and breach of equality of arms), Article 3 (failure to duly consider serious health conditions), and Article 8, alone and with Article 13 (restriction of family contact and lack of effective remedy).

**Case: Mohammed v. Austria (Application no. 2283/12), Judgment of 6 June 2013**

The applicant, Salaheldin Mohammed, a Sudanese national born in 1981, arrived in Austria on 9 October 2010 via Greece and Hungary and applied for asylum. On 5 January 2011, the Austrian Federal Asylum Office found that Hungary had jurisdiction under the Dublin II Regulation, rejected his asylum application as inadmissible, and ordered his transfer to Hungary. The applicant did not appeal that decision. He later went into hiding and thwarted a planned detention and transfer in May 2011. On 21 December 2011 he was detained in Vienna, and the following day the Vienna Federal Police Authority ordered his detention pending forced transfer to Hungary.

On 30 December 2011, the applicant lodged a second asylum application. It had no suspensive effect on the existing transfer order. He relied on the Austrian Asylum Court’s practice and reports concerning reception conditions and access to asylum proceedings in Hungary. On 2 January 2012, he complained against the detention order, referring to a 1 December 2011 Asylum Court decision that had granted suspensive effect to an Algerian asylum-seeker’s appeal against transfer to Hungary. That decision was based on a UNHCR letter of 17 October 2011 concerning detention conditions in Hungary and the risk of refoulement to Serbia. On 5 January 2012, the Vienna Independent Administrative Panel dismissed the applicant’s detention complaint as unfounded.

On 9 January 2012, the applicant asked the Vienna Federal Police Directorate to establish that his transfer to Hungary would create a risk under the Immigration Police Act. The request was rejected because no proceedings concerning a return decision, deportation, or residence ban were pending. On 10 January 2012, the Administrative Court refused to grant suspensive effect to his complaint. It said it would not review the lawfulness of the transfer itself, but noted that the immigration police would have to refrain from transferring him if the current situation in Hungary for Dublin returnees would breach Article 3 of the Convention. His transfer was scheduled for 12 January 2012. On 11 January 2012, the European Court of Human Rights applied an interim measure under Rule 39, staying the transfer until further notice.

The alleged Article 3 violation concerned the risk that forced transfer to Hungary under the Dublin Regulation would expose the applicant to torture or inhuman or degrading treatment. Relevant facts included UNHCR and Hungarian Helsinki Committee reports documenting routine detention of asylum-seekers in Hungary, high-security detention regimes, alleged daily police ill-treatment and harassment, systematic drugging with tranquilisers, ineffective judicial review of detention, and handcuffing during administrative matters. Dublin returnees were often treated as second applicants, whose asylum claims lacked automatic suspensive effect and who could be deported to third countries before a merits examination. Hungary also treated Serbia as a safe third country and returned asylum-seekers who had transited Serbia without substantive asylum proceedings, creating a risk of refoulement. Austrian Asylum Court decisions in late 2011 had, in several cases, quashed Dublin transfer decisions or granted suspensive effect because of these concerns.

The alleged Article 13 violation concerned the lack of an effective remedy. The applicant argued that his second asylum application did not suspend transfer, his detention complaint was dismissed, his non-refoulement assessment request was rejected as inadmissible, and the Administrative Court refused suspensive effect. He therefore claimed he could be transferred to Hungary without any substantive domestic review of whether the transfer would breach Article 3. The Government argued that domestic remedies had not been exhausted, particularly because he had not appealed the first asylum decision and because his second asylum proceedings were pending. The Court joined that objection to the merits and declared the application admissible.

The applicant alleged under Article 3 that forced transfer to Hungary would expose him to inhuman or degrading treatment, given Hungary’s detention and reception conditions and the risk of refoulement. He also alleged under Article 13 that he lacked an effective remedy capable of staying the transfer, especially because his second asylum application had no suspensive effect. The Government argued non-exhaustion, saying he had failed to appeal the first asylum decision and that second asylum proceedings were still pending. The applicant maintained that the relevant reports on Hungary emerged after the appeal deadline and that available remedies did not protect him from transfer.

UNHCR reported in October 2011 that asylum-seekers and Dublin transferees were routinely detained, judicial review was merely formal, and there were allegations of daily police abuse, drugging, handcuffing, and restricted access to asylum procedures. They also indicated that Hungary treated Serbia as a safe third country and returned asylum-seekers there without a merits examination. Dublin transferees were treated as second applicants, whose appeals did not automatically suspend deportation. Austrian Asylum Court decisions in late 2011 had quashed several Dublin transfers to Hungary or granted suspensive effect because those reports raised serious Article 3 concerns.

The applicant also alleged under Article 13 that he lacked an effective remedy in the proceedings concerning his second asylum application to suspend his transfer. He argued that the second application had no suspensive effect, that the immigration police’s refusal to examine the transfer risk was discretionary and not judicially reviewable, and that he had no way to have changed circumstances considered before removal. The Court joined the exhaustion objection to the merits and declared the application admissible. **Summary of Pyrantienė v. Lithuania (Application no. 45092/07)**

The case of *Pyrantienė v. Lithuania* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Ms. Kotrina Pyrantienė, a Lithuanian national, alleging a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention (protection of property). The core of her complaint was that she was deprived of her property and subsequently received inadequate compensation.

The key facts are as follows: In 1994, a local authority assigned a 0.5-hectare plot of land to the applicant. In 1996, she purchased this plot from the State for 61 "single-use investment vouchers," and the sale was officially confirmed and registered in her name. The case of *Beltram and Beltram Cerovšek v. Slovenia* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by two Slovenian nationals, Mr. Marijan Beltram and Mrs. Anuška Beltram Cerovšek, on 9 February 2010. The applicants alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial within a reasonable time) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights, stemming from the excessive length of civil proceedings they initiated in Slovenia.

The facts relevant to the alleged violations are as follows: On 2 October 2007, the applicants filed a civil claim against an individual, O.J., before the Ljubljana District Court regarding defects in an apartment they had purchased. Despite requesting a hearing on 2 April 2008, the court informed them on 4 April 2008 that their case could not be prioritized and that a hearing would not occur until the end of 2008.

On 6 February 2009, after fourteen months of inaction, the applicants lodged a supervisory appeal, noting that under the Court Rules, a first-instance decision should be issued within eighteen months. This appeal was dismissed on 26 February 2009 by the President of the Ljubljana District Court, who reiterated that the case was not a priority and indicated a hearing might be scheduled in the second half of 2009. Subsequently, on 5 March 2009, the applicants filed a motion for a deadline with the Ljubljana Higher Court, which was dismissed on 27 March 2009, again citing the case’s non-priority status. A constitutional appeal alleging a violation of their right to a trial within a reasonable time was also dismissed by the Constitutional Court on 3 November 2009.

The proceedings eventually progressed with a main hearing on 22 January 2010, where a construction expert was appointed. However, further delays ensued, including the dismissal and replacement of the expert, postponed hearings, and an appeal by a third-party construction company, K.Z., which was granted on 17 February 2011, causing further delay. Additional expert appointments and hearings occurred over the next two years. The first-instance judgment was finally delivered on 15 March 2013, granting the applicants' claim in large part. This decision was served on 17 April 2013, and both parties appealed. The proceedings remained pending before the Ljubljana Higher Court at the time of the European Court’s judgment.

The Government contested the application, arguing that the applicants had failed to exhaust domestic remedies, specifically those provided by the Act on the Protection of the Right to a Trial without Undue Delay. The Government claimed that the applicants had lodged their acceleratory remedies prematurely and could seek just satisfaction after the final resolution of the case.

The European Court examined the period from 2 October 2007, which had lasted almost six years across two levels of jurisdiction. It found that the case was not complex, that no significant delays were attributable to the applicants, and that the domestic courts took over two years to hold the first hearing and three and a half more years to deliver a judgment. Regarding the Article 13 complaint, the Court noted that the applicants’ acceleratory remedies were dismissed as premature after fourteen months of inactivity, and that due to the domestic system, they lacked prompt access to a compensatory remedy. Consequently, the Court found that the overall length of the proceedings was excessive, violating the "reasonable time" requirement, and that the domestic remedies available to the applicants had proven ineffective, in violation of Article 13.

In *Brzuszczyński v. Poland*, the applicant, Piotr Brzuszczyński, a Polish national, complained under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights that his criminal trial was unfair. The central issue was the domestic courts’ reliance on out-of-court statements by R.N., the actual killer, who died before trial and was never available for questioning by the defence.

The underlying facts concerned the murder of E.U. in May 2001. R.N. killed E.U. after pretending to sell him a car. The applicant and R.N. were arrested on 6 June 2001; R.N. had a loaded gun. R.N. was interrogated four times: twice on 7 June, again on 8 June, and on 25 July 2001. In his first statements, he confessed to the murder, claimed that Brzuszczyński had supplied the gun, and said they had planned to split the victim’s money. He repeated those allegations on 8 June and 25 July. On 25 July he changed some details, mentioned an unnamed man present at the killing, said he himself had been kidnapped and ordered to dig his own grave, then stopped and said he would write to the prosecutor. On 31 August 2001 R.N. committed suicide in his prison cell. Because of his death, he was never heard in court, and the applicant could not cross-examine him.

In May 2002 the applicant was indicted for aiding and abetting murder by providing the gun, illegal possession of a firearm with a silencer, and attempted extortion of ransom from the victim’s family. He denied all involvement, stating that he had never possessed or supplied any gun. In May 2003 the Warsaw Regional Court convicted him of aiding and abetting armed robbery, illegal possession of the gun, and aiding and abetting extortion, sentencing him to eight years’ imprisonment. The court relied heavily on R.N.’s investigation statements, found them credible, and noted that hearing R.N. in court would have been useful but was impossible because of his death.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the trial court had selectively used parts of R.N.’s testimony and ignored contradictory evidence. R.N.’s friends and ex-wife testified that R.N. had possessed a gun long before the murder; other witnesses said R.N. never told the truth, and one said he used drugs. The prosecutor also appealed, arguing that the evidence supported a murder conviction.

In December 2003 the Warsaw Court of Appeal quashed the judgment. It found that the first-instance court had failed to examine all evidence and that its assessment lacked consistency. Because R.N. could not be heard in court, the trial court was required to assess his statements with particular thoroughness. It had failed to address numerous witnesses. The appellate court instructed the lower court to determine whether the gun had been provided by the applicant or had already been in R.N.’s possession, consider fingerprint evidence, and establish whether the applicant had a gun permit.

On retrial, after 19 hearings, the Regional Court convicted the applicant in November 2007 of aiding and abetting murder, illegal possession of a gun, and aiding and abetting extortion, sentencing him to 15 years’ imprisonment. It again relied on R.N.’s statements, supported by about 40 witnesses and documentary evidence. It found that the applicant and R.N. were close, financially troubled friends; that R.N. planned to kill a buyer; and that the applicant knew of the plan, provided the gun, and expected half the proceeds. It found R.N.’s early statements spontaneous, detailed, and corroborated, and rejected defence evidence suggesting R.N. had possessed the gun earlier.

The alleged Article 6 violation therefore arises from the conviction being based significantly on the untested statements of a deceased witness, R.N., whom the applicant never had an opportunity to examine.

In *Brzuszczyński v. Poland* (Application no. 23789/09), the applicant, Piotr Brzuszczyński, a Polish national, complained under Article 6 of the Convention that his criminal trial was unfair. The case arose from the murder of E.U. on 19 May 2001 by R.N., who was arrested with the applicant on 6 June 2001 and was found carrying a loaded gun. R.N. was questioned four times. On 7 June 2001 he broke down and confessed, stating that the applicant had provided the gun to commit the murder and that they had planned to split the victim’s money. He repeated this account on 8 June and 25 July 2001, specifying that the handover had occurred in Kobyłka near the Zepter warehouse. On 25 July he slightly changed his account, referring to an unnamed man at the killing and claiming he had been kidnapped and ordered to dig a grave; he then stopped and said he needed to think and would write to the prosecutor. On 31 August 2001 R.N. committed suicide in prison, so he could never be examined at the applicant’s trial.

The prosecution indicted the applicant in 2002 for aiding and abetting murder by supplying the gun, illegal possession of the gun, and attempted ransom extortion. In 2003 the Warsaw Regional Court convicted him of aiding and abetting armed robbery, illegal gun possession, and extortion, sentencing him to eight years. It relied heavily on R.N.’s pre-trial statements, finding no irrefutable proof that the applicant knew the gun would be used to kill. The Court of Appeal quashed that judgment in December 2003, finding the evidence assessment flawed. It stressed that, because R.N. could not be heard in court, his statements required particularly thorough scrutiny, and the trial court had failed to address numerous witnesses and to establish key matters such as who supplied the gun, fingerprint evidence, and whether the applicant had a gun permit.

On retrial, after 19 hearings, the Regional Court in 2007 convicted the applicant of aiding and abetting murder, illegal gun possession, and extortion, imposing 15 years. The court again relied on R.N.’s statements, together with about 40 witnesses and documentary, forensic and firearms evidence. It found the applicant had financial motives, was close to R.N., maintained contact while R.N. hid from creditors, supplied him with clothes and hygiene items, and gave contradictory explanations about debts and the gun. It found R.N.’s early statements credible because they were immediate, detailed, self-incriminating, and corroborated by other evidence, including the handover location, the victim’s burial site, autopsy, and firearms expert evidence. The absence of fingerprints was explained by the gun being handed over in a plastic bag. The court discounted witnesses who later suggested R.N. already had a gun, finding their testimony biased or inconsistent.

The alleged Article 6 violation was that the applicant had no opportunity to cross-examine R.N., the central witness against him, and that the domestic courts selectively relied on R.N.’s untested pre-trial statements while ignoring inconsistencies and exculpatory evidence. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 6 § 1 read together with Article 6 § 3(d), concluding that reliance on the deceased witness’s statements was not sufficiently counterbalanced by procedural safeguards.

In *Brzuszczyński v. Poland* (Application no. 23789/09), the applicant, a Polish national, complained under Article 6 of the Convention that his criminal trial was unfair. The case arose from the murder of E.U. on 19 May 2001 by R.N. The applicant and R.N. were arrested on 6 June 2001; R.N. had a loaded gun. R.N. was questioned four times between 7 June and 25 July 2001. On 7 June he confessed to the murder and implicated the applicant, stating that the applicant had provided the gun, knew it would be used to kill, and that they planned to split the victim’s money. He repeated this account on 8 June and 25 July. On 31 August 2001, before trial, R.N. committed suicide in his prison cell. He therefore could not be examined in court.

The applicant was charged with aiding and abetting murder, illegal possession of a gun with a silencer, and attempted extortion of ransom. He denied involvement, claiming he never possessed or supplied a gun. A co-accused, P.D., also denied involvement in the extortion.

In the first trial, the Warsaw Regional Court on 27 May 2003 convicted the applicant of aiding and abetting armed robbery, illegal gun possession, and aiding extortion, sentencing him to eight years. It relied on R.N.’s pre-trial statements, finding them credible, and held there was no irrefutable evidence that the applicant knew the gun would be used to kill. On appeal, the Warsaw Court of Appeal quashed the judgment on 9 December 2003. It found the trial flawed: the court had not examined all evidence, the assessment lacked consistency, and because R.N. could not be heard in court, his statements required particularly thorough scrutiny. It instructed the trial court to establish whether the applicant or R.N. had provided the gun, consider fingerprint evidence, and verify whether the applicant had a gun permit.

On retrial, after 19 hearings, the Regional Court on 27 November 2007 convicted the applicant of aiding and abetting murder, illegal gun possession, and aiding extortion, sentencing him to 15 years. The court again relied heavily on R.N.’s statements, finding them credible because they were made immediately after arrest, were detailed, incriminated R.N. himself, and were corroborated by other evidence, including witnesses, autopsy, site inspection, and firearms expert opinion. The applicant pleaded not guilty and refused to testify. The defence argued that R.N.’s statements were unreliable and could not prove guilt: R.N. had not been cross-examined; parts of his accounts were inconsistent; other witnesses said R.N. had possessed a gun earlier, had lied, or used drugs; and no fingerprints were found on the gun.

The alleged Article 6 violation therefore concerned the fairness of relying on the pre-trial statements of a deceased witness who could not be confronted or cross-examined at trial, where those statements were central to the conviction. The ECtHR had to assess whether counterbalancing safeguards ensured a fair trial.

**Summary of Sizarev v. Ukraine (Application no. 17116/04)**

The case of *Sizarev v. Ukraine* originated from an application lodged against Ukraine with the European Court of Human Rights on 14 May 2004 by Mr. Konstantin Konstantinovich Sizarev, a Ukrainian national born in 1958. The applicant, a former court assistant with no prior criminal record, raised multiple complaints under the Convention, including the lawfulness and length of his pre-trial detention, the conditions of his detention, the authorities’ failure to ensure his physical safety and to investigate an assault against him, and being handcuffed while in hospital.

The facts relevant to the alleged violations began on 3 October 2003, when a certain Mr. K. complained to the police that the applicant had beaten him. Initially, no prosecution was initiated. However, on 24 February 2004, the Yevpatoriya City Prosecutor’s Office opened a criminal case against the applicant on suspicion of deliberately inflicting bodily harm of medium severity on Mr. K. — an offence punishable by up to three years’ imprisonment.

On 18 March 2004, the applicant was ordered not to leave town, and on 25 March 2004 he appointed his wife, Ms. D., as his representative. From 8 to 29 April 2004, the applicant was on sick leave due to a leg injury and consequently failed to appear before the investigator when summoned.

On 19 April 2004, the investigator applied to the Saky City Court requesting the applicant’s pre-trial detention as a more appropriate preventive measure, citing the applicant’s failure to comply with the summons and the fact that his actual place of residence was unknown. On 22 April 2004, the court ordered the police to ensure the applicant’s appearance.

On the morning of 27 April 2004, the applicant was arrested. On the same date, the Saky City Court held a hearing, attended by the applicant and the prosecutor, to consider the investigator’s detention request. The applicant’s request for his wife to be present was rejected.

In ordering the applicant’s pre-trial detention, the Saky Court acknowledged that detention was normally ordered where the likely penalty exceeded three years’ imprisonment, but found it possible to make an exception in this case. It noted that the applicant had failed to appear in response to several summonses, did not actually live at the address he had given to the authorities, and had left Yevpatoriya on many occasions without informing the investigator, in breach of the obligation not to leave town. Additionally, the victim, Mr. K., complained that the applicant had threatened him. The court concluded that these factors sufficed to consider the case exceptional within the meaning of Article 155 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and ordered pre-trial detention pending trial.

Also on 27 April 2004, Ms. D. lodged an appeal on the applicant’s behalf. She argued that pre-trial detention was contrary to criminal procedural legislation given the minor nature of the crime. She contended that the Saky Court had failed to consider medical records confirming the applicant had been undergoing treatment since 8 April 2004, providing a valid reason for his failure to attend the investigation. She further pointed out that the court had disregarded the fact that the applicant had two minor children and that she, his wife, was disabled. Finally, she complained that the hearing had taken place in her absence.

These facts form the basis of the applicant’s complaints before the European Court regarding the lawfulness of his detention and the fairness of the proceedings leading to it.

Azerbaijan* (Application no. 16133/08), the European Court of Human Rights examined an application by Ali Binnat oglu Insanov, an Azerbaijani national and former Minister of Health Care from 1993 to 2005. The applicant complained about detention conditions, inadequate medical treatment in detention, unfairness of civil proceedings concerning his detention conditions, unfairness of the criminal proceedings against him, and other Convention violations. The Court communicated complaints under Article 3 (conditions of detention and lack of adequate medical treatment), Article 6 (fairness of civil and criminal proceedings), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property), while declaring other parts inadmissible.

The criminal case began in October 2005. After being questioned at the Ministry of National Security, Insanov was detained on suspicion of abuse of official authority, embezzlement of public funds, and complicity in an attempted coup allegedly planned after the November 2005 parliamentary elections. He was formally charged with offences including preparation to organise public disorder, actions aimed at usurping State power, high-level embezzlement, abuse of official authority, and repeated and high-level bribe-taking. His pre-trial detention was extended several times by the Nasimi District Court until April 2007; his appeals were dismissed. A search of his home found large amounts of cash in various currencies, gold and jewellery, and property deeds. In January 2007, a new indictment was issued and a separate criminal case was severed and sent to the Assize Court. The charges concerned, among other matters, unlawfully creating conditions for privatisation of State health-care property worth about €23.5 million, receiving bribes, embezzling public funds to publish a book, taking bribes for pharmacy licences, failing to comply with final domestic judgments, and forgery in public office.

Key fair-trial complaints arose before and during the trial. The defence alleged it could not properly familiarise itself with the case file or photocopy materials. The Prosecutor General rejected this, saying the defence had access to all 43 volumes and signed a record of familiarisation. The Assize Court refused to suspend proceedings on this ground. During hearings from February to April 2007, the applicant complained that he could not confer confidentially with his lawyers, that he was not allowed meetings at the detention facility at weekends, and that he was forced to discuss defence strategy in the presence of prosecutors and judges. He also alleged that the court repeatedly refused short adjournments for confidential consultations. The Government maintained that the court had adjourned once on 30 March 2007 and had reminded the MNS Detention Facility of his right to meet his lawyers.

A further central issue was the refusal to summon defence witnesses. Insanov repeatedly asked the Assize Court to hear experts and officials to challenge three audit reports of June, August, and December 2006, which concluded that he had abused his powers to unlawfully privatise State health-care assets. These reports were decisive evidence for his conviction. He argued that the reports were contradictory, that some experts had refused to sign or had reservations, and that privatisation authority lay with the State Committee for Management of State Property and the Ministry of Economic Development. He claimed his role was limited to submitting proposals and confirming non-objection, so those agencies’ officials were responsible for any unlawful privatisation. The handling of these witness requests formed a key part of his Article 6 complaint.

Overall, the case concerns whether the applicant’s detention and medical treatment violated Article 3, whether the criminal and civil proceedings were fair under Article 6, and whether his property rights were breached under Protocol No. 1.

In *Insanov v. Azerbaijan* (Application no. 16133/08), the applicant, Ali Binnat oglu Insanov, an Azerbaijani national and former Minister of Health Care (1993–2005), lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 31 March 2008. He complained principally about conditions of detention, the lack of adequate medical treatment in detention, the unfairness of civil proceedings concerning his detention conditions, the unfairness of the criminal proceedings against him, and violations of his property rights. The Court communicated complaints under Article 3 (conditions and medical treatment), Article 6 (fairness of civil and criminal proceedings), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The criminal case arose on 20 October 2005, when Insanov was summoned to the Ministry of National Security, questioned, and detained on suspicion of abuse of official authority, embezzlement of public funds, and complicity in an attempted coup allegedly planned after the 6 November 2005 parliamentary elections and masterminded by former Parliament Speaker R. Guliyev. He was dismissed from office that same day. On 22 October 2005 he was formally charged with offences including preparation to organise public disorder, actions aimed at usurping State power, high-level embezzlement, abuse of official authority, and repeated and high-level bribe-taking. His detention was repeatedly extended by the Nasimi District Court until April 2007, and his appeals were dismissed. A search of his home found large amounts of cash in various currencies, gold and jewellery, and deeds to residential properties.

In January 2007, a new indictment was issued and a separate criminal case was severed from the original one. The charges included creating conditions for the unlawful privatisation of State health-care property worth approximately AZN 27,221,574 (about EUR 23.5 million), falsifying documents, using dummy companies, and reselling assets to family members and acquaintances. He was also accused of receiving bribes totaling USD 200,000 in connection with those transactions; embezzling AZN 115,240 to publish a book; taking bribes of USD 76,900 and AZN 2,800 for issuing pharmacy licences, keeping 70% for himself; and continually failing to comply with seven final domestic judgments ordering the reinstatement of unlawfully dismissed Ministry employees.

Before trial, the defence complained that it had not been allowed to properly familiarise itself with the case file or take photocopies. The Prosecutor General rejected the complaint, stating that the defence had access to all 43 volumes, video tapes, photographs, and other material evidence. The Assize Court refused to suspend proceedings on this ground.

Insanov was tried with ten co-defendants, and a civil claim was advanced against him and others. Around twenty civil defendants—current private owners of the allegedly unlawfully privatised property—were also involved. Hearings took place from February to April 2007, with more than 120 witnesses and extensive documentary and expert evidence. Three 2006 audit reports on the Ministry’s financial activities were decisive, concluding that Insanov had abused his powers and enabled unlawful privatisation.

Relevant to the fair-trial complaint, Insanov alleged that he could not confer confidentially with his lawyers during hearings, was denied meetings at the detention facility on weekends and non-working days, and was forced to confer in the presence of prosecutors and judges. He also requested that the court summon auditors and officials from privatisation agencies, arguing that the audit reports were contradictory and that responsibility for privatisation lay with other State bodies, not him. These complaints and refused witness requests formed key facts behind his alleged Article 6 violations.

**Case: Insanov v. Azerbaijan** (Application no. 16133/08), European Court of Human Rights, First Section, judgment of 14 March 2013, final on 14 June 2013.

**Summary of N.M.B. v. Sweden (Application no. 68335/10)**

The case of N.M.B. v. Sweden concerns an Iraqi national's application to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging that his deportation from Sweden to Iraq would violate Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment.

The applicant, born in 1973, is a Christian academic from Baghdad. He arrived in Sweden in December 2007 and applied for asylum. He claimed that his work on a university committee, established to develop research methods, led to accusations of cooperating with Americans. In June 2006, he accused a colleague affiliated with the Iraqi Islamic Party (IIP) of corruption. Following this, he alleged a series of threats and incidents: an attempted kidnapping of his daughter, threatening letters calling his family Christian traitors, and the kidnapping and killing of the committee head. The applicant and his family fled to Syria in October 2006. He later claimed his parents were attacked in Baghdad, and he received online threats from a militia within the IIP. His asylum claim was based on a risk of persecution due to his Christian faith and his profile as an academic.

The Swedish Migration Board rejected his application in March 2009, questioning the credibility of his account and finding that his work with the committee had ended years ago, with no remaining work-related threat. The Migration Court upheld this decision in June 2010, noting that the incidents did not constitute religious persecution and that his story contained exaggerations. The Migration Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal in November 2010. Subsequent claims of impediments to deportation were also rejected.

Before the European Court, the applicant argued that he would face a real risk of being killed or tortured by Islamic extremist groups in Iraq due to his Christian beliefs and status as a university professor. He asserted that the general situation in Iraq was unsafe and that the Iraqi authorities could not protect Christians. He also claimed that the threats against him were personal and would follow him even to the Kurdistan Region.

The Swedish Government acknowledged the serious security situation in central and southern Iraq and that Christians were a vulnerable group. However, they maintained that there was no general need for protection for all Christians. They questioned the applicant's credibility, pointing to inconsistencies and late additions to his story. Crucially, the Government argued that the applicant could reasonably relocate to the Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI), which is relatively safe, and where Christians are generally respected and can enter without a sponsor. They noted he was a healthy adult capable of supporting himself.

The Court's assessment focused on the possibility of internal relocation. It found that while the general situation in Iraq remained difficult, it was not so extreme as to preclude all returns from a violation of Article 3. It noted that Christians faced heightened risks in southern and central Iraq. However, the Court determined that relocation to the Kurdistan Region was a viable alternative. The KRI was considered safer, with Christians facing preferential treatment at borders and no requirement for a sponsor. The Court concluded that there was no indication that living conditions in the KRI for a Christian settler would be unreasonable or amount to treatment prohibited by Article 3.

The Court examined the applicant's personal circumstances. It noted that the incidents he described occurred in Baghdad and that his claims of personal threats following him to the KRI were unsubstantiated. His former employment at the university had ended over six years prior, and he had not been politically active, making it unreasonable to assume he would still be of interest to his former threats. Consequently, the Court concluded that the applicant could reasonably relocate to the Kurdistan Region, where he would not face a real risk of treatment contrary to Article 3. Therefore, his deportation to Iraq would not involve a violation of Article 3. The interim measure under Rule 39 was to remain in force until the judgment became final.

N.M.B. v. Sweden (App. no. 68335/10, 27 June 2013) concerned whether Sweden’s deportation of an Iraqi Christian to Iraq would violate Article 3 ECHR. The applicant, born 1973, was a Christian academic from Baghdad. He arrived in Sweden in December 2007 and sought asylum. He claimed that while working for a university committee accused of cooperating with Americans, he wrote to the Ministry of Education accusing a colleague linked to the Iraqi Islamic Party (IIP) of corruption. He then received threats, armed men attempted to kidnap his daughter, and he received a letter calling his family Christian traitors and threatening death unless he quit. He reported the incidents to police, moved his family, and later learned the committee head had been kidnapped and killed. In October 2006 he fled to Syria. Later, his parents were attacked, his father kidnapped and tortured to reveal the applicant’s whereabouts, and online threats from the Islamic Brigade warned him not to return.

Swedish authorities rejected asylum. The Migration Board accepted he was Christian and had done committee work, but found it unlikely this made him suspected of cooperating with Americans; any work-related threat had ended; his accusation probably did not harm the IIP; and the alleged attack on his parents was not credible. It noted improved security. The Migration Court upheld, finding no religious persecution, some exaggeration, limited committee work, long delay, no political activity, and no individual threat. The Migration Court of Appeal refused leave. The Board later declined reconsideration based on the general situation for Christians and November 2010 attacks.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged a real risk of killing or torture by Islamic extremists because of his Christian faith and status as a high-level scholar. He argued Iraq was generally unsafe and Iraqi authorities could not protect Christians, citing the October 2010 Baghdad church massacre. He also claimed his personal threats would follow him even in the Kurdistan Region.

The Government acknowledged serious security problems and that Christians were vulnerable, but insisted on individual assessment. It questioned his credibility due late or inconsistent allegations, found no link between the incidents and his work or religion, and stressed his employment had ended years earlier. It argued he could relocate internally to the Kurdistan Region (KRI), a safer area where he could enter, settle, work, and access services.

The Court declared the complaint admissible. It reiterated that expulsion violates Article 3 if substantial grounds show a real risk of prohibited treatment; general violence alone only in extreme cases. It noted Iraq’s situation was slowly improving and Christians were vulnerable in central and southern Iraq, with attacks escalating and authorities often unable to protect them. However, it did not decide whether all Christians faced such risk because relocation to the KRI was viable. The KRI was relatively safe, Christian rights were generally respected, many Christians had found refuge there, entry was possible without sponsor, identity documents were obtainable, and jobs and support existed. Relocation hardship did not reach Article 3 severity.

On personal circumstances, the applicant’s incidents occurred in Baghdad. His claim that threats would reach him in the KRI was unsubstantiated, and risks based solely on Christian faith were unsupported for the KRI. His university work had ended over six years earlier and he had no political activity, so he was unlikely still to interest former threats. Thus, despite being part of a vulnerable minority, he could reasonably relocate to the KRI. Deportation would not violate Article 3. The Rule 39 interim measure remained in force until final judgment.

In N.M.B. v. Sweden (ECtHR, 27 June 2013), the applicant was an Iraqi Christian academic born in 1973, from Baghdad. He arrived in Sweden in December 2007 and applied for asylum. He alleged that deportation to Iraq would violate Article 3 ECHR, which prohibits torture or inhuman or degrading treatment.

He claimed that in April 2006 he joined a university committee developing research methods, which was soon accused of cooperating with Americans. In June 2006 he wrote to the Minister of Education accusing a colleague, allegedly a member of the Iraqi Islamic Party (IIP), of corruption. He said this led to threats. Armed men allegedly tried to kidnap his daughter on 27 June 2006; on 30 June he received a letter calling his family Christian traitors and threatening death unless he quit. He reported the incidents to police and moved with relatives. The committee head was later kidnapped and killed. In October 2006 he fled with his family to Syria. In January 2008 his parents in Baghdad were allegedly attacked, and his father kidnapped and tortured to reveal the applicant’s whereabouts. In late 2008 he allegedly received online threats from the Islamic Brigade, an IIP militia, warning him not to return.

The Swedish Migration Board rejected asylum in March 2009. It accepted that he was Christian and had worked for the university committee, but found it unlikely that this work made him suspected of cooperating with Americans, especially since he had left years earlier. It doubted the impact of his corruption accusation, questioned the alleged attack on his parents, and noted improved security. The Migration Court upheld the rejection in June 2010, finding no religious persecution, some exaggeration, limited committee work, no political activity, and no individual threat. The Migration Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal in November 2010. Reconsideration requests based on the general situation for Christians and November 2010 attacks were refused in January 2011.

Before the ECtHR, N.M.B. complained that return to Iraq would expose him to a real risk of killing or torture by Islamic extremists because of his Christian faith and status as a university professor. He argued the general situation was unsafe and Iraqi authorities could not protect Christians. He also said relocation to Kurdistan would not help because his threats were personal and could reach him there. The Government accepted that the situation was serious and that Christians and professionals were exposed, but maintained that protection needs required individual assessment. It questioned his credibility due to inconsistencies and late-added claims, found no link between the incidents and his religion or former work, and proposed an internal flight alternative in the Kurdistan Region.

The Court declared the application admissible but found no violation of Article 3. It assumed he might face risk in southern or central Iraq as a Christian, but held that relocation to the Kurdistan Region was a viable alternative. Christians could generally enter, settle, and live there without sponsor requirements; the region was relatively safe; and his personal circumstances—no recent political activity, employment ended over six years earlier, and unsubstantiated personal threats—did not make relocation unreasonable. Therefore, deportation would not violate Article 3.
