In *Jeznik v. Slovenia* (Application no. 32238/08), judgment of 20 June 2013, the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints concerning the length of civil proceedings and the effectiveness of domestic remedies in Slovenia. The applicant, Marija Jeznik, born in 1940 and living in Vuzenica, began investing in commercial papers of Kompas Consulting d.d. through Kompas Maribor D.O.O. in 1994. Although such trading was prohibited at the end of 1994 by the Securities Market Act, she continued until 1996. In 1996 she brought enforcement proceedings against Kompas Maribor, seeking payment for lost investments. She alleged that the company had failed to inform her of the legislative amendments and had continued trading commercial papers. She also complained that because Kompas Consulting d.d. was bankrupt, she could recover only a small proportion of her investment in bankruptcy proceedings.

On 14 October 1996 the Maribor District Court issued a writ of execution. After an objection, the case was referred to contentious proceedings on 12 November 1996. On 4 February 1998 the District Court rejected the applicant’s request. She appealed. On 24 November 1998 the Maribor Higher Court upheld the appeal and remitted the case, finding that the applicant had clarified in the appeal that she sought damages only, which was a new fact for the first-instance court to consider. On 24 October 2001 the District Court again ruled against her, finding that Kompas Maribor could not be held responsible because of the contractual arrangements. The applicant appealed. On 15 September 2004 the Higher Court upheld that judgment. She then lodged an appeal on points of law. On 25 January 2007 the Supreme Court rejected it. Her constitutional appeal was rejected on 10 December 2007.

The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 that the proceedings exceeded a reasonable time, and under Article 13 that Slovenia lacked an effective remedy for excessive length. The Court noted that the relevant period began on 14 October 1996 and ended on 10 December 2007, lasting eleven years and two months across four levels of jurisdiction. Considering the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicant and authorities, and what was at stake, the Court found the length excessive and contrary to the reasonable-time requirement.

As to Article 13, the Government offered a settlement under section 25 of the 2006 Act, acknowledging the delay, but the applicant refused. The Court held that section 25 did not provide a remedy because her proceedings continued before the Supreme Court after the new legislation. Under section 19, because the proceedings had been finally resolved before the 2006 Act became operational and later continued before the Supreme Court, she could not claim compensation for delays. The Court found the 2006 Act remedies ineffective, as were earlier remedies. It therefore declared the complaints admissible and found violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 13.

In *Jeznik v. Slovenia* (Application no. 32238/08), the European Court of Human Rights delivered judgment on 20 June 2013. The applicant, Ms Marija Jeznik, a Slovenian national born in 1940, complained about the excessive length of civil proceedings and the lack of effective domestic remedies for that delay.

The underlying dispute began in 1994, when the applicant invested in commercial papers of Kompas Consulting d.d. through Kompas Maribor D.O.O. At the end of 1994, such trading was prohibited by the Securities Market Act, but she continued until 1996. In 1996 she brought enforcement proceedings before the Maribor District Court against Kompas Maribor, seeking compensation for lost investments. She alleged that the company had failed to inform her of the legislative changes and had continued trading commercial papers. She also claimed that Kompas Consulting was bankrupt and that she could recover only a small proportion of her investments through bankruptcy proceedings.

On 14 October 1996 the Maribor District Court issued a writ of execution. After an objection, the case was referred to contentious proceedings on 12 November 1996. On 4 February 1998 the District Court rejected her claim. The Maribor Higher Court allowed her appeal on 24 November 1998 and remitted the case, finding that her clarification on appeal that she sought damages only constituted a new fact requiring re-examination. On 24 October 2001 the District Court again ruled against her, holding that Kompas Maribor could not be held responsible for damages given the contractual arrangements. The Higher Court upheld that judgment on 15 September 2004. Her appeal on points of law was rejected by the Supreme Court on 25 January 2007, and the Constitutional Court rejected her constitutional appeal on 10 December 2007.

The Court calculated that the proceedings lasted from 14 October 1996 to 10 December 2007 — eleven years and two months — across four levels of jurisdiction. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, claiming the length was incompatible with the “reasonable time” requirement, and Article 13, claiming that Slovenian remedies for excessive proceedings were ineffective.

The Government offered a settlement under section 25 of the 2006 Act, acknowledging a violation of the right to a trial within a reasonable time, but the applicant did not accept. The Court found that section 25 did not provide a remedy because the proceedings continued before the Supreme Court after the new legislation took effect. Other provisions, especially section 19, were also unavailable because the case had been finally resolved before the 2006 Act became operational and then continued only before the Supreme Court. Thus the applicant could not claim compensation for delays. The complaint was declared admissible.

On the merits, applying the criteria of complexity, conduct of the parties, and what was at stake, the Court found no justification for the delay and concluded that the length of proceedings was excessive, violating Article 6 § 1. It also found that Article 13 required an effective remedy for the alleged unreasonable-length breach; since the applicant had no access to compensation and the 2006 Act remedies were ineffective, and prior remedies were ineffective under *Lukenda v. Slovenia*, the Court found a violation of Article 13.

**Case Name:** Jeznik v. Slovenia (Application no. 32238/08)

**Summary:**

The case of *Jeznik v. Slovenia* originated from an application lodged against the Republic of Slovenia with the European Court of Human Rights by Ms. Marija Jeznik, a Slovenian national, on 1 July 2008. The applicant alleged violations of Articles 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial within a reasonable time) and 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights, focusing on the excessive length of domestic civil proceedings and the lack of effective remedies for such delays.

The factual background begins in 1994 when the applicant invested in commercial papers of the company Kompas Consulting d.d. through Kompas Maribor D.O.O. Although such trading was prohibited by the Securities Market Act at the end of 1994, the applicant continued until 1996. In 1996, she initiated enforcement proceedings against Kompas Maribor, seeking compensation for lost investments. She claimed the company failed to inform her of legislative changes and continued trading, while Kompas Consulting had gone bankrupt, leaving her able to recover only a small portion of her investments.

The domestic proceedings commenced on 14 October 1996 with the issuance of a writ of execution by the Maribor District Court. Following an objection, the case was referred to contentious proceedings on 12 November 1996. On 4 February 1998, the District Court rejected the applicant’s request. The applicant appealed, and on 24 November 1998, the Maribor Higher Court upheld the appeal and remitted the case for re-examination. The Higher Court noted that the applicant had clarified during the appeal that she sought only compensation for damages, constituting a new fact for the first-instance court to consider.

On 24 October 2001, the Maribor District Court rendered a judgment, finding that Kompas Maribor could not be held responsible for the damages due to contractual arrangements. The applicant appealed, and on 15 September 2004, the Maribor Higher Court upheld the first-instance judgment. The applicant then lodged an appeal on points of law with the Supreme Court, which rejected it on 25 January 2007. Subsequently, she filed a constitutional appeal, which was rejected by the Constitutional Court on 10 December 2007.

In its admissibility assessment, the Court noted that the Government offered a settlement proposal under section 25 of the 2006 Act, acknowledging the violation of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. However, the applicant did not accept it. The Court found that the remedial provisions, including section 25, did not apply because the proceedings continued before the Supreme Court after the legislation became operational. Similarly, section 19 did not provide a compensation claim since the case was finally resolved before the Act. Thus, the applicant had no effective remedy. The complaint was declared admissible.

On the merits regarding Article 6 § 1, the Court determined the relevant period began on 14 October 1996 and ended on 10 December 2007, totaling eleven years and two months across four levels of jurisdiction. Assessing reasonableness based on case complexity, conduct of parties, and stakes, the Court referenced similar cases finding violations. It concluded that the Government failed to provide persuasive arguments, and the length was excessive, violating the "reasonable time" requirement.

For Article 13, the Court reiterated that effective remedies are required for alleged breaches of reasonable time under Article 6 § 1. It found the remedies under the 2006 Act ineffective and, consistent with prior cases like *Lukenda v. Slovenia*, determined there was a violation. The case highlights systemic issues in Slovenia’s legal system regarding prolonged proceedings and inadequate redress.

**Case of Moskalenko and Others v. Ukraine** (Application no. 1270/12 and 249 other applications) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, on 18 July 2013. The case concerned 250 applications lodged by Ukrainian nationals against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention.

The applicants complained, expressly or in substance, under Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, about the lengthy non-enforcement of final domestic court decisions given in their favour and about the lack of effective domestic remedies for those complaints. The domestic courts had delivered decisions entitling the applicants to various pecuniary amounts or requiring certain actions to be taken in their favour. These decisions became final and enforceable. However, the applicants were unable to obtain their enforcement in due time. Some applicants also submitted complaints concerning factual and legal matters unrelated to the non-enforcement issue.

Procedurally, two applicants died, and their spouses expressed the wish to continue the proceedings; the Court accepted that the next-of-kin had standing to pursue those applications. Two other applicants also died. The Government informed the Court of their deaths, but no heir requested permission to pursue the applications and no replies were received. The Court therefore struck those two applications out of its list under Article 37 § 1 (a) of the Convention, finding no special circumstances requiring continued examination. Another application was declared inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded: the applicant complained that from 1 November 2011 the debtor had stopped enforcing a judgment of 21 January 2011 concerning recalculation and payment of his pension. However, the Government showed that the Donetsk Administrative Court of Appeal had amended the judgment on 11 May 2011, limiting the relevant recalculation and payment period to 22 July 2011. Therefore, the original judgment did not cover the period complained of.

For the remaining applications, the Court joined those raising similar principal legal issues. The Government argued that no violation had occurred because Ukrainian legislation and a Cabinet of Ministers resolution had reduced the budget allocations for enforcing judgments awarding social payments, and that the applicants’ entitlements under the relevant legislation were accordingly reduced. The Government therefore considered the complaints manifestly ill-founded. The Government also submitted documents seeking to show that certain judgment debts had been paid. The Court requested confirmation. In three applications, the Government failed to establish full payment: in two, documents showed only partial payment before particular dates; in one, an order from the ministry to a bank was submitted without confirmation from the bank that the order had been carried out.

The Court reiterated that the judgments at issue were final and enforceable, yet had not been complied with by the State for a lengthy period, for which the State authorities remained responsible. It held that regulations on the allocation of budgetary resources did not affect that position. It also recalled its established case-law that a State’s failure to comply with enforceable judgments because of a lack of budgetary funds cannot justify non-enforcement. The Court accordingly rejected the Government’s objection and declared the relevant complaints admissible, finding they were not manifestly ill-founded or inadmissible on any other grounds.

In essence, the case concerned systemic non-enforcement in Ukraine of final domestic decisions, principally concerning social or pecuniary entitlements, and the absence of effective remedies, in alleged violation of Article 6 § 1, Article 13, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The case *Moskalenko and Others v. Ukraine* (application no. 1270/12 and 249 other applications) was a 2013 European Court of Human Rights judgment concerning 250 applications brought by Ukrainian nationals. The applicants complained about final domestic court decisions issued in their favour that had not been enforced in due time. Those decisions entitled them to various pecuniary amounts or required certain actions to be taken by State authorities. The decisions became final and enforceable, but the applicants were unable to secure timely enforcement. The applicants relied, expressly or in substance, on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, Article 13, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, alleging lengthy non-enforcement and lack of effective domestic remedies.

Procedurally, some applicants died. In two applications, the deceased applicants’ spouses sought to continue, and the Court accepted that next-of-kin had standing. In two other applications, the applicants died and no heir requested permission to pursue the proceedings; the Court struck those applications out under Article 37 § 1 (a). One application, no. 29644/12, was declared inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded: the applicant complained that from 1 November 2011 the Pension Fund stopped enforcing a 21 January 2011 judgment, but the Donetsk Administrative Court of Appeal had amended that judgment to limit the recalculation and payment period to 22 July 2011. Therefore, the judgment did not cover the period in dispute.

The remaining applications were joined because they raised the same principal legal issue. The Court declared them admissible. It noted that the domestic decisions were final and enforceable but had not been complied with for a lengthy period, for which the State authorities were responsible.

The Ukrainian Government opposed the complaints. It argued that no violation had occurred because the 2011 amendments to the State Budget Law and Cabinet Resolution No. 745 reduced the amounts allocated for enforcement of judgments awarding social payments and reduced the applicants’ entitlements. It therefore considered the complaints manifestly ill-founded. The Court rejected that argument. It reiterated that final and enforceable judgments must be complied with and that budgetary allocation rules do not affect the State’s responsibility. Under its constant case-law, a State cannot justify non-enforcement by lack of budgetary funds (see *Voytenko v. Ukraine*; *Tsibulko and Others v. Ukraine*).

The Government also claimed certain judgment debts had been paid. However, the evidence showed only partial payment before November 2011 in application no. 41016/12, partial payment before July 2011 in no. 52222/12, and in no. 41356/12 only an order from the ministry to a bank without confirmation that it had been carried out. The Government thus failed to prove full payment in those cases.

Accordingly, the Court rejected the Government’s admissibility objection and found the applicants’ complaints under Articles 6 and 13 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 not manifestly ill-founded. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were that final domestic judgments in the applicants’ favour remained unenforced for a lengthy period, that the State was responsible, and that the absence of effective remedies and budgetary shortfalls could not excuse the failure to enforce.

In Moskalenko and Others v. Ukraine, the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, Committee) considered 250 applications (no. 1270/12 and 249 others) lodged by Ukrainian nationals against Ukraine. The applicants complained, expressly or in substance, under Article 6 §1 and Article 13 of the European Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, about the lengthy failure of Ukrainian authorities to enforce final domestic court decisions given in their favour. Some decisions awarded them pecuniary amounts; others required specific actions to be taken for their benefit.

The central facts were similar. On dates listed in appended tables, domestic courts issued decisions entitling the applicants to various payments or actions. Those decisions became final and enforceable. Despite this, the applicants could not obtain enforcement in due time. Some applicants also submitted complaints concerning unrelated factual or legal matters, but the principal issue was non-enforcement of the final judgments.

Procedurally, two applicants, Mr Vasiliy Grunskiy and Mr Petro Plyaka, died; their spouses asked to continue the proceedings. The Court accepted that the next-of-kin had standing. Another two applicants, Mr Viktor Motuzkov and Ms Olga Moroz, also died. The Government informed the Court, but no heir requested permission to pursue their applications. Since there were no special circumstances, the Court struck those applications out under Article 37 §1(a).

One application, no. 29644/12, was declared inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded. The applicant alleged that from 1 November 2011 the debtor stopped enforcing a 21 January 2011 judgment ordering the Pension Fund to recalculate and pay his pension. The Government showed that on 11 May 2011 the Donetsk Administrative Court of Appeal amended that judgment, limiting the recalculation and payment period to 22 July 2011. The judgment therefore did not cover the later period complained of.

For the remaining applications (Appendix 3), the Government argued that no violation had occurred. It relied on the Law of Ukraine of 14 June 2011 amending the State Budget and Cabinet Resolution No. 745, which reduced budget allocations for enforcing judgments awarding social payments. The Government claimed the applicants’ entitlements were correspondingly reduced and their complaints were manifestly ill-founded.

The Court rejected that argument. It noted that the judgments at issue were final and enforceable, yet the State had failed to comply with them for a lengthy period, for which the State authorities remained responsible. Regulations on allocation of budgetary resources did not alter that position, and a State’s lack of budgetary funds cannot justify non-enforcement of enforceable judgments (citing Voytenko v. Ukraine and Tsibulko and Others v. Ukraine).

The Court also examined the Government’s claims that certain debts had been paid. In application no. 41016/12, documents showed only part payment before November 2011; in no. 52222/12, only part payment before July 2011; and in no. 41356/12, the Government submitted a ministry order to a bank without confirmation that the bank had carried it out. Thus, in those three cases, the Government failed to prove full payment.

Accordingly, the Court joined the similar applications, found the complaints in Appendix 3 not manifestly ill-founded and admissible, and rejected the Government’s objections based on budget reductions. The key alleged violation was the State’s lengthy non-enforcement of final and enforceable domestic decisions, engaging the applicants’ rights to a fair trial, an effective remedy, and protection of property.

**Summary of *Tarasov v. Ukraine* (Application no. 17416/03)**

**Key Facts Relevant to Alleged Violations**

The case originated from an application against Ukraine by Mr. Aleksey Gennadyevich Tarasov, concerning events in January 2000. On 13 January 2000, the applicant was arrested by police in Makiyivka and detained until 25 January 2000. During this period, he alleged that he was subjected to severe ill-treatment, including beatings with fists, kicks, and a stick; being trussed with belts; having a plastic bag and an ammonia-filled gas mask placed over his head; and having electric wires attached to his genitals and right hand, with shocks applied. This treatment was allegedly inflicted to force him to confess to theft and robbery. He claimed he had no access to a lawyer during this time.

On 14 January 2000, an ambulance was called, and hospital medical reports recorded abdominal trauma and bruising in the lumbar region, injuries consistent with his allegations. The applicant was transferred to the SIZO (pre-trial detention center) on 25 January 2000. He alleged that the SIZO doctor, after speaking with a police officer, failed to record his injuries properly.

On 25 May 2000, the prosecutor’s office refused to institute criminal proceedings regarding the ill-treatment, citing lack of proof. This decision was quashed on 2 August 2000 due to an incomplete investigation. A subsequent refusal on 7 September 2000 was also quashed by a court on 6 November 2003, which noted significant investigative failures, including the lack of records on the applicant’s health upon arrival at SIZO and the unexamined origin of his injuries. A final refusal on 15 June 2005 cited unavailable documentation and conflicting witness statements.

A court-ordered forensic examination (July-August 2000) found scars and marks, including a dotted-line scar on the penis and a brown mark on the wrist. The expert concluded that some marks could be healing bruises from 13 January 2000 and that the scars on the penis and wrist were consistent with the applicant’s account of electric shocks. This finding was corroborated by the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT), which visited Ukraine in September 2000 and reported a case matching the applicant’s description, noting visible marks consistent with electrical shocks.

During his criminal trial for theft and robbery, which began in March 2000, the applicant retracted his confessions, claiming they were obtained under duress. He sought to examine witnesses who had heard his screams and the ambulance doctor, but the latter request was rejected. The trial court, in convicting him on 25 December 2001, relied on his prior confessions alongside other evidence and rejected his ill-treatment complaint, dismissing the testimony of two witnesses because of their relationship with him (his cohabitant and her mother). The applicant also faced difficulties attending hearings due to severe health issues, requiring transport on a stretcher. His appeals were repeatedly rejected for procedural non-compliance.

**Alleged Violations**

The applicant complained under Article 3 that he had been tortured by police and that the state failed to conduct an effective investigation. Under Article 6, he alleged that his conviction was based on self-incriminating statements obtained under duress and without a lawyer, that he was forced to attend trial despite his poor health, and that key defense witnesses were not summoned. The European Court of Human Rights found the complaints admissible, ultimately holding that the State had not provided a plausible explanation for his injuries, classifying the treatment as torture for which the Government bore responsibility, and that the investigation into his allegations was ineffective and deficient.

Case of *Tarasov v. Ukraine* (App. No. 17416/03) concerned a Ukrainian national, Mr Aleksey Tarasov, arrested on 13 January 2000 by Makiyivka police and held in police custody until 25 January 2000. He alleged that during this period he had no access to a lawyer and was repeatedly beaten, suffocated with a plastic bag and gas mask, and subjected to electric shocks to his genitals and right wrist in order to force him to confess to theft and robbery. The Government claimed he was informed of his procedural rights and signed waivers of legal representation. On 14 January 2000, an ambulance was called; hospital records noted abdominal trauma and bruising in the lumbar region. Between 13 and 19 January, he was questioned and participated in on-site reconstructions, confessing to several offences. On 2 March 2000, once represented by a lawyer, he retracted his confessions, denied guilt, and claimed they had been obtained under duress.

At trial, which began on 17 March 2000, Tarasov repeated his ill-treatment allegations. Two witnesses testified that they had heard him screaming at the police station and seen him after beatings. His request to summon the ambulance doctor was rejected. A forensic medical examination conducted in July–August 2000 found marks on his wrist and penis, as well as brown pigmentation in the lumbar/coccyx area; the expert considered these consistent with healing bruises from 13 January 2000 and with his account of electric shocks. A 2000 CPT report also described a detainee matching Tarasov’s account and noted visible marks consistent with electric shocks.

Investigations into his complaints were repeatedly closed for lack of proof. In 2003, a domestic court quashed one refusal, finding that the origin and time of his injuries had not been properly established, cellmates had not been questioned, and health records were missing. A later 2005 refusal relied on destroyed records and conflicting statements. Meanwhile, on 25 December 2001, the local court convicted Tarasov of theft and robbery and sentenced him to five years’ imprisonment. Although the court noted his denial and cited other evidence, it also referred to his earlier confessions. His appeals and cassation appeal failed.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Tarasov complained under Article 3 that he had been tortured by police and that the authorities had failed to investigate effectively. He also complained under Article 6 that his conviction was based on coerced self-incriminating statements made without a lawyer, that he could not properly challenge the evidence, that witnesses were not summoned, and that he was forced to attend court despite poor health. The Court found that the Government had not provided a plausible explanation for injuries sustained while he was under police control; given their serious nature, the treatment amounted to torture. It also found the investigation ineffective. The failure to expressly disregard his confessions, combined with the violation of his defence rights, rendered the criminal proceedings unfair. The Court accordingly found violations of Article 3 and Article 6.

In *Tarasov v. Ukraine* (Application no. 17416/03, judgment 31 October 2013), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by Ukrainian national Aleksey Tarasov that police ill-treated him and that his defence rights were violated. The key violations alleged were torture/inhuman treatment and an ineffective investigation under Article 3, and an unfair trial under Article 6, particularly through the use of self-incriminating statements obtained under duress and without a lawyer.

On 13 January 2000, police from the Makiyivka Police Department arrested Tarasov and held him in police custody until 25 January 2000. He alleged that during interrogations he had no access to a lawyer and was forced to confess to theft and robbery. He claimed repeated severe beatings, kicking and punching, being tied up, suffocation with a plastic bag and a gas mask containing ammonia, and electric shocks applied to his genitals and right hand. The Government maintained that his procedural rights, including the right to counsel and freedom from self-incrimination, were explained to him, that he signed waivers, and that he confessed voluntarily to car theft, scrap-metal theft and robbery. He also participated in filmed on-site reconstructions.

Medical evidence was central. On 14 January 2000, an ambulance was called because Tarasov was weak and suffering lumbar and rib pain. Hospital reports recorded abdominal trauma and bruising in the lumbar region. A forensic examination in July–August 2000 found a mark on his wrist and a scar on his penis consistent with electric shocks, and bruising that could have been inflicted on 13 January 2000. Later examinations noted numerous scars and pigmentation. A CPT report describing a man arrested in Makeyevka on 13 January 2000 mirrored his allegations, including visible marks consistent with electric shocks.

On 2 March 2000, with lawyer M. present, Tarasov denied guilt and stated that his earlier confessions had been obtained under duress. At trial, which began on 17 March 2000, he repeated his torture allegations and sought witnesses. Two women testified that they had heard him screaming at the police station, but the court rejected their evidence because of their relationship with him. The court refused to summon the ambulance doctor but ordered a forensic medical examination. Tarasov’s health deteriorated, and in December 2001 he was brought to court on a stretcher. On 25 December 2001, the local court convicted him of theft and robbery and sentenced him to five years’ imprisonment. It relied on his prior confessions along with co-accused testimony, victim testimony and material evidence, and rejected his ill-treatment complaint. Appeals and a cassation appeal failed.

Prosecutorial investigations into the alleged ill-treatment were repeatedly refused. In 2003, a domestic court quashed one refusal, noting that the origin and time of his injuries had not been established, health records on arrival at detention were missing, and cellmates had not been properly questioned. By 2005, some records had been destroyed, and the prosecutor again refused to open proceedings.

The ECtHR found that the Government had failed to provide a plausible explanation for injuries sustained while Tarasov was under police control. It concluded that he had been subjected to torture, in violation of Article 3, and that the domestic investigation was ineffective, also violating Article 3. The Court further found that the failure of the domestic courts to expressly disregard his confessions, together with violations of his defence rights, rendered the criminal proceedings unfair under Article 6.

Case Qama v. Albania and Italy (Application no. 4604/09) is a European Court of Human Rights case decided by the Fourth Section on 8 January 2013, final on 8 April 2013. The applicant, Flamur Qama, an Albanian national born in 1960 and living in Durrës, lodged the application on 23 December 2008 against Albania and Italy. He alleged breaches of Articles 6 § 1 and 8 of the Convention because the Albanian and Italian authorities allegedly failed to secure his right of contact with his child, who was in Italy. The application was communicated to the respondent governments on 21 September 2009, and the Court decided to examine admissibility and merits together.

The applicant had a son born on 25 August 1994. In September 1999, the applicant’s late spouse, who was suffering from a serious disease, entered Italy irregularly with the son in order to obtain medical treatment. The applicant later joined them in Italy. In August or September 2002, after disagreements with his in-laws, the applicant was expelled from Italy because he did not have a residence permit. His wife and son remained in Italy, as their status had not yet been regularised. The wife died on 7 October 2002.

Following the mother’s death, custody proceedings began in Italy. On 17 October 2002, the applicant’s sister-in-law, Z., applied to the Ancona Youth Court seeking custody of the child. On 30 December 2002, a report from the local social health centre stated that the child feared returning to live with his father because of the father’s alleged ill-treatment of the deceased mother. The report also said the father had abandoned the child and spouse without notice when they most needed him.

On 4 June 2003, the Italian court granted Z.’s request. It entrusted Z. with custody of the child under the supervision of the Social Service of Senigallia and appointed the Mayor of Senigallia as temporary guardian. The court suspended the parents’ parental rights, reasoning that they had allowed the child to leave Albania without addressing the serious difficulties he would face. It prohibited the child’s removal from Italian territory and assigned the International Social Service (ISS), an NGO, to investigate the applicant’s family situation. Crucially, the court made no provision for the applicant’s visiting or contact rights with his child.

On 25 September 2003, the ISS, after attempting to contact the applicant, informed the Italian court that he refused to speak to them and simply requested that the child be returned to him. From contacts with neighbours, the ISS reported that the applicant had remarried, his new wife was pregnant, he was unemployed, and he was living on his spouse’s income. On 22 March 2004, the Italian social services updated the court: the child’s status in Italy had been regularised and his situation appeared balanced.

The applicant’s central complaint was that, despite being the father, he was left without effective contact with his son in Italy. He argued that both Albania and Italy failed to protect his family life and his right of access to the child, raising issues under Article 8, and that the proceedings did not satisfy Article 6 § 1. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the father’s expulsion, the mother’s death, the Italian custody order suspending parental rights without contact arrangements, the child’s placement with the aunt, the ISS investigation, and the applicant’s limited ability to maintain or restore contact from Albania.

**Case Qama v. Albania and Italy (Application no. 4604/09)** concerns an Albanian national, Flamur Qama, who alleged that the Albanian and Italian authorities failed to secure his right of contact with his child in Italy, in breach of Articles 6 § 1 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant was born in 1960 and lived in Durrës. His son was born on 25 August 1994. In September 1999, the applicant’s late spouse, who was suffering from a serious disease, entered Italy irregularly with their son in order to obtain medical treatment. His wife and son remained in Italy, where their immigration status had not yet been regularised. The applicant’s wife died on 7 October 2002.

On 30 December 2002, a local social health centre report stated that the child feared returning to live with his father because of the father’s alleged ill-treatment of the deceased mother and because the father had abandoned the child and spouse without notice when they needed him most.

On 4 June 2003, the Italian court granted Z.’s request. It entrusted Z. with custody of the child, under the supervision of the Social Service of Senigallia. It appointed the Mayor of Senigallia as the child’s temporary guardian. The court suspended the parents’ parental rights, finding that they had allowed the child to leave Albania without addressing the serious difficulties he would later face. It also prohibited the child’s removal from Italian territory and assigned the International Social Service, an NGO, to investigate the applicant’s family situation. Critically, the court made no provision for the applicant’s visiting or contact rights with his child.

On 25 September 2003, after trying to contact the applicant, the ISS informed the Italian court that he refused to speak to them. He simply requested that the child be returned to him. Following contacts with neighbours, the ISS reported that the applicant had re-married, that his wife was expecting a child, and that he was unemployed and living on his spouse’s income. On 22 March 2004, the Italian social services updated the court: the child’s status in Italy had been regularised and his situation appeared balanced.

The applicant’s central complaint was that the Italian and Albanian authorities failed to secure his right of contact with his son. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore that the Italian court placed the child with a maternal relative and suspended parental authority without arranging any contact, while the applicant, who had been expelled from Italy, remained in Albania and was left without any practical means of maintaining family life with his child. The child was under Italian jurisdiction, and the applicant’s requests for contact or return were not matched by effective measures to facilitate contact or to review the absence of contact arrangements. The cross-border element and the child’s expressed fear and refusal of contact were also central to how the authorities handled the case.

The application was communicated to both respondent Governments, and the Court decided to rule on admissibility and merits together. Ultimately, the Court examined whether Italy and Albania had complied with their positive obligations under Article 8 to protect the applicant’s family life and whether the proceedings concerning custody and contact satisfied Article 6. The case is primarily relevant for the alleged failure to secure contact between a non-custodial parent and a child living in another Contracting State.

Rozhenko and Others v. Ukraine (Application no. 2644/04 and 23 other applications) is a European Court of Human Rights case involving 24 Ukrainian nationals. The applications were lodged under Article 34 of the Convention. The central legal issue was Ukraine’s lengthy failure to enforce final domestic court decisions given in the applicants’ favour. The domestic courts had delivered judgments on dates listed in appended tables. These judgments became final and enforceable. They entitled the applicants either to various pecuniary amounts or to have certain actions taken in their favour. However, the applicants could not obtain timely enforcement because State authorities failed to comply with those decisions. Some applicants also made submissions about factual and legal matters unrelated to the non-enforcement issue, but the principal alleged violation concerned the non-enforcement itself.

Two applicants, in applications nos. 17176/07 and 48229/07, died during the proceedings. Their relatives, heirs, or next-of-kin continued the applications. The Court held that those persons had standing to pursue the proceedings. Because the applications raised a similar principal legal issue, the Court joined them. The Ukrainian Government was represented by its Agent, Mr Nazar Kulchytskyy. The Government submitted unilateral declarations aimed at resolving the non-enforcement issues and asked the Court to strike out the applications under Article 37 § 1(c) of the Convention. The Court examined the declarations but rejected the Government’s request.

The applicants complained, expressly or in substance, under Article 6 of the Convention, Article 13 of the Convention, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Article 6 guarantees a fair hearing within a reasonable time in the determination of civil rights and obligations. Article 13 guarantees an effective remedy before a national authority for Convention violations. Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. The applicants alleged that the final judgments in their favour had not been enforced for lengthy periods and that they had no effective domestic remedy to address or prevent that delay. They therefore claimed violations of their right to a reasonable-time hearing, their right to an effective remedy, and their property rights.

The Government contested admissibility, arguing that the complaints were inadmissible or partly inadmissible for various reasons. The applicants disagreed. The Court noted that similar objections had already been dismissed in prior case-law, citing Voytenko v. Ukraine. The Court also noted that the underlying legal issue was already the subject of well-established case-law, referring to Yuriy Nikolayevich Ivanov v. Ukraine.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were: final and enforceable domestic decisions existed in the applicants’ favour; the State failed to enforce them in due time; the delay was attributable to State authorities; the applicants lacked effective domestic remedies for the non-enforcement; and the Government’s unilateral declarations did not persuade the Court to strike out the applications. These facts formed the basis of the alleged breaches of Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The case thus concerned systemic non-enforcement of domestic judgments in Ukraine and the adequacy of domestic remedies for that problem.

In *Rozhenko and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 2644/04 and 23 other applications), the European Court of Human Rights examined 24 applications lodged by Ukrainian nationals. The central factual complaint was that final domestic judgments given in the applicants’ favour were not enforced for lengthy periods because of the State’s failure to comply with those decisions.

According to the appended tables, domestic courts had delivered judgments entitling the applicants to various pecuniary amounts or requiring certain actions to be taken in their favour. These judgments became final and enforceable. However, the applicants were unable to obtain timely enforcement, not because of any private dispute, but because the State authorities failed to comply with the binding decisions. This prolonged non-enforcement formed the principal legal issue in the case.

The applicants complained, expressly or in substance, under Article 6 of the Convention, Article 13 of the Convention, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Article 6 protects the right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time. Article 13 guarantees an effective remedy before a national authority for alleged Convention violations. Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. The applicants alleged not only that the final judgments in their favour remained unenforced for excessive periods, but also that there was no effective domestic remedy available to address that non-enforcement. The Court noted that the underlying legal issue was already the subject of well-established case-law, referring in particular to *Yuriy Nikolayevich Ivanov v. Ukraine* (no. 40450/04, 15 October 2009).

Procedurally, the applications were communicated to the Ukrainian Government on various dates. The Government submitted unilateral declarations aimed at resolving the non-enforcement issues and requested that the Court strike the applications out of its list under Article 37 § 1(c) of the Convention. The Court examined those declarations and rejected the Government’s request. The Government also raised objections to admissibility, arguing that the applicants’ complaints were inadmissible or partly inadmissible for various reasons. The Court observed that similar objections had already been dismissed in a number of its judgments, including *Voytenko v. Ukraine* (no. 18966/02, §§ 32-35, 29 June 2004). The applicants disagreed with the Government’s submissions.

Two applicants, in applications nos. 17176/07 and 48229/07, died during the proceedings. The Court held that their heirs or next-of-kin had standing to continue the proceedings in their stead, citing *Mironov v. Ukraine*. Some applicants also made submissions concerning factual and legal matters unrelated to the non-enforcement issues, but the main focus remained the failure to enforce final domestic decisions.

Because the applications raised similar principal legal issues, the Court joined them. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore: final and enforceable domestic judgments in the applicants’ favour; lengthy State failure to enforce those judgments; the applicants’ resulting inability to obtain the awarded sums or actions; and the alleged absence of effective domestic remedies for that non-enforcement. These facts engaged Article 6, Article 13, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, and the Court proceeded in light of its established case-law on Ukraine’s systemic non-enforcement problem.

CASE OF ROZHENKO AND OTHERS v. UKRAINE (Application no. 2644/04 and 23 other applications) is a 2013 European Court of Human Rights judgment concerning Ukraine. It originated in 24 applications lodged by Ukrainian nationals under Article 34 of the Convention. Two applicants died, and their relatives or heirs continued applications nos. 17176/07 and 48229/07; the Court accepted that they had standing to proceed.

The central facts common to the applications concerned the non-enforcement of final domestic court decisions. On dates listed in appended tables, Ukrainian domestic courts delivered judgments in the applicants’ favour. These judgments entitled them either to various pecuniary amounts or to have certain actions taken in their favour. The decisions became final and enforceable. Despite this, the applicants could not obtain enforcement in due time. The failure was attributed to the State’s failure to comply with the domestic decisions. As a result, the applicants did not receive what the courts had awarded, and enforcement was delayed for lengthy periods. Some applicants also made submissions concerning factual and legal matters unrelated to the non-enforcement issues, but the main legal issue across the applications was similar.

Before the Court, the applicants complained, expressly or in substance, under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, Article 13, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Article 6 guarantees a fair hearing within a reasonable time; Article 13 guarantees an effective remedy before a national authority; and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. The applicants alleged that the lengthy failure to enforce the judgments violated their right to a fair hearing and their property rights, and that no effective domestic remedy existed for these complaints. These allegations were based on the State’s inability or failure to execute binding court decisions in their favour.

During the proceedings, the Government submitted unilateral declarations aimed at resolving the non-enforcement issues and asked the Court to strike out the relevant applications under Article 37 § 1 (c) of the Convention. The Court examined the declarations but rejected the Government’s request. The Government also raised admissibility objections, arguing that the complaints were inadmissible or partly inadmissible for various reasons. The Court noted that similar objections had already been dismissed in earlier case-law, such as Voytenko v. Ukraine. The Court joined the applications because they raised the same principal legal issue.

The Court further noted that the underlying legal issue was already the subject of well-established case-law, particularly Yuriy Nikolayevich Ivanov v. Ukraine (no. 40450/04, 15 October 2009), which addressed Ukraine’s systemic problem of non-enforcement of final domestic decisions. Accordingly, the key facts relevant to the alleged violations were the existence of final and enforceable domestic judgments in the applicants’ favour, the State’s lengthy failure to enforce them, and the absence of effective domestic remedies for that non-enforcement.

Davit Jashi, a Georgian national born in 1973, was arrested on 28 September 2005 for drug possession and detained in Tbilisi No. 5 Prison. Prior to these proceedings, he had suffered serious cranial traumas that deteriorated his mental health. On 28 December 2005, a psychiatric report concluded that a definitive diagnosis required a comprehensive examination in an appropriate medical setting. Acting on this, the Zugdidi District Court ordered on 20 January 2006 that Jashi be admitted to Poti Psychiatric Hospital for a forensic psychiatric examination, specifying that his trial could only resume after obtaining results. Despite this final ruling, authorities refused to enforce it.

On 9 March 2006, Jashi was transferred to Zugdidi Prison under a strict regime. His representatives requested interim measures from the European Court of Human Rights on 7 April 2006, seeking enforcement of the psychiatric examination order. The Court declined to indicate interim measures but gave urgent notice to the Government on 26 April 2006, requesting explanations for non-enforcement and documentation of medical treatment provided.

A subsequent court order on 23 May 2006 directed Jashi's admission to the National Forensic Bureau's psychiatric ward, where he was transferred on 31 May 2006. A panel of State psychiatric experts issued a report on 14 June 2006 finding that Jashi had an organic personality disorder but retained criminal responsibility and did not require compulsory psychiatric treatment. He was returned to Zugdidi Prison the following day.

After his return, Jashi attempted suicide on 15 June 2006 by slashing his wrists and exhibited aggressive behaviour. Neither he nor his lawyers had been informed of the medical report's contents. On 4 July 2006, the Court applied Rule 39, indicating that Jashi's mental health should be examined by a parity-based panel of psychiatric experts in an appropriate medical establishment, with adequate medical treatment to follow.

Jashi made further suicide attempts on 12 July 2006 (drug overdose) and 22 July 2006 (slashing wrists with electrical wiring). He was transferred to the NFB psychiatric ward from 27 July to 18 August 2006, where a parity-based panel issued a report largely reiterating the previous findings but noting depressive symptoms and suicidal ideation. The prison authority then admitted him to the prison hospital's psychiatric ward, where he remained until 31 August 2008.

While in the prison hospital, medical examinations conducted between August 2007 and June 2008 revealed serious cardiac conditions including cardiac ischemia, class III-IV angina, arterial hypertension, and grade II-III heart failure. Medical reports recommended treatment in a specialised cardiology hospital and a coronary angiogram. In July 2008, Jashi was diagnosed with viral hepatitis C. Although offered an angiogram in a private hospital on 15 July 2008, he declined.

The applicant's representatives repeatedly requested transfer to a cardiology hospital. On 9 December 2008, the Court indicated that Jashi should be placed in a cardiology hospital for treatment consistent with the second medical report's recommendations. Prison authorities offered transfers on multiple occasions in December 2008 and January 2009, which Jashi refused without explanation. He was finally transferred to Guli Hospital, a private cardiology facility, on 3 April 2009, where he remained until 15 May 2009. Due to his iodine allergy, a coronary angiogram was deemed imprudent, but supervised cardiology drug treatment significantly improved his condition. Subsequent hepatitis C treatment with antiviral drugs from July to December 2009 proved successful.

**Jashi v. Georgia (Application no. 10799/06, judgment of 8 January 2013)** concerned a Georgian national, Davit Jashi, who complained under the European Convention on Human Rights about, among other things, inadequate medical care in prison. His initial 2006 application alleged poor detention conditions and lack of adequate medical treatment under Article 3, along with complaints under Articles 5, 6 and 13. The Court later restored only the complaint concerning the adequacy of medical treatment in prison and gave notice of that issue under Articles 2 and 3.

The applicant had a history of serious cranial trauma and deteriorating mental health. In September 2005 he was arrested for drug offences and detained in Tbilisi No. 5 Prison. A December 2005 psychiatric report stated that a definite diagnosis required a comprehensive psychiatric examination in an appropriate medical setting. In January 2006 the Zugdidi District Court ordered his admission to Poti Psychiatric Hospital for one month for a forensic psychiatric examination, ruling that his trial could resume only after the results were obtained. Although the ruling was final, the authorities refused to enforce it despite repeated complaints. In March 2006 he was transferred to Zugdidi Prison under a strict regime.

After the applicant sought interim measures, in May 2006 the domestic court ordered his admission to the psychiatric ward of the National Forensic Bureau. He was transferred on 31 May 2006, but his request that two experts of his choice participate was refused. A State psychiatric panel report of 14 June 2006 found an organic personality disorder but concluded that he could be held responsible and did not require compulsory psychiatric treatment. He and his lawyers were not informed of the report at the time. On 15 June 2006 he attempted suicide by slashing his wrists and became aggressive. On 4 July 2006 the European Court indicated under Rule 39 that his mental health should be examined in an appropriate establishment by a parity panel of experts and that he should receive adequate medical treatment. Further suicide attempts followed in July and August 2006, including drug overdoses and wrist-slashing. A second parity-panel examination largely repeated the earlier diagnosis but noted depression and suicidal ideation. He was then admitted to the prison hospital’s psychiatric ward until August 2008.

Later medical reports in 2007–2008 documented severe cardiac problems, including ischaemia, angina, hypertension and heart failure, as well as vein diseases, personality disorder, suicidal tendencies, and later hepatitis C. Two National Forensic Bureau reports recommended treatment in a cardiology hospital and a coronary angiogram. Despite requests, the prison authorities did not transfer him. In December 2008 the Court indicated under Rule 39 that he be placed in a cardiology hospital for treatment consistent with the second medical report. The authorities offered transfer for an angiogram in December 2008 and January 2009, but the applicant refused. In April 2009 he was transferred to a private cardiology hospital, where his cardiac condition improved; an angiogram was avoided because of an iodine allergy. HCV treatment was later offered and, after initial postponement, successfully completed in 2009–2010.

International reports by the CPT (2007) and Human Rights Watch (2006) criticised psychiatric care in Georgian prisons, citing shortages of psychiatrists, restrictions on psychotropic medication, and inadequate treatment of prisoners with mental disorders. The case therefore focused on whether Georgia fulfilled its positive obligations to provide adequate psychiatric and cardiac medical care and to enforce the court-ordered psychiatric examination, under Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention.

In *Abdi v. the United Kingdom* (Application no. 27770/08, judgment 9 April 2013), the applicant was a Somali national who arrived in the UK in May 1995 and claimed asylum. Although his asylum claim was refused, he received exceptional leave to remain until February 2000. In July 1998 he was convicted of rape and indecency with a child and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. In May 2002 the Secretary of State decided to deport him and authorised his detention pending deportation. His asylum and deportation appeals were exhausted by December 2003. His prison sentence ended automatically in September 2003, but he remained in immigration detention.

A deportation order was issued in April 2004. The applicant claimed to be a member of the Isaaq tribe from Somaliland. The authorities initially sought to return him to Somaliland, but this required clan bio-data which he did not provide. Enforced removals to Somalia became impossible in August 2004 after the last willing carrier withdrew; only voluntary returns were possible. The applicant refused to sign a voluntary-return disclaimer in November 2004. Enforced removals resumed in July 2006 after an agreement with African Express Airlines, and the first enforced removal took place in November 2006. The applicant remained in immigration detention until released on bail in April 2007; the application concerned this first period of detention, particularly from 3 December 2004 onward.

Domestically, the Administrative Court held that his detention from December 2004 to June 2006 was unlawful due to its length, the impossibility of removal during that period, and misleading information given to decision-makers. However, it found detention after June 2006 lawful because removal had again become possible. The Court of Appeal reversed this, holding the entire period lawful because the applicant could have returned voluntarily and posed a high risk of reoffending. Meanwhile, from April 2006 the Home Office operated an unpublished “secret” policy creating a near-blanket presumption in favour of detaining foreign national prisoners, contrary to the published policy presuming release. There was also a failure to conduct regular monthly detention reviews required by published policy. The UK Supreme Court later held in *Lumba and Mighty* that the secret policy was unlawful, and in *Kambadzi* that failure to conduct required reviews made detention unlawful under domestic law.

The applicant complained under Article 5 § 1(f) of the Convention that his detention was unlawful and arbitrary, that it was not genuinely “with a view to deportation” because removal was impossible for much of the time, and that his refusal to return voluntarily should not justify the length of detention. The Government contested the claims but accepted that some required detention reviews had not been carried out and that, following *Kambadzi*, the detention was not authorised under domestic law.

The European Court of Human Rights found the complaint concerning detention before 3 December 2004 inadmissible for failure to exhaust domestic remedies. However, for the period from 3 December 2004 to mid-April 2007, it held that because the Government accepted that the required regular reviews were not conducted, the detention was not “lawful” under domestic law. It therefore found a violation of Article 5 § 1 of the Convention. The Court did not separately decide whether the length of detention also violated Article 5, but noted that refusal to return voluntarily cannot operate as a trump card where removal is impossible or legal challenges are pending.

His appeals were exhausted by December 2003, and although his release from prison became automatic in September 2003, he remained in immigration detention pending deportation. A deportation order was issued in April 2004. The application concerned his first period of immigration detention, which ended in mid-April 2007.

Somaliland authorities required clan bio-data, which he did not provide. He argued that he was not detained “with a view to deportation” because removal was impossible for much of the time; that his detention was not in accordance with a procedure prescribed by law due to missed reviews and the secret policy; and that its length was arbitrary and lacked due diligence. The Government accepted that some required reviews had not been carried out and that, following *Kambadzi*, his detention was not authorised under domestic law for that reason. It denied that the secret policy had applied to him.

The Court declared the complaint admissible only from 3 December 2004; it found the earlier period inadmissible for failure to exhaust domestic remedies. On the merits, it did not need to decide whether he was a person against whom deportation action was being taken. It held that from 3 December 2004 until mid-April 2007, the failure to conduct the required regular detention reviews meant his detention was not “lawful” under domestic law and breached Article 5 § 1. The Court made no separate finding on length, but noted that a refusal to return voluntarily could not justify indefinite detention where removal was impossible or legal challenges were pending.

Case of Abdi v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 27770/08), ECtHR Fourth Section, judgment of 9 April 2013.

The applicant, Mr Mustafa Abdi, was a Somali national who arrived in the United Kingdom in May 1995 and claimed asylum. Although asylum was refused, he was granted exceptional leave to remain until February 2000. In July 1998 he was convicted of rape and indecency with a child and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. In May 2002 the Secretary of State decided to make a deportation order and authorised his detention. His appeal against deportation and fresh asylum claim were unsuccessful, with appeal rights exhausted in December 2003. In September 2003 his prison sentence ended automatically, but he remained in immigration detention under the 2002 detention authority. A deportation order was issued in April 2004.

The applicant claimed Isaaq/Somaliland origins, although he was born in Mogadishu. Returning him to Somaliland was difficult because the authorities required detailed clan/bio-data and the applicant did not co-operate. In August 2004 the last carrier willing to take enforced returns to Somalia withdrew; only voluntary returns remained possible. In November 2004 the applicant refused to sign a disclaimer confirming voluntary return. Bail was refused in December 2004. Further asylum representations in 2005 were refused. In October 2005 an immigration judge was wrongly told that enforced removals to Somalia would soon be possible. In July 2006 the Government reached an agreement with African Express Airlines, making enforced removals possible; the first enforced removal occurred in November 2006. Removal directions issued for the applicant were cancelled pending judicial review.

Domestically, the Administrative Court in December 2006 held that detention was lawful up to August 2004, unlawful from December 2004 to June 2006 because removal was impossible and decision-makers had been misled, and lawful after June 2006 because removal again appeared possible. The Court of Appeal reversed in July 2007, holding that the December 2004–June 2006 period was lawful because the applicant could have returned voluntarily, and because he posed a high risk of reoffending. The House of Lords refused permission to appeal in December 2007.

The present Strasbourg application concerned only the first period of immigration detention, ending shortly after the applicant was released on bail on 13 April 2007. He alleged that this detention violated Article 5 § 1(f) ECHR, both because it exceeded a reasonable period and because it was not “lawful” under domestic law.

Two key detention-policy issues arose. First, Home Office policy required regular monthly reviews and written reasons for continued detention. The Government accepted that, following the Supreme Court’s decision in Shepherd Kambadzi, the required reviews had not been carried out, so the applicant’s detention from 3 September 2003 to shortly after 13 April 2007 was not lawful under domestic law. Second, from April 2006 an unpublished “secret” policy created a near-blanket presumption in favour of detaining foreign national prisoners, contrary to the published presumption of release. In Lumba and Mighty the Supreme Court later found that policy unlawful, though the Government disputed whether it applied to Abdi.

On admissibility, the Government argued non-exhaustion because the applicant had not brought a false-imprisonment tort claim after Lumba/Kambadzi and had not challenged detention before 3 December 2004. The ECtHR rejected the tort argument, since he had already pursued judicial review and those Supreme Court decisions postdated his application. However, it found the pre-3 December 2004 period inadmissible for non-exhaustion, while noting he had already been detained 15 months by that date.

On the merits, the Court found that from 3 December 2004 until mid-April 2007 the applicant’s detention was not “lawful” under domestic law because the required reviews were not conducted. This breached Article 5 § 1. The Court did not make a separate finding on length. It nevertheless observed that refusal to return voluntarily is not a “trump card”: where return is impossible for extraneous reasons, refusal has no causal effect; where return is possible and legal challenges are pending, continued detention may be reasonable.
