In **Tomić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina** (Application no. 14284/08, judgment of 15 January 2013), the European Court of Human Rights examined the prolonged non-enforcement of a final domestic judgment awarding war damages. The five applicants were citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina living in Milići. They alleged violations of Article 6 of the Convention (right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property).

The key facts concerned a judgment of the Srebrenica First Instance Court of 13 March 2001. That court ordered the Republika Srpska, an Entity of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to pay the applicants 31,500 convertible marks (BAM) in respect of war damage, together with default interest at the statutory rate, within 15 days. The judgment became final on 20 April 2001. On 1 April 2002 the Banja Luka District Court issued a writ of execution. Nevertheless, the judgment was not enforced for a prolonged period.

The applicants complained to the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. On 26 June 2007, the Constitutional Court found a breach of Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. However, the applicants did not claim compensation, and the Court noted that even if they had, such a claim would most likely have been refused under existing domestic practice. This was relevant to whether they could still be considered victims of the alleged violation.

Later, after an information campaign concerning settlement of the Republika Srpska’s public debt, three applicants—Ms Ljeposava Kovačević, Mr Marko Tomić, and Mr Janko Tomić—agreed on 18 January 2010 to be paid only legal costs in cash, while the principal debt and default interest would be paid in government bonds. Bonds were issued to them on 15 June 2010, and they sold some or all of those bonds on the Stock Exchange. Ms Dobrinka Jovanović did not accept government bonds and was not issued any. Ms Ruža Tomić had died; as her close relatives did not seek to pursue her case, that part of the application was struck out.

The Government argued that the three applicants who accepted bonds could no longer claim victim status because the domestic judgments had been enforced partly in cash and partly through government bonds. The Court distinguished the earlier case of **Čolić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina**, because in that case the applicants had not accepted government bonds. Since the three applicants here had accepted bonds, received legal costs in cash, and sold some or all bonds, the domestic judgments were considered enforced. However, the Court held that a favourable measure alone does not remove victim status unless the national authorities have acknowledged the breach and afforded appropriate redress. Although the Constitutional Court had acknowledged the breach, the applicants could not obtain compensation for the delayed enforcement. Therefore, they remained victims in relation to the period during which the judgments remained unenforced.

On the merits, the Court found that the case was practically identical to **Runić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina** as regards the three applicants who accepted bonds. The non-enforcement lasted almost eight years after Bosnia and Herzegovina ratified the Convention. The Court found violations of Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. As regards Ms Dobrinka Jovanović, her situation was identical to **Čolić and Others**, and the Court likewise found violations of both provisions due to the non-enforcement of the final and enforceable domestic judgment awarding war damages.

In essence, the case concerned a final war-damages judgment that remained unenforced; partial enforcement through government bonds accepted by some applicants did not eliminate the violation because no compensation was provided for the delay.

In *Tomić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Application no. 14284/08), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint by five Bosnian citizens about the failure of the Republika Srpska, an Entity of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to enforce a final domestic judgment awarding them war damages. On 13 March 2001, the Srebrenica First Instance Court ordered the Republika Srpska to pay the applicants 31,500 convertible marks (BAM), within 15 days, plus statutory default interest. The judgment became final on 20 April 2001, and on 1 April 2002 the Banja Luka District Court issued a writ of execution. Nevertheless, the judgment was not enforced. The applicants complained to the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. On 26 June 2007, that court found violations of Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 because of the non-enforcement. The applicants did not claim compensation, and the ECtHR noted such a claim would most likely have been refused. The case was later brought to Strasbourg under Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

A key factual development concerned the settlement of Republika Srpska’s public debt. After an information campaign, on 18 January 2010, three applicants—Ms Ljeposava Kovačević, Mr Marko Tomić, and Mr Janko Tomić—agreed to receive their legal costs in cash and the principal debt and default interest in government bonds. Bonds were issued on 15 June 2010, and they sold some or all of them on the Stock Exchange. Ms Dobrinka Jovanović did not receive or accept bonds. Ms Ruža Tomić died during proceedings; the remaining applicants did not seek to pursue her part, so the Court struck out her application.

The Government argued that the three bond-accepting applicants were no longer victims because the domestic judgment had been enforced partly in cash and partly through bonds. The Court distinguished *Čolić and Others*, where applicants had not accepted bonds. Since these applicants accepted and sold the bonds, and received legal costs, the Court considered the judgment enforced. However, they could still claim victim status in relation to the period of delayed enforcement because, although the Constitutional Court had acknowledged the breach, they had obtained no compensation for the delay. Their complaints were therefore admissible.

On the merits, the Court found no reason to depart from its case-law. For Ms Kovačević, Mr Marko Tomić, and Mr Janko Tomić, the case was practically identical to *Runić and Others*, where violations of Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 were found. The period of non-enforcement was almost eight years after Bosnia and Herzegovina ratified the Convention. For Ms Dobrinka Jovanović, the case was identical to *Čolić and Others*, as she had not accepted bonds and the final, enforceable domestic judgment awarding war damages remained unenforced. The Court accordingly found violations of Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 in respect of the remaining applicants. The central alleged violation was the failure to enforce a final domestic judgment, causing prolonged uncertainty and deprivation of possessions.

Tomić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina (Application no. 14284/08) is a European Court of Human Rights judgment of 15 January 2013 concerning the non-enforcement of final domestic judgments awarding war damages. Five citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina—Ruža Tomić, Ljeposava Kovačević, Dobrinka Jovanović, Marko Tomić, and Janko Tomić—lodged the application on 18 February 2008. They alleged violations of Article 6 of the Convention (fair trial within a reasonable time) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) because the Republika Srpska failed to enforce a final judgment in their favour.

The key facts are as follows. On 13 March 2001, the Srebrenica First Instance Court ordered the Republika Srpska to pay the applicants 31,500 convertible marks (BAM), plus statutory default interest, for war damage within 15 days. That judgment became final on 20 April 2001. On 1 April 2002, the Banja Luka District Court issued a writ of execution. Despite this, the judgment remained unenforced. The applicants complained to the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which on 26 June 2007 found breaches of Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. However, the applicants did not claim compensation, and the European Court noted that such a claim would most likely have been refused.

After an information campaign about settling the Republika Srpska’s public debt, three applicants—Ljeposava Kovačević, Marko Tomić, and Janko Tomić—informed authorities on 18 January 2010 that they agreed to receive legal costs in cash and the principal debt plus default interest in government bonds. Bonds were issued on 15 June 2010, and they sold some or all of them on the Stock Exchange. Dobrinka Jovanović did not accept bonds or receive them. Ruža Tomić died during the proceedings, and that part of the application was struck out.

The Government argued that the three bond-accepting applicants could no longer be considered victims under Article 34 because the domestic judgments had been enforced: legal costs in cash and the debt and interest through bonds. The Court distinguished Čolić and Others, where applicants had not accepted bonds. Because these three applicants accepted and partly sold bonds and received cash costs, the Court considered the judgments effectively enforced. Nonetheless, they retained victim status because the domestic authorities, although acknowledging the breach, had not provided compensation for the delayed enforcement. Their complaints were admissible.

On the merits, for the three bond-accepting applicants, the Court found the case practically identical to Runić and Others and found violations of Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The non-enforcement lasted almost eight years after Bosnia and Herzegovina ratified the Convention. For Dobrinka Jovanović, who did not accept bonds, the case was identical to Čolić and Others, and the Court likewise found violations due to non-enforcement of the final and enforceable war-damages judgment. The Domestic Debt Act 2012 was irrelevant to the bond applicants because the 2004 Act applied when bonds were issued.
001-116827:
This case originated in an application (no. 50254/07) lodged by Mr Lampros Papadakis, a Greek national, against the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia. The applicant alleged violations of Article 6 of the Convention concerning his defence rights, particularly because evidence was given by an undisclosed undercover witness, and of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning a court order that he reimburse storage costs for his seized car.

The criminal proceedings arose from an investigation into suspected drug trafficking involving Greek and Macedonian nationals. On 10 November 2005 the public prosecutor authorised special investigative measures, including secret surveillance, audio-visual recording, and undercover agents. The order permitted DEA undercover agents from Athens to take part. According to the investigation, the applicant allegedly met undercover agents and co-accused persons in Skopje and Thessaloniki. On 10 November 2005, a meeting took place in a Skopje café bar where the sale of about 10 kg of cocaine was allegedly discussed. On 14 November 2005, a cocaine sample was allegedly handed to an undercover agent in Thessaloniki. On 18 November 2005, the applicant was arrested in Skopje, while other suspects were arrested elsewhere and cocaine was found in a car at the border.

On 19 November 2005, an investigating judge opened an investigation. The applicant remained silent when questioned. An undercover agent, whose identity was not disclosed, gave evidence in Greek with Macedonian interpretation. He implicated the applicant and described meetings and negotiations concerning the drug deal. In December 2005, the public prosecutor indicted the applicant and others for drug trafficking.

At trial, the applicant sought a direct confrontation with the undercover agent who had testified during the investigation. The prosecution said the agent’s identity was unknown to it, and the court attempted to secure the witness’s attendance through the Ministries of Justice of the respondent State and Greece. On 21 June 2006, a different undercover agent appeared in a specially secured room. The applicant and his lawyers were not present during the examination. The witness, a DEA agent, testified in English with Macedonian translation and described the operation, the applicant’s alleged role, and the alleged drug negotiations.

After the testimony, the court provided a transcript and gave the accused and their lawyers one hour to prepare written questions. Defence counsel requested at least 24 or 48 hours, arguing that the evidence was new and that they had not been given prior notice. The court refused, noting that the witness had only a 24-hour leave to remain. When the time expired, the applicant and his lawyers stated that they could not formulate questions. The applicant later submitted five written questions, but on 11 July 2006 the trial court refused to admit them, stating that the defence had already been given an opportunity to question the witness. The defence insisted that direct questioning of both undercover agents was necessary, especially because their statements allegedly contained inconsistencies.

These facts formed the basis of the Article 6 complaint: the use of an unidentified undercover witness, the inability to confront or effectively cross-examine him, the lack of adequate time to prepare questions, and the rejection of later questions. The applicant also complained that he had been ordered to pay storage costs for his seized car, which he alleged amounted to an unjustified interference with his property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

**Summary of the Case of Papadakis v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia**

The case originated from an application lodged by Mr. Lampros Papadakis, a Greek national, against the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia. The applicant alleged violations of his defence rights under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to a fair trial) and his property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The facts stemmed from a drug trafficking investigation initiated in November 2005. The Macedonian public prosecutor authorized special investigative measures, including secret surveillance and the use of undercover agents from the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), to investigate a suspected drug network involving Greek and Macedonian nationals. The applicant was arrested on 18 November 2005 in Skopje, following a series of meetings and a drug sample exchange in Thessaloniki, Greece. He was charged with drug trafficking.

The core of the applicant's complaint concerned the criminal proceedings against him. During the pre-trial investigation, an undercover DEA agent, whose identity was not disclosed, testified before an investigating judge. The applicant was present but remained silent. At trial, the prosecution sought to have this undercover agent, along with another, testify. However, the authorities faced difficulties in securing the attendance of the first agent, whose identity remained anonymous. The trial court eventually heard evidence from a different DEA undercover agent on 21 June 2006.

This hearing became central to the alleged violation. The applicant and his lawyers were not present during the direct examination of this anonymous witness. Instead, after the witness testified for several hours, the court provided a transcript to the defence and gave them only one hour to prepare written questions to be submitted through the presiding judge. The applicant and his co-accused argued this time was insufficient, especially given the lack of prior notice, and stated they could not formulate questions. The court refused requests for more time or for a direct confrontation. When the applicant later submitted written questions, the trial court rejected them, stating the opportunity to question the witness had already passed.

The applicant also raised a property complaint. He alleged that a court order requiring him to reimburse the storage costs for his seized car violated his property rights. This seizure was connected to the criminal proceedings.

The European Court of Human Rights communicated the case to the Government in June 2011, focusing on the fairness of the criminal proceedings regarding the anonymous witness evidence and the interference with the applicant's property rights. The applicant's primary argument was that the procedure adopted by the trial court, which prevented his lawyers from directly questioning the anonymous undercover agent and gave them inadequate time and facilities to prepare counter-questions, fundamentally undermined his defence rights and rendered the trial unfair.

In **Papadakis v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia** (Application no. 50254/07, judgment of 26 February 2013), the applicant, a Greek national, alleged violations of Article 6 of the Convention—specifically his defence rights regarding evidence from an undisclosed witness—and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning a court order that he reimburse storage costs for his seized car.

The case arose from a drug-trafficking investigation. On 10 November 2005, the public prosecutor authorised secret surveillance, audio-visual recording, and undercover agents, based on suspicion that Greek and Macedonian nationals were involved in cocaine trafficking. The order permitted DEA undercover agents from Athens to take part. Police reports stated that undercover agents met Mr B.V., the applicant, and others in Skopje on 10 November 2005 to discuss the sale of 10 kg of cocaine. Later, in Thessaloniki, a cocaine sample was handed over, and delivery was arranged for 18 November 2005 in Skopje, with payment to be shown in Thessaloniki. On 18 November, several co-accused were arrested at the Bulgarian border with cocaine; the applicant was arrested in Skopje, and Mr B.V. was arrested in Thessaloniki.

An investigation was opened. On 19 November 2005, an investigating judge heard the applicant, who remained silent, and an undercover agent whose identity was not disclosed. The agent testified in Greek with Macedonian translation, described the meetings, and identified the applicant from photographs. In December 2005, the public prosecutor indicted the applicant and others. The evidence included the surveillance order, an expert report, search reports, photographs, DVDs, and reports on the special investigative measures.

At trial, the applicant was represented. He viewed some video material and received a copy of the undercover agent’s pre-trial deposition. He requested a direct confrontation with that agent. The authorities attempted to secure the witness’s attendance, including through Greek authorities. On 21 June 2006, a different undercover agent attended and was examined in a secured room. Neither the applicant nor his lawyers were present. They received a transcript and were given only one hour to read it, consult, and prepare written questions to be put through the court. The applicant’s lawyer objected that the time was too short, that there had been no prior notice of this evidence, and that translation and preparation conditions were inadequate. After the time expired, the accused and lawyers stated they could not formulate questions. On 10 July 2006, the applicant submitted five written questions, but on 11 July 2006 the trial court refused to put them to the witness, stating that the defence had already had an opportunity to question him. The defence also sought direct questioning of both undercover agents, arguing inconsistencies and that their statements were largely based on presumptions.

These facts underpinned the Article 6 complaint: the use of evidence from a witness whose identity was undisclosed and the inability of the applicant and his counsel to examine or confront him effectively. Separately, the applicant complained that the order requiring him to reimburse storage costs for his seized car interfered with his property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The application was lodged on 22 October 2007. The Greek Government was informed but did not intervene. On 8 June 2011, the Court communicated the Article 6 and property complaints to the Macedonian Government and decided to examine admissibility and merits together.
001-122187:
**Rudnichenko v. Ukraine (Application no. 2775/07)** concerned complaints by Sergey Vladimirovich Rudnichenko about unlawful and excessively long pre-trial detention, and about unfair criminal proceedings due to judicial bias and inability to question a key witness.

The detention facts arose on 6 January 2006, when the applicant was caught by N. while breaking into N.’s car and attempting to dismantle equipment. N. handed him over to police. The arresting officer’s report referred to the car theft, N.’s complaint, and the applicant’s apprehension and arrest; it noted that the applicant was drunk and had been handcuffed. On 7 January 2006, however, the Leninskyy District Court ordered the applicant’s administrative detention for three days for being drunk in a public place at 6 p.m. on 6 January. On 9 January 2006, the same day that administrative detention expired, an investigator arrested him on suspicion of robbery based on the events of 6 January. On 12 January 2006 the court remanded him in custody for two months, citing that he had been caught in flagrante delicto, was drunk, had a criminal record, had committed the offence within a year of release, and was unemployed.

The applicant alleged that his detention from 6 to 12 January 2006 was unlawful. He argued that from 6 to 9 January he had in reality been detained as a criminal suspect, not merely for an administrative offence, and that from 9 to 12 January he had been held without a court order. A domestic court on 29 March 2006 acknowledged that the authorities knew the applicant had been arrested immediately after a criminal offence but delayed formal arrest as a criminal suspect until 9 January; nevertheless, it rejected his complaint. The Court of Appeal upheld that decision. The European Court of Human Rights later found that the administrative detention had been used as an artificial pretext to hold the applicant for criminal investigation purposes, violating Article 5 § 1. It also found that this manipulation undermined the lawfulness of the subsequent detention without a court order from 9 to 12 January.

The applicant further complained that his pre-trial detention was unreasonably long. He repeatedly sought release or a less restrictive measure. In March 2006 his lawyer argued that continued detention after 6 March 2006 was unlawful because the initial two-month period had expired. In September 2006 the applicant offered an undertaking not to abscond, provided an address, and stated he had worked in construction. These requests were rejected, mainly because of his criminal record, unemployment, and lack of permanent residence.

The fairness complaint concerned events of 22 October 2005, when two people attempted to break into K.’s car and K. caught one of them, B. On 7 February 2006, Judge R. convicted B. of robbery, relying on B.’s statements that the applicant—called “Sergey”—had initiated car thefts, taught him techniques, and participated in threatening K. with scissors, a knife, and a bottle. The applicant was not a party to B.’s trial. Later, after the applicant was indicted for robberies involving K. and N., his case was assigned to the same Judge R. On 12 October 2007 Judge R. sought recusal, stating she had already examined B.’s case and expressed an opinion about the incident involving the applicant and B. The court president rejected the recusal.

On 14 November 2007 Judge R. convicted the applicant of robbery in conspiracy with B., sentencing him to seven years, and relied on B.’s statements from the separate trial, which were read out. The applicant unsuccessfully requested B.’s attendance and questioning. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction, and the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal. The European Court found violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 6 § 3 (d) because the judge was not impartial and the applicant could not cross-examine the key witness against him.

**Case Summary: Rudnichenko v. Ukraine (Application no. 2775/07), ECtHR, 11 July 2013**

The case concerned Sergey Rudnichenko, a Ukrainian national, who complained about unlawful and lengthy pre-trial detention and about unfairness in his criminal trial.

On 6 January 2006, at about 6 p.m., the applicant was caught inside N.’s car trying to dismantle equipment. N. handed him over to the police. The arresting officer’s report referred to a car theft, N.’s complaint, and the applicant’s apprehension; it noted that the applicant was drunk and had to be handcuffed. Despite this, on 7 January 2006 the Leninskyy District Court ordered his administrative detention for three days for being drunk in a public place. On 9 January 2006, after that administrative detention expired, an investigator arrested him on suspicion of robbery. On 12 January 2006 the same court remanded him in custody for two months, citing that he had been caught in flagrante delicto, was drunk, was unemployed, and had committed the offence within a year of release from prison. From 13 January he had a lawyer.

The applicant alleged that his detention from 6 to 12 January 2006 was unlawful. He argued that his initial administrative detention was an artificial pretext used to hold him as a criminal suspect, and that his detention from 9 to 12 January lacked a court order. A domestic court later acknowledged that the authorities knew he had been arrested for a criminal offence but had documented it as an administrative offence; nevertheless, it rejected his complaint. The Court of Appeal upheld that rejection.

Separately, on 22 October 2005, two men attempted to break into K.’s car. K. caught one of them, B. On 7 February 2006, Judge R., sitting alone, convicted B. of robbery. She relied on B.’s account that the applicant was his accomplice, had initiated car thefts, had threatened K. with scissors, and had hit him with a bottle. The applicant was not a party to those proceedings. Later, K. and B. identified the applicant as the second thief.

In March 2006 the applicant was indicted for robberies concerning K. and N. After delays, his case was assigned in April 2007 to Judge R., the same judge who had tried B. On 12 October 2007 Judge R. asked to withdraw, stating that she had already expressed an opinion about the incident involving the applicant and B. The President of the Leninskyy Court refused her recusal. On 14 November 2007 Judge R. convicted the applicant of robbery in concert with B. regarding K. and sentenced him to seven years’ imprisonment. The conviction relied on B.’s statements from B.’s earlier trial, which were read out at the applicant’s trial. The applicant had requested B.’s attendance and questioning, but B. was not summoned. The applicant was acquitted regarding the N. incident because it was classified as attempted petty theft, an administrative rather than criminal offence.

The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction in July 2009, finding B.’s prior statements concordant with other evidence. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal in January 2010.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged violations of Article 5 §§1 and 3 (unlawful and unreasonably long detention) and Article 6 §§1 and 3(d) (lack of judicial impartiality and inability to examine key witness B.). The key facts relevant to those complaints were the authorities’ artificial use of administrative detention to hold a criminal suspect, the lack of a court order for part of the detention, the prolonged remand, Judge R.’s prior involvement in B.’s case, and the use of B.’s untested statements from a separate trial to convict the applicant. The ECtHR found violations of Article 5 §1 and Article 6 §§1 and 3(d), and also addressed the length of detention under Article 5 §3.

In *Rudnichenko v. Ukraine* (no. 2775/07), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by Sergey Rudnichenko that his pre-trial detention was unlawful and unreasonably long, and that his criminal trial was unfair because the trial judge was not impartial and he could not obtain the attendance of a key witness.

The detention complaint concerned 6–12 January 2006. On 6 January 2006, the applicant was caught breaking into N.’s car and handed over to police. The arresting officer’s report referred to the car theft and the applicant’s apprehension as a criminal suspect; it noted that he was drunk and had been handcuffed. Instead of recording a criminal arrest, on 7 January the Leninskyy District Court ordered three days’ administrative detention for being drunk in public. On 9 January, after that administrative detention expired, an investigator arrested him on suspicion of robbery relating to the 6 January incident. On 12 January the court remanded him in custody for two months, citing that he had been caught in flagrante delicto, had acted while drunk, was unemployed, and had committed the offence within a year of release from prison. The applicant alleged that the 6–9 January detention was an artificial administrative pretext and that the 9–12 January detention had no court authorisation. A domestic court later admitted that the authorities knew he had been arrested immediately after a criminal offence but delayed his formal criminal arrest until 9 January; nevertheless it rejected his complaint. The Strasbourg Court found that the administrative detention was closely linked to the criminal suspicion and was used in bad faith as a pretext, breaching Article 5 §1 and undermining the lawfulness of the subsequent detention. He remained in custody during the proceedings; release requests in April and September 2006 were rejected, and the case was delayed after the original judge’s term expired in December 2006.

The fair-trial allegations arose from an earlier incident on 22 October 2005 involving an attempted break-in of K.’s car. K. caught one thief, “B.”, while the other escaped. On 7 February 2006, Judge R. convicted B. of robbery, relying on B.’s statements implicating the applicant: B. said the applicant initiated car thefts, threatened K. with scissors, and hit him with a bottle. The applicant was not a party to B.’s trial. Later, the applicant was charged with robberies concerning K. and N. On 25 April 2007, his case was assigned to the same Judge R. On 12 October 2007, Judge R. asked to recuse herself, stating that she had already expressed an opinion about the incident involving both the applicant and B. The court president refused. On 14 November 2007, Judge R. convicted the applicant, relying on B.’s prior testimony read out at the hearing. The applicant’s request to summon and question B. was refused. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction, finding B.’s statements consistent with other evidence. The applicant alleged violations of Article 6 §1 and §3(d). These facts—the prior judicial involvement of Judge R., her refused recusal, and the reliance on untested witness statements—formed the core of his alleged fair-trial violations.

In **Majs Eksport-Import v. Serbia** (Application no. 35327/09), the European Court of Human Rights delivered judgment on 5 November 2013. The applicant was a Serbian company. It had concluded a contract on 7 March 2000 with Beogradski Pamučni Kombat (“the debtor”). The debtor failed to perform. On 11 December 2001, the Commercial Court in Belgrade opened insolvency proceedings against the debtor; this was published on the court notice board on 19 December 2001. On 12 March 2002, the applicant lodged a pecuniary claim in the insolvency proceedings. Because the claim was disputed, on 11 October 2002 the applicant began a separate civil action before the Commercial Court to have its claim determined.

The domestic courts eventually ruled in the applicant’s favour. On 2 September 2004, the Commercial Court determined part of the claim and ordered the debtor to pay EUR 6,686.15. That judgment became final. On 4 April 2005, the court determined the remainder, ordering payment of EUR 11,409 plus 80,500 Serbian dinars in costs. That judgment became final on 9 June 2005. On 30 September 2009, the applicant applied to enforce the costs award from the 4 April 2005 judgment. The Commercial Court allowed the application and issued an enforcement order the same day. However, the 2 September 2004 judgment and the remainder of the 4 April 2005 judgment were to be enforced through the insolvency proceedings. The debtor had been predominantly socially owned before the insolvency and remained registered as such throughout. Insolvency was terminated on 18 December 2009, final on 11 January 2011, and the debtor was erased from the Companies Register on 1 June 2011. The judgments remained unenforced.

The applicant complained that the respondent State had failed to enforce two final judgments in its favour and had not provided an effective remedy. It relied on Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time), Article 13 (right to an effective remedy), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of possessions).

The Government raised two main objections. First, it argued the application was out of time: the six-month period should run from 19 December 2001, when the insolvency was announced, or at latest from 3 March 2004, when the Convention entered into force for Serbia. The Court rejected this. The case concerned non-enforcement of final judgments; the judgments became final and enforceable in 2004 and 2005 and remained unenforced. At the time of application, no effective domestic remedies existed. The situation was therefore continuous. Second, the Government argued that Serbia could not be responsible for the debtor, a separate legal entity. The Court rejected this too, citing established case-law that the State is liable for debts of socially owned companies. The application was declared admissible.

On the merits, the Court found the case similar to *Adamović v. Serbia*. The Government had not offered facts or arguments to justify a different outcome. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It did not find it necessary to examine the essentially same complaint under Article 13. The key facts for the alleged violations were the final domestic judgments in the applicant’s favour, the debtor’s socially owned status, the insolvency and later erasure, and the State’s continued failure to enforce those judgments without an effective remedy.

**Case Summary: Majs Eksport-Import v. Serbia**

The case of *Majs Eksport-Import v. Serbia* (Application no. 35327/09) concerns a Serbian company’s complaint against the respondent State for its failure to enforce two final domestic judgments and the lack of an effective remedy in this regard. The applicant relied on Articles 6 and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The key facts are as follows: On 7 March 2000, the applicant company entered into a contract with Beogradski Pamučni Kombat (the debtor), which subsequently failed to fulfil its contractual obligations. On 11 December 2001, the Commercial Court in Belgrade initiated insolvency proceedings against the debtor, a fact published on its notice board on 19 December 2001. The debtor company was predominantly socially owned both before and throughout these proceedings.

The applicant lodged a pecuniary claim within the insolvency proceedings on 12 March 2002. As the claim was disputed by the insolvency administrator, the applicant was required to file a separate civil suit before the Commercial Court in Belgrade on 11 October 2002 to have its claim formally determined.

This civil suit resulted in two favorable judgments for the applicant. On 2 September 2004, the Commercial Court determined one part of the claim, ordering the debtor to pay the applicant EUR 6,686.15. This judgment became final. Subsequently, on 4 April 2005, the court determined the remainder of the claim, ordering the debtor to pay an additional EUR 11,409 and 80,500 Serbian dinars for the costs of the civil proceedings. This second judgment became final on 9 June 2005.

The central issue arose from the non-enforcement of these final and enforceable judgments. The judgment of 2 September 2004 and the remainder of the judgment of 4 April 2005 were to be enforced within the context of the ongoing insolvency proceedings. The applicant made efforts to enforce the costs awarded in the 2005 judgment by lodging a separate application for enforcement on 30 September 2009, which was allowed by the court.

However, the debtor’s financial situation deteriorated further. On 18 December 2009, the Commercial Court terminated the insolvency proceedings, a decision that became final on 11 January 2011. Consequently, on 1 June 2011, the debtor company was erased from the Companies’ Register. As a result, the applicant’s final judgments remained completely unenforced.

Before the European Court, the Serbian Government raised two main objections. First, they argued that the application was lodged outside the six-month time-limit, which they claimed started when the insolvency proceedings were announced. Second, they contended that the State could not be held responsible for the debts of the debtor, as it was a separate legal entity.

The Court rejected both arguments. It found that the non-enforcement of final judgments constituted a continuous situation, making the application timely. Furthermore, the Court reiterated its established case-law that the State is liable for the debts of socially-owned companies. Consequently, the Court declared the application admissible and, on the merits, found a violation of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, consistent with its prior jurisprudence. It did not find it necessary to examine the complaint under Article 13 separately.

**Majs Eksport-Import v. Serbia** (Application no. 35327/09, judgment of 5 November 2013) concerned a Serbian company’s complaint that Serbia failed to enforce final domestic judgments in its favour and provided no effective remedy. The applicant had concluded a contract with Beogradski Pamučni Kombat (“the debtor”) on 7 March 2000. The debtor failed to fulfil its contractual obligations.

On 11 December 2001, the Commercial Court in Belgrade instituted insolvency proceedings against the debtor; this was published on the court’s notice board on 19 December 2001. On 12 March 2002, the applicant lodged its pecuniary claim within the insolvency proceedings. Because the claim was disputed, on 11 October 2002 the applicant filed a separate civil suit before the Commercial Court in Belgrade seeking determination of its claim.

On 2 September 2004, the Commercial Court determined one part of the claim and ordered the debtor to pay the applicant EUR 6,686.15. That judgment later became final. On 4 April 2005, the court determined the remainder of the claim and ordered the debtor to pay EUR 11,409 plus 80,500 Serbian dinars in costs. This judgment became final on 9 June 2005. On 30 September 2009, the applicant applied to enforce the costs part of the 4 April 2005 judgment; the Commercial Court allowed the application and issued an enforcement order the same day. However, the substantive amounts under the 2004 judgment and the remainder of the 2005 judgment were to be enforced within the insolvency proceedings and remained unenforced.

The debtor was predominantly socially owned before and throughout the insolvency proceedings. On 18 December 2009, the Commercial Court terminated the insolvency proceedings; that decision became final on 11 January 2011. On 1 June 2011, the debtor was erased from the Companies’ Register.

The applicant lodged its application with the European Court of Human Rights on 11 June 2009. It complained about the respondent State’s failure to enforce two final judgments rendered in its favour and about the lack of an effective remedy. It relied on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, Article 13 of the Convention, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The Government objected that the application was out of time, arguing that the six-month period ran from the publication of the insolvency proceedings on 19 December 2001, or at latest from 3 March 2004 when the Convention entered into force for Serbia. The Court rejected this objection. It held that the case concerned the non-enforcement of final judgments which became final and enforceable in 2004 and 2005 and remained fully unenforced. At the time the application was introduced, there were no effective domestic remedies for such complaints. The alleged violation therefore constituted a continuing situation.

The Government also argued that the State could not be held responsible for the debtor, a separate legal entity. The Court rejected that argument, relying on its established case-law that Serbia is liable for debts of socially owned companies in comparable circumstances.

The Court declared the application admissible. On the merits, it found the case similar to *Adamović v. Serbia*, where it had found violations of Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Government had not presented facts or arguments capable of leading to a different conclusion. The Court therefore found a breach of Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to the failure to enforce the final judgments. It did not consider it necessary to examine the essentially same complaint under Article 13.

**Summary of Mijanović v. Montenegro (Application no. 19580/06)**

The case of *Mijanović v. Montenegro* concerns the failure of Montenegrin authorities to enforce a final domestic judgment, resulting in violations of the applicant's rights under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The applicant, Mr Borislav Mijanović, a Montenegrin national born in 1930, filed a compensation claim against "Radoje Dakić," a joint-stock company predominantly owned by State capital. On 24 September 2003, the Court of First Instance in Podgorica ruled in his favour, ordering the debtor to pay EUR 159,879.33 plus statutory interest, along with EUR 6,216.26 for legal costs. This judgment was upheld by the High Court on 6 July 2004 and became final when the Supreme Court dismissed the debtor's appeal on 27 December 2005.

Despite the final judgment, enforcement proved impossible. On 24 September 2004, the Court of First Instance issued an enforcement order via bank account transfer. However, on 31 October 2005, the Central Bank informed the court that the judgment could not be enforced due to insufficient funds in the debtor's account. The Minister of Justice confirmed this in February 2006 and invited the applicant to provide details of other accounts used by the debtor.

The applicant supplied information about several additional accounts on 9 March 2006. Subsequently, on 16 March 2006, the Court of First Instance ordered the Central Bank to block all the debtor's accounts and provide data on available funds, prioritising payment from the designated account. Despite these orders, on 24 March 2006, the Central Bank attached the debt to an account with no funds, rendering enforcement impossible. The applicant complained about the delay on 3 and 13 April 2006. Although the Court of First Instance reaffirmed its decision on 26 April 2006, and the Central Bank confirmed blocking other accounts on 28 April 2006, no funds were forthcoming. By 13 September 2006, the Central Bank stated that enforcement awaited an inflow of funds, noting that fifteen other claims had priority over the applicant's.

In March 2007, the applicant sought to change the means of enforcement. The court requested him to specify his request within eight days; when his representative failed to do so, the case was archived on 24 April 2007, though the enforcement order remained registered. On 4 May 2009, the applicant filed a new enforcement request proposing the sale of the debtor's immovable assets. An enforcement order was issued on 15 July 2009, but no attempt was made to enforce it. The proceedings remain ongoing.

The debtor's status is significant: between March 2004 and the end of 2005, the State owned 52.196% of its stocks; from 2006 onwards, the State and its bodies owned 50.579%. The applicant alleged that the debtor had substantial income, including land sales totaling EUR 9,018,000, a government grant of EUR 1,200,000, and profits of approximately EUR 2,000,000, yet avoided using its official bank account.

The applicant passed away on 21 April 2010. His daughter, Mrs Marina Mijanović Markuš, was declared his sole heir regarding the judgment debt and continued the proceedings.

The Court found that the debtor, despite being a separate legal entity, lacked sufficient independence from the State, which retained majority ownership and control. It held that the authorities failed to take necessary measures to enforce the judgment, citing the Central Bank's failure to attach other accounts, the courts' inactivity, and the State's inability to cite lack of funds as an excuse. Consequently, the Court found violations of both Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In **Mijanović v. Montenegro** (Application no. 19580/06), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint by Borislav Mijanović, a Montenegrin national, concerning the failure of Montenegrin authorities to enforce a final domestic judgment in his favour and the resulting violation of his property rights. The debtor was “Radoje Dakić,” a joint-stock company in which the State and State bodies held a majority stake—52.196% between March 2004 and the end of 2005, and 50.579% from 2006. The Government’s Privatisation Council managed the company’s privatisation and income, and the applicant alleged that the debtor had substantial assets and income but avoided enforcement through other bank accounts.

On 24 September 2003, the Court of First Instance in Podgorica ordered the debtor to pay the applicant EUR 159,879.33 plus statutory interest and EUR 6,216.26 in legal costs. The High Court upheld this judgment on 6 July 2004, and it became final when the Supreme Court dismissed the debtor’s appeal on points of law on 27 December 2005.

On 24 September 2004, the Court of First Instance issued an enforcement order by bank account transfer. In October 2005, the Central Bank informed the court that the judgment had not been enforced because the debtor’s account lacked funds. In February 2006, the Minister of Justice repeated that no funds were available and invited the applicant to identify other accounts. The applicant provided details in March 2006. The court then ordered the Central Bank to block all the debtor’s accounts and to pay the applicant primarily from the specified account, and, if necessary, from other accounts. However, the Central Bank attached the claim to an account without funds and later stated that enforcement awaited an inflow of funds. It also noted that fifteen other claims had priority. The applicant repeatedly complained about the delay.

In 2007, the court asked the applicant to specify a proposed change in the means of enforcement within eight days or the request would be considered withdrawn. His representative failed to do so, and the case was archived. Nevertheless, the original enforcement order remained registered and awaiting funds. In May 2009, the applicant filed a new enforcement request, proposing sale of the debtor’s immovable assets. An order to that effect was issued in July 2009, but there is no evidence that the domestic bodies made any attempt to enforce it, and the proceedings remained ongoing.

The applicant died in April 2010. His daughter, Marina Mijanović Markuš, was declared sole heir to the amount owed under the 2003 judgment and was permitted to continue the proceedings.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained that the non-enforcement of the final judgment violated Article 6 of the Convention (right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time, including execution of final judgments) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The Government argued that the case was complex, that the applicant contributed to delay, and that other claims and failed auctions explained the delay.

The Court found that enforcement proceedings must be expeditious, that the case was not especially complex, and that the delay could not be fully attributed to the applicant because the original order remained in force. The Central Bank never attached the debt to other known accounts, and the later enforcement order was never pursued. Because the debtor was State-controlled and the State could not rely on lack of funds or the debtor’s indigence, the Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1 and a separate violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In Mijanović v. Montenegro (App. no. 19580/06, judgment 17 September 2013), Borislav Mijanović, a Montenegrin national, obtained a final compensation judgment against “Radoje Dakić,” a joint-stock company in which the State and State bodies held a majority stake. On 24 September 2003 the Podgorica Court of First Instance ordered the debtor to pay him €159,879.33 plus statutory interest and €6,216.26 for legal costs. The High Court upheld the judgment on 6 July 2004, and the Supreme Court dismissed the debtor’s appeal on 27 December 2005.

On 24 September 2004 the applicant requested enforcement by bank-account transfer. The Central Bank later reported that the debtor’s account lacked funds. In February 2006 the Minister of Justice also said the judgment could not be enforced for lack of funds and asked the applicant to identify other accounts. After he supplied details, on 16 March 2006 the Court of First Instance ordered the Central Bank to block all the debtor’s accounts and to pay first from the designated account and then from other accounts if necessary. However, the Central Bank attached the debt to an account with no funds, while other accounts were merely blocked. Further complaints and court orders did not lead to payment. In September 2006 the Central Bank stated that enforcement awaited an inflow of funds and that fifteen other claims had priority. In March 2007 the applicant sought a change in the means of enforcement, but his representative failed to amend the request within eight days; in April 2007 the case was archived as withdrawn, although the original enforcement order remained registered and awaiting funds. In May 2009 the applicant filed a new request to enforce by selling the debtor’s immovable assets. An order was issued in July 2009, but the file contains no evidence that domestic authorities attempted to enforce it. The enforcement proceedings were still ongoing.

The debtor’s State connection was key. Between March 2004 and the end of 2005, the State and its bodies owned 52.196% of the debtor’s shares; from 2006 onward, they owned 50.579%. Privatisation was managed by a State Privatisation Council. The applicant alleged that the debtor had sold land for large sums, received a State grant, made substantial profits, and used unofficial bank accounts to avoid enforcement. He complained repeatedly to various State officials.

The applicant alleged that the non-enforcement of the final judgment violated Article 6 §1 of the Convention, because final judgments must be executed within a reasonable time, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, because it breached his property rights. After his death in April 2010, his daughter was declared his sole heir to the judgment debt and continued the proceedings.

The Government argued that enforcement was complex, that courts acted, that the applicant caused delay by failing to amend his 2007 request, and that auctions failed due to lack of investors. The Court found the debtor lacked sufficient independence from the State, so Montenegro was responsible. It held enforcement must be expeditious; the case was not complex; the delay was not attributable to the applicant because the original order remained in force; the Central Bank never attached other accounts; the later order was never enforced; and the State could not rely on lack of funds or the debtor’s indigence. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 §1 and a separate violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

**Case summary: *Eremia v. the Republic of Moldova* (ECtHR, 28 May 2013)**

The applicants were Lilia Eremia and her daughters, Doina and Mariana. They alleged that Moldova failed to fulfil its positive obligations under Articles 3, 14 and 17 of the European Convention on Human Rights to protect them from domestic violence by a private individual and to punish the aggressor. The first applicant’s husband, “A,” was a police officer. According to the applicants, A. frequently came home drunk and assaulted Lilia, often in the presence of their daughters. After the birth of their second daughter, the violence worsened.

On 2 July 2010, Lilia petitioned for divorce after A. assaulted her and verbally abused their teenage daughters. A. then became more violent, regularly assaulting and insulting Lilia and the daughters. On 30 August 2010, Lilia reported being punched in the head. A. was fined only 200 Moldovan lei by an administrative court on 18 September 2010 and received a formal warning from the Ministry of Internal Affairs on 30 September 2010. On 5 November 2010, A. assaulted Lilia again. On 11 and 12 November 2010, he assaulted her in front of the daughters and nearly suffocated her, causing her to lose her voice for a day and a half. A forensic examination on 23 November 2010 found no injuries.

On 9 December 2010, the Călăraşi District Court issued a protection order. It found that A. had beaten, insulted, threatened and psychologically abused Lilia, mistreated the family pet, and that his violence in front of the daughters harmed their psychological well-being. A. was ordered to stay away from the home for 90 days, with a 500-metre exclusion zone and a prohibition on contacting the applicants or committing violence. The order was served on 12 December 2010.

Despite the order, A. harassed Lilia on 16 December 2010 and entered the family home on 19 December 2010. The Government claimed the applicants permitted this; the applicants denied it and said A. assaulted Lilia, destroyed possessions and verbally abused the third applicant. On 10 January 2011, police allegedly pressured Lilia to withdraw her criminal complaint because a criminal record could harm A.’s job and their daughters’ prospects. On 11 January 2011, a meeting with the prosecutor took place with A. present. The next day, the prosecutor refused to initiate a criminal investigation.

On 13 January 2011, A. returned home, assaulted Lilia, simulated strangling her, and threatened to kill her and her aunt if she did not withdraw the complaint. A medical expert found haematomas on her neck and clavicle consistent with her account. In *Schädler-Eberle v. Liechtenstein* (Application no. 56422/09), the applicant, Karolina Schädler-Eberle, a Liechtenstein national born in 1925 living in Triesenberg, owned two plots of land. In February 2000, the Municipality of Triesenberg adopted its first land development plan by referendum. The plan placed the applicant’s plots in a zone where construction was not authorised. The applicant objected in March 2000, arguing that the plan breached her rights to equality and property protection and requesting that the plots be designated as building land.

In November 2000, the municipality dismissed her objection. It found that the plots were not fully developed because water installations were incomplete, that they lay outside the year-round inhabited area, and that environmental and landscape protection justified the non-building designation. It also distinguished other fully developed areas. The decision was sent to the applicant in January 2001. In April 2004, the Liechtenstein Government dismissed her complaint, upholding the plan. It stated that even if the plots had been building land under provisional 1983 rules, she had no claim to have them so designated in the municipality’s first land development plan, and it found no need to hear the parties or inspect the property.

The applicant then appealed to the Administrative Court in May 2004. She requested that documents be obtained, that a public oral hearing be held, that witnesses be examined to show the referendum had been manipulated, that her plots be designated building land or compensation be granted, and that the referendum be declared void. The court obtained observations and documents but, on 30 June 2004, dismissed her complaint without holding a public oral hearing. It found no breach of legitimate expectations. Even if municipal officials had raised hopes that the plots might become building land, the adopted plan did not so designate them; therefore, the offered evidence and a hearing were unnecessary. It also found no proof that the referendum had been manipulated.

The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint in August 2004. She complained under Article 6 of the Convention that the Administrative Court had refused to take evidence in an adversarial manner in a public oral hearing, contrary to its practice in comparable cases, and had not examined her named witnesses. She also complained about the referendum procedure and alleged a disproportionate interference with her property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Administrative Court replied that it did not usually hold public hearings in land development cases, that the facts were clear from the file and photographs, and that the applicant had had written opportunity to comment.

The Constitutional Court held a public hearing in May 2006, but its composition later changed without a new hearing despite the applicant’s request. In November 2008, it dismissed her request to declare the referendum void as inadmissible because she had not lodged a separate complaint with the Government. It rejected the remainder of her complaints. It did, however, find ex officio that the length of the proceedings before it had violated the reasonable-time guarantee and awarded costs. On the lack of a public hearing before the Administrative Court, the Constitutional Court held that Liechtenstein’s reservation to Article 6 § 1 concerning public hearings was valid and covered the National Administrative Justice Act 1922. Therefore, no public or oral hearing was required. Alternatively, it found no fair-trial violation because the facts and legal issues were clear and not complex.

The applicant applied to the European Court of Human Rights in October 2009. Her main complaint was that the Administrative Court’s refusal to take evidence in an adversarial public oral hearing violated Article 6. The Government argued that the reservation barred the complaint. The applicant argued that the reservation was invalid, obsolete, too general, and inapplicable to the new Administrative Court. The ECtHR examined admissibility and merits together, focusing on whether Liechtenstein’s reservation complied with Article 57 and whether Article 6 required a public oral hearing in her case.

**Schädler-Eberle v. Liechtenstein (Application no. 56422/09)**

The applicant, Ms Karolina Schädler-Eberle, a Liechtenstein national born in 1925, owned two plots of land in Triesenberg. On 28 March 2000, the applicant objected to the Municipality, arguing the plan breached her right to equality and protection of property, and requested that her plots be designated as building land. On 15 November 2000, the Municipality dismissed the objection, finding that the plots were not fully developed for lack of complete water installations, were situated outside the year-round inhabited area, and were excluded for environmental and landscape protection reasons. The decision was sent on 22 January 2001.

On 7 February 2001, the applicant complained to the Liechtenstein Government. On 27 and 28 April 2004, the Government dismissed the complaint, endorsing the Municipality's reasoning and finding that the applicant had no claim to have her undeveloped plots designated as building land in the first land development plan. The Government considered it unnecessary to hear the parties in person or inspect the property.

The Municipality submitted observations and further documents. On 30 June 2004, without holding a public oral hearing, the Administrative Court dismissed the complaint. It found nothing indicated a breach of legitimate expectations, and even if municipal officials had raised hopes about future building designation, the plan clearly did not designate the plots as building land. It therefore deemed it unnecessary to take the offered evidence or hold a public hearing, and found no proof the referendum had been manipulated.

On 26 August 2004, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint. She complained under Article 6 of the Convention that, despite her express request and the fact that no prior authority had held an oral hearing, the Administrative Court refused to take evidence in an adversarial manner in a public oral hearing, contrary to its practice in comparable cases, and failed to examine her witnesses. She also complained about the procedure of adopting the land development plan and, under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, that the unlawful plan disproportionately interfered with her property rights. She requested an oral hearing.

On 4 November 2008, it dismissed the request to declare the referendum void as inadmissible (no separate complaint had been lodged with the Government), and rejected the remaining complaints as ill-founded. It found ex officio a violation of the right to a hearing within a reasonable time due to excessive length, ordering Liechtenstein to bear the applicant's costs.

The National Administrative Justice Act of 21 April 1922 applied to the Administrative Court, and the reservation covered that Act. Therefore, the public and oral hearing requirement did not apply. The right to a fair trial, however, was not covered by the reservation. The Constitutional Court found the Administrative Court could determine all factual and legal questions from written observations and documents, and the legal question regarding alleged referendum manipulation was not complex. Applying Strasbourg case-law, it concluded the refusal to hold a public oral hearing did not violate the applicant's right to a fair trial.

The applicant lodged her application with the European Court of Human Rights on 14 October 2009.

**Tuncer Güneş v. Turkey** (Application no. 26268/08) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section), delivered on 3 September 2013. The applicant was Gülizar Tuncer Güneş, a Turkish national and lawyer born in 1966, living in Istanbul.

The key facts concerned her surname after marriage. On 30 March 2005, the applicant married and, under Article 187 of the Turkish Civil Code, took her husband’s surname. Article 187 provided that married women “shall bear their husband’s name,” but could keep their maiden name in front of the husband’s surname by written declaration. The applicant did so, using her maiden name before her husband’s surname. However, she wanted to use only her maiden name, “Tuncer.”

On 9 May 2007, she brought proceedings before the Şişli Court of First Instance seeking permission to use only her maiden name. On 18 July 2007, that court dismissed her request, holding that under Article 187 married women were required to bear their husband’s name throughout the marriage and were not entitled to use their maiden name alone. The applicant appealed, but on 22 November 2007 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment.

The relevant domestic law included Article 187 of the Civil Code, as well as Article 10 of the Turkish Constitution, which guarantees equality before the law and equal rights between women and men, and Article 90, which gives precedence to international human rights agreements in cases of conflict with domestic law. The Constitutional Court had also considered an objection to Article 187 and dismissed it in a decision of 10 March 2011.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged that the refusal by domestic courts to allow her to bear only her maiden name unjustifiably interfered with her right to respect for private life under Article 8 of the Convention. She further alleged that Turkish law allowed married men, but not married women, to bear only their own surname after marriage. According to the applicant, this difference in treatment constituted discrimination on grounds of sex, contrary to Article 14 of the Convention. She also complained under Article 13 that the domestic courts had disregarded the Court’s earlier judgment in *Ünal Tekeli v. Turkey* and had failed to amend domestic law, thereby denying her an effective remedy.

The Court considered it appropriate to examine the case under Article 14 taken together with Article 8. It declared the complaints admissible, finding they were not manifestly ill-founded. On the merits, the Government argued that the domestic courts were bound by Article 187, that the applicant had not suffered discrimination in daily or business life, and that draft legislation was being consulted upon to align Article 187 with the Convention. The Court, however, noted that *Ünal Tekeli v. Turkey* had raised similar issues and had found that the difference in treatment on grounds of sex between persons in an analogous situation breached Article 14 taken in conjunction with Article 8. The Government failed to put forward any fact or argument capable of persuading the Court to reach a different conclusion.

Accordingly, the key violation alleged was that the mandatory husband’s-surname rule for married women, as applied to the applicant, discriminated against her on the basis of sex and interfered with her private life. The Court concluded that there had been a violation of Article 14 of the Convention taken together with Article 8, consistent with its earlier case-law.

In *Röman v. Finland* (Application no. 13072/05, ECtHR, 29 January 2013), the applicant, Ms Mirja Anneli Röman, born in 1954 out of wedlock, complained that Finnish law prevented her from legally establishing her biological father’s paternity. At birth she bore her mother’s maiden name. The same year, her mother and biological father signed a child-support agreement verified by social services. In 1956 her mother married another man, and in 1961 the applicant’s surname was changed to her mother’s husband’s; the family agreed never to mention her biological father.

In 1976 Finland’s Paternity Act entered into force. Transitional provisions allowed paternity proceedings for children born before the Act only within five years—by 1 October 1981—and barred claims after the putative father’s death. Children born after the Act were not subject to this restriction. The applicant became curious about her origins only later. In 2001 she discovered that the church register listed her mother’s husband as her stepfather, while the state population register listed him as her father. She also located the child-support agreement, which helped identify her biological father. The population register was corrected in September 2002.

In February 2003, at age 48, the applicant began paternity proceedings against her biological father. The District Court dismissed the claim as time-barred, finding that during the five-year period she had been an adult and could have checked the church register or asked her mother. The Court of Appeal upheld that decision, and in October 2004 the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal. The Parliamentary Ombudsman later found no basis to intervene. In 2007 a private DNA test confirmed with 99.99% certainty that the man was her biological father; he died in 2008.

The applicant alleged violations of Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention, arguing that the absolute five-year time-limit deprived her of the ability to have her biological father’s paternity legally established and discriminated against children born before the 1976 Act. She maintained that she had no reason to suspect her origins during the limitation period and would have brought proceedings had she known. The Government accepted that the impossibility of establishing paternity interfered with her private life but argued that the time-limit pursued legitimate aims: legal certainty, finality in family relations, and protection of putative fathers from stale claims.

The European Court of Human Rights held that Article 8 was applicable because the right to know one’s ascendants and personal identity falls within private life. Although the time-limit was lawful and pursued a legitimate aim, the Court found that the fair balance required by Article 8 had not been struck. The limitation was applied rigidly, with no exceptions and no opportunity for domestic courts to weigh the applicant’s interest in knowing her biological father against the father’s and society’s interests. Because the applicant had no realistic opportunity to bring proceedings during the five-year period, the strict application impaired the essence of her Article 8 right. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 8.

**Case: Röman v. Finland (Application no. 13072/05), European Court of Human Rights, 29 January 2013**

The applicant, Mirja Anneli Röman, was a Finnish national born in 1954 out of wedlock. In the same year, her mother and biological father concluded a verified child support agreement. In 1956, her mother married another man, and in 1961 the applicant’s surname was changed to that of her mother’s husband. The family agreed that the biological father was never to be mentioned. The applicant grew up believing, or at least being officially registered as, the daughter of her mother’s husband.

On 1 October 1976, Finland’s Paternity Act entered into force. Its transitional provisions allowed paternity proceedings for children born before the Act, but only if initiated within five years—by 1 October 1981. No claim could be examined after the putative father’s death. Children born after the Act’s entry into force were not subject to this restriction.

In 2001, the applicant began investigating her biological background. She discovered that the church register, until 1993 the official population register, listed her mother’s husband as her stepfather, while the later State population register listed him as her father. She also found the child support agreement, which enabled her to identify her biological father. In September 2002, the population register was corrected. In February 2003, at age 48, she initiated paternity proceedings against her biological father. She claimed she had only learned in December 2001 that her mother’s husband was not her biological father.

The Vantaa District Court dismissed her claim as time-barred. It found that during the five-year period she had been an adult and could have questioned her mother or checked the church register, which had contained correct information. The Helsinki Court of Appeal upheld that decision, and in October 2004 the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal. The Parliamentary Ombudsman later declined to intervene, finding the courts had acted within their margin of appreciation. In 2007, a private DNA test confirmed with 99.99% certainty that the identified man was her biological father. He died in 2008.

The applicant complained under Articles 8 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights that she had been unable to have her biological father’s paternity legally established because of the five-year time-limit applicable to children born before the 1976 Paternity Act, and that she suffered discrimination. The Government accepted that the impossibility of establishing paternity after the time-limit interfered with her private life, but argued it pursued legitimate aims: legal certainty, finality in family relations, and protection of putative fathers from stale claims.

The Court found Article 8 applicable, since the right to know one’s ascendants and have paternity determined falls within “private life.” It accepted that the time-limit pursued a legitimate aim. However, it held that a fair balance was not struck. The applicant had learned the biological truth only in December 2001, after the limitation period expired, and during the five-year period she had no reason to suspect her origins; her mother had never told her, and the family had agreed not to mention the biological father. The time-limit was rigid and absolute, with no exceptions or possibility of restoration. National courts merely declared the claim time-barred, without balancing the applicant’s right to identity against the father’s or family’s interests or general legal certainty. The Court noted a trend against inflexible limitation periods and that Finland’s Supreme Court later changed its practice in KKO 2012:11. It therefore found a violation of Article 8: the applicant was deprived of a practical and effective opportunity to obtain judicial determination of her paternity.

In 2001 the applicant began investigating her origins. She also found the child-support agreement and was able to identify her biological father. The population register was corrected in September 2002. In February 2003, aged 48, she initiated paternity proceedings against her biological father, claiming she had learned only in December 2001 that her stepfather was not her biological father.

The domestic courts dismissed her claim as time-barred. The District Court found that during the five-year period she had been an adult and could have initiated proceedings or inquired into her origins. The Court of Appeal upheld that decision, and the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal in October 2004. The Parliamentary Ombudsman later declined to intervene. In 2007 a private DNA test confirmed with 99.99% certainty that the alleged man was her biological father; he died in July 2008.

Before the Strasbourg Court, the Government accepted that the impossibility of establishing paternity interfered with the applicant’s private life, but argued that the five-year limit pursued legitimate aims: legal certainty, finality in family relations, and protection of putative fathers from stale claims. The applicant contended that she had no reason to suspect her origins during the limitation period and that the absolute time-bar made her right illusory.

The Court held Article 8 applicable, since the right to know one’s ascendants and biological identity falls within “private life.” Although the time-limit was lawful and pursued a legitimate aim, the Court found its application disproportionate. The national courts applied it rigidly, without balancing the applicant’s right to know her origins against the interests of the putative father or legal certainty, and no alternative remedy existed. Because the applicant had not had a realistic opportunity to bring proceedings within the five-year period, the absolute limitation impaired the essence of her Article 8 rights. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 8.

In *Grupa Zastava Vozila, A.D. v. Slovenia* (App. no. 67793/10, 25 April 2013), the European Court of Human Rights examined a Serbian company’s complaints that Slovenian civil proceedings lasted unreasonably long and that domestic remedies for delay were ineffective, contrary to Article 6 §1 and Article 13 of the Convention.

On 1 December 1997, PS ZA AVTO sued before the Ljubljana District Court seeking annulment of the contract and notarial protocol. The court inquired about service in October 1998, and in November 1998 the Ministry said it was still awaiting a reply from Serbian authorities. In 2000, third-party intervention requests and another service inquiry occurred. The applicant’s representative filed an authority form and joinder request in June 2000, and the applicant requested a hearing in May 2001. A hearing set for October 2001 was postponed. Third parties were allowed to participate in June 2002.

The applicant lodged a counterclaim in September 2002, causing postponement. A settlement hearing in February 2003 failed. The first hearing was held on 14 April 2003. The applicant obtained an extension to submit documents. A financial expert was appointed in November 2003 and reported in May 2004. After another hearing in October 2004, the Ljubljana District Court on 13 December 2004 ruled in the applicant’s favour, maintaining the contract and notarial protocol. The plaintiff appealed. The Constitutional Court rejected the applicant’s constitutional appeal as unfounded on 13 May 2010.

The Government offered a settlement under section 25 of the 2006 Act on Protection of the Right to a Trial without Undue Delay, but the applicant rejected it.

Although the case had some complexity and service abroad caused difficulties, the first-instance court took over five years to hold the first hearing and another two years to issue judgment, with almost two years of total inactivity. That delay was unreasonable. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 §1.

On Article 13, the Court held that the 2006 Act did not provide the applicant an effective remedy because the proceedings continued before the Supreme Court and Constitutional Court after the Act became operational. Pre-2006 remedies were also ineffective under its case-law, notably *Lukenda v. Slovenia*. The Court thus found a violation of Article 13.

Grupa Zastava Vozila, A.D. v. The applicant requested joinder in June 2000 and a hearing in May 2001. A hearing scheduled for 11 October 2001 was postponed. The applicant filed a counterclaim in September 2002, causing another postponement. A settlement hearing in February 2003 failed. The first hearing was held on 14 April 2003.
