The plaintiff appealed. On 7 November 2006 the Ljubljana Higher Court reversed the first-instance judgment and ruled against the applicant. The Supreme Court upheld that decision on 12 May 2008. The applicant’s constitutional appeal was rejected as unfounded on 13 May 2010.

The proceedings therefore began on 1 December 1997 and ended on 13 May 2010, lasting twelve years and five months at four levels of jurisdiction. The Government offered a settlement under section 25 of the 2006 Act on Protection of the Right to a Trial without Undue Delay, but the applicant refused it. The Court found the complaints admissible. It held that section 25 did not provide a remedy because the proceedings continued before the Supreme Court and Constitutional Court after the 2006 Act became operational.

On the merits, the Court accepted that the case had some complexity and that service in Serbia was difficult. However, it found that the first-instance court took more than five years to hold the first hearing and an additional two years to deliver judgment, with almost two years of inactivity. This was unreasonable. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 §1. It also found no effective remedy for the excessive length, because the 2006 Act remedies were ineffective in the applicant’s situation and pre-2006 remedies had already been found ineffective in Lukenda v. Slovenia. Accordingly, it found a violation of Article 13 as well.

**Grupa Zastava Vozila, A.D. v. Slovenia** (Application no. 67793/10), judgment of 25 April 2013, concerned a Serbian company’s complaint that civil proceedings in Slovenia lasted unreasonably long and that domestic remedies for delay were ineffective.

In 1996 the applicant company concluded a notarised contract with PS ZA AVTO p.o. concerning joint investments. On 1 December 1997, PS ZA AVTO brought proceedings before the Ljubljana District Court seeking annulment of the contract and notarial protocol. On 14 July 1998, the court ordered the claim to be served on the applicant in Serbia through the Ministry of Justice and diplomatic channels. Service became a source of delay: in October 1998 the court asked the Ministry about service, and in November 1998 the Ministry said it was still awaiting a reply from the Serbian authorities. In May 2000, a third party sought to intervene; in June 2000 the court made another inquiry about service, and the applicant’s representative submitted an authority form and a joinder request. In May 2001 the applicant requested a hearing. The first hearing, scheduled for 11 October 2001, was postponed. In October 2001 the State Attorney’s Office sought third-party intervention; the court allowed both third parties to participate in June 2002. The applicant lodged a counterclaim in September 2002, causing another postponement. A settlement hearing in February 2003 failed, and the first hearing was held in April 2003. A financial expert was appointed in November 2003, granted an extension in February 2004, and submitted a report in May 2004. A further hearing took place in October 2004.

In December 2004 the first-instance court ruled in favour of the applicant company, preserving the contract and notarial protocol. The plaintiff appealed. In November 2006 the Ljubljana Higher Court reversed the judgment and ruled against the applicant. The applicant appealed on points of law, but in May 2008 the Supreme Court upheld the appeal court’s decision. A constitutional appeal was rejected as unfounded on 13 May 2010.

The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the length of the proceedings violated the “reasonable time” requirement, and under Article 13 that there was no effective domestic remedy for excessive delay. The Government offered a settlement under section 25 of the 2006 Act on the Protection of the Right to a Trial without Undue Delay, but the applicant refused it. The European Court of Human Rights found the application admissible. It noted that section 25 did not provide a remedy because the proceedings continued before the Supreme Court and Constitutional Court after the 2006 Act entered into force.

On the merits, the Court considered the period from 1 December 1997 to 13 May 2010—twelve years and five months across four levels of jurisdiction. Applying the criteria of complexity, conduct of the parties and authorities, and what was at stake, the Court observed that the first-instance court took more than five years to hold the first hearing and another two years to deliver judgment, with almost two years of total inactivity. Although the case had some complexity and there were difficulties in serving the claim in Serbia, those factors did not justify the delay. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1. It further found that the available remedies, including those under the 2006 Act and prior remedies, were ineffective, violating Article 13.
001-121573:
**Case Name:** N.M.Y. and Others v. Sweden  
**Application no.:** 72686/10  
**Court:** European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section  
**Judgment:** 27 June 2013; Final: 27 September 2013

The applicants were three Iraqi Christian siblings—two women and one man, born in 1963, 1966 and 1971—from Baghdad. They arrived in Sweden on 17 September 2008 and applied for asylum two days later. They alleged that deportation to Iraq would violate Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention, protecting the right to life and prohibiting torture, inhuman or degrading treatment.

In support, they claimed regular harassment and insults as Christians. The two female applicants had allegedly been forced to wear a veil to avoid trouble. In 2006, armed men stopped a car carrying the two women and their mother; after seeing a hanging cross, the men forced the passengers out and seized the car. On 17 August 2008, armed men came to the applicants’ house and told another brother that the applicants had to convert to Islam before 1 September 2008, the start of Ramadan, or be killed. They wrote the same message on the house wall. The applicants left Iraq on 20 August 2008.

The Swedish Migration Board rejected their asylum applications on 30 December 2008. It accepted that there was a threat based on their Christian beliefs and the difficult situation in Baghdad, but found the threat limited to Baghdad. Because the applicants had no prominent professional or religious position, they were not of particular interest outside Baghdad and could relocate to central or northern Iraq. The Migration Court upheld that decision on 16 September 2009, finding the incidents were criminal acts linked to the general security situation in Baghdad. It noted that two years had passed and Baghdad’s security had improved, so there was no concrete, individual threat. The Migration Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal on 9 November 2009.

Before the European Court, the applicants argued that they would face a real risk of attacks, threats, kidnappings and massacres because of their Christian faith. They said Iraqi authorities could not protect them and that Christians were vulnerable throughout Iraq. The Government accepted that Christians were exposed and that southern and central Iraq remained dangerous, but argued that not all Christians required protection and that the 2008 threats were no longer valid. It relied on an internal flight alternative in the Kurdistan Region—Dahuk, Erbil and Sulaymaniyah—as safer, stable and accessible, with no sponsor requirement and access to work and services.

The Court found that general violence in Iraq did not alone bar all returns, and that Christians were vulnerable in southern and central Iraq. However, it did not decide whether all Christians could return because relocation to the Kurdistan Region was available. The KRI was relatively safe, Christian rights were generally respected, many Christians had found refuge there, entry was possible and Christians often received preferential treatment. Documents could be obtained, no sponsor was required, and living conditions were not unreasonable. The applicants’ past incidents occurred in Baghdad; their claims about deteriorating conditions in the KRI were unsubstantiated; they could support each other as siblings; they were aged 42–50 and had no health problems. Therefore, although they belonged to a vulnerable minority, they could reasonably relocate to the Kurdistan Region and would not face a real risk under Articles 2 or 3. Deportation would not violate the Convention. The Rule 39 interim measure remained in force until the judgment became final.

Sweden* (Application no. 72686/10, 27 June 2013), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Sweden’s planned deportation of three Iraqi Christian siblings to Iraq would breach Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention. The applicants—two women and one man born in 1963, 1966, and 1971—were Iraqi nationals from Baghdad. They arrived in Sweden on 17 September 2008 and applied for asylum two days later.

Their claims were based on their Christian faith and experiences in Baghdad. They alleged regular harassment and insults, and the female applicants said they had been forced to wear a veil to avoid trouble. In 2006, armed men stopped a car carrying the two women and their mother, saw a hanging cross, forced them out, and took the car. On 17 August 2008, armed men came to the family home and told another brother that the applicants had to convert to Islam before 1 September 2008, the start of Ramadan, or be killed. The men also wrote the same warning on the house wall. The applicants left Iraq on 20 August 2008.

Sweden’s Migration Board rejected the asylum applications on 30 December 2008. It accepted that there was a threat based on their Christian beliefs and the difficult situation in Baghdad, but considered the threat limited to Baghdad. Since the applicants had no prominent professional or religious profile, the Board found no particular risk outside Baghdad and concluded they could relocate to central or northern Iraq. It also noted that, because the siblings had shared a household, the female applicants would not lack a male relative on return. The applicants appealed, arguing that Iraqi authorities could not protect them and that Christians faced persecution throughout Iraq, so there was no internal flight alternative. The Board suggested relocation to the Kurdistan Region, noting direct flights from Sweden to Erbil. On 16 September 2009, the Migration Court upheld the rejection, finding the incidents were criminal acts tied to Baghdad’s general security situation, that two years had passed, and that security had improved; there was no concrete, individual threat. The Migration Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal on 9 November 2009.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants alleged that deportation to Iraq would violate Articles 2 and 3. The Court declared the complaint admissible and applied Rule 39 to prevent deportation during proceedings. On the merits, it accepted that Christians were a vulnerable minority in southern and central Iraq and that attacks on them had escalated, with authorities often unable to protect them. However, it did not decide whether return to those areas would breach Articles 2 or 3 because it found a viable internal relocation alternative in the Kurdistan Region (Dahuk, Erbil, and Sulaymaniyah).

The Court found the Kurdistan Region relatively safe, with Christians’ rights generally respected and many Christians having sought refuge there. Christians could enter without a sponsor and obtain identity documents. Although relocation involved hardship, jobs, healthcare, and support existed. The applicants’ past incidents occurred in Baghdad; their claims of risk in Kurdistan were unsubstantiated. They could support one another and were aged 42–50 with no health problems affecting work. The Court therefore held that deportation to Iraq would not violate Articles 2 or 3.

They alleged regular harassment as Christians. The female applicants had been forced to wear veils. On 17 August 2008, armed men came to their house and told a brother that the applicants must convert to Islam by 1 September 2008, the start of Ramadan, or be killed; they wrote the same message on the wall. The applicants left Iraq on 20 August 2008.

The Migration Board rejected asylum on 30 December 2008. It accepted a religion-based threat and the difficult situation in Baghdad but found the threat limited to Baghdad. Because the applicants held no prominent professional or religious positions, they were not of particular interest elsewhere. They could relocate to central or northern Iraq; the women would not lack a male relative because the siblings had shared a household. On appeal, the applicants argued Iraqi authorities could not protect them, the risk was nationwide, and there was no internal flight alternative. The Board proposed relocation to the Kurdistan Region, noting direct flights to Erbil. On 16 September 2009, the Migration Court upheld the rejection, finding the incidents were criminal acts linked to general Baghdad insecurity, two years had passed, security had improved, and there was no concrete individual threat. The Migration Court of Appeal refused leave on 9 November 2009.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants said return to Baghdad would risk attacks, threats, kidnappings, and massacres due to their Christian beliefs. They claimed police could not protect them. They opposed relocation, arguing Christians were vulnerable throughout Iraq and the Kurdistan Region was not reasonable under UNHCR Guidelines because of poor living conditions, unemployment, and hostility. The Government accepted that the security situation in southern and central Iraq remained serious and Christians were exposed, but said no general protection need applied to all Christians; assessments had to be individual. The threats dated from August 2008 and were no longer shown valid. An internal flight alternative existed in the three northern Kurdistan governorates, where they could enter, settle, work, and access services. Domestic authorities had made thorough assessments with legal counsel and interpreters.

The Court found general violence in Iraq did not alone preclude return. Christians were vulnerable in southern and central Iraq and attacks had escalated, but the Court did not decide whether all Christians faced Article 3 risk there because relocation to the Kurdistan Region was viable. Relocation involved hardship but not unreasonable conditions. Individually, the incidents occurred in Baghdad; alleged KRI risk was unsubstantiated; the siblings could support each other; they were aged 42–50 with no health issues. Therefore deportation would not violate Articles 2 or 3. The Rule 39 interim measure remained in force until final.
001-127813:
**Case Summary: Belousov v. Ukraine (Application no. 4494/07)**

The case of *Belousov v. Ukraine* concerns allegations of unlawful detention, torture, and an ineffective investigation, in violation of Articles 3 and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant, Mr. Vyacheslav Belousov, was a Ukrainian national living in a Kharkiv hostel. On 18 July 2005, at approximately 11 a.m., several police officers in civilian clothes came to his hostel and invited him to accompany them to the Kominternivskyy District police station. He was questioned regarding complaints from two mothers who implicated him in the sexual abuse of their minor daughters.

At around 5 p.m. that same day, the applicant confessed to the offence and signed permission for police to inspect his home. At approximately 6 p.m., police officers took him back to the hostel, searched his room, seized several items, and returned him to the police station. No formal arrest report was drawn up at that time. The applicant first met with a lawyer, hired by his relatives, at about 7 p.m. on 19 July 2005. A formal arrest report was only drawn up at 8:40 p.m. that evening, stating he was arrested as a crime suspect. He was brought before a judge on 22 July 2005, remanded in custody for ten days, and released on 29 July 2005 subject to an undertaking not to abscond. One of the complainants later withdrew her complaint against him, stating it had been lodged under police pressure.

The core of the applicant’s complaints centres on his treatment during this period, particularly his initial unrecorded detention. During the evening of 18 July 2005, neighbours informed a human rights group that when they had seen the applicant leaving with police at 11 a.m., he was sober, neatly dressed, and in good health. Seven hours later, when police brought him back for the search, they observed he was limping, stooping, had bruises and swellings on his face, and his clothes were dirty. Some neighbours noted he arrived handcuffed.

On 19 July 2005, a forensic examination certified that the applicant was suffering from minor bodily injuries, including soft tissue swelling, numerous bruises and scratches on his body, particularly on his face and groin area. The expert concluded these injuries had been inflicted by blunt objects within the past one to three days.

On 20 July 2005, the applicant lodged a formal complaint, alleging that upon arrival at the police station, three officers had urged him to confess under threat of torture. He stated they had placed him on a desk, twisted his arms, punched him, and squeezed his genitals. Three additional officers then joined, taking turns to beat and strangle him. Unable to withstand the torture, he confessed by 5 p.m.

On 1 August 2005, the District Prosecutor’s Office instituted criminal proceedings regarding his complaints. However, the investigation was plagued by delays, suspensions, and discontinuations. The proceedings were stayed on multiple occasions because the perpetrators could not be identified, and repeatedly renewed. The police officers implicated were questioned only as witnesses, not as suspects. The investigation was eventually discontinued in December 2009 for lack of evidence, a decision later quashed and remitted.

The applicant complained to the European Court that the police had unlawfully detained him, tortured him, searched his home, failed to bring him promptly before a judge, and conducted an ineffective investigation into his torture complaint. The Government argued his torture complaint was premature as a domestic investigation was pending. The Court noted the investigation’s numerous delays and failures, ultimately concluding that no serious effort had been made to investigate his ill-treatment allegations, violating the procedural limb of Article 3.

In *Belousov v. Ukraine* (Application no. 4494/07, ECtHR, 7 November 2013), the applicant, Mr Vyacheslav Belousov, alleged that Ukrainian police unlawfully detained him, tortured him to obtain a confession, searched his home unlawfully, failed to bring him promptly before a judge, and then conducted an ineffective investigation into his torture complaint.

On 18 July 2005, at about 11 a.m., several plainclothes police officers came to the hostel where the applicant lived and invited him to accompany them to the police station. He went with them. At the station, he was told that two mothers had accused him of sexually abusing their minor daughters and was questioned. By about 5 p.m., he had confessed and signed permission for police to inspect his home. At about 6 p.m., police took him back to the hostel, searched his room, seized a bed cover, a rug and personal belongings, and returned him to the station. No arrest record was drawn up at that stage.

The applicant remained in police custody. He first met a lawyer hired by relatives at about 7 p.m. on 19 July 2005. Only at about 8.40 p.m. that day did an investigator draw up an arrest report under Article 115 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On 22 July 2005 he was brought before a judge, who remanded him in custody for ten days; he was released on 29 July 2005 subject to an undertaking not to abscond. One of the complaining mothers later withdrew her complaint, saying it had been made under police pressure.

The key alleged violation facts concerned torture. The applicant claimed that, after arriving at the station around noon on 18 July, officers S.B., A.O. and V.M. urged him to confess under threat of torture. He said they cleared a desk, covered it with a blanket, placed him on it with his hands handcuffed behind his back, twisted his arms, punched him and squeezed his genitals. Three more officers allegedly joined and took turns beating and strangling him. He confessed by 5 p.m. Neighbours later reported that when police brought him back for the search, he was limping, stooping, had facial bruises and swelling, and was handcuffed; earlier that day he had been sober, neatly dressed and in good health.

On 19 July 2005 a forensic examination found minor bodily injuries, including soft tissue swelling, bruises and scratches on his face and groin, inflicted by blunt objects within the previous one to three days. The applicant said police caused them; police said they were self-inflicted. He lodged a formal complaint on 20 July 2005, and criminal proceedings were opened on 1 August 2005. However, the investigation was marked by delays, suspensions, renewals and repeated discontinuations. Officers were questioned as witnesses rather than suspects; the applicant received injured-party status only in November 2005; reconstructions and confrontations occurred months later. In December 2009 the prosecutor accepted that the applicant had been de facto arrested on 18 July but documented only on 19 July, yet treated this as at most a disciplinary matter; it found insufficient evidence of torture and considered the home visit a lawful inspection with consent. Courts repeatedly quashed discontinuances and remitted the case, but the investigation remained unresolved.

The European Court of Human Rights joined the Government’s non-exhaustion objection to the merits. It found the investigation ineffective, citing numerous delays, inactivity, suspensions, discontinuations, repeated remittals and the passage of more than eight years. It referred to systemic problems identified in *Kaverzin v. Ukraine*, which allowed officials who ill-treated suspects to go unpunished, and concluded that no serious effort had been made to investigate the applicant’s ill-treatment allegations, violating the procedural limb of Article 3.

**Belousov v. Ukraine (no. 4494/07)** concerned Mr Vyacheslav Belousov, a Ukrainian national who alleged that police unlawfully detained him, tortured him, searched his home unlawfully, failed to bring him promptly before a judge, and conducted an ineffective investigation into his torture complaint.

On 18 July 2005 at about 11 a.m., several plainclothes police officers came to the hostel where Belousov lived and invited him to their office. He went to the Kominternivskyy District police station, where he was told that two mothers had accused him of sexually abusing their minor daughters. He was questioned, and at about 5 p.m. he confessed and signed permission for police to inspect his home. At about 6 p.m., seven or eight officers took him back to the hostel, examined his room, seized a bed cover, rug and personal belongings, and returned him to the police station. No arrest record was drawn up at that stage. Belousov remained at the station. He first met a lawyer hired by his relatives at about 7 p.m. on 19 July. Only at about 8:40 p.m. on 19 July did an investigator draw up an arrest report stating that he had been arrested as a crime suspect under Article 115 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. He was brought before a judge on 22 July, remanded for ten days, and released on 29 July subject to an undertaking not to abscond. In September 2005, one of the complaining mothers withdrew her complaint, saying it had been lodged under police pressure.

The alleged ill-treatment was supported by witness and medical evidence. On the evening of 18 July, the hostel concierge and three neighbours told the Kharkiv Human Rights Group that when Belousov left with police around 11 a.m. he had been sober, neatly dressed and in good health. About seven hours later, when police brought him back for the search, he was limping, stooping, had bruises and swellings on his face, and his clothes were dirty and wrinkled. Some neighbours saw him handcuffed and prevented from explaining what was happening. At about 10 p.m., an anonymous caller complained to the police hotline. At about 10:30 p.m., Deputy Chief M.K. interviewed Belousov, who complained of ill-treatment; the officers claimed he had injured himself. On the morning of 19 July, a forensic expert found minor bodily injuries, including soft tissue swelling, numerous bruises and scratches, especially on his face and groin, inflicted by blunt objects within the past one to three days. Belousov said the police caused them; the police said they were self-inflicted.

On 20 July, represented by counsel, Belousov formally complained about his unrecorded detention until 8:40 p.m. on 19 July and about torture. He named officers S.B., A.O. and V.M. and said he could identify others. He later added that his home had been unlawfully searched. On 1 August 2005, the District Prosecutor’s Office opened criminal proceedings. When questioned on 6 August, Belousov alleged that three officers had threatened and tortured him to obtain a confession. He said they placed him handcuffed on a blanket-covered desk, twisted his arms, punched him, squeezed his genitals, and were joined by three other officers who beat and strangled him. He confessed by 5 p.m. The implicated officers were questioned only as witnesses and claimed he became agitated and injured himself; their accounts varied.

The investigation was repeatedly delayed, suspended, discontinued and renewed. In December 2009, the prosecutor’s office discontinued the case, acknowledging that Belousov had been de facto arrested on 18 July but documented only on the evening of 19 July. It treated this as a possible disciplinary matter, found insufficient evidence of torture, and classified the home visit as a lawful inspection with consent. The decision was later quashed, but proceedings continued to stall. The European Court of Human Rights concluded that no serious effort had been made to investigate the ill-treatment allegations, citing systemic problems in Ukraine and the investigation’s failure to meet effectiveness requirements, violating the procedural limb of Article 3.
001-122892:
Lay Lay Company Limited v. Malta (Application no. 30633/11) concerned a Maltese-registered company’s complaint that it was denied access to court under Article 6 § 1 to contest the refusal of its building permit, and that this also violated its property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In 1984, A., for the applicant company, and C. purchased about 4,500 sq. m of land in Ghaxaq. The company claimed it was a building site under the Building Development Areas Act 1983. In August 1984 an application to build garages with upper floors was lodged in C.’s name before the Planning Area Permits Board (PAPB). In September 1985 the applicant company acquired C.’s share and became sole owner, but did not inform the PAPB.

On 10 July 1986 the PAPB approved the application as per plans, subject to payment of road contribution costs. The company began building. However, the contribution bill was sent to C. and remained unpaid. A 1987 minute noted that no permit had been issued because the applicant had failed to pay and works were in hand. C. was warned that construction was not covered by a permit. In 1992 a fresh bill (about EUR 7,962) was sent to C., passed to A., and paid by the applicant on 14 December 1992. Clearance was issued.

After the PAPB was replaced by the Planning Authority (later MEPA) in 1993, the file was moved, lost, and not acted upon. On 7 October 1996, a Development Control Unit manager wrote that the permit could not be issued because the 1986 bill had “fallen through” and the 1992 payment came after a decision not to accept payment six years after billing. The applicant did not appeal within thirty days or seek judicial review then, later claiming it did not understand this as a formal refusal.

In 1999, after more delays, the company filed a judicial protest. MEPA issued a stop notice. In 2003 the Development Appeals Board rejected the company’s appeal, finding that the PAPB had never issued a permit, its recommendation was not a permit, and payment of the contribution did not automatically lead to approval. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal in 2004. It emerged that MEPA treated the 1996 letter as the refusal, which had become final because the thirty-day appeal period had lapsed.

In constitutional redress proceedings begun in 2004, the company complained under Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the failure to issue the permit, the stop notice, and the absence of a contestable decision. The First Hall rejected the claims: the company had no permit and no possession of development rights; it had built without a permit; enforcement was proportionate. On Article 6, it found the company could have challenged the authority’s conduct or the 1996 letter but failed to do so. In 2011 the Constitutional Court upheld this, finding no permit and no legitimate expectation, and that the 1996 letter sufficiently conveyed a refusal. The company remained passive and did not appeal. Meanwhile, a 2006 local plan placed the property outside the development zone, and the contribution payment was not refunded.

The applicant, Lay Lay Company Limited, is a Maltese-registered company. In July 1984, A. (on the company’s behalf) and a co-owner, C., purchased about 4,500 sq. m of land in Ghaxaq, described in the deed as a “field.” The company claimed the land was a building site under the Building Development Areas Act 1983 because it fronted a public road and lay within 120 metres of a built-up area. In August 1984, an application was lodged in C.’s name with the Works Department for examination by the Planning Area Permits Board (“PAPB”) to build garages with upper floors. In September 1985, the applicant bought C.’s share and became sole owner, but the PAPB was not informed.

In July 1986, the PAPB approved the application “as per plans submitted,” subject to payment of road contribution costs. The applicant began building. A road contribution bill was sent to C. in May 1987 and a final notice in June 1987, but no payment was made. A minute in June 1987 recorded that no permit had been issued because the applicant had failed to pay and works were in hand. In July 1987, C. was warned that construction was not covered by a permit. The applicant’s architect later sought information, but the file had allegedly been transferred to the Attorney General’s office for criminal proceedings. Criminal proceedings for illegal construction began in April 1988 but were suspended in November 1998 without judgment.

Legislative changes followed. The 1988 Act introduced temporary building provisions, and the 1992 Development Planning Act replaced the PAPB with the Planning Authority, later MEPA. In May 1992, reminders were sent to C. In August 1992, a fresh road contribution bill of about EUR 7,962 was issued to C., who passed it to A.; the applicant paid it in December 1992, and clearance was issued. Despite this, the file was mishandled, misplaced, and no permit was issued.

In May 1996, the applicant’s new architect asked the Development Control Commission to issue the permit and informed it that the company now owned the land. In October 1996, a manager, G.C., replied that the permit could not be issued because the 1986 bill had “fallen through” and the 1992 clearance came after a decision not to accept payment six years after billing. MEPA later treated this letter as a refusal.

In June 1999, the applicant filed a judicial protest. That same day, MEPA issued a stop notice. The applicant appealed to the Development Appeals Board, which in August 2003 rejected the appeal, finding that the PAPB had never issued a permit; its 1986 decision was only a recommendation, and payment of the contribution did not amount to a permit. The Court of Appeal dismissed a further appeal in June 2004. During those proceedings, it emerged that MEPA regarded the October 1996 letter as a refusal, meaning the thirty-day appeal period had long expired.

In September 2004, the applicant brought constitutional redress proceedings, alleging that the failure to issue the permit, the stop notice, and the manner of refusal without a proper appealable decision violated Article 6 § 1 (access to court) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (property). The Civil Court rejected the claims in 2009, and the Constitutional Court upheld that judgment in 2011. The domestic courts found that the applicant never held a permit, had no possession or legitimate expectation of one, that payment did not oblige MEPA to issue a permit, and that the October 1996 letter sufficiently indicated a refusal which the applicant could have appealed or challenged by judicial review but did not. The contribution paid was not refunded, and by 2006 the property fell outside the development zone under the South Malta Local Plan.

The case concerns an application against Malta by Lay Lay Company Limited, a Maltese company. In July 1984 the company and a co-owner, C., purchased about 4,500 sq. m of land in Ghaxaq. In August 1984 an application for permission to build garages with overlying dwellings was lodged in C.’s name with the Works Department, for examination by the Planning Area Permits Board (PAPB). In September 1985 the applicant bought C.’s share and became sole owner, but the PAPB was not informed at the time.

On 10 July 1986 the PAPB approved the application subject to payment of road contribution costs, stating there was no objection to the garages and overlying dwellings subject to conditions and plans. The applicant then began building. A contribution bill was sent to C. in May 1987, followed by a final notice in June 1987. No payment was made. A June 1987 minute recorded that no permit had been issued because the contribution bill was unpaid and works were in hand. In July 1987 C. was warned that the construction was not covered by a permit. Criminal proceedings for illegal construction began in April 1988 but were suspended in 1998 without judgment.

Meanwhile, legislative changes replaced the PAPB with the Planning Authority/MEPA. In August 1992 a fresh contribution bill of about EUR 7,962 was issued to C.; C. passed it to the applicant, which paid in December 1992. Clearance was issued. In January 1993 the applicant’s architect submitted a transitional notice to the new Authority, still naming C. as owner. The file was later misplaced and no permit was issued. In May 1996, after the applicant’s new architect requested the permit and informed the authority that the applicant owned the land, the Development Control Unit manager, G.C., replied on 7 October 1996 that the permit could not be issued because the 1986 bill had “fallen through” and the 1992 clearance came after a decision not to accept late payment. MEPA later treated this letter as a refusal; the thirty-day appeal period expired.

The applicant complained that it had been denied access to court under Article 6 § 1 to contest the refusal of its building permit and that its property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 had been violated. In June 1999 it lodged a judicial protest seeking issuance of the permit and damages. MEPA issued a stop notice. The applicant appealed to the Development Appeals Board, which in 2003 held that no permit had ever been issued: the PAPB’s 1986 decision was only a recommendation, payment of the contribution did not amount to approval, and the development was unauthorised. The Court of Appeal dismissed its appeal in 2004.

In constitutional redress proceedings begun in 2004, the applicant repeated that the authorities’ failure to issue the permit, the stop notice, and the manner of refusing the permit—without a proper decision or opportunity to contest it—violated Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The domestic constitutional courts rejected the claims, finding no permit, possession, or legitimate expectation; the control of use was lawful and proportionate; and the applicant could have appealed the 1996 letter or sought judicial review but remained passive. In 2006 the South Malta Local Plan placed the property outside the development zone. The contribution paid was not refunded.
001-115981:
In **Claes v. Belgium** (App. no. 43418/09, judgment 10 April 2013), the applicant, André Claes, was a Belgian national born in 1952 with severe mental disabilities and chronic behavioural disorders. He had an IQ of 72 and was classified as “mentally disabled.” He also had a history of sexual offences against minors. In 1978, a criminal court found him not criminally responsible and ordered his committal. After periods of release and further offences, from 1994 he was detained in the psychiatric wing of Merksplas Prison under Belgium’s Social Protection Act. He alleged that his prolonged detention in a prison setting unsuitable for his disability violated Article 3 (inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 5 §§ 1(e) and 4 (lawful detention of persons of unsound mind and access to judicial review).

The key facts concerned the adequacy and suitability of his detention. The Mental Health Board repeatedly decided that he required placement in a suitable psychiatric or disability institution. It extended his detention pending such placement. From 1998 onwards, the authorities tried to find a non-prison facility willing to accept him, but no institution did so, largely because of his aggressive behaviour, sexual offending risk, and need for intensive supervision. Medical and psychological reports described him as mentally deficient, immature, manipulative, and potentially dangerous. They also noted growing distress and frustration because he had no realistic prospect of rehabilitation. In prison, his treatment consisted mainly of periodic consultations with psychiatrists or psychologists—often only about once a month and sometimes with different practitioners—and participation in activities organised by social workers. Reports from 2007 and 2008 confirmed worsening suffering, limited understanding of his condition, and a need for close personal supervision. Conditions in the F block included a dormitory shared with twenty-four others and unsatisfactory sanitation. The Government claimed he was later placed in the new “De Haven” secure unit, but the applicant disputed this, and the Court found that any such stay lasted at most two months and was not decisive.

The applicant sought an injunction ordering the State to find him a suitable institution. Domestic courts dismissed his applications, holding that the urgent applications judge had no jurisdiction and that decisions on placement lay exclusively with the Mental Health Board. The Mental Health Board confirmed that continued detention was necessary to protect society, especially children, but acknowledged that treatment was not always sufficient and that it lacked power to order the authorities to provide a suitable place. In September 2009, he was released on a trial basis to the Martine van Camp Centre, but in June 2011, after aggressive behaviour, he was returned to the psychiatric wing of Louvain Prison.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 3. It emphasised that mentally ill detainees are especially vulnerable and that it is not enough merely to examine or diagnose them; suitable treatment and medical supervision must be provided. The applicant had been held in prison psychiatric wings for many years without appropriate care and with no real hope of change. Although the authorities had made efforts to find an outside placement, the applicant’s plight resulted from a structural problem: insufficient care in prison psychiatric wings and a lack of places in suitable external facilities. The Court concluded that the national authorities had not taken sufficient care of his health and that his long detention in these conditions subjected him to degrading treatment.

The case *Claes v. Belgium* (Application no. 43418/09) concerned André Claes, a Belgian national born in 1952. He suffered from severe mental disabilities, with an IQ of 72, chronic behavioural disorders and a history of sexual offences. In 1978 the Louvain Criminal Court found him not criminally responsible for repeated rapes of his under-age sisters and committed him to psychiatric care. After conditional release, he was detained again in 1982 for sexually assaulting a child. Following placements in psychiatric institutions and further incidents, including indecent assault in 1987 and sexual incidents in a psychiatric hospital in 1994, the Mental Health Board ordered his return to the psychiatric wing of Merksplas Prison. He remained there until September 2009, when he was trial-released to the Martine van Camp Centre; in June 2011 he was returned to the psychiatric wing of Louvain Prison after aggressive behaviour.

The applicant alleged that his detention in a place unsuitable for a person with his disability violated Article 3 and Article 5 §§ 1(e) and 4 of the Convention. He claimed he received inadequate treatment and support, had no realistic prospect of rehabilitation, and suffered from being held long-term in a prison psychiatric wing. He described being held in an ordinary prison block, sleeping in a dormitory with twenty-four others, unsatisfactory sanitation, and only limited consultations with rotating psychiatrists. Reports from 2004 to 2008 documented unsuccessful attempts to find an outside residential institution. Medical and psychological opinions described him as vulnerable, increasingly distressed by the lack of placement, and in need of close personal supervision. The Mental Health Board repeatedly extended his detention until an appropriate institution could accept him, but no non-prison facility was willing to take him because of his aggressive behaviour, sexual offending history and the shortage of places. The domestic courts dismissed his requests for an injunction, finding that the urgent applications judge lacked jurisdiction and that the Mental Health Board had exclusive power over placement.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the Government argued that Claes had received proper treatment and that authorities had made efforts to place him elsewhere. The Court rejected a formalistic approach, emphasising that mentally ill detainees are especially vulnerable and may be unable to complain coherently. It found that mere psychiatric consultations were insufficient; proper treatment and suitable medical supervision were required. The Court noted a structural problem: prison psychiatric wings were generally unsuitable, with insufficient staff, poor continuity of treatment, overcrowding and lack of outside capacity or legal powers to compel placement. The applicant’s difficult behaviour did not relieve the State of its obligations. Detention for a significant period in such conditions, with no real hope of change and without appropriate care, caused distress exceeding the unavoidable suffering inherent in detention. The Court concluded that Claes had been subjected to degrading treatment, in violation of Article 3 of the Convention. The Article 5 complaints concerned the lawfulness and review of his continued detention/placement, but the central violation turned on the prolonged unsuitable prison detention and failure to provide adequate care or transfer.

In *Claes v. Belgium*, the applicant, André Claes, a Belgian national born in 1952, alleged that his prolonged detention in prison psychiatric wings unsuitable for his mental disability violated Article 3 and Article 5 §§ 1(e) and 4 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The key facts began in 1978, when the Louvain Criminal Court found Claes not criminally responsible for the repeated rape of his under-age sisters between 1973 and 1977 because of severe mental disabilities. He was first committed in April 1978. After release, he was detained again in 1982 for sexually assaulting a child. The Mental Health Board attempted various placements, including a private psychiatric clinic, Merksplas Prison, and a trial release to a psychiatric institute. In 1987 he was arrested for indecent assault on a young girl and placed in Turnhout Prison’s psychiatric wing.

In 1994, following incidents involving young girls and female staff, and after psychological reports described him as manipulative, potentially dangerous, and incapable of living in society, the Mental Health Board ordered his return to the psychiatric wing of Merksplas Prison. He remained there from 1994 until 2009, apart from a disputed short stay in the “De Haven” unit. In 2009 he was released on trial to the Martine van Camp Centre, but in 2011 he was returned to Louvain Prison’s psychiatric wing after aggressive behaviour.

Testing in 1998 showed an IQ of 72, and he was classified as “mentally disabled.” Reports between 2002 and 2008 documented ongoing behavioural problems, limited insight, growing suffering, and a need for close, personalised supervision. From 1998 onward, authorities repeatedly tried to find a non-prison psychiatric institution willing to accept him, but none would. Although he attended activities run by the “‘t Zwart Goor” association and some improvement was noted in 2005, the Mental Health Board repeatedly extended his detention until a place in the Flemish disability care system could be found. Conditions at Merksplas included sharing a dormitory with 24 others, unsatisfactory sanitation, and only limited psychiatric consultations, often with different psychiatrists.

Claes sought injunctions in ordinary courts ordering the State to place him in a suitable institution. In 2008 the urgent applications judge dismissed his requests, and in 2009 the Antwerp Court of Appeal held that ordinary courts lacked jurisdiction because the Mental Health Boards had exclusive power over placement. Appeals to the Higher Mental Health Board and Court of Cassation also failed.

The Government argued that he received proper treatment and that his aggression and sexual problems made placement difficult. Claes argued that prison psychiatric care was unsuitable, not personalised, and offered no realistic rehabilitation prospect for over fifteen years. The European Court of Human Rights found that his serious mental deficiency, long detention in prison psychiatric wings, and lack of appropriate treatment caused acute hardship. It noted national and international consensus that prison psychiatric wings are unsuitable for mentally disordered detainees due to staff shortages, poor treatment continuity, overcrowding, and structural capacity problems. The Court concluded that Belgium had subjected him to degrading treatment contrary to Article 3. The Article 5 complaints concerned the alleged unsuitability of his detention and the lack of an effective remedy or placement.
001-126918:
**Case Summary: Budrevich v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 65303/10)**

**Key Facts**

The applicant, Andrei Budrevich, a Belarusian national, left Belarus in October 2006 using an assumed name and entered the Czech Republic, where he sought asylum. He alleged that he had faced state pressure in Belarus for importing advertisements supporting opposition candidate Aliaxandr Milinkevich, resulting in detention, fines, confiscation of his car and passport, and repeated police visits to his home warning his family of criminal proceedings.

Czech authorities rejected his first asylum request in September 2007, finding his allegations contradictory and not credible. They noted he had only engaged in a one-off activity for financial reward, had not been politically active, and had already been punished—with no indication of future risk. This decision was upheld through subsequent appeals, with the Supreme Administrative Court dismissing his cassation appeal in June 2009 due to his failure to cooperate with his lawyer.

In December 2009, Czech police sent his fingerprints to Belarus, revealing his true identity. In November 2009, Belarus requested his extradition for drug-related offences. Critically, on 23 April 2010, the Plzeň Regional Court refused extradition, finding reasonable fears that criminal proceedings in Belarus would violate his rights under Articles 3 and 6 of the Convention. The court relied on reports documenting political persecution, lack of judicial independence, inhuman detention conditions, ill-treatment by police, and fair trial violations in Belarus.

Separately, the applicant was convicted of theft in multiple criminal proceedings. On 5 November 2008, the Prague 10 District Court sentenced him to thirty months’ expulsion. On 13 March 2009, the Prague 8 District Court imposed a one-year prison sentence and five years’ expulsion. He served his prison sentence from December 2008 to 4 October 2010—the first date his expulsion could be executed.

The applicant lodged multiple subsequent asylum requests, all rejected as inadmissible repeat applications lacking new circumstances. In September 2010, he requested suspension of his expulsion, which was initially granted pending asylum review but cancelled on 25 October 2010 after his third asylum request was dismissed. His appeal was rejected as belated. On 4 October 2010, his attempted expulsion was prevented only by a suicide attempt before boarding the plane.

On 9 November 2010, the applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights, alleging violations of Article 3 (risk of ill-treatment in Belarus) and Article 13 (no effective remedy against expulsion). The Court applied Rule 39, indicating to the Government not to remove him pending proceedings. The applicant was subsequently granted subsidiary protection on 17 October 2011, extended on 3 June 2013 for twenty-four months.

**Alleged Violations**

The applicant complained that his expulsion to Belarus would expose him to a real risk of ill-treatment contrary to Article 3, and that he lacked an effective domestic remedy under Article 13 to challenge that risk in light of the extradition refusal and new evidence of persecution.

**Case Summary: Budrevich v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 65303/10)**

The applicant, Andrei Budrevich, a Belarusian national born in 1979, entered the Czech Republic in October 2006 using an assumed name and applied for asylum. He claimed he had fled Belarus after facing pressure, detention, fines, confiscation of his car and passport, and repeated police searches because he had imported advertisements supporting opposition presidential candidate Aliaxandr Milinkevich. He alleged that police had warned his mother and sister that criminal proceedings would be brought against him, and he feared imprisonment if returned.

Czech authorities rejected his first asylum request in September 2007, finding his account contradictory and not credible. The Hradec Králové Regional Court upheld that decision in May 2008, and the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed his cassation appeal in June 2009 because he failed to provide proper grounds.

Separately, the applicant was convicted of several thefts in 2008 and 2009. These convictions resulted in sentences of expulsion from Czech territory—first for thirty months, later for five years. He served a prison sentence from December 2008 until October 2010.

A key development occurred in November 2009, when Belarus requested his extradition for drug-related offences. In April 2010, the Plzeň Regional Court refused extradition, finding reasonable fears that criminal proceedings in Belarus would violate his rights under Articles 3 and 6 of the Convention. It relied on reports documenting political persecution, ill-treatment by police, inhuman detention conditions, and unfair trials in Belarus. This became central to his alleged risk of ill-treatment if returned.

The applicant lodged further asylum requests in January, September, and November 2010. The second and third were rejected or terminated as repeated requests lacking new circumstances. Although judicial review was available, it generally did not have suspensive effect. His expulsion was initially stayed pending asylum proceedings, but the stay was cancelled in October 2010 after his third asylum request was dismissed. A removal apparently scheduled shortly afterward did not occur because he attempted suicide before boarding a plane. On 9 November 2010, the European Court of Human Rights issued an interim measure under Rule 39 preventing his removal. His fourth asylum request ultimately led to subsidiary protection in October 2011, later extended in 2013.

Before the Court, the applicant alleged that expulsion to Belarus would violate Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment) and that he lacked an effective domestic remedy under Article 13. The Government argued that he had lost victim status because subsidiary protection barred expulsion and that effective remedies had existed.

The Court rejected the Article 3 complaint as manifestly ill-founded: subsidiary protection legally prevented his expulsion, so he no longer faced a current risk and had lost victim status. However, it declared the Article 13 complaint admissible. It found that his Article 3 claim was arguable between April 2010, when extradition was refused, and November 2010, when he applied to the Court. Ordinary criminal appeals were unavailable because the expulsion sentences had become final before the new risk evidence emerged. A waiver under Article 350h and a constitutional appeal lacked suspensive effect. A fresh asylum request could have suspended expulsion, but the Ministry dismissed his third request in one day with brief reasoning and failed to examine the new extradition-related risk with the required close and rigorous scrutiny. The Court therefore found that the Czech authorities had not provided an effective remedy, resulting in a violation of Article 13 in conjunction with Article 3.

**Summary of *Budrevich v. The Czech Republic* (Application no. 65303/10)**

The case of *Budrevich v. the Czech Republic* concerns a Belarusian national, Mr. Andrei Budrevich, who alleged that his expulsion from the Czech Republic would violate Article 3 (prohibition of ill-treatment) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant entered the Czech Republic in October 2006 using an assumed name. He claimed to have fled Belarus due to state pressure and persecution related to his involvement with opposition political activities during the presidential elections. After his true identity was revealed in December 2009, the Czech authorities began processing an extradition request from Belarus, where he was sought for prosecution on drug-related charges.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are as follows:

1.  **Asylum Proceedings:** The applicant lodged four asylum requests between 2006 and 2010. His initial request was rejected as not credible, a decision upheld on appeal. His subsequent requests were largely dismissed as inadmissible "repeated requests" without new circumstances, although the courts later found procedural flaws in how these were handled by the Ministry of the Interior. Crucially, his fourth request, lodged in November 2010, resulted in the granting of **subsidiary protection** on 17 October 2011, which was later extended.

2.  **Criminal Convictions and Expulsion Orders:** Between 2008 and 2009, the applicant was convicted of several thefts. Two separate criminal judgments sentenced him to expulsion from the Czech Republic—first for thirty months and later for five years.

3.  **Extradition Proceedings:** In November 2009, Belarus requested the applicant’s extradition for drug offenses. On 23 April 2010, the Plzeň Regional Court **refused the extradition request** as inadmissible. The court found reasonable fears that the criminal proceedings in Belarus would violate the applicant's rights under Articles 3 and 6 of the Convention, citing reports from Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International regarding political persecution, lack of judicial independence, and ill-treatment in Belarus.

4.  **Deportation Attempts:** The execution of the expulsion order was stayed pending asylum decisions. However, on 25 October 2010, the Prague 10 District Court cancelled the suspension after his third asylum request was dismissed. A deportation attempt on 4 October 2010 was thwarted only by the applicant's suicide attempt. Following his application to the European Court, an interim measure under Rule 39 was applied, preventing his removal.

The applicant complained that, between the Plzeň Regional Court's refusal to extradite him (23 April 2010) and the lodging of his application (9 November 2010), he faced a real risk of ill-treatment if expelled and had no effective domestic remedy to challenge the expulsion on that basis. The Czech Government contested this, arguing that the applicant had access to various remedies in criminal and asylum proceedings and had ultimately lost his "victim" status upon being granted subsidiary protection. The Court found the Article 3 complaint inadmissible but declared the Article 13 complaint admissible to examine whether an effective remedy existed at the relevant time.
001-118045:
**Summary of *Julius Kloiber Schlachthof GmbH and Others v. Austria***

The case of *Julius Kloiber Schlachthof GmbH and Others v. Austria* (Applications nos. 21565/07, 21572/07, 21575/07, and 21580/07) concerns four Austrian companies operating in the slaughter of cattle and pigs. The applicants challenged the imposition of surcharges on unpaid contributions owed to the national agricultural marketing board, Agrarmarkt Austria (AMA), arguing that the proceedings failed to comply with Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Under the Agricultural Market Act, the applicant companies were liable to pay marketing charges based on the number of animals slaughtered. In 2006, AMA issued payment orders against all four companies for outstanding contributions from 2003 to 2006, along with surcharges for non-payment. These surcharges ranged from 10% to 60% of the unpaid contributions. The first applicant was ordered to pay EUR 56,573.62 plus a 10% surcharge; the second applicant EUR 12,556.43 plus 10%; the third applicant EUR 5,936.01 plus 10%; and the fourth applicant EUR 96,050.48 plus 60%.

The companies appealed, contending that the AMA contribution system violated European Union state aid rules and requesting oral hearings. The Federal Minister of Agriculture, Forestry, the Environment and Water dismissed their appeals on 17 July 2006 without holding hearings. The Minister relied on a European Commission decision of 30 June 2004, which approved AMA’s quality assurance scheme as compatible with the Common Market, and an Administrative Court decision from 20 March 2006 confirming the compliance of AMA contributions with EU law. The Minister also stated that a hearing was unnecessary because such hearings were only held when a panel decided appeals against tax office or regional finance directorate decisions.

The applicant companies then lodged complaints with the Constitutional Court and the Administrative Court. Before the Constitutional Court, they alleged a violation of their constitutional right to property. Before the Administrative Court, they argued that the appeal authority was not a court within the meaning of European Court of Justice case-law, preventing them from obtaining a preliminary ruling under Article 234 of the EC Treaty. They further complained that the authorities failed to establish the objective and subjective elements of the offence when imposing surcharges, that there was no public hearing, and that the criminal charges were not decided by an impartial tribunal established by law, relying on Article 6 of the Convention.

On 25 September 2006, the Constitutional Court declined to entertain the complaints for lack of prospects of success. On 30 January 2007, the Administrative Court dismissed the complaints, referencing its earlier decision and holding that Article 6 of the Convention was not relevant. The court decided without further proceedings in camera.

The key issue before the European Court of Human Rights was whether the proceedings concerning the surcharges violated Article 6 § 1, specifically whether the applicants had access to a tribunal as required for criminal charges. The Court found Article 6 applicable under its criminal head, as the surcharges imposed for non-payment of parafiscal contributions carried a punitive element. Neither AMA nor the Federal Minister qualified as a tribunal. Furthermore, relying on its prior judgment in *Steininger v. Austria*, the Court held that the Administrative Court’s limited power of review was insufficient for criminal proceedings, and the Constitutional Court’s refusal to entertain the complaint excluded it from being a judicial body with full jurisdiction. Consequently, the applicants lacked access to a tribunal satisfying Article 6 § 1 requirements.

This case involved four Austrian companies that slaughtered cattle and pigs. Under the Agricultural Market Act, they were liable to pay agricultural marketing contributions to Agrarmarkt Austria (“AMA”), calculated by the number of animals slaughtered. In 2006 AMA issued payment orders against them for unpaid contributions for 2003–2006 and imposed surcharges for non-payment: 10% for the first three applicants and 60% for the fourth. The applicants appealed, arguing that the contribution system breached EU state aid rules and requesting oral hearings.

On 17 July 2006 the Federal Minister of Agriculture, Forestry, the Environment and Water, acting as appeal authority, dismissed the appeals without holding a hearing. The Minister relied on a 2004 European Commission decision approving AMA’s quality scheme and on a prior Administrative Court judgment holding that AMA contributions complied with EU law. He also stated that a hearing was unnecessary because the appeal had not been decided by a panel, unlike appeals from tax offices or finance directorates.

The companies then complained to the Constitutional Court and the Administrative Court. They alleged, among other things, that the appeal authority was not a court for EU law purposes; that the surcharge findings were insufficient, including failure to establish the objective and subjective elements of the offence; and, under Article 6 of the Convention, that there had been no public hearing and that the criminal charge against them had not been decided by an impartial tribunal established by law. The Constitutional Court declined to deal with the complaints for lack of prospects of success. In January 2007 the Administrative Court dismissed them in separate decisions, referring to its earlier decision and holding that Article 6 was irrelevant; it decided in camera without a hearing.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants complained only about the surcharge proceedings, not the underlying contributions. They alleged violations of Article 6 § 1: the proceedings had not been decided by a tribunal, and there had been no public hearing. The Government argued that Article 6 did not apply because the surcharges were administrative parafiscal charges rather than criminal penalties; alternatively, there was no violation because the Administrative Court had full jurisdiction. The Government also contended that domestic remedies had not been exhausted.

The Court held that Article 6 applied under its criminal head, following Steininger v. Austria and Jussila v. Finland, because surcharges imposed for non-payment of parafiscal contributions had a punitive character. It rejected the Government’s admissibility objections, finding that the applicants had sufficiently raised Article 6 domestically. On the merits, neither AMA nor the Federal Minister was a tribunal. The Constitutional Court, which declined to entertain the case, and the Administrative Court, whose review was limited, did not qualify as a judicial body with full jurisdiction in criminal proceedings. Applying Steininger, the Court found that the applicants had no access to a tribunal within the meaning of Article 6 § 1. The lack-of-hearing complaint was linked to that issue and was declared admissible. The central violation was therefore the absence of adequate review by an independent and impartial tribunal.

The case concerned four Austrian companies—Julius Kloiber Schlachthof GmbH, Fa. Pöll Günter, Pöll-Fleisch GmbH, and Schweinespezialbetrieb Innviertel GmbH—engaged in cattle and pig slaughtering. Under the Agricultural Market Act, they were liable to pay agricultural marketing contributions to Agrarmarkt Austria (“AMA”), calculated by the number of animals slaughtered.

In 2006 AMA issued payment orders against the companies for unpaid contributions and imposed surcharges for non-payment. On 5 July 2006, the first applicant was ordered to pay EUR 56,573.62 for 2003–2004 plus a 10% surcharge. On 30 May 2006, the second applicant was ordered to pay EUR 12,556.43 for 2004–2005 plus 10%; the third EUR 5,936.01 for 2005–2006 plus 10%; and the fourth EUR 96,050.48 for 2005–2006 plus a 60% surcharge.

The companies appealed, arguing that the contribution system breached EU state-aid rules and requesting oral hearings. On 17 July 2006, the Federal Minister of Agriculture, Forestry, Environment and Water dismissed the appeals without a hearing. The Minister relied on a European Commission decision of 30 June 2004 and an Administrative Court judgment of 20 March 2006, which had found the AMA contributions compatible with EU law. The Minister also stated that a hearing was only required where a panel decided an appeal against a tax office or regional finance directorate decision, which was not the situation here.

The companies then lodged complaints with the Constitutional Court and the Administrative Court. Before the Constitutional Court, they alleged that the surcharges violated their constitutional right to property. Before the Administrative Court, they argued that the appeal authority had not been a court within the meaning of EU case-law, preventing review of the Commission decision via Article 234 EC Treaty. They also complained that the authorities had not sufficiently established the objective and subjective elements of the offence, and that under Article 6 of the Convention there had been no public hearing and no impartial tribunal established by law to decide the criminal charge against them. They specifically requested a public hearing before the Administrative Court. On 25 September 2006, the Constitutional Court declined to entertain the complaints for lack of prospects of success. On 30 January 2007, the Administrative Court dismissed the complaints in separate decisions, referring to its earlier decision and Section 43(2) of the Administrative Court Act, and held that Article 6 was irrelevant.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the Government argued that Article 6 did not apply because the surcharges were parafiscal administrative charges, not criminal penalties, and that the applicants had not exhausted domestic remedies. The Court rejected these objections. Relying on Steininger v. Austria and Jussila v. Finland, it found that Article 6 applied under its criminal head to proceedings concerning surcharges for AMA contributions. It also found that the applicants had sufficiently raised their Article 6 complaint domestically.

On the merits, the Court reiterated that decisions by administrative authorities not satisfying Article 6 must be subject to subsequent review by a judicial body with full jurisdiction. AMA and the Federal Minister were administrative authorities, not tribunals. In Steininger, the Court had already found that neither the Constitutional Court nor the Administrative Court qualified as a tribunal for such criminal proceedings: the Constitutional Court declined to deal with the case, and the Administrative Court’s review was limited and insufficient for criminal penalties. The Court found the same deficiencies here. Accordingly, the applicants had not had access to a tribunal within the meaning of Article 6 § 1. The related complaint concerning the lack of a public hearing was likewise declared admissible and linked to the same violation.
001-119972:
In *Zeynalov v. Azerbaijan* (App. No. 31848/07, ECtHR, 30 May 2013), the applicant, Ahmadshah Zeynalov, an Azerbaijani farmer, was involved in a land ownership dispute with Sadan Municipality over 0.8 hectares in the former Davachi district. The Municipality claimed the land; the applicant claimed it was part of his family’s 50-hectare farming business. Criminal proceedings were brought against him under Article 188 of the Criminal Code for unauthorised occupation/cultivation of land. On 29 December 2004 the Davachi District Court convicted him and fined him 100 conventional financial units (approximately AZN 110 / EUR 84), relying on witness statements and information from the State Committee of Land and Cartography. The Court of Appeal upheld that judgment on 18 March 2005.

The applicant appealed on points of law. In *Zeynalov v. Azerbaijan* (Application no. 31848/07, judgment of 30 May 2013), the European Court of Human Rights examined an Article 6 complaint about the composition of the Supreme Court panel in the applicant’s criminal case.

On 29 December 2004, the Davachi District Court convicted him and fined him 100 conventional financial units—approximately 110 new Azerbaijani manats or EUR 84. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 18 March 2005.

The applicant appealed on points of law. The alleged violation concerned Judge N.H.’s participation in both Supreme Court cassation examinations of the same criminal case. The applicant argued that this breached domestic law and deprived him of an impartial tribunal. The Government admitted that the same judge sitting twice in the same case was contrary to domestic law, but argued that Article 6 had not been violated because the Supreme Court had reached different decisions and the proceedings were otherwise fair.

Domestic law, Article 109 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, required a judge to be disqualified if he or she had already participated in examination of the same criminal case at first-instance, appellate, or Supreme Court level. The applicant’s separate complaint about lack of free legal assistance was dismissed as manifestly ill-founded.

Article 109.2 required automatic self-disqualification. The applicant maintained his complaint.

The European Court of Human Rights considered the key issue to be whether the second Supreme Court panel could be regarded as a “tribunal established by law.” It reiterated that while Article 6 does not require states to create cassation courts, if such courts exist, their proceedings must comply with Article 6. The phrase “established by law” includes compliance with rules governing the composition of the bench. Since the Government conceded that Judge N.H.’s repeated participation breached Article 109 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and domestic case-law, the Court concluded that the panel was not a “tribunal established by law” under Article 6 § 1. It therefore found a violation, without separately deciding the issue of objective impartiality.

On admissibility, the Government asked whether the applicant had suffered a “significant disadvantage” under Article 35 § 3 (b). The Court found that the criminal conviction made the issue one of principle and objectively important for the applicant, despite the relatively small fine and his status as a small farmer.
