During questioning, officers invoked s.2 of the Offences Against the State (Amendment) Act 1998, which allows inferences to be drawn from a suspect’s failure to answer material questions. After being warned of the consequences, Donohoe refused to answer any questions.

At trial before the SCC, the prosecution relied on four strands of evidence: (1) the sworn belief evidence of Chief Superintendent PK that Donohoe was an IRA member on 10 October 2002; (2) evidence associating him with the Corke Abbey activities; (3) documents found at his home; and (4) inferences from his silence during interviews. PK said his belief was based on confidential oral and written information from police and civilian sources, independent of Corke Abbey. When asked to identify those sources, he claimed privilege, stating that disclosure would endanger lives and State security.

The defence applied for an inquiry into PK’s sources, arguing that without knowing the evidence against him, Donohoe could not have a fair trial. The SCC accepted that some inquiry was necessary to reconcile privilege with defence rights. It directed PK to produce all relevant documentation to the court. The SCC reviewed the material in camera, without showing it to either the prosecution or the defence. It concluded that PK had adequate and reliable information for his belief and that nothing in the files would assist the defence. It later said it had excluded that material from its deliberations when weighing PK’s evidence.

The SCC convicted Donohoe. It held that it would not convict on PK’s belief alone, so it sought corroboration. It found that the Corke Abbey evidence and documents showed association with unlawful activity, though not necessarily subversive activity. It also drew inferences from Donohoe’s failure to answer material questions, treating that silence as corroboration of PK’s belief. Donohoe appealed unsuccessfully to the Court of Criminal Appeal, which held that the privilege claim did not automatically breach fair trial rights and that the trial court’s review and requirement of corroboration were sufficient safeguards.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Donohoe complained under Article 6 that the non-disclosure of PK’s source material seriously restricted his defence rights and was not counterbalanced by adequate safeguards. He also alleged that the trial court’s in camera review was inadequate and that no effective safeguards were available to him. The key fair-trial issue was whether the secret review of undisclosed material, combined with reliance on belief evidence and inferences from silence, deprived him of a fair hearing.
001-119055:
Saint-Paul Luxembourg S.A., publisher of the Portuguese-language weekly *Contacto Semanário*, published an article on 17 December 2008 about families who had lost custody of their children. The article alleged that the Central Social Welfare Department (SCAS) had instigated the custody withdrawals. It named two teenagers and the social worker involved and disclosed sensitive details: the girl had reportedly suffered attempted rape and the boy had allegedly burnt a friend with a cigarette. The article was signed “Domingos Martins.” The official list of recognised journalists contained no such name, but included “De Araujo Martins Domingos Alberto,” who worked for *Contacto* and whose name contained all the elements of the pseudonym.

The social worker complained to the SCAS director, who complained to the Attorney General, alleging defamation of the social worker and of Luxembourg’s judicial and social system. A separate complaint followed on 5 January 2009. On 30 January 2009 the public prosecutor opened a judicial investigation for breach of section 38 of the Youth Welfare Act—which prohibited publishing facts likely to disclose the identity or personality of minors subject to youth measures—and for defamation or calumny. On 30 March 2009 an investigating judge issued a search and seizure warrant for the applicant company’s registered office as publisher. The warrant authorised seizure of “any documents and items, in whatever form and on whatever medium, connected with the offences charged,” including material identifying the article’s author or the *Contacto* employee who wrote it.

Police executed the warrant on 7 May 2009. The Government said the sole aim was to identify the author. The journalist handed over a copy of the newspaper, a notebook, documents, a computer file and a CD. He signed the search report. The applicant later claimed cooperation was forced, but an internal report indicated the journalist had no objection, the editor suggested giving an electronic version, and a police officer inserted a USB stick into the journalist’s computer while the applicant’s lawyer was present and did not object. The police report stated cooperation was voluntary, polite and without pressure, lasting 12–15 minutes, and that the items exonerated the journalist and did not mention sources. The domestic courts did not question the report’s accuracy.

The applicant and journalist sought annulment of the warrant and its execution. On 11 May 2009 the investigating judge discontinued the seizure and ordered the return of items. The *chambre du conseil* dismissed the annulment application, and the Court of Appeal upheld that decision on 27 October 2009. The applicant complained under Article 8 (right to respect for its “home,” including business premises) and Article 10 (freedom of expression).

The Government argued non-exhaustion, claiming the applicant should have sued the State under the 1988 State liability law. The Court dismissed this, finding no demonstrated effective remedy for challenging the necessity of an investigative measure.

On Article 8, the Court found the search and seizure interfered with the company’s registered office as its “home.” Although lawful and pursuing legitimate aims—preventing disorder and crime and protecting the rights of minors and the social worker—it was unnecessary. The pseudonym “Domingos Martins” closely matched De Araujo Martins Domingos Alberto on the official list, exclusively and linked to *Contacto*. Less intrusive steps could have confirmed the author’s identity. The search was therefore disproportionate.

On Article 10, the Court emphasised that protecting journalistic sources is a cornerstone of press freedom. The warrant’s broad wording allowed seizure of “any documents and items” connected with the offences, without narrow limits or safeguards; police alone assessed what to seize. Even if the aim was not to uncover sources, the broad warrant and USB insertion could access unpublished, source-identifying information. A narrower warrant limited to identifying the author would have sufficed. The search and seizure were disproportionate, violating both Article 8 and Article 10.

In *Saint-Paul Luxembourg S.A. v. Luxembourg* (Application no. 26419/10, 18 April 2013), the applicant was a Luxembourg company that published the Portuguese-language weekly *Contacto Semanário*. On 17 December 2008, *Contacto* published an article about families who had lost custody, allegedly involving the Central Social Welfare Department (SCAS). The article named two teenagers and the social worker handling their case, and was signed “Domingos Martins.” No journalist with that exact name appeared on Luxembourg’s official press list, but the list contained “De Araujo Martins Domingos Alberto,” who worked for *Contacto*. The social worker and SCAS complained that the article defamed the social worker and the judicial/social system and breached the Youth Welfare Act. On 30 January 2009, the public prosecutor opened a judicial investigation for defamation or calumny and breach of the Youth Welfare Act.

On 30 March 2009, an investigating judge issued a search and seizure warrant for the applicant’s registered office as publisher, seeking documents and items connected with the alleged offences, including material identifying the article’s author or the *Contacto* employee who wrote it. Police executed the warrant on 7 May 2009. The journalist gave them a copy of the newspaper, a notebook, documents, and an electronic copy of the article; a USB stick was inserted into his computer. A lawyer and the editor-in-chief were present. The police report said the cooperation was voluntary and aimed only at identifying the author; the applicant later claimed cooperation was effectively forced under threat of a search. On 11 May 2009, the investigating judge discontinued the seizure and ordered the return of the items. The applicant and journalist unsuccessfully sought annulment before the *chambre du conseil* and the Court of Appeal.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Article 8, claiming the search infringed its right to respect for its registered office as its “home,” and Article 10, claiming the measure interfered with freedom of expression and could expose journalistic sources. The Government contested admissibility for non-exhaustion and argued that the search was lawful, justified, necessary, and based on voluntary cooperation. The Court declared the application admissible, finding the Government had not shown an effective domestic remedy.

On Article 8, the Court held that a company’s registered office may constitute a “home” and that the search and seizure was an interference. Cooperation did not remove its intrusive character because refusal could have led to forced execution. Although the measure was in accordance with law and pursued legitimate aims—preventing disorder or crime and protecting the rights of others—it was not necessary. The author could likely be identified through the official journalists’ list, so a less intrusive measure should have been used first. The search was disproportionate.

On Article 10, the Court stressed that protecting journalistic sources is a cornerstone of press freedom. Though the Government denied seeking sources, the warrant’s broad wording—“any documents and items, in whatever form and on whatever medium”—gave police extensive access to unpublished material and potential source-identifying information. The USB procedure could also retrieve unrelated data. A narrower warrant aimed only at confirming authorship would have sufficed. The Court therefore found violations of Article 8 and Article 10.

**Case: Saint-Paul Luxembourg S.A. v. Luxembourg (Application no. 26419/10), ECtHR, 18 April 2013**

The applicant, Saint-Paul Luxembourg S.A., was a Luxembourg company that published the Portuguese-language newspaper *Contacto Semanário*. On 17 December 2008, *Contacto* published an article about families who had lost custody of their children, alleging that the Central Social Welfare Department (SCAS) had instigated the custody withdrawals. The article named a social worker and two teenagers and described sensitive details, including an attempted rape of the girl and the boy allegedly burning a friend with a cigarette. It was signed “Domingos Martins,” a name not appearing on the official list of recognised Luxembourg journalists. That list did, however, include “De Araujo Martins Domingos Alberto,” who worked for *Contacto*.

The social worker complained to the SCAS director, who complained to the Attorney General, alleging defamation of the social worker and the Luxembourg judicial and social system. The social worker also lodged a complaint. On 30 January 2009, the public prosecutor opened a judicial investigation for breach of section 38 of the Youth Welfare Act and defamation/calumny. On 30 March 2009, an investigating judge issued a search and seizure warrant for the applicant company’s registered office, as publisher of *Contacto*, to seize any documents or items connected with the alleged offences, including anything identifying the article’s author or the *Contacto* employee who wrote it.

On 7 May 2009, police executed the warrant at the newspaper’s premises. The Government claimed the sole aim was to identify the author. The journalist handed over a copy of the newspaper, a notebook, documents, a computer file and a CD. A police officer inserted a USB stick into the journalist’s computer; the applicant’s lawyer was present and did not object. The applicant later argued that cooperation was effectively forced because the warrant gave no real choice. The police report stated that the journalist cooperated voluntarily, without pressure, and that the search lasted 12–15 minutes. On 11 May 2009, the investigating judge discontinued the seizure and ordered the return of all items. The applicant and journalist unsuccessfully sought annulment of the warrant and its execution before the *chambre du conseil* and Court of Appeal.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 8 (right to respect for its “home,” including its registered office) and Article 10 (freedom of expression, including protection of journalistic sources). The Government objected that domestic remedies had not been exhausted, specifically an action for damages against the State under the 1988 Law. The Court dismissed that objection, finding the Government had not shown that remedy was effective for challenging the necessity of an investigative measure.

On Article 8, the Court held that the search and seizure interfered with the applicant’s “home.” Cooperation under threat of a search did not remove the interference. Although the measure was lawful and pursued legitimate aims—preventing disorder/crime and protecting others’ rights—it was not necessary or proportionate. The journalist’s identity could likely have been confirmed from the official list, given the name similarity and connection to *Contacto*. A less intrusive measure should have been tried first. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 8.

On Article 10, the Court emphasised that protecting journalistic sources is a cornerstone of press freedom. The warrant was too broad, covering “any documents and items, in whatever form and on whatever medium, connected with the offences charged.” This allowed access to unpublished information and possible source-identifying material. The USB insertion could retrieve unrelated data. Even if the aim was only to identify the author, the warrant was not sufficiently narrow. The search and seizure were disproportionate. The Court accordingly found a violation of Article 10.
001-119049:
**Summary of the Case**

The case of *Kristiansen and Tyvik AS v. Norway* (Application no. 25498/08) concerned a complaint against Norway regarding the excessive length of national patent proceedings and its impact on the applicants' right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

On 30 November 1990, the first applicant, Mr Arne Kristiansen, submitted a patent application (no. 19905214) to the Norwegian Industrial Property Office (NIPO) for a method of propulsion for aircraft and sea vessels. In March 1991, NIPO issued a preliminary opinion stating that the application was not patentable because it did not reveal a concrete solution to achieve the desired effect, and questioned whether the invention had any effect at all. NIPO required the applicant to perform practical tests at an independent research institute and submit test documentation. The applicant disputed the need for testing, citing high costs, and instead submitted theoretical views and a 1965 research report as evidence of the technical effect.

Between 1992 and 1994, correspondence continued regarding confidentiality and national security concerns. In February 1995, NIPO reiterated its request for test evidence. The applicant again refused, claiming tests were superfluous. He complained about delays in November 1996, and NIPO apologised and prioritised the matter. Despite further exchanges and the applicant's continued refusal to conduct tests, NIPO maintained its position and gave him until 5 November 1999 to comply. Having received no compliance, NIPO shelved the application in November 1999, though it later clarified in February 2000 that the application had been received on time but was shelved due to failure to meet substantive requirements.

Following a complaint to the Parliamentary Ombudsman, NIPO annulled its discontinuation decision in August 2001 but subsequently refused the application in October 2001 on the ground that the applicant had not made probable the alleged technical effect. The applicant appealed to NIPO's Board of Appeals in November 2001. The Board's first meeting occurred only in September 2004, after approximately thirty months of case file circulation. The Board took a different view from NIPO and indicated a possible patentable formulation limited to sea vessels, but the applicant was unwilling to amend the claims accordingly.

In November 2005, the Board set aside NIPO's decision, finding the invention had a technical effect, and referred the case back to NIPO for further consideration. NIPO then concluded in November 2005 that the subject-matter lacked novelty. Further correspondence and complaints to the Ombudsman followed. On 20 June 2007, NIPO formally refused the application due to lack of novelty. The applicants appealed again to the Board of Appeals, which confirmed the refusal on 22 September 2008, finding the application did not fulfil patent conditions as presented. The applicants did not challenge this decision before the Norwegian courts.

The total processing time was eighteen years. The Government conceded that NIPO was responsible for delays totalling nearly six years across specific periods. Critically, under section 40 of the Patents Act, patent protection would have expired twenty years from filing—on 30 November 2010—just over two years after the Board's final decision. The applicants argued that the excessive length of proceedings, combined with the twenty-year limitation, rendered their right of access to a court illusory. The Court agreed, finding that by the time the applicants could institute court proceedings, the patent protection period had effectively expired, impairing the very essence of their right of access to a court. This constituted a violation of Article 6 § 1.

**Summary of Kristiansen and Tyvik AS v. Norway**

The case of *Kristiansen and Tyvik AS v. Norway* (Application no. 25498/08) concerns a complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights regarding the excessive length of patent proceedings and its impact on the right of access to a court.

**Key Facts:**

On 30 November 1990, Mr. Arne Kristiansen (the first applicant) filed a patent application (no. 19905214) with the Norwegian Industrial Property Office (NIPO) for a method of aircraft and sea vessel propulsion. In March 1991, NIPO issued a preliminary opinion stating the application lacked a concrete solution and questioned whether the invention had any technical effect. NIPO required the applicant to perform practical tests at an independent research institute to demonstrate the invention's effect.

The applicant disputed the need for testing, citing high costs, and offered to test prototypes in NIPO's presence. From 1992 to 1994, correspondence continued regarding confidentiality, and NIPO confirmed the application need not be kept secret on national security grounds. NIPO reiterated its testing requirement multiple times (1995, 1996, 1999), which the applicant consistently contested, submitting theoretical views and academic statements instead.

In November 1999, NIPO discontinued examination due to the applicant's failure to comply with the testing deadline. After the applicant petitioned the Parliamentary Ombudsman, NIPO annulled its discontinuation decision in August 2001 but ultimately refused the application on 2 October 2001 for failure to demonstrate technical effect.

The applicant appealed to NIPO's Board of Appeals in November 2001. The Board first met on the case in September 2004—nearly three years later—and indicated a possible patent for sea vessels only, requiring claim modifications. The applicant was unwilling to make these changes. In November 2005, the Board set aside NIPO's decision and referred the case back for reconsideration. NIPO then refused the application again in June 2007 for lack of novelty.

A second appeal followed. On 22 September 2008, the Board of Appeals confirmed the refusal, finding the application lacked novelty for aviation but could have succeeded for sea transport if claims had been properly limited. The applicants did not challenge this decision in Norwegian courts.

**Relevant Violation:**

The applicants complained that the proceedings' excessive length—18 years—rendered their right of access to a court illusory. Under section 40 of the Patents Act, patent protection would have expired on 30 November 2010, twenty years from filing. Since the final administrative decision came only in September 2008, any court review would have been meaningless.

The Court found the administrative delays largely attributable to NIPO, with the Government conceding responsibility for nearly six years of delays. The Court held that the length of proceedings impaired the very essence of the applicants' right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1.

**Summary of Kristiansen and Tyvik AS v. Norway (Application no. 25498/08)**

The case of *Kristiansen and Tyvik AS v. Norway* concerns a complaint brought before the European Court of Human Rights regarding the excessive length of national patent proceedings and its impact on the applicants' right of access to a court. The first applicant, Mr. Arne Kristiansen, is a Norwegian national, and the second applicant, Tyvik A/S, is a Norwegian limited liability company.

The key facts center on a patent application filed by Mr. Kristiansen with the Norwegian Industrial Property Office (NIPO) on 30 November 1990. The application, numbered 19905214, was for a method of propulsion for aircraft and sea vessels. In March 1991, NIPO issued a preliminary opinion stating the application lacked a concrete solution and questioned its effect. NIPO required the applicant to perform tests at an independent research institute to demonstrate the invention's technical effect, pursuant to patent regulations.

A protracted dispute ensued. The applicant consistently refused to perform the required tests, citing high costs and arguing they were unnecessary. He instead provided theoretical views and statements from academics. Despite intermittent apologies from NIPO for delays, the core disagreement over testing remained unresolved for years. In November 1999, NIPO decided to shelve the application due to the applicant's failure to comply with a deadline to provide test evidence. This decision was later annulled following an inquiry by the Parliamentary Ombudsman, but NIPO ultimately refused the application in October 2001 for failure to demonstrate the alleged technical effect.

The applicant appealed to NIPO's Board of Appeals in November 2001. The appeal process itself was slow; the first meeting was not held until September 2004. The Board indicated that a modified patent claim might be patentable for sea vessels only, but the applicants were unwilling to amend their claims accordingly. In a decision of November 2005, the Board found the invention had a technical effect but referred the case back to NIPO for further consideration, without deciding on other patent requirements.

Following further exchanges, NIPO formally refused the application again in June 2007 due to a lack of novelty. A second appeal to the Board of Appeals was lodged. On 22 September 2008, the Board confirmed the refusal, concluding the application lacked novelty for aviation, though it might have succeeded for a limited area of sea transport if the claims had been amended. The applicants did not challenge this final administrative decision in the Norwegian courts.

The applicants complained to the European Court that the proceedings before NIPO and the Board of Appeals lasted approximately eighteen years. They argued that this excessive delay, combined with the twenty-year limitation on patent protection from the filing date under Norwegian law, rendered their right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention illusory, as any potential court remedy after the final administrative decision would be meaningless.

The Norwegian Government contested this, arguing that the applicants had failed to exhaust domestic remedies by not bringing the matter before Norwegian courts. They also attributed much of the delay to the applicants' own intransigence in refusing testing and amendments. The Court rejected the non-exhaustion plea, finding the government had not established an effective remedy. On the merits, the Court observed that the eighteen-year administrative processing time was exceptionally long. It accepted that while the applicants contributed to delays, NIPO was responsible for significant periods of inactivity. The Court found that the lengthy proceedings, coupled with the patent's twenty-year term expiring shortly after the final administrative decision, effectively impaired the very essence of the applicants' right of access to a court, amounting to a violation of Article 6 § 1.
001-118590:
Case of Trunk v. Slovenia (Application no. 41391/06, 18 April 2013) concerned a Slovenian national, Franc Trunk, who complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that domestic proceedings involving him exceeded a reasonable time, and under Article 13 that Slovenia lacked an effective domestic remedy for excessive length.

The case arose from two sets of proceedings. In the first set, the applicant was a public servant at the Centre for Educational and Extracurricular Activities. After being laid off following disciplinary proceedings, on 11 October 1996 he brought proceedings before the Ljubljana Labour and Social Court against the Ministry of Education and Sport and the Centre. He sought annulment of the termination of his employment contract and related rights and benefits. The proceedings became protracted. After the first hearing in February 1998, the first-instance court rejected his claim in December 1999. On appeal, in April 2002 the Ljubljana Higher Labour and Social Court partly upheld his appeal and remitted the case because a preliminary submission by the defendant had not been served on him, preventing him from commenting. In June 2002 the first-instance court issued a new judgment. It found the first-instance disciplinary decision lawful but the second-instance decision unlawful. It concluded that although the employment contract had been lawfully terminated, the termination decision became final only when the judgment became final; the applicant was therefore entitled to employment rights and benefits for the relevant period. Further appeals followed. In August 2004 the Higher Labour and Social Court dealt with appeal issues, including treating one request as a request for a supplementary judgment. The applicant pursued an appeal on points of law; after procedural rejection and a successful appeal, the Supreme Court rejected it on 25 October 2005. He then lodged a constitutional appeal. On 7 June 2006 the first-instance court issued another judgment, which was rejected on appeal in October 2006. On 12 February 2007 the Constitutional Court rejected his constitutional appeal.

In the second set of proceedings, the applicant’s former employer sued him in December 1996 for restitution of work-related material. That case involved transfers between courts, a counterclaim, a stay, jurisdictional decisions, hearings, partial judgments, appeals, and remittals, continuing until 2008.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged that the first set of proceedings had lasted too long and that no effective domestic remedy existed. The Court found the Article 6 § 1 period ran from 11 October 1996 to 12 February 2007—ten years and four months at four levels of jurisdiction. Applying the criteria of complexity, conduct of the applicant and authorities, and what was at stake, the Court held that the length was excessive and failed the “reasonable-time” requirement. On Article 13, the Court found the available remedies ineffective. The first set had been finally resolved before the 2006 Act entered into force but later continued before the Supreme and Constitutional Courts; similar to Kovinar, the Government gave no convincing reason to distinguish the case. The 2006 Act remedies were ineffective, and pre-2006 remedies were also ineffective under Lukenda. The second set was declared inadmissible because it was pending at second instance on 1 January 2007 and continued for more than three months, following Grzinčič and Nezirovič.

The Court therefore found violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 in respect of the first set of proceedings.

**Case: Trunk v. Slovenia (Application no. 41391/06), European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, Judgment of 18 April 2013.**

The applicant, Franc Trunk, a Slovenian national and former public servant at the Centre for Educational and Extracurricular Activities, was laid off after disciplinary proceedings. He complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that domestic court proceedings involving him had lasted excessively long, and under Article 13 that Slovenia lacked an effective domestic remedy for such delay.

**First set of proceedings (III Pd 489/96).** On 11 October 1996 the applicant sued the Ministry of Education and Sport and the Centre before the Ljubljana Labour and Social Court, seeking annulment of the termination of his employment and related rights and benefits. The first hearing was held in February 1998. After the applicant withdrew his claim against the Ministry, a decision was issued in September 1998. Between October 1998 and November 1999 several hearings took place, though two were postponed at the defendant’s request. In December 1999 the first-instance court rejected the applicant’s request. On appeal, the Ljubljana Higher Labour and Social Court in April 2002 partly upheld the appeal and remitted the case because a preliminary submission by the defendant had not been sent to the applicant. On remand, the first-instance court issued a judgment in June 2002, followed by a corrigendum in September 2002. The appeal court delivered judgment in August 2004; the Supreme Court rejected the applicant’s appeal on points of law in October 2005; and the Constitutional Court rejected his constitutional appeal on 12 February 2007. The proceedings thus lasted ten years and four months across four levels of jurisdiction. The Court noted that the applicant repeatedly lodged new requests concerning rights and benefits, but still found the overall length excessive. It declared this part admissible and, applying the criteria of complexity, conduct of the parties, and what was at stake, found a violation of the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1.

**Second set of proceedings (VP 371/96).** On 20 December 1996 the applicant’s former employer sued him before the Ljubljana District Court for restitution of work-related material. The case was transferred to the Piran District Court due to lack of jurisdiction. The applicant filed a counterclaim for computer updates and car expenses. The proceedings were stayed in January 2001 and resumed in April 2001. After the plaintiff withdrew the claim, the applicant pursued his counterclaim, and the case was transferred to the Ljubljana Labour Court. Hearings were held between 2002 and 2003; the first-instance judgment partly upheld the applicant’s request. On appeal, the Higher Labour and Social Court remitted the case in November 2004. In March 2007 the Labour Court again partly upheld the request, and the Higher Labour and Social Court delivered judgment in September 2008. Because these proceedings were still pending at second instance on 1 January 2007 and continued for more than three months, the Court declared the Article 6 and Article 13 complaints inadmissible under Article 35, following *Grzinčič v. Slovenia* and *Nezirovič v. Slovenia*; the applicant should have used remedies under the 2006 Act.

**Article 13 and conclusion.** As to the first set, the Court found that the domestic proceedings had been finally resolved before the 2006 Act but continued before the Supreme and Constitutional Courts. Following *Kovinar d.o.o. v. Slovenia*, the available remedies were ineffective. The Government offered no convincing distinction. The Court therefore found violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention concerning the excessive length of the first set of proceedings and the lack of an effective domestic remedy.

CASE OF TRUNK v. SLOVENIA (App. no. 41391/06) is a European Court of Human Rights judgment delivered on 18 April 2013 and final on 18 July 2013. The applicant, Franc Trunk, a Slovenian national born in 1957, complained under Article 6 § 1 that domestic proceedings involving him exceeded a reasonable time, and under Article 13 that Slovenia lacked an effective domestic remedy for excessive length.

The case concerned two sets of proceedings. The first, III Pd 489/96, arose from the applicant’s dismissal as a public servant at the Centre for Educational and Extracurricular Activities. On 11 October 1996 he sued the Ministry of Education and Sport and the Centre before the Ljubljana Labour and Social Court, seeking annulment of the termination of his employment contract and related rights and benefits. The first hearing was not held until 23 February 1998. In September 1998 he withdrew his claim against the Ministry. Between October 1998 and November 1999 hearings took place, some postponed at the defendant’s request. On 22 December 1999 the first-instance court rejected his claim.

On appeal, on 5 April 2002 the Ljubljana Higher Labour and Social Court partly upheld the appeal and remitted the case because a preliminary submission had not been served on the applicant. On 18 June 2002 the first-instance court held a hearing and issued judgment, finding the first-instance disciplinary decision lawful and the second-instance decision unlawful. It concluded that the employment contract had been lawfully terminated, but the termination became final only when the judgment became final; the applicant was therefore entitled to employment rights and benefits for the relevant period. The applicant appealed. After a corrigendum, on 27 August 2004 the Higher Labour and Social Court treated one request as a request for a supplementary judgment and rejected the remainder of the appeal. The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law, which was initially rejected on procedural grounds, then upheld on appeal and sent to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court rejected it on 25 October 2005. The Constitutional Court rejected the constitutional appeal on 12 February 2007. The first set of proceedings thus lasted from 11 October 1996 to 12 February 2007—ten years and four months across four levels of jurisdiction.

The second set, VP 371/96, began on 20 December 1996 when the applicant’s former employer sued him for restitution of work-related material. The case was transferred between courts, stayed and resumed, and included the applicant’s counterclaim after the plaintiff withdrew. Proceedings continued through 2008.

The Court declared the complaints concerning the second set inadmissible because those proceedings were pending at second instance on 1 January 2007 and continued for more than three months; under Grzinčič and Nezirovič, the Article 6 and Article 13 complaints were inadmissible. The first-set complaints were admissible. The Government failed to distinguish the case from Kovinar d.o.o. v. Slovenia, where remedies were ineffective for cases finally resolved before the 2006 Act but later continued before the Supreme and Constitutional Courts.

On the merits under Article 6 § 1, considering complexity, the conduct of the parties and authorities, and what was at stake, the Court found the length of the first proceedings excessive and contrary to the “reasonable-time” requirement. Under Article 13, it found that the applicant had no effective domestic remedy: he could not access compensation, the 2006 Act remedies were ineffective, and pre-2006 remedies were ineffective under Lukenda v. Slovenia. The Court accordingly found violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 13.
001-128204:
In *Putistin v. Ukraine* (App. no. 16882/03, ECtHR, 21 November 2013), the applicant, Vladlen Putistin, complained that Ukrainian courts refused to rectify allegedly defamatory information about his late father. His father, Mikhail Putistin, was a former Dynamo Kyiv footballer who played in the legendary 1942 “Death Match” between FC Start and a German Flakelf team. After FC Start’s victory, several players were arrested and sent to the Syrets concentration camp, where four were eventually executed.

In April 2001, the newspaper *Komsomolska Pravda* published an article titled “The Truth about the Death Match.” The article discussed a planned film about the match and included interviews with its future director and producer. It also reproduced a 1942 match poster containing players’ names. The article stated that the Start team had only four Dynamo players, who were executed, while “other players worked in the police, collaborated with the Gestapo.” The applicant’s father was not named in the text, and the names on the reproduced poster were illegible. The applicant argued that the article implied his father had collaborated with the occupying police and Gestapo, thereby damaging his father’s memory and the family’s reputation. He submitted archival evidence showing no information or criminal proceedings concerning his father’s alleged collaboration, while confirming his father had participated in the Death Match and been detained at Syrets.

The applicant sued the newspaper and journalist, seeking rectification and non-pecuniary damages. On 25 December 2001, the Obolonskyy District Court of Kyiv rejected the claim, finding that the applicant was not directly affected, that the article concerned a film script, and that it neither named his father nor alleged he had collaborated with the Gestapo. The Kyiv City Court of Appeal upheld that judgment on 13 March 2002, and the Supreme Court rejected a cassation appeal on 15 November 2002. The applicant also pursued proceedings against other newspapers, with some rectification orders issued, but the ECtHR focused on the *Komsomolska Pravda* proceedings.

Although the applicant invoked Articles 6 and 10, the Court considered the complaint under Article 8, concerning the right to respect for private and family life. The Government accepted that the reputation of a deceased relative could fall within Article 8 but argued that the domestic courts had struck a fair balance with freedom of expression under Article 10. The ECtHR noted that reputation is part of private life and that a deceased family member’s reputation may, in certain circumstances, affect a person’s private life and identity. The case therefore required balancing the State’s positive obligation to protect the applicant’s private life against the newspaper’s Article 10 rights.

On the merits, the Court found the article addressed a matter of public and cultural interest—the historical “Death Match” and a proposed film about it. It was neither provocative nor sensationalist. The applicant’s father was not named in the text, and his name on the poster photograph was illegible. The article did not suggest that he had collaborated with the Gestapo. Any adverse inference would require a reader to know independently that his name appeared on the original poster. Thus, the impact on the applicant’s Article 8 rights was indirect and remote. The domestic courts had reasonably concluded that he was not directly affected and that no allegation had been made against his father. Balancing the newspaper’s freedom of expression against the marginal interference with the applicant’s private life, the Court held that the domestic courts had not failed to strike an appropriate balance. It declared the complaint admissible but found no violation of Article 8. The judgment became final on 21 February 2014.

**Case: Putistin v. Ukraine (Application no. 16882/03), European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, judgment of 21 November 2013, final 21 February 2014.**

The applicant, Vladlen Mikhaylovich Putistin, a Ukrainian national born in 1934, was the son of Mikhail Putistin, a former Dynamo Kyiv footballer who played in the 1936 USSR championship and participated in the legendary 1942 “Death Match” between FC Start and a German team composed of Luftwaffe pilots, air-defence soldiers and airport technicians (“Flakelf”). FC Start won 5–3. The match allegedly led to reprisals: several players were arrested, sent to the Syrets concentration camp, and four were executed. In 2002 Kyiv commemorated the match’s 60th anniversary, attracting wide media coverage.

On 3 April 2001, the newspaper *Komsomolska Pravda* published an article titled “The Truth about the Death Match,” written by journalist O.M., about a planned film on the events. It included an interview with director A.S. and producer D.K., and reproduced a 1942 match poster containing players’ names, though the names were illegible in the newspaper reproduction. The article named four executed Dynamo players but did not name the applicant’s father. In one passage, D.K. stated that only four Dynamo players were in the Start team and “these [were the players who] were executed. And other [football] players worked in the police, collaborated with the Gestapo.”

The applicant claimed this falsely implied that his father had collaborated with the occupying police and Gestapo, damaging his father’s memory and his own reputation. In July 2001 he sued the newspaper and journalist for rectification and non-pecuniary damages. He submitted archival documents from Ukraine’s State Security Service and Kyiv Regional State Archives showing no information that his father had collaborated with the occupying police or Gestapo, and confirming that he had played in the Death Match and was detained at Syrets.

On 25 December 2001, the Obolonskyy District Court of Kyiv rejected the claim. It found that the applicant was not directly affected by the publication; the article concerned a film script; it did not mention the applicant or his father; and it made no allegation that his father had collaborated with the Gestapo. The Kyiv City Court of Appeal upheld that judgment on 13 March 2002, and the Supreme Court rejected a further appeal on 15 November 2002. Other defamation proceedings against different newspapers had varying outcomes, but the ECtHR complaint concerned only *Komsomolska Pravda*.

Although the applicant invoked Articles 6 and 10, the Court examined the substance under Article 8, the right to respect for private and family life. The Government accepted that the reputation of a deceased relative could, in certain circumstances, fall within Article 8, but argued that the article did not name the applicant’s father or allege his collaboration, and that a fair balance had been struck with freedom of expression.

The ECtHR declared the complaint admissible but found no violation. It accepted that reputation forms part of private life and that a deceased family member’s reputation may affect a person’s private life. However, the State’s positive obligation to protect reputation had to be balanced against Article 10. The article addressed a matter of public interest—the historical and cultural heritage of Dynamo Kyiv and the Death Match. It was neither provocative nor sensationalist. Although suggesting Gestapo collaboration was serious, the article did not refer to the applicant’s father; his name appeared only on an illegible poster. A reader could infer adverse conclusions only with outside knowledge that his father’s name was on the original poster. The interference was therefore indirect and remote. The domestic courts had not failed to strike an appropriate balance. There was no violation of Article 8.

**Putistin v. Ukraine (no. 16882/03)** concerned an alleged breach of the right to protection of reputation and family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Vladlen Putistin, was the son of Mikhail Putistin, a former Dynamo Kyiv footballer who participated in the legendary 1942 “Death Match” between FC Start and a German team. After the match, several FC Start players were arrested and sent to the Syrets concentration camp, where four were executed.

In April 2001, the newspaper *Komsomolska Pravda* published an article titled “The Truth about the Death Match,” concerning a planned film about the 1942 events. The article included an interview with the film’s director and producer. The producer was quoted as saying that only four Dynamo players were in the Start team and that those four were executed, while other players “worked in the police, collaborated with the Gestapo.” The article did not name the applicant’s father in the text. It also reproduced a 1942 match poster containing the players’ names, but the reproduction was illegible.

The applicant sued the newspaper and journalist, seeking rectification of allegedly false information and non-pecuniary damages. He claimed the article implied that his father had collaborated with the occupying police and Gestapo. In support, he submitted State Security Service and Kyiv archive documents showing no information that his father had collaborated with the occupying authorities, while confirming that he had played in the “Death Match” and had been detained at Syrets.

The domestic courts rejected the claim. The Obolonskyy District Court of Kyiv found that the applicant was not directly affected by the publication, that the article concerned a film script, that it did not name his father, and that it did not allege that his father had collaborated with the Gestapo. The Kyiv City Court of Appeal upheld that judgment, and the Supreme Court rejected a cassation appeal in November 2002. Separate proceedings against other newspapers had sometimes resulted in rectification concerning the applicant’s father, but not in the case against *Komsomolska Pravda*.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant invoked Articles 6 and 10, but the Court examined the complaint in substance under Article 8, concerning private and family life. The Government accepted that the reputation of a deceased relative could, in certain circumstances, fall within Article 8, but argued that the domestic courts had struck a fair balance with freedom of expression.

The Court declared the complaint admissible. On the merits, it accepted that a person’s reputation forms part of private life and that a deceased family member’s reputation may affect a living person’s private life. However, it found that the article did not suggest that the applicant’s father had collaborated with the Gestapo. Neither the producer’s quoted words nor the article itself referred to the applicant’s father. To draw such an inference, a reader would have needed to know that his name appeared on the original 1942 poster, but the published reproduction was illegible. The applicant was therefore affected only indirectly and remotely. The article concerned a matter of public and cultural interest—the historical “Death Match” and a proposed film—and was neither provocative nor sensationalist. Weighing the marginal and indirect effect on the applicant’s Article 8 rights against the newspaper’s and journalist’s Article 10 rights, the Court concluded that the domestic courts had not failed to strike an appropriate balance. It found no violation of Article 8. The judgment was delivered on 21 November 2013 and became final on 21 February 2014.

The case of *Bandaletov v. Ukraine* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr. Gennadiy Vitalyevich Bandaletov, a Ukrainian national, on 18 May 2006. The applicant alleged a violation of his right to a fair trial, specifically complaining that he had not been legally represented during the initial stage of the pre-trial investigation.

The underlying events began on the evening of 20 April 2005, when an elderly couple, Mr. and Ms. L., were murdered in their apartment. The applicant lived in the flat below them. On 21 April 2005, a criminal investigation was launched, and police questioned several individuals, including the applicant's stepson and wife, as well as the son of one of the victims. On that same day, the applicant himself was questioned by police and confessed to the double murder. He claimed a longstanding conflict with Ms. L. over noise from his flat refurbishment had culminated in a violent confrontation, during which he stabbed both victims. He also admitted to disposing of the knife, a broken stool, and his blood-stained T-shirt.

A critical fact relevant to the alleged violation is that this initial confession on 21 April 2005 was made without a lawyer present. The applicant was not formally arrested as a suspect until the following day, 22 April 2005, at 11:30 a.m. It is not recorded where the applicant was or whether he was in custody between the questioning on the 21st and his formal arrest on the 22nd; the applicant did not claim he was detained during this period.

Following his arrest on 22 April, a lawyer, Mr. T., was appointed for him. Approximately thirty minutes after the arrest, the applicant signed a report acknowledging that he had been informed of his defence rights. From noon to 1 p.m. that day, he was questioned again in the presence of his lawyer and confirmed his earlier confession. Later that afternoon, a videotaped crime reconstruction was conducted, again with his lawyer present, where he repeated his testimony and stated he was acting of his own free will. The applicant was subsequently formally charged on 29 April and continued to cooperate with the investigation, repeating his confession with his lawyer present.

At his trial, which began in August 2005, the applicant was represented by a new lawyer and maintained his confession, expressing sincere remorse. He was ultimately convicted and was serving a life sentence at the time of the European Court's judgment.

The central factual issue before the Court was therefore the lack of legal assistance during the applicant's first interrogation on 21 April 2005, a time when he was a suspect but had not yet been formally arrested or charged. The applicant's subsequent confessions were all made with a lawyer present, but his initial, unassisted confession formed a key part of the prosecution's case. The case hinges on whether this initial questioning, which yielded a confession later used at trial, violated his right to legal assistance under Article 6 of the Convention.

**Case: Bandaletov v. Ukraine (Application no. 23180/06), European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, judgment of 31 October 2013.**

The applicant, Mr Gennadiy Vitalyevich Bandaletov, a Ukrainian national born in 1961, was serving a life sentence. His principal complaint was that he had not been legally represented during the initial stage of the pre-trial investigation, specifically when he was first questioned and confessed.

On the evening of 20 April 2005, the applicant’s upstairs neighbours, Mr and Ms L., were killed in their apartment. On 21 April 2005, a criminal investigation was launched into the murders as having been committed by unknown persons. Police inspected the scene and questioned neighbours and relatives. The applicant’s stepson said he had seen the applicant drinking after midnight and noticed he had a black eye; he also mentioned conflicts in the victims’ family and that Mr L.’s son had previously served a prison sentence. The applicant’s wife said she had seen nothing suspicious. The victims’ son and his friend provided alibi statements.

The applicant was also questioned on 21 April 2005. Without a lawyer present, he confessed to the double murder. He described a longstanding dispute with Ms L. over noise and renovations. He said that on the evening of 20 April, after hearing Ms L. swearing and mentioning his name, he took a knife, went upstairs, argued with her, and stabbed her. When Mr L. attacked him with a stool, the applicant struck him with the stool and stabbed him. He then disposed of the knife, broken stool legs, and his blood-stained T-shirt. His statement noted that Article 63 of the Constitution had been explained. He signed each page and wrote that it had been accurately recorded from his words and that he was willing to repeat it in court. He also made an additional statement confirming his account and invoking Article 63 not to make further statements.

On 22 April 2005 at 11:30 a.m., the applicant was arrested as a suspect. About half an hour later, he and a lawyer, Mr T., appointed that day, signed a report confirming that he had been informed of his defence rights. From noon to 1 p.m., he was questioned in the lawyer’s presence and repeated his confession. From 2:40 to 4 p.m., a videotaped crime reconstruction took place with his lawyer present; he again confessed and said he was testifying freely. He was then placed in a temporary detention centre. Also on 22 April, his stepson gave further written explanations, stating that he had learned of the murder that morning and later noticed a kitchen knife missing.

On 29 April 2005, the applicant was formally charged with double murder. On 30 April, with his lawyer present, he again repeated his confession. The pre-trial investigation was then declared complete, and both he and his lawyer signed that they had studied the file and had no remarks. The trial began on 8 August 2005. On 25 August, he was represented by a new lawyer, Mr N., and maintained his confession, expressing remorse. On 5 September, his lawyer argued in mitigation that he had voluntarily confessed, shown remorse, cooperated, not absconded, had no previous record, and supported two minor children.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore the 21 April 2005 questioning without counsel, during which the applicant confessed, and the fact that he was not formally arrested until the following day, when a lawyer was appointed. All later investigative acts took place with legal representation, but the initial uncounselled confession formed the core of his complaint.

Case Bandaletov v. Ukraine (Application no. 23180/06) concerned criminal proceedings arising from a double murder. On 20 April 2005 the applicant’s upstairs neighbours, Mr and Ms L., were killed in their apartment. On 21 April 2005 a murder investigation was launched. Police inspected the scene and questioned neighbours and relatives, including the applicant. The applicant was questioned at the police station without a lawyer and confessed to killing both victims. He described a longstanding conflict with Ms L. over noise from refurbishment and a balcony roof. He said he heard swearing and his name mentioned, took a knife, went upstairs, argued and fought with Ms L., stabbed her, then killed Mr L. when attacked, and later disposed of the knife, stool legs and his blood-stained T-shirt. His statement noted that Article 63 of the Constitution, concerning the right not to incriminate oneself, had been explained. He signed each page, stated that the record was accurate and that he was willing to repeat his statements in court, and added a written statement confirming this and saying he did not wish to make further statements. It is unclear where he was between questioning on 21 April and arrest on 22 April; he did not allege that he was detained during that period.

On 22 April 2005 at 11:30 a.m. the applicant was arrested as a suspect. He wrote that he had no statements or complaints. About half an hour later, together with lawyer Mr T., who had been appointed earlier that day, he signed a report confirming that he had been informed of his defence rights. From noon to 1 p.m. he was questioned in the lawyer’s presence and signed a typed summary similar to his earlier confession. From 2:40 to 4 p.m. a videotaped reconstruction of the crime took place in the lawyer’s presence; the applicant repeated his confession and said he was testifying of his own free will. At 4:30 p.m. he was placed in the Kerch Temporary Detention Centre. Also on 22 April the applicant’s stepson gave further explanations: he had learned of the murder from police on the morning of 21 April, when he and the applicant were invited for questioning, and later noticed that a kitchen knife was missing. On 29 April the applicant was formally charged with double murder. On 30 April, with his lawyer present, he again repeated his confession. The pre-trial investigation was declared complete that day, and the applicant and his lawyer studied the file without remarks. The trial began on 8 August 2005. On 25 August he was represented by a new lawyer, Mr N., did not object, and maintained his confession and remorse. On 5 September his lawyer argued that he had voluntarily confessed, shown remorse, cooperated, not absconded, had no previous record, and had two minor children to support.

The alleged violation was that the applicant had not been legally represented during the initial stage of the pre-trial investigation, particularly when he first confessed on 21 April 2005, before formal arrest and before a defence lawyer had been appointed. The case therefore focused on whether the absence of counsel at that early questioning, and the subsequent use of his self-incriminating statements, breached his fair-trial rights under Article 6 of the Convention, including the right to legal assistance. The Court gave notice of the application to the Government on 9 September 2010. The applicant, granted legal aid, was represented by lawyers, and was serving a life sentence at Ladyzhynska Prison No. 39.

In *Orožim v. Slovenia* (Application no. 49323/06), the applicant, a Slovenian national born in 1939, complained under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights that domestic proceedings involving her had lasted excessively long, and under Article 13 that Slovenia lacked an effective domestic remedy for that delay.

The proceedings began in 1993, when DOMPLAN Kranj instituted enforcement proceedings against the applicant before the Kranj Basic Court. An enforcement order was issued on 20 April 1993. The Convention entered into force for Slovenia on 28 June 1994. The case was later transferred to the Radovljica District Court. In December 1994 the enforcement order was served on the applicant, who objected. In September 1995 the enforcement order was annulled and the matter was to be decided in contentious proceedings. In October 1995 the creditor lodged another enforcement request, and an enforcement order was issued later that month. The two cases were joined in January 1999. A hearing was held in April 2001, and in July 2001 the first-instance court upheld the creditor’s requests. The applicant appealed, but in April 2002 the Ljubljana Higher Court rejected the appeal.

In October 2002 the creditor sought enforcement of the July 2001 judgment, and an enforcement order was issued. The applicant objected and requested postponement of enforcement, expressing willingness to settle. Her objection was sent to the creditor only in September 2003, and the creditor responded in March 2004. In May 2006 the first-instance court held a hearing and decided on the objection; the creditor appealed. In March 2007, following an out-of-court settlement, the creditor requested termination of the proceedings, and the proceedings ended on 16 March 2007.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the Government argued that the enforcement proceedings and the contentious proceedings should be considered separately. The Court disagreed. It treated the proceedings as comprising three stages: initial enforcement proceedings, contentious proceedings ending with the first-instance judgment of 9 July 2001, and subsequent enforcement proceedings based on that judgment, ending on 16 March 2007. The Court reiterated that execution of a judgment is an integral part of the “trial” for Article 6 purposes. It therefore took the relevant period as beginning on 28 June 1994, when the Convention entered into force for Slovenia, and ending on 16 March 2007—a total of twelve years and nine months.

Applying the criteria of complexity, conduct of the applicant and authorities, and what was at stake, the Court observed that the longest period of inactivity attributable to the State ran from October 1995 to June 2001. The applicant herself contributed approximately two years of delay, from October 2002 to May 2006, by requesting postponement and failing to settle promptly. Nevertheless, the overall length of the proceedings was excessive and failed to satisfy the “reasonable-time” requirement under Article 6 § 1.

The Court also examined the complaint under Article 13 and recalled that Article 13 requires an effective domestic remedy for an alleged breach of the Article 6 § 1 reasonable-time guarantee. In light of its case law, including *Maksimovič v. Slovenia*, it found that the applicant did not have an effective domestic remedy and therefore found a violation of Article 13 as well. The application was declared admissible, and the Court concluded that Slovenia had violated both provisions.

Rousk v. Sweden concerned a Swedish national, Jim Rousk, who owned a close company and was required to file a special income tax return for tax year 2002 by 31 March 2002. He failed to do so. After he ignored an order to file, the Tax Authority made a discretionary assessment in November 2002, imposing taxes, tax surcharges and a delay charge totaling SEK 232,572, payable by 26 February 2003. He did not appeal or request respite at that time. Because tax debts to the State are immediately enforceable, the claim was sent to the Enforcement Authority in April 2003.

On 28 May 2003, the Enforcement Authority issued a writ of execution attaching the applicant’s site-leasehold right and the house where he and his wife lived. The property’s 2002 tax value was SEK 1,372,000, with a mortgage of SEK 960,200. The applicant apparently learned of the writ only in July or August 2003. On 10 August 2003, he appealed, arguing that the tax debt was not final, that he had not been served, that he would file his return, and that he had requested respite. He also claimed that selling his home would cause serious economic, social and medical consequences. He suffered from depression and was receiving antidepressants. The District Court rejected the appeal, and the Court of Appeal later refused leave to appeal.

Meanwhile, the applicant repeatedly asked for respite from payment and for a stay of the sale. On 3 September 2003, the Tax Authority granted him respite from the taxes and surcharges and registered the decision the same day. However, it did not directly notify the Enforcement Authority. The public auction took place on 3 September at 1:45 p.m.; the property was sold for SEK 1,600,000. The applicant later argued that the respite decision was registered at 2:02 p.m. and that the Enforcement Authority could have verified it during a pause in the bidding. A later re-assessment reduced the tax debt, though surcharges remained.

The applicant’s appeals against the sale and refusal to stay were unsuccessful. He was ordered to vacate by 1 October 2003 but refused. On 6 October 2003, the Enforcement Authority decided to evict him. His requests for respite, based on poor health and lack of alternative housing, were rejected. The eviction was enforced on 22 October 2003 with police and professional movers. Contents were stored, but some items were destroyed or thrown away; his cat and car were also removed. The eviction cost SEK 71,115. His appeals failed.

The distribution of the sale proceeds initially listed a tax debt of SEK 256,352, but was later corrected to SEK 6,721 because the Enforcement Authority knew of the respite, even though it was not registered in its database. The applicant ultimately received SEK 524,343 after debts and costs.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, concerning peaceful enjoyment of property, and Article 8, concerning respect for private and family life and home. The key facts were the attachment, auction sale and eviction of his home; the timing and communication of the Tax Authority’s respite decision; the proportionality of the enforcement measures; his health and housing situation; and the coordination between the Tax Authority and Enforcement Authority. The Government later offered a unilateral declaration of EUR 80,000, but the applicant objected and asked the Court to continue examining the case.

**Case of Rousk v. Sweden** (Application no. 27183/04) concerned a Swedish national, Jim Rousk, who alleged that enforcement measures taken by Swedish authorities violated his right to peaceful enjoyment of his property under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and his right to respect for his private and family life and home under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Rousk owned a close company and was required to file a special income tax return for the 2002 assessment year by 31 March 2002. After he failed to do so, the Tax Authority ordered him to file within two weeks. When he still did not comply, the Tax Authority prepared a discretionary assessment. Rousk did not comment on the proposal or appeal. In November 2002, the Tax Authority imposed taxes, tax surcharges and a delay charge totaling SEK 232,572, due by 26 February 2003. Rousk neither appealed nor requested respite from payment at that time. Because tax debts to the State are immediately enforceable, the claim was sent to the Enforcement Authority in April 2003.

On 28 May 2003, the Enforcement Authority issued a writ of execution attaching Rousk’s site-leasehold right and the house where he and his wife lived. The property’s tax value was SEK 1,372,000, with a mortgage of SEK 960,200. Rousk apparently learned of the writ only in July 2003. On 10 August 2003, he appealed, arguing that the tax debt was not final, that he had not been served, that he intended to file his return and had requested respite, and that selling his home was disproportionate given his and his wife’s serious depression. The District Court rejected the appeal, and the Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal.

The Enforcement Authority also decided to sell the property at public auction. Rousk requested a stay on 28 July 2003, citing illness, his pending respite request, and payment of another debt. The request was rejected, as was his later appeal. An independent valuation placed the property at SEK 1,850,000–2,150,000. At the public auction on 3 September 2003 at 1:45 p.m., it sold for SEK 1,600,000. On the same day, the Tax Authority granted Rousk respite from payment of the tax debt, registered at 2:02 p.m. The Enforcement Authority did not verify this before the auction. Rousk’s appeals against the sale failed.

Rousk refused to vacate by 1 October 2003. On 6 October, the Enforcement Authority ordered his eviction. His request for respite, based on poor health and lack of alternative housing, was rejected, and further appeals failed. On 22 October 2003, the eviction was enforced with police and movers. Some belongings were stored, but others—including food, flowers and a bed too large to remove—were destroyed or thrown away; his cat and car were also removed. Eviction costs amounted to SEK 71,115. His complaints about the eviction and destruction were rejected.

After the sale, the distribution protocol initially included the tax debt of SEK 256,352. Because of the respite, it was later corrected to SEK 6,721. Rousk ultimately received SEK 524,343 after mortgage, costs and debts were paid. He died in June 2011, and his wife continued the application. The Government offered a unilateral declaration of EUR 80,000, which the applicant opposed. The central alleged violations arose from the attachment, auction sale and eviction of Rousk’s home despite his illness, pending tax return and request for respite.

On 3 September 2003, the Tax Authority granted him respite and later re-assessed his income, reducing the tax and surcharges substantially.
