The applications were lodged in 2006–2007, joined, and given priority because the Court examined whether the delays reflected

**Vlad and Others v. Romania** (Applications nos. 40756/06, 41508/07 and 50806/07) concerned three Romanian nationals—Mihai Vlad, Flaviu Plaţa, and Vasilica Bratu—whose cases were joined by the European Court of Human Rights. The central alleged violations were the excessive length of criminal and civil proceedings under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and, for Plaţa and Bratu, the absence of effective domestic remedies under Article 13. The Court also examined whether the delays reflected a systemic problem in Romania.

**Mr Mihai Vlad** was taken into police custody in January 1994 on suspicion of first-degree murder and indicted in November 1994. His criminal proceedings were marked by repeated remittals between courts and prosecution authorities. In 1995 the case was sent back for further investigation; in 1996 he was convicted, but the appeal court quashed the judgment and remitted the case. He was convicted again in 1997, but in 1998 the High Court of Cassation and Justice sent the case back because the investigation was incomplete. A new indictment followed in 1999, then another conviction in 2000, which was again sent back by the High Court. In 2001 a further indictment was issued; after an impartiality request, the case was transferred to the Dolj County Court. He was convicted in 2003, but appeal proceedings were delayed by repeated failures to properly summon him. In 2005 the Court of Appeal rejected his appeal as time-barred; the High Court ordered a retrial, and the final dismissal occurred in April 2006. Thus, his criminal proceedings lasted over twelve years, with delays caused mainly by repeated remittals, investigative deficiencies, and procedural adjournments.

**Mr Flaviu Plaţa** faced a civil inheritance-division lawsuit filed in March 1997. The first-instance proceedings were delayed by difficulties in clarifying claims and paying stamp duty. The case was transferred to another Bucharest district court in 1998. Hearings were repeatedly adjourned because public authorities failed to submit court-ordered documents. The case was stayed in January 1999 and resumed in November 1999. Further delays arose over service of process in China and the annulment of procedural acts carried out without the applicant. A first-instance decision was given in December 2001. The appeal was delayed by a constitutional review (2002–2003) and an expert report. In November 2003 the appeal was dismissed, but in January 2005 the Court of Appeal allowed an appeal on points of law because the expert report had been prepared without the applicant. The case was remitted, then further delayed. A final decision on the merits came in June 2006, upheld in March 2007. The civil proceedings therefore lasted about ten years.

**Mrs Vasilica Bratu** was questioned in May 1998 on suspicion of misconduct in public office and indicted in June 1998. The district court rejected the prosecution’s forensic accounting report and ordered a new one, causing adjournments. She was convicted in July 2000. On appeal, the criminal conviction was upheld in June 2001, but the civil part was remitted. The civil appeal involved twenty-two hearings awaiting documents from the Ministry of Public Finance and prosecutors. In November 2004 the County Court increased compensation, but in January 2005 the Court of Appeal set aside the decision for insufficient evidence and remitted the case. The retrial was adjourned seventeen times due to improper service and missing documents; a prosecutor was fined, yet the documents arrived nineteen months later. The final decision came in May 2007, ending proceedings that had lasted nearly nine years.

The Government disputed admissibility, arguing that Plaţa had suffered no significant disadvantage and had not exhausted remedies, and that Bratu’s complaint regarding her criminal conviction was lodged out of time. The case also raised broader concerns about Romania’s structural delays and inadequate remedies.
001-117134:
Salakhov and Islyamova v. Ukraine (App. no. 28005/08, ECtHR, 14 March 2013) concerned complaints under Articles 2 and 3 ECHR. The first applicant, Mr Salakhov, was HIV-positive (diagnosed in 2005) but had not registered for monitoring. In November 2007 he was arrested and detained in an ITT and later a SIZO. He allegedly disclosed his HIV status; the authorities claimed he did not. Initial examinations found no complaints. From March 2008 his health deteriorated sharply, with high fever, digestive problems and weight loss. Detention doctors initially treated him for a respiratory infection. On 31 May an infectious disease specialist recommended an HIV test, but it was not carried out because of a transfer.

On 3 June a hospital diagnosed an ulcer, gastrointestinal hemorrhage and suspected HIV. On 5 June an infectious disease specialist diagnosed pneumocystis pneumonia, esophageal candidiasis and HIV at clinical stage IV, yet concluded there was no urgent need for hospitalisation. His lawyer applied for release on 6 June, but the court refused. A further specialist on 13 June also said urgent hospitalisation was unnecessary. On 16 June the applicants asked the European Court to indicate an interim measure under Rule 39. On 17 June the Court indicated that Mr Salakhov should be transferred immediately to a hospital or medical institution for appropriate treatment. Despite this, on 18 June a hospital doctor again stated that urgent hospitalisation was not required, and the domestic court rejected release.

On 20 June he was examined at the Aids Centre, which found HIV stage IV, systemic candidiasis, continuous fever, significant weight loss and a need for inpatient treatment. He was then placed in Central Hospital under police guard, allegedly handcuffed to his bed. On 26 June he was transferred to Hospital No. 7, where diagnoses included pneumocystis pneumonia, anaemia, severe immunosuppression and encephalitis. He remained handcuffed during treatment from 26 June to 18 July, although it was unclear whether this was constant. Antiretroviral therapy began on 10 July. On 18 July the security measures were lifted and his mother took him home; he was rehospitalised the next day, taken home again on 1 August, and died on 2 August 2008. His mother continued the application and added her own Article 3 complaint.

The alleged violations were: failure to provide prompt and adequate medical care in detention, jeopardising his life; failure to comply with the Rule 39 interim measure requiring immediate hospitalisation; handcuffing him in hospital; an ineffective domestic investigation into his death; and the mother’s own suffering under Article 3. Domestic investigations repeatedly refused criminal proceedings. A March 2009 health ministry commission blamed the delay in his seeking care and disease severity. However, a November 2010 forensic report found that the 5 June diagnosis had not reflected the severity of his condition and that urgent hospitalisation was required; it also found he required urgent hospitalisation on 18 June. In December 2010 the prosecutor opened a criminal investigation into alleged negligence by Central Hospital doctors, citing delayed hospitalisation as contributing to deterioration. The file contained no final outcome. Investigations concerning ITT/SIZO staff were repeatedly quashed and remitted for further inquiry.

In *Salakhov and Islyamova v. Ukraine* (ECtHR, no. 28005/08, 14 March 2013), the first applicant, Linar Salakhov, an HIV-positive Ukrainian national, was arrested in November 2007 and detained in an ITT and later SIZO pending criminal proceedings. He alleged that he informed investigators of his HIV status; the Government claimed he did not. Initial detention medical examinations recorded no complaints or visible health problems. However, from March 2008 his health allegedly deteriorated sharply, with high fever, digestive problems, and weight loss. Ambulance assistance was reportedly called repeatedly, but the nature of interventions remained unclear.

On 31 May 2008 a SIZO infectious disease specialist recommended an HIV test, scheduled for 2 June, but his transfer prevented it. On 2 June he complained of weakness, fever, and back pain; only antipyretics were given. On 3 June hospital tests led to diagnoses including ulcer, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, chronic bronchitis, and suspected HIV. On 5 June an infectious disease specialist diagnosed HIV at the fourth clinical stage, pneumocystis pneumonia, and oropharyngeal/esophageal candidiasis. Although he was assessed as “moderately severe” and needing treatment, the doctor concluded there was no urgent need for hospitalisation.

On 6 June his lawyer requested release because his life was in danger, but the court refused. On 13 June another specialist revised the diagnosis to HIV stage 2 and again said urgent hospitalisation was unnecessary; further tests were ordered. On 16 June the applicants asked the European Court to indicate an interim measure under Rule 39. On 17 June the Court indicated that Salakhov “should be transferred immediately to a hospital or other medical institution” for appropriate treatment. On 18 June his lawyer again sought release citing Rule 39, but the hospital’s chief doctor stated he did not require urgent hospitalisation, and the court rejected release.

On 20 June the Aids Centre diagnosed HIV stage 4, systemic candidiasis, continuous fever, intoxication, and over 15% weight loss, and concluded he required inpatient treatment. He was transferred to Central Hospital under police guard and allegedly handcuffed to his bed. On 26 June he was moved to Hospital No. 7, where diagnoses included pneumocystis pneumonia, severe immunosuppression (CD4 count 48), anaemia, and encephalitis. He remained handcuffed from 26 June to 18 July 2008. On 4 July he was convicted of fraud and fined, but remained detained until the judgment became final. Antiretroviral therapy began on 10 July; he allegedly refused medication on one occasion. On 18 July security measures were lifted and his mother took him home, but he was rehospitalised the next day due to deterioration. He died on 2 August 2008.

The domestic investigation into his death involved repeated refusals and reversals. A 2010 forensic report found that the 5 June and 18 June 2008 conclusions—that urgent hospitalisation was unnecessary—were incorrect and that by 18 June he required urgent inpatient treatment. In December 2010 a criminal investigation was opened into alleged negligence by Central Hospital doctors, while investigations concerning ITT/SIZO staff were repeatedly refused or remitted.

The applicants alleged violations of Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention: failure to provide prompt and adequate medical care in detention, jeopardising Salakhov’s life; failure to comply with the Rule 39 interim measure; his handcuffing in hospital; the lack of an effective domestic investigation into his death; and the mother’s own suffering under Article 3.

In *Salakhov and Islyamova v. Ukraine* (ECtHR, Fifth Section, App. no. 28005/08, judgment 14 March 2013), the first applicant, Linar Salakhov, was HIV-positive, having tested positive in September 2005 and been informed in February 2006, but he did not register for medical monitoring. On 20 November 2007 he was arrested on suspicion of robbery and detained in the Bakhchysaray police temporary detention facility and later Simferopol Pre-Trial Detention Centre (SIZO). Initial medical examinations recorded no health complaints.

From March 2008 his health allegedly deteriorated sharply, with high fever, digestive problems and weight loss. In late May 2008 he was diagnosed with an acute respiratory viral infection. On 31 May an infectious disease specialist noted fever and weight loss over two months and recommended an HIV test, scheduled for 2 June, but his transfer prevented it. On 2 June he complained of weakness, fever and back pain. On 3 June hospital tests led to diagnoses including ulcer, gastrointestinal haemorrhage, haemorrhoids, chronic bronchitis and suspected HIV. On 5 June an infectious disease specialist diagnosed pneumocystis pneumonia, oropharyngeal/oesophageal candidiasis, ulcer and HIV at clinical stage IV, but concluded there was no urgent need for hospitalisation. His lawyer’s request for release was refused.

On 13 June another doctor concluded HIV stage II and no urgent hospitalisation. On 16 June the applicants asked the European Court to indicate an interim measure under Rule 39. On 17 June the Court indicated that Salakhov “should be transferred immediately to a hospital or other medical institution” for appropriate treatment. The Government was notified the same day. On 18 June, despite the Rule 39 indication, the Chief Doctor again stated that urgent hospitalisation was not required, and the domestic court refused release.

On 20 June the Aids Centre found HIV stage IV, systemic candidosis, continuous fever, intoxication, significant weight loss and seborrheic dermatitis, requiring inpatient treatment. He was transferred to Central Hospital under police guard, allegedly handcuffed to his bed. From 26 June to 18 July he was treated in Hospital no. 7; official correspondence confirmed he was handcuffed there during treatment, though whether constantly was unclear. On 4 July he was convicted of fraud, fined, but remained detained pending final judgment. Antiretroviral therapy began on 10 July. On 18 July security measures were lifted and his mother took him home; he was rehospitalised the next day and died on 2 August 2008.

After his death, the second applicant complained about lack of timely adequate medical care. Investigations were repeatedly refused and reopened. A Ministry of Health commission blamed the delay in seeking care after HIV diagnosis and the severity of the disease, finding no link between treatment/conditions and death. However, a November 2010 forensic report found that the 5 June diagnosis had not been based on a thorough examination and that the conclusion that urgent hospitalisation was unnecessary did not correspond to the diagnoses; pneumocystis pneumonia alone warranted urgent inpatient care. It also found that by 18 June he required urgent hospitalisation. In December 2010, a criminal investigation was opened into alleged negligence by Central Hospital doctors, stating delayed hospitalisation contributed considerably to deterioration. Investigation into detention facility staff was refused, later quashed and remitted, with no final outcome shown.

The applicants alleged violations of Articles 2 and 3: failure to provide prompt, adequate medical care in detention; failure to comply with the Rule 39 interim measure requiring immediate hospitalisation; inhuman handcuffing in hospital; ineffective domestic investigation into the death; and the mother’s own suffering under Article 3.

**Case Summary: Klinovská v. Slovakia (Application no. 61436/09)**

**Parties and Background**
The applicant, Ms. Margita Klinovská, a Slovak national born in 1969, filed an application against the Slovak Republic on 10 November 2009. The case concerned the excessive length of civil proceedings she initiated on 15 November 2004. The applicant sought damages from the Ministry of Finance and several other public authorities for financial losses incurred from failed investments in private non-banking institutions. These institutions operated in Slovakia during the 1990s, soliciting public funds with promises of high returns before collapsing. The applicant argued that the defendants failed in their supervisory duties, thereby enabling the institutions' illicit activities and making them liable for her losses.

**Proceedings Before Domestic Courts**
The domestic proceedings were procedurally complex. Throughout the case, the applicant submitted new evidence, was asked to provide further particulars, and requested to add more defendants, eventually bringing the total to eight. The first hearing on the merits was not held until 15 March 2012, over seven years after the action was lodged. Two more hearings followed, and on 9 November 2012, the Bratislava I District Court discontinued proceedings against three defendants and dismissed the action against the others. The applicant appealed, and this appeal was still pending at the time of the European Court's judgment. The total duration of the proceedings before domestic courts, spanning two levels of jurisdiction, exceeded eight years and seven months.

**Complaints Regarding Delays**
In response to the protracted proceedings, the applicant first complained to the President of the District Court on 16 March 2009. In an April 2009 response, the President acknowledged undue delays, attributed them mainly to objective factors, apologized, and instructed the presiding judge to prevent further delays while monitoring the case's progress.

Subsequently, on 25 May 2009, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint, alleging a violation of her right to a hearing within a reasonable time. On 11 June 2009, the Constitutional Court declared her complaint inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded. It reasoned that her complaint to the District Court President had proven to be an effective remedy, as the President had reacted adequately and taken necessary measures. The Constitutional Court stated that the District Court was proceeding properly and advised that any future delays could be raised in a new constitutional complaint without needing to first address the President.

**Violations Alleged and Court’s Findings**
Before the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR), the applicant alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial within a reasonable time) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the Convention. The Government argued that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies, both by not meeting formal requirements for her constitutional complaint and by not seeking damages under the State Liability Act.

The ECtHR dismissed the Government's objections, citing its prior judgments in similar cases (*Ištván and Ištvánová v. Slovakia* and *Komanický v. Slovakia (no. 6)*). The Court found the application admissible, noting the proceedings had lasted over 8 years and 7 months. Assessing the merits, the Court considered the case's complexity, the conduct of the parties, and what was at stake. It concluded that the length of the proceedings was excessive and failed to meet the "reasonable time" requirement, thus violating Article 6 § 1.

Consequently, given its conclusions on the failure to exhaust domestic remedies for the Article 6 complaint, the ECtHR also found a violation of Article 13, as the applicant lacked an effective domestic remedy for the length of the proceedings.

In *Klinovská v. Slovakia* (Application no. 61436/09), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered judgment on 8 October 2013. The applicant, Margita Klinovská, a Slovak national born in 1969 and living in Rabčice, complained under Articles 6 § 1 and 13 of the Convention that her civil proceedings had lasted unreasonably long and that she had no effective domestic remedy for that delay.

The underlying dispute began on 15 November 2004, when Klinovská lodged an action for damages with the Bratislava I District Court against the Ministry of Finance and three other public authorities; the number of defendants eventually stabilized at eight. She relied on the State Liability Act. Her claim arose from a failed investment with two private non-banking investment institutions that had operated in Slovakia in the 1990s. Those institutions had solicited and accepted money from the public on a large scale, promising unusually high returns through private-law contracts outside the banking and investment sectors, and eventually collapsed. Klinovská alleged that the defendant public authorities had failed to exercise their supervisory functions, thereby enabling the institutions to carry on illicit activities, and were therefore liable for her financial loss.

The proceedings were marked by significant delay and procedural activity. The applicant submitted new evidence, was repeatedly asked to provide further particulars, did so, and sought to add defendants. Observations were obtained, and at one point fresh observations were needed because of an error in the District Court’s summonses. Two levels of jurisdiction were involved. The first hearing on the merits was not held until 15 March 2012. Two further hearings followed. On 9 November 2012, the District Court discontinued proceedings as against three defendants and dismissed the action against the remaining defendants. The applicant appealed, and that appeal was still pending at the time the ECtHR examined the case. The period under review therefore began on 15 November 2004 and had not ended, lasting more than eight years and seven months for two levels of jurisdiction.

As to domestic remedies, on 16 March 2009 the applicant complained about delays to the President of the District Court. In a letter of 16 April 2009, the President acknowledged undue delays, attributed them mainly to objective factors, apologized, instructed the judge to avoid further delays, and said she would monitor the case. On 25 May 2009 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint under Article 127 of the Constitution, alleging violation of her right to a hearing within a reasonable time. On 11 June 2009 the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded. It held that her complaint to the President had been effective, that the President had reacted adequately, and that any further delays could be raised anew in the Constitutional Court without first complaining to the President again.

The Government argued that the applicant had failed to exhaust effective remedies, both because her constitutional complaint did not comply with formal requirements and because she had not sought damages under the State Liability Act. The ECtHR rejected those objections, relying on its earlier judgments in *Ištván and Ištvánová v. Slovakia* and *Komanický v. Slovakia (no. 6)*. It declared the application admissible. On the merits, the Court found that the length of the proceedings was excessive and failed the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1. Given its findings on exhaustion, it also found a violation of Article 13 because the applicant had not had an effective domestic remedy for the length complaint.

She sued the Ministry of Finance and three other public authorities, later expanding the number of defendants to eight. Those institutions had operated in Slovakia in the 1990s, soliciting money from the public on a large scale by promising unusually high returns under private-law contracts outside the banking and investment sectors, before collapsing. The applicant argued that the defendant public authorities had failed to exercise their supervisory functions, thereby enabling the institutions to carry out illicit activities, and were therefore liable for her loss.

The civil proceedings were lengthy and procedurally complex. The applicant repeatedly submitted new evidence, was asked to provide further particulars of her claim, and requested that additional defendants be joined. The number of defendants eventually stabilised at eight. On the merits, applying the criteria of complexity, conduct of the parties, and what was at stake, the Court held that the length of the proceedings was excessive and failed to satisfy the “reasonable time” requirement, violating Article 6 § 1. Since the domestic remedies were also ineffective for the delay complaint, the Court found a further violation of Article 13.

In *Slyusar v. Ukraine* (Application no. 39797/05, judgment of 17 January 2013), the European Court of Human Rights examined the applicant’s complaint that Ukraine failed to conduct an effective investigation into his twin brother Se.’s death. The Court considered the allegation under the procedural limb of Article 2 of the Convention.

The key facts concerned Se.’s disappearance between 16 and 17 April 2003. On 15 April 2003, Se. had made a will in the applicant’s favour, leaving him an apartment and other property. The applicant spoke to Se. by telephone around 8 p.m. on 16 April and they agreed to meet the next day, but Se. could not be reached thereafter. Se. had continued to share an apartment with his former wife, G., despite a sham divorce. G. stated that she did not know whether Se. was at home when she left on the morning of 17 April. Friends who visited the apartment claimed the carpet was missing, that Se.’s son, S., had a wound on his hand, and that G. and S. appeared very nervous.

On 18 April 2003, the applicant and G. reported Se.’s disappearance to the police. Police examined the apartment on 18, 22, and 23 April, seizing stained wallpaper, traces of a brown substance from a radiator and door, a bathroom pipe, a stool, a T-shirt, S.’s running shoes and trousers, property deeds, cash, and Se.’s passport. On 26 April, police refused to open criminal proceedings for lack of evidence. On 20 May, a prosecutor quashed that decision and opened proceedings on suspicion of kidnapping. Neighbours testified that between 2 and 3 a.m. on 17 April they heard a water heater, running water, and sounds resembling cleaning. Forensic examinations were inconclusive: some items had no blood; blood on the door may have been female; blood on the radiator and wallpaper possibly belonged to S. or G., but a later examination excluded both. S. and G. were arrested in July 2003 but released and proceedings against them terminated. In August, the kidnapping case was suspended; in October it was reclassified as murder, with authorities noting it appeared Se. had been killed. The applicant was recognized as a victim in December 2003.

The investigation was repeatedly criticised. The Prosecutor General’s Office found delays, tactical mistakes, unsubstantiated decisions to drop the case, chaotic conduct, failure to preserve evidence, and failure to verify the applicant’s allegations against G., S., and M. M. was first questioned only in 2006; he claimed G. had told him S. killed Se. with a dumbbell, cut up the body, and hid it. S. denied this. The case was transferred many times and handled by sixteen different investigators. Lie-detector records were lost. S. left for Australia in 2008. Se.’s body was never found, and the proceedings remained pending. The applicant alleged that the authorities failed to act promptly, did not secure evidence, delayed critical steps, and did not sufficiently involve him. The Government argued that the investigation had been diligent, but the Court found that the procedural obligation under Article 2 had been violated because the investigation into Se.’s death was ineffective.

In *Slyusar v. Ukraine* (Application no. 39797/05, judgment of 17 January 2013), the European Court of Human Rights examined a Ukrainian applicant’s complaint that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into his twin brother Se.’s suspected death. The applicant alleged that Se. was killed by his former wife G. and son S. on the evening of 16 April 2003 in their apartment, that S. removed and hid the body with M.’s help, and that G. and S. avoided prosecution through bribery. The Court considered the complaint under the procedural limb of Article 2 of the Convention.

The underlying facts were suspicious. On 15 April 2003 Se. made a will in the applicant’s favour, covering an apartment and other property. He disappeared between 16 and 17 April. The applicant last spoke to him by phone around 8 p.m. on 16 April. G., who continued sharing the flat after a sham divorce, said Se. was using the phone when she went to bed but she did not know whether he was home the next morning. On 17 April, friends noticed a missing carpet and a wound on S.’s hand; G. and S. appeared nervous. The applicant and G. reported the disappearance on 18 April.

Police searched the apartment on 18, 22 and 23 April, seizing stained wallpaper, brown traces from a radiator and door, a bathroom pipe, a stool, S.’s T-shirt, shoes and trousers, property deeds, cash and Se.’s passport. On 26 April police refused to open criminal proceedings for lack of evidence. On 20 May the prosecutor quashed that decision and opened a kidnapping case. Neighbours later testified they heard running water and cleaning sounds from Se.’s flat between 2 and 3 a.m. on 17 April. Forensic tests in June–July 2003 were inconclusive: no blood was found on some items, blood on S.’s shoes was unidentifiable, and findings concerning blood on the wallpaper and radiator were conflicting.

S. and G. were arrested on 9 July 2003 but released on 18 July, and proceedings against them ended on 21 July. The kidnapping case was suspended in August and reclassified as murder on 15 October 2003. The applicant was recognised as a victim in December 2003. The investigation was repeatedly criticised. Officers were disciplined; the case was transferred between authorities, including to Zhytomyr and back; by 2005 the applicant said sixteen investigators had handled it. In January 2006 the General Prosecutor’s Office found the investigation improper, chaotic and delayed, saying the applicant’s allegations against S., G. and M. had not been properly checked, witnesses were questioned perfunctorily, and the possible financial motive was not investigated.

M. later claimed G. had told him S. killed Se. with a dumbbell, cut up the body and hid it. Confrontations followed, and S. was briefly arrested in February 2006. Lie-detector records were reportedly lost. S. left for Australia in 2008. Se.’s body was never found, and the proceedings remained pending.

The Government argued the authorities had acted diligently and that insufficient evidence existed to charge anyone. The applicant argued the investigation was not proactive, was delayed and chaotic, failed to secure evidence, and did not allow him effective participation. The Court declared the complaint admissible and assessed whether Ukraine had complied with its Article 2 duty to conduct an effective official investigation where death occurs in suspicious circumstances. It ultimately found a violation of the procedural limb of Article 2.

**Slyusar v. Ukraine** (Application no. 39797/05) concerned the applicant’s complaint that Ukraine failed to conduct an effective investigation into the disappearance and presumed death of his twin brother, Se. In April 2003 Se. made a will in the applicant’s favour, leaving him an apartment and other property. Se. disappeared between 16 and 17 April 2003 while living with his former wife, G., and son, S. The applicant last spoke to him by phone at about 8 p.m. on 16 April and arranged to meet the next day, but his brother did not answer calls the following morning. G. said Se. had been using the phone when she went to bed, but because they slept in separate rooms and his door was closed, she did not know whether he was home when she left on 17 April.

On the evening of 17 April, friends visiting the flat noticed the carpet was missing, that S. had a wound to his hand, and that G. and S. seemed very nervous. The applicant and G. reported Se.’s disappearance on 18 April 2003. Police examined the flat on several occasions and seized stained wallpaper, traces of a brown substance from a radiator and door, a bathroom pipe, a stool, a T-shirt, S.’s shoes and trousers, deeds for apartments, cash, and Se.’s passport. On 26 April the police refused to open criminal proceedings for lack of evidence. On 20 May the prosecutor quashed that decision and opened a kidnapping investigation, which was later replaced by a murder investigation on 15 October 2003 after authorities concluded Se. had likely been killed. The applicant was recognised as a victim in December 2003.

The investigation was repeatedly criticised as ineffective. Neighbours said they heard water and cleaning sounds in the early hours of 17 April, but a later reconstruction found those sounds could not have been heard from the neighbours’ flat. Forensic examinations were inconclusive or contradictory: no blood was found on several seized items, blood on S.’s shoes could not be attributed, and wallpaper stains initially possibly linked to S. or G. were later excluded. G. and S. were arrested in July 2003 but released, and proceedings against them were terminated. S. underwent a lie-detector test in 2005, but the results were allegedly lost. M., a friend of G., was first questioned only in 2006 and claimed G. had told him S. killed Se. with a dumbbell, cut up the body, and hid it; S. denied this. S. was briefly arrested in 2006 and later left for Australia in 2008. Se.’s body was never found.

The prosecution service repeatedly found serious shortcomings: unjustified refusals to investigate, delays, tactical mistakes, chaotic handling, frequent transfers between investigators—reportedly sixteen—failure to preserve evidence, and failure to properly check the applicant’s allegations against G., S., and M., including a possible financial motive. Disciplinary sanctions were imposed on some officers. Relying on Articles 2, 6, 8 and 13, the applicant alleged that the investigation was ineffective, delayed, failed to secure evidence, and did not involve him adequately. He also claimed S. and G. escaped prosecution through bribery, though this was unsubstantiated. The Government argued that authorities acted diligently and that no charges were brought because evidence was insufficient. The Court examined the central complaint under the procedural limb of Article 2, which requires an effective official investigation where death occurs under suspicious circumstances, and declared it admissible.

In *Rooney v. Ireland*, the applicant, John Rooney, an Irish farmer and barrister, complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that two civil actions he brought in 1987 and 1995 had exceeded the “reasonable time” requirement, and under Article 13 that Ireland provided no effective domestic remedy for that delay.

The 1987 proceedings arose after some of Rooney’s cattle were destroyed under a Government scheme to eradicate Bovine Tuberculosis. In November 1987 he began a High Court action challenging the scheme’s constitutionality. The litigation became procedurally complex, involving partial discovery, repeated amendments to pleadings, motions to join defendants, applications for judgment in default of defence, strike-out applications, and a special case referred by the Supreme Court. In December 1991 the Supreme Court rejected appeals nos. 111/1990 and 224/1991, but it failed to determine the part of appeal no. 111/1990 concerning the refusal of judgment in default of defence. Over the following decade Rooney sought to reopen the appeals because of that omission. In 2001 the Supreme Court refused his motions and made a vexatious litigant order against him. In 2007 the High Court refused to hear a motion to amend his statement of claim because of that order. In March 2010 the Supreme Court found that claims outside the special case could still proceed and that the High Court’s 2007 refusal was incorrect. It also accepted that there had been a clear “oversight” in failing to determine the default-judgment part of appeal no. 111/1990 and said it would hear submissions on how to deal with it most quickly. The 1987 action began on 19 November 1987 and had still not ended by the time of the Strasbourg judgment, lasting almost 26 years across two levels of jurisdiction.

The 1995 proceedings concerned the restriction of Rooney’s herd under the same TB scheme from April 1993 to July 1996. In November 1995 he began a High Court action alleging that the restriction was unlawful and that the scheme was contrary to statute, the Constitution, the Convention, and EU law. Discovery was obtained in 1997. A Notice to Admit Facts was served in 2002 and refused. A Notice of Trial was served in December 2002. The High Court heard the action over ten days in May and June 2004 and dismissed his claims in July 2004. Rooney appealed in August 2004. He filed written submissions in July 2006 and a Certificate of Readiness in January 2007. In May 2009 the Registrar stated that the waiting time after certification was 31 months and no hearing date had been allocated. The appeal was eventually heard in October 2009. After judgment in another appeal was delivered in March 2010, the Supreme Court initially treated the 2004 appeal as covered by that judgment, but the State Solicitor agreed it had been omitted. The appeal was finally dismissed on 18 November 2010. The 1995 action thus lasted 15 years for two levels of jurisdiction.

Rooney alleged that both delays violated Article 6 § 1 and that he had no effective domestic remedy under Article 13. The Government argued that delay stemmed mainly from Rooney’s own numerous motions. The Court declared the application admissible. Applying the criteria of complexity, conduct of the applicant and authorities, and what was at stake, it found that although Rooney made many applications, significant delay was also caused by structural delays before the Supreme Court and by errors that court accepted it had made. Relying on *McFarlane v. Ireland*, the Court held that the length of both proceedings was excessive, violating Article 6 § 1, and that there was no effective domestic remedy, violating Article 13.

The case *Rooney v. Ireland* (ECHR, 2013) concerns John Rooney, an Irish national, farmer and barrister, who complained that two civil actions he began in 1987 and 1995 were not determined within a reasonable time, contrary to Article 6 §1 of the Convention, and that Ireland lacked an effective domestic remedy for that delay, contrary to Article 13.

The 1987 proceedings arose after some of Rooney’s cattle were destroyed under a Government scheme to eradicate bovine tuberculosis. In November 1987, he brought a High Court action challenging the scheme’s constitutionality. The case involved numerous procedural steps: discovery, repeated amendments, joinder motions, and multiple hearings. In 1990, the High Court refused his motions for judgment in default of defence, struck out his case against some defendants, and refused to appoint a shorthand writer. Rooney appealed to the Supreme Court. A special case was directed to the High Court, which was rejected in 1991; the Supreme Court then rejected the related appeals in December 1991. However, it failed to deal with the High Court’s refusal of judgment in default of defence. Over the next decade, Rooney sought to reopen the appeals. In 2001, the Supreme Court made a vexatious litigant order against him. In 2010, the Supreme Court accepted that there had been a clear “oversight”: the part of appeal no. 111/1990 concerning default judgment had not been determined and still could be. Thus, the 1987 action had lasted almost 26 years for two levels of jurisdiction and had not been shown to have ended.

The 1995 proceedings concerned restrictions placed on Rooney’s cattle herd from April 1993 to July 1996 under the same TB scheme. In November 1995, he sued State defendants, claiming the herd restriction was unlawful and that the scheme breached statute, the Constitution, the Convention, and EU law. Discovery was ordered in 1997. In 2002, he served a Notice to Admit Facts, which the Chief State Solicitor refused, and then a Notice of Trial. The High Court heard the action over ten days in 2004 and dismissed his claims. Rooney appealed in August 2004. He filed written submissions in 2006 and a Certificate of Readiness in January 2007. In 2009, the Registrar stated that the waiting time after certification was 31 months. The appeal was eventually heard in October 2009 together with another appeal. In March 2010, the Supreme Court gave judgment only on the other appeal; later it claimed the 2004 appeal was covered. The State Solicitor agreed it had been omitted. After further listings, the Supreme Court finally dismissed the 2004 appeal on 18 November 2010. That action therefore lasted 15 years for two levels of jurisdiction.

The Government argued that the delay was mainly due to Rooney’s own numerous motions and procedural applications. The Strasbourg Court accepted that he had made many applications, but found that significant delay was also caused by structural delays before the Supreme Court and by errors or oversights which that court itself acknowledged. Applying established case law, especially *McFarlane v. Ireland*, the Court held that the length of both proceedings was excessive, violating Article 6 §1, and that Rooney had no effective domestic remedy, violating Article 13.

However, the Supreme Court failed to deal with the High Court’s refusal of judgment in default of defence. Over the following decade, the applicant repeatedly tried to reopen the appeals. The Supreme Court refused in 2000 and 2001, and in October 2001 made a vexatious litigant order against him. In 2010, the Supreme Court acknowledged a clear “oversight” in not determining that part of the earlier appeal and indicated it would hear submissions on how to proceed. By the time of the Strasbourg judgment, the 1987 action had still not been shown to have ended; it had lasted almost 26 years for two levels of jurisdiction.

**The 1995 proceedings.** From 1993 to 1996 the applicant’s herd was restricted under the same TB scheme. In November 1995 he began another High Court action against State defendants, claiming the restriction was unlawful and that the scheme breached statute, the Constitution, the Convention, and EU law. Discovery was ordered in 1997. A notice to admit facts was served in 2002 and refused. A notice of trial was served in December 2002. The High Court heard the action over ten days in May and June 2004 and dismissed the claims in July 2004. The applicant appealed in August 2004. He filed written submissions in 2006 and a certificate of readiness in January 2007. A request to prioritise the appeal was refused in November 2007. In 2009 the Registrar indicated a 31-month waiting period after certification. The appeal was eventually heard with another appeal in October 2009. In March 2010 the Supreme Court gave judgment only on the other appeal; the applicant later established that the 2004 appeal had been omitted. After further initiatives, the Supreme Court finally dismissed the 2004 appeal in November 2010. That action had lasted 15 years for two levels of jurisdiction.

**Alleged violations and Court’s conclusion.** The applicant alleged that both actions breached the “reasonable time” guarantee of Article 6 § 1 and that Ireland provided no effective domestic remedy under Article 13. The Government argued that the delay was mainly caused by the applicant’s own numerous motions and procedural choices. The Court found the application admissible. Applying the criteria of complexity, conduct of the applicant and authorities, and what was at stake, it accepted that the applicant had made many applications, but held that significant delay was also caused by the authorities—particularly long delays before the Supreme Court due to structural problems and acknowledged errors by that court. The Court concluded that the length of the proceedings was excessive, violating Article 6 § 1, and that there was no effective domestic remedy, violating Article 13.

**Summary of *Lavrechov v. the Czech Republic* (Application no. 57404/08)**

The applicant, Mr Evgueni Lavrechov, a Russian national born in 1952, was a representative of a Russian company that acquired a share in a Czech company, S. He served on the Board of Directors from August 1995 and as chairman from February 1996. After being illegally dismissed by Czech board members in late 1996, the company later became insolvent.

In June 2001, the applicant was charged with insider trading and fraud, accused of concluding contracts disadvantageous to company S. and causing damage of approximately EUR 3.5 million. He was placed in pre-trial detention on 20 June 2001.

On 8 January 2002, the applicant requested release on bail, offering CZK 4 million and declaring awareness of Article 73 § 3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure regarding bail forfeiture conditions. On 17 January 2002, the Ostrava Regional Court granted bail at CZK 10 million (EUR 400,000), citing the gravity of charges and high risk of absconding. After payment, he was released on 22 February 2002, with conditions including residing at a Czech address and attending hearings.

The applicant made three authorised trips to Russia between February and June 2002, always returning. On 7 June 2002, the Regional Court permitted another trip until 18 June 2002, conditional on attending a hearing scheduled for 19-21 June 2002. However, on 17 June 2002, the applicant informed his lawyer that his passport had been stolen in Moscow on 14 June 2002, and he was arranging a replacement. The hearing was adjourned.

Summonses sent to the applicant's Czech address were returned undelivered. His lawyer informed the court on 30 July 2002 that he lacked direct contact details for the applicant in Russia. Hearings were repeatedly cancelled or adjourned as the applicant failed to attend, citing lack of a new passport and later health problems and new lawyers, but he never provided a clear address for service in Russia.

The applicant received a new passport (date disputed: February or April 2003) but did not inform the court. The Regional Court made extensive efforts to summon him through Interpol and Russian authorities. In December 2005, the court decided to conduct proceedings in absentia, finding the applicant had been avoiding prosecution by staying abroad and had frustrated delivery of official letters.

Hearings proceeded in absentia in 2006, and on 23 October 2006, the Regional Court fully acquitted the applicant, finding no criminal offence. This was upheld on appeal in June 2007.

In November 2007, the Regional Court ordered the bail returned, finding the applicant had not been duly informed of forfeiture consequences. However, on 5 December 2007, the Olomouc High Court quashed this and ruled the bail forfeited. It held the applicant must have known of forfeiture possibilities, had failed to collect correspondence at addresses he provided, and had avoided prosecution by remaining abroad without maintaining contact with the court.

The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant's appeal on 3 June 2008. The applicant then complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the bail forfeiture violated his property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, particularly given his acquittal.

In *Lavrechov v. the Czech Republic* (App. no. 57404/08, 20 June 2013), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether the forfeiture of a Russian national’s bail violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 6 of the Convention.

The applicant, Mr Lavrechov, was a representative of a Russian company and chairman of the board of a Czech company, S. In June 2001 he was charged with insider trading and fraud and placed in pre-trial detention. In January 2002 the Ostrava Regional Court released him on bail of CZK 10,000,000 (about EUR 400,000), citing the gravity of the charges and flight risk. His bail conditions required him to stay at a Czech address, receive mail there, and attend hearings. He declared that he knew bail could be forfeited if he breached those conditions.

In June 2002 the court allowed him to travel to Russia until 18 June, on condition that he attend a hearing on 19–21 June. He reported that his passport and Czech visa had been stolen in Moscow. The hearing was adjourned, but summonses sent to his Czech address were returned undelivered. His lawyer later sent documents showing his registered Russian address in Udomlya, but did not provide a clear address for service. Further hearings were cancelled. The court made inquiries through Interpol and Russian authorities. The date he received a new passport was disputed—the Government said February 2003, the applicant said April 2003—but he did not inform the court. In 2004 a summons was sent to an address in Podolsk; Russian authorities said he neither lived nor was registered there. He learned of a September 2004 hearing and obtained a visa, but faxed the court seeking adjournment due to health problems and new lawyers, again without giving a Russian address. A summons for a November 2005 hearing was not served until January 2006, in Udomlya, too late.

In December 2005 the Regional Court ordered that he be tried in absentia, finding that he had avoided proceedings by staying abroad, failed to comply with bail conditions, and not maintained contact. In October 2006 he was fully acquitted, and that acquittal was upheld in June 2007.

The applicant then sought return of his bail. In November 2007 the Regional Court ordered its return, finding that he had not been duly informed of the consequences of non-compliance and that the statutory conditions for forfeiture were not met. In December 2007 the Olomouc High Court reversed that decision and ordered forfeiture. It found that he must have known of the possibility of forfeiture from his earlier declarations; although initially unable to return after losing his passport, he later failed to collect correspondence, avoided prosecution by remaining abroad, and failed to keep in contact with the court. The Constitutional Court dismissed his appeal in June 2008.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged that forfeiting the bail violated his property rights, particularly because he had been acquitted, and complained under Article 6 that the domestic decisions were insufficiently reasoned. The Court found that the forfeiture was lawful, pursued the legitimate aim of ensuring the proper conduct of criminal proceedings, and was proportionate. Acquittal did not make forfeiture unjust: bail secured appearance, not punishment. After receiving a new passport, the applicant had ample time to contact the court but failed to provide a clear address or remain in contact. The domestic proceedings were adversarial and adequately reasoned. There was therefore no violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, and the Article 6 complaint was manifestly ill-founded.

Lavrechov v. the Czech Republic concerned a Russian national charged in 2001 with insider trading and fraud relating to a Czech company, with alleged damage of CZK 88 million. He was placed in pre-trial detention and later released in February 2002 on bail of CZK 10 million (approximately EUR 400,000). The bail conditions required him to reside at a Czech address and attend hearings.

In June 2002 the applicant was permitted to travel to Russia on condition that he attend a hearing. He reported that his passport had been stolen in Moscow and did not return to the Czech Republic. The date he obtained a new passport was disputed, but he did not inform the court. Summonses sent to his Czech address were returned, and attempts to serve him in Russia failed because his whereabouts or correct address could not be established. The court warned that his conduct could lead to forfeiture of bail and to trial in absentia. In September 2004 the applicant obtained a visa but asked for an adjournment, citing health problems and new lawyers, without providing an address in Russia. In December 2005 the court decided to try him in absentia. He was acquitted in October 2006, and the acquittal was upheld in 2007.

In November 2007 the Regional Court ordered the bail returned, finding that the applicant had not been duly informed of the consequences and that statutory grounds for forfeiture were absent. In December 2007 the High Court reversed that decision and ordered forfeiture. It found that the applicant knew of the possibility of forfeiture, had avoided prosecution by remaining outside the country, had failed to collect correspondence or provide a proper address, and had frustrated service of official documents. The Constitutional Court dismissed his appeal in June 2008.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that forfeiture of his bail violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, especially because he had been acquitted. He argued that he had not been properly warned, had not been hiding, and had objective reasons for his absence. He also complained under Article 6 that the domestic decisions were insufficiently reasoned.

The Court declared the property complaint admissible. It found that forfeiture was an interference with his possessions but was lawful, pursued the legitimate aim of ensuring the proper conduct of criminal proceedings and fighting crime, and was proportionate. The EUR 400,000 bail was substantial, but the time to assess the amount was when bail was set, not when forfeited; the applicant had not challenged the initial amount. Acquittal did not automatically make forfeiture unjust, because bail secures participation in proceedings, and prosecution may rest on reasonable suspicion even if it does not lead to conviction. The applicant’s conduct significantly hampered the proceedings: he missed hearings, caused cancellations, failed to maintain contact, and failed to provide a reliable address. The forfeiture followed adversarial proceedings with reasoned decisions.

The Court therefore found no violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Article 6 complaint was rejected as manifestly ill-founded.
001-118388:
Case Ternovik and Others v. Ukraine (Application no. 19430/06 and 19 other applications) is a European Court of Human Rights judgment delivered by the Fifth Section Committee on 11 April 2013, rectified on 5 June 2013. The case concerned 20 applications against Ukraine. Most applicants were Ukrainian nationals; the applicant in application no. 64583/09 was a Russian national. The Russian Government declined to intervene.

The central factual complaint concerned the lengthy failure of Ukrainian authorities to enforce domestic court decisions given in the applicants’ favour. In each application, domestic courts had delivered judgments entitling the applicants either to specific pecuniary amounts or to have certain actions taken in their favour. These judgments became final and enforceable. However, the applicants could not obtain timely enforcement because State authorities failed to take necessary budgetary or regulatory measures. Enforcement was further obstructed by bans on the attachment and sale of property belonging to State-owned or State-controlled companies. As a result, despite having binding judicial decisions in their favour, the applicants either remained unpaid or did not receive the required actions.

The enforcement status varied. In four applications—nos. 25358/06, 1777/08, 20895/09, and 64583/09—the domestic judgments were eventually enforced, respectively on 2 June 2011, 18 April 2008, 9 July 2009, and 18 January 2011. In all other applications, the domestic decisions had not been enforced in full. Some applicants also made submissions on unrelated factual and legal matters, but the principal common issue was the non-enforcement of final domestic judgments.

Procedurally, the applications were communicated to the Ukrainian Government on various dates. The Government submitted unilateral declarations aimed at resolving the non-enforcement issues and requested that the Court strike the applications out under Article 37 § 1(c) of the Convention. The Court examined those declarations and rejected the request. The Court joined the applications because they raised the same principal legal issue and noted that the underlying issue was already covered by well-established case-law, referring to Yuriy Nikolayevich Ivanov v. Ukraine (no. 40450/04, 15 October 2009).

The applicants complained, expressly or in substance, under Article 6 of the Convention, Article 13 of the Convention, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Article 6 guarantees a fair hearing within a reasonable time in the determination of civil rights and obligations. Article 13 guarantees an effective remedy before a national authority for Convention violations. Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

The applicants’ core allegations were twofold: first, that the final domestic judgments in their favour were not enforced for a lengthy period; and second, that they lacked effective domestic remedies for that non-enforcement. The Court found these complaints admissible, not manifestly ill-founded, and not inadmissible on any other grounds. On the merits, the Court found that the judgments in the applicants’ favour had not been enforced in due time and that the State authorities were responsible for the delay. This was directly relevant to the alleged violations: the prolonged failure to execute final domestic decisions deprived the applicants of the practical benefit of their judicial awards and possessions, while no effective domestic remedy addressed the systemic non-enforcement. The Court’s findings followed established case-law concerning Ukraine’s failure to enforce domestic judgments.

In *Ternovik and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 19430/06 and 19 other applications), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) examined 20 applications lodged under Article 34 of the Convention. These judgments became final and enforceable. However, the applicants were unable to obtain timely enforcement. The non-enforcement resulted from the authorities’ failure to take specific budgetary or regulatory measures and from bans introduced on the attachment and sale of property belonging to State-owned or State-controlled companies. In four applications—nos. 25358/06, 1777/08, 20895/09 and 64583/09—the judgments were eventually enforced on 2 June 2011, 18 April 2008, 9 July 2009 and 18 January 2011 respectively. In all other applications, the domestic decisions had not been enforced in full. Some applicants also raised unrelated factual and legal matters, but these were not the central issue.

The applicants complained, expressly or in substance, under Article 6 of the Convention, Article 13 of the Convention, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Under Article 6, they alleged that the failure to enforce final judgments violated their right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time in the determination of their civil rights. Under Article 13, they alleged the absence of an effective domestic remedy for the non-enforcement. Under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, they alleged that the prolonged non-enforcement interfered with their right to peaceful enjoyment of their possessions, because the final judgments represented enforceable entitlements.

During the proceedings, the Ukrainian Government submitted unilateral declarations aimed at resolving the non-enforcement issues and requested that the Court strike the applications out under Article 37 § 1 (c). The Court examined the declarations but rejected the Government’s request. It also joined the applications because they raised the same principal legal issue. The Court noted that the underlying legal issue was already the subject of well-established case-law, referring to *Yuriy Nikolayevich Ivanov v. Ukraine* (no. 40450/04, 15 October 2009).

The Court found the applicants’ complaints admissible: they were not manifestly ill-founded and were not inadmissible on other grounds. On the merits, the Court found that the judgments in the applicants’ favour had not been enforced in due time and that the State authorities were responsible for that delay. The case therefore concerned systemic non-enforcement of final domestic decisions and the alleged lack of effective remedies, engaging the applicants’ rights under Article 6 § 1, Article 13, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The central alleged violation was not the substance of the domestic judgments themselves, but the State’s failure to secure their timely enforcement.

**Case: Ternovik and Others v. Ukraine** (App. no. 19430/06 and 19 other applications) is a 2013 European Court of Human Rights judgment delivered by the Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee. The judgment was adopted on 19 March 2013 and delivered on 11 April 2013, later rectified on 5 June 2013. It concerned 20 applications lodged under Article 34 of the Convention. All applicants were Ukrainian nationals except the applicant in application no. 64583/09, who was Russian. The Russian Government declined to intervene.

The central alleged violation was the lengthy failure of Ukrainian authorities to enforce final domestic court decisions given in the applicants’ favour, together with the lack of effective domestic remedies for that non-enforcement. The Court noted that the underlying legal issue was already the subject of well-established case-law, particularly *Yuriy Nikolayevich Ivanov v. Ukraine* (no. 40450/04, 15 October 2009).

On the facts, domestic courts had delivered judgments on various dates entitling the applicants to various pecuniary amounts or requiring certain actions in their favour. These judgments became final and enforceable. However, the applicants could not obtain timely enforcement. The authorities failed to take specific budgetary or regulatory measures necessary for enforcement. In addition, bans were introduced on the attachment and sale of property belonging to State-owned or State-controlled companies, which further obstructed enforcement.

Four applications were eventually enforced: no. 25358/06 on 2 June 2011; no. 1777/08 on 18 April 2008; no. 20895/09 on 9 July 2009; and no. 64583/09 on 18 January 2011. In all other applications, the domestic decisions had not been enforced in full. Some applicants also made submissions concerning factual and legal matters unrelated to the non-enforcement issue.

Procedurally, the applications were communicated to the Ukrainian Government on various dates. The Government submitted unilateral declarations aimed at resolving the non-enforcement issues and asked the Court to strike the applications out under Article 37 § 1 (c) of the Convention. The Court examined the declarations but rejected the Government’s request. It then considered joinder because the applications raised the same principal legal issue.

The applicants complained, expressly or in substance, under Article 6 of the Convention, Article 13 of the Convention, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Article 6 guarantees a fair hearing within a reasonable time; Article 13 guarantees an effective remedy for Convention violations; and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. The applicants alleged that the lengthy non-enforcement of final judgments violated these rights and that no effective domestic remedy existed.

The Court found that the complaints were not manifestly ill-founded and were not inadmissible on any other grounds, so it declared them admissible. On the merits, the Court found that the judgments in the applicants’ favour were not enforced in due time, for which the State authorities were responsible. The case therefore concerned repeated or systemic non-enforcement of domestic decisions against the State or State-controlled entities, caused by budgetary and regulatory failures and property attachment bans, and the absence of effective remedies for such delays.

In *Mežnarič v. Slovenia* (ECtHR, App. No. 41416/06, judgment of 18 April 2013), the applicant, Marijan Mežnarič, complained under Article 6 § 1 that domestic proceedings involving him lasted unreasonably long. He also complained under Article 13 that Slovenia lacked an effective domestic remedy for excessive length.

The underlying proceedings began on 13 June 1995, when Žiri Municipality brought enforcement proceedings against the company KODA SPAAR d.o.o. before the Kranj Basic Court. A writ of execution was issued on 28 June 1995, but the company objected, and on 5 September 1995 the first-instance court annulled the writ. On 6 November 1995 the case was referred to the Kranj District Court for contentious proceedings. From 1999 to 2000, the case was affected by jurisdictional confusion: in November 1999 the Kranj District Court declared it lacked jurisdiction and referred the case to Škofja Loka Local Court, which initiated a jurisdictional dispute. In August 2000, the Ljubljana Higher Court assigned the case back to the Kranj District Court. This created a lengthy period of inactivity attributable to the State.

On 17 October 2000, the court received an extract from the Register of Companies showing that KODA SPAAR had been struck out under Article 580 §§ 5–6 of the Companies Act for failing to align its operations with new legislation. On 8 January 2001, the creditor asked to continue the proceedings against the applicant as the company’s founder and owner. On 27 August 2001, the first-instance court granted continuation against the applicant. He appealed and sought exemption from court fees; the Higher Court rejected the appeal on 24 October 2001. His request for protection of legality was also rejected.

The proceedings were stayed from 27 August 2002 until 17 January 2003, pending a Constitutional Court decision concerning the Financial Operations of Companies Act. Hearings followed in December 2003 and February 2004. In February 2004, the first-instance court annulled the writ of execution, but the Higher Court remitted the case in February 2005. In August 2005, the first-instance court upheld the writ, and on 21 June 2006 the Higher Court upheld the applicant’s appeal and annulled the writ. On 4 September 2006, the applicant sought reimbursement of legal costs; his request was rejected on 10 October 2006. The total duration was therefore from 13 June 1995 to 10 October 2006—eleven years and four months.

The Government argued that only the period after 27 August 2001, when the case continued against the applicant personally, should count. It claimed the applicant was not a victim for the earlier period against the company and that five years at two levels was not excessive. The Court rejected this. Because the company had been struck out ex officio and former shareholders became personally liable as universal successors under the Constitutional Court’s case-law, the applicant replaced the company in the domestic proceedings and could claim victim status for the entire period.

On the merits, the Court applied the reasonable-time criteria. The longest inactivity attributable to the State was four years, and the applicant did not substantially contribute to delays. The Court found the length excessive, violating Article 6 § 1. Regarding Article 13, it relied on *Ribič v. Slovenia* and found no reason to distinguish the case, concluding that Slovenia lacked an effective remedy for excessive length, in violation of Article 13.

Mežnarič v. Slovenia (application no. 41416/06) is a European Court of Human Rights case decided on 18 April 2013. The applicant, Marijan Mežnarič, a Slovenian national born in 1950, complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that domestic proceedings involving him lasted excessively. He also complained, in substance, under Article 13 that Slovenia lacked an effective domestic remedy for excessive length of proceedings.

The underlying dispute began on 13 June 1995, when the Žiri Municipality instituted enforcement proceedings against the company KODA SPAAR d.o.o. before the Kranj Basic Court. A writ of execution was issued on 28 June 1995, but the company objected. On 5 September 1995 the first-instance court annulled the writ. On 6 November 1995 the case was referred to the Kranj District Court to be decided as contentious proceedings. On 21 November 1999 the court found it lacked jurisdiction and referred the case to the Škofja Loka Local Court, which on 25 November 1999 initiated a jurisdictional dispute. On 30 August 2000 the Ljubljana Higher Court assigned the case to the Kranj District Court.

On 17 October 2000 the first-instance court received an extract showing that KODA SPAAR d.o.o. had been struck out of the Register of Companies under Article 580 §§ 5 and 6 of the Companies Act. On 8 January 2001 the creditor requested continuation of the proceedings against the applicant, because he had been the company’s founder and owner. On 27 August 2001 the first-instance court decided to continue the proceedings against the applicant. The applicant appealed and requested an exemption from court fees; his appeal was rejected on 24 October 2001. His later request for protection of legality was also rejected.

On 27 August 2002 the Kranj District Court stayed the proceedings pending a Constitutional Court decision concerning the Financial Operations of Companies Act. The proceedings resumed on 17 January 2003. A settlement hearing was held on 17 December 2003, where the applicant sought legal aid, a fee exemption, and filed a counterclaim for damages. On 11 February 2004 the first-instance court annulled the 1995 writ of execution; an appeal followed. On 16 February 2005 the Ljubljana Higher Court remitted the case for re-examination. On 31 August 2005 the first-instance court upheld the writ, but on 21 June 2006 the Higher Court allowed the applicant’s appeal and annulled the writ. On 4 September 2006 the applicant requested reimbursement of legal costs; that request was rejected on 10 October 2006.

The Government argued that only the period after the proceedings were continued against the applicant, from 27 August 2001, should count, and that the earlier period concerned the company. The Court rejected that argument. It noted that the company had been struck out ex officio, that former shareholders became personally liable for its debts, and that under the Constitutional Court’s case-law they were universal successors. Because the company’s assets, rights, and obligations had passed to the applicant, he replaced the company in the domestic proceedings and could claim victim status for the earlier period.

On the merits, the Court applied the reasonableness criteria: complexity, conduct of the applicant and authorities, and what was at stake. It found the longest period of state-attributable inactivity was four years, while the applicant had not substantially contributed to delays. The length was therefore excessive and violated Article 6 § 1. As to Article 13, the Court reiterated that an effective domestic remedy was required for complaints about excessive length. Relying on Ribič v. Slovenia and finding no grounds to distinguish the case, it found a violation of Article 13 as well.

His request for protection of legality was rejected on 20 December 2001.

On 27 August 2002 the Kranj District Court stayed the proceedings pending the Constitutional Court’s decision concerning part of the Financial Operations of Companies Act.
