001-108680:
In *Varapnickaitė-Mažylienė v. Lithuania* (no. 20376/05, judgment 17 January 2012), the applicant complained under Article 8 that her private life was violated by disclosure of information to the media, and under Article 13 that she lacked an effective domestic remedy. The background was a custody dispute concerning her son.

Before the alleged violation, the applicant had herself publicly disclosed extensive private details. On 31 March 2001, the newspaper *Respublika* published, at her expense, an open letter she had written to the Children’s Rights Ombudsman complaining about the Children’s Welfare Service (“CWS”). The letter named her, her son and her former husband, gave her son’s date of birth, described the custody litigation, and discussed her son’s psychiatric treatment and medical reports, including allegations about his father’s negative influence. On 3 April 2001, *Lietuvos Aidas* published an interview in which she repeated private details and named CWS employees involved in the case.

The alleged violation arose from a *Lietuvos Aidas* article of 15 June 2001 about the CWS’s general work. Its director described everyday child-protection problems and, as an illustration, referred to a custody case involving a thirteen-year-old boy. The article did not name the applicant, her son or her former husband, and used no initials or residence. It said the mother lived with another man, rarely met the child and did not know his telephone number. It also cited the child’s medical records, stating that the boy was hostile towards his mother because she had allegedly betrayed the family by marrying another man; that conflicts had arisen with her new husband; that the mother suspected sexual abuse but no signs were found; and that the mother had pulled the boy’s hair and bitten him.

The applicant claimed she was identifiable and that the CWS unlawfully disclosed private and health information. The Inspector of Journalistic Ethics warned the newspaper that, despite apparent anonymity, the applicant was recognisable and negatively portrayed. The Child Development Centre said the CWS had acted unethically by disclosing medical records. However, the Children’s Rights Ombudsman found that the applicant herself had breached her son’s privacy by publicising family matters.

The applicant sued the CWS for damages. Domestic courts dismissed her claim, finding that the 15 June article did not sufficiently identify her or her son and that she had not proved deliberate disclosure of private information. The Supreme Court upheld the dismissal but issued a separate ruling criticising the CWS for publicly commenting on a particular child’s health and private relations, saying this was incompatible with the child’s interests.

Before the European Court, the Government argued there was no interference because the article contained no identifying data and much information had already been made public. The Court agreed: the article concerned general CWS problems; no names or initials were given; the medical diagnosis was not sufficiently distinctive; and the domestic courts’ findings were not arbitrary. Since almost all disputed information was already public, there was no Article 8 interference.

On Article 13, the Court found that a legal framework for privacy protection existed and the applicant had proceedings at three levels. Dismissal for lack of proof did not make the remedy ineffective. The Supreme Court’s separate ruling addressed general secrecy issues, not a proven violation. The complaint about witness refusal was not in the original application and was weak. The Article 13 complaint was therefore manifestly ill-founded and inadmissible.

In *Varapnickaitė-Mažylienė v. Lithuania* (App. no. 20376/05, 17 January 2012), the applicant complained under Article 8 that Lithuanian authorities disclosed information about her private life and her minor son’s health, and under Article 13 that she lacked an effective remedy. The European Court of Human Rights found no violation.

The disputed publication appeared in *Lietuvos Aidas* on 15 June 2001. It concerned the daily work of the Vilnius Children’s Welfare Service (CWS). Its director, N.S., described general child-protection issues but used, as an example, a custody dispute involving a thirteen-year-old boy. The article said the mother was divorced, lived with another man, rarely met her son, and that the child did not want to see her. It then quoted the boy’s medical records from the Vilnius Child Development Centre Psychiatric Unit, stating he was hostile towards his mother because she had “betrayed the family,” that conflicts had arisen with her current husband, and that on one occasion the mother had pulled the boy’s hair and bitten him, though she claimed self-defence. It did not give names, initials, professions, workplaces, appearances, or places of residence.

The applicant claimed she and her son were identifiable. She relied on earlier self-publicity: on 31 March 2001 *Respublika* published a paid open letter from her to the Children’s Rights Ombudsman, naming her, her son, and former husband, giving the son’s date of birth, and describing the custody litigation and psychiatric treatment. On 3 April 2001 *Lietuvos Aidas* published an interview in which she again named family members and criticised CWS employees. The Government also said she disclosed similar information on television.

She sued the CWS for non-pecuniary damages. The domestic courts dismissed her claim, finding that the 15 June article did not contain identifying data and that she had not proved deliberate disclosure of private information. The Supreme Court upheld that outcome. However, in a separate ruling, it criticised the CWS for publicly commenting on a particular child’s private relations and health, saying this was incompatible with the child’s interests, even though the applicant had not proved she was identifiable. The Inspector of Journalistic Ethics had earlier warned the newspaper, and the Child Development Centre said the CWS acted unethically.

Before the ECtHR, the key Article 8 issue was whether the article amounted to an interference with the applicant’s private life. The Court noted the absence of names or initials; Vilnius had about 122,000 children; the medical diagnosis was not sufficiently distinctive; and no other identifying details appeared. The domestic courts’ conclusion was not arbitrary. Moreover, most disputed information had already entered the public domain through the applicant’s own publications. Thus the applicant had not shown that she or her son were identifiable from the article, and there was no interference with Article 8.

On Article 13, the Court found that a legal privacy framework existed and the applicant had access to three levels of courts. An unfavourable outcome did not make the remedy ineffective. The Supreme Court’s separate ruling addressed general future practice and did not contradict the dismissal. The complaint about witnesses was manifestly ill-founded. The application was therefore rejected as inadmissible under Article 13, and no Article 8 violation was found.

**Summary of *Varapnickaitė-Mažylienė v. Lithuania* (Application no. 20376/05)**

The applicant, Ms Jolanta Varapnickaitė-Mažylienė, a Lithuanian journalist, lodged an application against Lithuania alleging violations of Articles 8 and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights concerning her right to privacy and access to an effective remedy. The case centred on the publication of an article in the daily newspaper *Lietuvos Aidas* on 15 June 2001, which she claimed disclosed private information about her and her minor son.

The background involved contentious custody proceedings between the applicant and her former husband over their son's residence. Prior to the disputed article, the applicant herself had publicly disclosed extensive details about her family life. On 31 March 2001, she paid for an open letter in *Respublika* complaining about the Children's Welfare Service (CWS). She revealed her and her son's full names, her former husband's name, his date of birth, and described the custody litigation, including psychiatric treatment her son received. On 3 April 2001, *Lietuvos Aidas* published an interview with her containing similar information and criticism of CWS employees.

The allegedly violating article, published on 15 June 2001 in *Lietuvos Aidas*, reported on the general work of the CWS. Its director, N.S., described typical issues, using an anonymised case as an illustration. This example described a thirteen-year-old boy in a custody dispute, detailing his mother's alleged behaviour: that she rarely met the child, did not know his telephone number, and had started attending school meetings only after his grades dropped. The article further cited the child's medical records from a psychiatric unit. These records stated the boy was hostile towards his mother because she "betrayed the family by marrying another man," mentioned conflicts with her new husband, an incident where the husband hit the boy, and an occasion where the mother pulled the boy's hair and bit him, claiming self-defence. Crucially, the article did not name the applicant, her son, or her former husband, nor did it provide other identifying details like their address or professions.

The applicant sued the CWS for non-pecuniary damages, arguing that despite the lack of names, she was identifiable from the article's details, thus violating her private life. She pointed to an apology printed by the newspaper and a response from a medical institution as proof of her identifiability. The domestic courts at three levels dismissed her claim. They found that the article did not contain any data permitting her clear identification. The Supreme Court noted that the details were insufficient for third parties to identify her or her son.

However, on the same day it dismissed her cassation appeal, the Supreme Court issued a separate ruling. While not overturning the finding on identifiability, it expressed disapproval of the CWS employees' actions. It stated that publicly commenting in detail on a specific child's health and family circumstances was incompatible with the child's interests. It noted that publicising such details would cause distress to the child, who would recognize the article as being about his parents. The ruling emphasised that there was no legitimate public interest warranting the publication of such information.

Before the European Court, the applicant maintained that the CWS's disclosure interfered with her Article 8 right to respect for private life. She argued she was recognisable from the article's content. The Government contended there was no interference, as the article contained no identifying information and largely reiterated details the applicant had already made public herself.

The Court ultimately found no violation of Article 8. It reasoned that the applicant and her son were not sufficiently identifiable from the article, noting it lacked names, initials, or other identifying specifics like profession or residence. It also considered that most of the disputed information had already been disseminated by the applicant herself. Consequently, there was no interference with her private life. As the Article 8 complaint failed, the related Article 13 complaint regarding the lack of an effective remedy was also rejected as manifestly ill-founded.

**M. and Others v. Italy and Bulgaria** (ECtHR, Application no. 40020/03, judgment 31 July 2012) concerned four Bulgarian nationals of Roma origin: L.M. (the first applicant, a minor at the time), her parents S.M. and I.I., and her sister-in-law K.L. They alleged violations primarily under Article 3, and also under Articles 4, 13 and 14 of the Convention, arising from events in Italy in May–June 2003.

According to the applicants, the first three travelled to Italy after X., a Serbian Roma man living in Italy, promised work. They stayed at a villa in Ghislarengo, Vercelli. X allegedly proposed that his nephew Y. marry L.M. When her parents refused, X threatened them with a loaded gun. The parents alleged they were beaten, threatened with death and forced to return to Bulgaria on 18 May 2003, leaving L.M. behind. L.M. alleged that she was kept under constant surveillance, forced to steal, beaten, threatened with death and repeatedly raped by Y. while tied to a bed. During one forced robbery she allegedly had an accident and was taken to hospital, but the family removed her before treatment.

On 24 May 2003 the mother returned to Italy with K.L. and complained to Turin police that she and her husband had been beaten and threatened and that L.M. had been kidnapped; she feared L.M. might be forced into prostitution. Police later accompanied her to identify the villa in Ghislarengo. The applicants complained of police slowness. On 11 June 2003—after the complaint, police surveillance and an apparent delay—police raided the villa, found L.M. and made arrests.

The applicants alleged that during police questioning L.M. was treated roughly and threatened with accusations of perjury and libel. She was allegedly forced to say she did not want her alleged kidnappers prosecuted, to answer “yes” to questions, and to sign documents in Italian she did not understand. They claimed no proper interpreter or lawyer was present, and that Y. was present during parts of her questioning. The mother also alleged threats and ill-treatment during her interview. Later that evening L.M. was questioned again without an interpreter or lawyer, held in a cell, and then placed in a shelter. On 12 June 2003 the applicants returned to Bulgaria.

The Italian Government disputed this account. It stated that the complaint was promptly transmitted to Vercelli police and prosecutors; police inspected and surveilled the villa and raided it on 11 June. Questioning allegedly revealed discrepancies with the mother’s kidnapping complaint. Photographs were said to show a wedding and payment of a bride price by X. to the father. The prosecutor concluded that no kidnapping had occurred, but rather an agreement about marriage. Proceedings were therefore opened against L.M. and her mother for perjury and false accusations. L.M.’s juvenile case was later dropped as socially irrelevant; the mother was acquitted in 2006 because the evidence did not establish guilt.

The applicants submitted medical reports dated June 2003 indicating that L.M. suffered post-traumatic stress disorder, a bruise, an elbow wound, a broken rib, loss of virginity and a vaginal infection; the doctor considered the injuries consistent with her account. They also complained that the Bulgarian consular authorities merely served as a communication channel and did not adequately assist them.

The Bulgarian Government, relying largely on Italian evidence, described a consensual marriage and bride-price arrangement, with the parents leaving after celebrations; it said the Bulgarian authorities acted promptly after receiving the complaint on 31 May 2003.

The central factual disputes were whether L.M. was kidnapped, trafficked, raped and forced into labour by the Serbian family; whether Italian authorities failed to protect her and investigate effectively; whether police ill-treated L.M. and her mother and denied procedural safeguards; and whether discriminatory treatment based on Roma ethnicity or Bulgarian nationality occurred.

The case *M. and Others v. Italy and Bulgaria* (Application no. 40020/03), judgment of 31 July 2012, concerned four Bulgarian nationals of Roma origin: L.M. (the first applicant, then a minor), her parents S.M. and I.I., and her sister-in-law K.L.

In May 2003 the first three applicants travelled to Italy after X, a Serbian Roma man living there, promised work. They stayed at a villa in Ghislarengo, Vercelli. The applicants alleged that X and his family threatened them with a gun, beat the parents, and forced them to return to Bulgaria on 18 May, leaving the first applicant behind. The first applicant claimed she was held under constant surveillance, forced to steal, beaten, threatened with death, and repeatedly raped by X’s nephew Y while tied to a bed. After an accident during a forced robbery, she was allegedly taken to hospital but not left for treatment.

On 24 May the third applicant returned to Italy with the fourth applicant and complained to Turin police that she and her husband had been beaten and threatened and that her daughter had been kidnapped and might be forced into prostitution. Police later identified the villa. On 11 June 2003, eighteen days after the complaint, police raided the house, found the first applicant, and made arrests.

The applicants alleged that during police questioning in Vercelli the first applicant was treated roughly, threatened with perjury and libel charges, forced to say she did not want her alleged kidnappers prosecuted, and made to sign documents in Italian without translation or understanding. They said the interpreter failed to assist and that Y was present during parts of the questioning. The third applicant similarly alleged threats and rough treatment when she refused to sign. The first applicant was questioned again without an interpreter or lawyer, held in a cell, and later transferred to a shelter. Medical reports of 22 and 24 June 2003 recorded post-traumatic stress disorder, a bruise, an elbow wound, a broken rib, loss of virginity, and a vaginal infection, and concluded the injuries were consistent with her account.

The Italian Government disputed this narrative. It said the first applicant’s statements differed from her mother’s complaint and that photographs showed a wedding party at which the second applicant received money. The prosecutor concluded that no kidnapping but an agreement about marriage had occurred. X, Y and Z stated that Y and the first applicant had entered a consensual marriage. Consequently, proceedings against unknown kidnappers were converted into proceedings against the first and third applicants for perjury and false accusations. The first applicant’s case was discontinued in 2005 as socially irrelevant; the third applicant was acquitted in 2006 because the evidence did not establish guilt. The Bulgarian Government relied on similar statements and said the first applicant had agreed to marriage and a bride price had been negotiated.

Before the European Court, the applicants complained under Articles 3, 4, 13 and 14. In particular, they alleged that Italy failed to take adequate steps to prevent the first applicant’s ill-treatment by securing her swift release and failed to conduct an effective investigation into the alleged abuse. They also alleged ill-treatment by Italian police during questioning, lack of lawyers and interpreters, being forced to sign unknown documents, discriminatory treatment because of their Roma origin and Bulgarian nationality, and inadequate assistance from Bulgarian consular authorities, who allegedly served only as a communication channel.

The case of *Scoppola v. Italy (No. 3)* (Application no. 126/05) concerns an application lodged by Franco Scoppola, an Italian national, alleging that his disenfranchisement following a criminal conviction violated Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights (right to free elections).

In September 1999, following a violent family dispute, the applicant killed his wife and injured one of his sons. He was arrested the next day. In November 2000, under the summary procedure he had elected, the Rome preliminary hearings judge found him guilty of murder, attempted murder, ill-treatment of his family, and unauthorised possession of a firearm. Although the judge noted that life imprisonment was warranted, the summary procedure reduced the sentence to thirty years' imprisonment and a lifetime ban from public office under Article 29 of the Italian Criminal Code. The judge found aggravating circumstances, including that the crimes were committed against his own family and triggered by a trivial incident, and no remorse. Both the prosecution and the applicant appealed. In January 2002, the Rome Assize Court of Appeal sentenced him to life imprisonment, and in January 2003 the Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal.

Under Italian law, a life sentence entails a lifetime ban from public office, which in turn results in permanent forfeiture of the right to vote under section 2 of Presidential Decree no. 223/1967. The applicant's disenfranchisement was not mentioned in the judgments against him. In April 2003, the electoral committee deleted his name from the electoral roll.

In June 2004, the applicant lodged a complaint with the electoral committee, citing *Hirst v. the United Kingdom (no. 2)*, alleging that his disenfranchisement was incompatible with Article 3 of Protocol No. 1. The complaint was rejected, and his appeal to the Rome Court of Appeal was dismissed in November 2004. The Court of Appeal distinguished *Hirst*, noting that unlike the UK's blanket ban, Italian law applied the voting ban only where the offence was punishable by a particularly heavy sentence, including life imprisonment; the automatic application to any custodial sentence was lacking. The applicant appealed on points of law, arguing that the disenfranchisement was an automatic consequence of the ancillary penalty, had nothing to do with the offence committed, and the courts had no power to decide whether to apply it. In January 2006, the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal, referring to the Grand Chamber's *Hirst* judgment and noting that in Italian law only offenders sentenced to at least three years' imprisonment were deprived of the right to vote, with temporary bans for sentences of three to five years and lifelong bans for sentences of five years to life.

Separately, in *Scoppola v. Italy (no. 2)*, the Grand Chamber found violations of Articles 6 and 7 regarding his life sentence, and in April 2010 the Court of Cassation reduced his sentence to thirty years' imprisonment. However, the disenfranchisement remained the subject of the present application.

In November 2000, using the summary procedure he had elected, the Rome preliminary hearings judge found him guilty of all charges. The judge noted that the appropriate sentence was life imprisonment but, because the summary procedure had been used, imposed thirty years’ imprisonment and a lifetime ban from public office under Article 29 of the Criminal Code. The judge took into account aggravating circumstances, including that the crimes were committed against his own family and triggered by a trivial incident, and found no remorse. In January 2002, the Rome Assize Court of Appeal sentenced him to life imprisonment. The Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal in January 2003.

The applicant’s disenfranchisement was not mentioned in the criminal judgments; it followed automatically from the sentence. In April 2003, the electoral committee removed his name from the electoral roll. In June 2004, relying in part on *Hirst v. the United Kingdom (no. 2)*, he complained to the electoral committee that his disenfranchisement breached Article 3 of Protocol No. 1. The complaint was rejected. His appeal to the Rome Court of Appeal was dismissed in November 2004. Italy (no. 2)* (2009), the Grand Chamber found violations of Articles 6 and 7 because the applicant’s life sentence had been affected by retroactive sentencing legislation. Following that judgment, the Court of Cassation in April 2010 replaced the life sentence with thirty years’ imprisonment. Nevertheless, because a sentence of five years or more still entailed a lifetime ban from public office under Article 29, his disenfranchisement continued.

The applicant therefore maintained that the automatic and permanent loss of his voting rights—imposed as an ancillary penalty without any individualised judicial assessment of proportionality—was incompatible with Article 3 of Protocol No. 1. The key issue was whether Italy’s regime of disenfranchising persons convicted of serious offences and sentenced to long terms of imprisonment was compatible with the right to free elections. The Grand Chamber ultimately examined this complaint and found no violation of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1.

This case, *Scoppola v. Italy (No. 3)*, application no. 126/05, is a Grand Chamber judgment of the European Court of Human Rights delivered on 22 May 2012. The applicant, Franco Scoppola, an Italian national, alleged that his disenfranchisement following a criminal conviction violated Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, which guarantees the right to free elections.

The facts arose from a violent family incident on 2 September 1999. After a domestic dispute, Scoppola killed his wife and injured one of his sons. He was arrested the next day. The Rome prosecution charged him with murder, attempted murder, ill-treatment of his family, and unauthorised possession of a firearm. Scoppola elected to be tried under the summary procedure. On 24 November 2000, the Rome preliminary hearings judge found him guilty of all charges. Although the judge noted that the offences warranted life imprisonment, the summary procedure allowed a reduced sentence of thirty years’ imprisonment. The judge also imposed a lifetime ban from public office under Article 29 of the Criminal Code. In doing so, the judge relied on aggravating circumstances: the crimes were committed against his own family and triggered by a trivial incident, he showed no remorse, and there was evidence of prior domestic violence.

Both the prosecution and Scoppola appealed. On 10 January 2002, the Rome Assize Court of Appeal sentenced him to life imprisonment, upholding the earlier findings on aggravating and mitigating circumstances. The Court of Cassation dismissed his further appeal on 20 January 2003, making the conviction final.

The key consequence for the alleged violation was the loss of voting rights. Under Article 29 of the Italian Criminal Code, a life sentence or imprisonment of at least five years entails a lifetime ban from public office. Under Article 28, that ban deprives the convicted person of the right to vote. Section 2 of Presidential Decree no. 223/1967 provides that persons under a lifetime ban from public office cannot vote, and that criminal judgments produce loss of voting rights once final. The disenfranchisement was not mentioned in the criminal judgments. On 2 April 2003, the electoral committee deleted Scoppola’s name from the electoral roll under section 32 of Decree no. 223/1967.

Scoppola challenged this. On 30 June 2004, he complained to the electoral committee, citing *Hirst v. the United Kingdom (no. 2)* and arguing that his disenfranchisement was incompatible with Article 3 of Protocol No. 1. The complaint was rejected. On 16 July 2004, he appealed to the Rome Court of Appeal. That court dismissed the appeal on 29 November 2004, distinguishing *Hirst*: unlike the UK’s blanket ban on all prisoners, Italian law applied disenfranchisement only to serious offences, including those punishable by life imprisonment. Scoppola then appealed on points of law, arguing that the voting ban flowed automatically from the ancillary public-office ban, bore no relation to the offence, and left the courts no discretion. On 17 January 2006, the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal. It noted that Italian law deprived only offenders sentenced to at least three years of the vote, with temporary disenfranchisement for shorter sentences and lifelong disenfranchisement for sentences of five years to life.

Separately, in *Scoppola v. Italy (No. 2)*, the Grand Chamber found violations of Articles 6 and 7 concerning his life sentence. On 28 April 2010, the Court of Cassation replaced the life sentence with thirty years’ imprisonment. However, under Italian law, a thirty-year sentence still triggered a lifetime ban from public office and thus continued disenfranchisement.

The Grand Chamber case concerned whether this automatic and permanent loss of voting rights following conviction and ancillary penalty breached Article 3 of Protocol No. 1. The Chamber declared the application partly admissible on 24 March 2009, and the Grand Chamber accepted referral on 20 June 2011. A public hearing was held on 2 November 2011.
001-110949:
**Julin v. Estonia** concerned four applications brought by Vyacheslav Julin, an Estonian national serving a prison sentence. He alleged ill-treatment by prison officers and the absence of an effective investigation; denial of access to court regarding prison conditions and officers’ actions; a humiliating strip-search violating private life; and ill-treatment through restraint measures.

**Application no. 16563/08:** In 2007, while in Murru Prison, the applicant was placed in punishment cells nos. 140 and 122. He complained of degrading conditions: dirty, unopenable windows, poor ventilation, cold, dim or no lighting, high noise, inadequate plumbing and toilet facilities, bad smells, and dirty bedding. On 11 July 2007 he was assaulted by fellow prisoners and sustained thirteen stab wounds. After hospital treatment, he returned to Murru Prison and was held for ten days in cell no. 147 in the closed disciplinary section, where he again complained of poor conditions. On 7 August 2007 he was transferred to Tartu Prison on the day of a planned family visit, so the visit did not occur. In Tartu’s reception section, he later sewed his mouth shut and began a hunger strike, mainly due to fears about a cellmate; he was then placed in a locked isolation cell and subjected to additional restrictions. His administrative complaints about prison conditions and the family visit were blocked because courts refused to exempt him from the State fee, finding his claims not sufficiently important or likely to succeed. His complaints were returned for non-payment.

**Application no. 40841/08:** In 2007 the applicant was punished for a prohibited transaction and placed in cell no. 155 in Murru Prison. He complained of similar degrading conditions and challenged the lawfulness of the punishment. Again, his request for exemption from the State fee was refused, and his complaint was returned for non-payment.

**Application no. 8192/10:** On 26 May 2009, after returning from a court hearing to Tartu Prison, the applicant was strip-searched. He alleged that, although seven prisoners were escorted together, only he was searched that way; five officers were present. He said he was ordered to undress, lift his sexual organ and squat, and was laughed at. Officer O. wanted to perform a digital rectal examination, but the applicant refused, insisting a doctor should do it. He was taken to the medical unit, where a female doctor performed the rectal examination in the presence of two officers. His request for a male doctor was rejected, and he was warned force could be used. The Government disputed his account. His compensation claim was refused by the prison, and the administrative court declined to examine it for failure to comply with the mandatory pre-litigation procedure.

**Application no. 18656/10:** On 22 October 2009, a conflict arose over tobacco. Prison reports stated the applicant became aggressive, threatened officers, used foul language, banged on the door, and struck an officer’s hand. He was placed in a restraint bed from 10:40 a.m. to 7:30 p.m., monitored hourly. The applicant alleged he was provoked, did not resist, was subdued by masked officers, handcuffed and restrained, and was denied food, drink and toilet access for nine hours. Further handcuff restrictions were imposed. On 23 October 2009, officers reported that he refused to be handcuffed and used offensive language; force was used. A nurse recorded an abrasion near his left eye and bluish marks on his neck. The applicant alleged officers hit him with a shield, pushed his face against bars, grabbed his neck, put fingers in his nostrils, and forced him down. Disciplinary proceedings led to two twenty-day punishment-cell sanctions. Prosecutors refused to open a criminal investigation, relying on prison reports and finding the force lawful; the applicant was not interviewed and was refused legal aid.

These facts formed the basis of his complaints under the Convention concerning ill-treatment, ineffective investigation, humiliating search, and lack of access to court.

**Case: Julin v. Estonia** (Applications nos. 16563/08, 40841/08, 8192/10 and 18656/10), judgment of 29 May 2012. The applicant, Vyacheslav Julin, an Estonian national and prisoner, alleged mainly that: (1) he had been ill-treated by prison officers and there had been no effective investigation; (2) he had been denied access to court regarding prison conditions and officers’ actions; and (3) he had been strip-searched in a humiliating manner, in breach of private life.

In 2007, while serving a sentence in Murru Prison, Julin was placed in punishment cells and complained of degrading conditions: dirty, unopenable windows, poor ventilation, cold, dim lighting, high noise, inadequate plumbing, an open toilet near the washbasin, and dirty bedding. In July 2007 he was assaulted by fellow prisoners and suffered thirteen stab wounds. After hospital treatment he was returned to Murru Prison and held for ten days in cell no. 147 in the closed disciplinary section, where he again complained of poor conditions. He was transferred to Tartu Prison on 7 August 2007, the day a previously authorised family visit was to begin, so the visit did not take place. In September 2007, after sewing his mouth shut and starting a hunger strike, apparently due to fears about a cellmate, the prison imposed additional security measures: locked isolation, no personal clothing or effects, and monthly review.

Julin sought compensation in administrative courts for prison conditions, the transfer, and related violations. In most cases the courts refused to exempt him from the State fee of EEK 1,000 (approximately EUR 64), reasoning that his non-pecuniary damage claims were not important or lacked prospects of success. After the Supreme Court declined to hear his appeals, he failed to pay the fee and his complaints were returned. In one family-visit case he received only partial exemption and still could not proceed. Thus he was effectively unable to obtain court review of many complaints.

In the second application, Julin challenged a May 2007 disciplinary punishment of nineteen days in a punishment cell for a prohibited transaction, and complained about conditions in cell no. 155. His request for exemption from the State fee was refused and the complaint was returned.

In the third application, on 26 May 2009, Julin was strip-searched on returning to Tartu Prison from a court hearing. He alleged that, although seven prisoners were escorted together, only he was searched in that manner, in the presence of five officers. He was ordered to undress, lift his sexual organ and squat, and to open his mouth while his ears were inspected; officers allegedly laughed. An officer wanted a digital rectal examination, but Julin refused and was taken to the medical unit, where a female doctor performed the procedure in the presence of officers. His request for a male doctor was rejected. The Government disputed parts of this account. A search report confirmed a “full search” and recorded Julin’s objection that being naked degraded his dignity. His compensation claim was rejected, and the administrative court refused to examine it because the required prior extra-judicial procedure had not been satisfied.

In the fourth application, incidents occurred on 22 and 23 October 2009. On 22 October, after a dispute over tobacco in a punishment cell, officers reported that Julin became aggressive, used offensive language, banged on the door and struck an officer’s hand. He was confined to a restraint bed from 10:40 a.m. to 7:30 p.m., monitored hourly, with medical checks. Julin alleged that masked officers with shields stormed his cell, threw him down, handcuffed him and confined him, denying food, drink and toilet access for nine hours. Additional handcuff measures were imposed. On 23 October, after he allegedly refused handcuffing, force was used; a medical report noted an abrasion near his eye and bluish marks on his neck. Julin alleged he was hit with a shield, pushed against window bars, grabbed by the neck, and had fingers placed in his nostrils, causing severe pain. He received disciplinary penalties of twenty days in a punishment cell for each incident. The prosecutor refused to initiate criminal proceedings, finding the force lawful and the injuries possibly caused by resisting officers. Appeals and legal aid were refused. Administrative complaints were later withdrawn.

001-114244:
In *Hode and Abdi v. the United Kingdom* (Application no. 22341/09, ECtHR, 6 November 2012), the applicants were Mr Ilyas Elmi Hode, a Somali national, and Ms Hawa Aden Abdi, a Djibouti national. The first applicant arrived in the UK in February 2004 and was granted asylum in March 2006. Because the Immigration Rules changed on 30 August 2005, he received five years’ limited leave to remain, expiring 16 March 2011, rather than indefinite leave to remain (ILR), along with a Refugee Convention Travel Document. The second applicant remained in Djibouti.

In June 2006 the applicants were introduced. In February 2007 the first applicant travelled to Djibouti; they married on 5 April 2007 and lived together there until he returned to the UK on 15 May 2007. The second applicant applied for a visa to join him. As a refugee, the first applicant could only be joined under paragraph 352A of the Immigration Rules if the marriage had taken place before he left his country of habitual residence. Since the marriage was post-flight, she did not qualify for family reunion. She also applied under paragraph 281 as the spouse of a person present and settled in the UK. On 18 November 2007 the Entry Clearance Officer refused because the first applicant had only limited leave and was therefore not “present and settled.” In February 2008 the second applicant gave birth to their son.

On appeal, the Immigration Judge accepted that the marriage was genuine and that the first applicant could maintain and accommodate his wife and child. He also accepted that the refusal engaged Article 8. However, he dismissed the appeal because the second applicant had never enjoyed family life in the UK and there were no obstacles to the first applicant living in Djibouti, apart from language and likely employment difficulties. Reconsideration was refused by the Asylum and Immigration Tribunal in August 2008 and by the Administrative Court in October 2008.

The first applicant’s limited leave expired in March 2011, after which he obtained ILR. In April 2011 the Rules were amended to allow refugees with limited leave to be joined by post-flight spouses under paragraph 319L, subject to conditions. The second applicant did not reapply. Their second child was born in July 2011.

The applicants complained under Article 8 ECHR that the refusal violated their right to respect for family life, and under Article 14 read with Article 8 that they were discriminated against. The alleged discrimination arose from the Immigration Rules’ treatment of post-flight spouses of refugees: refugees with limited leave could not be joined by a spouse married after they fled, while spouses of other persons with limited leave, such as students or workers, could join them without any pre-flight marriage requirement. The rules also distinguished between refugees with limited leave and refugees with ILR or pre-2005 refugees, who were considered settled. Domestic cases such as *A (Afghanistan)* and *FH (Iran)* had noted the apparent lack of justification for this disadvantage. The central issue was whether this difference in treatment, which prevented the applicants from enjoying family life in the UK during the first applicant’s initial five-year leave period, was objectively justifiable or discriminatory.

The case concerned two applicants: Mr Ilyas Elmi Hode, a Somali national living in Leeds, and Ms Hawa Aden Abdi, a Djibouti national living in Djibouti. The first applicant arrived in the United Kingdom on 18 February 2004 and was granted asylum in March 2006. Under the rules in force before 30 August 2005, successful asylum seekers received Indefinite Leave to Remain together with refugee status. However, after that date the Immigration Rules changed: refugees were granted an initial five-year period of Leave to Remain, after which they could apply for Indefinite Leave to Remain. Consequently, the first applicant received five years’ leave to remain, expiring on 16 March 2011, and a Refugee Convention Travel Document.

They lived together there until he returned to the United Kingdom on 15 May 2007. The second applicant then applied for a visa to join him. Because the marriage took place after the first applicant had left his country of former habitual residence to seek asylum, the couple could not qualify for family reunion under paragraph 352A of the Immigration Rules, which applied only to spouses who had formed part of the refugee’s family unit before flight. She therefore applied under paragraph 281 as the spouse of a person present and settled in the United Kingdom.

On 18 November 2007 the Entry Clearance Officer refused the application. The reason was that the first applicant, having only five years’ Leave to Remain, was not “present and settled” for the purposes of paragraph 281. A child was born to the couple on 17 February 2008, and the first applicant was named as the father.

The second applicant appealed. The Immigration Judge accepted that the marriage was genuine and that the first applicant could maintain and accommodate his wife and child. He also accepted that the refusal engaged Article 8 rights. Nevertheless, he dismissed the appeal, finding that the refusal was not a disproportionate interference with Article 8. He noted that the second applicant had never enjoyed family life in the United Kingdom and that there were no obstacles preventing the first applicant from living in Djibouti, apart from language difficulties and limited employment prospects. Reconsideration was refused in August and October 2008.

The first applicant later obtained Indefinite Leave to Remain after his original leave expired. In April 2011 the Immigration Rules were amended to allow refugees with limited leave to be joined by post-flight spouses under paragraph 319L, subject to conditions. The second applicant did not re-apply. A second child was born in July 2011.

The applicants complained of violations of Article 8 alone and Article 8 read together with Article 14 of the Convention. They alleged that the immigration rules prevented their family life in the United Kingdom and discriminated against them. In particular, refugees with limited leave were treated less favourably than other categories of persons with limited leave, whose spouses could join them without a pre-flight marriage requirement, and less favourably than settled persons or refugees with indefinite leave. The Government argued that the complaints were manifestly ill-founded, but the European Court of Human Rights declared the application admissible, finding that the complaints were not manifestly ill-founded and were not inadmissible on any other grounds.

In *Austin and Others v. the United Kingdom* (Applications nos. 39692/09, 40713/09 and 41008/09), Grand Chamber, 15 March 2012, four applicants complained under Article 5 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights that their confinement inside a police cordon—known as “kettling”—during a demonstration in central London amounted to a deprivation of liberty.

The events occurred on 1 May 2001. The applicants were caught within a police cordon at Oxford Circus, at the junction of Regent Street and Oxford Street. The first applicant, Lois Austin, was a demonstrator and member of the Socialist Party. She needed to leave at about 3:45 p.m. to collect her 11-month-old daughter from a crèche, but police refused to let her out; she arranged for a friend to collect the child and was released at about 9:30 p.m. The second applicant, George Black, was a passer-by trying to reach a bookshop. He was directed away from Oxford Street, then forced into the cordon by riot police. He asked to leave and was told there was an exit at Bond Street, but when he went there no exit existed. He was released at about 9:20 p.m. The third applicant, Bronwyn Lowenthal, had no connection with the demonstration. She worked in the Oxford Circus area and was on her lunch break when police blocked her return to work and then blocked other exits. She was held until about 9:35 p.m. The fourth applicant, Peter O’Shea, also worked nearby and was caught in the cordon during his lunch break; he was released at about 8 p.m. All applicants repeatedly asked to leave but were told no one could pass.

The police cordon was imposed at about 2 p.m. in response to intelligence that the May Day protest would involve serious disorder. Police relied on previous anti-globalisation demonstrations in London and abroad, intelligence that 500 to 1,000 hard-core demonstrators sought confrontation, and the organisers’ lack of cooperation. Nearly 6,000 officers were deployed. Once the cordon was in place, those inside could not leave without police permission. Conditions became uncomfortable: it was cold and wet, with no food, water, toilets or shelter. There was space to move and no crushing. Individual releases took place, mostly before 4 p.m., with around 400 individual releases recorded. Collective release was repeatedly delayed because of missile-throwing, attempts to break the cordon, and disorder nearby. Police kept the possibility of release under review.

In domestic proceedings, Austin and another claimant acted as test cases. The High Court found that the containment did amount to a deprivation of liberty under Article 5 § 1, but that it was lawful because it was necessary to prevent a breach of the peace and justified under Article 5 § 1(c). It dismissed claims for false imprisonment and breach of Article 5. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that the initial containment did not amount to a deprivation of liberty, comparing it to crowd control at a football match or a motorway hold-up. The applicants then applied to the European Court of Human Rights. The Grand Chamber ultimately found no violation of Article 5 § 1, concluding that the containment did not amount to a deprivation of liberty in the exceptional circumstances, or was not arbitrary, as the police acted in good faith to prevent serious disorder and injury.

Austin and Others v United Kingdom concerned four applicants who were confined by a police cordon at Oxford Circus, London, on 1 May 2001. They alleged that the containment measure—known as “kettling”—for up to seven hours amounted to a deprivation of liberty in breach of Article 5 §1 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

On 1 May 2001, a May Day demonstration against capitalism and globalisation took place in central London. Police intelligence indicated that 500–1,000 hard-core demonstrators intended confrontation and violence. Previous similar protests had caused serious disorder, injury and property damage. Nearly 6,000 officers were deployed. Around 2 p.m., after demonstrators gathered at Oxford Circus, police imposed a cordon to contain the crowd, relying on common-law powers to prevent a breach of the peace. A full cordon was in place by about 2:20–2:25 p.m. No announcement was made until 4 p.m. Conditions inside were uncomfortable: cold, wet, and with no food, water, toilets or shelter. Attempts at controlled release were repeatedly delayed by violence, missile-throwing, attempts to break the cordon, and disorderly crowds outside. Some individual releases occurred, but many people remained held for hours. Release in groups resumed around 7–8 p.m. and was almost complete by 9:45 p.m. Over 100 arrests were made.

The first applicant, Ms Austin, was a protester. She arrived at Oxford Circus about 2 p.m. At 3:45 p.m. she needed to leave to collect her 11-month-old daughter from a crèche. Police refused to let her leave, and a friend had to collect the child. She was released about 9:30 p.m. The second applicant, Mr Black, was a passer-by going to a bookshop. He was advised to take an alternative route but was forced into the cordon by riot police. He asked to leave and was told there was an exit at Bond Street, but no exit existed there. He left about 9:20 p.m. The third applicant, Ms Lowenthal, had no connection with the demonstration. She worked in the Oxford Circus area and was on her lunch break when police prevented her from returning to work. She was held until 9:35 p.m. and told police had orders to allow no one to pass. The fourth applicant, Mr O’Shea, also worked in the area and was caught in the cordon during his lunch break; he left about 8 p.m.

In domestic proceedings, the High Court found that the containment amounted to a deprivation of liberty under Article 5 §1, but held it was lawful under Article 5 §1(c) and that the false-imprisonment claim was defeated by necessity. The police had no alternative at 2 p.m. and the action was proportionate. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that there was no deprivation of liberty, comparing the situation to containment of football crowds or motorway closures. The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights that their restriction within the cordon violated Article 5 §1. The Grand Chamber ultimately held that the containment did not amount to a deprivation of liberty under Article 5 §1, so there was no violation.

Austin and Others v. the United Kingdom (ECtHR Grand Chamber, 15 March 2012) concerned the police crowd-control tactic known as “kettling.” Four applicants were caught inside a police cordon at Oxford Circus, London, on 1 May 2001, during a May Day protest against capitalism and globalisation. They alleged that being confined for up to seven hours amounted to a deprivation of liberty in breach of Article 5 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Before the event, police had intelligence that 500–1,000 “hard-core” demonstrators intended violence. Previous similar protests in London and abroad had caused serious disorder, injuries and property damage. The May Day organisers did not cooperate with police and allegedly encouraged masks and disorder. Nearly 6,000 officers were deployed. By about 2 p.m., over 1,500 people had gathered at Oxford Circus. Police, surprised by the crowd’s size, imposed a cordon to prevent a breach of the peace. It took 20–25 minutes to complete. No announcement was made until 4 p.m. because police feared the cordon was not yet strong enough.

The applicants’ experiences varied. Austin, a demonstrator, needed to leave at 3:45 p.m. to collect her 11-month-old daughter from a crèche. Police refused to let her out, so a friend collected the child. She was released around 9:30 p.m. Black, a passer-by going to a bookshop, was directed by police toward Oxford Circus and then trapped. He was told there was an exit at Bond Street, but when he went there, none existed. He left around 9:20 p.m. Lowenthal, who worked in the area, was on her lunch break and was prevented from returning to work; she was held until about 9:35 p.m. O’Shea, also a local worker on lunch break, was caught in the cordon and released around 8 p.m. The group therefore included both demonstrators and uninvolved bystanders.

Inside the cordon, people could move around and there was no crushing, but conditions became uncomfortable: cold, wet weather, with no food, water, toilets or shelter. Police kept release under review, but controlled dispersal was repeatedly delayed by missile-throwing, violence, attempts to break the cordon and disorderly crowds outside. Around 392–400 people were individually released, including pregnant women, elderly people and children. Collective release began around 7 p.m., was paused and resumed, and dispersal was almost complete by 9:45 p.m. Over 100 arrests were made.

In domestic proceedings, the High Court found the containment was a deprivation of liberty under Article 5 but was lawful. The Court of Appeal held it was not a deprivation of liberty, comparing it to crowd control at football matches or motorway closures. The Grand Chamber ultimately found no violation of Article 5 § 1, holding that the containment did not amount to deprivation of liberty within the Convention. The case thus focused on whether a lengthy police cordon imposed for public-order and safety reasons crossed the threshold from restriction of movement into Article 5 detention.

Dimitar Ivanov v. Bulgaria (Application no. 19418/07, judgment of 14 February 2012) concerned a Bulgarian national, born in 1974, who alleged violations arising from criminal proceedings and a travel ban. He complained that the criminal charges against him had not been determined within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, that he had no effective domestic remedy for that delay under Article 13, and that the prohibition on leaving Bulgaria was unlawful and unjustified.

The criminal proceedings began on 6 October 1994, when the applicant confessed before the police to committing robbery earlier that day with two other individuals. The stolen goods were confiscated the same day. Formal criminal proceedings were instituted only on 4 October 1995. The case then remained dormant until 5 October 2004, when witnesses were questioned. Between 2001 and 2004, the applicant left Bulgaria on several occasions and returned each time. On 6 October 2004, while he was abroad, an ex officio lawyer was appointed and the applicant was charged in absentia with robbery. The first hearing was held on 14 January 2005 in his presence. On 12 April 2006, the Pazardzhik District Court convicted him and sentenced him to one year’s imprisonment, suspended for three years. Following an appeal by a co-defendant, the Pazardzhik Regional Court upheld the conviction and sentence in a final judgment of 12 October 2006.

For the length complaint, the relevant period ran from 6 October 1994, when the applicant confessed, to 12 October 2006, the final judgment. The proceedings therefore lasted about twelve years, including a preliminary investigation and two levels of jurisdiction. The Court found that the case was not particularly complex and that the authorities were responsible for a large part of the delay, especially because the case had remained dormant at the pre-trial stage for approximately nine years. It concluded that the length was excessive and violated the “reasonable time” requirement of Article 6 § 1. It also found a violation of Article 13 because there was no effective domestic remedy for the length of criminal proceedings, consistent with its pilot judgment in Dimitrov and Hamanov v. Bulgaria.

Separately, on 9 March 2007, the Pazardzhik Regional Police Directorate banned the applicant from leaving Bulgaria on account of his conviction and pending rehabilitation. The order relied on section 76(2) of the 1998 Bulgarian Identity Papers Act. The applicant challenged the ban, arguing that he could not provide for his family in Bulgaria and that he had employment opportunities in Serbia. On 25 May 2007, a border police official refused him passage when he attempted to leave Bulgaria despite the prohibition. By a final judgment of 10 October 2007, the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the ban. It reasoned that imposing such a restriction fell within the administrative authority’s discretion, that its assessment was not subject to judicial control, and that the law permitted the ban where a conviction existed prior to rehabilitation. It further held that other factors, such as the applicant’s inability to find employment in Bulgaria, were irrelevant.

The travel-ban facts were central to the applicant’s complaint that the restriction was unlawful and unjustified. The Court’s analysis referred to its case-law in Nalbantski v. Bulgaria concerning travel bans on convicted persons pending rehabilitation. In essence, the applicant’s complaint concerned an automatic or administratively controlled restriction on leaving the country after conviction, with limited or no effective judicial review of the measure’s necessity or proportionality. The Court found violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 and also found a violation regarding the prohibition on leaving Bulgaria under Article 2 of Protocol No. 4.

The Court found the complaint admissible. Bulgaria and found that Bulgaria lacked an effective remedy for complaints about the length of criminal proceedings, resulting in a violation of Article 13.

On 25 May 2007, a border police official refused him passage despite the prohibition. By a final judgment of 10 October 2007, the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the ban. It reasoned that imposing such a restriction fell within the administrative authority’s discretion and was not subject to judicial control, that the law permitted the ban where a conviction existed and rehabilitation had not yet occurred, and that other factors, such as difficulty finding employment in Bulgaria, were irrelevant. Applying the principles from Nalbantski v. Bulgaria, the Court found that this automatic travel restriction, without effective judicial review of its proportionality or the individual circumstances, amounted to a violation of Article 2 of Protocol No. 4.

**Case H. v. Finland (Application no. 37359/09), European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, 13 November 2012 (later referred to the Grand Chamber).**

The applicant, a Finnish national born male in 1963, had always felt she was female but initially coped with her situation. In 1996 she married a woman, and in 2002 they had a child. In 2004 her condition worsened; in 2005 she sought medical help, and in April 2006 she was diagnosed as transgender. She began living as a woman, changed her first names, passport and driving licence in 2006, and underwent gender reassignment surgery in 2009. However, she could not change her male identity number, which continued to indicate that she was male.

In June 2007 the applicant asked the local Register Office to confirm her as female and issue a female identity number. The office refused. Under the Finnish Act on Confirmation of the Gender of a Transsexual, confirmation requires that the person is not married or in a civil partnership, unless the spouse consents to the marriage being converted into a registered civil partnership. The applicant’s wife did not consent to such a conversion. The couple preferred to remain married, and divorce would have conflicted with their religious convictions. The applicant also argued that a civil partnership did not provide the same security as marriage and would affect their child’s legal position.

The applicant appealed to the Helsinki Administrative Court, which rejected her appeal in May 2008. It found that same-sex partners could obtain family-law protection through civil partnership and that the law did not violate constitutional rights. She then appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court, reiterating that the State was violating her private life by requiring her to divorce or convert her marriage. She argued that the male identity number revealed her transgender status every time it was used, and that transgenderism was a medical condition falling within private life. She also claimed that converting the marriage into a civil partnership would mean she could not be a legal father or mother to her child, since a child could not have two mothers. In February 2009 the Supreme Administrative Court rejected her appeal, holding that Finnish law allowed marriage only between a man and a woman, that civil partnership was essentially comparable to marriage, and that the matter fell within the State’s margin of appreciation. A subsequent extraordinary appeal was also refused in August 2010.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention. She complained that her right to private and family life was violated because full recognition of her new gender was made conditional on transforming her marriage into a civil partnership. She also alleged discrimination, since the refusal to give her a female identity number forced her to reveal her transgender status and treated her differently from others. The Court also examined the case under Article 12, concerning the right to marry.

The Government accepted that there had been an interference with private life but argued it was lawful, pursued legitimate aims, and was proportionate. It maintained that the applicant could obtain a new identity number if her spouse consented to a civil partnership, or she could divorce; civil partnership offered nearly identical legal protection. The Chamber agreed. It found that Article 8 was applicable, but that a fair balance had been struck. It noted that Articles 8 and 12 do not require States to allow same-sex marriage, and that the applicant’s situation was not sufficiently similar to others for Article 14 discrimination. The Chamber therefore found no violation of Article 8, no separate issue under Article 12, and no violation of Article 14. The case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 16 July 2014.

In *H. v. Finland*, the applicant, Ms H., was born male in 1963 but identified as female. She married a woman in 1996, and they had a child in 2002. In 2006 she was diagnosed as transgender, began living as a woman, and later underwent gender reassignment surgery in September 2009. Although she changed her first names, passport, and driver’s licence in 2006, her Finnish identity number remained male.

In June 2007, H. asked the local Register Office to confirm her female gender and change her identity number. The office refused. Under the Act on Confirmation of the Gender of a Transsexual, confirmation requires that the person be unmarried or that the spouse consent to transforming the marriage into a civil partnership. H.’s wife did not consent; the couple wished to remain married. H. appealed, arguing that the refusal violated her private and family life. She said divorce would contradict their religious convictions, that a civil partnership did not provide the same security as marriage, and that it would adversely affect their child, including the child’s legal position and the fact that a child could not have two mothers. She also claimed that the male identity number revealed her transgender status in everyday situations, violating her privacy. The Administrative Court and Supreme Administrative Court rejected her appeals. They held that Finnish law permits marriage only between a man and a woman, that same-sex couples may register a civil partnership, and that changing the marriage institution was for Parliament. The Supreme Administrative Court refused an extraordinary appeal in 2010. Separately, reimbursement of hormone treatment costs was initially refused because she lacked a new identity number, but the Social Security Appeal Board later granted reimbursement.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, H. alleged violations of Articles 8 and 14, and the Court also considered Article 12. She argued that conditioning full legal recognition of her female gender on transforming her marriage into a civil partnership breached her right to respect for private and family life and discriminated against her. The Government accepted that there was an interference with private life because she could not obtain a female identity number, but argued that it was lawful and pursued legitimate aims. It said she could obtain a new identity number if her spouse consented to convert the marriage into a civil partnership; otherwise she could remain married or divorce. Civil partnership was substantially equivalent, and parental rights would not be altered.

The Court found Article 8 applicable and accepted there was an interference. However, it balanced H.’s private-life interest against Finland’s interest in maintaining the traditional institution of marriage. Since Finnish law did not permit same-sex marriage, allowing H. to remain married as a woman would create a same-sex marriage. The Court held that Article 12 did not require States to grant same-sex couples access to marriage, and that regulating the effects of gender reassignment on marriage fell within the State’s margin of appreciation. Requiring spousal consent—or, if absent, divorce—was not disproportionate. It also found no separate Article 12 issue and no Article 14 discrimination, because H. was not in a relevantly similar situation to others and the core issue was the absence of same-sex marriage. The Chamber therefore found no violation.

In *Wenerski v. Poland (No. 2)* (Application no. 38719/09, judgment of 24 July 2012), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by Ernest Wenerski, a Polish national with a long criminal record and continuous detention since 1 September 2004. He alleged that his detention in Łódź Remand Centre violated Article 3 of the Convention, mainly because of overcrowding, poor sanitary conditions, and inadequate medical care for his epilepsy and personality disorder. The relevant periods in Łódź Remand Centre were 1 September 2004–10 March 2005; 20 May–30 November 2005; 14 December 2005–19 January 2007; 5 February–22 July 2007; and 8 January 2009–June 2010—altogether about four years.

Medical experts concluded that his epilepsy did not by itself make detention impossible, but recommended a bottom bunk in a non-overcrowded cell. Psychiatric and psychological reports found a mild personality disorder with emotional outbursts and self-injury, though the disorder was considered largely independent of overcrowding. Domestic courts nevertheless accepted that overcrowding may have affected his personality disorder and increased the risk of injury during seizures.

On detention conditions, domestic courts established that from 2002 to 2006 the minimum space per prisoner in Łódź Remand Centre was significantly reduced because of nationwide overcrowding and renovations. During his first four terms, Wenerski occupied 14 different cells measuring 10.5–12 sq m, shared by four to six prisoners, giving him only about 2–2.4 sq m per person. The overcrowding was not temporary but lasted years. Some cells designed for two or four prisoners held six. The cells were allegedly dirty, poorly ventilated, mouldy, and bug-infested; toilet areas were separated only by cloth, causing a lack of privacy and bad odours. On one occasion he was placed on a top bunk despite medical advice and without a ladder or safety rail.

As to medical care, Wenerski suffered numerous epileptic seizures causing cut lips, bruises, abrasions, head bumps, and a bitten tongue. Fellow inmates usually provided first aid, with an in-house doctor or ambulance called later. On at least two occasions he received no medical help after a seizure. In March 2007 a warden allegedly told cellmates to turn him on his side and put something in his mouth. In another cell, staff gave no assistance because they believed he was simulating. He also had a self-mutilation record but received adequate treatment after self-injury.

Wenerski brought a civil action in 2005 seeking 70,000 PLN. In 2009 the Regional Court found a breach of his personal rights due to severe, long-term overcrowding, awarding 2,000 PLN. The Court of Appeal increased this to 5,000 PLN (about EUR 1,180), with roughly EUR 240 ordered for lawyer’s fees. The ECtHR found this redress insufficient—about 25% of its usual award—so he remained a “victim.” It declared the Article 3 complaint admissible and found a violation: the cumulative effects of poor living conditions and his vulnerable health, requiring frequent medical assistance, amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment. No separate Article 8 issue arose, and the remaining Article 6 and 13 complaints were rejected as manifestly ill-founded.

In the case of **Wenerski v. Poland (No. 2)** (Application no. 38719/09, ECtHR Fourth Section, 24 July 2012), the applicant, Ernest Wenerski, a Polish national born in 1970, complained about conditions in Łódź Remand Centre. He was detained there in five periods between 1 September 2004 and June 2010, altogether about four years, and had been continuously detained since 2004. He suffered from epilepsy, regular seizures, and a personality disorder. He alleged that overcrowding and inadequate medical care amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment under Article 3 of the Convention. He also complained under Article 8 about his physical and mental integrity and privacy, and under Articles 6 and 13 about the civil compensation proceedings.

The key medical facts were that the applicant had numerous epileptic fits while in Łódź Remand Centre, often causing injuries such as cut lips, bruises, skin abrasions, head bumps, a bitten tongue, and a head cut from the edge of a bed. Fellow inmates usually provided first aid, while staff later called an in-house doctor or ambulance. On at least two occasions he received no medical help after a seizure. Once, a warden told cellmates to turn him on his side and put something in his mouth; in another cell, a warden considered him to be simulating and no assistance was given. Medical experts found his epilepsy did not itself require special detention conditions, but recommended a bottom bunk in a non-overcrowded cell. His personality disorder was independent of overcrowding but involved emotional outbursts and self-injury.

The domestic courts established that from 2002 to 2006 the minimum space per prisoner in Łódź Remand Centre was significantly reduced because of nationwide overcrowding and renovation. The applicant occupied fourteen different cells measuring 10.5–12 sq m, shared by four to six prisoners. His personal space was only 2–2.4 sq m per person. The overcrowding was not temporary: he spent several years with approximately 2 sq m. Some cells designed for two or four prisoners held six. The cells were dirty, poorly ventilated, and infested with bugs and mould. Toilet annexes were separated only by a sheet of fabric, giving no privacy and causing foul odours. On one occasion he was assigned a top bunk without a ladder or security rail despite medical advice.

In a civil action, the Łódź Regional Court in 2009 found that his right to dignity and humane treatment had been breached by severe, long-term overcrowding and awarded him PLN 2,000. The Court of Appeal increased this to PLN 5,000 (about EUR 1,180), but he was ordered to reimburse about EUR 240 in lawyer’s fees. The ECtHR found this redress insufficient—about 25% of what it would likely award—so he remained a “victim.”

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 3. It noted the structural overcrowding in Polish prisons identified in Orchowski and Norbert Sikorski. For several years the applicant had less than 3 sq m of personal space. Although experts said his epilepsy was independent of detention conditions, his vulnerability meant overcrowding exacerbated distress, tension, personality disorder, and risks during seizures. The Court also criticised shifting responsibility for first aid to cellmates. The cumulative effects amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment. No separate Article 8 issue arose, and the remaining complaints were manifestly ill-founded.

The European Court of Human Rights case *Wenerski v. Poland (No. 2)* (App. no. 38719/09, 24 July 2012) concerned Ernest Wenerski, a Polish national with a long criminal record. He complained under Article 3 that his detention in Łódź Remand Centre, in five periods between 1 September 2004 and June 2010 (about four years), was inhuman and degrading because of overcrowding and inadequate medical care. He suffered from epilepsy with regular seizures and had a personality disorder.

Domestic civil proceedings established the key facts. From 2002 to 2006 the minimum space per prisoner at Łódź Remand Centre was reduced due to nationwide overcrowding and renovation. During the first four periods the applicant occupied fourteen cells of 10.5–12 sq. m shared by four to six prisoners; his personal space was about 2–2.4 sq. m. Overcrowding was not temporary: a cell designed for two was shared by six; a 12 sq. m cell designed for four held six. Courts found overcrowding harmed health and sanitation, increased stress and aggression, and the applicant was involved in fights and disciplinary punishments. Cells were dirty, poorly ventilated, infested with bugs and mould; toilet areas were separated only by fabric, causing odour and no privacy.

Medical expert reports said epilepsy alone did not require special detention conditions, though a bottom bunk in a non-overcrowded cell was recommended. Psychiatry and psychology experts found a personality disorder partly independent of detention conditions. Still, during detention the applicant had numerous epileptic fits, causing injuries such as a bitten tongue, cut head, cut lips, bruises and abrasions. Cellmates usually gave first aid; doctors or ambulances were called later. On at least two occasions he received no help after a seizure. Once the warden told cellmates to put something in his mouth; on another occasion staff allegedly considered he was simulating.

The applicant brought a civil tort action seeking PLN 70,000. In 2009 the Regional Court found his dignity and right to humane treatment breached by severe, long-term overcrowding and awarded PLN 2,000. The Court of Appeal raised this to PLN 5,000 (about EUR 1,180), but he had to reimburse about EUR 240 in lawyer’s fees. No cassation appeal was available. Complaints to penitentiary authorities were rejected as manifestly ill-founded.

The Government made no observations before the ECtHR. The Court found that although domestic courts acknowledged the overcrowding, the compensation was insufficient—about 25% of what it would likely award—so the applicant remained a victim. Relying on its pilot judgments on structural overcrowding in Polish prisons from 2000 to mid-2008, the Court found he had been held for years with less than 3 sq. m of space. His epilepsy and personality disorder made him more vulnerable; overcrowding increased tension and distress, and seizure injuries were worsened by cluttered cells. The practice of relying on cellmates for first aid was criticized. The cumulative conditions and inadequate care amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment, violating Article 3. No separate issue arose under Article 8; complaints under Articles 6 and 13 were manifestly ill-founded.
