In *Drakšas v. Lithuania* (App. no. 36662/04, judgment 31 July 2012), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by Algirdas Drakšas, a Lithuanian politician and founding member of Rolandas Paksas’s Liberal Democrats, that his telephone conversations were intercepted and publicly disclosed, contrary to Article 8, and that he lacked an effective domestic remedy under Article 13.

Key facts: On 16 March 2003 the State Security Department (“SSD”) intercepted a call between Drakšas and Jurij Borisov (“J.B.”), a major contributor to President Paksas’s electoral campaign. The tap had been authorised for J.B.’s telephone. In the call J.B. complained that President Paksas had failed to appoint him as adviser, threatened to recover his money and go public, and claimed he had recordings. Drakšas largely said he did not know about these matters.

On 17 September 2003 the SSD sought authority to tap Drakšas’s telephone, citing contacts with J.B. and A.Z., both campaign contributors, and with Russian citizen V.F., alleged by the SSD to have been expelled from Spain for spying. The Attorney General applied to the Vilnius Regional Court, relying on possible participation in smuggling strategic goods and other crimes. The court granted a secret three-month order. Later it emerged that the request also concerned alleged unlawful attempts to take over shares of “Žemaitijos keliai”.

On 1 November 2003 the SSD declassified the 16 March call and sent it to the Attorney General’s Office. The next day, 2 November, the recording was broadcast by national television channels LTV and LNK. The SSD denied leaking it. Between 18 September and 11 November, the SSD also intercepted Drakšas’s calls with the State President, presidential advisers and business partners, including five calls with the President. The Attorney General warned that intercepting the President’s communications was prohibited and ordered the recordings destroyed and kept confidential, but did not establish whether disclosures had already occurred.

In March 2004 recordings and transcripts were deposited with the Constitutional Court for President Paksas’s impeachment proceedings. At a public hearing on 19 March 2004, some recordings were played and broadcast. Prosecutors refused to open a criminal investigation because the disclosure occurred in public court proceedings and contained no private-life information. Drakšas’s attempts to challenge the tapping order, obtain records, or complain about leaks were unsuccessful; courts held that tapping orders were not appealable and later refused access due to criminal proceedings.

The Court found that the interception itself was an Article 8 interference but was lawful, judicially authorised, necessary for national security and crime prevention, and not exploratory. Interception of calls with the President was incidental and did not make the measure unlawful. Disclosure during the Constitutional Court public hearing was lawful, served public scrutiny of impeachment, and involved public figures; there was no Article 8 violation. However, the leak of the 16 March conversation with J.B. to television was not in accordance with law: despite declassification, it should have remained confidential during the pre-trial investigation, and the authorities never identified the leaker. That disclosure violated Article 8. The Court further found a violation of Article 13 because Drakšas had no effective domestic remedy to challenge the lawfulness of the surveillance or the disclosure.

In **Drakšas v. Lithuania** (Application no. 36662/04), the applicant was a Lithuanian politician, a founding member of the Liberal Democrats party led by Rolandas Paksas, and a member of the Vilnius City Municipal Council. He complained under Article 8 that his telephone conversations had been intercepted and publicly disclosed, and under Article 13 that he had no effective domestic remedy.

The case arose during political tensions surrounding President Paksas. On 16 March 2003, the State Security Department (SSD) intercepted a call between Drakšas and Jurij Borisov (J.B.), a major campaign contributor to President Paksas. J.B.’s telephone had been tapped under court authorisation. In the call, J.B. complained that the President had failed to appoint him as an adviser, threatened to recover money, and said he would go public with damaging information. Drakšas largely replied that he did not know the facts. J.B. was later convicted of threatening the President.

On 17 September 2003, the SSD asked the Attorney General to authorise tapping Drakšas’s telephone. The Attorney General applied to the Vilnius Regional Court, which issued a secret three-month order based on suspected involvement in smuggling strategic goods and other crimes, and links with J.B., A.Z., and Russian citizen V.F. Later, the investigation also concerned alleged unlawful attempts to take over shares of the road-building company “Žemaitijos keliai.” The order was not disclosed to Drakšas. Between 18 September and 11 November 2003, the SSD intercepted his calls, including conversations with the President, presidential advisers, and business partners. Some transcripts contained swearing. Lithuanian law prohibited operational activities targeting the President.

On 1 November 2003, the SSD declassified the 16 March call and sent it to prosecutors. On 2 November, it was broadcast on national television LTV and LNK. The SSD denied leaking it. The Attorney General later ordered that recordings with the President be destroyed and stressed confidentiality. Drakšas complained to prosecutors, the SSD, and courts, but could not effectively challenge the secret tapping order or obtain access to the material. Authorities said the surveillance was lawful and advised him to seek civil damages or SSD information.

In March 2004, recordings and transcripts were sent to the Constitutional Court for President Paksas’s impeachment proceedings. On 19 March 2004, some recordings were played in a public hearing broadcast on television. Drakšas complained, but prosecutors refused to open criminal proceedings, saying the disclosure was lawful in public court proceedings and contained no private-life information.

The European Court of Human Rights held that the interception itself had a legal basis, was judicially authorised, and was necessary for national security and crime prevention; incidental interception of the President did not make it unlawful regarding Drakšas. However, disclosure of the 16 March 2003 conversation with J.B. to the media violated Article 8: even if declassified, it should have remained confidential as pre-trial investigation material, and the leak was never identified or remedied. Disclosure during the Constitutional Court hearing did not violate Article 8 because it was lawful, prosecutor-authorised, in public proceedings, and involved public figures. The Court also found a violation of Article 13 because Drakšas had no effective domestic remedy to challenge the interference or disclosure.

The case *Drakšas v. Lithuania* (no. 36662/04, judgment 31 July 2012) concerned Algirdas Drakšas, a Lithuanian national, founding member of the Liberal Democrats party led by Rolandas Paksas, and a member of Vilnius City Municipal Council. He complained under Article 8 of the Convention that his telephone conversations had been intercepted and publicly disclosed, and under Article 13 that he lacked an effective domestic remedy.

On 16 March 2003, the State Security Department (“SSD”), while lawfully tapping Jurij Borisov, a major contributor to President Paksas’s electoral campaign, recorded a call between Borisov and the applicant. Borisov complained that the President had betrayed him, threatened to recover money and go public; the applicant largely said he did not know the facts and urged calm. On 17 September 2003, the SSD asked the Attorney General to tap the applicant’s telephone, citing operational information about his contacts with Borisov, A.Z., and Russian citizen V.F. The Attorney General then obtained a secret order from the Vilnius Regional Court under the Law on Operational Activities, based on suspected smuggling of strategic goods and other crimes. The order was not disclosed to the applicant. Later it emerged that the request also concerned alleged unlawful attempts to take over shares in the company “Žemaitijos keliai.” The court authorised interception for three months.

Between 18 September and 11 November 2003, the SSD intercepted the applicant’s calls, including calls with the State President, presidential advisers, and business partners. Some transcripts contained swearing. The Attorney General later stated that Article 6 § 3 of the Law on Operational Activities prohibited operational measures against the President and ordered that such recordings not be disclosed and be destroyed.

On 1 November 2003, the SSD declassified the 16 March 2003 conversation with Borisov and sent it to prosecutors. The next day, it was broadcast on national television channels LTV and LNK. The SSD denied leaking it, and no effective investigation ever identified the source. During the President’s impeachment proceedings before the Constitutional Court in March 2004, recordings and transcripts of the applicant’s calls were deposited with the court, and some were played at a public hearing on 19 March 2004, broadcast nationally. Prosecutors refused to open a criminal case, saying the disclosure occurred in a public court hearing and contained no private-life information.

The applicant unsuccessfully challenged the tapping order and sought access to the recordings. Domestic courts held that secret surveillance orders could not be appealed; the SSD and administrative courts refused access, partly because the material had become evidence in criminal proceedings and disclosure was restricted. Complaints about the media leak produced no remedy, and the authorities never established who leaked the 16 March conversation.

The European Court of Human Rights found that the interception itself had a legal basis and did not violate Article 8. However, it found a violation of Article 8 because the authorities failed to keep the 16 March 2003 conversation confidential and it was leaked to the media. It found no violation regarding disclosure during the Constitutional Court’s public impeachment hearing, as this was lawful and involved public figures. It also found a violation of Article 13 because the applicant had no effective domestic remedy to challenge the surveillance and disclosure.

**Case: Levin v. Sweden (Application no. 35141/06), European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, judgment of 15 March 2012.**

The applicant was a Swedish mother of three children, T. (born 1999), S. (born 2001) and D. (born 2002). In 2005, social services investigated concerns about the children’s home environment. The home was found to be in a chaotic and destitute condition, with little furniture and no electricity or running water. The applicant was in a confused state and was briefly committed to compulsory psychiatric care. The children were placed in a temporary family home, and later all three were taken into public care. In October 2005, a permanent care order was granted on the basis that the applicant lacked the ability to care for her children, who had already suffered harm to their health and development. That decision was upheld on appeal in January 2006.

Initially, the applicant had relatively frequent contact with the children: T. for one hour every other week, S. every third week, and D. weekly. After she moved approximately 1,100 km away in May 2006, she visited them about once a month. In December 2006, however, the Social Council restricted her contact rights. Because the children’s father also had contact rights, the Council allocated contact so that each parent would meet the children once every three months, meaning the applicant effectively saw her children only twice a year. The Council relied on an investigation, made in consultation with child psychiatric services, which found that the children had suffered severe harm due to earlier care deficiencies and showed serious negative reactions before, during and after meetings with the applicant. These included anxiety, bedwetting, nightmares, stomach aches, developmental regression and, in S.’s case, clear fear of his mother. The children needed stability and calm in their family homes.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the restrictions violated her right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. She claimed she was a loving mother, that the children would forget her, and that the restrictions were contrary to their best interests. The domestic courts rejected her appeals: the County Administrative Court in April 2007, the Administrative Court of Appeal in October 2007, and the Supreme Administrative Court refusing leave to appeal in December 2007. The Social Council reviewed the restrictions every three months and maintained them. In August 2008, the applicant appealed again, and in November 2008 the County Administrative Court increased contact to four visits per year for four hours each, a decision upheld on appeal in May 2009.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged a breach of Article 8 concerning the contact restrictions. The Government accepted that there had been an interference with family life but argued that it was lawful, pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the children, and was necessary in a democratic society.

The Court found that the restrictions interfered with the applicant’s family life but were in accordance with Swedish law and aimed at protecting the children’s health, morals and rights. Applying stricter scrutiny because the children had been taken into care, the Court nevertheless stressed that the children’s best interests were of crucial importance. It relied on the domestic findings of the children’s severe negative reactions to contact, the need for stability, the father’s competing contact rights, and the children’s own expressed wishes not to see their mother more often or alone. The authorities had not severed all family links and later increased contact. The Court concluded that the restrictions were proportionate and within Sweden’s margin of appreciation. It declared the complaint admissible but found no violation of Article 8.

In *Levin v. Sweden* (Application no. 35141/06, ECtHR, 15 March 2012), the applicant, Eleonor Levin, alleged that Sweden violated Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights by severely restricting her contact with her three children after they were taken into public care.

The applicant was the mother of three children, T. (born 1999), S. (born 2001), and D. (born 2002). Social services had been aware of the family since 2002. In May 2005, an emergency visit revealed that the home was destitute, with no electricity or running water, and the applicant was in a confused state. The children were placed with her in a temporary family home, and she was briefly committed to compulsory psychiatric care. During summer 2005, contact between the applicant and the children became chaotic. After she withdrew consent to voluntary placement, the Social Council took T. and D. into provisional public care, and in October 2005 the County Administrative Court granted permanent care orders for all three children. The courts found that the applicant lacked the ability to care for them, that their health and development had already been impaired, and that there was a serious risk of further harm. Appeals were unsuccessful.

Initially, the applicant had regular but limited contact, including visits and telephone calls. After moving about 1,100 km away in May 2006, she visited roughly once a month. In December 2006, following her request for more contact, the Social Council restricted her contact rights to all three children. Each parent was allowed to meet the children once every three months, meaning the applicant could meet them only once every six months, in a neutral environment with family-home parents and a social worker present. The decision relied on an investigation and consultation with child psychiatric services. It found the children had suffered severe harm, were vulnerable, and reacted negatively to contact: T. became tired, anxious, and wet her bed; S. had stomach pains, vomiting, and fear of his mother; D. regressed, wet her bed, and had sleeping difficulties. The council concluded that limited contact was necessary for the children’s best interests.

The applicant appealed, arguing she had a close relationship with her children, that an earlier custody report had raised no concerns, and that she needed at least monthly contact so they would not forget her. The administrative courts upheld the restrictions in 2007, and the Supreme Administrative Court refused leave to appeal. The Social Council reviewed the restrictions every three months and maintained them. In 2008, the applicant appealed again, and in November 2008 the County Administrative Court increased contact to four times per year, four hours each time; this was upheld in May 2009.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained that the contact restrictions violated her right to respect for family life under Article 8. The Government accepted that there was an interference but argued it was lawful, legitimate, and necessary to protect the children’s best interests.

The Court declared the application admissible. On the merits, it found that the contact restrictions interfered with family life but were based on Swedish law and pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the children’s health and rights. Although the restrictions were severe, the Court stressed that the children’s best interests were crucial. The authorities had not severed all family links: siblings continued to meet, the father had contact, letters and postcards were allowed, and guardianship remained. The children’s negative reactions and expressed wishes, especially T.’s and S.’s reluctance and S.’s fear, supported the restrictions. The applicant was legally represented, and contact was later increased. The Court concluded that the restrictions were proportionate and within the domestic authorities’ margin of appreciation. There was no violation of Article 8.

Levin v. Sweden (Application no. 35141/06), judgment of 15 March 2012, concerned a Swedish mother’s complaint under Article 8 ECHR that contact restrictions imposed after her three children were taken into public care violated her right to respect for family life.

The applicant was the mother of T. (born 1999), S. (born 2001), and D. (born 2002). She separated from the children’s father, B., in 2003 and obtained sole custody, while B. had contact rights. She later married J. Social services had known the family since 2002. In spring 2005, day-care staff reported that the children arrived hungry and dirty, behaved hyperactively, and that the applicant seemed stressed and distracted. On 3 May 2005, emergency social services, accompanied by police and a psychiatrist, found the home destitute—little furniture, no electricity or running water—and the applicant in a confused state. The children were placed with the applicant in a temporary family home. The applicant was briefly committed to compulsory psychiatric care but released after a week.

During summer 2005, contacts between the applicant and children were chaotic. After she withdrew consent to voluntary placement, the Social Council took the children into public care. On 19 October 2005, the County Administrative Court granted permanent care orders for all three children, finding that the applicant lacked the ability to care for them, that their health and development had already been impaired, and that there was a serious risk of further harm. Appeals were rejected, and the Supreme Administrative Court refused leave to appeal in February 2006.

Initially, the applicant had relatively frequent but supervised contact: T. once every other week, S. once every third week, and D. weekly. After moving to Göteborg in May 2006, she visited about once a month. The children were placed in three separate family homes. In November 2006, the applicant requested more contact. On 11 December 2006, the Social Council restricted her contact to meetings once every three months per parent in a neutral environment with family-home parents and a social worker present; in practice, the applicant saw her children roughly twice a year. The decision relied on a BUP consultation and investigation finding that the children had suffered severe harm and had negative reactions to contact: T. became tired, wet her bed, and was anxious after telephone calls; S. had stomach pains, vomiting, fear, stuttering, and aggression; D. regressed, wet her bed, and had sleep difficulties. The Council concluded that limited contact was necessary for the children’s secure development.

The applicant appealed, arguing that she had a close prior relationship with the children and that the restrictions were too severe. The County Administrative Court rejected her appeal in April 2007; the Administrative Court of Appeal upheld that decision in October 2007; and the Supreme Administrative Court refused leave to appeal in December 2007. The Social Council reviewed the restrictions every three months and maintained them. After the applicant appealed again in August 2008, the County Administrative Court increased contact in November 2008 to four times per year for four hours each, finding improvements but continued limitations necessary. The Administrative Court of Appeal upheld this in May 2009.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged an Article 8 violation. The Government accepted an interference but argued it was lawful, legitimate, and necessary in the children’s best interests. The Court found an interference with family life, but accepted that it was lawful and pursued legitimate aims. Assessing necessity, the Court emphasised the children’s best interests, their severe negative reactions, and their own views—T. and S. did not want more than twice-yearly contact or to be alone with their mother, and S. showed fear of her. Although the restrictions were severe, all links were not severed: siblings met monthly, the father had contact, letters were allowed, and parental guardianship remained. The applicant was legally represented, and contact was later increased. The Court concluded the restrictions were proportionate and within Sweden’s margin of appreciation, finding no violation of Article 8.

In *G v. Germany* (Application no. 65210/09, ECtHR, 7 June 2012), the applicant was a German national born in 1968. In 1992, the Frankfurt am Main Regional Court convicted him, as a first offender, of three murders and one attempted murder committed between 1988 and 1990. The victims were four young women unknown to him, killed or attacked in his car, treacherously and for sexual motives, mainly by strangulation. The court found he suffered from a serious mental abnormality, sadistic sexual deviation, lack of empathy and brain damage, and acted with diminished criminal responsibility. It sentenced him to fifteen years’ imprisonment and ordered his placement in a psychiatric hospital under Article 63 of the Criminal Code. Although the conditions for preventive detention under Article 66 were also met, the court did not order it, relying on Article 72(1) because psychiatric hospital placement appeared the more suitable corrective and preventive measure.

He was transferred to a psychiatric hospital in 1992. In 1994, after therapy failed, the court ordered him to serve his prison sentence first. He served the full sentence and was transferred back to a psychiatric hospital in 2006. In April 2007, the Kassel Regional Court terminated his psychiatric hospital placement under Article 67d(6), finding that he had in fact never suffered from the condition diminishing criminal responsibility that had justified the placement. On the same day, he was provisionally detained pending a decision on retrospective preventive detention.

In March 2008, the Frankfurt Regional Court ordered retrospective preventive detention under Article 66b(3) of the Criminal Code, a provision introduced in 2004. It found that he had originally been placed in a psychiatric hospital for several murders; that the placement had been terminated because the qualifying mental condition never existed; and that a comprehensive assessment and expert reports showed a very high risk that he would again commit serious offences, including sexual murders, if released. He refused examination and therapy, and less restrictive measures were considered insufficient. His appeal was dismissed by the Federal Court of Justice in September 2008, and in August 2009 the Federal Constitutional Court rejected his constitutional complaint. It held that retrospective preventive detention was not a penalty but a preventive measure, did not breach the ban on retrospective punishment or legitimate expectations, and that public protection outweighed his interests. It considered that an indefinite psychiatric hospital placement had merely been replaced by another indefinite preventive measure.

The applicant complained under Article 7 §1 of the European Convention on Human Rights that the retrospective order for, and execution of, his preventive detention violated the prohibition on imposing a heavier penalty retrospectively. He argued that preventive detention was in substance a penalty; that retrospective preventive detention was impossible at the time of his offences and 1992 conviction; that Article 66b was enacted only in 2004; that the sentencing court had expressly declined preventive detention; and that he had legitimately expected not to be subjected to it. He further argued that because his psychiatric placement was terminated on the basis that the mental condition never existed, his prior hospital detention could not be treated as a mere transfer to another preventive measure. The Government contended that preventive detention was not a penalty under German law, did not amount to a heavier penalty, and that he remained dangerous; release would breach positive obligations to protect potential victims. The ECtHR declared the complaint admissible, rejected the Government’s objections on exhaustion and victim status, and examined whether the retrospective preventive detention violated Article 7 §1. The Court ultimately found a violation of Article 7 §1.

Case G v. Germany (Application no. 65210/09, judgment 7 June 2012) concerned retrospective preventive detention. The applicant, a German national born in 1968, was convicted in February 1992 by the Frankfurt am Main Regional Court, as a first offender, of three murders and one attempted murder committed between 1988 and 1990. He had killed or attempted to kill four young women unknown to him, treacherously and for sexual motives. He received a 15-year prison sentence and was ordered to be placed in a psychiatric hospital under Article 63 of the Criminal Code. The court found he suffered from a serious mental abnormality, acted with diminished criminal responsibility, and remained dangerous. It also found the conditions for preventive detention were met, but chose psychiatric hospital placement under Article 72 as the more suitable measure.

In March 1992 he was transferred to a psychiatric hospital. In 1994, because therapy had not succeeded, the court ordered him to serve his prison sentence first. He served the full sentence, completed in March 2005. In April 2006 he was returned to the psychiatric hospital. On 5 April 2007 the Kassel Regional Court terminated his psychiatric placement under Article 67d § 6, finding he had in fact never suffered from a condition diminishing criminal responsibility. The same day, he was provisionally detained pending a decision on retrospective preventive detention; that order became final in July 2007.

On 13 March 2008 the Frankfurt am Main Regional Court ordered his retrospective preventive detention under Article 66b § 3, a provision introduced in 2004. The court found he had been placed in a psychiatric hospital after several murders listed in Article 66 § 3, and that termination of placement was sufficient even if the original diagnosis had been wrong. Based on a comprehensive assessment and two psychiatric expert reports—prepared from case files because the applicant refused examination—the court found it very likely he would again commit serious offences, including sexual murders, if released. Less restrictive measures were deemed insufficient.

The applicant’s appeal was dismissed by the Federal Court of Justice in September 2008. His constitutional complaint argued that Article 66b § 3 and the retrospective order violated the Basic Law’s prohibition on retrospective increased punishment, protection of legitimate expectations, the ban on double punishment, and his right to liberty. In August 2009 the Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the complaint, holding that preventive detention was not a penalty but a preventive measure. It found that replacing an indefinite psychiatric placement with an indefinite preventive detention order caused only limited disadvantages and that public protection outweighed the applicant’s expectations.

In December 2009 the applicant lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights, alleging a breach of Article 7 § 1 of the Convention. The key alleged violation was that his retrospective preventive detention and its execution imposed a heavier penalty after his 1992 conviction and sentence had become final. The applicant stressed that retrospective preventive detention was not possible at the time of his offences, that the 2004 law created the basis for it, and that the 1992 sentencing court had expressly declined to order preventive detention. He argued that, without the later law, he would have been released. The Government contended that preventive detention was not a penalty and that he was merely transferred from one indefinite preventive measure to another because he remained dangerous.

The Court rejected the Government’s objections on exhaustion of domestic remedies and victim status, noting that later 2011 domestic remedies could not redress the prior detention at issue. It declared the Article 7 § 1 complaint admissible and proceeded to examine whether the retrospective preventive detention amounted in substance to a penalty.

**Summary of G v. Germany (Application no. 65210/09)**

The case of *G v. Germany* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by a German national, Mr. G, on 9 December 2009. The applicant alleged that the retrospective order for his preventive detention and its subsequent execution violated Article 7 § 1 of the Convention, which prohibits the retrospective imposition of a heavier penalty.

The key facts are as follows. In 1992, the Frankfurt am Main Regional Court convicted the applicant, a first-time offender, of three counts of murder and one count of attempted murder, committed between 1988 and 1990. He was sentenced to fifteen years' imprisonment. The court, relying on expert psychiatric testimony diagnosing him with a serious mental abnormality and diminished criminal responsibility, ordered his placement in a psychiatric hospital under Article 63 of the Criminal Code. While the court also found that the conditions for preventive detention were met, it opted for the psychiatric hospital placement as the more suitable measure for correction and prevention.

After his prison sentence was served, the applicant was transferred back to a psychiatric hospital. However, in April 2007, the Kassel Regional Court terminated this placement. Based on a new expert assessment, the court found that the applicant had never actually suffered from the mental disorder that would have warranted his hospital placement. Despite this, the court ordered his provisional detention pending a decision on retrospective preventive detention, as he was still considered highly dangerous.

In March 2008, the Frankfurt am Main Regional Court ordered the applicant’s retrospective preventive detention under Article 66b § 3 of the Criminal Code. This provision, enacted in 2004, allowed for preventive detention if a person's placement in a psychiatric hospital was terminated because the condition it was based on had never existed, and if a comprehensive assessment showed a high likelihood of the person committing serious future offences. The court found the applicant posed a high risk of committing further murders for sexual motives if released.

The applicant exhausted domestic remedies, but his appeal to the Federal Court of Justice and his constitutional complaint to the Federal Constitutional Court were both dismissed. The Federal Constitutional Court ruled that the retrospective preventive detention did not breach the prohibition on retrospective punishment, as preventive detention was a purely preventive measure aimed at protecting the public, not a penalty.

Before the European Court, the applicant argued that his preventive detention amounted to a "penalty" for the purposes of Article 7. He stressed that at the time of his offences, a retrospective order for preventive detention was not legally possible. Furthermore, the original sentencing court had deliberately declined to order his preventive detention in 1992. He argued that the legal basis for his current detention, Article 66b of the Criminal Code, was only enacted in 2004, thus imposing a heavier penalty retrospectively. The government contested this, arguing that preventive detention is not a penalty and that the applicant was merely transferred from one indefinite measure of correction (psychiatric hospital) to another (preventive detention) due to his persisting dangerousness.

In **Andreşan v. Romania** (ECtHR, 30 October 2012), the applicant, Ilie Andreşan, alleged that Romanian police ill-treated him and that the ensuing investigation was ineffective, contrary to Article 3 of the Convention.

The key facts began on 30 April 2001. The applicant’s employer, I.N., informally told two police officers, N.D. and C.B., that money had been stolen from his house and that he suspected Andreşan. The officers arrested Andreşan in the street, handcuffed him in front of other people, and took him to the police station. According to Andreşan, officers kept him handcuffed and beat him continuously to force him to confess to the theft. He signed a confession. He was then taken, still handcuffed, to his parents’ house, where police searched the home and seized 1,000,000 Romanian lei, which they gave directly to I.N. Andreşan alleged that officers continued beating him in front of his parents to make him reveal where the rest of the money was hidden. When he refused, he was returned to the police station and beaten again until I.N. asked the officers to release him. I.N. reportedly said the applicant had been so severely beaten that he felt pity for him. On 2 May 2001, after I.N. lodged an official theft complaint, Andreşan was again taken to the police station, where he alleged the abuse continued.

In October 2001, Andreşan retracted his confession and accused N.D. and C.B. of beating and threatening him on 30 April and 2 May to obtain statements. He complained of abuse of position and wrongful arrest. A military prosecutor investigated. Two witnesses said they knew nothing; one said he saw the applicant being hit and arrested; a neighbour said an officer hit Andreşan and pushed him into the car “like a bag of potatoes.” The accused officers and I.N. denied the allegations.

On 12 June 2002, the military prosecutor dismissed the complaint. He noted the absence of medical evidence, said it was “hard to believe” the victim would not have sought forensic examination if injured, noted the applicant had not earlier complained against the police, and found witness statements contradictory. The applicant objected that his parents and other key witnesses had not been questioned, that he and his lawyer could not participate in interviews or question witnesses, and that witnesses had been pressured. His complaints were rejected. In 2004, the Târgu-Mureş Court of Appeal upheld the dismissal based almost exclusively on the investigation file and refused to re-examine witnesses. The High Court of Cassation and Justice dismissed his appeal in November 2004, reasoning that the pending theft proceedings against him made parallel investigations into the police impossible.

Separately, Andreşan was indicted for theft in November 2002. In March 2005, the Luduş District Court acquitted him. It found the house search and seizure unlawful, excluded evidence obtained thereby, and held, based on witness statements, that Andreşan had been subjected to violence on 30 April 2001 and that his confession was made under duress from police and I.N. This judgment became final in January 2006.

Before the European Court, the Government argued non-exhaustion, claiming Andreşan could have sought reopening or civil damages after the 2005 acquittal. The Court found the investigation ineffective: the military prosecutor’s independence was doubtful, supporting witness statements were discarded, civilian courts relied on the military file without hearing witnesses, and the 2005 acquittal did not amount to an effective investigation because the police were not parties. On the substantive claim, the domestic courts and the Government effectively acknowledged ill-treatment, and witness evidence supported it. The Court concluded that Andreşan suffered treatment contrary to Article 3 and that the investigation was ineffective.

In *Andreşan v. Romania*, the applicant alleged that Romanian police ill-treated him to obtain a confession and that the subsequent investigation was ineffective, in violation of Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

On 30 April 2001, the applicant’s employer informally told two police officers that money had been stolen from his home and that he suspected the applicant. The officers arrested the applicant in the street, handcuffed him in public, and took him to the police station. He alleged that officers kept him handcuffed and beat him continuously until he signed a confession. He was then taken, still handcuffed, to his parents’ house, where police searched the premises, seized 1,000,000 Romanian lei, and handed the money directly to the employer. The applicant claimed the officers continued beating him in front of his parents to make him reveal where the rest of the money was hidden. He was taken back to the station and beaten again until the employer intervened and took him home. The employer allegedly said the applicant had been beaten so severely that he felt pity for him. On 2 May 2001, after the employer filed a formal theft complaint, the applicant was again taken to the police station, where the alleged abuse continued.

On 8 October 2001, the applicant retracted his confessions and accused the two police officers of beating and threatening him on 30 April and 2 May to force a confession. He also complained of wrongful arrest. The case was handled by a military prosecutor. Some witnesses said they knew nothing; one said he saw the applicant being hit and arrested; a neighbour said an officer hit the applicant and pushed him into the car “like a bag of potatoes.” The accused officers and the employer denied the abuse. On 12 June 2002, the military prosecutor dismissed the complaint, citing the lack of medical evidence, the applicant’s failure to complain earlier, and contradictory witness statements. The applicant’s challenge was rejected, and civilian courts later upheld the prosecutor’s decision, relying almost exclusively on the investigation file and refusing to re-examine witnesses. The High Court of Cassation and Justice dismissed his appeal in November 2004, reasoning that parallel investigations were not possible while theft proceedings against the applicant were pending.

Meanwhile, the applicant was indicted for theft. In March 2005, the district court acquitted him, finding the house search and seizure unlawful and holding that his confession had been made under duress. It also found, based on witness statements, that he had been subjected to violence by police and the employer. That judgment became final in January 2006.

Before the European Court, the Government argued that the applicant should have sought reopening of the investigation or civil damages. The Court rejected these arguments and found a violation of Article 3. It held that the investigation was ineffective: the military prosecutor’s independence was doubtful, courts relied on the file without hearing witnesses, and the later acquittal merely incidentally acknowledged ill-treatment without punishing the officers. On the substantive issue, the Court found that the evidence supported the applicant’s account and that the domestic authorities had effectively acknowledged police ill-treatment. The absence of a medical certificate was not fatal, since the criminal courts still found that police violence had occurred. The Court concluded that the applicant had suffered treatment contrary to Article 3 and that the State had failed to conduct an effective investigation.

The officers arrested the applicant in the street, handcuffed him in front of others, and took him to the police station. There, he alleged, he was kept handcuffed and repeatedly hit to force him to confess to the theft. He signed a confession. The applicant claimed the beatings continued in front of his parents as officers tried to make him reveal where the rest of the money was hidden. He was taken back to the station and beaten again until the employer took pity on him and asked for his release. The employer allegedly later said he had taken the applicant home because he had been so severely beaten. On 2 May 2001, after the employer lodged an official theft complaint, the applicant was again taken to the police station, where abuse allegedly continued.

On 8 October 2001, the applicant retracted his confessions and accused officers N.D. and C.B. of beating and threatening him on 30 April and 2 May to obtain statements. He lodged a complaint for abuse of position and wrongful arrest. The military prosecutor investigated. Some witnesses said they saw the applicant being hit and arrested; a neighbour stated that an officer hit him and pushed him into the car “like a bag of potatoes.” The accused officers and the employer denied the allegations. On 12 June 2002, the military prosecutor dismissed the complaint, noting the absence of medical evidence, the applicant’s failure to complain earlier, and contradictory witness statements. The applicant complained that key witnesses, including his parents, had not been questioned and that he and his lawyer could not participate. His complaints were ultimately dismissed. The Court of Appeal relied exclusively on the investigation file, refused to re-examine witnesses, and upheld the dismissal. The High Court dismissed his appeal on 24 November 2004, reasoning that criminal proceedings against the applicant were still pending, so parallel proceedings against the officers were not possible.

Meanwhile, the applicant was indicted for theft on 5 November 2002. On 1 March 2005, the Luduş District Court acquitted him. It found the house search and seizure unlawful, struck the resulting evidence, and held, based on witness statements, that on 30 April 2001 the applicant had been subjected to violence and that his confession had been obtained under duress from police officers and the employer. This was upheld on appeal and became final on 18 January 2006.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 3. Procedurally, the investigation was ineffective: the military prosecutor’s independence was doubtful, the investigators disregarded evidence of abuse, and the civilian courts relied almost exclusively on the file and never heard witnesses despite requests. The 2005 acquittal did not cure this, because the police officers were not parties and the finding of abuse was incidental. Reopening and civil remedies were too equivocal to require exhaustion. Substantively, domestic courts and the Government acknowledged the ill-treatment, witness evidence supported the applicant, and the absence of a medical certificate was not fatal. The Court concluded that the applicant had suffered treatment contrary to Article 3 and that the investigation had been ineffective.

In **Ball v. Andorra** (Application no. 40628/10), the applicant, Mr Toby Nigel Ball, a British national living in Andorra, complained about the Andorran courts’ failure to enforce a final contact schedule allowing him to see his two children. He relied on Article 6 § 1 (fair hearing) and Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) of the Convention.

The applicant married in February 2003 and had two children, a son born in 1992 and a daughter born in 2003. He left the family home in March 2004, and the children remained with their mother. In the ensuing legal separation proceedings, the separation judge on 13 June 2005 granted custody to the mother and set up a contact schedule for the applicant. In July 2006, following criminal complaints by the mother, psychological reports and a public prosecutor’s submission, the judge provisionally suspended the contact schedule, allowing only telephone contact.

In December 2006 the mother petitioned for divorce. The applicant sought restoration of contact. On 2 April 2007 the separation judge restored the contact schedule for the daughter and appointed a psychologist to examine the family with a view to restoring contact with the son. The mother appealed. On 19 June 2008 the High Court of Justice partially reversed that decision, striking down the psychologist’s appointment but upholding the restoration of the contact schedule established by the separation judgment. The applicant then applied for enforcement.

However, on 24 July 2008 the separation judge again provisionally suspended the contact schedule, relying on a psychologist’s report that said contact was not desirable pending treatment. On 21 October 2008 the divorce judgment was delivered. It granted custody to the mother and established a contact schedule that remained suspended pending a psychologist’s assessment and possible treatment; the judge relied on reports and the son’s testimony that he did not want contact with his father. The applicant appealed.

On 12 February 2009 the High Court, hearing the appeal against the July 2008 suspension, held that because a divorce judgment had now been delivered, the separation judgment should be set aside and the divorce judgment enforced. It deprived the July 2008 decision of effect. The applicant asked for clarification, specifically whether the 19 June 2008 decision in the separation proceedings should be enforced while the divorce judgment was not yet final or enforceable. On 23 April 2009 the High Court refused clarification, stating that during a suspensive appeal against the divorce judgment, neither that judgment nor previous decisions adopted in separation proceedings were enforceable. Thus, despite the earlier final contact decision, no contact schedule could be enforced during the pending divorce appeal.

The applicant’s subsequent appeal for annulment was dismissed on 28 May 2009. He then lodged a constitutional appeal, arguing that the impossibility of enforcing the final 19 June 2008 decision while the divorce appeal was pending denied him a fair hearing and violated his right to meaningful contact with his children. On 12 October 2009 the Constitutional Court declared the appeal inadmissible as devoid of constitutional content, finding the High Court’s decisions neither arbitrary nor illogical. A final appeal was dismissed on 21 December 2009.

The key alleged violation was therefore that the domestic courts’ procedural handling created a prolonged deadlock: the applicant had a final contact decision in his favour, but it became unenforceable due to the pending divorce proceedings and suspensive appeal, preventing him from maintaining meaningful contact with his children. The case was communicated to the Andorran Government in April 2011, and the United Kingdom waived its right to intervene.

**Summary of *Ball v. Andorra* (Application no. 40628/10)**

The case of *Ball v. Andorra* originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr. Toby Nigel Ball, a British national residing in Andorra, against the Principality of Andorra. The applicant alleged violations of Articles 6 § 1 (right to a fair hearing) and 8 (right to respect for private and family life) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The core of his complaint was that the Andorran High Court of Justice’s refusal to enforce a final judicial decision setting up a parent-child contact schedule denied him a fair hearing and violated his right to maintain meaningful contact with his two children.

The factual background is complex, involving protracted separation and divorce proceedings. The applicant married in 2003 and had two children. Following his departure from the family home in 2004, legal separation proceedings began. A separation judgment in June 2005 granted custody to the mother and established a contact schedule for the applicant. However, this schedule was provisionally suspended in July 2006, based on criminal complaints by his wife, a psychological report indicating the son's mental stability was at risk, and a proposal by the public prosecutor for a psychological examination before contact resumed. Telephone contact was permitted.

In December 2006, divorce proceedings were initiated. Both parties sought custody. In April 2007, a judge restored the contact schedule for the daughter and appointed a psychologist to facilitate restoring contact with the son. This decision was partially upheld on appeal in June 2008, which confirmed the separation judgment's contact schedule should be restored but struck down the psychologist's appointment. Despite this, in July 2008, the separation judge again provisionally suspended the contact schedule, citing a psychologist's report that contact was not desirable until the children underwent comprehensive treatment.

A critical development occurred in October 2008 when the divorce judgment was issued. It granted custody to the mother and set up a new contact schedule, which was to remain suspended pending a psychologist's assessment aimed at restoring contact. The applicant appealed. While this appeal was pending, he sought enforcement of the final June 2008 decision. In a decision of 23 April 2009, the High Court of Justice clarified that due to the suspensive effect of the appeal against the divorce judgment, neither the divorce judgment's measures nor those from the prior separation proceedings were enforceable until the appeal was decided.

The applicant's subsequent appeals, including a constitutional appeal, were dismissed. The Andorran courts held that the procedural rules mandated awaiting the outcome of the divorce appeal before enforcing any contact measures, and that this interpretation did not infringe his right to a fair hearing. The Constitutional Court found the appeal inadmissible, stating the lower courts' decisions were not arbitrary.

The Andorran judicial system's procedural framework effectively suspended the enforcement of the earlier final decision until the divorce case, including its appeal, was fully resolved. This created a situation where the applicant was deprived of court-ordered contact with his children for an extended period, forming the basis of his complaint that the State failed to enforce his right to family life and denied him an effective remedy to secure that enforcement, contrary to Articles 8 and 6 § 1 of the Convention.

In *Toniolo v. San Marino and Italy*, the applicant, Giuseppe Toniolo, was an Italian national resident in San Marino. In 2009 Italian authorities were prosecuting him, inter alia, for money laundering. On 3 July 2009 the Rome Tribunal ordered his preventive detention. On 10 August 2009 the Rome Prosecutor asked the San Marino authorities to extradite Toniolo and place him in preventive detention, relying on the 1939 Italy–San Marino Convention on Friendship and Good Neighbourhood. The Italian Ministry of Justice was also asked to authorize the extradition request.

On 12 August 2009 the Commissario della Legge (CL) accepted the request and ordered Toniolo’s arrest and preventive detention pending extradition under the 1939 Convention, noting that San Marino had also ratified the 1957 European Convention on Extradition. Toniolo was arrested and notified that day. On 14 August the CL asked the Captains Regent to authorize extradition pending the official Italian request. On 20 August Toniolo and his lawyer were heard, and a request for house arrest was refused. On 26 August Italy’s embassy informed San Marino that San Marino had become party to the 1957 Convention on 16 June 2009 and that Italy would submit its formal extradition request within the Convention’s 40-day period, requesting an extension if necessary.

Toniolo challenged the detention on 24 August, arguing that there were no urgent grounds under the 1939 Convention. On 7 September the appeal judge dismissed this, holding that preventive detention facilitated extradition and that urgency arose from the risk of absconding and San Marino’s geographical situation. The judge nevertheless stated that the applicable law was now the 1957 Convention. He noted that San Marino had made a reservation when ratifying the 1957 Convention that its bilateral agreement would prevail, but Italy had neither made nor acknowledged such a reservation. The same day Toniolo sought release after 30 days under the 1939 Convention. On 11 September the CL rejected this, saying the 1957 Convention prevailed and allowed up to 40 days.

On 18 September Italy submitted the formal extradition request and documents. The CL found the 1957 conditions fulfilled, the Captains Regent authorized extradition under the 1957 Convention, and the CL ordered Toniolo’s extradition. He was extradited on 19 September. He was picked up at 12:50 a.m. and notified of the extradition order ten minutes later, but refused to sign, claiming it should be given to his lawyer. He was transferred to Italian police at 2:45 p.m.; the order was notified to one of his lawyers at 4:15 p.m.

Toniolo brought domestic proceedings challenging both the preventive detention and the extradition. He argued that there was no danger, flight risk or need to protect the community; that the charges were unfounded; that the extradition request had been improperly submitted; and that the authorities had wrongly mixed the 1939 and 1957 Conventions. Because San Marino’s reservation made the 1939 Convention prevail for it while Italy applied the 1957 Convention, he claimed the legal basis was conflicting and unworkable. He also alleged defence-rights breaches: he was not heard before extradition, his lawyers were not notified of or allowed access to him during the extradition, and he was not notified of the relevant authorizations except the 18 September order.

The domestic courts rejected his complaints. The Terza Istanza Penale held that the 1957 Convention governed, that any reliance on the 1939 Convention did not prejudice his liberty, that Toniolo and his lawyers had been properly notified and had access, and that the extradition request was sufficiently justified. It confirmed the detention and extradition orders. Toniolo was released by the Italian courts on 12 February 2010 after statutory detention time-limits expired. Before the European Court of Human Rights, he alleged that his preventive detention and subsequent extradition breached Article 5 § 1 of the Convention.

Giuseppe Toniolo, an Italian national resident in San Marino, was the subject of an extradition request from Italy. On 10 August 2009, the Prosecutor of the Rome Tribunal informed San Marinese authorities that criminal proceedings for money laundering had been instituted against Toniolo and that the Rome Tribunal had ordered his preventive detention. Italy requested his extradition and detention under the bilateral 1939 Convention on Friendship and Good Neighbourhood.

On 12 August 2009, the Commissario della Legge (CL) accepted the request and ordered Toniolo's arrest and preventive detention pending extradition. He was arrested the same day. The CL noted that San Marino had ratified the 1957 European Convention on Extradition. On 14 August, the CL requested authorization from the Capitani Reggenti (CR), but no reply was received. Toniolo and his lawyer were heard on 20 August, and his request for house arrest was rejected.

A key legal issue arose regarding which convention governed the proceedings. On 26 August, the Italian embassy noted San Marino's recent accession to the 1957 Convention, stating the extradition request would follow its 40-day timeline. The applicant appealed his detention on 24 August, arguing there were no urgent reasons under the 1939 Convention. On 7 September, the appeal judge dismissed this, holding that while initial steps followed the 1939 Convention, the 1957 Convention now applied. The court acknowledged San Marino had made a reservation for its bilateral agreement to prevail, but noted Italy had not made a reciprocal reservation. Toniolo's request for release after 30 days under the 1939 Convention was rejected on 11 September, with the CL stating the 1957 Convention's 40-day limit prevailed.

On 18 September 2009, the Italian Ministry of Justice submitted the formal extradition request. The CL confirmed the conditions of the 1957 Convention were met and requested authorization. The CR authorized the extradition, and the CL ordered it the same day. Toniolo was extradited to Italy on 19 September 2009. He was notified of the extradition order in the early hours, transferred to Italian police later that day, with his lawyer notified in the afternoon.

Toniolo initiated two parallel sets of proceedings challenging the legality of his detention and extradition. In the first, he argued before the Terza Istanza Penale that there was no risk of absconding, that charges were unfounded, and that the extradition was vitiated by the application of the wrong convention and procedural breaches. In a judgment of 20 November 2009, the court confirmed the arrest and detention orders. It reasoned that the conflicting application of the two conventions created an unworkable situation, but found the detention was legitimate under both and that the extradition process caused no prejudice.

In the second set of proceedings, Toniolo appealed the extradition order directly. This was rejected on 23 November 2009 as duplicating arguments. He appealed this rejection, and on 8 February 2010, the Terza Istanza Penale confirmed the extradition order. The court found that Toniolo and his lawyers had been properly notified and had access to documents, and that all proceedings were governed by the 1957 Convention, which had not prejudiced his rights. Toniolo was released by Italian authorities on 12 February 2010 upon expiration of his detention time-limits.

**Summary of Harkins and Edwards v. the United Kingdom (Applications nos. 9146/07 and 32650/07)**

The case of Harkins and Edwards v. the United Kingdom concerns two separate applications brought against the United Kingdom before the European Court of Human Rights. Both applicants faced extradition to the United States and alleged that, if extradited, they would be at risk of sentences incompatible with Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. Specifically, they argued that the death penalty or life imprisonment without parole (LWOP) would violate this provision.

The first applicant, Phillip Harkins, a British national born in 1978, was sought by the United States for a murder committed in Jacksonville, Florida, in August 1999. Harkins was indicted for first-degree murder and attempted robbery with a firearm. The prosecution initially filed a notice to seek the death penalty, but this was later withdrawn. The case against him relied heavily on the testimony of a co-accused, Terry Glover, who claimed Harkins shot the victim during a robbery. Harkins maintained that the shooting was accidental and denied being present. Under Florida’s felony murder rule, a defendant can be convicted of murder without premeditation if a death occurs during a serious felony such as armed robbery. The maximum penalty for first-degree murder in Florida is life imprisonment without parole.

Harkins was arrested in the United Kingdom in 2003. The United States requested his extradition, and in 2005, the US Embassy provided a diplomatic note assuring that the death penalty would not be sought or imposed. The Secretary of State ordered his surrender in 2006. Harkins challenged this decision, arguing that the assurance was inadequate and that he could still face the death penalty or an irreducible life sentence. The High Court rejected his claim in 2007, finding no real risk of the death penalty and that any life sentence would not be grossly disproportionate given the seriousness of the alleged offence. Further representations were refused in 2010, and judicial review was dismissed in 2011.

The second applicant, Joshua Daniel Edwards, a United States national born in 1987, was sought by the United States for charges arising from a 2006 incident in Maryland. He was indicted on eleven counts, including first-degree murder, attempted murder, and assault. The allegations were that Edwards, after being mocked, left an apartment and returned with others, producing a handgun and firing shots that killed one man and wounded another. The prosecution indicated it would not seek the death penalty but might seek life imprisonment without parole. Diplomatic notes assured that the death penalty would not be sought or carried out.

Edwards was arrested in the UK in 2007, and the Secretary of State ordered his extradition. He appealed, arguing that a sentence of life imprisonment without parole would violate Article 3. The High Court dismissed his appeal, relying on existing domestic precedent. Both cases raised questions about the compatibility of harsh sentencing regimes with the Convention’s prohibition on inhuman or degrading treatment in the context of extradition.

**Mr Harkins**, a British national, was sought by the United States for a 1999 murder and attempted armed robbery in Jacksonville, Florida. The victim, Joshua Hayes, was shot in the head during an alleged robbery. The prosecution relied largely on the testimony of a co-accused, Terry Glover, who said Harkins shot Hayes after Hayes refused to hand over money. Harkins denied being present, claiming he had lent his car to another participant. Initially, Florida prosecutors filed notice that they would seek the death penalty, but this was later withdrawn. US diplomatic notes assured the UK that the death penalty would not be sought or imposed. Harkins nevertheless argued that, under Florida’s felony murder rule, he could be convicted of first-degree murder without premeditation and possibly face death sentencing. Later affidavits and a Florida trial judge’s order confirmed that no death penalty proceedings would occur and that the maximum sentence would be life imprisonment. Harkins then focused on the alleged risk of mandatory LWOP. He argued that such a sentence would be grossly disproportionate and irreducible, especially given his youth at the time and a diagnosis of severe personality disorder. UK authorities and courts rejected this, finding that clemency was available, the sentence was not irreducible, and the alleged offence—a killing during armed robbery—was grave enough that LWOP would not clearly violate Article 3.

Prosecutors anticipated seeking LWOP, but the sentencing judge retained discretion to impose LWOP, life with parole, or a suspended sentence, and could consider mitigation such as youth and lack of serious criminal history. The central issue was whether extradition to the United States, with assurances against the death penalty but with possible very severe life sentences, would breach Article 3. The UK courts had emphasized the extradition context, the reliability of US assurances, the availability of clemency or sentencing discretion, and the gravity of the alleged offences. Harkins denied being present, claiming he had lent his car to another man, and alternatively suggested the gun discharged accidentally. Florida law permitted a first-degree murder conviction either by premeditated design or under the felony murder rule, which allowed conviction for a killing committed during a serious felony such as armed robbery, even without premeditation. The possible sentence was death or life imprisonment without parole. The United States gave diplomatic assurances that the death penalty would not be sought or imposed, and the Florida trial judge later stated that no death-penalty sentencing proceedings would be held, so the maximum sentence would be life imprisonment. Harkins nevertheless argued that extradition would breach Article 3 because he risked mandatory LWOP under the felony murder rule, which he said would be irreducible and grossly disproportionate. UK courts rejected that argument, noting that clemency or commutation was available and that his alleged conduct was grave.

In 2006, a Maryland grand jury indicted him on eleven counts arising from the killing of Mr Rodriguez, the non-fatal shooting of Mr Perry, and assault of Mr Broadhead. The allegation was that Edwards, after being mocked about his stature and appearance, left an apartment and returned with three other men. While Broadhead was restrained, Edwards allegedly produced a handgun and shots were fired, killing Rodriguez and wounding Perry. The first-degree murder count carried a maximum sentence of life imprisonment; the death penalty did not apply. Diplomatic notes assured the UK that the death penalty would not be sought or carried out. However, a Maryland prosecutor stated that the State anticipated seeking LWOP, and that the sentencing judge had discretion to impose LWOP, life with parole, or a suspended sentence. Edwards argued that extradition would violate Article 3 because he faced a real risk of LWOP. The UK High Court dismissed that ground, considering itself bound by domestic authority.

Both applicants lodged applications with the European Court of Human Rights in 2007. The Court applied Rule 39 interim measures, indicating to the UK Government that they should not be extradited pending the proceedings. The key alleged violation was Article 3 ECHR: that extradition would expose them to death-penalty or LWOP sentences amounting to inhuman or degrading treatment. For Harkins, the death-penalty risk was said to have been addressed by assurances and the trial judge’s order, but the alleged LWOP risk remained under Florida’s felony murder rule. For Edwards, the death-penalty risk was excluded, but the alleged LWOP risk remained because Maryland could seek LWOP and the judge had sentencing discretion. It granted amnesty for criminal offences committed in connection with the war in Croatia between 17 August 1990 and 23 August 1996, except for the gravest breaches of humanitarian law or war crimes, including genocide. Pursuant to that Act, the criminal proceedings against Tarbuk were discontinued on 7 October 1996, and he was immediately released.

On 9 June 1998, Tarbuk brought a civil action against the State in the Zagreb Municipal Court, seeking damages for his detention. He relied on Article 480 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which provided that a person who had been in pre-trial detention but against whom criminal proceedings had not been instituted or had been discontinued by a final decision was entitled to compensation.

While that civil claim was pending, Croatia amended the Code of Criminal Procedure. On 2 June 1999, a new Article 484(a) was enacted, providing that no compensation was to be granted in respect of detention where criminal proceedings had been discontinued pursuant to a pardon or amnesty under special laws or decisions. A further amendment on 27 October 1999 specified that this exclusion applied to criminal offences committed between 17 August 1990 and 23 August 1996.

On 31 January 2006, the Zagreb County Court dismissed his appeal, reasoning that Article 484(a) extinguished his compensation claim and had retroactive effect. On 28 August 2007, the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal on points of law, expressly confirming that Article 484(a) applied retroactively. On 19 November 2007, Tarbuk lodged a constitutional complaint, arguing that the retroactive application of Article 484(a) to a civil action filed a year before that provision came into force had extinguished his right to compensation. On 5 November 2009, the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint, endorsing the lower courts’ reasoning. It held, in substance, that the constitutional right to compensation concerned unlawful deprivation of liberty; amnesty did not render the detention unlawful, and the legislature could exclude amnesty beneficiaries from compensation.

The Government maintained that the domestic courts had correctly applied the relevant law.
