Milan Sýkora v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 23419/07) concerned a Czech national with a psycho-social disability who alleged violations of his right to liberty and private life arising from the removal of his legal capacity and his involuntary detention in a psychiatric hospital.

In 2000, the Brno Municipal Court deprived Mr Sýkora of legal capacity at the request of the City of Brno, relying on a 1998 expert report diagnosing paranoid schizophrenia. He was not summoned to appear, was not served with the decision, and was represented by a court employee who had never met him. The judgment became final in December 2000. After he learned of it and appealed, the Regional Court quashed the decision in August 2001. However, in November 2004, the Municipal Court again deprived him of legal capacity and appointed the City of Brno as his guardian. This second decision relied on a 2004 expert report by the same doctor, who had not examined him because he refused medical examinations. The court did not hear him, the judgment was not served on him, and it became final in January 2005. He learned of it in June 2006, appealed, and in October 2006 the Regional Court quashed the decision, criticising the expert opinion because it had been prepared without examining him. In September 2007, the Municipal Court declined to deprive him of legal capacity, based on a new expert report finding that he was mentally ill but not schizophrenic and was fully capable of making legal assessments. In total, he was deprived of legal capacity for about two years and six months.

The detention at issue occurred in November 2005. After a verbal, non-violent argument with his partner, she called the police and an ambulance. Although the police found no signs of violence and the partner confirmed he had not been aggressive, an ambulance doctor took him to Brno-Černovice Psychiatric Hospital. On admission, two examinations concluded he suffered from schizophrenia. He insisted there was no reason for detention and warned that neuroleptic medication harmed his eyesight, but medication was administered by injection after he refused it. The hospital notified the Municipal Court so it could review the lawfulness of his involuntary admission. However, on 14 November 2005, his guardian—the City of Brno—consented to his detention. The employee who signed the consent had never met him and did not inform him. Under domestic law, this made him a voluntary patient, so the court did not review the involuntary hospitalisation. He was released on 29 November 2005 after twenty days. Later attempts to obtain judicial review failed because the courts considered that no proceedings had been instituted, that the guardian had consented, and that he was no longer detained.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Mr Sýkora complained under Article 5 §§ 1 and 4 that his psychiatric detention was unlawful and lacked sufficient safeguards against arbitrariness, and that he had no opportunity to seek judicial review of his detention. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore the absence of any effective court review, the detention’s reliance solely on the guardian’s retrospective consent without consulting Mr Sýkora, and the broader context of his legal-capacity deprivation, which left him unable to challenge the detention himself.

**Case: Sýkora v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 23419/07)**

Milan Sýkora, a Czech national born in 1949 with a psycho-social disability, was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia and had prior psychiatric hospitalisations. In 2000, the Brno Municipal Court deprived him of legal capacity at the request of the City of Brno, relying on an expert report by Dr H. The applicant was aware of the proceedings but was not summoned or served with the decision. He was represented by a court employee who never met him and took no substantive part. After an appeal, the Regional Court quashed that decision, but in 2004 the Municipal Court again deprived him of legal capacity. The new expert report was prepared without examining him because he refused medical examinations. The judgment was not served on him, and the City of Brno was appointed guardian. In total, he was deprived of legal capacity from December 2000 to August 2001 and from January 2005 to October 2006—about two and a half years. In 2007, following a fresh expert opinion that he was mentally ill but not schizophrenic and was capable of making legal assessments, the court decided not to deprive him of capacity.

The detention at issue occurred on 9 November 2005, after a verbal argument with his partner. Police found no violence, and the partner confirmed he had not been aggressive. Nonetheless, an ambulance doctor took him to Brno-Černovice Psychiatric Hospital. The applicant disagreed but did not resist. On admission, two examinations concluded he suffered from schizophrenia. He insisted there was no reason for detention and warned that neuroleptic medication harmed his eyesight. When he refused medication, it was administered by injection; he later claimed his eyesight deteriorated. His complaint letter to the hospital director was retained by staff and never answered. The hospital notified the Municipal Court of his involuntary admission, but then contacted his guardian, the City of Brno, which consented to detention on 14 November 2005. The employee who signed the consent had never met the applicant and did not inform him. He was moved to a more lenient ward but still could not leave. On 14 November, a lawyer from the Mental Disability Advocacy Center told the court the detention was unlawful and requested release. He was released on 29 November 2005.

After release, the applicant tried to obtain judicial review. A judge indicated that a power of attorney had to be signed by his guardian; the guardian refused. His request for review was answered that no proceedings had been instituted because the guardian had consented. Complaints and constitutional appeals were unsuccessful. In January 2012, the Constitutional Court held that the courts had rightly not instituted review proceedings because the guardian had consented and because the applicant was no longer detained; it suggested civil damages against the hospital.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of his right to liberty and private life due to the removal of legal capacity and psychiatric detention. The key complaints were under Article 5 § 1—that his detention was unlawful and arbitrary because it rested solely on his guardian’s retrospective consent, without court approval or sufficient safeguards—and under Article 5 § 4—that he had no opportunity to seek judicial review of the lawfulness of his detention. The Court noted that the 20-day detention was involuntary, that no domestic court reviewed it because domestic law treated him as voluntary once the guardian consented, and that the guardian had never met or consulted him. It found that such consent was not a sufficient safeguard against arbitrariness and that no proceedings existed by which the lawfulness of his detention could be determined or his release ordered.

In *Sýkora v. the Czech Republic*, the European Court of Human Rights examined the involuntary psychiatric detention and removal of legal capacity of Milan Sýkora, a Czech national born in 1949 with a psycho-social disability and a history of schizophrenia.

In 2000, the Brno Municipal Court deprived Mr Sýkora of legal capacity at the request of the City of Brno. The decision relied on an expert report diagnosing paranoid schizophrenia. Although aware of the proceedings, he was not summoned, not served with the judgment, and was represented by a court employee who never met him and took no substantive part. After an appeal, the Regional Court quashed the decision in 2001, but in 2004 the Municipal Court again deprived him of legal capacity and appointed the City of Brno as his guardian. A new expert report relied on the earlier findings because Mr Sýkora refused examination. The expert recommended that the judgment not be served on him. The court did not hear him; the judgment became final in January 2005. He learned of it in June 2006 and successfully appealed. In September 2007, the court restored his legal capacity. In total, he was deprived of legal capacity for about two years and six months.

The detention facts arose on 9 November 2005, after a verbal argument with his partner. Police found no violence, and the partner confirmed he had not been aggressive. Nevertheless, an ambulance doctor took him to the Brno-Černovice Psychiatric Hospital. Two admission examinations concluded he suffered from schizophrenia. He insisted there was no reason for detention and warned that neuroleptic medication harmed his eyesight, but medication was administered by injection. He alleged his eyesight deteriorated.

The hospital notified the Municipal Court of the involuntary admission so that the lawfulness of detention could be reviewed. However, the hospital also contacted Mr Sýkora’s guardian, the City of Brno, which consented to the detention on 14 November 2005. The employee who signed the consent had never met him and did not inform him. Under domestic law, the guardian’s consent meant Mr Sýkora was treated as a voluntary patient, so the court did not review the detention. A Mental Disability Advocacy Center lawyer requested his release, but he remained hospitalised until 29 November 2005—twenty days. Later attempts to obtain judicial review failed: courts said no review proceedings had been instituted because the guardian had consented, and after release no proceedings could continue. The Constitutional Court dismissed his appeals, one for non-exhaustion and another as unsubstantiated. In separate damages proceedings, the Ministry of Justice awarded CZK 102,000 for the unreasonable length of the incapacitation proceedings and acknowledged procedural failures, but not a violation of his liberty. Ordinary courts rejected further damages claims.

Before the European Court, Mr Sýkora alleged violations of Article 5 § 1 and Article 5 § 4 of the Convention. He argued that his psychiatric detention was unlawful and arbitrary because it rested solely on retrospective guardian consent, without court approval or safeguards. The Government contended he had lost victim status and had not exhausted domestic remedies. The Court rejected those objections.

On the merits, the Court found that although initial medical expertise existed, the detention lacked sufficient safeguards against arbitrariness. No domestic court reviewed the lawfulness of detention; the guardian’s consent was the only safeguard, and the guardian had never met or consulted him. Thus, the detention was not “lawful” under Article 5 § 1. The Court also found a violation of Article 5 § 4 because Mr Sýkora had no opportunity to seek judicial review of his detention or to have his release ordered. The case illustrates the need for judicial review of guardians’ consent to deprivations of liberty of incapacitated persons.

In *Harroudj v. France* (Application no. 43631/09), the European Court of Human Rights examined France’s refusal to allow a French national to adopt an Algerian child placed in her *kafala* care.

The applicant, Katya Harroudj, a French national born in 1962, lived in Villeurbanne. The child, Zina Hind, was born in Algeria on 3 November 2003, abandoned anonymously by her mother. Because her father was also unknown, she became a ward of the Algerian State in December 2003, with the director of social services in Boumerdès appointed as guardian. On 13 January 2004, the President of the Boumerdès court granted Harroudj, then aged 42 and unmarried, the right to take the child into *kafala* care and authorised the child to leave Algeria and settle in France. A subsequent Algerian decision allowed the child to take Harroudj’s surname, becoming Hind Harroudj. The child arrived in France on 1 February 2004 and lived continuously with the applicant and the applicant’s mother.

In November 2006, Harroudj applied for full adoption, arguing that adoption best served the child’s interests under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and the Hague Convention on Intercountry Adoption. In March 2007, the Lyons *tribunal de grande instance* dismissed the application. It noted that *kafala* gave the applicant parental authority and enabled her to protect the child’s interests, but under Article 370-3 of the French Civil Code, a foreign minor could not be adopted where the child’s personal law prohibited adoption, unless the minor was born and habitually resident in France. Algerian law prohibited adoption (*tabanni*) under Article 46 of the Family Code, while permitting *kafala*. The Lyons Court of Appeal upheld that decision in October 2007, finding the choice-of-law rule compatible with Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention and with international law. It held that *kafala* was not equivalent to adoption and preserved the child’s interests. In February 2009, the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s appeal on points of law.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged violations of Article 8 alone and Article 14 taken together with Article 8. She argued that the refusal to recognise a legal parent-child relationship between her and Hind—whom she regarded as her daughter—was a disproportionate interference with her family life. She pointed to consequences such as lack of inheritance rights, difficulties regarding guardianship after her death, and obstacles to the child’s acquisition of French nationality. She also alleged discrimination based on the child’s nationality or national origin, because children from countries that did not prohibit adoption could be adopted in France.

The Government disputed that there was any interference with family life, noting that *kafala* gave the applicant rights comparable to guardianship and that family life continued. It stressed that the Convention does not guarantee a right to adopt and that the refusal was consistent with the child’s best interests and international obligations. It relied on Article 20 of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, which recognises *kafala* as a form of alternative care, and on the Hague Convention’s requirement that a child be adoptable under the law of the State of origin. It also noted that French law offered ways to alleviate the prohibition, including an exception for children born and habitually resident in France and the possibility of acquiring French nationality after five years’ care by a French national, which could then permit adoption.

The ECtHR found no violation of Article 8 and no separate issue under Article 14. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were the child’s Algerian nationality, Algerian law’s prohibition of adoption, the judicially granted *kafala*, the child’s continuous residence in France, the refusal of full adoption, and the alleged effects on the applicant’s family life and equal treatment.

**Harroudj v. France** (ECtHR, 4 October 2012) concerned a French national, Ms Katya Harroudj, who was granted **kafala**—an Islamic-law guardianship arrangement—over an Algerian child, Zina Hind. The child was born in Algeria on 3 November 2003, abandoned anonymously by her mother, with no known father, and became a ward of the Algerian State. In January 2004, an Algerian court granted the applicant kafala, authorised the child to leave Algeria for France, and later permitted a name change to Hind Harroudj. The child arrived in France in February 2004, aged about three months, and lived continuously with the applicant and the applicant’s mother.

In November 2006, the applicant applied for the child’s **full adoption**. French courts refused. The Lyons tribunal de grande instance in 2007 and the Lyons Court of Appeal later that year held that adoption was unavailable because Algerian law prohibited it. Under Article 370-3 of the French Civil Code, adoption of a foreign minor cannot be ordered where the child’s personal law prohibits adoption, unless the minor was born and habitually resides in France. Hind was born in Algeria and did not fall within that exception. Algerian law permits **kafala** but prohibits **tabanni** (adoption), stating that adoption is prohibited by the Sharia and by legislation. The Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s appeal in February 2009, finding no violation of the Convention and noting that kafala is recognised by Article 20 of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child as a form of alternative care.

The applicant complained before the European Court of Human Rights under **Article 8** (right to respect for family life) and **Article 14** (prohibition of discrimination). She argued that the refusal to allow adoption denied her and Hind a legal parent-child relationship, despite their de facto family life. She claimed this interfered disproportionately with her family life and affected the child’s inheritance rights, nationality prospects, and continuity of care. She also alleged discrimination based on the child’s national origin, because children from countries that permit adoption could be adopted in France, while Algerian children in kafala care could not.

The French Government argued that there was no interference with family life, since kafala gave the applicant parental authority and enabled her to act in the child’s interests. It stressed that the Convention does not guarantee a right to adopt, that adoption must consider the child’s best interests, and that international law recognises kafala as a valid alternative care arrangement. It also noted that French law offered ways to alleviate the effects of non-adoption: a name change, a will, appointment of a guardian, and possible acquisition of French nationality after five years of care, after which adoption might become possible.

The ECtHR found **no violation of Article 8**. It treated the case as concerning positive obligations rather than direct interference. Given the lack of European consensus and the recognition of kafala in international instruments, France enjoyed a wide margin of appreciation. The Court found that France had struck a fair balance by respecting the child’s Algerian personal law while allowing integration through mechanisms such as nationality and name change. It also found **no separate issue under Article 14**, since the discrimination complaint was essentially the same as the Article 8 complaint already rejected.

In *Harroudj v. France* (ECtHR, 4 October 2012), the applicant, Ms Katya Harroudj, a French national living in Villeurbanne, complained about France’s refusal to allow her to adopt a child of Algerian nationality placed in her *kafala* care. The child, Zina Hind, was born in Algeria in 2003, abandoned anonymously by her mother, with no known father, and became a ward of the Algerian State. In January 2004 an Algerian court granted the applicant *kafala* and authorised the child to leave Algeria; the child later took the applicant’s surname, Harroudj. She arrived in France in February 2004 and lived with the applicant and the applicant’s mother.

In November 2006 the applicant applied for full adoption. In 2007 the Lyons courts refused. They relied on Article 370-3(2) of the French Civil Code, which bars adoption of a foreign minor where the child’s personal law prohibits adoption, unless the child was born and habitually resides in France. Hind was born in Algeria, and Algerian Family Code Article 46 prohibits adoption (*tabanni*) while permitting *kafala*. The Court of Cassation upheld the refusal in 2009. It noted that *kafala* was recognised by Article 20(3) of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child as an alternative care arrangement and that it preserved the child’s best interests, even though it did not create a legal parent-child relationship.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged violations of Articles 8 and 14. Under Article 8, she argued that refusing adoption denied her and Hind a legal parent-child relationship, interfered with their established family life, and harmed Hind’s interests: no intestate inheritance, uncertainty on guardianship after the applicant’s death, no immediate nationality, and a lack of full legal security. She said adoption best served the child’s best interests. Under Article 14, she alleged discrimination based on the child’s national origin, because children whose countries do not prohibit adoption could be adopted in France.

The Government argued that *kafala* already gave the applicant parental authority and allowed family life to continue; the Convention does not guarantee a right to adopt. The refusal allegedly protected the child’s best interests and respected international adoption safeguards, including the Hague Convention’s requirement that the State of origin find the child adoptable.

The ECtHR accepted that family life existed but found the refusal to equate *kafala* with adoption did not amount to an interference; it examined the case as a positive obligation. It noted a wide margin of appreciation because no European consensus equates *kafala* with adoption. International law recognises *kafala*, and French law provided mitigating measures: name change, a will, appointment of a guardian, and possible later adoption once the child acquired French nationality. The Court concluded France had struck a fair balance and found no violation of Article 8. No separate Article 14 issue arose, since the discrimination complaint was essentially the same as the Article 8 complaint.

**PETA Deutschland v. Germany** (Application no. 43481/09), European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, judgment of 8 November 2012.

The applicant, PETA Deutschland, the German branch of the animal-rights organisation PETA, complained that German civil injunctions prohibiting its planned poster campaign violated its right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention.

In March 2004 PETA planned a campaign titled “The Holocaust on your plate,” similar to one previously run in the United States. The campaign consisted of seven posters juxtaposing photographs of Holocaust victims with photographs of animals in factory farming. One poster showed emaciated, naked concentration-camp inmates beside starving cattle under the heading “walking skeletons.” Another showed piled human bodies beside slaughtered pigs under “final humiliation.” Another showed inmates on stock beds beside hens in laying batteries under “if animals are concerned, everybody becomes a Nazi.” A further poster showed a starving inmate beside starving cattle with the title “The Holocaust on your plate” and text stating that 12 million humans were killed in the Holocaust, while as many animals are killed every hour in Europe for human consumption.

Three individuals—P.S., C.K. and S. Korn—then president and vice-presidents of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, all Holocaust survivors, and C.K. having lost family in the Holocaust—sought an injunction preventing publication of the posters via the internet, public exhibition or otherwise. They alleged the campaign was offensive and violated their human dignity and personality rights.

The Berlin Regional Court granted an injunction in March 2004 and confirmed it in the main proceedings. The Berlin Court of Appeal rejected PETA’s appeals, and in February 2009 the Federal Constitutional Court rejected PETA’s constitutional complaint. The Federal Constitutional Court doubted whether the campaign violated human dignity, but upheld the injunction on the basis that the posters banalised the fate of Holocaust victims and violated the plaintiffs’ personality rights as Jews living in Germany. It accepted that Jews in Germany formed a group singled out by fate and owed a special moral obligation, and that the lower courts had given sufficient reasons for preferring the plaintiffs’ rights over PETA’s freedom of expression.

Before the European Court, PETA argued that the posters did not equate humans and animals but merely showed disturbing similarities; that it had no intent to debase Holocaust victims; that the campaign addressed a matter of public interest—animal welfare; and that the Austrian Supreme Court had refused a similar injunction. The German Government argued that the injunction was prescribed by law, pursued the legitimate aim of protecting personality rights, and was necessary in a democratic society, especially given Germany’s historical responsibility.

The European Court found the interference prescribed by law and pursuing a legitimate aim. On necessity, it noted that the campaign concerned animal protection and was therefore in the public interest, requiring weighty reasons for restriction. However, it emphasised the historical and social context, particularly Germany’s special obligation toward Jews. The domestic courts had carefully balanced the competing interests and gave relevant and sufficient reasons. They found no intent to debase, but held that PETA had instrumentalised the plaintiffs’ suffering and banalised the Holocaust, aggravated by depicting victims in a vulnerable state. The civil injunction covered only seven posters, was not criminal, and left PETA other means to publicise its cause. The Court therefore held there was no violation of Article 10. PETA’s remaining complaints under Articles 6 and 14 were rejected as manifestly ill-founded.

Case: PETA Deutschland v. Germany (ECtHR, 8 Nov 2012, app. no. 43481/09). The applicant, the German branch of PETA, planned in March 2004 an advertising campaign called “The Holocaust on your plate.” It used seven posters juxtaposing photographs of Holocaust victims with images of factory-farmed animals. One showed emaciated, naked concentration-camp inmates next to starving cattle under “walking skeletons.” Another showed heaped human corpses next to slaughtered pigs under “final humiliation.” Another placed inmates lying on camp bunks next to hens in laying batteries under “if animals are concerned, everybody becomes a Nazi.” A further poster showed a starving, naked male inmate beside starving cattle and stated: “Between 1938 and 1945, 12 million human beings were killed in the Holocaust. As many animals are killed every hour in Europe for the purpose of human consumption.” PETA said the campaign aimed to criticise mass animal farming and encourage abstention from animal products.

Three Holocaust survivors, who were president and vice-presidents of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, sought an injunction from the Berlin Regional Court. One had lost her family in the Holocaust. They argued the posters were offensive, equated their suffering with that of animals, and violated their human dignity and personality rights. The Regional Court granted the injunction, later confirmed in main proceedings; the Berlin Court of Appeal rejected PETA’s appeals, and the Federal Constitutional Court dismissed PETA’s constitutional complaint in February 2009. The German courts accepted that the posters were expressions of opinion on a matter of public interest and did not primarily aim to debase Holocaust victims. However, they found the campaign placed Holocaust victims on the same level as animals, instrumentalised their suffering for animal-protection purposes, banalised the Holocaust, and violated the plaintiffs’ personality rights. The Federal Constitutional Court doubted a direct human-dignity violation but found sufficient justification based on banalisation, personal honour, and the special status of Jews in Germany.

Before the ECtHR, PETA complained mainly under Article 10 that the civil injunction violated its freedom of expression. It also complained under Article 6 that the domestic courts arbitrarily misassessed the facts and failed to follow relevant case-law, and under Article 14 that it was stigmatised as anti-Semitic. PETA argued that the posters did not intend to debase anyone, that Holocaust comparisons were used in public debate, and that the Austrian Supreme Court had refused a similar injunction.

The ECtHR found that the injunction was an interference with Article 10. It was prescribed by German law (Civil Code §823/§1004 and Criminal Code §185), pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the plaintiffs’ personality rights, and was necessary in a democratic society. Although animal protection is public interest, the Court stressed Germany’s historical context and special obligation toward Jews. Domestic courts had carefully weighed the interests and gave relevant, sufficient reasons: PETA had instrumentalised and banalised Holocaust suffering. The civil injunction was proportionate, limited to seven posters, and left other means of expression. Thus no Article 10 violation. The Article 6 and 14 complaints were manifestly ill-founded.

**Case: PETA Deutschland v. Germany (App. no. 43481/09, ECtHR, 8 Nov. 2012)**

PETA Deutschland, the German branch of the animal-rights organisation PETA, planned in March 2004 an advertising campaign titled “The Holocaust on your plate.” The campaign used posters juxtaposing black-and-white photographs of concentration-camp inmates and Holocaust victims with colour photographs of animals in mass-farming conditions. Captions included “walking skeletons,” “final humiliation,” “if animals are concerned, everybody becomes a Nazi,” and “The Holocaust on your plate,” with text comparing the 12 million human victims of the Holocaust with the number of animals killed hourly in Europe for food. PETA’s aim was to criticise factory farming and encourage public reflection on animal suffering.

Three individuals—the president and two vice-presidents of the Central Council of Jews in Germany—sought an injunction before the Berlin Regional Court to stop publication of seven specified posters. All three had survived the Holocaust as children; one had lost her family in it. They argued that the campaign was offensive and violated their human dignity, personality rights, and the personality rights of one plaintiff’s dead family members.

The Berlin Regional Court granted the injunction and confirmed it. It accepted that the posters were expressions of opinion protected by freedom of expression and related to a matter of public interest. It also found no primary intent to debase Holocaust victims. However, it held that an ordinary viewer would understand the posters as equating the fate of Holocaust victims with that of animals. In light of the German Basic Law’s central commitment to human dignity, this comparison was arbitrary and exploited the suffering of concentration-camp victims to advocate better treatment of animals. The Berlin Court of Appeal rejected PETA’s appeals in 2004 and 2005. In 2009, the Federal Constitutional Court rejected PETA’s constitutional complaint. It doubted that the campaign violated human dignity, but found the injunction justified by the plaintiffs’ personality rights: the campaign banalised the Holocaust, and Jews living in Germany could rely on a self-image as a group singled out by fate and owed a special moral obligation. The lower courts had sufficiently weighed the competing interests.

PETA applied to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging mainly a violation of Article 10 (freedom of expression). It also complained under Article 6 that domestic courts arbitrarily assessed the facts, and under Article 14 that it was stigmatised as anti-Semitic. PETA argued that the posters did not equate humans and animals, showed only disturbing similarities, were not intended to insult, and that Holocaust comparisons were part of public debate. It noted that the Austrian Supreme Court had refused a similar injunction. The German Government maintained that the injunction was prescribed by law, pursued protection of the plaintiffs’ personality rights, and was necessary and proportionate given Germany’s historical responsibility.

The ECtHR found an interference with Article 10. It was prescribed by German law and pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the reputation or rights of others. On necessity, the Court noted that the campaign concerned animal farming, a public-interest issue, and that offensive or shocking expression is protected. However, the domestic courts had carefully examined freedom of expression and found that PETA instrumentalised Holocaust victims’ suffering for animal protection, aggravating the violation because the victims were shown in a vulnerable state. The Court emphasised Germany’s specific historical and social context and its special obligation toward Jews living in Germany. The domestic courts gave relevant and sufficient reasons. The injunction was civil, not criminal, limited to seven posters, and PETA had other means to publicise its cause. The interference was therefore proportionate. There was no Article 10 violation; the remaining complaints were manifestly ill-founded.

**Milić v. Montenegro and Serbia** (Application no. 28359/05, ECtHR, 11 December 2012) concerned the prolonged non-enforcement of a final domestic judgment ordering the applicant’s reinstatement, and the alleged absence of an effective domestic remedy.

The applicant, Ivan Milić, a Serbian national born in 1966, had been employed by the Clinical Centre of Montenegro, a State-run medical institution in Podgorica. On 20 June 2002, the Court of First Instance in Podgorica ordered the Clinical Centre to reinstate him. That judgment became final on 4 February 2003 and was confirmed by the Supreme Court on 16 December 2003.

Despite the final judgment, enforcement did not occur. On 23 April 2003, the Clinical Centre informed the applicant that it could not comply and would instead seek an “alternative solution.” An enforcement order was issued on 22 May 2003 and confirmed on 26 June 2003. However, on 19 August 2003, the Clinical Centre concluded an agreement with the Special Hospital in Risan—another State-run institution—whereby the Risan hospital accepted the applicant as an employee. On 17 October 2003, the Risan hospital issued a decision making him its employee as of 30 October 2003. The applicant had already informed the State Prosecutor on 30 September 2003 that he did not approve this arrangement. Under domestic labour law, transfer to another employer required the employee’s consent, which was absent.

Separately, in May 2004, the Court of First Instance ordered the Clinical Centre to pay the applicant EUR 4,456 in salary arrears for September 2001 to 3 February 2003. That judgment was upheld in October 2004 and apparently later enforced. The applicant also began working at the Clinical Centre of Serbia on 3 February 2003, initially temporarily and later permanently.

On 21 October 2009, according to the Montenegrin Government, the applicant signed an Agreement on Termination of Employment with the Clinical Centre, terminating his employment retroactively from 3 February 2003 and waiving further claims. On 26 October 2009, he withdrew his enforcement request, and on 5 November 2009 the enforcement proceedings were terminated. The applicant claimed he was effectively forced to settle because enforcement had been pending for over five years and he needed to regularise his new employment. He argued that this did not remove his complaint about the delay.

The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 19 July 2005 against both Montenegro and Serbia. He complained under Articles 6 § 1 and 13 of the Convention about the non-enforcement of the final reinstatement judgment and the lack of an effective domestic remedy.

The Court declared the complaints against Serbia inadmissible as incompatible *ratione personae*, because the enforcement proceedings were conducted solely by Montenegrin authorities. Montenegro’s objections that the applicant was no longer a victim, or had failed to exhaust domestic remedies, were rejected. The Court found that the 2009 settlement did not address the alleged length of non-enforcement, and that the suggested remedies—request for review, action for fair redress, constitutional appeal—were either introduced after the application or ineffective for length complaints.

On the merits, the relevant period ran from 3 March 2004, when the Convention entered into force for Montenegro, to 26 October 2009, when the applicant withdrew the enforcement request—over five years and seven months. The Court stressed that final judgments must be enforced, that enforcement proceedings must be urgent, and that employment disputes require exceptional diligence. The Montenegrin authorities made no real attempt to enforce the reinstatement judgment, while the applicant did not contribute to the delay. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1 and also found that there was no effective domestic remedy, contrary to Article 13.

**Milić v. Montenegro and Serbia** (Application no. 28359/05, ECtHR, 11 December 2012) concerned the prolonged non-enforcement of a final domestic judgment ordering the applicant’s reinstatement and the absence of an effective domestic remedy.

The applicant, Ivan Milić, a Serbian national born in 1966, was ordered reinstated by the Court of First Instance in Podgorica on 20 June 2002 to his position at the Clinical Centre of Montenegro, a State-run medical institution. That judgment became final on 4 February 2003 and was confirmed by the Supreme Court on 16 December 2003. On 23 April 2003, the Clinical Centre informed the applicant that it could not comply and would seek an “alternative solution.” An enforcement order was issued on 22 May 2003 and confirmed on 26 June 2003.

On 19 August 2003, the Clinical Centre agreed with the Special Hospital in Risan, another State institution, that the latter would take the applicant as an employee. The applicant objected on 30 September 2003. On 17 October 2003, the Risan hospital decided he would become its employee from 30 October 2003; he received that decision on 20 October 2003. Under domestic labour law, such a transfer required the employee’s consent, which was absent.

Later, on 21 October 2009, the applicant concluded an Agreement on Termination of Employment with the Clinical Centre, terminating his employment as from 3 February 2003 and waiving further claims. On 26 October 2009 he withdrew his enforcement request. Enforcement proceedings were terminated on 5 November 2009, final on 17 November 2009. A separate judgment for salary arrears was enforced. The applicant had also begun working at the Clinical Centre of Serbia in February 2003, later on a permanent basis.

On 19 July 2005, the applicant lodged an application against Montenegro and Serbia, complaining about non-enforcement of the final reinstatement judgment and the lack of an effective domestic remedy. The Court examined the complaints under Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention.

Serbia was dismissed as a respondent because the enforcement proceedings were conducted solely by Montenegrin authorities. Montenegro argued that the applicant had lost victim status due to the 2009 termination agreement, waiver and withdrawal of enforcement. The Court rejected this: the agreement did not address the length of the non-enforcement, so the applicant remained a victim for that complaint.

Montenegro also argued that the applicant failed to exhaust domestic remedies, including a request for review, an action for fair redress under the 2007 Right to a Trial within a Reasonable Time Act, and a constitutional appeal. The Court rejected these objections. The request for review had not been shown effective for proceedings already long pending before the Act; the action for fair redress was introduced after the application and had no transitional provision for pending Strasbourg cases, and was time-barred; the constitutional appeal was not effective for length complaints.

On the merits, the Court reiterated that Article 6 § 1 protects the execution of final, binding judicial decisions and requires effective, expeditious enforcement. The relevant period ran from 3 March 2004, when the Convention entered into force for Montenegro, to 26 October 2009, when the applicant withdrew the enforcement request — over five years and seven months, with more than nine months already elapsed before that date. The reinstatement issue was important and not exceptionally complex. After the Convention entered into force, the authorities made no real attempt to enforce the judgment, and the proposed transfer required consent that was lacking. The applicant did not contribute to the delay. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1. It also found that Montenegro had not provided an effective domestic remedy for the length/non-enforcement complaint, resulting in a violation of Article 13.

**Falter Zeitschriften GmbH v. Austria (No. 2)** concerned an Article 10 complaint by the publisher of the Vienna weekly *Falter* after Austrian courts ordered it to pay damages under the Media Act for defamation of a judge.

The case arose from criminal proceedings against H.P., a security officer at the Traiskirchen Reception Centre, who was accused of raping K., a Cameroonian asylum seeker. In May 2005 the Wiener Neustadt Regional Court acquitted H.P. on the principle of *in dubio pro reo*. The written judgment included a passage noting K.’s alleged prior prostitution in her country of origin, which the court said allowed an inference that she might have become involved with the accused to gain some advantage.

In issue 19/05, *Falter* published an article titled “‘Sex with a nigger woman’” about the case. The article described K.’s background, her asylum claim, her rape complaint, and the investigation and trial. It strongly criticised the proceedings, reporting that police had called K. “the nigger woman,” that she was repeatedly linked to prostitution, and that the accused gave shifting accounts. It also referred to the Court of Appeal’s earlier finding that rape and coercion appeared made out and its order that H.P. be prosecuted. The article criticised Judge I.K., who presided over the acquittal, claiming that she had alleged K. had immoral motives, attributed “the basest intentions” to her without proof, ignored relevant evidence, and delivered a scandalous judgment. It contrasted the acquittal reasoning with the Court of Appeal’s assessment and accused the trial court of failing to address evidence such as the torn red underpants and the fact that the accused admitted locking the room and removing the key.

Judge I.K. brought defamation proceedings under section 6 of the Media Act and Article 111 of the Criminal Code. She claimed the article stated that she had grossly misused her office and sought compensation and retraction. The applicant argued that the statements were true and that the article was protected criticism, focused not on the acquittal itself but on the treatment of the victim and the judgment’s reasoning. It sought to prove truth through witnesses and case files, and unsuccessfully sought the assigned judge’s disqualification because the claimant’s lawyer had previously represented that judge.

The Vienna Regional Court found for Judge I.K. It held that the article gave a biased account, sided with K., and treated contrary evidence as incredible. The applicant had not proved the truth of the impugned statements. The court found that the criminal judgment had assessed the evidence extensively, that the prostitution reference had some basis in the file, and that it could not be established that the judge made base insinuations or disregarded evidence. The accusation that a judge had acted without factual basis and from racist motives deliberately to acquit an accused was a severe defamation. The “scandal” value judgment was based on factual assertions that had been disproved. Applying *Prager and Oberschlick v. Austria*, the court accepted that the press could criticise the justice system but held that this attack exceeded permissible limits and endangered public confidence in the judiciary. It ordered EUR 7,000 compensation plus publication of a summary. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal.

The applicant company complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the Media Act judgment ordering it to pay damages infringed its right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention.

Falter Zeitschriften GmbH v. Austria (No. 2) concerned an Article 10 complaint by the publisher of the Austrian weekly newspaper Falter after it was ordered to pay damages for defaming a judge. The applicant company alleged that the Media Act judgment ordering compensation infringed its right to freedom of expression.

The case arose from criminal proceedings before the Wiener Neustadt Regional Court in May 2005. H.P., a security officer at the Traiskirchen Reception Centre, was acquitted of raping K., a Cameroonian asylum seeker, on the basis of in dubio pro reo. The presiding judge was Judge I.K. The written judgment contained a passage referring to K.’s alleged past prostitution and suggesting that the accused’s claim—that K. might have become involved with him to gain an advantage—could not be excluded.

Falter then published an article in issue 19/05 highly critical of the case. The article described K.’s background and the alleged failings at the Traiskirchen centre, and sharply attacked Judge I.K.’s handling of the trial. It claimed that the judge and lay assessors had no doubt about K.’s guilt, had “unfinished business” with the African woman, attributed the basest motives to her without proof, ignored relevant evidence, and delivered a scandalous judgment. It contrasted the acquittal reasoning with a Court of Appeal decision that had found rape and coercion made out beyond doubt. It also criticized the judge’s treatment of bakery witnesses, the torn red underpants, and the security officer’s changing statements. Judge I.K. regarded these statements as accusing her of grossly misusing her judicial office.

Judge I.K. sued the applicant under section 6 of the Media Act and Article 111 of the Criminal Code, seeking compensation and retraction. The applicant argued that the impugned statements were true and protected by Article 10. It claimed it had criticized not the acquittal itself but the treatment of the victim and the written judgment’s neglect of evidence and suggestion that K. was a prostitute. It sought to prove truth through witnesses and case files. It also unsuccessfully sought the disqualification of Judge N.F. because the claimant’s lawyer had previously represented N.F. The Regional Court refused some proposed witnesses.

On 12 December 2005, the Regional Court found for Judge I.K. It held that the article was a biased account, took K.’s side, and portrayed the judge as acting arbitrarily and out of racist motives, while presenting the alleged rape as proven. This was not an objective critique. The applicant had failed to prove truth: the file showed the judge had dealt with all evidence extensively, so allegations of baseless insinuations or disregard of evidence were not established. The reference to prostitution came from K.’s own examination statement, even if a translation error could not be excluded. The accusation that a judge deliberately disregarded evidence out of racist motives to acquit a domestic accused was a severe defamation. “Scandal of justice” was a value judgment based on disproven factual assertions. Citing Prager and Oberschlick v. Austria, the court said the press may criticize the justice system but must protect public confidence; this critique lacked sufficient factual basis and was excessive. It awarded EUR 7,000 compensation and ordered publication of a summary. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 19 June 2006.

The applicant therefore complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the Media Act judgment requiring compensation infringed its Article 10 rights. The key issue was whether the domestic courts’ interference—damages and retraction for criticism of a judge’s conduct in a criminal case—was justified, given the public interest in press scrutiny of the judiciary and the factual basis for the article’s value judgments.

In *Falter Zeitschriften GmbH v. Austria (No. 2)*, the applicant company published the Vienna weekly newspaper *Falter*. The case arose from an article about criminal proceedings against H.P., a security officer at the Traiskirchen Reception Centre, who had been accused of raping K., a Cameroonian asylum seeker. In May 2005, the Wiener Neustadt Regional Court acquitted H.P. under the principle *in dubio pro reo*. Its written judgment contained a passage suggesting that K. had previously been engaged in prostitution in her country of origin, which allowed an inference that she might have become involved with the accused because she expected some advantage.

*Falter* published an article strongly critical of the case and its handling. It described K. as a traumatised asylum seeker, recounted her allegations in detail, criticised police terminology—including references to “the nigger woman”—and scrutinised the security officer’s changing statements. The article also attacked Judge I.K., who had presided over the acquittal. It claimed that the judge and lay assessors had no doubt about the woman’s guilt, had “unfinished business” with the African woman, attributed the basest intentions to her without proof, ignored relevant evidence, and delivered a “scandalous” judgment. It further stated that the judge had failed to refute the suggestion that K. was a prostitute, although even the accused had not claimed that.

Judge I.K. brought defamation proceedings under section 6 of the Media Act and Article 111 of the Criminal Code. She sought compensation and a retraction, arguing that the article accused her of grossly misusing her judicial office. The applicant company argued that the statements were true and constituted permissible criticism on a matter of public interest. It sought to prove the truth of its claims by calling witnesses and admitting the files from K.’s asylum proceedings and the criminal case against H.P. The Regional Court refused some witness requests, rejected a motion to disqualify the judge assigned to the media case, and ultimately found against the applicant company.

The Regional Court held that the article had not been an objective critique but a biased account portraying Judge I.K. as arbitrary and racist, ignoring evidence, while presenting K.’s rape allegation as proven and the judgment as absurd. It found that the applicant had failed to prove the truth of the impugned statements. According to the case file, the judge had dealt with all evidence and assessed it extensively; there were no base insinuations or disregard of evidence. The reference to prostitution had some basis in K.’s witness statement, though a translation error could not be excluded. The accusation that a judge deliberately disregarded evidence out of racist motives in order to acquit a domestic accused was a severe defamation. The phrase “scandal of justice” was a value judgment, but rested on factual assertions that had been disproved.

The Regional Court awarded Judge I.K. EUR 7,000 in compensation and ordered publication of a summary of the judgment. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant company’s appeal and upheld the decision. The applicant company then complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the domestic judgment under the Media Act, ordering it to pay damages, infringed its right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention. The key factual dispute was therefore whether the newspaper’s sharp criticism of a judge, in the context of public concern about the justice system and the treatment of an asylum seeker, had a sufficient factual basis or exceeded the permissible limits of press criticism.
001-114473:
**Summary: Van Colle v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 7678/09)**

**Background and Parties**

The applicants, Mr. and Mrs. Van Colle, are British nationals whose son, Giles Van Colle, was murdered in November 2000. They brought a claim against the United Kingdom under Articles 2 (right to life) and 8 (right to private and family life) of the European Convention on Human Rights, alleging that the police failed to protect their son's life from a known threat posed by Daniel Brougham, an individual facing criminal proceedings in which Giles was a witness.

**Key Facts**

In September 1999, Giles Van Colle, an optometrist, hired Daniel Brougham (using the alias "Lee Jordan"), who concealed a criminal record including common assault. After a dispute over equipment repairs and Brougham's departure, Brougham was arrested and charged in April 2000 with theft offences involving Giles and other victims. He was released on unconditional bail.

Beginning in summer 2000, Brougham attempted to bribe multiple witnesses—including Mr. H, Mr. P, and Mr. A—to drop charges or not give evidence. On 13 October 2000, Brougham telephoned Giles directly, stating: "I know where you live... If you don't drop the charges you will be in danger." Giles reported this threat to Detective Constable Ridley between 16-18 October. Additional incidents followed: fires at Mr. P's car and premises on 28-29 October (initially deemed accidental but later found to be deliberate), and a second aggressive call to Giles on 9 November 2000 demanding he get Alpha Optical to drop charges.

DC Ridley took witness statements but failed to arrest Brougham on witness intimidation charges. Critically, he never considered witness protection measures despite the escalating pattern of intimidation, was unaware of the Hertfordshire Constabulary's Witness Protection Policy, and had received no training on it. On 22 November 2000, Brougham shot Giles Van Colle dead outside his workplace.

**Procedural History**

A police disciplinary panel found DC Ridley guilty of failing to perform duties diligently regarding witness intimidation. The High Court and Court of Appeal subsequently found violations of Articles 2 and 8, applying a lowered threshold based on Giles being a vulnerable state witness. However, the House of Lords unanimously overturned these decisions, holding that the standard Osman test applied—requiring a "real and immediate risk" to life of which authorities knew or ought to have known. The House of Lords concluded this high threshold was not met, emphasizing that Brougham's offences were minor, his record showed only petty offending, and the threats, while concerning, did not objectively signal imminent lethal violence.

**Relevance to Alleged Violations**

The case centrally concerns whether the police's admitted operational failures—failure to investigate, arrest, or consider protective measures—breached positive obligations under Article 2 to protect life. The key dispute involved the appropriate legal threshold for state protective duties and whether a witness in criminal proceedings constitutes a special category warranting a lower risk threshold.

In *Van Colle v. the United Kingdom* (App. No. 7678/09), the applicants were the parents of Giles Van Colle, an optometrist murdered on 22 November 2000 by Daniel Brougham. They alleged that the UK police violated Articles 2 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights by failing to protect their son’s life from Brougham, who was the accused in criminal proceedings in which Giles was a witness.

In September 1999 Giles hired Brougham, who used the alias Lee Jordan and concealed a criminal record. After a dispute over equipment, Brougham left. In February 2000 police found optical equipment at Brougham’s garage; Giles identified some as his. Brougham was charged in April 2000 with theft and obtaining property by deception concerning Giles, Southern Counties and Alpha Optical. He was released on bail.

From summer 2000, Brougham tried to deter witnesses. He offered Mr H £1,000 not to testify; offered Mr P £650 and later a bribe not to give evidence; and offered Mr A £400 not to give evidence. Most were reported to DC Ridley, the officer in the case. On 13 October 2000 Brougham telephoned Giles, saying he knew where Giles, his businesses and parents lived, and that if Giles did not drop the charges “you will be in danger.” Giles reported this as a death threat. DC Ridley recorded it and took statements from Giles and Mr P on 19 October. Although there was evidence of witness intimidation, DC Ridley did not arrest or contact Brougham and did not consider protective measures. On 9 November 2000 Brougham again telephoned Giles, demanding that Alpha Optical drop the charges. Giles reported it; DC Ridley planned to arrest Brougham after taking a formal statement arranged for 23 November.

Other relevant incidents included a fire damaging Giles’s car on 24 September 2000, initially treated as accidental and not reported to DC Ridley; and fires at Mr P’s car and premises on 28–29 October 2000, reported to DC Ridley but considered unlikely to be linked to Brougham and possibly accidental. Later forensic investigation after the murder showed the fires were deliberate. On 22 November 2000, before the arranged statement, Brougham shot Giles dead. Brougham was convicted of murder in 2002.

A police disciplinary panel found DC Ridley guilty of failing to perform his duties diligently regarding the intimidation of Giles and Mr P. It found an escalating situation of witness intimidation, that DC Ridley was in a unique position to see the developing picture, and that he failed to investigate thoroughly, analyse links, or consider arresting Brougham. He was fined five days’ pay.

The applicants brought a Human Rights Act claim against the Chief Constable. The High Court and Court of Appeal found a violation of Article 2, holding that police should have appreciated a real and immediate risk and taken preventive steps. Mr. and Mrs. Van Colle, British nationals, lodged an application against the United Kingdom under Articles 2 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The case concerned the failure of the police to protect their son, Giles Van Colle, who was murdered in November 2000 by Daniel Brougham, a man facing theft charges in which Giles was a key witness.

The facts centered on an escalating pattern of witness intimidation by Brougham. In September 1999, Giles, an optometrist, hired Brougham under a false name. After an aggressive incident and a dispute over equipment, Brougham's employment ended. In February 2000, Brougham was arrested for theft, and some of Giles's property was recovered. He was later charged with thefts totaling £4000, including from Giles, and released on bail.

From mid-2000, Brougham began attempting to dissuade witnesses. He offered bribes to two other witnesses, Mr. H and Mr. P, who did not report the initial approaches. On 13 October 2000, Brougham directly threatened Giles in a phone call, stating, "I know where you live... If you don't drop the charges you will be in danger." Giles reported this "death threat" to the police. Detective Constable (DC) Ridley, the investigating officer, took a statement from Giles on 19 October, noting the credible threat but failed to arrest Brougham.

On 28 and 29 October, fires occurred at the property and business of witness Mr. P. Brougham was suspected, but DC Ridley deemed the fires accidental and did not link them to the ongoing intimidation.

On 9 November, Brougham made a second threatening call to Giles, demanding he get the charges dropped. Giles reported this to DC Ridley and provided a written account. DC Ridley intended to arrest Brougham for witness intimidation after taking a formal statement, which was scheduled for 23 November. However, on the evening of 22 November 2000, Brougham shot and killed Giles Van Colle as he left work.

A police disciplinary panel later found DC Ridley guilty of failing to diligently investigate the witness intimidation and failing to consider arresting Brougham. It described the events as an "escalating situation of intimidation" and found there was sufficient evidence to justify arrest, which was "necessary and proportionate."

The applicants brought a claim under the Human Rights Act 1998. Initially, the High Court and Court of Appeal found a violation of Article 2, ruling that the police should have known there was a "real and immediate" risk to Giles's life and failed in their duty to protect him. However, the House of Lords overturned this. Applying the stringent *Osman* test from the European Court, they held that the threshold for a "real and immediate risk" to life was not met. They concluded that while DC Ridley made errors of judgment, the intelligence available at the time did not indicate an imminent threat to life that the police were obliged to prevent under Article 2. The applicants then took their case to the European Court of Human Rights.

**Case: Malkhasyan v. Armenia (Application no. 6729/07), European Court of Human Rights, Judgment of 26 June 2012.**

The applicant, Vardan Malkhasyan, an Armenian national, was prosecuted after giving a speech on 2 December 2006 at an assembly of an NGO, the Unity of Armenian Volunteers. In the speech, he allegedly called the authorities “bandits and internal enemies” and urged that they be removed by any means, including armed struggle and rebellion. On 8 December 2006, the National Security Service opened criminal proceedings under Article 301 of the Criminal Code for public calls for a violent overthrow of the government.

On 9 December 2006, the applicant’s flat was searched. He alleged that he was taken to the NSS immediately afterwards. On 10 December 2006, he was questioned as a suspect and, at 2:30 p.m., an arrest record was drawn up. His passport was seized. On 12 December 2006, he was formally charged under Article 301. The same day, the District Court ordered his detention for two months, finding a risk that he might abscond or unlawfully influence persons involved in the proceedings. The applicant appealed unsuccessfully and later sought release on bail, arguing he had a permanent residence, family and property in Armenia and had never absconded. Bail was refused.

The applicant’s detention was extended on 7 February 2007 for two months. He complained that the statutory time-limits for seeking and deciding extension had not been respected and that he was absent from the hearing. The Court of Appeal acknowledged that the time-limits had not been observed but considered this a minor procedural defect. A further extension was granted on 5 April 2007. Meanwhile, on 3 April 2007, the applicant was registered as a parliamentary candidate. He argued that his continued detention violated the Electoral Code because it required the Central Election Committee’s consent and prevented him from campaigning equally. The Court of Appeal rejected this, distinguishing imposition of detention from extension.

On 5 June 2007, the prosecutor approved the indictment and sent the case to court. On 10 June 2007, the detention period authorised by the 5 April decision expired. On 13 June, the applicant asked the detention facility for release. On 19 June, its chief refused, stating the case had been transmitted to the District Court. On 22 June 2007, the judge scheduled the trial and stated that the preventive measure remained unchanged.

Before the European Court, Malkhasyan alleged violations of Article 5 § 1 and Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. Under Article 5 § 1, he claimed his detention between 10 and 22 June 2007 was unlawful because no court decision authorised it. The Court agreed, following its earlier judgment in *Poghosyan v. Armenia*, and found a violation. It rejected as manifestly ill-founded his complaint about the February 2007 extension, finding the brief delay in complying with domestic time-limits was formal and did not affect the lawfulness of detention.

Under Article 5 § 3, the applicant complained that the domestic courts failed to give relevant and sufficient reasons for his continued detention. The Court found a violation. The District Court and Court of Appeal repeatedly relied in an abstract and stereotyped way on risks of absconding and obstructing justice, without addressing the applicant’s concrete arguments, such as his family ties, property, seized passport, and the existence of a recording of his speech. A general reference to the seriousness of the charge was insufficient. The Court therefore found violations of Article 5 §§ 1 and 3.

**Summary of Malkhasyan v. Armenia (no. 6729/07, ECtHR, 26 June 2012)**

The case concerned an Armenian applicant charged under Article 301 of the Criminal Code with public calls for the violent overthrow of the government. On 2 December 2006, at an assembly organised by the NGO “Unity of Armenian Volunteers,” the applicant gave a speech calling the authorities “bandits and internal enemies of the people” who had to be removed by any means, including arms, armed struggle and rebellion. Criminal proceedings were instituted on 8 December 2006. His flat was searched on 9 December, he was questioned as a suspect on 10 December, and an arrest record was drawn up that same day. He was formally charged on 12 December 2006.

The investigator sought a two-month detention order, alleging that the applicant, if released, could abscond or exert unlawful pressure on persons involved in the proceedings. The District Court granted the motion on 12 December 2006. The applicant objected, arguing that his statements had been made while intoxicated and on the spur of the moment, that there was no evidence he would abscond or obstruct the investigation, and that the authorities already had a recording of his speech. His appeals and bail requests were dismissed. Later, the Court of Appeal also relied on the fact that a co-accused, V.A., had been detained on weapons charges.

The applicant’s detention was extended on 7 February 2007 and again on 5 April 2007. He complained that the 7 February extension breached domestic time-limits: the investigator filed the motion on 1 February, but the court decided on 7 February, whereas the law required a decision not later than five days before expiry of detention on 10 February. The Court of Appeal admitted the time-limits had not been observed but found this did not affect the outcome.

A key alleged violation concerned the period 10–22 June 2007. The detention authorised by the 5 April decision expired on 10 June 2007. On 13 June the applicant asked the detention facility to release him, but on 19 June the chief refused, saying the case had been transmitted to the District Court. On 22 June a judge scheduled the trial and stated that the preventive measure remained unchanged. The applicant therefore remained detained between 10 and 22 June without a fresh court decision authorising his detention.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Article 5 § 1 (unlawful detention) and Article 5 § 3 (failure to provide reasons for continued detention). On the time-limit complaint concerning the 7 February extension, the Court found the complaint manifestly ill-founded. Although there had been procedural delays, the previous detention order was still valid, and the competent court had acted before expiry; the shortcomings were formal and minor.

However, regarding 10–22 June 2007, the Court found a violation of Article 5 § 1. Applying Poghosyan v. Armenia, it held that the detention was not based on a court decision and was therefore unlawful; transmission of the case to court did not authorise continued detention after the order expired.

The Court also found a violation of Article 5 § 3. The domestic courts relied abstractly and stereotypically on the risks of absconding and exerting unlawful pressure on witnesses, without concrete reasons or engagement with the applicant’s arguments. The seriousness of the charge alone was insufficient, and the co-accused’s detention was not clearly relevant to the risk that the applicant would abscond.

**Case: Malkhasyan v. Armenia (Application no. 6729/07), European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, judgment of 26 June 2012.**

The applicant, Vardan Malkhasyan, an Armenian national born in 1953, was prosecuted after giving a speech on 2 December 2006 at an assembly organised by the NGO “Unity of Armenian Volunteers” in Yerevan. About 150 people attended. In his speech, Malkhasyan called the authorities “bandits and internal enemies of the people” and said they had to be removed by any means, including arms, armed struggle and rebellion. He also called for blood and fire against the enemy and stated that the country had to be liberated from the internal enemy.

On 8 December 2006 the National Security Service opened criminal proceedings under Article 301 of the Criminal Code for public calls for a violent overthrow of the government. On 9 December the applicant’s flat was searched. On 10 December he was questioned as a suspect and allegedly admitted making the statements. At 2:30 p.m. an arrest record was drawn up, and his passport was seized. On 12 December he was formally charged under Article 301. Another speaker, Z.S., was also charged, including with illegal possession of firearms and ammunition. The applicant claimed that his statements had been made while intoxicated and confused, on the spur of the moment, and without intent to incite rebellion.

On 12 December the investigator sought a two-month detention order, alleging that the applicant could abscond or unlawfully pressure persons involved in the proceedings. The District Court granted the motion, mainly on the risk of obstruction. Appeals and a bail request were unsuccessful; the Court of Appeal referred to the co-accused’s firearms charges and the seriousness of the offence.

The detention was extended several times. On 1 February 2007 the investigator sought an extension before the existing period expired on 10 February. On 7 February the District Court granted a two-month extension, although the domestic time-limits under Article 139 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure—requiring the motion not later than ten days and a court decision not later than five days before expiry—were not met. The Court of Appeal acknowledged this but treated it as minor. A further extension was granted on 5 April. Meanwhile, the applicant was registered as a parliamentary candidate on 3 April. He argued that extending his detention required the Central Election Committee’s consent under the Electoral Code, but the Court of Appeal dismissed that argument, distinguishing detention from its extension.

The indictment was approved on 5 June 2007, and the case was sent to court. The authorised detention period expired on 10 June 2007. The applicant requested release, but the detention facility refused on 19 June because the case had been transmitted to court. On 22 June a judge listed the case for trial and stated that the preventive measure remained unchanged.

The applicant alleged under Article 5 § 1 that the 7 February extension violated domestic time-limits and that his detention between 10 and 22 June 2007 was unlawful because it lacked court authorisation. Under Article 5 § 3, he alleged that the courts failed to provide relevant and sufficient reasons for his continued detention.

The Court rejected the time-limit complaint as manifestly ill-founded, finding the procedural delay formal and minor. However, it found a violation of Article 5 § 1 regarding the 10–22 June detention, which was not based on a court decision. It also found a violation of Article 5 § 3 because the domestic courts relied on abstract, stereotyped risks of absconding and witness pressure, without factual assessment or proper response to the applicant’s arguments.
