In *Madah and Others v. Bulgaria* (ECtHR, 10 May 2012), the applicants were Mohammad Rasoul Madah, an Iranian national, his Bulgarian partner Maria Kerkenezova, and their son Daniel, a Bulgarian national. Madah had visited Bulgaria since the 1990s, obtained a permanent residence permit in 2001, and from 2005 lived with Kerkenezova. Their son was born in 2006 and had fragile health.

On 27 December 2005, the head of the National Security Service ordered Madah’s expulsion on the ground that he posed a threat to national security. The order deprived him of residence rights and banned him from entering Bulgaria for ten years. It gave no factual grounds and relied on a classified internal document of 15 December 2005, which was not served on him. That document alleged that Madah was involved in drug trafficking to finance the militant Kurdish separatist group Kongra-Gel, formerly the PKK. The expulsion order also provided for his detention pending expulsion, stated it was immediately enforceable, and said it was appealable to the Minister of Internal Affairs but not subject to judicial review.

Madah was served with the order and detained on 21 February 2006. He was held in Sofia and later transferred to a special detention facility outside the city. He was released on 28 October 2006. After release, he was allegedly interviewed at the Iranian embassy about suspected links to a Kurdish separatist organisation.

Madah challenged the expulsion before the Sofia City Court on 9 March 2006, citing unlawfulness and his difficult family situation. His separate appeal to the Minister was returned as out of time. In court, he submitted a certificate that no criminal proceedings were pending against him, denied the allegations, and relied on his family life and *Al-Nashif v. Bulgaria*. The National Security Service submitted the internal document, but the court did not order further information or evidence. On 26 July 2007, the Sofia City Court dismissed the appeal, treating the internal document as a binding official certification that Madah threatened national security. On 28 May 2008, the Supreme Administrative Court upheld that judgment, endorsing the lower court’s reasoning without examining the evidence supporting the security assessment.

Madah also challenged his detention. On 16 October 2006, the Sofia City Court suspended the detention order, noting the authorities had not shown necessity, that detention had lasted eight months, and that his family situation was relevant. He was released. However, in a final judgment of 23 February 2009, the Supreme Administrative Court discontinued the proceedings without merits review, holding that the detention order was subordinate to the expulsion order and not independently reviewable.

The applicants alleged violations of Article 8 (expulsion interfering with family life), Article 13 (lack of effective remedy), Article 3 and 13 (risk of ill-treatment in Iran), and Articles 5, 6 and 8 regarding detention. The ECtHR found a genuine family life and held that deportation would interfere with it. The interference could not be considered “in accordance with the law” because the national-security assessment was based on undisclosed internal information, lacked factual grounds, and was not meaningfully scrutinised by domestic courts. Thus, enforcement of the deportation order would violate Article 8. The Court also found a violation of Article 13 because judicial review did not examine the executive’s factual allegations or proportionality. The Article 3 and 13 complaints were rejected as manifestly ill-founded because Madah provided only general statements and never raised a real-risk claim before Bulgarian authorities. The remaining detention-related complaints were also rejected as manifestly ill-founded.

In *Madah and Others v. Bulgaria* (Application no. 45237/08, judgment 10 May 2012), the European Court of Human Rights examined Bulgaria’s expulsion of an Iranian national and its effect on his Bulgarian partner and child.

The first applicant, Mohammad Rasoul Madah, an Iranian national, had visited Bulgaria since the 1990s and obtained a permanent residence permit in 2001. In 2004 he met the second applicant, Maria Kerkenezova, a Bulgarian national; they began living together in 2005. Their son, the third applicant, was born in 2006 and suffered from fragile health.

On 27 December 2005, the head of the National Security Service ordered the first applicant’s expulsion, deprived him of residence rights, and banned him from Bulgaria for ten years. The order gave no factual grounds and relied on a classified internal document dated 15 December 2005. That document alleged that the first applicant was involved in drug trafficking to finance the Kurdish separatist group Kongra-Gel, formerly the PKK. The order stated he should be detained pending expulsion, was immediately enforceable, and could be appealed to the Minister of Internal Affairs but not judicially reviewed. He was served on 21 February 2006 and detained the same day, remaining in detention until 28 October 2006.

The first applicant sought judicial review before the Sofia City Court, citing his family situation and denying involvement in the alleged activities. He submitted a certificate that no criminal proceedings were pending against him. The National Security Service produced only the internal document. The Sofia City Court dismissed the appeal on 26 July 2007, treating the internal document as an official certification that he threatened national security and as binding. On 28 May 2008, the Supreme Administrative Court upheld that judgment without examining the evidence allegedly supporting the security assessment. It found the deportation lawful and justified because he had been able to challenge it before a court.

The applicants complained under Article 8 that deportation would unlawfully and disproportionately interfere with their family life; under Article 13 that they lacked effective remedies; and under Article 3 that the first applicant risked ill-treatment in Iran. He also challenged his detention under Articles 5 and 6, and the applicants complained that the detention interfered with Article 8.

The Court found that the applicants had genuine family life in Bulgaria and that deportation would interfere with it. However, the interference would not be “in accordance with the law” because the expulsion was based on undisclosed internal information and the domestic courts did not examine its factual basis or proportionality. They effectively accepted the executive’s national-security certification without meaningful scrutiny, leaving no minimum protection against arbitrariness. The Court therefore found that enforcing the deportation order would violate Article 8. It also found a violation of Article 13 because judicial review of the expulsion did not provide an effective remedy: the courts neither meaningfully examined the security allegations nor assessed proportionality.

The Article 3 complaint was rejected as manifestly ill-founded. The first applicant had not shown substantial grounds for believing he would face a real risk of ill-treatment in Iran, and he had not raised that complaint before Bulgarian authorities. Consequently, no arguable Article 3 claim required an Article 13 remedy. The remaining complaints concerning detention were also rejected as manifestly ill-founded. The Court indicated that Bulgaria should adopt general measures, including legislative and judicial changes, to ensure that national-security deportations are subject to thorough judicial scrutiny, including with classified information, and proportionate balancing with affected individuals’ family rights.

**Madah and Others v. Bulgaria** (Application no. 45237/08, ECtHR, 10 May 2012) concerned the proposed expulsion of an Iranian national and its effect on his Bulgarian partner and their child.

The first applicant, Mr Mohammad Rasoul Madah, an Iranian national, had visited Bulgaria since 1990, obtained a temporary residence permit in 1992 on business grounds, and was granted permanent residence in 2001. In 2004 he met the second applicant, a Bulgarian national, and they began living together in early 2005. Their son, the third applicant, was born in April 2006 after a complicated pregnancy and suffered from fragile health, including frequent pulmonary disease.

On 27 December 2005, the head of the National Security Service ordered the first applicant’s expulsion on the ground that he posed a threat to national security. The order deprived him of residence rights and banned him from Bulgaria for ten years. It gave no factual grounds and relied on a classified internal document dated 15 December 2005, which was not served on him. That document alleged that he was involved in drug trafficking to finance the Kurdish separatist group Kongra-Gel, formerly the PKK. The expulsion order was immediately enforceable, and the applicant was told he could appeal to the Minister of Internal Affairs, but not to a court.

The first applicant was served with the order on 21 February 2006 and was arrested and detained pending expulsion the same day. He remained in detention, later in a special facility outside Sofia, until 28 October 2006. After release, he was reportedly interviewed at the Iranian embassy about alleged connections with a Kurdish separatist organisation.

He challenged the expulsion order before the Sofia City Court, arguing that it was unlawful and referring to his family situation and his partner’s difficult pregnancy. He also submitted a certificate that no criminal proceedings were pending against him and denied involvement in the alleged activities. The National Security Service submitted the internal document, and the court refused his request for further evidence. In July 2007, the Sofia City Court dismissed his appeal, treating the internal document as a binding official certification that he was a national security threat. In May 2008, the Supreme Administrative Court upheld that judgment, accepting the national security basis without examining the supporting evidence.

The applicants alleged violations of Article 8 (family life), Article 13 (effective remedy), and, for the first applicant, Articles 3 and 13 (risk of ill-treatment in Iran). They also complained about his detention under Articles 5, 6, and 8.

The European Court of Human Rights found that the applicants had a genuine family life in Bulgaria and that deportation would interfere with it. However, the interference was not “in accordance with the law” under Article 8 § 2 because the domestic proceedings lacked even minimum protection against arbitrariness. The expulsion rested on undisclosed internal information, and the courts did not scrutinise the factual basis or proportionality of the measure. The Court therefore found that there would be a violation of Article 8 if the deportation order were enforced. It likewise found a violation of Article 13 because judicial review did not provide an effective remedy.

By contrast, the first applicant’s Article 3 complaint was rejected as manifestly ill-founded: he had not provided evidence that he faced a real risk of ill-treatment in Iran and had never raised such claims before Bulgarian authorities. The remaining complaints regarding detention were also rejected.

**Case of Hartman v. Slovenia** (Application no. 42236/05), European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, judgment of 18 October 2012.

The applicant, Andrej Hartman, a Slovenian national born in 1972, complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the criminal proceedings against him were excessively long, and under Article 13 that Slovenia lacked an effective domestic remedy for such delay. The application was lodged on 15 November 2005.

The relevant facts began on 14 November 1997, when the Ministry of the Interior issued a detention decision and the applicant was arrested. On 16 November 1997 he was brought before an investigating judge and remanded in custody. A criminal investigation was opened on 27 November 1997. On 11 May 1998, after the investigation ended, an indictment was lodged. The applicant was charged with six criminal offences involving unlawful manufacture of and trade in heroin. Six other accomplices were charged with about twenty similar offences. The case concerned an organised drug-trafficking network.

The first-instance trial before the Kranj District Court began on 6 October 1998. Between then and 15 March 2000, the court held sixty-nine hearings, heard forty-eight witnesses, reviewed video cassettes, secret surveillance reports, wiretaps, and documents from several countries, including Spain, the United Kingdom, Hungary, Austria, Bulgaria, and Romania. On 15 March 2000, the first-instance judgment sentenced the applicant to fifteen years’ imprisonment. He appealed on 21 April 2000. On 30 November 2000, the Ljubljana Higher Court largely upheld the judgment, reduced the sentence to fourteen years, and remitted part of the case. The applicant, who had been under house arrest, fled the country, and an arrest warrant was issued on 3 December 2000.

On 31 March 2001, the applicant’s attorney lodged a request for protection of legality with the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court received the case file on 25 May 2001. The applicant later returned to Slovenia and surrendered; he was brought to prison on 10 December 2002. On 21 December 2004, the Supreme Court rejected the request for protection of legality. That judgment was served on 7 January 2005. The applicant then filed a constitutional complaint on 1 March 2005. The Constitutional Court rejected it as unfounded on 5 May 2006, and the decision was served on 11 May 2006.

The Court excluded from its length calculation the applicant’s later requests for reopening and extraordinary mitigation of sentence, because Article 6 § 1 does not apply to post-final review or reopening proceedings. The relevant period therefore ran from 14 November 1997, the day of arrest, to 11 May 2006, the service of the Constitutional Court’s decision—a total of eight years and six months across four levels of jurisdiction.

The Government argued that the case was complex: six accused, more than twenty offences, a large-scale drug-trafficking network, a file of over 7,000 pages, and novel legal issues. The Court accepted that the case was complex. The first-instance court took two years and three months, and the appeal court seven months. However, the Supreme Court took almost four years—three years and eight months—to decide the protection-of-legality request. Although that remedy was extraordinary and decided in camera on the file, the Court found this delay excessive. The applicant’s flight did not excuse it, because his presence or involvement was not required.

The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1 owing to the excessive length of proceedings. It further found, in substance, a violation of Article 13 because there was no effective domestic remedy for the excessive length, referring to its case-law in *Ribič v. Slovenia*.

**Case: Hartman v. Slovenia (Application no. 42236/05)**  
**Court:** European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section  
**Judgment:** 18 October 2012; final 18 January 2013

The applicant, Andrej Hartman, a Slovenian national born in 1972, complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that criminal proceedings against him had been excessively long. In substance, he also complained under Article 13 that Slovenia lacked an effective domestic remedy for the excessive length of proceedings.

The relevant facts began on 14 November 1997, when the Ministry of the Interior’s Kranj Criminal Police Unit issued a detention decision and Hartman was arrested. On 16 November he was brought before an investigating judge and remanded in custody. The prosecution requested a criminal investigation against Hartman and six others, and the investigation opened on 27 November 1997. On 11 May 1998, after investigation, Hartman was indicted for six criminal offences related to unlawful manufacture of and trade in narcotic drugs, specifically heroin. Six other accomplices faced about twenty similar offences. The case concerned an organised drug-trafficking network.

The first-instance hearing began on 6 October 1998 before the Kranj District Court. Between then and 15 March 2000, the court held sixty-nine hearings, heard forty-eight witnesses, reviewed video cassettes, secret surveillance reports, wiretaps, and documents sent from Spain, the United Kingdom, Hungary, Austria, Bulgaria and Romania. In December 1999 Hartman was placed under house arrest. On 15 March 2000 the District Court sentenced him to fifteen years’ imprisonment. He appealed. On 30 November 2000 the Ljubljana Higher Court largely upheld the judgment, remitted part of the case, and reduced his sentence to fourteen years. Hartman later fled while under house arrest; an arrest warrant was issued on 3 December 2000. He returned and turned himself in in December 2002.

On 31 March 2001 Hartman’s attorney lodged a request for protection of legality with the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court received the file on 25 May 2001 but did not reject the request until 21 December 2004, with the judgment served on 7 January 2005. Hartman then lodged a constitutional complaint, which the Constitutional Court rejected as unfounded on 5 May 2006, served on 11 May 2006. Later requests for reopening and for extraordinary mitigation of sentence were not counted toward the Article 6 length calculation because Article 6 does not apply to reopening or post-final sentence-review proceedings.

The Court calculated the relevant period from Hartman’s arrest on 14 November 1997 to 11 May 2006, when the Constitutional Court’s decision was served. That amounted to eight years and six months at four levels of jurisdiction. The Government argued the case was complex: six accused, more than twenty offences, a major first drug-trafficking case, a file exceeding 7,000 pages, and the applicant’s flight. The Court accepted the case was complex; first instance took two years and three months and the appeal court seven months. However, the Supreme Court phase lasted almost four years, with three years and eight months of deliberation, which the Court found excessive. The protection-of-legality request was an extraordinary remedy decided in camera on the file, so Hartman’s flight did not affect it.

The Court therefore found that the length of proceedings violated the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1. It also examined Article 13 in light of its case-law, particularly *Ribič v. Slovenia*, concerning the absence of an effective domestic remedy for excessive length.

**Case summary: Hartman v. Slovenia (Application no. 42236/05)**

In *Hartman v. Slovenia*, the European Court of Human Rights considered complaints by Andrej Hartman, a Slovenian national, that criminal proceedings against him were excessively long, contrary to Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, and that Slovenia lacked an effective domestic remedy for that delay, contrary to Article 13.

The relevant facts began on 14 November 1997, when the Ministry of the Interior issued a detention decision and Hartman was arrested. On 16 November 1997 he was brought before an investigating judge and remanded in custody. The prosecution requested a criminal investigation against Hartman and six others, which was opened on 27 November 1997. On 11 May 1998 an indictment was lodged. Hartman was charged with six criminal offences relating to the unlawful manufacture of and trade in heroin. Six co-accused faced approximately twenty similar offences. The case concerned an organised drug-trafficking network.

The first-instance hearing began on 6 October 1998 before the Kranj District Court. Between that date and 15 March 2000, the court held sixty-nine hearings and heard forty-eight witnesses. It also reviewed numerous video cassettes, secret surveillance reports, wiretaps, and documents from Spain, the United Kingdom, Hungary, Austria, Bulgaria, and Romania. On 30 December 1999 Hartman was placed under house arrest. On 15 March 2000 the first-instance judgment sentenced him to fifteen years’ imprisonment. The judgment was served on 11 April 2000. Hartman and other parties appealed.

On 30 November 2000 the Ljubljana Higher Court mainly upheld the first-instance judgment, remitted part of the case for re-examination, and reduced Hartman’s sentence to fourteen years. In December 2000 Hartman fled while under house arrest, and an arrest warrant was issued. The second-instance judgment was served on his attorney on 3 January 2001. On 31 March 2001 his attorney lodged a request for protection of legality with the Supreme Court, which received the file on 25 May 2001. Meanwhile, the remitted part of the proceedings was terminated on 5 June 2002 after the indictment was withdrawn. Hartman later returned to Slovenia and was taken to prison on 10 December 2002.

The Supreme Court rejected the protection-of-legality request on 21 December 2004, and the judgment was served on 7 January 2005. Hartman filed a constitutional complaint on 1 March 2005. The Constitutional Court rejected it as unfounded on 5 May 2006, served on 11 May 2006. Hartman also later sought reopening and extraordinary mitigation of sentence, but the Court excluded those post-finality proceedings from the length calculation.

The Court took the relevant period as running from Hartman’s arrest on 14 November 1997 to 11 May 2006—eight years and six months across four levels of jurisdiction. The Government argued that the case was complex: six accused, over twenty offences, a file exceeding 7,000 pages, and the first large-scale drug-trafficking case in Slovenia. It also relied on Hartman’s flight. The Court accepted the case’s complexity and found that the first-instance and appeal stages were not excessively long. However, the Supreme Court took almost four years—three years and eight months—to decide the protection-of-legality request. That delay was excessive, and Hartman’s flight was irrelevant because that phase was decided in camera without requiring his participation. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1. It further found, in substance, that no effective domestic remedy existed for the excessive length of proceedings, violating Article 13.

Genderdoc-M v. Moldova (Application no. 9106/06) concerned a Moldovan NGO that provided information and assistance to the LGBT community. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects freedom of peaceful assembly.

The key facts arose in 2005. On 7 April 2005, Genderdoc-M applied to Chișinău Municipal Council for authorisation to hold a peaceful demonstration in front of Parliament on 27 May 2005. The stated purpose was to encourage the adoption of laws protecting sexual minorities from discrimination. On 27 April 2005, the Municipal Council rejected the application, saying the demonstration was baseless because a law on the protection of national minorities had already been adopted. On 6 May 2005, the Mayor’s Office also refused permission, again relying on the existing national-minorities law and on legal provisions identifying who had the power of legislative initiative.

Genderdoc-M challenged the Mayor’s Office decision, arguing that the ban was illegal and discriminatory. On 2 June 2005, the Chișinău Court of Appeal allowed its action and declared the Mayor’s Office decision void. The court found that domestic law did not provide the grounds relied on for refusing authorisation. It held that whether to authorise an assembly should not depend on the nature or status of the problems the participants intended to raise. However, the court rejected other complaints, including an alleged breach of the 48-hour notification rule.

The Mayor’s Office appealed. It argued that many individuals and associations had objected strongly to the demonstration and to any law legalising homosexual partnerships, invoking the protection of marriage and the family. On 7 September 2005, the Supreme Court of Justice allowed the appeal, quashed the Court of Appeal decision and remitted the case for re-examination. Before the Court of Appeal, the Mayor’s Office argued that an assembly promoting sexual minority rights would endanger public order and social morality, and that the organisers had not accepted responsibility for managing the demonstration. On 14 June 2006, the Court of Appeal found against Genderdoc-M. On 18 October 2006, the Supreme Court of Justice upheld that decision. It found that the applicant had failed to give undertakings required by assembly law, such as respecting the law, designating persons in charge, creating a group with police to maintain order, marking the site, paying Municipal Council fees, establishing routes, providing police access, and forbidding certain persons from participating. The stated aim was to encourage the adoption of laws protecting sexual minorities from discrimination. On 27 April 2005, the Municipal Council rejected the application, saying the demonstration was baseless because a law on the protection of national minorities had already been adopted. On 6 May 2005, the Mayor’s Office also refused permission, relying on the same national-minorities law and on legal provisions governing who could exercise legislative initiative.

Genderdoc-M challenged the Mayor’s Office decision, arguing that the ban was illegal and discriminatory. On 2 June 2005, the Chișinău Court of Appeal allowed the action and declared the 6 May 2005 decision void. It found that the refusal grounds were not provided for by law, and that authorisation could not depend on the nature or status of the problems the participants wished to raise. The court nevertheless rejected other complaints, including an alleged breach of the 48-hour time-limit for notifying a refusal.

The Mayor’s Office appealed. It argued that many individuals and associations had objected to the demonstration and opposed any law legalising homosexual partnerships, invoking marriage and family protection. On 7 September 2005, the Supreme Court of Justice allowed the appeal, quashed the Court of Appeal judgment and remitted the case for re-examination.

Genderdoc-M again argued that the ban was illegal and discriminatory. On 14 June 2006, the Court of Appeal ruled against the applicant. On 18 October 2006, the Supreme Court upheld that decision. It found that Genderdoc-M had failed to give undertakings required by the law on assemblies, such as respecting the law, designating persons in charge, creating an order-maintenance group with police, marking the site, paying fees, establishing routes, providing police access, and forbidding certain persons from participating. It also considered that there was a risk of a breach of public order.

Relevant domestic law included Law no. 560-XIII on assemblies, which required notification at least 15 days before an assembly and allowed the Mayor’s Office to grant or refuse permission, with judicial review within five days. Local public administration law allowed the Mayor to forbid or suspend demonstrations contradicting legal order and morals. The Constitution permitted restrictions only by law and only where necessary and proportionate for interests such as public order, health or morals and the rights of others. The Civil Code required associations to pursue purposes consistent with public order and good morals.

Genderdoc-M complained that the ban was not in accordance with the law, pursued no legitimate aim and was not necessary in a democratic society. The Government initially accepted that there had been an interference but argued it was justified, noting that 98% of Moldova’s population was Christian Orthodox and submitting public requests to ban the assembly. Later, on 1 April 2010, the Government conceded that Article 11 had been violated. The Court declared the complaint admissible as not manifestly ill-founded.

The applicant association, Genderdoc-M, provides information and assistance to the LGBT community. On 7 April 2005, it applied to the Chişinău Municipal Council for authorisation to hold a peaceful demonstration in front of Parliament on 27 May 2005. The stated aim was to encourage the adoption of laws protecting sexual minorities from discrimination.

On 27 April 2005, the Municipal Council rejected the application, saying the proposed demonstration was baseless because a law on the protection of national minorities had already been adopted. On 6 May 2005, the Mayor’s Office also refused permission, relying on the same national-minorities law and on legal provisions governing who has the power to initiate legislation. The applicant challenged the refusal, arguing that the ban was illegal and discriminatory.

On 2 June 2005, the Chişinău Court of Appeal annulled the Mayor’s Office decision. It found the refusal legally unfounded because Moldovan law did not provide such grounds for refusing an assembly. It also held that authorisation should not depend on the nature or status of the problems the participants intended to raise. The Mayor’s Office appealed. Before the Supreme Court, it argued that many individuals and associations opposed the demonstration and same-sex partnerships, invoking marriage and family protection. On 7 September 2005, the Supreme Court quashed the favourable decision and remanded the case.

On remand, the Mayor’s Office argued that an assembly promoting sexual minority rights would endanger public order and social morality, and that the organisers had not assumed responsibility for the demonstration’s good management. Genderdoc-M again argued that the ban was illegal and discriminatory. On 14 June 2006, the Court of Appeal ruled against the applicant. On 18 October 2006, the Supreme Court upheld that decision, finding that Genderdoc-M had failed to undertake various statutory obligations for assemblies: to respect the law, designate responsible persons, create a public-order group with police, mark the site, pay municipal fees, establish routes, provide police access, and forbid certain persons. It also found a risk of breach of public order.

Relevant domestic law required advance notification for assemblies and allowed the mayor to grant or refuse permission. Local administration law empowered the mayor to forbid public demonstrations contradicting legal order and morals. The Constitution permitted restrictions only by law and only where necessary for, among other things, public order, health or morals, or the rights of others.

Before the Court, Genderdoc-M complained under Article 11 that the ban violated its right to peaceful assembly. It argued that the refusal was not in accordance with law, pursued no legitimate aim, and was not necessary in a democratic society. The Government initially accepted that there was an interference but claimed it was justified; it emphasised that most of Moldova’s population was Christian Orthodox and submitted public requests asking for the ban. Later, on 1 April 2010, the Government agreed that there had been a violation of Article 11. The International Commission of Jurists intervened as a third party.

The Court declared the complaint admissible and examined the merits. It ultimately found a violation of Article 11, concluding that the refusal and subsequent domestic court decisions were not shown to be necessary in a democratic society. Moral or religious opposition and vague or speculative risks of disorder could not justify suppressing a peaceful assembly advocating LGBT rights.

**Parties and Allegation**

Mr Zdeněk Jirsák, a Czech national born in 1953, lodged an application against the Czech Republic on 13 February 2008, alleging that the conditions of his detention in Valdice Prison were inhuman and degrading, in violation of Article 3 of the Convention. He was represented by Mr W. Firla; the Government by Mr Vít A. Schorm.

**Detention Conditions**

The applicant served his sentence in Sections C and D of Valdice Prison between 2000 and 2005. Between 10 November 2000 and 29 January 2001, he shared cell no. 223—measuring 35.816 sq. m. including a separate toilet—with nine other prisoners, yielding roughly 3.58 sq. m. of living space per inmate. The cell had bunk beds along both long walls, two windows (each 1.44 sq. m., partially openable) covered externally with yellow translucent fibreglass, ten lockers, two tables, and ten chairs. The applicant worked nine hours each working day in the prison laundry, had one hour of daily outdoor exercise, could shower twice weekly, received one warm meal daily (plus two hot meals four times weekly), and had access to cultural activities, sports, books, and newspapers.

On 28 January 2001 at 7:30 p.m., the applicant broke his ankle while climbing down from his bunk bed, which he attributed to dizziness caused by stuffy air. He did not immediately seek help, taking Ibuprofen instead. The next morning, unable to walk, he was taken to the infirmary. The prison doctor visually examined him, deemed him heavily intoxicated with medicaments without testing, declined an x-ray because the operator was on holiday, and sent him to solitary confinement rather than a hospital. On 30 January he was finally x-rayed, his fracture confirmed, and he was transferred to Prague Prison Hospital, where he was operated on 31 January 2001. Treatment lasted seven months, and he later developed arthritis.

On 26 March 2001 the applicant was found guilty of self-intoxication, receiving five days under the closed regime (he did not appeal), and was dismissed from his prison job for absence due to intoxication. He also was not paid sickness benefit.

In November 2001 the applicant filed a criminal complaint against the prison director. The Regional Prosecutor's Office found it unjustified (1 February 2002). The High Prosecutor's Office later expressed doubts about the authorities' conduct and forwarded the matter to the Ministry of Justice, noting concerns that the applicant had not been x-rayed despite a medical report showing he was no longer intoxicated, and that he had been punished without consideration of his painkiller use. In February 2004, responding to an overcrowding complaint, the High Prosecutor's Office acknowledged that some Valdice sections were overcrowded. An October 2005 complaint to the Prison Directorate General was found unsubstantiated.

**Summary**

In *Kotsev and Ermenkova v. Bulgaria* (Application no. 33864/03, judgment 10 May 2012), the applicants were two Bulgarian nationals who jointly owned a building and plot of land in Sofia with B.I.’s parents. In 1992, B.I.’s parents sold him one quarter of the property. In 1993, B.I. began constructing an adjoining building. The authorities repeatedly ordered the construction to be halted or demolished, in 1996, 1999, and 2005. B.I. challenged those orders by judicial review, resulting in two main sets of proceedings in which the applicants participated as interested parties because the outcome affected their property rights.

In the first set, arising from a March 1996 demolition order, B.I. sought review by the Sofia City Court. The applicants joined in March 1999. At least fifteen hearings were held between June 1999 and October 2007, at intervals of four to eight months. Five hearings failed because parties were not properly summoned. At least six hearings between January 2005 and October 2007 were adjourned because a newly added party in Toronto, Canada, had to be summoned by letter rogatory. The Sofia City Court gave judgment in 2010, and by October 2010 the case was pending on appeal. The proceedings had lasted about thirteen years for two levels of jurisdiction.

In the second set, in June 1999 the building control authorities ordered B.I. to pull down the building. B.I. and his wife sought judicial review, and the applicants intervened in November 1999. About twenty hearings took place until February 2006, at intervals of two to nine months. At least four hearings were adjourned due to improper summoning, including of B.I.’s brother in Canada. After the brother died in 2002, at least six hearings were adjourned because his widow in Canada had not been summoned by letter rogatory. As of October 2010, the proceedings were still pending before the Sofia City Court, after about twelve years and five months at first instance.

The applicants complained three times—in 2000, 2002, and 2007—to the Sofia City Court and the Supreme Judicial Council about the slow progress. In 2007 the Ministry of Justice said no delays were attributable to the authorities. However, in 2002 the Ministry had informed local authorities that an inspection found a delay caused by B.I.’s abuse of process and the Sofia City Court’s heavy caseload.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged that the length of both sets of proceedings violated their right to a hearing within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1, that they lacked an effective remedy under Article 13, and that there was an interference with their possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Government argued non-exhaustion, saying the applicants had not filed a “complaint about delays” under Article 217a of the 1952 Code of Civil Procedure, and that the delays were not attributable to the authorities.

The Court found Article 6 § 1 applicable because, although the applicants were not formal plaintiffs or defendants, the proceedings were decisive for their civil property rights. On the merits, the cases were not particularly complex, and the authorities caused substantial delays through improper summoning and lengthy intervals between hearings. **Summary of *Seta v. Greece and Germany* (Application no. 30287/09)**

The case of *Seta v. Greece and Germany* originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 6 April 2009 by Mr. Selim Seta, a Kosovar national born in 1942. The primary complaint concerned the length of criminal proceedings in Greece, which the applicant alleged violated the "reasonable time" requirement under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The facts relevant to the alleged violation began on 14 June 2002, when the applicant was arrested by Greek authorities at the Greek-Albanian border. He was charged with drug trafficking after 25 kilograms of heroin were discovered in the car he was driving. The Ioannina First Instance Prosecutor ordered his detention on remand the same day. The applicant maintained that his arrest was a set-up orchestrated by a German national with whom he had prior disagreements, and that the drugs were placed in his vehicle without his knowledge.

On 20 May 2003, the Ioannina First Instance Criminal Court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to twenty years' imprisonment. He subsequently appealed the decision. On 5 June 2007, the Ioannina Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment. The applicant then lodged an appeal on points of law with the Court of Cassation on 8 September 2007. Notably, no complaint was raised in the grounds of appeal regarding the interpretation service at the time of his arrest or during subsequent proceedings.

The Court of Cassation hearing, initially scheduled for 12 March 2008, was adjourned to 19 November 2008. According to the case file, these proceedings remained pending before the Court of Cassation at the time of the European Court's judgment.

Regarding the Article 6 § 1 complaint, the European Court determined that the period to be considered began on 14 June 2002, when the applicant was arrested and criminal proceedings were brought, and had not yet ended because the proceedings were still pending before the Court of Cassation. This period had thus lasted more than nine years and nine months across three levels of jurisdiction. The Court found this complaint admissible and, on the merits, concluded that the length of proceedings was excessive and failed to meet the "reasonable time" requirement. The Greek Government submitted no observations capable of persuading the Court to reach a different conclusion.

The Court also addressed other complaints. Although the application was brought against both Greece and Germany, no complaint was raised against Germany, rendering that part manifestly ill-founded. The applicant further complained about his lawyer's alleged mishandling of the case and lack of professionalism, but the Court noted this was directed against a private individual, for which no State liability arose under the circumstances. Additionally, the applicant claimed inadequate interpretation services. However, since the domestic proceedings remained pending before the Court of Cassation, this complaint was deemed premature and rejected for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies. The Court ultimately found a violation of Article 6 § 1 concerning the excessive length of the criminal proceedings.

The European Court of Human Rights case **Seta v. Greece and Germany** (Application no. 30287/09, First Section, judgment of 3 May 2012) concerned **Selim Seta**, a Kosovar national born in 1942 and living in Besian. He was arrested by Greek authorities on **14 June 2002** at the Greek-Albanian border after **25 kg of heroin** was found in the car he was driving. The same day, the Ioannina First Instance Prosecutor charged him with illegal drug trafficking and ordered his detention on remand. Seta alleged that his arrest was a set-up by a German national with whom he had disagreements in Germany, and that the drugs were placed in the car without his knowledge.

Domestically, on **20 May 2003**, the Ioannina First Instance Criminal Court convicted Seta and sentenced him to **twenty years’ imprisonment**. On **5 June 2007**, the Ioannina Court of Appeal upheld the conviction. On **8 September 2007**, Seta lodged an appeal on points of law with the Court of Cassation. Importantly, his grounds of appeal did **not** complain about the interpretation service at the time of his arrest or during the later proceedings. The Court of Cassation hearing was initially set for **12 March 2008** but was adjourned to **19 November 2008**. According to the case file, the cassation proceedings were still pending when the ECtHR decided the case.

Seta lodged his application with the ECtHR on **6 April 2009**, naming both Greece and Germany. The application was communicated to the Greek Government on **5 July 2011**. Greece was represented by its Agent, and no observations were submitted by the Government.

The main alleged violation was under **Article 6 § 1** of the Convention, namely that the length of the criminal proceedings before the Greek courts violated the “reasonable time” requirement. The Court found that the relevant period began on **14 June 2002**, when Seta was arrested and criminal complaints were brought, and had not ended because the proceedings remained pending before the Court of Cassation. The total duration had therefore exceeded **nine years and nine months** across three levels of jurisdiction. The Court declared this complaint admissible and, on the merits, found that the length was excessive and failed to meet the “reasonable time” requirement. It noted that the Government had not put forward any fact or argument capable of justifying the delay.

The Court rejected the other complaints. Although Germany was named in the application, no complaint was actually raised against Germany, so that part was manifestly ill-founded. Seta also complained about his Greek lawyer’s alleged mishandling of the case, lack of professionalism and impartiality. The Court held that this was directed against a private individual, so no State liability arose, making it incompatible *ratione personae*. Finally, he alleged inadequate interpretation at arrest and during the proceedings. The Court recalled that fairness of criminal proceedings is assessed as a whole, but because the domestic proceedings were still pending before the Court of Cassation, this complaint was premature and rejected for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies.

Thus, the only substantive violation found was the **excessive length of proceedings under Article 6 § 1**; the remaining complaints were inadmissible.

**Case summary: Seta v. Greece and Germany (Application no. 30287/09), ECHR, 3 May 2012**

The applicant, Selim Seta, a Kosovar national born in 1942 and living in Besian, lodged an application on 6 April 2009. Although the case title names Greece and Germany, the Court noted that no actual complaint was raised against Germany; that part was later rejected as manifestly ill-founded.

The underlying facts concerned Greek criminal proceedings. On 14 June 2002, Greek authorities arrested Seta at the Greek-Albanian border. He was driving a car in which 25 kg of heroin were found. The same day, the Ioannina First Instance Prosecutor charged him with illegal drug trafficking and ordered his detention on remand. Seta denied responsibility, alleging that his arrest had been a set-up by a German national with whom he had disagreements in Germany, and that the drugs had been placed in the car without his knowledge.

On 20 May 2003, the Ioannina First Instance Criminal Court convicted him and sentenced him to twenty years’ imprisonment. He appealed. On 5 June 2007, the Ioannina Court of Appeal upheld the conviction. On 8 September 2007, he lodged an appeal on points of law with the Court of Cassation. Importantly, his grounds of appeal did not raise any complaint about the interpretation service at the time of arrest or during the proceedings. The Cassation hearing, initially set for 12 March 2008, was adjourned to 19 November 2008. According to the case file, the proceedings remained pending before the Court of Cassation at the time of the Strasbourg judgment.

Before the ECtHR, the main alleged violation was under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention: that the length of the Greek proceedings was incompatible with the “reasonable time” requirement. The Greek Government submitted no observations. The Court found the relevant period began on 14 June 2002, when the applicant was arrested and criminal charges were brought, and had not ended because the Cassation appeal was still pending. The proceedings had therefore lasted more than nine years and nine months across three levels of jurisdiction. Applying the criteria of complexity, the applicant’s conduct, and the conduct of the authorities, and noting similar prior case-law, the Court declared the complaint admissible and found a violation of Article 6 § 1. It held that the length was excessive and failed to meet the reasonable-time requirement.

The applicant also made other complaints. First, the part concerning Germany was manifestly ill-founded because no complaint against Germany was identified; it was rejected under Article 35 §§ 3 (a) and 4. Second, he complained about his lawyer before the Greek courts for allegedly mishandling the case and lacking professionalism and impartiality. The Court held this inadmissible *ratione personae*, because it concerned acts of a private individual for which the State could not generally be liable. Third, he complained that no adequate interpretation was provided at arrest and during the proceedings. The Court found this complaint premature: fairness of criminal proceedings must be assessed as a whole, and the criminal proceedings were still pending before the Court of Cassation. It therefore rejected that part for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies under Article 35 §§ 1 and 4.

Thus, the only successful claim was the excessive length of proceedings under Article 6 § 1; the remaining complaints were inadmissible or ill-founded.

**Summary of Shuvalov v. Estonia**

The case of *Shuvalov v. Estonia* (Applications nos. 39820/08 and 14942/09) originated from two applications lodged by Mr. Ardi Shuvalov, an Estonian national and a former judge at Harju County Court, against the Republic of Estonia. The applicant alleged a violation of his right to the presumption of innocence under Article 6 § 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights, stemming from public statements made by the prosecution during criminal proceedings against him.

The underlying facts concern a criminal case presided over by the applicant since 2003, involving a businessman, D., charged with multiple offences. In January 2006, the security police received a statement from D. alleging that his business partner, N., had claimed he could arrange a favourable judgment through the applicant in exchange for a bribe. N. allegedly demanded 200,000 Estonian kroons (EEK) as a "good-will gesture" and a further 900,000 EEK for D.'s acquittal. Based on this information, the police initiated a criminal investigation into bribery offences in January 2006.

Authorities authorized covert surveillance, interception of communications, and undercover audio recording of both N. and the applicant. Crucially, they also authorized a simulation of the offence of giving a bribe to entrap the applicant and N. On 27 February and 6 April 2006, D. provided N. with funds totaling 600,000 EEK, with the second transfer leading to N.'s immediate arrest. N. then claimed the applicant had demanded the money. Prosecutor V., who led the investigation, made numerous public statements to television, newspapers, and news agencies over the following months. These statements asserted that the criminal proceedings were initiated based on specific information, that a successful simulation had occurred, that the main evidence was gathered, and that it was the applicant who had demanded the bribe. A second press release on 6 October 2006 announced the case had been sent to court, reiterating the charges that the applicant demanded a large bribe and promised a favourable judgment.

The applicant argued that these public statements by the prosecutor, an authoritative source, violated his presumption of innocence. He contended the prosecutor presented the allegations as established fact, gave legal assessments that he had committed the crime, and disclosed details from the preliminary investigation. The applicant also filed a separate claim for non-pecuniary damage against the Public Prosecutor’s Office in administrative courts, arguing the statements infringed his presumption of innocence and right to private life. Both the Tallinn Administrative Court and the Tallinn Court of Appeal dismissed his claim, finding that the Public Prosecutor’s Office had acted lawfully, that there was elevated public interest given the suspect was a judge, and that the information released did not exceed the objective need to inform the public or amount to an opinion on his guilt. The case thus reached the European Court of Human Rights regarding the alleged infringement of the presumption of innocence due to these pre-trial and trial-phase public communications.

**Case: Shuvalov v. Estonia (Apps. nos. 39820/08 and 14942/09), ECtHR, 29 May 2012**

In January 2006, D. told the security police that his business partner N., who owed D.’s company money, had claimed he knew Shuvalov from law studies and could arrange a favourable judgment if D. did not insist on repayment. N. allegedly demanded EEK 200,000 as a “Christmas good-will gesture” and a further EEK 900,000 for D.’s acquittal.

The police opened a bribery investigation, authorised covert surveillance and interception, and later simulations of bribe-giving and bribe-arranging. D. paid N EEK 200,000 in February and EEK 400,000 in April 2006. N. was arrested and told police that Shuvalov had demanded the money. Acting under police instructions, N. met Shuvalov with recording equipment and gave him EEK 200,000. Shuvalov was arrested, released the next day, and surrendered the money.

The alleged violation concerned public statements and press releases. On 9 April 2006, the Public Prosecutor’s Office published a press release titled “A judge suspected of accepting a bribe.” It said a Harju County Court judge had been arrested on suspicion of demanding a large bribe through an intermediary for a more favourable judgment. It stated that he had accepted part of the sum during a simulated offence, that the exact amount could not be disclosed, and that a large bribe was at least EEK 300,000. Shuvalov’s identity soon became known.

Prosecutor V. then made media statements. On television, she said the suspicion emerged when the person from whom the bribe was allegedly demanded contacted the security police, and that the simulation was successful. In newspapers, she said the case had not been provoked, that surveillance began in January, and that the applicant himself had demanded the money. She described him as “very careful.”

After the bill of indictment was submitted in October 2006, the Prosecutor’s Office issued another press release, “The judge’s criminal case has arrived at the court.” It stated that Shuvalov was charged with demanding a large bribe, that the established facts showed he promised decisions in the accused’s favour and acquittal, that he accepted EEK 200,000, and that he had committed the offence and breached the rule-of-law principle that justice is administered impartially. Further media statements named D. and gave the total alleged sum as EEK 1.1 million, asserting the initiative came from the judge and there was no provocation.

He separately sued the Public Prosecutor’s Office for non-pecuniary damage, arguing that the statements violated his presumption of innocence and private life. The domestic administrative courts dismissed the claim, finding elevated public interest because the suspect was a judge, and that the information was limited, based on suspicion or the indictment, and did not amount to a subjective opinion on guilt. The Supreme Court declined review.

The European Court of Human Rights joined the applications, declared parts inadmissible, and examined the complaint under Article 6 § 2. It found that certain public statements by the prosecutor and press releases went beyond objective information and effectively presented Shuvalov as guilty before a final conviction, violating his presumption of innocence.

**Summary of *Murtić and Ćerimović v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (App. No. 6495/09)**

The case originated in an application by Mr. Fikret Murtić and Ms. Raska Ćerimović, two citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, against the State for the non-enforcement of a domestic human rights decision. The core of their complaint concerned the violation of their property rights, specifically their inability to exercise rights attached to shares they held in a company, Agrokomerc.

The facts relevant to the alleged violation began in 1991 when the applicants, employees of Agrokomerc, acquired "internal shares" as part of the company's reorganisation from a socially-owned to a joint-stock company. Their shares were paid for through permanent deposits and deductions from their salaries between 1991 and 1994. This process created a significant internal share capital held by employees.

However, in August 1994, amidst armed conflict, the State took control of Agrokomerc's management. Following this takeover, the applicants were effectively prevented from exercising any shareholder rights, despite the company's balance sheets continuing to list their privately-held capital until 1999. Their employment was also suspended in 1995, and they were never re-hired.

In 2000, the applicants appealed to the Human Rights Chamber for Bosnia and Herzegovina. In its decision of 8 March 2002, the Chamber found that the applicants had acquired protected "possessions" in the form of their paid-up internal shares under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights. It ruled that the subsequent transfer of ownership to the State, based on an audit that invalidated the internal shares without the applicants' effective participation, violated their property rights and their right to a fair hearing under Article 6 of the Convention.

The Chamber ordered the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina to take specific remedial steps, including employing international auditors to determine the company's complete and accurate ownership structure, establishing the value of the applicants' shares, and formally registering them so the applicants could exercise their shareholder rights.

The enforcement of this decision was fraught with delay. An initial audit by Deloitte & Touche in 2003 still failed to assign the value of the applicants' shares, preventing them from attending the 2004 shareholders' meeting. It was not until 2007—more than five years after the Chamber's binding decision—that the applicants were finally issued individual share certificates and their shares were formally registered. By this time, their shares were assigned a market value (BAM 4,510 for the first applicant and BAM 10,000 for the second).

Finally, in 2009, the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina concluded that the Human Rights Chamber's decision had been fully implemented. This was despite the significant and prolonged delay.

The key violation alleged by the applicants was not the original State takeover of their shares, but the State's failure to promptly and effectively enforce the 2002 decision that was meant to remedy that initial violation. The applicants complained that the non-enforcement of the domestic decision in their favour violated their rights under the Convention. The central issue for the European Court of Human Rights was whether this belated implementation, taking over six years, constituted a failure by the State to comply with its positive obligation to enforce a final and binding domestic decision, thereby perpetuating the initial violation of their property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

**Case summary: Murtić and Ćerimović v. Bosnia and Herzegovina**  
*(ECtHR, Fourth Section, Application no. 6495/09, judgment of 19 June 2012)*

The applicants, Fikret Murtić and Raska Ćerimović, two Bosnian citizens living in Velika Kladuša, complained to the European Court of Human Rights about Bosnia and Herzegovina’s non-enforcement of a decision of the Human Rights Chamber dated 8 March 2002. The application was lodged on 6 October 2005 and communicated to the Government on 7 May 2009.

Both applicants had been employed by Agrokomerc, an agricultural company in Velika Kladuša. In August 1991, during the company’s reorganisation from socially owned to joint-stock status, the workers’ council decided to issue internal shares to employees. One third of employees’ salaries was allocated to instalment payments for those shares. In March 1993, the company’s management board adopted resolutions retaining earnings and increasing internal share capital. As a result, internal share capital reached 80.9% of the company’s total capital, with the remainder held by the State. In August 1994, after armed conflict in north-western Bosnia, the State took over the company’s management. From then on, the applicants were effectively unable to exercise their shareholder rights, although the company continued to record privately held internal share capital on its balance sheets until 30 June 1999. In August 1995, their employment was suspended and they were placed on a waiting list, but they were never re-employed.

In June 2000, the applicants complained separately to the Human Rights Chamber. In March 2001, an audit by Revsar concluded that the measures creating internal share capital from 1991 to 1994 had been unlawful and that the internal share capital had never been formed; the company was therefore 100% State-owned. In July 2001, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina placed the company under its control based on State-owned capital.

On 8 March 2002, the Human Rights Chamber joined the applicants’ cases with others and held that the applicants had acquired protected “possessions” in their paid-up internal shares. It found violations of Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Chamber reasoned that the renewed Revsar audit had cancelled all internal shares in favour of State capital, thereby depriving the applicants of their possessions. It also found that the Federation’s exclusive control over the company’s management interfered with the applicants’ rights to participate in management and share in profits, and that they had no real or effective means to participate in determining the ownership structure or to access a court for determination of their civil rights.

The Chamber ordered the Federation to recognise the applicants as holders of internal shares, employ internationally recognised auditors to determine the complete ownership structure, establish and register the value of their shares, issue individual share certificates, and maintain interim management measures. Implementation was delayed. A 2003 Deloitte & Touche audit found 90.33% State ownership and 9.67% private ownership, with only 3.34% assigned to individual shareholders. The applicants’ share value was not established, so they could not attend the March 2004 shareholders’ meeting. Interim measures were lifted in May 2004. In May 2005, ownership changes were registered; in February 2006, unassigned private capital was distributed; and in October 2007, the applicants finally received share certificates. The first applicant received 451 shares worth BAM 4,510; the second received 1,086 shares worth BAM 10,000. In January 2009, the Constitutional Court found the Human Rights Chamber’s decision fully implemented. Nevertheless, the applicants’ ECtHR complaint concerned the alleged failure to enforce that decision.

The case of *Murtić and Ćerimović v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* concerns the failure of the respondent State to enforce a final decision of the Human Rights Chamber. The applicants, Fikret Murtić and Raska Ćerimović, were employees of Agrokomerc, a large agricultural company in Velika Kladuša. The key facts revolve around their ownership of "internal shares" in the company and the subsequent loss of their shareholder rights.

Between 1991 and 1994, as part of the company's reorganisation from a socially-owned to a joint-stock company, the applicants acquired internal shares. Their ownership was based on the allocation of parts of their salaries and the distribution of profits, for which they made payments. This process was halted in August 1994 when, following the armed conflict, the company's management was taken over by the State. After this takeover, the applicants were effectively unable to exercise any of their rights as shareholders. Subsequently, on 7 August 1995, their employment was suspended, and they were never re-employed.

In 2000, the applicants appealed to the Human Rights Chamber. A crucial development occurred in 2001 when an audit by the firm Revsar declared that the creation of the internal share capital had been unlawful, concluding that the company was 100% State-owned. This effectively erased the applicants' ownership.

On 8 March 2002, the Human Rights Chamber ruled in favour of the applicants. It found that they had acquired protected "possessions" in the form of their paid-up internal shares and that the Federation's actions, particularly the Revsar audit and its exclusive control over the company, had violated their rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) and Article 6 (right to a fair trial) of the Convention. The Chamber ordered the Federation to take specific steps to remedy the situation, including employing internationally recognised auditors to determine the company's complete ownership structure, establishing the value of the applicants' shares, formally registering them, and issuing individual share certificates.

The enforcement of this decision was protracted. A new audit by Deloitte & Touche in 2003 found that only 9.67% of the company was privately owned and failed to assign the applicants' specific share values, preventing them from attending a key shareholder meeting in 2004. Eventually, after years of delay, the applicants were finally issued individual share certificates on 29 October 2007 and were subsequently able to attend shareholder meetings.

On 15 January 2009, the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which had taken over supervision of the enforcement, concluded that the Human Rights Chamber's decision had been fully implemented. The applicants, however, brought their case to the European Court of Human Rights, complaining primarily about the non-enforcement of the 2002 decision in their favour. The central alleged violation was the State's failure to promptly and effectively implement the domestic human rights body's binding decision, which had recognised their property rights and right to a fair trial.

**Summary of *Hatice Duman v. Turkey* (Application no. 43918/08)**

The case of *Hatice Duman v. Turkey* concerns an application lodged against the Republic of Turkey with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicant, Ms. Hatice Duman, a Turkish national born in 1974, alleged violations of her rights under Article 5 §§ 3 and 4 of the Convention, specifically regarding the excessive length of her pre-trial detention and the lack of an effective remedy to challenge its continuation.

The key facts are as follows: On 9 April 2003, the applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership in the MLKP (Marxist-Leninist Communist Party), an illegal organisation. She was brought before a public prosecutor and an investigating judge on 13 April 2003, who subsequently ordered her pre-trial detention. On 23 July 2003, the public prosecutor at the Istanbul State Security Court filed an indictment against the applicant and eight others, charging them with attempting to undermine the constitutional order of the State and membership of, or aiding and abetting, an illegal organisation.

Following the abolition of State Security Courts, the case was transferred to the Istanbul Assize Court. Throughout the proceedings, the Assize Court repeatedly prolonged the applicant’s pre-trial detention and rejected her requests for release. These decisions were based on reasonable suspicion that she had committed the offence, the severity of the charges, and the state of the evidence. A significant event occurred at the hearing on 1 April 2009, when the court again rejected the applicant’s claim that her detention was unreasonably lengthy. The applicant objected to this decision.

The circumstances surrounding the review of this objection form the basis of her second complaint. The applicant alleged that during the review proceedings before the 13th Chamber of the Istanbul Assize Court, neither she nor her lawyer was given the opportunity to make oral submissions. Crucially, they were not notified of the written observations submitted by the public prosecutor, which argued for the continuation of her detention. On 17 April 2009, the 13th Chamber rejected her objection, relying on the nature of the charge and the existence of reasonable suspicion.

On 4 May 2011, the Istanbul Assize Court convicted the applicant of attempting to undermine the constitutional order under the former Criminal Code and sentenced her to life imprisonment. An appeal to the Court of Cassation was pending at the time of the European Court's judgment.

Regarding Article 5 § 3, the Court noted that the applicant was held in pre-trial detention from 9 April 2003 until her conviction on 4 May 2011, a period exceeding eight years. The Government argued that a compensation claim under domestic law was an available remedy. However, the Court rejected this preliminary objection, citing its established case-law (*Barış v. Turkey*, *Tunce and Others v. Turkey*) that such a claim cannot end excessively long detention while proceedings are pending and is therefore not an effective remedy. The Court found the length of detention excessive, violating Article 5 § 3.

Regarding Article 5 § 4, the Court reiterated that detention review proceedings must be adversarial and ensure "equality of arms." It found that the 13th Chamber ruled on the applicant’s objection after receiving the public prosecutor’s opinion, which was not communicated to the applicant or her lawyer, denying them any opportunity to respond. This failure to respect the principle of equality of arms led the Court to conclude that the procedure did not meet the requirements of Article 5 § 4, finding a violation.

**Case: Hatice Duman v. Turkey (Application no. 43918/08), European Court of Human Rights, Second Section, Judgment of 22 May 2012.**

The applicant, Hatice Duman, a Turkish national born in 1974, was serving a sentence in Gebze Prison at the time of the case. On 9 April 2003 she was arrested on suspicion of membership of the MLKP (Marxist-Leninist Communist Party), an illegal organisation. On 13 April 2003 she was brought before the public prosecutor and an investigating judge, who ordered her pre-trial detention. On 23 July 2003 the public prosecutor at the Istanbul State Security Court filed an indictment against her and eight other persons, charging them with attempting to undermine the constitutional order of the State and membership of, or aiding and abetting, an illegal organisation.

Following the abolition of the State Security Courts, the criminal proceedings resumed before the Istanbul Assize Court. During the proceedings, that court repeatedly prolonged the applicant’s pre-trial detention and rejected her requests for release pending trial. It relied on the existence of reasonable suspicion that she had committed the offence, the severity of the charge, and the state of the evidence. At a hearing on 1 April 2009, the Assize Court again rejected her claim that her detention had been unreasonably lengthy and refused to release her. The applicant objected to that decision before the higher division of the Assize Court.

The applicant alleged that, in the proceedings reviewing her continued detention, neither she nor her lawyer was given an opportunity to make oral submissions against the lawfulness of her detention, and that they were not notified of the public prosecutor’s written observations. On 17 April 2009 the 13th Chamber of the Istanbul Assize Court dismissed her objection, taking into account the nature of the criminal charge and the existence of reasonable suspicion. On 4 May 2011 the Istanbul Assize Court convicted the applicant of attempting to undermine the constitutional order under Article 146 § 1 of the former Criminal Code and sentenced her to life imprisonment. Her appeal to the Court of Cassation was pending.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained under Article 5 § 3 that the length of her pre-trial detention had been excessive. The Government preliminarily objected that she had failed to exhaust domestic remedies, arguing that she could have sought compensation under Law no. 466 or Article 141 of the new Code of Criminal Procedure. The Court rejected that objection, finding that a compensation claim would not end detention of excessive length while criminal proceedings were pending and therefore was not an effective remedy for the Article 5 § 3 complaint.

On the merits, the Court noted that the applicant had been detained on 9 April 2003 and convicted on 4 May 2011, meaning her pre-trial detention lasted over eight years. The Government argued that continued detention was justified by the severity of the charges, reasonable suspicion, protection of evidence, risk of absconding, and complexity of the proceedings. The Court, relying on its established case-law, found that the length of the applicant’s pre-trial detention was excessive and that the Government had not provided facts or arguments capable of leading to a different conclusion. It therefore found a violation of Article 5 § 3.

The applicant also complained under Article 5 § 4 that there was no effective remedy by which she could effectively challenge her continued pre-trial detention. In particular, she argued that she had not been afforded a fair and adversarial hearing before the 13th Chamber of the Istanbul Assize Court, because no oral hearing was held and the public prosecutor’s written opinion against her release was not communicated to her or her lawyer. The Government contested this.

The Court reiterated that proceedings reviewing a detainee’s continued detention under Article 5 § 4 must be adversarial and must ensure equality of arms between the prosecutor and the detained person. It observed that the 13th Chamber ruled on the applicant’s objection after receiving the public prosecutor’s opinion recommending continued detention, but that opinion was not communicated to the applicant or her lawyer, depriving them of any opportunity to respond. The higher court then decided in accordance with the prosecutor’s opinion and dismissed the objection. The Court held that the applicant and her lawyer had been denied an adversarial hearing and that the principle of equality of arms had not been respected. This was sufficient to find that the review procedure did not meet the requirements of Article 5 § 4. Accordingly, the Court found a violation of Article 5 § 4 of the Convention.

The case *Hatice Duman v. Turkey* (Application no. 43918/08) concerned a Turkish national, Ms Hatice Duman, born in 1974 and later detained in Gebze Prison. On 9 April 2003 she was arrested on suspicion of membership in the MLKP, an illegal Marxist-Leninist Communist Party. On 13 April 2003 she was taken before the public prosecutor and an investigating judge, who ordered her pre-trial detention. On 23 July 2003, the public prosecutor at the Istanbul State Security Court indicted her and eight others, charging her with attempting to undermine the constitutional order of the State and with membership of, or aiding and abetting, an illegal organisation. After the State Security Courts were abolished, the criminal proceedings resumed before the Istanbul Assize Court.

During the proceedings, the Istanbul Assize Court repeatedly extended the applicant’s pre-trial detention and rejected her requests for release. It relied on reasonable suspicion that she had committed the offence, the seriousness of the charges, and the state of the evidence. On 1 April 2009, the Assize Court again rejected her claim that her detention had become unreasonably lengthy and refused to release her pending trial. The applicant challenged that decision before the higher division of the Assize Court. In that review, she alleged that neither she nor her lawyer was given an opportunity to make oral submissions against the lawfulness of her continued detention and that they were not notified of the public prosecutor’s written observations. On 17 April 2009, the 13th Chamber of the Istanbul Assize Court dismissed her objection, relying on the nature of the charge and the existence of reasonable suspicion. On 4 May 2011, the Istanbul Assize Court convicted her of attempting to undermine the constitutional order under Article 146 § 1 of the former Criminal Code and sentenced her to life imprisonment. Her appeal was pending before the Court of Cassation.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 5 § 3 that the length of her pre-trial detention was excessive, and under Article 5 § 4 that she had no effective remedy by which to challenge her continued detention and that the review proceedings were not adversarial. The Government objected that she had failed to exhaust domestic remedies, arguing that she could have sought compensation under Law no. 466 or Article 141 of the new Code of Criminal Procedure. The Court rejected that objection, reasoning that a compensation claim could not end detention of excessive length while criminal proceedings were pending and therefore was not an effective remedy for Article 5 § 3 purposes.

On the merits, the Government maintained that detention was justified by the severity of the charges, reasonable suspicion, protection of evidence, risk of absconding, and the complexity of the case. The Court noted that the applicant was detained on 9 April 2003 and convicted on 4 May 2011, meaning her pre-trial detention lasted over eight years. It found a violation of Article 5 § 3 because the detention was excessive. As to Article 5 § 4, the Court held that detention review proceedings must be adversarial and ensure equality of arms between the prosecutor and the detained person. The 13th Chamber had ruled after receiving the public prosecutor’s opinion supporting continued detention, but that opinion was never communicated to the applicant or her lawyer, so they could not respond to it. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 5 § 4, as the applicant and her lawyer had been denied an adversarial hearing and equality of arms.
