In *Levinta v. Moldova (No. 2)*, two Moldovan nationals, Pavel and Vitalie Levinta, complained under Article 5 about their detention after their criminal convictions were quashed. They had been arrested in Russia in October 2000, extradited to Moldova, ill-treated to obtain self-incriminating statements, and convicted. In 2008 the European Court of Human Rights found violations of Articles 3 and 6 in the first *Levinta* case. Relying on that judgment, on 3 April 2009 the applicants lodged an extraordinary appeal seeking annulment of their convictions.

On 8 February 2010 the Plenary Supreme Court of Justice quashed all previous judgments, ordered a re-hearing, and stated that the applicants “shall continue to be detained.” Critically, it did not issue arrest warrants, specify the legal basis or purpose of detention, give reasons, or set a time limit. It also left the issue of preventive measures to the Chisinau Court of Appeal. The applicants therefore remained in custody without a new detention order.

On 13 April 2010 the applicants’ lawyer asked the Court of Appeal to release them because no valid detention order existed. The prosecutor then requested a thirty-day detention pending trial. The court postponed hearings on 14 and 16 April, and on 19 April rejected the release request and ordered detention for thirty days from 14 April. It cited reasonable grounds to believe the applicants had committed exceptionally serious crimes and risks that they might abscond or obstruct proceedings. The lawyer appealed, arguing there was no legal basis for detention, that the presumption of innocence had been breached, that the detention exceeded the maximum allowed, and that the prosecution had submitted no supporting evidence. On 13 May 2010 the Supreme Court of Justice rejected the appeal.

A separate issue arose the same day. The prosecution had filed a request on 7 May 2010 to extend detention by sixty days. According to the applicants, their lawyer was called at 2 p.m. on 13 May and told a Court of Appeal hearing would be held at 4 p.m. He was in Anenii Noi on another case and could not attend. The applicants were absent—one refused to attend and the other said he was unfit. A State-appointed lawyer represented them and briefly objected. The Court of Appeal granted the extension for essentially the same reasons as before. A dissenting judge noted that the prosecution had failed to inform the defence of the request despite opportunities to do so, that no specific danger had been shown, and that the applicants’ defence rights had been breached. On 3 June 2010 the Supreme Court rejected the appeal, finding no breach because the applicants had refused to appear and their chosen lawyer had been informed but unavailable.

The applicants later made regular release requests, while the prosecution sought extensions. The courts continued to extend detention until December 2010, when it was replaced by house arrest, and in February 2011 by an undertaking not to leave the country.

The alleged violations concerned Article 5 § 1 (unlawful detention after the convictions were quashed, and a brief alleged period without a valid warrant), Article 5 § 3 (lack of relevant and sufficient reasons for detention pending trial), and Article 5 § 4 (inability to be represented by their chosen lawyer at the 13 May 2010 hearing). The Court found the two-hour detention complaint inadmissible; found a violation of Article 5 § 1 for the period 8 February to 19 April 2010 because the Supreme Court ordered continued detention without legal basis or reasons; found no Article 5 § 3 violation after 19 April because the Supreme Court cited the applicants’ prior absconding and international wanted status; and found a violation of Article 5 § 4 because the prosecution and court failed to notify the chosen lawyer of the extension request and hearing, leaving him insufficient time to prepare.

In *Levinta v. Moldova (No. 2)* (App. no. 50717/09, 17 January 2012), two Moldovan applicants alleged unlawful detention and procedural breaches after their convictions were quashed. They had been arrested in Russia in 2000, extradited to Moldova, ill-treated, and convicted partly on self-incriminating statements. In *Levinţa v. Moldova* (2008), the ECtHR had already found violations of Articles 3 and 6. In April 2009, relying on that judgment, the applicants filed an extraordinary appeal seeking annulment of their convictions.

On 8 February 2010, the Plenary Supreme Court of Justice quashed all previous judgments, ordered a re-hearing, and directed verification of the ill-treatment complaint. In its operative part, it stated that the applicants “shall continue to be detained; the trial court shall decide on the preventive measure.” It issued no arrest warrant, gave no reasons, and set no duration. The applicants’ lawyer immediately complained to the Minister of Justice and Prosecutor General, seeking release because no valid detention order existed. The Prosecutor General referred to the 8 February judgment; the Ministry said it had no record of a relevant judgment after 2002. The case was sent to the Chişinău Court of Appeal in March.

On 13 April 2010, the lawyer again sought release. The prosecutor then requested 30 days’ detention pending trial. After postponements, on 19 April the Court of Appeal rejected release and ordered detention for 30 days, starting from 14 April, citing reasonable grounds, the seriousness of the charges, and risks that the applicants might abscond or obstruct proceedings. The applicants therefore remained detained from 8 February to 19 April without a reasoned court order or warrant. This formed the core of their Article 5 § 1 complaint.

On 13 May 2010, the Supreme Court rejected their appeal against the 19 April detention. That same day, the applicants’ chosen lawyer was allegedly given very short notice—by phone—of a Court of Appeal hearing on the prosecution’s 7 May request to extend detention by 60 days. He could not attend because he was in Anenii Noi on another case. At the hearing, the applicants were absent (one refused, one claimed unfit), their chosen lawyer was absent, and a State-appointed lawyer represented them, merely “objecting” to the request. The court granted the extension for essentially the same reasons. A dissenting judge noted that the prosecution’s request reached the Supreme Court only on 11 May, lacked specific evidence of danger, and that the same prosecutor had failed to inform the defence despite attending the morning Supreme Court hearing. The Supreme Court later upheld the extension, citing the applicants’ prior absconding, international wanted status, extradition, and lack of social ties, income, or employment. Later detention was extended monthly; in December 2010 it became house arrest, then an undertaking not to leave.

The ECtHR rejected as manifestly ill-founded the complaint about an alleged two-hour unlawful detention gap. Under Article 5 § 1, it found the detention from 8 February to 19 April 2010 incompatible with the Convention: quashing the convictions ended detention “after conviction,” and the Supreme Court’s bare instruction to continue detention lacked legal basis, reasons, and duration. The Government’s claim that the Supreme Court could not give reasons was rejected, because a court empowered to detain must justify detention. Under Article 5 § 3, the Court did not examine the initial period due to the § 1 violation; after 19 April, the Supreme Court’s reliance on the applicants’ prior absconding was a relevant specific fact. Under Article 5 § 4, it found a violation because the chosen lawyer could not effectively challenge the 13 May extension: the prosecution failed to notify the defence, and the late/no notice left no time to prepare, while the State-appointed lawyer lacked prior knowledge.

**Summary of *Levinţa v. Moldova (No. 2)* (Application no. 50717/09)**

The case of *Levinţa v. Moldova (No. 2)* concerns two Moldovan applicants, Pavel and Vitalie Levinţa, who were arrested in Russia in October 2000, extradited to Moldova, and convicted based on self-incriminatory statements obtained through ill-treatment. In a prior judgment (*Levinţa v. Moldova*, no. 17332/03, 16 December 2008), the European Court of Human Rights found violations of Articles 3 and 6 of the Convention. Based on that judgment, the applicants lodged an extraordinary appeal, and on 8 February 2010, the Plenary Supreme Court of Justice quashed all prior convictions, ordering a re-hearing. Critically, the Supreme Court's operative ruling stated only that the applicants "shall continue to be detained" and that the trial court would decide on preventive measures, without providing legal grounds, justification, or a time limit for detention.

Following the quashing of their convictions, the applicants' lawyer immediately requested their release, arguing there was no valid detention order. The Prosecutor General's Office and Ministry of Justice offered inconsistent responses, and no proper arrest warrant was issued. On 13 April 2010, the lawyer again sought release, while the prosecution requested a thirty-day detention order. On 19 April 2010, the Chişinău Court of Appeal rejected the release request and ordered detention for thirty days, citing reasonable grounds to believe the applicants committed serious crimes and risks of absconding or obstructing proceedings—though without specific evidence. The court also relinquished jurisdiction to the Supreme Court of Justice.

On 13 May 2010, the applicants' lawyer received a late-morning call about an appeal hearing at noon after the Supreme Court rejected their appeal. Later that afternoon, he was contacted again about a 4 p.m. hearing on the prosecution's request to extend detention. Unable to attend due to another case, the applicants were represented by a State-appointed lawyer who objected without meaningful argument. The Court of Appeal granted a sixty-day extension based on the same reasoning as before. A dissenting judge noted the prosecution failed to notify the defence of its request and that the chosen lawyer was prevented from effectively representing the applicants.

The applicants appealed, but on 3 June 2010, the Supreme Court of Justice rejected it, finding no breach of defence rights and noting the prior detention order had not expired. It cited specific facts—that the applicants had previously absconded and were internationally wanted—as justifying detention. Subsequent monthly extensions occurred until house arrest replaced detention on 28 December 2010, followed by an undertaking not to leave the country on 4 February 2011.

The applicants alleged violations of Article 5 §§ 1, 3, and 4 of the Convention. Under Article 5 § 1, they argued detention lacked legal basis after the quashing of convictions, and that they were held two hours unlawfully on 13 April 2010. The Court declared the two-hour complaint inadmissible but found the broader detention between 8 February and 19 April 2010 incompatible with Article 5 § 1, as the Supreme Court failed to justify detention under any listed ground, leaving it arbitrary. Under Article 5 § 3, given the Article 5 § 1 violation for the initial period, the Court examined post-19 April detention and found no violation, as the Supreme Court cited relevant facts about absconding. Under Article 5 § 4, the Court found a violation due to the applicants' inability to be represented by their chosen lawyer at the 13 May 2010 hearing, as insufficient notice prevented effective preparation, undermining their right to challenge detention speedily.
001-114514:
**I.G. and Others v. Slovakia** concerned three Slovak nationals of Roma origin—I.G., M.K., and R.H.—who alleged that they were sterilised in Krompachy Hospital without their informed consent and that Slovak authorities failed to provide effective redress. They complained under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 8 (private and family life), 12 (right to marry and found a family), 13 (effective remedy), and 14 (non-discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The alleged violations arose from tubal ligations performed during Caesarean deliveries. The first applicant, born in 1983, was sterilised on 23 January 2000 during her second Caesarean section, when she was 16 years old. She claimed she was not told about the sterilisation; the next morning she was asked to sign a document because “all women who had Caesarean sections had to sign it.” She only learned of the sterilisation in 2003 while reviewing her medical file. A typewritten “Request for authorisation of sterilisation,” dated the day of delivery and bearing her signature, was in the file, together with a sterilisation committee decision citing medical reasons. She later suffered serious infection and underwent a hysterectomy. Her civil claim was dismissed because the later hysterectomy was found to have broken the causal link between the unlawful sterilisation and her infertility.

The second applicant, born in 1981, was sterilised on 10 January 1999 during her second Caesarean section, when she was 17 and unmarried. She alleged that neither she nor her parents were advised beforehand or consented. She learned four years later, during a criminal investigation, that her file contained a “Request for sterilisation” with her signature dated 9 January 1999 and a committee approval. She suffered medical side-effects, her partner left her, and her social status in her Roma community declined. In civil proceedings, a court eventually found that hospital staff had acted unlawfully by not obtaining her guardians’ approval, but awarded only EUR 1,593.3, refusing a higher award for alleged social exclusion.

The third applicant, born in 1972, was sterilised on 11 April 2002 during her fourth delivery, a Caesarean section for twins. She claimed she was given pre-medication, felt dizzy, and was asked to sign a paper she could not read. She was allegedly told only after discharge that she had been sterilised. She learned details during police questioning in 2003. She died in 2010, and her children sought to continue the application; the domestic court discontinued her civil action because the right claimed had extinguished on death.

The applicants also alleged inferior, segregated treatment at Krompachy Hospital, including “Gypsy rooms,” separate bathrooms and dining facilities, and verbal abuse. They linked this to racial prejudice and cited the *Body and Soul* Report on coercive sterilisation of Roma women in Slovakia. The Government disputed the allegations and relied on a Ministry of Health expert report and hospital statistics denying forced sterilisation.

Their attempts to obtain redress included criminal complaints from 2003. The investigation was repeatedly discontinued, including findings that no criminal offence had been committed and that the sterilisations complied with the 1972 Sterilisation Regulation. Constitutional complaints led to partial findings: in 2005 the Constitutional Court found a breach of Articles 3 and 13 concerning rejection of their complaint, and in 2006 it found procedural violations of Articles 3 and 8 and ordered reinvestigation. Nevertheless, later prosecutorial decisions again found no offence. Civil claims largely failed or produced minimal compensation, and constitutional complaints were mostly rejected as manifestly ill-founded.

The key alleged violations were therefore the non-consensual sterilisation of Roma women in a public hospital, particularly minors without guardian consent, and the State’s failure to investigate effectively and provide adequate compensation.

# Summary of I.G. and Others v. Slovakia (Application no. 15966/04)

**Parties and Allegations:** The case was brought by three Slovakian nationals of Roma ethnic origin—I.G. (born 1983), M.K. (born 1981), and R.H. (born 1972)—against the Slovak Republic. The applicants alleged violations of Articles 3, 8, 12, 13, and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights on account of their sterilisation in a public hospital and the failure of Slovakian authorities to provide appropriate redress. R.H. died in October 2010, and her three children expressed the wish to pursue the application in her stead.

**Key Facts:** All three applicants were sterilised by tubal ligation during Caesarean sections at Krompachy Hospital, a facility then under the authority of the Ministry of Health.

The **first applicant** was sterilised on 23 January 2000 during her second delivery by Caesarean section. She was 16 years old at the time—a minor—and her legal guardians had not consented to the operation. She was not informed that she had been sterilised. The next morning, a doctor asked her to sign a document, telling her that all women who had Caesarean sections had to sign it. She later suffered post-surgery complications, and on 9 February 2000 underwent a life-saving hysterectomy. She first learned of her sterilisation in January 2003 while reviewing her medical files, which contained a "Request for authorisation of sterilisation" dated 23 January 2000 bearing her signature, along with a decision of the district sterilisation committee approving the procedure.

The **second applicant** was sterilised on 10 January 1999 during her second Caesarean delivery. She was 17 years old, a minor, and not legally married. Neither she nor her parents were advised of or consented to the sterilisation. She learned only four years later, during a criminal investigation, that her medical record contained a "Request for sterilisation" with her signature dated 9 January 1999. Her partner left her upon learning she could not have more children, and her social status in the Roma community fell.

The **third applicant** was sterilised on 11 April 2002 during her fourth delivery (twins) by Caesarean section. Before the operation, a nurse gave her a pre-medication injection, after which she felt dizzy. A nurse then asked her to sign a paper, telling her she had to sign it because she was having a Caesarean delivery. She was unable to read its contents. She learned she had been sterilised only later, during police questioning on 14 August 2003. The sterilisation request form was dated 10 April 2002.

The applicants also alleged they received inferior treatment at the hospital, including being accommodated separately in "Gypsy rooms," being prevented from using the same bathrooms and toilets as non-Roma women, and experiencing verbal abuse. The chief gynaecologist allegedly admitted categorising patients by "adaptability" and hygiene. The Government disputed these allegations.

**Attempts to Obtain Redress:** Following publication of the Body and Soul Report, a criminal investigation was initiated in 2003 but was repeatedly discontinued. The Constitutional Court found violations of the applicants' rights under Articles 3 and 8 (procedural aspect) in 2005 and 2006, quashing decisions and ordering re-examination. However, the investigation was again discontinued in 2007, and the General Prosecutor's Office concluded that no criminal offence had been committed.

In civil proceedings, the first applicant's claim was dismissed on the basis that the subsequent hysterectomy, not the sterilisation, had caused her infertility, breaking the causal link. The second applicant was awarded EUR 1,593.30, the Regional Court finding this appropriate and refusing to increase it for alleged impairment of social position. The third applicant's proceedings were discontinued after her death.

The case thus concerns allegations of forced or coerced sterilisation of Roma women without informed consent and the failure of domestic authorities to provide effective investigation and adequate redress.

**I.G. and Others v. Slovakia** concerned three Slovak Roma women—I.G. (b. 1983), M.K. (b. 1981), and R.H. (b. 1972)—who alleged that they were sterilised without informed consent in Krompachy Hospital, a public health institution then under the Ministry of Health, and that Slovak authorities failed to provide adequate redress. They invoked Articles 3, 8, 12, 13, and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

**Key facts.** Each applicant underwent tubal ligation during a Caesarean section. I.G. was sterilised on 23 January 2000, during her second Caesarean delivery, when she was 16 years old. She said she was not told about the sterilisation; after waking, she was told she had a girl, and the next day was asked to sign a document because all women who had Caesareans had to sign it. Her medical file later contained a typewritten “Request for authorisation of sterilisation,” dated the same day and signed by her, plus a sterilisation committee approval citing medical reasons, two children, prior Caesarean, and a small pelvis. She later suffered post-surgical infection and underwent a life-saving hysterectomy.

M.K. was sterilised on 10 January 1999 during her second Caesarean delivery, at age 17 and unmarried. She claimed neither she nor her parents were advised beforehand or signed any consent. She learned four years later, during a criminal investigation, that her file contained a “Request for sterilisation” with her signature dated 9 January 1999, citing pelvic varicose veins, and committee approval. Her partner left her after learning she could not have more children, and she reported social and medical consequences.

R.H. was sterilised on 11 April 2002 during her fourth delivery, a Caesarean birth of twins. She said she was given pre-medication, felt dizzy, and was asked by a nurse to sign a paper she could not read; she signed because she was told it was required for the Caesarean. After discharge, a doctor allegedly said the paper confirmed sterilisation. She only saw the typewritten request and committee decision on 14 August 2003 at a police station; it cited medical reasons and three children.

The applicants also alleged inferior, segregated treatment as Roma patients, including “Gypsy rooms,” separate bathrooms and dining areas, and verbal abuse. The Government disputed these claims.

**Redress efforts.** After publication of the *Body and Soul* report, criminal proceedings began in 2003 but were repeatedly discontinued. The Constitutional Court found violations of Articles 3 and 8 in their procedural aspect in 2006, quashed a prosecutor’s decision, and awarded EUR 1,430 to each applicant. Nevertheless, investigators again concluded in 2007–2008 that no criminal offence had occurred and that the sterilisations were lawful; prosecutors also said the applicants were not injured parties. Civil claims largely failed or produced minimal compensation. I.G.’s claim was dismissed because courts found no causal link between the sterilisation and later infertility, attributing infertility to the hysterectomy. M.K. was eventually awarded EUR 1,593.30, upheld on appeal. R.H.’s action was discontinued after her death and was pursued by her children.

The ECtHR declared the application admissible on 22 September 2009. The core alleged violations were the applicants’ involuntary sterilisation in a public hospital and the State’s failure to investigate and provide appropriate redress, raising issues of degrading treatment, private and family life, reproductive autonomy, effective remedy, and discrimination.

Dadiani and Machabeli v. Georgia (Application no. 8252/08) is a European Court of Human Rights Third Section judgment delivered on 12 June 2012 and final on 12 September 2012. The applicants are Georgian nationals Elene Dadiani (born 1923) and her nephew David Machabeli (born 1964), both living in Tbilisi. The first applicant’s mother was deprived of land and other assets by the Soviet authorities in the 1920s. In 2004, the applicants sued the relevant local authority seeking restitution of their ancestral lands. They relied on archival documents confirming their ancestor’s title and on general property and inheritance rules in the Civil Code, the Constitution, and international human-rights treaties ratified by Georgia.

On 31 January 2005, the Gurjaani District Court recognized the applicants as joint owners of plot no. 604 in the village of Bakurtsikhe. The local authorities did not appeal, and the judgment became binding. On 15 February 2005, their lawyer obtained the enforcement writ. On 26 October 2005, the applicants submitted the final judgment and writ to the Gurjaani Public Registry for enforcement. By letter of 2 November 2005, the registrar refused registration, stating that the documentation was incomplete: the judgment did not indicate the size or category of plot no. 604, and the lawyer was at fault. The registrar requested the lawyer’s identity document, authority form, the original enforcement writ, and a cadastral plan. The applicants claimed their lawyers visited the registry several times and explained that they could not produce an amended court decision. The registry continued to refuse registration. The judgment remains unenforced.

In a second set of proceedings, on 25 May 2005 the applicants lodged another action, on the same legal basis, claiming ownership of adjacent plot no. 646. The action was registered by the Gurjaani District Court the same day, but, according to the applicants, examination never began.

Before the Court, the applicants complained under Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the failure to enforce the 2005 judgment. They also alleged violations of Articles 6 and 13 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to the unexplained delay in the second proceedings, and a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 regarding expropriation of ancestral lands by the Soviet authorities.

The Government objected. As to the second proceedings, it argued Article 6 was inapplicable because Georgian law did not create a right to restitution for property expropriated by the Soviet authorities. The Court agreed, relying on Kiladze v. Georgia and Andronikashvili v. Georgia, and rejected that complaint as incompatible ratione materiae. As to the first proceedings, the Government argued non-exhaustion of domestic remedies: a damages claim under Civil Code Article 1005 §1, a criminal complaint under Criminal Code Article 381 for non-execution of a judicial decision, and administrative review under General Administrative Code Article 177 §3 of the 2 November 2005 letter. It also alleged the application was late under the six-month rule.

The Court found Article 6 §1 applicable to enforcement, which is an integral part of the “trial.” It held the suggested remedies inadequate: damages were not a proper alternative to enforcement; the criminal remedy could not order enforcement; and administrative review was unavailable because the General Administrative Code expressly excluded executive activities related to enforcement of final judgments. The six-month rule did not apply because non-enforcement was a continuing situation, and the 2 November 2005 letter did not terminate enforcement; the judgment remained binding and enforceable. The Article 6 §1 complaint concerning the first set of proceedings was declared admissible.

Case Dadiani and Machabeli v. Georgia (Application no. 8252/08; judgment of 12 June 2012) concerned two Georgian nationals, Elene Dadiani and David Machabeli, who sought restitution of ancestral lands. The first applicant’s mother had been deprived of land and other assets by the Soviet authorities in the 1920s. In 2004, the applicants brought an action against the relevant local authority for restitution, relying on archival documents confirming their ancestor’s title and on Georgian civil, constitutional, and international human-rights provisions.

On 31 January 2005, the Gurjaani District Court established the applicants’ joint ownership of land in the village of Bakurtsikhe, identified as plot no. 604. The local authorities did not appeal, so the judgment became final and binding. On 15 February 2005, the applicants’ lawyer obtained an enforcement writ. On 26 October 2005, the lawyer submitted a copy of the writ and the final judgment to the Gurjaani Public Registry for enforcement. By a letter of 2 November 2005, the registrar refused to register the land in the applicants’ names, stating that the documentation was incomplete. According to the registrar, the judgment did not indicate the size of plot no. 604 or whether it was agricultural or non-agricultural, and the lawyer had to submit his identity document, authority form, the original enforcement writ, and a cadastral plan of the land.

The applicants maintained that their lawyers visited the Gurjaani Public Registry repeatedly and objected to the failure to enforce the judgment. They argued that they could not produce an amended final court decision. The registry continued to refuse registration for various reasons, and the judgment of 31 January 2005 remained unenforced.

In a second set of proceedings, on 25 May 2005, the applicants lodged another action claiming ownership of plot no. 646, adjacent to plot no. 604, on the same legal basis. The action was registered by the Gurjaani District Court the same day, but, according to the applicants, examination of the case never began.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about the authorities’ failure to enforce the final domestic judgment in their favour. They also alleged violations of Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 regarding the delay in the second set of proceedings, and a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning the Soviet-era expropriation of their ancestral lands. The Government objected that Georgian law did not provide a right to restitution for property expropriated by the Soviet authorities, that domestic remedies had not been exhausted, and that the application was late.

The Court rejected the complaint concerning the second set of proceedings as incompatible ratione materiae, because Georgian law did not create a right to restitution for Soviet-era expropriations. As to the first set, the Court held that enforcement of a binding judgment is an integral part of Article 6. It dismissed the Government’s objections: a damages claim, criminal complaint, or administrative review would not have provided adequate redress, and administrative review was unavailable for enforcement of final judgments. The six-month rule did not apply because non-enforcement created a continuing situation. The complaint concerning the first set of proceedings was therefore declared admissible. The central alleged violation was the prolonged failure to enforce a final judgment granting the applicants ownership of plot no. 604.

**Case: Dadiani and Machabeli v. Georgia (Application no. 8252/08, ECtHR, 12 June 2012)**

The case concerned two Georgian nationals, Elene Dadiani and David Machabeli, an aunt and nephew. The first applicant’s mother had been deprived of her land and other assets by the Soviet authorities in the 1920s. In 2004 the applicants sued the relevant local authority seeking restitution of their ancestral lands, relying on archival documents confirming their ancestor’s title and on general property and inheritance rules in Georgian and international law.

On 31 January 2005 the Gurjaani District Court recognized the applicants as joint owners of plot no. 604 in the village of Bakurtsikhe. The local authorities did not appeal, and the judgment became binding. On 15 February 2005 the applicants’ lawyer obtained the enforcement writ. On 26 October 2005 they submitted the writ and the final judgment to the Gurjaani Public Registry for enforcement. By letter of 2 November 2005, the registrar refused to register the land in their names, saying the documents were incomplete: the judgment did not indicate the size or category of plot no. 604, and the lawyer needed to provide identity documents, authority to represent the applicants, the original enforcement writ, and a cadastral plan.

The applicants claimed that their lawyers repeatedly visited the registry and objected to the failure to enforce the judgment. They said they could not produce an amended court decision, and the registry continued to refuse registration for various reasons. The judgment of 31 January 2005 remains unenforced.

Separately, on 25 May 2005 the applicants filed another action seeking ownership of plot no. 646, adjacent to plot no. 604, on the same legal basis. The action was registered by the Gurjaani District Court the same day, but according to the applicants its examination never began.

The applicants complained under Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the authorities’ failure to enforce the first judgment. They also alleged violations of Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning the delay in the second set of proceedings and the Soviet-era expropriation of their ancestral lands.

The Government contested admissibility on several grounds. Regarding the second set of proceedings, the Court held that Georgian law did not provide a right to restitution of property expropriated by the Soviet authorities. Therefore, the complaint about delay in those proceedings was incompatible *ratione materiae* with Article 6 § 1 and had to be rejected.

Regarding the first set of proceedings, the Government argued that Article 6 did not apply, that domestic remedies had not been exhausted, and that the six-month time-limit had expired. The Court held that enforcement of a final judgment is an integral part of the “trial” for Article 6 purposes, so the provision applied. It dismissed the exhaustion objection: a damages claim would not secure registration; a criminal complaint could not directly enforce the judgment; and administrative review was unavailable because Georgian law excluded executive activities related to enforcement of final court judgments from the relevant administrative procedure. The six-month objection also failed because non-enforcement was a continuing situation and the letter of 2 November 2005 did not terminate enforcement proceedings. The Article 6 § 1 complaint concerning non-enforcement of the first judgment was therefore declared admissible.

In *Michaud v. France*, the applicant was a French lawyer and member of the Paris Bar, specialising in financial and tax law. He challenged French regulations that implemented EU anti-money-laundering directives. These directives extended obligations to independent legal professionals. France transposed them into the Monetary and Financial Code. On 12 July 2007, the National Bar Council adopted regulations imposing on all French lawyers duties of due diligence, internal procedures, and reporting suspicions when participating in specified financial or real-estate transactions—such as buying or selling property or businesses, managing client funds, opening accounts, and forming or administering companies or trusts. The rules did not apply when lawyers acted as legal counsel or in judicial proceedings. Lawyers were still required to respect professional confidentiality. Failure to comply could lead to disciplinary sanctions, including being struck off.

On 10 October 2007, the applicant asked the Conseil d’Etat to set aside the Bar Council’s decision. He argued that the Bar Council lacked regulatory power; that the undefined term “suspicions” breached Article 7 of the Convention (legal certainty); and that the reporting obligation violated lawyer-client privilege and professional confidentiality under Article 8. He requested a preliminary reference to the Court of Justice of the European Union. On 23 July 2010, the Conseil d’Etat rejected most claims. It held that “reporting suspicions” was sufficiently clear by reference to the Monetary and Financial Code and that the obligation did not excessively interfere with confidentiality, given the exceptions for judicial proceedings and legal advice and the general interest in combating money laundering. It declined to refer the matter to the CJEU.

The applicant then applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 19 January 2011, alleging a violation of Article 8. He claimed that, as a lawyer, he was required—subject to disciplinary action—to report clients who came to him for advice, which was incompatible with lawyer-client privilege and professional confidentiality. The Government argued that he was not a “victim” because the law had not been applied to him and that the application was time-barred, running from an earlier 2008 Conseil d’Etat judgment. The ECtHR declared the complaint admissible. It found that the applicant was directly affected: the Bar Council decision had the force of law and applied to all French lawyers. As a financial and tax lawyer, he was especially exposed. He faced a dilemma: comply and compromise privilege, or refuse and risk sanctions. The six-month time-limit ran from the 23 July 2010 final domestic decision, not the 2008 judgment.

On the merits, the applicant argued that the interference was not “in accordance with the law”—because “suspicions” was undefined and the activities were vaguely described—and was not “necessary in a democratic society”. He stressed that lawyer-client confidentiality was indivisible. The Government disagreed. The ECtHR examined whether the French system struck a fair balance under Article 8. It considered the limited scope of the obligation, which applied only to certain financial and real-estate activities, the exclusion of legal advice and judicial proceedings, and the procedural safeguards, including the role of the Bar Council in receiving reports. The Court ultimately found no violation of Article 8, holding that the interference was prescribed by law, pursued the legitimate aim of preventing crime, and was proportionate in the circumstances.

In *Michaud v. France* (Application no. 12323/11, judgment of 6 December 2012), the applicant, Patrick Michaud, was a French lawyer and member of the Paris Bar. He challenged French anti-money-laundering rules that imposed compliance and reporting obligations on lawyers. The rules stemmed from EU Directives 91/308/EEC, as amended by 2001/97/EC and replaced by 2005/60/EC, which extended anti-money-laundering duties to independent legal professionals when they took part in certain financial, real-estate, or corporate transactions. France transposed these obligations into the Monetary and Financial Code.

A National Bar Council decision of 12 July 2007 adopted regulations requiring all French lawyers, when carrying out covered business activities, to show due diligence, create internal procedures, adopt written rules, train staff, and set up internal monitoring to ensure compliance with the obligation to report suspicions of money laundering or terrorist financing. Lawyers remained required to respect professional confidentiality. Failure to comply could lead to disciplinary sanctions, including being struck off.

On 10 October 2007, Michaud asked the Conseil d’Etat to annul the National Bar Council decision. He argued that the Bar Council lacked regulatory power; that the term “suspicions” was undefined and violated the legal-certainty requirement; and that the obligation to report suspicions breached Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights and lawyer-client privilege. He also requested a preliminary ruling from the Court of Justice of the European Union.

By judgment of 23 July 2010, the Conseil d’Etat rejected most of his arguments. It found that “suspicions” was sufficiently defined by reference to the Monetary and Financial Code. On Article 8, it concluded that any interference with professional confidentiality was justified by the general interest in combating money laundering. It relied on safeguards excluding information obtained by lawyers in judicial proceedings or while acting as legal counsel, unless the lawyer participated in money laundering, the advice was given for money-laundering purposes, or the lawyer knew the client sought advice for that purpose.

Michaud applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 19 January 2011, alleging a violation of Article 8. The Government argued that he was not a “victim” because the rules had not been applied to him individually, and that the application was lodged out of time, since the six-month period should run from an earlier 2008 Conseil d’Etat judgment.

The Court declared the application admissible. It held that Michaud was directly affected: the National Bar Council decision had force of law, applied to all French lawyers, and exposed him to disciplinary sanctions if he did not comply. As a lawyer specialising in financial and tax law, he was particularly affected. The six-month period ran from the Conseil d’Etat’s 23 July 2010 judgment, so the application was timely.

On the merits, Michaud argued that the interference was not “in accordance with the law” because “suspicions” and the covered activities were vague, and that legal professional confidentiality was indivisible. He accepted that the measure pursued a legitimate aim but denied that it was necessary in a democratic society. He further argued that the *Bosphorus* presumption of equivalent protection did not apply because EU directives left a margin of appreciation to member States and because the CJEU had examined only fair-trial concerns, not Article 8.

The Court ultimately found no violation of Article 8. It held that the French system was in accordance with the law and necessary in a democratic society, and that adequate safeguards protected legal professional privilege.

**Case Summary: Michaud v. France (Application no. 12323/11)**

**Background and Legal Framework**
The applicant, Patrick Michaud, is a French lawyer specializing in financial and tax law and a member of the Paris Bar. The case concerns the transposition of European Union Anti-Money Laundering (AML) Directives into French law. Specifically, EU Directive 91/308/EEC, as amended by Directive 2001/97/EC and replaced by Directive 2005/60/EC, extended AML obligations beyond financial institutions to include "independent legal professionals."

These directives required lawyers, when participating in specific financial or real-estate transactions (e.g., buying/selling property, managing client funds, creating companies), to implement customer due diligence measures and report suspicious transactions to authorities. In France, these obligations were codified in the Monetary and Financial Code. To implement these statutory duties, the National Bar Council adopted a regulatory decision on 12 July 2007, establishing internal procedures for lawyers to comply with the "obligation to report suspicions" regarding money-laundering and terrorist financing.

**The Applicant's Complaint**
Michaud challenged the National Bar Council's decision before the *Conseil d'Etat* (French supreme administrative court) on 10 October 2007. He argued that the regulations exceeded the Bar Council's powers, lacked legal certainty, and violated legal professional privilege and confidentiality. He contended that compelling lawyers to report suspicions about their clients, under threat of disciplinary sanctions including being struck off, contravened Article 8 (right to respect for private life and correspondence) and Article 7 (no punishment without law) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The *Conseil d'Etat* rejected his claims on 23 July 2010. It found the term "suspicions" sufficiently defined by reference to the Monetary and Financial Code. Regarding Article 8, it held that the obligation did not constitute excessive interference with professional confidentiality, citing the general interest in combating money-laundering and the safeguard excluding information obtained in judicial proceedings or legal counsel activities (unless the lawyer is involved in money-laundering).

**Proceedings Before the European Court of Human Rights**
Michaud applied to the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) on 19 January 2011, reiterating that the reporting obligation violated Article 8. The French Government contested the application's admissibility, arguing he was not a direct "victim" as the law had not been applied to him, and that the application was lodged outside the six-month time-limit.

**Key Facts Relevant to Alleged Violations**
The crux of the alleged Article 8 violation is the mandatory "obligation to report suspicions." Lawyers are required, under threat of disciplinary action, to report transactions they suspect may be linked to money-laundering. They must also establish internal procedures to ensure compliance. The applicant, specializing in financial law, argued he was directly affected by these rules, facing a dilemma: either comply and breach client confidentiality, or refuse and face sanctions. The ECtHR found him to be a victim belonging to a class directly affected by the regulations. The application was deemed timely as it was filed within six months of the *Conseil d'Etat's* final judgment in the domestic proceedings. The core violation alleged is that the mandatory reporting duty, imposed on lawyers, interferes with the confidentiality of lawyer-client relations protected under Article 8.

**Epners-Gefners v. Latvia** (Application no. 37862/02) concerned a Latvian national, Mr Aivars Epners-Gefners. He was arrested on 1 October 1999 on suspicion of aggravated robbery. On 11 April 2002 the Kurzeme Regional Court convicted him of aggravated robbery and sentenced him to six years and one month’s imprisonment. His appeal was essentially upheld by the Supreme Court on 5 June 2002, and his cassation appeal was dismissed on 20 September 2002. He was released early under a pre-release scheme on 23 August 2004.

The applicant lodged his application on 2 October 2002. He alleged that he had not received appropriate dental treatment and that he had been unable to receive long-term family visits in detention. He also complained about the length of his pre-trial detention under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. On 17 June 2009 the Government submitted a unilateral declaration admitting that the length of his pre-trial detention had violated Article 5 § 3. The Court accepted that declaration on 25 May 2010 and struck out that part of the application. The remaining complaints concerning dental care and family visits were declared admissible, and the Government’s preliminary objection as to the scope of domestic law was joined to the merits.

As to dental care, the applicant first complained on 29 June 2000. A prison doctor prescribed Ibuprofen and advised him to consult a dentist. On 16 August 2000 he again complained of toothache and received Analgin. On 18 August 2000 a dentist found caries in one tooth, noted two missing teeth and the remains of twenty-one damaged teeth, leaving only eight healthy teeth. The applicant refused the recommended treatment. On 10 August 2001 he complained again and received Analgin. On 19 September 2001 a psychiatrist linked his headaches to dental cavity problems and advised dental consultation. On 25 October 2001 a dentist diagnosed periodontal disease, and four teeth were extracted.

On 26 November 2001 the applicant complained to the General Inspectorate that he had not received appropriate dental care and needed dental prosthetics. On 11 December 2001 the Prisons Administration replied that the extractions had been free, that he had only eight teeth left, that poor dental care before detention was presumed, and that dental prosthetics could be provided only at his own expense because no state funds were allocated for that purpose. A further complaint to the President’s Chancery led to the same response on 12 February 2002.

As to family visits, the applicant’s wife gave birth to their son on 18 May 2000. During his pre-trial detention he received only two short-term visits from his wife, on 16 November 2000 and 20 November 2001, and four short-term visits from his aunt. He was able to receive long-term visits only while serving his sentence, beginning on 5 October 2002. Until his release, he received six long-term visits from his wife, each lasting about sixteen hours.

Domestic rules for remand prisons allowed only short-term visits, generally one per month and up to one hour, with permission from the authority dealing with the criminal case. A 2009 Constitutional Court judgment found no obligation to provide long-term visits for detainees, but held that a blanket one-hour restriction on monthly short-term visits was disproportionate; it was abrogated in December 2009. Medical rules provided convicted persons with free minimum health care, including emergency dental care, but did not require free dental prosthetics.

The Court therefore examined whether the dental treatment and restrictions on long-term family visits disclosed violations of the Convention, particularly Articles 3 and 8, while the Article 5 § 3 complaint had already been resolved by the unilateral declaration.

**Case: Epners-Gefners v. Latvia** (Application no. 37862/02), European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, judgment of 29 May 2012.

The applicant, Aivars Epners-Gefners, a Latvian national born in 1964, was arrested on 1 October 1999 on suspicion of aggravated robbery. On 11 April 2002 the Kurzeme Regional Court convicted him of aggravated robbery and sentenced him to six years and one month’s imprisonment. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction on 5 June 2002, and the Senate of the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal on points of law on 20 September 2002. On 23 August 2004 he was released early under a pre-release scheme.

The applicant lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 2 October 2002. He complained that he had not received appropriate dental treatment in detention and that he had been unable to receive long-term family visits while in detention. A separate complaint concerning the length of his pre-trial detention under Article 5 § 3 was later resolved when the Latvian Government submitted a unilateral declaration admitting a violation; the Court accepted that declaration on 25 May 2010 and struck that complaint out. The remaining complaints—dental care and long-term family visits—were declared admissible, and the Government’s preliminary objection concerning the scope of domestic law was joined to the merits.

As to family visits, the applicant’s wife gave birth to their son on 18 May 2000. During his pre-trial detention in a remand prison, he received only short-term visits: two from his wife, on 16 November 2000 and 20 November 2001, and four from his aunt. Under the applicable remand-prison rules, detainees could receive only one short-term visit per month, lasting up to one hour, and only with written permission from the authority handling the criminal case. Long-term visits were not available to remand detainees. The applicant began receiving long-term visits only after he started serving his sentence, from 5 October 2002. Until his release on 23 August 2004, he received six long-term visits from his wife, each lasting about sixteen hours. His complaint therefore centred on the absence of long-term family visits during the pre-trial/remand period.

As to dental care, the applicant first complained of dental problems on 29 June 2000. A prison doctor gave him Ibuprofen and advised him to see a dentist. On 16 August 2000 he again complained of toothache and received Analgin. On 18 August 2000 a dentist found caries in one tooth and noted that the applicant had two missing teeth and the remains of twenty-one damaged teeth; only eight teeth were healthy. The applicant refused the recommended treatment. On 10 August 2001 he complained again and received pain relief. On 19 September 2001 a psychiatrist considered that his headaches were linked to dental cavities and advised him to consult a dentist. On 25 October 2001 a dentist diagnosed periodontal disease, and four teeth were extracted. On 26 November 2001 the applicant complained to the General Inspectorate that he had not received appropriate dental care and needed prosthetics. On 11 December 2001 the Prisons Administration replied that the extractions had been free, that he had eight teeth left, and that dental prosthetics could be provided only at his own expense because no state funds were allocated for that purpose. Further complaints in December 2001 and February 2002 produced the same response.

Under Cabinet Regulation no. 358 (1999), convicted persons were entitled to minimum health care free of charge, including emergency dental care, while detained persons received medical care excluding planned in-patient treatment, with acute cases only. The applicant alleged that this regime resulted in inadequate dental treatment and that the denial of long-term family visits violated his rights, principally under Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention.

Further complaints to the President’s Chancery produced the same answer on 12 February 2002. Domestic rules at the time provided free minimum health care and emergency dental care for detainees, but not planned in-patient treatment or prosthetics.

001-114085:
Paweł Pawlak, a Polish national born in 1965 and owner of a pawnshop, was arrested on 11 June 2001. He was suspected of large-scale fraud while leading an organised criminal group, extortion and threatening witnesses. The Lublin District Court remanded him in detention, relying on strong suspicion, the likelihood of a severe sentence and the risk that he would obstruct proceedings. More charges followed: aggravated fraud, attempted fraud, illegal possession of a gas gun, amphetamine possession, document forgery and corrupting a police officer. In December 2002 the prosecution filed an indictment containing twelve charges against him and eleven co-defendants. His pre-trial detention was repeatedly extended until 14 March 2006—about four years and nine months—on grounds including the severity of the charges, the complexity of the case, the organised nature of the alleged crimes and the risk of interference with witnesses. Some periods overlapped with a sentence in another case. Ultimately, several charges ended in acquittals, discontinuance or reclassification/time-barring; appellate courts criticised the investigation as relying on unreliable witnesses.

The Article 3 complaint concerned the “dangerous detainee” regime. On 1 February 2002, at the prosecutor’s request, the Radom Remand Centre classified the applicant as a dangerous detainee, citing alleged organised crime, illegal gun possession, risk of corruption and escape. He was placed in a high-security ward. He alleged he was held in a solitary cell, had only solitary walks, was subjected to body searches—including anal inspection—each time he left or entered his cell, and was shackled when escorted outside, later preventively shackled for walks, baths, visits and court. The regime was repeatedly extended. Domestic courts quashed some decisions: on 3 December 2002 and 11 December 2003, the Lublin Regional Court found the reasons inadequate or unlawful, noting that fraud/gun charges did not justify dangerous status and fears of corruption were hypothetical. Despite this, the applicant said he remained in a dangerous cell until 24 December 2003. Prison authorities later admitted that after the 11 December 2003 ruling he should have been transferred immediately to an ordinary cell. The Government disputed some claims, saying it could not establish whether he was always solitary and that CCTV was not installed in all cells or sanitary facilities.

As to Article 5 § 3, the applicant complained that his pre-trial detention was excessively long. The extensions relied on the likely severe sentence, complexity, risk of obstructing proceedings and the organised nature of the alleged group. He appealed unsuccessfully, citing the lengthy detention and deterioration of family ties.

The Article 8 complaint concerned restrictions on family contact during the dangerous-detainee regime. The applicant claimed his mother was refused visits between December 2002 and September 2003 because she was to testify, and that he received only closed visits from his wife, daughter and mother. The Government maintained that from February 2002 to December 2003 he received numerous visits, but all were conducted without direct contact and lasted 60–90 minutes. The President of the Lublin District Court justified temporary visit bans by the need to secure the proceedings, the risk of pressure on co-accused witness R.P., and the applicant’s aggressive behaviour towards R.P.; the mother’s visit was refused because she was a witness. Thus the key facts concern prolonged pre-trial detention, the harsh and repeatedly reviewed “dangerous detainee” regime (isolation, searches, shackles), and severe no-contact restrictions on family visits.

Paweł Pawlak v. Poland (Application no. 13421/03) concerned a Polish national, a pawnshop owner, arrested on 11 June 2001 on suspicion of large-scale fraud while leading an organised criminal group, extortion and threatening witnesses. He was remanded in detention on 12 June 2001. Additional charges followed, including aggravated fraud, attempted fraud, unlawful possession of a gas gun and amphetamines, document forgery, corrupting a police officer and putting forged bank notes into circulation. On 5 December 2002 the prosecution filed a bill of indictment against him and eleven co-defendants. His pre-trial detention was extended repeatedly by the Lublin District Court and Court of Appeal until he was released on 14 March 2006. The courts relied on the reasonable suspicion against him, the likelihood of a severe sentence, the risk of obstructing proceedings, witness pressure, the organised nature of the alleged crimes and the complexity of the case. The Government noted that during two periods he was serving a prison term imposed in another case. He alleged that the length of his pre-trial detention violated Article 5 § 3.

The main Article 3 complaint concerned the “dangerous detainee” regime. On 31 January 2002 the prosecutor asked the Radom Remand Centre to classify the applicant as dangerous. On 1 February 2002 the Penitentiary Commission did so, relying on charges of leading a criminal gang and unlawful possession of a gun, plus risks that he would corrupt prison or justice officials or attempt to escape. Under the 1998 Ordinance, dangerous detainees were held in special high-security wards or cells, subjected to a personal check each time they left or entered the cell, had their cells searched more often, took segregated one-hour outdoor walks, and were shackled when escorted outside. The applicant alleged that he was held in a solitary cell, constantly monitored by CCTV, and subjected to humiliating body searches including anal inspection. The Government disputed some details but confirmed that all visits were non-contact.

The regime was repeatedly extended. Courts quashed some decisions: on 3 December 2002 and 11 December 2003, finding insufficient reasons or no factual basis. In December 2003 the Lublin Regional Court stated that the charges did not warrant classifying him as posing a serious danger to society or prison security, and that his personal file showed rewards and only a minor disciplinary warning. Nevertheless, he remained in a dangerous-detainee cell after the quashing decisions—until 12 December 2002 and until 24 December 2003—and prison authorities later admitted an erroneous application of the rules. The regime finally ended on 24 December 2003.

As to Article 8, the applicant alleged severe restrictions on family contact during the regime. His mother was refused visits between December 2002 and 1 September 2003 because she was to testify as a witness. He claimed he received only closed visits from his wife, daughter and mother. The Government submitted that numerous visits took place, each lasting 60 minutes except one lasting 90 minutes, but all without direct contact. The President of the Lublin District Court justified a temporary ban by the need to secure the proceedings and the risk of pressure on a co-accused, R.P., referring also to the applicant’s aggressive behaviour towards R.P. at a hearing.

Later criminal proceedings produced mixed results: convictions for forged bank notes, unlawful possession of a gas gun, amphetamines and coal-mine fraud, but acquittals in 2007 for corrupting a police officer based on unreliable witnesses P.K. and R.P. The appellate court criticised the prosecution’s investigation as grossly violating objective evidence assessment. In 2010 he was acquitted of attempted fraud and related charges; in 2011 the extortion and witness-threat charges were discontinued or became time-barred, and he was acquitted of one fraud charge. These facts were relevant to the alleged unreasonableness of his detention and dangerous classification.

Paweł Pawlak v. Poland (no. 13421/03) concerned a Polish national, born in 1965, who owned a pawnshop in Lublin. He was arrested on 11 June 2001 on suspicion of large-scale fraud while allegedly leading an organised criminal group, as well as extortion and threatening witnesses. He was remanded in custody on 12 June 2001. Additional charges followed, including aggravated fraud, attempted fraud, unlawful possession of a gas gun and amphetamines, document forgery, corrupting a police officer, and putting forged bank notes into circulation. His pre-trial detention was repeatedly extended on grounds including the likely severe sentence, risk of obstructing proceedings, influencing witnesses, and case complexity. He remained in detention until 14 March 2006. Ultimately, many charges were discontinued, time-barred, or resulted in acquittal; the charge of leading an organised group was discontinued because it was not a crime under the old Criminal Code then applicable. Some convictions for fraud, weapons, drugs, and forged bank notes were upheld, but later courts criticised the investigation, particularly reliance on unreliable witnesses P.K. and R.P., one of whom had made false allegations. This protracted detention formed the basis of the applicant’s Article 5 § 3 complaint.

The main Article 3 complaint concerned the “dangerous detainee” regime. Initially held in Lublin Remand Centre with increased protection, he was transferred to Radom Remand Centre. On 31 January 2002, the Organised Crime Department of the Lublin Regional Prosecutor’s Office requested that he be classified as a dangerous detainee, citing charges of leading a criminal gang and unlawful gun possession, plus risks that he would corrupt prison or justice officials or attempt to escape. On 1 February 2002 the Radom Penitentiary Commission classified him as a “dangerous detainee.” The regime involved placement in a high-security or solitary cell, hand and foot shackles when escorted outside, solitary walks, frequent cell searches, and personal checks—including anal inspection—each time he left or entered his cell. He alleged constant CCTV monitoring of cells and sanitary facilities; the Government disputed this, stating only Radom had CCTV and sanitary facilities were not monitored. Cultural and educational activities were severely limited; he could read, listen to prison radio, and play board games. The regime was periodically extended. Some decisions were quashed by courts for lack of factual reasons or unlawful application, yet he reportedly remained in dangerous-detainee cells after such rulings until administrative correction. The regime was formally lifted on 24 December 2003. Before 1 September 2003 it was governed by the 1998 Ordinance; afterwards by Articles 212a–212b of the Code of Execution of Criminal Sentences. CPT reports criticised the regime for absence of organised activities, lack of human contact, routine handcuffing as disproportionate and punitive, and lack of physical contact during family visits.

The Article 8 complaint concerned restrictions on family contact during the dangerous-detainee regime. The applicant claimed his mother was refused visits between December 2002 and 1 September 2003 because she was to testify at his trial. He stated he received only closed visits from his wife, daughter, and mother, without direct contact. Government records showed numerous visits—for example, from his mother on 22 March and 28 December 2002 and 1 September 2003, and from his wife and daughter on several dates—but all were conducted so as to prevent direct contact. Authorities justified temporary refusals by the need to secure the proper conduct of proceedings, the risk of pressure being exerted through third parties on co-accused R.P., and the applicant’s aggressive behaviour toward R.P. at a hearing on 11 July 2003. The case therefore centred on whether the prolonged “dangerous detainee” conditions amounted to inhuman or degrading treatment under Article 3, whether the pre-trial detention exceeded a reasonable time under Article 5 § 3, and whether the visit restrictions breached Article 8.

**Case: Tonov and Others v. Bulgaria (Application no. 48704/07), ECtHR, 30 October 2012**

The applicants were three Bulgarian nationals: Iliya Tonov, Vatka Udvareva, and Pena Karalakova. The case concerned the loss of a flat in Sofia after a restitution claim under Bulgaria’s Restitution Law.

In 1968, the second applicant, Ms Udvareva, and her husband bought a 97-square-metre flat from the Sofia municipality. The flat had previously become State property through the nationalisations carried out by the communist regime after 1947. In March 1998, after the time-limit under section 7 of the Restitution Law had been renewed, the pre-nationalisation owner sued Udvareva and her husband, seeking to have their title declared null and void. While the proceedings were pending, Udvareva’s husband died. His grandson, Mr Tonov, inherited his share, so Tonov and Udvareva each owned one half of the flat, and Tonov joined the civil proceedings.

On 23 April 2007, the Supreme Court of Cassation gave a final judgment declaring Udvareva and Tonov’s title null and void ab initio. The domestic courts found that the 1968 sale had been flawed because a document related to it had not been signed by the municipality official in whom the relevant power was vested. Udvareva, who had been living alone in the flat, later vacated it. On 20 September 2007, Udvareva and Tonov requested compensation bonds, but their request was rejected because it had not been made within two months of the final judgment, as required by domestic law.

The applicants complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Articles 6 § 1, 13, and 14 of the Convention that they had been arbitrarily deprived of their property, following unfair judicial proceedings and without adequate compensation. The Court decided to examine the complaint solely under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The Government argued that the applicants had failed to exhaust domestic remedies because they had not sought municipal housing or permission to buy a flat at a regulated price. The Government also argued that the deprivation was not arbitrary and that compensation bonds could have provided adequate compensation. The Court rejected the non-exhaustion objection. It found that municipal tenancy could not amount to adequate compensation and that regulated-price purchase was not a remedy designed for the applicants’ situation. However, the third applicant, Ms Karalakova, was not an owner of the disputed flat and was not affected by the events, so her application was inadmissible ratione personae. The complaint of Tonov and Udvareva was declared admissible.

On the merits, the Court accepted that the Restitution Law pursued an important public interest aim: restoring justice after the totalitarian regime. However, the interference was not proportionate. The action against Udvareva and her husband was not brought within the initial one-year time-limit after the 1992 Restitution Law, but only in March 1998 after the time-limit had been renewed. Under Velikovi and Others v. Bulgaria, section 7 measures could be proportionate only as an exceptional transitional step of short duration. In Tsonkovi and Georgieva, the Court had held that belated actions after the renewal departed from the transitional nature of restitution legislation and from legal certainty. Therefore, nothing short of compensation reasonably related to the market value of the lost flat could maintain a fair balance under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Tonov and Udvareva had not received such compensation, and the Government had not shown that the bonds scheme would have provided it with sufficient clarity and certainty.

The Court therefore found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 in respect of Mr Tonov and Ms Udvareva. The key violation arose from the retroactive nullification of a long-held property title through a belated restitution claim, combined with the failure to provide compensation reasonably related to the flat’s market value.

Tonov and Others v. Bulgaria (Application no. 48704/07, judgment of 30 October 2012) concerned three Bulgarian nationals. The third applicant, Ms Karalakova, was not an owner of the disputed flat and was held inadmissible ratione personae. The relevant applicants were Mr Tonov and Ms Udvareva.

In 1968 Ms Udvareva and her husband bought a 97-square-metre flat in Sofia from the Sofia municipality. The flat had become State property through communist-era nationalisations after 1947. In March 1998, after the time-limit for claims under section 7 of the Restitution Law had been renewed, the pre-nationalisation owner sued Ms Udvareva and her husband, seeking to have their title declared null and void. During the proceedings, Ms Udvareva’s husband died. His grandson, Mr Tonov, inherited his share, so Tonov and Udvareva each owned half of the flat; Tonov joined the civil proceedings. On 23 April 2007 the Supreme Court of Cassation finally declared their title null and void ab initio. The domestic courts found that the 1968 sale was flawed because a related document had not been signed by the municipality official vested with the relevant power. Ms Udvareva subsequently vacated the flat.

On 20 September 2007 Tonov and Udvareva requested compensation bonds. Their request was rejected because it was made outside the two-month period following the final judgment. The applicants complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Articles 6, 13 and 14 that they had been arbitrarily deprived of their property after unfair proceedings and without adequate compensation. The Court examined the complaint solely under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The Government argued non-exhaustion: the applicants had not sought municipal housing or purchase at a regulated price, and the deprivation was lawful with bonds available as compensation. The Court rejected this objection. It found that municipal tenancy or regulated-price purchase might alleviate the situation but did not amount to adequate compensation for the lost property and was not a remedy designed for this situation.

On the merits, the Court noted the case concerned the same restitution legislation considered in Velikovi and Others. The interference pursued a legitimate public-interest aim: restoring justice and respect for the rule of law after the totalitarian regime. However, the proportionality question was decisive. The action against Udvareva and her husband was not brought within the initial one-year time-limit after the 1992 Restitution Law, but in March 1998, after the limit had been renewed. Under Velikovi, section 7 measures allowing challenges to decades-old property titles could be proportionate only as an exceptional transitional step of short duration. In Tsonkovi and Georgieva and Mukareva, similar late claims after the expiry and renewal of the initial time-limit were found to depart from the transitional nature of restitution legislation and from legal certainty. Such interferences could not fall within the legitimate aims of the restitution legislation. Nothing short of compensation reasonably related to the market value of the lost flats could maintain a fair balance.

The Court applied that approach: the interference with Tonov and Udvareva’s property rights disregarded legal certainty, and only market-value-related compensation could restore the required fair balance. They had not received such compensation, and the Government had not shown that the bonds scheme secured it with sufficient clarity and certainty. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In *Tonov and Others v. Bulgaria* (Application no. 48704/07), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint by three Bulgarian nationals: Mr Iliya Tonov, Ms Vatka Udvareva, and Ms Pena Karalakova. The case concerned a 97-square-metre flat in Sofia. In 1968, Ms Udvareva and her husband purchased the flat from Sofia municipality. The flat had earlier become State property through the nationalisations carried out by Bulgaria’s communist regime after 1947.

In March 1998, after the time-limit under section 7 of the Restitution Law had been renewed, the pre-nationalisation owner sued Ms Udvareva and her husband, seeking a declaration that their title was null and void. During the proceedings, Ms Udvareva’s husband died. His grandson, Mr Tonov, inherited his share, so Mr Tonov and Ms Udvareva each owned half the flat, and Mr Tonov joined the civil proceedings. The proceedings ended with a final judgment of the Supreme Court of Cassation on 23 April 2007. The domestic courts found that Ms Udvareva’s and Mr Tonov’s title was null and void *ab initio* because the 1968 sale had been flawed: a related document had not been signed by the municipality official vested with the relevant power. Ms Udvareva, then living alone in the flat, later vacated it.

On 20 September 2007, Ms Udvareva and Mr Tonov requested compensation bonds. Their request was dismissed because it had not been made within two months of the Supreme Court of Cassation’s final judgment, as required by domestic law.

The applicants complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Articles 6 § 1, 13, and 14 of the Convention that they had been deprived of their property arbitrarily, through unfair judicial proceedings, and without adequate compensation. The Court decided to examine the complaint solely under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, which protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions and permits deprivation only in the public interest and subject to law.

The Government argued that the applicants had failed to exhaust domestic remedies because they had not sought municipal housing or the right to buy a flat at a regulated price. It also argued that the deprivation was not arbitrary, that the restitution rules balanced competing interests, and that compensation bonds could provide adequate compensation. The Court rejected the non-exhaustion objection in respect of Mr Tonov and Ms Udvareva, finding that municipal tenancy or regulated purchase did not amount to adequate compensation or a remedy for their grievance. As for Ms Karalakova, the Court found that she was not an owner of the flat and was not affected by the events, so her application was incompatible *ratione personae* and inadmissible.

On the merits, the Court noted that the case concerned the same legislation and issues as *Velikovi and Others v. Bulgaria*. The interference was based on the Restitution Law, which pursued an important public interest: restoring justice and respect for the rule of law after the totalitarian regime. However, the Court found a proportionality problem. The action was not brought within the initial one-year time-limit after the 1992 Restitution Law, but in March 1998, after the time-limit had been renewed. Under *Velikovi*, section 7 measures allowing challenges to decades-old property titles could be proportionate only as an exceptional transitional step of short duration. In similar cases such as *Tsonkovi* and *Georgieva and Mukareva*, the Court held that actions brought after the initial time-limit and its 1997 renewal departed from the transitional nature of restitution legislation and violated legal certainty. Nothing short of compensation reasonably related to the market value of the lost flat could maintain a fair balance under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

Applying that approach, the Court found that the interference with Mr Tonov’s and Ms Udvareva’s property rights disregarded legal certainty. They had not received compensation reasonably related to the market value of their flat, and the Government had not shown that the bonds scheme would have provided such compensation with sufficient clarity and certainty. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.
