**Standard Verlags GmbH v. Austria (No. 3)** (Application no. 34702/07) concerned an alleged violation of Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights, protecting freedom of expression. The applicant company owns the Vienna daily newspaper *Der Standard*.

On 4 April 2006, *Der Standard* published an article in its economics section about an investigation into massive speculative losses at Hypo Alpe-Adria Bank. The headline stated that “Haider’s Hypo” was now also facing criminal investigation. The article reported that the Klagenfurt public prosecutor’s office had opened an investigation into suspected embezzlement by senior Hypo managers; that Jörg Haider had criticised the judicial authorities as overzealous and politically motivated; and that losses of approximately EUR 328 million from swap deals had previously been blamed on Christian Rauscher, the head of the bank’s treasury department and son of a former SPÖ regional government member responsible for finance. It stated that Rauscher had not been dismissed in 2004 but demoted and transferred, and was relieved of duties only after the losses became known. The article also described the roles of other bank officials, auditors, and related companies.

Rauscher brought proceedings against the applicant under section 7a of the Austrian Media Act, which permits damages where a medium discloses details likely to reveal the identity of a person suspected or convicted of a punishable offence, if the person’s legitimate interests are injured and there is no predominant public interest in disclosure due to the person’s position in society, connection with public life, or other reasons. Rauscher argued that he was not a public figure, that his bank position did not justify naming him, that disclosure harmed his professional advancement, and that he had acted under instructions and supervision. The applicant argued that the article portrayed him as a scapegoat rather than as responsible, that he had held a leading position, and that his father’s political role created a public connection. It also claimed the reporting was neutral.

The Vienna Regional Criminal Court dismissed Rauscher’s action. It found that he had headed the treasury department when the losses occurred, had authority over foreign-currency transactions, and was answerable only to the executive board. Although he was not a public figure, there was a sufficient connection with public life because the Land of Carinthia owned 45% of the bank and taxpayers bore a substantial share of the losses. The court held that the public had an overriding interest in knowing who was responsible.

The Vienna Court of Appeal reversed, ordering the applicant to pay EUR 5,000 in compensation and costs. It agreed that Rauscher had been presented as a suspect in a large-scale embezzlement. Applying a strict standard, it found that the public had no general right to know his identity. At the time of publication, the investigation was at an early stage, no proceedings had been brought against Rauscher, and the accusations were only rumours from senior bank officials. Naming him had no independent informative value; it served mainly to connect him with his father and create a sensational story. Given the vague suspicion, negative consequences, and wide circulation of *Der Standard*, compensation was appropriate.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the Court of Appeal’s judgment violated its Article 10 rights. The ECtHR declared the application admissible and examined whether the interference was prescribed by law and necessary in a democratic society for protecting the reputation or rights of others. The central issue was whether Austria had struck a fair balance between press freedom and the public interest in reporting an economic scandal, on the one hand, and Rauscher’s privacy and presumption of innocence, on the other. The Court ultimately found a violation of Article 10.

**Standard Verlags GmbH v. Austria (No. 3)** (Application no. 34702/07), a First Section European Court of Human Rights judgment of 10 January 2012, concerned an alleged violation of Article 10 (freedom of expression). The applicant company, based in Vienna, owned the daily newspaper *Der Standard*. It complained that an Austrian court order requiring it to pay compensation for revealing a person’s identity in a news article breached its right to freedom of expression.

The relevant facts began on 4 April 2006, when *Der Standard* published an economics article titled “Haider’s Hypo now also facing criminal investigation.” The article reported that the Klagenfurt public prosecutor’s office had opened an investigation into suspected embezzlement at Hypo Alpe-Adria Bank following massive speculative losses from swap deals, estimated at EUR 288–328 million. It named Christian Rauscher, the former head of the bank’s treasury department, stating that Hypo executives and Jörg Haider had previously blamed him for the losses. The article noted that Rauscher was the son of a former SPÖ regional government member responsible for finance, that he had been demoted and transferred in 2004 rather than dismissed, and that he had been relieved of his duties only after the losses became known. It also discussed the bank’s ownership structure, supervisory board, and auditing issues.

Rauscher sued the applicant company under section 7a of the Austrian Media Act, which allows damages where a medium discloses the identity of a person suspected of a punishable offence and the person’s legitimate interests are injured, unless there is a predominant public interest in publication. Rauscher argued that he was not a public figure, that his role did not justify naming him, and that publication harmed his professional advancement. The applicant company contended that the article did not portray him as solely responsible but rather as a “scapegoat,” and that the public interest in identifying a senior bank official responsible for huge losses—especially given the bank’s partial state ownership and Rauscher’s political family connection—outweighed his privacy interest.

The Vienna Regional Criminal Court dismissed Rauscher’s claim. It accepted that he was not a public figure but found an overriding public interest in disclosing his name because the Land of Carinthia owned 45% of the bank, taxpayers bore a share of the losses, and Rauscher had headed the treasury department responsible for the transactions. On appeal, however, the Vienna Court of Appeal reversed on 14 February 2007, ordering the applicant company to pay EUR 5,000 in compensation plus costs. It held that the article had presented Rauscher as a suspect of embezzlement; that the public interest in reporting a crime did not by itself justify naming him; that the investigation was at an early stage and no proceedings had been brought against him; and that disclosure of his name had little informative value and mainly served to create a sensational story by linking him to his father. The court found the negative consequences for Rauscher and the newspaper’s wide circulation justified compensation.

The applicant company complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 10. It alleged that the Austrian courts’ order was an unjustified interference with its freedom of expression. The Government contested the claim. The Court declared the application admissible and examined whether the interference was prescribed by law, pursued a legitimate aim, and was necessary in a democratic society. Weighing the public interest in reporting the scandal against Rauscher’s reputation and privacy rights, and considering the early stage of the criminal investigation, the limited informational value of naming him, and the modest compensation award, the Court ultimately found **no violation of Article 10**, holding that the Austrian courts had struck a fair balance within the State’s margin of appreciation.

Standard Verlags GmbH v. Austria (No. 3) (Application no. 34702/07), decided by the European Court of Human Rights on 10 January 2012, concerned an alleged violation of Article 10 freedom of expression. The applicant company owns the Vienna daily newspaper Der Standard.

On 4 April 2006, Der Standard published an economics article entitled “Haider’s Hypo now also facing criminal investigation.” The article reported that, following a Financial Market Authority audit, the Klagenfurt public prosecutor’s office had opened an investigation into suspected embezzlement by senior managers at Hypo Alpe-Adria Bank. It described massive speculative losses of approximately EUR 328 million from swap deals and mentioned political reactions, including Jörg Haider’s criticism of the “judicial authorities’ overzealousness.” The article named Christian Rauscher, head of the bank’s treasury department, as the person previously blamed by Hypo’s executive board and Haider for the losses. It noted that Rauscher was the son of a former SPÖ regional government member responsible for finance, that he had been demoted and transferred rather than dismissed in 2004, and that he was relieved only after the losses became known. It also discussed the bank’s supervisory and audit arrangements and its interest in Bank Burgenland.

Rauscher sued the applicant company under section 7a of the Media Act. That provision allows damages where a medium publishes details liable to disclose the identity of a person suspected of a punishable offence, if the person’s legitimate interests are injured and there is no predominant public interest in disclosure based on the person’s position in society or another connection with public life. Rauscher argued that he was not a public figure, that his position at the bank did not justify naming him, that he had acted under instructions and supervision, and that publication of his name harmed his professional advancement and was not justified by public interest.

The Vienna Regional Criminal Court dismissed the action. It found that Rauscher had headed the treasury department, had authority over foreign currency transactions, and had been responsible for the department that incurred the losses. Although he was not a public figure, the court found a public-life connection: the Land of Carinthia owned 45% of the bank, so taxpayers bore a share of the losses, and the public had an overriding interest in identifying those responsible. The court therefore held that naming Rauscher was justified.

On 14 February 2007, the Vienna Court of Appeal reversed. It agreed the article presented Rauscher as suspected of embezzling a large sum, but found the Regional Court had wrongly weighed the interests. It held that public interest must be assessed objectively and with reference to the person’s identity; general interest in reporting crime was insufficient. At the time of publication, the investigation was at an early stage, no proceedings had been brought against Rauscher,

Vikulov and Others v. Latvia (Application no. 16870/03) concerned three Russian nationals—Sergey Vikulov, his wife Galina, and their son Anton—who were detained and deported from Latvia in September 2003. They complained under Article 3 (inhuman/degrading treatment), Article 5 § 1(f) (detention pending deportation), and Article 8 (private and family life) about their detention in Rīga and Olaine.

The first applicant had been a Soviet army officer responsible for supervising the Soviet radar station at Skrunda. He and his wife entered the Latvian SSR in 1985. After Latvia regained independence and Russia assumed jurisdiction over former Soviet forces, the applicants became Russian citizens. In 1994, Latvia and Russia signed treaties on the withdrawal of Russian armed forces and the Skrunda radar station. The first applicant was demobilised in November 1998, and the family’s service visas expired on 30 November 1998.

In October 1998, the applicants applied for residence permits, relying on family ties and the son’s schooling. In April 1999, the Office of Citizenship and Migration Affairs refused, stating that they had entered Latvia due to military service and had no legal basis for permanent residence. Appeals failed. In May 2000, the authorities ordered them to leave by 12 June 2000 and imposed a five-year re-entry ban. National courts upheld this, finally on 19 February 2003. The deadline was later extended to 15 June 2003 so the son could finish the school year.

On 3 September 2003, Border Guard officers arrested the applicants while executing the leave orders under section 51(1)(1) of the Immigration Law. The applicants refused to sign the arrest records because they were in Latvian, which they claimed not to understand. They were placed in the State Border Guard Service detention unit in Rīga. On 8 September 2003, the Office of Citizenship and Migration Affairs ordered their deportation under section 47; the decision was not appealable. On 12 September, a court extended their detention until 19 September, noting that at arrest they had no identity documents and, according to their Russian passports, no lawful basis to reside in Latvia. They were transferred to the Olaine accommodation centre from 12 to 15 September, then returned to Rīga, and deported to Russia on 17 September 2003.

The applicants alleged that the Rīga cell was small, dirty, poorly ventilated, foul-smelling due to the lavatory, lit 24 hours a day, and that they had only two 10–15 minute outside walks during fourteen days. They complained of poor and insufficient food, mouldy potatoes, ants, limited family visits, and no opportunity to collect belongings before deportation. They also alleged that other detainees were placed in their family cell—a woman for about 24 hours, and later a man, forcing the first applicant to sleep on the floor. At Olaine, they alleged similarly poor conditions, dirty cells, graffiti, high fencing, and inadequate food. They further complained of insufficient medical assistance; the second applicant suffered heart attacks on the deportation day, received injections, but an ambulance reportedly concluded she had not had a heart attack. They described a five-hour trip in a stuffy minivan without food.

The Government disputed many allegations. Documents showed the Rīga cell measured 14.6 sq. m, the window was at least 0.8 m wide, and the lavatory was separated by a brick partition 1.2 m high. Pest control was monthly; visits and parcels were authorised; officers offered to take the applicants to collect documents, but they refused; and the first applicant executed a notary power of attorney on 16 September. Medical records showed the second applicant received treatment for headaches, neuralgia, and tachycardia on 15–17 September.

The Court found the cell size and furnishings compatible with Article 3, ventilation likely functioning, and no organised walks but not severe enough for Article 3. It found family unity was largely preserved and temporary placements were not intended to humiliate. It considered the Article 8 privacy complaint under Article 3. The provided text does not include the final judgment outcome.

Vikulov and Others v. Latvia (Application no. 16870/03) is a European Court of Human Rights case concerning three Russian nationals—Sergey, Galina, and Anton Vikulov—who were detained and deported from Latvia in 2003. The applicants alleged violations of Article 3, Article 5 § 1(f), and Article 8 of the Convention, focusing on their detention in Rīga and Olaine.

Sergey Vikulov had been a Soviet army officer responsible for supervising the Skrunda radar station. The family entered the Latvian SSR in 1985 and remained after Latvia regained independence and Russian forces withdrew. After their 1998 request for residence permits was refused, Latvian authorities ordered them to leave by 12 June 2000 and imposed a five-year re-entry ban. Appeals were exhausted by February 2003. The deadline was later extended to 15 June 2003 to allow their son to finish the school year.

On 3 September 2003, while executing the leave orders, State Border Guard officers arrested the applicants and placed them in the State Border Guard Service detention unit for illegal immigrants in Rīga. The arrest records relied on the Immigration Law; the applicants refused to sign them because they were in Latvian. On 8 September 2003, the Office of Citizenship and Migration Affairs ordered their deportation under section 47(1)(1), and the decision was not appealable. On 12 September, a district court extended detention until 19 September. From 12 to 15 September they were held at the Olaine accommodation centre for foreign detainees, then returned to Rīga. On 17 September 2003 they were deported to Russia.

The applicants’ main complaints concerned the lawfulness and conditions of detention, medical assistance, and privacy/family life. They alleged that the Rīga cell was small, dirty, foul-smelling, poorly ventilated, with sanitary facilities inadequately separated, 24-hour lighting, and only two 10–15 minute outdoor walks. They complained of poor and sometimes mouldy food, ants, limited family visits, and being prevented from collecting belongings. They also alleged that other detainees were placed in their family cell—a woman for up to two days and a man before deportation—violating their privacy. The second applicant claimed heart problems and inadequate medical care, including during transport to the border. At Olaine, they described dirty cells with graffiti, grilles, high fences, and self-cooking with limited facilities.

The Government disputed much of this. Inventory documents showed the Rīga cell measured 14.6 sq m, with a window at least 0.8 m wide and a brick partition at least 1.2 m high. Pest-control inspections were monthly. Records showed authorized family visits and parcels, and medical treatment given to the second applicant on 15, 16, and 17 September. The Court partly accepted the Government’s records. It found the cell size and furnishings not incompatible with Article 3, ventilation at least partly functioning, and no evidence of deliberately humiliating placement of other detainees; such placements lasted less than 24 hours. Although no organized outdoor walks were provided, the Court considered this shortcoming did not reach Article 3 severity in the circumstances. Some allegations, including restrictions on collecting belongings, were not established beyond reasonable doubt. The Court assessed all circumstances together under Article 3, including the Article 8 privacy complaint. The Russian Government intervened as a third party. The application had been partly declared admissible on 31 August 2006, and the Government’s non-exhaustion objection was dismissed.

In Sarkizov and Others v. Bulgaria, four Bulgarian nationals complained under Article 6 §§1 and 3(d) that their conviction for sexual procurement was based decisively on anonymous witness testimony and that they could not effectively examine their accusers. The second and fourth applicants also complained about post-release travel bans and lack of effective remedies under Articles 8 and 13 and Article 2 §§2–3 of Protocol No. 4.

The investigation began in October 2004. Four non-anonymous witnesses were questioned before a judge without the applicants or their lawyers present. The authorities later granted anonymity to three witnesses (nos. 15, 16 and 17). Witnesses 15 and 16 testified that the third and fourth applicants had induced them into prostitution, arranged travel abroad and received money; witness 17 implicated the first, second and fourth applicants. They were questioned before a judge. Immediately afterward, the records were shown to the applicants and their lawyers, who were invited to ask questions but stated in writing that they had none. Some applicants attended witness 17’s interview but again declined to question her.

At trial, the anonymous witnesses repeatedly failed to appear; some were reported abroad or could not be found. The applicants’ lawyers asked the court to locate and question them. The court ordered efforts to secure their attendance, but in March 2006 read out and admitted their pre-trial statements. The District Court convicted the applicants, imposing imprisonment and fines. It relied on the victims’ statements but found them corroborated by other evidence: other witness testimony, international money-transfer reports, border-control records and secret surveillance material. The Regional Court upheld the conviction and refused to question the anonymous witnesses. The Supreme Court of Cassation later refused reopening, noting the applicants had been offered but declined the chance to question the anonymous witnesses and that their testimony was not sole or decisive.

Regarding travel bans, the second applicant was released in April 2007 and in June 2007 was prohibited from leaving Bulgaria pending rehabilitation. The fourth applicant received a similar ban in April 2008. Both appealed unsuccessfully. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld the bans, reasoning that they were lawful for convicted persons pending rehabilitation and, for the fourth applicant, that the administrative assessment was not subject to judicial control and no reasons were required. The bans would have lasted until rehabilitation, but were cancelled by a 2009 amendment effective July 2010.

Before the European Court, the Government argued the applicants had been given the opportunity to question the anonymous witnesses at the pre-trial stage but refused, and that the conviction was supported by other evidence. The applicants argued anonymity was unnecessary because they knew the witnesses’ identities and that authorities failed to secure their trial attendance. The Court found the Article 6 complaint admissible. Applying Al-Khawaja and Tahery, it accepted that anonymity was reasonably justified by fear of reprisals, that the applicants had waived their right to question the witnesses by expressly declining to do so, and that the conviction was not based solely or decisively on anonymous testimony. It also found the domestic courts made reasonable efforts to locate the witnesses.

In *Sarkizov and Others v. Bulgaria*, four Bulgarian nationals complained under Article 6 §§1 and 3(d) that their convictions for sexual procurement were based to a decisive extent on anonymous witness testimony and that their defence rights were unfairly restricted. The second and fourth applicants also challenged post-release travel bans under Articles 8 and 13 and Article 2 §§2–3 of Protocol No. 4.

The investigation began in October 2004. Prosecutors alleged the applicants induced, procured or transported several women, including three anonymous witnesses (nos. 15–17), into prostitution in Bulgaria and abroad. The anonymous witnesses were questioned before a judge at the pre-trial stage. Afterwards, the applicants and their lawyers were shown the records and given the opportunity to put questions. They expressly stated they had no questions for those witnesses. At trial, the anonymous witnesses did not appear. The prosecution reported that two were abroad and one could not be found. The applicants asked the court to locate and question them and disputed the continued need for anonymity. The domestic courts found the reasons for anonymity persisted, made efforts to summon the witnesses, and when they remained absent read their pre-trial statements into evidence. Prior testimony of other absent witnesses, including some questioned before a judge, was also read.

In March 2006 the District Court convicted the applicants of inducing or procuring prostitution. It relied on the anonymous statements but also on other evidence: witness testimony, international money-transfer reports, border-control records, and secret-surveillance material. The Regional Court upheld the conviction in July 2006. The Supreme Court of Cassation later refused reopening, finding no procedural breach and that the anonymous testimony was not the sole or decisive evidence.

Before the ECtHR, the Government argued the applicants had waived their right to question the anonymous witnesses by declining to ask questions at the pre-trial stage, and that anonymity was necessary to protect victims. The applicants argued anonymity was unnecessary because they already knew the witnesses’ identities and that authorities failed to secure their trial attendance to avoid changed testimony. Applying *Al-Khawaja and Tahery*, the Court found the Article 6 complaint admissible but concluded the proceedings were fair: the witnesses had been questioned before a judge, the defence had an opportunity to question them and declined, the conviction was corroborated by substantial other evidence, and the domestic courts had made reasonable efforts to secure attendance.

As to the travel bans, the second applicant was conditionally released in April 2007 and in June 2007 was prohibited from leaving Bulgaria pending rehabilitation. The fourth applicant was similarly banned in April 2008 after release. Both appealed. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld the bans; for the fourth applicant it held that the administrative assessment was not subject to judicial control and that no reasons needed to be given. The bans were tied to rehabilitation and would have lasted until about October 2010 or 2011, but a 2009 amendment ended such bans from July 2010. The applicants alleged these restrictions violated their freedom of movement and lacked effective domestic remedies.

**Summary of Sarkizov and Others v. Bulgaria (Apps. nos. 37981/06, 38022/06, 39122/06, 44278/06)**

The case originated in four applications lodged against Bulgaria by four Bulgarian nationals (Mr Sarkizov, Mr Vasilev, Mr Petkov, and Mr Marinkov) between August and September 2006. The applicants alleged violations of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (d) of the Convention concerning anonymous witness testimony, and the second and fourth applicants additionally alleged violations of Articles 8 and 13 and Article 2 §§ 2 and 3 of Protocol No. 4 regarding unjustified travel bans.

**Criminal Proceedings**

On 12 October 2004, a preliminary investigation was opened against the applicants for sexual procurement. Between 13 and 18 October 2004, four witnesses (Mr Zh.M., Mr N.P., Ms R.M., and Ms D.M.) were questioned before a judge without the applicants or their lawyers present. Subsequently, the prosecution decided to keep the identities of three other witnesses (nos. 15, 16, and 17) secret.

Witness no. 15 stated that the third applicant had taken her to a hotel room where a man paid to have sex with her while she was underage, and that the third and fourth applicants later suggested she work for them as a prostitute. Witness no. 16 stated that the fourth applicant contacted her about working as a prostitute and that the first, second, and fourth applicants arranged her travel abroad to Denmark and France. Witness no. 17 stated that she accepted work as a prostitute for the first, second, and fourth applicants, who arranged her travel to Denmark, Norway, and France.

Witnesses nos. 15 and 16 were questioned before a judge who verified their identities. Immediately after the interviews, the records were presented to the applicants and their lawyers, who were given the opportunity to put questions. They stated in writing that they had no questions. Witness no. 17 was questioned before a judge with the first, second, and fourth applicants and some lawyers participating; they also expressly stated they had no questions.

**Trial and Conviction**

At trial, the anonymous witnesses did not appear. The District Court read out and admitted their pre-trial statements, along with those of other absent witnesses. On 28 March 2006, the District Court convicted the applicants of inducing, procuring, or transporting the anonymous witnesses and other women into prostitution. The court found the victims' statements were corroborated by other evidence, including international money transfer reports, border control records, secret surveillance information, and other witness statements. The Regional Court upheld the convictions on 17 July 2006.

**Travel Bans**

After release from prison, the second applicant (on 4 June 2007) and fourth applicant (on 7 April 2008) were prohibited from leaving Bulgaria pending rehabilitation. Their appeals were dismissed by the Supreme Administrative Court. The bans were lifted following a 2009 amendment to the Bulgarian Identity Papers Act.

**Alleged Violations**

The applicants alleged that their conviction was based to a decisive extent on anonymous witness testimony and that their defense rights were unacceptably restricted. They argued anonymity was unnecessary as they knew the witnesses' identities and that authorities failed to secure the witnesses' attendance at trial. The second and fourth applicants alleged the travel bans were unjustified and lacked effective domestic remedies.
