In **Boulois v. Luxembourg** (Application no. 37575/04, Grand Chamber, 3 April 2012), the applicant, Thomas Boulois, a French national, was imprisoned in Luxembourg. In October 2001, the Court of Appeal sentenced him to 15 years’ imprisonment, three years suspended, for assault occasioning actual bodily harm, rape, and false imprisonment accompanied by acts of torture committed in December 1998. While detained at Schrassig Prison, he made several requests for prison leave. These refusals formed the basis of his complaint to the European Court of Human Rights.

In October 2003, Boulois requested one-day prison leave to complete administrative tasks, including obtaining passport photographs, renewing his driving licence and consular registration, visiting a bank, tax office, police station, lawyer, and his flat, and meeting friends. On 5 November 2003, the Prison Board refused the request. It cited a risk of deportation because an application had been made to the Ministry of Justice, a risk that he might abscond, his failure to reflect on his crime, and his failure to begin paying the civil party. In January 2004, he renewed the request. On 17 March 2004, the Board maintained the refusal.

Boulois applied to the Administrative Court for judicial review of both refusals. On 23 December 2004, the Administrative Court declined jurisdiction. It reasoned that a distinction had to be drawn between administrative measures concerning prison treatment and decisions altering the nature or scope of a sentence imposed by ordinary courts. It held that granting or refusing prison leave altered the “scope” of the sentence and was therefore judicial, not administrative, and thus outside administrative court review. On 14 April 2005, the Higher Administrative Court upheld that ruling. It stated that prison leave concerned the execution of the sentence and was judicial in nature. It also found that Article 6 § 1 of the Convention did not apply because the administrative courts had no power to rule on the merits, and that there was no denial of justice.

Before the ECtHR, Boulois alleged that he had been deprived of his right to a fair hearing and his right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1 in connection with the decisions refusing his prison-leave requests. The central issue was whether proceedings concerning prison leave attracted Article 6 guarantees, particularly access to a court, given that no domestic court had accepted jurisdiction to review the refusals.

Under Luxembourg law, the Law of 26 July 1986 listed prison leave as one means of executing a custodial sentence. Section 6 defined it as permission to leave prison for part of a day or for 24-hour periods, counting towards the sentence. Section 7 described it as a privilege for family reasons, preparation for rehabilitation and reintegration, or trial before conditional release. Section 12 provided that, for sentences over two years, such measures were taken by the Attorney-General or representative in accordance with a majority of the Prison Board, comprising a judge and a public prosecutor. Section 13 required consideration of the prisoner’s personality, progress, and risk of further offence, but granting leave remained discretionary.

The Ombudsman had recommended creating a post-sentencing judge with appeal and adversarial proceedings. International recommendations encouraged prison leave and review of refusals. Boulois eventually received leave in 2008, was transferred to semi-open prison, and was granted conditional release in 2009 and suspension in 2010. The key alleged violation concerned the absence of any court review of the repeated refusals of prison leave.

In *Boulois v. Luxembourg* (ECtHR, Grand Chamber, 3 April 2012), the applicant, Thomas Boulois, a French national born in 1972, was detained in Schrassig Prison, Luxembourg. In October 2001 he was sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment, three years suspended, for assault occasioning actual bodily harm, rape, and false imprisonment accompanied by torture, committed in December 1998. While serving his sentence, he requested prison leave. His first request, in October 2003, sought one day’s leave to complete various administrative and personal tasks, including obtaining passport photos, renewing his driving licence, visiting the embassy, bank and tax offices, meeting his lawyer, and collecting documents. Two psychologists supported the request, noting that he had undertaken psychotherapy and wished to understand his offences and avoid reoffending.

On 5 November 2003, the Prison Board refused the request through the Attorney-General’s representative. The reasons were a risk of deportation, a risk of absconding, a failure to reflect on his crime, and the fact that he had not yet paid the civil party. A second request in January 2004 repeated the same proposed programme. On 17 March 2004, the Prison Board confirmed that the earlier refusal remained valid.

The applicant sought judicial review of both refusals before the Administrative Court. That court raised the issue of jurisdiction of its own motion. On 23 December 2004, it declined jurisdiction. It distinguished measures relating to the treatment of prisoners from decisions altering the nature or scope of a sentence. It held that granting or refusing prison leave altered the scope of the sentence and was therefore a judicial, not administrative, decision. On 14 April 2005, the Higher Administrative Court upheld that ruling. It stated that prison leave concerned the execution of the sentence and was judicial in nature; the administrative courts had no jurisdiction; there was no denial of justice; and Article 6 §1 of the Convention did not apply before a body lacking power to rule on the merits.

Consequently, the applicant had no court review of the decisions refusing his prison leave. Before the ECtHR, he alleged that this deprived him of a fair hearing and his right of access to a court under Article 6 §1. Further requests between 2004 and 2006 were also refused, on grounds including failure to compensate the victim, inability to show why courses could not be attended in prison, and risk that he would not return. He was eventually granted leave in October 2008, transferred to Givenich semi-open prison in March 2009, granted conditional release in September 2009, and had his sentence suspended in July 2010.

Domestic law provided that prison leave could be granted by the Attorney-General or Prison Board on discretionary grounds, taking into account the prisoner’s personality, progress, and risk of reoffending. No statutory appeal was available. International recommendations encouraged prison leave and review of refusals. The Grand Chamber ultimately held that Article 6 §1 was not applicable to proceedings concerning prison leave, so there was no violation of the applicant’s right of access to a court or fair hearing.

**Boulois v. Luxembourg** (Application no. 37575/04, Grand Chamber, 3 April 2012) concerned a French national, Thomas Boulois, who was detained in Schrassig Prison, Luxembourg. In 2001 he was sentenced by the Court of Appeal to fifteen years’ imprisonment, three years suspended, for assault occasioning actual bodily harm, rape, and false imprisonment accompanied by acts of torture committed in December 1998.

While serving his sentence, Boulois sought temporary prison leave. His first request, made in October 2003, was for one day to complete administrative tasks: obtain passport photos, renew his driving licence and consular registration, visit his lawyer, attend to tax and banking matters, meet friends, and collect documents. Psychologists certified that he was engaged in psychotherapy and wanted to avoid reoffending. In November 2003 the Prison Board refused the request, citing a risk of deportation, a risk of absconding, his failure to reflect on his offence, and his failure to begin paying damages to the civil party.

Boulois renewed the request in January 2004, again emphasising rehabilitation and his need to arrange repayment of debts. In March 2004 the Prison Board confirmed its earlier refusal. He then applied to the Administrative Court for judicial review. In December 2004 that court declined jurisdiction, holding that decisions granting or refusing prison leave altered the “scope” of the sentence and were therefore judicial, not administrative, in nature. In April 2005 the Higher Administrative Court upheld that ruling. It reasoned that prison leave concerned the execution of a sentence, not an administrative measure, and that Article 6 § 1 of the Convention did not apply because the administrative courts had no power to rule on the merits. The applicant thus had no judicial review of the refusals.

Further requests for prison leave were made and refused between 2004 and 2006. Reasons included lack of substantial efforts to compensate the victim, unclear visiting rights regarding his children, failure to give reasons, risk of non-return, and non-compliance with conditions. Later, from 2008 onwards, Boulois was granted prison leave, transferred to Givenich semi-open prison, granted conditional release in 2009, and had his sentence suspended in 2010.

The alleged violation concerned Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights: the right to a fair hearing and access to a court. Boulois complained that the refusals of prison leave could not be challenged before any court, because the administrative courts declined jurisdiction and no other remedy existed. He argued that prison-leave decisions affected his prospects of rehabilitation and reintegration, and that the absence of judicial review denied him a fair hearing.

The Government maintained that prison leave was a discretionary measure concerning the execution of sentence, granted by the Attorney-General and the Prison Board under the Law of 26 July 1986. Domestic law allowed leave for family, rehabilitation, or reintegration purposes, considering the prisoner’s personality, progress, and risk of reoffending. International recommendations encouraged prison leave and review of refusals, but did not require full judicial proceedings.

The key issue for the Grand Chamber was whether Article 6 § 1 applied at all to proceedings concerning prison leave. If it did not, the absence of court review would not breach the Convention. The applicant’s central complaint therefore turned on whether prison-leave decisions involved the determination of civil rights or a criminal charge. The Grand Chamber ultimately examined that question, with the earlier Chamber having found a violation of Article 6, before the case was referred to the Grand Chamber.
001-114439:
The case arose after the Netherlands daily newspaper *De Telegraaf* published articles on 21–22 January 2006 by journalists Joost de Haas and Bart Mos. The articles revealed alleged State secrets from the Dutch General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) concerning criminal Mink K., suspected corruption, and AIVD informants. The newspaper claimed the documents had circulated in criminal circles and said it had returned them to the AIVD. The AIVD then lodged a criminal complaint concerning unlawful disclosure of State secrets.

On 26 January 2006, the National Police Internal Investigations Department ordered the publisher to surrender documents and/or copies containing State secrets about operational activities of the BVD/AIVD. To protect the journalistic source, the originals were sealed and placed with an investigating judge pending objection proceedings. The publisher objected under Article 10 of the Convention, arguing that surrender would breach journalistic source protection. The Regional Court dismissed the objection, reasoning that the documents existed independently of the journalists’ will and were themselves the object of a criminal act. The Supreme Court upheld that decision in 2008. It found that the documents contained State secret information and that source protection, though important, was not absolute and could yield to weighty State interests, including protection of national security.

In parallel, the applicants alleged that the AIVD used special surveillance powers—telephone tapping and observation—against De Haas and Mos from late January 2006 onwards in order to identify their journalistic source. The State refused to confirm or deny such use. The applicants brought civil injunction proceedings under Articles 10 and 8 of the Convention, seeking cessation of the measures, destruction of data, and an order preventing transfer of information to the Public Prosecution Service. The Provisional Measures Judge assumed surveillance had occurred and found it contrary to Article 10, ordering provisional measures. The Court of Appeal held that surveillance against journalists was not per se unlawful, but became unlawful insofar as it continued after another target had been identified; it also ordered that data not be handed to the prosecution until the Supervisory Board for Intelligence and Security Services found it lawfully obtained. The Supreme Court upheld that approach, stressing that national security and prevention of dissemination of confidential information could justify interference, but only with extreme reticence and an overriding public-interest need.

The Supervisory Board later found the AIVD investigation broadly lawful but identified lapses: tapping a non-target breached subsidiarity; unrelated conversations were transcribed and retained; some tapping occurred before ministerial consent; and some numbers were wrongly attributed. The Minister declared the complaint partly well-founded regarding excessive transcription and retention, but unfounded on the main points, maintaining that special powers against the journalists were lawful, though they indirectly interfered with source protection.

The journalists were later questioned as witnesses in criminal proceedings against suspected leakers. They refused to answer questions capable of revealing their source and were initially ordered detained for non-compliance, but the Regional Court released them, recognising source protection and noting that the State-security issue was diminished because the leak had already become public. In the criminal case against one suspect, forensic examination of the seized documents found no traces.

The applicants alleged violations of Article 10 due to measures, including special surveillance powers, used to identify journalistic sources. The second and third applicants additionally alleged a violation of Article 8 resulting from surveillance.

Case: *Telegraaf Media Nederland Landelijke Media B.V. and Others v. the Netherlands* (App. no. 39315/06). The applicants were the publisher of the daily newspaper *De Telegraaf*, journalists Joost de Haas and Bart Mos, and two journalists’ associations (later declared inadmissible). They alleged violations of Article 10 (and Article 8 for the two journalists) arising from State measures, including special surveillance powers, used to identify journalistic sources after *De Telegraaf* published leaked AIVD state secrets.

On 21 January 2006, *De Telegraaf* published a front-page article by De Haas and Mos reporting that state secrets from AIVD investigations into drug criminal Mink K. were circulating in criminal circles. It alleged corruption, weapons stockpiles, and AIVD informants; an inside article named informant code names. Further articles followed. The AIVD filed a criminal complaint for unlawful disclosure of state secrets.

On 26 January 2006, the National Police Internal Investigations Department ordered the publisher to surrender documents and copies containing state secrets about BVD/AIVD operations. Fearing source identification, the publisher sealed the originals with a notary and handed them to the investigating judge pending objection. It invoked Article 10 journalistic source protection. The Regional Court dismissed the objection on 31 March 2006, reasoning that surrender did not require the journalists’ active cooperation and that the documents existed independently and were the object of a crime. The Supreme Court upheld this on 25 March 2008, finding that protecting state secrets was a weighty interest justifying the interference. It noted that fingerprint identification was not necessary because the AIVD could identify the leak from the documents’ content, already known to it.

In parallel, the journalists claimed that from late January 2006 the AIVD had subjected them to telephone tapping and observation, apparently to identify their source. The State refused to confirm or deny this. In civil injunction proceedings, the Provisional Measures Judge on 21 June 2006 assumed surveillance had occurred and held it contrary to Article 10, ordering cessation, destruction of data, and no handover to the prosecution. The Court of Appeal on 31 August 2006 held that surveillance was not per se impermissible, but was unlawful insofar as it continued after a target other than the applicants had been identified. It barred handover to the prosecution until the Supervisory Board found the material lawfully obtained. The Supreme Court on 11 July 2008 dismissed appeals, accepting that the initial AIVD investigation could be justified by national security and that source protection is not absolute; it required “extreme reticence” in using special powers but did not exclude them.

The Supervisory Board found the AIVD investigation largely lawful but identified lapses: tapping a non-target violated subsidiarity; too many unrelated conversations were transcribed; some tapping occurred before ministerial consent; and two numbers were wrongly attributed. It nevertheless concluded that official reports were based on lawfully obtained data. The Minister declared the complaint partly well-founded and said unlawfully recorded data had been destroyed. The journalists were later questioned as witnesses in criminal proceedings against alleged leakers; they refused to answer questions identifying their source, were briefly detained for non-compliance, and then released by the Regional Court.

The central alleged violations were that the surrender order and surveillance measures interfered with journalistic source protection under Article 10 without sufficient justification or safeguards, and that the surveillance violated the journalists’ private life under Article 8. The key factual dispute was whether the State’s national-security interest in tracing the AIVD leak could justify measures that foreseeably undermined confidential journalistic sources.

Case: Telegraaf Media Nederland Landelijke Media B.V. and Others v. the Netherlands (App. no. 39315/06), ECtHR, 22 November 2012. The applicants were the publisher of the daily De Telegraaf, two journalists (Joost de Haas and Bart Mos), and two journalist associations; the associations were later declared inadmissible.

On 21 January 2006, De Telegraaf published articles by De Haas and Mos reporting that AIVD/BVD state secrets concerning an investigation into drug and weapons dealer Mink K. and alleged corruption in the police and prosecution were circulating in criminal circles. The articles disclosed operational details and informant code names. The AIVD filed a criminal complaint for unlawful disclosure of state secrets. Authorities then issued a surrender order to the publisher for documents containing state secrets about BVD/AIVD operational activities. The publisher objected, invoking Article 10 protection of journalistic sources. To avoid source identification through fingerprints or other traces, copies were returned, and the originals were sealed and placed with an investigating judge pending review. The Regional Court and Supreme Court dismissed the objection. They held that the documents were state secrets and the object of a criminal act; source protection was not absolute, and surrender was justified by weighty State interests. The prosecution accepted that examining the documents to find the source was not its first priority but said it would use that opportunity if available.

Separately, the journalists suspected that the AIVD used special surveillance powers—telephone tapping and observation—against them from late January 2006 to trace the leak and source. The State refused to confirm or deny this. In civil injunction proceedings, the Provisional Measures Judge accepted the claim and held that such surveillance was contrary to Article 10, ordering cessation, destruction of data, and no handover to the prosecution. The Court of Appeal accepted that the use of powers was credible, found interference with Articles 8 and 10, and held it unlawful after another target had been identified. However, it allowed the State’s appeal in part, preventing handover to the prosecution until the Supervisory Board assessed lawfulness. The Supreme Court upheld this approach, stressing that source protection is not absolute and may yield to national security and the prevention of dissemination of confidential information, subject to strict necessity, subsidiarity and proportionality.

The Supervisory Board later found the AIVD investigation largely lawful but identified lapses: tapping a non-target violated subsidiarity; unrelated conversations were transcribed and retained; some tapping occurred before ministerial consent; and wrong numbers were tapped. The Minister declared the main complaint unfounded but partly well-founded regarding overbroad transcription and retention; unlawfully recorded data were destroyed. The journalists were also summoned as witnesses in criminal proceedings against suspected leakers. They refused to answer questions identifying their source and were briefly detained before release.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants alleged violations of Article 10 concerning measures, including special powers and the surrender order, aimed at identifying journalistic sources, and Article 8 concerning surveillance. The Court ultimately found violations of both Articles, holding that the Dutch legal framework for using special powers against journalists lacked sufficient safeguards, particularly prior judicial authorization, to protect journalistic sources and private life.
001-112529:
**Case: Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania**  
**ECtHR, Fourth Section, judgment of 31 July 2012 (revised 4 November 2014)**

The case originated in four applications brought by twenty Albanian nationals against Albania. The applicants complained that the Albanian authorities failed to enforce final administrative decisions recognising their inherited property rights and awarding them compensation in lieu of restitution. They alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (fair hearing/access to court), Article 13 (effective remedy), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) to the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicants’ claims arose from Albania’s post-communist property restitution and compensation scheme. Under the relevant legislation, local property commissions could recognise former owners’ rights and, where the original property could not be restored because it was occupied or otherwise unavailable, award compensation through various statutory forms. Although the commissions issued decisions in the applicants’ favour, those decisions were not enforced.

In application no. 604/07, the Vlora Commission in 1995 recognised the applicants’ inherited title to a 5,000 sq. m plot and decided they would be compensated. The applicants wrote to the Commission in 1995, 1996 and 2002 but received no official response. In 2007 the Agency stated that it was still preparing property valuation maps and allocating funds. In 2008 the Agency’s director decided ex officio to verify the lawfulness of the 1995 decision. No further decision followed, and the 1995 decision remains unenforced.

In application no. 43628/07, the Lezhë Commission recognised the applicants’ title to 3,434 sq. m in 1994, restoring 713 sq. m and awarding compensation for the remaining 2,721 sq. m. The applicants challenged the decision, and in 1996 the Lezhë District Court ordered an additional 1,187 sq. m to be restored, bringing the restored total to 1,900 sq. m. However, the remaining 1,534 sq. m remained uncompensated.

In application no. 46684/07, the Korçë Commission recognised title to 4,000 sq. m in 1996 and, because the land was occupied, decided compensation was due. In 1999 the same Commission recognised title to 59,546 sq. m of agricultural land and awarded compensation in State bonds of 1,018,236 Albanian leks. No bonds or other compensation were provided. The Government claimed that in 2009 the applicants received ALL 2,000,000 from the Financial Compensation Fund for 200 sq. m, but submitted no supporting document.

In application no. 34770/09, the Tirana Commission in 1995 recognised the applicant’s title to two plots of 63 sq. m and 597 sq. m, deciding that because they were occupied he would be compensated and had a right of first refusal over two buildings. Another 1995 decision recognised 800 sq. m, of which 178 sq. m were restored, leaving 622 sq. m to be compensated. In 2009 the Agency rejected his compensation claim because he had already benefited from the 178 sq. m restitution. He did not appeal within the statutory 30-day period.

Domestically, the 1993 and 2004 Property Acts created complex restitution and compensation mechanisms, later administered by the Agency. Constitutional Court case-law held that commission decisions were final, enforceable, and capable of creating legal expectations similar to court decisions, and that the Agency director could not annul them ex officio. Nevertheless, compensation remained largely unimplemented due to incomplete valuation maps, insufficient funds, fragmented legislation, and repeated delays. The alleged violations therefore centred on the prolonged non-enforcement of final administrative compensation decisions, the absence of effective remedies, and unjustified interference with the applicants’ property rights.

**Summary of *Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania***

The case of *Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania* (Applications nos. 604/07, 43628/07, 46684/07 and 34770/09) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights by twenty Albanian nationals against the Republic of Albania. The applicants alleged violations of Articles 6 § 1 and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, stemming from the non-enforcement of final administrative decisions that awarded them compensation in lieu of property restitution.

The applicants were former owners whose property had been expropriated, nationalised, or confiscated by the communist regime prior to 1944. Following the enactment of property restitution laws, various local Commissions recognised their inherited property titles but determined that, since the original plots were occupied or unavailable, they were entitled to compensation under the law.

**Application no. 604/07 (Manushaqe Puto and Others):** On 27 July 1995, the Vlora Commission recognised the applicants' inherited title to 5,000 sq. m. of land and decided they would be compensated. Despite the applicants' repeated inquiries in 1995, 1996, and 2002, no compensation was provided. In 2008, the Agency's director decided to verify the 1995 decision *proprio motu*, and to date, the decision remains unenforced.

**Application no. 43628/07 (Dani and Others):** On 31 October 1994, the Lezhë Commission recognised the applicants' title to 3,434 sq. m., restoring 713 sq. m. and awarding compensation for the remaining 2,721 sq. m. A subsequent court decision in 1996 increased the restored area to 1,900 sq. m. The applicants, however, have not received compensation for the remaining 1,534 sq. m.

**Application no. 46684/07 (Ahmatas and Others):** The Korçë Commission issued two decisions: on 19 January 1996, recognising title to 4,000 sq. m. and awarding compensation; and on 15 January 1999, recognising title to 59,546 sq. m. and awarding 1,018,236 Albanian leks in State bonds. The applicants received no compensation for either decision, though the Government claimed they received 2,000,000 leks from the Financial Compensation Fund in 2009 for 200 sq. m., without providing supporting documentation.

**Application no. 34770/09 (Muka):** On 7 June 1995, the Tirana Commission recognised the applicant's title to two plots (63 sq. m. and 597 sq. m.), awarding compensation and a right of first refusal for buildings. On 16 August 1995, the Commission recognised title to another 800 sq. m. plot, restoring 178 sq. m. and awarding compensation for the remaining 622 sq. m. In 2009, the Agency dismissed Muka's compensation claim, citing the prior restitution, and no appeal was filed.

The core factual pattern across all applications is the recognition of property rights and entitlement to compensation by final, enforceable administrative decisions, followed by prolonged failure of Albanian authorities to provide the awarded compensation. The domestic legal framework, including the 1993 and 2004 Property Acts, established compensation mechanisms such as the Financial Compensation Fund and In-kind Compensation Fund, but these proved ineffective in practice. The Government's Action Plan of 2011 acknowledged systemic issues, including lack of inter-institutional coordination, fragmented legislation, and absence of a unified property database, contributing to the non-enforcement of decisions. The case highlights a systemic failure in Albania's property compensation process, forming the basis for the applicants' complaints before the Court.

In **Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania** (ECtHR, Fourth Section, judgment 31 July 2012), twenty Albanian nationals brought four applications (nos. 604/07, 43628/07, 46684/07 and 34770/09). They alleged breaches of Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, essentially complaining that final administrative decisions awarding them compensation in lieu of restitution of their properties had not been enforced.

The applicants’ claims arose from property nationalised or confiscated under Albania’s former communist regime. After the transition, property commissions recognised their inherited title to various plots. Because the original land was often occupied or not restorable, the commissions decided that the applicants should receive compensation in one of the forms provided by law. Those decisions were final but were not implemented.

In **Puto (no. 604/07)**, on 27 July 1995 the Vlora Commission recognised the applicants’ inherited title to 5,000 sq. m of land and decided they would be compensated. The applicants wrote to the Commission in 1995, 1996 and 2002 without official response. In March 2007 the Agency said it was still preparing valuation maps and funds. In October 2008 the Agency’s director decided ex officio to verify the lawfulness of the 1995 decision. No further decision followed, and the 1995 decision remained unenforced.

In **Dani (no. 43628/07)**, on 31 October 1994 the Lezhë Commission recognised title to 3,434 sq. m, restored 713 sq. m, and provided compensation for the remaining 2,721 sq. m. After the applicants challenged the extent of restitution, the Lezhë District Court on 10 December 1996 ordered an additional 1,187 sq. m restored, bringing total restitution to 1,900 sq. m. However, no compensation was provided for the remaining 1,534 sq. m.

In **Ahmatas and Others (no. 46684/07)**, the Korçë Commission on 19 January 1996 recognised title to 4,000 sq. m and, because the land was occupied, ordered compensation. On 15 January 1999 it recognised title to 59,546 sq. m of agricultural land and ordered compensation in State bonds worth 1,018,236 Albanian leks. Neither decision was implemented. The Government claimed that in 2009 the applicants received 2,000,000 leks from the Financial Compensation Fund for 200 sq. m, but submitted no supporting document.

In **Muka (no. 34770/09)**, the Tirana Commission on 7 June 1995 recognised title to two plots of 63 sq. m and 597 sq. m, ordered compensation because they were occupied, and recognised a right of first refusal over buildings. On 16 August 1995 it recognised title to another 800 sq. m, restored 178 sq. m, and ordered compensation for 622 sq. m. In February 2009 the Agency rejected Muka’s compensation claim on the ground that she had already benefited from the 178 sq. m restitution. No appeal was lodged within the statutory 30-day period.

Domestically, the 1993 and 2004 Property Acts created restitution and compensation schemes, including a Financial Compensation Fund and in-kind compensation. Implementation was delayed by missing valuation maps, inadequate funds, fragmented legislation and administrative reorganisations. Constitutional Court decisions later held that Commission decisions were final and enforceable and could not be re-examined ex officio by the Agency director. The applicants therefore alleged that the prolonged non-enforcement of final decisions deprived them of effective judicial protection, an effective remedy, and their property-related compensation entitlement.
001-114243:
**Summary of the Case**

The case of *Ališić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Serbia, Slovenia and the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia* (Application no. 60642/08) originated from an application lodged on 30 July 2005 by three citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina—Ms Emina Ališić, Mr Aziz Sadžak, and Mr Sakib Šahdanović—against five successor states of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (SFRY). The applicants alleged that they were unable to withdraw their "old" foreign-currency savings deposited before the dissolution of the SFRY, in violation of their rights under the European Convention on Human Rights.

Before the SFRY's disintegration, the applicants had deposited foreign currency—primarily German marks—in banks that were part of the Yugoslav banking system. Ms Ališić and Mr Sadžak held accounts at the Sarajevo branch of Ljubljanska Banka, while Mr Šahdanović had accounts at the Tuzla branch of Investbanka. The balances in their accounts were approximately DEM 4,715.56, DEM 129,874.30, and DEM 63,880.44 respectively, with Mr Šahdanović also holding small amounts in US dollars and Austrian schillings.

The deposits were made under a system where banks were required to "redeposit" foreign currency with the National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY). Under this scheme, Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo shipped foreign currency to its parent bank, Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana in Slovenia, on a monthly basis. Between 1984 and 1991, DEM 244,665,082 was shipped to Ljubljana, but less than 17% (DEM 41,469,528) was returned to Sarajevo. Similarly, funds from Investbanka's Tuzla branch likely ended up in Serbia.

Following the SFRY's dissolution in 1991/92, the successor states adopted different approaches to "old" foreign-currency savings. In 1990, Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo became a branch without legal personality of Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana, with the parent bank assuming its rights and liabilities. After the war, Bosnia and Herzegovina's Entity governments assumed liability for savings in domestic banks but expressly excluded branches of Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana and Investbanka. The 2006 Old Foreign-Currency Savings Act confirmed this exclusion, though it obligated the State to help clients recover savings from Slovenia and Serbia.

Slovenia assumed the SFRY's guarantee for savings in domestic branches of all banks in 1991. After nationalising and restructuring Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana in 1994, a new bank (Nova Ljubljanska Banka) took over domestic assets and liabilities, while the old bank retained liability for "old" foreign-currency savings in branches in other successor states. In 1997, proceedings concerning these savings were stayed pending succession negotiations. However, in 2009, Slovenia's Constitutional Court declared this measure unconstitutional, and Slovenian courts subsequently ordered the old Ljubljanska Banka to repay savings with interest, holding that the relationship was of a private-law nature.

Serbia made a bankruptcy order against Investbanka in 2002, activating the State guarantee on "old" foreign-currency savings. However, 322 clients of Bosnian-Herzegovinian branches of Investbanka unsuccessfully applied for repayment within the bankruptcy proceedings.

Despite the 2001 Agreement on Succession Issues, which included provisions requiring successor states to negotiate the distribution of SFRY guarantees of foreign-currency savings under the auspices of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), negotiations failed. By 2002, the BIS terminated its involvement, and subsequent attempts to revive negotiations proved unsuccessful.

The applicants alleged that the respondent states' failure to enable them to withdraw their savings violated their rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy). The Court joined the issue of exhaustion of domestic remedies to the merits and declared the application admissible.

The case originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 30 July 2005 by three citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, one of whom also held German citizenship. The applicants alleged that they were still unable to withdraw their “old” foreign-currency savings from accounts held before the dissolution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Ms Ališić and Mr Sadžak had deposits at the Sarajevo branch of Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana, while Mr Šahdanović had deposits at the Tuzla branch of Investbanka. Their balances were approximately DEM 4,715.56, DEM 129,874.30 and DEM 63,880.44 respectively, plus small amounts in US dollars and Austrian schillings.

Before the break-up of the SFRY, the banking system consisted of basic and associated banks. Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo was a basic bank linked to the associated Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana. Foreign-currency deposits were encouraged, guaranteed by the SFRY, and largely “redeposited” with the National Bank of Yugoslavia. In 1990, Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo became a branch without legal personality of Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana, which took over its rights, assets and liabilities. Investbanka became an independent bank headquartered in Serbia, with its Tuzla branch remaining a branch without legal personality. After the SFRY disintegrated in 1991/92, these deposits became known as “old” or “frozen” foreign-currency savings.

After dissolution, the successor States adopted different and conflicting measures. Bosnia and Herzegovina assumed the statutory guarantee only for savings in domestic banks and expressly excluded the branches of Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana and Investbanka. Its courts and later legislation stated that the State should help clients recover their savings from Slovenia and Serbia, respectively, rather than repay them. In 2004, a domestic court found that the local Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo was not the successor of the Sarajevo branch and was not liable for those savings.

Slovenia assumed the SFRY guarantee for domestic branches, restructured Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana, and left the old bank with liability for “old” savings in branches in other successor States, including Sarajevo. Slovenian proceedings concerning such savings were initially stayed pending succession negotiations. Later, Slovenian courts ordered the old bank to pay some clients, but enforcement and recovery remained uncertain.

Serbia allowed repayment of old savings in domestic banks for its own citizens and citizens of non-successor States, but kept savings of successor-State citizens and savings in branches located in other successor States frozen. Investbanka was declared bankrupt in 2002. Some 322 clients of its Bosnian branches unsuccessfully sought payment in the bankruptcy proceedings, which remained pending. Croatia and Macedonia repaid savings in their own domestic banks or local branches, but the applicants’ accounts were not in those branches.

The 2001 Agreement on Succession Issues provided that SFRY guarantees of hard-currency savings should be negotiated under the auspices of the Bank for International Settlements. Those negotiations failed, and no agreement allocated responsibility among the successor States.

The applicants alleged that this legal vacuum left them unable to withdraw their savings for years, violating their property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and their right of access to a court and/or an effective remedy. The key factual issue was which successor State bore responsibility: the deposits were originally in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but the parent banks or related assets and liabilities were linked to Slovenia and Serbia, while Bosnia excluded liability and Slovenia and Serbia disputed it.

In **Ališić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Serbia, Slovenia and the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia** (App. no. 60642/08), three applicants—Emina Ališić, Aziz Sadžak and Sakib Šahdanović—complained that they could not withdraw their pre-dissolution “old” foreign-currency savings. Before the break-up of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (SFRY), they deposited foreign currency with Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo and the Tuzla branch of Investbanka. Their balances were approximately DEM 4,715.56, DEM 129,874.30 and DEM 63,880.44, plus small amounts in US dollars and Austrian schillings. After the SFRY dissolved, such savings became known as “old” or “frozen” foreign-currency savings.

The banking history is central. Under the SFRY system, Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo was originally a basic bank founded by Bosnian companies; in 1990 it became a branch without legal personality of Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana, which took over its rights, assets and liabilities. Investbanka became an independent bank headquartered in Serbia, with branches in Bosnia and Herzegovina, including Tuzla. The deposits had been guaranteed by the SFRY, but from 1990–91 emergency measures severely restricted withdrawals. After 1992, each successor State dealt differently with old savings.

Bosnia and Herzegovina assumed the guarantee for savings in domestic banks, but expressly excluded savings in the Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana and Investbanka branches. Its courts held that neither the State nor its Entities were liable, and legislation required only that the State assist clients to recover from Slovenia and Serbia. A domestic Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo initially administered the Sarajevo branch savings, but in 2004 a court found it was not the successor and not liable; its bankruptcy proceedings remained pending. The Tuzla branch closed in 1992. Investbanka was declared bankrupt in Serbia in 2002; 322 former clients of Bosnian-Herzegovinian branches sought payment unsuccessfully, and the bankruptcy remained pending.

Slovenia assumed the SFRY guarantee for old savings in domestic branches regardless of depositor citizenship. In 1994 it restructured Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana: a new bank took domestic assets and liabilities, while the old bank retained liability for branches in other successor States. Proceedings concerning those branches were stayed in 1997 pending succession talks; Slovenia’s Constitutional Court later found the stay unconstitutional. Some Slovenian courts ordered the old bank to repay Sarajevo and Zagreb branch savings, and at least one Sarajevo-branch judgment became final. Serbia, by contrast, repaid old savings in domestic branches for its own citizens and non-successor-State citizens, but froze savings of successor-State citizens and savings in branches located in those States pending succession. Croatia and the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia generally repaid old savings in their domestic banks or local branches of foreign banks, regardless of citizenship, but certain Ljubljanska Banka Zagreb clients remained affected.

The 2001 Agreement on Succession Issues made SFRY guarantees of hard-currency savings a matter for negotiation under the Bank for International Settlements. Negotiations failed, and the BIS ended its role in 2002. The applicants therefore alleged that their inability to withdraw their savings, and the absence of an effective remedy, violated their rights under the Convention, particularly the right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The case concerned which successor State or States bore responsibility for those frozen savings.
001-113648:
Mitkus v. Latvia concerned Andris Mitkus, a Latvian national, who alleged violations arising from criminal proceedings, two civil cases, his HIV/hepatitis C infection in prison, and press publication of his identity and health information.

Criminal proceedings: On 20 July 1999 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of extortion. While detained, on 26 November 1999 he was charged with robbery committed on 18 July 1999. He protested his innocence, saying neighbours could confirm he had been working in his yard. In July 2000 a confrontation took place with witness M.B., who implicated him; the applicant denied involvement. After the pre-trial investigation ended in August 2000, he requested an identity parade, but a prosecutor refused in September 2000 because the victim had said he could not recognise his attackers. At trial in June–July 2002, the victim and M.B. did not appear. The victim’s pre-trial statements were read because he claimed disability prevented attendance. M.B., though ordered to be brought by police, could not be found, so his pre-trial statements were also read despite the applicant’s objection; M.B.’s evidence directly implicated him. The applicant also claimed M.B. had a motive to lie. The court convicted him of robbery on 2 July 2002 and sentenced him to eight years, relying on co-accused, the victim, M.B., and other witnesses, and rejecting alibi witnesses because they were called by him and recalled events after a long delay. His appeals complained about absent witnesses, including S.K-a and S.K-s, but the Supreme Court rejected them; the Senate noted he had not repeated some requests at the appeal hearing. He also complained of delay, and the Ministry of Justice referred to the court’s heavy workload.

Infection and civil claim against Central Prison: In March 2003 the applicant learned he was HIV positive from 2002 tests and later that he had hepatitis C. He denied drug use or homosexual activity and believed he was infected in Central Prison. Prison records showed a negative HIV test on arrival in July 1999 and a positive test in September 2002. The prison suggested a possible “window” period, pre-arrest infection, or infection in prison through hygiene/sex; it said single-use syringes had been used. The applicant alleged a multiple-use glass syringe was used for his 1999 blood sample. His damages claim was rejected in February 2004; the nurse testified that single-use syringes were used. On appeal, he requested to attend, but the Supreme Court heard the case on 30 September 2004 in his absence because he was detained. His cassation appeal was dismissed without addressing that absence. He also complained to prosecutors, but no criminal investigation into the infection was opened.

Newspaper civil claim: In November 2003 the newspaper Rīgas Balss published an article, “Prison Doctors Accused of Injecting AIDS,” naming “prisoner Andris M.,” describing his alleged infection claim, convictions and sentence, and printing a recognisable photo of him behind bars. The applicant had asked that his identity not be disclosed; the court later prohibited media from revealing it. He sued for non-pecuniary damages. The first-instance court found the publication contravened data-protection law but dismissed for lack of proved damage. The appeal court heard the case in his absence on 2 February 2006 and dismissed it, holding media not subject to data-protection legislation; cassation was refused.

He therefore alleged breaches of Articles 6 and 8 concerning unfairness, length, exclusion from hearings, failure to investigate/protect against infection, and disclosure of sensitive private information.

**Summary of Mitkus v. Latvia (Application no. 7259/03)**

The case of *Mitkus v. Latvia* concerns an application lodged by Mr. Andris Mitkus, a Latvian national, against the Republic of Latvia on 19 February 2003. The applicant raised several complaints under the European Convention on Human Rights, primarily concerning the fairness and length of criminal proceedings against him, the fairness of civil proceedings, his alleged infection with HIV and hepatitis C while in prison, and a violation of his right to respect for private life.

**Criminal Proceedings:** On 20 July 1999, the applicant was arrested on suspicion of extortion. While in detention, he was subsequently charged with robbery committed on 18 July 1999. The applicant maintained his innocence, citing an alibi supported by neighbours who claimed he was at home on the day of the robbery. During the trial in the Rīga Regional Court in 2002, several witnesses testified in his defence. However, two key witnesses for the prosecution—the victim and a witness named M.B.—did not appear in court. The victim cited a disability, and M.B. could not be located by police. Over the applicant's objections, the court read out their pre-trial statements. M.B.'s statement implicated the applicant in the robbery. On 2 July 2002, the applicant was convicted of robbery and sentenced to eight years' imprisonment. His appeals to the Supreme Court and the Senate were rejected, with the courts largely relying on the first-instance judgment and not specifically addressing his complaints about the absent witnesses. The applicant also complained about the lengthy proceedings, receiving a letter from the Ministry of Justice acknowledging delays due to the court's heavy workload.

**Civil Proceedings Against Central Prison:** In March 2003, the applicant was informed that a 2002 blood test showed he was HIV positive, and further tests revealed hepatitis C. He believed he had been infected in Central Prison due to negligence by prison staff, specifically alleging that a multiple-use syringe had been used to draw his blood in 1999. He lodged a claim for damages. Central Prison denied the allegation, stating that single-use syringes had been used since the 1990s. The Rīga Regional Court rejected the applicant's claim in February 2004, finding that the prison had proven a single-use syringe was used and that it was impossible to pinpoint when he contracted hepatitis C. The applicant's appeal to the Supreme Court was dismissed on 30 September 2004; the court noted his absence at the hearing because he was detained but did not address it further. His subsequent appeal on points of law was also dismissed.

**Civil Proceedings Against Newspaper Publisher:** During the civil case against Central Prison, the applicant initially left the decision on a public hearing to the court, which chose a closed session. Later, at the applicant's request, the trial was opened to the public on the condition that his identity was not disclosed. On 25 November 2003, the newspaper *Rīgas Balss* published an article titled "Prison Doctors Accused of Injecting AIDS," which included the applicant's name, details of his health status, criminal record, and a recognizable photograph of him. The applicant sued the publisher for non-pecuniary damages. The first-instance court found that the newspaper had contravened data protection laws but dismissed the claim as the applicant failed to prove any specific damage. The Supreme Court upheld this decision on appeal, further ruling that media were not subject to data protection legislation. The applicant's appeal on points of law was dismissed. In both this and the prison case, the applicant's requests to be present at the appeal hearings were not granted.

**Case: Mitkus v. Latvia (Application no. 7259/03), European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, judgment of 2 October 2012.**

The applicant, Andris Mitkus, a Latvian national, complained about the length and fairness of criminal proceedings against him, the fairness of two sets of civil proceedings, the substantive and procedural handling of his HIV and hepatitis C infection, and an alleged violation of his right to respect for private life.

**Criminal proceedings.** On 20 July 1999 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of extortion. On 26 November 1999, while in detention, he was charged with robbery committed on 18 July 1999. He claimed an alibi: neighbours had seen him working in the yard of his home on the day of the robbery. In July 2000 a confrontation took place with witness M.B., who implicated him; the applicant asked no questions. After the pre-trial investigation ended in August 2000, he requested an identity parade, but the prosecutor refused because the victim said he could not recognise his attackers. In April 2001 the applicant was convicted of extortion. In the robbery trial in June–July 2002, the victim did not attend, citing disability, and the court read his pre-trial statements despite the applicant’s objection. Witness M.B. also failed to appear; police could not find him, and the court read his pre-trial statements even though the applicant insisted on questioning him because M.B. directly implicated him. Several alibi witnesses testified, but the court disbelieved them, partly because too much time had passed and because they had been requested by the applicant. On 2 July 2002 the applicant was convicted of robbery and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. His appeal was rejected in February 2003 without specific analysis of his complaints, and the Senate rejected his appeal on points of law in April 2003, noting that he had not repeated his request for the victim and M.B. to be summoned at the appeal stage. The Ministry of Justice later cited the court’s heavy workload as causing delay.

**Civil proceedings concerning infection.** In 2003 the applicant was informed that a 2002 blood test showed he was HIV positive and that he was also infected with hepatitis C. He believed he had been infected in Central Prison, stating that he had never used intravenous drugs and was not homosexual. He sued Central Prison, alleging that in 1999 prison medical staff had used a multiple-use syringe to take his blood, infecting him with HIV and later hepatitis C. The prison claimed single-use syringes had been used since the early 1990s; his 1999 HIV test was negative and the 2002 test positive, possibly due to the “window” period or infection before or inside prison. In February 2004 the first-instance court rejected his claim, accepting a nurse’s testimony that single-use syringes had been used since 1996/97. On appeal in September 2004, the Supreme Court heard the case in his absence because he was detained and not escorted, and dismissed the appeal. The Senate later dismissed his appeal on points of law without addressing his absence.

**Civil proceedings against a newspaper.** During the prison civil trial, the hearing was initially closed but later opened at the applicant’s request, with a ban on photographs. On 25 November 2003 the newspaper *Rīgas Balss* published an article entitled “Prison Doctors Accused of Injecting AIDS,” identifying “prisoner Andris M.,” publishing a recognisable photograph, and disclosing his HIV claim, criminal record, and sentence. The applicant sued the publisher for non-pecuniary damages. In December 2004 the first-instance court found that data protection law applied, that he had not consented, and that sensitive data had been unlawfully published, but dismissed the claim for lack of proven damage. In February 2006 the Supreme Court proceeded in the applicant’s absence and held that the media were not subject to data protection law and that there were no grounds for compensation. The Senate dismissed his further appeal in April 2006 without addressing his absence.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints before the European Court of Human Rights.
001-114082:
*Catan and Others v. Moldova and Russia* (Applications nos. 43370/04, 8252/05 and 18454/06) was a Grand Chamber case brought by Moldovan nationals living in Transdniestria. The applicants were children attending three Moldovan/Romanian-language schools in the separatist “Moldavian Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”) and their parents. They alleged violations of Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education), Article 8 (private and family life), alone and read with Article 14 (discrimination), arising from the closure and harassment of their schools by the MRT authorities. The applications were lodged in 2004, joined, declared partly admissible in 2010, and heard by the Grand Chamber in 2012.

Transdniestria is an unrecognised separatist region of Moldova. After the 1991–92 conflict, the MRT exercised de facto control there. Russian military forces—formerly the Soviet 14th Army, later the Russian Operational Group—remained, and Russian peacekeepers operated under the 1992 ceasefire. The applicants alleged that Russia also gave political, economic and military support to the MRT, including arms, energy, pensions/aid and Russian citizenship. The MRT imposed a language policy requiring “Moldavian” to be written in Cyrillic. Latin-script schools were banned, and from 1999 schools linked to foreign states had to register with the MRT or lose recognition. In July 2004 the MRT began closing Latin-script schools.

The individual facts concerned three schools.

**Evrica School, Rîbniţa (Catan and Others):** It used premises on Gagarin Street built with Moldovan public funds and followed Moldova’s curriculum in Latin script. It refused MRT registration because that would require Cyrillic and an MRT curriculum. In February 2004 the building was transferred to the MRT education department. In July 2004 MRT police stormed the school and evicted women and children; parents were allegedly pressured to withdraw children, with threats to jobs and parental rights. After OSCE intervention, the school registered as a foreign private school and reopened in a rented former kindergarten, which was inadequate. Requests to return to Gagarin Street were refused. It suffered vandalism and intimidation, and enrolment fell from 683 (2002–03) to 345 (2008–09).

**Alexandru cel Bun School, Tighina/Bender (Caldare and Others):** The school was warned it would close if it did not register. In July 2004 its water and electricity were cut and it was told to leave its premises. Teachers, pupils and parents occupied the building; MRT police failed to retake it. Utilities were restored after international negotiations. The school reopened in three separate rented buildings lacking proper facilities. Enrolment fell from 1,751 to 901.

**Ştefan cel Mare School, Grigoriopol (Cercavschi and Others):** Originally Cyrillic, it sought to switch to Latin script in 1996. The MRT responded with hostile media, intimidation and threats. In August 2002 police stormed the school and evicted teachers, pupils and parents. A pupil committee president was arrested and given 15 days’ administrative imprisonment. About 300 pupils left. The school was relocated to Doroţcaia, under Moldovan control, with pupils bused daily; they faced searches, identity checks and harassment. Enrolment fell from 709 to 169.

The applicants complained to both respondent Governments. Russia generally urged negotiations between Moldova and the MRT; Moldova said it could do no more. The key factual dispute for the alleged violations was whether these interferences with education and private life were attributable to Moldova and/or Russia and whether they amounted to discrimination.

They complained that the separatist Transdniestrian authorities (“MRT”) closed their schools and harassed them, violating Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education) and Article 8 (private and family life), alone and in conjunction with Article 14 (discrimination). **Summary of the Case**

The case of *Catan and Others v. Moldova and Russia* (Applications nos. 43370/04, 8252/05, and 18454/06) was a Grand Chamber judgment delivered by the European Court of Human Rights on 19 October 2012. It concerned the closure of Moldovan-language schools in the separatist region of Transdniestria and the alleged failure of both respondent states to protect the applicants’ rights under Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education) and Article 8 (right to private life), taken alone and in conjunction with Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination).

The applicants were Moldovan nationals—pupils and their parents—living in Transdniestria, a region that had declared independence in 1990 but remained internationally recognised as part of Moldova. The "Moldavian Republic of Transdniestria" (MRT) was not recognised by the international community, yet it exercised effective control over the region with significant military, economic, and political support from Russia.

The dispute arose from the MRT’s 1992 law mandating that the Moldovan language be written in Cyrillic script. In 1994, the MRT banned Latin-script education. By 1999, schools using the Latin script were required to register with MRT authorities, which would force them to adopt the Cyrillic script and MRT curriculum. The three applicant schools—Evrica in Rîbniţa, Alexandru cel Bun in Tighina, and Ştefan cel Mare in Grigoriopol—refused registration and continued using the Latin script under the Moldovan Ministry of Education.

In July 2004, the MRT authorities began forcibly closing these schools. At Evrica, police stormed the school, evicted occupants, and pressured parents to transfer their children. The school was eventually relocated to inadequate rented premises. At Alexandru cel Bun, utilities were cut off and the building seized; it reopened in scattered, unsuitable buildings. At Ştefan cel Mare, police stormed the school in 2002, evicted teachers and pupils, and arrested a student leader. The school was relocated to a village under Moldovan control, with pupils facing daily harassment at checkpoints.

Across all cases, the applicants alleged systematic harassment, intimidation, vandalism, and pressure from MRT authorities, including threats of job loss and removal of parental rights. The schools’ pupil numbers declined sharply. Complaints to Russian and Moldovan authorities yielded only general statements urging negotiation, with no effective protection.

The applicants argued that both Moldova and Russia were responsible. Moldova was alleged to have failed to protect their rights despite its sovereignty over Transdniestria. Russia was alleged to have effective control over the MRT through military presence, economic dependence (especially gas supplies), and political support, and thus had jurisdiction and responsibility under the Convention.

The case was declared partly admissible in 2010 and relinquished to the Grand Chamber. The Court examined the historical context of the Transdniestrian conflict, the ceasefire agreement, the 1997 Memorandum, and Russia’s commitments to withdraw troops—which it failed to honour. It also considered the MRT’s “laws” and administrative measures targeting Latin-script schools, and the applicants’ specific experiences of closure, relocation, and harassment. The Court ultimately found violations of the right to education and private life, holding Russia responsible for its effective control over the MRT and Moldova responsible for failing to fulfil its positive obligations to protect the applicants’ rights.
001-115396:
The case **F.N. and Others v. Sweden** (Application no. 28774/09) concerned a family of four Uzbek nationals—F.N., his wife, and their two minor children—who arrived in Sweden in December 2005 and applied for asylum. They alleged that deportation to Uzbekistan would expose them to a real risk of arrest, torture, or other ill-treatment, contrary to Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The first applicant claimed a long history of persecution. In 1995 he was allegedly arrested during a mosque raid, held in solitary confinement, and later placed under a travel ban. In 1998 he was reportedly detained for six months and convicted as a Muslim separatist, but released after clemency and placed on an authorities’ blacklist. In May 2005 he claimed to have attended the Andijan demonstrations as a member of the local organisation Akrami. When police opened fire, he fled to Tashkent. Two days later, police allegedly arrested him at home, threatened and tortured him to extract a confession, and released him only after bribery. He was hospitalized for head injuries, then hid for six months before the family left Uzbekistan. The second applicant claimed she was interrogated and subjected to degrading treatment because of her husband, and that her brother was imprisoned. The third child, fragile from birth, reportedly developed anxiety, headaches, and learning and concentration difficulties.

The applicants submitted driving licences, employment books, a summons calling the first applicant as a witness, a Tashkent medical certificate, and wanted posters bearing the first applicant’s photograph and name among persons sought after Andijan. Later they produced a Ministry for Interior Affairs decision dated June 2005 stating that a search of his home had found extremist material and cartridges and that he was wanted. Medical certificates documented the third child’s psychological and neurological problems.

Swedish authorities rejected the asylum claims. The Migration Board found identities unproven and doubted the first applicant’s credibility, noting implausibilities in his travel from Andijan, the wanted posters’ low evidentiary value, and that the summons identified him only as a witness. The Migration Court, after an oral hearing, found the applicants’ accounts vague, inconsistent, and progressively escalated. It held that they had not shown a risk of persecution and that the third child could receive care in Uzbekistan. The Migration Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal in April 2009.

Further re-examination requests raised new claims: that the first applicant faced criminal charges in Uzbekistan over the Andijan events; that relatives had been visited by authorities; and that he had briefly joined the opposition party Birdamlik in Sweden and participated in demonstrations before leaving the party. The Migration Board and courts rejected these, finding no new circumstances showing an impediment to deportation. They considered his political activity limited, found no proof the Uzbek authorities knew of it, and reasoned that return could be arranged via Russia or Kazakhstan without revealing asylum status. The Migration Board’s contact with the Uzbek Embassy for travel documents did not, in their view, necessarily disclose that the family were asylum seekers.

The Court applied Rule 39, staying deportation. Country information before the Court described endemic torture in Uzbekistan, particular vulnerability of persons linked to Andijan, surveillance of returnees and failed asylum seekers, and criminal penalties for illegal exit. The applicants therefore maintained that deportation would violate Article 3. The Court declared the application admissible.

**CASE OF F.N. AND OTHERS v. SWEDEN**  
*(Application no. 28774/09, judgment of 18 December 2012)*

The case concerned four Uzbek nationals—F.N., his wife, and their two minor children—who arrived in Sweden in December 2005 and applied for asylum. They alleged that deportation to Uzbekistan would expose them to arrest, torture, or inhuman and degrading treatment, contrary to Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The third applicant’s poor health and need for medical treatment were also invoked.

The first applicant claimed that in 1995 he was arrested during a mosque raid and held in solitary confinement; in 1998 he was detained for six months and convicted as a Muslim separatist, then granted clemency and placed on a blacklist. In May 2005 he allegedly participated in the Andijan demonstrations as a member of Akrami. After police opened fire, he fled to Tashkent, but two days later police allegedly arrested him at home, beat and tortured him to extract a confession, and released him only after his parents bribed officials. He was hospitalized for injuries, then hid for six months before the family fled Uzbekistan.

The second applicant claimed she had been summoned and interrogated about her husband and subjected to degrading treatment. Her brother was imprisoned. The third child, fragile from birth, reportedly developed fever and stopped speaking after the first applicant’s arrest, later suffering headaches, anxiety, and learning difficulties.

The applicants produced employment books, a summons, a Tashkent medical certificate, wanted posters showing the first applicant among Andijan suspects, and a Ministry of Interior decision stating that a search of his home found extremist material and cartridges and that he was wanted. Swedish authorities rejected the asylum claim. The Migration Board doubted their credibility and identity, found the wanted posters unreliable, and noted the summons indicated witness status. The Migration Court in 2008 found vague, inconsistent, and escalating accounts, and held that the child’s health did not warrant residence. The Migration Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal in 2009, and later re-examination requests were rejected.

While in Sweden, the first applicant briefly joined the opposition party Birdamlik and attended demonstrations, then left, claiming Uzbek authorities knew through spies and had visited his parents. Swedish authorities found his political activity limited and not shown to be known to Uzbekistan. However, country information before the Court—including UN reports, Human Rights Watch, and Swedish Migration Board reports—described endemic torture, targeting of persons connected to Andijan, surveillance by the SNB and Mahalla system, and risks for failed asylum seekers and illegal exits. The European Court of Human Rights applied Rule 39, staying deportation.

The Court declared the application admissible and found that deportation to Uzbekistan would violate Article 3. It considered the first applicant’s specific history, his alleged involvement in Andijan, the documents indicating he was wanted, and the serious country conditions. It concluded there were substantial grounds for believing he faced a real risk of torture or inhuman or degrading treatment, and that the family’s removal would therefore breach Article 3.

The case *F.N. and Others v. Sweden* (Application no. 28774/09, judgment of 18 December 2012) concerns four Uzbek nationals—F.N., his wife, and their two minor children—who arrived in Sweden in December 2005 and applied for asylum and residence permits. They alleged that deportation to Uzbekistan would expose them to arrest, persecution, and treatment contrary to Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The first applicant claimed a long history of persecution. In 1995 he was allegedly arrested during a mosque raid and held in solitary confinement. In 1998 he was arrested again, detained for six months, and convicted as a Muslim separatist, but was granted clemency and placed on an authorities’ blacklist. In May 2005 he allegedly attended a demonstration in Andijan as a member of Akrami; police opened fire on demonstrators. He fled to Tashkent, but two days later police reportedly arrested him at home, detained him for four days, threatened and tortured him to extract a confession, and released him only after bribery. He was hospitalised for injuries, then hid for six months before the family fled Uzbekistan illegally. He claimed police identified him after arrested friends gave his name under torture, and that he was wanted for Andijan-related crimes.

The second applicant claimed she had been interrogated and subjected to degrading treatment because of her husband’s activities; her brother was imprisoned and allegedly used as leverage to locate the family. The third child suffered from physical and psychological problems. The applicants submitted employment books, a summons (as a witness), a medical certificate, wanted posters showing the first applicant, and later a Ministry of Interior decision stating that a search of his home had found extremist material and ammunition and that he was wanted.

Swedish authorities rejected the asylum claims. The Migration Board found identities unproved and the first applicant’s account not credible: his travel after Andijan was implausible, the posters had low evidentiary value, and the summons described him as a witness, not a suspect. The Migration Court upheld the rejection, citing vague, inconsistent and escalating accounts and changing details. Appeals and re-examination requests failed. A Rule 39 stay prevented deportation.

Later, the applicants invoked new risks: failed asylum seekers returning to Uzbekistan faced arrest, interrogation and possible ill-treatment; illegal exit was punishable under Article 223 of the Uzbek Criminal Code; and the first applicant had joined the opposition party Birdamlik in Sweden, participated in demonstrations, then resigned. They claimed Uzbek authorities knew of his activities and had visited his parents. The Swedish Migration Board had contacted the Uzbek Embassy in Riga for travel documents. Domestic authorities again found no new impediments, noting limited political activity, no proof the Uzbek authorities knew, unproved identity, and possible return via Russia or Kazakhstan.

International reports described endemic torture, pervasive surveillance through the Mahalla system and security services, and heightened vulnerability for persons linked to the Andijan events or returned asylum seekers. UNHCR urged caution. The applicants alleged a real and personal risk of persecution, arrest, torture or death if returned, contrary to Article 3.
001-108580:
Ustyantsev v. Ukraine (App. No. 3299/05, judgment 12 January 2012) concerned a Ukrainian national, Mr Sergey Ustyantsev, born in 1972. He complained under the Convention that conditions of his detention in the Odessa Remand Centre (SIZO) breached Article 3; that his pre-trial detention and trial were excessively long; and that he could not receive compensation for the lengthy detention.

The criminal proceedings began in September 2001. On 7 September a group allegedly including the applicant burgled a house. On 12 September the applicant stole a car, was involved in a collision, and was arrested; he was charged with car theft the next day. On 14 September the Leninskyy District Court ordered his detention on remand. After the car-theft investigation was completed, the case was sent to court. On 11 January 2002 the court discovered that burglary charges were also pending against him, remitted the car-theft case for joinder, and confirmed his further detention. On 2 February 2002 he was formally charged with burglary; the joined case was sent to court by 14 March 2002.

The proceedings were repeatedly delayed. Hearings were rescheduled because victims and witnesses failed to appear; the court complained that authorities did not enforce attendance orders and noted that delays extended detention in an overcrowded SIZO. On 3 March 2003 the applicant was convicted and sentenced to nine years. On appeal, on 31 July 2003, the burglary conviction was quashed and remitted, and the car-theft sentence was reduced to five years and six months. The Supreme Court dismissed his cassation appeal on 22 March 2005. At retrial on the burglary charge, hearings were again delayed by absent lawyers and witnesses. In 2005 a handwriting examination found that the applicant’s signatures had been forged on key procedural documents from early 2002; the case was remitted, and on 4 October 2005 the proceedings were discontinued for lack of proof.

Regarding detention conditions, the applicant was held in the SIZO from 15 September 2001 to 20 August 2003 and from 2 October 2003 to 20 November 2005, with shorter later periods, and in various correctional colonies. He alleged that in a temporary detention centre detainees were fed once daily and lights stayed on. In the SIZO he claimed severe overcrowding—about one square metre per person (a 7.5–10 square metre cell held four, with 1.5 square metres occupied by toilet and washstand)—constant lighting, a concrete floor, no facilities to prepare his defence, and lack of basic necessities, medical care, press, gym, and private correspondence. He also complained of overcrowded prison vans and poor conditions in the court’s detainee room. He said his health deteriorated, citing chronic prostatitis, thrombophlebitis, and a venereal disease. The Government disputed this, claiming at least 2.5 square metres per detainee, basic furniture, separated toilets, adequate light and ventilation, food, daily walks, eight hours’ sleep, weekly baths, and a library. The applicant also tried to obtain compensation for detention conditions, but his civil claim was dismissed on 17 April 2006 for procedural shortcomings, and his appeal was dismissed on 11 September 2006 as lodged out of time. He claimed authorities refused to provide copies of court decisions and his medical file. The Court later rejected as time-barred his complaints about the temporary detention centre (detention ended by 17 July 2002; application lodged 1 November 2004) and found his complaints about prison vans and the court detainee room unclear and lacking detail.
