Case Hristozov and Others v. Bulgaria (Applications nos. 47039/11 and 358/12) concerned ten Bulgarian nationals, most of whom suffered from terminal cancer. They had exhausted conventional treatments—surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and hormone therapy—or had been advised that such treatments would not work or were unavailable in Bulgaria. They approached a private Sofia clinic, the Medical Centre for Integrative Medicine OOD, which told them about MBVax Coley Fluid, an experimental anti-cancer product developed by the Canadian company MBVax Bioscience Inc. The product had not been authorised in any country, but had been allowed for “compassionate use” in several countries. The company offered to supply it free of charge to the clinic for patients who could no longer benefit from conventional treatment, in exchange for data on its effects.

Each applicant applied to the Bulgarian authorities for permission to use the product. In letters dated June, July and August 2011, the Director of the Medicines Executive Agency refused. He stated that MBVax Coley Fluid was an experimental product not authorised or undergoing clinical trials in any country. Under Bulgarian Regulations no. 2 of 2001, unauthorised medicines could not be authorised for use in Bulgaria. Bulgarian law made no provision for compassionate use outside clinical trials, unlike some other European countries. The Minister of Health agreed with that position, as did the Ombudsman in relation to some applicants. The applicants did not seek judicial review.

One applicant, Mr Petrov, travelled to Germany, obtained the product free of charge and received it seven times, but returned to Bulgaria because he could not afford living expenses or clinic fees. Four applicants—Mr Hristozov, Mr Petrov, Mr Behar and Ms Pencheva—died after lodging their applications, and their heirs continued the proceedings. The Government disputed whether MBVax Coley Fluid was a medicinal product and whether it was undergoing clinical trials. The applicants argued that it was undergoing a phase one clinical trial in Germany, relying on United States National Cancer Institute and National Library of Medicine websites, and therefore complied with Article 83 § 2 of Regulation (EC) no. 726/2004 on compassionate use. The Government rejected that assertion.

The applicants alleged that the authorities’ refusal to allow them to use the experimental medicinal product for compassionate use breached their right to life, amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment, and violated their right to respect for private and family life. They also alleged that they had no effective remedy in that respect. The Court joined the applications, declared them partly inadmissible, and gave the Government notice of the complaints concerning the refusal to permit use of the product and the alleged lack of effective remedies. It decided to examine the merits together with admissibility. The central factual issue was whether Bulgaria’s refusal to permit compassionate use of an unauthorised but potentially life-saving experimental medicine, when conventional treatment had failed and the applicants were terminally ill, unjustifiably interfered with their Convention rights.

Hristozov and Others v. Bulgaria (Applications nos. 47039/11 and 358/12) concerned ten Bulgarian nationals who were terminally ill with various types of cancer. The first applicant in application no. 47039/11 and all eight applicants in application no. 358/12 had terminal cancer; the second applicant in the first application was the first applicant’s mother. Four applicants died shortly after lodging their applications, and their heirs sought to continue the proceedings. The applicants had either undergone conventional treatments—surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and hormone therapy—or had been told that such treatments would not work in their cases or were unavailable in Bulgaria. They approached a private Sofia clinic, the Medical Centre for Integrative Medicine OOD, and were told about MBVax Coley Fluid, an experimental anti-cancer product developed by the Canadian company MBVax Bioscience Inc. The product had not been authorised in any country, but had been allowed for “compassionate use” in several countries. The company offered to provide it free of charge to the clinic for cancer patients who could no longer benefit from conventional treatment, in exchange for data on each patient’s adverse and beneficial effects.

Each applicant applied to the Bulgarian authorities for permission to use MBVax Coley Fluid. In June, July and August 2011, the Director of the Medicines Executive Agency refused. The Director stated that the product was experimental, had not been authorised or undergone clinical trials in any country, and could not be authorised in Bulgaria under Regulations no. 2 of 2001. Bulgarian law made no provision for the use of unauthorised medicines outside clinical trials; unlike some other European countries, compassionate use was not possible. The Director also said that EU law did not oblige Bulgaria to adopt a harmonised approach. The Minister of Health agreed, and the Ombudsman similarly advised that access was possible only through a clinical trial. One applicant, Mr Petrov, travelled to Germany, where he received the product seven times free of charge, but returned to Bulgaria because he could not afford living expenses or the clinic fees. The applicants did not seek judicial review of the refusals.

Under Bulgarian law, only authorised medicinal products may generally be used for treatment. Regulations no. 2 allowed unauthorised products only if they were authorised in other countries and intended for rare or specific diseases where authorised treatment had proved fruitless. Because MBVax Coley Fluid was not authorised anywhere, the authorities considered it ineligible. Under EU law, Article 83 of Regulation (EC) no. 726/2004 permits Member States to allow compassionate use of certain unauthorised products, but does not require them to do so. Article 5(1) of Directive 2001/83/EC permits individual patient use under strict conditions. Comparative material showed that many Contracting States had rules allowing access to unauthorised medicines outside clinical trials, especially for terminally ill patients, though practices varied.

The applicants alleged that the refusal to authorise compassionate use breached their right to life under Article 2, amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment under Article 3, and breached their right to respect for private and family life under Article 8. They also alleged a lack of an effective remedy under Article 13. The Court joined the applications, granted them priority, declared them partly inadmissible, and gave notice of the complaints concerning the refusal to allow use of the experimental product and the alleged lack of effective remedies. The key factual issue was whether the State’s refusal to permit access to an unauthorised, experimental medicine for terminally ill patients, when no domestic compassionate-use procedure existed, violated the Convention.

The Court joined the applications, declared them partly inadmissible, and communicated the complaints concerning the refusal of access and the alleged lack of effective remedies.

The case of *Khoniakina v. Georgia* concerned a Georgian national and former Supreme Court judge, Mrs Adelina Khoniakina, born in 1926. She had served as a Supreme Court judge from 1956 and retired in May 2000. Under the original version of section 36 of the Supreme Court Act, she received a life-long pension equal to her final salary, adjustable in line with changes in the salaries of serving Supreme Court judges. In 2001, section 36 was amended to remove that adjustment clause. Later amendments reintroduced adjustment, but a December 2005 amendment, effective 1 January 2006, rephrased section 36 to provide retired Supreme Court judges with State compensation fixed at GEL 1,200 (EUR 551). The 2005 amendment was given retroactive effect. From February 2006, the State Social Insurance Fund applied it to the applicant, reducing her pension from the previously adjustable level.

The applicant brought two pension disputes. In the first, begun in 2004, she challenged the removal of the adjustment clause. On 21 February 2006, a majority of the Supreme Court’s Administrative Division ruled in her favour, holding that the 2001 amendment could not retroactively deprive already-retired judges of their adjustment right and ordering arrears up to December 2005. Judge S. dissented, arguing that the amendment did not necessarily worsen her position and that her pension should be adjusted only between March 2005 and January 2006.

In the second dispute, the applicant challenged the application of the December 2005 amendment to her pension from February 2006. On 31 May 2006, she sued the Fund, arguing that the retroactive reduction of her pension was unlawful. The Tbilisi City Court dismissed her claim on 19 September 2006, and the Tbilisi Regional Court dismissed her appeal on 6 March 2007, stating that Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 did not guarantee a pension of a particular amount. The applicant lodged a cassation appeal on 9 July 2007, relying on the Convention case-law against retroactive interference with civil rights and arguing that the domestic courts had resolved an analogous issue inconsistently with the Supreme Court’s 21 February 2006 judgment.

On 10 October 2007, a Supreme Court bench composed of Judge S. and two other judges declared her cassation appeal inadmissible without a hearing and without addressing her arguments. The applicant requested that the decision be set aside, complaining that Judge S. should not have participated because he had already expressed a clear opinion on the same legal issue in the earlier pension dispute. She relied on domestic provisions allowing a judge’s exclusion where impartiality could be doubted. On 26 December 2007, the Supreme Court rejected that request, finding that Judge S.’s earlier dissenting opinion was not evidence of actual or implied bias.

The applicant complained before the European Court of Human Rights under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, alleging bias because Judge S. participated in the cassation decision after having already expressed an opinion on the same issue, and under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, alleging that the retroactive December 2005 amendment and fixed GEL 1,200 pension unlawfully interfered with her retirement pension rights and legal certainty. The Court gave notice of these complaints to the Georgian Government on 8 April 2009.

Case Summary: Khoniakina v. Georgia (Application no. 17767/08)

The applicant, Adelina Khoniakina, a Georgian national born in 1926, is a retired Supreme Court judge. She served on Georgia’s Supreme Court from 1956, first under the Soviet Union and then after independence, and retired on age grounds in May 2000. Under the original section 36 of the 1999 Supreme Court Act, retired Supreme Court judges were entitled to a life-long pension equal to their final salary, adjustable in line with salary increases for serving Supreme Court judges. Her initial pension was GEL 1,073 (EUR 492), corresponding to her final salary.

The legal regime changed repeatedly. A 16 March 2001 amendment removed the adjustment clause. A 10 March 2005 amendment reintroduced it in altered form. Most importantly, a 23 December 2005 amendment, effective 1 January 2006, replaced section 36 with a fixed State compensation of GEL 1,200 (EUR 551) for retired Supreme Court judges. It also added section 40(7)(1), which gave the new provision retroactive effect, unlike earlier amendments.

In her first pension dispute, begun in September 2004, the applicant challenged application of the 2001 amendment and sought pension adjustment and arrears. On 21 February 2006, the Supreme Court’s Administrative Division, by majority, allowed her claim in full up to December 2005. It held that the 2001 amendment could not be applied retroactively to judges who had already retired and acquired pension rights under the original section 36. Judge S. dissented, arguing that the 2001 amendment merely redefined the pension amount and did not breach legal certainty; he considered adjustment due only between 10 March 2005 and 1 January 2006. The judgment debt was paid.

From February 2006, relying on the 23 December 2005 amendment, the Fund reduced the applicant’s pension to GEL 1,200. She brought a second action on 31 May 2006, challenging the retroactive application of that amendment. The Tbilisi City Court dismissed her claim on 19 September 2006; the Tbilisi Regional Court dismissed her appeal on 6 March 2007, stating that Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 does not guarantee a pension of a particular amount and that the earlier Supreme Court judgment had concerned only the 2001 amendment. On 9 July 2007, she lodged a cassation appeal, arguing that retroactive interference with a civil right violated the Convention and that the case-law was inconsistent.

On 10 October 2007, a Supreme Court bench including Judge S. and two judges who had not sat in the first dispute declared the cassation appeal inadmissible without an oral hearing. The applicant requested that the decision be set aside, complaining that Judge S. should have been disqualified because he had already expressed an opinion on the same issue in his earlier dissent. On 26 December 2007, the Supreme Court rejected that request, finding that a prior dissenting opinion did not prove actual or implied bias.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, concerning the allegedly biased participation of Judge S. in the examination of her second pension case, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, concerning the retroactive reduction of her retirement pension as a former Supreme Court judge to a fixed amount, which she claimed interfered with her possessions and legitimate expectations.

Khoniakina v. Georgia concerned Adelina Khoniakina, a Georgian national and former Supreme Court judge. She retired on age grounds in May 2000. Under the original section 36 of the Supreme Court Act, she was granted a lifelong pension equal to her final salary, adjustable in line with changes in serving Supreme Court judges’ salaries. The bench included Judge S., who had already dissented in her first pension dispute, and two judges who had not previously participated. The decision was made without an oral hearing and without addressing her cassation arguments. The applicant then sought annulment, complaining that Judge S. should have been excluded because he had already expressed an opinion on the same issue. On 26 December 2007 the Supreme Court rejected that request, holding that a prior dissenting opinion did not prove actual or implied bias.

She also complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the retroactive 23 December 2005 amendment reduced her pension from a final-salary-linked entitlement to GEL 1,200, amounting to an unjustified interference with her possessions. The key facts therefore concerned the repeated involvement of the dissenting judge in reviewing her pension case and the retroactive legislative reduction of her retirement pension.
001-109572:
Gas and Dubois v. France (Application no. 25951/07) concerned two French nationals, Ms Valérie Gas and Ms Nathalie Dubois, a same-sex couple who had cohabited since 1989 and registered a civil partnership in 2002. In September 2000, Ms Dubois gave birth in France to a daughter, A., conceived in Belgium through anonymous donor insemination. The child had no established legal tie to a father, was formally recognised only by her mother, and lived continuously with both applicants, who jointly raised her.

In March 2006, Ms Gas applied to the Nanterre tribunal de grande instance for a simple-adoption order in respect of A., with Ms Dubois’s consent. The public prosecutor objected under Article 365 of the Civil Code. The first-instance court found that the statutory conditions for adoption were met and that Ms Gas was actively involved in the child’s emotional and material well-being. Nevertheless, it refused the application because a simple adoption of a minor would transfer parental responsibility entirely to the adoptive parent and deprive Ms Dubois, the birth mother, of her parental rights. Under Article 365, joint parental responsibility following such an adoption is possible only where the adoptive parent is married to the child’s mother or father. The Versailles Court of Appeal upheld that refusal in December 2006, finding the adoption contrary to the child’s interests and noting that a later delegation of parental responsibility would not sufficiently remedy the mother’s loss of rights. The applicants’ further appeal on points of law was not pursued and was declared forfeited.

French law distinguishes full adoption from simple adoption. Simple adoption does not sever the child’s original family ties but creates an additional legal parent-child relationship. For a minor, however, it vests parental responsibility exclusively in the adoptive parent, except where a married person adopts the child of his or her spouse, in which case the spouses may share parental responsibility. Marriage was not available to same-sex couples in France. Civil partnership, although conferring certain rights, had no effect on adoption or parental responsibility. Assisted reproduction was available only to opposite-sex couples, which explains why the child was conceived in Belgium and had no legal father. Court of Cassation case-law consistently refused simple adoption by the civil partner of a child’s mother, and in 2010 the Constitutional Council upheld Article 365 as so interpreted.

The applicants alleged discrimination based on sexual orientation, relying on Article 14 of the Convention taken together with Article 8. They argued that no legal means existed in France for same-sex couples to obtain second-parent adoption, whereas heterosexual couples—especially married couples—could secure a legal tie and shared parental responsibility through adoption of a spouse’s child. They claimed this breached their right to respect for private and family life. The Government preliminarily objected that Article 8 does not guarantee a right to adopt, so Article 14 could not apply. The Court dismissed that objection, finding that the applicants enjoyed family life under Article 8 and that sexual orientation fell within the personal sphere protected by Article 8; the facts thus fell within the ambit of Article 8 for Article 14 purposes. On the merits, the Court ultimately found no violation of Article 14 taken in conjunction with Article 8, giving France a margin of appreciation in the area of second-parent adoption and child-protection arrangements.

**Gas and Dubois v. France (ECtHR, 2012)**

The case concerned two French women, Valérie Gas and Nathalie Dubois, who had lived together since 1989 and entered a civil partnership in 2002. In 2000 Dubois gave birth in France to a daughter, A., conceived in Belgium through anonymous donor insemination. A. had no legal father and lived with both women, who jointly raised her.

In 2006 Gas applied for a simple adoption of A., with Dubois’s consent, to give legal recognition to her relationship with the child. Under French law, simple adoption creates an additional parent-child relationship but, for a minor, normally transfers parental responsibility to the adoptive parent alone. Article 365 of the Civil Code contains an exception where the adopter is married to the child’s mother or father: in that case, parental responsibility can be shared. Because same-sex marriage was not available in France, Gas could not benefit from that exception as Dubois’s civil partner.

The public prosecutor objected. The Nanterre tribunal de grande instance refused the application in 2006, finding that although the statutory conditions were met and Gas was actively involved in A.’s upbringing, the adoption would deprive Dubois of her parental rights by transferring them to Gas. The Versailles Court of Appeal upheld that refusal in December 2006. It accepted that Gas contributed to the child’s emotional and material well-being, but held that the legal consequences of adoption would contradict the applicants’ intention that both women continue to share parenting. A later delegation of parental responsibility would not remove the risk caused by the mother’s loss of parental responsibility. The applicants’ appeal to the Court of Cassation was not pursued, and their right to appeal was declared forfeited.

French case-law and a 2010 Constitutional Council decision confirmed that Article 365’s mechanism for sharing parental responsibility applied only to married spouses. Same-sex couples could enter a civil partnership, but that status did not create adoption or parental responsibility rights comparable to marriage.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Gas and Dubois alleged discrimination based on sexual orientation, relying on Article 14 taken together with Article 8. They argued that no legal means existed in France for same-sex couples to access second-parent adoption, whereas heterosexual married couples could adopt a spouse’s child and share parental responsibility. They relied on their established family life with A. and the refusal to give that family relationship legal recognition through adoption.

The Government argued that Article 8 did not guarantee a right to adopt or to create legal ties, so Article 14 could not apply. The Court held, however, that the applicants had “family life” within Article 8 and that sexual orientation fell within the personal sphere protected by that Article. The facts therefore came within the ambit of Article 8, making Article 14 applicable, and the Government’s preliminary objection was dismissed.

The key alleged violation was thus not a complete ban on adoption by gay or lesbian individuals, but differential treatment between same-sex civil partners and married opposite-sex couples regarding access to simple, second-parent adoption of a partner’s child. The French refusals rested on the legal effects of simple adoption, the absence of a marriage tie, and the aim of protecting the child’s existing legal relationship with her biological mother. The ECtHR ultimately examined whether this difference in treatment was objectively justified and found no violation of Article 14 combined with Article 8.

The case of Gas and Dubois v. France concerned two French nationals, Ms Valérie Gas and Ms Nathalie Dubois, who had cohabited since 1989 and registered a civil partnership in 2002. In 2000, Ms Dubois gave birth in France to a daughter, A., conceived in Belgium through anonymous donor insemination. The child therefore had no legal tie to her biological father and lived all her life with both applicants.

In 2006, Ms Gas applied for a simple-adoption order in respect of her partner’s daughter, with Ms Dubois’s express consent. Under French law, simple adoption creates an additional legal parent-child relationship but, where the adoptee is a minor, normally vests parental responsibility in the adoptive parent alone. Article 365 of the Civil Code provides an exception allowing joint parental responsibility only where the adoptive parent is married to the child’s mother or father. Same-sex marriage was not available in France, and a civil partnership did not produce equivalent adoption or parental-responsibility effects.

The public prosecutor objected to the application. The Nanterre tribunal de grande instance found that the statutory conditions for adoption were met and that the applicants were jointly involved in the child’s upbringing, providing care and affection. It nevertheless refused the adoption because its legal effect would be to transfer parental responsibility to Ms Gas and deprive Ms Dubois, the birth mother, of her rights, contrary to the child’s interests and the applicants’ own intentions. The Versailles Court of Appeal upheld that refusal in December 2006. It accepted that Ms Gas contributed to the child’s emotional and material well-being, but held that the adoption would deprive Ms Dubois of all rights in relation to her child. It also considered that a later delegation or sharing of parental responsibility could not eliminate the risks and that the application essentially reflected the applicants’ wish to have their joint parenting recognised and legitimised. A further appeal to the Court of Cassation was declared forfeited.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged discrimination based on sexual orientation, relying on Article 14 of the Convention taken together with Article 8. They argued that no legal means existed in France allowing same-sex couples to access second-parent adoption, whereas heterosexual married couples could use Article 365 to allow one spouse to adopt the other’s child while sharing parental responsibility. They claimed this denied legal recognition of their family life and discriminated against them compared with heterosexual couples in a comparable situation.

The Government objected that Article 8 did not guarantee a right to adopt or to found a family, and that Article 14 therefore could not apply. The Court declared the application admissible. It found that examination of the applicants’ specific situation disclosed “family life” within the meaning of Article 8, and that sexual orientation fell within the personal sphere protected by Article 8. Consequently, the facts fell within the ambit of at least one Convention Article, making Article 14 applicable in conjunction with Article 8. The Court dismissed the Government’s preliminary objection and proceeded to the merits. Ultimately, the Court examined whether the refusal of second-parent adoption amounted to discriminatory treatment. The key alleged violation was that French law, by reserving joint parental responsibility following simple adoption to married spouses and excluding same-sex civil partners, treated the applicants differently on grounds of sexual orientation without sufficient justification, in breach of their right to respect for family life without discrimination.

In *Bajsultanov v. Austria* (ECtHR, First Section, 12 June 2012), the applicant was a Russian national of Chechen origin who arrived in Austria with his family in July 2003 and applied for asylum. He claimed he had supported Chechen fighters during the first war (1994–96), did not take part in the second war, and in 2003 was sought during a “cleaning operation”; his father was beaten and the family house burned. In 2005 the Austrian Independent Federal Asylum Panel granted him asylum, finding a real risk of ill-treatment in Chechnya. His wife was granted asylum in 2007, and his two children also received asylum.

The applicant was later convicted of several criminal offences: attempted theft in 2005; attempted resistance to public authority, aggravated damage to property, and aggravated bodily harm in 2006; and aggravated bodily harm in 2008, for which he received a twelve-month prison sentence and his probation was revoked. He was released in August 2009.

In 2008 the Federal Asylum Office lifted his asylum status and ordered his expulsion to the Russian Federation under the 2005 Asylum Act. It found that his convictions were final and concerned particularly serious offences, that he presented a danger to society, and that the public interest outweighed his interest in asylum protection. It also concluded that the security situation in Chechnya had improved and that he would not face a real risk of treatment contrary to Article 3. As regards family life, it found he had not integrated well into Austrian society and still had strong ties to Chechnya. The Asylum Court dismissed his appeal in 2009, and the Constitutional Court refused to hear his complaint in 2010.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that expulsion to Russia would violate Article 3 because he would face a real risk of ill-treatment, and Article 8 because it would separate him from his wife and two children, who had independent asylum status in Austria. The Court applied an interim measure under Rule 39 to stay his expulsion.

On Article 3, the Court accepted that country reports continued to show serious human rights problems in Chechnya, including risks for former rebels, their relatives, critics of the Kadyrov regime, human rights activists, and returnees. However, it found that the applicant’s individual circumstances did not establish a real and personal risk. His support role had ended in 1996; he had not fought in the second war; much time had passed; and his parents and six siblings had remained in Chechnya without reported harassment. He had maintained regular telephone contact with his father, suggesting he would have known of any reprisals. He provided no substantial new evidence. The Court also noted that the definition of a “particularly serious offence” was not decisive under Article 3, since the prohibition of ill-treatment is absolute, but no substantial grounds existed here. It found no violation of Article 3.

On Article 8, the applicant argued that his wife and children could not reasonably be expected to follow him to Russia because of their independent asylum status, making family life impossible. The Court accepted that the expulsion interfered with his family life, but held that the Austrian authorities had properly balanced the competing interests. Given his repeated violent offences, poor integration, and continued ties to Chechnya, the public interest in expulsion justified the interference. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 8.

**Bajsultanov v. Austria** (Application no. 54131/10, judgment of 12 June 2012) concerned a Russian national of Chechen origin whose asylum status in Austria was lifted after criminal convictions, leading to a planned expulsion to the Russian Federation. He alleged that expulsion would violate **Article 3** (real risk of ill-treatment) and **Article 8** (disruption of family life with his wife and two children in Austria).

The applicant arrived in Austria with his family on 25 July 2003 and immediately sought asylum. He claimed that he had supported Chechen fighters during the first Chechen war (1994–1996) but did not participate in the second war. In summer 2003, during a “cleaning operation,” mercenaries allegedly came looking for him based on a file created after the first war. When they did not find him, they beat his father, and the family’s house was later burned down. His father advised him to leave Chechnya. In 2005, the Austrian Independent Federal Asylum Panel granted him asylum, finding his account credible, the security situation in Chechnya dangerous, and no viable domestic alternative elsewhere in Russia. His wife was granted asylum in 2007; his daughter, born in 2004, and son, born in 2007, were also granted asylum in 2007. The family therefore had independent refugee status in Austria.

Between 2005 and 2008, the applicant was convicted of several offences: attempted theft (2005); attempted resistance to public authority, aggravated damage to property, and aggravated bodily harm (2006); and aggravated bodily harm (2008) for hitting a prostitute with a bottle. His final sentence was twelve months’ imprisonment, with an earlier probation order revoked. He served his sentences and was released in August 2009.

In October 2008, the Federal Asylum Office lifted his asylum status and ordered his expulsion to Russia. It found that his convictions were for particularly serious offences, that he was dangerous, and that the public interest outweighed his interest in protection. It also found that the situation in Chechnya had improved and that he faced no real Article 3 risk. In August 2009, the Asylum Court upheld that decision. It accepted that serious human rights problems persisted in Chechnya but found no general Article 3 risk and no individual risk because his role in the first war had been minor, his family remained in Chechnya without reported harassment, and he had weak integration in Austria. It also rejected his Article 8 claim, noting his continuing ties to Chechnya and his children’s adaptability. The Constitutional Court declined to hear his complaint.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant argued that the Austrian authorities had failed to properly assess the current risk in Chechnya and that returnees and former rebels faced ill-treatment. The Government argued that domestic authorities had thoroughly examined updated country information and his individual circumstances. The Court applied an interim measure under Rule 39 to stay his expulsion.

The European Court found the complaints admissible. On Article 3, it accepted that Chechnya remained unsafe and that returnees could face questioning, harassment, or worse. However, the applicant’s support role ended in 1996, he did not fight in the second war, and his close family remained in Chechnya without reported reprisals. There were therefore no substantial grounds to believe he faced a real personal risk of ill-treatment. The Court also noted that Russia is itself a High Contracting Party to the Convention. It found **no violation of Article 3**. On Article 8, although expulsion interfered with family life, the Court considered his serious repeated violent offences, weak integration, and the State’s right to control residence, and found the interference proportionate. It accordingly found **no violation of Article 8**.

The case concerns Ruslan Bajsultanov, a Russian national of Chechen origin, who arrived in Austria with his family in July 2003 and applied for asylum. He claimed that he had supported Chechen fighters during the first Chechen war (1994–96) and that in 2003 security forces conducting a “cleaning operation” sought him, beat his father, and burned the family home. In 2005 the Independent Federal Asylum Panel granted him asylum, finding that Chechnya remained unsafe, that there was no realistic domestic alternative, and that he faced a real risk of ill-treatment. His wife and two children later received independent asylum status in Austria.

The applicant was subsequently convicted of several criminal offences: attempted theft in 2005; attempted resistance to public authority, aggravated damage to property, and aggravated bodily harm in 2006; and aggravated bodily harm in 2008, for striking a prostitute with a bottle. He received custodial sentences, served them, and was released in August 2009. He then lived in Graz with his wife and children.

In October 2008 the Federal Asylum Office lifted his asylum status and ordered his expulsion to Russia under the 2005 Asylum Act. It relied on his convictions as “particularly serious offences,” found that the situation in Chechnya had improved, and concluded that he would not face a real Article 3 risk. It also held that his criminal record and weak integration meant the public interest outweighed his family-life interests. In August 2009 the Asylum Court dismissed his appeal, finding no general Article 3 risk in Chechnya, no individual risk because his role in the first war was minor and his family remained safe there, and no disproportionate Article 8 interference given his ties to Chechnya and his children’s adaptability. The Constitutional Court declined to hear his complaint in 2010.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that expulsion to Russia would violate Article 3 because he faced a real risk of ill-treatment, and Article 8 because it would separate him from his wife and two children, who had independent asylum status in Austria. The Court applied an interim measure under Rule 39 staying his expulsion.

On Article 3, the Court accepted that country reports still described serious abuses in Chechnya, including abductions, ill-treatment, impunity, and risks for returnees and alleged rebels’ relatives. However, it found that the applicant’s individual circumstances did not show substantial grounds for a real risk. His support role was in the first war, which ended in 1996; he did not participate in the second war; his parents and siblings remained in Chechnya without reported harassment; and he maintained regular contact with them. The Austrian authorities had obtained updated country information and thoroughly examined his case. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 3.

It nevertheless assessed whether the interference was justified under Article 8 § 2, taking into account the State’s right to control residence, the applicant’s criminal convictions, his limited integration, his remaining ties to Chechnya, and the family’s circumstances. In *Keskinen and Veljekset Keskinen Oy v. Finland* (Application no. 34721/09, ECtHR, 5 June 2012), the applicants were Vesa Petteri Keskinen and Veljekset Keskinen Oy, a Finnish limited liability company. In February 2005 they organised an ice-fishing competition on a rented lake. The entry fee was €20, and the lake had been stocked with 5,551 marked salmon. Prizes depended on the weight of the marked fish caught: €1 million for a 5-kg salmon, and gift certificates of €20,000, €2,000, and €200 for 3-kg, 2-kg, and 1-kg salmon respectively. More than 27,000 people participated, and 2,188 marked salmon were caught. The applicants had organised the event several times before.

The regulatory background was central. In 2003, the Ministry of the Interior had concluded that the competition was partly a lottery within the meaning of the Lotteries Act because prizes were awarded for catching marked salmon. That view was sent to the county administrative board and local police, but no legal consequences followed. Before the 2005 event, the Ministry again told the applicant company that the competition might constitute a lottery. The police were informed, and the applicants informed the police in advance. Although the police could have prohibited an illegal event, they did not do so.

In 2006, criminal proceedings were brought. The public prosecutor charged the first applicant with organising a lottery without a permit, arguing that the outcome was partly based on luck. The prosecutor also sought forfeiture of the profit gained by the applicant company. On 5 June 2006, the Seinäjoki District Court held an oral hearing and dismissed all charges and the forfeiture request. It found that the lottery had been illegal, but that the first applicant’s misinterpretation of the law was excusable because the provisions were unclear, similar events had been organised before, and the authorities had not prevented the event.

The prosecutor appealed to the Vaasa Appeal Court, reiterating the charges and requesting an oral hearing. He wanted two Ministry of the Interior civil servants heard about the Ministry’s role, the question of intent, and the applicants’ reactions to the Ministry’s queries and guidelines. He also argued that an oral hearing was needed to assess the evidence and the amount of profit for forfeiture. The applicants also appealed and requested an oral hearing. They wanted witnesses heard about the nature, content, and organisation of the competition, and the company’s financial manager heard about the financial outcome. If no hearing was held, they asked for an opportunity to submit further comments. Both parties had an opportunity to comment on the other’s appeal.

On 8 August 2007, the Vaasa Appeal Court refused to hold an oral hearing. It convicted the first applicant of breaching the lottery provisions and sentenced him to 50 day-fines, amounting to €13,300. It also ordered forfeiture of the company’s profit. The Appeal Court reasoned that the facts and background were undisputed, the written correspondence between the Ministry and the applicants was already in the District Court judgment, and the Ministry’s role as supervisory and expert authority was apparent from the Lotteries Act. It found that an oral hearing was not necessary and that further comments were not needed.

The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. They alleged that their right to a fair trial had been violated because the Appeal Court, without holding an oral hearing, convicted the first applicant and ordered forfeiture against the applicant company. The key issue was whether the Appeal Court could properly reverse an acquittal and impose criminal sanctions and forfeiture on the basis of the written record alone, despite the applicants’ requests to hear witnesses on disputed issues such as intent and the financial amount subject to forfeiture. The ECtHR found a violation of Article 6 § 1, holding that the lack of an oral hearing before the Appeal Court was not justified in the circumstances.

In *X v. Finland* (Application no. 34806/04), the applicant was a Finnish paediatrician, X, who continued in private practice after retirement. In 1995, V’s mother brought V to X, suspecting that V had been sexually abused by her father; X examined the child and took photographs. In 2000, V was taken into public care. In December 2000, V’s mother failed to return her to the support centre, and V stayed with her mother until found in April 2001. X examined V on 26 December 2000.

In April 2001, X was arrested as a suspect in depriving V of liberty from 16 December 2000. Her home and practice were searched; she was remanded in custody on 20 April and released on 25 April. A restraining order was issued in May 2001 but quashed in June 2001. In April 2002, X was charged with aggravated deprivation of liberty or, alternatively, aiding and abetting it. The prosecution alleged that her opinions, advice and actions contributed to the mother’s abduction of V and that X unlawfully isolated V. The trial was held in camera in October 2002. X rejected her appointed public defender and defended herself. The District Court rejected her requests to hear several witnesses relevant to the background of the charge.

In October 2002, the District Court ordered a psychiatric assessment of X and V’s mother. X went into hiding and failed to attend hospital, leading to detention orders in absentia. In October 2004, she was arrested and taken to Vanha Vaasa Hospital for assessment. Dr A.K. concluded that X suffered from delusional disorder, had not been criminally responsible at the time of the alleged offence, and needed a guardian for the criminal proceedings. In February 2005, the Forensic Psychiatry Board ordered involuntary treatment under the Mental Health Act. The District Court released X from detention, but she remained hospitalised.

X refused medication. From March 2005, she was forcibly injected with antipsychotics—first Zyprexa, then Risperdal Consta every two weeks—with dosage changes. She alleged an assault during forced medication in July 2005. She was moved to an open ward in November 2005, discharged in January 2006, and involuntary care officially ended in June 2006.

For Article 6, the key facts are that the Board found X’s capacity reduced and that she needed a guardian. On 2 March 2005, the District Court appointed her public defender, M.S., as guardian without an oral hearing, relying on the psychiatric assessment. X opposed this. Her appeals were rejected without an oral hearing, and the Supreme Court refused leave. She also complained that she could not examine witnesses appearing on her behalf.

For Articles 5 and 8, X alleged that her involuntary admission and forced medication were unlawful and unnecessary. She appealed the February 2005 confinement to the Supreme Administrative Court, which held an oral hearing in October 2005 but dismissed her appeal, finding reliable medical evidence that she was mentally ill, needed treatment, and that other services were inadequate. Later continuation decisions were upheld, some without oral hearings. X relied on contrary opinions from Drs K.A., E.P. and M-P.H., but they were not accepted.

For Article 13, X alleged no effective remedy against forced medication. She complained to the National Forensic Medical Authority, the Chancellor of Justice/Parliamentary Ombudsman, the police, and the State Provincial Office. The Authority found no deviation from accepted practice; the police closed the investigation; the Ombudsman declined because matters were pending elsewhere; and the State Provincial Office found no further measures necessary. Some decisions were not appealable.

X v. Finland (Application no. 34806/04) concerned a Finnish paediatrician, born in 1943, who continued private practice after retirement. The District Court released her from detention, but she remained hospitalised. Before the European Court of Human Rights, she alleged violations of Article 6 (no oral hearing on the need for a guardian, and no opportunity to examine witnesses on her behalf), Articles 5 and 8 (unnecessary and unlawful involuntary admission and forcible medication), and Article 13 (no effective remedy against forced medication).

Hardy and Maile v. the United Kingdom concerned the construction and operation of two liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminals at Milford Haven harbour. The applicants, Alison Hardy and Rodney Maile, were Milford Haven residents and members of Safe Haven, a local group opposed to the LNG developments. They complained under Articles 2 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that the United Kingdom had failed in its positive obligations to regulate hazardous activities adequately and to disseminate relevant safety information.

The terminals—the Dragon site (Petroplus) and the South Hook site (Qatar Petroleum/ExxonMobil)—required planning permission and hazardous substances consent. Applications made between 2002 and 2004 were publicised; environmental statements were prepared; local authorities consulted statutory bodies including the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) and the Milford Haven Port Authority (MHPA); and public comments were considered. Planning permissions and hazardous substances consents were granted between March 2003 and December 2004.

A central factual issue was the treatment of marine risks. The HSE assessed shore-side risks, such as storage, regasification and transfer of LNG to shore, but did not assess risks from LNG vessels at sea or while approaching or moored at the jetty. It stated that it had no legal competence over ships under the master’s direction. The Maritime and Coastguard Agency had a general maritime safety role, while MHPA had navigational jurisdiction over the waterway and responsibility for managing shipping movements. MHPA participated in extensive risk-assessment work, including marine traffic analyses, simulator trials, navigation risk assessments and collision/damage studies. It concluded that LNG vessels could be handled safely subject to conditions such as pilotage, tugs, weather limits and passing distances. However, MHPA refused to disclose several commissioned reports, citing commercial confidentiality. Local authority reports recorded public concern about the lack of a comprehensive quantitative risk assessment for tankers, the possibility of a ship collision at the jetty, and blurred responsibility between the HSE, MCA and MHPA. HSE’s chief executive later clarified that it had examined only shore-side operations and had advised local authorities to consult others about marine risks. MHPA explained that it operated an open-ports policy, had no say in site selection, and engaged in continuing risk assessment rather than producing a single “go/no-go” document.

In March 2005 the applicants sought judicial review of the planning permissions and hazardous substances consents. In July 2005 the High Court refused leave, finding the challenge was not prompt, involved undue delay and would cause substantial prejudice to the operators and detriment to good administration.

The European Court of Human Rights examined whether the United Kingdom’s regulatory framework and its practical implementation satisfied Articles 2 and 8. It found no violation. The Court considered that an adequate legislative and administrative framework existed for regulating the LNG terminals, assessing risks and providing information. The authorities had consulted and assessed hazards, and the applicants had not shown that the State failed to protect life or private life or to disseminate relevant information. The case is therefore important for the scope of positive obligations in environmental and hazardous-activity cases.

Planning permissions were granted for the Dragon site in 2003 and 2004 and for South Hook in 2003. Hazardous substances consents were granted in 2004.

Environmental statements considered operational safety, fire, explosion and marine risks. They referred to risk assessments, marine simulations and mitigation measures, and concluded that risks were tolerable or acceptable. However, the HSE assessed only shore-based risks. It stated that it had no legal competence to assess risks from ships at sea or under the shipmaster’s control, and advised local authorities to consult others, including the Maritime and Coastguard Agency (“MCA”). The MCA’s role concerned shipboard standards and Port State Control. MHPA had navigational jurisdiction over the Haven and participated in risk assessments, simulations, pilot training and reports. It accepted responsibility for managing shipping safely but said it could not refuse ships access under the UK’s “open ports” policy, only impose conditions. It refused to disclose several risk assessment reports, citing commercial confidentiality.

The applicants and other objectors raised concerns about the adequacy of marine risk assessment, the absence of a single overriding authority, possible conflicts between LNG ships and other vessels, and the need for public access to health and safety information. They alleged that the authorities failed to carry out a comprehensive environmental impact assessment of the project as a whole, failed to consider marine traffic risks and alternative locations, misunderstood LNG characteristics, and failed to disseminate relevant information.

In March 2005 the applicants sought judicial review of the planning permissions and hazardous substances consents. The High Court refused leave in July 2005 because the challenge was not brought promptly and was unduly delayed; most decisions were more than three months old and the applicants knew of them by August–October 2004. The court also found that quashing the decisions would cause substantial prejudice and hardship to the operators and be detrimental to good administration.

The European Court of Human Rights examined whether the UK had complied with its positive obligations under Articles 2 and 8 in regulating hazardous LNG activities and providing information. Key facts included the hazardous nature of LNG, public concern, the division of responsibility between the HSE, MCA and MHPA, the non-disclosure of MHPA risk reports, the public environmental statements and consultations, and the domestic delay. The Court ultimately found no violation of Articles 2 or 8, concluding that the State had not failed in its regulatory or information duties.

In *Hardy and Maile v. the United Kingdom* (App. no. 31965/07, judgment 14 February 2012), the applicants were two British nationals living in Milford Haven and members of “Safe Haven,” a local residents’ group opposed to two liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminals: the Dragon terminal, proposed by Petroplus, and the South Hook terminal, proposed by Qatar Petroleum and ExxonMobil. They alleged that the United Kingdom had failed in its positive obligations under Articles 2 and 8 of the Convention by inadequately regulating hazardous activities and by failing to disseminate information about the risks associated with the LNG terminals.

The factual background concerned the planning and hazardous-substances consent process for both sites. Construction and operation required planning permission and hazardous substances consent, with statutory consultation of bodies including the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) and the Milford Haven Port Authority (MHPA). The HSE assessed shore-based risks—LNG transfer to shore, storage, and regasification—but stated that it had no legal competence to assess risks from ships at sea or under the ship master’s control. It began preliminary work on marine spill scenarios but stopped because marine risks fell outside its remit. Responsibility for marine navigation and shipping safety rested with the MHPA, while the Maritime and Coastguard Agency had broader maritime regulatory functions.

For the Dragon site, planning permission was granted in March 2003, with extensions and amendments approved in September 2004; hazardous substances consent followed in December 2004. For South Hook, planning permissions were granted in November and December 2003, and hazardous substances consent in April and August 2004. Environmental statements and public consultations took place, and the HSE did not object on safety grounds. MHPA strongly supported both projects and said it had no safety or navigation concerns. However, objectors, including the applicants, complained about the absence of a comprehensive quantitative risk assessment for marine LNG risks and the lack of public access to risk information. Local authority reports acknowledged a possible gap: HSE covered shore-based activities, while MHPA and MCA were responsible for ship-related risks. MHPA later confirmed it had carried out and commissioned numerous risk assessments, simulations, and studies concerning LNG shipping, but refused disclosure of many reports, citing commercial confidentiality. It also stated that there was no single “go/no-go” document, because its role was to manage shipping safely within an “open ports” policy, not to decide whether LNG ships could use the port.

The applicants brought judicial review in March 2005, challenging the grants of planning permission and hazardous substances consent. They alleged failure to carry out a comprehensive environmental assessment, failure to consider marine traffic risks and alternative locations, and misunderstanding of LNG risks. In July 2005, the High Court refused leave, finding undue delay, prejudice to the terminal operators, and detriment to good administration. The ECtHR application was lodged on 24 July 2007. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore the division of regulatory responsibility, the HSE’s limited assessment of marine risks, MHPA’s extensive but undisclosed risk assessments, and the applicants’ claim that these gaps and non-disclosures breached the State’s duties to regulate hazardous activities and provide relevant risk information under Articles 2 and 8.

**Balogun v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 60286/09)**

**Background and Immigration History**

The applicant, Mr Moshood Abiola Balogun, a Nigerian national born in 1986, claimed to have arrived in the United Kingdom at age three. However, no official record of his presence existed until 1994, when he was eight, after a family court sought clarification of his immigration status during a residence order application by his aunt. In January 2003, his aunt applied for indefinite leave to remain with the applicant as her dependant. A separate application by Southwark Social Services stated the applicant had been thrown out by his aunt in January 2002 and placed in foster care, and alleged he had suffered beatings by his aunt and her boyfriend since age three. He was granted indefinite leave to remain outside the immigration rules in December 2003. He lived in foster care until eighteen, then in council accommodation.

**Criminal Convictions and Deportation Proceedings**

On 21 February 2007, at age twenty, the applicant was convicted of two counts of possession of Class A drugs with intent to supply. He pleaded guilty on the basis that he had been coerced into letting his premises be used for drug preparation and sale by a group he feared, following a 2005 shooting. He received three years' imprisonment. His prior record included possession of Class A and B drugs (February 2004), handling stolen goods (April 2004), and possession of Class C drugs (June 2005).

In October 2007, the Secretary of State notified him of the intention to deport him, finding no evidence of continuous presence since age three and only four years with valid leave. His appeal was dismissed by the Asylum and Immigration Tribunal in March 2008, which rejected claims of a serious relationship with his girlfriend, close ties to a second aunt (who was unaware of his conviction), and a meaningful relationship with his half-brother. The Tribunal found no protected family life and that his private life ties were insufficient to render deportation disproportionate. A deportation order was signed in October 2008; his human rights application was rejected in June 2009, and judicial review was refused in October 2009.

**Article 3 Complaint (Suicide Risk)**

Following the refusal of his human rights application, the applicant attempted suicide on 13 August 2009 and was diagnosed with moderate depression. He was detained on 10 November 2009 with removal directions set for 19 November. On 13 November 2009, he sought interim measures under Rule 39, which the Court granted, preventing expulsion pending its decision.

The Government submitted that the applicant failed to exhaust domestic remedies by not raising the suicide risk in his appeal or judicial review. The Court found it unnecessary to rule on exhaustion, as the complaint was manifestly ill-founded. It noted the high threshold for Article 3 in expulsion cases and the measures outlined by the Government: constant supervision if detained, trained medical escorts during removal, and adequate psychiatric care in Nigeria. The Court concluded there was no real and imminent risk of treatment reaching the Article 3 threshold.

**Article 8 Complaint (Private and Family Life)**

The applicant claimed deportation would breach his right to family and private life. The Court accepted he enjoyed private life in the UK but found no family life, given the Tribunal's findings regarding his girlfriend and relatives. The deportation was in accordance with law and pursued the legitimate aim of crime prevention.

Applying the *Üner* criteria, the Court noted the serious nature of the drug offence and that most offences were committed as an adult, distinguishing the case from *Maslov*. However, it accepted the applicant had resided in the UK since age three, was a settled migrant entitled to "very serious reasons" for expulsion, and had stronger social and cultural ties to the UK than Nigeria. Nonetheless, weighing his repeated drug-related offending and the careful consideration by domestic authorities, the Court found the interference with private life was not disproportionate. There was no violation of Article 8.

The applicant claimed he had arrived in the UK aged three, although the first official record of his presence was in 1994, when he was eight. He lived with an aunt; in 2002 social services stated that the aunt had thrown him out and he entered foster care, alleging beatings by the aunt and her boyfriend. In 2003 he was granted indefinite leave to remain outside the immigration rules. He had previous convictions, including drug and stolen-goods offences, and in February 2007 was convicted of two counts of possession of Class A drugs with intent to supply. He pleaded guilty on the basis that he had been coerced and feared a group after being shot in 2005. He received three years’ imprisonment. In October 2007 the Secretary of State notified him of the intention to deport him, finding no evidence he had been in the UK since age three, noting only four years with valid leave, believing his mother remained in Nigeria, and finding no family life and sufficient independence.

His appeal was dismissed in March 2008. The Asylum and Immigration Tribunal found that his claimed relationship with his girlfriend was not serious or permanent, that his ties to an aunt and half-brother were exaggerated, and that he had no protected family life; his private-life ties were insufficient to make deportation disproportionate. A deportation order was signed in October 2008. His human rights revocation request was refused in June 2009, and judicial review was refused in October 2009. In November 2009 he was detained and removal directions set. He applied to the ECtHR and obtained a Rule 39 interim measure. A psychiatric report stated that he had attempted suicide in August 2009 after refusal of his human rights claim and suffered moderate depression.

On Article 3, the applicant alleged deportation would expose him to a real risk of suicide and inhuman or degrading treatment. The Government said it had safeguards in detention, would use trained/medical escorts during removal, and that psychiatric care was available in Nigeria. The Court found the complaint manifestly ill-founded/inadmissible. Although suicide risk can engage Article 3, the threshold is high; adequate protective measures and available treatment in Nigeria meant no real and imminent risk of treatment reaching Article 3 severity.

On Article 8, the Court found no family life but accepted private life. The deportation was lawful and pursued crime prevention. Applying *Üner/Boultif*, it accepted he had likely lived in the UK since age three and was a settled migrant, with stronger UK social/cultural ties than Nigerian ties. However, his drug-supply offence was very serious, his offending was repeated and mostly adult, and public-interest considerations justified deportation. The interference with private life was therefore proportionate. There was no violation of Article 8.

**Case: Balogun v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 60286/09), European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, judgment 10 April 2012.**

The applicant, Moshood Abiola Balogun, a Nigerian national born in 1986, claimed to have arrived in the United Kingdom at age three, although the first official record of his presence was in 1994 when he was eight. He was placed in foster care after being thrown out by his aunt in 2002 and alleged abuse by her and her boyfriend from age three. In 2003 he was granted indefinite leave to remain outside the immigration rules. He lived independently in council accommodation from age eighteen.

His criminal record included convictions for drug and stolen goods offences. Most relevantly, on 21 February 2007, at age twenty, he was convicted of two counts of possession of Class A drugs with intent to supply and sentenced to three years’ imprisonment. He pleaded guilty, claiming coercion by people he feared after being shot in 2005. In October 2007 the Secretary of State notified him of an intention to deport him. His appeal was dismissed in March 2008; the Asylum and Immigration Tribunal found he had no protected family life in the UK and that deportation was proportionate. A deportation order was signed in October 2008. His human rights application to revoke it was refused in June 2009, and judicial review was refused in October 2009.

The alleged Article 3 violation concerned the risk of suicide upon deportation. A psychiatric report of 14 September 2009 stated that the applicant had attempted suicide on 13 August 2009 after refusal of his human rights claim and suffered moderate depression. He was detained on 10 November 2009, with removal set for 19 November. He sought interim measures under Rule 39, which the Court granted. The Government said it had not known of the suicide attempt but outlined precautions: constant supervision in detention, trained and medical escorts during removal, accompaniment to Nigeria, and available psychiatric care in Nigeria. The applicant later claimed a minor overdose on 29 December 2009; he was assessed and released in January 2010. The Court found the Article 3 complaint manifestly ill-founded. Although suicide risk could engage Article 3, the high threshold was not met because the UK authorities were aware of the risk and could be relied on to take adequate preventive measures at all three stages: detention, transit, and arrival. Adequate psychiatric care existed in Nigeria.

For Article 8, the applicant claimed family life with his girlfriend, aunt, and half-brother, and private life based on long residence, education, work, and ties to the UK. The domestic tribunal rejected family life, finding the girlfriend relationship not serious or permanent and the other relationships exaggerated. The Court accepted that deportation interfered with his private life. It was in accordance with law and pursued the legitimate aim of preventing crime. Applying Üner criteria, the Court accepted he had lived in the UK since age three and was a settled migrant, so very serious reasons were needed. His ties to the UK were stronger than to Nigeria. However, his drug offence was very serious, he had previous convictions, and most offences were committed as an adult. Considering the careful domestic consideration and his repeated drug-related offending, the interference was not disproportionate. The Court found no violation of Article 8.

In *Kaperzyński v. Poland* (Application no. 43206/07), the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) examined the applicant’s complaint under Article 10 of the Convention. The applicant, Przemysław Kaperzyński, a Polish national born in 1964, was at the material time editor-in-chief of the local weekly newspaper *Iławski Tydzień*.

On 17 October 2005, the newspaper published an article co-authored by the applicant, entitled “Municipality in danger; authorities fail to see problem.” The article concerned the sewage system in the Iława municipality. It alleged that the sanitary situation posed significant public health risks; that extensive investment was needed but funds were lacking; that municipal authorities were acting slowly and incompetently; that they prioritized saving money over preventing health risks; that water quality was unsatisfactory; and that the mayor, despite two terms in office, had failed to address the problems properly.

On the same day, the mayor of Iława sent a letter complaining about the article. Its first paragraph was ironic and questioned the applicant’s intentions, suggesting he had acted in his own personal interest. The mayor also criticized the article’s tone, doubted whether the newspaper had readers, and then requested publication of a rectification under section 31 § 1 read with section 32 of the Press Act 1984. He asserted that developing the sewage network was a municipal priority, listed completed projects from the previous five years and planned projects for 2007–2013, stated that water quality was monitored by appropriate services, and referred to modernization and overhaul projects.

The applicant neither replied to nor published the mayor’s letter. The municipality later brought a private bill of indictment against him before the Elbląg District Court for failure to publish a rectification or reply, an offence under section 46 § 1 of the Press Act. The applicant argued that the mayor’s letter could not reasonably be treated as a rectification: it was not factual or objective, contained personal criticism and innuendo, resembled a “reply,” exceeded the permitted length, and infringed his and other journalists’ personal rights. He also relied on section 33 of the Press Act, which required refusal of publication if the content was incompatible with principles of social coexistence.

On 13 December 2006, the District Court found the applicant guilty. It held that he was clearly obliged to publish the letter as a rectification or reply, knew of that obligation, and had no objective grounds for refusing. It emphasized that he neither published the letter nor explained his refusal. He was sentenced to four months’ restriction of liberty, in the form of twenty hours’ community service per month, suspended for two years; deprived of the right to practise journalism for two years; and the judgment was ordered to be displayed at the Iława Municipal Office. The court reasoned that his failure prevented a fair public debate and undermined confidence in the democratically elected municipal executive. On 29 March 2007, the Elbląg Regional Court upheld the judgment.

Relevant domestic law under the Press Act obliged an editor-in-chief to publish, free of charge, a factually based rectification of untrue or inaccurate statements, or a factually based reply to material infringing personal rights. Section 46 criminalized refusal. Constitutional Court judgments in 2004 and 2010 found related provisions imprecise; in 2010, sections 46 § 1, 31, and 32 § 1 were declared incompatible with Article 46 of the Polish Constitution, though they remained applicable for up to eighteen months. The applicant alleged that his criminal conviction for refusing to publish the mayor’s letter breached his right to freedom of expression under Article 10.

The first paragraph was ironic, questioning the applicant’s intentions, suggesting personal interest, and doubting whether the newspaper had readers. The mayor then invoked the Press Act 1984 and requested publication of a rectification. He asserted that sewage development was a priority, listed projects undertaken in the previous five years and planned for 2007–2013, and stated that water quality was monitored by the appropriate services. The applicant neither replied nor published the letter.

The Iława municipality brought a private bill of indictment against the applicant under section 46 § 1 of the Press Act for failing to publish a rectification or reply required by section 31. The applicant argued that the mayor’s letter was not a valid rectification request: it lacked a factual and objective character; contained innuendoes and attacks on his and other journalists’ professionalism and integrity; and was more than twice the length of the contested article. He contended it was more like a “reply” expressing the mayor’s value judgments and should have been refused under section 33 because its form and content were incompatible with principles of social coexistence.

On 13 December 2006, the Elbląg District Court convicted the applicant. It found he was obliged to publish the letter or at least explain his refusal. It noted that he knew his obligations from previous rectifications and that no objective grounds prevented compliance. The court sentenced him to four months’ restriction of liberty, in the form of twenty hours’ community service per month, suspended for two years; deprived him of the right to practise as a journalist for two years; and ordered the judgment displayed at the Iława Municipal Office. The court reasoned that the failure harmed the municipality by preventing fair public debate and undermining confidence in the democratically elected executive. On 29 March 2007, the Elbląg Regional Court upheld the conviction.

The applicant alleged before the European Court of Human Rights that this criminal conviction breached his right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention. The key issue was whether the State could criminally punish an editor-in-chief for refusing to publish a mayor’s requested rectification or reply concerning a newspaper article on a matter of public interest. Relevant domestic law included Press Act sections 31–33 and 46. Section 31 required publication of a factually based rectification of untrue or inaccurate statements, or a factually based reply to statements infringing personal rights. Section 33 required refusal if those requirements were not met, together with written notice of the reasons. Section 46 criminalized refusal. The Constitutional Court had noted serious practical difficulties in classifying requests as “rectification” or “reply,” and later found certain provisions, including section 46 § 1, unconstitutional for lack of precision, with delayed effect.

On 17 October 2005 the newspaper published an article co-authored by him, “Municipality in danger; authorities fail to see problem.” It concerned the sewage and sanitation situation in the Iława municipality. It alleged serious public-health risks, insufficient investment and funds, slow and incompetent municipal action, unsatisfactory water quality, and that the mayor had failed to solve the problems despite two terms in office.

The same day, the mayor of Iława wrote to the newspaper complaining about the article. The letter was partly ironic, questioned the applicant’s intentions and suggested personal interest, criticised the article’s tone, and doubted whether the newspaper had readers. Relying on sections 31 § 1 and 32 of the 1984 Press Act, the mayor requested publication of a rectification. He asserted that developing the sewage network was a priority, listed projects from the previous five years and planned for 2007–2013, and said water quality was monitored and systems were being modernised.

The Iława municipality brought a private bill of indictment against him for failure to publish a rectification or reply under section 46 § 1 of the Press Act. The applicant argued that the mayor’s letter was not a valid rectification request: it was not factual or objective, contained personal attacks and innuendo, resembled a value-laden “reply,” and was more than twice the length of the article, contrary to section 33. He also claimed it infringed his and other journalists’ personal rights, making refusal justified.

On 13 December 2006 the Elbląg District Court convicted him under section 46 § 1 read with section 31 § 1. It sentenced him to four months’ restriction of liberty, consisting of twenty hours’ community service per month, suspended for two years; deprived him of the right to practise journalism for two years; and ordered the judgment displayed at the Iława Municipal Office. The court found that he was obliged to publish the mayor’s letter as a rectification or reply, knew of the obligation, and had no objective grounds for refusing. He also did not explain his refusal to the mayor. The court reasoned that the article raised an important public issue and that a diligent editor should have published the rectification or given reasons for refusal. The failure, it said, prevented fair public debate and undermined confidence in the democratically elected municipal executive. On 29 March 2007 the Elbląg Regional Court upheld the conviction.
