**Summary of the Case of Vidgen v. the Netherlands**

The case of *Vidgen v. the Netherlands* (Application no. 29353/06) concerns an allegation that a criminal conviction was based to a decisive extent on the statements of a witness whom the applicant was unable to effectively cross-examine, thus violating Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (d) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant, Mr. Nicholas Otto Vidgen, a British national, was convicted by the Utrecht Regional Court on 5 September 2003 as a co-perpetrator in the transport of ecstasy (XTC) from the Netherlands to Australia. The drugs were to be hidden in motor car engines shipped to a business, H. Autosport, which the applicant had set up in Sydney. He was sentenced to five years' imprisonment.

The applicant did not deny his involvement in shipping the engines but consistently maintained he had no knowledge of the drugs being smuggled inside them, denying any criminal intent. His conviction, therefore, hinged on proving this intent.

The primary evidence against him consisted of statements made by a co-suspect named M. to German prosecutors and later to Dutch police. M. had made a full confession implicating several individuals, including the applicant. The applicant had no opportunity to question M. when these initial statements were made. Although M. was later questioned before the Amsterdam Court of Appeal on 6 August 2004, he repeatedly invoked his right not to testify, citing pending proceedings against him in the Netherlands. He refused to answer substantive questions, making the cross-examination futile for the defence.

Despite this, the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal on 13 December 2004. It ruled that M.'s refusal to testify did not, in itself, violate the applicant's rights, as long as his earlier statements were largely corroborated by other evidence. The court found this corroboration existed, citing the confession of another co-suspect (A.), intercepted telephone conversations, and the applicant's own admission of his business operations in Australia. However, the supporting evidence largely implicated others in the smuggling operation without directly establishing the applicant's criminal intent. The Supreme Court upheld this decision on 6 June 2006.

The essential facts for the alleged violation centre on whether the conviction was based "solely or to a decisive extent" on M.'s untested statements. The applicant argued that his criminal intent, the sole point of dispute in the case, was proven only through M.'s testimony, which he could not challenge. The statements were central to proving the applicant's knowledge and role in the drug smuggling conspiracy, as opposed to merely shipping engines. The European Court of Human Rights was therefore tasked with assessing whether the use of this untested, decisive evidence, coupled with the lack of sufficient counterbalancing factors, rendered the trial as a whole unfair under the Convention.

In *Vidgen v. the Netherlands* (ECtHR, 10 July 2012), the applicant, Nicholas Otto Vidgen, a British national, was convicted by the Utrecht Regional Court on 5 September 2003 as a co-perpetrator of transporting MDMA/XTC from the Netherlands to Germany, intended for eventual shipment to Australia. The drugs were hidden in car engines sent to H. Autosport in Sydney, a business the applicant had set up. He was sentenced to five years’ imprisonment. Vidgen admitted involvement in shipping engines but denied knowing they were used to smuggle XTC and denied any criminal intent.

The prosecution’s case on intent relied heavily on statements by M., a co-accused who had been convicted in Germany. M. had given detailed confessions to German prosecutors and later to Netherlands police, implicating Vidgen. Vidgen and his counsel were not present when M. made these statements. Although attempts were made to question M. in Germany, the German investigating judge conducted the questioning and M. refused to answer or repeat his statements. Vidgen repeatedly requested an opportunity to put his own questions to M.

At trial, the Regional Court admitted M.’s statements and German trial records. It found that Vidgen had been able to question M. twice—without specifying when or where—and that M.’s refusal to testify did not breach Article 6. It also found M.’s statements sufficiently supported by other evidence. Vidgen appealed.

Before the Amsterdam Court of Appeal, A. and M. were summoned. At the hearing on 6 August 2004, A. denied involvement, invoked his right not to testify, and said M. had lied. M. admitted being questioned by Dutch police and having a prior perjury conviction, but refused substantive questions, invoking his privilege against self-incrimination due to pending extradition/proceedings in the Netherlands. The Court of Appeal dismissed Vidgen’s appeal. It held that M.’s refusal did not automatically violate the defence’s right to examine him; M. had at least confirmed making the police statements. The court required M.’s confessions to be “largely corroborated” on disputed points and found sufficient support from A.’s German confession, intercepted communications, engine discoveries, and the handwritten note. The Supreme Court later dismissed Vidgen’s cassation appeal, finding no Article 6 § 3(d) violation because M. appeared and could be questioned, though it reduced the sentence by six months for excessive cassation length.

The alleged violation concerned Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d): Vidgen’s conviction was said to be based solely or decisively on M.’s statements, which he had no effective opportunity to examine. The ECtHR agreed that M.’s statements to German police were the only evidence connecting Vidgen to criminal intent regarding the XTC. Other evidence implicated others or showed only lawful engine shipping and business activity. The Court thus found M.’s untested statements were the “sole” evidence of criminal intent and “decisive” for the conviction. Although reasonable attempts had been made to allow questioning, M.’s persistent silence made questioning futile, and there were no effective counterbalancing procedural safeguards. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d).

# Summary of Vidgen v. the Netherlands (Application no. 29353/06)

**Judgment: 10 July 2012**

The applicant, Nicholas Otto Vidgen, a British national born in 1958, was convicted on 5 September 2003 by the Utrecht Regional Court as a co-perpetrator in the transportation of MDMA (ecstasy) tablets from the Netherlands to Germany, intended for ultimate shipment to Australia. He was sentenced to five years' imprisonment. The tablets were concealed in car engine cylinders and crankcases destined for H. Autosport in Sydney, a business the applicant had established to import engine parts from Europe.

At trial, the applicant did not deny involvement in shipping engines to his Australian business but denied all knowledge that they were being used to smuggle ecstasy, thus denying criminal intent. The prosecution's case rested significantly on statements made by M., a co-accused, to German prosecutors and Netherlands police investigators during the pre-trial stage. M. had made full confessions implicating the applicant, including regarding a handwritten note bearing the H. Autosport address found in his dwelling.

The applicant repeatedly requested to question M., as neither he nor his counsel had been present when M. made these statements. Although the applicant traveled to Germany to question the witnesses, the German investigating judge conducted all questioning, and M. refused to answer questions or repeat his earlier statements. At the Court of Appeal hearing on 6 August 2004, M. was questioned but invoked his right not to testify due to pending extradition proceedings in the Netherlands. He did confirm having made the statements recorded by police but refused substantive questioning. Co-accused A. also invoked his right not to testify and claimed M.'s statements were lies.

The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 13 December 2004, finding that M.'s refusal to testify did not violate the applicant's rights and that M.'s statements were sufficiently corroborated by other evidence. The Supreme Court upheld this on 6 June 2006, noting M. had appeared at the hearing and the applicant could have questioned him, though M. invoked his right not to testify. The Supreme Court reduced the sentence by six months due to excessive cassation proceedings.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d), claiming his conviction was based solely or decisively on statements by a witness he could not examine.

The Court examined the evidence and found that of the 21 items relied upon, only four mentioned the applicant. Only M.'s statements connected him to the smuggling attempt; the others merely established his business activities in Australia and that he had met A. The remaining seventeen items implicated various individuals but not the applicant. Consequently, the Court concluded that M.'s statements were the "sole" evidence of the applicant's criminal intent and thus "decisive" for his conviction. While reasonable attempts were made to allow questioning, M.'s persistence in remaining silent rendered questioning futile. The handicaps under which the defence laboured were not offset by effective counterbalancing procedural measures.

Solomakhin v. Ukraine (no. 24429/03) is a European Court of Human Rights judgment delivered on 15 March 2012. The applicant, Mr Sergey Solomakhin, a Ukrainian national from Donetsk, alleged that court proceedings in his case were excessively lengthy and that his health suffered due to medical malpractice. After his death in September 2010, his mother pursued the application.

In November 1998 the applicant sought treatment at Donetsk City Hospital No. 16 and was diagnosed with an acute respiratory disease. On 27 November he was tested for reaction to diphtheria vaccination, and on 28 November he was vaccinated against diphtheria. He claimed the vaccination was contraindicated, was administered while he was ill and against his will, and involved poor-quality, uncertified, expired and improperly stored vaccine. Afterward, he developed chronic conditions, including pancreatitis, cholecystitis, hepatitis and colitis, and spent more than six months in medical institutions from late December 1998. On 4 February 1999 the hospital’s chief doctor reprimanded a doctor and nurse for vaccinating him despite his objections and while he was being treated for an acute respiratory infection, finding that vaccination rules had been violated.

In April 1999 the applicant sued the local public health department and the hospital, seeking compensation. He alleged the vaccination caused his chronic diseases, that medical records were falsified and that negative effects were concealed. Several medical expert examinations were conducted between 2000 and 2003. In June 2003 the domestic court dismissed his claim. It found no causal link between the vaccination and his diseases; only urticaria appeared more than eight months later and was unrelated. It noted he had no acute symptoms at vaccination, the epidemic situation justified diphtheria vaccination, no physical force was used, and as an adult he could have refused. The vaccination was performed outside the vaccination room, but by a qualified nurse in a doctor’s presence after prior testing and caused no negative side-effects. Allegations about vaccine quality and falsified records were unsubstantiated. Appeals were rejected in March and August 2008.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 about the length of proceedings and, in substance, about health damage from medical malpractice, which the Court examined under Article 8. On Article 6, the proceedings lasted from 26 April 1999 to 22 August 2008—nine years and almost four months across three levels. The Government argued the case was complex because of expert examinations. The Court found a violation: although complex, the length, including almost five years before the court of appeal, was not justified.

On Article 8, the Court held that physical integrity falls within “private life” and that compulsory vaccination—an involuntary medical treatment—interferes with Article 8 § 1. The parties agreed there was an interference. The Government argued it was justified under the 1994 Health Act and guidelines, pursuing protection of public health against diphtheria amid a serious epidemiological situation. The Court accepted that the interference was provided by law and pursued a legitimate aim. It found the interference necessary: medical staff checked suitability, the applicant could have refused as he had before, and no evidence showed the vaccination harmed his health. Domestic courts thoroughly examined the evidence and relied on expert reports; their findings were not arbitrary. There was therefore no violation of Article 8.

In *Solomakhin v. Ukraine* (no. 24429/03, 15 March 2012), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints about excessive length of civil proceedings and compulsory vaccination/medical malpractice. The applicant, Sergey Solomakhin, a Ukrainian national, died in September 2010; his mother pursued the application.

The key facts concerned events in 1998–1999. On 23 November 1998 the applicant sought treatment at Donetsk City Hospital No. 16 and was diagnosed with an acute respiratory disease. On 27 November he was tested for reaction to diphtheria vaccination; the test showed no susceptibility to diphtheria antigens. On 28 November he was vaccinated against diphtheria, despite claiming the vaccination was contraindicated. On 30 November a doctor noted improvement and diagnosed tracheobronchitis, later confirmed. From 28 December 1998 he spent over half a year in various medical institutions for chronic diseases such as pancreatitis, cholecystitis, hepatitis and colitis. On 4 February 1999 the hospital’s chief doctor reprimanded a doctor and nurse for vaccinating the applicant although he had objected and was being treated for an acute respiratory infection, finding that vaccination rules had been violated.

On 26 April 1999 the applicant sued the local public health department and the hospital in the Budyonnovskiy District Court, seeking compensation for damage to his health. He alleged that the vaccination while he was ill caused chronic diseases; that the vaccine was uncertified, expired, of poor quality and improperly stored; and that doctors falsified medical records to conceal negative effects. Several medical expert examinations were conducted between 2000 and 2003. On 2 June 2003 the court dismissed his claim. Relying on expert conclusions, it found no causal link between the vaccination and his diseases. Only urticaria appeared more than eight months later and could not be linked. It found no acute symptoms at vaccination, no violation of medical rules, and that the epidemic situation required diphtheria vaccination. No physical force was used, and the applicant, an adult, could have refused as he had previously. The vaccination was performed outside the vaccination room, but by a qualified nurse in a doctor’s presence after checking his reaction, and caused no side effects. Allegations about vaccine quality were speculative, and falsification claims unsubstantiated. Appeals were dismissed on 19 March 2008 and 22 August 2008.

At the ECHR, the application was lodged on 22 July 2003. On 6 May 2008 the Court partly declared it inadmissible and communicated the Article 6 length complaint and Article 8 complaint. Under Article 6, the proceedings lasted from 26 April 1999 to 22 August 2008—nine years and almost four months over three levels. Although the Government argued the case was complex due to expert examination, the Court found a violation because the complexity could not justify the delay, including almost five years before the court of appeal.

Under Article 8, the applicant complained of health damage from medical malpractice. The Court treated compulsory vaccination as an interference with private life/physical integrity. The Government conceded interference but argued it was lawful and justified by public health protection against diphtheria, the epidemiological situation, and the absence of force. The Court found the interference lawful and legitimate. Medical staff had checked suitability; the applicant failed to explain why he did not object; there was no evidence the vaccination harmed his health; and domestic findings based on expert reports were not arbitrary. The only irregularity—vaccination outside the special room—did not affect health. Thus, the Court found no violation of Article 8, but a violation of Article 6 § 1.

The case *Solomakhin v. Ukraine* (Application no. 24429/03, ECtHR, 15 March 2012) concerned a Ukrainian applicant who alleged that court proceedings in his civil case were excessively lengthy and that medical malpractice had damaged his health. The applicant died in 2010, and his mother pursued the application before the Court.

In November 1998, the applicant sought treatment at Donetsk City Hospital No. 16 and was diagnosed with an acute respiratory disease. On 27 November 1998 he was tested for a reaction to diphtheria vaccination. On 28 November 1998 he was vaccinated against diphtheria. The applicant claimed that the vaccination had been contraindicated, administered while he was ill and against his will, and that the vaccine was uncertified, expired, and improperly stored. He alleged that it caused chronic diseases including pancreatitis, cholecystitis, hepatitis, and colitis. On 4 February 1999, the hospital’s chief doctor reprimanded a doctor and nurse for vaccinating the applicant despite his objections and while he was being treated for an acute respiratory infection, finding that vaccination rules had been violated.

In April 1999, the applicant sued the local health department and the hospital, seeking compensation for damage to his health. Between 2000 and 2003, several medical expert examinations were conducted. In June 2003, the Budyonnovskiy District Court dismissed his claim. Relying on expert conclusions, the court found no causal link between the vaccination and his diseases. The only condition possibly associated with vaccination, urticaria, appeared more than eight months later and could not be linked. The court found that the applicant had no acute symptoms at the time of vaccination and that the epidemic situation in Donetsk required diphtheria vaccination. It noted that he was an adult of sound mind and could have refused, as he had previously done. Although the vaccination was not performed in the vaccination room, it was administered by a qualified nurse in a doctor’s presence after prior verification, and caused no negative side-effects. Allegations about vaccine quality were speculative, and claims of falsified medical records were unsubstantiated. The Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court upheld the judgment in 2008.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 about the length of proceedings and under Article 8 about damage to his health from medical malpractice. On the length complaint, the Court noted that the proceedings lasted from 26 April 1999 to 22 August 2008—nine years and almost four months across three levels of jurisdiction, including almost five years before the court of appeal. Although the case was complex and required medical expert examination, the Court found that this did not justify the total delay. It therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1.

On the health complaint under Article 8, the Court treated compulsory vaccination as an interference with private life and physical integrity. The Government conceded interference but argued it was lawful and justified by public health concerns. The Court accepted that the interference was provided by law and pursued the legitimate aim of protecting health. It was also necessary: public health considerations and the need to control infectious diseases justified it; medical staff had checked the applicant’s suitability; he could have objected; and there was no evidence that the vaccination harmed him. Domestic courts had thoroughly examined his allegations using multiple expert reports and found them unsubstantiated. The only procedural irregularity—vaccination outside the special room—did not affect his health. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 8.

**Aleksejeva v. Latvia** (Application no. 21780/07), European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, judgment of 3 July 2012, concerned a Latvian female prisoner who alleged violations of Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention.

The applicant, Jeļena Aleksejeva, was detained on 18 October 2006 in Iļģuciema Prison, Latvia’s only female prison. Her mother had worked there for about 25 years and, until 19 October 2006, was an assistant to the prison governor. Because the applicant was the relative of a prison employee, prison staff warned her that other prisoners might pose a danger if they learned of her family ties. A guard removed a photograph of her mother from her cell to prevent disclosure. The applicant said she lived in constant fear that her connection to her mother would be discovered, since prisoners were generally hostile toward relatives of prison, police, or court staff. She later alleged that an inmate, L.A., had used derogatory language and veiled threats toward her and implied that a prison staff member, T.J., had revealed her family relationship. Another former inmate, V.M., allegedly witnessed this but was afraid to provide written evidence.

The applicant was moved to a two-person cell and began her sentence in the lowest, most restrictive regime. In February 2007 she complained to the Ombudsman, asking for transfer to an open prison or isolation because her mother’s former employment could endanger her. A deputy governor told her separation from other prisoners was impossible unless she was kept in complete isolation, which both agreed would amount to additional punishment. Before an April 2007 commission hearing about transfer to the medium regime, she signed a pre-typed form waiving legal representation and added in her own hand that she did not object to sharing a cell if transferred. In May 2007 she was transferred to the medium regime and placed with first-time prisoners for safety reasons. In August 2007 the Ombudsman found sufficient safeguards and no threat to her life or health. The Government argued that her Article 3 complaint was hypothetical and unsupported, while she argued that Latvia’s prison system could not properly separate vulnerable female prisoners and that her consent to sharing a cell had been given under duress or fraud.

As to Article 8, on 26 February 2007 the prison governor refused the applicant’s request for a long-term visit from a man she described as her partner. She was told that by law she could receive long-term visits from non-close relatives only if her close relatives did not visit her, and she was asked to prove her divorce from her husband. On 28 February 2007 an official confirmed the refusal despite a court statement that her divorce was pending. The applicant also said prison staff told her that visits from her mother would be “problematic” because other prisoners would discover their relationship. Her mother therefore did not visit, though the applicant used her four monthly phone calls to speak with her. After her divorce on 16 April 2007, between 26 April and 22 September 2007 she was allowed five long-term and six short-term visits from her partner. From 29 August to 5 September 2007 she was granted leave to visit her mother. In January 2008 she was transferred to Vecumnieki Open Prison and later released.

The case therefore centred on whether Latvia failed to protect the applicant from potential prisoner violence under Article 3 and whether the restrictions on visits from her partner and mother breached her right to respect for private and family life under Article 8.

The case originated in application no. 21780/07, lodged against Latvia by Latvian national Jeļena Aleksejeva on 13 April 2007. She alleged violations of Articles 3 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights: first, that the national authorities failed to protect her from potential attacks by other prisoners; second, that they violated her right to respect for private and family life by not allowing her to receive visits from her partner and her mother.

On 18 October 2006 the applicant was detained in Iļģuciema Prison, Latvia’s only female prison. Her mother had worked there for approximately twenty-five years and in 2006 was an assistant to the prison governor; she retired on 22 October 2006. On arrival, the applicant was allegedly told by the head of security that this was the first time a relative of a staff member had been detained there. She was advised to conceal this information because she might be in danger. A guard later removed a photo of her mother from her cell, explaining that it could reveal their relationship and endanger her. The applicant lived in constant fear that other detainees would discover her mother’s former employment, since prisoners were hostile towards relatives of prison, police or court staff. One inmate knew who her mother was; that inmate was released in 2007. The applicant later claimed that a former inmate, V.M., had witnessed another inmate, L.A., using derogatory language and veiled threats towards her, implying that she had learned of the applicant’s family ties from a prison staff member, T.J.

On 5 February 2007 the applicant complained to the Ombudsman, seeking transfer to an open prison or isolation because her situation could become dangerous. A deputy governor told her that separation from other prisoners was impossible unless she was kept in complete isolation, which both agreed would amount to additional punishment. On 12 April 2007, before a commission was to decide whether to transfer her to the medium regime, the applicant signed a pre-typed form waiving her right to a lawyer and added in her own hand that, if transferred, she did not object to sharing a cell. On 8 May 2007 she was transferred to the medium regime and placed with other prisoners; the Government said she was placed with first-time prisoners for safety reasons. In August 2007 the Ombudsman found sufficient safeguards and no threat to her life or health.

As to visits, on 26 February 2007 the prison governor refused her request for a long-term visit from a man she described as her partner. She was told that, by law, non-close relatives could receive long-term visits only if her close relatives did not visit her, and she was asked to prove her divorce. On 28 February a prison official maintained the refusal even though her divorce case was pending. The applicant’s mother did not visit because prison staff said it would be “problematic” and would reveal their relationship to other prisoners. The applicant used her monthly phone calls instead. After her divorce on 16 April 2007, between 26 April and 22 September 2007 she received five long-term and six short-term visits from her partner. In August–September 2007 she was granted leave to visit her mother. In January 2008 she was authorised to serve her sentence under the highest regime and transferred to Vecumnieki Open Prison; she was later released.

The relevant legal context included CPT standards on protecting prisoners from inter-prisoner violence and Latvian rules requiring separate detention for certain vulnerable detainees, including former law-enforcement or judicial staff and their close relatives, though that provision applied to detainees whose conviction was not final. The Government argued that the Article 3 complaint was hypothetical and unsupported by credible evidence, while the applicant claimed the system could not separate vulnerable female prisoners and that her consent had been given under duress. The Article 8 complaint concerned the restrictions on visits from her partner and mother.

In *Aleksejeva v. Latvia* (Application no. 21780/07), the applicant, a Latvian national, complained under Articles 3 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. She alleged that prison authorities failed to protect her from potential attacks by other prisoners and violated her private and family life by refusing visits from her partner and effectively preventing visits from her mother.

**Article 3 facts.** On 18 October 2006 the applicant was detained in Iļģuciema Prison, Latvia’s only female prison. Her mother had worked there for about 25 years and was assistant to the prison governor until 19 October 2006, retiring shortly afterwards. On arrival, the head of security allegedly told the applicant that this was the first time a staff member’s relative had been detained there and advised her to conceal the relationship because she might be in danger if other employees or detainees learned of it. The next day a guard removed a photo of her mother from her cell for the same reason.

The applicant served her sentence in the lowest, most restrictive regime. She was initially placed in a two-person cell with a former bailiff and later shared with another detainee. She encountered other prisoners during walks, cooking classes, showers and laundry visits. She claimed she lived in constant fear because prisoners generally held negative attitudes toward relatives of prison, police or court staff. One inmate knew who her mother was. She later alleged that a former inmate had witnessed another prisoner, L.A., using derogatory language and veiled threats toward her, implying she had learned of the applicant’s family ties from a prison staff member, T.J.

In February 2007 the applicant complained to the Ombudsman, seeking transfer to an open prison where she could be separated from other prisoners and where her mother’s former employment would not cause problems. A deputy governor told her that separation from other prisoners could only be ensured by complete isolation, which both agreed would amount to additional punishment. In April 2007, before a commission decided on her transfer to the medium regime, she signed a pre-typed form waiving legal representation and added in her own hand that she did not object to sharing a cell if transferred. In May 2007 she was transferred to the medium regime and placed with other prisoners, reportedly first-time prisoners for safety reasons. In August 2007 the Ombudsman found sufficient safeguards and no threat to her life or health. The Government argued that the authorities were aware of her situation, took protective measures, and that her complaints were hypothetical and unsupported. The applicant argued that Latvia’s prison system could not separate vulnerable female prisoners due to inadequate infrastructure and that her consent to sharing a cell was obtained under duress or by fraud.

**Article 8 facts.** In February 2007 the prison governor refused the applicant a long-term visit from her alleged partner, stating that non-close relatives could receive such visits only if close relatives did not visit; she was asked to prove her divorce. A prison official later maintained the refusal even though a court confirmed her divorce was pending. The applicant said prison staff told her that visits from her mother would be “problematic” because other prisoners would discover their relationship, so her mother did not visit. The applicant used her four monthly phone calls instead. After her divorce in April 2007, between late April and September 2007 she received five long-term and six short-term visits from her partner. In August–September 2007 she was granted leave to visit her mother. In January 2008 she was transferred to Vecumnieki Open Prison under the least restrictive regime and later released.

The relevant legal context included CPT standards on protecting prisoners from inter-prisoner violence, Latvian rules requiring separate detention of certain vulnerable detainees and their close relatives, and Sentence Enforcement Code provisions limiting long-term visits mainly to close relatives unless none visited.

**Case Summary: Boukrourou and Others v. France (Application no. 30059/15)**

This case originated from an application lodged against France by six family members of Mr. M.B., who died on 12 November 2009 following a police intervention. The applicants alleged violations of Articles 2 (right to life) and 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) of the European Convention on Human Rights, claiming the police used disproportionate force leading to their relative's death.

The key facts are as follows. M.B., a 41-year-old man with a known history of psychiatric disorders including paranoid psychosis, entered a pharmacy to exchange medicine. He became agitated, shouting incoherently, and the pharmacist, feeling threatened, called the police. Four police officers arrived at 4:53 p.m. They were aware M.B. suffered from psychiatric disorders. After M.B. refused repeated requests to leave, officers seized him, and a physical struggle ensued. On the pharmacy doorstep, he fell to the ground. While he continued to struggle, one officer struck him twice in the abdomen, described as "diversionary blows," to facilitate handcuffing. He was handcuffed with his hands in front.

The officers then forced the resisting M.B. into a police van. Inside the van, he continued to struggle. To restrain him, officers employed controversial techniques: one officer positioned himself across M.B.'s shoulders, another on his legs, and a third stood on his buttocks. He was attached to the van's interior fixtures with multiple pairs of handcuffs. Five minutes after arriving, at 4:58 p.m., the police requested assistance from the fire brigade and emergency medical services (SAMU), informing them M.B. was in a highly agitated state.

When paramedics arrived at 5:07 p.m., they found M.B. face down, restrained as described. He had calmed down, but his heart stopped. Despite immediate resuscitation efforts, he was pronounced dead at 6:02 p.m.

An autopsy and subsequent expert reports concluded that M.B.’s death was caused by sudden cardiac rhythm disorders triggered by a coronary spasm. This was attributed to "intense and prolonged emotional and physical stress" acting on a pre-existing, but unknown, severe heart condition (70% stenosis of a coronary artery). The experts ruled out mechanical asphyxia as the cause of death but noted traumatic injuries consistent with the force used.

The applicants argued the police were negligent for removing him when he was calm, used disproportionate force, and failed to properly account for his psychiatric vulnerability, causing fatal stress. The police officers were charged with manslaughter but were ultimately cleared. The investigating judges and the Court of Appeal found no case to answer, holding that while some restraint techniques were "objectionable," they were not the direct cause of death. Crucially, they found that the police could not have foreseen the fatal outcome as they were unaware of M.B.'s heart disease. The Court of Cassation dismissed the applicants' final appeal in November 2014.

Before the European Court, the applicants maintained that the force used and the failure to adapt their conduct to a vulnerable person violated the State’s positive obligation to protect life under Article 2. The French Government contended that the use of force was absolutely necessary and strictly proportionate to the threat posed by M.B., and that the officers promptly sought medical aid.

In *Boukrourou and Others v. France* (ECtHR, 16 November 2017), six family members of M.B. alleged violations of Articles 2 and 3 after M.B. died during a police intervention. M.B. suffered from serious psychiatric disorders, including delusional/paranoid psychosis, and regularly collected neuroleptic medication from a pharmacy in Valentigney. On 12 November 2009, he went to exchange medicine, became angry when staff explained that his medication had become less effective due to addiction, threw boxes, spoke incoherently about “night visits,” and threatened to file a complaint. The pharmacist asked staff to call the police, who were told that an individual with psychiatric disorders was causing an incident.

Four police officers arrived at 4:53 p.m. and repeatedly asked M.B. to leave. He refused. Officers seized him; a struggle followed. At the pharmacy entrance M.B. fell to the ground. Constable M. punched him twice in the solar plexus while trying to handcuff him, and M.B. was eventually handcuffed in front with interlinked handcuffs. Officers forced him into a police van. Inside, he continued struggling. Officer L. positioned himself over M.B.’s shoulders, while officers D. and M. restrained his legs and buttocks; one stood on his buttocks. At 4:58 p.m., five minutes after arriving, police requested the fire brigade and emergency medical service. The fire brigade arrived at 5:07 p.m.; police refused to transfer M.B. to them because he remained agitated. Firemen noted he had calmed, but his heart rate could not be measured and his breathing/circulation stopped. He was taken back into the pharmacy, where defibrillation and cardiac massage were attempted. An emergency doctor pronounced him dead at 6:02 p.m.

Expert reports concluded that M.B. likely died from heart failure caused by cardiac rhythm disorders/coronary spasm triggered by intense and prolonged emotional and physical stress, in a person with pre-existing 70% coronary artery stenosis. Experts ruled out mechanical asphyxia or chest compression as the direct cause and found that superficial injuries did not directly contribute to death. Witness accounts conflicted: pharmacists said police did not hit M.B.; a shopkeeper and her son alleged punches, kicks and truncheon blows; police described using taught “diversionary blows” and restraint techniques. The Ombudsman criticised the van immobilisation as dangerous, disproportionate and amounting to inhuman/degrading treatment under Article 3, recommending disciplinary action and better police training. A manslaughter investigation led to charges against four officers, but investigating judges found no case to answer; the Court of Appeal upheld that decision, and the Court of Cassation dismissed the family’s appeal.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants argued that police knew of M.B.’s psychiatric vulnerability but removed him when he was calm and no imminent danger existed, used force and dangerous restraint, prolonged his stress and caused decompensation of his heart condition. The Government argued that the force was absolutely necessary and proportionate, that there was no causal link to death, and that police promptly sought medical assistance. The Court examined Article 2 and found that the force was not intrinsically lethal. Even if a causal link could not be excluded, the fatal consequence was not foreseeable because police did not know of M.B.’s heart disease. As to the positive obligation to protect life, police knew he was vulnerable due to psychiatric disorder and had a duty of care, but they requested emergency assistance only five minutes after arriving and medical services responded quickly. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 2.

In *Boukrourou and Others v. France* (Application no. 30059/15, judgment of 16 November 2017), the European Court of Human Rights considered complaints brought by six French nationals, relatives of M.B., who died after a police intervention. The applicants alleged violations of Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention.

On 12 November 2009, M.B., who suffered from serious psychiatric disorders including delusional psychosis, went to a pharmacy in Valentigney. He became agitated, spoke incoherently, threw medicine boxes, accused the pharmacist of “night visits,” and refused to leave. The pharmacist called the police. Four officers arrived at 4:53 p.m., aware that M.B. had psychiatric disorders. They repeatedly asked him to leave. When he refused, officers seized him and a struggle followed. At the pharmacy entrance M.B. fell to the ground. Constable M. punched him twice in the solar plexus while attempting to handcuff him. M.B. was eventually handcuffed in front with two interlinking pairs of handcuffs. Officers then forced him into a police van. Inside, he continued struggling and shouting. He was restrained face down: one officer positioned himself across his shoulders, another held his legs, and another stood on his buttocks; he was also handcuffed to a fixed part of the van. At 4:58 p.m., only five minutes after arriving, the officers requested the fire brigade and SAMU. The fire brigade arrived at 5:07 p.m.; M.B.’s pulse could not be measured, his breathing stopped, and despite resuscitation he was pronounced dead at 6:02 p.m.

Medical evidence showed M.B. had pre-existing coronary heart disease with approximately 70% stenosis. The autopsy and expert reports ruled out mechanical asphyxia and concluded that death resulted from heart failure/cardiac rhythm disorders caused by a coronary spasm triggered by intense and prolonged emotional and physical stress. The injuries observed were not directly lethal. The Ombudsman criticized the police’s immobilisation and compression techniques in the van as dangerous and disproportionate, describing them as amounting to inhuman and degrading treatment. He recommended disciplinary proceedings and better training for dealing with mentally ill persons.

Domestic criminal proceedings for manslaughter were opened against the four officers. The investigating judges found no case to answer, holding that the force used was necessary and proportionate, that M.B.’s psychiatric state explained his agitation, and that the officers could not foresee the fatal combination of stress and unknown heart disease. The Court of Appeal upheld that decision, and the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicants’ appeal.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants argued that the police knew of M.B.’s psychiatric vulnerability, failed to exercise adequate vigilance, unnecessarily removed him from the pharmacy, used punches and dangerous restraint techniques, and thereby caused or hastened his death. The Government maintained that the force was absolutely necessary and proportionate, that no causal link existed, and that the officers promptly sought medical assistance.

The Court examined Article 2. It accepted that the force was not intrinsically lethal but could not exclude that the restraint contributed to death. However, the fatal consequence was not foreseeable because, although the officers knew M.B. had a psychiatric disorder, they did not know he had heart disease. As to the positive obligation to protect life, the Court found that the police, aware of his vulnerability, had a duty of care, but they requested emergency help only five minutes after arriving and medical services attended promptly. The authorities therefore did not fail in their obligation to protect M.B.’s life. The extract primarily addresses Article 2, while the application also alleged Article 3.

J.M. v. Denmark (App. no. 34421/09) concerned a Danish national born in 1991. On 13 September 2007, aged 15, he was arrested in Greenland and charged with rape and homicide committed on 26 May 2007 in Aalborg against an 85-year-old woman. The case attracted massive media coverage. He pleaded guilty from the outset. He was ordered into pre-trial detention, then transferred to Denmark and placed, under section 765 of the Administration of Justice Act, in a closed young offender institution and later in “Grenen”, a secure institution for 12–17-year-olds.

His detention was extended about every four weeks under section 762(2)(i), based on strong suspicion of an offence carrying at least six years’ imprisonment and the need, for law-enforcement/public-interest reasons, that he not be at large. After 1 July 2008, section 768a(2)(ii) also applied, limiting continuous pre-trial detention of juveniles under 18 for such offences to eight months unless “very special circumstances” existed.

Progress depended largely on forensic psychiatric examinations. A first report in January 2008 found him covered by Penal Code section 16(2) and recommended placement in an institution for persons with extensive mental disabilities; the Medico-Legal Council agreed. However, in April 2008 the Joint Council for the Mentally Disabled found the documentation inadequate and urged further examination. A second report was requested. In November 2008 it was submitted, and in December 2008 the Medico-Legal Council concluded that section 16(2) did not apply but that section 69 did, recommending structured socio-psychiatric treatment or ordinary punishment if unavailable. Trial was postponed until January 2009.

On 11 September 2008, after nearly ten months’ detention, the applicant first objected, relying on the eight-month juvenile limit in section 768a(2)(ii). The City Court extended detention, finding “very special circumstances”: the admitted, very serious offences and the need to clarify the most expedient sanction both for society and for him. The High Court upheld that decision. Subsequent extensions in November and December 2008 relied on similar reasons, including the need to obtain the second Medico-Legal Council opinion. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused. On 27 January 2009 he was convicted and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. Total pre-trial detention was one year, four months and fourteen days.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, J.M. complained under Article 5 §3 that the length of his detention on remand was excessive and routinely extended, especially after 1 July 2008 when it exceeded the eight-month juvenile limit, and that the psychiatric examination process lasted too long. He also raised Article 5 §1 in substance, but that complaint was rejected for non-exhaustion because he had not raised it in the domestic courts.

The Government argued that detention was justified by the gravity of the admitted rape and homicide, the public interest, and the need to complete mental-status examinations; releasing him would have offended public sense of justice. He was held in a less restrictive youth institution, and the authorities acted diligently with no significant inactivity. The Court agreed: the detention rested on relevant and sufficient grounds, the delay was due to complex but necessary psychiatric evaluations, the domestic courts regularly reviewed the detention, and after 1 July 2008 they expressly found very special circumstances under section 768a. The length was not excessive, and less restrictive measures and the applicant’s age were considered. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 5 §3.

Case J.M. v. Denmark (ECtHR, First Section, 13 Nov 2012) concerned a Danish national born 30 Nov 1991. On 13 Sep 2007, aged 15, he was arrested in Greenland and charged with rape and homicide committed on 26 May 2007 against an 85-year-old woman in Aalborg. The case received massive media coverage. J.M. pleaded guilty. He was initially remanded by Qaqortoq County Court, then transferred to Denmark. On 20 Sep 2007 Aalborg City Court extended detention under s.762(2)(i) of the Administration of Justice Act, ordered a forensic psychiatric examination, and directed placement in an appropriate home or institution. He was held in a closed young offender institution and then at “Grenen”, a secure institution for 12–17-year-olds. Detention was extended about every four weeks.

By Dec 2007 the investigation was largely complete, pending psychiatric assessment. In Jan 2008 the first forensic report concluded J.M. fell under s.16(2) of the Penal Code and recommended institutional placement. The Medico-Legal Council agreed in Mar 2008, but in Apr 2008 the Joint Council for the Mentally Disabled found the documentation inadequate and sought further examination. A second forensic report was therefore requested, delaying trial. On 1 July 2008, s.768a entered into force, limiting pre-trial detention of juveniles under 18 to eight months unless “very special circumstances” existed. By then J.M. had been detained almost 10 months. On 11 Sep 2008 he first objected, citing s.768a. The City Court extended detention, finding very special circumstances: the serious admitted offences and the need to clarify the appropriate sanction, both for society and for J.M. The High Court upheld that decision.

Further extensions followed. The second forensic report was submitted in Nov 2008. In Dec 2008 the Medico-Legal Council changed its conclusion, finding J.M. fell under s.69 (deficient development or mental impairment) rather than s.16(2), and recommended a structured socio-pedagogical measure or ordinary punishment. Trial began on 27 Jan 2009. J.M. was convicted and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. His pre-trial detention had lasted 1 year, 4 months and 14 days.

Before the ECtHR, J.M. alleged that the length of his detention on remand violated Article 5 §3. He also raised Article 5 §1(c)–(d), but that part was declared inadmissible for non-exhaustion because he had not raised it domestically. On the Article 5 §3 merits, the Court found no violation. It accepted that detention was justified by relevant and sufficient reasons: the gravity of the admitted rape and homicide, the public reaction/public sense of justice, and the need to complete complex psychiatric assessments to determine an appropriate sanction. The domestic courts regularly reviewed the detention; after s.768a entered into force, they expressly found “very special circumstances” and gave detailed reasons. There were no significant periods of inactivity. His age was considered, and he was placed in a secure youth institution rather than ordinary prison. In the circumstances, the length was not excessive, so there was no breach of Article 5 §3.

In *J.M. v. Denmark* (Application no. 34421/09, judgment 13 November 2012), the applicant was a Danish national born on 30 November 1991. On 13 September 2007, aged 15, he was arrested in Qaqortoq, Greenland, and charged with rape and homicide under the Danish Penal Code. The offences were committed on 26 May 2007 against an 85-year-old woman in Aalborg, where the applicant attended a youth school institution. The case received massive media coverage. The applicant pleaded guilty to both charges from the outset.

He was initially detained for four weeks in Greenland, then transferred to Denmark and brought before the Aalborg City Court. On 20 September 2007, the court extended his pre-trial detention, ordered a forensic psychiatric examination, and decided that he should be placed in an appropriate home or institution. He was placed first in a closed young offender institution and then in “Grenen,” a secure residential institution for young people aged 12–17. His detention was extended by four weeks repeatedly.

The investigation was largely complete by 21 December 2007 except for the psychiatric report. The first forensic psychiatric report in January 2008 concluded that the applicant fell under Article 16(2) of the Penal Code and recommended placement in an institution for persons with mental disabilities. The Medico-Legal Council broadly agreed in March 2008. However, the Joint Council for the Mentally Disabled found the documentation inadequate and requested further examination. A second forensic psychiatric report was submitted in November 2008, and in December 2008 the Medico-Legal Council concluded that the applicant fell under Article 69, recommending a structured socio-psychiatric measure or, if not feasible, ordinary punishment.

A key development was section 768a of the Administration of Justice Act, which entered into force on 1 July 2008. It limited pre-trial detention of juveniles under 18 to eight months for offences carrying six years’ imprisonment or more, unless “very special circumstances” existed. By then, the applicant had been detained almost 10 months. On 11 September 2008, he first objected to further extension. The City Court extended detention, finding very special circumstances: the admitted, very serious crimes; the need to clarify the most expedient sanction for society and the applicant; and the risk that release would offend the public sense of justice. The High Court upheld this. Further extensions followed, with the courts expressly stating that Article 5 § 3 was not breached. The trial began on 27 January 2009. The applicant was convicted and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. The High Court upheld the conviction and sentence on 4 June 2009. Total pre-trial detention lasted one year, four months and fourteen days.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 5 § 1(c)–(d) and Article 5 § 3. He argued that his pre-trial detention was excessively long, routinely extended, and that after 1 July 2008 he should have been released under section 768a. He also claimed that finding an expedient sanction was not a lawful ground for detention and that the psychiatric examination took too long.

The European Court of Human Rights declared the Article 5 § 1 complaint inadmissible for non-exhaustion, as he had not raised it domestically. The Article 5 § 3 complaint was admissible, but the Court found no violation. It accepted that detention was justified by the gravity of the offences, public reaction, his guilty plea, and the need to determine an appropriate sanction for an adolescent. The psychiatric delay was complex and not attributable to significant inactivity. Domestic courts regularly reviewed the detention and expressly found “very special circumstances” under section 768a. They also used a less restrictive measure—a secure youth institution. Thus, the length of detention did not breach Article 5 § 3.

**Summary of *Egill Einarsson v. Iceland* (Application no. 24703/15)**

The case of *Egil Einarsson v. Iceland* concerns an application brought by Mr. Egill Einarsson, an Icelandic national born in 1980, against the Republic of Iceland under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the Icelandic Supreme Court’s judgment of 20 November 2014 violated his right to respect for private life under Article 8 of the Convention.

The facts stem from events in late 2012. In November 2011 and January 2012, two women reported the applicant to the police for sexual offences. The Public Prosecutor dismissed both cases in June and November 2012, respectively, due to insufficient evidence. On 22 November 2012, *Monitor*, a magazine accompanying the newspaper *Morgunblaðið*, published an interview with the applicant, who was a well-known public figure in Iceland. He had gained prominence through articles, blogs, books, films, and television appearances, often under pseudonyms such as "Gillz" or "Gillzenegger." In the interview, the applicant discussed the rape accusation, claiming it was false and part of a conspiracy, while also stating he was not seeking revenge against his accuser. He made provocative comments, including about the accuser’s age, and criticized media coverage.

That same day, an 18-year-old man, referred to as X, published an altered version of the applicant’s front-page photograph on his Instagram account. The image featured an upside-down cross drawn on the applicant’s forehead, the word "loser" across his face, and the caption "Fuck you rapist bastard." X believed his posts were only accessible to his followers, but they were viewable by other Instagram users. The following day, the newspaper *Vísir* published an online article about X’s post, including the altered picture. The applicant’s lawyer demanded a retraction and apology; X’s lawyer responded that X had not distributed the image publicly and that it was shared without his consent, expressing regret.

On 17 December 2012, the applicant lodged defamation proceedings against X, seeking punishment under the Penal Code, a declaration that the statement was null and void, non-pecuniary damages of ISK 1,000,000, and publication costs. The District Court ruled against the applicant on 1 November 2013. It held that the applicant, as a public figure, had to accept public discussion, and that the altered picture and caption, taken together, constituted a value judgment rather than a factual statement of rape, falling within X’s freedom of expression. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court.

On 20 November 2014, the Supreme Court (by a majority of two to one) upheld the District Court’s judgment. It accepted that X’s post was a publication accessible to many users. However, it found that, given the context—including the applicant’s own provocative public statements and the public debate he had instigated—X’s expression was a value judgment protected under Article 10 of the Convention and Article 73 of the Icelandic Constitution. The Court noted that the applicant had launched a public debate and should have expected strong reactions. It emphasized that while the term "rapist" could imply a factual accusation, the overall context rendered it invective in a ruthless public debate. The minority opinion argued that the statement was a grave insinuation of a criminal offence that the applicant should not have to tolerate, especially since the investigation had been dismissed.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the Supreme Court’s judgment violated his right to private life under Article 8, arguing that the Icelandic courts failed to protect him from defamatory statements. The Government was communicated the application on 19 May 2016. The key legal issue centered on the balance between the applicant’s right to privacy and X’s freedom of expression, considering the applicant’s public role and the context of public debate.

**Summary of Einarsson v. Iceland (Application no. 24703/15)**

The case of *Egil Einarsson v. Iceland* originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 15 May 2015. The case concerns the balance between the right to private life and the right to freedom of expression in the context of a public figure facing defamatory online comments following sexual offence accusations.

The applicant was a well-known figure in Iceland, having published articles, blogs, and books and appeared in various media under pseudonyms, notably "Gillz" or "Gillzenegger." In late 2011 and early 2012, two women reported him to the police for sexual offences. After investigation, the Public Prosecutor dismissed both cases in June and November 2012, finding insufficient evidence likely to lead to a conviction. The applicant then filed a complaint against the women for false accusations, which was also dismissed.

On 22 November 2012, *Monitor* magazine published an interview with the applicant where he discussed the rape accusations, claiming they were false and part of a conspiracy against him. He stated he was not seeking revenge but criticized the media’s coverage. That same day, an individual named X posted an altered version of the applicant’s front-page photo on Instagram. The image had an upside-down cross drawn on the applicant’s forehead and the word "loser" written across his face, with the caption "Fuck you rapist bastard." X believed the post was only visible to his followers, but it was accessible to other Instagram users. The newspaper *Vísir* subsequently published an online article about the post, including the altered image.

The applicant lodged defamation proceedings against X, seeking punishment, a declaration that the statement was null and void, and non-pecuniary damages. The District Court ruled against the applicant on 1 November 2013. It held that the applicant, as a well-known person, had to accept public discussion. The court considered the altered picture and text as a whole to be X’s opinion—a value judgment rather than a factual statement—and thus within the bounds of freedom of expression.

The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court, which upheld the lower court’s decision on 20 November 2014. The majority accepted that the post was a publication but agreed it constituted a value judgment in the context of a ruthless public debate that the applicant himself had instigated through provocative comments. The court found that X enjoyed greater freedom to express himself under these circumstances, and the statement did not amount to a defamatory factual allegation of rape. The minority, however, dissented, viewing the comment as a grave insinuation of a serious criminal offence that the applicant should not have to tolerate, especially given the dismissed criminal investigations.

The applicant’s complaint to the European Court focused on this Supreme Court judgment, alleging that it failed to protect his private life under Article 8 by permitting the defamatory online post. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation include: the applicant’s status as a public figure who had engaged in public debate; the dismissal of sexual offence accusations against him; the publication of an offensive, altered image with a defamatory caption on social media; the domestic courts’ characterization of the post as a value judgment within permissible freedom of expression; and the Supreme Court’s majority finding that the applicant, by instigating public debate, had to tolerate stronger reactions.

In **Mažukna v. Lithuania** (no. 72092/12), the applicant, Aleksandras Mažukna, a Lithuanian welder, alleged that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into a workplace accident in which he was seriously injured. He relied on Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention; the Court also communicated the case under Article 3. After the applicant died, his son continued the proceedings.

The accident occurred on 17 April 2007 at a factory construction site in Klaipėda. The applicant and two co-workers were on scaffolding about two metres high, carrying or attaching a metal platform weighing approximately 200 kg to a reservoir tank. The scaffolding collapsed, and all three workers fell. The applicant hit his head on concrete, his helmet broke, and a co-worker and a metal tool fell on him. He lost consciousness. He alleged that, while he was unconscious, his employer had him moved and removed all traces of the accident. An ambulance was called at 4:53 p.m.; the other workers suffered only minor injuries.

A State Labour Inspectorate inspector examined the site the same day. By then the scaffolding was intact and no workers were present. The site manager said he had not seen the accident, and the safety officer said initial medical examination showed no serious injury. The inspector decided not to investigate. Later, after the applicant complained, the Inspectorate concluded that the accident had been caused by inappropriate organisation of dangerous work, because the scaffolding did not meet safety requirements.

In September 2007 the applicant asked the prosecutor to open a pre-trial investigation, which was opened the same day. Medical reports found head and facial cuts, facial fractures, a chest contusion, and later a large facial scar causing disfigurement; the injury was ultimately classified as serious health impairment. The applicant described the platform-carrying operation and the removal of traces. Co-workers generally said no platform was carried and none saw the fall.

In October 2008 the prosecutor discontinued the investigation, relying on the lack of scaffolding damage and witness testimony, and suggested the applicant may have fallen because of recklessness or leg numbness. The Klaipėda District Court reopened it in December 2008, calling that conclusion speculative. Further investigation followed. In May 2009 a co-worker, V.K., stated that the supervisor had ordered the platform work, the scaffolding was thin and unsafe, and the director told workers to repair it after the accident; he said his earlier testimony was given under employer pressure. In June 2009 the Inspectorate concluded the employer had breached safety rules.

The prosecutor discontinued again in July 2009, finding the workers acted recklessly. The court reopened it in October 2009, stressing the employer’s duty to supervise and investigate witness intimidation. A February 2010 forensic report found the platform exceeded the scaffolding’s weight limit, the scaffolding was unsuitable, workers were not properly instructed, and the employer breached safety requirements. Despite this, the prosecutor discontinued again in May 2010. The court reopened it in August 2010. In October 2010 V.J.S., the supervisor, was charged under Article 176 § 1 of the Criminal Code; an indictment followed in April 2011.

The trial was repeatedly adjourned because witnesses failed to appear and V.J.S. was ill or in rehabilitation. In May 2012 the prosecutor asked the court to terminate the case as time-barred. On 14 May 2012 the Klaipėda District Court terminated the case, did not examine the applicant’s civil claim, and told him to bring separate civil proceedings. His appeal was not admitted for procedural reasons. The applicant alleged that the investigation was ineffective and protracted, violating Article 6 § 1 and Article 13, and the Court considered the case under Article 3 as well.

In February 2007 the applicant began working for company N. On 17 April 2007, while at a factory construction site in Klaipėda, he and two co-workers were on scaffolding about two metres above ground, allegedly attaching a 200 kg metal platform to a reservoir tank. The scaffolding collapsed and all three fell. The applicant struck his head, lost consciousness and suffered facial fractures and a large facial scar, later classified as serious health impairment. He claimed that, while unconscious, his employer had him moved from the scene and that traces of the accident were removed.

A State Labour Inspectorate inspector visited the same day but found the scaffolding intact and no workers present. The site manager said he had not seen the accident, and a safety officer said the initial medical assessment showed no serious injury. The inspector therefore declined to investigate. After the applicant complained, the Inspectorate first blamed his recklessness, but in July 2007 concluded that the accident had been caused by inappropriate organisation of dangerous work and non-compliant scaffolding.

In September 2007 a pre-trial investigation opened. Medical experts confirmed serious facial injury. The applicant described carrying the platform, but co-workers denied carrying it or said they did not see the fall. In October 2008 the prosecutor discontinued the investigation, citing possible recklessness and no employer violation. Courts repeatedly reopened it, criticising speculative conclusions and the failure to address the Inspectorate’s findings. A key witness, V.K., later stated that a supervisor had ordered workers to attach the platform, that the scaffolding was unsafe, and that the employer had pressured witnesses to change testimony. In February 2010 a forensic report found the platform exceeded the scaffolding’s weight limit, the scaffolding was unsuitable, and the employer had breached safety rules.

Despite this, the prosecutor discontinued again in May 2010, finding that the supervisor was absent, had not ordered the task, and that the workers acted recklessly; only administrative liability was possible. He noted a separate investigation was needed into witness pressure, but none apparently opened. After further court reopenings, supervisor V.J.S. was charged in October 2010 under Article 176 of the Criminal Code, and an indictment followed in April 2011.

Trial delays accumulated due to absent witnesses and the accused’s repeated illness. The applicant asked to proceed in absentia but was refused. In May 2012 the prosecutor requested termination because the five-year limitation period had expired. On 14 May 2012 the Klaipėda District Court terminated the case as time-barred, did not examine the applicant’s civil claim, and told him to seek separate civil damages. His appeal was rejected on procedural grounds. The Prosecutor General’s Office found no substantial procedural violations. The applicant alleged that the investigation and proceedings were ineffective and protracted, denying him an effective remedy. He died in January 2016, and his son sought to continue the case.

In *Haarde v. Iceland*, the applicant, Geir Hilmar Haarde, was a long-serving Icelandic politician who served as Minister of Finance (1998–2005), Minister for Foreign Affairs (2005–2006), and Prime Minister (2006–2009). His complaints under Articles 6 and 7 of the European Convention on Human Rights arose from impeachment proceedings and his eventual conviction before Iceland’s Court of Impeachment following the October 2008 collapse of Iceland’s major banks.

After the banking collapse, Parliament established the Special Investigation Commission (SIC) in December 2008 to investigate the causes and assess whether mistakes or negligence had occurred. The SIC conducted an extensive inquiry, heard 147 individuals, met 183 others, and received testimony from Haarde in July 2009. In February 2010, the SIC informed Haarde that it considered he had acted negligently; he replied in writing. Its April 2010 report criticized several officials, including Haarde and two other ministers, for failing to respond appropriately to the impending financial danger.

Parliament then created a Parliamentary Review Committee (PRC) to assess ministerial accountability and possible impeachment. The PRC held 54 meetings, consulted experts and the deputy state prosecutor, Sigríður J. Friðjónsdóttir, who later became the prosecutor in Haarde’s case. It recommended impeachment against four former ministers. On 28 September 2010, Parliament voted 33–30 to impeach Haarde only; the other three ministers were not indicted. Haarde alleged this selective impeachment was arbitrary and politically motivated.

On 10 May 2011, Haarde was indicted. Counts 1.1–1.5 alleged serious neglect of his duties as Prime Minister, including failure to initiate a comprehensive analysis of financial risk, failure to ensure that a consultative group on financial stability worked effectively, failure to reduce the size of the banking system, and failure to ensure the transfer of Landsbanki’s Icesave accounts to a subsidiary. Count 2 alleged that he failed to hold ministerial meetings under Article 17 of the Constitution on important government matters between February and October 2008, despite the looming banking crisis. The charges invoked the Ministerial Accountability Act and, in the alternative, the General Penal Code.

Before trial, Haarde challenged the impartiality and independence of the eight lay judges on the Court of Impeachment because Parliament had extended their terms by law after the impeachment decision. He also complained that the investigation was defective: the SIC was not a criminal investigation; neither the PRC nor the prosecutor conducted genuinely independent investigative measures; he was not questioned before indictment; and the prosecutor had previously advised the PRC and allegedly prejudged his liability. He further argued that the indictment was vague, the applicable penal provisions were unclear, and the proceedings lacked foreseeability. The Court of Impeachment dismissed counts 1.1 and 1.2 for lack of clarity but rejected his other procedural challenges.

The trial began on 5 March 2012, with 40 witnesses and written evidence. On 23 April 2012, the Court of Impeachment unanimously acquitted Haarde of counts 1.3–1.5, but convicted him of count 2 by nine votes to six. It found that he had been grossly negligent in failing to hold ministerial meetings on the serious financial danger facing the State, contrary to Article 17 of the Constitution and section 8(c) of the Ministerial Accountability Act. He received no punishment. Haarde then applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 17 October 2012, alleging that the impeachment process and conviction violated his rights under Article 6 (fair trial, independent and impartial tribunal, adequate defence, legal clarity) and Article 7 (no punishment without law and foreseeability).

**Summary of Haarde v. Iceland (Application no. 66847/12)**

The case of *Haarde v. Iceland* concerns the impeachment and conviction of Mr. Geir Hilmar Haarde, former Prime Minister of Iceland, following the collapse of the Icelandic banking system in October 2008. The applicant alleged violations of Articles 6 (right to a fair trial) and 7 (no punishment without law) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant served as Prime Minister from 2006 to 2009, leading a coalition government. In early October 2008, Iceland's three largest banks collapsed, prompting emergency legislation that authorized the Financial Supervisory Authority to intervene in financial undertakings. Subsequently, Parliament established a Special Investigation Commission (SIC) to investigate the causes of the collapse and assess whether mistakes or negligence had occurred in implementing laws and rules regarding financial activities. The SIC's report, issued in April 2010, criticized the applicant and two other ministers for negligence in responding to the impending danger to the Icelandic economy.

A parliamentary review committee (PRC) was established to address the SIC report and assess grounds for impeachment. On 28 September 2010, by a vote of 33 to 30, Parliament approved impeachment proceedings against the applicant alone, despite the PRC proposal initially naming four ministers. The applicant was charged on six counts alleging serious neglect of his duties as Prime Minister, including failure to initiate comprehensive analysis of financial risk, failure to ensure the consultative group on financial stability was purposeful, failure to take measures to reduce the banking system's size, failure to follow up on transferring Icesave accounts, and failure to hold ministerial meetings on important government matters as required by Article 17 of the Constitution.

The Court of Impeachment dismissed counts 1.1 and 1.2 for insufficient clarity but proceeded on the remaining counts. During the trial, 40 witnesses testified. On 23 April 2012, the court unanimously acquitted the applicant of counts 1.3, 1.4, and 1.5. However, by nine votes to six, he was convicted of count 2—violation of section 8(c) of the Ministerial Accountability Act for gross negligence in failing to hold ministerial meetings on important government matters under Article 17 of the Constitution. He received no punishment.

The applicant complained that the impeachment proceedings and conviction violated his fair trial rights and the principle of legality. Key issues included: the alleged lack of clarity in the criminal provisions; the alleged defects in the investigation; the impartiality of the prosecutor who had advised the PRC; the alleged arbitrariness of Parliament's decision to indict him alone; and the retrospective extension of lay judges' terms.

The Court, sitting as a Chamber, examined these complaints and delivered its judgment on 23 November 2017, finding no violation of Article 6 or Article 7 of the Convention.

In *Tural Hajibeyli v. Azerbaijan* (Application no. 69180/11, judgment 28 September 2017), the applicant, an Azerbaijani national born in 1992, complained under Articles 5, 6, 11 and 13 of the Convention about his arrest, administrative conviction and the fairness of the proceedings following a demonstration in Baku. The complaints concerning those Articles were communicated to the Government; the remainder was declared inadmissible.

A demonstration was planned for 12 March 2011 in Baku. On 7 March 2011, opposition organisers notified the Baku City Executive Authority. The authority refused the proposed central location and suggested a driving school on the outskirts. The organisers nevertheless held the demonstration in central Baku. According to the applicant, the demonstration was peaceful and protested against corruption and demanded the President’s resignation. Police began dispersing participants shortly after it began. The applicant was arrested during the dispersal, around 2 p.m., and taken to three different police stations. He alleges he was not given access to a lawyer after arrest or while in police custody. A protester, Mr A.H., recorded the arrest and custody on a mobile phone.

On the day of arrest, police officer E.G. prepared an administrative-offence report stating that at about 2:55 p.m. at Fountains Square the applicant attempted to hold an unlawful demonstration and disobeyed a lawful police order. He was charged under Articles 298 and 310.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences. A separate police report by officers M.A. and H.A. stated that at around 4 p.m. they arrested ten people during the demonstration. The applicant alleged that his name was added later as the eleventh person on the list, in different handwriting. Official records claimed the administrative-offence report was based on that police report. The applicant says he was never served a copy of the administrative-offence report or other case documents.

The Sabail District Court heard the case the same day. A State-funded lawyer was appointed, but the record shows no oral or written submissions by him. No witnesses were questioned. The court convicted the applicant under Article 310.1 and sentenced him to eight days’ administrative detention. On appeal, the applicant argued that his arrest and conviction violated his right to freedom of assembly and that the hearing was unfair. He denied disobeying any police order. He asked the Baku Court of Appeal to summon witnesses A.H., A.M. and R.M., examine video recordings of his arrest and custody, and order a handwriting examination of the police report. On 18 March 2011, the Court of Appeal remitted the case for re-examination because the first-instance court had failed to examine the police report; only a photocopy existed, so expert examination was impossible. It did not address the witness or video requests.

On re-examination on 12 April 2011, the applicant was allegedly not allowed to appoint a lawyer of his choosing. A State-funded lawyer was appointed. Only police officers M.A. and E.G. testified. M.A. said the applicant was detained for unlawful assembly, noise and disobeying orders; E.G. said he prepared the administrative report. The court again convicted the applicant under Article 310.1, imposing seven days’ administrative detention. On appeal, the applicant complained that his arrest was unlawful, his assembly rights were violated, and the rehearing was unfair. He requested witnesses A.H., A.M., R.M. and R.B., asked the court to hear at least three persons listed in the police report, and sought examination of photographs and video recordings. He challenged the official records, noting a discrepancy in the arrest time and repeating that his name had been added later. He was not represented before the Court of Appeal. On 28 April 2011, the appellate court dismissed the appeal and upheld the conviction, without addressing his requests.
