This case concerns Tural Hajibeyli, an Azerbaijani national, arrested during a Baku demonstration on 12 March 2011 and later sentenced to administrative detention. The ECtHR communicated complaints under Articles 5, 6, 11 and 13 of the Convention; other complaints were inadmissible.

A demonstration was planned for 12 March 2011. On 7 March, opposition organisers notified the Baku City Executive Authority. The BCEA refused the proposed central location and suggested a site on Baku’s outskirts. The organisers proceeded in central Baku. The applicant says the demonstration was peaceful; participants protested corruption and demanded the President’s resignation. Shortly after it began, police dispersed the crowd. The applicant was arrested and taken to three police stations consecutively.

That day, police officer E.G. prepared an administrative-offence report stating that at about 2:55 p.m. at Fountains Square the applicant attempted to hold an unlawful demonstration and disobeyed a lawful police order. He was charged under Articles 298 and 310.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences. Separately, officers M.A. and H.A. prepared a report stating that at about 4 p.m. they had arrested ten people during the demonstration. The applicant alleges his name—the eleventh on the list—was added later in different handwriting. Official records state the administrative-offence report was based on this police report. The applicant says he was never served with a copy of the administrative-offence report or other case-file documents and had no access to a lawyer after arrest or in police custody.

The same day, the Sabail District Court convicted him under Article 310.1 and sentenced him to eight days’ administrative detention. A State-funded lawyer was appointed, but the file contains no record that the lawyer made any oral or written submissions; no witnesses were questioned. On appeal, the applicant argued violations of freedom of assembly and an unfair hearing, denied disobeying police, and requested witnesses (A.H., A.M., R.M.), video recordings of his arrest and custody, and a handwriting examination of the police report. On 18 March 2011, the Baku Court of Appeal partly allowed the appeal and remitted the case because the first-instance court had not examined the police report; only a photocopy, not the original, was available. It did not address the witness or video requests.

On 12 April 2011, the Sabail District Court reheard the case. The applicant says he could not appoint a lawyer of his choosing; a State-funded lawyer was appointed. Only police officers M.A. and E.G. testified. The court again convicted him under Article 310.1, imposing seven days’ detention. His appeal repeated the assembly and unfair-trial complaints, challenged official records and timing discrepancies, repeated the alleged late addition of his name, and asked the appellate court to hear defence witnesses, including individuals listed in the police report, and examine photographs and video. He was unrepresented. On 28 April 2011, the Baku Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, without addressing those requests.

The file also notes that in August 2014, during criminal proceedings against the applicant’s ECtHR representative I. Aliyev, authorities searched his home and office and seized all pending ECtHR case files, including this one, without adequate inventory; the file was returned in October 2014. These facts underpin the applicant’s complaints about unlawful arrest and detention, unfair proceedings, interference with peaceful assembly, and lack of effective remedies.

Thuo v. Cyprus (Application no. 3869/07) concerned a Kenyan national who complained under Article 3 of the Convention about his conditions of detention in Cyprus, his ill-treatment during deportation, and the lack of an effective investigation into that ill-treatment.

The applicant entered Cyprus unlawfully in April 2005 through the “Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus.” On 6 April 2005 he was arrested at Larnaca Airport while trying to travel to London on a forged passport. He pleaded guilty and was sentenced to nine months’ imprisonment. While serving his sentence, he applied for asylum. In November 2005, the authorities issued detention and deportation orders against him as a “prohibited immigrant,” but enforcement was suspended pending his asylum claim. After his release on 14 November 2005, he was immediately re-arrested under those orders and held in Block 10 of Nicosia Central Prisons. His asylum claim was rejected in January 2006, his appeal was dismissed in April 2006, and he brought judicial review proceedings in May 2006. Deportation was delayed because he had no valid travel document and initially refused to cooperate. After Kenya issued a travel document in February 2007, new orders were issued and he was deported on 9 March 2007.

Regarding detention conditions, the applicant alleged that he was held for a long period in a shared cell of about 5.5 sq m, with no room for exercise, poor hygiene, toilet smells, uncleaned rubbish, and overcrowding. He also complained that after a fire in May 2006, Block 10 was covered in ash and smoke, and that detainees remained there during renovation and painting. The Government disputed this, describing a cell of about 2.73 m by 2 m with a bunk bed, window, air conditioning, communal areas, outdoor access, and cleaning facilities. IAIACAP material noted cells of 5.4 sq m, below the European standard of 7 sq m, and about one hour of daily exercise; in February 2007 Block 10 held up to 58 detainees.

As to the alleged ill-treatment, the applicant claimed that in the early hours of 9 March 2007 prison guards and two immigration officers insulted him as a “stupid mavro,” refused him a telephone call, pushed and hit him, held his neck, and pinched his testicles. After calling his lawyer, he was handcuffed and taken to Larnaca Airport. There, three men in military uniform, with immigration officers, allegedly beat him, forced him into a chair, held his neck, stuffed brown paper into his mouth, taped his mouth and neck with Cyprus Airways tape, and wrapped bandages around his head and neck. He complained to the Ombudsman and the IAIACAP. The IAIACAP initially declined because he was abroad, but after the Attorney General intervened, a formal investigation began in 2009. In June 2010 the applicant returned to Cyprus. Medical examinations were inconclusive: a maxillofacial surgeon could not link dental damage to ill-treatment; a urologist found no issues; a forensic pathologist considered ill-treatment minimal to negligible. A Kenyan medical certificate from March 2007 recorded injuries, but its evidentiary value was questioned. An identity parade was incomplete; the applicant identified N.S., Pa.P., and A.I. from photographs. The officers denied ill-treatment, later claiming he tried to self-harm and was bandaged only for protection. The investigator found possible excessive force but credibility problems and recommended disciplinary action; the IAIACAP and Attorney General found no criminal or disciplinary liability. The Chief of Police issued new recording instructions.

001-178877:
This case concerned Norwegian child welfare measures and the subsequent adoption of the first applicant’s son, X. The first applicant, Ms Strand Lobben, gave birth to X in September 2008 while in a difficult situation: she lacked stable housing and was staying with her parents, the fourth and fifth applicants. During pregnancy, the hospital notified child welfare authorities that she might need support. She agreed to stay at a family centre with X for three months after birth so her parenting capacity could be assessed.

Four days after X’s birth, they moved to the family centre. Staff soon became concerned: X lost weight, the mother did not appear to understand his needs, and he required checks every three hours to ensure feeding. On 17 October 2008, when X was about three weeks old, the mother withdrew consent and wanted to leave with him. The same day, child welfare authorities took X into emergency compulsory care and placed him in a foster home. The mother had supervised visits thereafter.

A family centre report stated that the mother could not provide satisfactory care, showed little empathy, expressed disgust toward the child, had inconsistent mental functioning, and was incapable of caring for him. The County Social Welfare Board rejected her appeal. In March 2009, the Board issued a care order, keeping X in foster care and limiting contact. The mother appealed. In August 2009, the City Court ordered reunification, but the authorities appealed and enforcement was suspended. In April 2010, the High Court confirmed the care order and reduced contact. It relied on expert evidence that the mother had cognitive impairment, learning difficulties, a history of epilepsy, and limited ability to plan, organise, and understand X’s needs. Experts found a risk of neglect and concluded that assistance measures would not suffice. X had also formed an attachment to his foster parents. The mother did not appeal further.

In July 2011, the authorities sought deprivation of parental responsibility and adoption by the foster parents. By then, the mother had married and given birth to Y in October 2011. A new municipality investigated and considered that she could probably care for Y with support. At the Board hearing, 21 witnesses testified. In December 2011, the Board deprived her of parental responsibility and allowed adoption. It found she remained unable to care for X, still viewed the case as a conspiracy, lacked empathy for X’s vulnerability, and that her care of Y did not prove capacity for X. X was attached to his foster family, and adoption was in his best interests.

The City Court upheld this in February 2012. It accepted that the mother’s general situation had improved, but found X had special needs and the mother could not understand his vulnerability. Contact sessions were stressful, with her outbursts and negative attitude. One expert believed return was best, but the court preferred other experts. X had lived with the foster parents since he was three weeks old and saw them as psychological parents; removal would cause serious problems. The High Court refused leave to appeal, and the Supreme Court refused in October 2012.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged that removing the mother’s parental authority over X and authorising his adoption violated Article 8. The key issues were whether the measures were necessary and proportionate to X’s best interests, whether the decision-making process adequately assessed the mother’s improved circumstances, and whether the permanent severance of family ties, without fixed post-adoption contact, struck a fair balance.

The case concerned an Article 8 complaint by a Norwegian mother, her two children, and the maternal grandparents. In May 2008 the first applicant, while pregnant and without stable housing, turned to child welfare authorities and agreed to stay at a family centre after giving birth so her parenting capacity could be assessed. Her son X was born on 25 September 2008. At the family centre, staff became seriously concerned: X lost weight, required feeding every three hours, and the mother showed limited understanding of his needs, little empathy, and apparent cognitive/mental difficulties. On 17 October 2008 she withdrew consent and wanted to leave with X. That same day, the child welfare authorities took X into immediate compulsory care and placed him in an emergency foster home. Reports stated that without close staff checks, X might not have survived. X was then three weeks old and remained with the same foster parents thereafter.

The emergency placement was upheld by the County Social Welfare Board and, in January 2009, by the City Court. In March 2009 the Board issued a care order, finding serious deficiencies in the mother’s care and limiting her contact to six supervised visits per year. On appeal, the City Court in August 2009 ordered reunification, suggesting X’s weight problems could have stemmed from an eye infection. The authorities appealed. In April 2010 the High Court reversed that decision, confirmed the care order, and reduced contact to four two-hour visits per year. It relied on the family centre report, a child psychiatry assessment, and expert evidence. The experts described the mother as having cognitive impairment, a history of serious epilepsy, weak learning capacity, and an inability to plan, organise, and understand X’s needs. Contact sessions were described as stressful and harmful to X, who had formed a strong attachment to his foster parents. The High Court found assistance measures insufficient, and the mother did not appeal.

In July 2011 the authorities sought deprivation of the mother’s parental responsibility for X and permission for the foster parents to adopt him. The mother sought termination of the care order or extended contact. She had meanwhile married and given birth to Y in October 2011. The new municipality observed generally adequate care of Y with some support, but this did not alter the assessment regarding X. In December 2011 the County Board granted deprivation of parental responsibility and adoption. It found no meaningful improvement in the mother’s ability to care for X, continued hostility towards the foster mother and authorities, and contact sessions that remained harmful. X was considered vulnerable and strongly attached to his foster family; long-term foster care was the alternative.

In February 2012 the City Court upheld the decision after a three-day hearing with 21 witnesses. It accepted that the mother’s general circumstances had improved, but found her fundamental care limitations persisted. X, then three and a half, had lived with his foster parents since he was three weeks old and regarded them as his psychological parents. Returning him would cause serious problems. Although one psychologist supported the mother, the court preferred other experts and recent infant research. Adoption was found to be in X’s best interests. The High Court refused leave to appeal in August 2012, and the Supreme Court refused leave in October 2012.

Before the European Court, the applicants alleged that removing the first applicant’s parental authority over X and authorising his adoption violated their rights under Article 8 of the Convention.

The applicants were a Norwegian mother, her children X and Y, and the maternal grandparents. Their Article 8 complaint centred on the child welfare authorities’ removal of the mother’s parental responsibility for X and the later decision allowing X’s foster parents to adopt him.

The case began when the mother, pregnant and in a difficult housing situation, contacted child welfare authorities. She agreed to stay at a family centre after X’s birth in September 2008 so her parenting could be assessed. Staff reported serious concerns: X lost weight, needed feeding every three hours, and the mother allegedly showed limited empathy and basic care skills. When she withdrew consent and wanted to leave with X, the authorities took X into emergency compulsory care on 17 October 2008, when he was three weeks old, and placed him in a foster home.

The care order was then litigated. The County Social Welfare Board upheld the emergency placement; the City Court initially ordered reunification in August 2009, but the High Court reversed in April 2010. It confirmed compulsory care and reduced contact to four supervised two-hour visits per year. The High Court relied on the family centre report, a child psychiatry report, a court-appointed psychologist, and contact supervisors. It found serious deficiencies in the mother’s care, linked to cognitive impairment and a history of severe epilepsy, and concluded that assistance measures could not sufficiently remedy them. X had also formed an attachment to his foster parents. The mother did not appeal that judgment.

In July 2011 the child welfare authorities sought to deprive the mother of parental responsibility for X and to allow X’s foster parents to adopt him. By then the mother had married and given birth to Y, and she argued her situation had improved. She opposed adoption and sought revocation of the care order or increased contact. In December 2011 the County Social Welfare Board granted adoption. It found no sufficient improvement in her ability to care for X, noted she denied neglect and viewed the case as a conspiracy, relied on negative contact sessions, and held that X was vulnerable and primarily attached to his foster parents. Long-term foster care was considered less beneficial than adoption, which would give X security and belonging.

In February 2012 the City Court upheld the adoption after a three-day hearing. It accepted that the mother’s general circumstances had improved but found she still did not understand X’s special vulnerability. Contact sessions had been stressful for X, who was attached to his foster parents as psychological parents. Removing him would cause serious problems, and adoption was in his best interests. The High Court refused leave to appeal in August 2012, and the Supreme Court refused in October 2012.

The applicants alleged that depriving the mother of parental authority over X and authorising his adoption violated Article 8. They argued the authorities failed to adequately consider less intrusive measures, reunification, or contact, and that the evidence on the mother’s parenting capacity and X’s best interests was insufficient. The case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment in 2019.
001-175645:
In *Kuc v. Slovakia* (Application no. 37498/14), the applicant, Ladislav Kuc, a Slovak national born in 1979, complained under Article 5 §§ 1(c), 3 and 4 of the Convention that his detention was excessively long, lacked relevant and sufficient grounds, and that the domestic courts failed to consider his mental (schizotypal) disorder and related personal circumstances when reviewing his continued detention.

Kuc was arrested on 1 January 2012 and charged with endangering public safety. The allegations concerned making homemade explosive devices, sending some with threats to veterinarians and a supermarket chain, and planting one near a fast-food outlet to promote animal rights. On 4 January 2012 the Košice I District Court remanded him in custody, relying on the nature of the charges and his long-term psychiatric treatment. Detention was repeatedly reviewed and extended on grounds of risk of reoffending and, later, risk of absconding. New charges were added, and the offences were reclassified as terrorism and firearms offences. Kuc was committed to the Trenčín hospital for charged and convicted persons twice in 2012 because of anxiety, suicide threats, and the need to examine his mental state.

In October 2012 he was indicted. In June 2013 the District Court convicted him and sentenced him to 25 years’ imprisonment. On 30 October 2013 the Regional Court quashed the conviction on appeal. It noted a conflict between expert reports: the first pre-trial report found no mental illness but a personality disorder, while a second report of 24 October 2013 concluded that Kuc suffered from a schizotypal disorder that prevented him from understanding or controlling his behaviour. The Regional Court ordered a third expert opinion to resolve whether he was criminally responsible.

After remittal, on 23 December 2013 Kuc applied for release. He relied on the second expert report, his need for daily medication and psychiatric treatment, and argued he posed no absconding risk because he had little education, no finances or job, had never travelled alone, and depended on his parents. He also claimed he would not reoffend if properly medicated or placed in a psychiatric institution. His parents offered guarantees and supervision. On 10 January 2014 the District Court heard him and asked the detention centre whether he was receiving prescribed drugs and treatment; the centre replied affirmatively. On 13 January 2014 the court dismissed his release application, upheld on 29 January 2014. The courts relied on the strong suspicion, systematic planning, severe potential sentence, alleged statements about fleeing, evidence suggesting possible ID counterfeiting, and the parents’ inability to prevent the offences. They rejected alternative measures but did not separately analyse his mental condition, and the detention-centre correspondence was not mentioned in their decisions.

Kuc’s constitutional complaint was dismissed as manifestly ill-founded on 2 April 2014. The Constitutional Court endorsed the ordinary courts’ reasoning and gave no answer to his argument about his specific mental-health situation. Later, a third expert report was filed in July 2014; he was convicted again in July 2014, but the Supreme Court later quashed those judgments. In September 2016 he was again convicted and sentenced to 23 years and 6 months; appeal proceedings remained pending.

Before the European Court, the key alleged violation was that his detention, particularly after the conflicting expert evidence emerged, was not justified by relevant and sufficient reasons and that his schizotypal disorder and personal circumstances were ignored. The Court assessed the complaint under Article 5 § 3, treating the relevant detention periods as a whole: 1 January 2012 to 19 June 2013, and 30 October 2013 to 2 April 2014, totalling about one year, ten months and twenty-eight days.

In *Kuc v. Slovakia*, the applicant, Ladislav Kuc, a Slovak national born in 1979, complained under Article 5 §§ 1(c), 3 and 4 of the Convention that his pre-trial detention was too long, lacked relevant and sufficient grounds, and failed to take account of his mental (schizotypal) disorder.

The applicant was arrested on 1 January 2012 and charged the next day with endangering public safety. The prosecution alleged that he had made homemade explosive devices, sent some with written threats to veterinarians and a supermarket chain’s head office, and planted one near a fast-food outlet, allowing it to explode to promote animal rights. On 4 January 2012 the Košice I District Court remanded him in custody to prevent further criminal activity, noting the charge and his long-term psychiatric treatment. His appeal failed.

During pre-trial detention, courts repeatedly upheld detention on grounds of risk of reoffending and absconding. They relied on new charges, witness testimony, evidence of systematic planning, the severe potential sentence, an alleged statement that he would flee if arrested, evidence suggesting he considered counterfeiting an ID, and later a witness statement that he had written a will expressing intent to commit a terrorist suicide attack. The charges were later reclassified as terrorism and firearms offences. Bail and parental supervision were rejected because his parents had not prevented the offences while he lived with them. He was twice hospitalized for psychiatric examination. He was indicted on 1 October 2012.

On 19 June 2013 the District Court convicted him and sentenced him to 25 years’ imprisonment. On 30 October 2013 the Regional Court quashed the conviction because expert reports conflicted: the first concluded he had no mental illness but a personality disorder; the second concluded he suffered from schizotypal disorder preventing him from understanding or controlling his behaviour. The Regional Court ordered a third expert opinion.

After remittal, on 23 December 2013 the applicant applied for release, relying on the second expert report, his psychiatric history since age 14, daily medication to prevent suicidal thoughts, his dependence on his parents, lack of money, job or travel history, and the absence of risk if medicated or institutionalized. His parents offered guarantees and parole supervision. On 10 January 2014 the District Court heard him and counsel, and asked the detention centre whether he received prescribed drugs and treatment; the director confirmed he did. On 13 January 2014 the court refused release, upheld on appeal on 29 January 2014.

The courts found a strong suspicion, serious planned offences, risk of reoffending and absconding, a severe potential penalty, and that alternative measures were unmet. They did not separately consider his mental condition, and the detention-centre correspondence was not mentioned in their decisions. On 2 April 2014 the Constitutional Court dismissed his complaint as manifestly ill-founded, endorsing the ordinary courts and not addressing his specific mental-health argument.

The Government argued that the courts were aware of his mental condition, had the expert reports and health information, and that adequate care was available; his mental condition affected criminal responsibility, not detention. The applicant maintained that he lacked proper psychiatric treatment and that his personal circumstances were not assessed in decisions on continued detention.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the complaint under Article 5 § 3, declared it admissible, and considered the overall detention period: 1 January 2012 to 19 June 2013, and 30 October 2013 to 2 April 2014, totaling about one year, ten months and twenty-eight days. It assessed whether the suspicion remained and whether other grounds were relevant, sufficient, and pursued with special diligence. The central alleged violation was the domestic courts’ failure to address the applicant’s mental disorder when deciding on his release.

Applicant Ladislav Kuc, a Slovak national born in 1979, was arrested on 1 January 2012 and charged with endangering public safety. The prosecution alleged that he had made homemade explosive devices, sent some with written threats to veterinarians and a supermarket chain’s head office, and planted one near a fast-food outlet, allowing it to explode to promote animal rights. On 4 January 2012 the Košice I District Court remanded him in custody to prevent further criminal activity, taking into account the nature of the charge and his long-term psychiatric treatment. The charges were later reclassified as terrorism and firearms offences.

The courts repeatedly reviewed and upheld his detention, relying on risks of reoffending and absconding. They cited the systematic planning of the alleged attacks, new charges, witness testimony, an alleged statement that he would flee if arrested, computer evidence suggesting possible ID counterfeiting, and a will allegedly expressing an intention to commit a terrorist suicide attack. Offers of bail and parental supervision were rejected because his parents had not prevented the offences while he lived with them. On 19 June 2013 the District Court convicted him and imposed a 25-year sentence. On 30 October 2013 the Regional Court quashed the conviction because two expert reports conflicted: the first found only a personality disorder, while the second concluded that he suffered from schizotypal disorder preventing him from understanding or controlling his conduct. The Regional Court ordered a third expert opinion. Detention continued on the same grounds.

He argued that he needed daily medication and psychiatric treatment, was dependent on his parents, had no job, money, or independent travel history, and would not abscond or reoffend if properly treated or placed in a psychiatric institution. His parents offered guarantees and supervision. On 10 January 2014 the District Court heard him and asked the detention centre whether he was receiving prescribed drugs and treatment; the director confirmed he was. On 13 January 2014 the District Court dismissed his release application, and the Regional Court upheld that decision on 29 January 2014. They rejected alternative measures but did not separately consider his mental condition as such; the detention-centre correspondence was not mentioned.

On 2 April 2014 the Constitutional Court dismissed his complaint as manifestly ill-founded, endorsing the ordinary courts’ reasoning and giving no answer to his argument about his mental disorder. Kuc complained under Article 5 §§ 1(c), 3 and 4 of the Convention that his detention had been too long and lacked relevant and sufficient grounds, and that the domestic courts had failed to take account of his mental disorder and personal circumstances when assessing continued detention. The European Court of Human Rights examined the complaint under Article 5 § 3. It considered two exhausted sub-periods: 1 January 2012 to 19 June 2013, and 30 October 2013 to 2 April 2014, totaling about one year, ten months and twenty-eight days. The central issue was whether the domestic authorities gave relevant and sufficient reasons for detention, particularly in light of his alleged schizotypal disorder and the conflicting expert evidence.

In *Brennan v. Ireland* (Application no. 44360/15), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention concerning the length of civil proceedings. The applicant, Ms Margaret Brennan, an Irish and British national born in 1947 and living in County Roscommon, purchased a newly built house in November 1999 through two agreements: one to buy the land from Mr and Mrs F for 5,000 Irish pounds, and one with T and C Developments Ltd, a company owned by the Fs, for 80,000 Irish pounds to build the house. Homebond provided a guarantee. After moving in in March 2000, she discovered major structural defects. She reported them to Homebond in September 2001; Homebond inspected and in September 2002 offered repairs under the guarantee, but the applicant claimed it refused to issue an engineer’s certificate/guarantee needed for any future sale.

In February 2003 she brought High Court proceedings against Mr and Mrs F, T and C Developments, Homebond, an engineer Mr Q, and later Mr Q’s company—six defendants in total. Her statement of claim was filed in May 2003, but service on Homebond was delayed until December 2003. Defences were repeatedly delayed. In December 2004 she obtained a default judgment against Mr Q and his company, but it was never enforced. Between 2005 and 2009 the case was effectively dormant as she engaged mainly with Homebond over its repair proposal. In April 2009 her solicitor ceased acting, and she continued as a lay litigant. She served notices of intention to proceed in April 2009, October 2010, and September 2011.

The High Court eventually heard the case in January 2013, but only Homebond and Mr Q appeared. In March 2013 Homebond was held liable under the guarantee, with damages of about €51,000 despite a €38,100 cap; the claim against Mr Q was dismissed. In May 2013 the Fs were held jointly and severally liable for €94,082. Appeals followed. Homebond’s appeal was allowed by the Court of Appeal in February 2015, and the applicant’s cross-appeal dismissed. The Fs’ appeal was also allowed in March 2015: the Court of Appeal held that the Fs were not liable because they had merely sold land and were not parties to the building agreement. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 29 July 2015.

The proceedings therefore lasted from 10 February 2003 to 29 July 2015—twelve years and five months across three instances. The applicant alleged that this violated the “reasonable time” requirement of Article 6 § 1. The Government denied a breach, arguing that the case was procedurally complex due to six defendants and numerous interim applications, and that the applicant’s litigation strategy and legal representatives’ errors caused much of the delay. It also argued that court delays were not excessive and that mediation was reasonably suggested.

The Court assessed complexity, the applicant’s conduct, the authorities’ conduct, and what was at stake. It found the case procedurally complex but not legally difficult. The applicant’s own conduct—especially the long dormancy from 2005 to 2009, delayed service, repeated procedural steps, and errors of her lawyers—had a critical impact on delay. The High Court’s handling after November 2011, including a reasonable mediation attempt, was not excessively delayed. The appellate courts, particularly the Court of Appeal, managed the appeals promptly after transfer. Although the subject matter affected the applicant’s quality of life, the overall duration was incommensurate with the relatively simple underlying claim and was largely generated by her own actions. The Court declared the complaint admissible but found no violation of Article 6 § 1.

Brennan v. Ireland (ECtHR, 2 November 2017) concerned a complaint under Article 6 § 1 that Irish civil proceedings exceeded a reasonable time. In November 1999, Margaret Brennan bought a newly built house. She bought the land from Mr and Mrs F and entered a building agreement with T and C Developments Ltd., which the Fs owned. Homebond guaranteed the house. After moving in March 2000, she found major structural defects. She reported them to Homebond in September 2001; in September 2002 Homebond offered repairs but allegedly refused to issue an engineer’s certificate on completion. In February 2003 she began High Court proceedings against six defendants: Mr and Mrs F, T and C Developments, Homebond, an engineer Mr Q, and Mr Q’s company. She filed her statement of claim in May 2003.

The proceedings were delayed by late defences, default judgment applications, an oversight in serving Homebond until December 2003, and a default judgment against Mr Q and his company in December 2004 that was never enforced. From 2005 to 2008 she dealt mainly with Homebond, and the case was effectively dormant. In April 2009 her solicitor ceased to act, and she continued as a lay litigant. She served notices of intention to proceed in April 2009, October 2010, and September 2011. The High Court heard the case in January 2013. In March 2013 it held Homebond liable under the guarantee for about €51,000 and dismissed the claim against Mr Q. In May 2013 it held Mr and Mrs F jointly liable for €94,082. Homebond’s appeal was transferred to the Court of Appeal and allowed in February 2015. The Fs’ appeal was also transferred; in March 2015 the Court of Appeal set aside the judgment against them, finding they were not liable because they had only sold land and were not parties to the building agreement. In July 2015 the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal. Overall, the proceedings lasted 12 years and 5 months through three instances.

The applicant alleged that this length violated Article 6 § 1. The Government denied a breach, citing procedural complexity from six defendants, numerous interim applications, the applicant’s litigation strategy, and no court backlog. The ECtHR declared the complaint admissible. Applying the criteria of complexity, applicant’s conduct, authorities’ conduct, and what was at stake, the Court found the case procedurally complex. It attributed much of the delay to the applicant, including the dormant period from 2005 to April 2009 and errors of her solicitors. After November 2011, the authorities did not cause excessive delay: the trial was listed reasonably, mediation was a legitimate proposal, and judgments were timely. The appellate courts, especially the Court of Appeal after transfer, actively case-managed the appeals; the final Supreme Court stage was prompt. Although the structural defects in her home were important, the litigation became incommensurate with the relatively simple underlying claim. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 6 § 1.

In *Brennan v. Ireland* (ECtHR, 2 November 2017), Margaret Brennan complained under Article 6 § 1 that Irish civil proceedings concerning defects in her home lasted unreasonably long. In November 1999 she bought a newly built house through two agreements: she purchased the land from Mr and Mrs F for IEP 5,000 and entered a building agreement with T and C Developments Ltd, owned by the Fs, for IEP 80,000. The house was covered by a Homebond guarantee. From March 2000 she observed major structural defects. She reported them to Homebond in September 2001; after inspection, Homebond offered repairs in September 2002, but she alleged it refused to provide an engineer’s certificate/guarantee upon completion.

In February 2003 she sued six defendants in the High Court: Mr and Mrs F, T and C Developments, Homebond, engineer Mr Q, and Mr Q’s company. Her statement of claim was filed in May 2003. The proceedings became procedurally protracted. The first three defendants delayed filing defences; Homebond was not served until December 2003 due to a solicitors’ oversight, and it defended in May 2004. In December 2004 Brennan obtained a default judgment against Mr Q and his company, but it was never enforced; she said she was advised to hold it over until damages were assessed.

Between 2005 and 2008 she focused mainly on Homebond under the guarantee, and the case was effectively dormant. In April 2009 her solicitor ceased acting and she became a lay litigant. She served notices of intention to proceed in April 2009, October 2010 and September 2011. In late 2011 she sought a trial date; a hearing was set for March/April 2012. Mediation was suggested and explored but abandoned by June 2012. The sixth defendant went into liquidation. The trial began on 29 January 2013, but only Homebond and Mr Q appeared. On 20 March 2013 the High Court held Homebond liable under the guarantee, awarding about €51,000 despite a IEP 30,000 cap, and dismissed the claim against Mr Q. On 15 May 2013 the first three defendants were held jointly and severally liable for €94,082.

Appeals ran from June 2013 to July 2015. Homebond appealed; service difficulties led to an extension granted on 14 June 2013. Brennan cross-appealed on costs. In October 2014 the appeal was transferred to the new Court of Appeal, which heard it on 23 February 2015; Homebond’s appeal was allowed and Brennan’s cross-appeal dismissed. The first and second defendants also appealed. After garnishee and judgment-mortgage proceedings, and a conditional Supreme Court stay that lapsed when €45,000 was not paid, that appeal was transferred to the Court of Appeal and heard on 9 March 2015. The Court of Appeal set aside the High Court judgment, holding that Mr and Mrs F were not liable because they had sold only the land and were not party to the building agreement; the remedy lay only against T and C Developments. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 29 July 2015.

The overall duration was twelve years and five months across three instances. The Government denied State responsibility, citing procedural complexity, six defendants, numerous applications, Brennan’s litigation strategy and solicitor errors. The Court found the case procedurally complex but not legally difficult. It attributed much of the delay to Brennan: delayed service, dormancy from 2005 to 2009, repeated notices to proceed, lay litigation, and her representatives’ errors. It found no excessive delay by the authorities once the case was actively prosecuted after November 2011; mediation was reasonable, and the Court of Appeal handled the appeals efficiently after transfer. Although the subject matter—structural defects in her home—was important, the Court considered the litigation’s scale and duration incommensurate with the simple underlying claim and largely generated by Brennan’s own conduct. It therefore found no violation of Article 6 § 1.

**Summary of *Traustason and Others v. Iceland* (Application no. 44081/13)**

The case of *Traustason and Others v. Iceland* originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 6 June 2013 by three Icelandic nationals: Reynir Traustason, Jón Trausti Reynisson, and Ingi Freyr Vilhjálmsson. At the material time, the first and second applicants were on the editorial board of the newspaper *DV*, and the third applicant was a journalist for the publication. The applicants alleged that Icelandic court judgments against them violated their right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention.

The facts centered on the bankruptcy of a prominent Icelandic industrial company in September 2010. Following the bankruptcy, the liquidator hired an accountancy firm to investigate the company’s accounts. On 31 January 2011, the firm finalized a report indicating a suspicion of criminal misconduct by the company’s board members, including its chairman, "A," who was also an assistant professor at the University of Iceland. The liquidator subsequently reported the suspected criminal misconduct to the police. Additionally, a holding company and a bank also filed reports concerning the company and A with the police.

On 14 March 2011, *DV* published a front-page picture of A under the headline "Black report on [the company]: Police investigate Assistant Professor," with a related article on pages 2 and 3 authored by the third applicant. The article's headline read "Assistant professor entangled in police investigation." The coverage was based on the accountancy firm's report, detailing the company's financial situation, alleged payments for A's expenditures unrelated to company operations, and the transfer of assets while insolvent. It noted the company owed approximately 1,100,000,000 ISK to a bank at the time of bankruptcy.

Crucially, on 16 March 2011, A's lawyer received an email from a police prosecutor confirming that the liquidator's complaint was being "examined" alongside two other complaints, but stating that no formal decision had been taken to instigate a police investigation. A's lawyer requested a correction from the first applicant, which was refused.

On 28 April 2011, A lodged defamation proceedings against the applicants and *DV* before the Reykjavík District Court. He requested that the statements "Police investigate Assistant Professor" and "Assistant Professor entangled in police investigation" be declared null and void, and sought compensation.

By judgment of 5 March 2012, the District Court found both disputed statements defamatory. It reasoned that, based on the email, no police investigation had been instigated against A, making the statements factually wrong. The court held that the statements damaged A's reputation by making readers believe he was a suspect in a police investigation. The court declared the statements null and void and ordered the applicants to pay A 200,000 ISK in non-pecuniary damages, 200,000 ISK for publishing the judgment, and 500,000 ISK for legal costs. The applicants appealed.

On 6 December 2012, the Supreme Court confirmed the District Court’s judgment, adding an order for the applicants to pay an additional 500,000 ISK for A’s legal costs before the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court agreed that the email could only be understood as meaning no investigation had been instigated and that the annulled statements were wrong and defamatory.

The applicants complained under Article 10 of the Convention about these judgments. The Court communicated the application to the Icelandic Government on 20 November 2015. The applicants' observations in reply and claim for just satisfaction, submitted on 30 June 2016, were excluded from the case file as they were made outside the granted time-limit and no extension had been requested.

**Case Summary: Traustason and Others v. Iceland**

**Introduction**
The case of *Traustason and Others v. Iceland* (Application no. 44081/13) originated from an application lodged against the Republic of Iceland with the European Court of Human Rights on 6 June 2013. The three applicants—Mr. Reynir Traustason, Mr. Jón Trausti Reynisson, and Mr. Ingi Freyr Vilhjálmsson—complained that judgments from the Icelandic District Court and Supreme Court violated their right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

**Factual Background**
At the time of the events, the first and second applicants were on the editorial board of the newspaper *DV*, and the third applicant was a journalist for the publication. On 30 September 2010, an Icelandic private limited company—one of the country's leading industrial firms in plastic packaging—was declared bankrupt. In October 2010, the bankruptcy estate's liquidator hired an accountancy firm to investigate the company's accounts.

On 31 January 2011, the accountancy firm finalised a report indicating suspicions of criminal misconduct by the company's board members. The chairman, identified as "A" (also an assistant professor at the University of Iceland), was implicated. The liquidator reported the suspected misconduct to the police, and two other entities—a holding company and a bank—also filed reports against the company and A.

**The Publication and Legal Proceedings**
On 14 March 2011, *DV* published a front-page picture of A under the headline "Black report on [the company]: Police investigate Assistant Professor." An accompanying article, authored by the third applicant, was headlined "Assistant professor entangled in police investigation." The article, based on the accountancy firm's report, detailed allegations that the company had paid for A's expenditures, that A and a co-owner knew of the company's grave financial situation before bankruptcy, and that assets had been transferred to another company owned by a co-owner while insolvent. The company owed approximately 1,100,000,000 ISK to a major Icelandic bank at the time of bankruptcy.

On 16 March 2011, A's lawyer received an email from a police prosecutor confirming receipt of the liquidator's complaint and stating it was being "examined," along with two other complaints. Critically, the prosecutor stated that no formal decision had been taken to instigate a police investigation. A's lawyer requested a correction, which the first applicant refused.

On 28 April 2011, A lodged defamation proceedings against the applicants and *DV* before the Reykjavík District Court. On 5 March 2012, the District Court found both statements defamatory, declared them null and void, and ordered the applicants to pay compensation, publication costs, and legal costs. The court reasoned that no police investigation had in fact been instigated against A, making the statements factually wrong. The court found the statements would make readers believe A was a suspect in a police investigation, damaging his reputation.

The applicants appealed, but on 6 December 2012, the Supreme Court confirmed the District Court's judgment, ordering additional legal costs. The Supreme Court reaffirmed that the statements were "wrong and defamatory" and attacked A's reputation "at a time when there were no grounds for it." Notably, by letter of 31 May 2013, the Special Prosecutor notified another company representative that the investigation into complaints against him and A had been closed and the case dismissed.
001-170467:
**Case summary: X v. Switzerland (Application no. 16744/14)**

The applicant, Mr X, is a Sri Lankan national of Tamil origin, born in 1979. During the 1990s he was a member of the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) and took part in armed resistance against the Sri Lankan Government. In late 2003 he was detained in Colombo for about three months, during which he alleged he was ill-treated. After release, he claimed he was threatened and kept under surveillance.

In April 2007 he left Sri Lanka for Italy, where he lived until May 2009. His wife later joined him. On 25 May 2009 they entered Switzerland illegally and applied for asylum, relying on his LTTE membership, armed resistance, detention and ill-treatment. On 1 June 2011 the Federal Migration Office (FMO) rejected the asylum application, finding insufficient evidence, and ordered their deportation to Sri Lanka, which it declared enforceable, lawful and reasonable.

The applicant and his wife appealed only the deportation order, not the refusal of asylum or refugee status. On 1 October 2012 the Federal Administrative Court dismissed the appeal. It accepted that the FMO had violated the right to be heard by withholding a country report on Sri Lanka, but held that later disclosure cured the defect. On the merits, it found no substantial likelihood that the applicant or his wife would face treatment contrary to Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights if returned. A request for reconsideration was rejected on 27 November 2012.

On 21 August 2013 the applicant and his family were deported to Sri Lanka. At Colombo airport they were detained and questioned for about thirteen hours. His wife and children were released, but the applicant was imprisoned and allegedly ill-treated at Boosa Prison. His wife later reported that his face appeared swollen, suggesting he had been beaten. In December 2013, a Swiss Embassy representative and a UNHCR protection officer visited him in prison; they observed that he was visibly afraid to speak and that a free conversation was impossible. He was later transferred to a so-called “rehabilitation” prison and released on 12 April 2015. He returned to Switzerland on 25 April 2015 and was granted asylum in a fresh application on 26 June 2015.

The applicant also highlighted a parallel case: another Tamil, Mr Y, had been deported from Switzerland to Sri Lanka on 25 July 2013, about a month before the applicant. Y was reportedly detained and ill-treated, requiring hospitalisation. On 2 August 2013, Y’s lawyer wrote to the Swiss Minister of Justice and the Migration Office asking that all deportations of Tamils to Sri Lanka be suspended.

Subsequent investigations were critical. A report by Prof. W. Kälin, commissioned by the FMO and delivered on 23 February 2014, concluded that due to several shortcomings by the Swiss authorities, the individual risk of ill-treatment for the two Tamils had not been properly assessed. A UNHCR assessment also identified shortcomings: the long delay between the 2009 asylum application and the 2013 deportation; significant changes in Sri Lanka after the civil war ended in 2009; involvement of several FMO employees over time; a partly superficial hearing; and failure to conduct additional investigations. These reports were made public on 26 May 2014.

Switzerland had resumed deportations of Tamils in 2011 but stopped them in September 2013 after the applicant’s and Y’s expulsions and ill-treatment. The FMO later changed its practice to assess risk using European Court of Human Rights criteria.

Before the Court, the applicant alleged that the Swiss authorities’ failure to properly assess his asylum application and his subsequent deportation to Sri Lanka violated Article 3. The application was lodged on 21 February 2014; the Article 3 complaint was communicated to the Government, and the remainder was declared inadmissible.

**Summary of X v. Switzerland (Application no. 16744/14)**

The case of *X v. Switzerland* concerns the alleged violation of Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. The applicant, Mr. X, is a Sri Lankan national of Tamil origin and a former member of the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), who claimed he had been detained and ill-treated in Sri Lanka in the early 2000s before fleeing to Italy in 2007 and later entering Switzerland in May 2009 with his wife to seek asylum.

In June 2011, the Swiss Federal Migration Office (FMO) rejected the applicant’s asylum application, finding insufficient evidence of persecution, and ordered his deportation to Sri Lanka, deeming it enforceable, legal, and reasonable. The applicant’s appeal to the Federal Administrative Court focused on the deportation order, not the asylum refusal. In October 2012, the court acknowledged a violation of the right to be heard due to delayed access to a country report but concluded the issue was remedied, and upheld the deportation, finding no substantial risk of Article 3 mistreatment upon return.

A request for reconsideration in November 2012 was rejected. On 21 August 2013, the applicant and his family were deported to Sri Lanka. Upon arrival in Colombo, they were detained and questioned for thirteen hours. While his wife and children were released, the applicant was incarcerated and allegedly ill-treated in Boosa Prison, where his wife later observed signs of beating. A December 2013 visit by Swiss Embassy and UNHCR representatives noted the applicant was visibly afraid and unable to speak freely. He was later transferred to a "rehabilitation" prison and released in April 2015.

The applicant highlighted a parallel case: another Tamil, Mr. Y, was deported to Sri Lanka in July 2013 and was detained and ill-treated upon arrival, prompting calls to suspend such deportations. Subsequent investigations, including an external report by Prof. W. Kälin and a UNHCR assessment, identified significant shortcomings in the Swiss authorities’ risk assessment. These included prolonged delays between the asylum application and deportation, failure to account for changed conditions in post-civil war Sri Lanka, and superficial hearings. The reports concluded that the individual risk of ill-treatment had not been properly evaluated.

Following these events, Switzerland suspended deportations of Tamils in September 2013 and revised its practice to align risk assessments with European Court of Human Rights criteria. The applicant eventually returned to Switzerland in April 2015 and was granted asylum in June 2015. The case underscores the failure of Swiss authorities to adequately assess the applicant’s risk of inhuman treatment prior to deportation, leading to his actual ill-treatment in Sri Lanka, and highlights systemic deficiencies in asylum decision-making processes.

In X v. Switzerland (ECtHR, 26 January 2017), the applicant was a Sri Lankan Tamil born in 1979 who complained that Switzerland violated Article 3 of the Convention by failing to properly assess his asylum application and by deporting him to Sri Lanka, where he was detained and ill-treated. He had been an LTTE member in the 1990s, participated in armed resistance against the Sri Lankan Government, and was detained in Colombo in late 2003 for about three months, during which he alleged ill-treatment. After release, he claimed he was threatened and surveilled. In 2007 he left Sri Lanka for Italy; his wife remained behind and allegedly faced police searches and questioning before joining him in 2009. In May 2009 they entered Switzerland and applied for asylum based on political persecution and his LTTE past.

In June 2011 the Federal Migration Office rejected the asylum application, finding insufficient evidence, and ordered their deportation to Sri Lanka as enforceable, legal and reasonable. The applicant and his wife appealed only the deportation order, not the refusal of asylum or refugee status. In October 2012 the Federal Administrative Court dismissed the appeal. It found a violation of the right to be heard because the FMO initially withheld a country report, but concluded this was cured by later access. On the merits, it held there was no substantial likelihood that the applicant or his wife would face Article 3 ill-treatment on return. A November 2012 request for reconsideration, supported by an LTTE magazine cover bearing his photograph, a sister’s letter, and confirmation of a complaint to the Sri Lankan Human Rights Commission, was rejected as an extraordinary remedy that could not introduce evidence available earlier.

On 21 August 2013 the family was deported to Sri Lanka. At Colombo airport they were detained and questioned for thirteen hours. The wife and children were released, but the applicant was imprisoned and allegedly beaten in Boosa Prison. His wife observed his swollen face when visiting. In December 2013 Swiss embassy and UNHCR representatives visited him and noted that he was visibly afraid and unable to speak freely. The family was later relocated to Switzerland; the applicant was transferred to a “rehabilitation” prison and released in April 2015. He returned to Switzerland, and a fresh asylum application was granted in June 2015.

The case was connected to another Tamil, Y, who was deported in July 2013 and allegedly detained, ill-treated, and hospitalized. Y’s lawyer asked Swiss authorities to suspend all Tamil deportations. An external report by Prof. W. Kälin in February 2014 concluded that, due to several shortcomings, the individual risk of ill-treatment for X and Y had not been properly assessed. A UNHCR assessment identified delays between the asylum application and deportation, changed conditions after the civil war, fragmented decision-making, a partly superficial hearing, and failure to conduct further investigations. Switzerland had resumed Tamil deportations in 2011 but stopped them in September 2013 after these cases, later modifying its practice to assess risk using ECtHR criteria. The central Article 3 issue was whether Switzerland adequately assessed and protected the applicant from a foreseeable risk of torture or ill-treatment before deporting him.

In the European Court of Human Rights case **Đuković v. Montenegro** (Application no. 38419/08, judgment of 13 June 2017), the applicant, Batrić Đuković, a Montenegrin and Serbian national born in 1939 and then serving a sentence in Spuž Penitentiary, alleged violations of Articles 6 §1 and 13 of the Convention. He complained that two sets of civil proceedings had lasted excessively long and that no effective domestic remedy existed for that delay.

The first set began on 25 March 1996, when the applicant sued the Municipality of Bar and a local primary school before the Court of First Instance in Bar, seeking compensation for damage caused by expropriation of his property. On 11 April 1996 his representative informed that court that he had started separate proceedings to determine the value of the damages. The Court of First Instance suspended the compensation proceedings pending the final resolution of that valuation matter. No documents showed whether the compensation proceedings had ended; apparently the two related sets remained pending before the Court of First Instance. This first set was the basis for the applicant’s admissible length complaint.

The second set began on 2 February 2004, when the applicant brought proceedings against his neighbour before the same court seeking demarcation of their two plots of land. He amended his claim on 25 March 2004. On 14 September 2004 the parties reached a friendly settlement, which the Court of First Instance approved the same day. The applicant lodged his application with the European Court on 10 June 2008.

The Government first objected that the applicant abused the right of petition by using insulting language about the domestic judiciary, such as “corrupted judges,” “bribed judges,” and “racketeering carried out by judges.” The Court rejected this objection, finding the remarks inappropriate and regrettable but not amounting to extraordinary circumstances justifying inadmissibility.

As to the second set, the Government argued that the complaint was lodged outside the six-month time limit. The proceedings had ended on 14 September 2004, whereas the application was introduced on 10 June 2008. The Government produced minutes showing the friendly settlement and that the applicant had signed them. The applicant did not comment. The Court held that he had sufficient knowledge of the final domestic decision and that the complaint concerning the second set was time-barred under Article 35 §1.

As to the first set, the Government argued that the Court lacked temporal jurisdiction because the proceedings had “ended” by 11 April 1996 and the Convention entered into force for Montenegro only on 3 March 2004. The applicant disagreed. The Court found that the first proceedings began in March 1996 and were suspended in April 1996 pending another civil suit concerning the same underlying issue, which was still pending. Applying its case-law, the Court held that the impugned proceedings fell within its competence ratione temporis from 3 March 2004. It rejected the Government’s objection and declared the complaint admissible.

On the merits, the Court took the relevant period as beginning on 3 March 2004, although the proceedings had started on 25 March 1996 and had not ended. By the time of judgment, they had lasted more than twelve years at one level of jurisdiction; when the Convention entered into force, they had already been pending for about seven years and eleven months. Considering the complexity, the parties’ conduct, and what was at stake, and finding no justification, the Court concluded that the length was excessive and failed the reasonable-time requirement. It found a violation of Article 6 §1 and did not separately examine the complaint under Article 13.

In *Đuković v. Montenegro* (Application no. 38419/08, judgment of 13 June 2017), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints brought by Mr Batrić Đuković, a Montenegrin and Serbian national born in 1939 who was serving a sentence in Spuž Penitentiary. He alleged under Article 6 §1 and Article 13 of the Convention that two sets of civil proceedings in Montenegro had exceeded a reasonable time and that there was no effective domestic remedy for that delay.

The first set of civil proceedings began on 25 March 1996, when the applicant brought a compensation claim against the Municipality of Bar and a local primary school for damage suffered as a result of the expropriation of his property. On 11 April 1996, his representative informed the Court of First Instance in Bar that separate proceedings had been initiated to determine the value of the damages. The Court of First Instance suspended the compensation proceedings pending the final resolution of that valuation matter. No documents were submitted showing whether the compensation proceedings had ended; it therefore appeared that the relevant proceedings were still pending.

The second set of civil proceedings began on 2 February 2004, when the applicant sued his neighbour before the Court of First Instance in Bar, seeking demarcation between their two plots of land. He amended his claim on 25 March 2004. On 14 September 2004, the applicant and the respondent reached a friendly settlement, which the Court of First Instance approved the same day.

The Government raised several preliminary objections. It argued that the applicant had abused the right of petition because he had used insulting expressions such as “corrupted judges,” “bribed judges,” and “the racketeering carried out by judges.” The Court rejected this objection, stating that although the language was inappropriate and regrettable, it did not amount to the extraordinary circumstances required to declare the application abusive.

The Government also argued that the complaints concerning the second set of proceedings were inadmissible under the six-month rule. Those proceedings had ended on 14 September 2004, but the applicant lodged his application with the Court on 10 June 2008. The Court agreed, finding that the applicant had sufficient knowledge of the final domestic decision and that the complaint was therefore introduced out of time.

As to the first set of proceedings, the Government argued that the Court lacked temporal jurisdiction because those proceedings had allegedly “ended” by 11 April 1996, before the Convention entered into force for Montenegro on 3 March 2004. The Court rejected this objection. It noted that the proceedings had been initiated in March 1996 and suspended in April 1996 pending the outcome of another civil suit concerning the same underlying issue, which was still pending. Under the Court’s case-law, the proceedings therefore fell within its competence *ratione temporis* as of 3 March 2004.

On the merits, the Court considered the period from 3 March 2004 onward. By that date, the proceedings had already been pending for approximately seven years, eleven months, and eight days. They had still not ended and had lasted more than twelve years before one level of jurisdiction. Applying the criteria of complexity, the conduct of the applicant and authorities, and what was at stake, the Court found no justification for the delay. It held that the length of the proceedings was excessive and violated the “reasonable time” requirement of Article 6 §1. Having reached that conclusion, the Court did not find it necessary to examine separately the essentially same complaint under Article 13 concerning the lack of an effective domestic remedy.

**Case Summary: Đuković v. Montenegro (Application no. 38419/08)**

The applicant, Mr Batrić Đuković, a Montenegrin and Serbian national born in 1939 and serving a sentence in Spuž Penitentiary, lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 10 June 2008. He complained under Articles 6 § 1 and 13 of the Convention about the excessive length of two sets of domestic civil proceedings and the lack of an effective domestic remedy.

**First set of civil proceedings:** On 25 March 1996, the applicant brought a compensation claim for damages arising from the expropriation of his property against the Municipality of Bar and a local primary school before the Court of First Instance in Bar. On 11 April 1996, the applicant's representative informed the court that separate proceedings had been initiated to determine the value of the damages. Consequently, the Court of First Instance suspended the compensation proceedings pending the final resolution of that related matter. No documentation was submitted confirming whether the compensation proceedings had concluded in the interim; it appeared that both sets of proceedings remained pending before the Court of First Instance. The Government argued that this complaint fell outside the Court's temporal jurisdiction, contending the proceedings had "ended" by 11 April 1996, whereas the Convention entered into force in respect of Montenegro on 3 March 2004. The Court rejected this objection, noting that the proceedings were suspended—not terminated—and remained pending. Applying its established case-law, the Court found the impugned proceedings fell within its competence ratione temporis as of 3 March 2004. On the merits, the Court observed that although the proceedings commenced in March 1996, the relevant period began only on 3 March 2004. By the time of judgment, the proceedings had lasted more than twelve years for one level of jurisdiction, with the case already pending some seven years and eleven months when the Convention entered into force. Finding no justification for the delay, the Court held that the length was excessive and failed to meet the "reasonable time" requirement under Article 6 § 1. Having reached this conclusion, the Court did not find it necessary to examine the essentially identical complaint under Article 13.

**Second set of civil proceedings:** On 2 February 2004, the applicant instituted proceedings against his neighbour seeking demarcation between their plots of land, amending his proposal on 25 March 2004. On 14 September 2004, the parties reached a friendly settlement approved by the Court of First Instance the same day. The Government argued that this complaint was lodged outside the six-month time-limit, as the proceedings ended on 14 September 2004 but the application was submitted on 10 June 2008. The Court agreed, noting the Government provided sufficient evidence (the signed hearing minutes) that the applicant had knowledge of the final decision, and that the complaint was introduced nearly four years later. Accordingly, this complaint was rejected as time-barred under Article 35 § 1.

**Additional issue:** The Government raised a preliminary objection alleging abuse of the right of petition due to the applicant's insulting remarks about the domestic judiciary ("corrupted judges," "bribed judges," "racketeering"). The Court acknowledged the statements were inappropriate and regrettable but held they did not rise to the extraordinary circumstances justifying rejection as abusive, and dismissed the objection.
001-177118:
**Summary of Kolar v. Slovenia (Application no. 33868/08)**

The case of *Kolar v. Slovenia* originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 8 July 2008 by Mr. Janko Kolar, a Slovenian national. The applicant alleged a violation of his right to a trial within a reasonable time and the lack of an effective domestic remedy for this grievance. These were the only complaints communicated to the Slovenian Government, with the remainder of the application declared inadmissible.

The facts stem from a property dispute that began in 1997. The Maribor unit of the Surveying and Mapping Authority issued several decisions concerning the delimitation of real estate belonging to the applicant and a company, D., and ordered changes to land use. The applicant appealed some of these decisions to the Ministry for the Environment and Spatial Planning. On 28 September 2000, the Ministry partially granted his appeal, annulling one decision but dismissing his appeal concerning two others.

On 23 November 2000, the applicant challenged the Ministry's decision before the Administrative Court. The Administrative Court ruled in his favor on 6 November 2003, annulling the contested part of the Ministry's decision and remanding the case. The applicant then appealed this judgment to the Supreme Court, which dismissed his appeal on 24 May 2006, upholding the lower court's decision. Subsequently, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint, which the Constitutional Court dismissed on 19 December 2007.

In total, the domestic judicial proceedings, from the applicant's initial challenge before the Administrative Court in November 2000 until the final decision of the Constitutional Court in December 2007, lasted over seven years. The core of the applicant's case before the European Court was that this duration was excessive and violated the "reasonable time" requirement under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

A further relevant fact concerns the domestic proceedings under the Protection of the Right to Trial without Undue Delay Act ("the 2006 Act"). Following the applicant's application to the European Court, the State Attorney's Office initiated a settlement procedure under section 25 of the 2006 Act. On 10 July 2015, they sent the applicant a settlement offer. In this offer, the State Attorney's Office acknowledged that the applicant's right to a trial within a reasonable time had been violated in the proceedings before the Administrative Court and the Supreme Court. However, the offer explicitly stated that the proceedings before the Constitutional Court could not have given rise to such a violation. As redress for the acknowledged delay, they offered to provide a written statement of this acknowledgment. The applicant did not accept this settlement offer.

**Summary of the Case of Kolar v. Slovenia**

The case of *Kolar v. Slovenia* (Application no. 33868/08) originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr. Janko Kolar, a Slovenian national, on 8 July 2008. The core of the applicant's complaint, which was communicated to the Slovenian Government, concerned the excessive length of judicial proceedings and the lack of an effective domestic remedy in that regard.

The facts stem from a property dispute that began in 1997. In that year, the Maribor unit of the Surveying and Mapping Authority issued several decisions regarding the delimitation of real estate belonging to the applicant and another company, ordering changes to land use. The applicant appealed some of these decisions to the Ministry for the Environment and Spatial Planning.

On 28 September 2000, the Ministry partially granted his appeal, annulling one decision but dismissing his appeal concerning two others. Subsequently, on 23 November 2000, the applicant initiated proceedings before the Administrative Court to challenge the part of the Ministry's decision that dismissed his appeal.

The domestic proceedings then progressed through several judicial levels over a period of nearly seven years. On 6 November 2003, the Administrative Court granted the applicant's appeal, annulled the challenged part of the Ministry's decision, and remitted the case for further consideration. The applicant then appealed this decision. On 24 May 2006, the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal, and this judgment was served on him on 4 July 2006. Following this, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint, which was dismissed by the Constitutional Court on 19 December 2007, with the decision served on 10 January 2008.

In total, the period under scrutiny for the applicant's "length of proceedings" complaint spanned from 23 November 2000, when he commenced proceedings before the Administrative Court, until 10 January 2008, when the Constitutional Court's decision was served. This amounts to over seven years for the domestic judicial review of his property dispute.

Separately, in 2015, following the application to the European Court, the State Attorney's Office attempted to settle the case under the Protection of the Right to Trial without Undue Delay Act (the 2006 Act). They offered the applicant a written statement acknowledging a violation of his right to a trial within a reasonable time in the proceedings before the Administrative and Supreme Courts. The applicant did not accept this settlement offer.

The European Court of Human Rights, sitting as a Committee, noted the significant duration of the proceedings before the national courts. The Court found that the applicant's right to a trial within a reasonable time, as guaranteed by Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, had been violated. It also held that the domestic legal remedies available to the applicant, including the settlement procedure under the 2006 Act, were not effective, constituting a violation of Article 13 of the Convention.

**Kolar v. Slovenia** (Application no. 33868/08) is a European Court of Human Rights case concerning the length of judicial proceedings and the alleged lack of an effective domestic remedy. The applicant, Janko Kolar, a Slovenian national born in 1949 and living in Serbia, was involved in a property and land-use dispute with a company referred to as D.

In 1997, the Maribor unit of the Surveying and Mapping Authority issued several decisions concerning the delimitation of real estate belonging to the applicant and company D., and ordering changes to land use. The applicant appealed some of those decisions. On 28 September 2000, the Ministry for the Environment and Spatial Planning partly granted his appeal, annulled one decision issued on 12 February 1997, but dismissed his appeal concerning two decisions issued on 31 January 1997.

On 23 November 2000, the applicant challenged the Ministry’s dismissing decision before the Administrative Court. On 6 November 2003, the Administrative Court granted his appeal, annulled the challenged part of the Ministry’s decision, and referred the case back to the Ministry, which in turn referred it to the Maribor unit. The applicant appealed. On 24 May 2006, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the Administrative Court’s judgment. That decision was served on the applicant on 4 July 2006.

The applicant then lodged a constitutional complaint. On 19 December 2007, the Constitutional Court dismissed it. The decision was served on the applicant on 10 January 2008. On 8 July 2008, the applicant lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights. On 13 May 2015, the Court communicated to the Government the complaints concerning the length of the judicial proceedings and the lack of an effective remedy in that connection. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

A further key fact relates to the domestic settlement procedure under the Protection of the Right to Trial without Undue Delay Act 2006. On 10 July 2015, the State Attorney’s Office sent the applicant a settlement offer under section 25 of that Act. Section 25 applies where an alleged violation of the right to a trial without undue delay had already ceased by 31 March 2007 and the party had sought just satisfaction before an international court before the Act entered into force. The State Attorney’s Office stated that the proceedings before the Constitutional Court could not have given rise to a reasonable-time violation. It offered a written statement acknowledging that the applicant’s right to a trial within a reasonable time had been violated in the proceedings before the Administrative Court and the Supreme Court. The offer was served on 24 July 2015, but the applicant did not accept it.

Under section 25, if a settlement offer is not accepted or no agreement is reached, the party may bring an action before the competent court within six months. The provisions on small claims apply. The central alleged violations therefore concerned the excessive duration of the proceedings before the Administrative Court and Supreme Court under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, and the absence of an effective domestic remedy for that delay under Article 13. The most relevant facts are the chronology of the domestic proceedings from 2000 to 2008, the applicant’s 2008 Strasbourg application, and the 2015 settlement offer, which he refused.
