In *Braga v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* (Application no. 76957/01, judgment of 17 October 2017), the applicant, Andrian Braga, a Moldovan national living in Râbniţa, was arrested on 28 July 1999 by a prosecutor of the self-proclaimed “Moldavian Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”). He was charged with fraud and incitement to bribery. On 17 May 2000, the Camenca District Court, acting under MRT jurisdiction, convicted him and sentenced him to five years’ imprisonment. He initially served his sentence in Tiraspol Prison no. 2.

On 25 October 2001, the applicant was transferred to Pruncul Prison Hospital, which was under the control of the Moldovan authorities. On 30 October 2001, he signed a form of authority allowing the Chişinău-based NGO Lawyers for Human Rights (LHR) to represent him before the European Court of Human Rights. On 20 November 2001, an LHR lawyer informed the Moldovan Prosecutor General’s Office that the applicant and seven others were being unlawfully held on the basis of MRT court convictions and requested their immediate release. The lawyer warned that transferring them back to the MRT would engage Moldova’s responsibility. A press conference was held the next day. Also on 21 November 2001, all eight detainees, including the applicant, were allegedly transferred back to MRT prisons. On 26 November 2001, the Moldovan Ministry of Justice said the detainees were not at Pruncul Prison Hospital. LHR’s later request to see the applicant in MRT custody received no reply. He was released on 22 January 2002 under an amnesty act.

The applicant alleged that he had been unlawfully arrested and convicted by the MRT authorities, ill-treated, held in inhuman conditions, and prevented from effectively communicating with the Court. Under Article 3, he complained that he had been severely beaten upon arrest and ill-treated to force a confession. He also described appalling detention conditions: being held with tuberculosis sufferers, risking infection, sharing a cell affected by parasitic insects, receiving no medication despite his category 3 disability, and being served food only once a day of very poor quality. He claimed that approximately 100 detainees had died of tuberculosis in Tiraspol Prison no. 2.

The Court rejected the complaint of ill-treatment upon arrest as manifestly ill-founded because the applicant provided no evidence and did not show that he had been prevented from complaining, including while under Moldovan control. However, it declared the complaint about inhuman conditions of detention admissible. On the merits, the Court found that the conditions amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment under Article 3, particularly because of parasitic insects and grossly inadequate food, which increased the risk of tuberculosis.

On jurisdiction, the Court held that Moldova retained jurisdiction over Transdniestria as the territorial State but had only positive obligations because it lacked effective control. Russia had jurisdiction because it had contributed militarily and politically to the creation of the MRT and the MRT depended on Russian support; Russia exercised effective control and decisive influence over the Transdniestrian authorities. The exception was the period between 25 October and 21 November 2001, when the applicant was in Moldovan-controlled custody.

As to responsibility, Moldova was not responsible for violations before 25 October 2001. But after the applicant’s transfer to Pruncul, Moldova had complete control over him. Despite LHR’s complaint to the Prosecutor General that his detention was unlawful and its warning not to return him to the MRT, Moldova failed to prevent his transfer back. Official documents had been destroyed, and no trace of an investigation existed. The Court therefore found that Moldova failed its positive obligation to ensure respect for the applicant’s Article 3 rights. Russia was responsible for the MRT’s treatment of the applicant outside the brief period of Moldovan control.

In **Braga v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia** (Application no. 76957/01), the applicant, Andrian Braga, was a Moldovan national living in Râbniţa, in the Transdniestrian region. On 28 July 1999 he was arrested by a prosecutor of the self-proclaimed “Moldavian Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”) and charged with fraud and incitement to bribery. On 17 May 2000 the Camenca District Court, an MRT court, convicted him and sentenced him to five years’ imprisonment. His appeal was rejected by the MRT Supreme Court. He initially served his sentence in Tiraspol Prison no. 2.

The key events relevant to jurisdiction and the alleged violations began on 25 October 2001, when Braga was transferred to Pruncul Prison Hospital, which was under the control of the Moldovan authorities. On 30 October 2001 he signed a form authorising Lawyers for Human Rights (LHR) to represent him before the European Court. His application reached the Court on 19 November 2001. On 20 November 2001, an LHR lawyer informed the Moldovan Prosecutor General’s Office and the Minister of Justice that Braga and seven others were being held in Pruncul on the basis of unlawful MRT convictions. The lawyer requested their immediate release and warned that transferring them back to the MRT would engage Moldova’s responsibility. On 21 November 2001, LHR held a press conference. That same day, Braga and the other detainees were allegedly transferred back to MRT prisons. On 26 November the Ministry of Justice stated that they were not then at Pruncul. On 7 December LHR sought permission from the MRT Ministry of Justice to see Braga, but received no reply. He was released on 22 January 2002 under an amnesty.

Braga alleged unlawful arrest and conviction by the MRT authorities, ill-treatment aimed at forcing a confession, inhuman conditions of detention, and interference with his communication with the Court. The Court rejected the ill-treatment complaint as manifestly ill-founded because there was no supporting evidence and no complaint had been made, at least while he was under Moldovan control. The complaint about inhuman detention conditions was declared admissible.

On jurisdiction, the Court held that Moldova had jurisdiction as the territorial State but only limited positive obligations because it lacked effective control over Transdniestria. Russia had jurisdiction over the MRT-controlled area because it had contributed militarily and politically to the separatist regime and continued to provide military, economic and political support, giving it decisive influence over the MRT. The exception was the period from 25 October to 21 November 2001, when Braga was in Moldovan-controlled Pruncul.

On the merits, the Court found that the conditions of Braga’s detention in MRT custody amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment under Article 3, particularly because of parasitic insects, grossly inadequate food, and exposure to tuberculosis. It held Moldova responsible for failing its positive obligation: although it had complete control over Braga at Pruncul, it did not prevent his transfer back to the MRT and failed to show any investigation into the serious allegations. Russia was responsible for the Article 3 breach while Braga was within its jurisdiction through the MRT, apart from the short Moldova-controlled period. The case therefore concerned both the unlawful detention and conviction by the MRT and, most importantly, the inhuman detention conditions and Moldova’s failure to protect the applicant when it had the opportunity.

**Case: Braga v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia (Application no. 76957/01), ECtHR Judgment, 17 October 2017**

The applicant, Andrian Braga, a Moldovan national born in 1971 and living in Râbniţa, complained that he had been unlawfully arrested and convicted by the authorities of the self-proclaimed “Moldavian Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”), ill-treated, held in inhuman conditions, and prevented from effectively communicating with the European Court of Human Rights.

On 28 July 1999, Braga was arrested in Râbniţa by a prosecutor of the MRT. He was charged with fraud and incitement to bribery. On 17 May 2000, the Camenca District Court, operating under the MRT, convicted him and sentenced him to five years’ imprisonment. His appeal to the MRT Supreme Court was rejected. He initially served his sentence in Tiraspol Prison No. 2. On 25 October 2001, he was transferred to Pruncul Prison Hospital, which was under Moldovan authorities’ control. On 30 October 2001, he signed a form authorising the Chișinău-based NGO Lawyers for Human Rights (LHR) to represent him before the Court; the application reached the Court on 19 November 2001.

On 20 November 2001, an LHR lawyer informed the Moldovan Prosecutor General’s Office that Braga and seven others were being held at Pruncul Prison Hospital on the basis of convictions by MRT courts. The lawyer sought their immediate release, arguing that they had been convicted by unlawful courts, and warned that transferring them back to the MRT would engage Moldova’s responsibility. A similar letter was sent to the Minister of Justice. On 21 November 2001, LHR held a press conference publicising the case. That same day, all eight detainees, including Braga, were allegedly transferred back to MRT prisons. On 26 November 2001, the Moldovan Ministry of Justice informed LHR that the detainees were not at Pruncul, but this did not contradict the alleged transfer. On 7 December 2001, an LHR lawyer wrote to the MRT Ministry of Justice seeking permission to visit Braga and stating an intention to lodge a Court application; no reply was received. Braga was released on 22 January 2002 under an amnesty.

Braga described severe ill-treatment upon arrest and detention conditions that he alleged violated Article 3. He complained of being held in a cell with tuberculosis sufferers, risking infection; approximately 100 detainees died of tuberculosis in Tiraspol Prison No. 2; parasitic insects; lack of medication despite a category 3 disability; and food served only once daily of very poor quality and quantity.

The Court rejected the ill-treatment complaint as manifestly ill-founded because Braga submitted no evidence and had not shown he was prevented from complaining. However, the complaint about inhuman conditions of detention was declared admissible. The Court found the conditions amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment, particularly due to parasitic insects, inadequate food, and increased tuberculosis risk.

On jurisdiction, the Court held that Moldova had territorial jurisdiction but only positive obligations regarding the Transdniestrian region. Russia exercised effective control and decisive influence over the MRT, so the applicant fell within Russian jurisdiction, except for the period between 25 October and 21 November 2001. Moldova was not responsible before 25 October 2001. However, after Braga was transferred to Pruncul, Moldova had full control over him. The Moldovan authorities failed to verify LHR’s unlawful-detention complaint or prevent his transfer back to the MRT, despite knowing an application had been lodged with the Court. The destruction of documents did not excuse that failure. Moldova therefore failed its positive obligation to ensure respect for Braga’s Article 3 rights, placing him back in incompatible detention conditions.

**Case:** *Ozols v. Latvia* (Application no. 61257/08), European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, judgment of 13 July 2017.

**Key facts relevant to the alleged violation**

The applicant, Jānis Ozols, was a Latvian customs official. In 2000, a criminal investigation began into irregularities in customs procedures involving the transit of vehicles, where falsified documents allegedly allowed foreign vehicles to be legalised in Latvia. Seven customs officials, including Ozols, were charged. Ozols was accused of negligence causing substantial harm to the State and public interest in connection with processing documentation for a used semi-trailer.

In December 2005, the Riga Regional Court convicted Ozols and fined him five minimum monthly salaries. It found that on 31 March 1999 he had acted contrary to customs regulations: he accepted a transit declaration from a person who was not the declarant’s authorised representative; failed to verify whether the person presenting a power of attorney was the person to whom it had been issued; failed to verify whether the semi-trailer was in the customs zone; failed to issue an administrative violation record for breach of the 48-hour delivery deadline; and processed incomplete documentation. The court relied on a State Revenue Service report and on the pre-trial statement of witness E.A., a purchaser of one of the vehicles. E.A. had been summoned but could not attend due to hospitalisation. His statement supported that the semi-trailer had not been at the customs warehouse and could not have been inspected by the customs officer, while the documentation showed Ozols processed it. The defence questioned why a certified copy of E.A.’s statement, rather than the original, was in the file; the prosecutor replied.

On appeal, E.A. again did not appear. Ozols initially asked that E.A. be summoned, but later his defence counsel withdrew that request, stating they no longer needed E.A., that the expert evidence was sufficient, and that there were no justifiable grounds for E.A.’s absence. Counsel also objected to reading E.A.’s pre-trial testimony. The appellate court nevertheless read it out under section 501 of the Criminal Procedure Law. After the reading, the defence said it had no requests and that the adjudication could be terminated. In February 2008, the appellate court upheld the conviction, relying on E.A.’s statement together with documentary evidence, the logbook, payment documents, and Ozols’s own statements. The Supreme Court dismissed his appeal on points of law in July 2008, finding that the appellate court had made efforts to secure E.A.’s attendance and had lawfully read his testimony.

**Alleged violation**

Ozols complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention that he and his defence counsel had been deprived of the opportunity to question witness E.A. and that the domestic courts had not sufficiently reasoned his guilt. The Government argued that Ozols had waived his right to summon E.A., that authorities had tried to secure his attendance, that E.A.’s evidence was not sole or decisive, and that the conviction rested on other evidence with detailed reasoning.

**ECtHR conclusion**

The Court declared the complaint admissible but found no violation. Although E.A.’s absence was not fully justified and more effort could have been made, Ozols had withdrawn his request to summon E.A. and could reasonably have foreseen that the court might read the statement. The evidence was not sole or decisive, and counterbalancing factors existed: Ozols was represented by counsel, could question another witness, had an opportunity to comment on or challenge E.A.’s statement, did not claim it was untrue, and the domestic courts treated it cautiously alongside corroborative evidence. The reasoning was also sufficient. Overall, the proceedings were fair.

In *Ozols v. Latvia* (ECtHR, 13 July 2017, App. No. 61257/08), the applicant, a Latvian customs official, was convicted in 2005 of negligence causing substantial harm to the State and public interest. The charge arose from a 2000 investigation into customs irregularities involving the transit of vehicles, in which falsified documents allowed foreign goods to be legalised. Seven customs officials were charged. Ozols was charged specifically over his processing of documentation for a used semi-trailer on 31 March 1999. The first-instance court found that he had accepted a transit declaration from a person who was not the declarant’s authorised representative, failed to verify the power of attorney, failed to check whether the semi-trailer was in the customs zone, failed to issue a violation record for breach of the 48-hour delivery deadline, and processed incomplete documents. It relied on a State Revenue Service report and the pre-trial statement of witness E.A., the purchaser, who was absent due to hospitalisation. E.A. had said the semi-trailer was not at the customs warehouse, could not have been inspected, and that clearance was performed by Ozols. The defence questioned how E.A.’s statement was included in the file.

On appeal, E.A. was summoned at the applicant’s request but failed to attend in September 2007 (hospitalisation) and February 2008 (abroad and car trouble), asking the court to read his pre-trial statements. At the February 2008 hearings, the prosecutor argued E.A. was avoiding court, so his testimony could be read. Defence counsel disagreed that it could be read, but also stated they no longer needed E.A., did not uphold the request to summon him, and considered there were no justifiable grounds for his absence. The appellate court read E.A.’s testimony under section 501 of the Criminal Procedure Law. After it was read, the defence said it had no requests and that adjudication could terminate. The appeal court upheld the conviction, relying on E.A.’s statement together with the logbook, the applicant’s own statements, and payment documents. The Supreme Court Senate dismissed the appeal on points of law, finding the appellate court had made efforts to secure E.A.’s attendance and acted under section 501.

The applicant complained under Article 6 §§1 and 3(d) that he and his counsel could not question E.A. and that the domestic courts had insufficiently reasoned his guilt. The Government argued waiver, adequate efforts to summon E.A., that E.A.’s evidence was not sole or decisive, and that other strong evidence supported conviction.

The ECtHR declared the complaint admissible but found no violation. Applying *Al-Khawaja*, *Schatschaschwili* and *Seton*, the Court noted that although authorities could have done more to compel E.A.’s attendance, the appellate court had consulted defence counsel, who expressly withdrew the request to summon him. The applicant could reasonably foresee that E.A.’s pre-trial statements might be read under domestic law, so the absence did not weigh heavily. However, because the defence had objected to reading the statement, the Court assessed overall fairness. E.A.’s evidence was not the sole or decisive basis for conviction; guilt rested on documentary evidence, the applicant’s statements, and other material. Counterbalancing factors existed: the applicant was represented by counsel who questioned another witness; he could give his own account and challenge E.A.’s statements; the first-instance court required the prosecutor to clarify the recording of E.A.’s statements and no further objection followed; the domestic courts treated the untested evidence cautiously and used it to corroborate other evidence; and the defence had an indirect opportunity to comment or ask questions but did not. The domestic decisions were sufficiently reasoned. Overall, the inability to question E.A. did not impair the fairness of the proceedings or render the reasoning arbitrary.

The applicant, Jānis Ozols, a Latvian customs official, was convicted in 2005 of negligence causing substantial harm to the State and public interest. The charge arose from a 2000 investigation into irregularities in customs procedures for vehicle transit. Ozols was accused of mishandling documentation for a used semi-trailer on 31 March 1999. Specifically, he allegedly accepted a transit declaration from someone not authorised to act for the declarant, failed to verify the identity of the person named in a power of attorney, failed to confirm whether the semi-trailer was in the customs zone, failed to issue a record for breach of the 48-hour delivery deadline, and processed incomplete documentation. The first-instance court relied on a State Revenue Service report and the pre-trial statement of witness E.A., the semi-trailer’s purchaser, who could not attend due to hospitalisation. E.A. said the semi-trailer had not been at the customs warehouse and could not have been inspected, while documents indicated Ozols processed the clearance. The defence challenged the use of a certified copy of E.A.’s statement, and the prosecutor provided an explanation.

On appeal, E.A. was again absent. Ozols initially asked that E.A. be summoned. E.A. was summoned for hearings in September 2007 and February 2008 but wrote asking to be excused because of hospitalisation, being abroad, and car trouble, and asked the court to read his pre-trial statements. At the February 2008 hearing, the prosecutor argued E.A. was avoiding court, providing grounds to read his testimony. Defence counsel objected to the reading, but then stated that E.A. was no longer needed, that the expert evidence was sufficient, and that the request to summon him was not upheld. The appellate court read E.A.’s testimony under section 501 of the Criminal Procedure Law. Afterwards, the defence said it had no requests and that adjudication could end. The appellate court upheld the conviction on 15 February 2008, finding that Ozols had inadequately verified the power of attorney and payment documents. The Government argued that Ozols had waived his right to summon E.A., that authorities had made efforts to secure his attendance, and that E.A.’s evidence was not sole or decisive.

The Court declared the complaint admissible but found no violation. Although the authorities could have done more to compel E.A. to attend, Ozols had expressly revoked his request to summon him and could reasonably have foreseen that the court might read the absent witness’s testimony. The Court therefore gave less weight to E.A.’s non-attendance. It further found that E.A.’s evidence was not the sole or decisive basis for conviction; Ozols’s guilt rested on a set of documentary and other evidence. Sufficient counterbalancing factors existed: Ozols was represented by counsel, questioned another witness, had an opportunity to comment on or challenge E.A.’s statements, and never claimed they were untrue. The appellate court treated E.A.’s evidence cautiously and used it to corroborate other evidence. The domestic decisions were also sufficiently reasoned. Consequently, the inability to question E.A. did not affect the overall fairness of the criminal proceedings.

**Case Summary: Ezgeta v. Croatia (Application no. 40562/12)**

**Background and Initial Proceedings**
The applicant, Ms. Iva Ezgeta, a Croatian national, purchased plots of land in 1999 from a company (the claimant) that had built residential buildings on land originally granted for use by the Novigrad Municipality in 1971. A dispute arose over land register records, leading the claimant to initiate civil proceedings against the Municipality in 2000 to correct the data, stating the claim's value as 5,000 Croatian kunas (HRK). The applicant joined these proceedings as an intervener in 2000, as her purchased property was directly affected.

**First-Instance and Appeal Proceedings**
During a hearing on 14 June 2001, the claimant raised the claim's value to HRK 105,000. The defendant did not object. The Buje Municipal Court initially ruled for the claimant in 2005, but this was quashed on appeal. In a retrial, the first-instance court dismissed the claim on 26 May 2009.

Crucially, the judgment noted that the case had been conducted and the judgment drafted by a court administrator, J.G., not a judge. The applicant appealed, arguing that a court administrator was not legally authorized to conduct such proceedings, violating her right to a tribunal established by law. She also contested the increased claim value for calculating costs.

**Key Facts Relevant to Alleged Violations**
The alleged violations stem from two core issues:

1.  **Lack of a Tribunal Established by Law (Article 6 § 1):** The applicant's primary complaint was that her civil case was heard and decided by a court administrator. According to the Civil Procedure Act and Courts Act in force at the time, court administrators were only authorized to conduct proceedings and propose decisions in specific, limited types of cases, primarily monetary claims below HRK 50,000. The applicant's case was a land register correction dispute and did not fall into this category. She argued that the administrator’s involvement meant her case was not determined by a legally constituted tribunal.

2.  **Denial of Access to the Supreme Court:** Despite the first-instance court and the Pula County Court (on appeal) proceeding on the basis that the claim's value was HRK 105,000, the Supreme Court, in a decision on 14 October 2011, declared the applicant's subsequent appeal on points of law inadmissible *ratione valoris*. It held that the relevant value was the original HRK 5,000 stated in the civil action, as the claimant had not formally amended the claim itself. This value fell below the statutory threshold for Supreme Court appeals. The applicant alleged this arbitrary re-evaluation by the Supreme Court deprived her of access to the highest court.

In *Ezgeta v. Croatia* (Application no. 40562/12, ECtHR, 7 September 2017), the applicant, Iva Ezgeta, a Croatian national, complained under Article 6 § 1 that her civil case had not been heard and decided by a tribunal established by law and that she had been deprived of access to the Supreme Court because her appeal on points of law was declared inadmissible *ratione valoris*.

The underlying dispute arose from land in Novigrad. In 1971 the municipality granted land to a company, G.P., for permanent use for residential construction. G.P. built and sold buildings and later sought corrections to the land register. After the municipality objected, the Buje Municipal Court instructed the parties in 2000 to bring civil proceedings. G.P. then sued the municipality to correct the register, initially valuing the claim at HRK 5,000. In 1999 the applicant bought surrounding plots from G.P.; in 2000 she joined the proceedings as an intervener, claiming a legal interest in the plots.

At a hearing on 14 June 2001 the first-instance court recorded that G.P. had increased the claim value to HRK 105,000; the municipality did not object. The court allowed the applicant to intervene. In 2005 the claim was allowed, but the Pula County Court quashed that judgment on appeal and remitted the case. In 2009 the Buje Municipal Court dismissed the claim. The judgment contained a note that the case had been conducted and the judgment drafted by J.G., a court administrator (*sudski savjetnik*).

The applicant appealed, complaining that a court administrator, who was not authorised to conduct such proceedings, had heard and decided the case. She proposed evidence from J.G. and others. She also disputed the litigation costs, arguing that the value of the claim remained HRK 5,000, not HRK 105,000. In 2010 the Pula County Court upheld the first-instance judgment. It accepted the HRK 105,000 value because the increase occurred before the defendant began arguing the merits, and stated that the file showed the proceedings had been conducted by a trial judge in the presence of the court administrator.

The applicant then filed a constitutional complaint and an appeal on points of law. She reiterated that the proceedings had not been conducted by a tribunal established by law, alleging that the judge had not been present at hearings and had signed the records afterwards. On 14 October 2011 the Supreme Court declared her appeal on points of law inadmissible *ratione valoris*. Contrary to the lower courts, it held that the relevant value was the original HRK 5,000, because the claimant could change it only if it also amended the claim; that amount fell below the HRK 100,000 statutory threshold. The applicant added this decision to her constitutional complaint, arguing that the Supreme Court had applied procedural rules arbitrarily. On 29 March 2012 the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint as manifestly ill-founded.

Relevant domestic law provided that court administrators could conduct first-instance litigation, assess evidence and propose decisions to a judge only in specified cases, including monetary claims up to HRK 50,000. The case therefore concerned whether the land-register claim fell within that authorisation and whether the inconsistent valuation of the claim unlawfully blocked access to the Supreme Court.

Ezgeta v. Croatia (Application no. 40562/12) concerned a Croatian land-register dispute and complaints under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant, Iva Ezgeta, was a Croatian national living in Novigrad. The underlying dispute arose from a 1971 contract under which a company, G.P., received plots from Novigrad Municipality for permanent use and built residential buildings, which were then sold. After land-register correction proceedings, the municipality objected, and on 2 October 2000 the Buje Municipal Court directed the parties to civil proceedings.

On 6 October 2000 G.P. sued Novigrad Municipality in the Buje Municipal Court, seeking correction of land-register data concerning the size and status of certain plots. It initially valued the claim at HRK 5,000. The applicant had bought surrounding plots from G.P. in December 1999 and, in October 2000, asked to join the proceedings as an intervener; this was allowed because she had a legal interest.

At a hearing on 14 June 2001, the claimant raised the value of the claim to HRK 105,000. The defendant did not object. On 25 February 2005 the Buje Municipal Court allowed the claim. On appeal, the Pula County Court quashed that judgment in 2007 and remitted the case. On 26 May 2009 the first-instance court dismissed the claim. Importantly, the judgment noted at the bottom that the case had been conducted and the judgment drafted by J.G., a court administrator (sudski savjetnik).

The applicant appealed, arguing that the court administrator had not been authorised to conduct the proceedings and that costs had been wrongly assessed using HRK 105,000 rather than the initial HRK 5,000. On 18 October 2010 the Pula County Court upheld the judgment. It found that the value of the claim was HRK 105,000 because it had been increased before the defendant began litigating on the merits, and stated that the file showed the trial judge had conducted the proceedings in the presence of the court administrator.

The applicant then filed both an appeal on points of law and a constitutional complaint. She alleged that she had not had a hearing before a tribunal established by law, because the proceedings had been conducted and the judgment drafted by a court administrator; she claimed the judge had not been present at hearings and had signed the records afterwards. On 14 October 2011 the Supreme Court declared her appeal on points of law inadmissible ratione valoris. Contrary to the lower courts, it held that the value of the claim was the original HRK 5,000, because the claimant could alter it only if it also amended its claim. Since that did not reach the statutory threshold of HRK 100,000, the appeal was inadmissible. The applicant added this decision to her constitutional complaint, but on 29 March 2012 the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint as manifestly ill-founded.

Under domestic law, the Civil Procedure Act and Courts Act allowed court administrators to conduct first-instance litigation, assess evidence, establish facts, and propose decisions to a judge. However, their authorisation in litigation was expressly limited to monetary claims not exceeding HRK 50,000, or commercial claims not exceeding HRK 500,000. Later Supreme Court case-law stated that court administrators were not authorised in other types of litigation, regardless of value. The applicant’s central Article 6 complaints were therefore that her case was decided by a tribunal not established by law and that she was denied access to the Supreme Court through the inadmissibility ruling based on the disputed valuation of her claim.

Case summary: **Ahmed v. the United Kingdom** (App. No. 59727/13)

The applicant, Liban Mohamud Ahmed, a Somali national born in 1977, left Somalia in 1992, lived in the Netherlands, and entered the UK in 1999, claiming asylum under a false name and history. He was granted exceptional leave to remain until 2004. Between 2001 and 2007 he received multiple criminal convictions, including a 2007 public-order offence and failure to surrender, for which he was imprisoned for four and a half months. In January 2008 the Secretary of State notified him of an intention to deport him; his appeal was dismissed in June 2008.

On 8 February 2008, after serving half of his custodial sentence, Ahmed was detained under Schedule 3 to the Immigration Act 1971 pending deportation. A deportation order was signed on 29 October 2008. Removal directions were set for June 2009, but on 16 June 2009 the European Court of Human Rights granted an interim measure under Rule 39, preventing his removal to Somalia. He remained in immigration detention until 13 July 2011—about two years and twenty-seven days after the Rule 39 measure.

During detention, monthly reviews stated that he could reduce his detention by withdrawing his ECtHR application and returning voluntarily under the Facilitated Return Scheme. Bail applications were refused; immigration judges found him a significant abscond risk. The domestic courts applied the *Hardial Singh* principles: detention must be for deportation, for a reasonable period, with release if removal cannot realistically occur within a reasonable time, and authorities must act with due diligence. The Administrative Court and Court of Appeal rejected his judicial review, finding that, despite the Rule 39 measure, there remained a reasonable prospect of removal within a reasonable time; that he posed substantial absconding and reoffending risks; that alternatives to detention were inadequate; and that continued detention after the *Sufi and Elmi* judgment (two weeks) was not unlawful. The Supreme Court refused leave in March 2013.

Before the ECtHR, Ahmed alleged a violation of Article 5 § 1(f). He argued that UK immigration detention law was not sufficiently precise, accessible or foreseeable; that during the last 25 months detention was not “with a view to deportation” because Rule 39 barred removal and no alternative destination was explored; that protracted inactivity showed a lack of due diligence; and that the overall length was excessive. The Government contended that the law was precise, that the *Hardial Singh* test was more protective than Article 5 § 1(f), and that the domestic courts had correctly found the detention lawful.

The ECtHR declared the complaint admissible. It noted that *J.N. v. the United Kingdom* had already rejected the quality-of-law argument. The central issue was whether detention became “arbitrary” between 16 June 2009 and 13 July 2011; the parties accepted it was lawful until 16 June 2009. The Court emphasised that removal must remain a realistic prospect and that a Rule 39 measure cannot justify indefinite detention. It examined the risk of absconding and reoffending, the availability of alternatives, the authorities’ diligence, and the possibility of voluntary return. The Court ultimately found **no violation** of Article 5 § 1(f), concluding that the applicant’s detention had not been arbitrary in the circumstances.

In **Ahmed v. the United Kingdom** (App. No. 59727/13, 2 March 2017), the applicant, a Somali national, complained that his immigration detention pending deportation from 8 February 2008 to 13 July 2011 violated Article 5 § 1(f) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The key dispute concerned the period after 16 June 2009, when the European Court of Human Rights granted an interim Rule 39 measure preventing his removal to Somalia.

The applicant arrived in the UK in December 1999 and claimed asylum using a false name and immigration history to avoid return to the Netherlands. Although asylum was refused, he obtained exceptional leave until 2004. Between 2001 and 2007 he received numerous criminal convictions, including public order and failing to surrender; in December 2007 he was imprisoned for four and a half months. In January 2008 the Secretary of State decided to deport him and refused indefinite leave to remain. His deportation appeal was dismissed in June 2008.

On 8 February 2008, after serving half his sentence, he was detained pending deportation; a deportation order was signed in October 2008. Removal directions were set for 17 June 2009, but on 16 June 2009 the ECtHR indicated a Rule 39 measure, so removal was cancelled. He remained detained until 13 July 2011. Monthly detention reviews repeatedly noted that the Rule 39 measure blocked removal but suggested he could reduce his detention by withdrawing his ECtHR application and returning voluntarily under the Facilitated Return Scheme. Bail applications were refused in November 2009, April 2010 and July 2010 because immigration judges found him a significant abscond risk. One judge noted that the latest detention period was due to delays with his own ECtHR application.

His further representations against removal were treated as an application to revoke the deportation order; the Secretary of State refused in November 2010, but withdrew that refusal in July 2011 after an appeal. In November 2010 he filed a judicial review alleging unlawful detention. Permission was granted in June 2011, but a further bail application was refused. He was released on bail on 13 July 2011, about two weeks after the ECtHR’s judgment in *Sufi and Elmi v. the United Kingdom* concerning removals to Mogadishu.

The domestic courts dismissed his challenge under the *Hardial Singh* principles. The Administrative Court found a substantial abscond risk (including six absconding convictions) and high reoffending risk; alternatives to detention were insufficient. It accepted that, despite the Rule 39 measure, there was still a realistic prospect of removal within a reasonable time. The Court of Appeal agreed, although one judge dissented on the two-week delay after *Sufi and Elmi*. The Supreme Court refused leave in March 2013.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant argued that his detention lacked a proper legal basis under Article 5 § 1(f), and that during the last 25 months it was not “with a view to deportation” because the Rule 39 measure prevented removal to Somalia and no other destination was explored. He also alleged failure to act with due diligence and excessive duration. The Government maintained that domestic law was precise and that the *Hardial Singh* test was stricter than Article 5 § 1(f). The Court declared the complaint admissible, rejected the quality-of-law argument by reference to *J.N. v. the United Kingdom*, and examined only the period from 16 June 2009 to 13 July 2011. It ultimately found a violation of Article 5 § 1(f), holding that during that period the detention could not be justified as action taken with a view to deportation given the Rule 39 measure and the lack of a realistic prospect of removal or due diligence.

**Ahmed v. the United Kingdom** (Application no. 59727/13), European Court of Human Rights, First Section, judgment of 2 March 2017.

The applicant, Mr Liban Mohamud Ahmed, was a Somali national born in 1977. He left Somalia in 1992 for the Netherlands, later entering the United Kingdom in December 1999 and claiming asylum under a false name and false immigration history to avoid return to the Netherlands. Although asylum was refused, he received exceptional leave to remain until 2004. Between 2001 and 2005 he received ten criminal convictions, and in December 2007 he was convicted of a public order offence and failing to surrender, receiving four and a half months’ imprisonment.

In January 2008 the Secretary of State indicated an intention to deport him and refused indefinite leave to remain. His appeal against deportation was dismissed in June 2008. On 8 February 2008, after serving half of his sentence, he was detained under immigration powers pending deportation. A deportation order was signed on 29 October 2008. Removal directions were set for 17 June 2009, but were cancelled after the European Court granted an interim measure under Rule 39 on 16 June 2009, preventing removal to Somalia. He remained detained until 13 July 2011, when he was granted bail shortly after the Court’s judgment in *Sufi and Elmi v. the United Kingdom*.

During detention, monthly reviews were conducted. Some review forms suggested that the applicant could reduce his detention by withdrawing his European Court application or volunteering to return to Somalia under the Facilitated Return Scheme. Bail applications were refused in November 2009, April 2010 and July 2010, with immigration judges finding him a significant abscond risk. He filed a judicial review claim in November 2010, and bail was eventually granted on 13 July 2011.

The applicant alleged a violation of Article 5 § 1(f) of the Convention for his detention from 8 February 2008 to 13 July 2011. He argued that domestic law was not sufficiently precise, accessible or foreseeable; that from 16 June 2009, when the Rule 39 measure was imposed, his detention was no longer “with a view to deportation” because removal to Somalia was impossible and no alternative destination was explored; that authorities failed to act with due diligence; and that the detention was excessive. The Government contended that the domestic *Hardial Singh* principles were stricter than Article 5 § 1(f) and that the detention was lawful.

The Administrative Court dismissed his claim in November 2011, finding a realistic prospect of removal within a reasonable time, a high risk of absconding and reoffending, and that alternatives to detention were insufficient. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal in October 2012, holding that the Rule 39 measure did not eliminate a realistic prospect of deportation, that no public law error vitiated the detention reviews, and that Article 5 § 1(f) added nothing. Lord Justice Elias dissented only as to the two-week delay after *Sufi and Elmi*. The Supreme Court refused leave in March 2013.

Before the European Court, the parties accepted that detention was lawful until 16 June 2009. The Court therefore examined arbitrariness only from 16 June 2009 to 13 July 2011—2 years and 27 days. It recalled *J.N. v. the United Kingdom*, rejecting the quality-of-law challenge to UK immigration detention. The key issue was whether detention remained “with a view to deportation” and non-arbitrary during the Rule 39 period, given that removal must be a realistic prospect and Rule 39 cannot justify indefinite detention. The Court ultimately found no violation of Article 5 § 1(f).

In *Svorcan v. Montenegro* (Application no. 1253/08, judgment of 13 June 2017), the European Court of Human Rights examined a Serbian national’s complaint about the excessive length of civil proceedings concerning the division of joint family property. The applicant, Olga Svorcan, lodged her application on 24 December 2007. The only complaint communicated to the Montenegrin Government was the length of the proceedings; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The underlying property dispute had two stages. On 18 September 1995, the applicant and her family members instituted proceedings before the Court of First Instance in Herceg Novi, seeking division of their joint property. On 5 May 1997, that court discontinued the proceedings and instructed the parties to initiate a separate civil case because of contentious issues. On 8 September 1997, the applicant’s cousins brought a claim against the applicant and her parents, followed by an additional claim on 30 December 1997. The claims were joined and examined in the same civil proceedings.

On 1 October 2002, the Court of First Instance ruled against the applicant and her parents. On 25 June 2004, the High Court in Podgorica upheld that judgment on appeal, making it final. It was served on the applicant on 15 July 2004. On 17 August 2004, the applicant lodged an appeal on points of law (*revizija*) with the Supreme Court of Montenegro. That appeal was misplaced until 20 January 2006, when her lawyers intervened and urged the authorities to locate it. On 12 January 2007, the applicant amended her appeal. On 14 February 2008, the Supreme Court rejected the appeal as unfounded, and the decision was served on the applicant on 6 March 2008. The proceedings overall therefore lasted from 18 September 1995 to 6 March 2008—more than twelve years and five months across three levels of jurisdiction.

The applicant alleged that this length was incompatible with the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. Montenegro had ratified the Convention on 3 March 2004. The Government objected that the complaint was incompatible *ratione temporis* because the proceedings began in 1997 and ended in 2008, and that domestic remedies had not been exhausted. The Court rejected both objections. It found that because the proceedings continued after 3 March 2004, they fell within its temporal jurisdiction from that date. As to exhaustion, the Court noted that no effective domestic remedy for length complaints existed when the application was lodged: the review request became effective in 2013, the fair-redress action in 2016, and the constitutional appeal in 2015. The fact that the Supreme Court stage ended after the application was lodged but before admissibility did not bar the complaint.

On the merits, the Court could examine only the period from 3 March 2004 to 6 March 2008—more than four years for two levels of jurisdiction. Applying the criteria of complexity, conduct of the applicant and authorities, and what was at stake, it found no justification for the delay. In particular, the delay before the Supreme Court lasted almost three years and seven months, with no explanation. The domestic authorities thus failed to act with the required diligence. The Court declared the complaint admissible and found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

**Case: Svorcan v. Montenegro (Application no. 1253/08), Judgment of 13 June 2017**

The applicant, Olga Svorcan, a Serbian national born in 1950 and living in Belgrade, lodged an application against Montenegro on 24 December 2007. She complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that civil proceedings concerning the division of joint family property had lasted unreasonably long, contrary to the “reasonable time” requirement. On 3 December 2014, the Court communicated only the length-of-proceedings complaint to the Government; the remainder was declared inadmissible. The Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

The factual background involved two sets of civil proceedings. On 18 September 1995, the applicant and her family members instituted proceedings before the Court of First Instance in Herceg Novi seeking division of their joint property. On 5 May 1997, that court discontinued the case and instructed the parties to initiate a separate civil case because of several contentious issues.

On 8 September 1997, the applicant’s cousins brought a claim against the applicant and her parents before the Court of First Instance in Herceg Novi. An additional claim concerning the same matter was lodged on 30 December 1997. Both claims were joined and examined together. On 1 October 2002, the Court of First Instance ruled against the applicant and her parents. On 25 June 2004, the High Court in Podgorica upheld that judgment on appeal, making it final. It was served on the applicant on 15 July 2004.

On 17 August 2004, the applicant lodged an appeal on points of law (*revizija*) with the Supreme Court of Montenegro. That appeal was misplaced until 20 January 2006, when the applicant’s lawyers intervened and asked the authorities to locate it. On 12 January 2007, the applicant amended her appeal. On 14 February 2008, the Supreme Court rejected the appeal as unfounded. Its decision was served on the applicant on 6 March 2008.

Before the European Court, the Government argued that the complaint was incompatible *ratione temporis* because the proceedings began in 1997 and ended in 2008, while Montenegro ratified the Convention on 3 March 2004. The applicant claimed the proceedings had begun in 1995. The Court rejected the Government’s objection, finding that because the proceedings continued after the ratification date, they fell within its competence from 3 March 2004 onward.

The Government also argued that the applicant had not exhausted domestic remedies, noting that the Supreme Court proceedings were still pending when she lodged her application. The Court rejected this objection. It recalled that at the relevant time there were no effective domestic remedies for length complaints: a request for review (*kontrolni zahtjev*) became effective on 4 September 2013, an action for fair redress (*tužba za pravično zadovoljenje*) on 18 October 2016, and a constitutional appeal on 20 March 2015. The last stage of domestic proceedings could occur after the application was lodged but before the Court decided admissibility.

On the merits, the total proceedings lasted from 18 September 1995 to 6 March 2008—more than twelve years and five months across three levels of jurisdiction. However, the Court could examine only the period from 3 March 2004 to 6 March 2008, which was still more than four years for two levels of jurisdiction.

Applying the criteria of complexity, the applicant’s conduct, the authorities’ conduct, and what was at stake, the Court found no justification for the delay. In particular, the delay before the Supreme Court lasted almost three years and seven months and was unexplained. The misplaced appeal and the authorities’ failure to act with required diligence led the Court to find a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.
001-171489:
The case of *Babak Hasanov v. Azerbaijan* (Applications nos. 43137/13 and 43153/13) concerns an Azerbaijani opposition activist's arrest, conviction, and administrative detention following two demonstrations in Baku.

The applicant, born in 1973, was a member of the opposition Popular Front Party. He participated in or attempted to participate in demonstrations on 17 November 2012 and 10 March 2013.

**First demonstration (17 November 2012):** Organizers notified the Baku City Executive Authority (BCEA), which refused authorization, citing general non-compliance with the Law on Freedom of Assembly and the venue's status as a public leisure area. Organizers proceeded anyway. The applicant stated the demonstration was peaceful and aimed at demanding democratic reforms and protesting impediments to freedom of assembly. Police dispersed it shortly after it began. The applicant was arrested—by people in plain clothes—taken to a police station, questioned, and issued an administrative-offence report under Article 310.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences (CAO) for deliberately failing to comply with a lawful police order. He refused to sign. He alleged he was never served with copies of reports or case documents and had no access to a lawyer after arrest or in custody.

**Second demonstration (10 March 2013):** No proper prior notice was given; information circulated via Facebook and the press. The demonstration protested soldiers' deaths. The applicant attended but, per witness M.M., was arrested before entering the assembly area. He was charged under Article 298.2 CAO (participation in a public assembly not organized in accordance with law). A document indicated a State-funded lawyer (Mr. T.A.) was instructed, but there was no evidence of pre-trial assistance; he only made brief oral submissions at trial. The applicant spent the night in police custody.

In both cases, hearings before the Sabail District Court were brief. The public was excluded without a formal closure decision. The applicant was not allowed to hire a lawyer of his choice; a State-funded lawyer was appointed. In the first case, the lawyer made no submissions and no witnesses were questioned. In the second, three police officers and witness M.M. testified. The applicant was convicted and sentenced to seven and six days' administrative detention, respectively. Appeals to the Baku Court of Appeal were dismissed on 26 November 2012 and 27 March 2013. He also raised that he had a second-degree disability and should not have received administrative detention.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 11 (freedom of assembly) in both cases, applying *Gafgaz Mammadov v. Azerbaijan*. For the first, it cited serious concerns about the foreseeability and precision of assembly legislation, doubts about Article 310.1 as a formal ground, failure to consider that the demonstration had been notified, lack of relevant and sufficient reasons for dispersing a peaceful demonstration, and failure to acknowledge that participating in an unauthorized peaceful demonstration is protected. For the second, although dispersal was lawful (the assembly was not shown to be spontaneous), the authorities still lacked relevant and sufficient reasons for dispersal and failed to recognize Article 11 protection.

The Court also found violations of Article 6 (fair trial) in both cases due to lack of adequate time and facilities, strong reliance on police reports, disregard of the peaceful nature of the demonstrations, absence of pre-trial legal assistance, denial of opportunity to appoint own counsel, and formalistic State-funded representation. It found a violation of Article 5 (liberty) in the first case, as the arrest and detention pursued aims unrelated to the formal ground and involved bad faith and arbitrariness.

**Case: Babak Hasanov v. Azerbaijan (Applications nos. 43137/13 and 43153/13), Judgment of 16 February 2017**

The applicant, Babak Hasanov, an Azerbaijani national and member of the opposition Popular Front Party, participated or attempted to participate in two opposition demonstrations in Baku: one on 17 November 2012, demanding democratic reforms and protesting restrictions on freedom of assembly, and one on 10 March 2013, protesting deaths of soldiers. He alleged both demonstrations were intended to be and were conducted peacefully.

For the first demonstration, the organisers gave prior notice to the Baku City Executive Authority (BCEA). The BCEA refused authorisation, citing general non-compliance with the Law on Freedom of Assembly, the proposed square being a public leisure area, and impracticality. For the second demonstration, no proper prior notice was given to the BCEA; information was circulated through Facebook or the press. The applicant argued that the second assembly was spontaneous, for which no prior written notification was required under domestic law.

In both cases, police dispersed the demonstrations shortly after they began. The applicant was arrested during the dispersal, taken to a police station, and questioned. In the first case, he alleged arrest by people in plain clothes. Administrative-offence reports were issued against him on the day of each arrest. In the first case, he was charged under Article 310.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences (CAO) for deliberately failing to comply with a lawful police order. In the second, he was charged under Article 298.2 of the CAO for participating in a public assembly not organised in accordance with the law. He refused to sign the first report. He claimed he was never served copies of the reports or case materials and had no access to a lawyer after arrest or in police custody. In the second case, documents indicated a State-funded lawyer was instructed, but there was no evidence he assisted before trial; he reportedly made only brief oral submissions at trial.

The applicant was brought before the Sabail District Court on the day of his first arrest, 17 November 2012, and the day after his second arrest, 11 March 2013. Hearings were brief, and the public was excluded even though no formal closed-hearing decision was taken. He was not allowed to hire a lawyer of his own choice. State-funded lawyers were appointed in both cases: in the first, the lawyer made no submissions; in the second, the lawyer stated generally that the applicant was not guilty. The first court heard no witnesses. The second court questioned three police officers, who said the applicant was arrested for staging an unauthorised demonstration, and a defence witness, M.M., who testified that he and the applicant were arrested before entering the assembly area.

The first-instance court convicted the applicant under Article 310.1 and sentenced him to seven days’ administrative detention. The second convicted him under Article 298.2 and sentenced him to six days’ administrative detention. On appeal, he argued that the demonstrations were peaceful, his arrests were unlawful, and the hearings were unfair. He also complained that, due to a second-degree disability, he should not have been sentenced to administrative detention. In the first appeal, he was represented by a lawyer of his choice; in the second, he was not represented. The Baku Court of Appeal dismissed both appeals on 26 November 2012 and 27 March 2013.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Articles 10 and 11 (dispersal, arrest and conviction for peaceful participation in unauthorised assemblies), Article 6 (unfair and non-public hearings, inadequate time and facilities, no own lawyer, no pre-trial legal aid, formalistic State representation, reliance on police reports), and Article 5 (arbitrary arrest, custody and detention, failure to inform promptly, denial of access to a lawyer and relatives, failure to serve the offence report, and plainclothes arrest in the first case). Other complaints communicated included Articles 3 and 7. The Court ultimately found violations of Article 11 in both cases, Article 6 in both, and Article 5 in the first case, following its earlier judgment in *Gafgaz Mammadov v. Azerbaijan*.

In *Babak Hasanov v. Azerbaijan* (Applications nos. 43137/13 and 43153/13, judgment 16 February 2017), the applicant was an Azerbaijani national and member of the opposition Popular Front Party. He participated or attempted to participate in two opposition demonstrations in Baku: one on 17 November 2012 and another on 10 March 2013.

For the first demonstration, the organisers notified the Baku City Executive Authority, which refused authorisation, saying the assembly would not comply with the Law on Freedom of Assembly and that the proposed square was a public leisure area. The organisers proceeded anyway. The demonstration was intended to be peaceful and demanded democratic reforms and protested impediments to freedom of assembly. For the second demonstration, no proper prior notice was given; information was spread via Facebook or the press. The applicant claimed it was spontaneous, for which no prior written notification was required by law. That demonstration protested deaths of soldiers. The applicant asserted both demonstrations were peaceful.

Police dispersed both demonstrations shortly after they began. The applicant was arrested at each and taken to a police station for questioning. In the first case, he was reportedly arrested by people in plain clothes. On each arrest day, an administrative-offence report was issued: in the first case under Article 310.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences (deliberate failure to comply with a lawful police order); in the second under Article 298.2 (participation in a public assembly not organised in accordance with the law). The applicant said he was not served copies of the reports or case documents and had no access to a lawyer while in custody. In the second case, records indicated a State-funded lawyer was appointed, but there was no evidence of pre-trial assistance; the lawyer only made brief submissions at trial.

The applicant was brought before the Sabail District Court on the day of his first arrest and the day after his second arrest. He claimed the hearings were very brief, the public was excluded without a formal closed-hearing decision, and he could not hire a lawyer of his own choice. In the first case, the State-funded lawyer made no submissions; in the second, the lawyer gave only a general denial. The first court convicted him under Article 310.1 and sentenced him to seven days’ administrative detention. The second convicted him under Article 298.2 and sentenced him to six days’ administrative detention. His appeals were dismissed by the Baku Court of Appeal in November 2012 and March 2013.

Relevant domestic law allowed spontaneous assemblies without prior written notification. Amendments to Article 298 introduced administrative detention and higher fines, while Article 310.1 allowed detention for up to fifteen days.

The European Court of Human Rights joined the applications. It found violations of Article 11 in both cases. In the first, it relied heavily on *Gafgaz Mammadov v. Azerbaijan*: serious concerns about the foreseeability and precision of assembly legislation, abusive bans or dispersals, dubious use of Article 310.1, failure to consider prior notification, lack of relevant and sufficient reasons for dispersing a peaceful demonstration, and failure to recognise that participation in an unauthorised peaceful demonstration is protected. In the second, although the Court accepted the dispersal was lawful because spontaneity was not substantiated, it still found no relevant and sufficient reasons and a failure to acknowledge Article 11 protection.

Under Article 6, the Court found the administrative-offence proceedings unfair as a whole: no pre-trial lawyer, no opportunity to choose counsel, formalistic State-funded representation, inadequate time and facilities, heavy reliance on police reports, disregard of the peaceful nature of the assembly, and exclusion of the public. Under Article 5, the first arrest, custody and detention were arbitrary and pursued aims unrelated to the formal ground invoked. Article 10 was not examined separately.
001-178701:
The case concerned two joined applications by Standard Verlagsgesellschaft mbH and derstandard.at GmbH against Austria, later merged into one applicant company. The applicant published the daily newspaper *Der Standard* and its online news portal. It complained that its conviction under the Austrian Media Act and a subsequent civil injunction violated its right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention.

The background involved the Carinthian Regional Hospital Operating Company (KABEG), a public-law institution operating hospitals in Carinthia. In 2011, I.M. was the KABEG board member responsible for human resources. K.S. was chairperson of the KABEG supervisory board, leader of the Freedom Party of Carinthia in the regional parliament, and brother of the Deputy Governor. Public debate had arisen over financial problems, rehirings, political interference, corruption, and alleged spying within KABEG. In October 2010, the medical director of Klagenfurt Regional Hospital criticised I.M. at a confidential doctors’ meeting and was dismissed without notice hours later.

In November 2011, the applicant published an article titled “Spying accusation against KABEG board of management.” It reported that I.M. was under pressure and that disclosed minutes suggested she had ordered the spying on the confidential doctors’ meeting by sending an informant, a trainee lawyer, to produce a transcript. The article added that K.S., chairperson of the supervisory board, who had also allegedly pressured journalists over critical KABEG reports, was “supposed to be the spiritus rector of the spying operation.”

K.S. brought private prosecution under the Media Act, claiming defamation and seeking compensation and publication of the judgment. He argued the statement was an untrue statement of fact. The applicant argued it was a permissible value judgment with a factual basis, intended to describe K.S.’s political role and the climate enabling such methods, not to allege that he personally ordered the spying. The Vienna Regional Criminal Court initially rejected the claim, but the Court of Appeal ordered proceedings, finding that readers would understand the phrase as suggesting K.S. was the initiator or “spin doctor” of the operation. The applicant refused to provide evidence of truth and maintained it was a value judgment. It was ultimately ordered to pay EUR 3,000 (EUR 1,500 for each publication) and to publish the judgment. Appeals and a renewal application to the Supreme Court failed.

In parallel, K.S. obtained a civil injunction under Article 1330 of the Civil Code ordering the applicant to refrain from repeating the allegation. The civil courts treated the final Media Act conviction as binding on the issues of fact and legal characterisation, so they did not re-examine the merits.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that the conviction and injunction breached Article 10. It argued that the statement was a value judgment, not a factual accusation, and that the binding effect of the criminal conviction prevented any meaningful civil review. The Government argued that the interference was justified and proportionate.

The Court found that the interference was prescribed by law and pursued the legitimate aim of protecting reputation. Although the issue was of public interest and K.S. was a public figure, the statement, in context, implied that K.S. played an active role in the spying operation. The domestic courts had reasonably classified it as a statement of fact, and the applicant had failed to prove its truth. The compensation was modest. The binding effect in the civil injunction was not disproportionate because the proceedings concerned the same parties and facts, and the applicant itself had requested suspension expecting that effect. The Court concluded that the interference was necessary in a democratic society and found no violation of Article 10.

Standard Verlagsgesellschaft mbH v. Austria concerned two applications brought by an Austrian newspaper publisher, Standard Verlagsgesellschaft mbH, and derstandard.at GmbH (later merged), alleging a violation of Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights—freedom of expression.

The applicant published the daily newspaper Der Standard and the online news portal derstandard.at. The case arose from reporting on KABEG, a public-law institution operating five hospitals in Carinthia. In 2010, public debate emerged over KABEG’s finances, rehiring of managers, political interference, corruption, and mismanagement. On 28 October 2010, the medical director of Klagenfurt Regional Hospital criticised I.M., the KABEG board member responsible for human resources, at a confidential meeting of hospital doctors. He was dismissed without notice only hours later.

On 25 and 26 November 2011, the applicant published an article titled “Spying accusation against KABEG board of management.” The article reported that minutes disclosed that I.M. had ordered the spying on the confidential doctors’ meeting. An informant—a trainee lawyer working under I.M.’s lawyer—had allegedly prepared a transcript. The article stated that the medical director, M.A., had accused KABEG management of using “Stasi methods” and was dismissed immediately after the meeting. It further stated that K.S., chairperson of KABEG’s supervisory board and leader of the Freedom Party of Carinthia in the regional parliament, who also pressured journalists over critical KABEG reports, was “supposed to be the spiritus rector of the spying operation.”

K.S. brought private prosecution for defamation under the Media Act, seeking compensation and publication of judgment, and also sought a civil injunction under Article 1330 of the Civil Code to prevent repetition of the allegation. The applicant argued that “spiritus rector” was a permissible value judgment with a factual basis: K.S. was close to I.M., linked to other spying accusations, and had publicly announced similar tactics. It claimed the article did not allege K.S. personally ordered the spy, but that he created a climate in which such methods were accepted.

The Vienna Regional Criminal Court initially dismissed K.S.’s Media Act claim, finding the phrase not defamatory. The Vienna Court of Appeal reversed, holding that in context the statement implied K.S. was the “spin doctor” or initiator of the spying operation and was therefore a defamatory statement of fact. In later proceedings, the applicant expressly declined to prove the truth of the allegation, maintaining it was a value judgment. The Regional Criminal Court ordered the applicant to pay EUR 3,000 (EUR 1,500 per publication) and publish the judgment. The Court of Appeal upheld that decision, and the Supreme Court rejected a renewal application.

In the civil injunction proceedings, the Commercial Court initially suspended the case pending the Media Act proceedings, then granted the injunction based on the binding effect of the criminal conviction. The Court of Appeal upheld this, and the applicant did not file an extraordinary appeal to the Supreme Court.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged that its conviction and the injunction violated Article 10. The Government argued non-exhaustion and that the interference was justified. The Court rejected the non-exhaustion objection, finding an extraordinary appeal had no reasonable prospect due to consistent Supreme Court case-law on binding effect. On the merits, the Court found the article concerned a matter of public interest and K.S. was a public figure, but agreed the phrase was a statement of fact implying active involvement in the spying operation. The applicant provided no truth evidence. The EUR 3,000 compensation was moderate. The binding effect in the civil injunction did not violate Article 10 because the proceedings involved the same facts and parties, and the applicant itself had requested suspension. The interference was necessary in a democratic society; no violation was found.

In *Standard Verlagsgesellschaft mbH v. Austria* (ECtHR, 23 November 2017), the applicant company owned the daily newspaper *Der Standard* and the news portal *derstandard.at*. It published an article on 25–26 November 2011 about alleged spying at KABEG, a public-law institution operating hospitals in Carinthia. The article reported that KABEG’s board of management, particularly I.M., had ordered spying on a confidential employees’ meeting of doctors at Klagenfurt Regional Hospital. It further stated that K.S., chairperson of KABEG’s supervisory board and leader of the Freedom Party of Carinthia’s parliamentary group, “was supposed to be the spiritus rector of the spying operation.” The article added that K.S. had also pressured journalists over critical KABEG reports.

K.S. brought two proceedings. First, he initiated a private prosecution under the Media Act for defamation, seeking compensation and publication of judgment. Second, he sought a civil injunction under Article 1330 of the Civil Code to prohibit the applicant from repeating the allegation. The applicant argued that “spiritus rector” was a permissible value judgment, not a factual accusation; it claimed the phrase described K.S.’s broader political influence and the climate surrounding the operation, not that he personally ordered the spying. It also relied on public interest and K.S.’s status as a powerful politician.

The Austrian courts disagreed. They interpreted the phrase, in context, as implying that K.S. was the initiator or “spin doctor” of the spying operation. They therefore classified it as a specific, sufficiently concrete statement of fact. Because the applicant expressly refused to provide evidence of its truth, the Vienna Regional Criminal Court ordered it to pay EUR 3,000 (EUR 1,500 for each publication) and to publish the judgment. The Court of Appeal and Supreme Court upheld that outcome. In the civil injunction proceedings, the Commercial Court and Court of Appeal granted the injunction, relying on the binding effect of the final Media Act conviction under Austrian Supreme Court case-law. They did not re-examine the merits.

The applicant complained before the ECtHR that both the Media Act conviction and the civil injunction violated Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression). It argued that the statement was a value judgment and that the binding effect of the criminal conviction improperly precluded a separate civil assessment. The Government maintained that the interference was justified to protect K.S.’s reputation.

The ECtHR joined the applications. It rejected the Government’s non-exhaustion objection concerning the civil proceedings, finding that an extraordinary appeal would have had no reasonable prospect of success given the Supreme Court’s consistent binding-effect case-law. On the merits, the Court held that the interference was prescribed by law and pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the reputation of others. Applying the necessity test, it accepted that the article concerned a matter of public interest and that K.S., as a politician and public figure, was subject to wider acceptable criticism. However, in context, readers would understand the “spiritus rector” allegation as accusing K.S. of playing an active role in the spying operation. It was thus a statement of fact, not a value judgment. The applicant neither proved its truth nor even alleged that K.S. had participated in the operation. The compensation was moderate, and the injunction’s reliance on the binding effect of the criminal conviction was not disproportionate because the proceedings involved the same facts and parties, the applicant itself had requested suspension due to that binding effect, and the injunction merely prevented repetition of an already established defamatory allegation. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 10.
