M.O. v. Switzerland concerned an Eritrean national born in 1990 who entered Switzerland illegally in June 2014 and applied for asylum. He alleged that his removal to Eritrea would breach Articles 3 and 4 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibit torture, inhuman or degrading treatment, and slavery, servitude and forced labour. His claim was based on his experiences in Eritrea and the general situation for returnees.

The applicant said he had been conscripted into Eritrea’s national service, tried to escape, was caught, beaten, and imprisoned in Wi’a. In his first interview he claimed detention from June 2012 to September 2013; later he said March to October 2013. He said he escaped from prison, stayed briefly with his parents, and left Eritrea illegally in October 2013 with a smuggler, crossing at Mereb. Ethiopian soldiers apprehended them, and he was later registered in the Hitsas refugee camp in Ethiopia. He submitted a student card, church deacon card, marriage certificate, son’s baptism certificate, and a UNHCR registration letter. He feared return because he had deserted or evaded military service and had left the country illegally, which he said would expose him to arrest, detention, torture, and forced labour.

Swiss authorities held three hearings. The State Secretariat for Migration rejected his asylum request on 8 March 2016 and ordered his removal. It found his account not credible because of contradictions and vagueness: the duration and dates of his detention, his schooling dates, his military training details, his inability to name a superior or unit, and shifting accounts of his departure—whether he left with a neighbour or a smuggler, how long he stayed at home, and how they lost their way. The Federal Administrative Court dismissed his appeal on 9 May 2016. It found the contradictions fundamental, held that he had not credibly shown illegal exit, and said the UNHCR camp registration did not prove individual risk. It also found removal possible, permitted

M.O. v. Switzerland (Application no. 41282/16) concerns an Eritrean national born in 1990 who entered Switzerland illegally on 23 June 2014 and applied for asylum the next day. He alleged that his removal to Eritrea would violate Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 4 (prohibition of slavery and forced labour) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court granted anonymity, priority, and applied Rule 39 to prevent his expulsion during the proceedings.

The applicant claimed that after failing school exams, he was summoned for national service. He reported for duty, attempted to escape, was caught, beaten, and imprisoned in Wi’a under poor hygiene conditions. He said he later escaped and left Eritrea illegally in October 2013, crossing at Mereb, before being apprehended by Ethiopian soldiers and registered in the Hitsas refugee camp. He submitted documents including a student card, church deacon attestation, marriage certificate, son’s baptism certificate, and UNHCR registration.

Swiss authorities held three asylum hearings. Credibility problems emerged. In the first hearing, he said he was detained from June 2012 to September 2013; in the second, he said March to October 2013. He gave limited detail about military training and prison conditions and could not name his superior, unit, or military number. His account of leaving Eritrea also changed: first he left with a neighbour, later with a smuggler; he gave differing details about losing their way before being caught by Amharic-speaking Ethiopian soldiers. He also gave inconsistent information about schooling and time spent at home after escaping prison.

On 8 March 2016, the State Secretariat for Migration rejected his asylum request and ordered his departure, finding his account not credible and concluding he had not proven or credibly demonstrated refugee status under the Asylum Act. The Federal Administrative Court dismissed his appeal on 9 May 2016. It found fundamental contradictions on key elements—detention duration, schooling, military training, and illegal exit—and held that he had not credibly shown he left Eritrea illegally. The UNHCR camp registration did not establish an individual risk of persecution. The court found removal possible, permitted, and reasonable, noting he was healthy and had family in Eritrea. The voluntary departure deadline expired on 17 July 2016.

The alleged violations depend heavily on country information about Eritrea. Reports described compulsory national service of indefinite duration, forced labour, and severe punishment for deserters, draft evaders, and illegal exiters. The UN Commission of Inquiry found that returnees are often treated as traitors, arrested, interrogated, tortured, detained in harsh conditions, and sent to military training or forced labour. It also found reasonable grounds to believe that Eritrean officials committed enslavement as a crime against humanity within national service. EASO reported that deserters and illegal exiters face extrajudicial punishment, usually detention for months to two years, followed by return to service, and that forcibly returned persons cannot regularise their status beforehand. Therefore, the key facts relevant to Articles 3 and 4 were the applicant’s alleged desertion, detention, and illegal exit; the Swiss authorities’ adverse credibility findings; and the general risk faced by returned Eritrean deserters and illegal exiters. The provided text does not include the Court’s final merits holding.

M.O. v. Switzerland (Application no. 41282/16) concerned an Eritrean national, born in 1990, who entered Switzerland illegally on 23 June 2014 and applied for asylum the next day. He alleged that his expulsion to Eritrea would violate Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 4 (prohibition of slavery and forced labour) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court applied Rule 39, indicating that he should not be expelled pending the proceedings.

The applicant claimed he had been prevented from continuing school after the eighth grade, was summoned for national service, tried to avoid it, reported for duty, but then attempted to escape. He said he was caught, beaten, and imprisoned in Wi’a under very poor hygiene conditions. In his first asylum hearing, he stated he was detained from June 2012 to September 2013; later he said March to October 2013. He escaped, stayed briefly in Eritrea, and left illegally on 3 October 2013 via Mereb with a smuggler or neighbour. He claimed they lost their way at night and were apprehended by Ethiopian soldiers, later registering in the Hitsas refugee camp. He submitted a student card, a church deacon card, a marriage certificate, his son’s baptism certificate, and UNHCR registration documents.

The Swiss State Secretariat for Migration rejected his asylum request on 8 March 2016, finding his account not credible. It cited contradictions about the duration and dates of detention, his schooling, military training, and departure, and found his descriptions of prison and escape lacking substance. The Federal Administrative Court dismissed his appeal on 9 May 2016. It found he had not credibly demonstrated refugee status or illegal exit. It accepted that legal exit from Eritrea required a passport and exit visa, rarely granted, and that illegal exit risked shooting and punishment. But because his account was not credible, it concluded he had not shown he left illegally. It also found removal possible, permitted, and reasonable, noting he was young, healthy, and had family in Eritrea.

The applicant relied on country evidence. UN Commission of Inquiry reports described indefinite national service, forced labour, torture, and enslavement in Eritrea. Conscripts served beyond 18 months; Wi’a was used for alleged traitors, school dropouts, and those caught fleeing. Deserters and draft evaders were severely punished, often tortured. Exit was tightly restricted, and illegal exit was treated as opposition. Returnees were often arrested, interrogated, tortured, detained in harsh conditions, forced to work, and returned to national service. An EASO report similarly stated that deserters and illegal exiters faced extrajudicial punishment, months to years of detention, and resumed service; forced returnees were treated more harshly than voluntary returnees.

The applicant argued that, if returned, he would face a real risk of ill-treatment because he had deserted, left illegally, and sought asylum in Switzerland. He also alleged that removal would expose him to forced labour contrary to Article 4. The Swiss courts’ rejection rested mainly on adverse credibility findings, which the applicant challenged as based on minor or explainable inconsistencies, his young age, poor education, and traumatic flight. The case therefore turned on whether the Swiss authorities properly assessed the risk of treatment contrary to Articles 3 and 4 in Eritrea despite doubting his account.
001-178352:
**Case Summary: Leuska and Others v. Estonia (Application no. 64734/11)**

**Parties and Background:**
The case involved four applicants from Estonia: Ms. K. Leuska, Mr. A. Leuska (the first and second applicants), and Ms. P. Esop and Ms. K.-B. Esop (the third and fourth applicants). The case stemmed from a fatal traffic accident on July 17, 2010, which resulted in the death of the first and second applicants' son and serious injuries to the fourth applicant (the third applicant is her mother).

**Key Facts:**
The applicants joined the criminal proceedings against the suspect, J., as victims. On December 9–10, 2010, they filed a civil action within the criminal proceedings, claiming compensation for non-pecuniary damage and reimbursement of legal costs incurred during the proceedings.

On January 28, 2011, the applicants concluded an out-of-court settlement with J., who paid compensation for damages. Subsequently, they agreed to a domestic settlement procedure (*kokkuleppemenetlus*). On February 4, 2011, the applicants’ consent to this procedure was recorded in a report signed by the prosecutor and their representatives. Crucially, the report noted that while they had given up their claims for non-pecuniary damage, they had not waived their claim for reimbursement of legal costs. The report also stated that victims could not withdraw consent to the settlement procedure. At that time, the applicants had not submitted an itemized list of legal costs.

On February 11, 2011, J. consented to the settlement procedure, and an agreement was signed stating that the victims had withdrawn their civil claims. On February 14, 2011, the Harju County Court scheduled a hearing for March 7, 2011, summoning only J., his counsel, and the prosecutor—not the applicants.

On March 4, 2011, the applicants submitted a claim for legal costs totaling 6,483.66 euros with supporting documents, received by the court on March 7, 2011. At the hearing, the trial judge disclosed this claim. J. argued it had been absorbed by the out-of-court settlement. The applicants alleged they were present in the court building but were not allowed to address the court.

In its judgment of March 7, 2011, the Harju County Court convicted J. of traffic violations, sentenced him to a suspended prison term, and ordered him to pay state expenses. It held that the victims had given up their civil claims but made no reference to their claim for legal costs.

**Appeals and Domestic Decisions:**
The applicants appealed, complaining they were not allowed to attend the hearing and that their cost claim was left undecided. On March 23, 2011, the Harju County Court refused to examine the appeal, finding the applicants were not parties to the proceedings and had no right to appeal. The Tallinn Court of Appeal upheld this decision on April 13, 2011, citing provisions that victims need not be summoned in settlement proceedings and cannot revoke consent. The Supreme Court refused to examine the appeal on October 3, 2011, but noted that courts should not overlook matters like legal costs not addressed in settlement agreements.

**Alleged Violations:**
The applicants complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the Harju County Court failed to decide on their claim for legal costs and did not hear oral evidence from them. They argued they were parties to the proceedings with rights to participate and appeal. The government contended that Article 6 was inapplicable, the applicants had abused the right of petition by not disclosing the out-of-court settlement, and they lacked victim status since their claims were covered by that settlement.

**Case: Leuska and Others v. Estonia (ECtHR, 7 November 2017)**

The case concerned four applicants: the parents of a young man killed in a traffic accident on 17 July 2010, the seriously injured fourth applicant, and her mother. The applicants joined the resulting criminal proceedings as victims. On 9–10 December 2010, they lodged a civil action within the criminal case against the suspect, J., seeking compensation for non-pecuniary damage and reimbursement of legal costs incurred in the criminal proceedings.

On 28 January 2011, the applicants concluded an out-of-court settlement with J. They then informed the prosecutor that the case could be settled through Estonia’s criminal settlement procedure. On 4 February 2011, their consent to that procedure was recorded in a prosecutor’s report. The report noted that they had given up their non-pecuniary damage claims but had **not** given up their claim for reimbursement of legal costs. At that stage, they had not yet submitted an itemised costs list or supporting documents. The report also stated that victims could not withdraw consent to the settlement procedure. J. consented on 11 February 2011, and the settlement agreement stated that the victims had withdrawn their civil claims.

The Harju County Court committed J. for trial and scheduled a hearing for 7 March 2011. Only J., his counsel, and the prosecutor were summoned; the applicants were not summoned. On 4 March 2011, the applicants filed a claim for legal costs of EUR 6,483.66 with supporting documents, received by the court on 7 March. At the hearing, the judge disclosed their costs claim. J. asked the court not to examine it, arguing it had been absorbed by the out-of-court settlement. The applicants alleged they were not allowed to address the court despite being in the court building.

In its judgment of 7 March 2011, the County Court convicted J. of traffic and driving violations and imposed a suspended prison sentence. It held that the victims had given up their civil claims, but made no reference to their claim for reimbursement of legal costs. The applicants appealed, complaining that they had not been allowed to attend the hearing and that their costs claim remained undecided. The County Court refused to examine their appeal, finding they were not parties to the settlement proceedings and had no right of appeal. The Tallinn Court of Appeal upheld that decision on 13 April 2011, relying on provisions providing that victims need not be summoned in settlement proceedings and cannot revoke consent. The Supreme Court declined to examine their further appeal but noted that courts should not overlook unresolved issues such as procedural costs in settlement proceedings.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the domestic courts had failed to decide their claim for legal costs and had not heard them. The Government argued that Article 6 was inapplicable, that the applicants had abused the right of application by omitting the out-of-court settlement, that they lacked victim status, and that they had not exhausted domestic remedies.

The Court found Article 6 § 1 applicable in its civil limb and rejected the Government’s preliminary objections. On the merits, it held that the applicants’ consent to the settlement procedure could be regarded as an unequivocal waiver of their right to be heard, so the failure to summon them to the hearing did not violate Article 6 § 1. However, the domestic courts’ failure to take any decision on their claim for reimbursement of legal costs amounted to a violation of their right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1.

In **Leuska and Others v. Estonia**, four applicants were victims in a fatal traffic accident on 17 July 2010. The first and second applicants’ son was killed, the fourth applicant was seriously injured, and the third applicant was the fourth applicant’s mother. They joined the criminal proceedings against the driver, J., as victims. On 9–10 December 2010 they lodged a civil action within the criminal case, claiming non-pecuniary damages and reimbursement of legal costs incurred in the criminal proceedings.

On 28 January 2011 the applicants concluded an out-of-court settlement with J., who paid compensation. They informed the prosecutor that they agreed to a settlement procedure. On 4 February 2011 their consent to the settlement procedure was recorded. The report stated that they had waived their non-pecuniary claims but not their claim for legal costs. It also stated that victims could not withdraw consent to the settlement procedure. At that stage, they had not submitted an itemised costs list or supporting documents.

J. consented on 11 February 2011. The prosecutor, J. and his counsel signed a settlement agreement stating that the victims had withdrawn their civil claims. On 14 February 2011 the Harju County Court committed J. for trial and scheduled a hearing for 7 March 2011. Only J., his counsel and the prosecutor were summoned; the applicants were not.

On 4 March 2011 the applicants submitted a legal costs claim of EUR 6,483.66 with supporting documents, received by the court on 7 March 2011. At the 7 March hearing, the judge disclosed the costs claim. J. asked the court not to examine it, arguing it was covered by the out-of-court settlement. The applicants alleged they were in the court building but were not allowed to address the court. In its judgment that day, the County Court convicted J. of traffic and driving offences, imposed a suspended prison sentence and withdrew his driving licence. It held that the victims had given up their civil claims but made no reference to their legal costs claim.

The applicants appealed, complaining that they had not been allowed to attend the hearing and that their costs claim had been left undecided. On 23 March 2011 the County Court refused to examine the appeal, finding that victims were not parties and had no right of appeal. On 13 April 2011 the Tallinn Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, relying on provisions that victims cannot revoke consent to settlement and need not be summoned in settlement proceedings. On 3 October 2011 the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal but noted that courts in settlement proceedings should not overlook unresolved matters such as procedural costs, and that costs decisions could be contested separately.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants complained under Article 6 § 1 that the County Court had failed to decide their legal costs claim and had not heard them. The Court found Article 6 applicable in its civil limb and rejected the Government’s objections. On the merits, it found that no decision had been taken on the costs claim even though the applicants had expressly reserved it and submitted an itemised list before the hearing. That failure violated their right of access to a court. However, because their consent to the settlement procedure amounted to an unequivocal waiver of procedural rights, the fact that they were not summoned or heard by the County Court did not violate Article 6 § 1.

In *Vučinić v. Montenegro* (App. No. 44533/10, ECtHR, 5 September 2017), the applicant, a Montenegrin national born in 1949, complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that two sets of civil proceedings concerning employment-related compensation had exceeded a reasonable time.

The background was that, after the breakup of Yugoslavia, the applicant’s employer closed its Podgorica office on 15 October 1991. Under domestic law, he was entitled to compensation equal to 24 monthly salaries. He founded a trading company in the former employer’s offices and on 25 March 1992 requested a certificate to continue providing services; he received it only on 3 October 1997. He then pursued two separate civil claims.

In the first set of proceedings, on 29 December 1998, he sued for pecuniary loss suffered while awaiting the certificate. The Court of First Instance rejected the claim for lack of competence in March 1999, but the High Court quashed that decision in September 1999. In April 2004, the first-instance court partly ruled in his favour, but the High Court overturned that decision and rejected his claim in January 2008. The Supreme Court quashed and remitted the case in May 2008. The High Court again rejected his claim in June 2009, and the Supreme Court upheld that rejection on 4 March 2010, served on 1 April 2010. He alleged that the length violated Article 6 § 1. The Government objected that the Court lacked temporal jurisdiction before 3 March 2004, when the Convention entered into force for Montenegro, and that domestic remedies had not been exhausted. The Court rejected these objections. It found no effective domestic remedy for length at the time of application and held it could examine the period from 3 March 2004. On the merits, the relevant period ran from 3 March 2004 to 1 April 2010—six years and one month across three levels—though the case had already been pending for five years and two months before that date. With no justification, and considering complexity, conduct, and what was at stake, the Court found the length excessive and a violation of Article 6 § 1.

In the second set, on 23 April 2002, the applicant claimed the 24 monthly salaries from the Municipality of Podgorica and the Republic of Montenegro. The first-instance court rejected the claim in February 2004; the High Court quashed and remitted in November 2004. The first-instance court rejected again in May 2006; the High Court partly quashed and remitted in May 2008. The Supreme Court rejected his appeal on points of law regarding the upheld part in March 2009. The first-instance court rejected the remitted part in January 2010; the High Court upheld in June 2010; the Supreme Court rejected his appeal on points of law on 18 January 2011, served on 7 February 2011. He lodged a constitutional appeal in 2011; the Constitutional Court rejected it on 19 April 2013, served on 28 May 2013.

He complained to the ECtHR about the length of the second set on 26 November 2013. The Court found this complaint inadmissible as out of time. A constitutional appeal was not an effective remedy for length at the relevant time; it became effective only on 20 March 2015. He should have applied within six months of service of the Supreme Court’s decision, i.e. by 7 August 2011. Accordingly, the second-set complaint was rejected under Article 35 §§ 1 and 4.

Overall, the Court declared the first-set length complaint admissible and found a violation of Article 6 § 1; the second-set complaint was dismissed as time-barred.

In *Vučinić v. Montenegro* (Application no. 44533/10, ECtHR, 5 September 2017), the applicant, Petar Vučinić, a Montenegrin national born in 1949, worked for an export trading company based in Ljubljana, Slovenia. After the breakup of the former Yugoslavia, his employer closed its Podgorica office on 15 October 1991. Under the domestic law then in force, he was entitled to compensation amounting to 24 monthly salaries. On 5 October 1991 he founded a trading company in his former employer’s offices. On 25 March 1992 he requested a certificate allowing his new company to continue providing services, which he received only on 3 October 1997.

**First set of civil proceedings.** On 29 December 1998, the applicant sued for pecuniary loss suffered while awaiting the certificate. The Court of First Instance rejected the claim for lack of competence on 10 March 1999, but the High Court quashed that decision on 17 September 1999. On 30 April 2004 the first-instance court partly ruled in his favour. On 24 January 2008 the High Court reversed that judgment and rejected his claim. The Supreme Court quashed the High Court’s judgment on 7 May 2008, but on 11 June 2009 the High Court again rejected the claim. The Supreme Court upheld that decision on 4 March 2010, served on 1 April 2010. The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 that the length of these proceedings violated the “reasonable time” requirement. The Government objected that the Court lacked temporal jurisdiction before the Convention entered into force for Montenegro on 3 March 2004 and that domestic remedies had not been exhausted. The Court rejected those objections. It found that the relevant period ran from 3 March 2004 to 1 April 2010, lasting about six years and one month across three levels of jurisdiction, although the proceedings had already been pending for five years and two months when the Convention entered into force. At the relevant time, no effective domestic remedy existed for length complaints: a request for review became effective only on 4 September 2013, an action for fair redress on 18 October 2016, and a constitutional appeal on 20 March 2015. On the merits, the Court found the length excessive and unjustified, violating Article 6 § 1.

**Second set of civil proceedings.** On 23 April 2002, the applicant sought payment of the 24 monthly salaries from the Municipality of Podgorica and the Republic of Montenegro. The first-instance court rejected the claim on 5 February 2004. The High Court quashed that decision on 9 November 2004. On 16 May 2006 the first-instance court again rejected the claim. On 27 May 2008 the High Court partly quashed that judgment. The Supreme Court rejected an appeal on points of law on 3 March 2009. The remitted part was rejected on 16 January 2010 and upheld on 4 June 2010. The Supreme Court rejected a further appeal on 18 January 2011, served on 7 February 2011. The applicant lodged a constitutional appeal in 2011; the Constitutional Court rejected it on 19 April 2013, served on 28 May 2013. The applicant’s complaint to the ECtHR regarding the length of this second set was introduced on 26 November 2013. The Court held that a constitutional appeal was not an effective remedy for length at the relevant time, becoming effective only on 20 March 2015. Therefore, he should have lodged his ECtHR complaint within six months of the Supreme Court decision being served, i.e. by 7 August 2011. The second complaint was thus inadmissible as out of time under Article 35 §§ 1 and 4. Only the first set resulted in a violation.

Vučinić v. Montenegro (ECtHR, Second Section, 5 September 2017, App. No. 44533/10) concerned an Article 6 § 1 complaint about the excessive length of civil proceedings. The applicant, Petar Vučinić, born in 1949 and living in Podgorica, had worked for an export trading company based in Ljubljana. After the breakup of Yugoslavia, his employer closed its Podgorica office on 15 October 1991. Under the law then in force, he was entitled to compensation of 24 monthly salaries. He founded a new trading company in the former employer’s offices and on 25 March 1992 requested a certificate allowing the new company to continue providing services. He received that certificate on 3 October 1997. Two sets of civil proceedings followed.

In the first set, on 29 December 1998 the applicant sued for pecuniary loss suffered while awaiting the certificate. In March 1999 the Court of First Instance rejected the claim for lack of competence; the High Court quashed that decision in September 1999. On 30 April 2004 the Court of First Instance partly ruled in his favour, but the High Court overturned that judgment on 24 January 2008 and rejected his claim. The Supreme Court quashed the High Court judgment on 7 May 2008 and remitted the case. On 11 June 2009 the High Court again rejected the claim, and on 4 March 2010 the Supreme Court upheld that decision. It was served on the applicant on 1 April 2010. Although the proceedings began in 1998, the Convention entered into force for Montenegro on 3 March 2004, so the Court assessed only the period from then. By that date the case had already been pending for over five years. From 3 March 2004 to 1 April 2010, the proceedings lasted six years and one month across three levels of jurisdiction. The Court found no justification for that delay and held that the length was excessive, violating Article 6 § 1. The Government’s objections on temporal jurisdiction and non-exhaustion were rejected because no effective domestic remedy for length existed when the application was lodged; relevant remedies became effective later.

In the second set, on 23 April 2002 the applicant claimed the 24 monthly salaries from the Municipality of Podgorica and the Republic of Montenegro. The Court of First Instance rejected the claim on 5 February 2004; the High Court quashed that decision on 9 November 2004. The Court of First Instance rejected the claim again on 16 May 2006. The High Court partly quashed that judgment on 27 May 2008. The Supreme Court rejected an appeal on points of law on 3 March 2009 concerning the upheld part. As to the remitted part, the Court of First Instance rejected the claim on 16 January 2010, the High Court upheld that decision on 4 June 2010, and the Supreme Court rejected the applicant’s appeal on points of law on 18 January 2011, served on 7 February 2011. The applicant then lodged a constitutional appeal; the Constitutional Court rejected it on 19 April 2013, served on 28 May 2013.

However, the applicant complained to the ECtHR about the second set only on 26 November 2013. At the relevant time, a constitutional appeal was not an effective remedy for length; it became effective only on 20 March 2015. He should have applied within six months of the Supreme Court decision served on him, i.e. by 7 August 2011. The second-set complaint was therefore inadmissible as out of time under Article 35 §§ 1 and 4. Overall, the Court found a violation only regarding the first set’s length; the second set was time-barred.
001-174404:
In *Arnarson v. Iceland* (App. No. 58781/13), the European Court of Human Rights examined an Icelandic journalist’s complaint that a domestic defamation judgment violated his right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention. The applicant, Ólafur Arnarson, was a journalist and freelance writer for the web-based media site *Pressan*. The dispute arose from public debate about the Federation of Icelandic Fishing Vessel Owners (“LIU”), an organisation representing fishing vessel owners and safeguarding their economic, legal and social interests. “A” was the LIU’s chief executive officer.

Arnarson claimed that a private website, “B,” published anonymous blogs that constantly lobbied for the LIU and discredited persons who spoke against it. On 21 July 2010, the newspaper *DV* published an article about rumours that the LIU was providing financial support to website B, allegedly ISK 1,500,000 per month. The article did not mention A. The same day, Arnarson published an article on *Pressan* under the headline “LIU pays 20 million for offensive material,” referring to the *DV* article. A sent a statement to *Pressan* denying that the LIU had supported website B; this was published on 23 July 2010.

On 24 July 2010, Arnarson published a response. He stated that A had to do better than merely denying direct payments and that the LIU, directed by A, was accountable for the offensive anonymous material on website B. He also questioned whether respectable representatives of the LIU’s member companies had agreed to the organisation’s funds being paid through intermediaries to “gossips” such as the owners of website B.

In a later article, Arnarson stated that the LIU supposedly supported website B with almost ISK 20 million annually through companies owned by Mr Y, who also owned website B. He added that he knew some LIU board members were unaware of the support because the payments were well disguised in the organisation’s financial records. He further wrote that he had been told it was possible that no LIU board members knew that the organisation’s millions were being used to support anonymous slander on website B, and that A alone had decided to use the funds that way. He noted that he had not received confirmation of that last statement. A photograph of A appeared beside the article.

On 28 December 2011, A lodged defamation proceedings before the Reykjaness District Court, requesting that four statements be declared null and void. On 29 November 2012, the District Court found that only one statement was defamatory: the statement that some LIU board members were unaware of the support because payments were well disguised, and that A alone may have decided to use the funds for anonymous slander. The court held that readers could understand this as implying accounting deception or fraud by abuse of position and negligence, namely that A had allocated LIU funds against the board’s will and without authorisation. Since Arnarson could not prove the statement true, the court declared it null and void and ordered him to pay A ISK 300,000 in non-pecuniary damages plus interest and ISK 450,000 in costs.

The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 25 February 2013. Arnarson complained under Article 10 that the District Court judgment—final after the refusal of leave—interfered with his right to freedom of expression and was not necessary in a democratic society. The key facts therefore concerned a journalist’s public-interest reporting on alleged lobbying, anonymous online attacks, and misuse of LIU funds by its CEO, balanced against the CEO’s reputation rights. The case raised whether the domestic courts properly considered the public debate, A’s public role, and whether the statements were factual accusations or value judgments/insinuations.

**Case: Arnarson v. Iceland (Application no. 58781/13)**

The applicant, Ólafur Arnarson, an Icelandic journalist and freelance writer for the web-based media site *Pressan*, complained under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights that a domestic defamation judgment interfered with his right to freedom of expression and was not necessary in a democratic society.

At the material time, the Federation of Icelandic Fishing Vessel Owners (“LIU”) represented fishing vessel owners and safeguarded their economic and legal interests. Its chief executive officer (“A”) participated publicly in debates on maritime affairs and advocated LIU policy. Arnarson claimed that a private website, “B,” published anonymous blogs that constantly lobbied for the LIU and discredited its opponents.

On 21 July 2010, the newspaper *DV* published an article about rumours that the LIU was financially supporting website B with ISK 1,500,000 per month. The article did not mention A. The same day, Arnarson published an article on *Pressan* headlined “LIU pays 20 million for offensive material,” referring to the *DV* article. A responded that the LIU had not supported website B; that statement was published on *Pressan* on 23 July 2010.

On 24 July 2010, Arnarson published a second article responding to A. He wrote that A had to do better than merely denying direct payments; that the LIU, directed by A, was accountable for the offensive anonymous material on website B; and he questioned whether respectable representatives of LIU member companies had agreed to LIU funds being paid through intermediaries to gossips such as the owners of website B.

On 26 July 2010, Arnarson published a third article. It stated that the LIU supposedly supported website B with about ISK 20 million annually through companies owned by Mr Y, who also owned website B. It further stated that not all LIU board members were aware of the support because payments were well-disguised in the organisation’s financial records. Arnarson added that he had been told it was possible no LIU board members knew that the organisation’s millions were being used to support anonymous slander on website B, and that A alone had decided to use the funds that way. He noted he had not received confirmation of that last statement. A picture of A appeared beside the article.

On 28 December 2011, A lodged defamation proceedings before the Reykjaness District Court, asking that four statements be declared null and void. By judgment of 29 November 2012, the District Court found only one statement defamatory, namely the statement concerning disguised payments, possible board ignorance, and A alone deciding to use LIU funds. The court reasoned that it applied directly to A and could be understood as insinuating accounting deception, fraud by abuse of position, or negligence at work—implying that A had allocated LIU funds against the board’s will and without authorisation. Since Arnarson had not proved the statement true, it was deemed defamatory and likely to damage A’s reputation and honour under Article 241(1) of the Penal Code. Arnarson was ordered to pay A ISK 300,000 in non-pecuniary damages, plus interest, and ISK 450,000 in costs; the statement was declared null and void.

The applicant sought leave to appeal to the Supreme Court, but leave was refused on 25 February 2013. He then lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 21 August 2013, alleging that the District Court judgment—final after the Supreme Court refusal—violated his Article 10 right to freedom of expression. The domestic courts had balanced freedom of expression against the right to reputation, in the context of public debate on fisheries management and A’s public role as LIU CEO. The application was communicated to the Icelandic Government on 20 November 2015.

**Arnarson v. Iceland** (Application no. 58781/13) concerned an Icelandic journalist’s complaint under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights that a domestic defamation judgment interfered with his freedom of expression and was not necessary in a democratic society.

The applicant, Ólafur Arnarson, was a journalist and freelance writer for the web-based media site *Pressan*. The Federation of Icelandic Fishing Vessel Owners (“the LIU”) represented fishing vessel owners and safeguarded their economic and legal interests. A was the LIU’s chief executive officer. The applicant claimed that a private website, B, published anonymous blogs that constantly lobbied for the LIU and discredited persons who spoke against it.

On the same day, the applicant published an article on *Pressan* under the headline “LIU pays 20 million for offensive material,” referring to the *DV* article. A responded with a short statement denying that the LIU had supported website B; *Pressan* published A’s statement on 23 July 2010.

On 24 July 2010, the applicant published a second article responding to A. He wrote that A had to do better than merely denying direct payments and that the LIU, directed by A, was accountable for offensive anonymous material on website B. He also questioned whether respectable representatives of the LIU’s member companies would accept that the organisation’s funds were being paid through intermediaries to “gossips” such as the owners of website B.

On 26 July 2010, the applicant published a third article. It stated that the LIU supposedly supported website B with almost ISK 20 million annually through companies owned by Mr Y, who also owned website B. It further stated that the applicant knew that some LIU board members were not aware of the support because the payments were well-disguised in the organisation’s financial records. It added that he had been told it was possible that no LIU board members knew that the organisation’s millions were being used to support anonymous slander on website B, and that A alone had decided to use the funds in that way. The applicant noted that he had not received confirmation of that last statement. A picture of A appeared beside the article.

In December 2011, A lodged defamation proceedings before the Reykjaness District Court, asking that four statements be declared null and void. By judgment of 29 November 2012, the District Court found only one statement defamatory—the statement that payments were well-disguised in the financial statements and that A alone may have decided to use LIU funds to support anonymous slander. The court reasoned that this statement directly concerned A and could imply accounting deception, fraud by abuse of position, or negligence, suggesting A allocated LIU funds against the board’s will and without authorisation. The applicant had not proved the statement true. The court declared it null and void and ordered the applicant to pay A ISK 300,000 in non-pecuniary damages plus interest, and ISK 450,000 for A’s costs.

The applicant sought leave to appeal, but the Supreme Court refused on 25 February 2013. He then applied to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging that the District Court judgment, upheld by the refusal of leave, amounted to an unjustified interference with his Article 10 right to freedom of expression. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation therefore centre on a journalist’s public-interest allegations about a powerful industry body, its CEO, and alleged hidden payments to an anonymous website, and the domestic court’s finding that one unproven accusation of financial misconduct was defamatory.

The case concerns Boštjan Koprivnikar, born in 1979 and detained in Slovenia. His application to the European Court of Human Rights alleged that imposing an overall thirty-year prison sentence on him breached Article 7 of the Convention (no punishment without law). The key facts arise from several convictions that were later combined into a single sentence.

On 17 September 2004, the Ljubljana District Court convicted the applicant of robbery and sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment. He served that sentence from 7 December 2007 to 7 December 2011. On 16 June 2009, he was convicted of paying with a bad cheque and fraudulent use of a bank card, receiving five months’ imprisonment; that judgment became final on 7 October 2009. In the meantime, on 9 April 2009, he was convicted of murder committed with another person on 15 September 2002. He was sentenced to thirty years’ imprisonment—the maximum under the 1994 Criminal Code applicable at the time of the offence. That conviction became final on 9 December 2009.

On 28 November 2011, the applicant asked the Ljubljana District Court to join the three prison terms into an overall sentence. On 13 January 2012, the District Court joined all three sentences, including the already-served robbery sentence, and imposed an overall sentence of thirty years. It applied the 2008 Criminal Code as it stood before the 2011 Amendment. Article 53 § 2 (2) of that Code provided that where prison sentences were imposed for all multiple offences, the overall sentence had to exceed each individual sentence but could not exceed the total sum of the sentences, nor twenty years’ imprisonment. The District Court acknowledged that this provision formally applied, but held that the legislature had made an obvious error. It reasoned that a twenty-year cap would be illogical because the 2008 Code allowed a single thirty-year sentence, meaning the overall sentence could be lower than one of the individual sentences. The 1994 Criminal Code had expressly provided that if one multiple offence carried thirty years, only that sentence was imposed. The 2011 Amendment later clarified the rules, providing that where one combined sentence was thirty years, the overall sentence would consist only of that term, and raising the overall maximum to thirty years.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the thirty-year overall sentence lacked a legal basis and violated the rule of law and the principle nullum crimen, nulla poena sine lege. He contended that the clear text of Article 53 § 2 (2) capped the overall sentence at twenty years and that any ambiguity should not be interpreted to his detriment. The Ljubljana Higher Court rejected his appeal on 29 May 2012. The Supreme Court rejected his request for protection of legality on 6 December 2012, relying on historical and systematic interpretation and stating that semantic interpretation had to yield where one individual sentence was thirty years. The Constitutional Court dismissed his complaint on 24 April 2013.

Later, on 24 March 2015, the applicant was convicted of another murder and sentenced to thirty years. A new overall sentence of thirty years was imposed, covering the earlier overall sentence, another four-month sentence, and the new thirty-year term. Appeals were unsuccessful, with the Supreme Court dismissing his protection-of-legality application on 2 June 2016.

The alleged violation was therefore that the domestic courts imposed a thirty-year overall sentence even though the law applicable at the time apparently prescribed a twenty-year maximum for such an overall sentence, thereby imposing a heavier penalty than that provided by law.

Koprivnikar v. Slovenia (Application no. 67503/13) concerned a complaint under Article 7 of the European Convention on Human Rights that the applicant, Boštjan Koprivnikar, had an overall thirty-year prison sentence imposed on him unlawfully. The applicant was born in 1979 and was detained in Dob pri Mirni.

The key facts relate to several criminal convictions. On 17 September 2004 the applicant was convicted of robbery and sentenced to four years’ imprisonment. He served that sentence between 7 December 2007 and 7 December 2011. On 16 June 2009 he was convicted of paying with a bad cheque and fraudulent use of a bank card, offences committed in 2005, and sentenced to five months’ imprisonment; that judgment became final on 7 October 2009. In the meantime, on 9 April 2009, he was convicted of murder committed with another person on 15 September 2002 and sentenced to thirty years’ imprisonment—the maximum under the 1994 Criminal Code as amended in 1999. That conviction became final on 9 December 2009.

On 28 November 2011 the applicant asked the Ljubljana District Court to join the three prison sentences into an overall sentence. On 13 January 2012 the District Court joined them and imposed an overall term of thirty years. It applied the 2008 Criminal Code as it stood before the 2011 Amendment. Under Article 53 § 2 (2) of that code, where prison sentences had been imposed for all multiple offences, the overall sentence had to exceed each individual sentence but could not exceed twenty years. A life sentence was imposed as an overall sentence only where two or more thirty-year sentences were being combined. There was no special rule for combining one thirty-year sentence with other sentences.

The District Court acknowledged that Article 53 § 2 (2) applied but found the provision unclear, ambiguous and deficient. It reasoned that the legislature could not have intended an offender sentenced to thirty years for one offence to receive an overall sentence ten years lower. It considered the 2011 Amendment, which later provided that if one of the sentences was thirty years, the overall sentence would consist only of that sentence, as rectifying an obvious legislative error.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the decision lacked a legal basis and violated the rule of law and the principle nullum crimen et nulla poena sine lege. He submitted that semantic interpretation should prevail and that any ambiguity should not be interpreted to his detriment. On 29 May 2012 the Ljubljana Higher Court dismissed the appeal. On 6 December 2012 the Supreme Court rejected his request for protection of legality, relying on historical and systematic interpretation. On 24 April 2013 the Constitutional Court dismissed his constitutional complaint.

The applicant alleged before the European Court that the overall thirty-year sentence breached Article 7 of the Convention. The central issue was whether the domestic courts could impose a thirty-year overall sentence despite the apparently clear twenty-year cap in the applicable 2008 Criminal Code, by relying on the legislature’s presumed intention and later amendment.

The case also noted that on 24 March 2015 the applicant was convicted of another murder and received a new overall thirty-year sentence covering the earlier overall sentence and another sentence. His appeal and request for protection of legality were dismissed, the latter by the Supreme Court on 2 June 2016.

Cela and Others v. Greece (Application no. 10244/14) is a European Court of Human Rights case brought by six Albanian and Greek nationals against Greece. The applicants lodged the application on 28 January 2014 while detained in Korydallos Prison, Athens. Their detention there occurred at various periods between January 2013 and August 2014, with temporary transfers to Ioannina, Komotini, and Chania Prisons. The core alleged violation was Article 3 of the Convention, based on allegedly inhuman and degrading conditions of detention in Korydallos, mainly in wings A and D.

The applicants alleged severe overcrowding: Korydallos held about 2,400 prisoners despite being designed for 700. Their cells measured 9 sq. m, including sanitary facilities, and housed three or four prisoners, leaving less than 3 sq. m per person. Toilets were only partially separated from living space. Heating and hot water were insufficient; inmates had to wash themselves, their dishes, and their clothes in a washbasin. Cells were dirty and infested with cockroaches and other pests, with no effective extermination. Rubbish was not properly collected, and food remains were left in cells and corridors for days. Prisoners were not adequately separated by health condition or drug use. Medical care, especially psychological care, was inadequate. Inmates were confined to their cells for sixteen hours per day, with no recreational or educational activities, ate poor-quality meals inside their cells, and faced understaffing that compromised safety.

The Government disputed these claims. It asserted that cells in wings A and D measured 9.60 sq. m and held three, or rarely four, detainees. The first applicant had also been held in wing E in cells of 10.44 sq. m and 42.78 sq. m; the larger cell housed between ten and twenty-two detainees only for a short period. According to the Government, cells had windows, sufficient light, washbasins, toilets, beds, tables, chairs, and shelves. Wings A–D had twelve communal showers each, wing E had nine, and each wing could provide 2,000 litres of hot water daily. Sheets and blankets were supplied. There was central heating and fans in summer. Cells were disinfected and cleaned twice daily by detainee cleaning crews, and all wings had rubbish bins. The infirmary was open twenty-four hours a day, with eighteen doctors and three nurses; transfers to prison hospitals or external hospitals were possible. Medical records showed the applicants had received treatment. Social services also assisted detainees. Meals were varied, and prisoners could spend four to five hours daily in the yard for sport. TVs, a lending library, book club, jobs, and a “second chance” school were available. The Government did not submit observations concerning the sixth applicant.

The CPT’s report following its April 2013 visit strongly supported the applicants. It found Korydallos held more than 2,300 prisoners against an official capacity of 840. Cells designed for one inmate (9.5 sq. m) routinely held three or four. Some prisoners slept on mattresses on the floor in toilet areas. One 36 sq. m cell held 27 inmates, leaving less than 1.5 sq. m each; nine slept on filthy mattresses on the concrete floor, two in the toilet area. Another cell with 14 beds held 19 prisoners. The CPT noted cockroaches, bed bugs, no artificial light at night, filthy toilets, uncollected food waste, and foul smells. Health care had deteriorated: no full-time doctor worked there; visiting GPs provided only about 15 hours weekly, with continuity problems. A wing of some 400 inmates was usually staffed by only one or two officers during the day, and only eight officers were on duty at night for the entire prison of over 2,300 inmates.

**Goldnagl v. Austria** (Application no. 6822/12), European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, judgment of 7 September 2017.

The applicant, Ingrid Goldnagl, an Austrian national born in 1939, married T.G. in 1965 and divorced him in 1996 on the ground of his sole fault. The case concerned primarily the length of spousal maintenance proceedings. On 2 August 1991 the applicant lodged a maintenance claim with the Döbling District Court and sought an interim order for provisional maintenance. T.G. objected. In February 1992 the District Court ordered T.G. to pay provisional maintenance; this was confirmed on appeal in June 1992. Because T.G. did not comply, enforcement proceedings were granted in July 1992.

The maintenance proceedings then continued for many years, with numerous hearings, expert reports, appeals, and remittals. In March 1997 the District Court partly granted and partly dismissed the claim, but the Regional Court quashed that judgment in October 1997. Further hearings followed, and a second expert was appointed in 1998; his report was submitted in 1999. Also in 1999, the applicant obtained a fresh interim maintenance order and a prohibition on payouts from T.G.’s pension fund and redundancy money. T.G. later sought reductions after retiring. In July 2003, private insolvency proceedings were opened against T.G. before the Salzburg Regional Court, and the maintenance proceedings were suspended. The applicant sought acknowledgement of her maintenance claim in the insolvency proceedings, but the liquidator refused. Litigation over interim orders continued up to the Supreme Court in 2004. In 2005 and 2007 the applicant requested acceleration of the proceedings. Swiss authorities supplied T.G.’s bank data in 2007, and further witnesses were questioned in 2009. In 2009 the applicant asked for suspension of the maintenance proceedings as from the opening of the insolvency proceedings; this was granted. In 2010 the District Court issued a partial judgment concerning maintenance until 10 July 2003, which was upheld in 2011. In October 2011 the applicant requested continuation of proceedings for the period after 10 July 2003. Further hearings took place in 2014 and 2015, but the proceedings apparently remained pending.

Separately, in December 2011 the applicant filed a fresh maintenance claim with the Salzburg District Court against the liquidator. That court rejected it as res judicata in February 2012, but the Regional Court quashed that decision. Hearings were held between 2013 and 2014, and in August 2015 the Salzburg District Court partly granted the applicant’s claim; an appeal remained pending.

The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the length of the proceedings violated the “reasonable time” requirement. On 12 May 2015, that complaint was communicated to the Government; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The relevant period began on 2 August 1991 and was still pending, lasting over 25 years and 11 months across three levels of jurisdiction, including remittals. The Court declared the complaint admissible.

On the merits, the Government argued that the case was complex because of T.G.’s complicated income and property situation, numerous hearings, about 30 witnesses, three expert opinions, and requests to Swiss authorities. It also claimed the applicant contributed to delay by amending her claim, requesting suspensions for over two years, and postponing hearings due to health, while T.G. challenged several interim decisions. The Court accepted that the proceedings were complex, partly because several sets of proceedings ran simultaneously, including the main maintenance case, provisional maintenance proceedings, T.G.’s insolvency proceedings, and later the Salzburg maintenance case. Some delays were caused by T.G., his liquidator, necessary procedural steps, or the applicant. However, major delays resulted from long periods of inactivity by the domestic courts. The complexity and conduct of the parties were insufficient to explain a total duration of over 25 years and 11 months. The Court therefore found that the length of the proceedings was excessive and violated Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

In *Goldnagl v. Austria* (Application no. 6822/12, judgment 7 September 2017), the European Court of Human Rights considered a complaint under Article 6 § 1 that Austrian spousal-maintenance proceedings had exceeded a reasonable time. The applicant, Ingrid Goldnagl, born 1939, married T.G. in 1965. They separated in 1990 and divorced in 1996 due to T.G.’s sole fault. On 2 August 1991 the applicant lodged a maintenance claim with the Döbling District Court and sought an interim provisional-maintenance order. T.G. objected. In February 1992 the District Court granted interim maintenance; this was confirmed on appeal in June 1992. When T.G. failed to comply, enforcement proceedings followed. Over the following years the court held numerous hearings and appointed experts to assess T.G.’s income. A 1997 judgment partly granted and partly dismissed the claim but was quashed on appeal. Further hearings and expert reports followed, including a second expert in 1998–1999. After T.G. retired in 1999, the applicant obtained a fresh interim order for monthly provisional maintenance and a bar on drawing from T.G.’s pension fund and redundancy payment. T.G. sought reductions and challenged interim decisions.

In July 2003 private insolvency proceedings were opened against T.G. The maintenance proceedings were suspended, and the applicant pursued her claim in the insolvency proceedings; the liquidator refused to acknowledge it. Litigation over interim orders continued. In 2005 the applicant requested acceleration of the main proceedings, and the Regional Court ordered a hearing within four weeks. Hearings continued, with evidence from Switzerland and witnesses questioned in 2009. In 2009 the applicant asked to suspend the proceedings from the opening of the insolvency proceedings; this was granted. In March 2010 the District Court issued a partial judgment covering maintenance until 10 July 2003, which became final in 2011 after appeal. The applicant requested continuation for the later period. Further hearings took place in 2014 and 2015, and the main proceedings apparently remained pending. In parallel, in December 2011 the applicant filed a fresh maintenance claim with the Salzburg District Court against the liquidator. It was initially rejected as res judicata, then quashed on appeal; after hearings in 2013–2015, the Salzburg court partly granted the claim, but appeals left it pending. T.G.’s insolvency proceedings also remained pending.

The alleged violation was the length of the maintenance proceedings under Article 6 § 1. The relevant period began on 2 August 1991 and was still pending at judgment—over 25 years and 11 months, involving three levels of jurisdiction and remittals. The Court declared the complaint admissible. The Government argued complexity: T.G.’s complicated income and property, numerous hearings, about 30 witnesses, three expert opinions and supplements, Swiss letters of request, the applicant’s amended claims, requested suspensions, and health-related postponements. The applicant argued the courts could have estimated T.G.’s income and fixed maintenance earlier. The Court accepted the case was complex, partly because several proceedings ran simultaneously. Some delays were caused by the parties and necessary procedural steps. However, major delays resulted from long periods of inactivity by the domestic courts. Complexity and party conduct could not justify the total duration. The Court therefore found that the length of the proceedings was excessive and violated the “reasonable time” requirement, consistent with earlier Austrian cases such as *Baumann*, *Eigenstiller*, and *Hauptmann*.

**Case: Goldnagl v. Austria (Application no. 6822/12), European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, Judgment of 7 September 2017.**

The applicant, Ingrid Goldnagl, an Austrian national born in 1939, married T.G. in 1965. They separated in 1990 and divorced in 1996 due to T.G.’s sole fault. The alleged violation concerned the length of civil proceedings under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees a hearing within a reasonable time.

The relevant proceedings began on 2 August 1991, when the applicant lodged a claim for spousal maintenance with the Döbling District Court and requested an interim order for provisional maintenance. T.G. objected. In February 1992 the District Court issued an interim maintenance order, later confirmed by the Vienna Regional Civil Court in June 1992. Because T.G. did not comply, enforcement proceedings followed.

Over the years, the maintenance case involved numerous hearings, several expert reports on T.G.’s income, appeals, and a 1997 judgment partly granting and partly dismissing the claim, which was later quashed by the Regional Court. A second expert was appointed, and further hearings and evidence-taking continued. In 1999 the applicant sought a fresh interim maintenance order and measures to prevent T.G. from drawing pension and redundancy funds. Disputes over provisional maintenance continued, including T.G.’s request for a reduction after retirement.

In July 2003 private insolvency proceedings were opened against T.G. The main maintenance proceedings were suspended, and the liquidator refused to acknowledge the applicant’s maintenance claim. The applicant requested continuation in November 2003. Further insolvency-related appeals and interim disputes followed. In 2005 and 2007 the applicant filed requests to accelerate the proceedings. The Regional Court partly granted the first request and ordered a hearing within four weeks. Evidence was still being gathered, including documents and witness statements via letters of request to the Zurich District Court.

In 2009 the applicant asked to suspend the maintenance proceedings from the date the insolvency proceedings were opened; this was granted. In 2010 the District Court issued a partial judgment covering maintenance until the insolvency opening. This was upheld in 2011, and the Supreme Court rejected the applicant’s extraordinary appeal. The applicant then requested continuation for the period after 10 July 2003. Further hearings took place in 2014 and 2015, but the proceedings were apparently still pending.

Separate maintenance proceedings were also filed in the Salzburg District Court in December 2011 against T.G.’s liquidator after he refused to acknowledge the claim. That case was initially rejected on res judicata grounds, then quashed on appeal, and remained pending. T.G.’s insolvency proceedings were also still pending.

The applicant complained that the proceedings had exceeded a reasonable time. The period began on 2 August 1991 and was still pending, lasting over 25 years and 11 months across three levels of jurisdiction, including remittals. The Government argued that the case was complex because of T.G.’s complicated income and property situation, numerous hearings, thirty witnesses, three expert opinions, Swiss requests for evidence, the applicant’s amended claims and suspensions, and T.G.’s use of appeals. The applicant argued that the courts could have estimated T.G.’s income earlier and fixed maintenance sooner.

The Court declared the complaint admissible. It accepted that the proceedings were quite complex, partly because several sets of proceedings ran simultaneously. Some delays were caused by T.G., his liquidator, necessary procedural steps, and the applicant herself. However, major delays resulted from long periods of inactivity by the domestic courts. The complexity and conduct of the parties could not justify an overall duration of 25 years and 11 months. The Court therefore found an excessive length of proceedings and a violation of Article 6 § 1.

**Ković and Others v. Serbia** (Applications nos. 39611/08, 50121/13, and 2490/14) is a 2017 European Court of Human Rights judgment concerning three Serbian nationals—Nikola Ković, Zoran Ranković, and Ivan Bojanić—who alleged excessive length of administrative and civil proceedings. They relied primarily on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees a hearing within a reasonable time; Ranković and Bojanić also complained under Article 13 about the lack of an effective domestic remedy.

The applications were lodged on 21 July 2008, 5 June 2013, and 16 December 2013. On 18 December 2014, the Court communicated the length-of-proceedings complaints to the Serbian Government, while declaring the remaining parts inadmissible. The Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

The central facts concerned what happened after each applicant obtained a decision from the Serbian Constitutional Court. In each case, the Constitutional Court found a violation of the right to a hearing within a reasonable time. The dispute before the European Court was therefore whether those domestic decisions—and any compensation awarded—deprived the applicants of “victim” status under Article 34 of the Convention.

For Nikola Ković, the Constitutional Court found a violation and, under the regulations then applicable, established his right to seek compensation for non-pecuniary damage before the Commission for Damage Compensation. Ković submitted a damages request to that Commission on 26 December 2010, but he never received a response. The Government argued that he could still pursue compensation and later bring civil proceedings if dissatisfied. The Court noted, however, that Ković had indeed submitted a request and received no answer. It also recalled that, for applications introduced before 7 August 2008, a constitutional appeal was not an obligatory remedy in Serbia under *Vinčić and Others v. Serbia*. Since Ković lodged his application on 21 July 2008, he had not been required to use the constitutional avenue.

For Zoran Ranković and Ivan Bojanić, the Constitutional Court awarded them specified sums in non-pecuniary damages. The amounts are set out in the appendix to the judgment. The European Court found that these sums were significantly lower than awards made in its own case-law for similar delays. Although domestic compensation may be lower than Strasbourg awards and may be paid more promptly, the Court assessed the awards in light of the duration of the proceedings, the standard of living in Serbia, and all circumstances. It concluded that the sums awarded to Ranković and Bojanić were not sufficient and did not constitute appropriate redress.

The Court reiterated that an applicant loses victim status only if domestic authorities have acknowledged the breach and provided adequate and sufficient redress. Here, the Constitutional Court had acknowledged the violations, but the redress was inadequate: Ković received no response to his compensation request, and Ranković and Bojanić received insufficient compensation. Consequently, none of the applicants lost victim status, and the Government’s objection was rejected.

On the merits, the Court concluded that the length of the proceedings at issue was excessive and failed to satisfy the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1. Having reached that conclusion, it did not find it necessary to examine the essentially same complaint raised by Ranković and Bojanić under Article 13. The judgment thus focused on the failure of domestic remedies to provide sufficient redress for lengthy proceedings, leaving the applicants as victims entitled to the Court’s finding of a violation.

**Summary of *Ković and Others v. Serbia* (Application nos. 39611/08, 50121/13, 2490/14)**

This case concerns three Serbian nationals—Mr Nikola Ković, Mr Zoran Ranković, and Mr Ivan Bojanić—who lodged applications against Serbia under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The central complaint, communicated to the Government on 18 December 2014, was that the length of separate administrative and civil proceedings to which each applicant was a party had been incompatible with the "reasonable time" requirement under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are as follows. All three applicants had previously pursued a constitutional appeal before the Serbian Constitutional Court. In each instance, the Constitutional Court found a violation of their right to a hearing within a reasonable time. This domestic acknowledgment of the breach formed the basis of the Government's primary objection before the European Court: that by obtaining these decisions, the applicants had lost their status as "victims" within the meaning of Article 34, as the finding of a violation and any awarded compensation constituted sufficient redress.

However, the subsequent treatment of each applicant differed significantly, which proved critical to the Court's analysis. For Mr. Ković, the Constitutional Court, applying the regulations in force at the time, did not directly award him compensation. Instead, it established his right to seek non-pecuniary damages before a separate body, the Commission for Damage Compensation. Mr. Ković submitted his request to this Commission on 26 December 2010, but the case file indicated he had received no response to date. The Court noted this failure, and further observed that because Mr. Ković lodged his application on 21 July 2008, before the Court's ruling in *Vinčić and Others* established the constitutional appeal as an effective remedy for all applications introduced after 7 August 2008, he had not been obliged to use that avenue at all.

For the other two applicants, Mr. Ranković and Mr. Bojanić, the Constitutional Court directly awarded them specified sums in non-pecuniary damages. Here, the Court's assessment focused on the adequacy of the redress. It reiterated that in length-of-proceedings cases, the amount of compensation is a key factor in determining whether an applicant has lost victim status. While States may award amounts lower than those the Court might grant under Article 41, the sums awarded to Mr. Ranković and Mr. Bojanić were found to be significantly lower than the Court's established case-law for similar delays. Considering the duration of the proceedings and the standard of living in Serbia, the Court concluded these amounts did not constitute "appropriate redress."

Consequently, the European Court rejected the Government's objection, finding that none of the applicants had lost their victim status. This conclusion was central to its finding that the length of the proceedings at issue was excessive and violated the "reasonable time" requirement of Article 6 § 1. Having reached this conclusion, the Court did not find it necessary to separately examine the essentially same complaint raised by two applicants under Article 13 concerning the lack of an effective remedy. The case was therefore decided in favor of the applicants on the core issue of the excessive length of domestic proceedings and the insufficiency of the domestic redress provided.

In **Ković and Others v. Serbia** (Applications nos. 39611/08, 50121/13 and 2490/14; ECtHR Third Section, 4 April 2017), three Serbian nationals—Nikola Ković, Zoran Ranković, and Ivan Bojanić—complained under Article 6 § 1 that administrative and civil proceedings involving them had exceeded a “reasonable time.” Ranković and Bojanić also complained under Article 13 that they lacked an effective domestic remedy. The applications were lodged on 21 July 2008, 5 June 2013, and 16 December 2013. The Court joined them because of their similar factual and legal background.

The key domestic facts concerned prior redress in Serbia. All three applicants had obtained decisions from the Constitutional Court of Serbia finding a violation of their right to a hearing within a reasonable time. For Ković, the Constitutional Court held that, under the regulations then applicable, he could seek compensation for non-pecuniary damage before the Commission for Damage Compensation. Ković submitted such a request on 26 December 2010, but by the time of the European Court’s judgment he had received no response. For Ranković and Bojanić, the Constitutional Court awarded specified sums of non-pecuniary damages.

The Serbian Government argued that the applicants could no longer be considered victims. It submitted that the Constitutional Court had acknowledged the breach and that the compensation, or the possibility of obtaining compensation, constituted sufficient redress. It further argued that Ković could later bring civil proceedings if he was dissatisfied with the Commission’s award. The applicants disagreed.

The ECtHR reiterated that an applicant loses victim status only where domestic authorities have acknowledged the alleged Convention infringement and provided appropriate redress. The Constitutional Court’s findings satisfied the acknowledgement requirement. The Court then examined whether the redress was adequate and sufficient. In length-of-proceedings cases, the amount awarded is important. Serbia’s constitutional remedy, designed both to expedite proceedings and to compensate, may award less than the ECtHR would under Article 41, provided the sums are not unreasonable.

The Court rejected the Government’s objection. As to Ković, he had actually submitted a damages request to the Commission but had received no response. Moreover, because he lodged his application on 21 July 2008, before the date from which the constitutional appeal was considered an effective domestic remedy in Serbia—7 August 2008—he had not been obliged to use that avenue. As to Ranković and Bojanić, the sums awarded by the Constitutional Court were significantly lower than those awarded by the ECtHR for comparable delays. Considering the duration of their proceedings, the value of the awards in light of Serbia’s standard of living, and the fact that domestic compensation is generally paid more promptly, the Court found those sums insufficient to amount to appropriate redress. Consequently, none of the applicants had lost victim status.

The Court therefore concluded that the length of the proceedings was excessive and violated the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1. Having reached that conclusion, it did not find it necessary to examine separately the essentially same complaint raised by Ranković and Bojanić under Article 13.
