**Case: Magát v. Slovakia (Application no. 44646/15), European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, Judgment of 25 July 2017.**

The applicant, Anton Magát, a Slovak national born in 1957, complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that civil proceedings concerning child maintenance had exceeded a “reasonable time.” The proceedings began on 28 February 2011, when the applicant’s son sued him before the Čadca District Court. The applicant was the defendant.

During the proceedings, the applicant made an incomplete submission in April 2011 and supplemented it the following month, saying he was waiting for a response from the Centre for Legal Aid regarding a legal-aid lawyer. He twice complained to the president of the District Court about delays, on 9 February 2012 and 29 February 2012, but these complaints were unsuccessful, as was his subsequent appellate review. The District Court took various steps: it requested information from public authorities such as the Social Security Authority and the Job Centre; between May 2012 and April 2014 it dealt with the appointment of a guardian because the applicant was undergoing ambulatory psychiatric treatment; the guardianship was revoked in September 2014 after a legal-aid lawyer was appointed in June 2014. The case file was also joined to another set of proceedings for several months, the judge changed in January 2014, and several hearings were adjourned or cancelled.

On 13 May 2015, the Constitutional Court rejected the applicant’s complaint about excessive length as manifestly ill-founded. It found that the District Court had proceeded actively and properly, apart from minor exceptions such as joining the file, changing the judge, and a procedural error at one hearing. After that decision, the District Court requested further information, including from the applicant’s employer. A hearing scheduled for 12 August 2015 was adjourned to 31 August 2015 and then postponed indefinitely because the court had to deal with a procedural request from the plaintiff, which was also appealed. No judgment on the merits had been delivered, and the proceedings remained pending.

The Government argued that the application was manifestly ill-founded and, regarding the period after the Constitutional Court’s decision, that the applicant should have complained again to the Constitutional Court. They relied on the Constitutional Court’s finding that by May 2015 the proceedings had lasted only four years and three months, that the applicant was merely a defendant, and that any shortcomings were minor. The applicant disagreed, arguing among other things that the guardian should not have been appointed without an expert opinion on his mental health and that he had an attorney.

The Court found the Government’s arguments intertwined. At the time of the Constitutional Court’s decision, the proceedings had lasted almost four years and three months before one level of jurisdiction with no merits decision. The subject matter—child maintenance—was not particularly complex. Although some steps taken by the District Court were relevant, they did not justify the overall duration. The Court noted specific delays: the file was joined to another case for almost five months, and the judge was changed. The applicant’s complaints to the District Court president were a lawful procedural right and did not cause excessive delay. The Court distinguished Horňák v. Slovakia. It concluded that the Constitutional Court’s decision was incompatible with Convention principles, so the applicant was not required to resort again to the Article 127 remedy. The period began on 28 February 2011 and, by March 2016, the proceedings had lasted more than six years before one level of jurisdiction. The complaint was admissible.

On the merits, applying the criteria of complexity, conduct, and what was at stake, the Court found that the length of the proceedings was excessive and failed to meet the “reasonable time” requirement. It therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

**Case: Magát v. Slovakia (Application no. 44646/15), European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, Judgment of 25 July 2017.**

The applicant, Anton Magát, a Slovak national born in 1957, complained under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights that the length of civil proceedings concerning child maintenance had violated his right to a hearing within a reasonable time. The proceedings began on 28 February 2011, when the applicant’s son sued him for child maintenance before the Čadca District Court. The applicant was the defendant.

During the proceedings, the applicant made an incomplete submission in April 2011 and later explained that he had been waiting for a response from the Centre for Legal Aid regarding his request for a legal-aid lawyer. He also lodged two complaints with the president of the District Court about excessive delays, on 9 and 29 February 2012. Those complaints were unsuccessful, as was his subsequent appellate review.

The District Court took various steps, including requesting information from public authorities such as the Social Security Authority and the Job Centre. Between May 2012 and April 2014, it dealt with the appointment of a guardian for the applicant, who was undergoing ambulatory psychiatric treatment. A guardian was appointed in April 2014 but revoked in September 2014, after the Centre for Legal Aid appointed a lawyer for the applicant in June 2014. The District Court also joined the case file to another set of proceedings for several months, changed the responsible judge in January 2014, and scheduled hearings that were adjourned or cancelled.

On 13 May 2015, the Constitutional Court rejected the applicant’s complaint about the length of proceedings as manifestly ill-founded. It found that the District Court had proceeded actively and properly, apart from minor shortcomings such as the joinder of the case file, the change of judge, and a procedural error at one hearing. It also noted that the applicant had complained to the District Court president and appealed further.

After the Constitutional Court’s decision, the District Court continued to take steps, including seeking information from the applicant’s employer. A hearing scheduled for 12 August 2015 was adjourned to 31 August 2015, then postponed indefinitely because the court had to deal with a procedural request from the plaintiff. No judgment on the merits had been delivered, and the proceedings remained pending.

Before the European Court, the Government argued that the applicant’s complaint was manifestly ill-founded, relying on the Constitutional Court’s findings. They also argued that, for the period after the Constitutional Court’s decision, the applicant should have lodged a new constitutional complaint and therefore had not exhausted domestic remedies. The applicant disagreed.

The European Court found that the Government’s arguments were intertwined. It first examined the Constitutional Court’s decision and concluded that it was not compatible with Convention principles. At the time of that decision, the proceedings had lasted almost four years and three months before one level of jurisdiction, without any decision on the merits. The subject matter—child maintenance—was not particularly complex. Although some steps taken by the District Court may have been relevant, they did not justify the overall duration. The Court also noted that the case had begun in February 2011 and still no merits decision had been given. Delays included a five-month joinder and a change of judge. The applicant’s use of domestic complaints did not cause excessive delay.

The Court held that the applicant was not required to resort repeatedly to the constitutional remedy, because the first use had not provided adequate redress. The period began on 28 February 2011 and, by March 2016, the proceedings had lasted more than six years before one level of jurisdiction. The Court declared the complaint admissible and found a violation of Article 6 § 1, holding that the length of the proceedings was excessive and failed to meet the “reasonable time” requirement.

The applicant was the defendant. In April 2011, he filed an incomplete submission, later supplemented, claiming he was waiting for the Centre for Legal Aid to assign him a lawyer. He twice complained to the president of the District Court about delay—on 9 and 29 February 2012—without success; appellate review of those complaints also failed.

During the proceedings, the District Court requested information from public authorities. From May 2012 to April 2014, it dealt with appointing a guardian for the applicant, who was undergoing ambulatory psychiatric treatment. That guardianship was revoked in September 2014 after a legal-aid lawyer was appointed for him in June 2014. No judgment on the merits had been delivered, and the proceedings were still pending.

Before the European Court, the Government argued that the complaint was manifestly ill-founded. It said the proceedings had lasted only about four years and three months at the time of the Constitutional Court’s decision, that the applicant was merely a defendant and the case was less significant for him, and that any delays were minor, relying on *Horňák v. Slovakia*. For the period after the Constitutional Court’s decision, it argued non-exhaustion because the applicant should have complained again to the Constitutional Court. The applicant disagreed, complaining in particular that a guardian had been appointed without an expert opinion on his mental health, and noting that he had an attorney.

The European Court found the Government’s arguments intertwined. At the Constitutional Court stage, the proceedings had lasted almost four years and three months before one level of jurisdiction without any merits decision. The child-maintenance subject matter was not complex. Although some steps were relevant, they did not justify the overall duration. The District Court caused delays, including joining the file for almost five months and changing judges. The applicant’s complaints to the District Court president were a procedural right and did not excuse the delay. *Horňák* was distinguishable.

The Court therefore disagreed with the Constitutional Court, finding the complaint not manifestly ill-founded. It also held that the applicant was not required to repeatedly use the Article 127 remedy where the first constitutional decision was incompatible with Convention principles. The period began on 28 February 2011 and, by March 2016, the proceedings were still pending after more than six years before one level of jurisdiction. The complaint was admissible and, on the merits, the length was excessive, violating Article 6 § 1.

In *Antović and Mirković v. Montenegro* (App. no. 70838/13, 28 Nov 2017), two professors at the School of Mathematics, University of Montenegro, alleged under Article 8 that video surveillance in university auditoriums where they taught violated their right to respect for private life.

On 1 February 2011, the Dean informed the School Council that video surveillance had been introduced in classrooms. On 24 February 2011, he issued a decision introducing cameras in seven amphitheatres and in front of the Dean’s Office. The stated aims were safety of property and people, including students, and monitoring teaching. Access was apparently limited to the Dean; data were meant to be stored for a year. Inspectors later found low-resolution cameras with no zoom or audio, and actual storage of about thirty days.

On 14 March 2011, the applicants complained to the Personal Data Protection Agency that their data were collected without consent and that surveillance was unnecessary. Inspectors initially found it compliant, citing past incidents. The applicants objected that they had not been notified in writing before surveillance began and that the decision came after surveillance started. On 28 April 2011, the Agency Council ordered removal of the cameras within fifteen days, finding the surveillance contrary to the Personal Data Protection Act, sections 10, 35 and 36. It held there was no evidence of danger to people, property or confidential data in the auditoriums, and monitoring teaching was not a lawful ground. The decision was served in January 2012; cameras were removed and data erased.

The applicants brought a civil compensation claim. On 27 December 2012, the Court of First Instance ruled against them. It held that although private life can include professional activities, university auditoriums were public working areas where no privacy expectation existed; there was no interference. The High Court upheld this on 17 July 2013. The applicants did not file a constitutional appeal.

The European Court held Article 8 applicable. Professional activities and workplace interactions can fall within private life, and video surveillance of an employee at work—covert or not—is a considerable intrusion. A constitutional appeal only became effective in Montenegro in March 2015, after their October 2013 application, so exhaustion was not required.

On the merits, the Court found an interference. The civil courts never examined lawfulness because they found no privacy interest. The Agency, however, found the surveillance unlawful. Section 35 allowed surveillance only of access areas to official premises, not amphitheatres. Section 36 permitted cameras in official or business premises only where safety of people, property or confidential data could not be protected otherwise. Monitoring teaching was not a lawful ground. The Agency found no evidence that people or property were endangered, and the Government offered no contrary evidence or proof that less invasive alternatives were considered. Therefore the interference was not “in accordance with the law,” sufficient to establish a violation of Article 8, without examining legitimate aim or necessity.

**Case: Antović and Mirković v. Montenegro (Application no. 70838/13, ECtHR, 28 November 2017)**

The applicants, Nevenka Antović and Jovan Mirković, were professors at the School of Mathematics, University of Montenegro. They alleged that the installation and use of video surveillance in the university auditoriums where they taught violated their right to respect for private life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

On 1 February 2011, the Dean informed the School Council that video surveillance had been introduced in the auditoriums. On 24 February 2011, the Dean issued a formal decision introducing cameras in seven amphitheatres and in front of the Dean’s Office. The stated aims were to ensure the safety of property and people, including students, and to monitor teaching activities. Access to recorded data was protected by codes known only to the Dean, and data was supposedly stored for one year, although in practice it was automatically deleted after thirty days.

On 14 March 2011, the applicants complained to the Personal Data Protection Agency, arguing that their data was collected without consent and that the surveillance was unnecessary. Inspectors initially found the surveillance compliant, citing incidents such as property damage, theft, and unauthorised entry. The applicants objected, and on 28 April 2011 the Agency Council ordered the School to remove the cameras within fifteen days. It found the surveillance contrary to the Personal Data Protection Act, notably sections 10, 35 and 36. In particular, there was no evidence that people or property were in danger, and monitoring teaching was not a lawful ground for video surveillance. The School was served with the decision in January 2012, and the cameras were removed by 27 January 2012.

The applicants also brought civil compensation proceedings against the University, the Agency, and the State. In December 2012, the Court of First Instance rejected their claim, holding that the university auditorium was a public working area, that teaching was a public activity, and that they could not reasonably expect privacy there. It further found that the recorded data did not amount to personal data and that no interference with private life had occurred. The High Court upheld that judgment in July 2013. The applicants did not file a constitutional appeal.

Before the ECtHR, the Government argued that the applicants had failed to exhaust domestic remedies and that Article 8 was not applicable because the surveillance concerned professional activity in a public institution. The Court rejected the exhaustion objection, noting that a constitutional appeal only became an effective remedy in Montenegro in March 2015, after the applicants lodged their application in October 2013.

The Court held that Article 8 was applicable. Private life includes professional and workplace activities, and video surveillance of an employee at work—whether covert or not—constitutes a considerable intrusion into private life. Since the domestic courts had found no interference, they never examined whether the surveillance was lawful. However, the Agency had expressly found it unlawful. The Court noted that section 35 permitted surveillance only of access areas to official premises, not amphitheatres, while section 36 allowed cameras in official or business premises only where safety of people or property could not be achieved otherwise. One stated aim—monitoring teaching—was not provided for by law. Moreover, there was no evidence that people or property were in jeopardy. The Government provided no contrary evidence and did not show that less invasive alternatives were considered.

The Court therefore concluded that the interference was not “in accordance with the law,” which sufficed to establish a violation of Article 8. It did not need to examine the remaining requirements of Article 8 § 2.

**Case summary: Antović and Mirković v. Montenegro**  
*Application no. 70838/13, ECtHR Second Section, judgment of 28 November 2017.*

The applicants, Nevenka Antović and Jovan Mirković, were professors at the School of Mathematics, University of Montenegro. They alleged that video surveillance installed in the university auditoriums where they taught violated their right to respect for private life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

On 1 February 2011, the Dean informed the School Council that video surveillance had been introduced in the auditoriums. On 24 February 2011, the Dean issued a formal decision introducing cameras in seven amphitheatres and in front of the Dean’s Office. The stated aims were to ensure the safety of property and people, including students, and to monitor teaching activities. Access to the collected data was allegedly protected by codes known only to the Dean. Although the decision said data would be stored for one year, the system actually stored recordings for about thirty days before automatic deletion.

On 14 March 2011, the applicants complained to the Personal Data Protection Agency that data about them was being collected without consent. They argued that the auditoriums were locked before and after classes, contained only fixed desks, chairs and a blackboard, and that there was no known safety risk. They also said other methods could protect people and property. Agency inspectors initially found the surveillance compliant, citing past incidents such as damage to property, unauthorized persons, animals, drinks and tobacco. They noted that the cameras produced low-resolution images, had no zoom, recorded no audio, and automatically deleted data after thirty days.

The applicants objected, saying they had not been notified in writing before surveillance began and that cameras could not ensure safety. On 28 April 2011, the Agency Council ordered the School of Mathematics to remove the cameras within fifteen days. It found violations of the Personal Data Protection Act, notably sections 10, 35 and 36. There was no evidence that the safety of people, property or confidential data was endangered, and surveillance of teaching was not a lawful ground for cameras. The decision was served in January 2012; the cameras were removed by 27 January 2012, and the data were erased.

The applicants then brought a civil compensation claim. In December 2012, the Podgorica Court of First Instance ruled against them. It accepted that private life could include professional activities, but held that university auditoriums were public working areas where professors were never alone, so no privacy right was violated. It also found that merely recording public activity, without publication, was not an interference. The High Court upheld that judgment in July 2013. The applicants did not file a constitutional appeal.

Before the ECtHR, the Government argued that Article 8 did not apply to public teaching activities and that the applicants had failed to exhaust domestic remedies. The Court found Article 8 applicable. Private life is broad and includes professional and workplace relationships. Video surveillance of employees at work, even non-covert, is a considerable intrusion into private life because employees cannot avoid the workplace. The constitutional appeal was not effective at the relevant time, so exhaustion did not require it.

On the merits, the Court found an interference with Article 8. It did not need to examine every justification because the surveillance was not “in accordance with the law.” The domestic courts had not examined lawfulness, having found no privacy interference. However, the Data Protection Agency explicitly found a violation. Section 35 allowed surveillance only of access areas to official premises, not amphitheatres. Section 36 allowed cameras in official or business premises only if safety or protection of confidential data could not be achieved otherwise; monitoring teaching was not a permitted aim. There was no evidence of danger to people or property, and no alternative measures were considered. Montenegro therefore violated Article 8.

In *Kemal Coşkun v. Turkey* (ECtHR, 28 March 2017), the applicant was a Turkish police officer dismissed from the force after a 2004 incident. As the applicant was taken to the station, he tried to discard a knife, hatchet and mobile phone. A later search of his car found a gun, duct tape, rope, a bloodstained towel, handcuffs and a truncheon.

Ç.V. told the prosecutor she had had an extramarital affair with the applicant, wanted to end it, and had agreed to meet him once more. She claimed he drove her out of the city without consent, hit her stomach with a truncheon, tied her hands with rope and threatened sexual assault. A medical report recorded a cut on her tongue, bruising on her neck, a chest lesion and thumb pain, making her unfit for work for seven days. She later submitted a written statement retracting the accusations, but, when summoned in person the same day, said the retraction had been made under duress and maintained her initial account. The applicant denied kidnapping or attempted rape, claiming Ç.V. had demanded money and behaved erratically, and that he had only hit her during a quarrel.

In March 2006 the Samsun Assize Court acquitted the applicant of false imprisonment and robbery and found no attempted rape, but convicted him of assault and battery. Meanwhile, parallel disciplinary proceedings led to the applicant’s dismissal from the police force in February 2005. The disciplinary bodies found that he had committed attempted rape, false imprisonment and threatening violence with a weapon. In September 2005 the Samsun Administrative Court upheld the dismissal, relying on Ç.V.’s initial statements, the medical report, the weapons found and the applicant’s attempt to conceal evidence. Although no witnesses corroborated Ç.V., the administrative court reasoned that the applicant had committed the alleged criminal acts. In April 2007 the Supreme Administrative Court upheld that decision, holding that acquittal in criminal proceedings did not preclude disciplinary sanctions.

The applicant complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 that his dismissal and the administrative courts’ judgments violated his right to a fair hearing and the presumption of innocence, since he had not been convicted of the charges. The administrative courts had made explicit, unqualified findings that he committed attempted rape, false imprisonment and related criminal offences, using criminal nomenclature without separating disciplinary liability from criminal guilt. The Supreme Administrative Court failed to correct this. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 2. It did not examine Article 6 § 1 separately. The later complaints under Articles 3 and 7 were rejected as out of time.

Case: Kemal Coşkun v. Turkey (ECtHR, 28 March 2017). The applicant, a Turkish police officer, was dismissed from the police force after disciplinary proceedings arising from a July 2004 incident. The woman, Ç.V., was crying and had blood around her mouth. She alleged that the applicant had kidnapped and beaten her. On the way to the station, the applicant was caught trying to discard a knife, a hatchet and a mobile phone. A later search of his car found a gun, duct tape, rope, a bloodstained towel, handcuffs and a truncheon. A medical report recorded a cut on Ç.V.’s tongue, neck ecchymosis, a chest lesion and thumb pain, rendering her unfit for work for seven days. Ç.V. initially accused the applicant of attempted rape, false imprisonment and threats; she then recanted, then claimed the recantation was made under duress and maintained her allegations, though she later withdrew the attempted sexual assault claim. The applicant denied the charges, claiming Ç.V. had blackmailed him and behaved aggressively.

The public prosecutor charged the applicant with attempted rape, false imprisonment and robbery. In March 2006, the Samsun Assize Court acquitted him of false imprisonment and robbery, found no attempted rape, but convicted him of assault and battery based on the same conduct. In September 2012, the Court of Cassation quashed the assault and battery conviction because the limitation period had expired and discontinued those proceedings, while upholding the acquittals.

In parallel, disciplinary proceedings were brought. The Samsun Police Disciplinary Council found that the applicant had committed false imprisonment, attempted rape and threatening violence with a weapon. On 15 February 2005, the Supreme Disciplinary Council dismissed him from the police force under section 8 §6 of the Disciplinary Regulations. On 29 September 2005, the Samsun Administrative Court upheld the dismissal, relying on Ç.V.’s initial statements, the medical report, the seized weapons and the applicant’s attempt to conceal evidence, even though the criminal proceedings were still pending and there were no witnesses. On 10 April 2007, the Supreme Administrative Court rejected his appeal, holding that an acquittal did not preclude disciplinary sanctions under Law no. 657.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 6 §2. Although disciplinary and criminal proceedings may run in parallel, the administrative courts had unequivocally pronounced the applicant guilty of false imprisonment, robbery and attempted rape while the criminal proceedings were still pending. They used criminal nomenclature and failed to distinguish disciplinary liability from criminal guilt, thereby breaching the presumption of innocence. The Court did not separately examine the Article 6 §1 complaint and rejected later Article 3 and 7 complaints as out of time. It stressed that it was not deciding whether dismissal itself was unjustified, but only that the grounds and language used violated the presumption of innocence.

Kemal Coşkun v. Turkey concerned a Turkish police officer, Kemal Coşkun, who was dismissed from the police force after a July 2004 incident and complained that the dismissal and related administrative judgments violated his rights under Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 of the Convention, particularly the presumption of innocence.

On 3 July 2004, the gendarmerie received a call about a woman crying for help in a white car. They located the car outside Samsun, driven by the applicant. The woman, Ç.V., was crying, had blood around her mouth, and said the applicant had kidnapped and beaten her. The applicant was seen trying to dispose of a knife, hatchet, and mobile phone. A search of his car found a gun, duct tape, rope, a bloodstained towel, handcuffs, and a truncheon. Ç.V. told the prosecutor that she and the applicant had had an extramarital affair, that she wanted to end it because of his threats, and that he had driven her out of the city without consent, hit her with a truncheon, tied her hands, and threatened sexual assault. The applicant denied kidnapping and attempted rape, claiming Ç.V. demanded money, behaved erratically, and that he hit her only after she threatened him. A forensic report documented a cut on her tongue, neck bruising, a chest lesion, and thumb pain, finding her unfit for work for seven days. Ç.V. later recanted in writing, then claimed she had recanted under duress and reasserted her allegations. At trial, she maintained her claims except for actual attempted sexual assault.

Criminal proceedings charged the applicant with attempted rape, false imprisonment, and robbery. In 2006, the Samsun Assize Court acquitted him of false imprisonment and robbery. It found no attempted rape but recharacterised his conduct as assault and battery and convicted him on that basis. In 2012, the Court of Cassation quashed that conviction because the five-year limitation period for assault and battery had expired, discontinued that charge, and upheld the acquittals.

In parallel, disciplinary proceedings led to the applicant’s dismissal. The Supreme Disciplinary Council found it established that he had committed attempted rape, assault, and threatening violence with a weapon, and dismissed him on 15 February 2005. The Samsun Administrative Court upheld the dismissal on 29 September 2005, relying on Ç.V.’s initial statements, the medical report, and the weapons/tools found in the car, even though there were no witnesses. It expressly found that the applicant had committed attempted rape, false imprisonment, and threatening with a weapon. On 10 April 2007, the Supreme Administrative Court rejected his appeal, holding that an acquittal in criminal proceedings did not preclude disciplinary sanctions under the Public Service Act. At that time, the criminal proceedings were still pending or not yet final.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that his dismissal and the administrative courts’ judgments violated Article 6 §§ 1 and 2. The Court found Article 6 § 2 applicable. Although disciplinary and criminal proceedings may run in parallel, public authorities must not pronounce a person guilty of a criminal offence before a competent criminal court has established guilt. Here, the administrative courts used criminal terminology and unequivocally found the applicant guilty of attempted rape, false imprisonment, and robbery/threatening with a weapon while criminal proceedings were pending, without limiting their findings to the disciplinary sphere. The Supreme Administrative Court failed to correct this. The Court therefore found a violation of the presumption of innocence. It did not decide whether the dismissal itself was unjustified. The Article 6 § 1 complaint was not examined separately, and later Article 3 and 7 complaints were rejected as out of time.

In *Porowski v. Poland* (Application no. 34458/03, judgment of 21 March 2017), the applicant, Dariusz Porowski, a Polish national, complained that his detention on remand had been unlawful and excessively long, that his correspondence with his lawyer was censored, and that criminal proceedings involving him and third persons were unfair and unreasonably lengthy.

The key facts concerned two overlapping criminal cases. In the first case, the applicant was arrested on 11 July 2000 and remanded in custody by the Jarosław District Court on suspicion of attempted extortion, false imprisonment and threats to kill. His detention was repeatedly extended. He was convicted on 13 December 2001 and sentenced to five years’ imprisonment, but that conviction was quashed on 23 April 2002. During the retrial, his detention continued and was extended through 2003. On 7 November 2003 he was again convicted and sentenced to five years; the judgment was upheld in March 2004, and his cassation appeal was dismissed in December 2004. He did not use the 2004 Act remedy for complaints about excessive length.

In the second case, on 10 November 2000—while already detained in the first case—the applicant was remanded in custody by the Mińsk Mazowiecki District Court on suspicion of armed robbery and false imprisonment. His detention was extended many times. A central issue was that the Polish courts treated the statutory two-year maximum for detention on remand as applying only to “effective” detention in a given case. Because the applicant was already deprived of liberty in the first case, the courts considered that his detention in the second case had not yet begun to run for the purposes of that limit. They therefore extended the measure beyond the ordinary two-year period, including while proceedings were stayed for psychiatric observation. In February 2003 his release was ordered in the second case, but he remained in custody because of the first case. He was convicted in September 2005, but that judgment was quashed in February 2006. He was ultimately released on 10 April 2008 after the appellate court quashed another conviction and lifted the preventive measure. He was later convicted again in October 2009.

He argued that the “effective detention” interpretation denied protection to detainees concurrently held in another case, and that the two-year limit did not protect detainees after a first judgment was quashed. The Constitutional Court discontinued part of the complaint after a related provision was declared unconstitutional in case SK 17/07; the remaining part was rejected for lack of standing.

He had reported alleged offences by Przemyśl Prison staff in June 2001, but the investigation was discontinued in November 2002, a decision upheld in February 2003. **Moreira Ferreira v. Portugal (No. 2)** (Grand Chamber, 11 July 2017) concerned a Portuguese woman convicted in 2007 of threatening and insulting conduct and sentenced to a fine. The Matosinhos District Court rejected her defence of diminished criminal responsibility, despite an expert report referring to limited intellectual and cognitive capacities. On appeal, the Oporto Court of Appeal upheld the conviction and reduced the fine, but it did not examine the applicant personally at the hearing.

In 2011, the European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 6 § 1 because the Court of Appeal should have heard the applicant in person, especially since her criminal responsibility and sentence were at issue. The Court awarded €2,400 in non-pecuniary damages. It also observed that a retrial or reopening, if requested, was in principle an appropriate remedy, and noted that Article 449 § 1 (g) of the Portuguese Code of Criminal Procedure allowed review where a conviction was irreconcilable with a binding international judgment or where such a judgment cast serious doubt on the conviction.

After that judgment, in October 2011, the applicant applied to the Supreme Court for review under Article 449 § 1 (g), arguing that her conviction was incompatible with the 2011 judgment. In March 2012, the Supreme Court refused. It held that the absence of a personal hearing was a procedural irregularity not amenable to review; that the conviction was not incompatible with the European Court’s judgment; and that no serious doubt had been cast on its validity. The Supreme Court reasoned that the European Court had compensated a procedural defect, not established that the conviction itself was unfair.

The applicant then lodged a new application, complaining that the Supreme Court’s dismissal of her review request violated Article 6 § 1 and amounted to a “denial of justice.” She argued that the Supreme Court had misinterpreted domestic law and the 2011 judgment, depriving her of the right to have her conviction reviewed. The Government objected that Article 46 prevented the Court from examining the complaint and that Article 6 did not apply to extraordinary review proceedings.

The Grand Chamber first held that Article 46 did not preclude examination. Although execution of judgments is supervised by the Committee of Ministers, the Supreme Court’s refusal raised a new issue: the validity of the conviction in light of the earlier violation. On applicability, the Court reiterated that there is normally no right to reopening and that extraordinary remedies fall outside Article 6. However, in criminal cases Article 6 may apply where the domestic court is called upon to determine the criminal charge or where the procedure leads to a full reconsideration. Here, the Supreme Court had to assess whether the final conviction was compatible with the European Court’s judgment and whether serious doubts existed, so Article 6 § 1 applied.

On the merits, however, the Court found no violation. The Supreme Court’s interpretation and application of Article 449 § 1 (g) were not arbitrary or manifestly unreasonable. The 2011 judgment had found a procedural violation, not that the conviction itself was substantively unfair, and it did not automatically require reopening. Just satisfaction had already been awarded, and domestic courts retained a margin in applying the review ground. The refusal therefore did not amount to a denial of justice.

Moreira Ferreira v. Portugal (No. 2) (Grand Chamber, 11 July 2017) concerned the aftermath of an earlier Strasbourg finding that Portugal had violated the applicant’s fair-trial rights. In 2007, Ms Moreira Ferreira was convicted by the Matosinhos District Court of threatening and insulting conduct after an altercation. Although an expert report noted limited intellectual and cognitive capacities, the court held her criminally responsible and imposed a fine. She appealed, arguing diminished responsibility. The Oporto Court of Appeal held a hearing in December 2007 but did not examine her personally. It upheld the conviction and reduced the fine.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the appellate court had not heard her in person. In its 2011 judgment, the Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1, reasoning that the Court of Appeal had to assess questions about her criminal responsibility and personal testimony. It awarded €2,400 in non-pecuniary damages. It noted that a retrial or reopening would, in principle, be an appropriate remedy, but it did not order one.

Portugal paid the award and proposed but did not enact a reform to ensure hearings in such appellate cases. In October 2011, the applicant asked the Portuguese Supreme Court to review the final conviction under Article 449 § 1(g) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. That provision permits review where a conviction is irreconcilable with a binding international judgment or where such a judgment casts serious doubt on the conviction. She argued that the 2007 Court of Appeal judgment was incompatible with the 2011 Strasbourg judgment. The prosecution supported review, citing doubts about sentencing. In March 2012, the Supreme Court refused. It held that the lack of a personal hearing was a procedural irregularity, not a matter amenable to review; the conviction itself was not incompatible with the Strasbourg judgment; and the Strasbourg Court had awarded compensation rather than requiring a retrial. It found no serious doubt about the conviction.

The applicant then lodged a new application, alleging that the Supreme Court’s refusal amounted to a denial of justice and violated Article 6 § 1. She claimed the Supreme Court misinterpreted both Portuguese law and the 2011 judgment, depriving her of any effective review of her conviction. The Government objected that the Court lacked jurisdiction because the complaint concerned execution of the 2011 judgment under Article 46, and that Article 6 did not apply to extraordinary review proceedings. The applicant argued that the Supreme Court’s decision was new information and that Article 6 applied.

The Grand Chamber first held that Article 46 did not bar examination. Although the review proceedings related to executing the 2011 judgment, they were new and subsequent, and the Supreme Court had decided a new issue: whether the conviction remained valid in light of the fair-trial violation. The pending supervision by the Committee of Ministers did not preclude review.

On the merits, however, the Grand Chamber held that Article 6 § 1 was not applicable to the Portuguese review proceedings. Reiterating that there is no Convention right to have a terminated case reopened, it found that extraordinary remedies seeking reopening generally do not involve determining a criminal charge. The Supreme Court was not deciding guilt or sentence; it was only assessing whether the statutory conditions for reopening were met. Therefore, Article 6 did not apply, and there was no violation of Article 6 § 1.

In *Moreira Ferreira v. Portugal (No. 2)*, the applicant, Ms Francelina Moreira Ferreira, was convicted in 2007 by the Matosinhos District Court of threatening and insulting conduct after an altercation. A psychiatric report noted limited intellectual and cognitive capacities but concluded she remained criminally responsible. The District Court rejected diminished responsibility, imposed 320 day-fines amounting to €640, and ordered damages. On appeal, she argued she lacked criminal responsibility due to psychiatric disorders and sought a fresh factual assessment and hearing. The Oporto Court of Appeal held a hearing attended by the prosecutor and her counsel, but did not examine her personally. It upheld the conviction while reducing the fine to 265 day-fines, totalling €530. She paid in instalments.

In her first Strasbourg application (no. 19808/08), she complained under Article 6 § 1 that she had not been heard in person by the appellate court. In 2011 the European Court of Human Rights found a violation. It held that the Court of Appeal should have held a public hearing and directly assessed her testimony on diminished responsibility. The Court awarded €2,400 in non-pecuniary damages, rejected pecuniary damage, and noted that reopening under Article 449 of the Portuguese Code of Criminal Procedure could be an appropriate remedy.

In October 2011, relying on Article 449 § 1(g) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the applicant applied to the Supreme Court for review, arguing that her conviction was irreconcilable with the 2011 Strasbourg judgment. The prosecution supported review, citing doubts about conviction and sentence. In March 2012 the Supreme Court refused. It held that review applied to judgments or convictions, not procedural irregularities; that the conviction was not incompatible with the Strasbourg judgment; that the lack of a hearing was a procedural defect; and that since the Court could not speculate on the outcome, no serious doubt attached to the conviction. The Court had compensated a procedural defect, not an unfair conviction.

The applicant then lodged a new application (no. 19867/12), relying on Articles 6 and 46. She alleged a denial of justice: the Supreme Court had misinterpreted the Code of Criminal Procedure and the 2011 judgment, depriving her of any review of her conviction. The Government objected that the Court lacked jurisdiction under Article 46, that no new facts existed, and that Article 6 did not apply to extraordinary review proceedings.

The Grand Chamber found that Article 46 did not preclude examination because the Supreme Court proceedings were new and raised a new issue: the validity of the conviction in light of the earlier violation. It then examined whether Article 6 § 1 applied to the review proceedings. It reiterated that the Convention does not guarantee a right to reopen terminated cases and that extraordinary remedies normally fall outside Article 6, unless they involve a full reconsideration or are akin to ordinary appeals, or the domestic court must determine the criminal charge. The key question was whether the Portuguese Supreme Court, in deciding the Article 449 § 1(g) review, was required to determine the criminal charge. The Grand Chamber ultimately held that Article 6 was not applicable to such review proceedings, and the applicant’s complaint was therefore inadmissible *ratione materiae*. The case clarified the limits of Article 6 in criminal review or reopening procedures following an ECtHR finding of a violation.

In **Mives DOO v. Serbia** (Application no. 48966/09), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint by Mives DOO, a Serbian limited liability company, that Serbian authorities had failed to enforce final domestic judgments in its favour and that it lacked an effective remedy. The applicant relied on Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time), Article 13 (right to an effective remedy), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property).

The underlying facts concerned a failed aircraft purchase. On 24 April 1997 and 3 September 1998, the Pančevo Commercial Court ordered DD Lola Utva Vazduhoplovna industrija, a socially-owned company based in Pančevo, to pay Mives DOO specified damages for an airplane that the applicant had bought but never received, plus the costs of the civil proceedings. These judgments became final on 4 June 1998 and 25 September 1998. On 5 June 2002, at the applicant’s request, the Pančevo Commercial Court ordered enforcement of the judgments and required the debtor to pay the enforcement costs.

Enforcement later stalled. On 11 February 2008, the Commercial Court noted that on 29 January 2008 the Privatisation Agency had ordered the restructuring of the debtor and stayed the enforcement proceedings until that process concluded. Information from the Serbian Business Registers Agency showed that the debtor remained an active company predominantly composed of State-owned capital. This state involvement was central to the case.

The Government objected to the application, arguing that the debtor was legally and financially independent from the State and that the restructuring could not be attributed to Serbia. It therefore contended that the State could not be held liable for the company’s debt, although it did not exclude possible liability for the length of the enforcement proceedings. The applicant maintained its complaints.

The Court rejected the Government’s objection. It recalled its established case-law that the State is liable for honouring the debts of socially-owned or State-owned companies established by final domestic court judgments. Since the debtor was predominantly State-owned and the judgments remained final, the Court saw no reason to depart from that jurisprudence. It declared the complaints admissible.

On the merits, the Court noted that the domestic judgments in the applicant’s favour had remained unenforced. It had repeatedly found violations of Article 6 § 1 and/or Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 in similar cases against Serbia involving non-enforcement of final judgments against socially/State-owned companies. The Government had not presented any convincing argument to justify a different outcome. The Court therefore found violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Having reached that conclusion, it did not consider it necessary to examine the essentially same complaint under Article 13.

The key violation was Serbia’s failure to enforce final court judgments in favour of the applicant, with responsibility engaged because the debtor was a socially/State-owned company and the restructuring stay did not absolve the State under the Convention.

Mives DOO v. Serbia (application no. 48966/09) is a European Court of Human Rights case decided on 10 January 2017 by a Committee of the Third Section. The applicant, Mives DOO, was a limited liability company based in Serbia, represented by Mr D. Simić. It lodged the application on 31 August 2009, complaining that Serbia had failed to enforce final domestic court judgments in its favour and that it had no effective remedy.

The key facts concerned unpaid damages for a purchased but undelivered airplane. On 24 April 1997 and 3 September 1998, the Pančevo Commercial Court ordered DD Lola Utva Vazduhoplovna industrija, a socially-owned company based in Pančevo (the debtor), to pay Mives specified amounts in damages, plus the costs of the civil proceedings. These judgments became final by 4 June 1998 and 25 September 1998 respectively. Thus, by the late 1990s, Mives held enforceable final court awards against the debtor.

On 5 June 2002, upon Mives’s request, the Pančevo Commercial Court ordered enforcement of those judgments and further ordered the debtor to pay the enforcement costs. However, the debtor did not pay. On 11 February 2008, the Commercial Court noted that on 29 January 2008 the Privatisation Agency had ordered the restructuring of the debtor and stayed the enforcement proceedings until the conclusion of that process. According to the Serbian Business Registers Agency website, the debtor remained an active company and was predominantly composed of State-owned capital.

Mives alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (fair hearing within a reasonable time), Article 13 (effective remedy), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions). The core alleged violation was the respondent State’s failure to enforce final court judgments rendered in the applicant’s favour, and the absence of an effective domestic remedy for that failure.

The Government objected. It argued that the debtor was legally and financially independent from the State, and that the debtor’s restructuring could not be attributed to the State. It therefore concluded that Serbia could not be held liable for the company’s debt. The Government did not exclude possible liability for the length of the enforcement proceedings, but maintained that the State was not responsible for the unpaid judgment debt itself. The Court rejected this objection, relying on its established case-law that the State is liable for honouring debts of socially-owned or State-owned companies where final domestic court judgments have established those debts. The application was declared admissible.

On the merits, the Court noted that the domestic judgments remained unenforced to date. It found that the Government had not put forward any fact or convincing argument to distinguish the case from its prior jurisprudence, in which similar failures had repeatedly led to findings of violations of Article 6 § 1 and/or Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court therefore found violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Having reached that conclusion, it did not examine the essentially same complaint under Article 13 separately.

The case *Mives DOO v. Serbia* (Application no. 48966/09, ECtHR Third Section, judgment of 10 January 2017) concerned an application lodged by Mives DOO, a Serbian limited liability company, against Serbia. The applicant complained that final domestic court judgments in its favour had not been enforced and that there was no effective domestic remedy for that failure.

The underlying facts concerned an aircraft purchase. Mives DOO had bought an airplane from DD Lola Utva Vazduhoplovna industrija, a socially-owned company based in Pančevo (“the debtor”), but the airplane was never delivered. On 24 April 1997 and 3 September 1998, the Pančevo Commercial Court ordered the debtor to pay Mives DOO specified amounts as damages for the undelivered airplane, plus the costs of the civil proceedings. These judgments became final by 4 June 1998 and 25 September 1998 respectively. On 5 June 2002, at the applicant’s request, the Pančevo Commercial Court ordered enforcement of the judgments and further ordered the debtor to pay the enforcement costs.

Enforcement was subsequently halted. On 11 February 2008 the Commercial Court noted that, on 29 January 2008, the Privatisation Agency had ordered the debtor’s restructuring and had stayed the enforcement proceedings until that process concluded. According to information from the Serbian Business Registers Agency, the debtor remained an active company predominantly composed of State-owned capital.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Mives DOO alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, Article 13 of the Convention, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Its central complaint was that the respondent State had failed to enforce final court judgments rendered in its favour and had failed to provide an effective remedy in that connection.

The Government objected to admissibility. It argued that the debtor was legally and financially independent from the State and that the debtor’s restructuring could not be attributed to the State. It therefore concluded that Serbia could not be held liable for the debtor’s obligations. The Government did not, however, exclude possible liability for the length of the enforcement proceedings. The applicant reaffirmed its complaints.

The Court rejected the Government’s objection. It recalled its established case law in comparable cases against Serbia that the State is liable for honouring the debts of socially-owned or State-owned companies established by final domestic court judgments. It saw no reason to depart from that jurisprudence. The complaints were neither manifestly ill-founded nor inadmissible on other grounds, and were declared admissible.

On the merits, the Court noted that the domestic judgments at issue had remained unenforced to date. It observed that it had frequently found violations of Article 6 of the Convention and/or Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 in cases raising similar issues. The Government had not put forward any fact or convincing argument capable of persuading the Court to reach a different conclusion. The Court therefore found violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Having reached that conclusion, it did not find it necessary to examine the essentially same complaint under Article 13.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore the final and enforceable domestic judgments in the applicant’s favour, the prolonged non-enforcement, the restructuring order that stayed enforcement, and the debtor’s status as a predominantly State-owned company.

In *Zdjelar and Others v. Croatia* (Application no. 80960/12, judgment 6 July 2017), nine Croatian nationals, all children of Milan Zdjelar, complained about their father’s killing and the failure of Croatian authorities to investigate it. Milan, an ethnic Serb, lived in Crni Potok, in the so-called Krajina. During Croatia’s Operation Storm (4–7 August 1995), most of the Krajina population fled. Milan remained with his daughter Dragica. On 8 August 1995, Dragica stated, they were outside their house when a military vehicle stopped. Three soldiers in camouflage approached; Milan ran, and she heard shots. She saw him shot in the chest and leg; he died soon afterwards. She alleged the soldiers were from the Croatian Army’s “Tigers” brigade. She hid for two days, then reported the matter; Croatian soldiers later buried her father.

The authorities learned of the killing in October 2001, when a list of persons killed during and after Operation Storm identified Milan as having been shot by “Tigers” brigade members. Police photographed the grave and interviewed Dragica. In 2002 the body was exhumed and a post-mortem was performed, but the cause of death was not established; the only noted injury was a broken collarbone. In 2004 Dragica repeated her eyewitness account. In 2005 the applicants and their mother filed a criminal complaint, alleging a war crime against a civilian and stressing that Milan was Serbian, unarmed, and not involved in military activity.

The investigation involved repeated police and State Attorney inquiries, interviews with neighbours and former Croatian soldiers, and requests to the Ministry of Defence. No perpetrator was identified. In 2012, witness Ž.L. alleged that members of his unit had killed civilians in Crni Potok with the acquiescence and participation of commanders, naming some officers. Police pursued those leads, but Ž.L. later refused to testify, citing health, time, and claiming he had not witnessed the crimes. In 2015 the investigation was transferred to the Osijek County State Attorney’s Office and remained active. Separately, in 2004 the applicants sued the State for compensation; the claim was dismissed as time-barred, a result upheld up to the Constitutional Court in 2012.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged substantive and procedural violations of Article 2, discrimination under Article 14, and lack of an effective remedy under Article 13. The Government argued non-exhaustion and failure to comply with the six-month time-limit.

The Court held that it lacked temporal jurisdiction over the substantive Article 2 complaint because the killing occurred before Croatia ratified the Convention on 5 November 1997. It rejected the Government’s exhaustion objection and found the procedural Article 2 complaint admissible. On the six-month rule, although the application was lodged in 2012, the investigation was still ongoing; there were no significant delays, and new evidence from Ž.L. in 2012 and later witness interviews meant the applicants could reasonably believe an effective investigation was continuing.

On the merits, the Court assessed the investigation as one of means, not results. Authorities had taken statements, interviewed traceable witnesses, pursued concrete leads, and sought military records. The absence of a prosecution did not itself render the investigation ineffective, especially given the post-war context and large number of war-crimes cases. The Court therefore found no violation of the procedural aspect of Article 2. The substantive killing complaint was inadmissible *ratione temporis*.

In **Zdjelar and Others v. Croatia** (no. 80960/12, 6 July 2017), nine Croatian nationals, the children of Milan Zdjelar, alleged that Croatia failed its procedural obligations under Articles 2 and 14 of the European Convention and provided no effective remedy under Article 13. The Court examined the complaints under Article 2 alone.

The case concerned the killing of Milan Zdjelar, a Serbian civilian, on 8 August 1995 in Crni Potok, shortly after Croatia’s Operation Storm. Milan had remained in the village with his daughter Dragica. Dragica later said that a military vehicle stopped near their house and three soldiers in camouflage uniforms, later described as members of the Croatian Army’s “Tigers” brigade, got out. Milan ran toward the woods. Dragica heard shots and saw her father struck in the chest and leg; he died soon afterwards. Croatian Army soldiers later buried him. Dragica hid for two days.

In October 2001, the State Attorney’s Office received a list naming Milan Zdjelar as having been shot by members of the “Tigers” brigade. Police photographed the grave and interviewed Dragica in 2001 and 2004. The body was exhumed in 2002, but an autopsy did not establish the cause of death and noted only a broken collarbone. In 2005, the family filed a criminal complaint alleging a war crime against a civilian, stressing that Milan was Serbian, unarmed, and not involved in military activity. The case was referred to the Sisak County State Attorney. From 2005 to 2008, police repeatedly reported no progress. In 2009, Dragica testified before an investigating judge; neighbours and former Croatian soldiers were interviewed. The Ministry of Defence provided information about brigade 153 and possible members, but several soldiers denied knowledge of the killing.

In 2012, a witness, Ž.L., alleged that members of the Third Battalion of the First Brigade had killed civilians in Crni Potok with the acquiescence and participation of commanders. He described a captured civilian called a “četnik,” shots heard, and an elderly man found shot in the back and head; a logistics officer allegedly said he shot him to “shorten his pain.” Police interviewed Ž.L., but he later refused to testify, citing health, the passage of time, and stating that his earlier allegations were unfounded. The investigation was transferred to the Osijek County State Attorney’s Office in 2015, and further inquiries occurred in 2016–17. The family’s civil compensation claim was dismissed as time-barred.

The Court held that it lacked temporal jurisdiction over the substantive Article 2 complaint because Milan died before Croatia ratified the Convention on 5 November 1997. The procedural complaint was admissible: domestic remedies were not effective, and the six-month rule did not bar it because the investigation remained active and new evidence had emerged. On the merits, however, the Court found no violation of the procedural aspect of Article 2. The authorities learned of the killing in 2001 and promptly investigated; they exhumed and autopsied the body, interviewed traceable witnesses, and pursued leads. Article 2 requires an effective investigation by means, not a successful result. The absence of a prosecution did not establish ineffectiveness, especially given the post-war situation, the large number of war-crimes cases, and the need for sufficient evidence. No significant omissions, bad faith, or lack of will were shown.

In **Zdjelar and Others v. Croatia** (App. no. 80960/12, judgment 6 July 2017), nine Croatian nationals, all children of Milan Zdjelar, complained about the killing of their father and the alleged failure of the Croatian authorities to investigate it effectively. Milan Zdjelar, a Serbian civilian, lived in Crni Potok, a village in the so-called Krajina. During Croatia’s Operation Storm (4–7 August 1995), Croatian forces retook the territory. On 8 August 1995, Milan was allegedly shot in the head and leg by members of the Croatian Army’s “Tigers” brigade. His daughter Dragica, one of the applicants, witnessed the killing: she stated that a military vehicle stopped near their house, three soldiers in camouflage approached, her father ran, she heard shots, and saw him shot in the chest and leg before dying. Soldiers later buried him.

The authorities learned of the killing in October 2001, when a person named S.K. submitted a list of persons killed during and after Operation Storm. The list named Milan and stated he had been shot by the “Tigers.” Police photographed the grave, interviewed Dragica in 2001 and 2004, and exhumed the body in 2002. The autopsy failed to establish the cause of death and noted only a broken collarbone. In 2005 the applicants and their mother filed a criminal complaint alleging a war crime against a civilian, emphasizing Milan’s Serbian ethnicity and that he was unarmed. The investigation continued slowly. Dragica repeated her evidence before an investigating judge in 2009. Former Croatian soldiers from the “Tigers” and other units were interviewed, mostly denying knowledge. In 2012, witness Ž.L. alleged that civilians in Crni Potok had been killed by the Third Battalion of the First Brigade with the acquiescence or participation of commanders, naming individuals. The authorities pursued these leads, but some potential witnesses had died or denied involvement. The investigation was transferred to the Osijek County State Attorney’s Office in 2015 and remained active. A civil compensation claim was dismissed as time-barred.

The applicants alleged violations of Articles 2, 13, and 14 of the Convention, claiming the State failed to conduct an effective investigation into the death and possible ethnic motive, and that no effective remedy existed. The Court examined the complaint under Article 2 alone. It found it had no temporal jurisdiction over the substantive Article 2 complaint because the death occurred before Croatia ratified the Convention on 5 November 1997. However, the procedural complaint was admissible. The Government’s objections on non-exhaustion and the six-month time-limit were rejected: although the application was lodged in 2012, the investigation was ongoing, significant steps had been taken in 2009–2014, and new evidence emerged in 2012.

On the merits, the Court found **no violation of the procedural aspect of Article 2**. It stressed that the obligation to investigate is one of means, not results. The authorities had promptly opened an enquiry in 2001, exhumed the body, conducted an autopsy, interviewed eyewitnesses and soldiers, pursued Ž.L.’s leads, and sought military records. No concrete lines of inquiry were ignored. The failure to identify or prosecute perpetrators did not itself render the investigation ineffective. The Court also considered Croatia’s post-war difficulties and the large number of war-crime cases. Thus, despite frustration over the lack of prosecutions, the investigation met the minimum standard.

In *Ilias and Ahmed v. Hungary*, two Bangladeshi nationals entered the Röszke transit zone on the Hungary-Serbia border on 15 September 2015 and applied for asylum. They had travelled through Greece, the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia and Serbia; Mr Ilias spent about 20 hours in Serbia, while Mr Ahmed spent about two days there. Once in the transit zone, they could not leave in the direction of Hungary. They alleged that they were effectively detained in a fenced area of about 110 square metres, guarded by officers, with a room of about 9 square metres containing five beds. They claimed no access to legal, social or medical assistance, television, internet, landline telephone or recreation, and that the conditions were unsuitable for a prolonged stay, especially given their psychological vulnerability. Hungary disputed this, saying the containers were 15 square metres, with five beds, heating, running water, three daily meals and medical care two hours daily. A CPT report found accommodation and healthcare generally satisfactory but questioned whether border asylum procedures had adequate safeguards against refoulement.

On the same day, the asylum authority interviewed the applicants. Both were illiterate. The first applicant was mistakenly interviewed in Dari, which he did not speak, and received a Dari information leaflet. The second applicant had an Urdu interpreter, but the interview lasted 22 minutes. The same day, the authority rejected their asylum applications as inadmissible, finding Serbia a “safe third country” under Government Decree no. 191/2015, and ordered their expulsion.

The applicants challenged the decisions. UNHCR lawyers were not allowed to enter the transit zone to consult them until after the 21 September 2015 court hearing. At that hearing, the applicants said Serbian documents they had received were in Serbian and unintelligible. The second applicant said he had applied for asylum in Serbia but his application had not been examined. The Szeged Administrative and Labour Court annulled the decisions and remitted the case, requiring the asylum authority to examine Serbia’s asylum system more thoroughly and to give the applicants three days and legal counsel to rebut the safe-third-country presumption.

Later, a psychiatrist diagnosed both applicants with PTSD; the second also had depression. The reports found no urgent treatment need but stated that confinement could worsen their mental state. In the resumed proceedings, the applicants’ lawyers allegedly received short notice and were absent; the applicants made no statement. On 30 September 2015, the asylum authority again rejected the applications. It found the psychiatric reports insufficient to show special treatment needs unmet in the transit zone and that the applicants had not rebutted Serbia’s safety with specific individual facts. On 5 October 2015, the court upheld that decision, finding Serbia generally safe, the applicants’ statements contradictory and incoherent, and the procedure lawful. The final decision was served on 8 October 2015, and the applicants were escorted to the Serbian border and left the transit zone.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged violations of Articles 3, 5 §§ 1 and 4, and 13 of the Convention. The key alleged violations were: (1) expulsion to Serbia exposed them to a real risk of inhuman or degrading treatment and chain-refoulement because the safe-third-country finding lacked a thorough, individualised assessment; (2) their protracted confinement in the transit zone, given their vulnerable status and conditions, amounted to inhuman treatment under Article 3; and (3) their deprivation of liberty was unlawful and lacked appropriate judicial review under Article 5. They also alleged the absence of an effective remedy under Article 13.

In *Ilias and Ahmed v. Hungary*, two Bangladeshi nationals arrived at the Röszke transit zone on the Hungary-Serbia border on 15 September 2015 and immediately applied for asylum. They had travelled through Pakistan, Iran, Turkey, Greece, the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, and Serbia, spending only about 20 hours and two days respectively in Serbia. Once in the transit zone, they were not allowed to leave in the direction of Hungary. They alleged they were effectively locked in a fenced, guarded area of about 110 square metres, with no access to legal, social or medical assistance, television, internet, telephone or recreation, and that they slept in a room of about 9 square metres with five beds. The Government disputed these conditions, describing containers of about 15 square metres, regular meals, running water and daily medical care. A CPT report described broadly satisfactory material conditions but expressed doubts about whether border asylum procedures provided effective safeguards against refoulement. A psychiatrist later diagnosed both applicants with PTSD and signs of anxiety, depression and despair, and considered their mental state liable to deteriorate because of confinement.

On the same day as their applications, the asylum authority rejected them as inadmissible, finding Serbia a “safe third country” under Government Decree no. 191/2015, and ordered their expulsion. The applicants were illiterate and Urdu-speaking. The first applicant was mistakenly interviewed with a Dari interpreter and given a Dari information leaflet; the second had a short Urdu-assisted interview. The Szeged Administrative and Labour Court initially annulled the decisions on 21 September 2015, holding that the authority had not sufficiently examined Serbia’s safety, had not informed the applicants of its conclusions, and had not allowed three days to rebut the safe-third-country presumption with legal counsel. Their lawyers were not allowed into the transit zone until after that hearing.

On remittal, the asylum authority held a hearing without the applicants’ representatives; the applicants declined to make statements. The authority again rejected the applications on 30 September 2015, finding the psychiatric reports insufficient to show “special treatment” needs and that the applicants had not rebutted Serbia’s safety in their individual cases. On 5 October 2015, the Szeged court upheld that decision, relying on country information and criticising the applicants’ allegedly contradictory statements. The applicants were expelled to Serbia on 8 October 2015.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged violations of Articles 3, 5 and 13 of the Convention. Under Article 3, they claimed that expulsion to Serbia exposed them to a real risk of inhuman and degrading treatment through chain-refoulement, and that their protracted confinement in the transit zone, given their vulnerable mental state and inadequate conditions, itself amounted to inhuman treatment. Under Article 5 §§ 1 and 4, they argued that their deprivation of liberty in the transit zone was unlawful and lacked appropriate judicial review. Under Article 13, they alleged the absence of an effective remedy to challenge the safe-third-country determination and the resulting risk of refoulement. They sought interim measures under Rule 39 to be released and to halt expulsion; these were refused, though the application was prioritised. The case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 21 November 2019.

In *Ilias and Ahmed v. Hungary* (Application no. 47287/15), two Bangladeshi nationals, Mr Md Ilias Ilias and Mr Ali Ahmed, complained about their treatment after arriving at the Röszke transit zone on the Hungary–Serbia border on 15 September 2015. They were illiterate Urdu speakers who had travelled through Pakistan, Iran, Turkey, Greece, Macedonia and Serbia. They applied for asylum immediately upon arrival in the transit zone.

The applicants were kept in the transit zone on Hungarian territory but were not allowed to leave toward Hungary. They described being confined in a fenced, guarded area of about 110 square metres, sleeping in a roughly 9-square-metre room with five beds. They alleged lack of access to legal, social or medical assistance and no telephone, internet, television or recreational facilities. The Government disputed some details, stating that containers measured about 15 square metres, with five beds, electric heating, three meals daily and medical care available for two hours daily. The CPT found the accommodation clean, with natural light, satisfactory sanitation and generally good health care. A psychiatrist later diagnosed both applicants with PTSD and depression and warned that their mental state could deteriorate because of the confinement.

The asylum authority interviewed them immediately. The first applicant was mistakenly interviewed with a Dari interpreter, which he did not understand, and received a Dari information leaflet. The second applicant had an Urdu interpreter. On the same day, 15 September 2015, the asylum authority rejected both applications as inadmissible, finding Serbia a “safe third country” under Government Decree no. 191/2015, and ordered their expulsion. The applicants alleged this was done without a thorough, individualised assessment of whether Serbia was safe for them and without proper consideration of the risk of chain-refoulement.

On judicial review, the Szeged Administrative and Labour Court annulled the decisions on 21 September 2015. It held that the asylum authority needed to examine Serbia’s actual asylum situation more thoroughly and give the applicants three days to rebut the safe-third-country presumption with legal assistance. On remand, a hearing was held, but the applicants’ lawyers were not present; the applicants declined to make statements. On 30 September 2015 the authority again rejected the applications, finding no special treatment needs and no sufficient individual rebuttal. The court upheld that decision on 5 October 2015, finding Serbia generally safe and the applicants’ statements vague and contradictory. The final decision was served on 8 October 2015; they were escorted to the Serbian border and left the transit zone for Serbia without physical coercion.

The applicants relied on Articles 3, 5 and 13 of the Convention. Under Article 3, they alleged that expulsion to Serbia exposed them to a real risk of inhuman or degrading treatment and chain-refoulement, and that the transit-zone conditions and prolonged confinement, given their vulnerable status, amounted to inhuman treatment. Under Article 5 §§ 1 and 4, they alleged unlawful deprivation of liberty without adequate judicial review. Under Article 13, they alleged the absence of an effective remedy against the safe-third-country finding and the associated refoulement risk. They sought interim measures to halt expulsion and secure release; these were not indicated, though the application was given priority and notice was sent to the Government. UNHCR and ECRE reports questioned Serbia’s safety as an asylum country, citing systemic deficiencies, possible readmission penalties and lack of safeguards. The Chamber judgment was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 21 November 2019.
