**Case: Alković v. Montenegro (Application no. 66895/10), ECtHR, 5 December 2017**

The applicant, Rizo Alković, a Montenegrin Roma and Muslim, lived with his family in Podgorica in an apartment for socially disadvantaged families. He alleged that between 26 May and 22 September 2009 the authorities failed to effectively investigate a series of ethnically and/or religiously motivated attacks and threats by neighbours, invoking Articles 8, 14, 9 and 13 of the Convention.

The key incidents began on 26 May 2009. While the applicant overheard his neighbour Y watching a kickboxing match involving a Bosnian Muslim contestant, Y allegedly said he would slaughter one of them. Another neighbour, X, allegedly fetched a gun. Y then said “turn it to the left,” toward the applicant’s terrace, and nine or ten shots were fired, followed by insults referring to the applicant’s “Turkish mother.” X, Y and Y’s family later collected the spent cartridges.

On 9 September 2009, the applicant overheard neighbours V, S and B discussing “cockroaches, frogs, nits and lice” brought by “those dirty gipsies.” V mentioned using a hammer, pruning knife and axe; S said “he is a Muslim, I have a sword”; B said whatever was available; V referred to an axe or sledgehammer “like the one used on pigs.”

On 15 September 2009, during an argument, X allegedly said that if he “saw red” he would kill M and his brother “like a dog,” adding “dirty gypsy” and “trash,” while pointing at the applicant’s apartment. M and D confirmed this.

On 22 September 2009, Ramadan Bayram, a large cross was drawn on the applicant’s door and a message written beside it: “move out or you’ll bitterly regret it.” The applicant called the police, who photographed the scene, and lodged a criminal complaint against several neighbours.

In October 2009 police interviewed neighbours. Most denied the allegations. X and Y admitted hearing shots but denied knowing who fired; Y claimed the children collected cartridges because they were interesting to play with. V claimed the 9 September discussion concerned another person sought by police and self-defence. M and D confirmed X’s threat. The prosecutor concluded that the 26 May and 9 September remarks were not directed at the applicant and that the 15 September incident was not a threat. The 22 September incident could amount to jeopardising security, so police were asked to find the perpetrator; prosecution would become time-barred by 22 September 2012.

The applicant’s attempts to pursue the case failed. The Higher State Prosecutor rejected his hate-crime complaint. The High Court dismissed his request for an investigation for lack of evidence, treating his video as inadmissible because it was obtained without a court order and faulting him for not providing evidence or calling police regarding 22 September. Appeals and a constitutional appeal were dismissed. Only in 2016 did police state that measures had been taken but no perpetrator found.

Other context included ongoing neighbour conflicts, prior convictions of the applicant, complaints against him, and later threats against his daughter in July 2010, after which the family moved out.

The Court found the legal framework sufficient in principle, but its implementation defective. The prosecutor ignored the 26 May shooting: no ballistics, gun check or motive inquiry. For 22 September, authorities did little beyond photographs; prosecution became time-barred, and courts blamed the applicant rather than assessing police inaction. Cumulatively, the shooting and threat remained virtually without legal consequences, denying protection of his psychological integrity. Especially given his Roma/Muslim identity and the repeated incidents, the Court found a violation of Article 8 in conjunction with Article 14. The linked Articles 9 and 13 complaints were admissible.

Alković v. Montenegro (ECtHR, Second Section, 5 December 2017) concerned Rizo Alković, a Montenegrin Roma Muslim living in Podgorica. He alleged that the authorities failed to effectively investigate a series of ethnically and/or religiously motivated attacks and threats by neighbours between 26 May and 22 September 2009, violating Articles 8 and 14, and also Articles 9 and 13.

Key incidents: On 26 May 2009, while neighbour Y watched a Montenegro–Bosnia kickboxing match, the applicant overheard Y and X make hostile remarks about the Bosnian Muslim/Turkish contestant. X allegedly fetched a gun, Y said “turn it to the left” toward the applicant’s terrace, and nine or ten shots were fired. Y then shouted insults about the applicant’s “Turkish mother.” X, Y and Y’s family picked up spent cartridges afterwards. The applicant had earlier installed a camera because of attacks on his car and apartment.

On 9 September 2009, the applicant overheard neighbours V, S and B discussing fighting “cockroaches, frogs, nits and lice” brought by “those dirty gipsies.” They referred to using a hammer, pruning knife, axe, sword and sledgehammer “like the one used on pigs”; S said “he is a Muslim, I have a sword.”

On 15 September 2009, during an argument, X allegedly said he would “kill both you and your brother here like a dog,” pointed toward the applicant’s apartment, and called him “dirty gypsy” and “trash.” This was witnessed by D, though it was unclear whether the applicant was present.

On 22 September 2009, Ramadan Bayram, a large cross was drawn on the applicant’s door and a message written: “move out or you’ll bitterly regret it.” Police came and photographed the scene; the applicant lodged a criminal complaint.

In the investigation, police interviewed neighbours in October 2009. Suspects denied the allegations. The prosecutor concluded that the 26 May and 9 September remarks were not aimed at the applicant, and that the 15 September incident was not a threat. The 22 September incident could amount to jeopardising security. The prosecutor asked police to find the perpetrator and noted prosecution would become time-barred on 22 September 2012. A hate-crime complaint was rejected. In March 2010 the High Court dismissed the applicant’s request for an investigation for lack of evidence; video evidence was inadmissible because it had been obtained without a court order, and the court faulted the applicant for not providing evidence or calling police to collect evidence regarding 22 September. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal in May 2010, saying police evidence-gathering was not for it to assess. The Constitutional Court dismissed his appeal in 2014. In 2016 police said measures had been taken but no material evidence found.

The ECtHR found the domestic legal framework sufficient but its implementation defective. The prosecutor omitted the 26 May shooting from his conclusion: no ballistics, no check whether X had a gun, and no motive inquiry. For 22 September, despite the time-bar warning, the investigation remained ineffective; courts blamed the applicant for police inaction, and police only reported measures in 2016. Cumulatively, the shooting and threat remained virtually without legal consequences. Given the applicant’s Roma and Muslim identity and repeated incidents, authorities failed to investigate possible racist motives. Although the neighbour conflict was mutual and the applicant contributed, this did not justify the insufficient response. The Court found a violation of Article 8 in conjunction with Article 14. The Articles 9 and 13 complaints were linked and declared admissible.

Case: **Alković v. Montenegro** (App. no. 66895/10), European Court of Human Rights, judgment of 5 December 2017. The applicant, Rizo Alković, was a Montenegrin Roma and Muslim living in Podgorica. He alleged that the authorities failed to effectively investigate a series of ethnically and religiously motivated attacks by private individuals between 26 May and 22 September 2009. He complained mainly under Articles 8 and 14, and also Articles 9 and 13.

The key incidents were as follows. On **26 May 2009**, the applicant overheard his next-door neighbour, Y, watching a kickboxing match with X. Anti-Muslim and anti-Turkish remarks were made. X allegedly fetched a gun, and Y said “turn it to the left,” toward the applicant’s terrace. Nine or ten shots were fired, after which Y shouted insults about the applicant’s “Turkish mother.” X, Y and Y’s family later collected the spent cartridges. On **9 September 2009**, neighbours V, S and B discussed on an adjacent terrace fighting “cockroaches, frogs, nits and lice” brought by “dirty gipsies.” They referred to using a hammer, pruning knife, axe and swords. S said “he is a Muslim, I have a sword,” and V mentioned an axe or sledgehammer “like the one used on pigs.” On **15 September 2009**, during an argument with M, X allegedly said that if he “saw red” he would “kill both you and your brother here like a dog,” pointing at the applicant’s flat, and called him a “dirty gypsy” and “trash.” M and D confirmed this. On **22 September 2009**, Ramadan Bayram, a cross was drawn on the applicant’s door and a message written: “move out or you’ll bitterly regret it.” The applicant called the police, who photographed the scene, and filed a criminal complaint.

Other reported incidents included a brick through his window in 2008; an attempt to hit his car in September 2009; threats in October 2009; gunshots near his apartment in December 2009; firecrackers damaging his car and a bottle and metal bar thrown at him and his son in January 2010; and in July 2010 X threatened the applicant’s daughter, who fainted and was hospitalised. The family then moved out.

In the domestic proceedings, police interviewed neighbours in October 2009. Suspects denied the allegations. Y said his remarks concerned the Bosnian kickboxer and that the cartridges were collected by children. V claimed the discussion concerned another person; B denied being present. M and D supported the applicant’s account of 15 September. The state prosecutor found that the 26 May and 9 September remarks were not directed at the applicant and that 15 September was not a threat, but considered 22 September capable of “jeopardising security.” Police were asked to find the perpetrator; the complaint was to be kept until 22 September 2012, when prosecution would be time-barred. The applicant’s request for an investigation was dismissed by the High Court for lack of evidence, with video evidence ruled inadmissible; the Court of Appeal upheld. The Constitutional Court dismissed his appeal in 2014. In 2016, police said they had taken measures but found no material evidence.

The ECtHR found the domestic legal framework sufficient, but its implementation defective. It focused on the 26 May shooting and the 22 September threat. The prosecutor omitted the shooting despite confirmed shots and available cartridges; no steps were taken to analyse shells, check for a gun or establish motive. The 22 September investigation was inadequate and became time-barred; courts blamed the applicant and police, while police only reported measures in 2016. Cumulatively, these failures left the incidents virtually without legal consequences, failing to protect the applicant’s psychological integrity, especially as a Roma Muslim facing repeated hostility. The Court found a violation of Article 8 in conjunction with Article 14; the Article 9 and 13 complaints were linked and admissible.
001-174119:
Van Wesenbeeck v. Belgium concerned two applications by a Dutch national, Mr Adrianus van Wesenbeeck, against Belgium. He alleged that his criminal proceedings violated Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention because he had no access to a separate confidential prosecution file and could not examine, or have examined, the undercover agents whose evidence contributed to his conviction.

The facts arose from an investigation into suspected drug trafficking, participation in an international criminal organisation, and money laundering. In May 2006 the Hasselt public prosecutor authorised a proactive investigation, including infiltration; observation was authorised later. Under Belgian law, a separate confidential case file was created for special investigative methods. It contained authorisations, implementation reports, and material whose disclosure could jeopardise the safety and anonymity of undercover agents or reveal police techniques. The defence was not allowed to consult this file throughout the proceedings. A criminal file accessible to the defence contained other reports and evidence. In September 2008 a judicial investigation was opened, and in June 2009 several suspects, including the applicant, were arrested.

Before trial, the Indictments Division of the Antwerp Court of Appeal reviewed the confidential file under Articles 235bis and 235ter of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It consulted the file, heard the Federal Prosecutor separately, then heard the defendants. It ordered certain documents, including confirmations of the observation and infiltration authorisations and a related report, to be added to the criminal file. By judgment of 24 June 2010, it declared the criminal file complete, found no nullity or irregularity, and held that the special investigative methods complied with legal conditions, including proportionality and subsidiarity. The applicant’s appeal to the Court of Cassation was dismissed.

At trial, the applicant was convicted of drug trafficking, membership of an international criminal organisation, and money laundering, and sentenced to ten years’ imprisonment and a fine. He requested a face-to-face meeting with the undercover agents to test their reliability and to verify whether they had incited him to commit offences. The trial court refused. It found questioning unnecessary for the truth or fair trial, stressed the agents’ safety and anonymity, noted a real risk of reprisals after long infiltration and internet exposure, and observed that the defence had not identified specific relevant questions. It also found no evidence of incitement. The Court of Appeal upheld this reasoning, adding that the agents’ statements had only relative evidentiary value and that guilt was established by other evidence. The Court of Cassation also dismissed the applicant’s complaints, holding that non-access to the confidential file did not automatically breach Article 6 and that the restriction was counterbalanced by the Indictments Division’s independent review. It further held that the right to question witnesses is not absolute and that domestic courts may assess whether hearing a witness is necessary.

The key alleged violations were therefore: (1) denial of access to the confidential file, preventing the applicant from checking whether observation and infiltration complied with subsidiarity, proportionality, and the prohibition on incitement; and (2) refusal to allow him to question the undercover agents. The European Court of Human Rights ultimately found no violation, considering the confidential-file system justified and sufficiently counterbalanced by the Indictments Division’s review, and the refusal to question the agents compatible with Article 6 in the circumstances.

**Summary of the Case of Van Wesenbeeck v. Belgium**

The case of *Van Wesenbeeck v. Belgium* concerns a Dutch national, Mr. Adrianus van Wesenbeeck, who was convicted in Belgium for drug trafficking, involvement in a criminal organisation, and money laundering. Following his conviction, he lodged applications with the European Court of Human Rights, alleging violations of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (d) of the Convention, which guarantee the right to a fair trial and the right to examine witnesses. The central issue was whether the use of evidence from a separate, confidential case file and the refusal to allow him to question undercover agents compromised the fairness of his trial.

The investigation began in May 2006 when the Hasselt public prosecutor authorised a proactive investigation, which included the use of undercover agents and observation. A key feature of the Belgian legal procedure was the establishment of a confidential file, kept by the prosecution, which contained authorisations and reports on these special investigative methods. This file was not accessible to the defence to protect the anonymity and safety of the undercover agents and to keep police methods secret. A parallel, "open" criminal file was maintained for the defence and the courts.

The applicant's trial was largely based on evidence gathered by these undercover agents. During the judicial investigation and subsequent trial proceedings, the applicant repeatedly requested a face-to-face meeting with the undercover agents to challenge the reliability of their statements and to verify whether they had incited him to commit crimes. The trial court dismissed this request, reasoning that it was unnecessary for establishing the truth, that the agents' safety and anonymity required protection, and that the applicant had failed to specify what questions he wanted to ask. The court also noted that the core of the agents' evidence was corroborated by other objective evidence, such as seized items and intercepted communications.

The applicant's appeals to the Court of Appeal and the Court of Cassation were unsuccessful. The Court of Cassation ruled that the restriction on the defence rights, while significant, was justified by the need to protect police techniques and the safety of agents. It found this restriction was counterbalanced by a mandatory review conducted by the Indictments Division, an independent court that verified the lawfulness of the investigative methods and ensured the non-confidential criminal file corresponded to the confidential one.

Before the European Court, the applicant argued that his defence rights were violated. He claimed he could not challenge the lawfulness of the investigation or the agents' conduct without access to the confidential file, and that the inability to question his accusers was a critical flaw in the proceedings. The Belgian Government countered that the procedures, particularly the judicial review by the Indictments Division, provided adequate safeguards.

The European Court examined the two main complaints: non-access to the confidential file and the inability to question the undercover agents. It assessed whether the proceedings as a whole were fair, balancing the rights of the defence with the public interest in prosecuting serious crime. The Court's judgment ultimately focused on whether the procedures followed by the Belgian judicial authorities sufficiently counterbalanced the restrictions placed on the applicant's defence rights.

**Summary of Van Wesenbeeck v. Belgium (Applications nos. 67496/10 and 52936/12)**

The case of *Van Wesenbeeck v. Belgium* concerns an application lodged against the Kingdom of Belgium by Mr. Adrianus van Wesenbeeck, a Dutch national, alleging violations of his right to a fair trial under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant was convicted in 2011 for drug trafficking, involvement in an international criminal organisation, and money laundering, and was sentenced to ten years' imprisonment and a substantial fine.

The core of the applicant's complaints stems from the investigative methods used and the subsequent legal proceedings. In 2006, the Hasselt public prosecutor authorized a proactive investigation into the applicant and other suspects, employing special investigative methods including infiltration and observation by undercover agents. A crucial element was the establishment of a separate and confidential case file, pursuant to Belgian law, to protect the anonymity and safety of the undercover agents and the secrecy of police techniques. This confidential file was not accessible to the defence at any stage.

The applicant's alleged violations are twofold. First, he complained that the non-disclosure of the confidential file violated his defence rights. He argued that without access to this file, he could not verify whether the special investigative measures were implemented lawfully, particularly concerning the principles of subsidiarity and proportionality, nor could he ascertain if the undercover agents had incited him to commit the crimes.

Second, he complained about his inability to question the undercover agents. Despite repeated requests for a face-to-face meeting to challenge the reliability of the agents' statements and to probe potential incitement, his requests were denied by the domestic courts. The trial court justified this refusal by citing the agents' safety and the need for anonymity, the lack of specific questions from the defence, and its own assessment that questioning was unnecessary given other corroborating evidence.

The Belgian judicial system provided a safeguard: the Indictments Division of the Antwerp Court of Appeal was tasked with reviewing the confidential file. It verified that the non-confidential criminal file was complete and corresponded to the confidential one, adding some documents but ultimately confirming the lawfulness of the investigative methods. The Court of Cassation later upheld the decisions, stating that while the restriction on defence rights was exceptional, it was counterbalanced by the review conducted by the independent Indictments Division.

In essence, the case centers on the tension between the state's interest in using covert methods to combat serious organised crime and the accused's right to an adversarial trial and to challenge the evidence and witnesses against him. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are the existence and use of a confidential police file inaccessible to the defence, and the domestic courts' refusal to allow the applicant to question the anonymous undercover agents whose testimonies contributed to his conviction.
001-171486:
In *Bayramli v. Azerbaijan*, the applicant, Gozal Oruj gizi Bayramli, an Azerbaijani national and deputy chairperson of the opposition Popular Front Party of Azerbaijan, complained about her arrest and administrative prosecution following two opposition demonstrations in Baku. The European Court of Human Rights communicated complaints under Article 3 (in the first application only) and Articles 5, 6, 10 and 11 (in both applications).

On 17 April 2011, the applicant attended a demonstration organised by the opposition. The organisers had notified the Baku City Executive Authority, but the authority refused the proposed central location and suggested an alternative site on the outskirts of Baku because of heavy traffic. The organisers nevertheless held the demonstration in the city centre. Participants demanded free and fair elections, democratic reforms, and protested against impediments to freedom of assembly. On 26 January 2013, the applicant attended another opposition demonstration. No prior notice had been given to the authorities; information about it was spread through Facebook or the press. Participants condemned the use of force by police against earlier demonstrators. According to the applicant, both demonstrations were peaceful.

Shortly after each demonstration began, police dispersed it and arrested the applicant. During the first arrest, she alleged that several police officers twisted her arms behind her back, held her head down, and forced her to move 20–25 metres to a police car, causing pain in her neck, arms, back and other parts of her body. At the police station she was kept handcuffed. She submitted a photograph allegedly showing her with both arms twisted behind her back and her body bent.

After each arrest, an administrative offence report was issued. In the first case, she was accused under Article 310.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences (CAO) of deliberately failing to comply with a lawful police order. In the second, she was accused under Article 298.1 of the CAO of breaching the rules on organising and holding assemblies as an organiser. She claimed she was never served with copies of the reports or other case documents and was not given access to a lawyer after arrest or in police custody.

In the first case, she was brought before the Nasimi District Court on 18 April 2011, the day after her arrest. In the second, she appeared before the Sabail District Court on 26 January 2013, the day of her arrest. She described both hearings as very brief. In the second case, the public was not allowed inside the courtroom even though no formal closure decision had been taken. She said she was not allowed to hire a lawyer of her choice in either case. State-funded lawyers were appointed, but the hearing records showed they only briefly stated that she was not guilty and/or asked for the case to be discontinued. The courts questioned only the police officers who had arrested her or issued the reports. Those officers testified that she had attempted to stage an unauthorised demonstration and, in the second case, had incited others to participate.

The first-instance courts convicted her. In the first case, she received five days’ administrative detention; in the second, a fine of 2,000 manats. She appealed to the Baku Court of Appeal, arguing that the demonstrations had been peaceful, her arrests unlawful, and the hearings unfair. In the first appeal, she requested a forensic examination of her alleged injuries and asked the court to examine video recordings, question police officers shown in them, and obtain her medical record; the court disregarded these requests. She had a lawyer of her choice in the first appeal but was unrepresented in the second. Both appeals were dismissed.

The applicant also complained to the General Prosecutor’s Office about police ill-treatment. The complaint was forwarded to the Baku City prosecutor’s office, and she was questioned. She said neither she nor her lawyer was informed of any investigative steps. Only in January 2012 did she obtain a copy of an investigator’s decision of 16 June 2011 refusing to open a criminal case. She did not challenge that refusal in court. At the relevant time, domestic law required no prior written notification for spontaneous assemblies, and the CAO provided lesser penalties for the relevant administrative offences than those ultimately imposed.

The case concerns Ms Gozal Oruj gizi Bayramli, an Azerbaijani national and deputy chairperson of the opposition Popular Front Party of Azerbaijan. She lodged two applications with the European Court of Human Rights (nos. 72230/11 and 43061/13) concerning her participation in two opposition demonstrations in Baku and the ensuing administrative arrests, prosecutions and alleged ill-treatment.

She was allegedly kept handcuffed at the police station. She submitted a photograph said to show her restrained by two officers with her arms twisted behind her back.

On the day of each arrest, an administrative offence report was issued. In the first case, she was accused under Article 310.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences (“CAO”) of deliberately failing to comply with a lawful police order. The courts questioned only the police officers who had arrested her or issued reports. They testified that she had attempted to stage an unauthorised demonstration and, in the second case, incited others to participate. 001-174414:
The European Court of Human Rights case *Centre for the Development of Analytical Psychology v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia* (Applications nos. 29545/10 and 32961/10), judgment of 15 June 2017, concerned a Skopje limited liability company owned and managed by psychiatrist Dr Marija Arsovska. In 1995 she established an independent psychiatric practice using Carl Jung’s analytical psychotherapy methods, with an individual tax number beginning 503. In 2004 that practice signed a contract with the State Health Insurance Fund for funding treatment provided to health insurance beneficiaries.

In 2006, after amendments to the Health Protection Act, the Ministry of Health’s inspectorate ordered the practice to re-register as a private health institution. The Ministry then registered a “new practice” at the same address, stating that the original 1995 registration would cease to be valid. The new practice received a different tax number, beginning 403. The inspectorate confirmed compliance, and the Central Registry recorded the new registration. In June 2006 the new practice notified the Fund of the changes. In November 2006 the Fund informed the new practice that it would not sign a new contract after the old one expired. In August 2007 the new practice transformed into the applicant company, retaining the 403 tax number. The link between the new practice and the applicant company was not disputed.

Two sets of domestic proceedings were brought against the Fund for alleged non-compliance with the 2004 contract. One was initiated by the original practice in January 2006; the new practice and later the applicant company continued it. The other was brought by the new practice in July 2006 for payment. In both cases, the Fund objected that the applicant company lacked standing because it was a different legal entity from the 2004 contracting party, relying on the different tax numbers. The domestic courts dismissed the claims solely on that basis. Appeals were rejected. Because the claim values fell below the statutory threshold for an appeal on points of law to the Supreme Court, the merits were never examined.

The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 that the dismissal for lack of standing violated its right of access to a court. It argued that the Fund had implicitly recognised legal continuity by accepting performance and terminating the contract through the new practice. The Government contended that the applicant had failed to prove succession and could have used cession to transfer claims, and that tax numbers ensured legal certainty.

The Court held that the right of access to a court is not absolute, but limitations must not impair its essence and must be proportionate. It noted that the original and new practices had the same owner, address, and activity, differing only by a minor name change and tax number. The Fund had been aware of the changes and had dealt with the new practice. Crucially, in separate proceedings involving the same parties and contract, the Supreme Court found that the applicant had standing because the Fund had terminated the contract by notice to the new practice. The ECtHR therefore found the domestic courts’ approach excessively formalistic, imposing an unjustifiable procedural obstacle and impairing the essence of Article 6 § 1. It found a violation.

The complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 was rejected as not ready for consideration, since the applicant could seek reopening of the domestic proceedings.

The case *Centre for the Development of Analytical Psychology v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia* (Applications nos. 29545/10 and 32961/10) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights on 15 June 2017. The applicant was a Skopje limited liability company owned and managed by Dr Marija Arsovska, a psychiatrist. It complained principally that domestic courts denied it access to a court under Article 6 § 1 by dismissing its contractual claims against the State Health Insurance Fund (“the Fund”) for lack of standing, and also alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In 1995 Dr Arsovska, then Marija Karanfilova, established an independent psychiatric practice using Carl Jung’s analytical psychotherapy. In 2004 that Practice signed a contract with the Fund for funded treatment. In 2006, after amendments to the Health Protection Act, the State Sanitation and Health Inspectorate ordered the Practice to re-register as a private health institution. Dr Arsovska applied, and the Ministry of Health issued a new registration decision for a private health institution at the same address. The Inspectorate confirmed compliance. The Central Registry registered the new Practice in 2006 with a new individual tax number. In 2007 the new Practice transformed into the applicant company, retaining the new Practice’s tax number. The Fund was notified of the changes. On 29 November 2006 the Fund told the new Practice that it would not sign a new contract after the old one expired.

The applicant company’s claims arose in two sets of civil proceedings against the Fund for non-adherence to the 2004 contract. In the first, the original Practice sued in January 2006; after re-registration and transformation, the new Practice and then the applicant company continued the case. The first-instance court partly granted the claim in 2008. On appeal, the Fund objected for the first time that the applicant lacked standing because it was a different legal entity, as shown by different tax numbers. The Court of Appeal remitted the case; the first-instance court then dismissed the claim for lack of standing, and the Court of Appeal upheld that decision in December 2009. In the second set, the new Practice sued in July 2006 for debt under the same contract; the applicant company continued the proceedings. The Fund again objected to standing. The first-instance court dismissed the claim in February 2009, and the Court of Appeal upheld the dismissal in December 2009, stressing that a tax number is a unique and unchangeable identifier. Both cases ended at second instance because their value was below the threshold for an appeal to the Supreme Court, so the merits were never examined.

The applicant argued that the original Practice, new Practice, and applicant company had legal continuity: they had the same owner/manager, address, and professional activity, with only a minor name change and different tax numbers. The Fund had accepted performance and sent the termination notice to the new Practice, implicitly recognizing continuity. The Government argued the applicant had failed to prove succession and could have used cession. The Court noted that in a separate case involving the same parties and contract, the Supreme Court had found standing because the contract was terminated by notice to the new Practice, which had the same tax number as the applicant. The ECtHR held that the domestic courts’ excessively formalistic reliance on the tax-number difference imposed an unjustifiable procedural obstacle, impaired the essence of the right of access to court, and violated Article 6 § 1. The Protocol No. 1 complaint was rejected as premature, since reopening remained possible.

**Case: Centre for the Development of Analytical Psychology v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia**  
(ECtHR, First Section, Applications nos. 29545/10 and 32961/10, judgment 15 June 2017)

The applicant was a Skopje limited liability company owned and managed by Dr Marija Arsovska, a psychiatrist. It originated from a private psychiatric practice established in 1995 by Dr Marija Karanfilova (later Arsovska), which used Carl Jung’s analytical psychotherapy methods and had individual tax number beginning 503. In 2004 that practice signed a contract with the State Health Insurance Fund for funding treatment of insured beneficiaries.

In February 2006 the Ministry of Health’s Sanitation and Health Inspectorate ordered the practice to re-register as a private health institution under amendments to the Health Protection Act. The Ministry then registered “Dr Marija Karanfilova’s Specialist Psychiatric Practice” at the same address as the earlier practice; the old registration was to cease. A March 2006 inspection found full compliance. In March/April 2006 the Central Registry recorded the new practice, which received a new tax number beginning 403. In June 2006 the new practice notified the Fund of its re-registration and name change. In November 2006 the Fund told the new practice that it would not sign a new contract after the existing one expired. In August 2007 the new practice transformed into the applicant company, retaining tax number 403.

The applicant company continued two sets of domestic proceedings against the Fund for breach of the 2004 contract. In both, the domestic courts dismissed its claims for lack of standing. They relied essentially on the difference between the original practice’s tax number (503) and the new practice/applicant company’s tax number (403). The Fund first objected to standing on appeal in the compensation proceedings. The Skopje Court of First Instance dismissed the claim in April 2009, and the Court of Appeal upheld that decision in December 2009. In the separate debt proceedings, the Fund objected in June 2008; the first-instance court dismissed the claim in February 2009, and the Court of Appeal upheld that in December 2009. Both cases ended before the second-instance courts because the amounts fell below the threshold for an appeal on points of law to the Supreme Court. The merits of the Fund’s alleged non-performance were therefore never examined.

The applicant argued that the re-registration was compulsory and that the entities had legal continuity: the same psychiatrist owned and managed both, the same address and professional activity continued, the Fund knew of the changes, accepted performance and reports, and terminated the contract by notice to the new practice. The Government argued that the applicant had failed to prove succession, that the tax number uniquely identified legal entities, and that a cession could have transferred claims. However, in separate proceedings involving the same contract, the Supreme Court in 2011 found that the applicant company did have standing, noting that the Fund had terminated the contract by notice to the new practice, which had the same tax number as the applicant company.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 6 § 1. Although assigning tax numbers pursues legal certainty, the domestic courts’ refusal to examine the merits solely because of different tax numbers was an excessively formalistic procedural obstacle that impaired the essence of the applicant’s right of access to a court. As to Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, the Court considered that complaint premature, since reopening was possible and it could not speculate on the contractual rights.
001-170050:
In *Salija v. Switzerland*, the applicant, Bljerim Salija, a national of “the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia,” complained under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that Switzerland’s revocation of his permanent residence permit and order of expulsion violated his right to respect for family life with his wife and children.

Salija arrived in Switzerland in 1989 through family reunification and held a permanent residence permit. In 1999 he married a Macedonian national who had arrived in Switzerland in 1990 and also held a permanent residence permit. They had two children, born in 2001 and 2005, who were also Macedonian nationals. After leaving school, Salija had no professional training and worked in various jobs, including postman, mailman, plasterer, and construction worker, with brief periods of unemployment.

His criminal record was central to the expulsion. In 2003 he was convicted of embezzlement for selling a rental car and received a suspended three-month sentence. More seriously, in 2004 the Supreme Court of the Canton of Zurich convicted him of homicide with indirect intent and serious traffic violations. In October 2000, while racing another car on a public road at at least 170 km/h, he lost control and crashed into a lamppost, killing his passenger. The court found he had deliberately taken the risk of killing the passenger and acted with a high degree of recklessness, sentencing him to five years and three months’ imprisonment. Appeals were dismissed in 2005 and 2006. He began serving the sentence in April 2006, was fined in 2007 for purchasing and consuming marijuana, and was released on parole in October 2009 after serving two thirds of his sentence.

In July 2009 the Migration Office of the Canton of Zurich revoked his permanent residence permit and ordered his expulsion. It found that the public interest in removal outweighed his interest in family life in Switzerland. The Canton of Zurich government and the Administrative Court dismissed his appeals. The Administrative Court noted the serious nature of the offence and that Salija was not well integrated despite his long stay. Although an expert prognosis was positive, it did not exclude reoffending. The court found he spoke Albanian, knew Macedonian culture, had spent part of his childhood there, and had visited since. His wife was also Macedonian, knew Albanian and the culture, and was not well integrated in Switzerland. Their children were five and nine and adaptable, so the family could reasonably relocate.

In July 2010 the Federal Supreme Court dismissed his appeal. It found intentional homicide particularly serious. Although Switzerland had been the centre of his life for over twenty years, he was neither professionally nor socially integrated: he had no stable employment, considerable debts, and his family had received significant social welfare. It concluded he could reasonably reintegrate in Macedonia, as could his wife, who had lived there until age twelve, still had relatives, and visited annually. She had no professional training, had received social welfare from 2005, and only began working in 2010. The children were of adaptable age. The public interest in removal outweighed his family-life interest; his wife and children could either relocate with him or remain in Switzerland and maintain contact through regular visits.

After the expulsion, Salija left Switzerland in October 2010. In December 2010 an entry ban of nine years was issued, later reduced to seven years in 2013. In late 2011 his wife and children moved to Macedonia to join him. In August 2015, after almost four years, they returned to Switzerland to avoid expiry of their permanent residence permits and because living conditions in Macedonia were difficult; they now live in Zurich.

The key facts relevant to the alleged Article 8 violation are therefore Salija’s long lawful residence and family ties in Switzerland, balanced against his serious criminal conviction, weak integration and financial dependency, his wife’s and children’s own Macedonian ties and adaptability, and the possibility of family relocation or maintaining contact.

In *Salija v. Switzerland* (ECtHR, Third Section, 10 January 2017), the applicant, Bljerim Salija, a national of “the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia” born in 1980, challenged Switzerland’s revocation of his permanent residence permit and its expulsion order. He alleged that these measures violated his right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, particularly his family life with his wife and two children.

The applicant arrived in Switzerland in 1989 through family reunification and held a permanent residence permit. In 1999 he married a national of “the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia,” who also held a permanent residence permit. They had two children, born in 2001 and 2005, both nationals of the same country. The applicant had no professional training and worked in various jobs, including postman, mailman, plasterer, and construction worker, with periods of unemployment. He had debts, and the family received social welfare.

His criminal record was central to the case. In 2003 he was convicted of embezzlement for selling a rental car and received a suspended three-month sentence. More seriously, in 2004 the Supreme Court of the Canton of Zurich convicted him of homicide with indirect intent and serious traffic violations. In October 2000, while racing on a public road at at least 170 km/h, he lost control of his car and crashed into a lamppost, killing his passenger. The court found he had acted with a high degree of recklessness and deliberately taken the risk of killing the passenger. He was sentenced to five years and three months’ imprisonment. Appeals were dismissed in 2005 and 2006. He began serving his sentence in April 2006. In 2007 he was fined 120 CHF for purchasing and consuming marijuana. He was released on parole in October 2009 after serving two-thirds of his sentence.

In July 2009, the Migration Office of the Canton of Zurich revoked his permanent residence permit and ordered his expulsion. It found that the public interest in removal outweighed his interest in family life in Switzerland. His appeals were dismissed by the Cantonal Government in September 2009 and by the Administrative Court in February 2010. The Administrative Court noted the serious offence, his weak integration despite long residence, a positive but not risk-free reoffending prognosis, and his familiarity with the language and culture of “the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia.” It also found that his wife was not well integrated, and that their children, aged five and nine, were adaptable and could reasonably relocate with him.

In July 2010, the Federal Supreme Court dismissed his final appeal. It accepted that Switzerland had become the centre of his life after over twenty years, but found he was neither professionally nor socially integrated. It cited his unstable employment, debts, and the family’s reliance on welfare. It concluded that he, his wife, and their children could reintegrate in “the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia,” where his wife had relatives and where the family had visited. The public interest in removal outweighed his Article 8 interests, especially since his wife and children could either follow him or remain in Switzerland and maintain contact through visits.

After leaving Switzerland in October 2010, he received a nine-year entry ban, later reduced to seven years in 2013. His wife and children moved to “the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia” in late 2011 but returned to Switzerland in August 2015 to avoid expiry of their permanent residence permits and because living conditions there were difficult. They now live in Zurich. The key Article 8 issue was whether Switzerland had struck a fair balance between public safety and the applicant’s family life.

In *Asatryan v. Armenia* (Application no. 3571/09, judgment of 27 April 2017), the European Court of Human Rights considered whether Ms Silva Asatryan received a fair trial under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention. The case arose from a bomb placed under the car of M.G., a businessman and former parliamentarian, which exploded on 29 December 2001. M.G. survived. He told police that he suspected the applicant’s ex-husband, A.G., with whom he had business disputes. A.G. denied involvement, and his son was briefly arrested but later released.

During the 2002 investigation, police took statements from several witnesses, including A.At., A.A., L.G. (the applicant’s daughter), and A.B. These statements concerned the applicant’s relationship with A.G., her attitude toward M.G., and alleged property or financial disputes. At that time, the applicant was not an accused.

In 2005, Y.W. was arrested after firearms and explosives were found at his home. He confessed to the attempted murder and claimed he had acted on the applicant’s orders. The applicant was arrested on 23 September 2005 and charged with instigating attempted murder and property damage. At trial, Y.W. retracted his pre-trial statements, saying they had been obtained under duress. The applicant denied any involvement, stating that she had divorced A.G. in 1999, lived separately with her daughter, and had no connection with A.G.’s business. Her daughter L.G. was initially listed as a witness but was removed after invoking her testimonial privilege.

The District Court convicted the applicant on 12 October 2007 and sentenced her to nine years’ imprisonment. It relied mainly on other evidence, including Y.W.’s trial statements, statements by S.A. and L.C., and court disputes showing that the applicant and A.G. had strained relations with M.G. The applicant appealed. On 18 June 2008, the Criminal Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal and upheld the conviction. In doing so, it additionally relied on the pre-trial statements of L.G., A.At., A.A., and A.B. to reject her defence that she had no family-like relationship with A.G. and therefore no motive. These pre-trial statements had not been read out or examined in court, and the applicant had no opportunity to question the witnesses.

The Government argued that the statements were not decisive and that A.A. had testified before the District Court, although the Court of Appeal relied on A.A.’s pre-trial statement rather than her trial testimony. The ECtHR found no evidence that the disputed pre-trial statements were read out or examined by either the District Court or the Court of Appeal. It held that the Court of Appeal’s reliance on them was relevant because they supported the finding that the applicant had a motive and undermined her defence. For A.At. and A.B., they were not examined at either stage and were not included in the witness call list. L.G. had testimonial privilege, but the Court of Appeal still used her pre-trial statement from a time before the applicant became an accused. There were no procedural safeguards, and the defence was not even aware that the appellate court intended to rely on this evidence.

The ECtHR concluded that the applicant’s right to a fair trial under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) had been violated. Other complaints were rejected as manifestly ill-founded.

**Case: Asatryan v. Armenia (Application no. 3571/09), ECtHR, 27 April 2017**

The applicant, Silva Asatryan, an Armenian national, was convicted of instigating the attempted murder of M.G., a businessman and former parliamentarian. On 29 December 2001, a bomb placed under M.G.’s car detonated as he started the engine; he survived. The investigation initially focused on the applicant’s ex-husband, A.G., because of business disputes with M.G. A.G.’s son, V.G., was briefly arrested but later released. In 2005, Y.W., a family friend, was arrested after firearms and explosives were found at his home. He confessed to the attempted murder and stated that he had acted on the applicant’s orders. The applicant was arrested on 23 September 2005 and charged with instigation of attempted murder and property damage.

At trial, Y.W. retracted his pre-trial statements, claiming they had been obtained under duress. The applicant denied involvement, stating that she had divorced A.G. in 1999, lived separately with their daughter L.G., and had no interest in A.G.’s business activities. L.G. was initially included in the witness call list, but she was later excluded after invoking her right not to testify against a close relative. In October 2007, the District Court convicted the applicant and sentenced her to nine years’ imprisonment. It relied mainly on the trial statements of S.A. and L.C. and on property disputes involving M.G. to establish motive.

On appeal, the Criminal Court of Appeal upheld the conviction in June 2008. In doing so, it additionally relied on pre-trial statements made in 2002 by L.G., A.At., A.A., and A.B. These statements were used to reject the applicant’s defence that she had no meaningful connection with A.G. and therefore no motive. However, those pre-trial statements were not read out or examined either before the District Court or before the Court of Appeal. Witnesses A.A., A.B., and A.At. were not included in the witness call list and were never examined by either court. L.G. had invoked testimonial privilege, yet the Court of Appeal still relied on her earlier pre-trial statement, made before the applicant was charged.

The applicant complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention that she had not received a fair trial because the appellate court relied on untested pre-trial witness statements and she had no opportunity to examine those witnesses. The Government argued that she had failed to exhaust domestic remedies and that the statements were not decisive. The European Court of Human Rights rejected the non-exhaustion objection, finding that the applicant had raised the complaint at the earliest possible stage in her appeal on points of law.

On the merits, the Court applied the principles from *Al-Khawaja and Tahery* and *Schatschaschwili*. It found that the Court of Appeal used the disputed statements to reinforce its finding on motive, giving them significant weight and potentially handicapping the defence. There was no shown good reason for the witnesses’ absence, no sufficient procedural safeguards, and the defence was not even aware that the appellate court would rely on that evidence. Although L.G. had a testimonial privilege, her pre-trial statement was still used against the applicant from a time when the applicant was not yet accused. The Court concluded that the applicant’s right to a fair trial had been breached, finding a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d). Other complaints were rejected as manifestly ill-founded.

In *Asatryan v. Armenia* (Application no. 3571/09, ECtHR, 27 April 2017), the applicant, Silva Asatryan, was convicted in Armenia of instigating the attempted murder of M.G., a businessman and former parliamentarian. The case began on 29 December 2001, when a bomb under M.G.’s car detonated; M.G. survived. The investigation initially focused on the applicant’s ex-husband, A.G., with whom M.G. had business disputes. In 2005, after Y.W., a family friend, was arrested following the discovery of firearms and explosives at his home, Y.W. confessed to the attempted murder and stated that the applicant had ordered it. The applicant was arrested in September 2005 and charged with instigation of attempted murder and property damage.

At trial, the applicant denied involvement. She claimed she had divorced A.G. in 1999, lived separately with their daughter L.G., and had no connection to A.G.’s business activities. Y.W. retracted his pre-trial statements, alleging duress, and later told the Court of Appeal that he had organized the explosion at the applicant’s request but had only intended to frighten M.G. In October 2007, the District Court convicted the applicant and sentenced her to nine years’ imprisonment. It relied mainly on trial statements by S.A. and L.C., and on the applicant’s involvement in property disputes with M.G. In June 2008, the Court of Appeal upheld the conviction.

The alleged violation concerned the Court of Appeal’s reliance on pre-trial witness statements that were not read out or examined in court, and the applicant’s inability to examine those witnesses. Specifically, the Court of Appeal referred to pre-trial statements by L.G. (the applicant’s daughter), A.At., A.A., and A.B. to conclude that the applicant had maintained a family-like relationship with A.G. and had a motive to kill M.G., thereby rejecting her defence. These statements were not read out or examined. L.G. had invoked testimonial privilege and was removed from the witness list, so she did not testify. A.A. had allegedly testified before the District Court, but the Court of Appeal relied on A.A.’s pre-trial statement, not her trial testimony. A.B. and A.At. were not included in the witness call list and were not examined by the first-instance or appellate courts. The applicant had no opportunity to question these witnesses, including during the investigation when she was not yet an accused.

The applicant raised these complaints in her appeal on points of law. The Court of Cassation rejected them, and after a Constitutional Court ruling, it reopened and again dismissed the appeal. The Government argued that the statements were not decisive and that other evidence supported the conviction. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d). It noted that no evidence showed the pre-trial statements were read out or examined, and although other evidence existed, the Court of Appeal found it necessary to rely on these statements to reinforce the motive finding. They therefore carried significant weight and may have handicapped the defence. No procedural safeguards compensated for this: the applicant could not challenge the witnesses during the investigation and could not reasonably have requested them at trial because some were not on the witness list. She was also not aware that the Court of Appeal intended to use the statements. L.G.’s testimonial privilege did not justify using her earlier pre-trial statement. The Court concluded that the applicant’s fair-trial rights were breached.

In *Güzelyurtlu and Others v. Cyprus and Turkey* (App. no. 36925/07), seven Cypriot nationals of Turkish Cypriot origin—relatives of Elmas, Zerrin and Eylül Güzelyurtlu—alleged that the Cypriot and Turkish authorities, including the authorities of the “Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus” (“TRNC”), failed to conduct an effective investigation into the 2005 killing of their family members. They relied on the procedural and substantive aspects of Article 2 of the Convention and on Article 13, complaining of the absence of an effective remedy. The Court communicated the procedural Article 2 complaints, both alone and in conjunction with Article 13.

The facts concerned the murder of Elmas Güzelyurtlu, his wife Zerrin and their daughter Eylül. The family, Turkish Cypriots, lived in Ayios Dometios in the government-controlled area of Nicosia. On 15 January 2005, their bodies were found on the Nicosia–Larnaca highway near the Athiainou exit. Zerrin and Eylül were in the back seat of the family car; Elmas was in a nearby ditch. All three were in pyjamas and slippers. Zerrin and Eylül had tape marks and bruises indicating they had been bound and had struggled. Post-mortems concluded that each died from close-range gunshot wounds to the head. Evidence suggested the victims had been kidnapped from their home at about 4:41 a.m. and murdered between 5:15 and 5:20 a.m. The crime appeared well planned, involving more than eight people and five vehicles.

The Cypriot authorities opened an investigation immediately. Police secured the crime scene and the victims’ home, collected forensic exhibits, conducted autopsies, and took statements. They identified several suspects, some linked by DNA found on the car and at the house. Arrest warrants, “stop list” messages, Interpol Red Notices and European arrest warrants were issued. The main suspects, however, were in the “TRNC” or Turkey. Cypriot authorities requested UNFICYP mediation for their transfer and later sent extradition requests to Turkey under the European Convention on Extradition. Turkey returned or refused to receive the requests, apparently because it did not recognise the Republic of Cyprus. One suspect was murdered in the “TRNC”; another was arrested in the south but released for lack of evidence. In 2008, the Cypriot investigation was classified as “otherwise disposed of” pending future arrests, although arrest warrants remained in force. An inquest was also delayed.

The Turkish and “TRNC” authorities conducted their own inquiries. “TRNC” police detained and questioned several suspects, searched homes and took statements, but all denied involvement and were released around 11 February 2005 for lack of evidence. A Turkish national suspect was arrested in Turkey but also released. The “TRNC” case was later classified as “non-resolved for the time being,” with the file remaining open pending further evidence. Subsequently, the first and second suspects were convicted of a separate murder; one allegedly made remarks implicating himself in the Güzelyurtlu killings, but the “TRNC” Attorney-General concluded there was insufficient evidence to charge anyone.

The applicants complained that, despite these steps, the authorities failed to cooperate effectively, failed to prosecute or surrender suspects, and left them without an effective investigation or remedy. The case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 29 January 2019.

Elmas Güzelyurtlu, his wife Zerrin and their daughter Eylül had lived in Ayios Dometios, in the area controlled by the Republic of Cyprus. Evidence indicated they had been abducted from their home at about 4.41 a.m. and murdered between 5.15 and 5.20 a.m.

The Cypriot authorities opened a detailed investigation. In *Güzelyurtlu and Others v. Cyprus and Turkey*, seven Cypriot nationals of Turkish Cypriot origin—relatives of Elmas, Zerrin and Eylül Güzelyurtlu—complained that Cypriot and Turkish authorities, including the authorities of the “Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus” (“TRNC”), failed to conduct an effective investigation into the 2005 murders and failed to provide an effective remedy. The case arose from the killing on 15 January 2005 of Elmas Güzelyurtlu, his wife Zerrin, and their daughter Eylül. The family lived in Ayios Dometios, Nicosia, in the government-controlled area of Cyprus. Early that morning, police found their black Lexus on the Nicosia–Larnaca highway. Zerrin and Eylül were dead in the back seat; Elmas was dead in a nearby ditch. All were in nightclothes. Tape and signs of binding and struggle were found. Post-mortems concluded that all three died from close-range gunshot wounds to the head and that the deaths were criminal.

The Cypriot investigation was immediate and extensive. Police secured the car and the family home, collected bullets, cartridge cases, a knife, tape and other exhibits, examined the security system, took statements, and conducted DNA and ballistics tests. Evidence indicated the victims were kidnapped around 4:41 a.m. and killed between 5:15 and 5:20 a.m. A BMW linked to suspects was seen, and crossing-point records showed a red BMW with “TRNC” plates entering and returning north. DNA of several suspects was found on exhibits and on the victims’ car. Eight suspects were ultimately identified, including Cypriot/“TRNC” citizens and Turkish nationals. Cypriot courts issued arrest warrants, European arrest warrants, and Interpol Red Notices. However, the suspects were in northern Cyprus or Turkey, outside the effective control of the Republic of Cyprus.

Cyprus sought UNFICYP’s help to hand over suspects and evidence and later sent extradition requests to Turkey under the European Convention on Extradition. Turkey returned the requests unprocessed, reflecting its non-recognition of the Republic of Cyprus. The Cypriot case was eventually “otherwise disposed of” pending arrest, and an inquest was held or adjourned. The applicants alleged that this left them without a meaningful investigation or remedy.

The “TRNC” authorities conducted a separate investigation. They questioned and detained several suspects, searched homes and the BMW, took statements, and checked border records. But suspects were released in February 2005 for lack of evidence linking them to the murders. A Turkish national suspect was also detained in Turkey and released. The “TRNC” investigation was later classified “non-resolved for the time being,” remaining open pending further evidence. The first and second suspects were later convicted in unrelated proceedings, but no murder charges resulted.

The central factual issue was the cross-border investigation: although Cyprus gathered substantial evidence identifying suspects in northern Cyprus/Turkey, it could not execute arrests there; Turkey and the “TRNC” authorities did not secure the suspects or transfer evidence, and extradition and cooperation efforts failed. The applicants argued that this fragmentation and lack of cooperation deprived them of an effective investigation and remedy for the unlawful killings.

**Case: Nikolić and Others v. Serbia** (Application no. 9235/11), European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, judgment of 24 January 2017. Fourteen applicants complained against Serbia under Article 6 § 1, Article 13, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that a final domestic judgment awarding them compensation for land was never enforced and that they lacked an effective remedy. The core alleged violations therefore concerned the prolonged non-enforcement of that final judgment, rather than the original deprivation of land.

In 1961, the applicants’ predecessors were deprived of certain land in favour of the State. In 2006, the Niš Municipal Court ordered PIK Niš—a company predominantly composed of socially-owned capital and the end user of the land—to pay specified compensation. The judgment became final and enforceable by 16 August 2006. On 25 October 2006 and 1 February 2007, following the applicants’ requests, the Niš Municipal Court ordered enforcement of the judgment and payment of enforcement costs. One applicant, Tomislav Đorđević, however, never lodged an enforcement request.

On 3 June 2009, the Niš Commercial Court opened insolvency proceedings against the debtor. Those proceedings were still ongoing. Only one applicant, Milica Nikolić Jajčević, duly submitted her claims in the insolvency proceedings. All applicants lodged constitutional appeals between 2009 and 2010. In 2011–2012, the Constitutional Court found a violation of the right to a hearing within a reasonable time in respect of all applicants except Tomislav Đorđević, but awarded no damages, stating that the applicants had not claimed non-pecuniary damages. It dismissed Tomislav Đorđević’s appeal because he had failed to request enforcement of the judgment.

Before the ECtHR, the Government objected that some applicants had failed to exhaust domestic remedies because they had neither initiated enforcement nor registered claims in the insolvency proceedings. It also argued that the remaining applicants had lost victim status because the Constitutional Court had acknowledged the delay. The Court rejected most objections. It held Tomislav Đorđević’s complaint inadmissible for non-exhaustion: he should have sought enforcement or filed a claim in the insolvency proceedings. For seven applicants, the Court found that they had in fact lodged enforcement requests, so the Government’s objection failed. As for the remaining seven, the application had been lodged on 15 December 2010, before 21 June 2012, when a constitutional appeal became effective in such cases. They were therefore not required to use that remedy and remained victims. The complaints were declared admissible.

On the merits, the Court noted that the domestic judgment remained unenforced. It relied on its established case law concerning the non-enforcement of final judgments against socially-owned companies. The Government offered no convincing argument to depart from that case law. The Court found violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Having reached that conclusion, it did not examine separately the Article 13 complaint. The key facts supporting the alleged violations were that the final, enforceable compensation judgment remained unsatisfied; the socially-owned debtor entered insolvency; the insolvency proceedings continued without payment; the Constitutional Court found delay but awarded no compensation; and one applicant’s failure to seek enforcement or register an insolvency claim led to his complaint being rejected for non-exhaustion.

In *Nikolić and Others v. Serbia* (Application no. 9235/11, Third Section, judgment of 24 January 2017), fourteen applicants alleged that Serbia had failed to enforce a final domestic judgment in their favour and had not provided an effective remedy. The case concerned land taken from their predecessors in 1961 in favour of the State. In 2006 the Niš Municipal Court ordered PIK Niš, a company predominantly composed of socially-owned capital and the end user of the land, to pay the applicants compensation. That judgment became final and enforceable by 16 August 2006. In October 2006 and February 2007, the Municipal Court further ordered enforcement of the judgment and required the debtor to pay enforcement costs. Despite this, the judgment remained unenforced.

In June 2009, the Niš Commercial Court opened insolvency proceedings against the debtor, which were still ongoing at the time of the European Court’s judgment. Only one applicant, Milica Nikolić Jajčević, duly submitted her claim in those insolvency proceedings. One applicant, Tomislav Đorđević, never lodged an enforcement request.

The applicants also pursued constitutional redress. Between 2011 and 2012, the Serbian Constitutional Court found a violation of the right to a hearing within a reasonable time for all applicants except Tomislav Đorđević. However, it awarded no damages because the applicants had not claimed non-pecuniary damages. It dismissed Tomislav Đorđević’s appeal because he had not requested enforcement of the judgment.

Before the European Court, the applicants complained under Article 6 § 1 (fair hearing within a reasonable time), Article 13 (effective remedy), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of possessions). The Government objected that certain applicants had failed to exhaust domestic remedies—either by not initiating enforcement proceedings or by not registering claims in the insolvency proceedings—and that others had lost victim status because the Constitutional Court had acknowledged a violation.

The Court rejected the Government’s objection as to six applicants, finding that they had in fact lodged enforcement requests. It also held that the constitutional appeal was not an effective domestic remedy for applications lodged before 21 June 2012. Since this application was lodged on 15 December 2010, the remaining seven applicants were still considered victims. However, Tomislav Đorđević’s complaints were rejected for non-exhaustion because he had neither requested enforcement nor reported his claim in the insolvency proceedings.

On the merits, the Court observed that the final domestic judgment remained unenforced. Applying its established case law concerning non-enforcement of final judgments against socially-owned companies, it found no convincing reason to depart from that jurisprudence. Consequently, the Court found violations of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Having reached that conclusion, it did not examine separately the complaint under Article 13. The case illustrates the State’s obligation to ensure enforcement of final judgments and the admissibility requirements arising from enforcement and insolvency remedies.

**Case Summary: Nikolić and Others v. Serbia (Application no. 9235/11)**

In *Nikolić and Others v. Serbia*, fourteen applicants lodged an application against Serbia on 15 December 2010 under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The case concerned the Serbian authorities’ failure to enforce a final domestic judgment rendered in the applicants’ favour and the alleged lack of an effective remedy for that failure. The applicants relied on Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The underlying facts began in 1961, when the applicants’ predecessors were deprived of certain land in favour of the State. In 2006, the Niš Municipal Court ordered PIK Niš—the debtor and end user of the land, a company predominantly comprised of socially-owned capital—to pay the applicants specified amounts as compensation for the land. That judgment became final and enforceable by 16 August 2006. Subsequently, on 25 October 2006 and 1 February 2007, the Niš Municipal Court ordered enforcement of the judgment and required the debtor to pay enforcement costs. However, one applicant, Mr Tomislav Đorđević, never lodged an enforcement request.

In June 2009, the Niš Commercial Court opened insolvency proceedings against the debtor. Those proceedings remained ongoing. Only one applicant, Ms Milica Nikolić Jajčević, duly submitted her claims in the insolvency proceedings.

Between March 2009 and June 2010, all applicants lodged constitutional appeals. The Serbian Constitutional Court found a violation of the right to a hearing within a reasonable time for all applicants except Mr Đorđević. However, it awarded no damages, stating that the applicants had not claimed non-pecuniary damages. In Mr Đorđević’s case, the Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal because he had failed to request enforcement of the judgment.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants complained that the respondent State had failed to enforce the final judgment in their favour and that no effective domestic remedy existed in that connection. The Government disputed admissibility. It argued that seven applicants had failed to exhaust domestic remedies because they had neither initiated enforcement proceedings nor registered their claims in the insolvency proceedings. It also argued that the remaining seven applicants had lost victim status because the Constitutional Court had acknowledged a violation of their right to a trial within a reasonable time.

The Court rejected the non-exhaustion objection concerning the applicants who had in fact lodged enforcement requests, finding that the Niš Municipal Court had ordered enforcement in 2006. However, it rejected Mr Đorđević’s complaints for non-exhaustion because he had failed either to seek enforcement or to report his claims in the insolvency proceedings. As for the remaining applicants, the Court held that they were not required to use the constitutional appeal because their application was lodged before 21 June 2012, when the Court’s case-law began treating that remedy as effective for Serbia. They therefore retained victim status, and their complaints were declared admissible.

On the merits, the Court noted that the final domestic judgment remained unenforced. It reiterated its established case-law finding violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 in similar cases involving unenforced judgments against socially-owned companies. The Government had advanced no convincing argument to justify a different conclusion. Accordingly, the Court found violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and did not examine the complaint separately under Article 13.
