Case: Ļutova v. Latvia (Application no. 37105/09), ECtHR Fifth Section, judgment of 9 November 2017. The applicant, Tatjana Seļezņova (later Ļutova), a Latvian national, lodged the application on 26 June 2009. The only complaint communicated to the Government was the length of civil proceedings under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention; the remainder was declared inadmissible.

The underlying dispute began on 24 November 2005, when Kurzemes Namu Apsaimniekotājs LLC sued the applicant for unpaid residential building maintenance charges, initially LVL 320 (about EUR 455). The applicant denied owing the debt, arguing that she had no maintenance-services agreement with the plaintiff and was free to choose another provider. She was represented by a non-lawyer.

The first-instance proceedings lasted from November 2005 until 6 November 2008, when the Riga City Kurzeme District Court dismissed the plaintiff’s claim as unsubstantiated. The proceedings involved twelve hearings and repeated postponements. The Government argued that six of the twelve hearings were adjourned at the applicant’s request, causing about one year and eight months of delay, and that her non-lawyer representative contributed to the length. The Court’s own itemisation noted four adjournments at the applicant’s request (almost one year), four at the plaintiff’s request (about ten months), and two due to further information from either party (over seven months). Minor delays of more than one month were attributable to the first-instance court itself, due to a change in judge and time needed to prepare judgment.

The plaintiff appealed. Although the appeal was admitted on 3 December 2008, the first hearing before the Riga Regional Court was not held until 13 September 2010—more than one year and nine months with no hearings. The plaintiff then increased the claim to LVL 3,173 (about EUR 4,515). On 22 December 2010, the Regional Court partly allowed the claim and ordered the applicant to pay LVL 2,854 (about EUR 4,059). It found that, although no maintenance agreement existed, domestic law obliged her to pay; she could have contested the bills but failed to do so, and had paid only some. The applicant appealed on points of law, but on 3 February 2012 the Supreme Court Senate remitted the appeal because she had not paid the required security deposit. After this was corrected, on 3 April 2012 the Senate refused to institute cassation proceedings. The proceedings thus lasted six years and more than four months across three levels of jurisdiction.

The Government objected that the applicant had suffered no significant disadvantage and had not exhausted domestic remedies. The ECtHR rejected both objections: the debt had increased substantially, the case raised a matter of principle—whether the applicant could be required to pay absent an agreement—and no comparable domestic examples of compensation for length violations were shown.

On the merits, the Court found the case was not complex. While the applicant’s conduct contributed to delays at first instance, the higher courts were responsible for long periods of inactivity: over one year and nine months before the appellate court and more than one year before the Supreme Court. Considering the total duration and lack of complexity, the Court concluded that the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1 had been violated.

**Case summary: Ļutova v. Latvia (Application no. 37105/09)**

The case concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights because of the excessive length of civil proceedings in Latvia. The applicant, Ms Tatjana Seļezņova (later Ļutova), a Latvian national living in Riga, was sued on 24 November 2005 by Kurzemes Namu Apsaimniekotājs, a residential building maintenance services provider, for an unpaid debt of LVL 320 (approximately EUR 455). The applicant disputed the claim, arguing that she had no maintenance services agreement with the plaintiff and was free to choose another provider. She was represented by Mr S. Seļezņovs, who was not a qualified lawyer. Civil proceedings were instituted the following day.

The first hearing was scheduled for 21 April 2006. During the proceedings, the claim was repeatedly increased, eventually reaching LVL 3,173 (approximately EUR 4,515). The first-instance court held twelve hearings. Several hearings were postponed: four at the applicant’s request, causing a delay of almost one year; four at the plaintiff’s request, causing around ten months’ delay; and two because further documents or information were needed, causing about seven and a half months’ delay. Minor delays were also attributable to the first-instance court, including a change in the court’s composition and time needed to prepare the judgment.

On 28 October 2008 the last first-instance hearing was held. On 6 November 2008 the Riga City Kurzeme District Court dismissed the plaintiff’s claim as unsubstantiated, finding that the plaintiff had not proved the expenses had been incurred or properly reflected services provided. The plaintiff appealed. The appeal was admitted in December 2008 and sent to the Riga Regional Court. However, the first appellate hearing took place only on 13 September 2010 — more than one year and nine months later. At that hearing, the plaintiff increased the claim to LVL 3,173 and submitted documents. The final appellate hearing was held on 8 December 2010; the plaintiff did not attend.

On 22 December 2010 the Regional Court partly allowed the claim and ordered the applicant to pay LVL 2,854 (approximately EUR 4,059). Although no maintenance agreement existed, domestic law obliged the applicant to pay for services; she could have contested the bills but had not, and had paid some bills selectively. The Regional Court refused a contractual penalty but awarded default interest of 6%. The applicant appealed on points of law on 18 January 2011. On 3 February 2012 the Senate of the Supreme Court remitted the appeal to the Regional Court because the applicant had not paid the security deposit; the deficiency was later rectified. On 3 April 2012 the Senate refused to institute cassation proceedings. The proceedings had thus lasted from 24 November 2005 to 3 April 2012 — six years and more than four months across three levels of jurisdiction.

The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 about the length of the proceedings. The Government objected that she had suffered no significant disadvantage and had not exhausted domestic remedies, arguing she could claim compensation under Article 92 of the Constitution and section 1635 of the Civil Law. The European Court of Human Rights rejected both objections. It found the financial impact and the principled issue — whether payment was required without an agreement — sufficient to show significant disadvantage, and found no comparable examples of effective domestic compensation claims.

On the merits, the Court noted the case was not complex. Although the applicant had contributed to delays before the first-instance court, the higher courts were responsible for long periods of inactivity: over one year and nine months before the first appellate hearing, and more than one year before the Supreme Court merely to remit the appeal for procedural defects. The Court therefore found a violation of the reasonable-time requirement under Article 6 § 1.

**Summary of Ļutova v. Latvia (Application no. 37105/09)**

The applicant, Ms Tatjana Ļutova (formerly Seļezņova), a Latvian national born in 1964 and residing in Riga, lodged an application against the Republic of Latvia on 26 June 2009, alleging a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention concerning the excessive length of civil proceedings. On 2 April 2014, the complaint regarding the length of proceedings was communicated to the Government, while the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The underlying dispute arose on 24 November 2005, when Kurzemes Namu Apsaimniekotājs, a residential building maintenance services provider, filed a claim against the applicant for recovery of a debt of 320 Latvian lati (approximately EUR 455) for its services. Civil proceedings were instituted the following day. The applicant contested the claim, arguing that no maintenance services agreement had been concluded between the parties and that she was free to choose another service provider. She was represented throughout by Mr S. Seļezņovs, who was not a qualified lawyer.

The case was pending before the Riga City Kurzeme District Court for nearly three years. Twelve hearings were held at regular intervals. Four hearings were postponed at the applicant's request, resulting in a delay of almost one year, as her representative needed time to examine legal norms and documents. Four hearings were postponed at the plaintiff's request, causing a delay of ten months, mainly because the plaintiff repeatedly increased the amount of its claim—from LVL 320 to LVL 426 and eventually to LVL 3,173 (approximately EUR 4,515)—and failed to submit supporting documents in a timely manner. Two further hearings were postponed due to additional information provided or requested by either party, resulting in a delay of approximately seven months. A few minor delays were attributable to the first-instance court itself, including a change in the court's composition. On 6 November 2008, the City Court dismissed the plaintiff's claim as unsubstantiated, finding that the expenses had not been proven.

The plaintiff appealed on 27 November 2008. A significant delay then occurred: the first hearing before the Riga Regional Court was not held until 13 September 2010—more than one year and nine months after the appeal was lodged—during which period no hearings took place. At that hearing, the plaintiff again increased its claim to LVL 3,173. On 22 December 2010, the Regional Court partly allowed the claim, ordering the applicant to pay LVL 2,854 (approximately EUR 4,059) plus default interest, despite finding that no maintenance services agreement had been concluded, because domestic law obliged her to pay for such services and she had failed to contest the bills.

The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law on 18 January 2011. The case then remained pending before the Senate of the Supreme Court for more than a year before being remitted to the Regional Court on 3 February 2012 because the applicant had not paid the required security deposit. After the deficiencies were rectified, the Senate refused to institute proceedings on points of law on 3 April 2012.

The proceedings thus lasted six years and more than four months across three levels of jurisdiction. The Court found the case was not complex, as it concerned a relatively small debt. While the applicant's conduct partially contributed to delays at first instance, the Court identified long periods of inactivity attributable solely to the higher courts, concluding that the "reasonable time" requirement under Article 6 § 1 had been violated.

In *Jóhannesson and Others v. Iceland* (Application no. 22007/11, judgment of 18 May 2017), the applicants were Jón Ásgeir Jóhannesson, Tryggvi Jónsson, and Fjárfestingafélagið Gaumur, an Icelandic limited company. They alleged that Iceland violated Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention (*ne bis in idem*) by punishing them twice for the same tax offences: first through tax surcharges imposed by the tax authorities and later through criminal proceedings for aggravated tax offences based on identical facts.

The tax investigation began in 2003. The Directorate of Tax Investigations audited the applicants’ tax returns and bookkeeping. Its reports concluded that the first and second applicants had failed to declare significant payments, car allowances, life-insurance payments, and profits from share sales in the Baugur Group. The third applicant had failed to account for salaries and allowances, withhold public levies, correctly declare share profits and losses, and had overdeclared expenditure. In December 2004 and December 2005, the Directorate of Internal Revenue re-assessed the applicants’ taxes for 1998–2002 and imposed 25% tax surcharges; the third applicant also received a further 10% surcharge for failing to withhold levies at source. The Internal Revenue Board largely upheld these surcharges in August and September 2007. The applicants did not seek judicial review, and the tax decisions became final in early 2008.

In parallel, in November 2004 the Director of Tax Investigations reported the matter to the National Police Commissioner. The police interviewed the applicants in August 2006 and treated them as suspects. In December 2008 the National Police Commissioner indicted them for aggravated tax offences. The criminal charges mirrored the tax findings: underdeclared income, unpaid allowances, failure to withhold and remit public levies, incorrect declaration of share profits and losses, and overdeclared expenditure.

In June 2010 the Reykjavik District Court accepted the applicants’ *ne bis in idem* objection. It found that the tax surcharge proceedings involved a “criminal charge” under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 and that the later indictment was based on the same facts already punished by the tax authorities. It dismissed those charges, relying on *Sergey Zolotukhin v. Russia*. The Acting National Commissioner appealed. In September 2010 the Supreme Court reversed, invoking dualism and section 2 of the ECHR Act. It held that domestic courts could not disapply the Icelandic system of tax surcharges followed by criminal proceedings, even for the same facts, because legislative amendment was required and ECtHR case-law was unclear.

The District Court then examined the merits. In December 2011 it convicted all three applicants on some charges, finding the first and second applicants had acted with gross negligence, but suspended penalty determination for one year, citing the excessive length of proceedings and the prior 25% surcharges. The first and second applicants and the prosecutor appealed; the third did not. In February 2013 the Supreme Court largely upheld the convictions, convicted the first applicant on two additional charges, revoked earlier suspended sentences, and imposed suspended prison terms and large fines. It considered the tax surcharges and excessive delay when fixing the fines.

The central alleged violation was that the tax surcharges amounted to a criminal penalty and that the subsequent criminal trial punished the applicants again for the same conduct, contrary to the prohibition on double jeopardy. The ECtHR ultimately found a violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 in respect of the first and second applicants; the third applicant’s case was struck out for failure to pursue it.

Iceland* (Application no. 22007/11), the applicants—Jón Ásgeir Jóhannesson, Tryggvi Jónsson, and Fjárfestingafélagið Gaumur—alleged that Iceland violated Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention (*ne bis in idem*). They claimed they had been tried twice for the same offence: first through tax surcharges imposed by tax authorities, and later through a criminal trial for aggravated tax offences based on identical facts.

Tax proceedings began on 17 November 2003, when the Directorate of Tax Investigations audited the applicants’ tax returns. Reports issued in 2004–2005 led the Directorate of Internal Revenue to rule on 30 December 2004 and 29 December 2005 that the first and second applicants had failed to declare significant payments, car allowances, life-insurance payments, and profits from share sales in the Baugur Group. It reassessed their taxes for 1999–2002 and imposed 25% tax surcharges. For the third applicant, the tax authority found failures to declare employee allowances, withhold public levies, declare share-sale profits/losses correctly, and overdeclared expenditure from 2000–2002. It reassessed taxes for 1998–2002, imposing a 25% surcharge and an additional 10% surcharge for failure to withhold levies. The Internal Revenue Board largely upheld these decisions on 29 August and 26 September 2007. The applicants did not seek judicial review, and the decisions became final in February and March 2008.

Meanwhile, on 12 November 2004, the tax investigation was referred to the National Police Commissioner. In August 2006 the applicants were interviewed by police and, according to the Government, informed they were suspects. On 18 December 2008 the National Police Commissioner indicted them for aggravated tax offences. The indictment covered substantially the same conduct: underdeclared income in 1999–2003, omitted payments from 1998–2002, car allowances, life-insurance payments, share-sale profits/losses, overdeclared expenses, and the company’s failure to declare salaries/allowances and withhold public levies.

On 1 June 2010, the Reykjavik District Court dismissed parts of the indictment. It found that the tax surcharge proceedings involved a “criminal charge” under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 and were based on the same facts as the criminal charges. Relying mainly on *Sergey Zolotukhin v. Russia*, it held that the later criminal proceedings were barred. The Supreme Court overturned that ruling on 22 September 2010. It reasoned that Icelandic law retained dualism, that the legislature would need to amend the dual system, and that ECtHR case-law on Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 was unclear. The District Court therefore examined the merits.

On 9 December 2011 the District Court convicted the applicants on some charges and suspended penalty determination for one year, citing excessive length and the prior 25% tax surcharge. On 7 February 2013 the Supreme Court upheld most convictions, convicted the first applicant on two additional charges, revoked earlier suspended sentences, and imposed suspended prison sentences and fines: 12 months and ISK 62 million for the first applicant; 18 months and ISK 32 million for the second. It considered the tax surcharges and excessive length when fixing sentence. The core alleged violation was that the tax surcharges and subsequent criminal convictions amounted to two criminal proceedings for the same conduct, contrary to the prohibition on double jeopardy.

**Jóhannesson and Others v. Iceland** (Application no. 22007/11) concerned three applicants—Jón Ásgeir Jóhannesson, Tryggvi Jónsson, and the Icelandic company Fjárfestingafélagið Gaumur. They alleged that Iceland violated Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the European Convention on Human Rights because they were tried and punished twice for the same tax offences: first through administrative tax surcharges, and later through criminal proceedings for aggravated tax offences.

In November 2003, the Directorate of Tax Investigations began auditing the applicants’ tax returns and bookkeeping. The resulting reports found that the first applicant had failed to declare significant payments received between 1998 and 2002, car allowances for 2000–2002, life-insurance payments, and profits from the sale of shares in the Baugur Group. The second applicant had failed to declare significant payments received from 1999 to 2002 and life-insurance payments made by Baugur. The third applicant had failed to account for salaries and car allowances enjoyed by the first applicant and other employees, failed to withhold and remit public levies, misreported profits and losses from share sales, and overdeclared expenditure.

On the basis of those findings, the Directorate of Internal Revenue re-assessed the applicants’ taxes and imposed 25% tax surcharges. The third applicant also received an additional 10% surcharge for failing to withhold levies at source. On appeal, the Internal Revenue Board largely upheld the surcharges in August and September 2007. The applicants did not seek judicial review, so those decisions became final in February and March 2008.

Separately, in November 2004, the Director of Tax Investigations reported the matter to the police. In August 2006, the applicants were interviewed and informed that they were suspects in a criminal investigation. In December 2008, the National Police Commissioner indicted them for aggravated tax offences. The indictment repeated essentially the same factual allegations: underdeclared income, unpaid withholding, incorrect share transactions, and overdeclared expenses.

In June 2010, the Reykjavik District Court dismissed parts of the indictment. It found that the criminal charges were based on the same facts as the tax surcharge decisions and that those tax proceedings involved a determination of a “criminal charge” under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. Relying on *Sergey Zolotukhin v. Russia*, the District Court held that the later prosecution was barred by *ne bis in idem*. The Supreme Court overturned that ruling in September 2010 and ordered the District Court to examine the merits. It reasoned that Icelandic dualism prevented domestic courts from invalidating the system of tax surcharges followed by criminal proceedings, and that Convention case-law was unclear, so legislative reform was required.

In December 2011, the District Court convicted the applicants on some charges, finding the first two applicants had acted with gross negligence, but suspended penalty determination because of excessive delay and the earlier 25% tax surcharges. In February 2013, the Supreme Court upheld most convictions, convicted the first applicant on additional counts, revoked earlier suspended sentences, and imposed suspended prison terms and fines: twelve months and ISK 62,000,000 for the first applicant, and eighteen months and ISK 32,000,000 for the second. The Supreme Court considered the excessive length of proceedings and the tax surcharges when fixing the fines.

The alleged violation therefore turned on whether the tax surcharges amounted to criminal punishment and whether the subsequent criminal trial for aggravated tax offences, based on identical facts, subjected the applicants to a second criminal proceeding contrary to Article 4 of Protocol No. 7.

In *Erol v. Germany* (Application no. 68250/11, 7 September 2017), the applicant, Ramazan Erol, a Turkish national living in Aachen, ran a café. On 20 April 2010, police searched the café and found him weighing and packaging about 400 grams of cocaine, with €2,325 in cash. He was arrested. The next day, the Aachen District Court issued a remand detention order, finding a strong suspicion of commercial trafficking in a substantial amount of drugs and a risk that he would abscond. It noted the possibility of a substantial prison sentence, his weak ties to Germany, his unemployment and reliance on social security, and the ease of fleeing to Turkey.

On 29 September 2010, the District Court convicted Erol on one count of commercial drug trafficking, acquitted him on two counts, sentenced him to two years and six months’ imprisonment, and continued his detention. Both Erol and the prosecutor appealed. Erol challenged his continued detention, arguing there was no risk of absconding: he had lived in Germany for twenty years, was married with two young children, and had parents and a brother in Germany. His only tie to Turkey was a family holiday home. The domestic courts maintained that the absconding risk remained because he faced a possibly longer sentence on the prosecutor’s appeal, had insufficient German, no employment, and family ties to Turkey. They considered that reporting conditions or security would not adequately address the risk.

The Cologne Court of Appeal indicated it might stay detention if security were furnished. It asked Erol to clarify the offer and required that the money be placed at his free disposal and its lawful origin shown. Erol’s counsel replied that his family was willing to deposit €10,000 directly with the court and prove its lawful origin, but not to put the money at Erol’s disposal. They feared the repayment claim could later be attached for authorities’ claims, including costs, meaning the security might be lost even if Erol did not abscond.

On 3 December 2010, the Cologne Court of Appeal dismissed Erol’s further appeal. It upheld the absconding risk, said it would consider staying detention if security were furnished, but refused the family’s direct deposit. It reasoned that the family’s unwillingness to entrust Erol with the money suggested a lack of confidence in him and that family ties were not strong enough to deter absconding. It also subsidiarily based detention on a risk of reoffending.

Erol later complained under Article 5 § 4 that the refusal to stay execution of the detention order breached his right to judicial review of the lawfulness of his detention. He argued the decision was arbitrary, especially because one month later the District Court accepted €5,000 from another person and released him, and because the family’s refusal was reasonable given the attachment risk. He also argued that relying on reoffending was unlawful.

The European Court of Human Rights declared the complaint admissible. Because Erol had already been convicted, his detention fell under Article 5 § 1(a), but Article 5 § 4 still applied because German law allowed detention review during appeal. The Court focused on whether the Court of Appeal’s insistence that Erol personally furnish security, rather than accepting third-party security, was arbitrary. It found that domestic and Convention case-law permit excluding third-party bail where the relationship may not deter absconding. The Court of Appeal gave detailed, relevant reasons and acted without bad faith. The later release involved different circumstances. The reoffending basis was a formal defect, not a gross and obvious irregularity rendering detention unlawful. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 5 § 4.

**Case: Erol v. Germany (Application no. 68250/11), ECtHR, 7 September 2017**

The applicant, Ramazan Erol, a Turkish national living in Aachen, Germany, was arrested on 20 April 2010 after police searched his café and found him weighing and packaging about 400 grams of cocaine, along with €2,325 in cash. On 21 April 2010, the Aachen District Court issued a detention order, finding a strong suspicion of commercial trafficking in a substantial amount of drugs and a risk of absconding. It noted the possible lengthy sentence, his weak ties to Germany, unemployment and reliance on social security, and the possibility that he could flee to Turkey.

In July 2010, the prosecution indicted him on three counts. On 29 September 2010, the District Court convicted him on one count, acquitted him on two, and sentenced him to two years and six months’ imprisonment, continuing his detention. Both the applicant and the prosecution appealed. The applicant also challenged his continued detention, arguing that there was no real risk of flight. He had lived in Germany for about twenty years, was married, had two young children, and his parents and brother lived in Germany. His only tie to Turkey was his parents’ holiday home.

The domestic courts nevertheless maintained detention. They cited the possibility of a longer sentence on the prosecution’s appeal, his unemployment and insufficient German, the fact that his wife was also Turkish, and the family’s holiday home in Turkey. The applicant offered €10,000 security. The Cologne Court of Appeal indicated it might stay execution if the applicant himself could dispose of the money and prove its lawful origin. His family was willing to deposit €10,000 directly with the court, but not to put it at the applicant’s disposal, fearing that authorities might attach the repayment claim to cover criminal proceedings costs.

On 3 December 2010, the Cologne Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s further appeal and refused to stay execution. It found a continuing flight risk and held that the family’s unwillingness to entrust the money to the applicant showed a lack of confidence in him and insufficient family ties to deter absconding. It also based detention subsidiarily on a risk of reoffending. The applicant complained that this breached Article 5 § 4 of the Convention, arguing that the flight-risk finding was wrong and the decision arbitrary. He also claimed that relying on a risk of reoffending violated domestic law.

The Government contested the complaint, arguing that detention had been reviewed repeatedly and that the refusal of third-party security was within the Court of Appeal’s discretion. It accepted that the subsidiary reliance on reoffending was a formal error but said the order remained valid, not void.

The European Court of Human Rights declared the complaint admissible. Since the applicant had already been convicted, his detention fell under Article 5 § 1 (a), but Article 5 § 4 was still applicable because domestic law allowed remand prisoners to seek review during appeal. The Court focused on whether the Court of Appeal’s refusal of his family’s offer of security was arbitrary. It found that domestic law and Convention case-law permitted courts to exclude third-party security where the guarantor relationship might not deter absconding. The Court of Appeal had given detailed, relevant reasons, and there was no bad faith. The later release on €5,000 security occurred after conviction became final and under different circumstances. As for the subsidiary reoffending ground, although prohibited, the flaw made the order defective but not void and did not amount to a gross and obvious irregularity. The Court therefore found **no violation of Article 5 § 4**.

In *Erol v. Germany* (ECtHR, 7 September 2017), the applicant, Ramazan Erol, a Turkish national living in Aachen, ran a café. On 20 April 2010, police searched the café and found him in a back room weighing and packaging about 400 grams of cocaine; he also had €2,325 in cash. He was arrested. The next day, the Aachen District Court issued a detention warrant on strong suspicion of commercial trafficking in a substantial amount of drugs and because of a risk that he would abscond. The court cited the possible lengthy sentence, his weak ties to Germany, unemployment and reliance on social security, and the ease of fleeing to Turkey.

On 29 September 2010, the District Court convicted Erol on one of three counts, acquitted him on two, sentenced him to two years and six months’ imprisonment, and ordered continued detention. Both Erol and the Public Prosecutor appealed. Erol also challenged the continued detention, arguing that he had lived in Germany for twenty years, was married with two young children, and had parents and a brother in Germany. His only tie to Turkey, he said, was a parents’ holiday home. The District and Regional Courts rejected this, finding a continuing risk of absconding because of the potential longer sentence, his insufficient German, unemployment and social security since 2001, his and his wife’s Turkish nationality, young children, and the Turkish holiday home.

The Cologne Court of Appeal then indicated it might stay execution of the detention order if security were furnished. It asked Erol to clarify the offer and required that the funds be placed at his own free disposal, with lawful origin shown. Erol’s family offered €10,000 directly to the court but refused to put the money at Erol’s disposal, fearing the authorities might attach the repayment claim for the costs of criminal proceedings. On 3 December 2010, the Court of Appeal refused to stay execution. It insisted that Erol himself furnish the security and inferred that his family’s unwillingness showed a lack of confidence in him, meaning family ties were not strong enough to prevent him from absconding. It also based detention subsidiarily on a risk of reoffending.

Erol complained under Article 5 § 4 that the Court of Appeal’s refusal to stay execution was arbitrary. He argued there was no real flight risk; direct third-party security was sufficient; the refusal served the authorities’ financial interest in recovering costs; and the subsidiary reoffending ground breached domestic law. The Government contested these claims, arguing that detention was reviewed repeatedly, the flight risk was properly assessed, domestic case-law allowed refusing third-party security, and any formal flaw did not make the order void.

The European Court of Human Rights found Article 5 § 4 applicable but focused narrowly on whether the Court of Appeal’s insistence on personal security was arbitrary. It held that domestic and Convention law permitted refusing bail or security from third parties where their relationship with the accused might not deter absconding. The Court of Appeal had given relevant, sufficient reasons and acted within its discretion. Its inference about the family’s lack of confidence was not arbitrary, and the later stay of execution for €5,000 was based on changed circumstances after conviction became final. The subsidiary reoffending ground was formally defective but not a gross and obvious irregularity. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 5 § 4.

In *Talpis v. Italy*, the applicant, Elisaveta Talpis, a Romanian and Moldovan national living in Italy, complained that the Italian authorities failed to protect her from domestic violence by her husband, A.T., leading to an attempt to murder her and the death of her son. The case concerned the alleged failure of the State to comply with its positive obligations to protect victims of domestic violence.

The applicant married A.T., a Moldovan national, and they had two children. She alleged that her husband, an alcoholic, had beaten her for years. In 2011 she followed him to Italy. On 2 June 2012, police intervened after A.T. assaulted the applicant and her daughter. The police report recorded that the applicant had been beaten and bitten in the face and leg and had bruises; her daughter had been injured while trying to protect her. The applicant alleged she was not informed of the possibility of lodging a complaint or contacting a shelter. No complaint was lodged at that stage.

On 19 August 2012, after receiving a threatening telephone call from A.T., the applicant left home. Later, A.T. broke into the cellar where she was staying, attacked her with a knife, and tried to force her to follow him. She managed to ask a police patrol for help. According to the applicant, the police merely checked their identity papers, told her to go home, told A.T. to stay away, and fined A.T. for unlawful possession of a knife. She was later taken to hospital with cranial trauma, a head injury, multiple abrasions, and a chest bruise.

On 5 September 2012, the applicant lodged a formal complaint against A.T. for bodily harm, ill-treatment, and threats. She asked the authorities to take prompt protective measures for her and her children and to prevent A.T. from approaching them. She stated that she had taken refuge in a women’s shelter and that A.T. was harassing her by telephone. A.T. was placed under investigation. In October 2012, the prosecution ordered urgent investigative measures, but according to the applicant no effective action followed. In March 2013, the prosecution again asked the police to investigate rapidly.

On 4 April 2013, seven months after the complaint, the applicant was questioned by police for the first time. She altered her earlier statements, minimising the violence. She later claimed she did so because of psychological pressure from A.T. In May 2013, the prosecution asked to close the ill-treatment and threats complaint. In August 2013, the investigating judge discontinued those charges, finding contradictions and that the alleged ill-treatment did not meet the requirement of repeated violence. The bodily harm proceedings continued; A.T. was committed for trial and later fined EUR 2,000.

On 18 November 2013, A.T. received notice of his committal for trial. In the night of 25 November 2013, police were called to a domestic dispute. They found a broken bedroom door and alcohol bottles, but no visible injuries. A.T. was intoxicated, taken to hospital, later left, was stopped by police at 2:25 a.m., fined, and released. At about 5 a.m., A.T. entered the family flat with a knife, stabbed his son three times, causing his death, and stabbed the applicant several times, severely injuring her. He was later sentenced to life imprisonment for murder, attempted murder, ill-treatment, and possession of a prohibited weapon.

The applicant alleged that the authorities knew of the repeated violence and her requests for protection but failed to act promptly and effectively, thereby failing to protect her and her children from foreseeable lethal violence.

**Summary of Talpis v. Italy (Application no. 41237/14)**

The case of *Talpis v. Italy* concerns a Moldovan-Romanian national, Ms. Elisaveta Talpis, who alleged that Italian authorities failed to protect her from domestic violence perpetrated by her husband, A.T., culminating in the attempted murder of the applicant and the murder of her son.

The applicant married A.T., an alcoholic who had subjected her to beatings since their marriage. In 2011, the family moved to Italy. On 2 June 2012, police intervened after A.T. assaulted the applicant and her daughter. The police report documented that the applicant had been beaten and bitten, sustaining bruises, while her daughter suffered injuries after intervening. The applicant alleged she was never informed of her right to lodge a complaint or access shelters for battered women. Although she stated an intention to seek hospital treatment, she ultimately did not go after waiting three hours.

Following this assault, the applicant began sleeping in the cellar of the family flat. On 19 August 2012, after a threatening phone call from A.T., she attempted to leave but was attacked by him with a knife in the cellar. He forced her to accompany him, allegedly intending to make her have sexual relations with his friends. When she sought help from a police patrol, officers merely checked identity papers and told A.T. to stay away from her, despite her assertions of threats and beatings. They fined A.T. for unauthorized possession of a lethal weapon but offered the applicant no assistance. Shortly afterward, she was hospitalized with cranial trauma, head injuries, multiple abrasions, and a chest bruise.

On 5 September 2012, the applicant formally lodged a complaint for bodily harm, ill-treatment, and threats, urging authorities to protect her and her children. A.T. was placed under judicial investigation. The prosecution ordered urgent investigative measures on 15 October 2012. However, despite repeated requests from the prosecution for police action—including a second request on 18 March 2013 noting that no investigative measures had been carried out—the applicant was not questioned until 4 April 2013, seven months after lodging her complaint.

During this interview, the applicant altered her statements, mitigating the seriousness of her allegations. She claimed A.T. had not threatened her with a knife during the August incident and that there had been no further violence. She later submitted that she had changed her account due to psychological pressure from her husband. On 30 May 2013, the prosecutor, relying on the applicant's revised statements, requested the closure of the ill-treatment complaint. On 1 August 2013, the investigating judge discontinued that part of the complaint, finding the events unclear and that the criterion of repeated violence was not met. Only the bodily harm charge proceeded.

On 18 November 2013, A.T. received notice of committal for trial for the August 2012 bodily harm. On the night of 25 November 2013, the applicant called police during a domestic dispute. Officers found a broken bedroom door and alcohol bottles, but neither the applicant nor her son showed signs of violence. A.T. was taken to hospital intoxicated, then left. Police later stopped him at 2:25 a.m. and released him after fining him. At 5 a.m., A.T. entered the family flat with a kitchen knife, intent on assaulting the applicant. Her son attempted to intervene and was stabbed three times, dying from his wounds. A.T. then chased the applicant into the street and stabbed her multiple times in the chest.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that Italian authorities failed to comply with their duty to protect her from domestic violence, which led to the attempted murder and her son's death.

**Talpis v. Italy** (Application no. 41237/14) concerned alleged failures by Italian authorities to protect a woman and her children from domestic violence. The applicant, Elisaveta Talpis, a Romanian and Moldovan national, lived in Italy with her Moldovan husband, A.T., an alcoholic who had allegedly abused her for years.

On 2 June 2012, police intervened after A.T. assaulted the applicant and her daughter. The police report recorded that the applicant had been beaten and bitten in the face and leg, with bruises, while her daughter suffered a neck injury and arm injuries after trying to protect her mother. The applicant later claimed she was not informed about lodging a complaint or contacting a shelter. She allegedly went to a hospital but left after waiting three hours. The Government disputed that she had gone to the hospital.

On 19 August 2012, after receiving a threatening call from A.T., the applicant left home but later returned to the cellar where she had been sleeping. She alleged A.T. attacked her there with a knife and tried to force her to have sexual relations with his friends. She sought help from a police patrol in the street. According to her account, police merely checked identity papers, told her to go home, and told A.T. to stay away; A.T. was fined for unauthorised possession of a knife. She then called emergency services and was taken to hospital, where doctors noted cranial trauma, a head injury, multiple abrasions and a chest bruise.

On 5 September 2012, the applicant lodged a formal complaint against A.T. for bodily harm, ill-treatment and threats. She expressly requested urgent protection for herself and her children and stated that A.T. was harassing her by telephone. A.T. was placed under investigation. On 15 October 2012, the prosecution ordered urgent investigative measures, but the applicant was not questioned until 4 April 2013 — seven months after her complaint. During that interview she substantially altered her statements, mitigating the seriousness of her allegations. She later claimed she did so because of psychological pressure from A.T.

On 30 May 2013, the prosecution asked to discontinue the ill-treatment complaint, noting that the applicant had retracted key allegations and that no further violent episodes had occurred. On 1 August 2013, the investigating judge discontinued the ill-treatment and threats charges, finding the events unclear and the offence of ill-treatment not made out because there had not been repeated episodes. The bodily harm charge continued. A.T. was committed for trial in October 2013 and eventually fined EUR 2,000 in October 2015.

Meanwhile, on the night of 25 November 2013, police intervened in a domestic dispute. A.T. was intoxicated and was taken to hospital but later left. He was stopped by police at 2:25 a.m. and released after an identity check and fine. At around 5 a.m., A.T. entered the family flat armed with a kitchen knife. He stabbed his son three times; the son died. He then chased the applicant into the street and stabbed her several times in the chest, attempting to murder her.

A.T. was later sentenced to life imprisonment for murder, attempted murder, ill-treatment and possession of a prohibited weapon, and ordered to pay the applicant EUR 400,000 in damages.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the Italian authorities had failed in their positive obligation to protect her from domestic violence, leading to the attempted murder and her son’s death. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are the repeated assaults, her explicit request for protection, the investigative delays, the discontinuance of ill-treatment charges, the absence of effective preventive measures, and the fatal attack that occurred despite prior police knowledge of the danger.
001-172665:
Claudio Podeschi, a San Marinese politician born in 1956, was investigated in joined criminal proceedings (nos. 769/12 and 184/14) for conspiracy and money laundering. On 23 June 2014 the inquiring judge issued detailed charges alleging that Podeschi had played a key role in a criminal organisation involving politicians, civil servants, entrepreneurs and bankers, using the San Marino Foundation for the Promotion of the Economy and Finances and other companies to conceal illicit funds. The judge ordered his arrest and detention on remand, finding serious evidence against him and risks of reoffending and tampering with evidence. He was imprisoned the same day.

On 24 June 2014, after requesting access to the files, his lawyers learned that file no. 769/12 was partially classified and file no. 184/14 entirely classified. Key material, including an Agency for Financial Information notification and annexes, was withheld. Only unclassified material was provided on the morning of questioning. On 25 June he appeared before the inquiring judge, remained silent, and complained that he could not examine the investigative material, had insufficient time with his lawyer, and had waited too long to appear. He challenged the detention, arguing that the secrecy time-limit had expired. The inquiring judge rejected this on 26 June. On 30 June the Judge of Criminal Appeals upheld his complaint about non-disclosure and ordered access to documents justifying detention, but on 18 July clarified that disclosure was only for the limited purpose of reviewing detention. The Third Instance Judge dismissed his complaints on 8 September 2014, finding the detention lawful and the information sufficient.

Further access requests were refused. On 15 September he sought revocation or a less restrictive measure; on 18 September the judge refused, citing continued tampering risks, alleged attempts to contact a private doctor, involve relatives, manipulate documents, and walkie-talkie communications with his co-accused. An appeal partly ordered declassification of further files on 13 October, but Podeschi claimed key evidence remained inaccessible. On 6 November the appeal court upheld detention, distinguishing pre-trial secrecy from trial rights and finding no need to repeat reasons.

In March 2015 he again sought release after a witness retracted testimony. This was refused because other grounds supported detention. On 9 March 2015, after new money-laundering charges, detention was prolonged due to risks of reoffending, flight and tampering, his support network, and evidence of favourable treatment in prison. The appeal court upheld this on 23 April 2015, noting San Marino law imposed no time-limit on pre-trial detention and that later charges arose from further investigations. House arrest was considered inappropriate. After partial declassification and an indictment, detention was revoked for indicted charges on 14 May but maintained for two new charges. On 2 July the Third Instance Judge suspended detention and ordered house arrest to protect defence rights and equality of arms. On 16 October 2015 house arrest was revoked and a travel ban imposed.

Regarding Article 3, Podeschi alleged that from 8 August 2014 he was isolated for 22 hours a day, lacked activities, could shower only weekly, and sometimes had no sanitary facilities, relying on CPT reports about the prison. He alleged violations of Article 3 (conditions of detention) and Article 5 §§ 3 and 4 (length/release pending trial and review of detention/equality of arms due to classified files). The Court communicated these complaints and declared the remainder inadmissible.

Claudio Podeschi, a San Marinese politician, applied to the European Court of Human Rights alleging violations of Articles 3 and 5 §§ 3 and 4 of the Convention arising from his pre-trial detention. He was investigated in two joined criminal proceedings concerning conspiracy and multiple money-laundering offences. In October 2012, one investigation file was classified under San Marino law because urgent investigative steps could be prejudiced by disclosure. On 23 June 2014, the inquiring judge charged Podeschi and others. The judge described evidence of a criminal organisation involving politicians, civil servants, entrepreneurs and bankers. Podeschi allegedly played a key role, using a San Marino foundation, shell companies, fictitious intermediary companies, frontmen and large transfers to conceal the criminal origins of funds. The judge ordered his arrest and detention on remand, finding a reasonable suspicion and risks of reoffending and tampering with evidence. Podeschi was imprisoned the same day.

As to Article 5 § 4 and equality of arms, on 24 June 2014 Podeschi’s lawyers requested access to the files and learned that file no. 769/12 was partially classified and file no. 184/14 was entirely classified. Withheld material included the initial notification by the Financial Information Agency, related notes and annexes. Only unclassified material in file no. 769/12 was provided on the morning of his questioning. On 25 June, Podeschi appeared before the inquiring judge but remained silent. He complained that he could not examine the investigative material, had had too little time with his lawyer, and had been delayed in appearing before the judge. He challenged his detention, sought release or a less restrictive measure, and requested declassification, arguing that the statutory secrecy period had expired. The inquiring judge rejected his requests on 26 June. On appeal, on 30 June 2014, the Judge of Criminal Appeals partially upheld his complaint and ordered disclosure of documents used to justify detention, with five days to submit observations. However, on 18 July it clarified that disclosure was only for the “limited aim” of challenging detention, and secrecy remained justified. The third-instance judge dismissed his complaints on 8 September 2014. Later, on 13 October 2014, the appeal judge ordered partial declassification of evidence underlying the refusal of bail, but Podeschi complained that the released documents did not substantiate the alleged grounds for continued detention, such as falsified documents, family collusion, simulated illness, or walkie-talkie conversations. On 6 November 2014, the appeal judge upheld detention, holding that pre-trial secrecy differed from trial and that equality of arms did not require further declassification. Further requests in April and May 2015 led only to partial disclosure; some material remained classified due to ongoing investigations and letters rogatory.

As to Article 5 § 3, Podeschi remained in pre-trial detention from 23 June 2014. He repeatedly challenged its lawfulness and sought release or house arrest. On 9 March 2015, the inquiring judge prolonged detention, citing further money-laundering charges and risks of reoffending, flight, tampering and his powerful network. The Judge of Criminal Appeals upheld this on 23 April 2015, noting that San Marino law imposed no time limit on pre-trial detention. On 2 July 2015, the third-instance judge suspended prison detention and ordered house arrest to protect defence rights and equality of arms. On 15 October 2015, he confirmed the earlier detention decisions but maintained house arrest; on 16 October 2015, house arrest was revoked and replaced by a travel ban.

As to Article 3, Podeschi was held at Carcere dei Cappucini. From 8 August 2014, he alleged isolation for twenty-two hours a day, no access to activities, only weekly showers, and periods without sanitary facilities, requiring him to relieve himself in a container in his cell. He described inhumane conditions and relied on CPT reports criticising the facility. He complained to the CPT on 30 June 2014.

The case of *Podeschi v. San Marino* concerned a San Marinese politician, Claudio Podeschi, who was investigated in two joined criminal proceedings (nos. 769/12 and 184/14) for conspiracy and money laundering. On 23 June 2014, the inquiring judge issued a detailed charging decision and ordered the applicant’s arrest and pre-trial detention, finding a risk that he would reoffend and tamper with evidence. The judge relied on evidence of large-scale transfers of money through the San Marino Foundation for the Promotion of the Economy and Finances, shell companies, frontmen and fictitious payment descriptions. He considered that the applicant had a key role in a criminal organisation involving politicians, civil servants, entrepreneurs and bankers, and that less restrictive measures would not prevent further money laundering or interference with evidence. The applicant was taken to prison the same day.

The applicant alleged violations of Articles 3 and 5 §§ 3 and 4 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Under Article 3, he complained about conditions of detention in the Carcere dei Cappucini. From 8 August 2014, he was allegedly isolated for twenty-two hours a day, had no access to other prison areas or activities, could shower only once a week, and for certain periods lacked sanitary facilities, having to relieve himself in a container in his cell. He relied on previous CPT reports criticising the facility and filed a complaint with the CPT on 30 June 2014.

Under Article 5 § 3, the applicant complained about the length of his pre-trial detention and the refusal to release him or impose a less restrictive measure. He was detained from 23 June 2014. His detention was repeatedly upheld on grounds of risk of reoffending, tampering with evidence and, later, possible flight. On 9 March 2015, the inquiring judge prolonged detention after further money-laundering charges were added. The Judge of Criminal Appeals upheld that decision on 23 April 2015, noting that San Marino law imposed no time-limit on pre-trial detention. On 2 July 2015, the third-instance judge suspended detention and ordered house arrest to protect defence rights and equality of arms; on 16 October 2015, house arrest was revoked and a travel ban imposed.

Under Article 5 § 4, the applicant alleged that he could not effectively challenge the lawfulness of his detention because of the secrecy/classification regime. On 24 June 2014, his lawyers learned that file no. 769/12 was partially classified and file no. 184/14 entirely classified. He was given only some material before questioning and complained of insufficient access. Although the Judge of Criminal Appeals on 30 June 2014 upheld his non-disclosure complaint and ordered access to documents justifying detention, a subsequent decision limited that access to the “limited aim” of the detention review. Later declassification orders in October 2014 and May 2015 were also partial. The applicant argued that the material disclosed did not include evidence said to support continued detention, such as alleged tampering, collusion with family members, simulated illness, or walkie-talkie conversations. The domestic courts held that secrecy was justified by the needs of the investigation and that the detention remained supported by sufficient grounds. The case therefore centred on whether the applicant’s detention conditions, its duration, and the restricted access to case materials violated Articles 3 and 5 §§ 3 and 4.
001-173103:
Krasniqi v. Austria concerned an application by Agron Krasniqi, a Kosovo national born in 1974, who alleged that Austria’s decision to expel him to Kosovo violated his right to respect for private and family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The facts relevant to that alleged violation centre on his long residence in Austria, his family ties there, his criminal record, his immigration status, and the domestic authorities’ proportionality assessment.

Krasniqi first entered Austria in January 1994, aged 19. In November 1994 he was arrested for illegal work and given a five-year residence ban. His 1995 asylum claim was dismissed, and he returned to Kosovo in September 1997. In July 1998 he returned to Austria with his wife and daughter and applied for asylum. Although asylum was refused, he and his family were granted subsidiary protection and temporary residence permits, which were extended several times. His permit expired in December 2009 after he failed to apply for renewal.

Between 2003 and 2012, Krasniqi received nine criminal convictions in Austria. These included bodily harm in 2003, 2006 and 2010; a brawl in 2004; aggravated burglary in 2003, for which he received twelve months’ imprisonment, mostly suspended; drugs offences and aggravated threat in 2007, resulting in ten months’ imprisonment with a suspended sentence revoked; another drugs offence in 2010; and aggravated threat in 2012, for which he received seven months’ imprisonment. In 2007, because of these convictions, the authorities issued a ten-year return ban, but it had no effect while his subsidiary protection remained valid.

In 2010, the Federal Asylum Office began proceedings to withdraw his subsidiary protection. At an interview, Krasniqi stated that he had four children, born between 1997 and 2006, that his parents and siblings lived in Austria, and that he and his wife both worked. He said he did not fear repression in Kosovo but had a “bad feeling” about returning. The Office withdrew his subsidiary protection, found no Article 2 or 3 risk, and declared his expulsion admissible. On Article 8, it accepted that his private and family life in Austria was established, but held that his numerous convictions—especially the drug offences—meant the public interest in expulsion outweighed his personal interests. It also noted his ties to Kosovo: he had grown up there, spoke Albanian, could work, and his father owned land and shops there. His wife had her own income, and he could send maintenance from Kosovo.

In 2011, the Asylum Court upheld that decision. It calculated that his fines amounted to 1,460 daily rates, equivalent to almost twenty-four months’ imprisonment, and his actual prison sentences totalled twenty-two months. Although he had strong family ties in Austria, the public interest in preventing crime outweighed them, particularly because he had reoffended after the return ban. It noted he could reapply for residence in 2017.

Krasniqi then complained to the Constitutional Court, adding that one daughter had been born from an extra-marital relationship with an Austrian citizen and lived with her Austrian mother; expulsion would make contact difficult. The Asylum Court replied that he had never previously mentioned this daughter, that she had never lived with him, and that he could pay maintenance from Kosovo. The Constitutional Court refused to deal with the complaint in December 2011.

Krasniqi was detained from June 2012 until January 2013 and was expelled to Kosovo on 5 January 2013. His family remained in Austria. The return ban remains in force until November 2017. He alleged that the expulsion violated Article 8.

Krasniqi v. Austria concerned a Kosovo national, Agron Krasniqi, who alleged that his expulsion from Austria to Kosovo violated his right to respect for private and family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. He first entered Austria in January 1994 at age 19. After an unsuccessful asylum claim and a five-year residence ban, he voluntarily returned to Kosovo in September 1997. In July 1998 he returned to Austria with his wife and daughter and lodged a fresh asylum claim. Although the asylum claim was rejected, he and his family were granted subsidiary protection and temporary residence permits, which were extended several times. His residence permit expired in December 2009 because he did not apply for renewal.

The case centered on his extensive criminal record in Austria. Between 2003 and 2012, he was convicted nine times, including for bodily harm, aggravated burglary, participation in a brawl, drug offences, aggravated threat, attempted bodily harm, and endangering the physical integrity of others. He received fines and prison sentences. In 2003 he was in pre-trial detention and prison from July to November; in 2007 he was imprisoned from May to November and later served the remainder of his sentence; in 2012 he was again in detention and prison. In September 2007, because of these convictions, the authorities issued a ten-year ban prohibiting his return to Austria. The ban, however, had no effect while his subsidiary protection status remained valid.

In March 2010 the Federal Asylum Office began proceedings to withdraw his subsidiary protection. In an interview, Krasniqi described his established life in Austria: he had four children born in 1997, 1999, 2000 and 2006; his parents, siblings and their families lived in the same city; his parents and older brother were recognised refugees; he and his wife worked and had regular income; and he lived with his parents. He said he would not know what to do in Kosovo and had a bad feeling about returning, though he did not fear repression. His wife and children would probably join him, but he preferred to stay in Austria because his children attended school there. He also stated that his father owned land and three shops in Kosovo, run by relatives.

In May 2010 the Federal Asylum Office withdrew his subsidiary protection, found no real risk of ill-treatment in Kosovo, and declared his expulsion admissible. Balancing Article 8, it acknowledged his private and family ties in Austria but found the public interest in preventing crime outweighed them, especially given his drug convictions. It noted his ties to Kosovo, his ability to work, and his wife’s income. In June 2011 the Asylum Court confirmed the decision, observing that his fines amounted to almost twenty-four months’ imprisonment and his actual prison sentences totaled twenty-two months. He had reoffended after the return ban, and could reapply for residence in 2017 when the ban expired.

The applicant later revealed that one daughter had been born from an extra-marital relationship with an Austrian citizen and lived with her Austrian mother, not with him. The Asylum Court found this family life less established and said he could pay maintenance from Kosovo. The Constitutional Court refused to hear his complaint in December 2011. Krasniqi was expelled to Kosovo in January 2013, while his family remained in Austria. The return ban remained in force until November 2017. The European Court of Human Rights communicated only the Article 8 complaint, declaring the remainder of the application inadmissible.

**Case: Krasniqi v. Austria (Application no. 41697/12), Judgment of 25 April 2017**

The applicant, Agron Krasniqi, a Kosovo national born in 1974, alleged that his expulsion from Austria to Kosovo violated his right to respect for private and family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court communicated only that complaint to the Austrian Government; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

Krasniqi first entered Austria in January 1994, aged 19. In November 1994 he was arrested for working illegally and received a five-year residence ban. His 1995 asylum claim was dismissed, and he voluntarily returned to Kosovo in September 1997. In July 1998 he returned to Austria with his wife and daughter and lodged a fresh asylum claim. Although the asylum claim was dismissed, he and his family were granted subsidiary protection and temporary residence permits, which were extended several times. His permit expired in December 2009 because he did not apply for renewal.

The applicant had an extensive criminal record in Austria. Between 2003 and 2012 he was convicted nine times, including for bodily harm, aggravated burglary, participating in a brawl, drug offences, aggravated threat, attempted bodily harm, and endangering physical integrity. His sentences included fines and imprisonment; he served prison terms in 2003, 2007, 2009–2010, and 2012. In September 2007, because of these convictions, a ten-year ban prohibiting his return to Austria was issued and confirmed in November 2007. The applicant did not appeal. However, the ban remained ineffective while his subsidiary protection status was valid.

In 2010 the Federal Asylum Office began proceedings to withdraw his subsidiary protection. In an interview, the applicant described his established life in Austria: he had four children born between 1997 and 2006; his parents, siblings, and their families lived in the same city; his parents and older brother were recognised refugees; he lived in the same house as his parents; he worked as a maintenance man and Albanian-German translator; and his wife also worked, giving them a regular income. He stated that if returned to Kosovo he would not know what to do or where to go, though he did not fear repression. His wife and children would probably join him if he were expelled, but he preferred to stay in Austria because his children attended school there. He later stated that one daughter had been born from an extra-marital relationship with an Austrian citizen and lived with her Austrian mother, making contact difficult if he were expelled.

In May 2010 the Federal Asylum Office withdrew his subsidiary protection, finding no longer a risk under Articles 2 or 3 if he returned to Kosovo, and declared his expulsion admissible. On Article 8, it accepted that his private and family life in Austria was well established, but found the public interest in expulsion outweighed his personal interest because of his numerous convictions, especially drug offences. It noted he still had ties to Kosovo: he had grown up there, spoke Albanian, his father owned land and three shops run by relatives, and he could work. It also assumed his wife’s income could support the family and that he could send maintenance from Kosovo.

In June 2011 the Asylum Court confirmed the decision. It treated his fines—1,460 daily rates—as equivalent to almost 24 months’ imprisonment, and his actual prison sentences totalled 22 months. Although he had strong family ties in Austria, the public interest in preventing crime outweighed them, particularly because he reoffended after the return ban. He could reapply for residence in 2017. The Constitutional Court refused to hear his complaint in December 2011. He was expelled to Kosovo on 5 January 2013, while his family remained in Austria; the return ban ran until November 2017.

The alleged violation was that this expulsion disproportionately interfered with his Article 8 rights. The Court ultimately found no violation of Article 8.
001-175121:
In *Satakunnan Markkinapörssi Oy and Satamedia Oy v. Finland* (Application no. 931/13), two Finnish companies alleged that Finland violated Article 10 (freedom of expression) and Article 6 § 1 (excessive length) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The first applicant, Satakunnan Markkinapörssi Oy, had since 1994 collected tax data from Finnish authorities and published individuals’ taxable income and assets in the *Veropörssi* newspaper. Under Finnish law, certain tax information—such as name, year of birth, municipality, earned and capital income, taxable net assets, and total taxes—was public and accessible to anyone.

In 2002, *Veropörssi* published 17 issues covering different geographical areas. Each issue listed alphabetically, by municipality and income bracket, the names of about 1.2 million people whose annual taxable income exceeded certain thresholds, mainly FIM 60,000–80,000 (approximately EUR 10,000–13,500), together with their income and taxable net assets rounded to the nearest EUR 100. In 2003, the first applicant transferred the published data on CD-ROMs to the second applicant, Satamedia Oy. With a mobile operator, Satamedia started an SMS service: by sending a person’s name to a service number, a user could receive that person’s tax information if it was in the database. From 2006, Satamedia also published *Veropörssi*.

The Data Protection Ombudsman advised the companies to stop publishing tax data in the manner and to the extent done in 2002, and to stop passing the data to the SMS service. He asked the Data Protection Board to prohibit the processing, arguing that the Personal Data Act applied and that the journalism derogation did not cover collecting and passing on tax data. The Board refused in 2004, finding that the journalism exception applied and that the SMS service used already published data. The Ombudsman appealed. The Helsinki Administrative Court rejected the appeal in 2005, interpreting the journalism derogation broadly and noting that the data were already public. The Ombudsman further appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court, which in 2007 requested a preliminary ruling from the CJEU.

In 2008, the CJEU held that the activities involved processing personal data. The journalistic-purpose exception had to be interpreted broadly, but privacy derogations could apply only so far as strictly necessary; whether the activities were journalistic was for the national court to decide. In 2009, the Supreme Administrative Court quashed the earlier decisions and referred the case back to the Data Protection Board, requesting a prohibition. It reasoned that the case concerned personal data processing, not public access to tax data or the right to publish as such. Collecting data in a background file for journalistic use could be protected if properly secured. However, publishing the background file almost verbatim on a large scale as municipality/income catalogues was not processing solely for journalistic purposes and was unnecessary for public debate. Passing the data to Satamedia for the SMS service was also not journalistic: it was not disclosure to the general public but an individual query about another person’s data.

The Board then prohibited the first applicant from processing tax data as in 2002 and from forwarding it to an SMS service, and prohibited the second applicant from collecting, storing or forwarding such data. Appeals were rejected by the Turku Administrative Court in 2010 and the Supreme Administrative Court in 2012, which reiterated that the measures did not amount to prior censorship or a ban on publishing tax information as such. The SMS service shut down and the newspaper later ceased or was heavily reduced. The companies alleged that these prohibitions breached Article 10 and that the domestic proceedings were excessively long under Article 6.

The case arose from the applicants’ publication and reuse of taxation data. Under Finnish law, information on individuals’ taxable income and net assets is public and accessible, but the Personal Data Act regulated processing of personal data and provided a derogation for journalism. The first applicant, Satakunnan Markkinapörssi Oy, collected tax data and published *Veropörssi*. In 2002 the newspaper appeared 17 times and listed the surnames and forenames of about 1.2 million persons whose annual taxable income exceeded certain thresholds, along with their earned and unearned income and taxable net assets. The data were arranged alphabetically and by municipality and income bracket. In 2003 the first applicant transferred the published data on CD-ROMs to the second applicant, Satamedia Oy, which with a mobile operator launched an SMS service: by sending a person’s name, a user could obtain that person’s tax information by text message.

After the Data Protection Ombudsman considered this unlawful processing rather than journalism, he asked the Data Protection Board to prohibit processing to the 2002 extent and passing data to the SMS service. The Board dismissed the request, finding the journalism derogation applied, and the Helsinki Administrative Court upheld that outcome. On the Ombudsman’s appeal, the Supreme Administrative Court sought a preliminary ruling from the CJEU. In 2008 the CJEU held that the activities were processing of personal data; the journalistic-purpose derogation had to be interpreted broadly, but privacy derogations only so far as strictly necessary, and the national court had to decide whether the sole object was disclosure to the public. In 2009 the Supreme Administrative Court quashed the earlier decisions and referred the matter back. It held that collecting and storing data in a background file before publication could be journalistic, but publishing the background file almost verbatim on a large scale as catalogues was not processing solely for journalistic purposes. Handing the data to the second applicant and the SMS service also fell outside the journalism derogation, because the SMS service provided individual data on request rather than disclosing information to the general public.

The Data Protection Board then prohibited the first applicant from processing tax data in the 2002 manner and from forwarding it to an SMS service, and prohibited the second applicant from collecting, storing or forwarding such data. The applicants’ appeals failed in the Turku Administrative Court in 2010 and in the Supreme Administrative Court in 2012. They complained to the ECtHR that these measures violated Article 10, amounting to censorship or prior restraint and an unjustified restriction on publishing public-interest information and operating the SMS service. They also alleged that the domestic proceedings were excessively long under Article 6 § 1, the first set running from 2004 to 2009 and the second from 2009 to 2012; the application was lodged on 18 December 2012. Central to the alleged Article 10 violation was the tension between publicly accessible tax data and data protection rules: Finnish law permitted access to the data, but the domestic authorities distinguished mere accessibility from lawful further dissemination and found the scale of publication and SMS reuse did not qualify for the journalism exemption.

In *Satakunnan Markkinapörssi Oy and Satamedia Oy v. Finland* (Application no. 931/13), two Finnish publishing companies alleged that Finland violated Article 10 (freedom of expression) and Article 6 § 1 (length of proceedings) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The first applicant, Satakunnan Markkinapörssi Oy, had since 1994 collected publicly accessible tax data from Finnish tax authorities and published it in the newspaper *Veropörssi*. In 2002 it published data on approximately 1.2 million natural persons whose annual taxable income exceeded thresholds of roughly EUR 10,000–13,500. The data included names, earned and unearned income, and taxable net assets, arranged alphabetically by municipality and income bracket. The second applicant, Satamedia Oy, received the published data on CD-ROMs and, with a mobile operator, launched an SMS service: by texting a person’s name, a user could obtain that person’s tax information.

The Data Protection Ombudsman considered these activities unlawful. In April 2003 he asked the Data Protection Board to prohibit the companies from processing tax data in the same manner and to the same extent as in 2002 and from passing it to the SMS service. He argued that the Personal Data Act’s journalism derogation did not apply because the collection and transfer of tax information were not for journalistic purposes. In January 2004 the Board refused, finding the journalism derogation applicable and the SMS service outside the Act because the data had already been published. The Helsinki Administrative Court upheld that decision in 2005, stressing that the data were publicly accessible and that publication served the public interest.

The Ombudsman appealed. In 2007 the Supreme Administrative Court sought a preliminary ruling from the CJEU. In December 2008 the CJEU held that the activities involved processing personal data under Directive 95/46/EC. The journalism derogation had to be interpreted broadly, but privacy protection could be derogated from only so far as strictly necessary. Whether activities were solely journalistic—i.e. disclosure of information, opinions or ideas to the public—was for the national court to determine.

In September 2009 the Supreme Administrative Court quashed the earlier decisions. It held that collecting and storing data in the pre-publication background file could be journalistic if properly protected. However, publishing the background file almost verbatim as large-scale catalogues was not solely journalistic. Nor was handing the CD-ROM to Satamedia or operating the SMS service journalistic: the SMS service did not disclose data to the general public but answered individual requests about other individuals. The applicants complained that this decision violated the constitutional prohibition of censorship and their right to freedom of expression, arguing that domestic law did not permit preventing publication based on the amount of information or the means used.

In November 2009 the Data Protection Board prohibited the first applicant from processing tax data as in 2002 and forwarding it to an SMS service, and prohibited the second applicant from collecting, storing or forwarding such data. The companies’ appeals were rejected by the Turku Administrative Court in 2010 and by the Supreme Administrative Court in 2012. They then applied to the ECtHR, alleging that the prohibitions breached their Article 10 right to freedom of expression and that the domestic proceedings had been excessively long under Article 6 § 1. The Grand Chamber heard the case in September 2016.
