The case arose from a defamation action against Independent Newspapers (Ireland) Limited, publisher of the *Evening Herald*. In late 2004 the newspaper published eleven articles over two weeks about Ms L, a public relations consultant hired by government departments while Mr C was minister. The articles questioned the tendering process, her qualifications, her remuneration and the work done, and referred to eight foreign trips including a UN conference. They also repeated rumours of an intimate relationship between Ms L and Mr C and used photographs, including a manipulated front-page photomontage and headline. The story became headline news and led to parliamentary questions and a 2005 report finding shortcomings but no specific infringement.

Ms L sued for defamation. In 2009 a High Court jury found that the articles meant she had had an extra-marital affair with Mr C, which was defamatory; it rejected a second alleged meaning. The jury awarded €1,872,000. Under Irish law, the trial judge could not suggest a figure or range to the jury. He told jurors to be fair, not to be overcome by generosity, and not to make a ridiculously large award, but gave no meaningful quantum guidelines. The applicant accepted the defamation finding, apologized, and appealed only the damages, arguing the award was disproportionate and violated its Article 10 right to freedom of expression. It submitted that €175,000 would have been sufficient.

Under the pre-2009 Irish regime, juries assessed defamation damages. The Supreme Court could set aside excessive awards, but intervention was limited and retrials were common; the Defamation Act 2009, which later permitted judicial directions and Supreme Court substitution, did not apply. In 2014 the Supreme Court found the award excessive and set it aside. The majority substituted €1.25 million; the dissenting judge would have ordered a retrial or awarded €1 million. The Court described the libel as a serious and sustained attack on Ms L’s business and personal integrity, widely published, with no pre-verdict apology and manipulated photographs, causing personal and professional harm, though not among the gravest libels. The applicant paid a further €500,000, bringing compensation to €1.25 million, plus €240,448.16 costs.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 10 that the award was disproportionately high and that domestic safeguards against excessive defamation damages were inadequate and ineffective. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation were that the jury received no effective guidance on quantum; the trial judge could not indicate any range; appellate review was deferential and intervened only where no reasonable jury could have made the award; and even after reduction the sum remained very high. The applicant argued this created a chilling effect on the press and failed to balance freedom of expression against reputation. The ECtHR found a violation of Article 10, holding that Irish law did not provide adequate safeguards against disproportionate defamation awards.

001-170361:
**Case Stamova v. Bulgaria (Application no. 8725/07)**

The applicant, Ms Elka Dimitrova Stamova, was a Bulgarian national and sole trader who rented a municipally-owned shop in Primorsko from 28 April 1993. The shop was a metal structure on a concrete foundation on municipal land. In September 1995 she asked Tsarevo Municipal Council to sell her the shop under the preferential privatisation procedure for tenants of State and municipal property, also expressing interest in buying the land. When the council did not reply, she sought judicial review of its tacit refusal.

In a final judgment of 4 November 2003, the Supreme Administrative Court quashed the lower court’s rejection and found that the applicant had a valid lease and that all statutory conditions for privatising the shop were met. It remitted the case with instructions that the municipal council open a privatisation procedure and offer to sell the shop to her. After administrative boundary changes, a second final judgment of 28 November 2005 again confirmed that she met the conditions and referred the matter to Primorsko Municipal Council. The council explicitly refused to sell in November 2005 and October 2006. In a third final judgment of 31 March 2008, the Supreme Administrative Court annulled those refusals as null and void, holding that the council was obliged to sell the shop to the applicant and noting that no evidence supported the council’s claim that the shop no longer existed.

Despite these judgments, the sale was never completed. Meanwhile, the authorities took steps against the applicant’s possession. In 1996 the municipal company managing the shop told her she had no lease for 1996 and asked her to vacate; its later rei vindicatio claim was dismissed in 2002, with the Supreme Court of Cassation holding that her lease could not be terminated pending privatisation. In 1999 the mayor ordered the shop demolished, but the regional governor revoked the order in 2000 because the mayor lacked competence absent a municipal council decision and because the lease could not be terminated pending privatisation. Also in 1999, the municipal company sold the shop to a private company. The buyer, assisted by municipal employees, prevented the applicant from entering. After she complained, the prosecutor found the buyer’s conduct abusive and police helped her regain possession. Electricity was cut off until 2001. The buyer’s rei vindicatio claim was dismissed in a final judgment of 14 October 2003, which found that the buyer had not acquired ownership and that the applicant was protected from eviction pending examination of her privatisation proposal.

Later, Primorsko Municipal Council deemed the shop dilapidated and unsafe due to corrosion and ordered its sale for demolition. In 2005 it sold the shop to an individual, and on 14 February 2006 the mayor ordered that buyer to demolish it. Although the mayor revoked his order the next day, the buyer dismantled the shop on 18 February 2006 with police assistance. The applicant learned of the demolition only from an acquaintance and had not known about the sale. The parties disputed what happened to her belongings: the Government said they were listed and taken for safekeeping; the applicant said they were destroyed.

In 2006 the applicant sought criminal proceedings against the mayor and council chairperson for breach of duties and obstruction of a final judgment. In February 2007 the prosecutor refused, reasoning that the refusals came from a collective body while criminal responsibility was personal. Further privatisation requests in 2006 and 2008 led the municipality to cite complexity and form a commission; the Privatisation Agency stated that the municipality remained obliged to comply with court judgments.

In 2011 the applicant claimed damages under the State and Municipalities Responsibility for Damage Act. Against the municipality concerning the demolition order, courts found she lacked standing because she was not its addressee. Against the municipal council, she sought pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages for failure to implement the final judgments, including rent paid from January 1998 to February 2006, destroyed belongings, lost income, lost investment opportunity, and stress and depression supported by medical records. The first-instance court declared the claims admissible in January 2014.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that the municipal authorities’ failure to sell the shop as ordered by three final judgments breached her right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, and that she lacked an effective remedy.

001-173091:
In *Sommer v. Germany* (Application no. 73607/13, judgment 27 April 2017), the European Court of Human Rights examined a German criminal defence lawyer’s complaint under Article 8 of the Convention. The applicant, Ulrich Sommer, defended a client in 2009. After those proceedings ended, the client’s fiancée transferred EUR 1,500 from her private bank account to Sommer’s professional account, with the reference “Prof Dr Sommer fees” and the client’s surname.

In 2010–2011, the Bochum public prosecution office investigated several people suspected of commercial gang fraud. One suspect was Sommer’s former client, who again retained Sommer as defence counsel. During the investigation, prosecutors inspected bank accounts of the client and his fiancée. They discovered that the fiancée had received EUR 7,400 suspected to be proceeds of crime and had transferred EUR 1,500 to Sommer’s account for legal fees. On that basis, the prosecutor contacted Sommer’s bank. In March 2011, he requested all transactions on Sommer’s professional account from 1 January 2009 onward and asked the bank not to inform Sommer. In April 2011, he requested further information, including other accounts, balances, rights of disposal, addresses, foreign transfers, credit cards, and all transactions from January 2009. The bank complied.

The information was analysed by police and prosecutors, and a list of 53 relevant transactions was placed in the investigation file. That file was accessible to others, including defence counsel for the co-accused, thereby revealing Sommer’s clients’ names and fees. Sommer only learned of the measures in January 2012 when he was granted access to the file. He asked the Chief Public Prosecutor to return and destroy the data, arguing that the measures lacked a legal basis and violated lawyer-client confidentiality. The prosecutor refused, relying on Article 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the suspicion that the transferred money came from illegal activity. The Regional Court refused Sommer’s application but restricted access to the documents. The Court of Appeal upheld that decision, finding the measure proportionate and the lawyer-protection provisions inapplicable. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to admit Sommer’s constitutional complaint.

Before the ECtHR, Sommer alleged that the public prosecution office had collected, stored, and made available information about his professional bank account in a disproportionate manner, violating Article 8. He argued that the information gave a complete picture of his professional activity and clients and circumvented his duty of confidentiality. The Government accepted that there had been a relatively minor interference but argued it was lawful under Article 161 CCP, pursued crime prevention, and was proportionate because the data was financial, only limited excerpts entered the file, access was restricted, and judicial review was available.

The ECtHR found that collecting, storing, and making available the applicant’s professional bank transactions interfered with his private life and professional confidentiality. It accepted that the measure pursued the legitimate aim of preventing crime. However, it found the interference disproportionate and not “necessary in a democratic society.” The requests were very broad, covering all transactions over more than two years and potentially private accounts. The legal threshold under Article 161 CCP was low, the bank’s compliance was not clearly voluntary because refusal could lead to coercive summons, banks were not treated as protected “persons assisting,” and the Article 160a safeguard for lawyers was suspended on a vague suspicion. There was no prior judicial authorisation or specific procedural safeguard for legal privilege, and Sommer was not notified. Although retrospective judicial review was possible, the Court concluded that the interference violated Article 8.

**Case: Sommer v. Germany (App. no. 73607/13, ECtHR, 27 April 2017)**

The applicant, Ulrich Sommer, is a German criminal defence lawyer. He complained under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that the Bochum public prosecution office had disproportionately collected, stored, and made available information about his professional bank account, thereby revealing information about his clients.

**Key facts.** In 2009, the applicant defended a client in criminal proceedings. After the proceedings ended, the client’s fiancée transferred EUR 1,500 in legal fees from her private account to the applicant’s professional account. The transfer reference stated: “Prof Dr Sommer fees (client’s last name).” In 2010–2011, the Bochum prosecution investigated several people, including the applicant’s former client, for commercial gang fraud. During the investigation, authorities inspected bank accounts of the client and his fiancée. They discovered that the fiancée had received EUR 7,400 suspected to come from illegal activity and had transferred EUR 1,500 to the applicant for legal fees.

On 1 March 2011, the prosecutor asked the applicant’s bank for a list of all transactions on his account from 1 January 2009 onward and asked the bank not to inform him. On 1 April 2011, the prosecutor sought further details: other accounts, rights of disposal, balances, addresses, foreign transfers, all transactions from 1 January 2009, and credit-card information. The bank complied. The prosecutor did not formally order production but warned of witness obligations and possible coercive consequences. The data were analysed, and a list of 53 relevant transactions was placed in the investigation file, accessible to others such as counsel for co-accused. The applicant learned of the measures only in January 2012 when he obtained access to the file.

The applicant asked the Chief Public Prosecutor to return and destroy the data. This was refused in May 2012 on the basis that the fee transfer justified investigating further transfers, and Article 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provided a legal basis. The Regional Court refused his application, finding the investigation lawful and the bank’s provision of information voluntary, though it later restricted access to the documents. The Court of Appeal confirmed, and the Federal Constitutional Court declined to admit his constitutional complaint in September 2013.

**Alleged violation.** The applicant alleged that the collection, storage, and disclosure of his professional banking information violated Article 8. He argued that the data covered nearly three years, gave a complete picture of his professional activity and clients, and circumvented lawyer-client confidentiality. He claimed there was no formal investigation or sufficient suspicion against him, that Article 161 CCP was an inadequate legal basis, and that Article 160a CCP protected lawyers from such measures. He also complained of disproportionate interference and the absence of judicial authorisation or safeguards for legal professional privilege.

The Government accepted a relatively minor interference. It said the data were financial only, access was limited, Article 161 CCP was a blanket clause for low-level measures, the fraud investigation was serious, the bank acted voluntarily, and safeguards existed under Article 160a and judicial review.

**Court’s conclusion.** The ECtHR found an interference with the applicant’s private life and professional confidentiality. Although the aim of investigating crime was legitimate, the interference was not “necessary in a democratic society.” The requests were wide, covering all transactions over more than two years and other accounts, giving a complete picture of his practice and clients. The bank’s voluntary compliance was doubtful because of the warning of coercive summons. Article 160a’s protection for lawyers was lifted on vague suspicion based merely on a fee transfer. There was no judicial authorisation and no specific procedural safeguards for legal professional privilege. The applicant was not notified and learned of the measure only from the file. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 8.

Sommer v. Germany (Application no. 73607/13, ECtHR, 27 April 2017) concerned a German criminal defence lawyer, Ulrich Sommer, who complained under Article 8 ECHR that the Bochum public prosecution office disproportionately collected, stored and disclosed information from his professional bank account, thereby revealing client information.

In 2009 the applicant defended a client in criminal proceedings. After those proceedings ended and the client was imprisoned, the client’s fiancée transferred €1,500 in legal fees from her private account to the applicant’s professional account. The transfer reference included the applicant’s name and the client’s surname.

In 2010–2011, the Bochum prosecution investigated several people suspected of gang-related commercial fraud. One suspect was the applicant’s former client, who again retained the applicant as defence counsel. During the investigation, authorities inspected accounts of several persons, including the client and his fiancée. They discovered that the fiancée had received €7,400 suspected to come from illegal activity and had transferred €1,500 to the applicant’s account for legal fees.

On that basis, on 1 March 2011 the prosecutor asked the applicant’s bank for a list of all transactions on his account from 1 January 2009 to date, and asked the bank not to reveal the request. On 1 April 2011, further questions sought information about other accounts, rights of disposal, balances, closed accounts, addresses, foreign transactions, all transactions from 2009, and credit cards. The bank complied. The prosecutor did not formally order disclosure but warned of witness obligations and possible coercive consequences. Police and prosecutors analysed the data; a list of 53 relevant transactions was placed in the investigation file as evidence. Consequently, others with file access, including counsel for co-accused, could see the applicant’s banking information and clients’ names.

The applicant only learned of the measures on 31 January 2012 when granted access to the file as defence counsel. He asked the Chief Public Prosecutor to return and destroy the data, stressing his role as a criminal defence lawyer and lawyer-client confidentiality, and arguing there was no legal basis. The prosecutor refused, citing a suspicion that the money transferred via the fiancée stemmed from crime and relying on Article 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, treating the public-law bank as an authority. The Regional Court and Court of Appeal upheld the measures, finding the bank had acted voluntarily, that seizure protections did not apply, and that the bank was not a “person assisting” under Article 53a of the CCP. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to admit the applicant’s constitutional complaint.

Before the ECtHR, the key issue was whether the collection, storage and disclosure of the professional bank account data violated Article 8. The Court found an interference with private life and professional confidentiality. Relevant factors included the broad scope of the requests, covering all transactions over more than two years and other possible accounts; the resulting complete picture of the applicant’s professional activity and clients; disclosure in the case file; lack of judicial authorisation and notification; the low threshold under the general “blanket clause” in Article 161 CCP; and weak safeguards for legal professional privilege. The lawyer-specific protection under Article 160a could be lifted without a formal investigation against the lawyer, based on vague suspicion arising essentially from the fee transfer. Although later access was restricted, that did not redress the ongoing interference. The ECtHR found a violation of Article 8 because the interference was disproportionate and not necessary in a democratic society.
001-177349:
In *Becker v. Norway* (Application no. 21272/12), the applicant, Ms C. Langum Becker, was a Norwegian journalist for DN.no, the online edition of *Dagens Næringsliv*. She alleged that Norwegian courts compelled her to give evidence capable of identifying one or more journalistic sources, violating her right under Article 10 of the Convention to receive and impart information.

The underlying facts concerned criminal proceedings against Mr X for market manipulation and insider trading under the 1997 Act on the Trade of Financial Assets. Mr X was accused of asking attorney Mr Y to draft a letter about the Norwegian Oil Company (DNO), addressed to a bond trustee company, suggesting that several bondholders were seriously concerned about DNO’s finances. In reality, the letter was written only on Mr X’s behalf; he owned just one bond, acquired the same day he requested the letter. On Friday 24 August 2007, Mr X faxed the letter to the applicant and spoke with her by telephone. The next day, she published an article entitled “Fears of DNO collapse,” which prominently relied on the letter. DNO stock fell by 4.1% on the next trading day. Other media reported on the matter, and the Oslo Stock Exchange suspected market manipulation. The Financial Supervisory Authority investigated; Mr X confirmed that he had initiated the letter and was the source of the DN article.

Police questioned the applicant in June 2008. She confirmed receiving the letter by fax at 5:35 p.m. on 24 August 2007 and the article’s publication time. She accepted the information was price-sensitive but refused further details, invoking journalistic source protection.

She also said she considered the information price-sensitive. However, she refused to give further information, invoking journalistic source protection.

The judge warned that this could lead to a fine. On 25 January 2012, the High Court fined her NOK 30,000, approximately EUR 3,700, or ten days’ imprisonment, for an offence against good order. She did not appeal that fine. Mr X was convicted the same day.

The key alleged violation was therefore that, despite Mr X having already admitted being the source and despite the order being limited to him, the applicant was compelled to confirm or deny source contact, with a criminal fine, contrary to Article 10’s protection of journalistic sources.

The minority dissented, stressing that source protection is absolute and protects the public interest in free information flow, not the source personally. It warned that allowing compelled testimony even where a person claims to be the source could reveal other sources and undermine press freedom.

In January 2012 the High Court heard Becker during Mr X’s appeal. She answered some questions but refused those about Mr X. The judge warned her of a fine. On 25 January 2012 the High Court fined her NOK 30,000 for contempt, with ten days’ imprisonment if unpaid. She did not appeal the fine. The same day, the High Court convicted Mr X. **Tsartsidze and Others v. Georgia (Application no. 18766/04, judgment 17 January 2017)**

The case was brought by thirteen Georgian nationals, all Jehovah’s Witnesses, who alleged religiously motivated violence and State failure to protect them. They relied on Articles 6, 8, 9, 11, 13, 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The application concerned five separate incidents. The Court held that cases nos. 1 and 4 were inadmissible as substantially the same as *Begheluri and Others v. Georgia*. Case no. 1 involved police blocking Jehovah’s Witnesses’ route to Marneuli on 16 September 2000 while allowing Orthodox extremists led by Father Basil to attack and burn religious literature. Case no. 4 concerned an April 2001 attack at a Borjomi bus stop watched by local officials. The remaining allegations concerned cases nos. 2, 3 and 5.

In case no. 2, on 26 October 2000 in Marneuli, police entered Mr Aliev’s home as about thirty Azerbaijani Jehovah’s Witnesses prepared a meeting. They insulted participants, ordered them out and confiscated religious books and Bibles. Mr Aliev and Mr Mikirtumov were taken to a police station, where Mikirtumov was told to leave Marneuli forever and Aliev was told not to hold religious gatherings. Their administrative complaint was dismissed. Domestic courts accepted police denials, rejected eyewitness evidence from fellow believers as interested, and found no intentional or negligent breach of duty.

In case no. 3, on 2 September 2000 in Kutaisi, Mr Dzamukov was stopped by uniformed police while carrying religious tracts. His literature was confiscated, he was taken to a police station, beaten, and later threatened and strangled with his tie. The next day Mr Gabunia, distributing tracts, was punched in the stomach by police, had his bag emptied, his literature torn, Bibles kept, and was threatened with being dumped in the Rioni River. Their complaint was dismissed. The court remarked that Jehovah’s Witnesses “blatantly violate” the Constitution by imposing their beliefs, rejected witness evidence as biased, and found no injury. The Supreme Court said administrative proceedings could not establish criminal guilt and suggested they should have brought criminal proceedings.

In case no. 5, on 27 March 2001 in Rustavi, Orthodox extremists led by Mr Bluashvili burst into Mr Gogelashvili’s flat during a Jehovah’s Witness meeting. They called the worshippers Satanists, confiscated and destroyed literature, threw benches from windows, and Mr Kurua was strangled by his tie. A police officer allegedly watched without intervening. The next day the literature was burned at Rustavi market while police patrolled without reaction. The applicants sued police for failing their professional duties. The case was initially struck out based on an allegedly forged withdrawal, then dismissed because the court found police presence or passivity not proven, although it acknowledged police went to the scene after the attack. Appeals upheld the dismissal.

The Government argued the complaints were manifestly ill-founded and non-exhausted, saying applicants should have used criminal proceedings. The Court rejected the non-exhaustion plea because the applicants had fully exhausted civil and administrative remedies and were not required to pursue every possible remedy. It declared the Article 9 complaints, alone and in conjunction with Article 14, admissible for cases nos. 2, 3 and 5. The central alleged violations were State toleration of religious violence against Jehovah’s Witnesses and inadequate, biased civil and administrative redress, amounting to failure to protect religious freedom and discriminatory treatment.

In *Tsyoge Fon Manteyfel v. Ukraine* (App. No. 29804/16), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by Ms Karina Volodymyrivna Tsyoge fon Manteyfel, a Russian national born in 1978, concerning her compulsory psychiatric detention in Ukraine. The applicant suffers from paranoid schizophrenia and had been charged with murder. In the criminal proceedings against her, a court ordered compulsory psychiatric treatment, and she was detained in various psychiatric hospitals under different supervision regimes from 23 August 2010 to 14 November 2017.

During that period, Ukrainian courts periodically reviewed her detention based on submissions from the hospitals and extended her compulsory inpatient treatment. The latest relevant order was issued by the Samarskyy District Court of Dnipropetrovsk on 19 August 2016. Under Ukraine’s Psychiatric Assistance Act, such orders had to be reviewed at least every six months. The applicant therefore argued that her detention became unlawful after 19 February 2017, when the six-month period expired without any further court decision extending it.

The Dnipro Psychiatric Hospital lodged requests on 13 January and 19 May 2017 for the applicant to continue compulsory inpatient treatment. Those requests were dismissed by the courts on 13 May and 2 November 2017, respectively, and outpatient treatment was ordered. She was discharged from hospital on 14 November 2017. However, during the disputed period after 19 February 2017, the courts did not examine her appeals against the detention orders or her requests for release because, under domestic law, she lacked *locus standi* to appeal or initiate a review of the lawfulness of her continued detention. Requests for immediate release made by her mother and lawyer after 19 February 2017 were dismissed by the hospital on the ground that no court decision had ordered her release.

In August 2017, the applicant brought a civil claim against the hospital. By a final judgment of 19 June 2019, the Supreme Court partly allowed the claim and declared that her continued detention after 19 February 2017—after expiry of the six-month period from the 19 August 2016 decision and in the absence of any further extension—had no basis in law. It emphasized that the six-month maximum period for extending compulsory medical measures was a guarantee against unlawful detention. The Supreme Court ordered the Dnipropetrovsk Court of Appeal to rule on compensation. In January 2021, the Court of Appeal awarded the applicant UAH 30,000 (approximately EUR 1,000) for non-pecuniary damage. That judgment became final, but the award remains unpaid.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained under Article 5 §§ 1, 4 and 5, and Article 46, that her confinement after 19 February 2017 was unlawful; that throughout her psychiatric detention she had no right under domestic law to challenge the lawfulness of her detention, request release, or obtain compensation; and that the case disclosed structural and systemic deficiencies. The Court examined the complaints solely under Article 5.

The Government argued that the applicant was no longer a victim under Article 5 § 1 because domestic authorities had acknowledged the unlawfulness of her detention and granted redress. The Court noted that the compensation was lower than awards in comparable cases, such as *M. v. Ukraine* (EUR 12,000), but found that she could not complain about the amount because she had not appealed it. Nevertheless, since the award remained unpaid, the Court concluded that she could still claim victim status in respect of her confinement after 19 February 2017 and accepted the national courts’ finding that her detention during that period was unlawful.

Ukraine* (Application no. 29804/16, judgment of 11 January 2024), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Article 5 of the Convention concerning compulsory psychiatric detention. The applicant, a Russian national suffering from paranoid schizophrenia, was charged with murder in criminal proceedings and ordered by a Ukrainian court to undergo compulsory inpatient psychiatric treatment. The latest extension order was issued by the Samarskyy District Court of Dnipropetrovsk on 19 August 2016. The Dnipro Psychiatric Hospital later requested continued compulsory inpatient treatment on 13 January and 19 May 2017. Those requests were eventually dismissed on 13 May and 2 November 2017, and the court ordered that the applicant be treated as an outpatient. She was discharged on 14 November 2017.

A key procedural issue was that the domestic courts did not examine the applicant’s subsequent appeals against the extension orders or her requests for release. Under Ukrainian law, she lacked locus standi to appeal or initiate a review of the lawfulness of her continued detention. Requests for immediate release lodged by her mother and lawyer after 19 February 2017 were rejected by the hospital because no court decision had ordered her release.

In August 2017, the applicant brought a civil claim against the hospital. By final judgment of 19 June 2019, the Supreme Court partly allowed the claim and declared that her continued detention after 19 February 2017—after expiry of the six-month period from the 19 August 2016 decision and without any further extension—had no basis in law. It noted that the statutory six-month limit for extending compulsory medical measures was a guarantee against unlawful detention. The Supreme Court remitted the case to the Dnipropetrovsk Court of Appeal to determine compensation. In January 2021, the Court of Appeal awarded the applicant UAH 30,000 for non-pecuniary damage. Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained under Article 5 §§ 1, 4 and 5, and Article 46, that her confinement after 19 February 2017 was unlawful; that throughout her psychiatric detention she had no effective domestic right to challenge the lawfulness of her detention, request release, or receive compensation; and that these problems disclosed structural and systemic deficiencies. The Court examined the complaints solely under Article 5.

The Government argued that the applicant was no longer a victim under Article 5 § 1 because the domestic authorities had acknowledged the unlawfulness of her detention and afforded redress. The applicant replied that the compensation proceedings were ineffective: the award was very low and, in any event, unpaid. The Court noted that the national courts had found the post-19 February 2017 hospitalisation unlawful and awarded UAH 30,000, then equivalent to about EUR 1,000, which was lower than ECtHR awards in comparable Ukrainian cases. However, because the applicant did not challenge the amount by an appeal on points of law and gave no explanation, she could not complain about the sum. Nevertheless, since there was no evidence that the award had been paid, the Court held that she could still claim victim status under Article 5 § 1 and accepted the national courts’ finding that her detention after 19 February 2017 was unlawful.

**M.L. v. Norway** (Application no. 43701/14) concerned a Norwegian mother’s complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that the domestic authorities had violated her right to respect for family life by placing her younger son, X, in a non-relative foster home rather than with the maternal grandmother and stepfather.

The applicant, born in 1987, had two sons, who were half-brothers. Her older son, born in 2008, was taken into permanent public care in 2010 and placed with the applicant’s mother and stepfather. Her younger son, X, was born in February 2012. The applicant had been diagnosed with a hyperkinetic disorder and had a history of psychiatric treatment.

In June 2012, after receiving notifications from authorities and a private individual about the applicant’s inability to care for X, the municipal child welfare authorities placed him in emergency foster care. The County Social Welfare Board upheld that emergency placement. The child welfare authorities then petitioned the Board for a public care order, requesting that X be placed in a foster home and that the applicant be granted supervised access.

Although the maternal grandmother and stepfather had previously been approved as foster parents for the older son, the authorities opposed placing X with them. They cited difficulties in cooperating with the grandmother, the couple’s relatively advanced age—born in 1962 and 1955 respectively—the grandmother’s recent illness, and her failure to prioritise visiting X. The applicant objected. She argued that the grandparents were suitable, that the alleged cooperation problems were merely disagreements, that age was not decisive, and that a family placement would keep the brothers together and be more stable and less stigmatising.

In October 2012, after hearing the parties and ten witnesses, the Board granted the public care order and decided that X should remain in the home where he had already been placed as an emergency measure. The Board accepted that family placement had many positives and that the grandparents were in many respects well suited. However, it found serious doubts: X might be inherently vulnerable and possibly have attention-related difficulties, given the applicant’s diagnosis and her brother’s ADHD; there had been some cooperation difficulties; the grandmother seemed uncertain about the applicant’s ability to care for X and had not attended contact sessions; and the grandparents were relatively old for long-term foster care of a small child while already caring for the older brother. The Board concluded that the disadvantages outweighed the advantages. X was transferred to a non-relative foster home in January 2013.

The applicant appealed. In July 2013, the City Court upheld the Board’s decision. It found serious deficiencies in the applicant’s care and agreed that public care was necessary. On the foster placement question, the City Court acknowledged the advantages of placing X with relatives and keeping the brothers together. However, the court-appointed psychologist did not recommend the grandparents. Key concerns included the applicant’s very different emotional ties to her two sons: she had largely renounced her role as mother to the older son but was expected to maintain contact with X. If X lived with the grandparents, the mother’s contact might increase and hinder his attachment to the foster home. The grandmother had also said she primarily wanted to be a mother to the applicant. The City Court further noted that X had already experienced two broken relationships, had formed an attachment to his new foster mother, was thriving, and would risk “contact injury” if moved again. It also cited the challenges of older foster parents caring for two preschool boys with different needs.

The High Court refused leave to appeal in October 2013, and the Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee rejected the appeal in December 2013. The applicant therefore alleged before the European Court that the refusal to place X with her mother and stepfather breached Article 8.

**Summary of M.L. v. Norway (Application no. 43701/14)**

Norway concerns a complaint brought by a Norwegian mother against the Norwegian authorities under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to respect for family life. The applicant alleged that the domestic authorities’ decision to place her younger son, X, in a foster home with non-relatives, rather than with his maternal grandmother and step-grandfather, violated her rights.

This decision was upheld by the County Social Welfare Board on 29 June 2012. The child welfare authorities subsequently petitioned for a public care order, requesting that X be placed in a foster home and that the applicant be granted supervised access.

A central issue in the proceedings was the choice of foster home. The child welfare authorities opposed placing X with his maternal grandmother and stepfather, despite their prior approval as foster parents for the older son. The authorities cited several concerns: conflicts between the grandmother and the child welfare services, the grandparents’ relatively advanced age (born in 1962 and 1955), the grandmother’s recent illness, and the view that she had not prioritized visiting X. The applicant objected to the public care order and argued that, if granted, X should be placed with her mother and stepfather. The Board concluded that the disadvantages outweighed the advantages.

The applicant appealed to the City Court, which upheld the Board’s decision in July 2013. The City Court heard testimony from a court-appointed psychology expert, T.B., who did not recommend placing X with his grandparents. The expert’s primary concern was that the applicant had very different emotional ties to her two sons. She had renounced her role as mother to the older son but was expected to maintain contact with X. If X lived with his grandparents, this could lead to an ever-increasing scope of contact between the applicant and X, hindering his ability to form a secure attachment to his foster home. The expert also noted the grandmother’s expressed primary desire to be a mother to the applicant. The City Court also emphasized the risk of "contact injury" to X from another broken relationship, as he had already formed an attachment to his new foster mother. It also considered the challenges of the grandparents’ age and the different needs of the two boys.

The High Court refused leave to appeal in October 2013, and the Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee rejected a further appeal in December 2013. The applicant then brought her case to the European Court of Human Rights.

However, it identified serious doubts: X might be vulnerable and at risk of attention-related difficulties; there had been some cooperation difficulties with the grandmother; the grandmother had not attended contact sessions and had not seen X since placement; the grandparents were relatively old for long-term foster care of a young child; and they already cared for the older son, so another foster child could create strain. The Board concluded that the disadvantages outweighed the advantages. X was transferred to a foster home in January 2013.

The applicant appealed. In June 2013, the City Court held an oral hearing with a professional judge, a psychologist, and a lay judge, and heard fourteen witnesses. It upheld the Board’s decision. The City Court found serious deficiencies in the applicant’s care of X and agreed that public care was necessary. On the foster-home choice, it accepted the Board’s reasoning and the court-appointed psychologist’s recommendation against placing X with the grandparents. The expert noted that the applicant had renounced her role as mother of the older son but still sought contact with X; placing X with the grandparents could allow mother-child contact to increase and hinder X’s attachment to foster care. The City Court also found that X had already experienced broken relationships and had formed an attachment to his new foster mother, so another move risked “contact injury.” It emphasised the grandparents’ age, the challenges of caring for two preschool boys, and the applicant’s different emotional ties to her sons.

The High Court refused leave to appeal in October 2013, and the Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee rejected the appeal in December 2013. The applicant alleged that the decision to place X with non-relatives rather than his maternal grandparents violated her rights under Article 8.

In *Melandri v. San Marino*, the applicant, an Italian national, was investigated after San Marino’s Financial Intelligence Agency reported suspicious banking transactions. Between September 2009 and March 2010, he deposited about €4,865,830 in cash and €500,000 in cheques into a San Marino bank account. Another person, L.C., opened an account for a wine company that received €310,000 from a company traceable to the applicant. The FIA linked these funds to the Italian “Operation Baccus” investigation, in which the applicant faced charges of money laundering, extortion, usury, and fraud against the Italian State and the EU through fictitious wine-sector invoices. An Italian court convicted him of issuing false invoices and criminal association, largely upheld on cassation.

San Marino opened criminal proceedings. Based on evidence obtained from Italy, the Investigating Judge charged the applicant with money laundering under Article 199 bis of the Criminal Code and seized a life insurance policy worth about €6.8 million, other accounts, and later a safe deposit box. The prosecution alleged that he transferred and concealed proceeds of tax fraud, EU fraud, and false invoicing through San Marino accounts and the insurance policy.

At trial, the applicant argued that the funds were lawful, partly from VAT refunds, and that self-laundering had only been introduced by Law no. 100/2013, after the alleged conduct. The first-instance court convicted him of money laundering only for acts after 29 July 2013, treating the offence as continuous until the seizure, and sentenced him to four years and six months. It ordered confiscation of the seized property under Article 147. On appeal, the Judge of Appeal upheld the first charge but reclassified the conduct as self-laundering, holding it prosecutable under Law no. 99/2010, which removed the self-laundering exception for false-invoice predicate offences. It found the offence occurred between 10 March 2011 and 27 December 2011, acquitted him of the second charge, reduced the sentence to four years and three months, and confirmed confiscation. The Enforcement Judge later ordered the assets, including the insurance policy and interest, forfeited to the San Marino treasury.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained under Article 6 §§1 and 3(a)(b) that he had been charged with money laundering but convicted of self-laundering, leaving him unable to understand the accusation and prepare his defence. He pointed to confusion over the predicate offences and the applicable law, noting that the first-instance court applied the 2013 law while the appeal court applied the 2010 law. The Government replied that money laundering and self-laundering were the same offence under Article 199 bis, that he had been fully informed of the transactions and legal basis, and that the appeal’s legal re-evaluation did not prejudice his defence.

The applicant also complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the confiscation and his inability to recover the money. The Court concluded that the confiscation was proportionate to the legitimate aim of combating money laundering and that procedural safeguards had been available in the domestic proceedings. It found no violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, and the Article 6 complaints did not disclose a violation.

San Marino* (ECtHR, First Section, 12 September 2024), the applicant, Vincenzo Secondo Melandri, an Italian national, complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(a) and (b) of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about San Marino criminal proceedings for money laundering and the confiscation of his assets.

L.C., introduced by the applicant, opened an account for wine company O.; between October and December 2010, EUR 310,000 was credited to company O. by company A.G., which was traceable to the applicant. Italian authorities said the funds deposited in San Marino were incompatible with the applicant’s lawful savings and resulted from mafia-linked activities, including false invoices.

San Marino opened criminal proceedings no. 865/2012. After obtaining Italian documents through letters rogatory, the Investigating Judge charged the applicant and L.C. in November 2013 with money laundering under Article 199 bis of the Criminal Code. The judge ordered preventive seizure of a life insurance policy containing roughly EUR 6,800,000, a bank account holding EUR 480, and other accounts traceable to the applicant. A safe deposit box was later seized.

The April 2015 indictment alleged two charges. First, the applicant transferred and concealed money derived from crimes including false invoices, tax fraud, and EU fraud, using account X deposits of EUR 6,132,577.39 in cash and EUR 1,768,915.53 in cheques, then investing and transferring funds, including into the life insurance policy. Second, with L.C., he transferred EUR 310,000 through company O.

At trial, the applicant argued there was no proof the funds were illicit and that self-laundering was only introduced by Law no. 100/2013, after the conduct. In January 2019, the first-instance court convicted him of money laundering for acts after Law no. 100/2013 entered into force on 29 July 2013, based on continuous concealment until seizure. He was sentenced to four years and six months and confiscation was ordered under Article 147. On appeal in November 2020, the Judge of Appeals upheld the first charge but changed its legal basis: it found self-laundering prosecutable under Law no. 99/2010, which excluded the self-laundering privilege for false invoice offences, and set the offence period from 10 March 2011 to 27 December 2011. The applicant was acquitted of the second charge, the sentence was reduced to four years and three months, and confiscation was confirmed. In December 2020, the enforcement judge ordered confiscation of the seized assets, including the life insurance policy and accrued interest.

The applicant alleged that he was charged with money laundering but convicted of self-laundering after legal changes, preventing him from preparing an adequate defence; he also complained that the two courts applied different legal bases and that the predicate offences were unclear. The Government maintained that the charges were sufficiently detailed, that money laundering and self-laundering were covered by the same provision, and that Law no. 99/2010 already removed the self-laundering privilege for false invoices. The Court also examined the confiscation under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, finding the measure proportionate to the legitimate aim of fighting money laundering, with procedural safeguards available.

In *L.B. v. Slovakia* (Application no. 5541/22), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section) examined a Slovak father’s complaints under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention concerning his right to contact with his minor son, the enforcement of interim orders, and the length of custody proceedings.

The applicant’s son was born in 2013. In February 2019, the child’s mother started proceedings in the Nové Mesto nad Váhom District Court seeking arrangements for parental rights and obligations. Interim orders in March and July 2019 allowed the applicant regular contact with his son, and that contact reportedly went smoothly until the end of September 2019.

On 6 March 2020, the District Court ordered regular contact between March and June 2020 at the Centre for Children and Family in Nové Mesto nad Váhom. Because the Centre was closed until late May 2020 due to the Covid-19 pandemic, the first meeting did not occur until 4 June 2020. On 3 June 2020, the Trenčín Regional Court varied the order so that contact would take place on Thursdays from 3 p.m. to 5 p.m. at the Centre. On 6 October 2020, after establishing on 25 August 2020 that scheduled contact had not taken place, the District Court ordered enforcement of the March 2020 interim order. On 20 October 2020, the Constitutional Court dismissed as manifestly ill-founded the applicant’s complaint about the protracted conduct of the District Court.

On 12 January 2021, the court ordered the parents, grandparents and child to attend regular social counselling sessions at the Centre and required the Centre to inform the court of each session. Contact scheduled for June, July and August 2021 did not take place. In its final report of 31 August 2021, the Centre stated that it had not been possible to re-establish contact and recommended further variation so it could work with the child individually, without the mother present. On 22 August 2021, the District Court discontinued enforcement of the March 2020 interim order because it had become unenforceable following the January 2021 interim order. On 22 September 2021, the court invited the mother to comply voluntarily. On 26 October 2021, the District Court again ordered counselling sessions, with the child to attend without his mother. On 11 November 2021, the Constitutional Court declared inadmissible the applicant’s second complaint, in which he alleged that his right to family life was violated because court inaction prevented contact with his son. The Centre later reported that scheduled contact in December 2021 and January and February 2022 had not occurred because the mother and child failed to attend.

On 10 February 2022, the District Court ordered that the child reside with the mother and that the applicant pay monthly maintenance of EUR 50. It also ordered both parents and the child to undergo three months of psychological counselling; after therapy, the applicant would be allowed contact every other weekend from Friday 3.30 p.m. to Sunday 6 p.m. On 16 February 2022, the court ordered the mother, under penalty of a fine, to ensure the child attended counselling under the October 2021 interim order. On 13 April 2022, the mother was fined EUR 100 for non-compliance. On 24 March 2022, the applicant was convicted of dangerous stalking of the child’s mother and obstructing execution of a court order, receiving a six-month suspended sentence. The Centre reported that the mother missed most counselling sessions between June and October 2022. On 2 August 2022, the mother was charged with obstructing execution of a decision by a public authority.

On 20 October 2022, the Regional Court upheld the October 2021 interim order. On 9 November 2022, it upheld the District Court judgment on counselling and ruled that, after therapy, the applicant would have contact every second Saturday from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. for two months, then every second week from Saturday 9 a.m. to Sunday 5 p.m. On 5 February 2023, the mother appealed on points of law to the Supreme Court, which apparently remains pending. The applicant complained under Article 8 that slow and inefficient court decision-making prevented him from obtaining regular contact with his son, and under Article 6 that the custody proceedings exceeded a reasonable time.

001-231088:
**Vlahović v. Montenegro (Application no. 62444/10)** concerned the prolonged non-enforcement of final domestic decisions in favour of the applicant, Mr Zoran Vlahović, a Croatian national. He was a co-owner of two plots in Herceg Novi, holding one third of plot no. 1084/4 and one half of plot no. 1084/10. In 2005 another co-owner, M.D., without the consent of the other owners or municipal authorisation, built a sewage collection system and paved the road with concrete. The applicant and another co-owner sued. A construction expert found that the concrete paving accelerated rainwater flow, drainage was inadequate, and the sewage system lacked authorisation and might not meet construction standards.

In February 2010 the Herceg Novi Court of First Instance found that M.D. had violated the applicant’s rights by unlawfully paving the plots and constructing the sewage system. It ordered M.D. to remove the constructions within fifteen days. In March 2010 the municipal police issued two decisions ordering removal of the unlawful sewage system and concrete paving; those decisions were upheld in April 2010. In May 2010 M.D. transferred his ownership share in the land to the municipality free of charge. In December 2010 the municipality requested expropriation of the plots.

The first-instance judgment became final in February 2011. However, enforcement failed. An April 2011 enforcement order was quashed in October 2011 because M.D. was no longer a co-owner and expropriation proceedings were pending. In 2012 the applicant’s request that the municipality enforce the judgment was dismissed because the judgment had been against M.D., not the municipality; he was advised to bring separate civil proceedings. The expropriation proceedings were rejected, restarted, and then stayed in 2015.

In April 2015 an interim measure prohibited removal of the concrete paving and sewage system until the expropriation proceedings ended, citing nearly irreparable damage to residents who depended on that road and infrastructure. Although the Supreme Court held in 2017 that expropriation could not obstruct enforcement, and the State Prosecutor’s Office later agreed, the decisions remained unenforced. In 2021 the High Court ordered urgent termination of the enforcement proceedings. The Court of First Instance then terminated enforcement and cancelled enforcement actions, finding that the original respondent no longer owned the land and advising new proceedings against the municipality. That decision was upheld in September 2021. Meanwhile, an August 2021 expropriation decision was quashed in November 2022 and remained pending before the Administrative Court in December 2023.

A 2022 Constitutional Court decision dismissed the applicant’s non-enforcement complaint, though in 2023 the Constitutional Court quashed a 2019 decision for failing to address his reliance on section 28 of the Enforcement Act, which allowed enforcement against a person not named as respondent where the relevant obligation had transferred.

By December 2023 the 2010 judgment and the two 2010 administrative decisions still had not been enforced, and the 2015 interim measure remained in force. The applicant alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, concerning access to court, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, concerning peaceful enjoyment of possessions. He argued that the State had allowed ownership transfers, expropriation proceedings, and interim measures to frustrate enforcement indefinitely. The Government submitted a unilateral declaration acknowledging only an Article 6 violation and proposing enforcement after the expropriation proceedings concluded, without compensation or acknowledgment of a Protocol No. 1 violation. The Court rejected that declaration, noting that a prior undertaking in 2016 had already been unfulfilled and the new proposal did not offer appropriate redress. It ultimately found violations based on the unjustified non-enforcement of the final domestic decisions.

**Vlahović v. Montenegro** (App. No. 62444/10, ECtHR, 22 February 2024) concerned the non-enforcement of final domestic decisions in favour of the applicant, Zoran Vlahović, a Croatian national and co-owner of two plots of land in Herceg Novi, Montenegro.

In 2005 another co-owner, M.D., without the applicant’s consent or municipal authorisation, built a sewage collection system and paved the plots with concrete, effectively creating a road. The applicant and another co-owner sued. An expert found that the concrete paving accelerated rainwater runoff and that inadequate drainage would likely cause flooding and damage to adjacent land; the sewage system also lacked prior authorisation and might not have met construction standards.

In February 2010 the Herceg Novi Court of First Instance found that M.D. had violated the applicant’s rights and ordered him to remove the unlawful sewage system and concrete paving within fifteen days. In March 2010 the municipal police issued two administrative decisions ordering the same removal; those decisions were upheld on appeal in April 2010. In February 2011 the Podgorica High Court upheld the civil judgment, making it final. Enforcement nevertheless did not occur.

Key facts relevant to the alleged violations concerned later ownership changes and proceedings that obstructed enforcement. In May 2010 M.D. transferred his shares in the land to the municipality free of charge. The municipality sought expropriation in December 2010. In April 2011 the Court of First Instance issued an enforcement order, but the High Court quashed it in October 2011 because M.D. was no longer a co-owner and expropriation proceedings were pending. In 2012 the applicant’s request to enforce against the municipality was dismissed, and he was advised to bring separate civil proceedings against the municipality. Expropriation requests were rejected or stayed.

In April 2015 an interim measure prohibited removal of the concrete and sewage system until the expropriation proceedings ended, citing serious consequences for occupants’ access, water supply, and sewage infrastructure. In 2017 the Supreme Court held that expropriation could not block enforcement of the removal decisions, but the decisions remained unenforced.

In April and September 2021 the enforcement proceedings were terminated because M.D. no longer owned the land; the applicant was again told to pursue claims against the municipality separately. Expropriation proceedings continued, with a 2021 expropriation decision later quashed and pending before the Administrative Court. The 2015 interim measure remained in force. By December 2023 the final judgment and the two administrative decisions in the applicant’s favour remained unenforced.

The Government submitted a second unilateral declaration in November 2021, acknowledging a violation of Article 6 and undertaking to enforce the decisions after expropriation or to bring the infrastructure into line with standards. It offered no compensation and did not acknowledge a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The applicant objected. The Court rejected the Government’s request to strike out the application, noting that an earlier declaration had already led to the case being struck out but had not been fulfilled, and that the new declaration was conditional, open-ended, and did not provide appropriate redress.

The case therefore concerned the alleged unjustified non-enforcement of final domestic decisions in the applicant’s favour, contrary to Article 6 § 1 (access to court) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions).

In *Vlahović v. Montenegro* (no. 62444/10, 22 February 2024), the applicant, Zoran Vlahović, a Croatian national, co-owned two plots of land in Herceg Novi. In June 2005, another co-owner, M.D., constructed a sewage collection system on one plot and paved both plots in concrete without the applicant’s consent or municipal authorization. The applicant and another co-owner sued. An expert found that the concrete paving accelerated rainwater runoff, that drainage was inadequate, and that flooding and soil deposits could damage adjacent land. The lack of authorization also raised concerns that the sewage system did not meet construction standards.

In February 2010, the Herceg Novi Court of First Instance found that M.D. had violated the applicant’s rights by unlawfully paving the plots and constructing the sewage system. It ordered M.D. to remove the unlawful objects within fifteen days. In March 2010, the municipal police issued two decisions ordering removal of the sewage system and concrete paving; these were upheld on appeal in April 2010. In May 2010, however, M.D. transferred his ownership share to the municipality free of charge. The municipality then sought to expropriate the plots in December 2010.

In February 2011, the Podgorica High Court upheld the first-instance judgment, making it final. An enforcement order was issued in April 2011 but was later quashed because M.D. was no longer a co-owner and expropriation proceedings were pending. In 2012, the court refused the applicant’s request to enforce against the municipality, holding that the judgment bound M.D., not the municipality, and advised the applicant to bring separate civil proceedings. Enforcement was further obstructed by repeated municipal police postponements, which were quashed, and by a 2015 interim measure prohibiting removal until the expropriation proceedings ended. That measure was based on the occupants’ need for access roads and water and sewage infrastructure.

Although the Supreme Court in 2017 and the State Prosecutor in 2022 stated that expropriation could not obstruct enforcement, the judgment and administrative decisions remained unenforced. In 2021, the enforcement proceedings were terminated because M.D. no longer owned the land, and the applicant was again told to pursue new civil proceedings against the municipality. Expropriation proceedings were still pending before the Administrative Court in December 2023, and the interim measure remained in force.

The applicant complained under Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the non-enforcement of the final judgment and two administrative decisions in his favour. The Government submitted a new unilateral declaration in 2021 acknowledging a violation of Article 6 and promising steps after the expropriation proceedings, but it did not acknowledge a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 or offer compensation. The applicant rejected the declaration. The Court refused to strike out the application, noting that the Government had already failed a similar undertaking after the case was previously struck out and later restored. It found the new declaration inadequate because it was conditional, dependent on pending expropriation proceedings, and offered no compensation. The Court therefore examined the non-enforcement and found violations of Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to the unjustified failure to enforce the final domestic judgment and administrative decisions in the applicant’s favour.
001-238269:
**Case: Kasım Özdemir and Mehmet Özdemir v. Türkiye**  
**ECtHR (Second Section), App. no. 18980/20, judgment 3 December 2024**

The case concerned two Turkish applicants, a father and son, who complained under Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention that a gendarmerie officer shot them in their village and that the State failed to conduct an effective investigation. The incident occurred on 10 November 2014 in Deliosman village, Gaziantep Province. Three gendarmerie officers on patrol had tried to stop an approaching vehicle. The driver ignored the warning, and the officers pursued the vehicle into the village. The vehicle was abandoned, and the officers allegedly found bags of smuggled cigarettes in the boot.

According to the applicants, officer C.Ç. began firing shots into the air after arriving in the village. The first applicant, the son, warned him not to shoot because it could scare the children; in response, C.Ç. shot him in the leg. The second applicant, the father, arrived after learning that his son had been shot and was also shot by C.Ç. The applicants denied resisting the officers or being involved in smuggling. According to official records and the officers’ statements, however, villagers surrounded and attacked the officers, threw stones, damaged their vehicle, and tried to take their rifles. The crowd allegedly grew to 50–60 people. C.Ç. stated that he fired warning shots and then aimed at the applicants’ feet only after they continued to advance and after one applicant tried to seize a rifle and the other tried to draw a wounded man’s weapon. The three officers suffered bruises and haematomas and received ten days’ medical leave. The applicants suffered serious tibia and fibula fractures; the second applicant’s injuries could seriously affect his daily life, but neither injury was life-threatening. Telephone intercepts of the suspect driver suggested villagers had been mobilised to prevent confiscation of smuggled goods and described a confrontation with the officer.

The domestic investigation began the same day. Authorities collected scene reports, witness statements, forensic swabs, gunshot residue and bullets. On 13 February 2015, the Kilis public prosecutor declined to prosecute C.Ç. for intentional bodily harm, finding that he had acted in self-defence and that the use of a firearm was lawful under section 16 of Law no. 2559. The applicants’ objection was dismissed on 23 March 2015. In separate criminal proceedings, the applicants were convicted of resisting public officers to impede their duties and sentenced to eight months and ten days’ imprisonment, suspended. The Constitutional Court examined their complaints under Article 17 of the Constitution and found no violation, accepting that the force was necessary and proportionate and that the investigation had been adequate. It rejected a second application concerning the fairness of the criminal proceedings as manifestly ill-founded.

Before the European Court, the applicants relied on Articles 2, 3, 8, 13 and 14. The Court held that the complaints fell only under Article 3, not Article 2, because the force used was not potentially lethal and the shots were controlled and aimed at the legs/feet, with injuries not life-threatening. On the merits, the Court found no violation of Article 3: there was sufficient evidence that the gendarmerie officer had acted in self-defence to protect his life and physical integrity and those of two other officers against a serious and imminent threat. The impugned use of force was considered indispensable and not excessive in the circumstances, and the investigation was effective. The ECtHR therefore concluded that there had been no violation of Article 3 of the Convention.

In *Kasım Özdemir and Mehmet Özdemir v. Türkiye* (App. No. 18980/20, judgment of 3 December 2024), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by a father and son that they were shot and seriously injured by a gendarmerie officer and that Türkiye failed to conduct an effective investigation, contrary to Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention.

The incident took place on 10 November 2014. Three gendarmerie officers on patrol in Gaziantep tried to stop a vehicle whose driver ignored their warning. They pursued it into Deliosman village. According to the applicants, officer C.Ç. began firing shots into the air. The first applicant, Kasım Özdemir, warned him not to shoot because it would frighten children, and C.Ç. then shot him in the leg. The second applicant, Mehmet Özdemir, the first applicant’s father, arrived after learning that his son had been shot and was also shot in the leg. The applicants claimed they had not resisted, threatened the officer, or been involved with smuggled goods.

The officers’ account was different. They stated that after finding smuggled cigarettes in the abandoned suspect vehicle, a crowd of villagers surrounded them, insulted them, threw stones, damaged their vehicle, and tried to seize their rifles. C.Ç. fired warning shots. When the first applicant allegedly tried to take his rifle and belt and threatened him, and the second applicant later tried to draw the wounded man’s weapon, C.Ç. shot at their feet in self-defence. Scene reports recorded blood stains, a severely damaged gendarmerie vehicle, stones, and missing cartridges. Intercepted telephone calls suggested the suspect driver had mobilised villagers to prevent confiscation of smuggled goods and that some speakers referred to villagers almost lynching the officer. Medical reports showed both applicants suffered serious leg fractures, though not life-threatening; the second applicant’s injuries required surgery and seriously affected daily life.

The Kilis public prosecutor declined to prosecute C.Ç., finding self-defence under section 16 of Law no. 2559. The magistrate dismissed the applicants’ objection. The Turkish Constitutional Court later found no violation of Article 17 of the Constitution, holding that the force was necessary and proportionate and the investigation adequate. The applicants were separately prosecuted for resisting public officers and received suspended sentences.

Before the ECtHR, the Court held that Article 2 was not applicable because the force was not potentially lethal: the shots were controlled and aimed at the applicants’ legs, and the injuries were not life-threatening. It examined the case under Article 3. The Court found sufficient evidence that C.Ç. had acted in self-defence to protect his life and physical integrity and those of two other officers against a serious and imminent threat. In the circumstances, the impugned use of force was indispensable and not excessive. The investigation into the shooting was also effective. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 3, either substantively or procedurally.

The applicants, Kasım Özdemir and Mehmet Özdemir, a son and father living in Kilis, complained under Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention that a gendarmerie officer had shot and seriously injured them during an incident in their village and that the ensuing investigation was ineffective.

On 10 November 2014, three gendarmerie officers conducting a road-safety patrol tried to stop a suspect vehicle. The driver ignored the warning and was pursued into Deliosman village. According to official records, the officers found bags of smuggled cigarettes in the abandoned vehicle. Villagers then gathered, confronted the officers, threw stones, damaged the gendarmerie vehicle, blocked escape routes and allegedly tried to seize the officers’ rifles. Officer C.Ç. fired warning shots and later shot the two applicants in the legs/feet. The applicants claimed a different sequence: C.Ç. began firing into the air upon entering the village; the first applicant warned him not to shoot because it would frighten children, and the officer shot him in the leg. The second applicant arrived after hearing that his son had been shot and was then shot as well. They denied resisting the officers.

The investigation examined both the shooting and the alleged attack on the officers. Scene reports described a severely damaged gendarmerie vehicle, stones, broken windows, and flattened tyres. Medical reports showed the officers suffered bruises and haematomas, while the applicants suffered serious leg fractures. The first applicant had tibia/fibula fractures and possible loss of function; the second had multiple fractures and later surgery, with serious impact on daily life, though neither injury was life-threatening. Gunshot residue was found on C.Ç. and the applicants, but not on the other officers. Intercepted telephone calls suggested the suspect driver had urged villagers to stop the officers from confiscating smuggled goods and later described the villagers as having nearly lynched the officer.

On 13 February 2015, the public prosecutor declined to prosecute C.Ç., finding that he had acted in self-defence and within lawful police powers to use firearms. The magistrate dismissed the applicants’ objection. Separately, the applicants and other villagers were prosecuted for resisting public officers; the applicants were convicted and their sentence was suspended. The Constitutional Court found no violation of the prohibition of ill-treatment, holding the force necessary and proportionate because of the crowd’s attack and finding the investigation independent.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the Court held that Article 2 was not applicable because the shots were not potentially lethal and were controlled, aimed at the applicants’ legs/feet. It examined the case under Article 3. On the substantive aspect, the Court found sufficient evidence that C.Ç. acted in self-defence to protect his life and physical integrity and those of two other officers against a serious and imminent threat. The use of force was therefore indispensable and not excessive. On the procedural aspect, it found the investigation effective. Accordingly, there was no violation of Article 3.
