In *Sacharuk v. Lithuania* (Application no. 39300/18, judgment of 23 April 2024), the applicant Aleksandr Sacharuk was a member of the Lithuanian Seimas from 2008 to 2012. Between 14 and 19 January 2010, while another MP, L.K., was abroad without parliamentary authorisation, Sacharuk used L.K.’s parliamentary identity card to register and vote electronically in L.K.’s place on several occasions. The Seimas Ethics and Procedures Commission found that he had violated the Seimas Statute requiring members to vote in person and proposed a warning. The Seimas Special Investigation Commission found possible criminal elements and asked the Prosecutor General to investigate. Prosecution was initially blocked because the Seimas did not lift Sacharuk’s immunity.

In impeachment proceedings, the Constitutional Court concluded in October 2010 that Sacharuk had grossly violated the Constitution and breached his parliamentary oath. The Seimas did not muster enough votes to remove him, although L.K.’s mandate was annulled. Sacharuk’s term ended in November 2012. After his immunity ended, the Prosecutor General opened a pre-trial investigation in November 2012. Sacharuk was charged with abuse of office (Article 228), forgery/use of a false document (Article 300), and unlawful use of an official document (Article 302) under the Criminal Code.

In 2015 the Vilnius Regional Court acquitted him; the Court of Appeal upheld the acquittal in 2016. Those courts found that voting for absent colleagues was a settled practice within political groups, that the Ethics Commission treated it as a disciplinary matter attracting at most a warning, and that Sacharuk’s conduct lacked criminal dangerousness and intent to commit a crime.

On the prosecutor’s cassation appeal, a Supreme Court panel in December 2016, presided over by Judge D.B., quashed the acquittal and remitted the case. It held that the lower courts had assessed the evidence one-sidedly; that the Seimas Statute unequivocally required personal voting; that the practice of mutual voting did not eliminate criminality; and that the applicant’s actions objectively involved document forgery. On remand, in June 2017 the Court of Appeal convicted Sacharuk of abuse of office and unlawful use of an official document, imposing a fine; the Article 300 charge was time-barred. It found direct intent, no valid settled-practice defence, and major non-pecuniary damage to the State and the Seimas’ authority.

Sacharuk appealed on points of law. The final Supreme Court panel included Judge D.B. as reporting judge—the same judge who had presided over the earlier cassation panel that quashed his acquittal and made findings prejudging his guilt. Sacharuk unsuccessfully requested her removal. In February 2018 the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal and upheld the conviction. It found the prosecution lawful after loss of immunity, that his acts were dangerous and contrary to law, that ignorance was no excuse, and that unequal treatment or wrongful practice could not justify acquittal.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 6 § 1 because objectively justified doubts arose as to the Supreme Court’s impartiality: Judge D.B. had already made strong findings on Sacharuk’s guilt in the earlier cassation proceedings, creating a legitimate fear of a preconceived view. It found no violation of Article 7: the conviction was reasonably foreseeable, the conduct violated domestic law, and the authorities’ past attitude did not amount to conscious toleration or a lawful tradition.

**Sacharuk v. Lithuania** (ECtHR, Application no. 39300/18, judgment 23 April 2024) concerned a former Lithuanian member of Parliament (Seimas), Aleksandr Sacharuk, elected for the 2008–2012 term. Between 14 and 19 January 2010, while another MP, L.K., was abroad without parliamentary authorisation, Sacharuk used L.K.’s parliamentary identity card to register and vote electronically in his place on several occasions.

The Seimas Ethics and Procedures Commission found that Sacharuk had breached the Seimas Statute by voting for another member and recommended a warning. The Special Investigation Commission later found possible criminal elements and asked the Prosecutor General’s Office to investigate under Criminal Code Articles 300 and 302. Because Sacharuk was an MP, prosecution required the Seimas to lift his immunity. In June 2010 the Seimas voted not to lift immunity, and the prosecutor refused to open a pre-trial investigation. Impeachment proceedings followed. On 27 October 2010 the Constitutional Court concluded that Sacharuk had deliberately voted for L.K. eight times, breached his parliamentary oath and grossly violated the Constitution. However, the Seimas failed to remove him: 80 votes were cast in favour, short of the required 85. L.K.’s mandate was annulled.

After the applicant’s parliamentary term ended on 16 November 2012, the prosecutor annulled the earlier refusal and opened a criminal investigation on 20 November 2012 under Articles 228 § 1 (abuse of office), 300 § 3 (forgery), and 302 § 2 (unlawful use of a document). The Vilnius Regional Court acquitted him in July 2015, and the Court of Appeal upheld the acquittal in May 2016. Both courts relied on evidence of a “settled practice” of MPs voting for absent colleagues, the disciplinary warning already imposed, and the absence of major damage.

On 20 December 2016, a three-judge Supreme Court panel presided over by Judge D.B. quashed the acquittal and remitted the case. The Supreme Court held that the alleged practice did not eliminate the criminal nature of the conduct, that voting records were documents, and that the lower courts’ assessment had been one-sided and unlawful, effectively making findings prejudging Sacharuk’s guilt. On remittal, the Court of Appeal convicted him in June 2017 under Articles 228 § 1 and 302 § 1, imposing a fine of €1,882; the Article 300 charge was time-barred.

The applicant appealed on points of law. A new Supreme Court panel was formed, again including Judge D.B., this time as reporting judge. Sacharuk unsuccessfully sought her removal because she had already presided over the earlier cassation panel that had quashed his acquittal and made adverse findings. On 13 February 2018, the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal and upheld the conviction. His conviction was later expunged in 2019.

Before the ECtHR, Sacharuk complained under Article 6 § 1 that the Supreme Court was not impartial and under Article 7 that his conviction was unforeseeable. The ECtHR found a violation of Article 6 § 1: although Judge D.B. was not legally bound by the earlier findings, her prior role created objectively justified doubts and a legitimate fear that she had already formed a preconceived view on his guilt. It found no violation of Article 7, holding that the prosecution was consistent with nullum crimen sine lege; the authorities had not consciously tolerated the practice, repeated violations did not amount to a tradition, and the law’s application, though novel, was not flagrantly arbitrary and was sufficiently foreseeable.

In *Sacharuk v. Lithuania* (App. no. 39300/18, judgment of 23 April 2024), the applicant, Aleksandr Sacharuk, was a member of the Lithuanian Parliament (Seimas) from 2008 to 2012. Between 14 and 19 January 2010, he used another MP L.K.’s parliamentary identity card to register and vote electronically in L.K.’s place while L.K. was abroad. The Seimas Ethics and Procedures Commission found that this breached Article 111 §4 of the Seimas Statute, which required MPs to vote in person, and the Code of Conduct; it recommended a warning. The Seimas Special Investigation Commission later found possible criminal elements and asked prosecutors to investigate under Criminal Code Articles 300 and 302. Prosecutors requested that the Seimas lift the applicant’s immunity, but in June 2010 the Seimas refused, so no pre-trial investigation began. In October 2010 the Constitutional Court concluded that the applicant had deliberately voted eight times for L.K. and had grossly violated the Constitution and his parliamentary oath. An impeachment vote failed to remove him, although L.K.’s mandate was annulled.

After the applicant’s parliamentary term ended in November 2012, he lost immunity. The prosecutor then opened a pre-trial investigation and charged him with abuse of office, forgery/use of a document, and unlawful use of an official document. In 2015 the Vilnius Regional Court acquitted him, and the Court of Appeal upheld the acquittal in 2016. Those courts found that voting for an absent MP from the same political group was settled practice, that the conduct had been treated as a disciplinary violation attracting only a warning, that there was no major damage, and that the applicant had not realised criminal liability could apply. On 20 December 2016, the Supreme Court quashed the acquittal and remitted the case. A panel including Judge D.B. as presiding judge held that unlawful practice did not eliminate criminality, that Article 111 §4 unequivocally required personal voting, that the voting records were objectively forged, and that the lower courts’ assessment raised doubts.

On retrial, the Court of Appeal convicted the applicant in June 2017 under Article 228 §1 (abuse of office) and Article 302 §1 (unlawful use of a document), imposing a fine of €1,882; the Article 300 charge was time-barred. The applicant appealed. In the final Supreme Court appeal, Judge D.B. again sat on the panel, now as reporting judge. The applicant asked for her removal because she had already participated in the first cassation and had made strong findings on his guilt. The Supreme Court refused, stating that prior involvement did not create impartiality doubts. On 13 February 2018 it upheld the conviction.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 6 §1 that the Supreme Court was not impartial, mainly because Judge D.B.’s repeated participation and earlier findings created objectively justified doubts that she had already formed a view on his guilt. He also complained under Article 7 that his conviction was unforeseeable, relying on the alleged Seimas practice of mutual voting and the disciplinary warning he had received. The ECtHR found a violation of Article 6 §1 because the impartiality doubts were objectively justified. It found no violation of Article 7, concluding that the conduct violated domestic law, was not consciously tolerated as a tradition, and that criminal liability was reasonably foreseeable.

A.I. and Others v. Greece (App. no. 13958/16), ECtHR Fifth Section, judgment 18 January 2024, concerned an Afghan father and his two minor children. They alleged violations of Article 3 regarding living conditions in Idomeni camp and Article 3 read with Article 13 regarding deficient access to the asylum procedure.

On 25 February 2016 the applicants were registered at Fylakio Reception and Identification Centre (RIC), Evros. The father suffered from a hip cyst and underwent surgery. On 2 March 2016 they left the RIC for Idomeni, intending to reach northern Europe; they considered Greece unsafe. They stayed in Idomeni until May 2016. They alleged severe overcrowding—over 10,000 people—exceeding the camp’s capacity. They lived in a tent without adequate weather protection and complained of poor hygiene and sanitation, infection risk, and inadequate food. They suffered bronchitis, fever and lung problems; the father’s cyst became infected and bled; they could not obtain medical assistance; the children were hungry. They claimed the authorities knew of their vulnerability—the father’s medical condition and the children’s ages (4 and 7)—and that conditions cumulatively breached Article 3.

As to asylum access, they alleged they were not informed about asylum procedures during police registration. The Greek Asylum Service made Skype the only way to express an intention to apply and schedule registration at the Regional Asylum Office (RAO). They had no internet or device, the Skype lines were overloaded, and in-person applications were no longer available. Even using Skype would not confer asylum-seeker status. On 3 March 2016 an administrative expulsion order was issued; enforcement was suspended for one month for the father and six months for the children. They claimed the suspension could be lifted before they could apply, exposing them to refoulement. An interim measure request to the ECtHR on 11 March 2016 was refused on 1 April 2016.

In May 2016 they moved to Diavata camp, living in a tent without electricity and with inadequate food. They received a pre-registration asylum-seeker card but kept no copy. The father was referred to hospital but no interpreter was available; the children could not attend school, became ill, and no pediatrician was available. They alleged authorities knew they were present, but they still could not submit an asylum request despite recorded interest. After Idomeni’s evacuation, pre-registration did not ensure access to asylum. These conditions, without safeguards for vulnerable persons, allegedly exceeded the Article 3 threshold and risked refoulement. In December 2016 they left for other countries; they returned to Greece in September 2018 and were homeless in Athens until December 2019. They applied for international protection on 12 October 2018 and were recognised as refugees on 22 April 2020.

The Government argued Greece faced an extraordinary humanitarian emergency caused by unprecedented migrant flows and the Western Balkan route closure. Idomeni was an unofficial camp built by NGOs, municipalities, IOM and UNHCR, with tents, toilets, showers, water, healthcare from hospitals/NGOs, and food from NGOs/shops. Police informed residents about border closure and transfers; the camp was evacuated on 24–26 May 2016 and residents moved to state facilities. Idomeni was never official accommodation; the applicants were not detained and went there voluntarily; no record of their presence existed. On asylum, pre-registration in June/July 2016 provided cards and health/education access; vulnerability was assessed; there was no indication authorities refused registration. During the RIC, applicants were informed they could apply before the RAO but did not express a wish. Their first application was on 12 October 2018, with no evidence earlier attempts were impossible. Skype appointments operated alongside personal appearance and did not preclude attendance at the RAO.

In **A.I. and Others v. Greece** (Application no. 13958/16, ECtHR Fifth Section, 18 January 2024), three Afghan nationals—a father and his two minor children, then aged 4 and 7—complained under Article 3, and Article 3 in conjunction with Article 13, about living conditions in Idomeni camp and shortcomings in access to the Greek asylum procedure.

The applicants registered at the Fylakio Reception and Identification Centre in Evros on 25 February 2016. The father had a cyst on his hip and had undergone surgery. On 2 March 2016 they left the RIC and went to Idomeni camp, intending to travel to northern Europe because they considered Greece and the Balkan route unsafe. They stayed at Idomeni between March and May 2016. They alleged that they lived in a tent without adequate protection from the weather; the camp was overcrowded, with more than 10,000 people despite capacity limits; hygiene and sanitation were inadequate; there was a risk of infection and insufficient nutrition. They suffered bronchitis, fever and lung problems; the father’s cyst became infected and bled; they could not obtain medical assistance; and the children were hungry. They argued that the authorities knew of their vulnerability—the father’s medical condition and the children’s young age—so the conditions, taken together with their status, amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment contrary to Article 3.

As regards asylum access, the applicants claimed they were not informed during police registration about how to apply for asylum. The Asylum Service had made Skype the only way to express an intention to apply and to schedule registration at the Regional Asylum Office. The applicants had no internet device and could not reach the overloaded Skype numbers; in-person application was no longer available. Even if they had reached Skype, they said they would not have been treated as asylum-seekers. On 3 March 2016 an administrative expulsion order was issued against them; enforcement was suspended for one month for the father and six months for the children, but they feared the suspension could be lifted before they could lodge an asylum request, exposing them to refoulement.

After leaving Idomeni, they moved in May 2016 to Diavata camp, where they lived in a tent without electricity and with inadequate nutrition. They received a pre-registration asylum-seeker card but kept no copy. The father was referred to hospital but no interpreter was available; the children could not enrol in school and fell ill, but no paediatrician was available. They stayed there until December 2016, then left Greece due to harsh conditions, returning in 2018. They were homeless in Athens until December 2019. They applied for international protection on 12 October 2018 and were recognised as refugees on 22 April 2020.

The Government contested the claims. It described an extraordinary humanitarian emergency caused by unprecedented migration flows and the closure of the Western Balkan route in February 2016. Idomeni was an unofficial camp created by NGOs and municipalities, later supported by IOM and UNHCR, with tents, toilets, showers, water, food and medical services. Police informed residents about border closures and transfer options, and the camp was evacuated in May 2016 to state accommodation. The Government argued Idomeni was never official, no record of the applicants existed, and they went there voluntarily. On asylum, it said pre-registration took place in June–July 2016, vulnerability was assessed, and the applicants were informed at the RIC of the possibility to apply but did not express a wish to do so; their first application was in 2018. The Court gave notice of the Article 3 and Article 13 complaints and declared the remainder inadmissible.

In *Wa Baile v. Switzerland* (Applications nos. 43868/18 and 25883/21, judgment of 20 February 2024), the applicant, Mohamed Shee Wa Baile, a Swiss national born in 1974, alleged that an identity check at Zürich railway station amounted to racial profiling.

On the morning of 5 February 2015, at around 7 a.m., the applicant was on his way to work when three municipal police officers stopped him for an identity check. The officer in charge later reported that his attention had been drawn by a “dark-skinned” man who seemed suspicious because he averted his gaze upon realising the officer was police and appeared to avoid him. The officer suspected a possible breach of the Federal Aliens Act and decided to check the applicant’s identity. The applicant refused to comply, said he had no identity document, repeatedly ignored police orders, and called the police racist, describing the check as vexatious. The officers took him aside, ordered him to raise his hands and spread his legs, and searched his pockets and backpack until they found a document confirming his identity. He was then allowed to leave. The applicant claimed that no one else in the mostly white crowd of commuters had been checked and that he was given no reason for the stop.

In the criminal proceedings, the applicant was fined 100 Swiss francs for refusing to comply with police orders, plus costs. The District Court found both the applicant’s and the officer’s accounts credible but held that, under domestic law, an unlawful police order still had to be obeyed unless it was null and void; it found no proof that skin colour was decisive. The Cantonal Court upheld the conviction, noting the context of Zürich railway station, suspected breaches of aliens law, and that weak grounds for the check did not make it manifestly unlawful. The Federal Supreme Court dismissed the discrimination complaint as inadmissible because it depended on facts not established by the lower court.

In separate administrative proceedings, the applicant sought a declaration that the identity check had been unlawful. The Administrative Court eventually declared the check unlawful because merely averting one’s gaze was insufficient, but it expressly left open whether the check had been discriminatory. The Federal Supreme Court then declared his further appeal inadmissible, reasoning that he had already obtained full satisfaction and merely sought additional reasoning.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 14 read in conjunction with Article 8, and under Article 13. The Court found that Article 14 + Article 8 were applicable: the identity check and search reached the severity threshold for interference with private life, and the applicant had an arguable claim of discrimination based on skin colour. The Government failed to rebut the presumption of discriminatory treatment. That presumption was strengthened by international reports showing racial profiling by police in Switzerland and was corroborated by third-party interveners. The domestic courts had failed to ascertain whether discriminatory motives were behind the check. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 14 read in conjunction with Article 8.

The Court also found a violation of Article 13, because the applicant had no effective remedy: although the Administrative Court declared the check unlawful, it left the discrimination question open, and the Federal Supreme Court’s inadmissibility ruling prevented any determination of whether racial profiling had occurred.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore the race-conscious stop of a dark-skinned man, the weak objective justification, the intrusive search, the refusal and fine, and the domestic authorities’ failure to examine discriminatory motive or provide an effective remedy.

**Summary of *Wa Baile v. Switzerland* (ECtHR, 20 February 2024)**

The case concerned Mohamed Shee Wa Baile, a Swiss national born in 1974, who alleged that an identity check at Zürich railway station was based on racial profiling. On the morning of 5 February 2015, at about 7 a.m., the applicant was on his way to work when three municipal police officers stopped him for an identity check. The officer in charge later reported that his attention had been drawn by a “dark-skinned, male individual” who seemed suspicious because he averted his gaze upon realising the officer was police and tried to avoid him. The officer suspected a possible breach of the Federal Aliens Act and decided to check his identity.

The applicant refused to comply. The officers took him aside, asked him to raise his hands and spread his legs, and searched his pockets and backpack until they found a document establishing his identity. He was then allowed to leave. According to the applicant, no one else in the crowd—which he described as almost entirely white—was subjected to an identity check, and he was not told why he had been stopped. He called the check racist and vexatious. He was subsequently fined CHF 100 for refusing to comply with police orders.

In the criminal proceedings, the District Court found both the applicant’s and the officer’s versions credible. It considered that skin colour had not been a decisive factor and held that, even if the check had been unlawful, the police order was not null and void, so the applicant had been obliged to comply. The Cantonal Court upheld the conviction, noting the context of Zürich railway station and suspected breaches of aliens legislation, and found no indication of manifestly discriminatory grounds. The Federal Supreme Court dismissed the discrimination complaint as inadmissible because it was bound by the lower court’s factual findings.

In parallel administrative proceedings, the applicant sought a declaration that the check had been unlawful. The Zürich Administrative Court eventually held that the check had been unlawful because merely looking away did not justify it, but it expressly left open whether discrimination on the ground of skin colour had occurred. The Federal Supreme Court then declared the applicant’s further appeal inadmissible, reasoning that he had already obtained full satisfaction and had no right to additional reasoning on the discrimination issue.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 14 read with Article 8 and under Article 13. The Court found that Article 14 read with Article 8 was applicable: the identity check and search reached the severity threshold for interference with private life, and the applicant had an arguable claim of discrimination based on skin colour. The key violation was that the domestic courts had failed to ascertain whether discriminatory motives lay behind the identity check. The Government was unable to rebut the presumption of discriminatory treatment during the check. That presumption was strengthened by international reports showing racial profiling by police in Switzerland, corroborated by third-party interveners. The Court also found a violation of Article 13, as the applicant had no effective remedy for his discrimination complaint.

In *Wa Baile v. Switzerland* (ECtHR, Third Section, 20 February 2024), the applicant, Mohamed Shee Wa Baile, a Swiss national born in 1974, complained about an identity check at Zürich railway station on 5 February 2015. Around 7 a.m., while on his way to work, he was stopped by three municipal police officers. The officer’s report stated that his attention was drawn by a “dark-skinned” man who seemed suspicious because he averted his gaze upon seeing police and tried to avoid them; the officer suspected a breach of the Federal Aliens Act. The applicant alleged he was the only person checked in a mostly white commuting crowd and was not told why he had been stopped. He refused to comply. The officers took him aside, ordered him to raise his hands and spread his legs, and searched his pockets and backpack until they found identity documents. He was then released.

Because of his refusal, he was fined CHF 100 for failing to comply with police orders, plus CHF 150 costs. In the criminal proceedings, he argued that the check was racial profiling. The District Court found both the applicant’s and officer’s accounts credible, but held there was nothing showing skin colour was decisive. It also held that even if the check were unlawful, the order was not null and void, so he was obliged to comply; administrative courts could later review its lawfulness. The Cantonal Court upheld the conviction, finding no indication of manifestly discriminatory grounds and accepting that the check was prompted by the applicant’s conduct. It noted the busy station context and that weak grounds did not make the check manifestly unlawful. The Federal Supreme Court dismissed his discrimination complaint as inadmissible because it contradicted the lower court’s factual findings.

In parallel administrative proceedings, the applicant sought a declaration that the check had been unlawful. After the criminal case ended, the authorities dismissed his request, saying they were bound by the criminal findings. In October 2020, the Zurich Administrative Court held the check unlawful because, even accepting the officer’s account that the applicant looked away, the check was not justified. However, it expressly left open whether the check was discriminatory on the ground of skin colour. The Federal Supreme Court then declared his further appeal inadmissible in December 2020, reasoning that he had already obtained full satisfaction and had no right to additional reasoning on discrimination.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged racial profiling and lack of an effective remedy. The Court found Article 14 read with Article 8 applicable: the identity check and search attained the severity threshold for private life, and he had an arguable claim of discrimination based on skin colour. The Government failed to rebut the presumption of discriminatory treatment. The Court stated that domestic courts had failed to ascertain whether discriminatory motives lay behind the check. This presumption was strengthened by international reports showing police racial profiling in Switzerland, corroborated by third-party interveners. The Court also found a violation of Article 13 because no effective remedy existed for his Article 14 + Article 8 complaint.

The case concerns an application by Verein KlimaSeniorinnen Schweiz, a Swiss association of older women, and four individual women against Switzerland. The applicants alleged that Switzerland’s inadequate climate-change mitigation policies violated their rights under Articles 2, 8, 6, and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The association’s members are predominantly women aged 64 and over, who claimed to be particularly vulnerable to heatwaves and other health effects of climate change. The applicants relied on scientific evidence that climate change causes rising temperatures, more frequent and intense heatwaves, and serious cardiovascular and respiratory risks, especially for elderly women. They argued that Switzerland, as a high-emitting state, had failed to adopt and implement sufficient greenhouse-gas reduction measures to meet its commitments under the Paris Agreement.

In November 2016, the applicants requested Swiss federal authorities—including the Federal Council, the Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications, the Federal Office for the Environment, and the Federal Office of Public Health—to take measures to reduce greenhouse-gas emissions, set a carbon budget, and protect vulnerable groups. The authorities rejected the request. The applicants appealed to the Federal Administrative Court, which dismissed their case, and then to the Federal Supreme Court, which also rejected their appeal. The domestic courts essentially treated the matter as political or found that the applicants lacked standing, without seriously engaging with the scientific evidence or the merits of the climate complaints.

Before the Grand Chamber, the applicants alleged that Switzerland’s failure to mitigate climate change violated the right to life (Article 2) and the right to respect for private and family life (Article 8), because it exposed them to serious adverse effects on their health and well-being. They also alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (access to court) and Article 13 (effective remedy), arguing that the domestic courts had refused to examine their claims.

The Grand Chamber held that the four individual applicants did not have victim status because they had not shown that they were personally and directly affected by the alleged failures; the threshold for victim status is especially high in climate-change cases. However, the applicant association had locus standi to act on behalf of its members. On the merits, the Court found Article 8 applicable and violated. Switzerland had failed its positive obligation to implement sufficient measures to combat climate change. There were critical lacunae in the Swiss regulatory framework: no carbon budget or quantified national greenhouse-gas emission limitations, and a failure to act in good time and in an appropriate and consistent manner in devising and implementing the relevant legislative and administrative framework. The State had exceeded its margin of appreciation.

The Court also found a violation of Article 6 § 1: the domestic courts had failed to engage seriously with the association’s action, failed to consider compelling scientific evidence and the issue of standing, and impaired the very essence of the right of access to court. The Court did not examine the Article 2 complaint separately and found it unnecessary to examine Article 13. Under Article 46, Switzerland was to assess specific measures with the assistance of the Committee of Ministers. The Court awarded costs and expenses to the association.
Verein KlimaSeniorinnen Schweiz and Others v. Switzerland (App. no. 53600/20, Grand Chamber

In *Verein KlimaSeniorinnen Schweiz and Others v. Switzerland*, the European Court of Human Rights Grand Chamber examined Switzerland’s response to climate change and its effects on Convention rights. The applicants were the Swiss association KlimaSeniorinnen Schweiz, representing older women concerned about heat-related health risks, and four individual women. They alleged that climate change—especially rising temperatures and heatwaves—disproportionately threatens older women’s health, well-being, and lives. They argued that Switzerland had failed to adopt sufficient measures to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and meet its climate commitments, violating Article 2 (right to life) and Article 8 (right to private and family life).

The applicants asked Swiss authorities to take stronger climate mitigation action, including adequate emission-reduction targets. Their requests were rejected. On appeal, the Federal Administrative Court and Federal Supreme Court dismissed their case, essentially finding that climate change affected the general public and that the women lacked victim status or a sufficiently protected legal interest. The domestic courts did not seriously examine the merits or the scientific evidence on climate change. This became central to the alleged access-to-court violation.

Before the ECtHR, the key admissibility issue was victim status and locus standi. The Court set out tailored criteria for climate-change cases. It found that the four individual applicants did not meet the particularly high threshold for victim status: they had not shown they were personally and directly affected in a sufficiently specific way. However, the applicant association had standing to act on behalf of its members. It had legal personality, was genuinely dedicated to protecting its members’ rights, and its members were exposed to serious adverse effects of climate change on their lives, health, well-being, and quality of life. The association could therefore pursue the complaints.

On the merits, the Court held Article 8 applicable and recognized a right to effective state protection from serious adverse effects of climate change. States have a positive obligation to implement adequate mitigation measures. While states enjoy a wide margin of appreciation as to the means chosen, that margin is reduced regarding the need to combat climate change and set aims. Switzerland had failed to comply. The Court identified critical lacunae in the Swiss regulatory framework: the authorities had failed to quantify national greenhouse gas emission limitations through a carbon budget or equivalent, and had failed to act in good time and in an appropriate, consistent manner in devising and implementing legislative and administrative measures. This exceeded the State’s margin of appreciation and violated Article 8.

The Court also found a violation of Article 6 § 1 (access to court). The domestic courts’ dismissal of the association’s action impaired the very essence of its right of access to court. They failed to engage seriously with the merits, gave no convincing reasons for not examining the complaints, and failed to consider compelling scientific evidence or properly examine the association’s standing. The Court stressed the key role of domestic courts in climate-change litigation and access to justice.

Under Article 46, Switzerland must assess specific measures to be taken, with the Committee of Ministers supervising execution. The judgment established important principles on collective action, intergenerational burden-sharing, and State obligations in the climate-change context.

In *Votta Ronza v. Italy* (Application no. 38083/10), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 14 November 2024. The case originated from an application against Italy lodged under Article 34 of the Convention on 7 July 2010. The applicant was represented by Mr G. Romano, a lawyer practising in Rome. The applicant’s details and the specific facts relevant to the application were set out in an appended table, which is not reproduced in the provided text.

In substance, she alleged that the failure to enforce the final domestic judgment deprived the proceedings of practical effect. She also raised other complaints under the Convention, in particular under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, concerning the non-enforcement of the same final domestic judgment. That complaint was examined under the Court’s well-established case-law.

It referred to *Hornsby v. Greece*, which confirms that the right to a fair hearing would be illusory if a final, binding judicial decision remained unenforced to the detriment of one party. The Court also relied on earlier judgments concerning non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of final domestic judgments, including *Ventorino v. Italy*, *De Trana v. Italy*, *Nicola Silvestri v. Italy*, *Antonetto v. Italy*, and *De Luca v. Italy*. In those leading cases, the Court had already found violations in respect of issues similar to those raised by the applicant.

Having examined all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on the admissibility and merits of the Article 6 § 1 complaint. It considered that, in the instant case, the Italian authorities had not deployed all necessary efforts to enforce fully and in due time the decision in the applicant’s favour. As to the complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, the Court found that it was not manifestly ill-founded within the meaning of Article 35 § 3 (a) and was not inadmissible on any other ground. Zdjelar v. Croatia (Application no. 58566/19) concerns an application brought by Cena and Robert Zdjelar, Croatian nationals living in Germany. In 1984 they bought a flat in Karlovac, Croatia, which they used during holidays. In autumn 1991, during the war in Croatia, I.B. and his family, internally displaced persons, occupied the flat. On 14 April 1992, the Karlovac Township authority allocated the flat to that family for temporary use; that decision was set aside on 5 July 1996.

On 27 September 1995, the Temporary Takeover and Administration of Certain Property Act (“the Sequestration Act”) entered into force. It provided that property in previously occupied territories belonging to persons who had left Croatia after 17 October 1990 could be sequestered by the State. Local authorities took possession of such property, and their sequestration commissions could temporarily accommodate others there. On 27 September 1996, Karlovac Township’s Sequestration Commission allocated the applicants’ flat for temporary use to Ms Đ.V.

The applicants applied for repossession on 1 March 1999. On 16 October 2000, the Karlovac Township Housing Commission set aside the 1996 allocation and ordered Đ.V. to vacate. After eviction proceedings, the flat was handed back to the applicants on 30 July 2001.

On 25 April 2002, the applicants sued Karlovac Township in the Karlovac Municipal Court for compensation for damage caused by the unlawful disposals of their flat. They claimed both the 1992 and 1996 decisions were unlawful and that the Township was liable for physical damage and lost rent. The Township denied liability. During the proceedings, the Municipal Court, at the applicants’ initiative, invited the State to intervene; the State declined on 11 May 2009.

After a remittal, the Municipal Court dismissed the action on 27 May 2013. On appeal, the Karlovac County Court on 8 January 2014 partly reversed. It allowed the claim for the period between 5 July 1996 and 30 July 2001. It found the 1996 allocation unlawful because Karlovac had never been occupied, the applicants had not left Croatia after 17 October 1990, and Đ.V. was not eligible for accommodation in sequestered property. It held the Township and the State jointly and severally liable. It upheld dismissal for the earlier period, finding the 1992 decision lawful. On 17 February 2014, the Township paid the applicants HRK 240,163.89 (EUR 31,875.26) as the judgment debt.

The Township, but not the applicants, appealed on points of law. The applicants replied, but the Municipal Court did not forward their reply to the Supreme Court. On 24 June 2014, the Supreme Court reversed the County Court and dismissed the claim for 5 July 1996 to 30 July 2001. It held that under section 13 of the State Administration System Act, the State was solely liable for damage caused not only by its own bodies but also by local authorities in administrative matters conferred on them. Since the State had conferred powers under the Sequestration Act on local authorities, and the applicants had sued only the Township, their claim had to be dismissed. On 18 April 2019, the Constitutional Court dismissed their constitutional complaint.

Meanwhile, the Township brought an unjust-enrichment action. By a judgment of 12 April 2017, final on 30 January 2020, the applicants were ordered to repay the amount received under the County Court’s judgment.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants complained that the Supreme Court’s dismissal of their civil action because they had sued the Township rather than the State violated Article 6 § 1 (right of access to a court) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (right to property). Complaints concerning the length of the civil proceedings and discrimination were declared inadmissible.

Case H.T. v. Germany and Greece (Application no. 13337/19), ECHR Fourth Section, judgment of 15 October 2024, concerned a Syrian national who had sought asylum in Greece, was removed from Germany to Greece the same day he was intercepted at the German-Austrian border, and was then detained in Greece.

The applicant first arrived in Greece on 30 June 2018 on Megisti island. He was detained and, on 4 July 2018, ordered removed to Türkiye under the EU-Türkiye Statement. On 18 July 2018 he applied for asylum in Leros. A geographical limitation confined him to Leros. He left the island; on 13 August 2018 the Greek Asylum Service discontinued his asylum application because he did not attend his interview.

On 4 September 2018 he attempted to enter Germany from Austria by bus. German Federal Police stopped him near the border. He presented a stolen Bulgarian identity card but also had a Syrian identity card, a Greek arrival certificate, and notes about refugee organisations in Germany. He was placed under provisional arrest on suspicion of unauthorised entry, unlawful residence and misuse of identity papers. He was informed of his rights and questioned with an Arabic interpreter. He expressed a wish to apply for asylum in Germany and to live with his brother in Dortmund. He refused consent to notify the Syrian mission.

German authorities refused him entry and returned him to Athens by plane the same day under the 2018 Administrative Arrangement between Germany and Greece. That arrangement applied where a person had expressed a wish for international protection and had a Eurodac hit showing a prior asylum request in Greece. It provided for return by air to Athens, generally within 48 hours, after notification to Greek authorities. No individual assurances were given by Greece. The applicant alleged that Germany did not register his asylum claim, did not provide a lawyer, gave contradictory information about whether he would be returned to Austria or Greece, and did not properly translate or explain the final refusal-of-entry decision. The Court found Germany violated Article 3 (procedural): there was insufficient basis at the material time for a general presumption that Greece offered an adequate asylum procedure protecting against refoulement and Article 3 treatment; the arrangement contained no guarantees; no individual assurances were obtained; Germany failed to conduct an individualised risk assessment; and the applicant was removed hastily without access to a lawyer.

After his return to Greece, the applicant was arrested and detained pending removal to Türkiye. He was held in the Attica Directorate for Foreigners, then at Leros police station and the Leros Reception and Identification Centre. He alleged degrading detention conditions: 24-hour confinement in a cell, no outdoor exercise, damp and poorly ventilated space, no phone access, lack of hygiene items, no recreation, and delayed medication. The Court found Greece violated Article 3 (substantive) because his detention in Leros police station for two months and seventeen days lacked amenities required for prolonged detention and amounted to degrading treatment. His overall detention in Greece pending deportation lasted two months and twenty-three days. The Court held this overall detention justified under Article 5 §1, but found a violation of Article 5 §4 because the legality of his detention was not examined. He was later identified as vulnerable, released on 27 November 2018, and recognised as a refugee in Greece in 2020. In parallel German proceedings, he eventually received subsidiary protection in Germany in 2022.

The European Court of Human Rights case H.T. v. Germany and Greece (no. 13337/19, judgment 15 October 2024) concerned the immediate removal of a Syrian asylum-seeker from Germany to Greece and his subsequent detention in Greece.

The applicant first arrived in Greece in June 2018 and applied for asylum on Leros in July 2018. He later left Greece, alleging poor reception conditions and lack of effective access to asylum, and travelled through Hungary to Germany. On 4 September 2018 he was stopped at the German-Austrian border. He told German police that he wished to seek asylum in Germany, where his brother lived. He carried a Syrian identity card, a Greek arrival certificate and a stolen Bulgarian identity card. Although he was questioned with an Arabic interpreter, his asylum request was not registered. Instead, German authorities refused him entry and returned him to Athens the same day under the 2018 Administrative Arrangement between Germany and Greece on refusing entry to persons seeking protection at the German-Austrian border. The return relied on a Eurodac hit showing that he had previously applied for asylum in Greece. Before removal, he had no lawyer; the later refusal-of-entry decision for asylum-seekers was not explained in Arabic, and he received contradictory information about whether he would be returned to Austria or Greece.

Before the Court, H.T. alleged that Germany violated Article 3 (procedural) by removing him to Greece without examining his asylum request or assessing the risk of refoulement and inhuman or degrading treatment. He argued that the administrative arrangement provided no individual guarantees and that Germany assumed, without adequate basis, that Greece would provide an adequate asylum procedure. The Court agreed. It found that, at the material time, there was an insufficient basis for a general presumption that Greece offered access to an adequate asylum procedure protecting against refoulement and Article 3 ill-treatment. Neither the administrative arrangement nor any individual assurance provided such guarantees. Germany also failed to conduct an individualised risk assessment before removal, and H.T. was removed hastily without access to a lawyer. Germany was therefore found to have violated Article 3 procedurally.

In Greece, upon return on 4 September 2018, H.T. was arrested and detained pending deportation. He was held in the Attica Directorate for Foreigners and then at Leros police station from 9 to 21 September 2018 and from 11 October to 27 November 2018, with an intervening period in a container at the Leros Reception and Identification Centre. His total detention pending deportation lasted two months and twenty-three days. He complained that during prolonged periods in the Leros police station he was confined to a cell almost all day, without outdoor exercise, adequate light, ventilation, hygiene items, recreational space or timely medication. A psychiatrist diagnosed an anxiety-depressive disorder, and EASO identified him as vulnerable, exempting him from the border procedure. He lodged objections against detention, which were rejected. The Court found that the conditions of his detention in the Greek police station amounted to degrading treatment, violating Article 3 substantively. It found his overall detention pending deportation justified under Article 5 §1, but that Greece failed to examine the legality of his detention as required by Article 5 §4. He was released on 27 November 2018 and later recognised as a refugee in Greece.

**H.T. v. Germany and Greece (Application no. 13337/19), ECtHR Judgment, 15 October 2024**

The applicant, H.T., a Syrian national, first entered Greece on 30 June 2018 at Megisti and was detained. On 4 July 2018 Greece ordered his removal to Türkiye under the EU-Türkiye Statement. On 18 July 2018 he applied for asylum in Leros and was subjected to a geographical limitation requiring him to remain on that island. He later left Leros, and on 13 August 2018 the Greek Asylum Service discontinued his asylum application because he failed to attend an interview.

On 4 September 2018, H.T. attempted to enter Germany via Austria. He was stopped by German federal police and expressed a wish to apply for asylum in Germany. The German authorities found a Greek arrival certificate and a Eurodac hit showing his prior Greek asylum request. The same day, Germany refused him entry under section 18(2) of the Asylum Act and returned him by plane to Athens under the 2018 Administrative Arrangement between Germany and Greece concerning refusal of entry to persons seeking protection at the German-Austrian border. His asylum request was not registered or processed in Germany.

The applicant alleged serious procedural defects: he was removed within hours, had no access to a lawyer before removal, received contradictory information about whether he would be returned to Austria or Greece, and the final refusal decision was not properly explained in Arabic. He also claimed that Germany made no individualised risk assessment before removing him to Greece. The German Government maintained that he was informed of his rights with an interpreter and that he agreed to voluntary return, though the final asylum-specific refusal notice was explained only orally in English shortly before departure.

Upon his return to Greece, H.T. was arrested and detained with a view to removal. He was held in the Attica Directorate for Foreigners and then, from about 9 September to 27 November 2018, at Leros police station and the Leros Reception and Identification Centre. His total detention in Greece lasted two months and twenty-three days, including two months and seventeen days at the police station. He alleged degrading conditions: being confined to a cell 24 hours a day, no outdoor exercise, damp and poorly ventilated accommodation, lack of hygiene items, no recreational activity, and delays in receiving prescribed medication. Greek authorities disputed these claims. His objections against detention were rejected by the Rhodes Administrative Tribunal, which found him a flight risk and considered his condition allegations unproven. EASO later identified him as vulnerable; he was released on 27 November 2018 and recognised as a refugee in Greece in April 2020. Germany later granted him subsidiary protection in 2022.

The European Court of Human Rights found that Germany violated Article 3 procedurally. At the material time, there was an insufficient basis to presume that Greece provided adequate asylum procedures protecting against refoulement and treatment contrary to Article 3. The administrative arrangement contained no guarantees, no individual assurances were given, and Germany failed to conduct an individualised risk assessment before removal. The applicant was also hastily removed without prior access to a lawyer. Greece violated Article 3 substantively because the conditions of his detention at Leros police station for a prolonged period amounted to degrading treatment. His overall detention pending deportation was justified under Article 5 § 1, but Greece violated Article 5 § 4 because there was no examination of the legality of that detention.

V.D. suffered from schizophrenia. On 11 November 2017 he left a psychiatric institution in Slovenia and entered Croatia. That same day, a hotel employee called the Metković police after V.D. fought with a guest and attacked people at the hotel, reporting that he was in mental distress. The responding officers were allegedly aware that the man could be V.D., a mentally disabled person dangerous to himself and others.

At the hotel carpark, four officers approached V.D. as he sat on his car, visibly distressed and mumbling. He complied with an order to empty his pockets but refused to turn around and spread his legs. He took out his phone, shouted that if they came closer he would press a button and “blow up” everyone, and then sat on the ground, still mumbling. After he refused repeated orders to drop the phone, Officer G. used pepper spray. V.D. lay on his side, held his face, bit his lips and tongue, and spat blood. Three officers then forced him onto his stomach and tried to handcuff him. He resisted, hit his head on the pavement, and bit off part of his little finger. Police called an ambulance around 2:35 p.m.; five officers held him in the prone position until it arrived about ten minutes later.

The doctor gave V.D. a sedative, noting he was bleeding, blue in the face, and had swallowed part of his finger. He was placed face down on the stretcher and restrained with three straps. During the approximately one-and-a-half-hour drive to Dubrovnik General Hospital, the doctor and nurse sat in front while three police officers sat in the back with V.D. Because he remained restless, the doctor gave another sedative; later she found he had died. The official autopsy concluded he died of natural causes—cardiac arrest—and that his injuries, though grave, had no causal link to death. A second autopsy arranged by the applicant and a later forensic report concluded that V.D. had suffered a violent death from mental trauma: prone restraint, police pressure on his back, self-harm, and medical handling aggravated his agitated mental state, leading to shock and cardiac arrest. That report found no medical negligence but said medical staff should have sat beside him during transport.

The applicant’s criminal complaints against police for serious bodily injury resulting in death and against medical staff for negligence were rejected. After review, an investigation was opened in 2020; a forensic report was obtained in 2021; but the State Attorney again rejected the complaint, finding the force lawful and proportionate and no negligence. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint, finding the investigation independent and thorough despite delay.

The key alleged violations under Article 2 concerned both substantive and procedural obligations. The applicant argued that police knew V.D. had mental health problems but failed to inform or request medical assistance as domestic guidelines required; used pepper spray despite it being prohibited for passive resistance; failed to show special care for a person in mental distress; kept him prone at the scene and in the ambulance for a prolonged period; inadequately monitored him during transport; lacked adequate training and experience; used force that was not “absolutely necessary”; and conducted an ineffective criminal investigation.

Croatia* (App. no. 47909/19), the European Court of Human Rights examined the death of the applicant’s partner, V.D., during a Croatian police intervention and the subsequent investigation. In *Tretyakov and Others v. Russia* (Applications nos. 33610/18 and 21 others), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee) delivered a judgment on 4 April 2024, adopted on 14 March 2024. The case arose from 22 applications lodged against Russia under Article 34 of the Convention. The Russian Government were given notice of the applications. The applicants’ principal complaint was that their pre-trial detention had been unreasonably long, in violation of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to trial within a reasonable time or to release pending trial. The appended table set out the applicants’ identities and the specific details of each application. Some applicants also raised additional complaints under other Convention provisions.

Because the applications concerned similar subject matter, the Court decided to examine them jointly in a single judgment. On jurisdiction, the Court observed that the facts giving rise to the alleged violations occurred before 16 September 2022, when the Russian Federation ceased to be a party to the Convention. Relying on *Fedotova and Others v. Russia*, the Court held that it still had jurisdiction to examine the applications.

As to the main complaint under Article 5 § 3, the Court recalled the general principles governing the right to trial within a reasonable time or release pending trial, as set out in cases such as *Kudła v. Poland* and *McKay v. the United Kingdom*. It noted that in the leading case of *Dirdizov v. Russia*, it had already found a violation in respect of similar issues. After examining all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of leading to a different conclusion. It therefore held that the length of the applicants’ pre-trial detention was excessive, in violation of Article 5 § 3.

Some applicants also submitted other complaints that raised issues already covered by well-established case-law. The Court declared these complaints admissible, finding they were not manifestly ill-founded. It concluded that they disclosed violations of the Convention in light of several prior judgments. These included: *Idalov v. Russia*, concerning lengthy review of detention matters; *Svinarenko and Slyadnev v. Russia*, concerning detention in a metal cage during court hearings; *Yaroslav Belousov v. Russia*, concerning extreme overcrowding inside a glass cabin, amounting to a violation of Article 3; *Andrey Smirnov v. Russia*, concerning restrictions on family visits in pre-trial detention facilities; *Tsvetkova and Others* and *Fortalnov and Others v. Russia*, concerning unlawful detention; *Tomov and Others v. Russia*, concerning conditions of transport of detainees and the lack of an effective domestic remedy; *Chaldayev v. Russia*, concerning discriminatory treatment regarding family visits in pre-trial detention; and *Mukhin v. Russia*, concerning conviction for making calls to participate in extremist activities.

In view of these findings, the Court considered that there was no need to deal separately with complaints under Article 13 about the lack of effective domestic remedies relating to the use of metal cages and other security arrangements in courtrooms, referring to *Valyuzhenich v. Russia*.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore that the applicants had been held in pre-trial detention in Russia; they alleged that detention was excessively long; and some additionally alleged specific procedural and detention-related abuses, including lengthy detention reviews, cage and glass-cabin confinement, overcrowding, family-visit restrictions and discrimination, unlawful detention, poor transport conditions, lack of remedies, and an extremist-speech conviction. The Court found a violation of Article 5 § 3 and additional violations based on established case-law.

001-233495:
In A.D. and Others v. Sweden (Application no. 22283/21), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section) considered whether Sweden could remove five Albanian nationals—a father, mother, and three children—to Albania without breaching Article 3 of the Convention. The family applied for asylum in Sweden on 6 December 2018; their request was refused and deportation ordered. They alleged that return would expose them to ill-treatment by non-State actors and that Albania could not or would not protect them.

The key facts concerned the first applicant’s work as an Albanian police officer from 1998 until November 2018, including anti-cannabis police activity. The family claimed that this work made them targets. In October 2017, the third applicant, the eldest daughter, was allegedly the victim of an attempted kidnapping by three masked men; she was traumatised and later developed depression. During 2017–2018, shots were fired at the family’s front door and a hand grenade exploded near their home. The applicants did not know who was responsible but believed the incidents were linked to the first applicant’s police work. They did not report these incidents to Albanian police, saying they distrusted law enforcement because of corruption and feared that reporting would worsen their situation. The first applicant had, however, been in direct contact with a senior police officer. The family left Albania shortly after he resigned.

In Sweden, the Migration Agency rejected the asylum request on 18 January 2019 and ordered deportation. It did not question that the incidents had occurred but found that the perpetrators and motives were unclear and treated the acts as crimes by unknown individuals. Based on country information, it concluded that Albania generally had the ability and willingness to protect citizens. It also found that the applicants had not taken reasonable steps to obtain domestic protection, especially because the attempted kidnapping had not been reported. The Migration Court upheld that decision on 28 April 2020, noting corruption problems but finding insufficient evidence that Albanian authorities lacked the will or ability to act, especially given the first applicant’s police connections. The Migration Court of Appeal denied leave to appeal in June 2020.

After the deportation order became final, the applicants raised new circumstances: an explosion at their Albanian home on 7 January 2020, injury to the first applicant’s mother, an anonymous call saying the first applicant “must pay debts,” and a second explosion on 12 July 2020. Albanian police documents linked the explosions to earlier incidents. The Migration Agency, upheld on appeal, refused residence permits or re-examination, treating the events as additions to previously assessed circumstances and finding no proof that available State protection had been exhausted.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants alleged that removal would breach Article 3 because they risked being killed or seriously assaulted by criminal networks and Albania could not protect them. They also complained of procedural deficiencies. The Government argued that the incidents were not disputed, but the perpetrators and motives were not established, and the applicants had not shown that effective State protection was unavailable.

The Court declared the complaint admissible but found no violation. It saw no indication that the domestic proceedings lacked effective guarantees against arbitrary refoulement or were otherwise flawed. It held that the applicants had failed to demonstrate that Albanian authorities were unable or unwilling to provide appropriate protection against the feared non-State actor risk.

In A.D. and Others v. Sweden (App. no. 22283/21, 7 May 2024), five Albanian nationals—a father, mother, and three children—complained that their deportation from Sweden to Albania after failed asylum requests would violate Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights. They alleged a risk of ill-treatment by non-State actors and that Albania was unable or unwilling to protect them.

The family applied for asylum in Sweden in December 2018. The father had been a police officer since 1998, working against cannabis production and trafficking, and resigned in November 2018. The family claimed the threats arose from that work. In October 2017, the eldest daughter was allegedly the victim of an attempted kidnapping by three masked men, which traumatized her and led to depression. In 2017–2018, shots were fired at their front door and a hand grenade exploded near their home. The perpetrators were unknown. The applicants believed the incidents were linked to the father’s anti-cannabis police work. They did not generally report the kidnapping to Albanian authorities, citing distrust and corruption, though the father had contacted senior police. They submitted a news article, a prosecutor report from August 2017 about threats by armed men, and a police document about the attempted kidnapping.

Sweden’s Migration Agency rejected asylum in January 2019. It did not dispute that the incidents occurred but found the perpetrators, motives, and connections unclear. It treated them as criminal acts by unknown individuals, primarily for Albanian authorities to prosecute. Country information showed corruption problems, but Albania had taken anti-corruption measures and authorities had a general ability and willingness to protect. The applicants had not exhausted domestic remedies by reporting the kidnapping. Since the father had left police work, threats related to that work should have ceased. The Migration Court upheld the decision in April 2020. It acknowledged corruption and doubts about general protection but assessed the case individually. Given the father’s police connections and contacts with police and prosecutors, the information did not show authorities lacked the will or ability to act. The Migration Court of Appeal denied leave in June 2020.

In July 2020, the applicants sought re-examination based on new incidents: an explosion at their Albanian home in January 2020 injuring the father’s mother, an anonymous call saying the father must pay debts, and a second explosion in July 2020. Police documents linked these to earlier incidents. The Migration Agency refused re-examination, treating the events as additions to previously examined circumstances. It said there was still no proof the applicants had exhausted State protection or that the new events were lasting impediments. The Migration Court upheld, and the Court of Appeal denied leave in September 2020.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants argued return would expose them to death or serious assault by criminal networks and that Albania was unable or unwilling to protect them. They also alleged procedural deficiencies. The Swedish Government argued the events were not established as linked to a known actor, and the key issue was effective State protection. It relied on country information showing a largely functioning legal system and reasonable ability and willingness to enforce the law.

The ECtHR declared the Article 3 complaint admissible but found no violation. It saw no indication that the domestic proceedings lacked effective guarantees against arbitrary refoulement or were otherwise flawed. The applicants failed to demonstrate that Albanian authorities were unable or unwilling to obviate any risk of ill-treatment by non-State actors by providing appropriate protection. Removal to Albania would therefore not breach Article 3.

**Case: A.D. and Others v. Sweden (Application no. 22283/21), European Court of Human Rights, First Section, judgment 7 May 2024 (final 7 August 2024).**

The applicants were five Albanian nationals—a father, mother, and their three children—who sought asylum in Sweden in December 2018. Their complaint concerned their proposed removal to Albania, which they alleged would violate Article 3 of the Convention because they faced a risk of ill-treatment by non-State actors and because the Albanian authorities were unable or unwilling to protect them.

The key facts arose from the first applicant’s work as an Albanian police officer, including involvement in operations against cannabis production and trafficking. He resigned in November 2018, and the family left Albania soon afterward. The applicants claimed that in October 2017 the eldest daughter was the victim of an attempted kidnapping by masked men; that shots were fired at their front door; and that a hand grenade exploded near their home during 2017–2018. They believed these incidents were linked to the first applicant’s police work and perceived statements by the kidnappers as threats. They did not report the incidents to the Albanian police or other authorities, saying they distrusted law enforcement due to corruption and feared making a report would worsen their situation. The first applicant, however, had direct contact with a senior police officer. They submitted documents to the Swedish Migration Agency, including a report to the district prosecutor’s office concerning an August 2017 threat and a police document about the attempted kidnapping.

In January 2019, the Migration Agency rejected their asylum request and ordered deportation. It did not doubt that the incidents occurred, but found that the perpetrators were unknown and their intentions unclear. It considered the acts criminal and held that the Albanian authorities generally had the ability and willingness to protect citizens. It also found that the applicants had not reported the attempted kidnapping or exhausted available domestic remedies. The Migration Court upheld the decision in April 2020. It noted country information showing a largely functioning Albanian judicial system but also corruption and police hesitation in some disputes. It concluded that effective protection could not be assumed generally, so an individual assessment was needed. Given the first applicant’s long police service and contacts with police and prosecutors, the court found insufficient evidence that the Albanian authorities lacked the will or ability to act. The Migration Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal in June 2020.

After the deportation order became final, the applicants sought re-examination, citing a January 2020 explosion at their family home in Albania, an anonymous threat to the first applicant’s mother that he “must pay debts,” and a second explosion in July 2020. Police documents linked these events to the earlier 2017 incidents. The Migration Agency refused re-examination, treating the new incidents as additions to previously assessed circumstances and finding no proof that the applicants had exhausted State protection. The Migration Court and Court of Appeal upheld that refusal.

Before the European Court, the applicants alleged that removal would breach Article 3 due to the risk from criminal networks and the Albanian authorities’ inability or unwillingness to protect them. They also complained of procedural deficiencies, including insufficient time, translation issues, refusal of an oral hearing, and refusal to re-examine new circumstances. The Government argued that the events were not disputed but that the perpetrators and underlying motive were never established; State protection was available; and the onus was on the applicants to show they could not obtain it.

The Court declared the application admissible but found no violation of Article 3. It saw no indication that the domestic proceedings lacked effective guarantees against arbitrary refoulement or were otherwise flawed. The applicants had failed to demonstrate that the Albanian authorities were unable or unwilling to obviate any risk of ill-treatment by non-State actors by providing appropriate protection.
