In *Cosovan v. the Republic of Moldova (No. 2)*, the applicant, Mr Serghei Cosovan, was the director of a company, V.G. A criminal investigation was opened against him on 15 January 2007 following complaints from the Chișinău municipality. Prosecutors suspected that he had operated a public car park between April and November 2006 without proper authorisation and without recording cash receipts or paying taxes. Tax authorities estimated the car park’s income at 116,428 Moldovan lei (about €7,080). The investigation also found that V.G. had failed to file tax returns since December 2004 and had been listed as a “delinquent” entity.

On 23 June 2011 the applicant asked for the criminal investigation to be discontinued because the limitation period had expired. On 27 June 2011 the prosecutor discontinued the proceedings as time-barred. In the same decision, however, the prosecutor stated that sufficient evidence confirmed the suspicion against the applicant, relying on witness statements, site records and tax-authority replies, and concluded that the income had been obtained through the criminal offence of illegal commercial activity under Article 241 § 2 (e) and (f) of the Criminal Code. Acting under the special-confiscation provisions, the prosecutor ordered the applicant to pay the State the equivalent of MDL 116,428, even though no money had been seized and no criminal penalty was imposed. The prosecutor characterised special confiscation as a precautionary measure.

The applicant challenged the confiscation. He argued that he had never admitted guilt, that his guilt had not been established by a court, and that he had not been properly informed that asking for discontinuance on limitation grounds would be treated as an admission. He complained that the confiscation violated his right to a fair trial and his right to be presumed innocent. He also noted that the confiscation had already been enforced.

A superior prosecutor dismissed his appeal on 6 April 2012. The prosecutor reiterated that the sum represented proceeds of criminal activity and could be subject to special confiscation. He further stated that discontinuance because of the expiry of the limitation period did not amount to rehabilitation, and that a request for such discontinuance indicated a waiver of the right to have guilt proved in criminal proceedings. On 15 January 2013 the investigating judge of the Buiucani District Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint. The court found that sufficient evidence had been gathered, that the applicant had been acknowledged as a suspect in 2008, that he had sought discontinuance, and that he had not contested the factual findings. It held that, even if no criminal penalty was imposed, special confiscation could apply where income was derived from an act prohibited by the Criminal Code.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 of the Convention about the confiscation despite the discontinuance of the criminal proceedings as time-barred and about the prosecutor’s statements implying his guilt. He died in 2021, and his wife pursued the application.

The Court examined whether the confiscation order amounted to a penalty or an affirmation of guilt. It found that, under domestic law, special confiscation was a precautionary measure directed against property rather than a person, intended to prevent the use of assets from an unlawful act. It did not amount to a penalty and did not require a finding of guilt for a criminal offence. The statements in the confiscation order, read in context, could not reasonably be understood as an affirmation of guilt to the criminal standard. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 6 § 2 of the Convention.

The case concerns an application by Mr Serghei Cosovan against the Republic of Moldova. In 2006 the Chișinău municipality complained that the applicant, acting as director of the company V.G., operated a public car park without authorisation, without a cash-recording system, and without paying taxes. On 15 January 2007 a criminal investigation was opened against him for illegal commercial activity under Article 241 of the Criminal Code. Tax authorities calculated the car park’s income for April–November 2006 at MDL 116,428 (about €7,080). V.G. had submitted no tax returns since December 2004 and was listed as a “delinquent” entity.

On 27 June 2011, after the applicant requested discontinuance because the limitation period had expired, the prosecutor discontinued the criminal investigation as time-barred. In the same decision, the prosecutor ordered special confiscation of the equivalent sum, MDL 116,428. The prosecutor relied on evidence said to confirm the suspicion: witness statements, site records, and tax-authority replies. He stated that the applicant had obtained the money through the criminal offence of operating an illegal car park and that, since the money had not been seized, its equivalent value should be transferred to the State as a precautionary measure under Articles 98 and 106 of the Criminal Code.

The applicant challenged only the confiscation. He argued that he had never admitted guilt, that his guilt had not been determined by a court, and that he had not been properly informed that requesting discontinuance as time-barred would be treated as an admission or waiver. He claimed the confiscation breached his right to a fair trial and the presumption of innocence. A superior prosecutor dismissed the appeal in April 2012, reasoning that discontinuance on limitation grounds was not rehabilitation and that the request implied a waiver of the right to have guilt proved in criminal proceedings.

In January 2013 the Buiucani District Court dismissed the applicant’s further complaint. It found sufficient evidence confirming the suspicion, noted that the applicant had been acknowledged as a suspect in 2008 and had declined to make a statement, and held that special confiscation could apply even without a criminal penalty where income derived from an act prohibited by the Criminal Code. The applicant did not contest the prosecutor’s factual conclusions, the court said, and the confiscation had already been enforced.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 6 §§1 and 2 that the confiscation order, made after proceedings were discontinued as time-barred, violated his fair-trial rights and the presumption of innocence. The Court examined whether the order amounted to a penalty or an affirmation of guilt. It noted that under Moldovan law special confiscation was a precautionary, in rem measure directed against property rather than a person, intended to prevent use of assets from an unlawful act. It did not require a finding of guilt or a criminal penalty. Read as a whole and against the correct domestic-law framework, the confiscation order’s statements could not reasonably be understood as affirming guilt to the criminal standard. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 6 §2.

In **Cosovan v. the Republic of Moldova (No. 2)**, the European Court of Human Rights examined whether a special confiscation order made after criminal proceedings were discontinued as time-barred violated Article 6 §§1 and 2, especially the presumption of innocence. The applicant, Serghei Cosovan, was a Moldovan national and director/operator of V.G., a company suspected of running a public car park in Chișinău without State authorisation, without recording cash receipts, and without paying taxes between April and November 2006. Prosecutors calculated income of MDL 116,428 (about €7,080). In January 2007 a criminal investigation was opened for illegal commercial activity under Article 241 of the Criminal Code. Evidence included a land lease, tax-authority records showing V.G. had submitted no tax returns since December 2004 and was listed as delinquent, site records, ten witness statements, and statements from car-park staff that the applicant took the income. The applicant was acknowledged as a suspect in February 2008 and refused to make a statement.

In June 2011 the applicant asked for the investigation to be discontinued because the limitation period had expired. On 27 June 2011 the prosecutor discontinued the case on that ground but simultaneously ordered special confiscation of MDL 116,428. The prosecutor stated that the sum had been obtained through the criminal offence of illegal commercial activity and that, under Moldovan law, special confiscation was a precautionary measure available even where the money had not been seized. The applicant challenged only the confiscation. He argued that he had never admitted guilt, that no court had established his guilt, and that the prosecutor had improperly treated his request for discontinuance as an admission. A superior prosecutor upheld the order, reasoning that discontinuance as time-barred was not rehabilitation and that requesting it indicated a waiver of the right to have guilt proved. In January 2013 the investigating judge dismissed the applicant’s complaint. The judge relied on the evidence said to confirm the applicant’s involvement and found that special confiscation could apply even without a criminal penalty where income derived from an act prohibited by the Criminal Code. The confiscation was already enforced.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained that the confiscation and the prosecutor’s reasoning amounted to a finding of guilt despite the absence of a conviction, violating his fair-trial rights and presumption of innocence. The Court examined the nature and purpose of special confiscation under Moldovan law. It found that it was a precautionary measure directed against property rather than a penalty against the person, intended to prevent the use of assets obtained from unlawful acts. It did not require a criminal conviction or a finding of guilt to the criminal standard. Read as a whole and in context, the confiscation order’s statements about the unlawful origin of the money could not reasonably be understood as an affirmation that the applicant was guilty of the criminal offence. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 6 §2, with no separate violation under Article 6 §1. The case illustrates the ECtHR’s distinction between non-punitive, in rem confiscation and criminal guilt determinations.
001-231078:
The European Court of Human Rights case **Lypovchenko and Halabudenco v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia** concerned alleged human-rights violations in the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transnistria” (“MRT”). The applicants were Oleksandr Lypovchenko, a Ukrainian national, and Oleg Halabudenco, a Moldovan national.

**Mr Lypovchenko’s case (no. 40926/16).** On 7 July 2015, de facto “MRT” authorities arrested him and charged him with extremism based on critical social-media posts and an old diary note. He was detained on warrants issued by the de facto “Tiraspol City Court” from 9 July 2015 until 28 March 2016. During proceedings, the de facto court refused to allow him to choose his own lawyer or represent himself because of an alleged schizophrenia diagnosis; in January 2016 he was removed from the courtroom until sentencing. On 28 March 2016 he was convicted and sentenced to three years and six months’ imprisonment, upheld on appeal in May 2016.

He alleged inhuman detention conditions, including overcrowding, smoking, only one hour’s daily outdoor exercise, unfit food and water, and weekly showers. Although sentenced to a semi-open prison, he was later transferred to a closed-regime prison. He went on hunger strike several times to protest his arrest, alleged ill-treatment and detention conditions. Authorities forcibly hospitalised him for psychiatric assessment and administered psychotropic drugs without consent in 2015 and 2016. He also alleged inadequate medical care for hepatitis C, thrombophlebitis, pancreatitis and other conditions, and refusal of external consultations. In April 2016 he alleged ill-treatment after refusing to hand over a copy of his sentence, which he intended for his lawyer. Authorities confirmed he could not give documents to his mother, and requests for his medical file were refused, hindering his application to the Court. Moldova later investigated his kidnapping, and the Moldovan Supreme Court quashed the “MRT” judgments. His complaints concerned Articles 3, 5, 6, 13 and 34.

**Mr Halabudenco’s case (no. 73942/17).** In April 2016, de facto “MRT” authorities arrested him, a part-time university lecturer in Tiraspol, on bribery charges. Bail was set at 18,400 Transnistrian roubles (about EUR 1,400). He paid and was released on 5 April 2016, after which he left for Chișinău. In December 2016 the case was sent to the de facto “Tiraspol City Court.” After he asked to be tried in absentia, in March 2017 the court revoked bail, ordered his preventive arrest, and issued a search-and-arrest warrant. In April 2017 the de facto “MRT Supreme Court” upheld that decision and forfeited his bail to the “MRT treasury.” Moldova opened a criminal investigation but suspended it; Russia replied that it had no jurisdiction. His complaints concerned Article 8, Article 13, Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, and Article 2 of Protocol No. 4.

The Court reaffirmed Russia’s jurisdiction and responsibility over the “MRT” due to its military presence and support, while Moldova had fulfilled its positive obligations. It found violations including unlawful arrest, detention and conviction by bodies not constituting a “tribunal established by law”; inhuman and degrading treatment; inadequate medical assistance; forced psychiatric hospitalisation; unlawful forfeiture of bail; and interference with freedom of movement. The judgment became final on 20 May 2024.

The case concerns two applications against Moldova and Russia arising from acts of the de facto “Moldovan Republic of Transnistria” (“MRT”). The Court found Russia responsible for the MRT authorities’ acts because of its ongoing military presence, economic and political support, while Moldova had complied with its positive obligations.

**Mr Lypovchenko (no. 40926/16)**, a Ukrainian national, was arrested on 7 July 2015 by de facto MRT authorities and charged with extremism based on social-media criticism of the MRT and an old diary note referring to UN forces. He was detained from 9 July 2015 until 28 March 2016 under warrants issued by the de facto “Tiraspol City Court.” During proceedings, he could not choose his own lawyer or represent himself because of an alleged schizophrenia diagnosis. In January 2016 he was removed from the courtroom until sentencing; on 28 March 2016 he was convicted and sentenced to three years and six months, upheld on appeal in May 2016.

He alleged inhuman and degrading detention conditions, including overcrowding, poor food and water, limited walks and showers, and exposure to smoking. Although sentenced to a semi-open prison, he was transferred to a closed-regime prison in 2016. He went on hunger strike several times and was forcibly hospitalised and psychiatrically assessed in 2015 and 2016, allegedly receiving psychotropic drugs without consent or information. He also alleged inadequate medical care for hepatitis C, thrombophlebitis and later other conditions. In April 2016 he was allegedly ill-treated for refusing to hand over a copy of his sentence; prison authorities also refused to let him pass documents to his mother for his application to the Court. Moldovan authorities investigated his kidnapping and the usurpation of powers by MRT officials, and in November 2016 the Moldovan Supreme Court quashed the MRT judgments as unconstitutional.

**Mr Halabudenco (no. 73942/17)**, a Moldovan national, was a part-time university lecturer in Tiraspol. On 2 April 2016 MRT authorities arrested and detained him on a bribe charge. On 5 April 2016 the de facto “Tiraspol City Court” set bail at 18,400 Transnistrian roubles, which he paid, and he was released. He then left Transnistria and lived in Chișinău. In December 2016 the case was sent for trial. In March 2017 the de facto court rescinded bail, ordered his preventive arrest, and issued a search-and-arrest warrant; in April 2017 the de facto “MRT Supreme Court” upheld that decision and forfeited his bail to the “MRT treasury.” He alleged that this interfered with his professional activities, restricted his freedom of movement, unlawfully deprived him of his money, and left him without effective remedies. Complaints to Moldova led to a criminal investigation, later suspended; Russia replied that it did not exercise jurisdiction over the MRT.

The applicants alleged violations of Articles 3, 5, 6, 8, 13 and 34 of the Convention, Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, and Article 2 of Protocol No. 4. The Court examined jurisdiction, responsibility and the lawfulness of the MRT authorities’ actions, including detention conditions, forced psychiatric treatment, unlawful conviction, property forfeiture, movement restrictions, and lack of effective remedies.

Case Lypovchenko and Halabudenco v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia (Apps nos. 40926/16 and 73942/17, ECtHR, 20 February 2024) concerned alleged human-rights violations in the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transnistria” (“MRT”), a separatist region of Moldova. The applicants complained against both Moldova and Russia.

Mr Lypovchenko, a Ukrainian national, was arrested on 7 July 2015 by de facto MRT authorities and charged with extremism based on critical social-media posts and an old diary note referring to UN forces in Transnistria. He was detained from 9 July 2015 to 28 March 2016 under warrants issued by the de facto “Tiraspol City Court”. Because of an alleged schizophrenia diagnosis, he was not allowed to choose his own lawyer or defend himself; he was removed from the courtroom until sentencing. On 28 March 2016 he was convicted and sentenced to three years and six months’ imprisonment, upheld on 10 May 2016. He alleged overcrowded and inadequate detention conditions, poor food and water, limited outdoor access, and only weekly showers. He was forcibly hospitalised and subjected to psychiatric assessment and psychotropic treatment without consent in 2015 and 2016, although one assessment said his condition did not require treatment. He also alleged inadequate medical care for hepatitis C, thrombophlebitis and other conditions, refusal of external consultations, ill-treatment during hunger strikes, and obstruction of his ability to send documents to the Court. Moldova’s Supreme Court later quashed the MRT judgments as unconstitutional; he was released in December 2018. He invoked Articles 3, 5, 6, 13 and 34.

Mr Halabudenco, a Moldovan national, was a part-time university lecturer in Tiraspol. In April 2016 the MRT authorities arrested him on a bribery charge. Bail was set at 18,400 Transnistrian roubles (about €1,400), which he posted, and he was released. He then left Transnistria for Chișinău. In March 2017 the de facto Tiraspol City Court rescinded the bail, ordered his preventive arrest and issued a search-and-arrest warrant; the MRT Supreme Court upheld this in April 2017 and ordered the bail forfeited to the MRT treasury. He alleged that this interfered with his professional activities, unlawfully deprived him of his property (the bail), restricted his freedom of movement, and left him without effective remedies. He relied on Article 8, Article 13, Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 2 of Protocol No. 4.

The Court reaffirmed that Russia had jurisdiction and responsibility for the acts of the MRT authorities because of its military presence, political and economic support; Moldova was not responsible, having fulfilled its positive obligations. It found violations against Russia of Article 3 (detention conditions, medical care, forced psychiatric treatment), Article 5 § 1 and Article 6 § 1 (unlawful arrest, detention and conviction by MRT bodies not constituting a tribunal established by law), Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (unlawful forfeiture of bail), Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 (unlawful movement restriction), and Article 13 (no effective remedy). It found no appearance of a violation of Article 34.
001-235475:
**Pasquinelli and Others v. San Marino** (App. no. 24622/22, ECtHR First Section, judgment of 29 August 2024) concerned 26 healthcare and social-health workers—19 San Marino nationals, six Italian nationals and one Moldovan national—employed by San Marino’s Social Security Institute (SSI). In May 2021, under Law no. 85/2021, they were urged to be vaccinated against COVID-19; all declined. The legislation was amended by Law no. 97/2021, ratified by Law no. 107/2021, which regulated the consequences for unvaccinated public healthcare and social-health personnel. Vaccination was not legally compulsory, but the law empowered the SSI to apply employment-related measures.

Under section 8 of Law no. 107/2021, the SSI first had to consider reorganizing services to minimize contact between unvaccinated staff and patients/users. If reorganization was possible, unvaccinated workers could remain on duty but had to undergo an antigen test every 48 hours at their own expense (€7 per test). If reorganization was not possible, the law offered alternatives: reassignment to other SSI services or vacant public posts with corresponding salary; use of accrued ordinary and other leave; or, as a last resort, temporary suspension from service with a gross monthly allowance of €600, plus family allowances, conditional on performing socially useful activities. Failure to perform those activities could result in loss of the allowance. Workers who could not be vaccinated for documented certified health reasons could be placed on fully paid leave. The specific measures applied to each applicant were listed in the appended table.

The applicants challenged the law before San Marino’s Constitutional Court, arguing that it breached equality and non-discrimination, the right to work, self-determination and health, and international instruments. They contended that the vaccines were experimental or conditionally authorized and that vaccinated persons could still transmit the virus. By judgment no. 11 of 2 November 2021, the Constitutional Court upheld the law. It found that vaccination was not mandatory, that the law merely established a limited difference in treatment between vaccinated and unvaccinated persons, and that the measures were justified by public health, protection of vulnerable service users, and social solidarity during the pandemic. It also considered the measures proportionate. Four suspended applicants later brought administrative proceedings; three were declared inadmissible on procedural grounds and one withdrew.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged that the employment-related measures imposed for refusing COVID-19 vaccination violated Article 8 (private life), alone and in conjunction with Article 14 (discrimination). The Court held that Article 8 was applicable because the choice whether to be vaccinated was sufficiently linked to personal autonomy and private life. On the merits, however, it found no violation. The impugned legislation did not make vaccination compulsory and did not impose statutory sanctions or automatic consequences for refusal. The measures were based on individual situations and could not be considered sanctions in disguise. The case was distinguishable from *Vavřička and Others v. the Czech Republic*, which concerned mandatory childhood vaccination and fines. The Court accepted that the measures pursued legitimate aims—protecting health and the rights and freedoms of others—and were justified and proportionate. In healthcare policy matters, especially during a pandemic, States enjoy a wide margin of appreciation. San Marino had not exceeded that margin.

In *Pasquinelli and Others v. San Marino*, the applicants were 19 San Marino nationals, six Italian nationals, and one Moldovan national, all employed as healthcare and social health workers by San Marino’s Social Security Institute (SSI). In May 2021, the SSI urged them to be vaccinated against COVID-19 under Law no. 85/2021. They declined. Law no. 97/2021, ratified by Law no. 107/2021 (in force 16 June 2021), then set out measures for unvaccinated healthcare and social health personnel. Vaccination was not compulsory. Under section 8, the SSI first had to consider reorganising services to minimise contact with users. If possible, unvaccinated workers remained on duty but had to take an antigen test every 48 hours at their own expense (€7 per swab). If reorganisation was not possible, options included reassignment to other SSI services or vacant public-sector posts with corresponding salary; using ordinary and other leave accrued in 2020; or, as a last resort, temporary suspension with a €600 monthly gross allowance plus family allowances. Suspended workers had to perform socially useful activities proportional to the allowance; refusal meant losing it. Those medically unable to be vaccinated, certified, could receive full-pay leave.

The measures applied to each applicant varied, as listed in the appended table. The applicants alleged that the law and resulting employment measures interfered with their private life and discriminated against them, violating rights to work, self-determination and health. They argued there was no legal or scientific justification for treating vaccinated and unvaccinated persons differently, since vaccinated persons could still spread the virus; that vaccines were experimental and only conditionally authorised; and that the measures breached equality and bioethics standards. Before the ECtHR, the case concerned Article 8 of the Convention, namely employment-related measures imposed for refusing vaccination.

A popular-initiative challenge was brought before San Marino’s Constitutional Court by citizens eligible to vote; the San Marino applicants took part, but the Italian and Moldovan applicants could not. By judgment no. 11 of 2 November 2021, the Constitutional Court upheld the law. It found vaccination was not obligatory, only recommended; the provisions created a limited, pre-specified difference in treatment; and the measures were justified by public health, collective protection and social solidarity. They were not disciplinary sanctions and were proportionate, striking a fair balance between the right to work and the right to health of service users, including vulnerable persons. It referred to *Vavřička and Others v. the Czech Republic* to note that even mandatory vaccination could be justified in serious disease contexts.

Four suspended applicants brought administrative applications to set aside their suspension. Three were declared inadmissible on procedural grounds concerning the authority form;

In *Pasquinelli and Others v. San Marino* (Application no. 24622/22, judgment of 29 August 2024), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints brought by nineteen San Marino nationals, six Italian nationals, and one Moldovan national. The applicants were healthcare and social health workers employed by San Marino’s Social Security Institute (SSI). They refused to be vaccinated against COVID-19 and, as a result, were affected by employment-related measures.

In May 2021, under section 14 of Law no. 85/2021, the SSI urged the applicants to be vaccinated. They declined. The legal framework was amended by Law no. 97/2021, ratified by Law no. 107/2021, which entered into force on 16 June 2021. Section 8 of Law no. 107/2021 provided that vaccination was not compulsory, but where SSI healthcare and social health personnel refused vaccination, the SSI had to consider how to protect service continuity and safety. It first had to examine whether the service could be reorganised to minimise contact between the unvaccinated employee and users. If reorganisation was possible, the employee remained on duty but was obliged to take an antigen test every 48 hours at his or her own expense, at a cost of €7 per swab at the SSI. If reorganisation was not possible, further alternatives applied: reassignment to other SSI services or to vacant public posts with the corresponding salary; use of ordinary and other leave or overtime accrued in 2020; or, as an extreme option, temporary suspension from service with a gross monthly suspension allowance of €600, plus family allowances. Suspended employees also had to perform socially useful activities, subject to proportionality with the allowance; refusal to do so meant loss of the allowance. Workers who could not be vaccinated because of documented health conditions could be placed on fully paid leave. The specific measures applied to each applicant were set out in an appended table.

The applicants challenged the law, mainly arguing that the difference in treatment between vaccinated and unvaccinated persons violated equality and discriminated against them, and that the measures breached their right to work, self-determination, and health. They claimed there was no legal or scientific certainty that vaccinated persons were immune or could not transmit the virus, and that the vaccines were experimental or conditionally authorised. In judgment no. 11 of 2 November 2021, the San Marino Constitutional Court upheld the law. It found that COVID-19 vaccination was not obligatory in San Marino and that the law merely created a limited difference in treatment. The measures were proportionate, not disciplinary sanctions, and aimed to balance the right to work with the right to health of vulnerable service users. Public health and social solidarity prevailed over temporary restrictions on individuals who refused vaccination. Some applicants also sought administrative review of their suspension, but those proceedings were declared inadmissible or withdrawn.

Before the European Court, the applicants alleged a violation of Article 8 of the Convention, concerning respect for private life. The Court held that Article 8 was applicable because the choice whether to be vaccinated was sufficiently linked to personal autonomy. However, it found no violation. The impugned legislation did not make vaccination compulsory and did not impose statutory sanctions or lead to automatic consequences. The measures were based on individual situations and could not be considered sanctions in disguise. The case was distinguishable from *Vavřička and Others v. the Czech Republic*. The measures pursued legitimate aims of protecting health and the rights and freedoms of others, and were justified and proportionate. In healthcare policy matters, States enjoy a wide margin of appreciation, which San Marino had not exceeded.
001-234259:
In *A.P. v. Armenia* (ECtHR, 18 June 2024), the applicant was a 14-year-old Armenian schoolgirl with a mild intellectual disability. A.G., a 49-year-old married man, was both the village administrative head and her State school sports teacher. Between November 2011 and February 2012, A.G. sexually abused A.P., including rape in the village office and at school, and indecent acts. On 22 February 2012, he took her to a classroom during a sports lesson. Another pupil, N.M., saw through a hole in the door A.G. pulling A.P. towards him and touching her bottom while she resisted. N.M. asked several teachers, including A.S., N.G. and H.B., and the headmistress for help, but they refused or failed to intervene. A.P. was later seen distressed and weak; her class teacher questioned her but did not protect her. Her mother reported the abuse the next day. A.G. was convicted in February 2013 of rape of a minor and indecent acts, and sentenced to eight years. Medical and psychological evidence confirmed A.P.’s disability and that she understood only superficially what had happened.

A.P. then sued the State for non-pecuniary damage. She alleged that Armenia had failed to establish an adequate legislative and regulatory framework to prevent, detect and report sexual abuse of minors—especially children with disabilities—and to train teachers and officials working with children. She also alleged that school authorities had failed to protect her despite clear warning signs. The first-instance court rejected the claim on formal grounds; the Civil Court of Appeal held that Armenian law did not provide compensation for non-pecuniary damage; the Court of Cassation found no merit.

Although A.P. had asked that the civil case be heard in camera and that her name not be published on Datalex, the official public judicial database, her full name and address and the complete texts of the judgments dismissing her claim were published there. Because the claim was directly linked to her sexual abuse, this left her and her family in constant fear that she could be identified as a victim of a sexual crime.

The ECtHR found violations of Article 3 (substantive), Article 8 and Article 13, read with Article 3. Under Article 3, the State failed to protect a 14-year-old pupil with an intellectual disability from sexual abuse by a teacher/public official in a State school; it failed to ensure an appropriate legal and regulatory framework for prevention, detection and reporting of sexual abuse of minors and training of persons working with children; and school authorities failed to take adequate protective measures. Under Article 8, publication of her full name and address and full decisions, despite her specific request, was an unjustified interference with private life not “in accordance with the law.” Under Article 13, she lacked an effective remedy because domestic law did not allow compensation for non-pecuniary damage for the ill-treatment suffered.

A.P. v. Armenia concerned a girl with a mild intellectual disability who, at fourteen, was a ninth-grade pupil at her local State school in Armenia. A.G., the then village administrative head and a married 49-year-old sports teacher at the school—thus both a teacher and a public official—sexually abused her between late 2011 and February 2012. The abuse included rape and indecent acts in the village administrative office and in school classrooms. On 22 February 2012, a fellow pupil, N.M., saw through a hole in the classroom door A.G. pulling the applicant towards him and touching her bottom while she resisted. N.M. tried to alert teachers and the headmistress, asking them to come and witness what was happening, but they refused or failed to intervene. The applicant was later seen in a distressed and tottering condition. Her mother reported the abuse to the police on 23 February 2012. Criminal proceedings followed. In 2013 A.G. was convicted of rape of a minor and indecent acts and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment; appeals were upheld. Another former pupil also alleged that A.G. had sexually exploited her while she was a pupil.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Articles 3, 8 and 13 of the Convention.

Under Article 3, the key facts were that the sexual abuse occurred in a State school, by a teacher who was also a public official, against a child with an intellectual disability. The State failed to ensure an appropriate legislative and regulatory framework for preventing, detecting and reporting sexual abuse of minors, failed to provide training for persons working in contact with children, and failed to ensure that school authorities took adequate protective measures once warning signs and reports emerged. Teachers and administrators refused to act when N.M. sought help, despite prior warnings about A.G.’s reputation and behaviour.

Under Article 8, after the criminal case the applicant brought a civil damages claim against the State for non-pecuniary damage. She specifically requested closed proceedings and that no information, including her name, be published in Datalex, the official online judicial database. Nevertheless, her full name and address, together with the complete texts of the judicial decisions dismissing her civil claim, were published on Datalex. Because the civil claim was directly linked to and a consequence of the sexual abuse, the disclosure left her and her family in constant uncertainty that she could be identified as a victim of a sexual crime. The Court found this interference not “in accordance with the law.”

Under Article 13, read with Article 3, the applicant had no effective remedy because Armenian law did not allow compensation for non-pecuniary damage. The lower courts rejected, or should have refused to admit, her civil claim, and the Court of Appeal expressly stated that domestic legislation provided no compensation for non-pecuniary damage. The Court of Cassation declared her appeal inadmissible. The State had therefore failed both its positive obligations and the applicant’s right to an effective remedy.

**Case: A.P. v. Armenia (ECtHR, Fourth Section, 18 June 2024)**

A.P. concerns a girl with a mild intellectual disability who, at age fourteen, was a ninth-grade pupil at a State school in an Armenian village. The alleged violations arose from her sexual abuse by A.G., her sports teacher. A.G. was also the village administrative head and therefore a public official. Between late November 2011 and February 2012, A.G. sexually abused A.P., including rape and indecent acts, in school classrooms and the village administrative office. On 22 February 2012, another pupil, N.M., saw through a hole in a classroom door A.G. pulling A.P. towards him and touching her bottom while A.P. resisted. N.M. urgently asked several teachers and the headmistress to come and witness what was happening, but they refused, ignored her, or declined to intervene. A.P. was later seen in a distressed and “tottering” state. Her mother reported the abuse the next day. Criminal proceedings ended in February 2013 with A.G.’s conviction for rape of a minor and indecent acts; he was sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. Evidence also showed that A.G. had previously sexually exploited another pupil, A.M., and was known at school and in the village as a “skirt-chaser.”

**Article 3:** A.P. complained that the State had failed to protect her from sexual abuse. The key facts were that she was a minor with an intellectual disability, dependent on a State school; the abuser was a teacher and public official with authority over her; the abuse occurred during school hours and in State premises; and when pupils alerted school staff, the staff failed to take adequate protective action. The Court found that Armenia had failed to ensure an appropriate legislative and regulatory framework for preventing, detecting, and reporting sexual abuse of minors and for training persons working with children. The school authorities also failed to take appropriate measures to protect A.P.

**Article 8:** After A.G.’s conviction, A.P. lodged a civil claim against the State for non-pecuniary damage. She specifically requested closed proceedings and that no information, including her name, be published in Datalex, the official public online judicial database. The District Court rejected the claim on procedural grounds. The Court of Appeal found that the claim should have been refused admission because Armenian law did not provide compensation for non-pecuniary damage. The Court of Cassation declared her appeal inadmissible. Despite her request, Datalex published her full name, address, and the complete texts of the judicial decisions dismissing her civil claim. This information was publicly accessible and directly linked to the sexual abuse. The disclosure left A.P. and her family in constant uncertainty that she could be identified as a victim of a sexual crime. The Court found the interference with her private life was not “in accordance with the law.”

**Article 13:** A.P. also complained of the lack of an effective remedy for the Article 3 ill-treatment. Because domestic law did not allow compensation for non-pecuniary damage, the courts refused to examine her claim for State compensation. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 13 in conjunction with Article 3.

In essence, the case concerned the State’s failure to protect a vulnerable minor from sexual abuse in school, the subsequent unlawful publication of her identity in a civil damages case, and the absence of any effective domestic remedy to obtain compensation for the harm suffered.
001-230878:
Case of Shylina v. Ukraine (Application no. 2412/19) concerned the suspension of social benefits to an internally displaced person (IDP) because she refused to open an account with a designated State bank, Oshchadbank.

The applicant, Ms Shylina, left Crimea in November 2014, moved to Government-controlled territory, and registered as an IDP with her family. She was entitled to a special monthly allowance under Cabinet Resolution No. 505 to cover living costs, including housing and municipal services. Initially, she received the allowance through a private bank account.

In April 2016, payments were suspended because she had not opened an Oshchadbank account. She successfully challenged that suspension for April–June 2016; the courts found no legal basis for it before July 2016. However, from 1 July 2016, amendments to Cabinet Resolution No. 637 required all social benefits to IDPs to be paid solely through Oshchadbank accounts, with periodic physical identification at Oshchadbank. Payments were again suspended because she refused to open such an account.

The applicant challenged Resolution No. 637, arguing that the Oshchadbank requirement was discriminatory and contrary to higher-ranking law. She claimed differential treatment compared with non-IDP benefit recipients, who did not have to open Oshchadbank accounts, and among IDPs themselves, depending on whether they already had such accounts. She also argued that the suspension imposed an excessive burden on her. Domestic courts dismissed her claims, reasoning that the Cabinet acted within its competence, the measure merely established practical payment arrangements, and it pursued legitimate aims: safeguarding social funds, preventing fraud and unlawful payments, and preventing terrorism financing. A 2017 amendment allowed IDPs to transfer or withdraw funds through other banks, but the initial benefit payment still had to go through Oshchadbank. The Supreme Court upheld the lower courts in September 2018. The applicant later closed her allowance file after becoming unemployed; payments to her family resumed when her husband opened an Oshchadbank account.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, she complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the suspension interfered with her peaceful enjoyment of possessions, and under Article 14 read with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that she was discriminated against. The Government maintained that the measure had a clear legal basis, pursued legitimate aims, and did not place an excessive burden on her.

The Court found the Article 1 Protocol No. 1 complaint admissible but no violation: the interference was lawful, pursued a legitimate aim, and was not disproportionate. States enjoy a wide margin of appreciation in social and economic policy, and the measure did not impose an individual or excessive burden. The Article 14 complaint was manifestly ill-founded. The applicant was not in an analogous or relevantly similar situation to recipients of social benefits without IDP status, because the special allowance was intended only for IDPs. Moreover, whether one held an Oshchadbank account was not an identifiable characteristic or “status” under Article 14, and she did not show different treatment compared with other IDPs. The case therefore ended without a finding of a Convention violation.

**Shylina v. Ukraine** (Application no. 2412/19), judgment of 15 February 2024, final 15 May 2024, concerned an internally displaced person’s (IDP) complaints under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) and Article 14 (non-discrimination) read with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The applicant, a Ukrainian national born in 1973, left Crimea in November 2014 after Russia’s occupation and moved to Government-controlled Ukraine. She and her family registered as IDPs and became entitled to a special monthly allowance under Cabinet of Ministers Resolution no. 505 of 1 October 2014, intended to cover living expenses, including housing and municipal services. Initially, the allowance was paid into her account at a private bank.

In April 2016, payment was suspended because the authorities had no information that she had opened an account with Oshchadbank, the designated State Savings Bank. She challenged that suspension, and domestic courts ordered payment for April–June 2016, which she received. From July 2016, however, amendments to Resolution no. 637 of 5 November 2014 required all social benefits to IDPs to be paid solely through Oshchadbank accounts, with periodic physical identification at Oshchadbank offices. The applicant refused to open such an account, and her allowance was again suspended.

The applicant challenged Resolution no. 637 before administrative courts. She argued that the requirement was discriminatory and incompatible with higher-ranking legislation. She claimed discrimination compared with non-IDP social benefit recipients, who did not need Oshchadbank accounts, and among IDPs themselves—those who already had Oshchadbank accounts and those who did not. She also alleged an unjustified interference with her property rights and an excessive burden on her family.

The domestic courts dismissed her claims. They found that the Cabinet of Ministers had acted within its competence and that the measure merely established practical payment arrangements. The appellate court stated that the measure pursued legitimate aims: safeguarding social payments to vulnerable IDPs, preventing fraud and unlawful actions, and preventing terrorism financing. It noted that Resolution no. 689 of 13 September 2017 later allowed IDPs to make further transactions through any bank in Government-controlled territory, though initial payment still had to be via Oshchadbank. The Supreme Court upheld the lower courts, finding no discrimination.

In November 2017, the applicant asked to close her file because she had become unemployed and was no longer entitled to the allowance. She nevertheless had not received payments for July 2016–November 2017 due to her refusal to open an Oshchadbank account. Payments later resumed when her husband opened such an account.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant argued that the interference lacked a sufficient legal basis, was incompatible with Resolution no. 505, pursued no proven legitimate aim, and imposed an excessive burden, especially given her family’s housing insecurity, minor daughter, and disabled husband. The Government maintained that the requirement was accessible and foreseeable, pursued legitimate aims, and did not impose an excessive burden.

The Court declared the Article 1 Protocol No. 1 complaint admissible. On the merits, it found that the suspension did not impose an individual and excessive burden. States enjoy a wide margin of appreciation in social and economic policies. The interference was lawful, pursued a legitimate aim, and was not disproportionate.

As to Article 14 read with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, the Court found the complaint manifestly ill-founded. The applicant was not in an analogous or relevantly similar situation to social benefit recipients without IDP status, because the special allowance was intended for IDPs only. Possession or non-possession of an Oshchadbank account was not an identifiable characteristic or “status” under Article 14. She also failed to show different treatment compared with other IDPs.

**Case: Shylina v. Ukraine (Application no. 2412/19), European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, Judgment 15 February 2024 (final 15 May 2024).**

The applicant, Ms Elvira Shylina, is a Ukrainian national who left Crimea in November 2014 after Russia’s occupation and moved to Government-controlled territory in Rivne. She and her family registered as internally displaced persons (IDPs). As IDPs, they were entitled to a special monthly allowance under Cabinet of Ministers Resolution no. 505 to cover living expenses, including housing and municipal services. Initially, the allowance was paid into the applicant’s account at a private bank, bank R.

In April 2016, payment was suspended because the authorities lacked information that the applicant had opened an account with Oshchadbank, the designated State Savings Bank. The applicant successfully challenged that suspension, and payments for April to June 2016 were made through bank R. However, from July 2016, her allowance was again suspended. This time the suspension was based on Resolution no. 637, as amended, which required that from 1 July 2016 all social benefits to IDPs be paid solely through accounts with Oshchadbank, with periodic physical identification at that bank. The applicant refused to open an Oshchadbank account.

The applicant challenged the relevant provisions of Resolution no. 637 before the domestic courts. She argued that they were discriminatory and incompatible with higher-ranking legislation, including the Law on Ensuring the Rights and Freedoms of Internally Displaced Persons and the Law on the Prevention of and Fight against Discrimination. She also relied on the Court’s discrimination case-law. She claimed unequal treatment compared with non-IDP benefit recipients, who did not have to open Oshchadbank accounts, and discrimination among IDPs themselves, depending on whether they already had such accounts.

The domestic courts dismissed her claims. The Kyiv Circuit Administrative Court held that the Cabinet of Ministers had acted within its competence and that the measure did not remove her rights but merely set practical payment arrangements. The Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal upheld that judgment, finding that the measure aimed to safeguard payments to socially vulnerable IDPs, ensure payment of pensions and benefits, prevent fraud and unlawful actions, and prevent the financing of terrorism. It also noted that IDPs could withdraw money and deposit it with another bank. A 2017 amendment allowed further transactions through any bank on Government-controlled territory, but the initial payment of social benefits still had to be made via Oshchadbank. In September 2018, the Supreme Court upheld the lower courts, finding no discrimination and stating that the measures were intended to ensure special protection for IDPs.

In November 2017, the applicant asked the Department to close her file because she had become unemployed and was no longer entitled to the allowance. She had still not received payments from July 2016 to November 2017 due to her refusal to open an Oshchadbank account. Later, payments to her family resumed when her husband opened an Oshchadbank account.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 alone and Article 14 taken together with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. She alleged that the suspension interfered with her peaceful enjoyment of possessions and was discriminatory. The Court declared the Article 1 Protocol No. 1 complaint admissible but found no violation: the interference was lawful, pursued a legitimate aim, and was not disproportionate, imposing no individual or excessive burden, especially given the State’s wide margin of appreciation in social and economic policy. The Article 14 complaint was manifestly ill-founded: the applicant was not in an analogous or relevantly similar situation to recipients without IDP status; the special allowance was intended only for IDPs; and having or not having an Oshchadbank account was not an identifiable “status” under Article 14. She also did not show different treatment compared with other IDPs.

Domenjoud v. France (ECtHR, Fifth Section, 16 May 2024) concerned two brothers, Cédric and Joël Domenjoud, placed under compulsory residence restrictions during France’s state of emergency after the November 2015 Paris terrorist attacks. The state of emergency was declared on 14 November 2015 and later extended; France lodged an Article 15 derogation. COP21 climate summit was held in Paris and Le Bourget from 30 November to 12 December 2015. On 25 November 2015, the Minister of the Interior ordered both applicants confined to their respective municipalities until 12 December 2015, requiring them to report to police three times daily and remain at home from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m.

The orders were based on general security concerns: the terrorist threat, COP21, calls for violent protests by “black bloc” activists, and the fact that security forces were heavily deployed against terrorism. Specific reasons described both men as main leaders of the radical left-wing protest movement in greater Paris, involved in violent protests and likely to disrupt COP21 violently. Cédric was accused of organising meetings in a squat, planning to block motorcades and target state institutions and sponsors, and participating in the August 2015 Bure anti-waste-site action where fibre-optic cables were cut, fencing torn down and Molotov cocktails thrown at gendarmes; he was also seen at a banned migrant rally on 22 November 2015 and allegedly broke a police roadblock. Joël was accused of activism against state and capitalist symbols, attending COP21 protest preparations, and co-organising the Bure camp where violence occurred.

Both challenged the orders before administrative courts. Cédric’s urgent application was dismissed; the Conseil d’État referred a constitutionality question, and the Constitutional Council upheld section 6 of the 1955 emergency law. The Conseil d’État held the measure was not a deprivation of liberty under Article 5 and not a manifest breach of Article 2 of Protocol No. 4, relying partly on notes blanches that were not seriously contested. Joël’s urgent application was initially dismissed for lack of urgency; the Conseil d’État quashed that but still rejected his case on the merits. His judicial review and appeal were also dismissed.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants alleged violations of Articles 5, 6 and 13, and alternatively Article 2 of Protocol No. 4, arguing the measures were not covered by the Article 15 derogation. The Court found the residence restrictions were mere restrictions, not deprivations, of liberty, so Article 5 was incompatible ratione materiae. Under Article 2 of Protocol No. 4, it assessed freedom of movement. For Cédric, there was no violation: although the measure lacked a direct link to countering terrorism, it was sufficiently linked to the state-of-emergency context in the specific COP21 circumstances, was relatively short, had adequate procedural safeguards, and rested on relevant and sufficient evidence showing a serious risk of participation in particularly violent disruptions; it was proportionate. For Joël, however, there was a violation: the essence of his procedural rights was not preserved, and there was no individual and detailed assessment of his conduct or acts allowing the risk to be characterised. His placement was not covered by the Article 15 derogation because it was not ordered to counter terrorism and was not strictly required by the exigencies of the situation.

The European Court of Human Rights case *Domenjoud v. France* (Applications nos. 34749/16 and 79607/17, judgment of 16 May 2024) concerned two brothers, Cédric and Joël Domenjoud, who were placed under compulsory residence orders during the state of emergency declared in France after the 13 November 2015 Paris terrorist attacks. The emergency was based on the Law of 3 April 1955, and France notified a derogation under Article 15 of the Convention. Despite the terrorist threat, France hosted the COP21 climate summit in Paris and Le Bourget from 30 November to 12 December 2015. To secure the summit, the Minister of the Interior ordered both applicants on 25 November 2015 to remain within their respective municipalities until 12 December 2015, report to a police station three times daily, and observe a curfew from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m.

The orders relied on general grounds: the serious terrorist threat, the heavy deployment of security forces, and fears of violent “black bloc” protests during COP21. The Minister also relied on specific allegations. Both applicants were described as leaders of radical left-wing protest movements in the Paris area, involved in past violent protest actions, and likely to disrupt COP21. As to Cédric Domenjoud, the Minister alleged that he organised meetings in a squat to prepare actions against the summit; that he helped organise the anti-authoritarian “summer camp” in Bure in August 2015; and that during the night of 3–4 August 2015 he took part in an attack on the ANDRA radioactive waste site, including severing fibre-optic cables, tearing down fencing, and throwing Molotov cocktails at gendarmes. He was also allegedly seen at a banned rally in Paris on 22 November 2015 and broke through a police roadblock. As to Joël Domenjoud, the Minister alleged that he had long been active against State bodies and capitalism, took part in preparatory meetings in a squat, helped organise the Bure camp, and was linked to the violent action against ANDRA during that camp.

The applicants complained of breaches of Articles 5, 6 and 13 of the Convention and, in the alternative, Article 2 of Protocol No. 4, arguing that the measures were not covered by Article 15. Domestic courts largely upheld the orders. In urgent proceedings, the Conseil d’État found that the residence restrictions did not amount to deprivation of liberty under Article 5 and were not manifestly incompatible with Article 2 of Protocol No. 4. The Constitutional Council also upheld the relevant law. For the second applicant, domestic courts relied on intelligence “notes blanches,” which he claimed he could not effectively rebut, despite producing evidence of no criminal record and statements describing his activism as peaceful.

Before the ECtHR, the Court held that Article 5 was incompatible *ratione materiae* because the residence restriction was a mere restriction, not a deprivation, of liberty. Under Article 2 of Protocol No. 4, the measure against the first applicant did not violate the Convention: it had adequate procedural safeguards, was sufficiently linked to the state-of-emergency context, was relatively short, and rested on relevant and sufficient reasons showing a serious risk of participation in particularly violent disruptions. However, the measure against the second applicant violated Article 2 of Protocol No. 4. The essence of his procedural rights was not preserved, and there was no individual and detailed assessment of his conduct or acts allowing the risk to be characterised. The Court further found under Article 15 that the second applicant’s placement was not covered by the derogation because it was not ordered to counter terrorism and was not strictly required by the exigencies of the situation.

In *Domenjoud v. France*, the European Court of Human Rights examined two compulsory residence orders imposed under French state-of-emergency legislation after the November 2015 Paris terrorist attacks. The applicants, brothers Cédric and Joël Domenjoud, were left-wing and environmental activists. Following the attacks, France declared a state of emergency and notified a derogation under Article 15 ECHR. Despite the terrorist threat, France hosted the COP21 climate summit in Paris and Le Bourget from 30 November to 12 December 2015. Authorities feared violent disruption by radical protesters, including “black bloc” activists.

On 25 November 2015, the Minister of the Interior placed both applicants under residence restrictions in their respective municipalities until 12 December 2015. They had to report to a police station three times daily and remain at home between 8 p.m. and 6 a.m. The orders relied on the general terrorist threat and the need to preserve security-force capacity during COP21, but also on individualised allegations. Both men were described as leaders of a radical protest movement. Cédric Domenjoud was accused of organising meetings in a squat, participating in the August 2015 Bure anti-nuclear protest against ANDRA—where fences and cameras were damaged and Molotov cocktails thrown—and attending a banned migrant rally on 22 November 2015, where he allegedly broke through a police roadblock. Joël Domenjoud was accused of taking part in preparatory meetings and helping organise the Bure camp where violence occurred. Much of the evidence came from unsigned intelligence “notes blanches.”

The applicants challenged the measures in administrative proceedings, alleging violations of Articles 5, 6 and 13 ECHR and Article 2 of Protocol No. 4, and arguing that the measures were not covered by the Article 15 derogation. The French courts generally found that the restrictions were lawful, proportionate and not a deprivation of liberty. The first applicant was granted some leave, including to attend a hearing and a job interview. The second applicant’s remedies failed; he emphasised that he had no criminal record and produced statements describing his activism as peaceful.

The ECtHR first held that the Article 5 complaints were incompatible *ratione materiae*: the residence restriction was a restriction, not a deprivation, of liberty given its duration, effects and implementation conditions. The central issue was therefore Article 2 of Protocol No. 4, protecting freedom of movement.

For the first applicant, the Court found adequate procedural safeguards. The measure was sufficiently linked to the very specific state-of-emergency context, was relatively short, and rested on relevant and sufficient reasons. The material evidence concerning his conduct and background reflected a serious risk of participation in particularly violent disruptions, so the measure was proportionate. There was no violation as to him.

For the second applicant, however, the Court found that the essence of his procedural rights had not been preserved. There had been no individual and detailed assessment of his conduct or acts sufficient to characterise him as posing the alleged risk. His placement was not ordered to counter terrorism and was not strictly required by the exigencies of the situation. It was therefore not covered by France’s Article 15 derogation. The Court accordingly found a violation of Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 as regards the second applicant. The case illustrates the limits of emergency powers when used for public-order policing rather than counter-terrorism, and the need for individualised, procedurally protected assessments.

**Jella and Others v. Albania** (Application no. 7564/07) concerns five Albanian nationals who alleged that Albania violated their right to the peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights. The core complaint was the non-enforcement of domestic decisions in their favour concerning restitution of nationalised land.

The applicants’ ancestor’s land was nationalised under the former communist regime. After communism fell, the applicants sought restitution from the Commission on Restitution and Compensation for Property. On 9 September 1994, the Commission recognised their property title over a plot of 43,100 square metres, of which 25,540 square metres were occupied. It ruled that 13,310 square metres, located within an unoccupied area of 17,560 square metres, were to be restituted to the applicants, who were to choose the exact location. That decision was never challenged and remained in force. However, the applicants never obtained possession of that land, and it was not registered in their name. The Commission also restored a house and adjacent plots of 430 and 400 square metres, which were registered in the Land Register.

The applicants later brought a court action against the Commission seeking clarification, restitution and/or compensation, including a claim over 290,700 square metres. On 17 May 2005, the Tirana District Court dismissed the claim as an administrative matter, and that decision became final. In 2005 and 2007, the applicants asked the Commission’s successor, the Agency for Restitution and Compensation of Property, to delimit the 13,310-square-metre plot and restitute remaining unoccupied land. On 26 June 2007, the Agency told them to submit a new application to its local office. Their objection was dismissed by the Agency’s director.

On 24 December 2009, the Tirana District Court ruled in the applicants’ favour, holding that the Agency had a duty to give a decision. That judgment became final. Nevertheless, on 25 October 2011, the Agency refused enforcement. It argued that the applicants had to choose the exact location of the plot, that it lacked jurisdiction to review a Commission decision, and that the applicants should bring a civil action. In 2015, the Tirana District Court dismissed their civil action for lack of conclusive evidence of their property right over the 13,310-square-metre plot. In 2017, the Tirana Appeal Court quashed that decision and remitted the case, noting that the Agency had not questioned the applicants’ ownership of that plot. By 2023, the case remained pending before the Supreme Court after the Agency appealed. In 2018, the Land Registry rejected the applicants’ request to register the 13,310-square-metre plot because the property plan did not clearly define its boundaries.

Separately, in 1996 the Commission recognised property rights in favour of a private family, the S. family. The applicants challenged that decision as overlapping with their land. On 19 May 2004, the Tirana District Court partly annulled the 1996 decision concerning 5,500 square metres that overlapped with the applicants’ property. That decision became final in 2006 after the Supreme Court dismissed an appeal. In 2011, the District Court dismissed another claim by the applicants against private parties concerning an overlap with the 13,310-square-metre plot, finding that in 1994 part of that land had been occupied by one Z.B.

The alleged violation therefore arose from the continued failure to enforce the 1994 Commission decision and the 2009 court decision, combined with registration obstacles and overlapping private claims, which prevented the applicants from effectively enjoying their possessions.

In *Jella and Others v. Albania* (Application no. 7564/07), five Albanian nationals complain under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that Albania violated their right to the peaceful enjoyment of their possessions by failing to enforce domestic decisions in their favour. The alleged violation therefore centres on the prolonged failure to enforce or give effect to the 1994 Commission decision and the 2009 court decision, leaving the applicants without possession or registration of the 13,310 sq. m plot.

On 26 June 2007, the Agency instructed them to submit a new application to its local office. Their objection was dismissed. 001-230627:
**Case: Bernotas v. Lithuania (App. no. 59065/21), ECtHR, Second Section, 30 January 2024**

In January 2010, the applicant, Jurgis Bernotas, accidentally shot Ž.K. while cleaning his rifle after a hunt. The victim suffered serious abdominal, hip and leg injuries, underwent multiple surgeries and a hip replacement, lost his job at the fire rescue service, and his working capacity was eventually assessed as diminished by 45%. The applicant was convicted of negligently causing serious damage to health, admitted guilt, received a suspended two-year sentence, and paid compensation to Ž.K. for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage.

Separately, the State Social Insurance Fund (“SSIF”) paid Ž.K. a lost working capacity pension from August 2010 onwards. Under Lithuanian law, social insurance authorities that pay allowances to an injured person may seek reimbursement from the person who caused the damage. Between 2011 and 2022, the SSIF made repeated claims against the applicant for reimbursement of the pension paid to Ž.K. The applicant sometimes agreed to pay in instalments, sometimes default judgments were issued, and one claim was settled amicably. Later claims were contested.

The applicant argued that the reimbursement obligation was unjustified and disproportionate. He stressed that the injury had been accidental, that he had already compensated Ž.K. in the criminal proceedings, that Ž.K. was employed and earning income, that the pension was social assistance rather than proof of actual damage, and that the pension amount kept increasing due to factors such as the victim’s length of service and changing economic conditions. He also complained about repeated court proceedings and unforeseeable future payments.

Domestic courts rejected these arguments. Relying on a forensic expert report confirming that Ž.K.’s diminished working capacity was directly caused by the accident, and on Constitutional Court and Supreme Court case-law, they held that the lost working capacity pension compensated lost income and additional injury-related expenses. The SSIF could therefore recover the amount corresponding to the victim’s pecuniary damage, up to the full pension paid. The courts found that the compensation paid in the criminal proceedings concerned damage at the time of the accident, distinct from the ongoing damage caused by diminished working capacity.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant relied on Articles 6, 7, 8 and 14 of the Convention, but the Court examined the complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions). It declared the application admissible but found no violation. The interference with the applicant’s property was lawful and pursued a legitimate aim. In assessing fair balance, the Court noted that domestic proceedings gave the applicant a reasonable opportunity to present his case, that there had been an individual assessment, and that he could seek reassessment or reduction of the compensation due. The authorities also acted flexibly, allowing instalments, deferrals, settlements, and staying enforcement. Although the reimbursement obligation lasted a long time, it was not disproportionate. A fair balance had been struck between the applicant’s property rights and the competing interests of the victim, the social security fund, and the public interest in tort liability.

In *Bernotas v. Lithuania* (Application no. 59065/21), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning Lithuania’s requirement that the applicant reimburse the State Social Insurance Fund (SSIF) for a lost working capacity pension paid to a man he had accidentally injured.

In January 2010, Jurgis Bernotas accidentally shot Ž.K. while cleaning his rifle after a hunt. Ž.K. suffered serious abdominal, hip, and leg injuries. Bernotas admitted guilt and was convicted of negligently causing serious damage to health, receiving a suspended two-year prison sentence. In the criminal proceedings, Ž.K. claimed pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages. Bernotas paid part of the compensation; the courts ultimately awarded Ž.K. approximately EUR 10,725 in non-pecuniary damages, plus pecuniary expenses.

Separately, Ž.K.’s working capacity was assessed as significantly diminished—initially by 60%, later reassessed at 50%, 45%, sometimes 30%, and finally 45% until retirement. The SSIF therefore paid him a lost working capacity pension from August 2010 onward. The pension amounts varied by period and generally increased over time.

Relying on Civil Code Article 6.290 § 3 and the Law on State Social Insurance, the SSIF repeatedly sought reimbursement from Bernotas for the pension paid to Ž.K. Between 2011 and 2022 it made successive claims covering different periods. Some claims resulted in default judgments when Bernotas did not respond; others led to settlements or installment agreements. Bernotas opposed the claims, arguing that he had already compensated Ž.K., that Ž.K. remained employed and sometimes earned more than before, that the working capacity assessments were questionable, and that the pension amount kept increasing due to Ž.K.’s length of service and economic changes. He contended that the reimbursement obligation was indefinite, unforeseeable, and disproportionate, potentially making him pay more than the damage he had accidentally caused.

Domestic courts largely rejected his arguments. A forensic examination confirmed that Ž.K.’s 45% diminished working capacity was directly caused by the accident. Courts held that the lost working capacity pension compensated pecuniary damage—lost income and additional injury-related expenses—which was distinct from the earlier compensation for damage at the time of the accident. Under Constitutional Court and Supreme Court case-law, the SSIF could claim reimbursement only up to the victim’s actual pecuniary damage, but here the pension corresponded to that damage. Courts also noted that the applicant could seek reduction due to financial hardship and that increases were justified by economic factors. Appeals and cassation requests were unsuccessful.

Before the ECtHR, Bernotas complained that the reimbursement obligation unjustifiably and disproportionately interfered with his possessions. The Court examined the complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It found the interference lawful and pursued a legitimate aim—allowing social security authorities to recover payments corresponding to damage caused by the applicant. The proceedings gave Bernotas a reasonable opportunity to contest liability and amount; domestic law allowed individual assessment, possible reduction, and installment arrangements. Although the obligation lasted a long time, it was not disproportionate on the facts. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In *Bernotas v. Lithuania* (ECtHR, Second Section, 30 January 2024), the applicant, Jurgis Bernotas, accidentally shot Ž.K. in January 2010 while cleaning his rifle after a hunt. The victim suffered serious abdominal, hip and leg injuries, underwent multiple surgeries, had a hip replacement, and suffered a lasting reduction in working capacity. The applicant was charged with negligently causing serious damage to health, admitted guilt, and was sentenced to two years’ imprisonment, suspended. In the criminal proceedings, the victim also obtained compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage; the applicant paid part of this and later paid the non-pecuniary award as reduced on appeal.

Separately, the State Social Insurance Fund (SSIF) granted Ž.K. a lost working capacity pension because the accident had diminished his working capacity. Initially assessed at 60%, this was later reassessed at various levels, eventually 45% until retirement. The SSIF paid the pension from August 2010 through at least April 2022. Relying on the Civil Code, the SSIF repeatedly sought reimbursement from the applicant for the pension amounts paid to the victim.

Between 2011 and 2022, the SSIF brought several claims or demands against the applicant. The applicant sometimes agreed to pay in instalments, but at other times objected that he had already compensated the victim; that the victim was employed and had not suffered actual loss of income; that the working-capacity assessments were doubtful; and that the pension amount was increasing and unpredictable. A forensic examination in 2018 confirmed that Ž.K.’s 45% diminished working capacity was directly caused by the accident. Domestic courts generally upheld the SSIF’s claims, treating the lost working capacity pension as compensation for pecuniary damage—lost income and additional injury-related expenses—and finding the SSIF entitled to recover the amounts it had paid. Some payment facilities were granted, including instalments and deferrals. The applicant’s appeals and cassation attempts were largely unsuccessful, and a later 2022 claim was adjourned pending the Strasbourg proceedings.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained under Articles 6, 7, 8 and 14 of the Convention, but the Court examined the case under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. He argued that the reimbursement obligation was an unjustified and disproportionate interference with his possessions. In particular, he claimed that he had already fully compensated the victim, that the injury was unintentional, that his obligation was indefinite and potentially lifelong, that the pension amount kept rising and was unforeseeable, and that he might ultimately pay more than the damage he had caused. He also complained that the repeated SSIF proceedings violated his fair-trial rights.

The ECtHR declared the application admissible but found no violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It emphasised that domestic proceedings had given the applicant a reasonable opportunity to put his case, including challenging the causal link and the working-capacity assessment. The courts conducted an individual assessment and the applicant could seek reassessment or reduction of compensation under domestic law, particularly if full payment would cause unacceptable and serious consequences or if he faced financial hardship. The authorities also acted flexibly by allowing instalments and deferrals and by retaining the possibility of waiving claims in appropriate social or economic circumstances. Although the interference lasted a long time, it was not disproportionate. The Court concluded that a fair balance had been struck between the applicant’s property rights and the public interest in allowing social security authorities to recover payments made as a result of his tortious conduct.
