**Case: Winther v. Denmark (ECtHR, Fourth Section, 12 November 2024)**

The applicant, Martin Treesh Winther, is a Syrian national born in 1994. He entered Denmark in September 2014 at age 20 and applied for asylum. In February 2015, he was granted a refugee residence permit until February 2020. At the time of the expulsion order, he had been lawfully resident in Denmark for less than four years.

In March 2019, the District Court convicted him of several offences: aggravated assault, blackmail, attempted duress, possession of cannabis for personal use and distribution, and importation of 91 forged €100 banknotes. The assault was particularly serious: jointly with others, he beat and kicked a victim, including with a bat or similar weapon and a bottle, even while the victim lay prostrate. The offences occurred on three days in November 2018 and related to debt collection for a third party. He was sentenced to seven months’ imprisonment and ordered expelled with a six-year re-entry ban.

The District Court found expulsion necessary for preventive purposes, law and order, and security, and proportionate under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The High Court upheld the judgment in January 2020. In August 2020, the Supreme Court increased the prison sentence to eight months but also upheld the expulsion order and six-year re-entry ban.

The Supreme Court conducted a proportionality assessment under Article 8. It noted that the applicant had lived in Denmark since September 2014 and had a Danish girlfriend and twin children born in March 2019. He had completed ninth grade, found employment, and lived with his family after release from custody. However, the court also found that he was born and raised in Syria, spoke and wrote Arabic, and retained strong ties there. His immediate family did not live in Denmark, though two aunts did. His ties to Denmark, apart from his partner and children, were relatively limited.

The Supreme Court acknowledged that expulsion would seriously interfere with his family life. His Danish partner had no ties to Syria and did not wish to move there. The children were young and expected to remain in Denmark with their mother. The court found that temporary physical separation from a young father was less harmful than if the children were older, and that contact could be maintained by telephone or internet. The six-year re-entry ban was limited, and family reunification in Denmark might be possible afterwards. Balancing the serious, planned nature of the offences against his short residence and family ties, the Supreme Court concluded that societal interests outweighed his private and family life. Expulsion was therefore not disproportionate under Article 8.

After serving his sentence, the applicant was released on parole in April 2021. In April 2022, the Aliens Appeal Board refused asylum but found that forced return to Syria was not possible, so he remained on tolerated stay. Later, authorities reported that he had absconded from a deportation centre in June 2022. He applied for asylum in the Netherlands in January 2023 and subsequently disappeared. He was arrested in Denmark in May 2024. The Government asked the Court to strike out the application because he had absconded, but the applicant contested this and wished to pursue the case. The Court dismissed the strike-out request.

The applicant complained that the expulsion order and six-year re-entry ban violated Article 8, arguing that the Danish courts failed to consider his lack of criminal past, his Danish partner and small children who needed his care, and his Syrian nationality. The Government argued that the domestic courts had thoroughly balanced all relevant factors and that the serious offences justified expulsion. The European Court of Human Rights found the application admissible and ultimately concluded that the expulsion order had relevant and sufficient reasons and that the domestic courts had duly assessed proportionality in light of the Court’s case-law. There was no violation of Article 8.

Denmark** (ECtHR, Fourth Section, 12 November 2024) concerned an Article 8 complaint by a Syrian national, born in 1994, who entered Denmark in September 2014 at age 20 and applied for asylum. In February 2015 he was granted a refugee residence permit until February 2020. In March 2019, the District Court convicted him of aggravated assault, blackmail, and attempted duress committed in November 2018. The offences arose from debt collection: with three co-accused, he beat and kicked a victim with a bat or similar weapon and a bottle, including while the victim lay prostrate. He was also convicted of cannabis possession (2.44 grams for personal use and 5.94 grams for distribution) and importing 91 forged 100-euro banknotes. He received seven months’ imprisonment, an expulsion order, and a six-year re-entry ban.

On appeal, the applicant stated he had a Danish girlfriend and twin children born in March 2019, one with health problems. After release from remand in April 2019, he lived with them, helped with childcare, completed ninth grade, and found work. His partner and children were Danish nationals; his partner did not wish to move to Syria. The High Court upheld expulsion in January 2020. In August 2020, the Supreme Court increased the sentence to eight months but upheld the expulsion and six-year re-entry ban.

The Supreme Court accepted that expulsion interfered with the applicant’s Article 8 §1 right to private and family life, but found it justified under Article 8 §2 for the prevention of disorder or crime. Applying the *Maslov v. Austria* criteria, it noted that he had lawfully resided in Denmark for only about three years and nine months; he was born and raised in Syria, spoke and read Arabic, and, although his family had fled, retained strong ties there. His ties to Denmark were relatively limited apart from his partner and children. The family relationship was fairly short, the children very young, and separation—though serious—was less harmful than if they were older; visits and communication remained possible. The six-year ban was limited, after which family reunification could be sought. The offences were serious and planned, not spontaneous. Societal interests therefore outweighed his private and family life.

Later, after parole in April 2021, he was required to live in a deportation centre away from his family. In April 2022, the Aliens Appeal Board refused asylum under section 7(1) but found forced expulsion currently impossible due to the general situation in Syria; he remained on “tolerated stay.” He was reported to have absconded in June 2022. In January 2023 he applied for asylum in the Netherlands; Danish authorities accepted readmission, but Dutch authorities reported him disappeared in July 2023. He was arrested in Denmark in May 2024. The Government asked the Court to strike out the application because he had absconded, but the applicant opposed this, and the Court dismissed the request.

The alleged violation was that the Supreme Court’s expulsion order with a six-year re-entry ban breached his Article 8 right to respect for private and family life. The applicant argued the domestic courts failed to weigh relevant circumstances: no criminal past, his partner and two small children needing care, their Danish nationality, and his Syrian nationality. The Government argued the application was manifestly ill-founded, that Danish courts had thoroughly applied the proportionality test at three levels in light of Article 8 case-law, and that the offences threatened public order. They also noted he could apply for family reunification after the ban. The Court declared the application admissible but found no violation of Article 8, as the domestic courts had given relevant and sufficient reasons and had duly assessed proportionality.

Acting with three others, he beat and kicked a victim with a bat or similar weapon and a bottle, including while the victim lay prostrate, in connection with debt collection. He was also convicted of possessing cannabis for personal use and distribution, and of importing 91 forged €100 banknotes. He was sentenced to seven months’ imprisonment and ordered expelled with a six-year re-entry ban.

The Supreme Court accepted that expulsion interfered with the applicant’s private and family life under Article 8 § 1, but found it justified under Article 8 § 2 for the prevention of disorder or crime. He had lived in Denmark for only about three years and nine months and had relatively limited ties apart from his Danish girlfriend and their twins, born in March 2019. The children were premature and one had health problems; the applicant had lived with his partner since January 2018 and helped care for the children. 001-237808:
**Case: Rybářství Třeboň a.s. and Rybářství Třeboň Hld. a.s. v. the Czech Republic**  
**Applications nos. 18037/19 and 33175/22 – ECtHR, 7 November 2024**

The case concerned the annulment without compensation of two privatisations of immovable property—fishponds and land totalling 232,312 m²—after approximately 26 and 25 years. The land had originally belonged to the Roman Catholic Parish of Novosedly nad Nežárkou and the Roman Catholic Parish of Lutová. In 1949, the Communist-era Třeboň District National Committee deprived those parishes of the land without compensation. The property was subsequently managed by the State-owned enterprise Státní rybářství Třeboň.

In 1992, under the Privatisation Act (Law no. 92/1991), the State-owned enterprise was privatised. The second applicant company was created by the National Property Fund and received the disputed land in its registered capital. A privatisation project was prepared by the State enterprise’s management under J.H., who later became a member of the second applicant’s board of directors. J.H. also signed the transfer record on behalf of the transferring State enterprise, the National Property Fund, and the acquiring applicant company, making independent verification impossible.

A 1994–95 Supreme Audit Office audit found that the privatisation had been unlawful. The project had included property that the State enterprise had no right to manage or that was subject to restitution, and State property worth at least CZK 349,715,895 had been unlawfully transferred. Importantly, the Privatisation Act contained a “blocking provision” prohibiting privatisation of property transferred to the State after 25 February 1948 from churches, religious orders or communities. After the 2013 Church Property Settlement Act, the parishes sued, seeking declarations that the land belonged to the State, not the applicant companies, because the privatisation had breached the blocking provision and was void *ab initio*.

Domestic courts agreed. They held that the applicant companies could not rely on good faith or acquisitive prescription because J.H. and others involved knew or should have known that the land had been church property before 1950. The 1994 audit also should have raised grave doubts. The transfer was therefore an “incurably void act *contra legem*.” The first applicant held the Novosedly land after a 2007 corporate split; the second applicant held the Lutová land. Administrative proceedings later ordered the State to surrender the land to the parishes or their successors.

The applicant companies complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. They alleged that the annulment of their ownership after more than two decades, without compensation, violated their property rights and fair-trial guarantees. They argued that they had a legitimate expectation of continued ownership and that the annulment imposed an excessive individual burden.

The European Court of Human Rights found no violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It held that the impugned legislation, as applied, served the fundamental public interest of restoring justice and respect for the rule of law after the communist regime. The applicants had no legitimate expectation of continued enjoyment of the land because the privatisation transfer was void *ab initio* and made in bad faith. The domestic courts’ decisions were not arbitrary or manifestly unreasonable. States enjoy a wide margin of appreciation in regulating complex property issues during transition to a democratic legal order. In the specific circumstances, the applicant companies did not bear an individual and excessive burden, and the fair balance between competing interests was not upset.

**Case: Rybářství Třeboň a.s. and Rybářství Třeboň Hld. a.s. v. the Czech Republic**  
*(Applications nos. 18037/19 and 33175/22, ECtHR Fifth Section, judgment of 7 November 2024, final 7 February 2025)*

The applicant companies are Czech private companies. The case concerns the annulment without compensation of their ownership titles to fishponds and land in Novosedly nad Nežárkou and Lutová, totaling 232,312 m². The land had originally belonged to the Roman Catholic Parishes of Novosedly and Lutová. In 1949, the communist-era district national committees deprived those parishes of the land without compensation. It later passed to the State-owned enterprise Státní rybářství Třeboň.

After the fall of communism, the 1992 Privatisation Act permitted transfer of State property. However, section 3(1) contained a “blocking provision”: property transferred to the State after 25 February 1948 from churches, religious orders, congregations or religious communities was not subject to privatisation. In 1992, the National Property Fund created the second applicant company, and the disputed land was included in its registered capital under a privatisation project approved by the Ministry. J.H., director of the State-owned enterprise, helped draft the project, later became a board member of the applicant, and signed the handover record on behalf of the State-owned enterprise, the National Property Fund, and the acquiring company.

A 1994 Supreme Audit Office audit found that the project had unlawfully included land the State enterprise did not have the right to manage or which was subject to restitution. It concluded that State property worth at least CZK 349,715,895 had been unlawfully transferred. It criticized the lack of verification and the conflict of interest arising from J.H.’s multiple roles. In 2007, the second applicant split, and the first applicant received the Novosedly land.

In 2013, the Church Property Settlement Act allowed churches to seek a court declaration that the State owned property if it had been transferred to private persons in breach of the blocking provision. In 2015, the Novosedly and Lutová Parishes sued. Domestic courts declared the privatisation void *ab initio*, holding that the land remained State property and that the applicant companies were not good-faith possessors. They found that J.H. and other managers knew or should have known that the land had been church property before 1950, and the 1994 audit should have raised grave doubts. The Supreme Court and Constitutional Court upheld those decisions. Later, land offices ordered the State to surrender the land to the parishes.

The applicant companies complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 6 § 1, alleging that annulment of their ownership after about 25–26 years without compensation violated their property rights and fair-trial guarantees. They argued they had legitimate expectations and bore a disproportionate burden.

The ECtHR found no violation. It held that the annulment served the fundamental public interest of restoring justice and the rule of law after the communist regime. Because the privatisation transfer was void *ab initio* and made in bad faith, the applicants had no legitimate expectation of continued enjoyment. The domestic courts’ decisions were not arbitrary or manifestly unreasonable. States enjoy a wide margin of appreciation in complex transitional property issues. In the circumstances, the applicants did not bear an individual and excessive burden, and the fair balance between competing interests was not upset.

In *Rybářství Třeboň a.s. and Rybářství Třeboň Hld. a.s. v. the Czech Republic* (ECtHR, Fifth Section, 7 November 2024), two Czech companies complained about the annulment, without compensation, of their ownership titles to fishponds and land in Novosedly nad Nežárkou and Lutová, totaling 232,312 m². The land had originally belonged to Catholic parishes but was taken without compensation in 1949 by the communist-era Třeboň District National Committee and later managed by the State-owned enterprise Státní rybářství Třeboň.

In 1992, under privatization legislation, the National Property Fund created the second applicant company and included the land in its registered capital. In 2007, part of the property, including the Novosedly land, passed to the first applicant company through a spin-off. However, the Privatisation Act contained a “blocking provision”: property transferred to the State after 25 February 1948 from churches, religious orders or communities was not subject to privatization. A 1994–95 Supreme Audit Office audit found that the privatization project had unlawfully included property the State enterprise had no right to manage or which should have been subject to restitution. State property worth at least CZK 349,715,895 was unlawfully transferred. The audit noted that J.H., director of the State enterprise, signed the handover record for the State enterprise, the National Property Fund, and the new company, and later sat on the applicant’s board. He knew some land had been church property before 1950.

In 2013, the Church Property Settlement Act enabled churches to seek a declaration that State-owned property belonged to the State, not private owners, where privatization had breached the blocking provision. In 2015, the Novosedly and Lutová Parishes sued. Domestic courts declared the privatizations void *ab initio*, holding that the land remained State property. They found the applicants lacked good faith, as those who prepared the privatization project knew of the land’s church origin, and the SAO audit should have raised grave doubts. The Supreme Court upheld the decisions, stressing that restitution claims could override completed property transfers. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicants’ appeals.

The applicants alleged violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, complaining of deprivation of property without compensation after more than twenty years, and Article 6 § 1 concerning fair proceedings. The European Court of Human Rights found no violation. It held that the annulment served the fundamental public interest of restoring justice and respect for the rule of law after the communist regime. The applicants had no legitimate expectation of continued enjoyment because the privatization transfer was void *ab initio* and made in bad faith. Domestic courts’ decisions were not arbitrary or manifestly unreasonable. States enjoy a wide margin of appreciation in regulating complex property issues during transition. On the facts, the applicants did not bear an individual and excessive burden, and the balance between competing interests was not upset.

The case of **Szustak and Others v. Poland** (Applications nos. 52773/22 and 3 others) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, First Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered on 8 February 2024. The applicants were individuals who had been parties to civil proceedings in Poland. They lodged applications against Poland under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms on various dates. The Polish Government were given notice of the applications.

The applicants’ central complaint was that the length of the civil proceedings in question was incompatible with the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. They also alleged that they had no effective remedy in domestic law for that complaint, contrary to Article 13. Because the applications raised similar subject matter, the Court joined them in a single judgment.

In all four applications, the Polish Government submitted unilateral declarations and asked the Court to strike the applications out under Article 37 § 1. The Court rejected that request. It held that the unilateral declarations did not offer a sufficient basis for finding that respect for human rights as defined in the Convention did not require continued examination of the cases. The Court therefore proceeded to examine the merits.

On the merits, the Court restated the criteria for assessing the reasonableness of proceedings: the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicants and the relevant authorities, and what was at stake for the applicants in the dispute. It referred to its case-law, particularly **Frydlender v. France**, and to its leading Polish case **Rutkowski and Others v. Poland**, where it had already found a violation of Article 6 in relation to excessive length of civil proceedings.

Having examined all material before it, the Court found no fact or argument capable of justifying the overall length of the proceedings at the national level. It concluded that the length was excessive and failed to meet the “reasonable time” requirement. It further noted that the applicants did not have at their disposal an effective remedy in respect of these complaints. Accordingly, the Court’s analysis supported findings of violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention.

The full text of the judgment does not reproduce the appended table, so the specific applicants’ names, exact lodging dates, durations of the civil proceedings, and the amounts awarded are not set out in the body of the judgment. Those details are contained in the appended list. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore that the applicants were involved in Polish civil proceedings that were unreasonably lengthy, and that Polish law did not provide them with an effective domestic remedy to complain about that length.

Under Article 41 of the Convention, the Court considered it reasonable to award the sums indicated in the appended table, having regard to its case-law, in particular **Rutkowski and Others**. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

In *J. Paul Getty Trust and Others v. Italy* (Application no. 35271/19), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section) considered a confiscation order concerning the “Victorious Youth,” a classical Greek bronze statue in the possession of the J. Paul Getty Trust. The applicants—the Trust and fourteen American trustees—alleged that the Italian confiscation order, and the risk of its enforcement in the United States, violated their right to the peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention.

The statue was discovered in 1964 in the Adriatic Sea off Pedaso by Italian fishermen and brought to Fano. It was later sold and disappeared, reappearing in Munich in 1973 at a German art dealer’s premises, held for a Liechtenstein company. Italian authorities investigated its alleged unlawful export, noting that no export licence had been issued. Earlier Italian criminal proceedings concerning stolen goods ended in acquittal in 1970 because it could not be proved that the statue had been found in Italian territorial waters or that the defendants knew of any unlawful origin. German criminal proceedings were also discontinued.

While the statue was in Germany, the Getty Trust negotiated its purchase. Mr. Getty Senior and his advisers were aware of possible legal complications and provenance doubts. The vendors’ Italian lawyers assured the Trust that Italy had no valid claim and provided translations of the Italian judgments. In July 1977 the Trust purchased the statue for USD 3,950,000 and imported it to the United States, where it has since been displayed at the Getty Villa in Malibu. Italy made repeated administrative and diplomatic attempts to recover it, including a 1989 demand, which the Trust refused.

In 2007, following a petition, the Pesaro public prosecutor’s office reopened proceedings. Initially, the preliminary investigations judge dismissed a confiscation request because the Trust was not involved in the offence and its good faith could not be ruled out. However, in enforcement proceedings, the GIP ordered confiscation in 2010, finding that the Trust had been at least negligent. After procedural challenges and remittal, the GIP upheld the confiscation in 2018, and the Court of Cassation made it final in 2019. The Cassation held that confiscation was not a penalty but had a recovery purpose, aimed at restoring public control over cultural heritage. It found the Trust had failed to conduct an independent inquiry and had relied only on the vendor’s assurances. It also concluded that the statue belonged to Italy’s cultural heritage and to the State, regardless of the exact discovery location, because it was found by an Italian-flagged vessel and had a sufficient cultural connection to Italy. Italy then sought recognition and enforcement of the confiscation in the United States, where proceedings remain pending.

The European Court of Human Rights found no violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It accepted that the Trust was sufficiently affected and that its proprietary interest amounted to a “possession.” The confiscation had a sufficiently clear and foreseeable legal basis, pursued the legitimate aim of protecting cultural heritage, and was supported by strong international consensus. The Italian authorities had reasonably shown that the statue formed part of Italy’s cultural heritage and legally belonged to the State. Their conclusions were not manifestly erroneous or arbitrary. Given the nature of the purchase, the Trust should have exercised high diligence, but it failed to do so. It had no legitimate expectation to retain the statue or obtain compensation. The authorities had acted in a legal vacuum at the time of export and purchase, and Italy had not overstepped its wide margin of appreciation in cultural heritage matters.

**Case: J. Paul Getty Trust and Others v. Italy (Application no. 35271/19), ECtHR First Section, judgment 2 May 2024, final 2 August 2024**

The case concerns an Italian confiscation order over the “Victorious Youth,” a classical Greek bronze statue held by the J. Paul Getty Trust at the Getty Villa in Malibu. The applicants were the Getty Trust and fourteen American members of its board of trustees. They alleged that the confiscation order, and the risk of its recognition and enforcement in the United States, violated their right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights.

The statue was discovered in 1964 in the Adriatic Sea off Pedaso by Italian fishermen and brought to Fano. It was later sold and then disappeared. Italian criminal proceedings concerning receiving and handling a stolen archaeological object ended in 1970 with acquittals because it could not be proved that the statue had been found in Italian territorial waters or that the defendants knew of its unlawful origin. The statue reappeared in Munich in 1973. Italian authorities investigated its alleged unlawful export, but German proceedings were discontinued. Between 1972 and 1977, the Getty Trust negotiated to buy the statue. Its representatives knew of possible legal complications and sought assurances from the vendor’s lawyers. In 1977 the Trust purchased the statue for USD 3,950,000 through a contract concluded in the United Kingdom. It entered the United States in 1977 and has since been displayed at the Getty Villa.

Italy maintained that the statue was part of its cultural heritage, that it had been exported without an export licence and without payment of customs duties, and that it legally belonged to the Italian State. Italian authorities made repeated criminal, administrative and diplomatic attempts to recover it, including through Interpol, letters of request to Germany, the United Kingdom and the United States, and negotiations with the Getty Museum.

In domestic confiscation proceedings, the Pesaro preliminary investigations judge initially ordered confiscation in 2010, finding that the statue had been found by an Italian-flagged vessel and thus within Italian territory, that Italy had acquired ownership, and that the Trust had been at least negligent. That order was later annulled for lack of a public hearing. On reopening, the judge upheld confiscation in 2018, and the Court of Cassation made it final in 2019. The Court of Cassation held that confiscation was primarily a recovery measure, not a penalty, and could be imposed even without a criminal conviction, including on a person not involved in the offence if they had been negligent or acted in bad faith. It found the Trust had failed to act with sufficient diligence: Getty officials had doubts about provenance, relied only on the vendor’s lawyers, and did not ask Italian authorities whether export and heritage-law requirements had been met. The court also found the statue fell within Italy’s cultural heritage because it had been found by an Italian-flagged vessel and had sufficient cultural connection to Italy.

Before the ECtHR, the key issue was whether the confiscation order breached Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court held that the provision was applicable and that the Trust was sufficiently affected even though the order had not yet been enforced in the United States. The interference had a sufficiently clear and foreseeable legal basis; the lack of a time-limit for recovery actions did not automatically make it arbitrary. Protecting Italy’s cultural and artistic heritage was a legitimate aim, supported by strong international consensus. The Italian authorities had reasonably shown the statue was part of Italy’s cultural heritage and legally belonged to the State when the order was issued. The domestic courts’ conclusions were not manifestly erroneous or arbitrary. Given the nature of the purchase, a high standard of diligence was required, and the Trust had failed to meet it. It had no legitimate expectation to retain the statue or obtain compensation. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The case concerns a confiscation order issued by Italian authorities in respect of the ancient Greek bronze statue known as the “Victorious Youth” (also the “Athlete of Fano” or “Lysippus of Fano”), held by the J. Paul Getty Trust. The applicants—the Trust and fourteen US national trustees—complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the order, and the risk of its enforcement in the United States, violated their right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

Key facts: In 1964 Italian fishermen found the statue in the Adriatic off Pedaso and brought it to Fano. It was later sold and disappeared. In 1966–1970 Italian criminal proceedings against fishermen and dealers for receiving stolen archaeological objects ended in acquittal: there was insufficient proof that the statue had been found in Italian territorial waters and that the defendants knew of its unlawful origin. The statue reappeared in Munich in 1973. Italian authorities sought its seizure and recovery; German authorities discontinued proceedings. While in Germany, the Trust negotiated its purchase from a Liechtenstein company through a German dealer. Getty Sr and Trust representatives knew of possible legal complications and provenance doubts. Vendor lawyers assured clear title, relying on the Italian acquittals, and argued Italy had no claim. In 1977 the Trust bought the statue for USD 3,950,000, exported it to the US, and displayed it at the Getty Villa in Malibu. Italy later established that no export licence had been issued and claimed unlawful export and unpaid customs duties. Italian investigations in the 1970s–1980s were discontinued or blocked abroad.

In 2007 new Italian criminal proceedings became time-barred. The initial confiscation request was dismissed because the Trust was not involved in the offence and good faith could not be excluded. On the prosecutor’s objection, the GIP in 2010 ordered confiscation “wherever located.” It found Italy owned the statue because it had been found by an Italian-flagged vessel, hence within Italian territory, and that the Trust had been negligent. After annulment for lack of a public hearing, the order was upheld in 2018 and made final by the Court of Cassation in 2019. The Cassation held confiscation was not a penalty but a recovery measure to restore public control over cultural heritage; it could apply to non-offenders who negligently or knowingly benefited from the unlawful export. It found the Trust had failed to make independent inquiries and relied only on vendor assurances. Italy then sought recognition and enforcement in the US; that procedure remained pending.

Before the ECtHR, the Court held Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 was applicable because the confiscation order sufficiently affected the Trust even though not yet enforced. On the merits, there was no violation. The interference had a sufficiently clear and foreseeable legal basis, pursued the legitimate aim of protecting Italy’s cultural heritage, and was proportionate. The Italian authorities had reasonably shown that the statue formed part of Italy’s cultural heritage and belonged to the State when confiscation was ordered. The domestic courts’ findings were not manifestly erroneous or arbitrary. Given the purchase context, high diligence was required; the Trust failed to act with requisite diligence, so it had no legitimate expectation to retain the statue or obtain compensation. The wide margin of appreciation in cultural heritage matters was not overstepped.

In *Carreto Ribeiro v. Portugal* (Application no. 20075/21), the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 25 April 2024. The applicant lodged the application against Portugal on 5 April 2021. He complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that disciplinary proceedings instituted against him by the Portuguese Bar Association had exceeded the “reasonable time” requirement. He also complained under Article 13 that there was no effective domestic remedy for that delay.

The central facts are that the Portuguese Bar Association brought disciplinary proceedings against the applicant, a lawyer. The proceedings lasted five years and seven months before the Bar Association reached a decision. During that period, the applicant did not know what disciplinary penalty would be imposed on him. The proceedings could affect his right to continue to practise as a lawyer. He later sought compensation in the Portuguese administrative courts for the unreasonable length of the proceedings, but his claim was dismissed. In the meantime, the disciplinary proceedings were eventually discontinued as time-barred.

The Government raised two main admissibility objections. First, it argued that the applicant had not suffered a significant disadvantage: he had not been prevented from exercising his profession during the proceedings, had not proved any damage or loss, and had not shown that his reputation or image was affected, especially given the confidential nature of the proceedings. The Court rejected this objection. It found that the five-year-and-seven-month delay, during which the applicant remained uncertain about the possible penalty, must have had a negative effect on his personal situation. It also reiterated that disciplinary proceedings liable to result in expulsion carry a significant degree of stigma. Therefore, the applicant could be said to have suffered a significant disadvantage.

Second, the Government argued that the applicant was no longer a “victim” because he had benefited from the delay: the disciplinary proceedings had been discontinued as time-barred. The Court also rejected this objection. Under settled case-law, a decision or measure favourable to an applicant does not automatically deprive him of victim status unless the national authorities have acknowledged a violation, either expressly or in substance, and afforded redress. Here, the applicant claimed compensation for the breach of the reasonable-time requirement, but the administrative courts dismissed his claim. Consequently, he could still claim to be a victim.

On the applicability of Article 6 § 1, the Court reiterated that disciplinary proceedings in which the right to continue exercising a profession is at stake involve “contestations” over civil rights. Because the disciplinary proceedings against the applicant put his right to continue practising as a lawyer at risk, Article 6 § 1 was applicable under its civil head.

Finally, the Court found that the complaints under Articles 6 § 1 and 13 were not manifestly ill-founded and were not inadmissible on any other grounds. It therefore declared them admissible. The judgment, adopted on 4 April 2024 and delivered on 25 April 2024, focused on the Government’s preliminary objections and the admissibility of the applicant’s complaints concerning excessive length of disciplinary proceedings and the absence of an effective domestic remedy.

**Case: Carreto Ribeiro v. Portugal (Application no. 20075/21)**

This case is a judgment of the Fourth Section of the European Court of Human Rights, sitting as a Committee, delivered on 25 April 2024. The applicant lodged his application against Portugal on 5 April 2021. The case concerned disciplinary proceedings instituted against the applicant by the Portuguese Bar Association. The applicant complained that the length of those proceedings was incompatible with the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. He also complained under Article 13 that there was no effective domestic remedy for the excessive length of the proceedings.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were as follows. The Portuguese Bar Association brought disciplinary proceedings against the applicant. Those proceedings took five years and seven months for the Bar Association to decide. During that entire period, the applicant did not know which disciplinary penalty, if any, would be applied to him. Eventually, the disciplinary proceedings were discontinued as time-barred. The applicant had sought compensation for the breach of the “reasonable time” requirement, but the administrative courts dismissed his claim. The applicant therefore remained affected by the prolonged uncertainty and by the fact that the disciplinary process had been pending against him for a substantial period.

The Government contested the admissibility of the application on two main grounds. First, they argued that the applicant had not suffered a significant disadvantage. They said he had not been prevented from exercising his profession during the disciplinary proceedings, had not proven any damages or losses caused by the proceedings, and had not shown that his reputation or image was affected, especially because the proceedings were secret. Second, the Government submitted that the applicant was no longer a “victim” because he had ultimately benefited from the delay, since the disciplinary proceedings had been discontinued as time-barred.

The Court rejected both objections. It found that the fact that it took five years and seven months for the Portuguese Bar Association to decide the disciplinary proceedings, during which time the applicant did not know what penalty would be applied, must have had a negative effect on his personal situation. It further reiterated that disciplinary proceedings liable to result in expulsion carry a significant degree of stigma. Therefore, the applicant could be said to have suffered a significant disadvantage. As to victim status, the Court recalled that a decision or measure favourable to an applicant does not in principle deprive him or her of victim status unless the national authorities have acknowledged a violation, either expressly or in substance, and afforded redress for it. Here, the applicant had claimed compensation for the breach of the reasonable-time requirement, but the administrative courts dismissed his claim. He could therefore still claim to be a victim.

The Court also addressed the applicability of Article 6 § 1. It reiterated that disciplinary proceedings in which the right to continue to exercise a profession is at stake give rise to “contestations” over civil rights within the meaning of Article 6 § 1. In this case, the institution of the disciplinary proceedings put the applicant’s right to continue practising as a lawyer at stake. Article 6 § 1 was therefore applicable under its civil head. The Court concluded that the complaints under Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 were not manifestly ill-founded and were not inadmissible on any other grounds. It accordingly declared them admissible.

**Carreto Ribeiro v. Portugal** (Application no. 20075/21) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, delivered on 25 April 2024. The applicant lodged his application against Portugal on 5 April 2021, relying on Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention. He complained principally that disciplinary proceedings brought against him by the Portuguese Bar Association had exceeded the “reasonable time” requirement and that he had no effective domestic remedy for that delay.

The key facts centred on the duration and nature of the disciplinary proceedings. The applicant was a lawyer, and the disciplinary proceedings concerned his right to continue practising his profession. The Bar Association took five years and seven months to decide the proceedings. During that period, the applicant did not know what disciplinary penalty would ultimately be imposed on him. Eventually, the proceedings were discontinued as time-barred. The applicant later sought compensation for the breach of the reasonable-time requirement, but the administrative courts dismissed his claim.

The Portuguese Government contested the application on two main grounds. First, it argued that the applicant had not suffered a “significant disadvantage” because he had not been prevented from exercising his profession during the proceedings, had not proven any damage or loss, and had not suffered damage to his reputation or image, particularly given the secrecy of the proceedings. Second, the Government submitted that the applicant was no longer a “victim” because he had benefited from the delay: the disciplinary proceedings had ultimately been discontinued as time-barred.

The Court rejected both objections. On significant disadvantage, it noted that a delay of five years and seven months, during which the applicant remained uncertain about the possible penalty, must have had a negative effect on his personal situation. It further reiterated that disciplinary proceedings which could result in expulsion carry a significant degree of stigma. Therefore, the applicant could be regarded as having suffered a significant disadvantage.

On victim status, the Court applied its established case-law: a favourable decision or measure does not normally deprive an applicant of victim status unless the national authorities have acknowledged, expressly or in substance, a violation of the Convention and afforded redress for it. Here, although the disciplinary proceedings were discontinued as time-barred, the applicant had claimed compensation for the excessive length, and the administrative courts had dismissed that claim. There had been no acknowledgment of a violation or adequate redress. The applicant therefore retained his victim status.

The Court then considered the applicability of Article 6 § 1. It reiterated that disciplinary proceedings in which the right to continue exercising a profession is at stake involve “contestations” over civil rights within the meaning of Article 6 § 1. Since the disciplinary proceedings against the applicant could affect his right to continue practising as a lawyer, Article 6 § 1 was applicable under its civil head.

Finally, the Court examined admissibility. It found that the applicant’s complaints under Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 were not manifestly ill-founded within the meaning of Article 35 § 3 (a) of the Convention and were not inadmissible on any other grounds. It accordingly declared the complaints admissible. The central alleged violations were therefore the excessive length of the disciplinary proceedings and the absence of an effective domestic remedy for that delay.

The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered a judgment in *Spahiu and Others v. Albania* on 18 July 2024. The case originated in three applications (nos. 79452/17, 39155/18 and 2248/19) lodged against Albania under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants complained principally of the non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of final domestic decisions given in their favour, relying expressly or in substance on Article 6 § 1. The applicants in applications nos. 79452/17 and 39155/18 also complained under Article 13 about the lack of domestic remedies to secure enforcement. Because the applications raised similar issues, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment.

The Court reiterated that execution of a judgment given by any court must be regarded as an integral part of a “hearing” for the purposes of Article 6. It referred to *Hornsby v. Greece* and to its earlier Albanian cases, including *Qufaj Co. Sh.p.k. v. Albania*, *Gjyli v. Albania*, *Elgakoti Sh.p.k and Others v. Albania*, and *Alsula and Others v. Albania*.

As to the facts, in application no. 79452/17, a Tirana Administrative Court decision of 25 March 2014 ordered the applicant’s transfer to another position. Enforcement proceedings began in July 2014. According to the Government, the decision was finally enforced on 9 February 2018, after slightly more than three and a half years. The applicant did not dispute that account.

In application no. 39155/18, a Tirana Administrative Court of First Instance decision of 30 March 2015 ordered the Central Technical Inspectorate to reinstate the applicant to her previous post and to pay salary arrears from the date of dismissal until reinstatement. The Government stated that the decision was fully enforced on 18 December 2018. Salary arrears were paid up to the date of her retirement, but she was not reinstated because she had retired in accordance with domestic requirements. Enforcement therefore took approximately twenty months. The applicant did not dispute the Government’s arguments. The Court found that these judgments were enforced or ceased to be enforceable, at least in part, due to changed circumstances.

In application no. 2248/19, a Tirana Administrative Court of First Instance decision of 28 April 2014 ordered the Public Administration Department to reinstate the applicant to her previous post and to pay salary arrears from dismissal until reinstatement. The Government said the decision was enforced in part on 4 July 2018, when she was appointed to a new position, and in part on 2 June 2022, when all salary arrears were paid. A bailiff then closed enforcement as fully enforced. On 28 February 2024, the applicant informed the Court that she had not been reinstated and that she should have received arrears and positions matching the judgment. However, she did not argue that she had contested the bailiff’s decision to close enforcement. The Court therefore accepted that enforcement ended on 2 June 2022, lasting almost five years.

Having examined the material, the Court found no reason to depart from its case-law. It concluded that the Albanian authorities did not deploy all necessary efforts to enforce the domestic decisions in the applicants’ favour in due time. It found a violation of Article 6 § 1. It found no need to give a separate ruling on the remaining Article 13 complaints.

**Case Name:** *Spahiu and Others v. Albania* (ECtHR, Third Section, Committee, 18 July 2024, App. no. 79452/17 and 2 others)

In *Spahiu and Others v. **Case: Spahiu and Others v. Albania**  
**Application no. 79452/17 and 2 others**  
**European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, judgment of 18 July 2024**

The applicants complained principally of the non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of final domestic decisions given in their favour. They relied, expressly or in substance, on Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which guarantees a fair hearing. The applicants in applications nos. 79452/17 and 39155/18 also complained under Article 13 about the lack of domestic remedies to secure enforcement. Because the applications raised similar issues, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment.

The alleged violation concerned Albania’s failure to execute final administrative court judgments in employment-related cases. Under the Court’s case-law, the execution of a judgment given by any court is an integral part of the “hearing” for Article 6 purposes. Unreasonable delay or complete non-enforcement of a final domestic judgment can therefore breach the right to a fair hearing. The Court referred to its earlier leading cases against Albania, including *Qufaj Co. Sh.p.k. v. Albania* and *Gjyli v. Albania*, and to more recent cases concerning delayed enforcement or non-enforcement of domestic judgments in Albanian employment disputes.

The key facts are as follows. In application no. 79452/17, a decision of the Tirana Administrative Court of 25 March 2014 ordered the applicant’s transfer to another position. Enforcement proceedings began in July 2014. According to the Government, the decision was finally enforced on 9 February 2018, slightly more than three and a half years later. The applicant did not dispute that account.

In application no. 39155/18, a decision of the Tirana Administrative Court of First Instance of 30 March 2015 ordered the Central Technical Inspectorate to reinstate the applicant to her previous post and to pay salary arrears from the date of dismissal until reinstatement. The Government submitted that the decision was fully enforced on 18 December 2018, approximately twenty months later. The applicant was paid salary arrears up to the date of her retirement. She was not reinstated because she had retired in line with domestic requirements. The applicant did not dispute the Government’s arguments.

In application no. 2248/19, a decision of the Tirana Administrative Court of First Instance of 28 April 2014 ordered the Public Administration Department to reinstate the applicant in her previous post and to pay her salary arrears from dismissal until reinstatement. The Government stated that the decision was enforced in part on 4 July 2018, when the applicant was appointed to a new position, and in part on 2 June 2022, when the authorities paid all salary arrears. A bailiff then closed the enforcement proceedings as fully enforced. On 28 February 2024, the applicant informed the Court that she had not been reinstated and that she should have been paid arrears and offered positions matching the 2014 decision. However, she did not argue that she had contested the bailiff’s decision to close the enforcement. The Court therefore accepted the Government’s position that enforcement ended on 2 June 2022, meaning the enforcement proceedings lasted almost five years.

Having examined the material, the Court found no fact or argument capable of leading to a different conclusion. It considered that the authorities had not deployed all necessary efforts to enforce the domestic decisions in due time. It therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention concerning the delayed or non-enforcement of the judgments. As to the remaining Article 13 complaints in applications nos. 79452/17 and 39155/18, the Court found that it had already examined the main legal question and that no separate ruling was needed.

The case *Taganova and Others v. Georgia and Russia* (ECtHR, 17 December 2024) concerns several applications by residents and property owners in Abkhazia, Georgia, who complained of losing access to their homes and possessions after the 1992–93 Abkhaz conflict and subsequent displacement or expulsion. Abkhazia was outside Georgia’s de facto control, while Russia was found to exercise effective control over the territory and the Abkhaz authorities.

The first and second applicants, Galina Taganova and Tariel Esartia, lived in Psakhara, Gagra District. Esartia owned half of a house at 185 Sukhumi Road and was registered there from 1977; a second house at 185a burned down in 1992. In 1992 Abkhaz fighters forced them out, and the old house was later given by de facto authorities to an ethnic Abkhaz man. From 1994 they complained to de facto Abkhaz administrative bodies and courts, but proceedings were stalled, rejected for procedural defects or unpaid State tax, or passed back and forth between authorities. In 2003 the de facto Supreme Court acknowledged their ownership but remitted the case; later the district court refused to examine it. The house was returned in August 2006, but it was allegedly stripped, uninhabitable, and again challenged by a third party. Esartia was also dismissed from his hospital post in 1993 amid dismissals of ethnic Georgians; his attempts to obtain reinstatement before de facto Abkhaz courts were not examined.

The third applicant, Ketevan Mekhuzla, lived in Sukhumi, owned a house at 7 Tavadze Street, and fled in October 1993. Her house was occupied and allegedly sold by an Abkhaz family. Georgian registration was refused because no local registry operated in Sukhumi, and her court request for recognition of ownership failed on procedural grounds. The fourth applicant, Ksenia Sanaia, fled Gagra in 1992; her house at 12 Sabcho Street was reportedly assigned to an Armenian family. The fifth and sixth applicants, Suliko Dvali and Marina Gogia, fled Sukhumi in 1993; their houses at 4 Lakerbaia Street, Sukhumi, and in Pshapi, Gulripshi Region, were occupied or assigned to Abkhaz families. All claimed IDP status and recorded their properties with Georgian authorities.

The applicants alleged violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property), Article 8 (home and family life), Article 6 § 1 (access to court, mainly concerning Esartia’s dismissal), and Articles 13 and 14. They complained of a continuing inability to access, control, use or enjoy their homes and property, lack of compensation, and lack of effective remedies.

The Court found Russia responsible for the Abkhaz authorities’ conduct because of its effective control over Abkhazia. It held that the loss of access to homes and property was a continuing situation and found violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 8 for applicants 2–6, as they were deprived of access to their property and homes without compensation. Article 6 § 1 was violated regarding the second applicant’s inability to have his dismissal examined by a lawful tribunal. Georgia, which lacked control over Abkhazia at the relevant time, satisfied its positive obligations and bore no responsibility.

Case *Taganova and Others v. Georgia and Russia* concerns five applications brought by residents and displaced persons from Abkhazia who alleged violations arising from the 1992–93 conflict and its aftermath. The applicants were Ms Taganova and Mr Esartia, both Russian nationals; Ms Mekhuzla, Ms Sanaia, Ms Dvali and Ms Gogia, all Georgian nationals. They owned homes and property in Abkhazia, including in Psakhara, Sukhumi, Gagra and Pshapi, and complained of prolonged inability to access, control or enjoy those homes and possessions after being forced to leave or displaced.

The first and second applicants lived at no. 185 Sukhumi Road, Psakhara. The second applicant, an ethnic Georgian who later acquired Russian nationality, owned half of the house; a new house on the same plot burned down in 1992. In 1992 Abkhaz fighters expelled the applicants, and the old house was later allocated to an ethnic Abkhaz man, N.B. From 1994 they complained to de facto Abkhaz administrative bodies and courts. Proceedings stalled: complaints were passed between authorities; the Gagra District Court declared their claim inadmissible for failure to identify the respondent; after the de facto Supreme Court acknowledged their ownership and remitted the case, the lower court refused to examine it because of procedural defects and unpaid State tax. In August 2006 the house was returned, but the applicants said it had been stripped and was uninhabitable, and it was again contested or taken away. The second applicant was also dismissed from his hospital post in 1993 amid dismissals of Georgian medical staff, and his complaints to de facto Abkhaz courts went unanswered. Russian authorities later indicated that Abkhaz laws permitted confiscation of abandoned property, and a Russia–Abkhaz Property Commission operated but reportedly rejected or obstructed claims by ethnic Georgians.

The third applicant built a house in Sukhumi, fled in October 1993, became an internally displaced person, and her house was occupied or sold. Georgian authorities refused registration because no local registry operated in Sukhumi, and Georgian courts rejected her application for procedural and jurisdictional reasons. The fourth applicant’s Gagra house was reportedly assigned to an Armenian family. The fifth and sixth applicants’ houses in Sukhumi and Pshapi were reportedly occupied by Abkhaz families. These applicants later made declarations to the Georgian Ministry for provisional registration of property.

The European Court of Human Rights found that Russia exercised effective control over Abkhazia and was responsible for the Abkhaz authorities’ conduct regarding applicants 2–6. Georgia lacked control but had positive obligations, which it was found to have satisfied. The main alleged violations were under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 8: continuous denial of access, control, use and enjoyment of homes and property without compensation. The second applicant also complained under Article 6 § 1 that he could not have his dismissal reviewed by de facto Abkhaz courts, which did not qualify as a “tribunal established by law.” The Court found no effective domestic remedies in Russia or Georgia for applicants 2–6, and found violations concerning property and home access, including an excessive individual burden on the second applicant.

In *Taganova and Others v. Georgia and Russia*, the European Court of Human Rights examined five applications brought by former residents of Abkhazia, Georgia, who were displaced or expelled during the 1992–1993 Georgian-Abkhaz conflict and later denied access to their homes and property. They complained mainly under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions), Article 8 (home and family life), Article 6 § 1 (access to court), and Articles 13 and 14.

The first and second applicants, Ms Taganova and Mr Esartia, lived in Psakhara, Gagra District. Esartia’s family house at 185 Sukhumi Road was partly registered in his name. In 1992 Abkhaz fighters forced them out; the house was later given to an ethnic Abkhaz man, N.B. They made repeated complaints to de facto Abkhaz administrative bodies and courts, but these were rejected or left unexamined for procedural reasons. In 2006 the de facto authorities returned the house after N.B.’s lease expired, but the applicants said it had been stripped and was uninhabitable, and N.B. challenged the return. Esartia was also dismissed from his hospital post in 1993, allegedly as part of a wave of dismissals of Georgian medical staff, and his attempts to obtain reinstatement through de facto Abkhaz courts were unsuccessful. They also complained to Russian and Georgian authorities without effective remedy.

The third applicant, Ms Mekhuzla, owned a house at 7 Tavadze Street, Sukhumi. She fled in October 1993; her house was occupied and allegedly sold. Georgia’s public registry refused registration because it had no local office in Sukhumi, and Georgian courts held they could not grant ownership or identify the occupants because Georgia did not control Abkhazia. She registered her claim with the Georgian Ministry for Displaced Persons. The fourth applicant, Ms Sanaia, fled Gagra in 1992 and her house at 12 Sabcho Street was reportedly assigned to an Armenian family. The fifth and sixth applicants, Ms Dvali and Ms Gogia, fled Sukhumi and Pshapi in 1993; their homes were occupied by non-Georgian families.

The applicants alleged a continuing denial of access to, control over, and enjoyment of their property and homes in Abkhazia, lack of compensation, and lack of access to court. The Court found that Russia exercised effective control over Abkhazia through a strong presence and the de facto authorities’ dependency on Russia. It therefore held Russia responsible for the continuing violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 8 concerning applicants nos. 3–6, and for applicant no. 2’s inability to access his home until its return. It also found a violation of Article 6 § 1 as regards the second applicant’s inability to have his dismissal reviewed by the de facto Abkhaz courts, but that situation was not attributable to Georgia. Georgia, which lacked control over Abkhazia, had satisfied its positive obligations; no violations were found against Georgia. There were no effective domestic remedies in Russia or Georgia for the property complaints.
