This case concerns Afgan Mukhtarli, an Azerbaijani freelance investigative journalist known for critical reporting on the Azerbaijani government. In January 2015, alleging harassment and persecution, he moved with his family to Georgia and sought asylum, while continuing to report on high-level corruption in Azerbaijan. On 29 May 2017, while walking home in Tbilisi, he allegedly was stopped by four Georgian-speaking men, three wearing Georgian criminal-police uniforms. They forced him into a silver Opel, handcuffed and beat him, then drove him past Tbilisi airport towards the Kakheti region. He was blindfolded, transferred between vehicles, and later realised he had been handed to Azerbaijani speakers; his captors reportedly referred to a “Mr General”. Around 10:40 p.m. he reached an Azerbaijani State Border Service unit in Balakan District. Border officials said he had illegally crossed the border and that €10,000 was found in his pocket; he denied the money was his. Azerbaijan claimed he was arrested at the border after fleeing and assaulting an officer, then administratively arrested and later criminally prosecuted in Baku. Georgian officials publicly called for a thorough investigation but denied institutional involvement. An Azerbaijani MP alleged Georgian-Azerbaijani intelligence cooperation, which Azerbaijan denied. The applicant alleged that his abduction, ill-treatment and forcible transfer from Georgia, and his arrest and detention in Azerbaijan, were intended to silence and punish him for his journalistic activities.

Georgia opened a criminal investigation into unlawful deprivation of liberty on 30 May 2017. Investigators interviewed the applicant’s wife and friends, many local witnesses, minibus drivers, border guards and customs officers, and collected CCTV footage. However, the European Court found serious shortcomings: key footage was unavailable or unreadable, vehicles and passengers were not adequately identified, the applicant and his wife were denied victim status or effective access at times, forensic and mutual-assistance steps were delayed or unanswered, and the core events could not be reconstructed. The Court held that Georgia failed to conduct an effective investigation into plausible allegations of abduction, ill-treatment and unlawful transfer, including any link to the applicant’s journalism. Because of those shortcomings, it could not establish with sufficient certainty what happened, nor conclude beyond reasonable doubt that Georgian authorities were actively or passively involved or acquiesced.

Regarding Azerbaijan, the Court could not establish that the arrest and initial detention before a judge were unlawful under Article 5 § 1. It did find a violation of Article 5 § 3 because Azerbaijani courts failed to give relevant and sufficient reasons for continuing pre-trial detention. It also found a violation of Article 8: the search of the contents of the applicant’s mobile phone by Azerbaijani investigators, without judicial authorisation and without judicial review, was not “in accordance with the law”.

Case Mukhtarli v. Azerbaijan and Georgia (no. 39503/17) concerns Afgan Mukhtarli, an Azerbaijani investigative journalist who reported critically on the Azerbaijani government for outlets including Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty. In January 2015, citing harassment and persecution, he moved with his family to Georgia and applied for asylum, but continued reporting on high-level corruption. On 29 May 2017 he disappeared in Tbilisi. He alleged that four Georgian-speaking men, three wearing uniforms resembling Georgian criminal police, forced him into a car, handcuffed and beat him, blindfolded him, drove him towards the airport and Sagarejo, changed vehicles twice, and handed him over to Azerbaijani men. He said he was taken to an Azerbaijani State Border Service unit in Balakan, where money was planted on him, his phone and cards were seized, and he was later transferred to Baku. Azerbaijan claimed he was arrested while illegally crossing the “green border,” that he resisted and assaulted an officer, and that EUR 10,000 was found on him. Georgia denied involvement. An Azerbaijani MP claimed the transfer resulted from Georgian-Azerbaijani intelligence cooperation, which Azerbaijan denied.

Georgia opened an investigation for unlawful deprivation of liberty. Investigators interviewed many witnesses, including café staff, neighbours, minibus drivers, border guards, customs officers, and a minibus driver who crossed into Azerbaijan that night. They sought CCTV from streets, border points, and nearby businesses. However, much footage was missing, deleted, switched off, damaged, or technically unreadable; the Tsodna border footage was initially unavailable; and a key request to Azerbaijan for DNA/forensic comparison went unanswered. The applicant’s lawyers complained of limited access to the file and denial of victim status.

The European Court of Human Rights found that Georgia failed to carry out an effective investigation into the applicant’s plausible allegations of abduction, ill-treatment, and unlawful transfer, violating the procedural obligations under Article 3 and Article 5. Because of these investigative shortcomings, it was impossible to establish with sufficient certainty the events leading to his disappearance from Georgia and reappearance in Azerbaijan. The Court could not conclude beyond reasonable doubt that the alleged acts occurred with the involvement or acquiescence of Georgian authorities, so no substantive violation was established against Georgia.

As regards Azerbaijan, the Court could not establish that the arrest and initial detention before a judge were unlawful under Article 5 § 1. It nevertheless found a violation of Article 5 § 3 because the Azerbaijani courts failed to give relevant and sufficient reasons for the need to keep the applicant in pre-trial detention. It also found a violation of Article 8: the search of the contents of the applicant’s mobile phone by Azerbaijani investigating authorities was conducted without judicial authorisation and without judicial review, and was therefore not “in accordance with the law.” The case therefore concerns primarily Georgia’s ineffective investigation of a cross-border disappearance and transfer, and Azerbaijan’s unjustified pre-trial detention and unlawful phone search.

Case: Mukhtarli v. Azerbaijan and Georgia (ECtHR, Fifth Section, Application no. 39503/17, judgment 5 September 2024). The applicant, Afgan Mukhtarli, was an Azerbaijani investigative journalist known for critical reporting on the Azerbaijani Government. After alleged harassment and persecution, he moved with his family to Georgia in January 2015, applied for asylum, and continued reporting on high-level corruption in Azerbaijan.

On 29 May 2017, while walking home in Tbilisi, he alleged that four unknown men—three wearing Georgian criminal police uniforms and speaking Georgian—forced him into a car, handcuffed and beat him, then blindfolded him. They drove through Georgia, changed vehicles, and eventually handed him to Azerbaijani-speaking men. He said he was taken to a State Border Service unit in Balakan District, Azerbaijan, accused of illegally crossing the border, and had EUR 10,000 allegedly planted in his pocket; his mobile phone and cards were seized. The Azerbaijani Government claimed border guards caught him crossing the “green border” illegally, that he resisted and punched an officer, and that he was administratively arrested. The Georgian Government denied involvement and called his allegations unsubstantiated.

Georgian authorities opened a criminal investigation into unlawful deprivation of liberty. Investigators interviewed the applicant’s wife, friends, café owner, numerous local witnesses, minibus drivers, border guards, customs officers and border-checkpoint staff; reviewed CCTV footage; requested telephone data; and sought mutual legal assistance from Azerbaijan. Many witnesses saw nothing unusual, and CCTV evidence was often unavailable because cameras were not working, footage had been deleted, or files could not be opened. The applicant’s lawyer alleged police involvement, sought transfer of the case to the Chief Prosecutor’s Office, victim status, access to the file, and specific CCTV seizures. Some requests were refused or unanswered. Azerbaijani authorities largely did not answer Georgian mutual assistance requests.

The ECtHR found that Georgia failed to carry out an effective investigation into the applicant’s plausible allegations of abduction, ill-treatment and unlawful transfer from Georgia to Azerbaijan. Due to investigative shortcomings, the Court could not establish with sufficient certainty what happened between his disappearance in Georgia and reappearance in Azerbaijan. It could not conclude beyond reasonable doubt that the alleged acts occurred with the active or passive involvement, or acquiescence, of Georgian authorities. Georgia therefore violated procedural obligations under Articles 3 and 5, but no substantive attribution was established.

As regards Azerbaijan, the Court could not establish that the arrest and initial detention before he was brought before a judge were unlawful under Article 5 § 1. However, the Azerbaijani courts failed to provide relevant and sufficient reasons for his pre-trial detention, violating Article 5 § 3. Separately, the search of the contents of his mobile phone by Azerbaijani investigating authorities without judicial authorisation and without judicial review was not “in accordance with the law,” violating Article 8. The applicant’s broader claim that his abduction, transfer and prosecution were intended to silence and punish him for journalistic activities formed the context, but the Court’s violations concerned Georgia’s ineffective investigation and Azerbaijan’s detention and phone-search breaches.
001-236179:
Zavridou v. Cyprus concerns a Cypriot mother’s complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that the Cypriot authorities failed to protect her family life by securing her custodial rights and enforcing domestic court orders, resulting in the alienation of her two children from her.

The applicant and her husband separated in 2018. In July 2018 the Nicosia Family Court issued a temporary order granting both parents contact rights. On 20 November 2018, the order was amended to require the father to return the children to the applicant after contact and to establish the children’s residence with their mother. The father did not comply. The children regularly stayed overnight with him and had infrequent contact with the applicant. By March 2019, the applicant’s contact with the children stopped almost entirely.

In June 2019, following assessments by the Mental Health Services, reports found that the father had alienated the children from their mother. The MHS recommended immediately re-establishing contact between the applicant and the children without the father present. In September 2019, the Social Welfare Services recommended that custody and care be granted to the mother. On 25 October 2019, the Family Court granted the applicant custody and care of the children and made a residence order in her favour.

Between October 2019 and March 2020, the SWS attempted to enforce the order through meetings and cooperation with police, but the father was obstructive and the children were hostile towards the applicant. In December 2019, the applicant sought enforcement of the father’s compliance. A police complaint about psychological abuse led to recommendations, but no effective steps were taken because the father disagreed. A short meeting occurred in March 2020, but further visits were interrupted by COVID-19 measures. A habeas corpus petition was dismissed, and later enforcement attempts failed because the children opposed living with their mother.

On 5 June 2020, the Family Court ordered the father to surrender the children within four days, warning of imprisonment. An enforcement attempt on 12 June 2020 failed. A police report noted that the father had left the children unprepared and suggested investigating contempt and psychological violence. The SWS also considered temporary custody. In August 2020, the Ombudsman criticised the police and SWS. The police had failed to treat the court orders as mandatory and did not promptly investigate the father’s disobedience, losing valuable time and allowing alienation to deepen. The Ombudsman recommended immediate cooperation, reassessment of the children, possible partial removal of parental responsibility, and criminal investigations.

In February 2021, the Family Court found the father guilty of non-compliance, noting his systematic, deliberate and intentional alienation of the children from the applicant. He was sentenced to 45 days’ imprisonment. During his imprisonment, repeated attempts to enforce custody failed due to the children’s refusal, the presence of relatives, and the father’s continued negative influence. The Supreme Court refused a request to compel police to remove the children forcibly.

In January 2023, the father was convicted of disobedience and sentenced to one year’s imprisonment. The SWS temporarily removed the children to a state institution; the daughter later moved in with the applicant, but the son refused. After the father’s release, the children again became hostile, and they now reside with him, with the applicant’s contact limited.

The core alleged violation was that, despite clear court orders and expert findings, the authorities’ responses were not timely and depended on the father’s cooperation despite his systematic obstruction. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 8, holding that Cyprus failed its positive obligation to secure the mother’s custodial rights and enforce the relevant domestic court orders.

In *Zavridou v. Cyprus* (Application no. 14680/22, judgment 8 October 2024), the applicant, a Cypriot mother, complained under Article 8 that Cyprus authorities failed to secure her custodial rights and enforce domestic court orders, leading to the alienation of her two children, C.K. (born 2010) and A.K. (born 2012), from her.

The parents separated in 2018. In July 2018 the Nicosia Family Court issued a temporary order granting both parents contact rights. In November 2018 this was amended to require the father to return the children to the applicant after contact and to establish their residence with her. The father did not comply. The children stayed with him, and the applicant’s contact became infrequent and then stopped in March 2019.

In June 2019 the Mental Health Services concluded that the father had alienated the children from their mother and recommended immediately re-establishing contact without the father present. In September 2019 the Social Welfare Services recommended that custody and care be granted to the mother and that the father’s contact be gradually reduced. On 25 October 2019 the Family Court granted the applicant custody and made a residence order in her favour.

Between late 2019 and early 2020, the SWS, police, and multidisciplinary meetings attempted to enforce the order, but the children were hostile and the father was obstructive and not genuinely willing to comply. The applicant lodged enforcement proceedings in December 2019 and complained to the police of psychological abuse in January 2020. In March 2020 she had a short meeting with the children at the father’s home and in his presence. A February 2020 habeas corpus petition was refused, and an April 2020 attempt to collect the children failed due to their opposition.

In June 2020 the Family Court ordered the father to surrender the children within four days, warning of imprisonment, but enforcement failed. A police report suggested investigating contempt and psychological violence, and that the SWS consider temporary custody. In August 2020 the Ombudsman criticised the police for failing to promptly investigate disobedience of court orders and the SWS for insufficient action; she found a continuing breach of the applicant’s parental rights and growing alienation.

In February 2021 the Family Court found the father guilty of non-compliance, attributing the children’s opposition to his “methodical, systematic, deliberate and intentional” alienation of them from the applicant. He was sentenced to 45 days’ imprisonment in March 2021. During his imprisonment, SWS attempts to enforce custody still failed, the father continued to influence the children negatively from prison, and the children stopped attending school. In April 2021 the Supreme Court refused a mandamus petition seeking to compel police to remove the children.

After the applicant lodged her Strasbourg application in March 2022, further Family Court orders for increased contact and neutral-venue meetings without the father were not complied with. In January 2023 the father was convicted of disobedience and sentenced to one year’s imprisonment. The Family Court then assigned custody to the Director of the SWS, and the children were placed in a state institution. Some progress followed: A.K. moved in with the applicant in April 2023, but C.K. refused. After the father’s release in May 2023, an alternating overnight arrangement soon broke down; the children resumed hostility, including physical violence toward the applicant, and stopped residing with her. By 2024 they were living with the father, with only limited contact. Temporary SWS custody became absolute in April 2024, and the second custody application remained pending.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 8, holding that the domestic authorities failed to secure the mother’s custodial rights and enforce the relevant orders; their responses were either untimely or dependent on the father’s cooperation despite his systematic obstruction, resulting in the children’s alienation from the applicant.

In *Zavridou v. Cyprus* (ECtHR, Third Section, 8 October 2024), the applicant, a Cypriot mother, alleged under Article 8 that the domestic authorities failed to protect her family life by not securing her custodial rights or enforcing court orders, resulting in the alienation of her two children from her.

The applicant separated from the children’s father in 2018. In July 2018 the Nicosia Family Court issued a temporary contact order. In November 2018 it was amended to require the father to return the children to the applicant after contact and to establish their residence with her. The father did not comply, and by March 2019 the applicant’s contact with the children had effectively stopped.

In June 2019 the Mental Health Services reported that the father had alienated the children from their mother and recommended immediate re-establishment of contact without the father present. In September 2019 the Social Welfare Services recommended that custody be granted to the mother. In October 2019 the Family Court granted her custody and made a residence order in her favour. The father remained obstructive, and the children were hostile toward the applicant. Efforts by the SWS and police between October 2019 and March 2020 to enforce the order failed.

In December 2019 the applicant sought enforcement of the father’s compliance. In January 2020 she complained to police of psychological abuse. Meetings with the children occurred only sporadically, usually at the father’s home and in his presence. A habeas corpus petition was refused in February 2020. In June 2020 the Family Court ordered the father to surrender the children within four days, warning of imprisonment. Enforcement failed because the children refused. A police report noted that the father had not prepared them psychologically or practically and suggested investigating contempt and psychological violence, possibly placing the children temporarily with the SWS.

In August 2020 the Ombudsman found that police had failed to investigate disobedience promptly, treating orders as merely regulatory, and that the SWS had not done enough beyond preparing reports. The delay contributed to the children’s alienation.

In February 2021 the Family Court found the father guilty of non-compliance, citing his systematic and deliberate alienation of the children. He was sentenced to forty-five days’ imprisonment in March 2021. While he was imprisoned, repeated SWS attempts to enforce contact or remove the children failed; relatives were present and the father continued to influence the children negatively. The children stopped attending school. The applicant’s petition for mandamus compelling police to remove the children was dismissed, and the appeal was rejected in 2021. Visits continued mainly at the father’s home, at his insistence, and sometimes under camera surveillance.

In January 2023 a criminal court convicted the father of disobedience, describing tactics such as collecting the children early, hostility toward the applicant, false illness claims, recording the children crying, and failing to follow schedules. He was sentenced to one year’s imprisonment. The Family Court then temporarily assigned custody to the Director of the SWS, and the children were placed in a State Institution. One child later moved in with the applicant; the other refused. After the father’s release, alternate overnight stays briefly resumed, but the children became hostile, including physically violent, and stopped residing with the applicant. By 2024, the SWS retained custody, the children lived with their father, and the applicant’s contact was limited.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 8, holding that the authorities failed to fulfil their positive obligations to secure the mother’s custodial rights and enforce the relevant orders. Their responses were either untimely or dependent on the father’s cooperation despite his systematic obstruction, leading to the children’s alienation from their mother.

Case: Mirzoyan v. the Czech Republic (Apps. nos. 15117/21 and 15689/21), ECtHR Fifth Section, 16 May 2024. The applicant, Artur Mirzoyan, a Russian national born in 1966, had lived in the Czech Republic since 2006, initially on a long-stay visa and then a long-term residence permit for business. He lived in Karlovy Vary with his Armenian wife and four Russian-national children. His wife and three younger children held permanent residence since 2013; one daughter acquired Czech citizenship in 2020. The case concerned two refusals: (1) his 2011 application to extend his long-term residence permit for business purposes; and (2) his 2014 application for a new long-term residence permit for family purposes based on his wife’s permanent residence. The Ministry of Interior repeatedly dismissed both applications on the ground that his residence was not in the interests of the Czech Republic and posed a threat to national security and public order. The decisions relied on classified police information, including from the organised crime unit and NCOZ. Some classified material was made accessible to the applicant’s lawyer, but not to the applicant; other material, describing operational police activities, was withheld even from the lawyer. The Ministry considered the information credible and based on the applicant’s long-term conduct and contacts, even though he had no criminal record. The applicant argued that the refusals violated Article 8 (family life) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 7, adversely affecting his family and failing to consider the best interests of his children.

The domestic proceedings were protracted. Regional courts repeatedly annulled the Ministry’s decisions (2013, 2015, 2017, 2019), finding the classified information insufficiently specific or verifiable and lacking proof of criminal or subversive activity. The Supreme Administrative Court initially upheld those annulments. In 2020, however, it quashed the Regional Court’s judgment and found the classified information sufficient: it gave a long-term, consistent picture of the applicant’s contacts with a criminal community since 2011. On remand, the Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s actions. It held that the interference with family life was proportionate; the family could remain in the Czech Republic, his wife was financially independent, and the applicant had not shown exceptional circumstances or specified how separation would affect his children. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld that reasoning, stating that the applicant bore the burden of providing relevant private/family information and had remained passive. The Constitutional Court dismissed his complaints, finding that the children’s interests and family situation had been sufficiently considered and that the procedural limitations concerning classified information were counterbalanced by judicial review.

Before the ECtHR, the Court found no violation of Article 8. It noted that there was no expulsion order or withdrawal/revocation of a valid residence permit, so its expulsion case-law could not be automatically transposed. The domestic court proceedings offered sufficient guarantees to counterbalance the limited procedural rights before the administrative authorities, and the applicant was not deprived of an effective opportunity to challenge the executive’s national-security/public-order assertions. The domestic authorities had sufficiently considered his family ties and balanced the relevant interests, and the margin of appreciation was not overstepped.

In *Mirzoyan v. the Czech Republic*, the European Court of Human Rights examined the refusal of Czech authorities to extend or grant the applicant, a Russian national, long-term residence permits on national-security and public-order grounds based on classified information.

The applicant had lived in the Czech Republic since 2006, first on a long-stay visa and then on a long-term residence permit for business purposes. He lived there with his Armenian wife and four Russian-national children. His wife and three of the children had permanent residence in the Czech Republic from 2013; one daughter later acquired Czech citizenship. On 3 June 2011 he applied to extend his business-purpose long-term residence permit. Between 2012 and 2018 the Ministry of Interior repeatedly refused the application, finding that his residence was not in the interests or security interests of the Czech Republic. The refusals relied on classified police and organised-crime-unit information alleging long-term contacts and meetings with persons regarded as criminally involved. The applicant was never prosecuted and had no criminal record. Some classified material was made partly accessible to his lawyer, but other material was withheld because it described operational methods that could be compromised if disclosed.

Domestic administrative courts repeatedly intervened. The Regional Court annulled several Ministry decisions between 2013 and 2019, holding that the classified information was insufficiently specific, verifiable or credible. However, in March 2020 the Supreme Administrative Court reversed course, finding the classified material sufficiently conclusive, accurate and reliable. It described a long-term, consistent picture of the applicant’s contacts with a criminal community since 2011, based on meta-information derived from interceptions, video recordings and police statements gathered in criminal proceedings against other persons. On remand, the Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s action, the Supreme Administrative Court upheld that judgment, and the Constitutional Court dismissed his complaint.

Separately, in May 2014 the applicant applied for a long-term residence permit for family purposes based on his wife’s permanent residence. In February 2018 the Ministry refused it, relying on the same classified information and finding a reasonable risk that he could seriously disrupt public order through long-term immoral conduct, even if not criminal. The Ministry considered that his family could remain in the Czech Republic, that his wife was financially independent, and that his ties with Russia had not been disrupted. The administrative courts and Constitutional Court upheld that refusal.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 8 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 7, arguing that the refusals harmed his private and family life and that his children’s best interests had not been sufficiently considered. He also complained that the use of undisclosed classified information prevented him from effectively challenging the national-security and public-order grounds.

The Court found no violation of Article 8. Because there was no expulsion order and no withdrawal or revocation of a valid residence permit, its case-law on expulsion measures did not automatically apply. The domestic court proceedings provided sufficient procedural guarantees to counterbalance the limits before the administrative authorities. The applicant had been represented by a lawyer, some classified material was disclosed to the lawyer, and the courts reviewed the classified files. The authorities had also given sufficient consideration to his family ties and carried out a balancing of the relevant interests. The State’s margin of appreciation was therefore not overstepped.

In *Mirzoyan v. the Czech Republic* (ECtHR, Fifth Section, 16 May 2024), the applicant, a Russian national, had lived in the Czech Republic since 2006 and held a long-term residence permit for business purposes. He lived there with his Armenian wife and their children; several family members had permanent residence, and one daughter later acquired Czech citizenship. In 2011 he applied to extend his long-term business residence permit. In 2014 he applied for a long-term residence permit for family purposes based on his wife’s permanent residence.

Both applications were refused by the Ministry of Interior on the ground that the applicant’s residence was not in the Czech Republic’s interests or that he posed a threat to national security and public order. The decisions relied on classified information from the police organised crime unit and the National Centre against Organised Crime. The classified material alleged long-term contacts with a criminal community. Some classified documents were made accessible to the applicant’s lawyer, but not to the applicant himself; other documents were not disclosed at all because disclosure could compromise police operational methods. The Ministry considered family life but found that the applicant’s wife and children could remain in the Czech Republic and that the wife, a businesswoman, could provide for the family.

The applicant challenged the refusals. In several rounds, Czech administrative courts annulled the decisions because the classified information initially lacked sufficient credibility and verifiability. Eventually, the Supreme Administrative Court found the supplemented classified information sufficiently conclusive, accurate and reliable, describing a long-term and consistent picture of the applicant’s contacts with criminal circles since 2011. The Regional Court dismissed his actions, holding that the interference with his family life was proportionate and that no exceptional circumstances justified a different outcome. It noted that the children had long residence and social ties in the country but that the family could remain and was financially independent of the applicant. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld this, emphasising that the applicant had not submitted specific facts about his care for the children or how separation would affect them. The Constitutional Court dismissed his complaints, finding that the procedural limitations caused by non-disclosure were counterbalanced by judicial review and that the children’s interests had been sufficiently considered.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant relied on Article 8 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 7, arguing that the refusals violated his right to respect for family life and his children’s best interests, and that he could not effectively challenge the classified grounds. The Court noted that there was no expulsion order or withdrawal or revocation of a valid residence permit, so its expulsion case-law did not automatically apply. It found that the domestic court proceedings offered sufficient guarantees to counterbalance the limitation of his procedural rights before the administrative authorities. The applicant, through his lawyer, had access to parts of the classified file, and the courts reviewed the classified material. He was not deprived of an opportunity to effectively challenge the executive’s assertions that national security and public order were at stake. The authorities had given sufficient consideration to his family ties and had balanced the relevant interests. The Court therefore held that the Czech authorities had not overstepped their margin of appreciation and found no violation of Article 8.
001-233378:
**Case: Dias dos Santos Ferreira da Costa Cabral v. Portugal**  
**Application no. 25282/18 – European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section**  
**Judgment delivered: 30 April 2024**

The applicant, Maria Cristina Dias dos Santos Ferreira da Costa Cabral, is a Portuguese journalist born in 1957 who lives in Lisbon and works for the national daily newspaper *O Público*. She lodged an application against Portugal on 23 May 2018, alleging that her criminal conviction for publishing information subject to investigative secrecy violated her right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The facts concern an article written by the applicant and published in *O Público* on 4 February 2012, entitled “Two more former spies targeted by the Public Prosecutor’s Office.” The article reported on a criminal investigation into high-level corruption, illegal access, and abuse of power. According to the article, the investigation involved former senior officials of the intelligence services and high-ranking political figures who were allegedly involved in illegal operations aimed at taking control of a major Portuguese media group. The article also reported the search and seizure of the computers of two suspects in that investigation. It identified two former intelligence officials who had been hired as information technology experts by a media company whose operations were being investigated. The news item had already received media coverage before the applicant’s article was published.

At the relevant time, the judicial investigation was under investigative secrecy. This secrecy had been ordered by the investigating judge and applied during the period from 4 August 2011 to 7 May 2012. The domestic authorities considered that the applicant’s article disclosed information covered by that secrecy.

By judgment of the Lisbon District Court on 9 March 2017, the applicant was convicted of disclosing information covered by investigative secrecy in the news article at issue. She was sentenced to a 100-day fine, corresponding to a total amount of EUR 1,000. The Lisbon Court of Appeal upheld that conviction on 14 December 2017. After exhausting domestic remedies, the applicant brought her complaint to the European Court of Human Rights.

Before the Court, the applicant relied on Article 10 of the Convention, arguing that her criminal conviction and fine amounted to an unjustified interference with her right to freedom of expression. The central issue was whether the Portuguese courts had struck a fair balance between the protection of the secrecy of an ongoing criminal investigation and the public interest in press reporting on matters of serious public concern, including corruption, abuse of power, the intelligence services, and alleged attempts to control a major media group.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation include the applicant’s status as a journalist, the public-interest nature of the article, the fact that the information had already been the subject of media coverage, the identification of former intelligence officials hired by an investigated media company, the existence of a judicially ordered investigative secrecy during the relevant period, the domestic conviction for disclosure of secret information, and the resulting fine. The case therefore required the European Court to assess whether the criminal sanction imposed on the journalist was necessary and proportionate in a democratic society, or whether it disproportionately restricted her Article 10 rights.

This case, *Dias dos Santos Ferreira da Costa Cabral v. Portugal* (Application no. 25282/18), concerned an alleged violation of Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects freedom of expression. The applicant, Maria Cristina Dias dos Santos Ferreira da Costa Cabral, is a Portuguese national born in 1957, living in Lisbon. She works as a journalist for the national daily newspaper *O Público* and was represented by F. Teixeira da Mota. The application was lodged against Portugal on 23 May 2018. The Portuguese Government was represented by R. Bragança de Matos.

The facts relevant to the alleged violation began on 4 February 2012, when *O Público* published a news article written by the applicant. The article was entitled “Two more former spies targeted by the Public Prosecutor’s Office.” It reported that the computers of two suspects had been searched and seized in a criminal investigation into high-level corruption, illegal access and abuse of power. The investigation allegedly involved former senior officials of the intelligence services and high-ranking political figures who were suspected of illegal operations aimed at taking control of a major Portuguese media group. The news item, which had already received media coverage, identified two former intelligence officials who had been hired as information technology experts by a media company whose operations were being investigated.

At the time of publication, the judicial investigation was covered by investigative secrecy. An investigating judge had ordered secrecy for the period between 4 August 2011 and 7 May 2012. The applicant’s article was published during that period. Because it disclosed information covered by the secrecy order, the applicant was prosecuted. By judgment of the Lisbon District Court of 9 March 2017, she was convicted of disclosing information covered by investigative secrecy. The sentence was a 100-day fine, corresponding to EUR 1,000. The Lisbon Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 14 December 2017.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 10 of the Convention. She alleged that her criminal conviction for publishing the article violated her right to freedom of expression. The key facts relevant to that complaint were that the publication was by a journalist, concerned a matter of significant public interest—high-level corruption, abuse of power, the intelligence services and alleged attempts to control a major media group—and dealt with information that had already received some media coverage. The conviction was based specifically on the disclosure of information covered by judicial investigative secrecy, including the identification of two former intelligence officials. The domestic proceedings ended with a final fine of EUR 1,000.

The European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, sitting as a Committee, gave notice of the application to the Portuguese Government and considered the parties’ observations. In its judgment of 30 April 2024, the Court examined whether the applicant’s conviction and fine amounted to an unjustified interference with her Article 10 rights. The central question was whether the interference was prescribed by law, pursued a legitimate aim, and was necessary in a democratic society, balancing the protection of the secrecy of criminal investigations against the public-interest value of the journalistic publication.

In *Dias dos Santos Ferreira da Costa Cabral v. Portugal* (Application no. 25282/18), the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) examined an application lodged on 23 May 2018 by Maria Cristina Dias dos Santos Ferreira da Costa Cabral. The applicant is a Portuguese national, born in 1957, living in Lisbon, and working as a journalist for the national daily newspaper *O Público*. She was represented before the Court by Mr F. Teixeira da Mota, a Lisbon lawyer. The Portuguese Government was represented by Mr R. Bragança de Matos, Public Prosecutor.

The case concerned the applicant’s criminal conviction for publishing information covered by investigative secrecy. On 4 February 2012, *O Público* published an article written by the applicant entitled “Two more former spies targeted by the Public Prosecutor’s Office.” The article reported on the search and seizure of the computers of two suspects in a criminal investigation into high-level corruption, illegal access, and abuse of power. The investigation allegedly involved former senior officials of the intelligence services and high-ranking political figures who were suspected of taking part in illegal operations to take control of a major Portuguese media group. The news item, which had already received media coverage, identified two former intelligence officials who had been hired as information-technology experts by a media company whose operations were being investigated.

At the relevant time, the judicial investigation was subject to investigative secrecy under a decision of the investigating judge. That secrecy applied between 4 August 2011 and 7 May 2012. The applicant’s article was therefore found to have disclosed information covered by that secrecy.

By judgment of the Lisbon District Court on 9 March 2017, the applicant was convicted and sentenced to a 100-day fine, corresponding to EUR 1,000, for disclosing information covered by investigative secrecy in the article at issue. The Lisbon Court of Appeal upheld that judgment on 14 December 2017.

Relying on Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights, the applicant alleged that her criminal conviction violated her right to freedom of expression. The central issue was whether the interference with her journalistic expression—through a criminal conviction and fine for publishing information subject to judicial secrecy—was justified under the Convention. In particular, the Court would have to assess whether the conviction was prescribed by law and necessary in a democratic society, including whether it pursued a legitimate aim such as protecting the secrecy of criminal investigations or the rights of suspects, and whether it struck a fair balance between freedom of expression and the proper administration of justice.

The case was assigned to a Committee of the Fourth Section composed of President Tim Eicke, Judges Armen Harutyunyan and Ana Maria Guerra Martins, with Crina Kaufman as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The Court deliberated in private on 9 April 2024 and adopted its judgment on 30 April 2024. The judgment was final but subject to editorial revision. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore the applicant’s status as a journalist, the public-interest nature of the article, the pre-existing media coverage, the investigative secrecy then in force, and the criminal fine imposed for publication.

Case: Oghlishvili v. Georgia (Application no. 7621/19), European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, judgment 4 July 2024. The applicant, Nana Oghlishvili, complained under Articles 2, 3 and 13 that Georgia failed to protect her daughter, E.N., from domestic violence and failed to investigate her death effectively.

E.N. had lived since 2013 with her husband R.G., their daughter, and mother-in-law T.G. in Shilda. After about two years, relations deteriorated. T.G. accused E.N. of infidelity because she worked late and sometimes stayed out. On 12 October 2017 the applicant called police, reporting physical assault by T.G. and R.G. Police interviewed the family. E.N. said T.G. had punched her face during an argument and asked for restraining measures against T.G.; she said R.G. had never abused her. T.G. and R.G. claimed E.N. had hit T.G. A medical examination found only a minor bruise on E.N.’s left shoulder and no visible injury on T.G.

On 18 October 2017 E.N. was found hanged in the family wine cellar by G.G., R.G.’s brother. Police opened a criminal case for incitement to suicide under Article 115. The autopsy found death by asphyxia from strangulation. It documented numerous bruises and skin lesions on E.N.’s face, throat, jaw, forearm, wrist, abdomen, hips, thighs, buttock, vulva, legs and foot. Some were six or seven days old; others were inflicted shortly before death. No semen was found, but later tests found semen-stained trousers and socks in the cellar belonging to an unidentified man, a bra cut with a sharp object, and blue denim fibres under E.N.’s fingernails matching G.G.’s trousers.

Husband R.G. said E.N. had been depressed and had previously attempted suicide in the same cellar. G.G. said he found the body but was too shocked to call for help immediately; a neighbour saw him near the house at about 6:30 a.m. T.G. portrayed E.N. as unfaithful and emotionally unstable. Friends and neighbours described frequent altercations between E.N. and T.G., and some said G.G. visited E.N. late. On 21 October 2017 G.G. attempted suicide at E.N.’s funeral. R.G. then publicly accused G.G. of raping and murdering E.N., suggesting a motive linked to an affair.

Despite these leads, the investigation later stalled. After 6 February 2019 no significant investigative measures were taken; by April 2022 the case was still formally ongoing. The six-year limitation period for the less serious offence under Article 115 expired, making prosecution impossible. The ECtHR found a violation of Article 2 (procedural). It held that the authorities failed to explore adequately all credible lines of inquiry, particularly whether E.N.’s death involved sexual assault or homicide rather than simple suicide. The long unjustified inactivity was attributable to the investigating authority. The limitation period’s expiry stripped the continuing investigation of any utility and potential effectiveness. The failure to display particular diligence and vigour in a case involving violence against women could be read as unwillingness to establish the truth. The applicant also alleged a substantive Article 2 failure to protect E.N. before death; the Government objected that domestic remedies had not been exhausted, while the applicant argued such remedies were ineffective. The decisive finding was the procedural Article 2 violation.

Case *Oghlishvili v. Georgia* (no. 7621/19, judgment 4 July 2024) concerned the death of the applicant’s daughter, E.N., and the State’s response to alleged domestic violence and her alleged suicide. The applicant complained under Articles 2, 3 and 13 that Georgia failed to protect her daughter and to investigate her death effectively. The Court’s central finding was a violation of the procedural obligation under Article 2.

Key facts: E.N. married R.G. and from 2013 lived with him, their child, and his mother, T.G., in Shilda. After about two years, relations deteriorated because T.G. accused E.N. of infidelity, partly due to her working late. On 12 October 2017 the applicant made an emergency call reporting that T.G. and R.G. had physically assaulted her. Police came immediately and interviewed the family. E.N. said T.G. had punched her in the face during an argument about E.N. staying overnight with a friend; she asked police to take restraining measures against T.G. She also said R.G. had never physically or verbally abused her and that she had named him during the emergency call only because she was emotionally distressed. T.G. and R.G. denied E.N.’s account, claiming E.N. attacked T.G. and R.G. never assaulted her. A medical examination found a minor bruise on E.N.’s left shoulder but no visible injury on T.G.

On 18 October 2017 E.N. was found hanged in the family wine cellar by R.G.’s brother, G.G. Police opened a criminal investigation into incitement to suicide under Article 115 of the Criminal Code. The autopsy found numerous bruises and skin lesions on E.N.’s face, throat, knees, thighs, hips, genital area and legs; some had been inflicted days earlier and others shortly before death. Death was caused by asphyxia from strangulation. Family members said E.N. had been depressed and had attempted suicide in the same cellar in August 2017. R.G. suggested knee injuries came from a pig. Neighbours reported frequent verbal altercations between E.N. and T.G., knowledge of the earlier suicide attempt, and that G.G. had visited E.N. late when R.G. was away; one neighbour saw G.G. near the house around 6:30 a.m. on the day the body was found. At E.N.’s funeral, G.G. attempted suicide. R.G. then publicly accused G.G. of raping and murdering E.N. Forensic evidence showed no semen on E.N.’s body, but semen-stained trousers from an unknown male were found in the cellar; E.N.’s bra had been cut; blue fibres under her fingernails matched G.G.’s trousers.

Investigators questioned more than 25 witnesses, commissioned forensic examinations, and examined phone data. However, after 6 February 2019 no significant investigative measures were taken; by April 2022 the investigation remained ongoing. Under Georgian law, Article 115 was a less serious offence with a six-year limitation period, after which criminal liability expired if no charges were brought.

The Court found the investigation ineffective. Authorities failed to explore all credible lines of inquiry, especially evidence suggesting domestic violence and possible third-party involvement. There was a significant period of unjustified inactivity attributable to the investigative authority. The expiry of the limitation period stripped the continuing investigation of any possible utility and effectiveness. The failure to show particular diligence and vigour in a violence-against-women case could be read as unwillingness to establish the truth. Thus, Georgia violated the procedural limb of Article 2.

In *Oghlishvili v. Georgia* (ECtHR, 4 July 2024), the applicant, Nana Oghlishvili, complained that Georgian authorities failed to protect her daughter, E.N., from domestic violence and to conduct an effective investigation into her death. E.N. lived in Shilda with her husband, R.G., her mother-in-law, T.G., and her child. Her marriage became strained after T.G. accused her of infidelity because she worked late hours.

On 12 October 2017, the applicant made an emergency call reporting that she had been physically assaulted by T.G. and R.G. Police interviewed the family. E.N. stated that T.G. had punched her in the face during an argument and asked police to take restraining measures against T.G., but said her husband had never physically or verbally abused her. T.G. and R.G. claimed that E.N. had attacked T.G. A medical examination found a minor bruise on E.N.’s shoulder but no visible injury on T.G.

On 18 October 2017, E.N. was found hanged in the family wine cellar by R.G.’s brother, G.G. A criminal investigation was opened under Article 115 of the Criminal Code for incitement to suicide. Forensic reports revealed numerous bruises and skin lesions on E.N.’s face, throat, jaw, arms, abdomen, hips, thighs, buttock, vulva, legs, and foot. Most had been inflicted shortly before death, while some were six or seven days old. The cause of death was asphyxia by strangulation. Semen-stained trousers and socks found in the cellar did not match three tested men, including G.G.; E.N.’s black bra had been cut; and blue fibres under her fingernails matched G.G.’s denim trousers. G.G. attempted suicide at E.N.’s funeral. R.G. then publicly accused G.G. of raping and murdering E.N., and admitted an affair with G.G.’s former fiancée, suggesting a possible motive. Witnesses reported that G.G. visited E.N. late in the evening and one saw him near her house at 6:30 a.m. on the day her body was found. Others described E.N. as emotionally unstable and said she had previously attempted suicide.

Police initially conducted many investigative steps, including forensic examinations, questioning more than 25 witnesses, and retrieving telephone data. However, after 6 February 2019, no significant investigative measures were taken. By April 2022, the investigation remained ongoing, but the six-year limitation period for the less serious Article 115 offence expired, making prosecution impossible.

The applicant alleged violations of Articles 2, 3, and 13, mainly that police failed to protect E.N. from domestic violence and failed to investigate her death effectively. The Government argued non-exhaustion and that the investigation had been prompt, independent, and thorough. The European Court of Human Rights found a procedural violation of Article 2. It held that the authorities failed to explore all credible lines of inquiry, especially given the domestic-violence context and suspicious injuries. The significant unjustified period of inactivity was attributable to the investigative authority. The resulting expiry of the limitation period stripped the continuing investigation of any possible utility and effectiveness. The Court stressed that authorities must display particular diligence and vigour in investigating violence against women; their failure to do so could be read as unwillingness to establish the truth.
001-237811:
In Bakradze v. Georgia (no. 20592/21, ECtHR Fifth Section, 7 November 2024), applicant Maia Bakradze, a former Georgian judge, alleged discrimination in two judicial competitions before the High Council of Justice (HCJ). She claimed the rejections were due to her role as founder and President of the NGO “The Unity of Judges of Georgia” (“Unity”) and her critical views on the judiciary. She invoked Articles 10 and 11 read with Article 14, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12.

Bakradze served as a judge until September 2015, when her ten-year term expired; she had no disciplinary record. Unity, founded in 2013, monitored the HCJ and criticised its policies on judicial appointments, secondment, reserve lists, bonuses, and lack of reasoned decisions. In October 2015 and May 2016, she applied for Tbilisi Court of Appeal vacancies.

In the December 2015 interview, after brief education and experience questions, HCJ members spent about fifteen minutes on Unity: its aims, members, relations with the Association of Judges, and critical Facebook posts by Unity’s executive director. One member said he was personally offended by a post implying that managerial judges were “slackers” and suggested Bakradze, as Unity’s representative, was responsible. She was rejected on 28 December 2015 without reasons. In the June 2016 interview, she was asked about public criticism of judges, NGO campaigns against the judiciary, whether such criticism was healthy, and her salary as Unity president. She was rejected again on 14 July 2016 without reasons.

She brought a civil discrimination claim, arguing that the interviews were not aimed at assessing competence but at eliciting her critical views. She requested recordings and files of other candidates to compare interviews, but domestic courts refused. The Public Defender of Georgia, as amicus curiae, noted that discrimination claims require only facts creating an objective assumption of discrimination, after which the burden shifts to the respondent; he warned that unreasoned decisions and secret voting risked bias. The HCJ denied discrimination, citing statistics that many Unity members participated and some were appointed. Bakradze countered that Unity members, especially its executive council, had a much higher rejection rate.

Domestic courts dismissed her claim. They found no prima facie case, noted she had answered questions without objection, said questions could vary between candidates, and upheld the HCJ’s wide discretion. The Court of Appeal and Supreme Court added that secret voting protected HCJ independence and that different questions were not discrimination; they viewed the questions as testing legal analysis on judicial independence and freedom of expression.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 14 read with Articles 10 and 11. The applicant had demonstrated a prima facie case. The specific interview circumstances could lead an independent observer to infer that her NGO-related activities played a significant role in the non-reappointments. The questions went beyond testing integrity and showed bias or prejudice among individual HCJ members. Domestic courts failed to address the discrimination complaint with proper attention, ensure effective protection from potential bias, and shift the burden of proof onto the HCJ to dispel the perception of bias and show objective justification for any difference in treatment.

In **Bakradze v. Georgia** (Application no. 20592/21, judgment 7 November 2024), the applicant, Maia Bakradze, was a former Georgian judge and founder/President of the NGO “The Unity of Judges of Georgia.” She alleged that she was discriminated against in two judicial competitions in 2015 and 2016 because of her role in that NGO and her critical views of the High Council of Justice (HCJ) and the state of Georgia’s judiciary. She relied on Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention in conjunction with Article 14, and on Article 1 of Protocol No. 12.

Bakradze had served as a judge until September 2015, when her ten-year term expired. She had no disciplinary proceedings against her. In October 2015 and May 2016, she applied for vacant positions at the Tbilisi Court of Appeal. The HCJ accepted her applications but rejected her after interviews.

In the December 2015 interview, after initial questions about her education, experience and motivation, HCJ members questioned her extensively about Unity of Judges: its aims, organisation, membership, cooperation and disagreements with the Association of Judges, and critical Facebook posts by the NGO’s executive director. They asked whether those posts were made on behalf of the NGO, whether the applicant had agreed to them, and whether she agreed with their allegedly insulting content. One HCJ judge said he was personally offended by an NGO statement criticising bonuses for managerial judges, suggesting the applicant was responsible. Bakradze observed that the questions seemed unrelated to evaluating her judicial qualifications. She was rejected on 28 December 2015, without reasons.

In the June 2016 interview, questions again focused on public criticism of judges, NGO media campaigns allegedly aimed at discrediting the judiciary, whether such criticism was “healthy,” and her salary as President of Unity of Judges. She was rejected again on 14 July 2016, without reasons.

Bakradze brought a civil discrimination claim, seeking recordings and files of other candidates’ interviews to compare how interviews were conducted. Domestic courts refused access to that evidence. The HCJ denied discrimination, noting that some Unity of Judges members had been appointed. The applicant presented statistics suggesting that 41% of Unity members were refused reappointment, compared with 18% of non-members, and that most executive council members were rejected. The Public Defender of Georgia argued that the prima facie threshold was low and that secret voting, unreasoned decisions and lack of judicial review created risks of bias. A document by HCJ member V.M. alleged that appointments were used to undermine judges with opposing views and that “cancelled ballots” had been used against Unity members.

Domestic courts dismissed the claim. The Tbilisi City Court found no concrete evidence or causal link, noting the applicant answered the questions and did not challenge them. The Court of Appeal upheld that decision, finding questions varied between candidates, other interviews were irrelevant, no bias was shown, and the HCJ had wide discretion with secret voting. The Supreme Court rejected her appeal, relying on appointments of some Unity members and finding no specific discriminatory questions.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 14 read with Articles 10 and 11. It held that the applicant had demonstrated a prima facie case of discrimination: the specific interview circumstances could reasonably lead an independent observer to infer that her NGO activities played a significant role in the refusals. The questions went beyond testing integrity and showed bias or prejudice among HCJ members. The domestic courts failed to address the discrimination complaint with proper attention, did not shift the burden of proof to the HCJ, and did not require it to dispel the perception of bias or justify the difference in treatment.

In *Bakradze v. Georgia* (no. 20592/21, ECtHR, 7 Nov. 2024), Maia Bakradze, a former Georgian judge, alleged discrimination in two judicial competitions because of her role as founder/President of the NGO “The Unity of Judges of Georgia” and her critical views on the judiciary and High Council of Justice (HCJ). She relied on Articles 10 and 11 read with Article 14, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12.

Bakradze served as a judge from 2005, including at the Tbilisi Court of Appeal. In September 2015, her ten-year term expired and she was dismissed. She had no disciplinary record. She co-founded Unity of Judges in 2013; it monitored the HCJ and criticised judicial appointments, secondments, bonuses, and the lack of reasoned decisions. In October 2015 and May 2016, she applied for vacancies at the Tbilisi Court of Appeal. During HCJ interviews, after brief education/experience questions, much of the questioning focused on Unity of Judges: its aims, members, relations with the Association of Judges, and critical Facebook posts by its executive director. A HCJ judge said he was personally offended by NGO criticism of bonuses for managerial judges and suggested she was responsible. In the second interview, questions again focused on public criticism of judges and NGO media campaigns, and on her NGO salary. She was rejected both times without reasons.

She sued in the Tbilisi City Court, alleging discrimination. She sought recordings and files of other candidates to compare interviews, but courts refused. The Public Defender’s amicus brief noted the lower prima facie threshold in discrimination cases and warned that secret voting, unreasoned HCJ decisions, and limited judicial review created risks of bias. A HCJ member’s document alleged abuses in appointments to undermine judges with opposing views and “cancelled ballots” against Unity members. Bakradze’s statistics showed 41% of Unity members were refused reappointment versus 18% of non-members; five of seven executive council members were refused. The HCJ relied on statistics that 14 of 18 founding members participated and six succeeded, and 17 Unity members were appointed in 2013–2016.

Domestic courts dismissed her claim. They held she had not established a prima facie case, so the burden of proof never shifted to the HCJ. They found the HCJ had wide discretion over interview questions, no evidence of bias, and that she had not objected to the questions. The Supreme Court upheld that reasoning.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 14 read with Articles 10 and 11 (and Protocol No. 12). It held that Bakradze had demonstrated a prima facie case of discrimination. The interview circumstances allowed an independent observer reasonably to infer that her NGO-related activities played a significant role in the decisions not to reappoint her. The questions went beyond testing integrity/competency and showed bias or prejudice among individual HCJ members. Domestic courts failed to address the discrimination complaint properly, refused comparative evidence, and failed to shift the burden of proof to the HCJ to dispel the perception of bias or justify the difference in treatment.
