In **Dimović and Others v. Serbia** (Application no. 40238/16), four Serbian nationals lodged an application against Serbia with the European Court of Human Rights on 21 June 2016. They were represented by a lawyer. The case concerned criminal proceedings for attempted aggravated theft. The applicants were convicted and sentenced to imprisonment. They complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about the fairness of the appellate proceedings, specifically their inability to comment on written observations submitted by the Higher Public Prosecutor in reply to their defence statements of appeal before the Court of Appeal.

After the applicants’ first-instance conviction for attempted aggravated theft, both the applicants and the Subotica Basic Public Prosecutor’s Office filed appeals against the judgment. Those appeals were transmitted to the Novi Sad Court of Appeal. In addition, the Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office submitted written observations in the appellate proceedings. In those observations, the Higher Prosecutor asked the Court of Appeal to dismiss the appeals lodged by the applicants, to grant the appeal filed by the Subotica Basic Public Prosecutor’s Office, and to impose higher prison sentences on the applicants. The prosecutor’s observations were therefore not merely formal; they directly opposed the applicants’ appellate arguments and sought a more severe outcome.

The key procedural fact underlying the alleged violation is that the Court of Appeal did not provide the applicants with a copy of the written observations submitted by the Higher Public Prosecutor. As a result, the applicants had no opportunity to examine the prosecutor’s arguments or to respond to them before the appellate court reached its decision. The applicants only learned about the existence and content of the Higher Public Prosecutor’s reply to their appeal after they received the Court of Appeal’s final judgment. By that time, the appellate proceedings had concluded.

In its final judgment, the Court of Appeal upheld the applicants’ conviction but reduced the prison sentences in respect of all applicants. Nevertheless, the applicants considered that the failure to communicate the prosecutor’s observations violated their right to a fair trial, in particular the adversarial principle and equality of arms between the defence and the prosecution.

The applicants challenged this procedural defect before the Serbian Constitutional Court. On 26 November 2015, the Constitutional Court dismissed their constitutional complaint as manifestly ill-founded. It reasoned that the Code of Criminal Procedure did not require second-instance courts to provide an accused person with a copy of the prosecutor’s observations submitted in reply to that person’s appeal. The Constitutional Court therefore found no constitutional or Convention violation in the non-communication.

The applicants thereafter applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 21 June 2016. The Court gave notice of the application to the Serbian Government, represented by its Agent, and received the parties’ observations. The case was assigned to the Fourth Section, sitting as a Committee composed of President Tim Eicke and Judges Ana Maria Guerra Martins and Mateja Đurović, with Deputy Section Registrar Simeon Petrovski. The Committee deliberated in private on 22 October 2024 and delivered its judgment on 19 November 2024.

The central alleged violation before the European Court was therefore that the applicants were denied an opportunity to comment on the Higher Public Prosecutor’s written observations submitted in reply to their appeal, even though those observations sought dismissal of their appeal and heavier sentences. The case raises the question whether the domestic criminal procedure, as applied and as interpreted by the Constitutional Court, complied with Article 6 § 1’s requirements of a fair trial, adversarial proceedings, and equality of arms.

The case of *Dimović and Others v. Serbia* (Application no. 40238/16) concerns criminal proceedings in Serbia and an alleged breach of the right to a fair trial under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants were four Serbian nationals who were convicted of attempted aggravated theft and sentenced to imprisonment. After their conviction, both the applicants and the Subotica Basic Public Prosecutor’s Office lodged appeals against the first-instance judgment. The appeals were transmitted to the Novi Sad Court of Appeal.

In the appellate proceedings, the Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office submitted written observations responding to the applicants’ appeals. In those observations, the Higher Public Prosecutor asked the Court of Appeal to dismiss the applicants’ appeals, grant the appeal filed by the Subotica Basic Public Prosecutor’s Office, and impose higher prison sentences on the applicants. However, the Court of Appeal did not provide the applicants or their defence counsel with a copy of those written observations. As a result, the applicants had no opportunity to review or comment on the prosecution’s submissions before the appellate court decided the case.

The Court of Appeal ultimately upheld the applicants’ conviction but reduced the prison sentences for all applicants. The applicants only learned about the Higher Public Prosecutor’s written reply to their appeal after they received the Court of Appeal’s final judgment. This meant that the prosecution had been able to present additional arguments to the appellate court without the defence having any chance to respond.

The applicants challenged this procedure before the Serbian Constitutional Court. On 26 November 2015, the Constitutional Court dismissed their complaint as manifestly ill-founded. It noted that the Serbian Code of Criminal Procedure did not require second-instance courts to provide an accused person with a copy of the prosecutor’s observations submitted in reply to the accused’s appeal. The applicants therefore brought their complaint to the European Court of Human Rights, arguing that the non-communication of the Higher Public Prosecutor’s written observations violated their right to a fair hearing under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

The essence of the alleged violation is that the applicants were unable to comment on the written observations submitted by the Higher Public Prosecutor to the Court of Appeal. The applicants complained that this deprived them of the opportunity to respond to arguments made by the opposing party at a crucial stage of the appellate proceedings. Their complaint raises issues of adversarial proceedings and equality of arms: while the prosecution could make written submissions to the appellate court, the defence could not see or reply to them. The applicants argued that this procedural imbalance affected the fairness of the criminal proceedings against them, particularly because the prosecutor had sought higher sentences. The European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, communicated the application to the Serbian Government and considered the parties’ observations. The judgment was delivered on 19 November 2024. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore the appellate prosecutor’s secret written observations, the Court of Appeal’s failure to disclose them to the applicants, the applicants’ resulting inability to comment, and the Constitutional Court’s rejection of their complaint based on domestic criminal procedure rules.

Dimović and Others v. Serbia (Application no. 40238/16) is a European Court of Human Rights case brought by four Serbian nationals. They were convicted in domestic criminal proceedings of attempted aggravated theft and sentenced to imprisonment. The central complaint concerned Article 6 §1 of the Convention, specifically the fairness of the appellate proceedings. The applicants alleged that they were unable to comment on written observations submitted by the Higher Public Prosecutor in reply to their defence appeals before the Court of Appeal, which they argued violated the adversarial principle and equality of arms.

After the first-instance court convicted them, both the applicants and the Subotica Basic Public Prosecutor’s Office appealed against the judgment. The appeals were transmitted to the Novi Sad Court of Appeal. The Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office then filed written observations. In those observations, it asked the Court of Appeal to dismiss the applicants’ appeals, to grant the appeal of the Subotica Basic Public Prosecutor’s Office, and to impose higher prison sentences on the applicants.

However, the Court of Appeal did not provide the applicants with a copy of the Higher Public Prosecutor’s written observations. As a result, the applicants had no opportunity to review or respond to the prosecution’s arguments before the appellate court decided the case. The Court of Appeal subsequently issued a final judgment upholding the applicants’ conviction but reducing their prison sentences. The applicants only learned about the Higher Public Prosecutor’s reply after receiving the Court of Appeal’s judgment. This meant that any response they might have made could not have been considered in the appellate proceedings.

The applicants challenged this before the Serbian Constitutional Court. On 26 November 2015, the Constitutional Court dismissed their complaint as manifestly ill-founded. It reasoned that the Code of Criminal Procedure did not require second-instance courts to provide an accused person with a copy of the prosecutor’s observations submitted in reply to their appeal. The domestic constitutional decision thus confirmed the procedure followed by the Court of Appeal and rejected the applicants’ fair-trial objection.

The applicants then lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 21 June 2016. They complained under Article 6 §1 that the non-communication of the Higher Public Prosecutor’s observations deprived them of the opportunity to comment on submissions made by the opposing party in criminal appellate proceedings. The case was assigned to the Fourth Section of the Court. The Serbian Government, represented by its Agent, was given notice of the application and submitted observations. The applicants were represented by a lawyer practising in Subotica. The Court deliberated in private on 22 October 2024 and delivered its judgment on 19 November 2024.

The key issue was whether the failure to disclose the prosecutor’s written observations to the defence, combined with the impossibility of replying to them before the Court of Appeal ruled, was compatible with the right to a fair hearing under Article 6 §1. The facts therefore raise questions about the adversarial nature of criminal appeal proceedings, equality of arms between the defence and prosecution, and the opportunity for an accused person to comment on all material submitted to the court. The summary focuses on those facts that are directly relevant to the alleged Article 6 violation.
001-234516:
**Case: B.A. v. Cyprus (Application no. 24607/20), judgment 2 July 2024**

The applicant, B.A., a Syrian national born in 1996, entered Cyprus on 28 January 2019 with two relatives from Türkiye via the occupied areas. On 8 February 2019 they presented themselves at the Ledras Palace crossing point in Nicosia, stating they wished to apply for international protection. They were transferred to the Aliens and Immigration Service, where their photographs and fingerprints were taken. They were then placed at the Pournara Emergency Reception Centre.

On 11 February 2019 B.A. formally lodged an asylum application and received a confirmation document stating he was entitled to remain in government-controlled areas while his claim was examined. That same day, police interviewed him and his relatives. The authorities concluded he matched the profile of a “foreign fighter.” Indicators included his age, migration from a war zone, previous move to Al-Harra in Daraa Province, an area allegedly controlled by ISIS, and photographs found on his phone showing him and relatives holding Kalashnikov rifles and wearing military uniforms. A search warrant was obtained, and further information about relatives was gathered.

Also on 11 February 2019, the Director of the Civil Registry and Migration Department issued a detention order against B.A. under section 9ΣΤ(2)(e) of the Refugee Law on national security grounds. He was arrested and held at Lakatamia Police Station, then transferred on 22 February 2019 to the Menoyia Detention Centre for Prohibited Immigrants. He remained detained until 30 November 2021—a total of two years, nine months and twelve days—when he was released subject to regular police reporting and address notification.

B.A. challenged his detention. On 25 April 2019 the Administrative Court dismissed his recourse, finding the detention lawful and justified by national security. On 20 July 2021 the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal, holding that it could not question the executive’s national security assessment and relying on the CJEU’s judgment in N. (C-601/15 PPU). His asylum application was rejected on 28 May 2019 because he was suspected of war crimes; his recourse against that decision remained pending with suspensive effect. He also filed two habeas corpus petitions in 2019 and 2020, both dismissed, and an appeal dismissed in June 2021. Internal detention reviews maintained the order.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, B.A. complained under Article 5 § 1 that his detention was unlawful and arbitrary, and under Article 5 § 4 that he lacked a speedy review of its lawfulness. The Government argued that he had entered unlawfully, that detention was based on valid national security grounds under the Refugee Law, and that the length was justified by the security threat and asylum-case backlog.

The Court found a violation of Article 5 § 1. It held that there was no sufficiently close connection between the national security grounds relied on and the aim of preventing unauthorised entry. The detention was based solely on national security, was not linked to the outcome of his asylum application or right to stay, and amounted to a general preventive or protective mechanism. Its length was unjustified. The Court also found a violation of Article 5 § 4 because the review proceedings lasted over two years and were not “speedy”; delays included about ten months of authorities’ inaction before the Covid-19 pandemic.

Case B.A. v. Cyprus (App. no. 24607/20), ECtHR Third Section, judgment 2 July 2024, concerned the detention of a Syrian asylum-seeker on national security grounds and the speediness of judicial review.

The applicant entered Cyprus from Türkiye via the occupied areas on 28 January 2019. On 8 February 2019 he and two relatives went to the Ledras Palace crossing point and sought international protection. They were transferred to the Aliens and Immigration Service, registered as irregular entrants, and taken to the Pournara Emergency Reception Centre. On 11 February 2019 the applicant formally lodged an asylum application and received confirmation of his right to remain in Cyprus pending examination of his claim.

That same day, authorities interviewed him. They noted old shrapnel and bullet wounds, his age, his migration from a war zone, his prior move to Al-Harra in Daraa Province—an area mainly controlled by ISIS—and photos on his encrypted phone showing him and relatives holding Kalashnikov rifles and wearing military uniforms. They concluded he matched the profile of a “foreign fighter.” The Director of the Civil Registry and Migration Department then issued a detention order on national security grounds under section 9ΣΤ(2)(e) of the Refugee Law. The applicant was notified on 12 February 2019 and held at Lakatamia Police Station, then Menoyia Detention Centre until 30 November 2021—a total of two years, nine months and twelve days.

He challenged the detention. In April 2019 the Administrative Court dismissed his recourse, finding the detention lawful, based on national security, and that alternatives to detention would not suffice. In July 2021 the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal, holding that it could not question the executive’s national-security assessment and that detention was justified pending the asylum proceedings. His habeas corpus petitions in 2019 and 2020 also failed, and his appeal against refusal of habeas corpus was dismissed in June 2021. Meanwhile, in May 2019 the Asylum Service rejected his asylum claim, excluding him for war crimes; his recourse before the Administrative Court of International Protection remained pending with suspensive effect. The migration authorities reviewed his detention repeatedly and continued it until his release on 30 November 2021, subject to reporting conditions.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained under Article 5 § 1 that his detention was unlawful and arbitrary and could not be justified under Article 5 § 1(f). He argued that he had entered at an authorised crossing point, had been authorised to remain as an asylum-seeker, and was in effect detained for national security/criminal-investigation reasons rather than to prevent unauthorised entry. The Government argued that he had entered unlawfully, that the detention was lawful under the Refugee Law on national security grounds, and that its length was justified by the security threat and asylum backlog.

The Court found a violation of Article 5 § 1(f). It held that detention based solely on national security grounds lacked a sufficiently close connection to the aim of preventing unauthorised entry. The grounds were not linked to the outcome of the asylum application or to examination of his right to stay. National security was applied as a general preventive or protective mechanism, and the length of detention was unjustified.

The Court also found a violation of Article 5 § 4. The proceedings reviewing the lawfulness of his detention lasted over two years and did not comply with the “speediness” requirement. There were unjustified delays, including about ten months of authorities’ inaction before the Covid-19 pandemic.

In B.A. v. Cyprus (App. no. 24607/20, Third Section, judgment 2 July 2024, final 2 October 2024), the applicant, a Syrian national born in 1996, alleged that his detention as an asylum-seeker on national security grounds violated Article 5 § 1(f) and that he lacked a speedy judicial review of its lawfulness under Article 5 § 4.

On 28 January 2019 the applicant and two relatives travelled from Türkiye by air to the occupied areas of Cyprus, remaining until 8 February 2019. On 8 February they went to the Ledras crossing point in Nicosia and said they wished to apply for international protection. Police took their photographs and fingerprints and completed forms for migrants who had entered irregularly. The Counter Terrorism Office and Cyprus Intelligence Service were informed. Initial database checks found no relevant information, but the Aliens and Immigration Service suspected possible irregular immigration activity. They were transferred to the Pournara reception centre.

On 11 February 2019 the applicant lodged an asylum application and received confirmation that he could remain in the Government-controlled areas while his claim was examined. That day immigration officers, together with other police and intelligence bodies, interviewed him. Authorities noted old injuries or wounds, which he said came from Syrian munitions. They concluded he matched a “foreign fighter” profile because of his age, migration from a war zone, and prior move to Al-Harra in Daraa, an area mainly controlled by ISIS. A phone inspection revealed a password-encrypted application containing pictures of him and relatives holding Kalashnikov rifles and wearing military uniforms. Police obtained a search warrant to seize phones as part of an investigation into membership of terrorist or criminal organisations. Further checks revealed family links to a Cypriot identity card and older information about hosting or trafficking Muslim preachers.

That same day, the Civil Registry and Migration Department issued detention orders under section 9ΣΤ(2)(e) of the Refugee Law on national security grounds. On 12 February he was informed and detained at Lakatamia Police Station, later transferred to Menoyia Detention Centre, where he remained until release on 30 November 2021—about two years, nine months, and twelve days.

The applicant challenged the detention. The Administrative Court dismissed his recourse on 25 April 2019, relying partly on classified security documents not disclosed to him. It found detention lawful, necessary for national security, and that alternatives were ineffective. The Supreme Court dismissed his appeal on 20 July 2021, holding that it could not question the executive’s national security assessment. His asylum application was rejected in May 2019 on exclusion grounds for alleged war crimes; that recourse remained pending with suspensive effect. Two habeas corpus petitions and several internal reviews maintained his detention.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 5 § 1(f). Detention was based solely on national security grounds, with no sufficiently close connection to preventing unauthorised entry. The grounds were not linked to the asylum application or examination of his right to stay, and national security was used as a general preventive or protective mechanism. The length of detention was unjustified. The Court also found a violation of Article 5 § 4 because review proceedings lasted over two years and were not “speedy,” with unjustified delays, including about ten months of authorities’ inaction before the Covid-19 pandemic.

CASE OF SAAKASHVILI v. GEORGIA (Applications nos. 6232/20 and 22394/20) concerns former Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili, who was convicted in absentia in two separate criminal proceedings after leaving Georgia. He complained under Articles 6, 7 and 18 that the proceedings were unfair, that the tribunal was not independent or impartial, that he could not examine witnesses, that his convictions were retroactive, and that they were politically motivated.

In the first set of proceedings (App. 6232/20), the applicant was charged with complicity in criminal battery and misuse of authority by violence. The charges arose from the brutal attack on MP V.G. on 14 July 2005 by armed men in riot-police uniforms. V.G. had recently published an interview insulting the applicant and his wife. The original investigation was discontinued in 2005 but reopened in 2012 after the change of government. Witnesses included V.G., his bodyguard and driver, riot-police officers, secret-surveillance officers, and former high-ranking officials I.O. and N.B. Their evidence indicated that the applicant had ordered or was aware of the attack as retaliation. Mobile-phone data showed contacts between the applicant, the Interior Minister, the head of the Special Operative Department, and the riot-police chief before and after the incident. The International Prosecution Advisory Panel found sufficient material to prosecute. At trial, witnesses were heard in person in the presence of the applicant’s lawyer. He was convicted in absentia on 28 June 2018 and sentenced to six years’ imprisonment plus a two-year ban on public service. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction on 31 July 2019. The applicant argued that key witnesses I.O. and N.B. were political opponents whose evidence was unreliable and effectively hearsay.

In the second set of proceedings (App. 22394/20), the applicant was charged with abuse of official authority for granting presidential clemency to four former Constitutional Security Department officers convicted in the 2006 Girgvliani murder case. In November 2008, he reduced their sentences by half, and they were released on licence in September 2009. The ECtHR had earlier found an Article 2 procedural violation in Enukidze and Girgvliani and criticised the pardon. After a repeat investigation in 2012, the four officers stated that their supervisor D.A. had promised them presidential pardons in exchange for confessing and remaining silent about D.A. and the Interior Minister’s wife. Other former officials testified that the applicant knew the details and had promised pardons. Clemency Commission members said the applicant bypassed the Commission and granted pardons without applications or discussion. In 2014, he was charged with abuse of power for using the pardon to pervert justice. A single judge convicted him in absentia on 5 January 2018. He alleged that the single-judge court was not independent or impartial, that a judicial assistant performed judicial functions, and that his conviction violated Article 7 because presidential clemency was an absolute, non-justiciable power.

The ECtHR found no violation of Article 6 or Article 7. On Article 6, the single-judge composition was not objectively or functionally deficient, the assistant’s role was clerical/technical, witness statements were first-hand and could be confronted, and the judgments were reasoned and non-arbitrary. On Article 7, the conviction was reasonably foreseeable: the pardon power was not absolute immunity, domestic law and checks and balances allowed prosecution for abuse, and the courts reasonably assessed the applicant’s intent and constitutional limits of clemency.

**Case Summary: Saakashvili v. Georgia (Applications nos. 6232/20 and 22394/20)**

The case concerns two separate sets of criminal proceedings against Mikheil Saakashvili, former President of Georgia (2004-2013), who was convicted in absentia. The European Court of Human Rights examined alleged violations of Articles 6 (fair trial), 7 (no punishment without law), and 18 (limitation on rights restrictions) of the Convention.

**First Proceedings: Battery and Misuse of Authority (Application No. 6232/20)**

On 14 July 2005, V.G., a member of parliament, was brutally attacked by armed men in riot police uniforms. The victim suffered life-threatening injuries and permanent disfigurement. V.G. had recently published an interview containing offensive statements about Saakashvili's wife. During the attack, one assailant stated V.G. "would no longer be able to write anything about our President."

The original investigation was discontinued in September 2005 without verifying witness statements about possible riot police involvement. After the 2012 change of government, a new investigation was launched. Evidence emerged that Saakashvili had personally ordered the attack as retribution. Key witnesses included former Defence Minister I.O., who testified that Saakashvili explicitly ordered him to "exemplarily punish" V.G., and former Parliament President N.B., who recounted Saakashvili's satisfaction with the attack. V.Z., head of riot police, testified that Interior Minister Merabishvili praised him for the operation in Saakashvili's presence, with the President warmly thanking him.

The Tbilisi City Court convicted Saakashvili on 28 June 2018 of complicity in criminal battery and misuse of authority. He received six years' imprisonment. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction on 31 July 2019.

**Second Proceedings: Abuse of Official Authority (Application No. 22394/20)**

This case concerned the 2006 murder of Sandro Girgvliani by Interior Ministry officers following a café altercation involving the Interior Minister's wife. Four CSD officers were convicted in 2006. In November 2008, Saakashvili granted them presidential clemency, reducing their sentences by half; they were released in September 2009 after serving only three years.

Following the European Court's 2011 finding that Georgia violated Article 2 due to inadequate investigation, a repeat investigation was launched. The four officers revealed that their supervisor D.A. had promised them pardons in exchange for accepting sole responsibility and remaining silent about others' involvement. Witnesses including I.O. and N.B. testified that Saakashvili had prior knowledge of the murder details and promised pardons to protect his political team.

The Tbilisi City Court convicted Saakashvili on 5 January 2018 of abuse of power, finding he deliberately bypassed the Presidential Clemency Commission and issued prior pardon promises to pervert justice.

**Key Legal Findings**

The Court found no violation of Article 6, holding that the single-judge composition was independent and impartial, witness statements constituted first-hand testimony, and Saakashvili could confront witnesses. Regarding Article 7, the Court found his conviction reasonably foreseeable, rejecting claims of immunity for presidential acts. The Court gave deference to domestic courts' interpretation of presidential clemency powers within constitutional checks and balances.

He alleged violations of Articles 6, 7 and 18, including unfair trial, lack of an independent and impartial tribunal, inability to examine witnesses, and retroactive or undefined criminal liability.

The original investigation was discontinued in 2005 but reopened in November 2012 after the change of government. Evidence included testimony from V.G., his driver and bodyguard; former Defence Minister I.O., who said Saakashvili ordered V.G. be “exemplarily punished” after an insulting newspaper interview; former Parliament President N.B., who testified that Saakashvili said V.G. deserved the beating; riot-police chief V.Z., who said the Interior Minister praised the operation in Saakashvili’s presence; six riot officers; and mobile-phone data. In November 2014, Saakashvili was charged with complicity in criminal battery and misuse of authority. The Tbilisi City Court convicted him in absentia on 28 June 2018; the Supreme Court upheld the conviction on 31 July 2019, imposing six years’ imprisonment. He argued that the conviction relied on hearsay and politically hostile witnesses, and that he could not confront them. The ECtHR found the key statements were first-hand, not hearsay; he was represented and able to confront and challenge witnesses; domestic courts gave reasoned credibility assessments; and there was no arbitrariness.

In January 2006, Sandro Girgvliani was abducted and beaten to death after a café incident involving Interior Ministry officials and the Interior Minister’s wife. **Case:** *Executief van de Moslims van België and Others v. Belgium* (ECtHR, Second Section, 13 February 2024; final 24 June 2024).

The case concerned bans in Belgium’s Flemish and Walloon Regions on ritual slaughter of animals without prior stunning. The applicants were thirteen Belgian nationals and seven NGOs, including Muslim representative bodies, Turkish and Moroccan Muslim religious authorities, and Belgian Muslims and Jews. They alleged that the regional decrees breached Article 9 (freedom of religion) and Article 14 (non-discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The impugned measures were the Flemish Decree of 7 July 2017 and the Walloon Decree of 4 October 2018. Previously, Belgian federal law required stunning before slaughter but exempted slaughter prescribed by religious rite. The new regional decrees repealed that exemption. They now generally prohibit killing vertebrates without prior stunning, except in cases such as force majeure, hunting/fishing, and pest control. For ritual slaughter, stunning is permitted only if it is reversible and does not cause the animal’s death. The Flemish decree also allowed, transitionally, post-cut stunning for cattle until reversible stunning became practicable for that species. The Brussels-Capital Region retained the older exemption.

The applicants argued that Jewish and Muslim religious precepts require animals to be slaughtered without prior stunning, while conscious, and to die by bleeding. They claimed reversible stunning was religiously unacceptable and that the bans made it difficult or impossible to obtain ritually slaughtered meat in accordance with their beliefs. They also alleged discrimination because hunters and anglers were treated differently, and because the situation of practising Jews and Muslims differed from that of persons not following religious dietary rules.

Some applicants sought annulment before Belgium’s Constitutional Court. That court referred questions to the Court of Justice of the European Union. In *Centraal Israëlitisch Consistorie van België* (2020), the CJEU held that EU law did not preclude a member State from requiring reversible stunning in ritual slaughter, provided fundamental rights were respected. It found the measure pursued animal welfare, allowed a fair balance with religious freedom, and was proportionate, especially because non-stunned meat could still be imported. Following this, the Constitutional Court dismissed the annulment actions on 30 September 2021. It accepted that the decrees restricted religious manifestation but found the restriction justified by animal welfare/public morals, necessary and proportionate, with reversible stunning as a less restrictive alternative and no prohibition on importing non-stunned meat.

Before the ECtHR, the Court found Article 9 applicable. Although the decrees interfered with the manifestation of religion, the interference was prescribed by law and pursued the legitimate aim of protecting public morals through animal welfare. Noting no clear European consensus but a gradual evolution favouring greater animal welfare protection, the Court afforded Belgium a wide margin of appreciation. It found that the legislatures had considered Article 9 requirements and that the measures had undergone two-tier judicial review by the CJEU and the Constitutional Court. The reversible-stunning alternative and continued import possibility made the measure proportionate.

On Article 14, the Court found no discrimination. The applicants’ situation as practising Jews and Muslims was not analogous to that of hunters or anglers. They were not treated differently from individuals not adhering to religious dietary precepts. Nor was the situation of practising Jews relevantly different from that of practising Muslims merely because their dietary precepts differed. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 9 or Article 14.

The case, *Executief van de Moslims van België and Others v. Belgium*, concerned applications by thirteen Belgian nationals and seven NGOs, including Muslim representative bodies, Turkish and Moroccan Muslim religious authorities, and Belgian nationals of Muslim and Jewish faith. They challenged regional decrees in Flanders and Wallonia that prohibited the slaughter of animals without prior stunning, including in ritual slaughter, and alleged violations of Article 9 (freedom of religion) and Article 14 (non-discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Previously, Belgian federal law required animals to be stunned before slaughter but exempted slaughter prescribed by religious rites. After animal welfare became a regional competence in 2014, the Flemish Region adopted a Decree of 7 July 2017 and the Walloon Region a Decree of 4 October 2018. Both repealed the ritual-slaughter exemption. The Flemish provision required prior stunning; for slaughter under religious rites, stunning had to be reversible and could not cause death. A transitional rule allowed post-cut stunning for cattle until reversible stunning became practicable. The Walloon Code similarly required anaesthesia or stunning before killing, with exceptions for force majeure, hunting/fishing, pest control, and certain conservation killings; for religious rites, stunning had to be reversible and non-lethal. There was a transitional post-cut stunning regime for bovine animals until 31 December 2020. The Brussels-Capital Region retained the older federal exemption.

The applicants argued that Jewish and Muslim dietary precepts require animals to be slaughtered without prior stunning and to die by bleeding; even reversible stunning was said to be incompatible with those precepts for at least parts of both religious communities. They claimed the decrees restricted their right to manifest religion and made it harder to obtain meat consistent with their religious requirements. They also alleged discrimination: hunters and anglers were exempt from the stunning requirement, and the decrees allegedly treated Jews and Muslims differently, or religious believers differently from non-religious persons.

Domestically, some applicants sought annulment before the Belgian Constitutional Court. That court referred questions to the Court of Justice of the European Union. In *Centraal Israëlitisch Consistorie van België* (C-336/19), the CJEU held that EU law did not preclude national legislation requiring reversible, non-lethal stunning in ritual slaughter. It found such rules limited the manifestation of religion but respected the essence of religious freedom and were justified by animal welfare, with a broad margin of appreciation. It rejected discrimination arguments based on hunting and fishing because those situations were not comparable. The Belgian Constitutional Court then dismissed the annulment actions in 2021, finding the decrees pursued the legitimate aim of animal welfare/public morals, were necessary and proportionate, and did not discriminate. It noted that importation of ritually slaughtered meat was not prohibited.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the key issues were whether the bans breached Article 9 and whether they discriminated contrary to Article 14. The ECtHR found Article 9 applicable because ritual slaughter and dietary precepts are manifestations of religion. It distinguished *Cha’are Shalom Ve Tsedek v. France*, noting that the Convention does not protect animal welfare as such, but animal welfare could be linked to the legitimate aim of protecting public morals. Although there was no clear consensus among member States, there was a gradual evolution toward greater animal welfare protection, so the margin of appreciation was wide. The Court found the legislatures had considered Article 9, provided for reversible stunning, and their decisions had been reviewed by both the CJEU and the Constitutional Court. The measure was therefore proportionate and within the margin of appreciation. Under Article 14, the applicants’ situation was not analogous to hunters and anglers; they were not treated differently from persons not adhering to religious dietary precepts; and Jewish and Muslim applicants were not relevantly different solely because of differing dietary precepts. No violation was found.

In *Executief van de Moslims van België and Others v. Belgium* (ECtHR, Second Section, 13 February 2024), the applicants—organisations representing Belgian Muslim communities, Turkish and Moroccan Muslim religious authorities, and Belgian nationals of Muslim and Jewish faith—challenged regional bans in Belgium on ritual slaughter without prior stunning.

Following Belgium’s 2014 transfer of animal-welfare powers to the Regions, the Flemish Region adopted a Decree of 7 July 2017 and the Walloon Region a Decree of 4 October 2018. Both repealed the pre-existing federal exception allowing slaughter prescribed by religious rites without stunning. Under the new rules, vertebrates generally could not be killed without prior stunning. Exceptions remained for force majeure, hunting/fishing, pest control (and some nature-conservation killing in Wallonia). For ritual slaughter, the decrees required any stunning to be reversible and not to cause the animal’s death. The Flemish decree also permitted post-cut stunning for cattle until reversible stunning became practicable. The Brussels-Capital Region retained the earlier exemption, so the measures applied only in Flanders and Wallonia.

The applicants, with others, sought annulment before the Belgian Constitutional Court. They alleged the bans breached freedom of religion and equality/non-discrimination because Jewish and Muslim dietary precepts require animals to be slaughtered without prior stunning and to die from bleeding. The Constitutional Court referred questions to the CJEU. In *Centraal Israëlitisch Consistorie van België* (C-336/19, 17 December 2020), the CJEU held that EU Regulation 1099/2009 did not preclude a Member State from requiring reversible stunning in ritual slaughter. Such a rule limited religious manifestation but respected its essence, pursued animal welfare as a general interest, and was proportionate because it did not prohibit ritual slaughter as such and did not bar import of non-stunned meat. The CJEU also found no discrimination in treating hunters and anglers differently, since their situations were not comparable.

On 30 September 2021, the Constitutional Court dismissed the annulment actions. It held that the decrees restricted religious manifestation but pursued the legitimate aim of animal welfare/public morals; the restriction was necessary and proportionate; reversible stunning was a concession; and imports of ritually slaughtered meat remained possible. It rejected discrimination claims, finding Jewish and Muslim believers were not relevantly similar to hunters/anglers, and Jewish and Muslim applicants were not relevantly different from each other merely because their dietary precepts differed.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants complained under Articles 9 and 14. They alleged the prior-stunning obligation violated their freedom to manifest religion and discriminated against them. The Court found Article 9 applicable. It distinguished *Cha’are Shalom Ve Tsedek v. France*, linked animal welfare for the first time to the legitimate aim of protecting public morals, and noted a gradual European evolution favouring animal welfare but no clear consensus. It afforded Belgium a wide margin of appreciation. The legislature had considered religious requirements and adopted a proportionate alternative—reversible stunning—and the measures had undergone two-tier judicial review by the CJEU and the Constitutional Court. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 9. It also found no violation of Article 14: the applicants’ situation was not analogous to hunters/anglers, they were not treated differently from persons not adhering to religious dietary rules, and Jewish and Muslim applicants were not relevantly different solely because of differing dietary precepts.

S.F. v. Finland concerned an Eritrean refugee in Finland who complained under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that Finland’s refusal to grant family reunification to her husband violated her right to respect for family life.

The applicant and her three minor children were granted asylum in Finland on 27 October 2016 and were notified of the decision on 8 November 2016. She was recognised as a refugee because of a risk of political persecution in Eritrea. Her husband, also an Eritrean national, lived in Uganda, where he had refugee status. The applicant sought to sponsor him to join her in Finland.

Under the Finnish Aliens Act, family reunification generally requires the sponsor to have sufficient financial resources—the “maintenance requirement.” However, a refugee sponsor is exempt from that requirement if the family was established before the sponsor arrived in Finland and the family member applies within three months of the sponsor’s notification of the asylum decision. The asylum decision included information, in Finnish, about family reunification procedures and the three-month deadline. Immigration records indicated that the applicant discussed family reunification with a social worker in November 2016 and January 2017, assisted by a Tigrinya interpreter, and was specifically informed about the three-month time-limit and the consequences of exceeding it. She was also given application forms, contact details for the Finnish Embassy in Nairobi, and information about applying online.

The husband applied for a residence permit at the Finnish Embassy in Nairobi on 30 January 2018, about fifteen months after the applicant had been notified of her asylum decision. The Finnish Immigration Service refused the application on 20 February 2019. It accepted that the husband was a family member, but found that the applicant did not meet the maintenance requirement: her income consisted only of social security benefits, and she could not show the required EUR 2,900 per month or EUR 34,800 per year. The three-month exemption did not apply because the application was late. The Immigration Service also found no exceptionally serious grounds for derogating from the maintenance requirement. The husband claimed he had contacted Finland’s honorary consulate in Kampala in spring 2017 and was advised to apply in Nairobi, but he delayed. Passport stamps suggested he had travelled to Kenya and Eritrea before January 2018; he later alleged a middleman may have forged stamps and kept his passport, and raised health problems, but these claims were unsubstantiated and largely late. The children’s best interests were considered, but they lived with their mother, had little prior contact with their father, and no specific circumstances warranted a derogation.

The Administrative Court dismissed the appeal on 6 September 2019, and the Supreme Administrative Court refused leave to appeal on 26 February 2020.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant argued that the refusal ignored her vulnerable circumstances as a refugee and the children’s right to family life with their father. Applying the principles in Dabo v. Sweden, the Court examined whether the failure to apply within the three-month period was objectively excusable and whether Finland had struck a fair balance. It found that the applicant had received timely and adequate advice about the procedure and deadline; there were no objectively excusable reasons for the delay; the refusal was not irreversible, since a fresh application could be made if new or exceptional circumstances arose; and the children’s best interests had been considered. The Court held that Finland had not overstepped its wide margin of appreciation and found no violation of Article 8.

In *S.F. v. Finland* (App. no. 35276/20, ECtHR Second Section, judgment 8 Oct 2024, final 8 Jan 2025), the applicant, an Eritrean refugee in Finland, complained under Article 8 that Finland’s refusal of family reunification for her husband violated her right to respect for family life.

The applicant and her three minor children were granted asylum in Finland on 27 October 2016 and notified on 8 November 2016. The asylum decision included Finnish-language information on family reunification. It explained that a family member could apply for a residence permit without meeting the maintenance requirement if the application was submitted within three months of the sponsor’s notification of the positive asylum decision. In November 2016 and January 2017, the applicant discussed family reunification with a social worker through a Tigrinya interpreter. In January 2017 she was specifically informed of the three-month deadline and its consequences, and received application forms, contact details for the Finnish Embassy in Nairobi, and information about applying online.

Her husband, also Eritrean and a refugee in Uganda, applied for family reunification at the Finnish Embassy in Nairobi on 30 January 2018—nearly fifteen months after the applicant had been notified. On 20 February 2019, the Finnish Immigration Service refused the application. Although the family tie was accepted, the applicant did not meet the maintenance requirement under the Aliens Act. Her income consisted of social security benefits, while the required resources were EUR 2,900 per month and EUR 34,800 per year. It was assumed her husband would need social assistance. The three-month exemption did not apply because the application was late. The Immigration Service found no exceptionally serious grounds for derogation: the husband’s claimed difficulties with Finland’s honorary consulate in Kampala, the need to travel to Nairobi, and passport/middleman issues were not convincing; passport stamps suggested he could have travelled earlier; and alleged health problems were raised only on appeal and unsubstantiated. The children’s best interests did not warrant granting a residence permit: they lived with their mother, the father had little prior contact with them, and no contact during the five years before the refusal.

The Administrative Court dismissed the appeal on 6 September 2019, with a minority would have derogated from the maintenance requirement because the required income was unrealistic. The Supreme Administrative Court refused leave to appeal on 26 February 2020.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant argued that the authorities ignored her family’s vulnerable refugee circumstances, failed to give timely and adequate advice, and breached the children’s right to family life with their father. The Government stressed that the husband was healthy and settled in Uganda, the children lived with the applicant as primary caregiver, and their best interests had been assessed.

The Court declared the application admissible but found no violation of Article 8. Applying *Dabo v. Sweden*, it held that there were no objectively excusable reasons for missing the three-month period; the applicant had received timely and adequate advice; and the refusal was not irreversible, as a fresh application could invoke exceptional or new circumstances. A fair balance had been struck, and Finland had not overstepped its wide margin of appreciation.

In **S.F. v. Finland** (App. no. 35276/20, 8 October 2024), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Finland violated Article 8 by refusing family reunification to an Eritrean refugee who sought to have her husband join her.

The applicant, born in 1982, was granted asylum in Finland on 27 October 2016 and notified of the decision on 8 November 2016. Her three minor children were included. Her husband, also Eritrean, had fled Eritrea in 2014, was granted refugee status in Uganda, and lived in Kampala. The applicant sought a residence permit for him on family-reunification grounds.

Under Finnish law, family members of a refugee are normally subject to a maintenance requirement. However, the requirement does not apply if the family-reunification application is submitted within three months of the sponsor’s notification of the asylum decision, provided the family was established before the sponsor arrived in Finland and reunification is not possible in a third country. The asylum decision included information, in Finnish, about this procedure and deadline. Immigration records also showed that the applicant discussed family reunification with a social worker in November 2016 and January 2017, assisted by a Tigrinya interpreter. In January 2017 she was specifically informed of the three-month time-limit and the consequences of exceeding it, and was given application forms, embassy contact details, and information about applying online.

The husband applied for a residence permit at the Finnish Embassy in Nairobi only on 30 January 2018, nearly fifteen months after the applicant’s notification and well beyond the three-month exemption period. On 20 February 2019, the Finnish Immigration Service refused the application. It found that the applicant did not meet the maintenance requirement: she needed at least EUR 2,900 per month, or EUR 34,800 per year, but her income consisted only of social-security benefits, and she had not shown continuous income ensuring her husband’s subsistence without social assistance. No exceptionally serious grounds justified a derogation.

The husband claimed he could not apply earlier because Finland’s honorary consulate in Kampala did not handle residence permits. He said he had been advised to apply in Nairobi but delayed doing so. Passport stamps suggested he had travelled to Kenya and Eritrea before January 2018, undermining his explanation. Health problems raised later were unsubstantiated. The children’s best interests were assessed: they lived with their mother, had little or no prior relationship with their father, and were not dependent on his care.

The Administrative Court dismissed the appeal on 6 September 2019, with a minority favouring derogation. The Supreme Administrative Court refused leave to appeal on 26 February 2020.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged that the refusal breached her right to respect for family life under Article 8, arguing that she had not received timely and adequate advice and that her individual circumstances had been ignored. The Court declared the complaint admissible but found no violation. Applying the principles in *Dabo v. Sweden*, it held that there were no objectively excusable reasons for missing the three-month deadline; the applicant had received timely and adequate advice; the refusal was not irreversible; and she could make a fresh application if exceptional or new circumstances arose. The authorities had struck a fair balance between immigration control and family life, within Finland’s wide margin of appreciation.

In *Bielau v. Austria* (Application no. 20007/22, judgment of 27 August 2024), the applicant, an Austrian general practitioner in Styria with a “holistic medicine” website, complained under Article 10 of the Convention that a disciplinary sanction imposed for statements about vaccines violated his right to freedom of expression.

In June 2016, Bielau posted an article titled “Vaccination” on his practice website, describing himself as an expert on vaccinations and vaccine damage. The article stated, among other things, that pathogenic viruses were unproven, that people could not die from a tick bite, that meningitis symptoms were healing reactions, that chemical vaccinations could never protect against disease, that bacteria and viruses were not causes of illness but helpers or metabolic products, that nature knew no diseases, and that vaccination had not eradicated a single disease. He later claimed some formulations were provocative, intended to make people think, and reflected his holistic views.

In 2017, the Disciplinary Commission for Styria and Carinthia found him guilty of disciplinary offences under section 136(1)(1) and (2) of the Medical Practitioners Act. Relying on an expert immunologist’s report, it held that his statements contradicted established science and medical experience, were one-sided and negative, and violated section 53 of the Act and the Regulation on Medical Practitioners and the Public, which prohibit doctors from providing unobjective, untrue, or reputation-damaging information in connection with their profession. It imposed a EUR 2,000 fine, suspended for one year, plus EUR 1,500 costs.

The applicant challenged the decision, arguing that the statements were context-dependent, not advertising, and protected by Article 10. The Regional Administrative Court dismissed his complaint in 2018 after an oral hearing and a second expert opinion. It found the statements scientifically untenable, some contrary even to reason, and that his website served professional/advertising purposes. It held that such one-sided information could damage trust in doctors and public health. The Constitutional Court declined to hear the case, and in 2021 the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed his appeal, agreeing that the website had a professional/advertising connection and that the statements were unobjective, damaged the profession’s reputation, and breached professional duties. It considered the relatively low suspended fine proportionate.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Bielau alleged a violation of Article 10. The Government admitted the disciplinary sanction was an interference but argued it was justified under Article 10 § 2 for the protection of health, the reputation/rights of others, and public trust in medical expertise. It stressed that doctors may participate in public health debates but must not disseminate medically refuted, one-sided information in a professional/advertising context. Bielau argued the provisions did not apply to his website, that the interference lacked a legitimate aim, and that it was disproportionate and stifled alternative medical views.

The Fourth Section declared the complaint admissible. It found the interference was prescribed by law and pursued legitimate aims. The domestic courts had given relevant and sufficient reasons: the statements were scientifically untenable, made by a practising doctor on a website connected to his practice, and capable of undermining public health and trust in the medical profession. The Court found a fair balance had been struck between the applicant’s freedom of expression and the competing public/private interests, and that the suspended EUR 2,000 fine was proportionate. There was therefore no violation of Article 10.

In *Bielau v. Austria* (ECtHR, Fourth Section, 27 August 2024), the applicant, Klaus Bielau, was an Austrian general practitioner in Graz who also operated a “holistic medicine” website. On that site he posted a June 2016 article on vaccination, describing himself as an expert on vaccinations and vaccine damage. The article argued, among other things, that viruses are not pathogenic; that a tick bite cannot cause death; that meningitis symptoms are healing reactions; that chemical vaccinations never protect against disease; that bacteria and viruses do not cause illness; that nature knows no diseases; and that no disease had disappeared through vaccination. The text used provocative, one-sided language and was presented on a website connected to his medical practice.

In 2017, the Disciplinary Commission of the Austrian Medical Association found Bielau guilty of disciplinary offences under section 136(1)(1) and (2) of the Medical Practitioners Act, read with section 53(1) and the Regulation on Medical Practitioners and the Public. Relying on an expert report by a prominent immunologist, the Commission found that his statements contradicted established science and medical experience and were unobjective, one-sided, and capable of damaging the reputation of the medical profession. He was fined EUR 2,000, suspended for a one-year probationary period, and ordered to pay EUR 1,500 in costs.

The Regional Administrative Court upheld the decision after an oral hearing and a second expert opinion. It found that the statements were not in line with current medical science, and some were not even in line with reason. It stressed that doctors must provide objective information because patients rely on medical advice and because vaccination involves consent to an interference with physical integrity. It also held that the website served advertising purposes and was connected to the exercise of his profession. The Constitutional Court declined to hear the case, and the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed his further appeal. That court found that the unobjective information on the website could amount to professional misconduct, that the website had an advertising purpose, and that the relatively low suspended fine was proportionate under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Bielau complained under Article 10 that the disciplinary sanction violated his freedom of expression. He argued that his statements were provocative public-interest information, not advertising, and were not made in the exercise of his profession; even shocking or minority views should be protected. The Austrian Government accepted that the sanction was an interference but argued it was justified for the protection of public health and the reputation and rights of others, particularly given the trust placed in doctors and the international consensus on vaccination.

The Court declared the application admissible but found no violation of Article 10. It held that the disciplinary sanction was prescribed by law and pursued legitimate aims, namely protection of health and protection of the reputation of the medical profession. The domestic courts had given relevant and sufficient reasons: the statements were scientifically untenable, one-sided, and liable to undermine public trust in medical practice. The fact that they appeared on a website linked to his medical practice and served advertising purposes was significant. Finally, the sanction—a suspended EUR 2,000 fine—was proportionate. The Court therefore concluded that Austria had struck a fair balance between Bielau’s freedom of expression and the competing public interests, so there was no violation of Article 10.

**Bielau v. Austria** (Application no. 20007/22, ECtHR Fourth Section, judgment of 27 August 2024) concerned a practising Austrian doctor’s complaint under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights that disciplinary sanctions imposed for statements about vaccines violated his freedom of expression.

The applicant, Klaus Bielau, was a general practitioner in Graz with a “holistic medicine” website, on which he described himself as an expert on vaccinations and vaccine damage. In June 2016 he published an article titled “Vaccination” that made several scientifically contested claims. These included that viruses were not proven pathogens; that bacteria and viruses did not cause disease; that nature knew no diseases; that vaccination never protected against disease; and that no disease had disappeared through vaccination. The article also suggested that meningitis symptoms could be healing processes and criticised conventional vaccination narratives as fear-based and arbitrary.

On 27 June 2017, the Disciplinary Commission for Styria and Carinthia of the Austrian Medical Association found the applicant guilty of disciplinary offences under section 136(1)(1) and (2) of the Medical Practitioners Act. It relied on an expert report by a prominent immunologist, Dr G., concluding that the statements were not in line with medical science or experience and were one-sided and negative. The Commission held that the article violated section 53 of the Medical Practitioners Act and the Regulation on Medical Practitioners and the Public, which prohibit doctors from providing unobjective, untrue or reputation-damaging information. It imposed a fine of EUR 2,000, suspended for a one-year probationary period, plus EUR 1,500 costs.

The applicant challenged the sanction before the Regional Administrative Court, arguing that his statements were provocative but protected expression, not advertising, and not made in the exercise of his profession. That court heard a second expert, Dr K., and dismissed the complaint. It found the statements incompatible with current medical science—some even with reason—and one-sided. It held that the website was clearly connected to his medical practice and served advertising purposes, and that the statements could damage public trust in doctors. The Constitutional Court declined to hear the case, and the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed his appeal in October 2021. It emphasised that a doctor’s website could be professional advertising, that the statements were at least unobjective, and that the relatively low suspended fine was proportionate under Article 10.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant argued that the disciplinary sanction breached Article 10. He maintained that his statements concerned alternative medicine and vaccine risks, were not advertising, and should not attract professional discipline. The Government accepted that there had been an interference but argued it was justified under Article 10 § 2 for the protection of public health and the reputation and rights of others. It stressed that doctors could participate in public health debates but not disseminate clearly unobjective or untrue information in a professional/advertising context.

The Court declared the application admissible but ultimately found no violation of Article 10. It accepted that the interference was prescribed by law and pursued legitimate aims, notably public health and professional reputation. It found the domestic authorities’ reasons relevant and sufficient, particularly given the applicant’s professional status, the advertising character of his website, the scientifically untenable nature of the claims, and the potential to undermine public trust and health. The suspended fine of EUR 2,000 was considered modest and proportionate. A fair balance had therefore been struck between the applicant’s freedom of expression and the competing public and professional interests.

**M.B. v. the Netherlands** (Application no. 71008/16), European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, judgment of 23 April 2024 (final 23 July 2024).

The applicant, M.B., a Syrian national born in 1997, left Syria in December 2013, stayed in Türkiye until September 2015, and entered the Netherlands in October 2015. On 26 October 2015 he applied for asylum. While accommodated at a reception centre, two other asylum-seekers told police that M.B. had claimed involvement in a terrorist organisation in Syria and had detonated car bombs. A criminal investigation followed.

On 30 November 2015 M.B. was arrested on suspicion of participation in a terrorist organisation and placed in pre-trial detention. At trial, the public prosecutor argued there was lawful evidence but stated he was not convinced beyond reasonable doubt and sought acquittal. On 29 August 2016 the Rotterdam Regional Court nevertheless convicted M.B. and sentenced him to ten months’ imprisonment, reduced by time already spent in pre-trial detention. His criminal-law detention ended on 23 September 2016 because the sentence length had been reached.

On the same day, the Deputy Minister of Security and Justice ordered M.B.’s placement in immigration detention under section 59b(1)(b) and (d) of the Aliens Act 2000. The order was based on two grounds: detention was necessary to obtain information for assessing his asylum application, and M.B. posed a threat to national security or public order because of his criminal conviction. The Deputy Minister cited a genuine, present and sufficiently serious threat; risk of absconding; irregular entry; lack of fixed residence; insufficient resources; and the conviction itself. M.B. appealed, arguing that detention violated Article 5 § 1(f) of the Convention because there was no prospect of deportation to Syria, his asylum application remained pending, and no return decision had been issued. He relied on the CJEU’s judgment in *N.*, arguing it concerned a person already subject to a return decision.

On 10 October 2016 the Regional Court of The Hague dismissed the appeal. It held that section 59b transposed Article 8(3) of the EU Reception Conditions Directive; that the CJEU had upheld the public-order detention ground; and that no expulsion procedure was required. It found the risk-of-absconding ground insufficient under section 59b(1)(b), but held that section 59b(1)(d) alone provided a sufficient legal basis. The Council of State dismissed M.B.’s further appeal on 8 November 2016.

Later, on 13 December 2016, the Regional Court found that continued immigration detention had breached the statutory seven-day decision period from 19 November 2016, lifted the detention order and awarded compensation. In the criminal proceedings, the Court of Appeal acquitted M.B. in December 2017, and the Supreme Court confirmed that acquittal. In March 2018 he was granted an asylum-based residence permit retroactive to 26 October 2015.

The key alleged violation was the arbitrariness of M.B.’s immigration detention pending his asylum assessment on public-order grounds after criminal-law detention. The ECtHR found a violation of Article 5 § 1(f). Although the detention had a clear legal basis in EU and domestic law, it was arbitrary: it was not necessary to enable examination of his asylum claim upon initial entry, no steps had been taken to further that examination during the preceding ten months of criminal-law detention, and public order could not justify excessive immigration detention after criminal detention while the asylum application remained undecided. There was no sufficiently close connection between the aim of preventing unauthorised entry and the immigration detention.

**Case: M.B. v. the Netherlands (Application no. 71008/16)**

The applicant, M.B., a Syrian national born in 1997, left Syria in December 2013, stayed in Türkiye until late September 2015, and entered the Netherlands in October 2015. On 26 October 2015 he applied for asylum and was later housed in an asylum reception centre. Two other asylum-seekers told police that M.B. had said he had been involved in a terrorist organisation in Syria and had detonated car bombs. A criminal investigation followed, and on 30 November 2015 he was arrested on suspicion of participating in an organisation with intent to commit terrorist offences. He was placed in pre-trial detention.

M.B. was charged with participating in a terrorist organisation between March 2013 and October 2015. At trial, the public prosecutor argued that although there was lawful evidence, he was not convinced beyond reasonable doubt and sought acquittal. On 29 August 2016, the Rotterdam Regional Court nevertheless convicted M.B. and sentenced him to ten months’ imprisonment, deducting time already spent in pre-trial detention. The conviction relied on his statements, a witness statement, a 2013 tweet in which he said he belonged to Al Qaida, WhatsApp conversations from 2015, and photos and videos on his phone. Both M.B. and the prosecutor appealed.

On 23 September 2016, when the criminal detention had reached the length of the imposed sentence, he was released from criminal detention. The same day, the Deputy Minister of Security and Justice ordered his placement in immigration detention under section 59b(1)(b) and (d) of the Aliens Act 2000. The order relied on two grounds: that detention was necessary to obtain information for assessing his asylum application, particularly because of a risk of absconding, and that he posed a threat to national security or public order due to his criminal conviction for a terrorism-related offence. The Deputy Minister considered that the conviction showed a genuine, present and sufficiently serious threat, that less restrictive measures were inadequate, and that a prospect of deportation was not required for immigration detention under section 59b.

M.B. appealed, arguing that his immigration detention violated Article 5 § 1 (f) of the Convention because there was no prospect of deportation to Syria, his asylum application was still pending, and no return decision had been taken. He also argued that the Deputy Minister had relied on the conviction without addressing the prosecutor’s contrary view.

On 10 October 2016, the Regional Court of The Hague dismissed the appeal. It held that section 59b transposed Article 8(3) of the EU Reception Conditions Directive and that the CJEU’s judgment in *N.* upheld public-order detention under that provision. It found M.B.’s entry had not been authorised and that his detention was not arbitrary because of the criminal conviction. Although it found insufficient reasons for the absconding ground under section 59b(1)(b), it held that section 59b(1)(d), the public-order ground, provided a sufficient legal basis. The Council of State dismissed his further appeal on 8 November 2016.

After the application to the European Court of Human Rights, M.B. successfully challenged continued detention on procedural grounds; on 13 December 2016 the Regional Court found a breach of the seven-day decision rule from 19 November 2016, lifted the detention order, and awarded compensation. He was later subject to a freedom-restricting measure, which was lifted in January 2018. In December 2017, the Court of Appeal acquitted him of the relevant criminal charges, a judgment confirmed by the Supreme Court. On 29 March 2018, he was granted an asylum-based residence permit retroactive to 26 October 2015.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 5 § 1 (f). Although the immigration detention had a clear legal basis under the EU Reception Conditions Directive, it was arbitrary. It was not necessary to enable examination of his asylum claim upon initial entry, and no steps had been taken to examine that claim during the preceding ten months of criminal-law detention. Public order could not justify excessive immigration detention after criminal detention while the asylum application remained undecided, and there was no sufficiently close connection between the aim of preventing unauthorised entry and the immigration detention.

In *Kowalik v. Poland* (Application no. 37910/21), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 8 February 2024. The applicant lodged his application on 15 July 2021 under Article 34 of the Convention. He complained that the criminal proceedings involving him had been excessively long, contrary to Article 6 § 1, and that he had no effective remedy in Polish law for that complaint, contrary to Article 13. The full text does not reproduce the appended table containing the applicant’s personal details and the precise chronology, so the exact dates and total duration are not set out in the judgment’s body.

The Polish Government raised a preliminary objection that the applicant could no longer be regarded as a “victim” within the meaning of Article 34. It argued that the Warsaw-Praga Regional Court had already analysed the proceedings using the same criteria applied by the ECtHR, found delays attributable to the domestic authorities, concluded that the applicant’s right to a hearing without unjustified delay had been breached, and awarded him 2,000 Polish zlotys (approximately EUR 468) for the length of the proceedings. The applicant disagreed, considering that the domestic award was not satisfactory given the overall length of the proceedings.

The ECtHR examined the victim-status issue in light of its case-law in *Cocchiarella v. Italy* and *Scordino v. Italy*. It accepted that the domestic court had acknowledged a breach and awarded compensation. However, the Court found that the redress provided at the domestic level, assessed on the facts complained of before it, was insufficient. It relied on *Janulis v. Poland* and other examples. Consequently, it rejected the Government’s argument that the applicant had lost his victim status.

On the merits, the Court reiterated that the reasonableness of the length of proceedings must be assessed in light of the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicant and the relevant authorities, and what was at stake for the applicant. It referred to the leading case *Rutkowski and Others v. Poland*, where it had already found a violation of Article 6 concerning excessive length of criminal proceedings. After examining all the material, the Court found no fact or argument capable of justifying the overall length of the proceedings at the national level. It therefore concluded that the length was excessive and failed to meet the “reasonable time” requirement. The Court further found that the applicant did not have an effective remedy at his disposal for these complaints. Accordingly, it found violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were thus: the criminal proceedings were excessively long; the domestic authorities acknowledged delay and awarded only modest compensation, which was insufficient to remove the applicant’s victim status; and no effective domestic remedy existed for the length complaint. The ECtHR concluded that Poland violated the applicant’s right to a hearing within a reasonable time and his right to an effective remedy.
