**CASE OF GIANNAKOPOULOS v. GREECE** (Application no. 20503/20) concerns a Greek father’s complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that Greek courts violated his family life by rejecting his custody application for lack of jurisdiction after his children were taken to Germany.

The applicant, Georgios Giannakopoulos, married E.B., a German national, in 2009. They lived in Rhodes, Greece, and had two children, a girl born in 2010 and a boy born in 2012. After the couple separated, E.B. sought interim custody. In October 2013, the Rhodes One-Member Court of First Instance granted her custody (decision no. 590/2013) and set a contact schedule for the applicant. E.B. told the court she would remain in Rhodes with the children and had no intention of moving to Germany.

In December 2013, however, E.B. travelled with the children to Germany for what she said was a Christmas visit, promising to return by 13 January 2014. She did not return and settled permanently in Germany. The applicant later served the Greek custody/contact decision on the German authorities.

In September 2014, the applicant sought new interim orders. In January 2015, the Rhodes court granted him interim custody (decision no. 26/2015), finding that E.B. had misled the court and obstructed his contact rights by moving to Germany. The applicant obtained certificates of enforceability under the EU Brussels II bis Regulation. He also applied in Greece for sole custody and sought the children’s return under the Hague Convention.

In Germany, the Düsseldorf District Court initially ordered the children’s return in June 2015, but the Düsseldorf Court of Appeal overturned that decision in November 2015. It held that the return request had been lodged after the one-year time limit and that the children had settled in Germany, so they should remain with their mother.

Greek jurisdiction then became the central issue. In 2017, the Rhodes court rejected the applicant’s custody application as inadmissible, finding the children habitually resident in Germany. The Dodecanese Court of Appeal declined jurisdiction. In 2019, the Court of Cassation confirmed. It held that under Article 8 of the Brussels II bis Regulation the children were habitually resident in Germany; that Article 10 on child abduction did not apply because the mother had sole custody and could determine their residence; that Greece had not acquired jurisdiction under Article 12; and that the children had integrated into life in Germany through residence registration, social security, nursery/school attendance, language, and family ties.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that the Greek courts had misinterpreted the relevant provisions, wrongly found habitual residence in Germany, and dismissed his custody claim for want of jurisdiction. He stressed that the children had been taken to Germany in violation of his contact rights; that the mother had obtained custody by assuring she would stay in Greece; that Greek decision no. 26/2015 had granted him interim custody; that German courts had initially rejected the mother’s position; and that the children had lived in Germany only about a year.

The Court found no indication of arbitrariness. The domestic courts had assessed the relevant factors under Brussels II bis and the children’s best interests. The dismissal for lack of jurisdiction was therefore proportionate and did not violate Article 8.

Giannakopoulos v. Greece (Application no. 20503/20) concerned a Greek father’s complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that Greek courts violated his right to respect for family life by dismissing his custody application for lack of jurisdiction and ruling that his children were habitually resident in Germany.

The applicant, a Greek national living in Rhodes, married E.B., a German national. They had two children, born in 2010 and 2012. After separation, in 2013 the Rhodes One-Member Court of First Instance granted interim custody to the mother and set a contact schedule for the father. In her submissions, E.B. stated she would remain in Rhodes with the children and had no intention of moving to Germany. The court noted there was no evidence she would leave without the applicant’s consent.

In December 2013, E.B. travelled with the children to Germany, saying it was a Christmas visit and that she would return in January 2014. She did not return and settled permanently in Germany with the children. The applicant later served the Greek custody/contact decision on the German authorities. In January 2015, a Greek court granted him interim custody of the children, finding a substantial change of circumstances: E.B. had moved to Germany, misled the court by assuring she would stay in Greece, and obstructed the applicant’s contact rights. The applicant served that decision in Germany and obtained certificates of enforceability under the Brussels II bis Regulation. He then applied for sole custody in Greece.

Greek courts, however, declined jurisdiction. The Dodecanese Court of Appeal and later the Court of Cassation held that the children were habitually resident in Germany at the time the custody proceedings were initiated. They relied on factors including the children’s more than one year’s residence in Germany, their integration into nursery/school, their German nationality and language, their social and family ties there, and the mother’s lawful move while she had sole custody under the earlier Greek decision. The courts found no wrongful removal or retention under Article 10 of the Brussels II bis Regulation, and no prorogation of Greek jurisdiction under Article 12(3), because E.B. had not accepted Greek jurisdiction. The Greek interim custody decision was never enforced in Germany.

In parallel German proceedings, the applicant sought the children’s return under the Hague Convention. The Düsseldorf District Court initially ordered return in June 2015, but the Düsseldorf Court of Appeal reversed that decision in November 2015, refusing return because the application was lodged after the one-year time limit and the children had settled in Germany. The Federal Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint. Later German custody proceedings ultimately gave parental responsibility to the mother in 2021.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant argued that the Greek courts misinterpreted the relevant rules, wrongly found habitual residence in Germany, and ignored that the children had been taken to Germany in breach of his contact rights, that the mother had misled the Greek court, that he had obtained interim custody in Greece, and that German courts had initially ordered return. He alleged that the Greek courts’ refusal to hear his custody application violated Article 8.

The European Court found no violation. It held that the domestic courts’ findings were not arbitrary and that they had assessed all relevant factors under the Brussels II bis Regulation in light of the children’s best interests. The rejection of the applicant’s custody application for want of jurisdiction was therefore compatible with Article 8.

In *Giannakopoulos v. Greece* (ECtHR, Third Section, 3 December 2024), the applicant, a Greek national living in Rhodes, complained under Article 8 of the Convention that the Greek courts violated his right to respect for family life by rejecting his custody application for lack of jurisdiction. The applicant had two children with E.B., a German national. The family lived in Greece but separated in 2013. In interim proceedings, E.B. sought custody and assured the Rhodes court that she would remain in Rhodes with the children. By decision no. 590/2013, the Rhodes One-Member Court of First Instance granted her custody and set the applicant’s contact schedule, noting no evidence she would leave for Germany without his consent.

In December 2013, E.B. travelled with the children to Germany for Christmas, stating she would return in January 2014. She did not return and settled permanently in Germany. The applicant alleged that she misled the Greek court and obstructed his contact rights. In January 2015, the Rhodes court granted him interim custody by decision no. 26/2015, finding a substantive change of circumstances because E.B. had moved to Germany with the children and frustrated his contact. The applicant obtained enforceability certificates under the Brussels II bis Regulation and then sought sole custody in Greece.

In parallel German proceedings, the Düsseldorf District Court initially ordered the children’s return to Greece in June 2015 under the Hague Convention. However, the Düsseldorf Court of Appeal reversed that decision in November 2015, holding that the father’s return request was lodged after the one-year time-limit and that the children had settled in Germany. The German Constitutional Court later dismissed the applicant’s complaint.

Greek courts ultimately declined jurisdiction. The Rhodes court (decision no. 51/2017), the Dodecanese Court of Appeal (no. 302/2017), and the Court of Cassation (no. 927/2019) held that the children were habitually resident in Germany when the Greek custody application was lodged. They relied on the mother’s sole custody under decision no. 590/2013, her right to determine the children’s residence, the children’s registered residence in Germany in February 2014, social security coverage, nursery and school attendance, their adaptation to German life, language skills, and family and social ties there. The courts applied Article 8 of Brussels II bis. They found Article 10 on child abduction inapplicable because there had been no wrongful removal or retention: E.B. had sole custody when she moved, and decision no. 26/2015 had never been enforced in Germany. Article 12(3) did not apply because E.B. had not accepted Greek jurisdiction.

The applicant argued that the Greek courts misinterpreted the relevant provisions, wrongly found habitual residence in Germany, and ignored that the children had been taken in breach of his contact rights, that the mother had given false assurances, that decision no. 26/2015 granted him interim custody, and that German courts had initially rejected the mother’s attempt to disregard that decision.

The European Court of Human Rights found no indication of arbitrariness. The Greek courts had proportionately assessed all relevant factors under Brussels II bis and in accordance with the children’s best interests. Accordingly, the rejection of the applicant’s custody application for want of jurisdiction did not violate Article 8.

**Pasquariello v. Italy** (Application no. 57962/22) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, First Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered on 16 May 2024. The applicant lodged his application against Italy on 9 December 2022 under Article 34 of the Convention. The Italian Government were given notice of the application.

The applicant complained principally of the non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of domestic decisions given in his favour, relying on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to a fair hearing. He also raised other complaints under the Convention. The relevant domestic law concerned the “Pinto Act,” the Italian remedy for excessive length of proceedings, as previously examined in *Cocchiarella v. Italy* and *Di Giuseppe v. Italy*.

The key disputed decision was issued by the Naples Court of Appeal on 9 June 2016 (R.G. no. 624/2016). In relation to that decision, the Government argued that the applicant had failed to submit a declaration containing the necessary information for the authorities to proceed with payment of the judgment debt. They contended that such a declaration had to be submitted in order to obtain payment of sums awarded in “Pinto” decisions, as required by Article 5 sexies of the Pinto Act. The applicant did not comment on this argument and did not deny that he had failed to submit the required declaration.

The Court relied on its earlier decision in *Di Giuseppe v. Italy*, where it had established that the obligation to send the declaration and supporting documents under Article 5 sexies of the Pinto Act is a reasonable procedural step required of the creditor in order to obtain sums awarded by “Pinto” decisions. Failure by the creditor to comply with that obligation constitutes an obstacle to enforcement of the decision in his favour, for which the authorities cannot be held responsible. Since the applicant did not deny his failure to submit the declaration regarding the Naples Court of Appeal decision of 9 June 2016, the Court held that the respondent Government could not be held liable for the delayed enforcement of that decision. Consequently, that complaint was found manifestly ill-founded and rejected under Article 35 §§ 3 and 4 of the Convention.

As regards the remaining domestic decisions listed in the appended table, neither the Government nor the applicant submitted any observations. The Court reiterated that execution of a judgment given by any court must be regarded as an integral part of a “hearing” for the purposes of Article 6, referring to *Hornsby v. Greece*. It also referred to its established case-law concerning non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of final domestic judgments, including *Ventorino v. Italy*, *De Trana v. Italy*, *Nicola Silvestri v. Italy*, *Antonetto v. Italy*, and *De Luca v. Italy*, where similar issues had already resulted in findings of violations.

Having examined all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on the admissibility and merits of those remaining complaints. It considered that the Italian authorities had not deployed all necessary efforts to enforce fully and in due time the decisions in the applicant’s favour. Those complaints were therefore admissible and disclosed violations of the Convention.

The applicant also submitted other complaints raising issues under the Convention in light of well-established case-law. For the same reasons, the complaint concerning the Naples Court of Appeal decision of 9 June 2016 was manifestly ill-founded and rejected, while the complaints concerning the remaining domestic decisions were admissible and disclosed violations in light of *Ventorino*.

In summary, the Court found violations concerning the remaining domestic decisions due to non-enforcement or delayed enforcement, but rejected the complaint concerning the 9 June 2016 “Pinto” decision because the applicant’s failure to file the required declaration prevented payment and could not be attributed to the Italian authorities.

The European Court of Human Rights (First Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 16 May 2024 in *Pasquariello v. Italy*. The applicant lodged his application against Italy under Article 34 of the Convention on 9 December 2022. He complained principally of the non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of domestic decisions given in his favour, relying on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. He also raised other complaints under the Convention.

The case concerned two categories of domestic decisions. The first was a decision issued by the Naples Court of Appeal on 9 June 2016 (R.G. no. 624/2016). The second category consisted of remaining domestic decisions listed in an appended table to the judgment.

As regards the Naples Court of Appeal decision, the Italian Government argued that the applicant had failed to submit a declaration containing the necessary information for the authorities to proceed with payment of the judgment debt. The Government contended that such a declaration was required under Article 5 *sexies* of the Italian “Pinto Act” in order to obtain payment of sums awarded in “Pinto” decisions. The applicant did not comment on this point and did not deny that he had failed to submit the required declaration.

The Court noted that it had already examined this issue in *Di Giuseppe v. Italy* (Committee decision, no. 7997/21, 5 December 2023). In that case, the Court held that the obligation to send the declaration and supporting documents under Article 5 *sexies* of the Pinto Act constitutes a reasonable procedural step required of the creditor in order to obtain sums awarded by Pinto decisions. The failure of the creditor to comply with this obligation is an obstacle to enforcement of the decision in his favour, for which the authorities cannot be held responsible. Applying that principle, the Court found that the respondent Government could not be held liable for the delayed enforcement of the Naples Court of Appeal decision of 9 June 2016, because the applicant had failed to submit the required declaration. Accordingly, that complaint was manifestly ill-founded and was rejected under Article 35 §§ 3 and 4 of the Convention.

As regards the remaining domestic decisions listed in the appended table, neither the Government nor the applicant submitted any observations. The Court reiterated that the execution of a judgment given by any court must be regarded as an integral part of a “hearing” for the purposes of Article 6, referring to *Hornsby v. Greece* (no. 18357/91, § 40, 1997-II). It also referred to its established case-law on non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of final domestic judgments, including *Ventorino v. Italy*, *De Trana v. Italy*, *Nicola Silvestri v. Italy*, *Antonetto v. Italy*, and *De Luca v. Italy*, where similar issues had already resulted in findings of violations.

Having examined all the material, the Court found no fact or argument capable of leading to a different conclusion. It considered that the Italian authorities had not deployed all necessary efforts to enforce fully and in due time the decisions in the applicant’s favour. Therefore, the complaints concerning the remaining domestic decisions were not manifestly ill-founded and were admissible. On the merits, the Court concluded that they disclosed violations of the Convention in light of its findings in *Ventorino*.

The applicant’s other complaints under well-established case-law followed the same division: the complaint relating to the Naples Court of Appeal decision of 9 June 2016 was rejected as manifestly ill-founded, while the complaints concerning the remaining domestic decisions were declared admissible and found to disclose violations of the Convention.

In essence, the case turned on whether the applicant’s failure to comply with the Pinto Act declaration requirement excused the authorities from liability for delayed payment. For the Naples decision, it did; for the other decisions, the Court found that the authorities had failed to enforce the judgments in due time, resulting in violations of Article 6 § 1.

In *Levanov and Others v. Russia* (Applications nos. 40953/21 and 18 others), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered a Committee judgment on 25 April 2024. The case concerned multiple applications lodged against Russia under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates listed in the appended table. The applicants were organisers or participants in public assemblies in Russia. The central factual allegation was that the Russian authorities took disproportionate measures against them in connection with those assemblies: they were arrested in relation to the dispersal of the assemblies and subsequently convicted of administrative offences. They complained, expressly or in substance, that these measures violated Article 11 of the Convention, which protects freedom of assembly. Some applicants also raised additional complaints under other Convention provisions.

The Court joined the applications because they shared a similar subject matter. It first addressed jurisdiction. The facts giving rise to the alleged violations occurred before 16 September 2022, when the Russian Federation ceased to be a party to the Convention. Relying on *Fedotova and Others v. Russia*, the Court held that it had jurisdiction to examine the applications.

On the Article 11 complaint, the Court applied its established case-law on freedom of assembly, including *Kudrevičius and Others v. Lithuania*, and principles on proportionality from cases such as *Oya Ataman v. Turkey* and *Hyde Park and Others v. Moldova*. It noted that in leading cases such as *Frumkin v. Russia*, *Navalnyy and Yashin v. Russia*, and *Kasparov and Others v. Russia*, it had already found violations of Article 11 in respect of similar issues. After examining the material, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion. It held that the interferences with the applicants’ freedom of assembly—namely their arrest in relation to the dispersal of public assemblies and their administrative convictions—were not “necessary in a democratic society.” There was therefore a violation of Article 11.

The Court also considered other complaints raised by some applicants that fell under well-established case-law. These included complaints about unlawful deprivation of liberty of organisers or participants of public assemblies, citing *Butkevich v. Russia*, *Tsvetkova and Others v. Russia*, and *Korneyeva v. Russia*; the absence of a prosecuting party in proceedings under the Code of Administrative Offences, citing *Karelin v. Russia*; administrative convictions for making calls to participate in public events, citing *Elvira Dmitriyeva v. Russia*; and disproportionate measures against solo demonstrators, citing *Novikova and Others v. Russia*. The Court declared these complaints admissible and found violations in light of those precedents.

Some applicants also raised further Article 6 complaints concerning other aspects of fairness in the administrative-offence proceedings. Because the Court had already found violations in respect of the main and related complaints, it considered that there was no need to deal separately with those remaining Article 6 complaints. Overall, the judgment establishes that Russia’s dispersal of the assemblies, arrest of the applicants, and administrative punishment for their involvement violated their Convention rights, particularly Article 11, because the measures were disproportionate and unjustified.

In *Maļinovskis v. Latvia* (Application no. 46084/19), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, Committee) examined complaints under Article 3 of the Convention concerning alleged ill-treatment in prison and the State’s alleged failure to conduct an effective investigation. The applicant, Jānis Maļinovskis, a Latvian national born in 1969 and detained in Riga, was represented by lawyer J. Dadukina; the Latvian Government was represented by K. Līce.

The key incident occurred on 30 January 2013 at Riga Central Prison. Three prison guards used physical force to subdue the applicant in the prison yard when he attempted to collect a packet thrown to him from a prison cell window by another prisoner. The parties disputed the nature and degree of force used. The applicant alleged that he was forced to the ground, that his face was smashed into the concrete floor approximately twenty times, and that he received approximately twenty kicks. He alleged that his nose was broken as a result.

Medical evidence shortly after the incident showed bruising to the applicant’s forehead, head, left ear and nose, along with superficial scratches. The next day, after transfer to Daugavgrīva Prison, a doctor recorded scratches, a bruised face and chest, and a broken nose.

On 4 February 2013 criminal proceedings were instituted. The investigation went through six rounds, each ending with an investigator’s decision to terminate proceedings for lack of *corpus delicti*. All termination decisions except the last were quashed by a superior prosecutor. In the first four rounds, prosecutors found that the investigation had not been thorough. The first round included a forensic examination and interrogations of the applicant and several Riga Central Prison officials. In December 2013, a superior prosecutor instructed the investigator to identify potential prisoner witnesses. The second round involved additional witnesses, another forensic examination, and information gathering; in March 2015, further instructions were given to interrogate witnesses more thoroughly and identify additional witnesses. The third round included interrogation of a prison guard, but no new witnesses were identified. In the fourth round, a confrontation was held between the applicant and a witness, and a senior Prisons Administration official and other witnesses were interrogated. In November 2017, a prosecutor again instructed further investigative measures, found this round excessively lengthy, and requested an internal audit; the Prisons Administration and investigator admitted deficiencies.

In the fifth round, the investigator obtained information on the applicant and several guards, interrogated the applicant and witnesses, and terminated proceedings both for lack of *corpus delicti* and because the offence had become time-barred. That decision was quashed in February 2019 because the two grounds contradicted each other. In the sixth round, no investigative measures were taken. By final decision of 8 May 2019, a superior prosecutor upheld termination of the criminal proceedings.

Separately, on 8 March 2013 the applicant complained to the Prisons Administration about the use of force as an “action of a public authority.” After dismissal, he applied to the Administrative District Court, but those proceedings ended on 16 January 2015 after he withdrew his application.

The applicant applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 14 August 2019, complaining under Article 3 that prison guards had used excessive force against him and that the ensuing investigation had been ineffective and excessively lengthy. The Court gave notice of the ill-treatment and investigation complaints to the Government and declared the remainder inadmissible. The Government’s objection to examination by a Committee was rejected. The judgment was delivered on 6 June 2024.

In *Guðmundur Gunnarsson and Magnús Davíð Norðdahl v. Iceland* (Applications nos. 24159/22 and 25751/22, ECtHR Third Section, 16 April 2024), the applicants were candidates in Iceland’s 25 September 2021 parliamentary elections in the Northwest constituency. The first applicant led the Liberal Reform Party list; the second led the Pirate Party list. After the initial count, the first applicant appeared to have qualified for a nationally allocated levelling seat, while the second applicant narrowly missed election. The National Electoral Commission then flagged an extremely narrow margin and suggested a recount.

The recount in the Northwest constituency reduced the Liberal Reform Party’s votes from 1,072 to 1,063 and the Pirate Party’s from 1,082 to 1,081. This triggered a national reallocation of levelling seats: the first applicant lost his levelling seat, which went to the Centre Party, and the Liberal Reform Party ended up with no MP elected from that constituency. The second applicant remained unelected.

The applicants complained about the recount and election results. They alleged: no clear legal basis for the recount; ballots were not sealed and were left in open boxes in an unsupervised hotel room with three entrances, one unlocked, while hotel staff had keys and the electoral commission chairman spent time there alone; party agents were not informed of or present during the recount; valid, blank, and invalid ballot numbers changed between counts; counting procedures were inconsistent; and the minutes failed to record key events. They argued these defects could have affected the outcome or at least were liable to do so.

Domestically, the complaints went to the Preparatory Credentials Committee, composed of newly elected parliamentarians. It conducted a substantial inquiry, including meetings, witness hearings, expert input, and site visits. Its report identified serious irregularities, especially the insecure storage of ballots between counts, but the committee was divided on whether they affected the result. The Credentials Committee, all nine members of which had also sat on the Preparatory Committee, largely recommended confirming the election. A minority recommended annulling the Northwest constituency result or a nationwide re-election. Althingi debated for over five hours and voted 42–5, with 16 abstentions, to confirm the credentials. Notably, the MP who gained the Northwest levelling seat instead of the first applicant voted in favour, while several other levelling-seat MPs abstained or voted against.

The applicants alleged violations of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 (right to stand in free elections) and Article 13 (effective remedy). They argued that the recount irregularities undermined election reliability and that the parliamentary review was not fair, objective, or impartial. They also complained about limited access to material and insufficient participation. The Court dismissed Iceland’s non-exhaustion plea, finding that the Government had not shown that judicial review of Althingi’s election decisions existed in theory and practice.

On the merits, the European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1. Iceland had failed its positive procedural obligation to secure an effective examination of the applicants’ complaints. The procedure did not provide a fair and objective examination with a sufficiently reasoned decision, and it lacked adequate institutional and procedural safeguards of impartiality. The decision-making body enjoyed discretion not sufficiently circumscribed by precise domestic law. The Court also found a violation of Article 13, because the applicants lacked an effective remedy in the circumstances.

In *Gunnarsson and Norðdahl v. Iceland* (Apps. 24159/22 and 25751/22, ECtHR, 16 April 2024), the applicants were candidates in Iceland’s 2021 parliamentary elections in the Northwest constituency, the country’s smallest. Iceland elects 63 parliamentarians: 54 constituency seats and nine nationally allocated levelling seats. After the initial count, the first applicant, standing for the Liberal Reform Party, received 1,072 votes and appeared to qualify for a levelling seat. The second applicant, standing for the Pirate Party, received 1,082 votes and narrowly missed a constituency seat.

Because the margin was extremely narrow, the National Electoral Commission suggested a recount. The recount reduced Liberal Reform’s vote to 1,063 and the Pirate Party’s to 1,081. This triggered a national reallocation of levelling seats: the first applicant lost his levelling seat, and the Northwest levelling seat went to the Centre Party, leaving the Liberal Reform Party with no MP elected from that constituency.

The applicants complained about the recount and the election results. They alleged that there was no clear legal basis for the recount; that ballots were improperly stored and handled between the initial count and recount; that party agents were not informed and could not observe the recount; and that there were unexplained changes in party votes and in blank/invalid ballots. The storage issue was especially serious: ballots were not sealed and were left unattended in open boxes in a hotel room. One entrance could not be locked, hotel staff had keys, surveillance did not cover the area, and the chairman of the senior electoral commission spent about half an hour alone in the room.

A Preparatory Credentials Committee, composed of nine newly elected MPs, investigated. It found serious defects: unsecured ballot storage, a recount not expressly regulated by law, counting and recounting without agents present, changes in valid ballots, and inadequate minutes. However, it was divided on whether these defects affected the outcome. The Credentials Committee—containing the same nine members—mostly applied a “specific standard” requiring proof of actual effect, found no indication of tampering, and recommended confirming the election credentials. A minority recommended annulling the Northwest election or holding a nationwide re-election. Althingi rejected re-election and confirmed credentials by 42 votes to 5, with 16 abstentions. Notably, MPs whose seats were affected participated, abstained or voted; the member who gained the levelling seat instead of the first applicant voted in favour.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged violations of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 (right to free elections, including the right to stand) and Article 13 (effective remedy). The Court rejected the Government’s non-exhaustion argument, finding that a judicial remedy had not been shown to exist in practice. On the merits, it held that Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 imposes a positive procedural obligation to secure an effective examination of electoral complaints through a fair and objective procedure with adequate impartiality safeguards. The Court found that Iceland failed to discharge this obligation: the decision-making body consisted of newly elected parliamentarians whose own electoral interests were directly at stake, and its discretion was not sufficiently circumscribed by law. It therefore found violations of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 13. The judgment became final on 16 July 2024.

**Guðmundur Gunnarsson and Magnús Davíð Norðdahl v. Iceland** (ECtHR, Third Section, 16 April 2024) concerned the 2021 Icelandic parliamentary elections. The applicants stood in the Northwest constituency: Gunnarsson was the Liberal Reform Party’s top candidate and Norðdahl the Pirate Party’s top candidate. Althingi has 63 members: 54 constituency seats and 9 nationally allocated levelling seats. After the initial count on 26 September 2021, Liberal Reform received 1,072 votes and the Pirate Party 1,082 of 17,666. Gunnarsson appeared to qualify for a levelling seat; Norðdahl narrowly missed a constituency seat. Later that day, the National Electoral Commission flagged a two-vote margin and suggested a recount. The recount reduced Liberal Reform to 1,063 votes; a full recount gave the Pirate Party 1,081. The Northwest recount triggered nationwide reallocation of levelling seats: Gunnarsson lost his levelling seat, and the Northwest levelling seat went to the Centre Party.

The applicants alleged violations of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 (free elections/right to stand) and Article 13 (effective remedy). They complained of no legal basis for the recount; improper storage and handling of ballots between the first count and recount; failure to inform party agents, depriving them of the chance to observe; and unexplained changes in votes and blank/invalid ballots.

The Preparatory Credentials Committee’s 90-page report found serious irregularities: ballots were not sealed and were left unattended in a hotel room with an unlocked entrance, hotel staff access, no camera coverage, and the commission chairman alone there; the recount after public announcement was not expressly regulated; agents were not notified and the recount was not postponed; valid ballot numbers changed and agents were excluded from validity rulings; ballots were not mixed and counting began before polls closed in an insecure room; and minutes omitted key events. The Committee split on whether these defects affected the result. The Credentials Committee majority applied a “specific standard,” requiring actual effect, found no proof of tampering, and recommended confirming credentials. The minority recommended annulment of the Northwest election or nationwide re-election. Althingi rejected those proposals and confirmed credentials by 42 votes to 5, with 16 abstentions.

The Government argued non-exhaustion, claiming judicial review was available. The Court dismissed this: Article 46 of the Constitution gives Althingi power to decide election legality; no Icelandic court had ever ruled on such

In Tsaava and Others v. Georgia (ECtHR, 7 May 2024), twenty-six Georgian nationals lodged five applications concerning the police dispersal of a demonstration in front of the Georgian Parliament on 20–21 June 2019 and the subsequent criminal investigation. The protest was triggered by a Russian State Duma member and IAO president sitting in the Georgian Parliament Speaker’s chair and speaking in Russian. Initially peaceful, with about 12,000 people, the demonstration later became tense when some protesters tried to break the police cordon and enter Parliament. Scuffles involved bottles thrown at police, seizure of police shields and batons, and attempts to storm the building. Police used batons, shields, tear gas, water cannon, and rubber bullets. Rubber bullets and tear gas were fired simultaneously or in close sequence; shooting began around 11:55 p.m. without a warning. Dispersal lasted until about 6:45 a.m. Over 200 people were injured, including roughly eighty police officers and forty journalists; 342 were arrested.

The applicants were journalists, camera operators, photographers, and demonstrators. They complained under Articles 3, 10, 11 and 13 that police used excessive force and that the investigation was ineffective. Many were hit by rubber bullets while posing no threat, including while reporting or filming. Video and medical evidence showed: a journalist hit while filming calmly; another hit in the head; a demonstrator hit in the thigh while trying to calm others; a journalist wearing a press badge hit near the police cordon; another journalist lost an eye after being hit; one applicant suffered an open shoulder fracture and life-threatening injury; another had rubber bullets removed from a wound; and a further journalist was pushed and had equipment damaged in the Parliament yard despite identifying himself as press. Some demonstrators alleged physical ill-treatment, including beatings during arrest. Several applicants were refused victim status because authorities said it had not yet been established whether a crime had been committed against them.

On 22 June 2019, the General Prosecutor’s Office opened an ex officio investigation under Article 333 of the Criminal Code into alleged exceeding of official authority, by violence or weapons, by MIA officers during the dispersal. The investigation covered all incidents and was extended to unlawful interference with journalists’ professional activities. All applicants were questioned. The Public Defender’s Office monitored the investigation and recommended examining mid- and high-level officials and the supervision of rubber bullet use. By the time of the ECtHR judgment, the investigation had been ongoing for more than four and a half years. Some individuals who admitted violence against police were convicted through plea bargains.

The ECtHR found a procedural violation of Article 3 because the criminal investigation into injuries caused by rubber bullets and alleged ill-treatment was ineffective and still ongoing after more than four and a half years. However, the Court refrained from deciding the substantive complaints under Articles 3, 10 and 11, given the scope of the ongoing domestic investigation and the need for further factual elucidation at domestic level. It stressed subsidiarity and shared responsibility. The Court also indicated individual measures under Article 46. The case was referred to the Grand Chamber on 23 September 2024.

**Case: Tsaava and Others v. Georgia**  
*European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), judgment of 7 May 2024; referred to the Grand Chamber on 23 September 2024.*

The case concerns five applications by 26 Georgian nationals arising from the dispersal of a demonstration in Tbilisi on 20–21 June 2019 and the alleged failure to investigate effectively the force used by police.

**Background and protest.** On 20 June 2019, the Interparliamentary Assembly on Orthodoxy held a session in the Georgian Parliament. A Russian State Duma member and IAO president, S.G., sat in the Speaker’s chair and delivered a speech in Russian. This provoked widespread civic and political protest. By 7 p.m., around 12,000 people had gathered peacefully in front of Parliament. Police formed a cordon blocking the entrance. Around 9:49 p.m., tensions rose when several hundred demonstrators tried to break through the cordon; some threw plastic bottles, dismantled metal barriers, and seized police shields and batons. Police reinforced the cordon and used batons and shields. Official statements warned of unlawful actions, and the Interior Minister described the events as an attempted storming of State institutions.

A second escalation began around 11:22 p.m., with renewed attempts to break the cordon, thrown objects, and assaults on officers. At 11:55 p.m., shooting began without warning; tear gas or pepper spray was used, and later rubber bullets. Police used tear gas, rubber bullets, and a water cannon until about 6:45 a.m. In total, 342 people were arrested, and over 200 were injured, including approximately 80 police officers and 40 journalists.

**Applicants and alleged violations.** The applicants were journalists, camera operators, photographers, and demonstrators. Most alleged injuries from rubber bullets; some alleged physical ill-treatment by police. Medical evidence included serious injuries: loss of an eye, open shoulder fracture, broken jaw, facial fractures, eye rupture, and diminished eyesight. Several journalists were filming, wearing press badges, and reportedly posed no threat when hit. One journalist alleged assault and threats to his equipment inside the Parliament yard. Some demonstrator applicants were arrested and charged with administrative offences; some were acquitted, and one was convicted.

The applicants complained, explicitly or in substance, under Article 3 (prohibition of ill-treatment) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy). Some also raised Article 10 (freedom of expression) and Article 11 (freedom of assembly). The central allegations were excessive use of force by police during the dispersal and the absence of an effective criminal investigation.

**Domestic investigation.** On 22 June 2019, the General Prosecutor’s Office opened an ex officio criminal investigation under Article 333 of the Criminal Code concerning alleged exceeding of authority by Ministry of Internal Affairs officers during the dispersal. It covered all incidents and was extended to unlawful interference with journalists’ professional activities. All applicants were questioned. Some were denied victim status; others were granted it between 2020 and 2023. The Public Defender’s Office monitored the investigation and recommended examining mid- and high-level officials and the supervision of rubber bullet use.

**Court’s findings.** The ECtHR found a procedural violation of Article 3 because the criminal investigation remained ineffective and was still ongoing after more than four and a half years into injuries sustained from rubber bullets and alleged ill-treatment. The Court refrained from deciding the substantive Article 3, Article 10, and Article 11 complaints due to the scope of the ongoing investigation and the need for further factual elucidation at the domestic level, emphasising subsidiarity and shared responsibility. It also indicated individual measures under Article 46.

In *Tsaava and Others v. Georgia*, the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) examined five applications brought by twenty-six Georgian nationals concerning the police dispersal of a demonstration in Tbilisi on 20–21 June 2019 and the subsequent criminal investigation. The applicants included journalists, camera operators/photographers, and demonstrators. All relied on Article 3 and Article 13; some also raised Articles 10 and 11.

The protests began after a member of the Russian State Duma, S.G., addressed an Interparliamentary Assembly on Orthodoxy session from the Georgian Parliament Speaker’s chair in Russian. A large crowd gathered outside Parliament; it was initially peaceful, with around 12,000 people. Police formed a cordon at the Parliament entrance. Tensions arose when some protesters pushed toward the gate, threw bottles, dismantled metal barriers, and seized police shields and batons. Police reinforced the cordon and used batons and shields. Later, from around 11:55 p.m., police fired tear gas/pepper spray and rubber bullets to disperse the crowd; water cannon was also used. The first shooting was not preceded by a warning. Dispersal and clashes continued until about 6:45 a.m. Over 200 people were injured, including about 80 police officers and 40 journalists; 342 people were arrested.

The applicants alleged excessive use of force by police and, for some, ill-treatment during arrest. Many applicants were journalists reporting on the events; some wore press badges. Domestic prosecutor reports and video analyses indicated that several applicants were standing calmly, filming or photographing, and posed no threat when hit—mostly by rubber bullets. Injuries ranged from minor wounds to grave harm: one applicant suffered an open fracture and life-threatening injuries; another lost an eye; another sustained a fractured jaw; others suffered eye injuries, facial fractures, open wounds, and bruising. Three applicants alleged physical ill-treatment, including during arrest; some arrests led to administrative proceedings, with mixed outcomes.

On 22 June 2019 the General Prosecutor’s Office opened an ex officio investigation into possible excessive official authority by MIA officers during the dispersal. It was later extended to alleged unlawful interference with journalists’ professional activities. All applicants were questioned, but the investigation remained ongoing for more than four and a half years. Some applicants were granted victim status; others were refused because the authorities had not yet determined whether an offence had been committed against them. The Public Defender’s Office monitored the investigation and recommended examining the role of mid- and high-level officials and the supervision of rubber-bullet use.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 3 under its procedural limb: the criminal investigation was ineffective and still ongoing. However, given the scope of the ongoing domestic investigation and the need for further factual elucidation, the Court refrained from deciding the substantive complaints under Articles 3, 10, and 11, stressing subsidiarity and shared responsibility. It also indicated individual measures under Article 46.

The applicant complained of the excessive length of criminal proceedings and of the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law. The Government disputed the complaint. They submitted that the overall length of the proceedings had been caused by the applicant’s conduct. They also argued that delays attributable to the domestic authorities had not been significant. In other words, Poland sought to justify the duration by placing primary responsibility on the applicant rather than on the national courts or other authorities.

The Court reiterated the established criteria for assessing whether the length of proceedings is reasonable: the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicant and the relevant authorities, and what was at stake for the applicant in the dispute. Having examined all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of justifying the overall length of the proceedings at the national level. The Court further noted that the applicant did not have at his disposal an effective remedy in respect of these complaints. It accordingly found violations of both Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention.

**Al-Habeeb v. Denmark** (ECtHR, Fourth Section, 12 Nov 2024) concerned an Iraqi national who entered Denmark in 1998 aged seven, was granted subsidiary protection, and later permanent residence. He lawfully lived in Denmark for more than 21 years. His parents and siblings lived there; he spoke fluent Danish, had completed Danish schooling and technical training, and had worked, most recently for four years as an assistant social educator. He had a Danish wife/partner (married in a Muslim ceremony) and a Danish daughter born in March 2021. He had prior convictions: attempted robbery in 2010 (aged 17, eight months’ imprisonment), attempted aggravated violence in 2011 (three months), and repeated violence in 2019 (three months), when he was warned of the risk of expulsion.

In September 2021, he was convicted of assault of a particularly offensive, brutal or dangerous nature. With three masked co-offenders, he stabbed the victim five times in the back, groin and lung; one stab hit a lung and could have been fatal without medical treatment. He was sentenced to two years and three months’ imprisonment. The District Court ordered expulsion with a twelve-year re-entry ban. Under the Danish Aliens Act, a sentence exceeding one year and six months normally required a permanent re-entry ban, but courts could shorten it if the longer ban would “for certain” breach Denmark’s international obligations, including Article 8 ECHR. The District Court expressly reduced the permanent ban to twelve years, finding a permanent ban would be particularly burdensome given his strong ties to Denmark. Yet it found expulsion proportionate: there was a significant risk of future serious violence; he had prior violent convictions and had been warned the year before; and his family could maintain contact through visits, telephone and online communication. The High Court upheld the judgment, and the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal. He was expelled to Iraq in July 2022 and later moved to Sweden with his family; his wife became pregnant with their second child in August 2023.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged that the expulsion and twelve-year re-entry ban violated Article 8 (private and family life). The key issue was whether Denmark had struck a fair balance between his long residence and family life and the public interest in preventing serious crime. The Court considered it decisive that the ban was time-limited, not permanent. The domestic courts had examined his residence length, integration, family ties, criminal history, recidivism risk, and the consequences of expulsion. They had also reduced the permanent ban to twelve years specifically to avoid an Article 8 breach. The prospect of his re-entering Denmark after the ban, including through family reunification with a Danish spouse or long-term cohabiting partner, was not purely theoretical. The Court found the domestic courts had given relevant and sufficient reasons and had duly assessed proportionality under its case-law. It therefore found **no violation of Article 8**.

**Case: Al-Habeeb v. Denmark (Application no. 14171/23), European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, judgment 12 November 2024 (final 17 March 2025).**

The applicant, Hamza Azeem Thamer Al-Habeeb, an Iraqi national born in 1991, entered Denmark in 1998 at age seven. He was granted residence in 1999 under section 7(2) of the Danish Aliens Act (subsidiary protection) and permanent residence in 2002. By the time of the expulsion order, he had lawfully lived in Denmark for over 21 years. He married a Danish national in a Muslim ceremony in 2020, and they had a daughter in March 2021. His parents and siblings lived in Denmark. He spoke, read and wrote Danish fluently, had attended Danish schools, and had worked for several years, most recently as an assistant social educator. He had no relatives in Iraq and spoke only broken Arabic.

The applicant had prior convictions: attempted robbery in 2010, aged 17, sentenced to eight months; attempted aggravated violence in 2011, sentenced to three months; and repeated violence in 2019, sentenced to three months, when he was warned of the risk of expulsion.

The decisive conviction occurred on 28 September 2021. The District Court convicted him under Articles 245 § 1 and 247 § 1 of the Danish Penal Code of assault of a particularly offensive, brutal or dangerous nature. On 26 July 2020, jointly with three masked co-offenders, he had stabbed the victim five times in the back, groin and lung. One stab hit the lung and could have been fatal without medical treatment. He was sentenced to two years and three months’ imprisonment. The court also ordered his expulsion with a twelve-year re-entry ban.

Under the Aliens Act, because the sentence exceeded one year and six months, a permanent re-entry ban would normally have been imposed under section 32(4)(vii). However, section 32(5)(i) allowed the courts to reduce the ban if a permanent one would “for certain” breach Denmark’s international obligations, including Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The District Court reduced the ban to twelve years, finding that a permanent ban would certainly violate Article 8. It nevertheless found expulsion proportionate: the offence was serious, there was a significant risk of future serious violence, and he had been warned only a year earlier. It accepted that his ties to Denmark were stronger than to Iraq but found his family could maintain contact by visits, telephone or online communication. The High Court of Eastern Denmark upheld the judgment on 19 May 2022, and the Appeals Permission Board refused leave to appeal to the Supreme Court on 20 December 2022.

The applicant was expelled to Iraq on 5 July 2022. He later moved to Sweden to live with his family; in August 2023 his wife became pregnant with their second child.

Before the European Court, he complained under Article 8 that the expulsion order and twelve-year re-entry ban violated his right to private and family life. The key facts relevant to that alleged violation were his long lawful residence, strong integration and family ties in Denmark, his serious criminal record and future risk, the domestic courts’ reduction of the permanent ban to twelve years, and the possibility that he might later re-enter Denmark, including through family reunification. The Court found that the domestic courts had given relevant and sufficient reasons and had duly assessed proportionality, particularly because the re-entry ban was time-limited rather than permanent. It concluded that there was no violation of Article 8.

In *Al-Habeeb v. Denmark* (Application no. 14171/23, judgment of 12 November 2024), the applicant, an Iraqi national born in 1991, complained under Article 8 ECHR that his expulsion from Denmark with a twelve-year re-entry ban breached his right to respect for private and family life. He entered Denmark in 1998 at age seven, was granted subsidiary protection in 1999, and obtained permanent residence in 2002. He had lived lawfully in Denmark for over twenty-one years, spoke Danish fluently, attended Danish schools, had worked for four years as an assistant social educator, and had parents and siblings in Denmark. He had no relatives in Iraq, spoke only broken Arabic, and could not read or write Arabic.

His criminal record included: a 2010 conviction for attempted robbery at age 17, sentenced to eight months’ imprisonment; a 2011 conviction for attempted aggravated violence, sentenced to three months’ imprisonment; and a 2019 conviction for repeated violence, sentenced to three months’ imprisonment, when he was warned of the risk of expulsion. In September 2021, the District Court convicted him under Articles 245 § 1 and 247 § 1 of the Penal Code of a particularly offensive, brutal or dangerous assault committed in July 2020. With three masked co-offenders, he had stabbed the victim five times in the back, groin and lung; the lung wound could have been fatal. He was sentenced to two years and three months’ imprisonment and expelled with a twelve-year re-entry ban.

Under Danish law, serious offences normally triggered a permanent re-entry ban, but courts could reduce its length if a permanent ban would “for certain” breach Denmark’s international obligations, including Article 8. The District Court found expulsion justified by the gravity of the offence and a significant risk that he would commit further serious violent offences, especially given his prior convictions and the earlier expulsion warning. It acknowledged his strong ties to Denmark and the burden of expulsion, but concluded that a twelve-year, rather than permanent, ban made the measure proportionate. It noted that his wife and daughter could maintain contact through visits and remote communication. The High Court upheld the judgment in May 2022, and leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused in December 2022. He was expelled to Iraq in July 2022 and later moved to Sweden to live with his family; his wife became pregnant again in 2023.

Before the ECtHR, the key Article 8 issue was whether the expulsion and twelve-year re-entry ban struck a fair balance between the applicant’s private and family life and the State’s interest in public safety and immigration control. The Court emphasised that the length of the re-entry ban was decisive, and that a time-limited ban could render expulsion compatible with Article 8. It also examined whether the applicant could realistically re-enter Denmark after the ban. Although Iraq was a visa-group country with high immigration risk, the Court found that the prospect of re-entry on family reunification grounds for a foreigner with a Danish spouse or long-term cohabiting partner was not purely theoretical; statistics showed some expelled foreigners had later been granted residence permits, including for family reunification. The domestic courts had therefore given relevant and sufficient reasons and duly assessed proportionality in light of ECtHR case-law. The ECtHR found no violation of Article 8.

In *W.R. v. the Netherlands* (Application no. 989/18, judgment of 27 August 2024), the applicant alleged that his criminal proceedings were unfair under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) of the Convention because he did not have legal assistance during initial police interviews and an on-site visit.

The victim, the applicant’s ex-wife, disappeared in January 2014. When police visited the applicant on 11 January 2014, they noticed a strong smell of a combustible substance, an injury to his hand, blood spatter, and a partly burnt box. The applicant gave conflicting accounts about the box and his injury. He was arrested early on 12 January 2014 on suspicion of manslaughter. He was informed that a lawyer could be assigned free of charge before questioning, or that he could consult a lawyer of his choice. He did not respond, so the Legal Aid Duty Roster Service was notified. Later that morning, at about 10:30 a.m., he consulted his lawyer.

That evening, without his lawyer present, the applicant was questioned by police. After being informed of his right to remain silent, he gave a detailed confession, admitting that and how he had violently killed the victim. He also said he wished to cooperate and show police relevant locations. From 8:12 p.m. to 9:38 p.m., again without a lawyer, he took part in an on-site visit, during which police discovered the victim’s body, her bag, and two discarded tarpaulins. On 13 January 2014, again without a lawyer, he gave a further detailed account, including statements relevant to premeditation: he described feeling angry after a telephone call with the victim, considering scenarios, wanting to kill her, conceiving a plan, and laying out a knife and tarpaulins in the garage. He said he later “came to his senses” on the sofa but did not remove the items, and later killed the victim in the garage. Further police interviews occurred on 20 January, 29 January, and 6 February 2014, also without a lawyer.

On 14 January and 27 August 2014, the applicant appeared before an investigating judge with his lawyer. Initially he stood by his statements; later he retracted parts concerning premeditation, claiming they were based on assumptions or fragmented memories rather than fact. He denied a preconceived plan. The police interviews were audio-visually recorded, and records were made available to the defence.

At first instance, the Regional Court admitted the statements, found no irreparable procedural breach, convicted the applicant of manslaughter, and acquitted him of murder because premeditation was not sufficiently proved. The Court of Appeal reversed, convicted him of murder, and sentenced him to fourteen years’ imprisonment. It found no Convention violation under the then-applicable Dutch approach, noting he had consulted a lawyer before the first substantive interview, was informed of his right to silence, and gave reliable statements. The Supreme Court found an error in the exclusion reasoning but declined cassation because prior consultation had occurred; it reduced the sentence for a reasonable-time violation.

Before the European Court, the key issue was the lack of a lawyer during the initial interviews and on-site visit. The Court applied very strict scrutiny because the restriction occurred at the preliminary investigation stage without compelling reasons. Nevertheless, examining the overall fairness of the proceedings, it found no irretrievable prejudice: the applicant had prior lawyer consultation before the first substantive police interview, was repeatedly cautioned, the interviews were recorded and disclosed, a forensic psychologist found him fit, he had counsel at investigating-judge hearings, his later retractions were unconvincing, and objective evidence corroborated key facts. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c).

The Court of Appeal admitted the statements, convicted him of murder, and sentenced him to fourteen years, finding premeditation based largely on his own detailed statements. Although the Court applied very strict scrutiny, it found no violation in the circumstances: the applicant had prior lawyer consultation, was informed of his silence rights, received repeated cautions, gave detailed voluntary statements, was found fit by a psychologist, the interviews were recorded and disclosed, and he later had lawyer assistance at judicial hearings.

Rizzo Striano v. Italy (Application no. 54800/16) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, First Section, sitting as a Committee. The applicant, represented by Mr I. Toscano, lodged the application against Italy on 13 September 2016. The Italian Government was given notice of the application. The Court rejected the Government’s objection to examination by a Committee. The Committee comprised Krzysztof Wojtyczek (President), Lətif Hüseynov and Ivana Jelić, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The Court deliberated on 14 December 2023 and delivered judgment on 18 January 2024.

The key facts concern the non-enforcement of a domestic decision in the applicant’s favour. The applicant owned a plot of land that was occupied for the construction of an aqueduct. An aqueduct easement was also established over the land. A domestic decision awarded the applicant damages for the occupation of his plot and compensation for the establishment of the aqueduct easement. These sums were to be paid by the Reclamation Consortium of the Plain of Sybaris and the Middle Crati Valley (Consorzio di Bonifica della Piana di Sibari e della Media Valle del Crati). The Consortium is a public-law entity. Despite obtaining a favourable domestic decision, the applicant did not receive the damages and compensation. The domestic decision remained unenforced. The applicant’s further details and facts were set out in the appended table to the judgment.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained specifically about the failure to enforce that domestic decision. He relied on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees a fair trial and includes the right of access to court and the effective execution of final judicial decisions, and on Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, which protects property. The essence of his complaint was that the Italian State had failed to ensure that the final decision in his favour was executed, thereby depriving him of the practical benefit of the judgment and of the compensation owed for the interference with his land. The alleged violation therefore did not concern the original occupation or the easement as such, but the subsequent failure of the authorities to secure payment from the public Consortium.

In its assessment, the Court applied its settled case-law that execution of a judgment given by any court must be regarded as an integral part of the “trial” for the purposes of Article 6 § 1. A final and enforceable judicial decision cannot remain inoperative to the detriment of a litigant. The State is responsible for enforcing judgments against public bodies and cannot rely on internal difficulties, such as lack of funds or organisational problems, to justify prolonged non-enforcement. The failure also engaged Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 because it prevented the applicant from obtaining compensation that constituted a possession or at least a legitimate expectation under Italian law. The Government did not put forward facts or arguments capable of persuading the Court that the non-enforcement was justified or proportionate.

The Court therefore found violations of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The judgment is final, subject only to editorial revision.

In *Daugaard Sorensen v. Denmark* (App. No. 25650/22, ECtHR, 15 October 2024), the applicant reported to Danish police that she had been raped by A during the night of 6–7 June 2021. A was remanded in custody on 8 June 2021. Police investigated, including interviewing the applicant and witnesses, examining the scene and the applicant’s clothes, and searching A’s home. A was released on 18 June 2021. On 30 July 2021, the first-instance public prosecutor dropped the charges, finding insufficient evidence because there were two opposing statements and no conclusive corroborating evidence. The applicant appealed.

On 16 September 2021, the Regional State Prosecutor reversed that decision and decided to proceed with the prosecution. Under section 724(2) of the Danish Administration of Justice Act, notice of that decision had to be served on A within two months of the initial drop decision—by 30 September 2021—either through A’s compulsory Digital Post account or by registered letter. The prosecution then made at least three consecutive errors. First, a database typing error wrongly suggested that A could not receive Digital Post, so the prosecutor sent a registered letter. Second, another database error omitted A’s c/o address, so the letter was returned on 23 September 2021 marked “addressee unknown at this address.” Third, although internal guidelines required checking the returned letter, verifying A’s address, checking the time-limit, and considering another service attempt, another error meant no further address lookup or service attempt was made. A was therefore not notified before the 30 September deadline.

On 13 October 2021, the first-instance prosecutor filed an indictment. In November 2021, A’s defence lawyer asked for dismissal because the two-month time-limit had expired. The prosecutor agreed, and on 16 November 2021 the District Court dismissed the case. Prosecution for the alleged rape was no longer possible. The prosecutor later apologised for the procedural error.

The applicant sought compensation. On 15 November 2022, the Criminal Injuries Compensation Board rejected her claim, finding she had not sufficiently established that she was the victim of a crime. Under Chapter 93a of the Administration of Justice Act, the Director of Public Prosecutions indicated that she might claim compensation against the police or prosecution for administrative errors, though the scope was uncertain. On 31 January 2023, the applicant filed such a claim. On 24 April 2023, the prosecutor rejected it, holding that the claims fell outside Chapter 93a: rape-related damage did not fall within section 1018h, and the administrative-error claim was not covered because it did not arise from an official procedural act in the criminal prosecution of the claimant. The Director of Public Prosecutions upheld that decision on 30 June 2023, stating it was final but that the applicant could ask a court to decide the compensation claim or bring civil proceedings. The applicant did not bring civil proceedings.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Articles 3, 6, 8, and 13 of the Convention. The Court found violations of the positive obligations under Articles 3 and 8. It emphasised that the prosecution’s consecutive errors—especially the failure to comply with the statutory time-limit—led to the very serious consequence of preventing prosecution. Consequently, the applicant was not secured an effective prosecution or judicial review regarding the rape offence she had reported. The Court identified significant flaws in Denmark’s procedural response to her complaint.

**Case:** *Daugaard Sorensen v. Denmark* (Application no. 25650/22), European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section), judgment of 15 October 2024 (final 15 January 2025).

The applicant, a Danish woman, reported to police that she had been raped by A during the night of 6–7 June 2021. Police interviewed her and, on 8 June, A was remanded in custody on suspicion of rape and non-consensual sexual activity. A was released on 18 June. On 30 July 2021, the first-instance prosecutor dropped the charges under section 721(1)(ii) of the Administration of Justice Act, finding insufficient evidence and conflicting statements. The applicant appealed.

On 16 September 2021, the Regional State Prosecutor reversed that decision and decided to proceed with prosecution. Under section 724(2), notice of this decision had to be served on A before 30 September 2021—within two months of the original decision—either via A’s mandatory Digital Post account or by registered letter. However, at least three consecutive errors by the Prosecution Service prevented compliance. First, a typing error in the prosecutor’s database wrongly indicated that A could not receive Digital Post, so a registered letter was sent instead. Second, another database error omitted A’s c/o address from the letter, and it was returned on 23 September 2021 as “addressee unknown.” Third, although internal guidelines required the returned letter to be examined—including checking the address and the time-limit—the prosecutor’s office failed to look up A’s address again. A was therefore not notified before the deadline.

On 13 October 2021, the first-instance prosecutor filed an indictment. In November 2021, A’s lawyer argued that the case should be dismissed because the statutory two-month time-limit had not been met. The prosecutor agreed, and on 16 November 2021 the District Court dismissed the case. Prosecution of A for the alleged rape became impossible. The prosecutor later apologised for the procedural error.

The applicant then sought compensation. On 15 November 2022, the Criminal Injuries Compensation Board rejected her claim, finding she had not sufficiently established that she was the victim of a crime. She also brought a claim under Chapter 93a of the Administration of Justice Act against the prosecutor. On 24 April 2023, the prosecutor rejected it as outside the scope of that Chapter; the Director of Public Prosecutions upheld that decision on 30 June 2023. The applicant was told she could pursue ordinary civil proceedings, but she did not do so.

Before the Court, the applicant complained under Articles 3, 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention. The Court found violations of Articles 3 and 8 concerning the State’s positive obligations. The central issue was the withdrawal of charges caused by prosecutorial errors. The Court emphasised that at least three consecutive errors by the Prosecution Service—especially the failure to comply with the statutory time-limit—led to the very serious consequence of preventing prosecution. As a result, the applicant was not secured an effective prosecution or judicial review in respect of the rape offence she had reported. The Court identified significant flaws in Denmark’s procedural response. Although compensation mechanisms existed, they did not provide a sufficient remedy in the circumstances. The case illustrates how procedural failures by prosecutors can breach positive obligations to investigate and prosecute serious sexual offences under Articles 3 and 8.

Ms Emma Daugaard Sorensen reported to Danish police that she had been raped by A during the night of 6–7 June 2021. She was interviewed the same day. On 8 June 2021, the District Court remanded A in custody on reasonable suspicion of rape and non-consensual sexual activity other than intercourse. The police investigated, interviewing the applicant and witnesses, examining the scene and the applicant’s clothes, and searching A’s home. A was released on 18 June 2021.

On 30 July 2021, the first-instance prosecutor dropped the charges, finding insufficient evidence: there were opposing statements and no conclusive corroboration. The applicant appealed. On 16 September 2021, the Regional State Prosecutor reversed that decision and decided to proceed with the prosecution. Under Danish law, that decision had to be served on A within two months of the initial withdrawal decision—by 30 September 2021—either via his compulsory Digital Post account or by registered letter.

The prosecutor attempted notification but committed at least three consecutive errors. First, a database typing error wrongly indicated that A could not receive Digital Post, so a registered letter was sent instead. Second, another database error omitted A’s c/o address, causing the letter to be returned on 23 September 2021 marked “addressee unknown.” Third, although internal guidelines required the returned letter to be checked—including A’s address, the statutory deadline, and the possibility of a further attempt—a further error meant no proper re-check occurred. Consequently, A was not notified before the 30 September deadline.

On 13 October 2021, the first-instance prosecutor filed an indictment. In November 2021, A’s defence lawyer sought dismissal because the two-month time-limit had not been complied with. The prosecutor agreed, and on 16 November 2021 the District Court dismissed the case. It thus became impossible to prosecute A for the alleged rape. The prosecutor later apologised for the procedural error.

The applicant sought compensation from the Criminal Injuries Compensation Board, which rejected her claim on 15 November 2022, finding she had not sufficiently established that she was the victim of a crime. Later, the Director of Public Prosecutions indicated that compensation might be sought against the police or prosecution service under Chapter 93a of the Administration of Justice Act. The applicant claimed compensation under the summary procedure in section 1018h for pain and suffering, medical expenses, ruined clothes, and injury to feelings, the latter relating partly to the prosecution errors. On 24 April 2023, the prosecutor rejected the claim as outside Chapter 93a. The Director of Public Prosecutions upheld that decision, stating it was final but that the applicant could ask a court to decide or could bring civil proceedings. She did not bring civil proceedings.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Articles 3, 6, 8, and 13 that the withdrawal of charges and failure to prosecute violated the State’s positive obligations to investigate and prosecute rape and to protect her private life, and that available remedies were ineffective. The Court focused on Articles 3 and 8. It found significant flaws in Denmark’s procedural response. The prosecution errors—especially the failure to comply with the statutory time-limit—had the very serious consequence of preventing prosecution. The applicant was not secured an effective prosecution or judicial review in respect of the rape offence she reported. The Court therefore found violations of Article 3 and Article 8 of the Convention.
