The case of *Souroullas Kay and Zannettos v. Cyprus* (Application no. 1618/18) is a judgment of the Third Section of the European Court of Human Rights, delivered on 26 November 2024 and becoming final on 28 April 2025. The applicants, Gregoris Souroullas Kay and Venizelos Zannettos, are Cypriot nationals. They lodged their application against the Republic of Cyprus on 3 January 2018, alleging violations of Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights in the context of criminal proceedings that resulted in their convictions. The first applicant was convicted of money laundering and the second of extortion. The central issue was whether their trial was fair under Article 6 § 1 and whether their defence rights, including those under Article 6 § 3 (d), were respected.

The alleged violations arose from two main aspects of the criminal proceedings. First, the applicants complained that their convictions were based to a “most decisive” extent on the testimony of an accomplice. The accomplice was not prompted by any formal deal with the prosecution, but he was spared prosecution. The applicants argued that reliance on such testimony rendered the trial unfair, because the accomplice had a strong incentive to testify against them in order to avoid criminal liability. This raised questions about the reliability of the evidence and the fairness of the proceedings under Article 6 § 1.

Second, the applicants complained about their inability to access material held by the prosecution. Specifically, the domestic courts refused to give the defence access to a disk image held by the prosecution. The applicants contended that this refusal violated their rights of defence and their entitlement to adequate facilities to prepare their case, as guaranteed by Article 6 § 1 and Article 6 § 3 (d). They argued that without access to the disk image, they could not properly challenge the prosecution’s case or examine the evidence against them, thereby undermining the equality of arms between the prosecution and the defence.

The European Court of Human Rights gave notice to the Cypriot Government of these two complaints—namely, the inability to access prosecution material and the use of accomplice testimony—and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The parties submitted observations, and the Court deliberated in private on 13 February 2024 and 15 October 2024.

On the merits, the Court examined whether the criminal trial could be considered fair within the meaning of Article 6 § 1 despite the conviction being based decisively on accomplice testimony. It noted that the accomplice had not been prompted by any deal but had been spared prosecution. The Court found that this did not, in itself, render the trial unfair. It also considered the refusal to grant the defence access to the prosecution’s disk image. The Court concluded that this refusal did not amount to a breach of Article 6 § 1 or Article 6 § 3 (d). Accordingly, the applicants’ complaints were rejected.

The judgment is significant because it confirms that a conviction based to a decisive extent on accomplice evidence does not automatically violate the right to a fair trial, particularly where the accomplice was not induced by a formal deal. It also clarifies that denial of defence access to prosecution material, such as a disk image, will not necessarily breach Article 6 if the domestic courts’ refusal is compatible with the overall fairness of the proceedings and the rights of the defence. The case thus reinforces the Court’s contextual approach to Article 6, assessing fairness as a whole rather than applying automatic rules.

The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered judgment in *Souroullas Kay and Zannettos v. Cyprus* (Application no. 1618/18) on 26 November 2024; it became final on 28 April 2025. The applicants, Gregoris Souroullas Kay and Venizelos Zannettos, are Cypriot nationals. They were convicted in Cyprus—Souroullas Kay for money laundering and Zannettos for extortion. Their application alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (fair hearing in criminal proceedings) and Article 6 § 3 (d) (rights of defence, including adequate facilities to prepare a defence). The case concerned two main evidentiary and procedural issues.

First, the applicants complained about the use of accomplice testimony against them. The domestic convictions rested, to the “most decisive” extent, on testimony given by an accomplice. That accomplice had been spared prosecution—described in the judgment as immunity from prosecution—while the applicants were tried and convicted. The applicants argued that reliance on such testimony made their trial unfair under Article 6 § 1. The Court examined this complaint but found no violation. A key fact in its assessment was that the accomplice had not been prompted by any deal or inducement from the prosecution; although he was spared prosecution, his testimony was not obtained through a bargained-for agreement. In the Court’s view, this did not render the trial unfair despite the decisive weight of the accomplice’s evidence.

Second, the applicants complained about their inability to access material held by the prosecution. Specifically, the defence was refused access to a disk image in the prosecution’s possession. The domestic courts declined to order that the defence be given access to that disk image. The applicants argued that this refusal violated their rights of defence and their entitlement to adequate facilities to prepare their defence under Article 6 § 1 and Article 6 § 3 (d). The Court held that the domestic courts’ refusal to give the defence access to the prosecution’s disk image did not amount to a breach of Article 6. Accordingly, there was no violation on this ground either.

Procedurally, the application was lodged with the Court on 3 January 2018. The Court gave notice to the Cypriot Government of the applicants’ complaints concerning (i) their inability to access material held by the prosecution and (ii) the use of accomplice testimony against them. It declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The parties submitted observations. The Chamber deliberated in private on 13 February 2024 and 15 October 2024, adopting the judgment on the latter date. The judgment was prepared by the Registry and does not bind the Court.

In essence, the key facts relevant to the alleged violations were: the applicants’ convictions for money laundering and extortion respectively; the prosecution’s reliance to a decisive extent on an accomplice who was spared prosecution but not induced by any deal; and the defence’s denied access to a prosecution disk image. The Court concluded that neither the use of the accomplice’s testimony nor the refusal of access to the disk image rendered the criminal proceedings unfair or breached the applicants’ defence rights.

The case of **Souroullas Kay and Zannettos v. Cyprus** (Application no. 1618/18) concerned two Cypriot nationals, Mr Gregoris Souroullas Kay and Mr Venizelos Zannettos, who were convicted in Cyprus of money laundering and extortion respectively. They lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 3 January 2018, alleging violations of Article 6 of the Convention. The Third Section delivered judgment on 26 November 2024; it became final on 28 April 2025.

The applicants’ complaints had two main factual bases. First, their convictions were based to the “most decisive” extent on the testimony of an accomplice. The accomplice had been spared prosecution. The applicants argued that reliance on this evidence made their trial unfair under Article 6 § 1. The Court noted, however, that the accomplice had not been prompted by any deal or agreement with the prosecution; he was not induced to testify in exchange for immunity or other benefits. This was central to the Court’s assessment. Although the accomplice evidence was decisive, the absence of a prosecutorial deal meant that its use did not, by itself, render the criminal proceedings unfair.

Second, the applicants complained under Article 6 § 1 and Article 6 § 3 (d) about their inability to access material held by the prosecution. In particular, the domestic courts refused to give the defence access to a disk image held by the prosecution. The applicants alleged that this refusal infringed their rights of defence and denied them adequate facilities to prepare their case. They claimed that access to the disk image was necessary to challenge the prosecution’s evidence and to ensure equality of arms between the prosecution and the defence.

The European Court of Human Rights gave notice to the Cypriot Government of the applicants’ complaints concerning (i) the inability to access material held by the prosecution and (ii) the use of accomplice testimony against them. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

On the merits, the Court examined the fairness of the criminal proceedings as a whole. It found no violation of Article 6 § 1 in respect of the accomplice testimony: despite its decisive role, the accomplice had not been prompted by any deal, and the trial was not rendered unfair on that account. It also found no violation of Article 6 § 1 or Article 6 § 3 (d) concerning the refusal to give the defence access to the prosecution’s disk image. That refusal did not amount to a breach of the applicants’ defence rights or of the requirement to provide adequate facilities. Accordingly, the Court dismissed the applicants’ complaints, finding no violation of Article 6.

**Rizzo and Others v. Malta** (App. no. 36318/21) is a European Court of Human Rights case decided on 16 January 2024 (final 16 April 2024). The applicants were three Maltese nationals who held the perpetual utile dominium of a property in St Julian’s, inherited in 1994. In 1972, the property had been leased under a temporary sub-emphyteusis for 21 years. When that expired in 1993, the tenant, a Maltese citizen using the property as his ordinary residence, relied on the Housing (Decontrol) Ordinance, as amended by Act XXIII of 1979, to retain possession under a lease. The annual rent was initially about EUR 303, rising by law to EUR 454 in 2008, EUR 502 in 2013, and EUR 519 in 2016. The applicants complained that this old rent regime imposed an indefinite unilateral lease at a rent far below market value, breaching Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention.

In April 2019, the applicants brought constitutional redress proceedings before the First Hall, Civil Court (constitutional competence), alleging a breach of Article 1 Protocol No. 1 and seeking compensation for damage up to 31 December 2018. They did not seek the tenant’s eviction. A court expert valued the property at EUR 850,000 with development potential (EUR 320,000 as it stood) and assessed annual market rental values ranging from EUR 1,980 in 1993 to EUR 10,560 in 2018. In January 2021, the First Hall found a violation, holding that the applicants had suffered a disproportionate burden, and awarded EUR 30,000 in pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage for the period until 10 April 2018, when new Article 12B of the Ordinance provided a further remedy. No costs were imposed, and neither party appealed.

In parallel, after Act XXVII of 2018 introduced Article 12B, the applicants filed ordinary proceedings before the Rent Regulation Board. They sought recognition of the tenants, a means test, and either a rent increase up to 2% of open market value or eviction if the tenants failed the means test. In December 2020, the Board found the tenants satisfied the means test and increased the annual rent to EUR 5,000 for two years and EUR 7,500 for the next four; the Court of Appeal confirmed this in December 2021.

The applicants complained under Article 13 read with Article 1 Protocol No. 1 that they lacked an effective remedy. They argued that at the time to appeal in early 2021, a Constitutional Court appeal was not effective due to long-standing jurisprudence, despite changes in late 2020 and 2021. The Government argued that constitutional redress, especially appeal to the Constitutional Court, was effective; the applicants could have appealed the EUR 30,000 award, and recent case-law showed the Constitutional Court was increasing compensation and applying the *Cauchi* guidelines. The Government also noted the applicants had obtained higher future rent through Article 12B proceedings.

The Court found the Article 13 complaint admissible. It concluded that, as of 2021, following *Cauchi* and subsequent legal amendments, an appeal to the Constitutional Court had become an accessible and effective remedy capable of providing redress, with a reasonable prospect of success in old rent law cases. It found no violation of Article 13. However, given the timeline, the applicants were not expected to lodge a Constitutional Court appeal before the expiry of the appeal time-limit because the remedy had been ineffective at that time due to judicial practice. The Court found a violation of Article 1 Protocol No. 1 due to the disproportionate burden caused by the inadequate rent and the insufficient domestic redress at first instance.

**Rizzo and Others v. Malta** (Application no. 36318/21) concerned three Maltese nationals who owned the *utile dominium* of a property at 17, Triq Gort, Paceville, St Julian’s, inherited in 1994. In 1972, their predecessor leased the property under a temporary sub-emphyteusis for twenty-one years. When that expired in January 1993, the tenant—a Maltese citizen using the property as his ordinary residence—relied on the Housing (Decontrol) Ordinance, as amended by Act XXIII of 1979, to retain possession under a lease at the statutory annual rent of approximately EUR 303. The rent later rose by law to about EUR 454 in 2008, EUR 502 in 2013, and EUR 519 in 2016.

An expert valued the property at EUR 320,000 as it stood, or EUR 850,000 considering development potential. The annual market rental value was assessed at EUR 1,980 in 1993, EUR 3,120 in 1998, EUR 4,080 in 2003, EUR 6,360 in 2008, EUR 6,240 in 2013, and EUR 10,560 in 2018. The statutory rent was therefore substantially below market levels.

In April 2019, the applicants filed constitutional redress proceedings before the First Hall, Civil Court (constitutional competence). They alleged that the Ordinance, as amended, imposed a unilateral lease relationship for an indeterminate time without a fair and adequate rent, in breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. They limited their claims to 31 December 2018 and sought compensation, not eviction. In January 2021, the First Hall found a violation and a disproportionate burden, awarding EUR 30,000 in pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages for the violation up to 10 April 2018, when new Article 12B of the Ordinance provided a further remedy. No party appealed.

In parallel, Act XXVII of 2018 had amended the Ordinance and introduced Article 12B, effective August 2018. In April 2019, the applicants also instituted ordinary proceedings before the Rent Regulation Board, seeking recognition of the occupants as tenants, a means test, an increase in rent to no more than 2% of open market value, or eviction within five years if the tenant failed the means test. In December 2020, the Rent Regulation Board found the tenants satisfied the means test and increased the annual rent to EUR 5,000 for the first two years and EUR 7,500 for the following four years. The Court of Appeal confirmed that decision in December 2021.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants complained under Article 13, read with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, that they had no effective remedy. They argued that when their appeal deadline arose after the January 2021 judgment, an appeal to the Constitutional Court was not effective or practical. Although there were signs of change in late 2020, long-standing jurisprudence had treated that remedy as ineffective, and only after *Cauchi v. Malta* in March 2021 did the Constitutional Court begin consistently applying adequate-compensation guidelines. The Government contended that constitutional redress and an appeal to the Constitutional Court were effective, relying on 2020–2021 case-law where compensation was increased and *Cauchi* applied.

The Court declared the Article 13 complaint admissible. The case concerned whether an appeal to the Constitutional Court in old rent cases was an accessible and effective remedy as of 2021, and whether the applicants should have exhausted it. The headnote indicates that, as of 2021, such an appeal became effective under the *Cauchi* guidelines and subsequent amendments, but given the timeline and prior judicial practice, the applicants were not expected to lodge one before the appeal time-limit expired. The Court also found a disproportionate burden under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to inadequate rent and insufficient domestic redress at first instance.

**Case: Rizzo and Others v. Malta (ECtHR, Second Section, 16 January 2024)**

The applicants are three Maltese nationals who own the perpetual utile dominium of a property in St Julian’s, Malta, inherited in 1994. In 1972, their predecessor leased the property under a temporary sub-emphyteusis for 21 years. When that expired in 1993, the tenant relied on the Housing (Decontrol) Ordinance, as amended by Act XXIII of 1979, to retain the property as his ordinary residence under a statutory lease. The annual rent was initially about EUR 303, then increased to EUR 454 in 2008, EUR 502 in 2013, and EUR 519 in 2016.

In April 2019, the applicants brought constitutional redress proceedings before the First Hall, Civil Court (constitutional competence). They alleged that the Ordinance, as amended, forced them into a unilateral lease of indefinite duration at a rent that did not reflect fair market value, in breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. They limited their claim to 31 December 2018, sought compensation, and expressly did not seek the tenant’s eviction. A court-appointed expert estimated the property’s 2019 sale value at EUR 850,000 with development potential, or EUR 320,000 as it stood. Annual market rental values were estimated at EUR 1,980 in 1993 and EUR 10,560 in 2018.

By judgment of 25 January 2021, the First Hall found a violation of the applicants’ property rights and awarded EUR 30,000 in pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage for the period up to 10 April 2018, when new Article 12B of the Ordinance introduced a further remedy. No appeal was filed.

In parallel proceedings, Act XXVII of 2018 had introduced Article 12B. In April 2019, the applicants applied to the Rent Regulation Board seeking recognition of the tenancy, a means test, and either a rent increase up to 2% of the property’s market value or eviction within five years if the tenants failed the means test. In December 2020, the Rent Regulation Board found that the tenants satisfied the means test and increased the annual rent to EUR 5,000 for the first two years and EUR 7,500 for the following four years. The Court of Appeal confirmed this in December 2021.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants complained under Article 13, read with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, that they had no effective domestic remedy. They also complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the old rent laws imposed a disproportionate burden. The Government argued that an appeal to the Constitutional Court was an effective remedy, especially in light of 2020–2021 case-law applying the compensation guidelines from *Cauchi v. Malta*. The applicants contended that, at the time their appeal deadline expired, the Constitutional Court remedy was still ineffective due to long-standing judicial practice, and that recent awards remained inadequate.

The ECtHR held that, as of 2021, an appeal to the Constitutional Court was an accessible and effective remedy capable of providing redress and offering a reasonable prospect of success in old rent-law claims, with consistent application of *Cauchi* guidelines. The new Article 12B also provided a potentially effective procedure for eviction or higher future rent. Therefore, there was no violation of Article 13. However, the Court found that the rent imposed constituted a disproportionate burden on the applicants and that the first-instance domestic redress was insufficient, violating Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. On exhaustion, given the timeline, the applicants were not expected to lodge a Constitutional Court appeal before their time-limit expired because the remedy was ineffective at that time due to judicial practice.
001-237797:
The case of *Zahariev v. North Macedonia* (Application no. 26760/22), decided by the European Court of Human Rights on 5 November 2024, concerned the applicant’s complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that North Macedonian criminal courts failed to address his argument that he enjoyed immunity from criminal prosecution under the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations.

The applicant, Borislav Zahariev, was a Bulgarian national. Between 2004 and 2009 he worked as financial director of a telecommunications company in North Macedonia. From January 2007, his wife worked as an official at the Bulgarian Cultural and Information Centre attached to the Bulgarian embassy. In January 2012, an investigating judge opened an investigation against the applicant and another person for abuse of office and tax evasion allegedly committed in 2008 in connection with his work at the telecommunications company. He was indicted in February 2013.

In June 2013, the applicant and his lawyer informed the Skopje Court of First Instance that he held a special identity card issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs granting him absolute immunity from prosecution. The card stated that he enjoyed immunity from criminal jurisdiction, arrest or police custody in North Macedonia. The Ministry later explained that the card had been issued because of his wife’s status as an official of the Centre, and that under Article 37(2) of the Vienna Convention, family members of administrative and technical staff enjoyed certain immunities, but not for acts performed outside official functions. The applicant argued that this exception concerned only civil and administrative jurisdiction, not criminal jurisdiction.

The trial court convicted him in absentia in September 2015, finding that he did not enjoy immunity because the alleged offence was unrelated to official functions. The appellate court remitted the case for reconsideration of immunity. In the remitted proceedings, the applicant relied on the ICJ’s *Arrest Warrant* case, arguing that immunity from criminal jurisdiction made no distinction between official and private acts and could only be removed by waiver, cessation of functions, or prosecution by the sending State or an international court. None of those conditions applied.

The Ministry provided further information in 2018: the applicant had held special identity cards at various times; in 2010 the embassy had requested cancellation of his registration as spouse of an official; in January 2012 a card was again issued and later extended to May 2014; after June 2014, only his wife’s card was extended because criminal proceedings were pending against him. A Ministry representative stated in 2019 that the applicant’s immunity could be terminated because he had engaged in professional or commercial activity contrary to Article 42 of the Vienna Convention.

In December 2019, the trial court again convicted the applicant in absentia of abuse of office and sentenced him to five years’ imprisonment. It held that his immunity had ceased when he took private employment, contrary to Article 42, and that Article 31(1)(c) excluded immunity for acts outside official functions. The appellate court and Supreme Court upheld the conviction, reasoning that the applicant had lost or could not invoke immunity because of his employment and failure to invoke immunity earlier.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 6 § 1. Although the applicant had raised specific and arguable arguments under the Vienna Convention—particularly that immunity from criminal jurisdiction is not subject to the Article 31(1)(c) civil/administrative exception, that Article 42 does not automatically terminate immunity, and that only express waiver or cessation rules apply—the domestic courts failed to engage with those arguments. Instead, they relied on general findings that he had “lost” immunity through employment. This failure to address the core immunity argument rendered the proceedings unfair.

In *Zahariev v. North Macedonia* (Application no. 26760/22, ECtHR, 5 November 2024), the applicant was a Bulgarian national who worked as financial director of a telecommunications company in North Macedonia between 2004 and 2009. From January 2007, his wife worked as an official at the Bulgarian Cultural and Information Centre attached to the Bulgarian embassy. In January 2012, an investigating judge opened an investigation against the applicant for abuse of office and tax evasion allegedly committed in 2008 in connection with his telecom employment. He was indicted in February 2013.

The central factual issue was whether the applicant enjoyed immunity from criminal prosecution under the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations. In June 2013, the applicant and his lawyer told the Skopje Court of First Instance that he held a special identity card issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs granting him absolute immunity from prosecution, arrest, or police custody. The card was based on his wife’s status as a member of the administrative and technical staff of the embassy. The Ministry later confirmed that, under Article 37(2) of the Vienna Convention, family members of such staff enjoyed certain privileges and immunities, but that this did not cover acts performed outside official functions. The applicant argued that this exception concerned only civil and administrative jurisdiction, not criminal jurisdiction.

During the domestic proceedings, the applicant repeatedly argued that his immunity was absolute in criminal matters and could not be removed simply because he had worked for a private company. He relied on the ICJ’s *Arrest Warrant* judgment, arguing that criminal immunity made no distinction between official and private acts, and that prosecution could only occur in limited circumstances—none of which applied to him. He also stressed that he had held a valid special identity card when he was indicted in February 2013.

Ministry correspondence in 2018 stated that the applicant had been issued cards in 2007, 2009, and 2012, with the last extended until May 2014. In 2010, the embassy had asked to cancel his registration because of the Article 42 prohibition on diplomatic agents engaging in commercial activity. After 2014, only his wife’s card was extended because criminal proceedings were pending against him. A Ministry representative testified in 2019 that the applicant’s immunity could be terminated, including by professional or commercial activity contrary to Article 42, and invoked Article 31(1)(c).

In December 2019, the trial court convicted the applicant in absentia of abuse of office and sentenced him to five years’ imprisonment. It found that his immunity had ceased when he took private employment contrary to Article 42, that he had not invoked immunity during the investigation, that the embassy had not invoked it, and that his card had not been extended after 2014. The appellate court affirmed in March 2021, relying on Article 31(1)(c), and the Supreme Court affirmed in November 2021, finding that the applicant had lost the right to invoke privileges and immunities because of his employment.

The ECtHR case concerned Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant complained that the domestic courts failed to properly address his argument that he enjoyed immunity from criminal jurisdiction under the Vienna Convention. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation were that his immunity claim—supported by official identity cards and Ministry correspondence—was central to whether he could lawfully be prosecuted, yet the domestic courts rejected it mainly on Article 42 and Article 31(1)(c) grounds without adequately engaging with his arguments on criminal immunity, waiver, and the timing of his indictment. The Court found that this failure violated his right to a fair hearing.

**Summary of *Zahariev v. North Macedonia* (Application no. 26760/22)**

The case of *Zahariev v. North Macedonia* concerns a Bulgarian national, Mr. Borislav Zahariev Zahariev, who was convicted in North Macedonia for abuse of office. The central issue before the European Court of Human Rights was whether the domestic courts violated his right to a fair hearing under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention by failing to adequately address his argument that he enjoyed immunity from criminal prosecution under the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations.

The key facts are as follows. Between 2004 and 2009, the applicant worked as a financial director for a telecommunications company in North Macedonia. From January 2007, his wife was employed as an official at the Bulgarian Cultural and Information Centre, which was attached to the Bulgarian embassy. As the spouse of an administrative and technical staff member, the applicant was issued a special identity card by the North Macedonian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which indicated he enjoyed immunity from criminal jurisdiction.

In January 2012, an investigation was opened against the applicant for abuse of office and tax evasion related to his former employment at the telecommunications company, acts allegedly committed in 2008. He was indicted in February 2013. During the proceedings, the applicant and his lawyer repeatedly informed the trial court that he held a special identity card granting him absolute immunity from prosecution under international law. The applicant argued that, at the time of his indictment, he held a valid card, which was issued on 30 January 2012 and extended until 30 May 2014.

The domestic courts, however, rejected his immunity claim. They relied on a letter from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Article 37(2) of the Vienna Convention, which grants immunity to family members of administrative and technical staff but excludes acts performed outside their official functions. The courts further reasoned that under Article 42 of the Vienna Convention, which prohibits diplomatic agents from engaging in professional or commercial activities for personal profit, the applicant had lost his immunity when he took up employment with a private company. They noted that the Bulgarian embassy had never formally invoked immunity on his behalf and had not requested the extension of his special identity card after 2014.

The applicant consistently appealed, arguing that the Vienna Convention makes no distinction between official and private acts for immunity from criminal jurisdiction (unlike for civil and administrative jurisdiction) and that the *Arrest Warrant* case of the International Court of Justice supported his position. He also contended that Article 42 does not automatically terminate immunity and that Bulgaria had not waived his immunity.

The trial court convicted him in absentia in December 2019, a decision upheld by the appellate court in March 2021 and the Supreme Court in November 2021. The Supreme Court endorsed the lower courts' finding that the applicant had lost his immunity due to his employment, a fact it considered to be in breach of Article 42.

The European Court of Human Rights found that the domestic courts failed to properly engage with the applicant's specific and repeatedly raised arguments under the Vienna Convention, particularly his claim that he possessed a valid identity card granting immunity at the crucial time of his indictment. This failure to provide adequate reasoning constituted a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.
001-237504:
The case of *Agayev & Zulfugarzadeh Company v. Azerbaijan* (Application no. 31222/14) concerns alleged unlawful expropriation by the Baku City Executive Authority (“BCEA”) and the non-enforcement of a final domestic judgment. The applicant company, based in Baku, owned two rooms (34.83 sq. m in total) in a house that was shared with two individual co-owners, according to an ownership certificate issued by the Technical Inventory and Ownership Rights Registration Department of the BCEA.

The background is similar to *Khalikova v. Azerbaijan*. On 16 February 2011, the Head of the BCEA issued order no. 76, stating that buildings and houses on certain streets were to be demolished to construct a new garden-park complex known as the Winter Park, and that residents were to be relocated. On 23 September 2012, the BCEA began demolishing the house. The next day, the applicant company asked the State Land and Cartography Committee (“SLCC”) to issue a plan and measurements of the land underlying and attached to the house.

On the same date, the company brought proceedings against the BCEA and several other State authorities (“the first claim”). It sought invalidation of the BCEA order and compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. It claimed that its share in the house was actually 55.73 sq. m, rather than the 34.83 sq. m stated in the ownership certificate, and that 69.48 sq. m of the underlying and attached land belonged to it under domestic law. After the SLCC refused its request, on 22 November 2012 the company lodged a separate claim against the SLCC, asking the courts to order it to issue the relevant plan and measurements (“the second claim”). In November 2012, the house was completely demolished.

By final judgment of 17 October 2013, the Supreme Court dismissed the second claim. It found that the plot of land did not constitute the applicant company’s possessions because there were no legal grounds. Article 9 of the Law on Land Reform, which transferred land underneath private residential houses lawfully used by citizens from State ownership into the occupants’ private ownership, did not apply to the applicant company because it was a legal person. The court also found no evidence of an agreement with the co-owners concerning use of the land or their consent to the company’s privatisation of 69.48 sq. m.

By final judgment of 29 January 2014, the Supreme Court upheld the lower court’s judgment partly granting the first claim. It awarded the applicant company AZN 62,694 in compensation, calculated at AZN 1,500 per square metre for its share in the house plus an additional 20% under Presidential Decree no. 689. It dismissed the company’s claims concerning the additional surface area and the plot of land, holding that it had no rights over them. As of the latest communication with the parties in 2022, the Supreme Court’s judgment of 29 January 2014 remained unenforced.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant company complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the interference with its property rights was unlawful and unjustified. It further complained under Article 6 that the final judgment of 29 January 2014 had not been enforced. It also alleged violations of its right to a reasoned decision under Article 6 and its right under Article 13. The Court gave notice of the complaints under Article 6 § 1, Article 13, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, declaring the remainder inadmissible. The key factual issues concern the demolition and expropriation of the house, the scope of the company’s property rights in the land, the compensation awarded, and the failure to enforce the final compensation judgment.

**Agayev & Zulfugarzadeh Company v. Azerbaijan** (Application no. 31222/14) is a case before the European Court of Human Rights concerning an allegedly unlawful expropriation and demolition of property in Baku, and the subsequent failure to enforce a final domestic judgment. According to a certificate issued by the Technical Inventory and Ownership Rights Registration Department of the Baku City Executive Authority (“BCEA”), the applicant company owned two rooms totaling 34.83 sq. m, while the other co-owners held one room and the remaining part of the house. The facts were similar to those in *Khalikova v. Azerbaijan*.

On 16 February 2011, the Head of the BCEA issued order no. 76, stating that certain buildings and houses were to be demolished to construct a new garden-park complex known as the Winter Park, and that residents would be relocated. According to the applicant company, the BCEA began demolishing the house on 23 September 2012. By November 2012, the house had been completely demolished.

On 24 September 2012, the day after demolition began, the applicant company asked the State Land and Cartography Committee (“SLCC”) to issue a plan and measurements of the plot of land underlying and attached to the house. The applicant argued that its share in the house was actually 55.73 sq. m, rather than 34.83 sq. m, and that 69.48 sq. m of the underlying and attached land belonged to it under domestic law. After the SLCC refused its request, the applicant brought a separate claim against the SLCC on 22 November 2012, asking the courts to order the SLCC to issue the plan and measurements (“the second claim”).

By a final judgment of 17 October 2013, the Supreme Court dismissed the second claim. It held that the land underlying and attached to the house did not constitute the applicant company’s “possessions” because there was no legal basis. Article 9 of the Law on Land Reform, which transferred land beneath private residential houses lawfully used by citizens from State ownership into occupants’ private ownership, did not apply to the applicant because it was a legal person. The court also found no evidence of an agreement with the co-owners regarding land use or their consent to the company’s privatisation of 69.48 sq. m.

By a final judgment of 29 January 2014, the Supreme Court partly granted the first claim and awarded the applicant 62,694 Azerbaijani manats in compensation, calculated at AZN 1,500 per square metre for its share in the house, plus an additional 20% under Presidential Decree no. 689 of 26 December 2007. However, it dismissed the claim concerning the additional surface area and the plot of land, finding that the applicant had no rights over them. As of the latest communication with the parties in 2022, the Supreme Court’s judgment of 29 January 2014 remained unenforced.

The applicant company complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the interference with its property rights was unlawful and unjustified. It further complained under Article 6 that the final judgment of 29 January 2014 had not been enforced, and that it had been denied a reasoned decision under Article 6 and Article 13. The Court gave notice of the complaints under Article 6 § 1, Article 13, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

**Summary of *Agayev & Zulfugarzadeh Company v. Azerbaijan* (Application no. 31222/14)**

The case of *Agayev & Zulfugarzadeh Company v. Azerbaijan* concerns the allegedly unlawful expropriation and demolition of a privately owned house in Baku by state authorities. The applicant, a legal entity based in Baku, shared ownership of the property with two individuals. According to official ownership records, the applicant company owned two rooms totaling 34.83 square meters, while the other co-owners held the remaining portions of the house.

The central facts revolve around an order issued on 16 February 2011 by the Head of the Baku City Executive Authority (BCEA). Order no. 76 mandated the demolition of buildings and houses on certain streets to facilitate the construction of a new garden-park complex known as the "Winter Park," with residents to be relocated. On 23 September 2012, the BCEA commenced the demolition of the house. By November 2012, the structure had been completely demolished.

Following the start of demolition, the applicant company took legal action. On 24 September 2012, it applied to the State Land and Cartography Committee (SLCC) for a plan and measurements of the land underlying and attached to the house. On the same day, it initiated court proceedings against the BCEA and other state authorities. This first claim sought the invalidation of the demolition order and compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. The applicant argued that its share of the house was actually 55.73 square meters (not 34.83) and that, by virtue of domestic law, it also owned 69.48 square meters of the underlying and attached land.

After the SLCC refused its request for land documentation, the applicant filed a separate claim against the SLCC on 22 November 2012, seeking a court order for the SLCC to issue the plan and measurements. However, this second claim was ultimately dismissed by a final judgment of the Supreme Court on 17 October 2013. The Supreme Court reasoned that the land did not constitute the applicant company’s possessions. It held that Article 9 of the Law on Land Reform, which allowed for the transfer of land under private residential houses into occupants’ ownership, did not apply to legal persons such as the applicant company. Furthermore, the court found that the company had failed to provide evidence of an agreement with the house’s co-owners regarding land use or their consent for the company to privatize the land.

In a separate final judgment on 29 January 2014, the Supreme Court partly granted the applicant’s first claim. It awarded the company 62,694 Azerbaijani manats (AZN) in compensation, calculated at AZN 1,500 per square meter for its share in the house, plus an additional 20% as per a presidential decree. However, the court dismissed the applicant's claims regarding the additional surface area and the plot of land, reiterating that it held no rights over them.

A critical fact is that, as of 2022, the Supreme Court’s judgment of 29 January 2014, which awarded compensation, remained unenforced. The applicant company brought complaints before the European Court of Human Rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property), alleging that the interference with its property rights was unlawful and unjustified. It also complained under Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial) that the final judgment awarding compensation had not been enforced, and under Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) regarding the lack of a remedy for these grievances.

In *J.B. and Others v. Malta* (no. 1766/23, judgment 22 October 2024), six Bangladeshi nationals arrived in Malta by sea on 18 November 2022 after being rescued and were detained at the Ħal Far Initial Reception Centre (“China House”). They claimed to be unaccompanied minors aged 16–17. On 30 November 2022, the Principal Immigration Officer issued detention orders to verify identity/nationality, obtain asylum-related information, and prevent absconding. On 6 December 2022, the Immigration Appeals Board (IAB) held one mass hearing for the whole group and confirmed the detention as lawful. It noted that all applicants except the first were minors and that a guardian should be appointed.

The applicants alleged they were detained with adults in overcrowded rooms of 3–5 sq m, with insufficient and dilapidated washrooms, no meaningful outdoor/common/prayer space, limited phone access, no leisure or education, no heating, inadequate winter clothing and drinkable water, no information in a language they understood, and inadequate medical/psychosocial support. The Government disputed this, citing larger rooms, basic items, outdoor access, phone availability, games, prayer space, and winter clothing.

In January 2023, legal representatives obtained access, referred the applicants to AWAS, and sought urgent review of some detentions, which remained unanswered. On 11 January 2023, the European Court indicated interim measures under Rule 39 requiring conditions compatible with Article 3 and the applicants’ status as unaccompanied minors. The applicants were later moved to Safi Detention Centre, Block A, Zone 4, with other minors. They said conditions were similar, except for room size and one hour daily outside.

Age assessments concluded between 17 and 19 January 2023 that they were adults. The applicants challenged this as hasty, non-holistic, and involving an allegedly non-consensual bone test. IAB proceedings were confused: it was told some applicants wanted to withdraw appeals without consulting lawyers, and declarations of adulthood were signed without legal representatives or interpreters. Vulnerability reports later documented elevated anxiety, depression, acute stress/PTSD, and suicidal thoughts. Requests for release based on vulnerability were not answered in writing. In May 2023, the IAB found the first applicant adult based on a genuine passport showing birth in 2002, but confirmed the others’ minority. The first applicant was moved with adults; the rest were released to open accommodation for minors. His asylum claim was rejected, and he left Malta in August 2023; several others were later reported missing.

The applicants complained under Articles 3, 5 §§ 1 and 4, and 13, alleging inhuman or degrading detention conditions, unlawful or arbitrary detention, and ineffective remedies. The Court found that the first applicant’s conditions did not reach the Article 3 threshold, but the cumulative conditions for the remaining presumed minors amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment. The initial immigration detention was unlawful. The subsequent detention of the first applicant, ultimately found to be an adult, complied with Article 5 § 1, but continued detention of the remaining presumed minors pending asylum processing, without proper prior age assessment, was arbitrary. The IAB was not an effective Article 5 § 4 remedy because of inadequate independence, appointment safeguards, automatic review, and speed. Constitutional redress was ineffective for ongoing detention-condition complaints under Article 13. Under Article 46, Malta had to enact legislation ensuring IAB independence and impartiality and an effective domestic remedy for ongoing conditions of detention.

J.B. and Others v. Malta (Application no. 1766/23) concerned six Bangladeshi nationals who arrived in Malta by boat on 18 November 2022 after being rescued at sea. They claimed to be unaccompanied minors aged 16–17 and were initially detained at the Ħal Far Initial Reception Centre (HIRC/China House). They alleged that they were detained without proper documents or explanation, together with adults, in overcrowded rooms of about 3–5 sq m occupied by around four people. They complained of insufficient and dilapidated washrooms, no meaningful outdoor or common space, no prayer room or private space, very limited phone access, including to lawyers, no leisure or educational activities, no heating or suitable winter clothing, limited drinkable water, no information in a language they understood, and inadequate medical and psychosocial support.

On 30 November 2022, the Principal Immigration Officer issued detention orders to verify identity or nationality, obtain information for potential asylum claims, and because of an alleged risk of absconding. On 6 December 2022, the Immigration Appeals Board (IAB) confirmed the legality of their detention in a mass hearing. The IAB noted that all applicants except the first appeared to be minors and that a legal guardian should be appointed, yet it still upheld the detention. In January 2023, their lawyers obtained access, referred them to welfare authorities, and requested an urgent review of detention, which remained unanswered. The European Court of Human Rights then indicated interim measures requiring Malta to ensure conditions compatible with Article 3 and with their claimed status as unaccompanied minors. The applicants were later transferred to Safi Detention Centre with other minors, but alleged similar conditions apart from larger rooms and one hour daily outdoors.

Age-assessment proceedings in January 2023 concluded that they were adults. The applicants alleged the process was hasty and not holistic or multidisciplinary. One applicant had initially been assessed as a minor, but a bone test allegedly conducted without informed consent indicated he was 18. They appealed. The IAB proceedings were initially irregular: detention officers claimed some applicants wished to withdraw appeals, and some declarations of adulthood were signed without lawyers or interpreters. Ultimately, on 16 and 22 May 2023, the IAB found the first applicant to be an adult because he carried a genuine passport showing birth in 2002, but upheld the other five applicants’ minority. The first applicant was moved to an adult section on 16 May; the others were released to an open centre for minors on 19 May. Psychological reports disclosed elevated anxiety, depression, PTSD and, for some, suicidal thoughts, although later reports were less severe. The first applicant’s asylum claim was rejected and he left Malta in August 2023; several others were later reported missing.

The applicants complained under Article 3 about detention conditions, under Article 5 § 1 about unlawful initial and subsequent detention, under Article 5 § 4 about the IAB’s lack of effective review, and under Article 13 about the absence of an effective remedy for ongoing conditions. The Court found that the first applicant, ultimately determined to be an adult, did not show Article 3 ill-treatment. For the remaining applicants, presumed minors, the cumulative detention conditions amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment. Their initial detention was unlawful under Article 5 § 1; the subsequent detention of the first applicant complied, but the continued detention of the remaining applicants pending asylum processing without prior age assessment was arbitrary. The IAB was not an effective Article 5 § 4 remedy due to independence concerns, lack of full judicial jurisdiction, no automatic review, and delay. Constitutional redress was ineffective under Article 13 for ongoing detention conditions. Malta was required to adopt general measures concerning IAB independence and an effective domestic remedy for ongoing conditions.

**J.B. and Others v. Malta** concerned six Bangladeshi nationals who arrived in Malta by boat on 18 November 2022 after being rescued at sea. They claimed to be minors aged 16–17 and were detained at the Ħal Far Initial Reception Centre (“China House,” HIRC). They alleged unlawful detention in inadequate conditions: rooms of 3–5 sq. m. shared by around four people; detention with adults; insufficient and poorly maintained washrooms for 47 people; limited or no outdoor, common, prayer, or private space; restricted phone access, including to lawyers; no leisure or educational activities; no heating; inadequate winter clothing; limited drinkable water; no information in a language they understood; and inadequate medical and psychosocial support. The Government disputed this, describing larger rooms, basic supplies, winter vests, television, outdoor access, phone access, games, a multipurpose/prayer room, and potable water.

On 30 November 2022, the Principal Immigration Officer issued detention orders to determine identity/nationality, obtain asylum-related information, and address absconding risk. On 6 December 2022, the Immigration Appeals Board (IAB) confirmed the group’s detention in a mass hearing. The IAB noted that all applicants except the first were minors and that a guardian should be appointed. In January 2023, legal representatives accessed the applicants, referred them to AWAS, and sought urgent review of detention, which went unanswered. The European Court of Human Rights indicated interim measures on 11 January 2023. The applicants were then transferred to Safi Detention Centre, Block A, Zone 4, with other minors; conditions there were described as similar, though with one hour daily outside.

Age-assessment proceedings concluded between 17 and 19 January 2023 that the applicants were adults. They appealed. The IAB ultimately found the first applicant was an adult because he carried a genuine passport indicating birth in 2002, but upheld the other applicants’ minority. The first applicant was later moved with adults, while the remaining applicants were released to an open centre for minors. Psychological reports showed elevated anxiety, depression, PTSD, and suicidal thoughts among some applicants, though later reports were less severe.

The alleged violations centered on: (1) **Article 3** conditions of detention in HIRC and Safi, including detention of presumed minors with adults, lack of child-specific care, harassment, pressure to sign documents without interpretation, and mental harm. The Court found the first applicant’s conditions did not reach the Article 3 threshold, but the cumulative conditions for the remaining presumed minors amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment. (2) **Article 5 § 1**: initial immigration detention was unlawful; later detention of the first applicant, ultimately found adult, complied with the Convention, but continued detention of the remaining applicants pending asylum processing and age assessment was arbitrary. (3) **Article 5 § 4**: the IAB was not an effective remedy to review detention lawfulness, owing to lack of full judicial jurisdiction, unclear appointment criteria, insufficient independence guarantees, no automatic review, and lack of speedy decisions. (4) **Article 13 with Article 3**: constitutional redress was ineffective for ongoing detention-condition complaints. (5) **Article 46**: Malta was required to enact legislation ensuring the IAB’s independence/impartiality and to establish an effective domestic remedy for ongoing conditions of detention.

In **Maçi v. Albania** (Application no. 21051/10, ECtHR Third Section, 4 July 2024), the applicants were the heirs of Mr Sh.M. and complained that Albania failed to enforce final domestic property decisions in their favour. The case concerned two decisions: a 1996 Decision of a property restitution commission and a 2004 Judgment of the domestic courts.

The **1996 Decision** recognised Mr Sh.M.’s entitlement to property. Under its operative clause, one-third of a land plot was returned to him, while compensation was to be ensured for the remaining part. The **2004 Judgment** upheld Mr Sh.M.’s claim against the Immovable Property Registration Office (IPRO) and the Tirana Municipality and ordered IPRO to register his title to the entire 720 sq. m plot, as defined by a court-appointed expert. Mr Sh.M. died in 2004, and the applicants were recognised as his heirs, including in enforcement proceedings.

Enforcement problems arose in two main ways. First, regarding the **1996 Decision’s title clause**, the authorities did not register the applicants’ title to the one-third land plot. The Government argued that the applicants had not requested registration, or alternatively that registration would conflict with the rights of residents of a building who were allegedly co-owners of adjacent land. The Court found that the applicants had made requests to IPRO. It also held that the alleged conflict did not excuse non-enforcement: the authorities had not consulted the residents, and any conflict appeared to result from the State’s own inconsistent transfers of property rights. The Government’s non-exhaustion objection was dismissed, and the Court found a violation for failure to enforce this part of the 1996 Decision.

Second, regarding the **compensation clause of the 1996 Decision**, the Government argued that the applicants should have used the remedy under the 2015 Property Act. The Court accepted that this was an effective domestic remedy and rejected this part of the complaint for non-exhaustion.

As to the **2004 Judgment**, IPRO registered only 591 sq. m of the 720 sq. m plot. The authorities claimed the remaining 129 sq. m was public property—a road or square—following re-measurement. The Government argued the applicants should have started new proceedings against IPRO. The Court rejected that argument. The applicants’ predecessor had already obtained a final judgment against IPRO and the Municipality determining the size and borders of the plot. The applicants were recognised as his heirs. The authorities could not later dispute the expert measurements or claim that the 2004 Judgment merely described facts, especially since they had registered 591 sq. m on the basis of that same judgment. The 2004 Judgment clearly obliged IPRO to register title to the full 720 sq. m.

The applicants complained under **Article 6 § 1** and **Article 1 of Protocol No. 1** about non-enforcement of final decisions, and under **Article 13** about the lack of an effective remedy. The Court reiterated that execution of a final judgment is an integral part of a fair hearing and relied on similar Albanian non-enforcement case-law. It found that the Government failed to show it had deployed all necessary efforts to enforce the 1996 Decision’s title clause and the 2004 Judgment. Accordingly, the Court found violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning the non-enforcement of those final decisions. The compensation part of the 1996 Decision was rejected for non-exhaustion, and the Court found no need to rule separately on Article 13.

In *Maçi v. Albania* (Application no. 21051/10), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered judgment on 4 July 2024. The applicants are the heirs of Mr Sh.M. They alleged that Albania failed to enforce two final domestic decisions in their predecessor’s favour, relying on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The application was lodged on 9 April 2010.

The first decision was issued on 5 November 1996 by the Tirana Commission on Restitution and Compensation of Properties. The Commission found that Mr Sh.M. was the former owner of land confiscated during the communist era. A two-storey building and a road had been built on the plot. Under the operative clause, the Commission returned to Mr Sh.M. title to one-third of the land on which the building had been constructed, granted him the right to erect an additional third floor, and ordered registration of his ownership with the Immovable Property Registration Office (IPRO). It further ruled that he should receive compensation for the remainder of the land. The 1996 Decision became final in December 1996.

The second decision was the 2004 Judgment of the District Court of Tirana. Mr Sh.M. had sued the Ministry of Economy, the Municipality of Tirana and the IPRO to delimit the exact boundaries of his plot. An expert report identified a plot of 720 sq. m., bordering public property described variously as a “public square” or “public road.” The Municipality and IPRO accepted the claim; the Ministry did not express a position. The court upheld the claim and ordered the IPRO to register Mr Sh.M.’s title to the property as defined in the expert report. The judgment became final in June 2004, and an enforcement writ was issued. Mr Sh.M. died in May 2004, and the applicants were recognised as his heirs.

The alleged violations concerned non-enforcement. After the 2004 Judgment, the IPRO registered only 591 of the 720 sq. m. It claimed the remaining 129 sq. m. formed part of a public square owned by the Municipality and that the court expert had mismeasured the plot. The IPRO sought invalidation of the applicants’ title to that portion. Responsibility was passed between the State Attorney’s Office and the Municipality, and in 2023 the State Attorney was still considering whether to challenge the 2004 Judgment.

The Government argued that the applicants had failed to exhaust domestic remedies and that registration would conflict with building residents’ rights. The Court rejected those arguments. As to the 1996 Decision’s title clause, it found that the applicants had requested registration and that the authorities had not consulted residents or shown any actual conflict. The State could not avoid enforcement by pointing to conflicting property transfers it had itself created. However, regarding the 1996 Decision’s compensation clause, the Court accepted that the 2015 Property Act remedy before the Agency for Treatment of Property was effective and rejected that part for non-exhaustion.

As to the 2004 Judgment, the Court rejected the Government’s claim that the applicants should have brought identical proceedings against the IPRO. The predecessor had already obtained a final judgment against the relevant authorities, and the applicants were recognised heirs. Once the judgment settled the size and borders of the plot, the authorities could not dispute the expert measurements. The Government’s argument that the judgment merely described facts also conflicted with its own registration of 591 sq. m. and the operative clause requiring registration of the full 720 sq. m.

The Court found a breach of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to the authorities’ failure to deploy all necessary efforts to enforce the final domestic decisions. It found no need for a separate ruling on Article 13.

In *Maçi v. Albania* (Application no. 21051/10, judgment of 4 July 2024), the applicants were heirs of Mr Sh. M. They complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that Albania had failed to enforce two final domestic decisions in their predecessor’s favour.

The first decision was issued on 5 November 1996 by the Tirana Commission on Restitution and Compensation of Properties. The Commission found that Mr Sh. M. had been the former owner of land confiscated during the communist era. A two-storey building and a road had been built on the plot. By the operative clause, the Commission returned title to one-third of the land on which the building stood and granted him the right to erect a third floor. It also ordered the Immovable Property Registration Office (“IPRO”) to register his ownership. Paragraph (b) of the decision provided that he should receive compensation for the remainder of the plot in accordance with law. The decision became final on 5 December 1996.

The second decision was the 2004 Judgment. Mr Sh. M. sued the Ministry of Economy, the Municipality of Tirana and IPRO, seeking delimitation of the exact boundaries of his plot. An expert report set the plot at 720 sq. m and described its borders, including adjacent public property initially called a “public square” and later a “public road.” His title was confirmed by a 1994 ownership certificate. On 27 April 2004 the District Court of Tirana upheld his claim and ordered IPRO to register his title as defined in the expert report. Mr Sh. M. died on 17 May 2004, and the applicants were recognised as his heirs. The 2004 Judgment became final on 3 June 2004, and an enforcement writ followed.

Enforcement problems arose. IPRO registered only 591 of the 720 sq. m under the applicants’ name. It claimed that the remaining 129 sq. m formed part of a public square owned by the Municipality and that the court-appointed expert had mismeasured the plot. IPRO asked the State Attorney’s Office to invalidate the applicants’ title over those 129 sq. m. The State Attorney forwarded the request to the Municipality, which said the State Attorney should initiate proceedings. In 2023 the State Attorney was still considering whether to challenge the 2004 Judgment.

Before the European Court, the Government argued non-exhaustion. As to the 1996 Decision’s title clause, it said the applicants had not asked IPRO to register their rights; the Court found that requests existed and dismissed this. The Government also claimed a conflict with building residents. The Court found that the authorities had not consulted those residents and could not avoid enforcing the final decision merely because conflicting property rights may have arisen from State action.

As to the 1996 compensation clause, the Court accepted that the 2015 Property Act provided an effective remedy, so that part was rejected for non-exhaustion. As to the 2004 Judgment, the Government argued that the applicants should sue IPRO again. The Court rejected this: the predecessor had already obtained a final judgment against IPRO and the Municipality; the authorities recognised the applicants as heirs; and the authorities could not dispute the expert measurements after the final judgment. The 2004 Judgment clearly required registration of the entire 720 sq. m.

The Court therefore found that the authorities failed to deploy all necessary efforts to enforce the final domestic decisions, violating Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It made no separate ruling under Article 13.

In *Maisaia v. Georgia* (Application no. 75969/14), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Article 3 of the Convention concerning the applicant’s alleged ill-treatment in prison and the domestic authorities’ alleged failure to conduct an effective investigation. The applicant, Vakhtang Maisaia, a Georgian national born in 1972, lodged the application on 26 November 2014. The Court gave notice only of the Article 3 complaints and declared the remainder inadmissible. The Government’s objection to examination by a Committee was rejected.

The key facts concern events in Georgian detention. On 5 May 2009, the applicant was arrested and placed in police custody on suspicion of espionage, an offence for which he was later convicted. On 8 May 2009, he was transferred from police custody to Tbilisi Prison No. 8, known as Gldani Prison. During admission, a doctor examined him and recorded that he had no injuries, was in good health, and suffered from no medical condition.

On 25 August 2010, the applicant complained that prison guards had ill-treated him the previous day, 24 August 2010, in Gldani Prison. The Investigation Unit of the Ministry of Prisons opened a criminal investigation the same day. A medical examination was immediately commissioned and found marks of ill-treatment—multiple bruises and lesions on his face and body. Investigators questioned witnesses, including cellmates and prison guards. One cellmate confirmed that the applicant had been beaten by prison guards. Other witnesses claimed the applicant had inflicted the injuries himself by hitting his head and body against the wall and window bar in his cell.

When questioned on 25 August 2010, the applicant stated that, beyond the 24 August incident, he had been subjected to ill-treatment in Gldani Prison on a regular basis. He alleged systematic physical and psychological abuse between 8 May and 23 June 2009. He named the alleged abusers and provided further details about the circumstances of the 24 August ill-treatment. On 13 September 2010, the World Organisation Against Torture, an international human rights observer based in Geneva, issued a statement expressing concern about the applicant’s safety. Based on information from his family, the statement said that after reporting ill-treatment in Gldani Prison, he began receiving death threats from prison guards.

Between 22 September 2010 and May 2012, the applicant repeatedly enquired—at least four times—about the investigation’s progress with the Ministry of Prisons and the Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office. Relying on the medical opinion confirming injuries, he repeatedly requested aggrieved-party status. His letters were either unanswered or the authorities advised that the investigation was ongoing. In September 2012, footage of repeated ill-treatment of inmates in various prisons, including and in particular Gldani Prison, was disseminated in the Georgian media, a matter known as the “prison scandal.” On 13 January 2013, the applicant was released under an amnesty.

Between February 2013 and October 2014, the applicant made at least six further enquiries to the Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office about progress, if any, and again requested aggrieved-party status. These enquiries were either left unanswered or he was told to wait for certain investigative measures to be completed. According to the case file, the criminal investigation into his ill-treatment in Gldani Prison remained ongoing, but no other details about its progress were known.

The central Article 3 issues were whether the applicant suffered ill-treatment by prison guards, allegedly as part of large-scale and systematic prisoner abuse, and whether the State conducted an effective investigation. Key facts include the medical evidence of injuries after his complaint, conflicting witness accounts, his broader allegations of systematic abuse, threats after reporting, the wider prison scandal, and repeated delays and failures to grant him victim status or inform him of meaningful progress.

Maisaia v. Georgia (Application no. 75969/14) is a case before the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, with judgment delivered on 7 May 2024. The applicant, Vakhtang Maisaia, a Georgian national born in 1972 and living in Tbilisi, lodged the application on 26 November 2014. The Court gave notice of his complaints under Article 3 of the Convention to the Georgian Government and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. It also rejected the Government’s objection to examination by a Committee.

The case mainly concerns alleged ill-treatment in prison, said to form part of large-scale and systematic ill-treatment of prisoners at the material time, and the domestic authorities’ alleged failure to conduct an effective investigation. The applicant was arrested on 5 May 2009 on suspicion of espionage and later convicted. On 8 May 2009 he was transferred from police custody to Tbilisi prison no. 8, known as Gldani Prison. An admission medical examination recorded no injuries and noted that he was in good health.

The central alleged incident occurred on 24 August 2010, when the applicant claimed he was ill-treated by prison guards at Gldani Prison. On 25 August 2010 he complained, and the Investigation Unit of the Ministry of Prisons opened a criminal investigation. A medical examination was immediately commissioned and found multiple bruises and lesions on his face and body, establishing marks of ill-treatment. Investigators questioned witnesses, including cellmates and prison guards. One cellmate confirmed that the applicant had been beaten by guards. Other witnesses claimed that the applicant had inflicted the injuries himself by hitting his head and body against the wall and window bar in his cell.

When questioned on 25 August 2010, the applicant stated that, in addition to the 24 August incident, he had been subjected to regular ill-treatment in Gldani Prison. He alleged systematic physical and psychological abuse between 8 May and 23 June 2009. He named the alleged abusers and provided further details about the circumstances of the 24 August 2010 incident.

On 13 September 2010, the World Organisation Against Torture issued a special statement expressing concern about the applicant’s safety. It stated that, according to information from his family, after he reported the ill-treatment he began receiving death threats from prison guards. Between 22 September 2010 and May 2012, the applicant repeatedly—at least four times—asked the Ministry of Prisons and the Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office about the investigation. Relying on the medical opinion confirming injuries, he requested status as an aggrieved party. His letters were either unanswered or met with advice that the investigation was still ongoing.

In September 2012, media circulated footage of repeated ill-treatment of inmates at various prisons, particularly Gldani Prison, known as the “prison scandal.” The applicant was released on 13 January 2013 under an amnesty. From February 2013 to October 2014, he made at least six further enquiries to the Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office about progress in the investigation and again requested aggrieved party status. These enquiries were either unanswered or answered by saying that investigative measures still needed to be completed.

According to the case file, the criminal investigation into the applicant’s alleged ill-treatment in Gldani Prison remains ongoing, with no further details about its progress known. The alleged Article 3 violations therefore concern both the substantive ill-treatment—including claims of systematic abuse and threats after complaining—and the procedural obligation to conduct an effective, prompt investigation into credible allegations of torture or inhuman or degrading treatment. The key factual issues include the medical evidence of injuries, conflicting witness accounts, the applicant’s broader claims of regular abuse, and the prolonged lack of investigative progress.

The case of *Maisaia v. Georgia* (Application no. 75969/14) concerns complaints under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Vakhtang Maisaia, a Georgian national born in 1972, lodged the application on 26 November 2014. The case mainly concerns his alleged ill-treatment in prison—said to form part of a large-scale and systematic pattern of ill-treatment of prisoners at the time—and the domestic authorities’ alleged failure to conduct an effective investigation into his allegations. The European Court of Human Rights gave notice of the Article 3 complaints and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

On 5 May 2009 the applicant was arrested and placed in police custody on suspicion of espionage, an offence of which he was later convicted. On 8 May 2009 he was transferred from police custody to Tbilisi prison no. 8, known as Gldani Prison. During his admission procedure, a doctor examined him and recorded in his medical file that he had no injuries, was in good health, and did not suffer from any medical condition.

The central factual events concern an alleged incident on 24 August 2010, when the applicant claimed he was ill-treated by prison guards in Gldani Prison. On 25 August 2010, after he complained, the Investigation Unit of the Ministry of Prisons opened a criminal investigation into the alleged ill-treatment. A medical examination was immediately commissioned. Its results established marks of ill-treatment on the applicant, including multiple bruises and lesions on his face and body. Investigators questioned witnesses, including the applicant’s cellmates and Gldani prison guards. One cellmate confirmed that the applicant had been beaten by prison guards. Other witnesses stated that the applicant had inflicted the injuries himself by hitting his head and body against the wall and the window bar in his cell.

When questioned by investigators on 25 August 2010, the applicant stated that, in addition to the 24 August incident, he had been subjected to ill-treatment in Gldani Prison on a regular basis. He alleged that systematic physical and psychological abuse had lasted between 8 May and 23 June 2009. He gave investigators the names of the alleged abusers and provided further details about the circumstances of the 24 August 2010 incident.

On 13 September 2010, the World Organisation Against Torture issued a special statement about the applicant’s case, expressing concern for his safety in prison. The statement emphasised that, according to information received from the applicant’s family, after he reported his ill-treatment, he began receiving death threats from prison guards.

Between 22 September 2010 and May 2012, the applicant repeatedly inquired—at least four times—with the Ministry of Prisons and the Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office about the progress of the criminal investigation. Relying on the medical opinion confirming marks of ill-treatment, he repeatedly requested to be granted the status of aggrieved party. His letters were either left unanswered or he was told that the investigation was still ongoing.

In September 2012, footage of repeated acts of ill-treatment of inmates at various prison establishments, including and in particular Gldani Prison, was disseminated in the Georgian media, a matter referred to as the “prison scandal.” On 13 January 2013 the applicant was released from prison under an amnesty.

Between February 2013 and October 2014, the applicant filed repeated inquiries—at least six times—with the Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office about the progress of the investigation and again asked to be granted the status of an aggrieved party. These inquiries were either left unanswered or the prosecution authorities advised him that certain investigative measures still needed to be completed. According to the case file, the criminal investigation into the applicant’s alleged ill-treatment in Gldani Prison was still ongoing at the time, with no further details about its progress known.

The key alleged violations therefore concern whether the applicant was subjected to treatment contrary to Article 3, including systematic physical and psychological abuse, and whether the Georgian authorities failed to carry out an effective investigation into his credible allegations of ill-treatment.
