**Kornilova v. Ukraine** (Application no. 47283/14, judgment 12 November 2020) concerned an allegation that Ukrainian authorities failed to effectively investigate an assault on a Jehovah’s Witness and to unmask a possible religious motive, contrary to Articles 3, 9 and 14 of the Convention.

On 7 March 2013, the applicant, Ms Tetyana Kornilova, and a fellow Jehovah’s Witness, N.S., were doing door-to-door visits in Nosivka, distributing invitations to a religious service. The invitations showed Jesus Christ and the words “One Died for All,” with smaller text identifying the meeting as Jehovah’s Witnesses. At the house of V.S., a fifty-year-old man they did not know, V.S. saw the invitations and Bible. According to the applicant, he immediately cursed them, called them “shtundas”—a colloquial and derogatory term for evangelical Protestants—and punched her in the head. He allegedly threatened to set his dog on them. On 9 March, the applicant sought medical care, was diagnosed with concussion and a facial bruise, and remained in hospital until 19 March.

She reported the incident to the police the same day. A criminal investigation was opened under Article 125 § 2 of the Criminal Code, covering intentional infliction of minor bodily injury. The applicant consistently said the attack was unprovoked and religiously motivated. N.S. supported her account, stating that V.S. hit the applicant immediately and repeatedly called them “shtundas.” V.S.’s explanations changed over time. He first claimed the women refused to leave and kept trying to recruit him, so he slapped one. Later he said he acted due to the “sudden emergence of hostility,” then added that the applicant had insulted his “man’s health.” He denied any religious motive, said he did not know she was a Jehovah’s Witness, and claimed “shtundas” had no religious meaning. Medical evidence found minor injuries consistent with either a slap or a punch.

The applicant asked investigators and the trial court to reclassify the offence as discriminatory acts under Article 161 § 2 of the Criminal Code, or as hooliganism under Article 296, arguing that the authorities had a duty to investigate religious prejudice. The investigator refused, finding “sudden hostility” and no religious hatred. On 16 July 2013, the Nosivka District Court convicted V.S. under Article 125 § 2, fined him about EUR 78, and awarded the applicant about EUR 278 in non-pecuniary damages. The court found no aggravating circumstances and accepted the “sudden hostility” motive. Appeals were rejected, and in January 2014 the High Specialised Court upheld the lower decisions.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained that the authorities had not properly investigated the assault or the alleged religious motive. The Court found the incident sufficiently serious to fall within Article 3, because she was struck on the head during religious activity in the presence of a fellow believer and spent eleven days in hospital. It declared the complaint admissible. The Court recognised that States must take reasonable steps to unmask possible religious motives in violent incidents. It found the authorities had promptly investigated, identified and charged the perpetrator, completed proceedings within a year, imposed a proportionate sanction, and allowed the applicant to participate. Thus, there was no separate procedural violation of Article 3. However, the case turned on whether the investigation sufficiently addressed religious prejudice under Article 14 read with Article 3. The Court ultimately found a violation of Article 14 in conjunction with Article 3, because the domestic authorities failed to adequately investigate the alleged religious motive, accepting the defendant’s shifting explanation despite the religious context and the “shtundas” slur.

In *Kornilova v. Ukraine* (Application no. 47283/14, 12 November 2020), the applicant, a Ukrainian Jehovah’s Witness, alleged that Ukraine failed to effectively investigate a religiously motivated assault and to protect her rights under Articles 3, 9 and 14 of the Convention.

On 7 March 2013, Kornilova and another Jehovah’s Witness, N.S., were distributing door-to-door invitations to a religious service in Nosivka. The invitations showed Jesus Christ and referred to a Jehovah’s Witnesses’ meeting. At the house of V.S., a fifty-year-old man they did not know, V.S. met them at the gate. According to Kornilova and N.S., as soon as he saw the invitations and Bible, he punched Kornilova in the head, swore at them, and called them “shtundas,” a derogatory colloquial term for evangelical Protestants. He allegedly also threatened to set his dog on them. Kornilova was admitted to hospital on 9 March with concussion and facial bruising and remained an inpatient until 19 March.

Police opened a criminal case under Article 125 § 2 of the Criminal Code for intentional infliction of minor injury. Investigators questioned Kornilova, N.S., V.S., and other witnesses. V.S.’s account changed over time. Initially he said the women refused to leave and continued trying to recruit him, so he slapped one. Later he claimed Kornilova insulted his “man’s health,” that he did not know she was a Jehovah’s Witness, and that his use of “shtundas” had no religious meaning. He consistently denied religious hatred and attributed his act to the “sudden emergence of hostility.” Medical evidence found minor injuries that could have resulted from either a slap or a punch. The investigator refused Kornilova’s request to reclassify the offence as discriminatory acts under Article 161 § 2, finding no religious motive. In July 2013 the district court convicted V.S. under Article 125, fined him about EUR 78, and awarded damages. It found the motive to be sudden personal hostility, with no aggravating circumstances. Appeals upheld the conviction; the Court of Appeal said no religious motive had been established, and the High Specialised Court agreed in January 2014.

Before the ECtHR, Kornilova argued that the authorities accepted V.S.’s implausible and evolving account, failed to unmask religious prejudice, and allowed the initial Article 125 classification to narrow the investigation. She said her reclassification requests were dismissed without adequate reasoning, and no sufficient inquiry was made into whether V.S. had previously shown hostility

**Kornilova v. Ukraine** (App. no. 47283/14, ECtHR, 12 November 2020) concerned a Jehovah’s Witness who was assaulted while engaging in door-to-door religious outreach. The applicant, Ms Kornilova, lived in Nosivka, Ukraine. On 7 March 2013, she and a fellow believer, N.S., were distributing invitations to a Jehovah’s Witnesses meeting. The invitations showed an image of Jesus Christ and mentioned the meeting on the reverse. When they called at the home of V.S., a 50-year-old man unknown to them, he met them at the gate. According to the applicant, as soon as he noticed the invitations and Bible, he punched her in the head, cursed at the women, and called them “shtundas”—a colloquial and derogatory term used in Ukraine for evangelical Protestants. N.S. corroborated that V.S. struck the applicant immediately and repeatedly used that term. V.S. allegedly threatened to set his dog on them, and the women left.

On 9 March 2013, the applicant was hospitalized with concussion, dizziness, nausea, and a facial bruise. She remained an inpatient until 19 March. She complained to police that day, and a criminal investigation was opened under Article 125 § 2 of the Criminal Code—intentional infliction of minor bodily injury. The forensic examination concluded that her injuries had short-term health implications and could have resulted from either a slap or a punch.

The central dispute was whether the assault was motivated by religious prejudice. The applicant consistently stated that she had been attacked because she was a Jehovah’s Witness. N.S. and several fellow believers repeated her account. V.S. gave shifting explanations: first, that the women refused to leave and kept trying to recruit him; later, that he acted from “sudden hostility”; and eventually, that the applicant had insulted his masculinity. He denied any religious motive and claimed the word “shtundas” had no religious meaning. On 15 May 2013, the applicant asked the investigator to reclassify the offence as discriminatory acts under Article 161 § 2 of the Criminal Code. The request was refused on 17 May, the investigator finding only “sudden hostility” and no religious hatred.

At trial, V.S. pleaded guilty as charged. The applicant, represented by counsel, argued that the offence should be reclassified as discriminatory acts or hooliganism, invoking Articles 3, 9, and 14 of the Convention and the Court’s case law requiring authorities to unmask religious motives behind violence. On 16 July 2013, the Nosivka District Court convicted V.S. under Article 125 § 2, fined him about EUR 78, and awarded the applicant about EUR 278 in non-pecuniary damages. The Chernihiv Regional Court of Appeal upheld the judgment on 26 September 2013, and the High Specialised Court for Civil and Criminal Matters upheld it on 8 January 2014.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained under Articles 3, 9, and 14 that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into the assault, particularly by failing to uncover the alleged religious motive. She argued that the initial minor-injury classification narrowed the inquiry, that authorities accepted V.S.’s implausible and changing account, and that they failed to investigate his background or attitudes toward Jehovah’s Witnesses. The Government maintained that the investigation was prompt, thorough, and properly examined possible religious hostility, but found no such motive.

The Court held that Article 3 required an effective investigation even for ill-treatment by private individuals. While the authorities promptly investigated, identified, convicted, and punished the perpetrator—satisfying Article 3 taken alone—they failed to take reasonable steps to unmask a possible religious motive. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 3 read in conjunction with Article 14, with no separate issue arising under Article 9.

The case of *Livančić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* concerned eight applications (no. 15313/15 and seven others) lodged with the European Court of Human Rights against Bosnia and Herzegovina under Article 34 of the Convention. The applications were submitted on various dates. The Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina were given notice of the applications. The applicants all complained of the non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of domestic decisions that had been given in their favour. The specific applicants and the details of the relevant domestic decisions were set out in an appended table.

The applicants relied, expressly or in substance, on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees a fair hearing in the determination of civil rights and obligations, and on Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, which protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. They argued that the domestic authorities had failed to execute final decisions favourable to them, either altogether or within a reasonable time.

The Court joined the applications because they raised similar subject matter. It reiterated its established case-law that execution of a judgment given by any court must be regarded as an integral part of a “hearing” for the purposes of Article 6. It referred to *Hornsby v. Greece*, where it had held that the right to a court would be illusory if a final enforceable judgment remained unenforced. The Court also noted that the domestic decisions in these applications ordered specific action to be taken. For that reason, the decisions constituted “possessions” within the meaning of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1; the applicants had a legitimate expectation that the ordered action would be carried out.

In assessing the complaints, the Court relied heavily on its prior leading cases *Spahić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* and *Kunić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina*, both decided on 14 November 2017. In those cases, the Court had already found violations of the same Convention provisions in respect of similar problems of non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of final domestic decisions in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Court found no fact or argument in the present applications that would justify a different conclusion on admissibility or merits.

Having examined all the material, the Court concluded that the authorities had not deployed all necessary efforts to enforce fully and in due time the decisions in the applicants’ favour. The failure to enforce, or the delay in enforcing, final domestic decisions meant that the applicants did not receive the benefit of the judicial determinations they had obtained. This undermined the effectiveness of Article 6 § 1 and impaired their right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

Accordingly, the Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The judgment was adopted by the Fourth Section, sitting as a Committee, on 30 January 2020 and delivered on 20 February 2020. It was final but subject to editorial revision.

**Case summary: Livančić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina**  
*European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, 20 February 2020; Applications nos. 15313/15 and 7 others.*

The case originated in eight applications lodged against Bosnia and Herzegovina under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates listed in the appended table. The applicants complained of the non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of domestic decisions given in their favour. The Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina was given notice of the applications. Because the applications raised similar subject matter, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment.

The key facts, set out in the appended table, were that each applicant had obtained a final domestic decision—typically a court judgment or similar binding decision—that ordered specific action to be taken in their favour. These decisions were final and enforceable, and they created rights or entitlements that the applicants expected to enjoy. However, the domestic authorities either failed to enforce those decisions at all or enforced them late, partially, or otherwise not in full. As a result, the applicants did not receive the practical benefit of the domestic remedies they had successfully obtained.

The alleged violations therefore concerned not the fairness of the original domestic proceedings, but the failure of the State authorities to execute final domestic decisions. The applicants relied, expressly or in substance, on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees a fair hearing in the determination of civil rights and obligations, and on Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, which protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. They argued that the execution of a judgment is an integral part of the “hearing” for Article 6 purposes and that final domestic decisions in their favour constituted “possessions” within the meaning of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The Court reiterated its established case-law that the execution of a judgment given by any court must be regarded as an integral part of a “hearing” under Article 6. It referred to Hornsby v. Greece and to its leading judgments in Spahić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kunić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina, where it had already found violations in respect of similar issues. The Court further noted that the decisions in the present applications ordered specific action to be taken. It therefore considered that those decisions constituted “possessions” under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Consequently, the failure to enforce them engaged both Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

Having examined all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on admissibility or merits. Applying its case-law, it considered that the authorities had not deployed all necessary efforts to enforce fully and in due time the decisions in the applicants’ favour. The central violation was thus the State’s failure to ensure timely and complete execution of final domestic decisions, undermining the applicants’ fair-trial and property rights. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The judgment was final but subject to editorial revision.

Livančić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina (Applications nos. 15313/15 and 7 others) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, delivered on 20 February 2020. The case concerned eight applications lodged against Bosnia and Herzegovina under Article 34 of the Convention. The Government was given notice. Because the applications raised similar subject matter, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment.

The central facts were that each applicant had obtained final domestic decisions in their favour. The applicants complained that those decisions were either not enforced or were enforced only after delay. The domestic decisions were not merely declaratory; they ordered specific action to be taken by the respondent authorities. The applicants therefore alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees a fair hearing in the determination of civil rights and obligations, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, which protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. They relied expressly or in substance on both provisions.

The Court reiterated that execution of a judgment given by any court must be regarded as an integral part of a “hearing” for the purposes of Article 6. It referred to its established case-law, including Hornsby v. Greece, and to the leading Bosnia and Herzegovina cases Spahić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kunić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina. In those earlier cases, the Court had already found violations concerning similar failures by the authorities to enforce final domestic decisions.

Regarding Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, the Court noted that the decisions in the present applications ordered specific action to be taken. It therefore considered that the entitlements created by those decisions constituted “possessions” within the meaning of that provision. The alleged violation was not that the applicants had been formally deprived of property through legislation, but that final domestic decisions creating enforceable rights were left unexecuted or executed late.

In examining admissibility and the merits, the Court reviewed all material submitted. It found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion from its earlier case-law. It concluded that the domestic authorities had not deployed all necessary efforts to enforce fully and in due time the decisions in the applicants’ favour. In other words, the State failed to ensure effective and timely execution of binding judicial decisions, despite the applicants’ legitimate expectations.

Accordingly, the Court found violations of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision. The provided text does not include the full appended table, so individual applicant names, specific domestic decisions, exact dates, amounts, or the precise remedial action ordered are not detailed here. The key legally relevant facts are that final domestic decisions existed in the applicants’ favour, those decisions required specific action, and the authorities delayed or failed to enforce them, leading the Court to find a breach of the Convention and Protocol.
001-200213:
In *Aleksandrov v. Ukraine* (Application no. 56483/09), the European Court of Human Rights considered whether Ukrainian authorities hindered the applicant’s right of individual application under Article 34 of the Convention by failing to provide him with copies of documents from his criminal case file.

The applicant, Ruslan Alekseyevich Aleksandrov, was convicted on 25 December 2008 by the Court of Appeal of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea of two counts of rape and one count of murder. He was sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment. On 21 May 2009 the Supreme Court of Ukraine upheld that conviction. He was subsequently detained in Berdychiv correctional colony no. 70.

On 5 October 2009 the applicant informed the European Court of Human Rights of his intention to lodge an application. On 10 May 2010, the Court acknowledged receipt of his application form and attachments and requested that he submit copies of domestic court decisions and other relevant documents by 10 August 2010. Between 2009 and 2013, the applicant repeatedly asked the Crimea Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court of Ukraine to give him access to his case file or to send him copies of procedural documents, explaining that the Court required them.

The domestic authorities repeatedly refused. On numerous dates in 2009, 2010, 2011 and 2012, the Crimea Court of Appeal rejected his requests, stating that there was no legal basis for providing copies of documents from a criminal case file after a conviction became final. In February 2012, a judge told him that he had received all copies allowed by law and that, if he wanted additional procedural documents to send to the Court, he should provide confirmation that the Court had requested them and a list drafted by an authorised person. The applicant apparently misunderstood this and sent the Court’s Rules. In March 2012, the court rejected another request because the proceedings had ended. In November 2012, the applicant asked for his mother to be authorised to study the case file, but this was refused because only participants in criminal proceedings had access. In July 2013, a judge informed him that he could receive copies after paying a fee of 46 Ukrainian hryvnias. The applicant did not pay, saying he had no income and no legal counsel. He later claimed he had paid but provided no evidence.

The Government argued that the applicant could have copied documents before the criminal proceedings ended, that the February 2012 letter explained the procedure, and that the fee was not excessive. The Court rejected these arguments. It found the case similar to *Naydyon v. Ukraine*, *Vasiliy Ivashchenko v. Ukraine* and *Yakuba v. Ukraine*. Because the applicant was a prisoner without a lawyer and depended on the authorities, the State had an obligation not to hinder his Article 34 right of application. The February 2012 letter did not clearly explain any procedure, and the authorities denied access from 2009 to 2012. In 2013, the required fee was unaffordable for him, and no legal aid was available. The Court concluded that Ukraine had failed to comply with its Article 34 obligation to furnish all necessary facilities for the proper and effective examination of his application.

In *Aleksandrov v. Ukraine* (App. no. 56483/09, judgment of 9 January 2020), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Ukraine hindered the applicant’s right of individual petition under Article 34 of the Convention by failing to provide him with copies of documents from his criminal case file for use in his application to the Court.

The applicant, a Ukrainian national born in 1978, was convicted on 25 December 2008 by the Crimea Court of Appeal of two counts of rape and one count of murder and sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment. On 21 May 2009 the Supreme Court of Ukraine upheld that conviction. The applicant was serving his sentence in Berdychiv correctional colony no. 70.

On 5 October 2009 the applicant informed the Court of his intention to file an application. On 10 May 2010 the Court acknowledged receipt of his application form and asked him to submit copies of domestic court decisions and other relevant documents by 10 August 2010. Between 2009 and 2013, the applicant repeatedly asked the Crimea Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court of Ukraine for access to his case file or copies of procedural documents, stating that the Court had requested them.

On numerous occasions—including 2 February, 11 June, 7 and 9 July 2009; 10 March, 28 April, 1 and 21 July, 4 August and 5 November 2010; 16 March and 5 October 2011; and 10 May 2012—the Crimea Court of Appeal rejected his requests. It explained that domestic law did not provide for copies of documents from a criminal case file after a conviction had become final. On 29 February 2012 Judge G. told the applicant that he had received all documents allowed by law and that, if he wanted additional copies for the Court, he should submit a confirmation that the Court had requested them and a list, both drafted by an authorised person. The applicant claimed he made another request on 13 March 2012 and attached the Court’s Rules, but on 22 March 2012 the court rejected it because the proceedings had ended. On 4 December 2012 his request to authorise his mother to study the file was refused because only participants in criminal proceedings had access. On 11 July 2013 Judge T. told him he could receive copies if he paid a fee of 46 Ukrainian hryvnias; the applicant did not pay, saying he had no income and no legal counsel.

The Government argued that the applicant should have copied the documents before the criminal proceedings ended, that the 29 February 2012 letter explained the procedure, and that the fee was not excessive. The Court disagreed. It found the letter did not clearly explain the procedure and did not mention authorising a representative. It also noted that the applicant was denied access from 2009 to 2012 and was later asked to pay a fee despite having no income or legal aid. The authorities, without valid excuse, failed to take indispensable measures for the effective exercise of his right of application.

The Court therefore found a violation of Article 34, holding that Ukraine had failed to furnish all necessary facilities for a proper and effective examination of the applicant’s case.

**Case: Aleksandrov v. Ukraine (App. no. 56483/09), Judgment of 9 January 2020**

The applicant, Ruslan Alekseyevich Aleksandrov, a Ukrainian national born in 1978, was convicted by the Court of Appeal of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea on 25 December 2008 of two counts of rape and one count of murder. He was sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment. On 21 May 2009, the Supreme Court of Ukraine upheld that conviction. He was subsequently detained at Berdychiv correctional colony no. 70.

On 5 October 2009, while in detention, Aleksandrov informed the European Court of Human Rights of his intention to file an application. On 10 May 2010, the Court acknowledged receipt of his application and asked him to submit copies of domestic court decisions and other relevant case documents by 10 August 2010.

Between 2009 and 2013, the applicant repeatedly asked the Crimea Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court of Ukraine to provide him with access to his criminal case file or copies of procedural documents, explaining that the European Court had requested them. The domestic authorities refused on numerous occasions. They generally stated that there was no legal basis to provide copies after the conviction had become final, or that the proceedings had ended. On 29 February 2012, a judge of the Crimea Court of Appeal told him that he had already received the copies allowed by law and that, if he wanted additional documents to send to the European Court, he should present confirmation that the Court had requested them and a list of documents drafted by an authorised person. The applicant apparently misunderstood this and sent the Court’s Rules. Further requests in March 2012 and November 2012 were also rejected; the latter request to allow his mother to study the case file was refused because only participants in criminal proceedings had access.

In June 2013, the applicant again asked the Crimea Court of Appeal to send copies of documents, indicating that the European Court had requested them. On 11 July 2013, a judge replied that he had to pay a fee of UAH 46 and send proof of payment, after which the copies would be sent. The applicant did not pay, saying he had no income and no legal counsel. He later claimed he had paid the fee, but provided no evidence.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained under Article 34 of the Convention that the authorities had failed to provide him with copies of documents from his case file that he needed to substantiate his application. The Government argued that he could have copied documents before the criminal proceedings ended, that the procedure had been explained to him, and that the fee was not excessive.

The Court reiterated that Article 34 imposes an obligation on States not to hinder the effective exercise of the right of individual application. It found the case similar to earlier Ukrainian cases such as *Naydyon*, *Vasiliy Ivashchenko*, and *Yakuba*, where the domestic legal system lacked a clear and specific procedure for prisoners to obtain case documents after criminal proceedings had ended. It rejected the argument that the applicant should have made copies earlier. It also found that the 29 February 2012 letter did not clearly explain the necessary procedure and did not mention the possibility of authorising a representative. Finally, between 2009 and 2012 the applicant was denied access to the case file, and in 2013 he was required to pay a fee despite having no income or legal aid. The Government provided no contrary evidence.

The Court concluded that Ukraine had failed to comply with its obligation under Article 34 of the Convention to furnish all necessary facilities for the proper and effective examination of the applicant’s case.

The case concerned an application by the Religious Community of Jehovah’s Witnesses in Baku and Mr Oddvar Hansen, a Norwegian national. Hansen owned a private building and leased it without payment to the applicant community for religious meetings. On 24 December 2006, about 200 Jehovah’s Witnesses gathered for worship at their meeting hall on the second floor of that building. More than forty officials—including police officers, a representative of the State Committee for Work with Religious Associations, prosecutors and Ministry of National Security officials—raided the premises. According to a police investigator’s record, search and seizure procedures were carried out to prevent an unauthorised religious meeting. Eighteen items were seized, including computers and religious literature.

On 7 February 2007, the applicants lodged a complaint with the Khatai District Court in court-supervisory proceedings. Relying on the Code of Criminal Procedure and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, they asked the court to declare the search unlawful and to order the return of the seized computer equipment, religious literature and other property. The property was returned in March 2007. On 7 May 2007, the District Court partly allowed the complaint, holding that the search and seizure had been unlawful because they were carried out without a court order, contrary to the Code of Criminal Procedure. It also noted that the seized items had already been returned.

On 10 May 2007, the Khatai district prosecutor appealed, seeking to quash the favourable part of the decision. He argued that the authorities had not broken into the building, the doors had been open, and the owner had permitted entry. On 21 May 2007, the Baku Court of Appeal examined the case in the applicants’ absence, but in the presence of the prosecutor and a police representative. It said the applicants had been notified but had failed to appear. The Court of Appeal allowed the prosecutor’s appeal and found the search and seizure lawful under Article 177.6 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which provided that a court order was not required where the owner of the premises permitted entry. That decision was not amenable to further appeal.

The applicants alleged that they had received neither the notification nor a copy of the prosecutor’s appeal. Their lawyer reportedly learned only on 22 May 2007 that the first-instance decision had been appealed and quashed. Before the European Court of Human Rights, they complained under Article 6 § 1 that they had been unable to participate effectively in the appeal proceedings, and under Articles 9 and 14 that the domestic authorities had unlawfully interfered with their freedom of religion and discriminated against them as a religious minority.

The Court found Article 6 § 1 applicable under its civil head because the proceedings concerned the applicants’ civil rights to respect for their home and the peaceful enjoyment of their possessions. It found a violation of Article 6 § 1: the Government produced no proof that the applicants had been notified of the appeal hearing, and the appellate court did not verify whether they had been effectively informed. The applicants were therefore unable to attend, contest the prosecutor’s new argument about consent, or make submissions. This restricted their right to effective participation and equality of arms. The Article 9 and 14 complaints were rejected for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies, because the applicants had not raised religious freedom or discrimination, even in substance, before the domestic courts in those proceedings.

In *Religious Community of Jehovah’s Witnesses and Hansen v. Azerbaijan* (ECtHR, 30 January 2020), the applicants were a Baku-based Jehovah’s Witnesses community and Oddvar Hansen, a Norwegian national who owned a private building. Hansen leased the building to the community free of charge for religious meetings. On 24 December 2006, about 200 Jehovah’s Witnesses gathered there for worship. Authorities conducted a raid involving more than forty officials from the Khatai District police, the State Committee for Work with Religious Associations, the district prosecutor’s office and the Ministry of National Security. A police record stated that search and seizure were carried out to prevent an unauthorised religious meeting. Eighteen items were seized, including computers and religious literature.

On 7 February 2007 the applicants filed a court-supervisory complaint in the Khatai District Court, seeking a declaration that the search was unlawful and return of the property. The property was returned in March 2007. On 7 May 2007 the District Court partly allowed the complaint: the search and seizure were unlawful because they had been carried out without a court order, contrary to the Code of Criminal Procedure. On 10 May 2007 the district prosecutor appealed, arguing that the authorities had not broken in because the doors were open and the owner had permitted entry. On 21 May 2007 the Baku Court of Appeal heard the case in the applicants’ absence but with the prosecutor and a police representative present. It stated that the applicants had been notified but had failed to appear. It allowed the appeal and held that the search and seizure were lawful under Article 177.6 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which allowed entry without a court order when the owner consented. That decision was not subject to further appeal. The applicants alleged that they had not received notice of the appeal or a copy of the prosecutor’s appeal; their lawyer reportedly learned of the reversal only on 22 May 2007.

Before the Court, the applicants complained under Article 6 § 1 that they had not been informed of the appeal proceedings and could not participate. They also complained under Articles 9 and 14 that the authorities had unlawfully interfered with their freedom of religion and discriminated against them as a religious minority.

The Court found Article 6 applicable under its civil head because the proceedings concerned respect for the home and peaceful enjoyment of possessions. On the merits, the Government produced no proof that the applicants had been notified of the appeal hearing, and the appeal judgment or transcript did not show that the appellate court verified effective notification. Without notice, the applicants could not contest the prosecutor’s new consent argument or make submissions. The appellate decision was final and not subject to further review. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1: the applicants’ right to participate effectively and equality of arms were restricted.

As to Articles 9 and 14, the Court rejected the complaints for non-exhaustion. Although the case involved a religious assembly and seizure of religious literature, the applicants had not raised before the domestic courts, explicitly or in substance, any complaint of interference with freedom of religion or religious discrimination. No special circumstances excused that failure. Those complaints were therefore inadmissible under Article 35.

**Case: Religious Community of Jehovah’s Witnesses and Hansen v. Azerbaijan**  
**Application no. 52682/07, ECtHR Fifth Section, 30 January 2020**

The applicants were a local Jehovah’s Witnesses community in Baku and Oddvar Hansen, a Norwegian national who owned a private building used by the community as a meeting hall. On 24 December 2006, about 200 Jehovah’s Witnesses gathered there for worship. Authorities conducted a raid, search and seizure involving more than forty officials from the Khatai District Police, a police station, the State Committee for Work with Religious Associations, the district prosecutor’s office and the Ministry of National Security. The investigator’s record stated the measures were carried out to prevent an unauthorised religious meeting. Eighteen items were seized, including computers, computing equipment and religious literature, in the presence of attesting witnesses.

On 7 February 2007 the applicants complained to the Khatai District Court under the Code of Criminal Procedure and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, seeking a declaration that the search was unlawful and return of the seized property. The property was returned by March 2007. On 7 May 2007 the District Court partly allowed the complaint, holding that the search and seizure were unlawful because they had been conducted without a court order, contrary to the CCrP. It noted that the property had already been returned.

On 10 May 2007 the district prosecutor appealed, arguing that the authorities had not broken in; the doors had been open and the owner had permitted entry. On 21 May 2007 the Baku Court of Appeal examined the case in the applicants’ absence but with the prosecutor and a police representative present. It stated that the applicants had been notified but had failed to appear. The appellate court allowed the prosecutor’s appeal and found the search and seizure lawful under Article 177.6 of the CCrP, which provided that a court order was not required when the owner of the premises permitted entry. That decision was not subject to further appeal.

The applicants alleged that they had not received either the notification or a copy of the prosecutor’s appeal. Their lawyer reportedly learned only on 22 May 2007 that the first-instance decision had been appealed and quashed.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants complained under Article 6 § 1 that they had been deprived of a fair trial because they were not informed of the appeal hearing and could not participate. They also complained under Articles 9 and 14 that the authorities had unlawfully interfered with their freedom of religion and discriminated against them as a religious minority.

The Court held that Article 6 § 1 was applicable under its civil head, because the proceedings concerned the applicants’ civil rights to respect for their home and peaceful enjoyment of possessions, even though they were not criminally charged. On the merits, the Government provided no proof that the applicants had been notified of the appeal hearing, and neither the appeal judgment nor the hearing transcript showed that the appellate court verified effective notification. The Court therefore accepted that the applicants were unaware of the hearing and unable to attend. The appellate court heard only the prosecutor and allowed a new justification based on alleged consent, which the applicants could not contest. Since no further appeal lay against that decision, the Article 6 § 1 fair-trial guarantee was violated, particularly the right to participate effectively and the equality of arms.

As to Articles 9 and 14, the Court rejected those complaints for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies. The applicants had not raised freedom of religion or discrimination, explicitly or in substance, before the domestic courts in the relevant proceedings, and no special circumstances excused that failure.

In **Starishko v. Ukraine** (no. 61839/12, 15 October 2020), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by Mr Anatoliy Petrovych Starishko, a Ukrainian national born in 1980 and serving a life sentence in Vinnytsya Prison No. 1. On 14 December 1999, the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Court convicted him of several counts of aggravated murder and theft and sentenced him to death. On 30 May 2000, the Supreme Court replaced the death penalty with life imprisonment and upheld the rest of the verdict. The applicant lodged his application on 18 July 2012.

The applicant raised two main complaints. First, under Article 3, he alleged that his life sentence was irreducible because he had no genuine prospect of release. Second, under Article 8, he complained about restrictions on his visiting rights during post-conviction detention from 2000 to 2014. The Court declared the remainder of the application inadmissible and gave notice of these two complaints.

As to Article 3, the applicant relied on *Petukhov v. Ukraine (No. 2)*, where the Court had found that life imprisonment in Ukraine violated Article 3 because of its irreducible nature. The Government argued that presidential clemency offered a clear and foreseeable route to release. The Court rejected that argument, recalling that in *Petukhov* it had found the presidential clemency procedure—the only real possibility of mitigating a life sentence apart from commutation for terminal illness—lacked sufficient clarity, certainty and transparency. It was more akin to a prerogative of mercy based on humanity than a penological review mechanism with procedural safeguards. The existing regime for life prisoners was incompatible with rehabilitation. In the present case, the same systemic problem existed: the applicant, like Mr Petukhov, was deprived of any genuine prospect of release. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 3.

**Keaney v. Ireland** (Application no. 72060/17, ECtHR, 30 April 2020) concerned the excessive length of civil proceedings in Ireland and the absence of an effective domestic remedy for delay.

The applicant, Vincent Keaney, an Irish national born in 1955, purchased the Scotts Building in Cobh in 1996 after winning the national lottery. Between 2000 and 2003, the applicant and M.N. entered into a series of agreements, deeds and share transfers involving the premises and Titanic Queenstown Trading Company Ltd. Relations deteriorated, the business failed, and M.N. took possession of the premises.

In February 2006, with legal representation, Keaney commenced High Court proceedings against eighteen defendants. He alleged deceit, fraud, misrepresentation or undue influence arising from the 2000–2003 transactions and sought to set aside the agreements.

The proceedings became extensively delayed. In April 2006, the case was admitted to the Commercial List, and the applicant was ordered to deliver a properly pleaded statement of claim. Multiple amended statements followed. Defendants brought motions to strike out all or part of the claim, largely because the pleadings were poorly particularised. In January 2007, the High Court struck out claims against most defendants; by March 2007, claims against fourteen of the eighteen defendants had been struck out. Further disputes over amended statements continued through 2007 and 2008. A final statement of claim was delivered on 1 July 2008. On 19 December 2008, the High Court dismissed all remaining claims, noting that aspects of the applicant’s case bordered on an abuse of process.

Appeals to the Supreme Court caused further delay. Notices of appeal were issued between February 2007 and February 2009, but the books of appeal were not filed until March 2014 after Supreme Court directions. The first appeal was heard in June 2015 and judgment delivered in July 2015. The second appeal was heard in February 2017 and judgment delivered on 5 April 2017. The final judgment therefore came approximately eleven years after the proceedings were instituted in February 2006.

The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the length of the civil proceedings violated the “reasonable time” requirement. The case also raised Article 13 in conjunction with Article 6 § 1: whether Ireland provided an effective domestic remedy for complaints about length of proceedings.

Ireland* and *Nash v. DPP*, left unclear whether and when damages for delay would actually be available. In *Aggerholm v. Denmark* (Application no. 45439/18), the applicant, a Danish man born in 1985, suffers from paranoid schizophrenia. In 2005, he was convicted of five incidents of violence and threats against a public servant and was sentenced to committal to a psychiatric hospital. After periods in a high-security unit and an open ward, he was moved to a closed ward, P4, in September 2012. The case concerned his restraint on 8 February 2013, when at 1:15 p.m. he was strapped to a restraint bed with a belt, wrist straps and ankle straps. He remained restrained until 9 February at 12:05 p.m., approximately twenty-two hours and fifty minutes. He alleged that this breached Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits inhuman and degrading treatment. A previous restraint on 3 January 2013 was not at issue.

The restraint followed escalating events on 7–8 February. On 7 February, the applicant was described as very frustrated and angry. He made remarks about the chief physician, H.H., including “We have to do something about her,” which staff perceived as threats. H.H. was informed. On 8 February, she told him that his day release was revoked. He refused to sit down or talk, appeared pale, tense and full of pent-up anger. After attempts at dialogue failed and he remained extremely angry, H.H. considered him dangerous to others and decided on physical restraint. The applicant went voluntarily to the restraint room and lay down on the bed.

During the restraint, staff maintained a constant watch. Doctors checked him at 2:45 p.m., 6:55 p.m., 10:46 p.m. and 10:30 a.m. At 6:55 p.m., he appeared quieter and more talkative, so one foot strap was released and toilet visits were permitted. At 10:46 p.m., he was still considered potentially dangerous because of “instinctive anger.” He was released the next morning after becoming cooperative.

The Psychiatric Patients’ Complaints Board found both the January and February restraints unlawful, holding that an immediate risk of harm had not been documented. The State Administration dismissed his compensation claim and found no Article 3 violation. The Health Authority later found no lack of care by H.H. The Medico-Legal Council, however, stated that the conditions for restraint had been present, that medical checks were sufficiently frequent, and that H.H.’s assessment was justified. The City Court and High Court agreed that the restraint was necessary to prevent imminent harm and was lawful. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal. H.H. later acknowledged that the applicant had probably not been correctly medicated in early 2013 and that there may have been a medication failure.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the key issue was whether the restraint, especially its continuation for almost twenty-three hours, was “strictly necessary” and respectful of human dignity. The Court found a violation of Article 3. It accepted that the initial immobilisation may have been intended as a last resort to prevent imminent harm, but held that the domestic courts had not adequately examined crucial issues concerning continuation and duration: why such a long period was required, whether less intrusive measures were considered, whether the applicant’s calmer periods or the released foot strap showed restraint could have ended earlier, and how medication problems affected the necessity of the measure. The prolonged strapping was therefore not strictly necessary and did not respect his human dignity, amounting to inhuman and degrading treatment.

The alleged violation arose from an incident beginning on 8 February 2013. The evening before, the applicant had been very angry and had made remarks about the chief physician, H.H., which staff understood as threats, including “We have to do something about her” and, according to one witness, that she should have “a bullet through her head.” After speaking with a doctor, he appeared calm. The next day, staff decided he should not go on day release because of his anger. When H.H. told him his day release was revoked, he refused to talk, appeared white-faced and tense, and seemed to have pent-up anger. Attempts at dialogue over about one and a half hours failed, and he was considered dangerous. At 1.15 p.m. on 8 February 2013, he was strapped to a restraint bed with a belt and wrist and ankle straps—a five-point restraint. He went to the restraint room voluntarily and lay down.

He remained restrained for 22 hours and 50 minutes, until 12.05 p.m. on 9 February 2013. A staff member was constantly present. Doctors checked him four times. At 2.45 p.m. he still showed pent-up anger and latent aggression; at 6.55 p.m. he was quieter and one foot strap was released, with toilet and hygiene visits permitted; at 10.46 p.m. he was still considered potentially dangerous; and at 10.30 a.m. the next day he was cooperative, leading to release at 12.05 p.m.

The Psychiatric Patients’ Complaints Board found both the January 2013 restraint and the February 2013 restraint unlawful. For the February measure, it found it was not documented that the applicant had exposed himself or others to an immediate risk of harm to body or health. The State Administration dismissed his Article 3 compensation claim, and the Health Authority found no lack of care by H.H. In subsequent court proceedings, the Medico-Legal Council opined that the conditions for restraint had been present, that assessments were sufficiently frequent, and that the chief physician’s decision was justified. H.H. testified that the applicant had a history of violence, that restraint was a last resort, and later acknowledged he may have been under-medicated at the time. The City Court and High Court upheld the measure as necessary and proportionate.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 3. It held that restraining the applicant for almost 23 hours was not strictly necessary and was not respectful of his human dignity. Although domestic courts portrayed the immobilisation as a last resort and the only means of preventing immediate or imminent harm, they were silent on crucial issues relevant to whether continuing the restraint, and its very long duration, was strictly necessary—particularly after he calmed and less intrusive measures were used.

Glavinić and Marković v. Croatia (Apps. 11388/15 and 25605/15), ECtHR First Section, 30 July 2020, concerned two Croatian nationals who alleged that the length of their civil and enforcement proceedings was excessive and that Croatia lacked an effective remedy, contrary to Article 6 §1 and Article 13. Their applications were lodged on 27 February and 25 May 2015 and joined.

The first applicant, Jela Glavinić (b. 1947), was a defendant in a civil action filed on 8 January 2003 in the Zadar Municipal Court seeking annulment of a gift contract. She responded on 24 February 2003. The Municipal Court dismissed the claim only on 10 July 2014; the judgment was served on 9 September 2014 and became final on 20 April 2015. The proceedings thus lasted about 12 years and 2 months for one level of jurisdiction. On 24 October 2013 she used the 2013 Courts Act’s purely acceleratory remedy, requesting the court president to expedite. On 24 December 2013 the president found the request well-founded and ordered a decision within six months. When that time-limit expired, she sought compensation from the Zadar County Court. On 23 October 2014 the County Court awarded only HRK 1,000, found the length excessive, but held she had contributed to delay by failing to attend hearings on 9 April and 13 June 2014. She disputed that finding. The Supreme Court dismissed her appeal on 15 December 2014. She complained that the compensation was insufficient and that no effective remedy existed.

The second applicant, Aleksander Marković (b. 1936), applied on 20 July 2012 to enforce a judgment of 27 January 2010 requiring company T. to perform construction works. A writ of execution issued on 14 February 2013, but company T. appealed. The County Court decided the appeal only on 10 February 2017, quashed the writ and remitted the case. A new writ issued on 5 July 2017. Meanwhile, in April 2017 the Zagreb Commercial Court opened “emergency administration” proceedings against company T.’s parent and subsidiaries. This stayed enforcement, converted non-financial claims into financial claims, and required creditors to register. Marković registered HRK 1,400,000. Enforcement was stayed in October 2017. In July 2018 a settlement was approved giving him 14.4% (or 2.6% on liquidation) in financial instruments; implementation was ongoing. By 2020 the proceedings had lasted almost eight years. He had lodged a purely acceleratory request in September 2014; it was dismissed in November 2014, as was his Supreme Court appeal in December 2014. In February 2015 he lodged a constitutional complaint under section 63 of the Constitutional Court Act concerning the length of enforcement. The Constitutional Court treated it as a section 62 complaint against the Supreme Court’s remedial decision and declared it inadmissible.

The key issue was whether domestic remedies were effective and exhausted. The Government argued non-exhaustion. The ECtHR found that the first applicant could not reasonably have used a section 63 constitutional complaint because the relevant case-law change came after her deadline. For the second applicant, his complaint clearly invoked section 63 and challenged the length of the principal proceedings, but the Constitutional Court wrongly reclassified it as a section 62 complaint. The Court therefore found excessive length and a lack of effective domestic remedy, violating Article 6 §1 and Article 13.

**Case Summary: Glavinić and Marković v. Croatia**  
*(ECtHR, First Section, 30 July 2020)*

The case concerned two Croatian applicants who complained that their civil and enforcement proceedings had exceeded a reasonable time and that Croatia lacked an effective domestic remedy for length-of-proceedings complaints, contrary to Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention.

**First applicant (Glavinić):** In January 2003 a plaintiff sued her and others in the Zadar Municipal Court to annul a gift contract. She responded in February 2003. The Municipal Court did not deliver judgment until July 2014; it was served in September 2014 and became final in April 2015—about 12 years and 2 months at one level of jurisdiction. In October 2013 she used the 2013 Courts Act purely acceleratory remedy, asking the court president to expedite the case. In December 2013 the president found the request well-founded and ordered a decision within six months. When that deadline was missed, she sought compensation. In October 2014 the Zadar County Court awarded only HRK 1,000, finding the length excessive but stating that she had contributed to the delay by failing to attend two hearings in 2014. The Supreme Court dismissed her appeal in December 2014. She alleged that this compensation was insufficient.

**Second applicant (Marković):** In July 2012 he sought enforcement of a January 2010 judgment ordering company T. to carry out construction repairs. A writ of execution issued in February 2013; company T. appealed. In February 2017 the Karlovac County Court quashed the writ and remitted the case. A new writ issued in July 2017. However, in April 2017 the Zagreb Commercial Court opened “emergency administration” proceedings against company T.’s parent, company A., and its subsidiaries under emergency legislation. This stayed all civil and enforcement proceedings, converted non-financial creditor claims into financial claims, and required creditors to register claims. Marković registered HRK 1.4 million. In October 2017 the enforcement court stayed proceedings. In July 2018 a settlement was approved; Marković was entitled to 14.4% in financial instruments if successfully implemented, or 2.6% on liquidation. By the time of the application, the enforcement proceedings had lasted nearly eight years and remained unresolved. He had also used the 2013 acceleratory remedy in September 2014, but it was dismissed by the County Court and Supreme Court. In February 2015 he lodged a constitutional complaint under section 63 of the Constitutional Court Act alleging excessive length of the enforcement proceedings. The Constitutional Court, however, treated it as a section 62 complaint against the Supreme Court’s decision and declared it inadmissible in March 2015 for lack of jurisdiction.

The Government argued non-exhaustion, saying both applicants should have lodged constitutional complaints under section 63 after using the statutory length remedies. The Court rejected this. For the first applicant, the section 63 remedy had not been clearly available within the relevant time-limit because the Constitutional Court’s case-law change came later. For the second applicant, he had expressly invoked section 63, and the Constitutional Court wrongly reclassified his complaint. The Court found the applications admissible and concluded that the length of proceedings was excessive and that the available remedies—particularly the purely acceleratory remedy and the constitutional complaint—were ineffective, violating Article 6 § 1 and Article 13.

**Summary**

*Glavinić and Marković v. Croatia* (ECtHR, 30 July 2020) concerned two Croatian nationals who complained that the length of their civil and enforcement proceedings had been excessive and that domestic remedies for delay were ineffective.

The first applicant, Ms Glavinić, became involved in civil proceedings on 8 January 2003, when a plaintiff sued her and others in the Zadar Municipal Court seeking annulment of a gift contract. She responded on 24 February 2003. The Municipal Court did not deliver judgment until 10 July 2014, dismissing the claim. That judgment was served on her on 9 September 2014 and became final on 20 April 2015. The proceedings therefore lasted about twelve years and two months for one level of jurisdiction.

While the case was pending, she used the 2013 Courts Act’s purely acceleratory remedy on 24 October 2013, asking the President of the Zadar Municipal Court to protect her right to a hearing within a reasonable time. In December 2013 the president found the request well-founded and ordered the judge to decide within six months. When that deadline was missed, she sought compensation from the Zadar County Court. In October 2014 that court awarded her HRK 1,000, finding the length excessive but also stating that she had contributed to delay by missing two hearings. Her appeal was dismissed by the Supreme Court in December 2014. The Government later argued she had failed to exhaust domestic remedies by not lodging a constitutional complaint. The ECtHR rejected that argument, finding that the relevant constitutional remedy only became widely available after a Constitutional Court decision of 23 December 2014, published in January 2015, after her time-limit had expired.

The second applicant, Mr Marković, applied on 20 July 2012 for enforcement of a 2010 judgment requiring company T. to carry out construction works. In February 2013 the Karlovac Municipal Court issued a writ of execution, but company T. appealed. The appeal was not decided until February 2017, when the County Court quashed the writ and remitted the case. A new writ was issued in July 2017, but in April 2017 the Zagreb Commercial Court had opened “emergency administration proceedings” against company T.’s parent company and subsidiaries. This stayed enforcement proceedings and converted non-financial claims into financial claims. Marković registered a claim of HRK 1,400,000. In 2018 a settlement was approved entitling him to 14.4% or 2.6% of his claim depending on implementation.

By the time of the ECtHR judgment, the enforcement proceedings had lasted almost eight years and had not ended. Marković had used the acceleratory remedy in September 2014, but the President of the Karlovac County Court dismissed it in November 2014, and the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal in December 2014. In February 2015 he lodged a constitutional complaint expressly under section 63 of the Constitutional Court Act, complaining of the length of the principal enforcement proceedings. The Constitutional Court treated it as a section 62 complaint against the Supreme Court’s remedial decision and declared it inadmissible. The ECtHR found that he had clearly invoked section 63 and was complaining about the principal proceedings, not merely the remedial decision.

The applicants alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (reasonable time) and Article 13 (effective remedy). The Court joined the applications and found that the proceedings were excessively long and that the domestic remedies—particularly the purely acceleratory request and the constitutional complaint—did not provide effective redress, resulting in violations of both provisions.

In *Berkman v. Russia*, the applicant was a Russian national and LGBTI rights supporter in St Petersburg. On 27 September 2013, organisers notified the authorities of a public meeting to mark Coming Out Day on 12 October 2013 at the Field of Mars, expected to run from 2 p.m. to 3.30 p.m., with about 150 participants and some arriving at 1.30 p.m. to prepare. The authorities forwarded the notice to the police and warned organisers about liability for inciting hatred or promoting “non-traditional” sexual relationships to minors. The police deployed around 540 officers, including special-purpose units, anticipating clashes with counter-demonstrators, but apparently did not install crowd barriers or a perimeter fence.

On 12 October, police arrived at 11.30 a.m. The applicant arrived around 1 p.m. to help prepare. She said that 20–30 participants were unable to gather because more than 100 aggressive counter-demonstrators blocked the site. Many counter-demonstrators wore national costumes and carried whips; they insulted, pushed, punched, surrounded and followed the LGBTI participants. When participants asked police for help, the officers did not react until the counter-demonstrators insulted the police themselves. Police then arrested several counter-demonstrators, took them to a police bus and released them; the attacks continued. At 1.55 p.m., police surrounded a group of twelve demonstrators, including the applicant, alleging foul language and breach of public order. They ordered them onto a police bus and took them to central police station no. 28 under Article 27.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences. The Government said 93 people were arrested for disorderly conduct and taken to three stations before release; the applicant claimed only Coming Out Day participants were taken.

The applicant was detained from 2.30 p.m. to about 6.30 p.m. under Article 27.3. At around 6 p.m., police records stated she had been detained at 1.55 p.m. for disorderly conduct under Article 20.1 and taken to the station to ensure prompt and proper examination of her case. The grounds were that she had used foul language during the public meeting and ignored police warnings. She signed the records but noted her disagreement. On 8 November 2013, the Dzerzhinskiy District Court terminated the administrative proceedings against her for lack of evidence. Similar charges against other participants were also terminated; one conviction was quashed on appeal.

The applicant brought civil proceedings against police authorities, challenging the lawfulness of her arrest and detention and alleging that the authorities failed to ensure the personal safety of meeting participants. Domestic courts dismissed her claim. They found the arrest lawful as an interim measure due to tension between demonstrators and opponents, that detention did not exceed 48 hours, that no harm was caused, and that her claim was belated. Appeals and cassation attempts failed; the Supreme Court later said the case file had been destroyed.

The alleged violations concerned Articles 11 and 14: the authorities allegedly failed to ensure the peaceful conduct of the LGBTI awareness event, police passively allowed homophobic verbal attacks and physical pressure by counter-demonstrators, and the State failed its positive obligations in light of public hostility toward LGBTI people. The arrest allegedly breached negative obligations by preventing the applicant’s participation in the event. Under Article 5 § 1, the Court examined the lack of reasons and legal grounds for her arrest for a suspected administrative offence. It found no evidence that the arrests discriminatorily targeted only participants, since both participants and opponents were arrested.
