Berkman v. Russia (Application no. 46712/15) is an ECtHR Third Section judgment delivered on 1 December 2020 (final 1 March 2021). The applicant, Ms Yelena Berkman, complained about the Russian authorities’ handling of an LGBTI awareness event in St Petersburg marking Coming Out Day on 12 October 2013, and about her arrest, removal and detention.

On 27 September 2013, LGBTI rights activists notified the St Petersburg authorities of their intention to hold a meeting at the Field of Mars from 2 p.m. to 3:30 p.m. on 12 October 2013. About 150 people were expected, with preparations beginning at 1:30 p.m. The authorities forwarded the notice to the police and warned organisers about liability for inciting hatred or promoting “non-traditional” sexual relations to minors. The police deployed around 540 officers, apparently anticipating clashes with counter-demonstrators, but no crowd barriers or perimeter fence were installed.

When the applicant arrived around 1 p.m. to help prepare, about twenty or thirty participants were blocked by more than 100 aggressive counter-demonstrators. Some wore national costumes and carried whips. They insulted, pushed, punched, surrounded and followed the LGBTI participants. The participants asked police for help, but the officers initially failed to react. Police intervened only after counter-demonstrators insulted the police themselves. Several counter-demonstrators were briefly arrested and released, after which they resumed verbal attacks and physical pressure. At 1:55 p.m., police surrounded twelve demonstrators, including the applicant, accused them of using foul language in public and ordered them onto a police bus. They were taken to police station no. 28 under Article 27.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences. The Government said ninety-three people were arrested for disorderly conduct; the applicant alleged that only Coming Out Day participants were taken to police stations.

The applicant was detained from 2:30 p.m. to about 6:30 p.m. under Article 27.3. Records alleged she had used foul language and ignored police warnings; she signed while disputing the allegations. On 8 November 2013, the Dzerzhinskiy District Court terminated the administrative proceedings against her for lack of evidence. Similar charges against other participants were mostly terminated, and one conviction was later quashed. Her civil challenge to the arrest, detention and alleged failure to ensure participants’ safety was dismissed. The domestic courts found the arrest lawful as an interim measure because tension made it difficult to identify offenders immediately; they also relied on the statutory forty-eight-hour detention limit.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged violations of Article 5 § 1 (arbitrary and unlawful arrest/detention), Article 11 (freedom of assembly) and Article 14 (discrimination). The Court declared the complaints admissible. It found that the applicant’s arrest lacked sufficient reasons and legal grounds under Article 5. It also found that Russia failed its positive obligations under Articles 11 and 14 to ensure the peaceful conduct of the LGBTI awareness event, because police passively allowed homophobic verbal attacks and physical pressure by counter-demonstrators. The State also breached its negative obligation by preventing the applicant’s participation through unlawful arrest. However, the Court found no evidence that the arrests themselves were discriminatory as between the event participants and their opponents. The case therefore concerned both police failure to protect a vulnerable minority assembly and arbitrary interference with individual liberty.
001-206371:
**Parinov v. Ukraine (Application no. 48398/17), judgment of 10 December 2020**

The applicant, Mr Borys Parinov, a Ukrainian national, was a shareholder in a limited liability company. He withdrew from the company on 30 May 2005, but the other shareholder failed to return his share of the company’s funds, contrary to domestic law. In 2007–2008, a first set of proceedings confirmed that the applicant had withdrawn from the company. Meanwhile, the company sold two commercial buildings to third-party companies.

In June 2008, the applicant brought a second set of proceedings seeking reimbursement of the value of his share. He later amended his claim to challenge the validity of the property sale contracts. In 2010–2011, those proceedings ended: the Higher Commercial Court terminated the reimbursement claim because the issue was being examined in insolvency proceedings, and rejected the contract-invalidity claim for lack of standing.

Separately, in October 2010, insolvency proceedings were initiated against the company. In December 2010, the applicant lodged a creditor’s claim. On 11 April 2011, the Commercial Court recognised him as a creditor for UAH 4,100,439 (about EUR 356,560 at the time), corresponding to his share. The insolvency proceedings were then suspended at the applicant’s representative’s requests between April 2011 and June 2013 for a total of about one year, eleven months and fifteen days. In February 2014, the company was declared insolvent, liquidation began, and liquidator D. was appointed. A report in April 2014 indicated that the company owned only two vehicles whose location was unknown.

The Commercial Court did not operate from July 2014 to April 2015 because of the armed conflict in eastern Ukraine. It resumed work in Kharkiv, and in July 2015 reopened the insolvency case. The key delay then began: in August 2015, liquidator D. asked to be dismissed from his position. The creditors’ committee repeatedly failed to decide on his withdrawal or propose a new liquidator. Between 2015 and 2019, the Commercial Court issued numerous decisions ordering the committee to act and tried to find a new liquidator through the automatic system, but candidates either did not reply or refused. As a result, no new liquidator was appointed, and the liquidation remained effectively blocked. The applicant died in September 2018; his son and wife were permitted to pursue the application, and his wife was later admitted as a creditor/heir in the domestic proceedings.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 about the excessive length of the proceedings, under Article 13 about the lack of an effective remedy, and under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about being unable to recover his share. The Government argued that the insolvency proceedings were complex and that delays were caused by the parties and the liquidator, not the State.

The Court treated the proceedings as three separate sets. Complaints about the first and second sets were rejected as out of time because they had ended in 2008 and 2011, while the application was lodged in 2017. The insolvency proceedings, however, were still ongoing, so the complaint was admissible. On the merits, the relevant period began in December 2010 and had lasted about nine years and eleven months at one level of jurisdiction. The Court accepted that the suspensions and the period of armed conflict were not attributable to the State. However, the failure to appoint a new liquidator after August 2015—at least four and a half years—was attributable to Ukraine, especially since the Commercial Court could appoint a liquidator of its own motion. The Court found that this delay violated the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1 and that there was no effective domestic remedy under Article 13.

In *Parinov v. Ukraine* (no. 48398/17, judgment 10 December 2020), Mr Parinov, a Ukrainian national, complained under Articles 6 and 13 ECHR and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that domestic proceedings concerning his share in a limited liability company lasted excessively and prevented him from recovering that share.

He became a shareholder in 2000 and withdrew in May 2005, but the other shareholder failed to return his share. In December 2007 he brought proceedings to confirm his withdrawal; this was finally upheld in April 2008. Meanwhile, the company sold two commercial buildings to third companies. In June 2008 he began a second set of proceedings seeking reimbursement and invalidation of those sales. The commercial courts initially ruled partly in his favour, but in December 2011 the Higher Commercial Court terminated the reimbursement claim because the issue was being dealt with in insolvency proceedings and rejected the invalidity claim for lack of standing.

In October 2010 insolvency proceedings began against the company. In April 2011 the court recognised the applicant as a creditor for UAH 4,100,439 (about EUR 356,560), corresponding to his share. The insolvency case was suspended and resumed several times, partly at the applicant’s request. In February 2014 the company was declared insolvent and liquidator D. was appointed. A report showed the company had only two vehicles whose location was unknown. From July 2014 to April 2015 the court did not operate because of the armed conflict in eastern Ukraine; it later resumed in Kharkiv. In August 2015 D. asked to be dismissed. After that, no new liquidator was appointed for years: the creditors’ committee failed to act, and candidates found through the automatic system either did not respond or declined. The court repeatedly tried to resolve the vacancy through 2019. The proceedings remained ongoing. The applicant died in 2018; his son and wife were allowed to pursue the application.

The applicant also filed a criminal complaint against company officials in 2011; it was closed in 2014, reopened after being quashed in 2016, and remained under investigation.

Before the ECtHR, the Government argued that the first two sets of proceedings had ended long before the 2017 application and were time-barred. The Court agreed: the first ended in April 2008 and the second in December 2011, so complaints about them were out of time. The insolvency proceedings, however, were still pending, so the length complaint was admissible.

On the merits, the Court found the relevant insolvency period began in December 2010 and had lasted about nine years and eleven months at one level. Delays caused by the applicant’s suspension requests and the armed conflict were not imputable to Ukraine. But the failure from August 2015 to appoint a new liquidator blocked the proceedings; at least four and a half years of delay were attributable to the State. This violated Article 6 § 1’s reasonable-time requirement. The Court also found a violation of Article 13 because Ukrainian law provided no effective remedy for the length of proceedings. The key facts were therefore the prolonged insolvency, the liquidator vacancy, repeated appointment failures, and the absence of a domestic length remedy.

In *Parinov v. Ukraine* (no. 48398/17), the ECtHR examined complaints about prolonged proceedings over the applicant’s share in a company. The applicant became a shareholder in 2000 and withdrew in May 2005, but the other shareholder did not return his share. In December 2007 he brought first proceedings; in April 2008 a final ruling acknowledged his withdrawal. Meanwhile, the company sold two buildings to B., which resold them to K. In June 2008 the applicant began second proceedings seeking reimbursement of his share value and later challenged the sale contracts as invalid. In December 2011 a final decision terminated the reimbursement claim because it was covered by insolvency proceedings and rejected the contract challenge for lack of standing.

In October 2010 insolvency proceedings against the company began. In April 2011 the Commercial Court recognised the applicant as a creditor for UAH 4,100,439 (about EUR 356,560). In February 2014 the company was declared insolvent, liquidation began, and D. was appointed liquidator. D. later reported the company owned only two vehicles of unknown location. The court did not operate from July 2014 to April 2015 due to armed conflict and later resumed in Kharkiv. In August 2015 D. asked to be dismissed. The creditors’ committee failed to choose a replacement, and repeated attempts to appoint a new liquidator failed. D. moved to Odessa, liquidation was suspended, and by 2019 no new liquidator had been appointed. The applicant died in 2018; his son and wife pursued the application.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (excessive length), Article 13 (no effective remedy), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (inability to recover his share). The Court rejected as out of time complaints about the first two sets of proceedings, whose final decisions were in 2008 and 2011, while the application was lodged in 2017. It considered only the insolvency proceedings, which began in December 2010 and remained ongoing, lasting over nine years and eleven months at one level. Delays from the applicant’s suspension requests and the armed conflict were not attributed to the State. However, from August 2015 the proceedings were blocked because the liquidator withdrew and no replacement was appointed. This delay of at least four and a half years was attributable to Ukraine, as the State must organise its judicial system so courts can meet reasonable-time requirements. Complexity did not justify the delay.

Under Article 13, the Government argued the applicant could have complained about the liquidator’s inactivity. The Court found this ineffective because the main defect was the absence of any liquidator and the court’s failure to appoint one. The insolvency-length complaint under Article 6 and the Article 13 complaint were declared admissible. The key violation was the excessive length of the insolvency proceedings, caused principally by the State’s failure to ensure appointment of a new liquidator.
001-202750:
**M.S. v. Slovakia and Ukraine** concerned an Afghan national who alleged that he was a minor when detained, expelled by Slovakia to Ukraine, and later expelled by Ukraine to Afghanistan, where he feared persecution. He claimed his father, who had worked for Afghanistan’s National Security Department, was killed around 2005 by unknown persons possibly linked to the Taliban. In 2010, after his uncle received a threatening letter, arrangements were made for him to leave Afghanistan. Smugglers took him through Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Russia; he entered Ukraine in July 2010 and stayed in Kyiv for about three months. In September 2010 he crossed illegally into Slovakia with other Afghan nationals and was arrested.

Slovak border police interviewed him with interpretation from Slovak into English and then into Pashto by another Afghan in the group. The record stated his date of birth as 14 January 1992 and that he wished to go to Western Europe and was not seeking asylum in Slovakia. The applicant alleged that he had no proper interpreter or lawyer, was not informed about asylum procedures, and tried to say he was a minor and wanted asylum. Slovakia expelled him to Ukraine on 24 September 2010.

In Ukraine, he was held at the Chop border facility and later in Volyn. He alleged that he told officials he was fourteen and wanted to apply for asylum, but no action was taken. On 13 October 2010 a Ukrainian court ordered his expulsion and detention pending expulsion. The court relied on a 2008 UNHCR publication suggesting Afghanistan was not a country where crimes against persons occurred, concluded he would not be at risk, and noted he had not applied for asylum. The applicant claimed he was unaware of the proceedings, lacked legal representation and interpretation, signed a waiver without understanding, and was not served the decision, so he missed the appeal deadline.

On 23 February 2011 he applied for asylum in Ukraine, stating he would be “immediately killed” if returned to Afghanistan. On 9 March 2011 the Regional Migration Service rejected the application as inadmissible and manifestly unfounded. It found he did not meet the refugee definition, had not shown political, social or military targeting, had obtained an Afghan travel document suggesting protection in his country of origin, had not sought asylum while transiting other countries and only applied after being returned from Slovakia, indicating his aim was the United Kingdom, and lacked identity documents so his identity and country of origin could not be verified. The decision was notified to him on 11 March 2011, three days before his expulsion to Kabul on 14 March 2011. He alleged that after return, unknown persons searched for him and left a threatening letter.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the main complaints against Ukraine concerned Article 3: failure to examine his fear of persecution before expulsion, reliance on formal rejection grounds, contradictory conclusions about his identity document and country of origin, late notification of the asylum decision, and the domestic court’s irrational use of outdated country information. Under Article 5 §§ 2 and 4, he complained that he was not informed in a language he understood of the legal reasons for his detention or the related proceedings, and had no interpreter or lawyer. Under Article 34, he alleged that an NGO was denied access, preventing a request for an interim measure. Against Slovakia, he complained under Articles 3 and 13 that lack of interpretation and legal assistance denied him an opportunity to seek asylum and led to his return to Ukraine and risk of refoulement. The Court noted that the parties disputed his age: although he claimed to have been a minor, domestic records consistently recorded his birth date as 14 January 1992, while the copy of his Afghan identity document was illegible and contradicted those records.

**Case Summary: M.S. v. Slovakia and Ukraine (Application no. 17189/11)**

The applicant, M.S., is an Afghan national who alleged he was born in 1993 or 1994, making him a minor at the time of the events. He claimed his father, a former Afghan government employee, was killed by the Taliban around 2005, and that in 2010 his uncle received a threatening letter, prompting his flight from Kunduz province.

In September 2010, the applicant illegally crossed from Ukraine into Slovakia, where he was arrested by border police. He had no identity documents. According to Slovak authorities, he was interviewed with interpretation from Slovak to English, then English to Pashto by a fellow Afghan. The record noted his birth date as 14 January 1992 (making him 18) and stated he did not wish to seek asylum in Slovakia. The applicant disputed this, claiming he had no proper interpretation, no access to a lawyer, and that he repeatedly tried to request asylum and inform officials he was a minor. He was not given the opportunity to sign the interview record and was not provided with a written expulsion decision or informed of appeal options.

On 24 September 2010, Slovakia expelled him to Ukraine under a readmission agreement. In Ukraine, he was detained at a Border Guard facility in Chop, where he alleged overcrowded conditions. He claimed he informed a guard and a Caritas representative that he was a minor and wished to apply for asylum, but no action was taken.

On 13 October 2010, a Ukrainian court ordered his expulsion and detention pending expulsion. The court relied on outdated UNHCR country information from 2008, concluding Afghanistan was not a country where crimes against persons occurred. The applicant was not present, had no legal representation, and did not understand the proceedings. He signed a document waiving his right to appear without understanding its contents. The decision was not served on him, and he missed the appeal deadline.

On 23 February 2011, the applicant lodged an asylum application in Ukraine, stating he would be "immediately killed" if returned to Afghanistan. On 9 March 2011, the Regional Migration Service rejected it as inadmissible, finding his claims manifestly unfounded. Critically, the Service concluded that since he had no identity documents, it was impossible to identify him or his country of origin—despite simultaneously relying on an Afghan travel document issued to him. The decision was only notified to him on 11 March 2011, after he had been transferred in preparation for expulsion. On 14 March 2011, he was expelled to Kabul.

The applicant alleged that approximately three weeks after his return, unknown persons sought him at his home, leaving a threatening letter. He has since been forced to relocate frequently for fear of the people who killed his father.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations by Ukraine of Article 3 (failure to examine his fear of persecution before expulsion), Article 5 §§ 2 and 4 (failure to inform him of reasons for detention and inability to participate effectively in detention proceedings), and found Ukraine complied with Article 34. The Court's assessment focused on the Ukrainian authorities' formalistic rejection of his asylum claim, contradictory conclusions regarding his identity and origin, and the irrational reliance on outdated country information.

In *M.S. v. Slovakia and Ukraine* (ECtHR, 11 June 2020), the applicant was an Afghan national who claimed to have been born in 1993/94, making him a minor when detained and expelled. Slovak and Ukrainian authorities, however, consistently recorded his birth date as 14 January 1992. He lived in Kunduz. His father, who worked for Afghanistan’s National Security Department, was killed around 2005, possibly by Taliban-linked persons. In 2010 his uncle received a threatening letter and arranged his departure. Smugglers took him through Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Russia; he entered Ukraine in July 2010, stayed in Kyiv for three months, then crossed illegally into Slovakia on 23 September 2010 with three other Afghans.

Slovak border police arrested him without identity papers. At his interview, interpretation was provided from Slovak into English, with another Afghan translating into Pashto. He reportedly said he wanted to go to Western Europe and did not request asylum in Slovakia. His birth date was recorded as 14 January 1992. He did not sign the record. The next day Slovakia issued an expulsion order and a five-year entry ban and handed him over to Ukraine. He alleged he had no proper interpretation or legal assistance, tried to ask for asylum through a fellow Afghan who spoke French, told officials he was a minor, but was ignored; he received no written decision or appeal information.

In Ukraine, he was held at the Chop border facility. He alleged overcrowding and that he told a guard and a Caritas representative he was 14 and wanted asylum, but no action was taken. On 13 October 2010 a court ordered his expulsion and detention pending expulsion. It relied on his illegal entry, lack of means or relatives, and an outdated 2008 UNHCR publication suggesting Afghanistan was not a country where crimes against the person occurred, concluding his life would not be at risk. The applicant said he was unaware of the proceedings, had no lawyer or interpreter, signed a waiver without understanding it, was not served the decision, and missed the appeal deadline.

On 23 February 2011 he applied for asylum, saying he would be immediately killed if returned. After an interview, the Regional Migration Service rejected the application as inadmissible on 9 March 2011. It found the claim manifestly unfounded, said he did not meet the refugee definition, that an Afghan travel document showed protection in his country, that he had not sought asylum while travelling, and that without identity documents his identity and country of origin could not be established. The decision was notified only on 11 March 2011, three days before expulsion. On 12 March, NGO/UNHCR representatives were allegedly denied access to provide legal advice, preventing a Rule 39 request. On 14 March 2011 he was expelled to Kabul. He later alleged unknown persons sought him and left a threatening letter.

The alleged violations concerned Slovakia’s failure to provide adequate interpretation and legal assistance and its return of him to Ukraine despite refoulement risk (Articles 3 and 13). Against Ukraine, the complaints concerned expulsion to Afghanistan without examining his fear of persecution (Article 3), failure to inform him of the reasons for detention and to provide an interpreter or lawyer in detention proceedings (Article 5 §§ 2 and 4), and denial of NGO access (Article 34). The Court found Ukrainian authorities had complied with the Article 34 obligation not to hinder the right of application.

Social services and school staff reported that the children were distressed, scared of their father’s drunken and unpredictable behaviour, and had suffered “psychological ill-treatment.” Police warnings and preventive conversations failed to stop the incidents. In June 2016, the applicant sued to evict O.L. under Article 116 of the Housing Code, arguing that his systematic abuse made cohabitation impossible and exposed her and the children to continuing risk. It found hostile relations between the ex-spouses but held that there was no proof O.L. had systematically breached cohabitation rules or that corrective measures had been ineffective; eviction was too extreme. The Supreme Court upheld that decision in August 2018. The eviction proceedings lasted over two years across three levels of jurisdiction.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Articles 6, 8, and 13, with the core claim being that the domestic courts’ refusal to evict O.L. violated Ukraine’s positive obligation under Article 8 to protect her and her children from continuing harassment and violence. The Government argued that authorities had responded promptly, that the applicant had withdrawn complaints and rejected counselling, and that the eviction claim failed on the facts. The Court declared the complaint admissible and found a violation of Article 8. It held that the domestic courts had failed to conduct a comprehensive analysis of the situation and to assess the risk of future psychological and physical violence against the applicant and children. In *Albul and Others v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 18899/19 and 49871/19), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 18 June 2020. The case concerned complaints against Ukraine under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants alleged that the length of civil proceedings in Ukraine had been excessive and that they had no effective domestic remedy for that delay, in violation of Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention.

The individual facts for each applicant are set out in an appended table to the judgment, which is not reproduced in the supplied text. The body of the judgment states only that the applicants lodged their applications on the various dates indicated in that table and that the Ukrainian Government were given notice of the applications. The essential alleged facts relevant to the violations are therefore that each applicant was involved in civil proceedings in Ukraine; those proceedings concerned the determination of their civil rights and obligations; the proceedings lasted unreasonably long; and Ukrainian law provided no effective remedy through which they could complain about the excessive duration.

Article 6 § 1 guarantees that, in the determination of civil rights and obligations, everyone is entitled to a hearing within a reasonable time by a tribunal. Article 13 requires an effective remedy before a national authority for violations of Convention rights, even where the violation is committed by persons acting in an official capacity. The applicants relied on both provisions.

Because the applications raised similar complaints, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment. Case Walczak v. Poland (Application no. 45564/15), judgment of 9 July 2020, concerned a Polish national, Damian Walczak, who was detained on remand from 16 December 2014 on serious charges including membership and leadership of an organised criminal group, armed robbery and extortion. He complained under Article 8 of the Convention that during his detention he had been deprived of personal contact with his wife, M.W., for a significant period.

The key facts relate to M.W.’s repeated requests for prison visits. On 30 December 2014 she applied to visit the applicant. On 5 January 2015 the prosecutor refused because she was a witness in the proceedings. Her requests of 26 February and 17 March 2015 were also refused, the prosecutor citing the need to hear her evidence. On 3 April 2015 M.W. refused to testify at the investigation stage and again asked to visit the applicant. On 7 April the prosecutor refused, stating that the investigation was ongoing and she could still be asked to testify. A further request was refused on 5 June 2015. On 10 June 2015 M.W. applied again; on 15 June the prosecutor refused, saying a visit could impede the proceedings because she knew other witnesses and had access to the applicant’s computer. The applicant’s interlocutory appeal was dismissed on 28 August 2015. Further requests in June and July were also refused, as was the applicant’s own request of 29 June 2015. The applicant and M.W. did not appeal all of the refusal decisions; in particular, no appeal was lodged against several earlier refusals.

On 27 August 2015 the prosecutor allowed M.W. to visit, and the visit took place on 30 August 2015. On 3 September 2015 a bill of indictment was lodged. On 10 September 2015 the Poznań Regional Court refused M.W.’s visit request because she was a witness. Her appeal was dismissed on 24 September 2015. The court reasoned that she could change her mind and testify, and that the prosecutor’s earlier permission was irrelevant. On 2 October 2015 the court allowed a visit after M.W. stated she would rely on her right to refuse to testify against the applicant. She visited on 11 October 2015, and subsequent requests were granted. M.W. was not ultimately asked to testify at hearings after that date. The applicant was released from detention on 4 February 2016.

Under Article 217 of the Code of Execution of Criminal Sentences, a detainee needed permission for visits from the investigating prosecutor or, once trial began, from the court. An interlocutory appeal could be lodged by the detainee or by the person requesting the visit. Once a refusal was upheld, no further interlocutory appeal by the same person was possible if a new refusal was issued within three months of the upheld decision.

Before the Court, the Government raised a preliminary objection of non-exhaustion. It argued that the applicant could have challenged refusal decisions every three months but failed to do so, especially between 16 December 2014 and 15 June 2015. The applicant accepted that he had not appealed every decision but argued that such appeals would have had no prospect of success. The case therefore concerned whether the repeated refusal of prison visits, based on the wife’s status as a potential witness, breached the applicant’s right to respect for family life under Article 8.

**Case: Walczak v. Poland (Application no. 45564/15), Judgment of 9 July 2020**

The applicant, Damian Walczak, a Polish national born in 1971, complained under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that during his pre-trial detention he was deprived of personal contact with his wife for a significant period. The alleged violation centered on repeated refusals by Polish authorities to allow his wife, M.W., to visit him in detention, primarily because she was considered a witness in the criminal proceedings against him.

On 16 December 2014, the applicant was arrested on serious charges, including membership and leadership of an organised criminal group, robbery, extortion with a lethal weapon, severe assault, deprivation of liberty, and recidivism. He was remanded in custody by the Poznań-Nowe Miasto District Court until 16 March 2015. His detention was later extended by the Poznań Regional Court until 16 June 2015 and then until 16 September 2015.

On 30 December 2014, M.W. applied for permission to visit the applicant. On 5 January 2015, the prosecutor refused, stating that she was a witness in the proceedings. Neither the applicant nor M.W. appealed. Further applications on 26 February and 17 March 2015 were rejected on 27 February and 24 March 2015, respectively, because the prosecutor considered it necessary to hear evidence from M.W. Again, no appeals were lodged.

On 3 April 2015, M.W. refused to testify at the investigation stage and again applied for a visit. On 7 April 2015, the prosecutor refused because the investigation was ongoing and M.W. could still be asked to testify. No appeal followed. On 27 May 2015, M.W. applied again; the prosecutor refused on 5 June 2015, and no appeal was lodged.

On 10 June 2015, M.W. made another application. On 15 June 2015, the prosecutor refused, saying a visit could impede the proceedings because M.W. knew other witnesses and had access to the applicant’s computer. The applicant appealed, but on 28 August 2015 the Poznań Regional Prosecutor dismissed the appeal. Further applications by M.W. on 15 June and 15 July 2015 were refused on 25 June and 24 July 2015. The applicant’s own request of 29 June 2015 was also refused on 6 July 2015.

On 27 August 2015, the prosecutor finally allowed M.W. to visit the applicant, and the visit took place on 30 August 2015. On 3 September 2015, an indictment was filed. On 10 September 2015, the Poznań Regional Court dismissed M.W.’s visit application because she was a witness. On appeal, the Regional Court held on 24 September 2015 that it was irrelevant that M.W. had said she would not testify against her husband, since she could change her mind. It also said the prosecutor’s earlier decisions allowing visits could not be assessed by the court. A further request of 15 September 2015 was marked “examined” on 17 September 2015.

On 2 October 2015, the Regional Court allowed M.W. to visit the applicant after she stated she would rely on her right to refuse to testify. She visited him on 11 October 2015, and subsequent requests were granted. M.W. was not later asked to testify at hearings. The applicant was released on 4 February 2016.

Under domestic law, detainee visits required permission from the investigating prosecutor or trial court. Interlocutory appeals were possible, but if a refusal was upheld, no further interlocutory appeal could be lodged by the same person within three months. The Government argued that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies by not appealing decisions between December 2014 and June 2015. The applicant contended that any such appeals would have had no prospect of success.

**Case: Mugemangango v. Belgium** (Application no. 310/15), Grand Chamber, 10 July 2020.

The applicant, Germain Mugemangango, was chairman of the PTB in Hainaut and the top candidate on the PTB-GO! list for the Charleroi constituency in the 25 May 2014 elections to the Walloon Parliament. His list received 16,554 votes but needed 16,567.83 votes to qualify under the “related lists” system. It fell only 14 votes short. If a recount had added enough valid votes, the applicant could have won a seat. In Charleroi, 21,385 ballot papers had been declared blank, spoiled or disputed.

The applicant alleged serious irregularities in the counting process: long counting shifts causing fatigue, poor physical conditions, insufficiently trained polling/counting officers, ballots found days after the election, unclear marks caused by red pencils on pink ballots, and ballot papers wrongly declared spoiled despite valid votes. He asked the electoral boards for a recount. They refused, saying they lacked jurisdiction, and referred him to the Walloon Parliament.

On 6 June 2014, he lodged a complaint with the Walloon Parliament under section 31 of the Special Law of 8 August 1980, seeking re-examination and recount of the disputed ballots. The Walloon Parliament’s Credentials Committee, chosen by lot, heard the applicant. It initially split, then found his complaint admissible and well-founded by three votes to one. It proposed that the Interior Department check and recount the ballots and that credentials in Hainaut not be approved. A committee note indicated that the distribution of seats could change if the 21,385 ballots were recounted and some were held valid.

On 13 June 2014, however, the plenary Walloon Parliament rejected the committee’s findings by 43 votes to 32 and approved all elected representatives’ credentials by 43 votes to 28. All members voted, including MPs elected in the applicant’s constituency and province whose seats could have been affected by a recount. Parliament reasoned that most alleged irregularities were general, not recorded officially, supported only by late witness statements or press articles, and insufficient to show that the outcome was affected.

The applicant complained under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 (right to stand in free elections) and Article 13 (effective remedy). He argued that the Walloon Parliament acted as both judge and party, because MPs whose elections could be questioned decided his complaint. He also alleged lack of impartiality, insufficient legal precision, and absence of procedural safeguards such as a fair hearing, adversarial procedure, and reasoned impartial decision. No judicial remedy existed.

The Grand Chamber found violations. Under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1, election disputes must be examined by a body offering sufficient impartiality and safeguards. The Walloon Parliament, as a not-yet-constituted decision-making body, included MPs whose election could be called into question, so impartiality was not guaranteed. Its discretion was not sufficiently circumscribed by law, and safeguards were discretionary. Parliamentary autonomy must be exercised in accordance with the rule of law. Since the applicant’s allegations were serious and arguable and a recount could have led to his election, Belgium violated Article 3 of Protocol No. 1. It also violated Article 13 by failing to provide an effective remedy to challenge the election results and seek a recount.

**Case Summary: Mugemangango v. Belgium (Application no. 310/15)**

In *Mugemangango v. Belgium*, the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights considered a post-election dispute concerning the Walloon Parliament elections of 25 May 2014. The applicant, Germain Mugemangango, was chairman of the Hainaut branch of the Workers’ Party of Belgium (PTB) and the top candidate on the PTB-GO! list in the Charleroi constituency. His list received 16,554 votes. To qualify for the “related lists” system, which could have allowed it to take over unused votes in Hainaut Province and win a seat, it needed 16,567.83 votes—only about fourteen votes more. If the list had qualified, the applicant would have been elected.

In the Charleroi constituency, 21,385 ballot papers were declared blank, spoiled, or disputed. The applicant alleged irregularities in the count, including counting-station fatigue, poor physical conditions, hurriedly set-up stations, insufficient training, ballots found days after the election, unclear marks caused by red pencils and ballot size, and ballots wrongly declared spoiled. He asked the electoral boards for a recount, but they refused jurisdiction and referred him to the Walloon Parliament. He then lodged a complaint under section 31 of the Special Law of 8 August 1980, requesting re-examination and recount of the disputed ballots.

The Walloon Parliament’s Credentials Committee heard the applicant and initially rejected his complaint, but later found it admissible and well-founded by three votes to one. It proposed checking and recounting the ballots and not approving credentials in Hainaut Province. A note indicated that a recount could change seat distribution in Charleroi and, through the related-lists system, elsewhere in Hainaut. However, on 13 June 2014, the full Walloon Parliament rejected the committee’s findings by 43 votes to 32. All members voted, including MPs elected in the applicant’s constituency whose seats could have been affected. The Parliament then approved all credentials. It reasoned that possible irregularities were not sufficiently serious or officially recorded, that some scenarios showed the applicant still far short, and that press articles and later witness statements were not adequate evidence.

The applicant complained under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 (right to stand in free elections) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy). He argued that the only decision-making body—the Walloon Parliament—lacked impartiality because it acted as both judge and party, since its members had a direct interest in the outcome. He also alleged a lack of procedural safeguards: no hearing before the plenary, no adversarial procedure, and excessive, imprecisely defined discretion. No judicial appeal was available; Belgian courts consistently declined jurisdiction over parliamentary election disputes.

The Government defended the system as rooted in parliamentary independence and separation of powers, arguing that the alleged irregularities were not serious enough to affect the outcome and that the procedure was lawful.

The Grand Chamber found violations of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 13. It held that the complaint concerning a recount was examined by a body lacking sufficient impartiality, through a procedure without adequate safeguards. The Court noted that it could not be ruled out that the applicant could have been elected after a recount, making the allegations serious and arguable. The decision-making body’s discretion was not circumscribed with sufficient precision, and safeguards were afforded only on a discretionary basis. Parliamentary autonomy, the Court stressed, must be exercised in accordance with the rule of law. The absence of an effective remedy to challenge election results and seek a recount also breached Article 13.

Mugemangango v. Belgium concerned a post-election dispute over the 25 May 2014 elections to the Walloon Parliament. The applicant, Germain Mugemangango, was the top candidate on the PTB-GO! list in Charleroi. His list received 16,554 votes, but needed 16,567.83 votes to qualify under the “related lists” system; if it had reached that figure, he would have won a seat. In the same constituency, 21,385 ballot papers were declared blank, spoiled or disputed. He asked the electoral boards for a recount, but they said they had no jurisdiction and referred him to the Walloon Parliament.

On 6 June 2014, he lodged a complaint with the Walloon Parliament under section 31 of the Special Law of 8 August 1980, seeking re-examination of the 21,385 ballots and a recount of votes wrongly declared void. He alleged irregularities: counters suffering fatigue after long shifts; poor counting conditions; hastily set-up stations and inadequate training; ballots found days later; ballot design and red pencils causing unclear marks; and valid ballots wrongly declared spoiled because of non-identifying marks. He relied on witness accounts and press articles. The Credentials Committee, chosen by lot, heard him and his lawyer at a public sitting, then deliberated in private. It ultimately found his complaint admissible and well-founded by three votes to one, proposing an Interior Department check and a full recount in Charleroi. It noted that a recount could change the distribution of seats in Charleroi and, through related lists, elsewhere in Hainaut.

On 13 June 2014, however, the plenary Walloon Parliament rejected the committee’s findings by 43 votes to 32. All members, including those elected in the applicant’s constituency, took part. It then approved all elected representatives’ credentials by 43 votes to 28. In its reasoned decision, Parliament accepted that the seat distribution could change in some scenarios but said the vote shortfall varied (15 to 1,582), the grievances were general, press articles were not admissible evidence, and witness statements should have been recorded officially. It also noted that blank/spoiled ballots were fewer than in 2009, and that annotations generally spoiled ballots. The applicant was notified on 24 June 2014.

He complained under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 13. The key alleged violation was that the only decision-making body, the Walloon Parliament, was not independent or impartial: it acted as judge and party, and MPs whose election could be called into question voted on the result. There was also no effective judicial remedy, no adequate procedural safeguards, and the body’s discretion was not sufficiently circumscribed by domestic law. Under Belgian law, the Constitution and Special Law gave Parliament exclusive power to examine credentials and election disputes, and Belgian courts declined jurisdiction. The Grand Chamber found violations of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 13, holding that parliamentary autonomy must be exercised under the rule of law and that the recount complaint had been examined by a body lacking sufficient impartiality and safeguards.
001-203165:
In *Stavropoulos and Others v. Greece* (Application no. 52484/18), the European Court of Human Rights considered whether a birth-registration entry disclosed the parents’ religious beliefs by revealing that their child had not been christened. The applicants were three Greek nationals—Mr Nikolaos Stavropoulos, Ms Ioanna Kravari, and their daughter, Ms Stavroula-Dorothea Stavropoulou—living in Oxford, United Kingdom.

On 17 August 2007, the father, authorised by the mother, registered the third applicant’s birth at the Amarousio registry office. The registrar entered the child’s forename and added, in brackets, an abbreviation of the Greek word for “naming” (*ονοματοδοσία*). The applicants complained that this note disclosed that their daughter had not been christened and therefore revealed their religious beliefs, namely their choice not to have her baptised. They alleged a violation of Article 9 of the Convention (freedom of religion, including its negative aspect) and Article 8 (protection of sensitive personal data).

On 19 October 2007, the applicants applied to the Supreme Administrative Court for annulment of the birth registration in so far as it contained the “naming” note. They argued that it referred to the absence of a christening, revealed their religious beliefs, and could lead to discrimination. On 6 March 2018, the Supreme Administrative Court rejected the application as inadmissible, finding that the applicants lacked legal interest. It relied on Law no. 344/1976, Articles 25 and 26, holding that a child’s first name is acquired through “naming”—a declaration by the parents or guardians before the registry office—regardless of whether the child is later christened. A christening is recorded separately in the side section of the birth act. The note “naming” therefore merely repeated the title of Article 25 and reflected the only legal way of acquiring a name; it did not, in the domestic court’s view, cause harm or discrimination.

The relevant legal framework distinguished civil naming from religious christening. Article 25 provided that a newborn’s name is recorded after a parental declaration. Article 26 provided that a christening is recorded in the birth register’s margin after a priest’s declaration. A State Legal Council opinion (no. 431/2006) stated that if the name was not declared simultaneously with or before the christening, parents had to make a separate naming declaration; registration of a christening alone did not confer a first name. A Ministry of the Interior circular of 24 October 2006 similarly stated that a christening declaration could not be treated as a naming declaration unless the statutory conditions were met. The Greek Ombudsman, intervening in the case, criticised the practice and the view that only non-christened children are “named” or that christened children need not be named, saying it forced citizens to inadvertently register a religion.

Before the European Court, the central issue was whether the “naming” note amounted to an interference with Article 9. The Court observed that birth registration acts are frequently used public documents. Adding the note disclosed the parents’ choice not to christen their child, thereby revealing their religious beliefs or lack thereof, and exposed them and the child to a risk of discriminatory treatment in dealings with administrative authorities. The interference stemmed from a widespread practice of domestic registry offices rather than from a clear legal requirement. The Court found that this interference was not “prescribed by law”: Greek law regulated naming and the registration of christenings, but it did not require or authorise registrars to specify that a name had been acquired by civil “naming” rather than by christening. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 9, regarding the negative aspect of freedom of religion. In light of that finding, it did not consider it necessary to examine separately the complaint under Article 8 concerning sensitive personal data.

**Case: Stavropoulos and Others v. Greece (Application no. 52484/18)**

The applicants were three Greek nationals: Nikolaos Stavropoulos and Ioanna Kravari, the parents, and their daughter Stavroula-Dorothea Stavropoulou, born in 2007. The family lived in Oxford, United Kingdom.

On 17 August 2007, the father, authorised by the mother, went to the Amarousio registry office in Greece to register their daughter’s birth. A registry employee entered the child’s forename in the birth register and added, in parentheses, an abbreviated note meaning “naming” (ονοματοδοσία). The applicants alleged that this note disclosed that their daughter had not been christened and thereby revealed the parents’ religious beliefs—specifically, their choice not to have her baptised in the Greek Orthodox Church.

On 19 October 2007, the applicants applied to the Supreme Administrative Court to annul the birth registration insofar as it included the “naming” note. They argued that it constituted a reference to the absence of a christening and thus revealed sensitive religious information. On 6 March 2018, the Supreme Administrative Court rejected the application as inadmissible, finding that the applicants lacked legal interest. It reasoned that under Law no. 344/1976, a child’s first name is registered by a “naming” declaration made by the parents or guardians before the registry office, irrespective of whether the child is later christened. Therefore, the note merely repeated the title of Article 25 of that Law and reflected the only legal way for a child to acquire a name. It could not, in the court’s view, amount to discrimination or harm.

The relevant legal framework included Law no. 344/1976. Article 25 provided that a newborn’s name is recorded following a declaration by the parents exercising parental responsibility. Article 26 provided that a christening is recorded in the side section of the birth registration act after a declaration by the officiating priest. A State Legal Council opinion (no. 431/2006) stated that where a child’s name is not declared at or before the christening, the parents must make a separate naming declaration; merely recording the name at christening does not suffice. A Ministry of the Interior circular similarly stated that a christening declaration cannot be treated as a naming declaration unless the legal conditions are met.

The Greek Ombudsman intervened, noting that the view that only non-christened children are “named,” or that christened children need no separate naming, “results in forcing citizens to inadvertently register a religion.” The Ombudsman also observed that administrative inflexibility and misunderstandings about state religious neutrality continued to create religious-freedom problems.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants complained under Article 9 (freedom of religion) and Article 8 (respect for private life) of the Convention. The Court examined the case under Article 9, focusing on the negative aspect of religious freedom—the right not to manifest or disclose one’s religion or belief. It found that the birth registration act revealed the parents’ choice not to christen their child. Because birth registration documents are frequently used in dealings with administrative authorities, the disclosure exposed the applicants to a risk of discriminatory treatment. The interference arose from a widespread practice of domestic registry offices rather than from a specific legal requirement. The Court held that the interference was not prescribed by law and therefore violated Article 9 of the Convention.

**Case: Stavropoulos and Others v. Greece** (Application no. 52484/18), ECtHR, First Section, judgment 25 June 2020.

The case concerned the Greek practice of adding the notation “naming” (ονοματοδοσία), often abbreviated and placed in brackets, beside a child’s forename in the birth register when the name was given by a parental declaration rather than through christening. The applicants were Nikolaos Stavropoulos and Ioanna Kravari, parents, and their daughter Stavroula-Dorothea Stavropoulou, Greek nationals living in Oxford. In August 2007, the father, authorised by the mother, registered their daughter’s birth at the Amarousio registry office. The registrar entered the child’s forename with the disputed “naming” note.

Because Greek law records a christening in the side section of the birth registration act and treats christening as the usual religious context for naming, the presence of a separate “naming” notation could indicate that the child had not been christened. The applicants alleged that this disclosed their decision not to christen their child and therefore revealed their religious beliefs in a public document. They argued that no law required registry offices to specify whether a child was named by a civil act or a Christian ceremony, and that the notation breached their rights under Articles 8 and 9 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

In October 2007, the applicants sought annulment of the birth registration insofar as it contained the “naming” note before the Supreme Administrative Court. In March 2018, that court rejected the application as inadmissible for lack of legal interest. It reasoned that under Law no. 344/1976, a first name is acquired through a parental “naming” declaration, irrespective of later christening. Article 26 separately allowed a christening to be recorded in the birth register. The domestic court therefore considered that the note merely repeated the legal basis for naming and could not cause discrimination or harm.

The relevant legal framework supported the applicants’ concern. Article 25 of Law no. 344/1976 provided that a newborn’s name is registered following a declaration by the parents or guardians. Article 26 provided that a christening is recorded in the side section of the birth act. State Legal Council opinion no. 431/2006 and a Ministry of the Interior circular stated that a christening declaration did not itself constitute a naming declaration unless made by the parents in the required form. The Greek Ombudsman, intervening in the case, observed that the practice could force citizens inadvertently to register a religion and criticised administrative inflexibility regarding the religious neutrality of the State.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the key issue was whether the registry practice interfered with the negative aspect of Article 9—the right not to manifest religion or belief. The Court found that the birth registration act, a frequently used public document, revealed the parents’ choice not to christen their child and exposed them to a risk of discriminatory treatment in dealings with administrative authorities. The interference arose from a widespread registry-office practice, but it was not prescribed by Greek law. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 9 of the Convention.
001-206159:
In *Project-Trade d.o.o. v. Croatia*, the applicant was a Croatian limited liability company and shareholder of Croatia Bank, holding 1,251 shares with a nominal value of HRK 200 each. The case arose after the Croatian Government adopted a decision on the recovery and restructuring of the bank, which resulted in the cancellation of all existing shares and the issuance of new shares to the State Agency for Deposit Insurance and Bank Resolution (DAB). The alleged violations concerned deprivation of property, lack of access to court, and excessive length of proceedings.

The bank was privately owned. In February 1999 the Croatian National Bank appointed a temporary administrator. Based on an expert report that the bank’s debts largely outweighed its capital and posed a risk to financial stability, the CNB proposed recovery. On 23 September 1999 the Government adopted the Decision on recovery and restructuring, published on 27 September 1999. The Decision cited risky investments, potential losses, disputed claims, and operating losses. It provided that on publication all existing shares were revoked and cancelled; new shares would be issued entirely to DAB; and the powers of the bank’s governing bodies and shareholder rights based on existing shares were extinguished. DAB funded the recovery and recapitalisation.

The applicant claimed it was a lawful shareholder, that the bank had been in good standing, that statutory conditions had not been met, and that it had been deprived of property without participation or compensation. It argued that the Government Decision was unconstitutional and economically unjustified. The applicant was not among the shareholders who filed constitutional review petitions in 1999–2000. In 2003 the Constitutional Court discontinued those proceedings because the underlying 1994 Act had been repealed. It noted that the Decision was subordinate legislation but affected individual rights, and said shareholders could seek protection in civil proceedings. Dissenting judges disagreed, stating that no effective judicial remedy existed.

On 12 September 2003 the applicant brought a civil action against the bank and DAB in the Zagreb Commercial Court. It sought a declaration that it remained holder of 1,251 shares, an order that DAB transfer equivalent shares, and registration in the bank’s shareholder register. It repeated that the Government Decision was unjustified and contrary to the Constitution. On 21 February 2006 the Commercial Court dismissed the action, finding that the shares had been cancelled and no longer existed. On 18 June 2008 the High Commercial Court dismissed the appeal, upholding that DAB had acquired new shares through recapitalisation. The judgment was served in September 2008.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged that the cancellation and revocation of its shares violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1; that it had no access to a court to challenge the Government Decision under Article 6 § 1; and that the civil proceedings were excessively long. The Court upheld the applicant’s victim status, finding that the share cancellation directly affected its property right and went beyond merely affecting its governance position. It found that the Government Decision was not reviewable by any judicial authority, so the civil proceedings could not provide effective access to court. It also found the length of proceedings excessive, lasting almost five years at one level of jurisdiction. The case therefore concerned a State restructuring measure extinguishing private shareholdings, a lack of judicial review over that measure, and prolonged civil litigation.

Project-Trade d.o.o. v. Croatia concerned the 1999 State restructuring of Croatia Banka d.d. and the resulting loss of shareholders’ shares without effective judicial review. The applicant, a Croatian limited liability company, held 1,251 shares in Croatia Banka, each with a nominal value of HRK 200. The bank was privately owned.

In early 1999, the Croatian National Bank appointed a temporary administrator, taking over the bank’s governing bodies. After an expert report concluded that the bank’s debts greatly outweighed its share capital and threatened financial stability, the CNB proposed recovery and restructuring. On 23 September 1999, the Croatian Government adopted the Decision on the Recovery and Restructuring of Croatia Banka, published on 27 September 1999. The Decision recorded large risky investments, disputed claims and operating losses; wrote off losses; provided for funding and recapitalisation by the State Agency for Deposit Insurance and Bank Resolution (DAB); and, critically, revoked and cancelled all existing shares. New shares were to be issued entirely to DAB. The Decision also extinguished the powers of the general meeting, supervisory board and management board, as well as the rights of existing shareholders. The applicant did not participate in the process and received no compensation.

Other shareholders challenged the Decision before the Constitutional Court. In 2003, that court discontinued the review because the underlying 1994 Act had been repealed. Although it described the Decision as subordinate legislation that directly interfered with individual rights, it stated that former shareholders could seek judicial protection in civil proceedings. Dissenting judges argued that no effective remedy existed and that civil courts could not invalidate the Decision.

The applicant brought a civil action on 12 September 2003 in the Zagreb Commercial Court against the bank and DAB. It sought a declaration that it remained the holder of 1,251 shares, an order that DAB transfer equivalent shares, and registration in the shareholder register. It argued that the Government Decision was economically unjustified, that statutory conditions were not met, and that it violated constitutional rights to property and entrepreneurial freedom. The Commercial Court dismissed the action on 21 February 2006, treating the shares as extinguished by the Decision. The High Commercial Court dismissed the appeal on 18 June 2008, served on 16 September 2008. It upheld the finding that the old shares no longer existed and that DAB owned the new shares, so the applicant could not have them returned. The courts thus applied the Decision without examining its legality or constitutional merits.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 6 § 1. The key alleged violations were: (1) deprivation or control of property through cancellation of shares without compensation or effective review; (2) lack of access to court because the Government Decision could not be challenged before a judicial authority; and (3) excessive length of the civil proceedings. The Court found that cancellation and revocation of the shares directly affected the applicant’s property rights, going beyond merely altering its position in the bank, and upheld its victim status. It found violations concerning control of property and access to court, since the Government Decision was not reviewable by any judicial authority. It also found a violation of Article 6 § 1 due to the excessive length of proceedings, which lasted almost five years at one level of jurisdiction.

In *Project-Trade d.o.o. v. Croatia* (ECtHR, 19 November 2020), the applicant was a Croatian limited liability company and a shareholder in Croatia Bank, a private joint-stock bank. It held 1,251 shares, each with a nominal value of HRK 200. In 1999, following financial difficulties, the Croatian National Bank appointed a temporary administrator and proposed recovery/restructuring. On 23 September 1999, the Croatian Government adopted a Decision on the recovery and restructuring of Croatia Bank, published on 27 September 1999. The Decision revoked and cancelled all existing shares, extinguished the rights of shareholders and the powers of the bank’s governing bodies, and provided that new shares would be issued to and owned by the State Agency for Deposit Insurance and Bank Resolution (DAB). The recovery process ended in September 2000.

The applicant alleged that the Government Decision deprived it of its property without justification or compensation and that it had no effective access to court to challenge the measure. Earlier, five other shareholders had asked the Constitutional Court to review the Decision’s constitutionality and legality. In 2003, the Constitutional Court discontinued those proceedings because the underlying 1994 Recovery and Restructuring of Banks Act had been repealed. It nevertheless stated that former shareholders could seek judicial protection in civil proceedings. The applicant had not been a party to those constitutional proceedings.

In 2003, the applicant brought a civil action in the Zagreb Commercial Court against the bank and DAB. It sought a declaration that it remained the holder of its 1,251 shares, an order that DAB transfer equivalent shares to it, and registration in the bank’s shareholder register. It argued that the bank had been economically sound, that statutory conditions for recovery were not met, and that the Government Decision was unconstitutional and unlawful. The Commercial Court dismissed the claim in February 2006. The High Commercial Court dismissed the appeal in June 2008, with service in September 2008. The domestic courts treated the Government Decision as decisive, holding that the applicant’s shares had been cancelled and no longer existed. They did not review the Decision’s legality or constitutionality.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the key complaints concerned Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The Court found that the cancellation and revocation of the applicant’s shares directly affected its property rights and went beyond merely affecting its position in the bank’s governance structure; the applicant was therefore a victim. It further held that the Government Decision was not reviewable by any judicial authority. The civil proceedings did not provide effective access to court because the domestic courts simply applied the Decision without examining its validity. The Court also found a violation of Article 6 § 1 due to the excessive length of the civil proceedings, which lasted almost five years at one level of jurisdiction. The case thus concerned both an unjustified interference with property rights through the share cancellation and procedural failures: the absence of judicial review of the restructuring decision and unreasonable delay in the applicant’s civil case.
001-206511:
In *Yukhymovych v. Ukraine* (App. no. 11464/12, ECtHR, 17 December 2020), the applicant’s son, Ruslan Yukhymovych, was shot and killed by police on 4 March 1999 during an attempted arrest. The case began after B. complained that unknown persons had threatened her and extorted USD 25,000. Police identified Ruslan and his friend Z. as suspects, allegedly members of an organised criminal group. The DCOC approved an operation to arrest them at B.’s house using officers in civilian clothes.

On 4 March 1999, Ruslan and Z. arrived at B.’s house. Z. entered first, followed by Ruslan. Police officer M. shouted “Freeze, police!” and officers arrested Z. Ruslan disobeyed and fled. Officers M. and O. chased him to the garden gate. O. shot Ruslan twice; he died from his injuries. The central disputed issue was whether Ruslan had a gun and posed a threat. Police testimony said he pointed a gun at M.; other evidence was contradictory. A “Valtro” gas gun was allegedly found near the body and had fingerprints linked to Ruslan, but scene witnesses did not clearly see it. The taxi driver initially said Ruslan had a gun but later withdrew this. Z. initially said Ruslan had left his gun in the car, then changed his account. Forensic reports differed as to the order and location of the shots, and later examination was hampered because Ruslan’s clothes had been returned to the applicant and destroyed.

The investigation was criticised as delayed and ineffective. For nearly a month after the shooting, the circumstances were examined only in a pre-investigation inquiry. On 25 March 1999 the prosecutor refused to open a criminal investigation, accepting the internal DCOC conclusion that O. had used his weapon lawfully. On 31 March 1999 the regional prosecutor set that decision aside and opened criminal proceedings, but the investigation then suffered repeated terminations and reopenings. Domestic courts repeatedly found failures: the scene was not secured; the car was towed without permission; investigators failed to resolve contradictions about whether Ruslan was armed; witnesses were not properly questioned; instructions were not followed; and the applicant’s complaints were not answered. The proceedings remained pending for more than nineteen years.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the complaints under Article 2. It found the application admissible. On the procedural limb, the Court held that the investigation was not prompt or effective. The initial pre-investigation inquiry excluded the applicant’s effective participation and unnecessarily delayed a proper criminal investigation. The subsequent investigation was marked by repeated discontinuations and reopenings, failure to follow judicial instructions, loss of evidence, and failure to clarify whether the son posed a threat justifying lethal force. The length of over nineteen years also breached the requirement of expedition. The Court therefore found a procedural violation of Article 2.

On the substantive limb, the Court also found that the operation had not been planned and conducted so as to minimise recourse to lethal force. In light of the investigative omissions and contradictory material, the Government had not provided a satisfactory and convincing explanation or solid evidence that the shooting was absolutely necessary. The Court thus found a violation of Article 2, both for the unjustified use of lethal force and for the failure to conduct an effective investigation.

In *Yukhymovych v. Ukraine* (Application no. 11464/12), the European Court of Human Rights examined the death of the applicant’s son, Ruslan Yukhymovych, during a police arrest attempt and the domestic authorities’ failure to conduct a prompt and effective investigation, contrary to Article 2 of the Convention.

The incident arose after B. complained to the Lviv anti-organised-crime police that unknown persons had threatened her and extorted USD 25,000. Police allegedly identified Ruslan and his friend Z. as suspects and planned an arrest operation. On 4 March 1999, officers in civilian clothes waited at B.’s house. When Ruslan and Z. arrived, Z. entered the house and was arrested after an officer shouted “Freeze, police!” Ruslan fled. Officers M. and O. chased him. O. shot Ruslan twice, and he died from his injuries.

The Government claimed O. fired because Ruslan had a gun and pointed it at M., justifying the use of lethal force. The applicant maintained that his son posed no danger and was shot twice in the back while fleeing. The evidence about whether Ruslan was armed was contradictory. A “Valtro” gas gun was allegedly found near his body, and some fingerprints linked it to Ruslan; a taxi driver also said he saw a gun. However, Z. initially said Ruslan had no weapon and had left his gun in his car, and other witnesses did not clearly see a gun. Forensic reports found two gunshot wounds to the back, including a fatal wound to the back of the right shoulder, and noted additional injuries.

The domestic investigation was heavily criticised. For nearly a month after the death, the circumstances were examined only through a pre-investigation inquiry. An internal police inquiry concluded that O. had used his weapon lawfully, and on 25 March 1999 the prosecutor refused to open criminal proceedings. That decision was set aside on 31 March 1999, and criminal proceedings were opened. However, the investigation was repeatedly terminated and reopened. Courts identified serious shortcomings: failure to secure the scene, failure to resolve contradictions over whether Ruslan was armed, failure to address additional injuries, superficial reconstructions, reliance on an internal inquiry by an interested police body, loss of evidence, and failure to follow investigative instructions. By 2018, the investigation had been pending for more than nineteen years.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 2 both procedurally and substantively. Procedurally, the investigation was not prompt or effective: the initial pre-investigation stage excluded effective participation and delayed the criminal investigation, while the later proceedings were marked by repeated discontinuations, unresolved key questions, and excessive length. Substantively, the operation was not planned or conducted so as to minimise recourse to lethal force. The Government failed to provide a satisfactory and convincing explanation, supported by solid evidence, that the shooting was absolutely necessary. In light of the investigative omissions and contradictory material, the burden of proof shifted to the Government. The Court therefore concluded that Ukraine had violated Article 2 in respect of both the use of lethal force and the inadequate investigation into the applicant’s son’s death.

In *Yukhymovych v. Ukraine* (ECtHR, 17 December 2020), the applicant’s son, Ruslan Yukhymovych, was shot and killed by police on 4 March 1999 during an attempted arrest. The applicant complained under Article 2 that State agents killed his son and that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation. The Court examined the case under Article 2 and found both substantive and procedural violations.

Background: B. complained that unknown men, allegedly Ruslan and Z., had extorted USD 25,000. Police in the DCOC approved an operation by the “Sokil” special unit to arrest the alleged extortionists at B.’s house. On 4 March 1999, officers in civilian clothes waited inside. When Z. entered, officer M. shouted “Freeze, police!” and Z. was arrested. Ruslan, at the entrance, fled. Officers M. and O. chased him; O. shot him twice. He died.

The key disputed fact was whether Ruslan was armed and threatening. A “Valtro” gas gun was allegedly found near his body and later placed in a plastic bag inside B.’s house; his fingerprints were found on it. But evidence was contradictory. The taxi driver initially said he saw a gun in Ruslan’s hand, then withdrew that statement. Z. said Ruslan had left his gun in the car and that the gun produced was not his. Police said Ruslan pointed a gun at M., justifying O.’s shots. Witnesses to the scene inspection did not clearly see a gun. Forensic reports identified two gunshot wounds, including one to the back/right shoulder and another at close range/back, but experts disagreed about order and distance. Additional injuries on Ruslan’s head and lip were noted but not fully investigated.

Procedurally, for nearly a month after the death, authorities conducted only a pre-investigation inquiry, not a full criminal investigation. On 25 March 1999 the district prosecutor refused to open a criminal case, relying partly on an internal DCOC inquiry that found O.’s use of force lawful. On 31 March 1999, the regional prosecutor set that refusal aside and opened criminal proceedings. However, the investigation was repeatedly terminated and reopened. Domestic courts repeatedly found failures: not securing the scene; not resolving contradictions about whether Ruslan was armed; not properly investigating B.’s extortion complaint; inadequate reconstruction; failure to answer the applicant’s complaints; and loss of evidence. As of 13 March 2018, the proceedings were still pending—more than 19 years after the killing.

The ECtHR found the investigation ineffective, lacking promptness and expedition, and incapable of determining whether the lethal force was justified. It also examined the planning and control of the operation and the actual use of force. The operation was not planned or conducted so as to minimize recourse to lethal force. The Government failed to provide a satisfactory and convincing explanation or solid evidence justifying the shooting. In light of investigative omissions and contradictory material, the burden of proof shifted to the Government. The Court therefore held that Ukraine violated Article 2 both substantively—because the death resulted from unjustified lethal force during an inadequately planned arrest—and procedurally—because the authorities failed to conduct a prompt and effective investigation.
001-200815:
In *Klopcovs v. Latvia* (Application no. 26902/13), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint by Mr Boriss Klopcovs, a Latvian national, that the length of domestic proceedings concerning interference with his prison correspondence violated Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant had been detained in Riga Central Prison pending trial in 2005. During June, July and August 2005, the prison administration controlled and stopped his correspondence to private persons and institutions. In September 2005 he complained to the Prisons Administration, but his complaints were rejected in October 2005. The Ministry of Justice later found the prison administration’s actions and the Prisons Administration’s answers lawful.

On 22 September 2006, the applicant brought administrative proceedings against the Ministry of Justice; the Prisons Administration later joined. He sought a finding that the actions were unlawful and claimed 5,406 Latvian lats (approximately EUR 7,692) in pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages. On 21 October 2008, the Administrative District Court found the prison administration’s actions unlawful but rejected the damages claim.
