The case arose from Iceland’s 2008 financial collapse. The applicant, Sigríður Elín Sigfúsdóttir, was director of corporate banking at Landsbanki and a member of its credit committee. On 3 October 2008, four days before Landsbanki collapsed, she approved a loan enabling Imon ehf. to purchase Landsbanki shares. She was later indicted by the Special Prosecutor for fraud by abuse of position and market manipulation. In June 2014 the Reykjavik District Court acquitted her, but in October 2015 the Supreme Court overturned the acquittal, convicted her, and sentenced her to 18 months’ imprisonment. The Supreme Court panel consisted of five justices: M.S., V.M.M., E.T., H.I.J. and Þ.Ö.

In December 2016, media reports revealed that some Supreme Court justices had owned shares in Icelandic banks before the crash. The applicant said this was the first time she learned of possible conflicts of interest. She requested information and learned that Justice M.S. had not owned Landsbanki shares, though he had owned Glitnir shares and other investments lost in the crisis. Justice E.T. had owned Landsbanki shares with a nominal value of ISK 87,383, worth about ISK 1,738,922 at the time of collapse, plus Glitnir shares. Justice V.M.M. had owned Landsbanki shares with a nominal value of ISK 428,075, purchased for ISK 14,753,256 and last valued at ISK 8,518,692 before becoming worthless. His loss—about EUR 62,860—was substantial relative to his earnings. V.M.M. and E.T. became Supreme Court justices in 2010 and 2011, after those losses, and were not obliged to notify pre-appointment holdings.

The applicant sought reopening of her case, arguing that the judges’ financial interests violated her right to an impartial tribunal under Article 6. In May 2019, the Committee on Reopening of Judicial Proceedings accepted reopening, finding that V.M.M.’s substantial Landsbanki loss justified reasonable fears of partiality. The reopening remained pending before the Supreme Court.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 about lack of impartiality and breach of the presumption of innocence. The Government argued non-exhaustion and that the application was late. The Court rejected those objections: the applicant had not been required to investigate judges’ undisclosed finances, reopening was not an effective remedy for exhaustion purposes, and the six-month period began only when the media disclosed the issue in December 2016.

On the merits, the Court applied subjective and objective impartiality tests. It found no proof of subjective bias. Objectively, M.S. had no direct Landsbanki interest; his Glitnir losses were irrelevant. E.T.’s Landsbanki holding was modest and below the ISK 3,000,000 notification threshold, so no objectively justified fear arose. V.M.M., however, had suffered a substantial loss in Landsbanki—the very bank whose management conduct was at issue. The relevant loss was that at the time of collapse, not the judge’s later financial position. His participation created legitimate doubt about the Supreme Court’s impartiality. The fact that he sat on a five-judge panel was not decisive because deliberations were secret and his influence could not be measured. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1. The Article 6 § 2 complaint, alleging preconceived guilt and burden-shifting, was manifestly ill-founded and inadmissible.

**Case: Mirgadirov v. Azerbaijan and Turkey (ECtHR, Fifth Section, 17 September 2020)**

The applicant, Rauf Mirgadirov, is an Azerbaijani journalist and political analyst. He left Azerbaijan in 2010 and was based in Ankara, Turkey, working as a correspondent for the newspaper *Zerkalo*. Turkey granted him a press card and residence permit valid through 2014. On 8 April 2014, however, the Turkish Press and Information Directorate annulled his press card without providing written reasons, and steps were taken to revoke his residence permit.

On 18 April 2014, while travelling with his family from Ankara to Georgia, the applicant’s bus was stopped by police. Because his residence permit had been revoked, he was detained for illegal residence. He alleged that he was not properly notified of the deportation or detention decisions, was refused access to a lawyer, and was not allowed to contact his wife. On 19 April 2014, police took him to Esenboğa Airport, informed him of a twelve-month entry ban, and placed him on a flight to Baku under police control. The official deportation and administrative detention decision was only issued on 21 April 2014, after his removal.

Upon arrival at Baku Airport on 19 April 2014, the applicant was arrested by Azerbaijan’s Ministry of National Security. At 5:15 p.m. he was recorded as a suspect of high treason under Article 274 of the Criminal Code. He was questioned in the presence of a State-appointed lawyer. He admitted meeting L.B., an Armenian NGO head, and D.S., a former Armenian intelligence official, to discuss the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict and regional issues, but denied providing State secrets or committing espionage. On 21 April 2014, he was formally charged with high treason by espionage. The prosecution alleged that he had been recruited by Armenian intelligence, collected information on Azerbaijan’s socio-political, economic, and military situation, and met Armenian agents in Armenia, Turkey, and Georgia between 2008 and 2009, supplying information, photographs, and technical drawings.

On the same day, the Nasimi District Court ordered his pre-trial detention for three months at the prosecutor’s request. The court cited the serious nature of the charge and risks that he would abscond or obstruct the investigation.

The alleged violations concerned both Turkey and Azerbaijan. Against Turkey, the applicant complained about unlawful detention on 19 April 2014, lack of reasons for detention, failure to bring him before a judge, inability to challenge the lawfulness of detention, and violation of Article 10 as a journalist. Against Azerbaijan, he complained of the absence of a reasonable suspicion for his arrest, a 16-hour pre-trial detention without judicial authorisation, unjustified continued detention, inadequate judicial review, breach of the presumption of innocence through investigators’ statements to the press, unlawful restrictions during investigation on receiving and subscribing to socio-political magazines and newspapers, and on meetings, correspondence, and telephone calls with family and the outside world, and ulterior purpose under Article 18 read with Article 5.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations against Azerbaijan: lack of legal basis for restrictions on socio-political publications; unjustified restrictions on family and outside contact; failure to meet the minimum standard of reasonable suspicion; a 16-hour pre-trial detention without any authorising judicial order; inadequate review of the lawfulness of detention; violation of the presumption of innocence; and unsubstantiated allegations of an ulterior purpose behind his arrest and detention.

**Shebaldina v. Ukraine** (ECtHR, Fifth Section, 18 June 2020) concerned a Ukrainian teacher’s complaint that domestic courts refused to award her statutory social allowances, allegedly violating her property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and her right to an effective remedy under Article 13.

The applicant, Ms Alla Petrivna Shebaldina, was employed from 1988 to 2006 as a teacher at a State specialised child-care centre. Under Article 57 of the 1991 Education Act, she was entitled to seniority and recreation allowances. She claimed that between 1997 and 2002 she did not receive these allowances, leaving arrears of UAH 2,244.30.

In December 2007 she sued the centre and the regional department of the State Treasury, seeking the arrears, an index-linked adjustment of UAH 4,336.17, non-pecuniary damages of UAH 10,000, and costs of UAH 1,484. In October 2010, the Bilgorod-Dnistrovskyy Town Court partly allowed her claim. It found she was entitled to the allowances and that the centre owed her UAH 2,244.30, plus UAH 4,336.17 in indexation and UAH 1,400 in legal costs. Because the non-payment resulted from a lack of State budget funding, the court said the centre could seek reimbursement from the State budget. Her non-pecuniary damage claim was dismissed.

In April 2011, the Odessa Regional Court of Appeal quashed that judgment and dismissed her claim. It found that although she had worked in an institution with dual healthcare and educational status and had not received the Article 57 allowances in 1997–2002, the 2004 Act on the Restructuring of Indebtedness under Article 57 classified such payments as a State debt payable from the State budget. The centre was therefore not liable, as it had not received the relevant funds. The Treasury was not a proper defendant, and indexation and non-pecuniary damages were not provided by the 2004 Act. In July 2011, the Higher Specialised Civil and Criminal Court declined to examine her appeal on points of law.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant argued that the unpaid allowances were a “possession” or at least a legitimate expectation under domestic law. She noted that both domestic courts had accepted that the State guaranteed payment and that the refusal was based only on a lack of budget funds. She also stressed that the arrears represented 30% of her monthly salary and were significant, especially given Ukraine’s economic situation in 1997–2002. In 2002, UAH 2,244.30 was equivalent to about EUR 450.

The Government contested admissibility. It argued that the amount at stake—about EUR 204—was below the “significant disadvantage” threshold, that the application was late under the six-month rule, and that she had not been entitled to the allowances because she was a pedagogical employee of a healthcare institution, not an educational institution. The applicant replied that she had filed within time on 1 December 2011, that the amount was not negligible, and that the State could not rely on a lack of funds to evade its obligations.

The Court considered the Government’s significant-disadvantage objection. It found no indication that the amount sought, representing 30% of her monthly salary, was insignificant for her, and the Government did not show otherwise. It also noted that the euro equivalent would have been much higher in 2002 had she been paid on time, and that she should not be blamed for exchange-rate changes caused by the authorities’ lengthy non-payment. The Court therefore did not accept the significant-disadvantage objection on that basis. The case centrally concerned whether the domestic courts’ refusal to award the statutory allowance arrears breached the applicant’s property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In *Baz v. Ukraine* (Application no. 40962/13, judgment of 5 November 2020), the European Court of Human Rights examined a Turkish national’s complaint under Article 5 § 1(f) of the Convention that his detention in Ukraine pending extradition to Turkey was unlawful. The applicant, born in 1976, left Turkey in 1998 and arrived in Ukraine in 2004. In March 2011 he was granted refugee status. However, in October 2012 the State Migration Service revoked that status, finding that he had provided false information: he claimed political persecution in Turkey but concealed that he was wanted by Turkish law-enforcement authorities on suspicion of a criminal offence. Ukrainian courts at three levels rejected his challenge to that revocation, with a final decision on 3 April 2013. Meanwhile, on 14 March 2013, he applied for subsidiary protection. That application was rejected in August 2013 as inadmissible because his refugee status had been revoked. In February 2014, however, a court quashed that rejection and ordered the authorities to examine the application on the merits; the later outcome is not recorded in the case file.

The extradition proceedings began when, on 20 June 2011, the Istanbul 13th Higher Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for the applicant on suspicion of participation in terrorist and separatist activities on 5 August 1998. On 3 October 2012 that court requested his extradition from Ukraine. The request stated that the criminal charge would become time-barred on 15 August 2013 and assured that the applicant’s Convention rights would be respected. On 14 November 2012 the applicant was detained by the State Security Service of Ukraine with a view to extradition. Two days later, the Mykolaiv Tsentralny District Court ordered his detention pending extradition.

Separately, the applicant faced Ukrainian criminal proceedings for using documents he knew to be forged. On 14 March 2013 the Kharkiv Leninsky District Court convicted him and sentenced him to two months’ imprisonment; the outcome of his appeal is unknown. Because he was transferred to Kharkiv in connection with those proceedings, the Kharkiv Zhovtnevy District Court became competent to review his detention. On 17 July 2013 that court held that continued detention was justified, relying on two Turkish arrest warrants and the extradition request. It noted that the prosecution had carried out an extradition inquiry and found no impediments to extradition. It also referred to the applicant’s Ukrainian conviction, though it had not become final.

On 30 August 2013 the Zhovtnevy Court released the applicant. It found that the limitation period for the Turkish offences had expired on 15 August 2013 and that, under Article 10 of the European Convention on Extradition, extradition could not be granted. On 23 September 2013 the Ministry of Justice of Ukraine rejected the extradition request.

Before the European Court, the applicant argued that his detention pending extradition violated Article 5 § 1(f) because: (i) until 3 April 2013 his appeals against revocation of refugee status were pending, meaning he could not be extradited; (ii) from 14 March 2013 his subsidiary protection application was pending, which also barred extradition; and (iii) from 15 August 2013 onward his prosecution in Turkey had become time-barred. Relevant Ukrainian law prohibited extradition of refugees or persons under subsidiary protection and barred an extradition decision while such an application remained pending without a final decision. The Government submitted no observations within the time-limits. The Court declared the complaint admissible, finding it neither manifestly ill-founded nor inadmissible on other grounds.

**Summary of Baz v. Ukraine (Application no. 40962/13)**

The case of *Baz v. Ukraine* concerns an application lodged by Mr. Mekhmet Takhır Dıno Baz, a Turkish national, against Ukraine under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant alleged that his detention in Ukraine, pending the examination of a Turkish extradition request, violated Article 5 § 1 (f) of the Convention, which permits lawful detention "with a view to extradition."

The applicant arrived in Ukraine in 2004 and was granted refugee status on 23 March 2011. However, on 18 October 2012, the State Migration Service revoked this status, claiming he had provided false information by concealing that he was wanted by Turkish law enforcement for a criminal offence. This revocation was upheld by the High Administrative Court on 3 April 2013. Meanwhile, on 14 March 2013, the applicant applied for subsidiary protection. This application was initially rejected as inadmissible, but on 27 February 2014, the Odessa Circuit Administrative Court quashed that decision and ordered a merits examination.

Separately, in Turkey, the Istanbul 13th Higher Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for the applicant on 20 June 2011, suspecting him of terrorist and separatist activities related to events in 1998. On 3 October 2012, the Turkish court sent an extradition request to Ukrainian authorities, noting the criminal charge would become time-barred on 15 August 2013. On 17 June 2013, a second Turkish arrest warrant was issued on the same charge.

On 14 November 2012, the applicant was detained by Ukraine's State Security Service with a view to extradition. The following day, migration authorities confirmed he was not a Ukrainian national, a prerequisite for extradition under Ukrainian law. On 16 November 2012, the Mykolaiv Tsentralny District Court ordered his detention pending extradition.

The applicant was later transferred to Kharkiv for separate criminal proceedings in Ukraine (using forged documents). On 17 July 2013, the Kharkiv Zhovtnevy District Court reviewed his detention and found it justified, citing the Turkish arrest warrants and extradition request. The court noted the prosecution had conducted an extradition inquiry and found no impediments. However, on 30 August 2013, the same court released the applicant, observing that the limitation period for the alleged Turkish offences had expired on 15 August 2013. Consequently, under Article 10 of the European Convention on Extradition, extradition could not be granted. On 23 September 2013, Ukraine's Ministry of Justice formally rejected Turkey's extradition request.

The applicant complained that his detention was unlawful under Article 5 § 1 (f) for three reasons: first, until 3 April 2013, his appeals against the revocation of refugee status were pending, meaning he could not be extradited; second, from 14 March 2013, his pending subsidiary protection application barred extradition under Ukrainian law; and third, from 15 August 2013, his prosecution in Turkey became time-barred, rendering further detention unlawful. The Ukrainian Government failed to submit observations on admissibility or merits.

The European Court of Human Rights declared the complaint admissible, finding it neither manifestly ill-founded nor inadmissible on other grounds. The case proceeded to a merits examination concerning whether the applicant's detention complied with Article 5 § 1 (f).

**Case: Smbat Ayvazyan v. Armenia (Application no. 49021/08, ECtHR, 8 October 2020)**

The case concerned an Armenian opposition activist and former MP, Smbat Ayvazyan. After the disputed 19 February 2008 presidential election, supporters of opposition candidate Levon Ter-Petrosyan held daily protests at Freedom Square in Yerevan. Ayvazyan, a member of an opposition party’s political council and a Ter-Petrosyan supporter, actively attended the rallies and sit-ins, including spending the night of 23–24 February 2008 at Freedom Square.

On 24 February 2008, while returning home, his car was stopped by masked police officers. He was taken to a police anti-organised-crime unit on suspicion of illegal arms possession. Police recorded finding a spring baton in his coat; Ayvazyan alleged it was planted and that he was coerced into admitting ownership by threats to prosecute his friends instead. A Makarov pistol found in his car was later found to be defective and not a firearm. That night, after a toxicology examination, three police officers alleged that Ayvazyan insulted and threatened them and punched officer K.H. at Kentron Police Station. Ayvazyan denied any incident, stating he was handcuffed, protested his unlawful arrest, and that relatives, a lawyer and a journalist were nearby. A criminal case was opened for non-life-threatening assault on a public official, and he was charged and detained.

Domestic courts repeatedly extended his detention, citing risks that he might abscond, obstruct the investigation or reoffend. His case was joined to a broader investigation into the 1–2 March 2008 post-election clashes; authorities suggested he had helped organise unlawful demonstrations and conspire to usurp power. A new charge of illegally carrying a cold weapon—the baton—was later added. After the investigation ended and the case was sent for trial, the Court of Appeal refused to examine his detention appeal solely because the case was no longer at the pre-trial stage.

At trial, the District Court convicted Ayvazyan in November 2008 under Article 316 § 1 and Article 235 § 4, relying mainly on statements by police officers K.H., E.P., A.S. and later S.H. and A.H. The applicant sought to call defence witnesses—relatives, supporters, a journalist and two detainees who allegedly saw or heard no incident—but the court refused, finding them irrelevant or unnecessary. He was also unable to question officers S.H. and A.H. properly. He received two years’ imprisonment and a fine; appeals were rejected and the Court of Cassation refused review. He was later amnestied and released.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 5 § 1 because there was no court decision for a short period of continued detention; Article 5 § 3 because domestic courts failed to give relevant and sufficient reasons for continued detention; Article 5 § 4 because his detention appeal was unjustifiably refused; Article 6 § 1 because his conviction was secured decisively on testimony of police officers actively involved in the contested events, without verification; and Article 11 because his prosecution and conviction were linked to his participation in the protest movement, forming part of a repetitive pattern of artificial, politically motivated arrests and prosecutions of opposition activists.

In *Smbat Ayvazyan v. Armenia* (no. 49021/08, 8 October 2020), the European Court of Human Rights examined the arrest, detention, prosecution and conviction of an Armenian opposition activist following the disputed 19 February 2008 presidential election. The applicant was a former member of parliament and government minister, a member of an opposition party’s political council, and a supporter of opposition candidate Levon Ter-Petrosyan. After the election, daily protests and sit-ins were held at Freedom Square in Yerevan. Ayvazyan actively participated and spent the night of 23–24 February 2008 at the square.

On 24 February 2008, while returning home, his car was blocked by masked police officers and he was taken to the police anti-organised-crime department on suspicion of illegal arms. A spring baton was allegedly found in his coat; he claimed it was planted and that he was coerced into admitting it belonged to him. A Makarov pistol found in his car was later found to be defective and not a firearm, and drug tests were negative. Later that night, after a forensic examination, three police officers alleged that Ayvazyan insulted and punched officer K.H. at Kentron Police Station. Ayvazyan denied the incident, saying he was handcuffed and that relatives, a lawyer and a journalist nearby could confirm his account.

A criminal case was opened under Article 316 of the Criminal Code for assaulting a public official. He was arrested and placed in two-month detention. Domestic courts repeatedly extended detention on generic grounds that he might abscond, reoffend or obstruct the investigation. His case was joined to proceedings concerning the March 2008 mass disorder, then disjoined; in June 2008 a new charge of illegally carrying a cold weapon was added. At trial, the District Court convicted him in November 2008, relying heavily on police testimony. It refused to summon defence witnesses—relatives, supporters, a journalist and fellow detainees—and did not allow him to question two police witnesses, S.H. and A.H., whose written statements were used. Appeals failed; he was later released under amnesty.

The ECtHR found violations. Under Article 11, the applicant’s prosecution and conviction were arbitrary and linked to his participation in a protest movement, reflecting a repetitive pattern of artificial, politically motivated arrests and prosecutions of opposition activists. Under Article 5 § 1, a period of continued detention lacked a court decision; after 15 July 2008 the judge failed to address detention when setting the case for trial and later relied on an alleged typographical error. Under Article 5 § 3, the domestic courts failed to give relevant and sufficient reasons for continued pre-trial detention. Under Article 5 § 4, an appeal against extended detention was unjustifiably refused solely because the case was no longer considered pre-trial. Under Article 6 § 1, the conviction was secured to a decisive extent by testimony of police officers actively involved in the contested events, and the domestic court failed to verify their incriminating statements. The case thus concerned politically motivated restrictions on assembly, unlawful and unreasoned detention, and fair-trial defects.

In *Smbat Ayvazyan v. Armenia* (no. 49021/08, ECtHR, 8 October 2020), the applicant was an Armenian opposition politician and former MP/minister who supported Levon Ter-Petrosyan in the disputed February 2008 presidential election. After the election, daily opposition protests and sit-ins were held in Freedom Square, Yerevan. Ayvazyan was an active participant and spent the night of 23–24 February 2008 at the square.

On 24 February 2008, as he drove home, police blocked his car and took him to the anti-organized crime department, allegedly acting on an anonymous tip that he was armed. A search allegedly found a spring baton in his coat; he claimed it was planted and that he confessed only after threats to prosecute his friends. A Makarov pistol found in his car was later found defective and not a firearm; drug tests were negative. That night, after a forensic examination, police alleged that he insulted, pushed and punched officer K.H. at Kentron Police Station. Ayvazyan denied any assault, saying he was handcuffed and that relatives, friends, a lawyer and a journalist waiting outside could confirm his account. A medical examination of K.H. found no injuries.

A criminal case was opened under Article 316 §1 of the Criminal Code (non-life-threatening assault on a public official). Ayvazyan was arrested on 25 February and placed in detention on 27 February. Courts repeatedly extended detention, citing risks of absconding or obstruction and sometimes linking him to a broader case concerning the 1–2 March 2008 protests and mass disorder. A further charge of illegally carrying a cold weapon was added. The case was disjoined and sent to trial in July 2008.

At trial, the conviction rested decisively on statements of police officers involved in the events, including K.H., E.P., A.S., and guards S.H. and A.H. The court refused to summon defense witnesses—relatives, a journalist, and passengers who said no assault occurred—and did not allow proper questioning of S.H. and A.H.; their written statements were admitted instead. In November 2008 Ayvazyan was convicted and sentenced to two years’ imprisonment for the assault and fined for the weapon offence. Appeals were dismissed, and the Court of Cassation declared his appeal inadmissible. He was released under amnesty in June 2009. He died in 2014, and his widow continued the application.

The ECtHR found violations. Under Article 11, the prosecution and conviction were arbitrary and linked to his participation in the opposition protest movement, forming part of a repetitive pattern of artificial, politically motivated arrests of opposition activists. Under Article 5 §1, his continued detention after 15 July 2008 lacked a valid court decision; the judge’s later claim of a typographical error did not cure this. Article 5 §3 was violated because domestic courts failed to give relevant and sufficient reasons for continued pre-trial detention. Article 5 §4 was violated because the Court of Appeal refused to examine his detention appeal solely on the ground that the case was no longer at the pre-trial stage. Finally, Article 6 §1 was violated because the assault conviction was based to a decisive extent on testimony of police officers actively involved in the contested events, and the domestic court failed to verify their incriminating statements.

In *M.A. and Others v. Bulgaria* (Application no. 5115/18, ECtHR, 20 February 2020), five Chinese nationals of Uighur Muslim origin from Xinjiang complained that Bulgaria’s intended expulsion to China would expose them to arbitrary detention, ill-treatment or death, in violation of Articles 2 and 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicants said they had fled China fearing persecution because of their Uighur ethnicity, religion and perceived disloyalty. Their accounts included arrests, police monitoring, torture, threats, family detention and punishment for practices such as praying, wearing a beard, teaching Uighur, or breaching family-planning rules. After leaving China, they lived in Turkey but fled again in 2017, believing improved Turkish-Chinese relations created a risk that Uighurs would be deported to China. They entered Bulgaria unlawfully in July 2017 and were detained. Bulgarian authorities issued repatriation decisions and the applicants received suspended sentences and fines for illegal entry.

The applicants then applied for asylum in December 2017. Their applications were rejected by the State Refugees Agency and, on judicial review, by the Haskovo Administrative Court in January 2018. The Administrative Court found no proof of past persecution or a real future risk. It considered that China’s measures in Xinjiang were justified counter-terrorism responses, that any problems the applicants had faced were ordinary law-enforcement or family-planning issues rather than ethnic or religious persecution, and that there was no indication Turkey intended to return Uighurs to China. Some applicants also complained that they had not had interpretation from Uighur during the asylum process, though interpreters were provided in the court proceedings.

In parallel, the State Agency for National Security ordered their expulsion on national security grounds in January 2018. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld the expulsions of the second, third and fourth applicants. The case **Pasquini v. San Marino (No. 2)** (Application no. 23349/17) concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 § 2 (presumption of innocence) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Enrico Maria Pasquini, an Italian national residing in San Marino, was chairman and sole shareholder of S.M.I., a fiduciary company. Following a June 2011 Central Bank inspection of S.M.I., criminal proceedings were brought against Pasquini and B., the company’s director.

Pasquini was charged with exercising fiduciary activity without a licence, three counts of obstruction of surveillance, misreporting to shareholders and supervisory boards, and continuing aggravated embezzlement. As to embezzlement, the prosecution alleged that between April 2009 and March 2010 Pasquini, as beneficial owner of company S., withdrew EUR 2,633,055.77 from a fiduciary account administered by S.M.I. The funds were allegedly paid through fictitious invoices and simulated brokerage services to foreign companies, including entities in tax-haven countries, to the detriment of S.M.I. S.M.I., then in compulsory liquidation, joined the criminal proceedings as a civil party.

On 8 April 2014, the first-instance judge convicted Pasquini and B. on all charges. Pasquini was sentenced to four years’ imprisonment and a fine, and ordered to compensate S.M.I.; an interim compensation order of EUR 2,633,055.77 was made. The judge found that the accused had created a complex system of foreign broker companies, used fictitious commissions and invoices, and moved money through accounts effectively traceable to themselves. The payments were not genuine commissions, and S.M.I.’s patrimony had been abused for their benefit.

On appeal, Pasquini argued that the limitation period for embezzlement had expired. On 1 December 2015, the Judge of Criminal Appeals accepted that the limitation period had expired but referred a constitutional question concerning Article 196 of the Code of Criminal Procedure: whether an appeal judge could decide civil compensation claims after an offence became time-barred. Law No. 189/2015 then introduced Article 196 bis, allowing the Judge of Criminal Appeals, when declaring an offence time-barred, to decide civil obligations deriving from it. The Constitutional Court returned the file.

On 19 September 2016, the Judge of Criminal Appeals applied the new provision, acquitted Pasquini of some charges, confirmed others, and ruled that obstruction of surveillance, misreporting, and aggravated embezzlement were time-barred and discontinued. Nevertheless, the judge upheld the compensation order. Although the embezzlement charge had been discontinued, he examined the first-instance findings solely to decide civil compensation and stated that the earlier reasoning had not shown the facts never occurred or that the accused had not committed them.

Pasquini complained under Article 6 § 2 that, despite no finding of guilt, the appeal judgment conveyed the judge’s conviction that he was guilty and made him pay damages on that basis. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation. It held that the judge’s remarks were not merely unfortunate language but amounted to an imputation of criminal liability. The Court emphasised that extra care must be exercised when formulating reasoning in a civil judgment following discontinuation of criminal proceedings.

Pasquini was sentenced to four years’ imprisonment and a fine, and an interim compensation order of EUR 2,633,055.77 was made in favour of S.M.I. On appeal, Pasquini argued that the embezzlement charge was time-barred. In December 2015, the Judge of Criminal Appeals accepted that the limitation period had expired but referred a constitutional question concerning whether the appeal judge could still decide civil compensation claims after discontinuing a time-barred offence. While the matter was pending, Law No. 189/2015 introduced Article 196 bis of the Code of Criminal Procedure, allowing the Judge of Criminal Appeals, when declaring an offence time-barred, to decide civil obligations arising from that offence. In doing so, he examined the evidence underlying the discontinued embezzlement charge solely to decide the civil claims, noting that the first-instance reasoning had not shown that the facts never occurred or that the accused had not committed them.

Although no criminal conviction was entered because the charges were time-barred, he alleged that the Judge of Criminal Appeals’ reasoning effectively treated him as guilty and required him to pay damages on that basis, without guilt having been established in criminal proceedings.

Pasquini was sentenced to four years’ imprisonment and a fine, and was ordered to compensate S.M.I., with an interim compensation order of €2,633,055.77. The judge found that the accused had created a complex system of foreign broker companies, simulated business operations, and fictitious commissions, and that bank accounts formally held by the broker companies were actually traceable to Pasquini and B. The judge rejected Pasquini’s argument that, as sole shareholder, he had merely taken his own funds.

Pasquini appealed, arguing that the embezzlement charge was time-barred. In December 2015 the Judge of Criminal Appeals accepted that the limitation period had expired, but referred a constitutional question concerning whether an appellate judge could still decide civil compensation claims after declaring an offence time-barred. A new law, Article 196 bis of the Code of Criminal Procedure, subsequently allowed the appellate judge to decide civil obligations deriving from a time-barred offence. The Constitutional Court returned the case, and in September 2016 the Judge of Criminal Appeals applied the new law.

The appellate judgment acquitted Pasquini and B. of unlicensed fiduciary activity and acquitted Pasquini of one obstruction count for lack of evidence. It confirmed other obstruction counts and ruled that the obstruction, misreporting, and aggravated embezzlement charges were time-barred, discontinuing them. Nevertheless, it upheld the first-instance judgment, including the compensation order. Importantly, the appellate judge examined the evidence underlying the discontinued aggravated embezzlement conviction solely in order to decide civil compensation. He noted that the first-instance reasoning had not indicated that the alleged facts never occurred or that the accused had not committed them, so the only possible finding was to declare the charges discontinued. He then scrutinised the elements of aggravated embezzlement for the civil decision.

Pasquini complained that, despite the absence of a criminal conviction on the time-barred charges, the appellate judge’s reasoning effectively treated him as guilty and imposed civil damages on that basis. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 6 § 2. It held that the judge’s remarks were not merely unfortunate language but amounted to an imputation of criminal liability. The Court stressed that judges must exercise extra care when formulating reasoning in civil judgments delivered after criminal proceedings have been discontinued, especially where limitation has prevented a finding of guilt.

Case D. v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 25397/09, ECtHR, 8 December 2020) arose from the aftermath of Moldova’s 5 April 2009 parliamentary elections. Protests against alleged electoral fraud began peacefully in Chișinău on 7 April but later turned violent; police restored order early on 8 April. The applicant, a young Moldovan woman, went to the Great National Assembly Square on the evening of 7 April 2009 with her roommate R. and relative V. Boboc. She alleged that around 1 a.m. on 8 April, while she and about fifty young people stood peacefully discussing events, they were surrounded by police, masked special forces and plain-clothed officers armed with automatic rifles and rubber sticks. The group was ordered to lie on the ground and then kicked and severely beaten. The applicant’s head was hit against the pavement and she received multiple blows. She saw police kicking Boboc, who was unconscious; he later died.

The applicant and others were taken to police detention centres. At Buiucani police station, she alleged that around twenty young men and three young women, including her, were made to stand against a wall with their hands up and were beaten when they moved or spoke. Male detainees were taken individually to an office, ordered to lower their trousers, and were heard being beaten and screaming; they returned with visible injuries, one completely naked. The three women were insulted and shouted at but not physically assaulted. No reason was given for the applicant’s arrest, and she was not allowed to inform relatives. She was released around 5 a.m. on 8 April, after over five hours’ detention, and advised to leave the city.

On 14 April 2009 a doctor found a 16x15 cm injury to her right foot; fearing for her life, she falsely claimed she had been attacked by an unknown person. Between 4 and 15 May 2009, the Memoria Rehabilitation Centre examined her and reported headaches, vertigo, insomnia, nightmares, anxiety, flashbacks, post-traumatic stress disorder and possible consequences of cranial trauma. On 4 May 2009 she complained to the Prosecutor General about ill-treatment and unlawful detention without explanation or access to relatives. A criminal investigation into her allegations began on 22 July 2009, was joined to other cases in March 2010, and was suspended on 15 January 2013 because authorities could not identify which officer had used force against which victim. Separately, officer G. was convicted of negligence for failing to act when detainees, including the applicant and R., were brought to Buiucani police station and some were ill-treated; this was upheld in 2016. The Government also paid the applicant MDL 7,000 (about EUR 447) under a 2012 compensation scheme.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained under Articles 3 and 13 that she was ill-treated by police during arrest and that the investigation was ineffective; under Article 5 that her detention was unlawful; and under Articles 2 and 13 that her life was endangered after witnessing Boboc’s death and that authorities refused witness protection. The Government disputed her account, argued lack of evidence, non-exhaustion and loss of victim status due to compensation. The Court rejected the Article 2/13 complaint as manifestly ill-founded, finding no sufficiently serious and immediate danger to life. It declared the Article 3/13 complaint admissible, rejected the Government’s preliminary objections, and proceeded to examine the merits of the alleged ill-treatment and ineffective investigation.

In *D. v. the Republic of Moldova* (Application no. 25397/09, judgment of 8 December 2020), the applicant was a Moldovan woman born in 1990. The case arose from the post-election protests in Chișinău following Moldova’s 5 April 2009 general elections. After disputed results, protests began on 6 April and grew the next day. On 7 April the demonstration initially remained peaceful but later became violent, with some protesters attacking and occupying government buildings. After midnight on 8 April, police and special forces launched a mass operation to restore order. According to a later parliamentary inquiry, excessive force was used and many people present in the main square were arrested regardless of whether they had been violent.

On the evening of 7 April 2009, the applicant went to the Great National Assembly Square with her roommate, R., and her relative, V. Boboc. She alleged that at about 1 a.m. on 8 April, her group of about fifty young people was surrounded by police, masked special forces, and plain-clothed officers. The group was ordered to lie on the ground and was kicked and beaten with rubber sticks and rifles. The applicant claimed her head was struck against the pavement and she received multiple blows. While being taken to a police car, she saw officers kicking Mr Boboc, who was unconscious and unresponsive; he later died.

At Buiucani police station, about twenty young men and three young women, including the applicant and R., were allegedly forced to stand facing a wall with their hands up. They were reportedly beaten when they tried to speak or move. The young men were taken one by one into an office and ordered to lower their trousers; sounds of beating and screaming followed. Men returning showed clear signs of ill-treatment, and one was completely naked. The three women were insulted and shouted at but allegedly not physically assaulted. The applicant said she was detained for over five hours without being told why she was arrested or allowed to contact relatives, and was released around 5 a.m. and advised to leave the city.

On 13 April 2009 the applicant gave an anonymous television interview about the events. Authorities sought to discover her identity, but journalists and Mr Boboc’s relatives/lawyer refused to reveal it. Fearing for her safety, she saw a doctor on 14 April and claimed she had been attacked by an unknown person; the doctor found one injury to her right foot. On 4 May 2009 she complained to the Prosecutor General about her alleged ill-treatment and unlawful detention. Between 4 and 15 May 2009, the Memoria Rehabilitation Centre examined her and documented headaches, vertigo, insomnia, nightmares, anxiety, flashbacks, signs of post-traumatic stress disorder, and possible consequences of cranial trauma.

A criminal investigation into her allegations began on 22 July 2009 and was later joined with other cases concerning alleged police beatings. On 15 January 2013 it was suspended because authorities could not identify which officer had used force on which victim or whether the force was necessary. The applicant said she was not informed of decisions in the investigation. In parallel proceedings, officer G. was convicted in 2015—upheld in 2016—of negligence for witnessing ill-treatment at the Buiucani police station, with reference to the applicant’s and R.’s statements. In 2012 the Government awarded the applicant MDL 7,000 (about €447) as ex gratia compensation.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained under Articles 2 and 13 that her life was at risk after witnessing Mr Boboc’s death and that witness protection was refused; the Court rejected that part as manifestly ill-founded. She also complained under Articles 3 and 13 of ill-treatment during arrest and an ineffective investigation; that part was declared admissible. She further alleged unlawful detention under Article 5. The Government disputed her account and evidence, but the Court rejected several preliminary objections, including non-exhaustion and loss of victim status.

Case D. v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 25397/09, judgment of 8 December 2020) concerned alleged police ill-treatment and unlawful detention during Moldova’s April 2009 post-election protests. The applicant, a Moldovan national born in 1990, was arrested in Chișinău on the night of 7–8 April 2009.

After the 5 April 2009 elections, protests erupted over alleged electoral fraud. On the evening of 7 April, the applicant went to the Great National Assembly Square with her roommate R. and met her relative V. Boboc. Around 1 a.m. on 8 April, she alleged that she was part of a group of about fifty young people standing peacefully in the street. Police guarding the Government building, masked special forces, and plain-clothed officers armed with automatic rifles and rubber sticks surrounded the group. The group was ordered to lie down. The applicant claimed she was kicked and severely beaten with rubber sticks and rifles; her head was hit against the pavement and she received several blows. She and R. saw police kicking Boboc while he was unconscious. Boboc later died.

The applicant said she was taken to Buiucani police station with about twenty young men and three young women, including R. They were allegedly ordered to stand facing a wall with their hands up and were beaten whenever they spoke or moved. Young men were taken one by one into an office and ordered to lower their trousers; those who returned showed signs of ill-treatment, and one was released completely naked. The three women were insulted and shouted at but not physically assaulted. At about 5 a.m. on 8 April the women were released and advised to leave the city. The applicant alleged she was detained for over five hours without being told the reason for her arrest or being allowed to inform relatives.

On 13 April 2009, the applicant gave a TV interview with her identity concealed, describing what she had witnessed. Authorities then asked journalists and Boboc’s father and lawyer to reveal her identity, which they refused. Fearing for her life, on 14 April she told a doctor she had been attacked by an unknown person; the doctor recorded one injury to her right foot, measuring 16 by 15 centimetres. On 4 May 2009 she complained to the Prosecutor General about her ill-treatment and unlawful detention. Between 4 and 15 May 2009, the Memoria Rehabilitation Centre examined her and found headaches, vertigo, insomnia, nightmares, anxiety, flashbacks, possible cranial trauma, and signs of post-traumatic stress disorder.

A criminal investigation into her ill-treatment allegations began on 22 July 2009, was joined to another case in March 2010, and was suspended on 15 January 2013 because authorities could not identify which officer used force against which victim. A police officer, G., was later convicted of negligence for failing to carry out duties at Buiucani police station while detainees, including the applicant and R., were brought there and some ill-treated; that conviction was upheld in 2016. The applicant received MDL 7,000 (about EUR 447) under a government compensation scheme.

The applicant alleged violations of Articles 3 and 13 (ill-treatment and ineffective investigation), Article 5 (unlawful detention), and Articles 2 and 13 (failure to protect her life after she witnessed Boboc’s death and refusal of witness protection). The Court declared the Article 3 complaint admissible, but rejected the Article 2/13 complaint as manifestly ill-founded.

**Stafeyev v. Russia** (Application no. 32984/06) is a European Court of Human Rights case concerning the fairness of Russian criminal proceedings. The applicant, Vyacheslav Vladimirovich Stafeyev, complained under Article 6 § 1 taken together with Article 6 § 3 (c) of the Convention that he lacked effective legal assistance during his appeal, and also about the poor quality of the video link used before the Supreme Court. The Court gave notice of these complaints to the Russian Government and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

The underlying case concerned the murder of a family—a man, his wife, and their thirteen-year-old son—whose bodies were found in their flat on 19 February 2001. The applicant was detained in November 2004 for another crime. His fingerprints were later found to match prints discovered in the victims’ flat, and a search of his home allegedly recovered items stolen from the victims. Police officers questioned him informally at the detention facility, and he eventually confessed. According to the applicant, the confession was made under duress; according to the Government, he voluntarily admitted guilt after being told about the fingerprint match.

On 10 December 2004 the applicant was informed of his rights and waived his right to a lawyer. He was interviewed as a suspect without a lawyer and repeated his confession. He did so again on 16 December 2004. In January 2005, assisted by a lawyer, he retracted his confession. At trial, the Sverdlovsk Regional Court excluded his statements of 10 and 16 December 2004 because they were made without a lawyer and later retracted, but it admitted his earlier confession of 8 December 2004. On 14 December 2005 the Regional Court convicted him of three counts of murder, robbery, and destruction of property, and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The conviction relied on fingerprint evidence, the stolen items found at his home, police testimony, and the 8 December confession. The applicant denied guilt, claiming he had visited the family on 16 February 2001, not 18 February, and that his confession had been coerced.

The alleged violation arose mainly from the appeal proceedings. The applicant’s trial lawyer filed a seventeen-page appeal raising factual and legal issues. The appeal hearing was set for 15 May 2006, and the applicant was transferred to Moscow. His trial lawyer did not appear. The applicant, who was present, asked for a new lawyer. The Supreme Court assigned lawyer R. and adjourned the hearing to 29 May 2006. On 23 May 2006 R. visited the applicant in detention, but the applicant claimed the meeting lasted only fifteen minutes and was repeatedly interrupted by a guard. On 25 May 2006 the applicant asked the detention facility to transmit a request to the Supreme Court for an additional meeting with R. The Government disputed that the Supreme Court received this request before the appeal; a copy was postmarked as received on 5 June 2006, after the hearing. On 29 May 2006 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the life sentence. R. was present, and the applicant participated by video link. The applicant claimed he asked the Supreme Court to admit his 25 May request but was refused. The Government later stated that the applicant complained about poor video transmission and insufficient consultation time on 30 and 31 May 2006, while a Supreme Court IT certificate recorded no video failures during the hearing.

The key issue before the Court was whether the applicant had effective legal assistance on appeal, particularly given the late appointment of R., the very limited consultation before the hearing, the refusal of an additional meeting, and the conditions of his participation by video link. The Government argued non-exhaustion, contending that the applicant had not timely raised the insufficient consultation time before or at the appeal hearing. The applicant maintained that he had requested an additional consultation and brought the matter to the Supreme Court’s attention during the hearing.

**Stafeyev v. Russia** (Application no. 32984/06, European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, 8 December 2020) concerned complaints under Article 6 § 1 read with Article 6 § 3(c) of the Convention about the lack of effective legal assistance on appeal and the poor quality of a video link before the Russian Supreme Court.

The applicant, Vyacheslav Vladimirovich Stafeyev, a Russian national born in 1978, was detained in November 2004 following conviction for another crime. He later became a suspect in the 2001 murder of the Sh. family—a man, his wife, and their thirteen-year-old son. After his fingerprints were entered into a police database, they were found to match fingerprints discovered in the victims’ flat. A search of the applicant’s flat reportedly found items stolen from the victims.

Between 8 and 10 December 2004, police officers visited the applicant in detention and questioned him informally about the murders. The Government claimed that on 8 December 2004 he spontaneously and voluntarily confessed. The applicant claimed that he confessed on 10 December 2004 under duress. On 10 December 2004, at 3 p.m., he was informed of his rights and waived his right to a lawyer. He was then interviewed as a suspect without counsel and reiterated his confession. On 16 December 2004, he was again interviewed without a lawyer after waiving counsel, and again repeated the confession. On 20 January 2005, assisted by a lawyer, he retracted his confession.

At trial before the Sverdlovsk Regional Court, the applicant denied guilt. He maintained that he had visited the Sh. family on 16 February 2001, not 18 February 2001, and that his confession had been coerced. On 15 September 2005, the Regional Court declared his statements of 10 and 16 December 2004 inadmissible because they were made without a lawyer and retracted at trial. However, it admitted his alleged confession of 8 December 2004. On 14 December 2005, the Regional Court convicted him of three counts of murder, robbery, and destruction of property, sentencing him to life imprisonment. The judgment relied on fingerprint evidence, seized stolen items, police testimony that he had voluntarily confessed after being told about the fingerprints, and the 8 December confession.

The alleged violation arose during appeal proceedings. The applicant’s trial lawyer filed a seventeen-page appeal on 14 November 2005. On 30 March 2006, the lawyer was informed that the appeal hearing would take place on 15 May 2006. The applicant was transferred to Moscow. On 15 May 2006, his lawyer failed to appear. The applicant, who was present, requested a new lawyer. The Supreme Court assigned lawyer R. and adjourned the hearing to 29 May 2006.

On 23 May 2006, R. visited the applicant in detention. The applicant alleged that the meeting was limited to fifteen minutes and was repeatedly interrupted. On 25 May 2006, he submitted a request to the Supreme Court for an additional meeting with R., claiming the time was insufficient. The Government said the case file contained no information that he made such a request to the Supreme Court, but produced a copy dated 25 May, registered as outgoing on 26 May, and received by the Supreme Court on 5 June 2006.

On 29 May 2006, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, with R. present and the applicant participating via video link. The applicant alleged that he asked the court to admit his 25 May request but was refused. The Government said he complained on 30 and 31 May about poor video transmission and insufficient consultation time. A Supreme Court IT certificate stated that no video transmission failures had been recorded during the hearing. The Government argued non-exhaustion, while the applicant maintained that he had raised the issue during the hearing.

**Stafeyev v. Russia** (Application no. 32984/06) is a European Court of Human Rights case decided by the Third Section Committee on 8 December 2020. The applicant, Vyacheslav Vladimirovich Stafeyev, a Russian national born in 1978 and detained in Kharp, complained principally under Article 6 § 1 taken together with Article 6 § 3 (c) about the lack of effective legal assistance during his appeal. The Court also gave notice to the Government of his complaint about the poor quality of the video link used before the Supreme Court; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The underlying criminal case concerned the 2001 murder of a family—a man, his wife and their thirteen-year-old son—whose bodies were found in their flat. In 2004, while the applicant was detained for another crime, his fingerprints were matched to prints found in the victims’ flat. A search of his flat allegedly found items stolen from the victims. The applicant initially confessed on 8 December 2004. He later said that confession was made under duress. On 10 December 2004 he was informed of his rights and waived his right to a lawyer; he then repeated his confession in interviews on 10 and 16 December 2004 without a lawyer. On 20 January 2005, assisted by a lawyer, he retracted his confession.

At trial, the Sverdlovsk Regional Court on 15 September 2005 excluded the applicant’s statements of 10 and 16 December 2004 because they were made without a lawyer and later retracted. However, it admitted his 8 December 2004 confession. On 14 December 2005 the Regional Court convicted him of three counts of murder, robbery and destruction of property and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The conviction relied on fingerprint evidence, items found at his home, police testimony, and the 8 December confession.

The appeal proceedings are central to the alleged violation. On 14 November 2005 the applicant’s trial lawyer filed a seventeen-page appeal raising factual and legal issues. On 30 March 2006 the lawyer was informed that the appeal hearing would be held on 15 May 2006. The applicant was transferred to a Moscow detention facility to participate. On 15 May 2006 his trial lawyer did not appear. The applicant, who was present, asked for a new lawyer. The Supreme Court assigned lawyer R. and adjourned the hearing to 29 May 2006.

On 23 May 2006 R. visited the applicant in detention. The applicant alleged that his communication with R. was limited to fifteen minutes and that a guard repeatedly interrupted them. On 25 May 2006 he submitted a request through the detention facility authorities asking the Supreme Court to grant an additional meeting with R. because the time had been insufficient. The Government argued that the case file contained no information that he made a relevant request to the Supreme Court on that date, though it produced a copy of the request dated 25 May, registered as outgoing correspondence on 26 May, and received by the Supreme Court on 5 June 2006—after the appeal.

On 29 May 2006 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the conviction. R. was present, and the applicant participated via video link. The applicant claimed that during the hearing he asked the Supreme Court to admit his 25 May request to the case file, but was refused. The Government stated that on 30 and 31 May 2006 the applicant complained about poor video transmission and insufficient time to consult R. on 23 May. A Supreme Court IT certificate dated 28 August 2013 said no video transmission failures had been recorded during the 29 May 2006 hearing.

The Government also pleaded non-exhaustion, arguing that the applicant did not timely raise his complaint about insufficient consultation time before or at the appeal hearing, and that his later complaints were received after the appeal. The applicant maintained that he had submitted the request through the detention facility, raised it during the video-link hearing, and was denied admission of a copy. The Court examined these facts in determining whether the applicant had effective legal assistance on appeal and whether the video link was adequate.

In *Talalikhina v. Ukraine* (Application no. 13919/12), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) delivered a judgment on 22 October 2020. The applicant, Olga Vasilyevna Talalikhina, was a Ukrainian national born in 1954 and living in Sevastopol. She was represented by R. Martynovskiy. The case concerned the lawfulness and length of her pre-trial detention, the length of criminal proceedings, and the alleged lack of effective remedies.

The relevant facts began on 5 September 2007, when criminal proceedings were instituted against the applicant for theft. She was questioned as a suspect and signed an undertaking not to abscond. On 30 October 2007 the theft case was sent to court. On 13 April 2009, while that case was pending, she was involved in a drunken brawl with her cohabitant. She allegedly hit him with a hammer; he was taken to hospital and died a few days later. On 17 April 2009 she was arrested and questioned about the incident. On 20 April 2009 the Leninskyy District Court of Sevastopol ordered her pre-trial detention.

On 15 June 2009 the Sevastopol City Prosecutor approved a bill of indictment charging her with aggravated infliction of serious bodily harm resulting in death and referred the case to the District Court. The applicant remained in custody. Under Article 156 of the 1960 Code of Criminal Procedure, detention during pre-trial investigation could not exceed two months, although a judge could extend it upon request. Therefore, after about 20 June 2009, the April detention order had expired. The domestic courts did not revisit her detention until 6 July 2009, when the Nakhimovskiy District Court of Sevastopol committed her for trial and ruled that the preventive measure should remain in place, without giving any justification.

The applicant complained under Article 5 § 1 of the Convention that (a) her pre-trial detention after the termination of the investigation in June 2009 was not based on any court order until 6 July 2009, and (b) the 6 July 2009 decision authorising further detention was arbitrary. The Government argued that she had not exhausted domestic remedies because she could have appealed the initial 20 April 2009 detention order. The Court rejected that objection, finding that the complaint concerned a different period not covered by that order. It declared the Article 5 § 1 complaint admissible.

On the merits, the Court noted that after the expiry of the 20 April 2009 order, the applicant’s continued detention rested merely on the fact that the bill of indictment had been submitted to the District Court. No court reviewed the detention until 6 July 2009, when the District Court extended it without justification. The Court found this incompatible with the principles of legal certainty and protection from arbitrariness under Article 5 § 1, relying on *Kharchenko v. Ukraine*. It saw no reason to depart from that case-law and found a violation.

Other facts noted were that her release applications were dismissed on 5 August 2011 and 10 May 2012; on 20 June 2012 the custodial measure was changed and she was released with relatives as guarantors. On 19 September 2012 the theft charge was dropped. On 6 February 2013 she was convicted of the unintentional homicide of her cohabitant and sentenced to two years’ imprisonment. The judgment’s focus, however, was the unlawful gap and arbitrary extension of her pre-trial detention under Article 5 § 1.

**Talalikhina v. Ukraine** (Application no. 13919/12, judgment of 22 October 2020) concerned the lawfulness and length of the applicant’s pre-trial detention, the length of criminal proceedings against her, and the alleged lack of effective remedies. The applicant, Ms Olga Vasilyevna Talalikhina, a Ukrainian national born in 1954 and living in Sevastopol, was represented by counsel.

In September 2007, criminal proceedings were instituted against the applicant on suspicion of theft. She was questioned as a suspect and signed an undertaking not to abscond. In October 2007, the theft case was referred to court for trial.

A separate, more serious incident occurred in April 2009. During a drunken brawl with her cohabitant at home, the applicant allegedly struck him with a hammer. The man was hospitalised and died a few days later. On 17 April 2009, the applicant was arrested and questioned in connection with that incident. On 20 April 2009, the Leninskyy District Court of Sevastopol ordered her pre-trial detention.

On 15 June 2009, the Sevastopol City Prosecutor approved a bill of indictment charging the applicant with aggravated infliction of serious bodily harm resulting in death, and referred the case to the District Court. The applicant remained in custody. On 6 July 2009, the Nakhimovskiy District Court of Sevastopol committed her for trial and ruled that the preventive measure—continued detention—should remain in place.

Under Article 156 of the 1960 Code of Criminal Procedure, pre-trial detention during investigation could not exceed two months, though a judge could extend it upon request.

The applicant complained under Article 5 § 1 of the Convention that: (a) after the investigation was terminated in June 2009, her continued pre-trial detention was not based on any court order until 6 July 2009; and (b) the 6 July 2009 court decision authorising further detention was arbitrary. The Government argued that she had failed to exhaust domestic remedies because she had not appealed the initial 20 April 2009 detention order. The applicant replied that her complaint concerned other periods of detention not covered by that order. The European Court of Human Rights dismissed the Government’s objection, finding that the remedy invoked did not address the substance of her complaint.

On the merits, the Court noted that after the 20 April 2009 detention order expired—its validity could not exceed two months—the applicant’s further detention was based merely on the fact that a bill of indictment had been submitted to the District Court. The domestic courts did not address her detention again until 6 July 2009, when the District Court prolonged it without providing any justification. The Court found this situation incompatible with the principles of legal certainty and protection from arbitrariness under Article 5 § 1, relying on its earlier case-law, notably *Kharchenko v. Ukraine*. It saw no reason to depart from those findings.

Other relevant facts included that the applicant’s applications for release were dismissed in August 2011 and May 2012 as unfounded. On 20 June 2012, the custodial measure was changed and she was released on relatives’ guarantees. In September 2012, the theft charge was dropped for lack of constituent elements. In February 2013, she was convicted of unintentional homicide of her cohabitant and sentenced to two years’ imprisonment. The Government claimed it could not properly comment because the case file was in Crimea, outside Ukraine’s control at the time; the applicant noted that electronic copies were available in the official judicial register. The Court proceeded on the file as it stood.

**Case:** *Talalikhina v. Ukraine* (Application no. 13919/12), European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, Judgment of 22 October 2020.

The applicant, Ms Olga Vasilyevna Talalikhina, a Ukrainian national born in 1954 and living in Sevastopol, complained principally about the lawfulness and length of her pre-trial detention, the length of criminal proceedings against her, and the lack of effective remedies. The judgment excerpt focuses on her complaint under Article 5 § 1 of the Convention.

**Key facts.** On 5 September 2007 criminal proceedings were instituted against the applicant on charges of theft. She was questioned as a suspect and signed an undertaking not to abscond. On 30 October 2007 the theft case was referred to court.

Separately, on 13 April 2009 the applicant was involved in a drunken brawl with her cohabitant at home. She allegedly hit him with a hammer; he was taken to hospital and died a few days later. On 17 April 2009 she was arrested and questioned in connection with that incident. On 20 April 2009 the Leninskyy District Court of Sevastopol ordered her pre-trial detention.

On 15 June 2009 the Sevastopol City Prosecutor approved a bill of indictment charging the applicant with aggravated infliction of serious bodily harm resulting in death, and referred the case to the District Court. She remained in custody. On 6 July 2009 the Nakhimovskiy District Court of Sevastopol committed her for trial and ruled that the preventive measure should remain in place. The applicant later applied for release, but on 5 August 2011 and 10 May 2012 the District Court dismissed those applications as unfounded. On 20 June 2012 the custodial measure was changed and she was released, with relatives acting as guarantors. On 19 September 2012 the theft charge was dropped for lack of constituent elements. On 6 February 2013 she was convicted of unintentional homicide of her cohabitant and sentenced to two years’ imprisonment.

**Relevant legal framework.** At the relevant time, Article 156 of the 1960 Code of Criminal Procedure provided that detention during pre-trial investigation should not exceed two months. A judge could, however, extend pre-trial detention upon request.

**Alleged violation.** The applicant complained under Article 5 § 1 that: (a) her pre-trial detention after the termination of the investigation in June 2009 was not based on any court order until 6 July 2009; and (b) the court decision of 6 July 2009 authorising her further pre-trial detention had been arbitrary.

**Admissibility and merits.** The Government argued that she had not exhausted domestic remedies because she could have appealed the initial detention order of 20 April 2009. The Court dismissed that objection, finding that the complaint concerned other periods of detention not covered by the 20 April 2009 order. It declared the complaint admissible.

On the merits, the Court noted that the detention order of 20 April 2009 could not validly exceed two months. After its expiry, the applicant’s further detention was based only on the fact that a bill of indictment had been submitted to the District Court. The domestic courts did not revisit the detention issue until 6 July 2009, when the District Court prolonged detention without providing any justification. The Court found this incompatible with the principles of legal certainty and protection from arbitrariness under Article 5 § 1, relying on *Kharchenko v. Ukraine*. It saw no reason to depart from that case-law, indicating a violation of Article 5 § 1.
