In *Chernov v. Ukraine* (ECtHR, 10 December 2020), the applicant was arrested on 20 June 2007 for an administrative offence. On 21 June 2007 the Zarichnyy District Court of Sumy found him guilty of “minor disorderly acts” under Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences. It found that at about 10 p.m. on 20 June 2007 on Prokofyeva Street, Sumy, he was drunk, uttered obscenities, reacted aggressively to police remarks, cursed officers, and attempted to start a fight. He was sentenced to three days’ administrative detention. That decision became final, and he served the sentence from 21 to 23 June 2007.

Despite this, on 16 July 2007 a prosecutor opened a criminal case under Article 296 of the Criminal Code for “disorderly acts” based on the same events. The prosecution alleged that Chernov had caused minor physical injuries to Mu. and P. during the incident. Forensic examinations of Mu. and P. were carried out on 22 June and 14 September 2007, indicating minor injuries possibly inflicted on 20 June 2007. Chernov was arrested in December 2007 and indicted in January 2008 under Article 296 § 3.

On 28 January 2008, the prosecutor lodged an objection against the June 2007 administrative decision. On 6 February 2008 the Zarichnyy District Court annulled its earlier administrative decision; this was upheld on appeal on 25 February 2008. The judge who had decided the administrative case later withdrew from hearing the criminal case.

In the criminal proceedings, Chernov was convicted on 14 July 2008 and sentenced to two years’ imprisonment, but the Sumy Regional Court of Appeal quashed the conviction on 7 October 2008 and remitted the case. On 29 December 2008 the first-instance court convicted him again under Article 296 § 3 and sentenced him to two years and one month. On 10 March 2009 the appellate court upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence to two years. On 24 September 2009 the Supreme Court upheld that decision, finding no double jeopardy because the administrative decision had been annulled.

Chernov complained under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention that he had been tried and punished twice for the same offence. He argued that the administrative and criminal cases concerned the same facts—same date, time, place, and conduct—and that the injuries relied on in the criminal case were known to police and prosecutors by 21–22 June 2007, so they were not newly discovered facts. The Government argued that the two cases concerned different conduct: the administrative case involved drunkenness, obscenities, and aggression toward police, while the criminal case involved physical injuries and property damage. It also claimed the criminal proceedings were justified as a reopening based on new facts and the annulment of the administrative decision.

The European Court of Human Rights declared the complaint admissible and found a violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. It held that the administrative offence was criminal in nature for Convention purposes, especially given the three-day detention. The facts underlying both convictions were substantially the same and inextricably linked. The administrative conviction had been final, and Chernov had already served his sentence before the criminal case began. The reopening exception did not apply because the police and prosecutor knew of the fight and injuries shortly after 20 June 2007; no new facts were discovered. Annulling the administrative decision after the sentence had been served did not cure the duplication. Thus, Ukraine breached the *ne bis in idem* principle.

In *Chernov v. Ukraine* (Application no. 16432/10, judgment of 10 December 2020), the European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention, which protects the right not to be tried or punished twice for the same offence.

The applicant, Oleksandr Chernov, was arrested on 20 June 2007 after an incident in Sumy. At about 10 p.m., while drunk on Prokofyeva Street, he uttered obscenities, reacted aggressively to police officers’ remarks, cursed them, attempted to start a fight, and breached public order and the peace. On 21 June 2007, the Zarichnyy District Court of Sumy found him guilty of “minor disorderly acts” under Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences and sentenced him to three days’ administrative detention. That decision became final and could not be appealed. Chernov served the sentence from 21 to 23 June 2007.

Subsequently, the authorities pursued criminal proceedings based on the same incident. On 16 July 2007, a prosecutor opened a criminal case under Article 296 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine for “disorderly acts,” later alleging that Chernov had caused physical injuries to two people, Mu. and P., and damaged property. The applicant was arrested on 23 December 2007 and indicted on 29 January 2008 under Article 296 § 3.

Meanwhile, on 28 January 2008, a prosecutor lodged an objection against the earlier administrative decision. On 6 February 2008, the Zarichnyy District Court annulled its own decision of 21 June 2007, and the Sumy Regional Court of Appeal upheld that annulment on 25 February 2008.

In the criminal case, Chernov was convicted on 14 July 2008 and sentenced to two years’ imprisonment. That conviction was quashed on 7 October 2008 and remitted for fresh examination. On 29 October 2008, Judge Ma., who had decided the administrative case, withdrew from hearing the criminal case because she had annulled the administrative decision after criminal elements became apparent. On 29 December 2008, the district court again convicted Chernov under Article 296 § 3 and sentenced him to two years and one month’s imprisonment. On 10 March 2009, the appellate court upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence to two years. The Supreme Court of Ukraine upheld that outcome on 24 September 2009, reasoning that the administrative decision had been annulled and the administrative case “closed,” so there had been no double trial.

Before the ECtHR, Chernov complained that he had been tried and punished twice for the same conduct: first through the administrative offence and three-day detention, then through the criminal conviction. The Government argued that the administrative and criminal cases concerned different facts—drunkenness, obscenities, and aggression toward police in the administrative case, versus physical injuries and property damage in the criminal case—and that the criminal proceedings were justified as a reopening based on newly discovered facts.

The Court found that the administrative proceedings were criminal in nature for Convention purposes. The administrative decision had been final, and the sentence had already been served before the criminal proceedings concluded. The facts underlying both sets of proceedings were substantially the same: the same date, time, place, public-order breach, and continuous disorderly conduct. The later criminal case added injuries and property damage, but those facts were already known to police and prosecutors by 21–22 June 2007. Therefore, the annulment of the administrative decision after Chernov had served his detention did not justify a second punishment. The Court concluded that Ukraine violated the *ne bis in idem* principle.

**CASE OF CHERNOV v. UKRAINE**  
*European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, Judgment of 10 December 2020 (Application no. 16432/10)*

The applicant, Oleksandr Chernov, a Ukrainian national, complained that he had been tried and punished twice for the same offence, contrary to Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention, which protects the right not to be tried or punished twice (*ne bis in idem*).

On 20 June 2007, at about 10 p.m. on Prokofyeva Street in Sumy, the applicant was arrested following an incident while he was drunk. On 21 June 2007 the Zarichnyy District Court of Sumy found him guilty of “minor disorderly acts” under Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences. The court established that he had uttered obscenities, reacted aggressively to police remarks, cursed the officers and attempted to start a fight. He was sentenced to three days’ administrative detention, which he served from 21 to 23 June 2007. That decision became final and could not be appealed.

On 28 January 2008, however, the prosecutor lodged an objection against the administrative decision, arguing that the same facts gave rise to criminal liability. On 6 February 2008 the Zarichnyy District Court annulled its earlier decision, and this annulment was upheld on appeal on 25 February 2008.

In the meantime, criminal proceedings had been initiated. On 16 July 2007 a prosecutor opened a criminal case under Article 296 of the Criminal Code concerning disorderly acts on 20 June 2007 at the same time and place, including physical injuries allegedly inflicted on two victims, Mu. and P. Forensic examinations on 22 June and 14 September 2007 found that both victims had minor physical injuries. The applicant was arrested on 23 December 2007 and indicted on 29 January 2008. On 14 July 2008 he was convicted under Article 296 § 3 and sentenced to two years’ imprisonment. That conviction was later quashed on appeal on 7 October 2008 because of factual inconsistencies and because the sentence was considered too lenient. On 29 October 2008 the judge who had dealt with the administrative case withdrew from hearing the criminal case. On 29 December 2008 the applicant was again convicted and sentenced to two years and one month’s imprisonment; on appeal, the conviction was upheld but the sentence was reduced to two years. On 24 September 2009 the Supreme Court of Ukraine upheld that outcome, reasoning that because the administrative decision had been annulled, the applicant had not been tried twice.

Before the European Court, the applicant argued that the administrative and criminal proceedings concerned substantially the same facts. The Government contended that the administrative case concerned drunkenness, obscene language and aggression toward police, while the criminal case concerned physical injuries and property damage. They also argued that the criminal proceedings were justified as a reopening based on newly discovered facts.

The Court found the complaint admissible. It held that the administrative proceedings were criminal in nature for the purposes of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7, especially because the applicant had served three days’ detention. The administrative decision had been final before the later criminal conviction. Applying the “same offence” test, the Court found that both proceedings arose from the same continuous conduct, on the same date, time and place. Although the criminal case included additional elements such as injuries and property damage, those facts arose from the same incident. The reopening exception did not apply because the police and prosecutor already knew of the fight and injuries by 21–22 June 2007; no genuinely new facts had been discovered. Annulling the administrative decision after the criminal proceedings began did not cure the duplication, particularly since the applicant had already served his administrative sentence.

The Court therefore found a violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention.

In *Lopata and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 84210/17 and 23 others), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee) delivered judgment on 10 December 2020. The case originated in 24 applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates. The Ukrainian Government was given notice. Because the applications raised similar issues, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment.

The applicants complained principally under Article 3 that they were serving life sentences with no prospect of release. Some applicants also raised other complaints under other Convention provisions. The excerpt does not reproduce the appended table of applicants and individual details, but the judgment indicates that they had been convicted of especially serious crimes, such as murder, and sentenced to life imprisonment. The central alleged violation was therefore not the imposition of a life sentence as such, but its irreducible character: the applicants claimed that their imprisonment lacked any realistic possibility of review or release, amounting to inhuman or degrading punishment.

The Court reiterated its settled case-law: the Convention does not prohibit life imprisonment for especially serious crimes. However, for a life sentence to be compatible with Article 3, it must be reducible both *de jure* and *de facto*. This means there must be both a prospect of release and a possibility of review. The review must not be merely formal; it must allow authorities to assess whether there remain legitimate penological grounds for continued detention. Those grounds include punishment, deterrence, public protection, and rehabilitation. The Court emphasised that the balance among these grounds can shift over time. What may justify detention at the outset may not justify it after many years, and rehabilitation is especially important under contemporary European penal policy, Council of Europe standards, and international materials. The Court relied on *Vinter and Others v. the United Kingdom* and noted that in *Petukhov v. Ukraine (no. 2)*, it had already found a violation of Article 3 in respect of similar issues concerning irreducible life sentences in Ukraine.

In the present case, the Court examined the material and found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on admissibility or merits. It therefore found a violation of Article 3 in respect of the applicants’ life sentences with no prospect of release. As to the additional complaints raised by some applicants under various Convention Articles, the Court considered them either inadmissible under Articles 34 and 35 of the Convention or disclosing no appearance of a violation of Convention rights or Protocols. Those parts of the applications were accordingly rejected under Article 35 § 4. The judgment records that Article 41 of the Convention was also invoked, but the provided excerpt does not include the Court’s detailed ruling on just satisfaction. In short, the key facts relevant to the violation were that the applicants were serving life sentences in Ukraine under a regime that did not provide an adequate *de jure* and *de facto* review mechanism, leaving them without a realistic prospect of release and thus subjecting them to treatment contrary to Article 3.

**Case: Filozofenko v. Ukraine (Application no. 72954/11)**

The applicant, Ms Lina Alekseyevna Filozofenko, is a Ukrainian national born in 1938 who lives in the Odessa Region. She held the special status of a “child of war” under the Children of War Social Protection Act in force as of 1 January 2006. Section 6 of that Act entitled her to a special supplement to her pension amounting to 30% of the minimum pension.

On 11 December 2008, the applicant sued the State Pension Fund in the domestic administrative courts. She asked for recalculation of her pension under section 6 for the years 2006–2008 and payment of the outstanding arrears.

On 10 June 2009, the Odessa Circuit Administrative Court partly allowed her claim. It held that in 2006 section 6 had been suspended by the State Budget Act 2006. Although later amendments empowered the Cabinet of Ministers to create a mechanism for a pension increase, no such mechanism had been set up. Her claims for 2006 were therefore rejected. As to 2007 and 2008, section 6 had been suspended and modified by the 2007 and 2008 State Budget Acts. However, the Constitutional Court had found that suspension and modification unconstitutional on 9 July 2007 and 22 May 2008 respectively. The court therefore ordered recalculation only for the periods from 9 July to 31 December 2007 and from 22 May to 31 December 2008.

On 1 November 2010, the Odessa Regional Administrative Court of Appeal partly amended that judgment. It upheld the rejection of the 2006 claims. It also upheld the applicant’s right to a pension increase for 2007 and 2008, but found that she had missed the one-year statutory time-limit for lodging her claim. Consequently, the 2007 claim was allowed only for the period from 11 to 31 December 2007. On 18 May 2011, the Higher Administrative Court upheld that judgment, making it final.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, alleging that the domestic courts had refused to acknowledge in full her claims for a pension increase for 2006–2008. She argued that the refusals concerning 1 January to 31 December 2006, 1 January to 11 December 2007, and 1 January to 22 May 2008 were unlawful and ungrounded.

The Government contended that the application had been lodged out of time because the final domestic decision was delivered on 18 May 2011, while the application was lodged on 23 January 2012. Alternatively, they argued that the complaint was manifestly ill-founded. They relied on *Sukhanov and Ilchenko v. Ukraine* regarding the periods 1 January to 9 July 2007 and 1 January to 22 May 2008, argued that the period from 9 July to 11 December 2007 was inadmissible because the applicant had missed a time-limit, and described the 2006 complaints as manifestly ill-founded.

The applicant replied that she had sent her first letter to the Court on 17 November 2011, within six months of the final domestic decision, and submitted a completed application form on 23 January 2012, as directed by the Court. The Court noted that the first letter was sent on 18 November 2011, within six months, and that the completed form was submitted on 23 January 2012 within the time-limit set by the Court.

The key alleged violation therefore concerned the State’s failure to pay the full statutory pension supplement to a “child of war” after Constitutional Court rulings invalidated budget-law restrictions, and the domestic courts’ partial refusal of her claims due to suspension of the provision and late-claim limitations.

Case Makuchyan and Minasyan v. Azerbaijan and Hungary (App. no. 17247/13), decided by the ECtHR Fourth Section on 26 May 2020, concerned the 2004 axe murder in Budapest of Armenian officer G.M. and the attempted murder of Armenian officer Hayk Makuchyan by Azerbaijani officer R.S. The applicants were Armenian nationals: Makuchyan, a course participant, and Samvel Minasyan, G.M.’s uncle (later represented by his family after his death).

In January 2004, Armenian and Azerbaijani officers attended a NATO Partnership for Peace English-language course in Budapest. On 19 February 2004, R.S. killed G.M. while he slept, striking him at least twelve times with an axe. He then tried to break down Makuchyan’s door, allegedly shouting anti-Armenian threats. R.S. had bought the axe and a sharpening stone two days earlier. In Hungarian criminal proceedings, he admitted disliking Armenians because of the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict and killed G.M. because of his Armenian origin. In 2006, the Budapest High Court convicted him of exceptionally cruel, premeditated murder committed with vile motives exclusively because of the victims’ Armenian nationality, and of preparation to murder Makuchyan. He received life imprisonment, with possible release after thirty years; the conviction was upheld on appeal in 2007.

In 2012, Azerbaijan requested R.S.’s transfer to serve his sentence in Azerbaijan. Under the Council of Europe Convention on Transfer of Sentenced Persons, Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Justice assured Hungary that the sentence would continue without conversion and that life imprisonment could be paroled only after at least twenty-five years. Hungary approved the transfer on 17 August 2012. On 31 August 2012, upon arrival in Azerbaijan, R.S. was immediately released by presidential pardon. He was then promoted to major by the Minister of Defence, granted a State flat, awarded salary arrears, and publicly celebrated by high-ranking Azerbaijani officials as a hero and patriot. Hungarian authorities later expressed disapproval.

The applicants alleged that Azerbaijan violated Article 2 by failing to enforce the prison sentence, granting a pardon, and rewarding R.S., thereby creating impunity. They also alleged Article 14 read with Article 2, because the Armenian ethnicity of the victims motivated the murder and the subsequent discriminatory treatment. Hungary was alleged to have violated Article 2 by transferring R.S. without binding assurances that he would continue serving his sentence.

The Court found Azerbaijan had violated Article 2 procedurally: its unjustified failure to enforce the sentence and its measures securing impunity were incompatible with the State’s obligation to effectively deter offences against life. It found no substantive Article 2 violation under State responsibility rules, because Azerbaijan’s approval and endorsement did not meet the high threshold of clearly and unequivocally acknowledging and adopting R.S.’s private crime as its own. The Court did find an Article 14 violation: Azerbaijan failed to disprove an arguable allegation of discrimination, and the impunity measures had a causal link to the victims’ Armenian ethnicity; R.S. had been glorified by officials for an extremely cruel hate crime. Hungary was not found in violation: it followed the Transfer Convention, and there was no evidence it was or should have been aware that Azerbaijan would release R.S.

**Summary of *Makuchyan and Minasyan v. Azerbaijan and Hungary* (Application no. 17247/13)**

The case concerns the 2004 murder of Armenian Lieutenant G.M. and the attempted murder of Armenian officer H.M. by Azerbaijani officer R.S. in Budapest, Hungary. He then attempted to break down the door of the first applicant's room, allegedly shouting threats to kill all Armenians.

Hungarian authorities arrested R.S., who admitted killing G.M. due to his Armenian ethnicity, citing the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict. He showed no remorse. Psychiatric examinations found him fit to stand trial. In 2006, the Budapest High Court convicted R.S. of exceptionally cruel, premeditated murder and preparation of murder, committed with vile motives based on the victims' Armenian nationality. He received life imprisonment with eligibility for parole after thirty years. The conviction was upheld on appeal in 2007.

In 2012, after Hungary rejected two prior transfer requests, Azerbaijan sought R.S.'s transfer under the Council of Europe Convention on Transfer of Sentenced Persons. Azerbaijan's Ministry of Justice assured Hungary that the sentence would continue without conversion and that life imprisonment required at least twenty-five years before parole eligibility. Hungary approved the transfer on 17 August 2012.

Upon arrival in Azerbaijan on 31 August 2012, R.S. was immediately pardoned by presidential decree, released, promoted to major, provided a state flat, and awarded salary arrears. Azerbaijani officials and public figures glorified him as a patriotic hero, with statements celebrating the killing and calling for similar acts against Armenians.

They also alleged Hungary violated Article 2 by transferring R.S. without binding assurances he would serve his sentence.

The Court found Azerbaijan violated Article 2 procedurally by failing to enforce the prison sentence, granting impunity incompatible with the obligation to deter offences against life. It also found Azerbaijan had sufficient evidence to disprove the discrimination allegation, violating Article 14 combined with Article 2. However, Azerbaijan's actions did not meet the high threshold of "acknowledgement and adoption" of the crimes as its own under Article 2 substantively.

Regarding Hungary, the Court found no violation, as Hungary followed the Transfer Convention procedures entirely and had no evidence Azerbaijani authorities would release R.S.

**Case: Romanov v. Ukraine (Application no. 63782/11)**

The applicant, Ilya Romanov, a Russian national, was a communist revolutionary involved with a group that printed and distributed newspapers in Ukraine during anti-Kuchma protests. The publications, including *Soviet of Workers’ Deputies* and *Rada of Workers’ Deputies*, contained articles calling for armed revolt, civil war, overthrow of the constitutional order, and Soviet rule. In October 2002, an explosive device was detonated near the SBU headquarters in Kyiv.

In December 2002, Romanov was arrested in Kakhovka after police reportedly found a gun, bullets, a homemade explosive device, and a detonator. He alleged unrecorded detention and said he requested a lawyer, Chet. On 21 December 2002, at SBU premises in Mykolayiv, he made a handwritten “explanation” confessing to the SBU explosion, manufacturing explosives, and distributing the newspapers. He claimed the investigator dictated the statement after psychological ill-treatment. He later confirmed confessions during a crime reconstruction with lawyer Sk., but alleged Sk. was investigator-chosen, not effective, and that his self-incriminating statements were coerced and obtained in breach of defence rights. A co-defendant, Sm., also confessed and implicated him.

Charges were changed in May 2003 to include dissemination of material calling for violent overthrow of the constitutional order, banditry, terrorism, illegal drug production/possession, and unlawful possession of firearms and explosives. In July 2004, the Odessa Regional Court convicted Romanov of terrorism, dissemination, banditry, and weapons offences; he was acquitted of drug offences and sentenced to ten years. In July 2005, the Supreme Court quashed the banditry conviction but upheld the rest.

Romanov complained that his trial was unfair: he lacked adequate time and facilities to prepare his defence, was denied chosen counsel during key investigative steps, was represented ineffectively, could not participate effectively, and was convicted for his political beliefs. He also alleged a lack of effective remedies for these complaints.

As to detention, he was held in Odessa SIZO from March 2003 to November 2005. He alleged overcrowding, a cold cell with an unglazed window, sleeping on the floor, poor sanitation, lack of hot water and bedding, and a flooded disciplinary cell. The Government denied this, describing ordinary cells with toilet, heating, light, weekly showers, and daily walks. Romanov also alleged superficial medical care and untreated spine problems later recognised as a disability. During court transfers, he claimed early-morning departures, long waits in unheated windowless assembly cells, missed meals, and exhaustion preventing proper preparation. The Government described shorter hearings and arranged meals.

In 2006, his transfer from Yenakieve to Polytska Prison took nearly two months via several SIZOs. He alleged overcrowded, unventilated train compartments, no food, water, or sanitary access for long periods, poor transit cells, beatings, disrespect, and correspondence problems. The Government said relevant travel documents were destroyed but claimed conditions were adequate.

The Court gave notice of complaints concerning Odessa SIZO conditions and transfer to Polytska; adequate defence facilities; effective participation and legal representation; conviction for political beliefs; and lack of effective remedies. These implicated Articles 3, 6, 9/10/11, and 13 of the Convention.

In *Avto Atom Doo Kochani v. North Macedonia* (Application no. 21954/16, judgment of 28 May 2020), the European Court of Human Rights considered a company’s complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention that it had been unlawfully deprived of its right to deduct input VAT because of its supplier’s failure to register for VAT.

The applicant company, Avto Atom Doo Kochani, was a limited-liability passenger bus transport company registered for VAT. It declared VAT on outgoing invoices and claimed deductions on incoming invoices. In March–April 2007, the Internal Revenue Office audited its VAT obligations for 2004–2005. The audit found that one of its suppliers, a petrol station, had not been registered for VAT. However, the supplier’s invoices contained its tax number and declared VAT. The applicant paid those invoices in full and claimed the related VAT deduction. It otherwise complied with its VAT obligations.

On 2 May 2007, relying on the audit, the IRO issued a payment order imposing an additional VAT demand of 3,266,792 Macedonian denars (MKD). The authorities claimed the applicant had unlawfully deducted VAT based on invoices from the unregistered supplier. The applicant contested the order but paid the amount in instalments during 2007–2008. Its administrative claim was dismissed by the Administrative Court on 28 January 2015, which held that the applicant was not entitled to a deduction because the supplier had not been VAT-registered; the fact that the supplier had declared VAT on the invoices was considered irrelevant. The Higher Administrative Court dismissed the appeal on 20 October 2015.

Other relevant facts were that the supplier had been founded in 2003 and struck off the companies register in 2006. Its founder and sole owner was convicted in 2009 for failing to register for VAT (tax evasion), received a suspended sentence, and paid a tax debt of 595,470 MKD (approximately €9,650). The supplier itself was not prosecuted because it had been liquidated.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant argued that the State had not been diligent in collecting VAT from the supplier; it had no practical way to verify the supplier’s VAT compliance, and charging the applicant amounted to a second payment of the same tax. The Government argued that the interference was lawful and in the public interest, aimed at protecting the stability of the VAT system. It claimed the applicant should have checked the supplier’s VAT status through online IRO records, the companies register, the central registry, or by requesting a tax certificate.

The Court declared the complaint admissible, rejecting the Government’s non-exhaustion objection by reference to *Euromak Metal Doo v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia*. On the merits, the Court accepted that the applicant’s right to deduct input VAT amounted at least to a legitimate expectation falling within “possessions” under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It found that VAT had been declared on the supplier’s invoices, the applicant had paid them, had not been charged with tax offences, and had complied with its reporting duties. The Government failed to show that the suggested verification methods were supported by domestic law or practice, or that they would have revealed the supplier’s non-registration. The applicant had no reason to suspect unlawful conduct and no reasonably available means to monitor the supplier’s VAT compliance. Moreover, since the supplier’s owner was convicted and paid part of the VAT debt, it was unclear why the State did not seek the full amount from him. Domestic law also made an entity that declared VAT despite non-registration liable for that VAT. A civil claim against the supplier was impossible because it had been struck off. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

**Case: Avto Atom Doo Kochani v. North Macedonia**  
**ECtHR, First Section, App. No. 21954/16, Judgment of 28 May 2020**

The applicant, Avto Atom Doo Kochani, was a North Macedonian limited-liability company providing passenger bus transport. It was registered for VAT and regularly declared VAT on outgoing and incoming invoices, allowing it to make periodic deductions from its VAT liabilities.

In March–April 2007, the Internal Revenue Office audited the company’s VAT obligations for 2004–2005. The audit found that one of its fuel suppliers, a petrol station, had not been registered for VAT. The supplier’s invoices nevertheless included its tax number and separately stated VAT. The applicant paid those invoices in full and claimed the corresponding input VAT deduction. The IRO treated the deduction as unlawful solely because the supplier was not VAT-registered. On 2 May 2007, it issued a payment order imposing an additional VAT demand of MKD 3,266,792. The applicant contested the order but paid it in instalments during 2007–2008. After two remittals, the Administrative Court dismissed its claim on 28 January 2015, and the Higher Administrative Court dismissed its appeal on 20 October 2015. The supplier had been founded in 2003, struck off the companies register in 2006, and its owner was later convicted of tax evasion in 2009, receiving a suspended sentence and paying MKD 595,470 (about EUR 9,650) of the tax debt.

The applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the domestic authorities deprived it of its right to deduct VAT paid on goods received, effectively punishing it for an error committed by its supplier. The Government first objected that domestic remedies had not been exhausted, but the Court rejected that objection, relying on *Euromak Metal Doo v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia*. On the merits, the Government argued the interference was lawful and in the general interest of maintaining VAT stability. It claimed the applicant should have checked the supplier through the IRO online system, the companies register, annual tax reports, or by requesting a VAT registration certificate.

The Court held that the applicant’s right to claim a VAT deduction amounted at least to a legitimate expectation and thus a possession. VAT had been declared on the supplier’s invoices; the applicant paid them, was never charged with tax offences, and otherwise complied with VAT reporting. The central issue was whether the applicant had been sufficiently diligent. The Court found the Government failed to show that an online IRO verification was available in law or practice, or that any suggested check would have revealed the supplier’s non-registration. The applicant reasonably relied on invoices containing the supplier’s tax number and VAT. It did not know and had no reason to know of the supplier’s tax evasion. Thus it had no reasonably available means to monitor or ensure the supplier’s VAT compliance.

The Court also noted that domestic law makes an entity liable for VAT it declares even if unregistered, and the supplier’s owner was convicted for the same tax fraud but only part of the debt was collected from him. It was unclear why the State did not seek the full amount from him rather than charging the applicant again. A civil claim against the supplier was impossible because the company had been struck off. The Court therefore concluded that refusing the applicant’s input VAT deduction was not justified by the need to secure tax payment, and found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

Avto Atom Doo Kochani v. North Macedonia (Application no. 21954/16) is a European Court of Human Rights First Section Committee judgment of 28 May 2020. The applicant is a limited-liability company in Kochani specialising in bus passenger transport. It was registered for VAT and declared VAT on its outgoing invoices; it also declared VAT on incoming invoices and deducted that input VAT from its VAT obligations.

In 2004–2005 the applicant bought fuel from a petrol station supplier. The supplier was not registered for VAT, but issued invoices containing its tax number and separately declaring VAT. The applicant paid those invoices in full and claimed the related VAT deduction. In March–April 2007, the Internal Revenue Office audited the applicant’s VAT obligations for 2004–2005. The audit found that the supplier had not been VAT-registered. On 2 May 2007 the IRO issued a payment order imposing additional VAT of 3,266,792 Macedonian denars, on the basis that the applicant had unlawfully deducted VAT from invoices issued by an unregistered supplier. The applicant contested the order but paid the amount in instalments in 2007–2008.

The applicant’s administrative challenge ultimately failed. On 28 January 2015 the Administrative Court dismissed its claim, holding that the applicant had not been entitled to deduct VAT because the supplier was not VAT-registered; the fact that VAT had been declared on the invoices was irrelevant. The Higher Administrative Court dismissed the appeal on 20 October 2015.

Other relevant facts: the supplier was founded on 19 August 2003 and struck off the companies register on 30 June 2006. Its founder and sole owner was convicted on 25 December 2009 of failing to register for VAT (tax evasion) and received a suspended sentence. He paid tax debt of 595,470 MKD, about EUR 9,650. The supplier itself was not prosecuted because it had been liquidated. Domestic law provided that an entity which declared VAT on an invoice despite not being VAT-registered nevertheless owed that declared VAT.

The applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the domestic authorities had deprived it of the right to deduct VAT paid on received goods because of an error committed by its supplier. The Government objected that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies, arguing it should have pursued criminal or civil action against the supplier or its owner. The Court rejected that objection, relying on Euromak Metal Doo v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, and declared the complaint admissible.

On the merits, the Court treated the applicant’s right to claim a VAT deduction as at least a “legitimate expectation” amounting to a “possession.” It noted that VAT was declared on the supplier’s invoices, that the applicant had paid them, that it had not been charged with tax offences, and that it had otherwise complied with its VAT reporting obligations. The key dispute was whether the applicant had been sufficiently diligent. The Government claimed it could have checked the supplier’s VAT status through the IRO online system, the companies register, tax reports, or by asking the supplier for a certificate. The Court found these checks were not supported by domestic law or practice, and the Government did not show they would have revealed the supplier’s non-registration. The applicant reasonably relied on invoices containing the necessary data and VAT declarations, and there was no proof it knew or should have known of the supplier’s tax evasion. It therefore had no reasonably available means to monitor the supplier’s VAT compliance. The Court also found it unclear why the State had not sought the full VAT from the supplier’s owner, who had been convicted for the same fraud, especially since domestic law made the issuer liable for declared VAT. A civil claim against the supplier was impossible because it had been struck off. The Court consequently found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention.

**CASE OF N.H. AND OTHERS v. FRANCE** (ECtHR, Fifth Section, 2 July 2020) concerned five single adult asylum-seekers in France who complained under Article 3 that administrative delays in registering their asylum claims and issuing residence documents left them without the material reception conditions required by French and EU law. Unable to work while their claims were pending, they depended entirely on State support. They alleged they were forced to live rough for months in degrading conditions. Some also invoked Article 13 (effective remedy) and Article 8.

The key facts varied by applicant. **N.H.**, an Afghan national, arrived in France in March 2013. He obtained a mailing address but his prefecture appointment was set for 9 July 2013, about three months later. Without asylum-seeker status, he received no in-kind or financial support. He lived rough under bridges for around nine months, often sleeping only two or three hours, and had his belongings stolen. Emergency accommodation through the “Atlas bus” was inadequate and later unavailable. He wrote to authorities on 6 April, 19 August, and 6 September 2013 but received no reply. He was refused the Temporary Waiting Allowance (TWA). He later received subsidiary protection in December 2013 and accommodation.

**S.G., G.I., and K.T.**, in Carcassonne, lodged asylum claims but were told there were no Asylum Reception Centre places. The 115 emergency helpline was at capacity, so they lived in tents by the Aude river. S.G. and G.I. eventually received TWA of €11.20 per day after about one to two months; K.T. later. Domestic interim-relief judges denied accommodation, reasoning that they were young, single, healthy men with no dependants and that priority had to go to vulnerable people.

**A.J.**, an Iranian journalist, arrived in September 2014. His prefecture appointment was delayed to 7 January 2015. Without status or support, he lived rough near Gare de l’Est, was assaulted, and had his bags stolen. He occasionally used emergency shelters. He received TWA in February 2015, accommodation in April 2015, and refugee status in April 2015.

The systemic background was that asylum-seekers could not lawfully work while their claims were pending. French law and the EU Reception Directive required in-kind or financial support, but administrative delays prevented access. Emergency accommodation was insufficient and prioritised particularly vulnerable persons. The Court noted there was no humanitarian emergency arising from an exceptional migration crisis. The authorities had been repeatedly put on notice but failed to provide an appropriate official response. Domestic courts consistently denied relief on the ground that the applicants were single young adults in good health without dependent family members.

The Court found that the conditions endured by **N.H.** and **A.J.** reached the severity threshold of Article 3, amounting to degrading treatment, because they were left without resources for several months. For the other applicants, who received financial support after about two months, the threshold was not reached. It found no violation of Article 13 or Article 8. The case established that systemic administrative delays causing asylum-seekers to live rough may violate Article 3, even absent a migration crisis, where no adequate official response is provided.

In *Minyaylo and Others v. Ukraine*, the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) examined three applications (nos. 59356/10, 61038/10 and 59824/12) lodged by Ukrainian nationals Anatoliy Minyaylo, Igor Kindra and Leonid Kharchenko. The judgment, delivered on 24 September 2020 and rectified on 20 November 2020, concerned allegations that the applicants had been ill-treated by police and that the authorities had failed to investigate their complaints effectively, contrary to Article 3 of the Convention. The applicants also raised complaints under Articles 5 §§ 1 and 5 and 6 § 1. Because the applications concerned similar subject matter, the Court examined them jointly.

The key facts relevant to the alleged Article 3 violations were set out in appended tables. In each application, the applicants claimed that police had subjected them to inhuman and degrading treatment. Those allegations triggered a positive obligation on Ukraine to carry out an effective official investigation aimed at establishing the origin of the applicants’ injuries and identifying and punishing those responsible if the allegations proved true. However, the domestic investigations did not reflect any serious effort to determine the relevant facts. The Court noted numerous shortcomings in those investigations, which failed to produce a reliable account of the alleged incidents.

In Mr Minyaylo’s case, the Government argued that he had not exhausted domestic remedies because he had not appealed against a conviction of 24 December 2010. It also contended that his complaint was lodged outside the six-month time-limit, calculated from 15 November 2007, when the prosecutor’s office last decided not to institute criminal proceedings into his ill-treatment allegations. The Court rejected those objections, relying on earlier Ukrainian cases such as *Kaverzin v. Ukraine*. It found the complaint admissible. Medical documents confirmed that Minyaylo had sustained injuries. In the applications brought by Mr Kindra and Mr Kharchenko, the Government raised no admissibility objections. It also filed no comments on the merits regarding Mr Kindra’s application.

On the merits, the Court found that all applicants had raised arguable ill-treatment claims at the domestic level. The State therefore had to provide a plausible explanation for injuries sustained by persons under police control. The applicants’ accounts of the alleged ill-treatment were detailed and coherent. By contrast, the investigation results, given their many shortcomings, did not disprove those accounts. The Court referred to its earlier finding in *Kaverzin* that the reluctance of Ukrainian authorities to ensure a prompt and thorough investigation of ill-treatment complaints against police constituted a systemic problem. The present facts were another example of that failure.

Because the domestic authorities neither properly investigated nor plausibly explained the applicants’ injuries, the Court concluded that Ukraine was responsible for the ill-treatment. The applicants had been subjected to inhuman and degrading treatment. There were therefore violations of Article 3 of the Convention under both its substantive limb—the ill-treatment itself—and its procedural limb—the ineffective investigation. The judgment also addressed other complaints under Articles 5 §§ 1 and 5 and 6 § 1, which fell within the Court’s well-established case-law.

In short, the case concerns three Ukrainian men who alleged police ill-treatment; the Court found that the State failed to investigate those allegations effectively and failed to account for their injuries, resulting in Article 3 violations.

In Minyaylo and Others v. Ukraine (ECtHR, Fifth Section, 24 September 2020), three Ukrainian nationals—Anatoliy Minyaylo, Igor Kindra, and Leonid Kharchenko—brought applications (nos. 59356/10, 61038/10, and 59824/12). The case mainly concerned alleged police ill-treatment and the allegedly ineffective investigation of their complaints. The applicants invoked Articles 3 and 13, and also raised other complaints under Articles 5 §§1 and 5 and 6 §1. The Court examined the ill-treatment complaints under Article 3 only.

The facts for each applicant were set out in appended tables. In substance, each applicant alleged that police had ill-treated him and that domestic authorities had failed to investigate properly. The Government contested admissibility only in Minyaylo’s case. It argued that he had not exhausted domestic remedies because he had not appealed his conviction of 24 December 2010. Alternatively, it argued that his complaint was out of time, calculated from the prosecutor’s decision of 15 November 2007 not to institute criminal proceedings into his ill-treatment allegations. The Government also said his complaint was manifestly ill-founded. Minyaylo disagreed.

The Court rejected the non-exhaustion and six-month objections, relying on prior Ukrainian cases including Kaverzin, Buglov, and Zyakun. It found no reason to depart from those findings. On manifest ill-foundedness, the Court noted medical documents confirming Minyaylo’s injuries, found his complaints not entirely without basis, and held that they raised issues requiring merits examination. For Kindra and Kharchenko, the Government made no admissibility objections. The Court declared all Article 3 complaints admissible.

On the merits, the applicants alleged violations of Article 3 under both substantive and procedural limbs. The Government filed no comments on Kindra’s application and contested the others. Applying Bouyid v. Belgium, the Court held that the applicants had raised arguable ill-treatment claims domestically. That triggered an obligation on national authorities to conduct an effective official investigation to establish the origin of the applicants’ injuries and to identify and punish those responsible if the allegations were true.

The documents showed that the domestic investigations did not reflect any serious effort to determine the relevant facts. The Court recalled Kaverzin, where it had found that Ukrainian authorities’ reluctance to ensure prompt and thorough investigation of ill-treatment complaints against police constituted a systemic problem under Article 46. It concluded that the present applications were another example of that failure.

The Court further found that the applicants’ accounts of their alleged ill-treatment were detailed and coherent, and that the investigations—given their numerous shortcomings—did not disprove those allegations. Since the State had an onus to provide a plausible explanation for injuries sustained by persons under police control, the Court concluded that State responsibility for the applicants’ injuries was engaged. Those findings were sufficient to establish that the applicants had been subjected to inhuman and degrading treatment. The Court therefore found violations of Article 3 of the Convention in respect of the alleged police ill-treatment and the ineffective domestic investigations. The judgment was final and was rectified on 20 November 2020.

In *Minyaylo and Others v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 59356/10, 61038/10 and 59824/12), the European Court of Human Rights’ Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 24 September 2020 (rectified on 20 November 2020). The applicants were three Ukrainian nationals: Anatoliy Anatolyevich Minyaylo, Igor Aleksandrovich Kindra and Leonid Oleksiyovych Kharchenko. They lodged applications under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates. The Ukrainian Government was represented by Agent I. Lishchyna.

The case primarily concerned alleged ill-treatment by police and the allegedly ineffective investigation of the applicants’ respective complaints. The applicants also raised other complaints under the Court’s well-established case-law, namely Articles 5 §§ 1 and 5 and Article 6 § 1. Because the applications involved similar subject matter, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment.

The relevant alleged violations centred on Article 3. The applicants claimed they had been ill-treated by police and that their complaints had not been properly investigated, invoking Articles 3 and 13. The Court, as master of the characterisation of the facts, examined the complaints only under Article 3, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

On admissibility, the Government objected only to Mr Minyaylo’s application. It argued that he had failed to exhaust domestic remedies because he had not appealed against his conviction of 24 December 2010. Alternatively, it argued that if no effective remedy existed, his complaint was lodged outside the six-month time-limit, calculated from the prosecutor’s last decision of 15 November 2007 not to institute criminal proceedings into his ill-treatment allegations. The Government also said the complaint was manifestly ill-founded. The Court rejected the non-exhaustion and time-limit objections, relying on prior Ukrainian cases such as *Kaverzin*, *Buglov* and *Zyakun*. It found that medical documents confirming injuries meant the claim was not entirely without basis and required examination on the merits. For Mr Kindra and Mr Kharchenko, the Government filed no admissibility objections under Article 3. The Court declared all Article 3 complaints admissible.

On the merits, the applicants alleged violations of both the substantive and procedural limbs of Article 3. The Government filed no comments for Mr Kindra and contested the remaining applications. Applying general principles from *Bouyid v. Belgium*, the Court found that the applicants had raised arguable ill-treatment claims. Those claims triggered an obligation on national authorities to conduct an effective official investigation to establish the origin of the injuries and to identify and punish those responsible if the allegations were true.

The domestic investigations, however, did not reflect any serious effort to determine the relevant facts; individual details were set out in appended tables. The Court recalled that in *Kaverzin v. Ukraine* it had found a systemic problem under Article 46 concerning authorities’ reluctance to ensure prompt and thorough investigation of ill-treatment complaints against police. It considered the present facts another example of that failure.

The Court also found the applicants’ accounts detailed and coherent. The investigation results, given their numerous shortcomings, did not disprove the allegations. Since the applicants were under police control, the State had an onus to provide a plausible explanation for their injuries (*Bouyid*; *Adnaralov*; *Kulik*; *Yaroshovets*). The Court concluded that State responsibility for the injuries was engaged. These findings sufficed to establish that the applicants had been subjected to inhuman and degrading treatment, in violation of Article 3, and that the investigation was ineffective.

Ukraine* (Applications nos. 59552/11 and 7096/12), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) delivered judgment on 2 July 2020 (rectified on 27 August 2020). The applicants were two Ukrainian nationals. The first, Mykola Mykhaylovych Dmytrenko, born in 1943 and living in Donetsk, lodged his application on 12 September 2011. The second, Mykhaylo Gerasymovych Bezdorozhniy, born in 1936, lodged his application on 29 January 2012. He died in 2015; his son and heir, Yuriy Mikhaylovich Bezdorozhniy, was allowed to continue the proceedings because the property right at issue was transferable to heirs. The Government was represented by its Agent, I. Lishchyna.

Both applicants had the special status of “child of war” under the Children of War Social Protection Act, in force from 1 January 2006. That status applied to persons who were no more than 18 years old on 2 September 1945. Article 6 of the Act entitled them to a special supplement to their pension equal to 30% of the minimum pension.

The applicants brought court proceedings against the Pension Fund of Ukraine, claiming this pension supplement for the period between 2 April and 31 December 2006. By final decisions of 13 May and 18 August 2011, the Higher Administrative Court of Ukraine and the Donetsk Administrative Court of Appeal rejected their claims. The domestic courts found that amendments to the State Budget Act 2006, effective from 2 April 2006, provided that the supplement was to be introduced gradually during 2006 in accordance with a procedure to be elaborated by the Cabinet of Ministers. Because no such procedure had been adopted in 2006, the courts held there was no basis for allowing the claims.

There was also a separate domestic judgment: on 31 December 2010 the Kuybyshevskyy District Court of Donetsk ordered the Pension Fund to calculate and pay the second applicant the supplement for 9 July–31 December 2007 and 22 May 2008–31 December 2010. That judgment became final on 18 August 2011 but remained unenforced. The Strasbourg complaint, however, concerned only the failure to pay the 2006 supplement.

The applicants complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention that the State had failed to pay the pension supplement for the period between 2 April and 31 December 2006, as required by Article 6 of the Children of War Act. The Court gave notice of that complaint to the Government and declared the remainder of the applications inadmissible. The Government argued that the amount claimed, about EUR 159, was negligible, less than EUR 200, and not the applicants’ primary source of income, so there was no significant disadvantage. The Court noted that it was for the Cabinet of Ministers to determine the size of the supplement in 2006, but no relevant decision had been made. The relevant domestic law and practice were set out in *Sukhanov and Ilchenko v. Ukraine*. The applications were joined because of their similar subject matter. The central alleged violation was therefore the State’s failure to pay a statutory pension supplement for the 2006 period after domestic courts rejected the claims because the required Cabinet procedure had never been adopted.

Before the Court, the Government argued that the complaint should be rejected because the amount claimed was negligible—approximately EUR 159 in total—and had not constituted the primary source of income for either applicant. Relying on *Svystun v. Ukraine*, they submitted that the applicants had not suffered a significant disadvantage. The Court noted that under *Sukhanov and Ilchenko v. Ukraine*, it was for the Cabinet of Ministers to determine the size of the pension supplement in 2006, but no relevant decision had been made. The provided excerpt ends at that point and does not set out the final violation finding.

In *Potoroc v. Romania*, the European Court of Human Rights examined the detention of Ioan Potoroc, a Romanian national born in 1953, despite his severe medical condition. He suffered from brain damage after strokes, hemiparesis, prostate problems, impaired hearing, severe psycho-organic syndrome, and depression. He was wheelchair-bound and required permanent assistance and continuous medical care. In 2009, he was convicted of international drug trafficking and sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment.

The applicant alleged that his continued detention and the conditions in which he was held violated Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits inhuman and degrading treatment. The key facts concerned his detention, particularly after his reimprisonment in 2015, and the adequacy of medical care and daily assistance available in prison.

Potoroc had already been imprisoned in 2011. Between February 2011 and August 2012, he spent 350 days out of 529 in prison hospitals. In 2012, a forensic report recommended Colibaşi Prison Hospital, stating that prison medical wings could provide adequate treatment, though it could not guarantee that treatment would actually be provided. The Argeş County Court subsequently interrupted his sentence because of his “deplorable” health, and his release was upheld in 2013. Later medical reports noted that he needed permanent care and supervision and that Colibaşi Prison alone could not provide adequate care, though the National Prison Service hospital network could.

In December 2014, the Bucharest County Court reassessed his health. A report by ten forensic experts concluded that the prison hospital network could provide adequate care, including in a chronic-illness unit, and that he needed a personal assistant. The report found that the criteria for interrupting his sentence were not met. The court accepted that the prison network could provide care and that the prison service had confirmed it could provide a personal assistant. Potoroc was reimprisoned in January 2015 and again in March 2015 after the judgment became final.

During his later detention, he was held in several prisons and prison hospitals, mostly at Mioveni/Colibaşi Prison Hospital for one year and eleven months. The Government stated that he generally had at least 4.22 sq. m of personal space, except for thirteen days in Giurgiu Prison, where he had 3.06 sq. m. The Giurgiu room was not fit for a disabled person, although ramps existed. Prison hospitals were equipped for disabled inmates. Assistance in Colibaşi was provided by a team of inmates rather than an individually allocated assistant; in Jilava, another inmate appointed as his “personal assistant” also helped two other inmates.

In 2016, Potoroc again sought interruption of his sentence. A forensic report said prison healthcare could provide necessary treatment and frequent hospitalisation, and that he needed constant assistance. The Argeş County Court dismissed his application, finding that the need for a personal assistant did not justify interruption because he had benefited from such assistance. He appealed, claiming he had no personal assistant and could not go outside because he was on the first floor. The appeal was dismissed. However, in October 2016, a court allowed his transfer to Colibaşi Prison Hospital, finding his health so precarious that Article 3 was engaged and the prison could not provide all necessary safeguards. He was released in September 2017 after his sentence was quashed following an earlier finding of a fair-trial violation.

The European Court of Human Rights found a substantive violation of Article 3. It held that Romania had failed to provide adequate medical care and assistance during his detention. Domestic courts had relied on medical reports confirming his ability to remain in prison under the impugned conditions, but no adequate measures accommodated his daily assistance needs, despite help from other inmates. The conditions were incompatible with respect for human dignity.

**Summary of *Potoroc v. Romania* (Application no. 37772/17, judgment of 2 June 2020)**

In *Potoroc v. Romania*, the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Romania violated Article 3 of the Convention by continuing to detain a seriously ill and disabled applicant in conditions allegedly incompatible with human dignity.

The applicant, born in 1953, suffered from brain damage following several strokes, hemiparesis, prostate problems, impaired hearing, and severe psycho-organic syndrome comparable to pre-senile dementia. He was wheelchair-bound, needed permanent daily assistance, and required continuous medical care. In 2009, he was convicted of international drug trafficking and sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment.

The applicant was held at Rahova Prison from February 2011. Because the medical wing was on the first floor and lacked ramps, he refused placement there and was held in a regular cell. Between February 2011 and August 2012, he spent 350 out of 529 days in prison hospitals. In November 2011 and March 2012, disability commissions found that he did not require a personal assistant and had no functional deficiency. He was released on health grounds in August 2012, but suffered an ischemic stroke in October 2012. He was reimprisoned in January 2015, briefly released, and then reimprisoned in March 2015 after his sentence became final.

From March 2015 until September 2017, he was held mainly in Mioveni (Colibași) Prison Hospital for one year and eleven months, but also in Rahova, Jilava, Giurgiu, and Colibași prisons. The Government stated that he generally had at least 4.22 sq. m of personal space, except for thirteen days in Giurgiu Prison, where he had 3.06 sq. m. The Giurgiu room was not adapted for disabled persons, although ramps existed. Prison hospitals were said to be equipped for disabled inmates. He received help from other inmates, and in March 2017 another inmate, V.I., was appointed as his “personal assistant,” but V.I. also assisted two other inmates.

The applicant repeatedly sought interruption of his sentence on health grounds. In 2012, the Argeș County Court allowed his release, finding his health “deplorable.” That decision was confirmed in 2013. After a reassessment in 2014, an NIFM report concluded that the prison hospital network could provide adequate care, that he needed a personal assistant, but that the criteria for interrupting his sentence were not met. The domestic courts relied on that report and on the National Prison Service’s confirmation that a personal assistant would be provided. His appeals were dismissed.

A further application in 2016 was also rejected. A medical report again stated that prison healthcare could treat his serious ailments and that he needed constant assistance. The courts found that he had had such assistance since reimprisonment. In September 2016, however, a court allowed his transfer to Colibași Prison Hospital. He was released in September 2017 after his sentence was quashed following an earlier finding of an Article 6 violation; he was acquitted in 2018.

The ECtHR found a substantive violation of Article 3. The key facts were that the applicant was seriously ill, wheelchair-bound, and in need of permanent assistance, yet the domestic courts accepted that he could remain in detention based on medical reports about the prison system’s capacity to provide care. In reality, no adequate measures were taken to accommodate his daily assistance and mobility needs. He depended on other inmates, lacked individual assistance, and faced conditions—including limited access to fresh air and, at least briefly, insufficient personal space—that were incompatible with respect for human dignity. His continued detention for two years and seven months under these conditions amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment.

The applicant, Ioan Potoroc, a Romanian national born in 1953, was convicted in 2009 of international drug trafficking and sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment. He suffered from severe medical conditions, including brain damage after several strokes, hemiparesis, prostate adenoma, impaired hearing, and a severe psycho-organic syndrome comparable to pre-senile dementia. He was confined to a wheelchair and required permanent daily assistance and continuous medical care.

The alleged violation concerned his continued detention and the conditions in which he was held despite his serious illness. He was initially placed in Rahova Prison in February 2011. Although he was sometimes hospitalised, he spent 350 of 529 days between February 2011 and August 2012 in prison hospitals. He refused placement in Rahova’s medical wing because it was on the first floor and lacked ramps, making outdoor access difficult, and was instead placed in a regular cell. In November 2011 a disability commission found he did not require a personal assistant, a conclusion confirmed in March 2012.

In August 2012, in proceedings to interrupt his sentence on health grounds, the Argeş County Court ordered his release, describing his health as “dreadful” and relying on humanitarian considerations. That decision was upheld in September 2013, although with restrictions. He suffered an ischemic stroke after release in October 2012. He was reimprisoned in January 2015, briefly released when the judgment was not final, then reimprisoned on 9 March 2015 after the judgment became final. He remained detained until 20 September 2017.

During that period, he was held mainly in Mioveni (Colibaşi) Prison Hospital for about one year and eleven months, with shorter periods in Rahova Prison, Jilava Prison Hospital, Rahova Prison Hospital, Giurgiu Prison, and Colibaşi Prison. The Government submitted that his personal space was generally at least 4.22 sq. m, except for thirteen days in Giurgiu Prison when it was 3.06 sq. m. In Giurgiu, the room was not adapted for physically disabled persons. Medical assistance was sometimes provided collectively by other inmates; one inmate, V.I., was appointed as his “personal assistant” in 2017 but also assisted two other inmates.

Domestic courts repeatedly relied on medical reports, including NIFM reports in 2006 and 2014 and an NIFM report in April 2016, which concluded that the prison medical network could provide adequate care. In 2014 the Bucharest County Court found that prison hospitals could care for him and that the National Prison Service could provide a personal assistant; the appeal was dismissed in February 2015. A further application to interrupt his sentence in 2016 was dismissed, with the courts finding that his need for assistance did not justify interruption because he allegedly had assistance in detention. In October 2016, however, a court allowed his transfer to Colibaşi Prison Hospital, finding that his precarious health engaged Article 3 and that prison could not provide necessary care. He was released in September 2017 after his sentence was quashed on review following a prior finding of an unfair trial, and acquitted in April 2018.

The European Court of Human Rights found a substantive violation of Article 3. The key facts were the detention for two years and seven months of a seriously ill, wheelchair-bound person; inadequate medical care and daily assistance; domestic courts’ reliance on medical reports confirming his ability to remain in prison under the impugned conditions; and the lack of adequate measures to accommodate his needs, despite help from other inmates. The conditions were incompatible with respect for human dignity.
