In *Bilal Akyıldız v. Turkey* (ECtHR, 2020), the applicant complained under Article 5 § 1 of the Convention that he had been arrested and remanded in custody without reasonable suspicion of having committed an offence.

In 2002, Turkish authorities investigated a series of sexual assaults and attempted abductions of minors in Istanbul, attributed to the so-called “Ümraniye pervert.” On 16 November 2002, following an anonymous call reporting a man resembling the perpetrator’s photofit, gendarmes arrested the applicant in Samandıra. The arrest and search report stated he was arrested on suspicion of attempted child abduction and had been notified of his rights, but it mistakenly indicated he had a criminal record (later corrected). A separate handwritten report claimed he had been arrested during a routine patrol for failing to produce his identity card. That same day, an identification parade was held: one child witness identified the applicant with certainty, while two child victims said he strongly resembled the perpetrator.

DNA testing soon showed the applicant was not responsible for the sexual assaults. When questioned on 18 November, he denied the attempted abductions, noted the DNA exclusion, and declined a lawyer. The gendarmerie commander forwarded the file to the prosecutor, noting the parade had used two gendarmes in civilian clothes and that the victims and witness may have been influenced by press coverage of the “Ümraniye pervert,” identifying the applicant because of his resemblance to the photofit. That same day, a judge ordered the applicant’s pre-trial detention based on the evidence and the seriousness of the alleged offences.

The applicant’s lawyer objected, arguing that the DNA results excluded him from the sexual assaults, that the victims’ accounts were contradictory, that the identification parade was irregular—especially because the applicant had a partially burned face while the others had no distinguishing features—and that the victims had not identified him with certainty. The objection was rejected on 21 November. The applicant was charged on 22 November with attempted abduction of minors. On 11 December, a victim’s father petitioned the court, saying his daughter had been influenced by media coverage and, after seeing the actual suspect on television, was convinced the applicant was not the perpetrator. On 13 December, the victims unequivocally stated the applicant was not the perpetrator. He was acquitted and released after 27 days in detention.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged not only the absence of reasonable suspicion but also that the gendarmes lacked competence, the arrest reports were irregular, the identification parades were improper, he was not informed of charges, lacked access to a lawyer, could not notify his family, and was publicly exposed as the “Ümraniye pervert.” Domestic compensation proceedings under Act No. 466 awarded him small sums for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage, and an administrative court later awarded TRY 80,000 for breach of confidentiality.

The ECtHR rejected the complaints about the lawfulness of the deprivation of liberty—competence, clerical error, the false handwritten report, and the identification parade—as manifestly ill-founded. It found the applicant remained a “victim” despite the compensation, because Act No. 466 compensation followed automatically from acquittal and did not involve a finding that his detention violated Article 5. On the central complaint, the Court held that the arrest and pre-trial detention were supported by sufficient evidence at the time: the applicant resembled the photofit and had been identified by two victims and a witness during the parade. His subsequent acquittal and the victims’ retraction did not retroactively undermine the reasonable suspicion existing at the time of detention. There was therefore no violation of Article 5 § 1.

**Case: Bilal Akyıldız v. Turkey (Application no. 36897/07), ECtHR, 15 September 2020**

The case concerned the arrest and pre-trial detention of Bilal Akyıldız in Istanbul in 2002 on suspicion of a series of sexual assaults and attempted abductions of minors, before his acquittal 27 days later. The applicant complained mainly under Article 5 § 1 of the Convention that there had been no reasonable suspicion that he had committed an offence.

In 2002, several children were sexually assaulted in Ümraniye, Istanbul, and two attempted child abductions occurred in Samandıra on 25 October and 6 November 2002. On 16 November 2002, following an anonymous call reporting a person resembling the photofit of the alleged perpetrator, gendarmes arrested the applicant in Samandıra because of that resemblance. The official arrest and search report, signed by the applicant, stated that he was arrested on suspicion of attempted child abduction. A separate handwritten report said he had been arrested during a routine patrol for failing to produce his identity card.

On the same day, an identification parade was held. Child victims and a child witness identified the applicant as the perpetrator of the attempted abductions. The witness identified him with certainty; the two victims said he strongly resembled the perpetrator. DNA testing later showed that the applicant was not responsible for the sexual assaults. When questioned on 18 November, he acknowledged the resemblance but denied the attempted abductions and pointed to the DNA result. The gendarmerie commander sent the file to the public prosecutor, noting that the applicant had no criminal record and that the victims, witness and families may have been influenced by press reports about the “Ümraniye pervert” and identified the applicant because of his resemblance to the photofit.

On 18 November 2002, the Kartal Criminal Court judge ordered the applicant’s pre-trial detention in light of the evidence and the nature and seriousness of the alleged offences. Counsel objected, arguing that DNA excluded him, that witness descriptions were contradictory, that the identification parade was irregular because the applicant was presented alongside two men with no distinguishing features while his face was partially burned, and that the victims had not identified him with certainty. The objection was rejected. The applicant was charged on 22 November 2002.

On 11 December 2002, the father of one victim stated that his daughter had been influenced by media coverage and that, after seeing another person arrested on television, they believed the applicant was not the perpetrator. On 13 December 2002, the victims unequivocally stated in court that the applicant was not the perpetrator. The Assize Court acquitted him. He had spent 27 days in detention.

The applicant alleged that his arrest and detention lacked reasonable suspicion, that the gendarmes lacked competence, that the reports were irregular, and that the identification parades were improper. The Government argued non-exhaustion and that compensation under Act No. 466 removed his victim status. The European Court of Human Rights rejected those objections, finding that the compensation was an automatic consequence of acquittal and did not recognise an Article 5 violation.

On lawfulness, the Court found the gendarmes’ alleged lack of competence unsubstantiated, the criminal-record error clerical and rectified, and the handwritten report not a gross or obvious irregularity. The official arrest report was proper, and no procedural invalidity in the identification parade was established. Those complaints were rejected as manifestly ill-founded.

On reasonable suspicion, the Court found no violation of Article 5 § 1. At the time of arrest and initial detention, there was sufficient evidence to persuade a neutral observer: the applicant resembled the photofit, was identified by two victims and a witness, and a judge reviewed the file. The later acquittal, based on the victims’ retraction after media influence and another arrest, did not retroactively eliminate the reasonable suspicion existing at the time of detention.

In *Bilal Akyıldız v. Turkey* (ECtHR, Second Section, 15 September 2020), the applicant complained under Article 5 § 1 that his arrest and pre-trial detention lacked any reasonable suspicion that he had committed an offence. In 2002, several children were sexually assaulted in Ümraniye, Istanbul, and there were two attempted child abductions in Samandıra. On 16 November 2002, after an anonymous caller reported seeing someone resembling the photofit of the suspected perpetrator, gendarmes arrested the applicant in Samandıra because of that resemblance. The arrest report stated he was suspected of attempted child abduction and that his rights had been notified, but it wrongly indicated that he had a criminal record. A separate handwritten report claimed he had been detained during a routine patrol for failing to produce his identity card.

On the same day, an identification parade was held. Two child victims and a child witness identified the applicant as the perpetrator of the attempted abductions; the witness was certain, while the victims said he strongly resembled the perpetrator. A DNA test taken in custody excluded him as the perpetrator of the sexual assaults. On 18 November, when questioned, the applicant acknowledged his resemblance to the photofit but denied the attempted abductions and pointed to the DNA result. He had no criminal record and declined a lawyer. The gendarmerie commander sent the file to the public prosecutor, noting the DNA exclusion and stating that the victims, witness and families may have been influenced by press coverage of the “Ümraniye pervert” and had identified the applicant because of his resemblance to the photofit.

That same day, a judge ordered the applicant’s pre-trial detention based on the evidence and the seriousness of the alleged offences. His lawyer objected, arguing that the DNA test excluded him, the victims’ descriptions were contradictory, the identification parade was irregular, and the victims had not identified him with certainty. The objection was rejected. The applicant was charged with attempted abduction of minors. On 11 December 2002, the father of one victim stated that his daughter had been influenced by media coverage and, after seeing the actual suspect on television, no longer believed the applicant was the perpetrator. At a hearing on 13 December 2002, the victims unequivocally stated that the applicant was not the perpetrator. The court acquitted him; he had been detained for 27 days.

Subsequently, the public prosecutor investigated the applicant’s complaints but found no ill-treatment or irregularities and decided not to prosecute. Three gendarmes were charged with abuse of authority over the inaccurate handwritten report, but the proceedings became time-barred. Under Act No. 466, the applicant received compensation for his detention, including TRY 697 for pecuniary damage and TRY 1,000 for non-pecuniary damage, with legal fees later increased; the total paid was TRY 4,443. In separate administrative proceedings, he was eventually awarded TRY 80,000 for non-pecuniary damage caused by breach of confidentiality and exposure to the press.

Before the ECtHR, the Government argued non-exhaustion and loss of victim status, but the Court rejected those objections. On the lawfulness complaints, the Court found no substantiation that the gendarmes lacked jurisdiction, the criminal-record error was a clerical mistake that was corrected, the inaccurate handwritten report was not a “gross or obvious irregularity” rendering detention unlawful, and no procedural irregularity in the identification parade was established. Regarding reasonable suspicion, the Court held that the applicant’s physical resemblance to the photofit and the identification by two victims and a witness provided sufficient evidence at the time to persuade a neutral observer that he may have committed the attempted abductions. His later acquittal, after the victims retracted, did not retroactively negate that reasonable suspicion. There was therefore no violation of Article 5 § 1.

In *Arkania v. Georgia* (Application no. 2625/12), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Article 3, and initially Article 5, that Georgian police ill-treated Lasha Arkania during an unrecorded detention in order to extract a confession, and that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation.

According to official records, Arkania was arrested on 15 June 2011 at 3 a.m. in Muzhava, Tsalenjikha district, on suspicion of unlawful firearm possession. The arrest and search report noted scratches on his face and head, which he allegedly said predated arrest. He was taken to Jvari police department and questioned between 4:55 and 5:25 a.m. without a lawyer, during which he confessed to firearms and drug offences. Upon admission to Zugdidi temporary detention centre, bruises, reddish spots on his back and behind his ears, and a haematoma on his left eye were recorded. He signed a report stating the injuries predated arrest and that he had no complaints. On 16 June, an ambulance was called because his condition worsened; a doctor diagnosed a post-concussion condition. He was then formally charged with arms and drug offences.

Arkania later complained to the prosecutor that he had actually been arrested on 14 June around 10 p.m. by plain-clothes officers, ill-treated, and forced through physical and psychological duress to sign a self-incriminating statement. He claimed he was taken to an abandoned factory, beaten with a rifle butt, then taken to Jvari police where the ill-treatment continued; he was threatened with rape and lost consciousness. He identified or claimed he could identify several alleged perpetrators, including investigator I.A., who allegedly beat him and forced the confession.

Public Defender representatives documented injuries, including alleged cigarette burns under his armpits. Forensic examinations found multiple haematomas and scars, possibly dating to 15 June, and later scars under both armpits. He was diagnosed with post-concussion syndrome and post-traumatic stress disorder. Domestic courts ordered pre-trial detention on 17 June 2011, finding no procedural irregularities, but did not examine his ill-treatment allegations. He was convicted on 23 August 2011 and sentenced to thirteen years’ imprisonment; appeals were unsuccessful. He was released in January 2013 under an amnesty.

An investigation into the alleged ill-treatment was opened only on 17 August 2011 for aggravated torture. Arkania was questioned repeatedly, identified nine police officers in photo identification procedures in February 2013, and was granted victim status in May 2013. Several police officers denied the allegations, but some duty officers and other witnesses said they saw him brought to Jvari police handcuffed, injured, and/or beaten. His lawyer’s requests for identification procedures and further witness questioning were dismissed, and progress updates were vague. The proceedings remained ongoing.

The Government denied ill-treatment beyond reasonable doubt, relying on official reports that the injuries predated arrest, the absence of an immediate complaint or medical request, allegedly contradictory statements, inconclusive medical evidence, and possible self-harm. It argued the investigation began promptly, all relevant steps were taken, and the ongoing investigation complied with Article 3. Arkania maintained that the ill-treatment was intended to extract a confession and that the investigation never genuinely sought to identify and punish those responsible. The Court declared the Article 3 complaint admissible.

**Case: Arkania v. Georgia (Application no. 2625/12), European Court of Human Rights, 25 June 2020.**  
The applicant, Lasha Arkania, a Georgian national, complained under Article 3 that police ill-treated him during an initial unrecorded detention lasting four to five hours in order to extract a confession, and that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into that ill-treatment.

According to the official record, Arkania was arrested on 15 June 2011 at 3 a.m. in Muzhava, Tsalenjikha district, on suspicion of unlawful firearm possession. A search allegedly found a Kalashnikov rifle, nineteen cartridges, and a paper bag containing a greyish substance. The detention and search report noted scratches on his face and head; Arkania said these had been sustained before arrest. He was taken to the Jvari police department. Between 4:55 and 5:25 a.m., while questioned by investigator I.A. without a lawyer, he pleaded guilty to unlawful possession of firearms and drugs. On transfer to the Zugdidi temporary detention centre, a visual examination noted bruises and reddish spots on his back and behind his ears and a haematoma on his left eye. The report, signed by Arkania, stated that the injuries predated arrest and that he had no complaints. On 16 June, an ambulance was called after his condition worsened; the doctor diagnosed a post-concussion condition. He was formally charged with arms and drug offences. He then complained to the Zugdidi district prosecutor that he had actually been arrested on 14 June around 10 p.m. by several police officers who ill-treated him and forced him, through physical and psychological duress, to sign a self-incriminating statement. He protested his innocence and requested a medical examination.

Arkania’s account alleged that on 14 June 2011, after a phone call, he went to meet an acquaintance with his neighbour R.Kh. and friend K.A. Plainclothes police forced him into a car, took him to an abandoned factory in Tchale, and beat him with a rifle butt. He was then taken to the Jvari police department, where the ill-treatment continued; he was threatened with rape and lost consciousness several times. He identified alleged perpetrators, including S.A., head of the Jvari police, R.K. from the Tsalenjikha prosecutor’s office, police officer G.S., and investigator I.A., whom he accused of beating him and forcing a confession. Public Defender’s Office reports documented his injuries. Later reports noted cigarette burns under both armpits, which he attributed to the Jvari police chief and two officers, saying he had not reported them earlier because of threats against his family.

A criminal investigation into aggravated torture was opened on 17 August 2011. Forensic examinations found multiple haematomas and scars dating to 15 June 2011, and later scars under the armpits. A psychiatric examination diagnosed post-concussion syndrome and post-traumatic stress disorder. Witnesses R.Kh. and K.A. confirmed he was forced into a car around 10–11 p.m. Several police officers testified that they saw Arkania brought handcuffed to the Jvari police department with facial injuries and then beaten. Other officers denied the allegations, and detention-centre staff said he made no complaints. In February 2013, photo identification procedures led Arkania to identify numerous officers. He was granted victim status in May 2013, but the investigation remained ongoing. In his criminal trial, he was convicted in August 2011 and sentenced to thirteen years’ imprisonment; appeals were unsuccessful, though he was released in January 2013 under an amnesty. The ECtHR declared his Article 3 complaint admissible. The Government disputed the allegations, arguing the injuries were pre-existing, the medical evidence inconclusive, his statements contradictory, and the investigation compliant.

In *Arkania v. Georgia* (Application no. 2625/12, judgment of 25 June 2020), the applicant, Lasha Arkania, alleged that Georgian police ill-treated him during an initial unrecorded detention lasting four to five hours and that authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation, contrary to Article 3 of the Convention; Article 5 was also initially invoked.

According to official records, the applicant was arrested on 15 June 2011 at 3 a.m. in Muzhava, Tsalenjikha district, on suspicion of unlawful possession of firearms. A search allegedly found a Kalashnikov rifle, cartridges and a grey substance. The detention report noted scratches on his face and head, which he reportedly said predated arrest. He was taken to the Jvari police department and, between 4:55 and 5:25 a.m., questioned without a lawyer; he pleaded guilty to firearms and drug offences. On admission to the Zugdidi temporary detention centre, staff noted bruises, red spots on his back and behind his ears, and a haematoma on his left eye. A report signed by him stated the injuries were pre-arrest and that he had no complaints. The next day, an ambulance was called due to deterioration; he was diagnosed with post-concussion condition.

The applicant later claimed his real arrest occurred on 14 June 2011 around 10 p.m., when several police officers seized him, ill-treated him and forced him to confess. A Public Defender’s Office report described him being lured to a meeting, forced into a car, taken to an abandoned factory in Tchale, beaten with a rifle butt, then taken to Jvari police department where beatings continued, including threats of rape and loss of consciousness. He identified the head of Jvari police, S.A., a prosecutor’s employee, R.K., and officer G.S., and said beatings occurred in the presence of investigator I.A.

Medical examinations found multiple haematomas and minor scars possibly dating to 15 June 2011, later scars under both armpits alleged to be cigarette burns, and diagnoses of post-concussion syndrome and post-traumatic stress disorder. Witnesses partially corroborated his account: neighbour R.Kh. and friend K.A. described his forcible detention by car between 10 and 11 p.m.; police officers T.K., L.P. and L.G. described him being brought handcuffed around 11:30 p.m. with visible facial injuries, blood and torn clothes, and being beaten. His first defence lawyer also saw injuries. Detention-centre staff recalled injuries but said he did not complain and claimed they predated arrest. In 2013, photo identification procedures led him to identify several officers.

An investigation into aggravated torture opened on 17 August 2011. The applicant was questioned repeatedly, eventually granted victim status on 5 May 2013, but many investigative requests were dismissed and the investigation remained ongoing. At trial, he repeated the ill-treatment allegations, but was convicted on 23 August 2011 and sentenced to thirteen years; appeals failed, and he was released in January 2013 under an amnesty. The domestic courts relied on official records and did not examine his ill-treatment claims.

The Government disputed the allegations, arguing injuries predated arrest, medical evidence was inconclusive, his accounts were contradictory, and the investigation was prompt and thorough. The Court declared the Article 3 complaint admissible.

**Chernika v. Ukraine (Application no. 53791/11)**

The applicant, Mykhaylo Chernika, a former police investigator, was convicted in Ukraine of stealing opium seized as evidence in a case he was investigating, diluting the remaining liquid, and soliciting help to sell the stolen drugs on the black market. The prosecution's case relied heavily on three key witnesses: N.Sh., who allegedly facilitated the drug transfer; V.G., who transported the drugs to Crimea; and I.S., who was found with the opium.

During the pre-trial investigation, all three witnesses gave statements implicating the applicant, and confrontations were held between them and the applicant. However, the applicant and his lawyers did not have access to the investigation file at that stage. At the original trial before Judge V.D., N.Sh. affirmed her pre-trial statement and was examined. V.G. and I.S. failed to appear despite repeated summons; the Security Service could not locate them. The trial court nevertheless read out their pre-trial statements and convicted the applicant.

On appeal, the Volyn Regional Court of Appeal quashed the conviction because the trial court had read V.G.'s statement without information as to why he failed to appear. The case was remitted for retrial before a different judge (Judge V.B.).

At the retrial, none of the three key witnesses appeared. N.Sh. could not be found. V.G. and I.S. were reported to be seriously ill: V.G. was hospitalised, and I.S. had infectious tuberculosis; their health reportedly prevented them from travelling from Crimea to Lutsk. The trial court ordered the Security Service to locate the witnesses, but they remained unavailable.

The retrial court relied on the pre-trial statements of N.Sh., V.G., and I.S., finding them reliable because they corroborated each other and were confirmed during pre-trial confrontations with the applicant, who had been able to examine them and put questions. The court also cited testimony from other witnesses who knew the applicant and N.Sh., as well as documentary and expert evidence regarding the opium. The applicant was convicted again and sentenced to eight years' imprisonment. The Court of Appeal and Supreme Court upheld the conviction.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) that the proceedings were unfair because the domestic courts admitted statements from three witnesses who were not examined at the retrial: N.Sh. had only been examined at the original trial, and V.G. and I.S. never appeared before any trial court. The Court found that the conviction was based decisively on the untested evidence of these absent witnesses, that there were no good reasons for the non-attendance of at least one of them, and that there were insufficient counterbalancing safeguards—particularly because the new trial judge had not heard the witnesses directly and had to rely on transcripts. The overall fairness of the proceedings was therefore impaired, violating the applicant's rights under Article 6.

**Case of Chernika v. Ukraine** (Application no. 53791/11, judgment of 12 March 2020) concerned the fairness of criminal proceedings under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention. The applicant, a former Ukrainian police investigator, was convicted of stealing opium that had been seized as evidence in another case, diluting the remaining liquid, and arranging through his friend N.Sh. for V.G. and I.S. to transport the opium to Crimea for sale. The prosecution’s case rested heavily on pre-trial statements made by N.Sh., V.G., and I.S.

During the pre-trial investigation, confrontations were held between the applicant and these three witnesses. However, the applicant and his lawyers did not at that stage have access to the investigation file. The applicant later argued that this prevented the confrontations from being an effective substitute for cross-examination at trial, because he could not fully test the witnesses’ statements against the case material.

At the first trial before Judge V.D., N.Sh. appeared and affirmed her pre-trial statement. V.G. and I.S. were repeatedly summoned but failed to appear, and the Security Service could not locate them. The court read out their pre-trial statements and convicted the applicant on 26 August 2008. On appeal, the Volyn Regional Court of Appeal quashed the conviction because the trial court had read V.G.’s statement without knowing the reasons for his absence. The case was remitted for retrial before a different judge.

At the retrial before Judge V.B., none of the three key witnesses appeared. V.G. and I.S. were reported to be seriously ill—V.G. hospitalised and I.S. suffering from infectious tuberculosis—and unable to travel from Crimea to Lutsk. No explanation was provided for N.Sh.’s absence; she could not be found. The retrial court again relied on the pre-trial statements of N.Sh., V.G., and I.S., finding them reliable and corroborated by other witnesses such as Y.G., Z., O.O., and police officer O.G., as well as documentary and expert evidence. However, those other witnesses largely testified about the applicant’s relationship with N.Sh. or overheard conversations; they did not directly establish the alleged drug transfer. On 11 December 2009 the applicant was convicted again and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. Appeals were dismissed, and the Supreme Court rejected a further appeal in 2011.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained that the domestic courts had admitted the statements of N.Sh., V.G., and I.S. even though N.Sh. had been examined only at the original trial, not at the retrial before the new judge, and V.G. and I.S. had never appeared before any trial court. He argued that the pre-trial confrontations were insufficient because he lacked access to the file at that time. The Government contended that the conviction rested on a wide range of evidence and that the applicant had confronted the three witnesses during the investigation.

The Court found a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d). The conviction on retrial was decisively based on testimony by absent witnesses. There was no good reason for at least one key witness’s non-attendance at the retrial, and there were no particularly strong safeguards to ensure that the new judge properly understood the absent witnesses’ evidence. Although the applicant had confronted the witnesses pre-trial, and N.Sh. had been cross-examined at the first trial, those safeguards did not compensate for the handicaps at the retrial. Overall, the proceedings were unfair.

**CASE OF CHERNIKA v. UKRAINE** (Application no. 53791/11) concerned a Ukrainian former police investigator, Mykhaylo Chernika, convicted of stealing opium seized as evidence in a case he investigated, diluting the remainder, and arranging for the stolen opium to be sold through his friend N.Sh. and two men from Crimea, V.G. and I.S. The prosecution’s case rested significantly on statements made by N.Sh., V.G., and I.S. during the pre-trial investigation. Confrontations between these witnesses and Chernika took place pre-trial, but at that time neither he nor his lawyers had access to the investigation file. He later argued that this limited his ability to challenge their evidence effectively.

At the first trial before Judge V.D., N.Sh. appeared and affirmed her pre-trial statement. V.G. and I.S. were repeatedly summoned but failed to appear; the Security Service could not locate them. The trial court nevertheless read out their pre-trial statements and convicted Chernika, sentencing him to eight years’ imprisonment. On appeal, the Volyn Regional Court of Appeal quashed the conviction because the trial court had read V.G.’s statement without information about the reason for his latest non-attendance. The case was remitted for retrial before a different judge.

At the retrial before Judge V.B., all three key witnesses—N.Sh., V.G., and I.S.—were repeatedly summoned but did not appear. V.G. and I.S. were shown to be seriously ill: V.G. had been hospitalised and I.S. had infectious tuberculosis; their health prevented travel from Crimea to Lutsk. No explanation was provided for N.Sh.’s absence, and she could not be found. The retrial court again convicted Chernika, relying essentially on the same evidence, particularly the pre-trial statements of N.Sh., V.G., and I.S. It reasoned that those statements were confirmed by the pre-trial confrontations, where Chernika had been able to question them, and found no breach of defence rights or the principle of immediacy. Other witnesses—Y.G., Z., O.O., and O.G.—gave corroborating evidence

In *Čivinskaitė v. Lithuania*, the applicant was a Deputy Chief Prosecutor at the Kaunas City District Prosecutor’s Office. She was disciplined over her role in supervising a high-profile pre-trial investigation into allegations that a minor had been sexually abused. The case attracted intense public, political and media attention, especially after related deaths and the emergence of serious investigative failures.

In January 2009, after a review identified shortcomings, the Kaunas Regional Prosecutor’s Office took over the investigation and said it should be entrusted to a qualified prosecutor. The Chief Prosecutor of the Kaunas City District Prosecutor’s Office instructed the applicant to entrust the investigation to prosecutor G.R.; the applicant did so. From late January to June 2009, G.R. conducted the investigation under the applicant’s supervision. In February 2009, the applicant partly allowed suspect A.Ū.’s complaint against G.R.’s refusal to grant him access to the investigation file. A later inquiry found that the police and G.R. had failed to act promptly and thoroughly, causing loss of evidence. It also blamed the applicant for entrusting the case to G.R. despite doubts about G.R.’s competence, failing to properly supervise or instruct her, improperly handling A.Ū.’s access complaint instead of directing it to a pre-trial judge, and granting access contrary to relevant recommendations. Disciplinary proceedings found that the applicant had committed disciplinary offences and recommended demotion. On 30 October 2009, the Prosecutor General ordered her demotion, and she was transferred to a lower prosecutor post.

A parallel parliamentary inquiry was conducted by the Seimas Legal Affairs Committee. Its January 2010 report found the investigation incompetent, criticised the Kaunas City District Prosecutor’s Office, and referred to responsible officials including the Deputy Chief Prosecutor. The Seimas endorsed the findings and concluded that the Prosecutor General and various prosecutors had failed to perform their duties. The President publicly demanded personal accountability and harsher decisions against those responsible. The media extensively covered the “paedophilia scandal” and the disciplinary outcomes, sometimes reporting proposed penalties before final decisions. The applicant argued that her demotion was not genuinely based on her performance but was influenced by political statements and media pressure.

She challenged the demotion before the administrative courts. She alleged that the penalty was disproportionate and that the proceedings were unfair because of political and media interference. In June 2010, the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court dismissed her complaint. It overturned some findings but upheld others, including that she had failed to properly supervise G.R. and had overstepped her remit regarding the suspect’s access to the file. It found demotion proportionate. The court did not address her complaint about political statements and media coverage. In October 2011, the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed her appeal, also without commenting on those interference allegations.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 6 §§1 and 2 that the disciplinary proceedings were unfair because the parliamentary inquiry, public statements by high-ranking politicians, and extensive media coverage had prejudged her guilt and compromised the impartiality of the administrative courts. The ECtHR held that Article 6 §1 was applicable under its civil head, but Article 6 §2 was inapplicable. It found no violation: the parliamentary inquiry, political statements, and media coverage did not compromise the administrative courts’ independence or impartiality, and the domestic courts’ failure to explicitly address her interference argument did not render the proceedings, taken as a whole, unfair.

In *Čivinskaitė v. Lithuania* (no. 21218/12), the applicant was a Lithuanian prosecutor and Deputy Chief Prosecutor of the Kaunas City District Prosecutor’s Office. The case arose from a high-profile pre-trial investigation into alleged sexual abuse of a minor. In January 2009, after earlier shortcomings, the Kaunas Regional Prosecutor’s Office took over the investigation and directed that it be assigned to a qualified prosecutor. The Chief Prosecutor instructed Čivinskaitė to entrust the investigation to prosecutor G.R.; she did so and supervised G.R. from January to June 2009. During this period, G.R. dismissed a suspect’s request for access to the case file; on appeal, Čivinskaitė partly granted the suspect access.

In October 2009, a Prosecutor General’s Office inquiry found serious shortcomings throughout the investigation. It criticized G.R. for poor supervision and Čivinskaitė for failing to properly supervise G.R., not giving instructions, and wrongly handling the suspect’s access complaint. Disciplinary proceedings followed. The Prosecutor General’s Office concluded that Čivinskaitė had committed disciplinary offences, harmed the prosecutor office’s reputation, and recommended demotion. The Prosecutor General ordered her demotion, and she was transferred to a lower prosecutor post.

In parallel, the Lithuanian Parliament conducted a parliamentary inquiry into the investigation’s handling. Its January 2010 report endorsed the disciplinary findings, criticized the Kaunas prosecution office, and stated that responsible prosecutors included Čivinskaitė. The Seimas adopted a resolution finding that prosecutors who conducted or supervised the investigation had failed to perform their functions. High-ranking politicians, including the President, publicly demanded accountability and harsher decisions. Media coverage was extensive and included statements about the applicant’s demotion and the alleged failings.

Čivinskaitė challenged the demotion before administrative courts. She argued the penalty was disproportionate and that the proceedings were unfair because of political and media interference: the parliamentary inquiry, public statements by politicians, and extensive press coverage had prejudged her case. The Vilnius Regional Administrative Court partly annulled some findings but upheld the core findings that she failed to supervise the investigation and improperly allowed access to the file; it found demotion proportionate. It did not address her political/media interference complaint. The Supreme Administrative Court dismissed her appeal, also without addressing those complaints. Later reopening requests were refused.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Čivinskaitė complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 that the disciplinary proceedings were unfair. The Court held that Article 6 § 1 applied under its civil head, but Article 6 § 2 did not. It examined whether the administrative courts’ independence and impartiality were compromised by the parliamentary inquiry, politicians’ statements, or media coverage. The Court found no such compromise. Although the domestic courts had not explicitly addressed her political/media interference argument, that omission did not make the proceedings, taken as a whole, unfair. The alleged Article 6 violation was therefore not established.
001-205538:
In *Haziyev and Others v. Azerbaijan* (ECtHR, 5 November 2020, Applications nos. 3650/12 and four others), five Azerbaijani nationals complained mainly under Article 3 that they had been ill-treated by police or security officials and that the authorities failed to investigate effectively. The first applicant also complained under Article 10; the second under Articles 5 and 8.

The first applicant, a journalist for the opposition newspaper *Azadlig*, was detained before an unauthorized Baku protest on 15 May 2010 and given seven days’ administrative detention. On 17 May 2010, at the Binagadi district police detention centre, a warder allegedly took him to a cell where two plainclothes men questioned him about critical articles on the President, threatened him, pushed him against a wall, struck him 10–15 times, beat his legs, and forced him to stand spread-eagled until he fainted. His complaints led to repeated refusals to open a criminal case. Investigators questioned only detention officers who denied the beating, not cellmates who saw his condition. Courts upheld the refusals, citing the absence of complaint in his departure record. He also alleged a violation of freedom of expression.

The second applicant, charged with hooliganism, was arrested at home on 23 March 2011 while sick with a high fever. Eight plainclothes officers allegedly demanded a bribe, insulted and hit him, and took him to the police station in underclothes without shoes. There he was allegedly handcuffed, beaten, his head hit against a wall, and denied medicine, water, a phone call, and a lawyer. Medical evidence noted a head injury and later hospital treatment for acute asthenoneurotic syndrome caused by a closed head injury; a forensic report found only wrist injuries from handcuffs. The refusal to prosecute relied on six police officers and did not question his wife or adequately address his medical evidence. He also complained under Article 5 about unlawful detention and lack of effective review, and under Article 8 about home intrusion.

The third applicant, arrested for suspected theft in September 2012, alleged three officers beat him in a police station room to extract testimony: they made him sit with legs outstretched, placed a chair over his legs, beat his soles with a rubber truncheon, punched him, threatened rape with the truncheon, and continued beating him. His lawyer was initially denied access. When later seen, injuries including haematomas on his soles were observed, and a judge was asked to order an examination. A delayed forensic examination found only a pigmentation spot on his thigh. The refusal relied on the accused officers and limited forensic findings; courts upheld it.

The fourth applicant, a NIDA activist, alleged police/MNS ill-treatment during the January–March 2013 protests: beating on 11 January, punches and dragging on 7 March, forced self-incriminating statements, and on 14 March, after retracting them, being handcuffed, slapped, punched, kicked, and beaten with truncheons, causing limping and temporary hearing damage. Because injuries healed and he lacked access to family and a lawyer, he declined forensic examination. The refusal relied on absence of injuries and officers’ denials.

The fifth applicant, an opposition activist, was stopped on 11 August 2014 by plainclothes narcotics/police officers, allegedly beaten, handcuffed, and had drugs planted on him. At the Sabirabad police station he was allegedly beaten with a truncheon on his soles, back, legs, and thigh for about an hour to force a confession. A detention-centre record noted a large violet thigh bruise and his statement that police violence caused it. A later forensic report found no injury; the refusal relied on police testimony and that report; courts upheld it.

Commonly, the applicants alleged cursory investigations: reliance on accused officers, failure to secure CCTV, question witnesses or cellmates, conduct timely forensic examinations, or address documented injuries.

Haziyev and Others v. Azerbaijan (ECtHR, 5 November 2020) concerns five Azerbaijani applicants who complained mainly under Article 3 that they had been ill-treated in police custody and that domestic authorities failed to investigate effectively. The first applicant also relied on Article 10; the second also complained under Articles 5 and 8.

The first applicant, a journalist for the opposition newspaper Azadlig, was detained in May 2010 before an opposition protest and given seven days’ administrative detention. He alleged that on 17 May 2010, at the Binagadi police detention centre, a warder took him to a cell where two plainclothes men questioned him about his critical articles on the President, threatened him, pushed him against a wall and beat him repeatedly, including on his legs. They allegedly forced him to stand spread-eagled until he fainted. His complaints led to a decision not to open a criminal case, later annulled for lack of thoroughness but then effectively restored. Investigators relied on officers’ denials, failed to question his cellmates or check CCTV, and the courts upheld the refusal. He also alleged a violation of his freedom of expression.

The second applicant was arrested at home in March 2011 in a hooliganism case while ill with a high fever. He alleged that eight plainclothes officers demanded he either accompany them or pay a bribe, insulted and hit him, and took him half-dressed to the police station. There, he claimed, he was handcuffed, beaten, had his head struck against a wall, and was denied medicine, water, a phone call and a lawyer. He complained of unlawful detention without a court order, no prior summons, no risk of absconding, and unlawful intrusion into his home. A forensic report found only wrist injuries from handcuffing. The prosecutor refused a criminal case based on six officers’ testimony. He also complained of inadequate detention review under Article 5 and breach of private life/home under Article 8.

The third applicant was arrested in September 2012 on theft suspicion. He alleged that three officers beat him in a police station room, made him stretch out his legs, sat on a chair over them, struck the soles of his feet with a rubber truncheon to extract testimony, punched him to the ground, threatened to rape him with the truncheon, and continued beating him. His lawyer was allegedly denied access, and medical evidence was delayed. A later forensic examination found only an ambiguous thigh mark. The prosecution refused a case relying on that report and police denials, and the courts upheld the decision.

The fourth applicant, a NIDA activist, alleged ill-treatment in January and March 2013. He claimed police punched, kicked and beat him with a truncheon before a protest; later, MNS officers dragged him into a car, punched him, forced him to incriminate himself and NIDA under threats, and after he retracted his testimony handcuffed and beat him, causing limping, ear pain and hearing damage. The prosecutor refused a case based on absence of injuries and police denials; courts dismissed his complaints.

The fifth applicant, an opposition activist, was stopped in August 2014. He alleged plainclothes officers dragged him from a car, beat him, handcuffed him, and planted narcotics on him before a search. At the police station, he was allegedly beaten for about an hour with a truncheon on his soles, back, legs and thigh to force a confession. A detention-centre medical record noted a large violet bruise on his thigh and his statement that police caused it. A later forensic report found no injury, and the prosecutor refused a case based mainly on police testimony. Courts dismissed his complaints.

Across the applications, the key alleged violations were ill-treatment and ineffective investigations relying predominantly on police denials, delayed or inconclusive medical evidence, failure to question witnesses or obtain CCTV, and obstacles to legal access.

**Haziyev and Others v. Azerbaijan** (Apps. nos. 3650/12 and 4 others) concerns five Azerbaijani nationals who alleged ill-treatment and ineffective domestic investigations, mainly under Article 3 ECHR. The first applicant also alleged an Article 10 violation; the second also alleged breaches of Articles 5 and 8.

The **first applicant, Seymur Haziyev**, was a journalist for the opposition newspaper *Azadlig*. He was detained on 15 May 2010, hours before an unauthorised opposition protest in Baku, and sentenced to seven days’ administrative detention. On 17 May 2010, at the Binagadi district police detention centre, he was allegedly taken to another cell, where two unidentified plainclothes men questioned him about his critical articles on the President, threatened him, pushed him against a wall, beat him ten to fifteen times, and forced him to stand with legs spread until he fainted. His complaints led to repeated decisions refusing criminal proceedings, then annulment and further refusals. Investigators relied on officers’ denials and allegedly failed to question cellmates or examine transfer/security records.

The **second applicant, Magrub Badalli**, faced hooliganism proceedings. He was arrested at home on 23 March 2011 while ill with fever. Eight plainclothes officers allegedly demanded a bribe, insulted and hit him, and took him to the station in underclothes and without shoes. At the police station he was allegedly handcuffed, beaten, had his head struck against a wall, and was denied medicine, water, a lawyer, and a phone call. Medical evidence noted wrist injuries from handcuffs; he later received hospital treatment for acute asthenoneurotic syndrome caused by a closed head injury. The refusal to open a case relied on six police officers and found the arrest lawful.

The **third applicant, Abdulla Yolbarsov**, was arrested in September 2012 on theft suspicion. He alleged that three officers beat him in officer A.M.’s room, made him sit with legs outstretched, beat the soles of his feet with a rubber truncheon to extract testimony, punched him, removed his trousers, threatened rape with the truncheon, and beat him on the ground. His lawyer was initially denied access. A delayed forensic report found only pigmentation, and the case was refused based mainly on police testimony.

The **fourth applicant, Mammad Azizov**, a NIDA civic movement member, alleged beatings during arrests around January–March 2013. He claimed police punched and kicked him before a protest; MNS officers later allegedly forced him to incriminate NIDA under threats, and after he retracted his statement on 14 March 2013, officers handcuffed, slapped, punched, kicked, and beat him with truncheons, causing limp, ear pain, and temporary hearing damage. The investigation refused to open a case, citing no bodily injuries and officers’ denials, though he said injuries had faded and he lacked access to medical certification.

The **fifth applicant, Murad Adilov**, an opposition activist, was stopped in August 2014 by plainclothes narcotics and police officers. He alleged they beat him, handcuffed him, planted drugs on him, and later beat him with a truncheon on his soles, back, legs, and thigh for about an hour to force a confession. A detention-centre medical record noted a large violet bruise on his left thigh and his account of police violence. A later forensic report found no injury, and the prosecutor refused a criminal case based on police testimony and that report.

All applicants alleged that domestic authorities failed to conduct effective investigations into their ill-treatment complaints.
001-205170:
In *Suur v. Estonia*, the applicant, Tarvo Suur, complained under Article 8 of the Convention that Estonia violated his right to respect for family life by ending his joint custody over his son R.S. (born 2008) and by restricting his contact with the child. The child’s mother, K.T., ended her relationship with the applicant in 2009, when R.S. was almost two. R.S. remained living with K.T., who later had a long-term partner referred to as the child’s stepfather. The applicant last saw R.S. in January 2011.

In October 2015 K.T. applied to the Pärnu County Court to terminate joint custody and grant her full custody. The applicant objected and later counterclaimed for fixed contact arrangements. He alleged that K.T. had changed her residence and phone numbers, hindered contact, and portrayed him negatively to the child. He admitted he had not contacted authorities earlier, hoping the parents could resolve matters themselves.

During the proceedings, the child’s guardian ad litem reported that R.S. was wary of his biological father and opposed forced communication. Pärnu City Government considered ending joint custody extreme but noted the child’s unwillingness and need for stability. Tarvastu Rural Municipality thought ending joint custody premature. In October 2016 the court interviewed R.S., who said he did not want contact, believed his father had shown no interest, and mentioned hearing that the applicant had yelled at K.T. The court stayed proceedings for family counselling. Six sessions took place; R.S. attended two and met the applicant once. Therapist A.T. concluded that further meetings were not in R.S.’s interests because the child was stressed and reluctant, and suggested indirect communication such as texts or emails instead. The applicant’s requests for further counselling, a different therapist, and a special guardian were rejected.

In May 2017 the Pärnu County Court terminated joint custody, granted full custody to K.T., dismissed the contact application, and restricted direct meetings to those with K.T.’s knowledge and consent. It relied on the mother’s continuous care, the long absence of contact, the child’s unwillingness, and the applicant’s earlier use of bank accounts opened in his son’s name while his own accounts were frozen. It found forced contact could harm R.S. but left letters, calls, emails, and texts available. The Tallinn Court of Appeal upheld the decision, stressing the child’s expressed unwillingness. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, clarifying that the child’s best interests, not merely his wishes, were decisive, and that forcing contact might jeopardise future restoration. A dissenting judge argued the courts had effectively left contact to the custodial mother and failed to facilitate restoration.

The applicant alleged that the custody and contact decisions were disproportionate and effectively precluded contact. He blamed K.T.’s influence for the child’s reluctance and argued the courts failed to ascertain the true reasons or restore the relationship. The Government maintained that extensive procedural steps had been taken and that the decisions were justified by R.S.’s best interests. The ECtHR ultimately found no violation of Article 8, considering the domestic reasons relevant and sufficient and noting that future contact remained possible and arrangements could be revised.

In *Suur v. Estonia*, the applicant, Tarvo Suur, complained under Article 8 that Estonia violated his right to respect for family life by ending joint custody of his son R.S. (born 2008), granting full custody to the child’s mother K.T., and restricting his contact to meetings only with K.T.’s knowledge and consent.

The applicant and K.T. separated in 2009 when R.S. was one year and nine months old. R.S. remained with K.T., who later lived with a partner described as the child’s stepfather. The applicant last saw R.S. in January 2011. The applicant was partially incapacitated for work, received a State allowance, and paid 45 euros monthly child support. It was also alleged that he had opened bank accounts in R.S.’s name and used them while his own accounts were frozen due to debts.

In October 2015 K.T. sought termination of joint custody and full custody. The applicant objected and counterclaimed for contact, alleging K.T. had changed her residence and phone numbers, hindered contact, and portrayed him negatively. At a 2016 hearing, he admitted he had not contacted authorities after losing contact in 2011, hoping to resolve matters privately, and agreed to partial transfers of custody.

During proceedings, the child’s guardian ad litem said R.S. was wary and should not be forced to communicate; any meetings should occur with the mother or a social worker present. Pärnu City Government considered ending joint custody extreme but favored stable living arrangements and no forced contact; Tarvastu Rural Municipality thought termination premature. In May 2016 the county court ended joint custody, granted full custody to K.T., and allowed limited monthly contact in the presence of a familiar person and therapy. The Court of Appeal quashed this, finding insufficient assessment and noting K.T.’s possible role in estrangement.

On remand, R.S. was interviewed in October 2016. He said he did not want contact with the applicant, even with others present. He was unsure why but thought the applicant had shown no interest and mentioned a claim that the applicant had yelled at K.T. The court stayed proceedings for family counselling with psychologist-family therapist A.T. Six sessions occurred; R.S. attended two, meeting the applicant once. A.T. reported that the applicant was a stranger to R.S., the child was stressed and anxious afterwards, and continued meetings were not in R.S.’s interests. Pärnu City supported modifying custody and opposed forced contact; Tarvastu opposed ending joint custody but considered enforceable contact impossible; the guardian ad litem opposed forced communication.

In May 2017 the county court terminated joint custody, granted full custody to K.T., dismissed the applicant’s contact request, and restricted contact to meetings with K.T.’s knowledge and consent. It cited K.T.’s continuous care, the long absence of contact, R.S.’s unwillingness, and the applicant’s prior use of the child’s bank accounts. It found forced contact threatened R.S.’s mental health, while letters, calls, emails and texts remained possible. The Court of Appeal and Supreme Court upheld the decision. The Supreme Court stressed that R.S.’s best interests, not merely his wishes, were decisive, and that forced contact at that time could harm future restoration. A dissent argued that contact had been effectively excluded and that the courts had not sufficiently examined other experts or the mother’s influence.

The ECtHR found no violation of Article 8. It considered that the domestic process had aimed at an amicable solution in the child’s best interests with the applicant’s meaningful participation, and that the courts gave relevant and sufficient reasons for ending joint custody and for not ordering forced contact. Future meetings remained possible, and contact arrangements could be revised.

Case *Suur v. Estonia* concerns an Article 8 ECHR complaint by Tarvo Suur, an Estonian father, about the ending of joint custody over his son, R.S. (born 2008), the granting of full custody to the child’s mother, K.T., and restrictions on his contact with the child.

The parents separated in 2009, when R.S. was one year and nine months old. R.S. remained with K.T., who later lived with a long-term partner referred to as the child’s stepfather. Suur last saw his son in January 2011. He was certified as partially incapacitated for work, received a state allowance, and paid 45 euros monthly child support. During the later dispute, it was also noted that he had opened bank accounts in his son’s name and used them while his own accounts were frozen due to debts—a fact relied on in the custody proceedings.

In October 2015 K.T. applied to the Pärnu County Court to terminate joint custody and grant her full custody. Suur objected and counterclaimed for contact arrangements. He alleged that K.T. had changed her residence and phone numbers, hindering contact, and said he had learned of his son’s whereabouts via the internet in 2015 but had not interfered. At a June 2016 hearing, he agreed to partial transfer of custody, including K.T.’s custody over property and power to decide the child’s place of stay in Estonia. The guardianship authority and the child’s guardian ad litem described R.S. as wary and estranged from his father and opposed forced contact. Tarvastu Rural Municipality considered ending joint custody premature.

In May 2016 the first-instance court ended joint custody, granted full custody to K.T., and fixed limited contact: monthly meetings of two to three hours in 2016 and six to seven hours in 2017, in a familiar place and with K.T. or another known person present, plus father-son therapy. The Tallinn Court of Appeal quashed that decision, finding insufficient reasoning and failure to assess the mother’s possible role and the child’s wishes.

In October 2016 R.S. was interviewed. He said he did not want contact with his father, even with others present, and thought his father had shown no interest in him. He also mentioned that his stepfather had told him the applicant had yelled at K.T. The court stayed proceedings for counselling. Six sessions took place; R.S. attended two and met the applicant once. Psychologist A.T. reported that the child was stressed and that further meetings were not in his interests, though text or email contact could leave the child a choice.

In May 2017 the Pärnu County Court again ended joint custody, granted full custody to K.T., dismissed the contact application, and restricted meetings to those with K.T.’s knowledge and consent. It cited the mother’s long-term care of the child, the years without contact, the child’s unwillingness, the applicant’s earlier agreement to the mother’s decisions, and his misuse of the son’s bank accounts. It did not restrict letters, emails, phone calls, or texts because the child could choose whether to respond. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal in September 2017, relying heavily on the child’s unwillingness and A.T.’s opinion. The Supreme Court dismissed the further appeal in April 2018, holding that the child’s interests, not merely his will, were decisive, and that forced contact was then not in R.S.’s interests and might harm future restoration. One judge dissented, finding that the lower courts had effectively excluded contact and failed to facilitate restoration.

Suur complained under Article 8 that full custody and the contact restriction violated his family life. He alleged maternal alienation, reliance on the mother’s statements and premature expert conclusions, and insufficient State efforts to restore contact. The Government argued that the authorities had consulted local bodies, appointed a guardian ad litem, heard the child, attempted counselling, and based decisions on the child’s best interests. The ECtHR found no violation: the domestic process sought an amicable, child-centred solution with meaningful participation by the applicant, and the courts gave relevant and sufficient reasons. Future meetings remained possible, other contact was not banned, and arrangements could be revised.
001-206268:
Case Makhmudova v. Russia (Application no. 61984/17), decided by the European Court of Human Rights on 1 December 2020, concerned Russia’s failure to enforce a final order returning two children to Estonia under the 1980 Hague Convention. The applicant, an Estonian national, married a Russian national, A., in 2006. They had two sons, born in 2010 and 2014, who held both Estonian and Russian nationality. The family lived in Estonia, but the children visited A. in Dagestan, Russia. In August 2015 the applicant told A. she intended to divorce him; he threatened to take the children. She hid their passports, but in early 2016 A. obtained new Estonian passports for them. On 4 February 2016, while the applicant was at work, A. took the elder son from home and the younger son from kindergarten and crossed from Estonia to Russia with them, travelling via St Petersburg to Makhachkala in Dagestan.

The applicant sought assistance under the Hague Convention. In Estonia, the Harju County Court suspended A.’s joint parental responsibility, granted the applicant the right to determine the children’s residence, and ordered A. to return them. In Russia, the Pyatigorsk Town Court on 20 July 2016 ordered the children’s immediate return to their habitual residence in Estonia and required A. to hand over their passports. That judgment was upheld on appeal on 20 January 2017. A. did not comply voluntarily.

Enforcement proceedings began in April 2017. Repeated attempts failed. On 22 May 2017 the applicant travelled to Makhachkala, but A. had left with the children for Rostov-on-Don. A later court found that he had evaded enforcement and that no evidence supported his claimed medical reason for travelling. Fines were imposed on A., including a RUB 5,000 execution fee and a RUB 2,500 administrative fine, but these proved ineffective. The applicant complained about delays and alleged sabotage, and requested enforcement without her presence and transfer of the children to Moscow; her requests were dismissed. In September 2017 the case was transferred to a special bailiff department, and A. was temporarily barred from leaving Russia.

On 7 November 2017 another enforcement attempt took place with A., the applicant, childcare authorities and a psychologist. The children refused to go to the applicant. The psychologist reported that they spent over two hours with her without displaying a positive emotional attitude and that forcible transfer could cause serious psychological trauma. She recommended counselling and regular contact over two months before another attempt. Later attempts on 22 May and 18 June 2019 also failed because the children refused to go to the applicant; the applicant alleged violent actions by local officials on one occasion. The return order remained unenforced.

In 2019 the applicant asked the Town Court to modify the enforcement method, seeking safe removal of the children regardless of their wishes, transport to St Petersburg, psychological adaptation counselling, contact arrangements, and departure to Estonia. On 9 August 2019 the Town Court refused, finding that A. had not been inactive, that the children had refused to go, that forcible transfer would be harmful, and that the children had spent over three and a half years in Russia, exceeding the Hague Convention’s one-year limit. The Regional Court dismissed her appeal on 5 December 2020.

The applicant complained that the Russian authorities’ failure to enforce the return order violated her right to respect for family life under Article 8. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation, citing delays, failure to ensure preparatory measures and regular contact pending proceedings, the children’s unwillingness, lack of effective coordination among authorities, and inadequate and ineffective enforcement measures.

In *Makhmudova v Russia* (no. 61984/17), the applicant, an Estonian national, complained under Article 8 that Russian authorities failed to enforce a Russian judgment ordering the return of her two sons to Estonia under the Hague Convention. The children, born in 2010 and 2014, held Estonian and Russian nationality and lived in Estonia with her. Their father, A., a Russian national from Dagestan, visited them and partly lived in Estonia. After the applicant told A. in August 2015 that she intended to divorce him, he threatened to take the children. On 4 February 2016, while she was at work, A. took the elder son from home and the younger from kindergarten and crossed into Russia, going to Dagestan.

In Estonia, the Harju County Court suspended A.’s joint parental responsibility, granted the applicant residence rights, and ordered him to return the children. In Russia, on 20 July 2016 the Pyatigorsk Town Court ordered their immediate return to Estonia under the Hague Convention; the Stavropol Regional Court upheld this on 20 January 2017. A. did not comply voluntarily.

Enforcement began in April 2017. A. was served with a compliance request but denied obstructing return. The applicant travelled to Makhachkala for an enforcement attempt on 22 May 2017, but A. had left with the children for Rostov-on-Don. Small fines and an execution fee were imposed, but enforcement remained ineffective. On 7 November 2017, with a childcare authority and psychologist present, the children refused to go to the applicant. The psychologist reported no positive emotion toward her and that forced transfer risked serious psychological trauma; she recommended counselling and two months of contact before another attempt. Attempts on 22 May and 18 June 2019 also failed because the children refused. The applicant alleged she and her representative were subjected to violent actions by local officials. The return order remains unenforced.

The applicant repeatedly complained that bailiffs acted inefficiently and allegedly sabotaged enforcement. She asked for enforcement without her participation, transfer of the children to Moscow, and an external enforcement team. The proceedings were transferred in September 2017 to a special department, and A. was temporarily barred from leaving Russia, but these steps did not secure return. In 2019 she sought modification of enforcement: safe removal regardless of the children’s wishes, transport to St Petersburg, psychological adaptation, and contact arrangements. On 9 August 2019 the Town Court refused. It found A. had not been inactive, had appeared with the children, and had not pressured them; the children simply refused to go. It relied on the trauma risk and noted that over three and a half years had passed, exceeding the Hague Convention’s one-year period. The Regional Court upheld that decision on 5 December 2020.

Before the ECtHR, the key facts relevant to the alleged Article 8 violation were the authorities’ delays; failure to ensure effective coordination; failure to take preliminary measures to prepare the children and maintain regular contact with the applicant pending proceedings; the children’s unwillingness to go to her; and inadequate, ineffective enforcement measures. The Court declared the application admissible and found a violation of Article 8, holding that Russia had failed its positive obligation to enforce the return order.

In *Makhmudova v Russia* (no. 61984/17, 1 December 2020), the applicant, an Estonian national, married a Russian national, A., in 2006. They had two sons, born in 2010 and 2014, who held Estonian and Russian nationality and lived in Estonia. In August 2015, when the applicant informed A. of her intention to divorce him, he threatened to take the children. In February 2016, while she was at work, A. took the elder son from home and the younger from kindergarten, crossed into Russia, and flew to Makhachkala in Dagestan.

Estonian authorities responded: the Harju County Court suspended A.’s joint parental responsibility, granted the applicant the right to determine the children’s residence, ordered A. not to remove them from Estonia, and ordered their immediate return. In Russia, the applicant applied under the 1980 Hague Convention. On 20 July 2016, the Pyatigorsk Town Court ordered the children’s immediate return to Estonia and required A. to hand over their passports; this was upheld on appeal in January 2017.

A. did not comply voluntarily. In spring 2017, Russian bailiffs opened enforcement proceedings. A. claimed he was not obstructing the transfer. The first enforcement attempt, scheduled for 22 May 2017, failed because A. left with the children for Rostov-on-Don. The applicant travelled from Estonia to Makhachkala for nothing. Her complaints about inefficiency were dismissed. In June 2017, bailiffs located the children’s residence, imposed an administrative fine on A., but refused the applicant’s request for enforcement without her presence and transfer of the children to Moscow. She repeatedly complained of delays and requested an external enforcement team.

In September 2017, the case was transferred to a special federal bailiff department; A. was temporarily barred from leaving Russia. On 7 November 2017, a further enforcement attempt took place with A., the applicant, childcare authorities, and a psychologist. The children spent over two hours with the applicant but refused to go to her. The psychologist warned that forced transfer could cause serious psychological trauma and recommended counselling and two months of contact before another attempt. Later attempts in May and June 2019 also failed because the children refused to go; the applicant alleged officials used “violent actions.” The return order remained unenforced.

In 2019, the applicant sought modification of the enforcement method, including safe removal of the children regardless of their wishes, transport to St Petersburg, psychological family adaptation, contact arrangements, and departure to Estonia. On 9 August 2019, the Town Court refused. It found A. had not been inactive, the children had refused to go, and forced transfer risked trauma. It also noted the children had spent over three and a half years in Russia, exceeding the Hague Convention’s one-year period. The Regional Court upheld that decision in December 2020.

The applicant complained under Article 8 that Russia failed to enforce the return order, violating her right to respect for family life. The key alleged failures were prolonged non-enforcement, inadequate and ineffective measures, poor coordination among authorities, failure to ensure regular contact and preparation of the children pending proceedings, and failure to address their unwillingness to return. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 8.
