In *Karesvaara and Njie v. Spain*, the applicants—a Finnish national and a Gambian national legally resident in Spain—complained under Article 6 §1 of the Convention that they were denied access to a court. The case arose from eviction proceedings brought by a bank over an apartment in Fuengirola.

On 1 July 2010 the applicants jointly signed two lease-purchase agreements with the bank for two apartments. The contracts stated that the rented apartments would be the tenants’ habitual and permanent residence and that, for future communications, service on the tenants would be valid at the relevant apartment’s address. The contracts’ header also mentioned another address: Calle Las Viñas, Fuengirola. In January 2012 the bank’s insurer sent a burofax to the Avenida de Mijas apartment demanding arrears. A missed-delivery slip was left, but the applicants did not collect the post.

On 11 April 2012 the bank began eviction proceedings regarding the Avenida de Mijas apartment, claiming arrears. The bank designated that apartment as the address for service. On 15 October 2012 a court officer went to the apartment to serve the summons. Finding nobody there, he left an official notice in the letterbox requiring the applicants to collect the summons at the court. The court document noted a second attempt and that names of other individuals appeared on the letterbox. The applicants did not collect the summons. The first-instance court then ordered service by public announcement on the court bulletin board. The applicants did not appear or oppose the claim.

On 9 January 2013 the court allowed the bank’s claims, ordered eviction, and held the applicants liable for arrears. The decision became final. The eviction was initially suspended in March 2013. In September 2013 the bank initiated enforcement proceedings, again designating the Avenida de Mijas apartment for service. In October 2013 the court issued an enforcement order and seized assets. A public-registry search revealed that the applicants owned an apartment on Calle Las Viñas, used that address as their fiscal address, and that Mr Njie had a bank account.

On 15 November 2013 Mr Njie discovered his bank account had been frozen. He went to the court, where he was served for the first time with the enforcement decisions. He gave a current address in Mijas. In December 2013 the applicants accessed the eviction case file and learned for the first time of the January 2013 final judgment. They filed an action to annul the eviction proceedings. They argued that they had returned the keys to the bank before the proceedings, that the bank knew they did not live in the apartment, and that they had never been summoned. They submitted tax returns, a residence-permit card, and a census certificate showing they had been registered at another address since October 2011.

On 7 February 2014 the first-instance court dismissed the annulment action. It held that the applicants could have contested enforcement and that the service attempts complied with procedural law and the contractual address, so they were effective. The applicants lodged an amparo appeal under Article 24 of the Spanish Constitution. On 2 February 2015 the Constitutional Court declared it inadmissible for lack of special constitutional significance; a subsequent súplica appeal by the public prosecutor was dismissed on 1 June 2015.

The alleged violation concerned the right of access to a court under Article 6 §1. The key issue was whether the Spanish courts failed to ensure effective notification of eviction proceedings, given that service was made only at a contractual address despite indications the applicants no longer lived there, resulting in a default judgment and inability to oppose the bank’s claim.

**Case: Karesvaara and Njie v. Spain (Application no. 60750/15), ECtHR, 15 December 2020**

The case concerned the applicants’ right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights in the context of Spanish eviction proceedings. The applicants were a Finnish national, Ms Karesvaara, and a Gambian national, Mr Njie, both legally resident in Spain.

In July 2010 the applicants entered into two lease-purchase agreements with a bank for two apartments in Fuengirola. Clause 13 of both contracts designated the rented apartment as the address for service of future communications, while clause 4 stated that the apartments would be the tenants’ habitual and permanent residence. The contract header also mentioned another address of the applicants, Calle Las Viñas, Fuengirola.

In January 2012 the bank’s insurer sent a burofax to the Avenida de Mijas apartment demanding payment of arrears. A missed-delivery slip was left, but the applicants did not collect the post. In April 2012 the bank initiated eviction proceedings against the applicants regarding that apartment, claiming arrears of EUR 6,215.44. The bank designated the rented apartment as the address for service.

In October 2012 a court officer went to the Avenida de Mijas apartment to serve the summons. Finding nobody there, he left an official notice in the letterbox. The court officer noted that names other than the applicants’ appeared on the letterbox. The applicants did not collect the summons. The first-instance court then ordered service by public announcement on the court bulletin board. The applicants did not appear or oppose the claim.

On 9 January 2013 the first-instance court allowed the bank’s claims, ordered eviction and held the applicants liable for arrears. The decision became final. In March 2013 the bank applied to suspend the eviction, which the court allowed.

In September 2013 the bank initiated enforcement proceedings, again designating the Avenida de Mijas apartment as the service address. In October 2013 the court issued an enforcement order and ordered seizure of the applicants’ assets. A registry search revealed that the applicants owned property at Calle Las Viñas, used that address as their fiscal address and residence on their driving licences, and had been registered as sole traders. It also identified a bank account in Mr Njie’s name.

On 15 November 2013 Mr Njie discovered that his bank account had been frozen. He went to the court, where the enforcement decisions were served on him for the first time, and provided a new address in Mijas. In December 2013 the applicants obtained access to the eviction case file and learned for the first time of the January 2013 eviction judgment. They then applied to annul the proceedings, arguing that they had returned the keys to the apartment before the eviction proceedings began, that the bank knew they did not live there, and that the summons had never been personally served. They submitted tax returns, a residence-permit card and a census certificate showing they had been registered at another address since October 2011.

In February 2014 the first-instance court dismissed the annulment action, finding that the service attempts had been lawful because they were made at the contractually agreed address. The applicants’ amparo appeal to the Constitutional Court was declared inadmissible for lack of special constitutional significance in February 2015, and a subsequent súplica appeal was dismissed in June 2015.

The key alleged violation was that the failure to personally serve the eviction summons deprived the applicants of any effective opportunity to participate in the proceedings and oppose the bank’s claim, thereby breaching their right of access to a court.

In *Karesvaara and Njie v. Spain* (ECtHR, Third Section, App. No. 60750/15, judgment of 15 December 2020), the applicants were a Finnish national and a Gambian national legally resident in Spain. They complained of a violation of their right of access to a court under Article 6 of the Convention in the context of private eviction proceedings in which the summons had not been personally served on them.

The dispute concerned two lease-purchase agreements entered into with a bank in July 2010 for two apartments in Fuengirola. Clause 13 of the contracts designated each rented apartment as the address for service of future communications, and clause 4 stated that the apartments were to be the tenants’ habitual and permanent residence. Another address, Calle Las Viñas, appeared on the contract header.

After arrears accumulated, the bank’s insurer sent a certified fax to the Avenida de Mijas apartment on 3 January 2012. No one was present; a missed-delivery slip was left, but the applicants did not collect the post. On 11 April 2012 the bank initiated eviction proceedings concerning the Avenida de Mijas apartment, claiming rent arrears, and again designated that apartment as the address for service. On 15 October 2012 a court officer attempted service there, found nobody, left an official notice in the letterbox giving a deadline to collect the summons at the court, and noted that other names appeared on the letterbox. The applicants did not collect the summons. The court then ordered service by public announcement on the courthouse bulletin board. The applicants did not appear or oppose the claim.

On 9 January 2013 the first-instance court allowed the bank’s claim, ordered the applicants’ eviction and held them liable for arrears. The decision became final because no appeal was lodged. The eviction was later suspended on the bank’s application.

In September 2013 the bank commenced enforcement proceedings, again using the Avenida de Mijas apartment as the address for service. On 16 October 2013 the court issued an enforcement order and ordered seizure of assets. A search of public registries revealed that the applicants owned an apartment on Calle Las Viñas, had that address as their fiscal address and driving-licence residence, and that Mr Njie had a bank account. On 15 November 2013 Mr Njie learned his account had been frozen. He went to court and was served for the first time with the 16 October decisions, which started the ten-day period to contest enforcement. He provided a current address in Mijas.

On 3 December 2013 the applicants accessed the eviction case file and learned for the first time of the eviction proceedings and the final judgment of 9 January 2013. On 17 December 2013 they sought annulment of the eviction proceedings. They argued that they had returned the keys to the Avenida de Mijas apartment before the proceedings began, that the bank knew they did not live there, and that the summons had never been served on them. They submitted tax returns, a residence-permit card, and a census certificate showing that since October 2011 they had been registered at their current Mijas address with their children.

On 7 February 2014 the first-instance court dismissed the annulment application. It held that the applicants should have contested enforcement rather than bringing a separate action, and that service had complied with procedural law and the contractual address. Their amparo appeal to the Constitutional Court, based on Article 24 of the Spanish Constitution, was declared inadmissible on 2 February 2015 for lack of special constitutional significance; a prosecutor’s *súplica* was dismissed on 1 June 2015. The Constitutional Court stated that the right-of-access perspective did not meet the special-significance threshold.

Spanish law, notably sections 155 and 156 of the Civil Procedure Act, and Constitutional Court case-law indicated that using the rented home as the default address for service does not relieve courts of their duty to inform the defendant of proceedings. The central alleged violation was therefore that service at the contractual address, without personal notice, prevented the applicants from participating in and defending the eviction claim.

**Tamrazyan v. Armenia** concerned an Armenian national, Babken Tamrazyan, who had possessed and cultivated a plot of about 1,300 sq.m. adjacent to Teghut village since 1986. He fenced the land, built a garden shed, planted fruit trees, and arranged water supply. The land was initially registered in his name in the Kuybishev collective farm register from 1986 to 1990. In 1994 Teghut separated from Haghartsin, but the plot was not included within the administrative boundaries of either village. From 1995 until 2007, except 1998–1999, the applicant paid rent to the Teghut community administration, which transferred the money to the State budget.

In April 2007, the Tavoush Regional Administration sold the plot at public auction to a third person, A.H. The Governor’s decision was dated 27 March 2007; a sale contract was concluded on 3 April 2007, and A.H. registered title on 23 April 2007. The applicant learned of the sale in April 2008 and later obtained official confirmation. A newspaper announcement in February 2007 had described the plot as measuring 1,394 sq.m.

In 2009 the applicant brought a claim before the Administrative Court seeking annulment of the sale and registration of A.H.’s title, and an order that the Governor conclude a direct sale agreement with him. He argued that, under Articles 65, 66, 67 and 72 of the Land Code, he had a pre-emptive right to acquire the land because he had used State land continuously, openly and in good faith for more than ten years. He relied on Court of Cassation case-law, particularly decision no. 3-537 (VD) of 30 March 2007, concerning adverse possession of State and community property.

The Administrative Court granted his claims. It found that from at least 1995 until the Governor’s decision, the applicant had possessed the land continuously, openly and in good faith for more than ten years. It concluded that he had a pre-emptive right to acquire the property, and that the Governor had unlawfully sold it at auction rather than by direct sale to the person holding that right. The court also referred to Cassation case-law stating that continuous, open and good-faith possession for ten years could prevail over another person’s ownership.

A.H. appealed on points of law. On 2 April 2010 the Court of Cassation quashed the Administrative Court’s judgment and rejected the applicant’s claims. It reasoned that the applicant’s rent payments to Teghut community were not essential because the land was outside Teghut’s administrative boundaries, so they could not substantiate continuous, open and good-faith possession for more than ten years. It further held that Article 72 § 3 of the Land Code referred adverse possession of land owned by another person to the Civil Code, but that Article 187 of the Civil Code did not apply to land owned by the State or communities, citing decision no. 3-153 (VD). Therefore, the applicant had no pre-emptive right.

The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 that the Court of Cassation failed to give adequate reasons. In particular, it rejected both Article 187 of the Civil Code and Article 72 of the Land Code but did not identify any other legal basis for denying his pre-emptive right. It also allegedly ignored his key arguments concerning his possession and the Cassation’s own case-law on State land, and failed to address Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. He further complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the alienation of the land to a third person violated his peaceful enjoyment of possessions and his pre-emptive right after about twenty-three years of possession. The Government argued that the reasons were sufficient and that the Cassation had implicitly applied the Land Code while distinguishing prior case-law. The Court declared the Article 6 complaint admissible.

In *Tamrazyan v. Armenia* (App. no. 42588/10, 19 March 2020), the applicant, an Armenian national born in 1931, lived in Teghut village. From 1986 to 2009 he possessed about 1,300 sq.m. of land adjacent to Teghut, in the Tavoush region. He enclosed it, built a garden shed, planted fruit trees, and arranged water supply. The land was registered in his name in the Kuybishev collective-farm register from 1986 to 1990. In 1994 Teghut separated from Haghartsin, but the plot was not included within the administrative boundaries of either village. From 1995 to 2007, except 1998–99, he paid rent to Teghut community administration, which transferred the money to the State budget.

In April 2008 the applicant learned that in April 2007 the Tavoush Regional Administration had sold the plot at public auction to a third person, A.H. A newspaper announcement of 21 February 2007 advertised an auction on 20 March 2007 for a plot said to measure 1,394 sq.m. By a decision of 27 March 2007, the Governor declared A.H. the auction winner; a sale contract was concluded on 3 April 2007, and A.H. registered title on 23 April 2007. The applicant claimed he obtained a copy of the Governor’s decision only in 2009.

On 21 April 2009 the applicant sued in the Administrative Court, seeking annulment of the sale and registration and an order for direct sale to him. He relied on Articles 65, 66, 67 and 72 of the Land Code and Court of Cassation case-law, arguing that his continuous, open and good-faith use of State land for more than ten years gave him a pre-emptive right to acquire the plot by adverse possession. On 8 July 2009 the Administrative Court allowed his claims in full. It found that from at least 1995 he had possessed the land continuously, openly and in good faith; under Article 72(2) he had a pre-emptive right; and the Governor should have sold directly to him under Article 66, not by auction under Article 67.

A.H. appealed on points of law. On 2 April 2010 the Court of Cassation quashed the lower judgment and rejected the applicant’s claims. It held that rent payments to Teghut were not essential because the land lay outside Teghut’s administrative boundaries, so they could not prove continuous, open, good-faith possession for over ten years. It further stated that under Article 72(3) of the Land Code, adverse possession of land owned by another person is governed by the Civil Code, and that Article 187 of the Civil Code did not apply to State or community land, citing decision no. 3-153 (VD).

The applicant alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (fair trial) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions). Under Article 6, he complained that the Court of Cassation failed to give adequate reasons: after rejecting both Civil Code Article 187 and Land Code Article 72, it did not identify the legal basis for denying his pre-emptive right, did not address his arguments on adverse possession and Protocol No. 1, and did not explain its departure from its own case-law (notably decisions nos. 3-1835(A) and 3-537(VD)) or its reliance on no. 3-153. Under the property complaint, he alleged unlawful alienation of land he had possessed for about twenty-three years and for which he claimed a statutory pre-emptive right. The Court declared these complaints admissible; the remainder of the application was inadmissible.

**Case: Tamrazyan v. Armenia (Application no. 42588/10), ECtHR, 19 March 2020**

The applicant, Mr Babken Tamrazyan, an Armenian national living in Teghut village, complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the alienation to a third person of land he had possessed for about twenty-three years and about the Court of Cassation’s failure to give adequate reasons.

From 1986 until 2009, the applicant possessed a plot of about 1,300 sq.m. adjacent to Teghut village, in the Tavoush region. He fenced it, built a garden shed, planted fruit trees and arranged water supply. From 1986 to 1990, the land was registered in his name in the Kuybishev collective farms register. In 1994 Teghut became a separate administrative unit from Haghartsin, but the plot was not included within the administrative boundaries of either village. From 1995 to 2007, except 1998 and 1999, the applicant paid rent to the Teghut community administration, which transferred the money to the State budget. He continued to possess and cultivate the land.

In April 2008, he learned that in April 2007 the Tavoush Regional Administration had sold the plot to a third person, A.H., at public auction. A letter from the State Real Estate Registry stated that A.H. had registered title on 23 April 2007. The applicant later found that an announcement had been published on 21 February 2007 for an auction on 20 March 2007; the Governor’s decision was dated 27 March 2007; a sale contract was concluded on 3 April 2007. He allegedly obtained a copy of the Governor’s decision only in 2009.

The applicant claimed a pre-emptive right to acquire the State-owned land by adverse possession under domestic law, particularly Article 72 § 2 of the Land Code, because he had used it continuously, openly and in good faith for more than ten years. He sought annulment of the sale and an order that the Governor conclude a direct sale agreement with him.

On 8 July 2009, the Administrative Court granted his claims. Relying on a village head’s certificate, rent payment evidence and witness testimony, it found that from at least 1995 until the auction, he had possessed the land continuously, openly and in good faith for over ten years. It held that he had a pre-emptive right under Article 72 § 2 and that the Governor had wrongly auctioned the land instead of selling it directly to him under Article 66. It relied on Court of Cassation decision no. 3-537 (VD).

A.H. appealed on points of law. On 2 April 2010, the Court of Cassation quashed the Administrative Court’s judgment and rejected the applicant’s claims. It reasoned that rent payments to Teghut were not essential because the land lay outside Teghut’s administrative boundaries. It further held that Article 72 § 3 referred adverse possession of land owned by another person to the Civil Code, and that Article 187 of the Civil Code did not apply to State or community land, citing decision no. 3-153 (VD). It therefore found no pre-emptive right.

The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 because the Court of Cassation failed to state the applicable law, address his key arguments, or explain its departure from its own case-law, especially decisions no. 3-537 (VD) and no. 3-1835 (A). Having rejected both Civil Code Article 187 and Land Code Article 72, it identified no other legal basis for denying his pre-emptive right and did not address his continuous, open, good-faith possession or his Protocol No. 1 argument. He also alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to the alienation of land he had possessed for around 23 years. The Government argued that the Cassation Court’s reasons were sufficient and that it had distinguished its earlier case-law on the facts. The Court declared the Article 6 and property complaints admissible; the remainder was inadmissible.
001-200214:
In *Sargsyan and Others v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 54012/07 and two others), the European Court of Human Rights’ Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 9 January 2020. The case concerned three applications against Ukraine lodged under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants alleged that they had been ill-treated by police and that Ukrainian authorities had failed to carry out effective investigations into their respective allegations. They relied on Articles 3 and 13, but the Court examined the complaints under Article 3 only, as it is master of the legal characterisation of the facts. Certain other complaints in applications nos. 54012/07 and 25697/08 were declared inadmissible under Rule 54 § 3. The Government did not object to examination by a Committee.

Because the applications raised similar issues, the Court joined them in a single judgment. The judgment’s main body does not set out each applicant’s individual facts in detail; instead, it refers to appended tables. The key common facts are that each applicant claimed to have suffered police ill-treatment and that the domestic authorities failed to investigate those claims effectively. The applicants therefore alleged violations of Article 3 under both its substantive and procedural limbs. The Government contested those allegations.

On admissibility, the Government filed no objections to the Article 3 complaints. The Court found the complaints not manifestly ill-founded and admissible.

On the merits, the Court applied its established case-law, especially *Bouyid v. Belgium*, concerning credible ill-treatment claims. It held that where an applicant raises a credible claim of ill-treatment, the national authorities must carry out an effective and thorough investigation to establish the origin of any physical injuries or emotional trauma and, if the allegations are true, identify and punish those responsible. The Court found that the applicants had raised credible ill-treatment claims at the domestic level. However, the domestic investigations did not reflect a serious effort to determine the relevant facts. The Court recalled its earlier finding in *Kaverzin v. Ukraine* that the reluctance of authorities to ensure prompt and thorough investigation of ill-treatment complaints against police constituted a systemic problem under Article 46 of the Convention. The present cases were another example of that failure.

The Court further found that the applicants’ accounts of their alleged ill-treatment were detailed and coherent, and that the investigations, given their numerous shortcomings, did not disprove those allegations. In such circumstances, the State had an onus to provide a satisfactory and convincing explanation for injuries sustained by persons under police control. Since no such explanation was provided, the Court concluded that the State’s responsibility for the applicants’ ill-treatment was engaged. This established a substantive violation of Article 3, while the failure to conduct an effective investigation established a procedural violation.

The Court also considered whether the treatment amounted to “torture.” It found no conclusive evidence concerning the circumstances in which the applicants were injured or the exact nature and degree of force used against them. Accordingly, it could not find beyond reasonable doubt that the treatment reached the level of torture. Nevertheless, the ill-treatment and the defective investigations violated Article 3. The judgment is final but subject to editorial revision.

The case *Sargsyan and Others v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 54012/07 and two others) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, Committee) on 9 January 2020. The applicants lodged three applications against Ukraine, complaining principally that they had been ill-treated by police and that Ukrainian authorities failed to conduct effective investigations into their allegations. Notice was given to the Government regarding those complaints and other well-established case-law complaints. Parts of applications nos. 54012/07 and 25697/08 were declared inadmissible under Rule 54 §3.

The Court joined the applications because they raised similar issues. Although the applicants relied on Articles 3 and 13, the Court, as master of legal characterisation, examined the complaints only under Article 3, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. The Government did not object to admissibility. The Court declared the Article 3 complaints admissible, finding they were not manifestly ill-founded.

On the merits, the applicants alleged violations of both the substantive and procedural limbs of Article 3 in each case: that police had ill-treated them and that domestic authorities had failed to investigate properly. The Government contested this. The Court reviewed the facts against principles from *Bouyid v. Belgium* and other case-law.

The Court found that the applicants had raised credible ill-treatment claims at the domestic level. Those claims triggered a positive obligation on Ukraine to carry out an effective and thorough investigation to establish the origin of their physical injuries and, where appropriate, emotional trauma, and to identify and punish those responsible if the allegations were true. However, the documents before the Court showed that the domestic investigations did not reflect a serious effort to determine the relevant facts. The Court noted its earlier finding in *Kaverzin v. Ukraine* that the reluctance of authorities to ensure prompt and thorough investigations of ill-treatment complaints against police constituted a systemic problem under Article 46 of the Convention. It considered the present applications another example of that failure.

The Court further observed that the applicants’ accounts of their alleged ill-treatment were detailed and coherent, while the investigations, given their numerous shortcomings, did not disprove those allegations. It reiterated that the State must provide a satisfactory and convincing explanation for injuries sustained by persons under police control. On that basis, the Court concluded that the State’s responsibility for the applicants’ ill-treatment was engaged under Article 3. It therefore found a substantive violation in that respect and a procedural violation due to the ineffective investigations.

At the same time, the Court noted that there was no conclusive evidence about the exact circumstances in which the applicants were injured or the precise nature and degree of force used against them. Consequently, it could not find beyond reasonable doubt that the treatment reached the level of “torture” under Article 3. The key facts therefore concern alleged police violence against persons in custody, documented injuries or trauma giving rise to credible claims, and systemic failures by Ukrainian authorities to investigate those claims promptly and thoroughly. The Court’s focus was on Ukraine’s dual failure: the ill-treatment itself (substantive Article 3) and the inadequate response to it (procedural Article 3), while stopping short of a torture finding.

In *Sargsyan and Others v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 54012/07 and two others), the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 9 January 2020. The case originated in three applications against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants alleged that they had been subjected to police ill-treatment and that the Ukrainian authorities had failed to carry out effective investigations into their respective allegations. They invoked Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention. However, the Court, as master of the legal characterisation of the facts, examined the complaints solely under Article 3, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. Notice of the ill-treatment and ineffective-investigation complaints was given to the Ukrainian Government, together with notice of several other complaints falling under the Court’s well-established case-law. The remainder of applications nos. 54012/07 and 25697/08 was declared inadmissible under Rule 54 § 3. The Government did not object to examination by a Committee.

Because the applications concerned similar subject matter, the Court joined them. The Government filed no objections to the admissibility of the Article 3 complaints. The Court found that those complaints were not manifestly ill-founded and were not inadmissible on any other grounds, and therefore declared them admissible.

On the merits, the applicants alleged violations of Article 3 under both its substantive and procedural limbs: they claimed that police had ill-treated them and that the State had failed to investigate effectively. The Government contested those claims. Applying the general principles established in *Bouyid v. Belgium*, the Court considered that the applicants had raised credible ill-treatment claims at the domestic level. Those claims triggered an obligation on the national authorities to carry out an effective and thorough investigation aimed at establishing the origin of the applicants’ physical injuries and possible emotional trauma, and at identifying and punishing those responsible if the allegations proved true.

The Court found from the documents that the domestic investigations did not reflect a serious effort to determine the relevant facts. Individual details were set out in the appended tables. The Court referred to *Kaverzin v. Ukraine*, where it had found that the reluctance of the Ukrainian authorities to ensure prompt and thorough investigation of ill-treatment complaints against police constituted a systemic problem under Article 46 of the Convention. The present applications, in the Court’s view, were another example of that same failure.

The Court further found that the applicants’ accounts of their alleged ill-treatment were detailed and coherent, and that the investigation results, given their numerous shortcomings, did not disprove those allegations. It emphasised the onus on the State to provide a satisfactory and convincing explanation for injuries sustained by persons under police control, citing *Bouyid* and cases such as *Adnaralov v. Ukraine*, *Kulik v. Ukraine*, and *Yaroshovets and Others v. Ukraine*. Accordingly, the State’s responsibility for the applicants’ ill-treatment was engaged.

At the same time, the Court noted that there was no conclusive evidence concerning the circumstances in which the applicants were injured, in particular the exact nature and degree of force used against them. Therefore, the case files did not allow the Court to find beyond reasonable doubt that the treatment reached the level of “torture.”

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were that each applicant allegedly suffered ill-treatment while under police control, made credible complaints, and faced domestic investigations that were neither prompt nor thorough. The authorities failed to establish the facts, explain the injuries, or punish those responsible. The Court found a systemic problem in Ukraine concerning the investigation of police ill-treatment and concluded that the State was responsible for the ill-treatment and that the investigations were procedurally deficient, while not finding that the treatment amounted to torture.

**Nicolaou v. Cyprus** (Application no. 29068/10, judgment 28 January 2020) concerned the death of Athanasios Nicolaou, a 26-year-old Cypriot national performing mandatory military service. The applicants—his parents and siblings—complained that the investigation into his death was inadequate, violating the procedural aspect of Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which requires an effective official investigation where death may involve State responsibility.

On 28 September 2005, Nicolaou was granted overnight leave from Camp Evmenios Panayiotou. He returned home, left around 6:30 a.m. on 29 September, but failed to report back to camp. After his mother reported him missing, police found his car near a bridge in Alassa and his body under the bridge later that afternoon. A forensic pathologist, Dr P.S., attended the scene. According to police records, P.S. indicated on-site that the death appeared to be suicide by falling from the bridge and that no criminal act was suspected. P.S. later denied saying this, but the initial police investigation was reportedly oriented toward an ordinary unnatural death rather than a potential criminal case.

P.S.’s post-mortem concluded that death resulted from multiple injuries consistent with a fall from a height and found no signs of criminal activity. The first police investigation took statements from over fifty witnesses, including soldiers, but concluded there was no evidence of crime and did not substantively address the deceased’s alleged difficulties with fellow soldiers, including bullying, humiliation, and his being called “the English” or “an Australian.” A parallel military investigation also concluded suicide and proposed closing the case. In 2007, the first inquest found no criminal liability and that death occurred under conditions resembling suicide.

The family challenged this. In 2008, the Supreme Court quashed the coroner’s verdict, holding that a finding of suicide required evidence that the deceased intended to kill himself and that the coroner had not properly excluded other possibilities. A second inquest (2009) found insufficient evidence to conclude suicide or criminal act, but stated that death resulted from injuries caused by falling from a height. The Attorney General then decided there were no grounds for criminal proceedings.

The family obtained several private forensic and criminological opinions criticizing the post-mortem and police investigation. Experts questioned the compatibility of the injuries with a fall from the bridge, noted possible signs of third-party involvement, and pointed to omissions such as failure to test stomach contents, vomit, sand/water in the mouth, and DNA from glasses, watch, wallet, clothing, and the car. They also criticized the lack of scene protection and failure to pursue the bullying allegations.

In 2011, the Council of Ministers appointed criminal investigators. Their 2012 report identified serious initial deficiencies: the scene was not properly cordoned off and was contaminated; blood found three metres from the body was not adequately explained; gastric fluid was unsealed and untested; mobile phone data was not properly recovered; not all soldiers were interviewed; and police accepted P.S.’s suicide assessment too readily. An independent forensic expert, M.M., concluded that the cause of death was indeterminable and that criminal involvement could not be ruled out. The investigators proposed a fresh police investigation.

The Attorney General initially declined, but in 2014 ordered further investigation. A second police investigation followed, though DNA from two soldiers did not match unknown male DNA found on the deceased’s clothing. Ultimately, the ECtHR found a violation of Article 2 under its procedural limb, holding that the investigation into Nicolaou’s death was undermined by serious initial omissions and the passage of time.

In *Nicolaou v. Cyprus*, five Cypriot nationals—the parents and siblings of Athanasios Nicolaou—complained under Article 2 of the Convention that Cyprus failed to conduct an effective investigation into his death. Nicolaou, aged 26, was serving mandatory military service. On 29 September 2005 he was on overnight leave and was due back at camp at 6:50 a.m. He failed to return. His car was later found near a bridge in Alassa, and his body was found under the bridge. A forensic pathologist, P.S., attended the scene and reportedly suggested the death was suicide from a fall and that no criminal act was suspected. The post-mortem concluded that death resulted from multiple injuries consistent with a fall from a height, with no signs of criminal activity.

The initial police investigation treated the case as an ordinary unnatural death/suicide. It was carried out by local police rather than specialist crime investigators. The family alleged that Nicolaou had been bullied and humiliated at camp, including being called “Australian,” and suggested he may have been killed by fellow soldiers. Statements were taken from over fifty witnesses, but the police report found no evidence of crime. A parallel military investigation also concluded suicide. A first inquest in 2007 found death under conditions resembling suicide. However, in 2008 the Supreme Court quashed that verdict, holding there was insufficient evidence of suicide, and ordered a second inquest. In 2009 the second coroner found that death resulted from injuries caused by a fall from a height, but concluded there was insufficient evidence of either suicide or a criminal act. The Attorney General found no grounds for criminal proceedings.

The family obtained private forensic opinions that strongly criticised the investigation. These experts noted that the scene had not been properly secured, no DNA samples had been taken from the car, glasses, watch, wallet or clothing, the gastric-fluid vial had not been sealed, stomach contents and vomit had not been tested, blood found three metres from the body had not been explained, and the absence of expected external or skeletal injuries cast doubt on the fall-from-height theory. They suggested possible third-party involvement.

In 2011 the Council of Ministers appointed criminal investigators. An independent forensic pathologist, M.M., found the scene inspection, post-mortem and police investigation substandard. He considered the fall theory unreliable, said the cause of death was indeterminable, and did not rule out a criminal act. The investigators identified serious initial omissions: failure to cordon the scene, contaminated or lost evidence, no proper DNA testing or mobile-phone data recovery, and failure to trace all soldiers. They recommended police re-examination. The Attorney General initially declined but later ordered a second police investigation in 2015. Further DNA testing found unknown male DNA on the deceased’s clothes, but no match to two soldiers tested; by then, time had degraded the evidence.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of the procedural aspect of Article 2. The investigation into Nicolaou’s death was ineffective and undermined by serious initial omissions—especially the early assumption of suicide, failure to secure the scene and preserve evidence—and by the passage of time. The State had not fulfilled its positive obligation to conduct an adequate and effective investigation capable of establishing the cause of death and, if appropriate, identifying and punishing those responsible.

In *Nicolaou v. Cyprus* (App. no. 29068/10, judgment 28 January 2020), the applicants—the parents and siblings of Athanasios Nicolaou—complained under Article 2 of the Convention that Cyprus failed to carry out an effective investigation into his death. Nicolaou, a 26-year-old Cypriot national, was performing mandatory military service. After being granted overnight leave on 28 September 2005, he left home early the next morning to return to camp but never reported. His car was found near a bridge in Alassa, and his body was found under the bridge. The initial forensic pathologist, P.S., reportedly said at the scene that the death was suicide from a fall and that no criminal act was suspected, although he later denied stating “suicide.” This early view oriented the police towards treating the case as an ordinary unnatural death, and it was handled by local police rather than specialist crime investigators.

The initial investigation suffered from serious omissions relevant to the Article 2 complaint. The scene was not immediately secured, leading to contamination. No DNA samples were taken from the car. The area was not thoroughly examined despite blood later being found three metres from the body. The gastric-fluid vial was not sealed and stomach contents were not tested; vomit, sand and water in the mouth were not analysed; DNA was not taken from the deceased’s glasses, watch, wallet or clothing; and mobile phone data was not properly recovered. Many soldiers were not interviewed. The first inquest in 2007 found no evidence of third-party criminal liability and concluded that death occurred under conditions resembling suicide.

The family challenged that verdict. The Supreme Court quashed it because suicide required evidence of intent, and ordered a second inquest. In 2009, the second coroner found that death resulted from injuries caused by a fall from a height, but found insufficient evidence of suicide or a criminal act. The Attorney General later decided that no criminal proceedings were warranted.

The family obtained private forensic opinions from O.P., P.K., D.G. and M.G. These experts criticised the autopsy and police investigation. They noted unexplained bruising, intact glasses after an alleged high fall, blood away from the body, failure to test key samples, and opined that the injuries were not clearly consistent with a fall and could indicate third-party violence or a criminal act. In 2011 the Council of Ministers appointed criminal investigators and independent pathologist M.M. M.M. found the original scene inspection, autopsy and police investigation substandard. He concluded that the cause of death was indeterminate and that a criminal act had not been ruled out. The investigators identified serious police omissions, considered that death may possibly have been criminal, and recommended a fresh police investigation. The Attorney General initially declined because of the long delay, but in 2014 ordered further investigation. The second police investigation took some steps, including DNA testing and a new forensic opinion, but the passage of time and the initial failures made the cause of death impossible to resolve.

The applicants alleged that Cyprus violated the procedural limb of Article 2 by failing to conduct an effective official investigation capable of establishing the cause of death and identifying those responsible. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation, holding that the investigation into the conscript’s death had been undermined by serious initial omissions and the passage of time.

In *Bezzina Wettinger and Others v. Malta* (Application no. 52673/15, judgment of 21 January 2020), six Maltese applicants complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that, five decades after expropriation, they had still received no compensation and that the compensation fixed by the Land Arbitration Board (“LAB”) was inadequate.

The applicants and/or their ancestors held a perpetual emphyteusis over “Tal-Ħriereb,” about 23,606 sq m of land in Birkirkara and Msida. In 1961 the Governor declared about 7,531 sq m required for a public purpose, to be acquired by outright purchase. The applicants held most of the affected land under emphyteusis, jointly owning one third. In 1964 Notices to Treat offered £631 (about EUR 1,470) jointly to the dominus and the emphyteutae; they refused. The matter was referred to the LAB in 1964. In 1978 the LAB awarded MTL 1,161 (about EUR 2,704) and fixed a date for transfer. On rectification in 1981, the LAB acknowledged that its earlier decision had relied on a wrong measurement of the expropriated land and ordered correction, but left the compensation unchanged. It refused to apportion the compensation between the dominus and the emphyteutae, leaving that to the ordinary courts. Because the parties disagreed on their shares, the compensation was never apportioned or paid.

In 2005 the Constitutional Court rejected the applicants’ claims. In 2008 the European Court of Human Rights found an Article 6 violation concerning the length of the LAB proceedings ending in 1981 for the direct victims, but rejected other complaints: the complaint about inadequate compensation failed for non-exhaustion, and the complaint about non-payment was manifestly ill-founded because the applicants had failed to take steps to divide the compensation. In 2011 the applicants brought fresh constitutional redress proceedings challenging the quantum of compensation under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. They sought annulment of the LAB award, adequate compensation, refund of ground rent, and damages. Their architect valued the land at about EUR 8,805,000 in 2006, EUR 17,319 in 1964, and EUR 121,210 in 1978. The Government’s architect valued it as agricultural/outside the development zone at about EUR 3,610 in 1961.

The first-instance court in 2014 rejected the claim. It noted that the applicants were not challenging the compensation law itself; they had paid about 0.08 euro cents per sq m and received about 0.41 euro cents per sq m, more than the acquisition price. It found no proof that the award was inadequate. In 2015 the Constitutional Court confirmed. It held that the applicants only challenged the amount; non-payment since 1981 was due to their failure to determine shares and pursue ordinary proceedings, as confirmed in 2008. Ground rents had been repaid. The land was agricultural at the time of taking, so a fair balance had been struck.

The European Court declared the complaint admissible and found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It stressed that domestic law tied compensation to the value of the land at the time of the Notice to Treat (1964), even though the award was determined in 1981 and payment delayed further, with only 5% interest. This raised proportionality concerns, and similar Maltese cases had found such LAB awards inadequate. Even accepting that the land was agricultural, the award was strikingly low—lower than the Government architect’s own estimate. The 1981 rectification left compensation unchanged despite acknowledging that the earlier measurement was about 10% too small. The constitutional courts did not remedy this. Although delay after 1981 was attributable to the applicants, the 1981 award itself was not adequate, violating Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The case *Bezzina Wettinger and Others v. Malta* (ECtHR, 21 January 2020) concerned six Maltese applicants and an alleged breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 arising from the expropriation of land and allegedly inadequate compensation.

In 1960 the applicants and/or their ancestors, together with others, acquired the right of perpetual emphyteusis over land known as “Tal-Ħriereb”, measuring about 23,606 sq.m, between Birkirkara and Msida. The applicants jointly held one third. In 1961 the Governor declared part of the land, about 7,531 sq.m, required for a public purpose, to be acquired by outright purchase. In 1964 Notices to Treat offered the emphyteutae and the dominus £631 (about €1,470) jointly. The offer was refused, and the matter was referred to the Land Arbitration Board (LAB). In 1978 the LAB awarded MTL 1,161 (about €2,704). In 1981, on rectification, the LAB acknowledged that its earlier decision had relied on a wrong measurement but left the compensation unchanged. It also declined to apportion the compensation between the dominus and the emphyteutae, leaving that issue to the ordinary courts. Because the parties disagreed over their shares, the compensation was not apportioned or paid.

The applicants first brought constitutional redress, complaining under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 6 about delay. In 2005 the Constitutional Court rejected their claims. In 2008 the European Court found a violation of Article 6 concerning the length of the LAB proceedings from 1964 to 1981 for certain direct victims, but declared the remaining complaints inadmissible. In particular, the complaint about inadequate compensation was rejected for non-exhaustion, and the complaint about non-payment was found manifestly ill-founded because the applicants had failed to take steps to divide the compensation.

In 2011 the applicants brought fresh constitutional redress proceedings challenging the quantum of compensation. They argued that the award was derisory: the land had development potential, but it had been valued as agricultural land; domestic law limited compensation to the value at the time of the Notice to Treat, without accounting for the decades before payment; and they had paid ground rent while remaining unpaid. Their architect estimated the 2006 open-market value at about €8,805,000, the 1964 value at about €17,319, and the 1978 value at about €121,210. The first-instance court rejected the claim in 2014, finding the compensation closer to the price originally paid and accepting that the expert had used open-market rather than expropriation value. The Constitutional Court confirmed in 2015, holding that the land was agricultural at the time, that ground rents had been repaid, and that the post-1981 delay was the applicants’ fault.

Before the ECtHR, the Court declared the Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 complaint admissible. It reiterated that compensation terms are central to the fair-balance assessment and that taking property without payment reasonably related to its value will normally be disproportionate. It recalled that the delay from 1964 to 1981 was attributable to the authorities, but the delay from 1981 onwards was attributable to the applicants. The key issue was whether the 1981 LAB award itself was adequate. The Court noted that valuing the land at 1964 values despite payment decades later, with only 5% interest, raised proportionality concerns and had led to findings of inadequacy in similar Maltese cases. Although it accepted doubts about the land’s development status, the award was strikingly low—lower even than the Government’s own agricultural valuation. The LAB had also admitted a wrong measurement, smaller by about 10%, without increasing compensation. The Court concluded that the compensation determined more than two decades after the taking was not adequate, violating Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In *Bezzina Wettinger and Others v. Malta* (App. no. 52673/15), six Maltese nationals complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that, decades after their land was expropriated, they remained unpaid and the compensation fixed was inadequate.

In 1961 the Governor declared part of the land—about 7,531 sq m—required for a public purpose, to be acquired by outright purchase. In 1964 Notices to Treat offered £631 (about €1,470) jointly to the dominus and the emphyteutae. The offer was refused. The matter went to the Land Arbitration Board (LAB) in 1964. In 1978 the LAB awarded MTL 1,161 (about €2,704), fixed a date for the transfer deed, but did not apportion the compensation. A 1981 rectification corrected a measurement error but left the amount unchanged and reserved the shares issue for ordinary courts. Because the dominus and emphyteutae disagreed over their respective shares, the compensation was not divided or paid.

The applicants brought constitutional redress, alleging breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and excessive length under Article 6. In 2005 the Constitutional Court rejected their claims. In 2008 the European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 6 concerning the length of proceedings before the LAB ending in 1981. It rejected the compensation-inadequacy complaint for non-exhaustion and found the non-payment complaint manifestly ill-founded because the applicants had failed to take steps to divide the compensation.

In 2011 the applicants brought fresh constitutional proceedings challenging the quantum. They argued that the LAB award was inadequate because it treated the land as agricultural despite development use/potential, ignored inflation, ground rents paid, and the long delay between taking and payment. They also argued that Maltese law restricted compensation to the value at the time of the declaration/Notice to Treat, without accounting for later payment. Their architect valued the land much higher. The first-instance court rejected the claim in 2014, finding the compensation closer to what the empyhteutae had paid and not shown inadequate. In 2015 the Constitutional Court confirmed, holding that the applicants challenged only the amount, that non-payment resulted from their failure to determine shares and institute ordinary proceedings, that ground rents had been repaid, and that the land was agricultural at the time.

Before the Strasbourg Court, the complaint was declared admissible. The Court reiterated that compensation terms are material to fair balance, and taking property without payment reasonably related to its value will normally be disproportionate. It noted that the 2008 judgment had found most delay before 1981 attributable to the authorities, but delay after 1981 attributable to the applicants. The key issue was whether the 1981 LAB award itself was adequate. Domestic law valued the land at the 1964 Notice to Treat despite payment decades later, plus 5% interest, raising proportionality concerns. The Court accepted the land was not indisputably developable and had been treated as agricultural domestically. However, the award was strikingly low—lower than the Government’s own agricultural valuation—and the rectification kept the same amount despite acknowledging a wrong measurement. The Court therefore found the compensation fixed more than two decades after the taking was not adequate, breaching Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.
