In *Rasiński v. Poland* (Application no. 42969/18), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section) delivered judgment on 28 May 2020. The applicant, Artur Rasiński, a Polish national born in 1972, was detained in Łowicz Prison. He lodged an application on 31 August 2018, complaining under Article 3 of the Convention that the conditions of his detention—particularly overcrowding—between 18 July 2013 and 16 April 2015 (one year, eight months and twenty-eight days) amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment. He alleged that the space per person in his cells fell below the Polish statutory minimum of 3 sq. m. According to the domestic courts’ reasoning, he had indeed been held in overcrowded cells during that period; the cells were poorly equipped, not properly ventilated, and had mold on the walls.

The Government contested those findings. It argued that the national courts had not received sufficient information from the State Treasury’s representative and had relied solely on the applicant’s submissions and general statistics. The Government also submitted Prison Service information on cell surface area and cell occupancy, claiming the applicant had not been held in overcrowded cells.

Before applying to Strasbourg, the applicant brought a civil action against the State Treasury on 1 July 2016 for infringement of personal rights and compensation for detention in overcrowded cells. He claimed PLN 300,000 (approximately EUR 75,000). On 13 April 2017, the Łódź Regional Court awarded him PLN 5,000 (approximately EUR 1,250) and dismissed the remainder. It found that he had been detained in overcrowded cells and that prison authorities had dismissed all his complaints, thus violating his personal rights. On 23 February 2018, the Łódź Court of Appeal dismissed appeals by both the applicant and the State Treasury, upheld the lower court’s factual and legal findings, and excluded the State Treasury’s evidence as filed out of time. On 7 May 2018, a court-appointed lawyer advised that there were no grounds for a cassation appeal.

In the ECtHR proceedings, on 7 February 2019 the Government were given notice of the complaint concerning detention in overcrowded cells; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible under Rule 54 §3. The Government raised two main objections: first, that the applicant had lost his victim status because he had received PLN 5,000 compensation; second, that the treatment did not reach the minimum level of severity required by Article 3 due to mitigating factors. These included that he served his sentence in a semi-open penitentiary institution, his cell was open during the day and could be opened at night, he had freedom of movement outside the cell, could attend out-of-cell activities, and from 17 July 2014 to 16 April 2015 had a job and stayed outside the cell during working hours. The Court noted, however, that these submissions were not confirmed by evidence.

The Court reiterated that a favourable national decision does not deprive an applicant of victim status unless the authorities acknowledged, expressly or in substance, and afforded redress for the Convention breach. It considered the Government’s objections closely linked to the merits and joined them to the merits. The key alleged violation therefore concerned prolonged overcrowding and inadequate detention conditions, the domestic courts’ recognition of that violation, the adequacy of the compensation awarded, and the Government’s challenge to the factual basis and Article 3 severity.

**Summary of *Rasiński v. Poland* (Application no. 42969/18)**

The case of *Rasiński v. Poland* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr. Artur Rasiński, a Polish national born in 1972, against the Republic of Poland. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment, specifically regarding the conditions of his detention at Łowicz Prison between 18 July 2013 and 16 April 2015—a period of one year, eight months, and twenty-eight days.

The applicant submitted that during this period, he was held in cells where the space per person fell below the Polish statutory minimum standard of 3 square meters. He further alleged that the cells were poorly equipped, inadequately ventilated, and had mold on the walls. These claims were corroborated by the findings of domestic courts, which confirmed that he had indeed been detained in overcrowded conditions and that his complaints to prison authorities had been dismissed.

Following his detention, on 1 July 2016, the applicant brought a civil action against the State Treasury, seeking 300,000 Polish zlotys (approximately EUR 75,000) in damages for the infringement of his personal rights. On 13 April 2017, the Łódź Regional Court awarded him PLN 5,000 (approximately EUR 1,250) in compensation, acknowledging that the overcrowding had violated his personal rights. The court dismissed the remainder of his claim. On 23 February 2018, the Łódź Court of Appeal upheld this judgment, dismissing appeals by both the applicant and the State Treasury. The Court of Appeal also rejected evidence submitted late by the State Treasury, which attempted to contest the overcrowding findings.

In its observations to the European Court, the Government contested the national courts' findings, asserting that the applicant had not been held in overcrowded or inadequately furnished cells. They argued that the domestic courts had relied solely on the applicant's submissions and general statistics, and submitted a Prison Service statement claiming the applicant did not experience overcrowding. Additionally, the Government contended that the applicant had lost his victim status because he had been awarded compensation by the domestic courts. They also argued that the treatment did not reach the minimum level of severity required under Article 3, citing mitigating factors such as the semi-open nature of the penitentiary institution, freedom of movement outside his cell, and opportunities for work and out-of-cell activities. However, these submissions were not supported by evidence.

The European Court of Human Rights considered the Government's objections regarding victim status and the severity of the treatment. The Court noted that a favorable decision or measure does not automatically deprive an applicant of victim status unless the national authorities have acknowledged the breach and afforded sufficient redress. It found that the Government's arguments were closely linked to the merits of the complaint and decided to join these objections to the merits of the case for further examination. The case thus proceeded to determine whether the conditions of the applicant's detention amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment under Article 3 and whether the compensation awarded constituted sufficient redress.

In *Rasiński v. Poland* (Application no. 42969/18), the European Court of Human Rights examined a Polish national’s complaint under Article 3 of the Convention concerning allegedly inhuman and degrading detention conditions in Łowicz Prison. The applicant, Artur Rasiński, born in 1972 and detained in Łowicz Prison, lodged his application on 31 August 2018. On 7 February 2019, the Government were given notice of the complaint concerning his detention in overcrowded cells; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The alleged violation concerned the applicant’s detention in Łowicz Prison from 18 July 2013 to 16 April 2015—one year, eight months and twenty-eight days. The applicant claimed that he had been held in cells where the space per person was below the Polish statutory minimum of 3 square metres. According to the reasoning of the domestic courts, he had indeed been detained in overcrowded cells during that period. The cells were also described as poorly equipped, not properly ventilated, and with mold on the walls. The applicant stated that his complaints about these conditions had been dismissed by the prison authorities.

The Government contested the domestic courts’ findings. They argued that the national courts had not received sufficient information from the State Treasury’s representative and had relied solely on the applicant’s submissions and general statistics. The Government submitted a Prison Service statement concerning the surface area of the applicant’s cells and the number of persons incarcerated with him, asserting that he had not been held in overcrowded cells. The Government also argued that the applicant had lost his victim status because the domestic court had awarded him compensation. Alternatively, they submitted that the complaint was manifestly ill-founded because the treatment did not reach the minimum level of severity required by Article 3. In support, they cited mitigating factors: the applicant was held in a semi-open penitentiary institution; his cell was open during the day and could have been opened at night; he enjoyed freedom of movement outside his cell; he could attend out-of-cell activities; and between 17 July 2014 and 16 April 2015 he had a job and stayed outside his cell during working hours. The Court noted, however, that these submissions were not confirmed by any evidence.

At the domestic level, on 1 July 2016 the applicant brought a civil action against the State Treasury for infringement of personal rights and compensation for detention in overcrowded cells, claiming PLN 300,000 (approximately EUR 75,000). On 13 April 2017, the Łódź Regional Court awarded him PLN 5,000 (approximately EUR 1,250) and dismissed the remainder of his action. It found that he had been detained in overcrowded cells and that his complaints had been dismissed by the prison authorities, violating his personal rights. On 23 February 2018, the Łódź Court of Appeal dismissed appeals by both the applicant and the State Treasury. It excluded the State Treasury’s evidence—the Prison Service information on cell surface and inmate numbers—as filed out of time, and upheld the lower court’s factual and legal findings. On 7 May 2018, a court-appointed lawyer advised the applicant that there were no grounds to lodge a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained that the overcrowding and conditions of detention amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment under Article 3. The Court reiterated that a favourable domestic decision does not automatically deprive an applicant of victim status unless the national authorities acknowledged the breach and afforded adequate redress. It found that the Government’s objections—loss of victim status and failure to meet the minimum severity threshold—were closely linked to the merits of the complaint. The Court therefore joined those objections to the merits. The excerpt provided ends at that procedural stage.
001-191487:
**Summary of *Šaranović v. Montenegro* (Application no. 31775/16)**

**Case Background and Facts**

The applicant, Mr. Slobodan Šaranović, a Montenegrin national born in 1938, lodged an application against Montenegro on 2 June 2016. The case concerned his pre-trial detention, which he alleged was unlawful and excessively long, and that the decisions extending it lacked proper reasoning.

The events began after the murder of the applicant's brother in 2009 and the subsequent murder of an individual named "X" in Belgrade in 2013. The Serbian Organised Crime Prosecution opened an investigation in July 2013, suspecting the applicant of arranging X's murder as revenge, given that X's brother was believed responsible for the applicant's brother's death. The applicant was arrested in Montenegro, and Serbia sought his extradition. However, in January 2014, the Montenegrin High Court refused extradition, and he was released in February 2014. In April 2014, the Supreme State Prosecution of Montenegro authorised his prosecution domestically.

**Detention and Alleged Violations**

On 8 April 2014, the applicant was arrested in Montenegro. The High State Prosecutor opened an investigation on 9 April 2014. The following day, an investigating judge ordered his detention for one month based on reasonable suspicion of aggravated murder through incitement, citing risks of witness interference and threat to public peace and order due to the crime's gravity. His detention was extended monthly by the High Court, relying on the same grounds: reasonable suspicion, potential witness influence, the gravity of the offence (punishable by ten years or more), and the risk to public order.

An indictment was issued on 7 October 2014, one day before the six-month statutory limit for detention without an indictment expired. The High Court extended his detention "until a further decision of the court." However, the indictment was returned for further investigation on 22 October 2014.

A critical period at issue was between 15 November and 15 December 2014. Under domestic law (Article 179 § 2 of the Criminal Procedure Code), the court had a duty to review the reasons for detention and issue a decision every 30 days before the indictment entered into force. The applicant argued that no such review occurred, rendering his detention unlawful. The High Court finally extended his detention on 15 December 2014, stating it reviewed the case of its own motion. The Court of Appeals dismissed the applicant's appeal, holding that while the 30-day time-limit was breached, this did not automatically render the detention unlawful or mean it had ceased.

The applicant further alleged that his detention, lasting over two years, exceeded the six-month maximum without an indictment. The Government argued that once the indictment was issued (even if returned), the detention regime under Article 179 applied, allowing detention up to three years. The courts also repeatedly extended the investigation. The applicant complained that all decisions extending his detention were insufficiently reasoned, merely copying earlier reasoning without a genuine examination of why the reasons persisted, and failing to consider his personal circumstances (age, health, family). He raised these issues in a constitutional appeal, which the Constitutional Court dismissed on 29 May 2015, finding the decisions were reasoned and non-arbitrary.

The applicant's detention continued until 9 December 2016, when it was revoked. He was murdered on 11 March 2017. His wife expressed a wish to pursue the application. The European Court of Human Rights declared the complaints concerning the lawfulness and length of detention, and the lack of reasoning in the decisions, admissible.

In *Šaranović v. Montenegro* (Application no. 31775/16), the applicant was a Montenegrin national born in 1938. The case concerned his pre-trial detention in Montenegro on suspicion of aggravated murder through incitement. Serbian authorities had investigated him over the 2013 murder of X, allegedly arranged in revenge for the murder of the applicant’s brother. After Serbia’s extradition request was refused, Montenegro authorised prosecution. He was arrested on 8 April 2014, and an investigation was ordered on 9 April 2014. On 10 April 2014 the investigating judge ordered one month’s detention under Article 175 § 1(2) and (4) of the Criminal Procedure Code, citing reasonable suspicion, risk of witness interference, the gravity of the offence, and a threat to public peace and order. Detention was then extended repeatedly on similar grounds.

The central alleged Article 5 violation concerned the period from 15 November to 15 December 2014. On 7 October 2014 an indictment was issued and detention was extended “until a further decision,” but that decision was quashed. On 17 October 2014 detention was again extended under Article 175 § 1(4), relying on the same reasons plus possible absconding. On 22 October 2014 the indictment was returned for further investigation. The Court of Appeals upheld the detention on 31 October, finding that the six-month limit had been complied with because the investigation began on 9 April and the indictment was issued on 7 October; the fact that the indictment was later returned was considered irrelevant.

The applicant argued that his detention became unlawful on 15 November 2014 because, under Article 179 § 2 CPC, the court had to review detention every 30 days before the indictment entered into force. No such decision was issued until 15 December 2014, when he sought release. On that same day, the High Court extended detention “until a further decision,” invoking Article 179 § 2 and the same grounds as before. On 25 December 2014 the Court of Appeals dismissed his appeal, holding that failure to review within 30 days did not mean detention had ceased and that detention remained lawful.

The applicant further complained that detention could last at most six months without an indictment, yet lasted over two years without the indictment ever entering into force. He also alleged that the extension decisions were insufficiently reasoned, that the reasoning was merely copied from one decision to another, and that the courts failed genuinely to examine whether the grounds for detention persisted. He raised these issues in constitutional appeals. The Constitutional Court dismissed his first appeal on 29 May 2015, served in January 2016, finding the decisions reasoned and not arbitrary. He later challenged continued extensions, citing *Mugoša v. Montenegro*; that appeal may have remained pending.

Detention continued through 2015–2016. Indictments were returned three times, and investigation time limits were extended many times. The applicant was repeatedly hospitalised. On 9 December 2016 detention was revoked because the grounds no longer persisted: the indictment had been returned for a third time, it was uncertain when or whether it would enter into force, and detention could last three years at most. The applicant was murdered on 11 March 2017. His wife pursued the application before the ECtHR. Domestic proceedings were terminated, and the indictment never entered into force.

Before the Court, the Government argued that review deadlines were not mandatory and that the absence of a written extension decision for a period did not make detention unlawful. The applicant argued that the deadlines were mandatory and that the prosecutor had abused the six-month rule by issuing an indictment just before the deadline and then repeatedly returning it. The Court declared admissible the complaints concerning the lawfulness and length of detention and the alleged lack of reasoning.

In *Šaranović v. Montenegro* (ECtHR, App. No. 31775/16, judgment 5 March 2019), the applicant was Slobodan Šaranović, a Montenegrin national born in 1938. The case concerned his pre-trial detention in Montenegro and alleged violations of Articles 5 and 6 of the Convention.

The background involved a revenge killing. In 2009 the applicant’s brother was murdered in Belgrade, and Šaranović publicly offered a reward for information. In April 2013 a man, X, was murdered in Belgrade. X’s brother had been identified by Serbian authorities as an organised-crime leader linked to the 2003 murder of Serbia’s Prime Minister. In July 2013 Serbia opened an investigation suspecting that Šaranović had arranged X’s murder because he believed X’s brother was responsible for his own brother’s death. The applicant was arrested in Montenegro, and Serbia requested his extradition. Montenegro refused extradition in January 2014, and he was released in February 2014. In April 2014 Montenegrin authorities authorised his prosecution locally.

On 8 April 2014 the applicant was arrested again. The next day the High State Prosecutor ordered an investigation for aggravated murder through incitement. On 10 April 2014 an investigating judge ordered detention for up to one month under Article 175 § 1(2) and (4) of the Criminal Procedure Code. The grounds were reasonable suspicion, risk of influencing witnesses, the gravity of the offence, and the risk that release would seriously disturb public peace and order. His detention was extended monthly during the investigation on essentially the same grounds.

On 7 October 2014 the prosecutor issued an indictment, within the six-month investigation period, and detention was extended. The indictment was later returned for further investigation. On 17 October 2014 the High Court again extended detention “until a further decision,” relying on Article 175 § 1(4), adding a risk that the applicant might abscond. The Court of Appeals upheld this, treating the absconding finding as an obvious error but irrelevant, and noting that the indictment had been issued within six months.

The key alleged violation concerned the period 15 November to 15 December 2014. Under Article 179 § 2 CPC, while the indictment had not entered into force, the court had to review detention every 30 days and issue a decision extending or revoking it. No such decision was issued by 15 November 2014. On 15 December 2014 the applicant sought release, arguing that his detention had been unlawful since 15 November. The same day the High Court extended detention until further decision, repeating earlier reasons, especially the public peace and order ground. On appeal, the Court of Appeals held that failure to review within the time-limit did not mean detention had ceased, and that the indictment had been issued within six months; its later return was irrelevant.

The applicant also complained that detention could last at most six months without an indictment, yet his detention lasted over two years without any indictment entering into force. He further alleged that the extension decisions and the Constitutional Court’s decision lacked adequate reasoning and merely copied identical reasoning without considering his age, health, family circumstances, or the overall length of detention. His constitutional appeal was dismissed in May 2015.

Detention continued through many further extensions and was revoked on 9 December 2016. The applicant was murdered on 11 March 2017; his wife was permitted to pursue the application. The Court declared admissible the complaints about the lawfulness and length of detention and the alleged lack of reasoning in the detention decisions and the Constitutional Court’s decision, examining them under Articles 5 and 6.
001-195540:
In *Dobrovitskaya and Others v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* (ECtHR, Second Section, 3 September 2019), six applications were joined. The applicants were eleven Moldovan and Russian nationals who alleged violations arising from events in the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Transdniestrian Republic” (“MRT”).

Each applicant, except Mrs Galina Samatova in application no. 8064/11, was detained by “MRT” authorities. Most applicants complained of unlawful detention. Some also alleged inhuman conditions of detention, unfair trial, and the lack of effective remedies for their complaints. One applicant, Mr Serghei Boltenco (application no. 28972/13), additionally complained under Article 2 that the authorities failed to provide him with necessary medical assistance, exposing him to a real risk to his life.

Procedurally, the applications were lodged between 2010 and 2014. The Russian Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection. On admissibility, the Court first addressed Mrs Galina Samatova’s complaint. Because her son, Mr Ivan Samatov, was alive and could pursue the application himself, her own complaints as a direct or indirect victim were incompatible *ratione personae* and rejected. Mr Boltenco died in November 2014; his wife was permitted to continue the application.

The Russian Government argued that several applications were lodged outside the six-month time-limit. The Court held that complaints concerning ongoing detention, conditions of detention, and lack of effective remedies amounted to a “continuing situation” while the applicants remained detained, so they were timely. However, Mr Ursu’s complaints under Article 3 concerning alleged ill-treatment and under Article 6 concerning his conviction were based on a final judgment of 29 June 2010; since he applied only on 11 April 2011, those specific complaints were time-barred. For the applicants in application no. 6151/12, their Article 6 complaint was timely because the “MRT” Supreme Court upheld their conviction on 19 July 2011, less than six months before they applied.

The Moldovan Government argued non-exhaustion of domestic remedies in Moldova, but the Court rejected this on the same grounds as in *Mozer v. Moldova and Russia*. The Russian Government also argued non-exhaustion before Russian courts. The Court rejected that objection because Russia did not identify which courts had jurisdiction, the legal basis for such complaints, or how decisions would be enforced, and because Russia denied involvement in the Transdniestrian events.

On jurisdiction, the Court reaffirmed *Ilaşcu*, *Catan*, and *Mozer*. Moldova, as the territorial State, had jurisdiction but lacked effective control over Transdniestria; its obligations were positive measures. Russia had jurisdiction because it contributed to the creation of the “MRT” and continued to provide military, economic, and political support, exercising effective control and decisive influence over the “MRT” authorities. Thus, the applicants fell within Russia’s jurisdiction under Article 1.

The Court declared Mr Boltenco’s Article 2 complaint concerning denial of medical assistance admissible. The judgment then proceeded to determine whether the alleged violations engaged the responsibility of Moldova and/or Russia.

**Dobrovitskaya and Others v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia** (ECtHR, Second Section, 3 September 2019) concerned six applications brought by eleven Moldovan and Russian nationals. The case arose from events in Transdniestria, controlled by the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Transdniestrian Republic” (“MRT”). Except Galina Samatova (application no. 8064/11), each applicant had been detained by MRT authorities. All applicants except those in application no. 28972/13 complained of unlawful detention; several also alleged inhuman conditions of detention, unfair trial, and lack of effective remedies. Application no. 28972/13, brought by Serghei Boltenco, concerned the authorities’ alleged failure to provide medical assistance for his condition, exposing him to a real risk to life under Article 2. Boltenco later died, and his wife continued the application.

The applications were lodged from 2010 onward. Between 2014 and 2016, certain complaints were communicated, while other parts were declared inadmissible. The Russian Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection. Admissibility issues included victim status, death of an applicant, the six-month rule, exhaustion of domestic remedies, and jurisdiction.

Galina Samatova’s own complaints were rejected as incompatible *ratione personae*: her son, Ivan Samatov, was alive and could pursue his own application. Boltenco’s death did not terminate the case; his wife was permitted to continue it.

On the six-month rule, the Court found Ursu’s complaints about ill-treatment under Article 3 and unfair conviction under Article 6 time-barred. His final MRT Supreme Court judgment was on 29 June 2010, but he applied on 11 April 2011. However, complaints by Samatov, Ursu, Boltenco and the four applicants in application no. 6151/12 about detention conditions, lawfulness of detention, and lack of remedies were treated as “continuing situations” because they remained in detention. For application no. 6151/12, the MRT Supreme Court upheld convictions on 19 July 2011, and the application was lodged on 18 January 2012; given the lack of effective MRT remedies, it was timely.

Moldova argued non-exhaustion, claiming applicants could seek compensation or quashing in Moldovan courts. The Court rejected this, following *Mozer*. Russia also argued non-exhaustion, but the Court found Russia had not shown available and effective remedies, especially while denying involvement in Transdniestria.

On jurisdiction, the Court reaffirmed that Moldova, as the territorial State, had jurisdiction, but its obligations were positive and limited to measures within its power. Russia had jurisdiction because it contributed militarily and politically to the MRT’s creation and continued to exercise effective control and decisive influence over MRT authorities through military, economic and political support. The applicants therefore fell within Russia’s jurisdiction under Article 1. The Court dismissed Russia’s objections *ratione personae* and *ratione loci*.

The Court then declared Boltenco’s Article 2 complaint about lack of medical assistance admissible, as not manifestly ill-founded. The case proceeded to determine whether the alleged violations engaged the responsibility of Moldova and/or Russia. The key facts concerned MRT detention and criminal proceedings, allegedly inhuman detention conditions, unfair trial, lack of effective remedies, and one life-threatening medical neglect claim, set against the broader issue of dual jurisdiction in Transdniestria.

In *Dobrovitskaya and Others v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* (ECtHR, Second Section, 3 September 2019), six joined applications were brought by eleven Moldovan and Russian nationals. The case concerned detentions, criminal proceedings, and detention conditions imposed by the authorities of the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Transdniestrian Republic” (“MRT”) in the Transdniestrian region of Moldova.

Each applicant, except Mrs Galina Samatova in application no. 8064/11, was detained by MRT authorities. All applications except no. 28972/13 included complaints of unlawful detention. Some applicants also alleged inhuman conditions of detention, unfair trial, and the lack of effective remedies. The applications were lodged between 2010 and 2014 and communicated to the respondent Governments between 2014 and 2016. The Russian Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

The alleged violations centred on the conduct of MRT detention authorities. In application no. 28972/13, Mr Serghei Boltenco complained under Article 2 that the authorities failed to provide him with requisite medical assistance for his condition, exposing him to a real risk to his life. He died from a heart attack on 19 November 2014, and his wife expressed the wish to continue the application. The Court allowed her to do so and continued to refer to him as the applicant.

Several admissibility issues arose. Mrs Samatova lodged application no. 8064/11 in her own name and on behalf of her son, Ivan Samatov, who was isolated in an MRT prison. The Court held that her personal complaints—inhuman conditions, unlawful detention, and lack of effective remedies—were incompatible *ratione personae* because her son was alive and could pursue the application himself.

The Russian Government argued that several applications were late under the six-month rule. The Court distinguished between instantaneous acts and continuing situations. Mr Ursu’s complaints under Article 3 concerning alleged ill-treatment and under Article 6 concerning his conviction were rejected as out of time: his final conviction was on 29 June 2010, but he applied on 11 April 2011. However, complaints about ongoing detention conditions, lawfulness of detention, and lack of effective remedies were treated as continuing situations and were timely. The Article 6 complaint in application no. 6151/12 was also timely because the MRT Supreme Court upheld the conviction on 19 July 2011, less than six months before the application was lodged.

On exhaustion of domestic remedies, Moldova argued that the applicants should have used Moldovan remedies. The Court rejected this objection, following its earlier case-law in *Mozer*. Russia argued that the applicants had failed to exhaust remedies before Russian courts, but the Court dismissed that objection because Russia denied involvement in Transdniestria and did not identify accessible and effective remedies. The Court also found that no effective remedies existed within the MRT.

On jurisdiction, the Court held that both respondent States had jurisdiction under Article 1 of the Convention. Moldova, as the territorial State, had jurisdiction, but its responsibility was limited to positive obligations to take measures within its power. Russia had jurisdiction because it had contributed militarily and politically to the creation of the separatist regime and continued to exercise effective control and decisive influence over the MRT authorities through military, economic, and political support.

The Article 2 complaint brought by Mr Boltenco was declared admissible and not manifestly ill-founded. The Court then proceeded to determine whether the alleged violations engaged the responsibility of either respondent State.

In *Burlakov and Lysenko v. Ukraine* (no. 19103/11, ECtHR, 17 Dec 2019), two Ukrainian nationals were arrested on 25 June 2010 by State Security Service officers on drug-trafficking suspicion. They alleged they were beaten and ill-treated during and after arrest. The first applicant was examined by ambulance and hospital doctors, who noted bruises on his right thigh, lumbar and patellar regions; an expert later found minor bruises on his arms, trunk and left leg, caused by blunt objects three to five days earlier. The second applicant was examined on 29 June 2010; the expert found minor bruises on his head, right arm and right leg, caused five to eight days earlier.

Domestic authorities refused criminal proceedings into the ill-treatment. For the first applicant, an investigator found no crime, noted the injuries were minor, and said officers were empowered to use special means during arrest; courts upheld this, suggesting injuries could have resulted from resisting lawful arrest. Later, another investigator refused proceedings against him for resisting arrest, finding no resistance but non-criminal disobedience. For the second applicant, an investigator also refused proceedings, dating his injuries to 21–24 June 2010 and relying on police powers during arrest; courts upheld this.

The applicants complained under Article 3 of ill-treatment and ineffective investigation; Article 13 of no effective remedies; Article 3 of poor transport/detention conditions; Article 5 §§3–5 of pre-trial detention; Article 3 of inadequate medical assistance for the second applicant; and Article 34 of hindered communication with the Court. Pre-trial detention was repeatedly extended for case complexity, serious charges, and risks of absconding, obstruction or reoffending. In *Burlakov and Lysenko v. Ukraine* (App. No. 19103/11), two Ukrainian nationals arrested on 25 June 2010 by State Security Service officers on suspicion of drug trafficking alleged ill-treatment during and after arrest. The first applicant was quickly examined: ambulance and hospital doctors noted bruises on his thigh, lumbar and patellar regions; a later expert found minor bruises on his arms, trunk and left leg, caused by blunt objects three to five days earlier. The second applicant was examined on 29 June 2010; an expert found minor bruises on his head, right arm and right leg, caused five to eight days earlier.

Domestic authorities refused to open criminal proceedings into both ill-treatment claims in August and September 2010. They found no constituent elements of a crime and noted that officers could use special means and other measures to arrest suspects. The first applicant’s refusal was upheld by the Chervonozavodskyy District Court in April 2011 and the Kharkiv Regional Court of Appeal in July 2011, which suggested he might have been injured while resisting lawful arrest. Yet a separate May 2011 inquiry found he had not resisted arrest but had shown disobedience—a contradiction. The second applicant’s refusal was also upheld on appeal, relying on the expert’s injury timeline. These inquiries were only pre-investigation checks, not full criminal investigations.

The applicants also challenged their pre-trial detention. Courts authorized and repeatedly extended it based on the case’s complexity, serious charges, risk of absconding, obstructing the investigation, or reoffending. In July 2011 they were committed for trial; detention continued. In August 2014 they were convicted of drug trafficking and sentenced to over nine years’ imprisonment.

As to conditions, they alleged that during transport to and from hearings they were held in prison vans and court transit cells with poor ventilation, no fresh air, high summer temperatures, tobacco smoke, no food, and sometimes with detainees suffering from tuberculosis. Prosecutors rejected some complaints but confirmed one transport with a TB detainee due to lack of information; the Ombudsman partly substantiated the second applicant’s transit-cell conditions and said authorities planned sanitation and ventilation improvements. The second applicant received treatment for spinal disc herniation, a gall bladder polyp and other illnesses. The applicants further alleged hindrance of communication with the ECtHR, including difficulty meeting representatives and limited access to the case file.

Before the ECtHR, complaints concerned Articles 3 and 13 (ill-treatment, ineffective investigation, lack of effective remedies), Article 3 (poor transport/detention conditions), Article 5 §§3, 4, 5 (pre-trial detention), Article 3 (inadequate medical assistance for the second applicant), and Article 34 (hindrance of communication). The Court declared these admissible. On ill-treatment, it reiterated that force during arrest must be indispensable and not excessive. The medical evidence raised arguable ill-treatment claims, triggering an effective-investigation duty. However, evidential gaps and possible legitimate force made causation hard to establish—difficulty stemming from the authorities’ failure to investigate. The contradictions about resistance and the use of limited pre-investigation inquiries fell short of minimum standards of independence, thoroughness, promptness and public scrutiny. The Court concluded that no serious effort was made to investigate the applicants’ ill-treatment allegations.

**Burlakov and Lysenko v. Ukraine** (App. no. 19103/11, ECtHR, 17 December 2019) concerned two Ukrainian nationals arrested late on 25 June 2010 by State Security Service officers on suspicion of drug trafficking. They alleged that officers beat and ill-treated them during and after arrest. Medical evidence partly supported the claims. The first applicant was seen by ambulance doctors early on 26 June 2010 with bruises to the right thigh, lumbar and patellar areas. An expert examination between 29 June and 2 July 2010 found minor bruises on his arms, trunk and left leg, caused by blunt objects three to five days earlier. The second applicant was examined on 29 June 2010 and had minor bruises on his head, right arm and right leg, caused five to eight days earlier.

Domestic authorities handled the ill-treatment claims through pre-investigation inquiries rather than full criminal investigations. On 21 August 2010 an investigator refused to open proceedings over the first applicant’s alleged ill-treatment, finding no crime and noting that officers could use special means to arrest a suspect. On 14 April 2011 a district court upheld that decision, suggesting the first applicant might have been injured while resisting lawful arrest. However, on 20 May 2011 another investigator refused to open proceedings against the first applicant for resisting arrest, finding that he had not resisted but merely disobeyed officers. The second applicant’s complaint was similarly rejected on 10 September 2010 and upheld by courts in December 2010 and July 2011.

The applicants also complained about other matters: poor conditions in prison vans and court transit cells—lack of fresh air and ventilation, high summer temperatures, tobacco smoke, no food, and transport with tuberculosis-infected detainees; their pre-trial detention and its extensions, which courts based on the complexity of the case, seriousness of charges, and risks of absconding, obstruction, or further offences; the second applicant’s allegedly inadequate medical care for spinal disc herniation, gall bladder polyp and other illnesses; and alleged hindrance of their communication with the ECtHR, including restrictions on meeting representatives and accessing the case file. The prosecution dismissed some transport complaints, while the Ombudsman partly substantiated the second applicant’s complaint about transit-cell conditions. In August 2014 the applicants were convicted of drug trafficking and sentenced to more than nine years’ imprisonment.

Before the ECtHR, the complaints given notice concerned Articles 3 and 13 (ill-treatment, ineffective investigation, lack of remedies), Article 3 (conditions of transport/detention on hearing days and inadequate medical assistance for the second applicant), Article 5 §§ 3, 4 and 5 (pre-trial detention), and Article 34 (hindrance of communication with the Court). The Court declared the ill-treatment and related Article 13 complaints admissible. It reiterated that force in arrest is permitted only if indispensable and not excessive. The applicants’ documented injuries raised arguable ill-treatment claims, triggering an obligation to investigate. Although evidential gaps and possible legitimate force made causation hard to establish, the Court held that this difficulty resulted from the authorities’ failure to investigate effectively. It criticised the use of limited pre-investigation inquiries, incompatible with effective-remedy standards, and the contradictory findings about whether the first applicant resisted arrest. It concluded that no serious effort was made to investigate the ill-treatment allegations.
001-192985:
In *Tasev v. North Macedonia* (ECtHR, 16 May 2019), the applicant, Slavčo Tasev, was a judge of the Štip Court of Appeal. The case concerned the refusal of the authorities to register his self-declared ethnicity—Macedonian—in the electoral roll for judges, where he had previously been recorded as Bulgarian since 1995.

In September 2012, a vacancy notice announced the election of five members to the State Judicial Council (SJC) from among sitting judges. Although ethnicity was not a formal eligibility requirement, the SJC electoral system included general candidate lists and a separate list for judges belonging to ethnic-minority communities. After the election announcement, on 28 September 2012, Tasev asked the Ministry of Justice to change his ethnicity entry from Bulgarian to Macedonian. On 15 October 2012, when the electoral roll was made available for inspection, he filed a fresh request under section 17 of the State Judicial Act.

On 18 October 2012, the Ministry of Justice refused the request. It reasoned that the request had been submitted after the election announcement and was aimed at securing an electoral right in the SJC election. It also said allowing the change would put other judges at a disadvantage. The Administrative Court upheld that decision on 26 October 2012, finding that the requested change was not a mere “rectification” and that Tasev had previously declared himself Bulgarian in the 2006, 2008 and 2010 electoral rolls. On 5 November 2012, the Higher Administrative Court dismissed his appeal, repeating that the refusal did not restrict his right to ethnic identity because the request came after the election announcement. Later, the SJC struck Tasev from the general list of candidates because his declared Macedonian ethnicity did not match official records showing him as Bulgarian.

Tasev complained under Article 6 of the Convention that he had not had an opportunity to examine and comment on the 2006, 2008 and 2010 electoral-roll extracts submitted by the Ministry and relied on by the Administrative Court. He also complained that the refusal to change his ethnicity violated his right to ethnic identity. The European Court of Human Rights treated that latter complaint as falling under Article 8, the right to respect for private life.

The Government argued that Tasev had abused his right to self-identification in order to improve his chances in the SJC election. They noted that he had declared himself Bulgarian since 1995 and that his request came only after the election announcement. Tasev maintained that ethnicity was a personal right, that his self-identification as Macedonian was genuine, and that he would not have gained an advantage because he could stand on a general candidate list regardless of ethnicity.

The Court held that ethnic identity is an aspect of private life protected by Article 8. The refusal to change his ethnicity entry therefore amounted to an interference with that right. The central issue was whether the interference was “in accordance with the law.” Under section 17 of the State Judicial Act, the electoral roll was made available only after the election was announced, and judges could seek rectification of their details within a short period. Nothing in that provision barred judges running for the SJC from requesting rectification after the announcement. Yet the domestic authorities refused Tasev’s request essentially because of its timing, without a clear statutory basis. Although the law was accessible, its application was not foreseeable. The Court therefore found that the interference was not “in accordance with the law” and violated Article 8. It did not need to examine the other requirements of Article 8 § 2.

In *Tasev v. North Macedonia* (App. no. 9825/13, 16 May 2019), the applicant was Slavčo Tasev, a judge of the Štip Court of Appeal. In September 2012, a vacancy notice announced elections for five State Judicial Council (SJC) members to be elected by sitting judges. Ethnicity was not an express requirement for the posts. On 28 September 2012, Tasev asked the Ministry of Justice to change his ethnicity entry in the judicial electoral roll from Bulgarian to Macedonian. After the roll was made available for inspection on 15 October 2012, he lodged a fresh request under section 17 of the State Judicial Act. The Ministry refused on 18 October, reasoning that the request was submitted after the election announcement, was intended to secure an electoral right in the SJC election, and would disadvantage other judges. The Administrative Court upheld that decision on 26 October, adding that the change was not a mere rectification and that extracts from the 2006, 2008 and 2010 electoral rolls showed him registered as Bulgarian. On 5 November 2012, the Higher Administrative Court dismissed his appeal, stating that changing ethnicity after the election announcement could not be regarded as restricting his ethnic identity and that, as a Bulgarian, he had enjoyed election-related rights.

Meanwhile, Tasev had applied for election to the SJC on 5 October 2012, submitting a statement that he was Macedonian and applying on the general list for judges within the Štip Court of Appeal’s jurisdiction. On 3 December 2012, the SJC struck him from that list because his declared Macedonian ethnicity conflicted with official records showing Bulgarian ethnicity since 1995. He complained under Article 6 that he had not been able to examine or comment on the old electoral rolls relied on by the Administrative Court, and under Article 8 that the refusal to change his ethnicity entry violated his private life and ethnic identity. The Court analysed the latter complaint under Article 8.

The Court observed that ethnic identity falls within private life. Since domestic law required or allowed judges to declare ethnicity in the electoral roll for SJC elections, the authorities’ refusal to record Tasev’s declared ethnicity interfered with Article 8. The Government did not deny that interference. The central issue was whether the refusal was “in accordance with law.” The domestic authorities relied mainly on the timing of the request—after the election announcement and while Tasev was a candidate—and on alleged disadvantage to other judges. Yet they cited no relevant statutory provision. The Higher Administrative Court cited the State Judicial Council Act and the General Administrative Procedure Act, but those provisions did not govern the electoral roll or rectification of entries. Section 17, which did govern rectification, allowed judges to seek correction after the roll was made available, which necessarily occurs after the election announcement. It contained no clause excluding candidates or limiting requests based on election timing. Tasev could not reasonably have foreseen that his request would fail on those grounds. The legal basis was accessible but not foreseeable. The Court therefore found that the interference was not “in accordance with law” under Article 8 § 2 and found a violation, without needing to examine legitimate aim or necessity. The key facts were thus the timing of his ethnicity rectification request, his simultaneous SJC candidacy, the authorities’ reliance on prior Bulgarian registration, and the absence of a clear legal rule justifying refusal.

In *Tasev v. North Macedonia* (Application no. 9825/13, judgment 16 May 2019), the applicant, Slavčo Tasev, was a judge at the Štip Court of Appeal. In September 2012, a vacancy notice was published for five posts on the State Judicial Council (SJC), to be filled by sitting judges elected by their peers. Although ethnicity was not a formal requirement, the SJC electoral roll recorded each judge’s ethnicity and included a separate list for judges from ethnic-minority communities. The Ministry of Justice administered the roll. Under section 17 of the State Judicial Act, after an SJC election was announced, the roll was made available for inspection, and judges could seek rectification of their personal details, including ethnicity, within three days.

On 28 September 2012, after the election announcement, Tasev asked the Ministry to change his ethnicity entry from Bulgarian to Macedonian. On 15 October, after inspecting the roll, he repeated the request, relying on section 17. On 18 October, the Ministry refused. It reasoned that the request had been submitted after the election announcement and was intended to secure an electoral right in the SJC election; allowing it would place other judges at a disadvantage. The Administrative Court upheld that decision. It added that the request was not a “rectification” of an obvious error and noted that Tasev had declared himself Bulgarian in the 2006, 2008, and 2010 electoral rolls. The Higher Administrative Court dismissed his appeal, citing the State Judicial Act and the General Administrative Procedure Act. It stated that changing ethnicity after the election announcement would disadvantage other judges and that the refusal did not restrict his right to assert his ethnic identity.

Meanwhile, on 5 October 2012, Tasev applied for election to the SJC as a Macedonian. On 3 December 2012, the SJC removed his name from the general list because his declared Macedonian ethnicity did not match official records, which had listed him as Bulgarian since 1995.

Tasev complained under Article 8 of the Convention that the refusal to register his self-declared ethnicity violated his right to respect for private life and ethnic identity. He also complained under Article 6 that he had not been given an opportunity to examine or comment on the 2006, 2008, and 2010 electoral roll extracts submitted by the Ministry and relied on by the Administrative Court.

The European Court of Human Rights treated the ethnicity complaint as an Article 8 issue. It recalled that ethnic identity falls within private life. The Government did not dispute that the refusal interfered with Tasev’s Article 8 rights. The Court therefore examined whether the interference was “in accordance with the law.” It found that the main reason for refusal was the timing of the request, tied to Tasev’s candidacy in the SJC election. However, the domestic authorities initially cited no statutory basis; the Higher Administrative Court later cited provisions that did not actually regulate the electoral roll. The relevant provision, section 17, allowed rectification after the roll was made available, which necessarily occurred after the election announcement, and contained no clause excluding judges running for election from seeking rectification of their ethnicity. Thus the refusal’s legal basis was accessible but not foreseeable. The Court concluded that the interference was not “in accordance with the law” and therefore violated Article 8, without needing to examine the other requirements of Article 8 § 2.

In **Panteleiciuc v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia** (Application no. 57468/08, judgment 2 July 2019), the applicant, a Moldovan farmer who sold potatoes, complained mainly about unfair administrative proceedings before the authorities of the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”) and about the lack of effective remedies.

The key facts arose on 5 February 2008. While selling potatoes in Varnița, a village under Moldovan control near Bender/Tighina, which is controlled by the MRT, the applicant was approached by plainclothes MRT customs officers. They demanded documents for the goods, including proof of payment of taxes for importing merchandise into the MRT. The applicant said he had all relevant documents and had paid taxes to the Moldovan local authorities in Varnița. More MRT customs and security officers arrived. When the applicant’s brother said he had called the Moldovan police, the applicant was attacked, forced into an MRT car and driven away. The Moldovan police arrived only after the incident. Later that evening, MRT customs seized the applicant’s car and remaining merchandise; according to the applicant, a Moldovan police officer was present but did not intervene. The applicant maintained that he had been arrested on Moldovan territory and had not seen any signs that he was crossing into MRT-controlled territory.

On 6 February 2008, an MRT court in Bender found him guilty of resisting customs officers and sentenced him to three days’ detention. The applicant alleged that the hearing was conducted in Russian, which he understood only to a limited degree, and without an interpreter. He was refused the right to a lawyer while preparing for the hearing; a court-appointed lawyer was present at the hearing but did not assist him. He did not receive a copy of the arrest record before the court examined it, nor a copy of the court decision. The sentence was enforced immediately, and he served the three days until 8 February 2008. He later appealed, but only obtained a copy of the decision on 17 March 2008. On 18 March 2008, the MRT Supreme Court quashed the decision for failure to specify the exact place of the offence and sent the case back, but the applicant was not informed. After an extraordinary appeal, the case was again sent for re-examination, again without informing him. On 27 May 2008, he received by fax a letter dated 12 May summoning him to a Supreme Court hearing that same day at 10 a.m.; because of the late notice, he could not attend. The court then rejected his appeal, finding that he had been arrested in Bender after refusing MRT customs orders.

The applicant’s brother also filed criminal complaints with Moldovan authorities about the unlawful arrest by MRT officers. A Moldovan criminal investigation began but was suspended in August 2008 because the Moldovan authorities could not effectively prosecute persons in MRT-controlled territory. It was resumed in 2013.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the Court found that both Moldova and Russia had jurisdiction under Article 1 of the Convention. Russia had effective control and decisive influence over the MRT; Moldova had positive obligations as the territorial State. The Governments’ non-exhaustion objections were dismissed. However, the applicant’s Article 5 complaints were rejected as lodged out of time, because he was released on 8 February 2008 but applied on 27 November 2008, more than six months later. The Article 13 complaint was found manifestly ill-founded because the Article 5 claim was not “arguable.” The remaining admissible complaint concerned Article 6 §§ 1 and 3: the alleged lack of an interpreter, inadequate legal assistance, insufficient time and facilities to prepare, and inability to attend the appeal hearing. The Court did not examine the separate claim that the MRT courts were unlawful because it had not been raised in the initial application.

He was not given a copy of the arrest record before the court examined it, nor a copy of the decision. On 18 March 2008, the MRT Supreme Court quashed the lower decision because it failed to specify the exact place of the offence and sent the case for re-examination. The applicant was not informed. On 25 April 2008, an extraordinary appeal was accepted, again without informing him. On 27 May 2008, he received a fax dated 12 May 2008 summoning him to a hearing that same day at 10 a.m. Because of the late summons, he could not attend. The court then rejected his appeal, finding that he had been arrested in Bender after refusing MRT customs orders.

The applicant’s brother also made a criminal complaint to Moldovan authorities about the unlawful arrest, and complaints were sent to several embassies, including Russia’s. A Moldovan criminal investigation into the abduction began on 28 February 2008. Witnesses confirmed the forced removal and identified two MRT officers. The investigation was suspended in August 2008 because Moldovan authorities could not effectively prosecute persons in MRT-controlled territory; it was resumed in 2013 and remained pending.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 about unfair proceedings, lack of adequate time and facilities, denial of legal assistance, and absence of an interpreter. The Court dismissed jurisdiction and exhaustion objections, finding both Moldova and Russia had jurisdiction—Moldova as the territorial State with positive obligations, and Russia because of its effective control over the MRT. Nikolyan v. Armenia (Application no. 74438/14) concerned an Armenian national, Gurgen Nikolyan, born in 1939, who was declared legally incapable amid a family dispute over divorce and property. In April 2012, he brought proceedings in the Shengavit District Court seeking to divorce his wife and evict her from his flat, claiming that he was the sole owner and that cohabitation had become unbearable. In July 2012, his wife responded by filing “special” civil proceedings under Article 168 of the Code of Civil Procedure to declare him legally incapable. She alleged that he had become argumentative, suspicious, threatening, and that his divorce and eviction claim demonstrated mental disorder. She claimed the family needed protection because he might evict them. Neighbours signed a statement describing strange behaviour and suspected mental disorder. The court ordered a psychiatric examination.

On 25 September 2012, a psychiatric panel diagnosed the applicant with “delusional disorder” and concluded that he could not understand the meaning of his actions or control them. In November 2012, his son also applied to have him declared incapable. The divorce and eviction proceedings were stayed. In December 2012, the District Court rejected the wife’s application, finding a conflict of interest and holding that the expert opinion was necessary but insufficient. However, on 8 February 2013, a differently composed District Court granted the son’s application and declared the applicant incapable. He was not notified of the application or hearing, and no appeal was lodged; the judgment became final in March 2013. The son was then appointed guardian.

After learning of the judgment, the applicant appealed. In July 2013, the Civil Court of Appeal reversed the judgment because he had not been notified of the hearing and ordered a new examination. The District Court later joined the wife’s and son’s applications. On 29 November 2013, it again declared him incapable, relying on the September 2012 expert opinion. His appeals failed, and in April 2014 the Court of Cassation declared his appeal on points of law inadmissible. As guardian, the son later withdrew the applicant’s divorce and eviction claim, and in October 2014 the District Court terminated those proceedings. The applicant was thus effectively prevented from pursuing his own family and property claim through the courts.

The applicant also tried to restore his legal capacity. In 2014, the Ministry of Health said it could not order a new examination, a psychiatric hospital did not respond, and the District Court refused, citing Article 173 § 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, which allowed only a guardian, family member, or psychiatric institution to apply. In April 2015, the Constitutional Court declared that provision unconstitutional insofar as it denied persons seeking restoration of legal capacity the right to be heard and to participate personally. In May 2015, the applicant began restoration proceedings, which remained pending. Later expert examinations in 2015–2016 suggested possible delusional disorder and ultimately advised continued incapacity.

He also challenged his son’s guardianship. The Administrative Court and Administrative Court of Appeal found that he lacked standing because he had been declared incapable. In September 2016, the Court of Cassation quashed that approach, noting conflict between the applicant and his son, the failure to hear the applicant before appointing the guardian, and that requiring him to act only through his guardian was ineffective and violated his right of access to court. The case was remitted and remained pending.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged: denial of access to court in the determination of his divorce and eviction claim and for restoration of legal capacity; unfairness in the proceedings depriving him of legal capacity, including lack of adversarial procedure and reliance on outdated expert evidence; and that the deprivation of legal capacity breached his right to private life under Article 8. These complaints were communicated to the Government.

In *Nikolyan v. Armenia* (Application no. 74438/14, judgment 3 October 2019), the applicant, Gurgen Nikolyan, born in 1939, lived in a Yerevan flat with his wife of 15 years, their son, daughter-in-law, and grandchild. In April 2012 he filed for divorce and sought his wife’s eviction, claiming the flat was his sole property and that their relationship had become unbearable after 12 years of conflict. In July 2012 his wife responded by initiating “special” civil proceedings to declare him legally incapable. She alleged that he had become aggressive, suspicious, argumentative, threatening, and that his divorce and eviction claim was itself a sign of mental disorder. Four neighbours signed a statement supporting her account. The District Court ordered a psychiatric examination.

On 25 September 2012, a psychiatric panel diagnosed the applicant with “delusional disorder,” concluding that he could not understand the meaning of his actions or control them. In November 2012, his son also applied to have him declared incapable. The divorce and eviction proceedings were stayed.

On 13 December 2012, the District Court rejected the wife’s incapacity application, noting the conflict of interest between the spouses and finding the expert opinion necessary but insufficient. However, on 8 February 2013, a differently composed District Court granted the son’s application and declared the applicant incapable, relying solely on the same 2012 expert opinion. The applicant was not notified of the son’s application or the hearing. That judgment became final and the son was appointed guardian.

After learning of the judgment, the applicant appealed. In July 2013, the Court of Appeal reversed it because he had not been notified of the hearing, and ordered a fresh examination. The wife’s application was also remitted. In October 2013 the applications were joined, and in November 2013 the District Court again declared the applicant incapable, again relying on the 2012 expert opinion. His appeals failed. Subsequently, the son, as guardian, withdrew the applicant’s divorce and eviction claim, and the proceedings were terminated in October 2014 because domestic law allowed a guardian to withdraw an incapable person’s claim.

The applicant attempted to restore his legal capacity. In 2014 the Ministry of Health said it could not order a new examination; a hospital did not respond; and the District Court said only a guardian, family member, or psychiatric institution could apply for restoration under Article 173 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In April 2015, the Constitutional Court declared that provision unconstitutional insofar as it prevented persons in his position from being heard personally. The applicant then began restoration proceedings through lawyers. Psychiatric examinations followed; one 2015 panel was inconclusive, and a December 2016 panel found intellectual retardation and advised incapacity. Those proceedings remained pending.

The applicant also challenged his guardianship. In February 2015, the Administrative Court declared his application inadmissible because, as an incapable person, he lacked standing. In September 2016, the Court of Cassation quashed that approach, finding that he should have access to court to contest the guardian’s appointment; the case was remitted and remained pending.

The alleged violations concerned: denial of access to court in his divorce/eviction and restoration claims; unfair proceedings leading to deprivation of legal capacity, including lack of notification, reliance on outdated expert evidence, his third-party status, and guardian conflicts; and breach of his right to private life through the deprivation of legal capacity.

**CASE OF NIKOLYAN v. ARMENIA**  
*(Application no. 74438/14, judgment of 3 October 2019)*

The applicant, Gurgen Nikolyan, an Armenian national born in 1939, lived in a Yerevan flat with his wife, son, daughter-in-law and grandchild. In April 2012 he brought divorce and eviction proceedings against his wife, claiming the flat was his sole property and that their relationship had become unbearable. On 4 July 2012 his wife filed “special” civil proceedings seeking to declare him incapable. She alleged that he had become aggressive, suspicious and threatening, and that his divorce and eviction claim was evidence of mental disorder. Neighbours signed a statement supporting her account. The District Court ordered a psychiatric examination. On 25 September 2012 the expert panel diagnosed “delusional disorder” and concluded that he could not understand the meaning of his actions or control them.

On 14 November 2012 the applicant’s son also applied to have him declared incapable. The divorce and eviction case was stayed. On 13 December 2012 the District Court rejected the wife’s application, finding a conflict of interest and insufficient evidence. She appealed. On 8 February 2013, in a different composition, the District Court granted the son’s application and declared the applicant incapable, relying on the September 2012 expert opinion. The applicant was not notified of the son’s application or the hearing. That judgment became final on 11 March 2013. On 20 March 2013 the guardianship body appointed the son as guardian. The Civil Court of Appeal later reversed the rejection of the wife’s application and remitted it, because the final incapacity judgment had not existed at the earlier hearing. The applicant appealed the 8 February 2013 judgment; on 11 July 2013 the Court of Appeal reversed it because he had not been notified and ordered a fresh examination. The wife’s and son’s applications were then joined. On 29 November 2013 the District Court again declared him incapable, relying on the 2012 expert opinion. His appeal was rejected in March 2014 and the Court of Cassation declared his appeal on points of law inadmissible on 30 April 2014.

Because of the incapacity declaration, the son, as guardian, withdrew the applicant’s divorce and eviction claim in June 2014. On 1 October 2014 the District Court terminated those proceedings. The applicant tried to challenge the guardian appointment, but the Administrative Court declared his application inadmissible in February 2015 because, as an incapable person, he lacked standing. In 2016 the Court of Cassation held that an incapable person should be able to contest guardian appointment, finding that the contrary approach violated access to court; the case was remitted and remained pending.

The applicant also tried to restore his legal capacity. In 2014 the Ministry of Health and the District Court stated they could not order a new psychiatric examination. In April 2015 the Constitutional Court declared Article 173 § 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure unconstitutional insofar as it prevented persons seeking restoration of legal capacity from personally being heard. He began restoration proceedings in May 2015. In December 2016 a new expert panel found a mental disorder and advised continued deprivation of capacity; those proceedings remained pending.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged denial of access to court concerning his divorce and eviction claim and restoration of legal capacity, unfairness in the incapacity proceedings, and that deprivation of legal capacity breached his right to private life. Those complaints were communicated to the Government; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The case *Sobco and Ghent v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* (Applications nos. 3060/07 and 45533/09, judgment of 18 June 2019) concerned two applicants, Serghei Sobco and Serghei Ghent, who in 2005 were dismissed from employment. They brought reinstatement proceedings against their employers before the courts of the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”). Those proceedings ended with final judgments of the MRT Supreme Court on 15 June 2006 and 19 February 2009, dismissing their claims. The applicants complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that they had been denied a fair trial by a court that did not qualify as an “independent tribunal established by law.” The second applicant also alleged that the same Supreme Court judge had examined his appeal on points of law three times after repeated quashing and re-examination by lower courts, and that he had not had access to the case-file materials.

The Court joined the applications. The first issue was jurisdiction under Article 1. Moldova, as the territorial State, had jurisdiction even though it lacked effective control over Transdniestria; however, its obligations were positive—to take diplomatic, economic, judicial and other measures within its power and compatible with international law. Russia denied jurisdiction. The Court, relying on *Ilaşcu*, *Catan* and *Mozer*, found that Russia had contributed militarily and politically to the creation of the separatist regime in 1991–1992, and that until July 2010 the “MRT” could survive only because of Russian military, economic and political support. This dependency showed that Russia exercised effective control and decisive influence over the MRT authorities. The applicants therefore fell within Russia’s jurisdiction, and Russia’s objections *ratione personae* and *ratione loci* were dismissed.

On the merits, Article 6 § 1 requires a fair hearing by an independent tribunal established by law. The Court recalled that courts of an unrecognised entity may qualify only if they form part of a judicial system operating on a constitutional and legal basis reflecting a judicial tradition compatible with the Convention. In *Mozer*, the Court had already found that the MRT judicial system did not meet that standard. No new evidence suggested otherwise. Thus, the MRT courts that decided the applicants’ employment cases could not qualify as a “tribunal established by law” under Article 6 § 1. The complaint was admissible.

Moldova accepted that the MRT courts were not “tribunals established by law” but argued that the breach was not attributable to it. The Court agreed that Moldova did not fail its positive obligations. Moldova had taken all measures in its power to re-establish control before July 2010, and the events occurred before that date. As for ensuring the applicants’ individual rights, the applicants showed no evidence that they had informed the Moldovan authorities of their problem, so Moldova’s non-involvement could not be held against it.

Russia, by contrast, exercised effective control over the MRT during the relevant period. Because of its continued military, economic and political support—without which the MRT could not survive—Russia’s responsibility under the Convention was engaged. The Court therefore found that the determination of the applicants’ civil rights by MRT courts violated Article 6 § 1. There was no violation by Moldova, but a violation by Russia.

**Summary of *Sobco and Ghent v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* (Applications nos. 3060/07 and 45533/09)**

The case of *Sobco and Ghent v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* originated from two applications lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr. Serghei Sobco, a Moldovan national, and Mr. Serghei Ghent, a Russian national, on 15 December 2006 and 19 August 2009, respectively. The applicants, both residents of the Transdniestrian region of Moldova, were dismissed from their employment in 2005. In response, they initiated reinstatement proceedings against their employers before the courts of the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”).

These proceedings concluded with final judgments from the Supreme Court of the “MRT” on 15 June 2006 (for Mr. Sobco) and 19 February 2009 (for Mr. Ghent), which dismissed the applicants’ actions. Consequently, the applicants complained to the European Court that they had been denied a fair trial by a court that did not qualify as an independent and impartial “tribunal established by law” within the meaning of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The second applicant (Ghent) also raised specific issues, including that a single judge of the “MRT” Supreme Court had examined his appeal on points of law three times following repeated re-examinations by lower courts, and that he was denied access to the case-file materials.

A central legal issue was the question of jurisdiction. The Court reaffirmed its established case-law concerning the Transdniestrian region. It held that the Republic of Moldova, as the territorial State, had jurisdiction but its responsibility was limited to fulfilling positive obligations—taking diplomatic, economic, and judicial measures within its power to secure Convention rights. Regarding the Russian Federation, the Court noted its prior findings that Russia had contributed militarily and politically to the creation of the separatist regime and continued to provide crucial military, economic, and political support, upon which the “MRT” was dependent. This support indicated that Russia exercised effective control and a decisive influence over the Transdniestrian authorities. Therefore, the Court concluded that the applicants fell within the jurisdiction of the Russian Federation. The Russian Government's objections on grounds of jurisdiction (*ratione personae* and *ratione loci*) were dismissed.

On the merits, the Court assessed the complaint under Article 6 § 1. It recalled its previous judgment in *Mozer v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia*, which held that the judicial system of the “MRT” was not a system reflecting a judicial tradition compatible with the Convention. In the absence of any new evidence to the contrary, the Court concluded that the “MRT” courts that decided the applicants’ cases could not be considered a “tribunal established by law” for the purposes of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

The Court then examined the responsibility of each respondent State. For Moldova, it found that the applicants had not provided evidence that they had informed the Moldovan authorities of their situation. Therefore, the Moldovan authorities' non-involvement could not be held against them, and the Court concluded that Moldova did not fail to fulfil its positive obligations. For Russia, the Court, having established that it exercised effective control over the “MRT” during the relevant period, held that by virtue of its continued support for the “MRT,” its responsibility under the Convention was engaged for the violation of the applicants’ rights.
