In *Berardi and Mularoni v. San Marino* (ECtHR, 10 January 2019), the applicants were two San Marino nationals, Paolo Berardi and Davide Mularoni, who worked as officials responsible for construction-site safety supervision. A parliamentary commission investigating organised crime found collusion involving a company linked to B. and corrupt payments to safety officials to avoid inspections. The applicants were charged in December 2012 with the continuing offence of bribery under Articles 50, 73 and 373 of the Criminal Code. They were accused of periodically receiving cash payments in order to omit their duties—failing to inspect B.-controlled construction sites and not sanctioning violations—with the charges covering events up to 1 January 2010. In September 2014, they were convicted of direct bribery under Article 373 § 1 and sentenced to imprisonment, bans on public office and political rights, and fines. The appeal court upheld the convictions in January 2016 but reduced the penalties.

The alleged violation concerned Article 7 of the Convention, which prohibits retroactive criminal liability and heavier penalties. The applicants argued that before Law No. 92 of 17 June 2008, which entered into force on 23 September 2008, San Marino law did not clearly criminalise “bribery inducing omission”—payment to an official to omit or delay a legitimate act. They claimed that their pre-2008 conduct should at most have been classified as indirect bribery, a lesser offence, or as no offence at all. Thus, applying the post-2008 wording to facts occurring before that date allegedly applied the criminal law retroactively to their disadvantage.

The Government denied retroactivity. It argued that the offence was a continuing one, linked by the same criminal plan, and persisted until 1 January 2010, after the amendment entered into force. Under Articles 50 and 55 of the Criminal Code, the offence was deemed committed when the criminal activity ceased. The Government also maintained that the applicants’ conduct was not mere omission but acts of commission and favouritism contrary to official duties, already covered by the old Article 373 § 1. Both the old and new versions carried the same penalty; the amendment merely provided a more specific definition.

The ECtHR declared the Article 7 complaint admissible. It reiterated that criminal offences must be clearly defined and foreseeable at the time of the conduct, although judicial interpretation may gradually clarify the law, especially in a first prosecution, if consistent with the essence of the offence. The domestic courts disagreed on whether bribery inducing omission fell under old Article 373 § 1 or § 2, but both found the applicants had accepted money to act contrary to their official duties by not inspecting sites and not sanctioning violations. Both the pre-2008 and post-2008 versions of Article 373 § 1 defined bribery similarly: receiving undue profit or a promise in order to carry out an act contrary to official duties. Whether characterised as omission or commission, the applicants’ conduct fell within that provision before and after the amendment. The Court found it foreseeable that receiving payments to avoid safety inspections constituted bribery. Because a legal basis existed both before and after 2008 and the penalties were the same, the continuing-offence issue was irrelevant. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 7.

**Case summary: Berardi and Mularoni v. San Marino (ECtHR, 10 January 2019)**

The applicants, Paolo Berardi and Davide Mularoni, were San Marino nationals and public officials responsible for supervising safety on construction sites. Following a parliamentary inquiry into organised crime, a commission reported corrupt collusion between public officials and companies linked to B., a notary/lawyer. It found that officials were bribed to omit compulsory safety checks and avoid sanctioning violations on construction sites connected to B.’s companies.

The applicants were charged with the continuing offence of bribery under Articles 50, 73 and 373 of the San Marino Criminal Code. They were accused of periodically receiving cash payments in exchange for failing to inspect construction sites controlled by B. and for abstaining from sanctioning irregularities. The charges covered events up to 1 January 2010. In 2014, the first-instance judge convicted them of direct bribery under Article 373 § 1, finding that they had exercised their discretionary powers in an aberrant way and acted contrary to their official duties. They received prison sentences and fines. On appeal in 2016, the conviction was upheld but the sentences were reduced.

The alleged violation concerned Article 7 of the Convention, which prohibits retroactive criminal liability. The applicants argued that before Law No. 92 of 17 June 2008—which entered into force on 23 September 2008—San Marino law did not specifically criminalise “bribery inducing omission,” namely accepting payment to omit or delay a legitimate official act. They claimed that conduct occurring before that amendment could at most be classified as the lesser offence of indirect bribery, or was not criminal as charged. Thus, they alleged that they had been convicted on the basis of a criminal provision applied retroactively to their disadvantage.

The Government denied retroactivity. It argued that the 2008 amendment did not create a new offence but merely clarified the definition of direct bribery. The old Article 373 § 1 already covered acts contrary to the duties of a public official. The Government also relied on domestic rules on continuing offences: because the bribery was a single continuing offence linked by the same criminal plan and lasted until 1 January 2010, the post-2008 wording applied. It further contended that the applicants’ conduct involved acts of commission and favouritism, not mere omissions.

The domestic appeal court held that the bribery constituted one continuing crime based on a corrupt pact, renewed by each payment. It found that the 2008 amendment did not create a new crime but clarified direct bribery, and that the applicants’ conduct—omitting checks and favouring B.’s companies contrary to official duties—was already covered by the old Article 373 § 1. The ECtHR agreed that both the old and new versions defined bribery similarly: receiving undue profit or a promise in order to carry out an act contrary to official duties. Although the domestic courts disagreed on whether bribery by omission fell under § 1 or § 2 before 2008, both characterised the applicants’ conduct as acts contrary to their official duties. The Court found it foreseeable that accepting money to avoid inspections and sanctions constituted bribery. Because the legal characterisation and penalty were essentially the same before and after the amendment, the continuing-offence issue was not decisive. The ECtHR therefore found **no violation of Article 7**.

In *Berardi and Mularoni v. San Marino* (Applications nos. 24705/16 and 24818/16, judgment 10 January 2019), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether San Marino violated Article 7 of the Convention by convicting two public officials for bribery based on criminal-law wording that the applicants claimed had not been in force at the time of some of the conduct.

The applicants, Paolo Berardi and Davide Mularoni, were officials responsible for construction-site safety (*Sicurezza Antinfortunistica*). A parliamentary commission investigating organised crime found evidence of collusion between company F., linked to notary/lawyer B., and public officials. The commission reported a corrupt practice in which construction companies bribed safety officials to avoid mandatory inspections. Criminal proceedings followed. On 12 December 2012, the applicants were charged with the continuing offence of bribery under Articles 50, 73 and 373 of the Criminal Code. They were accused of periodically receiving cash payments in order to omit their duties, namely by failing to inspect construction sites of companies controlled by B. and by abstaining from sanctioning violations. The charges covered events up to 1 January 2010.

On 19 September 2014, the first-instance judge convicted them of continuing bribery. The judge classified the conduct as direct bribery under Article 373 § 1, finding that the applicants had exercised discretionary powers in an aberrant way, contrary to their official duties, in exchange for money. They were sentenced to five years and six months’ imprisonment, a four-year prohibition on public office and political rights, and a EUR 25,000 fine. Evidence included witness statements, bank deposits from 2005–12, and testimony about short meetings with company representatives.

On appeal, the applicants argued that before Law No. 92 of 17 June 2008 (in force 23 September 2008), “bribery inducing omission” — payment to omit or delay a legitimate act — was not expressly criminalised. They claimed that pre-2008 conduct should at most have been indirect bribery, a lesser offence, or should not have been punished at all. The Judge of Criminal Appeals upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence to five years, a four-and-a-half-year prohibition, and a EUR 20,000 fine. It reasoned that the corrupt pact with B. constituted one continuing offence, renewed by each payment, and lasted until the last payment. Although conceding that bribery inducing omission might previously have fallen under Article 373 § 2, the court found the applicants had also been paid to carry out acts contrary to their duties, conduct covered by the old Article 373 § 1. The 2008 amendment did not create a new crime but clarified an existing one.

Before the Strasbourg Court, the applicants alleged retroactive application of criminal law contrary to Article 7. The Government argued that the continuing offence persisted until 1 January 2010, so the amended provision applied, and that the old law already covered the conduct with the same penalty.

The Court declared the complaint admissible but found no violation. It noted that both the pre- and post-2008 versions of Article 373 § 1 defined bribery similarly: receiving undue profit or a promise to carry out an act contrary to official duties. The domestic courts had reasonably characterised the applicants’ conduct — accepting money to avoid inspections and sanctions — as acts contrary to their duties, covered by the old provision. Whether framed as omission or commission, the legal basis remained Article 373 § 1. The interpretation was foreseeable, even if this was San Marino’s first bribery prosecution. The continuing-offence issue was therefore not decisive. The Court concluded that the applicants’ conviction did not violate Article 7.

The case *Bradarić v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Application no. 84721/17) is a European Court of Human Rights judgment, Fourth Section, delivered on 3 December 2019. The applicant, Nedžad Bradarić, born in 1954 and living in Tuzla, complained about the non-enforcement of a court-approved settlement. On 26 April 2012, he and his former employer, a private Tuzla company, concluded a settlement before the Tuzla Municipal Court concerning his severance pay. On 29 August 2012, he requested enforcement of that settlement. The enforcement did not proceed effectively.

On 20 March 2017, the applicant lodged a constitutional appeal about the non-enforcement. On 15 June 2017, the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and ordered the Tuzla Municipal Court to expedite the enforcement. It also awarded him 1,000 convertible marks (BAM), about 500 euros, for non-pecuniary damage. Despite this, enforcement remained unresolved. On 27 September 2017, after a third party—a company suing the applicant’s former employer in separate proceedings—made a request, the Tuzla Municipal Court postponed enforcement until those separate proceedings ended. The applicant appealed. On 15 November 2017, the Tuzla Cantonal Court overturned the postponement, rejected the third party’s request, and ordered the third party to pay the applicant BAM 1,053 in costs. As of 28 June 2019, the enforcement proceedings were still pending.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged non-enforcement of the settlement under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, guaranteeing a hearing within a reasonable time in civil matters, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, protecting peaceful enjoyment of possessions. The Government argued that he was no longer a “victim” because the Constitutional Court had acknowledged the breach and awarded BAM 1,000, which it considered sufficient.

The Court rejected that objection. It reiterated that a favourable domestic decision removes victim status only if the authorities have acknowledged the breach and provided appropriate and sufficient redress. The Constitutional Court had acknowledged the breach and ordered expedition, but the compensation was not adequate compared with what the European Court would likely award under Article 41. Moreover, the order to expedite remained unenforced and the enforcement proceedings were still pending. The applicant could therefore still claim victim status. The Government’s objection was dismissed, and the complaint was declared admissible as not manifestly ill-founded. The case concerned the prolonged failure to enforce a final settlement and whether the domestic redress had been sufficient.

In **Bradarić v. Bosnia and Herzegovina** (Application no. 84721/17, judgment of 3 December 2019), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint about the failure of the domestic authorities to enforce a final court-approved settlement. The applicant, Nedžad Bradarić, was born in 1954 and lived in Tuzla. On 26 April 2012, he and his former employer, a private company based in Tuzla, concluded a settlement before the Tuzla Municipal Court concerning the applicant’s severance pay. On 29 August 2012, the applicant filed a request with the Tuzla Municipal Court for enforcement of that settlement.

The enforcement proceedings subsequently remained unresolved for an extended period. On 20 March 2017, the applicant lodged a constitutional appeal complaining about the non-enforcement. On 15 June 2017, the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, holding that the applicant’s right to enforcement within a reasonable time had been breached. It ordered the Tuzla Municipal Court to expedite the enforcement proceedings and awarded the applicant BAM 1,000 (approximately EUR 500) in respect of non-pecuniary damage.

Despite that ruling, enforcement did not proceed promptly. On 27 September 2017, following a request by a third party—a company that had brought civil action against the applicant’s former employer in separate proceedings—the Tuzla Municipal Court postponed the enforcement proceedings until the end of the third-party proceedings. The applicant appealed. On 15 November 2017, the Tuzla Cantonal Court overturned that decision, rejected the third party’s request, and ordered the third party to pay the applicant BAM 1,053 in legal costs. Nonetheless, as of 28 June 2019, the latest information before the European Court, the enforcement proceedings in the applicant’s case were still pending.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained of the non-enforcement of the court-approved settlement under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. Article 6 § 1 guarantees a fair hearing within a reasonable time in the determination of civil rights and obligations. Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

The Government argued that the applicant could no longer claim to be a “victim” because the Constitutional Court had acknowledged the breach and awarded him BAM 1,000. The Court disagreed. It reiterated that a favourable domestic decision only removes victim status if it acknowledges the relevant breach and affords appropriate and sufficient redress. Although the Constitutional Court had acknowledged the violation and ordered the proceedings to be expedited, the compensation awarded was lower than what the European Court would likely have awarded under Article 41 of the Convention. Moreover, the Constitutional Court’s order to expedite enforcement remained unexecuted, with the enforcement still pending in June 2019.

The Court therefore dismissed the Government’s objection and held that the applicant could still claim to be a victim within the meaning of Article 34 of the Convention. It further found that the application was neither manifestly ill-founded nor inadmissible on any other grounds, and declared the application admissible. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were the prolonged non-enforcement of a final, court-approved settlement, the Constitutional Court’s finding of a violation but inadequate compensation and ineffective expedition order, and the continued pendency of enforcement despite domestic remedies having been pursued. These circumstances formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints under Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

Oddone and Pecci v. San Marino concerns two Italian nationals, David Oddone, a journalist, and Alessandro Pecci, a lawyer, who complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention that they had been unable to cross-examine two co-accused, G and L, whose incriminating statements were used against them.

San Marino authorities investigated suspicious car accidents involving Oddone. Between 2008 and 2011 he was the driver in three accidents in the same small town; two occurred on the same street, caused the same injuries, and involved different cars and insurers. The investigation focused on the 2009 and 2011 accidents. In July 2012 the police questioned G, the truck driver in the 2011 accident, and L, the driver in the 2009 accident, as witnesses without counsel. Initially both described ordinary accidents, but then changed their accounts and admitted the accidents were staged to claim insurance compensation. G said Oddone planned the fraud and paid him. L said Pecci, her then boyfriend, recruited her into a staged crash with Oddone and that Oddone later gave her about EUR 5,000.

On 31 August 2012 the investigating judge questioned G and L again, with counsel but without the applicants present. The case file had been classified as secret on 6 August 2012, without reasons, and was not declassified until 29 November 2013. The applicants were notified of the charges in December 2013. When summoned in February 2014, they requested that the investigation be reopened so they could cross-examine G and L. The judge refused on 26 February 2014, stating that only G and L’s statements before the investigating judge had been used, that co-accused could not participate in questioning, and that the applicants had made only generic requests. The applicants, G and L were indicted for insurance fraud. The trial court automatically admitted the investigation file as evidence.

At trial the applicants repeatedly objected and sought to cross-examine G and L, and also police officer J.B., whom Oddone alleged was hostile and had influenced the investigation. The trial judge rejected the requests, holding that questioning of co-accused was a defensive guarantee, not evidence-gathering, and that G and L’s statements were not the sole basis for conviction because other evidence existed: repeated accidents, the same street, phone records, and Oddone’s acquaintance with participants. The applicants were convicted in August 2015; the appeal court upheld the convictions in October 2016, although L’s case became time-barred after a confession mitigation.

The alleged violation is that the applicants never had an adversarial opportunity to challenge G and L. Although G and L were co-accused, their statements implicating the applicants functioned as witness testimony under Article 6 § 3(d). The domestic secrecy regime meant the applicants did not know of or participate in the investigating judge’s questioning, and the trial court refused cross-examination. Domestic law had no exclusionary rule; courts could freely assess evidence regardless of how it was obtained. The second applicant also argued the classification regime was unlawful, unreasoned, discriminatory, and prolonged. The first applicant alleged police bias. The Court declared the Article 6 complaint admissible, rejecting the Government’s non-exhaustion objection based on the extraordinary revision remedy.

Oddone and Pecci v. San Marino (Apps. 26581/17 and 31024/17) concerned two Italian nationals, David Oddone, a journalist, and Alessandro Pecci, a lawyer, charged in San Marino with insurance fraud arising from allegedly staged car accidents. Their complaint under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (d) alleged that they were unable to cross-examine two co-accused, G. and L., whose incriminating statements were used against them.

Police investigated suspicious accidents involving Oddone on 26 May 2008, 18 October 2009 and 28 September 2011. Oddone was always the driver, often with his parents, and the accidents followed a similar pattern: different cars and insurers but similar circumstances, injuries and location. In July 2012, police questioned G., the truck driver in the third accident, and L., the driver in the second accident, as witnesses and without counsel. Both initially described ordinary accidents, then retracted and admitted the events had been simulated to obtain insurance compensation. G. said Oddone planned the fraud, recruited him, and later paid him about EUR 2,000. L. said Pecci, her boyfriend at the time, and Oddone planned the second accident; she intentionally rear-ended Oddone’s car and later received about EUR 5,000. She also stated that Pecci had persuaded her to participate and that she needed money.

The investigating judge opened a fraud investigation. On 31 August 2012, the judge questioned G. and L. with counsel but without the applicants present. Both confirmed their earlier statements and added details, including alleged attempts by the applicants to persuade them to withdraw or deny the accusations. The case file had been classified from 6 August 2012 without reasons and was not declassified until 29 November 2013. The applicants were informed of the charges on 2 December 2013 and summoned for questioning.

On 20 February 2014, the applicants’ counsel requested that the investigation be reopened so they could cross-examine G. and L.; the applicants remained silent. On 26 February 2014, the investigating judge refused. She reasoned that G. and L. had also made statements before her, that co-accused persons could not participate in questioning of other co-accused, and that the investigation was sufficient. The applicants and G. and L. were indicted for fraud. The prosecution witness list named only police officer P.

At trial, the investigation file was automatically admitted as evidence. The applicants again objected and requested cross-examination of G. and L., also challenging the secrecy regime and their exclusion from the investigation. The first-instance judge rejected these requests, holding that questioning co-accused was a defence instrument rather than evidence collection and that San Marino law contained no exclusionary rule; the judge could freely assess evidence regardless of how it had been obtained. On 19 August 2015, the applicants were convicted and sentenced to imprisonment. G. and L. were also convicted, though L. later received a reduced, time-barred penalty based on her “useful and spontaneous confession.”

On appeal, the applicants repeated that the inability to cross-examine G. and L. violated their defence rights, especially because their statements were central. In 2016, the Judge of Criminal Appeals upheld the convictions. It accepted that the classification decision lacked reasons but found no nullity followed. It also held that the investigating judge could question G. and L. without the applicants and that the Code of Criminal Procedure imposed no admissibility restrictions. The appeal court treated G. and L.’s statements as admissible and reliable, regarding them as confirmed by other elements such as phone records and the unusual accident pattern. The applicants then brought their Convention complaint, alleging denial of the opportunity to examine witnesses against them.

In **Oddone and Pecci v. San Marino** (ECtHR, 17 October 2019), two Italian nationals, David Oddone and Alessandro Pecci, complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) that they had been convicted without any opportunity to cross-examine two co-accused, G. and L., whose incriminating statements were used against them.

San Marino police investigated suspicious car accidents. Oddone, a journalist, had been the driver in three accidents over three and a half years—2008, 2009 and 2011—usually with his parents as passengers, using different cars and insurers, with similar injuries, in the same town and twice on the same street. In July 2012, police questioned G., the truck driver in the 2011 accident, and L., the driver in the 2009 accident, as witnesses without counsel. Both initially described ordinary accidents but then admitted they had simulated the crashes to obtain insurance payouts. G. said Oddone planned the fraud and later gave him €2,000. L. said Pecci, then her boyfriend, recruited her into the scheme, and Oddone later gave her about €5,000. L. also alleged Pecci later asked her to retract her statements; G. alleged Oddone told him to deny their connection and confirm the accident was real. Both cited financial need.

A fraud investigation was opened. On 6 August 2012 the investigating judge classified the file, making it secret, without giving reasons. On 31 August 2012 the judge questioned G. and L. with counsel present, but the applicants were not present and could not cross-examine them. G. and L. confirmed their earlier accounts. The file was declassified on 29 November 2013. The applicants were then charged and summoned. In February 2014 their counsel requested that the investigation be reopened so they could cross-examine witnesses, especially G. and L. The investigating judge refused, stating that co-accused persons could not participate in the questioning of other co-accused; that only G. and L.’s statements before her had been used; and that the request was generic. The applicants were indicted with G. and L. for insurance fraud. The investigation file was automatically admitted as evidence at trial.

At trial, the applicants again objected that they had been unable to question G. and L., and that the secret investigation and lack of cross-examination violated their defence rights. The first-instance judge rejected these arguments. He treated the questioning of G. and L. before the investigating judge as an interrogation rather than evidence-gathering, so the applicants had no right to participate. Domestic law contained no exclusionary rule, and the convictions did not rest solely on G. and L.: other evidence included the suspicious pattern of accidents and phone records showing contacts before the 2011 crash. Both applicants were convicted. On appeal, the Judge of Criminal Appeals upheld the convictions. It accepted that the classification decision lacked reasons but found no nullity, and held that San Marino’s Code of Criminal Procedure did not regulate admissibility, leaving evidence to the judge’s free assessment regardless of how it was obtained. It found G. and L.’s statements corroborated by other evidence, not decisive alone. L.’s sentence was later reduced and time-barred as a “useful and spontaneous confession”; G. withdrew his appeal. Oddone’s later revision attempt was rejected in January 2019.

The alleged violation therefore centred on the use of incriminating statements by G. and L.—co-accused whom the applicants regarded as witnesses—without the applicants ever having a chance to examine or have them examined at the investigation or trial, particularly after the secrecy regime was lifted.

In *Kálovics v. Hungary* (Application no. 46030/18), the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 19 September 2019. The applicant, Kálovics, was represented by Ms L. Horgos, a lawyer practising in Budapest. The application was lodged against Hungary under Article 34 of the Convention on 3 September 2018. Notice of the application was given to the Hungarian Government.

The applicant’s principal complaint concerned the excessive length of civil proceedings in Hungary. He relied on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees that, in the determination of civil rights and obligations, everyone is entitled to a hearing within a reasonable time by a tribunal. The Court reiterated the established criteria for assessing the reasonableness of the length of proceedings: the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicant and the relevant authorities, and what was at stake for the applicant in the dispute. It referred to *Frydlender v. France* and, importantly, to its leading judgment in *Gazsó v. Hungary*, which had already found a violation in respect of similar issues concerning lengthy civil proceedings in Hungary.

Having examined all the material submitted to it, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on admissibility or merits. It therefore held that the length of the proceedings in the applicant’s case was excessive and failed to meet the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1. The Court’s finding was based on its well-established case-law, particularly *Gazsó*, rather than on any newly identified factual circumstances.

The applicant also raised a complaint under Article 13 of the Convention, alleging the absence of an effective domestic remedy in respect of the excessive length of the civil proceedings. The Court noted that this complaint raised an issue under its well-established case-law, specifically *Gazsó v. Hungary*. The applicant further raised other complaints under Article 6 of the Convention. The case of *Strand Lobben and Others v. Norway* concerns a challenge under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights regarding the severance of family ties between a mother and her child.

The first applicant, Ms. Trude Strand Lobben, contacted child welfare services in May 2008 during a difficult pregnancy. She had a history of serious health issues, including epilepsy and a brain injury, which had resulted in cognitive impairments. With her consent, she moved to a parent-child institution after giving birth to her son, X, in September 2008, to be assessed for her parenting abilities.

Almost immediately, staff at the institution raised serious concerns. They reported that X was not gaining weight, lacked energy, and appeared dehydrated. The mother struggled to meet his basic needs, such as feeding and hygiene, despite repeated guidance. Reports from the institution described her as having significant cognitive limitations, a lack of empathy for her son, and an inability to understand his needs. They concluded she was incapable of providing adequate care.

Consequently, in October 2008, the child welfare services placed X in an emergency foster home. A report noted that upon arrival, X was undernourished, pale, and weak, but that he developed well in the care of his foster parents. The County Social Welfare Board upheld the emergency placement, and the City Court agreed, concluding that X would suffer material harm if returned to his mother.

In March 2009, the Board issued a formal care order, authorizing X's placement in a foster home. Critically, they determined that due to the mother’s fundamental and limited potential for change, X would likely grow up in foster care. Therefore, they set very restrictive contact rights—two hours, six times per year—to avoid disrupting his attachment to his foster parents. The Board viewed the foster parents as X’s psychological parents.

However, the municipality appealed to the High Court, which granted leave. During this period, an expert psychologist appointed by the High Court conducted a comprehensive assessment. Her report concluded that the mother suffered from a fundamental cognitive impairment, with a stable low IQ and lasting socio-emotional problems. **Case summary: Strand Lobben and Others v. Norway**

The case concerned Norwegian child welfare measures that culminated in the adoption of a young boy, X, against his mother’s wishes, and the mother’s complaint that this violated her right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The first applicant, Ms Trude Strand Lobben, was a young woman with epilepsy and cognitive/learning difficulties. In 2008, while pregnant and without stable housing, she contacted the child welfare services and agreed to a voluntary stay at a parent-child institution after giving birth. Her son, X, was born on 25 September 2008. They moved to the institution on 29 September 2008. Staff soon reported concerns: X was not gaining sufficient weight; he appeared weak and dehydrated; the mother needed repeated basic guidance on feeding, hygiene and care; and she showed little empathy or understanding of the baby’s needs.

On 17 October 2008, after the mother said she wanted to leave the institution with X, the child welfare services placed X in emergency foster care. The County Social Welfare Board upheld the emergency placement. The City Court later found that X had shown clear signs of neglect and that returning him to his mother would create a risk of material harm.

In November 2008, the municipality applied for a care order. On 2 March 2009, the County Social Welfare Board granted the care order, finding serious deficiencies in the mother’s care capacity and limited potential for change. X was placed in foster care, later described as enhanced foster care, with contact rights set at two hours, six times per year. The mother appealed.

In August 2009, the City Court revoked the care order, doubting the strength of the evidence and suggesting, among other things, that X’s weight problems might have been linked to an eye infection. However, the High Court granted leave to appeal, stayed enforcement, and after further expert reports, the care order was ultimately maintained. X remained with his foster parents.

Later, the child welfare authorities sought to withdraw the mother’s parental responsibilities and authorise X’s adoption by his foster parents. The domestic bodies considered that X had become attached to the foster parents, that the mother’s care difficulties were fundamental and longstanding, and that adoption would give X stability. The mother appealed, but the adoption decision was upheld through the domestic courts.

Before the European Court, the mother and X alleged that the refusal to lift the care order, the withdrawal of parental responsibilities and the authorisation of adoption breached Article 8. They argued that the authorities had not done enough to reunite the family, had relied on old or insufficient expert evidence, had set very limited contact, and had turned to adoption without properly considering less restrictive alternatives. The grandparents’ complaints were declared inadmissible.

The Grand Chamber found a violation of Article 8 in relation to the adoption. It emphasised that adoption severing family ties must be justified by exceptional circumstances and must follow a genuine proportionality assessment. In this case, the domestic authorities had not sufficiently assessed the mother’s current capacity, had not adequately explored reunification or less intrusive measures, and had relied heavily on historical evidence. The adoption was therefore not supported by sufficient reasoning, despite the child’s best interests being central.

**Summary of Ryabinin and Shatalina v. Ukraine (Application no. 33006/07)**

The case of *Ryabinin and Shatalina v. Ukraine* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by two Ukrainian nationals: Mr. Valeriy Ryabinin (the first applicant) and his mother, Ms. Yuliya Shatalina (the second applicant). The case centers on the criminal proceedings against the first applicant for the murder of his acquaintance, "S," in June 2005.

**Key Facts:**

The body of S. was discovered dismembered in a river near the applicants' home on June 23, 2005. Following a search of the property, the first applicant was summoned to the police station and arrested on suspicion of murder. Shortly after his arrest, and before being granted access to a lawyer, he provided a detailed written confession, admitting to killing S. during a drunken dispute, dissecting her body, and disposing of the remains. He was formally appointed a lawyer the following day.

The first applicant later retracted his confession, alleging it was coerced. He claimed that police officers beat him with sand-filled plastic bottles, attached electric cables to his testicles and lip, administered electric shocks, and threatened him with rape to force his confession. He also alleged he was shackled outside overnight and doused with cold water. He argued that his initial confession was dictated to him and that his clothes, soiled with blood from the alleged beating, were destroyed on the investigator's orders.

The first applicant was convicted of aggravated murder and sentenced to life imprisonment in February 2006. The trial court primarily relied on his consistent pre-trial confessions, which were made in the presence of his lawyer, and other physical evidence. His complaints of ill-treatment were investigated by the prosecutor's office multiple times and each time dismissed for lack of evidence. The domestic courts noted that the first applicant had no visible injuries during a crime scene reconstruction on June 24, 2005, and that his initial confession contained no legal citations.

The second applicant complained about the arbitrary seizure and prolonged retention of her mobile telephone by the investigator. The phone was taken from her son upon his arrest, and while she was told it would be returned, it was only given back in August 2007. Her subsequent legal claims for this delay were rejected by domestic courts on jurisdictional grounds.

**Alleged Violations:**

Before the European Court, the first applicant alleged violations of:
- **Article 3 (Prohibition of torture):** He claimed he was ill-treated by police and that the domestic investigation into his allegations was ineffective.
- **Article 6 (Right to a fair trial):** He argued his trial was unfair, primarily because his conviction was based on a self-incriminating confession given without a lawyer and under duress.
- **Article 8/34:** He also complained about routine monitoring of his correspondence in detention and hindrances in obtaining case file documents to substantiate his application.

The second applicant complained under **Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (Protection of property)** and **Article 13 (Right to an effective remedy)** regarding the seizure of her phone and the lack of an effective remedy for that interference.

The Court ultimately declared the application inadmissible, finding the first applicant's ill-treatment complaint manifestly ill-founded and his fair trial complaint inadmissible, as he failed to provide evidence for his allegations or demonstrate compelling reasons for the lack of legal assistance during his initial confession.

**Case summary: Ryabinin and Shatalina v. Ukraine (no. 33006/07)**

The case concerned two Ukrainian nationals: Valeriy Ryabinin (“the first applicant”), who was serving life imprisonment, and his mother, Yuliya Shatalina (“the second applicant”). The first applicant alleged police ill-treatment and an ineffective investigation under Article 3; an unfair trial under Article 6 because he confessed without a lawyer; routine monitoring of his correspondence in detention; and refusal of access to case-file documents needed for his Strasbourg application. The second applicant alleged arbitrary seizure and retention of her mobile telephone in the criminal proceedings against her son and the absence of an effective remedy.

The underlying events began in June 2005, after body parts of S. were recovered from the river Ingulets. On 23 June 2005 police searched the applicants’ home and seized a hacksaw, blades, a handcart, a TV and a kitchen cabinet. The second applicant telephoned her son, and he went to the police station, where he was arrested at 7.20 p.m. on suspicion of murder.

The first applicant alleged that, after arrest, police beat him with plastic bottles filled with sand and liquid to extract a confession. He claimed electric cables were attached to his testicles and lower lip and that he was shocked until he fainted; officers also allegedly threatened him with rape. He eventually wrote a dictated confession. He further alleged that he was later shackled to a motorcycle outside overnight while cold water from a fire hose poured over him. The next morning, he said, he was made to change into clean clothes and his blood-stained clothes were destroyed by his mother on the investigator’s instruction. The Government denied coercion and noted that detention records from the police station had been destroyed in 2012 after expiry of the storage period.

On 23 June 2005, without a lawyer, the first applicant gave a 14-page handwritten confession admitting the murder and dismemberment of S., use of her bank card and taking property. He said it was voluntary. That evening he signed a rights form requesting a lawyer. A lawyer was appointed on 24 June, and he repeated his confession during questioning and a reconstruction; photographs and video showed no visible injuries. He maintained his confession throughout the pre-trial investigation, including during a psychiatric examination. At trial in February 2006, however, he pleaded innocent and retracted the confession, alleging torture. He was convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment; the Supreme Court upheld the conviction in August 2006.

Domestically, he complained in August 2005 of “moral coercion” and threats to relatives, but prosecutors repeatedly refused to institute criminal proceedings, and courts upheld those refusals. The European Court of Human Rights found the Article 3 complaint manifestly ill-founded: the applicant failed to specify injuries or provide supporting evidence, and his account had inconsistencies—no visible injuries, delayed complaints, omissions about the night outside, and an initial confession not containing legal quotations as alleged.

Regarding Article 6, the Court found that by the time of the first confession a “criminal charge” existed. He had not waived his right to a lawyer and had requested one. No compelling reasons justified the restriction, and domestic law required mandatory representation where life imprisonment was possible.

The other allegations concerned automatic monitoring of prisoner correspondence—later exempting Court mail—and refusal of case-file copies, which were eventually provided in 2013 after administrative litigation. The second applicant’s telephone, seized from her son though belonging to her, was returned in August 2007; her civil and administrative claims were refused, and prosecutors found no violation.

In *Ryabinin and Shatalina v. Ukraine* (App. no. 33006/07, 7 Nov. 2019), the first applicant, Valeriy Ryabinin, and his mother, Yuliya Shatalina, complained about criminal proceedings and related matters. Ryabinin had been released in 2004 after serving a murder sentence. In 2005 he began a relationship with S. After S. disappeared, body parts were found in the Ingulets River. On 23 June 2005 police searched the applicants’ home, seized a hacksaw, handcart, TV, and cabinet, and asked Shatalina to call her son to the police station. He went and was arrested on suspicion of S.’s murder.

**Case: O’Leary v. Ireland (Application no. 45580/16), ECtHR, 14 February 2019**

The applicant, Alan O’Leary, an Irish national born in 1986, suffers from severe brain damage and lacks legal capacity. He was represented by his sister and guardian. It was alleged that his condition was caused by a measles vaccination administered in 1988 when he was 15 months old. The complaints given notice to the Irish Government concerned the length of the domestic civil proceedings and the lack of effective remedies for that delay; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

In November 2002—14 years after the vaccination—the applicant’s mother began proceedings on his behalf against four defendants: the local health authority, the State, the Attorney General (together the “State defendants”), and the doctor who administered the vaccine. In August 2003 the High Court made a limited discovery order against the local health authority, seeking records about the applicant, the vaccine used, adverse effects, the manner in which consent was obtained, and family health. Although discovery was to be complied with within eight weeks, the authority only complied in June 2008, a delay of over four and a half years.

The applicant appealed the scope of that discovery order, leading to a further limited discovery order in January 2004 against all four defendants. A further appeal against that order was dismissed by the Supreme Court in July 2006, with only a minor amendment. In December 2007 the applicant’s mother died. The applicant later argued that this caused grave prejudice because she had been a vital witness and essential evidence was lost. Settlement was proposed but not agreed.

In May 2008 the applicant sought to have the State defendants’ defence set aside; the High Court refused in March 2010. The trial involved ten days of hearings. No factual evidence was called for the applicant, but independent medical witnesses gave evidence after reading his medical records, and documentary discovery evidence was before the court. On the eleventh day, 19 July 2011, the judge accepted the defendants’ application to strike out the case for failure to establish a prima facie case. As regards the doctor, the applicant accepted there was insufficient evidence of negligence in administering the vaccine, and the claim against him was dismissed. Against the State defendants, the judge found no evidence supporting the applicant’s grounds. The High Court proceedings terminated on 19 December 2011.

The applicant appealed on 30 grounds. After the Court of Appeal was established in October 2014, the case was transferred there. Submissions were filed by the doctor in February 2015 and by the State defendants in September 2015. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 10 February 2016, finding that the trial judge had correctly approached the strike-out application and noting the many legal hurdles the applicant faced. The proceedings ended on 10 May 2016 when the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal.

Relevant domestic law included Nash v. D.P.P. (October 2016), which recognised that the constitutional right to a timely trial was well established and that damages might be available for breach in appropriate circumstances, including under the European Convention on Human Rights Act 2003 where no other damages remedy existed. However, that judgment post-dated the applicant’s proceedings.

The key alleged violations were therefore the excessive duration of the civil proceedings—from November 2002 to May 2016, approximately 13.5 years—and the absence of an effective domestic remedy for that delay. The facts emphasised prolonged discovery delays, interlocutory appeals, the death of a crucial witness, the applicant’s vulnerability, and the eventual strike-out of his case.

*Carpov v. the Republic of Moldova* (Application no. 6338/11, judgment of 12 February 2019) concerned a Moldovan national, Mr Sergiu Carpov, who had obtained a civil judgment against a company undergoing insolvency. In September 2009, the applicant initiated civil proceedings against the company. On 18 December 2009, the Drochia District Court ruled in his favour, ordering the company to pay him 24,957 Moldovan Lei (MDL) (approximately EUR 1,413) in pecuniary damages and MDL 749 (approximately EUR 42) in costs and expenses. The defendant company’s representative was not present at that hearing.

On 28 December 2009, the secretariat of the Drochia District Court sent a copy of the reasoned judgment to the defendant company by ordinary mail. On 11 January 2010, an enforcement writ was issued to the applicant in respect of the 18 December 2009 judgment. On 10 February 2010, in separate insolvency proceedings involving the same defendant company, the company’s insolvency administrator updated the list of creditors and expressly referred to the 18 December 2009 judgment and the exact amounts awarded. The court dealing with the insolvency issued a decision concerning the updated creditor list on the same date.

On 26 April 2010, the insolvency administrator of the defendant company lodged an appeal against the 18 December 2009 judgment. The applicant objected that the appeal was time-barred. Under Article 362 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an appeal had to be lodged within twenty days from service of the reasoned judgment. The applicant argued that the defendant company had known of the judgment at least since 10 February 2010, when its insolvency administrator referred to it in the insolvency proceedings.

On 28 September 2010, the Bălţi Court of Appeal admitted the appeal and quashed the 18 December 2009 judgment. After re-examining the merits, it dismissed the applicant’s action against the defendant company. The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law, repeating his objection that the appeal had been lodged out of time. On 26 January 2011, the Supreme Court of Justice dismissed his appeal and upheld the lower court’s judgment, without commenting on the late-appeal objection.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, claiming that his right to a fair trial had been breached because a final judgment in his favour had been quashed following an appeal lodged out of time. The Government argued that the defendant company’s representative had learned of the judgment only on 23 April 2010, when he requested a copy, and had appealed three days later, within the twenty-day statutory period. The Government did not deny that the judgment had been sent on 28 December 2009, but said there was no evidence it had been received. The Court found no plausible explanation for the insolvency administrator’s knowledge of the exact award by 10 February 2010 and concluded that the defendant company had received the judgment at the latest by that date. Therefore, the 26 April 2010 appeal was clearly outside the twenty-day time-limit. By allowing it and quashing the final judgment, the domestic courts infringed the principle of legal certainty and breached Article 6 § 1.

The applicant also complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court reiterated that a judgment debt constitutes a “possession” and that quashing a final judgment interferes with the beneficiary’s right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions. It found the interference unjustified because a fair balance had not been preserved and the applicant had to bear an individual and excessive burden. Violations of both Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 were found.

In *Carpov v. the Republic of Moldova* (ECtHR, Second Section, 12 February 2019, App. No. 6338/11), the applicant, Sergiu Carpov, complained that Moldovan courts violated his fair-trial and property rights by allowing an out-of-time appeal and quashing a final civil judgment in his favour.

In September 2009 Carpov sued a company undergoing insolvency. On 18 December 2009 the Drochia District Court awarded him MDL 24,957 (about EUR 1,413) in pecuniary damages and MDL 749 (about EUR 42) in costs. The defendant company’s representative was absent from that hearing. On 28 December 2009 the court secretariat sent a copy of the reasoned judgment to the defendant company by ordinary mail. On 11 January 2010 an enforcement writ was issued in Carpov’s favour.

The key factual dispute concerned when the defendant company learned of the judgment. On 10 February 2010, in separate insolvency proceedings, the company’s insolvency administrator updated the creditors’ list, expressly referring to the 18 December 2009 judgment and the exact amounts awarded. The insolvency court issued a decision on that updated list the same day.

On 26 April 2010 the insolvency administrator appealed against the 18 December 2009 judgment. Carpov objected that the appeal was time-barred. Under Article 362 of the Civil Procedure Code, an appeal had to be lodged within twenty days from service of the reasoned judgment. He argued that the administrator had known of the judgment since at least 10 February 2010.

On 28 September 2010 the Bălţi Court of Appeal admitted the appeal and quashed the 18 December 2009 judgment. After re-examining the merits, it dismissed Carpov’s action. Carpov appealed on points of law, repeating his objection that the appeal had been late. On 26 January 2011 the Supreme Court of Justice dismissed his appeal and upheld the lower court’s decision. It made no comment on the lateness objection.

Before the ECtHR, the Government argued that the defendant’s representative had not been present at the December 2009 hearing and had learned of the judgment only on 23 April 2010, when he requested a copy from the court secretariat. The appeal three days later was therefore, they claimed, within the twenty-day limit. They did not deny that the court had sent a copy on 28 December 2009, but said there was no evidence it had been received.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. It emphasised the principle of legal certainty and res judicata: a final judgment should not be called into question. Although receipt of the mailed copy was disputed, the Government offered no plausible explanation for how the insolvency administrator knew of the judgment and its exact amounts by 10 February 2010. The Court therefore found it established that the defendant company had received the judgment by that date at the latest. The 26 April 2010 appeal was clearly outside the twenty-day time-limit. By allowing it and quashing the final, enforceable judgment, the Court of Appeal and Supreme Court set at naught an entire judicial process and breached Carpov’s right to a fair hearing.

The ECtHR also found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. A final judgment debt constitutes a “possession.” Quashing the judgment after it had become final and unappealable interfered with Carpov’s peaceful enjoyment of that possession. Even if the interference pursued a public interest, it was not justified: a fair balance was not preserved, and Carpov bore an individual and excessive burden.

**Carpov v. the Republic of Moldova** (Application no. 6338/11, 12 February 2019) concerned a Moldovan applicant whose final, favourable civil judgment was later quashed after an allegedly late appeal.

In September 2009, Sergiu Carpov brought civil proceedings against a company undergoing insolvency. On 18 December 2009, the Drochia District Court awarded him 24,957 Moldovan lei (approximately EUR 1,413) in pecuniary damages and 749 lei (approximately EUR 42) in costs. The defendant company’s representative was not present at the hearing. On 28 December 2009, the court secretariat sent a copy of the reasoned judgment to the defendant by ordinary mail. On 11 January 2010, an enforcement writ was issued in the applicant’s favour.

On 10 February 2010, in separate insolvency proceedings involving the same defendant, the insolvency administrator updated the list of creditors and expressly referred to the 18 December 2009 judgment and the exact amounts awarded. The insolvency court issued a decision on the updated list that same day. On 26 April 2010, the insolvency administrator appealed against the 18 December 2009 judgment. The applicant objected that the appeal was time-barred. Under Article 362 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an appeal had to be lodged within twenty days from service of the reasoned judgment; the administrator had known of the judgment since at least 10 February 2010. On 28 September 2010, the Bălţi Court of Appeal admitted the appeal and quashed the judgment in the applicant’s favour. After re-examining the merits, it dismissed his action. On 26 January 2011, the Supreme Court of Justice dismissed the applicant’s appeal on points of law, upholding the lower court’s decision and not commenting on the late-appeal objection.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. He argued that the Court of Appeal’s decision to quash a final judgment in his favour following an appeal lodged out of time breached his right to a fair trial and the principle of legal certainty. The Government submitted that the defendant’s representative had not been present at the hearing and had learned of the judgment only on 23 April 2010, when he requested a copy. He lodged the appeal three days later, allegedly within the twenty-day period. The Government did not deny that a copy had been sent on 28 December 2009 but claimed there was no evidence of receipt.

The Court found no plausible explanation for how the insolvency administrator knew the exact amounts awarded by 10 February 2010. It therefore concluded that the defendant company had received the judgment at the latest on 10 February 2010. The appeal of 26 April 2010 was thus clearly outside the twenty-day time-limit. By allowing it, the Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court set aside a final and enforceable judgment, infringing the principle of legal certainty and res judicata. A violation of Article 6 § 1 was found.

The applicant also complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that quashing the judgment deprived him of a possession. The Court agreed that a judgment debt may constitute a possession and that quashing a final judgment imposed an individual and excessive burden. It therefore also found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In *Abdi Ibrahim v. Norway* (Application no. 15379/16), the applicant was a Somali national who left Somalia in 2009 while pregnant, gave birth to her son, X, in Kenya under traumatic circumstances, and later sought asylum in Norway with him. She was granted refugee status in June 2010. After concerns arose about her care of X, he was placed in emergency foster care in late 2010. In December 2010, the County Social Welfare Board issued a care order and placed X with a Christian foster family. The applicant was granted limited contact: two hours, four times yearly. On appeal, the District Court upheld the care order in September 2011 but reduced contact to one hour, six times yearly, noting X’s need for stability and uncertainty about the applicant’s care skills. She did not appeal further at that stage.

In September 2013, the child welfare services applied to withdraw the applicant’s parental responsibilities and consent to X’s adoption by his foster parents. The Board granted the request in March 2014, finding that X had become strongly attached to his foster parents, that the applicant would be permanently unable to provide proper care, and that adoption was in X’s best interests. The District Court upheld the decision in November 2014. The High Court upheld it in May 2015, finding that X was vulnerable, had special care needs, and had shown negative reactions to contact with the applicant, including screaming and anxiety. It found adoption would provide stability and security. The High Court acknowledged the cultural and religious differences—the applicant was Muslim, while the foster parents were Christian and intended to baptise X and change his name—but concluded these factors did not outweigh adoption. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal in September 2015.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 8 (respect for family life) and Article 9 (freedom of religion), arguing that the withdrawal of parental responsibility and consent to adoption, especially by a Christian family, unlawfully severed her ties with X. The European Court of Human Rights examined the cultural and religious issues under Article 8. It accepted that the measures interfered with family life and were lawful and aimed at protecting X’s rights, but found them disproportionate.

Key to the violation was the decision-making process. From the outset, contact had been extremely limited, undermining the duty to maintain and strengthen family ties. Although reunification was not realistically imminent, the authorities had taken no real longer-term measures to facilitate it before resorting to adoption, the most far-reaching measure. The few contact sessions provided a limited basis for concluding that future contact would be harmful. Experts disagreed about the causes of X’s reactions, yet little was done to clarify or treat them. The High Court also focused more on the effects of returning X to his mother than on terminating all contact, and gave significant weight to the foster parents’ opposition to “open adoption.” The Court concluded that insufficient weight was given to the applicant’s and X’s family life, especially considering their cultural and religious background, and that the decision-making process had not duly taken account of all the applicant’s views and interests. It found a violation of Article 8.

In *Abdi Ibrahim v. Norway*, the applicant was a Somali national who arrived in Norway in 2010 with her infant son, X, after fleeing traumatic circumstances. She was granted refugee status. A parent-child institution soon reported concerns that X was at risk in her care. X was placed in emergency foster care and, in December 2010, a County Social Welfare Board issued a care order. He was placed with an ethnically Norwegian Christian foster family. The mother was granted contact of only two hours, four times yearly; the District Court later reduced this to one hour, six times yearly. It noted the importance of X’s cultural background and uncertainty over the care order’s long-term nature, but found his need for stability limited frequent contact. The applicant did not appeal that contact regime.

In 2013, child welfare services sought to withdraw the mother’s parental responsibilities and consent to adoption by the foster parents, alternatively to deny contact. The Board granted adoption in March 2014, finding X attached to his foster parents and that removal would cause serious problems; adoption would provide stability and security. The District Court upheld that decision. In May 2015, the High Court also upheld adoption. It found X, then about five and a half, had lived with the foster parents since age one, regarded them as his parents, and was vulnerable with special care needs. It accepted he had negative reactions after contact with his mother, including screaming, agitation, and anxiety, and that contact had stopped in 2013. The majority also considered cultural and religious factors: the mother was Muslim, while the foster parents were Christian and intended to baptise X and change his name. The foster parents opposed an “open adoption” with future contact. The majority concluded adoption was in X’s best interests. The minority disagreed that the grounds for adoption were sufficiently compelling but favoured no contact at that time. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal.

The applicant complained under Articles 8 and 9 that withdrawal of parental responsibility, adoption, and X’s Christian upbringing violated her rights to family life and religion. The Court examined the religious and cultural complaint under Article 8. It accepted that the measures interfered with family life, were lawful, and pursued legitimate aims, but assessed proportionality.

The Court found a violation of Article 8. It emphasised that even though the applicant did not seek immediate reunification, the authorities still had a positive duty to facilitate family life, at minimum through regular contact where compatible with X’s best interests. From the outset, contact was extremely restrictive. The domestic decisions relied on X’s attachment to his foster parents and negative reactions to contact, but the evidence on those reactions was limited and experts disagreed about their causes. Little was done to clarify or improve contact. The High Court focused largely on the consequences of returning X to his mother rather than on why all future contact should be permanently ended, and gave significant weight to the foster parents’ opposition to open adoption. Considering the gravity of severing family ties and the cultural and religious background militating in favour of preserving some possibility of contact, the Court held that insufficient weight had been given to the applicant and X’s family life and that the decision-making process had not duly taken all the applicant’s views and interests into account.

In *Abdi Ibrahim v. Norway* (App. no. 15379/16), ECtHR Second Section, 17 December 2019, the applicant, a Somali national, fled to Norway in 2010 with her son X, born in Kenya in 2009. She had been unaccompanied and pregnant; X’s father did not acknowledge paternity. When X was an infant, a parent-child institution notified child welfare that he was at risk. X was placed in emergency foster care and, in December 2010, a care order was issued. Contact was set at two hours, four times yearly. X was placed with a Christian family. The applicant had asked for placement with her cousin or a Somali/Muslim foster home, but this was not granted; she later dropped that alternative claim.

In 2011 the District Court upheld the care order but reduced contact to one hour, six times yearly. It considered X’s cultural background but found his vulnerability and need for stability did not support frequent contact. No appeal followed. In September 2013 the child welfare services applied to withdraw the applicant’s parental responsibility and consent to adoption. The Board granted this in March 2014; the District Court upheld it in November 2014; the High Court upheld it in May 2015; and the Supreme Court refused leave in September 2015.

The High Court found X strongly attached to his foster parents and that removal would cause serious problems. X was vulnerable, had special care needs, possible early attachment disorder, and showed trauma reactions after contact with the applicant. Adoption would provide stability, security, identity, and equal membership in the family. The foster parents would not agree to an “open adoption.” The applicant was Muslim; the foster parents were Christian and intended to baptise X and change his name. The High Court majority found particularly compelling reasons for adoption; the minority did not.

The applicant alleged violations of Articles 8 and 9, arguing the adoption severed family ties and disregarded her and X’s cultural and religious background. The Government argued the measures were necessary and in X’s best interests.

The ECtHR examined the cultural and religious complaints under Article 8. It found the adoption and withdrawal of parental responsibility interfered with family life, were lawful and pursued legitimate aims, but proportionality was decisive. Article 8 requires family unity and positive steps toward reunification; adoption entails final severance and requires very exceptional circumstances. Although the applicant did not seek X’s return, she opposed adoption and sought continued contact. From the outset, contact was very limited—two hours four times yearly, then one hour six times yearly. This created a serious risk that family ties would be broken. Before adopting, the authorities took no real measures to facilitate reunification. The sparse contact gave limited basis to conclude future contact would harm X. The High Court relied largely on foster parents’ reports about X’s negative reactions; experts disputed the causes, and little was done to clarify or treat them. The High Court focused more on the effects of returning X than on terminating all contact, and gave more weight to the foster parents’ opposition to open adoption than to the applicant’s interests. The cultural and religious background militated in favour of preserving some contact. Thus the decision-making process failed to duly take account of the applicant’s views and interests. The Court found a violation of Article 8; the Article 9 complaint was not separately examined.
