**Case Summary: Svitlana Ilchenko v. Ukraine (Application no. 47166/09)**

Svitlana Ilchenko, a Ukrainian national living in Kyiv, had used a one-car brick garage in the courtyard of her apartment building since 1980. In 1983 the Kyiv Leninsky District Council authorised her to use the garage. Between 1993 and 1998 she rented the relevant part of the courtyard under a written lease. In January 1995 the district executive committee stated it had no objection to her registering the garage, and in February 1995 the Kyiv Technical Inventory Bureau registered it in her name. A 2002 municipal certificate confirmed that she owned the 34 sq. m brick garage. She later bought her flat privately and paid land tax.

In 2002 the city and a private developer began planning a new housing project on the site where her garage stood. In 2003 the Kyiv City Council allocated the land to the city’s Housing Directorate. The Directorate then told Ilchenko that she was using the garage without legal grounds, that her registration was invalid, and that the garage would have to be demolished. It said no alternative space was available and offered monetary compensation, inviting her to negotiate. She did not follow up on that offer.

In July 2003 the Directorate sued for demolition. Ilchenko counterclaimed, seeking recognition of her title to the land under the garage and annulment of the development documents. In February 2004 the Brovary Court dismissed the Directorate’s claim, finding that Ilchenko owned the garage, had used the land openly since 1980, had acquired title by adverse possession, and that the development approvals were irregular. In July 2005 the Kyiv Regional Court of Appeal reversed the decision. It found that Ilchenko had not proved a right to the land, that the adverse-possession period did not apply as she claimed, and ordered her to vacate the land by demolishing the garage.

Ilchenko appealed and sought suspension of enforcement, arguing demolition would be irreversible. On 12 August 2005, before the suspension was granted, State bailiffs demolished the garage. The suspension was granted on 19 August 2005. In February 2006 the Supreme Court quashed the lower judgments, noting that Ilchenko owned the garage, had paid land tax, and had used the land openly. The case was remitted. In May 2007, however, the Kyiv Shevchenkivsky District Court again found for the Directorate, holding that the 1983 decision had only been temporary permission and that no land right had been properly granted. The court ordered her to vacate the land. This was upheld on appeal in October 2008 and by the Supreme Court in March 2009. A separate claim against the bailiffs was dismissed.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Ilchenko alleged that demolition of her garage violated her right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Government argued she had failed to exhaust domestic remedies because she had not claimed compensation. The Court rejected that objection, noting that domestic courts treated her as a squatter under the Land Code, which provided no compensation and could even require her to pay demolition costs.

On the merits, the Court found an interference with her possessions amounting to deprivation of property. Although domestic courts found the demolition lawful, the Court found no strong public interest justifying uncompensated taking: the project was primarily private commercial housing. Since Ilchenko was treated as a squatter, she had no legally guaranteed compensation and no adequate procedure to assess market value. Her failure to negotiate an ex gratia settlement was not a waiver. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In *Svitlana Ilchenko v. Ukraine* (Application no. 47166/09, judgment 4 July 2019), the applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the demolition of her garage deprived her of her possessions without compensation.

The applicant lived in a flat in central Kyiv and had used a one-car brick garage in the courtyard of her house since 1980. In April 1983 the Leninsky District executive committee authorised her use of the garage. From 1993 to 1998 she rented the part of the courtyard occupied by the garage under a signed lease. In January 1995 the district executive committee stated it had no objection to her registering the garage in her name, and in February 1995 the Kyiv Technical Inventory Bureau registered the garage in her name. She later privatised her flat. In October 2002 a municipal housing agency certificate confirmed that she owned a 34 sq. m brick garage in the courtyard. She also paid land tax.

In 2002 the city and a private developer began planning a new housing project on the site, including the garage. In April and July 2003, Kyiv City Council allocated land for the project to the city’s Housing Directorate. In May 2003 the Directorate told the applicant that the land had been designated for new housing, that she was using the garage without legal grounds, and that her registration was invalid. The garage would have to be demolished. It said there was no alternative placement and offered monetary compensation, inviting her to negotiate. The applicant did not follow up on that offer.

In July 2003 the Directorate sued for demolition. The applicant counterclaimed for title to the land and annulment of the development documents. In February 2004 the Brovary Court found for the applicant: she owned the garage, had used the land openly since 1980, had acquired title by adverse possession, and the development approvals were irregular. In July 2005 the Kyiv Regional Court of Appeal reversed, holding that she had not proved a right to the land and had never been properly granted use of it. It ordered her to vacate the land by demolishing the garage. The applicant sought suspension of enforcement on 8 August 2005, but bailiffs demolished the garage on 12 August; suspension was granted on 19 August.

In February 2006 the Supreme Court quashed the lower judgments and remitted the case, noting that the applicant owned the garage, paid land tax, and could rely on adverse possession. Nevertheless, in 2007 and 2008 the lower courts again found for the Directorate, holding that the 1983 decision was merely temporary permission and that she had no valid land right. The Kyiv City Court of Appeal upheld that outcome in October 2008, and the Supreme Court upheld it in March 2009. Her separate claim against the bailiffs also failed.

The European Court of Human Rights found an interference with the applicant’s possessions and classified it as deprivation of property, not a mere control measure. Her registered title had never been invalidated, and the garage had not been unlawfully constructed at the time. The domestic courts treated her as a squatter under Article 212 of the Land Code, meaning she had no right to compensation and could even owe demolition costs. Although the Government claimed the project served public housing interests, the Court found no demonstrated strong public interest; the project was primarily for private commercial gain. No compensation or procedural safeguards ensuring market-value compensation were provided. Her failure to follow up on the city’s ex gratia offer did not waive her rights because there was no legal entitlement or proper procedure. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

**Svitlana Ilchenko v. Ukraine** (Application no. 47166/09), judgment of 4 July 2019, concerned the demolition of the applicant’s garage in Kyiv and her complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention.

The applicant lived in a flat in central Kyiv and had used a one-car brick garage in her courtyard since 1980. In 1983 the local executive committee authorised her to use the garage. From 1993 to 1998 she leased the part of the courtyard occupied by the garage. In January 1995 the district committee stated it had no objection to her registering the garage in her name, and in February 1995 the Kyiv Technical Inventory Bureau registered it in her name. She later bought her flat privately. In October 2002 a municipal housing agency certified that she owned the 34 sq. m brick garage.

In 2002 the city and a private developer began planning a new housing project on the site, including the garage. In 2003 the Kyiv City Council allocated land to the city’s Housing Directorate. In May 2003 the Directorate told the applicant that the land was designated for development, that her use of the garage was without legal grounds and her registration invalid, and that the garage would be demolished. It offered monetary compensation and invited her to negotiate. She did not follow up.

The Directorate sued in July 2003 seeking demolition. The applicant counterclaimed for recognition of her title to the land and annulment of development documents. In February 2004 the Brovary Court dismissed the Directorate’s claim, finding that the applicant owned the garage, had used the land openly since 1980, and had acquired title by adverse possession. It also found irregularities in the development approval, including that the project was commercial rather than public.

In July 2005 the Kyiv Regional Court of Appeal reversed, finding no proved land right, holding that the adverse-possession period ran only from 2002, and ordering her to vacate the land by demolishing the garage. After she sought suspension of enforcement on 8 August 2005, bailiffs demolished the garage on 12 August; suspension was granted on 19 August. In February 2006 the Supreme Court quashed the lower judgments, noting she owned the garage, paid land tax, and adverse possession applied. On remittal, however, the District Court in May 2007 again found for the Directorate, holding that the 1983 decision was only temporary permission and that no proper land right had been granted. The Court of Appeal upheld this in October 2008, acknowledging the garage had been registered as her property but finding no proper land-use right. The Supreme Court upheld that outcome in March 2009. Her separate claim against the bailiffs was dismissed.

Before the European Court, the Government argued she had not exhausted remedies because she had not claimed compensation. The Court rejected this: domestic courts treated her as a squatter under Article 212 of the Land Code, which provided no compensation and even made squatters liable for demolition costs.

The Court found an interference with her possessions and applied the deprivation-of-property rule, not mere control, because her registered title was regular, never invalidated, and the garage’s construction was not unlawful. The “unauthorised” land use largely resulted from Ukraine’s post-Soviet legal transition. The domestic lawfulness interpretation was not arbitrary. However, the Government failed to show a strong public-interest justification; the project mainly served private commercial high-value housing. No compensation or procedural safeguards were provided. Therefore, the demolition imposed a disproportionate burden, and there was a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

**Balsamo v. San Marino** (Applications nos. 20319/17 and 21414/17, ECtHR, 8 October 2019) concerned two Italian sisters, Valentina and Angela Balsamo, who complained about confiscation orders imposed in San Marino criminal proceedings even though they were ultimately acquitted.

The case arose from a San Marino investigation into ongoing money laundering against B. (the applicants’ father) and the applicants under Articles 50, 73 and 199 bis of the Criminal Code. Prosecutors alleged they had laundered assets worth €2,150,000 obtained by B. through crimes committed in Italy.

In July 2011, an investigating judge seized a current account, a bonds account and the contents of a safe-deposit box registered in Valentina’s name but subject to mandates held by B. and later Angela. The seized assets totalled €1,920,785.50. Most funds had been deposited in cash: Valentina deposited €500,000 in December 2004 at age eighteen, then €150,000 in August 2005 and €400,000 in March 2006; B. deposited €950,000 in April 2006; and Angela deposited €150,000 in July 2008. Italian authorities later supplied documents, including a 2008 Brescia Court of Appeal judgment convicting B. of theft and receiving stolen goods, with proceeds of €750,000. San Marino authorities archived proceedings against B. but indicted the applicants for money laundering.

In November 2014, the first-instance criminal judge convicted both applicants. Valentina was sentenced to two years and six months’ imprisonment and Angela to one year; both were fined €5,000 and temporarily banned from public office. The judge confiscated the seized €1,920,785.50 under Article 147(3) of the Criminal Code and ordered Valentina to pay an equivalent confiscation of €499,000 for sums she had withdrawn before seizure. The judge found the assets had illicit origins. Although the proven Italian predicate offence involved only €750,000, he relied on B.’s long criminal record, a disproportion between the family’s lawful income and the assets, inconsistent explanations, and the use of San Marino accounts to hide origins.

On appeal, in October 2016, the Judge of Criminal Appeals acquitted both applicants because it was not proved beyond reasonable doubt that they knew the criminal origin of the assets, especially given their youth. Nevertheless, the appeal court found the deposited funds had criminal origins absent any legitimate explanation and upheld the confiscation of the seized sums. Thus the applicants faced confiscation despite acquittal.

Before applying to the ECtHR in March 2017, the applicants had in January 2017 sought revision before San Marino’s judge for extraordinary remedies, raising the same Convention complaints. They did not inform the ECtHR of those domestic proceedings. In May 2017, the judge rejected the revision, finding the complaints arguable but no violation. He characterized the confiscation as preventive rather than punitive, aimed at preventing illicit funds from recirculating, and held it lawful, foreseeable and proportionate under international anti-money-laundering obligations.

The applicants alleged that the confiscation following acquittal was not in accordance with the law and was disproportionate. The communicated complaints concerned Articles 6 §2 and 7 §1, alone and with Article 13, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Government also raised an abuse-of-petition objection based on the applicants’ failure to disclose the pending revision proceedings. The key facts for the alleged violations were the acquittal on mens rea, the continued confiscation based on findings of illicit origin, the equivalent confiscation, and the applicants’ claim that no effective remedy existed.

**Balsamo v. San Marino** (Applications nos. 20319/17 and 21414/17) is a European Court of Human Rights case brought by two Italian nationals, Valentina and Angela Balsamo. The case arose from a San Marinese criminal investigation into ongoing money laundering involving the applicants and their father, “B.” The prosecution alleged that assets obtained in Italy by B. through multiple offences, totaling about EUR 2,150,000, had been laundered.

In July 2011, the investigating judge seized a current account, a bonds account, and the contents of a safe deposit box registered in the first applicant’s name, over which B. and later the second applicant had mandates. The seized assets totaled EUR 1,920,785.50. The first applicant had opened the account in December 2004 at age eighteen and deposited EUR 500,000 in cash; further cash deposits of EUR 150,000 and EUR 400,000 followed. B. deposited EUR 950,000 in April 2006, and the second applicant deposited EUR 150,000 in July 2008. Italian authorities later supplied documents, including a 2008 Brescia Court of Appeal judgment convicting B. of theft and receiving stolen goods, with proceeds estimated at EUR 750,000.

In February 2014, proceedings against B. were archived, while the applicants were indicted for money laundering. In November 2014, the first-instance criminal judge convicted both applicants. Valentina Balsamo was sentenced to two years and six months’ imprisonment; Angela Balsamo to one year. Both were fined EUR 5,000 and barred from public office and political rights. The judge confiscated the seized sums under Article 147 § 3 of the Criminal Code and ordered an additional equivalent confiscation of EUR 499,000 against the first applicant for funds withdrawn before seizure. The judge found the money had a criminal origin based on the Italian judgment against B., B.’s criminal record, the disproportion between legitimate income and assets, contradictory explanations, and the suspicious use of foreign bank accounts.

On appeal, in October 2016, the Judge of Criminal Appeals acquitted both applicants for lack of evidence of the subjective element—mens rea—because it was not proved beyond reasonable doubt that they knew the assets were of criminal origin, particularly given their young age. Nevertheless, the appeal judge upheld the confiscation, finding that the money had a criminal origin absent any explanation and that transferring it to San Marino showed an attempt to hide its origin.

The applicants complained to the ECtHR in March 2017 that the confiscation imposed after their acquittal was unlawful and disproportionate. Their communicated complaints concerned Article 6 § 2 (presumption of innocence), Article 7 § 1 (no punishment without law), Article 13 (effective remedy), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The remainder of the applications was declared inadmissible.

A procedural issue arose because the applicants had also applied in January 2017 to San Marino’s judge for extraordinary remedies for revision of the October 2016 judgment, raising similar Convention complaints, but did not inform the Court. The Government later argued that this omission amounted to an abuse of petition. The applicants contended that the revision remedy was extraordinary and did not need to be exhausted. In May 2017, the domestic judge rejected the revision request, holding that the confiscation was preventive rather than punitive, lawful, foreseeable, and proportionate, and that the illicit origin of the funds had been established in fair proceedings.

**Balsamo v. San Marino** (Applications nos. 20319/17 and 21414/17) is a European Court of Human Rights case brought by two Italian nationals, Valentina and Angela Balsamo. They alleged that confiscation orders imposed on them after their acquittal were not in accordance with the law and were disproportionate. They relied on Article 6 §2 (presumption of innocence), Article 7 §1 (no punishment without law), Article 13 (effective remedy), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The Italian Government did not intervene.

The case arose from a San Marino criminal investigation against the applicants’ father, B., and the two applicants for ongoing money laundering. The prosecution alleged that they had laundered assets worth approximately EUR 2,150,000 obtained by B. through offences committed in Italy. In July 2011 the investigating judge seized a current account, a bonds account and a safe deposit box registered in the first applicant’s name, over which B. and later the second applicant had mandates. The seized assets totalled EUR 1,920,785.50. The first applicant had opened the account in December 2004, at age eighteen, depositing EUR 500,000 in cash; further cash deposits of EUR 150,000 and EUR 400,000 followed. B. deposited EUR 950,000 in April 2006, and the second applicant deposited EUR 150,000 in July 2008. In January 2012, Italian authorities supplied documents, including a Brescia Court of Appeal judgment of November 2008 convicting B. of theft and receiving stolen goods, with proceeds assessed at EUR 750,000.

In February 2014 proceedings against B. were archived, and the applicants were indicted for money laundering. In November 2014 the first-instance criminal judge found both applicants guilty. They received prison sentences and fines. The judge confiscated the seized sums (EUR 1,920,785.50) under Article 147 §3 of the Criminal Code and also ordered the first applicant to pay an equivalent confiscation of EUR 499,000 for sums withdrawn before seizure. The judge found the assets had a criminal origin, relying on the Italian judgment against B., his criminal record, the disproportion between the applicants’ legitimate income and the assets, the absence of evidence of a lawful origin, and the unexplained transfer of money to San Marino.

On appeal, in October 2016, the Judge of Criminal Appeals acquitted both applicants because the evidence did not prove beyond reasonable doubt that they knew of the criminal origin of the assets, particularly given their young age. Nevertheless, the appeal judge upheld the confiscation. He found that the money had had a criminal origin, as no adequate explanation for its origin had been provided, and that transferring it to San Marino showed an attempt to hide its origin.

Before applying to the Strasbourg Court, the applicants sought revision in January 2017 before San Marino’s judge for extraordinary remedies, raising the same Convention complaints. They lodged their ECtHR applications in March 2017 but did not inform the Court about the pending domestic revision. In May 2017 the judge for extraordinary remedies rejected the revision after considering the merits. He held that the confiscation was preventive rather than punitive, lawful, proportionate and foreseeable, and that the illicit origin of the funds had been established in fair proceedings. The Government later argued that the applicants had abused the right of petition by omitting this pending domestic remedy. The key factual issues relevant to the alleged violations were therefore whether the confiscation after acquittal could be justified as a preventive measure based on findings of illicit origin, and whether the applicants had an effective domestic remedy.

The case *Deli v. the Republic of Moldova* (Application no. 42010/06), decided by the European Court of Human Rights on 22 October 2019, concerned complaints under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about an impartial tribunal and a fair hearing. The applicant, Teodor Deli, a Moldovan national, represented party X in civil proceedings before the Ciocana District Court against party Y. At the hearing of 15 June 2006, presided over by Judge B., Deli objected to what he described as the judge’s intimidating manner toward X. He alleged that the judge threatened to have him removed from court or jailed. When Deli requested Judge B.’s recusal, alleging bias, hostility, and favouritism toward Y, the judge dictated a decision into the minutes of the hearing. That decision fined Deli 200 Moldovan lei (about 12 euros) for contempt of court, citing disrespect, disturbing order, unacceptable expressions, shouting, and failure to heed warnings. Deli maintained that no such warnings had occurred, that the fine was never delivered publicly, and that he never received a copy of the decision. His client supported his account.

The same day, another judge rejected Deli’s recusal request, finding that the grounds did not fall within Article 50 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The civil case then continued. On 23 June 2006 Deli objected to the minutes, claiming they omitted his requests that the judge stop shouting at and intimidating X, his repeated recusal request, and the judge’s threats. He also asserted that the contempt fine had merely been dictated to the court assistant in response to his legitimate complaints, rather than being a properly delivered court decision. He received no reply. On the same day he lodged a cassation appeal, arguing that the decision breached domestic administrative-offence provisions and Article 6 of the Convention, and that he had not received a copy of the sanctioning decision. On 6 July 2006 the Chișinău Court of Appeal rejected the appeal. It reiterated the lower court’s decision, stated that Deli had been summoned, and upheld the fine without further details. That decision was final.

The relevant domestic framework allowed recusal where circumstances gave rise to doubts about a judge’s impartiality, but contempt cases under Article 2007 of the Code of Administrative Offences were examined by the court against which the offence was committed. Appellate decisions in such cases did not require reasoning. The ECtHR found violations of Article 6 § 1. First, the same judge before whom the alleged contempt took place imposed the sanction and was the subject of Deli’s bias complaint, while the domestic courts failed to examine his impartiality allegations. Second, the Court of Appeal failed to properly summon Deli, impairing his right to a fair hearing. The case therefore focused on the lack of impartial review in contempt proceedings and procedural unfairness on appeal.

In *Deli v. the Republic of Moldova* (Application no. 42010/06, judgment of 22 October 2019), the applicant, Teodor Deli, a Moldovan national, represented a party, X, in civil proceedings before the Ciocana District Court against another party, Y. The hearing of 15 June 2006 was held before a single judge, Judge B. According to the applicant, during the hearing he objected to Judge B’s intimidating manner towards X. The judge allegedly threatened to have the applicant removed from the courtroom or even jailed. When the applicant requested the judge’s recusal, Judge B dictated a decision into the minutes of the hearing. That decision fined the applicant 200 Moldovan lei (about EUR 12 at the time) for contempt of court under Article 200/7 of the Code of Administrative Proceedings. It stated that he had shown disrespect by disturbing order, using unacceptable expressions, shouting, and failing to heed warnings.

The applicant disputed this account. He claimed that he had been sanctioned in retaliation for challenging the judge and that the fine had never been delivered publicly, but had simply been dictated to the court assistant. He also alleged that the minutes omitted key events, including his request that the judge stop shouting at and intimidating X, his repeated request for Judge B’s recusal, and the judge’s threats against him. His client supported these objections. On 15 June 2006 another judge rejected the recusal request, finding that the grounds relied on did not correspond to any ground for challenging a judge under Article 50 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The civil proceedings then continued.

On 19 June 2006 the applicant asked for a copy of the hearing minutes. On 23 June 2006 he submitted objections to the minutes, complaining of the omissions and the manner in which the fine had been imposed. He received no reply. Also on 23 June 2006 he lodged a cassation appeal with the Ciocana District Court, which forwarded it to the Chișinău Court of Appeal. He argued, among other things, that he had not received a copy of the sanctioning decision and that the decision breached Article 2651 of the Code of Administrative Offences and Article 6 of the Convention.

On 6 July 2006 the Chișinău Court of Appeal rejected the appeal. It reiterated the lower court’s decision, stated that the applicant had been summoned, and upheld the fine without further details or reasoning. That decision was final. The applicant later complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the judge who convicted him of contempt lacked impartiality and that the Court of Appeal had not properly summoned him to its hearing.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. In particular, the same judge before whom the alleged contempt had occurred imposed the sanction, and the domestic courts failed to examine the applicant’s allegations of bias. The Court also found that the applicant had not been properly summoned to the Court of Appeal hearing, violating his right to a fair hearing. The underlying civil case between X and Y was later settled.

In *Deli v. the Republic of Moldova* (Application no. 42010/06, ECtHR Second Section, judgment of 22 October 2019), the applicant, Teodor Deli, a Moldovan national, complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the judge who fined him for contempt of court lacked impartiality and that the Chișinău Court of Appeal failed to properly summon him.

The facts arose from civil proceedings before the Ciocana District Court, where Deli represented party X against party Y. At a hearing on 15 June 2006 before single Judge B., a dispute occurred. Deli alleged that the judge behaved intimidatingly toward X and, when he objected, threatened to remove him from the courtroom or jail him. Deli then requested the judge’s recusal. In response, Judge B. dictated a contempt decision into the minutes, stating that Deli had been cautioned for inappropriate behaviour, disrespectful remarks toward Y’s representative, disturbing order, using unacceptable words, shouting, and ignoring warnings. The judge fined Deli 200 Moldovan lei (about €12) under Article 200/7 of the Code of Administrative Proceedings for showing disrespect to the court. Deli claimed the sanction was retaliatory, that he had not actually been warned, and that the fine was never delivered publicly but simply dictated to the court assistant.

On the same day, another judge rejected Deli’s recusal request, finding no grounds under Article 50 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The civil case continued. On 19 and 23 June 2006, Deli requested and then objected to the minutes. He argued that they omitted his requests that the judge stop shouting at and intimidating his client, his repeated recusal request, and the judge’s threats against him. He also objected that the minutes falsely recorded prior cautions and that the fine had not been pronounced publicly. He received no reply to these objections. He then lodged a cassation appeal with the Chișinău Court of Appeal, arguing that he had not received a copy of the sanctioning decision and that the proceedings breached Article 2651 of the Code of Administrative Offences and Article 6 of the Convention.

On 6 July 2006, the Chișinău Court of Appeal rejected the appeal. It repeated the lower court’s account, stated that Deli had been summoned, and upheld the fine without further reasoning. That decision was final. Deli alleged before the European Court that he had not been properly summoned to the Court of Appeal hearing.

Relevant domestic law included Article 50 of the Code of Civil Procedure, which allowed recusal where circumstances raised doubts about a judge’s objectivity or impartiality; Article 196, which permitted cautions, removal, and fines for repeated disturbance of court order; Article 200/7 of the Code of Administrative Offences, which penalised contempt of court; Article 209, which provided that such cases be examined by the court against which the offence was committed; Article 2651, requiring recusal where impartiality was doubted; and Article 2827, allowing appellate decisions in administrative-offence cases to be issued without reasoning.

The ECtHR found violations of Article 6 § 1. First, the same judge before whom the alleged contempt took place had imposed the sanction, and the domestic courts failed to examine the applicant’s allegations of bias. Second, the Court of Appeal failed to properly summon Deli, undermining his right to a fair hearing.

In **Duranspahić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina** (Application no. 47761/16 and nine others), the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section, sitting as a Committee) delivered judgment on 9 May 2019. The applicants, represented by Mr S. Zaklan, lodged applications against Bosnia and Herzegovina under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates. Notice was given to the Government.

The central factual complaint was the **non-enforcement of final domestic decisions** issued in the applicants’ favour. The judgment states that the list of applicants and relevant details are set out in an appended table, though that table is not reproduced in the provided text. The applicants complained that the domestic authorities had failed to execute decisions that had become final and that ordered specific action to be taken. They relied, expressly or in substance, on **Article 6 § 1 of the Convention** (right to a fair hearing in the determination of civil rights and obligations) and **Article 1 of Protocol No. 1** (protection of property and peaceful enjoyment of possessions).

Because the applications raised similar subject matter, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment. On the merits, the Court reiterated its established case-law, particularly **Hornsby v. Greece**, that execution of a judgment given by any court must be regarded as an integral part of a “hearing” for the purposes of Article 6. It also recalled its case-law on non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of final domestic judgments. The Court noted that it had already found violations in similar cases, specifically **Spahić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina** and **Kunić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina** (both 14 November 2017). It found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on admissibility or merits.

A key point for the alleged violation under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 was that the domestic decisions in question ordered specific action to be taken. The Court therefore considered that those decisions constituted “possessions” within the meaning of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. This meant that the applicants’ entitlements under the final decisions were protected as property, and the State’s failure to enforce them engaged the positive obligation to protect property rights, not merely a procedural fair-hearing issue.

The Court concluded that the authorities did not deploy all necessary efforts to enforce fully and in due time the decisions in the applicants’ favour. It therefore found a violation of **Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1**. The judgment was final but subject to editorial revision. The case forms part of the Court’s repetitive case-law concerning Bosnia and Herzegovina’s failure to enforce final domestic decisions, confirming that such non-enforcement breaches both the right to a fair hearing and the right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

**Summary of Duranspahić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina**  
*(Application no. 47761/16 and 9 others, ECtHR, Fourth Section, 9 May 2019)*

This case concerned a group of applications lodged against Bosnia and Herzegovina under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applications were filed on various dates and were joined by the Court because they raised the same subject matter. The applicants were represented by Mr S. Zaklan, a lawyer practising in Mostar. Notice of the applications was given to the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The central complaint was the non-enforcement of domestic decisions given in the applicants’ favour. The applicants relied, expressly or in substance, on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees a fair hearing in the determination of civil rights and obligations, and on Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, which protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. The appended table to the judgment lists the individual applicants and the relevant details of their applications, but the essential factual pattern was that each applicant had obtained a domestic decision in his or her favour and that those decisions had not been enforced, or had been enforced only with delay.

A key fact for the alleged violations was that the domestic decisions in question ordered specific action to be taken. Because of this, the Court considered that those decisions constituted “possessions” within the meaning of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The failure to enforce them therefore engaged not only the applicants’ right to a fair hearing under Article 6 § 1 but also their property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In its legal reasoning, the Court reiterated that execution of a judgment given by any court must be regarded as an integral part of a “hearing” for the purposes of Article 6 § 1. It also referred to its established case-law on the non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of final domestic judgments, notably Hornsby v. Greece. The Court then noted that in the leading cases of Spahić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kunić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina, it had already found violations in respect of similar issues. The present applications therefore fell within the same systemic problem of non-enforcement by the respondent State.

The Court examined all material submitted and found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on admissibility or merits. It considered that the authorities had not deployed all necessary efforts to enforce fully and in due time the decisions in the applicants’ favour. Accordingly, the Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore: final domestic decisions in the applicants’ favour, imposing specific obligations; the failure or delay by the Bosnian authorities in enforcing those decisions; and the resulting interference with the applicants’ rights to a fair hearing and to the peaceful enjoyment of their possessions.

The case of Duranspahić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina (Application no. 47761/16 and 9 others) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section), sitting as a Committee, in a judgment dated 9 May 2019. The Committee comprised Georges Ravarani, President, Marko Bošnjak and Péter Paczolay, judges, with Liv Tigerstedt, Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The applicants were represented by Mr S. Zaklan, a lawyer practising in Mostar. Notice of the applications was given to the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The applications were lodged under Article 34 of the Convention against Bosnia and Herzegovina on various dates listed in the appended table. Because they raised the same subject matter, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment. The appended table contained the list of applicants and the relevant details of each application, but the core complaint common to all was the non-enforcement of final domestic decisions given in the applicants’ favour.

The applicants relied, expressly or in substance, on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Article 6 § 1 guarantees the right to a fair hearing in the determination of civil rights and obligations. Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. The applicants alleged that the domestic authorities had failed to enforce domestic decisions issued in their favour, thereby depriving them of the benefit of those decisions and of their possessions.

The Court reiterated its established case-law that the execution of a judgment given by any court must be regarded as an integral part of a “hearing” for the purposes of Article 6. It also referred to its case-law concerning non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of final domestic judgments, notably Hornsby v. Greece. The Court further noted that it had already found violations of similar issues in the leading cases of Spahić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kunić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina, both decided on 14 November 2017.

A key point in the Court’s reasoning was that the domestic decisions in the present applications ordered specific action to be taken. Consequently, the Court considered that those decisions constituted “possessions” within the meaning of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. This meant that the failure to enforce them engaged both the fair-trial guarantee under Article 6 § 1 and the property-protection guarantee under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The Court examined all the material submitted by the parties and found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on the admissibility and merits of the complaints from the one adopted in its earlier case-law. Having regard to that case-law, the Court considered that the authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina had not deployed all necessary efforts to enforce fully and in due time the decisions in the applicants’ favour. In other words, the domestic authorities failed to ensure the timely and complete execution of final and binding decisions that had already determined the applicants’ rights in their favour.

Accordingly, the Court found that the non-enforcement of the domestic decisions amounted to a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The case is therefore an example of the Court’s settled approach to Bosnia and Herzegovina concerning the failure to enforce final domestic decisions, particularly where those decisions order specific action and create enforceable individual entitlements.
001-191721:
**Bigović v. Montenegro** (Application no. 48343/16) concerned Ljubo Bigović, a Montenegrin national born in 1976. He was arrested on 16 February 2006 on suspicion of criminal enterprise, attempted extortion, and aiding and abetting the aggravated murder of a high-ranking police officer, S.Š., who had been killed in August 2005. On 19 February 2006 an investigating judge ordered his detention, initially for one month, under Article 148 § 1(1) of the then Code of Criminal Procedure, mainly because the gravity of the offences created a risk that he would abscond.

The applicant’s detention became the core of his later complaints. It was extended repeatedly—on 16 March, 15 April, 16 May, 15 June, and 12 July 2006, and again on 15 August 2006, 21 October 2008, and 11 March 2009. Many extensions relied on the same grounds: the gravity and number of offences, possible sentence, risk of absconding, and, later, risk to public order. Several decisions were issued collectively for multiple defendants, sometimes without specifying the duration of the extension, and often with brief or boilerplate reasoning.

An indictment was filed on 14 August 2006. The applicant was convicted at first instance on 7 August 2009 and sentenced to 30 years’ imprisonment, but that judgment was quashed on 17 February 2010. A second conviction on 9 May 2011 was also quashed on 30 December 2011. A third first-instance conviction on 9 October 2012 was upheld in 2013, then quashed by the Supreme Court on 2 April 2014. Throughout, his detention continued.

Relevant to the alleged Article 5 violations, the applicant argued that his detention was unlawful because it was not regularly reviewed and because decisions extending it were insufficiently reasoned. In particular, from 2012 the High Court extended detention “until further notice” under Article 179 § 2 of the 2009 Code, relying on risk of absconding and public-order grounds. On 1 August 2014 he applied for release, complaining about the length of detention, lack of regular review, insufficient reasoning, poor conditions, and lack of medical care. He repeatedly urged the courts to decide, but no timely ruling followed. The Court of Appeal eventually dismissed the request on 13 February 2015 after hearing a medical expert. On 20 February 2015 the Court of Appeal extended detention under Article 175 § 4, but the Supreme Court quashed that extension on 12 March 2015 because that provision did not exist and the decision lacked reasoning on his health. A new extension followed on 16 March 2015. His constitutional appeal was dismissed on 28 December 2015, served on 25 March 2016.

Relevant to the Article 3 complaints, the applicant suffered from serious ulcerative colitis, diagnosed in 2013, requiring a special diet and Vedolizumab (VDZ), which was not registered in Montenegro. Treatment was delayed, he was hospitalised repeatedly, and his family sometimes purchased doses abroad. Medical experts warned that stress, inadequate diet, and detention conditions could worsen his illness and even threaten his life. He also had eye surgery, knee problems, and psychiatric issues. He alleged overcrowding, lack of running water, limited outdoor exercise, lack of special diet and disinfectant, and inadequate medical care. The Government disputed this, describing improved cells and available care. The ECtHR later communicated his complaints concerning conditions of detention, medical care, unlawfulness and length of detention, irregular review, insufficient reasoning, and lack of a speedy decision on release.

**Bigović v. Montenegro** (Application no. 48343/16) concerned Ljubo Bigović, a Montenegrin national born in 1976, detained in 2006 in connection with an organised crime investigation. The background involved explosions at a hotel construction site in 2005 and the murder of a high-ranking police officer, S.Š., who had been investigating the case. On 16 February 2006 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of criminal enterprise, attempted extortion and aiding and abetting aggravated murder. On 19 February 2006 the High Court in Podgorica ordered his detention for one month, relying on the risk that he might abscond and the gravity of the offences.

His detention was repeatedly extended between 2006 and 2015. Early extensions were usually based on the risk of absconding, the seriousness and number of offences, and the potential sentence. Later extensions also invoked the risk that release would seriously breach public order and peace. Some extension decisions did not specify how long detention would last; others extended detention “until further notice.” The applicant was convicted and sentenced to thirty years’ imprisonment in 2009, 2011 and 2012, but those judgments were quashed or reheard. The Supreme Court ultimately upheld the conviction in 2015.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights about the conditions of his detention, especially the lack of adequate medical care; the unlawfulness of his detention due to irregular reviews of whether it remained justified; insufficient reasoning in the extension decisions; the excessive length of detention; and the failure to decide speedily on his applications for release. These complaints principally concerned Articles 3 and 5 of the Convention.

Key facts relevant to the alleged violations included that, although he applied for release on 1 August 2014, the High Court did not decide the application until 13 February 2015, despite repeated urgings. The Court of Appeal upheld the refusal. On 20 February 2015 the Court of Appeal extended his detention, but the Supreme Court quashed that order because it relied on a non-existent provision, Article 175 § 4 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and because there was no reasoning on whether the applicant’s health affected his continued detention. On 16 March 2015 the Court of Appeal again extended detention, finding his health irrelevant because the prison provided medical care and nutrition.

The applicant suffered from serious ulcerative colitis, diagnosed in 2013, as well as eye, knee and psychiatric problems. He required a special diet and Vedolizumab, a medication unavailable in Montenegro. There were delays in providing it; his family bought some doses abroad, and the prison later obtained some doses. Medical experts stated that stress and prison conditions worsened his illness and could be life-threatening. He also alleged overcrowding, lack of water, limited outdoor exercise, a toilet not separated from the cell, lack of running water and showers, medical examinations conducted in the presence of guards, a colonoscopy without anaesthesia, lack of disinfectant alcohol, and the prison’s inability to provide his prescribed diet. The Government disputed many conditions, citing cell sizes, outdoor areas and improvements after a CPT visit.

The Constitutional Court dismissed his appeal on 28 December 2015, finding the extension decisions not arbitrary and that the lawfulness of detention could be assessed only until the first-instance judgment. It did not address his complaints about detention conditions, regular review, or the delayed ruling on his release application. The ECHR communicated the applicant’s complaints to the Government on 25 January 2018.

**Bigović v. Montenegro** (Application no. 48343/16) concerned Ljubo Bigović, a Montenegrin national born in 1976, detained in the Institution for the Execution of Criminal Sanctions in Spuž. He was arrested on 16 February 2006 on suspicion of criminal enterprise, attempted extortion, and aiding and abetting the aggravated murder of a high-ranking police officer, S.Š. On 19 February 2006 an investigating judge ordered his detention under Article 148 § 1(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, mainly because of a risk that he might abscond, initially for one month.

His detention was repeatedly extended—in March, April, May, June and July 2006, and after the August 2006 indictment. Extensions often relied on the gravity and number of offences, prescribed sentences, risk of absconding, and public-order concerns. Some decisions failed to specify the duration of extension; others relied on Article 175 § 1(1) and (4) of the 2009 CCP. In 2015 the Supreme Court quashed one extension because the relied-upon Article 175 § 4 did not exist and because the decision lacked reasoning on the applicant’s health.

The applicant complained under Articles 3, 5 and 6 of the Convention about: conditions of detention, especially lack of medical care; unlawfulness of detention due to irregular reviews of its justification; insufficient reasoning in extension decisions; the length of detention; and lack of a speedy decision on his release. He alleged that extensions were not regularly reviewed under Article 179 § 2 of the CCP and that decisions were generic, collective, and failed to address his personal circumstances.

A key health issue arose in September 2013, when he was diagnosed with ulcerative colitis, an incurable inflammatory bowel disease. Medical experts stated it required a special diet, specific medication, and the least stressful environment possible; detention conditions in the IECS increased the risk of complications and could be life-threatening. He was prescribed Vedolizumab (VDZ), unavailable and unregistered in Montenegro. He received some doses bought by his family in Germany, costing tens of thousands of euros, and later some provided by the authorities, but with significant delays—for example, a dose planned for March 2016 was not administered until October 2016. He was hospitalised several times. He also suffered eye problems requiring private cataract/retinopathy surgery, knee and orthopedic issues, and anxiety-depression requiring psychiatric treatment.

As to conditions, the applicant alleged overcrowding, lack of water, insufficient daily exercise, inadequate diet and medical care. The Government disputed this, providing cell measurements and describing available facilities and medical treatment.

On 1 August 2014 the applicant applied for release, citing Article 5, the length of detention, insufficient reasoning, lack of regular review, lack of medical care, poor conditions, and his colitis. He repeatedly urged the High Court and Court of Appeal to rule; the Court of Appeal dismissed the application on 13 February 2015. Further release requests were dismissed in June and July 2015. The Constitutional Court dismissed his constitutional appeal on 28 December 2015, served on 25 March 2016, finding the detention decisions not arbitrary but not addressing the conditions, regular review, or failure to rule on his release application.

The European Court of Human Rights gave notice of the complaints to the Government on 25 January 2018; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.
001-198884:
In *Pikhun v. Ukraine* (Application no. 63754/09), the applicant, a Ukrainian national and former police officer, complained under Articles 3, 5 and 6 of the Convention about police ill-treatment and the lack of an effective investigation, unlawful detention on remand, and the unreasonable length of criminal proceedings against him.

The criminal case began on 25 September 2006 with an investigation into illegal arms possession. The applicant was later charged with murder, threats and abuse of power, and was arrested and released several times under court orders, most recently on 13 March 2009. On 30 November 2009 he was arrested in connection with new charges of firearms theft. On 3 December 2009 the Leninskyy District Court ordered his detention on remand.

The Article 3 complaint concerned events on 30 November 2009. The applicant went to the prosecutor’s office with his lawyer, where new firearms-theft charges were brought. He alleged that, after refusing to answer questions, three police officers physically assaulted him: they throttled him, handcuffed him, hit his head against a parked car, and continued ill-treating him at the police station. They allegedly stubbed a cigarette out on his left hand and demanded that he not assert his rights in the investigation. A temporary detention centre report of 22 December 2009 recorded a head wound, scratches on his head and neck, bruises on his wrists, and complaints of headache and stomach sickness; an ambulance was called. The applicant repeatedly requested medical documents, but he said these were not provided.

From 1 December 2009 he made numerous ill-treatment complaints. According to the Government, on 29 January 2010 an investigator refused to institute criminal proceedings against the police officers, finding no offence: the officers had allegedly stopped and handcuffed him after he tried to flee, the wrist bruises came from handcuffs, and no cigarette burns were found. The applicant claimed he was never given this decision and could not challenge it. Prosecutors later stated that his complaints would be examined during the trial. In 2013 the trial court noted that the events could indicate ill-treatment and notified the regional prosecutor. In 2014 the Regional Court quashed that ruling and instructed the trial court to examine the ill-treatment complaints carefully; it was unclear whether this was done.

As to detention, on 28 January 2010 the District Court extended the applicant’s detention until 30 March 2010 in his and his lawyer’s absence. His appeal was returned without examination because the case was before the trial court. On 26 February 2010, during a preparatory hearing, the court remitted the case for additional investigation and continued his detention without giving reasons or time-limits. The case returned to the trial court in July 2010. He was convicted in October 2011 and sentenced to four years, but the sentence was quashed in December 2011 and he was released under an undertaking not to abscond. Later proceedings ended in December 2018 when charges were dropped.

On length, the proceedings lasted from 2006 until 2018. The trial court held 86 hearings on the merits. Sixty-six hearings were adjourned because the prosecution, victim, expert or witnesses failed to appear; 21 because the applicant or his lawyer was absent; and 18 because the judge could not sit, adding about one year and six months.

The Court gave notice of the Article 3, 5 and 6 complaints in February 2018. It joined the Government’s non-exhaustion argument to the merits and declared the Article 3 complaints admissible.

In *Pikhun v. Ukraine* (Application no. 63754/09, ECtHR, 12 December 2019), the applicant, a Ukrainian national and former police officer, alleged violations of Articles 3, 5, and 6 of the Convention. The case arose from criminal proceedings begun in September 2006 for illegal arms possession, later expanded to murder, threats, abuse of power, and firearms theft.

**Article 3 alleged ill-treatment and ineffective investigation.** On 30 November 2009 the applicant attended the prosecutor’s office with his lawyer and was charged with firearms theft. After refusing to answer questions, he claimed three police officers assaulted him: they throttled him, handcuffed him, hit his head against a parked car, continued beating him at the police station, stubbed a cigarette out on his left hand, and demanded he not assert his rights. A temporary detention centre report recorded a head wound, scratches on his head and neck, and wrist bruises; he complained of headache and stomach sickness and received ambulance care. From 1 December 2009 he made numerous ill-treatment complaints. The Government said an investigation ended on 29 January 2010 when an investigator refused to institute criminal proceedings, finding police had restrained him after an attempted flight, wrist bruises resulted from handcuffs, and no cigarette burns existed. The applicant claimed he never received that decision and could not challenge it. Prosecutors later said his complaints would be examined during his trial. In 2013 the trial court noted possible ill-treatment and notified the regional prosecutor, but the appellate court quashed that ruling in 2014 and instructed the trial court to examine the complaints; it was unclear whether this was done. The ECtHR declared the Article 3 complaints admissible and joined the Government’s non-exhaustion objection to the merits.

**Article 5 alleged unlawful detention on remand.** After his arrest on 30 November 2009, the District Court ordered his detention on 3 December 2009. On 28 January 2010 it extended detention until 30 March 2010 in the absence of the applicant and his lawyer. His appeal was returned unexamined because the case had been transferred to the trial court. On 26 February 2010, during a preparatory hearing, the court remitted the case for additional investigation and continued his detention without giving reasons or time-limits. He remained detained until 13 December 2011, when the Regional Court quashed his conviction and released him, substituting an undertaking not to abscond. He alleged his detention on remand was unlawful.

**Article 6 alleged unreasonable length of proceedings.** The criminal proceedings were lengthy. Initiated in 2006, they involved multiple charges and repeated remittals. In 2011 he was convicted, but that conviction was quashed. In 2013 he was convicted of firearms theft but exempted from liability because the statutory time-limit had expired; that decision was quashed in 2014. According to the applicant, proceedings were terminated in 2018 after charges were dropped. The trial court held 86 merits hearings, but 66 were adjourned because the prosecution, victim, expert, or witnesses failed to appear; 21 because the applicant or his lawyer was absent; and 18 because the judge could not hear the case, causing about one year and six months’ delay. The applicant complained of unreasonable length.

In *Pikhun v. Ukraine* (Application no. 63754/09), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints brought by Mr Denis Pikhun, a Ukrainian national and former police officer, concerning alleged police ill-treatment, ineffective investigation, unlawful detention on remand, and the excessive length of criminal proceedings.

The applicant’s criminal proceedings began in 2006 with an investigation into illegal arms possession. He was arrested and released several times, and later faced charges including murder, threats, and abuse of power. On 30 November 2009, while attending the prosecutor’s office with his lawyer in connection with new firearms-theft charges, the applicant alleged that he was assaulted by three police officers. According to him, after refusing to answer questions, the officers throttled him, handcuffed him, hit his head against a parked car, and continued beating him. At the police station, they allegedly stubbed a cigarette out on his left hand and told him to stop asserting his rights. He later felt sick, and an ambulance was called at the temporary detention centre.

A detention centre report dated 22 December 2009 recorded that upon admission on 30 November 2009 the applicant had a head wound, scratches on his head and neck, and bruises on his wrists. He complained of headaches and stomach sickness. The applicant repeatedly requested medical documents and complained to prosecutors from 1 December 2009. On 29 January 2010, an investigator refused to institute criminal proceedings against the police, finding no constituent elements of an offence. The investigator said the police had forcibly stopped and handcuffed the applicant after he tried to flee; no cigarette burns were found, and wrist bruises were attributed to handcuffs. The applicant claimed he never received that decision and could not challenge it. Prosecutors later said his ill-treatment complaints would be examined during his criminal trial. In 2013, the trial court noted that the events could indicate ill-treatment and notified prosecutors, but the appellate court later quashed that ruling and instructed the trial court to examine the complaints. It was unclear whether that instruction was implemented. The Court declared the Article 3 complaints admissible and joined the Government’s non-exhaustion objection to the merits.

As to detention, the applicant was arrested on 30 November 2009. On 3 December 2009, a district court ordered his detention on remand. On 28 January 2010, the court extended his detention for four months in the absence of both the applicant and his lawyer. His appeal was returned unexamined because the case was already before the trial court. On 26 February 2010, the trial court remitted the case for further investigation and continued his detention without giving reasons or setting time-limits. He was convicted in 2011, but that conviction was quashed and he was released; further proceedings continued until 2018, when the case was terminated after charges were dropped.

Regarding the length of proceedings, the trial court held 86 hearings on the merits. However, 66 hearings were adjourned because the prosecution, victim, expert, or witnesses failed to appear; 21 were adjourned due to the applicant’s or his lawyer’s absence; and 18 were adjourned because the judge could not sit. The judge-related adjournments alone extended the proceedings by about eighteen months. The applicant complained under Articles 3, 5, and 6 of the Convention about police ill-treatment, the lack of an effective investigation, unlawful detention on remand, and unreasonable length of the criminal proceedings.
001-192424:
In *Ifandiev v. Bulgaria* (App. no. 14904/11, 18 April 2019), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint under Article 10 of the Convention concerning freedom of expression. The applicant, Mr Georgi Menelaev Ifandiev, was a Bulgarian journalist and writer born in 1950 and living in Sofia.

In 2003, the applicant published a book entitled *The Shadow of Zion*, discussing Judaism, Zionism, Freemasonry and their alleged influence on world history. On pages 69–70, the book stated that after Bulgaria’s “democratic changes” many Freemasons were former communists or people connected with communist secret services. It listed several names, including K.T., a well-known political figure and long-time leader of Bulgaria’s second-largest trade union, calling him a “pseudo trade unionist.” A footnote cited a 2002 article by another author.

In 2005, K.T. brought tort proceedings against the applicant. He claimed that the statements—that he was a Freemason, a communist connected with the former secret services, and a “pseudo trade unionist”—were untrue and defamatory. K.T. said he was a devout Orthodox Christian, had never been a member of the Communist Party or linked to the secret services, and had spent his life fighting for democracy and human rights. The applicant argued that he had relied on earlier publications, that K.T. had himself said he belonged to the Maltese Order, and that witnesses would prove the secret-service link. He also contended that the statements were not offensive or defamatory and that no non-pecuniary damage had been shown. He was legally represented throughout the domestic proceedings.

In 2008, the Sofia City Court allowed K.T.’s action and ordered the applicant to pay BGN 15,000 (EUR 7,670) in moral damages plus default interest. It found the allegations untrue: K.T.’s Orthodox faith was treated as incompatible with Freemasonry; official archives disproved the secret-service link; the applicant’s witnesses were unconvincing; and “pseudo trade unionist” was a gratuitous offence aimed at discrediting K.T. The court also said an insult was subjective, so K.T.’s feeling offended sufficed, and found that the publication had harmed his honour and dignity and worsened his health. The Sofia Court of Appeal upheld the judgment in 2009, adding that prior publication did not make the allegations less defamatory and that K.T.’s status as a public figure justified higher damages. In 2010, the Supreme Court of Cassation refused to accept the applicant’s appeal on points of law.

Enforcement later calculated the total due, including principal, interest and costs, at BGN 31,549 (EUR 16,100). K.T. eventually abandoned enforcement in 2016, and only BGN 4.55 (EUR 2.32) was seized from the applicant.

Before the ECtHR, the Government argued that the application was an abuse of process because of insulting comments the applicant later posted about the Court and judges, and that he had suffered no significant disadvantage. The Court rejected these objections. The Government also invoked Article 17, alleging anti-Semitism, but the Court found it inapplicable because that argument did not concern the specific statements about K.T. that led to liability.

On the merits, the Court accepted that the interference was prescribed by law and pursued the legitimate aim of protecting K.T.’s reputation. The decisive issue was proportionality. Although the factual allegations were untrue, the Court found them not especially scandalous or shocking. K.T. was a public official and political figure, so the limits of acceptable criticism were wider. Even assuming a pressing social need, the damages—amounting to over EUR 16,000, about 117 minimum monthly salaries—were manifestly disproportionate and risked a chilling effect on a writer and journalist. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 10.

**Case: Ifandiev v. Bulgaria (ECtHR, no. 14904/11, 18 April 2019)**

The applicant, Georgi Menelaev Ifandiev, a Bulgarian journalist and writer, published in 2003 a book titled *The Shadow of Zion*, concerning Judaism, Zionism and Freemasonry. In one passage, after discussing Freemasons, Nazis and communists, he wrote that after the “democratic changes” many Freemasons were former communists and people linked to the communist secret services. He listed several names, including K.T., whom he described as a “pseudo trade unionist.” K.T. was a prominent Bulgarian political and trade-union figure, leader of a large trade union and a member of international trade-union bodies.

In September 2005 K.T. brought a tort action against the applicant. He claimed the allegations—that he was a Freemason, a communist connected with the former secret services, and a “pseudo trade unionist”—were untrue and defamatory. K.T. stated he was a devout Orthodox Christian, had never been a member of the Communist Party or its youth organisation, and had never been linked to the secret services. The applicant argued that he had relied on earlier publications, one cited in a footnote; that K.T. had himself said he belonged to the Maltese Order; and that he intended to prove the secret-service link through witnesses. He also contended the expressions were not offensive or defamatory.

In July 2008 the Sofia City Court allowed K.T.’s action and ordered the applicant to pay BGN 15,000 (about EUR 7,670) in moral damages plus interest. Although it referred to Article 10 of the Convention, it found the applicant had overstepped acceptable criticism. It concluded that the Freemason allegation was refuted by K.T.’s Orthodox faith, that the secret-service allegation was disproved by official archive attestations and unconvincing witnesses, and that “pseudo trade unionist” was a gratuitous offence aimed at discrediting K.T. The court added that an insult was subjective and that K.T.’s feeling offended sufficed. It justified the damages by finding serious harm to K.T.’s honour and dignity and aggravated health problems. The Sofia Court of Appeal upheld the judgment in 2009, and the Supreme Court of Cassation refused to accept a further appeal in 2010. Enforcement later calculated the total due at BGN 31,549 (about EUR 16,100), though only BGN 4.55 was actually seized; proceedings were discontinued in 2016.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 10. The Government argued that Article 17 should apply because of anti-Semitic material and that the application was abusive due to insulting blog comments about the Court and judges, and that there was no significant disadvantage. The Court rejected these objections: Article 17 did not concern the impugned statements about K.T., and the blog comments, though provocative, did not make the application intolerable to handle.

On the merits, the Court accepted that the interference was prescribed by law and pursued protection of K.T.’s reputation. It accepted that the factual allegations were untrue, while “pseudo trade unionist” was a value judgment. Although the statements were objectionable, they were not especially scandalous or shocking, and K.T., as a public figure, had to tolerate wider criticism. The decisive issue was the severity of the sanction: damages exceeding EUR 16,000, equivalent to about 117 minimum monthly salaries, created a chilling effect on a writer and journalist and were manifestly disproportionate. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 10.

**Case of Ifandiev v. Bulgaria (no. 14904/11), ECtHR, 18 April 2019**, concerned Article 10 freedom of expression. The applicant, a Bulgarian journalist and writer, published in 2003 the book *The Shadow of Zion*. In a passage, he wrote that after the democratic changes Freemasons were “all communists and people connected with their gloomy secret services,” then listed K.T., calling him a “pseudo trade unionist,” implying he was a Freemason and linked to the communist secret services. A footnote cited a 2002 magazine article. K.T. was a prominent political figure, long-time leader of Bulgaria’s second-largest trade union (about 150,000 members), and active in international trade-union bodies.

In 2005 K.T. brought a tort action, claiming the statements were untrue and defamatory. He said he was a devout Orthodox Christian and could not be a Freemason; he had never been a Communist Party member or connected to the communist secret services; and he had fought for human rights and democracy. Ifandiev defended himself: he had relied on earlier publications, including the cited article; K.T. had himself said he belonged to the Maltese Order; he intended to prove the secret-service link through witnesses; and the expressions were not offensive or defamatory and caused no proven damage.

The domestic courts found against Ifandiev. In 2008 the Sofia City Court ordered him to pay BGN 15,000 (about €7,670) in moral damages plus interest. It held the statements untrue and beyond acceptable criticism: K.T.’s Orthodox faith refuted Freemasonry; official archive attestations and unconvincing witnesses disproved the secret-service allegation; and “pseudo trade unionist” was a gratuitous insult. It added that insult was subjective, so K.T.’s feeling offended sufficed. Damages were justified by reputational harm among trade unionists and internationally, and by K.T.’s worsened health/hospitalisation. The Sofia Court of Appeal upheld this in 2009, saying earlier publications did not make the allegations less defamatory and K.T.’s public status justified a higher award. In 2010 the Supreme Court of Cassation refused leave to appeal, confirming that offensiveness depended on how the addressee and his circle perceived the statement.

Enforcement later calculated the total due, including principal, interest, and costs, at BGN 31,549 (about €16,100) by October 2011; only BGN 4.55 (€2.32) was seized, and proceedings were discontinued in 2016. Before the ECtHR, the Government argued Article 17 abuse, abuse of the right of application due to Ifandiev’s insulting blog comments about the Government and judges, and no significant disadvantage because he paid almost nothing. The Court rejected those objections.

On the merits, the ECtHR accepted the interference was prescribed by law and aimed at protecting K.T.’s reputation. It assumed a pressing social need could exist, but found the civil award manifestly disproportionate. The statements, though objectionable, were not especially shocking or calumnious; K.T. was a public official, so wider criticism was acceptable; and the damages—equivalent to about 117 minimum monthly salaries—risked a chilling effect on a writer and journalist. Bulgaria thus violated Article 10.
001-193251:
In *Liblik and Others v. Estonia*, six applications were brought by four Estonian nationals—Tullio Liblik, Kalev Kangur, Toomas Annus, and Villu Reiljan—and two companies, E.L.L. Kinnisvara AS and AS Järvevana. They complained under Article 6 of the Convention that criminal proceedings against them were excessively long, and some applicants complained under Article 8 that secret surveillance authorisations had been retrospectively justified, violating their right to respect for private life and correspondence.

The underlying criminal case concerned suspicions of high-level corruption involving the exchange of land in conservation areas for development land. Proceedings were instituted on 18 August 2005 without the applicants being informed. Between August 2005 and October 2006, Estonia’s Internal Security Service carried out secret surveillance of the first, second, and third applicants. The third applicant was also a supervisory board member of the two applicant companies, and communications between the fourth applicant and surveillance targets were intercepted. The surveillance rested on 44 prosecutor authorisations (for covert observation and communication data) and 21 preliminary investigation judge authorisations (for covert listening and interception). The judges’ authorisations contained only general, boilerplate reasoning, while the prosecutors’ decisions contained no reasoning at all.

A related issue concerned the third applicant: he had been subject to secret surveillance in earlier criminal proceedings from September 2004 to January 2005, which were later terminated without prosecution. In December 2006, material from that surveillance was placed in the surveillance file of the present case.

Pre-trial proceedings ended on 31 March 2009. On 19 June 2012, Harju County Court acquitted all applicants, finding the surveillance unlawful and the resulting evidence inadmissible. It did not decide whether the authorisations had been sufficiently reasoned when issued. The Court of Appeal, after examining the surveillance files, convicted the applicants on 19 June 2013. It found that the prosecutors’ applications had contained enough information to justify surveillance, that the surveillance was lawful, and that the evidence was admissible.

On 30 June 2014, the Supreme Court upheld the convictions. It acknowledged that the judicial and prosecutorial authorisations had not been properly reasoned under domestic law. However, it held that insufficient reasoning did not amount to a lack of authorisation and did not automatically render evidence inadmissible. Instead, courts could conduct an *ex post facto* review of the substantive conditions. After examining the surveillance files, the Supreme Court concluded that probable cause and the *ultima ratio* requirement had been satisfied when the authorisations were issued. This retrospective justification was central to the Article 8 complaint.

As to length, the Supreme Court identified the relevant starting points as when each applicant was substantially affected: 25 September 2005 for the second applicant (when he found a surveillance device); 3 October 2006 for the first applicant, second applicant company, and third applicant regarding some incidents; 20 September 2007 for the first applicant company and third applicant regarding other incidents; and 16 October 2007 for the fourth applicant (when questioned as a suspect). The proceedings ended on 30 June 2014, producing durations ranging from about six years and eight months to eight years and nine months. The domestic courts found the case complex, with no significant delays attributable to the State, and concluded the length was close to excessive but still reasonable. The applicants alleged this violated Article 6 § 1. The European Court of Human Rights declared the length and retrospective-surveillance complaints admissible.

# Summary: Liblik and Others v. Estonia (Applications nos. 173/15 and 5 others)

**Parties and Proceedings:** Six applications were lodged against Estonia by four individuals—Tullio Liblik, Kalev Kangur, Toomas Annus, and Villu Reiljan—and two companies, E.L.L. Kinnisvara AS and AS Järvevana. The applicants complained under Article 6 of the Convention about the excessive length of criminal proceedings, and under Article 8 that the retrospective justification of secret surveillance authorisations violated their right to respect for private life and correspondence.

**Facts:** On 18 August 2005, criminal proceedings were instituted without informing the applicants, concerning suspicions of high-level corruption involving the exchange of plots of land in conservation areas for developable plots. From 2 September 2004 to 2 January 2005, secret surveillance had been conducted on the third applicant (Annus) in separate proceedings later terminated without prosecution; that material was placed in the surveillance file of the present case on 4 December 2006. Between 23 August 2005 and 11 October 2006, the Internal Security Service conducted surveillance on the first, second, and third applicants, intercepting communications involving the fourth applicant. These activities rested on 44 prosecutor authorisations (covert observation, communication data) and 21 preliminary investigation judge authorisations (covert listening, interception).

The authorisations were critically deficient: the judges' decisions contained only generic, formulaic reasoning (e.g., citing the gravity of the offence and difficulty of gathering evidence otherwise), while the prosecutors' decisions contained no reasoning whatsoever.

Pre-trial proceedings lasted three and a half years, ending 31 March 2009. The Harju County Court heard 92 hearing days, ultimately acquitting all applicants on 19 June 2012, finding the surveillance unlawful and the evidence inadmissible—but not addressing whether the authorisations had been sufficiently reasoned. On appeal, the Court of Appeal convicted the applicants on 19 June 2013, holding that the prosecutors' applications had contained sufficient information and the surveillance was lawful. The Supreme Court upheld the convictions on 30 June 2014, finding the evidence admissible.
