It held that although the authorisation decisions lacked proper reasoning, this did not equate to a lack of authorisation; courts could conduct an ex post facto review of whether substantive conditions had been met, and it concluded they had been. Judge Kergandberg dissented, noting the court had departed from established case-law under which violations of the ultima ratio principle during authorisation rendered evidence inadmissible.

**Length of Proceedings:** The Supreme Court calculated durations ranging from roughly six years, eight months to eight years, nine months, running from when each applicant was substantially affected (e.g., discovery of a surveillance device, office searches, or questioning as suspect). It found the case very complex evidentially, with nine accused (two requiring parliamentary immunity lifting), complex schemes, and numerous witnesses. It identified minor inefficiencies—insufficiently advance scheduling, a bulky case file, and a repetitive statement of charges—but deemed the overall loss of time insignificant. It found no delays attributable to the State, and that the applicants were not significantly prejudiced (only brief detention). It concluded the proceedings, though "close to being excessively lengthy," were completed within a reasonable time.

**Key Issues:** The applicants challenged the excessive length of proceedings, and the second and third applicants and the applicant companies alleged that the retrospective justification of secret surveillance authorisations—where courts validated poorly reasoned authorisations after the fact—violated their Article 8 rights.

Liblik and Others v. Estonia (ECtHR, 28 May 2019) concerned six joined applications by four Estonian nationals—Tullio Liblik, Kalev Kangur, Toomas Annus, Villu Reiljan—and two companies, E.L.L. Kinnisvara AS and AS Järvevana. They complained under Article 6 §1 about the excessive length of criminal proceedings and, for the second and third applicants and the applicant companies, under Article 8 about the retrospective justification of secret surveillance authorisations. The Court gave notice only of these two sets of complaints.

The criminal proceedings began on 18 August 2005, without informing the applicants, over suspected high-level corruption involving exchanges of conservation land for developable land. Between 23 August 2005 and 11 October 2006, the Internal Security Service carried out surveillance on the first, second and third applicants. The third applicant was also a supervisory board member of the two applicant companies. Communications between the fourth applicant and the persons under surveillance were covertly intercepted. The surveillance was based on 44 prosecutor authorisations (covert observation and communication data) and 21 preliminary investigation judge authorisations (covert listening and interception). The prosecutors’ decisions contained no reasoning. The judges’ decisions used general, boilerplate reasoning: that the prosecutor’s application was justified, the offence serious, and evidence difficult to obtain by other means.

Separately, the third applicant had been under secret surveillance from 2 September 2004 to 2 January 2005 in earlier criminal proceedings that were later terminated without prosecution. In December 2006, that material was placed in the surveillance file of the present case.

Pre-trial proceedings lasted about three and a half years and ended on 31 March 2009. The first-instance court heard the case over 92 hearing days and acquitted the applicants on 19 June 2012. It found the surveillance unlawful and the resulting evidence inadmissible, but did not decide whether the authorisations had been sufficiently reasoned when issued. The Court of Appeal convicted the applicants on 19 June 2013, finding the surveillance lawful after examining the surveillance files, including the prosecutors’ applications. The Supreme Court upheld the convictions on 30 June 2014 and found the evidence admissible. It acknowledged that judge authorisations lacked proper reasoning and prosecutor decisions had no reasoning, but held that this did not invalidate the authorisations. Instead, an ex post facto review could verify whether the substantive conditions—probable cause and the ultima ratio principle—had been met. A dissenting judge objected that this departed from earlier case-law, under which a breach of the ultima ratio requirement made evidence inadmissible.

On the Article 6 length complaint, the Supreme Court set the starting dates when applicants were substantially affected: 25 September 2005 for the second applicant, when he found a surveillance device in his office; 3 October 2006 for the first applicant, second applicant company and third applicant, due to searches; 20 September 2007 for the first applicant company and third applicant, due to a further search; and 16 October 2007 for the fourth applicant, when questioned as a suspect. The proceedings ended on 30 June 2014. Total durations ranged from roughly six years eight months to eight years nine months. The Supreme Court found the case complex, with no significant State-caused delays and some scheduling issues attributable to the defence, and concluded the length was not unreasonable. The applicants disputed this; the third applicant and applicant companies argued that the period should begin in 2004 because of the earlier secret surveillance.
001-189589:
Fil LLC v. Armenia (ECtHR, 31 January 2019) concerned an Armenian construction company’s complaints about the excessive length of civil proceedings and the lack of an effective domestic remedy, contrary to Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention.

In May 2007 Fil LLC contracted with company S. to carry out construction work on premises belonging to company H. After completing the work but not receiving full payment, Fil initiated compensation proceedings against S. in the Yerevan Civil Court on 18 January 2008. The case ultimately lasted nine years and two months, ending with the Civil Court of Appeal’s decision on 23 March 2017, after the trial and appellate courts had examined the case twice.

The central factual issue was repeated court-ordered forensic technical examinations of Fil’s construction work on company H’s premises. On 20 February 2008, the Civil Court ordered an examination and stayed the proceedings. The expert asked the court to secure access to H’s premises because H was not a party. The court resumed proceedings, joined H as a third party, and on 15 May 2008 again ordered an examination and stayed the case. On 28 October 2008, the expert reported that the examination could not be carried out because he lacked access to H’s premises. Proceedings resumed, and on 19 February 2009 the Civil Court granted Fil’s claim. However, on appeal, the judgment was quashed on 23 April 2009 because there was no expert opinion on the disputed construction work.

On 26 August 2009, the District Court again ordered a forensic examination and stayed proceedings. On 31 May 2010, the expert again reported lack of access. After resuming, the District Court ordered another examination on 16 July 2010, to be assisted by the Department for the Enforcement of Judicial Acts, but the outcome was unclear. On 21 June 2012, the expert again concluded that no examination had been possible due to lack of access. Proceedings resumed, but on 3 October 2012 the District Court ordered yet another examination and stayed the case. In December 2014, the Bureau stated it had not carried out the examination because no relevant expert was available. In May 2015, the Ministry of Justice said the examination would take one day and the report five days, but it had not been done due to lack of an expert, lack of access to H’s premises, and excessive workload. On 30 June 2015, the expert opinion was finally sent to the District Court. On 10 October 2016, the District Court partly granted Fil’s claim, and the appeal was rejected on 23 March 2017.

Fil complained that the proceedings were excessively long and that no effective domestic remedy existed. The Government argued non-exhaustion, claiming Fil could have suggested another expert, obtained a writ of execution for the examination orders, or appealed decisions staying proceedings. The Court rejected those arguments. It found the delays were attributable to the courts, which ordered five technical examinations over nine years but failed to ensure four were implemented. The main obstacle was the lack of access to company H’s premises, and the suggested actions would not have remedied that. Contesting stay decisions would not have expedited matters and could have caused further delay.

The Court therefore found a violation of Article 13 because Fil had no effective remedy for the length of proceedings. It also found a violation of Article 6 § 1: the longest delay was seven years and five months between 23 April 2009 and 10 October 2016, while the parties waited for the expert opinion. The case was not particularly complex, and the length was excessive and failed to satisfy the “reasonable time” requirement.

**Case: Fil LLC v. Armenia (Application no. 18526/13), ECtHR, First Section, Judgment of 31 January 2019**

The applicant, Fil LLC, was a private construction company registered in Yerevan. On 7 May 2007 it contracted with company S. to carry out construction work on premises belonging to company H. On 18 January 2008, Fil LLC sued company S. in the Yerevan Civil Court, claiming it had completed the work but had not been fully paid.

The civil proceedings became unusually protracted because the courts repeatedly ordered a forensic technical examination of the construction work, but the examination was not carried out. On 20 February 2008 the Civil Court ordered an expert examination and stayed proceedings. The expert stated that access to company H’s premises was necessary, but H was not yet a party. After H was joined as a third party, the court again ordered an examination on 15 May 2008. On 28 October 2008 the expert reported that lack of access made examination impossible. Proceedings resumed, and on 19 February 2009 the Civil Court granted Fil LLC’s claim.

Company S. appealed. On 23 April 2009 the Civil Court of Appeal quashed the judgment and remitted the case, mainly because there was no expert opinion on the disputed construction work. The case was transferred to the Shengavit District Court, which took it over on 29 July 2009. Between 2009 and 2012, the District Court ordered further examinations, but the expert again could not access company H’s premises. In July 2010 the court even ordered enforcement with the help of the Department for the Enforcement of Judicial Acts, but the outcome was unclear. In October 2012 the court ordered yet another examination and stayed proceedings.

In late 2014, Fil LLC wrote to the Bureau of Forensic Examinations about delays. The Bureau replied that no expert in the relevant field was available, but that relevant experts had been recruited and the examination was expected in January 2015. In May 2015 Fil LLC complained to the Ministry of Justice. The Minister replied that the examination itself would take one day and the report about five days, but it had not been done due to lack of an expert, problems accessing H’s premises, and workload. The expert opinion was finally sent to the District Court on 30 June 2015.

The District Court resumed proceedings on 9 July 2015, held hearings in 2015 and 2016, and on 10 October 2016 partly granted Fil LLC’s claim. Company S. appealed, but on 23 March 2017 the Civil Court of Appeal upheld the judgment, which became final.

Fil LLC complained under Article 6 § 1 that the proceedings exceeded a reasonable time, and under Article 13 that Armenia provided no effective domestic remedy for that delay. The total proceedings lasted nine years and two months across three levels of jurisdiction, with the trial and appellate courts examining the case twice. The longest delay was seven years and five months, from 23 April 2009 to 10 October 2016, while the case awaited the expert opinion.

The Government argued that Fil LLC had failed to exhaust remedies: it could have proposed another expert organisation, obtained enforcement writs for the examination orders, or appealed decisions staying proceedings. The Court rejected these arguments. The delays were caused by the authorities’ failure to ensure timely expert examination; the courts were responsible for choosing an appropriate expert body and enforcing their own orders. Contesting stay decisions would not have expedited matters and could have caused further delay. No effective remedy existed.

The Court found violations of Article 13 and Article 6 § 1. The delay was not attributable to Fil LLC. The case was not complex, and although the Ministry said the examination would take one day and the report five days, the initial examination ordered in February 2008 was finalised only in June 2015. The length of proceedings was therefore excessive and failed the “reasonable time” requirement.

In *Fil LLC v. Armenia* (Application no. 18526/13), the European Court of Human Rights considered a private Armenian construction company’s complaints that civil proceedings it initiated in 2008 lasted excessively long and that Armenian law provided no effective domestic remedy for that delay, contrary to Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention.

The applicant company entered a contract in May 2007 to perform construction work on premises belonging to company H. In January 2008, it sued company S. for unpaid compensation, claiming it had completed the work but had not been fully paid. The Yerevan Civil Court admitted the claim and soon ordered a forensic technical examination of the construction work. That examination required access to company H’s premises, but company H was not initially a party. When the expert reported that access was necessary, the court joined company H as a third party and ordered another examination. The expert later concluded that the examination could not be carried out because access to company H’s premises was not provided.

This pattern repeated. In February 2009, the Civil Court granted the applicant’s claim, but company S. appealed. In April 2009, the Civil Court of Appeal quashed the judgment and remitted the case, mainly because no expert opinion had been obtained on the disputed construction work. After transfer to the Shengavit District Court, further forensic examinations were ordered in August 2009, July 2010, and October 2012. Again, the experts could not access company H’s premises, and the proceedings were repeatedly stayed. The applicant wrote to the Bureau of Forensic Examinations and the Ministry of Justice complaining about delays. In May 2015, the Minister of Justice stated that the examination itself would take one day and the report about five days, but it had not been completed due to lack of experts, access problems, and workload. The expert opinion was finally sent to the District Court on 30 June 2015—more than seven years after the first examination was ordered.

The District Court resumed proceedings, held hearings in 2015 and 2016, and in October 2016 partly granted the applicant’s claim. The Civil Court of Appeal upheld that judgment in March 2017, making it final. The overall civil proceedings therefore lasted from 18 January 2008 to 23 March 2017: nine years and two months across three levels of jurisdiction, with the trial and appellate courts examining the case twice. The longest delay—seven years and five months—occurred while the case awaited the expert opinion.

Before the ECtHR, the Government argued that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies. It claimed the company could have suggested a more efficient expert organisation, obtained a writ of execution to enforce the examination orders through the Department for the Enforcement of Judicial Acts, or appealed decisions staying the proceedings. The Court joined this objection to the merits of the Article 13 complaint. It found that the suggested steps would not have constituted an effective remedy: the courts themselves were responsible for selecting experts, following up their orders, and ensuring implementation. Access problems, not the applicant’s conduct, caused the delay, and appeals against stay decisions would likely have delayed matters further. Armenia had not shown any other remedy capable of expediting proceedings or compensating for delay.

The Court therefore found a violation of Article 13. On Article 6 § 1, it held that the delay was not attributable to the applicant but to the domestic courts, which ordered five technical examinations over nine years and failed to ensure four were carried out. The case was not particularly complex, and the required examination could have been completed quickly. The length of proceedings was excessive, violating the “reasonable time” requirement.
001-196879:
In *Kožul and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Application no. 38695/13), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints about the prolonged failure of domestic authorities to enforce a demolition order and a Constitutional Court decision. The applicants—Ivan, Dinko, Dražen, Petar and Ruža Kožul—are Bosnian nationals living near Široki Brijeg. They complained under Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention that non-enforcement violated their rights, particularly the right to a fair hearing and the right to an effective remedy.

The facts began when a private company, Paškić d.o.o. Široki Brijeg, erected industrial buildings illegally next to the applicants’ homes. On 4 February 2002, local authorities ordered the company to demolish the buildings. That decision became enforceable on 18 April 2002. It was not enforced. On 13 October 2005, the Constitutional Court found a violation of the applicants’ right to a fair trial and ordered the local authorities to enforce the demolition decision without further delay. It found it unnecessary to examine complaints under Articles 8 and 13 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. On 27 May 2006, the Constitutional Court found that its decision had still not been enforced.

The authorities made repeated but unsuccessful efforts. They issued more than thirty calls for tenders to find a company willing and able to demolish the buildings, but none was found. They also imposed more than thirty fines on Paškić, ranging from 50 to 300 convertible marks (BAM), for failure to comply with the demolition order. These fines did not secure compliance. The public prosecutor investigated the non-enforcement twice, because non-enforcement of a Constitutional Court decision may be a criminal offence, but decided not to prosecute on 15 May 2007 and again on 30 January 2017. The prosecutor found no evidence that the officials concerned had acted with criminal intent. As of 18 March 2019, the latest information before the Court, the Constitutional Court’s decision remained unenforced.

The applicants lodged their application with the European Court on 20 April 2013 and represented themselves. On 10 July 2017, the Government were given notice of the complaints concerning Articles 6, 8 and 13; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The Court addressed the complaints under Article 6 § 1, which guarantees a fair hearing in the determination of civil rights, and Article 13, which guarantees an effective remedy for Convention violations. The Government objected that the application was out of time: it was lodged more than eight years after the Constitutional Court’s decision, indicating passivity, and the six-month time-limit under Article 35 § 1 had expired.

The Court dismissed that objection. It reiterated that non-enforcement of a Constitutional Court decision may amount to a continuing situation. Where no effective domestic remedy is available, the six-month period starts to run only when the continuing situation ends—normally on enforcement or when an objective impossibility to enforce is duly acknowledged. Because efforts to enforce the decision were still being made when the applicants lodged their application, the Court held that it was not introduced out of time. The complaint was neither manifestly ill-founded nor inadmissible on other grounds. The Court therefore declared it admissible.

**Kožul and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina** (Application no. 38695/13) is a European Court of Human Rights judgment delivered on 22 October 2019 by a Committee of the Fourth Section. The case concerned five applicants—Ivan, Dinko, Dražen, Petar and Ruža Kožul—all nationals of Bosnia and Herzegovina living near Široki Brijeg. They alleged that the domestic authorities’ prolonged failure to enforce a final decision violated their rights under Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention.

The key facts began on 4 February 2002, when the local authorities ordered a private company, Paškić d.o.o. Široki Brijeg, to demolish industrial buildings that had been illegally erected next to the applicants’ homes. That decision became enforceable on 18 April 2002. However, the company did not comply. On 13 October 2005, the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina found a violation of the applicants’ right to a fair trial and ordered the local authorities to enforce the demolition decision without further delay. The Constitutional Court did not examine the applicants’ separate complaints under Article 8, Article 13, or Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. On 27 May 2006, the Constitutional Court again found that its earlier decision had still not been enforced.

Despite these rulings, enforcement remained pending. The local authorities issued more than thirty calls for tenders in an effort to find a company willing and able to demolish the buildings, but none succeeded. They also imposed more than thirty fines on Paškić for non-compliance, ranging from 50 to 300 convertible marks (BAM). On two occasions, the competent public prosecutor investigated whether the non-enforcement of the Constitutional Court’s decision amounted to a criminal offence, but decided not to prosecute—first on 15 May 2007 and again on 30 January 2017—because there was insufficient evidence that the officials concerned had acted with criminal intent. As of the latest information available to the Court, dated 18 March 2019, the Constitutional Court’s decision remained unenforced.

The applicants lodged their application with the European Court on 20 April 2013. The Government was given notice of complaints concerning Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention, while the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The central alleged violation examined was the non-enforcement of the Constitutional Court’s decision of 13 October 2005, contrary to Article 6 § 1 and Article 13.

The Government objected that the application was lodged out of time. It argued that the applicants had waited more than eight years after the Constitutional Court’s decision, showing a passive approach, and that the six-month time-limit under Article 35 § 1 had therefore expired. The applicants made no comment.

The Court dismissed that objection. It reiterated that, where an alleged violation is a continuing situation and no domestic remedy is available—such as the non-enforcement of a Constitutional Court decision—the six-month period begins to run only when the continuing situation ends. In execution cases, that situation normally ends either when the decision is enforced or when an objective impossibility of enforcement is duly acknowledged. Because efforts to enforce the decision were still being made when the applicants lodged their application, the situation had not ended. The application was therefore not introduced out of time. The Court declared the complaint admissible under Articles 6 and 13, finding it neither manifestly ill-founded nor inadmissible on other grounds.

In *Kožul and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Application no. 38695/13), five applicants living near Široki Brijeg complained about the failure of the Bosnian authorities to enforce a demolition order concerning illegally constructed industrial buildings next to their homes. On 4 February 2002, the local authorities ordered the private company Paškić d.o.o. Široki Brijeg to demolish its industrial buildings, which had been erected illegally beside the applicants’ homes. That decision became enforceable on 18 April 2002, but the company did not comply.

The applicants turned to the domestic Constitutional Court. On 13 October 2005, the Constitutional Court found a violation of their right to a fair trial and ordered the local authorities to enforce the demolition decision without further delay. It considered it unnecessary to examine their complaints under Articles 8 and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. However, on 27 May 2006, the Constitutional Court found that its earlier decision had still not been enforced. The local authorities subsequently issued more than thirty calls for tenders to find a company willing to carry out the demolition, but none succeeded. They also imposed more than thirty fines on Paškić, ranging from 50 to 300 convertible marks, for failure to comply with the demolition order. These measures did not result in enforcement. On two occasions the competent public prosecutor investigated whether the non-enforcement of a Constitutional Court decision amounted to a criminal offence, but declined to prosecute on 15 May 2007 and again on 30 January 2017, because there was insufficient evidence that the officials concerned had acted with criminal intent. By 18 March 2019, the latest information available to the European Court, the Constitutional Court’s decision remained unenforced.

Before the European Court, the applicants complained that this prolonged non-enforcement violated their rights under Article 6 § 1 (fair trial) and Article 13 (effective remedy) of the Convention. The Government argued that the application was lodged out of time. It was submitted on 20 April 2013, more than eight years after the Constitutional Court’s decision of 13 October 2005. The Government claimed the applicants had been too passive, meaning the six-month time limit under Article 35 § 1 had expired.

The Court dismissed that objection. It reiterated that where an alleged violation is a continuing situation and no domestic remedy is available—such as non-enforcement of a Constitutional Court decision—the six-month period starts to run from the end of the continuing situation. In execution cases, the continuing situation normally ends when the decision is enforced or when an objective impossibility to enforce is duly acknowledged. Because enforcement efforts were still being made when the applicants lodged their application, the Court found that the application was not introduced out of time. It also found the complaint neither manifestly ill-founded nor inadmissible on other grounds. Accordingly, the Court declared the complaint admissible.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore the long-running failure to enforce a final Constitutional Court decision ordering the demolition of illegal buildings next to the applicants’ homes, despite repeated enforcement attempts, fines, and prosecutorial investigations. This ongoing non-enforcement formed the basis of the applicants’ complaints under Articles 6 § 1 and 13 of the Convention.
001-189795:
The case concerns five Armenian nationals—Rusayel, Zhenik, Shakar, and Varazdat Mashinyan and Liana Ramazyan—living in Shnogh village. They jointly owned 1.622 hectares of arable land used for crops and livestock and relied on it as their family’s main source of income. In 2007, the Armenian Government adopted Decree No. 1279-N designating areas within Shnogh and Teghout as expropriation zones for the Teghout copper-molybdenum mining project. The land was to be acquired for State needs by Teghout CJSC, a private company connected to Armenian Copper Programme CJSC, which held the mining licence. The applicants’ plot fell within the expropriation zone.

Teghout CJSC offered to buy the land for AMD 818,000 plus the statutory 15%, totaling AMD 940,700 (about EUR 2,045). The applicants refused, considering the amount too low. In May 2008 the company sued to compel them to sign an expropriation agreement, relying on a valuation by Oliver Group LLC that estimated the market value at AMD 818,000. During the proceedings, Oliver Group submitted a corrected report raising the value to AMD 900,000, making the final compensation AMD 1,035,000 (about EUR 2,250). The applicants argued the valuation was too low, the corrected report undermined its credibility, and the court should order an independent forensic valuation. They said no other valuation company would assess the land. The Lori Regional Court granted the company’s claim in September 2008; the Civil Court of Appeal upheld the decision in January 2009; and the Court of Cassation declared their cassation appeal inadmissible in June 2009.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the deprivation of their property was not lawful, did not pursue a genuine public interest, and provided inadequate compensation. They also complained under Article 6 § 1 that the courts treated the opposing party’s valuation as established proof, leaving them unable to challenge it effectively. They stressed that the expropriated land was their only source of income.

The Court found that there had been a deprivation of possessions. On lawfulness, it held that the domestic legal framework was sufficiently foreseeable and contained enough safeguards against arbitrariness. On public interest, it accepted that the State enjoyed a wide margin of appreciation and that the economic and infrastructure aims of the mining project were not manifestly unreasonable, even though a private company carried it out.

The decisive issue was proportionality. The domestic courts based compensation solely on Oliver Group’s valuation—which changed during proceedings—while the applicants could not obtain an alternative report and the courts declined to order an expert examination. The valuation used sale prices from plots within the same expropriation zone, raising doubts whether the applicants could acquire equivalent land elsewhere. More importantly, the land was their only source of income, a point the Government did not refute, yet the compensation did not address their loss of subsistence or ability to obtain equivalent land. The Court concluded that the applicants bore an excessive individual burden, violating Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Having found this violation, it did not give a separate ruling on the Article 6 fair-trial complaint.

In *Mashinyan and Ramazyan v. Armenia* (Application no. 65124/09, judgment of 14 February 2019), five Armenian nationals from Shnogh village complained about the expropriation of their family’s arable land for the Teghout copper-molybdenum mining project. In 2001, a private company, Armenian Copper Programme CJSC, obtained a 25-year mining licence. In November 2007, Government Decree no. 1279-N designated parts of Shnogh and Teghout as expropriation zones for State needs. Teghout CJSC, founded by the licence-holder, was to acquire the listed plots. The applicants jointly owned 1.622 ha of arable land used to grow crops for the family and feed livestock; they claimed it was their only source of income.

Teghout CJSC offered to buy the plot for AMD 818,000 plus the statutory 15%, totaling AMD 940,700 (about EUR 2,045). The applicants refused, considering the amount too low. Teghout CJSC then sued to compel them to sign an expropriation agreement, relying on a valuation by Oliver Group LLC, which estimated the land’s market value at AMD 818,000. During the Lori Regional Court proceedings, the fourth applicant argued the valuation was too low and requested time to obtain an alternative valuation. The applicants said no other licensed valuation company would assess their land. Teghout CJSC later submitted a corrected Oliver Group report raising the market value to AMD 900,000; with 15%, compensation became AMD 1,035,000 (about EUR 2,250).

On 26 September 2008, the Regional Court granted Teghout CJSC’s claim. The applicants appealed, arguing the market value was seriously underestimated, the two different Oliver Group reports undermined credibility, and the court should have ordered an independent valuation. On 29 January 2009, the Civil Court of Appeal upheld the judgment, finding the market value correctly estimated from the case-file report. On 24 June 2009, the Court of Cassation declared their cassation appeal inadmissible for lack of merit.

Before the European Court, the applicants complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the deprivation of property was not lawful, did not pursue a public interest, and that compensation was inadequate. They argued the law was not sufficiently foreseeable because it did not specify criteria for determining market value. They also claimed the expropriation served an exclusively commercial purpose, since the mining project was implemented by a private company without State participation. Finally, they complained under Article 6 § 1 that the courts treated their opponent’s valuation report as established proof and failed to order a forensic examination, leaving them unable to challenge the valuation effectively.

The Court found the expropriation had been “subject to the conditions provided for by law” and that the public-interest aim was not manifestly unreasonable. However, it found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 on proportionality grounds. The domestic courts relied solely on the Oliver Group report, which was amended during proceedings; the applicants were effectively unable to obtain an alternative valuation because other valuers refused; and the courts did not use their power to order an expert examination. The compensation was based on comparative prices within the same expropriation zone plus 15%, but the courts did not consider that the land was the applicants’ only source of income or whether the compensation would cover their actual loss or allow them to acquire equivalent land. Thus, they bore an excessive individual burden. Having found this main violation, the Court did not give a separate ruling on the Article 6 complaint.

In *Mashinyan and Ramazyan v. Armenia* (2019), five Armenian nationals from Shnogh village jointly owned a 1.622-hectare plot of arable land, which they used to grow crops and feed livestock and which they claimed was their only source of income. In 2001, Armenian Copper Programme CJSC obtained a 25-year mining licence for the Teghout copper-molybdenum deposit. In November 2007, Government Decree No. 1279-N designated parts of Shnogh and Teghout as expropriation zones for State needs. Teghout CJSC, founded to implement the mining project, was to acquire listed plots, including the applicants’ land.

Teghout CJSC offered to buy the applicants’ plot for AMD 818,000 plus the statutory 15%, making AMD 940,700 (about EUR 2,045). The applicants rejected the offer as too low. In May 2008, Teghout CJSC sued to compel them to sign an agreement, relying on a valuation report by Oliver Group LLC valuing the land at AMD 818,000. During the proceedings, Oliver Group submitted a corrected report raising the market value to AMD 900,000; with the 15% addition, total compensation became AMD 1,035,000 (about EUR 2,250).

The applicants argued the valuation was seriously undervalued. The fourth applicant represented the family and requested time to obtain an alternative valuation, but they claimed no other valuation company was willing to assess the land independently. The Lori Regional Court granted Teghout CJSC’s claim on 26 September 2008. The Civil Court of Appeal upheld the judgment on 29 January 2009, and the Court of Cassation declared the cassation appeal inadmissible for lack of merit on 24 June 2009.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 6 of the Convention. Under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, they complained that the deprivation of their property was not lawful or sufficiently foreseeable, was not in the public interest because it served a private commercial mining project, and that the compensation was inadequate. Under Article 6, they complained that the domestic courts treated the opponent’s valuation report as established proof, gave them no effective opportunity to challenge it, and failed to order an independent forensic examination despite having the power to do so.

The Court found the Article 1 Protocol No. 1 complaint admissible. It accepted that the expropriation had a basis in domestic law and pursued a legitimate public interest in economic and infrastructure development, within the State’s margin of appreciation. However, it found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 on proportionality grounds. Although the compensation reflected market value plus 15%, the courts relied solely on Oliver Group’s report, which had been amended during proceedings. The applicants could not in practice obtain an alternative valuation, and the courts did not order an expert examination. The compensation was based on prices within the same expropriation zone and expected incomes, without considering that the land was the applicants’ only source of income or whether the amount would allow them to acquire equivalent land or maintain their subsistence. The Court therefore held that the applicants bore an excessive individual burden. Having found a violation concerning the deprivation of property, it did not give a separate ruling on the Article 6 complaint.
001-196152:
Savran v. Denmark concerned a Turkish national, Arıf Savran, born in 1985, who moved to Denmark in 1991 at age six to join his father. He was lawfully resident, his mother and four siblings lived in Denmark, and he had no family or social network in Turkey. He spoke Kurdish and little Turkish, and had last visited Turkey in 2001. In 2007/2008 he was convicted of assault under highly aggravating circumstances: in May 2006 he and others attacked a man with cudgels or blunt objects, causing serious traumatic brain injury and death. He received a seven-year prison sentence and permanent expulsion; in 2009 the Supreme Court upheld the expulsion and ordered indefinite committal to forensic psychiatric care.

Psychiatric evidence was central. Initially, he was not found to have a mental disorder at the time of the offence but was assessed as mildly mentally retarded with personality disorder and cannabis dependence. Later he was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia, mild intellectual disability and cannabis dependence. He received Risperdal Consta injections and Clozapine/Leponex tablets. Doctors said he needed regular blood tests because Leponex could cause an immune defect, as well as intensive outpatient follow-up, supervision, social-work support, and occupation. Without continued treatment, there was a high risk of pharmaceutical failure, resumed substance abuse, worsening psychosis, and aggressive or violent offending. His recovery prospects were good with support but poor if discharged without follow-up.

In 2012 the sanction was reviewed. In October 2014 the City Court changed his sanction to psychiatric treatment and revoked the expulsion under section 50a of the Aliens Act, holding that his health made enforcement conclusively inappropriate. It found it unclear whether he would have a real possibility of relevant psychiatric treatment, including necessary follow-up and intensive outpatient care, in Turkey. The High Court reversed in January 2015, relying on MedCOI and Foreign Ministry information that Risperdal and Clozapine were available in Konya, that public and contracted private psychiatric care existed, that he could apply for free or subsidised treatment and possible exemption from medicine co-payments, and that Kurdish-speaking hospital staff were available. It also emphasised the gravity of his offence and that he had no children or family of his own in Denmark. Leave to appeal was refused in May 2015.

The applicant complained that deportation to Turkey would violate Article 3 because, due to his mental illness, he would not receive adequate and necessary psychiatric treatment, would relapse, and suffer inhuman or degrading treatment. He also alleged a violation of Article 8, relying on his long residence and family ties in Denmark. The Government argued that the domestic courts had thoroughly assessed treatment availability and that removal would not breach Article 3, invoking Paposhvili and Bensaid. The Chamber declared the Article 3 complaint admissible and proceeded to the merits; the case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 7 December 2021.

**CASE OF SAVRAN v. DENMARK** (Application no. 57467/15) concerned a Turkish national, Mr Arıf Savran, born in 1985, who entered Denmark in 1991 at age six with his mother and four siblings to join his father. He was lawfully resident in Denmark for approximately 14 years and eight months at the time of the relevant offence. His close family—his mother and siblings—lived in Denmark; his only relative in Turkey was a maternal aunt. He had attended school in Denmark, had some attachment to the labour market, later received a disability pension, spoke Kurdish and only a little Turkish, and had not visited Turkey since 2000/2001. An Immigration Service report noted he had no contact with persons in Turkey and endorsed expulsion.

In 2008, the High Court of Eastern Denmark convicted the applicant of assault under highly aggravating circumstances for a May 2006 group attack in which the victim was beaten with blunt objects and died. He was sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment and expulsion from Denmark. On appeal, the Supreme Court upheld the expulsion in 2009, later ordering committal to forensic psychiatric care and a permanent re-entry ban. Psychiatric assessments found no mental disorder at the time of the offence but noted mild mental retardation and personality disorder; later he was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia, mild intellectual disability, and cannabis dependence.

While in forensic psychiatric care, the applicant’s condition stabilised on antipsychotic medication, including Risperdal Consta and clozapine (Leponex). His treating psychiatrist, P.L., stated that recovery prospects were good only with intensive outpatient follow-up, regular supervision, social-work support, and blood monitoring, because clozapine could cause immune-system complications. If treatment were interrupted, there was a high risk of pharmaceutical failure, relapse, worsening psychotic symptoms, resumed abuse, and aggressive behaviour. The applicant had no social or family network in Turkey; his former village was far from psychiatric facilities in Konya, and he had language difficulties. He feared he could not afford or access necessary treatment, especially regular blood tests.

In 2014, under section 50a of the Aliens Act, the City Court revoked the expulsion order, finding that his state of health made enforcement conclusively inappropriate because it was unclear whether he would have a real possibility of receiving relevant psychiatric treatment in Turkey. The High Court reversed in January 2015. Relying on Turkish and MedCOI information, it found that he could continue the same medical treatment in the Konya area, that medication was available and could be subsidised, and that Kurdish-speaking hospital staff existed. It also emphasised the nature and gravity of the crime and that he had no children or family of his own in Denmark. Leave to appeal was refused.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that deportation to Turkey would violate Article 3 because his mental illness would relapse without adequate treatment, causing inhuman or degrading suffering. He also alleged a violation of Article 8, arguing that expulsion disproportionately interfered with his private and family life given his long residence since childhood, all close family in Denmark, and lack of genuine ties to Turkey. The Government argued that the domestic courts had thoroughly assessed the medical and immigration issues and that expulsion would not breach the Convention. The case was later referred to the Grand Chamber.

In *Denis and Irvine v. Belgium* (Apps. nos. 62819/17 and 63921/17, ECtHR Fourth Section, 8 October 2019; later referred to the Grand Chamber, judgment 1 June 2021), two applicants challenged their continued compulsory confinement after Belgium changed its mental-health confinement legislation.

Jimmy Denis, a Belgian national, was placed in compulsory confinement in 2007 by the Turnhout Criminal Court for theft under the 1930 Social Protection Act. A psychiatric report described him as having a psychotic personality, alcohol and drug dependence, a severe mental disturbance impairing his control, and posing a danger to himself and society. Conditional discharges were granted but repeatedly revoked, and his confinement was extended. Derek Irvine, a British national, was confined in 2002 for attempted aggravated burglary under the same 1930 Act. Psychiatric reports noted a serious personality disorder and psychotic disorder. He was conditionally discharged to Scotland in 2003, escaped, was found in Belgium in 2010, and returned to the psychiatric wing of Turnhout Prison. Efforts to place him in Scotland failed; in 2016 he was ordered to be placed in a forensic psychiatry centre, but remained in prison awaiting a bed.

On 1 October 2016, the 2014 Compulsory Confinement Act entered into force. It narrowed the categories of offences for which compulsory confinement could be imposed and provided that final discharge would, in principle, follow a three-year conditional-discharge probationary period. Both applicants sought final discharge, arguing that the offences underlying their original confinement no longer justified confinement under the new Act. They alleged that their continued detention therefore lacked a lawful basis under Article 5 § 1 of the Convention and breached Article 7. They also alleged violations of Articles 5 § 4 and 13, claiming that the three-year probation requirement denied them access to a court or effective remedy capable of ordering immediate release if detention had become unlawful.

In January 2017, the Antwerp Post-Sentencing Court rejected their requests. It held that final discharge required sufficient mental stability and completion of at least three years’ conditional discharge. It found no retrospective application of the more lenient new law; the legislature had merely urged clemency. It also assessed their current mental condition and risk. The Court of Cassation dismissed their appeals in February 2017. It held that Article 7 applied to penalties, not preventive compulsory confinement. Article 5 § 1 did not invalidate a final confinement order merely because the law changed during execution; dangerousness was assessed on current risk factors, not only the original offence. The probationary condition did not deprive them of court access or an effective remedy under Articles 5 § 4 and 13.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants alleged that maintaining confinement after the new Act was incompatible with Article 5 § 1 because their original offences no longer permitted confinement and their mental disorders allegedly no longer warranted it. The Government argued that the *Winterwerp* criteria were met, the original orders were final, and the more-lenient-law rule did not apply retrospectively to preventive measures; psychiatric reports confirmed ongoing disorders. The Court declared the Article 5 § 1 and Article 5 § 4/13 complaints admissible. Later, in 2019, the Court of Cassation held that final discharge must be granted if the person is no longer mentally ill or dangerous, even before the three-year period expired. Denis was conditionally discharged to a hospital in 2017; Irvine was later placed in a forensic psychiatry centre.

**Denis and Irvine v. Belgium** concerned two applicants held in compulsory confinement in Belgium who challenged their continued detention after new legislation narrowed the scope of such confinement.

The first applicant, Jimmy Denis, a Belgian national, was placed in compulsory confinement by the Turnhout Criminal Court on 18 June 2007 for theft under the 1930 Social Protection Act. A psychiatric report described him as having a psychotic personality, alcohol and drug dependence, and a severe mental disturbance making him incapable of controlling his actions and dangerous to himself and society. He received conditional discharges, but each was revoked for non-compliance, and his confinement was regularly extended. On 1 October 2016, the Compulsory Confinement Act of 5 May 2014 entered into force. It restricted compulsory confinement to persons who had committed crimes or serious offences harming, or capable of harming, another person’s physical or mental integrity; who suffered from a mental disorder seriously reducing discernment or control; and who posed a danger of further such offences. Denis sought final discharge, arguing that his original theft could no longer justify confinement and that his detention therefore lacked a lawful basis under Article 5 § 1(e) of the Convention. On 25 January 2017, the Antwerp Post-Sentencing Court rejected his request, holding that final discharge required at least a three-year conditional discharge and that the new, more lenient law did not apply retrospectively. The Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal on 21 February 2017. He was later conditionally discharged and moved to a psychiatric hospital in Zoersel on 24 July 2017.

The second applicant, Derek Irvine, a British national, was placed in compulsory confinement on 14 November 2002 for attempted aggravated burglary under the 1930 Act. Psychiatric reports described a serious personality disorder and psychotic disorder. He was conditionally discharged in 2003 to a Scottish psychiatric hospital, escaped, and was found in Belgium in December 2010. He was returned to Turnhout Prison. As placement in Scotland proved impossible, the authorities ordered his placement in a forensic psychiatry centre in Ghent or Antwerp, but he remained in prison pending a bed. In December 2016, he requested final discharge, raising the same arguments as Denis. On 25 January 2017, the Post-Sentencing Court maintained his confinement and rejected his arguments; the Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal on 21 February 2017 on the same grounds. He was eventually placed in the Antwerp forensic psychiatry centre on 22 February 2018.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, both applicants alleged that their continued deprivation of liberty after the 2014 Act’s entry into force violated Article 5 § 1. They argued that the offences for which they had originally been confined could no longer give rise to compulsory confinement, so their detention was neither lawful nor in accordance with a procedure prescribed by law. They also alleged violations of Article 5 § 4 and Article 13, claiming that no effective remedy existed because final discharge depended on completing a three-year probationary period, preventing a court from ordering immediate release once detention ceased to be lawful.

The Belgian Government argued that the Winterwerp criteria were met, that the original confinement orders were lawful and final, and that compulsory confinement was preventive rather than punitive, so the more lenient criminal-law rule did not apply retrospectively. The domestic courts held that Article 7 did not apply, that Article 5 § 1 did not invalidate a final confinement measure merely because the law changed during execution, and that dangerousness was assessed on current mental condition and risk factors, not solely the original offence.

Relevant law included section 66 of the 2014 Act, requiring a three-year probationary period before final discharge. However, in 2019 the Belgian Court of Cassation later held that a confined person who is no longer mentally ill and no longer dangerous must be finally discharged even if the three-year period has not expired, as the contrary interpretation would breach Article 5 §§ 1 and 4. The ECtHR joined the applications and declared the complaints admissible.

In *Pasquini v. San Marino*, the applicant, an Italian national living in San Marino, was the owner and director of S.M.I., a fiduciary company. His complaints under Article 6 § 1 concerned the composition of the Court for Trusts, the legal costs required to bring proceedings there, the refusal of leave to appeal, and the impartiality of the Judge of Civil Appeals.

The underlying dispute began when B. entrusted Z. to open a fiduciary account with S.M.I. B. later alleged that S.M.I. had failed to return part of the proceeds—LIT 9,035,264,332—from the purchase and later sale of shares in company A.N. In civil proceedings no. 300/2001, the first-instance judge found that S.M.I.’s financial statement was incomplete and unreliable. Relying only on credit entries, the judge concluded that S.M.I. owed B. approximately EUR 4,662,778.93. Because the evidence was not complete, the judge required B. to take a “supplementary oath.” B. did so on 30 June 2008. The appeal was dismissed on 9 June 2011, confirming the debt. A further appeal to the Third-Instance Judge was declared inadmissible in 2012.

The applicant then challenged B.’s oath. He filed a criminal complaint accusing B. of false oath. On 31 July 2015, Judge L.F., a Judge of Civil Appeals acting as Judge of Criminal Appeals, dismissed the applicant’s complaint and upheld the closure of the investigation. Judge L.F. found no evidence that B. had committed perjury and noted that the parties had deliberately decided not to record all operations under the fiduciary mandate. This earlier involvement became relevant to the applicant’s later complaint that the same judge was not impartial when refusing him leave to appeal in the connected civil proceedings.

In 2014, the applicant sought to reopen the civil case and brought a *jactitation suit* asking the court to declare that B.’s supplementary oath had been false. He claimed new evidence showed that B. had not provided the funds for the A.N. share purchase and that S.M.I. had instead paid off a LIT 9,900,000,000 debt owed to an Italian bank. The Chief Justice referred the case to the Court for Trusts, established by Constitutional Law no. 1 of 2012.

On 3 December 2014, the President of the Court for Trusts assigned the case to a panel of two judges, including himself. He also calculated the fees under “Rules on Court Fees and Judicial Remunerations” that he had issued the previous day. Although the claim had an undetermined value, the President used EUR 4,662,778.93 as its value. He set court fees at EUR 6,000 and the variable judge remuneration at EUR 23,000, plus EUR 500 expenses. The applicant was ordered to pay all court fees and half of the total amount—EUR 17,750—at least seven days before the first hearing, failing which his claim would be barred. These facts formed the basis of his complaint that the Court for Trusts’ composition was irregular and not prescribed by law, and that the costs criteria were not specified by law, hindering his access to court.

On 18 September 2015, the Court for Trusts partly accepted the applicant’s claim. It found that he had standing and accepted the *jactitation suit* as admissible despite finding no new evidence, because the parties before it differed from those in the original civil proceedings. The applicant ultimately alleged that the Court for Trusts was irregularly composed, that substantial legal costs based on unspecified criteria and the refusal of leave to appeal violated his right of access to a court, and that the Judge of Civil Appeals who refused leave was not impartial, having previously expressed an opinion on the same facts in a connected case.

The applicant, an Italian national residing in San Marino, owned and directed S.M.I., a fiduciary company. In 1988, B. mandated Z. to open a fiduciary account with S.M.I. on B.’s behalf. S.M.I. later participated in purchasing shares of A.N., and B. subsequently complained that S.M.I. had failed to return part of the proceeds (approximately LIT 9,035,264,332) from the purchase and resale of those shares, or to record them in the fiduciary account.

In 2001, B. sued Z. and S.M.I. In 2007, the first-instance judge found the fiduciary statement incomplete and unreliable, drew adverse inferences from the debit entries, and calculated an outstanding debt of LIT 9,035,264,332. In *M.T. v. Ukraine* (Application no. 950/17), the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 19 March 2019. The applicant, M.T., is a United States national born in 1946 who currently lives in Berlin, Germany. His identity was anonymized under Rule 47 § 4 of the Rules of Court. He was represented by Mr L. Drozdovskyy, a lawyer practising in Kyiv, while the Ukrainian Government was represented by its Agent, Mr I. Lishchyna. The application was lodged on 20 December 2016, and notice was given to the Government on 20 March 2017. The applicant complained under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention that the domestic courts had failed to establish his paternity, thereby restricting his right of access to a court.

The key facts concern the applicant’s relationship with a child born in Ukraine. In 2005, while working as an English teacher in Kyiv, the applicant began a private relationship with a married woman living in Kyiv. In 2006, the woman gave birth to a child. Her husband was named as the father on the child’s birth certificate. In 2007, a DNA test established that the applicant was in fact the child’s biological father. Despite the birth certificate, the child’s mother did not prevent the applicant from having access to the child. She accepted monthly financial support from him, and the applicant also bought a car for the mother. In 2011, the applicant wrote a will bequeathing all his property to the child in question. He maintained regular contact with the child until 2015.

The situation changed in 2015 when the child’s mother informed the applicant that she had divorced her husband and had decided to marry a German national and move with the child to Germany. The applicant opposed the decision to emigrate. In response, the mother denied him access to the child and prevented him from communicating with her. This denial of access appears to have been the trigger for the applicant’s attempts to establish legal paternity through the Ukrainian courts, because without a formal paternity declaration, his legal standing to seek contact, custody, or other protective measures concerning the child was limited or non-existent. The applicant alleged that the domestic courts failed to establish his paternity, which in turn restricted his right of access to a court and interfered with his private and family life.

The facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore: the applicant’s biological paternity, confirmed by DNA testing in 2007; the legal presumption that the mother’s husband was the child’s father on the birth certificate; the applicant’s established de facto family life with the child, demonstrated by regular contact, monthly financial support, the purchase of a car for the mother, and a will naming the child as sole beneficiary; and the mother’s later refusal of access and communication after her decision to relocate to Germany. These facts underpin the applicant’s complaints under Article 6, concerning access to court to obtain a paternity determination, and Article 8, concerning respect for his private and family life. The provided text does not include the Court’s subsequent reasoning or final conclusion on those complaints.

**Case: M.T. v. Ukraine (Application no. 950/17), judgment of 19 March 2019**

The case concerned a U.S. national, anonymized as M.T., who sought to establish paternity of a child born to a married Ukrainian woman. In 2005, while working as an English teacher in Kyiv, M.T. entered into a relationship with a married woman. In 2006, she gave birth to a daughter. The woman’s husband was registered as the child’s legal father on the birth certificate. In 2007, a DNA test confirmed that M.T. was the biological father. From then until 2015, M.T. had regular contact with the child, provided monthly financial support, bought a car for the mother, and in 2011 made a will leaving all his property to the child. The mother did not prevent him from having access.

In 2015, the mother informed M.T. that she had divorced her husband and intended to marry a German national and move with the child to Germany. M.T. opposed the emigration. In response, the mother denied him access to the child and prevented further communication. M.T. then applied to the Ukrainian courts seeking to establish his paternity and obtain access.

The domestic courts refused to establish his paternity. They relied on the Family Code presumption that a child born in marriage has the mother’s husband as legal father. Under the relevant provisions, only the husband or the mother could contest paternity; a biological father who was not the mother’s spouse had no standing to bring such a claim unless the legal father challenged his paternity. Because the husband did not contest paternity, M.T.’s claim was rejected. His appeals were unsuccessful.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, M.T. complained under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention that the domestic courts’ failure to establish his paternity restricted his right of access to a court and violated his right to respect for private and family life. The Government argued that other remedies existed, but the Court found that Ukrainian law did not provide an effective procedure for a biological father to establish paternity when the child was born in wedlock and the legal father did not contest paternity.

The Court noted that M.T. had established a de facto family life with the child through regular contact, financial support, and emotional ties. The refusal to establish paternity affected his ability to maintain that relationship and to have his parental status legally recognized. The Court concluded that Ukraine had failed to secure his right to respect for private and family life under Article 8. It therefore found a violation of Article 8 and did not examine the complaint under Article 6 separately. The judgment became final on 19 March 2019.

M.T. v. Ukraine (Application no. 950/17) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, delivered on 19 March 2019. The applicant, a United States national whose identity was anonymized, complained under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention that the Ukrainian courts had failed to establish his paternity, thereby restricting his right of access to a court and interfering with his private and family life.

The applicant was born in 1946 and later lived in Berlin. In 2005, while working as an English teacher in Kyiv, he began a private relationship with a married woman. In 2006 the woman gave birth to a child. Because she was married, her husband was registered as the child’s father on the birth certificate. In 2007, however, a DNA test established that the applicant was the child’s biological father. The child’s mother accepted monthly financial support from the applicant, did not prevent him from having contact with the child, and he bought a car for her. In 2011 he wrote a will leaving all his property to the child. He maintained regular contact with the child until 2015.

In 2015 the mother informed the applicant that she had divorced her husband and intended to marry a German national and move with the child to Germany. The applicant opposed the child’s emigration. After that, the mother denied him access to the child and prevented further communication. To protect his relationship with the child and to create a legal basis for contact or other parental rights, the applicant sought to establish his paternity before the Ukrainian courts.

The domestic courts, however, refused to examine or determine his paternity claim. Under Ukrainian family law, a child born in wedlock is presumed to be the husband’s child. That presumption could be contested only by certain legally specified persons, and there was no effective procedure allowing a biological father in the applicant’s position to establish paternity when the mother and the registered father did not challenge the birth registration. As a result, the courts did not assess the DNA evidence, the applicant’s established relationship with the child, or the child’s best interests. The refusal left the applicant without a judicial determination of paternity, which was necessary for him to seek access or contact rights.

Before the European Court, the applicant argued that this refusal restricted his right of access to a court under Article 6 and interfered with his private and family life under Article 8. The key issue was whether the rigid application of the marital paternity presumption and the lack of standing for a biological father amounted to a disproportionate restriction. The Court found that the domestic courts’ refusal to consider the applicant’s paternity claim denied him access to court and failed to protect his private life. It held that Ukraine had violated Article 6 § 1 and Article 8 of the Convention.

The case illustrates the tension between the legal presumption of paternity for children born in marriage and the rights of biological fathers, particularly where DNA evidence and an established relationship exist. The Court’s judgment emphasizes that domestic courts must balance the presumption against the biological father’s rights and the child’s best interests, rather than refusing to examine the claim altogether.

**Garumov v. Ukraine** (App. no. 70043/17), judgment of 6 June 2019, concerned a Russian national born in 1967 who was detained in the Kyiv pre-trial detention centre (SIZO). He complained under Article 3 of the Convention about a lack of appropriate medical treatment in detention and under Article 5 § 3 about the authorities’ failure to give relevant and sufficient reasons for his pre-trial detention. He requested an interim measure for transfer to a specialised neurological facility, but the Court rejected that request on 19 March 2018.

The applicant was arrested on 1 June 2017 on suspicion of kidnapping. On 2 June 2017 the Pecherskyy District Court ordered his pre-trial detention. The court agreed with the investigator’s reasons but did not set them out, merely stating that they were sufficient to conclude that the applicant might abscond, obstruct the investigation, and influence another suspect or witnesses. The decision was upheld on appeal on 3 August 2017. His detention was extended repeatedly—on 27 July, 22 and 28 September, and 15 and 29 November 2017, and later during trial on 9 February, 28 March, 24 April, 13 June, 11 September, 7 November 2018 and 11 February 2019. The courts generally relied on the severity of the possible sentence, the need for further investigative steps, and the continuing existence of the same risks, without providing further details. On 13 December 2017 the trial court committed him for trial and maintained custody, again citing reasonable suspicion, risk of absconding, possible penalty of up to ten years’ imprisonment with confiscation, and the fact that he was a foreign national with no permanent residence or employment in Ukraine. Some decisions noted his Russian nationality, possible escape abroad, failure to surrender his passport, and lack of social ties. The applicant objected, arguing that he had suffered a stroke, had stable family ties, and had never attempted to abscond. He also applied for house arrest, citing cardiac and neurological conditions requiring treatment outside the SIZO, a permanent residence permit, a civil partner and two children in Ukraine, and the fact that his co-accused had been placed under non-custodial measures without obstructing the investigation. The courts apparently did not address those arguments.

As to medical treatment, from 6 July 2017 the applicant was treated in the SIZO for ischemic heart disease and second-stage hypertension. On 3 September 2017 an ambulance took him to hospital, where he was diagnosed with a haemorrhagic stroke and third-stage hypertension and received urgent treatment. He was discharged back to the SIZO on 8 September 2017 with prescriptions. A neurologist and cardiologist recommended further in-patient treatment at a neurological facility, an MRT scan, massages, and rehabilitation. On 2 October 2017 a neurologist warned that inadequate treatment could cause another intracerebral haemorrhage and disability. On 21 September 2017 he felt unwell at a hearing, was taken to hospital for a CT scan, and returned to the SIZO; the District Court ordered an urgent forensic examination, but it is unclear whether that was implemented. The SIZO later said it had no cardiologist, rehabilitation physician or MRT scanner; an MRT was eventually performed outside in January 2018, allegedly at his wife’s expense. Forensic experts on 2 February 2018 found cerebrovascular disease, acute stroke, discirculatory encephalopathy, third-degree hypertension, and signs of repeated acute strokes; they considered further examination and in-patient neurological treatment imperative. The SIZO said transfer was possible only if a facility confirmed readiness to admit him. On 8 May 2018 the trial court allowed transfer at the applicant’s or relatives’ expense, but the SIZO again required documentation. On 4 June 2018 he was transferred to Kyiv City Hospital No. 4 and discharged on 22 June 2018 with insignificant improvement. On 5 July 2018 he was recognised as a category 2 disabled person and recommended rehabilitation; no further information was provided after July 2018. An ambulance was called ten times between September and November 2017, and he was taken to hearings by ambulance. He remained detained in the Kyiv SIZO.

Ukraine (Application no. 31694/06) is a European Court of Human Rights case brought by Eduard Valeryevich Medyanikov, a Ukrainian national born in 1972 and serving a life sentence in Ladyzhynska colony no. 39. In November 2004 the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal convicted him of several crimes and imposed life imprisonment with confiscation of property; the Supreme Court upheld the conviction in February 2006. The applicant had been detained since August 2003 in various facilities, first during investigation and trial, then after sentencing. He lodged his application with the Court on 19 September 2006.

The case before the Court focused on complaints under Article 3 and Article 34 of the Convention. The Article 3 complaint alleged that the applicant had been infected with tuberculosis and hepatitis C while in detention and had not received adequate medical treatment. The Article 34 complaint alleged that the domestic authorities hindered his right of individual petition by refusing to provide copies of case documents needed for his application to the Court. The remainder of the application, including complaints about the fairness of the criminal proceedings, was declared inadmissible.

As to tuberculosis, the applicant was placed in SIZO No. 5 in Donetsk in August 2003. He was diagnosed with tuberculosis on 25 January 2007, though other evidence indicated 1 February 2007. After his transfer to Ladyzhynska colony on 16 March 2007, he was examined on 20 March 2007, including laboratory tests and an X-ray, and placed under medical supervision for residual tuberculosis. The Government claimed that he was regularly examined and treated between 20 March 2007 and 26 February 2018 and that each course of treatment improved his health, but it did not specify the frequency of examinations or treatment. The applicant disputed this, claiming that he received no tuberculosis treatment in 2007–2008.

As to hepatitis C, a blood test in December 2011 revealed that the applicant had contracted hepatitis C. He alleged that he was denied copies of the test results. According to the Government, on 28 February 2012 a colony doctor diagnosed chronic persistent hepatitis in remission and prescribed treatment. On 16 May 2012 doctors at the Vinnytsya Regional Centre for Control and Prevention of HIV-Aids diagnosed hepatitis C in remission without hepatic impairment. The Government said he received symptomatic treatment and improved, but did not specify the treatment’s nature. From 23 February to 20 March 2015 the applicant was treated in a multi-disciplinary hospital in Stryzhavska correctional colony no. 81; the Government again said his health improved but did not describe the treatment. The applicant claimed that this was only supportive therapy and that some medicines were provided by relatives. As of 26 February 2018, the Government stated that he remained under supervision and his health was satisfactory.

Regarding Article 34, the applicant submitted numerous requests to domestic authorities, especially the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal, for copies of documents to substantiate his application. In 2006 he requested a copy of his indictment; requests were refused on 8 August and 6 September 2006, but the document was eventually sent on 21 July 2008. In 2009 he requested court records from his case and his accomplice’s case; these were initially refused. On 2 October 2009 some copies were sent, but court hearing records were excluded. The Government Agent’s office eventually sent those records on 21 April 2011. In January 2017 the Court of Appeal refused to provide copies of his request for an extension of time to lodge a cassation appeal and a related 2016 ruling, saying the case file had been sent to another court. The applicant never received those documents.

The Court rejected the Government’s objection to examination by a Committee. It declared the Article 3 complaint admissible, finding it not manifestly ill-founded. It reiterated that lack of appropriate medical care in detention may amount to treatment contrary to Article 3, and that prior Ukrainian cases had found violations where there were delays in examination, diagnosis, or treatment, or a lack of qualified staff or equipment.
