In *P.R. v. Austria* (Application no. 200/15, judgment 21 November 2019), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Austria violated Article 8 (right to private life) by refusing to issue the applicant a new or amended university diploma certificate after he changed his surname.

The applicant, an Austrian national born in 1968, completed legal studies at Karl-Franzens-University, Graz. In February 1997 he was awarded the academic degree *Magister iuris* and received a diploma certificate (*Sponsionsurkunde*). In 2010 he asked the Vienna Municipality to change his surname from S. to R. under the Name Amendment Act 1988. He claimed he suffered unacceptable economic and social disadvantages and discrimination because of the “oriental origin” of his former surname. On 12 February 2010, the Vienna Municipality granted the name change.

The applicant then asked the University of Graz to issue a rectified diploma certificate or a notice of award bearing his new surname. On 19 August 2010, the university’s Director of Studies refused, finding no legal basis. The degree had been awarded under the law in force in 1997; the later name change had no retroactive effect; and issuing a new notice would imply a second award of the same degree. The university Senate dismissed his appeal on 11 November 2011, holding that the surname change did not affect the degree and did not oblige the university to amend the certificate. The Constitutional Court declined to hear the complaint on 11 June 2012, finding no sufficient indication of a rights violation and noting that anti-discrimination laws existed. On remittal, the Administrative Court dismissed the complaint on 26 June 2014. It held that the right to use an academic degree attaches to the person awarded it and that there was no subjective right to have previously issued documents changed after a name change.

Before the ECtHR, P.R. complained under Article 8 that the refusal to issue a new diploma certificate violated his private life. He argued that, although his name change was legally recognised, he still had to reveal his former surname when proving his qualifications to employers, the Lawyer’s Chamber and others. A Central Personal Status Register excerpt was not always sufficient, especially in legal employment. This forced disclosure caused explanations, stigmatisation and discrimination, defeating the purpose of his name change. The Government argued that Article 8 was not engaged because an academic degree is not part of a name; the applicant could use his degree and prove it via the register. Any interference was necessary and proportionate, and anti-discrimination remedies were available.

The Court found Article 8 applicable. In Austria, academic degrees are closely linked to a person’s name and form part of personal identity. Refusing a document showing his new name affected his private life. The Court also rejected the non-exhaustion argument: a register excerpt might not suffice where an official university graduation document is required, and anti-discrimination remedies did not address this specific problem. On the merits, the Court applied the State’s positive obligation to ensure respect for private life. The requested measure—amending or duplicating a diploma certificate—was narrow and precise, while the impact on the applicant was significant. There was no evidence that amendment would undermine legal certainty or facilitate abuse, and the refusal was based on formal considerations without balancing the competing interests. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 8.

P.R. v. Austria (Application no. 200/15) concerned an Austrian national, born in 1968, who completed legal studies at Karl-Franzens-University Graz. In February 1997 he was awarded the academic degree Magister iuris at a graduation ceremony (Sponsion) and received a diploma certificate (Sponsionsurkunde) bearing his then surname, S. In 2010, he applied to the Vienna Municipality to change his surname from S. to R under section 2(1)(10) of the Name Amendment Act 1988, which permits a name change to avoid unacceptable economic or social disadvantages. He claimed discrimination because of the “oriental origin” of his former name and submitted empirical studies. On 12 February 2010 the Municipality granted the change.

The applicant then asked the University of Graz to issue a rectified diploma certificate or an award decision showing his new surname. The University’s Director of Studies refused on 19 August 2010, stating there was no legal basis: his degree had been awarded under the law in force at the time; the name change had no retroactive effect; and issuing a new notice would imply a second award of the same degree. The University Senate dismissed his appeal in November 2011, finding that the right to hold the degree remained linked to the person and that the Municipality’s decision did not oblige the University to amend certificates. The Constitutional Court declined to hear the case in June 2012, noting that anti-discrimination laws existed. The Administrative Court dismissed his complaint in June 2014, holding there was no subjective right to have previously issued documents changed after a surname change and no provision requiring university action.

Before the ECtHR, P.R. alleged that Austria’s refusal to issue an amended or new diploma certificate violated Article 8, the right to respect for private life. He argued that although his name change was legally recognized, he remained forced to reveal his former “oriental-sounding” surname whenever he needed to prove his law degree, especially to employers and the Lawyer’s Chamber when seeking trainee registration. This exposed him to explanations and social stigmatisation, undermining the purpose of the name change. The Government contended Article 8 was not applicable because an academic degree is not part of a name and he could prove his degree through an excerpt from the Central Personal Status Register. They also argued domestic anti-discrimination remedies were available.

The Court declared the complaint admissible and found Article 8 applicable. It noted that academic degrees can be closely related to a person’s name and identity in Austria, and that refusal to provide an accepted document showing the new name affected private life. Register excerpts might not suffice where official university proof of a law degree was required. On the merits, the Court examined the State’s positive obligation to strike a fair balance. The impact on the applicant was significant, while the requested measure—amending or duplicating an existing certificate—was narrow and not burdensome. Legal certainty concerns did not justify refusing merely to update an already awarded certificate, and the authorities had made no real balancing of interests. The Court therefore held that Austria violated Article 8 by failing to provide a new or amended diploma certificate bearing the applicant’s changed surname.

**Case of Haddad v. Spain (Application no. 16572/17)** concerned an alleged violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights—the right to respect for family life—after Spanish authorities placed the applicant’s daughter in foster care with a view to adoption and refused him contact.

The applicant, Mr Wael Haddad, a Syrian national, arrived in Spain in January 2012 with his Spanish wife and three minor children after fleeing the armed conflict in Syria. One month later, his wife lodged a domestic-violence complaint. On 2 February 2012, the Coslada judge no. 1 issued a temporary protection order barring the applicant from approaching or communicating with his wife and children, requiring a tracking bracelet, and temporarily withdrawing his parental responsibility and contact rights. Despite the order, the wife twice returned to live with him, and he was arrested for violating the order but released. Shelter reports later described serious emotional, educational and behavioural deprivation in the children’s relationship with their mother.

On 15 June 2012, following a request from the mother stating she could no longer care for the children, the Madrid regional government declared all three children abandoned and assumed guardianship, placing them in residential care. The applicant was not informed of the abandonment declaration or related care decisions. The children were moved to Murcia. In February 2013, the Spanish Muslim Association wrote on the applicant’s behalf, saying he had no information about his children and requesting contact; the child protection department refused outsider visits and said return to the birth family was not planned.

In April 2013, the applicant was notified by public edict of a guardianship confirmation hearing and was contacted by telephone. He did not attend and said he would appeal if necessary. Later reports noted alleged abuse by the applicant and the mother’s vulnerabilities. On 20 September 2013, the regional child protection board decided to place the daughter in temporary foster care with a view to adoption. She was placed with a foster family on 24 September 2013, with no provision for birth-family visits.

Crucially, on 27 September 2013, a criminal court acquitted the applicant of all domestic-violence charges and set aside the protection order and civil measures. The acquittal became final on 8 November 2013. The criminal judge found the wife’s allegations vague, witness evidence imprecise, and expert reports insufficiently specific to rebut the presumption of innocence.

On 19 November 2013, with a lawyer, the applicant contacted child protection services, informed them of his acquittal, stated he had stable work and income, and requested permission to see his children. A February 2014 report nevertheless proposed refusing visits to his daughter and provisionally refusing visits to his sons, noting the daughter had adjusted well to pre-adoption fostering and the sons showed fear and distrust. The applicant appealed the daughter’s foster placement in May 2014.

On 11 February 2015, a first-instance judge authorised the daughter’s foster care with a view to adoption, citing her best interests. The applicant appealed, arguing that he had been acquitted, that the abandonment arose from the mother’s conduct and the war, and that his own parenting capacity had never been assessed. The regional government responded that he had shown no interest and had not appealed earlier care decisions.

On 7 April 2016, the Murcia Audiencia Provincial dismissed the appeals, relying on the applicant’s alleged lack of interest, lack of contact, and the child’s strong bonds with her foster family. It warned that removing her would seriously harm her development and found the return of his sons to him irrelevant. In fact, the sons had been returned to the applicant in February 2016. His amparo appeal was declared inadmissible in October 2016.

The ECtHR ultimately found a violation of Article 8, concluding that Spain had failed to strike a fair balance and to adequately involve the father in decisions regarding his daughter after his acquittal.

In *Haddad v. Spain* (Application no. 16572/17), the applicant, a Syrian national living in Madrid, complained under Article 8 of the Convention about the placement of his daughter in foster care with a view to adoption and the resulting interference with his family life.

The applicant and his Spanish wife left Syria in January 2012 with their three minor children because of the armed conflict. One month after arriving in Spain, the wife lodged a criminal complaint against the applicant for domestic violence. In February 2012 the Coslada investigating judge issued a protection order barring him from approaching or communicating with his wife and children and temporarily suspending his parental responsibility and contact rights. Despite the order, the wife twice left an emergency shelter and returned to live with him. He was arrested for breaching the order on two occasions but released. Shelter reports in April and May 2012 described serious emotional, educational and behavioural deprivation in the children’s relationship with their mother, and in June 2012 the wife filed a further violence complaint.

On 15 June 2012 the Madrid regional government declared the three children abandoned and took over their guardianship under the urgent procedure, following the wife’s request that she could no longer care for them due to family conflict and lack of resources. The children were placed in residential care and then moved to Murcia. The applicant was not informed of the abandonment declaration or the care decisions. In July 2012 the Murcia authorities assumed guardianship. In February 2013 the Spanish Muslim Association wrote on the applicant’s behalf seeking information and possible contact; the child protection department replied that there were no plans to return the children to their birth family and that visits by outsiders were undesirable. In April 2013 the applicant was notified by edict in the Murcia official gazette of a hearing to confirm guardianship, and was later contacted by telephone, but he did not attend.

Reports in June and July 2013 referred to alleged abuse by the applicant, the protection order, and the mother’s vulnerable personality and lack of parenting capacity. They recommended placing the daughter in temporary foster care with a view to adoption and suspending birth-family visits. On 20 September 2013 the regional child protection board so decided, and the daughter was placed with a foster family on 24 September 2013.

Crucially, on 27 September 2013 the Alcalá de Henares criminal court acquitted the applicant of all charges and set aside the earlier criminal and civil measures. The acquittal became final in November 2013. The court cited vague allegations, imprecise witness evidence and generic expert reports. In November 2013 the applicant contacted child protection services, provided the acquittal judgment, said he had stable work and income, and asked to see his children.

In February 2014 the child protection department refused contact with his daughter and provisionally refused contact with his sons, noting the applicant had had no contact with the children between June 2012 and November 2013 and that the daughter had adjusted well to pre-adoptive fostering. The applicant appealed the daughter’s foster placement. In February 2015 the Murcia first-instance court authorised foster care with a view to adoption, finding it beneficial for the child. The applicant appealed, arguing that his acquittal removed the basis for the earlier measures and that his own parenting capacity had never been assessed. In April 2016 the Murcia Audiencia Provincial dismissed the appeal, relying on his alleged lack of interest, the child’s strong bonds with the foster family, and the risk of serious harm if the placement ended. The applicant’s sons were returned to him in February 2016.

His constitutional amparo appeal was declared inadmissible in October 2016 for failing to demonstrate special constitutional significance. The central Article 8 issue was whether Spain had unjustifiably interfered with the applicant’s family life by maintaining pre-adoptive foster care and refusing contact/restoration, particularly after his acquittal and despite his sons’ return.

The applicant claimed that he did not receive adequate medical care while in detention. The Court noted that he suffered from serious medical conditions, as indicated in the appended table, and that these affected his everyday functioning. It reiterated that the adequacy of medical assistance is difficult to determine but requires authorities to ensure prompt and accurate diagnosis and care. Where required by the nature of a medical condition, supervision must be regular and systematic and must involve a comprehensive therapeutic strategy aimed at successfully treating the detainee’s health problems or preventing their aggravation. Prison medical treatment must be appropriate and comparable to the quality the State has committed to providing to the general population, though detainees are not guaranteed the same level as the best outside health establishments.

Ukraine* and *Sergey Antonov v. Ukraine*, where similar issues had produced Article 3 violations. The applicant also complained under Article 13 that there were no effective domestic remedies for his complaint about the quality of medical care in detention. Article 13 guarantees an effective remedy before a national authority for violations of Convention rights. The Court observed that it had repeatedly found a lack of effective domestic remedies in Ukraine for complaints about medical treatment in detention, citing cases including *Melnik v. Ukraine*, *Koval v. Ukraine*, and *Savinov v. Ukraine*. In those cases, none of the remedies suggested by the Government were capable of preventing the alleged violations, stopping their continuation, or providing adequate redress. In *Samoylenko v. Ukraine* (Application no. 45050/10), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by Ukrainian national Oleg Nikolayevich Samoylenko, born in 1962. The applicant alleged that the authorities failed to give relevant and sufficient reasons to justify his pre-trial detention; that court decisions extending his detention in April and June 2010 were taken in his and his lawyer’s absence; and that no effective procedure was available to challenge the lawfulness of his detention. The application was lodged on 2 August 2010. The Government was notified on 9 December 2015. The applicant died on 6 October 2017, and on 9 November 2017 his wife, Tatyana Samoylenko, expressed the wish to pursue the proceedings.

On 8 February 2010 the Dnipropetrovsk regional prosecutor’s office arrested the applicant on suspicion of fraudulent business activities. On 11 February 2010 the Zhovtneviy District Court of Dnipropetrovsk extended his custody to ten days for a personality assessment. On 18 February 2010 the District Court ordered his detention on remand. It noted that he was unemployed, had poor character references from his place of residence, and could potentially influence witnesses and abscond. Represented by a lawyer, the applicant appealed, arguing that he had no prior criminal record, a permanent residence, and a family to support, including a pregnant wife and ailing elderly parents, and that he suffered from health conditions that could deteriorate in detention. On 24 February 2010 the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Court of Appeal upheld the detention order, finding no evidence that his health was incompatible with detention and noting that the alleged offence was serious, punishable by up to five years’ imprisonment.

On 6 April 2010 the District Court extended the applicant’s detention until 8 June 2010, citing the need for further investigation and the absence of grounds for release. The hearing was held in the presence of the prosecutor but without the applicant or his lawyer; according to the applicant, they had not been summoned. The applicant said he appealed, and that on an unspecified date the Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal in a hearing attended by the prosecutor, again without summoning him or his lawyer. He did not submit a copy of that decision.

On 7 June 2010 the Court of Appeal, acting as a first-instance court, extended the applicant’s detention until 8 July 2010, finding no grounds for release. That hearing was also held in the prosecutor’s presence; the applicant and his lawyer were allegedly not summoned. The decision was not subject to appeal.

The criminal case was later transferred to the trial court, and the applicant was committed for trial. The trial court maintained his detention on remand. On 6 September and 28 October 2010 the applicant applied for release pending trial. On 2 November 2010 the trial court dismissed the applications as unfounded. It found that the crimes imputed to him were sufficiently serious to potentially warrant a prison sentence of ten years or more, that he pleaded not guilty and refused to give testimony, and, without providing details, that he might influence witnesses and obstruct proceedings if released.

These facts underpinned the alleged violations: the lack of relevant and sufficient reasons for pre-trial detention, the holding of detention-extension hearings without the applicant or his lawyer, and the absence of an effective procedure to challenge the lawfulness of detention. The Fifth Section Committee adopted its judgment on 24 October 2019.

**Summary of A.S. v. Norway (Application no. 60371/15)**

The case of A.S. v. Norway concerns a Polish national, A.S., residing in Norway, who challenged the Norwegian authorities' decision to permanently sever her legal ties with her son, X, and deny her contact and information about his whereabouts. The applicant alleged that these measures violated her and her child's right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The key facts are as follows: The applicant gave birth to X in December 2009. From April 2010, Norwegian child welfare services received numerous notifications of concern from health visitors and the applicant's family regarding a lack of interaction between the applicant and her son. After attempting various assistance measures, X was placed in an emergency foster home on 27 March 2012, at the age of two years and three months.

On 18 September 2012, the County Social Welfare Board issued a long-term care order, granting the applicant only two hours of supervised contact twice a year. This decision was confirmed by the City Court on 25 February 2013. The court found pervasive deficiencies in the applicant's ability to provide care, noting that X had suffered extensive and serious neglect, resulting in significant developmental and emotional problems.

In 2014, the applicant requested that the foster care placement be terminated or, alternatively, that her contact rights be extended. On 5 November 2014, the County Social Welfare Board rejected her request, revoked all contact rights, and determined she should not be informed of X's whereabouts.

The applicant brought the case before the City Court, which heard testimony from fourteen witnesses over two days in March 2015. The court's judgment of 27 March 2015 found that the applicant would not be able to provide X with proper care, either at that time or in the future. The court emphasized X's special needs and vulnerability, noting that he had been diagnosed with symptoms consistent with developmental disorders and had suffered relational trauma while in his mother's care. Since living in the foster home, X had shown significant improvement in his motor skills, communication, socialisation, and emotional regulation. He had developed a secure attachment to his foster parents, whom he called "mum and dad."

The court found that X's reactions to contact sessions with the applicant were severe, including regression to baby behaviour, bed-wetting, and retching when eating, lasting up to two months after the final session. The court concluded that contact posed a serious risk to X's mental health and that the applicant's need to know X's whereabouts must yield to the child's interests.

The High Court refused leave to appeal on 22 May 2015, and the Supreme Court's Committee on Leave to Appeal rejected the applicant's further appeal on 3 July 2015. The applicant then brought her case to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging that the severing of parent-child ties without adequate decision-making processes violated Article 8 of the Convention.

**A.S. v. Norway** (Application no. 60371/15) concerned a Polish national, A.S., living in Norway, and her son X, born in December 2009 after artificial insemination. A.S. had sole parental responsibility. From April 2010, when X was under four months old, health visitors and family members raised concerns about a lack of interaction between A.S. and X. After assistance and guidance measures, X was placed in an emergency foster home on 27 March 2012, aged two years and three months.

In September 2012, the County Social Welfare Board ordered that X remain in foster care, assuming the placement would be long-term. Contact was initially set at two hours twice a year, supervised, with the purpose of letting X know his roots rather than maintaining attachment to A.S. In February 2013, the City Court confirmed the care order. It found pervasive care deficiencies and extensive physical and emotional neglect. It agreed that long-term foster care was appropriate and that reunification was not then an aim. Contact was set at one hour twice a year under supervision.

In spring 2014, A.S. sought termination of the foster placement or, alternatively, extended contact. On 5 November 2014, after a two-day oral hearing with eleven witnesses, the Board rejected her request, denied her contact, and decided she should not be given information about X’s whereabouts. A.S. appealed to the City Court, which heard the case on 2–3 March 2015. The court included a professional judge, a psychologist expert, and a lay person. A.S. testified and fourteen witnesses were heard, including her GP, psychiatrist, a counsellor, and two private psychologists. Before the hearing, the City Court refused to appoint its own expert or allow A.S.’s privately engaged psychologists to observe her and X together, accepting the municipality’s arguments.

In its judgment of 27 March 2015, the City Court refused to revoke the care order. It found that A.S. could not provide X with proper care, either then or in the future. X was a vulnerable child with special needs, likely suffering relational or developmental trauma from his early care. He had improved significantly in foster care and had formed a secure attachment to his foster parents. Removing him risked serious harm to his mental health. Contact had caused severe reactions—insecurity, sleep disturbance, regression, bed-wetting, and retching—lasting about two months after the last session. The court concluded that the risk of harm from continued contact was too great, denied contact, and withheld the foster parents’ address because unannounced contact would disproportionately affect X. The High Court refused leave to appeal on 22 May 2015, and the Supreme Court’s committee rejected the appeal on 3 July 2015.

A.S. alleged that Norway violated Article 8 of the Convention, both her and X’s right to respect for family life. She complained that the authorities refused to terminate the foster placement and denied her contact and information about X’s whereabouts, effectively severing their parent-child ties without an adequate decision-making process. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation were the long-term foster placement, the very limited and then total denial of contact, the withholding of address information, reliance on X’s severe reactions to contact, and the procedural refusals concerning expert assessment and observation. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 8, holding that the parent-child ties had been severed without an adequate decision-making process.

In *Korban v. Ukraine* (ECtHR, 4 July 2019), the applicant was a Ukrainian politician, former deputy head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional State Administration, and leader of the UKROP party, which sharply criticised President Poroshenko. He complained under Article 3 about ill-treatment during transport, forced participation in court hearings after heart surgery, and confinement in a metal cage; under Article 5 §§ 1, 3, 4 and 5 about unlawful detention; under Article 18 read with Article 5 about politically motivated detention; and under Article 6 § 2 about public statements breaching the presumption of innocence.

From August 2014, criminal proceedings were opened against him concerning alleged kidnapping of officials, car theft, embezzlement of charity funds, creation of a criminal organisation, and interference with an electoral officer. On 31 October 2015, a Prosecutor General’s Office investigator, accompanied by special forces, forced entry into his home in Dnipropetrovsk and arrested him. The arrest report relied on a template ground that eyewitnesses had identified him as the offender, but left the space for “specific facts and data” blank. He was taken to Kyiv. On 2 November 2015, he was transported 150 km to Chernigiv in an ordinary minibus; he alleged he was held from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. without food, water or toilet access, while the Government denied this.

On 3 November, when the 72-hour arrest period expired, he was released in the courtroom but immediately re-arrested at 8:42 a.m. on a new charge of aggravated interference with an electoral officer, again using the same template arrest ground. He complained that both arrests were unlawful and arbitrary, but domestic courts rejected or failed to properly examine the complaints. On 6 November he was placed under 24-hour house arrest with an electronic tag; on 28 December this was replaced by pre-trial detention.

On 25 December 2015 he was admitted to the Amosov Institute with ischemic heart disease, hypertensive crisis, acute coronary syndrome and unstable angina, and underwent urgent coronary angioplasty with two stents. Despite his postoperative condition, hearings were held from 26 to 28 December 2015 on changing his preventive measure. He was brought to court in a wheelchair with a medication infusion device; the hearings ran through the weekend and night, lasting about thirty hours. The judge ordered his detention to secure attendance. He alleged that being forced to participate while so weak amounted to Article 3 ill-treatment. During hearings on 13, 22 and 25 January 2016, he was held in a metal cage, later replaced by a transparent box.

Under Article 5, he alleged unlawful arrest and re-arrest without judicial warrant, ineffective judicial review, and lack of compensation. Under Article 18 read with Article 5, he argued his detention was politically motivated: he led an opposition party, ran in elections, and was arrested after criticising the President; officials publicly described him as a criminal-group leader. Under Article 6 § 2, he cited statements by the President, the Head of the Security Service, the Prosecutor General’s assistant, and an investigator calling him the leader of a criminal group involved in kidnappings, embezzlement and illegal arms, before any conviction. Several charges were later discontinued for lack of evidence; he had earlier entered a friendly settlement and received a suspended sentence for one kidnapping charge.

Case Korban v. Ukraine (Application no. 26744/16) concerned Ukrainian politician Gennadiy Korban. From March 2014 to March 2015 he was Deputy Head and Chief of Staff of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional State Administration. In July 2015 he became leader of UKROP, a political party sharply critical of President Poroshenko. After electoral losses in 2015, several criminal proceedings were brought against him.

The charges arose from alleged incidents: the kidnapping of R., head of the State Agency of Land Resources, in Korban’s office on 14 August 2014 concerning an appointment; the alleged kidnapping of V., a Dnipropetrovsk City Council official, in February 2015 aimed at forcing a resignation; alleged embezzlement of charity funds; and alleged interference with electoral officials, including threats to an election commission head. On 31 October 2015 a Prosecutor General’s Office investigator, accompanied by special forces, forced entry into Korban’s home and arrested him. He was suspected of embezzlement by an organised group, creating a criminal organisation, aggravated car theft, and two counts of hostage-taking. The arrest report used a pre-printed ground that eyewitnesses, the victim, or obvious signs indicated he had committed an offence; the space for specific facts was left blank.

On 2 November 2015 he was transported from Kyiv to Chernigiv, about 150 km, in a regular minibus. He alleged he was held from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. without food, water or toilet access; the Government disputed this. On 3 November 2015, when the 72-hour arrest limit expired, he was released in court but immediately re-arrested at 8:42 a.m. on suspicion of aggravated interference with an electoral officer, again relying on the same pre-printed arrest ground.

On 6 November 2015 the Pecherskyy Court ordered 24-hour house arrest with an electronic tracking device, later upheld on appeal. On 7 December 2015 he was hospitalised for hypertensive crisis, acute coronary syndrome and unstable angina. On 25 December 2015, while at the Amosov Institute, he underwent urgent coronary angioplasty with two stents. The prosecution sought to replace house arrest with pre-trial detention, alleging abuse of medical treatment, tracker tampering and witness intimidation. Despite his post-operative condition, court hearings were held from 26 to 28 December 2015, with orders for his detention and compulsory attendance. He was brought in a wheelchair; the hearing lasted about 30 hours. On 28 December 2015 the Dniprovskyy Court ordered pre-trial detention. In January 2016 he was held in a metal cage during hearings on 13, 22 and 25 January; later a transparent box was used.

Korban complained under Article 3 about the transport conditions, being forced to attend hearings after heart surgery, and cage confinement. He complained under Article 5 §§1, 3, 4 and 5 about unlawful arrest, re-arrest and detention, and lack of effective judicial review. Under Article 18 taken with Article 5, he alleged that his liberty was deprived for ulterior political motives. Finally, under Article 6 §2, he complained that public statements by high-ranking officials—including the President, Prosecutor General’s assistants, the SBU head and an investigator—described him as leader of a criminal group involved in kidnappings, embezzlement and illegal arms handling, thereby breaching his right to the presumption of innocence.

In **Korban v. Ukraine** (Application no. 26744/16, judgment 4 July 2019), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints brought by Gennadiy Korban, a Ukrainian politician, former deputy head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional State Administration, and leader of the UKROP party. His political activity—especially UKROP’s criticism of President Poroshenko—forms the background to his allegations that criminal proceedings against him were politically motivated.

Between 2014 and 2015, several criminal cases were opened against Korban, including allegations of kidnapping a State Agency official, kidnapping a Dnipropetrovsk City Council official, embezzlement of charity funds, and interference with an electoral officer. On 31 October 2015, investigators from the Prosecutor General’s Office, with special forces, forced entry into his home and arrested him. He was taken to Kyiv and charged with embezzlement by an organised group, creating a criminal organisation, aggravated car theft, and two counts of hostage-taking. The arrest report used a pre-printed ground—that eyewitnesses or obvious indications pointed to him—but left blank the space for “specific facts and data.” On 2 November 2015, he was transported 150 km from Kyiv to Chernigiv in a regular minibus; he alleged he was held from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. without water, food, or toilet access, while the Government denied this.

On 3 November 2015, when the 72-hour arrest limit expired, he was released in the courtroom but immediately re-arrested on a new charge of aggravated interference with an electoral officer. Again, the arrest report relied on the same pre-printed ground. He was later placed under 24-hour house arrest with an electronic tracking device. On 25 December 2015, after being hospitalised with acute coronary syndrome and unstable angina, he underwent urgent coronary angioplasty with two stents. Despite post-operative inpatient treatment, court hearings were held on 26–28 December 2015. He was brought to court in a wheelchair with a medication infusion device; the hearing lasted about 30 hours, including overnight sessions, and ended with an order for pre-trial detention. In January 2016, he was held in a metal cage during hearings on 13, 22, and 25 January.

Korban complained under Article 3 about the transport conditions on 2 November 2015, his forced participation in court hearings while weak after heart surgery, and the metal cage. Under Article 5 §§1, 3, 4 and 5, he challenged the lawfulness of his arrest and re-arrest, the detention orders, and judicial review. Under Article 18 read with Article 5, he alleged his detention pursued ulterior political motives. Under Article 6 §2, he complained that public statements by high-ranking State officials—including the President, the Head of the Security Service, prosecutors, and investigators—called him the leader of a criminal group and linked him to kidnappings and corruption before conviction, breaching the presumption of innocence. The Court granted the case priority and communicated the complaints to the Government in March 2018.

In *Kardava v. Ukraine* (Application no. 19886/09, judgment of 17 December 2019), the applicant, Tamaz Kardava, a Georgian national born in 1967 who had lived in Kyiv since 1993, was arrested by Kyiv police on 7 August 2008 on suspicion of robbery. Narcotic drugs were found on him. His arrest was initially documented under the Code of Administrative Offences for a drug-circulation violation. On 10 August 2008 an investigator ordered his detention on suspicion of robbery and drug possession, and on 12 August 2008 the Shevchenkivskyy District Court remanded him in custody. His detention was later extended, and his case was referred to trial on 27 July 2009. He remained in detention until his death on 7 April 2010.

The applicant alleged under Article 3 that police officers beat him during his arrest and continued to beat and abuse him at the police station, particularly on 11 August 2008, in order to obtain a confession. Medical evidence supported his account: on 11 August 2008 a medical assistant recorded haematomas on his right shoulder and left thigh and a closed chest injury. On 15 August 2008 his health deteriorated and he was hospitalised, where doctors found a closed head injury, multiple blunt internal injuries including kidney contusion, and a broken rib. He was also diagnosed with chronic internal haemorrhoids, discirculatory encephalopathy and chronic hepatitis C. A later forensic report of 22 December 2008 confirmed only encephalopathy and hepatitis C and did not confirm the other diagnoses.

The applicant, his family and his lawyer complained repeatedly to courts, prosecutors and the Ombudsman about police ill-treatment. Between 2008 and 2010 the prosecutor’s office refused several times to open criminal proceedings, finding his allegations unfounded. Higher prosecutors or courts quashed those refusals because the inquiries were not full or objective. In particular, on 30 March 2010 the Shevchenkivskyy District Court noted that the December 2008 forensic report had not analysed the August–October 2008 medical records and that further verification was needed. On 24 June 2010 the prosecutor’s office again refused to open proceedings, relying on the December 2008 report. The Court found that the State had not provided a plausible explanation for the injuries and that the investigation had been ineffective, consisting only of repeated pre-investigation inquiries for about three years.

The applicant also complained under Articles 2 and 3 that the authorities failed to provide adequate medical assistance in detention, endangering his health and life. He was held mainly in the Kyiv pre-trial detention centre (SIZO). From 15 August to 2 October 2008 he was treated in a public hospital for his injuries and illnesses; doctors noted improvement but recommended continued inpatient neurological treatment. Later SIZO doctors diagnosed him with, among other things, the after-effects of a head injury, chronic hepatitis C, coronary heart disease, hypertension, circulatory deficiency, encephalopathy and chronic gastritis. On 25 November 2009 he was placed in the SIZO medical unit because of cirrhosis of the liver and portal hypertension; doctors found no grounds for urgent external hospitalisation but considered it “advisable” as his health deteriorated. On 8 February 2010 he was taken to hospital with active cirrhosis, hepatocellular failure, hepatorenal syndrome, portal hypertension, ascites and other conditions. On 1 March 2010 he returned to the SIZO medical unit under intense observation. He refused transfer to a hospital in Bucha Correctional Colony, claiming solitary confinement and lack of necessary facilities. On 1 April 2010 he was taken to Kyiv Emergency Hospital, where he died on 7 April 2010. An autopsy attributed death to pulmonary heart disease, pneumonia with abscess, splenomegaly and cirrhosis.

After the applicant’s death, his sister pursued the application. The authorities also refused to open criminal proceedings into his death, though one refusal was quashed as unfounded. These facts formed the basis of the complaints concerning ill-treatment, failure to investigate, and inadequate medical care in detention.

In *Kardava v. Ukraine* (Application no. 19886/09, judgment 17 December 2019), the applicant, Tamaz Kardava, a Georgian national, was arrested in Kyiv on 7 August 2008 on suspicion of robbery, with narcotics found on him. He alleged that police officers beat him during arrest and at the police station, and that on 11 August 2008 they beat and abused him to obtain a confession.

Key medical evidence was central. After being placed in police custody on 11 August 2008, a medical assistant recorded haematomas on his right shoulder and left thigh and a closed chest injury. On 15 August his health deteriorated; hospital doctors diagnosed a closed head injury, multiple blunt internal injuries including kidney contusion, and a broken rib, along with chronic hepatitis C and other conditions. A forensic report of 22 December 2008 later did not confirm some injuries, but domestic authorities themselves found it incomplete because it omitted medical records from August–October 2008 and required further inquiry.

The applicant, his family and his lawyer repeatedly complained to prosecutors, courts and the Ombudsman about ill-treatment and unlawful detention. From September 2008 to December 2009, the district prosecutor’s office repeatedly refused to open criminal proceedings, finding the allegations unfounded. Higher prosecutors or courts quashed those refusals as not full or objective, citing failure to obtain and verify medical evidence and to question the applicant and doctors. On 24 June 2010, relying again on the December 2008 report, the prosecutor refused once more to open proceedings.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 3 regarding ill-treatment. Because the injuries arose while the applicant was under State control, the authorities had to provide a satisfactory explanation and disprove his allegations. They failed to do so; the December 2008 report did not effectively discredit the earlier medical evidence. The investigation was also ineffective: it consisted only of pre-investigation inquiries over about three years, during which supervising authorities repeatedly found important investigative steps missing. The Court noted similar patterns and a systemic problem in Ukraine.

As to medical care, the applicant was held mainly in Kyiv SIZO. He was treated in a public hospital from 15 August to 2 October 2008, but doctors recommended further neurological inpatient treatment. SIZO doctors later noted after-effects of head injury, hepatitis C and gastroduodenitis, yet deemed him fit for custody. By October 2009 he had heart disease, hypertension, encephalopathy and other conditions. In November 2009 he was placed in the SIZO medical unit with cirrhosis and portal hypertension; doctors found no grounds for urgent external hospitalisation but noted it might be advisable. In February 2010 he was hospitalised with active cirrhosis, hepatocellular failure, hepatorenal syndrome, portal hypertension and ascites, then returned to the SIZO. On 11 and 31 March 2010 the SIZO suggested transfer to Bucha Correctional Colony hospital; he refused, citing solitary confinement and lack of surgical facilities. On 1 April 2010 he was taken to Kyiv Emergency Hospital, where he died on 7 April 2010. Autopsy found pulmonary heart disease, pneumonia with abscess, splenomegaly and cirrhosis. Authorities refused to open criminal proceedings over his death, though one refusal was quashed. The applicant’s sister continued the case and was accepted as having standing.

Alleged violations: Article 3 (police ill-treatment and failure to investigate) and Articles 2 and 3 (failure to provide adequate medical assistance in detention, endangering health and life). The Court’s extracted reasoning confirms a violation of Article 3 concerning the ill-treatment and inadequate investigation.

He alleged that police officers beat him during his arrest and later at the Shevchenkivskyy District police station, especially on 11 August 2008, in order to obtain a confession. On 11 August a medical assistant recorded haematomas on his right shoulder and left thigh and a closed chest injury. On 15 August his health deteriorated and hospital doctors diagnosed a closed head injury, multiple blunt internal injuries including kidney contusion, and a broken rib. He also suffered from chronic hepatitis C and other conditions.

From 14 August 2008 onwards, the applicant, his family members and his lawyer complained to prosecutors, courts and the Ombudsman that he had been ill-treated by police and unlawfully detained. Prosecutors repeatedly refused to open criminal proceedings in 2008–2009, but higher prosecutors or courts quashed those decisions because the inquiries were not full or objective. A forensic report of 22 December 2008 did not confirm the injuries, but domestic authorities later criticised it for failing to analyse relevant medical records. On 24 June 2010 another refusal relied on that report. The European Court of Human Rights found that the State had to provide a plausible explanation for the applicant’s injuries, which occurred while he was under police control. Since no satisfactory explanation was given, the Court held that the State was responsible for ill-treatment classified as inhuman and degrading. It also found the investigation ineffective, as it consisted only of pre-investigation inquiries, the applicant had no formal victim status, and repeated remittals revealed serious deficiencies.

As to medical care, after being remanded in custody on 12 August 2008 and having his detention extended, the applicant was held mainly in Kyiv pre-trial detention centre (SIZO). He was hospitalised from 15 August to 2 October 2008 for his injuries and illnesses. Doctors recommended continued neurological inpatient treatment, but later SIZO doctors considered him fit to remain in custody. In 2009 he was examined by specialists for after-effects of head injury, hepatitis C, heart problems and other conditions. In November 2009, after his health worsened with cirrhosis and portal hypertension, he was placed in the SIZO medical unit. SIZO doctors found no grounds for urgent external hospitalisation but noted it might be advisable. In February 2010 he was taken to hospital with active cirrhosis, liver failure, hepatorenal syndrome and other conditions. He returned to the SIZO in March 2010, where he received medication and was placed under intense observation. The SIZO proposed transferring him to a hospital in Bucha Correctional Colony; he refused, citing solitary confinement and lack of surgical facilities. On 1 April 2010 he was taken to Kyiv Emergency Hospital and died on 7 April 2010. An autopsy attributed death to pulmonary heart disease, pneumonia, splenomegaly and cirrhosis. Investigations into his death were refused in October 2010, quashed in March 2011, and refused again in April 2011.

After the applicant’s death, his sister pursued the application, and the Court accepted that she had standing. The alleged violations concerned Article 3 (ill-treatment and failure to investigate) and Articles 2 and 3 (failure to provide adequate medical assistance during detention, endangering his health and life). The Court declared the Article 3 complaint admissible and found violations concerning the ill-treatment and the ineffective investigation.

**Case: Kamenova v. Bulgaria (Application no. 61731/11)**

The applicant, Ms Hristina Georgieva Kamenova, a Bulgarian national born in 1947, complained that restitution proceedings concerning her father’s former land had lasted excessively long and had still not been completed. She relied on Articles 6 § 1 and 7 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The European Court of Human Rights examined the complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 alone.

In 1991, after the Agricultural Land Act provided for restitution of formerly collectivised land, the applicant applied to recover land previously owned by her father. By decision of 20 May 1996, the Oryahovo land commission recognised the applicant and her sister as entitled to restitution of an 11,800 sq m plot classified as “forest.” The decision stated that the plot was “situated in an area under section 4” of the Act’s transitional provisions. Section 4 concerned land formerly offered for use to private persons; restitution to pre-collectivisation owners was to occur only after a detailed cadastral plan and a plan of newly created plots were prepared. From 1996 onward, the applicant repeatedly wrote to authorities seeking completion of the procedure. She was told to await the relevant plans. Those plans for Oryahovo municipality were approved only in 2010.

In 2012, the Ministry of Agriculture informed her that the municipality was competent. In April 2013, however, the municipality stated that her plot was not within the section 4 area and was not covered by the new-plots plan; the land was considered State property managed by the Ministry. Subsequent correspondence created confusion. The Oryahovo Agriculture Department said the municipality lacked competence and that the applicant had either to have the exact borders identified in another procedure or apply under the Forests Restitution Act, whose time-limit had expired. In April 2017, the Department said the 1996 decision was final and could no longer be revoked or rectified. Later in 2017, the Department and superior bodies indicated that she could use the section 45d procedure and listed required documents: a written request, inheritance certificate, notarial deeds, court decisions or other title documents, municipal documents concerning section 4, and a geodesist’s plan showing exact borders. The applicant submitted only the written request, not the remaining documents. Authorities sent further instructions and requested some documents ex officio from the municipality. No final restitution decision followed.

The Government argued that the 1996 decision was null and void because forest land fell under the Forests Restitution Act, so the applicant had no legitimate expectation or possession. The Court rejected this. The 1996 decision had never been challenged or annulled domestically, and authorities had generally treated her as entitled to restitution. It therefore gave rise to a legitimate expectation and constituted a possession under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The application was admissible.

On the merits, the Court distinguished cases of outright refusal to comply with restitution decisions. It found that after 2013 the appropriate avenue was section 45d and that the applicant, having been instructed, failed without explanation to provide the required documents. Delays after 2013 were therefore attributable to her, not the authorities. Nevertheless, the Court found a violation because of the earlier delay: from 1996 to 2013—about seventeen years—the procedure was delayed due to the land commission’s erroneous indication that the plot was covered by section 4, which required her to await plans that ultimately proved inapplicable. The Government did not show the delay was inevitable. This substantial unjustified delay caused prolonged uncertainty, breaching Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In *Kamenova v. Bulgaria* (Application no. 61731/11, judgment of 16 May 2019), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint about delays in a post-communist land restitution procedure.

The applicant, Hristina Georgieva Kamenova, born in 1947 and living in Vratsa, applied in 1991 under the Agricultural Land Act for restitution of land formerly owned by her father. On 20 May 1996, the Oryahovo land commission decided that the applicant and her sister, as heirs, were entitled to restitution of, among other things, an 11,800-square-metre plot classified as “forest.” The decision said the heirs had established their father’s property title by notarial deed and that the plot was “situated in an area under section 4” of the transitional provisions of the Agricultural Land Act. Section 4 concerned land previously offered for use to private persons by the Communist authorities; restitution there was to occur only after preparation of a detailed cadastral plan and a plan of newly created plots.

After 1996, the applicant repeatedly wrote to authorities seeking completion of restitution. She was told to await the relevant plans. Those plans for Oryahovo municipality were approved in 2010. In 2012 the Ministry of Agriculture and Forests told her the municipality was competent. In April 2013, however, the municipality informed her that her plot was not within the section 4 area and was not covered by the new-plots plan; it considered the plot State property managed by the Ministry. In August 2013, the Oryahovo Agriculture Department confirmed the municipality lacked competence but said the applicant had either to identify the exact borders in a different procedure, concerning land not covered by section 4, or to seek restitution under the Forests Restitution Act, whose time-limits had expired. In April 2017 the Department stated that the 1996 decision was final and could no longer be revoked or rectified.

Later in 2017, after further complaints, the Ministry and the Vratsa Regional Directorate of Agriculture directed the applicant to use the procedure under section 45d of the Regulations on the Application of the Agricultural Land Act. The Oryahovo Agriculture Department listed the required documents: a written section 45d request, an inheritance certificate, notarial deeds and other title documents, municipality documents concerning section 4, and a certified geodesist’s plan showing exact borders. On 19 September 2017 the applicant submitted only the written request, without the remaining documents. The Department repeatedly asked for them in October and November 2017 and also sought documents ex officio from the municipality. No further relevant developments occurred.

Before the Court, the applicant alleged under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, and Articles 6 and 7 of the Convention, that the restitution procedure had lasted too long and remained unfinished. The Government argued that the 1996 decision was null and void because forest land fell under the Forests Restitution Act, so the applicant had no “possession” or legitimate expectation. The Court rejected that objection: the 1996 decision had never been challenged domestically, and the authorities had treated the applicant as entitled to restitution. It therefore created a legitimate expectation and amounted to a “possession.”

On the merits, the Court found that the authorities were not responsible for the procedure remaining unfinished after 2013, because the applicant failed to comply with the section 45d formalities without explanation. However, the delay from 1996 to 2013—about seventeen years—was caused by the land commission’s erroneous indication that the plot was covered by section 4, which forced the applicant to await inapplicable plans. That delay was unjustified and created prolonged uncertainty. The Court accordingly found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In *Kamenova v. Bulgaria* (ECtHR, Fifth Section, 16 May 2019, App. No. 61731/11), the applicant, a Bulgarian national born in 1947, complained that restitution proceedings concerning her late father’s land had lasted excessively and remained unfinished. In 1991, under the Agricultural Land Act, she applied for restitution of formerly collectivised property. On 20 May 1996, the Oryahovo land commission recognised the applicant and her sister as heirs entitled to restitution of an 11,800 sq m plot classified as “forest.” The decision stated that the plot was situated in an area under section 4 of the Act’s transitional provisions. Section 4 concerned land previously offered for private use by the Communist authorities; restitution of such plots was to be completed only after adoption of a detailed cadastral plan and a plan of newly created plots.

After 1996, the applicant repeatedly sought completion of the procedure. Authorities told her to await the relevant plans. Those plans for Oryahovo municipality were approved only in 2010. In 2012, the Ministry of Agriculture and Forests said the municipality was competent for section 4 plots. In April 2013, however, the municipality informed her that her plot was not within the section 4 area or the new plan, and was considered State property managed by the Ministry. The Ministry then directed her to the Oryahovo Agriculture Department. In August 2013, that Department confirmed the municipality lacked competence but said she either had to identify the plot’s exact borders in a different completed procedure for land outside section 4, or apply under the Forests Restitution Act, whose deadlines had expired. Later, in April 2017, the Department stated that the 1996 decision was final and could no longer be revoked or amended. The Ministry and superior agricultural bodies then instructed the applicant to use the procedure under section 45d of the Regulations on the Application of the Agricultural Land Act. In September 2017, she submitted a section 45d request but omitted required supporting documents, including an inheritance certificate, title documents, municipality documents, and a geodesist’s plan showing exact borders. Authorities repeatedly told her what to submit and requested some documents ex officio from the municipality, but the procedure was not completed.

The applicant complained under Articles 6 and 7 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the lengthy unfinished restitution. The Court examined the case under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 alone. The Government argued that the 1996 decision was null and void because forest land had to be restituted under the Forests Restitution Act, and that the applicant therefore had no “possession” or legitimate expectation. The Court rejected this objection. The 1996 decision had never been challenged domestically, and the authorities had treated the applicant as entitled to restitution. It gave her a legitimate expectation and thus a “possession” under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

On the merits, the Court found that the authorities could not be blamed for the procedure remaining unfinished after 2013, because the applicant failed to comply with the section 45d formalities despite clear instructions. However, the delay from 1996 to 2013—about seventeen years—was attributable to the authorities. The land commission had erroneously stated that the plot was covered by section 4, causing the applicant to await an inapplicable procedure and plans. That delay was unjustified and substantial, placing her in prolonged uncertainty. The Court accordingly found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to the authorities’ delay up to 2013.

In *Beketov v. Ukraine* (Application no. 44436/09), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by Yuriy Beketov, a Ukrainian national, under Article 3 and Article 13 of the Convention. The key facts concern his arrest, alleged police ill-treatment, the ensuing investigation, and his detention conditions and medical care.

In February 2008 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of abduction and murder and held at the Shevchenkivskyy district police station in Kyiv. The parties disputed whether he was arrested on 9 or 10 February, but it was undisputed that he remained under police control until 16 February. Beketov alleged that during that period police officers beat him to force a confession. Specifically, Officer G., the station’s first deputy head, allegedly kicked him in the face and abdomen, injuring the area of a 2007 umbilical hernia operation. On 16 February he confessed and signed undated documents. On arrival at the temporary detention facility, a medical examination recorded a bruise under his right eye. The pre-trial detention centre initially refused to admit him because of his poor health. He was treated at an emergency hospital from 20 to 25 February for “contusion to the abdomen and facial tissue.” A SIZO doctor later described his condition as a “post-operative condition.”

The applicant’s lawyer complained of ill-treatment in May 2008. Investigative authorities repeatedly refused to institute criminal proceedings—ultimately eight times before May 2013—and each refusal was quashed by courts or prosecutors. The main defects were failure to question the applicant, Officer G., other officers and witnesses, and failure to establish the origin of the injuries. The applicant was not questioned until August 2010, more than two years after the complaint. After the 2012 Code of Criminal Procedure entered into force, a full pre-trial investigation began in May 2013, but termination decisions were again quashed for non-compliance with court instructions. The investigation remained unresolved at least until April 2014. The Court found that the authorities made no serious effort to investigate the alleged ill-treatment and failed to meet promptness requirements. It also concluded that the injuries were sufficiently established to have occurred while the applicant was under police control, and the Government offered no satisfactory explanation or justification.

Separately, Beketov alleged inadequate medical treatment in detention. He suffered ongoing abdominal pain, navel fistula, omphalitis and suture sinus. He received various treatments in the SIZO medical unit and hospitals, and surgery was recommended in July 2009. In September 2009 an ambulance suspected peritonitis, but the prison escort allegedly refused hospitalisation. The Court indicated an interim measure under Rule 39 in October 2009 requiring appropriate medical treatment; this was lifted in December 2009. In January 2010 he underwent surgery to remove the navel fistula. The Government failed to provide medical records after February 2010, saying they were lost.

Beketov also complained about material detention conditions: cells allegedly lacked natural light, had dim electric light constantly on, beds without mattresses or linen, and poor food. He further alleged no food or water was provided on court hearing days. Relying on Article 3, he alleged ill-treatment, ineffective investigation, inadequate medical care, poor conditions, and lack of food/water on hearing days. Under Article 13, he complained of no effective domestic remedies. The Court reviewed the facts and found violations concerning the police ill-treatment and the ineffective investigation.

Beketov v. Ukraine (App. no. 44436/09) concerned a Ukrainian national’s complaints under Article 3 and Article 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights. He alleged police ill-treatment, an ineffective investigation, inadequate medical care in detention, poor material conditions, and lack of food and water on court hearing days.

On 9 or 10 February 2008, the applicant was arrested on suspicion of abduction and murder. Although the parties disputed the exact date and place of arrest, it was undisputed that he was under police control at the Kyiv Shevchenkivskyy district police station from 10 to 16 February 2008. He claimed that during this period police officers beat him to force a confession. In particular, Officer G., the station’s first deputy head, allegedly kicked him in the face and abdomen, injuring the area of a 2007 umbilical hernia operation. On 16 February he confessed and signed undated documents. A medical examination at the Kyiv Temporary Detention Facility (ITT) that day noted a bruise under his right eye. On 19 February, the Kyiv Pre-trial Detention Centre (SIZO) allegedly refused to admit him due to poor health. He was returned to the ITT and then taken by ambulance to Kyiv Medical Emergency Hospital, where he stayed from 20 to 25 February 2008 and was treated for “contusion to the abdomen and facial tissue.” On 26 February he was admitted to the SIZO, where a doctor described his condition as a post-operative condition following the hernia operation.

In May 2008, the applicant’s lawyer complained to prosecutors about the alleged police ill-treatment. A July 2008 forensic examination found no injuries attributable to 9–16 February, but noted liquid leaking from his navel and recommended a surgical examination. The investigation into the ill-treatment was repeatedly refused and restarted. From 2008 to 2013, authorities conducted only a pre-investigation inquiry under the 1960 Code of Criminal Procedure, in which the victim had no formal status and could not effectively participate. The investigating officer refused to institute criminal proceedings eight times; each decision was quashed, mainly for failure to question the applicant, Officer G., other officers, cellmates, medical staff, and witnesses, or to comply with court instructions. The applicant was first questioned only in August 2010, over two years after complaining. After the 2012 Code came into force, proceedings were again terminated and quashed; the investigation remained incomplete at least until 2014. The Court found the injuries occurred while he was under police control, with no satisfactory explanation from the Government, amounting to a substantive Article 3 violation. It also found the investigation ineffective and not prompt.

As to medical care, the applicant suffered persistent abdominal pain, navel fistula, omphalitis, urachal cyst, and suture sinus. He received outpatient medication and antiseptic treatment, but surgery was delayed. On 24 September 2009, an ambulance suspected peritonitis and recommended urgent hospitalisation, but the prison escort refused. The Court issued a Rule 39 interim measure in October 2009, lifted in December 2009. He finally underwent surgery to remove the navel fistula on 20 January 2010. The Government failed to provide medical records after 26 February 2010, saying they were lost.

Regarding conditions, he alleged SIZO cells lacked natural light, had dim constantly lit electric light, and beds had no mattresses or linen; food was inadequate. He also alleged no food or water on hearing days because domestic law and court facilities did not provide for it. He complained under Article 13 that no effective domestic remedies existed for these violations.

**Case: Beketov v. Ukraine** (App. no. 44436/09, judgment 19 February 2019). The applicant, Yuriy Beketov, a Ukrainian national born in 1970, had undergone surgery for an umbilical hernia in April 2007. In February 2008 the police arrested him on suspicion of abduction and murder. Although the parties disputed the exact arrest date, it was undisputed that he was under police control from 10 to 16 February 2008 at the Shevchenkivskyy district police station in Kyiv. He alleged that officers beat him to force a confession. In particular, Officer G., the first deputy head of the police station, allegedly kicked him in the face and abdomen, injuring the area of his 2007 hernia operation. On 16 February 2008 he confessed and signed undated documents. The same day he was transferred to the Kyiv Temporary Detention Facility (ITT), where medical staff noted a bruise under his right eye.

On 19 February 2008 the SIZO allegedly refused to admit him because of his poor health. He was taken to the Kyiv Medical Emergency Hospital, where he stayed from 20 to 25 February 2008 and was treated for “contusion to the abdomen and facial tissue.” On 26 February 2008 he was admitted to the SIZO; a doctor diagnosed a “post-operative condition” following the 2007 hernia operation. In May 2008 his defence lawyer complained to the prosecutor’s office about police ill-treatment. A July 2008 forensic examination found no injuries from the relevant period but noted navel discharge and recommended a surgical examination.

The investigation was repeatedly criticised. From May 2008 to May 2013 the complaint was handled as a pre-investigation inquiry under the old Code of Criminal Procedure, which limited the victim’s procedural participation. The prosecutor refused to institute criminal proceedings eight times; those decisions were repeatedly quashed by courts and superior prosecutors for failure to question the applicant and Officer G., to follow instructions, and to establish the origin of the injuries. The applicant was first questioned only in August 2010, more than two years after complaining. From May 2013 a new CPC investigation began, but termination decisions were again quashed for similar failures. The case was still ongoing in April 2014. The Court found no serious effort to investigate and no valid explanation for the delay.

As to medical treatment, the applicant suffered constant abdominal pain, a navel fistula, omphalitis, a urachal cyst, and a suture sinus. The SIZO provided outpatient and medical-unit treatment, and surgeons recommended elective surgery. On 24 September 2009 an ambulance suspected peritonitis and recommended urgent hospitalisation, but the prison escort allegedly refused. On 30 October 2009 the European Court indicated an interim measure under Rule 39 that he be placed in an appropriate medical facility; this was lifted on 4 December 2009. On 20 January 2010 he underwent an operation at Buchanska Prison Hospital to remove the navel fistula; he was discharged on 26 February 2010. The Government later said post-February 2010 medical records were lost.

Regarding detention conditions, the applicant alleged that SIZO cells lacked natural light, had dim electric light constantly on, and beds had no mattresses or bed linen. Food was allegedly inadequate: tea and bread in the morning, porridge in the afternoon, and boiled water in the evening. On hearing days he allegedly received no food or water because Ukrainian law made no provision and courts had no facilities.

He complained under Article 3 ECHR of police ill-treatment, ineffective investigation, inadequate medical treatment, poor material conditions, and lack of food/water on hearing days. Under Article 13 he complained of the lack of effective domestic remedies. The Court declared the complaints admissible and, on the ill-treatment and investigation aspects, found the injuries occurred under police control, the Government gave no satisfactory explanation, the force was unjustified, and the investigation was neither effective nor prompt.

In *Korol and Others v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 54503/08 and seven others), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 7 March 2019. The case concerned multiple applications against Ukraine lodged under Article 34 of the Convention. Because the applications raised similar issues, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment.

The principal complaint was under Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. The applicants alleged that they did not receive adequate medical care while in detention. Some applicants also raised other Convention complaints. The Court noted that the applicants suffered from serious medical conditions that affected their everyday functioning. Their central allegation was not that they received no medical care at all, but that the care provided in detention was inadequate, delayed, incomplete, or not sufficiently adapted to their serious health needs.

The Court applied its established case-law on medical care in detention. It reiterated that authorities must ensure that diagnosis and care are prompt and accurate. Where required by the nature of a medical condition, supervision must be regular and systematic and must involve a comprehensive therapeutic strategy aimed at successfully treating the detainee’s health problems or preventing their aggravation. Medical treatment in prison must be appropriate and comparable to the quality of treatment the State has committed to providing to the general population, although detainees are not necessarily entitled to the same level of treatment available in the best health establishments outside prison.

Having examined the material submitted, including the details listed in the appended table, the Court identified shortcomings in the applicants’ medical treatment. It relied on earlier cases against Ukraine, such as *Nevmerzhitsky*, *Melnik*, *Logvinenko*, *Sergey Antonov*, and *Pivovarnik*, where similar failures had already been found to violate the Convention. On the facts, the Court concluded that the applicants did not receive comprehensive and adequate medical care while in detention. It therefore found a violation of Article 3 of the Convention.

Two applicants, in applications nos. 54503/08 and 38721/10, also complained under Article 13 that they had no effective domestic remedy for their complaints about the quality of medical care in detention. Article 13 guarantees an effective remedy before a national authority for arguable Convention violations. The Court reiterated its well-established case-law that Ukraine lacked effective domestic remedies for complaints about inadequate medical treatment in detention. The legal avenues suggested by the Government had previously been found not to prevent or stop the alleged violations, nor to provide adequate redress. The Court saw no reason to depart from that case-law and found a violation of Article 13 for those two applicants.

In addition, the applicants in applications nos. 65987/09, 29273/10, and 38721/10 raised other complaints which, in light of the Court’s well-established case-law, disclosed Convention issues. The Court found these complaints neither manifestly ill-founded under Article 35 § 3(a) nor inadmissible on any other ground.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore the applicants’ serious medical conditions while in detention, the State’s failure to provide timely, systematic, comprehensive, and adequate medical treatment comparable to that available to the general population, and, for two applicants, the absence of an effective domestic remedy to challenge the quality of that care.

In *Svit Rozvag, TOV and Others v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 13290/11 and 2 others), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) delivered judgment on 27 June 2019, final on 27 September 2019. The applicants were two Ukrainian companies and one Ukrainian national. They held prepaid multi-year gambling licences, each having paid the equivalent of EUR 150,000, and generally operated gambling businesses. The first applicant operated at least fifteen gambling establishments in Kharkiv.

The case arose from Ukraine’s 2009 gambling ban. In late 2008 the Cabinet proposed a new regulatory system that would allow existing licensees time to comply and preserve licences for their issued terms. In March 2009 two MPs introduced a competing bill for total prohibition of gambling from 1 January 2010, citing crime and youth gambling. On 7 May 2009 a fire at a gambling establishment in Dnipro killed nine people and injured eleven, drawing public attention. That same day the Cabinet instructed the Ministry of Finance to suspend all gambling licences for one month. On 8 May the Ministry suspended all licences until 7 June 2009. On 15 May Parliament adopted the Prohibition Law, banning gambling except limited activities such as lotteries, with no compensation provision. The President vetoed it, citing property protections, lack of grounds for collective licence revocation, and committed business expenses; Parliament overrode the veto on 11 June. The law entered into force on 25 June 2009, and the applicants’ licences were deemed revoked by operation of law.

The applicants sought compensation in domestic courts but failed. The first applicant claimed damages initially about UAH 11,461,690 (about EUR 905,426), later increased to about EUR 3,219,900, for unused licence fees, gambling equipment, tax-control software, premises refurbishment, and lost profit. It argued that the five-year licence was a guaranteed property right, that the Licensing Law allowed only individual revocation on specified grounds, and relied on Civil Code provisions including the “Legislative Takings Clause” requiring compensation for lawful termination of property rights. The commercial courts dismissed the claim, finding no unlawful State action, noting the Prohibition Law had not been declared unconstitutional and provided no compensation; appeal courts also did not address Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 or ECtHR case-law.
