**Summary of *Svit Rozvag, TOV and Others v. Ukraine* (App. Nos. 13290/11 and 2 others)**

The case concerns applications lodged against Ukraine by two Ukrainian companies and one Ukrainian national. The applicants held multi-year gambling licences, for which they had paid fees equivalent to €150,000 each, prepaid for the entire licence period. They operated gambling businesses under these licences. The core of their complaint relates to the Ukrainian State's termination of their gambling operations.

In late 2008, Parliament began considering a bill to comprehensively regulate gambling. However, a parallel bill proposing a total prohibition on gambling was introduced in March 2009. A pivotal event occurred on 7 May 2009, when a fire at a gambling establishment in Dnipro killed nine people. The following day, the Ministry of Finance, acting on a Cabinet of Ministers instruction, suspended all gambling licences for one month. Then, on 15 May 2009, Parliament passed the "Prohibition Law," banning all gambling operations except lotteries, with no provisions for compensating licence holders. After a presidential veto was overridden, the law entered into force on 25 June 2009, at which point the applicants' licences were revoked by operation of law.

The applicants alleged violations under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property), Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial), and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights. Specifically, they argued that the revocation of their valid, prepaid licences constituted a disproportionate interference with their possessions. The second applicant also complained about the pre-emptive one-month suspension of her licence.

The applicants pursued compensation claims in domestic courts, arguing that the State was obligated to compensate them for the revoked licences under the Civil Code's "Legislative Takings Clause" and citing Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. They relied on the European Court's case-law, notably *Tre Traktörer AB v. Sweden*, which recognized licences as "possessions." However, their claims were systematically dismissed. The domestic courts reasoned that the Prohibition Law was a lawful exercise of Parliament's constitutional power, was not declared unconstitutional, and did not itself provide for any compensation. The courts rejected arguments based on the Legislative Takings Clause and did not substantively address the applicants' references to the Convention or the Court's case-law. Consequently, the applicants alleged before the European Court that the revocation of their licences violated their property rights and that the domestic proceedings failed to provide a reasoned decision or an effective remedy for these violations.

On 8 May 2009 the Ministry of Finance suspended all gambling licences until 7 June 2009 with immediate effect.

The law contained no provisions compensating licence holders. The President vetoed it, noting that the Licensing Law did not permit blanket revocation on the ground that an activity had been banned; that the law conflicted with constitutional property protections; and that it ignored businesses’ already-committed expenses. **Andreyeva v. Ukraine** (Application no. 24385/10), judgment of 29 January 2019, concerned the death of the applicant’s son and the effectiveness of the investigation in Ukraine. The applicant, Yevdokiya Ivanovna Andreyeva, a Ukrainian national, complained under Articles 2, 3 and 6 of the Convention. The Court examined the case under Articles 2 and 3.

On 14 January 2004, the applicant’s son, born in 1967, was found dead in her barn. The same day, police inspected the scene and reported that he had committed suicide by hanging. On 24 January 2004, the Snizhne Prosecutor’s Office refused to initiate criminal proceedings, finding no elements of a crime. On 11 February 2004, a forensic expert concluded that death was caused by strangulation by a rope loop, possibly due to the body’s weight pulling against the rope, and that there were no other injuries. On 5 April 2005, the Donetsk Regional Prosecutor’s Office quashed the refusal as premature and unfounded, noting that possible reasons for suicide had not been examined and that relatives and acquaintances had not been questioned.

Between 2005 and 2012, the authorities conducted only pre-investigation inquiries. They questioned various people and ordered additional medical examinations. Experts later found numerous fractures, which they said had been inflicted after death, possibly during exhumation. The applicant’s husband stated that when he saw his son’s body, it was in a sitting position and the rope loop had not been tightened. The applicant denied suicide and alleged a violent murder. She suspected, among others, police security guards who allegedly took her son from a bar, a local police officer with whom he had a dispute, a female employee and her husband, his brothers-in-law, a business partner, and people from a local gambling club.

Investigators repeatedly refused to initiate criminal proceedings—on 25 April 2005, 26 March 2006, 20 August 2008, 17 February and 12 December 2011, 15 February 2012 and 17 September 2012. Each refusal was quashed by supervising authorities as unsubstantiated, with further investigative measures ordered. On 7 December 2012, after the applicant requested an investigation under the new Criminal Procedure Code, criminal proceedings were finally instituted. They were then terminated on 24 December 2012, 22 July 2013 and 30 September 2013, but each termination was quashed. On 5 December 2013, the Snizhne Town Court quashed the latest closure, finding the investigation not thorough or comprehensive: the police-involvement theory had not been properly examined, the brother-in-law’s role had not been clarified, the applicant had not been fully questioned, and evidence of suicidal tendencies had not been assessed. On 1 April 2014, the proceedings were closed again for lack of evidence of a crime.

The Government argued that the applicant’s allegations of police torture and murder were unsupported. The Court found no evidence of police involvement, no objective information that the son had been in contact with police before death, and no medical evidence of ill-treatment. It therefore dismissed the substantive Article 2 and 3 complaints as manifestly ill-founded.

However, the procedural complaint under Article 2 was admissible. The Court held that the investigation was ineffective: for nearly nine years, the matter was handled only through pre-investigation inquiries, which lacked sufficient scope and effective victim participation. Supervising authorities repeatedly found the inquiries unthorough and remitted them, revealing serious deficiencies. A full investigation began only in late 2012, followed by repeated unsuccessful closures. By December 2013, almost ten years after the death, the domestic court still noted major shortcomings concerning the basic circumstances. The Court thus found a violation of the procedural aspect of Article 2, and no separate issue under the procedural aspect of Article 3.

**Summary of the Case of Bjarni Ármannsson v. Iceland**

The case of *Bjarni Ármannsson v. Iceland* (Application no. 72098/14) concerns an Icelandic national, Mr. Bjarni Ármannsson, who was the CEO of Glitnir, one of Iceland's largest banks, from 1997 to 2007. The case centers on his complaint that he was subjected to double punishment—both administrative tax penalties and criminal sanctions—for the same tax offences, violating the principle of *ne bis in idem* under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the European Convention on Human Rights.

The events began in July 2009 when Iceland’s Directorate of Tax Investigation initiated an audit of the applicant’s tax returns, focusing on whether he had declared profits from selling shares received upon stepping down as CEO. After questioning the applicant and concluding its investigation in October 2010, the Directorate referred the matter to the Directorate of Internal Revenue for possible tax reassessment and informed the applicant of potential criminal proceedings. In May 2011, the Internal Revenue notified the applicant of reassessed taxes for 2007–2009, but this was later amended in January 2012, cancelling the reassessment related to the share sale profits.

On 15 May 2012, the Directorate of Internal Revenue issued a final ruling, finding that the applicant had failed to declare significant capital income from 2006 to 2008. It revised his tax returns upward, re-assessed his taxes, and imposed a 25% surcharge. The applicant paid both the taxes and the surcharge and did not appeal, so the decision became final in August 2012.

Meanwhile, in March 2012, the Directorate of Tax Investigation had referred the matter to the Special Prosecutor for criminal investigation. Despite objections from the applicant’s lawyer, the Special Prosecutor proceeded, and on 17 December 2012, indicted the applicant for aggravated tax offences for failing to declare income in his 2007–2009 tax returns, including capital income from property sales, dividends, interest, and foreign exchange gains from 2006 to 2008.

The applicant sought dismissal of the criminal case, arguing it violated Article 4 of Protocol No. 7, but the District Court rejected this on 23 April 2013. On 28 June 2013, the District Court convicted him, finding gross negligence sufficient for criminal liability under tax law. He was sentenced to six months’ imprisonment, suspended for two years, and fined ISK 38,850,000 (approximately EUR 241,000). The fine accounted for the tax surcharges already imposed, though no calculation was detailed.

The applicant appealed, and on 15 May 2014, the Supreme Court upheld the conviction and fine but increased the suspended prison sentence to eight months. The Supreme Court also rejected his *ne bis in idem* claim.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are that the applicant was first subjected to a final administrative tax penalty (re-assessment and 25% surcharge) for failing to declare income, and subsequently prosecuted and criminally punished for the same conduct. This dual process—administrative and criminal—for identical tax offences forms the basis of his complaint under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7, which prohibits being tried or punished twice for the same offence. The domestic courts rejected this argument, leading to his application to the European Court of Human Rights.

It revised upwards his declared capital for tax years 2007–2009, reassessed his taxes, and imposed a 25% surcharge under Section 108 of the Income Tax Act. The applicant paid the taxes and surcharge and did not appeal; the decision became final in August 2012.

The applicant’s lawyer protested, arguing that the deadline for objecting to the Internal Revenue’s reassessment had not expired and that the referral was ill-founded. The Directorate replied that the deadline had expired and that the Special Prosecutor would independently assess whether to indict.

In September 2012, the Special Prosecutor interviewed the applicant, informing him that the investigation concerned the case as concluded by the Internal Revenue and that certain reported aspects had been dropped. On 17 December 2012, the Special Prosecutor indicted him for aggravated tax offences, alleging failure to declare income in his 2007–2009 tax returns, including the same capital income from 2006–2008. The applicant sought dismissal under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7, but the District Court rejected that claim in April 2013. In June 2013, he was convicted for gross negligence, sentenced to six months’ imprisonment suspended for two years, and fined ISK 38,850,000 (approximately EUR 241,000). The court had regard to the tax surcharges imposed, without detailing the calculation.

The applicant appealed. In May 2014, the Supreme Court rejected his Article 4 Protocol No. 7 argument, upheld the conviction, confirmed the fine, but increased the suspended prison sentence to eight months. The applicant then lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights in November 2014.

The key factual issue was therefore the overlap between two punitive proceedings: the final administrative tax reassessment with a 25% surcharge and the later criminal conviction for substantially the same failure to declare income. In Ēcis v. Latvia (Application no. 12879/09, judgment 10 January 2019), the European Court of Human Rights examined an alleged breach of Article 14, read in conjunction with Article 8. The applicant, Mārtiņš Ēcis, complained that Latvia discriminated against him on grounds of sex through the prison regime applied to him, leading to refusal of leave to attend his father’s funeral.

In 2001 the applicant was convicted of kidnapping, aggravated murder, and aggravated extortion and sentenced to twenty years’ imprisonment. Under section 504(1) of the Sentence Enforcement Code, as a man sentenced for serious or especially serious crimes, he began serving his sentence in a closed prison at maximum-security level. He was later transferred to the medium-security level within that closed prison. Women convicted of comparable intentional crimes were placed in partly-closed prisons under section 505(1). This difference affected prison privileges. In particular, prisoners in closed prisons, regardless of security level, were not eligible for prison leave. Only prisoners at medium- or minimum-security level in partly-closed prisons could obtain leave, up to seven days per year, including up to five days for the death or life-threatening illness of a close relative.

On 30 September 2008 the applicant learned that his father had died. On 2 October 2008 he requested leave to attend the funeral. The prison director refused, stating that he had no authority because the applicant was serving his sentence at the medium-security level of a closed prison and was therefore ineligible under the Code. The applicant alleged that if he had been a woman convicted of the same crimes, he would have been placed in a partly-closed prison and would have been eligible for compassionate leave. He claimed that his sex was the decisive reason he could not attend his father’s funeral, which interfered with his family life and amounted to discrimination.

He pursued complaints before the Ministry of Justice, the Ombudsperson, and the Constitutional Court. The Ministry found no sex discrimination because both sexes were imprisoned and subjected to restrictions. The Ombudsperson considered the restriction proportionate because closed-prison inmates were regarded as particularly dangerous. The applicant filed three constitutional complaints. The third expressly alleged sex discrimination and added the funeral refusal, arguing that men and women convicted of the same offences were in comparable situations. The Constitutional Court declined to institute proceedings, finding the legal reasoning evidently insufficient, particularly because the applicant had not explained why men and women convicted of serious crimes should be subject to the same sentence-enforcement rules.

Before the ECtHR, the Government accepted that the refusal interfered with family life but argued it was lawful, aimed at public safety and crime prevention, and proportionate. It submitted that male and female prisoners were not in comparable situations because women generally posed lower security risks, and that gender-sensitive prison regimes were justified. It also noted that at the same security level male and female inmates had similar privileges. The applicant maintained that his sex alone caused the refusal, that he had committed no regime breaches, and that later, under a different regime, he was granted prison leave four times without incident. The Court dismissed the Government’s non-exhaustion objection, finding that the third constitutional complaint had raised the discrimination claim in substance. Focusing on the concrete refusal to allow the applicant to attend his father’s funeral, the Court ultimately found a violation of Article 14 read in conjunction with Article 8.

In **Ēcis v. Latvia** (Application no. 12879/09), the applicant, Mārtiņš Ēcis, a Latvian national born in 1981, was convicted in 2001 of kidnapping, aggravated murder, and aggravated extortion and sentenced to twenty years’ imprisonment. The sentence became final in 2002. Under section 504(1) of the Latvian Sentence Enforcement Code, he was initially placed at the maximum-security level in a closed prison and later transferred to the medium-security level of that closed prison.

The applicant alleged that Latvia’s prison regime discriminated against him on grounds of sex. Under domestic law, men convicted of serious or especially serious crimes began serving their sentences in closed prisons, whereas women convicted of the same categories of crimes began serving their sentences in partly-closed prisons. This distinction affected prisoners’ rights, particularly eligibility for prison leave. Prisoners in closed prisons—regardless of security level—were not eligible for leave. By contrast, prisoners at the medium- or minimum-security level in partly-closed prisons could, with permission, leave prison for up to seven days per year, or up to five days because of the death or life-threatening illness of a close relative.

The key event occurred after the applicant’s father died on 30 September 2008. On 2 October 2008, the applicant asked to leave prison to attend the funeral. The prison director refused on the same day, stating that he had no authority to grant leave because the applicant was serving his sentence at the medium-security level of a closed prison. Only prisoners in partly-closed prisons at medium or minimum security were eligible. The applicant therefore could not attend his father’s funeral.

The applicant complained that this refusal resulted from sex-based discrimination in the applicable prison regime. He argued that women convicted of the same crimes and given similar sentences would have been held in partly-closed prisons and could have been granted compassionate leave. The applicant also claimed that the prison regime differences affected visits, phone calls, progression to more lenient regimes, and access to leave. He invoked Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights, read in conjunction with Articles 5, 8, and 10. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 14 read in conjunction with Article 8, concerning respect for private and family life.

Domestically, the Ministry of Justice rejected his complaint, saying both sexes were deprived of liberty and their rights restricted. The Ombudsperson found the refusal proportionate, reasoning that closed-prison inmates were particularly dangerous. The Constitutional Court declined to institute proceedings three times, finding the legal reasoning insufficient. It stated that the applicant had failed to show why men and women convicted of serious crimes should be treated as comparable groups and, in the first complaint, had not specified the human right in conjunction with which discrimination was alleged. In his third complaint, the applicant expressly added the funeral refusal and argued that women in his situation could have attended.

Before the Court, the Government argued non-exhaustion of domestic remedies because the Constitutional Court had not properly examined the issue. The Court dismissed that objection, finding the third constitutional complaint had raised the substance of the discrimination claim and that the Constitutional Court had, at least partly, addressed its merits. The Government further argued that different regimes were justified because women prisoners generally posed lower risks, were less violent, and had distinct needs recognized by international standards, including the Bangkok Rules. The applicant maintained that his sex was the sole reason for the refusal and that later, under a different regime, he was granted leave four times without incident.

The central alleged violation was therefore sex-based discrimination in prison regimes, specifically the blanket ineligibility of male closed-prison inmates for compassionate leave, which prevented the applicant from attending his father’s funeral, contrary to Article 14 read with Article 8.

In 2008 the applicant discovered that men and women convicted of comparable serious crimes were treated differently. Male prisoners convicted of serious or especially serious crimes started their sentences in closed prisons. Female prisoners convicted of intentionally committed crimes, including comparable offences, started in partly-closed prisons under section 505(1). This distinction affected restrictions on visits, telephone calls, progression to more lenient security levels, and, critically, eligibility for prison leave. Prisoners in closed prisons, regardless of security level, could not obtain leave. Only prisoners at the medium- or minimum-security level in partly-closed prisons could leave temporarily for up to seven days per year, or up to five days for the death or life-threatening illness of a close relative.

The alleged violation arose from a specific event. On 30 September 2008 the applicant was informed that his father had died. On 2 October 2008 he asked for permission to leave prison to attend the funeral. The prison director refused the same day, explaining that he had no authority to grant leave because the applicant was serving his sentence at the medium-security level of a closed prison. The applicant claimed that this refusal was based solely on the prison regime applicable to him and, indirectly, on his sex. He argued that a woman convicted of the same offences would have been placed in a partly-closed prison and would therefore have been eligible for compassionate leave. He complained that this was discrimination on the ground of sex contrary to Article 14, read in conjunction with Article 8, the right to respect for family life.

Domestically, the Ministry of Justice rejected his complaint, saying both male and female inmates were deprived of liberty and both had rights restricted. The Ombudsperson found the restriction proportionate and necessary because closed-prison inmates were considered particularly dangerous. The applicant lodged three constitutional complaints. The Constitutional Court declined to institute proceedings each time, finding the legal reasoning evidently insufficient. It repeatedly stated that he had not sufficiently shown why men and women convicted of equally grave crimes were in comparable situations; the third complaint also mentioned the funeral refusal.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant’s discrimination complaint was communicated to the Latvian Government under Article 14 read with Article 8; the remainder was declared inadmissible. The Government objected that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies, but the Court dismissed this objection. It found that the third constitutional complaint had in substance raised the same discrimination issue and that the Constitutional Court had partly addressed it. The Court limited its examination to the refusal to allow the applicant to attend his father’s funeral, rather than comparing the entire prison regimes generally. The applicant was later granted one prison-leave day per year in 2012–2015 and was conditionally released on 11 September 2015.

**Summary of *Živanović and Others v. Serbia* (Application nos. 29171/16 and 8 others)**

**Case Background and Core Complaint**
The case of *Živanović and Others v. Serbia* was brought before the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) by nine applicants against the Republic of Serbia. The applications were lodged on various dates and were jointly examined due to their similar subject matter. The applicants were represented by Ms. R. Dugošija, a lawyer from Žabari.

The central complaint of all applicants was the excessive length of civil proceedings in which they were involved. They alleged that the duration of these proceedings was incompatible with the "reasonable time" requirement guaranteed by Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which ensures the right to a fair and public hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal.

**Key Facts and Procedural History**
The specific details of each applicant's case are set out in an appended table to the judgment. The proceedings in question were identified as labour disputes. Under Serbian domestic law, such disputes are considered urgent and are meant to be resolved swiftly. Despite this, the applicants' civil cases had been pending for a substantial period.

When the applicants' cases reached the Serbian Constitutional Court, they had already been ongoing for between six and eight years, spanning two levels of jurisdiction. This significant delay was a critical fact in the ECtHR's assessment.

**Proceedings before the Constitutional Court**
A pivotal aspect of the case concerned the admissibility of the applications before the ECtHR. The Serbian Government argued that the applications should be rejected because the applicants had failed to properly exhaust domestic remedies. Specifically, the Government claimed the applicants did not adequately substantiate their length-of-proceedings complaint before the Serbian Constitutional Court.

The ECtHR, however, disagreed with the Government's position. The Court examined the applicants' constitutional appeals and found that they had expressly complained about the excessive length of the proceedings. The applicants had provided the Constitutional Court with key information, including the total duration of the proceedings, the number of jurisdictional levels involved, the nature of the disputes as urgent labour cases, and copies of the decisions rendered.

The ECtHR noted that the Constitutional Court had acknowledged the length complaint but dismissed it on the grounds that it was not sufficiently substantiated. The ECtHR found this reasoning to be problematic. It held that given the proceedings had already lasted six to eight years for only two levels of jurisdiction, the cases were *prima facie* meritorious. Consequently, the Constitutional Court should have examined the merits of the complaints. The ECtHR emphasised that complaints about the length of proceedings, unlike other more complex issues, do not normally require extensive elaboration. If more information was needed, the Constitutional Court could have requested it from the applicants or the relevant authorities.

**Conclusion on Admissibility**
The ECtHR concluded that the applicants had provided the national authorities with the opportunity to remedy the alleged violations, thereby satisfying the requirement to exhaust domestic remedies under Article 35 § 1 of the Convention. The Government's preliminary objection was therefore rejected. Finding that the applications were not manifestly ill-founded and not inadmissible on any other grounds, the Court declared them admissible.

In *Živanović and Others v. Serbia* (ECtHR, Third Section, 19 September 2019), the Court considered nine applications (no. 29171/16 and eight others) against Serbia. The applicants were represented by Ms R. Dugošija. Because the applications raised the same complaint, the Court joined them. The applicants alleged that the length of civil proceedings in Serbia had violated their right to a hearing within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. Article 6 § 1 provides that, in determining civil rights and obligations, everyone is entitled to a hearing within a reasonable time by a tribunal.

The relevant facts were set out in the appended table, but the judgment identifies the underlying proceedings as labour disputes. Under Serbian law, such disputes were urgent. The applicants’ cases had proceeded through two levels of jurisdiction. By the time the Serbian Constitutional Court examined their constitutional appeals, the proceedings had already lasted between six and eight years. In their constitutional appeals, the applicants expressly complained about the excessive length. They indicated the total length, the number of jurisdictional levels, and the fact that the proceedings were urgent labour disputes. They also provided the Constitutional Court with the decisions rendered in the proceedings.

The Government argued that all applications were inadmissible for failure to exhaust domestic remedies. It claimed the applicants had not properly complained before the Constitutional Court and that the Constitutional Court was bound by the request formulated in the constitutional appeal. The Court rejected that preliminary objection. Under Article 35 § 1, exhaustion requires that complaints intended for Strasbourg be raised before the appropriate domestic body, at least in substance, and in compliance with domestic formal requirements and time limits (*Vučković and Others v. Serbia*). Here, unlike cases where a complaint was not raised at all, the applicants expressly complained of length. The Constitutional Court itself noted the length complaint but considered it insufficiently substantiated. The ECtHR found, however, that the applicants had provided enough: total duration, levels of jurisdiction, urgent nature, and decisions. Since the proceedings had lasted six to eight years for two levels, the cases were prima facie meritorious. The Constitutional Court should therefore have examined the merits; if it needed more information, it could have requested it. Complaints about length normally do not require much elaboration (*Šaćirović and Others*; contrast *Golubović and Others*).

Consequently, the applicants had given the national authorities an opportunity to put right the alleged violations. The applications were not manifestly ill-founded or inadmissible on any other ground. The Court declared them admissible. The key issue was exhaustion of domestic remedies in Serbian length-of-proceedings cases. The case shows that an express length complaint before the Constitutional Court, supported by basic details, can satisfy Article 35 § 1, especially where delays are long and the proceedings are urgent. The provided text ends at the admissibility stage and does not set out the final merits finding.

**Case: Živanović and Others v. Serbia**  
**Applications nos. 29171/16 and 8 others**  
**European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, Committee Judgment, 19 September 2019**

The case concerned nine applications lodged against Serbia under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants were represented by Ms R. Dugošija, a lawyer practising in Žabari. Notice of the applications was given to the Serbian Government. Because the applications raised similar subject matter, the Court decided to examine them jointly in a single judgment.

The applicants’ central complaint was the excessive length of civil proceedings. They relied on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which provides that, in the determination of civil rights and obligations, everyone is entitled to a hearing within a reasonable time by a tribunal. The specific applicants and details of each application were set out in an appended table.

The main legal dispute at the admissibility stage concerned whether the applicants had exhausted domestic remedies. The Serbian Government argued that all applications should be rejected as inadmissible because the applicants had failed to properly complain before the Constitutional Court. The applicants disagreed.

The European Court reiterated its established rule under Article 35 § 1 that complaints intended to be made before it must first have been made to the appropriate domestic body, at least in substance and in compliance with formal requirements and time-limits. The Court then examined the applicants’ constitutional appeals. It found that the applicants had expressly complained about the length of the impugned proceedings before the Constitutional Court. Therefore, the Government’s argument that the Constitutional Court was “bound” by the request formulated in the constitutional appeal was irrelevant.

The Constitutional Court had noted that the applicants raised a length-of-proceedings complaint but considered that they had not sufficiently substantiated it. The European Court disagreed with that assessment. It observed that the applicants had indicated the total length of the proceedings and the number of levels of jurisdiction. They had also underlined that the proceedings were labour disputes, which were urgent under domestic law. They provided the Constitutional Court with the decisions rendered in the proceedings.

At the time the Constitutional Court examined the cases, the proceedings had already lasted between six and eight years for two levels of jurisdiction. The European Court considered that the cases were therefore prima facie meritorious. In such circumstances, the Constitutional Court should have examined the merits. If it needed additional information or documents, it could have invited the applicants or the relevant authorities to provide them. The Court also noted that complaints about the length of proceedings, unlike some other Convention complaints, normally do not require much elaboration.

Consequently, the Court found that the applicants had provided the national authorities with an opportunity, as intended by Article 35 § 1, to put right the violations alleged against them. Since the applications were not manifestly ill-founded within the meaning of Article 35 § 3 (a) and were not inadmissible on any other grounds, the Court declared them admissible.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation were therefore: multiple civil proceedings, two levels of jurisdiction, durations of six to eight years at the time of constitutional review, the urgent nature of labour disputes under domestic law, and the applicants’ attempts to raise the length complaint before the Constitutional Court. These facts made the length complaint sufficiently arguable and required domestic merits review. The provided text deals with the admissibility stage; it does not include any subsequent merits finding.

**Summary of Clasens v. Belgium (Application no. 26564/16)**

The case of *Clasens v. Belgium* originated from an application lodged by Mr. John Clasens, a Belgian national born in 1983, against the Kingdom of Belgium on 13 May 2016. The applicant was serving a final criminal sentence at Ittre Prison. His complaint centered on the conditions of his detention during a prison staff strike that occurred from 25 April to 22 June 2016, which he alleged violated Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The strike, affecting prisons in Brussels and Wallonia, led to the suspension of the ordinary prison regime due to the lack of guaranteed minimum services. The applicant described severe deteriorations in detention conditions. On 2 May 2016, he and other inmates filed an urgent application to compel the State to reinstate normal prison operations. An order issued on 3 May 2016 by the President of the Walloon Brabant Court of First Instance documented the conditions: limited telephone access and showers, reduced exercise, no family visits, and a threat to food supplies due to picket lines. The court partly granted the request, ordering the State to provide, under penalty of fine, three meals daily, showers and phone access every other day, two family visits per week, and access for lawyers and the Supervisory Board.

Despite this order and subsequent measures like police reinforcements, the strike's impact persisted. A report by the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT), following a visit from 7-9 May 2016, confirmed prisoners faced confinement to cells 24 hours a day, limited showers, no visits, and interrupted supplies. The strike ended on 22 June 2016. The Ittre Prison Supervisory Board later concluded that inmates had no family visits for most of the period, only one meal a day, and were confined to their cells for days at a time.

The applicant argued that the State failed to take effective action to change the situation despite judicial orders. The Government contended that the applicant had not exhausted domestic remedies, arguing he should have also pursued a damages claim. The Court rejected this objection, noting that a compensatory remedy would not have altered his conditions during the strike. The merits of the case focused on whether the State fulfilled its positive obligation to ensure detention conditions compatible with human dignity, particularly given the recurring nature of such strikes and the known severe consequences, as highlighted by the CPT and domestic courts.

**Clasens v. Belgium** (Application no. 26564/16) concerned a Belgian national, Mr John Clasens, who was detained in Ittre Prison under a final criminal conviction. He alleged that his conditions of detention during a prison staff strike from 25 April to 22 June 2016 amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment contrary to Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights. He also complained that he lacked an effective remedy under Article 13 in respect of that complaint.

The strike affected prisons in Brussels and Wallonia. Because Belgian law did not guarantee minimum services in prisons during strikes, ordinary prison regimes were suspended to varying degrees. At the time, Ittre Prison held 386 prisoners with a capacity of 420 places. Most cells were single-occupancy, measuring 9 m², with wash basins and partitioned toilets.

On 2 May 2016, the applicant and other prisoners lodged an urgent application with the President of the Walloon Brabant Court of First Instance, asking the State to restore the ordinary prison regime and relying on Article 3. On 3 May 2016, the urgent-applications judge described the regime in Ittre since 26 April: telephone calls only on 26, 29 and 30 April and 1 May; showers on 27 and 29 April and 1 May; exercise yard on 28 and 30 April; normal healthcare and medicine distribution; no family visits; and pickets blocking food deliveries, threatening food supplies from 5 May. The judge ordered the State to provide three meals per day, one hot; showers every other day; telephone access every other day; two family visits per week; and two days per week for lawyers and the Supervisory Board, subject to fines. The State appealed, and on 26 April 2017 the Brussels Court of Appeal largely upheld the order, reducing the fines.

A CPT delegation visited Ittre from 7 to 9 May 2016. Its report noted limited access to showers, anxiety and stress medication, collective exercise once a week, 24-hour cell confinement, interrupted canteen supplies, no cleaning or hygiene products, no visits, and insufficient staff to top up telephone accounts. After the strike ended, the Ittre Prison Supervisory Board reported on 23 June 2016 that prisoners had no lawyer visits before 16 June and no family visits except on the weekends of 4–5 and 11–12 June; only one meal a day was distributed; outside contact was limited to about one telephone call every three days; until 16 June prisoners left their cells only once every three days for exercise or a shower; and no other activities were provided.

A CFI visit report also noted that staff presence varied from 4 to 20, with police reinforcements covering shifts. The night regime kept prisoners in their cells, and regular service normally required 45 staff members.

The Brussels Court of Appeal, relying on Vasilescu v. Belgium and Muršić v. Croatia, found that the conditions during the strike attained the severity required for a prima facie finding of degrading treatment. It stated that prisoners were treated like objects, at the mercy of staff refusing to work, uncertain of the strike’s duration, confined without activities, deprived of family and lawyer contact, and forced to accept irregular exercise, contact and basic healthcare, causing distress beyond the suffering inherent in imprisonment.

The Government argued that the applicant had not exhausted domestic remedies because he should also have sought damages under Article 1382 of the Civil Code. The Court rejected that objection, finding that a compensatory remedy would not have changed the detention conditions and was not effective for complaints about poor conditions. It declared the Article 3 complaint admissible. On the merits, the applicant stressed that domestic courts had already found a violation and that prison strikes were recurrent and foreseeable, while the Government argued that conditions varied and improved through reinforcements and that minimum-service legislation was being prepared. At the material time, no guaranteed minimum service existed; a 2019 Act later introduced such a system.

**Case Name:** *Clasens v. Belgium* (Application no. 26564/16)

**Summary:**

The case of *Clasens v. Belgium* originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr. John Clasens, a Belgian national, on 13 May 2016. The applicant alleged that his conditions of detention in Ittre Prison during a prison staff strike were incompatible with Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits inhuman and degrading treatment. He also claimed a violation of Article 13, alleging he lacked an effective domestic remedy for this complaint.

The central facts revolve around a prison staff strike that affected prisons in Brussels and Wallonia from 25 April to 22 June 2016. Due to a lack of guaranteed minimum service, the ordinary prison regime was suspended. The applicant was serving a final criminal sentence in Ittre Prison during this period. The prison, with a capacity of 420, held 386 prisoners at the time, mostly in single-occupancy cells of 9 m² equipped with basic sanitation.

The strike severely impacted detention conditions. On 2 May 2016, the applicant and other inmates filed an urgent application with the Court of First Instance (CFI), citing a violation of Article 3 due to the conditions. On 3 May 2016, the President of the CFI issued an order describing the conditions since 26 April, which included severely restricted access to showers (twice in the first week), the exercise yard (twice), and telephone calls, as well as a complete suspension of family visits. The order mandated the State to provide specific minimum services, including three meals daily (one hot), showers every other day, telephone access every other day, two family visits per week, and lawyer access.

Despite this order, which was largely upheld on appeal in April 2017, the situation remained dire. The European Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT), which conducted a visit in May 2016, reported limited shower access, confinement to cells for 24 hours a day, interrupted canteen supplies, and no visits. A subsequent report by the Ittre Prison Supervisory Board on 23 June 2016 confirmed that inmates had no family visits until mid-June, received only one meal a day, and were confined to their cells for most of the day, leaving only once every three days for exercise or a shower.

The applicant relied on Article 3 of the Convention, arguing that the State failed to take effective action despite judicial orders. The Government objected, claiming non-exhaustion of domestic remedies, as the applicant had not also sought damages under Article 1382 of the Civil Code. However, the Court rejected this objection, noting that a compensatory remedy would not have changed the applicant’s situation during the strike and is not considered effective for complaints about poor detention conditions. The Court declared the application admissible, focusing on the substantiated facts of the applicant's physical conditions of detention during the strike, which were the core of the alleged Article 3 violation.

In *Baralija v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Application no. 30100/18, Fourth Section, judgment of 29 October 2019), the applicant was Irma Baralija, a Bosnian national living in Mostar and president of the local branch of the political party “Naša stranka”. She complained that she was unable to vote or stand in Mostar’s local elections, alleging discrimination based on her place of residence contrary to Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 to the European Convention on Human Rights.

Mostar, one of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s largest cities with a population of about 105,797, last held local elections in 2008. In 2010, the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina declared unconstitutional several provisions of the Election Act 2001 (sections 19.2 and 19.4) and the Statute of the City of Mostar (section 17(1)) governing elections to the Mostar City Council. The Constitutional Court found that the electoral arrangements failed to ensure equal suffrage and were discriminatory, notably because voters in different city areas had unequal voting weights and residents of the Central Zone could vote for fewer councillors. It gave the Parliamentary Assembly six months to amend the legislation.

Parliament failed to comply. In January 2012, the Constitutional Court adopted a ruling on non-enforcement, and the unconstitutional provisions ceased to have legal effect on 28 February 2012. No replacement legal framework was adopted. As a result, local elections in Mostar could not be held in 2012 or 2016, and by September 2019 the relevant Election Act provisions had still not been enacted. The applicant therefore remained unable to vote or stand in local elections solely because she lived in Mostar, unlike citizens elsewhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The prolonged deadlock also affected city governance. The mayor, elected by the city council in 2009, remained in a “technical mandate” after 2012. Because no city council could be constituted, the mayor assumed budget-adoption functions, and from 2014 the Federation Parliament annually renewed exceptional legislation allowing the Mostar mayor to adopt the city budget. International bodies, including the High Representative, the Council of Europe, and the European Commission, repeatedly criticised the absence of local elections in Mostar and urged authorities to resolve the legal vacuum.

Before the European Court, the Government argued that the application was an *actio popularis* and that domestic remedies had not been exhausted. The Court examined the complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 12. It found a violation: the applicant’s inability to vote or stand in local elections, caused by the State’s failure to adopt the necessary legislation, amounted to a difference in treatment based on residence. There was no sufficient, objective, or reasonable justification for keeping Mostar residents disenfranchised for such a prolonged period while citizens elsewhere could participate in local elections. The Court held that Bosnia and Herzegovina must take general measures, including legislative amendment, to secure the right to vote and stand in local elections in Mostar.

The case of *Baralija v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Application no. 30100/18), decided by the European Court of Human Rights on 29 October 2019, concerned the prolonged inability of residents of Mostar to vote in or stand for local elections. The applicant, Irma Baralija, born in 1984, lived in Mostar and was president of the local branch of the political party “Naša stranka.” She complained that she could not vote or stand as a candidate in local elections, relying on Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 to the Convention, which prohibits discrimination on grounds such as “other status”—including, in this context, residence.

The key facts began with the 2008 local elections in Mostar, the last held before the application. In 2010, the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina declared certain provisions of the Election Act 2001 and the Statute of the City of Mostar unconstitutional. These provisions governed elections to the Mostar City Council through a city-wide constituency and six city-area constituencies based on former municipalities. Among other problems, the Constitutional Court found that residents of the Central Zone could vote only for city-wide councillors, while residents of six city municipalities could also vote for area councillors, resulting in unequal suffrage. The Constitutional Court ordered the Parliamentary Assembly to amend the unconstitutional provisions within six months.

When the Parliamentary Assembly failed to act, the Constitutional Court issued a ruling on non-enforcement on 18 January 2012. The relevant provisions of the Election Act 2001 ceased to have legal effect on 28 February 2012. As a result, no legal framework existed to hold local elections in Mostar. Consequently, local elections could not be held in the 2012 or 2016 election cycles. By September 2019, the Government confirmed that the necessary provisions had still not been adopted.

The practical consequences were significant. The mayor of Mostar, elected by the city council in 2009, remained in a “technical mandate” after 2012. Because the city council could not be constituted, the mayor substituted for it in adopting the city budget in 2013. From 2014 onward, the Parliament of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina repeatedly amended budget legislation to allow the mayor, with consent of the finance official, to adopt the budget in lieu of the city council. International bodies, including the High Representative, the Council of Europe Congress, the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, and the European Commission, repeatedly urged authorities to restore local democracy in Mostar.

Before the European Court, the Government argued that the application was an actio popularis and that domestic remedies had not been exhausted. The applicant disputed those objections. The Court gave notice of the complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 12.

The alleged violation was that the applicant’s inability to vote and stand in local elections amounted to discrimination based on her place of residence. Residents of Mostar were treated differently from citizens elsewhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina who could participate in local elections. The Court found that this difference in treatment lacked sufficient, objective, and reasonable justification, and that the State had failed to adopt measures to hold democratic elections. It found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 and required Bosnia and Herzegovina to take general measures, including legislative amendment, to remedy the situation.

**Case: Baralija v. Bosnia and Herzegovina (Application no. 30100/18), European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, Judgment of 29 October 2019 (final 29 January 2020).**

The applicant, Irma Baralija, born in 1984, is a national of Bosnia and Herzegovina living in Mostar and president of the local branch of the political party “Naša stranka.” She lodged her application on 4 June 2018, complaining that she was unable to vote or stand as a candidate in local elections in Mostar. She relied on Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 to the Convention, alleging discrimination on the ground of her place of residence. On 15 January 2019, the Court gave notice of the complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 12; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The key factual background concerns the prolonged failure to hold local elections in Mostar. Mostar is one of the largest cities in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the cultural and economic capital of Herzegovina. Its last local elections were held in 2008 under provisions of the Election Act 2001 and the Statute of the City of Mostar.

On 26 November 2010, following a request from the Croat caucus, the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina declared several provisions of the Election Act 2001 and the Statute of Mostar unconstitutional. The challenged system created a 35-member City Council: 17 councillors elected from a city-wide constituency and three councillors elected from each of six city-area constituencies based on former city municipalities. The Constitutional Court found that this arrangement failed to secure equal suffrage, particularly for residents of the Central Zone of Mostar. Central Zone residents could vote only for the 17 city-wide councillors, while residents of the six city areas could also vote for area councillors. The Central Zone was also not represented on council committees. The Constitutional Court found this inequality incompatible with Article 25 of the ICCPR and the constitutional prohibition on discrimination, and ordered the Parliamentary Assembly to amend the relevant provisions within six months.

After the Parliamentary Assembly failed to comply, the Constitutional Court issued a ruling on non-enforcement on 18 January 2012. The unconstitutional provisions ceased to have legal effect on 28 February 2012. As a result, no local elections could be held in Mostar in the 2012 or 2016 election cycles. According to the Government’s latest information of 13 September 2019, the necessary provisions regulating elections to the Mostar City Council had still not been adopted.

Because no City Council could be constituted, the mayor elected in 2009 continued in a “technical mandate” after 2012. In 2013, the mayor substituted the city council in adopting the city budget. From 2014 onwards, the Parliament of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina repeatedly amended budget legislation to allow the mayor, with the consent of the finance official, to adopt Mostar’s budget in place of the city council.

The applicant alleged that this state of affairs left her and other Mostar residents unable to exercise the right to vote and stand in local elections, unlike citizens in other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. She argued that this difference of treatment based on residence lacked sufficient, objective and reasonable justification. The Government objected that the application was an actio popularis and that domestic remedies had not been exhausted.

The Court’s judgment concerned Article 1 of Protocol No. 12, finding a violation based on the impossibility of voting and standing in local elections for a prolonged period, the difference of treatment depending on residence, and the absence of sufficient justification. Under Article 46, the State was required to take general measures, including legislative amendment, to enable democratic local elections in Mostar.

In *Kopytets and Shtopko v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 9706/19 and 9709/19), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 17 October 2019. The applications were lodged by two Ukrainian applicants under Article 34 of the Convention. The Ukrainian Government were given notice. Because the applications raised similar issues, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment.

The factual background, set out in the appended table rather than in the main text of the judgment, concerned criminal proceedings brought against the applicants in Ukraine. The applicants’ principal alleged violation was that the criminal proceedings against them had been excessively long. They relied on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees a hearing within a reasonable time in the determination of a criminal charge. They also complained under Article 13 that they had no effective remedy in domestic law for the excessive length of those proceedings. In application no. 9709/19, the applicant additionally raised a complaint under Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 to the Convention, which protects freedom of movement and the right to leave a country.

In assessing the length complaint, the Court reiterated the established criteria: the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicants and the relevant authorities, and what was at stake for the applicants. It referred to its leading judgment in *Merit v. Ukraine*, where it had already found violations of the Convention concerning similar issues—namely, excessively long criminal proceedings and the absence of an effective domestic remedy in Ukraine. After examining all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion. It therefore held that the length of the criminal proceedings in the present case was excessive and failed to meet the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1. It further held that the applicants did not have at their disposal an effective remedy for that complaint, in violation of Article 13.

As to the additional complaint under Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 in application no. 9709/19, the Court noted that it raised issues covered by its well-established case-law. It found that this complaint was not manifestly ill-founded within the meaning of Article 35 § 3 (a) and was not inadmissible on any other ground. The Court therefore considered it admissible for examination. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore that the applicants faced criminal proceedings that were not concluded within a reasonable time and that Ukrainian law did not provide them with an effective remedy to challenge that delay. One applicant also had an additional complaint under Protocol No. 4 concerning freedom of movement. The Court’s findings followed its settled case-law on Ukraine’s systemic problems with lengthy criminal proceedings and inadequate domestic remedies.

**Summary of *Kopytets and Shtopko v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 9706/19 and 9709/19)**

The case of *Kopytets and Shtopko v. Ukraine* was a judgment delivered by the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) on 17 October 2019. The case originated from two separate applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The primary subject of the complaints was the excessive length of criminal proceedings and the absence of an effective domestic remedy to address this delay.

The applicants, Kopytets and Shtopko, were involved in criminal proceedings in Ukraine. The specific details of the charges and the course of the proceedings are outlined in an appended table to the judgment, but the core issue was the prolonged nature of these proceedings. The applicants alleged that the duration of the criminal proceedings against them was incompatible with the "reasonable time" requirement stipulated by Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to a fair and public hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal. Furthermore, they contended that Ukrainian law did not provide any effective remedy by which they could challenge or seek redress for this excessive length, thereby violating Article 13 of the Convention, which ensures the right to an effective remedy before a national authority for violations of Convention rights.

In addition to the complaints concerning the length of proceedings, the applicant in application no. 9709/19 raised a separate complaint under Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 to the Convention. This article guarantees the right to freedom of movement, including the right to leave any country and to enter one's own country. The judgment notes that this particular complaint raised issues that were well-established in the Court's case-law, as detailed in the appended table.

The Court, sitting as a Committee, joined the two applications due to their similar subject matter. In its legal assessment, the Court reiterated the established criteria for evaluating the reasonableness of the length of proceedings: the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicants and the relevant authorities, and what was at stake for the applicants in the dispute. The Court referenced its leading case of *Merit v. Ukraine* (2004), where it had previously found a violation of similar issues.

Upon examining the material submitted, the Court found no facts or arguments that would lead it to a different conclusion. It held that the length of the criminal proceedings in the applicants' cases was indeed excessive and failed to meet the "reasonable time" requirement under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. Consequently, the Court also found that the applicants did not have at their disposal an effective remedy in domestic law to address these complaints, constituting a violation of Article 13. Regarding the complaint under Article 2 of Protocol No. 4, the Court determined that it was not manifestly ill-founded and was admissible.

The judgment was final and subject to potential editorial revision. This case serves as a clear example of the European Court of Human Rights' consistent jurisprudence concerning the unreasonable length of judicial proceedings in Ukraine and the systemic failure to provide an effective domestic remedy for such delays, as well as addressing ancillary complaints regarding other Convention rights.

*Kopytets and Shtopko v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 9706/19 and 9709/19) is a 17 October 2019 judgment delivered by a Committee of the Fifth Section of the European Court of Human Rights. The case originated in two applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Ukrainian Government were given notice of the applications. Because the applications raised similar subject matter, the Court examined them jointly in a single judgment.

The key alleged violations concerned the length of criminal proceedings and the absence of an effective domestic remedy. The applicants complained principally that the criminal proceedings against them had exceeded the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. They also complained under Article 13 that Ukrainian law did not provide them with any effective remedy for that delay. In application no. 9709/19, the applicant additionally raised a complaint under Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 to the Convention, which protects freedom of movement.

The judgment states that the applicants’ names, lodging dates, and the relevant procedural details are set out in an appended table. That table is not reproduced in the provided text, so the exact chronology of the criminal proceedings—including their total duration and the specific stages of investigation or trial—is not visible from the excerpt. What is clear, however, is that the alleged violations arose from criminal proceedings in Ukraine that the applicants considered excessively long, combined with the lack of any effective domestic mechanism to challenge that delay or obtain redress.

In assessing the Article 6 § 1 complaint, the Court reiterated the established criteria for determining whether the length of proceedings is reasonable: the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicants and the relevant authorities, and what was at stake for the applicants. It referred to the leading case of *Merit v. Ukraine* (no. 66561/01, 30 March 2004), where the Court had already found violations in respect of similar issues. After examining all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of leading to a different conclusion. It therefore held that the length of the proceedings in the present case was excessive and failed to meet the “reasonable time” requirement. This amounted to a violation of Article 6 § 1.

The Court further found that the applicants did not have at their disposal an effective remedy in respect of these complaints. Accordingly, there was also a violation of Article 13 of the Convention.

As for the additional complaint under Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 in application no. 9709/19, the Court noted that it raised issues in light of its well-established case-law. It held that this complaint was not manifestly ill-founded within the meaning of Article 35 § 3 (a) and was not inadmissible on any other ground. The provided excerpt does not include the final merits disposition of that Protocol No. 4 complaint beyond the admissibility finding. The judgment was final, though subject to editorial revision.

In short, the key facts relevant to the alleged violations are that the applicants faced lengthy criminal proceedings in Ukraine, lacked an effective domestic remedy for that delay, and one applicant also complained of a violation of freedom of movement under Article 2 of Protocol No. 4. The Court found violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 13, and found the Protocol No. 4 complaint admissible/not manifestly ill-founded.

**Milovanović v. Serbia** (Application no. 56065/10) concerned a Serbian mother’s complaint that the authorities failed to enforce domestic custody and contact decisions and to facilitate her reunion with her twin son and daughter after her former husband took them in January 2002 and systematically prevented contact. She alleged violations of the right to respect for family life and the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time.

The applicant left the matrimonial home in March 2001. In January 2002, while returning from a medical check-up, her husband intercepted her, took the children, and thereafter blocked contact, using threats of violence. She applied for divorce, sole custody and maintenance. In June 2002 the first-instance court granted her divorce and custody, but the District Court quashed the custody part. In February 2003 the Municipal Court issued an interim custody order requiring the father to hand over the children within 24 hours. It became enforceable in June 2003 but was never enforced. In October 2005 the court granted the applicant sole custody, regulated the father’s contact, ordered maintenance, and prohibited father-child contact for three months because of the father’s destructive behaviour and the children’s appalling living conditions. That judgment became final in November 2006 and enforceable in January 2007.

Enforcement efforts were repeatedly ineffective. The father failed to comply; fines were imposed in 2003 and 2004, but bailiffs found no assets and the house was often empty. Reunion attempts in 2003, 2004 and 2005 failed. At a June 2005 school transfer, the children were terrified and rejected their mother; social services sent a lawyer rather than an expert team, and the applicant urged that the children not be forcibly handed over without psychologists. A September 2005 social services report acknowledged her parental capacity but criticised her lack of efficiency and concluded that disrupting the children’s existing placement was not in their best interests. Enforcement was terminated in September 2005, then quashed in April 2006. Later, in 2007, social services advised that enforcement was in the children’s best interests. In February 2008 the interim enforcement was terminated because the final judgment existed; the applicant then sought enforcement of the 2005 judgment. An enforcement order was issued in March 2008, but the father appealed and the appeal was rejected only in April 2009. Further delays resulted from case-file transfers, court inactivity, adjournments, and the father’s obstruction. In 2009–2010 the court ordered counselling and limited weekend contact, but contact remained irregular and the final custody judgment remained unenforced.

The father was convicted in 2006 of parental child abduction for failing to hand over the children between 2003 and 2005, receiving a suspended sentence. Further criminal proceedings ended in acquittal in December 2012, with appeal pending. Social services also sought deprivation of his parental rights in 2007; a 2008 decision was later quashed and the request withdrawn.

In February 2009 the applicant filed a constitutional appeal complaining of non-enforcement and delay. In May 2012 the Constitutional Court found a violation of the right to a fair trial because the enforcement proceedings concerning the 2005 custody judgment had been protracted, and ordered the enforcement court to act. It dismissed complaints about the interim order as out of time and about the criminal proceedings because she had not sought damages as a civil party. The European Court of Human Rights later examined the length of the constitutional proceedings, noting they lasted nearly three years and five months and that the Constitutional Court’s excessive caseload could not justify the delay. The key alleged violations thus concerned the State’s failure to enforce custody and contact decisions and to facilitate family reunification, as well as the excessive length of the constitutional proceedings.

**Milovanović v. Serbia** (ECtHR, 8 October 2019) concerns a Serbian mother’s complaints that authorities failed to enforce court decisions granting her custody of her twin children and to facilitate their reunion, and that her constitutional appeal took too long.

The applicant and her husband had twins, a boy and a girl, in May 1996. She left the matrimonial home in March 2001. In January 2002, while she was taking the children to a medical check-up, her husband intercepted them and took them away. From then until 2010 he systematically prevented her from having contact with them, using threats of violence. He moved with the children to a house he was building.

In 2002 the applicant sought divorce, sole custody, and maintenance. In June 2002 the municipal court divorced the couple and granted her custody, but the district court later quashed the custody part. In February 2003 the municipal court issued an interim custody order requiring the husband to hand over the children within twenty-four hours pending the civil proceedings. It became enforceable in June 2003 but was never enforced.

In October 2005 the municipal court granted the applicant sole custody, set the father’s contact rights, ordered maintenance, and temporarily prohibited contact between the father and children to help restore emotional ties. The court cited the father’s destructive behaviour and appalling living conditions. The judgment became final in November 2006 and enforceable in January 2007, but it remained unenforced.

Enforcement efforts were protracted and largely ineffective. The father failed to comply. Fines were imposed in 2003–2004, but bailiffs found no valuable assets or an empty house. Reunion attempts failed. In June 2005 a transfer at the children’s school was aborted because the children were terrified, crying, and no expert team was present. Social services gave conflicting reports: initially they considered the mother better suited for custody, but later noted the children were alienated and advised against forcible enforcement. In September 2005 enforcement of the interim order was terminated based on the children’s objections, but this was quashed in April 2006. In 2007 social services said enforcement would be in the children’s best interests. In February 2008 the interim enforcement was terminated as no longer valid, and a new enforcement request for the final judgment was filed in March 2008. Delays continued, with case files transferred to criminal and constitutional courts and hearings postponed. Contact remained limited; the children eventually saw the applicant more often but did not want to live with her. The 2005 custody judgment remained unenforced.

Separately, the father was convicted in 2006 of parental child abduction and given a suspended sentence, but was acquitted in 2012. Deprivation of parental rights proceedings also took place. The applicant complained repeatedly to the enforcement court, Ministry of Justice, prosecutors, and social services.

In February 2009 she filed a constitutional appeal alleging non-enforcement of the final custody judgment and the interim order, and the length of criminal proceedings. In May 2012 the Constitutional Court found a violation of the right to a fair trial due to the protracted enforcement of the final custody judgment, ordered the enforcement court to act, and dismissed the rest. The interim complaint was out of time, and the criminal complaint was barred because she had not claimed damages as a civil party.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged failures to enforce custody decisions and facilitate reunion since 2002. The Court also examined the length of the constitutional proceedings—from February 2009 to July 2012, nearly three years and five months. The Government blamed the Constitutional Court’s excessive caseload. The ECtHR found this delay excessive and violated Article 6 § 1, stressing that exceptional diligence is required in child custody cases.

**Case Summary: Milovanović v. Serbia (Application no. 56065/10)**

The case of *Milovanović v. Serbia* concerns a Serbian national’s complaint that state authorities failed to enforce court decisions granting her custody of her children and to facilitate their reunion, thereby violating her right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant also alleged a violation of Article 6 regarding the length of proceedings.

The key facts are as follows: The applicant, Mirjana Milovanović, had twins in 1996. In January 2002, her husband forcibly took the children and systematically prevented her from having any contact with them for years. In June 2002, a municipal court granted the applicant a divorce and awarded her sole custody. While the divorce was upheld on appeal, the custody decision was quashed and remitted.

In February 2003, the court issued an interim custody order, ordering the respondent to hand over the children within 24 hours. This order became enforceable in June 2003 but was never enforced. The respondent repeatedly ignored the order, and fines imposed on him proved ineffective as he had no seizable assets. Attempts to transfer the children in 2005 failed; the children were found to be terrified and rejected the idea of reunification. The social care centre (RSCC) reported that the children were alienated from the applicant and that forcible enforcement would not be in their best interests.

In October 2005, the court granted the applicant final, sole custody, finding the respondent’s living conditions and destructive behaviour required the children’s immediate removal. This judgment became enforceable in January 2007, but it also remained unenforced.

The enforcement court’s proceedings were marked by significant delays. The case file was frequently tied up in other proceedings, including a criminal case against the respondent for child abduction. Hearings were postponed, sometimes due to the unavailability of judges or the RSCC experts. The RSCC, which was tasked with providing expert opinions, gave conflicting advice. It initially recommended enforcement, but later advised against it due to the children’s resistance, recommending counselling instead. By 2010, the enforcement court had reduced the applicant’s contact rights to short visits, and the final custody judgment remained unenforced.

The applicant filed a constitutional appeal in February 2009. In May 2012, the Constitutional Court found a violation of the right to a fair trial solely on account of the excessive length of the enforcement proceedings, ordering the court to expedite the case. It dismissed the complaint regarding the interim custody order as out of time and did not consider a violation of family life rights. The applicant then turned to the European Court of Human Rights.

The ECtHR noted that the proceedings before the Serbian Constitutional Court lasted nearly three years and five months. It found that this length was excessive and failed to meet the "reasonable time" requirement of Article 6, especially given the exceptional diligence required in child custody cases. The Government's justification of an excessive caseload was not accepted.
