**Case summary: Radzevil v. Ukraine (App. no. 36600/09)**

The case concerned criminal proceedings arising from a fatal road accident in Ukraine. On 12 September 2002 the applicant, Mr Boris Radzevil, was driving a white Toyota to work. As he approached a pedestrian crossing, a pedestrian, G., began crossing the road. The applicant claimed that G. suddenly fell into his traffic lane after an oncoming red car passed at high speed, and that G. may have been hit by that unidentified car, slipped, or fallen for another reason. The investigation and domestic courts, however, concluded that G. had been struck by the applicant’s car. The applicant stopped, placed G. in the rear seat, and an ambulance took G. to hospital. G. died later that day. The applicant left the scene before police arrived.

The self-incrimination complaint focused on events after the accident. The applicant later went to the hospital to ask about G.’s condition. A police officer, T., said the applicant admitted that he had accidentally hit G. with his car and agreed to show police the accident site. Police took him there, but no traces of the accident were found. The applicant later disputed having participated because his signature did not appear on the scene inspection report. On the same day, 12 September 2002, he signed an “explanation” to Illichivsk police stating that G. had unexpectedly emerged and fallen onto the bonnet of his car. The document noted that he had been informed of Article 63 of the Ukrainian Constitution, which protects the right not to incriminate oneself. The applicant claimed he did not have his glasses, signed without reading, denied making those statements, and said the Article 63 note was added later in different ink.

On 20 September 2002 criminal proceedings were instituted against the applicant. A licensed advocate, K., was later admitted as defence counsel. On 11 December 2002 formal charges were brought, and the applicant’s status changed from suspect to accused. According to the applicant, during questioning that day in the presence of his lawyer, he retracted the 12 September explanation, saying it had been given under psychological pressure. Although the self-incriminating statement was formally excluded from the case file, the applicant complained that the domestic courts indirectly relied on it, contrary to his right not to incriminate himself.

As to legal assistance, the applicant complained under Article 6 § 3 (c) that he was not represented on appeal by lawyers of his own choosing. The European Court of Human Rights examined whether this, together with the alleged indirect reliance on the excluded statement, undermined the overall fairness of the proceedings.

The length complaint concerned the prolonged criminal proceedings. The case was sent to the Illichivsk Town Court, then remitted for additional pre-trial investigation on 31 July 2003. It returned to court on 15 October 2003. Hearings were adjourned several times because witnesses were absent. On 19 April 2004 the court ordered forensic medical, technical, and reconstruction examinations, but some were only carried out on 24 February 2005. The trial judge’s term expired on 30 March 2005, and a new judge began hearing the case on 29 November 2005. A fresh reconstruction was ordered on 4 July 2006 because the earlier order had not been implemented; it was carried out on 10 July 2006. Throughout, the applicant denied breaching traffic rules or hitting G., arguing there was no expert evidence that his car had touched G.’s body.

On 13 December 2006 the Illichivsk Court convicted the applicant, sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment and a two-year driving ban, but granted amnesty. The ECtHR ultimately found that the alleged reliance on the excluded self-incriminating statement and the inability to use chosen counsel on appeal did not undermine the overall fairness of the trial, but it found a violation of the right to a hearing within a reasonable time. The applicant died in January 2016, and his wife pursued the application.

In *Yakuba v. Ukraine* (no. 1452/09), the applicant, a Ukrainian national with prior drug convictions, was convicted in 2007 of selling opioids to an undercover police agent, P., on three occasions: 26 February and 6 and 9 March 2007. Police used a test-purchase operation; P. allegedly received marked cash and returned with syringes. The first transaction was video-recorded by a hidden camera. On 9 March the applicant was arrested. He admitted having a drug-filled syringe and trying to destroy evidence; police pushed him down and handcuffed him. He alleged that after being immobilised they dragged and beat him. A medical examination on 15 March recorded abrasions on his right hand, shin and knees, consistent with the arrest date. Prosecutors refused to open a criminal case against the police, and domestic courts found the force lawful because the applicant had tried to destroy evidence. The ECtHR declared the Article 3 complaint inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded, finding no reason to doubt that the force was strictly necessary due to the applicant’s own conduct.

The main fair-trial complaints concerned non-disclosure of the video and the absent undercover agent. On 20 April 2007 an investigator viewed the video with witnesses and summarised it in a report. The applicant’s lawyer asked to see it, but on 27 April the investigator refused, citing protection of P.’s identity. Nevertheless, the bill of indictment listed P. as a trial witness and the investigator’s video summary as evidence. At trial the applicant denied selling drugs on two occasions and asked the court to disclose the video and examine P., a possible defence witness B., and the forensic expert. Those requests were refused for unspecified reasons. The conviction relied on the police officer who arranged the test purchase, an attesting witness, P.’s untested pre-trial statements, a banknote found on the applicant, and drug traces. Appeals and cassation review upheld the conviction.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(b) and (d). There was no convincing good reason for P.’s absence; as the only direct participant in the alleged sales, his evidence was decisive. Counterbalancing factors were insufficient. The video was central, yet the prosecution alone controlled its meaning through an investigator’s summary, without judicial scrutiny or real examination of the need to protect P. The proceedings were therefore overall unfair.

Finally, the applicant complained under Article 34 that authorities refused to provide copies of procedural documents, hearing records and his cassation appeal for his Strasbourg application. The trial court refused in October 2008, March 2009 and May 2013, and the Court of Appeal refused in October 2008, saying domestic law had no procedure for a convict to examine the case file after criminal proceedings ended. The Court found that this hindered his effective exercise of the right of individual application, contrary to Article 34.

In *Yakuba v. Ukraine* (no. 1452/09, judgment 12 February 2019), the applicant was a Ukrainian national with prior drug convictions. Police targeted him through an undercover test-purchase operation. Agent P., allegedly recruited by police, was given cash before attesting witnesses and, out of their sight, made three alleged purchases of opium from Yakuba on 26 February and 6 and 9 March 2007. The first purchase was video-recorded by hidden camera. On 9 March 2007 Yakuba was arrested. Police reported that force was used and handcuffs applied because he tried to destroy evidence—a drug-filled syringe. Yakuba alleged that after being pushed to the ground and handcuffed, police dragged him, causing pain and humiliation. On 15 March 2007, at his lawyer’s request, a medical expert examined him and noted abrasions on his right hand, shin and both knees, which could have been sustained on 9 March and could have resulted from a fall. On 8 May 2007 prosecutors refused to open criminal proceedings against the arresting officers. Yakuba did not appeal that refusal but continued to raise ill-treatment before the criminal courts, which rejected it as unsubstantiated and found the force lawful. The ECtHR later declared the Article 3 complaint manifestly ill-founded, accepting that the force was strictly necessary because of Yakuba’s own attempt to destroy evidence.

The criminal proceedings raised the main fair-trial issues. Yakuba admitted that on 9 March he had bought and kept drugs for personal use and was accompanied by B., but denied selling drugs on three occasions. He asked the investigator to find and examine B. as a witness; police searched unsuccessfully. P. was questioned at pre-trial stage and described the three purchases. The bill of indictment listed P. as a trial witness and identified a police report summarising the video recording of the first test purchase as evidence. Yet when the defence asked to watch the video, the investigator refused on 27 April 2007, saying it would reveal P.’s identity and endanger him. At trial, Yakuba requested disclosure of the video and examination of P., B. and a forensic expert. The trial court refused these requests for unknown reasons. On 26 June 2007 Yakuba was convicted of drug trafficking and sentenced to eight years. The conviction relied on the test-purchase police officer and an attesting witness, P.’s pre-trial statements, a banknote found on Yakuba, and forensic traces.

The applicant complained under Article 6 that he could not examine P. or view the video. The ECtHR found no convincing good reason for P.’s absence, noting the contradiction between the identity-protection claim and P.’s listing as a trial witness. P.’s evidence was decisive because he alone directly participated in the alleged sales, and other evidence did not sufficiently compensate. The video procedure worsened the unfairness: only the investigator had viewed the tape and prepared the summary, so the prosecution alone defined its incriminating meaning, without judicial scrutiny of the need to protect P.’s identity. The Court therefore found the proceedings overall unfair under Article 6.

Finally, Yakuba alleged under Article 34 that authorities refused to give him copies of procedural documents, hearing records and his cassation appeal needed for his Strasbourg application. The trial and appellate courts replied that domestic law did not allow a convict to examine the case file after proceedings ended.

Yakuba v. Ukraine (no. 1452/09, 12 February 2019) concerned a Ukrainian man with prior drugs-related convictions who was targeted in an undercover test-purchase operation. A police-recruited agent, P., was given cash in front of attesting witnesses and, out of their sight, allegedly bought opium-filled syringes from the applicant on three occasions: 26 February and 6 and 9 March 2007. The first purchase was secretly video-recorded. The applicant was arrested on 9 March 2007. He initially admitted having a drug-filled syringe and trying to destroy it, but later denied having it at arrest, while still admitting he had bought drugs for personal use. Police pushed him to the ground, handcuffed him, and, according to the applicant, dragged him after he was immobilised. Officers reported using force to prevent him destroying evidence. A medical examination found abrasions on his hand, shin and knees, consistent with the arrest date. Prosecutors refused to open criminal proceedings against the police, and the domestic courts rejected his ill-treatment complaint as unsubstantiated, finding the force lawful and necessary.

In the criminal proceedings, the investigator viewed the video with attesting witnesses and recorded that it showed the applicant selling drugs to P. The applicant’s lawyer was refused access to the video because P.’s identity needed protection. P. was questioned during the investigation but never examined at trial. Although the indictment listed him as a witness, the trial court refused requests to call him, to disclose the video, to call the forensic expert, and to locate B., a witness the applicant said could confirm he had bought drugs for personal use. The applicant was convicted of drug trafficking and sentenced to eight years. The conviction relied on police and attesting-witness testimony, P.’s untested pre-trial statements, a banknote found during arrest, and forensic traces. Appeals were rejected; the Court of Appeal and Supreme Court also relied on the investigator’s report about the video. The applicant further asked domestic courts for copies of procedural documents—hearing records and his appeal—to substantiate his Strasbourg application, but was refused on the ground that domestic law provided no procedure for a convict to access the case file after trial.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged ill-treatment by police under Article 3, unfair trial under Article 6 because he could not examine the video or P., and obstruction of his right of individual petition under Article 34. The Court declared the Article 3 complaint inadmissible. It found that force had been used, but that it was strictly necessary because the applicant had attempted to destroy evidence, and the medical evidence supported the domestic authorities’ findings.

The Court found a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(b) and (d). There was no convincing reason for P.’s absence; as the only direct participant in the alleged sales, his evidence was decisive. The counterbalancing factors were insufficient, especially because the prosecution alone viewed the video and the investigator’s summary determined its meaning without independent or judicial scrutiny. The domestic courts made no real assessment of whether P.’s identity truly required protection. The proceedings were therefore overall unfair. The Court also found a violation of Article 34 concerning the refusal to provide copies of documents needed for the application.

**Summary**

The case concerned three joined applications (nos. 315/10, 1153/10 and 1158/10) brought by six Moldovan, Russian and Ukrainian nationals. The applicants complained principally under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights about inhuman and degrading conditions of detention in facilities controlled by the separatist “MRT” authorities in Transdniestria, Moldova. One applicant also alleged ill-treatment and denial of medical assistance.

In application no. 315/10, Evghenii Antonov was arrested in Tiraspol in August 2009 and accused of possessing a hunter’s knife and marijuana. He was held in IVS Tiraspol and later Hlinaia prison in Grigoriopol. He told Iryna Antonova that he was in a dark, damp cell without basic hygiene and asked her to bring food and warm clothes. She was refused visits. On 19 October 2009, the OSCE was denied access to IVS Tiraspol, where about 90 detainees, including Antonov, were on hunger strike protesting ill-treatment and inhuman conditions. Complaints to Moldovan, Russian and “MRT” authorities failed. When she saw him at a court hearing in December 2009, he appeared tired and weak. He was convicted in November 2010, with appeal proceedings pending.

In application no. 1153/10, Alexandru Băluţă was arrested in Tiraspol in December 2004 and accused of murder and arson. He alleged he was severely beaten. Released in 2007, he was rearrested in September 2009 and held in IVS Tiraspol, then Hlinaia. He allegedly endured a dark, damp cell without hygiene or daily walks. Food and items sent by Tamara Băluţă, except bread, did not reach him, and visits were refused. In October 2009, detainees went on hunger strike; he alleged riot police entered on 16 October and beat prisoners. The OSCE was again denied access. The “MRT” prosecutor refused relative visits without giving reasons.

In application no. 1158/10, Oleksandr Bezrodnii was arrested in July 2009 and accused of stealing roses and endangering militia officers. On 29 July 2009, Liudmila Bezrodnyaya saw him at court with blood on his face, a green substance on his head, and bruises. He said he had been ill-treated to extract self-incriminating statements. He later described a basement cell without daylight, shared with detainees having HIV and tuberculosis, insufficient beds, one shower per month, a dirty in-cell toilet, dampness, poor ventilation, insects, no hygiene products, mouldy and insect-infested food, and no medical help for his injuries. Food and items sent to him were rejected or destroyed. On 13 October 2009, she was told detainees were on hunger strike and that riot police would be called. A Moldovan anti-torture committee member reported the strike and ill-treatment. On 16 October, riot police entered the prison; she could not learn what happened to him. The OSCE was denied access on 19 October. In February 2010, Bezrodnii complained to the Tiraspol city court that he had been severely beaten at arrest, with bruises, head blows, and a swollen leg, and had been taken to a medical facility. He was convicted in July 2010, but the sentence was later quashed and the case was pending.

The Court found that both Moldova and Russia had jurisdiction: Moldova as the territorial State with positive obligations, and Russia because it exercised effective control over the “MRT” through military, economic and political support. On Article 3, the Court found that the applicants’ detention conditions amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment. For Bezrodnii, it also found ill-treatment and a failure to provide medical assistance. The respondent Governments did not contradict the applicants’ accounts, and the same “MRT” prisons had previously been found substandard. The Article 3 complaints were declared admissible, and responsibility was assessed against both respondent States.

The case concerned three joined applications by six Moldovan, Russian, and Ukrainian nationals alleging violations of Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights in the Transdniestrian region of Moldova, controlled by the separatist “MRT” authorities. All three first applicants were detained in “MRT” facilities, initially at IVS Tiraspol and later at Hlinaia prison in Grigoriopol, where they allegedly suffered inhuman conditions and ill-treatment.

In Application no. 315/10, Evghenii Antonov was arrested in Tiraspol in August 2009 and accused of possessing a hunter’s knife and marijuana. He described being held in a dark, damp cell without basic hygiene. His mother, Iryna Antonova, was refused permission to see him. On 19 October 2009, the OSCE was denied access to IVS Tiraspol, where about 90 detainees, including Antonov, were on hunger strike protesting ill-treatment and inhuman detention conditions. Complaints to Moldovan, Russian, and “MRT” authorities were unsuccessful. She later saw him at a court hearing in December 2009 and said he appeared tired and weak.

In Application no. 1153/10, Alexandru Băluţă was arrested in Tiraspol in December 2004 for murder and arson and allegedly severely beaten. Released in 2007, he was rearrested in September 2009 and held in the same facilities. He allegedly endured dark, damp cells without basic hygiene or daily walks. His mother, Tamara Băluţă, claimed food and items she sent did not reach him, except bread, and all visits were refused. She reported an October 2009 hunger strike and alleged that riot police entered the prison and beat detainees. The OSCE was again denied access, and complaints were unsuccessful. The “MRT” prosecutor’s office stated that investigators were not obliged to authorize family visits and had refused them.

In *Romeva v. North Macedonia* (App. no. 32141/10), the applicant, Ms Olgica Romeva, complained that she had been deprived of her retirement pension and ordered to repay previously paid sums, breaching legal certainty and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, and she also relied on Article 6 § 1. The key facts concerned a pension granted in 2000 and retroactively annulled in 2007.

In May 2000 the Employment Bureau instructed the applicant, then unemployed and receiving unemployment social benefits, to apply for a retirement pension. She lodged an application containing only basic personal information; she supplied no employment records. On 23 May 2000 the Pension and Disability Fund granted her a monthly pension, finding she had completed 35 years, 10 months and 24 days of service—the sole criterion at the time. The decision became final and she received payments. Under domestic law, employers had to submit employment data, and the Fund had to maintain those records; employees were not responsible for supplying or verifying them.

In 2007 an internal Fund audit found incomplete records for several pensioners. In the applicant’s case, her employment booklet was missing, and the Fund could not obtain further evidence about her alleged employment between 1963 and 1967. Nevertheless, on 18 October 2007 the Fund annulled its 2000 decision and refused her pension, finding she had not in fact worked during 1963–1967 and therefore lacked the required 35 years. Her pension payments stopped.

The applicant appealed. Initially, the Administrative Court quashed the refusal because section 145-A, which allowed annulment of final pension decisions, had entered into force in June 2006 and could not be applied retroactively. However, in 2009 the Second-Instance Commission dismissed her appeal again, relying on reopening grounds under the Administrative Proceedings Act: it said erroneous documents had been used in the pension proceedings and that the applicant had “endorsed” them by applying. The Administrative Court and Supreme Court upheld that outcome. No finding was made that the applicant had personally supplied false employment information.

The Fund also sued for reimbursement of the full pension paid between 2000 and 2007—MKD 645,138—on unjust-enrichment grounds. The civil courts upheld the claim and enforcement proceedings began. A criminal complaint against the applicant was rejected because the limitation period had expired. The applicant’s pension had been her sole income since 2006. In November 2009, after legislative changes, she was granted a new pension under the age criterion.

Before the ECtHR, the central issue was whether the retroactive withdrawal of the pension and the repayment order violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court found that the final grant of the pension created a protected “possession.” The applicant had acted in good faith: she did not provide the employment data, the authorities were responsible for checking eligibility and maintaining records, and there was no evidence she had misled the Fund. The Government argued the measure was in the public interest and part of a campaign against wrongly granted pensions, alleging bad faith, but the Court rejected that. The interference, especially requiring repayment of seven years of pension that had been her sole income, imposed an excessive individual burden for the authorities’ mistake. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The decision became final, and she received monthly payments.

The Fund attempted to verify her alleged employment between 1963 and 1967 with the employer but apparently obtained no further evidence. On 18 October 2007 the Fund annulled its 2000 decision, refused her pension request, and discontinued payments. It claimed that the information about her 1963–1967 employment had been incorrect and that she therefore did not meet the minimum 35-year service requirement. The right had been generated by the Fund’s favourable decision in 2000, and she had acted in good faith. She had not provided the employment data; under domestic law, employers supplied such information and the Fund maintained the records. There was no evidence she misled the authorities or acted in bad faith. The 2007 annulment and the repayment order therefore interfered with her property rights. Although the measure pursued a legitimate aim of correcting wrongly granted pensions and protecting public funds, it imposed an excessive individual burden on the applicant. The mistake was attributable to the authorities, not to her, and she lost her sole source of income and was required to repay seven years of pension. **Summary of *Romeva v. North Macedonia* (Application no. 32141/10)**

**Key Facts:**

The applicant, Ms Olgica Romeva, born in 1947, was granted a retirement pension by the Pension and Disability Fund ("the Fund") on 23 May 2000, amounting to 6,462 denars monthly. The Fund determined she had completed the requisite service period of thirty-five years, ten months and twenty-four days based on records in its possession. The applicant had lodged her pension application following an instruction from the Employment Bureau, providing only basic personal information without any employment documentation. The decision became final and she received regular payments.

Under domestic law, employers bore responsibility for submitting employment data to the Fund, which maintained individual records. The applicant had no role in compiling or submitting this information.

Between February and July 2007, the Fund conducted an internal audit revealing incomplete records for several pension recipients. Regarding the applicant, the audit found her employment booklet was missing and questioned her employment between 1963 and 1967. On 18 October 2007, the Fund annulled its 2000 decision and refused her pension, finding she had not actually been employed during that period and therefore lacked the minimum thirty-five-year service requirement. Payments ceased immediately.

The applicant's appeals were ultimately unsuccessful. The Administrative Court initially ruled in her favour, finding retroactive application of legislation, but subsequent decisions upheld the Fund's position. The Supreme Court dismissed her final appeal on 26 April 2010.

Critically, the Fund also brought a civil action seeking reimbursement of MKD 645,138 paid between 2000 and 2007 on grounds of unjust enrichment. This claim was upheld through all instances, becoming final on 8 January 2014, and enforcement proceedings commenced. The applicant's pension had been her sole income source since 2006.

The Fund lodged a criminal complaint against the applicant in 2012, which was rejected due to the expired statutory limitation period.

In November 2009, following legislative changes introducing new age criteria, the applicant qualified for and received a new pension of MKD 10,384.50 monthly.

**Relevant Violation:**

The applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that she was retroactively divested of her pension, violating legal certainty. The Court found the Fund's decision generated a property right because the applicant acted in good faith—she neither supplied employment information nor could control the Fund's records. The authorities bore responsibility for verifying eligibility. The Court noted no evidence the applicant misled the Fund or acted in bad faith.

The Court concluded the applicant bore an excessive individual burden, having lost her sole income and facing reimbursement demands for seven years of payments due to administrative errors beyond her control.

In evaluating the Article 3 complaint, the Court applied its established case-law on prison conditions. It referred in particular to the principles in **Muršić v. Croatia** [GC], no. 7334/13, §§ 96–101, ECHR 2016. Under *Muršić*, a serious lack of space in a prison cell weighs heavily in determining whether detention conditions are “degrading” for the purposes of Article 3. Such a lack of space may disclose a violation by itself or when taken together with other shortcomings. The Court also cited **Ananyev and Others v. Russia**, nos. 42525/07 and 60800/08, §§ 149–159, 10 January 2012, concerning conditions of detention and the effectiveness of remedies.

The Court noted that in the leading case of **Melnik v. Ukraine** (no. 72286/01, 28 March 2006), and more recently in **Beketov v. Ukraine** (no. 44436/09, 19 February 2019), it had already found violations in respect of issues similar to those raised by the applicants. After examining all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on the admissibility and merits of the complaints.

Consequently, the Court considered that the applicants’ conditions of detention were inadequate, in violation of Article 3. It further found that the applicants did not have at their disposal an effective remedy in domestic law in respect of those complaints, contrary to Article 13. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore that the applicants were detained in poor conditions—primarily involving serious lack of space and associated deficiencies—and that no effective domestic remedy existed to challenge those conditions. The Court accordingly found violations of Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention.
001-196897:
The case **J.D. and A v. the United Kingdom** (Applications nos. 32949/17 and 34614/17) concerned the UK’s 2012 Housing Benefit under-occupancy rules, often called the “bedroom tax.” Regulation B13 reduced Housing Benefit for social housing tenants with more bedrooms than the state considered necessary by 14% for one extra bedroom and 25% for two or more. Both applicants had three-bedroom homes for two people and suffered a 14% reduction. They alleged violation of Article 14 ECHR (non-discrimination), taken with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of possessions), on grounds of disability and gender.

**J.D.** lived in a three-bedroom social rented property with her adult daughter since 1993. Her daughter had severe brain damage from oxygen deprivation, severe physical and learning disabilities, used a wheelchair, and was registered blind. J.D. cared for her full time. The house was specifically adapted: wide doors, internal lift, ramps, ceiling hoists, an accessible bathroom, and a changing bed. Under the bedroom criteria, they were entitled to two bedrooms, so the third was treated as spare. The 14% reduction left J.D.’s Housing Benefit insufficient to cover rent. She received discretionary housing payments (DHPs) only temporarily; her last award expired on 31 March 2017, and no smaller accommodation suitable for her daughter’s needs was available.

**A** had lived in a three-bedroom social rented house with her son for over 25 years. She had been allocated the three-bedroom home because of a shortage of two-bedroom properties. She had briefly been involved with a man, X, who was extremely dangerous and had served a long prison sentence for attempted murder. After release, X attacked and raped her; her son was conceived as a result. In 2012 X contacted and threatened her again. Police referred her to the Sanctuary Scheme, which adapted her home, including converting the attic into a “panic room,” and arranged police tagging and multi-agency support. Her Housing Benefit was also reduced by 14% for the spare bedroom. She obtained temporary DHPs, but in early 2015 a DHP refusal led to an eviction threat. The Secretary of State intervened, and the local authority reversed its decision, accepting that it had failed to consider the home’s special adaptations.

In domestic proceedings, courts accepted that the regulation discriminated against disabled people and, in A’s case, women needing Sanctuary Scheme protection. However, the Divisional Court, Court of Appeal, and ultimately the Supreme Court in 2016 dismissed the claims, applying the “manifestly without reasonable foundation” test for welfare measures. The Supreme Court found a reasonable foundation for using DHPs rather than blanket exemptions. Lady Hale and Lord Carnwath dissented for A.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants argued that the reduction discriminated against them by failing to accommodate their disability- and gender-related needs. The ECtHR, applying the wide margin of appreciation in social and economic policy and the manifestly without reasonable foundation test, found **no violation** of Article 14 taken with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It considered that the UK’s choice to rely on a discretionary scheme rather than specific exemptions was not beyond its margin.

**J.D. and A v. the United Kingdom** concerned two British social housing tenants whose Housing Benefit was reduced under the UK’s 2012 under-occupancy rules, often called the “bedroom tax.” Regulation B13 reduced Housing Benefit by 14% where a tenant was deemed to have one spare bedroom, and by 25% for two or more. Affected claimants could apply for Discretionary Housing Payments (“DHPs”), but these were discretionary, temporary, cash-limited, and did not provide a statutory right of appeal. The applicants alleged that the reduction discriminated against them contrary to Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights, taken with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, on grounds of disability and gender.

The first applicant, J.D., had lived since 1993 in a three-bedroom social rented property with her adult daughter. The daughter had severe physical and learning disabilities, was a permanent wheelchair user, was registered blind, and required full-time care. Their home had been specially adapted to her needs, including wide doors, an internal lift, wheelchair access, ceiling hoists, an accessible bathroom, and a changing bed. Because there were two people in a three-bedroom house, J.D. was treated as under-occupying by one bedroom. Her Housing Benefit was cut by 14%, leaving a shortfall between benefit and rent. She received DHPs only on a temporary basis; her last award had expired by March 2017, and no suitable smaller accommodation had been offered.

The second applicant, A, had lived for over 25 years in a three-bedroom social rented house with her son. She had been allocated the larger house because of a shortage of two-bedroom properties. A had previously been violently attacked and raped by X, a dangerous man convicted of attempted murder. Her son was conceived as a result of that rape. After X threatened her again in 2012, police referred her to a Sanctuary Scheme, which adapted her home to include a modified attic “panic room” where she and her son could retreat. Her Housing Benefit was likewise reduced by 14% for under-occupancy. DHPs covered the shortfall only temporarily. In 2015, a DHP refusal led to an eviction threat; the Secretary of State intervened, and the local authority reversed its decision, acknowledging that it had failed to consider the special adaptations.

Domestically, courts agreed the measure produced prima facie discrimination on grounds of disability and sex but differed on justification. The Supreme Court dismissed both claims, holding that the correct test was whether the policy was “manifestly without reasonable foundation” and that DHPs were an acceptable way to address individual needs. Lady Hale dissented in part, especially for A, reasoning that her need was not extra space but to remain in a safe adapted home, and that DHPs were inadequate.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants complained that the benefit reduction, without exemptions for severely disabled tenants or victims of gender-based violence in Sanctuary Schemes, violated Article 14 read with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court ultimately found no violation, giving the UK a wide margin of appreciation in social and economic policy. It accepted that the DHP scheme provided a mechanism for vulnerable tenants’ circumstances to be considered, and that the failure to create specific exemptions was not manifestly without reasonable foundation.

In *J.D. and A v. the United Kingdom* (ECtHR, First Section, 24 October 2019), two British social-housing tenants challenged the UK’s 2012 “bedroom tax” under Article 14 of the Convention, read with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, alleging discrimination on grounds of disability and gender. The measure, Regulation B13 of the Housing Benefit Regulations 2006, reduced Housing Benefit for social-sector tenants deemed to have one spare bedroom by 14% (and by 25% for two or more). Its aims were to incentivise moves to smaller accommodation and reduce public expenditure. Discretionary Housing Payments (DHPs) could cover shortfalls, but were discretionary, cash-limited, temporary, and not appealable as of right.

The first applicant, J.D., had lived since 1993 in a three-bedroom social rented property with her adult daughter. Her daughter has severe brain damage, physical and learning disabilities, is a wheelchair user, and is registered blind. The home was specially adapted to her needs, including wide doors, an internal lift, ramps, ceiling hoists, an accessible bathroom, and a changing bed. Because two people occupied three bedrooms, J.D.’s Housing Benefit was reduced by 14%. No smaller suitable accommodation was available, and her DHPs were temporary and had expired, leaving a rent shortfall. She alleged disability discrimination.

The second applicant, A, lived for over 25 years in a three-bedroom social house with her son. She had been allocated the larger house because of a shortage of two-bedroom properties. A had been violently attacked and raped by X, a man convicted of attempted murder; her son was conceived as a result. After further threats in 2012, she was placed in a Sanctuary Scheme, and her home was adapted with a secure “panic room,” police tagging, and multi-agency support. She suffered PTSD and suicidal ideation. Her Housing Benefit was also cut by 14% for under-occupancy. DHPs were awarded only temporarily; in 2015 a refusal led to an eviction threat and was reversed only after the Secretary of State intervened because the home’s adaptations had not been considered. She alleged gender-based discrimination.

Domestic courts accepted prima facie discrimination. The Supreme Court ultimately dismissed both claims, applying the “manifestly without reasonable foundation” test for welfare policy. It held that the absence of blanket exemptions for disabled tenants or Sanctuary Scheme victims was justified; DHPs were a reasonable alternative, and A needed to remain in her home rather than to have a third bedroom as such. Lady Hale and Lord Carnwath dissented in A’s case.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants complained that the benefit reduction, without exemptions for their circumstances, discriminated against them contrary to Article 14 taken with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court considered the UK’s wide margin of appreciation in social and economic policy and whether the scheme was manifestly without reasonable foundation. It found no violation: the UK had not exceeded its margin, and the failure to make special provision for these vulnerable categories was not discriminatory in breach of the Convention.
001-193259:
Van de Kolk v. the Netherlands (ECtHR, 28 May 2019) concerned a Dutch national arrested on 19 August 2009, aged 19, on suspicion of distributing child pornography involving three photographs of a 16-year-old girl. He was informed of his right to consult a lawyer. While in police custody, before his lawyer was available but with his consent, police conducted a “social interview” about personal circumstances and personality, not the suspected offence. He disclosed a brain disorder—cavernous hemangiomas in his brain and spinal cord—and said it might affect his trust in others. When his lawyer became available, the interview was suspended so he could consult by telephone. Following that advice, he refused further questions and the interview ended.

On 20 August 2009, police interviewed him twice, including about the suspected offence. At the start he asked to have his lawyer present. He was told this was impossible, and questioning proceeded; he answered questions. During the interview, officers noticed a spasm-like arm movement and asked whether he was having an epileptic fit. He confirmed it; the interview was interrupted, a doctor was called, and questioning later resumed. A final interview occurred on 21 August 2009. All interviews were audio-recorded, and he was released that day.

Domestically, the Regional Court of The Hague convicted him on 25 March 2011 and imposed a suspended two-week prison sentence plus 80 hours’ community service. It found he should have been allowed to consult a lawyer before the first police interview, but treated this as a procedural defect only because later interviews were not substantially different. On appeal, the Court of Appeal of The Hague quashed that decision, convicted him again, and imposed 40 hours’ community service. It rejected the complaint about lawyer presence, holding that as an adult he was not entitled to a lawyer during police interviews under Salduz. Counsel had claimed he had the mental age of a 15- or 16-year-old and suffered from a brain disorder, but the Court of Appeal found no substantiating medical data and no indication that officers should have viewed him as vulnerable or underage. It also found officers properly consulted a doctor after the suspected seizure. The Supreme Court dismissed his further appeal on 18 November 2014 with summary reasoning.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) that he had been denied legal assistance during police questioning. The Government submitted a unilateral declaration admitting a breach and offering compensation, seeking strike-out. The applicant opposed this because Dutch law allowed revision of a final conviction only after an ECtHR judgment finding a violation, not after a strike-out. The Court declined to strike out.

On the merits, the ECtHR focused on the 20 August 2009 interviews because statements from that day were used for his conviction. It found he had a right to be assisted by a lawyer during police interviews unless compelling reasons existed. No compelling reasons appeared; the only reason was the then-existing Dutch rule denying adult suspects legal assistance during police questioning. Such a general mandatory restriction is not compelling. The absence of compelling reasons weighed heavily, and the Government bore the burden of showing that overall fairness was not irretrievably prejudiced. The Government made no substantive argument. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c): denying the applicant his lawyer during the 20 August 2009 interviews rendered the proceedings as a whole unfair.

In *Van de Kolk v. the Netherlands* (ECtHR, Third Section, 28 May 2019, App. no. 23192/15), the applicant, a Dutch national born in 1990, complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) that he was denied a lawyer during police questioning. On 19 August 2009, aged nineteen, he was arrested on suspicion of distributing child pornography—three pictures of a sixteen-year-old girl—in April 2009. He was informed of his right to consult a lawyer. At the police station, before his lawyer was available, but with his consent, police began a social interview about his personal circumstances and personality, not the suspected offence. He disclosed a brain disorder (cavernous hemangiomas in his brain and spinal cord), which might affect his trust in others, and said he could not head a football. When his lawyer became available, the interview was suspended for a telephone consultation. Afterward, on his lawyer’s advice, he refused to answer further questions, and the interview ended. He met his lawyer later that day.

The next day, 20 August 2009, he was interviewed twice, including about the suspected distribution. At the start, he said he would prefer his lawyer to be present. He was told this was not possible, and questioning proceeded; he answered. During the interview, officers noticed a spasm-like arm movement and asked whether he was having an epileptic fit. He confirmed he was. The interview was interrupted and a doctor called. He said the seizure might have been caused by stress, and the interview resumed. A final interview took place on 21 August 2009; all interviews were audio-recorded. He was released from custody that day.

Domestically, the Regional Court convicted him in 2011, but found he should have been allowed to consult a lawyer before the first police interview; it considered the procedural defect sufficient because later interviews did not substantially differ. The Court of Appeal quashed and convicted him in 2013, sentencing him to forty hours’ community service. It rejected the claim that officers should have viewed him as vulnerable or underage, noting no medical evidence, and held that as an adult he was not entitled to a lawyer’s presence during police interviews under the then-applicable *Salduz* case-law. His conviction relied partly on his 20 August police statements about sending photographs, along with the victim’s complaint and statements, a third party’s statement, and a police record of images online. The Supreme Court dismissed his appeal in 2014 under summary reasoning.

At the relevant time, Dutch law did not grant adult suspects the right to have a lawyer present during police interviews. The ECtHR found no compelling reason to restrict the applicant’s right; the only basis was the general domestic rule. Because the Government failed to show that the overall fairness of the proceedings was not irretrievably prejudiced, the Court found a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c).

**Case: Van de Kolk v. the Netherlands (Application no. 23192/15), ECtHR, 28 May 2019**

The applicant, Hugo van de Kolk, a Dutch national, complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (c) of the Convention that he had been denied legal assistance during police questioning.

On 19 August 2009, the applicant, then 19 years old, was arrested on suspicion of distributing child pornography—specifically three photographs of a 16-year-old girl. He was informed of his right to consult a lawyer. At the police station he was taken into police custody. Before his lawyer was available, but with his consent, police conducted a “social interview” about his personal circumstances and personality, not about the suspected offence. He disclosed that he had a brain disorder—cavernous hemangiomas in his brain and spinal cord—which might affect his trust in others; he could play football but not head the ball. When his lawyer became available, the interview was suspended so he could consult by telephone. On his lawyer’s advice, he then refused to answer further questions, and the interview ended. He later met his lawyer.

On 20 August 2009, the applicant was interviewed twice, including about the suspected distribution of child pornography. At the start, he asked for his lawyer to be present. He was told this was not possible, and the interview proceeded; he answered questions. During the interview, officers noticed a spasm-like arm movement and asked whether he was having an epileptic fit. He confirmed he was. The interview was interrupted and a doctor was called; the applicant said the seizure could have been caused by stress and other factors. The interview then resumed. A final interview took place on 21 August 2009. All interviews were audio-recorded. He was released on 21 August 2009.

In domestic proceedings, the Regional Court of The Hague convicted him in 2011 of distribution of child pornography and imposed a suspended two-week prison sentence and 80 hours’ community service. It found he should have been allowed to consult a lawyer before the first interview, but considered that a finding of procedural defect sufficed because later interviews did not substantially differ. The Court of Appeal in 2013 quashed that judgment but convicted him again, imposing 40 hours’ community service. It rejected the complaint about lack of a lawyer during police interviews, holding that he was an adult, that claims about his mental age and brain disorder were unsubstantiated, and that the officers did not have to treat him as vulnerable or underage. It relied, among other evidence, on the victim’s statements, the applicant’s 20 August 2009 police statement that he had sent photographs, a third party’s statement, and a police record showing images online. The Supreme Court dismissed his further appeal in 2014 with summary reasoning.

Before the ECtHR, the Government submitted a unilateral declaration admitting a breach of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (c) and offered compensation. The applicant opposed strike-out because Dutch law permits revision of a final conviction only on the basis of an ECtHR judgment finding a violation, not a strike-out decision. The Court refused to strike the case out.

On the merits, the Court focused on the 20 August 2009 interviews because statements from that day were used to convict the applicant. It found that he was charged and in custody, so he had a right to a lawyer during police interviews unless there were compelling reasons. When he requested his lawyer’s presence, he was told it was impossible. The only reason was the absence at the time of a domestic right to legal assistance during police questioning for adult suspects. Such a general, mandatory restriction did not constitute a compelling reason. The absence of compelling reasons weighed heavily, and the Government had to show that overall fairness was not irretrievably prejudiced. It made no substantive argument. The Court therefore found that denying the applicant legal assistance during the 20 August 2009 police interviews rendered the proceedings as a whole unfair, violating Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (c).

001-208280:
**Gawlik v. Liechtenstein** (Application no. 23922/19, judgment 16 February 2021) concerned the dismissal without notice of Dr Lothar Gawlik, a German national and deputy chief physician at the Liechtenstein National Hospital, the only public hospital in Liechtenstein. His complaint alleged a violation of Article 10 (freedom of expression) after he was dismissed for reporting suspicions that the hospital’s chief physician, Dr H., had practised active euthanasia.

In September 2014, Gawlik examined electronic medical files and concluded that four patients had died after morphine administration and that Dr H. may have practised active euthanasia. He raised this suspicion with the President of the Parliamentary Control Committee and, on his advice, filed a criminal complaint against Dr H. with the Public Prosecutor’s Office. He later added six more suspected cases based on electronic records. He claimed he acted to protect patients and the hospital and in accordance with medical ethics.

The hospital had an internal Critical Incident Reporting System (CIRS), but it was unclear whether staff knew that Dr H. no longer handled such reports. Gawlik did not use it. The hospital commissioned an external palliative-care expert, who reviewed the paper files and heard Dr H. and concluded that no active euthanasia had occurred. The expert found the morphine treatment was justified for palliative purposes, though some prescriptions were imprecise. He stated that if Gawlik had consulted the complete paper files, which were accessible, he would have immediately realized his suspicions were unfounded. Gawlik was dismissed without notice in October 2014 for serious breach of trust, mainly for failing to verify his allegations and failing to use internal channels first.

Criminal proceedings against Dr H. were discontinued in December 2014. Proceedings against Gawlik for casting false suspicions were also discontinued in 2016. Domestic courts split: the Regional Court upheld the dismissal; the Court of Appeal found it unjustified; the Supreme Court reversed, holding that Gawlik’s failure to verify serious allegations before external disclosure destroyed trust. The Constitutional Court rejected Gawlik’s Article 10 complaint, applying the *Heinisch v. Germany* whistleblowing criteria. It accepted a public interest in hospital treatment and no personal motive, but found Gawlik acted irresponsibly by not checking the paper files before making grave, unfounded allegations.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the key issue was whether the dismissal was a justified interference with Article 10. The Court found an interference, prescribed by the Civil Code, pursuing the legitimate aim of protecting the reputation and rights of the hospital and Dr H. Applying whistleblowing factors—public interest, authenticity/verification, damage to the employer, whether external disclosure was a last resort, motive/good faith, and severity of sanction—the Court concluded that the domestic courts had struck a fair balance. Gawlik’s good-faith but unverified complaint did not outweigh the detriment to the employer hospital and the accused chief physician. There was therefore **no violation of Article 10**.

**Case: Gawlik v. Liechtenstein (Application no. 23922/19), European Court of Human Rights, Second Section, Judgment of 16 February 2021 (final 31 May 2021).**

The applicant, Lothar Gawlik, a German doctor, worked as deputy chief physician in the internal medicine department of the Liechtenstein National Hospital, a public-law foundation, under a private-law employment contract. His superior was Dr H., the chief physician.

In September 2014, the applicant examined electronic medical files and concluded that four patients had died after being administered morphine and that Dr H. had practised active euthanasia. He met the President of the Parliamentary Control Committee and, on his advice, filed a criminal complaint against Dr H. with the Public Prosecutor’s Office. He later added suspicions concerning six more patients. The police seized paper medical files and questioned Dr H.; the applicant was also questioned. The hospital had an internal reporting system, CIRS, but the applicant did not use it, fearing that Dr H. might still be responsible for receiving reports, and did not first consult the patients’ paper files.

Hospital-commissioned external experts and an expert appointed in the criminal investigation concluded that no active euthanasia had occurred. The patients had been in palliative situations, and morphine had been administered for pain or breathing difficulties. The experts found that if the applicant had read the paper files, which were accessible and contained complete information, he would have realised his suspicions were clearly unfounded. The criminal proceedings against Dr H. were discontinued in December 2014; proceedings against the applicant for making false suspicions were discontinued in 2016.

The hospital suspended the applicant and then dismissed him without notice on 17 October 2014, stating that trust had been irretrievably destroyed because he had failed to verify his serious allegations internally before raising them externally. The applicant sued for wrongful dismissal, claiming about CHF 600,000 in damages. The Regional Court dismissed his claim. The Court of Appeal reversed, finding the dismissal unjustified and holding that the external disclosure was protected by freedom of expression. The Supreme Court reversed again, holding that the applicant, a senior employee, had relied only on incomplete electronic files and failed to verify his serious allegations, amounting to a serious breach of trust. The Constitutional Court dismissed his complaint, accepting that Article 10 applied indirectly but finding no violation. It noted the public interest in proper hospital treatment and the absence of personal motives, but held that the applicant had acted irresponsibly by not checking the paper files before making grave, unfounded allegations.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that his dismissal violated Article 10 of the Convention. The Court found that the dismissal constituted an interference with his freedom of expression, was prescribed by law, and pursued the legitimate aims of protecting the reputation and rights of the hospital and Dr H. Applying its whistle-blowing case-law, notably Guja v. Moldova and Heinisch v. Germany, the Court examined the public interest in the information, its authenticity, the damage caused, whether external disclosure was a last resort, the applicant’s motives, and the severity of the sanction. It concluded that the domestic courts had struck a fair balance. Although the applicant acted in good faith, he had failed to verify his suspicions to the extent permitted by the circumstances. The public interest in unverified information did not outweigh the detriment to the employer hospital and the accused chief physician. There was therefore no violation of Article 10.

In *Gawlik v. Liechtenstein* (Application no. 23922/19, judgment 16 February 2021), the applicant, Lothar Gawlik, a German doctor, was deputy chief physician at the Liechtenstein National Hospital, the only public hospital in Liechtenstein. Employed from June 2013 under an indefinite contract with six months’ notice, he was directly supervised by Dr H., chief physician of internal medicine.

On 9 September 2014, while researching electronic medical files, the applicant found that four patients had died after morphine administration. He concluded that Dr H. had practised active euthanasia. The same day, he met the President of the Parliamentary Control Committee and voiced his suspicions. On 11 September 2014, on advice, he lodged a criminal complaint against Dr H. with the Public Prosecutor’s Office. Police seized paper medical files and questioned Dr H. On 19 September 2014, after further electronic-file research, the applicant reported suspicions concerning six additional patients, alleging morphine had been given without pain indication, deaths occurred shortly after treatment began, and treatment was labelled “supportive.” He stated his aim was to avert damage to patients.

The hospital had an anonymous Critical Incident Reporting System (CIRS), but the applicant did not use it. An internal hospital review of the paper files concluded that all patients had been in a palliative situation, that morphine treatment was justified, and that the applicant would have realised his suspicions were clearly unfounded had he consulted the complete paper files. All interviews were video-recorded but conducted without the solicitor physically present. Neither Doyle nor his solicitor requested the solicitor’s presence during questioning; it was later confirmed that, under police practice at the time, such a request would have been refused. Another solicitor arrived at 11:00 a.m. and represented him from then on.

He initially made no admissions. During interviews on 25–26 February, police told Doyle that his former girlfriend, G, the mother of his child, had been arrested and was being detained and questioned. They emphasised her hardship and separation from her daughter and the innocence of the victim.

In interview 14 he again asked to speak to his solicitor and complained that the earlier consultation had not been proper. The interview continued for a time. His solicitor later arrived and consulted him. According to a police memo, the solicitor told police, off the record, that Doyle would admit the murder if G were released. Police replied that they wanted the truth and that a confession obtained by inducement would not be accepted. After further consultations, the solicitor said Doyle would not admit before G’s release and left. **Case: Gražulevičiūtė v. Lithuania (Application no. 53176/17), ECtHR, 14 December 2021**

The applicant, Edita Gražulevičiūtė, was a Lithuanian rheumatologist and clinical researcher. In 2011 she took part in a clinical trial of tocilizumab. During the trial, a patient, V.S., died. After V.S.’s daughters complained, the State Medicines Control Agency (SMCA) inspected the trial. In December 2011, inspectors found two “critical (dangerous)” violations of the Good Clinical Practice Rules: failure to arrange an unscheduled appointment for V.S. and failure to report serious side effects. They also found other significant and minor violations. In January 2012, the SMCA suspended the applicant from two clinical trials and prohibited her from starting new trials; the suspension and the alleged critical violations were published on the SMCA website.

The applicant challenged the suspension. On 6 December 2013, the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court fully annulled the suspension orders. It found the inspectors’ conclusions incorrect. A forensic report in related criminal proceedings concluded that V.S. died from acute sepsis, not from the applicant’s actions. A colleague confirmed that the applicant had insisted V.S. go to hospital, and the applicant and the colleague had examined V.S., contrary to the inspection finding. The court also found no failure to report serious side effects: ankle pain was not a serious side effect, and the sponsor was informed once septic arthritis was suspected. The decision became final on 21 December 2013.

The applicant then claimed damages from the State for unlawful suspension. In November 2015, the first-instance administrative court partly allowed her claim, relying on the final 2013 decision under domestic res judicata rules. It awarded EUR 6,128 in pecuniary damage and EUR 200 in non-pecuniary damage. On the SMCA’s appeal, however, the Supreme Administrative Court on 30 January 2017 reversed and dismissed the claim. It held that annulment of an administrative decision did not automatically establish State liability under Article 6.271 § 4 of the Civil Code. A broader tortious-liability assessment was required. The Supreme Administrative Court re-examined the same circumstances, concluded that the SMCA had acted within its competence and for lawful protective aims—protecting trial participants and ensuring data reliability—and found that data supported at least the first critical violation. It therefore held that the suspension order had not been unlawful ab initio.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 that the Supreme Administrative Court had failed to respect the res judicata effect of the final 2013 decision. She also complained under Article 8 about lack of compensation and reputational harm, and under Article 13 about an effective remedy.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 6 § 1. It held that, although domestic law permitted certain verification in damages proceedings, the Supreme Administrative Court had reassessed the very factual circumstances already conclusively determined between essentially the same parties in the 2013 proceedings, without reopening those earlier proceedings. By doing so, it rendered the first final decision largely devoid of legal effect. This breached the principle of res judicata and the applicant’s right to a fair hearing. The Court found no separate issue under Article 8 and did not need to examine Article 13 separately.

Lithuania*, the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Lithuanian courts violated Article 6 § 1 of the Convention by failing to respect the res judicata effect of a final administrative judgment. The applicant was a rheumatologist and clinical researcher. In 2011, a patient, V.S., died during a clinical trial of tocilizumab. After V.S.’s daughters complained to the State Medicines Control Agency (SMCA), an inspection found two “critical (dangerous)” violations of the Good Clinical Practice Rules: failure to arrange an unscheduled appointment and failure to report serious side-effects. On that basis, the SMCA suspended the applicant from two clinical trials, prohibited her from starting new trials, and published information about the suspension.

The applicant challenged the suspension. On 6 December 2013, the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court fully allowed her claim and annulled the suspension orders. It found the inspectors’ critical conclusions unfounded: the applicant had advised V.S. to go to hospital, had examined V.S. together with another doctor, and had not failed to report serious side-effects. The court held that the restrictions had been imposed unjustly. That decision was not appealed and became final on 21 December 2013.

The applicant then sought damages from the State, represented by the SMCA. On 4 November 2015, the first-instance administrative court partly granted her claim, relying on the final 2013 judgment. Under Lithuanian law, facts established by an effective court decision did not need to be proved again in later proceedings between the same parties. The court awarded EUR 6,128 for lost income concerning the first clinical trial and EUR 200 in non-pecuniary damages, finding that the suspension had caused her damage. It dismissed her claim concerning the second trial.

On the SMCA’s appeal, the Supreme Administrative Court, by ruling of 30 January 2017, allowed the appeal, rejected the damages claim, and dismissed the applicant’s appeal. It held that annulment of an administrative decision did not by itself mean that the State institution had acted unlawfully under Article 6.271 of the Civil Code. In its view, damages proceedings required a “broader legal assessment” of the same circumstances. It re-examined the two critical violations, found that the SMCA had acted within its competence and in accordance with law to protect clinical trial participants and data reliability, and concluded that the suspension order had not been unlawful ab initio. Thus, no State liability arose.

The applicant complained to the ECtHR that the Supreme Administrative Court had reassessed the same factual circumstances already decided in the final 2013 judgment and had effectively overturned her exculpation without reopening the first set of proceedings. She alleged a breach of the principle of res judicata and Article 6 § 1. She also complained under Article 8 that she had not been compensated for reputational and private-life harm caused by the suspension and publication of the SMCA order.

By reassessing the same facts and reaching opposite conclusions in the damages proceedings, without reopening the earlier proceedings, it rendered the first final judgment largely devoid of legal effect. The key facts for the violation were therefore the final 2013 annulment, the later damages claim, and the Supreme Administrative Court’s fresh assessment of the same critical violations to deny compensation.

**Summary of *Gražulevičiūtė v. Lithuania* (Application no. 53176/17)**

The applicant, Ms. Edita Gražulevičiūtė, is a Lithuanian rheumatologist and clinical researcher. The case concerns her suspension from clinical trials in 2012 following the death of a patient and the subsequent conflict between two final domestic court decisions.

In 2011, the applicant was a researcher in a clinical trial for the drug tocilizumab. A patient, V.S., in the trial died on 14 April 2011. Following a complaint by the patient's daughters, the State Medicines Control Agency (SMCA) conducted an inspection, which identified two "critical" violations of Good Clinical Practice Rules attributed to the applicant: failure to arrange an unscheduled appointment for the patient and failure to report serious side-effects. Based on these findings, the SMCA suspended the applicant from two clinical trials in January 2012.

The applicant challenged her suspension in administrative court. In a decision of 6 December 2013, the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court annulled the suspension orders. Critically, this court found that the inspectors' conclusions were incorrect and contradicted the factual circumstances. It relied on a forensic report showing the patient died of sepsis unrelated to the trial, and found that the applicant had not committed the alleged violations. This decision was not appealed and became final on 21 December 2013, thus acquiring the force of *res judicata*.

The applicant then filed a separate civil claim for damages against the State, arguing that her unlawful suspension had caused pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. A first-instance court initially awarded her damages, relying on the binding findings of the 2013 final decision. However, on appeal, the Supreme Administrative Court reversed this ruling on 30 January 2017. It held that the annulment of the suspension order did not automatically mean the SMCA's actions were unlawful for the purpose of State liability.

Crucially, the Supreme Administrative Court conducted a new assessment of the same facts. It re-evaluated the circumstances of the patient's death and the alleged violations, concluding this time that the SMCA had acted lawfully and within its competence to protect patient safety. It found the applicant had an "increased duty of care" and that the inspectors' conclusions provided a sufficient factual basis for the suspension order, regardless of the order's subsequent annulment. By reassessing the core facts without reopening the first set of proceedings, the Supreme Administrative Court effectively rendered the final 2013 judgment devoid of its legal effect.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair hearing) and Article 8 (right to private life). The Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1, holding that the Supreme Administrative Court's failure to respect the *res judicata* effect of the final 2013 decision was a fundamental breach of the principle of legal certainty. By re-examining the same factual circumstances and reaching a contradictory conclusion, the later court undermined the finality of the earlier, binding judgment.

He was represented by Mr O. Eterović, a lawyer practising in Sarajevo. The Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina were given notice of the application.

The judgment’s factual section is brief. It states that the applicant’s details and information relevant to the application are set out in an appended table, which is not reproduced in the full text provided. The central fact, however, is that a domestic decision had been given in the applicant’s favour and was not enforced. The Court treated that decision as one ordering specific action to be taken. The applicant complained that this non-enforcement breached his rights.

Article 6 § 1 guarantees a fair hearing in the determination of civil rights and obligations. Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

The Court reiterated its established case-law that the execution of a judgment given by any court must be regarded as an integral part of a “hearing” for the purposes of Article 6. It referred to *Hornsby v. Greece*, which confirms that the right to a court includes the right to enforcement of final judgments. It also referred to its prior cases concerning non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of final domestic judgments, particularly *Spahić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* and *Kunić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina*, where it had already found violations in respect of similar issues.

As regards Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, the Court noted that the domestic decision in the present case ordered specific action. It therefore considered that the decision constituted “possessions” within the meaning of that provision. This meant that the failure to enforce it engaged the applicant’s right to peaceful enjoyment of his possessions.

Having examined all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on the admissibility and merits of these complaints. It concluded that the authorities had not deployed all necessary efforts to enforce fully and in due time the decision in the applicant’s favour. The key alleged violations were therefore the non-enforcement of a final domestic decision, contrary to Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court’s reasoning followed its established case-law concerning Bosnia and Herzegovina, where systemic failures to enforce domestic decisions had previously led to findings of violations.
