He relied, expressly or in substance, on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees a fair hearing in the determination of civil rights and obligations, and on Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, which protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. The domestic decision at issue ordered specific action to be taken. The applicant alleged that the authorities failed to enforce that final decision, thereby depriving him of the benefit of the judgment and interfering with his property rights.

In its legal assessment, the Court reiterated that execution of a judgment given by any court must be regarded as an integral part of a “hearing” for the purposes of Article 6. It referred to its well-established case-law, notably *Hornsby v. Greece*, concerning non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of final domestic judgments. The Court also noted that similar issues had already been examined in the leading cases of *Spahić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* and *Kunić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina*, both decided on 14 November 2017, in which violations were found. Those cases concerned comparable failures by Bosnia and Herzegovina to enforce final domestic decisions.

The Court further observed that the decision in the present application ordered specific action to be taken. Consequently, it considered that the decision constituted “possessions” within the meaning of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. This was significant because the applicant’s complaint was not merely that he had been denied a court victory, but that a final enforceable decision had not been translated into actual relief. Having examined all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on admissibility or merits. Applying its existing case-law, it concluded that the domestic authorities had not deployed all necessary efforts to enforce fully and in due time the decision in the applicant’s favour.

Accordingly, the Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The case is a committee judgment of the Fourth Section, composed of Judges Armen Harutyunyan, Jolien Schukking and Ana Maria Guerra Martins, with Liv Tigerstedt as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The Court deliberated in private on 21 January 2021 and adopted the judgment on that date; it was delivered on 11 February 2021 and is final, though subject to editorial revision. The key violation was therefore the failure of the Bosnia and Herzegovina authorities to ensure full and timely execution of a final domestic decision in the applicant’s favour, which breached both his right to a fair hearing and his right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

The European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section, Committee) delivered judgment in *Efendić v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Application no. 37130/19) on 11 February 2021. The applicant lodged the application under Article 34 of the Convention on 28 June 2019 and was represented by Mr O. Eterović, a lawyer practising in Sarajevo. The Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina were given notice. The judgment’s statement of facts is brief: the applicant’s details and information relevant to the application are set out in an appended table, which is not included in the supplied text. The essential factual allegation is therefore that a domestic decision was given in the applicant’s favour but was not enforced by the respondent State.

The applicant complained of the non-enforcement of that domestic decision. He relied, expressly or in substance, on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Article 6 § 1 guarantees a fair hearing in the determination of civil rights and obligations. Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions and prohibits deprivation except in the public interest and subject to law. The applicant’s complaint was that the final domestic decision in his favour remained unexecuted, thereby denying him the benefit of the judicial determination and interfering with his property rights.

The Court reiterated established case-law that execution of a judgment given by any court must be regarded as an integral part of a “hearing” for Article 6 purposes. It referred to *Hornsby v. Greece*, where the Court held that the right to a court would be illusory if a final judicial decision remained unenforced. It also referred to its case-law on non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of final domestic judgments. The Court noted two leading cases against Bosnia and Herzegovina—*Spahić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* and *Kunić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina*—in which it had already found violations concerning similar issues.

A significant point was that the domestic decision in the present application ordered specific action to be taken. Because it imposed a specific obligation and was final, the Court considered that the decision constituted “possessions” within the meaning of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. This brought the non-enforcement within the protection of property as well as the fair-hearing guarantee.

Having examined all material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on admissibility and merits. Applying its case-law, it concluded that the authorities did not deploy all necessary efforts to enforce fully and in due time the decision in the applicant’s favour. The failure to enforce a final domestic decision therefore amounted to a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In essence, the key facts relevant to the alleged violations are: a final domestic decision existed in the applicant’s favour; it ordered specific action; the State authorities failed to enforce it fully or promptly; and that failure deprived the applicant of the practical benefit of the decision and of possessions protected under Protocol No. 1. The Court treated the case as another instance of the repetitive problem of non-enforcement of domestic judgments in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The excerpt does not provide further details such as the exact domestic decision, the authority responsible, the length of delay, or the just satisfaction award.
001-213406:
M.F. v. Norway (Application no. 5947/19, ECtHR, 25 November 2021) concerned an Article 8 complaint by a Norwegian mother about the public care order for her daughter X and her restricted contact rights. The applicant already had two older children, Y and Z. From 2013, child welfare services had been involved due to concerns about the children’s hygiene, school lateness and absence, and the applicant’s care capacity. Various assistance measures were implemented. In 2016 the applicant moved in with B, who had a criminal record and substance-abuse issues. Police stopped a car driven by B, suspected of drug driving, and found illegal drugs; their apartment was described as chaotic and unhygienic. The applicant was pregnant at the time. X was born in December 2016. After the birth, child welfare services and a hospital midwife raised concerns about the applicant’s hygiene, lack of routines, indifference to X’s needs, and B’s drug use. Reviews and home visits followed. The relationship with B ended in spring 2017.

In May 2017, child welfare services applied for a care order for X, envisaging long-term foster placement and possible later adoption, with limited contact to ensure X’s security and attachment. The County Social Welfare Board held a hearing and in December 2017 found serious shortcomings in the applicant’s care. It found she failed to see X’s needs, that her older children had suffered “gross educational neglect,” that she blamed others for care failures, and that further assistance measures would not improve her care skills. Contact was set at two hours, three times per year, under supervision.

On District Court review, a court-appointed psychologist reported. In February 2018 the District Court upheld the care order. It found the applicant had a damaged ability to form relationships and impaired “mentalising,” affecting her emotional care. It relied on prior assessments concerning Y and Z, expert views that she could not read children’s signals and could “mentally disappear,” and evidence that X showed lack of attachment and emotional neglect—turning away, poor eye contact, inadequate feeding, sleep and diaper routines, and prolonged chair sitting. The expert found X well-functioning in foster care but vulnerable; she recognised the applicant but showed stronger attachment to the foster parents. The court concluded treatment would take years, X could not wait, and X’s best interests favoured the care order. Contact remained limited because X was in a critical attachment phase and placement was likely to last her whole childhood. The High Court refused leave to appeal in May 2018, and the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal in July 2018.

After lodging the ECtHR application, the applicant sought to lift the care order. The Board refused in January 2020, but in June 2020 the District Court lifted it, and X returned to the applicant in July 2020. The County Governor also identified several shortcomings in child welfare’s handling of the case.

The applicant alleged that the care-order proceedings violated her right to respect for family life under Article 8. The Court declared the complaint admissible, finding it not manifestly ill-founded. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are the care order, evidence of parenting deficiencies and emotional neglect, the very limited contact rights, and the subsequent lifting of the order.

**M.F. v. Norway (Application no. 5947/19)** concerns an Article 8 complaint by a Norwegian mother, M.F., about the foster-care placement of her daughter, X, and the restrictions on her contact rights.

The applicant had two older children, Y and Z, with an ex-partner, C, and later X (born December 2016) and a son (born December 2017) with an ex-partner, B. Child welfare services had been involved since March 2013, when they reviewed her care of Y and Z due to concerns about poor hygiene and school attendance. Assistance measures were implemented, but concerns about school absence persisted after she moved municipalities in 2016.

In October 2016, police stopped a car driven by B and suspected him of driving under the influence; drugs were found in their apartment, which police described as chaotic and unhygienic. The applicant was pregnant. In November 2016, child welfare services raised concerns about the unborn child, citing earlier measures and B’s criminal record and substance abuse. After X’s birth in December 2016, they began a care-skills review. A midwife reported that B lacked interest in X and the applicant, and that the applicant showed inadequate hygiene, indifference to X’s needs, and a careless attitude toward B. Further visits and concerns about B’s drug use led to more assistance measures.

The relationship with B ended in early 2017. The applicant and the children moved to her mother’s home, where child welfare services continued visits and measures. On 29 May 2017, the child welfare services applied for a care order for X, intending a long-term placement and possible adoption. They argued contact should be limited to help X attach to foster parents.

In September 2017, the County Social Welfare Board held a hearing and, in December 2017, found serious care shortcomings. It concluded that the applicant failed to see X’s needs, had caused “gross educational neglect” to Y and Z, blamed others, and lacked boundaries. It found her caregiving problems were linked to her personality and that further assistance would not improve her skills. It set contact at two hours, three times per year, under supervision.

The applicant challenged the decision in the District Court. A court-appointed psychologist reported in January 2018, and the District Court held a hearing in February 2018. It upheld the care order, finding X had suffered emotional neglect. It relied on the applicant’s mental health, damaged ability to form relations, and impaired capacity to “mentalise” X’s needs. Evidence from prior proceedings concerning Y and Z included expert findings that she could not read her children’s signals and could “mentally disappear” from the relationship. Child welfare reports noted X turned away and lacked eye contact as an infant, and that the applicant failed to establish feeding, sleep, and hygiene routines. The expert found X well-functioning in foster care but vulnerable due to early instability, and more attached to foster parents than to the applicant. The District Court concluded assistance measures could not create adequate care in the near future because treatment would take years. It maintained the care order and restricted contact, citing X’s critical attachment phase and the likelihood of placement throughout her childhood.

The High Court refused leave to appeal in May 2018, and the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal in July 2018. A County Governor review later identified shortcomings in the child welfare services’ handling. After lodging the application, the applicant successfully applied to lift the care order; X was returned to her in July 2020. The Court declared her Article 8 complaint admissible.

**M.F. v. Norway** (Application no. 5947/19, ECtHR Fifth Section, 25 November 2021) concerned a Norwegian mother’s complaint under Article 8 of the Convention that the child welfare proceedings relating to her daughter, X, and the resulting care order and contact restrictions violated her right to respect for family life.

The applicant had four children. Her older children, Y and Z, were from a previous relationship. Child welfare services had been involved with the family since 2013 because of concerns about the children’s hygiene and school attendance. Assistance measures were repeatedly offered to improve the applicant’s care skills. In 2016 the applicant lived with her then partner, B, and became pregnant with X, born in December 2016. Concerns about the unborn child were raised because of B’s criminal record and substance abuse, and because of the prior child welfare measures.

After X’s birth, a midwife reported that B lacked interest in X and the applicant, and that the applicant showed inadequate hygiene and indifference to the newborn’s needs. Child welfare services visited the home and received further reports that B used illegal drugs. In October 2016, police had stopped a car driven by B, suspected B of driving under the influence, and found illegal drugs in the family’s apartment, which police described as chaotic and unhygienic. The relationship between the applicant and B ended in early 2017, after which the applicant and children moved in with her mother. Child welfare services continued visits and support measures.

In May 2017, the child welfare services applied for a care order for X, envisaging placement until adulthood and possible adoption, with limited contact to ensure X’s security and attachment to foster parents. The County Social Welfare Board heard the case in September 2017 and ordered public care in December 2017. It found serious shortcomings in the applicant’s care, including failure to see X’s needs, “gross educational neglect” of Y and Z due to school absence, blaming others, and failure to set boundaries. It concluded that further assistance measures would not improve her care skills. Contact was set at two hours, three times per year, under supervision.

On judicial review, the District Court upheld the care order in February 2018. It emphasised the child’s best interests and found the applicant’s ability to form relations damaged, affecting her emotional care. Experts referred to her difficulty reading children’s signals, possible emotional withdrawal, and serious neglect of her older children. As to X, reports described lack of emotional attachment, poor eye contact, turning away from the applicant, lack of routines for feeding and sleep, missed diaper changes, and excessive time in chairs. A court-appointed expert found X well-functioning in foster care but vulnerable due to early instability, and more attached to foster parents. Treatment for the applicant would likely take years, and X could not wait. Contact remained limited because X was in a critical attachment phase and placement was likely long-term. The High Court refused leave to appeal in May 2018, and the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal in July 2018.

Later, the County Governor identified shortcomings in the child welfare services’ handling. In 2019 the applicant sought to lift the care order; the Board refused in January 2020, but the District Court lifted it in June 2020, and X returned to the applicant in July 2020. The ECtHR declared the Article 8 complaint admissible.

In E.H. v. Norway, the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Norway violated a father’s Article 8 right to respect for family life by withdrawing his parental responsibilities for his son, X, and authorising X’s adoption by his foster parents.

X was born in June 2015. His mother, B, and the applicant father were no longer in a relationship. During pregnancy and after birth, midwives and clinic staff raised serious concerns about both parents’ caregiving abilities. X was placed in emergency foster care shortly after birth and, in October 2015, the County Social Welfare Board issued a care order. The Board found B had mild mental retardation and an expressive language disorder, low functioning, and lacked basic caregiving capacity; assistance measures could not sufficiently protect X. The applicant had cognitive limitations and difficulty interacting with X, including low frustration tolerance, but accepted the care order and was considered more able than B to benefit from guidance. Contact was limited and supervised. An expert later found X had epilepsy, severe eczema, and significant far-sightedness, requiring extraordinary care. X remained with foster parents from about three weeks old, formed a strong attachment to them, and had no attachment to his biological parents. The parents agreed reunification was unrealistic and would likely seriously harm X; the foster parents were considered fit.

In November 2017 the child welfare services sought withdrawal of both parents’ parental responsibilities and adoption by the foster parents. The Board granted this in January 2018, finding adoption in X’s best interests because of his lack of attachment to his natural parents, strong foster-home attachment, vulnerabilities, need for stability, difficult contact sessions, and the risk of future proceedings and uncertainty if long-term foster care continued. The parents agreed all adoption conditions except whether adoption was in X’s best interests. The City Court upheld the decision in July 2018. It declined to appoint a further expert, relying instead on general research and the concrete case, and found adoption would give X the safety he needed. A lay judge dissented, warning that reliance on general research could make adoption automatic for children placed early. The High Court refused leave to appeal, and the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained under Article 8 that removing his parental responsibilities and authorising adoption violated his family life. He accepted that X would grow up in foster care, but argued adoption was not in X’s best interests and should not have been ordered without an updated expert assessment. He contended that the domestic courts had relied on general research rather than an individual assessment. The Government argued the measure was necessary in a democratic society: the applicant did not seek X’s return or increased contact, agreed to continued foster care and to all adoption conditions except best interests, and the domestic courts had a sufficient basis to conclude adoption was in X’s best interests. The Court declared the application admissible and ultimately found no violation of Article 8, holding that the domestic authorities had acted within their margin of appreciation and that adoption was justified by X’s best interests.

E.H. v. Norway is a European Court of Human Rights case concerning a Norwegian father’s complaint under Article 8 of the Convention that the withdrawal of his parental responsibilities for his son, X, and the authorisation of X’s adoption by his foster parents violated his right to respect for family life.

X was born in June 2015. His parents were no longer in a relationship at the time of his birth. During the mother’s pregnancy, a midwife notified child welfare services of concerns about both parents’ caregiving abilities. After X’s birth, further serious concerns were raised. In June 2015, when X was about three weeks old, an emergency placement decision was made and X was placed in an emergency foster home. A care order was later issued in October 2015. The applicant, X’s father, did not oppose the care order but sought more extensive contact rights.

A psychologist’s expert report in March 2016 found that X had extraordinary care needs, including epilepsy, severe atopic eczema and significant far-sightedness. He needed regular specialist health care and a stable, capable care environment. The report concluded that the mother could not meet X’s ordinary or special needs and that X would be at risk of emotional and physical neglect if he stayed with her. As to the applicant, the report found clear cognitive limitations, difficulties with reflection and “mentalising”, a weak ability to interact with X, and low tolerance for stress and frustration, sometimes causing him to become loud and hot-tempered towards X. However, he was positive towards the child, more able than the mother to use help and guidance, and had potential for improvement. The expert recommended that X remain in foster care but maintain knowledge of his biological parents, with contact limited to three two-hour supervised sessions per parent yearly.

In November 2017, when X was two and a half years old and had lived with his foster parents since shortly after birth, the child welfare services applied to withdraw both parents’ parental responsibilities and authorise X’s adoption by his foster parents. The parents opposed the application. In January 2018, the County Social Welfare Board granted the adoption. It found that reunification with the biological parents was unrealistic and that X had no attachment to his natural parents, was closely attached to his foster parents, and needed stability. Contact sessions had been challenging for him, and adoption would eliminate uncertainty and the risk of future proceedings. The Board considered that the biological parents’ interests had to yield.

The applicant and mother appealed to the City Court. They argued that an updated expert assessment should be obtained, but did not formally request one. The City Court upheld the adoption in July 2018. It noted that the parties agreed the parents would be permanently unable to provide proper care and that the foster parents were fit to raise X. The court found X exceptionally vulnerable and in need of a stable care situation. Although adoption was a far-reaching measure, X would otherwise remain in foster care throughout childhood, had close ties to his foster parents, and relocation could cause serious problems. The court relied on general research and knowledge rather than a new expert assessment. One lay judge dissented, arguing that general research was insufficient to justify adoption. The High Court refused leave to appeal, and the Supreme Court dismissed further appeals.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant accepted that X would grow up in foster care but argued that adoption was not in X’s best interests and should not have been ordered without an updated expert assessment. The Government maintained that the adoption decision was necessary in a democratic society and that the domestic courts had sufficient basis for finding adoption to be in X’s best interests. The Court declared the application admissible and examined whether the interference with the applicant’s Article 8 rights was justified.
001-211777:
In *Sanchez v. France* (Application no. 45581/15), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether the criminal conviction of Julien Sanchez, a French local councillor and Front National candidate in the 2011 parliamentary elections in Nîmes, violated his right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention.

Sanchez personally managed a publicly accessible Facebook wall, which was open to comments from approved “friends” (1,829 at the relevant time). On 24 October 2011 he published a political post about an opponent, F.P. Third parties then posted comments on his wall that associated Muslims with drug dealing, prostitution, crime, insecurity and the alleged “Islamisation” of Nîmes. One comment included “kisses to Leila,” referring to F.P.’s partner, L.T., whose North African-sounding forename was said to associate her with the racist message.

L.T. discovered the comments on 25 October 2011, felt personally insulted, and filed a criminal complaint. S.B., one of the commenters, deleted his own comment after L.T. confronted him, but L.R.’s comments remained visible until at least 6 December 2011. On 27 October Sanchez posted a general warning asking users to be careful about their comments, but he did not delete the existing offending posts. He later restricted public access to his Facebook page.

Sanchez, S.B. and L.R. were prosecuted for incitement to hatred or violence on grounds of religion. All were convicted. Sanchez was fined EUR 4,000, reduced to EUR 3,000 on appeal, and ordered to pay damages and costs. The domestic courts found that the comments specifically targeted Muslims and were likely, by their meaning and scope, to arouse rejection, hostility, hatred or violence. The reference to L.T. was also capable of associating her with the alleged transformation of Nîmes and arousing hatred against her.

As regards Sanchez, the courts applied French law under which the “producer” or administrator of a public online communication service may be criminally liable for third-party messages only if aware of them before posting or if, upon becoming aware, he fails to act promptly to delete them. They found Sanchez had knowingly made his wall public, controlled who could post, consulted it daily, and, as a political figure, should have been especially vigilant. He did not promptly delete the comments, and L.R.’s remained for weeks. The Court of Cassation upheld the conviction, holding that the remarks fell within the restrictions permitted by Article 10.

Before the ECtHR, Sanchez argued that his conviction for comments written by others violated his freedom of expression. He claimed he had not authored the remarks, could not monitor all comments, had not been promptly aware, and that the comments were political speech on immigration and insecurity, not a personal attack on L.T. He also argued that criminal liability for third-party content would chill political expression.

The Court considered that the interference was prescribed by law, pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the rights of others, and was necessary in a democratic society. It found the domestic courts’ reasons relevant and sufficient: the comments amounted to hate speech or incitement against Muslims and L.T.; Sanchez had a separate responsibility as the Facebook account holder; the authors themselves were also convicted; and he failed to delete promptly despite controlling the page. His status as a public figure and election candidate increased his duty of care. The fine and damages were not disproportionate. The Chamber therefore found no violation of Article 10. The case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 15 May 2023.

**Case of Sanchez v. France (Application no. 45581/15)** concerned an alleged violation of Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights (freedom of expression). The applicant, Julien Sanchez, was a French local councillor, mayor of Beaucaire, Front National regional councillor, and FN candidate in the 2012 parliamentary elections in Nîmes. He personally managed a publicly accessible Facebook account.

On 24 October 2011 Sanchez posted a political message criticising an opponent, F.P., a UMP MEP and deputy mayor of Nîmes. Third parties then posted comments on the public “wall” of Sanchez’s Facebook page. S.B. wrote that Nîmes had become “Algiers,” referring to kebab shops, mosques, drug dealers, prostitutes, and sharia, and ended with “Thanks [F.] and kisses to Leila ([L.])”—a reference to F.P.’s partner, L.T., whose forename sounded North African. L.R. added three comments associating Muslims with crime, drug trafficking, insecurity, veiled women, and the alleged decline of Nîmes.

L.T. saw the comments, felt personally insulted, and complained. S.B. deleted his comment after L.T. confronted him, but L.R.’s comments remained. On 26 October 2011 L.T. lodged a criminal complaint against Sanchez, S.B., and L.R. for incitement to hatred or violence. On 27 October Sanchez posted a general warning asking users to be careful about their comments, but he did not delete the existing comments. L.R.’s comments were still visible to investigators on 6 December 2011. Sanchez later restricted his Facebook wall to friends only. He claimed he could not monitor all comments, had more than 1,800 friends, had not written the offending comments, and did not know L.T.’s forename.

French courts convicted all three individuals. The Nîmes Criminal Court, on 28 February 2013, found that the comments targeted Muslims and L.T. and were likely to arouse rejection or hostility, linking L.T. to her partner and to the alleged Islamisation and insecurity of Nîmes. Sanchez was convicted as principal under section 93-3 of the Law of 29 July 1982 and sections 23 and 24 of the Law of 29 July 1881. He was fined €4,000, reduced to €3,000 on appeal, and ordered to pay L.T. €1,000. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 18 October 2013, finding that as a public political figure Sanchez knowingly made his wall public, was responsible for its content, consulted it daily, was alerted to the issue, and failed to act promptly. The Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal on 17 March 2015, holding that the offence was established and that Article 10 did not protect the comments.

The key issue before the European Court of Human Rights was whether criminally punishing Sanchez for failing to promptly delete third-party hate-speech comments on his public Facebook page violated his freedom of expression. The Court considered his public figure status, his control over the Facebook page, the public nature of the wall, his awareness or constructive awareness of the comments, the delay in deletion, and the hateful content targeting Muslims and L.T. The Chamber found no violation of Article 10, concluding that the interference was prescribed by law, pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the rights of others, and was based on relevant and sufficient reasons. The fine was proportionate. The case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 15 May 2023.

**Sanchez v. France** (Application no. 45581/15) concerns the criminal conviction of a French local councillor for failing to promptly delete third-party comments constituting incitement to hatred, in violation of Article 10 (freedom of expression) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant, Julien Sanchez, was at the material time a local councillor, mayor of Beaucaire, and a Front National candidate for the French parliamentary elections in Nîmes. He maintained a publicly accessible Facebook account with approximately 1,829 "friends" who could post comments on his "wall."

On 24 October 2011, Sanchez published a post criticizing a political opponent, F.P., a Member of the European Parliament and first deputy mayor of Nîmes. In response, third parties posted comments on his wall. One comment by S.B. stated that F.P. had "turned Nîmes into Algiers," referencing kebab shops, mosques, drug dealers, prostitutes, and sharia, and concluded with "Thanks [F.] and kisses to Leila ([L.])"—a reference to F.P.'s partner, L.T., whose forename sounded North African. Another user, L.R., posted three comments associating Muslims with drug trafficking, insecurity, veiled women, and crime in Nîmes.

On 25 October 2011, L.T. discovered the comments, felt personally insulted, and confronted S.B. at his hairdressing salon. S.B., unaware the page was public, deleted his comment. L.T. lodged a criminal complaint on 26 October 2011 against Sanchez, S.B., and L.R. On 27 October 2011, Sanchez posted a message urging users to be careful with their comments but did not delete the existing comments. L.R.'s comments remained visible as of 6 December 2011, when investigators examined the page.

Sanchez was interviewed on 28 January 2012. He stated he had not written the comments, had not had time to monitor the large volume of comments, had not been aware of L.R.'s comments until summoned, and had removed public access to his wall shortly before the interview. He argued the comments fell within freedom of expression.

The Nîmes Criminal Court convicted Sanchez, S.B., and L.R. on 28 February 2013, fining each €4,000. Sanchez was convicted as principal under section 93-3 of the Law of 29 July 1982, which imposes liability on the "producer" of an online public communication service who fails to act promptly to delete offending messages upon becoming aware of them. The court found the comments specifically targeted Muslims and were likely to arouse rejection or hostility, and that Sanchez, having voluntarily created a public forum, was responsible for monitoring it. The Nîmes Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 18 October 2013, reducing the fine to €3,000, finding Sanchez had knowingly made his wall public, consulted it daily, and deliberately left the comments. The Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal on 17 March 2015, holding the comments fell within the restrictions of Article 10 § 2.

Sanchez complained that his conviction violated his right to freedom of expression under Article 10. The key issue was whether his separate liability as a Facebook account holder for third-party comments—when the comment authors were also convicted—constituted a proportionate interference with his freedom of expression.

Case Cauchi v. Malta (Application no. 14013/19, judgment 25 March 2021) concerned whether Maltese rent-control legislation imposed a disproportionate burden on a landlord and whether the available domestic remedies were effective.

The applicant, Catherine Cauchi, owned a property in Ħal Għaxaq. In 1967 she leased it under a temporary emphyteusis for seventeen years at 25 Maltese liras (about €58) per year. Through a sub-emphyteusis, a couple, A., came to occupy the property as their sole ordinary residence and carried out substantial refurbishment. When the emphyteusis ended in 1984, the tenants relied on Act XXIII of 1979, amending the Housing (Decontrol) Ordinance, to retain possession as tenants. The law capped rent increases by reference to inflation but not above double the previous rent. From 1999 the rent should have risen to about €116 yearly, but the tenants continued paying MTL 50 because the applicant did not seek an increase. From 2010, following Act X of 2009, they paid €185 yearly; later €197.31, and from 2017 €200 yearly. The tenants owned no other property; Mr A. had a low wage, periods of unemployment, and later a pension of €515 monthly.

In 2017 the applicant brought constitutional redress proceedings. She alleged that the Ordinance, as amended, imposed a unilateral lease relationship for an indefinite period without enabling her to obtain fair and adequate rent, contrary to Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Government’s expert valued the refurbished property at €174,000 in 2017 and estimated rental value at €398.75 monthly (€4,785 yearly). The court-appointed expert valued it at €165,000, with annual rental values estimated at €701 in 1984, €1,828 in 1999, €3,463 in 2009, and €5,775 in 2017.

It awarded €20,000 compensation and declared that the tenants could no longer rely on the relevant law to retain title. It found that the lease had not been entered into voluntarily but imposed by law; that the difference between market rental value and the rent received remained “enormous if not shocking”; and that the law lacked procedural safeguards. The court refused to order eviction but barred the tenants from relying on Article 12(2)(b)(i) of the Ordinance in future eviction proceedings. Compensation reflected the lengthy disproportionality, uncertainty as to recovery of the property, the applicant’s delay in instituting proceedings until 2017, and the State’s inertia. The applicant did not appeal, asserting that the Constitutional Court was not an effective remedy because it systematically reduced awards.

After the judgment, Act No. XXVII of 2018 prevented eviction despite a favourable court judgment unless the owner first used a new procedure. In 2019 the applicant applied to the Rent Regulation Board under Article 12B seeking a rent increase; proceedings remained pending in May 2020. If the tenant failed the means test, the tenant received five years to vacate and the owner received double the old rent; if the tenant passed, the Board set rent considering the tenant’s means and age and any disproportionate burden on the landlord. Article 12B(11) specifically applied where a prior lease had lapsed due to a proportionality judgment but the tenant still occupied, barring eviction without using the new procedure.

It also found a violation of Article 13 because the aggregate remedies were ineffective in the applicant’s case.

In **Cauchi v. Malta**, the applicant, Catherine Cauchi, a Maltese national born in 1941, owned a property at 19 Dar il-Bebbux Street, Ħal Għaxaq. Couple A. continued paying MTL 50 per year after 1999 even though the legal rent should have risen to MTL 100; following Act X of 2009 they began paying EUR 185 per year from 2010, EUR 197.31 from 2013, and EUR 200 per year from 2017. She alleged that the Ordinance, as amended, imposed a unilateral lease relationship for an indefinite period without enabling her to obtain fair and adequate rent, in breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Despite the first-instance order, Act No. XXVII of 2018 prevented her from seeking eviction without first using the new procedure under Article 12B of the Ordinance. That provision allowed an owner to ask the Rent Regulation Board to revise the rent to a maximum of 2% per annum of the open market freehold value, subject to a means test, possible gradual increases, and other conditions. It also found a violation of Article 13, since the available remedies, taken together, were ineffective in her case. **Cauchi v. Malta** concerns an elderly Maltese property owner, Catherine Cauchi, who complained that Maltese rent-control legislation imposed a disproportionate burden on her property rights and that domestic remedies were ineffective.

They relied on the Housing (Decontrol) Ordinance, as amended by Act XXIII of 1979, to retain the property under a lease. The law allowed them to keep possession at a controlled rent, initially increased only in line with inflation and capped at double the previous rent. The tenants carried out substantial works to make the property habitable, with the applicant’s permission.

From 2010, following Act X of 2009, they paid EUR 185 per year; this rose to EUR 197.31 in 2013 and EUR 200 in 2017. The tenants owned no other property, and Mr A had a low income before retiring on a pension of EUR 515 per month.

She alleged that the Ordinance created a unilateral lease of indefinite duration without fair rent, contrary to Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. She sought compensation since 1984 and eviction. Expert evidence showed a stark imbalance. A government expert valued the refurbished property at EUR 174,000 in 2017 and estimated its rental value at EUR 398.75 per month, or EUR 4,785 per year. A court-appointed expert valued it at EUR 165,000 and estimated annual rental values rising from EUR 701 in 1984 to EUR 5,775 in 2017. Thus, the rent actually received—EUR 200 per year—was far below market levels.

On 31 October 2018 the Civil Court found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It held that the lease had not been entered into voluntarily but imposed by law, that the rent was not fair or adequate, and that the law lacked procedural safeguards. In 2019 she filed an application before the Rent Regulation Board seeking increased rent under Article 12B, but those proceedings were still pending.

Article 12B allows owners to request rent of up to 2% of the property’s open-market freehold value, subject to a means test. If the tenant fails the means test, the tenant may receive five years to vacate, with compensation at double the old rent. If the tenant passes, the Board sets rent while considering the tenant’s means, age, and any disproportionate burden on the landlord. Rent is fixed for six years, after which it may be revised.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 because the inadequate rent imposed by law placed a disproportionate burden on the applicant and domestic redress was insufficient. **Velichko v. Ukraine** (Application no. 22273/12, judgment 28 January 2021) concerned complaints under Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention about the lack of medical treatment in detention and the absence of an effective remedy. The applicant, a Ukrainian national born in 1973 with disabled status (group III), had been diagnosed with HIV in 1996.

On 22 October 2010, the applicant was detained on remand at the Izmayil Detention Centre (“Izmayil SIZO”) on suspicion of theft. On 25 October 2010, he informed the facility doctor that he had HIV. Between October 2010 and May 2011, he was diagnosed with HIV clinical stage IV, hepatitis C, and other conditions. He received some treatments, but no antiretroviral treatment (“ART”) was provided. On 18 May 2011, the head of Izmayil SIZO wrote to the judge that the applicant’s health was deteriorating and he urgently needed ART at the Odesa regional AIDS centre, which was impossible at Izmayil SIZO. The judge suspended the criminal proceedings and ordered his transfer to Odesa SIZO for examination and treatment. He was transferred on 27 May 2011.

On 7 June 2011, the applicant was offered ART and tuberculosis chemotherapy but refused. On 10 June 2011, the regional AIDS centre confirmed HIV and diagnosed tuberculosis; out-patient treatment and ART were prescribed at Odesa SIZO, but a certificate recorded his refusal. On 24 June 2011, he again refused out-patient treatment. On 12 August 2011, the head of Odesa SIZO reported that the applicant had refused out-patient ART three times and proposed transferring him back. On 16 August 2011, the Izmayil Court allowed the transfer, noting that his refusal could be seen as deliberately protracting the criminal case, and resumed the proceedings. Upon arrival at Izmayil SIZO, the applicant stated he would refuse ART there and in any penitentiary institution, certified in writing by staff.

On 8 November 2011, he complained to the Ombudsman that, despite his critical condition, authorities refused in-patient ART and treatment for concomitant diseases in a specialised hospital. On 1 and 20 December 2011, he and his lawyer sought a change of preventive measure to allow in-patient treatment. On 12 January 2012, a forensic examination was ordered to determine whether he could remain in detention. On 19 January 2012, he complained to the Odesa Regional Prosecutor about the lack of ART. On 27 January 2012, he was transferred to Odesa SIZO for forensic examination. On 8 February 2012, his CD4 count was 79 cells/mm³.

On 15 and 22 March 2012, the head of Odesa SIZO informed his lawyer of numerous diagnoses and offered treatment, again referring to the applicant’s refusals; he stated treatment would be provided fully if the applicant consented. On 21 March 2012, the prosecutor rejected the complaint as unfounded due to the refusals. On 16 April 2012, the applicant sought an interim measure under Rule 39. On 23 April 2012, the Court indicated to the Government that he should immediately receive appropriate in-patient treatment in a hospital specialising in AIDS and concomitant diseases, and requested his medical file. On 23 April 2012, a forensic report found his diseases not incompatible with detention. On 28 April 2012, a public hospital doctor concluded he did not need in-patient care. On 14 May 2012, he was admitted to the Infectious Hospital of Izmayil District. On 16 May 2012, the Izmayil Court released him with an undertaking not to abscond due to poor health. On 6 July 2012, the Rule 39 measure was lifted.

The Court found the refusals genuine. It held that between 7 and 24 June 2011, the authorities took necessary measures, interrupting the continuing situation. Since the application was filed on 12 April 2012, complaints concerning 22 October 2010 to 24 June 2011 were time-barred. The period from 25 June 2011 to 16 May 2012 was admissible. The Court ultimately found violations of Article 3 and Article 13 concerning inadequate medical treatment in detention and the lack of an effective remedy.

Between October 2010 and May 2011, he was diagnosed with HIV (clinical stage IV), hepatitis C, and other conditions. On 18 May 2011, the head of Izmayil SIZO informed the trial judge that the applicant’s health was deteriorating and that he urgently needed ART at the regional AIDS centre in Odesa. The judge suspended the criminal proceedings and ordered his transfer to Odesa SIZO for examination and treatment. The applicant was transferred on 27 May 2011.

On 10 June 2011, he was examined at the regional AIDS centre; doctors confirmed HIV and diagnosed tuberculosis, prescribing outpatient tuberculosis treatment and ART within the SIZO. On 12 January 2012, the court ordered a forensic examination to determine whether he could remain in detention. On 19 January 2012, he complained to the prosecutor about the lack of ART. On 27 January 2012, he was transferred to Odesa SIZO for forensic examination. On 8 February 2012, his CD4 count was 79 cells/mm³. The period from 25 June 2011 to 16 May 2012 was declared admissible. The Government maintained that he had been examined, that medications were available, and that he had refused offered treatment.

Ukraine* (Application no. 22273/12), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Articles 3 and 13 that Ukrainian detention authorities failed to provide adequate medical treatment and an effective remedy. The applicant, Mr Vladyslav Velichko, born in 1973, was disabled (group III) and had been diagnosed with HIV in 1996. On 22 October 2010 he was remanded in custody

**Case: Baranin and Vukčević v. Montenegro** (Applications nos. 24655/18 and 24656/18), ECtHR Fifth Section, judgment of 11 March 2021. The applicants complained under Articles 3 and 13 about ill-treatment by unidentified police officers on 24 October 2015 in Podgorica and the alleged lack of an effective investigation and remedy.

On that night, opposition protests outside Parliament turned violent. The applicants, Momčilo Baranin and Branimir Vukčević, were in the vicinity but did not participate. At about 10:30 p.m., while avoiding protesters, they walked toward police in a side street. Several masked police officers ordered them to lie on the ground, verbally insulted them and kicked them. One officer pressed the second applicant’s head to the ground with his foot. A Special Anti-Terrorist Unit (SAU) Hummer was present. The incident was filmed from a nearby office and posted on YouTube. Medical reports later documented large painful haematomas on both applicants: the first had 30 cm and 20 cm thigh haematomas and an eyelid haematoma; the second had ribcage and knee haematomas.

The applicants reported the incident on 30 October 2015. The State prosecutor’s office (SPO) opened a case against unknown SAU officers. The SAU’s initial report of 25 October 2015 omitted the incident. The investigation faced difficulties: officers wore masks and helmets; video quality was poor; police said radio communications had not been recorded; and attempts to obtain nearby pharmacy footage failed. The SPO repeatedly asked the Police Directorate and Minister of the Interior to identify officers.

On 21 June 2017, the Montenegrin Constitutional Court found violations of both the substantive and procedural aspects of Article 3. It held that the applicants had suffered inhuman and degrading treatment by unidentified SAU officers, with excessive and disproportionate force, and that the investigation had not been thorough, independent or prompt. The SPO had not interviewed journalists or SAU officers and had relied on the Police Directorate—part of the same chain of command—to identify the perpetrators. The Police Directorate had likewise failed to investigate its own officers effectively. The court ordered a fresh investigation.

After that decision, the SPO interviewed a journalist, TV director, pharmacy owner, SPU commander and 54 SAU officers. However, the SAU officers were questioned “as citizens,” not as witnesses, and were not obliged to answer. In November 2017 the SPO reported that an offence had undoubtedly occurred but the perpetrators could not be identified. The investigation remained ongoing. Separately, the SAU commander was convicted of aiding perpetrators by giving false information and allowing a joint report; his five-month sentence became final in May 2017. In civil proceedings, the applicants were awarded EUR 5,000 each, upheld in March 2020, for excessive force violating Article 3.

Before the ECtHR, the Government argued the applicants had lost victim status because the Constitutional Court found violations and they received compensation. The Court struck out the substantive Article 3 complaint in light of those domestic findings and damages. It examined only the procedural aspect of Article 3. The ECtHR found a violation: the investigation remained not prompt, thorough or independent and did not afford sufficient public scrutiny. Consequently, the applicants retained victim status due to the continuing ineffectiveness of the investigation.

In *Baranin and Vukčević v. Montenegro* (ECtHR, 11 March 2021), the applicants complained under Articles 3 and 13 of ill-treatment by unidentified police officers during protests in Podgorica on 24 October 2015, and of the lack of an effective investigation.

That night, an opposition protest outside Parliament turned violent. Police deployed Special Police Unit and Special Anti-Terrorist Unit (SAU) officers. Around 10:30 p.m., the applicants were near the protests but did not participate. While heading toward police in a side street, several masked police officers ordered them to lie down, insulted them, and kicked them. One officer pressed the second applicant’s head to the ground with his foot. The incident was recorded from a nearby office and posted online. The applicants later sought medical help: the first had large haematomas on both inner thighs and near his left eyelid; the second had haematomas on his left ribcage and behind his left knee. A medical expert later classified the injuries as minor bodily injuries caused by blunt force, fists or feet.

On 30 October 2015 the applicants reported the incident. The State Prosecutor’s Office (SPO) opened a case against unknown SAU officers. Investigative steps were slow and largely ineffective. The SAU’s report on the night’s use of force did not mention the applicants. Requests for GPS data, video footage, and radio communications yielded little: SAU vehicles could not be linked to perpetrators, radio recordings did not exist, and video evidence was poor. Officers allegedly wore masks and helmets, making identification impossible. The SPO repeatedly asked the Police Directorate and Interior Ministry to identify those involved, but no one was identified. In January 2017 the applicants lodged constitutional appeals.

On 21 June 2017 the Montenegrin Constitutional Court found violations of both the substantive and procedural aspects of Article 3. It held that the applicants had suffered inhuman and degrading treatment by unidentified SAU officers, without provocation, and that the force was excessive and disproportionate. It also found the investigation was not thorough, independent or prompt: the SPO had failed to interview journalists or SAU officers for a long time and had relied on police authorities to investigate their own subordinates. The court ordered a fresh, thorough, prompt and independent investigation and a report within three months.

After that decision, the SPO interviewed a journalist, TV staff, a pharmacy owner, the SPU commander and 54 SAU officers. The SAU officers were questioned only “as citizens” and were not obliged to answer. Almost all claimed they could not identify anyone because of masks, helmets and chaotic conditions. In November 2017 the SPO reported that some officers had undoubtedly committed an offence, but none could be identified. The investigation remained ongoing.

Separately, the SAU commander was convicted of aiding perpetrators by giving false information and allowing a joint report; he received five months’ imprisonment. In civil proceedings, the applicants were later awarded EUR 5,000 each because the domestic courts found excessive force violated Article 3.

Before the ECtHR, the Government argued the applicants had lost victim status. The Court struck out the substantive Article 3 complaint because domestic courts had found a violation and awarded damages, but it maintained the procedural complaint. It found that the investigation remained ineffective, not prompt, thorough or independent, and lacked sufficient public scrutiny. The applicants therefore had not lost victim status. The Court found a violation of the procedural aspect of Article 3.

**Case: Baranin and Vukčević v. Montenegro (Applications nos. 24655/18 and 24656/18), European Court of Human Rights, Judgment of 11 March 2021 (final 11 June 2021).**

The case concerned the ill-treatment of two Montenegrin nationals, Momčilo Baranin and Branimir Vukčević, by unidentified Special Anti-Terrorist Unit (SAU) police officers on 24 October 2015, and the subsequent failure to conduct an effective investigation. On that date, opposition protests took place in Podgorica in front of Parliament. The protests became violent, with some protesters throwing stones and Molotov cocktails. Police, including the SAU and Special Police Unit, were deployed. The applicants were in the vicinity but did not participate in the protests. At about 10:30 p.m., while walking away from a group of protesters, they encountered police in a side street. Several masked police officers ordered them to lie on the ground, verbally insulted them, and kicked them. One officer pressed the second applicant’s head to the ground with his foot. The incident was filmed from a nearby office and posted on YouTube.

The applicants sought medical assistance on 27 and 28 October 2015. Medical reports documented painful haematomas on the first applicant’s thighs and eyelid, and on the second applicant’s ribcage and knee. They reported the incident to police on 30 October 2015. The State Prosecutor’s Office (SPO) opened a case against unknown SAU officers. However, an SAU report of 25 October 2015 omitted the incident. The Court struck out the substantive Article 3 complaint because domestic courts had found a violation and awarded compensation. However, it examined the procedural complaint and found that the investigation remained ineffective—not prompt, thorough, independent, or subject to sufficient public scrutiny. **Poltoratskyy v. Ukraine** (Application no. 11551/13) is a European Court of Human Rights case decided by the Fifth Section in a Committee judgment on 22 April 2021. The applicant, Mr Boryslav Yevgenovych Poltoratskyy, is a Ukrainian national born in 1976 who is serving a life sentence in Vinnytsya Prison No. 1. He was granted legal aid and represented by Mr Gennadiy Tokarev. The Ukrainian Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Ivan Lishchyna.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are largely undisputed. On 12 December 1995, the Ivano-Frankivsk Regional Court found the applicant guilty of several counts of aggravated murder and robbery and sentenced him to death. On 22 February 1996, the Supreme Court upheld that verdict. On 2 June 2000, following legislative amendments, the Ivano-Frankivsk Court commuted the applicant’s death sentence to life imprisonment. The applicant’s parents have visited him in prison in accordance with the applicable legal rules.

The applicant lodged his application with the European Court on 21 August 2012. He complained under Article 3 of the Convention that his life sentence lacked any genuine prospect of release. He relied on **Petukhov v. Ukraine (no. 2)** (no. 41216/13, 12 March 2019), in which the Court had found a violation of Article 3 because life imprisonment in Ukraine was irreducible. He also complained under Article 8 that restrictions on his right to family visits during his sentence—restrictions in force until the 2014 legislative amendments—had unlawfully interfered with his private and family life. Finally, he complained under Article 13 that there were no effective domestic remedies for these grievances.

The Government were given notice of the complaints under Articles 3, 8 and 13, while the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The Government stated that they were not in a position to provide observations on the admissibility and merits. The applicant submitted observations.

On the Article 3 complaint, the Court declared it admissible and noted that the circumstances disclosed the same systemic problem identified in **Petukhov**: like Mr Petukhov, the applicant was a life prisoner deprived, for the time being, of any genuine prospect of release. The Government did not contest this issue substantively, referring instead to the ongoing legislative process concerning life sentences in Ukraine.

On the Article 8 complaint, the applicant alleged that the pre-2014 restrictions on family visits violated his right to respect for private and family life. The applicable legal framework on visiting entitlement was set out by reference to **Trosin v. Ukraine**, **Bigun v. Ukraine**, and **Starishko v. Ukraine**. The case therefore concerned both the irreducibility of the applicant’s life sentence and the prison visiting regime applicable to him before the 2014 amendments, together with the alleged absence of effective domestic remedies for those complaints.

**Poltoratskyy v. Ukraine** (Application no. 11551/13, judgment 22 April 2021) concerned a Ukrainian life prisoner’s complaints under Articles 3, 8 and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Boryslav Yevgenovych Poltoratskyy, born in 1976, was serving a life sentence in Vinnytsya Prison No. 1.

The key facts were as follows. On 12 December 1995 the Ivano-Frankivsk Regional Court convicted the applicant of several counts of aggravated murder and robbery and sentenced him to death. On 22 February 1996 the Supreme Court upheld that verdict. On 2 June 2000, following legislative amendments, the Ivano-Frankivsk Court commuted the death sentence to life imprisonment. The applicant’s parents visited him in prison in accordance with the applicable legal rules. He lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 21 August 2012. The Court gave notice to the Ukrainian Government of the complaints under Articles 3, 8 and 13 and declared the remainder inadmissible. The Government stated that they were not in a position to provide observations on admissibility or merits; the applicant, represented by lawyer Gennadiy Tokarev, submitted observations.

The main alleged violation was under Article 3, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. The applicant argued that his life sentence was incompatible with Article 3 because it offered no genuine prospect of release. He relied on *Petukhov v. Ukraine (no. 2)*, where the Court had found a violation of Article 3 on account of the irreducible nature of life imprisonment in Ukraine. The Court declared the complaint admissible and, on the merits, noted that the circumstances disclosed the same problem: like Mr Petukhov, the applicant was a life prisoner deprived, for the time being, of any genuine prospect of release. The Government did not contest the facts, citing an ongoing legislative process. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 3.

Under Article 8, the applicant complained that restrictions on his right to family visits during his sentence, in effect until the 2014 legislative amendments, had been contrary to his right to respect for family life. Although his parents had visited him under the prison rules, the complaint concerned the restrictive legal regime applicable to such visits. The Court considered this complaint admissible and examined whether the interference was justified.

Under Article 13, the applicant complained that there was no effective domestic remedy for his Article 3 and Article 8 grievances—namely, no domestic avenue to challenge either the irreducible nature of his life sentence or the restrictions on family visits. The Court also examined this complaint.

The facts most relevant to the alleged violations were therefore: the commutation of the death penalty to life imprisonment in 2000; the absence under Ukrainian law of a genuine release mechanism for life prisoners; the pre-2014 prison visit regime limiting family contact; the fact that the applicant’s parents visited him only in accordance with those restrictive rules; and the lack of effective domestic remedies for those complaints. The judgment is final, subject to editorial revision.

Case Budimir v. Croatia (App. no. 44691/14), judgment of 16 December 2021, concerned Jovan Budimir, an ethnic Serb car mechanic and certified motor vehicle inspector in Beli Manastir. He held a special licence issued in 1997. On 5 October 1998 he inspected a tractor and certified it roadworthy. Ten days later the tractor collided with a police car; a later inspection found defective brakes. In March 1999 the Ministry of the Interior filed a criminal complaint alleging he had falsified the inspection record. He was charged but acquitted on 23 May 2001 because the court could not establish the offence; expert evidence suggested the brakes could have become defective during the intervening ten days.

Meanwhile, on 16 March 1999, the Ministry revoked his licence to carry out vehicle inspections. His employer summarily dismissed him on 30 March 1999 because the loss of licence made continued employment impossible. Budimir challenged the revocation. The Administrative Court quashed the Ministry’s decision on 23 May 2001 for failure to establish all relevant facts and remitted the case. On 29 August 2001 the Ministry again revoked his licence, relying on an expert opinion that the brakes could not have failed after the inspection. On 4 December 2003 the Administrative Court quashed that decision too, finding that he had not been allowed to comment on the expert findings and that contradictions between the criminal and administrative expert evidence had not been resolved. **Budimir v. Croatia** (Application no. 44691/14, ECtHR, 16 December 2021) concerned the protracted revocation of the applicant’s professional licence and his resulting inability to work as a certified motor vehicle inspector, which he alleged violated his right to respect for private life under Article 8 of the Convention.

The applicant, a Croatian national and car mechanic, worked as a certified motor vehicle inspector for a private company in Beli Manastir. In May 1997 he was issued a special licence. On 5 October 1998 he inspected a tractor and certified it as roadworthy. On 15 October 1998 the same tractor collided with a police car. A day later, an extraordinary inspection by a colleague found that the tractor’s braking system had been defective.

In March 1999 the Ministry of the Interior filed a criminal complaint alleging that the applicant had falsified the vehicle inspection record. He was charged in July 1999. In May 2001 he was acquitted because the court could not establish that he had committed the offence. The court relied mainly on expert testimony indicating that the brakes could have become defective in the ten days between the inspection and the accident.

Meanwhile, on 16 March 1999, the Ministry revoked the applicant’s licence to carry out vehicle inspections. The decision became final, and his employer dismissed him on 30 March 1999 because the loss of his licence made continued employment impossible. The applicant challenged the revocation. In May 2001 the Administrative Court quashed the first revocation for failure to establish all relevant facts and remitted the case. In August 2001 the Ministry again revoked the licence, relying on an expert opinion that the brakes could not have become defective in the intervening period. In December 2003 the Administrative Court again quashed that decision, finding that the Ministry had failed to let the applicant comment on the expert findings and had not resolved contradictions between expert evidence in the criminal and administrative proceedings. On 10 May 2004 the Ministry returned his licence, taking into account his criminal acquittal. He had therefore been without his professional licence for about five years.

The applicant’s labour challenge failed. In 2005 the Zagreb Municipal Court found that his summary dismissal had been lawful and that his employer had not been obliged to offer him another post pending the criminal and administrative proceedings. This was upheld in 2006.

In 2006 the applicant sought damages from the State under section 13 of the State Administration Act for unlawful or wrongful conduct by administrative authorities. Domestic courts dismissed his claim. In 2013 the Supreme Court held that the revocation had not amounted to “unlawful conduct” because the Ministry had acted under the Road Safety Act based on reasonable doubt, and the later quashing of administrative decisions for procedural or factual reasons did not necessarily mean the State had acted unlawfully. His constitutional complaint was declared inadmissible in 2014.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained that he could not obtain compensation for the damage caused by the allegedly unlawful revocation of his licence. This had led to his immediate dismissal, prolonged unemployment, loss of income, reputational harm, inability to develop professional relationships, financial dependence on family, and worsened health. The Government argued that he had not exhausted domestic remedies and that Article 8 was inapplicable.

The Court found Article 8 applicable because the protracted withdrawal of his professional licence and consequent inability to work had serious repercussions on his private life. Croatia had failed its positive obligations: it provided no solution pending establishment of his actual liability, no effective legal framework for equitable relief, and no comprehensive assessment of his right to respect for private life. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 8.

He was charged but acquitted on 23 May 2001, mainly because expert evidence showed the brakes could have become defective in the ten days between the inspection and the accident.

Meanwhile, on 16 March 1999 the Ministry of the Interior revoked his licence to carry out vehicle inspections. That decision became final, and his employer dismissed him on 30 March 1999. The applicant challenged the revocation. On 23 May 2001 the Administrative Court quashed the decision for failure to establish all relevant facts and remitted the case. On 29 August 2001 the Ministry again revoked his licence, relying on a forensic opinion that the brakes could not have become defective in the intervening period. On 4 December 2003 the Administrative Court again quashed that decision, finding that the Ministry had failed to allow the applicant to comment on the expert findings and had failed to resolve contradictions between expert evidence in the criminal and administrative proceedings. On 10 May 2004 the Ministry returned his licence, taking into account his criminal acquittal. He had therefore been unable to work as a certified inspector for about five years.

His labour complaint failed. In 2005–2006 the domestic courts found that his summary dismissal had been lawful because the loss of his licence made continued employment impossible, and his employer had not been obliged to offer him another post while proceedings were pending. In 2006 he brought a civil action for damages against the State for unlawful or wrongful administrative conduct, alleging that the licence withdrawal had caused his dismissal, unemployment and loss of income. The Municipal Court dismissed the claim in 2009; the County Court upheld that decision in 2011; and the Supreme Court dismissed his further appeal in 2013. The Supreme Court held that the Ministry had acted under the Road Safety Act on reasonable doubt, and that the later quashing of administrative decisions did not amount to unlawful conduct, even though damage and causation existed. His constitutional complaint, alleging fair-hearing and right-to-work violations, was declared inadmissible in 2014 as raising no constitutional issue.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 8 that he could not obtain compensation for the unlawful revocation of his licence and its consequences: dismissal, prolonged unemployment and no income. The Government argued non-exhaustion and that Article 8 was inapplicable, since the case concerned compensation for loss of a professional licence and he had not shown effects on private life or pursued adequate labour remedies. The applicant argued that he had raised the substance of the complaint and that the revocation harmed his reputation, professional relationships, finances and health.

The Court found Article 8 applicable under a consequence-based approach, because the protracted withdrawal of his professional licence and his consequent inability to work as a certified motor vehicle inspector had serious repercussions on his private life. Croatia had failed to provide him with any solution pending determination of his actual liability and lacked an effective legal framework for claiming equitable relief. The absence of a comprehensive assessment of his right to respect for private life was inconsistent with any acceptable margin of appreciation. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 8.

It concluded that these parts of the applications were incompatible *ratione personae* with the Convention and rejected them.
