Centrum för rättvisa v. Sweden (Application no. 35252/08) is a Grand Chamber judgment of the European Court of Human Rights delivered on 25 May 2021. The applicant is a Swedish foundation that represents clients in proceedings concerning Convention rights and participates in public debate. It communicates daily, often on sensitive matters, with individuals, organisations and companies in Sweden and abroad. It alleged that Swedish legislation and practice on signals intelligence violated its rights under Article 8 of the Convention and that it had no effective remedy under Article 13. It did not bring domestic proceedings, claiming that no effective remedy existed.

The Swedish regime is governed by the Foreign Intelligence Act and the Signals Intelligence Act 2008. The National Defence Radio Establishment (FRA) conducts signals intelligence in support of Swedish foreign, defence and security policy. It may intercept cross-border cable-based communications using selectors, subject to permits from the Foreign Intelligence Court. Emergency permits may be issued by the FRA but must be reviewed by the court. A permit lasts up to six months. Interception must concern foreign circumstances and may not be used for ordinary law enforcement. Selectors directly relating to a specific natural person may be used only if exceptionally important. The regime contains rules on destruction of certain intercepted material, oversight by the Foreign Intelligence Inspectorate (SIUN), a privacy protection representative, data protection rules, notification of affected individuals, and judicial review. Intelligence may be shared with foreign states or international organisations when necessary for international defence and security cooperation, subject to secrecy.

The applicant argued that, as a body scrutinising State actors, its sensitive communications were at risk of being intercepted and examined through bulk signals intelligence. It complained that the regime allowed bulk interception, that safeguards were inadequate, and that secrecy meant individuals could not learn whether they had been surveilled or obtain an effective remedy.

The Grand Chamber adapted its Article 8 case-law for bulk interception. It held that such regimes require a global assessment focusing on “end-to-end safeguards,” because intrusion increases as material moves through the different stages of interception, processing, storage, use, transmission and destruction. Applying that test, the Court found shortcomings in the Swedish regime. First, there was no clear rule requiring destruction of intercepted material that did not contain personal data. Second, when deciding whether to transmit intelligence material to foreign partners, there was no requirement to consider the privacy interests of the individuals concerned. Third, the Foreign Intelligence Inspectorate had a dual role, and its ex post facto control did not include reasoned decisions; these defects were not sufficiently compensated by other safeguards. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 8. It did not examine Article 13 separately. The judgment is significant for setting out the “end-to-end safeguards” approach to bulk interception regimes under Article 8.
001-207136:
Shuaib Khan, a Pakistani national born in Denmark in 1986, complained under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that Denmark’s order expelling him with a six-year re-entry ban violated his right to respect for private life. He had lived in Denmark his entire life; his parents and four siblings lived there, and he had no family of his own. His ties to Pakistan were limited: he spoke broken Punjabi, could not read it, and had visited Pakistan only briefly, most recently in 2007, although his family owned property there and his Pakistani ID listed a permanent address there.

Khan had a lengthy criminal record since 2003, with thirteen convictions. These included fines for knife possession and criminal damage; imprisonment for driving and weapons offences; violence in prison; drug possession; and several serious violent offences. In 2008 he was sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment for aggravated violence, including fatal violence. In 2013 he received three years and six months for aggravated violence and theft. In 2015 he received six months’ imprisonment for aggravated violence and was issued a suspended expulsion order with a two-year probation period. He was released in March 2017. He was also the leader of the gang Loyal to Familia (LTF), later dissolved as an unlawful association operating through violence.

In July 2017, police established stop-and-frisk zones due to gang conflict. On 31 July 2017, while in such a zone at Blaagaard Square, Khan, as LTF leader, was frisked. He allegedly confronted a police inspector and made threatening remarks such as “Remember his face”, “Watch out”, and “Watch your back”, while an LTF affiliate photographed the officer. The atmosphere was tense and his manner threatening. He was charged under Article 119(1) of the Penal Code for threatening a public official, and also with staying in Denmark without a valid permit due to a lapsed residence permit, later renewed.

In October 2017 the City Court convicted him, imposed three months’ imprisonment and a fine, but issued only a suspended expulsion order. It found that his birth and upbringing in Denmark required very serious reasons and that the spontaneous, short-sentence offence did not justify expulsion despite his past. The High Court upheld the conviction, reduced the prison term to 60 days, and also found expulsion disproportionate. On further appeal, the Supreme Court in November 2018 increased the sentence to three months and ordered unconditional expulsion with a six-year re-entry ban. The majority found that although his ties to Denmark were stronger than to Pakistan, his long history of serious violent crime, gang leadership, continued offending during probation, and risk of future violence constituted very serious reasons. It held that the short length of the latest sentence did not preclude expulsion. A dissenting judge considered the latest offence too minor to make expulsion proportionate.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Khan alleged that the expulsion violated Article 8. The Court assessed proportionality under its case-law and found no violation. There were very serious reasons for expelling a settled migrant; the nature of the offence and his long history of serious and violent criminality were central; and there was no minimum requirement as to the sentence or seriousness of the offence triggering expulsion. The Danish Supreme Court had duly assessed proportionality.

**Case: Khan v. Denmark (Application no. 26957/19)**

The applicant, Shuaib Khan, was a Pakistani national born in Denmark in 1986 who had lived in Denmark his entire life. His parents and four siblings lived in Denmark; he had no spouse or children. He had a criminal record since 2003 and had been convicted thirteen times, including for knife possession, criminal damage, driving and weapons offences, drug possession, repeated violence, aggravated violence, and fatal violence. In 2008 he received eight years’ imprisonment for aggravated violence, including fatal violence; in 2013 he received three years and six months for aggravated violence and theft; and in 2015 he received six months for aggravated violence committed in prison. On that last occasion he was given a suspended expulsion order with a two-year probation period. He had served approximately ten years in prison. Khan was also the leader of the gang Loyal to Familia (LTF), later found by Danish courts to be an unlawful association operating through violence.

The offence giving rise to the case occurred on 31 July 2017. Police had established stop-and-frisk zones in Copenhagen, including Blaagaard Square, because of an ongoing violent gang conflict involving firearms. Khan, as LTF leader, was present with other LTF members and was frisked. Afterwards, he turned to a police inspector on duty and made threatening remarks, including “Remember his face,” “Watch out,” “Watch out carefully,” and “Watch your back,” while at least one LTF member photographed the inspector. The atmosphere was tense. He was charged under Article 119(1) of the Danish Penal Code for threatening a police officer on duty, and also for residing in Denmark without the required permit due to a lapse in renewing his residence permit.

In October 2017 the Copenhagen City Court convicted him, sentenced him to three months’ imprisonment and a fine, and issued a suspended expulsion order with a two-year probation period. It found that, although he was born and raised in Denmark and therefore required very serious reasons for expulsion, the recent offence was spontaneous and short, and his ties to Pakistan were limited. On appeal, the High Court upheld the conviction, reduced the prison sentence to 60 days, and found that immediate expulsion with a six-year re-entry ban would be disproportionate.

The Supreme Court, by judgment of 20 November 2018, increased the sentence to three months’ imprisonment and imposed unconditional expulsion with a six-year re-entry ban. Because Khan had committed a new offence during the probation period of his suspended expulsion and proceedings began before its expiry, the Aliens Act required expulsion unless it would clearly violate Denmark’s international obligations. The Supreme Court majority found that, despite the short sentence, very serious reasons justified expulsion: his long history of serious and violent crime, approximately ten years’ imprisonment, leadership of LTF, offence committed only months after release and during probation, weak integration, and risk of future violent offending. It also noted his ties to Pakistan were not nonexistent: he spoke Punjabi, knew Pakistani culture, had family property there, and a Pakistani ID card listed a permanent address there. A dissenting judge considered the latest offence too minor to justify expelling a lifelong resident.

Khan complained that the expulsion order violated Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, respect for private life. The European Court of Human Rights found no violation. It held that there is no minimum sentence or seriousness requirement for expulsion. The Supreme Court had properly assessed proportionality under the Court’s case-law, and very serious reasons existed for expelling him despite the three-month sentence, notably the nature of the offence against an on-duty police officer in a gang-violence context and his long history of serious violent criminality. The six-year re-entry ban did not make the measure disproportionate.

**Khan v. Denmark (Application no. 26957/19) – Summary**

The applicant, Shuaib Khan, is a Pakistani national born in Denmark in 1986. He lived in Denmark his entire life, where his parents and four siblings also reside. He has no family of his own—no spouse or children. Although he completed the ninth grade of Danish primary and lower secondary school and took some classes during imprisonment, he never obtained further education or employment. He speaks broken Pakistani Punjabi, cannot read the language, and had visited Pakistan only two or three times, most recently in 2007. He was lawfully resident in Denmark for approximately 20 years and 10 months, though his criminal record dates back to 2003 and included thirteen convictions.

The applicant’s criminal history was extensive and serious. In 2006, he was convicted of driving without a license, illegal weapons possession, and attempted obstruction of a police officer. In 2007, he was convicted of violence against a fellow inmate. In 2008, he received an eight-year prison sentence for two counts of aggravated violence as a repeat violent offender, one involving fatal violence. In 2013, he was sentenced to three years and six months for aggravated violence and theft. In 2015, he was convicted of aggravated violence for assaulting a person with six accomplices and was issued a suspended expulsion order with a two-year probation period. He was released in March 2017.

The applicant was the leader of a gang called "Loyal to Familia" (LTF), which was later dissolved by a City Court judgment in January 2020 for having an unlawful purpose and functioning through violence.

The events giving rise to the case occurred on 31 July 2017, when the applicant, in a stop-and-frisk zone at Blaagaard Square in Copenhagen, threatened a police inspector on duty with violence. The zone had been established due to an ongoing violent conflict between LTF and another gang. The applicant, surrounded by other LTF affiliates, told them to "Remember his face," then directed at the inspector: "Watch out," "Watch out carefully," and "Watch your back," while at least one affiliate photographed the officer. His voice and demeanor were threatening, and the atmosphere was tense. The offence occurred approximately four months after his release from prison and during the probation period of his suspended expulsion order.

The Supreme Court of Denmark, by judgment of 20 November 2018, convicted the applicant under Article 119(1) of the Penal Code and sentenced him to three months' imprisonment and a fine. Critically, the majority (six of seven judges) also ordered his unconditional expulsion with a six-year re-entry ban. The majority found that although the applicant was poorly integrated, his ties with Denmark were significantly stronger than with Pakistan, and there were "very serious reasons" to justify expulsion despite the short sentence. They emphasized his long history of serious violent criminality, his leadership of a violent gang, his demonstrated unwillingness to integrate despite prior warnings, and the reasoned assumption that he would commit further violent offences if not expelled. The minority judge dissented, finding the most recent offence insufficiently serious to justify expulsion of a settled migrant born and raised in Denmark. The applicant complained that the expulsion order breached Article 8 of the Convention.

**CASE OF ASANOVIĆ v. MONTENEGRO** (Application no. 52415/18) concerned Nebojša Asanović, a Montenegrin lawyer and long-time representative of an opposition media outlet. He alleged that he had been unlawfully deprived of liberty and lacked an effective domestic remedy, relying on Articles 5 § 1 and 13 of the Convention. The European Court of Human Rights found a breach of Article 5 § 1 because his detention on suspicion of a criminal offence did not comply with domestic law requirements.

The facts began on 23 December 2016, when the Tax Administration reported to the police that there were indications the applicant had committed tax evasion in connection with his professional activities. The case was forwarded to the State Prosecution Office in January 2017. On 12 September 2017, a state prosecutor allegedly gave an oral order to police officer G.M. to gather information from the applicant “as a citizen,” since he was suspected of the offence. The next morning, G.M. informed the prosecutor that the applicant had not been found at his address and that his phone was switched off. Apparently believing the applicant was hiding, the prosecutor ordered the police to find him and deprive him of liberty.

At around 9:30 on 13 September 2017, G.M. and three other officers approached the applicant in front of the Court of First Instance in Podgorica. They served him with a summons requiring him to appear at the Police Directorate “at once” to provide information as a citizen, warning that he would be brought by force if he did not comply. The applicant claimed he was placed in a vehicle and taken to the police station; the Government claimed he was merely offered a ride without force.

After giving a statement, the police served an official report stating that the applicant had been deprived of liberty at 10:40 on the prosecutor’s order in relation to tax evasion and would be brought before the prosecutor. His fingerprints and photograph were taken, his belongings including his glasses were seized, and he was placed in a windowless cell. At 12:10 he was handcuffed and taken to the prosecutor, who questioned him from 12:30 to 13:54. He denied the offence and was then released. A criminal complaint was filed the same day.

Domestically, the applicant filed a constitutional appeal on 15 September 2017. The Bar Association protested. The Council for Civic Control of Police found the police had acted unlawfully, particularly because, as a lawyer, the applicant could not be deprived of liberty without a court decision under the Bar Act. On 2 October 2018, the Ombudsperson also found a breach, reasoning that the applicant should first have been allowed to comply with the summons; that de facto deprivation began at 9:30; and that no grounds for detention under Article 175 of the Criminal Procedure Code existed. The Constitutional Court dismissed his appeal on 11 July 2018, finding the police and prosecution acted lawfully and that he had failed to comply with the summons, with deprivation occurring at 10:40.

The applicant also brought civil proceedings on 12 October 2018 for unlawful deprivation, seeking compensation and publication, but these were later stayed pending criminal proceedings. He clarified that the civil claim concerned honour, reputation, and the right to liberty rather than damages for unlawful deprivation. He separately obtained €1,500 in civil proceedings concerning his right to defence.

The Government argued non-exhaustion, saying the civil action was effective. The applicant maintained he had exhausted other remedies and that the civil claim was different. The Court found that the summons did not authorize immediate de facto detention, no Article 175 detention grounds were shown, and domestic law required a court decision before depriving a practising attorney of liberty for offences related to his practice. Police control therefore began at 9:30, despite the official report recording detention only at 10:40.
001-212829:
W.A., a Swiss national born in 1960, was convicted by the Zurich Jury Court in 1993/1995 of murder and intentional manslaughter and sentenced to 20 years’ imprisonment. The offences were violent: in 1983 he murdered a man in a particularly violent manner, and in 1990 he induced his partner to strangle an acquaintance and later dismembered the corpse. Psychiatric expert G. found that a personality disorder and alcohol intoxication had substantially diminished his criminal responsibility. The sentencing court declined preventive detention under former Article 43 § 1(2) of the Criminal Code, considering a long prison term a better way to protect society because preventive detention in practice rarely lasted more than five years.

He served his sentence until 8 October 2010. In 2009, the prosecution applied for subsequent preventive detention under Article 65 § 2 of the Criminal Code, introduced in 2007. In 2012 the Federal Court found new facts justified reopening the proceedings to his detriment: a 2009 report by psychiatric expert P., using methods unavailable in the 1990s, concluded that W.A. had not been alcohol-addicted but suffered from dissocial personality disorder and psychopathy, was untreatable, and posed a very high risk of further violent offences. The case was reopened. In 2013 the Zurich District Court ordered subsequent preventive detention under Article 65 § 2 read with Article 64 § 1(b) and transitional provisions/old Article 43. Relying on P. and a 2013 report by expert R., it found a serious mental disorder, high recidivism risk, and no realistic therapeutic prospects, and that the requirements had already been met at conviction. Appeals were dismissed in 2014 and 2015. W.A. remained in ordinary prison and refused therapy.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, W.A. alleged violations of Article 5 § 1 (right to liberty), Article 7 § 1 (no retrospective heavier penalty), and Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 (double punishment/ne bis in idem). For Article 5, the key facts were that he was detained after completing his sentence, the later detention rested on his mental-health condition and recidivism risk rather than simply the original conviction, and he was held in ordinary prison rather than a therapeutic institution. For Article 7, the preventive detention was imposed retrospectively under the 2007 law for offences and a conviction predating it; Swiss courts treated it as no heavier than the old law, but W.A. argued it was retrospective punishment. For Article 4 of Protocol No. 7, the issue was whether the limited reopening to his detriment and the subsequent preventive detention order was a permissible reopening under Article 4 § 2 or a second punishment after final conviction. The Swiss courts reasoned that new facts justified reopening, the original judgment was quashed, and the new order became part of that judgment. The ECtHR found no sufficient causal link under Article 5 § 1 and that ordinary prison detention was not justified by unsound mind; it found an Article 7 § 1 violation and held that the limited reopening was not a reopening for Article 4 § 2 purposes.

In **W.A. v. Switzerland** (Application no. 38958/16, judgment 2 November 2021), the European Court of Human Rights examined the applicant’s subsequent preventive detention after he had completed a 20-year prison sentence for violent offences.

The applicant, born in 1960, was convicted by the Zurich Jury Court in 1993, as amended in 1995, of murder and intentional manslaughter. In 1983 he had murdered a man in a particularly violent manner. In 1990 he induced his then partner to strangle an acquaintance and later dismembered the corpse. Psychiatric expert G. found that the applicant’s capacity to appreciate the wrongfulness of his acts was substantially diminished owing to a personality disorder and alcohol intoxication. At sentencing, the court declined to order preventive detention under the former Article 43 §1 of the Criminal Code. It considered that a long prison term better protected society because preventive detention in practice rarely lasted more than five years.

The applicant served his sentence until 8 October 2010. He was then held on remand pending a 2009 prosecution application for subsequent preventive detention under Article 65 §2 of the Criminal Code, introduced in 2007. In 2012 the Federal Court found that new facts permitted a reopening to the applicant’s detriment. A 2009 report by expert P., using methods unavailable in the 1990s, concluded that the applicant had not been alcohol-addicted at the time of the offences but suffered from dissocial personality disorder and psychopathy, which were untreatable and carried a very high risk of further violent offending. These facts had not and could not have been known at the original conviction.

In the reopened proceedings, the Zurich District Court ordered subsequent preventive detention in 2013 under Article 65 §2 read with Article 64 §1(b). Relying on expert P. and a 2013 report by expert R., it found that the applicant suffered and had suffered from a serious mental disorder, posed a very high risk of serious violent offences, and that psychiatric treatment had little or no prospect of success. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal in 2014, and the Federal Court dismissed his further appeal in 2015. The applicant remained in ordinary prison in Regensdorf and had refused therapy.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged violations of Article 5 §1 (right to liberty), Article 7 §1 (no retrospective heavier penalty), and Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 (ne bis in idem). The key facts for those alleged violations were that the preventive detention was imposed only after the original sentence had been fully served, was based on later psychiatric findings about his mental disorder and recidivism risk, and was executed in an ordinary prison rather than a therapeutic institution. The domestic courts argued that the reopening made the subsequent detention part of the original conviction and that the old law would also have permitted preventive detention in 1993. The European Court disagreed in material respects: it found no sufficient causal link between the 1993 conviction and the later preventive detention for Article 5 §1, and held that detention in an ordinary prison could not be justified as detention of a person of unsound mind. It also found that the subsequent order amounted to a retrospective heavier penalty under Article 7 §1, and that the limited reopening leading to preventive detention was not a reopening for the purposes of Article 4 §2 of Protocol No. 7.

In **W.A. v. Switzerland** (Application no. 38958/16, judgment 2 November 2021), the applicant was convicted by the Zurich Jury Court in 1993/1995 of murder and intentional manslaughter and sentenced to 20 years’ imprisonment. The offences included a particularly violent 1983 murder and a 1990 killing in which he induced his partner to strangle an acquaintance. Psychiatric expert G. diagnosed a personality disorder and alcohol intoxication, finding substantially diminished criminal responsibility. Although the court considered W.A. very dangerous and difficult to treat, it declined to order preventive detention under the old Article 43 § 1 of the Criminal Code. It preferred a long prison sentence because preventive detention in practice rarely lasted more than five years.

W.A. served his sentence until October 2010. In 2009, while he was still imprisoned, the prosecution applied for his subsequent preventive detention under Article 65 § 2 of the Criminal Code, which entered into force in 2007. That provision permits post-conviction preventive detention where new facts or evidence show that the offender met the requirements for preventive detention at the time of conviction but those facts could not then have been known. A new 2009 psychiatric report by expert P., using methods unavailable in the 1990s, concluded that W.A. had not been addicted to alcohol but suffered from dissocial personality disorder and psychopathy, which were untreatable and created a very high risk of further violent offences.

In 2012 the Federal Court allowed the proceedings to be reopened, finding these new facts sufficient. In the reopened proceedings, the Zurich District Court ordered W.A.’s subsequent preventive detention in 2013 under Article 65 § 2 read with Article 64 § 1(b) of the Criminal Code and transitional provisions. Relying on the 2009 report and a 2013 report by expert R., the court found that the requirements for preventive detention had been met both at the time of conviction and currently: W.A. suffered from a serious mental disorder, posed a very high risk to others, and treatment under Article 59 had little or no prospect of success. His appeals were dismissed by the Court of Appeal in 2014 and the Federal Court in 2015. He remained detained in an ordinary prison, Pöschwies/Regensdorf, and had refused therapy.

W.A. complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 5 § 1 (right to liberty), Article 7 § 1 (no retrospective heavier penalty), and Article 4 § 1 of Protocol No. 7 (ne bis in idem). The domestic courts rejected these complaints, holding that the reopening created a sufficient link to the original conviction, that the new preventive detention was not heavier than the old law, and that the initial judgment had been quashed so there was no double punishment.

The ECtHR found violations. Under Article 5 § 1, the subsequent preventive detention lacked a sufficient causal link to the original conviction: it was based not on the punitive conviction but on his mental health condition and future dangerousness. Detention in an ordinary prison was also not justified as detention of a person “of unsound mind.” Under Article 7 § 1, the retrospective order amounted to imposing a heavier penalty than the law applicable at the time of the offences. Under Article 4 § 1 of Protocol No. 7, the limited reopening leading to a preventive detention order was not a reopening of the case within the meaning of Article 4 § 2, so the applicant was punished twice for the same offences.
001-209373:
E.G. v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 37882/13, judgment 13 April 2021) concerned Moldova’s failure to enforce a sentence imposed on one of three men convicted of sexually assaulting the applicant. In February 2008, E.G. was sexually assaulted by P.G., R.G., and V.B. In June 2009, the Centru District Court convicted the three of gang sexual assault and imposed suspended sentences. On appeal in December 2009, the Chișinău Court of Appeal affirmed the convictions, additionally convicted P.G. and R.G. of gang rape, and sentenced P.G. to six years, R.G. to five and a half years, and V.B. to five years’ imprisonment. The judgment was immediately enforceable. P.G. and R.G. were taken into custody from the courtroom; V.B., who was absent, was not.

V.B.’s case became central to the alleged violation. A wanted notice was issued for him in May 2010. In April 2011, V.B. applied for amnesty under the 2008 Amnesty Act. A similar amnesty claim by R.G. had been rejected because his conviction post-dated the Act. In December 2011, the District Court rejected V.B.’s claim for the same reason. On appeal, however, the prosecution supported V.B.’s amnesty claim, and in May 2012 the Chișinău Court of Appeal granted him amnesty, finding that the offence pre-dated the Act. This allowed V.B. to avoid serving his sentence. The amnesty proceedings later became tangled: the decision was reopened, set aside, restored, and eventually revoked. In October 2012, V.B. was arrested but released the same day on the basis of the May 2012 amnesty decision. In September and November 2013, the courts finally set aside the amnesty, noting that the earlier court had not known V.B. had breached the conditions of his release against security. By then, V.B. had left Moldova for Ukraine on 16 November 2013.

After the final revocation, E.G. asked whether V.B. was serving his sentence. In January 2014, police told her lawyer that no wanted notice had been issued and no search measures had been taken because neither the prosecuting authority nor the Court of Appeal had directed a search. The prosecution then asked police to enforce the decision. In late January 2014, police resumed inquiries and determined that V.B. had left Moldova. A CIS wanted notice was issued only in February 2014, and an international notice in April 2015. As of March 2020, V.B. had still not been found. Domestic law required courts to forward immediately enforceable decisions to enforcement authorities within ten days.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, E.G. complained under Articles 3 and 8 that Moldova had failed its positive obligations to give practical effect to V.B.’s conviction and sentence. She alleged two linked failures: the grant of amnesty to V.B. and, during periods when he had no amnesty, the authorities’ failure to search for him effectively. The Government argued that the application was late because the six-month period should run from the final amnesty decision of 22 May 2012.

The Court declared the complaints admissible. It found that the alleged failures—the amnesty grant and the authorities’ inaction in locating V.B.—were inextricably linked and amounted to a continuing situation of non-enforcement of the criminal sanction. The period therefore had to be considered as a whole for the six-month rule. The Court ultimately found breaches of the procedural positive obligations under Articles 3 and 8. While amnesty and pardon generally fall within domestic law and are not contrary to international law unless they concern grave breaches of fundamental human rights, here the lack of coordination between State authorities and the unjustified delay in issuing wanted notices allowed V.B. to leave Moldova and remain at large.

In *E.G. v. the Republic of Moldova* (no. 37882/13), the European Court of Human Rights examined Moldova’s failure to enforce a sentence imposed for a sexual assault, raising positive obligations under Articles 3 and 8. E.G. was sexually assaulted by three men, P.G., R.G., and V.B., on 9–10 February 2008. After prosecution, they were initially detained but released pending trial; V.B. was released on 12 March 2008 against security.

On 17 June 2009, the Centru District Court convicted all three of gang sexual assault under Article 172 §2(c) and imposed suspended sentences. E.G. appealed. On 2 December 2009, the Chișinău Court of Appeal affirmed but additionally convicted P.G. and R.G. of gang rape under Article 171 §2(c), sentencing them to six and five and a half years, and sentenced V.B. to five years. The judgment was immediately enforceable. P.G. and R.G. were taken into custody from court; V.B. was absent and not detained. The Supreme Court affirmed on 7 December 2010. A wanted notice for V.B. was issued on 14 May 2010.

The key violation concerned V.B.’s non-enforcement. On 18 April 2011, V.B. sought amnesty under the 2008 Amnesty Act. R.G.’s similar request had been rejected because his conviction post-dated the Act. On 20 December 2011, the Centru District Court rejected V.B.’s request for the same reason. On appeal, however, the prosecution supported him. On 22 May 2012, the Chișinău Court of Appeal granted amnesty, finding section 5 applicable because the offence pre-dated the Act. V.B. was arrested on 22 October 2012 but released the same day based on that decision.

The amnesty was later set aside. On 29 June 2012, the Court of Appeal reopened and reversed it, but that decision was quashed by the Supreme Court for lack of jurisdiction. On 4 September 2013, the Centru District Court reopened the proceedings and set aside the 22 May 2012 amnesty; the Court of Appeal affirmed on 18 November 2013, noting the earlier court had not known V.B. breached his release conditions.

Enforcement then stalled. In a letter of 10 January 2014, police told E.G.’s lawyer that no wanted notice had been issued and no search steps taken because no competent authority had directed one. On 28 January 2014, the prosecution asked police to enforce the decision setting aside amnesty. On 31 January 2014, police learned V.B. had left Moldova for Ukraine on 16 November 2013. The prosecution admitted courts had failed to forward the final decision for enforcement within ten days. A CIS wanted notice was issued only on 20 February 2014 and an international notice on 29 April 2015. By March 2020, V.B. had not been found.

The Government argued the application was time-barred, six months from the 22 May 2012 amnesty. The Court rejected this, finding the amnesty grant and failure to search were inextricably linked and amounted to a continuing situation; the non-enforcement period had to be viewed as a whole. The complaints were admissible. The Court found Moldova breached its procedural positive obligations. Although amnesty and pardon fall within domestic law, they cannot bar accountability for grave human rights breaches. The amnesty enabled V.B. to leave the country, and authorities showed lack of coordination and unjustified delay in issuing wanted notices, leaving E.G. without effective enforcement of the sentence.

In *E.G. v. the Republic of Moldova* (App. no. 37882/13, judgment 13 April 2021), the applicant complained under Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention that Moldova failed to enforce the sentence imposed on one of the men who sexually assaulted her, resulting in his de facto impunity.

The underlying facts concerned a gang sexual assault. On the night of 9–10 February 2008, E.G. was sexually assaulted by P.G., R.G. and V.B. Criminal proceedings were opened. V.B. was initially detained but was released on 12 March 2008 against a security deposit. On 17 June 2009, the Centru District Court convicted all three defendants of gang sexual assault and imposed suspended sentences. On appeal, on 2 December 2009, the Chișinău Court of Appeal additionally convicted P.G. and R.G. of gang rape and sentenced them to six and five and a half years’ imprisonment respectively. V.B. was sentenced to five years’ imprisonment. The judgment was immediately enforceable. P.G. and R.G. were taken into custody from the courtroom; V.B. was not present and was not detained. The Supreme Court of Justice affirmed the judgment on 7 December 2010.

The enforcement problems concerning V.B. were central to the alleged violations. A wanted notice for V.B. was issued only on 14 May 2010. In April 2011, V.B. applied for amnesty under the 2008 Amnesty Act. After an initial rejection, the Chișinău Court of Appeal granted him amnesty on 22 May 2012. That decision was later reopened and eventually set aside. On 4 September 2013, the Centru District Court reopened the amnesty proceedings and set aside the 22 May 2012 decision; the Chișinău Court of Appeal affirmed on 18 November 2013. The Court of Appeal noted that the earlier court had not known that V.B. had breached the conditions of his release against security.

The Government argued that the application was out of time because the main complaint concerned the final amnesty decision of 22 May 2012. The Court disagreed. The Court found Article 6 applicable and admissible, but no violation: the applicant was not substantially disadvantaged or placed at an inequality of arms by appearing via video-link when he could not enter Norway.

In *Mucha v. Slovakia* (Application no. 63703/19, ECtHR, 25 November 2021), the applicant, Pavel Mucha, was allegedly a mid-ranking member of an organised criminal gang operating in Bratislava and elsewhere in Slovakia. In 2012, he and nine others were charged with setting up, conceiving and maintaining a criminal enterprise, along with multiple violent offences. Although the prosecution was initially joint, eight co-perpetrators were separately prosecuted because they entered into plea-bargaining agreements with the Public Prosecution Service. These agreements required confessions, were supported by the case file, and had to be approved by the Specialised Criminal Court (SCC).

The same three-judge chamber of the SCC approved all the plea bargains and convicted the eight co-perpetrators in judgments dated 19 December 2012 and 7 March 2013. The operative factual findings in those judgments referred to the applicant by initials or an alias, and in the underlying agreements by his full name. They described him as a mid-ranking member who gave instructions, ordered extortion, imposed and enforced internal penalties, arranged a forcible taking of money, and received or distributed proceeds. The judgments contained no ordinary evidentiary reasoning; they mainly recited the procedural history, confirmed compliance with plea-bargaining rules, and endorsed the agreed penalties. They became final on delivery and bound only the convicted persons.

The applicant was later tried separately by the SCC before a chamber with identical composition. On 7 August 2013, he was convicted as charged and sentenced to 23 years’ imprisonment. The factual definitions of his offences were essentially identical to those in the co-perpetrators’ judgments. The trial court noted that the co-perpetrators’ convictions were “a factual and homogenous part” of the case under examination and contained in the file. It relied on documentary, expert and witness evidence, including testimony from co-perpetrators, some of whom were cooperating “penitents.”

The applicant appealed, lodged an appeal on points of law, and later filed a constitutional complaint. He argued that his right to an impartial tribunal and his right to be presumed innocent had been violated because the same judges had earlier convicted his alleged co-perpetrators based on plea bargains and because those judgments prejudged his guilt. All remedies were dismissed, with the Constitutional Court delivering the final decision on 25 June 2019.

The domestic courts relied on a Supreme Court unifying decision (no. 15/2017), which held that a court approving a plea bargain takes no evidence, its decision binds only the convicted person, and the judge is not disqualified from later hearing a co-accused’s case. It also stated that the later court must make an autonomous assessment of evidence and cannot rely on the approved agreement. Slovak law later expressly provided that a prior decision concerning a co-accused does not constitute bias, and that plea-bargain references should not interfere with the presumption of innocence. EU law, including Directive 2016/343 and CJEU case-law, similarly required caution in referring to non-signatory co-perpetrators.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 6 § 1. The key facts were that the same chamber had previously issued convicting judgments against co-perpetrators, expressly identifying and incriminating the applicant, then sat in his trial; those earlier judgments were final and placed in his file. The higher courts failed to remedy the resulting objectively justified doubts about the tribunal’s impartiality and the prejudice to the applicant’s presumption of innocence.

Mucha v. Slovakia (Application no. 63703/19, ECtHR 25 November 2021) concerned Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, specifically the right to an impartial tribunal and the presumption of innocence in criminal proceedings.

The applicant, Pavel Mucha, a Slovak national, was allegedly a mid-ranking member of an organised criminal gang operating in Bratislava and other regions of Slovakia. In 2012 he and nine others were charged with setting up, conceiving and maintaining a criminal enterprise, as well as multiple violent offences. Although the prosecution was initially to be conducted jointly, eight co-perpetrators reached plea-bargaining agreements with the prosecution and were prosecuted separately.

The Specialised Criminal Court (SCC) approved those plea bargains in three judgments: one on 19 December 2012 and two on 7 March 2013. All three were delivered by the same three-judge chamber. The judgments were drafted like ordinary convicting judgments: they found the co-perpetrators guilty and included precise factual findings. Those findings referred to Mucha — by initials, alias, and in the underlying agreements by full name — as a mid-ranking superior who gave instructions on criminal activities, was to receive a percentage of extortion proceeds, imposed a financial penalty on a gang member and ordered its enforcement, and ordered or facilitated forcible debt collection and received/distributed its proceeds. The judgments contained no substantive reasoning on evidence; they merely recounted procedure, cited plea-bargain rules, and endorsed the agreements. They became final on delivery.

Mucha was later tried separately by an SCC chamber with an identical composition. On 7 August 2013 he was convicted as charged and sentenced to twenty-three years’ imprisonment. The factual definitions of his offences were essentially identical to those in the co-perpetrators’ judgments. The trial court noted that the co-perpetrators’ convictions were “a factual and homogenous part of the case under examination” and were contained in the file. The conviction relied largely on evidence from co-perpetrators who had agreed to collaborate with police, known as “penitents,” though the court said this was supported by indirect evidence.

Mucha appealed, lodged an appeal on points of law, and then a constitutional complaint. He argued that the same judges who had convicted his co-perpetrators based on plea bargains had already prejudged his guilt, violating his right to an impartial tribunal and the presumption of innocence. The higher courts dismissed his complaints. They relied on a Supreme Court unifying decision (no. 15/2017), which held that approving a plea bargain involved no evidence-taking, bound only the convicted person, and did not disqualify the judge or violate the presumption of innocence of others. The Constitutional Court found no constitutional defect and distinguished Ferrantelli, noting that Mucha had not argued the trial court cited extracts from the earlier judgments.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 6 § 1. The key facts were that the same chamber had already issued final conviction judgments against co-perpetrators containing detailed findings implicating Mucha, then tried him; those judgments used conviction language; and the trial court treated them as part of his case. The higher courts failed to remedy the resulting objectively justified doubts about the tribunal’s impartiality and the prejudice to Mucha’s right to be presumed innocent.

In *Mucha v. Slovakia*, the applicant, Pavel Mucha, was alleged to be a mid-ranking member of an organised criminal gang operating in Bratislava and other parts of Slovakia. On 1 February and 23 May 2012, he and nine others were charged with setting up, conceiving and maintaining a criminal enterprise and with multiple violent offences. Although the prosecution was initially joint, eight co-accused were later prosecuted separately because they were prepared to enter plea-bargaining agreements with the prosecution. Under Slovak law, such agreements required a confession and judicial approval; the approving court had to examine whether the alleged act occurred, whether it constituted an offence, whether the accused committed it, and whether the proposed penalty was adequate.

All eight co-perpetrators’ plea agreements were approved by the same three-judge chamber of the Specialised Criminal Court in judgments dated 19 December 2012 and 7 March 2013. These judgments became final on delivery. Crucially for the alleged violations, the operative factual findings in those judgments referred to Mucha. Although he was sometimes identified only by initials or an alias, the underlying plea agreements named him fully. The findings described him as a middle-ranking member who gave instructions for criminal activities, was to receive a percentage of an extortion, imposed and enforced a financial penalty on a group member, and ordered and arranged the forced taking of money from another member, later receiving and distributing its proceeds. The judgments contained no substantive reasoning beyond reciting the procedural history, the plea-bargaining rules, and the court’s conclusion that the agreements were not unjust and the penalties adequate.

In August 2013, the Specialised Criminal Court heard Mucha’s case separately. The chamber had the same composition as the one that had approved his co-perpetrators’ plea bargains. It convicted him as charged and sentenced him to twenty-three years’ imprisonment. The four sets of criminal actions for which he was convicted corresponded to the factual definitions already set out in the earlier co-perpetrator judgments. His conviction was based on documentary, expert and witness evidence, including testimony and statements from co-perpetrators. Some refused to testify; others incriminated him to varying degrees. The trial court expressly noted that the co-perpetrators’ convictions were “a factual and homogenous part of the case under examination” and were contained in the file. It also acknowledged that incriminating evidence came mainly from cooperating “penitents,” though it found that evidence supported by other material.

Mucha appealed, lodged an appeal on points of law, and ultimately filed a constitutional complaint. He argued that he had been denied an impartial tribunal and the presumption of innocence because the earlier judgments convicting his co-perpetrators—delivered by the same judges—had prejudged his role and prejudiced the assessment of his case. Domestic authorities dismissed his complaints. The Constitutional Court relied on a Supreme Court unifying decision holding that a judge approving a plea bargain does not violate the presumption of innocence of other persons mentioned in the factual definition and is not excluded from later related proceedings; it also noted that the plea-bargain court took no evidence and its judgment bound only the convicted person.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 6 § 1. It held that objectively justified doubts existed as to the trial court’s impartiality because the same court had previously convicted Mucha’s co-perpetrators based on plea bargains whose wording was prejudicial to his presumption of innocence, referring to him as a participant and organiser. The higher courts’ failure to remedy those defects was central to the violation.

**Case: Golub v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia (App. no. 48020/12), ECtHR Judgment, 30 November 2021**

The applicant, Nikolay Golub, a Russian national born in 1993 and living in Lunga, complained about compulsory military service in the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”). He alleged that his service amounted to forced labour under Article 4, unlawful detention/restrictions on liberty under Article 5 and Article 2 of Protocol No. 4, and a lack of effective remedies under Article 13.

In September 2011 the applicant was called up for compulsory military service in the “MRT.” As the sole caretaker of his disabled mother, he was entitled under “MRT” law to deferral. Instead, he and his mother opted for his enrolment in a military education institution under the “MRT” Ministry of Defence, which counted as military service and allowed him to obtain a diploma. As a cadet, his passport was taken away, he was issued a recruit card, and he could not leave the premises without the commander’s authorisation.

In November 2011 he left the military institute several times to seek medical treatment after alleged ill-treatment or to care for his mother. On his return, from 17 to 24 November 2011, he was disciplined for absence without leave and placed in isolation in the Tiraspol Military Command. There he was held in a cell with eight other persons and could leave only once per day to use the toilet.

On 2 December 2011 the “MRT” authorities opened a criminal investigation against him for absence without leave; it was discontinued on 27 January 2012 on non-rehabilitation grounds. On 20 December 2011 he was excluded from the military institute for lack of discipline and unwillingness to continue, and sent to “MRT military unit no. 40896” in Dubăsari to complete compulsory service. On 25 December 2011 he returned several hours late from authorised leave. According to him, he was asked to dig a trench as an informal sanction; when he refused, he was disciplined and isolated from 26 December 2011 to 9 January 2012 in the unit’s prison (“гауптвахта”). On 25 February 2012 the “MRT” Minister of Defence granted his request for early dismissal as sole caretaker of his disabled mother; he was informed on 27 February and left the unit.

In May 2012 the applicant complained to the Moldovan and Russian Prosecutor General’s Offices about unlawful deprivation of liberty. The Russian Military Prosecutor redirected the complaint to the Moldovan and “MRT” authorities. On 19 June 2012 the Moldovan Prosecutor General’s Office initiated a criminal investigation, but suspended it on 17 August 2012 until identification of the perpetrators.

Regarding Article 4, the applicant argued that compulsory service in an unrecognised entity constituted forced labour and was not covered by the military-service exception; he claimed his enrolment was not voluntary because draft evasion was criminal. The Moldovan Government argued he had voluntarily enrolled despite being entitled to deferral and that Moldova did not recognise “MRT” military obligations; the Russian Government made no specific submissions. The Court found the Article 4 complaint manifestly ill-founded, as the applicant had “offered himself voluntarily” and later obtained early dismissal.

As to Article 5 and Article 2 of Protocol No. 4, the applicant argued that all restrictions were unlawful because ordered by unrecognised “MRT” authorities and that he had not consented since military service was compulsory. He distinguished the military institute period, the isolation in Tiraspol, and the Dubăsari unit period. The Moldovan Government conceded that Article 5 applied to the isolation periods and that there was a violation because the detention was ordered by unrecognised authorities; it argued the remaining period fell under Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 and involved consent. The Russian Government made no specific submissions.

The Court also addressed jurisdiction: Moldova had jurisdiction but only positive obligations; Russia exercised effective control and decisive influence over the “MRT,” so the applicant fell within Russian jurisdiction. Exhaustion objections were rejected.

Lacatus v. Switzerland (no. 14065/15) is a 2021 European Court of Human Rights judgment concerning Switzerland’s blanket criminal ban on begging and its impact on a poor Roma woman. The applicant, Violeta-Sibianca Lacatus, a Romanian national, lived for periods in Geneva from 2011. Unable to find work, she resorted to begging. Under section 11A of the Geneva Criminal Law Act, begging on public highways is punishable by a fine. On 22 July 2011 she was fined CHF 100; CHF 16.75 was confiscated from her after a police body search. Between February 2012 and January 2013 she received eight further CHF 100 penalty notices for begging with a cup. On two occasions she was taken into police custody for three hours. Each fine could be replaced by one day’s imprisonment for non-payment. After objecting, in January 2014 the Geneva Police Court convicted her, imposed a consolidated CHF 500 fine convertible into five days’ imprisonment, and upheld the confiscation. The Criminal Appeals Division and the Federal Supreme Court dismissed her appeals. The Federal Supreme Court held that the ban did not violate Article 8 or 14; it found her begging had little communicative value under Article 10 because it was non-verbal, private, and lacked political or symbolic content. It also rejected indirect discrimination, stating there was no proof the law targeted Roma, and noted social assistance was available. In March 2015, after non-payment, Lacatus was imprisoned for five days in Champ-Dollon short-term prison.

Before the ECtHR, she alleged violations of Articles 8 (private life/personal liberty), 10 (freedom of expression), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination). The facts central to those complaints were her extreme poverty and vulnerability as a Roma woman; her resort to unintrusive begging to survive; the absence of aggressive, organised, or exploitative conduct on her part; and the automatic criminal sanction culminating in detention because she could not pay.

The ECtHR found Article 8 applicable and violated. It held that the right to call on other people for assistance falls within private life. Switzerland’s blanket criminal ban was exceptional among Council of Europe member States. Applied to a poor and vulnerable Roma woman for unintrusive begging, it produced a serious, automatic, and virtually inevitable sanction that diminished her human dignity. The Court found no sound public-interest reasons for punishing her specific conduct. Domestic courts had failed to conduct an in-depth examination of her individual situation, including her poverty and vulnerability. The measure was disproportionate for combating organised crime and protecting the rights of passers-by, residents, and shopkeepers, especially because less restrictive measures were available. Switzerland therefore overstepped the narrow margin of appreciation. The case establishes that criminalising non-aggressive begging and imposing imprisonment for non-payment can breach Article 8 when applied to highly vulnerable persons reduced to begging to survive.

**Lacatus v. Switzerland** (Application no. 14065/15), European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, judgment of 19 January 2021.

The applicant was a Romanian national and member of the Roma community. From 2011 she lived for periods in Geneva but, unable to find work, resorted to begging. Under section 11A of the Geneva Criminal Law Act, begging on the public highway was an offence punishable by a fine. In July 2011 she received an initial CHF 100 fine, and CHF 16.75 found on her was confiscated. Between February 2012 and January 2013 she received eight further CHF 100 fines for begging on the public highway using a cup. She was also twice taken into police custody for three hours. Each fine could be replaced by one day’s imprisonment if unpaid.

The applicant objected. In January 2014 the Police Court of the Canton of Geneva convicted her of begging and ordered her to pay CHF 500, replaceable by five days’ imprisonment, while upholding the confiscation. Her appeals failed. In April 2014 the Criminal Appeals Division held that the ban did not breach freedom of expression because she could make her social situation known by other means, and that there was no indirect discrimination because the law did not target only Roma people and poverty was not a protected ground. In September 2014 the Federal Supreme Court held that the ban violated neither Article 8 nor Article 14 of the Convention. It found that begging was non-verbal conduct lacking political or general symbolic content, conveying only her private need for help, and therefore was not protected by Article 10. It also found the confiscation not arbitrary. In March 2015 the applicant was imprisoned for five days for non-payment of the fine.

Before the ECtHR, she alleged violations of Articles 8, 10 and 14 of the Convention. Article 8 concerned respect for private life, personal liberty and human dignity; Article 10 concerned freedom of expression; Article 14 concerned discrimination, particularly indirect discrimination against Roma and poor people.

The domestic authorities justified the ban as necessary to maintain public order, safety and tranquillity, prevent harassment, protect passers-by, residents and shopkeepers, combat exploitation and organised crime, and protect minors. They also relied on the existence of social assistance and on the Federal Supreme Court’s earlier abstract approval of the Geneva ban. The ECtHR, however, found Article 8 applicable to the right to call on others for assistance. It emphasised that the applicant was poor and vulnerable and that her begging was unintrusive. The fine and subsequent imprisonment for non-payment amounted to a serious, automatic and virtually inevitable sanction that diminished her human dignity. The domestic courts had failed to conduct an in-depth examination of her specific situation or to consider less restrictive measures. There were no sound public-interest reasons justifying the blanket criminal ban in her case. The Court found the measure disproportionate for combating organised crime and protecting the rights of passers-by, residents and shopkeepers. It therefore held that Switzerland had violated Article 8 and had overstepped the narrow margin of appreciation. The judgment underscores that blanket criminal bans on non-aggressive begging by highly vulnerable persons may breach the Convention’s protection of private life and dignity.

**Lacatus v. Switzerland** (Application no. 14065/15) concerned Violeta-Sibianca Lacatus, a Romanian national of Roma origin, born in 1992 and living in Bistrita-Nassaud, Romania. From 2011 she spent periods in Geneva but, unable to find work, resorted to begging. Under section 11A of the Geneva Criminal Law Act, begging on the public highway is an offence punishable by a fine. On 22 July 2011 she received an initial CHF 100 fine, and CHF 16.75 was confiscated from her after a police body search. She received eight further CHF 100 fines on various dates between February 2012 and January 2013 for begging on the public highway using a cup. On two occasions she was taken into police custody for three hours. Each fine could be replaced by one day’s imprisonment if unpaid.

Lacatus, represented by counsel, objected to the penalties. In January 2014 the Police Court of the Canton of Geneva convicted her of begging and ordered her to pay CHF 500, replaceable by five days’ imprisonment if she failed to pay. It also upheld confiscation of the CHF 16.75. She appealed, arguing inter alia violations of freedom of expression, personal liberty, human dignity, and indirect discrimination under Article 14 of the Convention read with section 11A. In April 2014 the Criminal Appeals Division dismissed her complaints, finding no infringement of freedom of expression and no indirect discrimination because the law did not target only Roma persons. The Federal Supreme Court dismissed her further appeal in September 2014. It held that the begging ban breached neither Article 8 nor Article 14, and that her conduct lacked sufficient communicative or symbolic content to attract Article 10 protection. It also found the confiscation was not arbitrary. From 24 to 28 March 2015 Lacatus was imprisoned in Champ-Dollon short-term prison for non-payment of the fine.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, she alleged violations of Articles 8, 10, and 14 of the Convention. The Court focused on Article 8, which protects private life, and found a violation. It considered that Article 8 was applicable because the right to call on other people for assistance—through begging—falls within the scope of private life. The Court emphasized that the applicant was a poor and vulnerable Roma woman who had been reduced to begging to survive. The Swiss blanket ban, enforced through criminal law, was exceptional among Council of Europe member States. The fine and subsequent imprisonment for unintrusive begging amounted to a serious, automatic, and virtually inevitable sanction that diminished her human dignity. The Court found no sound public-interest reasons justifying the measure in her specific case. Domestic courts had failed to conduct an in-depth examination of her particular situation, including her poverty, possible eligibility for social assistance, and the availability of less restrictive measures. The Court held that the blanket criminal ban was disproportionate as a means of combating organised crime and protecting passers-by, residents, and shopkeepers. Switzerland had overstepped its narrow margin of appreciation. The judgment became final on 19 April 2021.

Case No. 76892/14, *Șcerbinina v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia*, concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Ms Irina Șcerbinina, is a Moldovan national born in 1981 who lives in Tiraspol. In 2013 she was dismissed from employment. She brought civil proceedings against her employer seeking reinstatement, but she did so before the courts of the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”). Those proceedings ended on 5 June 2014 with a final judgment of the MRT Supreme Court dismissing her action. The central alleged violation is that the civil proceedings before the MRT courts did not satisfy Article 6 § 1 because those courts could not qualify as “independent tribunals established by law.” Thus, the key facts concern not the dismissal itself, but the judicial forum in which her reinstatement claim was heard and finally rejected.

After the MRT proceedings, the applicant complained to the authorities of the Republic of Moldova. The Bender District Prosecutor’s Office initiated a criminal investigation into her complaints, but the proceedings were later discontinued on the ground that the facts did not disclose the elements of a criminal offence. The applicant lodged her application with the European Court of Human Rights on 4 December 2014 against both the Republic of Moldova and Russia. She was represented by Ms N. Hriplivîi, a lawyer practising in Chișinău.

Because the application was directed against two respondent States, the Court first had to determine jurisdiction under Article 1 of the Convention. The applicant submitted that both Governments had jurisdiction. The Moldovan Government submitted that they had positive obligations to secure the applicant’s rights. The Russian Government argued that the applicant did not fall within Russian jurisdiction and that the application should therefore be declared inadmissible *ratione personae* and *ratione loci* in respect of Russia. This jurisdictional dispute is central because the alleged Article 6 violation arose in Transdniestria, a region whose status and control are disputed between Moldova and Russia.

The background to the case includes the Transdniestrian armed conflict of 1991–1992 and subsequent events, as set out in *Ilaşcu and Others v. Moldova and Russia* and *Catan and Others v. Moldova and Russia*. The relevant legal framework, including reports by inter-governmental and non-governmental organisations, Moldovan domestic law and practice, and other documents, was summarised in *Mozer v. Moldova and Russia*. These materials provide context for assessing whether the MRT courts could be considered “independent tribunals established by law” and whether either respondent State bore responsibility.

Procedurally, the Court gave notice of the application to both Governments. The Russian Government objected to the examination of the application by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection. The parties submitted observations. The Second Section, sitting as a Committee composed of Judges Ranzoni, Kūris and Koskelo, with Hasan Bakırcı as Deputy Section Registrar, deliberated in private on 8 June 2021 and delivered the judgment on 29 June 2021. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

In essence, the case focuses on the applicant’s unsuccessful civil reinstatement proceedings before the MRT Supreme Court, the finality of that judgment on 5 June 2014, her related but discontinued criminal complaint in Moldova, and her claim that these proceedings denied her a fair trial before a tribunal established by law. The main legal issue is whether the respondent States had jurisdiction and responsibility under the Convention in respect of that alleged violation.

In *Șcerbinina v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* (Application no. 76892/14, judgment of 29 June 2021), the European Court of Human Rights examined an application brought by Ms Irina Șcerbinina, a Moldovan national born in 1981 and living in Tiraspol. The case concerned an alleged denial of a fair trial under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention as a result of civil proceedings before the courts of the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”). The applicant argued that those courts could not qualify as “independent tribunals established by law” within the meaning of Article 6 § 1.

The broader factual background concerns the Transdniestrian armed conflict of 1991–1992 and subsequent developments, as already described in *Ilaşcu and Others v. Moldova and Russia* and *Catan and Others v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia*. In 2013, the applicant was dismissed from her employment. She then initiated reinstatement proceedings against her employer before the courts of the MRT. Those proceedings ended with the final judgment of the Supreme Court of the “MRT” on 5 June 2014, which dismissed her action. Since the applicant lived in Tiraspol and the proceedings took place within the MRT judicial system, her central complaint was that she had been denied a fair hearing before a tribunal meeting Convention standards. She later complained to the Moldovan authorities, and the Bender District Prosecutor’s Office initiated a criminal investigation into her complaints. However, those criminal proceedings were discontinued on the ground that the facts complained of did not disclose the elements of a criminal offence.

The applicant lodged her application under Article 34 of the Convention on 4 December 2014 against both the Republic of Moldova and Russia. Both Governments were given notice of the application. The Russian Government objected to the examination of the application by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection. The applicant submitted that both respondent Governments had jurisdiction. The Moldovan Government submitted that it had positive obligations to secure the applicant’s rights. The Russian Government, by contrast, argued that the applicant did not fall within its jurisdiction and that the application should therefore be declared inadmissible *ratione personae* and *ratione loci* in respect of Russia.

As a preliminary issue, the Court had to determine whether the applicant fell within the jurisdiction of the respondent States for the purposes of the matters complained of, within the meaning of Article 1 of the Convention. The relevant legal framework, including reports by inter-governmental and non-governmental organisations, Moldovan domestic law and practice, and other pertinent documents, was summarised in *Mozer v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia*.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore: the applicant’s 2013 dismissal from employment; her attempt to obtain reinstatement through civil proceedings before the MRT courts; the final MRT Supreme Court judgment of 5 June 2014 dismissing her action; and the fact that those proceedings allegedly took place before a judicial system that was not an independent tribunal established by law under Article 6 § 1. The case also raises complex issues of jurisdiction and attribution, namely whether Moldova and/or Russia can be held responsible under the Convention for the operation of the MRT judicial system in Transdniestria.

In the case of Șcerbinina v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia (Application no. 76892/14), the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) delivered judgment on 29 June 2021. The applicant, Ms Irina Șcerbinina, is a Moldovan national born in 1981 who lives in Tiraspol. She complained that she had been denied a fair trial, contrary to Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, because civil proceedings concerning her employment were conducted before the courts of the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”), which could not qualify as “independent tribunals established by law.”

The factual background involves the Transdniestrian armed conflict of 1991–1992 and the establishment of the unrecognised MRT within Moldova. The Court had previously set out this context in Ilaşcu and Others v. Moldova and Russia and Catan and Others v. Moldova and Russia. Relevant domestic law, practice and international reports were summarised in Mozer v. Moldova and Russia.

The key facts are that in 2013 the applicant was dismissed from her employment. She brought reinstatement proceedings against her employer before the MRT courts. Those proceedings ended with a final judgment of the MRT Supreme Court on 5 June 2014, which dismissed her action. Thus, her civil employment dispute was finally determined by a court system of an unrecognised entity. The applicant later complained to the Moldovan authorities. A criminal investigation was initiated by the Bender District Prosecutor’s Office, but it was subsequently discontinued on the ground that the facts complained of did not disclose the elements of a criminal offence. No effective redress followed.

The alleged violation therefore centres on the fact that the applicant was required to pursue her civil claim before MRT courts that allegedly lacked the independence and legal basis required by Article 6 § 1. Because the MRT is not an internationally recognised state, the Court first had to determine whether the applicant fell within the jurisdiction of Moldova and/or Russia under Article 1 of the Convention. The applicant argued that both respondent Governments had jurisdiction. The Moldovan Government submitted that it had positive obligations to secure the applicant’s rights. The Russian Government argued that the applicant did not fall within its jurisdiction and that the application should be declared inadmissible ratione personae and ratione loci in respect of Russia. The Russian Government also objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

The Court’s assessment thus concerned whether the respondent States could be held responsible for the acts of the MRT authorities and its courts. The facts relevant to the alleged violation are that the applicant’s employment dispute was adjudicated by an unrecognised court system, her final appeal was dismissed by the MRT Supreme Court in June 2014, and her complaint to Moldovan authorities led to a criminal investigation that was discontinued without redress. The case forms part of the ECtHR’s Transdniestria jurisprudence, in which the Court examines Russia’s effective control over the region and Moldova’s positive obligations to protect Convention rights. The application was lodged on 4 December 2014.
