**Case: Špadijer v. Montenegro** (Application no. 31549/18, ECtHR, 9 November 2021)

The applicant, Daliborka Špadijer, worked as a prison guard at the Institute for the Execution of Criminal Sanctions in Podgorica, Montenegro. From June 2012 she temporarily covered the position of head of shift in the women’s prison. In January 2013 she reported five colleagues for indecent conduct on New Year’s Eve. Disciplinary proceedings later established that male guards had entered the women’s prison, that one had had “physical contact” with two inmates, and that some female guards had tolerated this.

After her report, the applicant alleged a campaign of retaliation and bullying. On 12 January 2013 a colleague, N.R., allegedly warned her that she should not have reported the others, that many colleagues were against her, and that she should be prepared for anything. The next night the windscreen of her car was smashed. In March 2013 a prison driver refused to take her home and allegedly said she was “known for [her] sharp tongue and behaviour.” In June 2013 another colleague, A.V., allegedly insulted her, spat near her, and called her a “stinking bitch.” She reported this, but the governor allegedly told her the cameras were not working, although another officer said they were.

Between January and August 2013 she also claimed that she was forbidden to organise duty shifts, that colleagues ignored her and failed to perform tasks she assigned, that her reports about prisoners were ignored, and that she was ordered to make coffee for a prisoner. In August 2013 she formally requested protection against bullying. The mediator dismissed her request as unfounded, finding that the conduct was not continuous, that some incidents occurred outside the workplace, and that her transfer was due to poor performance. Civil proceedings followed. An expert found that she suffered post-traumatic stress disorder and an adjustment disorder, with a permanent 20% reduction in functioning. In February 2015, shortly before the civil court ruled, she was assaulted in a car park; the attacker told her, “Be careful what you’re doing.” She reported it the next morning, but the perpetrator was never identified.

In February 2015 the Court of First Instance ruled against her. It accepted her factual claims but held that the conduct did not amount to bullying because it lacked the required frequency—at least once a week for six months. It also failed to examine several alleged incidents. The High Court and Supreme Court upheld that judgment, and the Constitutional Court dismissed her appeal in 2017. The Constitutional Court made no reference to her criminal complaints or the authorities’ alleged failure to act on them.

The ECtHR examined the complaint under Article 8 of the Convention. It found Article 8 applicable and held that Montenegro had violated its positive obligation to protect the applicant from bullying. The domestic authorities had implemented civil and criminal law in a flawed manner, applied an overly rigid frequency requirement, failed to consider the cumulative effect of the incidents, and ignored the overall context, including the possibility that the alleged bullying was retaliation for her whistle-blowing. The Court also criticised the failure to deal properly with her criminal complaints concerning the car damage and the assault.

In *Špadijer v. Montenegro* (Application no. 31549/18, judgment 9 November 2021), the applicant, Daliborka Špadijer, was a Montenegrin prison guard at the Institute for the Execution of Criminal Sanctions in Podgorica and temporarily covered the position of head of shift at the women’s prison. In January 2013 she reported five colleagues for indecent conduct on New Year’s Eve: male guards had entered the women’s prison, one had physical contact with two inmates, and some female guards tolerated it. Afterward, colleague N.R. warned her that she should not have reported them, that many colleagues were against her, and that she should be prepared for anything. On 13 January 2013 her car windscreen was smashed outside her home; video footage apparently showed the perpetrator. Police interviewed N.R., but the prosecutor found no criminal or misdemeanour elements. She later reported other workplace irregularities without response. In March 2013 a driver refused to take her home and insulted her. The reported colleagues were later disciplined. In June 2013 A.V. insulted her as a “stinking bitch,” said she would look acceptable if she lost 50kg, and spat near her. Her report led to no effective action; an assistant governor said she would be transferred and no longer be head of shift. The governor confronted A.V.; cameras were said not to be working although the applicant learned they were.

From January to August 2013 she alleged further bullying: she was barred from organising duty shifts, colleagues ignored her and refused allocated tasks without sanction, her report about a prisoner was ignored (the prisoner said the applicant would soon be fired), she was ordered to make coffee for a prisoner, and was criticised for complaining. On 16 August 2013 she requested protection against bullying, describing continuous insults, humiliation and health problems. She went on sick leave in September 2013. The mediator dismissed her request as unfounded, finding the conduct insufficiently continuous, the car and N.R. incidents outside the workplace, and her transfer due to poor job performance.

She brought civil proceedings in November 2013. An expert found PTSD and an adjustment disorder with reactive psychosis, causing permanent 20% reduction in functioning. On 10 February 2015, shortly before the civil judgment, she was assaulted in a car park; the attacker said “Be careful what you’re doing.” She suffered injuries, but police and the prosecutor could not identify the attacker. On 19 February 2015 the civil court ruled against her. It accepted her account but found no bullying because the incidents were not frequent enough—requiring repetition at least weekly for six months—and did not amount to systematic ill-treatment. It failed to examine several allegations. Appeals were dismissed; the Supreme Court suggested bullying as discrimination required treatment based on personal characteristics. The Constitutional Court dismissed her appeal without addressing the criminal complaints.

The ECtHR examined the case under Article 8, concerning psychological integrity and positive obligations. The key alleged violation was the State’s failure to protect her from workplace bullying and its flawed implementation of civil and criminal law. The Court found that the domestic authorities applied an overly rigid frequency test, ignored the overall context and cumulative effect of the incidents, failed to consider that she may have been targeted as a whistle-blower, and did not properly deal with her criminal complaints. It found a violation of Article 8.

In *Špadijer v. Montenegro* (Application no. 31549/18), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Montenegro failed to protect the applicant from workplace bullying, in violation of her psychological integrity under Article 8. The applicant, Daliborka Špadijer, worked as a prison guard and temporarily as head of shift at the Institute for the Execution of Criminal Sanctions in Podgorica. In January 2013, she reported several colleagues for indecent behaviour on New Year’s Eve at the women’s prison. Retaliation followed.

On 12 January 2013, a colleague, N.R., warned her that she should not have reported the others, that many colleagues were against her, and that she should “prepare for anything.” The next night, the windscreen of her car was smashed outside her home. She complained to the police and provided video footage, but the State prosecutor found no criminal offence or misdemeanour. In February 2013, she allegedly reported other work irregularities but received no response. On 8 March 2013, a prison driver refused to take her home, referring to her “sharp tongue and behaviour.” On 20 March 2013, the colleagues she had reported were disciplined and fined.

On 24 June 2013, one of the reported colleagues, A.V., insulted her, called her a “stinking bitch,” said she would look acceptable only if she lost 50 kilograms, and spat near her. When she reported this, the assistant governor said she would be transferred and would no longer be head of shift. The governor later confronted A.V.; when the applicant suggested checking CCTV, the governor claimed the cameras were not working, although an officer said they were. Between January and August 2013, she also alleged that she was prevented from organising shifts, ignored by colleagues, that subordinates refused tasks without sanction, that her report on a prisoner was ignored, and that she was ordered to make coffee for a prisoner. On 16 August 2013, she requested protection against bullying (“mobbing”).

In November 2013, the employer’s mediator dismissed her request as unfounded, finding the alleged conduct insufficiently continuous. The incidents involving N.R. and her car were deemed outside the workplace, and her transfer was attributed to poor performance. She then brought civil proceedings. An expert found that she suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder, adjustment disorder, and reactive psychosis, with a permanent 20% reduction in functioning linked to conflict at work.

On 10 February 2015, shortly before the civil judgment, she was assaulted in a car park; the attacker struck her neck, back, elbow, and thighs and said, “Be careful what you’re doing.” Police and the prosecutor failed to identify the attacker. On 19 February 2015, the civil court ruled against her despite accepting her factual submissions and the expert’s link to workplace conflict. It held that bullying required systematic repetition—at least once a week for six months—which the incidents lacked. Appeals were dismissed. The Supreme Court suggested bullying as discrimination required treatment based on personal characteristics. The Constitutional Court dismissed her appeal in November 2017 without addressing the criminal complaints.

The applicant was on sick leave from September 2013 and retired in May 2016 due to complete loss of working capacity; the Pension Fund noted her psychological problems began in 2013 after work stress. The Ombudsman found no rights violation. The ECtHR held there had been a violation of Article 8: the authorities failed to protect her from bullying, flawed the civil and criminal law implementation, and failed to consider the overall context, including possible whistle-blowing.

**Case:** *Moroşanu and Others v. Romania* (Applications nos. 84271/17 and four others), European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, judgment of 16 March 2021.

The case concerned five Romanian nationals who complained under Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights that Romania failed to conduct an effective investigation within a reasonable time into the events of the Romanian Revolution in December 1989 in Bucharest and Reșița. During those events, the applicants or their close relatives were shot and either injured or killed while taking part in demonstrations that led to the fall of the communist regime.

The applicants’ circumstances differed. Mr Moroşanu (application no. 84271/17) was injured by gunshot, required medical care for one year and three months, and was left with a permanent infirmity. Mr Iordan (application no. 2666/18) was also shot and needed between twenty-three and twenty-five days of medical care. The remaining applicants’ close relatives were killed by gunshot during the same events. The applicants alleged that the shootings formed part of a violent crackdown on civilian demonstrators and that the subsequent State investigation was unreasonably prolonged and ineffective.

In 1990, the military prosecutor’s office attached to the High Court of Cassation and Justice opened, on its own motion, a criminal investigation into illegal detention, ill-treatment, injury, and related events of December 1989. This became the main investigation, file no. 97/P/1990, later renumbered 11/P/2014. Between 1991 and 2006, in separate proceedings concerning the applicants or their relatives, prosecutors either declined to open an investigation or discontinued proceedings. Those cases were nevertheless examined within the main criminal investigation, and the applicants brought civil claims.

The main investigation progressed slowly. On 14 October 2015, the military prosecutor’s office closed it, finding that some complaints were statute-barred, some covered by amnesty, some ill-founded, some not classifiable as offences, and some res judicata. That closure decision was annulled by the Prosecutor General on 5 April 2016, confirmed by the High Court of Cassation and Justice on 13 June 2016. On 1 November 2016, the military prosecutor ordered a fresh *in rem* investigation for crimes against humanity concerning the same facts. On 5 April 2019, the military prosecutor’s office sent to trial several former high-ranking officials—including a former president, a former prime minister, and a former commander of the Romanian air force—for crimes against humanity. It discontinued proceedings against other individuals because some charges were res judicata, some suspects had died, or some facts could not be classified as criminal offences. Those proceedings remained pending before the Preliminary Chamber of the High Court of Cassation and Justice.

Before the European Court, the applicants relied mainly on Article 2, which protects the right to life and requires an effective official investigation where individuals are killed or seriously injured. They argued that the Romanian authorities had failed to carry out such an investigation within a reasonable time. The Government accepted that Mr Iordan had been shot but contended that his injuries were not life-threatening and should be analysed under Article 3. The Court, as master of the legal characterisation of the facts, considered the massive use of firearms against civilian demonstrators and decided to examine all complaints under Article 2. It found the complaint neither manifestly ill-founded nor inadmissible on other grounds and declared it admissible.

**Liebscher v Austria** (App. no. 5434/17), European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, judgment of 6 April 2021 (final 6 July 2021).

The applicant, Christoph-Herwig Liebscher, an Austrian national born in 1957, divorced by mutual consent in 2013. Under section 55a(2) of the Austrian Marriage Act, he and his former wife concluded a divorce settlement before the Döbling District Court, acting as the family court. The settlement regulated the division of matrimonial assets, custody and residence of their two minor children, and alimony, and contained an overview of the applicant’s assets and income.

In December 2015, the applicant asked the same court, acting as the land register court, to enter into the public land register the transfer of his share in the former matrimonial real estate to his ex-wife. Instead of the full divorce settlement, he submitted a partial engrossment/excerpt issued by the family court. The excerpt was expressly labelled “excerpt from the … divorce settlement” and reproduced only the chapter concerning “real estate.” It also stated that it contained all agreements pertaining to the real estate property.

The land register court rejected the application. Under section 87(1) of the Land Register Act, an application for registration must be accompanied by the “originals” of the relevant documents. For court settlements, the engrossment is deemed the original, but it must be presented in full; an excerpt is not sufficient. Under section 94(1), the land register court must comprehensively examine the application and supporting documents and may approve the entry only if the request is justified by the enclosed documents and those documents are in the required form. The court held it could not determine from the excerpt whether the full settlement contained conditions or legally relevant facts affecting registration. The Vienna Regional Civil Court upheld that decision. The Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s extraordinary appeal, relying on earlier precedent that a partial engrossment is insufficient and that the family court could not bind the land register court by confirming that the excerpt contained everything relevant.

The applicant alleged a violation of Article 8 of the Convention. He argued that requiring the entire divorce settlement would make highly personal and sensitive data publicly accessible in the land register’s document archive, because the Austrian land register is open to the public. That data included the names and places of residence of his minor children and former spouse, alimony amounts, custody arrangements, and his financial circumstances. He claimed there was no legitimate aim or sufficient public interest outweighing his privacy rights, and relied on the Data Protection Act and EU Charter. He also complained under Article 13 that no effective domestic remedy existed, and under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that refusal of the transfer impaired his property rights.

The Supreme Court rejected the Article 8 complaint, stating that examination of the entire document was mandatory under sections 87 and 94 of the Land Register Act and served the protection of registered property rights. It also found no reason to refer the case to the CJEU or Constitutional Court.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 8. It held that the requirement to submit the full divorce settlement, containing personal data, fell within the ambit of Article 8 and engaged Austria’s positive obligations. However, the domestic courts failed to conduct a comprehensive assessment of whether that requirement was compatible with the applicant’s effective enjoyment of his privacy rights, and they failed to address the Convention issue at stake.

**CASE OF LIEBSCHER v. AUSTRIA**  
*(Application no. 5434/17, European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, judgment of 6 April 2021)*

The applicant, Christoph-Herwig Liebscher, an Austrian national living in Vienna, divorced by mutual consent on 21 May 2013. Before the Döbling District Court, sitting as a family court, he and his former wife concluded a divorce settlement under section 55a(2) of the Marriage Act. The settlement regulated the division of matrimonial assets, custody and residence of their two minor children, alimony, and included an overview of the applicant’s assets and income. It therefore contained highly personal and sensitive data.

In December 2015, the applicant asked the same court, acting as the land register court, to register the transfer of his share in the former couple’s joint real property to his divorced wife. Instead of the full divorce settlement, he submitted a partial engrossment designated as an “excerpt from the divorce settlement,” reproducing only the chapter on real estate. The family court noted that the excerpt contained all agreements pertaining to the real estate.

The land register court rejected the application on 25 February 2016. It held that a partial engrossment was not the “original” required by section 87 of the 1955 Land Register Act (LRA). Under section 94(1) LRA, the land register court had to examine the application and supporting documents comprehensively. With only an excerpt, it could not verify whether the settlement contained conditions or other legally relevant facts affecting registration. Only the complete version could count as the original. The court also noted that the land register is public under section 7(1) LRA.

The applicant appealed. He argued that the refusal infringed his right to dispose of his property. He further claimed that requiring the full settlement would make personal data publicly accessible in the land register’s document archive, including the names and addresses of his minor children and former wife, alimony amounts, and custody arrangements. He alleged a violation of Article 8 of the Convention, the Austrian Data Protection Act, and Article 52 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, arguing that no legitimate aim or public interest justified publishing such private data.

The Vienna Regional Civil Court rejected the appeal on 25 April 2016, confirming that an excerpt did not satisfy section 87(1) LRA and that the land register court itself had to examine the complete document. It found a legal basis for any interference with data protection rights. On 24 June 2016, the applicant filed an extraordinary appeal with the Supreme Court, repeating his data-protection arguments and requesting referrals to the Court of Justice of the European Union and the Constitutional Court. The Supreme Court rejected the appeal on 11 July 2016. It held that submission of a partial engrossment was insufficient and that the family court could not bind the land register court on whether the excerpt contained all relevant agreements. It dismissed the Article 8 concerns, stating that examination of the entire document was mandatory under sections 87(1) and 94(1) LRA and served the protection of property rights. The inclusion of documents in the land register’s document archive was not the subject of the decision.

The case concerned the obligation to file the full divorce settlement—containing personal data—with the public land register to transfer property. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 8, holding that the domestic courts had failed to comply with their procedural obligation to conduct a comprehensive assessment of whether that requirement was compatible with the effective enjoyment of the applicant’s privacy rights and to address the Convention issue at stake.

In **Liebscher v. Austria** (Application no. 5434/17), the applicant, an Austrian national born in 1957, divorced by mutual consent in May 2013. The divorce settlement, concluded before the Döbling District Court acting as a family court, regulated the division of matrimonial assets, custody and residence of the two minor children, alimony, and included an overview of the applicant’s assets and income. In December 2015, the applicant asked the same court, acting as a land register court, to register the transfer of his share in the former couple’s joint real property to his ex-wife. Instead of the full settlement, he submitted a partial engrossment described as an “excerpt from the divorce settlement,” reproducing only the chapter on real estate and noting that it contained all agreements pertaining to the property.

The land register court rejected the application in February 2016. It held that under section 87 of the Land Register Act, the “original” document had to be presented and that an excerpt was insufficient. It also relied on section 94(1), which required comprehensive examination of the application and attachments, including whether the settlement contained conditions or other legally relevant facts affecting registration. Because only an excerpt was submitted, the court could not conduct that examination. The Vienna Regional Civil Court dismissed the appeal in April 2016, confirming that a partial engrossment was not the original and that the land register court, rather than the family court, had to determine whether all relevant property agreements were included. In July 2016, the Supreme Court rejected an extraordinary appeal, relying on prior case-law that a full engrossment was mandatory. It also rejected the applicant’s data-protection objections, stating that examination of the entire document was required by sections 87(1) and 94(1) and served the protection of registered property rights.

The alleged violations mainly arose from the public nature of the Austrian land register. Under section 7(1) of the Land Register Act, the register is open to the public and may be consulted without restriction; documents supporting entries are kept in the document archive, now stored electronically. The applicant complained that requiring the full divorce settlement to be submitted and archived would make highly personal and sensitive data publicly accessible, including the names and residences of the minor children and his former wife, alimony amounts, custody arrangements, and details of his assets and income. He argued that this breached his right to respect for private life and personal data under Article 8 of the Convention, was not justified by any legitimate aim outweighing his privacy interests, and violated national and EU data-protection law. He also alleged that no effective domestic remedy existed under Article 13 and that refusal to register the transfer interfered with his property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The European Court of Human Rights found that the requirement to enter the full divorce settlement containing personal data into the public land register fell within the ambit of Article 8 and engaged Austria’s positive obligations. The domestic courts, however, failed to conduct a comprehensive assessment of whether that requirement was compatible with the effective enjoyment of the applicant’s privacy rights and failed to address the Convention issue at stake. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 8 based on this procedural failure.
001-209358:
**Omdahl v. Norway** concerned an Article 6 § 1 complaint that the administration of a deceased person’s estate in Norway exceeded the “reasonable time” requirement. The applicant, Olav Omdahl, was a Norwegian national whose grandfather, O.A. Knutsen, died on 24 April 1993. The estate was substantial: assets worth approximately NOK 100 million, debt of about NOK 10 million, including property, shares, securities and moveable property. The heirs were three children and two grandchildren. Public administration began before the Probate Court on 5 May 1993 and lasted 22 years and 4 months, ending in 2015.

The administration was exceptionally complex. Early disputes concerning the will and codicil, especially heirs’ rights to receive assets in kind, prevented the realisation of estate assets until around 2005/06. Probate Court decisions to convert assets into cash were quashed or amended on appeal. A Bahamas trust, managed by a London bank, emerged after the applicant’s mother died in 2002; in December 2005 each child and grandchild received NOK 5.5 million from it. The trust also generated disputes over whether funds belonged to the estate and led to complex tax questions, clarified by tax authorities only in 2010.

An interim distribution occurred on 1 July 2010, giving each branch NOK 10 million; the appeal was dismissed in 2011. Disputes over the sale of shares, property companies and a fish oil factory continued, with sales mostly completed in 2013 and remaining companies wound up in December 2013. Final distribution was decided on 1 August 2014, upheld by the High Court in November 2014, with the Supreme Court refusing leave to appeal in April 2015. Final disbursement followed on 16 April 2015, giving each family branch approximately NOK 18.9 million. A later distribution in August 2015 entailed no payments.

The applicant sued the Norwegian Government in 2016, seeking a declaratory judgment and compensation for the alleged Article 6 violation. The City Court found no violation, noting the estate’s complexity, the litigiousness of other heirs, no proven inactivity, and no blame attributable to the State. The High Court agreed in 2018 that Article 6 applied but found no violation: the administration was extraordinary and highly complex, there were no pure periods of inactivity, the State could not legally have done more, and interim distributions had reduced the disadvantages. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal in June 2018.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant argued that the sheer length indicated inactivity or ineffective activity, particularly claiming that a 1997 High Court ruling blocked progress on priority claims and assets in kind. He said the estate could have been finalised earlier. The Government argued that estate administration was a service and framework for multiple disputes, not ordinary proceedings, and that this was an unprecedented, complex case in which no structural shortcomings existed. The applicant and other heirs had also engaged in litigation, while interim payments partly protected heirs’ interests.

The ECtHR held that Article 6 was applicable because estate administration involved a mixture of contentious and non-contentious elements and could determine civil rights. The application was admissible, but on the merits the Court found no violation. It emphasised the exceptional complexity, the numerous disputes, the absence of inactivity attributable to the authorities, the fact that the length was not caused by shortcomings in the legal or procedural framework, and that interim distributions reduced the heirs’ disadvantages. Although the administration lasted over 22 years, the Court concluded that, in these extraordinary circumstances, the duration was not excessive.

Omdahl v Norway concerned whether the administration of a deceased’s estate over 22 years and 4 months violated the Article 6 §1 “reasonable time” requirement. The applicant, Olav Omdahl, was a grandson of O.A. Knutsen, who died in April 1993. The estate was worth about NOK 100 million, with NOK 10 million debt, and consisted mainly of property, shares, securities, and wholly or partly owned companies. The heirs included three children and two grandchildren; Omdahl’s mother died before final distribution.

Public estate administration began on 5 May 1993 before the Probate Court, with an appointed administrator. The process generated numerous disputes. Early disputes over the will and codicil, especially heirs’ rights to receive assets in kind, tied up proceeds until 2005/06, and Probate Court liquidation decisions were quashed or amended on appeal. A Bahamas trust managed by a London bank came to light after the applicant’s mother died in 2002; in December 2005 each child and grandchild received NOK 5.5 million. The trust also raised ownership and tax disputes, clarified with tax authorities by winter 2010. An interim distribution on 1 July 2010 gave NOK 10 million per family branch; appeals were dismissed in 2011. Further disputes over share sales, a property company, a fish-oil factory, and judicial impartiality ended by 2012; sales were largely completed in 2013 and remaining companies wound up in December 2013. Final distribution was decided on 1 August 2014, upheld after appeals, and disbursed on 16 April 2015, with about NOK 18.9 million per branch. Administration ended after 22 years and 4 months.

In 2016 the applicant sued the Norwegian Government, seeking a declaration and compensation for an Article 6 violation. The City Court found no violation despite the length, citing complexity, numerous legal actions by heirs, no proven inactivity, and no State blame. The High Court accepted Article 6 applied but also found no violation. It described the administration as extraordinary: very large assets, multiple complex disputes, trust and tax complications, property-sale difficulties, and no periods of pure inactivity. The Probate Court had attempted progress, including interim distributions, and no alternative material steps were available to the State. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal in June 2018.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant argued that the length itself showed inactivity or ineffective activity, particularly because a 1997 High Court ruling allegedly blocked asset realisation. The Government argued that estate administration was an administrative service and framework for disputes, that the case was extraordinarily complex, that there were no structural shortcomings, and that interim payments partly protected the applicant’s pecuniary interests.

The ECtHR held Article 6 applicable because estate administration mixed contentious and non-contentious elements and could decisively determine heirs’ civil rights. On the merits, considering the exceptional complexity, numerous disputes, absence of inactivity, interim distributions, and no shortcomings in the legal/procedural framework, the overall length was not excessive. There was no violation of Article 6 §1.

In **Omdahl v. Norway** (ECtHR, Fifth Section, 22 April 2021; final 6 September 2021), the applicant, Olav Omdahl, complained that the administration of his grandfather’s estate lasted so long that it breached the “reasonable time” guarantee in Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

The deceased, O.A. Knutsen, died on 24 April 1993. His estate was substantial: assets worth approximately NOK 100 million and debts of about NOK 10 million, including property, shares, securities and movable property. The heirs were three children and two grandchildren. Public administration began on 5 May 1993 before the Probate Court, with an advocate appointed as administrator. It ended 22 years and 4 months later, after the final distribution in April 2015.

The delay arose from numerous legal disputes among the heirs. Early disputes concerned rights to receive assets in kind under the will and a codicil; these effectively tied up proceeds until 2005/06. Probate Court decisions to convert assets into cash were quashed or amended on appeal. A Bahamas trust, discovered after the applicant’s mother died in 2002, generated further disputes over whether funds belonged to the estate and complicated tax questions, which were clarified by the tax authorities in 2010. An interim distribution of NOK 10 million per family branch took place on 1 July 2010; appeals were dismissed by the High Court

**Sławiński v. Poland** (Application no. 61039/16) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights (First Section), delivered on 15 April 2021. The case concerned the alleged unreasonable length of criminal proceedings against the applicant, Mr Mariusz Grzegorz Sławiński, a Polish national born in 1958, and the alleged lack of an effective remedy for that delay.

In 2001 the Toruń District Prosecutor began investigating alleged fraud by the applicant’s company, which dealt with debt recovery. The applicant and a business partner were suspected of failing to transmit to a bank several hundred monthly instalment payments collected from individuals who had taken consumer loans. On 26 February 2002 the applicant was charged with fraud and placed under police supervision. On 24 June 2002 he and one co-accused were indicted before the Toruń District Court.

The first hearing took place only on 4 December 2003, approximately eighteen months after indictment. The trial involved about 100 hearings. By 7 March 2006 the District Court had heard over 300 witnesses listed in the indictment. Despite the main evidence having been gathered by then, the case continued for several more years. On 30 October 2013 the Toruń District Court convicted the applicant of defrauding payments from over 300 persons and sentenced him to one year and eight months’ imprisonment, suspended on probation, plus a fine. On appeal, on 23 October 2014 the Toruń Regional Court quashed the judgment and remitted the case.

After remittal, the trial court held four hearings between 9 April and 16 June 2015. On 22 June 2015 it acquitted the applicant of some charges and convicted him of fraud in a more limited scope, imposing one year’s imprisonment, suspended, and a fine. The applicant appealed again. On 17 March 2016 the Toruń Regional Court quashed the conviction and discontinued the proceedings because the offences had become time-barred. The judgment was given at a hearing attended by the applicant and his lawyer. The court informed the parties that written reasons would be prepared within fourteen days and gave the main grounds orally. The applicant was served with the written grounds, containing detailed factual findings and legal reasoning, on 12 April 2016.

Relevant to the effective-remedy complaint, on 6 July 2015 the applicant lodged a complaint under the 2004 Act concerning undue delay. On 20 August 2015 the Toruń Regional Court partly allowed the complaint, found that the length of proceedings had been excessive, and awarded 2,000 Polish zlotys (about EUR 475). It noted that the first hearing was scheduled almost eighteen months after indictment; that after 7 March 2006 the court had, over seven and a half years, heard only four more witnesses and requested some bank evidence, amounting to a flagrant lack of procedural efficiency; and that the trial court had taken excessively long to prepare written reasons for the 30 October 2013 judgment. It also noted that the applicant and his lawyer had contributed to some delays, and found no further court-attributable delays after remittal.

Before the ECtHR, the Government objected that the application was lodged out of time under the six-month rule, arguing that the final judgment was delivered on 17 March 2016 and that the applicant was not automatically entitled to written reasons. The Court held that the relevant period ran from 26 February 2002 to 17 March 2016, lasting fourteen years and one month. It found that the six-month period began when the applicant was served with the written grounds on 12 April 2016, because only then could he learn the full content of the judgment. The application, lodged on 11 October 2016, was therefore timely, and the length complaint was declared admissible.

In *Sławiński v. Poland* (Application no. 61039/16), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints that criminal proceedings against the applicant were unreasonably long and that there was no effective domestic remedy. The applicant, Mariusz Grzegorz Sławiński, was a Polish national born in 1958.

In 2001 the Toruń District Prosecutor began investigating alleged fraud by the applicant’s debt-vindication company. He and a business partner were suspected of failing to transfer to a bank several hundred monthly instalments collected from individuals with consumer loans. On 26 February 2002 the applicant was charged with fraud and placed under police supervision. This date began the period relevant to the length complaint. On 24 June 2002 he and a co-accused were indicted before the Toruń District Court.

The trial was slow. The first hearing was held only on 4 December 2003, about eighteen months after indictment. The court then held about 100 hearings and, by 7 March 2006, had heard over 300 witnesses. Afterwards, progress stalled: over the next seven and a half years, the court heard only four more witnesses and sought some bank evidence. On 30 October 2013 the District Court convicted the applicant of defrauding payments from over 300 persons and imposed a suspended prison sentence and fine. Preparation of the written reasons also took an excessively long time. On appeal, on 23 October 2014, the Toruń Regional Court quashed the judgment and remitted the case.

After remittal, the District Court held four hearings between 9 April and 16 June 2015. On 22 June 2015 it acquitted the applicant of some charges and convicted him in a more limited scope, again imposing a suspended sentence and fine. The applicant appealed. On 17 March 2016 the Regional Court quashed the conviction part and discontinued the proceedings because the offences had become time-barred. The applicant and his lawyer were present when the final judgment was delivered. The court stated that written reasons would follow within fourteen days and gave oral grounds. The applicant was served with written reasons on 12 April 2016.

Relevant to the alleged remedy violation, on 6 July 2015 the applicant lodged a complaint under the 2004 Act concerning undue delay. On 20 August 2015 the Toruń Regional Court partly allowed it, finding the length excessive and awarding 2,000 Polish zlotys (about EUR 475). It criticised the eighteen-month delay before the first hearing, the long period after March 2006 during which almost no evidence was taken, the court’s failure to secure attendance of the applicant and his lawyer, and the delayed preparation of written reasons for the 2013 judgment. It found no further delays after remittal.

The applicant applied to the Strasbourg Court on 11 October 2016. The Government argued that the application was out of time because the final judgment had been delivered in his presence on 17 March 2016. The Court disagreed, holding that, because the written reasons contained the full facts and legal reasoning, the six-month period began when he was served on 12 April 2016. The application was therefore admissible. The proceedings had lasted fourteen years and one month at two levels of jurisdiction.

**Sławiński v. Poland** (Application no. 61039/16, ECtHR, 15 April 2021) concerned complaints that criminal proceedings against the applicant were unreasonably long and that he lacked an effective domestic remedy for that delay.

The applicant, a Polish national born in 1958, was investigated in 2001 in connection with alleged fraud by his debt-collection company. He and a business partner allegedly failed to transmit to a bank hundreds of monthly instalment payments collected from individuals who had taken out consumer loans. On 26 February 2002 the applicant was charged with fraud and placed under police supervision. On 24 June 2002 he and one co-accused were indicted before the Toruń District Court.

The first hearing was held on 4 December 2003, almost eighteen months after the indictment. The trial court then held approximately 100 hearings. By 7 March 2006 it had heard over 300 witnesses listed in the indictment. However, after that point the proceedings slowed dramatically. During the following seven and a half years, the court heard only four more witnesses and requested some evidence from a bank. This lengthy period of near-inactivity was later described by the Toruń Regional Court as a “flagrant lack of procedural efficiency.”

On 30 October 2013 the Toruń District Court convicted the applicant of defrauding payments from over 300 persons. He was sentenced to one year and eight months’ imprisonment, suspended on probation, and a fine. He appealed. On 23 October 2014 the Toruń Regional Court quashed the judgment and remitted the case. In 2015 the trial court held four hearings and, on 22 June 2015, acquitted the applicant of some charges while convicting him of fraud in a more limited scope, imposing a suspended one-year sentence and a fine. The applicant appealed again. On 17 March 2016 the Toruń Regional Court quashed the conviction and discontinued the proceedings because the offences had become time-barred. The judgment was delivered orally at a hearing attended by the applicant and his lawyer, and the court stated that written reasons would be prepared within fourteen days. The applicant was served with the written grounds on 12 April 2016.

Separately, on 6 July 2015, the applicant lodged a complaint under the 2004 Act concerning undue delay. On 20 August 2015 the Toruń Regional Court partly allowed the complaint, found that the proceedings had been excessively long, and awarded him 2,000 Polish zlotys (approximately EUR 475). It criticised the eighteen-month delay before the first hearing, the seven-and-a-half-year period after March 2006 in which little evidence was taken, and the delay in preparing written reasons for the 2013 judgment. It also noted that the applicant and his lawyer had contributed to some delays, and found no further court-attributable delays after remittal.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the period examined ran from 26 February 2002 to 17 March 2016—fourteen years and one month across two levels of jurisdiction. The Government argued that the application was late under the six-month rule because the applicant had been present when the final judgment was delivered. The Court disagreed, holding that the six-month period began when the applicant was served with the written grounds on 12 April 2016, because only then could he know the full content of the judgment. The application, filed on 11 October 2016, was therefore within time. The Court declared the complaint admissible as not manifestly ill-founded.

In *Valdís Fjölnisdóttir and Others v. Iceland*, the applicants were two Icelandic women—then a married couple—and a child born in California in February 2013 through gestational surrogacy. The child was conceived using donor gametes and had no biological link to either intended parent. The surrogate waived legal parenthood. The first two applicants were named as parents on the US birth certificate and obtained a US passport for the child. Three weeks after birth, they returned to Iceland and applied to Registers Iceland to register the child in the national register using the US birth certificate, later disclosing the surrogacy.

Registers Iceland refused registration on 18 June 2013. Under Icelandic law, the woman who gives birth is the legal mother, and surrogacy is prohibited. The child was therefore not automatically an Icelandic citizen and was treated as a foreign national. The Ministry of the Interior upheld that decision in March 2014.

Because the child was considered a foreign unaccompanied minor, the child protection committee took custody and appointed a legal guardian. The child was initially placed with the first two applicants as foster carers. After the applicants divorced in 2015, foster arrangements changed: temporary care alternating between them, then permanent foster care with the first applicant and her spouse from December 2019, with equal access to the second applicant. In 2015, Parliament granted the child Icelandic citizenship by legislation, and he was registered as a citizen, but the first two applicants were still not registered as his parents.

The applicants also attempted to adopt the child. The adoption application was put on hold while the parentage/registration dispute continued. The District Commissioner considered the surrogate mother, and possibly her husband, to be the legal parents whose consent was required, and raised issues under the Adoption Act concerning payments to the surrogate. The applicants withdrew the adoption request after divorcing in 2015.

Domestic courts rejected the applicants’ claims for annulment and registration. The District Court (2016) accepted that family life existed and that the refusal interfered with Article 8 rights, but found the interference justified by Iceland’s ban on surrogacy and the need to protect others, including children’s access to origins. It noted counterbalancing measures: foster care preserving the bond, residence/citizenship, and the likely possibility of adoption had the applicants not divorced. The Supreme Court (2017) upheld the rejection but held that no protected family life existed when Registers Iceland decided, because the relationship had not been established lawfully under Icelandic law; only the later foster arrangement was protected.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged a violation of Article 8 on respect for private and family life. The Government argued they had not exhausted domestic remedies because they could still pursue adoption after divorce, and that the complaint was manifestly ill-founded. The applicants replied that adoption was not an effective or appropriate remedy, was no longer available jointly after divorce, and would risk severing the child’s ties with one parent. The Court considered Article 8 family life applicable but found that Iceland had struck a fair balance between the applicants’ family life and the general interests protected by its ban on surrogacy, especially because the authorities preserved the practical bond through foster care while refusing formal parent-child recognition.

**Case: Valdís Fjölnisdóttir and Others v. Iceland (ECtHR, 18 May 2021)**

The case concerned two Icelandic women, a married couple, and a child born in California in February 2013 through gestational surrogacy using donor gametes. The child was not biologically related to either intended mother. Under the US arrangement, the intended mothers were registered as the child’s parents on the Californian birth certificate, and the surrogate waived any legal parenthood claim.

Three weeks after the birth, the applicants returned to Iceland and applied to register the child in Iceland’s national register as an Icelandic national born abroad. Registers Iceland refused in June 2013. It treated the woman who gave birth—the surrogate—as the child’s mother under Icelandic law. Since the surrogate was a US citizen and no Icelandic biological father was shown, the child was not automatically entitled to Icelandic citizenship. The Ministry of the Interior upheld that refusal in March 2014.

As a result, the child was initially treated as a foreign unaccompanied minor. The child protection committee assumed custody, appointed a legal guardian, and placed the child in foster care with the first two applicants. Later, in 2015, Parliament granted the child Icelandic citizenship, and he was entered in the national register as a citizen. However, the first two applicants were still not registered as his parents.

The applicants challenged the refusal to register them as parents. They also tried to adopt the child, but the adoption process stalled and was withdrawn after the couple divorced in 2015. Domestic courts rejected their claims. The District Court accepted that family life existed and that the refusal interfered with Article 8, but found the interference justified by Iceland’s ban on surrogacy and the need to protect the rights of others. It noted counterbalancing measures: the child remained in foster care with the applicants, received citizenship, and adoption might have been possible had the couple not divorced.

The Supreme Court upheld the refusal but found that no protected family life existed at the time of the registration decision because the relationship had not been established in accordance with Icelandic law.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged a violation of Article 8 regarding private and family life and discrimination. The key issue was whether Iceland violated Article 8 by refusing to recognise the intended mothers as legal parents while preserving the child’s bond with them through foster care.

The ECtHR held that Article 8 family life was applicable because a de facto family bond existed. However, it found that Iceland had struck a fair balance between the applicants’ family life and the general interests protected by the ban on surrogacy. The authorities had not separated the child from the applicants; instead, they facilitated foster care, granted citizenship, and considered the child’s best interests. Accordingly, the non-recognition of the parental link did not violate Article 8. The case illustrates that States may refuse legal parentage arising from surrogacy abroad when it conflicts with fundamental domestic family-law principles, provided that the child’s de facto family ties are adequately protected.

In *Valdís Fjölnisdóttir and Others v. Iceland* (2021), the applicants were Valdís and Eydís, an Icelandic married couple, and X, a child born in California in February 2013 through gestational surrogacy. The couple used a US surrogacy agency and donor gametes; neither intended mother had a biological link to the child. The surrogate mother waived legal parenthood. California authorities registered Valdís and Eydís as X’s parents and issued a birth certificate and US passport.

Three weeks after X’s birth, the family travelled to Iceland. Valdís and Eydís applied to Registers Iceland to register X in the national register, relying on the US birth certificate. In June 2013, Registers Iceland refused registration. It reasoned that, under Icelandic law, the woman who gives birth is the child’s legal mother; surrogacy is prohibited; and X was not automatically entitled to Icelandic citizenship because neither the surrogate nor the biological father was Icelandic. The Ministry of the Interior upheld that decision in March 2014.

Because X was treated as a foreign unaccompanied minor, the local child protection committee took legal custody and appointed a guardian. X was initially placed in the care of Valdís and Eydís as foster carers. After their divorce in 2015, foster care arrangements changed: X was temporarily fostered by each applicant in turn, with equal access to the other. From December 2019, X was permanently fostered by Valdís and her spouse, while continuing equal access to Eydís and her spouse.

Although X was granted Icelandic citizenship by Act No. 128/2015 and entered in the national register as a citizen, Valdís and Eydís were still not registered as his parents. Earlier, they had applied to adopt X, but the District Commissioner indicated that the surrogate mother and her husband would need to consent and that payments related to surrogacy could bar adoption. After the couple divorced, they withdrew the adoption application.

The applicants sought judicial review, asking for annulment of the refusal and a declaration that Registers Iceland must register Valdís and Eydís as X’s parents. The District Court rejected the claims in 2016. It found that Icelandic family law treats the birth mother as the legal mother and that recognising foreign surrogacy arrangements would create a loophole around Iceland’s surrogacy ban. It accepted that the refusal interfered with family life but found it justified and mitigated by foster care and citizenship. The Supreme Court upheld the rejection in 2017, holding that no family life protected by the Constitution or Article 8 existed at the time of the refusal because the parent-child ties had not been established lawfully under Icelandic law.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants complained under Article 8 that non-recognition of the parent-child relationship violated their right to respect for private and family life, and also alleged discrimination. The key facts were that a strong de facto family bond existed, X’s best interests were engaged, and the US birth certificate named the intended mothers as parents, but Icelandic law refused legal recognition because of the surrogacy ban and the absence of biological or gestational links.

The European Court held that Article 8 family life was applicable. However, it found that Iceland had struck a fair balance between the applicants’ family life and the general interests protected by the ban on surrogacy. The authorities had preserved the bond through foster care and had granted X citizenship, while maintaining the legal principle that the birth mother is the mother. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 8.

In *Caamaño Valle v. Spain* (ECtHR, 11 May 2021), the applicant, Maria del Mar Caamaño Valle, challenged the disenfranchisement of her daughter, M., a young woman with intellectual disability born in 1996. In December 2013, as M. approached majority, the applicant sought extended guardianship but expressly asked that M. retain her right to vote. On 2 September 2014, a First-Instance Judge in Santiago de Compostela placed M. under the mother’s extended partial guardianship and revoked her voting rights. The judge relied on a forensic/medical report, court examination, and hearing. Applying Spanish electoral law (LOREG), the judge stressed that loss of suffrage was not automatic but required an express judicial finding that the person was incapable of exercising it. He found M. unable to make a free, self-determined electoral choice: she was highly influenceable, unaware of voting consequences, and had intellectual capacity equivalent to a child aged six to eight. The decision was not based on lack of political knowledge or irrational preferences, but on her incapacity in political/electoral matters.

The applicant appealed, arguing that Articles 12 and 29 of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) guaranteed voting rights for persons with disabilities and required support. The Regional Court of A Coruña dismissed the appeal on 11 March 2015, finding the disenfranchisement lawful and CRPD-compatible because it followed individualised judicial review and was sufficiently reasoned. The Supreme Court dismissed a further appeal on 17 March 2016. The Constitutional Court dismissed amparo on 28 November 2016, reasoning that Spanish universal suffrage did not preclude individual disenfranchisement under LOREG sections 3(1)(b) and 3(2), provided a court assessed the person’s specific circumstances and found them unable to exercise suffrage. It distinguished the CRPD’s broad concept of disability from Spanish “incapacity,” and held that only persons lacking the minimum understanding and will to vote freely could be deprived. It found no arbitrariness and noted the reinforced reasoning required for fundamental-rights restrictions.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged violations of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 (right to free elections), alone and read with Article 14 ECHR and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 (discrimination). She argued the disenfranchisement was disability-based discrimination, lacked a legitimate aim, and was disproportionate. The Government maintained that Spanish law distinguished disability from legal incapacity, did not automatically disenfranchise disabled people, and required an individualised judicial decision with guarantees. It noted that Institutional Law 2/2018 later abolished this disenfranchisement and restored voting rights. The Council of Europe Human Rights Commissioner intervened, arguing that international standards, especially CRPD Article 29, prohibit withdrawing political rights based on disability.

The Court declared the application admissible and refused to strike it out, since M. had been unable to vote in several elections between 2014 and 2018, despite the later reform. On the merits, the Court found no violation. It held that disenfranchisement was justified because domestic courts had conducted a thorough, individualised assessment and concluded that M. was effectively unable to make a free and self-determined electoral choice. States enjoy a margin of appreciation, but disenfranchisement of persons with mental disabilities must apply only to those effectively unable to vote freely. The difference in treatment based on mental capacity was therefore justified, and no discrimination under Article 14 or Protocol No. 12 was established.

In **Caamaño Valle v. Spain** (Application no. 43564/17, judgment 11 May 2021), the European Court of Human Rights examined the disenfranchisement of M., the intellectually disabled daughter of the applicant, Ms Maria del Mar Caamaño Valle.

In December 2013, as M. approached adulthood, her mother applied for a declaration of incapacity and extension of guardianship, but expressly asked that M. retain her right to vote. On 2 September 2014, the First-Instance Court in Santiago de Compostela placed M. under extended partial guardianship and revoked her voting rights. The judge relied on medical expert evidence, a personal examination, and a hearing. He found M. was not capable of exercising suffrage: she was highly influenceable, unaware of the consequences of voting, and had intellectual ability equivalent to that of a child aged six to eight. The judge stressed that disenfranchisement was not automatic; it required an individualised, reasoned assessment and remained subject to review. The Regional Court of A Coruña dismissed an appeal on 11 March 2015; the Supreme Court dismissed an appeal on 17 March 2016; and the Constitutional Court rejected an *amparo* appeal on 28 November 2016. M. was therefore unable to vote in the 2014 European Parliament elections and the Spanish general elections of 2015 and 2016.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 (right to free elections), alone and read with Article 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12. She argued that depriving her daughter of the vote because of disability was discriminatory and contrary to Articles 12 and 29 of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD), which guarantee political rights and require support for their exercise.

The Government argued that Spanish “incapacity” is not equivalent to the CRPD’s broad concept of “disability.” Under the Spanish electoral law (LOREG), disenfranchisement required a final judicial decision expressly finding that the person was incapable of exercising suffrage. The procedure involved a judge, medical evidence, examination of the person, and the possibility of revision. The Government invoked the State’s margin of appreciation and noted that Institutional Law 2/2018 amended the LOREG to guarantee voting rights for persons with disabilities and annulled prior restrictions. The Court refused to strike out the application because M. had been unable to vote in several elections before 2018.

The Commissioner for Human Rights argued that international standards had evolved against withdrawing political rights on the basis of disability, and that Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 should be interpreted in light of CRPD Article 29. The applicant agreed.

The key issue was whether Spain’s system, which allowed courts to disenfranchise persons with mental disabilities only after individualised judicial assessment, violated Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 and the non-discrimination provisions. The Court found the disenfranchisement justified: it was not automatic or group-based, but based on a thorough, individualised assessment by domestic courts and applied only to persons effectively unable to make a free and self-determined electoral choice, as in M.’s case. Accordingly, there was no violation of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1, and the difference in treatment based on mental capacity was justified under Article 14 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12.

**Feilazoo v. Malta** (Application no. 6865/19) concerned a Nigerian national, Joseph Feilazoo, who had been sentenced in Malta in 2010 to twelve years’ imprisonment and a fine for drug-related offences. After serving his sentence, on 10 April 2018 he was released from prison but immediately taken to the Immigration Office. There he was declared a prohibited immigrant under the Immigration Act and issued a Return Decision and Removal Order based on his criminal conviction. He resisted being detained and placed in a van; a scuffle followed, pepper spray and restraints were used, and he was taken to hospital with injuries. Criminal proceedings were later brought against him for assaulting and resisting correctional officers. In February 2019 he was convicted, and in May 2019 his appeal resulted in a suspended sentence and an order for immediate deportation.

The facts most relevant to the alleged violations arose mainly after 16 May 2019, when the applicant was transferred from prison to a closed immigration detention centre. Although a fine was later converted into six months’ imprisonment, he was returned to immigration detention at Safi in September 2019. He remained in immigration detention into late 2020. The authorities sought emergency travel documents from Nigeria by notes verbale in May and December 2019, but no documents were issued. Deportation became increasingly unlikely, particularly as Nigerian consular officers were unable to meet him or secure travel documents. The applicant also refused to leave detention unless given a passport or travel document.

For the **Article 3** complaint, the applicant alleged inadequate conditions in immigration detention. He complained of overcrowding, poor hygiene, inadequate food, limited healthcare, lack of clothing and communication facilities, and difficulties accessing medical records. More significantly, he was subjected to an excessively stringent and long period of de facto isolation, including transfers between security regimes that restricted contact with others and impeded access to legal assistance. During the Covid-19 pandemic, he was also unnecessarily placed in quarantine with new arrivals, exposing him to health risks. The Court found these conditions amounted to degrading treatment.

For the **Article 5 § 1** complaint, the key issue was whether his immigration detention remained lawful. Although the initial detention was based on the removal order and his prohibited-immigrant status, the Court examined whether the grounds remained valid throughout the whole period. It found that the Maltese authorities failed to take active and diligent steps towards deporting him. Despite the notes verbale to Nigeria, no effective progress was made, and once deportation had become unlikely, continued detention lacked a valid basis under Article 5 § 1.

For the **Article 34** complaint, the applicant alleged that Malta hindered his right of individual application to the European Court. Correspondence between the Court and the applicant passed through prison or detention authorities and was allegedly interfered with or tampered with. He also suffered ineffective legal representation through the domestic legal aid system. Although a legal aid lawyer was appointed for the Strasbourg proceedings, she failed to contact him adequately, submitted no observations, and eventually sought to withdraw, telling the detention authorities to stop him contacting her. The Court ultimately removed her under Rule 36 § 4(b) and granted legal aid directly. These facts supported the finding that Malta interfered with the effective exercise of his right of application.

In summary, the case concerned the applicant’s prolonged immigration detention, the inadequate and isolating conditions he endured, the lack of realistic prospect of deportation, and obstacles placed in the way of his communication with and representation before the Court.

**Feilazoo v. Malta** concerned a Nigerian national, Joseph Feilazoo, who alleged violations of the Convention arising from his immigration detention and from obstacles to his application before the European Court of Human Rights. In 2010, the applicant was convicted in Malta of drug-related offences and sentenced to twelve years’ imprisonment plus a €50,000 fine, converted into further imprisonment if unpaid. Shortly before completing his sentence in April 2018, he was questioned about his post-release intentions. He wished to return to Spain, where he had previously held a residence permit, but the Spanish authorities apparently refused to accept him.

On 10 April 2018, upon release from prison, the applicant was taken to the Immigration Office rather than to emergency accommodation. He was declared a prohibited immigrant under Maltese law because of his criminal conviction, and a Return Decision and Removal Order were issued. He was ordered to be detained pending removal to Nigeria. His request for voluntary departure was refused on grounds including risk of absconding and threat to public policy. When he objected to detention, a scuffle occurred with correctional officers. The applicant alleged that he was pepper-sprayed, restrained, beaten, kicked, and handcuffed, causing injuries including a fractured left radial head, bruising, and abrasions. The officers alleged that he assaulted and bit them. He was taken to hospital and later charged with assault, violent resistance, disobeying lawful orders, and disturbing public order. In February 2019 he was convicted; on appeal in May 2019, his sentence was reduced to two years’ imprisonment suspended for three years and a €4,000 fine. Immediate deportation was ordered. Because he could not pay the fine, it was converted into six months’ imprisonment.

After release, the applicant was transferred to closed immigration detention. His passport had expired, and Malta requested emergency travel documents from Nigeria. By late 2020, deportation had become unlikely. The Government stated he would be released once medically cleared; he received clearance in November 2020 but refused to leave unless given a travel document, remaining in detention until December 2020, when he was offered accommodation at an open centre.

Relevant to **Article 3**, the applicant complained about inadequate conditions in immigration detention, an excessively stringent and long period of de facto isolation, transfers to high-security regimes, limited access to medical records and legal assistance, and placement in Covid-19 quarantine with new arrivals, exposing him to health risks. Relevant to **Article 5 §1**, he argued that his immigration detention ceased to have a valid legal basis once deportation was no longer realistic, and that the authorities failed to take active and diligent steps to deport him during detention. Relevant to **Article 34**, he alleged interference with correspondence between himself and the Court through prison authorities, and ineffective domestic legal aid representation. Although a legal aid lawyer was appointed for the Strasbourg proceedings, she allegedly failed to contact him, file observations, or represent him effectively, and sought to withdraw. The Court eventually removed her and appointed a new lawyer. It found violations of Article 3 (substantive), Article 5 §1, and Article 34.

In *Feilazoo v. Malta*, the applicant was a Nigerian national who had been serving a twelve-year drug-related sentence in Malta, with fines converted into additional imprisonment. As his sentence was ending in April 2018, he was questioned about his post-release intentions and said he wished to return to Spain. When Spain reportedly refused to accept him, Malta treated him as a prohibited immigrant and issued a removal order. On 10 April 2018, instead of being taken to emergency accommodation, he was escorted to the Immigration Office and told he would be detained pending removal to Nigeria. He objected, and a scuffle followed with correctional officers; pepper spray was used, and he sustained a fractured elbow, bruises, abrasions and other injuries. He was charged with assaulting and resisting officers, convicted in February 2019, and on appeal in May 2019 his sentence was suspended, with immediate deportation ordered. A fine was later converted into six months’ imprisonment. From May 2019 he was held in immigration detention, moving between Safi detention centre and Corradino prison.

His passport had expired, and Malta sent notes verbales to Nigeria in May and December 2019 seeking emergency travel documents. Nigeria later refused documents unless consular officers met him, which he allegedly refused. By late 2020 deportation was unlikely; he was medically cleared in November 2020 but remained in detention until December 2020.

The alleged Article 3 violations concerned inadequate detention conditions, particularly an excessively stringent and long period of de facto isolation, and exposure to Covid-19 health risks through unnecessary placement with new arrivals in quarantine. He also complained about hygiene, food, overcrowding, access to medical records, and transfers to high-security regimes. The Government claimed the transfers were due to unruly behaviour but submitted no documentation.

Under Article 5 §1, he alleged his immigration detention was unlawful because the grounds ceased to be valid once deportation became unrealistic. He argued the authorities failed to take active and diligent steps to deport him, with delays and missing documents attributable to them. He also disputed the effectiveness of domestic remedies and legal aid.

Under Article 34, he initially applied to the European Court of Human Rights unrepresented in August 2019. A domestic legal aid lawyer was appointed but allegedly failed to maintain contact, did not submit observations, and pressured him to drop the case; she later asked detention authorities to stop him contacting her and sought revocation. The Court removed her and appointed new representation. He further alleged prison authorities interfered with his correspondence with the Court, refused medical reports, restricted legal aid and phone access, and moved him between regimes to impede his application. The Government denied these claims, saying transfers were disciplinary. The judgment, delivered on 11 March 2021 and final on 11 June 2021, focused on Malta’s compliance with Articles 3, 5 §1 and 34 of the Convention.

**Case Summary: Sandu and Others v. Romania**  
*European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, 16 December 2021*

This case concerned 20 applications lodged against Romania under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights, led by Application no. 27855/17. The applicants complained about the inadequate conditions of their detention, relying on Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. Because the applications raised similar issues, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment.

One procedural issue arose in application no. 2673/18. The applicant, Mr Tudor, died on 26 July 2021 after the case had been communicated to the Romanian Government. His children, Ms Daniela-Loredana Tudor and Ms Mihaela-Simona Tudor, informed the Court that they wished to continue the application. They submitted notarial documents showing they had accepted the inheritance. The Government did not comment. The Court found that the heirs had legal standing and a legitimate interest in obtaining findings on the alleged violations, and allowed them to pursue the application.

The central facts concerned the applicants’ detention in Romanian custody. The Court stated that the applicants had been kept in detention in poor conditions. The specific details—such as the detention periods, prison facilities, cell space, and other material circumstances—were set out in an appended table, which is not reproduced in the provided text. The applicants alleged that these conditions amounted to inhuman or degrading treatment under Article 3. The Government disputed the complaints and raised an objection concerning non-exhaustion of domestic remedies.

In its assessment, the Court relied on established case-law on inadequate detention conditions, particularly *Muršić v. Croatia* and *Ananyev and Others v. Russia*. It reiterated that a serious lack of space in a prison cell weighs heavily in determining whether detention conditions are “degrading” under Article 3. Such a lack of space may disclose a violation either alone or in combination with other shortcomings. The Court also noted that in the leading Romanian case *Rezmiveș and Others v. Romania* it had already found a violation concerning similar issues.

After examining all the material and the parties’ arguments, including the Government’s non-exhaustion objection, the Court found no fact or argument capable of leading to a different conclusion on admissibility or merits. Referring also to *Polgar v. Romania*, it concluded that the applicants’ conditions of detention, as described in the appended table, were inadequate. Consequently, the Court found a violation of Article 3 in respect of those complaints.

The judgment also addressed remaining complaints. In applications nos. 42881/17, 44495/17, 67182/17, 81285/17, 2668/18, 2673/18, 4561/18 and 8476/18, the applicants raised other Article 3 complaints. The Court found these either inadmissible under Articles 34 and 35 of the Convention or disclosing no appearance of a violation, and rejected that part of the applications under Article 35 § 4. The provided text does not include the full Article 41 just satisfaction section, so any award of compensation or costs is not summarized here.

**Key facts relevant to the alleged violation:** the applicants were detained in conditions the Court classified as poor and inadequate, with particular emphasis on serious overcrowding or lack of cell space and possible accompanying deficiencies. The Court treated these conditions as meeting the threshold for degrading treatment under Article 3.

**Case: Sandu and Others v. Romania**  
**Application no. 27855/17 and 19 others**  
**European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, 16 December 2021**

The case concerned twenty applications lodged against Romania under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights.
