**Case Apap Bologna v. Malta** (Application no. 47505/19, ECtHR, 9 December 2021) concerned a unilaterally imposed commercial lease under Chapter 69 of Malta’s laws and whether the applicant received sufficient redress for a breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The applicant, a Maltese national, owned a shop at 295/296 Republic Street, Valletta. He originally inherited a half share in 1980 and later became full owner of no. 296 after a partition. The premises had been leased in 1922 for four years at GBP 100 per year. After temporary tenant-protection laws in 1925–26, Act XXI of 1933—today Chapter 69—introduced perpetual protection, renewing the lease indefinitely at the old rent and leaving owners without legal grounds to evict. In 1964 the rent was negotiated up to GBP 150. The tenancy later passed to three tenants not recognised by the landlords, and eviction attempts failed.

Rent remained very low. From April 2001 rent was deposited in court: MTL 2,828.84 covered 1982–2001, after which MTL 150 (about EUR 395) per year was deposited until 2009. Act X of 2009 raised rent by 15% annually for 2010–2013, reaching EUR 611.11 for the whole shop. From 2014, because the Index of Commercial Value of Property was never published, rent rose 5% yearly, reaching EUR 818.95 by 2019. In constitutional proceedings, a court-appointed architect valued the property in 2017 at EUR 1,500,000 and its annual market rent at EUR 86,540, considering its prime location, condition and going-concern status. The lawful rent then was about EUR 743. Total market rent since 1986 was estimated at EUR 1,603,499.

On 22 February 2017 the applicant filed constitutional redress, alleging that the controlled lease breached Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 as regards no. 296 because the low rent imposed a disproportionate burden compared with the property’s real rental value. On 4 June 2018 the Civil Court (First Hall), in its constitutional jurisdiction, found a violation of property rights and awarded EUR 100,000 in pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages, with costs split equally. It considered the property’s location, rent paid and increases, market value, disproportion, the lease ending in 2028, the duration of interference, and the applicant’s delay in bringing proceedings.

On appeal, the Constitutional Court on 29 March 2019 confirmed the violation but reduced compensation to EUR 55,000 (EUR 50,000 pecuniary, EUR 5,000 non-pecuniary). It refused eviction as outside its jurisdiction, but declared Chapter 69 provisions without effect between the applicant and tenants, meaning the tenants could no longer rely on them to justify occupation. It noted the architect’s valuation covered the entire shop while the applicant’s interest was limited to his divided part. Costs at first instance remained split; appeal costs were divided half between the Attorney General and the applicant, while tenants bore their own cross-appeal costs.

Afterward, the applicant negotiated a new lease at EUR 140 daily—about EUR 51,100 annually—effective 1 October 2019, and the tenant paid a lump sum for fair rent from the Constitutional Court judgment until the new agreement. The applicant said he was satisfied with the fair rent. Later, due to COVID-19, a new agreement set rent at EUR 50 daily.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained that the compensation was insufficient and claimed victim status for the period until the Constitutional Court judgment. The Government argued he had lost victim status because domestic courts acknowledged the violation, awarded compensation, and the declaration allowed eviction. The ECtHR found the acknowledgment sufficient in principle, but the EUR 55,000 global award was insufficient for a decades-long breach involving property with an estimated 2017 rental value exceeding EUR 40,000. In *Barseghyan v. Armenia* (Application no. 17804/09, judgment of 21 September 2021), the applicant, Levon Barseghyan, was a journalist, political activist, and chairman of a journalists’ club in Gyumri, Armenia’s second-largest city. He complained under Article 11 of the Convention that his right to freedom of peaceful assembly had been violated when he was prevented from holding or participating in a rally and later fined for disobeying police orders.

The case arose after the disputed 19 February 2008 presidential election. Opposition supporters held daily protests in Yerevan. On 1 March 2008, police cleared Freedom Square; violence escalated, resulting in ten deaths, injuries, and property damage. The President then declared a 20-day state of emergency in Yerevan, banning meetings, rallies, demonstrations, marches, and other mass events. Armenia notified a derogation under Article 15 of the Convention, but the decree and derogation referred specifically to Yerevan.

On 2 March 2008 at around 12:30 p.m., the applicant went to Theatre Square in central Gyumri and tried to enter in order to hold a protest. Police officers stationed there to prevent demonstrations refused him entry. It was alleged that he called on people at the square to gather and hold a demonstration. Police ordered him to leave and stop inciting others to assemble. He did not comply and was taken to a police station. An administrative case was opened under Article 182 of the Code of Administrative Offences for disobeying lawful police orders. The police claimed there had been no proper notification or authorisation for a demonstration and relied on the tense post-1 March situation in Armenia.

The applicant counter-claimed that he had not intended to organise a rally, that no rally occurred, and that merely “calling on people” was not unlawful. He also argued that the law did not require prior notification for assemblies of fewer than 100 people, and that no evidence showed such a threshold had been met. On 10 June 2008, the Administrative Court granted the police claim and fined him 50,000 Armenian drams. It found there was no legal basis for the demonstration because no notification had been submitted. Although the state of emergency applied only to Yerevan, the court reasoned that a mass event in Gyumri could endanger public order and public health, especially after the events in the capital, and that police restrictions were therefore lawful. The Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal in October 2008.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the Government argued that the Article 15 derogation barred the complaint, claiming that an emergency effectively existed in Gyumri too and that restrictions were necessary because of the close link to Yerevan. It also argued that because the applicant said he had no assembly intent, he could not be a victim and had suffered no significant disadvantage. The applicant replied that the emergency and derogation applied only to Yerevan, while Gyumri had experienced no violence or emergency situation.

The Court held that Article 15 was inapplicable *ratione loci*: the emergency and derogation covered only Yerevan, not Gyumri. On Article 11, it found a violation. The domestic authorities had failed to give relevant and sufficient reasons for banning the assembly and for the applicant’s arrest and fine. In particular, the domestic court had wrongly relied on the situation in the capital to justify a blanket ban on peaceful assembly in another city.

The case of *Barseghyan v. Armenia* concerns an alleged violation of Article 11 (freedom of peaceful assembly) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Levon Barseghyan, is a journalist, political activist, and chairman of a journalists’ club in Gyumri, Armenia’s second-largest city.

The events occurred in the aftermath of the disputed 19 February 2008 presidential election in Armenia. Following the election, the main opposition candidate, Mr. Ter-Petrosyan, called for protests in Yerevan’s Freedom Square. From 20 February 2008, daily rallies were held, with hundreds of demonstrators camping in the square. On 1 March 2008, a police operation cleared Freedom Square. Later that day, the situation escalated into violent clashes between protesters and law enforcement in Yerevan, resulting in ten deaths, numerous injuries, and property destruction.

On the same date, the incumbent President issued a decree declaring a state of emergency in Yerevan for twenty days. This decree included a prohibition on holding meetings, rallies, demonstrations, marches, and other mass events—but only within Yerevan. The following day, 2 March 2008, the applicant arrived at Theatre Square in central Gyumri around 12:30 p.m., intending to hold a protest. He was refused entry by police officers stationed there to prevent demonstrations. According to the police, the applicant began calling on people present to gather and hold a demonstration, but was ordered to leave and stop inciting others to assemble. He did not obey and was taken to a police station.

An administrative case was initiated against the applicant under Article 182 of the Code of Administrative Offences for disobeying lawful orders of police officers. The police claimed that the Gyumri Mayor’s Office had not been duly notified of the demonstration and no authorisation had been obtained. On 10 June 2008, the Administrative Court granted the police claim, fining the applicant 50,000 Armenian Drams (approximately €110).

Crucially, the Administrative Court’s judgment relied on the events in Yerevan to justify the restriction in Gyumri. It noted that in connection with the events in the capital on 1 March 2008, a state of emergency had been declared in Yerevan, and concluded that conducting a mass public event in Gyumri, “the second largest city of the country,” could have endangered public order and public health, especially since no notification had been submitted. The court found the police orders lawful. The applicant’s appeal was declared inadmissible by the Court of Cassation on 2 October 2008.

Before the European Court, the Government argued that Armenia had derogated under Article 15 from its Article 11 obligations, and that although the derogation referred specifically to Yerevan, a state of emergency had also effectively existed in Gyumri. The applicant countered that the state of emergency and derogation applied only to Yerevan, where the violent events occurred, while Gyumri experienced no violence or emergency situation.

The central issue was whether the state of emergency declared in Yerevan could justify restrictions on assemblies in Gyumri. The Court found that the derogation inapplicable *ratione loci* to events outside Yerevan, and that domestic courts failed to provide relevant and sufficient reasons for banning the assembly and arresting the applicant, improperly relying on the situation in the capital to justify a blanket ban in another city.

The case *Aslanian v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* (Application no. 74433/11) is a European Court of Human Rights judgment delivered on 13 July 2021 by the Second Section. The applicant, Rostom Aslanian, is a Russian national born in 1989 who lives in Vărăncău, Moldova. He is a member of the Jehovah’s Witnesses religious community in the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (the “MRT”), a separatist region of Moldova.

The facts relevant to the alleged violations arose when Aslanian became eligible for military draft. Because of his religious conscience and beliefs, he asked the MRT authorities to be assigned to civilian service instead of compulsory military service. In December 2010, the MRT authorities rejected his request and opened a criminal investigation against him for draft evasion. On 29 March 2011, the Rîbnița City and Region Court convicted him of draft evasion and sentenced him to one year’s imprisonment. He was taken into custody in the courtroom. On 7 June 2012, the MRT Supreme Court upheld the first-instance judgment. Aslanian was released on 29 March 2012, having fully served his sentence.

Before the ECtHR, Aslanian complained under Article 9 of the Convention that his conviction for opposing military service on religious grounds—despite his willingness to perform alternative service—violated his freedom of thought, conscience, and religion. He also invoked Article 14, alleging discrimination. The central alleged violation was therefore that the MRT’s refusal to recognize conscientious objection and to provide alternative service amounted to an unjustified interference with his religious freedom.

The judgment also addressed jurisdiction under Article 1. The Court recalled its case law on Transdniestria. Moldova, as the territorial State, had jurisdiction but only positive obligations to take diplomatic, economic, judicial, and other measures within its power, since it lacked effective control over the region. Russia, by contrast, had contributed militarily and politically to the creation of the separatist regime and continued to provide military, economic, and political support. The MRT’s high dependency on Russian support indicated that Russia exercised effective control and decisive influence over the Transdniestrian authorities. The Court thus found that Aslanian fell within Russia’s jurisdiction under Article 1, as well as Moldova’s jurisdiction subject to positive obligations.

On admissibility, both Governments argued that Aslanian had failed to exhaust domestic remedies. Moldova said he had not notified Moldovan authorities; Russia said he had not exhausted remedies before Moldovan or Russian courts. The applicant argued that no effective remedies existed. The Court dismissed these objections, relying on *Mozer v. Moldova and Russia*, *Vardanean*, and *Bobeico*, noting that the Governments did not identify specific available remedies and presented no new arguments. It declared the Article 9 complaint admissible as not manifestly ill-founded and not inadmissible on any other ground. The case proceeded to determine whether the conviction engaged the responsibility of either respondent State. The key facts—his religious objection, request for alternative service, denial, criminal conviction, imprisonment, and the jurisdictional link to the MRT and Russia—formed the basis for the alleged Article 9 violation.

In *Aslanian v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* (Application no. 74433/11), the European Court of Human Rights examined the conviction of a Jehovah’s Witness for refusing compulsory military service in the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”). The applicant, Rostom Aslanian, a Russian national born in 1989 and living in Vărăncău, Moldova, was a member of the Jehovah’s Witnesses in the MRT. When he became eligible for the draft, he requested assignment to civilian service instead of compulsory military service, relying on his religious conscience and beliefs. In December 2010, the MRT authorities rejected his request and opened a criminal investigation for draft evasion.

On 29 March 2011, the “Rîbnița City and Region Court” convicted the applicant of draft evasion and sentenced him to one year’s imprisonment. He was taken into custody in the courtroom. On 7 June 2012, the “MRT” Supreme Court upheld the first-instance judgment. The applicant was released on 29 March 2012 after fully serving his sentence. He complained under Articles 9 and 14 of the Convention, alleging that his criminal conviction for opposing military service on religious grounds—despite his willingness to perform alternative service—violated his freedom of thought, conscience, and religion and amounted to discrimination.

The Court first addressed jurisdiction under Article 1. The applicant and the Moldovan Government argued that both respondent States had jurisdiction; the Russian Government denied jurisdiction. Moldova submitted that it had positive obligations to secure the applicant’s rights and that Russia had jurisdiction due to its continuous military presence in the region. Applying its earlier case-law in *Ilaşcu and Others*, *Catan and Others*, and *Mozer*, the Court held that Moldova, as the territorial State, had jurisdiction even though it lacked effective control over Transdniestria, but its responsibility was limited to positive diplomatic, economic, judicial, and other measures within its power and consistent with international law. Russia had jurisdiction because it had contributed militarily and politically to the creation of the separatist regime, and the MRT depended on Russian military, economic, and political support. That dependency indicated that Russia continued to exercise effective control and decisive influence over the Transdniestrian authorities. The applicant therefore fell within Russia’s jurisdiction, and the Court would later assess whether either State bore responsibility for the alleged violations.

On admissibility, both Governments objected that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies. Moldova argued that he had not notified the Moldovan authorities; Russia argued that he had not exhausted remedies before either Moldovan or Russian courts. The applicant contended that no effective remedies existed. The Court dismissed these objections, noting that similar objections had been rejected in *Mozer*, *Vardanean*, and *Bobeico and Others*. The Governments did not specify which domestic remedies should have been exhausted and offered no new arguments. The Article 9 complaint was not manifestly ill-founded or otherwise inadmissible, so the Court declared it admissible.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are thus: the applicant’s Jehovah’s Witness faith and conscientious objection to military service; his formal request for civilian alternative service; the MRT’s refusal in December 2010; the criminal investigation; his conviction and one-year prison sentence in March 2011; the unsuccessful appeal in June 2012; and his full imprisonment until March 2012. The case centrally concerns whether punishment for conscientious objection breached Article 9 and whether Moldova and/or Russia bore Convention responsibility given the special jurisdictional situation in Transdniestria.

In *Ibrišimović and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (application no. 15634/20 and three others), the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 11 February 2021. The applicants, represented by Sarajevo lawyer O. Eterović, lodged applications under Article 34 of the Convention against Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Government was given notice. Because the applications raised similar subject matter, the Court joined them for examination in a single judgment.

The core alleged violation was the non-enforcement of final domestic decisions issued in the applicants’ favour. The appended table listed the applicants and relevant details of each application; the provided text does not reproduce those individual facts, but the common factual basis is that domestic authorities failed to enforce final decisions, or failed to enforce them fully and in due time. The applicants complained expressly or in substance under Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair hearing) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). Article 6 § 1 guarantees a fair hearing in the determination of civil rights and obligations, while Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

The Court reiterated that execution of a judgment given by any court must be regarded as an integral part of a “hearing” for Article 6 purposes, citing *Hornsby v. Greece*. It also referred to its case-law on non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of final domestic judgments. In the earlier leading cases *Spahić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* and *Kunić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina*, the Court had already found violations concerning similar issues. Those cases concerned Bosnia and Herzegovina’s persistent failure to enforce final domestic decisions.

The Court further noted that the decisions in the present applications ordered specific action to be taken. Consequently, the decisions constituted “possessions” within the meaning of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court examined all material submitted and found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on admissibility or merits. Having regard to its established case-law, it considered that the domestic authorities did not deploy all necessary efforts to enforce fully and in due time the decisions in the applicants’ favour. That failure formed the basis for the alleged violations.

Thus, the key facts relevant to the alleged violations were not complex: final domestic decisions had been rendered in the applicants’ favour; those decisions required specific action; and the authorities failed to secure their timely and complete enforcement. That non-enforcement engaged both the fair-hearing guarantee under Article 6 § 1 and the property-protection guarantee under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court’s review was framed as a repetitive non-enforcement case, following its prior jurisprudence against Bosnia and Herzegovina. The judgment was adopted on 21 January 2021, delivered on 11 February 2021, and became final, subject to editorial revision. The provided extract does not include the appended table’s individual details or the final just-satisfaction disposition, but it indicates the Court found the complaints admissible and substantiated by the authorities’ failure to enforce domestic decisions fully and in due time.

**Application no. 15634/20 and three others – European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section Committee – Judgment of 11 February 2021.**

The case originated in four applications lodged against Bosnia and Herzegovina under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants were represented by Mr O. Eterović, a lawyer practising in Sarajevo. The Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina were given notice of the applications. Because the applications raised the same essential complaint, the Court decided to examine them jointly in a single judgment.

The central factual allegation was that the respondent State had failed to enforce final domestic decisions issued in the applicants’ favour. The full list of applicants and the specific details of each application were set out in an appended table, but the key common feature was that domestic authorities or courts had rendered decisions granting the applicants relief, and those decisions had not been enforced, or had not been enforced fully and in due time. The domestic decisions were not merely declaratory; they ordered specific action to be taken. This fact was important because it meant the applicants had enforceable entitlements rather than merely expectations.

Before the Court, the applicants complained of the non-enforcement of those domestic decisions. They relied, expressly or in substance, on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to a fair hearing in the determination of civil rights and obligations, and on Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, which protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. Their argument was that the failure to execute final decisions in their favour deprived them of the practical benefit of the judicial proceedings and interfered with their property rights.

The Court reiterated its established case-law that the execution of a judgment given by any court must be regarded as an integral part of a “hearing” for the purposes of Article 6. It cited *Hornsby v. Greece*, confirming that the right to a fair hearing would be illusory if a final, binding judicial decision remained unenforced to the detriment of a party. The Court also referred to its previous leading cases concerning Bosnia and Herzegovina, namely *Spahić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* and *Kunić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina*, in which it had already found violations concerning similar issues of non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of final domestic judgments.

The Court further observed that the domestic decisions in the present applications ordered specific action to be taken. Consequently, the entitlements they created constituted “possessions” within the meaning of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Having examined all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on admissibility or merits. In particular, it considered that the authorities had not deployed all necessary efforts to enforce fully and in due time the decisions in the applicants’ favour. The State therefore failed to comply with its positive obligation to ensure effective and timely execution of final domestic decisions.

Accordingly, the Court found that the non-enforcement of the domestic decisions violated Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The judgment was final but remained subject to editorial revision. The key violation was the authorities’ failure to secure full and timely enforcement of binding decisions that had already established the applicants’ rights.

In *Ibrišimović and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Application no. 15634/20 and 3 others), the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 11 February 2021. The case originated in four applications lodged against Bosnia and Herzegovina under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants were represented by Mr O. Eterović, a lawyer practising in Sarajevo. The Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina was given notice of the applications.

The applicants’ central complaint was the non-enforcement of domestic decisions given in their favour. Although the judgment does not reproduce the full individual facts—these are set out in an appended table—the key facts are that the applicants had obtained domestic decisions ordering specific action to be taken, and the authorities allegedly failed to enforce those decisions fully and in due time. The applicants relied, expressly or in substance, on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees a fair hearing in the determination of civil rights and obligations, and on Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, which protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

Because the applications raised similar subject matter, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment. The Court reiterated that execution of a judgment given by any court must be regarded as an integral part of a “hearing” for the purposes of Article 6. It referred to *Hornsby v. Greece* and to its leading cases *Spahić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* and *Kunić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina*, in which it had already found violations concerning non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of final domestic judgments. The Court further noted that the decisions in the present applications ordered specific action to be taken and therefore constituted “possessions” within the meaning of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

Having examined all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on the admissibility or merits of the complaints. It considered that the authorities had not deployed all necessary efforts to enforce fully and in due time the decisions in the applicants’ favour. That failure engaged both Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court therefore concluded that there had been a violation of those provisions.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are thus: the existence of domestic decisions ordering specific action in the applicants’ favour; the State’s failure to enforce those decisions fully and promptly; and the resulting interference with the applicants’ right to a fair hearing and their right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions. The judgment is final, though it may be subject to editorial revision. The Committee was composed of Armen Harutyunyan (President), Jolien Schukking, and Ana Maria Guerra Martins, judges, with Liv Tigerstedt as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The Court deliberated in private on 21 January 2021 and adopted the judgment on 11 February 2021.

In **Milošević v. Croatia** (ECtHR, First Section, Application no. 12022/16, judgment of 31 August 2021), the applicant, Milan Milošević, a Bosnia and Herzegovina national, owned a truck. On 29 June 2012, an inspection by the Vukovar Customs Office, assisted by police, found that the truck was using red-tinted, state-supported heating oil, which Croatian law prohibited as motor fuel. The same day, the Customs Office issued a minor-offence penalty notice under section 74(2) of the Excise Duties Act, found him guilty of using the heating oil illegally, and fined him HRK 4,800 (about EUR 640). He did not appeal, the decision became final, and he paid the fine.

Also on 29 June 2012, the Customs Office sent the inspection and sampling records to its administrative department to calculate tax surcharges. On 2 July 2012, the Osijek Customs Office ordered the applicant to pay HRK 123,000 (about EUR 16,700) in excise duties, representing the duty on the oil quantity multiplied by one hundred under section 76(2) of the Excise Duties Act because of the illegal use. The applicant challenged this. On 31 October 2013, the Ministry of Finance quashed the decision because the quantity of heating oil had not been properly determined. On 15 January 2014, the Osijek Customs Office issued a fresh decision for HRK 83,025 (about EUR 11,300), again applying the 100-fold increase. This was upheld on appeal. The applicant’s administrative action was dismissed by the Osijek Administrative Court on 20 January 2015, and the High Administrative Court upheld that ruling. He then lodged a constitutional complaint alleging double punishment contrary to Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. On 20 January 2016, the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded without addressing the ne bis in idem complaint.

The relevant law provided that labelled gas oils could only be used as heating oil. Section 74(2) prohibited their use as motor fuel. Section 80(3) made that a minor offence punishable by a fine for natural persons. Section 76(2) required the owner of a vehicle found using such oil illegally to pay excise duties on the relevant quantity multiplied by one hundred. In 2015, the Act was amended to remove the 100-fold increase; the amendment noted that the increase had been contrary to the ne bis in idem principle and CJEU case-law.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged a violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7, arguing that the minor-offence and administrative tax proceedings punished the same conduct and were based on the same legal provision. He maintained that the 100-fold excise increase showed the tax measure was criminal in nature, not merely preventive. The Government argued that the two proceedings formed a single integrated response: the minor offence protected traffic safety because heating oil damages engines, while the tax proceedings collected excise duties and combated tax evasion, since heating oil is cheaper due to tax advantages. The Government also argued the proceedings were foreseeable, linked in time, and the minor-offence fine was near the legal minimum.

The Court rejected the Government’s non-exhaustion objection because the applicant had raised the ne bis in idem complaint in his constitutional complaint. On the merits, it found a violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. The two sets of proceedings were not sufficiently linked in substance to form a coherent whole, and the applicant suffered disproportionate prejudice by being subjected to both minor-offence punishment and administrative excise duties increased one hundred times.

In *Milošević v. Croatia* (Application no. 12022/16, judgment 31 August 2021), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether the applicant was tried and punished twice for the same conduct, contrary to Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention. The applicant, Milan Milošević, a national of Bosnia and Herzegovina living in Bosanski Brod, owned a truck.

On 29 June 2012, an inspection by the Vukovar Customs Office, assisted by police, found that the truck was using special state-supported heating oil, which Croatian law prohibited as motor vehicle fuel. The same day, the Customs Office found the applicant guilty of a minor offence under section 74(2) of the Excise Duties Act and fined him HRK 4,800 (about EUR 640). The penalty notice stated that non-payment could be enforced and, if unsuccessful, converted into 16 days’ imprisonment. The applicant did not appeal, the decision became final, and he paid the fine.

Also on the same day, the Customs Office sent the inspection and sampling records to its administrative department to calculate tax surcharges. On 2 July 2012, the Osijek Customs Office ordered the applicant to pay HRK 123,000 (about EUR 16,700) in excise duties. This amount represented the excise duty for the oil in question multiplied by one hundred because of its illegal use, under section 76(2) of the Excise Duties Act. The applicant challenged the decision. On 31 October 2013, the Ministry of Finance quashed it because the quantity of oil had not been properly determined. On 15 January 2014, a fresh decision ordered payment of HRK 83,025 (about EUR 11,300), again with the hundredfold increase. That decision was upheld on appeal, and the applicant’s administrative action was dismissed by the Osijek Administrative Court on 20 January 2015, upheld by the High Administrative Court.

The applicant then lodged a constitutional complaint alleging double punishment contrary to Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. On 20 January 2016, the Constitutional Court declared it inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded without addressing the *ne bis in idem* complaint.

Under the relevant Excise Duties Act, labelled gas oils could only be used for heating. Section 80(3) provided a minor-offence fine of HRK 2,000–10,000 for a natural person. Section 76(2) required the owner of a vehicle found using such oil to be charged excise duties for the fuel-tank volume multiplied by one hundred. In 2015, the Act was amended to remove this hundredfold increase; the final proposal noted that it had been contrary to the *ne bis in idem* principle and EU case-law.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant argued that both proceedings concerned the same event and legal provision. The hundredfold increase allegedly showed that the tax measure was criminal/punitive, not merely preventive. The Government claimed the two proceedings formed a single integrated response: the minor offence protected traffic safety, while the tax proceedings collected excise duties and prevented tax evasion; they were linked in time and law, with no duplication of evidence.

The Court dismissed the Government’s exhaustion objection because the applicant had raised the complaint domestically. It declared the complaint admissible and ultimately found a violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. The two sets of proceedings were not sufficiently linked in substance to form a coherent whole, and subjecting the applicant to both the minor-offence and administrative tax proceedings, with excise duties increased one hundred times, caused disproportionate prejudice.

In *Milošević v. Croatia* (Application no. 12022/16), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether the applicant was punished twice for the same conduct, contrary to Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention. The applicant, Milan Milošević, was a national of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

On 29 June 2012, an inspection by the Vukovar Customs Office, assisted by police, found that a truck owned by the applicant was using special state-supported heating oil. Under the Croatian Excise Duties Act, such labelled gas oil could be used only for heating, not as fuel for motor vehicles. The same day, the Customs Office issued a minor-offence penalty notice finding the applicant guilty under section 74(2) of the Act for using red-tinted heating oil as fuel. He was fined HRK 4,800 (about EUR 640). The notice stated that non-payment could be enforced and, if enforcement failed, converted into imprisonment. The applicant did not appeal, the decision became final, and he paid the fine.

Also on the same day, the Customs Office sent the inspection and sampling records to its administrative department to calculate tax surcharges. On 2 July 2012, the Osijek Customs Office ordered the applicant to pay HRK 123,000 (about EUR 16,700) in excise duties. This amount consisted of excise duties for the quantity of oil used, multiplied by one hundred because of its illegal use, under section 76(2) of the Excise Duties Act. The applicant challenged that decision. The Ministry of Finance quashed it because the quantity of oil had not been properly determined. On 15 January 2014, a fresh decision ordered payment of HRK 83,025 (about EUR 11,300), again applying the hundredfold increase for the same incident. That decision was upheld on appeal. The applicant’s administrative action was dismissed by the Osijek Administrative Court on 20 January 2015 and upheld by the High Administrative Court. His constitutional complaint alleging double punishment under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 was declared inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded on 20 January 2016, without a substantive reply on the *ne bis in idem* issue.

The legal framework allowed a minor-offence fine of HRK 2,000 to HRK 10,000 for illegal use of heating oil. Section 76(2) required the vehicle owner to be charged excise duties corresponding to the fuel-tank volume multiplied by one hundred. In 2015, the Act was amended to remove that hundredfold increase; the final proposal noted that the increase had been contrary to *ne bis in idem* and EU standards.

The applicant argued that both proceedings concerned the same event and same legal provision, and that the hundredfold excise charge showed the administrative measure was criminal in nature, not merely tax collection. The Government argued that the two proceedings formed a single integrated response: the minor offence protected traffic safety, while the tax proceedings collected excise duties and prevented tax evasion. It also relied on foreseeability, close timing, and the absence of duplicated evidence.

The Court declared the complaint admissible, finding that the applicant had exhausted domestic remedies by raising it in his constitutional complaint. On the merits, it found a violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. Although the proceedings arose from the same facts, they were not sufficiently linked in substance to form a coherent whole. The applicant suffered disproportionate prejudice, especially because the administrative tax proceedings increased excise duties one hundred times for conduct already punished in the minor-offence proceedings.
001-210332:
**Summary of the Case**

The case of *Norwegian Confederation of Trade Unions (LO) and Norwegian Transport Workers’ Union (NTF) v. Norway* concerns an alleged violation of Article 11 (freedom of association) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The dispute arose from a trade union boycott intended to pressure a foreign-owned company to enter into a Norwegian collective agreement, a move that Norwegian courts ultimately declared unlawful for conflicting with the right of freedom of establishment under the European Economic Area (EEA) Agreement.

**Key Facts:**
The applicants, NTF and LO, were parties to a longstanding collective "Framework Agreement" for dockworkers, which established a system of priority engagement for registered dockworkers at major Norwegian ports. This system, rooted in ILO Convention No. 137, was managed at the port of Drammen by the Administration Office, which employed all permanent dockworkers.

Holship Norge AS, a wholly-owned Norwegian subsidiary of a Danish freight forwarding group, operated in the port of Drammen. It was not a member of the relevant employer organisation or a party to the Framework Agreement. In 2013, instead of using the Administration Office’s services, Holship employed its own workers to perform loading and unloading tasks.

In response, NTF demanded that Holship enter into a collective agreement, specifically to accept the Framework Agreement and its priority-of-engagement clause. When Holship refused, NTF issued a notice of boycott, threatening a blockade of ships at the port of Drammen where Holship was involved in loading or unloading. The stated purpose was to secure a collective agreement enshrining the dockworkers' priority rights.

The case proceeded through Norwegian courts. While the Drammen City Court and the Borgarting High Court found the notified boycott to be lawful, the Supreme Court, in a 10-7 plenary decision on 16 December 2016, ruled it unlawful. The Supreme Court’s majority held that the boycott’s primary objective, while aimed at protecting workers, was to enforce a priority-of-engagement system that restricted Holship’s right to freedom of establishment under Article 31 of the EEA Agreement. This restriction was not sufficiently justified and failed the proportionality test. The majority reasoned that the system shielded the Administration Office from competition and was detrimental to Holship's own employees, and that the protection of working conditions could be achieved by less restrictive means. The court also referenced an advisory opinion from the EFTA Court, which found the system likely to constitute a restriction on freedom of establishment.

The applicant unions then lodged a complaint with the European Court of Human Rights, arguing that the Norwegian Supreme Court’s decision to declare their planned boycott unlawful violated their right to freedom of association under Article 11 of the Convention.

In *Norwegian Confederation of Trade Unions (LO) and Norwegian Transport Workers’ Union (NTF) v. Norway*, the applicants were Norwegian trade unions challenging a Norwegian Supreme Court ruling that declared an announced boycott unlawful.

The dispute concerned dockwork in Norway. The unions had a collective framework agreement with the Confederation of Norwegian Enterprise (NHO) covering dockworkers. The agreement included a priority-of-engagement clause: for vessels of 50 dwt or more sailing between Norwegian and foreign ports, loading and unloading had to be carried out by dockworkers, except at a company’s own facilities using its own employees. In Drammen, this system was managed by the Administration Office, a non-profit entity employing registered dockworkers with permanent employment and pay protections.

Holship Norge AS, a Norwegian subsidiary of a Danish freight group, was based in Drammen but was not an NHO member and was not party to the Framework Agreement. In 2013, instead of using the Administration Office, Holship used four of its own employees for loading and unloading. NTF demanded that Holship enter into a collective agreement accepting the Framework Agreement. After mediation failed, NTF notified a boycott/blockade of ships calling at Drammen where Holship was involved in loading or unloading. The stated purpose was to secure a collective agreement and enforce priority of engagement for Administration Office dockworkers. NTF also said it was willing to negotiate to limit harm to Holship’s employees.

NTF sought a declaration that the boycott was lawful. The Drammen City Court and Borgarting High Court ruled in its favour, finding the purpose was to protect dockworkers’ permanent employment and conditions, including under ILO Convention No. 137, and that there was no unlawful purpose or violation of negative freedom of association.

Holship appealed to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court sought an advisory opinion from the EFTA Court, which indicated that the priority system likely restricted freedom of establishment under Article 31 EEA and that the boycott did not genuinely aim at improving Holship employees’ conditions. The Supreme Court, by 10 votes to 7, declared the boycott unlawful. The majority held that the priority-of-engagement demand restricted Holship’s EEA freedom of establishment. Although protection of workers could justify restrictions, the boycott’s primary effect was to limit market access and shield the Administration Office from competition, not to protect Holship’s employees. It therefore failed proportionality. The minority found the boycott justified as a legitimate means of protecting dockworkers.

The unions complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 11, alleging that the Supreme Court’s decision violated their freedom of association. The ECtHR held that the planned boycott was capable of falling within Article 11, but found no violation. The domestic decision was well-founded. The Court assumed, only for this case, that the *Bosphorus* presumption did not apply to EEA law. It held that EEA rights should not be treated as a competing right to be balanced against Article 11, but rather considered as one element in the proportionality assessment. Economic consequences of collective action were not decisive. Overall, declaring the boycott unlawful was a proportionate and justified restriction on freedom of association.

The case concerned an Article 11 ECHR complaint by the Norwegian Confederation of Trade Unions (LO) and the Norwegian Transport Workers’ Union (NTF) against Norway. The dispute arose after Norway’s Supreme Court declared an announced trade union boycott unlawful.

The unions had a collective framework agreement with the Confederation of Norwegian Enterprise (NHO) regulating pay and working conditions for dockworkers. Clause 2(1) gave registered dockworkers priority of engagement for loading and unloading on vessels of 50 dwt or more sailing between Norwegian and foreign ports, except at a company’s own facilities. In Drammen, an Administration Office for Dock Work employed permanent dockworkers and assigned them to port users, who paid fees. Holship Norge AS, a Norwegian subsidiary of the Danish Holship group, was not an NHO member and was not bound by the framework agreement. Until 2013 it used the Administration Office; in 2013 it employed four workers who also performed loading and unloading for Holship.

In April 2013 NTF demanded that Holship enter into a collective agreement and accept the framework agreement. After mediation failed, NTF notified a boycott/blockade of ships calling at Drammen where Holship was involved in loading or unloading. NTF stated the aim was to secure a collective agreement and enforce the priority-of-engagement clause for Administration Office dockworkers. NTF applied to the Drammen City Court for an advance declaration that the boycott was lawful. The City Court and Borgarting High Court found it lawful, relying on Norway’s ILO Convention No. 137 obligations and the historical dockworker scheme. Holship appealed.

The Supreme Court sought an advisory opinion from the EFTA Court. The EFTA Court found that the priority clause and Administration Office system likely restricted EEA freedom of establishment under Article 31 EEA, went beyond the core of collective bargaining, protected only a limited group of dockworkers to the detriment of others, and could affect negative freedom of association. The Norwegian Supreme Court, sitting plenary, ruled by ten votes to seven that the boycott was unlawful. The majority balanced Article 11 freedom of association against EEA freedom of establishment. It accepted that protecting workers could justify restrictions, but found the boycott’s principal effect was to restrict Holship’s market access and shield the Administration Office from competition. Priority of engagement was not sufficiently justified; ILO Convention No. 137 did not require it, and EEA freedom of establishment took precedence. The boycott therefore had an unlawful purpose under the Boycott Act. The minority found the boycott justified and lawful.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the unions alleged a violation of Article 11. The Court assumed the announced boycott fell within the scope of Article 11, but found no violation. The domestic decision was prescribed by law, pursued legitimate aims, and was proportionate. The Court held that EEA freedom of establishment was not to be balanced against Article 11 as an external right, but should be considered as one element in the proportionality assessment. Economic consequences of collective action were not decisive. The non-inclusion of the EU Charter in the EEA Agreement was not determinative of the Bosphorus presumption, and the Court assumed for this case that Bosphorus did not apply to EEA law. Ultimately, the declaration that the boycott was unlawful was well-founded, and there was no violation of Article 11.

In *Monir Lotfy v. Cyprus*, the applicant was an Egyptian national with a long immigration history in Cyprus. He had been deported twice and had his Cypriot citizenship revoked. After re-entering Cyprus unlawfully, he was arrested on 10 February 2013 during a random identity check. On 11 February 2013, detention and deportation orders were issued under the Aliens and Immigration Law because he was considered a prohibited immigrant. He was held in immigration detention in several facilities, mainly the Menoyia detention centre, until his deportation to Egypt on 8 July 2014.

The key Article 5 complaint arose from his continued detention after a habeas corpus ruling. On 11 July 2013, the applicant challenged the lawfulness of his detention, arguing that it had lasted more than five months without progress toward deportation. The Government did not file an objection. On 30 July 2013, the Supreme Court ordered his immediate release. It found that the Government had failed to show that his continued detention was lawful, had not explained what steps had been taken to execute the deportation order, and had not informed the court whether the Minister of the Interior had reviewed the detention. The Government did not appeal. However, on the same day, while the applicant was still at court, he was rearrested and returned to detention. The Director of the Civil Registry and Migration Department annulled the old orders and issued new deportation and detention orders on substantially the same grounds. Internal notes suggested that the first habeas corpus application had failed only because the authorities had not supplied relevant information, and that the Supreme Court might have decided differently had it known the full facts. A second habeas corpus application was rejected in January 2014; the Supreme Court treated the detention as continuous and lawful, citing ministerial extensions and delays in obtaining a travel document due to the situation in Egypt and the applicant’s refusal to cooperate. The applicant was eventually deported after Egyptian authorities issued a travel document without his consent.

For Article 3, the central issue concerned conditions at Menoyia detention centre. The applicant was held there from 18 February to 6 July 2013 and again from 30 September 2013 to 8 July 2014. The cells measured 18.36 square metres and were used to hold up to eight inmates. During his detention, he shared with four to seven other detainees, meaning his personal space could fall well below acceptable minimum standards, sometimes to around 2.3–3.7 square metres. Other facilities, such as Nicosia Central Prisons Block 10 and various police stations, offered more space, but the prolonged overcrowding at Menoyia was significant. The applicant also alleged ill-treatment, lack of medical treatment, and solitary confinement, but the Court’s principal Article 3 finding concerned the reductions in required minimum personal space at a specialised immigration detention centre. Those reductions were not short, occasional, or minor.

Overall, the case concerns two main alleged violations: arbitrary continued detention after a habeas corpus writ ordering immediate release, contrary to Article 5 § 1(f), and degrading treatment due to insufficient personal space at Menoyia detention centre, contrary to Article 3.

In *Monir Lotfy v. Cyprus* (Application no. 37139/13, judgment of 29 June 2021), the applicant was an Egyptian national with a long immigration history in Cyprus. He first arrived in 1991, was deported twice, and although he had been granted Cypriot citizenship, that citizenship was later revoked and his challenges to the revocation failed. After his second deportation in June 2012, he re-entered Cyprus unlawfully. On 10 February 2013 he was arrested during a random identity check, and on 11 February detention and deportation orders were issued under the Aliens and Immigration Law on the basis that he was a prohibited immigrant. He was held in immigration detention from 11 February 2013 until his deportation on 8 July 2014, mostly at the Menoyia detention centre but also in Nicosia Central Prisons Block 10 and various police stations.

The Article 5 § 1(f) complaint concerned the arbitrariness of his continued detention with a view to deportation after a habeas corpus writ ordered his immediate release. On 11 July 2013 the applicant lodged a habeas corpus application. On 30 July 2013 the Supreme Court ordered his immediate release, finding that the Government had failed to show that his detention for more than five months remained lawful: it had not explained the steps taken to deport him, why deportation had not occurred, or whether the Minister had reviewed the detention. Nevertheless, on the same day, while still at the court, the applicant was rearrested and returned to Block 10. An internal note from the Director of the Civil Registry and Migration Department stated that the habeas application had been served late, that the detention was considered lawful, and that the earlier orders were annulled and new deportation and detention orders were issued on the same grounds. A second habeas corpus application was rejected in January 2014. The Minister extended detention repeatedly, and the applicant was deported in July 2014 after the Egyptian authorities issued a travel document without his consent. The Court found that re-detaining him immediately after the Supreme Court’s release order, on materially identical grounds and without changed circumstances, rendered the continued detention arbitrary under Article 5 § 1(f).

The Article 3 complaint focused on conditions of detention, especially at Menoyia. That centre opened in January 2013 and was designed for periods of up to two months, but the applicant was held there long-term. At Menoyia, cells measured 18.36 sq m and were used for up to eight detainees; the applicant shared with four to seven others. This reduced available personal space below acceptable minimum standards and was not “short, occasional and minor,” leading to a violation of Article 3. Other placements included Block 10 (9 sq m shared by two), Aradippou police station (6.9 sq m shared by two), and single cells at Polis Chrysochous and Ayia Napa (10.8 and 9.4 sq m). The applicant also alleged ill-treatment, denial of medical treatment, hunger strikes, and solitary confinement; the Government disputed these claims, and many incidents could not be fully investigated after his deportation. The Court’s key findings therefore concerned the arbitrary post-habeas detention and the degrading conditions caused by overcrowding and inadequate personal space at Menoyia.

**Monir Lotfy v. Cyprus** (Application no. 37139/13, 29 June 2021) concerned an Egyptian national with a long immigration history in Cyprus. He had first arrived in 1991, was deported twice, had Cypriot citizenship revoked, and later re-entered Cyprus unlawfully. On 10 February 2013 he was arrested during a random identity check. The next day, deportation and detention orders were issued under Cyprus’s Aliens and Immigration Law because he was a prohibited immigrant. He was held in immigration detention in several facilities, principally Menoyia detention centre, but also Nicosia Central Prisons Block 10, Aradippou, Polis Chrysochous, and Ayia Napa police stations. He remained detained until his deportation to Egypt on 8 July 2014.

The applicant challenged his detention through two habeas corpus applications. In his first application, filed on 11 July 2013, he argued that detention exceeding five months was unlawful because no progress had been made toward deportation. On 30 July 2013 the Supreme Court ordered his immediate release, finding that the authorities had failed to justify continued detention or to show what steps had been taken to execute the deportation order or whether the Minister of the Interior had reviewed it. However, on the same day, while still at the court, he was rearrested. The Director of the Civil Registry and Migration Department annulled the old orders and issued new, essentially identical deportation and detention orders based on the same grounds. A second habeas corpus application was rejected in January 2014. The Supreme Court held that detention had continued for the same reasons and that the Minister had extended it. The applicant also brought judicial review proceedings and an asylum claim, both ultimately unsuccessful.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 5 § 1(f) concerning the arbitrariness of his continued detention after the habeas corpus writ ordering his release. The authorities’ immediate re-detention using identical orders circumvented the Supreme Court’s binding decision without adequate justification. This undermined the protection against arbitrary detention in expulsion cases.

The Court also found a violation of Article 3 regarding conditions at Menoyia detention centre. The applicant was held in a multi-occupancy cell measuring 18.36 sq m, shared with four to seven other detainees, with capacity for up to eight. The Government provided no occupancy records. The Court found that the resulting reductions in personal space were not “short, occasional and minor,” and therefore amounted to degrading treatment. Other complaints, including alleged ill-treatment and denial of medical care, were not central to the violations found. The case established that re-detaining an immigration detainee immediately after a habeas corpus release order, using substantively identical orders, can breach Article 5 § 1(f), and that overcrowded personal space in immigration detention may breach Article 3.
001-209438:
**Alimpiev v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia** (Application no. 48802/08, ECtHR, 27 April 2021) concerned a Russian national, Alexandru Alimpiev, born in 1950 and living in Tiraspol. He had been president of the Tiraspol People’s Court in the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”). On 31 August 2006 the “MRT” prosecutor’s office opened a corruption investigation against him. He was arrested and charged on 17 May 2007 and remained in detention pending trial until 25 December 2008, when the “MRT” Supreme Court convicted him and sentenced him to seven years’ imprisonment. The conviction was upheld on 18 March 2009, but on 24 July 2009 the sentence was reduced to five years and he was released under an amnesty.

The application alleged violations under Article 3 (inhuman detention conditions and lack of medical assistance; being held in a metal cage during trial), Article 5 §§ 3 and 4 (rights during pre-trial detention), Article 6 § 1 (fair trial), Article 8 (censorship of correspondence), and Article 13 (effective remedy). The key facts relevant to those alleged violations included the following.

While detained pending trial, the prosecutor repeatedly sought extensions of detention, which a judge granted. The applicant’s lawyer was unable to obtain copies of the extension decisions. On 21 July 2008 he asked the president of the “MRT” Supreme Court for a copy of a 18 July 2008 extension decision; the reply stated that “MRT” law did not give defence representatives a right to obtain copies of such decisions. A request to copy parts of the criminal file was also refused. On 18 August 2008 the lawyer asked for copies of all extension decisions, stressing that he had not been involved at the pre-trial stage and needed them to prepare an effective defence. Applications to replace detention with another preventive measure relied on Articles 3, 5, 6, 8 and 13 and argued that the “MRT” courts had cited only abstract risks without evidence. On 11 November 2008 the lawyer issued a press release publicising the case.

As to conditions, the applicant described detention in an IVS in Tiraspol and UIN-3 prison: no separate toilet or shower, no hygiene products or bed linen, parasite-infested cells, bad tap water, a small window letting in damp and cold air, very short daily walks, and a 30 kg monthly parcel limit including bottled water. He said the food was inedible and amounted to torture through hunger. During trial he was held in a metal cage. A medical certificate showed that on 23 June 2008 an emergency team diagnosed respiratory problems and moderate persistent asthma; his cellmates smoked heavily, worsening his condition. He also alleged all correspondence was censored; an envelope from his lawyer bore the stamp “Verified. Censor (signature), 8/09/2008”.

On jurisdiction, the Court followed its case-law on Transdniestria. Moldova had jurisdiction as the territorial State but only positive obligations. Russia’s objection was dismissed because Russia exercised effective control and decisive influence over the “MRT” through military, economic and political support. However, the application against Moldova was rejected for non-exhaustion: the press release did not properly inform the Moldovan authorities or request assistance. On Article 3, the Court found that the applicant’s conditions of detention—severe overcrowding, lack of sanitation, insufficient daylight and inadequate medical assistance, exacerbated by passive smoking and asthma—breached the Convention. Holding him in a metal cage throughout trial was also inherently degrading and breached Article 3, with no security justification offered. Russia was held responsible for these violations.

Alimpiev v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia (Application no. 48802/08) concerned a Russian national, born in 1950 and living in Tiraspol, who had been president of the Tiraspol People’s Court in the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”). On 31 August 2006 the “MRT” prosecutor’s office began a corruption investigation into him. He was arrested on 17 May 2007 and charged with corruption. He remained in pre-trial detention until 25 December 2008, when the “MRT” Supreme Court convicted him and sentenced him to seven years’ imprisonment. That judgment was upheld on 18 March 2009, but on 24 July 2009 the sentence was reduced to five years and he was released under an amnesty.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 3 (inhuman and degrading treatment), Article 5 §§ 3 and 4 (rights in pre-trial detention), Article 6 § 1 (fair trial), Article 8 (correspondence), and Article 13 (effective remedy). The key facts concerned his detention conditions, medical care, court cage, inability to obtain detention-extension decisions, and censorship of correspondence.

As to detention conditions, the applicant described the IVS in Tiraspol and prison UIN-3 as severely inadequate: the cell had no separate toilet or shower, no hygiene products or bed linen, parasites, bad tap water, a very small window letting in damp and cold air, and only very short daily walks. Relatives could send only 30 kg of items per month, including bottled water, and the food was inedible, which he said amounted to torture through hunger. During his trial he was held in a metal cage. He asked to sit next to his lawyer instead of in the cage, arguing this was necessary for an effective defence. It was unclear whether he received a reply.

On medical care, an emergency medical team attended him on 23 June 2008 and diagnosed respiratory problems and moderate persistent asthma; medication was prescribed. He stated that his cellmates smoked heavily, exposing him, a non-smoker, to passive smoking, and that his health worsened.

Regarding pre-trial detention, the prosecutor periodically sought extensions, which judges granted. The applicant could not obtain copies of any extension decisions. His lawyer’s requests were refused. For example, on 21 July 2008 the lawyer asked the “MRT” Supreme Court president for a copy of the 18 July 2008 extension decision and invoked Article 34 of the Convention, but was told “MRT” law did not give defence representatives the right to obtain copies of such decisions. On 15 August 2008 a request to copy parts of the criminal file was also refused. On 18 August 2008 the lawyer asked for copies of all detention-extension decisions, noting he had not been involved at the pre-trial stage and needed them for an effective defence. In applications to replace detention, the lawyer argued that the courts merely cited possible risks—absconding, reoffending, interfering with the investigation—without evidence.

On correspondence, the applicant alleged all his mail was censored. He submitted a lawyer’s letter with an envelope stamped “Verified. Censor (signature), 8/09/2008.”

The Court found Moldova had jurisdiction but its responsibility was limited to positive obligations; the case against Moldova was rejected for non-exhaustion because a press release did not properly inform the Moldovan authorities. Russia, however, exercised effective control over the “MRT” through military, economic, and political support, so the applicant fell within Russian jurisdiction. On the merits, the Court found a breach of Article 3 due to inhuman detention conditions, lack of required medical assistance, and the unjustified use of a metal cage during trial. Russia was held responsible.

**Summary of *Alimpiev v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* (Application no. 48802/08)**

Alexandru Alimpiev, a Russian national born in 1950 and residing in Tiraspol, served as president of the Tiraspol People's Court in the self-proclaimed "Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria" ("MRT"). On 31 August 2006, the "MRT" prosecutor's office initiated a criminal investigation into corruption allegations against him. He was arrested on 17 May 2007 and formally charged with corruption.

From his arrest until his conviction on 25 December 2008, Alimpiev was detained pending trial. During this period, the prosecutor periodically sought extensions of his detention, which a judge granted each time. However, the applicant was unable to obtain copies of any decisions extending his detention. His lawyer's requests for copies were repeatedly rejected on the basis that "MRT" law did not provide for the right of defence representatives to obtain copies of such decisions. On 18 August 2008, the lawyer again requested copies of all detention extension decisions, emphasising he had not been involved at the pre-trial stage and needed them to organise an effective defence. He also relied on Article 34 of the Convention. The lawyer filed applications to replace detention with alternative measures, invoking Articles 3, 5, 6, 8, and 13 of the Convention, and arguing that "MRT" courts extended detention by citing legal provisions without reference to evidence confirming specific risks in the applicant's case.

Regarding conditions of detention, Alimpiev described his cells in the Tiraspol temporary detention facility (IVS) and prison (UIN-3) as lacking separate toilets or showers, hygiene products, and bed linen. The cells were infested with parasites, tap water quality was poor, and windows were small, allowing damp and cold air inside. Daily walks were very short. A 30 kg monthly weight limit on items sent by relatives, combined with inedible facility food, meant he was often subjected to "torture through hunger." During trial, he was held in a metal cage. A medical certificate confirmed that on 23 June 2008, an emergency team diagnosed respiratory problems and moderate persistent asthma. His cellmates smoked heavily, subjecting him to passive smoking.

Additionally, Alimpiev alleged that all his correspondence was censored during detention. He submitted an envelope from a letter sent by his lawyer bearing a stamp reading "Verified. Censor (signature), 8/09/2008."

On 25 December 2008, the "MRT" Supreme Court convicted him and sentenced him to seven years' imprisonment. This was upheld on 18 March 2009, but on 24 July 2009, the plenary "MRT" Supreme Court reduced his sentence to five years and ordered his release under an amnesty.

The Court found Moldova had jurisdiction but that the applicant failed to exhaust domestic remedies against it by not properly informing Moldovan authorities. Regarding Russia, the Court held it exercised effective control over the "MRT" and bore responsibility. The Court declared admissible the complaints under Article 3 concerning inhuman detention conditions, lack of medical assistance, and being held in a metal cage during trial, finding violations of Article 3.

Rovshan Hajiyev v. Azerbaijan (Applications nos. 19925/12 and 47532/13) concerned a journalist’s access to State-held information about the environmental and public-health impact of the Gabala Radar Station. Hajiyev was an Azerbaijani journalist and editor of the newspaper Azadlıq. The Gabala Radar Station was a Soviet-era military early-warning radar located in Azerbaijan and operated by Russia under a lease until 2012. It allegedly caused serious environmental and health problems in the Gabala District and nearby areas.

By presidential orders in 2001 and 2003, Azerbaijan created commissions—chaired by the Minister of Healthcare—to assess the station’s impact on the environment and public health. In July 2010, invoking the Law on Access to Information, Hajiyev asked the Ministry of Healthcare whether the relevant State commission was still active and requested copies of reports prepared by the commissions. The Ministry replied that a report prepared under the 2001 order had been transmitted to the Cabinet of Ministers. Hajiyev considered this an inadequate response and sued, seeking an order requiring the Ministry to provide the report. The Ministry argued that it no longer possessed the report and had therefore given a comprehensive reply. The domestic courts dismissed his claim, holding that the Ministry had complied with its obligations because it no longer held the report and had assisted him by identifying the Cabinet of Ministers as the holder.

Separately, in December 2010, Hajiyev wrote to the Cabinet of Ministers requesting a copy of the same report. The Cabinet received the request but did not respond. He sued, arguing that the failure breached the Law on Access to Information and Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights. During the proceedings, the Cabinet of Ministers did not appear or submit written pleadings. In December 2011, Baku Administrative Economic Court No. 1 dismissed the claim, reasoning that Article 29.1 of the Law did not oblige an information owner to disclose reports of commissions created for a specific purpose. Hajiyev appealed, arguing that Article 29.1 merely listed categories of information that must be proactively disclosed; it did not limit the right to request other non-restricted, public-interest information. The Baku Court of Appeal upheld the dismissal in March 2012, and the Supreme Court upheld it in July 2012.

Under the Law, State bodies were “information owners.” They were required to respond to requests, assist applicants in locating information, and, if refusing access, provide clear and substantiated written reasons with legal references and notice of the right to challenge. Article 29.1 listed types of information to be proactively disclosed, including environmental information, while Article 34 distinguished open from restricted information.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 10. It emphasised that the applicant, as a journalist, sought information of public interest concerning environmental and health risks from a former military radar station. The domestic authorities failed to consider the procedural requirements of the access-to-information law and did not indicate any substantive ground for denying access. The courts’ interpretation of Article 29.1—effectively treating it as removing any duty to disclose reports of specially created commissions—was manifestly unreasonable and resulted in an arbitrary denial of State-held information. Azerbaijan therefore breached Hajiyev’s right to receive information under Article 10.

**Case: Rovshan Hajiyev v. Azerbaijan (Applications nos. 19925/12 and 47532/13), European Court of Human Rights, 9 December 2021**

The applicant, Rovshan Hajiyev, was an Azerbaijani journalist and editor of the newspaper *Azadlıq*. The case concerned his attempts to obtain State-held information about the environmental and public-health impact of the Gabala Radar Station, a former Soviet military early-warning radar located in Azerbaijan and operated by Russia under a lease until 2012. A joint Azerbaijani-Russian commission had been created by presidential orders in 2001 and 2003 to assess the station’s impact on the environment and public health. According to the applicant, independent studies indicated serious health problems in Gabala and nearby districts.

In July 2010, relying on Azerbaijan’s Law on Access to Information, Hajiyev wrote to the Ministry of Healthcare asking whether the relevant State commission was still active and requesting copies of reports prepared by commissions concerning the radar station. He stated that the information was needed for analysis and public discussion of the station’s environmental and health effects. By letter of 6 August 2010, the Ministry replied that a report prepared under the 2001 presidential order had been transmitted to the Cabinet of Ministers, but it did not provide a copy.

The applicant brought court proceedings seeking an order requiring the Ministry to provide the report. The Ministry argued that it no longer possessed the report and had given a comprehensive reply. In February 2011, the Nasimi District Court dismissed the claim, finding that because the Ministry no longer held the report and had informed the applicant that it had been sent to the Cabinet of Ministers, it had complied with its disclosure obligations. The Baku Court of Appeal upheld that judgment in May 2011, and the Supreme Court upheld it in September 2011.

Separately, in December 2010, the applicant asked the Cabinet of Ministers for a copy of the same report. The Cabinet received the request but did not respond. He then sued the Cabinet, arguing that its failure to respond breached the Law on Access to Information and Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Cabinet did not participate in the proceedings or submit written pleadings. In December 2011, the Baku Administrative Economic Court No. 1 dismissed the claim, reasoning that Article 29.1 of the Law on Access to Information did not oblige an information owner to disclose reports of commissions created for a specific purpose. The Baku Court of Appeal upheld that decision in March 2012, and the Supreme Court upheld it in July 2012.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained under Article 10 that the refusal to grant him access to information of public interest violated his right to receive and impart information. He argued that the requested report was not lawfully restricted and that, as a journalist, he needed it to exercise his professional functions. The Government did not raise admissibility objections other than contesting the merits.

The Court examined the applications jointly and found a violation of Article 10. It held that the domestic authorities had failed to consider the procedural requirements of the Law on Access to Information and had not indicated any substantive grounds for denying access. Their interpretation and application of the relevant domestic law were manifestly unreasonable, particularly regarding the refusal to provide the requested report of public interest concerning environmental and health impacts.

In *Rovshan Hajiyev v. Azerbaijan*, the applicant was an Azerbaijani journalist and editor of the newspaper *Azadlıq*. He sought information about the Gabala Radar Station, a former Soviet military early-warning radar located in Azerbaijan and leased to Russia until 2012. The station had raised public concern about environmental and public-health effects. Presidential orders in 2001 and 2003 created State commissions to assess its environmental impact and monitor public health, chaired by the Minister of Healthcare.

On 27 July 2010, Hajiyev wrote to the Ministry of Healthcare under the Law on Access to Information, identifying himself as editor and requesting: whether the State commission assessing the radar station’s environmental and public-health impact was still active; and what reports had been prepared or published, including copies. He stated the information was needed for analysis and public discussion. On 6 August 2010, the Ministry replied only that a report prepared under the 2001 presidential order had been transmitted to the Cabinet of Ministers.

Hajiyev sued the Ministry, arguing that the reply breached the access law. The Ministry claimed it no longer possessed the report and had given a comprehensive response. On 3 February 2011, the Nasimi District Court dismissed the claim, finding the Ministry had complied by stating it lacked the report and answering other questions. The Baku Court of Appeal upheld this on 2 May 2011, adding that Article 17.2 required an information owner without the information to help locate it, which the Ministry did by pointing to the Cabinet. The Supreme Court upheld that judgment on 5 September 2011.

Separately, on 6 December 2010, Hajiyev asked the Cabinet of Ministers for a copy of the same commission report. The Cabinet received the request but did not respond. After further unanswered requests in April 2011, he brought administrative proceedings seeking an order that the Cabinet execute the request. The Cabinet did not appear or submit pleadings. On 23 December 2011, Baku Administrative Economic Court No. 1 dismissed the claim, reasoning that Article 29.1 of the Law on Access to Information did not oblige an information owner to disclose reports of commissions created for a specific purpose.

On appeal, Hajiyev argued that Article 29.1 merely listed categories of information to be proactively published and did not restrict individual requests for other non-restricted information. He contended the report was public-interest information needed for his journalistic work under Article 10. The Baku Court of Appeal upheld the dismissal on 15 March 2012, and the Supreme Court upheld it on 11 July 2012.

The alleged violations concerned the denial of access to State-held information of public interest and, in the first application, the fairness of the domestic proceedings. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 10. It held that the domestic authorities had failed to consider the procedural requirements for refusing access and had not indicated any substantive grounds for denial. Their interpretation and application of the domestic access law were manifestly unreasonable, particularly in treating Article 29.1 as excluding the requested report from disclosure despite its public environmental and health interest.
