In *Avci v. Denmark* (Application no. 40240/19), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Denmark’s expulsion of a settled migrant with a permanent re-entry ban violated Article 8 of the Convention, which protects private and family life. The applicant, Cihan Avci, was a Turkish national born in Denmark in 1993 and had lived there for about twenty-five years. He was unmarried and had no children. His parents and three siblings lived in Denmark. He had not completed the ninth grade or any further education, had worked in various jobs, and was receiving unemployment benefits when arrested. He spoke Danish better than Turkish or Kurdish, had visited Turkey only as a tourist, and had some relatives there, including a maternal grandfather; his earlier claim about a maternal aunt was disputed.

In October 2013, Avci received a suspended 20-day sentence for attempting to free a detainee and, as part of a crowd, causing public insecurity. More significantly, in September 2018 the District Court convicted him of serious drug offences under section 191 of the Penal Code. Between January and April 2017, as part of an organised network, he had received, possessed, and transferred one kilogram of cocaine through extensive sales and deliveries to identified and unidentified buyers. He was sentenced to four years’ imprisonment and given a warning about expulsion.

On appeal, in January 2019 the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence but ordered his expulsion with a permanent re-entry ban. It found the drug offences very serious, committed over several months and in an organised network, and that his behaviour represented a genuine and sufficiently serious threat to fundamental societal interests. It also found a risk of reoffending if he remained in Denmark, rejecting his explanation that he had acted because of gambling debt. The High Court acknowledged that he was born and raised in Denmark, that his family lived there, and that permanent expulsion would be a particular burden. However, it found he had certain ties to Turkey, including holidays, a grandfather, some Kurdish language ability, and knowledge of customs and culture. Although his personal and cultural ties to Denmark were stronger, he had the prerequisites to establish a life in Turkey, and family contact could continue by phone or internet. The court therefore concluded that compelling circumstances outweighed those against expulsion and that it was not disproportionate under Article 8.

The Appeals Permission Board refused leave to appeal to the Supreme Court in March 2019. The deportation order was enforced in January 2020. Avci complained to the ECtHR that the expulsion and permanent re-entry ban breached Article 8. The Government argued non-exhaustion because he could later seek revocation under section 50 of the Aliens Act, but the Court held that he had exhausted domestic remedies by challenging the expulsion in the criminal proceedings. The application was declared admissible.

On the merits, the applicant argued that the domestic courts had failed to weigh properly his strong ties to Denmark, weak ties to Turkey, minor criminal past, and lack of a prior conditional expulsion order. The Government maintained that the order was lawful, pursued the legitimate aim of preventing disorder and crime, and was necessary, with domestic courts having conducted a fair Article 8 balancing exercise. The ECtHR ultimately found no violation of Article 8, holding that very serious reasons justified expelling the settled migrant and that the domestic courts had duly assessed proportionality.

In *Avci v. Denmark* (Application no. 40240/19), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Denmark’s expulsion of a settled migrant with a permanent re-entry ban violated Article 8 of the Convention, protecting private and family life.

The applicant, Cihan Avci, was a Turkish national born in Denmark in 1993. He had lived in Denmark for approximately twenty-five years. In 2013, he received a suspended 20-day sentence for attempting to free a detainee and, as part of a crowd, causing public insecurity. More seriously, by a District Court judgment of 12 September 2018, he was convicted of serious drug offences under section 191(2) read with section 191(1) of the Danish Penal Code, committed between January and April 2017. As part of an organised network, he had received, possessed, and transferred one kilogram of cocaine through extensive sales and deliveries to identified and unidentified buyers. He was sentenced to four years’ imprisonment and given a warning about expulsion.

The Immigration Service gathered information on his personal circumstances. He was born and raised in Denmark and lived there with his parents and three siblings. He was unmarried and had no children. He had not completed the ninth grade or any subsequent education, although he later passed ninth-grade final exams while in remand. He had worked in various jobs, including in a supermarket and as a waiter, and was receiving unemployment benefits when arrested. He had a maternal aunt and grandfather in Turkey, spoke Turkish/Kurdish but less well than Danish, and had visited Turkey on holidays. Before the High Court, he disputed some of this: he said his father’s sister had died, he had no maternal aunt in Turkey, his maternal grandfather suffered from dementia and he had no relationship with him, he spoke only a little Kurdish and mostly Danish with his parents, and he did not really speak Turkish. He claimed he committed the offences because of a gambling debt.

On appeal, the High Court, by judgment of 17 January 2019, unanimously confirmed the conviction and sentence but ordered his expulsion with a permanent re-entry ban. It found that the drug offences were very serious, committed as part of organised drug dealing over several months, and that his behaviour represented a genuine and sufficiently serious threat to the fundamental interests of society. It also found a risk that he would reoffend in Denmark if not expelled. Although his personal and cultural ties with Denmark were stronger than those with Turkey, the High Court considered that he had certain ties to Turkey and the prerequisites to establish a life there. Family in Denmark could maintain contact by phone and the internet. It concluded that the circumstances favouring expulsion were sufficiently compelling and that a permanent re-entry ban would not be disproportionate under Article 8 ECHR or Article 14(1) of the Association Agreement. The Appeals Permission Board refused leave to appeal to the Supreme Court on 8 March 2019, and the deportation order was enforced on 24 January 2020.

Before the ECtHR, Avci complained that the expulsion violated Article 8. The Government argued non-exhaustion, because he could seek revocation under section 50 of the Aliens Act, and that the complaint was manifestly ill-founded. The Court declared the application admissible, finding that challenging the expulsion in criminal proceedings exhausted domestic remedies. On the merits, the applicant argued that the domestic courts failed to give proper weight to his strong ties to Denmark, weak ties to Turkey, limited criminal past, and the absence of a prior conditional expulsion order. The Government maintained that the expulsion was lawful, pursued the legitimate aim of preventing disorder and crime, and was necessary, with domestic courts having carefully balanced the relevant interests under Article 8. The Court ultimately found no violation, holding that there were very serious reasons for expelling a settled migrant and that the domestic courts had duly assessed proportionality.

In *Avci v. Denmark* (Application no. 40240/19), the applicant, Cihan Avci, a Turkish national born in Denmark in 1993, complained under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that Denmark’s order expelling him with a permanent re-entry ban violated his right to respect for private and family life. The expulsion was imposed in criminal proceedings following his conviction for serious drug offences.

The applicant had lived in Denmark for approximately 25 years. His parents and three siblings lived there; he was unmarried and had no children. He had worked in various jobs, including in a supermarket and as a waiter, and was receiving unemployment benefits when arrested. He had not completed further education, though he later passed his ninth-grade exams while in custody.

His criminal history included a 2013 suspended 20-day sentence for attempting to free a detainee and, as part of a crowd, causing public insecurity. In September 2018, the District Court convicted him under section 191 of the Penal Code for serious drug offences committed between January and April 2017 as part of an organised network. He had received, possessed and transferred one kilogram of cocaine through extensive sales and deliveries to identified and unidentified buyers. He was sentenced to four years’ imprisonment and given a warning about expulsion.

On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence but ordered his expulsion with a permanent re-entry ban. It found the offences very serious, involving organised drug dealing over several months, and that his conduct represented a genuine and sufficiently serious threat to society’s fundamental interests. It also found a risk of reoffending if he were not expelled, noting his prior convictions. Although his personal and cultural ties to Denmark were stronger than those to Turkey, the High Court found he could establish a life in Turkey: he had visited several times, spoke some Kurdish, had a maternal grandfather there, and was deemed to have knowledge of Turkish customs and culture. Family contact could continue by phone or internet. It concluded that the circumstances favouring expulsion were sufficiently compelling and that a permanent ban was not disproportionate under Article 8.

The applicant argued that the courts failed to properly weigh his lack of a significant criminal past, the absence of a prior conditional expulsion warning, his strong Danish ties, and his weak Turkish ties. He submitted that there were no “very compelling reasons” for expulsion. The Government maintained that the order was lawful, pursued the legitimate aim of preventing disorder and crime, and struck a fair balance between competing interests. It invoked the subsidiarity principle, arguing that the domestic courts had carefully assessed the case under Article 8 and the Court’s case-law.

The Court dismissed the Government’s objection that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies. It found that he had properly challenged the expulsion order in the criminal proceedings, and it was immaterial that he could later seek revocation under section 50 of the Aliens Act based on changed circumstances. On the merits, the Court considered that the Danish courts had duly assessed proportionality in light of its case-law and found no violation of Article 8. The expulsion order was enforced on 24 January 2020.

In *K.I. v. France* (ECtHR, Fifth Section, 15 April 2021), the applicant was a Russian national of Chechen origin, born in 1994. He fled Russia in 2011 after alleging three arrests, beatings and threats by Russian law-enforcement officers, who pressured him to infiltrate Chechen rebels and threatened his family because of his deceased father’s past involvement with Chechen guerrilla fighters. France granted him refugee status in January 2013, based on his family ties to Chechen separatists and his refusal to cooperate with the Russian authorities.

In November 2013, about nine months after obtaining refugee status, K.I. was arrested in France in a terrorism investigation. In April 2015, the Paris Criminal Court convicted him of participation in a criminal conspiracy to commit acts of terrorism between September 2012 and November 2013. The court found that he had helped organise and had undertaken travel to Syria, passing through Germany, Poland, Ukraine and Turkey, in order to undergo military training and join a jihadist group composed of Chechen, Dagestani and Ingush fighters. He was sentenced to five years’ imprisonment.

Following this conviction, OFPRA revoked K.I.’s refugee status in June 2016 under Article L. 711-6 2° of the Immigration and Asylum Code, on the grounds that he had been finally convicted in France of a terrorism offence and that his presence constituted a serious threat to society. The CNDA upheld that revocation in January 2019, and the Conseil d’État later dismissed his appeal in July 2020. Importantly, under subsequent domestic and EU case-law, revocation of refugee status under that provision did not mean the person was no longer a refugee; he remained entitled to Geneva Convention protections, including non-refoulement.

A deportation order had been issued in November 2015. In February 2019, the prefect set Russia as the destination country. K.I. alleged that removal to Russia would violate Articles 2 and 3 ECHR. He claimed that Russian and Chechen authorities still targeted him because of his family’s ties to fighters, his refusal to collaborate, his membership of an allegedly anti-regime *teip*, his past ill-treatment, and his conviction in France. He relied on statements that police or FSB officers had repeatedly visited or summoned relatives, asked about him, threatened that he would be imprisoned upon arrival, and allegedly arrested a friend who returned to Russia. The Government disputed the evidence as insufficient, undated or unauthenticated, and argued he had not shown a real and personal risk; they also noted he had used his Russian passport to travel to Syria and there was no proof he was wanted or charged in Russia.

Domestic courts rejected his risk claim. In May 2019, the Lille Administrative Court found he had not demonstrated a real and personal risk of ill-treatment if returned, noting that he no longer appeared linked to an at-risk group and that reports merely showed returnees from Syria were monitored. The ECtHR nevertheless found a violation of the procedural limb of Article 3. The central failure was that the French authorities did not take into account that the applicant remained a refugee despite revocation and that the non-refoulement principle still applied. They also failed to conduct a comprehensive *ex nunc* assessment of the risks he would face on return, in light of his continued refugee status and his alleged membership in a targeted group.

K.I. v. France (ECtHR, 15 April 2021) concerned a Russian national of Chechen origin who faced deportation to Russia after France revoked his refugee status following a terrorism conviction. The applicant, born in 1994, claimed that in 2010–2011 Russian security officers arrested and beat him three times, sought to force him to infiltrate Chechen rebels, and threatened his family when he refused. His father had been a Chechen guerrilla fighter. He fled Russia in 2011, transited Poland, and arrived in France aged 17. In January 2013, OFPRA granted him refugee status based on his family ties to Chechen separatists and his refusal to cooperate with the Russian authorities. He received a residence permit.

In November 2013, nine months after recognition, he was arrested in France in a terrorism investigation. In April 2015, the Paris Criminal Court convicted him of participation in a criminal conspiracy to commit acts of terrorism and sentenced him to five years’ imprisonment. It found that he had travelled to Syria in August–September 2013 via Germany, Poland, Ukraine and Turkey, joined a jihadist group of Chechen, Dagestani and Ingush fighters, and prepared and organised his departure with an accomplice. In June 2016, OFPRA revoked his refugee status under Article L.711-6 of the Immigration and Asylum Code, on the grounds that he had a final terrorism conviction and that his presence constituted a serious threat to society. The CNDA upheld that revocation in January 2019. The Conseil d’État later dismissed his appeal in July 2020, noting that under EU law revocation did not mean he was no longer a refugee; he remained a refugee and the non-refoulement principle applied.

Meanwhile, in November 2015 the prefect issued a deportation order based on public safety. In February 2019 the prefect designated Russia as the destination country. The applicant alleged that removal would violate Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention. He relied on continuing threats: Russian and Chechen police and FSB officers had repeatedly questioned and pressured his relatives, including after his conviction and imprisonment; he claimed to belong to a targeted group because of family ties to Chechen fighters, his refusal to collaborate, his teip/clan, and his profile as a Chechen returned from Syria with a terrorism conviction. The Government disputed the evidence, citing undated witness statements and lack of proof of identities or family relationships.

Domestic courts rejected his challenges. In May 2019, the Lille Administrative Court held that because his refugee status had been revoked, he had to prove a real and personal risk. It found he had not demonstrated links to an at-risk group or that he was wanted or charged in Russia, although reports showed returnees from Syria were monitored and persons linked to insurgents or Salafism could be at risk. The ECtHR indicated interim measures under Rule 39 to prevent removal.

The central alleged violation concerned the procedural assessment under Article 3. The Court found that the French authorities failed to take into account that, despite revocation, the applicant remained a refugee and was protected by the non-refoulement principle. They also failed to conduct a comprehensive ex nunc assessment of the risks he would face as a refugee and member of a targeted group. There was accordingly a violation of Article 3 (procedural limb), without a final ruling on the actual risk of ill-treatment upon return.

K.I. v. France (ECtHR, Fifth Section, 15 April 2021) concerned a Russian national of Chechen origin who had been granted refugee status in France in 2013. He claimed that in Chechnya he had been arrested, beaten and threatened by Russian security officials who tried to force him to infiltrate rebel groups, partly because of his father’s past role as a Chechen guerrilla fighter and his own refusal to collaborate. He fled Russia in 2011 and was recognised as a refugee in France in January 2013.

In November 2013, about nine months after obtaining refugee status, K.I. was arrested in France. In April 2015, the Paris Criminal Court convicted him of participation in a criminal conspiracy to commit acts of terrorism. The court found that he had helped organise and had undertaken travel, via Germany, Poland, Ukraine and Turkey, to Syria between August and September 2013, where he joined and trained with a jihadist group composed of Chechen, Dagestani and Ingush fighters. He was sentenced to five years’ imprisonment.

Following that conviction, OFPRA revoked his refugee status in June 2016 under French law on the ground that he had been finally convicted of a terrorism offence and that his presence constituted a serious threat to society. The CNDA upheld the revocation in January 2019, and the Conseil d’État dismissed his appeal in July 2020, clarifying that revocation of refugee status did not mean that the person was no longer a refugee and did not remove the protection against refoulement under the Geneva Convention.

In the meantime, a deportation order was issued in November 2015, and in February 2019 the authorities designated Russia as the destination country. K.I. was detained and a Russian consular laissez-passer was issued. He invoked Articles 2 and 3 ECHR, alleging that return to Russia would expose him to persecution, detention, ill-treatment or death. He relied on continuing pressure on his family, visits and summonses by FSB/Chechen police, threats that he would be imprisoned on arrival, and the arrest of a friend who had returned to Russia. The Government disputed the reliability and authenticity of much of that evidence.

The domestic administrative court upheld the removal to Russia, finding that K.I. had not shown a real and personal risk. It accepted that returnees from Syria might be monitored and that persons linked to insurgents or Salafism could be at risk, but found no evidence that K.I. himself was wanted or charged in Russia. It also noted that he had used his Russian passport to travel to Syria. The applicant complained that the authorities failed to recognise that, despite revocation, he remained a refugee and benefited from non-refoulement, and failed to conduct a comprehensive ex nunc assessment of the risks in light of that status and his alleged membership of a targeted group.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of the procedural limb of Article 3. It held that the French authorities, when ordering and reviewing deportation to Russia, failed to take into account that the applicant remained a refugee and that the non-refoulement principle still applied. They did not carry out a comprehensive ex nunc assessment of the risks he would face on return, particularly because he was a refugee and allegedly belonged to a targeted group. The judgment became final on 15 July 2021.

In *Toțchi and Others v. the Republic of Moldova, Russia and Ukraine* (App. no. 8833/10, judgment of 15 June 2021), the applicants—two Russian nationals, Mr Iurie Toțchi and Mrs Tatiana Toțcaia, and one Ukrainian national, Mr Marc Fașcevschii—were the parents and husband of Ms Iana Faşcevscaia. They complained under Article 2 of the Convention that the authorities failed to protect the victim’s right to life and failed to conduct an effective investigation into her death after she ate poisonous mushrooms.

The key facts concern a fatal mushroom poisoning in Tiraspol, in the self-proclaimed Moldovan Republic of Transnistria (“MRT”). On 6 July 2001, two sellers, K.S. and K.V., collected mushrooms in the woods and sold them at a Tiraspol market. On 8 July 2001, two people who had eaten mushrooms from those sellers were admitted to the Republican Clinical Hospital in Tiraspol with poisoning. On 9 July 2001 at 10:35 a.m., hospital staff urgently informed the Republican Centre for Hygiene and Epidemiology about the incident and the marketplace where the mushrooms had been bought. Later that day, at around 5 p.m., Ms Iana Faşcevscaia bought mushrooms from the same sellers. They showed her a veterinary-sanitary laboratory certificate confirming the mushrooms were suitable for consumption. She prepared dinner for her family. Early on 10 July she became ill, was admitted to hospital, and was later transferred to Chișinău, where she died on 15 July 2001.

The investigation revealed serious failures. On 19 July 2001, the Tiraspol Prosecutor’s Office opened criminal proceedings against the sellers and the market laboratory expert. On 31 May 2002, both investigations were discontinued. The sellers could not have known that some mushrooms were poisonous, especially as they had a certificate. The laboratory expert had used only a rudimentary method—visual inspection and boiling mushrooms with an onion—and no market laboratory in the MRT had equipment for biochemical mushroom testing. Prosecution of the expert was barred by amnesty. Investigations against the sellers were reopened and discontinued several times, eventually ending because the limitation period expired.

The investigation was also extended to three officials from the Centre, accused of negligence for failing to react promptly to the 9 July warning and for not preventing further sale of the dangerous mushrooms. On 14 May 2009, the Tiraspol city court convicted two officials, finding that proper performance of their duties would have prohibited further sale and avoided the victim’s death. They received three-year sentences but were released because the limitation period had expired. The court further noted serious systemic shortcomings: old regulations on veterinary-sanitary laboratories no longer applied, no new regulations had been adopted, laboratories operated without a legal basis, and they lacked food-testing equipment. It also criticised prosecution delays, including requesting key documents only in October 2004, which allowed responsible persons to escape liability. The MRT Supreme Court upheld the judgment on 30 July 2009. Moldova’s Supreme Court later refused to review the case because the judgments came from unconstitutional courts.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged violations of Article 2: that the authorities failed to establish an adequate legal and administrative framework to protect life, failed to provide testing equipment and properly trained personnel, failed to act on the earlier poisoning warning, and failed to conduct an effective investigation. The Court found Ukraine had no jurisdiction. Moldova had jurisdiction as the territorial State but only limited positive obligations due to its lack of effective control over Transnistria. Russia had jurisdiction because of its military, economic, and political support for, and decisive influence over, the MRT. On the merits, the Court considered it established that the State failed to provide effective deterrence against threats to life and that the investigation was ineffective because those responsible avoided accountability through limitation periods or amnesty, largely due to official delays. These facts supported a violation of Article 2.

In *Toțchi and Others v. the Republic of Moldova, Russia and Ukraine* (Application no. 8833/10, judgment of 15 June 2021), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Article 2 of the Convention concerning the death of Ms Iana Faşcevscaia after she ate poisonous mushrooms bought at a public market in Tiraspol, in the self-proclaimed Moldovan Republic of Transnistria (“MRT”). The applicants were her parents, two Russian nationals, and her husband, a Ukrainian national.

The key facts were as follows. On 6 July 2001, two sellers, K.S. and K.V., collected mushrooms in the woods and sold them at a Tiraspol market. On 8 July 2001, several people who had eaten mushrooms from those sellers were admitted to intensive care in the Republican Clinical Hospital in Tiraspol. On 9 July 2001 at 10:35 a.m., hospital staff urgently informed the Republican Centre for Hygiene and Epidemiology about the poisonings and the market where the mushrooms had been bought. Nevertheless, at about 5 p.m. that same day, the victim bought mushrooms from the same sellers. They showed her a certificate from the market’s veterinary and sanitary laboratory confirming the mushrooms were suitable for consumption. She cooked dinner for her family; early on 10 July she became ill and was admitted to hospital. Her condition worsened, she was transferred to a hospital in Chișinău, and she died on 15 July 2001.

The alleged violations concerned the State’s failure to protect the victim’s right to life and to conduct an effective investigation. On 19 July 2001, the Tiraspol Prosecutor’s Office opened criminal investigations against the sellers and the laboratory expert. These were discontinued on 31 May 2002. The sellers could not have known that some mushrooms were poisonous, especially given the laboratory certificate. The expert had used only a rudimentary visual and boiling method; no market laboratory in the MRT had equipment for biochemical mushroom testing. She was also covered by an amnesty law. Later, the investigation against the sellers was reopened and discontinued several times, eventually ending because the limitation period had expired.

The investigation was later extended to three officials from the Centre, accused of negligence for failing to react promptly to the hospital’s alert and for not preventing further sales despite having time to do so. On 14 May 2009, the Tiraspol city court convicted two officials, finding that proper performance of their duties would have stopped the sale and avoided the death. They received three-year sentences but were released because the limitation period had expired. The court also noted serious systemic shortcomings: old laboratory regulations no longer applied, no new rules had been adopted, laboratories lacked testing equipment, and prosecution delays had allowed responsible persons to escape criminal liability. The MRT Supreme Court upheld the judgment in July 2009. Moldovan courts refused to examine the applicants’ later appeal on the ground that the MRT judgments came from unconstitutional courts.

On jurisdiction, the Court found Ukraine had no relevant jurisdiction. Moldova had jurisdiction as the territorial State but lacked effective control over Transnistria, so its responsibility was limited to positive obligations. Russia had jurisdiction because the MRT depended on Russian military, economic, and political support, giving Russia effective control and decisive influence.

On the merits, the Court found the authorities had failed to put in place an adequate legal and administrative framework to protect life, and the investigation was ineffective because those responsible avoided accountability through limitation and amnesty resulting from delays. The case therefore concerned established violations of Article 2.
The case concerned the death of Iana Faşcevscaia after she ate poisonous mushrooms bought at a market

In *Ancient Baltic Religious Association “Romuva” v. Lithuania*, the applicant was a registered Lithuanian religious association practising the old Baltic pagan faith. It sought the status of a State-recognised religious association. Under Lithuanian law, mere registration allows worship and cultural/charitable activity, but State-recognised (and traditional) associations receive extra privileges: religious education in public schools, religious marriages with civil effect, national broadcaster airtime, State pensions for clergy, and land-tax exemptions. Non-traditional associations may obtain recognition if they have operated for 25 years since initial registration, have support in society, and their teaching and practices do not contravene law or public morals. The Ministry of Justice assesses eligibility; the Seimas (Parliament) makes the final decision by resolution.

Romuva was registered as an association in 2002, though one constituent community dated from 1992. Its statute described it as continuing the original Baltic faith, revering nature as divine, practising polytheism, and respecting other religions. In 2018, the Ministry of Justice concluded that Romuva met the legal criteria: it had existed over 25 years, its teachings were lawful and moral, and it had sufficient public support. It was the largest non-traditional religious group in Lithuania, with over 5,000 adherents in the 2011 census and more than some traditional associations. Parliamentary committees, the Government, and the Seimas Law Department supported a draft resolution granting recognition. In June 2019, the Seimas debated the draft; a preliminary vote approved the text (46 for, 19 against, 18 abstentions), with a final vote scheduled for 27 June.

Crucially, on 26 June 2019, the president of the Lithuanian Bishops’ Conference—the Roman Catholic Church authority in Lithuania—sent a letter to a Seimas member who chaired the 81-member parliamentary group “For the Family.” The letter opposed recognition, arguing that there had never been a uniform ancient Baltic faith, that Romuva’s beliefs were not a comprehensive set of teachings, and that public support was not established. The member forwarded it to the group.

During the final debate, opponents cited the Catholic letter and made statements that Romuva was not genuinely religious, historically unfounded, opposed to Christianity, linked to Soviet/KGB efforts to strengthen paganism, and lacking sufficient public support. The final vote was 40 for, 31 against, and 15 abstentions, so the resolution was not adopted. Later, the Seimas Ethics Commission found that one member had knowingly spread false defamatory claims linking Romuva to the Kremlin/KGB; the administrative court upheld that finding but held there was no basis to order a retraction.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) read with Article 9 (freedom of religion). It held that denying State recognition to a pagan religious association that met the legal eligibility criteria, on grounds incompatible with the State’s duty of neutrality and impartiality, amounted to discrimination. The Court stressed that domestic law lacked safeguards against arbitrariness because the decision was entrusted to a political body, Parliament, without adequate legal criteria or judicial control. It also treated the involvement of a Catholic authority in the parliamentary procedure as significant, along with hostile and prejudicial characterisations of the applicant’s beliefs. Other complaints, including under Article 13, were inadmissible or not separately examined.

In *Romuva v. Lithuania* (App. No. 48329/19, 8 June 2021), the European Court of Human Rights examined Lithuania’s refusal to grant State recognition to the Ancient Baltic religious association “Romuva,” a registered pagan/neo-pagan group practising the old Baltic faith. One constituent community was registered in 1992; the association itself was registered in 2002. Its statute describes continuity with ancient Baltic traditions, the sanctity of nature, polytheism, ancestors, and harmony. Lithuanian law distinguishes traditional, State-recognised, and other religious associations. State recognition carries significant privileges: religious education in public schools, religious marriages with civil effect, national-broadcaster airtime, pension eligibility for clergy, and land-tax exemption. Non-traditional associations may seek recognition after twenty-five years if they have support in society and their teaching and practices do not contravene law or public morals. The Ministry of Justice assesses eligibility; the Seimas (Parliament) decides by resolution.

In 2017 Romuva sought State recognition. In 2018 the Ministry of Justice concluded that it met the legal criteria: it had operated for more than twenty-five years, its teachings were lawful, and it had sufficient public support. The Ministry noted that Romuva was the largest non-traditional religious group in Lithuania, with over 5,000 adherents in the 2011 census, growing numbers, and positive public surveys. The draft resolution was supported by the Seimas Law Department, relevant parliamentary committees, and the Government.

During Seimas debates on 25 and 27 June 2019, supporters invoked freedom of religion, pluralism, and Lithuania’s historical traditions. Opponents questioned whether Romuva had existed long enough or had sufficient public support, argued that it was a cultural/heritage organisation rather than a religion, warned that recognition could hollow out the concept of religion, and sometimes portrayed it as opposed to Christianity or linked to Soviet/KGB interests. On 25 June, a preliminary vote approved the text (46 for, 19 against, 18 abstained). The next day, the president of the Lithuanian Bishops’ Conference sent a letter to the chair of the parliamentary group “For the Family,” which was forwarded to its eighty-one members. The letter argued that there had never been a uniform ancient Baltic faith, that Romuva’s beliefs were not a comprehensive doctrine, and that public support could not be established by census data. On 27 June 2019, the Seimas voted 40 for, 31 against, 15 abstained; the draft was not adopted. Later, the Seimas Ethics Commission found that one MP’s statements alleging KGB/Kremlin links were false and defamatory; courts upheld that finding but held that no retraction could be ordered.

The applicant alleged violations of Articles 9, 13, and 14 of the Convention. The central complaint was that the refusal of State recognition, despite Romuva meeting statutory criteria, discriminated against it on grounds of religion or belief. It argued that the parliamentary decision lacked safeguards against arbitrariness and that the involvement of the Catholic Bishops’ Conference in the parliamentary process breached the State’s duty of neutrality and impartiality. The ECtHR found a violation of Article 14 taken together with Article 9, holding that the denial was discriminatory and incompatible with the State’s obligation to remain neutral and impartial in matters of religion.

The case *Ancient Baltic Religious Association “Romuva” v. Lithuania* (no. 48329/19, ECtHR, 8 June 2021) concerned the refusal by the Lithuanian Parliament, the Seimas, to grant State-recognised religious association status to Romuva, a registered pagan/neo-pagan association following the old Baltic faith. Romuva was registered in 2002, with one constituent community registered in 1992. Under Lithuanian law, non-traditional religious associations may seek State recognition after 25 years if they have support in society and their teaching and practices do not contravene law or public morals. Recognition carries privileges: religious education in public schools, religious marriages with civil effect, national broadcaster airtime, State pensions for clergy, and land tax exemptions.

In 2017–2018 Romuva sought recognition. The Ministry of Justice concluded it met the legal criteria: it had operated for more than 25 years, its teachings were lawful, and it had sufficient public support. The Ministry noted census data showing over 5,000 people professed a “Baltic faith” in 2011, a fourfold increase since 2001; it was the sixth largest religious movement in Lithuania and viewed positively in surveys. A draft resolution was supported by several Seimas committees and the Government.

Debates took place on 25 and 27 June 2019. Supporters cited Romuva’s connection to Lithuanian history and traditions, freedom of religion, and pluralism. Opponents questioned whether it had existed long enough or had sufficient public support. They argued recognition concerned additional privileges, not freedom of religion; claimed Romuva was more a cultural/heritage organisation than a religion; warned of hollowing out the concept of religion; asserted incompatibility with Christianity; and made hostile allegations, including false claims of KGB/Kremlin links. The Seimas Ethics Commission later found one member had knowingly spread false defamatory claims, though a retraction order was overturned on parliamentary immunity grounds.

Crucially, on 26 June 2019, the president of the Lithuanian Bishops’ Conference—the Roman Catholic Church authority in Lithuania—emailed a Seimas member who chaired the parliamentary group “For the Family” (81 members), who forwarded it to the group. The letter opposed recognition, denying a uniform ancient Baltic faith, dismissing practices as superstition, and questioning Romuva’s teachings and public support.

On 27 June 2019, 86 of 141 Seimas members were present: 40 voted for, 31 against, and 15 abstained. The draft resolution was not adopted. Domestic remedies were uncertain: administrative courts generally could not review Seimas governance acts, and an individual constitutional complaint required a prior decision violating rights, which was absent.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 14 read with Article 9. It held that denying State recognition to a religious association that met the eligibility criteria, on grounds incompatible with the State’s duty of neutrality and impartiality, constituted discrimination. Domestic law lacked safeguards against arbitrariness because the decision was made by a political body, Parliament, with vague criteria and no effective judicial review. The involvement of a Catholic authority in the parliamentary procedure further undermined State neutrality. The case is significant for minority pagan and neo-pagan religions and State recognition regimes.

**Case Summary: Lambertné Bársony v. Hungary (Application no. 48689/10)**

**Court:** European Court of Human Rights (Second Section)
**Judgment Date:** 25 March 2014

**Key Facts and Alleged Violations:**

The applicant, Ms. Klára Lambertné Bársony, a Hungarian national born in 1955 and residing in Miskolc, lodged an application against the Republic of Hungary on 18 August 2010. The case concerned a civil dispute initiated by the applicant on 20 April 1998, seeking the division of property from her common-law partnership with a Mr. F.

The domestic proceedings traversed three levels of jurisdiction. The first-instance case was heard by the Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén County Court. An appeal followed before the Debrecen Court of Appeal. The final judgment in the matter was delivered by the Supreme Court on 2 March 2010.

The primary alleged violation centered on the length of these civil proceedings. The applicant complained that the duration was incompatible with the "reasonable time" requirement stipulated under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Government contested this argument.

In its assessment, the Court determined that the relevant period for consideration began on 20 April 1998, when the applicant filed her initial action, and concluded on 2 March 2010, with the Supreme Court's final judgment. This period amounted to nearly twelve years of litigation across three judicial instances.

The Court declared this complaint admissible, noting its extensive case-law establishing violations of Article 6 § 1 in cases with similar lengthy proceedings. It found that the Government had failed to present any convincing argument or fact that would lead to a different conclusion. Consequently, the Court held that the length of the proceedings was excessive and failed to meet the "reasonable time" requirement, thereby violating Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

Additionally, the applicant raised a complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, concerning the outcome of the litigation and its effect on her property rights. The Court rejected this part of the application as manifestly ill-founded. It reasoned that the domestic courts had adjudicated a civil-law dispute between private parties, and their decisions, being free from any appearance of arbitrariness, did not constitute an interference with the applicant's property rights.

Regarding just satisfaction under Article 41, the applicant claimed approximately EUR 211,000 for pecuniary damage and EUR 23,000 for non-pecuniary damage. The Court dismissed the pecuniary damage claim, finding no causal link between the violation of the Convention (the excessive length) and the alleged financial loss. However, it accepted that the applicant had sustained non-pecuniary damage due to the protracted proceedings. Ruling on an equitable basis, the Court awarded her EUR 5,400 for non-pecuniary damage. The applicant also claimed EUR 5,300 for costs and expenses incurred before the domestic courts and the Strasbourg Court. The Court awarded EUR 500 for costs and expenses, considering this sum reasonable given that the applicant was not represented by a lawyer.

**Case:** *Lambertné Bársony v. Hungary* (Application no. 48689/10), European Court of Human Rights, Second Section, judgment of 25 March 2014.

The applicant, Klára Lambertné Bársony, a Hungarian national born in 1955 and living in Miskolc, brought a civil action on 20 April 1998 seeking division of the property of her common-law partnership with Mr F. The case was heard at first instance by the Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén County Court, on appeal by the Debrecen Court of Appeal, and finally by the Supreme Court, which gave judgment on 2 March 2010. The applicant lodged her application with the European Court of Human Rights on 18 August 2010.

The principal alleged violation concerned the length of the domestic civil proceedings. Relying on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, the applicant complained that the proceedings had not been concluded within a “reasonable time.” The Court noted that the relevant period began on 20 April 1998, when the action was brought, and ended on 2 March 2010, when the Supreme Court delivered final judgment. The proceedings therefore lasted almost twelve years across three levels of jurisdiction. The Government contested the complaint, but the Court declared it admissible.

Having examined the submissions, the Court found that the Government had not put forward any fact or convincing argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion. Referring to its established case-law, including *Frydlender v. France*, the Court held that the length of the proceedings was excessive and failed to satisfy the “reasonable time” requirement of Article 6 § 1. It therefore found a violation of that provision. The key facts supporting the violation were the very long duration—nearly twelve years—and the fact that the case passed through three judicial instances, with no adequate justification from the Government for the delay.

The applicant also complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the outcome of the litigation, essentially alleging an interference with her property rights. The Court rejected this part of the application. It observed that the domestic courts had decided a civil-law dispute between private parties. Since their decisions were free of any appearance of arbitrariness, they could not be regarded as constituting an interference with the applicant’s property rights. Consequently, that complaint was manifestly ill-founded within the meaning of Article 35 § 3 (a) and was rejected under Article 35 § 4.

As to just satisfaction under Article 41, the applicant claimed approximately EUR 211,000 in pecuniary damage and EUR 23,000 in non-pecuniary damage. The Government contested these claims. The Court found no causal link between the violation of the length requirement and the alleged pecuniary damage, so it rejected that claim. However, it considered that the applicant must have sustained some non-pecuniary damage and, ruling on an equitable basis, awarded her EUR 5,400 under that head. She also claimed EUR 5,300 for costs and expenses; the Court awarded EUR 500, noting that she had not been represented by a lawyer. Default interest was set at the European Central Bank marginal lending rate plus three percentage points.

In summary, the case concerned primarily the excessive length of civil proceedings in Hungary. The Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1 due to nearly twelve years of litigation, while rejecting the property-rights complaint as manifestly ill-founded.

**Case Kiisa v. Estonia** (ECtHR, 13 March 2014) concerned two Estonian nationals, Karin and Aare Kiisa, formerly married from 1989 to 2006. Their child K. was born in September 2002, and the second applicant was registered as the father. On 25 October 2004 the first applicant sued the second applicant in the Harju County Court for child alimony. On 27 April 2005 the second applicant brought a separate filiation action seeking to establish that he was not the child’s father and to contest the civil-status record.

Because of the filiation proceedings, the second applicant requested suspension of the alimony case. The first applicant did not oppose suspension, and on 14 October 2005 the County Court suspended the alimony proceedings until judgment in the filiation case. In the filiation proceedings, the court ordered DNA testing, but the first applicant failed to take the child for testing despite court orders and unsuccessful appeals. The filiation action was eventually dismissed in 2012. On 14 June 2007 the first applicant asked for the alimony case to resume, citing Supreme Court practice that contesting paternity did not affect the duty to provide child support. The alimony proceedings resumed on 20 June 2007.

The alimony case then proceeded through repeated hearings, evidence submissions, amendments, interim measures and appeals. On 11 January 2008 the County Court ordered the second applicant to pay monthly alimony. Both parties appealed. The Court of Appeal upheld the judgment on 9 May 2008, but the Supreme Court quashed it on 19 November 2008 and remitted the case to the Court of Appeal. On 21 May 2009 the Court of Appeal quashed the lower judgment and remitted the case to the County Court. The first applicant’s further appeal was refused in September 2009. In 2010 the first applicant amended her claim and obtained an interim alimony order. On 5 July 2010 the County Court ordered monthly alimony of EEK 5,000; on 6 October 2010 the Court of Appeal reduced it to EEK 3,550. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 26 January 2011. The proceedings had therefore lasted from 25 October 2004 to 26 January 2011—about six years and three months across three court levels.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged that the length of the civil proceedings violated the “reasonable time” requirement of Article 6 § 1 and that there was no effective domestic remedy for that delay, contrary to Article 13. The Government asked the Court to strike the applications out based on a unilateral declaration in which it acknowledged only the Article 6 delay and offered payment. The Court refused because the declaration did not acknowledge the Article 13 complaint, which was inseparably linked to the Article 6 complaint.

The Government also argued that the applicants had failed to exhaust domestic remedies, relying on a remedy developed after the Supreme Court’s *Osmjorkin* judgment of 22 March 2011, which allowed compensation claims for excessive length in administrative courts. The Court rejected this: the first applicant had lodged her application on 4 March 2010, before that remedy existed, and the second applicant lodged on 31 May 2011, only two months after the judgment—too soon to expect awareness of the new case-law. There were also no transitional provisions and few similar Estonian cases.

On the merits, the Court found the alimony case was not complex and required special diligence. Although the applicants contributed to delays through amendments, adjournment requests and appeals, their use of appeal rights was not blameworthy. The remittals were caused by lower-court errors and were imputable to the authorities. The overall length was excessive, violating Article 6 § 1, and no effective remedy existed, violating Article 13.

In *Kiisa v. Estonia* (Applications nos. 16587/10 and 34304/11, judgment of 13 March 2014), two Estonian nationals—formerly married and parents of a child, K., born in 2002—complained about the excessive length of civil alimony proceedings and the lack of an effective domestic remedy.

On 25 October 2004, the first applicant brought an action against the second applicant in the Harju County Court seeking child alimony. On 27 April 2005, the second applicant commenced separate filiation proceedings to establish that he was not the child’s father and to contest the civil-status record. On 2 June 2005, he requested suspension of the alimony proceedings, referring to the pending filiation case; the first applicant did not oppose suspension. On 14 October 2005, the County Court suspended the alimony proceedings until judgment in the filiation case. Earlier, on 12 May 2005, the court had ordered DNA testing; the first applicant was required to take the child for samples but did not do so. Her appeals against that decision failed, and the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 31 January 2007.

On 14 June 2007, the first applicant asked that the alimony proceedings be resumed, relying on then-recent Supreme Court practice that contesting a civil-status record did not remove the obligation to pay child support. The proceedings resumed on 20 June 2007. Various hearings were postponed and evidence exchanged. On 11 January 2008, the County Court ordered monthly alimony. Both parties appealed. The Tallinn Court of Appeal upheld the judgment on 9 May 2008, but the Supreme Court quashed it on 19 November 2008 and remitted the case. On 21 May 2009, the Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance judgment and remitted the case for fresh examination; the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 7 September 2009. The first applicant amended her claim and submitted new evidence in January 2010. An interim alimony measure was imposed on 17 February 2010. On 5 July 2010, the County Court ordered monthly alimony; the Court of Appeal varied the amount on 6 October 2010. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 26 January 2011. The proceedings therefore lasted from 25 October 2004 to 26 January 2011—six years and three months across three levels of jurisdiction.

The applicants alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (reasonable time) and Article 13 (effective remedy). The Government argued that delays were caused by the applicants’ conduct, including the suspension request, repeated adjournments, new evidence, amendments, and appeals. The Government also claimed that a new domestic remedy existed through administrative-court compensation following the Supreme Court’s *Osmjorkin* judgment of 22 March 2011. The Government made a unilateral declaration acknowledging the length violation but not the Article 13 complaint; the Court refused to strike out the applications because the two complaints were inseparably linked.

On exhaustion, the Court held that the first applicant lodged her application on 4 March 2010, before the *Osmjorkin* remedy developed. The second applicant lodged on 31 May 2011, only two months after *Osmjorkin*, too soon for him to be expected to know of the new case-law. Given the absence of transitional provisions and few similar Estonian cases, the Court declined to depart from the general rule and dismissed the Government’s exhaustion objection.

On the merits, the Court found the alimony case was not complex and required special diligence. Although the applicants contributed to delays, they could not be blamed for using available appeals. The remittals for re-examination were attributable to the authorities. The Court found the length excessive, violating Article 6 § 1, and, because no effective remedy was available that the applicants were required to exhaust, also found a violation of Article 13.

**Kiisa v. Estonia** (Applications nos. 16587/10 and 34304/11) concerned two Estonian nationals, Karin and Aare Kiisa, formerly married from 1989 to 2006. Their child K. was born in September 2002, and the second applicant was registered as the father. In October 2003 the first applicant began divorce and marital-property proceedings. On 25 October 2004 she sued the second applicant for child alimony in the Harju County Court.

On 27 April 2005 the second applicant brought a separate filiation action, seeking to establish that he was not K.’s father and to contest the civil-status record. He then requested suspension of the alimony case pending the filiation proceedings. The first applicant did not oppose suspension, and on 14 October 2005 the County Court suspended the alimony proceedings until judgment in the filiation case. In the meantime, DNA testing had been ordered, but the first applicant did not take the child for samples, and her appeals against that order failed.

On 14 June 2007 the first applicant asked to resume the alimony proceedings, relying on Supreme Court practice that contesting paternity did not remove the obligation to support the child. The case resumed on 20 June 2007. Thereafter, hearings were postponed, evidence was exchanged, and the second applicant made a compromise proposal. On 11 January 2008 the County Court ordered monthly alimony of 3,000 EEK. Both parties appealed. The Tallinn Court of Appeal upheld the judgment on 9 May 2008. On 19 November 2008 the Supreme Court quashed the appeal judgment and remitted the case. On 21 May 2009 the Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance judgment and remitted the case for fresh examination. The first applicant’s further appeal was refused on 7 September 2009.

In early 2010 the first applicant amended her claim and sought interim measures. On 17 February 2010 the County Court ordered interim monthly alimony of 2,175 EEK. On 5 July 2010 the County Court ordered 5,000 EEK monthly. On 6 October 2010 the Court of Appeal reduced this to 3,550 EEK. On 26 January 2011 the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal. The domestic proceedings therefore lasted from 25 October 2004 to 26 January 2011—six years and three months across three levels of jurisdiction.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged that the length of the civil proceedings violated the “reasonable time” requirement of Article 6 § 1 and that there was no effective domestic remedy for that complaint, contrary to Article 13. The Government submitted a unilateral declaration acknowledging only the Article 6 length violation and offered payment, requesting that the applications be struck out. The applicants rejected the offer as inadequate. The Court refused to strike out the applications because the Government had not acknowledged the Article 13 complaint, which was inseparably linked to the Article 6 complaint.

On exhaustion of domestic remedies, the Government relied on an administrative-court compensation remedy developed after the Supreme Court’s *Osmjorkin* judgment of 22 March 2011. The Court held that the first applicant had lodged her application before that remedy existed. The second applicant lodged only two months after the judgment, too soon to expect awareness of the new case-law. Given the small number of similar Estonian cases and no transitional provisions, the Court applied the general rule that exhaustion is assessed at the date of lodging and found the applicants were not required to use that remedy.

On the merits, the Court found the alimony case not especially complex but requiring special diligence. Although the applicants contributed to delays through amendments, adjournment requests, and appeals, using appeal rights was not blameworthy. Remittals caused by lower-court errors were imputable to the authorities. The overall length was excessive, violating Article 6 § 1. Since no effective remedy existed, Article 13 was also violated.

**Summary of *Taraneks v. Latvia* (Application no. 3082/06)**

The case of *Taraneks v. Latvia* concerns an application lodged by Mr Aivars Taraneks, a Latvian bailiff, who alleged that his criminal trial for corruption was unfair due to police incitement and the use of improperly obtained evidence, violating Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. He also claimed a violation of his right to respect for private life under Article 8 concerning the recording of his conversations and the search of his office.

The events began in November 2001 amid a commercial dispute between companies R.L. and M. A court ordered M.’s property, primarily fur coats, to be seized. The applicant, the senior bailiff in his office, was involved in a dispute over storage costs. He requested an advance payment of LVL 500 from R.L. for purported storage expenses. The seizure order was later quashed, but R.L. lodged an ancillary complaint, which suspended the property’s return.

On 14 December 2001, O.V., the director of R.L., complained to the police, alleging that the applicant and another bailiff were soliciting a bribe to prevent the return of the seized property. Subsequently, the police conducted undercover operations. They recorded telephone conversations between O.V., R.L.’s lawyer S.Ž., and the applicant. On 18 December 2001, a prosecutor approved an "investigative test." O.V., equipped with marked banknotes and a recording device, visited the applicant's office. During their conversation, which was secretly recorded, O.V. offered the applicant LVL 500. The applicant instructed O.V. to divide the money and left to stamp a document. After O.V. departed, the police detained the applicant. Marked banknotes were found hidden under books on his desk, and traces of a luminescent substance were detected on his hands.

The applicant was charged and convicted of demanding a bribe, receiving a five-year prison sentence. Throughout the proceedings, he argued that he had been incited by the police and that the evidence, particularly the audio recordings and the search of his office, was illegally obtained and inadmissible. He contended that the recordings made before the formal approval of the investigative test were unlawful and that the search was conducted without proper judicial authorization.

The Supreme Court of Latvia upheld his conviction, rejecting the incitement claim as speculation. It ruled that the recordings made by private individuals (O.V. and S.Ž.), even with police-supplied equipment, did not constitute a state "operational activity" requiring legal authorization. It also found the search lawful, as it was authorized by a prosecutor in an urgent case with a judge notified within the required timeframe. The applicant's subsequent complaints to prosecutors about the legality of these actions were largely dismissed, with some information classified as a state secret.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations center on the police's use of undercover tactics, including the active involvement of O.V. in offering the bribe, the timing and legal basis for recording private conversations, and the procedures followed for the office search. The applicant's core argument was that these state actions amounted to entrapment and a violation of his fair trial rights, as the courts failed to adequately scrutinize the legality of the evidence obtained through what he described as incitement.

**Taraneks v. Latvia** (Application no. 3082/06) concerned a Latvian bailiff, Mr Aivars Taraneks, who was convicted of corruption and later complained to the European Court of Human Rights that his criminal trial was unfair and that his private life was violated.

In November 2001, in a commercial dispute between companies R.L. and M., a court ordered M.’s movable property to be seized. The applicant was the senior bailiff in the office handling the matter, although the actual seizure was entrusted to another bailiff, G.P. The seized property, mainly fur coats, was transported and stored with O.V., the director of R.L. Taraneks allegedly requested an advance payment of LVL 500 from R.L. for storage and valuation costs. On 28 November the seizure order was quashed and the property was ordered returned to M., but R.L.’s ancillary complaint had suspensive effect.

On 14 December 2001 O.V. complained to the police that Taraneks and G.P. were demanding LVL 500 as a bribe to avoid returning the coats. Police recorded telephone conversations between R.L.’s lawyer S.Ž. and G.P., then between S.Ž. and Taraneks, and an office meeting involving O.V. and S.Ž. On 18 December a prosecutor approved an investigative test. O.V. was given marked LVL 500 and a recording device and went to the bailiffs’ office. Taraneks allegedly took the money, placed it under books on his desk, and later traces of luminescent substance were found on his hands. A search of his office found the marked money under books. The search was authorised by a prosecutor’s resolution, and a judge was informed the following day. Taraneks claimed the search was unlawful because it was not authorised by a judge and because urgency had not been assessed.

At trial, Taraneks denied wrongdoing. He claimed the LVL 500 was a legitimate advance payment, that recordings had been edited, and that he had not touched the money. In March 2005 the Riga Regional Court convicted him of demanding a bribe and sentenced him to five years’ imprisonment with confiscation. It relied on O.V., ten witnesses, recordings and documents, and acknowledged certain procedural “imperfections” but found them irrelevant. The Supreme Court in January 2006 quashed the abuse-of-office conviction but upheld the bribe conviction. The Senate of the Supreme Court in March 2006 dismissed final appeals, holding that recordings made by O.V. and S.Ž. as private parties were not operational activities requiring judicial authorisation, and that the prosecutor-authorised search was lawful.

Before the ECtHR, Taraneks alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 because he had been incited by police through O.V. and because his conviction was based on improperly obtained evidence. He argued that O.V., acting on police instructions, insisted on meeting him and offered the marked money, and that recordings made before the investigative test was approved were inadmissible. He also alleged under Article 8 that the secret recording of his conversations and the search of his office violated his right to respect for private life. Prosecutors refused to disclose operational documents, claiming State secret. The application was lodged on 14 December 2005 and communicated to the Latvian Government on 9 November 2010.

In *Taraneks v. Latvia* (no. 3082/06), the applicant, a Latvian bailiff, was convicted of corruption and sentenced to five years’ imprisonment. His complaints to the European Court of Human Rights centred on allegations of police incitement, an unfair criminal trial based on improperly obtained evidence, and violations of his right to respect for private life through secret recordings and an office search.

The case arose from enforcement proceedings in November 2001. In a commercial dispute between companies R.L. and M., a court ordered the seizure of M.’s movable property, mainly fur coats. Bailiff G.P. seized the property and entrusted its storage to O.V., R.L.’s director. M. asked the applicant, senior bailiff, to ensure proper storage. The prosecution alleged that on 20 November 2001 the applicant requested LVL 500 from O.V. as a bribe, disguised as an advance payment for non-existent storage and valuation costs. On 28 November the seizure order was quashed and return of the property was ordered. R.L. lodged an ancillary complaint, which suspended execution. On 14 December O.V. complained to police that the applicant and G.P. were demanding LVL 500, failing which the seized property would be returned to M.

Police then recorded telephone conversations between R.L.’s lawyer S.Ž. and G.P., and between S.Ž. and the applicant. S.Ž. and O.V. also visited the applicant’s office, where their conversation was secretly recorded. On 18 December a prosecutor approved an investigative test. O.V., equipped with marked LVL 500 banknotes and a recording device, went to the bailiffs’ office. The recorded conversation included O.V. saying he had the money, the applicant discussing how it should be divided, and the applicant leaving to obtain a seal. According to O.V., the applicant placed the money between books on his desk. The applicant later claimed he never touched it and assumed O.V. had taken it back. After O.V. left, police detained the applicant; luminescent traces from the marked notes were found on his hands. A filmed search of his office, authorised by a prosecutor, found LVL 500 under books. A judge was informed the next day.

The applicant was charged in January 2002 with extortion by an organised group and abuse of office. Proceedings against G.P. were terminated. In March 2005 the Riga Regional Court convicted the applicant of demanding a bribe, relying on O.V., ten witnesses, the recordings, the marked money, and the search. It acknowledged certain procedural “imperfections” but found the evidence reliable. The Supreme Court upheld the bribe conviction in January 2006, rejected the incitement claim as speculation, and held that recordings made by private individuals were not operational activities requiring judicial authorisation. The Senate dismissed his final appeal in March 2006, also finding the search lawful because a prosecutor had authorised it and a judge was later notified.

The applicant alleged that O.V. and S.Ž. had acted as police agents inciting him to crime; that the recordings made before prosecutor approval of the investigative test were inadmissible; that the search was illegal because it required prior judicial authorisation absent urgency; and that the secret recordings and search violated his private life. Prosecutors replied that recordings by private individuals needed no judicial authorisation, operational activities could begin before a criminal case, and operational details were secret.

The case of **S.J. v. Belgium** (Application no. 70055/10; Chamber judgment of 27 February 2014, later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 19 March 2015) concerned a Nigerian national who alleged that her expulsion to Nigeria would violate **Article 3** (risk of inhuman or degrading treatment), **Article 8** (right to private and family life), and **Article 13** (lack of an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

S.J. arrived in Belgium in summer 2007, when she was eight months pregnant, and applied for asylum on 30 July 2007. She claimed she had fled Nigeria after the family of M.A., the father of her child and the man in whose home she had lived since age eleven, pressured her to have an abortion. EURODAC records showed she had already applied for asylum in Malta on 29 June 2007. Belgium requested Malta to take charge under the Dublin II Regulation, and Malta accepted in September 2007. S.J. nevertheless remained in Belgium while proceedings continued.

In August 2007, during antenatal care, she was diagnosed HIV-positive with a serious immune deficiency requiring antiretroviral treatment. From October 2007 she received ARV therapy at St Pierre University Hospital. She gave birth to her first child in September 2007, a second child in April 2009, and a third in November 2012; M.A. was the father of all three. Medical certificates documented fluctuating CD4 counts and viral loads, changes in treatment, and periods of uncontrolled infection. By 2012–2013, doctors described her situation as worrying for both her and her children, requiring multidisciplinary HIV care, regular blood tests, and medication. She also received psychosocial support from the association Lhiving. M.A. spent occasional periods in Belgium without a residence permit.

Her asylum claim was rejected in May 2010 because of inconsistencies, and the Aliens Appeals Board upheld that rejection in October 2010. Separately, in November 2007, S.J. sought leave to remain on medical grounds under section 9ter of the Aliens Act. The Aliens Office initially considered treatment available in Malta; later, after deciding to examine her asylum claim, it considered treatment and monitoring available in Nigeria. In September/October 2010 the Aliens Office refused her medical regularization, finding HIV medication available in Nigeria, subsidized or free in public hospitals, and that she likely had family support there. On 22 November 2010 she was ordered to leave Belgium by 20 December 2010.

S.J. lodged an extremely urgent request for a stay of execution and an application to set aside the decisions, alleging violations of Articles 3, 8 and 13. The Aliens Appeals Board rejected the stay on 27 November 2010, finding extreme urgency not established because she was not detained and no removal date had been set. The Conseil d’État declared her appeal inadmissible in January 2011, noting that ordinary stay and interim measures were available. Her set-aside application remained pending. She applied to the European Court, which indicated under Rule 39 on 17 December 2010 that Belgium should not expel her and her children pending the proceedings.

The key facts underlying the alleged violations were her severe HIV status and dependence on ARV treatment, the disputed availability and accessibility of equivalent treatment in Nigeria, her three minor children and family ties in Belgium, the risk of irreversible health deterioration if expelled, and the alleged inadequacy of domestic remedies because appeals did not automatically suspend removal. The Chamber declared the application admissible on 18 December 2012.

In **S.J. v. Belgium** (Application no. 70055/10), the applicant was a Nigerian national who arrived in Belgium in summer 2007, then eight months pregnant, and applied for asylum. She claimed she fled Nigeria after the family of the child’s father, M.A., pressured her to have an abortion. EURODAC checks showed she had already applied for asylum in Malta in June 2007. Belgium requested Malta to take charge of her asylum claim under the Dublin II Regulation, and Malta accepted. She nevertheless remained in Belgium while her parallel residence proceedings continued. In 2009, Belgium decided to examine her asylum claim itself. In May 2010, the Commissioner General rejected the claim as inconsistent: she had denied applying in another country, could not explain her travel, did not know how long she had spent in Malta, and did not know the identities of people she had lived with in Nigeria. The Aliens Appeals Board upheld that rejection in October 2010.

The facts relevant to the alleged violations centred on her health and family life. In August 2007, she was diagnosed HIV-positive with a serious immune deficiency requiring antiretroviral treatment. She gave birth to her first child in September 2007, a second child in April 2009, and a third child in November 2012; M.A. was the father. M.A. spent occasional periods in Belgium without a residence permit. The applicant received ARV treatment at St Pierre University Hospital and psychosocial support from the association Lhiving. Medical certificates showed a fluctuating condition: in November 2010 her CD4 count was 447 with an undetectable viral load; by December 2011 it was 269 with a viral load of 42,900, possibly due to treatment failure or poor adherence; in June 2012, while pregnant, she had uncontrolled HIV with a viral load of 18,900 and T4 count of 126, described as worrying; by February 2013, after adding Norvir, her T4 count had risen to 200. Doctors stressed the need for multidisciplinary HIV care and psychosocial support.

In November 2007, she requested leave to remain on medical grounds under section 9ter of the Aliens Act. Initially, after finding treatment available in Malta, the Aliens Office refused. That decision was later revoked, and the Office explored treatment options in Nigeria. In September 2010, its medical adviser concluded that although untreated HIV posed a real risk, treatment and monitoring were available in Nigeria, so there was no medical objection to return. On 27 September 2010, the Aliens Office refused leave, relying on information from the Nigerian embassy and medical sources: ARV medication was available, subsidised, and free in public hospitals; two hospitals existed in Ogun State; and she likely had family support. After her asylum rejection, the refusal was confirmed on 20 October 2010. On 22 November 2010, she and her children were ordered to leave Belgium by 20 December 2010.

She challenged the refusal and order, alleging violations of Articles 3, 8 and 13 ECHR. She claimed expulsion to Nigeria would expose her to inhuman or degrading treatment because she would lack adequate access to HIV treatment and monitoring, and would infringe her private and family life with her children in Belgium. She also alleged the domestic remedies were ineffective because they did not suspend removal. The Aliens Appeals Board rejected her extremely urgent stay request on 27 November 2010, finding no extreme urgency: she was not detained, no repatriation date was set, and ordinary stay or interim measures remained available. On 6 January 2011, the Conseil d’État declared her appeal inadmissible and manifestly unfounded, stating that urgency was for the first-instance court and effective remedies existed. Her application to set aside remained pending. Meanwhile, the European Court applied Rule 39, indicating she and her children should not be expelled pending proceedings.

S.J. v. Belgium (Application no. 70055/10) concerned a Nigerian national, S.J., who arrived in Belgium in summer 2007 while eight months pregnant and applied for asylum. She had previously applied for asylum in Malta in June 2007; Belgium requested Malta to take charge under the Dublin II Regulation, and Malta accepted. Belgium ultimately examined the asylum claim itself. In May 2010 the Commissioner General rejected it for inconsistencies: S.J. had denied applying elsewhere, could not explain her travel or time in Malta, and gave vague details about Nigeria. The Aliens Appeals Board upheld that rejection in October 2010. The Chamber judgment of 27 February 2014 was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 19 March 2015.

The central facts concerned S.J.’s HIV-positive status. In August 2007 she was diagnosed with HIV and a serious immune deficiency requiring antiretroviral (“ARV”) treatment. She began ARV therapy in Belgium and was monitored by a Brussels university hospital and an NGO, Lhiving. She gave birth to three children, all fathered by M.A. Medical certificates showed fluctuating CD4 counts and viral loads, treatment changes, episodes of uncontrolled infection, and the need for regular blood tests, medication and multidisciplinary HIV care, especially during pregnancy.

In November 2007 S.J. applied for leave to remain on medical grounds under section 9ter of the Aliens Act. Initially, the Aliens Office refused because treatment was available in Malta. After revoking that decision, it examined whether treatment was available in Nigeria. In September 2010 its medical adviser concluded that, although untreated HIV posed a real risk to life, treatment and monitoring were available in Nigeria and there were no medical objections to return. The Aliens Office therefore refused her medical leave application on 27 September 2010 and confirmed that refusal on 20 October 2010, relying on information that ARV drugs, laboratory tests and specialist monitoring were available in Nigeria, partly free of charge, and that she likely had family support in Ogun State. On 22 November 2010 an order to leave Belgium by 20 December 2010 was served on her.

S.J. alleged that expulsion to Nigeria would violate Article 3 because she would lack effective access to appropriate HIV treatment, leading to severe suffering and risk to life. She also alleged violation of Article 8, relying on her private and family life in Belgium with her three young children, her social ties, and the psychosocial support she received. She alleged violation of Article 13, arguing that domestic remedies did not effectively suspend removal.

She sought a stay of execution under the extremely urgent procedure, but the Aliens Appeals Board rejected it on 27 November 2010, finding no extreme urgency because no repatriation date had been fixed and she was not detained. The Conseil d’État declared her appeal inadmissible in January 2011, noting that ordinary stay and interim measures remained available. Her main application to set aside the removal decisions remained pending. Meanwhile, the European Court of Human Rights applied Rule 39, indicating to Belgium not to expel S.J. and her children pending the proceedings. These facts framed the alleged violations: medical risk in Nigeria under Article 3, family/private life under Article 8, and lack of a suspensive effective remedy under Article 13.
