In **Milinković v. Bosnia and Herzegovina** (Application no. 21175/13), the European Court of Human Rights examined the failure of the authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina to enforce a final domestic judgment in favour of the applicant, Mr Dragan Milinković. The applicant, born in 1977, lived in Banja Luka. The case concerned the non-enforcement of a final and enforceable judgment against the Republika Srpska, an Entity of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and fell within a special legal regime governing the Republika Srpska’s general obligations. The Court noted that the case was similar to *Momıć and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina*, which also concerned non-enforcement of final domestic judgments under that regime.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations began with a judgment of the Banja Luka Court of First Instance of 23 February 2009. That court ordered the Republika Srpska to pay the applicant, within 15 days, 34,000 convertible marks (BAM) in respect of non-pecuniary damage, together with default interest at the statutory rate, and BAM 4,667 in respect of legal costs, also with default interest. The judgment became final on 11 May 2009. On 29 June 2009, the Banja Luka Court of First Instance issued a writ of execution. Despite the judgment being final and enforceable, it was not enforced.

The applicant complained to the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina about the non-enforcement. On 16 January 2013, the Constitutional Court found a breach of Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. However, the final judgment in the applicant’s favour remained unenforced at the time the case was considered by the European Court. The applicant therefore lodged an application with the European Court on 13 February 2013, alleging continued non-enforcement. He relied on Article 6 of the Convention, which guarantees a fair and public hearing within a reasonable time in the determination of civil rights and obligations, and on Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, which protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

The Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina contested the application. It sought to distinguish the case from the *Čolić and Others* line of authority. The Government argued that the final judgment did not concern war damage but instead represented general obligations of the Republika Srpska, which were to be paid in cash under the relevant settlement plan. It further submitted that the size of the Republika Srpska’s public debt justified postponing enforcement, because immediate enforcement would jeopardise macroeconomic stability and fiscal sustainability. The Government also objected to the examination of the application by a Committee of the Court, but the Court rejected that objection.

The European Court declared the application admissible, finding that it was not manifestly ill-founded and that no other inadmissibility ground applied. On the merits, the Court observed that the present case was practically identical to *Momıć and Others*. In that earlier case, the Court had already found violations of Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 in circumstances involving the non-enforcement of final domestic judgments falling under the Republika Srpska’s special obligations regime. Since the final judgment in the applicant’s case had still not been enforced and the situation had already lasted more than five years, the Court saw no reason to depart from its previous case-law. Accordingly, the Court found that the non-enforcement constituted a violation of Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In *Milinković v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Application no. 21175/13), the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section, sitting as a Committee) delivered judgment on 8 July 2014. The applicant, Mr Dragan Milinković, a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina born in 1977 and living in Banja Luka, complained about the continued non-enforcement of a final domestic judgment in his favour. He was represented by Ms R. Plavšić, while the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina was represented by its Agent, Ms M. Mijić.

The key facts concerned a judgment of the Banja Luka Court of First Instance of 23 February 2009, which became final on 11 May 2009. Under that judgment, the Republika Srpska—an Entity of Bosnia and Herzegovina—was ordered to pay the applicant, within 15 days, 34,000 convertible marks (BAM) in respect of non-pecuniary damage, together with default interest at the statutory rate, and BAM 4,667 in respect of legal costs, also with statutory default interest. On 29 June 2009, the Banja Luka Court of First Instance issued a writ of execution. Despite the judgment being final and enforceable, it was not enforced.

The applicant complained to the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. On 16 January 2013, the Constitutional Court found a breach of Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. Nevertheless, the final judgment in the applicant’s favour remained unenforced. The applicant then lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 13 February 2013.

Before the Strasbourg Court, the applicant relied on Article 6 of the Convention, which guarantees a fair and public hearing within a reasonable time in the determination of civil rights and obligations, and on Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, which protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. In substance, he alleged that the domestic authorities had failed to enforce a final and enforceable judgment awarding him compensation and costs. The case was linked to *Momić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina*, which also concerned non-enforcement of final judgments falling under a special legal regime governing the Republika Srpska’s general obligations.

The Government objected to the examination of the application by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection. On the merits, the Government sought to distinguish the case from *Čolić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina*, arguing that the judgment did not concern war damage but instead represented general obligations of the Republika Srpska that were to be paid in cash under the relevant settlement plan. The Government further argued that postponement of enforcement was justified by the size of the Republika Srpska’s public debt, since immediate payment could jeopardise macroeconomic stability and fiscal sustainability. The applicant, by contrast, invited the Court to apply the *Čolić and Others* case-law.

The Court declared the application admissible, finding it neither manifestly ill-founded nor inadmissible on any other grounds. It observed that the present case was practically identical to *Momić and Others*, in which it had already found violations of Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Since the final judgment had still not been enforced and the situation had lasted more than five years, the Court saw no reason to depart from that case-law. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The key violation was the prolonged failure of the respondent State to enforce a final domestic judgment in the applicant’s favour, notwithstanding the Constitutional Court’s earlier finding of a breach.

**Summary of Milinković v. Bosnia and Herzegovina (Application no. 21175/13)**

The case of *Milinković v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* concerns the failure of the respondent State to enforce a final domestic judgment in favor of the applicant, Mr. Dragan Milinković, a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina residing in Banja Luka. The application was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 13 February 2013, alleging violations of Article 6 of the Convention (right to a fair trial) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) due to the non-enforcement of a binding court decision.

The key facts are as follows: On 23 February 2009, the Banja Luka Court of First Instance issued a judgment ordering the Republika Srpska—one of the two Entities of Bosnia and Herzegovina—to pay the applicant 34,000 convertible marks (BAM) in non-pecuniary damages, plus default interest at the statutory rate, and BAM 4,667 for legal costs, also with default interest. This judgment became final on 11 May 2009. Subsequently, on 29 June 2009, the same court issued a writ of execution to enforce the decision.

Despite the finality and enforceability of the judgment, the Republika Srpska failed to comply. The applicant then turned to the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which, on 16 January 2013, found a breach of both Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to the non-enforcement. However, this finding did not lead to the execution of the original judgment. As of the Court’s deliberation, the final judgment in the applicant’s favor remained unenforced, a situation that had persisted for over five years.

The applicant’s complaints before the European Court centered on this prolonged non-enforcement. He relied on Article 6 § 1, which guarantees a fair and public hearing within a reasonable time in the determination of civil rights and obligations, and on Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, which protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. The Court noted that the application was admissible, as it was not manifestly ill-founded.

In examining the merits, the Court considered the arguments. The applicant urged the application of the *Čolić and Others* jurisprudence, which addressed similar issues of non-enforcement. The Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina attempted to distinguish the case, arguing that the judgment did not relate to war damage but to general obligations of the Republika Srpska, which were to be paid in cash under a settlement plan. They further claimed that postponement of enforcement was justified due to the Entity’s large public debt, warning that immediate enforcement could jeopardize macroeconomic stability and fiscal sustainability.

The Court, however, found the case to be practically identical to *Momiić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina*, where it had already established violations of Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 in circumstances involving the non-enforcement of final judgments against the Republika Srpska under a special legal regime. Given that the final judgment in the present case had not been enforced for more than five years, the Court saw no reason to depart from its established case-law. It therefore concluded that there had been a violation of both Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The summary highlights the core issue: the systemic failure to execute a final and enforceable domestic judgment, leading to a breach of the applicant’s rights to a fair trial and property protection.
001-145068:
Fernández Martínez v. Spain (App. no. 56030/07, Grand Chamber, 12 June 2014) concerned a Spanish married Catholic priest who taught Catholic religion and ethics in a State secondary school. The applicant was ordained in 1961. In 1984 he asked the Vatican for dispensation from celibacy but received no immediate reply. In 1985 he married civilly and later had five children. From 1991 he taught Catholic religion and ethics in Murcia under renewable one-year contracts. Under the 1979 Spain–Holy See Agreement and a 1982 Ministerial Order, such teachers were appointed annually on the proposal of the diocesan Ordinary, with automatic renewal unless the Ordinary objected or serious academic/disciplinary reasons existed.

In November 1996, the Murcian newspaper La Verdad published an article about the Movement for Optional Celibacy of priests (MOCEOP). It reported that married priests, including the applicant, had gathered at La Luz monastery to advocate optional celibacy and a more democratic Church, and it set out their views on abortion, birth control, divorce and sexuality. This article publicly disclosed the applicant’s status as a married priest and father and his MOCEOP membership. In August 1997 the Vatican granted his long-pending dispensation from celibacy. The rescript stated that he lost clerical status and was barred from teaching Catholic religion in public institutions unless the local bishop decided otherwise, prudently and provided there was no scandal. He was notified in September 1997.

The Diocese of Cartagena then declined to propose him for the 1997/98 school year. The Ministry of Education terminated his employment with effect from 29 September 1997. In November 1997 the Diocese explained that, once the applicant’s situation became public and commonly known, the bishop could no longer exercise the rescript powers; signing the authorization would risk scandal, especially for parents. It also noted his entitlement to unemployment benefit. The school board had supported him and considered his teaching satisfactory.

An employment tribunal found that he had been discriminated against because of his marital status and MOCEOP membership, and that press publicity had caused the dismissal; it declared the dismissal null and ordered reinstatement. It found no discrimination or private-life violation because he had voluntarily made his situation public, and held that the interference with his rights was justified by the Catholic Church’s collective religious freedom and parents’ rights to choose religious education, with the State remaining neutral.

The Chamber found no violation of Article 8 § 1; the Grand Chamber ultimately also found no violation of Article 8.

**Case Summary: Fernández Martínez v. Spain (Application no. 56030/07)**

The case of *Fernández Martínez v. Spain* concerns the non-renewal of a Catholic religion teacher’s contract in a Spanish state school and the alleged violation of his rights under Article 8 (right to private life) of the European Convention on Human Rights, both taken separately and in conjunction with Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination).

The applicant, José Antonio Fernández Martínez, was born in 1937 and ordained as a Catholic priest in 1961. In 1984, he applied for dispensation from celibacy but received no immediate response. The following year, he married in a civil ceremony and went on to have five children. From 1991 onwards, he was employed under a renewable one-year contract to teach Catholic religion and ethics in a state-run secondary school in Murcia. Under a 1979 Agreement between Spain and the Holy See, such teachers are appointed by the educational authority from candidates proposed by the local bishop. The appointment is renewed annually unless the bishop provides an opinion to the contrary.

In November 1996, a regional newspaper published an article about the Movement for Optional Celibacy (MOCEOP), which reported on a gathering of married priests. The article identified the applicant by name—referring to him as a "former seminary director"—and detailed his public advocacy for optional celibacy and a more democratic Church. It also reported his critical views on Church teachings regarding abortion, birth control, and divorce. The article made public both his family situation as a married priest and father, and his membership in MOCEOP. His personal circumstances were reportedly already known to the school community and Church authorities.

In August 1997, the Vatican granted his 1984 request for dispensation from celibacy. The rescript stipulated that he lost his clerical status and was barred from teaching Catholic religion in public institutions unless the local bishop decided otherwise, provided there was no scandal. In September 1997, the Diocese of Cartagena informed the Ministry of Education that it would not propose the applicant for renewal. The Diocese later stated that once his situation became publicly known, the bishop could no longer authorize him to teach, citing the need to avoid scandal and respect parental sensitivity. The Ministry terminated his employment effective September 1997.

The applicant challenged the decision in administrative and employment courts. While an employment tribunal initially found his dismissal null and void, citing discrimination based on marital status and union (association) activity, the Murcia High Court of Justice overturned this, holding that the bishop’s decision was based on the necessary bond of trust and the avoidance of scandal. The applicant then filed an *amparo* appeal with the Constitutional Court, alleging violations of his rights to equality, privacy, and freedom of expression and religion.

In June 2007, the Constitutional Court dismissed his appeal. It held that the non-renewal was justified by the Catholic Church’s right to religious freedom in its collective dimension and the right of parents to choose their children’s religious education. The Court found the reasons for non-renewal to be exclusively religious in nature, related to the applicant’s public conduct which contravened Church rules. It emphasized that the State must remain neutral in internal Church disputes and that the requirement for religious teachers to profess the faith they teach is reasonable. Consequently, the interference with the applicant’s rights was deemed proportionate and necessary to protect the Church's rights. The applicant then brought his case to the European Court of Human Rights.

José Antonio Fernández Martínez, a Spanish national born in 1937, was ordained as a Catholic priest in 1961. In 1984 he asked the Vatican for dispensation from celibacy; after receiving no immediate answer, he married civilly in 1985 and had five children. From 1991 he taught Catholic religion and ethics in a State-run secondary school in Murcia under annually renewable contracts. Under the 1979 Spain–Holy See Agreement, such teachers were appointed by the education authority from candidates proposed each year by the diocesan Ordinary. Renewal was automatic unless the Ordinary objected.

In November 1996, a Murcian newspaper reported a gathering of the Movement for Optional Celibacy (MOCEOP). The article named the applicant as a married priest and former seminary director and attributed to participants views advocating optional celibacy, a more democratic Church, and liberal positions on contraception and abortion. His marital situation and MOCEOP membership were already known to Church authorities, but the newspaper article made them public.

In August 1997, the Vatican granted the applicant dispensation from celibacy and loss of clerical status. The rescript barred him from teaching Catholic religion in public lower-level schools unless the local bishop decided otherwise, prudently and with no scandal. In September 1997 the Diocese of Cartagena informed the Ministry that he should cease teaching, and the Ministry terminated his employment. The Diocese later explained that once the applicant’s situation became public and common knowledge, the bishop could no longer sign the annual authorization because of the risk of scandal and sensitivity of parents. It also noted the religious nature of the decision. The school board supported him and said his teaching had been satisfactory.

The applicant challenged the non-renewal. In 2000 an employment tribunal held that he had been discriminated against because of his marital status and MOCEOP membership, and that publicity had caused his dismissal. The Murcia High Court reversed, finding that teaching Catholic religion rests on a bond of trust with the bishop, that the bishop had exercised his canonical prerogative, and that the temporary contract had simply expired. In 2007 the Constitutional Court dismissed his amparo appeal. It found no discrimination, emphasized that he had voluntarily publicized his situation, and held that the non-renewal was justified by the Catholic Church’s collective religious freedom and parents’ rights. The reasons were exclusively religious; the State had to remain neutral and could not adjudicate internal Church disputes.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that the non-renewal unjustifiably interfered with his private life under Article 8, separately and in conjunction with Article 14, and was incompatible with Articles 9 and 10. He argued that the real cause was publicity about his family and personal situation as a married priest. A Chamber found no violation of Article 8 § 1. On referral, the Grand Chamber ultimately also found no violation of Article 8, giving weight to the Church’s autonomy and the State’s margin of appreciation in the specific context of religious education.

Beganović v. Slovenia (Application no. 6625/10) was a European Court of Human Rights judgment delivered on 3 April 2014. The applicant, Nenad Beganović, a Slovenian national born in 1986, alleged that the conditions of his detention in Ljubljana prison violated Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), and that he had no effective domestic remedy under Article 13.

The applicant served his sentence in Ljubljana prison from 1 July to 4 November 2009, after which he was transferred to Celje prison until 9 December 2009. He was then held in the Section Novo mesto of Ljubljana prison until 1 April 2010. His complaints concerned only Ljubljana prison, including the Novo mesto section.

From 1 July to 23 September 2009, he was held in the closed section of Ljubljana prison. He occupied cells measuring between 16.8 and 18 square metres, each including a small separate sanitary facility. Each cell had five sleeping places. According to the applicant, five prisoners were held in each cell, while the Government said the number varied between four and five. The applicant thus had approximately 3 to 3.26 square metres of personal space, further reduced by furniture. Sentenced prisoners in the closed section were locked in their cells and could leave only for certain activities; there was only one 50-square-metre recreation room per floor, for up to ten inmates. Summer temperatures were also high: average late-afternoon temperatures in July and August 2009 were around 28°C and exceeded 30°C on seven days.

From 23 September to 4 November 2009, the applicant was held in the semi-open section. He had about 3.4 square metres of personal space. Cell doors were generally unlocked, and prisoners could move in the corridor, other prisoners’ living quarters, or exercise areas, except at night. However, although he was transferred to the semi-open section because of overcrowding, he was not granted outside visits or unsupervised leave.

From 9 December 2009 to 1 April 2010, the applicant was held in the closed section of Section Novo mesto. He was placed in unit 5, measuring 58.83 square metres and containing four rooms, including a smaller room with three beds and a larger room with five or occasionally six beds. Seven prisoners shared the unit. They could move freely within the unit at all times because the inner doors were unlocked, and from 3.30 p.m. to 10.00 p.m. they could also use a shared corridor and recreation areas. The applicant spent six hours per day outside the unit.

The Court declared admissible the complaint concerning the physical conditions in the closed section of Ljubljana prison and the related lack of an effective remedy under Article 13. It found a violation of Article 3 regarding the closed section, because the overcrowding, very limited out-of-cell time, and high summer temperatures cumulatively exceeded the threshold of severity. It rejected as manifestly ill-founded the complaints about the semi-open section and the Section Novo mesto, inadequate health care and psychiatric support, insufficient security, and the Article 8 complaints, including restrictions on telephone calls and outside contact. It also found no separate Article 8 issue arising from the admissible Article 3 complaint. Finally, as in similar cases, it found that the applicant had no effective domestic remedy for his Article 3 complaint concerning the closed section.

Beganović v. Slovenia (Application no. 6625/10) is a 2014 European Court of Human Rights case concerning prison conditions. He was then transferred to Celje Prison until 9 December 2009, after which he returned to Ljubljana Prison’s Novo mesto Section until 1 April 2010. He did not complain about Celje Prison. His allegations concerned violations of Articles 3, 8, and 13 of the Convention.

From 1 July to 23 September 2009, Beganović was held in the closed section of Ljubljana Prison. He occupied cells measuring 16.8 to 18 square metres, including a small separate sanitary facility, and each cell had five sleeping places. He claimed five prisoners were held in each cell; the Government said the number varied between four and five. His personal space was therefore about 3 to 3.26 square metres, further reduced by furniture. Out-of-cell time was very limited: prisoners were locked in their cells unless they applied for activities, with only one 50-square-metre recreation room per floor for up to ten inmates. In summer 2009, late-afternoon cell temperatures averaged about 28°C and exceeded 30°C on seven days. He had three general practitioner consultations and one psychiatric treatment, and never requested a psychologist or dentist.

From 23 September to 4 November 2009, he was in the semi-open section, with about 3.4 square metres of personal space. Cell doors were unlocked except at night, and he could move in a 35.7-square-metre corridor and exercise areas. However, because he had been transferred there due to overcrowding, he was not granted outside visits or unsupervised leave.

From 9 December 2009 to 1 April 2010, he was in the closed Novo mesto Section. Unit 5 measured 58.83 square metres and included four rooms, a sanitary facility, and an ante-chamber. Seven prisoners were held in the unit. The applicant could move freely inside the unit at all times and use shared corridors and recreation areas from 3:30 p.m. to 10:00 p.m. He spent six hours per day outside the unit, including two hours outdoors.

Before the Court, Beganović alleged that severe overcrowding, lack of personal space, poor sanitary conditions and ventilation, excessive restriction on out-of-cell time, high cell temperatures, inadequate health care and psychiatric support, insufficient protection from violence by other inmates, and restrictions on telephone calls violated Articles 3 and 8. He also argued that the inadequate prison conditions were systemic and that he had no effective domestic remedy, contrary to Article 13.

The Court rejected as manifestly ill-founded the complaints concerning the semi-open section, the Novo mesto Section, health care, psychiatric support, security measures, telephone restrictions, and other Article 8 contact issues. It found, however, that the conditions in the closed section of Ljubljana Prison violated Article 3. The applicant’s personal space was only about 3 to 3.26 square metres, out-of-cell time was severely limited, and summer temperatures were high. Considering the cumulative effects, the hardship exceeded the unavoidable level inherent in detention. The Court also declared admissible the Article 13 complaint concerning the lack of an effective remedy for the inadequate physical conditions in the closed section, and, consistent with Štrucl and Others, found no effective domestic remedy. No separate issue arose under Article 8 for the conditions already examined under Article 3.

Beganović v. Slovenia (App. No. 6625/10), ECHR Fifth Section, judgment of 3 April 2014. His complaints did not concern Celje prison.

From 1 July to 23 September 2009, the applicant was in the closed section of Ljubljana prison. He was held in cells measuring 16.8 or 18 square metres, including a separate sanitary facility of 1.72 square metres. Each cell had five sleeping places. The applicant claimed five prisoners were held in each cell; the Government said the number varied between four and five. His personal space in the closed section was about 3 or 3.26 square metres, further reduced by furniture. Out-of-cell time was very limited: sentenced prisoners were locked in their cells and could leave only by applying for activities, most of which took place in a single 50-square-metre recreation room per floor. In late July and August 2009, average late-afternoon cell temperatures were about 28°C, exceeding 30°C on seven days.

From 23 September to 4 November 2009, he was in the semi-open section, in an 18-square-metre cell with about 3.4 square metres of personal space. Cell doors there were unlocked except at night, and prisoners could move in the corridor, other prisoners’ quarters, and exercise areas. He had been transferred there due to overcrowding but was not granted outside visits or unsupervised leave.

From 9 December 2009 to 1 April 2010, he was in the closed section of Section Novo mesto. He was held in a unit of 58.83 square metres containing four separate rooms, with seven prisoners total. He was mostly in a larger room with three other prisoners. The unit’s inner doors were unlocked, allowing free movement within the unit 24 hours per day; from 3.30 p.m. to 10 p.m. prisoners could also use shared corridors and recreation areas. It rejected as manifestly ill-founded the complaints concerning the semi-open section, Section Novo mesto, health care, psychiatric support, security, and contact restrictions. On the merits, the Court found that the cumulative conditions in the closed section—about 3–3.26 square metres of personal space, reduced by furniture, very limited out-of-cell time, and high summer temperatures—exceeded the unavoidable level inherent in detention, violating Article 3. Article 8 raised no separate issue regarding the admissible Article 3 matters, and the remaining Article 8 complaints were rejected. Finally, following Štrucl and Others v. Slovenia, the Court found that no effective remedy existed for the closed-section conditions, violating Article 13.

In *Vajnai v. Hungary (No. 4)* (Application no. 6061/10), the European Court of Human Rights considered an Article 10 complaint by Attila Vajnai, a Hungarian left-wing politician. On 18 May 2009, while participating in a peaceful demonstration, Vajnai wore a five-pointed red star on his jacket. Police officers present called on him to remove it and then confiscated it. Vajnai complained to the Head of National Police, without success. He then challenged the police measure in court.

On 29 June 2010, the Budapest Regional Court dismissed his action. It held that displaying the red star contravened section 269/B of the Hungarian Criminal Code and that confiscation was justified under sections 115(1) and 151(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On review, the Supreme Court upheld the decision on 8 June 2011. It found the police measure lawful despite the European Court’s earlier judgment in *Vajnai v. Hungary* (no. 33629/06, 2008). According to the Supreme Court, applying the contextual scrutiny required by that earlier judgment was not a task for the police officers present. The applicant incurred approximately EUR 1,115 in legal costs.

Vajnai lodged an application with the ECtHR on 23 January 2010, alleging that the police measure for wearing the red star violated his right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention. The Government argued that the present case differed from the earlier *Vajnai* judgment: here the issue was whether police officers had the duty or possibility to carry out contextual scrutiny of the applicant’s conduct as required by *Vajnai*. It maintained that the police measure was lawful and justified because the officers reasonably assumed that the applicant’s conduct constituted an offence under section 269/B, which still prohibited display of a red star. The applicant disputed this and relied on the earlier *Vajnai* judgment.

The Court recalled that in *Vajnai v. Hungary* it had already found that prosecution of the applicant for displaying the red star was an admissible complaint and constituted a violation of Article 10. The impugned national provision was the same as in the present case, and the circumstances of the interference were virtually identical. The Court therefore saw no reason to depart from its earlier conclusion. Accordingly, it found a violation of Article 10. The case thus turned on the continued application and enforcement of the same criminal-law prohibition already held incompatible with freedom of expression, even though in this instance the interference occurred through a police confiscation rather than a criminal prosecution. The Court rejected the Government’s attempt to distinguish the case based on the police’s limited role, because the underlying interference with the applicant’s expression was materially the same. The judgment was delivered on 23 September 2014.

In *Sociedade de Construções Martins & Vieira, Lda and Others v. Portugal*, five applications were joined. The applicants were a Portuguese construction company and its two managing partners. They complained under Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention that fiscal criminal proceedings against them had exceeded a reasonable time and that they had no effective domestic remedy.

In September 1999, Portuguese authorities began investigating the company’s tax activity for 1994–1997. Two sets of fiscal criminal proceedings were brought, before the Porto and Barcelos Criminal Courts. On 20 December 1999 the applicants were made defendants in both.

In the Porto proceedings, charges were filed on 5 November 2003 against the company and the third applicant for tax fraud relating to 1997. The trial began on 27 September 2005 but was adjourned because defence witnesses were absent. It was later adjourned again after the applicants’ representative resigned. In June 2006 the applicants appointed new counsel. On 14 November 2006 they informed the Porto Criminal Court that they had sought judicial review before the Porto Administrative and Fiscal Court concerning a tax adjustment for 1994–1997. On 29 November 2006 the Porto Criminal Court suspended the criminal proceedings under Article 50 § 1 of the RJIFNA, which required suspension pending final resolution of the tax review.

In the Barcelos proceedings, on 28 April 2003 the prosecutor charged all three applicants with tax fraud and abuse concerning 1994–1996. On 1 October 2003 the applicants contested the charges and sought suspension pending the tax review. On 17 November 2003 the Barcelos Criminal Court suspended the proceedings under Article 50 § 1 and requested information from the administrative court. In December 2006 and October 2008, the administrative court confirmed that the tax review was still pending. On 23 April 2007 the Barcelos Criminal Court suspended the proceedings until a final decision was reached.

In December 2008 the applicants asked the High Council of Magistrates to expedite both criminal cases. In May 2009 and January 2009, respectively, the requests were dismissed. The Council considered that the delay was attributable to the administrative and fiscal court and that the applicants should have applied to the High Council of the Administrative and Fiscal Courts. In October 2006 the applicants also brought tort proceedings against the State in the Porto and Braga Administrative and Fiscal Courts, claiming damages for excessive length; those proceedings were still pending in February 2014.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 13. The Government argued that the complaint was incompatible *ratione materiae* because the delay resulted from the tax judicial review, not the criminal proceedings, and that the applicants had contributed to delays. The Court joined the applications. It found that the relevant period began on 20 December 1999 and had not ended, already lasting fourteen years and nine months at one level of jurisdiction. The cases were not particularly complex. The applicants caused only minor delay through a change of counsel in 2006, with no real impact. The domestic courts, however, were inactive for nearly four years before charges were brought and for about two years in the Porto case before trial. Although awaiting parallel tax proceedings can be reasonable, the suspension became indefinite, keeping the accused in prolonged uncertainty. The Court therefore found violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 13.

**Sociedade de Construções Martins & Vieira, Lda and Others v. Portugal**  
*(Applications nos. 56637/10, 59856/10, 72525/10, 7646/11 and 12592/11)*

The case concerned a Portuguese construction company and its two managing partners. In September 1999, Portuguese authorities began investigating the applicant company’s tax activity for 1994–1997. This led to two sets of fiscal criminal proceedings before the Porto and Barcelos Criminal Courts. On 20 December 1999, the applicants were formally made defendants. Charges were later brought in 2003: the Porto proceedings concerned tax fraud relating to 1997 activity, while the Barcelos proceedings concerned tax fraud and abuse relating to 1994–1996.

A central factual issue was that the applicants challenged a tax adjustment before the Porto Administrative and Fiscal Court. Under Article 50 § 1 of the RJIFNA, Portuguese law required fiscal criminal proceedings to be suspended until the tax judicial review became final. The Porto Criminal Court suspended its proceedings in November 2006, and the Barcelos Criminal Court suspended its proceedings in April 2007. The administrative tax review remained pending for years, and both criminal proceedings were still pending before the domestic courts. The applicants asked the High Council of Magistrates to expedite the criminal proceedings, but their requests were dismissed because the delay was attributed to the administrative/fiscal courts and because the suspension was lawful. The applicants also brought separate tort proceedings against the State claiming damages for excessive length; those proceedings were also still pending.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants complained that the length of the criminal proceedings violated the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and that they lacked an effective remedy under Article 13. The Government argued that the complaint was incompatible *ratione materiae* with Article 6 because the delay resulted from the tax judicial review, to which Article 6 did not apply. They also claimed the applicants contributed to delays.

The Court joined the applications and declared the length complaint admissible. It found that the relevant period began on 20 December 1999, when the applicants were made defendants, and had not yet ended. The proceedings had therefore lasted over fourteen years and nine months at one level of jurisdiction. The Court treated the fiscal criminal proceedings as criminal in nature and subject to autonomous analysis under Article 6.

On the merits, the Court noted that the cases were not shown to be particularly complex. The applicants were responsible for only minor delay, such as a change of lawyer in 2006, which had no real impact. By contrast, the domestic courts showed serious inactivity: almost four years passed between December 1999 and the 2003 charges, and a further two years passed in the Porto proceedings before trial. More importantly, the criminal proceedings were suspended indefinitely from 2006/2007 pending the tax review, leaving the applicants in prolonged uncertainty. While awaiting parallel proceedings may sometimes be reasonable, the Court emphasized that suspension must be proportionate and not indefinite. Article 6 § 1 requires States to organise their legal systems so that courts can hear cases within a reasonable time. A statutory suspension rule, such as Article 50 § 1 RJIFNA (later Article 47 § 1 RGIT), cannot dispense national courts from ensuring an expeditious trial or from imposing a reasonable time-limit on the suspension. The alleged violations therefore centred on the prolonged, indefinite suspension of criminal proceedings and the absence of an effective remedy for that delay.

Slovenia** (Application no. 32863/05), European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, judgment of 12 June 2014, concerned a Slovenian woman with a long-standing psychotic disorder who had been hospitalised several times since 2000. Under Article 8, she alleged that forced medication and other therapeutic procedures interfered with her physical and mental integrity, and that no remedy existed to challenge them.

In July 2005, police told the applicant’s family physician that she had broken into an unoccupied house and was difficult to communicate with. She was referred to Idrija Psychiatric Hospital and admitted the same day to its closed ward. Although she signed a consent form, she expressed delusions—claiming she was possessed by people through cameras operated by President Bush—and was diagnosed with schizophrenia. She received antipsychotic and sedative medication. The hospital notified the Idrija Local Court. The court appointed a lawyer and held a hearing on 15 July, where the applicant said she would rather be at home and did not understand why she had been hospitalised. Later, through lawyer D.P., she stated that treatment was against her will but that she feared refusing because medication might be forced on her. D.P. notified the hospital that the applicant did not consent and asked that forced medication stop. On 8 August 2005 she was transferred to the open ward, and the court terminated the confinement proceedings. She was discharged on 12 August at her own request. Her constitutional complaint was rejected for failure to exhaust remedies.

In August 2005, police took her to emergency services, and she was transferred to Ljubljana Psychiatric Hospital. Admission notes recorded paranoid and megalomanic delusions and stated that she “accepted hospitalisation owing to the situation (the staff being present),” with no compulsory measures initially deemed necessary. From 17 August she was placed in the closed ward and treated with Haldol, Akineton, Lorsilan, Moditen and Leponex. On 21 August she notified the local court of her confinement and sought release and termination of treatment; she also lodged a constitutional complaint. The court appointed counsel. At a 25-minute hearing on 23 August, an expert found a paranoid delusional system and recommended closed-ward treatment for up to one month. The Local Court ordered confinement until 23 September. Interlocutory relief was refused. On appeal, the Higher Court set aside the decisions on 9 September due to inadequate reasoning, noting that injunctive relief was possible and that stopping treatment required separate consideration. Around 3–4 September she was transferred to the open ward. **Case Summary: S.A.S. v. France (ECtHR, Grand Chamber, 1 July 2014)**

The applicant, S.A.S., is an anonymised French national born in 1990 who lives in France. She described herself as a devout Muslim and said she wore the burqa and niqab in accordance with her religious faith, culture and personal convictions. The burqa is a full-body covering that includes a mesh over the face; the niqab is a full-face veil leaving only the eyes visible. She stressed that neither her husband nor any family member pressured her to dress this way. She wore the niqab both in public and in private, but not systematically: she might not wear it when visiting the doctor, meeting friends in public, or socialising. She wanted the freedom to wear it when she chose, particularly during periods of heightened spiritual feeling such as Ramadan, in order to express her faith and feel inner peace. She did not claim a right to keep it on during security checks, at banks or in airports, and accepted that she should show her face for necessary identity checks.

The alleged violation arose from Law no. 2010-1192 of 11 October 2010, which entered into force throughout France on 11 April 2011. The Law prohibited anyone from concealing their face in public places. Public places were defined broadly to include the public highway and any places open to the public or assigned to a public service. Exceptions existed for clothing prescribed or authorised by law, justified for health or occupational reasons, or worn during sports, festivities, artistic or traditional events. Breach of the ban was punishable by a fine of up to 150 euros, with a possible citizenship course instead of or in addition to the fine. The Law also created a criminal offence for anyone forcing another person to conceal their face by threats, duress, coercion or abuse of authority on account of gender.

The applicant complained that the ban deprived her of the possibility of wearing the full-face veil in public. She alleged violations of Articles 3, 8, 9, 10 and 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights, taken separately and in conjunction with Article 14. In essence, she argued that the general ban interfered with her private life, religious freedom, expression and assembly, and discriminated against her.

The case reached the Grand Chamber after being relinquished by a Chamber of the Fifth Section. The Court considered the legislative background: a 2010 parliamentary report estimated that about 1,900 women wore the full-face veil in France by the end of 2009, mostly under 40, two-thirds French nationals, and one-quarter converts. The report framed the practice as contrary to Republican values of liberty, equality, fraternity, dignity, gender equality and “living together.” By contrast, the National Advisory Commission on Human Rights opposed a general absolute ban, warning of stigmatisation and exclusion, and the Conseil d’État doubted the legal viability of banning the full veil alone. The Constitutional Council upheld the Law, subject to a reservation protecting religious freedom in places of worship.

The key Convention question was whether France’s general prohibition on face concealment in public places unjustifiably interfered with the applicant’s rights. The Grand Chamber ultimately found no violation of Articles 8 and 9, and no separate violation under the other provisions.

She did not claim a right to keep it on during security checks, at banks, or in airports, and agreed to show her face for necessary identity checks.

Her core complaint was that the general ban interfered with her private life, religious freedom, expression, and association, and discriminated against her. She argued that her wearing of the veil was voluntary, spiritually motivated, and not a threat to public order.

The Government relied on domestic parliamentary and constitutional materials. A 2010 parliamentary report estimated that about 1,900 women wore the full-face veil in France. It characterised the practice as contrary to Republican values—liberty, equality, fraternity, human dignity, gender equality, and “living together” (*vivre ensemble*). The Constitutional Council upheld the law but reserved that the ban could not restrict religious freedom in places of worship open to the public. Official circulars instructed authorities on enforcement, identity checks, and avoiding intervention near places of worship.

The Grand Chamber ultimately found no violation of Articles 8 and 9, and no violation of Article 14 taken in conjunction with those Articles; it found no separate issue under Articles 10 and 11, and declared the Article 3 complaint inadmissible. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were the applicant’s voluntary religious practice, the absence of family pressure, her willingness to reveal her face for identity checks, the small number of women affected, and the State’s asserted aims of public safety, gender equality, human dignity, and social cohesion.

**S.A.S. v. France** (Application no. 43835/11, Grand Chamber, 1 July 2014) concerned a French national Muslim woman who challenged France’s ban on concealing one’s face in public places. The applicant stated that she was a devout Muslim and wore the burqa and niqab in accordance with her religious faith, culture, and personal convictions. She stressed that neither her husband nor any family member pressured her to dress this way. She wore the niqab in public and private, but not systematically: she might not wear it when visiting a doctor, meeting friends, or socialising. She wished to be able to wear it when she chose, especially during religious periods such as Ramadan, for spiritual reasons and inner peace. Importantly, she did not claim a right to keep her face covered during security checks, at banks, or at airports, and accepted showing her face when required for identity checks.

The relevant French law was Law no. 2010-1192 of 11 October 2010, in force from 11 April 2011, which prohibits anyone from wearing clothing designed to conceal the face in public places. “Public places” included the public highway and any place open to the public or assigned to public service. The law contained limited exceptions, such as clothing prescribed by law, justified for health or occupational reasons, or worn in sports, festivities, artistic or traditional events. Breach was punishable by a fine of up to 150 euros and/or an obligation to follow a citizenship course. A separate offence punished anyone who forced another person to conceal their face by threat, duress, coercion, or abuse of authority.

The ban followed lengthy domestic debate. A 2010 parliamentary report found that the full-face veil was a recent phenomenon in France, involving around 1,900 women, and characterised it as contrary to Republican values of liberty, equality, and fraternity, as well as to gender equality, human dignity, and “living together.” The National Advisory Commission on Human Rights opposed a general and absolute ban, warning of stigmatisation and exclusion. The Conseil d’État doubted that a ban on the full veil alone would be legally sound, suggesting instead targeted public-order restrictions and penalties for forcing women to conceal their faces. The National Assembly adopted a resolution denouncing radical practices, and the bill’s explanatory memorandum argued that systematic face concealment was incompatible with the minimum requirements of social life, public order, safety, and the dignity of others. The Constitutional Council upheld the law but reserved the exercise of religious freedom in places of worship open to the public.

The applicant complained that the ban deprived her of the possibility of wearing the full-face veil in public. She alleged violations of Articles 3, 8, 9, 10, and 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights, taken separately and in conjunction with Article 14. The key factual issue was thus whether a general ban on face concealment in public places could be justified against her voluntary religious and personal practice, given her willingness to uncover her face for identity and security checks. The case required the Grand Chamber to balance her rights to private life, religious manifestation, expression, and assembly against France’s asserted aims of public safety, public order, gender equality, dignity, and “living together.”

**Avotiņš v. Latvia** (Application no. 17502/07) concerned a Latvian applicant’s complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights that Latvia violated his right to a fair hearing by recognising and enforcing a Cypriot default judgment obtained against him without proper service and without allowing him to exercise his defence rights.

In 1999, the applicant signed a deed of acknowledgement of debt with F.H. Ltd., a Cypriot company, declaring that he owed USD 100,000, with interest, to be repaid by 30 June 1999. The deed was governed by Cypriot law and gave Cypriot courts non-exclusive jurisdiction. In 2003, F.H. Ltd. sued the applicant in the Limassol District Court in Cyprus. Because the applicant did not reside in Cyprus, the company applied ex parte for permission to serve him abroad. Its lawyer stated by affidavit that the applicant habitually resided at an address in G. Street, Riga. The Cypriot court ordered service at that address, requiring the applicant to appear within thirty days.

The summons was allegedly sent by recorded delivery on 16 November 2003 to G. Street, and a postal slip indicated receipt on 18 November 2003—a Latvian national holiday and non-working day. The applicant denied receiving it. He claimed G. Street was merely the address where he had signed the loan documents in 1999, not his home or business premises. He did not appear, and on 24 May 2004 the Limassol District Court entered a default judgment ordering him to pay USD 100,000 plus 10% annual interest and costs. The judgment was finalised on 3 June 2004 but did not state whether it was final or what remedies were available.

In February 2005, F.H. Ltd. sought recognition and enforcement in Latvia. Its request gave the applicant’s address as Č. Street, Riga, different from G. Street. The Latvian District Court noticed this discrepancy. The company later explained that Č. Street was the applicant’s officially declared residence, while G. Street had been assumed to be his actual residence. On 27 February 2006, the Riga City Latgale District Court, sitting without the parties, allowed the request in full, recognised the Cypriot judgment, and entered a charge on the applicant’s property in Garkalne.

The applicant only learned of the Cypriot judgment and the Latvian enforcement order on 16 June 2006. He appealed the enforcement order. The Latgale District Court extended the time-limit, finding that he had not received the 27 February 2006 order and no longer lived at his declared address. On 2 October 2006, the Riga Regional Court allowed his appeal and refused recognition, relying on Article 34(2) of the Brussels I Regulation and Latvian law: a default judgment could not be recognised if the defendant was not served in sufficient time to arrange his defence. The Regional Court also found defects concerning proof that the Cypriot judgment was enforceable.

F.H. Ltd. appealed to the Senate of the Supreme Court. At the hearing on 31 January 2007, it submitted a certificate dated 18 January 2007 stating that the applicant had been served on 27 November 2003; the section identifying the person against whom the judgment was enforceable was left blank. The Senate quashed the Regional Court’s judgment and allowed enforcement. It reasoned that the applicant had not appealed against the Cypriot judgment, so his complaints about notification were irrelevant, and that the foreign judgment could not be reviewed on the merits under Article 36 of the Regulation. A writ of execution followed on 14 February 2007, and the applicant paid approximately LVL 90,244.62 (around EUR 129,000).

The applicant alleged that Latvia breached Article 6 § 1 by enforcing the Cypriot default judgment without ensuring that he had been properly served and able to defend himself. The application initially also concerned Cyprus, but that part was declared inadmissible for failure to comply with the six-month time-limit. The key issue was whether the Latvian courts properly examined the service and defence-rights concerns before recognising and enforcing the foreign default judgment.

It held the Cypriot judgment was final, that because the applicant had not appealed in Cyprus his complaint about notification was unimportant, and that Article 36 barred review of the substance. **Summary of Avotiņš v. Latvia (Application no. 17502/07)**

The case concerned a Latvian national, Pēteris Avotiņš, who complained that a Cypriot default judgment ordering him to repay a debt was enforced in Latvia without proper service of proceedings, thereby breaching his right to a fair hearing under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The application was initially lodged against Cyprus and Latvia, but the complaint against Cyprus was declared inadmissible for failure to comply with the six-month time-limit. The Court examined only the complaint against Latvia.

In May 1999 the applicant signed a deed before a Cypriot notary acknowledging that he had borrowed USD 100,000 from F.H. Ltd., a Cypriot company, and undertaking to repay it with interest by 30 June 1999. The deed was governed by Cypriot law and gave Cypriot courts non-exclusive jurisdiction. In 2003 F.H. Ltd. sued the applicant in the Limassol District Court for non-repayment. Because the applicant did not live in Cyprus, the company applied ex parte for service abroad. Its lawyer stated in an affidavit that the applicant was habitually resident at an address in G. Street, Riga, and that service could be effected there. The applicant later claimed that this address was merely the place where he had signed the 1999 documents, not his home or business address, and that it was objectively impossible for him to receive the summons there.

The Cypriot court ordered service at G. Street. A law firm employee’s affidavit stated that the summons was sent by recorded delivery on 16 November 2003 and that a post office slip showed receipt by the applicant on 18 November 2003, a Latvian public holiday. The applicant denied receiving it. He did not appear, and on 24 May 2004 the Limassol District Court entered a default judgment ordering him to pay USD 100,000 or its Cypriot pound equivalent, plus 10% annual interest from 30 June 1999, costs, and further interest. The judgment stated that he had been duly informed but had not attended. It contained no reference to its finality or available remedies.

In February 2005 F.H. Ltd. sought recognition and enforcement in Latvia. Its application gave a different Riga address for the applicant, Č. Street. The Latvian court initially returned the request because of defects, but after a corrigendum and an appeal by the company, the Riga City Latgale District Court on 27 February 2006 allowed recognition and enforcement without the parties being present. The applicant learned of the Cypriot judgment and the Latvian enforcement order only on 16 June 2006. He did not challenge the Cypriot judgment in Cyprus, but appealed in Latvia.

He argued that enforcement breached Article 34(2) of the Brussels I Regulation and Latvian law because, in a default judgment, recognition must be refused if the defendant was not served in sufficient time and in such a way as to enable him to arrange his defence. He also argued that the judgment had not been shown to be enforceable in Cyprus, that no required certificate had been produced, and that the judgment did not mention finality or remedies. The Riga Regional Court accepted these arguments on 2 October 2006 and refused enforcement. However, the Senate of the Latvian Supreme Court reversed that decision on 31 January 2007. At that hearing F.H. Ltd. produced a certificate dated 18 January 2007, stating that the initiating document had been served on 27 November 2003. The Senate held that the Cypriot judgment was final and that, because the applicant had not appealed in Cyprus, his complaints about notification were irrelevant. Enforcement followed, and the applicant paid approximately EUR 129,000.

The key alleged violation was therefore that Latvia enforced a Cypriot default judgment despite unresolved questions about defective service, without adequately verifying whether the applicant had been able to arrange his defence, contrary to Article 6 § 1.

**Summary of the Case of Radu v. the Republic of Moldova**

The case of *Radu v. the Republic of Moldova* (Application no. 50073/07) concerns an alleged violation of the right to respect for private life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Ms. Liliana Radu, a Moldovan national born in 1969, was a lecturer at the Police Academy in Chişinău.

At the time of the events, the relationship between the applicant and her superiors at the Police Academy was tense, with prior employment-related civil proceedings between them. In 2003, the applicant underwent artificial insemination and became pregnant with twins. On 3 August 2003, due to an increased risk of miscarriage, she was hospitalized and subsequently placed under close medical supervision. Her absence from work was certified by a sick note citing pregnancy and risk of miscarriage as reasons.

On 5 November 2003, the President of the Police Academy requested detailed information from the No. 7 Centre for Family Doctors (CFD), a state-owned hospital, regarding the applicant’s medical leave. Specifically, he asked who had ordered her hospitalization, the dates, the initial and final diagnoses, and the treatment received. In a letter dated 7 November 2003, the CFD disclosed extensive confidential medical information to the applicant’s employer without her consent. The letter revealed that the applicant had been hospitalized due to an increased risk of miscarriage, that it was her first pregnancy, that she was carrying twins, that the pregnancy resulted from artificial insemination, and that she had hepatitis B and a negative blood type. A detailed copy of her medical file was also annexed.

Following this disclosure, the applicant suffered a miscarriage. According to a medical report, stress was a contributing factor. The applicant alleged that the information was not kept confidential and was disseminated throughout the Police Academy, causing her severe stress and anxiety. Her husband, also an employee there, was forced to resign.

In January 2004, the applicant initiated civil proceedings against the CFD and the Police Academy, claiming compensation for the breach of her private life. She argued that her employer had sufficient information about her medical leave and was not entitled to seek further private details, and that the disclosed information was not kept confidential.

On 6 July 2004, the Centru District Court dismissed her action, finding the disclosure lawful due to the employer’s ongoing investigation. The applicant appealed. On 2 November 2006, the Chişinău Court of Appeal quashed the judgment, found her action well-founded, and ordered the CFD and the Police Academy to pay her compensation. The court held that the CFD had disclosed more information than requested. However, on 10 May 2007, the Supreme Court of Justice upheld an appeal by the CFD, dismissing the claims against it. The Supreme Court ruled that the CFD had acted lawfully in providing the medical information, as it was obliged to do so in the context of the employment relationship between the Police Academy and the applicant, and considered the laws on patient rights and reproductive health not pertinent to the case.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the State had failed to fulfil its obligation to secure respect for her private life, as a state-owned hospital disclosed her medical condition without her consent.

The CFD also annexed a copy of her medical file, containing detailed descriptions of all medical procedures and analyses.

The applicant alleged that this information was private and was not kept confidential but was spread throughout the Police Academy, including among students. According to a medical report, stress was one of the factors contributing to the miscarriage. Her husband, also employed at the Police Academy, allegedly had to resign and accept a lower-paid job.

It found that the CFD had disclosed more information than had actually been requested.

In May 2007, however, the Supreme Court of Justice upheld the CFD’s appeal on points of law and dismissed the applicant’s claims against it. The Supreme Court held that the CFD had acted lawfully in providing the medical information to the Police Academy, in the context of the employment and criminal-law relationship between the Academy and the applicant. It also considered that laws on reproductive health and patients’ rights were not pertinent to the case.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the State had failed to fulfil its obligation to secure respect for her private life. Specifically, she alleged that a State-owned hospital had disclosed information about her medical condition without her consent, contrary to Article 8 of the Convention. The key issue was whether Moldova had taken adequate measures to protect confidential medical information, given domestic laws on medical confidentiality, patient rights, reproductive health, and access to personal data.

In *Lakatoš and Others v. Serbia* (App. no. 3363/08, judgment of 7 January 2014), five Serbian nationals complained of violations of Articles 3, 5, 6 § 2 and 8 of the Convention in the context of criminal proceedings.

The case arose from an investigation into numerous robberies committed in northern Serbia during 2006–2007, mainly targeting elderly people, some of whom suffered grievous bodily harm. On 5 November 2007, after a robbery in Kucura, police stopped a suspicious vehicle and arrested one person, PN; the first, second and third applicants allegedly escaped. The next morning, the fourth and fifth applicants allegedly went to give them a lift back to Subotica. Police stopped the vehicle before the town and arrested all five applicants, taking them to Novi Sad Police Station.

On 6 November 2007, the investigating judge ordered DNA samples to be taken. The fifth applicant was later released. On 7 November, police reports stated that the applicants had resisted arrest or tried to escape, so force had been used. Injuries were noted: the first and third applicants had excoriations on their foreheads; the second had redness around his forehead and right eye; the fourth had an excoriation on the left side of his head. The first and third were not given medical assistance because they did not ask for it.

On 8 November 2007, the first to fourth applicants were brought before the investigating judge and complained, in the presence of the public prosecutor, of being beaten by police during arrest and at the police station. The judge recorded injuries to the second and fourth applicants, including neck excoriations and bruises to the shoulder and face. Their lawyer photographed the injuries. The fourth applicant was released; the first, second and third were remanded in custody on suspicion of numerous robberies, based on the severity of the potential sentence and the nature of the alleged crimes. On the same day, police held a press conference. Senior officers allegedly described the applicants as members of a criminal group responsible for the robberies, released their photographs to the press, and said local residents had begun forming “village guard units.” These facts are relevant to the Article 6 § 2 presumption-of-innocence and Article 8 complaints.

On 13 November 2007, court-ordered medical examinations found multiple bruises and haematomas on the first, second and third applicants, including on their heads, ears, necks, arms, legs, shoulders, backs and feet. The fourth applicant did not attend, but earlier photographs showed bruises and excoriations on his shoulder, back and abdomen. The fifth applicant later stated she had been slapped by police on arrest. A later expert report concluded that the injuries had been caused by repeated mechanical force, ruled out a fall, and estimated they were inflicted roughly three, seven and three days before the examination. However, it also noted no clear temporal stages and some discrepancies with the photographs.

On 29 February 2008, the public prosecutor indicted the first, second and third applicants, plus PN, for numerous robberies and attempted robberies; the second was also charged with causing grievous bodily harm to a police officer with intent to resist arrest. The fourth and fifth applicants were not prosecuted. In 2009, the first, second and third applicants were convicted and sentenced to long prison terms. In 2011, the Appeals Court quashed the convictions and ordered a retrial, but they were again convicted in November 2011 and the judgment was upheld in June 2012. A constitutional appeal remained pending, and they were released in December 2012 under an amnesty.

Their pre-trial detention was repeatedly extended from December 2007 to June 2009 on the same grounds: the severity of the potential sentence and the nature of the alleged crimes. The Constitutional Court rejected challenges, finding the detention grounds compatible with the equivalent constitutional right. Additionally, the fourth and fifth applicants’ DNA samples remained stored, with no specific legislation governing their destruction absent a court decision. This formed part of the Article 8 complaint.

**Lakatoš and Others v. Serbia (Application no. 3363/08)**

**Key Facts Relevant to the Alleged Violations**

The case originated from an application lodged against Serbia by five Serbian nationals concerning their arrest, detention, and subsequent criminal proceedings in 2007. The applicants were suspected of a series of robberies targeting elderly individuals in northern Serbia.

On 5 November 2007, following a robbery in Kucura, police arrested one suspect (PN), while the first, second, and third applicants allegedly escaped. The next morning, the fourth and fifth applicants were arrested while reportedly giving the others a lift. All five were taken to the Novi Sad Police Station.

On 6 November 2007, the investigating judge ordered DNA samples to be taken. The fifth applicant was released later that day. On 7 November 2007, police officers filed reports stating the applicants had resisted arrest, justifying the use of force that resulted in injuries. These injuries included excoriations on the foreheads of the first and third applicants, redness on the second applicant’s face, and an excoriation on the fourth applicant’s head. The reports noted that medical assistance was not provided to the first and third applicants because they did not request it.

On 8 November 2007, the first four applicants appeared before the investigating judge and complained of being beaten by police during arrest and at the station. The judge documented visible injuries on the second applicant (neck excoriations and laceration) and fourth applicant (bruises on shoulder and face). Photographs were taken. The first, second, and third applicants were remanded in custody on suspicion of numerous robberies, based on the severity of the potential sentence and the nature of the crimes. The fourth applicant was released. That same day, police held a press conference where high-ranking officers reportedly referred to the applicants as members of a criminal group and released their photographs to the media.

On 13 November 2007, court-ordered medical examinations revealed extensive injuries: the first applicant had bruises on his head, ear, arms, and legs; the second on his forehead, ear, neck, and legs; and the third on his forehead, shoulder, back, and foot. The fourth applicant did not attend but his injuries were documented by earlier photos. The fifth applicant later stated she had been slapped by police.

A subsequent medical report in September 2008 concluded the injuries were inflicted by “repeated use of mechanical force,” ruling out falls. It estimated the first and third applicants’ injuries were sustained three days prior to 13 November (i.e., around 10 November), and the second applicant’s seven days prior (i.e., around 6 November), though noting the imprecision of such estimates.

On 29 February 2008, the public prosecutor indicted the first, second, third applicants and PN on multiple robbery charges; the second applicant was also charged with causing grievous bodily harm to a police officer. The fourth and fifth applicants were not prosecuted. The first three applicants were convicted in July 2009, but this was quashed in March 2011 and remanded for retrial. They were convicted again in November 2011, and this judgment was upheld in June 2012. They were released in December 2012 under a general amnesty.

Regarding pre-trial detention, it was repeatedly extended between December 2007 and June 2009 based on the severity of the potential sentence and the nature of the crimes. The applicants’ appeals were rejected, and the Constitutional Court dismissed their constitutional appeals concerning detention.

Other relevant facts include: the fourth and fifth applicants’ DNA samples remained stored without specific legislation governing their destruction; a co-suspect’s criminal complaint alleging police abuse was rejected for lack of evidence.

The applicants alleged violations of Articles 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman treatment), 5 (right to liberty and security), 6 § 2 (presumption of innocence), and 8 (right to respect for private life) of the Convention, all arising from these events.

On 29 February 2008, the public prosecutor indicted the first, second, and third applicants on multiple robbery charges, with the second also accused of causing grievous bodily harm to resist arrest. The fourth and fifth applicants were not prosecuted.

On 10 July 2009, the Novi Sad District Court convicted the first three applicants, sentencing them to lengthy imprisonment terms. This judgment was quashed on 1 March 2011 due to procedural deficiencies, and a retrial ordered. On 11 November 2011, the High Court again convicted them, finding their injuries resulted from resisting arrest or escape attempts. This was upheld on 4 June 2012. The applicants’ constitutional appeal remained pending, and they were released on 28 December 2012 under a general amnesty.

In *Filatova and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 12424/06 and 15 others), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, Committee) delivered a judgment on 31 July 2014 concerning 16 applications lodged by Ukrainian nationals and Ukraine-based companies. The central factual background was that domestic courts in Ukraine had issued decisions in the applicants’ favour. Those decisions entitled the applicants either to receive various pecuniary amounts or to have certain actions taken in their favour. The decisions became final and enforceable under domestic law. However, the applicants were unable to obtain enforcement of those decisions in due time. The Court found that the State authorities were responsible for this failure. This prolonged non-enforcement formed the core of the applicants’ complaints before the Strasbourg Court.

The applicants alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights, Article 13 of the Convention, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. In substance, they complained that the final domestic decisions in their favour had not been enforced for a lengthy period and that Ukraine lacked effective domestic remedies to address that non-enforcement. Some applicants also made submissions on factual and legal matters unrelated to the non-enforcement issues, but the principal legal issue before the Court was the failure to execute final judicial decisions.

Procedurally, the applications were communicated to the Government on various dates. The Government, represented by its Agent, submitted unilateral declarations in certain applications aimed at resolving the non-enforcement issues. The declarations were submitted on 15 December 2011 in application no. 7436/08 and on 15 September 2011 in application no. 40893/09. The Government asked the Court to strike the applications out of its list under Article 37 § 1(c) of the Convention. The Court examined the terms of the declarations and concluded that they did not provide a sufficient basis for finding that respect for human rights did not require continuing the examination of the applications. It therefore did not strike them out on that basis.

Two applications, nos. 12424/06 and 23509/08, involved applicants who died during the proceedings. Their next-of-kin expressed the wish to continue. The Court noted that these applications concerned a property right that was in principle transferable to heirs, and it held that the applicants or their next-of-kin had standing to continue the proceedings. Because the applications raised similar principal legal issues, the Court joined them.

On admissibility, the Court found that the complaints concerning lengthy non-enforcement and lack of effective domestic remedies were not manifestly ill-founded within Article 35 § 3(a). They were not inadmissible on any other grounds, so the Court declared them admissible. On the merits, the Court found that the decisions in the applicants’ favour had not been enforced in due time and that the State authorities were responsible. It relied on its well-established case-law, including *Yuriy Nikolayevich Ivanov v. Ukraine*. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore the existence of final and enforceable domestic decisions granting the applicants rights or entitlements, the State’s failure to enforce them promptly, and the absence of effective domestic remedies for that failure.
