In *Filatova and Others v. Ukraine*, the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee) delivered judgment on 31 July 2014 in application no. 12424/06 and 15 other applications. The applicants were Ukrainian nationals and companies based in Ukraine. They complained under Article 34 of the Convention about the lengthy non-enforcement of final domestic court decisions given in their favour. They relied, expressly or in substance, on Article 6 § 1 (fair trial, including execution of judgments), Article 13 (effective remedy), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property).

The key facts were largely undisputed. On dates set out in the appendix, Ukrainian domestic courts issued decisions entitling the applicants to various pecuniary amounts or requiring certain actions to be taken in their favour. These decisions became final and enforceable. However, the applicants could not obtain their enforcement in due time. The State authorities were responsible for the failure to enforce. Some applicants also raised unrelated factual and legal matters, but the principal legal issue was the same across all applications: prolonged non-enforcement of binding domestic judgments and the absence of effective domestic remedies to address that problem.

Procedurally, two applicants—applications nos. 12424/06 and 23509/08—died during the Strasbourg proceedings. Their next-of-kin expressed a wish to continue. The Court held that the applications concerned a property right that was in principle transferable to heirs, so the applicants or their next-of-kin had standing to continue. The Court also joined the applications because of the similarity of the main legal issues.

The Ukrainian Government attempted to resolve the non-enforcement complaints in two applications—nos. 7436/08 and 40893/09—by submitting unilateral declarations in 2011 and asking the Court to strike those applications out under Article 37 § 1 (c). The Court examined the declarations and found they did not provide a sufficient basis for concluding that respect for human rights did not require continued examination. It therefore did not strike out the applications on that basis.

On admissibility, the Court found that the complaints were not manifestly ill-founded within Article 35 § 3 (a) and were not inadmissible on any other grounds. They were declared admissible. On the merits, the Court found that the decisions in the applicants’ favour were not enforced in due time and that the State authorities were responsible. It referred to its well-established case-law on non-enforcement of domestic judgments in Ukraine, particularly *Yuriy Nikolayevich Ivanov v. Ukraine*. The Court’s reasoning indicated that the prolonged failure to enforce final judgments, combined with the lack of effective domestic remedies, gave rise to violations of Article 6 § 1, Article 13, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The critical facts for the alleged violations were that binding domestic court decisions had been issued in the applicants’ favour, that those decisions became final and enforceable, that the applicants failed to obtain timely enforcement, and that the State was responsible for the delay and did not provide effective remedies. In *Grespik v. Hungary* (Application no. 47018/10), the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) delivered judgment on 22 April 2014. The applicant, László Grespik, a Hungarian national born in 1964 and living in Budapest, complained that the length of domestic proceedings concerning his dismissal and related employment disputes violated the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

The relevant facts began in 2002. At the time, the applicant was head of the Budapest Public Administration Authority. On 22 February 2002, he was dismissed from the civil service as a disciplinary measure. In the ensuing labour action, the parties reached a friendly settlement on 22 March 2002: the applicant was reinstated and received damages. However, on the same day, the Prime Minister revoked his mandate to preside over the Authority, and the applicant consequently left the Authority.

This labour dispute generated four sets of proceedings. On 2 May 2002, the applicant brought a labour action claiming that the revocation of his mandate had been unlawful. In parallel, the Authority brought a civil action against him, seeking a declaration that the friendly settlement was invalid and demanding reimbursement of the compensation he had received. The applicant also brought labour proceedings challenging the lawfulness of the disciplinary measure imposed on 22 February 2002 and claiming salary arrears.

The friendly settlement was annulled by a final judgment of the Baranya County Regional Court, sitting as a second-instance court, on 3 November 2005. On 2 February 2010, the same court adopted a final judgment establishing that the revocation of the applicant’s mandate on 22 March 2002 had been unlawful. In the labour action concerning the disciplinary measure, the Zalaegerszeg Labour Court issued an interim judgment on 3 April 2007 in the applicant’s favour, finding the sanction unlawful. As for the applicant’s salary-arrears claim and the Authority’s action for repayment of compensation, the proceedings were apparently still pending before the Kúria and the Budapest Surroundings High Court, respectively.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged that the proceedings had lasted unreasonably long. The Government contested that argument. The Court noted that the period to be considered began on 2 May 2002 and had apparently not yet ended, lasting almost eleven years and eleven months across three levels of jurisdiction. Given that length, the complaint was admissible.

The Court reiterated that reasonableness must be assessed in light of the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicant and the authorities, and what was at stake for the applicant. It emphasised that special diligence is required in employment disputes. Having examined the material, the Court found that the Government had not advanced any fact or convincing argument justifying the delay. It therefore concluded that the length of the proceedings was excessive and failed to satisfy the “reasonable time” requirement, in violation of Article 6 § 1.

Under Article 41, the applicant claimed approximately EUR 16,700 in pecuniary damage and EUR 33,400 in non-pecuniary damage. The Court rejected the pecuniary claim for lack of a causal link to the violation, but awarded EUR 7,000 for non-pecuniary damage. It also awarded EUR 500 for costs and expenses, despite a claim of EUR 3,300, since the applicant was not represented by a lawyer. Default interest was to be calculated using the ECB marginal lending rate plus three percentage points.

In *Margaretić v. Croatia* (Application no. 16115/13, judgment of 5 June 2014), the applicant, Bruno Margaretić, was a Croatian police officer in the Osijek-Baranja Police Department. On 23 March 2012 he was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy and abuse of power and authority. The next day, an investigating judge of the Zagreb County Court ordered his pre-trial detention for two months under Article 123 § 1(2) and (3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, citing risk of collusion and reoffending, or alternatively bail of HRK 700,000. The judge found that further evidence was needed, that the second suspect was still at large, and that the applicant might suborn witnesses or reoffend given his police employment. The State Attorney’s Office appealed the bail decision; on 4 April 2012 a three-judge panel reversed it, holding detention necessary to prevent collusion and reoffending. On 6 April 2012 the applicant’s appeal was dismissed, with the panel relying on the risk that he might coordinate his defence with the second suspect, interfere with evidence, and suborn nine police witnesses.

The applicant’s detention was extended repeatedly. On 23 April 2012 the investigating judge extended it for two months on the ground of risk of collusion only, dropping the reoffending risk because the applicant had been suspended from duty. Further extensions followed, largely justified by the need to question the nine witnesses. The applicant repeatedly argued that the witnesses could have been questioned earlier and that his detention was no longer justified. On 9 October 2012 the investigating judge ordered the State Attorney’s Office to question the nine witnesses within fourteen days, noting that the applicant had been detained for over six months and that the prosecution had repeatedly relied on the need to question those very witnesses. The State Attorney’s Office questioned eight witnesses on 20 October 2012 and the last on 24 October 2012. On the same day, it sought an extension on a new ground: the risk that the applicant might coordinate his defence with the second suspect, who was still at large. Detention was extended on that basis despite the applicant’s objections and requests for less restrictive measures. He was finally released on 21 May 2013, after almost fifteen months, subject to a ban on contacting the second accused and seizure of his travel documents. The criminal proceedings remained pending.

In parallel, on 24 March 2012 the applicant was suspended from duty pending the criminal proceedings. His appeal to the Ministry of the Interior was dismissed on 17 April 2012. He brought an administrative action, but on 18 September 2012 the Osijek Administrative Court held a hearing in the absence of the applicant and his representative, refused an adjournment request, and dismissed his action as ill-founded, considering the adjournment request a delaying tactic.

The case thus concerned alleged violations of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention (length of pre-trial detention and whether the grounds remained relevant and sufficient), Article 5 § 4 (judicial review of detention), and Article 6 § 1 (fairness of the administrative proceedings concerning his suspension). The key facts were the repeated extensions based on risk of collusion, the delay in questioning witnesses, the belated shift to the second-suspect ground, the failure to consider alternative measures, and the administrative court’s refusal to adjourn the hearing.

Bruno Margaretić, a Croatian police officer, was arrested on 23 March 2012 on suspicion of conspiracy and abuse of power. He was placed in pre-trial detention by an investigating judge of the Zagreb County Court for two months under Article 123 § 1(2) and (3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, on grounds of risk of collusion and risk of reoffending, with an alternative option of release on bail of 700,000 Croatian kunas (HRK). The judge cited the need to collect further evidence, prevent coordination with a second suspect still at large, and prevent witness subornation.

On appeal by the State Attorney’s Office, a three-judge panel reversed the bail option on 4 April 2012, finding detention was the only way to prevent collusion and reoffending. The applicant’s own appeal was dismissed on 6 April 2012, with the court citing risks of coordinating his defence with the fugitive second suspect, interfering with evidence, and suborning nine police officer witnesses.

On 23 April 2012, the investigating judge extended detention for two months solely on the ground of risk of collusion, dropping the reoffending risk since the applicant had been suspended from duty. The detention was repeatedly extended throughout 2012 and into 2013 on the basis that the applicant might suborn the nine witnesses—who had not yet been questioned—and later, that he might coordinate his defence with the second suspect, who remained at large.

A critical development occurred on 9 October 2012, when the investigating judge ordered the State Attorney’s Office to question the nine witnesses within fourteen days, noting the applicant had been detained over six months and that the prosecution could have questioned them earlier. The witnesses were subsequently questioned in late October 2012. Following this, the detention rationale shifted back to the risk of collusion with the second suspect.

The applicant’s appeals and constitutional complaints were largely dismissed. Notably, on 25 October 2012, the Constitutional Court declared one complaint inadmissible because a new detention decision had been adopted in the meantime. On 12 April 2013, the Supreme Court quashed a detention extension for failing to consider less severe preventive measures and for setting excessive bail. On 21 May 2013, the Zagreb County Court released the applicant under preventive measures, including seizure of travel documents and a ban on contacting the second accused, after nearly fifteen months in detention.

Parallel disciplinary proceedings led to the applicant’s suspension from duty on 24 March 2012. His challenge was dismissed by the Ministry of the Interior and later by the Osijek Administrative Court, which held a hearing in his absence after refusing an adjournment request.

The case concerns the applicant’s prolonged pre-trial detention, primarily based on the risk of collusion, and the alleged failure of domestic authorities to justify his continued detention and consider alternative measures.

Bruno Margaretić, a Croatian police officer in the Osijek-Baranja Police Department, was arrested on 23 March 2012 on suspicion of conspiracy and abuse of power and authority. The following day, a Zagreb County Court investigating judge ordered his pre-trial detention for two months under Article 123 § 1(2) and (3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, citing risk of collusion and risk of reoffending. The judge alternatively set bail at HRK 700,000, but the State Attorney’s Office successfully appealed, and bail was reversed. The applicant’s own appeal was dismissed on 6 April 2012. The courts found he might coordinate his defence with a second suspect still at large, interfere with evidence, suborn nine police witnesses, and reoffend.

His detention was repeatedly extended. After the applicant was suspended from duty, the reoffending ground was dropped. In July 2012, the investigating judge also stopped relying on coordination with the second suspect because all suspects had given their defences, leaving only the risk that the applicant might suborn nine police witnesses. The applicant repeatedly argued that the witnesses could have been questioned and that detention was no longer justified.

On 9 October 2012, the investigating judge ordered the State Attorney’s Office to question the nine witnesses within fourteen days. She noted that the applicant had already been detained for more than six months and that, throughout that period, the prosecution had repeatedly relied on the need to question those same witnesses, who could clearly have been questioned earlier. The witnesses were eventually questioned on 20 and 24 October 2012. Immediately afterwards, the prosecution sought further extension of detention on the ground that the applicant might coordinate his defence with the second suspect, who was still at large. The applicant argued that the second suspect lived in Serbia and offered to surrender his passport and accept preventive measures. The domestic courts nevertheless continued his detention, finding that, as a police officer, he had many contacts and could easily reach the second suspect, and that preventive measures would not suffice. Bail was at one point set at HRK 1,500,000. The Supreme Court twice quashed extension decisions for lack of reasoning and failure to consider less restrictive measures. On 21 May 2013, the Zagreb County Court released the applicant under measures prohibiting contact with the second suspect and seizing his travel documents; the Supreme Court upheld that decision on 12 June 2013. The criminal proceedings remained pending.

The applicant also lodged constitutional complaints. Some were declared inadmissible because a new detention decision had been adopted, while others were dismissed as ill-founded.

In parallel, on 24 March 2012, the Chief of the Osijek-Baranja Police Department suspended the applicant from duty pending the criminal proceedings. His appeal was dismissed by the Ministry of the Interior on 17 April 2012. He brought an administrative action. On 17 September 2012, his lawyer requested an adjournment of the hearing scheduled for the next day because the applicant was in detention. On 18 September 2012, the Osijek Administrative Court held the hearing in the absence of both the applicant and his representative and dismissed the action as ill-founded, holding that the adjournment request was merely dilatory and that the representative had failed to appear without justification.

The case therefore concerns alleged violations of Article 5 of the Convention regarding the lawfulness and length of the applicant’s pre-trial detention, the relevance and sufficiency of the grounds relied on, and the failure to consider less restrictive measures, as well as an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 concerning the fairness of the administrative proceedings relating to his suspension, particularly his inability to attend the hearing while in detention.
001-147037:
**CASE OF ZALEVSKIY v. UKRAINE**

**Key Facts Relevant to the Alleged Violation**

The applicant, Viktor Zalevskiy, was a Ukrainian national born in 1964 who shared a flat in Vinnytsya with his former wife, S., following their 2001 divorce. Their cohabitation was marked by ongoing disputes, and in December 2005, a local court found the applicant guilty of domestic violence against S. and their son.

The central events occurred on the night of 14-15 February 2006. At approximately 11 p.m., three police officers arrived at the flat after receiving a call about a domestic disturbance. According to the Government, the applicant was shouting and threatening S. with a knife. The applicant refused to open the door, as the officers did not identify themselves and it was late. The police attempted to enter but failed.

At around 2 a.m. on 15 February 2006, two of S.'s brothers arrived and persuaded the applicant to open the door. Once he did, the brothers and three police officers burst into the flat. What happened next is disputed. The applicant alleged that he was immediately beaten, did not resist, and that officers twisted his arms and broke his right arm while handcuffing him. The Government claimed that the applicant tried to close the door, was pushed backwards, fell onto a chair and the floor, and that his arm was unintentionally broken while officers applied force to overcome his resistance during arrest.

After being taken to the police station, the applicant complained of a broken arm and was taken to a hospital. He was diagnosed with a fractured right humerus, neuritis of the radial nerve, crushed soft tissue, and bruises on his wrists and jaw. He underwent surgery and remained hospitalised until 1 March 2006.

The applicant complained to the prosecutor's office on 21 February 2006, alleging ill-treatment by police and S.'s brothers. What followed was a series of refusals to institute criminal proceedings, which were repeatedly quashed by supervising authorities as unfounded or incomplete, and then re-issued. A crucial development occurred on 18 August 2006, when a panel of experts concluded that the arm fracture resulted from a rotary application of force—consistent with arms being twisted behind the back—and could not have been caused by a fall, as the police alleged.

Despite this, on 12 February 2007, the district prosecutor's office again refused to institute proceedings, finding that the force used was lawful and necessary given the applicant's resistance. This decision was upheld by domestic courts, including the Supreme Court in 2008.

**Alleged Violation**

The applicant complained under Article 3 of the Convention that he had been ill-treated during his arrest and that no effective investigation had been carried out. The key factual issues for the Court were: (1) whether the force used by police was excessive and unnecessary, given the medical evidence contradicting the official version of events; and (2) whether the domestic investigation was effective, as evidenced by the repeated quashing of decisions for incompleteness and the failure to properly reconcile the expert findings with the authorities' narrative.

In *Zalevskiy v. Ukraine* (no. 3466/09, ECtHR 16 October 2014), the applicant, a Ukrainian national born in 1964, lived in Vinnytsya. In 1995 he was given a flat by local authorities; he married S. that year, and they had a son in 1997. They divorced in 2001 but continued living in the same flat, with frequent disputes. In December 2005 a court fined the applicant for domestic violence against his son and former wife.

The alleged violation arose from events on 14–15 February 2006. After S. complained, three police officers arrived at the flat around 11 p.m. The applicant refused them entry, allegedly because they did not identify themselves, it was late, and the corridor was dark. The police could not enter. At about 2 a.m. on 15 February, S.’s two brothers arrived, claimed the police had left, and persuaded the applicant to open the door. The applicant alleged that once he opened it, the brothers and three police officers burst in and beat him. He said he did not resist, but police twisted his arms and broke his right arm while handcuffing him; he was also allegedly ill-treated on the way to the police station and there.

The Government’s account differed: it claimed the applicant saw the police, tried to close the door, was pushed backwards, and fell onto a chair and floor; because he resisted arrest, police, assisted by S.’s brothers, used force, and his arm was unintentionally broken during handcuffing. At the police station he complained of arm pain and was taken by ambulance to hospital. He was diagnosed with a fractured right humerus with displacement, radial nerve neuritis, crushed soft tissue, and bruises on both wrists and jaw. He underwent surgery on 16 February and remained in hospital until 1 March 2006.

Separately, S. complained that the applicant had threatened to kill her and their son. Police questioned witnesses and inspected the scene; S. had a bruise on her leg. Initially, criminal proceedings against the applicant were refused after S. withdrew her complaint. Later, in September 2006, a criminal case was instituted against him for threat to kill under Article 129 of the Criminal Code, but it was closed for lack of evidence.

On 21 February 2006 the applicant complained to the prosecutor about ill-treatment by police and S.’s brothers. The prosecutor repeatedly refused to institute criminal proceedings. Those decisions were several times quashed by higher prosecutors or courts as incomplete or unfounded. Medical evidence was important: an August 2006 expert panel found the arm fracture resulted from a rotary force, when the arm was twisted about its axis, consistent with the applicant’s account and not with a direct fall as police claimed. A later expert said wrist bruises could have come from handcuffs; other bruises might have resulted from a fall. In February 2007 the prosecutor again refused proceedings, finding police and the brothers acted lawfully and force was necessary because the applicant was strong and resisted. Courts upheld that decision through 2008.

The applicant lodged his ECtHR application on 19 December 2008, alleging under Article 3 that he had been ill-treated during arrest and that no effective investigation had followed. The Government argued the investigation was effective and force lawful and necessary. The applicant argued it was superficial and that the facts had been wrongly established. The Court declared the complaint admissible and assessed whether the investigation met the required standards of independence, impartiality, thoroughness, promptness, and public scrutiny.

In **Zalevskiy v. Ukraine** (App. no. 3466/09, 16 October 2014), the applicant, a Ukrainian national living in Vinnytsya, alleged that he had been ill-treated during his arrest and that Ukraine had failed to conduct an effective investigation, contrary to Article 3 of the Convention.

The applicant had been allocated a flat in 1995. He married S. that year, and they had a son in 1997. They divorced in 2001 but continued to live in the same flat, leading to frequent domestic disputes. In December 2005, a district court found the applicant guilty of domestic violence against S. and his son and fined him.

The alleged violation arose on 14–15 February 2006. Late on 14 February, police came to the flat after a call reporting that the applicant was shouting and threatening S., allegedly with a knife. The applicant refused to open the door, saying the officers had not identified themselves, it was late, and the corridor light was off. At about 2 a.m., S.’s two brothers arrived and persuaded him to open, saying the police had left. The applicant claimed that once he opened the door, the brothers and three police officers burst in and beat him. He did not resist, but officers twisted his arms and broke his right arm. He also alleged further ill-treatment on the way to and at the police station.

The Government gave a different account. It said the applicant resisted arrest and tried to shut the door; police and S.’s brothers pushed in; he fell onto a chair and the floor; and his arm was unintentionally broken while officers used necessary force to handcuff him. S.’s brothers allegedly helped restrain him.

The applicant was diagnosed with a fractured right humerus with displacement, radial nerve neuritis, crushed soft tissue, and bruises on both wrists and his jaw. He had surgery on 16 February 2006 and stayed in hospital until 1 March 2006. Medical evidence later became important. In August 2006, experts concluded that the fracture resulted from a rotary force, when the arm was twisted around its axis, consistent with the applicant’s account of having his arms twisted behind his back. They said it could not have been caused by direct force, including a fall when the door was pushed open. In September 2006, another expert stated that the wrist bruises could have been caused by handcuffs, while other bruises might have resulted from the fall.

On 21 February 2006, the applicant complained to the prosecutor about ill-treatment by police and S.’s brothers. The prosecutor refused to institute criminal proceedings several times: on 14 March, 6 May, and 26 September 2006, and finally on 12 February 2007. Earlier refusals were quashed as unfounded or incomplete, and further enquiries were ordered. The final refusal found that police and the brothers had acted lawfully, that force was necessary because the applicant resisted, and that the injuries were accidental or caused

**Summary of *Osakovskiy v. Ukraine* (Application no. 13406/06)**

The case of *Osakovskiy v. Ukraine* concerns an application lodged by Mr Sergey Valeryevich Osakovskiy, a Ukrainian national, against Ukraine. The applicant alleged several violations of the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically under Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 5 § 3 (right to trial within a reasonable time or release pending trial). The facts stem from two sets of criminal proceedings.

**First Set of Proceedings (F.'s Murder):**
In June 2004, the applicant was arrested by Leninskiy District police in Kharkiv for the murder and robbery of a cashier, F. The applicant confessed but later retracted, claiming the confession was coerced through ill-treatment, including electric shocks and suffocation with a gas mask. He was initially represented by a legal-aid lawyer, later replaced by a private lawyer in July 2004. On 14 December 2004, the District Court released him against an undertaking not to abscond, citing a lack of evidence that he posed a flight risk. However, on 16 March 2005, the same court remanded him in custody again, stating he might hide from authorities. This detention continued despite appeals. The applicant’s ill-treatment complaints were repeatedly investigated and rejected by the prosecutor’s office between 2004 and 2006. On 18 August 2006, the District Court acquitted the applicant, finding that his initial confession was unreliable due to inadequate legal representation during the investigation. This acquittal was overturned in 2007, and further investigation was ordered. The proceedings were suspended in 2008 and resumed in 2012, remaining pending as of June 2013.

**Second Set of Proceedings (D.'s Murder):**
While in pre-trial detention, the applicant became a suspect in another murder case (D.). In August 2004, the Chuguiv police notified the SIZO. On 25 August 2004, the applicant sustained razor cuts to his left arm. He claimed cellmates beat him and inflicted the cuts to pressure him into confessing to D.'s murder. The SIZO authorities, however, concluded he had self-inflicted the injuries during an anxiety attack. Shortly after, on 21 September 2004, the applicant confessed to killing D. to SIZO authorities. He was indicted but the charges were dropped in October 2004 for lack of evidence. He later complained that he was subjected to unlawful pressure and ill-treatment in the SIZO to extract this false confession. His complaints were repeatedly rejected by the prosecutor’s office, though some decisions were revoked for further inquiry.

**Key Findings by the European Court:**
Regarding the ill-treatment by Leninskiy police, the Court declared the complaint inadmissible, finding no objective evidence and noting the applicant’s detailed account was lacking. However, regarding the ill-treatment in the SIZO, the Court found a violation of Article 3. It held that the Government failed to provide a satisfactory explanation for the applicant's injuries and his subsequent false confession to a murder he did not commit. The authorities' version relied largely on statements from implicated persons and lacked objective evidence. The Court also found a violation of Article 5 § 3 concerning the second period of detention (16 March 2005 to 18 August 2006). It ruled that the domestic courts relied on the gravity of the charges and used formulaic grounds without sufficient justification for keeping him in custody, especially after he had complied with release conditions previously.

**Osakovskiy v. Ukraine** (Application no. 13406/06) concerned a Ukrainian national, Sergey Osakovskiy, who alleged ill-treatment in custody, unreasonable pre-trial detention, lack of judicial review of detention, and excessive length of criminal proceedings. The Strasbourg Court focused on Article 3 and Article 5 § 3.

In August 2003, F., a cashier at a game-machine arcade, was found unconscious with head injuries and later died. On 8 June 2004, the applicant was arrested by Leninskiy District police and allegedly confessed to injuring F. and robbing the arcade. He later claimed the confession was false and had been extracted by electric shocks, suffocation with a gas mask, beatings, and other torture. A legal-aid lawyer was appointed, and the applicant participated in a confrontation, a crime-scene reconstruction, and questioning. On 10 June 2004, he was indicted and remanded in custody. A SIZO medical examination on 11 June 2004 found no bodily injuries. In July 2004, a psychiatric assessment diagnosed a mixed personality disorder but found he could understand and control his actions. After a privately hired lawyer replaced the legal-aid lawyer, the applicant retracted his confession on 31 July 2004, alleging duress. The prosecutor refused to investigate his ill-treatment complaint on 4 August 2004. On 14 December 2004, he complained in court and was released on an undertaking not to abscond. On 16 March 2005, however, the case was remitted for further investigation and he was remanded again on the ground that he might hide. Later release requests were refused, largely citing the gravity of the charges. In September 2005, a forensic examination found an old scar but could not establish June 2004 injuries. In February 2006, the prosecutor again refused to pursue ill-treatment allegations, finding the account inconsistent and improbable. On 18 August 2006, the applicant was acquitted, the court doubting his initial confession and noting procedural breaches. The acquittal was quashed in 2007, and further investigation continued, still pending as of 2013.

Separately, after D. was found strangled in May 2004, the applicant was identified as a suspect while detained in Kharkiv SIZO. On 25 August 2004, he sustained razor cuts to his left arm. The authorities said he self-inflicted them during an anxiety attack; he later alleged that cellmates and wardens beat and pressured him to confess to D.’s murder. On 21 September 2004, he confessed to killing D.; he was indicted and pleaded guilty in October, but the charges were soon dropped and proceedings discontinued for lack of evidence. He complained that ill-treatment in the SIZO had coerced his false confession. Prosecutors repeatedly refused to institute criminal proceedings.

The Court declared the complaint about police ill-treatment inadmissible: there was no objective medical evidence, the applicant was legally represented, and he failed to provide a detailed, coherent account. However, it found a violation of Article 3 regarding SIZO ill-treatment. The Government failed to give a convincing objective explanation for his injuries and false confession to a murder he did not commit; authorities relied on implicated persons and did not conduct an independent medical examination.

Under Article 5 § 3, the Court considered only the second detention period, 16 March 2005 to 18 August 2006. The courts had earlier released him because no risk of absconding was shown, then remanded him again without specific reasons. Subsequent refusals were formulaic and based mainly on the gravity of the charges. The Court found the detention unreasonable, violating Article 5 § 3.

Osakovskiy v. Ukraine (Application no. 13406/06, ECtHR 17 July 2014) concerned a Ukrainian national who faced two criminal investigations. The applicant alleged ill-treatment in custody, unreasonable detention, lack of a procedure to review detention, and excessively lengthy criminal proceedings.

In the first case, F., a cashier at a game-machines arcade, was found unconscious with head injuries in August 2003 and later died. On 8 June 2004 the Leninskiy District police arrested the applicant, who confessed to injuring F. and robbing the arcade. He later claimed the confession was false and had been extracted by ill-treatment, including electric shocks, suffocation in a gas mask, and beatings. A legal-aid lawyer was assigned that day. The applicant participated in witness confrontations and, on 9 June, a crime-scene reconstruction, confirming his statements. On 10 June he was indicted and remanded in custody because of the serious charges and lack of steady employment. A SIZO medical examination on 11 June found no injuries. In July, after a privately hired lawyer replaced the legal-aid lawyer, the applicant retracted his confession, alleged duress, and pleaded innocent. Prosecutors refused to open an inquiry into the ill-treatment complaint. In December 2004 he was released on an undertaking not to abscond, but in March 2005 the case was remitted for further investigation and he was re-remanded because he might abscond. He remained detained until acquitted in August 2006. The acquittal was later quashed, and proceedings remained pending. The ECtHR found the police ill-treatment complaint inadmissible but found a violation of Article 5 §3 because the re-remand and detention from March 2005 to August 2006 rested on the gravity of charges and formulaic reasons, despite his compliance while released.

The second case concerned D., found strangled in a river in May 2004. While the applicant was in Kharkiv SIZO, police identified him as a suspect. On 25 August 2004 his cellmates reported he had self-injured; a medical examination recorded razor cuts to his left arm. The applicant and cellmates said he cut himself during an anxiety attack over divorce and a possible long sentence. The SIZO governor sent records to forensic experts, who classified the injuries as minor and consistent with that account; the governor concluded they were self-inflicted. 001-146047:
**Summary of *Husayn (Abu Zubaydah) v. Poland* (Application no. 7511/13)**

The case of *Husayn (Abu Zubaydah) v. Poland* concerns the alleged complicity of Poland in the CIA’s secret “High-Value Detainees” (HVD) programme and the ill-treatment of the applicant, a stateless Palestinian and alleged senior Al-Qaeda operative, on Polish territory.

The applicant was captured in Pakistan in March 2002 and held in CIA custody in Thailand until December 2002. On 4–5 December 2002, he was transferred to a secret CIA detention facility in Stare Kiejkuty, Poland, where he was held until 22 September 2003. The core of the case revolves around his detention and treatment during this period.

The facts, as established by the Court primarily through evidence from parallel proceedings (*Al Nashiri v. Poland*), international investigations, and witness testimony, indicate that the applicant was subjected to what the CIA termed “Enhanced Interrogation Techniques.” These included prolonged sleep deprivation, dietary manipulation, stress positions, and waterboarding. The applicant was held incommunicado, with no access to the outside world, legal counsel, or any judicial authority. He alleges that during his detention in Poland, he was subjected to these techniques, constituting torture and inhuman and degrading treatment.

Key to Poland’s alleged violation is its knowledge and facilitation of the operation. The Court examined evidence that Polish authorities, including the intelligence services and military, provided logistical support for the transfer and detention. This included securing the remote facility at Stare Kiejkuty, granting the CIA a free hand, and ensuring the operation remained secret. Flight logs and other evidence placed the CIA aircraft at the Szymany airport near the facility. The applicant’s stay in Poland was part of a wider renditions network, and his subsequent transfer to other secret facilities, and eventually to Guantánamo Bay in 2006, followed the same pattern.

The case also details the aftermath, highlighting Poland’s failure to conduct an effective investigation into these allegations. The Polish criminal investigation was marked by delays, lack of cooperation with international bodies, and was ultimately discontinued. The government consistently refused to disclose key information, citing state secrecy.

The applicant alleged violations of several Articles of the European Convention on Human Rights, including:
- **Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment):** For the ill-treatment he suffered in Poland.
- **Article 5 (right to liberty and security):** For his unlawful and incommunicado detention.
- **Article 8 (right to respect for private life):** For the lack of any legal basis for his detention and the secrecy surrounding it.
- **Article 13 (right to an effective remedy):** Due to Poland’s failure to conduct a thorough and effective investigation into his credible allegations of serious human rights violations.
- **Article 6 (right to a fair trial):** For the impossibility of challenging the lawfulness of his detention.

In its judgment, the Court found that Poland had violated the applicant’s rights under Articles 3, 5, 8, and 13 of the Convention. It held that Poland had failed to prevent the applicant’s torture and ill-treatment, and had failed to conduct a proper investigation, thereby acting in violation of its obligations under the Convention. The case is a landmark ruling on state responsibility for complicity in extraterritorial human rights abuses committed in the context of counter-terrorism operations.

In *Husayn (Abu Zubaydah) v. Poland* (App. No. 7511/13, 24 July 2014), the European Court of Human Rights examined Poland’s alleged complicity in the CIA’s High-Value Detainee (HVD) Programme. After the 11 September 2001 attacks, the CIA established a secret detention and interrogation programme for suspected terrorists. Detainees were held in black sites, subjected to “enhanced interrogation techniques” authorized by the US Department of Justice, and denied access to courts, family, or the ICRC. The applicant, Zayn al-Abidin Muhammad Husayn (Abu Zubaydah), a stateless Palestinian, was captured in Faisalabad, Pakistan, on 27 March 2002. He was first held in Thailand, where he was subjected to waterboarding and other techniques, and then transferred to Poland on 4/5 December 2002 by a CIA-chartered flight that landed at Szymany airport. Polish border guards and airport officials were aware of the flight. He was detained at a secret CIA facility in Stare Kiejkuty, near Szymany, until 22 September 2003.

The facility was a former military intelligence training base. The applicant was held in a cell with no natural light, under constant surveillance, and was subjected to 24-hour interrogations. During his detention in Poland, he was held incommunicado and subjected to ill-treatment, including walling, stress positions, sleep deprivation, prolonged nudity, dietary manipulation, and confinement in small boxes. These acts caused severe physical and psychological suffering and amounted to torture. The Polish authorities allegedly facilitated the CIA’s activities by allowing flights through Szymany airport, providing logistics, and permitting the use of the Stare Kiejkuty facility. Although he was never formally in Polish custody, the Court found Poland had jurisdiction because its authorities knew of the CIA’s activities and failed to prevent them. After Poland, he was transferred to other CIA black sites and ultimately to Guantánamo Bay in September 2006.

Poland’s investigation into the CIA black site began in 2008 but was repeatedly delayed and hampered by secrecy. It was extended but failed to produce meaningful results. The Polish Government denied that the applicant had been detained in Poland and refused to cooperate fully with the Strasbourg Court, withholding key documents and invoking state secrecy. The Court found this failure violated Article 38 of the Convention. International inquiries, including the Council of Europe’s Marty Report and European Parliament investigations, had identified Poland as a likely host of a CIA black site, increasing pressure on Polish authorities. The applicant complained under Articles 3, 8, 13, and 38. The Court held that Poland had violated Article 3 both substantively, by failing to comply with its positive obligation to prevent torture and inhuman treatment, and procedurally, by failing to conduct an effective investigation. It also found violations of Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) due to the secret detention and isolation, and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy). The case established that states can be held responsible for enabling CIA secret detentions and torture on their territory, even without formal custody, and that failure to investigate such acts breaches the Convention.

In *Husayn (Abu Zubaydah) v. Poland* (Application no. 7511/13), the European Court of Human Rights delivered judgment on 24 July 2014. The applicant, Zayn al-Abidin Muhammad Husayn, known as Abu Zubaydah, was a stateless Palestinian suspected of terrorist links. He was captured in Pakistan in March 2002 and placed in the CIA’s secret “High-Value Detainee” programme. After initial detention in Thailand, he was transferred to Poland on 4–5 December 2002 and held in a CIA “black site” at Stare Kiejkuty until 22 September 2003. During this period, he was held incommunicado, without access to family, lawyers, the Red Cross, or any court. He alleged that he was subjected to enhanced interrogation techniques amounting to torture and inhuman or degrading treatment, including waterboarding, sleep deprivation, stress positions, prolonged isolation, threats, and confinement in a small box.

The case concerned Poland’s role in facilitating and enabling this secret detention and ill-treatment. Evidence before the Court included flight logs, testimony, and international reports indicating CIA aircraft movements and the existence of the Stare Kiejkuty facility. The Court found that Polish authorities knew or should have known that the CIA was operating a secret detention site on Polish territory and that the applicant faced a real risk of torture. Poland provided logistics, security, and other support, allowed the detention and transfers to occur, and failed to prevent the ill-treatment or to intervene. After leaving Poland, the applicant was transferred to other CIA sites and eventually to Guantánamo Bay in September 2006.

The alleged violations arose under the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant complained that Poland had subjected him to torture and inhuman or degrading treatment (Article 3); unlawfully deprived him of liberty (Article 5); violated his right to respect for private and family life through incommunicado detention and isolation (Article 8); and failed to provide an effective remedy (Article 13). He also alleged that Poland failed to conduct an effective investigation into credible allegations of serious human rights violations on its territory, contrary to the procedural obligation under Article 3. A further key issue was Poland’s failure to cooperate with the Court: despite requests, the Government withheld relevant information and documentary evidence, including classified materials and records concerning the CIA facility. This gave rise to a complaint under Article 38 of the Convention, which requires States to furnish necessary facilities for the effective examination of a case. The Polish parliamentary inquiry and criminal investigation were also criticised as limited by secrecy and ineffective in establishing responsibility.

The Court concluded that Poland had violated Article 3 both substantively, by enabling and failing to prevent the applicant’s torture and inhuman treatment, and procedurally, by failing to carry out an effective investigation. It also found violations of Article 5, Article 8, Article 13, and Article 38. The judgment established that a State cannot escape responsibility by allowing a foreign intelligence agency to operate secret detention and torture on its territory, and that it must investigate credible allegations and cooperate fully with the Court.

Estonia** (App. no. 66393/10, ECtHR, 13 February 2014) concerned an Estonian life prisoner, Andrei Tali, who alleged that prison officers ill-treated him on 3 and 4 July 2009, violating Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant had a lengthy criminal record, including murder convictions and earlier attacks on prison officers, and was assessed as a dangerous and aggressive prisoner.

On **3 July 2009**, the applicant was told he would be transferred to a punishment cell. He refused, claiming a pending complaint before the Chancellor of Justice, and warned that he would resist unlawful force. Guards went to his cell with a shield, flak jackets and helmets. The applicant alleged that they pressed a shield into his chest, twisted his arms, forced him down, kicked his ribs, pressed his neck, covered his mouth and nose, and poked his eyes. The guards claimed the applicant attacked them and that one guard suffered minor injuries; they denied kicking or strangling him. Medical evidence noted possible crepitation near the seventh left rib, but an X-ray showed no clear fracture. Domestic criminal proceedings were discontinued after the prosecutor found the force lawful and proportionate. Administrative courts initially found some measures unlawful, but the Court of Appeal reversed that finding and the Supreme Court declined review. The ECtHR rejected this part of the application as manifestly ill-founded, finding the force used on 3 July did not exceed what was necessary in the circumstances.

The main alleged violation concerned **4 July 2009**. Guards came to take back a mattress from the applicant’s punishment cell. The applicant said nurses had certified that he needed it; the prison maintained he had not been authorised to keep it. After he refused and allegedly threatened officers, six guards arrived. According to the Government, the applicant pushed guard AR, so VG used pepper spray. According to the applicant, VG sprayed him without warning; he ran into the corridor, was forced to the floor, handcuffed, and then VG struck him several times with a telescopic baton. He was later strapped to a restraint bed from 8:40 a.m. to 12:20 p.m.

Medical evidence recorded stripe-shaped haematomas on his back, haematomas on his arm and shin, a swollen wrist, crepitation around ribs 8–9, and blood in his urine. A forensic expert considered the back haematomas likely resulted from baton blows, possibly on 4 July. Witness statements differed on whether the baton blows occurred before or after handcuffing. Domestic authorities discontinued criminal proceedings, finding the force lawful because of the applicant’s resistance and threats. The ECtHR declared the 4 July complaint admissible and found a violation of Article 3. It emphasised that force against detainees must be strictly necessary and not excessive, and that authorities must provide satisfactory explanations for injuries occurring under their control. The Court concluded that the force used on 4 July—including pepper spray, baton blows and the restraint bed—was excessive or insufficiently justified, particularly given the applicant’s restrained state and the inconsistent explanations for his injuries.
