In *Tali v. Estonia*, the applicant, Andrei Tali, an Estonian national serving a life sentence for murder and attempted manslaughter, complained under Article 3 of the Convention that prison officers ill-treated him on 3 and 4 July 2009. He had a long record of criminal convictions, including attacks on prison officers and prisoners, numerous disciplinary punishments, and was assessed in prison as dangerous and lacking self-control.

On 3 July 2009, guards informed Tali that he would be transferred to a punishment cell. He objected, saying he would resist if unlawfully attacked. Three officers, equipped with a shield, flak jackets and helmets, went to his cell. Tali alleged that they pressed a shield into his chest, twisted his arms, forced him to the floor, compressed his neck, covered his mouth, poked his eyes and kicked his ribs; he was then handcuffed and taken to the punishment cell. The guards claimed Tali attempted to hit them and struggled, causing minor injury to one officer, but denied kicking or strangling him. Medical evidence showed no visible injuries, but crepitation near the left seventh rib; a fracture was suspected but not confirmed by X-ray. The European Court of Human Rights rejected this part as manifestly ill-founded, finding the force did not exceed what was necessary given Tali’s threats and resistance.

The central admissible events occurred on 4 July 2009. Tali had a mattress in the punishment cell. Guards sought to remove it, claiming medical staff had not authorised its continuous use; Tali said a nurse had certified he needed it because of a suspected broken rib. Six guards came to his cell. Guard AR grabbed Tali’s hand to take the mattress; Tali pulled away. Guard VG then pepper-sprayed Tali’s face. Tali ran into the corridor, where several guards forced him to the floor. He was handcuffed, and VG struck him three times with a telescopic baton. Tali alleged he was beaten after being handcuffed, could not breathe, and fainted. The guards alleged he pushed AR, resisted, struggled, and threatened to kill them; VG said the baton was used to overcome resistance. Witness accounts differed on whether the baton blows came before or after handcuffing.

Medical evidence recorded stripe-shaped haematomas on Tali’s back, haematomas on his right upper arm and shin, swelling of the left wrist, crepitation of the eighth and ninth ribs, and blood in his urine. X-ray showed no clear traumatic changes. A forensic expert considered the stripe haematomas likely resulted from baton blows on 4 July, and other injuries from blunt force; a rib fracture was possible but unconfirmed. Tali was then strapped to a restraint bed from 8:40 a.m. to 12:20 p.m., monitored hourly, recorded as aggressive and then calm.

Domestic criminal proceedings were discontinued: prosecutors and courts found the guards’ use of force, pepper spray, handcuffs, baton and restraint bed lawful and proportionate because Tali disobeyed orders, threatened officers and resisted. An administrative court initially found the restraint and special equipment unlawful but denied compensation; the Court of Appeal reversed, finding the measures lawful.

The ECtHR declared the 4 July complaint admissible and ultimately found a violation of Article 3. It held that the force used on 4 July—particularly pepper spray in a confined space and baton blows—was excessive and disproportionate in the circumstances, even accounting for Tali’s behaviour and dangerous history. The 3 July complaint was rejected.
001-141434:
Ruiz Rivera v. Switzerland (no. 8300/06) concerned a Peruvian national, Carlos Humberto Ruiz Rivera, who in 1995 killed his wife in Zurich. The applicant had stabbed her 49 times, cut off her head, and thrown it from a window. Toxicological evidence showed he acted under the influence of alcohol and cocaine. A 1995 psychiatric report diagnosed chronic paranoid schizophrenia and drug addiction, found the offence directly related to his illness and drug abuse, and concluded he lacked criminal responsibility. In 1996 the Zurich District Court found he had killed his wife but was fully not criminally responsible and ordered his confinement under the Criminal Code. He was held at Pöschwies Prison from August 1996.

His discharge was repeatedly refused (1997, 1998, 1999, 2000, 2002, 2003). A second psychiatric report in June 2001 confirmed chronic paranoid schizophrenia. It noted that the positive symptoms were less visible in the “not very stimulating” prison setting but that he retained delusional interpretations of the offence. It found no basis for alternative measures or discharge on probation. In March 2004, two psychologists from the Judicial Enforcements Office’s Psychiatry and Psychology Service, one of whom had treated him, issued an annual therapy report. They confirmed the 2001 conclusions, reported an unfavourable prognosis, and noted that he denied being ill and refused prescribed neuroleptic treatment.

On 24 June 2004, after interviewing the applicant, the Judicial Enforcements Office refused discharge on probation, relying on the 2004 therapy report and the 2001 psychiatric assessment. The applicant, assisted by counsel, appealed and requested a fresh neutral psychiatric assessment, an oral hearing, and legal aid. The Directorate of Justice and Internal Affairs denied legal aid in September 2004 because his appeal seemed hopeless. The Administrative Court dismissed his appeal in January 2005, holding that the 2001 expert report was still valid, that no expert hearing was necessary, and that legal aid had been properly refused. The Federal Court dismissed his further appeal in October 2005. It found no fresh assessment was required, rejected his public-hearing complaint as not formally raised, and denied legal aid because the appeal had no prospects; it also noted that Article 5 § 4 review intervals can be longer for persons of unsound mind.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Article 5 § 4 and Article 13. He complained that the procedure refusing discharge lacked a fresh psychiatric assessment, despite the 2001 report being outdated; that the 2004 therapy report was not an objective independent assessment; and that he was denied a hearing, cross-examination of the 2001 expert, and legal aid.

The Court treated Article 5 § 4 as lex specialis and did not examine Article 13 separately. It found a violation of Article 5 § 4. Under the Winterwerp principles, continued confinement of a person of unsound mind requires reliable and sufficiently recent medical expertise. The 2001 psychiatric assessment was more than three years old when the 2004 refusal was taken and over three and a half years old when the Administrative Court ruled. The 2004 therapy report was not an independent psychiatric assessment: it was prepared by institutional psychologists, one treating the applicant. Given the deadlock and breakdown of trust reflected in his refusal of treatment, the authorities should at least have sought an external medical expert. Without that, they lacked sufficient information to justify refusing discharge. Thus the refusal to order a fresh assessment breached Article 5 § 4.

In *Ruiz Rivera v. Switzerland* (ECtHR, 18 February 2014), the applicant, a Peruvian national living in Zurich, was confined after killing his wife in 1995. He stabbed her 49 times, cut off her head, and was under the influence of alcohol and cocaine. A 1995 psychiatric report diagnosed chronic paranoid schizophrenia and drug addiction, linked the offence to his illness, found him totally lacking criminal responsibility, and recommended confinement because of serious danger to public safety. In 1996 the Zurich District Court found that he had killed his wife but was not criminally responsible and ordered his confinement under Article 43 of the Criminal Code. He was held from August 1996 at Pöschwies Prison, and his discharge was refused repeatedly between 1997 and 2003.

In 2001, external psychiatrists at the Rheinau Cantonal Psychiatric Clinic issued a second assessment. They confirmed chronic paranoid schizophrenia, found that positive symptoms had become less noticeable in prison but that he still held delusional interpretations of the offence, and concluded that little had changed since 1995. In March 2004, two psychologists from the Judicial Enforcements Office—one of whom had treated him—issued an annual therapy report confirming the 2001 findings, noting an unfavourable prognosis, his denial of illness, and his refusal to take prescribed neuroleptic treatment. In June 2004 the Judicial Enforcements Office refused discharge, relying on the prison report, the 2004 therapy report, and the 2001 assessment. The applicant appealed, requesting a fresh psychiatric assessment, a hearing, and legal aid. Legal aid was denied because his appeal appeared hopeless. The Administrative Court dismissed his appeal in January 2005, finding the 2001 report still valid and no need for the expert to testify. The Federal Court dismissed his further appeal in October 2005, holding that a fresh assessment was unnecessary because later therapy reports confirmed the diagnosis and no change had occurred. It also found his public-hearing complaint inadmissible for lack of a formal request, and upheld the denial of legal aid because Article 5 § 4 scrutiny is required only at reasonable intervals, which may be longer for mentally ill detainees.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Article 5 § 4 and Article 13. He complained specifically that the authorities refused to order a fresh psychiatric assessment even though the 2001 report was outdated; that they refused a hearing where he could present observations orally and question the 2001 expert; and that denial of legal aid impaired his access to court. The Government argued that no systematic requirement existed for a recent independent expert opinion, that the therapy report was objective, that the applicant had been heard by the Office, and that no proper hearing request had been made.

The Court treated Article 5 § 4 as the relevant provision. It reiterated that confinement of a person of unsound mind requires reliable proof of a mental disorder warranting confinement and that the disorder persists; a deprivation of liberty cannot comply with Article 5 without a sufficiently recent medical expert opinion. The 2004 therapy report was not an independent psychiatric assessment. The 2001 assessment was more than three years old when discharge was refused and nearly three years and seven months old when the Administrative Court ruled. Although older opinions may sometimes suffice if confirmed by institutional psychologists, here the applicant’s refusal of therapy was explained by a breakdown of trust and a deadlock. The authorities should at least have sought an external expert opinion. They therefore lacked sufficient information to establish that discharge conditions were unmet. The Court found a violation of Article 5 § 4 due to the refusal to order a fresh assessment, and did not examine Article 13 separately.

**Case: Ruiz Rivera v. Switzerland (Application no. 8300/06), ECtHR, 18 February 2014**

The applicant, Carlos Humberto Ruiz Rivera, a Peruvian national living in Zurich, was involved in criminal proceedings after his wife was found dead in April 1995. According to toxicological examinations, he was under the influence of alcohol and cocaine at the time. He had stabbed his wife 49 times, cut off her head, and thrown it out of a window. A 1995 psychiatric report by Dr. R. diagnosed chronic paranoid schizophrenia and drug addiction, found the offence directly related to his illness and drug abuse, and concluded that he had not been criminally responsible. Because he represented a serious danger to public safety, the psychiatrist recommended confinement.

In May 1996, the District Court of Zurich found that the applicant had killed his wife but had been totally lacking in criminal responsibility. It ordered his confinement under Article 43 of the Criminal Code. He was placed at Pöschwies Prison from August 1996. His discharge was refused repeatedly in 1997, 1998, 1999, and 2000. A second psychiatric assessment in June 2001 again diagnosed chronic paranoid schizophrenia. It noted that the positive symptoms had become less noticeable in the “not very stimulating” prison atmosphere, but that he still displayed delusional interpretations of his offence. Because he received no treatment, the experts saw no basis for alternative arrangements or discharge on probation. Further discharge requests were refused in 2002 and 2003.

The relevant alleged violations arose from the 2004 refusal to discharge him. On 23 March 2004, two psychologists from the Psychiatry and Psychology Service of the Judicial Enforcements Office—one of whom had treated the applicant—issued a therapy report. It confirmed the 2001 findings, described an unfavourable legal prognosis, and noted that the applicant denied being ill and refused prescribed neuroleptic treatment. On 24 June 2004, the Judicial Enforcements Office refused discharge on probation, relying on the prison administration report, the 2004 therapy report, and the 2001 psychiatric assessment.

The applicant appealed, arguing that a fresh expert assessment by a neutral doctor was necessary. He also sought legal aid, a hearing, and an opportunity to question the author of the 2001 report. Legal aid was denied because his appeal appeared devoid of prospects. The Administrative Court dismissed his appeal in January 2005, finding the 2001 report still valid and no need for the expert to testify. The Federal Court dismissed his further appeal in October 2005. It held that a fresh psychiatric assessment was unnecessary because the diagnosis had been confirmed by later therapy reports and no change could be identified. It also found the complaint about the lack of a public hearing inadmissible because no formal request had been made, and upheld the denial of legal aid.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Article 5 § 4 and Article 13 of the Convention. He complained that the procedure refusing his discharge lacked a fresh psychiatric assessment, a hearing where he could make oral submissions, and the possibility of cross-examining the 2001 expert. He also complained about the refusal of legal aid. The Court treated Article 5 § 4 as the relevant provision, as a lex specialis in relation to Article 13.

The Court recalled the Winterwerp principles: a person cannot be confined as of unsound mind unless reliably shown to be of unsound mind, the disorder must warrant confinement, and continued confinement depends on persistence of the disorder. Continued detention must be based on a sufficiently recent medical expert opinion. The 2004 therapy report was not an independent psychiatric assessment; it merely confirmed the 2001 assessment, which was over three years old when the 2004 and 2005 decisions were taken. Given the applicant’s refusal of therapy and the breakdown in trust, authorities should at least have sought an external medical expert. The Court thus found a violation of Article 5 § 4 due to the refusal to order a fresh assessment of the applicant’s mental health.
001-140769:
Cēsnieks v. Latvia (Application no. 9278/06) concerned a Latvian national, Valters Cēsnieks, who complained that he was ill-treated by police in March 2002 and that evidence obtained through that ill-treatment was later used to convict him. The European Court of Human Rights initially examined complaints under Article 3 (prohibition of ill-treatment), Article 13 (effective remedy), and Article 6 § 1 (fair trial). In 2012, after the Latvian Government made a unilateral declaration acknowledging ill-treatment and a lack of effective investigation, the Court struck out the Article 3 and 13 complaints. The remaining issue was whether the criminal proceedings were fair under Article 6 § 1 because the applicant’s allegedly coerced statements were admitted at trial.

Key facts: On 21 March 2002 police telephoned Cēsnieks and asked him to come to the State Police station in connection with the murder of Ģ.Č. He alleged that, before any formal charges were laid, officers accused him of the murder and used physical force to obtain a confession. He claimed he was beaten and his nose was broken. He made a written confession. On 22 March he wrote another confession and was questioned as a suspect, without a lawyer, confirming and expanding his statements. He was taken into custody on 21 March at 8 p.m. but remained at the Riga police station until 1 a.m. on 23 March, when he was transferred to a short-term detention facility. Expert reports later confirmed bodily injuries while in custody.

At first instance, the Riga Regional Court found that Article 3 had been violated regardless of the terminated criminal case against police officers. It noted the unexplained detention at the police station and the medical evidence of injuries. It found the applicant’s 22 March statements contradictory and excluded them from use in his conviction. It acquitted him, finding no other evidence that he had organised, assisted, or incited the murder.

On appeal, the Supreme Court of Latvia overturned the acquittal on 26 April 2005 and convicted Cēsnieks of aggravated murder. It admitted the 22 March 2002 confession and statements and relied on them. It reasoned that there was no impartial evidence that the statements resulted from ill-treatment, that the case against police officers had been terminated, and that an expert report found no indication the confession was written under anxiety, fear, or ill-treatment. He was sentenced to eleven years’ imprisonment.

The applicant’s appeal on points of law argued that the conviction violated Articles 3 and 6 because the pre-trial confession had been coerced. On 26 August 2005 the Senate of the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal without a hearing, holding that re-evaluation of evidence was outside its competence and that the Convention argument was formal.

Before the ECtHR, the key question was whether the domestic courts, especially the Supreme Court, properly examined the ill-treatment allegation before admitting the confession. The Government had already acknowledged ill-treatment and ineffective investigation. The ECtHR ultimately found a violation of Article 6 § 1. The case illustrates that statements obtained through ill-treatment must be excluded and that courts must effectively examine such allegations rather than relying on them.

In *Cēsnieks v. Latvia* (Application no. 9278/06, judgment of 11 February 2014), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by Valters Cēsnieks that Latvian police ill-treated him to obtain a confession, that there was no effective investigation, and that the confession was used to convict him, allegedly violating Articles 3, 13, and 6 § 1 of the Convention. The Article 3 and 13 complaints were later struck out after the Government made a unilateral declaration acknowledging that the applicant had been ill-treated in police custody and that there had been no effective investigation. The Court therefore examined the remaining complaint under Article 6 § 1 concerning the fairness of the criminal proceedings.

The key facts were as follows. On 21 March 2002 the State Police telephoned the applicant and asked him to come to the police station. Before any formal charges were laid, police officers accused him of murdering Ģ.Č. The applicant alleged that officers used physical force to make him confess. He was taken into custody at 8 p.m. on 21 March but was not transferred to a detention facility until 1 a.m. on 23 March, remaining at the Riga police station in the meantime. Expert reports later confirmed that he had suffered bodily injuries while in custody.

On 22 March 2002 the applicant wrote a confession stating that he had financial difficulties and had asked his acquaintance O.O. to kill Ģ.Č. during a trip to Moscow. In later questioning as a suspect, he confirmed and expanded on that confession, saying he had sought the killing to obtain money. The transcripts recorded that he wished to give statements without a lawyer. At trial, however, he retracted the statements, claiming they had been given after police beat him and broke his nose.

On 23 May 2002 the police opened an investigation into the alleged misconduct of police officers. On 25 June 2005 a prosecutor concluded that the complaint was no longer subject to review, referring to the Supreme Court’s judgment of 26 April 2005, which had dismissed the ill-treatment allegation.

The first-instance Riga Regional Court acquitted the applicant on 11 October 2004. It found his account of ill-treatment credible, noting the unexplained detention at the police station after he had been questioned as a witness and the expert reports confirming injuries. It found that Article 3 had been violated, excluded the 22 March 2002 statements from use in conviction, and held that there was no other evidence that the applicant had organised, assisted, or incited the murder.

On appeal, the Supreme Court reversed the acquittal on 26 April 2005. It held that the Regional Court had groundlessly rejected the confession and the expert report. It found no impartial evidence supporting the ill-treatment claim, noted that the criminal case against the police officers had been terminated, and relied on an expert report finding no signs that the confession had been written under anxiety, fear, or ill-treatment. It admitted the 22 March 2002 statement into evidence and convicted the applicant of aggravated murder, sentencing him to eleven years’ imprisonment.

The defence appealed on points of law, arguing that the conviction violated Articles 3 and 6 because it rested on statements obtained through ill-treatment, that the injuries remained unexplained, and that there was no other evidence of guilt. On 26 August 2005 the Senate of the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal without a hearing, stating that it could not re-evaluate evidence and that the Convention argument was merely formal.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 6 § 1. It held that once an applicant raises an arguable complaint of ill-treatment, the authorities must ensure that statements allegedly obtained through such treatment are not used in criminal proceedings. The domestic courts had admitted and relied on the confession despite credible evidence of ill-treatment and without adequately examining its voluntariness. The trial was therefore unfair.

Case Cēsnieks v. Latvia (Application no. 9278/06, ECtHR, 11 February 2014) concerns Valters Cēsnieks, a Latvian national. He alleged that on 21 March 2002, after State Police asked him to attend their station, officers ill-treated him before any formal charge to force him to confess to the murder of Ģ.Č. He claimed officers beat him and broke his nose, and that as a result he made a written confession on 22 March 2002. He was transferred to a short-term detention facility on 23 March. On 23 May 2002 the police opened an investigation into the officers’ alleged misconduct, but in June 2005 a prosecutor ended the review, citing the Supreme Court’s judgment of 26 April 2005, which dismissed the ill-treatment allegation.

At trial before the Riga Regional Court with co-accused O.O., V.Z. and J.G., the applicant pleaded not guilty and retracted his pre-trial statements, saying they were given under ill-treatment. On 11 October 2004 the Regional Court acquitted the applicant and O.O.; V.Z. and J.G. were convicted of aggravated murder. The Regional Court found an Article 3 violation as regards the applicant. It noted he had been questioned as a witness on 21 March from 5.20 p.m. to 6.40 p.m., taken into custody at 8 p.m., but not transferred to a detention facility until 1 a.m. on 23 March, remaining at the Riga police station. Police witnesses could not explain why he had not been released. Expert reports confirmed bodily injuries suffered in custody. The court found his 22 March statements contradictory, rejected an expert report concluding no signs of anxiety, fear or ill-treatment because it lacked a study section, and ruled that the 22 March statements could not be used to convict him. It found no other evidence that he had organised, assisted or incited the murder.

On appeals by the prosecution, victim and co-accused, the Supreme Court on 26 April 2005 overturned the acquittal, convicted the applicant of aggravated murder and sentenced him to eleven years’ imprisonment. The Supreme Court held that the Regional Court had groundlessly rejected the confession. It said the file contained no impartial evidence that the statements resulted from physical or psychological ill-treatment or were dictated by police; the criminal case against the police had been terminated and the defence had not disputed that decision; and the expert report properly found the confession was written in the applicant’s free style and showed no signs of coercion. The Supreme Court admitted the 22 March 2002 statement in evidence and relied on it. The defence’s appeal on points of law argued that the conviction violated Articles 3 and 6 because the confession and statements were obtained through ill-treatment and no other evidence supported guilt. On 26 August 2005 the Senate of the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal without a hearing, stating that it sought re-evaluation of evidence and was outside cassation competence.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged ill-treatment contrary to Article 3, an ineffective investigation contrary to Article 13, and use at trial of evidence obtained in violation of Article 3, contrary to Article 6 § 1. On 6 March 2012, after the Government submitted a unilateral declaration acknowledging ill-treatment and lack of effective investigation, the Court struck out the Article 3 and Article 13 complaints. The remaining Article 6 § 1 complaint concerned whether reliance on the allegedly coerced confession and statements rendered the criminal proceedings unfair.
001-142515:
Duško Ivanovski v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (Application no. 10718/05) concerned a Macedonian national’s complaint that his criminal conviction for drug trafficking violated his right to a fair trial. He alleged that the domestic courts relied on unlawfully obtained evidence and denied him the opportunity to examine defence witnesses and obtain alternative expert evidence. The application was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 18 March 2005.

On 4 February 2003, police apprehended and personally searched Ivanovski in Skopje without a court warrant and without witnesses. They seized 13 keys and a mobile phone. The same day, an investigating judge issued two search warrants for two apartments and other premises owned by Ivanovski’s father, based on suspicion of drug trafficking. During searches attended by his father and two neighbours, seven packages were found. The record for one apartment stated that the packages had been found in cellar no. 10, which belonged to another apartment and was opened with a key seized from Ivanovski. Ivanovski was not present when the cellar was searched; he was brought there later and signed a confiscation certificate. Expert examinations by the Criminal Investigations Bureau of the Ministry of the Interior concluded that the padlock was damaged and could be opened with any object, including the seized keys; that five packages contained 2.296 kg of heroin; and that a fingerprint on one package matched Ivanovski’s right middle finger.

Ivanovski was charged with drug trafficking. At trial, he denied any connection with the drugs and said cellar no. 10 belonged to a third party. He claimed that police had forced him to touch the packages so they could photograph him and obtain his fingerprints, and that he had been physically ill-treated. His father testified that police opened cellar no. 10, found the packages in a ventilation shaft, brought Ivanovski, and pushed him against a metal sheet, causing him to touch the packages. He also said police forced him to sign a search record. On 20 March 2003, the trial court convicted Ivanovski and sentenced him to two and a half years’ imprisonment, relying on the search records, confiscation certificate, expert reports, and fingerprint evidence. It rejected the father’s account as biased.

On appeal, Ivanovski argued that the conviction was based on inadmissible evidence because cellar no. 10 had been searched without a court warrant and because the expert examinations had been carried out by the Bureau, a body within the Ministry of the Interior that had initiated the criminal proceedings. He claimed this made the expert evidence biased. He also sought alternative expert examinations of the fingerprint and the drugs and requested that the police officers, experts, and neighbour witnesses be examined. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal on 20 May 2004, finding the searches and expert evidence lawful and the witnesses unnecessary because they had signed the records. The Supreme Court dismissed his extraordinary review request on 2 November 2004.

The key alleged violations were therefore: use of unlawfully obtained evidence, particularly from the warrantless personal search and the cellar search; reliance on allegedly biased expert reports from a police-body bureau; refusal to allow alternative expert examinations; and refusal to examine witnesses—police officers, experts, and neighbours—whom the defence needed to challenge the fingerprint and search evidence.

In *Duško Ivanovski v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia*, the applicant, a Macedonian national born in 1971, was convicted of drug trafficking and sentenced to two and a half years’ imprisonment. He complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the criminal proceedings against him were unfair, alleging that the domestic courts relied on unlawfully obtained evidence, denied him the opportunity to examine witnesses in his defence, and refused alternative expert evidence.

The events began on 4 February 2003, when police apprehended and personally searched the applicant in Skopje. The personal search was carried out without a court warrant and without witnesses, under statutory provisions permitting such a search on reasonable suspicion. Police seized 13 keys and a mobile phone. The same day, an investigating judge issued search warrants for two apartments and other premises owned by the applicant’s father, based on suspicion of drug trafficking. During the searches, conducted in the presence of the applicant’s father and two neighbours as witnesses, seven packages were found. The record for apartment no. 9 noted that the packages had been found in the cellar belonging to apartment no. 10, which was opened with a key confiscated during the applicant’s personal search. The applicant was not present during the cellar search; he was brought later and signed the confiscation certificate.

Police expert reports concluded that the padlock was damaged and could be opened with any key, including those confiscated from the applicant; that five packages contained 2.296 kg of heroin and two contained substances commonly mixed with heroin; and that a fingerprint on one package matched the applicant’s right middle finger. The Ministry of the Interior filed a criminal complaint. At trial, the applicant denied any connection with the drugs. He claimed the cellar belonged to a third party and that police forced him to touch the packages so they could photograph him and later beat him to obtain his fingerprints. His father testified that police opened cellar no. 10 with a key taken from the applicant, although the cellar belonged to another person; that police pushed the applicant against the packages, causing him to touch them; and that officers initially handled the packages without gloves.

The defence objected that neither the personal search nor the cellar search had a valid warrant; that no eyewitness directly linked the applicant to the drugs; that the fingerprint evidence was unclear and obtained without an expert present; that no fingerprints were found on the padlock or in the cellar; and that the drug analysis was unreliable and conducted by the Bureau within the Ministry of the Interior, which was not impartial. The defence requested examination of the police officers, experts and neighbours, and alternative expert examinations of the fingerprint and the substance. The trial court convicted the applicant, relying on the search records, fingerprint evidence, signed confiscation certificate and expert reports, and dismissed the father’s testimony as biased. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction, finding the searches lawful and the Bureau’s expert examinations competent; it held the neighbours need not be examined because they had signed the records without objection. The Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s further review request.

The alleged violations therefore centred on Article 6: use of unlawfully obtained evidence, inability to examine key witnesses, and refusal of alternative expert evidence.

**Summary**

In *Duško Ivanovski v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia* (Application no. 10718/05), the applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention that his drug-trafficking conviction was based on unlawfully obtained evidence and that he was denied the opportunity to examine witnesses and obtain alternative expert evidence.

On 4 February 2003, police apprehended and personally searched Ivanovski in Skopje without a court warrant and without witnesses. They seized 13 keys and a mobile phone. Later that day, an investigating judge issued search warrants for two apartments and other premises owned by Ivanovski’s father, based on suspicion of drug trafficking. The searches were conducted in the presence of the father and two neighbours as witnesses. Seven packages were found. The record concerning apartment no. 9 stated that the packages had been found in cellar no. 10, which belonged to a third party, and that the cellar had been opened with a key seized from Ivanovski. Ivanovski was not present when the cellar was searched; he was brought there later. He alleged that police forced him to touch the packages so they could photograph him, and later beat him and forced him to touch the drugs again to obtain his fingerprints. He signed a confiscation certificate.

Expert reports by the Ministry of the Interior’s Criminal Investigations Bureau concluded that the padlock on cellar no. 10 was damaged and could be opened with any key, including those taken from Ivanovski; that five packages contained 2.296 kg of heroin; and that a fingerprint on one package matched Ivanovski’s right middle finger.

At trial, Ivanovski denied any connection with the drugs. He claimed the cellar belonged to a third person and that police had manipulated the fingerprint evidence. His father testified that police opened cellar no. 10 with keys, found the bags in a ventilation shaft, pushed Ivanovski against a metal sheet containing the packages, and forced the father to sign the search record. The defence argued that the personal search and cellar search lacked court warrants; that the drugs were found in a third party’s cellar; that the fingerprint evidence was unreliable and obtained without an expert; that the expert reports were not impartial because they were prepared by a police body; and that the courts refused to examine police officers, experts, and neighbours, or to order alternative expert examinations.

The trial court convicted Ivanovski, relying on the search records, his possession of the keys, the fingerprint expert opinion, and the signed confiscation certificate. It dismissed his father’s account as biased and found the police acted lawfully. The Court of Appeal and Supreme Court upheld the conviction, holding that the personal search was lawful without a warrant under domestic law, the home searches were based on a warrant and witnesses, and the expert reports were admissible. The courts also found no need to examine the neighbours because they had signed the records, and no basis for alternative expert evidence.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Ivanovski alleged that these facts amounted to a violation of his right to a fair trial: the domestic courts had based his conviction on unlawfully obtained evidence, including evidence from the warrantless personal search and the disputed cellar search, and had denied him the opportunity to examine witnesses and obtain alternative expert evidence.
001-145788:
**Case: Tershiyev v. Azerbaijan (ECtHR, 31 July 2014).** Applicant Ramazan Tershiyev, a Russian national of Chechen origin, was serving a 14-year prison sentence in Azerbaijan after his 2011 conviction for offences including membership in an illegal armed unit, illegal border crossing, weapons/explosives possession, and setting up safe flats for Chechen fighters. In 2011 Russia opened criminal proceedings against him under Article 208 §2 of the Russian Criminal Code for allegedly participating in an illegal armed unit in Chechnya from 2000 to 2007. Russia charged him, placed him on a search list, remanded him in absentia, and in August 2012 requested his extradition under the Minsk Convention, alternatively temporary extradition for three months because he was imprisoned in Azerbaijan. The request contained assurances that he would be prosecuted only for the charged offence, not tortured or ill-treated, and returned within three months.

In November 2012 Azerbaijan’s First Deputy Prosecutor General granted temporary extradition. The applicant appealed, claiming a real risk of torture or ill-treatment in Russia as a Chechen and former rebel. He had sought UNHCR asylum in January 2012; UNHCR rejected it at first instance but his appeal was pending. UNHCR requested suspension of forced return until a final decision. In January 2013 Sabayil District Court dismissed his appeal, reasoning there were no grounds to block temporary extradition, he had no refugee status, and Russian assurances sufficed. It refused to examine his torture risk because he submitted no evidence. The Baku Court of Appeal upheld in February 2013, without addressing the pending UNHCR appeal or torture-risk allegations. No further appeal was available. The ECtHR later applied Rule 39 to prevent extradition during proceedings.

Alleged violations: Article 3 (extradition would expose him to torture/ill-treatment) and Article 13 (no effective domestic remedy to challenge extradition on Article 3 grounds). The Government and Russia relied on extradition assurances, including no torture, no third-country extradition, consular access, notification, and return; Russia intervened as a third party. On Article 3, the Court considered reports of serious problems in Russia and Chechnya, including abuse of suspects, arbitrary violence, and ill-treatment in pre-trial detention. However, it found no general bar to extraditing Chechens. The temporary nature of the extradition, the obligation to return him within three months, his non-prominent role, and weak supporting evidence—such as unsubstantiated Chankayev claims and an undetailed Chechen Refugee Council list—meant no real personal risk was established. Thus no Article 3 violation.

On Article 13, the Court found the Article 3 complaint arguable. Although domestic law allowed judicial review of extradition decisions, the first-instance court refused to examine the risk of torture/ill-treatment, and the appellate court was silent on it. The courts therefore failed to conduct independent and rigorous scrutiny of the applicant’s Convention claim. The Court held that Azerbaijan violated Article 13 in conjunction with Article 3, while finding no violation of Article 3.

The case of *Tershiyev v. Azerbaijan* concerned the proposed extradition of Mr. Ramazan Tershiyev, a Russian national of Chechen ethnic origin, from Azerbaijan to Russia. The applicant was serving a fourteen-year prison sentence in Azerbaijan for serious crimes, including membership in an illegal armed unit and illegal border crossing, committed in 2009. In parallel, Russian authorities sought his extradition to face charges under Article 208 § 2 of the Russian Criminal Code for allegedly participating in an illegal armed unit in Chechnya between 2000 and 2007.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations centered on the extradition proceedings in Azerbaijan. In August 2012, the Russian Deputy Prosecutor General requested the applicant's extradition. As an alternative, because the applicant was serving a sentence in Azerbaijan, Russia requested his "temporary extradition" for three months under the Minsk Convention. The Russian request included assurances that the applicant would not be subjected to torture or ill-treatment and would be returned to Azerbaijan within the specified period.

In November 2012, the Azerbaijani First Deputy Prosecutor General granted the request and ordered the applicant's temporary extradition. The applicant appealed this decision, arguing a real risk of torture or ill-treatment in Russia, particularly given his Chechen ethnicity and alleged past involvement in armed conflict. He submitted that he was a former rebel and referenced the case of another Chechen extradited from Azerbaijan, who claimed to have been tortured. He also pointed to a statement from the Chechen Refugee Council alleging a pattern of ill-treatment for extradited Chechens.

However, his appeals were dismissed. The Sabayil District Court rejected his appeal, noting that his asylum claim had been rejected by the UNHCR and that Russia had provided necessary assurances. Crucially, the court refused to examine his specific complaints of a risk of torture, stating he had failed to submit evidence. The Baku Court of Appeal upheld this decision without addressing his arguments regarding the risk of ill-treatment.

The applicant also had a pending asylum application with the UNHCR, which had been rejected at first instance. The UNHCR had requested that his forced return be prevented until a final decision was made. This information was before the domestic courts but was not considered in their rulings. The applicant alleged that his extradition would violate Article 3 (prohibition of torture) and that he lacked an effective domestic remedy to challenge the extradition on this basis, in violation of Article 13.

The European Court of Human Rights found no violation of Article 3, concluding that the applicant had not established a real risk of ill-treatment. However, it found a violation of Article 13. The Court held that the domestic courts failed to provide an effective remedy because they did not conduct a rigorous scrutiny of the applicant's arguable claim that he faced a real risk of torture if extradited, effectively refusing to examine the substance of his complaint.

Case of *Tershiyev v. Azerbaijan* concerned a Russian national of Chechen ethnic origin who was serving a prison sentence in Azerbaijan and faced temporary extradition to Russia. He alleged that extradition would expose him to a real risk of torture or ill-treatment, contrary to Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and that Azerbaijan provided no effective domestic remedy to challenge that risk, contrary to Article 13.

The applicant arrived in Azerbaijan in 2009 and was arrested in July 2009 while attempting to cross illegally into Russia. In April 2011, the Assize Court convicted him and others of serious offences committed in Azerbaijan in 2009, including creating an illegal armed unit, illegal border crossing, illegal possession of firearms and explosives, and creating clandestine flats in Baku for members of armed units operating in Chechnya. He received fourteen years’ imprisonment.

In Russia, in September 2011, an investigator instituted criminal proceedings against the applicant under Article 208 § 2 of the Russian Criminal Code, suspecting him of participation in an illegal armed unit in the Vedeno district of Chechnya between 2000 and 2007. He was later charged, placed on an international search warrant, and remanded in custody in absentia by a Chechen court.

In January 2012, the applicant applied to the UNHCR in Baku for asylum. Because of an arrangement between the UNHCR and Azerbaijan concerning Chechen asylum-seekers, his application was handled by the UNHCR. His application was rejected at first instance, and an appeal remained pending. In August 2012, the Russian Deputy Prosecutor General requested his extradition under the Minsk Convention, alternatively requesting temporary extradition for three months because he was serving a sentence in Azerbaijan. Russia gave assurances that he would be prosecuted only for the charged offence, would not be subjected to torture or ill-treatment, and would be returned to Azerbaijan within three months.

On 26 November 2012, the Azerbaijani First Deputy Prosecutor General granted temporary extradition. The applicant appealed, arguing a serious risk of torture or ill-treatment in Russia
001-139995:
In *Lindström and Mässeli v. Finland* (ECtHR, Fourth Section, 14 January 2014), two Finnish prisoners at Riihimäki Prison complained about treatment during isolation. The first applicant was serving a two-year-eight-month sentence for aggravated drug offence, aggravated theft and a firearms misdemeanour. The second was serving four years and three months for attempted manslaughter. The first was isolated from 13 to 16 November 2004 after an unsupervised family visit because he was suspected of concealing drugs inside his body. The second was isolated from 9 to 16 May 2004 after returning from leave on the same suspicion.

While in isolation, both had to wear closed overalls covering them from feet to neck, sealed by prison staff with plastic strips. They could not remove the overalls themselves or draw their hands inside the sleeves. To use the toilet, they had to call guards to escort them and remove the overalls. The first applicant claimed that guards did not come quickly enough and he had to relieve himself in the overalls. The second claimed that he was given laxatives, with his consent but without prior medical consultation; when they took effect, guards allegedly delayed taking him to the toilet, so he defecated in the overalls. He said he then had to put the same dirty overalls back on, was not allowed to wash, and suffered skin irritation; the first also alleged skin irritation. The applicants said they had not been involved in drug smuggling. The prison authorities justified the overalls as necessary to observe prisoners suspected of concealing drugs and to prevent smuggling and health risks.

In February 2005 the applicants reported the matter to the police. In 2007 the public prosecutor charged the prison director and two chief guards with breach of official duty. On 15 June 2007 the Riihimäki District Court dismissed the charges. It found the use of overalls acceptable for controlling and preventing drug smuggling, that defecation was intended to occur in supervised toilets, that there was no evidence guards delayed response, and that the applicants had not shown they lacked washing facilities or had to wear dirty overalls. The Kouvola Appeal Court upheld the judgment on 30 September 2008, and the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 4 November 2009.

Before the European Court, the applicants alleged inhuman and degrading treatment under Article 3 because of the closed and allegedly dirty overalls. The Court declared the complaint admissible but found no violation of Article 3. It accepted that maintaining prison security and protecting prisoners’ health could justify an observation system, and that the overalls were not intended to humiliate. The applicants had failed to substantiate their claims about delayed toilet access, dirty overalls, lack of washing or skin injuries. The use of closed overalls during relatively short isolation did not reach the Article 3 threshold.

The Court also examined Article 8 (private life) ex officio. The parties agreed the overalls interfered with private life. The key issue was whether the interference was “in accordance with the law.” The Court found it was not. Although the Government relied on Chapter 2, section 9d, of the Act on Execution of Sentences, that provision only regulated isolation, not the use of closed overalls. The measure was regulated at the material time only by internal rules issued by the Riihimäki Prison director. The Parliamentary Ombudsman later concluded there was no sufficient legal basis, and the Court found the rules were not sufficiently accessible or foreseeable and lacked safeguards. There was therefore a violation of Article 8.

**Lindström and Mässeli v. Finland** (ECtHR, Fourth Section, 14 January 2014) concerned two Finnish prisoners at Riihimäki Prison. The first applicant, serving a sentence for aggravated drug offence, aggravated theft and a firearms misdemeanour, was isolated from 13 to 16 November 2004 after an unsupervised family visit. The second applicant, serving a sentence for attempted manslaughter, was isolated from 9 to 16 May 2004 after returning from leave. Both were suspected of concealing drugs or other unlawful substances inside their bodies. Finnish law permitted isolation for up to seven days in such cases.

While in isolation, the applicants had to give up normal clothing and wear closed overalls covering them from feet to neck, sealed by prison staff with plastic strips. They could not remove the overalls themselves or draw their hands inside the sleeves. To use the toilet, they had to call guards, who escorted them and removed the overalls. The first applicant alleged that guards did not come quickly enough, so he had to relieve himself in the overalls. The second applicant was given laxatives with his consent; when they took effect, he called for a guard, but the delay allegedly forced him to defecate in the overalls. He claimed he then had to put the same dirty overalls back on and could not wash. Both applicants alleged they were unable to wash during isolation and that the dirty overalls caused skin irritation; the second said his skin broke. They denied having smuggled drugs.

In 2005 the applicants reported the matter to the police. In 2007 the prosecutor charged the prison director and two chief guards with breach of official duty. The District Court dismissed all charges in June 2007, finding the use of overalls acceptable for controlling and preventing drug smuggling. It found no evidence that guards delayed responses to toilet calls. It concluded that the first applicant had defecated in the overalls as a protest, while the second simply did not reach the toilet in time. The Appeal Court upheld the judgment in 2008, and the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal in 2009.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants complained under Article 3 that the forced use of closed overalls, especially dirty ones, was inhuman and degrading. The Court accepted that the system could pursue legitimate security and health aims and did not itself reach the Article 3 threshold during relatively short isolation. It relied on the domestic courts’ findings that the applicants had not proved delays, lack of washing, or skin injuries. There was therefore no violation of Article 3.

The application was also examined under Article 8. Both parties agreed that the use of closed overalls interfered with the applicants’ private life. The Government relied on Chapter 2, section 9d, of the Act on Execution of Sentences and prison rules. The ECtHR found no sufficient legal basis at the relevant time: the provision addressed only the grounds and duration of isolation, not the modality of closed overalls. The rules were issued by the prison director and were likely not accessible or foreseeable to prisoners. The Parliamentary Ombudsman had similarly found in 2012 that closed overalls lacked a clear legal basis, and their use was prohibited from March 2013. The ECtHR therefore held that the interference was not “in accordance with the law” and violated Article 8.

**Lindström and Mässeli v. Finland** (ECtHR, Fourth Section, 14 January 2014) concerned two Finnish prisoners at Riihimäki Prison. The first applicant, serving a sentence for aggravated drug offence, aggravated theft and a firearms misdemeanour, was placed in isolation from 13 to 16 November 2004 after an unsupervised family visit. The second applicant, serving a sentence for attempted manslaughter, was isolated from 9 to 16 May 2004 after returning from prison leave. Both were suspected of concealing drugs or other unlawful substances inside their bodies.

While in isolation, the applicants had to wear closed overalls covering them from feet to neck. The overalls had integrated plimsolls, a rear zipper and sleeves sealed with plastic strips, so the prisoners could not remove them or draw their hands inside. To use the toilet, they had to call guards, who escorted them and removed the overalls. The first applicant claimed that guards did not come quickly enough and he had to relieve himself in the overalls. The second applicant claimed that after taking laxatives, which he consented to, he had to defecate in the overalls because a guard arrived too late; he allegedly then had to wear the same dirty overalls and was not allowed to wash. Both applicants claimed they could not wash during isolation, that the overalls caused skin irritation or broken skin, and that the treatment was degrading.

In February 2005 the applicants reported the matter to the police. Charges were brought against the Riihimäki Prison director and two chief guards for breach of official duty, and the applicants also pressed charges for coercion and defamation. In June 2007 the District Court dismissed all charges. It found that using closed overalls was acceptable to control and prevent drug smuggling and health risks; that defecation was intended to occur in supervised toilets; that there was no evidence guards delayed responses; and that the first applicant had defecated as a protest while the second did not reach the toilet in time. It also found no proof that the applicants were denied washing or had to continue wearing dirty overalls. The Appeal Court upheld the judgment in September 2008, and the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal in November 2009.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged inhuman and degrading treatment under Article 3. The Court accepted that using closed overalls during relatively short isolation could serve legitimate prison-security and prisoner-health aims and was not intended to humiliate. It acknowledged that forced defecation in overalls, dirty overalls, or denial of washing could raise Article 3 issues, but the domestic courts had found no evidence supporting those allegations. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 3.

The application was also examined under Article 8 concerning private life. The Government conceded that the use of closed overalls interfered with the applicants’ private life but argued it had a legal basis in the Act on Execution of Sentences and prison rules. The Court disagreed. The relevant statutory provision only regulated isolation where concealment of drugs was suspected; it did not regulate the modalities of isolation or the use of closed overalls. The only specific basis was the Riihimäki Prison director’s internal rules of 18 March 2004, addressed to staff, which were not sufficiently accessible or foreseeable to prisoners. The law was also unclear and provided no effective remedy. The Parliamentary Ombudsman later found that closed overalls required a clear legal basis, and their use was prohibited from 15 March 2013. The Court accordingly found a violation of Article 8.

In *Vieira Gomes Bezerra v. Portugal* (Application no. 60786/10, judgment of 28 January 2014), the European Court of Human Rights examined an application by Ms Tomásia Vieira Gomes Bezerra, a Portuguese national residing in Bonn, Germany. The case concerned civil proceedings she brought in Portugal over land she claimed as her own and alleged occupation by two companies. The main alleged violation was the excessive length of those proceedings under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention; she also complained of a violation of her right to property under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The facts relevant to the length complaint were as follows. On 28 February 2007, the applicant started civil proceedings before the Court of Vila Nova de Gaia against two companies, concerning occupation of land she claimed to own (domestic proceedings no. 1908/07.8TBVNG). The defendants contested the claim. The court ordered an expertise to analyse the size of the land, and this procedural step ended on 18 December 2007. In the first trimester of 2008, an attempt at conciliation took place. On 18 July 2008, the domestic court suspended the proceedings because the property was not registered in the applicant’s name at the Land Registry Office. On 20 January 2010, the court ordered the proceedings to be interrupted. On 18 July 2010, the applicant submitted an additional supporting document informing the court that the land had been registered; the judge then ordered the proceedings to resume. According to the last information before the Strasbourg Court, dated 3 May 2013, the proceedings were still pending.

The applicant lodged her application with the European Court on 4 October 2010. The Portuguese Government contested the complaint, arguing that the delay was due to the applicant’s failure to register the disputed land in her name. The Court declared the application admissible. On the merits, it recalled that the reasonableness of the length of proceedings must be assessed in light of the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicant and the relevant authorities, and what was at stake for the applicant. The Court found that the Government had not put forward any fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion. Although the applicant could be held responsible for some delays, the overall length of the proceedings was excessive. The period to be considered began on 28 February 2007 and had not ended, lasting approximately six years and ten months for one level of jurisdiction. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

As to the applicant’s further complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning her right to property, the Court declared it inadmissible for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies. Because the domestic proceedings were still pending, the applicant had not exhausted the remedies available at national level, as required by Article 35 §§ 1 and 4 of the Convention. The judgment thus primarily concerned the violation of the reasonable-time guarantee, while the property complaint was rejected on admissibility grounds.

The Court noted that the period to be considered began on 28 February 2007 and had not yet ended, meaning the proceedings had already lasted six years and ten months for one level of jurisdiction.
