001-147875:
**Case Summary: Stauder and Gabl v. Austria (Application no. 10711/09)**

The case of Stauder and Gabl v. Austria concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 10 February 2009 by Mr. Wolfgang Stauder, a German national born in 1948, and Mr. Bernhard Gabl, an Austrian national born in 1964. The applicants alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, specifically that the length of criminal proceedings against them was incompatible with the "reasonable time" requirement.

The underlying facts date back to 1997, when the Wels Regional Court instituted preliminary investigations against the applicants and several other persons on suspicion of aggravated fraud. The allegations involved setting up and managing an internationally operated gambling system based on a pyramid scheme. On 19 January 1999, the Regional Court separated the proceedings against the applicants from those of their co-suspects to avoid delays.

Regarding Mr. Stauder, an international arrest warrant was issued on 9 December 1997. He was detained on remand from 26 to 27 May 1998. On 18 February 2008, he filed a request for acceleration of proceedings under Section 91 of the Courts Act. The Linz Court of Appeal dismissed this request on 11 September 2008, stating that it could only be directed against delays caused by the courts, not the Public Prosecutor. Mr. Stauder was ultimately acquitted of all charges on 2 May 2013, with the decision served on his counsel on 15 October 2013.

Regarding Mr. Gabl, an international arrest warrant was issued on 18 April 1997. He was detained on remand from 22 May 1997 until 6 August 1999. On 12 April 2002, the preliminary investigations against him were closed and the file was transferred to the Wels Public Prosecutor. However, no indictment was initially brought. On 4 December 2007, Mr. Gabl filed a request for acceleration of proceedings, which was also dismissed by the Court of Appeal on 11 September 2008 for the same reason. On 2 April 2010, the Public Prosecutor brought an indictment against him. Mr. Gabl appealed, and on 28 February 2011, the Court of Appeal rejected the indictment but did not discontinue the proceedings. On 13 October 2011, the Public Prosecutor finally discontinued the proceedings.

The Court assessed the reasonableness of the length of proceedings based on the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicants, and the conduct of the relevant authorities. It noted that the cases were complex due to the initially significant number of accused and the international dimension of the alleged crimes. However, the Court found that these factors alone could not justify the overall duration of the pre-trial proceedings—approximately fifteen years and ten months for Mr. Stauder and fourteen years and six months for Mr. Gabl, both involving only one level of jurisdiction. Importantly, the Court found no discernible delays caused by the applicants, whereas there were significant periods of inactivity on the part of the investigative bodies.

The Court declared the application admissible and, having regard to its established case-law on the subject, concluded that the length of the proceedings was excessive and failed to meet the "reasonable time" requirement. Accordingly, it found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

**Summary of *Stauder and Gabl v. Austria* (Application no. 10711/09)**

The case of *Stauder and Gabl v. Austria* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by two individuals, Mr. Wolfgang Stauder (a German national) and Mr. Bernhard Gabl (an Austrian national), against the Republic of Austria. The central violation alleged by the applicants was a breach of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically the right to a hearing within a "reasonable time." The case originated from lengthy criminal proceedings related to a complex fraud investigation.

The facts of the case date back to 1997, when the Wels Regional Court in Austria initiated preliminary investigations against the applicants and several others. The suspects were accused of aggravated fraud for having established and managed an internationally operated gambling system based on a pyramid scheme. Due to the complexity and number of suspects, the court separated the proceedings against Stauder and Gabl from those of their co-suspects in January 1999 to avoid delays.

For the first applicant, Mr. Stauder, the relevant period began on 9 December 1997, when an international arrest warrant was issued for him. He was briefly held in detention on remand in May 1998. In an attempt to move the case forward, he filed a request for the acceleration of proceedings in February 2008. This request was dismissed by the Linz Court of Appeal in September 2008, on the grounds that such a request could only target delays caused by the courts, not by the Public Prosecutor. The proceedings against Mr. Stauder were not concluded until 2 May 2013, when he was acquitted of all charges. This acquittal was served on his counsel on 15 October 2013, resulting in proceedings that lasted a total of 15 years, 10 months, and 10 days for a single level of jurisdiction.

For the second applicant, Mr. Gabl, the timeline was similarly protracted. An international arrest warrant was issued for him on 18 April 1997. He was in detention on remand for a substantial period, from 22 May 1997 until 6 August 1999. The preliminary investigations against him were closed in April 2002, and the file was transferred to the Wels Public Prosecutor. However, no indictment was brought for several years. Like Mr. Stauder, Mr. Gabl filed a request to accelerate the proceedings in December 2007, which was also dismissed by the Court of Appeal on the same procedural grounds in September 2008. An indictment was finally brought against him in April 2010, but this was rejected by the Court of Appeal in February 2011. Ultimately, the Public Prosecutor discontinued the proceedings against Mr. Gabl on 13 October 2011. His proceedings lasted a total of 14 years, 5 months, and 29 days for one level of jurisdiction.

In its judgment, the European Court of Human Rights found that the application was admissible. It reiterated that the reasonableness of the length of proceedings must be assessed based on the complexity of the case and the conduct of the applicants and authorities. The Court acknowledged that the case was complex due to the number of accused and its international dimension. However, it ruled that these factors could not justify such an extreme duration, noting significant periods of inactivity by the investigative bodies, while there were no apparent delays caused by the applicants. Consequently, the Court found that the length of the proceedings in both cases was excessive and failed to meet the "reasonable time" requirement, violating Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

In *Stauder and Gabl v. Austria* (Application no. 10711/09, judgment of 13 November 2014), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by Wolfgang Stauder, a German national, and Bernhard Gabl, an Austrian national, that the length of criminal proceedings against them in Austria violated the “reasonable time” requirement of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

The proceedings originated in 1997, when the Wels Regional Court opened preliminary investigations against the applicants and several others on suspicion of aggravated commercial fraud. The allegation was that they had set up and managed an internationally operated gambling system based on a pyramid scheme. In January 1999, the proceedings against the applicants were separated from those involving co-suspects to avoid delays.

As regards the first applicant, Mr Stauder, the Regional Court issued an international arrest warrant on 9 December 1997. He was held in detention on remand from 26 to 27 May 1998. On 18 February 2008, he filed a request under Section 91 of the Courts Act seeking acceleration of the proceedings. The Linz Court of Appeal dismissed the request on 11 September 2008, holding that such a request could only target delays caused by the courts, not by the Public Prosecutor. On 2 May 2013, the Regional Court acquitted Mr Stauder of all charges, and the decision was served on his counsel on 15 October 2013. The period relevant to the length complaint therefore ran from 9 December 1997 to 5 October 2013, lasting 15 years, 10 months and 10 days for one level of jurisdiction.

As regards the second applicant, Mr Gabl, an international arrest warrant was issued on 18 April 1997. He was in detention on remand from 22 May 1997 until 6 August 1999. On 12 April 2002, the preliminary investigations against him were closed and the file was transferred to the Wels Public Prosecutor, but no indictment followed at that stage. On 4 December 2007, Mr Gabl also filed a request for acceleration of proceedings. The Court of Appeal dismissed it on 11 September 2008 for the same reason as in Mr Stauder’s case: the request could not be directed against delays attributable to the Public Prosecutor. On 2 April 2010, the Public Prosecutor indicted Mr Gabl. He appealed against the indictment and moved for discontinuation. On 28 February 2011, the Court of Appeal rejected the indictment but did not discontinue the proceedings. On 13 October 2011, the Public Prosecutor discontinued the proceedings against him. The relevant period ran from 18 April 1997 to 13 October 2011, lasting 14 years, 5 months and 29 days for one level of jurisdiction.

Before the European Court, the Government did not comment on admissibility or merits. The Court declared the application admissible. On the merits, it applied the criteria of complexity, the applicants’ conduct, and the conduct of the authorities. It accepted that the cases were complex because of the initially large number of accused and the international dimension of the alleged crimes. However, it found that these factors alone could not explain the overall duration. There were no discernible delays caused by the applicants, whereas there were significant periods of inactivity by the investigative bodies.

The Court concluded that the length of the proceedings was excessive and failed to satisfy the “reasonable time” requirement, violating Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.
001-146697:
In *Volyanyk v. Ukraine* (Application no. 7554/10), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) delivered judgment on 2 October 2014. The applicant, Mr Oleg Markiyanovych Volyanyk, a Ukrainian national, worked as a deputy chief guard at “Lviv Railways,” a State-owned company. On 26 October 2009 the police instituted criminal proceedings against him, suspecting that he had accepted bribes to cover up thefts from the company’s premises in conspiracy with two individuals, S. and D.

On 3 November 2009 the Galytskyy District Court of Lviv ordered the applicant’s pre-trial detention. It stated that he had committed serious crimes, did not admit guilt, and, if at liberty, would influence witnesses and others involved. The court also said that because the applicant worked as a policeman, he was well aware of how to obstruct the investigation and justice. However, the case file contained no evidence that he had ever worked as a policeman. It was also unclear whether S. and D. had been arrested or remained at liberty. The Lviv Regional Court of Appeal upheld the detention on 9 November 2009.

The detention was repeatedly extended. On 25 December 2009 the Galytskyy Court extended it until 26 February 2010, citing that not all accomplices had been detained, complaints from bribe-givers were still being received, and the applicant might obstruct the investigation or abscond. This was upheld on 30 December 2009. On 22 February 2010 the detention was extended until 26 April 2010 on grounds that the applicant had committed serious crimes, refused to testify, and—given his higher education and extensive work experience as a guard—might influence witnesses, obstruct the investigation, or abscond. On 22 April 2010 the Court of Appeal prolonged detention until 26 July 2010, citing the need for further investigative measures, serious charges, and risks of absconding, obstruction, or continued criminal activity.

After the investigation was completed and the case sent to the Sykhiv District Court of Lviv for trial, that court on 17 August 2010 upheld the preventive measure without giving reasons and without fixing a time-limit for detention. On 16 February 2012 the Sykhiv Court changed the measure on health grounds, and the applicant was released on an undertaking not to abscond.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 5 § 1 of the Convention, arguing that the detention decisions and extensions were unlawful and groundless. The Government denied this, claiming reasonable suspicion, lawful procedure, relevant grounds, and that domestic courts had examined the case files and heard the parties.

The European Court of Human Rights declared the application admissible and found a violation of Article 5 § 1. It reasoned that relying on the applicant’s refusal to admit guilt or testify as a ground for detention contradicted the presumption of innocence and the privilege against self-incrimination. As to obstruction, there was no evidence he was a policeman or could interfere in that capacity; being a guard with higher education might show skills, but not intent. The domestic courts did not verify any actual attempt to intimidate witnesses, and the allegations lacked proof, names, or details. It was not established whether S. and D. were at liberty or who other accomplices were. Risks of absconding or reoffending were unsupported. The seriousness of charges alone could not justify detention, nor could a bare need for investigative measures. Finally, the detention from 17 August 2010 to 16 February 2012 rested on a decision without grounds or a time-limit, which was incompatible with Article 5 § 1(c).

In *Volyanyk v. Ukraine* (Application no. 7554/10), judgment of 2 October 2014, the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) examined a Ukrainian national’s complaint under Article 5 §1 of the Convention about allegedly unlawful and groundless pre-trial detention.

The applicant, Oleg Markiyanovych Volyanyk, worked as a deputy chief guard at “Lviv Railways,” a State-owned company. On 26 October 2009 the police instituted criminal proceedings against him. They suspected that he had accepted bribes to cover up thefts from the company’s premises in conspiracy with two individuals, S. and D.

On 3 November 2009 the Galytskyy District Court of Lviv ordered his pre-trial detention. The court said he had committed serious crimes, did not admit guilt, and if at liberty would influence witnesses and other persons involved. It also stated that because he “works as a policeman,” he knew how to obstruct the investigation and justice. However, the case file contained no evidence that the applicant had worked as a policeman before or during the relevant events. It was also unclear whether S. and D. had been arrested or remained at liberty. The Lviv Regional Court of Appeal upheld this decision on 9 November 2009.

The detention was repeatedly extended. On 25 December 2009 the Galytskyy Court extended it until 26 February 2010, citing that not all alleged accomplices were detained, that complaints were still being received from persons who had paid bribes, and that the applicant might obstruct the investigation or abscond. On 22 February 2010 it extended detention until 26 April 2010, referring to the seriousness of the charges, the applicant’s refusal to admit guilt or testify, and his higher education and extensive work experience as a guard, which supposedly meant he might influence witnesses, obstruct the investigation, or abscond. On 22 April 2010 the Lviv Regional Court of Appeal prolonged detention until 26 July 2010, citing the need for further investigative measures, the serious charges, and risks of absconding, obstruction, or continued criminal activity.

After the investigation was completed and the case sent to the Sykhiv District Court of Lviv for trial, that court on 17 August 2010 upheld the preventive measure without giving any reasons and without fixing a time-limit. On 16 February 2012 the court allowed a change of preventive measure on health grounds, and the applicant was released on an undertaking not to abscond. His detention from 17 August 2010 to 16 February 2012 therefore rested on a decision lacking reasons and a time-limit.

The applicant alleged that the detention decisions violated Article 5 §1. The Government denied any violation, arguing reasonable suspicion, lawful procedure, and judicial consideration. The Court declared the application admissible but found a violation. It held that requiring the applicant to admit guilt or testify as a basis for detention conflicted with freedom from self-incrimination and the presumption of innocence. The obstruction, absconding, and reoffending risks were not supported by concrete evidence; seriousness of charges alone and the mere need for investigative measures were insufficient. Finally, the detention from 17 August 2010 to 16 February 2012, based on an unreasoned decision with no time-limit, was incompatible with Article 5 §1(c).

Volyanyk v. Ukraine (no. 7554/10, 2 October 2014) concerned a Ukrainian national, Mr Oleg Volyanyk, who worked as a deputy chief guard at “Lviv Railways,” a State-owned company. On 26 October 2009 the police opened criminal proceedings against him, suspecting that he had accepted bribes in exchange for covering up thefts from the company’s premises in conspiracy with two individuals, S. and D.

On 3 November 2009 the Galytskyy District Court of Lviv ordered his pre-trial detention. It cited the serious nature of the charges, the applicant’s denial of guilt, the risk that he would influence witnesses and others, and—incorrectly—that he worked as a policeman and therefore knew how to obstruct the investigation and justice. The case file contained no evidence that he had ever worked as a policeman. It was also unclear whether S. and D. had been arrested or remained at liberty. The detention decision was upheld on appeal.

The detention was repeatedly extended. On 25 December 2009 it was extended until 26 February 2010 because not all accomplices had been detained, complaints were still being received from bribe-givers, and the applicant might obstruct the investigation or abscond. On 22 February 2010 it was extended until 26 April 2010 on grounds including serious charges, refusal to admit guilt or testify, and his higher education and extensive guard experience, which supposedly made it possible that he would influence witnesses, obstruct the investigation, or abscond. On 22 April 2010 the Lviv Regional Court of Appeal prolonged detention until 26 July 2010, citing the need for investigative measures, serious charges, and risks of absconding, obstruction, or continuing criminal activity.

After the investigation was completed and the case sent to the Sykhiv District Court of Lviv, that court on 17 August 2010 upheld the preventive measure at a preliminary hearing without giving any reasons or fixing a time-limit for detention. On 16 February 2012, the applicant’s request to change the preventive measure on health grounds was allowed, and he was released on an undertaking not to abscond. He had therefore remained in detention from 17 August 2010 to 16 February 2012 under an unreasoned, open-ended decision.

The applicant complained under Article 5 § 1 of the Convention that his detention and its extensions were unlawful and groundless. The Government argued that there had been reasonable suspicion, proper procedure, and judicial review. The Court declared the application admissible.

On the merits, the Court found the reasons used to justify detention deficient. The ground that the applicant refused to admit guilt or testify contradicted fair-trial principles, including freedom from self-incrimination and the presumption of innocence. As to obstruction, there was no evidence that he had worked as a policeman; being a guard with higher education showed capability but not intent. Although organised-crime cases may create a high risk of witness pressure, the domestic courts never verified actual attempts, named witnesses, or explained how he could influence them. Uncertainty about S., D., and other accomplices further weakened the allegation. Risks of absconding or reoffending also lacked plausible evidence. The seriousness of charges alone cannot justify lengthy detention, and the need for investigative measures alone is not sufficient. Finally, the period from 17 August 2010 to 16 February 2012 was based on a decision lacking any grounds and time-limit, which was incompatible with Article 5 § 1(c). The Court therefore found a violation of Article 5 § 1(c) of the Convention.

**Summary of *Császy v. Hungary* (Application no. 14447/11)**

The case of *Császy v. Hungary* concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to respect for family life. The applicant, Mr. Zsolt Béla Császy, a Hungarian national, complained that the Hungarian authorities' refusal to allow him to attend his stepmother's funeral while he was under arrest constituted an unjustified interference with his family life.

The key facts are as follows: On the morning of 31 August 2010, the applicant was apprehended at his home, and a house search was conducted. During this time, he informed the police officers of his intention to attend a funeral later that day. He claimed his request was "unofficially" dismissed, an allegation the Government denied. After the search, he was taken to the Central Investigating Prosecutor’s Office, located about seven kilometers from the cemetery.

At 1:35 p.m., his interrogation as a suspect in a case of attempted misappropriation of funds began. At the outset, he formally requested permission to attend his stepmother's funeral, scheduled for 2:15 p.m. that same day. The authorities rejected his request, stating that granting it would "have contravened the purpose of the arrest." The interrogation concluded at 2:29 p.m., after the funeral had already started.

The applicant subsequently complained to the Attorney General. This complaint was rejected on 10 September 2010. The Attorney General's office reasoned that the relevant legal decree did not permit arrestees—as distinct from those in pre-trial detention—to attend funerals, and therefore the refusal was lawful.

In its judgment, the European Court of Human Rights focused on whether the refusal was "necessary in a democratic society." The Government argued that the restriction was lawful, pursued the legitimate aim of preventing disorder and crime, and was proportionate, given that the nature of a police arrest is incompatible with granting leave for outside activities.

The Court accepted that the measure was lawful and pursued a legitimate aim. However, it found that the refusal was not "necessary." The Court emphasized that any limitation on a detainee's rights must be justifiable and correspond to a pressing social need. It noted that the applicant could not have anticipated that his arrest would coincide with the funeral and thus could not have made alternative arrangements.

The Court found that allowing the applicant, who had just been apprehended, to attend the funeral under police escort would not have been unreasonable. It pointed out that the short distance between the prosecutor's office and the cemetery would have facilitated this task, even with the short notice. The Court also found it noteworthy that the authorities' reasoning created an illogical situation where pre-trial detainees could potentially receive such leave, while arrestees—whose cases are at an earlier stage—could not.

Crucially, the Court determined that the authorities failed to conduct any balancing exercise between the interests of the ongoing investigation and the applicant's right to family life. Instead, they relied on a vague argument that the request was incompatible with the purpose of the arrest. The Court concluded that, in the specific circumstances, the refusal was disproportionate and did not correspond to a pressing social need. Consequently, it found a violation of Article 8 of the Convention. The applicant's separate complaint under Article 13 regarding an effective remedy was rejected as manifestly ill-founded.

In *Császy v. Hungary* (Application no. 14447/11, judgment of 21 October 2014), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Hungarian authorities violated Article 8 by refusing a newly arrested suspect permission to attend his stepmother’s funeral.

On 31 August 2010, police apprehended the applicant at his home at 8:04 a.m. and searched the premises until 11:12 a.m. During the search, the applicant told officers that he intended to attend a funeral later that day. He claimed this request was immediately dismissed informally; the Government denied that allegation. After the search, he was taken to the Central Investigating Prosecutor’s Office, about seven kilometres from the cemetery. From 1:35 p.m., he was interrogated as a suspect in an attempted misappropriation of funds case. At the beginning of the interrogation, he formally requested leave to attend his stepmother’s funeral, scheduled for 2:15 p.m. that same day. The request was rejected because granting it would allegedly contravene the purpose of the arrest. The interrogation ended at 2:29 p.m. The applicant complained to the Attorney General, whose office rejected the complaint on 10 September 2010. It stated that the relevant domestic decree did not allow arrestees—as opposed to persons in pre-trial detention—to attend funerals, so the refusal was lawful.

The applicant alleged that the refusal unjustifiably interfered with his right to respect for family life under Article 8. The Government argued that the restriction was lawful, pursued the legitimate aim of preventing disorder and crime, and was proportionate, since police arrest was incompatible with allowing an arrestee to leave custody for activities such as attending a funeral. The applicant argued that the measure was disproportionate and that allowing him to attend under police escort would have been proportionate. He also noted that the authorities never explained what “contravened the purpose of the arrest” meant.

The Court declared the Article 8 complaint admissible. It accepted that the measure was lawful and pursued the legitimate aim of crime prevention. However, it found that the refusal was not “necessary in a democratic society.” The applicant could not have known that the funeral would coincide with his arrest, so he could not have made alternative arrangements. The authorities could reasonably have allowed him to attend under police escort, especially given the short distance between the interrogation site and the cemetery. The Court also observed that, under the Attorney General’s reasoning, pre-trial detainees could receive such leave, while arrestees normally at an earlier stage could not. Crucially, the authorities did not balance the interests of the ongoing investigation against the applicant’s family-life interests; they merely asserted that the request conflicted with the purpose of the arrest. While Article 8 does not guarantee an unconditional right for detainees to attend relatives’ funerals, and domestic authorities enjoy a margin of appreciation, each request must be assessed on its merits. In the particular circumstances, the refusal was neither proportionate nor based on a pressing social need. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 8.

The applicant also complained under Article 13, read with Article 8, that the Attorney General decided his complaint only ten days after the funeral, meaning there was no effective remedy. The Court rejected this complaint as manifestly ill-founded, finding that the Attorney General had issued a reasoned decision on the merits and that the short time available did not show the remedy was ineffective.

The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) decided **Császy v. Hungary** (Application no. 14447/11) on 21 October 2014; the judgment became final on 21 January 2015. The applicant, Zsolt Béla Császy, a Hungarian national, complained under Article 8 that the authorities refused his request to attend his stepmother’s funeral while he was under arrest, allegedly interfering unjustifiably with his family life. He also alleged a violation of Article 13 read with Article 8 concerning the lack of an effective remedy.

The key facts were as follows. On 31 August 2010 at 8:04 a.m., the applicant was apprehended at his home and a house search was conducted until 11:12 a.m. During the search, he told officers that he intended to attend a funeral later that day. He claimed this request was immediately and “unofficially” dismissed; the Government denied that. After the search, he was taken to the Central Investigating Prosecutor’s Office, about seven kilometres from the cemetery. From 1:35 p.m., he was interrogated as a suspect in an attempted misappropriation-of-funds case. At the beginning of the interrogation, he formally requested leave to attend his stepmother’s funeral, scheduled for 2:15 p.m. that same day. The request was rejected on the ground that granting it would contravene the purpose of the arrest. The interrogation ended at 2:29 p.m. The applicant complained to the Attorney General, but on 10 September 2010 that office rejected the complaint, stating that the relevant decree did not permit arrestees—unlike those in pre-trial detention—to attend funerals, so the refusal was lawful.

The Government argued that the restriction was lawful, pursued the legitimate aim of preventing disorder and crime, and was proportionate. It contended that the nature of police arrest was irreconcilable with granting leave to attend activities at large. The applicant argued that the refusal was disproportionate and that allowing him to attend under police escort would have been an acceptable minimum measure.

The Court declared the Article 8 complaint admissible. It accepted that the interference was lawful and pursued the legitimate aim of crime prevention. However, it found that the refusal was not “necessary in a democratic society.” The State had to demonstrate a pressing social need. The funeral coincided with the applicant’s arrest and interrogation; he could not have foreseen this and could not have made alternative arrangements. The Court considered that allowing a newly apprehended person to attend the funeral under police escort would not have been unreasonable. Although time was short, the cemetery was close to the interrogation site. The Court also noted the anomaly that pre-trial detainees could obtain such leave, while arrestees could not. Crucially, the authorities did not balance the investigation’s interests against the applicant’s family life; they merely relied on the vague “purpose of the arrest.” While Article 8 does not guarantee an unconditional right to attend a relative’s funeral, the refusal in this case was not proportionate. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 8.

As to Article 13, the applicant complained that the Attorney General decided his complaint ten days after the funeral, leaving him without an effective remedy. The Court found that the Attorney General had issued a reasoned decision on the merits and that the short time available did not show the remedy was ineffective. That complaint was rejected as manifestly ill-founded.

Germany (no. 68919/10), ECtHR, 4 September 2014, concerned the alleged excessive length of proceedings before the Federal Constitutional Court and the lack of an effective remedy. The applicant, a German national born in 1948, entered a civil partnership in October 2001; his partner died in June 2002. He applied for a survivor’s pension in September 2002. The pension fund rejected his claim, and the Fulda Social Court dismissed his challenge in November 2004, holding that a surviving civil partner was not a “widower” under the Social Security Code and that the partnership had not lasted a year. During the appeal, the fund acknowledged his pension from January 2005 after legislative amendments.

Case of Peter v. Germany (ECtHR, 4 September 2014) concerned a German man whose same-sex civil partner died in June 2002. The applicant had entered a civil partnership in October 2001. In September 2002 he applied for a survivor’s pension. The German Pension Fund rejected the claim in November 2002 and dismissed his administrative appeal in February 2003. His case then went to the Fulda Social Court, which dismissed it in November 2004, reasoning that a surviving civil partner could not be considered a “widower” under the Social Security Code and that the partnership had not lasted one year. During the appeal, the respondent acknowledged his pension from January 2005, when amendments to the Civil Partnership Act took effect. The Federal Social Court dismissed the remaining leapfrog appeal in December 2005, leaving only the period July 2002 to December 2004 at issue.

In January 2006 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court. The FCC postponed handling his complaint pending a 2007 case concerning surviving civil partners’ pension rights. In July 2009 the FCC ruled in that 2007 case that denying such pension rights violated the Basic Law’s non-discrimination principle. The applicant then requested a similar decision. On 11 June 2010, a three-judge panel declined to review his complaint, explaining that the relevant social security provision had already been amended and that the FCC could not grant redress even if the former provision had been unconstitutional. The decision was served on 13 July 2010. The FCC proceedings had lasted four years and six months.

The applicant alleged that this duration violated Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees a hearing within a reasonable time. He also complained of a lack of an effective domestic remedy. In December 2011 Germany enacted the Remedy Act, creating compensation for protracted court proceedings, including before the FCC. The applicant filed a compensation complaint in February 2012. In October 2012 the FCC complaints panel dismissed it. The panel accepted that the four-and-a-half-year duration was unusually long, but held it was not excessive given the FCC’s special constitutional role, binding decisions, limited structural flexibility, and need to prioritize important constitutional issues. It found the delay reasonable in phases, including waiting for the related 2007 case, although that case later proved not decisive.

The ECtHR declared the length complaint admissible. Applying the criteria of complexity, conduct of the applicant and authorities, and what was at stake, the Court noted that the applicant had not caused delay and was not required to remind the FCC of its duty to proceed promptly. What was at stake was pension arrears, not subsistence, because he received a monthly pension from 2005. The underlying discrimination issue was complex. The FCC’s decision to await a related pilot case was prima facie reasonable, and the new judge’s limited time explained further delay. The Court accepted the FCC panel’s assessment that the proceedings were unusually long but not unreasonably so, especially because the domestic panel had applied the Court’s criteria and given a reasoned decision. It therefore found no violation of Article 6 § 1. The case illustrates deference to constitutional courts’ special functions while requiring reasoned domestic remedies for length complaints.

**Peter v. Germany** concerned a German national’s complaint that proceedings before the Federal Constitutional Court lasted unreasonably long, in violation of Article 6 §1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant had entered into a civil partnership in October 2001; his partner died in June 2002. In September 2002 he applied for a survivor’s pension. The German Pension Fund rejected the claim in November 2002, and his administrative appeal was dismissed in February 2003.

The applicant then sought judicial review before the Fulda Social Court, arguing that the term “widow or widower” in the Social Security Code should include a surviving civil partner. In November 2004 the Social Court dismissed his claim, finding that a civil partner could not be regarded as a “widower” and that the partnership had not lasted longer than one year, which would also have excluded married couples. During the appeal, the respondent accepted the applicant’s entitlement to a survivor’s pension from January 2005, when amendments to the Civil Partnership Act took effect. The remaining appeal concerned only arrears for July 2002 to December 2004. The Federal Social Court dismissed the leapfrog appeal in December 2005.

In January 2006 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint. In July 2009 the Federal Constitutional Court decided a separate 2007 case, holding that denying a surviving civil partner a survivor’s pension under the civil servants’ scheme violated the constitutional equality principle. The applicant asked for a similar decision. In June 2010, however, a three-judge panel declined to review his complaint. It reasoned that the relevant social security provision had since been amended and that no pressing constitutional question remained; even if the provision had violated the Constitution, the Court could not require the legislature to amend an already void provision. The decision was served in July 2010. The constitutional proceedings had thus lasted four years and six months.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights about the length of those proceedings. Germany introduced a new domestic remedy in December 2011 for protracted court proceedings. The applicant then filed a compensation complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court in February 2012. In October 2012 the complaints panel dismissed it. It accepted that the proceedings were unusually long but not excessive, considering the Constitutional Court’s special constitutional role, its limited capacity, the need for careful drafting of decisions with general effect, and the decision to await the 2007 pilot case. It distinguished three phases: over one year before awaiting the pilot case, two years until that decision, and eleven months until the applicant’s complaint was decided. A new judge rapporteur had inherited the case and had to finish higher-priority matters.

Before the Strasbourg Court, the applicant argued that the delay was excessive and that the domestic panel had failed to remedy it. The Government relied on the Constitutional Court’s special function and the reasonable use of pilot cases.

The European Court of Human Rights found the complaint admissible. Assessing complexity, conduct, and what was at stake, it accepted that the pension issue was complex and that the Constitutional Court could reasonably prioritize a related pilot case. The applicant had not contributed to the delay and was not required to remind the court of its duties. However, what was at stake was not subsistence, because he was already receiving a monthly pension and the complaint concerned arrears. The Court accepted that awaiting the pilot case was prima facie reasonable, even though it later proved not directly relevant, and that the new rapporteur’s handling was understandable. It concluded that the proceedings, though unusually long, were not unreasonably long. There was therefore no violation of Article 6 §1.

In *Placì v. Italy* (Application no. 48754/11, 21 January 2014), Luigi Placì was called up for compulsory military service in 1993. A pre-conscription psychological and physical examination on 3 December 1993 declared him fit, although the detailed report—not disclosed to him until 2010—noted that he was slow in understanding and executing tasks, logical but prone to giving up, and scored only 4/10 in language, culture, motivation, mental performance and behaviour. A further examination on 14 June 1994 again found him fit. He was assigned to Battalion No. 123 in Chieti for intensive physical and mental training, including firearms. In July 1994 he was transferred to Aquila, where he remained until December 1994. There he received at least eight punishments for minor disciplinary breaches, amounting to about 29 days of confinement (*consegna semplice/rigore*), including solitary confinement. He was also hospitalised several times.

In December 1994, after transfer to Lecce, a commander noticed nervous tics, difficulty socialising and learning, and absent-mindedness, and ordered a specialist medical assessment. In January 1995 Placì was hospitalised with anxiety disorder. A February 1995 NHS report found affection-relational problems, learning difficulties, low aptitude, isolation, cognitive deficits (IQ 67), incapacity for positive relationships, and fear of fellow soldiers. It warned that longer service would worsen his anxiety. In April 1995 he was diagnosed with dysphoria and borderline personality disorder and discharged as unfit. Later diagnoses included chronic OCD, and his doctor alleged that military service or the punishments caused or aggravated his condition. In 1999–2000 military Medical Commissions concluded the OCD was pre-existing and not service-related, and the Ministry of Defence rejected damages.

In domestic administrative proceedings, the TAR in 2007 found the 1994 fitness examination inaccurate but accepted the pre-existing condition. The first-instance expert had failed to produce a report; the TAR refused replacement and decided the case. In 2011 the Supreme Administrative Court relied on a Defence Ministry Medical Board report finding no causal link and rejected the appeal.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 3 (lack of proper pre-conscription assessment and ill-treatment through training and repeated punishments), Article 8 (damage to private/family life), and Article 6 (unfairness: the expert Medical Board was not independent or impartial—composed mostly of military doctors and dependent on the Ministry of Defence, the opposing party—and relevant documents were not disclosed). The ECtHR found no Article 3 violation concerning the pre-conscription assessment, as there were no substantial grounds at that time to foresee a real risk of prohibited treatment. However, it found a violation of Article 3 after conscription: the military failed to detect his vulnerability, gave no timely psychological support or protective procedures, and subjected him to repeated punishments, causing distress exceeding the unavoidable hardship of military service. Article 8 was not examined separately. The Court also examined the Article 6 complaints and found a violation of Article 6 § 1 due to the lack of independence and impartiality of the Medical Board.

In *Placì v. Italy*, Luigi Placì, born 1975, was called up for compulsory military service in 1993 at age 18. A December 1993 pre-conscription psychological and physical examination found him fit, although the report noted he was slow in understanding and executing tasks, prone to giving up, and scored only 4/10 in language/cultural skills, motivation, mental performance, and behaviour. This report was not disclosed to him until 2010. A further June 1994 examination found him fit and suffering from no illness. He was assigned to Battalion No. 123 in Chieti for intensive physical and mental training, including firearms use.

In July 1994 he was transferred to the provincial command in Aquila, where he remained until December 1994. During roughly six months, he was subjected to at least eight punishments, including about 24–28 days of “consegna semplice” (restriction to base) and one day of “consegna di rigore” (confinement to a specified area), sometimes involving solitary confinement, for minor disciplinary matters such as negligent care of his bed area or informal behaviour. He was also hospitalised at least four times for unrelated medical care.

In December 1994 he was transferred to Lecce. A commander there noted nervous tics, difficulty socialising and learning, and absent-mindedness, and ordered a specialised medical assessment. In January 1995 he was hospitalised and diagnosed with anxiety disorder and a fragile mental state. A February 1995 NHS report described affection-relational problems, learning difficulties, insecurity, isolation, cognitive deficits, an IQ of 67, and an inability to perform assigned tasks or form positive relationships. It stated that military life caused him anxiety and fear and that longer service would worsen his condition. In April 1995 he was found to suffer from dysphoria and borderline personality disorder and was discharged as unfit. Later diagnoses included chronic obsessive-compulsive disorder.

The applicant sought damages, alleging that his mental illness was caused or aggravated by military service. Bari Medical Commissions in 1999 and 2000 found his OCD pre-existing and not caused by service, and the Ministry of Defence rejected his claim. Before the Regional Administrative Tribunal, an expert appointed in 2002 never filed a report; in 2007 the TAR refused to replace him, found the infirmity pre-existing, but also found the June 1994 fitness examination inaccurate. On appeal, the Supreme Administrative Court ordered an assessment by the Defence Ministry’s Medical Board, composed mainly of military doctors. That Board found the condition pre-existing and not caused or aggravated by military service. The CS rejected the appeal, deferring to the Board and refusing to review its merits.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Placì alleged violations of Article 3, arguing that the State failed to properly assess his fitness before conscription and then forced him into military service, training, and repeated punishments despite his vulnerability. He also complained under Article 6 that the Medical Board was not independent or impartial because it was an organ of the defendant Ministry of Defence, that key documents were not disclosed, and that he could not effectively challenge the Board’s report. He further relied on Article 8 regarding the impact on his private and family life.

The Court dismissed the Government’s non-exhaustion objection. On Article 3, it found no violation concerning the pre-conscription assessment, as there were no substantial grounds at that time to foresee a real risk of prohibited treatment. However, it found a violation after conscription: during his first six months in Aquila, the military repeatedly punished him without timely detection of his vulnerability, psychological support, or any framework to prevent such harm. As a vulnerable conscript, his suffering exceeded the unavoidable hardship inherent in military discipline. The Court also found a violation of Article 6 § 1 concerning the Medical Board’s lack of independence and impartiality, and held that no separate issue arose under Article 8.
001-142185:
**Case: Karagjozi and Others v. Albania** (ECtHR, Fourth Section, 8 April 2014)

Ten applications were lodged by 52 Albanian nationals between 2006 and 2009. They alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, principally because final administrative decisions awarding them compensation in lieu of restitution of their properties had not been enforced. The Court noted that the underlying legal issue was already covered by well-established case-law, notably *Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania*.

The facts followed a similar pattern. In the 1990s, local commissions recognised the applicants’ inherited title to plots of land. Where land was free, portions were restored. Where land was occupied by embassies, stadiums, national parks, buildings, or third parties, the applicants were to receive compensation in State bonds, in kind, rent, or another form provided by law. The decisions were final but remained unenforced.

Key individual facts:

- **Karagjozi and Others:** In 1996, the Tirana Commission recognised title to 1,214 sq. m. The land was occupied by buildings housing foreign embassies, so compensation was due. The decision remained unenforced.
- **Budini:** In 1995, the Mat Commission recognised title to 7,984 sq. m.; 4,797 sq. m. were restored, while 3,187 sq. m. were occupied and subject to State bond compensation. The decision remained unenforced. A separate claim over 11,112 sq. m. was dismissed by the Court of Cassation in 1996.
- **Koco:** In 1995, the Tirana Commission recognised title to 1,154.62 sq. m. A stadium had been built on the land, so compensation was due. It was not enforced.
- **Hajnaj:** In 1994, the Tirana Commission recognised title to 8,900 sq. m.; 7,727 sq. m. were to be restored and 1,173 sq. m. compensated in kind. The 7,727 sq. m. was occupied by Urban Transportation Company buildings. Later court decisions annulled the restitution and substituted compensation. Constitutional appeals were rejected in 2005–2006. The applicant sold several plots, but compensation for 6,342 sq. m. remained unenforced.
- **Shehu:** In 1994, the Vlora Commission recognised title to 3,600 sq. m. Two warehouses and two 820 sq. m. plots were restored; 2,240 sq. m. were occupied and subject to compensation. The decision remained unenforced.
- **Dvorani and Dume:** In 1993, the Korça Commission recognised title to 2,250 sq. m.; 278 sq. m. were restored, and 1,972 sq. m. were occupied and subject to State bonds. The decision remained unenforced.
- **Sallabanda and Hoxha:** In 1996, the Tirana Commission recognised title to 10,056.7 sq. m., occupied by a national park. Compensation was due, but the decision remained unenforced.
- **Goga and Others:** In 1996, the Durrës Commission recognised title to 12,000 sq. m., awarding State bonds for 4,950 sq. m. and in-kind compensation for 5,000 sq. m.; 600 sq. m. were restored. Compensation for 9,350 sq. m. remained unenforced.
- **Tartari:** In 1995, the Tirana Commission recognised title to 1,100 sq. m.; 142 sq. m. were restored, and 958 sq. m. were occupied and subject to compensation. A third party obtained a building permit in 1997. In 2009, the Agency dismissed the compensation claim for lack of funds. The applicant later received ALL 6,000,000 for another plot.
- **Okaj:** In 1995, the Shkodër Commission restored 8,430 sq. m., awarded compensation for 2,833 sq. m., and recognised a right of first refusal for 14,537 sq. m. Third parties challenged the title; the Supreme Court dismissed their action in 2001. No compensation was paid for 2,833 sq. m., and the properties remained occupied.

The Committee of Ministers described a longstanding structural problem: non-enforcement of final decisions on restitution or compensation and lack of an effective remedy. The pilot judgment in *Manushaqe Puto* set a deadline of 17 June 2014 for Albania to establish an effective compensation mechanism. The core alleged violations therefore arose from the authorities’ failure to enforce final property compensation decisions, affecting fair-trial, remedy, and property rights.

The case *Karagjozi and Others v. Albania* (ECtHR, Fourth Section, 8 April 2014) concerned ten applications brought by fifty-two Albanian nationals. They alleged principally that Albania failed to enforce final administrative decisions awarding them compensation in lieu of physical restitution of properties nationalised during the communist regime. They relied on Articles 6 § 1 and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court noted that the underlying legal issue was already the subject of well-established case-law, particularly *Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania*.

The facts followed a common pattern. Albanian commissions on restitution and compensation recognised the applicants’ inherited property titles, but because the original plots were occupied or could not be restored, the commissions ordered compensation in one of the forms provided by law, such as State bonds, compensation in kind, or another statutory method. In application no. 25408/06 (*Karagjozi and Others*), the Tirana Commission in 1996 recognised title to 1,214 sq m occupied by buildings housing foreign embassies; compensation remained unpaid. In no. 37419/06 (*Budini*), the Mat Commission in 1995 recognised title to 7,984 sq m, restored 4,797 sq m and awarded State bonds for 3,187 sq m; the decision remained unenforced. In no. 49121/06 (*Koco*), the Tirana Commission recognised title to 1,154.62 sq m occupied by a stadium; no compensation was provided. In no. 1504/07 (*Hajnaj*), the Tirana Commission recognised title to 8,900 sq m; although 7,727 sq m were initially to be restored, domestic courts later annulled that restoration because the land was occupied by UTC buildings and held that compensation was due. That decision remained unenforced for 6,342 sq m, and construction was later allowed on the plot. In no. 19772/07 (*Shehu*), the Vlora Commission recognised title to 3,600 sq m, restored parts but awarded compensation for 2,240 sq m occupied by buildings; the decision remained unenforced. In no. 46685/07 (*Dvorani and Dume*), the Korça Commission recognised title to 2,250 sq m, restored 278 sq m and awarded State bonds for 1,972 sq m; the decision remained unenforced. In no. 49411/07 (*Sallabanda and Hoxha*), the Tirana Commission recognised title to 10,056.7 sq m occupied by a national park; compensation was due but remained unenforced. In no. 27242/08 (*Goga and Others*), the Durrës Commission recognised title to 12,000 sq m and awarded compensation for 9,350 sq m; the decision remained unenforced. In no. 61912/08 (*Tartari*), the Tirana Commission recognised title to 1,100 sq m, restored 142 sq m and awarded compensation for 958 sq m; a third party obtained a building permit, and in 2009 the Agency rejected the applicant’s compensation claim for lack of funds. In no. 15075/09 (*Okaj*), the Shkodër Commission restored 8,430 sq m and awarded compensation for 2,833 sq m; third parties occupied the properties, and despite injunctions and the final dismissal of the third parties’ claims, no compensation was paid and the applicants could not enjoy possession.

The common alleged violation was therefore the authorities’ continued non-enforcement of final Commission decisions awarding compensation. The domestic compensation mechanism was described as ineffective, and Council of Europe materials noted the structural problem and the Court’s pilot-judgment deadline for Albania to establish an effective compensation mechanism.

The case of *Karagjozi and Others v. Albania* concerns ten applications brought by fifty-two Albanian nationals against the Republic of Albania. The applicants alleged violations of Articles 6 § 1 and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, primarily due to the non-enforcement of final administrative decisions that awarded them compensation for properties nationalized during the communist regime.

The core facts across the applications follow a consistent pattern: Albanian Commissions on Restitution and Compensation of Properties recognized the applicants' inherited property titles but, because the original plots were occupied by buildings, embassies, stadiums, or other developments, the decisions provided for compensation in various forms (state bonds, in-kind, or other legal means) rather than physical restitution. These Commission decisions, which became final, remained unenforced.

In Application no. 25408/06 (Karagjozi and Others), the Commission recognized title to 1,214 sq. m. occupied by foreign embassies, ordering compensation. This decision was never enforced.

Application no. 37419/06 (Budini) involved a Commission decision recognizing title to 7,984 sq. m., with 3,187 sq. m. designated for compensation in State bonds due to occupation. This also remained unenforced.

In Application no. 49121/06 (Koco), title to 1,154.62 sq. m. was recognized, but a stadium's presence meant compensation was ordered instead of restitution. The decision was not enforced.

Application no. 1504/07 (Hajnaj) was more complex. A 1994 decision restored 7,727 sq. m., but this land was occupied by buildings belonging to the Urban Transportation Company (UTC). Subsequent domestic court proceedings annulled the restitution part, confirming compensation would be provided. Despite this, the decision remained unenforced for a 6,342 sq. m. plot, and the applicant reported unauthorized construction on his land.

For Application no. 19772/07 (Shehu), a 1994 decision restored some property but ordered compensation for 2,240 sq. m. occupied by buildings. This decision was unenforced.

Similarly, in Application no. 46685/07 (Dvorani and Dume), a 1993 decision restored a small portion of land but awarded State bonds for 1,972 sq. m. of occupied land. This remained unenforced.

Application no. 49411/07 (Sallabanda and Hoxha) involved a 1996 decision recognizing title to 10,056.7 sq. m. occupied by a national park, leading to a compensation order that was never enforced.

In Application no. 27242/08 (Goga and Others), a 1996 decision ordered compensation in State bonds and in-kind for 9,350 sq. m. of a 12,000 sq. m. plot. This decision remained unenforced.

Application no. 61912/08 (Tartari) concerned a 1995 decision that restored 142 sq. m. but ordered compensation for 958 sq. m. of occupied land. Despite this, a third party was granted a building permit for the land. The applicant's later claim for compensation was dismissed by the Agency due to lack of funds.

Finally, Application no. 15075/09 (Okaj) involved a 1995 decision that restored title to three plots (8,430 sq. m.) and ordered compensation for another (2,833 sq. m.). The applicants faced occupation of their restored properties by third parties, and the compensation for the 2,833 sq. m. plot was never paid.

The Court noted that this issue of non-enforcement of compensation decisions for nationalized property is a well-established structural problem in Albania, already addressed in its pilot judgment *Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania*.

The case *Yavorovenko and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 25663/02 and 30 others) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights’ Fifth Section on 17 July 2014. It concerned 31 applications against Ukraine brought by Ukrainian and Russian nationals and by companies registered in Ukraine, Cyprus, and Romania. The applicants complained, expressly or in substance, under Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, primarily alleging the lengthy non-enforcement of final domestic court decisions given in their favour and the absence of effective domestic remedies for that non-enforcement.

The central facts were similar across most applications. Domestic courts in Ukraine issued decisions entitling the applicants either to various pecuniary amounts or to have certain actions taken in their favour. Those decisions became final and enforceable. However, the applicants were unable to obtain enforcement in due time. The Court found that the State authorities were responsible for the delays. Some applicants also raised factual and legal issues unrelated to the non-enforcement complaints, but the principal common issue was the failure to enforce binding domestic judgments.

Several procedural developments were relevant. In applications nos. 23056/07 and 24245/10, the Court had earlier accepted Government unilateral declarations and struck the applications out. Later, the applicants informed the Court that Ukraine had paid the compensation but still failed to enforce the underlying domestic judgments—specifically, a Shevchenkivskyy District Court of Kyiv judgment of 4 February 2005 and an Oleksandriya Court judgment of 22 October 2010. The Government confirmed the judgments remained unenforced. The Court restored both applications; in application no. 23056/07, enforcement proceedings were later terminated on 17 April 2013 after full enforcement.

The Court also addressed locus standi. In applications nos. 26330/09 and 34384/05, involving deceased applicants, the Court allowed heirs or next of kin to continue because the property rights were transferable. In application no. 30843/08, a successor company could proceed on behalf of a liquidated creditor company. However, one applicant, Ms Klavdiya Mykolayivna Galayda in application no. 54769/08, died and no one wished to pursue her application, so it was struck out. In application no. 18330/05, the second applicant, Mr Vadym Yevgenovych Mykhaylenko, was not a party to the domestic proceedings; his complaint was declared inadmissible. In that same application, the judgment of the Higher Arbitration Court dated 26 December 2000 was enforced only after 5 years and 4 months, with UAH 701,926 transferred to the first applicant’s account on 16 May 2006.

The Court joined the applications because of the similarity of the principal legal issues. It declared admissible—except for the above-mentioned exceptions—the complaints concerning lengthy non-enforcement and lack of effective domestic remedies. It found that the final decisions in the applicants’ favour were not enforced in due time and that the State authorities were responsible. The Court therefore examined the case under its well-established case-law on non-enforcement, particularly *Yuriy Nikolayevich Ivanov v. Ukraine*, and found violations of Article 6 § 1, Article 13, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In *Yavorovenko and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 25663/02 and 30 others), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) examined 31 applications against Ukraine. The applicants included Ukrainian and Russian nationals and companies registered in Ukraine, Cyprus, and Romania. The central complaint was that final and enforceable domestic court decisions in the applicants’ favour were not enforced in due time by State authorities.

According to the facts, domestic courts had ordered various pecuniary amounts to be paid to the applicants or required certain actions to be taken in their favour. Those decisions became final and enforceable. However, the applicants were unable to obtain timely enforcement. This failure formed the principal factual basis of the alleged violations. Some applicants also raised unrelated factual and legal matters, but the Court focused on the common issue of non-enforcement.

Procedurally, the Court joined the applications because they raised similar principal legal issues. Two applications, nos. 23056/07 and 24245/10, had previously been struck out after the Government made unilateral declarations. Later, the applicants informed the Court that although compensation had been paid, the domestic judgments remained unenforced. The Government confirmed that the relevant judgments were still unenforced; in application no. 23056/07, enforcement proceedings were eventually terminated on 17 April 2013, after full enforcement. The Court restored both applications to its list of cases under Rule 43 § 5.

The Court also addressed standing and admissibility issues. In applications nos. 26330/09 and 34384/05, the original applicants had died, but the property rights at issue were transferable to heirs, and the next of kin or successors were permitted to continue. In application no. 30843/08, a company claimed to be the lawful successor of a liquidated creditor company; the Court accepted its standing because the property right was transferable. By contrast, in application no. 18330/05, the second applicant, Mr Mykhaylenko, had not been a party to the domestic court proceedings. The Court agreed with the Government that he could not claim to be a victim and declared his complaints inadmissible. In application no. 54769/08, one applicant, Ms Galayda, died after lodging her application, and no one wished to pursue it; her application was struck out.

On the merits, the remaining applicants complained about the lengthy non-enforcement of the decisions given in their favour and about the lack of effective domestic remedies. They relied expressly or in substance on Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court found that these complaints were not manifestly ill-founded and were not inadmissible on any other grounds. They were therefore declared admissible.

The Court further found that the decisions in the applicants’ favour had not been enforced in due time and that the State authorities were responsible for that failure. Referring to its well-established case-law, notably *Yuriy Nikolayevich Ivanov v. Ukraine*, the Court concluded that the prolonged non-enforcement violated the applicants’ rights under the Convention, particularly their right to a fair trial and protection of property, and that they lacked effective domestic remedies. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore the finality of the domestic judgments, the State’s failure to enforce them promptly, and the absence of adequate domestic redress.

In *Yavorovenko and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 25663/02 and 30 others), the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, examined 31 applications lodged against Ukraine. The applicants were Ukrainian and Russian nationals, as well as companies registered in Ukraine, Cyprus, and Romania. They complained under Article 6 § 1, Article 13 of the Convention, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the lengthy non-enforcement of final domestic court decisions and the lack of effective domestic remedies for that non-enforcement.

The central facts were that domestic courts had issued decisions in the applicants’ favour, entitling them to various pecuniary amounts or requiring certain actions to be taken for their benefit. These decisions became final and enforceable. However, the applicants were unable to obtain enforcement in due time, and state authorities were responsible for the delays. Some applicants also raised unrelated factual and legal matters, but the principal complaint concerned the failure to enforce binding judgments.

Several procedural issues arose. In two applications (nos. 23056/07 and 24245/10), the Court had earlier accepted the Government’s unilateral declarations and struck the cases out. Later, the applicants informed the Court that although compensation had been paid, the domestic judgments remained unenforced. The Court restored these applications under Rule 43 § 5. The Government confirmed continued non-enforcement, though in application no. 23056/07 the relevant enforcement proceedings were terminated on 17 April 2013 after full enforcement. In application no. 24245/10, the complaint concerned non-enforcement of the Oleksandriya Court judgment of 22 October 2010.

The Court also addressed locus standi. In application no. 34384/05, the applicant died but the next of kin wished to continue. In application no. 54769/08, one applicant, Ms Galayda, died and no one sought to maintain her application, so it was struck out. In applications nos. 26330/09 and 30843/08, the Court allowed successors to continue because the property rights at issue were transferable. In application no. 18330/05, the second applicant, Mr Mykhaylenko, was not a party to the domestic proceedings and could not claim victim status; his complaint was inadmissible under Article 35 § 3 (a). The first applicant company in that case had obtained enforcement after five years and four months.

The Court joined the applications because of similar principal legal issues. It declared the remaining complaints admissible, finding they were not manifestly ill-founded. On the merits, the Court found that the decisions in the applicants’ favour had not been enforced in due time and that the State authorities were responsible. It relied on its well-established case-law, particularly *Yuriy Nikolayevich Ivanov v. Ukraine*. The key alleged violations were therefore the prolonged failure of Ukrainian authorities to enforce final domestic judgments, contrary to Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, and the absence of effective domestic remedies, contrary to Article 13. The case illustrates systemic non-enforcement of court decisions in Ukraine and the related procedural treatment of succession, death, and victim status.

In *Sukhanov and Ilchenko v. Ukraine* (ECtHR, 26 June 2014), two Ukrainian nationals born in 1938, both recognized as “children of war,” complained that they had not received a pension supplement in the amount they claimed. Under section 6 of the Children of War Social Protection Act, in force from 1 January 2006, “children of war” were entitled to a supplement of 30% of the minimum pension. Section 3 stated that these social guarantees could not be limited or annulled by other legal acts. However, the State Budget Acts for 2006–2008 suspended or modified section 6, creating disputes over payment.

The first applicant, Sukhanov, sued in May 2008, seeking recalculation of his pension for 2006–2008, payment of arrears, future payments, damages, and legal costs. On 22 July 2008, the Lugansk Regional Administrative Court rejected his claims for 2006 because section 6 had been suspended by the State Budget Act 2006 and no mechanism had been established by the Cabinet of Ministers. For 2007–2008, the court relied on Constitutional Court decisions of 9 July 2007 and 22 May 2008, which found the Budget Act modifications unconstitutional, and ordered recalculation for 9 July–31 December 2007 and from 22 May 2008. This was upheld in December 2008, and his appeal on points of law was dismissed on 28 July 2010.

The second applicant, Ilchenko, sued in December 2009 for recalculation from January 2006. On 2 March 2010, the Zhovtovodsky Town Court awarded him the supplement only from 9 July 2007, ordering recalculation for 9 July–31 December 2007 and 22 May 2008–2 March 2010. The Dnipropetrovsk Regional Court of Appeal upheld this on 10 August 2010, making it final. In a later suit, Ilchenko obtained payment from 3 March 2010; this was upheld on 14 October 2011.

Domestic practice, summarized by the Higher Administrative Court on 1 May 2009, indicated that 2006 benefits were not implemented because the Cabinet never adopted the required decision. For 2007–2008, supplements were awarded only from the dates of the Constitutional Court decisions, since those decisions were not retrospective.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, complaining about the failure to pay the supplement at the statutory 30% rate between 1 January 2006 and 9 July 2007, and between 1 January and 22 May 2008. The Court accepted that their entitlement to the supplement as such was a “possession,” but the amount was disputed.

The Court divided the periods. For 1 January–2 April 2006, 1 January–9 July 2007, and 1 January–22 May 2008, it found no legitimate expectation to the claimed amount. The claims lacked sufficient basis in national law, no settled domestic case-law supported them, and the domestic courts’ decisions were not arbitrary or unreasonable. Although the Constitutional Court criticized the use of Budget Acts to change substantive entitlements, Parliament could redefine benefits, and the decisions were not retroactive. That part was inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded. For 2 April–31 December 2006, however, the amended State Budget Act 2006 used mandatory wording, so the applicants could legitimately expect the Cabinet to set a supplement level. That complaint was declared admissible on the merits.
