In *Göthlin v. Sweden* (Application no. 8307/11, judgment 16 October 2014), the European Court of Human Rights considered the detention of a Swedish national who refused to disclose the location of property attached by the Enforcement Authority.

The applicant, born in 1943, owed enforceable tax debts of approximately SEK 246,199. In September 2009, the Enforcement Authority issued a writ of execution attaching his mobile sawmill, valued at about SEK 300,000. The sawmill remained in his possession, but he was forbidden to sell, dispose of, or otherwise reduce its value. His appeals against the attachment were ultimately unsuccessful; the writ became final on 6 May 2010 when the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal.

In April 2010, while the Authority was planning to sell the sawmill, the applicant removed and hid it. On 5 May 2010, the Authority visited his property, confirmed the sawmill was missing, and served him with a summons and an injunction under Chapter 4, section 14, of the Enforcement Code. The injunction ordered him to provide information necessary to recover the sawmill and warned that detention could be requested if he failed to cooperate. At questioning on 7 May 2010, the applicant admitted he knew the sawmill was attached and that he could not dispose of it, but he refused to reveal its location because he believed the tax debt and attachment were wrong. He said he had acted alone, that no one else knew where the sawmill was, and that he took full responsibility. His wife was also questioned but said she did not know its whereabouts.

On 17 May 2010, the Authority asked the District Court to detain the applicant. The District Court initially refused, finding no extraordinary reasons and noting that less severe measures, such as a conditional fine, had not been tried. The Court of Appeal reversed that decision on 28 June 2010, finding extraordinary reasons and that detention was proportionate given the substantial debt, the hidden property, and the applicant’s continued refusal. The applicant was detained on 29 June 2010.

His detention was reviewed every two weeks. He maintained his refusal to disclose the location, citing health problems including high blood pressure, panic anxiety, prostate cancer, and asthma. On 9 August 2010, the District Court found continued detention disproportionate and ordered his immediate release. He had been detained for 42 days. A separate police investigation concerning his hiding of the attached property was later discontinued, and the writ of execution was eventually revoked in October 2011.

The applicant complained under Article 5 § 1 that his detention was disproportionate. He argued that less intrusive measures should have been used and that detention served no purpose because the authorities did not search for the sawmill or question him or his family during detention. The Government submitted that the detention fell under Article 5 § 1(b), was lawful and proportionate, and was necessary to secure his legal obligation to provide information so the tax debt could be enforced. A conditional fine would have been futile, they said, because he had no other assets.

The Court declared the complaint admissible, finding domestic remedies exhausted through the Chancellor of Justice. On the merits, the Court examined the detention under Article 5 § 1(b). It found an unfulfilled legal obligation to provide information and that detention aimed to secure compliance, not to punish him; the separate criminal investigation concerned hiding the property. Considering proportionality, the Court noted the importance of tax enforcement, the applicant’s repeated refusal, the futility of a conditional fine, and that he would have been released immediately had he cooperated. Although 42 days was relatively long, detention was reviewed every two weeks. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 5 § 1. His Article 3 complaint about detention conditions was rejected as manifestly ill-founded for lack of substantiation.

In *Göthlin v. Sweden* (ECtHR, 2014), the applicant, a Swedish national born in 1943, owed tax debts of approximately SEK 246,199. In September 2009, the Enforcement Authority attached his mobile sawmill, valued at about SEK 300,000, but left it in his possession while forbidding him to sell, dispose of, or otherwise reduce its value. His appeals were ultimately rejected, and the attachment became final on 6 May 2010.

In late April/May 2010, the applicant removed and hid the sawmill. He told the Authority that he had acted alone and refused to reveal its location. On 7 May 2010, after being summoned and served with an injunction requiring him to provide information needed to recover the sawmill, he admitted he knew the attachment was binding but said he had hidden the sawmill because he believed the attachment was wrong. He accepted responsibility but continued to refuse to disclose its whereabouts. His wife was also questioned and said she did not know where it was. The Authority then requested his detention under the Enforcement Code for failure to comply with his legal duty to provide information.

On 27 May 2010, the District Court refused the detention request, finding no “extraordinary reasons” and noting that a less severe measure, such as a conditional fine, had not been tried and that the matter had only recently become final. The Court of Appeal reversed on 28 June 2010, finding extraordinary reasons and proportionality based on the size of the debt, the value of the hidden property, and the applicant’s persistent refusal to cooperate. He was detained on 29 June 2010. A hearing on 30 June maintained the detention, subject to review every two weeks; he would be released immediately if he revealed the location, and detention could not exceed three months.

Reviews on 13 and 27 July continued his detention. The applicant raised health problems, including high blood pressure, panic anxiety, prostate cancer treatment, and asthma, but submitted no medical evidence. On 9 August 2010, the District Court found continued detention disproportionate and ordered his immediate release. He had been detained for 42 days. The police report concerning his removal of the attached property was later discontinued by waiver of prosecution, and the writ of execution was revoked in October 2011.

The applicant complained under Article 5 § 1 that his detention was disproportionate. He argued that less intrusive measures should have been used, that he was not interrogated during detention, and that the Authority did not search for the sawmill. The Government argued that the detention fell under Article 5 § 1(b) and was lawful and proportionate, aimed at compelling him to provide information to enforce a substantial tax debt.

The Court examined the detention under Article 5 § 1(b). It found that the obligation to disclose the sawmill’s location was prescribed by law, that the detention was aimed at securing compliance rather than punishing him, and that he would have been released immediately if he had cooperated. It found no violation: enforcing tax debts was in the general interest; a conditional fine would have been pointless because he had no available assets and had already refused to cooperate; the Authority had already questioned him and his wife and had little information from which to search; and although 42 days was relatively long, he could have ended the detention at any time and reviews occurred every two weeks. His Article 3 complaint about detention conditions was rejected as manifestly ill-founded for lack of evidence. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 5 § 1 and declared the Article 3 complaint inadmissible.

**Case: Göthlin v. Sweden** (ECtHR, Fifth Section, 16 October 2014)

The applicant, Mr Göthlin, born 1943, owed unpaid taxes of approximately SEK 246,199. In September 2009, the Swedish Enforcement Authority attached his mobile sawmill, valued at about SEK 300,000, but left it in his possession on condition that he not sell or dispose of it. His appeals against the attachment failed, and the writ of execution became final on 6 May 2010.

In late April 2010, the applicant removed and hid the sawmill. After being summoned and questioned on 7 May 2010, he admitted hiding it, acknowledged that he knew it was attached and that he could not dispose of it, but refused to reveal its location. He said he alone was responsible, that his wife did not know where it was, and that he had even considered setting fire to it. The Enforcement Authority served an injunction requiring him to provide information needed to recover the sawmill and warned that it would ask the District Court to detain him if he refused. His wife was also questioned but gave no information.

The District Court initially refused detention on 27 May 2010, finding no “extraordinary reasons” and noting that less severe measures, such as a conditional fine, had not been tried. The Court of Appeal reversed on 28 June 2010, finding extraordinary reasons and that detention was proportionate given the size of the tax debt, the value of the hidden property, and the applicant’s persistent refusal. He was detained on 29 June 2010.

During detention, the applicant continued to refuse to disclose the sawmill’s location unless the tax and attachment decisions were corrected. He claimed health problems, including high blood pressure, panic attacks, prostate cancer, and asthma, but submitted no substantiating medical evidence and did not show he had complained to prison authorities. His detention was reviewed every two weeks by the District Court, with oral hearings and opportunities to appeal. On 9 August 2010, the District Court found continued detention disproportionate and ordered his immediate release. He had been detained for 42 days. The Enforcement Authority later revoked the writ, and a police investigation into breach of an official order was discontinued. The Chancellor of Justice rejected his compensation claim.

The main alleged violation was Article 5 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant argued that his detention was disproportionate: authorities should have used less intrusive measures, he was not interrogated during detention, no search for the sawmill was made, and detention served only to force him to confess or disclose information. The Government maintained that detention fell under Article 5 § 1(b) as lawful detention for non-compliance with a lawful order and was necessary to secure fulfilment of his legal obligation to provide information, thereby enabling recovery of tax debt.

The Court found the detention lawful and procedurally proper, with counsel, hearings, and periodic review. Its purpose was to secure compliance with the obligation to reveal the sawmill’s location, not to punish him, and release would have been immediate upon compliance. Proportionality weighed in favour of the State: tax recovery is an important general interest; a conditional fine would likely have been futile because he had no other assets and had firmly refused; and no useful search was possible without location information. Although 42 days was relatively long, it resulted from his refusal and was regularly reviewed. Thus, no Article 5 § 1 violation was found.

The applicant also alleged Article 3 inhuman or degrading treatment due to isolation, denied medication, and being held with dangerous criminals. The Court rejected this as manifestly ill-founded because he provided no evidence or complaints to domestic authorities.
001-140020:
F.G. v. Sweden (Application no. 43611/11) concerns an Iranian national, born in 1962, who sought asylum in Sweden and alleged that his expulsion to Iran would violate Articles 2 and 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights—the right to life and the prohibition of torture, inhuman or degrading treatment. The application was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 12 July 2011. The applicant was granted anonymity. On 25 October 2011, the Court applied Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, indicating to the Swedish Government that he should not be expelled to Iran during the proceedings. The provided text is the Fifth Section Chamber judgment of 16 January 2014; the case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 23 March 2016.

F.G. applied for asylum and a residence permit in Sweden on 16 November 2009. He claimed that in Iran he had worked with individuals connected to universities who opposed the regime, mainly by creating and publishing web pages. He said he was arrested in April 2007 with another person, released after 24 hours, and then hospitalised for ten days due to high blood pressure. Before the 12 June 2009 presidential elections, he worked with the Green Movement, which supported Mousavi, spreading its message via the Internet. The day before the elections, he and friends were arrested, questioned, and detained overnight at a polling station. After the elections, he participated in demonstrations and other activities. In September 2009 he was arrested again and imprisoned for twenty days. In October 2009 he was taken before the Revolutionary Court, which released him after one day on condition that he cooperate with the authorities and spy on his friends. He agreed, gave his business premises as a guarantee, and promised not to participate in demonstrations and to respond to their summons.

After his release in a park, he found that his business premises had been searched. He had kept politically sensitive material there, which the authorities must have noticed, and his passport and other documents were gone. On 2 November 2009 he was summoned to appear before the Revolutionary Court. He contacted a friend, who arranged for a smuggler to help him leave Iran. He later converted to Christianity after arriving in Sweden. He submitted a summons from the Revolutionary Court requiring him to present himself at Evin prison in Tehran on 2 November 2009.

On 29 April 2010, the Swedish Migration Board rejected his request. It found that he had not proven his identity but that his Iranian citizenship was probable. On the asylum claim, the Board held that participation in demonstrations or affiliation with the Green Movement could not by itself give rise to a risk of persecution, ill-treatment, or punishment on return to Iran. It also raised credibility concerns: the applicant had changed parts of his story, particularly the number of times he had been arrested, and could not name the park where he said he had been released, leading the Board to question whether he had been arrested at all. The Board further considered his political activities limited, noting that after the 2007 questioning and until the 2009 elections he had been able to continue working on web pages containing critical material even though the authorities were allegedly aware of his activities.

These facts were central to the alleged Articles 2 and 3 violation. F.G. claimed that removal to Iran would expose him to serious harm, including possible death, torture, or ill-treatment, because of his political activities, his forced agreement to cooperate with the authorities, the Revolutionary Court summons, and his conversion. The Swedish authorities’ refusal rested on credibility findings and their assessment that his activities did not establish a real risk. The Court therefore had to decide whether expelling him would breach Sweden’s Convention obligations.

In *F.G. v. Sweden* (Application no. 43611/11), the applicant was an Iranian national, born in 1962, who applied for asylum and a residence permit in Sweden on 16 November 2009. He alleged that his expulsion to Iran would violate Articles 2 and 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, because he would face death, torture, or inhuman or degrading treatment. The European Court of Human Rights applied Rule 39 on 25 October 2011, indicating to Sweden that he should not be expelled during the proceedings. The application had been lodged on 12 July 2011.

The facts said to create the alleged risk were as follows. In Iran, the applicant claimed he had worked with people connected to different universities who opposed the regime. His main work was creating and publishing web pages. In April 2007 he and another person were arrested; he was released after 24 hours and then hospitalised for ten days due to high blood pressure. Before the presidential elections of 12 June 2009, he worked with the Green Movement, which supported Mousavi, by spreading its message via the Internet. The day before the elections, he and friends were arrested, questioned, and detained overnight in a polling station. After the elections, he participated in demonstrations and other activities. In September 2009 he was arrested again and imprisoned for twenty days. In October 2009 he was taken before the Revolutionary Court, which released him after one day on condition that he cooperate with the authorities and spy on his friends. He agreed, gave his business premises as a guarantee, promised not to participate in demonstrations, and promised to respond to summonses. After being released in a park, he found that his business premises had been searched. He had kept politically sensitive material there, which the authorities must have noticed, and his passport and other documents were gone. On 2 November 2009 he was summoned to appear before the Revolutionary Court. A friend then helped him leave Iran through a smuggler. After arriving in Sweden, he converted to Christianity. He submitted, among other things, a summons from the Revolutionary Court requiring him to present himself at Evin prison in Tehran on 2 November 2009.

The Swedish Migration Board rejected his request on 29 April 2010. It found that he had not proven his identity but that he had made his identity and Iranian citizenship probable. On the asylum claim, the Board held that participation in demonstrations or affiliation with the Green Movement could not, by itself, create a risk of persecution, ill-treatment, or punishment on return to Iran. It also found reason to question his credibility: he had changed parts of his story, particularly the number of times he had been arrested, and could not name the park where he claimed to have been released. The Board therefore doubted whether he had been arrested at all. It further considered that his political activities had been limited, noting that after the 2007 questioning and until the 2009 elections he had continued working on web pages containing critical material, even though the authorities were allegedly aware of his activities.

Thus, the key facts relevant to the alleged Articles 2 and 3 violation were his political and internet activities, claimed arrests and detention, the Revolutionary Court summons and conditions of release, the search of his premises and missing documents, his departure via smuggler, and his post-arrival conversion to Christianity. He argued that these matters would expose him to serious harm if returned. The Swedish authorities’ refusal rested largely on credibility doubts and the view that his activities did not establish a real risk. The case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 23 March 2016.

In *Aleksandr Vladimirovich Smirnov v. Ukraine* (no. 69250/11, judgment 13 March 2014), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by a Russian national concerning (1) inhuman and degrading conditions of detention in the Slavyanoserbsk Colony and (2) breach of his right to mount a defence in criminal proceedings.

**Criminal proceedings and Article 6 complaint.** On 5 December 2002 Smirnov was stopped by police at an Odessa bus station for lacking identity documents and detained. He alleged that until 23 December he was held alternately in a vagrants’ holding facility and police detention facilities in Kakhovka, Kherson and Mykolayiv, questioned off the record about an alleged terrorist/communist group, and beaten and tortured. Official records showed he was medically examined on 9 and 14 December with no injuries or complaints noted; he was held in Kakhovka from 14 to 18 December, questioned as a witness on 14–15 December about the communist movement and the newspaper *Soviet rabochikh deputatov*, and took part in a confrontation on 17 December. On 23 December he gave a handwritten confession to the Security Service of Ukraine in Mykolayiv, admitting distribution of the newspaper and involvement with two others in an October 2002 rubbish-bin explosion near the SSU headquarters in Kyiv. He was arrested the same day as a terrorist suspect, notified of his right to a lawyer, and said he wished to consult one before questioning. On 24 December, minutes after again confirming that wish, he signed a waiver and was questioned without a lawyer, repeating and expanding his confession. A lawyer engaged by his mother was admitted on 26 December. At trial he pleaded not guilty, alleged unlawful detention and torture from 5 to 23 December, and claimed his self-incriminating statements were false. In 2004 he was convicted, with the court relying on his 23 and 24 December statements, and sentenced to eight years from 5 December 2002. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction in 2005. The ECtHR found a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c): despite the official arrest date, the applicant had been de facto in custody and treated as a suspect from 5 December; he had no lawyer access until 23 December without compelling reason; his 24 December waiver was not unequivocal because it came minutes after requesting a lawyer and before access; and the statements obtained were used as a basis for conviction, irretrievably prejudicing his defence.

**Detention conditions and Article 3 complaint.** From November 2005 to September 2007 Smirnov was held in Slavyanoserbsk Colony No. 60, in maximum-security cell no. 201. He alleged the cell, about 30 square metres, held 10 to 16 inmates, with confinement all day except one hour’s exercise. He complained of passive smoking without ventilation, winter temperatures around 8°C, poor lighting due to non-transparent windows and weak bulbs, inadequate food requiring parcels, refused transfer or fan, and inadequate medical care, including delayed dental treatment until his mother supplied materials in May 2007. The Government disputed this, claiming the cell measured 32 square metres for eight inmates, with adequate ventilation, heating of 19–22°C, sufficient food, and regular medical checks. The Court found the physical conditions violated Article 3, mainly because the Government did not rebut allegations of severe overcrowding—2 to 3 square metres per inmate versus the CPT-recommended 4 square metres—and poor ventilation, heating, lighting and nutrition over nearly two years. It rejected the medical-assistance complaint as manifestly ill-founded.

Aleksandr Vladimirovich Smirnov v. Ukraine (Application no. 69250/11) concerned a Russian national prosecuted in Ukraine for communist- and terrorist-related offences and later detained in the Slavyanoserbsk Correctional Colony. He alleged violations of Article 3 of the Convention due to detention conditions and of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) due to breach of his right to mount a defence.

**Criminal proceedings and right to defence.** On 5 December 2002 the applicant was stopped by police at an Odessa bus station for lacking identity documents and detained. He alleged that until 23 December 2002 he was held in various police facilities, questioned off the record about alleged involvement with a terrorist/communist group, and beaten and tortured. Official records stated he was arrested only on 23 December 2002, but Kakhovka police later admitted he had been held there as an “arrestee under investigation” from 14 to 18 December. He was questioned as a witness on 14–15 December and participated in a confrontation on 17 December. On 23 December he gave a handwritten confession that he had distributed the newspaper *Soviet rabochikh deputatov* and, with others, had blown up a rubbish bin near the Security Service of Ukraine headquarters in Kyiv in October 2002. He was then arrested, notified of his right to counsel, and expressed a wish to consult a lawyer. On 24 December, however, minutes after again confirming that wish, he signed a waiver and was questioned without a lawyer, reiterating his confession. A lawyer was admitted on 26 December. At trial he pleaded not guilty, alleging unlawful detention, torture, and false self-incriminating statements. On 19 July 2004 the Regional Court convicted him, relying significantly on his 23–24 December statements, and sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment from 5 December 2002. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction in 2005.

The European Court of Human Rights found that the applicant had been de facto in custody and treated as a suspect from 5 December 2002, despite the official arrest date. He should therefore have had access to a lawyer before his first questioning. No compelling reason justified denying him access from 5 to 23 December. His waiver on 24 December, made minutes after requesting a lawyer and without prior legal consultation, was not unequivocal. The later use of those confessions at trial irretrievably prejudiced his defence, notwithstanding his later legal representation and retraction. Article 6 was therefore violated.

**Detention conditions.** From November 2005 to September 2007 the applicant was held in the Slavyanoserbsk Colony’s maximum-security unit. He alleged that his cell, about 30 square metres, held 10–16 inmates, leaving only 2–3 square metres per person; that he was confined all day except for one hour’s exercise; and that there was no ventilation, heavy passive smoking, poor heating down to 8°C, inadequate lighting, insufficient food, and inadequate medical care, including delayed dental treatment. The Government disputed these claims, saying the cell was designed for eight inmates and conditions were adequate.

The Court found the physical-conditions complaint admissible. Because the Government failed to provide rigorous evidence rebutting the applicant’s detailed allegations, and because the personal space fell below the CPT-recommended minimum of 4 square metres, the Court held that the physical conditions amounted to degrading treatment in violation of Article 3. The medical-assistance complaint was rejected as manifestly ill-founded: the dental delay was not urgent and did not reach the Article 3 severity threshold.

**Case: Aleksandr Vladimirovich Smirnov v. Ukraine (Application no. 69250/11), judgment 13 March 2014.**

The applicant, a Russian national, was stopped by police in Odessa, Ukraine, on 5 December 2002 for lacking identity documents and placed in a holding facility for vagrants. He alleged that from 5 to 23 December 2002 he was held in various police detention facilities, questioned off the record about alleged involvement with a terrorist/communist group, and beaten and tortured. Official records stated he was arrested only on 23 December 2002, after giving a handwritten confession to the Security Service of Ukraine (SSU) that he had distributed the newspaper *Soviet rabochikh deputatov* and, with others, had blown up a rubbish bin near the SSU headquarters in Kyiv in October 2002. He was then arrested on suspicion of a terrorist offence and remanded.

Upon arrest, Smirnov was informed of his right to legal assistance and said he wished to consult a lawyer before questioning. On 24 December 2002, however, minutes after again confirming that he wanted a lawyer, he signed a waiver and was questioned without one, reiterating and expanding his earlier statements. A lawyer engaged by his mother was admitted on 26 December 2002. On 29 December, with counsel present, he admitted communist movement affiliation but denied the rubbish-bin explosion or terrorist activity. He later changed lawyers and, at trial from 2003, pleaded not guilty, alleging unlawful detention and torture between 5 and 23 December 2002, with false self-incriminating statements extracted through ill-treatment. Prosecutors refused to investigate his complaints. On 19 July 2004, the Odessa Regional Court convicted him, relying partly on his 23 and 24 December 2002 statements, finding no indication they were obtained by ill-treatment or in breach of procedural rights. He was sentenced to eight years, calculated from 5 December 2002. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction on 26 July 2005, dropping only the charge of membership in a criminal association.

Separately, from November 2005 to September 2007, Smirnov was detained in the Slavyanoserbsk Colony. He alleged that his cell, about 30 square metres, held 10–16 inmates; they were confined all day except one hour’s exercise; smoking was rampant without ventilation; heating was poor, sometimes around 8°C; daylight and artificial light were inadequate; and food was insufficient, requiring parcels from his mother. He also alleged inadequate medical care, including an ignored 2006 request for examination and delayed dental treatment until May 2007, when his mother bought supplies. The Government claimed the cell measured 32 square metres, was designed for eight inmates, had adequate heating, lighting, ventilation and food, and that medical check-ups showed satisfactory health; the dental treatment was non-urgent and eventually provided.

The European Court of Human Rights found the medical-care complaint manifestly ill-founded. On the physical conditions, the Government’s submissions were general and failed to rebut allegations of overcrowding—only 2–3 square metres per inmate versus the CPT-recommended 4 square metres—and poor ventilation, heating, lighting and nutrition. Given nearly two years in maximum security and most time spent in the cell, the conditions amounted to degrading treatment, violating Article 3.

Under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c), the Court found Smirnov was de facto in custody and treated as a suspect from 5 December 2002, despite the official arrest date, as confirmed by the sentence calculation. He had no lawyer from 5 to 23 December without compelling reason. His 24 December waiver was not unequivocal because it came minutes after requesting a lawyer and before access. Since his 23 and 24 December confessions were used as a basis for conviction, his right to mount a defence was irretrievably prejudiced, violating Article 6.
001-145575:
In *Ališić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Serbia, Slovenia and the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia* (Application no. 60642/08), three Bosnian citizens—Emina Ališić, Aziz Sadžak, and Sakib Šahdanović—complained that they could not withdraw their pre-dissolution foreign-currency savings from banks in Bosnia and Herzegovina after the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (SFRY) disintegrated. They relied on Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property), Article 14 (non-discrimination), and Article 13 (effective remedy).

Before the SFRY dissolved, Ališić and Sadžak had deposited foreign currency at Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo. In 1990 that bank became a branch, without legal personality, of Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana, a Slovenian bank, which assumed its rights, assets, and liabilities. By 31 December 1991 their balances were DEM 4,715 and DEM 129,874. Šahdanović had deposited money at the Tuzla branch of Investbanka, a Serbian bank; by 3 January 2002 his balances were DEM 63,880, 4 Austrian schillings, and USD 73.

Under the SFRY system, foreign-currency deposits were state-guaranteed and withdrawable on demand with interest. Banks commonly “redeposited” foreign currency with the National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY), which assumed currency risk. After the 1989–90 reforms, Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo became a branch of the Slovenian parent bank, while Investbanka became an independent Serbian bank with branches in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Following the SFRY’s dissolution in 1991–92, such deposits became “old” foreign-currency savings and were frozen or placed under special regimes in the successor states.

The applicants could not withdraw their savings. Their accounts were in branches located in Bosnia and Herzegovina but belonging to banks headquartered in Slovenia and Serbia. Bosnia and Herzegovina later assumed liability for old savings in domestic banks but expressly excluded savings in branches of foreign banks such as Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana and Investbanka. It said those were the responsibility of the successor states where the banks had their seats, though it offered assistance. A new domestic Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo briefly assumed liability in 1993, but a 2004 court decision held it was not the successor; bankruptcy followed. The Tuzla branch of Investbanka closed in 1992, and Investbanka entered bankruptcy in Serbia, where many savers failed to recover.

Serbia froze old savings and later repaid certain categories, but its 1998 and 2002 laws excluded citizens of other SFRY successor states and savings in foreign branches, and ceased related proceedings. Slovenia assumed state responsibility for old savings in domestic branches of all banks and restructured Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana, leaving the old bank with liability for branches in other successor states; it initially stayed proceedings pending succession talks, though Slovenian courts later ordered payment for the Sarajevo branch. Croatia and Macedonia took measures concerning their own branches, but the applicants’ accounts were not in those states.

The 2001 Agreement on Succession Issues provided that SFRY/NBY guarantees of hard-currency savings in commercial banks and their branches in any successor state would be negotiated under the Bank for International Settlements, protecting individual savers. Negotiations failed and the BIS withdrew. The applicants alleged that all five respondent states were responsible for the continued inability to withdraw their savings, violating property rights, discriminating against them, and failing to provide an effective remedy.

Case no. 60642/08, *Ališić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Serbia, Slovenia and the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia* (Grand Chamber, 16 July 2014), concerned three applicants—Emina Ališić, Aziz Sadžak and Sakib Šahdanović—citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina (the first also German) living in Germany. Before the dissolution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (SFRY), Ališić and Sadžak held foreign-currency savings at Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo, which in 1990 became a branch of Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana, a Slovenian bank. Šahdanović held foreign-currency savings at the Tuzla branch of Investbanka, a Serbian bank. Their balances included DEM 4,715 and DEM 129,874, and DEM 63,880 plus 4 Austrian schillings and 73 US dollars. After the SFRY broke up in 1991–92, these became “old” or “frozen” foreign-currency savings. The applicants could not withdraw them and alleged violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, alone and in conjunction with Article 14, and Article 13, against all five respondent States.

The background concerned SFRY banking. Foreign-currency deposits were encouraged, earned high interest, and were guaranteed by the State; savers could normally withdraw at any time. From the mid-1970s, banks used a “redepositing” scheme, transferring citizens’ foreign-currency deposits to the National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY), which assumed currency risk. In practice, funds were often recorded by accounting entries rather than physically transferred. For Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo, funds were transferred monthly to Ljubljana for Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana; only a small part returned. The unrepaid funds were recorded as claims against the NBY.

The 1989–90 reforms abolished the basic/associated bank system. Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo became a branch without legal personality of Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana, which assumed its rights and liabilities. Investbanka became an independent Serbian bank with a Tuzla branch in Bosnia and Herzegovina. After dissolution, emergency measures restricted withdrawals.

The successor States adopted differing measures. Bosnia and Herzegovina assumed the guarantee only for domestic banks; later laws expressly excluded branches of Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana and Investbanka. A new domestic Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo assumed liability in 1993, but in 2004 a court found it was not the successor and deleted the register entry; it later went bankrupt. The Tuzla branch of Investbanka closed in 1992. Serbia allowed repayment for some categories but excluded citizens of other successor States and savings in foreign branches; proceedings concerning old savings ceased. Investbanka became State-owned and bankrupt; savers were largely unsuccessful. Slovenia assumed the guarantee for domestic branches and restructured Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana; the old bank retained liability for branches in other successor States. Proceedings were stayed pending succession negotiations, though Slovenia’s Constitutional Court later declared the stays unconstitutional and Slovenian courts ordered payment to Sarajevo branch clients. Croatia and the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia took other repayment measures. The 2001 Agreement on Succession Issues required negotiation over SFRY/NBY guarantees, but BIS-assisted talks failed. The alleged violations therefore centre on the continuing legal obstacles, exclusions and frozen proceedings that prevented the applicants from withdrawing their savings.

In *Ališić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Serbia, Slovenia and the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia* (Application no. 60642/08), the European Court of Human Rights Grand Chamber delivered judgment on 16 July 2014. The applicants—three citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina residing in Germany—complained that they could not withdraw their pre-dissolution “old” foreign-currency savings from bank accounts in Bosnia and Herzegovina after the breakup of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (SFRY).

Two applicants, Ms Ališić and Mr Sadžak, had deposits at the Sarajevo branch of Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana. Before the 1989–90 banking reforms, that branch had been Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo, a basic bank. In 1990 it became a branch without legal personality of Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana, a Slovenian bank, which assumed its rights, assets and liabilities. Their balances were approximately DEM 4,715 and DEM 129,874. The third applicant, Mr Šahdanović, held accounts at the Tuzla branch of Investbanka, a Serbian bank, with balances of about DEM 63,880, 4 Austrian schillings and USD 73.

Before the SFRY dissolved, foreign-currency deposits were encouraged and guaranteed by the State. Banks often redeposited such funds with the National Bank of Yugoslavia under a “redepositing” scheme. After dissolution in 1991–92, these deposits became “old” or “frozen” foreign-currency savings. The successor States adopted different measures. Bosnia and Herzegovina excluded liability for savings in local branches of foreign banks such as Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana and Investbanka, stating that liability lay with the State where the bank had its seat, while offering only assistance. A domestic Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo was incorporated in 1993 and initially assumed liability, but a 2004 court decision found it was not the successor. Investbanka’s Tuzla branch closed in 1992; Investbanka later entered bankruptcy in Serbia.

Slovenia restructured Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana. The old bank retained liability for “old” savings in its branches outside Slovenia, but proceedings were stayed pending succession negotiations; later Slovenian courts ordered it to pay some clients. Serbia treated Investbanka as State-owned and in bankruptcy, and froze savings of citizens of other successor States pending succession negotiations, also halting related proceedings.

The applicants alleged that all five respondent States violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property), alone and in conjunction with Article 14 (non-discrimination), and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy). They argued that their inability to withdraw their savings amounted to an unjustified interference with their possessions and that no effective remedy existed.

The key issue was which successor State(s) bore responsibility for “old” foreign-currency savings deposited in branches located in one State but belonging to banks headquartered in another. The Grand Chamber ultimately held that Slovenia and Serbia were responsible for the applicants’ savings in the Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana and Investbanka branches respectively. It found violations by Slovenia and Serbia of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 13. The complaints against Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia and the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia were not sustained.

In *Bokal v. Slovenia* (Application no. 34386/10, judgment of 3 April 2014), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by Ms Lidija Bokal, a Slovenian national born in 1955, that her civil proceedings lasted unreasonably long and that Slovenia lacked an effective remedy for excessive length.

On 21 July 1997 the applicant began civil proceedings before the Ljubljana Local Court against M.P. and N.M. She sought a determination that a sale contract concerning an apartment in a building partially owned by her was invalid and requested that a note on dispute be entered in the Land Register. She stated the disputed value as SIT 500,000 (about EUR 2,100). On 20 August 1997 the court rejected her request to enter the note on dispute. Her appeal was dismissed by the Ljubljana Higher Court on 4 March 1998. Service problems arose, and documents were posted on the court notice board.

The proceedings then stagnated. Although the applicant requested a hearing in April 1998 and priority in March 2000, the court dismissed her priority request in April 2000. In June 2000, a third party, D.S., who had bought the apartment, joined the proceedings. In March 2002, D.S. also complained through a supervisory appeal that the pending case prevented disposal of the apartment. The first hearing was not scheduled until 13 February 2004, then postponed to 26 March 2004—more than six and a half years after the claim was filed. At that point the applicant increased the disputed value to SIT 1,100,000 (about EUR 4,600), and the court modified the value accordingly. Further hearings occurred between April and June 2004, and on 4 June 2004 the court partially upheld the applicant’s claim. Service of the judgment again caused difficulties.

The applicant appealed on 27 September 2004. In December 2005 the Higher Court returned the file, instructing the Local Court to serve the first defendant and decide an interim-order request. In March 2006 the judgment and appeal were served by posting. The Local Court dismissed the interim-order request; the Higher Court dismissed the applicant’s appeals on 21 June 2006. The applicant then lodged an appeal on points of law. On 23 October 2008 the Supreme Court rejected it on procedural grounds, finding that the lower court had wrongly allowed the increase in disputed value, so the threshold for that appeal had not been met. The Constitutional Court dismissed her constitutional appeal on 26 November 2009, served on 1 December 2009.

The Government argued the application was out of time, claiming the case ended in July 2006 when the appeal on points of law was rejected on procedural grounds. The ECtHR disagreed: the applicant could not be penalized for trusting the lower court’s decision on value, and the proceedings ended only on 1 December 2009. The application was therefore admissible.

On the merits, the ECtHR found the relevant period ran from 21 July 1997 to 1 December 2009—twelve years and four months across four levels of jurisdiction. Considering the case’s complexity, the applicant’s conduct, the authorities’ conduct, and what was at stake, and noting the Government’s failure to present arguments on those criteria, the Court held that the length was excessive and violated Article 6 § 1’s “reasonable time” requirement. It further found a violation of Article 13 because Slovenia’s available remedies for excessively long proceedings were ineffective, as established in prior cases such as *Tomažič v. Slovenia* and *Robert Lesjak v. Slovenia*.

In *Bokal v. Slovenia* (Application no. 34386/10, judgment 3 April 2014), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Article 6 § 1 (right to a hearing within a reasonable time) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) arising from lengthy civil proceedings in Slovenia.

On 21 July 1997, Ms Lidija Bokal instituted civil proceedings before the Ljubljana Local Court against M.P. and N.M. She sought a determination regarding the validity of a sale contract concerning an apartment in a building partially owned by her and proposed that a note on dispute be entered in the Land Register. She initially indicated the disputed value as SIT 500,000 (approximately EUR 2,100). On 20 August 1997, the court rejected her proposal to enter the note; her appeal was dismissed on 4 March 1998. After a supervisory appeal to the Ministry of Justice, the court reported on 18 February 1998 that the case could not be given priority. On 21 April 1998, the applicant requested a hearing, and on 27 March 2000 she requested priority; that request was dismissed on 5 April 2000.

In June 2000, a third-party intervener, D.S., who had bought the apartment, joined the proceedings. In March 2002, the third party also lodged a supervisory appeal, stating that the pending proceedings prevented her from disposing of the apartment. The first hearing was scheduled for 13 February 2004 but postponed to 26 March 2004. Shortly before it, on 18 March 2004, the applicant raised the disputed value to SIT 1,100,000 (approximately EUR 4,600). At the first main hearing on 26 March 2004, the court modified the value as requested. Further hearings were held between April and June 2004, and on 4 June 2004 the court partially upheld the applicant’s claim.

The applicant appealed on 27 September 2004. On 7 December 2005, the Ljubljana Higher Court returned the file, instructing the lower court to serve appeal documents properly and decide on the applicant’s interim-order request. On 6 January 2006, the Local Court asked the applicant to pay fees and supplement her interim-order proposal. On 3 March 2006, the judgment and appeal were served on the first defendant by posting them on the court’s notice board. On 20 March 2006, the Local Court dismissed the interim-order request; the applicant appealed. On 21 June 2006, the Higher Court dismissed her appeals. She then lodged an appeal on points of law. On 23 October 2008, the Supreme Court rejected it on procedural grounds, holding that the lower court had wrongly allowed the disputed value to be modified late, meaning the value was below the threshold for such an appeal. The Constitutional Court dismissed her constitutional appeal on 26 November 2009, served on 1 December 2009.

The Government argued that the application was out of time because the appeal on points of law had been rejected on procedural grounds and the proceedings had effectively ended in 2006. The Court rejected that argument, finding that proceedings capable of influencing the outcome fell within Article 6 and that the applicant could not be penalized for trusting the lower court’s value modification. The proceedings therefore ended on 1 December 2009, and the application was admissible.

On the merits, the Court found that the proceedings lasted from 21 July 1997 to 1 December 2009—approximately 12 years and 4 months across four levels of jurisdiction. Considering the complexity, the applicant’s conduct, the authorities’ conduct, and what was at stake, the Court found the length excessive, violating Article 6 § 1. It further found, relying on *Tomažič v. Slovenia* and *Robert Lesjak v. Slovenia*, that the available domestic remedies for excessive length were ineffective, violating Article 13.

**Case Bokal v. Slovenia (Application no. 34386/10, 3 April 2014)** concerned a Slovenian applicant, Ms Lidija Bokal, born in 1955, who complained that civil proceedings lasted unreasonably long and that Slovenia lacked an effective domestic remedy for excessive length, contrary to Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention.

On 21 July 1997, Bokal instituted civil proceedings before the Ljubljana Local Court against M.P. and N.M. She sought a declaration that a sale contract between the defendants concerning an apartment in a building partly owned by her was invalid, and requested that a note of dispute be entered in the Land Register. She stated the disputed value as SIT 500,000 (approximately EUR 2,100). On 20 August 1997, the court rejected her proposal to enter the note; her appeal was dismissed by the Ljubljana Higher Court on 4 March 1998. The case then remained pending with little progress. She requested a hearing in April 1998 and priority in March 2000, but her priority request was dismissed in April 2000. In June 2000, a third party, D.S., who had bought the apartment, joined the proceedings. In March 2002, the third party filed a supervisory appeal complaining that the pending case prevented her from disposing of the apartment. The first hearing was not scheduled until February 2004 and was postponed to 26 March 2004. In March 2004, Bokal increased the disputed value to SIT 1,100,000 (approximately EUR 4,600), and the court accepted that modification at the first main hearing. Further hearings were held between April and June 2004, and on 4 June 2004 the court partially upheld her claim.

Service problems followed. The judgment was served on the first defendant and third party by posting it on the court’s notice board. Bokal appealed in September 2004. In December 2005, the Higher Court returned the file, instructing the Local Court to serve documents properly and decide her interim-order request. In January 2006, the Local Court asked her to pay fees and supplement her interim-order proposal. In March 2006, the judgment and appeal were served on the first defendant by posting. Her interim-order request was dismissed in March 2006, and her appeal against that decision was dismissed by the Higher Court in June 2006. She then lodged an appeal on points of law. In October 2008, the Supreme Court rejected it on procedural grounds, holding that the Local Court had wrongly allowed her to modify the disputed value at a later stage; therefore the original value was below the threshold for an appeal on points of law. Her constitutional appeal was dismissed in November 2009 and served on 1 December 2009.

Before the European Court, Bokal alleged that the length of the proceedings violated Article 6 § 1 and that domestic remedies for excessive length were ineffective under Article 13. The Government argued the application was out of time, claiming the proceedings had ended in July 2006 because the appeal on points of law was rejected on procedural grounds. The Court rejected this, finding that proceedings capable of influencing the outcome fell within Article 6 and that Bokal should not be penalized for relying on the lower court’s acceptance of the value modification. The proceedings therefore ended on 1 December 2009, making the application timely.

On the merits, the Court found the relevant period lasted from 21 July 1997 to 1 December 2009—12 years and 4 months across four levels of jurisdiction. Considering the complexity, the applicant’s conduct, the authorities’ conduct, and what was at stake, and noting the Government’s lack of substantive arguments, the Court held that the length was excessive and violated Article 6 § 1. It further found a violation of Article 13 because no effective remedy existed for the excessive length of proceedings.
