In *Omelchenko v. Ukraine* (no. 34592/06, 17 July 2014), the applicant, a Ukrainian national, was convicted of robbery and murder for profit. The case mainly concerned Article 6 §§1 and 3(c) ECHR—the right to a fair trial, legal assistance, and the privilege against self-incrimination.

On 27 October 2004, V.’s body was found in Simferopol; she had knife wounds and missing belongings. On 28 October, police obtained an expert opinion that a fingerprint on V.’s notebook could belong to Omelchenko. On 29 October, officers searched his home about 120 km away, seized clothes, and took him to the police station in Simferopol. No formal arrest record was drawn up. On 29–30 October he was questioned as a witness, without a lawyer. On 30 October he confessed to murdering a passer-by to steal her belongings and said he killed V. with a kitchen knife.

On 31 October he was questioned as a suspect and signed a written waiver of legal assistance. A medical examination found no injuries. He was released under an undertaking not to abscond, but on 1 November he was immediately arrested for an administrative offence—swearing, spitting, and vagrancy—and detained for ten days. While in administrative detention, he was questioned again on 4, 9, and 10 November about the murder and robbery, each time signing a waiver of legal representation. He alleged that the administrative arrest was a pretext to keep him available for criminal questioning without procedural safeguards.

On 11 November a court remanded him in custody in the criminal case. A lawyer was admitted on 16 November but allegedly did not visit until 26 December. On 12 January 2005, the charge was reclassified from simple murder (Article 115 §1) to murder for profit (Article 115 §2), which could carry life imprisonment and required mandatory legal representation. On 28 February 2005, with a new lawyer present, he was first questioned as an accused. He retracted his confessions, pleaded innocent, and claimed they had been obtained under police pressure during unlawful detention. The prosecutor refused to investigate his allegations.

He was convicted in April 2005 and sentenced to 15 years. The Supreme Court quashed the conviction in July 2005, ordering closer examination of the confessions and contradictory evidence. On retrial in November 2005, he was again convicted; the courts relied on his early confessions, found no ill-treatment, and accepted the waivers as valid because he had initially been suspected only of simple murder. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction in March 2006.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 6 §§1 and 3(c). It held that the police already suspected him when they took him into custody, yet he was questioned as a witness without a lawyer and without an arrest record; the 30 October confession therefore breached his rights to legal assistance and against self-incrimination. The later waivers were not genuine or unequivocal: they were signed while he was in off-record detention or administrative arrest, vulnerable and without proper guarantees. The Court also condemned the practice of initially charging a lesser offence to avoid mandatory legal representation and later reclassifying it after obtaining confessions. Because the domestic courts used the confessions as a basis for conviction and failed to remedy the breach, the proceedings were unfair. Other complaints were rejected as manifestly ill-founded.

In *Omelchenko v. Ukraine* (Application no. 34592/06, judgment 17 July 2014), the European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 6 §§1 and 3(c) of the Convention. The case concerned the applicant’s criminal conviction in Ukraine for armed robbery and murder for profit, and his complaints that he was denied legal assistance at the start of the investigation and that self-incriminating statements obtained in breach of his defence rights were used to convict him.

On 27 October 2004, V.’s body was found in Simferopol; she had been stabbed and robbed. On 28 October, police obtained an expert opinion that a fingerprint on V.’s notebook could belong to the applicant. On 29 October, officers searched his home, seized clothing, and took him to the police station. No formal arrest record was drawn up. Although police already suspected him, he was questioned on 29–30 October as a witness, without a lawyer. On 30 October he confessed to murdering V. and stealing her belongings. He remained in unrecorded police custody until 1 November 2004.

On 31 October he was questioned as a suspect. He was informed of his rights and signed a waiver of legal assistance. A medical examination found no injuries. An undertaking not to abscond was imposed, and he claimed he was released on 1 November. Immediately afterward, he was arrested for an administrative offence—swearing, spitting and vagrancy—and detained for ten days. While in administrative detention, on 4, 9 and 10 November, he was again questioned as a criminal suspect and again signed waivers of counsel. On 11 November he was remanded in custody in the murder case. A lawyer was admitted on 16 November but allegedly did not visit him until 26 December, and no questioning occurred in the lawyer’s presence.

On 12 January 2005, the charge was reclassified from simple murder under Article 115 §1 to murder for profit under Article 115 §2, which could carry life imprisonment and required mandatory legal representation. On 28 February 2005, with a new lawyer present, the applicant was first questioned as an accused. He retracted his confessions, pleaded innocent, and alleged police pressure, unlawful detention and threats. The prosecutor refused to investigate. He was convicted on 5 April 2005 and sentenced to fifteen years. The Supreme Court quashed the conviction on 21 July 2005, requiring verification of the confessions’ admissibility. On retrial, the court again convicted him on 18 November 2005, relying partly on the early confessions and finding the waivers valid. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction on 16 March 2006.

The ECtHR found the waivers problematic. Police had suspected the applicant from 28 October yet questioned him as a witness without a lawyer while he was held off the record. His first confession was therefore obtained without basic procedural guarantees against self-incrimination and without legal assistance. The later waivers, signed while he was in unrecorded or administrative detention, were not genuine and unequivocal; the administrative arrest appeared to be a pretext to keep him available for questioning, reflecting a structural problem in Ukraine. The initial simple-murder charge also appeared artificially chosen to avoid mandatory counsel, with the more serious charge added only after confessions were obtained. Although the applicant retracted his confessions once represented, the domestic courts used them as part of the evidence and failed to remedy the breach. The Court therefore held that his inability to obtain legal assistance at the beginning of the investigation and the use of his confessional statements as a basis for conviction breached Article 6 §§1 and 3(c). Other complaints were rejected as manifestly ill-founded.

In *Omelchenko v. Ukraine* (no. 34592/06, 17 July 2014), the European Court of Human Rights examined a Ukrainian national’s complaint that criminal proceedings against him breached his right to legal assistance and privilege against self-incrimination under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c). The applicant, Mr Omelchenko, was later convicted of armed robbery and murder for profit.

On 27 October 2004, V.’s body was found in Simferopol; she had multiple knife wounds and missing belongings. On 28 October, police obtained an expert opinion that a fingerprint on V.’s notebook possibly belonged to the applicant. On 29 October, officers searched his home some 120 km away, seized clothes, and took him to Simferopol police station. No formal arrest record was made. He was questioned on 29 and 30 October as a witness, not as a suspect, and without a lawyer. On 30 October he confessed to murdering V. and stealing her phone. He later alleged this confession was extracted under pressure during unlawful, unrecorded detention.

On 31 October he was questioned as a suspect, informed of his rights, and signed a written waiver of legal assistance. A medical assessment found no injuries. An undertaking not to abscond was imposed. On 1 November, after release, he was immediately arrested for administrative offences (swearing, spitting, vagrancy) and detained for ten days. While in administrative detention, on 4, 9 and 10 November, he was further questioned about the murder and robbery, signing fresh waivers before each session. On 11 November a court remanded him in custody in the criminal case. A lawyer was admitted on 16 November but, according to the applicant, did not visit until 26 December and did not attend questioning.

On 12 January 2005 the charge was reclassified from simple murder (Article 115 § 1), which allowed waiver of counsel, to murder for profit (Article 115 § 2), which could carry life imprisonment and required mandatory legal representation. On 28 February 2005, with new lawyer R. present, the applicant was first questioned as an accused; he retracted his earlier confessions, pleaded innocent, and alleged unlawful detention, threats and ill-treatment. The prosecution refused to investigate. In April 2005 he was convicted and sentenced to fifteen years. The Supreme Court quashed the conviction in July 2005, noting that the courts should have examined whether the confessions were admissible and whether his detention had ulterior motives. In November 2005 he was again convicted, with the courts relying partly on the early confessions; this was upheld in March 2006.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c). Police already suspected the applicant when they questioned him as a witness without a lawyer, and his first confession was taken in unrecorded police custody without basic procedural safeguards. His later waivers, signed during unrecorded detention and administrative arrest, were not genuine or unequivocal; the administrative arrest appeared a pretext to keep him available for questioning, reflecting a structural problem in Ukraine. He was also not fully aware of the consequences of waiver, and the initial simple murder charge artificially avoided mandatory legal representation until after confessions were obtained. Because the domestic courts used those confessions as a basis for conviction and failed to remedy the breach, the fair-trial guarantee was violated. Other complaints were rejected as manifestly ill-founded.
001-141910:
Beraru v. Romania (ECtHR, 18 March 2014) concerned an Israeli national, Sorin Schumel Beraru, charged in Romania with bribery linked to the 2001 acquisition of CICO, a Romanian company sold at a state auction. In May 2001 an international arrest warrant was issued against him. Prosecutor H.G. later reported being offered USD 1.5 million to revoke the warrant. Her husband, H.D., was contacted by police officers connected to Beraru’s alleged intermediary, S.H.; authorities authorised telephone monitoring. On 14 June 2002, officers B.R. and U.I. were arrested while handing H.D. USD 99,700 as part of a sting.

The prosecution alleged that Beraru asked S.H. to resolve his Romanian legal problems. S.H. allegedly met officers B.R. and U.I. through officer B.S.L.; they claimed connections to H.G. and H.D. Negotiations allegedly led to a USD 1.5 million offer, with S.H. and the officers travelling to Tel Aviv and later Antwerp for part of the money. Beraru denied the charges, claiming S.H. had motives against him, that he rejected S.H.’s proposal, that he told lawyer A.M. to notify Romanian authorities of a bribe offer, and that the confiscated money came from S.H., not him.

The key Article 6 complaints concerned fair-trial violations. First, defence access to the file was severely restricted. Before the Bucharest Military Tribunal and later the Court of Appeal, Beraru’s chosen lawyers were initially denied copies of the file; they were not given the indictment or the transcripts/audio tapes of intercepted calls. Photocopying was limited to thirty pages despite a file of several hundred pages and only short daily access hours. Their repeated requests for access were largely refused. In January 2004 they sought to withdraw because they could not properly prepare the defence.

Second, the trial panel changed. A single judge heard the co-defendants and witnesses in February–March 2003. In May 2003 a second judge was added after most evidence had been taken, but witnesses and recordings were not reheard. The second judge nevertheless deliberated and signed the conviction. The ECtHR found this undermined the principle of immediacy, since the conviction rested on evidence not directly heard by the deciding panel.

Third, the prosecution relied heavily on transcripts of intercepted telephone conversations. A Hebrew interpreter warned of discrepancies between the transcripts and recordings. The court ordered a forensic expert report, but INEC later reported that the tapes were not original and could be copies, mixes, or fabrications; voice identification required originals. Instead of resolving these doubts, the court revoked the expert order and relied on the transcripts. The defence could not fully listen to the recordings, obtain taped copies, or effectively challenge their authenticity. Requests to play the tapes, admit expert/A.M. evidence, or investigate the money’s origin were rejected.

The High Court of Cassation and Justice upheld the conviction without curing these defects. The ECtHR concluded that the proceedings as a whole were unfair, violating Article 6 §§1 and 3, due to lack of immediacy, restricted access to the file, and reliance on contested, non-adversarially examined recordings and transcripts.

**Case: Beraru v. Romania (Application no. 40107/04), ECtHR, 18 March 2014**

The applicant, Sorin Schumel Beraru, an Israeli national, complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 of the Convention that the Romanian criminal proceedings against him were unfair. The case concerned his alleged involvement in bribery linked to the acquisition of a Romanian company, CICO.

In 2001, Romanian prosecutors began investigating the applicant for serious financial crimes connected to CICO’s acquisition. An international arrest warrant was issued in May 2001. The prosecution’s case later focused on an alleged bribe offered to prosecutor H.G. to revoke that warrant. In February 2002, H.G. reported that she had been offered USD 1.5 million. Authorities then monitored and recorded telephone conversations among those involved. In June 2002, police officers B.R. and U.I. were caught handing USD 99,700 to H.G.’s husband, H.D., in a sting operation.

The applicant, S.H., and three police officers were charged. The prosecution alleged that the applicant had asked S.H. to resolve his legal problems in Romania and had negotiated, through S.H. and police intermediaries, a USD 1.5 million bribe. The applicant denied this. He claimed S.H. and the officers solicited money from him, that he refused, and that he informed his lawyer, A.M., who allegedly notified Romanian authorities. He also claimed the confiscated money came from S.H., not him.

The alleged fair-trial violations arose mainly from three areas.

First, the composition of the trial court changed. The Bucharest Court of Appeal initially sat as a single judge. After May 2003, a second judge was added, but by then most evidence—including co-defendants’ statements, witness testimony, and the playing of recorded telephone conversations—had already been heard. The new judge did not rehear that evidence, yet deliberated and signed the judgment. The ECtHR found this breached the principle of immediacy.

Second, the applicant’s lawyers lacked proper access to the case file. Before the Military Tribunal, they were denied photocopying facilities, initially without reasons; later they were allowed only limited copies, despite a file of several hundred pages. They could not obtain copies of the transcripts of tapped phone calls. Similar difficulties persisted before the Court of Appeal. Their inability to prepare properly was so serious that they asked to withdraw from representation.

Third, the evidence was not taken or assessed adversarially. The prosecution relied heavily on transcripts of recorded phone conversations. The applicant challenged their authenticity, accuracy, and translation. The court ordered a technical expert report, then later revoked that order. In January 2004, INEC reported that the tapes were not original and could be copies, mixes, or fabricated. Nevertheless, the first-instance court convicted the applicant on 26 January 2004, relying on the transcripts and stating they left “little room for doubt,” while acknowledging other evidence was subjective. It did not reopen proceedings for the parties to comment on the INEC report. Requests to play the tapes, obtain taped copies, hear lawyer A.M., or adduce evidence about the money’s origin were refused.

The High Court of Cassation and Justice dismissed the applicant’s appeal in May 2004, confirming the first-instance findings without conducting a new examination or addressing the defence complaints. The ECtHR concluded that the defects were not remedied on appeal and that the proceedings as a whole did not satisfy the requirements of a fair trial under Article 6.

Case Name: **Beraru v. Romania** (Application no. 40107/04), European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, judgment of 18 March 2014.

The applicant, Sorin Schumel Beraru, an Israeli national, was prosecuted in Romania for bribery linked to the acquisition of the state-owned company CICO. Criminal proceedings began in 2001, and an international arrest warrant was issued against him. The case arose after prosecutor H.G. reported an offer of USD 1.5 million to revoke the arrest warrant. A sting operation followed, and two police intermediaries were arrested while handing USD 99,700 to H.G.’s husband. The applicant was accused of offering the bribe through S.H. and other intermediaries. He denied the charge, claiming S.H. acted without authority, that he had rejected proposals, and that he had asked his lawyer A.M. to inform Romanian authorities about a bribe offer.

The applicant complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 of the Convention that his criminal trial was unfair. His main allegations concerned three areas: the composition of the trial panel, access to the case file, and the taking and assessment of evidence.

First, before the Bucharest Court of Appeal, his lawyers initially had no real access to the file while the case was before the Military Tribunal. They were not given a copy of the indictment, could not photocopy documents, and were limited to thirty pages although the file ran to hundreds. They could not copy transcripts of tapped telephone conversations. Later requests for tapes and transcripts were also refused or restricted.

Second, the panel changed during the proceedings. A single judge heard most of the evidence—co-defendants, witnesses, prosecutor H.G. and her husband—between February and March 2003. In May 2003, after a change in the law, a second judge joined the panel. The evidence was not reheard. The second judge therefore deliberated and signed the conviction without directly hearing the main evidence.

Third, the prosecution relied on recordings of telephone conversations in Romanian and Hebrew. A court interpreter warned of discrepancies between the transcripts and the recordings. The court ordered a forensic report by INEC, but later revoked that order. INEC eventually reported that the tapes were not original and could be copies, mixes, or fabricated; voice identification was impossible without originals and proper equipment. Despite this, the first-instance court convicted the applicant in January 2004, relying heavily on the transcripts and stating they left little doubt, while acknowledging other evidence was subjective. Requests to play the tapes fully or admit further evidence about the money’s origin and A.M.’s statement were rejected.

On appeal, the High Court of Cassation and Justice dismissed the appeal in May 2004. It confirmed the first-instance findings and relied on the same evidence without directly hearing it or addressing the complaints about the recordings’ lawfulness, authenticity, and use.

The ECtHR found that the proceedings as a whole did not satisfy Article 6 §§ 1 and 3. The key defects were the lack of immediacy due to the changed panel, inadequate access to the file for the defence, reliance on contested recordings without proper adversarial testing, and the appeal court’s failure to remedy these problems. The Court therefore found a violation of the right to a fair trial.
001-146399:
**Summary of *Karin Andersson and Others v. Sweden* (Application no. 29878/09)**

The case originated from an application lodged against Sweden by eighteen property owners living near Umeå, close to a Natura 2000 protected area. The applicants complained under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention that they were denied effective access to court regarding decisions permitting the construction of a 10 km railway section (part of the "Botniabanan" project). The dispute concerned the impact of the railway's location on their property, including noise, vibrations, and reduced property value.

The domestic planning process had three key stages. First, in June 2003, the Government granted the National Rail Administration permission to construct the railway within a specified "corridor," finding it permissible despite environmental harm to a Natura 2000 area because no alternative solutions existed and the project served public interest. No appeal lay against this decision, but judicial review could be sought in the Supreme Administrative Court.

Three applicants petitioned for such a review. In December 2004, the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed their petitions without examining the merits, finding that it could not yet determine who would be sufficiently affected until a detailed railway plan was adopted. The court stated that affected parties could obtain judicial review of the later railway plan decision.

Subsequently, the Environmental Court granted construction permits, considering itself bound by the Government's permissibility decision. Appeals to the Environmental Court of Appeal and Supreme Court upheld this binding nature, limiting review to environmental compensation measures rather than the railway's location.

In June 2005, the National Rail Administration adopted the railway plan. Twelve applicants appealed to the Government, which rejected their appeals, referring back to the 2003 permissibility decision. All applicants then sought judicial review by the Supreme Administrative Court. In December 2008, that court rejected their petition, holding that the railway plan complied with the Government's binding permissibility decision. It reasoned that the location was determined at the permissibility stage; subsequent proceedings could only address details within the designated corridor. The court stated that challenges to location should have been made against the permissibility decision itself, despite its earlier 2004 ruling that such challenges were premature.

A dissenting judge noted that the railway plan had direct consequences for individuals, including expropriation rights, and that the court should have examined all objections, including alternative locations.

Regarding compensation, at least ten applicants received payments for requisitioned land or reduced property value, and noise barriers were erected near some properties. However, the core alleged violation was the lack of a full judicial review of the Government's binding decision fixing the railway's location, which allegedly affected their civil rights under Article 6 § 1. The applicants exhausted domestic remedies through the available judicial review processes, but the courts consistently declined to examine the merits of the location decision due to its binding character and the timing of the challenges. The case thus concerned whether Sweden provided effective access to court for determining civil rights affected by the railway's location.

**Karin Andersson and Others v. Sweden** concerned the planning of a 10 km railway section near Umeå, part of the larger Botniabanan project. The eighteen applicants were Swedish nationals who owned homes or land near a Natura 2000 protected area. Six applicants owned property within the “corridor” proposed for the railway; the other twelve owned property outside it, though some land was as close as 50 metres to the corridor.

In 1999, the National Rail Administration applied to the Government for permission under the Environmental Code to construct the railway. In 2003, the Government granted permission for the railway within the proposed corridor, subject to conditions including adoption of a railway plan and environmental compensation measures. Crucially, the Government’s permissibility decision was binding on later proceedings: courts and authorities could not re-examine the general permissibility or location of the railway.

Three applicants sought judicial review of the 2003 decision in the Supreme Administrative Court. In December 2004, that court dismissed the petitions for lack of standing. It held that it could not yet be determined who would be sufficiently affected until the railway plan was adopted, and that affected owners could seek review later. One judge dissented, considering that standing should have been investigated because the Government’s decision would bind later stages.

Subsequent proceedings took place in several stages. The County Administrative Board and Environmental Court granted construction permits. The Environmental Court of Appeal quashed those decisions because compensation measures had not been properly examined, but on remand the Environmental Court again granted permits, considering itself bound by the Government’s permissibility decision. The Environmental Court of Appeal affirmed in 2007, and the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal in 2008.

In 2005, the National Rail Administration adopted the railway plan. Several applicants appealed to the Government, complaining about the specific route, noise and vibrations. The Government rejected the appeals, citing the 2003 permissibility decision. The applicants then sought judicial review in the Supreme Administrative Court. In December 2008, that court rejected the request, finding that the railway plan was within the permitted corridor and that the permissibility and general location could not be reviewed at that stage. A dissenting judge argued that the railway plan directly affected individuals, including through expropriation rights, and that a full review should have included alternative locations.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged violations of Articles 6 and 8. They claimed they had been denied effective access to court to challenge decisions on the railway construction that affected their homes, property, health and enjoyment of their land. The Government contested admissibility, arguing that twelve applicants outside the corridor were not sufficiently affected, that two applicants were not victims, and that domestic remedies had not been exhausted.

The Court rejected those objections. It found that complaints about noise, vibrations, property value and enjoyment of the home involved “civil rights” under Article 6. Even applicants outside the corridor could be sufficiently affected, especially as at least ten had received compensation. On exhaustion, the Court observed that the 2003 permissibility decision was binding, so challenging it was natural. However, the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed that challenge as premature and said review would be available later. Yet later courts treated the permissibility decision as binding and limited their review. Therefore, the judicial-review remedy was not effective at the relevant time. The core issue was the applicants’ lack of effective access to court to contest the railway’s permissibility and location.

This case concerns an application by eighteen Swedish nationals against Sweden under the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants owned homes or land near Umeå, close to a Natura 2000 nature-protection area. The National Rail Administration planned the final 10 km section of the Botniabanan railway through a river area. In 1999 it applied to the Government for permission under the Environmental Code to construct the railway within a defined “corridor,” presenting several route alternatives and recommending the “alternative east.” Some applicants owned property inside the corridor; others owned houses or land outside it, roughly 50 to 2,500 metres away.

In June 2003 the Government granted permissibility for the project, allowing construction in the corridor subject to conditions. The NRA had to adopt a railway plan before July 2009 and a plan for environmental compensation measures in the Natura 2000 areas. The Government stated that the project could proceed despite environmental harm if there were no alternative solutions and if it served public interest. Three applicants sought judicial review of this decision in the Supreme Administrative Court. In December 2004 that court dismissed their petitions, holding that it could not yet determine who would be sufficiently affected because the exact railway route had not been fixed. It said affected persons could seek review later when the railway plan was adopted. A dissenting judge considered that individual interests should have been examined because the Government’s decision would bind later proceedings.

In subsequent permit proceedings, the Environmental Court found itself bound by the Government’s 2003 permissibility decision. It granted construction permits, limiting its review mainly to environmental compensation measures. The Environmental Court of Appeal affirmed the permits in December 2007, and the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal in May 2008.

In June 2005 the NRA adopted a railway plan. Twelve applicants appealed to the Government, complaining about the chosen route and nuisance such as noise and vibrations affecting their property. In June 2007 the Government rejected the appeals, referring to its 2003 permissibility decision and finding the route within the permitted corridor. All applicants then sought judicial review in the Supreme Administrative Court. In December 2008 that court rejected the request, holding that the railway plan complied with the 2003 decision and that the permissibility and general location of the railway were binding and could not be reviewed at the plan stage. Only the precise location within the corridor could be examined. One judge dissented, noting that adoption of the railway plan had direct consequences, including possible expropriation, and that all objections should have been considered.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged that they had been denied effective access to court regarding the railway construction decisions, in violation of Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention. They claimed the 2003 decision effectively fixed the railway’s location and affected their civil rights, including enjoyment of their homes, health, property value, and exposure to noise and vibrations, yet no court had fully reviewed it. The Government argued that Article 6 did not apply to the twelve applicants outside the corridor; that two applicants were not victims; and that domestic remedies had not been exhausted, including possible compensation claims. The Court rejected those preliminary objections, finding the applicants’ civil rights sufficiently affected for Article 6 to apply. The central issue was whether Swedish judicial review provided effective court access to challenge the binding Government permissibility decision.
001-146409:
O.G. v. Latvia (Application no. 66095/09, 23 September 2014) concerned a Latvian national suffering from paranoid schizophrenia who alleged that he had been unlawfully confined to a psychiatric hospital and could not effectively challenge his detention. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 5 § 4 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to judicial review of the lawfulness of detention.

In a first set of criminal proceedings for Internet fraud, the applicant was initially found to have full mental capacity. Later, in April 2007, a psychiatrist diagnosed him with chronic paranoid schizophrenia and recommended outpatient treatment. In February 2008, the Riga Regional Court relieved him of criminal liability and imposed compulsory outpatient psychiatric treatment. That decision became final in March 2008.

In a second set of criminal proceedings for fraud, an October 2007 forensic psychiatric report again found chronic paranoid schizophrenia. It concluded that he was unable to participate in the investigation or give adequate statements, and recommended compulsory outpatient treatment. The prosecutor appointed D.A., a psychiatrist involved in his treatment, as his legal representative. At a hearing on 19 August 2008, the applicant was absent. He was represented by defence counsel A.Ā., although the applicant claimed he had not appointed him. D.A. and an expert psychiatrist testified that he posed a danger to society and recommended inpatient treatment. Defence counsel and the prosecutor agreed. On 20 August 2008, the Riga Regional Court relieved the applicant of criminal liability and ordered involuntary inpatient psychiatric treatment. The decision became final on 2 September 2008.

Although the decision was sent to a psychiatric hospital, the applicant was not actually detained until 22 October 2009, when police entered his flat and took him to the hospital. Between 2008 and 2009, medical panels had recommended continued outpatient treatment. The applicant claimed he never received a signed copy of the detention decision or an explanation of how to appeal. On 31 October and 15 November 2009, he petitioned the Supreme Court challenging his detention. Judge I.Š., the same judge who had ordered the detention, treated his requests as inadmissible appeals and rejected them, stating that he lacked standing because he had been absent from the hearing and had been represented by D.A. On 28 December 2009, the Regional Court decided to continue inpatient treatment; the applicant received that decision in January 2010 but did not appeal. He was released in June 2010.

Under domestic law, section 606(1) of the Criminal Procedure Law allowed only persons who had participated in the relevant hearing to appeal. Section 607 allowed a person subject to compulsory medical measures to request revocation or alteration, but the applicant’s requests were not examined on the merits. The Government argued that he had failed to exhaust domestic remedies, because he could have appealed through D.A., defence counsel, or a prosecutor. The Court rejected that argument. It held that because the applicant had been absent from the August 2008 hearing, he had no direct standing to appeal the detention order himself; any appeal depended entirely on others’ discretion. The Court emphasised that a person compulsorily detained for psychiatric treatment must be able to seek judicial review of his or her own motion, and that mental illness alone cannot be a blanket limitation on that right, especially where no court assessed his ability to participate. His later requests were effectively left without merits examination. Therefore, he lacked access to a speedy court review of the lawfulness of his detention, violating Article 5 § 4. The Government’s abuse-of-application argument based on an alleged threatening email was rejected.

**Summary of O.G. v. Latvia (Application no. 66095/09)**

The case of O.G. v. Latvia concerns an application lodged by a Latvian national, Mr. O.G., against the Republic of Latvia on 10 December 2009. The applicant alleged that he had been illegally confined to a psychiatric hospital, violating Article 5 § 4 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which guarantees the right to challenge the lawfulness of detention.

The facts involve two sets of criminal proceedings against the applicant for fraud. In the first set, initiated in March 2004 for internet fraud, the applicant initially underwent psychiatric examinations and was found to have full mental capacity. However, during appeal hearings in 2007, his behaviour was described as aggressive and illogical, prompting an outpatient psychiatric assessment. On 27 April 2007, a psychiatrist diagnosed him with chronic paranoid schizophrenia, recommending outpatient treatment. On 18 February 2008, the Riga Regional Court relieved him of criminal liability and imposed compulsory outpatient psychiatric treatment, which became final on 11 March 2008.

In the second set of proceedings, initiated on 1 March 2007 for fraud, the police learned that the applicant was registered as a psychiatric outpatient. On 8 October 2007, he was informed he was a suspect, and an additional forensic psychiatric assessment was requested. A report dated 29 October 2007 concluded that he suffered from chronic paranoid schizophrenia, was unable to take responsibility for his actions, and could not participate in the investigation, recommending compulsory outpatient treatment. The prosecutor decided to pursue proceedings for a compulsory medical measure. On 7 February 2008, the prosecutor allowed D.A., a psychiatrist, to serve as the applicant’s legal representative, as she had in the first proceedings.

A crucial hearing was held on 19 August 2008 in the Riga Regional Court. The applicant was absent, represented by defence counsel A.Ā., and D.A. also attended. The applicant claimed he had not appointed A.Ā. or anyone else as his counsel. D.A. testified that the applicant posed a danger to society and needed treatment. The expert psychiatrist G.S. recommended involuntary inpatient treatment. The defence counsel and prosecutor agreed. On 20 August 2008, the court relieved the applicant of criminal liability, deemed him a danger to society, and ordered his inpatient treatment in a psychiatric hospital. The decision was sent to D.A. on 25 August 2008, and became final on 2 September 2008 after no appeal was lodged. The applicant was not present at the hearing and later claimed he never received a copy of the decision.

On 9 September 2008, the applicant requested revocation of compulsory measures, but his letter only referenced the earlier decision of 18 February 2008. On 16 September 2008, judge I.Š. returned his complaint, noting he did not challenge the 20 August 2008 decision. On 13 March 2009, the applicant appealed against the "decision of 19 August 2008," but received no reply. On 9 April 2009, judge I.Š. explained that D.A. had not appealed, so the decision was final, and the applicant lacked locus standi to appeal. On 14 April 2009, another judge confirmed that only D.A. could appeal.

On 22 October 2009, police officers took the applicant from his flat to a psychiatric hospital based on the 20 August 2008 decision. On 31 October and 15 November 2009, the applicant petitioned the Supreme Court, arguing he was not present at the hearing, had no lawyer, and his detention was unlawful. Judge I.Š. responded on 5 and 23 November 2009, stating that his treatment as an outpatient had been erroneous and that his representatives had not appealed. On 28 December 2009, the Riga Regional Court decided to continue involuntary inpatient treatment, but the applicant did not appeal. He was released on 7 June 2010.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 5 § 4. It held that the applicant, having been absent from the hearing, had no right to appeal independently under domestic law, and any appeal depended entirely on intermediaries like D.A. or A.Ā. The court emphasized that compulsory psychiatric patients must have the right to seek judicial review of their detention. The applicant’s requests to the Supreme Court were not examined on the merits, and the government’s suggested remedies (complaining to the Bar Association or prosecutor) were ineffective. Thus, the applicant lacked access to a court to challenge the lawfulness of his detention, violating Article 5 § 4.

O.G. v. Latvia (ECtHR, 2014, no. 66095/09) concerned an applicant with paranoid schizophrenia who complained that he had been illegally confined to a psychiatric hospital and could not effectively challenge the lawfulness of his detention, contrary to Article 5 §4 of the Convention.

The applicant was initially prosecuted for Internet fraud in 2004. Two inpatient psychiatric examinations found him mentally fit, and he received a suspended sentence. On appeal in 2007, after reportedly behaving aggressively and making illogical statements, the Riga Regional Court ordered an outpatient psychiatric assessment. On 27 April 2007 a psychiatrist diagnosed chronic paranoid schizophrenia and said his participation in hearings was unhelpful. The court then began proceedings to apply compulsory medical measures. Because his illness allegedly prevented participation, the case was examined in his absence; his mother was appointed legal representative but did not attend, and psychiatrist D.A. replaced her. A November 2007 inpatient assessment found episodic paranoid schizophrenia with increasing residual symptoms, concluded he could not control his actions at the time of the offences, and recommended relief from criminal liability. In February 2008 the court ordered outpatient compulsory treatment.

Meanwhile, a second fraud case began in March 2007. In October 2007 a forensic psychiatric report found chronic paranoid schizophrenia and that he was unable to participate in the investigation or give adequate statements. It recommended outpatient treatment. The prosecutor again allowed D.A., a psychiatrist, to act as his legal representative.

On 19 August 2008 the Riga Regional Court held a hearing concerning compulsory medical measures. The applicant was absent. A lawyer, A.Ā., appeared for him, but the applicant later said he had not appointed him. D.A. told the court that the applicant was dangerous to society and should receive treatment. An expert psychiatrist recommended involuntary inpatient treatment, and defence counsel and the prosecutor agreed. On 20 August 2008 the court relieved the applicant of criminal liability and ordered involuntary inpatient treatment in a psychiatric hospital. The decision became final on 2 September 2008.

The applicant claimed he never received a copy. Under domestic law, because he had not attended the hearing, he could not personally appeal; only his legal representative, defence counsel, or a prosecutor could. His later requests were rejected or returned. A judge said D.A. had represented him, D.A. had not appealed, and he lacked locus standi. Although the decision was sent to the hospital, he apparently remained an outpatient until police took him to the psychiatric hospital on 22 October 2009. He then petitioned the Supreme Court, arguing his detention was unlawful and that he had not been present or represented by a lawyer at the hearing. The same judge who had ordered his detention treated his requests as inadmissible appeals and did not examine them on the merits.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 5 §4. Although Latvian law theoretically allowed a representative to appeal, the applicant himself had no direct opportunity to challenge his detention. The decision to appeal was left to intermediaries. The prior psychiatric assessments had not specifically assessed his ability to form an opinion about hospitalization, and the domestic court did not address that issue. His subsequent requests were not reviewed on the merits, and the later court-initiated review did not provide sufficiently certain access to a court. Consequently, the applicant did not have an effective procedure to have the lawfulness of his psychiatric detention speedily decided.
001-142305:
The case of *Luli and Others v. Albania* concerned six applications brought by Albanian nationals alleging that their property restitution and compensation proceedings were excessively long, in violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, and that their property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 were breached. The applications were joined by the European Court of Human Rights.

The applicants had sought recognition of inherited property rights and restitution or compensation under Albania’s property legislation. Their claims repeatedly passed between regional agencies, the Central Agency, and domestic courts, often being quashed and remitted for fresh examination.

In applications nos. 64480/09 and 64482/09, the applicants (Luli and Others) relied on a 2005 Durrës District Court decision recognising inherited rights to 400,000 sq. m of land, divided into Plot A (260,000 sq. m) and Plot B (140,000 sq. m). As to Plot B, in 2007 the Durrës Regional Agency recognised rights, restored 53,200 sq. m, provided compensation for 22,960 sq. m, and left 63,840 sq. m undecided. The Central Agency quashed that decision and remitted it. In 2008 the Regional Agency recognised only 76,160 sq. m and left 63,840 sq. m undecided. In 2011 the Central Agency again quashed the decision, and the matter was pending before the Tirana District Court. As to Plot A, similar repeated decisions occurred: in 2007 and 2008 the Regional Agency recognised rights to 242,600 sq. m and restored 7,788 sq. m, but the Central Agency quashed the decisions. In 2009 regional agencies were abolished and the Central Agency took over, but no further decision was taken. These proceedings began around 2007 and lasted over six years, largely due to repeated administrative remittals.

In application no. 12874/10 (Pistulli), a 1995 Lezhë Commission decision recognised the applicant’s father’s rights to 25,850 sq. m, restored 11,500 sq. m, and provided for compensation for 5,000 sq. m. The applicant registered 5,830 sq. m but could not use it because the Port Authority occupied it. In 2006 she sued to have the Port Authority vacate. The District Court ruled in her favour in 2007, but the Court of Appeal quashed the decision and remitted the case. The Supreme Court dismissed her appeal in 2010, and in 2011 the District Court discontinued the rehearing because she did not appear.

In application no. 56935/10 (Dushallari), a 2007 Gjirokastra Regional Agency decision recognised inherited property rights. The State Advocate’s Office appealed. In 2011 the Central Agency stayed proceedings pending a Constitutional Court decision, and in 2012 declared itself without jurisdiction. The case was pending before the Tirana District Court.

Application no. 3129/12 (Kekenezi) concerned property purchased in 1992, later allocated to another person under rehabilitation legislation. A final 1998 Court of Cassation decision ordered the applicant to vacate. Later attempts to annul related acts were rejected because he lacked locus standi. The Court found Article 6 § 1 inapplicable to the review/re-opening proceedings and rejected the complaint as out of time and incompatible *ratione materiae*.

The Government argued non-exhaustion of domestic remedies, citing Article 324 of the Civil Procedure Code, constitutional appeals, and complaints to the High Council of Justice. The Court rejected these objections, finding no effective remedy capable of providing redress for length. It found the length complaints admissible for Luli, Pistulli, and Dushallari. On the merits, the Court held that the repeated referrals for fresh examination revealed a serious deficiency in the Albanian legal system, and that the overall length of the proceedings violated Article 6 § 1.

**Case: Luli and Others v. Albania (ECtHR, 1 April 2014)**

The case concerned six applications by Albanian nationals alleging breaches of Article 6 §1 (reasonable time) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to lengthy property restitution and compensation proceedings. The Court joined the applications for its assessment of length.

**Luli and Others (nos. 31355/09, 64480/09, 64482/09)** involved inherited property in Durrës. In 1996 the Durrës Commission issued two decisions bearing the same number and stamp: one recognised rights to 174,000 sq m (4,200 restored, first refusal over 5,800, compensation for 158,200), while the other recognised 17,400 sq m (4,200 restored, first refusal over 5,800). The applicants later relied on the second decision. For Plot B (140,000 sq m), after a 2005 court finding of inherited rights to 400,000 sq m, the Regional Agency in 2007 restored 53,200 sq m, awarded compensation for 22,960 sq m, and left 63,840 sq m undecided. The Central Agency quashed and remitted. In 2008 the Regional Agency recognised only 76,160 sq m with compensation, again leaving 63,840 sq m undecided. In 2011 the Central Agency quashed again; the case was pending before the Tirana District Court. For Plot A (260,000 sq m), the applicants sought 242,600 sq m. In 2007 the Regional Agency restored 7,788 sq m and awarded compensation for 245,772 sq m, leaving 2,240 sq m undecided. The Central Agency quashed and remitted. In 2008 the Regional Agency restored 7,788 sq m and awarded compensation for 248,012 sq m. Later that year the Central Agency director quashed it again. After regional offices were abolished in 2009, no further decision was made. The Court found the first 1996 decision was not shown to be enforceable and rejected that complaint as manifestly ill-founded.

**Pistulli (no. 12874/10):** In 1995 the Lezhë Commission recognised her father’s rights to 25,850 sq m, restored 11,500 sq m, provided compensation for 5,000 sq m, and recognised first refusal. She registered 5,830 sq m, but the Port Authority occupied it. In 2006 she sued to vacate. The District Court ruled for her in 2007, but the Court of Appeal quashed and remitted. The Supreme Court dismissed her appeal in 2010. In 2011 the District Court discontinued the rehearing for non-appearance. Her complaint concerned the length.

**Dushallari (no. 56935/10):** In 2007 the Gjirokastra Regional Agency recognised inherited rights. The State Advocate appealed in 2008. In 2011 the Central Agency stayed proceedings pending a Constitutional Court decision, then in 2012 declared it lacked jurisdiction. The case was pending before the Tirana District Court after a March 2012 appeal.

**Kekenezi (no. 3129/12):** His property dispute dated back to a 1957 purchase and 1992 resale, later affected by rehabilitation laws. In 1998 the Court of Cassation ordered him to vacate. His later nullity action was rejected for lack of locus standi in 2007 and upheld in 2011. The Court found this akin to review/re-opening, so Article 6 did not apply, and the earlier complaint was out of time.

The Government argued non-exhaustion, citing CCP Article 324, the Constitutional Court, and the High Council of Justice, but the Court rejected these as ineffective. On the merits, for the remaining length complaints, the Court found the proceedings had lasted over six years and were delayed by repeated administrative remittals, revealing a serious deficiency in the Albanian legal system. The length complaints were admissible and the delays were not justified by complexity.

In *Luli and Others v. Albania*, six Albanian applicants complained under Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the length of property restitution and compensation proceedings and, in one instance, non-enforcement of an administrative decision. The European Court of Human Rights joined five applications raising the same length issue, while treating one separately.

The first application (no. 31355/09) concerned a 6 March 1996 decision of the Durrës Commission. On the same day, the Commission issued two conflicting decisions bearing the same number and stamp. The first recognised inherited rights to 174,000 sq. m, restored 4,200 sq. m, granted a right of first refusal over 5,800 sq. m and provided compensation for 158,200 sq. m. The second recognised rights to only 17,400 sq. m, restored 4,200 sq. m and granted first refusal over 5,800 sq. m. The applicants alleged that the first decision was enforceable but had not been enforced. The Court rejected this complaint as manifestly ill-founded, finding that the first decision could not be considered enforceable: it had never been mentioned in twenty years of domestic proceedings, and the applicants’ later claims implicitly relied on the second decision.

Applications nos. 64480/09 and 64482/09 concerned restitution of Plots B and A in Durrës. For Plot B, the Durrës Regional Agency recognised rights in 2007, but the Central Agency quashed and remitted the case. A 2008 decision was again quashed in 2011, and the case remained pending before the Tirana District Court. For Plot A, Regional Agency decisions in 2007 and 2008 recognised rights and restored 7,788 sq. m, with compensation for the remainder, but the Central Agency repeatedly quashed them, including on the director’s own motion. In 2009 regional offices were abolished and the Central Agency took over, yet no further decision was taken. These proceedings had lasted over six years, mainly because of repeated administrative remittals, which the Court described as a serious deficiency in the Albanian legal system.

In application no. 12874/10 (Pistulli), the Lezhë Commission in 1995 recognised the applicant’s father’s rights to 25,850 sq. m, restored 11,500 sq. m, and provided compensation for 5,000 sq. m. The applicant registered 5,830 sq. m, but the Port Authority occupied it. In 2006 she sued to vacate the land. The District Court ruled in her favour in 2007, but the Court of Appeal quashed the decision and remitted it. The Supreme Court dismissed her appeal in 2010, and in 2011 the District Court discontinued the rehearing because she did not appear. She complained of excessive length.

Application no. 56935/10 (Dushallari) concerned a 2007 decision of the Gjirokastra Regional Agency recognising inherited property rights. The State Advocate appealed in 2008. In 2011 the Central Agency stayed proceedings pending a Constitutional Court decision, and in 2012 it declared itself without jurisdiction. The case was then pending before the Tirana District Court.

Application no. 3129/12 (Kekenezi) arose from a property purchased in 1992 but later allocated to a political repression victim’s heir. A final 1998 Court of Cassation decision ordered the applicant to vacate and declared his sale contract void. His 2006 action seeking annulment of related acts was dismissed for lack of locus standi, upheld by the Supreme Court and Constitutional Court in 2011. The Court found Article 6 § 1 inapplicable to reopening or review and the 1998 complaint time-barred.

Overall, the alleged violations centred on whether Albania’s property restitution system, marked by repeated administrative reversals and uncertain review powers, failed to determine civil property rights within a reasonable time.
001-148673:
**Case summary: Horncastle and Others v. the United Kingdom (App. no. 4184/10)**

The applicants were four British nationals convicted in two separate English criminal cases. They alleged that the admission of absent witnesses’ statements at their trials violated their right to a fair trial under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the European Convention on Human Rights, particularly the right to examine witnesses against them.

In the first case, Mr Horncastle and Mr Blackmore were charged with causing grievous bodily harm with intent to P.R., a registered alcoholic. In May 2005, P.R. was attacked in his flat and suffered severe injuries. He gave a police statement in June 2005, saying he had drunk heavily, that his memory was vague, and describing three attackers, including “Horncastle” and a “bigger male” and a man on crutches. P.R. died in July 2006 from an alcohol-related illness before trial. The prosecution applied to read his statement under section 116(2)(a) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 because the witness was dead. The defence opposed this, arguing the statement was the only admissible evidence of participation, inherently unreliable due to P.R.’s intoxication and vague memory, and could not be cross-examined. The judge admitted it, finding the statutory condition satisfied and that the jury could be directed on the disadvantages. Horncastle and Blackmore admitted going to the flat to recover stolen property but denied involvement in the attack, blaming M. The jury convicted them after a third trial. The Court of Appeal accepted the statement was decisive but found sufficient counterbalancing safeguards; the Supreme Court dismissed their appeal.

In the second case, Mr Marquis and Mr Graham were charged with kidnapping H.M. in November 2007. Masked men entered her home, threatened her with a knife, stole items, and took her away while ransom demands were made. H.M. gave a detailed statement but did not identify the applicants. Graham was later seen on CCTV at the house and arrested in the victim’s partner’s stolen car; Marquis’s phone was linked to ransom calls, and an identical phone was seen in his hotel room. H.M. and her partner initially retracted their statements due to fear but later made video statements confirming their fear. The prosecution applied to read H.M.’s statement under section 116(2)(e) because she would not attend through fear. The defence argued the fear was caused not by the applicants but by police warnings about dangerous criminals. The judge found H.M. genuinely terrified and admitted her statement, while refusing the partner’s statement. Marquis and Graham were convicted. The Court of Appeal found H.M.’s evidence was not decisive because other evidence proved the kidnapping and linked the applicants; the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

The central alleged violation was that using absent witnesses’ statements, especially where sole or decisive, deprived the applicants of the opportunity to cross-examine, contrary to Article 6(3)(d). The UK courts held that the 2003 Act contained sufficient safeguards: judicial gatekeeping, exclusion powers, jury warnings, the power to stop a case under section 125, and appellate review. The European Court of Human Rights ultimately found no violation. It confirmed that confrontation is not absolute; where hearsay evidence is reliable or its reliability can be tested, and where sufficient counterbalancing measures exist, a conviction based significantly on an absent witness’s statement can still be fair.

This case concerned four British applicants convicted in criminal proceedings in England in which prosecution witnesses’ written statements were read at trial because the witnesses were unavailable. The applicants alleged that admitting those statements, without any opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses, rendered their trials unfair contrary to Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention.

The first two applicants, Mr Horncastle and Mr Blackmore, were charged with causing grievous bodily harm with intent. In May 2005, the victim, P.R., a registered alcoholic, was attacked in his flat and suffered extensive injuries. In June 2005 he made a police statement describing three attackers, including “Horncastle” and a “bigger male” alleged to be Blackmore. P.R. died in July 2006 from an alcohol-related illness before trial. The prosecution applied to read his statement under section 116(2)(a) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 (“the 2003 Act”) because the witness was dead. The defence objected under section 78 of PACE, arguing that the statement was unreliable—P.R. had been drunk, his memory was vague, and his description of Blackmore was questionable—and that it was the sole or decisive evidence against them. The judge admitted the statement. At trial there was other evidence, including admissions that the applicants had gone to the flat to recover stolen property, blood on a television removed by Horncastle, Blackmore stepping over the victim, and forensic evidence. The Court of Appeal accepted that the victim’s statement was decisive, but found sufficient safeguards. They were convicted.

The second pair, Mr Marquis and Mr Graham, were charged with kidnapping. In November 2007, H.M. was kidnapped from her home. She made police statements, but later retracted them and fled because she was frightened. Her partner, G.P., also failed to attend trial. The prosecution applied to read their statements under section 116(2)(e) of the 2003 Act on the basis that they would not give evidence through fear. The defence argued that the fear was not caused by the applicants but by police warnings about dangerous reprisals. The judge found H.M. genuinely terrified and admitted her statement, but refused to admit G.P.’s statement because he was not in fear. Other evidence included CCTV of Graham entering the house, his arrest in the stolen car, a knife, phone records linking Marquis, and hotel evidence. They were convicted of kidnapping.

On appeal, the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeals. It held that Article 6 § 3(d) does not create an absolute right to examine every witness. The 2003 Act contained safeguards: judicial gatekeeping, restrictions on hearsay, jury directions on the dangers of absent-witness evidence, the power to stop the case under section 125 if the evidence was unconvincing, and appeal rights. A conviction based solely or decisively on hearsay could still be fair if the evidence was reliable or its reliability could be tested and counterbalancing measures were sufficient. The Supreme Court dismissed further appeals, holding the statutory scheme compatible with fair trial rights.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the applications and found no violation of Article 6. It applied the principles from Al-Khawaja and Tahery. In Marquis and Graham, the absent witness evidence was not the sole or decisive basis for conviction. In Horncastle and Blackmore, although the victim’s statement was decisive, there were sufficient counterbalancing safeguards and strong independent evidence allowing the jury to assess reliability. The trials were therefore fair.

The case concerns four British nationals—Horncastle, Blackmore, Marquis, and Graham—who were convicted in two separate criminal trials in which the prosecution relied on written statements by absent witnesses who could not be cross-examined. They complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the admission of those statements rendered their trials unfair, contrary to Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention, which guarantees the right to examine witnesses.

In the first case, Horncastle and Blackmore were charged with causing grievous bodily harm to P.R., a registered alcoholic, who was attacked in his flat in May 2005. P.R. made a police statement in June 2005 describing the attack. He said he had drunk heavily, his memory was vague, and he described three attackers, naming Horncastle and describing Blackmore as the “bigger male.” P.R. died in July 2006 from an alcohol-related illness before trial. The prosecution applied to read his statement under section 116(2)(a) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 because the witness was dead. The defence opposed admission, arguing the statement was the sole or decisive evidence, inherently unreliable due to P.R.’s intoxication and vague memory, and could not be tested by cross-examination. The trial judge admitted it, noting that the defendants admitted being present at the flat to recover stolen property, that other evidence existed, and that the jury could be given special directions. At trial, further evidence included blood on a television removed by Horncastle, Blackmore’s admission that he stepped over the victim, forensic evidence, and defence evidence suggesting another man, M., may have carried out the attack. The jury convicted both applicants.

In the second case, Marquis and Graham were charged with kidnapping H.M. in November 2007. H.M. made a police statement but later retracted it, saying she was frightened. She and her partner, G.P., did not attend trial. The prosecution applied to read their statements under section 116(2)(e) of the 2003 Act, on the ground that they would not give evidence through fear. The defence argued that the fear was not caused by the applicants but by police warnings about dangerous offenders and relocation, and that H.M.’s statement was the only evidence that a kidnapping had occurred. The trial judge admitted H.M.’s statement, finding her genuinely terrified, but refused to admit G.P.’s statement. Other evidence against Marquis and Graham included CCTV footage, a stolen car, a knife, telephone records, hotel evidence, ransom calls, and testimony from H.M.’s father. They were convicted.

The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeals, holding that admitting hearsay evidence was not automatically unfair and that sufficient counterbalancing safeguards existed. The Supreme Court also dismissed the appeals, rejecting any absolute right to confrontation. It emphasised that the 2003 Act contained safeguards: judicial gatekeeping, restrictions on admissibility, the power to stop a case if hearsay evidence was unconvincing, jury directions, and appeal rights. The ECtHR ultimately examined whether the admission of the absent witnesses’ statements, especially where potentially sole or decisive, violated the applicants’ fair trial rights. It found no violation, concluding that the domestic courts had applied sufficient counterbalancing measures and that the trials, viewed as a whole, were fair.

Case Y v. Latvia (ECtHR, Fourth Section, no. 61183/08, 21 October 2014) concerned a Latvian woman’s complaint that municipal police officers subjected her to inhuman and degrading treatment on 1 November 2007 and that she could not obtain compensation.

The applicant, born in 1959 and living in Liepāja, was in the courtyard of her apartment building when two municipal police officers, J.M. and J.L., arrived in response to an alleged administrative violation—washing a car in a public courtyard. They spoke with her and asked her to approach their police car. According to the applicant, she suggested they talk in her apartment and began to walk away. The officers then grabbed her, twisted her arms behind her back, forced her toward the car, and tried to push her into the back seat. They released her after neighbours intervened.

She immediately experienced chest pain, high blood pressure, back, neck and head pain, and numbness in her hands. An ambulance was called and gave her an injection. The next day a doctor issued sick leave until 12 November 2007 and prescribed painkillers and sedatives. A forensic medical report found two haematomas on each upper arm, consistent with her account, though they were classified as minor injuries not causing health impairment beyond six days. Three eyewitnesses said the applicant ignored police requests and resisted, and that the officers twisted her arms until she stopped resisting.

The applicant complained to the prosecutor. Criminal proceedings were opened but terminated on 21 January 2008. The inspector found she had intentionally disobeyed a lawful police order and that the officers had grounds to detain her. However, the officers had breached section 13 in fine of the Law on Police, which prohibits special restraint techniques against women except in exceptional circumstances. The inspector accepted that their actions caused minor injuries. Nevertheless, he found no offence of exceeding official authority under section 317 of the Criminal Law because there was no substantial harm to state authority, administrative order or individual rights. The criminal case was terminated for absence of corpus delicti.

The letter advised the applicant that intentional infliction of minor injury under section 130 was subject to private prosecution and that she could apply to court. She attempted to do so in April/May 2008, seeking damages, but the courts refused because the six-month limitation period had expired and her complaint was insufficiently specific. The Regional Court’s decision became final on 2 June 2008, noting that a civil claim for compensation remained possible.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged that the police use of force amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment under Article 3 and that she had no possibility of compensation. The Government argued non-exhaustion, the six-month rule, and no significant disadvantage. On the merits, it accepted that the officers violated domestic law but argued the force was justified by her non-cooperation, was short, and did not intend to humiliate her.

The Court rejected the admissibility objections, finding that her attempt at private prosecution interrupted the six-month period and that she could choose a remedy addressing her essential grievance. It declared the Article 3 complaint admissible and reiterated that ill-treatment must reach a minimum level of severity, assessed by duration, physical and mental effects, and the victim’s sex, age and health. Physical force not strictly necessary by a person’s own conduct infringes Article 3; constraints may be justified only if the person resists or risks violence. The Court found the case raised serious Article 3 issues, particularly given the admitted breach of the domestic prohibition on using special techniques against women and the documented injuries. The Court ultimately found a violation of Article 3.
