In *M.E. v. Sweden*, the applicant was a Libyan national, born in 1982, who arrived in Sweden in July 2010 and applied for asylum. He initially claimed that he had been a soldier and guard at a military base in Tripoli and had transported illegal weapons for powerful clans. In November 2009 he was stopped, detained for about three weeks, interrogated and tortured, then transferred to a military prison. He escaped from a civil hospital with the help of a guard. He feared that if returned to Libya he would face at least ten years’ imprisonment for criminal offences and possible revenge from the clans whose names he had revealed under torture. He later stated that the clans were less interested in him after the 2011 changes in Libya.

In February 2011, the applicant added a new ground for asylum: he was homosexual and had a relationship with N., a transsexual person with a Swedish residence permit. They had met in Sweden, moved in together in December 2010, and married in September 2011. The applicant said his sexual orientation was unknown in Libya and that he had never had a homosexual relationship there. He claimed that if he were returned to Libya to apply for family reunion from there, his marriage to a man would become known, exposing him to persecution and ill-treatment. He later alleged that a Libyan in Sweden had told his brother about the marriage, that his uncle had threatened to kill him for shaming the family, and that homosexuals in Libya had been killed.

The Swedish Migration Board rejected the asylum application in December 2011. It accepted that the applicant was probably Libyan but found his account lacking credibility. It noted contradictions about his passport, inconsistent details about when he met N., a discrepancy in the name on the marriage certificate, and the late disclosure of his relationship. It also found that he had not substantiated a risk from the criminal accusations or the clans. As to family reunion, the Board applied the main rule that a residence permit on family-tie grounds must normally be applied for before entering Sweden. It found no reason to exempt him, concluding it was not unreasonable to require him to apply from Libya.

The Migration Court rejected his appeal in September 2012. It found the general situation in Libya serious but not enough for asylum without individual risk. The documents and scars did not prove future ill-treatment, and the court found the applicant not credible. It did not question that he was homosexual, but found no substantiated risk: his orientation was not known in Libya, it was unlikely that Libyans in Sweden would spread the information merely because he returned, and embassy staff were bound by confidentiality. One lay judge dissented, considering that a leak from an embassy could not be ruled out. The Migration Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal in October 2012.

A request for reconsideration was rejected in December 2012; the Migration Board found the alleged family threats did not constitute a permanent impediment to enforcement.

The applicant alleged that expulsion to Libya—or being required to apply for family reunion there—would violate Article 3 (risk of torture or inhuman or degrading treatment as a homosexual and/or due to his past) and Article 8 (right to private and family life with his spouse in Sweden). The Court applied Rule 39 to prevent deportation during proceedings. Relevant country evidence showed that same-sex acts were criminalised in Libya, homosexuality was socially taboo, and militias had abused gay men. Sweden’s only consulate in Libya, in Benghazi, was closed, although embassies in Algiers and Cairo and a consulate in Tunis handled residence-permit applications. These facts framed the alleged violations.

M.E., a Libyan national born in 1982, applied for asylum in Sweden on 29 July 2010. He claimed that he had been a soldier and guard at a military base in Tripoli and had transported illegal weapons for powerful southern Libyan clans. In November 2009, he was stopped, interrogated, tortured for about three weeks, and then transferred to a military prison on charges of illegal weapons possession and car theft. He escaped from a hospital while receiving treatment for an infected arm injury. He feared imprisonment and retaliation from the clans if returned to Libya.

In February 2011, while his asylum claim was pending, M.E. added a new ground: he was homosexual and in a relationship with N., a transsexual person with a Swedish residence permit. They later married in September 2011. M.E. stated that no one in Libya knew about his sexual orientation, but if he were returned there to apply for family reunion, his marriage and homosexuality would become known, exposing him to persecution and ill-treatment. He later claimed that a Libyan in Sweden had told his brother about the marriage, that his uncle had threatened to kill him for shaming the family, and that homosexual men were being killed in Libya.

The Migration Board rejected his asylum application in December 2011. It found his identity unproven and his account lacking credibility, citing contradictions about his passport, travel, date of arrival, and when he met N., as well as a name discrepancy on his marriage certificate. It accepted that the situation in Libya was serious but not an internal armed conflict, and concluded that he had not shown an individual risk. It also held that the main rule required family-reunion applications to be made before entry and that it was not unreasonable to require him to apply from Libya.

The Migration Court rejected his appeal in September 2012. In **O’Keeffe v. Ireland** (Application no. 35810/09, Grand Chamber, 28 January 2014), the applicant, Louise O’Keeffe, complained that Ireland’s primary education system failed to protect her from sexual abuse by a teacher in 1973 and that she had no effective domestic remedy. The key facts concerned the structure of Irish national schools and the State’s limited role in their management.

The applicant attended Dunderrow National School from 1968. The school was State-funded but owned, through trustees, by the Catholic Bishop of Cork and Ross and managed by a local parish priest. The manager, acting for the patron, controlled day-to-day management and teacher appointments. The State funded, regulated and inspected the school, but did not directly manage it or employ its teachers. In 1971, a parent complained to the manager that the school principal, L.H., had sexually abused her child. The complaint was not reported to the police, the Department of Education or any other State authority, and the manager did not act on it.

During the first six months of 1973, L.H. sexually assaulted the applicant approximately twenty times during music lessons. She and her parents were unaware of the 1971 complaint. In September 1973, other parents made similar allegations. L.H. went on sick leave and resigned, but again the allegations were not reported to the State. He later taught in another national school until 1995. The applicant suppressed the abuse. In 1996, police contacted her during an investigation of a 1995 complaint by a former pupil. She made a statement in 1997 and received counselling. L.H. was charged with 386 sexual offences involving about twenty-one former pupils. In 1998 he pleaded guilty to twenty-one sample charges and was imprisoned; his teaching licence was withdrawn. Around that time the applicant realised the connection between the abuse and her psychological difficulties.

In 1998 the applicant sued L.H. and the State defendants—the Minister, Ireland and the Attorney General. She alleged State negligence in the recognition, examination and supervision of the school and failure to put protective measures in place; vicarious liability for L.H.; and constitutional liability under Article 42 of the Irish Constitution. The High Court non-suited the negligence claim in 2004 and in 2006 rejected vicarious liability and the constitutional claim. The Supreme Court dismissed her appeal in 2008 by majority, holding that the “managerial system” meant L.H. was employed and controlled by the clerical manager, not the State, and that the State was not vicariously liable for L.H. or the manager’s failure to report the 1971 complaint. A dissent found a sufficient State-Church joint enterprise and relied on the role of school inspectors.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant principally alleged a violation of Article 3, arguing that the State’s primary education system failed to protect her from sexual abuse by a teacher in 1973, and Article 13, arguing that she lacked an effective domestic remedy. She also relied on Article 8 and Article 14 and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1. Complaints about the length of civil proceedings and the related remedy were settled. The Grand Chamber found violations of Article 3 and Article 13, holding that Ireland had failed in its positive obligation to protect children from sexual abuse in the national school system and that domestic law provided no effective remedy.

That complaint was not reported to the police, the Department of Education, or any other State authority, and the manager did not act on it. During the first half of 1973, L.H. sexually assaulted the applicant approximately twenty times during music lessons. She and her parents were unaware of the 1971 complaint. In September 1973, other parents raised similar allegations; after a parents’ meeting chaired by the manager, L.H. went on sick leave and resigned. Those allegations were also not reported to the State. In January 1974, the manager merely notified the Department that L.H. had resigned and named his replacement. L.H. later taught at another national school until 1995.

Between 1969 and 1973, a State inspector visited the school six times, met L.H. and the manager, and considered L.H.’s teaching satisfactory. No complaint about L.H. was made to him. In 1995, police investigated another former pupil’s complaint. The applicant made a statement in 1997. L.H. was charged with 386 sexual offences involving about twenty-one former pupils; in 1998 he pleaded guilty to twenty-one sample charges and was imprisoned. His teaching licence was withdrawn. Around 1998, the applicant connected her psychological difficulties with the abuse.

She also relied on Article 8 and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1, alone and with Article 14, and complained about the length of civil proceedings and lack of remedy under Article 6/13. The length/remedy complaints were struck out after a friendly settlement; the remaining complaints were declared admissible and referred to the Grand Chamber.

The applicant, Louise O’Keeffe, born in 1964, attended Dunderrow National School from 1968. The school was owned through trustees by the Catholic Bishop of Cork and Ross, who was recognised by the Department of Education as the school’s patron. The local parish priest acted as manager, with a second priest performing the role de facto because the named manager was elderly and infirm. The school had two teachers; one, L.H., was principal.

In 1971, a parent complained to the manager that L.H. had sexually abused her child. That complaint was not reported to the police, the Department, or any other State authority, and the manager did not act on it. During the first six months of 1973, the applicant was subjected to approximately twenty sexual assaults by L.H. during music lessons in his classroom. Neither she nor her parents knew of the 1971 complaint at that time.

In September 1973, other parents told the applicant’s parents about similar allegations against L.H. After a parents’ meeting chaired by the manager, L.H. went on sick leave and resigned. These allegations were again not reported to the police, the Department, or other State authorities. In January 1974 the manager merely notified the Department that L.H. had resigned and named his replacement. L.H. soon obtained a teaching post at another national school and taught until 1995.

Between 1969 and 1973 a school inspector visited Dunderrow six times, an above-average number. He met L.H. and the manager, attended parent meetings, and assessed L.H.’s teaching as satisfactory. No complaint about L.H. was made to him.

The applicant suppressed the abuse. Although she suffered significant psychological difficulties, she did not initially connect them to the abuse. In 1996 police contacted her during an investigation into a 1995 complaint by another former pupil. She made a statement in January 1997 and received counselling. L.H. was charged with 386 sexual offences involving about twenty-one former pupils over roughly ten years. In 1998 he pleaded guilty to twenty-one sample charges and was imprisoned; his teaching licence was withdrawn. Around June 1998 the applicant realised the link between her psychological problems and the abuse.

She applied to the Criminal Injuries Compensation Tribunal and accepted an ex gratia award. In 1998 she also brought a civil action against L.H., the Minister for Education, Ireland, and the Attorney General. Against the State defendants, she alleged negligence in the recognition, examination, and supervision of the school; failure to put in place measures and procedures to protect against and stop systematic abuse by L.H.; vicarious liability for L.H.; and liability for breach of her constitutional right to bodily integrity and the State’s duty under Article 42 of the Constitution to provide primary education.

The High Court dismissed the negligence claim and found the State was not vicariously liable because of the relationship between the State and denominational school management. The Supreme Court, by majority in 2008, upheld that conclusion, finding that the “managerial system” left day-to-day control of national schools to patrons and managers. The State funded and regulated education but did not employ or directly supervise teachers such as L.H.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant principally alleged that Ireland’s primary-education system had failed to protect her from sexual abuse in 1973, contrary to Article 3, and that she lacked an effective domestic remedy under Article 13. She also relied on Article 8 and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1, alone and with Article 14. Complaints about the length of the civil proceedings were settled. The key factual issue was whether the State’s regulatory and supervisory framework, given the 1971 complaint and the managerial structure, should have protected her from the abuse.

**Erla Hlynsdóttir v. Iceland (No. 2)** concerns an Icelandic journalist’s complaint under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights that her liability in domestic defamation proceedings violated her right to freedom of expression.

The applicant, Erla Hlynsdóttir, was a journalist for the newspaper *DV*. In its issue of 31 August–2 September 2007, *DV* published an article entitled “Satan’s attacks” about a high-profile criminal investigation involving Mr Y, the founder and director of a Christian rehabilitation centre called Byrgið, and his wife, Mrs X. In December 2006, a television programme had accused Mr Y of sexually abusing female patients and embezzling public funds. Three women subsequently filed police complaints against him. Both Mr Y and Mrs X were suspects in the criminal investigation.

The *DV* article contained interviews and comments from Ms A, one of the women who had complained to the police, and Mr B, the financial manager at Byrgið and a close friend of the couple. Ms A alleged that Mrs X had participated in sexual activities with her and Mr Y, had helped seduce female patients as part of their supposed “healing process,” and had sought sexual encounters with women herself. Ms A also criticised Mrs X’s work as a teaching assistant, stating that it was inappropriate that “the one who hunts for him works in a primary school.” Mr B similarly said that both Mr Y and Mrs X had sexually abused patients and that he found it strange that Mrs X was allowed to work with children. The article also included comments from the couple’s lawyer denying the accusations and from a police officer confirming that Mrs X had suspect status.

In February 2008, Mrs X brought defamation proceedings against Ms A, Mr B and the applicant under Articles 234, 235 and 236 of the Icelandic Penal Code. She sought annulment of the statements, criminal punishment and compensation. She argued that the applicant, as author of the article, was liable for its content.

The applicant relied on Article 73 of the Icelandic Constitution and section 15 of the Printing Act, arguing that responsibility lay with the named interviewees whose statements had been quoted directly. She also claimed the statements were true and accurate, noting that Mrs X had been a suspect in a sexual-offence investigation. The District Court, on 4 December 2008, found one statement attributed to Ms A defamatory but not proved to have originated from her. Only the applicant was ordered to pay Mrs X ISK 100,000 in non-pecuniary damages; the statement was annulled, and other claims were rejected.

Both parties appealed. On 18 February 2010, the Icelandic Supreme Court upheld most of the lower court’s findings. It held that some statements were substantiated or amounted to value judgments. However, it found the latter part of the statement that it was “not appropriate that the one who hunts for him works in a primary school” defamatory. According to the Supreme Court, those words implied that Mrs X was guilty of criminal conduct, which had not been proven. Because the applicant had been identified as the author, she was liable under section 15 of the Printing Act. She was ordered to pay ISK 300,000 in non-pecuniary damages, ISK 100,000 for publication costs, plus interest.

The applicant lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 17 August 2010. She complained that the Supreme Court’s judgment interfered with her Article 10 right to freedom of expression and was not “necessary in a democratic society.” The application was communicated to the Icelandic Government on 6 September 2012. The key issue was whether holding a journalist liable for publishing a named interviewee’s statement during public debate about a criminal investigation was justified under Article 10.

The case concerns Erla Hlynsdóttir, an Icelandic journalist working for the newspaper DV. In its weekend issue of 31 August to 2 September 2007, DV published an article entitled “Satan’s attacks” about a high-profile criminal investigation involving Mr Y, the founder and director of a Christian rehabilitation centre called Byrgið, and his wife, Mrs X. Mr Y had been publicly accused in a television programme of sexually abusing female patients at Byrgið and embezzling public funds. Three women subsequently filed police complaints against him. Both Mr Y and Mrs X were suspects in the criminal investigation.

The DV article contained interviews and comments from Ms A, one of the women who had complained to the police, and Mr B, Byrgið’s financial manager and a close friend of the couple. Ms A described Mrs X as having been active in the so-called sexual “games” organised by Mr Y, in which female patients were allegedly manipulated into participating as part of their “healing process.” According to Ms A, Mrs X helped seduce the women and also sought sexual encounters with them herself. Ms A further criticised Mrs X’s work as a teaching assistant in a school, stating, among other things, that Mrs X was “crazy” and that it was “not appropriate that the one who hunts for him works in a primary school.” Mr B also stated that both Mr Y and Mrs X had sexually abused several patients and questioned why Mrs X was allowed to work with children. The article also included comments from the couple’s lawyer denying the accusations and from a police officer confirming that Mrs X had the status of a suspect.

In February 2008, Mrs X instituted defamation proceedings against Ms A, Mr B, and the applicant before the Reykjavik District Court. She relied on Articles 234, 235, and 236 of the Penal Code and sought annulment of the statements, punishment, damages, and publication costs. The applicant argued that she was protected by Article 73 of the Icelandic Constitution on freedom of expression and by section 15 of the Printing Act, under which responsibility lay with the identified authors of statements. She claimed the statements were true and accurately quoted from named sources. Ms A denied making some of the statements or said she could not remember them.

In December 2008, the District Court found one statement attributed to Ms A defamatory but not proved to have originated verbatim from her. It therefore ordered only the applicant to pay Mrs X ISK 100,000 in non-pecuniary damages and declared the statement null and void, rejecting other claims. Both Mrs X and the applicant appealed. In February 2010, the Supreme Court upheld the outcome for Ms A and Mr B. It also upheld the applicant’s liability, but only for the latter part of the statement: “... not appropriate that the one who hunts for him works in a primary school.” The Supreme Court found that this implied Mrs X was guilty of criminal conduct, which had not been proven. It described the statement as a coarse insinuation published conspicuously in a widely read newspaper and likely to harm Mrs X’s dignity and professional reputation. Because the applicant was identified as the article’s author, she was liable under section 15 of the Printing Act and was ordered to pay ISK 300,000 in non-pecuniary damages and ISK 100,000 for publication costs.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 10 that the Supreme Court’s judgment interfered with her right to freedom of expression and was not “necessary in a democratic society.” The key alleged violation therefore concerns the domestic defamation ruling holding a journalist liable for publishing a source’s statement about a criminal suspect’s suitability to work in a primary school during a matter of public interest.

In *Miladinov and Others v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia* (ECtHR, 24 April 2014), three Macedonian nationals—private entrepreneurs—were among fifteen persons investigated on 23 December 2008 in connection with bankruptcy proceedings concerning company I. All applicants were charged with money laundering; the first applicant also faced charges of abuse of position, fraud, and forgery, and the third applicant faced fraud charges. An investigating judge ordered thirty-day pre-trial detention for nine accused, including the applicants, relying on all grounds under section 184(1)(1–3) of the Criminal Proceedings Act: risk of absconding, reoffending, and interfering with the investigation. The first and second applicants appealed; the panel dismissed the first applicant’s appeal and replaced the second applicant’s detention with house arrest.

The applicants’ detention was repeatedly extended. On 21 January, 19 February, and 20 March 2009, the panel ordered thirty-day extensions at private hearings. The first two relied on all three statutory grounds; the third excluded interference with the investigation after an indictment was lodged. The reasoning was largely generic, citing the gravity and nature of the offences, possible sentence, previous criminal record, pending proceedings, and the manner of offending through use of position or special powers. From 16 April to 16 September 2009, the panel issued six further thirty-day extensions on its own motion, in private, based on risk of flight and reoffending, often using identical boilerplate reasoning. Four orders also referred to the third applicant’s previous criminal record. Additional extensions followed between 15 October 2009 and 14 January 2010 for the first and third applicants, again in private and with similar reasoning.

The applicants appealed, arguing that the domestic courts had not given concrete, sufficient reasons for continued detention; that their family ties, permanent residence, the second applicant’s poor health, and the first applicant’s traffic-related previous conviction were ignored or mischaracterised; and that the wording of the decisions violated the presumption of innocence. The first and third applicants also requested notification of the Court of Appeal session. The Skopje Court of Appeal dismissed the appeals in private. It relied in part on written submissions by the public prosecutor that had not been communicated to the applicants and refused requests for a public session. Its decisions repeated that the nature, gravity, and manner of the offences, possible imprisonment, and the applicants’ lack of sufficient guarantees made flight risk real; as to reoffending, it cited the applicants’ ownership of or links to companies, pending proceedings, and previous convictions. It also stated that complaints denying the offences were irrelevant at that stage because only detention was at issue.

Other relevant facts included that on 28 May 2009 prison authorities retained a power of attorney signed by the first applicant and returned it only after eighteen days. On 18 September 2009, the second applicant’s house arrest was replaced by passport seizure. Ultimately, on 29 January 2010, the trial court convicted the applicants and sentenced the first and third to six and a half years’ imprisonment and the second to two years; the first and third remained in custody. On 24 September 2010, the Court of Appeal quashed the judgment and released the first and third applicants, finding no grounds for detention.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants alleged violations of Article 5 §§3 and 4—insufficient reasoning for continued detention, lack of oral and adversarial review, and non-communication of the prosecutor’s submissions—and Article 6 §2 concerning the presumption of innocence. These facts formed the basis of the alleged violations.

**Miladinov and Others v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia** (ECtHR, First Section, 24 April 2014; Applications nos. 46398/09, 50570/09 and 50576/09) concerned three Macedonian nationals and private entrepreneurs arrested in December 2008. An investigating judge of the Skopje Court of First Instance opened an investigation against fifteen people, including bankruptcy trustees, judges, lawyers, notaries and civil servants, concerning bankruptcy proceedings involving company I. The applicants were charged with money laundering; the first applicant also faced charges of abuse of position, fraud and forgery, and the third applicant also faced fraud charges. On 23 December 2008, the investigating judge ordered thirty-day pre-trial detention for nine accused, including the applicants, relying on all grounds under section 184(1)(1-3) of the Criminal Proceedings Act: risk of absconding, reoffending and interfering with the investigation. The judge cited the gravity of the charges, possible severe sentence and risk of influencing witnesses. The first and second applicants appealed; the first’s appeal was dismissed, while the second’s detention was replaced by house arrest.

The panel extended the applicants’ detention or house arrest every thirty days: on 21 January, 19 February and 20 March 2009, all at private hearings. The first two extensions were based on the investigating judge’s proposal and cited all three statutory grounds. The 20 March order, after an indictment was lodged, excluded interference with the investigation but continued to rely on risk of flight and reoffending. The reasons were largely generic and identically worded: the type, gravity and nature of the offences; the first applicant’s previous criminal record; the second applicant’s pending proceedings; and the alleged use of position and special powers. From 16 April to 16 September 2009, the panel issued six further thirty-day extensions on its own motion, again in private, using identical reasoning and adding that detention was “the most efficient measure” to secure attendance and had helped ensure trial within a reasonable time. Four more extensions for the first and third applicants followed between 15 October 2009 and 14 January 2010, again in private and with similar wording.

The applicants appealed to the Skopje Court of Appeal. They argued that the extension orders lacked concrete reasons, ignored their family ties and permanent residence, disregarded the second applicant’s poor health, and wrongly relied on the first applicant’s previous conviction, which concerned only a traffic offence. They also complained that the wording of the decisions violated the presumption of innocence. The first and third applicants requested notification of, or a public session under, section 388(1) of the Act. The Court of Appeal, sitting in private, dismissed the appeals in decisions from May to November 2009. It relied on written submissions from the public prosecutor requesting dismissal, but those submissions were not communicated to the applicants. It refused public sessions, finding section 388(1) inapplicable. Its reasoning repeated generic grounds: the nature, gravity and manner of the offences, the possibility of imprisonment, rejection of family and residence as irrelevant, and risk of reoffending based on company ownership or links, pending or previous proceedings, and use of position. It also stated that complaints denying the offences or criminal responsibility were irrelevant to detention review and would be examined at trial.

At trial on 29 January 2010, the applicants were convicted; the first and third received six and a half years’ imprisonment and the second two years, with the first and third remaining in custody. On 24 September 2010, the Court of Appeal quashed the judgment in a public session and ordered the release of the first and third applicants, finding no grounds for their detention.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants alleged violations of Article 5 §§3 and 4: insufficient concrete reasons for detention; no oral hearing in the detention-review proceedings before the panel and Court of Appeal; and non-adversarial proceedings because the prosecutor’s written observations were not disclosed. They also alleged an Article 6 §2 violation due to wording suggesting guilt. The Court joined the applications and declared the Article 5 complaints admissible.

Miladinov and Others v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia concerned three Macedonian nationals and private entrepreneurs—Dimitar Miladinov, Dimitrija Golaboski, and Georgi Miladinov—who complained under Articles 5 §§ 3 and 4 and Article 6 § 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights about their pre-trial detention and the review proceedings. On 23 December 2008 an investigating judge opened an investigation against fifteen people, including the applicants, in connection with alleged crimes relating to bankruptcy proceedings involving company I. All were charged with money laundering; the first applicant also faced charges of abuse of position, fraud, and forgery, and the third faced fraud charges. The investigating judge ordered nine accused, including the applicants, into thirty-day pre-trial detention based on all grounds under section 184(1)(1–3) of the Criminal Proceedings Act: risk of absconding, reoffending, and interfering with the investigation. The judge relied on the gravity of the charges, the potential severity of sentence, and the possibility of influencing witnesses, accomplices, and others.

The first and second applicants appealed, arguing that no concrete, individualized reasons had been given; both noted permanent residence and family ties, and the second cited poor health. The panel dismissed the first applicant’s appeal and replaced the second’s detention with house arrest. The panel then extended detention or house arrest every thirty days by decisions dated 21 January, 19 February, and 20 March 2009, all taken at private hearings. Initially, the extensions relied on all three statutory grounds; after the indictment on 20 March 2009, interference with the investigation was excluded. The reasoning was largely repetitive and generalized. For flight risk, the panel cited the gravity of charges, possible sentence, the first applicant’s previous criminal record, pending proceedings against the second, and said family and residence were insufficient guarantees. For reoffending, it cited the nature and manner of the offences and the applicants’ use of position and special powers. Later extensions added that detention was the most efficient measure to secure attendance. After April 2009, six more private thirty-day extensions followed, with similar reasoning and references to the third applicant’s prior conviction.

The applicants appealed to the Skopje Court of Appeal, complaining of insufficient reasoning, failure to address family and health circumstances, misuse of prior convictions, and wording that allegedly violated the presumption of innocence. They also requested notification or public sessions. The Court of Appeal, sitting in private, dismissed the appeals in several decisions between May and December 2009, finding sufficient reasons. It relied on written submissions from the public prosecutor that were not communicated to the applicants, and rejected requests for public sessions. It stated that complaints denying the offences or criminal responsibility were irrelevant at the detention-review stage and would be examined at trial. The criminal proceedings later ended in conviction in January 2010, but the appeal court quashed that judgment in September 2010 and released the first and third applicants, finding no grounds for detention.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants alleged violations of Article 5 § 3 (continued detention without relevant and sufficient reasons), Article 5 § 4 (review proceedings not adversarial and lack of oral hearing), and Article 6 § 2 (presumption of innocence). The Government argued that the reasons were sufficient and that detention secured attendance. The Court found the complaints admissible and reiterated that although reasonable suspicion is necessary, after time it no longer suffices; release is presumed and authorities must convincingly justify continued detention with specific reasons. The key facts were therefore the generic, repetitive detention-extension reasoning, private hearings, non-communicated prosecutor submissions, and failure to individualize justifications for each applicant.

**Case: Emin Huseynov v. Azerbaijan (No. 2) (Application no. 1/16)**

The applicant, Emin Huseynov, was an Azerbaijani independent journalist and chairman of the Institute for Reporters’ Freedom and Safety (IRFS), an NGO protecting journalists’ rights. In April 2014, the Prosecutor General’s Office opened criminal case no. 142006023 under the Criminal Code concerning alleged financial irregularities by several NGOs. In connection with those proceedings, the bank accounts of numerous NGOs and civil-society activists were frozen, and several human-rights defenders and activists were arrested. The applicant later learned that tax authorities had begun investigating IRFS.

On 5 August 2014, Huseynov was prevented from taking a flight from Baku to Istanbul. On 7 August, his mother received a call from prosecutors inviting him for questioning. Fearing imminent arrest, he went into hiding. On 18 August 2014, he secretly entered the Swiss embassy in Baku and remained there. The case of *Borovská and Forrai v. Slovakia* (Application no. 48554/10) originated from an application lodged against the Slovak Republic with the European Court of Human Rights on 16 August 2010. The applicants, Mária Borovská, Mária Buzová, and Štefan Forrai, were Slovak nationals and successors in title to a plot of land (no. 10610) in Košice-Sever. This land, along with other plots, had been expropriated in the 1980s by the socialist State to build a public sports centre, a decision the applicants later argued was legally invalid due to procedural flaws.

In 1994, the applicants filed a civil action seeking the removal of the constructions on their land, or alternatively, a judicial ruling to establish an easement for the sports centre's owner in return for financial compensation. In its 2008 judgment, the Košice I District Court agreed that the 1984 expropriation was legally ineffective and confirmed the applicants as the rightful owners. It also found the constructions were built without valid title. However, the court dismissed the claim for an easement. It reasoned that under the Civil Code, the sports facilities did not qualify as "buildings" (*stavba*) in the strict legal sense, and an easement could only be established for a building's owner. Since the applicants' claim was legally classified as seeking an easement, it had to be dismissed.

On appeal, the applicants argued that the District Court had failed to consider that other, generically similar claims concerning the same sports complex had been successful, with easements granted. They specifically cited a prior case (no. 15C 251/94) where an easement was established on comparable plots. The Košice Regional Court, however, dismissed the appeal on different grounds. While it agreed the expropriation was invalid, it ruled that the State had appropriated the land without legal title, a situation governed by the special Land Ownership Act (Law no. 229/1991 Coll.). This law required restitution claims to be filed by 31 December 1992, a deadline the applicants had missed. The Regional Court concluded that seeking redress under the general Civil Code was therefore impermissible. The applicants’ crucial argument regarding the inconsistent judicial practice went unanswered.

The applicants then lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court, alleging arbitrary dismissal and violations of their rights to a fair trial and property protection. They reiterated that their case fell outside the restitution laws and that the courts had ignored the divergent case-law. On 3 June 2010, the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded, again without addressing the applicants' argument about the conflicting judicial practice.

The applicants' core complaint to the European Court was that their rights under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair trial) were violated. They alleged that the domestic courts had arbitrarily dismissed their property claim and, critically, had failed to respond to their key argument: that a number of similarly situated claims concerning the same sports complex had been granted, creating a situation of legal uncertainty and unfairness. The case thus centered on whether the domestic courts' refusal to engage with this argument regarding inconsistent case-law constituted a violation of the right to a reasoned and fair judicial decision.

**Borovská and Forrai v. Slovakia (Application no. 48554/10)**

**Summary**

The applicants—three Slovak nationals—are successors in title to land in Košice-Sever that was expropriated in the 1980s by the socialist State, on which a public sports centre (including a tennis court, grandstand, water station and paved areas) was built. In 1994 the applicants sued the owner of the sports centre, seeking removal of the constructions on the ground that the 1984 expropriation decision was invalid, and alternatively seeking a judicial ruling establishing an easement over their land in return for compensation. The action was later extended to the municipality and a private company.

In 2008 the Košice I District Court found that the 1984 expropriation was legally ineffective, that the applicants were the lawful owners, that the constructions had been built without valid legal title, and that the applicants were entitled to redress under Article 135c of the Civil Code (which is not subject to any limitation period, unlike restitution legislation). However, the court dismissed the easement claim, holding that the constructions did not qualify as "buildings" in the civil-law sense and that an easement could only benefit the owner of a building.

On appeal, the applicants argued that the District Court had ignored the fact that the property formed part of a single sports complex; that numerous generically similar claims concerning other plots on the same complex had been fully or partly successful; and that in case no. 15C 251/94 the District Court had established an easement over similar plots, including plots without "buildings," with no distinction drawn. In 2010 the Regional Court dismissed the appeal on different grounds, holding that the case fell within the Land Ownership Act (restitution legislation), that claims had to be lodged by 31 December 1992, and that asserting property rights under general civil law was impermissible. The applicants' argument regarding divergent judicial practice went unanswered.

The applicants' constitutional complaint was declared inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded in June 2010. The Constitutional Court cited the Regional Court's reasoning at length but did not address the applicants' specific argument about inconsistent case-law.

Before the European Court, the applicants alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, arguing that their property claim had been arbitrarily dismissed and that the courts had failed to respond to their argument that a number of generically similar claims concerning other plots on which the same functional sports complex had been built had been granted.

The relevant domestic context reveals significant divergent judicial practice. While the Supreme Court had held in 2009 (case no. 4Cdo 130/07) that the Land Ownership Act was a lex specialis precluding subsidiary application of the Civil Code, the Constitutional Court in its judgment of 28 March 2012 reached the opposite conclusion—that original owners had not lost title and could assert it under the general Civil Code provisions. The Constitutional Court expressly found that contradictory conclusions in generically similar cases concerning the same sports centre amounted to divergent decision-making contrary to foreseeability and legal certainty, and was manifestly unfair.

The alleged violations thus centre on: (1) the arbitrary dismissal of the applicants' property claim; (2) the ordinary courts' failure to engage with the applicants' argument concerning inconsistent judicial practice; and (3) the broader inconsistency in domestic case-law regarding whether the Civil Code could be applied to property appropriated without legal title.

Case: *Borovská and Forrai v. Slovakia* (App. no. 48554/10), ECtHR Third Section, judgment 25 November 2014 (revised 16 February 2016).

The applicants were Slovak nationals and successors in title to land in Košice-Sever. In the 1980s the socialist State expropriated the land and built a public sports centre, including tennis courts, a grandstand, a water station and paved areas. After 1989, original owners and successors litigated property claims concerning the complex. In 1994 the applicants sued the owner of the sports centre, later adding the municipality and a private company, seeking removal of constructions on their plot. They argued that the 1984 expropriation decision was legally invalid, so they remained owners and the defendant had no lawful title. Alternatively, they sought an easement over their land for the sports centre owner in return for compensation.

In 2008 the Košice I District Court found the 1984 expropriation legally ineffective and recognised the applicants as owners; the constructions had been built without valid title. However, it refused an easement. Under Article 135c of the Civil Code, an easement could only be established for the benefit of the owner of a “building” in the legal sense, and the constructions on the applicants’ plots did not qualify. The claim was dismissed.

On appeal, the applicants argued that their claim was legally identical to similar claims concerning other plots under the same sports centre. They relied on case no. 15C 251/94, in which the District Court had established an easement over plots with similar constructions, without distinguishing plots with or without “buildings.” They contended that the only difference was the technical parameters of the plots, and that comparable claimants had been treated differently.

In February 2010 the Košice Regional Court dismissed the appeal but on different grounds. It agreed the expropriation was ineffective, but held that the State had therefore appropriated the land without legal title under section 6(1)(p) of the Land Ownership Act. Restitution claims had to be brought under that Act by 31 December 1992. Because the applicants had not done so, they could not assert property rights under general civil law. The Regional Court did not address their argument about inconsistent judicial practice.

The applicants complained to the Constitutional Court, alleging arbitrariness and violations of Article 6 §1 and property rights. They argued their case fell outside restitution laws and that Civil Code protection remained available. They again relied on case no. 15C 251/94 and other decisions accepting general civil law in identical contexts. They also noted the proceedings had lasted sixteen years. In June 2010 the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded, citing the Regional Court’s reasoning and again failing to answer the inconsistent-case-law argument.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants alleged in particular that Article 6 §1 was violated because their property claim was arbitrarily dismissed and because the domestic courts failed to respond to their central argument that generically similar claims concerning other plots on the same sports complex had been granted. The key facts for the alleged violation were therefore the allegedly inconsistent domestic case-law, the applicants’ explicit reliance on those comparable cases before the Regional and Constitutional Courts, and the domestic authorities’ failure to engage with that argument. The ECtHR found a violation of Article 6 §1.

**Katona and Závarský v. Slovakia** (Applications nos. 43932/19 and 43995/19) concerned two applicants—Mr László Katona, a Hungarian national, and Mr Tomáš Závarský, a Slovak national—who complained that Slovak insolvency legislation had made it impossible for them to recover debts owed to them by an individual debtor.

In 2005 the first applicant transferred part of his shares in a business entity to a debtor, who agreed to pay him in instalments. To secure payment, the debtor issued promissory notes in favour of the first applicant, who later transferred one note to the second applicant. The first applicant maintained that he had independent parallel claims against the debtor under both the share-transfer agreement and the promissory notes, but that he had not pursued the share-transfer claims and that they had become statute-barred. The second applicant had no claim under the share-transfer agreement.

After non-payment, the applicants sued the debtor over nine promissory notes, with a total principal amount of EUR 74,000. This resulted in four payment orders, which became final, binding and enforceable between 2016 and 2017. A further payment order was challenged, and those proceedings were ultimately terminated in 2019 without a decision on the merits because of the debtor’s later bankruptcy. The applicants initiated enforcement proceedings, but these yielded almost nothing: only EUR 1,399 was seized from the debtor’s monthly income in respect of the second applicant’s claim, of which EUR 1,092.93 was paid to him; no other sizeable assets were found.

A crucial development was the amendment to the Bankruptcy and Restructuring Code introduced by Law no. 377/2016 Coll., effective 1 March 2017. It made “debt discharge” part of bankruptcy proceedings and provided that claims based on promissory notes issued by the bankrupt before a certain date became incapable of being legally pursued. On 24 January 2019 the Bratislava I District Court issued a bankruptcy order against the debtor and granted him a debt discharge upon his request. The decision was not subject to appeal. By operation of law, the applicants’ enforcement proceedings were terminated, and the first applicant’s pending claim was also terminated. The bankruptcy court later confirmed that the applicants’ adjudicated promissory-note claims could not be registered or considered in the bankruptcy proceedings.

The applicants were not parties to the debtor’s bankruptcy or debt-discharge proceedings. They complained under Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that they had been unable to pursue their claims against the debtor in any legal proceedings and had no effective legal protection. The Court examined the case primarily under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The Government argued that the applicants should have sought cancellation of the debt discharge under Article 166f of the amended Code for lack of the debtor’s “honest aim.” The Court rejected that objection: the remedy focused on the debtor’s intention, not on the alleged disproportionate exclusion of the applicants’ claims, and the applicants lacked access to the bankruptcy file and had no clear grounds to challenge the discharge. The Court found the complaint admissible.

On the merits, the Court held that the legislative amendment, combined with the debtor’s discharge, imposed an absolute bar on the applicants’ ability to pursue their final and enforceable claims, without compensation, and without their participation in the bankruptcy proceedings. This imposed an excessive individual burden and failed to strike a fair balance between the competing interests. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

**Mesić v. Croatia (No. 2)** concerned former Croatian President Stjepan Mesić’s complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention that Croatia failed to protect his reputation when domestic courts dismissed his civil defamation action against the Internet news portal *Dnevno.hr*. The article, published on 17 February 2015, alleged his involvement in bribery connected to Croatia’s procurement of Patria armoured vehicles from Finland.

The background was Finnish criminal proceedings. In June 2013, the Finnish Prosecutor General’s press release stated that Patria employees were suspected of promising or giving bribes through intermediaries in exchange for actions by the President of Croatia and a Croatian state company director. On 16 February 2015, the Kanta-Häme District Court convicted two Patria employees of bribing the Croatian company director, but expressly found insufficient evidence that Mesić had been promised or given a bribe, although his name appeared in messages. The Turku Court of Appeal later acquitted the accused.

The next day, *Dnevno.hr* published an article asserting that Mesić had received €630,000 from persons just convicted of giving bribes; that the Finnish prosecutor had confirmed documents were sent to Croatia’s USKOK; that two Patria managers directly charged with bribing Mesić had been convicted; and that a joint investigation had “undoubtedly established” Mesić’s participation in criminal activities. It included quotes attributed to the Finnish Prosecutor General and excerpts from the Finnish indictment, and called on Croatian authorities to prosecute Mesić. Mesić requested a correction; the portal refused.

Mesić sued for non-pecuniary damage, arguing the statements were false and portrayed him as corrupt. The Zagreb Municipal Civil Court dismissed the claim in December 2015, and the County Court upheld that decision in April 2016. Applying the Media Act, the courts found the journalist had acted in good faith on sufficiently verified information from the Finnish press release, indictment, and alleged interview with the Finnish Prosecutor General. They held the article was in the public interest because Mesić was a public figure, and that the truth of the allegations did not need to be decided. They also found no breach of the presumption of innocence. The Constitutional Court dismissed his complaint in December 2016.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Mesić complained that dismissal of his defamation action violated Article 8’s positive obligation to protect private life and reputation. The Government argued non-exhaustion, saying his constitutional complaint relied on fair trial and presumption-of-innocence grounds, not Article 8 or Article 35 of the Croatian Constitution. Mesić replied that his reputation was the substance of his domestic claims.

The ECtHR ultimately found no violation of Article 8. It held that the domestic courts had struck a fair balance between the applicant’s Article 8 reputation interests and the media’s Article 10 freedom of expression. The article concerned a matter of public interest—alleged corruption in high-level arms procurement. The media’s “watchdog” role was particularly important where investigative journalism helped hold authorities accountable. Accordingly, dismissing the civil defamation claim did not breach Croatia’s positive obligations under Article 8.

**Case: Mesić v. Croatia (No. 2), Application no. 45066/17**

The applicant, Stjepan Mesić, was President of Croatia from 2000 to 2010. The case concerns an article published on 17 February 2015 by the Croatian internet news portal *Dnevno.hr*, alleging his involvement in criminal activity connected to Croatia’s procurement of armoured vehicles from the Finnish company Patria.

The background involved criminal proceedings in Finland. In 2013, Finnish prosecutors indicted several Patria employees for aggravated bribery in the sale of Patria AMV vehicles to Croatia. A Finnish Prosecutor General press release suggested that bribes had been promised or given through intermediaries in exchange for actions by the President of Croatia and a Croatian state-owned company director. In February 2015, the Kanta-Häme District Court convicted two Patria employees of promising and giving a bribe to the Croatian company director. However, the court expressly found insufficient evidence that a bribe had been promised or given to Mesić. The convictions were later overturned on appeal, and the accused were acquitted.

The day after the first-instance Finnish judgment, *Dnevno.hr* published an article stating, among other things, that Mesić had received a €630,000 bribe from persons “who have just been convicted of giving bribes”; that Patria managers had been directly charged with giving bribes to Mesić and the Croatian company director; and that the joint investigation had “undoubtedly established” that Mesić participated in criminal activities. The article also argued that Croatian authorities, particularly USKOK, were obliged to investigate and prosecute Mesić, and relied on an alleged telephone interview with the Finnish Prosecutor General and on the Finnish indictment.

Mesić requested a correction, claiming the statements were false and damaging. The portal refused. He then brought a civil defamation action against the company operating the portal, seeking compensation for non-pecuniary damage to his honour and reputation. He argued that the Finnish judgment showed he had not been convicted or even charged, and that the article falsely portrayed him as a corrupt politician and criminal.

The Croatian courts dismissed his claim. The Zagreb Municipal Civil Court found that the journalist acted in good faith and had based the article on sufficiently verified sources: the Finnish press release, the indictment, and the alleged interview with the Finnish Prosecutor General. It held that the article concerned a matter of public interest because Mesić was a public figure, and that his presumption of innocence had not been called into question. The Zagreb County Court upheld that judgment, and the Constitutional Court dismissed Mesić’s constitutional complaint.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Mesić complained that by dismissing his civil action, the Croatian courts had failed to protect his reputation as part of his right to respect for private life under Article 8 of the Convention. The Government argued that he had not exhausted domestic remedies because his constitutional complaint had not expressly relied on Article 8 or the corresponding Croatian constitutional provision protecting reputation. Mesić replied that he had in substance raised the reputation issue throughout the domestic proceedings.

The ECtHR examined the case under Article 8, focusing on Croatia’s positive obligation to protect reputation while balancing freedom of expression under Article 10. It considered that the article concerned a matter of public interest and that the media’s “watchdog” role, especially in investigative journalism, was particularly important. The domestic courts had weighed the competing interests using the Court’s criteria. The ECtHR concluded that a fair balance had been struck and found no violation of Article 8.

In *Mesi} v. Croatia (No. 2)*, the applicant, Stjepan Mesi}, was a former President of Croatia (2000–2010). He complained under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that Croatian courts dismissed his civil defamation action concerning an online article alleging his involvement in criminal activities during his presidency, thereby failing to protect his reputation and private life.

The case arose from the “Patria” affair. In 2013, Finnish authorities prosecuted Patria employees for bribery linked to Croatia’s procurement of armoured vehicles. A Finnish Prosecutor General press release stated that bribes had been promised or given through intermediaries in exchange for actions by the President of Croatia and a Croatian State-owned company director. In February 2015, the Kanta-Häme District Court convicted two Patria employees of bribing the Croatian company director, but found insufficient evidence that Mesi} had been promised or given a bribe. The Turku Court of Appeal later acquitted the accused.

On 17 February 2015, the Croatian internet news portal *Dnevno.hr* published an article suggesting Mesi} had participated in criminal activities. It claimed, among other things, that Mesi} had received €630,000 from persons convicted of giving bribes; that two Patria managers had been directly charged with giving bribes to Mesi} and the Croatian director and had been sentenced; and that the joint investigation had “undoubtedly established” that Mesi} participated in criminal activities. The article also said Mesi} had not been charged in Finland but argued Croatian authorities should investigate and prosecute him. Mesi} requested a correction; the portal refused and stood by the article.

Mesi} sued the portal for compensation, seeking 40,000 Croatian kunas (about €5,290) for non-pecuniary damage. He argued the statements were false and injured his honour and reputation by portraying him as a corrupt politician and criminal. The Zagreb Municipal Civil Court dismissed the claim. It found the journalist acted in good faith and relied on sufficiently verified sources: the Finnish Prosecutor General’s press release, the Finnish indictment mentioning Mesi}, and a telephone interview with the Finnish Prosecutor General. The court treated Mesi} as a public figure and the matter as one of public interest, and held that the article did not violate his presumption of innocence. The Zagreb County Court upheld that judgment, finding the information accurate, verified, and objectively reported. The Constitutional Court dismissed Mesi}’s constitutional complaint, finding no arbitrariness and no breach of the presumption of innocence.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Mesi} alleged that the dismissal of his civil action violated Article 8. The Government argued non-exhaustion, because his constitutional complaint had relied on fair-trial and presumption-of-innocence grounds rather than Article 8 or the corresponding constitutional provision on reputation. The applicant contended that he had in substance raised the reputation issue.

The Court examined Croatia’s positive obligation to protect private life/reputation while balancing Article 10 freedom of expression. It found that the domestic courts had struck a fair balance. The article concerned a matter of public interest, and the media’s “watchdog” role was particularly important where investigative journalism helped hold authorities accountable. Considering the Article 8 and Article 10 criteria, the Court concluded that the dismissal of the civil defamation action did not violate Article 8.

In *Strassenmeyer v. Germany* (Application no. 57818/18, judgment 2 May 2023), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) concerning the fairness of the applicant’s criminal conviction and his inability to examine a co-accused.

The case arose from the 1994 killing of G. in the Czech Republic. G. had run a clothing shop in Erfurt with F., who later committed suicide. In 2012, N., a former friend of F., told German police that F. had confided involvement in killing a co-worker in the Czech Republic. In 2014, police arrested K., who had also worked at the shop. Before questioning, K. was informed in writing of his rights to remain silent and to consult a lawyer, but, because an outdated form was used after a legislative change, he was not told of his right to have court-appointed counsel under Article 136 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

K. initially denied being present at the killing but later, with counsel, said he saw the applicant hit G. with a truncheon and place the unconscious body in a car boot. S. and V. were also questioned. V. provided a detailed account: the group had drugged G. with LSD, driven him to the Czech Republic, and, after G. threatened to report them, the applicant and M.S. beat him; V. handed the applicant a tonfa; later the applicant threw a rock at G.’s head; the body was burned. V., S. and the applicant were all informed of their rights in the same defective manner. After police questioning, they were brought before an investigating judge, assigned lawyers, and made no further statements.

At trial before the Erfurt Regional Court, the applicant made only a statement about drug abuse; the co-accused remained silent. The court therefore heard police officers about the pre-trial interviews, despite objections. It also heard N., L., B., Czech police officers, and forensic and pathological experts. V.’s account was partly contradicted—experts doubted G. could have moved after being set on fire, and the body’s distance from the cars differed from V.’s version—but the court found V.’s statement reliable due to corroboration with K., witness testimony, crime-scene evidence, and V.’s self-incriminating detail. In 2016, the applicant was convicted of murder and deprivation of liberty resulting in death and sentenced to life imprisonment. The conviction relied significantly on V.’s pre-trial statement.

The applicant appealed, arguing that he had been unable to examine the co-accused whose untested statements carried decisive weight, that counterbalancing factors were insufficient, and that the failure to inform him of the right to court-appointed counsel rendered the statements inadmissible. The Federal Court of Justice dismissed the appeal, noting the State’s strong interest in prosecuting serious crime, the unintentional nature of the error, and no indication that lack of funds prevented legal assistance. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider his complaint.

The ECtHR found no violation. Although the untested co-accused statements carried significant weight, the trial court had good reason to admit them, and sufficient counterbalancing factors allowed a fair and proper assessment of their reliability. The defence rights were not restricted to an extent incompatible with Article 6. The police’s failure to inform the accused of the right to court-appointed counsel did not, in the circumstances, affect the applicant’s conviction or the fairness of the proceedings; he had been informed in writing of the right to legal assistance, and there was no indication he lacked means to obtain a lawyer.

**Case: Strassenmeyer v. Germany (Application no. 57818/18, ECtHR, 2 May 2023)**

The applicant, Marco Straßenmeyer, was convicted in Germany of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment. The case concerned alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 6 § 3 (d) of the European Convention on Human Rights, namely the right to a fair hearing and the right to examine witnesses. The central issue was whether the applicant’s conviction could fairly be based on incriminating pre-trial statements made by co-accused who later refused to testify at trial, and whether the police’s failure to inform the accused of the right to court-appointed counsel affected the fairness of the proceedings.

In 1994, G. was killed in the Czech Republic. The investigation was revived in 2012. In 2014, German police arrested several suspects, including K., V., S., and the applicant. Before questioning, K. and the others were informed in writing of their rights to remain silent and to consult a lawyer. However, because police used an outdated form, they were not informed of their right to have court-appointed counsel under Article 136 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, despite a 2013 amendment implementing EU law.

K. initially implicated the applicant. Later, with counsel present, K. stated that he saw the applicant hit G. with a truncheon and place the unconscious body in a car. V. then gave a detailed statement describing the killing: a plan to drug G. with LSD over shop revenues, a trip to the Czech Republic, and a beating by the applicant and M.S., during which the applicant used a tonfa, threw a rock at G.’s head, and later burned the body. V.’s statement incriminated both himself and the applicant. The applicant denied knowing G. and denied being in the Czech Republic.

At trial, the applicant and co-accused exercised their right to remain silent. The Regional Court therefore heard police officers recount the pre-trial statements and considered other evidence, including witnesses L. and N., forensic experts, and crime-scene findings. The applicant objected to admission of the pre-trial statements and requested a psychological expert opinion on V.’s veracity, which the court refused. The Regional Court convicted the applicant, relying heavily on V.’s pre-trial statement, which it found reliable and corroborated by K., L., and forensic evidence. It admitted the statements despite the failure to warn about court-appointed counsel, citing the State’s strong interest in prosecuting serious crime, the unintentional nature of the oversight, V.’s stated willingness to speak without a lawyer, and no indication that lack of funds prevented counsel. The Federal Court of Justice and Federal Constitutional Court rejected the applicant’s appeals.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained that he could not examine the co-accused whose pre-trial statements were decisive, and that there were insufficient counterbalancing factors. He also argued that the failure to inform him and the others of the right to court-appointed counsel rendered the statements inadmissible.

The ECtHR found no violation. It accepted that the trial court had good reason to admit the untested statements because the co-accused refused to testify. It found sufficient counterbalancing factors allowed a fair assessment of reliability, including corroboration, forensic consistency, and witness testimony. Defence rights were not restricted incompatibly with Article 6. As to the missing court-appointed counsel warning, the Court found no indication that this omission affected the applicant’s conviction or the fairness of the proceedings; the accused had been informed in writing of their right to legal assistance, and there was no indication they lacked means to obtain a lawyer.

Strassenmeyer v. Germany (ECtHR, 2 May 2023) concerned a German national convicted of murder largely on the pre-trial statements of co-accused who later refused to testify. In 1994, G. was killed in the Czech Republic; his body was found in a wooded area. The investigation was revived in 2012 after N., a former friend of F., reported that F. had confessed involvement in killing a co-worker. In September 2014, police arrested K., who had worked at the shop run by G. and F. Before questioning, K. was informed in writing of his rights to remain silent and to consult a lawyer, but, owing to an outdated form, was not told of his right to have court-appointed counsel under Article 136 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. K implicated the applicant.

The applicant was arrested the next day and received the same defective warning. He denied knowing G. or visiting the Czech Republic. Other suspects, S. and V., were also warned in the same manner. V. then gave a detailed pre-trial statement: the group had planned to drug G. with LSD and drive him to the Czech Republic; once there, the applicant beat G. with fists and a tonfa, threw a rock at his head, and the body was burned. These police interviews were not video- or audio-recorded.

At trial before the Erfurt Regional Court, the applicant and co-accused exercised their right to remain silent. The court therefore heard police officers who recounted the pre-trial statements, over defence objections. The applicant could not examine V. or the other co-accused at any stage. The court also heard N., shop worker L., witness B., Czech police officers, and forensic and pathology experts. L. testified that the applicant had boasted about killing G.

The Regional Court convicted the applicant of murder and sentenced him to life imprisonment. It relied heavily on V.’s pre-trial statement, finding it reliable because it was corroborated by K.’s account, pathology evidence, and crime-scene details, and because it was unlikely V. would falsely incriminate himself. The court acknowledged some inaccuracies but found explanations for them. It refused a request for a psychological expert on V.’s veracity. It also declined to exclude the statements despite the failure to inform the accused of the right to court-appointed counsel, citing the gravity of the offence, the unintentional nature of the oversight, V.’s stated wish to speak without a lawyer, and no indication of lack of funds. The Federal Court of Justice and Federal Constitutional Court rejected further appeals.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (d): his conviction was based significantly on untested pre-trial statements of co-accused whom he could not examine, and the statements were obtained without informing him of the right to court-appointed counsel. The ECtHR found no violation. Although the untested statements carried significant weight, the trial court had good reason to admit them because the co-accused refused to testify, and sufficient counterbalancing factors allowed a fair assessment of reliability. The defence could challenge the evidence through police witnesses, other witnesses, and forensic evidence. As to the missing court-appointed counsel warning, the accused had been informed in writing of the right to legal assistance, and there was no indication that the omission affected the conviction or overall fairness.

In *Irodotou v. Cyprus* (ECtHR, Third Section, App. No. 16783/20, judgment 23 May 2023), the applicant, Marios Irodotou, complained that private criminal proceedings against him lasted an excessive time, contrary to Article 6 §1, and that Cyprus provided no effective domestic remedy, contrary to Article 13.

The underlying dispute began with a civil judgment of 18 June 2013 ordering Irodotou to pay the Cooperative Credit Company of Geroskipou and East Paphos EUR 300 monthly from 1 September 2013 until a debt was repaid. On 2 March 2015, Paphos Cooperative Savings Bank Ltd brought a private prosecution against him for failing to pay instalments due between 1 September 2013 and 1 January 2015. He was notified on 3 April 2015, pleaded not guilty, and the case was first set for hearing on 5 November 2015.

From 5 November 2015 to 22 March 2017, the hearing was adjourned four times, mainly because the District Court lacked time. The prosecuting entity then changed names because of mergers: Paphos Cooperative Savings Bank Ltd transferred assets and liabilities to Cooperative Central Bank Ltd, effective 1 July 2017; that company became Cyprus Cooperative Bank Ltd on 24 July 2017; and later became Cooperative Asset Management Company Ltd on 3 September 2018.

Further adjournments followed: on 6 November 2017 due to the court’s lack of time; on 29 March 2018 at the applicant’s request for health reasons; on 24 September 2018 because a prosecution witness was absent; on 15 November 2018 after the applicant challenged whether the prosecuting company could act as a legal entity; on 15 January 2019 to exchange documents; on 26 March 2019 to submit an agreed list of undisputed facts; and on 24 May 2019 without objection. No substantive trial hearing ever commenced.

On 5 September 2019, prosecution counsel applied to the Attorney General to discontinue the case. She explained that the mergers raised whether a non-existent prosecutor could validly pursue the prosecution, that the Supreme Court was considering that issue, that a similar case had ended in a pre-trial acquittal, and that continuation no longer served a purpose. She also said a dismissal could harm the merged entity’s rights in a future prosecution over unpaid instalments. On 23 September 2019, the Attorney General entered a *nolle prosequi*. On 2 October 2019, the District Court discontinued the case and discharged the applicant.

The applicant objected, arguing he had not been consulted; that he had already raised the legal-capacity issue on 15 November 2018; that the case had been repeatedly adjourned because of the court’s lack of time; and that he could not claim losses or expenses. He said he had appeared in court for four and a half years and had paid EUR 8 stamps for counsel’s appearances. The court replied that the *nolle prosequi* was an exclusive constitutional power of the Attorney General, not subject to judicial review, and made no costs order.

The relevant period ran from 2 March 2015 to 2 October 2019, about four years and seven months before one level of jurisdiction. The Government argued that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies, had lost victim status because the case was discontinued in his favour, and had suffered no significant disadvantage since no hearing began, he made only about fourteen formal appearances, the maximum penalty was a fine up to EUR 5,000, and costs were under EUR 2,000. The applicant maintained that he remained a victim, had suffered humiliation and insecurity, and had no effective remedy; he claimed legal fees of EUR 2,421.65 including VAT, which he could not recover after the *nolle prosequi*.

In *A.S. v. Italy* (Application no. 20860/20), judgment of 19 October 2023, the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee) examined an application lodged on 15 May 2020 by Mr A.S., a Tunisian national residing in Agrigento. The applicant was represented by Ms A. Brambilla, and the Italian Government was represented by Mr L. D’Ascia. The case concerned the applicant’s detention in the Italian hotspot at Contrada Imbriacola, on the island of Lampedusa, and the poor conditions of his stay there. The Lampedusa Early Reception and Aid Centre (CSPA) is one of Italy’s designated hotspots under section 17 of Decree-Law no. 13 of 17 February 2017.

The key facts are as follows. On 7 October 2019 the applicant reached the Italian coast aboard a makeshift vessel. On the following day, 8 October 2019, he was transferred to the hotspot at Lampedusa. He remained there until 25 October 2019. On 19 October 2019, while still in the hotspot, he expressed his wish to file an asylum request. On 25 October 2019 he was transferred to a reception centre in Agrigento and formally lodged his asylum request on the same date.

By decision of 29 October 2019, the Agrigento section of the Palermo Territorial Commission rejected the applicant’s asylum request as manifestly ill-founded. The decision was served on him on 2 November 2019. On that same date, he was served with an expulsion order issued by the Prefect of Agrigento, together with an order by the Agrigento police commissioner for his detention at the Caltanissetta Repatriation Detention Centre (CPR) for the time necessary to effect his repatriation.

On 5 November 2019, the Caltanissetta Justice of the Peace declined to approve the detention order for want of jurisdiction and referred the case to the Caltanissetta ordinary court. As a result, the applicant left the CPR. On 21 November 2019 he challenged the expulsion order before the Agrigento Justice of the Peace. By decision of 6 December 2019, the Agrigento Justice of the Peace revoked the expulsion order on procedural grounds.

The alleged violations before the Court centred primarily on the applicant’s stay in the Lampedusa hotspot from 8 to 25 October 2019. He complained that this amounted to a deprivation of liberty without a sufficient legal basis or adequate judicial review, contrary to Article 5 of the Convention. He also alleged that the material conditions in the hotspot were poor and amounted to inhuman or degrading treatment, contrary to Article 3 of the Convention.

The case therefore raised issues concerning Italy’s hotspot system, the de facto detention of migrants, and the reception conditions for persons arriving by sea before they can formally apply for international protection. The subsequent asylum rejection, expulsion order, and brief CPR detention provide context, but the core of the application concerns the lawfulness of the hotspot detention and the conditions there.

The case *A.S. v. Italy* (Application no. 20860/20) originated in an application lodged on 15 May 2020 by A.S., a Tunisian national born and living in Agrigento, Italy.
