The key facts are as follows. On 7 October 2019 the applicant reached the Italian coast aboard a makeshift vessel. The next day, 8 October 2019, he was transferred to the hotspot in Contrada Imbriacola. He remained there until 25 October 2019—approximately seventeen days. On 19 October 2019, while still in the hotspot, he expressed his wish to file an asylum request. On 25 October 2019 he was transferred to a reception centre in Agrigento, and on the same date he formally lodged his asylum application.

By decision of 29 October 2019, the Agrigento section of the Palermo Territorial Commission rejected the asylum request as manifestly ill-founded. The rejection was served on the applicant on 2 November 2019. On that same day, two further measures were served on him: an expulsion order issued by the Prefect of Agrigento, and an order by the Agrigento police commissioner for his detention at the Caltanissetta Repatriation Detention Centre (CPR) for the time necessary to effect his repatriation.

However, on 5 November 2019, the Caltanissetta Justice of the Peace declined to approve the detention order for lack of jurisdiction and referred the case to the Caltanissetta ordinary court. As a result, the applicant left the CPR. On 21 November 2019 he challenged the expulsion order before the Agrigento Justice of the Peace. By decision of 6 December 2019, the Agrigento Justice of the Peace revoked the expulsion order on procedural grounds.

The facts relevant to the alleged Convention violations therefore centre on two principal periods of deprivation of liberty: the applicant’s stay in the Lampedusa hotspot from 8 to 25 October 2019, including the conditions there and the legal basis for holding him; and his brief detention in the Caltanissetta CPR from 2 to 5 November 2019 following the expulsion and detention orders. The applicant’s asylum request, its rejection as manifestly ill-founded, the ensuing expulsion order, and the later revocation of that order on procedural grounds form the background against which the lawfulness of the measures and the adequacy of procedural safeguards must be assessed. The case was communicated to the Italian Government, which was represented by Mr L. D’Ascia. The Fifth Section Committee, composed of Judges Mourou-Vikström, Chanturia and Guyomar, deliberated in private on 28 September 2023 and delivered judgment on 19 October 2023.

The case of *A.S. v. Italy* concerns a Tunisian national, Mr A.S., who was detained in the Italian hotspot at Contrada Imbriacola on the island of Lampedusa and complained about the poor conditions of his stay. The application was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 15 May 2020. The applicant was born in and lived in Agrigento and was represented by a lawyer practising in Milan. The judgment was delivered by the Fifth Section on 19 October 2023.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are as follows. On 7 October 2019, the applicant reached the Italian coast aboard a makeshift vessel. The next day, 8 October 2019, he was transferred to the hotspot in Contrada Imbriacola, Lampedusa. That facility, the Early Reception and Aid Centre (CSPA), had been identified as an Italian hotspot under section 17 of Decree-Law no. 13 of 17 February 2017. That decision was served on him on 2 November 2019. On the same day, the Prefect of Agrigento issued an expulsion order, and the Agrigento police commissioner ordered his detention at the Caltanissetta Repatriation Detention Centre (CPR) for the time necessary to effect his repatriation. On 5 November 2019, the Caltanissetta Justice of the Peace declined to approve the detention order for want of jurisdiction and referred the case to the Caltanissetta ordinary court. The applicant therefore left the CPR. On 21 November 2019, he challenged his expulsion order before the Agrigento Justice of the Peace. By a decision of 6 December 2019, the Agrigento Justice of the Peace revoked the expulsion order on procedural grounds.

The alleged violations centre on the applicant’s detention in the Lampedusa hotspot and the conditions of his stay there. The key facts are that he was held in a designated hotspot for about 17 days, including a period of 11 days before he expressed an intention to seek asylum and a further 6 days after he did so. The case also involves his subsequent detention at the Caltanissetta CPR, which was not approved by the Justice of the Peace, and the later revocation of the expulsion order. These facts formed the basis for the applicant’s complaints under the Convention, particularly concerning the lawfulness of his detention and the adequacy of the conditions in the hotspot. The Court was therefore called upon to assess whether Italy had violated the applicant’s rights, notably in relation to the deprivation of liberty and the treatment he experienced in the hotspot.

**Case Summary: Kapitonov and Others v. Russia (Application nos. 16001/17 and 25 others)**

The case of *Kapitonov and Others v. Russia* was adjudicated by the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) in a judgment delivered on 9 November 2023. The case originated from 26 separate applications lodged against Russia under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms at various dates.

The central facts relevant to the alleged violations concern the treatment of the applicants as organisers or participants of public assemblies. The applicants complained primarily of disproportionate measures taken against them, specifically their arrest in connection with the dispersal of these assemblies and their subsequent conviction for administrative offences. The Russian Government was given notice of these applications.

The Court first addressed its jurisdiction, noting that the facts giving rise to the alleged violations occurred prior to 16 September 2022, the date on which the Russian Federation ceased to be a party to the Convention. Citing the precedent of *Fedotova and Others v. Russia*, the Court decided it had jurisdiction to examine the applications.

The applicants' principal complaint was that the measures taken against them violated their freedom of assembly, guaranteed by Article 11 of the Convention. They relied expressly or in substance on this Article. In examining the merits, the Court referred to its established case-law on freedom of assembly, particularly the principles outlined in *Kudrevičius and Others v. Lithuania* and the criteria for proportionality of interference as discussed in *Oya Ataman v. Turkey* and *Hyde Park and Others v. Moldova*.

A critical aspect of the Court's analysis was the precedent set by leading Russian cases, including *Frumkin v. Russia*, *Navalnyy and Yashin v. Russia*, and *Kasparov and Others v. Russia*. In these prior judgments, the Court had already found violations concerning issues similar to those raised in the present case. After examining all submitted material, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion. It concluded that the interferences with the applicants' freedom of assembly were not "necessary in a democratic society," thereby establishing a violation of Article 11.

Furthermore, the applicants submitted other complaints that raised issues under the Convention and its Protocols, consistent with the Court's well-established case-law. These complaints were deemed admissible, not being manifestly ill-founded. The Court concluded that these complaints also disclosed violations of the Convention. These findings were based on a body of prior case-law addressing various aspects of the treatment of assembly participants. Specifically, the Court identified violations in relation to:
- Aspects of unlawful deprivation of liberty (per *Lashmankin and Others*, *Butkevich*, *Tsvetkova and Others*, and *Korneyeva*).
- The absence of a prosecuting party in administrative offence proceedings (per *Karelin v. Russia*).
- Disproportionate measures taken against participants of solo manifestations (per *Novikova and Others v. Russia*).
- The lack of suspensive effect of an appeal against a sentence of administrative detention (per *Martynyuk* and *Tsvetkova and Others*).
- The right not to be tried and punished twice for the same offence (per *Korneyeva*).

Some applicants also raised additional complaints concerning other aspects of the fairness of their administrative-offence proceedings under Article 6. Given the findings of violations on the core issues, the Court found it unnecessary to deal separately with these remaining complaints. The Court ultimately found violations of Article 11 and other Articles of the Convention and its Protocols, based on the respondent State's actions against the applicants in the context of public assemblies.

**Summary of *Kapitonov and Others v. Russia* (Application nos. 16001/17 and 25 others)**

The case of *Kapitonov and Others v. Russia* was brought before the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) by 26 applicants against the Russian Federation. The applications were lodged on various dates under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Russian Government was given notice of the applications. The Third Section of the Court, sitting as a Committee, delivered its judgment on 9 November 2023.

The central facts of the case concern the applicants’ involvement in public assemblies. The applicants were either organisers or participants in these gatherings. The core of their complaint was that the Russian authorities took disproportionate measures against them. Specifically, these measures included their arrest in connection with the dispersal of the public assemblies and their subsequent conviction for administrative offences. The applicants alleged that these actions violated their right to freedom of assembly, as guaranteed by Article 11 of the Convention.

The Court first addressed the issue of jurisdiction. It noted that the facts giving rise to the alleged violations occurred prior to 16 September 2022, the date on which the Russian Federation ceased to be a party to the Convention. Relying on its established case-law (specifically the *Fedotova and Others v. Russia* judgment), the Court decided that it still had jurisdiction to examine the applications.

In examining the merits of the Article 11 complaint, the Court referred to its well-established principles regarding freedom of assembly, as outlined in cases like *Kudrevičius and Others v. Lithuania* and *Oya Ataman v. Turkey*. It also recalled its previous findings of violations in similar cases against Russia, such as *Frumkin v. Russia*, *Navalnyy and Yashin v. Russia*, and *Kasparov and Others v. Russia*.

After reviewing all the submitted material, the Court found no fact or argument that would lead it to a different conclusion from its prior case-law. It held that the interferences with the applicants’ freedom of assembly—namely their arrest and administrative conviction—were not “necessary in a democratic society.” Consequently, the Court found a violation of Article 11 of the Convention.

The applicants also raised several other complaints under various provisions of the Convention and its Protocols. These were based on well-established case-law and were found admissible. The Court concluded that these complaints also disclosed further violations. These included:
- **Unlawful deprivation of liberty:** Various aspects of the unlawful detention of organisers or participants of public assemblies, as per the cases of *Lashmankin and Others*, *Butkevich*, *Tsvetkova and Others*, and *Korneyeva*.
- **Unfair administrative proceedings:** The absence of a prosecuting party in proceedings under the Code of Administrative Offences, contrary to the *Karelin v. Russia* judgment.
- **Disproportionate measures against solo protesters:** As established in *Novikova and Others v. Russia*.
- **Lack of suspensive effect of appeals:** Concerning appeals against sentences of administrative detention, based on *Martynyuk v. Russia*.
- **Double jeopardy (*ne bis in idem*):** The right of organisers or participants of public assemblies not to be tried and punished twice for the same offence, as per *Korneyeva v. Russia*.

Some applicants also raised additional complaints under Article 6 concerning other aspects of the fairness of their administrative proceedings. Given the Court’s findings on the other violations, it decided there was no need to examine these remaining complaints separately.

**Summary of Kapitonov and Others v. Russia (Application nos. 16001/17 and 25 others)**

The case of *Kapitonov and Others v. Russia* was brought before the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) by 26 applicants against the Russian Federation. The applications, lodged on various dates, concerned events that occurred prior to 16 September 2022, when Russia ceased to be a party to the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court confirmed it had jurisdiction to examine the applications, citing *Fedotova and Others v. Russia*.

The central complaint raised by the applicants was that the Russian authorities had taken disproportionate measures against them as organisers or participants of public assemblies. Specifically, they alleged that they had been arrested in relation to the dispersal of these assemblies and subsequently convicted of administrative offences. The applicants relied, expressly or in substance, on Article 11 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to freedom of peaceful assembly.

In examining the merits, the Court referred to its established case-law on freedom of assembly, including the principles set out in *Kudrevičius and Others v. Lithuania*, and on the proportionality of interference with that right, as elaborated in *Oya Ataman v. Turkey* and *Hyde Park and Others v. Moldova*. The Court noted that in several leading cases against Russia—*Frumkin v. Russia*, *Navalnyy and Yashin v. Russia*, and *Kasparov and Others v. Russia*—it had already found violations in respect of issues similar to those in the present case.

Having examined all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion. It therefore held that the interferences with the applicants’ freedom of assembly had not been “necessary in a democratic society,” in violation of Article 11.

The applicants also raised other complaints under well-established case-law. These included various aspects of unlawful deprivation of liberty of organisers or participants of public assemblies (as in *Lashmankin and Others*, *Butkevich*, *Tsvetkova and Others*, and *Korneyeva*); the absence of a prosecuting party in proceedings under the Code of Administrative Offences (as in *Karelin v. Russia*); disproportionate measures against participants of solo manifestations (as in *Novikova and Others*); the lack of suspensive effect of an appeal against a sentence of administrative detention (as in *Martynyuk* and *Tsvetkova and Others*); and the right of organisers or participants not to be tried and punished twice for the same offence (as in *Korneyeva*). The Court declared these complaints admissible and found violations of the Convention and its Protocols in light of its established case-law.

Some applicants also raised additional complaints under Article 6 concerning other aspects of fairness in their administrative-offence proceedings. In view of the findings above, the Court considered there was no need to deal separately with these remaining complaints.

In conclusion, the Court found that Russia had violated the applicants’ rights under Article 11 of the Convention and other provisions, as established in its prior case-law.

In *Janáček v. the Czech Republic* (Application no. 9634/17, ECtHR, 2 February 2023), the applicant, a Czech national, complained under Article 6 § 1 that the Constitutional Court failed to communicate to him the written observations submitted by the general courts in his case, preventing him from commenting on them.

The underlying dispute concerned division of matrimonial property. On 17 December 2013, the Zlín District Court ordered the applicant to pay his former wife CZK 300,000 and CZK 1,759,627. Expert evidence was central. The court relied on expert S.’s report after another expert was unavailable, and despite an expert opinion submitted by the applicant from expert M. The presiding judge emailed expert S. for comments on M.’s opinion. On appeal, the Brno Regional Court on 24 March 2015 partially altered the judgment, ordering the applicant to pay a total of CZK 2,134,878. It relied on expert S.’s opinions, heard expert S. and two other experts, rejected an alternative expert report, and imposed costs. On 12 January 2016, the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal on points of law as manifestly ill-founded. Execution proceedings followed, including an order to sell the applicant’s immovable property.

On 14 April 2016, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint. He alleged, inter alia, that the lower courts had relied solely on expert S. without adequate justification, that the District Court judge had improper informal email contact with expert S., that the Regional Court wrongly refused an alternative expert opinion, and that the property division violated his fair-trial and property rights. The Constitutional Court invited the District, Regional, and Supreme Courts to submit comments on the complaint. Their written observations addressed expert S.’s appointment and evaluation, the courts’ reliance on his report, and the Supreme Court’s reasoning for rejecting the appeal. The District judge explained that his email contact with expert S. was intended to speed up proceedings.

On 19 July 2016, following a written procedure, the Constitutional Court dismissed the constitutional complaint as manifestly ill-founded. It stated that it had familiarised itself with the general courts’ observations. However, it did not send those observations to the applicant. After learning of the decision, the applicant’s lawyer inspected the file, and the applicant asked why he had not been allowed to comment. The Constitutional Court replied that, since the observations had not been sent, the judge rapporteur had probably considered they contained no new information or legal arguments.

The alleged violation was that the Constitutional Court’s failure to communicate the general courts’ written observations breached Article 6 § 1. The applicant could not respond to material possibly used in the Constitutional Court’s decision, undermining adversarial proceedings and equality of arms. The Government argued that any violation was merely formal because the observations contained no new or relevant arguments and the Constitutional Court did not rely on them. The applicant stressed that the case involved substantial property, not a trivial amount.

Domestic law treated lower courts as joined parties with rights to submit observations, and Constitutional Court practice, following *Milatová*, recommended sending observations to applicants when they contained or might contain new facts, allegations or arguments. The ECtHR found that the failure to communicate the observations, which the applicant could not comment on, violated Article 6 § 1.

The case *Janáček v. the Czech Republic* (ECtHR, Fifth Section, Application no. 9634/17, judgment of 2 February 2023) concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention—the right to a fair hearing in civil proceedings.

The applicant, Ladislav Janáček, was involved in proceedings for the division of matrimonial property between himself and his former wife. On 17 December 2013, the Zlín District Court ruled on the division and ordered the applicant to make substantial payments to his former wife. The court relied on expert evidence to value the property. Because an earlier expert opinion did not clearly assess the applicant’s business assets, the court appointed expert S., who submitted his report in November 2012. The applicant later obtained an expert opinion from expert M. On 5 December 2013, the presiding judge emailed expert S. asking him to comment on M.’s opinion; S. replied on 16 December 2013. The District Court accepted S.’s reasoning and declined to rely on M.’s opinion.

The applicant appealed. On 24 March 2015, the Brno Regional Court partially altered the judgment, ordering the applicant to pay CZK 2,134,878 in total. It admitted expert S.’s reply to comments, heard S. and other experts, and relied on S.’s opinions, rejecting the applicant’s objections and his request for an alternative expert report. On 12 January 2016, the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal on points of law as manifestly ill-founded.

On 14 April 2016, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint. He argued that the general courts had relied solely on expert S. without sufficient justification, referred to the email communication with S., complained that the Regional Court had refused an alternative expert report, and alleged that the courts’ formalistic approach had led to an incorrect division of property to his detriment. He invoked Czech Charter provisions and Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, among others.

The Constitutional Court invited the District Court, Regional Court, and Supreme Court to submit observations on the constitutional complaint. The Supreme Court judge replied on 11 May 2016, suggesting rejection of the complaint and waiving an oral hearing. The District Court judge replied on 17 May 2016, referring largely to earlier reasoning and explaining his contact with expert S.: he had approached S. only after other experts reported long delays, had not known him before, and had emailed him to speed up the process. A member of the Regional Court chamber submitted two-page comments on 25 May 2016 concerning S.’s appointment, valuation, and the reasons the Regional Court relied on his opinion.

On 19 July 2016, following a written procedure, the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s constitutional complaint as manifestly ill-founded. It stated that it had requested observations from the general courts and had familiarized itself with their contents. However, those observations had not been communicated to the applicant. On 18 August 2016, his lawyer inspected the file and discovered them. The applicant asked the Constitutional Court why he had not been allowed to comment. In reply on 29 September 2016, the Constitutional Court said the observations had not been sent because the judge rapporteur had probably considered that they contained no new information or legal arguments.

Under the Constitutional Court Act, parties and joined parties—including lower courts—could submit observations and inspect the file. Following *Milatová and Others v. the Czech Republic*, the Constitutional Court’s practice recommended sending such observations to applicants where they contained, or might contain, new facts, claims, or arguments.

The Government argued that any violation was merely formal, since the observations contained no new relevant arguments and the Constitutional Court had not relied on them. The applicant stressed that the case concerned substantial property and business assets, not a trivial amount.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 6 § 1: the Constitutional Court’s failure to communicate the general courts’ written observations to the applicant prevented him from commenting on them before his constitutional complaint was dismissed.

**Case: Janáček v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 9634/17), judgment of 2 February 2023**

The case concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights, namely the right to a fair hearing in civil proceedings. The applicant, Ladislav Janáček, complained that the Czech Constitutional Court failed to communicate to him the written observations submitted by the general courts involved in his case, thereby preventing him from commenting on them before the Constitutional Court decided his constitutional complaint.

The underlying dispute concerned the division of matrimonial property between the applicant and his former wife. In December 2013, the Zlín District Court ruled on the property settlement and ordered the applicant to pay his former wife substantial sums. The court relied on several expert opinions. After rejecting the applicant’s expert opinion, it based its valuation largely on an expert report prepared by expert S. The presiding judge had also contacted expert S by email to ask him to comment on the applicant’s expert report, which the applicant later challenged as irregular.

On appeal, in March 2015, the Brno Regional Court partially altered the first-instance judgment and increased the total amount the applicant was ordered to pay. It relied heavily on expert S’s opinion, rejected the applicant’s objections, and refused his request for an alternative expert report. In January 2016, the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal on points of law as manifestly ill-founded.

In April 2016, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint. He alleged, inter alia, that the ordinary courts had based their decisions solely on expert S’s report without adequate justification, that the Regional Court had wrongly refused an alternative expert opinion, and that the property division was unfair. He relied on fair-trial and property-protection provisions, including Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

The Constitutional Court invited the District Court, Regional Court, and Supreme Court to submit observations. In May 2016, the Supreme Court judge stated that the appeal on points of law had been rejected as inadmissible and suggested dismissing the constitutional complaint. The District Court judge explained his informal email contact with expert S, saying he did so to speed up proceedings. A Regional Court judge submitted comments defending the appointment and use of expert S and the Regional Court’s reliance on his opinion.

These written observations were not sent to the applicant. On 19 July 2016, following a written procedure, the Constitutional Court dismissed the constitutional complaint as manifestly ill-founded, stating that it had requested observations and familiarised itself with their contents. After learning of the decision, the applicant’s lawyer consulted the file. In September 2016, the applicant asked why he had not been allowed to see and comment on the observations. The Constitutional Court replied that, since the observations had not been sent, the judge rapporteur had probably considered that they contained no new information or legal arguments.

Before the European Court, the Government argued that any violation was merely formal because the observations contained no new or relevant arguments and the Constitutional Court had not relied on them. The applicant argued that the subject matter was not trivial, involving a significant matrimonial property settlement, and was distinguishable from cases involving minor sums.

The European Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1. The key issue was that the Constitutional Court received written observations from the general courts, considered them, but failed to communicate them to the applicant, thereby depriving him of any opportunity to respond. This procedural defect rendered the constitutional proceedings unfair.

Case **Axel Springer SE v. Germany** (ECtHR, Fourth Section, 17 January 2023) concerned an Article 10 freedom-of-expression complaint by Axel Springer SE, publisher of *Die Welt*, after German courts ordered it to publish a rectification by Ms K., a political official.

In October 2013, *Die Welt* published an article headlined “The Stasi woman by Gregor Gysi’s side.” It stated that Ms K., executive director of the party *die Linke*, had been a Stasi agent and discussed the disappearance of former East German Communist Party (SED) assets after 1989. The article said there was no evidence K. was involved in criminal activity, but added that documents showed she remained directly or indirectly involved with companies whose assets came from the SED/Honecker party’s heritage; that she held shares in such companies; that a 1995 Berlin Higher Administrative Court finding said two companies in which she held stakes managed PDS assets on a fiduciary basis; and that she was honorary chairwoman of the “Association of Friends of the ND.” Two days before publication, Springer sent K. questions, including about her role in that association. K. refused to answer.

On 11 October 2013, K. requested a rectification. She said she had nothing to do with the disappearance of SED assets after 1989; that FEVAC and Vulkan were founded in 1992 with PDS money and Treuhand approval; that she became a FEVAC shareholder only in 1998; that she had been a member of the Friends of the ND only since around 2000 and chair since 2002; and that she had not been a member of the party’s Federal Arbitration Commission since 1 January 2013. Springer refused to publish the reply.

K. sought an injunction. The Berlin Regional Court initially dismissed her application, finding the article did not expressly connect her to the disappearance of SED assets and that a possible interpretation was insufficient. On appeal, however, the Court of Appeal ordered Springer to publish the rectification under section 10 of the Berlin Press Act. In the main proceedings, the Regional Court again dismissed K.’s claim, but on 16 January 2014 the Court of Appeal again ordered publication on page 8 of the newspaper. It found that the average reader would infer that K. had been linked to the disappearance of SED assets, and that the article’s caveat that there was no evidence of criminal activity did not offset that implication. It held the rectification was limited to what was necessary and that K.’s refusal to answer press questions did not remove her legitimate interest. It also found the date on the rectification, 11 October 2013, was not manifestly incorrect despite later revisions. Springer published the rectification on 3 February 2014, adding an editor’s note that the information was correct and that the newspaper had no knowledge connecting K. to the disappearance of SED assets. In August 2017, the Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider Springer’s constitutional complaint.

Before the ECtHR, Springer argued that the order violated Article 10: the article had not associated K. with the disappearance of SED assets; the relevant statement was a value judgment; it had expressly said there was no evidence of criminal activity; K.’s refusal to answer undermined her legitimate interest; and the incorrect date harmed Springer’s reputation by suggesting deliberate delay. The Government maintained that the article covertly asserted K.’s involvement, that her refusal to answer did not defeat the right of reply, and that the date discrepancy was not significant.

The ECtHR declared the complaint admissible but ultimately found **no violation of Article 10**. It considered the domestic courts’ order justified and proportionate, well-reasoned, and consistent with its case-law, because the rectification was confined to correcting factual inaccuracies and did not require Springer to publish more than necessary.

In *Axel Springer SE v. Germany* (Application no. 8964/18, ECtHR, 17 January 2023), the applicant publishing house, which publishes *Die Welt*, complained that a German court order requiring it to publish a rectification/reply by Ms K. violated its right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention.

The dispute arose from an article published on 4 October 2013 under the headline “The Stasi woman by Gregor Gysi’s side.” K. was executive director of the political party die Linke and a political official. The article alleged that she had been an agent for the former GDR Ministry of State Security (Stasi). It also linked her name to the disappearance after 1989 of billions in assets belonging to the East German Communist Party (SED). The article stated there was no evidence K. had been involved in possible criminal activities, but added that, according to documents, she remained directly or indirectly involved with companies whose assets stemmed from the Honecker-party heritage. It further noted that in 1995 the Berlin Higher Administrative Court had found that two companies in which she held stakes managed assets for the PDS on a fiduciary basis. The article also identified K. as honorary chairwoman of the “Association of Friends of the ND,” which had promised large sums to support the newspaper *Neues Deutschland*.

Two days before publication, Axel Springer sent K. a list of questions, including about her membership in the “Association of Friends of the ND.” K. refused to answer. After publication, on 11 October 2013, K.’s lawyer requested a rectification, stating that K. had not been involved in the disappearance of SED assets, that she had not been a member of the party’s Federal Arbitration Commission since 1 January 2013, that FEVAC and Vulkan were founded in 1992 with PDS money and Treuhand approval and she became a FEVAC shareholder in 1998, and that she had joined the Friends of the ND around 2000 and chaired it since 2002. Axel Springer refused to publish the reply.

K. sought an injunction. The Berlin Regional Court initially dismissed her application, finding that the article had not expressly made the alleged connection between K. and the disappearance of SED assets. The Court of Appeal reversed and ordered Axel Springer to publish the rectification under section 10 of the Berlin Press Act. In the main proceedings, the Regional Court again dismissed K.’s request, but the Court of Appeal again ordered publication on page 8. It reasoned that the average reader would conclude that the article linked K. to the disappearance of SED assets, and the caveat that there was no evidence of criminal activity did not offset that implication. It found the rectification was limited to what was necessary, and K.’s earlier refusal to answer questions did not remove her legitimate interest in correcting the factual inaccuracy. The court also rejected Axel Springer’s objection that the rectification was dated 11 October 2013 even though the final version was submitted later, finding the core message unchanged.

Axel Springer published the rectification on 3 February 2014, with an editor’s note. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider its constitutional complaint. Before the European Court of Human Rights, Axel Springer argued that the article contained no factual allegation linking K. to the missing SED assets, that K.’s refusal to answer should bar rectification, and that the incorrect date harmed its reputation. The Government and K. maintained that the article covertly asserted K.’s involvement and that the rectification order was justified. The ECtHR declared the Article 10 complaint admissible but ultimately found no violation, holding that the domestic courts’ order was justified and proportionate and aimed at rectifying a factual inaccuracy.

**Case:** *Axel Springer SE v. Germany* (ECtHR, Fourth Section, 17 January 2023).

The applicant, Axel Springer SE, is a German publishing house that publishes the daily newspaper *Die Welt*. On 4 October 2013 it published an article headlined “The Stasi woman by Gregor Gysi’s side” about Ms K., the executive director of the political party die Linke and formerly the PDS. The article referred to K.’s alleged Stasi past and to the disappearance of assets belonging to the former East German Communist Party (SED) after 1989. It stated that there was currently no evidence that K. had been involved in possible criminal activities, but reported that documents allegedly showed she remained directly or indirectly involved with companies whose assets stemmed from the SED/Honecker-party heritage. It named companies FEVAC and Vulkan, said K. held shares in them, noted a 1995 finding by the Berlin Higher Administrative Court that two such companies managed PDS assets on a fiduciary basis, and stated that K. was honorary chairwoman of the “Association of Friends of the ND.”

Two days before publication, Axel Springer sent questions to K., including about her membership in the “Association of Friends of the ND.” K. refused to answer. After publication, on 11 October 2013, K.’s lawyer requested a rectification, denying that K. had anything to do with the disappearance of SED assets and explaining the origins of FEVAC and Vulkan and the dates of her involvement with the association. Axel Springer refused to publish it.

K. applied for an injunction. The Berlin Regional Court initially dismissed her application, finding the article had not made the alleged connection between K. and the disappearance of SED assets. The Court of Appeal reversed and ordered Axel Springer to publish K.’s rectification under section 10 of the Berlin Press Act. In the main proceedings, the Regional Court again dismissed K.’s request, but the Court of Appeal again ordered publication on 16 January 2014. It found that the average reader would infer that K. had been involved in the disappearance of SED party assets, despite the article’s caveat about criminal evidence. It also held that the rectification was limited to what was necessary, that K. could address the origin of the companies’ capital, that her refusal to answer the newspaper’s pre-publication questions did not remove her legitimate interest, and that the dated text was not manifestly incorrect. Axel Springer published the rectification on 3 February 2014, with an editor’s note stating the information was correct. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider Axel Springer’s constitutional complaint.

Axel Springer complained to the ECtHR under Article 10, arguing that the order to publish the rectification violated its freedom of expression. It claimed the article did not associate K. with the disappearance of SED assets, that the relevant statement was a value judgment rather than a factual allegation, that K.’s refusal to answer questions undermined her legitimate interest, and that the incorrect date harmed its reputation. The Government argued that the article contained a covert factual assertion of K.’s involvement and that the rectification order was justified. The third-party intervener K. argued that the editor’s note confirmed the truth of her reply and that there was no serious interference.

The ECtHR declared the complaint admissible but found **no violation of Article 10**. It held that the domestic courts’ order was justified and proportionate, well-reasoned, and gave due consideration to the Court’s case-law. The rectification was limited to correcting factual inaccuracies and struck a fair balance between press freedom and K.’s rights.

Case Abbasaliyeva v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 6950/13, ECtHR, 27 April 2023) concerned the alleged failure of Azerbaijani courts to protect the applicant’s reputation under Article 8 of the Convention. The applicant, Shahla Abbasaliyeva, was born in 1959 and lived in Gazakh. Her brother, Elchin Amiraslanov, had been head of the Gazakh regional OMON special police force and was convicted in connection with the March 1995 attempted coup d’état. He was sentenced to death, later commuted to life imprisonment.

On 19 August 2011 the applicant was appointed head physician of the outpatient clinic of Gazakh District Central Hospital. Between 23 August and 10 September 2011, the newspaper Gündəlik Bakı published several articles about her appointment. The articles linked her to her brother and suggested she did not deserve the post because of his conviction. Headlines and subtitles included “Relatives of the government’s enemies appointed to posts,” “The sister of an OMON member has become Gazakh’s head physician,” and “One of the twins serves the State, the other the coup d’état.” The articles stated that she had previously “maligned” State authorities when her brother was detained, questioned why she was appointed over other candidates, and implied that her appointment undermined State interests. They also referred to her by her maiden name, Amiraslanova.

According to the applicant, after publication, on 12 September 2011 the head of the Gazakh District Executive Authority asked her to resign. She refused. The same day she was dismissed from the head physician post and returned to her previous role as a physician. She brought labour proceedings seeking reinstatement and compensation, but the Gazakh District Court dismissed her claims on 18 November 2011, finding that her appointment had breached labour rules because no written contract had been concluded and the post was not in the staff schedule. The Ganja Court of Appeal and Supreme Court dismissed her appeals in February and July 2012.

The applicant also asked the newspaper’s editor-in-chief for a retraction, which was refused. In October 2011 she sued the editor and authors for a retraction, apology, and compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. She argued that the articles attacked her and that she had used the surname Abbasaliyeva for twenty-six years after marriage. On 8 February 2012 the Yasamal District Court dismissed her claims. On 25 May 2012 the Baku Court of Appeal upheld that decision. It accepted as facts that her maiden name was Amiraslanova, that her brother had been convicted, and that she had been appointed and later dismissed as head physician. It held that the opinions expressed in the articles were value judgments with a sufficient factual basis and were protected by the defendants’ right to freedom of expression. It also stated that public officials, including doctors, should be more tolerant of criticism. The Supreme Court dismissed her cassation appeal on 2 October 2012.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained that the domestic courts’ failure to grant her claims against the newspaper violated her right to reputation under Article 8. The Court found that the publications contained disparaging statements about her and affected her private and professional reputation sufficiently to engage Article 8. The complaint was admissible. The applicant argued that the articles were written in bad faith and intended to persecute her solely because of her brother’s conviction, and that the domestic courts dismissed her claims for the same reason. The Government did not submit particular arguments. The Court ultimately found a violation of Article 8, holding that the domestic courts had failed to protect the applicant’s reputation and had not conducted the required balancing exercise between her Article 8 rights and the newspaper’s freedom of expression in conformity with the Court’s case-law.

Case Name: Abbasaliyeva v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 6950/13), European Court of Human Rights, First Section, judgment 27 April 2023 (final 27 July 2023).

The applicant, Shahla Samad gizi Abbasaliyeva, an Azerbaijani national born in 1959 living in Gazakh, complained under Article 8 of the Convention that domestic courts failed to protect her reputation in civil proceedings against a newspaper. The background involved her brother, Elchin Amiraslanov, former head of the Gazakh regional OMON, who was arrested and convicted in connection with the March 1995 attempted coup d’état. He was sentenced to death; after abolition of capital punishment in 1998, his sentence was commuted to life imprisonment.

In August 2011, the applicant was appointed head physician of the outpatient clinic of the Gazakh District Central Hospital. Between 23 August and 10 September 2011, the newspaper Gündəlik Bakı published several articles about her appointment. The articles were headed with themes such as “Relatives of the government’s enemies appointed to posts,” and identified the applicant as the sister or twin sister of Elchin Amiraslanov, an OMON member convicted in the coup attempt. They questioned why she had been appointed and asserted that she did not deserve the post because of her brother’s conviction and her alleged past protest or hostility toward State authorities when he was detained. They suggested that more deserving candidates existed, implied that Health Minister O.S. and R.H., head of the Gazakh District Executive Authority, were responsible for an improper appointment, and described the appointment as undermining State interests. Some articles used her maiden name, Amiraslanova, although she had used Abbasaliyeva for twenty-six years after marriage.

After publication, on 12 September 2011, R.H. allegedly asked the applicant to resign; she refused. The same day, she was dismissed from the head physician post and returned to her previous post as a physician. She sued her employer for reinstatement and lost earnings, but the Gazakh District Court dismissed her claim on 18 November 2011, finding labour-law breaches in her appointment: no written contract and no head physician post in the staff schedule. The Ganja Court of Appeal and Supreme Court upheld that decision in February and July 2012.

The applicant also requested a retraction from the newspaper’s editor-in-chief, which was refused. In October 2011, she brought civil proceedings against the editor and authors, seeking a retraction, an apology, and compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. On 8 February 2012, the Yasamal District Court dismissed her claims. On 25 May 2012, the Baku Court of Appeal upheld that judgment. It treated as established facts that her maiden name was Amiraslanova, that her brother had been convicted, and that she had been appointed and later dismissed. It held that the opinions in the articles about her, her brother, and her appointment were value judgments with a sufficient factual basis, protected by the defendants’ freedom of expression and the right to criticise public officials, including doctors. It also stated that public officials, including doctors, should tolerate more criticism. The Supreme Court dismissed her cassation appeal on 2 October 2012.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant argued that the articles were written in bad faith and intended to persecute her solely because of her brother’s conviction, and that the domestic courts rejected her claims for the same reason. The Government did not submit particular arguments on this complaint. The Court found that the publications, including their headings, contained disparaging statements about the applicant and affected her private life sufficiently to engage Article 8. The complaint was admissible. The key alleged violation was the domestic courts’ failure, in the civil reputation proceedings, to protect her right to reputation. The Court ultimately found that the balancing exercise between freedom of expression and the applicant’s private life had not been conducted in conformity with its case-law, giving rise to a violation of Article 8.

**Case: Abbasaliyeva v. Azerbaijan (Application no. 6950/13), ECtHR, 27 April 2023**

The applicant, Shahla Abbasaliyeva, an Azerbaijani national born in 1959, complained under Article 8 that domestic courts had failed to protect her reputation in civil proceedings against a newspaper. Her brother, Elchin Amiraslanov, had been head of the Gazakh regional OMON special police and was prosecuted for the March 1995 attempted coup d’état. He was sentenced to death, later commuted to life imprisonment.

On 19 August 2011 the applicant was appointed head physician of the outpatient clinic of the Gazakh District Central Hospital. Between 23 August and 10 September 2011, the newspaper *Gündəlik Bakı* published several articles about her appointment. The articles carried headlines such as “Relatives of the government’s enemies appointed to posts,” “The sister of an OMON member has become Gazakh’s head physician,” “One of the twins serves the State, the other the coup d’état,” and “Undesirable fact in the Ministry of Health.” They identified her by her maiden name, Amiraslanova, linked her to her brother’s conviction, claimed she had protested against and “maligned” State authorities when her brother was detained, questioned why she had been appointed when eight candidates existed, suggested she did not deserve the post, and alleged that her appointment undermined State interests. The applicant had used her married surname, Abbasaliyeva, for twenty-six years.

After publication, on 12 September 2011, the head of the Gazakh District Executive Authority asked her to resign. She refused, and the same day she was dismissed from the head physician post and returned to her previous position as a physician. She sued her employer for reinstatement, but domestic courts dismissed her claims, finding that her appointment had breached labour law because no written contract had been concluded and the head physician post did not exist in the hospital’s staff schedule. Appeals were dismissed in February and July 2012.

The applicant also asked the newspaper’s editor-in-chief for a retraction, which was refused. She then sued the editor and authors, seeking a retraction, an apology, and compensation. On 8 February 2012 the Yasamal District Court dismissed her claims. On 25 May 2012 the Baku Court of Appeal upheld that decision. It found as facts that her maiden name was Amiraslanova, that her brother had been convicted, and that she had been appointed and later dismissed. It held that the opinions about her, her brother, and her appointment were value judgments with a sufficient factual basis, protected by the defendants’ right to freedom of expression and the right to criticise public officials, including doctors. It also stated that public officials and doctors should tolerate more criticism. On 2 October 2012 the Supreme Court upheld that reasoning.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant argued that the articles were written in bad faith and intended to persecute her solely because of her brother’s conviction. She claimed the domestic courts dismissed her claims for the same reason. The Government did not submit particular arguments on this complaint.

The Court considered that the articles contained disparaging statements about the applicant, affecting her social and professional reputation by asserting that she did not deserve her appointment because of her brother’s conviction and her alleged reaction to his imprisonment. Those statements reached the threshold of seriousness required to engage Article 8. The complaint was declared admissible. The Court ultimately found a violation of Article 8, holding that the domestic courts had failed to protect the applicant’s reputation and had not conducted the required balancing exercise between her right to reputation and the newspaper’s freedom of expression in accordance with the Court’s case-law.

**Case:** *Ohanjanyan v. Armenia* (Application no. 70665/11), European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, judgment of 25 April 2023.

The case concerned the death of the applicant’s son, T. Ohanjanyan, during compulsory military service in Armenia on 30 August 2007. The official account stated that after evening roll-call, T. Ohanjanyan left the armoury to go to a backup checkpoint. On the way, he allegedly accidentally touched the guy-wires of an antenna mast of an R-419 radio relay station at nearby military unit no. 28233, was electrocuted, and died instantly. A junior sergeant found him and reportedly also received an electric shock from the wire. An autopsy concluded that death resulted from electrocution, citing electrical wounds on the neck, left wrist, fingers, and right toe.

The investigation, however, failed to produce a coherent explanation. Initial military police measured a 180-volt current in the guy-wire, but a later Ministry of Defence inspection found no current and stated that the radio relay station had no direct mains connection. The scene was not properly inspected at night, and the radio relay station was dismantled before it could be examined. The specific station allegedly in use was never found, and attempts to examine a similar station years later were inconclusive because of the passage of time.

Expert evidence conflicted. An initial electrical expert concluded that damaged cable insulation and missing earthing caused the mast and guy-wires to become live. Later court-appointed and additional experts questioned this, finding that the subframe operated at 27 volts and that the alleged 180-volt transmission was not technically possible. The medical evidence also became uncertain: later reports could neither clearly confirm nor reject electrocution, and the toe injury had earlier been recorded as a laceration. The applicant produced photographs of his son’s body showing missing teeth, head, ear, jaw, and facial injuries, plus burns, which had not been recorded in the autopsy. The authenticity of the photographs was confirmed, but investigators largely failed to pursue the discrepancy, merely re-interviewing the autopsy expert, who dismissed the photos as poor quality.

Witness statements were inconsistent about T. Ohanjanyan’s movements, the timing of the incident, and whether he signed the roll-call register. There were also allegations that the military unit commander had slapped him. One witness maintained this account; the commander denied it, and no prosecution followed.

In 2008, two signal corps officers were charged with negligence. In 2010, the Regional Court acquitted them, finding key evidence inadmissible and the expert reports contradictory. The acquittal was upheld on appeal and the Cassation Court refused the prosecution’s appeal. Further investigation after 2010 was prolonged, repeatedly suspended, and reopened. Courts criticized it as ineffective, including for failing to address the applicant’s arguments and the photographic evidence. The applicant died in 2017; his widow continued the case. By 2022, the domestic investigation remained incomplete.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 2 of the Convention, both substantive and procedural. Substantively, the State failed to provide a plausible explanation for the death of a conscript under its control. Procedurally, the investigation was ineffective: it was delayed, failed to secure crucial evidence, produced irreconcilable expert findings, left key contradictions unresolved, and did not identify or punish those responsible.

**Ohanjanyan v. Armenia** (Application no. 70665/11, Fourth Section, judgment 25 April 2023, final 25 July 2023) concerned the death of the applicant’s son, T. Ohanjanyan, during compulsory military service in Armenia, and alleged violations of Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights, both substantive and procedural.

T. Ohanjanyan was drafted in November 2006 and transferred in May 2007 to military unit no. 28418. On 30 August 2007, after evening roll-call, he was found dead near the signal corps of nearby military unit no. 28233, lying under the guy-wires of an R-419 radio relay station antenna mast. The official account was that he accidentally touched live guy-wires and was electrocuted. A junior sergeant, A.G., said he heard moans, found the body, and later received an electric shock when he touched the same wire. Military police initially recorded a 180-volt current in the guy-wire. The autopsy concluded that death resulted from electrocution, noting electrical wounds on the neck, left wrist, fingers and right toe, plus abrasions.

However, later expert evidence undermined the official version. A Ministry of Defence inspection stated that the R-419 station had no direct mains connection and that no current should have been present. A court-ordered combined electrical and medical examination found that the station subframe could not produce 180 volts, questioned the electrical entry/exit wounds, and could not unequivocally confirm electrocution as the cause of death. It also noted that the toe injury had earlier been recorded as a laceration. The specific radio relay station was dismantled after the incident and later could not be located, preventing proper examination.

The investigation, opened on 31 August 2007 for military negligence, was marked by delays and omissions. The scene was not properly inspected at night; the guy-wire and clothing were submitted for biological examination weeks later, after traces had likely disappeared; no photographs were taken during the initial body inspection; and the mast was dismantled despite instructions to preserve the scene. Witness accounts conflicted about whether T. Ohanjanyan had been present at roll-call and why he left.

The applicant alleged that his son had been beaten. Witnesses stated that the former unit commander, S.S., had slapped T. Ohanjanyan, and there were reports of a prior fight and possible detention. Photographs taken by the applicant before the autopsy allegedly showed missing teeth, head, ear and jaw injuries, and foot burns not recorded by the forensic expert. The authorities declined to prosecute S.S. Charges were brought against Captain R.A. and Junior Sergeant K.T. for installing and operating the station in breach of technical requirements, but they were acquitted in January 2010; the acquittal was upheld because the prosecution’s electrical report conflicted with the later court-ordered expert findings.

Further investigation resumed and was repeatedly suspended. Additional expert reports were inconclusive or criticised; key evidence was lost; the applicant’s submissions were not properly addressed. Domestic courts in 2016 and 2018 found the investigation ineffective and insufficient to clarify the death. By 2022, proceedings were still incomplete. The applicant died in 2017, and his widow continued the case.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 2 both substantively and procedurally. The State failed to provide a plausible explanation for the death of a conscript under its control and failed to conduct an effective investigation capable of establishing the cause and any responsibility.

In *Ohanjanyan v. Armenia* (Application no. 70665/11, judgment 25 April 2023), the European Court of Human Rights examined the death of the applicant’s son, T. Ohanjanyan, during compulsory military service in Armenia and the subsequent investigation. The applicant, Suren Ohanjanyan, alleged violations of Article 2 of the Convention, both substantive and procedural.

T. Ohanjanyan was drafted in November 2006 and transferred in May 2007 to military unit no. 28418 in Gegharkunik. On 30 August 2007, according to the official account, he left the armoury after evening roll-call to go to a backup checkpoint of nearby military unit no. 28233. On the way, his neck and left wrist allegedly came into contact with guy-wires of the antenna mast of an R-419 radio relay station. He was electrocuted and died. A junior sergeant, A.G., found him, later touched the same wire and received an electric shock. The body was taken to a military hospital and then to Yerevan for autopsy.

Military police initially recorded that the guy-wire carried a 180-volt current when the station was switched on, but the record was drawn up without attesting witnesses. The next day, no current was found. An autopsy concluded death by electrocution, noting electrical wounds on the neck, left wrist, fingers and right toe, plus other abrasions. The applicant disputed this account. Photographs he took before autopsy allegedly showed additional injuries, including missing teeth and injuries to the head, ear, jaw and eye, which had not been recorded.

Criminal proceedings were opened for negligence under Article 376 § 2 of the Criminal Code. An initial electrical expert concluded that damaged insulation and lack of earthing had caused the mast and guy-wires to become live, and charges were brought against two signal corps officers, R.A. and K.T. However, a court-ordered combined electrical and medical examination later found that the subframe operated at 27 volts, could not produce 180 volts, and that an insulator existed. It could not unequivocally confirm electrocution as the cause of death and noted that the toe injury had been recorded earlier as a laceration. In 2010 the Regional Court acquitted the defendants, relying on conflicting evidence, inadmissible initial testing, and inconsistencies in witness statements about time and circumstances. Appeals upheld the acquittal.

Further investigation followed but was repeatedly suspended and resumed. In 2016 a district court found the post-acquittal investigation ineffective, not prompt, and criticized the failure to address the applicant’s photographs and unreported injuries. In 2018 the Criminal Court of Appeal found that the suspension decision was insufficient: the specific radio relay station had not been found or examined, electrocution had not been established, and other possible causes of death had not been investigated. The applicant died in 2017; his widow continued the case. By 2022, the investigation remained incomplete.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 2, both procedural and substantive. The key facts relevant to those violations were the death of a conscript in State custody, the State’s failure to provide a plausible explanation for how he died, conflicting expert and witness evidence, lost or dismantled equipment, delayed and incomplete investigative steps, repeated suspensions, and the overall failure to conduct an effective investigation capable of establishing responsibility.
