In *Luca v. the Republic of Moldova* (App. no. 55351/17, judgment 17 October 2023, final 17 January 2024), the European Court of Human Rights examined Moldova’s response to domestic violence and child-contact issues. The applicant, Lilia Luca, and A.I. were an unmarried couple in Italy; their two children were born in 2006 and the couple later married. In 2012 A.I. returned to Moldova with the children, while the applicant stayed in Italy to work and support the family, joining them in 2015. She alleged that A.I. began psychological and physical abuse in October 2015. She reported physical violence on 13 July and 4 November 2016, as well as verbal abuse, harassment, emotional abuse, utility cut-offs, and manipulation of the children against her.

On 1 August 2016 she sought a protection order. On 2 August the Ialoveni District Court granted a 90-day order requiring A.I. to leave the common residence, avoid contact, and stay at least 50 metres away; it was upheld on appeal in October 2016. The applicant repeatedly complained to police and child protection that A.I. breached the order—moving into his sister’s part of the same house, taking her belongings, cutting water, pressuring the children, and hindering her access. Police said her account was unconfirmed; on 7 October 2016 the prosecutor refused criminal proceedings, treating the conflict as civil/divorce-related. On 31 October she sought an extension. On 2 November the court refused, stating family misunderstandings were not violence and that the refusals confirmed a family dispute. Her appeal was dismissed in January 2017.

On 4 November 2016 A.I. assaulted her. A medical report noted bruises on her forehead, arms and buttocks, classified as minor, and she was hospitalised for eight days with concussion. Later protection requests in November 2016 and February 2017 were rejected. Courts found insufficient evidence or imminent danger, questioned her credibility, called her requests “overdramatic” and “aggressive”, warned against using domestic-violence proceedings as revenge, and pointed to the children’s wish to live with their father. Criminal proceedings for breach of the protection order and domestic violence were opened in November 2016, but in February 2017 the court refused the prosecutor’s requested protection measures, finding no evidence of violence or imminent danger and no need for State interference in private/family life. In November 2019 A.I. was convicted on both counts and received a suspended sentence; that became final in September 2021, five years after the events.

As to contact, the children moved in with A.I. in August 2016 and stopped answering the applicant. In September 2016 the child protection authority refused a contact schedule based on the children’s statements; a court ordered one in November 2016, and in January 2017 a schedule was set for every second week. The applicant complained A.I. did not comply, but police replied that the children voluntarily chose not to see her. A May 2017 child-protection visit recorded the children’s negative reaction and refusal of gifts. Divorce/custody proceedings ended with the children living with their father, final in 2022. A criminal complaint about psychological abuse of the children was discontinued in 2018 after experts found no mental trauma. The applicant alleged violations of Articles 3, 8 and 14. The Court found the authorities failed to protect her from domestic violence, conducted an ineffective investigation, failed to support contact and consider domestic violence in contact decisions, and exhibited discriminatory attitudes toward her as a woman.

Luca v. Republic of Moldova (Application no. 55351/17) is a European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) judgment delivered on 17 October 2023 and final on 17 January 2024. The applicant, Ms Lilia Luca, a Moldovan national, complained under Articles 3, 8 and 14 that the Moldovan authorities failed to protect her from domestic violence by A.I., failed to support her contact with her children, and discriminated against her as a woman.

The applicant and A.I. lived in Italy, where their two children were born in 2006, and later married. In 2012 A.I. returned to Moldova with the children; the applicant stayed in Italy to work and sent money, joining them in 2015. From October 2015, A.I. allegedly subjected her to psychological and physical abuse. She reported physical violence on 13 July and 4 November 2016, verbal abuse, harassment, emotional abuse, interference with utilities, and manipulation of the children against her.

On 1 August 2016 she sought a protection order. On 2 August 2016 the Ialoveni District Court issued a 90-day order requiring A.I. to leave the common residence, refrain from contact with her and the children, and stay at least 50 metres away; the Chișinău Court of Appeal upheld it in October 2016. The applicant complained to police and child protection services that A.I. did not comply: he moved into his sister’s part of the same house, the children moved in with him on 22 August, he took her belongings, and cut off water. The police said her account was unconfirmed; on 7 October 2016 the prosecutor refused criminal proceedings, treating the conflict as a civil family dispute.

On 31 October 2016 she sought extension of the protection order. On 2 November 2016 the court refused, finding family misunderstandings rather than violence and citing the refusal to prosecute. Her appeal was dismissed on 24 January 2017. On 4 November 2016 A.I. physically assaulted her, causing bruises and concussion; she was hospitalised for eight days. She again sought protection, but on 10 November 2016 the court rejected the request as unsubstantiated, accused her of using protection orders in financial and custody disputes, described her conduct as “overdramatic,” and questioned her credibility. Further requests in February 2017 were rejected on 13 February and on appeal on 13 April 2017, when the court found no physical or psychological violence, relied on A.I.’s presumption of innocence, and warned against using domestic-violence proceedings for revenge.

Criminal proceedings began on 2 November 2016 for breach of the protection order and on 24 November 2016 for domestic violence; they were joined. On 24 February 2017 the court refused protection measures as unsubstantiated and an unjustified interference with private life. Only on 14 November 2019 was A.I. convicted on both counts, receiving a suspended sentence; the conviction became final on 15 September 2021, five years after the events.

As regards contact, the children moved in with A.I. on 22 August 2016. On 5 September 2016 the applicant asked the child protection authority for a contact schedule. On 15 September 2016 it refused, relying on the children’s statements preferring their father. On 11 November 2016 a court ordered a schedule; on 26 January 2017 one was issued allowing contact every second week. The applicant complained that A.I. obstructed contact; police replied that the children themselves chose not to see her. A child protection visit in May 2017 reported the children’s negative reaction and refusal of gifts. Custody was later granted to the father in 2018, final in 2022.

The alleged violations concerned the authorities’ failure to conduct a proactive risk assessment, take preventative measures, investigate effectively, support contact, and avoid discriminatory stereotypes condoning domestic violence.

In *Luca v. the Republic of Moldova* (no. 55351/17, judgment 17 October 2023), the applicant, Lilia Luca, alleged that Moldovan authorities failed to protect her from domestic violence and to support her contact with her children. She had lived with A.I. in Italy, where their two children were born in 2006. A.I. returned to Moldova with the children in 2012; the applicant stayed in Italy to work and support the family, joining them in 2015. From October 2015, A.I. allegedly subjected her to physical and psychological violence, harassment, verbal abuse, and emotional abuse, including encouraging the children to reject her and cutting off utilities to her part of the home. She reported physical assaults on 13 July and 4 November 2016.

On 1 August 2016 the applicant sought a protection order. On 2 August 2016 the Ialoveni District Court issued a 90-day order requiring A.I. to leave the common residence, refrain from contact, and stay 50 metres away; this was upheld on appeal. The applicant repeatedly complained that A.I. breached the order: he moved into his sister’s part of the same house, the children moved in with him on 22 August 2016, he pressured them against her, took her belongings, and cut her water supply. Police said her allegations were unconfirmed; on 7 October 2016 a prosecutor refused criminal proceedings. On 2 November 2016 the court rejected her request to extend the protection order, calling the conflict a “family misunderstanding” without violence and suggesting she was using the order for financial and custody disputes. Her appeal was dismissed in January 2017.

On 4 November 2016 A.I. physically assaulted her, causing bruises, concussion, and an eight-day hospitalisation. Her later requests for protection orders were rejected. On 10 November 2016 the court found insufficient evidence and described her behaviour as “overdramatic,” undermining her credibility. On 13 February 2017 another court found no domestic violence or imminent danger, noting the last physical violence was on 4 November 2016 and that contact issues should be pursued through other legal means. The Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal in April 2017, saying there was no physical or psychological violence, that pending criminal proceedings were not proof, and that domestic violence law should not be used for “revenge.”

Criminal proceedings were delayed. After complaints, proceedings for breach of the protection order and domestic violence were opened in November 2016 and joined. In February 2017 the court refused protection measures in the criminal case as unsubstantiated and viewed State interference as unacceptable. Only on 14 November 2019 was A.I. convicted on both counts, receiving a suspended sentence and damages; the conviction became final on 15 September 2021, about five years after the key events.

Regarding contact, the children moved in with A.I. in August 2016 and stopped answering the applicant. On 15 September 2016 the child protection authority refused a contact schedule based on the children’s statements preferring their father. A court later ordered a schedule, issued on 26 January 2017, but the applicant complained A.I. refused compliance; police replied that the children voluntarily chose their father. A May 2017 school visit ended with the children refusing to speak to her or accept gifts. In divorce proceedings, A.I. obtained custody; the judgment became final in March 2022. A criminal complaint concerning psychological abuse of the children was discontinued in 2018 after experts found no trauma.

The alleged violations concerned: Article 3, for failing to conduct an autonomous, proactive, comprehensive risk assessment and to take coordinated preventive measures, allowing ill-treatment to continue and delaying effective investigation and punishment; Article 8, for failing to support the applicant’s contact with her children and ignoring domestic violence in contact decisions; and Article 14 read with Article 3, for discriminatory attitudes condoning domestic violence, shown by protection being denied through biased reasoning and A.I.’s later conviction on the same facts. The European Court of Human Rights found violations.
001-228357:
**A.M.A. v. the Netherlands** (Application no. 23048/19, ECtHR Third Section, judgment of 24 October 2023) concerned a Bahraini national who alleged that his expulsion from the Netherlands to Bahrain exposed him to a real risk of treatment contrary to Article 3 ECHR, and that the Dutch authorities failed properly to assess that risk in “last-minute” asylum proceedings.

The applicant, a Shiite Muslim from Bahrain, applied for asylum in the Netherlands in August 2017. He claimed membership of the opposition group “Barbar Revolutionary Youth,” involvement in publishing critical material, and fear of persecution because his brother was an activist sought by Bahrain. He said that after another group member was arrested and allegedly tortured, he feared being named and fled to Iran in February 2017. The Dutch Immigration and Naturalisation Service rejected his first asylum application as implausible. It found inconsistencies, noted he had left Bahrain legally on his own passport, and doubted his claimed online activities and his alleged link to his brother’s suspected terrorist activities. His judicial review was declared inadmissible because his grounds were allegedly filed late through the electronic system; the Regional Court found no special circumstances excusing the late filing.

In October 2018, the applicant’s removal to Bahrain was scheduled. He repeatedly refused voluntary return, saying he would be arrested. On 19 October 2018, shortly before removal, his lawyer sent him documents obtained from his brother: copies, in Arabic, bearing the letterhead of the Bahraini Public Prosecutor’s Office. The applicant claimed these showed he had been charged with participating in a terrorist organisation and that another person had named him under questioning. On 20 October 2018, at Schiphol Airport, he was interviewed about his subsequent asylum application. No lawyer attended. The interviewing officer had only asked an Arabic-speaking colleague about the documents beforehand. The applicant said he had just received the documents, could not explain exactly how his brother had obtained them, and did not know whether originals existed.

At the end of the interview, the officer orally rejected the application, stating that the documents were not originals and were in Arabic, that there was no time to obtain originals, and that no extension would be granted. A written decision the same day declared the subsequent application inadmissible because no new elements or findings had emerged. The Deputy Minister gave no probative value to the documents because they were untranslated, copies, and of unclear origin, and considered the application merely an attempt to delay removal. The decision stated that a copy had been faxed to his lawyer, but it appears to have been sent to a former lawyer, Mr B., at 3:13 p.m.; the flight had been scheduled for 2:10 p.m. The applicant was removed to Bahrain that day.

After removal, the applicant was arrested immediately. He was later convicted of weapons possession and terrorist activities, sentenced to life imprisonment, and initially stripped of his Bahraini nationality. He alleged torture to extract a confession, an unfair trial, and poor detention conditions. In 2023, he reportedly joined a hunger strike with other prisoners.

The applicant complained that the Dutch authorities had failed to sufficiently assess the Article 3 risk before expulsion and that he had no effective remedies to challenge that assessment. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of the procedural aspect of Article 3. The respondent State had failed to discharge its procedural obligation to properly assess, in the context of last-minute asylum proceedings, the alleged risk of treatment contrary to Article 3 before removing him to Bahrain. The risk he feared subsequently materialised.

A.M.A. v. the Netherlands (Application no. 23048/19), European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, judgment of 24 October 2023.

The applicant, a Bahraini national and Shiite Muslim, applied for asylum in the Netherlands in August 2017 during a layover en route to Ecuador. He claimed he had been a member of the opposition group “Barbar Revolutionary Youth” since 2012, wrote critical articles and gathered news for its social media. His brother was an activist who had fled to Germany. After another group member, X, was arrested in February 2017 and allegedly tortured, the applicant feared X would disclose his name. He fled to Iran on 10 February 2017 and later learned that his home had been searched and other members arrested. He feared persecution and ill-treatment by Bahraini authorities due to his political activities, religion, his brother’s activism, and the possibility that he was on a terrorist list.

The Dutch immigration service rejected his first asylum application on 23 August 2017, finding his account incoherent and implausible. It noted he had no evidence of online articles or posts, gave inconsistent explanations about X, left Bahrain legally with his own passport, and had not shown that his brother’s activities put him at risk. His judicial review was declared inadmissible because the grounds were filed late electronically. After a referral from the Council of State, the Regional Court again declared his appeal inadmissible in September 2018, finding no special circumstances under Bahaddar v. the Netherlands. He did not further appeal.

As removal approached, the Repatriation and Departure Service held return interviews. The applicant refused voluntary return to Bahrain, saying he feared immediate arrest, but was willing to go to Iran or Georgia. Those options proved impossible. A detention order was issued in October 2018. On 17 October his lawyer was told expulsion to Bahrain was scheduled for 20 October. At a final return interview on 18 October, he was told he could make a new asylum application, but this would not automatically cancel the flight. He tried unsuccessfully to consult his lawyer.

On 19 October his lawyer emailed documents from his brother to the detention centre: Arabic copies bearing the letterhead of the Bahraini Public Prosecutor’s Office. The applicant then submitted a subsequent asylum application. On the morning of 20 October he was transferred to Schiphol Airport and interviewed by the immigration service without a lawyer. The officer had an Arabic-speaking colleague review the documents beforehand. The applicant said he had just received them, could not explain exactly how his brother obtained them, but stated his name appeared and he had been charged with participating in a terrorist organisation. At the end of the interview, the officer orally rejected the application immediately, saying there was no time, the documents were not original and were in Arabic, and they could not serve as new evidence. A written decision the same day declared the subsequent application inadmissible: no new elements had emerged; the documents had no probative value because they were untranslated, not original, and unexplained; and the application was made just before removal to delay expulsion. The decision stated he had to leave immediately, was faxed to his former lawyer at 3:13 p.m., and advised that objection and interim relief were possible. The applicant did not use those remedies and was expelled to Bahrain later that day.

After removal, he was arrested and detained on arrival. His lawyer’s request to set aside the removal order and return him, based on a likely risk of torture, was refused. His subsequent asylum application was formally rejected in February 2019. In Bahrain he was convicted of weapons and ammunition possession and terrorist activities, sentenced to life imprisonment, and lost his nationality, later reinstated. He alleged torture to extract a confession, an unfair trial, and poor detention conditions.

Before the Court, he complained under Article 3 that the Dutch authorities had failed to sufficiently assess the risk of treatment contrary to Article 3 before expulsion, particularly in “last-minute” asylum proceedings, and under Article 13 that he had no effective remedy. The Court found that the Netherlands had failed to discharge its procedural obligation under Article 3 to properly assess the alleged risk before removing him to Bahrain.

**Case: A.M.A. v. the Netherlands (ECtHR, 24 October 2023)**

The case concerned the Netherlands’ assessment, shortly before removal, of whether returning a Bahraini asylum seeker to Bahrain would expose him to treatment contrary to Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, A.M.A., a Shiite Muslim from Bahrain, applied for asylum in the Netherlands in August 2017. He claimed he had been a member of the opposition group “Barbar Revolutionary Youth,” had written critical articles, and feared Bahraini authorities because his brother was an activist who had fled to Germany. He alleged that after another group member was arrested and tortured, he was implicated; that his home was searched; and that he feared being on a list of alleged terrorists linked to his brother.

The Dutch Immigration and Naturalisation Service rejected his asylum application as implausible. It found inconsistencies, noted he had left Bahrain legally with his own passport, and considered his fear based largely on assumptions about his brother. His judicial review was declared inadmissible because his grounds were not filed electronically within the time-limit; after a remittal, the Regional Court again ruled it inadmissible, and he did not appeal further.

The key events occurred in October 2018, as his expulsion to Bahrain approached. On 17 October, his lawyer was told the removal would take place on 20 October. On 18 October, during a final return interview, he was told he could make a subsequent asylum application but that this would not automatically cancel the flight. He could not reach his lawyer. On 19 October, his lawyer sent him documents obtained from his brother: Arabic copies bearing the letterhead of the Bahraini Public Prosecutor’s Office. The applicant said these documents named him, charged him with participating in a terrorist organisation, and arose from the questioning of someone who had implicated him. He received them only shortly before removal.

On 20 October, he was transferred to Schiphol Airport and interviewed by an IND officer without a lawyer. The officer had asked an Arabic-speaking colleague about the documents beforehand. The applicant said he had just received the copies, did not know how his brother had obtained them, and did not have originals. At the end, the officer orally and informally rejected the request, refused a one-week extension to obtain original documents, and said the documents could not serve as new evidence. A written decision the same day declared the subsequent application inadmissible: no new elements had emerged; the documents were not original or translated and their provenance was unexplained; and the late submission was intended to delay removal. The decision was faxed to an earlier lawyer and stated that objection and interim relief were possible, but the applicant did not pursue those remedies. He was removed to Bahrain.

After arrival, he was immediately arrested and detained. He was later convicted of weapons possession and terrorist activities, sentenced to life imprisonment, and alleged torture to extract a confession, poor detention conditions, and unfair trial. The applicant complained that the Dutch authorities had failed to properly assess the Article 3 risk before expulsion and that no effective remedy existed. The European Court of Human Rights found that the Netherlands had failed to discharge its **procedural obligation under Article 3** to properly assess the alleged risk of ill-treatment in the context of “last-minute” asylum proceedings before removing him to Bahrain.
001-228992:
The case *A.T. and Others v. Italy* (Application no. 47287/17) concerns the detention of thirteen applicants in the Taranto Early Reception and Aid Centre (*Centro di Soccorso e Prima Accoglienza* – CSPA), an Italian “hotspot,” and the poor conditions of accommodation there. The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee composed of Judges Mourou-Vikström, Chanturia and Guyomar, delivered judgment on 23 November 2023. The application was lodged against Italy on 5 July 2017. The applicants were represented by Mr D. Belluccio; the Italian Government by Mr L. D’Ascia. Defence for Children International, the International Commission of Jurists, the AIRE Centre, the European Council on Refugees and Exiles and the Dutch Council for Refugees submitted third-party comments. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The Taranto CSPA had been designated as an Italian hotspot under section 17 of Decree-Law no. 13 of 17 February 2017. On 22 May 2017 the applicants reached the Italian coast aboard a makeshift vessel. They alleged that they had declared that they were minors. Case *Zajmi v. Albania* (Application no. 83907/17, judgment 20 June 2023) arose from criminal proceedings against Ms Çetina Zajmi, an Albanian national. On 13 March 2013, the Tirana District Court convicted her of aggravated fraud and sentenced her to fourteen years’ imprisonment. The Tirana Appeal Court dismissed her appeal on 8 November 2013, and the Supreme Court dismissed her further appeal on 25 May 2015, making her conviction final.

The alleged violation concerned her inability to have a constitutional complaint examined by the Albanian Constitutional Court. At the relevant time, a constitutional complaint had to be lodged within two years. On 8 November 2016, Law no. 99/2016 was published. It shortened the time-limit from two years to four months from “obtaining knowledge of the interference” with a constitutional right or freedom. The new time-limit entered into force on 1 March 2017.

On 27 February 2017—before the new law entered into force—the applicant sent a constitutional complaint by post. She wrote the envelope address as “Gj – K.SH, Tirané”, which was incomplete. The postal service did not deliver it because the recipient could not be identified. The applicant later checked with the post office, learned of the non-delivery, and on 22 May 2017 re-sent the complaint to the Constitutional Court’s proper address. That date was still within the old two-year period counted from the Supreme Court’s decision of 25 May 2015, which would have expired on 25 May 2017. However, it was outside the newly introduced four-month period if counted from the Supreme Court’s decision.

On 16 June 2017, the Constitutional Court declared the applicant’s constitutional complaint inadmissible as lodged out of the four-month time-limit. On the same date, in two other cases, *Pajova* (decision no. 157) and *Ibrahimi* (decision no. 152), the Constitutional Court applied the new four-month time-limit to Supreme Court decisions adopted on 7 May 2015 and 25 June 2015 respectively, counting time from the date those Supreme Court decisions were adopted. This showed that the Constitutional Court was applying the shortened limitation period to cases in which the relevant Supreme Court decision predated the new law’s entry into force.

The key facts for the alleged violation were: the final Supreme Court decision of 25 May 2015; the statutory change shortening the constitutional complaint deadline; the applicant’s initial postal filing on 27 February 2017 before the new law took effect; the non-delivery due to the incomplete address; her re-filing on 22 May 2017 within the old two-year deadline; and the Constitutional Court’s retroactive application of the new four-month time-limit, as also illustrated by *Pajova* and *Ibrahimi*. The case of *Tepljakov v. Estonia* (Application no. 10753/21) concerns an Estonian national, Mr Jevgeni Tepljakov, born in 1976. In a judgment delivered by the Third Section of the European Court of Human Rights on 28 November 2023, the Court considered complaints under Articles 3, 8 and 10 of the Convention. The Court gave notice of these complaints to the Estonian Government and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

The applicant was held in pre-trial detention in Pärnu Arrest House in several separate periods between August 2016 and December 2018. These periods ranged from 6 days to 100 days at a time, amounting to 345 days in total. The remainder of his pre-trial detention was spent in Tallinn Prison.

Regarding the alleged violation of Article 3, the applicant complained about the physical conditions of detention in Pärnu Arrest House. The domestic courts found several shortcomings: ventilation and access to natural light were insufficient; the toilet was not adequately separated from the rest of the cell, which he sometimes shared with other detainees; and he had no possibility to spend time outdoors because the arrest house had no outside yard. These factors were relevant to whether the detention conditions reached the severity threshold under Article 3.

As to Article 8, the applicant complained about restrictions on meetings with family members. The domestic courts found that, without any fault on the applicant’s part, the authorities had limited his family meetings to approximately ten minutes at a time. This was relevant to his complaint that the detention regime unjustifiably interfered with his family life.

Under Article 10, the applicant complained about lack of access to an online legal database. The first-instance court initiated constitutional review proceedings. By judgment no. 5-19-41 of 18 December 2019, the Supreme Court of Estonia declared unconstitutional part of section 31(3) of Regulation no. 21 of the Minister of the Interior on the Internal Rules of the Arrest House. That provision allowed detainees to access an online database containing legal acts and court judgments “in so far as the arrest house had technical conditions for it.” The Supreme Court found that this restriction interfered with the constitutional right to freely obtain information disseminated for public use. It noted that the clause left it entirely to each arrest house to decide whether to provide access to the legal database. However, section 311 of the Imprisonment Act, as in force at the relevant time, provided that remand prisoners had the right to access that database. The Supreme Court held that the Imprisonment Act did not authorise the minister to impose further restrictions on such access. The impugned restriction was therefore not based on law and was unconstitutional.

When assessing all the shortcomings in conjunction, the domestic courts awarded the applicant EUR 1,500 in respect of non-pecuniary damage. The applicant had claimed EUR 3,450 before the Tallinn Court of Appeal. Before the European Court, the applicant invoked complaints about the physical conditions of detention in Pärnu Arrest House, the restrictions on meetings with family members, and the lack of access to the online legal database.

In *Cetinja v. Croatia* (Application no. 6959/17), a judgment of 9 May 2023, the European Court of Human Rights, Second Section, examined a Croatian applicant’s complaint that he had been convicted and fined for a minor offence after it had become time-barred. The applicant, Aleksandar Cetinja, a Croatian national born in 1988 and living in Rijeka, lodged the application on 17 January 2017.

The underlying facts concerned an incident on 28 August 2011. After a physical altercation with another person, the applicant, who was under the influence of alcohol, was taken to a local police station at 4 a.m. to sober up. He remained in police custody until 9 a.m., when he was released. By judgment of 12 October 2011, the Delnice Minor Offences Court found him guilty of a minor offence of breach of public peace. It imposed a fine of 728 Croatian kunas (HRK), approximately 97 euros (EUR). The five hours spent in police custody were credited as one day of imprisonment, corresponding to HRK 300, which was deducted from the fine. The applicant was therefore ordered to pay HRK 428 (about EUR 57), plus HRK 150 (about EUR 20) for costs. He later paid these amounts on 11 January 2017, together with HRK 75 charged by the domestic payment agency FINA for compulsory execution, totaling HRK 645.63.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations arose from the subsequent proceedings and the statutory limitation issue. The applicant appealed on 31 October 2011. The High Minor Offences Court dismissed his appeal on 27 May 2015, more than three and a half years later. Its judgment was served on him on 8 March 2016, more than nine months after it was adopted and more than four and a half years after the offence.

The applicant argued that the Minor Offences Act applicable at the time provided for a two-year relative prescription period and a four-year absolute prescription period, both running from the commission of the offence. The relative period could be interrupted only by an action of the relevant authority in relation to the minor offence. If interrupted, it began to run anew. He contended that the High Minor Offences Court’s failure to take any action for three and a half years meant the minor offence had become time-barred under the relative prescription rule. He relied on Supreme Court case-law and a Constitutional Court decision. He also argued that the inordinate delay in serving the High Court’s judgment suggested the judgment had been backdated to comply with the four-year absolute prescription period.

On 13 July 2016, the Constitutional Court declared his constitutional complaint inadmissible, without addressing his arguments, holding that the case did not raise a constitutional issue. That decision was served on his representative on 18 July 2016.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained under Articles 6 and 7 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that he had been convicted of a minor offence and ordered to pay a fine even though the offence had become time-barred. The Court gave notice of the complaints concerning property, fairness of the proceedings, and the principle of *nullum crimen sine lege*; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The central alleged violation was therefore that the domestic authorities penalized him despite the expiry of the statutory limitation period, and that the delayed proceedings and service undermined the fairness and legality of that conviction and the resulting fine.

Case of *Dimaksyan v. Armenia* concerned the death of the applicant’s 18-year-old son, M. Dimaksyan, during compulsory military service in the Armenian army. In November 2010, M. Dimaksyan was drafted and assigned to a military unit of the Nagorno-Karabakh armed forces near Hadrut. On 5 February 2012, while on watch duty at a base, he was shot by a fellow serviceman, G.A. Earlier that evening, after hearing a noise, G.A. loaded his assault rifle but later failed to close the trigger guard, ignoring M. Dimaksyan’s reminder that the weapon was still loaded. While moving during a second check, G.A.’s rifle discharged unintentionally; the bullet perforated M. Dimaksyan’s right shoulder girdle and chest. He died the same day.

After the shooting, other servicemen carried M. Dimaksyan to a dugout and then placed him in a truck driven by a major toward the military hospital. The road was bumpy and impassable, and 400 metres took about fifteen minutes. They met a medical vehicle with a paramedic and transferred him into it. The vehicle overheated, was stopped and repaired, overheated again, and M. Dimaksyan was transferred to another truck. Eventually they met a military hospital ambulance. Doctors tried emergency aid on the spot, but he was already dead. An autopsy concluded that death resulted from severe blood loss and also recorded non-ballistic bruises and abrasions inflicted around the time of death but not causing death.

A criminal investigation began the same day. G.A. was charged under Article 373 § 3 of the Criminal Code for breaching weapon-handling rules and causing death by negligence. In April 2013, he was convicted and sentenced to four years and six months’ imprisonment. The applicant participated as the victim’s legal successor but complained that the trial, held in Stepanakert, hindered his participation. He also argued that the courts failed to address the responsibility of the military unit’s administration, the non-ballistic injuries, the delay in evacuation, and whether prompt medical care could have saved his son. His appeals were rejected, and the Court of Cassation declared his appeal on points of law inadmissible.

A separate internal military investigation found significant shortcomings: some of G.A.’s signatures on safety-rule notices were forged; his individual file contained only standard entries; senior base staff had failed to perform duties properly; the military medical vehicle had technical problems; and poor supervision by the battalion administration and base staff contributed to the incident. The Government stated that six commanding officers, including the unit commander, received disciplinary penalties, but submitted no supporting documents.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 2 and Article 13 of the Convention. He claimed the State failed its positive obligation to protect his son’s life by not ensuring effective implementation of weapons-safety rules, proper training and supervision, and adequate emergency medical assistance. He also alleged that known risks inherent in military service, especially in an ongoing hostilities context, were not effectively averted. Procedurally, he argued the investigation was ineffective because it focused on G.A. and failed to identify all responsible officials or clarify whether timely medical care could have saved his son. Under Article 13, he complained that Armenian law made it impossible to claim compensation for non-pecuniary damage for the loss of a child.

The Government maintained that domestic law provided protective mechanisms, G.A. was adequately punished, the authorities could not have known of the risk, and evacuation was organized as quickly as possible. The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 2, both substantive and procedural, due to failures in safety regulation, emergency medical assistance, risk prevention, and investigation. It also found a violation of Article 13.

**Case: Dimaksyan v. Armenia (Application no. 29906/14), ECtHR, 17 October 2023**

The applicant, Aleksandr Dimaksyan, is the father of M. Dimaksyan, an 18-year-old conscript drafted into the Armenian army in November 2010. M. was assigned to military unit no. 38401 of the Nagorno-Karabakh armed forces near Hadrut. On 5 February 2012, while on watch duty at base no. 121 with fellow serviceman G.A., M. was shot and killed.

The key facts were largely undisputed. After hearing noises, G.A. loaded his assault rifle for security but later failed to close the trigger guard, despite M. reminding him that the rifle was loaded. When another noise was heard, G.A. moved to the right and M. to the left. As G.A. took his hands from his pockets and held the rifle’s handgrip, his finger touched the trigger. The rifle discharged unintentionally. The bullet entered M.’s right shoulder girdle and exited the left side of his chest, causing a perforating gunshot injury.

M. initially remained alive. Fellow servicemen carried him to a dugout, then placed him in a truck driven by Major V.S. toward the military hospital. The road was bumpy and difficult; 400 metres took about fifteen minutes. They then met a medical vehicle with paramedic A.G. and transferred M. to it. After about 6 kilometres, the vehicle overheated and stopped for water; it soon overheated again. M. was transferred to another truck and later met the military hospital ambulance. Doctors attempted emergency aid on the spot, but M. was already dead. The autopsy concluded that death resulted from severe blood loss. It also found non-ballistic bruises and abrasions on M.’s body, inflicted while he was alive or dying, but not linked to the cause of death.

A criminal investigation began the same day. G.A. was charged under Article 373 §3 of the Criminal Code for breaching weapon-handling rules causing death by negligence. The applicant was recognised as the victim’s legal successor. G.A. pleaded guilty. The Regional Court convicted him and sentenced him to four years and six months’ imprisonment. The court addressed only G.A.’s offence and sentence, not the responsibility of the military administration, the non-ballistic injuries, or the transport delays. The applicant’s appeals were rejected, and the Court of Cassation declared his appeal on points of law inadmissible.

An internal investigation by the Nagorno-Karabakh Defence Army found serious shortcomings: some of G.A.’s signatures on safety-rule notices were forged; entries in his individual file were standard or absent; the base’s senior staff failed to perform duties properly; the military medical vehicle had technical problems; and there was poor supervision by the battalion and base administration. Six commanding officers, including the unit commander, received disciplinary penalties. The Government later described these findings as preliminary and disciplinary, with no causal link to M.’s death, arguing that the accident resulted from G.A.’s personal error.

The applicant complained under Articles 2 and 13 that the State failed to protect his son’s life and to investigate effectively. He alleged failures in training, supervision, weapons-handling safety, and emergency medical assistance. He also complained that only G.A. was prosecuted, despite evidence of command failures, and that he could not claim compensation for non-pecuniary damage from the State. The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 2 both substantively and procedurally, and of Article 13 in conjunction with Article 2, due to the lack of an effective remedy for the loss of his child’s life.

In *Dimaksyan v. Armenia* (Application no. 29906/14, European Court of Human Rights, 17 October 2023), the applicant, Aleksandr Dimaksyan, complained about the death of his 18-year-old son, M. Dimaksyan, during compulsory military service in the Armenian army. M. was drafted in November 2010 and assigned to military unit no. 38401 of the Nagorno-Karabakh armed forces near Hadrut.

On 5 February 2012, M. was on watch duty at base no. 121 with fellow serviceman G.A. After hearing noises, G.A. loaded his assault rifle. Later, in breach of weapons-handling rules, he failed to close the trigger guard. While moving, his finger touched the trigger, the rifle discharged, and the bullet struck M. in the right shoulder/chest, causing a perforating gunshot injury. G.A. called for help. M. was first evacuated by truck over a rough road, then transferred to a medical vehicle with a paramedic. The medical vehicle overheated twice, requiring transfer to another truck. By the time an ambulance met them, M. was already dead. The autopsy found death resulted from severe blood loss; non-lethal blunt injuries were also found.

Criminal proceedings began the same day. G.A. was charged under Article 373 §3 of the Criminal Code for breaching assault-rifle handling rules causing death by negligence. In April 2013 he was convicted and sentenced to four years and six months’ imprisonment. Appeals were rejected, and the Court of Cassation declared the applicant’s appeal inadmissible in September 2013.

A separate internal military investigation in February 2012 found several shortcomings: some signatures on G.A.’s safety-rules notice were forged; his individual file entries were standard and lacked descriptions; the senior staff member at the base failed to perform duties properly; battalion administration and senior staff exercised poor supervision; and the military medical vehicle had technical problems, forcing a mid-route transfer. The Government stated that six commanding officers, including the unit commander, received disciplinary penalties, but provided no documents.

The applicant alleged violations of Articles 2 and 13. Under Article 2, he argued that the State failed its positive obligation to protect his son’s life. Specifically, the authorities did not effectively implement adequate safety regulations on handling weapons; commanders failed to train, supervise, or ensure observance of safety rules during watch duty, contrary to the Internal Service Regulations. He also alleged failure to organise effective emergency medical assistance: the transport was inadequate, the medical vehicle malfunctioned, and emergency equipment was lacking, potentially contributing to death. He further claimed the authorities knew or should have known of risks to conscripts, especially amid ongoing hostilities, but failed to avert them. He also complained the investigation was ineffective because only G.A. was prosecuted; it did not address command responsibility, the non-ballistic injuries, the delay, or whether timely medical care could have saved his son. Under Article 13, he complained that domestic law made it impossible to claim non-pecuniary damages from the State for the loss of his child’s life, leaving no effective remedy.

The Government argued that domestic law provided protective mechanisms, G.A. had been convicted, the shooting was an unpredictable individual error, the medical evacuation was prompt, and the internal shortcomings were disciplinary with no causal link. The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 2, both substantively and procedurally, and of Article 13, focusing on the failure to give effect to weapons-safety and emergency-medical frameworks, failure to avert known risks, ineffective investigation, and lack of a remedy for non-pecuniary damage.

In *Halet v. Luxembourg* (Application no. 21884/18, Grand Chamber, 14 February 2023), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Luxembourg violated Article 10 (freedom of expression) by criminally convicting and fining the applicant for disclosing confidential documents to the media.

The applicant, Raphaël Halet, worked for PricewaterhouseCoopers Luxembourg (PwC). In 2010, while still employed there, he accessed and copied confidential documents, including tax rulings and correspondence between PwC and the Luxembourg tax authorities concerning multinational companies. He provided these documents to journalist Edouard Perrin. The documents later formed part of the “LuxLeaks” revelations, which triggered significant national and European debate about Luxembourg’s tax practices and corporate tax avoidance.

After PwC filed a complaint, Luxembourg prosecuted Halet. He was convicted of theft and breach of professional secrecy and fined EUR 1,000. His appeals failed. The domestic courts accepted that the disclosed information had some public interest and that the Convention applied directly, but concluded that his disclosure was not protected. They found that he had other channels available, that he had breached professional secrecy, and that the disclosure harmed PwC and its clients. They also treated the public interest in the information as limited or already known.

Before the ECtHR, Halet alleged that the criminal-law fine violated Article 10. The Grand Chamber assessed the case under its whistleblower case-law, particularly *Guja v. Moldova*. It clarified that there is no abstract, general definition of a whistleblower; protection depends on the circumstances and context of each case. The relevant criteria—channels used, authenticity of the information, good faith, public interest, detriment caused, and severity of the sanction—must be assessed overall, without a rigid hierarchy.

Several facts were central to the alleged violation. The disclosed documents were authentic and concerned a matter of serious public interest: tax rulings and tax avoidance by multinational companies, already a subject of national and European debate. Halet was a private-sector employee bound by confidentiality, but he disclosed the documents to a journalist rather than making them fully public. There was no finding that PwC had engaged in illegal conduct. He acted in good faith, motivated by concern over tax practices rather than personal gain. However, the domestic courts gave an overly restrictive interpretation of the public interest and focused mainly on the detriment to PwC—theft of data, breach of professional secrecy, and harm to clients’ private interests—without adequately balancing the public interest in disclosure against those harms.

The Grand Chamber found that the public interest in disclosure outweighed the detrimental effects. Although the fine was relatively modest, the criminal conviction and fine were disproportionate and could deter whistleblowers. Luxembourg therefore violated Article 10. The judgment consolidated the Court’s approach to whistleblower protection, emphasizing flexible, context-sensitive balancing rather than an abstract definition of who qualifies as a whistleblower.

**Summary of the Case of Halet v. Luxembourg**

The case of *Halet v. Luxembourg* (Application no. 21884/18), decided by the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights on 14 February 2023, concerns a violation of Article 10 (freedom of expression) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant, Raphaël Halet, was an employee at PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) Luxembourg. Between 2008 and 2010, he copied numerous confidential documents belonging to his employer, which detailed tax practices—specifically, advance tax agreements—arranged for multinational companies. In 2012, he forwarded these documents to a journalist, Edouard Perrin, who used them as the basis for what became known as the "LuxLeaks" revelations. These disclosures sparked significant public debate in Luxembourg, across Europe, and internationally regarding corporate tax avoidance and the legality of such tax rulings.

Following an investigation, Halet was charged with theft, disclosure of professional secrets, money laundering, and fraud. He was subsequently convicted in a criminal court. On appeal, the Court of Appeal upheld his conviction but acknowledged his good faith, noting that he had no personal gain and acted out of a civic conviction. However, the court found that the public interest in the disclosure did not outweigh the harm caused to PwC and its clients. It emphasized that the documents contained confidential business information and that Halet had breached his duty of loyalty and professional secrecy. He was given a suspended fine of EUR 1,000. Critically, his co-defendant, Antoine Deltour, who faced similar charges, was ultimately acquitted by the Court of Cassation on procedural grounds.

Halet appealed to the European Court of Human Rights, arguing that his conviction constituted a disproportionate interference with his right to freedom of expression. The Grand Chamber assessed his case using the criteria established in *Guja v. Moldova* for whistle-blowers: the channels used for disclosure, the authenticity of the information, the applicant's good faith, the public interest in the information, the detriment caused to the employer, and the severity of the sanction.

The Court found that the domestic courts had failed to properly balance these interests. It held that the public interest in the LuxLeaks information—which concerned the tax practices of multinational companies and had made an essential contribution to a debate of major public importance—was overwhelmingly high. The domestic courts had interpreted this public interest too restrictively. Furthermore, the Court found that the sanctions imposed were disproportionate. It noted that the domestic courts had focused solely on the detriment to PwC, failing to consider the broader public interest or the fact that the disclosure had not harmed PwC's clients in a way that outweighed the public's right to know.

The Grand Chamber concluded that the criminal conviction and fine imposed on Halet were disproportionate and constituted a violation of Article 10. This judgment consolidated European Court case-law on whistle-blower protection, emphasizing that the *Guja* criteria must be assessed as a whole, without a rigid hierarchy, and that a strong public interest can justify the disclosure of confidential information even when the chosen channel is not the most appropriate one.

In *Halet v. Luxembourg* (Application no. 21884/18), the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Luxembourg violated Article 10 of the Convention by criminally fining Raphaël Halet €1,000 for disclosing confidential documents from his private-sector employer, PwC Luxembourg. The case formed part of the “LuxLeaks” revelations.

Halet, an accountant employed by PwC Luxembourg, had access to confidential documents concerning tax rulings and tax arrangements between PwC and multinational companies. In 2010–2011, he copied and transmitted such documents to a journalist. The documents were later used in media reports exposing Luxembourg’s tax practices and the role of major accounting firms in facilitating tax avoidance by multinationals. After the disclosures became public, PwC filed a criminal complaint.

Luxembourg prosecuted Halet for theft, breach of professional secrecy, and disclosure of business secrets. The domestic courts convicted him. Although the Court of Appeal acknowledged that the disclosed information concerned matters of public interest, it held that Halet’s disclosure was not protected as whistleblowing. It considered that he could have used internal reporting channels, that the documents were confidential and obtained through theft, and that the employer’s interests and professional secrecy outweighed the public interest. The final sanction was a criminal fine of €1,000. Halet’s appeals, including to the Court of Cassation, were unsuccessful.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Halet alleged that his criminal conviction and fine violated his right to freedom of expression under Article 10. He argued that he acted as a whistle-blower in the public interest, that the disclosed information revealed serious tax avoidance practices, and that the sanction was disproportionate. The Government maintained that the conviction was necessary to protect professional secrecy, business secrets, and the rights of PwC and its clients.

The Grand Chamber assessed the case under the criteria established in *Guja v. Moldova*: the channels used for disclosure, authenticity of the information, good faith, public interest, detriment caused, and severity of the sanction. It stressed that whistle-blower protection depends on the specific circumstances and context of each case and requires a fair balancing of competing interests.

The Court found that the domestic courts had interpreted the public interest too narrowly. The disclosed documents concerned tax practices of multinational companies and made an essential contribution to an existing public debate of national and European importance. While the disclosure involved theft of data, breach of professional secrecy, and harm to PwC’s private interests, the public interest in the information outweighed those detrimental effects. The domestic courts had focused mainly on the detriment to the employer rather than on the broader public interest.

The Grand Chamber concluded that the criminal conviction and fine imposed on Halet were disproportionate and not necessary in a democratic society. There was therefore a violation

**X and Others v. Ireland** (ECtHR, 22 June 2023) concerned two mothers lawfully present in Ireland but without a right to reside, who were refused child benefit because they did not meet the domestic “habitual residence” condition. They alleged discrimination contrary to Article 14 read with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 8 of the Convention.

Under the Social Welfare Consolidation Act 2005, child benefit is payable to a “qualified person” with whom a “qualified child” normally resides, provided the qualified person is habitually resident in Ireland. Section 246(5) provided that a person without a right to reside in the State could not be regarded as habitually resident. Section 246(6) recognised Irish and EU nationals, refugees, and certain family members as having a right to reside. Section 246(7) excluded asylum seekers and persons awaiting family reunification, and s.246(8) prevented backdating after status was granted.

In application no. 23851/20, X, a Nigerian national, arrived in Ireland in 2013 and sought asylum. Her daughter E was born in December 2014 and, through her Irish father, was an Irish citizen from birth. X and E lived in Ireland’s “direct provision” system for asylum seekers. In September 2015 X applied for residence as the mother of an Irish citizen child. In October 2015 she applied for child benefit for E; it was refused in November 2015 because she had no right to reside and so was not habitually resident. X was granted residence in January 2016, after which child benefit was paid. Her claim was therefore limited to the period from E’s birth until the residence grant, about twelve months.

In application no. 24360/20, Y, an Afghan national, arrived in Ireland in 2008 with her husband and first child and applied for asylum. The family initially used false Pakistani identity documents; their claim was rejected and removal orders issued, but they later established their true nationality and reapplied. Their youngest son, M, was born in April 2013. M was granted refugee status in December 2014, communicated in January 2015. While family reunification was pending, Y applied for child benefit in February 2015; it was refused in April 2015 because she lacked habitual residence. Family reunification was granted in September 2015, and child benefit was then paid from that date. The claim was limited to the roughly eight-month period between M’s asylum grant and Y’s residence permission.

During the relevant periods, both families received State support through direct provision, including accommodation, meals, healthcare, school access, and small weekly payments. The State argued that the habitual residence rule served legitimate immigration and social-policy aims, such as deterring welfare tourism and controlling migration, and applied equally to all claimants for child benefit.

Domestically, the High Court rejected the claims. The Court of Appeal held that excluding E, an Irish citizen child, from child benefit was unconstitutional, but rejected M’s claim. The Supreme Court reversed, holding that child benefit vested in the qualifying adult, not the child, and that the habitual residence requirement did not discriminate because all claimants were treated alike. It also found no obligation to backdate payment under the Constitution or Article 28 of the Qualification Directive.

Before the ECtHR, the Court accepted that child benefit was a proprietary interest within Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. However, under Article 14, the applicants were not in a relevantly similar position to persons with legal resident status. The differential treatment was objectively justified. As to Article 8, the benefit’s purpose was not to promote or organise family life, nor did it affect key aspects of daily life, so that complaint was inadmissible ratione materiae. There was therefore no violation.

In **X and Others v. Ireland** (Applications nos. 23851/20 and 24360/20, ECtHR, 22 June 2023), two mothers lawfully present in Ireland but without a recognised right to reside complained that the refusal of child benefit discriminated against them and their children, contrary to Article 14 ECHR read with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 8.

The first applicant, X, a Nigerian national, arrived in Ireland in November 2013 and applied for asylum. Her application was rejected. Her daughter, E, was born in December 2014 and was an Irish citizen because her father was Irish. X and E lived in Ireland’s “direct provision” system for asylum seekers. In September 2015, X applied for residence as the mother of an Irish citizen child. While that application was pending, she applied for child benefit for E in October 2015. It was refused in November 2015 because she did not satisfy the habitual residence condition: she had not yet been granted a right to reside. In January 2016, X was granted residence, after which child benefit was paid. Her claim therefore concerned only the period from E’s birth to the grant of residence, just over twelve months.

The second applicant, Y, an Afghan national, arrived in Ireland in May 2008 with her husband and first child and sought asylum. The family lived in direct provision. Her son, M, was born in April 2013. After initially using false identity documents, the family’s true nationality was established and M was granted asylum in December 2014, notified in January 2015. The rest of the family sought reunification. In February 2015, Y applied for child benefit for her four children, but it was refused in April 2015 because she did not meet the habitual residence condition. Family reunification was granted in September 2015, and child benefit was then paid from that date. Her claim covered the period from M’s asylum grant to the reunification decision, about eight months.

Domestically, the High Court rejected the claims, noting that direct provision met the families’ basic needs. The Court of Appeal found that excluding E, an Irish citizen child, from a universal child benefit lacked justification, and that Article 28 of the EU Qualification Directive required payment from M’s asylum grant. The Supreme Court reversed. It held that child benefit is payable to a “qualified person”—the parent—not the child; that the recipient must be habitually resident; and that a person without a right to reside cannot be habitually resident. The State could regulate migration and make entitlement prospective.

Before the ECtHR, the key issue was whether the habitual residence/right-to-reside rule discriminated against persons lawfully present but not yet granted a right to reside. The Court accepted that child benefit was a proprietary interest within Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. However, under Article 14 read with that provision, the applicants were not, at the material time, in a relevantly similar position to persons with legal resident status. The denial was therefore non-discriminatory. Under Article 14 read with Article 8, applying *Beeler v. Switzerland*, the Court found that the benefit’s purpose was not to promote or organise family life and did not represent a modality of exercising family life. Consequently, the Article 8 complaint was inadmissible *ratione materiae*.

Case: *Humpert and Others v. Germany* (ECtHR Grand Chamber, 14 December 2023, Applications nos. 59433/18, 59477/18, 59481/18 and 59494/18). The applicants were four teachers employed as civil servants (*Beamte*) in German State schools. They participated during working hours in strikes organised by their trade union, the Gewerkschaft Erziehung und Wissenschaft (GEW), to pursue occupational interests such as pay and working conditions. German law, reflecting the traditional civil-service principle and constitutional case-law, prohibits civil servants from striking. As a result, disciplinary proceedings were brought against the applicants, and they received disciplinary sanctions—reprimands and/or fines—for breaching their civil-service duties by taking part in the strikes. They challenged those sanctions before administrative courts and then the Federal Constitutional Court, arguing that the strike ban and penalties violated their trade-union rights. The Federal Constitutional Court upheld the ban and sanctions as compatible with both the Basic Law and Article 11 of the Convention. The applicants then complained to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging violations of Article 11 (freedom of association), Article 14 read with Article 11 (discrimination), and Article 6 §1 (fair trial).

The central alleged violation concerned Article 11. The applicants argued that punishing them for participating in strikes organised by their union, and maintaining a general ban on strikes for all civil servants, infringed their freedom of association, including the right to strike. The German Government maintained that the interference was prescribed by law and pursued legitimate aims: ensuring a stable administration, the proper functioning of the State and its institutions, a functioning school system, and the right to education protected by Article 2 of Protocol No. 1. It also relied on various domestic safeguards for civil servants’ unions.

The Grand Chamber found no violation of Article 11. It accepted that the disciplinary measures and the strike ban interfered with trade-union freedom. However, it held that the right to strike, though an important part of trade-union activity, is not absolute and is not automatically an essential element of Article 11 in every context; whether it is essential requires a context-specific assessment of all circumstances. In the civil-service context, Germany’s general prohibition pursued legitimate aims. The Court emphasised that German law provided a range of alternative institutional safeguards: civil servants could form and join trade unions; their unions had participatory rights in legislation, representation and co-determination; civil servants had a right to adequate maintenance; and individuals could work as contractual State employees with the right to strike. Although monitoring bodies under specialised international instruments had criticised the ban and a European trend against such bans was relevant, those factors were not decisive. Considering the safeguards in their totality and the limited severity of the sanctions, the Court found the interference proportionate.

The Court also found no violation of Article 14 read with Article 11 and no violation of Article 6 §1. The judgment is significant because the Grand Chamber upheld Germany’s general strike ban for civil servants, while stressing that restrictions on the right to strike require close, context-specific scrutiny.

**Case:** *Humpert and Others v. Germany* (Applications nos. 59433/18, 59477/18, 59481/18 and 59494/18), Grand Chamber, 14 December 2023.

The applicants were German State school teachers with civil-servant status. They participated, during their working hours, in strikes organised by their trade union. Under German law, civil servants are subject to a constitutional ban on strikes, based on the traditional principles of the civil service and the need to preserve the functioning of the State. Because the applicants took part in the strikes despite that prohibition, disciplinary sanctions were imposed on them.

The applicants challenged those sanctions before the administrative courts and then lodged constitutional complaints with the Federal Constitutional Court. The Federal Constitutional Court upheld the strike ban and the disciplinary measures, finding them compatible both with the German Basic Law and with Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants subsequently applied to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging violations of Article 11 (freedom of association, including the right to strike), Article 14 read in conjunction with Article 11 (discrimination), and Article 6 § 1 (fair hearing/access to court).

Before the Grand Chamber, the key issue was whether the disciplinary sanctions for participating in trade-union strikes breached the applicants’ freedom of association. The Court accepted that there had been an interference with Article 11. It emphasised that the right to strike, while an important aspect of trade-union activity, is not the only means by which trade unions and their members can protect occupational interests. Whether a strike prohibition affects an essential element of trade-union freedom is context-specific and requires an assessment of all the circumstances.

The Court found that the German ban pursued legitimate aims: ensuring the maintenance of a stable administration, the fulfilment of State functions, the proper functioning of the State and its institutions, and the functioning of the school system, thereby safeguarding the right to education under Article 2 of Protocol No. 1. It also noted that negative assessments by international monitoring bodies and a trend among Contracting States were relevant but not decisive.

In assessing necessity, the Court considered the nature and extent of the restriction and the alternative safeguards available in German law. Civil servants could form and join trade unions; they had participatory rights, rights of representation and co-determination, and a right to adequate maintenance. They could also work as State school teachers under contractual employee status, which carried a right to strike. In their totality, those safeguards enabled civil servants’ trade unions and civil servants to defend occupational interests effectively. The prohibition on strikes was therefore a general measure reflecting a balancing of competing constitutional interests, and the disciplinary sanctions imposed were proportionate.

The Grand Chamber accordingly found no violation of Article 11. It also found no violation of Article 14 read in conjunction with Article 11 and no violation of Article 6 § 1. The judgment is final, though subject to possible editorial revision.

**Case: Humpert and Others v. Germany**  
**Applications nos. 59433/18, 59477/18, 59481/18 and 59494/18**  
**Grand Chamber, 14 December 2023**

The applicants were German teachers holding civil-servant (*Beamte*) status. Under German law, civil servants are prohibited from striking, a rule rooted in the constitutional principle of a professional civil service. Despite this ban, the applicants participated in strikes organised by their trade union during their working hours to pursue occupational and pay interests. The authorities imposed disciplinary sanctions on them for breaching their civil-service duties. The applicants complained that the sanctions and the general strike ban violated their freedom of association under Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights. They also alleged discrimination contrary to Article 14 read in conjunction with Article 11, and unfairness under Article 6 § 1.

Domestic administrative courts upheld the disciplinary measures. The Federal Constitutional Court rejected the applicants’ constitutional complaints, holding that the strike ban for civil servants was compatible with both Article 9 § 3 of the Basic Law and Article 11 of the Convention. It stressed the special status of civil servants and the compensatory institutional safeguards available to them, including union representation and participation rights.

Before the European Court of Human Rights Grand Chamber, the central issue was whether the disciplinary sanctions for participating in strikes breached Article 11. The Court recalled that trade-union freedom is protected, but the right to strike, although important, is not absolute and is not necessarily an essential element of trade-union freedom in every context. Whether a strike prohibition affects an essential element requires a context-specific assessment of all circumstances. The Court found that the sanctions interfered with the applicants’ Article 11 rights. However, the interference was prescribed by law and pursued legitimate aims: maintaining a stable administration, ensuring the fulfilment of State functions, preserving the proper functioning of the State and its institutions, and securing a functioning school system, thereby protecting the right to education under Article 2 of Protocol No. 1.

On necessity, the Grand Chamber accepted that a general ban on strikes by all civil servants raises Convention issues. It noted that negative assessments by international monitoring bodies and a possible trend among Contracting States were relevant but not decisive. Strike action is an important means of protecting occupational interests, but it is not the only means. The Court examined German domestic safeguards in their totality: the right of civil servants to form and join trade unions; participatory rights of trade unions in the legislative process; the individual right to adequate maintenance; and rights of representation and co-determination. In the Court’s view, these safeguards enabled civil servants and their unions to defend their occupational interests effectively. The strike ban reflected a constitutional balancing of competing interests, and the disciplinary measures were not disproportionate.

The Court therefore found no violation of Article 11. It also found no violation of Article 14 read in conjunction with Article 11, and no violation of Article 6 § 1. The Grand Chamber thus upheld the German civil-service strike ban and the disciplinary sanctions as compatible with the Convention in the applicants’ circumstances.

Greece (Application no. 57378/18) concerned whether the Greek Court of Cassation violated Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights by failing to examine, without reasons, the applicant’s request to seek a preliminary ruling from the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU).

Criminal proceedings were brought against him for breach of duty. He faced three charges: (i) breach of his official duty of full and exclusive employment with ELSTAT because he allegedly continued to hold a position at the International Monetary Fund; (ii) breach of his duty to convene ELSTAT’s board from November 2010 to September 2011; and (iii) breach of official duty by releasing 2009 fiscal deficit information without first communicating it to ELSTAT’s administrative board or obtaining its consent.

On 1 August 2017, the Athens Court of Appeal convicted him only of the third charge and acquitted him of the rest. It imposed a two-year suspended prison sentence. The appellate court found that he had transmitted the data to Eurostat without communicating them to ELSTAT as a body and without obtaining its consent, in breach of Article 10 § 2A of Law no. 3832/2010. It further found that he acted intentionally to gain an illegal moral benefit by strengthening his power as president and effectively usurping the board’s powers.

By an additional grounds memorandum dated 21 March 2018, he requested that the Court of Cassation seek a preliminary ruling from the CJEU under Article 267 TFEU on the correct interpretation of Principle 1.4 of the European Statistics Code of Practice. He argued that if the court had any doubt about the provision’s meaning, it should refer the question; failure to do so would violate his right to a fair hearing under Article 6 ECHR. **Case: Georgiou v. Greece (Application no. 57378/18), ECtHR Third Section, 14 March 2023**

The appellate court found that he acted to gain an illegal moral benefit by strengthening his power as ELSTAT president and effectively usurping the board’s powers. They maintained that no preliminary ruling was necessary and that it would not have affected the outcome.
