001-224732:
**Ships Waste Oil Collector B.V. v. the Netherlands** (Application no. 2799/16) concerned the transmission and use, in competition-law proceedings, of data obtained through lawful telephone taps in a criminal investigation.

The applicant company was a Dutch waste-liquid collector operating in the Rotterdam port area. In late 2006, the VROM-IOD, a special investigative service under the public prosecutor’s authority, began criminal investigation “Toto” into another ship-waste collector, I. company, suspected of environmental offences. With authorization from an investigating judge, VROM-IOD intercepted telephone conversations, including calls between an I. company employee and an employee of the applicant. Some intercepted calls contained indications of price-fixing and were therefore potentially relevant to the Netherlands Competition Authority (NMA).

In April 2008, a VROM-IOD official drew up an official record noting those price-fixing indications and annexed summary transcripts. In October 2008, the public prosecutor approved transmission of the record and annexes to the NMA under the Judicial and Criminal Data Act (WJSG), initially by a handwritten note. The actual transmission occurred in June 2009. Further transcripts and audio files were transmitted in 2009–2010 after further prosecutor approvals; the case file showed contacts between VROM-IOD and NMA officials regarding selection of relevant data.

The NMA then investigated possible breaches of the Competition Act. In June 2010, NMA inspectors visited the applicant’s premises, questioned management under caution, and played a recording of an intercepted call. In November 2011, the NMA fined the applicant EUR 834,000, finding that between August 2005 and July 2007 it had coordinated with other companies to allocate contracts and limit price competition in ship-generated waste collection, contrary to section 6 of the Competition Act.

The applicant objected, arguing that the intercepted conversations were not “criminal data” capable of transmission under the WJSG because they were irrelevant to the criminal investigation. It also complained of the absence of prior judicial control and of a recorded balancing exercise before transmission. In 2013, the Rotterdam Regional Court allowed the appeal, excluded the transcripts as evidence, and quashed the NMA decisions, holding that the public prosecutor had merely given handwritten or pre-printed permission without reviewable reasoning.

On further appeal, the Supreme Administrative Court for Trade and Industry quashed that judgment in July 2015. It held that the telephone-tap data qualified as “criminal data” under the broad WJSG definition; a criminal file could relate to more facts than those prosecuted, and the data had been stored digitally. A compelling general interest existed—the economic well-being of the country—and the transmission served enforcement of competition law. The WJSG did not require written reasoning at the time of transmission; compliance could be reviewed ex post by courts. It found no violation of Article 8 ECHR and rejected objections that the NMA lacked interception powers or had helped select the data.

The applicant then applied to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging under Article 8 that the transmission and use of the data were not foreseeable and lacked sufficient safeguards, and under Article 13 that no effective remedy existed. The Third Section declared the complaints admissible but found no violation of Article 8 or Article 13. It considered the interference sufficiently foreseeable, subject to extensive ex post judicial oversight and adequate safeguards, and held that ex ante judicial authorization was not required in this context. The case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 1 April 2025.

**Case summary: Ships Waste Oil Collector B.V. v. the Netherlands (Application no. 2799/16)**

The applicant, Ships Waste Oil Collector B.V., was a Dutch company collecting waste liquids from ships in the Rotterdam port region. In 2006, the VROM-IOD, a special investigative service, began a criminal investigation codenamed “Toto” into another waste collector, the I. company, suspected of illegally disposing of polluted waste. With authorization from an investigating judge, VROM-IOD intercepted telephone calls involving I. company employees. Some intercepted calls were between an I. company employee and an employee of the applicant and contained indications of price-fixing.

VROM-IOD recorded these indications in an official report and annexed summary transcripts. In October 2008, the public prosecutor approved transmission of the report to the Netherlands Competition Authority (NMA) under the Judicial and Criminal Data Act (WJSG). The transmission occurred in June 2009. Further transcripts and audio files were transmitted to the NMA in 2009 and 2010, after contacts between VROM-IOD and NMA officials regarding the selection of data relevant to the competition investigation.

The NMA investigated and, in November 2011, fined the applicant EUR 834,000 for breaching section 6 of the Competition Act by coordinating behavior to allocate contracts and limit price competition in ship-generated waste collection. The applicant objected, arguing that the intercepted conversations were not “criminal data” transferable under the WJSG because they were irrelevant to the criminal investigation. It also complained that the transmission lacked prior judicial control and any recorded balancing of interests.

The Rotterdam Regional Court initially accepted these arguments, excluded the transcripts as evidence, and quashed the fines because the prosecutor had given permission by handwritten note or pre-printed form without reasons. The Consumer and Market Authority appealed. In July 2015, the Supreme Administrative Court for Trade and Industry quashed that judgment. It held that the phone-tap data qualified as “criminal data” under the broad WJSG definition, because a criminal file may cover more facts than those prosecuted and the data were digitally stored and processed. It found a compelling general interest in enforcing competition law, namely the economic well-being of the country. The WJSG did not require written reasons at the time of transmission, and lawfulness could be reviewed ex post by courts. It found no Article 8 violation, noting that the taps were judicially authorized and that civil and administrative review provided sufficient safeguards. The NMA’s lack of interception powers and its consultations on data selection did not render the transfer unlawful.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 8 that the transmission and use of data lawfully obtained in a criminal investigation, but irrelevant to it, were not foreseeable and lacked sufficient procedural safeguards, especially ex ante judicial authorization. It also complained under Article 13 about the absence of an effective remedy. The Government argued that because the data had been lawfully collected, lower safeguards sufficed, and that ex post judicial review was adequate.

The Court found the interference sufficiently foreseeable under Dutch law and supported by adequate safeguards. In this context, Article 8 did not require ex ante judicial authorization. The prosecutor’s balancing exercise plus extensive ex post judicial oversight were adequate to avoid abuse of power. The transmission pursued a compelling general interest—economic well-being—and was necessary and proportionate. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 8 and no violation of Article 13. The case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 1 April 2025.

It excluded the transcripts as evidence and quashed the fines.

It held that the tapped data qualified as “criminal data”; the term “criminal file” was broad, and the data were digitally stored and automatically processed. It found a compelling general interest in the economic well-being of the country, namely competition-law enforcement. Written reasoning at the time of transmission was not required, and ex post judicial review was sufficient. It found no violation of Article 8.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that the transmission and use were not foreseeable, that safeguards were insufficient, and that an ex ante judicial authorisation was required. It relied on cases such as *Dragojević*, *Sanoma*, and *Valenzuela Contreras*. It also alleged no effective remedy under Article 13. The Government argued that the law clearly set out what data could be transmitted, by whom, to whom, and why; that the data had been lawfully obtained; and that prosecutorial balancing plus ex post civil and administrative review provided adequate safeguards.

The Court declared the complaints admissible and found no violation of Article 8. The transmission was sufficiently foreseeable under Dutch law; extensive ex post facto judicial oversight and adequate safeguards existed; the domestic system was capable of preventing abuse; and Article 8 did not require ex ante court authorisation in this context. The balancing exercise was adequate, and the reasons for the interference were relevant and sufficient. It also found no violation of Article 13.

**Case: Efgan Çetin and Others v. Türkiye** (App. no. 14684/18), European Court of Human Rights, Second Section, judgment 3 October 2023, final 19 February 2024.

The five Turkish applicants complained that they could not access a court to challenge an administrative decision that no environmental impact assessment (EIA) was required for a geothermal plant near the first applicant’s olive grove and the other applicants’ residences. They relied on Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention; the Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1 concerning access to court.

The dispute concerned a geothermal plant with licence no. J-700. In 2012, the Aydın Governor’s Office issued an EIA non-requirement decision for another nearby plant, J-680. While the applicants and their lawyer attended an on-site inspection on 27 March 2015 in the J-680 proceedings, they noticed the J-700 plant already under construction. The parties later accepted that this was when the applicants learned of the second plant. On 6 May 2015, other claimants—not the applicants—asked the Governor’s Office under freedom-of-information law whether J-700 had undergone an EIA. On 18 May 2015, the office replied that on 24 July 2014 it had issued an EIA non-requirement decision for J-700.

On 19 June 2015, the applicants sued to annul the 24 July 2014 decision. They argued that geothermal projects could pollute water and air, harm health and the environment, and should not be exempt from EIA. The Administrative Court ordered an expert examination. The December 2015 expert report found the project file procedurally compliant but lacking scientific and technical detail; possible gas emissions and harm to flora, fauna, air quality and olive groves; no alternative-site survey; and construction commenced without necessary permits and was virtually complete.

On 26 February 2016, the Aydın Administrative Court dismissed the claim as out of time. Applying the 30-day fast-track limit for EIA-related decisions, it held that time began on 27 March 2015, when the applicants learned of the plant during the inspection, even though there was no evidence the EIA non-requirement decision had been notified to them. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld the dismissal on 17 November 2016. It noted that the administration had not shown the decision was publicly announced as required in the affected village or area, but still found the claim late because the applicants had learned of the construction in March 2015 and sued only on 19 June 2015 after the freedom-of-information reply. On 1 November 2017, the Constitutional Court rejected the applicants’ individual applications.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants alleged that this formalistic time-limit calculation denied them access to court. The Government argued that time-limits ensured legal certainty and that the applicants should have acted promptly once aware of the construction. The Court found Article 6 § 1 applicable in its civil limb, because the dispute concerned the right to live in a healthy environment and the outcome would directly affect the applicants. It rejected objections on victim status and exhaustion. On the merits, the Court held that domestic law required public announcement or notification of EIA decisions, which had not occurred. Requiring the applicants to sue within 30 days of merely learning by chance that a plant existed—before knowing the relevant decision—imposed a disproportionate burden and an excessively formalistic barrier. The Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1.

**Case:** *Efgan Çetin and Others v. Türkiye* (App. no. 14684/18), ECtHR Second Section, judgment of 3 October 2023.

The applicants were five Turkish nationals. The first applicant owned an olive grove, and the remaining applicants lived near a planned geothermal energy plant in Aydın. A private company sought to build a geothermal plant (licence J-700). On 24 July 2014, the Aydın Governorship issued an “EIA non-requirement decision,” meaning no environmental impact assessment was required. That decision was not served on the applicants or publicly announced as required under domestic law.

The applicants were already involved in separate litigation challenging an EIA non-requirement decision for an adjacent geothermal plant (J-680). On 27 March 2015, during an on-site inspection in that other case, they noticed the second plant (J-700) under construction nearby. On 6 May 2015, other claimants—not the applicants—submitted a freedom-of-information request to the Governor’s Office asking whether J-700 had undergone EIA. The Governor’s Office replied on 18 May 2015 that the 24 July 2014 EIA non-requirement decision existed. On 19 June 2015, the applicants sued to annul that decision. They argued that geothermal energy was not exempt from EIA and that the plant could cause chemical pollution, water-quality deterioration, and harm to health and the environment.

In the administrative proceedings, an expert report of 18 December 2015 found the project file lacked scientific, technical and legislative detail. It warned of adverse effects on flora, fauna and air quality, possible gas emissions harmful to human and animal health, irreversible damage to olive groves, no alternative-site survey, and construction begun without required permits and nearly completed. Nevertheless, on 26 February 2016 the Aydın Administrative Court dismissed the claim as out of time. It held that the 30-day fast-track time-limit ran from 27 March 2015, when the applicants allegedly learned of the plant. Although there was no proof the EIA non-requirement decision had been notified to them, the court said they should have acted within 30 days rather than waiting for the freedom-of-information reply. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld this on 17 November 2016, also noting the administration had not shown public announcement as required. The Constitutional Court dismissed the individual application on 1 November 2017.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (access to court) and Article 8 (private/family life and home). The Court found the Article 6 complaint admissible. It held that the dispute concerned a civil right—the right to live in a healthy environment as recognised in Turkish law—and that the outcome would be directly decisive for the applicants. The Government’s objections on victim status and non-exhaustion were rejected.

On the merits, the Court focused on the domestic authorities’ failure to announce or serve the EIA non-requirement decision and on the administrative courts’ excessively formalistic application of the 30-day time-limit. The applicants could not reasonably be expected to challenge a decision they had not been officially informed of; learning of the plant during another inspection was not the same as knowing the EIA decision. The time-bar therefore imposed a disproportionate burden, impairing the very essence of their right of access to court. The ECtHR found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

Efgan Çetin and Others v. Türkiye (no. 14684/18) is an ECtHR Second Section judgment delivered on 3 October 2023 (final 19 February 2024). The five applicants were Turkish nationals. The first owned an olive grove and the others lived near a planned geothermal energy plant in Aydın. They complained that they could not obtain judicial review of an administrative decision that an environmental impact assessment (EIA) was not required for the plant, alleging violations of Articles 6 and 8.

On 10 January 2012 the Governor of Aydın issued an EIA non-requirement decision for a first plant (J-680). A group including the applicants challenged that decision in the Aydın Administrative Court. On 27 March 2015, during an on-site inspection and expert examination in that case, they noticed a second geothermal plant (J-700) under construction nearby. The parties later accepted that date as when the applicants learned of the second plant. On 6 May 2015, some claimants—not the applicants—made a freedom of information request to the Governor’s Office asking whether the second plant had undergone an EIA procedure. On 18 May 2015 the Governor’s Office replied that on 24 July 2014 it had issued an EIA non-requirement decision for that second plant.

On 19 June 2015 the applicants challenged the 24 July 2014 decision. They argued that geothermal energy was not exempt from the EIA procedure and that the project could cause chemical pollution, deteriorate water quality, and harm health and the environment. The Administrative Court ordered an on-site inspection and expert examination. The expert report of 18 December 2015 found procedural compliance but missing scientific, technical, and legislative detail. It noted possible adverse effects on flora, fauna, and air quality; possible gas emissions harming human and animal health; irreversible damage to olive groves; no alternative site survey; and that construction had begun without necessary permits and was virtually complete and irreversible.

On 26 February 2016 the Aydın Administrative Court dismissed the claim as out of time. It held that the 30-day fast-track administrative time limit began on 27 March 2015, when the applicants became aware of the plant, rather than when they received the freedom of information reply. It noted no evidence that the EIA non-requirement decision had been notified, that construction was almost complete by March 2015, and that the applicants had been present at the inspection. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld this on 17 November 2016. It expressly noted that the administration had not shown the decision was publicly announced in the village or affected area, but still found the claim late. The Turkish Constitutional Court dismissed the individual applications on 1 November 2017.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants alleged that the domestic courts’ formalism denied them access to a court. The Government argued that time limits were clear, legal certainty was important, and the applicants should have acted after 27 March 2015. The Court held that Article 6 § 1 (civil) applied because the dispute over the EIA non-requirement decision affected their right to a healthy environment and was directly decisive for the first applicant’s property and the other applicants’ homes. It found that the domestic authorities failed to announce or serve the decision as required by domestic law, and that the courts’ excessively formalistic application of time limits precluded any examination on the merits. This imposed a disproportionate burden, impairing the very essence of the right of access to court. The Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1. The applicants also invoked Article 8 concerning home, private and family life, but the judgment’s principal finding was on access to court.
001-223027:
In *Y v. France*, the applicant, a French national born in 1951, was registered as “male” at birth. He states he is intersex: he was born with ambiguous sex characteristics, has no gonads or natural sex hormones, and did not undergo puberty. Medical certificates describe a male XY karyotype, hypogonadism, gonadal agenesis, micropenis, hypospadias, a rudimentary vagina and osteoporosis. Although raised male, he was perceived as female in early adulthood. At age 40, testosterone treatment produced a beard and deepened voice but left his genitalia ambiguous; he described this as trauma and an intrusion into his privacy and bodily integrity. He also identifies psychologically and socially as intersex, neither male nor female, and says he suffered from having to live behind a “borrowed” male identity. He is married and has an adopted child.

In January 2015 he asked the public prosecutor to replace the “male” marker on his birth certificate with “neutral” or, failing that, “intersex”. In August 2015 the Tours tribunal de grande instance granted the request. It found that his sex could not be defined genitally, hormonally or psychologically, that the male marker was fictitious, and that maintaining it violated Article 8 of the Convention. It treated “neutral” as correcting an error, not recognising a third sex.

The Orléans Court of Appeal reversed in March 2016. It accepted that he was sexually ambiguous but found his physical appearance and social behaviour to be male, noting his marriage and adopted child. It held that no domestic provision allowed a marker other than male or female; granting “neutral” or “intersex” would amount to recognising another sex category, a matter for the legislature. A fair balance between civil status and private life could permit no sex marker or a changed marker only where assigned sex did not match physical appearance and social behaviour, which was not the case.

In May 2017 the Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal. It stated that French law permits only male or female civil-status markers. While gender identity falls within Article 8, the binary marker pursued a legitimate aim and was a cornerstone of social and legal arrangements. Recognising a “neutral” sex would have far-reaching consequences and require multiple legislative amendments. The interference with his private life was not disproportionate.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained under Article 8 that the refusal violated his right to respect for private life, relying on the State’s positive obligations. The Court found no European consensus on intersex civil-status recognition, so France enjoyed a wide margin of appreciation. Emphasising public-interest considerations, it left the State to determine the speed and extent of meeting intersex people’s civil-status demands. It found no violation of Article 8.

**Case: Y v. France (ECtHR, Fifth Section, 31 January 2023)**

The applicant, a French national born in 1951 and living in Strasbourg, was registered as “male” at birth but states that he is intersex. He was born with ambiguous sex characteristics: sexual differentiation did not occur in utero, and it was impossible at birth to determine whether he was a boy or a girl. Medically, he has neither testicles nor ovaries and has never produced sex hormones. He did not go through puberty. Medical certificates from 1970, 1973 and 2014 described a total lack of genitalia, no gonads, intersex formation of the external genitalia, a rudimentary vagina, a micropenis, hypospadias, gonadal agenesis, and hypogonadism. Although he had a male XY karyotype, doctors found that male surgery would have been impossible and that his external genitalia retained both female and male aspects.

The applicant also described himself as psychologically and socially intersex. He said he had always maintained an intersex identity, neither male nor female, and had never regarded himself as anything other than intersex. A psychotherapist reported that he suffered from having to pretend to be a man, had no legal identity corresponding to his reality, and experienced exclusion because his community did not legally exist in France. He was married and had an adopted child. He also stated that, after being administratively assigned the male sex, he was prescribed testosterone treatment at around age 40, which changed his appearance and which he experienced as a violation of his bodily integrity and privacy.

The alleged violation arose from the refusal of French authorities to replace the “male” sex marker on his birth certificate with “neutral” or, failing that, “intersex.” In 2015, the President of the Tours tribunal de grande instance granted his request, holding that his sex could not be defined and that the male marker was fictitious. The Orléans Court of Appeal reversed that decision in 2016, finding that although he had a variation in sex development, his physical appearance and social behaviour were male; it also held that recognizing a third sex marker was a matter for the legislature. In 2017, the Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal, holding that French law permits only male or female markers, that the binary system pursued a legitimate aim, and that recognizing a neutral sex would have far-reaching legal consequences.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 8 that the refusal violated his right to respect for private life, because the discordance between his biological and legal identities caused suffering and anxiety. The Court noted that there was no European consensus on legal recognition of intersex people or on non-binary sex markers. It emphasized the wide margin of appreciation afforded to states in this sensitive area and the importance of public-interest considerations, including the structure of civil status and family law. The Court concluded that France had not exceeded its margin of appreciation in refusing to insert “neutral” or “intersex” on the birth certificate. It found no violation of Article 8, while stressing that states must keep the situation of intersex people under review and determine at what speed and to what extent to meet their civil-status demands.

**Case: Y v. France (Application no. 76888/17), ECtHR, 31 January 2023**

In *Y v. France*, the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) examined whether France violated Article 8 of the Convention by refusing to replace the “male” sex marker on an intersex applicant’s birth certificate with “neutral” or “intersex.” The applicant, born in 1951 and living in Strasbourg, was registered as male at birth but states that he is biologically, psychologically and socially intersex.

The key facts concern his intersex status. Medical certificates from 1970, 1973 and 2014 showed that he had ambiguous sex characteristics, no gonads or sex hormone production, atypical external genitalia—including a rudimentary vagina and micropenis—and hypogonadism with pubertal failure. Although raised as a boy, he never developed typical male or female secondary sex characteristics. At age 21 he was perceived socially as female, and later, after being administratively assigned the male sex, he was prescribed testosterone treatment that altered his appearance but did not resolve his ambiguous genitalia. He described this forced change as a violation of bodily integrity and a trauma. He also maintained an intersex identity, saying he was neither male nor female, and reported suffering, anxiety and exclusion because his legal sex did not match his biological and lived reality. He is married and has an adopted child.

In 2015, the applicant asked the Tours tribunal de grande instance to change his birth certificate from “male” to “neutral,” or alternatively “intersex.” The tribunal granted the request, accepting that his assigned male sex was fictitious and that Article 8 required respect for his identity. However, the Orléans Court of Appeal reversed the decision in 2016. It found that his physical appearance and social behaviour were male, that his request contradicted those facts, and that French law did not allow any sex marker other than male or female. Recognizing a third category, it said, was a matter for the legislature. In 2017, the Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal, holding that the binary sex marker system pursued a legitimate aim and was a cornerstone of French social and legal arrangements. A neutral marker would have far-reaching legal consequences, and the interference was not disproportionate.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained that the refusal violated his right to respect for private life under Article 8. The Court considered France’s positive obligations, including the protection of gender identity, and acknowledged that the discordance between his biological and legal identities caused suffering and anxiety. Nevertheless, it found no European consensus on how States should address intersex people’s civil-status demands. This lack of consensus widened France’s margin of appreciation. The Court stressed the importance of public-interest considerations in maintaining civil-status rules and held that the choice of society on whether and how quickly to recognize additional sex markers was left to the respondent State. Given the difficult situation of intersex people, France was entitled to determine the speed and extent of any reform. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 8. The judgment became final on 26 June 2023.

**Grima and Others v. Malta** (Application no. 18057/20) is a European Court of Human Rights case brought by eight Maltese nationals from the Grima and Parnis England families. The applicants jointly own a property at no. 35 Dingli Street, Sliema. The property was occupied by a tenant under a lease regime preserved by Act XXIII of 1979, which amended Chapter 158 of Maltese law (“the Ordinance”). Under Article 12(7) of the Ordinance, the tenant was able to remain in occupation under a lease. The rent paid was controlled and far below market levels: in March 1979 it was approximately €466 annually, increasing to €685 in 1994, €741 in 2009, €803 in 2013, and €819 in 2016.

A court-appointed expert assessed the annual market rental value as follows: €1,398 in 1977; €1,677 in 1982; €2,516 in 1987; €3,075 in 1992; €4,193 in 1997; €5,590 in 2002; €6,150 in 2007; €6,709 in 2012; and €7,268 in 2017. The rent actually received was therefore only a small fraction of the property’s market rental value. This disparity formed the core factual basis for the applicants’ complaint that the statutory lease regime imposed a disproportionate burden on their property rights.

The ownership history was complex. The Grima family’s predecessor in title acquired a half undivided share of the property in 1982, aware that it had been occupied under a temporary emphyteusis since 1960 for seventeen years, renewable once. That share belonged to him and his wife, the applicant Georgina Grima. His share was inherited *ab intestato* in 2015 by three applicants, Doreen, Georgina and Joseph Grima, in different shares. As a result, Georgina Grima now owns three-eighths of the undivided share of the entire property, while the siblings jointly own one-eighth. On the Parnis England side, the bare ownership of the other half undivided share vested in the siblings Nicholas, Robin and Stephen Parnis England and Johanna Petreski in 2004, as universal heirs of their father. Their mother, Margaret Parnis England, has a usufruct over the property following her husband’s death in 2004.

In 2019 the applicants lodged constitutional redress proceedings, complaining that they had suffered a breach of their property rights and requesting compensation for the period from 1977 to 2017. By judgment of 21 October 2019, the Civil Court (First Hall), in its constitutional competence, found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention and awarded €20,000 in compensation. However, despite contrary domestic case law (*Ian Peter Ellis v Maggur Cassar Reynaud*, Constitutional Court, 27 January 2017), the court considered that the applicants’ ancestors had never complained about the situation and that the applicants could not benefit financially from their predecessors’ passivity. It therefore held that compensation was due only from the dates when the applicants inherited the property: 2015 for the Grima family and 2004 for the Parnis England family.

The applicants then complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 alone and in conjunction with Article 13 of the Convention. They alleged that they remained victims of the violation already upheld domestically because the compensation awarded was too low and because the tenants had not been evicted. The Court gave notice of the complaints concerning the effects of Act XXIII of 1979 and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The key alleged violations thus concerned the ongoing disproportionate interference with the applicants’ property rights and the absence of adequate compensation or an effective remedy.

**Beltsios v. Greece (Application no. 57333/14)** concerns two alleged violations of the European Convention on Human Rights: the presumption of innocence under **Article 6 § 2** and the right to a “speedy” review of pre-trial detention under **Article 5 § 4**. The applicant, Ioannis Beltsios, a Greek national born in 1951, lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 29 July 2014.

The case arose from large-scale submarine procurement and repair contracts. In 2000, Hellenic Shipyards signed a contract with German consortium H.-F. for submarines worth over EUR 1.3 billion; in 2002, another contract for submarine repairs exceeded EUR 820 million. After German authorities investigated corruption, Greek criminal proceedings were opened on 30 October 2010 against 41 persons, including the applicant. In 2011, following a preliminary investigation, proceedings were instituted against Beltsios and others. He was accused of unlawfully assisting the German company to obtain the submarine contracts by promising and transferring money to former Defence Minister A.T. and top managers of Hellenic Shipyards. He was also accused of concealing the origin of over EUR 52 million and CHF 2.9 million, and of receiving and transferring those sums as proceeds of corruption.

On 29 September 2011 the criminal file was transferred to an Investigating Judge. The applicant was placed in preliminary detention on 13 January 2014, confirmed on 18 January 2014. On 23 January 2014 he lodged a recourse against the pre-trial detention, seeking replacement by other preventive measures. The prosecutor submitted a proposal to dismiss the recourse on 7 April 2014. The Indictment Division of the Athens Criminal Court of First Instance met on 27 May 2014 and, by order no. 1821/2014 published on 6 June 2014, rejected his recourse. On 10 July 2014, by order no. 2369/2014, his detention was extended for six months, until 13 January 2015. He remained detained until 27 March 2015, when his detention was replaced by preventive measures in connection with his referral to trial. These facts formed the basis of his Article 5 § 4 complaint that the authorities failed to decide “speedily” on his release application.

The Article 6 § 2 complaint concerned separate criminal proceedings against former Minister A.T. and eighteen co-accused, in which the applicant was not a defendant. On 7 October 2013, the three-member Athens Criminal Court convicted A.T. as charged. In its judgment, the court referred to the applicant as a member of a team used by German company F., a close associate and friend of A.T., and a former General Secretary at the Ministry of Interior. It stated that he had received bribe payments on behalf of A.T., had entered consulting contracts with company F. that concealed illegal transactions, and had received other bribes for A.T. The applicant later argued that these findings violated his presumption of innocence because they accepted his guilt before his own trial.

On 23 January 2019, the Athens Criminal Court convicted the applicant of aiding and abetting passive bribery of A.T. involving EUR 1,000,000, sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment, and rejected his objection of nullity based on the alleged breach of the presumption of innocence. He was acquitted of active bribery and money laundering. In 2021, the five-member Athens Court of Appeal allowed his appeal and held that the limitation period had expired, meaning he could no longer be prosecuted. The ECtHR examined whether the statements in the A.T. judgment and the delay in reviewing his detention violated Article 6 § 2 and Article 5 § 4 respectively.

Greece* (Application no. 57333/14, ECtHR, 28 November 2023), the applicant, Ioannis Beltsios, a Greek national, complained of violations of Article 6 § 2 (presumption of innocence) and Article 5 § 4 (speedy review of detention) of the Convention. Case Zammit and Busuttil v. Malta (Application no. 55102/20) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) in a judgment dated 12 September 2023. The applicants were Joseph Zammit and Anna Busuttil, two Maltese nationals born in 1944 and 1956 respectively, both living in Paola. The lease affected the applicants’ property as of 17 December 2007. At that time, the annual rent payable was EUR 291. In 2013, it increased to EUR 335 and would increase every three years thereafter.

A court-appointed expert later assessed the property’s annual market rental value as EUR 2,100 for the years 2007–2012 and EUR 5,800 for 2013–2018. Those figures were substantially higher than the controlled rent actually paid under the statutory lease.

On 27 September 2019, the applicants lodged constitutional redress proceedings. They complained that the application of Article 12(2) of the Ordinance breached their property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. They limited their claims to the period ending 31 December 2018, without prejudice to any future action challenging the 2018 amendments that introduced the new Article 12B. By judgment of 17 June 2020, the Civil Court (First Hall) in its constitutional competence found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 resulting from the application of the law until 2018. It awarded the applicants EUR 15,000 in compensation. The court noted that the applicants had limited their claims to December 2018 and considered that they had a new remedy to pursue in light of the 2018 amendments for the future. No costs were imposed on the applicants. Neither party appealed.

In the meantime, on 3 July 2019, the parties reached an agreement whereby the tenants would pay EUR 2,400 annually in light of the 2018 amendments. That agreement would come to an end when the tenants died.

They complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 alone and in conjunction with Article 13 of the Convention. They also invoked Article 13, arguing that the available domestic remedies had not provided adequate redress for the past violation of their property rights.

A court-appointed expert assessed the property’s annual market rental value at EUR 2,100 for 2007–2012 and EUR 5,800 for 2013–2018. The wide gap between controlled rent and market value was central to the alleged violation of property rights.

It noted that the applicants had limited their claims to December 2018 and considered that they had a new remedy under the 2018 amendments for the future. No costs were ordered against the applicants. Neither party appealed.

In the meantime, on 3 July 2019, the parties reached an agreement under the 2018 amendments. The tenants would pay EUR 2,400 annually, and the agreement would end when the tenants died. This agreement concerned the future and did not resolve the applicants’ complaint about the past period.

They complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 alone and in conjunction with Article 13 that they remained victims of the violation upheld by the domestic court because the compensation awarded was too low. Thus, the rent actually received by the applicants was substantially lower than what the property could have earned on the open market. This disparity formed the core of their complaint that the lease regime imposed a disproportionate burden on them as property owners.

On 27 September 2019, the applicants brought constitutional redress proceedings in Malta. They complained that the application of Article 12(2) of the Ordinance violated their property rights. Importantly, they limited their claims to the period until 31 December 2018, without prejudice to any future challenge to the 2018 amendments that introduced a new Article 12B. By judgment of 17 June 2020, the Civil Court (First Hall) in its constitutional competence found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 on account of the application of the law until 2018. It awarded EUR 15,000 in compensation. The court noted that the applicants had limited their claims to December 2018 and considered that they had a new remedy to pursue, in light of the 2018 amendments, for the future. No costs were ordered against the applicants. Neither party appealed.

In the meantime, on 3 July 2019, the parties reached an agreement under the 2018 amendments. Under that agreement, the tenants were to pay EUR 2,400 annually, and the agreement would come to an end when the tenants died.

The applicants then lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 11 December 2020. They complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 alone and in conjunction with Article 13 of the Convention that they remained victims of the violation already upheld by the domestic court. Their central allegation was that the compensation awarded—EUR 15,000—was too low to remedy the losses caused by the long period of below-market rent. They argued that the domestic finding of a violation had not provided adequate redress, so they continued to suffer the effects of the unlawful property interference. Article 13 was invoked because they alleged they lacked an effective remedy for that inadequate compensation.

The Court gave notice of the complaints concerning the effects of Act XXIII of 1979 under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 alone and in conjunction with Article 13, and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore: the unilateral lease, the statutorily controlled rent, the large discrepancy between actual and market rental values, the domestic court’s finding of a violation and award of EUR 15,000, the applicants’ limitation of claims to the period ending 31 December 2018, and the subsequent 2019 agreement under the 2018 amendments.

In *Pleshkov and Pleshkova v. Ukraine* (App. no. 5783/20, judgment of 9 March 2023), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) examined a complaint under Article 8 of the Convention concerning Ukraine’s failure to enforce domestic contact arrangements between a father and his daughter.

The applicants were Dmytro Pleshkov, born in 1974, and his daughter Alisa Pleshkova, born in 2011. They lived separately; the daughter lived with her mother, L. A judgment of the Dniprovskyi District Court of Kyiv of 24 October 2016, amended by the Kyiv Court of Appeal on 21 February 2017, set out contact arrangements between the applicants. L failed to comply with those arrangements.

Enforcement proceedings began in September 2018 and were still ongoing. Bailiffs imposed two fines on L, which she did not pay, and temporarily suspended her driving licence. Because L repeatedly failed to respond to summonses, the bailiffs unsuccessfully sought the initiation of criminal proceedings against her and a temporary ban on her leaving the country. On 10 November 2018, during the only meeting the bailiffs organised between the applicants in L’s presence, the daughter refused to communicate with her father because she was afraid of him. A psychological examination of the child on 26 June 2019, ordered by the bailiffs, concluded that her negative attitude toward her father was linked to the conflict between him and L. The psychologist stated that improving the father’s relationship with L was a precondition for re-establishing “psychological contact” between the applicants. The Government claimed that local child welfare services had been involved, but provided no further details.

The first applicant complained, on his own behalf and on behalf of the second applicant, that the 2016 judgment had not been enforced. He relied on Articles 8 and 46, arguing that the issue revealed structural and systemic deficiencies in the domestic legal system. The Government objected that the first applicant had abused his right of application by omitting relevant facts and that he was responsible for the lack of contact because he had failed to cooperate peacefully with L and had prematurely involved the police and bailiffs. It also argued that the bailiffs had acted reasonably given the animosity between the parents and that the father could have sought custody.

The Court examined the complaint solely under Article 8. It rejected the Government’s abuse objection, finding no indication that the first applicant had intended to mislead the Court. It declared the complaint admissible.

On the merits, the Court recalled that States have positive obligations to protect parent-child relationships. In previous cases against Ukraine, it had found that child-contact judgments were often poorly implemented because of a lack of developed legislative and administrative frameworks for voluntary compliance involving family and child welfare professionals, and because there were no appropriate, specific coercive measures subject to proportionality. The Court found those deficiencies relevant in this case.

Although it was promptly established, and later confirmed by a psychologist, that the child was unwilling to communicate with her father and appeared seriously alienated from him, the authorities took no further measures to assist her adaptation. In particular, no targeted professional support helped her become used to communicating with the first applicant or helped L understand that contact was in the child’s best interests under the binding judgment. The nature and extent of child welfare services’ involvement remained unclear. The authorities knew that L was obstructing contact, but the limited coercive measures imposed on her produced no results. While acknowledging the difficult strained relationship between the parents, the Court held that Ukraine had failed its positive obligation under Article 8 to enforce the contact arrangements. The first applicant could not be reproached for not applying for custody.

The Court awarded the applicants jointly EUR 4,500 for non-pecuniary damage and EUR 1,000 to the first applicant for costs and expenses, plus default interest.

**Summary of Pleshkov and Pleshkova v. Ukraine (Application no. 5783/20)**

The case of *Pleshkov and Pleshkova v. Ukraine* concerns the failure of Ukrainian authorities to enforce a court-ordered contact arrangement between a father and his daughter, in violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to respect for family life.

The applicants are Mr. Dmytro Pleshkov (the first applicant, born 1974) and his daughter, Ms. Alisa Pleshkova (the second applicant, born 2011). The first applicant and the second applicant’s mother, identified as “L,” were living separately. A judgment by the Dniprovskyi District Court of Kyiv on 24 October 2016, later amended by the Kyiv Court of Appeal on 21 February 2017, established a schedule for contact between the first and second applicants.

The central factual issue is that L. consistently failed to comply with this binding court order, obstructing contact between the applicants. To enforce the judgment, bailiffs initiated proceedings in September 2018, which remained ongoing. The coercive measures imposed on L. proved ineffective. The bailiffs fined her twice, but she did not pay. They also ordered a temporary suspension of her driving licence. Furthermore, because L. repeatedly ignored summons, the bailiffs unsuccessfully sought to initiate criminal proceedings against her and to impose a temporary travel ban.

A critical event occurred on 10 November 2018, during the only meeting the bailiffs managed to organise between the applicants. The second applicant, who was seven years old at the time, refused to communicate with her father, stating she was afraid of him. Subsequently, a psychological examination of the second applicant, ordered by the bailiffs and completed on 26 June 2019, concluded that her negative attitude toward the first applicant was linked to the conflict between him and L. The psychologist indicated that improving the relationship between the parents was a precondition for re-establishing psychological contact between the applicants.

In its assessment, the European Court of Human Rights noted that the Government’s objections, including claims that the first applicant had failed to cooperate peacefully, were unfounded. The Court focused on the State’s positive obligation to enforce contact arrangements, referencing its established case law against Ukraine which has repeatedly identified a systemic failure in this area. The domestic framework lacks effective measures to facilitate voluntary compliance or to coercively enforce judgments involving children.

The Court found that although the authorities were aware of the mother’s obstruction and the child’s alienation from her father, they took no effective measures to address the situation. The limited coercive measures against L. produced no results. Crucially, no professional, targeted support was provided to help the child adapt to the idea of communicating with her father or to help L. understand that compliance was in the child’s best interests. The involvement of child welfare services was unclear and insufficient.

Consequently, the Court unanimously found a violation of Article 8, concluding that the Ukrainian authorities failed to fulfil their positive obligation to enforce the applicants’ contact arrangements. The Court awarded the applicants jointly €4,500 for non-pecuniary damage and €1,000 to the first applicant for costs and expenses.

**Summary of the Case of Pleshkov and Pleshkova v. Ukraine**

Ukraine* (Application no. 5783/20) concerns the failure of Ukrainian authorities to enforce a court-ordered contact arrangement between a father (the first applicant, Mr. Dmytro Pleshkov) and his daughter (the second applicant, Ms. Alisa Pleshkova), who were living separately. The applicants alleged a violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to respect for private and family life.

The core facts are as follows: On 24 October 2016, the Dniprovskyi District Court of Kyiv issued a judgment, later amended by the Kyiv Court of Appeal on 21 February 2017, setting out specific contact arrangements between the first and second applicants. The second applicant lived with her mother, "L," who consistently failed to comply with these arrangements. This non-compliance triggered enforcement proceedings in September 2018, which remained ongoing at the time of the European Court's judgment.

In response to the mother's obstruction, the bailiffs took several coercive measures. They imposed two fines on L., which she did not pay, and temporarily suspended her driving licence. They also unsuccessfully sought to initiate criminal proceedings against her and impose a temporary travel ban due to her repeated failure to respond to their summons. A critical event occurred on 10 November 2018, during the only meeting the bailiffs managed to organize between the applicants. The second applicant refused to communicate with her father, stating she was afraid of him.

This refusal prompted the bailiffs to order a psychological examination of the child on 26 June 2019. The resulting report concluded that the second applicant's negative attitude towards her father was linked to the conflict between him and her mother. The psychologist emphasized that improving the relationship between the first applicant and L. was a precondition for re-establishing "psychological contact" between the applicants. While the government claimed that local child welfare services were involved, they provided no details on the nature or extent of this involvement.

In its assessment, the European Court noted that the first applicant complained about the non-enforcement of the 2016 judgment, arguing it revealed a systemic problem. The government countered that the first applicant had abused his right of application and was responsible for the lack of contact by failing to cooperate peacefully with L.

The Court dismissed the government's objection of abuse, finding no evidence of an intent to mislead. It then focused on the state's positive obligations under Article 8. The Court reiterated its established case law against Ukraine, which found that the inappropriate implementation of child contact judgments resulted from a lack of a developed legal and administrative framework. Such a framework should facilitate voluntary compliance with the help of family and child welfare professionals and provide for a proportionate range of coercive measures.

The Court found these systemic deficiencies present in this case. Although it was clear the child was unwilling to see her father due to alienation, the authorities took no further steps to help her adapt or to provide professional support to change her attitude, or to help her mother understand the child's best interests as determined by the binding court judgment. The coercive measures against the mother were ultimately ineffective. Consequently, the Court concluded that the Ukrainian authorities failed to fulfil their positive obligation under Article 8 to enforce the contact arrangements, finding a violation. The applicants were awarded EUR 4,500 in non-pecuniary damages and EUR 1,000 in costs.

The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) delivered judgment on 11 May 2023 in *Sharashkin and Others v. Russia* (applications nos. 57223/19 and 21 others). The applications, lodged under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates, were joined because they raised similar complaints. The Russian Government were given notice. The Court noted that the facts predated 16 September 2022, when Russia ceased to be a party to the Convention, and held that it still had jurisdiction under *Fedotova and Others v. Russia*.

Although the judgment refers to an appended table for each applicant’s details, the core facts concern public assemblies in Russia. The applicants were organisers and/or participants in these assemblies. The authorities took measures that the applicants described as disproportionate: dispersal of the assemblies, arrest, and subsequent conviction for an administrative offence. They complained principally that these measures violated their freedom of assembly under Article 11. Some also invoked Article 10, but the Court examined those complaints under Article 11.

The Court applied established case-law on freedom of assembly, including *Kudrevičius and Others v. Lithuania*, *Oya Ataman v. Turkey*, and *Hyde Park and Others v. Moldova*. It noted that in *Frumkin v. Russia*, *Navalnyy and Yashin v. Russia*, and *Kasparov and Others v. Russia* it had already found violations for similar issues. After examining the material, the Court found no fact or argument justifying a different conclusion. It held that the interferences with the applicants’ freedom of assembly—dispersal, arrest, and administrative conviction—were not “necessary in a democratic society.” Accordingly, it found a violation of Article 11.

The applicants also raised other complaints covered by well-established case-law. These concerned various aspects of unlawful deprivation of liberty of organisers or participants of public events, relying on *Butkevich v. Russia*, *Kalyapin v. Russia*, and *Korneyeva v. Russia*. They further complained about the examination of administrative-offence cases in the absence of a prosecuting party, contrary to *Karelin v. Russia*. The Court declared these complaints admissible and found violations in light of that settled case-law. Some applicants also raised additional Article 5 and 6 complaints about other aspects of detention and fairness of administrative proceedings. Because the Court had already found violations on the principal and related issues, it did not need to deal separately with those remaining complaints.

Finally, in applications nos. 57223/19, 6752/20, 10914/20, and 24997/20, the applicants raised further complaints under various Convention provisions. The Court examined them but found that they either did not meet the admissibility criteria under Articles 34 and 35 or disclosed no appearance of a violation. Those parts were rejected under Article 35 § 4.

Overall, the judgment is a repetitive case applying settled Russian assembly and administrative-justice case-law: the Russian authorities’ dispersal, arrest, and administrative punishment of public-assembly organisers and participants violated Article 11, and related detention and administrative-procedure defects also violated the Convention. **Case: Camara v. Belgium (Application no. 49255/22), European Court of Human Rights, Second Section, judgment 18 July 2023 (final 18 October 2023).**

The applicant, Abdoulaye Camara, a Guinean national born in 2001, arrived in Belgium on 12 July 2022 and applied for international protection on 15 July 2022. Under Belgium’s Reception Act, asylum-seekers are entitled to material support and accommodation from Fedasil, the federal reception agency. When Camara went to Fedasil, he was told the reception network was saturated and no place was available. He alleged that from 15 July to 4 November 2022—112 days—he lived on the streets of Brussels, sleeping in railway stations, parks, or on cardboard and makeshift mattresses. He relied on charity meals, had limited access to showers and toilets, often went hungry, suffered cold and rain, and had documents stolen. He said he had no support network in Belgium.

On 19 July 2022 his lawyer demanded accommodation from Fedasil. On 20 July he applied ex parte to the Brussels French-Language Employment Tribunal, alleging imminent serious and irreparable harm to his human dignity. On 22 July 2022 the tribunal ordered Fedasil to provide accommodation—in a reception centre, hotel, or other suitable establishment if necessary—and material support under the Reception Act, with a coercive fine of EUR 1,000 for each night spent outside the reception network or emergency accommodation. The order was immediately enforceable and not conditional on merits proceedings. Fedasil was notified on 29 July, did not lodge a third-party appeal, and the decision became final on 29 August 2022. It was not enforced.

The applicant served enforcement notices in October 2022. On 20 October he applied to the European Court of Human Rights for an interim measure under Rule 39. On 31 October the Court indicated to Belgium that he should be provided with accommodation and material support. On 3–4 November Fedasil assigned him to a Red Cross centre; he later moved to a Samusocial centre. He complained under Article 3 that he had been forced to live in inhuman and degrading conditions; under Article 6 § 1 that the final Employment Tribunal decision had not been enforced; and under Article 8 read with Article 13 that his private life and right to an effective remedy had been breached.

The Court focused on Article 6 § 1. It found the complaint admissible and Article 6 applicable: the applicant had a civil right to accommodation and material support, recognised by the Employment Tribunal; the decision was immediately enforceable and aimed to secure the same right as merits proceedings. The Court found that Belgium’s failure to enforce the tribunal’s final, enforceable decision impaired the essence of the applicant’s right to a court. It noted the State’s difficult situation due to increased asylum applications and insufficient reception capacity, but held that this did not justify non-enforcement. It also observed a systemic failure: thousands of similar orders remained unenforced, overburdening domestic courts and the ECtHR. Under Article 46, Belgium was required to address the systemic problem affecting its ability to comply with domestic law and final court decisions on asylum-seekers’ accommodation. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1 and required general measures.

Under Belgium’s Reception Act, asylum-seekers are entitled to material support and accommodation from the time they file their application. On 20 July 2022 the applicant applied ex parte to the Brussels French-Language Employment Tribunal. On 22 July 2022 the tribunal ordered Fedasil to provide him with accommodation—in a reception centre, hotel, or other appropriate establishment if necessary—and material support under the Reception Act, on pain of a €1,000 fine for each night spent outside the reception network. The decision was expressly immediately enforceable and remained so until the end of the asylum proceedings; it was not conditional on any proceedings on the merits. Fedasil was notified on 29 July and did not lodge a third-party appeal, so the decision became final on 29 August 2022. Nonetheless, Fedasil failed to enforce it. After a final notice in October, the applicant applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 20 October 2022. On 31 October the Court indicated an interim measure under Rule 39 requiring Belgium to provide accommodation and basic support. Fedasil then assigned him a place on 4 November 2022. Thus, he was accommodated only after the Strasbourg Court intervened.

The applicant complained under Articles 3, 6 § 1, 8 and 13 of the Convention. The Court focused on the Article 6 complaint that the immediately enforceable domestic decision had not been enforced. The parties agreed that Article 6 was applicable and that the right to accommodation and material support was civil in character. The Court found Article 6 applicable because the Employment Tribunal’s decision determined the same civil right as would be at stake on the merits and was immediately enforceable, even though no merits proceedings had been brought. The complaint was admissible.

The broader context was a systemic failure in Belgium’s reception system. The network had been saturated since September 2021. Fedasil maintained waiting lists for non-vulnerable single men and increasingly prioritized only those with court decisions or Rule 39 interim measures. By March 2023 more than 7,000 similar orders had been issued, Fedasil almost never appealed, and fines remained unpaid, heavily burdening the domestic courts and the ECtHR. The Government attributed the situation to a surge in asylum applications, insufficient reception capacity, Ukrainian arrivals, floods, staffing shortages and local resistance.

The Court accepted the difficult context but held that the refusal or failure to enforce an immediately enforceable judicial decision impaired the very essence of the right to a court. It found a violation of Article 6 § 1. Under Article 46, Belgium was required to adopt general measures to address the systemic problem affecting its ability to comply with domestic law and final court decisions on accommodation for asylum-seekers.

The judgment focuses on Article 6 § 1, concerning the right to a court and the failure to enforce a final, immediately enforceable domestic decision. The Court found Article 6 applicable: Belgian law gave asylum seekers a right to material support and accommodation; the Employment Tribunal had recognised the applicant’s right; the right was civil in character; and the decision was immediately enforceable and aimed to determine the same right as on the merits.

Belgium argued that non-enforcement was due to increased asylum applications, insufficient reception capacity, logistical and staff shortages, local-authority resistance, and other pressures. In *El-Asmar v. Denmark*, the applicant was a Danish national detained on remand at Enner Mark Prison in March 2017. His admission records noted possible dangerousness and aggressive behaviour, including threats and attempts to fight staff. Between 30 March and 3 April 2017, he was repeatedly placed in observation or security cells because of aggressive and threatening conduct. On 3 April he attempted to attack a guard with a pencil and later tried to kick guards when they entered his cell; he was restrained and placed in a security cell.

The key incident occurred on 4 April 2017, while the applicant was in an observation cell. The prison journal recorded that he threatened to kill officers if not given a television and cigarettes, shouted insults, threw food at the window, urinated under the door, destroyed his mattress, kicked the door, and shouted that he would kill staff. At about 4:20 p.m., guards D1 and M1 entered the cell. The official account stated that the applicant rushed at D1 and tried to punch him, so both guards used pepper spray. The guards said he remained agitated and resisted being moved to the security cell. The applicant disputed this: he claimed he had already surrendered and was passive, but the guards sprayed him in the face and back, causing him to faint briefly, before four guards dragged him to the security cell.

There was no video surveillance in the observation cell, security cell, or corridor. The prison doctor was contacted shortly after the spraying and reportedly said that if the applicant had only been exposed to pepper spray, there was no need to attend, though he asked to be updated. Later, the guard reported that the applicant appeared unharmed but agitated. The applicant refused examination by a prison doctor, considering them biased; he also later refused a police-requested medical examination.

The applicant reported the guards to the police for aggravated violence and separately complained to the Department of Prisons and Probation. The prison authorities and the Department found the use of pepper spray justified under the Sentence Enforcement Act as necessary to avert imminent violence and considered it gentler than manual force. They accepted that no warning had been given but found a warning was not possible due to the intensity of the attack. The police investigation interviewed the applicant in November 2017 and the two guards in January 2018. Finding contradictory accounts, no video evidence, no other witnesses, and no medical evidence, the police discontinued criminal proceedings in January 2018. The Regional Prosecutor upheld that decision.

In a separate procedural complaint, the police Management Secretariat acknowledged a seven-month delay as excessive and regrettable but found the investigation overall effective. It noted the lack of video, the applicant’s refusal of a medical report, and no other identifiable evidence. The Regional Prosecutor upheld that assessment.

The Court declared the complaint admissible, rejecting Denmark’s argument that he should have pursued a constitutional claim. El-Asmar v. Denmark (App no. 27753/19) is a European Court of Human Rights case (Fourth Section, judgment 3 October 2023; final 3 January 2024). D1 pushed him back, and D1 and M1 deployed pepper spray. The applicant alleged, by contrast, that he had been passive and had surrendered, yet both officers sprayed him in the face and on his back, causing him to faint; he was then dragged to the security cell. The officers denied that he fainted and said he remained abusive. There was no video surveillance in the observation cell, security cell or corridor, and no other witnesses. A separate complaint to the prison authorities was also rejected: the local prison and the Department of Prisons and Probation found the pepper spray justified under the Sentence Enforcement Act, accepting that the applicant was extremely violent, attacked staff, and that pepper spray was gentler than manual force and no warning was possible. The police Management Secretariat found a seven-month investigation delay excessive but overall effective; the Regional Prosecutor upheld.

The Court declared the application admissible and found a violation of Article 3 under both its substantive and procedural limbs. In *El-Asmar v. Denmark*, the European Court of Human Rights examined the use of pepper spray against a prisoner and the subsequent investigation. On 31 March he threatened to kill a guard; on 1 April he smeared toothpaste on his window and threatened a guard; on 2 April he threatened two guards; and on 3 April he attacked a guard with a pencil and clenched fist, requiring several officers to restrain him.

Prison records state that he shouted threats, threw food at the window, urinated under the door, destroyed his mattress, kicked the door, and shouted that he would kill staff. Four guards opened the cell door. The precise facts were disputed. Guards D1 and M1 said the applicant rushed at D1 and tried to punch him in the head, so pepper spray was used to avert imminent violence; no warning was given because of the intensity of the attack. The applicant claimed he was passive and had surrendered, but both guards sprayed him in the face and back, causing him to faint, before he was dragged to a security cell. There was no video surveillance in the observation cell, security cell, or corridor. A prison doctor was contacted at 4:27 p.m. and reportedly said no attendance was needed if only pepper spray had been used; later the applicant was reported unharmed but agitated. The prison authorities and the Department of Prisons and Probation found the force justified and the lack of warning unavoidable.

The applicant reported D1 and M1 to the police for aggravated violence. In the criminal investigation, the applicant refused examination by a prison doctor. He was interviewed in November 2017, the guards in January 2018. The applicant also complained that the investigation was ineffective: it was protracted, interviews were delayed, corridor video was not secured, and he was not examined by an independent doctor. The Court declared the application admissible, finding that such civil or damages proceedings were not effective remedies for substantive Article 3 complaints and could not review prosecution decisions.

The Court found that the authorities failed to demonstrate the deployment was made strictly necessary by the applicant’s conduct, particularly given the confined observation cell and absence of prior warning. It also found the investigation ineffective. The Court therefore found violations of both the substantive and procedural aspects of Article 3.

In *Bellotto and Others v. Italy* (Applications nos. 5170/21 and four others), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section, sitting as a Committee) delivered judgment on 16 November 2023. The applicants, represented by Mr N. Zampieri, lodged applications against Italy under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates. The Italian Government were given notice of the applications. Because the applications raised the same subject matter, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment.

The key facts concerned the applicants’ pending domestic proceedings against Italian administrative authorities. While those proceedings were still pending, Italy enacted section 1(218) of Law no. 266/2005 of 23 December 2005. That provision was applied retrospectively to pending cases. According to the applicants, this retrospective application settled the merits of their disputes with the administrative authorities with final effect. In practice, it meant that the domestic courts could no longer determine the disputes in the ordinary way, and the applicants were deprived of the possibility of obtaining a favourable judicial outcome. The applicants therefore complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the retrospective application infringed their right to a fair hearing. They also complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the retrospective nature of the provision deprived them of their property, because it definitively resolved their disputes with the State authorities.

The Court reiterated its established case-law on retrospective legislative interference in civil disputes. Although the legislature is not, in principle, prevented from regulating rights through new retrospective provisions, the rule of law and the notion of a fair trial under Article 6 preclude any interference by the legislature with the administration of justice designed to influence the judicial determination of a dispute, unless there are compelling grounds of the general interest. The Court emphasised that such dangers are particularly serious when the State is a party to the dispute and the retrospective legislation makes pending litigation unwinnable. In those circumstances, any reasons advanced to justify the measure must be treated with the greatest possible degree of circumspection, as stated in *Vegotex International S.A. v. Belgium*.

The Court referred to its earlier judgments concerning the same provision, including *Agrati and Others v. Italy*, *De Rosa and Others v. Italy*, *Caligiuri and Others v. Italy*, and *Cicero and Others v. Italy*. Having regard to that case-law and the documents submitted by the applicants, the Court saw no reason to reach a different conclusion on the admissibility of the complaints. On the merits, it found that section 1(218) of Law no. 266/2005 had resolved the merits of the dispute between the applicants and the State in the domestic courts with final retrospective effect. The legislature’s intervention was not justified by any compelling grounds of the general interest.

The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The case illustrates the Court’s consistent position that retrospective legislation which settles pending disputes involving the State, and thereby removes the possibility of a fair judicial determination, violates fair-trial and property rights. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.
