CASE OF SEMENYA v. SWITZERLAND (Application no. 10934/21) concerns Caster Semenya, a South African professional middle-distance runner with differences of sex development (DSD). Semenya was raised and competes as a woman. World Athletics’ Eligibility Regulations for the Female Classification (“DSD Regulations”) required female athletes with certain DSD conditions and naturally elevated testosterone to lower their natural testosterone, ordinarily through medication, to be eligible for international women’s competitions. She challenged these rules, arguing they discriminated on grounds of sex and sex characteristics and forced her to choose between unwanted medical treatment and exclusion from her profession.

The regulations were enforced through compulsory arbitration before the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS). In an award of 30 April 2019, CAS upheld the DSD Regulations, despite recognising discriminatory effects. Semenya then appealed to the Swiss Federal Supreme Court, which dismissed her appeal on 25 August 2020. Its review was very limited, essentially confined to whether the CAS award violated Swiss public policy. It did not conduct a full examination of her discrimination complaint under the European Convention on Human Rights.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Semenya alleged violations of Articles 8 (private life), 14 (non-discrimination), 3 (inhuman or degrading treatment), 13 (effective remedy), and 6 §1 (fair hearing). The central claim was discrimination under Article 14 read with Article 8: the DSD Regulations treated her differently from other female athletes by excluding her from the women’s category unless she altered her natural testosterone level. She also complained that compulsory CAS arbitration and the Swiss Federal Supreme Court’s highly limited review denied her an effective remedy and a fair hearing before an ordinary court.

The Third Section found a violation of Article 14 in conjunction with Article 8. Article 14 was applicable because the regulations interfered with her private life and right to practise her profession. She was in a comparable situation to other female athletes, but was treated differently because the DSD Regulations excluded her from competition. Discrimination on grounds of sex and sex characteristics requires “weighty reasons.” The Court found that CAS, although detailed in its reasoning, did not apply Convention provisions and left serious questions open about the validity of the DSD Regulations. The Swiss Federal Supreme Court’s review was too limited to provide sufficient institutional and procedural safeguards. It did not thoroughly examine the discriminatory treatment, did not adequately weigh all interests at stake, and did not address the failure to differentiate between transgender and intersex athletes. Given the high stakes—Semenya’s right to practise her profession—the margin of appreciation was overstepped, and the measure was neither objective nor proportionate to the aim pursued.

The Court also found a violation of Article 13. The Federal Supreme Court, owing to its very limited power of review, did not provide an effective response to Semenya’s substantiated and credible complaints of discrimination. The case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 10 July 2025.

In *Semenya v. Switzerland* (App. no. 10934/21), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Switzerland failed to protect a professional athlete with differences of sex development (DSD) from discriminatory eligibility rules imposed by World Athletics. Caster Semenya, a South African 800m runner and Olympic champion, was born with DSD, raised as female, and has natural testosterone levels in the male range. Under World Athletics’ DSD Regulations, to compete internationally in the women’s category in certain middle-distance events, she had to lower her natural testosterone below a specified threshold for at least six months, typically through hormonal medication. She refused, arguing the rules were discriminatory, medically harmful, and scientifically unjustified.

Semenya challenged the DSD Regulations before the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS). In April 2019, CAS dismissed her appeal by a 2-1 majority. It accepted that the regulations were necessary for fair competition in the female category, but also acknowledged scientific uncertainty and serious side effects, and left open important human-rights questions. The CAS did not apply the European Convention on Human Rights. Semenya then appealed to the Swiss Federal Supreme Court, which has only very limited review over CAS awards, essentially limited to whether the award violated Swiss public policy. In August 2020, the Federal Supreme Court rejected her appeal without a full examination of her discrimination complaint.

Before the ECtHR, Semenya alleged violations of Articles 8 (private life), 14 (non-discrimination), 3 (inhuman or degrading treatment), 13 (effective remedy), and 6 §1 (fair trial). She argued that Switzerland, by failing to provide effective institutional and procedural safeguards, allowed a non-State sports body to force her to undergo medically unnecessary treatment to pursue her profession. She claimed discrimination on grounds of sex and sex characteristics, because the DSD Regulations applied only to intersex athletes with DSD, not to other female athletes, and treated her differently from transgender athletes.

The Third Section found Article 14 in conjunction with Article 8 applicable and violated. It held that Semenya was in a relevantly similar situation to other female athletes but was treated differently by being excluded from competitions unless she lowered her natural testosterone. Although the DSD Regulations were adopted by World Athletics, Switzerland had a positive obligation to ensure adequate safeguards against discrimination in this context. The CAS, despite detailed reasoning, did not apply Convention provisions and left serious questions about the validity of the regulations unresolved. The Federal Supreme Court’s review was too narrow, confined to public policy, so it did not thoroughly examine the discrimination complaint or adequately weigh all interests at stake. It also failed to address the lack of differentiation between transgender and intersex athletes. Discrimination based on sex and sex characteristics requires weighty reasons. Given the high stakes—Semenya’s right to practise her profession—the narrow margin of appreciation was overstepped, and the measure was neither objective nor proportionate.

The Court also found a violation of Article 13 in conjunction with Articles 14 and 8, because the Federal Supreme Court did not provide an effective response to her substantiated and credible discrimination complaints, owing to its very limited power of review. The case was referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 10 July 2025.

I.B. repeatedly claimed D.K. was ill, failed to bring her, or brought her to the meeting place in a car with other adults only for D.K. to refuse contact and be driven away. Guardianship Institution assessments found a severe parental conflict, emotional harm to D.K., and that I.B. was not preparing the child for contact or facilitating it. **Case: Golovin v. Ukraine (Application no. 47052/18), ECtHR Fifth Section, judgment of 13 July 2023, final 13 October 2023.**

The applicant, Anatoliy Sergiyovych Golovin, a Ukrainian national born in 1952, was appointed by Parliament in August 2006 as a judge of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine for a non-renewable nine-year term. On 24 February 2014, Parliament dismissed him for “breach of his judicial oath” in connection with his participation in the Constitutional Court’s judgment of 30 September 2010. His dismissal was adopted by the same parliamentary resolution as that concerning the applicants in *Ovcharenko and Kolos v. Ukraine*.

Golovin challenged his dismissal before the Higher Administrative Court (“HAC”) under the Code of Administrative Justice. On 3 March 2014, he also submitted a resignation statement to Parliament. On 11 December 2017, the HAC declared the parliamentary resolution unlawful as regards his dismissal. It relied on international and domestic principles of judicial independence, the Constitutional Court Act provision that judges cannot be held liable for the results of their votes, procedural failures by Parliament, and the absence of any established individual liability.

Parliament appealed. On 14 March 2018, the Grand Chamber of the Supreme Court quashed the HAC judgment and dismissed Golovin’s claim. The Supreme Court found that the Constitutional Court had exceeded its powers in the 30 September 2010 judgment, had effectively changed the Constitution and constitutional system, and had undermined the legitimacy of State authorities. It concluded that Golovin’s participation in that judgment was manifestly inconsistent with his judicial oath. The Supreme Court also held that the dismissal procedure was compatible with the Constitution and parliamentary rules. It attempted to distinguish *Oleksandr Volkov v. Ukraine* by characterizing the Constitutional Court as more of a political body than a judicial one and therefore not a “court” within the meaning of Article 6 of the Convention. On that basis, it reasoned that the appointing body could apply political accountability to a Constitutional Court judge.

Before the ECtHR, Golovin complained under Article 6 that his dismissal case had not been examined by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law, that the right to a reasoned decision had been breached, and that legal certainty had been violated because no time-limits existed for imposing liability for “breach of oath.” Under Article 8, he complained that his unlawful dismissal violated his right to respect for private life. He also relied on Article 18. The Government argued, among other things, that his failure to inform the Court of his resignation application amounted to abuse of the right of application and that his resignation rendered the Article 8 complaint pointless. The ECtHR found no abuse and declared the complaints admissible.

On the merits, the Court observed that Golovin’s situation was nearly identical to that in *Ovcharenko and Kolos*. The only notable difference was the Supreme Court’s attempt to distinguish *Volkov* by calling the Constitutional Court primarily political. The ECtHR disagreed: that general characterization did not address the applicant’s specific dismissal for breach of his judicial oath. The legal framework was identical and lacked clarity and foreseeability as to what conduct constituted “breach of oath.” In particular, Section 28 of the Constitutional Court Act provided functional immunity for judges’ votes. Since Golovin was dismissed precisely for his vote in the 30 September 2010 judgment, it was crucial to clarify whether that immunity limited liability for “breach of oath,” but no authoritative clarification existed at the relevant time. Parliament and the Supreme Court failed to provide the required detailed analysis. The Court therefore found violations of Article 6 and Article 8, applying its findings in *Ovcharenko and Kolos v. Ukraine*.

**Case: Golovin v. Ukraine (App no. 47052/18), ECtHR Fifth Section, judgment 13 July 2023, final 13 October 2023.**

On 3 March 2014 he also submitted a resignation statement to Parliament. On 11 December 2017 the Higher Administrative Court declared the parliamentary dismissal unlawful. It relied on international and domestic principles of judicial independence, noted that the Constitutional Court Act provided that judges could not be held liable for the results of their votes, found procedural violations, and concluded that no individual liability of the applicant had been established. Parliament appealed.

It held that the Constitutional Court had acted beyond its powers in the 2010 judgment, had invalidated binding constitutional provisions, had failed to ensure the supremacy of the Constitution, had changed the constitutional system, and had undermined the legitimacy of State authorities. It concluded that the applicant’s participation in that judgment and its consequences were manifestly inconsistent with his judicial oath, and that the dismissal procedure had been compatible with domestic law. Ukraine*, characterising the Constitutional Court as primarily a political body rather than a court within the meaning of Article 6, and suggesting that the appointing body could apply political accountability.

Ukraine** (no. 15360/10, 1 July 2021), in which it had already found a violation in respect of similar issues.

After examining all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of justifying the overall length of the proceedings at the national level. Having regard to its case-law, the Court concluded that the length of the criminal proceedings in the applicants’ cases was excessive and failed to meet the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The Court further noted that the applicants did not have at their disposal an effective remedy in respect of these complaints, which constituted a violation of Article 13 of the Convention.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore: the applicants were involved in criminal proceedings in Ukraine; those proceedings lasted excessively long; the applicants complained of the delay to the European Court; and no effective domestic remedy existed to address the length complaint. The judgment does not, in the provided excerpt, set out the individual procedural histories or exact durations of each applicant’s criminal case, as those details are contained in the appended table. The Court’s central findings were that the prolonged criminal proceedings violated the applicants’ right to a hearing within a reasonable time and that Ukraine failed to provide an effective remedy for that violation. The excerpt provided ends before the Court’s final rulings on just satisfaction or costs, so those matters are not summarized here.

**CASE OF ZAGHINI v. SAN MARINO**  
*Application no. 3405/21, European Court of Human Rights, First Section, judgment 11 May 2023 (final 25 September 2023).*

The applicant, Gianluca Zaghini, an Italian national, complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention about the confiscation of €1,892,700 and his inability to recover it after criminal proceedings in San Marino for money laundering were brought against third parties, not against him.

The background began in 2003, when Italian authorities investigated the applicant for tax evasion and unjust profits of around €15 million. Italy requested international legal assistance from San Marino. San Marino investigations found a bank account in the applicant’s name; his father withdrew €939,500 and €1,006,700 in cash in December 2003. A safety deposit box in the name of G.A. contained €1,892,700. The money was seized in December 2003. In January 2004, San Marino opened money laundering proceedings against the applicant’s father, G.A. and P.A., but not the applicant. The applicant’s pre-trial statements in Italy included an admission that he had deposited around €1.8 million in San Marino obtained from illegal activity. San Marino investigators found that the applicant’s father delivered €1,903,700 to P.A., who asked G.A. to open a safety deposit box; €1,892,700 was deposited there, while the father and P.A. kept €12,000 and €11,000 respectively.

In 2005, the three co-accused were convicted of money laundering and the seized sum was confiscated. The appeal judgment in 2008 confirmed the guilt of the applicant’s father and former partner and the confiscation; proceedings against G.A. were discontinued as time-barred. The San Marino courts found that the money originated from the applicant’s crimes in Italy and that he had asked the accused to hide it while he was under house arrest. In December 2008, the Enforcement Judge ordered confiscation of €1,892,700 plus interest under Article 147(3) of the Criminal Code.

In Italy, the applicant’s criminal proceedings were later declared time-barred in 2016, and the Court of Appeal of Bologna ordered restitution of money that had been preventively seized. The applicant then asked the San Marino judge for international cooperation to release the sums to him. Those requests were rejected in 2017 and 2018 because the money had already been confiscated in the third-party criminal judgment. The authorities found that the applicant could not be considered an extraneous third party: he had only been spared money laundering charges as the author of the predicate offence, due to a domestic legal bar.

The applicant also sought annulment of the confiscation before the Enforcement Judge in 2018. That request was rejected. The Enforcement Judge found that the illicit origin of the funds had been established, that the applicant was not a good-faith third party, that he was aware of and had instigated the movement of the money, and that he had failed to show a licit origin. The appeal was rejected in January 2019: the Enforcement Judge was competent to protect post-judgment interests of third parties, and the applicant had had an adversarial opportunity, but his claim contradicted the final criminal judgment. The third-instance judge confirmed this in 2020.

Before the European Court, the Government argued non-exhaustion, saying the applicant should have sought revision under Article 200 of the Code of Criminal Procedure; the applicant replied that he was not entitled to do so. The Court found no violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The confiscation was proportionate to the legitimate aim of fighting money laundering, was based on a judicial assessment of the evidence, and the applicant had been given a reasonable opportunity to put his case to the domestic authorities, who examined his claims. There was no indication of arbitrariness.

In *Zaghini v. San Marino* (Application no. 3405/21, judgment of 11 May 2023), the applicant, Gianluca Zaghini, an Italian national, complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about San Marino’s confiscation of €1,892,700 and his inability to recover it after criminal proceedings against third parties for money laundering.

In 2003, Italian authorities investigating Zaghini for tax evasion and unjust profits of about €15 million sought legal assistance from San Marino. San Marino authorities investigated assets linked to Zaghini’s father, G.A., and P.A., and seized a safe-deposit box held in G.A.’s name containing €1,892,700. Earlier, Zaghini’s father had withdrawn €939,500 and €1,006,700 in cash from an account in Zaghini’s name; the money was allegedly delivered to P.A., who arranged for G.A. to open the box. Zaghini had admitted in Italian pre-trial statements that he deposited about €1.8 million in San Marino from illegal activity.

San Marino prosecuted Zaghini’s father, G.A., and P.A. for money laundering, not Zaghini, because domestic law then barred prosecution of the predicate offender for laundering. In 2005, they were convicted and the seized sum was confiscated. The 2008 appeal confirmed the conviction and confiscation, though G.A.’s proceedings were time-barred. In December 2008, the Enforcement Judge ordered confiscation of €1,892,700 plus interest under Article 147(3) of the Criminal Code, which made confiscation mandatory for money-laundering proceeds.

Meanwhile, in Italy, Zaghini’s tax proceedings ended in 2016 when declared time-barred; the Bologna Court of Appeal ordered restitution of money preventively seized in Italy. Zaghini then sought release of the San Marino funds. The judge for international cooperation rejected his requests because the sums had already been confiscated by final San Marino judgment. He was not an extraneous third party, having been spared laundering charges only as the predicate offender.

Zaghini then asked the Enforcement Judge to annul the confiscation based on the Italian judgment. This was rejected: the illicit origin had been established by San Marino courts; the Italian time-bar did not negate that; and Zaghini had not shown the funds were licit or that he was a good-faith third party. Appeals failed. The Judge of Criminal Appeals held the Enforcement Judge was competent to protect third-party interests *post rem iudicatam* and that Zaghini had had an adversarial opportunity, but the confiscation could not be annulled because it conflicted with final criminal findings. The third-instance judge rejected his remaining grounds and found his counsel had presented his case before the Enforcement Judge at first and second instance.

Before the ECtHR, Zaghini alleged the confiscation was unlawful or unjustified and that he lacked effective means to challenge it. The Government argued he had not exhausted domestic remedies, because he should have sought revision under Article 200 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which could potentially reverse the third-party convictions and revoke confiscation. Zaghini replied that Article 200 listed only entitled persons and he was not among them.

The Court found no violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The confiscation pursued the legitimate aim of fighting money laundering, was proportionate, rested on judicial assessment of evidence, and, in the circumstances, Zaghini had a reasonable opportunity to present his recovery claim to domestic authorities, who examined it as circumscribed. There was no indication of arbitrariness.

In *Zaghini v. San Marino*, the European Court of Human Rights examined the confiscation of EUR 1,892,700 following San Marino money-laundering proceedings against third parties, not the applicant. Gianluca Zaghini, an Italian national, had been investigated in Italy in 2003 for tax evasion and unjust profits of about EUR 15 million. Italian authorities sought mutual legal assistance from San Marino, whose authorities ordered asset investigations and seizures. They discovered a bank account in the applicant’s name; in December 2003 his father withdrew EUR 939,500 and EUR 1,006,700 in cash. A safety deposit box in G.A.’s name contained EUR 1,892,700 and was seized. In January 2004, San Marino opened money-laundering proceedings against the applicant’s father, G.A., and P.A. Evidence included the applicant’s pre-trial admission that he had deposited about EUR 1.8 million in San Marino from illegal activity. The father allegedly delivered EUR 1,903,700 to P.A.; she asked G.A. to open the box; G.A. deposited EUR 1,892,700, while the father and P.A. kept small sums. In August 2005 the sum was seized and the three were indicted. In November 2005 they were convicted, given suspended sentences, and the seized sum was confiscated. The May 2008 appeal judgment confirmed the convictions and confiscation; G.A.’s case became time-barred after his confession. In December 2008 the enforcement judge ordered confiscation of EUR 1,892,700 plus interest under Article 147(3) of the Criminal Code.

Meanwhile, in Italy, the applicant’s proceedings ended in 2016 with a time-bar and an order to return money preventively seized. The applicant then tried in San Marino to recover the confiscated funds. In November 2017 and early 2018, the judge for international cooperation rejected his requests, finding that the funds had already been confiscated in San Marino and that he was not a good-faith third party; he had been spared money-laundering charges only because he was the predicate offender. His appeals failed. In August 2018 he asked the Enforcement Judge to annul the confiscation based on the Italian judgment. That request was rejected in September and October 2018: the illicit origin had been established by San Marino courts, independently of the Italian predicate-offence outcome, and the applicant had been aware of and had instigated the money’s movement. The Criminal Appeals judge in January 2019 held that the Enforcement Judge was competent to hear third-party claims and that the applicant had enjoyed adversarial guarantees, but could not reopen final findings; revision might be available. The third-instance judge in 2020 rejected his appeal, noting that he had had an opportunity before the Enforcement Judge and that there was no power to revoke an enforced confiscation.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the confiscation was unlawful or unjustified and that he had no effective means to challenge it. The Court found no violation: the confiscation pursued the legitimate aim of fighting money laundering, was proportionate, was based on a judicial assessment of the evidence, and the applicant had been given a reasonable opportunity to present his claim for recovery to the domestic authorities, whose examination showed no arbitrariness.

The case of *V v. the Czech Republic* (Application no. 26074/18) concerns the death of the applicant’s brother, P.Z., a 30-year-old man suffering from paranoid schizophrenia. The events began on the evening of 5 November 2015, when P.Z. was admitted to the acute care unit of a psychiatric clinic after a family emergency call reported him as aggressive and threatening. He initially calmed down and agreed to anti-psychotic medication.

Early the next morning, P.Z. became restless after realising staff were preparing an intensive care (seclusion) room for him. A verbal altercation with an orderly escalated into a physical confrontation, during which P.Z. knocked the orderly to the ground and beat him severely, causing the orderly to fear for his life. P.Z. then began destroying fixtures, including a washbasin and doors, and started ripping out ceiling tiles and electrical wires, spraying water onto them. After two unarmed security guards failed to subdue him, a nurse called the police at 4:53 a.m.

Four police officers arrived at approximately 5:00 a.m. They briefly consulted a nurse who had not witnessed the attack and who provided limited information about P.Z.’s health status. The officers, using a mattress as a shield, forced P.Z. to the ground in a narrow corridor. Despite his physical strength, they were unable to restrain him or secure his hands. Officer T. fired his taser at P.Z.’s lower back after warning him. P.Z., however, continued to resist actively. At a colleague’s request, T. fired the taser two more times. The taser record showed three discharges lasting eight, eleven, and ten seconds, respectively. During the struggle, P.Z. was held in a prone position. Once his arm was partially immobilised, a nurse administered two injections of tranquilizers (Apaurin and Tisercin) as instructed by a doctor.

Shortly after the injections, at 5:05 a.m., P.Z. was turned onto his back and found to be cyanotic with no palpable pulse. Resuscitation efforts, including defibrillation and adrenaline, were unsuccessful, and P.Z. was pronounced dead at 6:08 a.m. The immediate cause of death was determined to be cardiac arrhythmia. A subsequent expert report noted that repeated tasering could be a possible contributory cause. The experts could not unequivocally determine the extent to which natural causes contributed, and they were not asked to comment on any possible interaction between the administered medication and the taser use.

The subsequent investigation by the General Inspectorate of the Security Forces (GISF) concluded that the police intervention had been lawful and that the use of the taser was justified and in compliance with regulations. This decision was upheld by the Regional Prosecutor’s Office, the High Prosecutor’s Office, and ultimately the Constitutional Court. However, a report by the Czech Public Defender of Rights was critical. It found that the use of a taser on a person already being restrained on the ground is generally unreasonable and unacceptable unless exceptional circumstances exist. It also highlighted systemic deficiencies, including inadequate training for police officers on the health risks of tasers, particularly concerning vulnerable persons, and the lack of a coordinated strategy between police and medical staff for intervening in psychiatric facilities. The report concluded that the police officers were not properly trained regarding the serious health risks associated with taser use, which contributed to the disproportionate force applied.

In *V v. the Czech Republic* (Application no. 26074/18, judgment of 7 December 2023), the European Court of Human Rights examined the death of P.Z., the applicant’s brother, a 30-year-old man with paranoid schizophrenia. On 5 November 2015, after becoming aggressive at home, P.Z. was taken by ambulance and police to a psychiatric clinic’s acute care unit. He initially calmed down and agreed to anti-psychotic medication (Haloperidol and Apaurin). Early the next morning, however, he became restless. Staff began preparing an intensive-care/seclusion room. P.Z. argued with staff, destroyed fixtures, broke doors and a washbasin, attacked a medical orderly—allegedly strangling him with a fire hose—knocked him down, beat him, and shoved a doctor. Two unarmed security guards failed to subdue him. A nurse called the police at 4:53 a.m.; four officers arrived around 5 a.m.

The police briefly consulted a nurse who had not witnessed the attack. They did not communicate with P.Z. or turn off the water or electricity. In a narrow corridor, using a mattress as a shield, two officers forced P.Z. to the ground. They could not restrain him or bring his hands behind his back. Officer T warned P.Z. and fired a taser at his lower back from about 1.5 metres. Although the darts connected, P.Z. continued resisting. At another officer’s request, T fired the taser repeatedly; records showed three discharges lasting 8, 11 and 10 seconds. While P.Z. was still prone and resisting, a nurse administered two injections (Apaurin and Tisercin). After he was turned onto his back, he was cyanotic and pulseless. Resuscitation failed; he was pronounced dead at 6:08 a.m. The immediate cause was cardiac arrhythmia. Experts viewed repeated tasering as a possible contributory cause, noted coronary anomalies, but could not determine unequivocally whether natural causes contributed; they were not asked about possible medication–taser interaction.

Domestic authorities investigated for negligent homicide but concluded that the police intervention was lawful and that no one was to blame. Prosecutors upheld this, and the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal. The Public Defender of Rights, however, criticised the classification of tasers as ordinary law-enforcement devices, inadequate police training on health risks, poor oversight, lack of coordination between police and medical staff, and the risks of prone restraint. She considered tasing a person already lying on the ground and being restrained generally disproportionate unless exceptional circumstances justified it, and noted the absence of a strategy to prevent and limit restraint in psychiatric settings.

The ECtHR found violations of Article 2. Substantively, the State had failed to put in place an appropriate legal and administrative framework: there was no strategy or measures to prevent and limit the use of means of restraint, including safeguards for prone restraint and taser use against mentally ill patients. Procedurally, the investigation into the death was inadequate. The case thus concerned not only the specific use of force but systemic deficiencies in protecting the life of a psychiatric patient during a police intervention.

**V v. the Czech Republic** (App. no. 26074/18, judgment 7 December 2023) concerned the death of the applicant’s brother, P.Z., a 30-year-old man with paranoid schizophrenia, after police used a taser and hospital staff administered tranquilizers while he was being restrained in a psychiatric hospital.

On 5 November 2015, P.Z. became aggressive at home and was taken by ambulance, accompanied by police, to the acute-care unit of Olomouc University Hospital psychiatric clinic. He initially calmed down and agreed to anti-psychotic medication. Early on 6 November, he became restless. Staff began preparing an intensive-care/seclusion room. P.Z. argued with staff, damaged fixtures and doors, attacked a medical orderly—allegedly trying to strangle him with a fire hose—and later ripped down ceiling tiles and sprayed water onto exposed electrical wires. After security guards failed to subdue him, police were called. Four officers arrived around 5 a.m.

The intervention took place in a narrow corridor. Using a mattress as a shield, officers forced P.Z. to the ground. Because of his size and intense resistance, they could not restrain him or secure his hands. Officer T. fired a taser at P.Z.’s lower back from about 1.5 metres, then fired repeatedly when P.Z. continued resisting. The taser record showed three discharges lasting eight, eleven and ten seconds. A nurse then injected P.Z. with Apaurin and Tisercin. Shortly afterwards he became cyanotic and pulseless; resuscitation failed and he was pronounced dead at 6:08 a.m.

A medical expert report concluded that the immediate cause of death was cardiac arrhythmia. It could not unequivocally determine whether or to what extent natural causes were responsible. Stress, psychotic episode, medication, and the repeated tasing were possible contributory factors. The experts were not asked to examine possible interaction between the medication and taser use, nor was positional asphyxia adequately investigated.

The General Inspectorate of the Security Forces opened a negligent-homicide investigation, gathered video and taser data, heard officers and staff, and obtained expert opinions. In April 2016 it discontinued the case, finding the police intervention lawful and the taser use justified because P.Z. posed a direct threat, especially by spraying water onto live wires. Prosecutors upheld that decision, and the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal.

The Public Defender of Rights later criticised Czech law and practice: tasers were treated as ordinary “less-lethal” police devices despite real death risks; training and oversight were inadequate; records lacked detail; and there was no sufficient strategy or coordination between police and hospitals to prevent and limit restraint of mentally ill patients. She considered taser use against a person already prone and held by officers generally unacceptable absent exceptional imminent danger.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 2 of the Convention. Substantively, the State had failed its positive obligation to protect life by not putting in place an appropriate legal and administrative framework and practical measures to prevent and limit the use of restraint, including prone restraint and tasers, particularly in psychiatric settings. Procedurally, the investigation was inadequate because it did not sufficiently examine key issues such as positional asphyxia, the interaction between repeated tasing and administered tranquilizers, and the overall tactics and proportionality of the intervention.

B.F. and Others v. Switzerland (ECtHR, 4 July 2023) concerned four applications by Eritrean nationals and one Tibetan-Chinese national living in Switzerland. All were recognised as refugees under the 1951 Convention but granted only provisional admission, not asylum, because Swiss authorities found their risk of persecution arose after departure and from their own illegal exit (“subjective post-flight grounds”). Under Swiss law, refugees granted asylum may reunite with nuclear family under section 51 of the Asylum Act without waiting periods or financial conditions. Provisionally admitted refugees, however, fall under section 85(7) of the Aliens Act, where reunification is discretionary and subject to cumulative requirements, notably a three-year waiting period and non-reliance on social assistance.

Each applicant requested family reunification, but the requests were refused mainly because the non-reliance-on-social-assistance condition was not met. They alleged violations of Article 8 (family life) and, in some cases, Article 14 read with Article 8, arguing discrimination compared with refugees granted asylum. They claimed the Swiss distinction caused de facto permanent separation, especially given their children’s vulnerable situations abroad and their own limited prospects of achieving financial independence.

In application no. 13258/18, B.F., an Eritrean mother, left her minor daughter D.E. behind; D.E. later lived precariously in Sudan. B.F. was illiterate, had health problems, relied fully on social assistance, and was later found 100% unfit to work. Her request failed for both the waiting period and financial independence. In no. 15500/18, a Tibetan applicant sought reunification with his wife and two children in India. He worked full-time as nursing staff but earned too little for a family of four; his wife had epilepsy. Authorities found the family could live in India and that reunification risked social assistance dependence. In no. 57303/18, an Eritrean mother sought reunification with her eldest daughter X, left first in Eritrea and later in Sudan. She cared alone for three minor children and worked part-time but remained largely reliant on social assistance. The request was also rejected for missing the time-limit for a child over 12 and for lack of financial independence. In no. 9078/20, an Eritrean mother sought reunification with two daughters in an Ethiopian refugee camp. She had health problems, had never worked in Switzerland, and was reliant on social assistance; authorities found she could work part-time but had not diligently sought employment.

Domestic courts accepted that the applicants had de facto settled status and that Article 8 applied, but held the refusals justified. They stressed the public interest in avoiding social assistance dependency, the applicants’ voluntary departure and foreseeable separation, the possibility of contact or visits abroad, and children’s increasing independence. They also noted some children could seek UNHCR assistance. The applicants emphasised the best interests of the child, trauma of separation, unsafe conditions abroad, and insurmountable obstacles to family life elsewhere.

The ECtHR assessed whether Switzerland struck a fair balance under Article 8 and whether the differential treatment breached Article 14. It found a violation of Article 8 in some but not all applications, and no breach concerning the duration of proceedings in one application. The core alleged violations concerned refusal of family reunification based on financial independence requirements and the distinction between provisionally admitted refugees and refugees granted asylum.

In *B.F. and Others v. Switzerland* (ECtHR, Third Section, 4 July 2023), five applicants—four Eritrean nationals and one Chinese national of Tibetan ethnicity—across four applications challenged Switzerland’s refusal of family reunification. All were recognised as refugees under the 1951 Convention but granted only provisional admission, not asylum, because Swiss authorities found the grounds for their refugee status arose after departure and from their own actions, such as illegal exit. Under Swiss law, refugees granted asylum could reunite with their nuclear family under section 51 of the Asylum Act without waiting periods or extra conditions. Provisionally admitted refugees, however, had no entitlement; reunification was discretionary under section 85(7) of the Aliens Act and subject to cumulative requirements, including a three-year waiting period and non-reliance on social assistance. The applicants sought reunification with spouses or minor children. Their requests were refused mainly because they did not satisfy the financial independence condition. They alleged violations of Article 8 (family life); some also alleged Article 14 discrimination compared with asylum refugees.

In application no. 13258/18, B.F., an Eritrean mother, sought her daughter D.E., who was living precariously in Sudan as an unaccompanied minor. B.F. was illiterate, had health problems, was fully reliant on social assistance and was later found 100% unfit for work. The refusal relied on both the waiting period and non-reliance on social assistance. In no. 15500/18, a Tibetan Chinese applicant sought his wife and two children in India. He worked full-time as a nursing assistant but earned too little to support the family without assistance; his wife had epilepsy. The domestic courts found he could reasonably live with them in India and that his integration was not above average. In no. 57303/18, an Eritrean mother sought her eldest daughter X in Sudan. She worked part-time (50%) in a hospital and cared alone for three children in Switzerland, but remained largely reliant on social assistance. Her request was also considered time-barred for a child over 12. In no. 9078/20, an Eritrean mother sought her two daughters in the Adi-Harush refugee camp in Ethiopia. She had serious health problems, had never found employment, and remained reliant on social assistance, though she was not fully unfit for work. The daughters were vulnerable and separated from both parents. She also complained about the length of the proceedings.

Domestic courts accepted that the applicants had de facto settled status and that Article 8 was engaged, but held that refusing reunification was justified by the public interest in avoiding long-term social assistance dependency. They noted that the applicants’ original persecution claims had been rejected, that separation was foreseeable, and that contact, visits, or alternatives abroad were possible.

Before the ECtHR, the Court held that States have a margin of appreciation in imposing a non-reliance on social assistance requirement on provisionally admitted refugees. But that margin is considerably narrower for refugees than for other protected persons, especially refugees *sur place*, because of international and European consensus that all 1951 Convention refugees should receive more favourable family reunification treatment. The particular vulnerability of refugees *sur place* must be adequately considered; obstacles to family life in the country of origin gain importance over time; and the financial condition must be applied flexibly. Refugees must not be required to do the impossible. The fair balance was struck in application no. 15500/18, but not in nos. 13258/18, 57303/18 and 9078/20, where the refusals violated Article 8. There was no breach regarding the duration of proceedings in no. 9078/20.

**Case: B.F. and Others v. Switzerland (ECtHR, 4 July 2023)**

The case concerned four applicants in Switzerland—three Eritrean nationals and one Chinese national of Tibetan ethnicity. All were recognised as refugees under the 1951 Refugee Convention, but none was granted asylum. Instead, they received “provisional admission” because Swiss authorities found that their refugee status arose after their departure from their countries of origin and because of their own actions—particularly illegal exit—so-called “subjective post-flight grounds.” Under Swiss law, refugees granted asylum can bring nuclear family members to Switzerland under the Asylum Act without a waiting period or financial conditions. Provisionally admitted refugees, however, must seek discretionary family reunification under the Aliens Act, subject to a three-year waiting period and non-reliance on social assistance. Their family reunification requests were refused mainly because they did not satisfy the financial independence condition. They alleged violations of Article 8 (family life), and some also alleged Article 14 discrimination compared with refugees granted asylum.

In application no. 13258/18, B.F., an Eritrean mother, left her daughter D.E. behind when she fled in 2012 and was provisionally admitted in 2014. She requested reunification in 2016. She was illiterate, had health problems, was fully reliant on social assistance, and was later assessed as 100% unfit to work. D.E. lived precariously in Sudan as an unaccompanied girl. The refusal relied on the incomplete waiting period and failure to meet the social assistance condition.

In application no. 15500/18, the Chinese/Tibetan applicant entered Switzerland in 2010 and was provisionally admitted. He sought reunification with his wife and two children in India. He worked full-time as nursing staff, but his income was insufficient; authorities found the family would likely depend on social assistance. His wife had epilepsy, limiting work. Authorities also found the family could live in India.

In application no. 57303/18, an Eritrean mother, provisionally admitted in 2010, sought reunification with her eldest daughter X in Sudan. She worked part-time while caring alone for three minor children; the father had disappeared. She remained largely dependent on social assistance. X lived precariously in Khartoum, was unschooled, and was exposed to abuse risks.

In application no. 9078/20, an Eritrean mother, provisionally admitted in 2014, sought reunification with two daughters in Ethiopia’s Adi-Harush refugee camp. She had health problems and was reliant on social assistance, though not completely unfit to work. The daughters lived in poor camp conditions and were vulnerable.

Domestic courts accepted that the applicants had de facto settled status and that Article 8 applied, but found no breach. They stressed the applicants’ voluntary departure, expected separation, limited integration, long-term reliance on social assistance, possibility of visits or contact, UNHCR options, and the public interest in avoiding social assistance. The applicants argued that strict application of the financial condition was impossible for them, caused permanent separation, and ignored the children’s best interests and vulnerability.

The ECtHR found that the fair balance had been struck in the Chinese applicant’s case but violated in the three Eritrean applications. It held that the margin of appreciation is narrower for refugees, especially vulnerable refugees sur place; authorities must apply the non-reliance on social assistance condition flexibly and cannot require refugees to do the impossible. It also found no breach concerning the duration of proceedings in one application.

The case concerns Giorgi Ugulava, former mayor of Tbilisi and a leader of the United National Movement, who complained under Article 5 §§1, 3, 4 and Article 18 that his pre-trial detention in Georgia was unlawful, arbitrary, unreasonably prolonged and politically motivated.

By 2014, several criminal cases were pending against him. On 2 July 2014, an investigator summoned him for questioning on 4 July in a money-laundering case. Ugulava allegedly told authorities he planned a brief trip to Kyiv and would return for questioning. On 3 July 2014, he was arrested at Tbilisi airport without a judicial warrant under Article 171 §2(e) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, based on flight risk, and charged with aggravated money laundering and later with offences relating to a violent incident at the Marneuli electoral commission. On 4 July 2014, Tbilisi City Court ordered his pre-trial detention, finding reasonable suspicion and risks of flight, witness interference and reoffending. It relied, inter alia, on his attempted departure, alleged witness pressure, and the fact that he allegedly committed new offences while on bail in other cases.

During the pre-trial conference, on 16 February 2015, Ugulava sought release, arguing that the investigation was complete, no real flight or witness risk remained, and he had been removed as mayor. On 18 February 2015, the court rejected the request orally, finding no new circumstances and that the original grounds remained valid. It also accepted that the risk of influencing witnesses had increased because the prosecution witness list had been confirmed, and that reoffending risk persisted.

Separately, in a fifth set of proceedings, new charges were brought in July 2014 and amended in March 2015. On 14 March 2015, while Ugulava’s existing nine-month pre-trial detention was due to expire on 2 April 2015, the prosecution requested a new detention order in the parallel case. On 15 March 2015, the Tbilisi City Court granted it. The Court of Appeal upheld it, reasoning that detention could be imposed separately in different criminal cases

In *Ugulava v. Georgia*, the applicant was a former Tbilisi mayor and a leader of the opposition United National Movement. After the Georgian Dream coalition took power in 2012, several criminal proceedings were opened against him. His Convention complaints concerned mainly his arrest and pre-trial detention in 2014–2015, which he alleged were unlawful, arbitrary, and politically motivated under Article 5 §§ 1 and 3 and Article 18.

The relevant events began on 2 July 2014, when an investigator in a money-laundering case summoned Ugulava for questioning on 4 July. Ugulava informed authorities that he had a pre-arranged trip to Kyiv but would return early on 4 July. On 3 July 2014 at 5:57 a.m., he was arrested at Tbilisi airport on suspicion of aggravated money laundering. The prosecution relied on the risk of flight under Article 171 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. His lawyers were initially denied prompt access to him. The next day, the money-laundering case was merged with a case concerning a violent incident at the Marneuli district electoral commission. Ugulava was charged with aggravated money laundering, use of a forged document, coercion, and organising or participating in group activity disrupting public order.

On 4 July 2014, the Tbilisi City Court ordered his pre-trial detention. The prosecution cited flight risk, witness tampering—based largely on a statement by G.K. that Ugulava had threatened him—and risk of reoffending because he was allegedly committing crimes while on bail in other cases. The court relied on the gravity of the charges, possible severe punishment, risk of obstructing evidence and influencing witnesses, and the fact that he had attempted to leave Georgia despite the summons. The Court of Appeal upheld the detention on 8 July 2014. The detention order did not fix a period, but domestic law set a maximum of nine months. The European Court of Human Rights found this aspect compatible with Article 5 § 1.

On 16 February 2015, during the pre-trial conference, Ugulava requested release or bail. He argued that the investigation was essentially complete, that risks of flight or witness interference were no longer real, and that he had been removed from office. The prosecution opposed, citing continuing flight risk, increased witness pressure because the witness list had been confirmed, and reoffending. On 18 February 2015, the City Court rejected the request orally, finding no new circumstances and that the original grounds remained valid. Ugulava received only an extract from the minutes. The ECtHR found a violation of Article 5 § 3 because the refusal was not based on relevant and sufficient reasons and the courts failed to conduct a fresh examination as time passed.

A further issue arose in March 2015. While Ugulava’s detention in the fourth case was due to expire on 2 April 2015, the prosecution sought a new pre-trial detention order in a fifth case concerning Imedi/Lynx charges. The defence argued that the nine-month maximum applied overall and that parallel proceedings could not extend detention. On 15 March 2015, the City Court granted the new detention; the Court of Appeal upheld it on 20 March, treating the nine-month limit separately for each case. Ugulava remained detained. After the Constitutional Court ruled in September 2015 that Article 205 § 2 was unconstitutional insofar as it allowed detention after nine months spent in any other pending case, he was released on 17 September 2015, having spent about fifteen months in pre-trial detention. The ECtHR found a violation of Article 5 § 1 regarding this second consecutive detention, as authorities failed to protect him from arbitrariness. It found no violation of Article 18, as no ulterior political purpose was established.

Ugulava v. Georgia concerned Giorgi Ugulava, a former Tbilisi mayor and leading member of the United National Movement. After the Georgian Dream coalition came to power in 2012, several criminal proceedings were opened against him. The European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Article 5 §§ 1, 3 and 4 and Article 18 that his arrest and pre-trial detention from 3 July 2014 to 17 September 2015 were unlawful, arbitrary, unreasonably prolonged and politically motivated.

In the fourth set of proceedings, investigators examined a June 2014 violent incident at the Marneuli district electoral commission and a money-laundering scheme involving offshore companies. On 2 July 2014, an investigator served Ugulava late at night with a summons to appear for questioning at 10 a.m. on 4 July. Ugulava said he had a pre-arranged trip to Kyiv but would shorten it and return on 4 July. Later that evening, witness G.K. alleged that Ugulava had threatened him. On 3 July at 5:57 a.m., Ugulava was arrested at Tbilisi airport under money-laundering charges. The arrest was based on the risk of flight. His lawyers were initially denied access to him for four to five hours and were also denied access to the case file. On 4 July charges were brought in a consolidated case, including money laundering, use of forged documents, coercion and disrupting public order.

On 4 July 2014 the Tbilisi City Court ordered Ugulava’s pre-trial detention. It relied on the gravity of the charges, the possible severe sentence, and risks of flight, obstruction, witness influence and reoffending. It cited G.K.’s statement about threats, Ugulava’s alleged attempt to leave Georgia despite the summons, and the fact that some alleged accomplices had fled. The Tbilisi Court of Appeal upheld the detention on 8 July. On 16 February 2015, during the pre-trial conference, Ugulava sought release or bail, arguing that the investigation was essentially complete and that no risks remained. On 18 February the judge rejected the request orally, finding no new circumstances and holding that the original grounds still applied. The judge also found that the risk of influencing witnesses had increased because the prosecution’s witness list had been confirmed. Ugulava received only an extract from the hearing minutes.

In the fifth set of proceedings, charges concerning the Imedi television company and Lynx Ltd were brought in July 2014 and amended in March 2015. With the first detention due to expire on 2 April 2015, prosecutors sought a new pre-trial detention in this separate case on 14 March 2015. The defence argued that the Constitution imposed a nine-month maximum overall and that a second period of detention was unlawful. On 15 March 2015 the Tbilisi City Court granted the request without addressing that argument. The Court of Appeal upheld it, reasoning that the nine-month period could be calculated separately for different criminal cases. On 15 September 2015 the Constitutional Court found Article 205 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure unconstitutional insofar as it allowed detention after nine months spent in any other pending case without safeguards against arbitrariness. Ugulava was released on 17 September 2015, after about fifteen months.

The key alleged violations were that the arrest and first detention were unlawful or arbitrary; that refusal of release during the first detention was not based on relevant and sufficient reasons and failed to consider new information; and that the second consecutive detention in parallel proceedings was arbitrary because the authorities failed to protect against manipulation of the nine-month limit. The Court found no established ulterior political purpose under Article 18.

**Locascia and Others v. Italy (no. 35648/10)** — European Court of Human Rights, First Section, judgment of 19 October 2023 (final 19 January 2024).

Nineteen Italian nationals living in Caserta and San Nicola La Strada, Campania, complained under Articles 2 and 8 that Italy had failed to manage municipal waste services properly and to minimise or eliminate pollution from the “Lo Uttaro” landfill. The Court examined the complaints under Article 8 (right to respect for home and private life).

The key facts concerned a prolonged waste-management crisis. From 11 February 1994 to 31 December 2009, a state of emergency was in place in Campania because of serious problems with municipal solid waste disposal. Management was entrusted to deputy commissioners and later to an under-secretariat. In Caserta, mayors’ orders in January 2008 described “huge heaps of waste piling up in the streets” after collection had stopped for more than twenty days. Fires were lit, releasing dioxin; the waste produced unbearable miasmas and impaired traffic. The situation was described as a public health emergency, leading to suspension of schools, kindergartens and local markets. In San Nicola La Strada, orders between 2007 and 2008 reported interrupted collection, waste accumulating on public roads, closure of a kindergarten and primary school, and suspension of the weekly fair.

After the emergency, decrees in 2009–2014 sought to improve waste treatment and disposal. The “Terra dei Fuochi” area was mapped for illegal waste pollution; Caserta was included, and San Nicola La Strada was placed “under observation.” By 2019, over 4 million tonnes of “ecobales” remained stored in Campania. CJEU judgments found Italy had failed to clean up illegal landfills and to establish an adequate waste-disposal network.

The “Lo Uttaro” landfill lay between Caserta and San Nicola La Strada. A site formerly operated by Ecologica Meridionale had already been found in 2001 to be “absolutely unsuitable” and seriously polluted. In 2007, during the emergency, the deputy commissioner authorised its reopening for non-hazardous waste. Civil proceedings led to an expert report finding groundwater already contaminated and warning that additional waste would worsen environmental and health risks. The mayor temporarily closed the site in November 2007. Criminal authorities seized it: the investigating judge found hazardous waste had been disposed of, certifications forged, groundwater contaminated, and safety measures omitted; the operation was illicit even in an emergency. In 2016, convictions followed for illegal waste trade and environmental disaster, though later proceedings were affected by limitation periods and remitted by the Court of Cassation.

ARPAC inspections found leachate and uncontrolled biogas emissions. Environmental characterisation in 2013–2016 confirmed groundwater contamination by arsenic, manganese, iron, fluorides and other substances. Mayors banned groundwater use in the area in 2013–2019 and restricted cultivation. By March 2020, no remediation had been completed; securing works and tenders were still pending.

The applicants alleged that the State’s failures caused serious environmental damage, endangered their health and lives, interfered with their home and private life through accumulated waste, and failed to inform them of risks from the landfill. The Court rejected the claims of several applicants for lack of proof of residence in the affected area. For the remaining applicants, it found a violation of Article 8: the authorities had been unable, for over fifteen years, to ensure proper waste collection, treatment and disposal, and the environmental nuisance adversely affected their private life. Regarding “Lo Uttaro,” the continuing pollution endangered health and upset the fair balance between competing interests, although the authorities had discharged their duty to inform those concerned. The Article 13 complaint concerning restitution of waste-collection taxes was manifestly ill-founded.

In *Locascia and Others v. Italy*, the ECtHR examined complaints by Italian nationals living in Caserta and San Nicola La Strada, Campania, about the regional waste crisis and the “Lo Uttaro” landfill. From 11 February 1994 to 31 December 2009, a state of emergency was in force because of municipal solid waste disposal problems. Management was entrusted to deputy commissioners and later an under-secretariat, but collection, treatment and disposal repeatedly failed. In Caserta, mayoral orders in January 2008 described huge piles of waste after collection stopped for over twenty days, fires releasing dioxin, unbearable miasmas, blocked traffic and a public-health emergency. Schools and markets were closed and waste moved to temporary sites. San Nicola La Strada mayors issued similar orders in 2007–08, citing waste on public roads and risks to health; a school and weekly fair were suspended.

The “Lo Uttaro” landfill lay between the two municipalities. The area had previously hosted a plant run by Ecologica Meridionale that exceeded authorised quantities and caused serious pollution. In 2001 a technical report found the area absolutely unsuitable for a new disposal plant. Nevertheless, in 2006 authorities signed a memorandum to open a new plant there, and in April 2007 the deputy commissioner authorised ACSA CE 3 to dispose of non-hazardous waste; operations began. Residents sought urgent civil relief. In July 2007 the Naples District Court stopped operations, finding no proper environmental impact assessment and health risks. An expert later reported that the area had been a public-health risk since the 1990s, groundwater was contaminated, and additional waste would worsen harm. The mayor closed the plant in November 2007. Criminal authorities seized it the same month, finding illegal hazardous-waste disposal, forged certifications, groundwater contamination and omitted safety measures. Later convictions were affected by limitation periods, while civil remediation and damages orders were disputed.

Subsequently, ARPAC found leachate problems, uncontrolled biogas emissions and contaminated groundwater. Mayors banned well water and cultivation near the site after arsenic, nickel, iron, manganese, mercury and other contaminants were detected. Remediation was repeatedly delayed; by 2020 substantial securing work remained incomplete. WHO/Italian studies indicated higher mortality from certain cancers and congenital malformations in waste-affected areas of Naples and Caserta.

The applicants alleged violations of Articles 2 and 8, claiming Italy failed to guarantee proper waste services and to minimise or eliminate pollution from Lo Uttaro, harming their health and home/private/family life, and failed to inform them of risks. The Court examined the case under Article 8. It found that the authorities’ protracted inability to ensure proper waste collection, treatment and disposal during a state of emergency lasting over fifteen years, and the continuing pollution from Lo Uttaro, adversely affected the applicants’ private life and home and endangered their health, upsetting the fair balance. It accepted that authorities had informed residents of risks. Some applicants lacked victim status for failing to prove residence in the affected area. The Article 13 complaint concerning taxes for waste services was manifestly ill-founded.

**Case: Locascia and Others v. Italy** (App. no. 35648/10), ECtHR First Section, judgment 19 October 2023.

Nineteen Italian nationals living in Caserta and San Nicola La Strada, Campania, complained under Articles 2 and 8 that Italy failed to ensure proper waste collection, treatment and disposal and to protect them from pollution from the “Lo Uttaro” landfill. The Court examined the complaints under Article 8, concerning the right to respect for home and private life, as positive obligations.

From 11 February 1994 to 31 December 2009, a state of emergency was in place in Campania because of serious municipal solid waste disposal problems. Management was entrusted to deputy commissioners and later to an under-secretariat. Waste collection repeatedly broke down. In Caserta, mayoral orders in January 2008 described huge heaps of waste in the streets after more than twenty days without collection; fires burned waste, releasing dioxin; unbearable miasmas spread; traffic was impaired; and a public health emergency was declared. Schools, kindergartens and universities were suspended, and markets closed. In San Nicola La Strada, mayoral orders between April 2007 and May 2008 reported interrupted collection due to closure of disposal sites, waste accumulating on all public roads, danger to public health, and temporary closure of a kindergarten and primary school.

The “Lo Uttaro” landfill lay between Caserta and San Nicola La Strada. A 2001 technical report found the area absolutely unsuitable for a new waste plant and already seriously polluted. Nevertheless, in 2006 a memorandum agreed to open a new waste disposal plant there. In 2007 the deputy commissioner authorised the ACSA CE 3 consortium to dispose of non-hazardous waste, and operations began. Residents sought an urgent injunction. In July 2007 the Naples District Court ordered operations to cease, finding no proper environmental impact assessment and that the area was already polluted. An expert report in October 2007 found groundwater contamination and concluded that additional waste would worsen risks. The mayor temporarily closed the site. Criminal proceedings led to preventive seizure in November 2007; the judge found hazardous waste had been disposed of, certifications forged, groundwater contaminated, and the site unsuitable. In 2016 the managing director and a deputy commissioner were convicted of illegal waste trade and environmental disaster, but in 2017 they were acquitted because the limitation period had expired; remediation and damages orders were upheld and later remitted by the Court of Cassation. ARPAC inspections (2008–2016) found leachate problems, uncontrolled biogas emissions, and groundwater contaminated by arsenic, manganese, iron, mercury and other substances. Mayors banned use of groundwater from wells in the area in 2013, 2014 and 2019, and cultivation was prohibited. The area was included in remediation plans and the “Area Vasta Lo Uttaro”. Remediation remained delayed; by 2020 no work had been completed and a tender was ongoing.

The Court rejected some applicants for lack of victim status because they did not prove residence in the affected area. For the remaining applicants, it found a violation of Article 8. The authorities’ protracted inability to ensure proper waste services during the fifteen-year emergency caused environmental nuisance affecting private life. Applicants were more vulnerable to illness because they lived in an area extensively exposed to waste in breach of safety standards. As to Lo Uttaro, pollution continued and endangered health, and the authorities failed to take all necessary protective measures, upsetting the fair balance. The authorities had, however, discharged their duty to inform residents of risks. The Article 13 complaint concerning restitution of waste taxes was manifestly ill-founded.

In *Lyapchev and Others v. Bulgaria* (Applications nos. 75478/13 and 30713/15), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 2 March 2023. The case originated in applications against Bulgaria lodged under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants complained of the forfeiture of alleged proceeds of crime. They relied, expressly or in substance, on Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, which protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions and permits deprivation only in the public interest and subject to law.

Because the applications raised similar issues, the Court joined them. The Bulgarian Government, without providing further details, invited the Court to decide the cases in line with the leading judgment *Todorov and Others v. Bulgaria* (2021). That judgment concerned forfeiture under the same legislation, the Forfeiture of Proceeds of Crime Act 2005. In *Todorov*, the Court identified several flaws in the 2005 Act and its application: its wide scope regarding predicate crimes and the periods for which defendants’ revenues and expenses were checked; the difficulty for defendants to prove “lawful” income during periods marked by inflation and economic change; and the presumption that any asset not shown to have had a “lawful” provenance was the proceeds of crime. Although those flaws did not automatically make every forfeiture contrary to Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, they placed a considerable burden on defendants and could tilt the balance in favour of the State. As a counterbalance, the Court held that national courts had to establish a causal link between the assets being forfeited and the defendants’ criminal conduct.

Applying those principles to the present applications, the Court found that the national courts had failed to justify such a causal link. In the *Lyapchevi* case, the national courts ordered forfeiture of assets acquired before Mr Lyapchev committed the predicate offence. They relied only on discrepancies between the applicants’ “lawful” income and expenses and on the fact that Mr Lyapchev was under further investigation. In the *Chupetlovski* case, the courts referred merely to the nature of the applicant’s unspecified “criminal activity.” The Court accepted that in cases of this type it would generally defer to the national courts’ assessment of whether a causal link existed between any criminal conduct and the assets subject to forfeiture. However, in these particular cases, the reasons provided to substantiate that link were clearly insufficient.

The Court therefore saw no reason to reach a different conclusion from *Todorov and Others*, where it had found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and criticised the national courts’ approach. Accordingly, it found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 in the present applications. The judgment was final but subject to editorial revision.

It concluded that Bulgaria had violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 in both applications. The judgment was final but subject to editorial revision. The Court also noted that the case concerned the application of Article 41 of the Convention, although the provided text does not detail any award or further relief.
