In *Burando Holding B.V. and Port Invest B.V. v. the Netherlands* (Apps. 3124/16 and 3205/16, ECtHR 16 May 2023), the applicants were Dutch waste-liquid collection companies operating in Rotterdam. Burando was Port Invest’s sole shareholder and board member, and Port Invest in turn controlled the I. company. In late 2006, VROM-IOD, a special investigative service, began criminal investigation “Toto” into I. company for suspected illegal disposal of polluted waste. With authorization from an investigating judge, VROM-IOD intercepted telephone calls of I. company employees and another ship waste collector. Some calls indicated price-fixing, so VROM-IOD prepared an official record on 21 April 2008 with summary transcripts and annexes.

On 21 October 2008, the public prosecutor approved transmission of that record to the Netherlands Competition Authority (NMA) under the Judicial and Criminal Data Act (WJSG), handwriting approval on the document. The transmission occurred on 29 June 2009. Further selections of transcripts and audio files were transmitted in 2009–2010 after prosecutor approvals and contacts between VROM-IOD and NMA officials about relevant data. The final approval was in August 2010, with transmission on 8/9 September 2010. Meanwhile, the criminal case against I. company ended through a settlement in March 2010; in July 2010 the Regional Court declared the prosecutor inadmissible.

The NMA used the intercepted data to investigate price-fixing. It concluded that between 2005 and 2007 several companies, including I. company, allocated contracts and restricted price competition contrary to section 6 of the Competition Act. In November 2011, the NMA fined I. company EUR 1,861,000, jointly and severally attributed to Port Invest, and EUR 621,000 to Burando, assuming decisive influence because of their corporate interconnectedness.

The applicants objected, arguing that the prosecutor had not carried out a knowable, reviewable balancing of interests and that there had been no prior judicial control over the transmission. In 2013, the Rotterdam Regional Court upheld their appeal, excluded the transcripts as evidence, and quashed the NMA decisions because no reviewable weighing of interests had been recorded. In 2015, the Supreme Administrative Court for Trade and Industry reversed. It held that the telephone tap data were “criminal data” under the WJSG; that transmission served a compelling general interest, namely the economic well-being of the country; and that the WJSG conditions were met. It found no requirement that the prosecutor’s balancing be recorded in writing at the time of transmission, because lawfulness could be assessed through ex post judicial review. It also rejected the argument that the criminal case had ended too early, holding that it ended only when the July 2010 ruling became final, so the transmissions fell within the relevant two-month period before destruction was required.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants complained under Articles 8 and 13 that the transmission and use of lawfully intercepted telephone data in competition-law proceedings were not foreseeable and lacked sufficient procedural safeguards, including prior judicial authorization. The Court found that the transmission was sufficiently foreseeable under Dutch law, that extensive ex post facto judicial oversight and other safeguards existed, and that ex ante court authorization was not required in this context. The authorities had adequately balanced the interests involved, and the interference was justified by the economic well-being of the country and proportionate. The Court found no violation of Article 8 and no violation of Article 13.

In *Burando Holding B.V. and Port Invest B.V. v. the Netherlands* (Apps. nos. 3124/16 and 3205/16, Third Section, 16 May 2023), two Dutch companies involved in collecting waste liquids from ships in Rotterdam complained under Articles 8 and 13 ECHR about the transmission and use, in competition-law proceedings, of data obtained through telephone tapping in a criminal investigation. Burando Holding was the sole shareholder and board member of Port Invest, which in turn was the sole shareholder and board member of I. company.

At the end of 2006, VROM-IOD, a special investigative service, began criminal investigation “Toto” into I. company on suspicion of illegally disposing of polluted waste. With an investigating judge’s authorization, VROM-IOD intercepted telephone conversations of I. company employees. Some calls indicated price-fixing, so VROM-IOD recorded those indications in an official record dated 21 April 2008, with summary transcripts annexed. On 21 October 2008 the public prosecutor approved transmission of the record to the Netherlands Competition Authority (NMA) under the Judicial and Criminal Data Act (WJSG). The transmission occurred on 29 June 2009. Further selections of transcripts and audio files were transmitted in 2009 and 2010, after contacts between VROM-IOD and NMA officials; the final transmission was approved in August 2010 and took place on 8/9 September 2010.

The NMA concluded that several companies, including I. company, had coordinated behaviour between 2005 and 2007 to allocate contracts and limit price competition, contrary to section 6 of the Competition Act. On 16 November 2011 it fined I. company EUR 1,861,000, jointly and severally attributed to Port Invest, and fined Burando Holding EUR 621,000, based on their decisive influence over I. company.

The applicant companies objected, arguing that the prosecutor had not made a knowable, reviewable balancing of interests and that there was no prior judicial control over the transmission. The Rotterdam Regional Court in 2013 upheld their appeal, finding the intercepted data were “criminal data” and that the prosecutor had merely given handwritten or pre-printed permission without reasoning. It excluded the transcripts as evidence and quashed the fines. The ACM appealed. In 2015 the Supreme Administrative Court for Trade and Industry quashed that judgment. It held that the data were criminal data, that the economic well-being of the country was a compelling general interest, and that the WJSG did not require written reasoning at the time of transmission. It found sufficient safeguards through ex post facto judicial review, including civil tort proceedings and review of the fine. It also held that transmissions after a criminal settlement were lawful because the criminal case ended only when the 5 July 2010 ruling became final, so the two-month destruction period under Article 126cc had not expired.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants alleged that the transmission and use of the tapped data were not foreseeable and lacked sufficient procedural safeguards. The Court found no violation of Article 8: the interference was provided for by law, sufficiently foreseeable, and subject to extensive ex post facto judicial oversight and adequate safeguards against abuse. Article 8 did not require ex ante judicial authorization in this context, and the domestic authorities had adequately balanced the interests. The Court also found no violation of Article 13, as effective remedies existed. The case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 1 April 2025.

In *Burando Holding B.V. and Port Invest B.V. v. the Netherlands*, the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Articles 8 and 13 of the Convention concerning the transfer of intercepted telephone data from a criminal investigation to the Netherlands Competition Authority (“NMA”) and its later use in competition-law proceedings.

The applicants were Dutch waste-collection companies operating in the Rotterdam port region. Burando Holding was the sole shareholder and board member of Port Invest, which in turn held the same position in the I. company.

At the end of 2006, the VROM-IOD, a special investigative service, began criminal investigation “Toto” into the I. company’s suspected involvement in illegal disposal of polluted waste. An investigating judge authorized telephone taps. Some intercepted conversations between an I. company employee and an employee of Ships Waste Oil Collector B.V. indicated possible price-fixing. In April 2008, VROM-IOD drew up an official report with summary transcripts of those conversations. In October 2008, the public prosecutor approved transmission of the report to the NMA under the Judicial and Criminal Data Act (“WJSG”); transmission occurred in June 2009. Further transcripts and audio files were transmitted in 2009 and 2010 after prosecutor approval. The NMA investigated possible breaches of the Competition Act and, in November 2011, fined the I. company EUR 1,861,000, jointly and severally attributed to Port Invest and Burando because of their decisive influence.

The applicants objected, arguing that the prosecutor’s balancing of interests was not knowable or reviewable and that there had been no prior judicial control over the data transmission. In 2013, the Rotterdam Regional Court found that the intercepted telephone data were “criminal data” under the WJSG, but that the prosecutor had merely given permission without a reviewable reasoning process. It therefore excluded the transcripts as evidence and quashed the fines. The Supreme Administrative Court for Trade and Industry reversed this in 2015. It held that the data fell within the broad definition of criminal data, that enforcement of competition law served a compelling general interest in the economic well-being of the country, and that the WJSG had been complied with. It further found that no written reasoning was required at the time of transmission and that sufficient safeguards existed: the taps had been authorized by an investigating judge, the transmission could be reviewed ex post by civil courts, the fine decision could be reviewed administratively, the ACM assessed the evidence, and the applicants were heard. It also rejected the claim that transmissions after the criminal settlement were unlawful.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants alleged that the transmission and use of lawfully intercepted data in competition proceedings were not foreseeable and lacked adequate procedural safeguards, including ex ante judicial authorization. The Court found no violation of Article 8 or Article 13. It held that the transmission was sufficiently foreseeable under domestic law, that extensive ex post facto judicial oversight and adequate safeguards existed, and that Article 8 did not require prior court authorization in this context. The domestic system was capable of avoiding abuse and had adequately balanced the privacy interests against the compelling public interest. The interference was justified by relevant and sufficient reasons showing necessity and proportionality.

**Case Name:** *Sholomytskyy and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 12260/15 and 2 others)  
**Court:** European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section (Committee)  
**Judgment:** Strasbourg, 30 November 2023

This case originated in several applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants complained principally of unlawful detention, relying expressly or in substance on Article 5 § 1 of the Convention. They also raised other complaints under the Convention. In application no. 60551/17, the applicant additionally raised further complaints under Article 5. Because the applications raised similar subject matter, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment. The specific applicants, dates, and details—including the relevant periods of detention—are set out in an appended table, which is not reproduced in the provided text.

The Ukrainian Government was given notice of the applications. The central alleged violation was that the applicants had been detained in circumstances that did not comply with Article 5 § 1, which guarantees the right to liberty and security and prohibits arbitrary or unjustified deprivation of liberty. The Court reiterated that Article 5, together with Articles 2, 3, and 4, ranks among the most fundamental Convention rights protecting the physical security of the individual. Its key purpose is to prevent arbitrary or unjustified deprivation of liberty.

The Court further recalled that, where the “lawfulness” of detention is at issue, including whether a procedure prescribed by law has been followed, the Convention refers essentially to national law and requires conformity with substantive and procedural rules. **Case J.A. and Others v. Italy** (Application no. 21329/18, judgment 30 March 2023) concerned four Tunisian nationals who left Tunisia by sea on 15 October 2017 and were rescued by an Italian ship, arriving in Lampedusa on 16 October 2017. They were placed in the Lampedusa hotspot at Contrada Imbriacola and remained there for ten days. They alleged that they could not lawfully leave, except occasionally through an opening in the fence, and had no meaningful interaction with authorities. They received some general information about asylum procedures and unaccompanied minors, but said they did not fully understand it. They described the material conditions as inhuman and degrading: overcrowding, inadequate sleeping arrangements, lack of common areas, and generally poor facilities. The hotspot had been designated under Decree-Law no. 13 of 2017. Domestic and international reports noted the uncertain legal nature of hotspots, the fact that Lampedusa was meant for very short stays of 24–48 hours, and that migrants were often not allowed to leave even after identification, resulting in de facto detention without judicial validation. The National Guarantor described the hotspot as a “limbo of legal protection.”

On the morning of 26 October 2017, the applicants and about forty others were woken, told to undress, searched, and transferred by bus to Lampedusa Airport. There they were asked to sign documents they allegedly did not understand and did not receive copies of. These were refusal-of-entry orders issued by the Agrigento police headquarters, dated 26 October 2017. Later, only the first two applicants obtained copies; requests concerning the third and fourth applicants went unanswered. The Government claimed the orders had been duly served, signed, and included information about the right to challenge them before the Agrigento District Court within thirty days. The applicants were then searched again, their wrists were secured with Velcro straps, and their mobile phones were taken. They were flown to Palermo, where the straps were removed and then reapplied. At Palermo Airport they met a Tunisian consulate representative who recorded their identities, and on the same day, 26 October 2017, they were forcibly removed to Tunisia by airplane.

The applicants complained under Article 3 (substantive) about their material conditions of detention; under Article 5 §§ 1(f), 2 and 4 about arbitrary deprivation of liberty; and under Article 4 of Protocol No. 4 about collective expulsion. The European Court of Human Rights found violations. It held that the ten-day stay in poor material conditions amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment under Article 3. Under Article 5 § 1(f), their detention to prevent unauthorised entry lacked a clear and accessible legal basis in domestic law and was not accompanied by a reasoned decision. They were not informed of the legal reasons for detention, contrary to Article 5 § 2, and could not effectively challenge the lawfulness of their de facto detention because they lacked sufficient information, contrary to Article 5 § 4. Finally, the refusal-of-entry and removal orders and the removal to Tunisia were issued and executed without proper regard to the applicants’ individual situations, amounting to a collective expulsion prohibited by Article 4 of Protocol No. 4. The case illustrates systemic failures in Italy’s hotspot system: unclear legal grounds for detention, inadequate conditions, lack of information and judicial review, and removal without individual assessment.

Finally, under Article 4 of Protocol No. 4, the removal to Tunisia was carried out without proper regard to the applicants’ individual situations when the refusal-of-entry and removal orders were issued, amounting to a collective expulsion. The Court therefore found violations of Article 3, Article 5 §§ 1, 2 and 4, and Article 4 of Protocol No. 4.

The case of J.A. and Others v. Italy concerns four Tunisian nationals who were rescued at sea and detained in the Lampedusa hotspot before being forcibly removed to Tunisia.

The applicants left the Tunisian coast on 15 October 2017 aboard makeshift vessels and were rescued by an Italian ship, arriving in Lampedusa on 16 October 2017. They underwent medical checks and identification procedures. During their ten-day stay at the Contrada Imbriacola hotspot, the applicants alleged they were unable to interact with authorities and could not lawfully leave the centre, though they occasionally exited through an opening in the surrounding fence. They described the material conditions as inhuman and degrading, including overcrowded dormitories, inadequate bedding, and lack of common areas.

There, they were asked to sign documents they allegedly did not understand and did not receive copies of. These documents were subsequently discovered to be refusal-of-entry orders issued by the Agrigento police headquarters. When the applicants' representatives requested copies, only those concerning the first two applicants were provided; requests regarding the third and fourth applicants went unanswered. The refusal-of-entry orders for the first two applicants were dated 26 October 2017.

The government maintained that the orders had been duly served, signed for, and included information about the right to challenge them before the Agrigento District Court within thirty days. However, the applicants' representatives had difficulty obtaining copies, raising concerns about whether the applicants were properly informed.

The applicants were then searched again, their wrists secured with Velcro straps, and their mobile phones confiscated. They were flown to Palermo, where they met a Tunisian consulate representative who recorded their identities. On the same day, 26 October 2017, they were forcibly removed to Tunisia by airplane.

The case raised issues under multiple Convention provisions. Regarding Article 3, the Court examined whether the material conditions at the Lampedusa hotspot constituted inhuman and degrading treatment during the applicants' ten-day detention. Under Article 5 §§ 1, 2, and 4, the Court considered whether the applicants' deprivation of liberty was arbitrary, lacking a clear and accessible legal basis, and whether they were informed of the reasons for detention and had the ability to challenge its lawfulness. The lack of sufficient information prevented them from effectively challenging their de facto detention.

Under Article 4 of Protocol No. 4, the Court examined whether the removal to Tunisia constituted collective expulsion, as the applicants were removed without proper regard to their individual situations when the refusal-of-entry and removal orders were issued. The applicants were part of a group of approximately forty individuals removed together, raising concerns about whether each person's circumstances were individually assessed.

The case highlighted systemic issues with Italy's hotspot system, including the uncertain legal nature of these facilities, the lack of clear legal framework governing detention, inadequate material conditions, and insufficient procedural safeguards for migrants facing removal.

**International Research and Exchange Board v. Azerbaijan** (Application no. 7668/15) is a European Court of Human Rights case decided by the First Section Committee on 2 March 2023. The applicant is the Baku representative office of the International Research and Exchanges Board (IREX), an international humanitarian organisation registered in Azerbaijan in 1998. The application was lodged on 30 December 2014 and concerned an order to search and seize the applicant’s property and an order freezing its bank accounts in the context of criminal proceedings against various local NGOs and representative offices of international organisations.

On 22 April 2014 the Prosecutor General’s Office opened criminal case no. 142006023 under Articles 308.1 (abuse of power) and 313 (forgery by an official) of the Criminal Code, alleging irregularities in the financial activities of several NGOs. The applicant organisation was mentioned in the decision opening the case but never had “suspect” status.

Regarding the bank accounts, on 26 July 2014 the Nasimi District Court issued an attachment order over all the applicant’s bank accounts pending the investigation. The court cited the need for a complete, comprehensive and objective investigation. The order was said to be appealable within three days. The applicant claimed that the hearing occurred without its representative because it was not notified, and that no copy of the order was sent to it. Because 27 July was a Sunday and 28–29 July were public holidays for Ramadan, the bank only informed the applicant of the freeze on 30 July. On 31 July the applicant obtained a copy of the order and appealed the next day, also requesting restoration of the time-limit. On 7 August the Nasimi District Court refused to restore the time-limit, finding no valid reasons for the delay, and on 18 August the Baku Court of Appeal upheld that refusal. The attachment was lifted only on 10 July 2020.

Regarding the search, on 4 September 2014 the Yasamal District Court authorised investigators to search the applicant’s office and seize legal, financial, accounting and bank documents relating to its activities and its receipt of grants and other financial aid, including documents stored on electronic devices. The court again relied on the need to ensure a complete, comprehensive and objective investigation. The search was carried out on 5 September 2014. Authorities seized twelve laptops, six computer system units, eight video cameras, two photo cameras, one mobile phone, forty-one CDs and DVDs, one hard drive, fifteen flash drives, one audio cassette and thirty-five boxes of documents. On 24 September 2014 the Baku Court of Appeal upheld the search warrant. After expert examinations, the seized items were returned on 13 November 2015, but the applicant alleged that the computers were not returned in working condition.

The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the freezing of its bank accounts. It complained under Article 8 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the search and seizure at its office. It also complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the retention of its computers for about a year and their allegedly unusable return. Finally, it complained under Article 18 that the restrictions were imposed for a purpose other than those permitted by the relevant provisions. The Court gave notice of the complaints under Articles 6, 8 and 18 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning the search, seizure and freeze, and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

In *Z.A. v. Ireland* (ECtHR, 2023), the applicant is a Nigerian national born in 1994 who came to Ireland in 2001, aged seven, to join his mother and siblings after his father died. His mother had obtained leave to remain as the parent of an Irish citizen and later became Irish; all six of the applicant’s siblings are Irish citizens. Z.A. had permission to remain as a dependant until 2010, then in his own right, subject to conditions including obeying Irish law.

In 2010, aged 16, he was charged with one sexual assault and two attempted defilements of a child under 17. The incidents involved a 14-year-old girl and other teenage boys. The trial took place in 2014, when he was 20; he pleaded guilty. The Circuit Court described the offences as serious and very distressing for the victim. A probation report assessed his risk of reoffending as moderate and noted that the convicted persons did not appreciate the harm caused. He received a two-year suspended sentence, suspended for three years, plus 12 months’ probation supervision. In 2014/2015 he also committed traffic offences—driving without a full licence and without insurance—and was fined €300.

In February 2015 the Minister for Justice proposed deportation under section 3 of the Immigration Act 1999. An April 2016 deportation order was challenged, revoked, and then reconsidered. In an April 2017 INIS analysis, the Minister accepted that deportation would interfere with Z.A.’s Article 8 private and family life, given his long residence, education, football career and family ties, including his mother, siblings and Irish girlfriend. However, the analysis found deportation proportionate to prevent disorder and crime. It relied on the serious sexual offences, the moderate risk assessment, his failure to undertake formal rehabilitative therapy, and the traffic offences as showing disregard for Irish law. It considered that he could reintegrate in Nigeria and that family ties could be maintained by relocation, visits or modern communication. The deportation order issued on 21 April 2017.

Z.A. sought judicial review. He alleged that deportation disproportionately interfered with his private and family life contrary to Article 8, and that Irish law lacked an independent review or appeal mechanism, contrary to Article 13. The High Court rejected these claims on 30 May 2019. Applying domestic case-law (*Meadows* and *ISOF*), it examined whether the Minister’s balancing exercise contained a flaw such that the conclusion plainly flew in the face of fundamental reason and common sense; it did not re-weigh proportionality afresh. It found no irrationality. It also held that High Court judicial review provided an effective Article 13 remedy. Leave to appeal was refused by the High Court on 11 July 2019 and by the Supreme Court on 13 November 2019.

Before the ECtHR, Z.A. had already left Ireland to play professional football in Vietnam. The Government did not contest the admissibility of his Article 8 complaint. The Court declared it admissible, noting that his departure would be considered on the merits. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore his long settled residence from childhood, strong family and private-life ties in Ireland, the serious sexual offences committed as a minor but with a moderate risk assessment, the later traffic offences, the absence of formal rehabilitation, and his complaint that domestic judicial review did not provide an independent or sufficient proportionality review under Article 8, nor an effective remedy under Article 13.

In **Nikolaev and Others v. Bulgaria** (Applications nos. 48806/11 and 11138/12), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on **12 January 2023**. The case concerned two applications against Bulgaria lodged under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants complained about the forfeiture of assets alleged to be proceeds of crime. They relied, expressly or in substance, on **Article 1 of Protocol No. 1**, which protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions and prohibits deprivation of possessions except in the public interest and subject to legal conditions.

The applicants and relevant factual details were listed in an appended table, which is not reproduced in the judgment. The essential facts are that national authorities ordered forfeiture of the applicants’ assets under the **Forfeiture of Proceeds of Crime Act 2005** (“the 2005 Act”). The Government did not provide further details and invited the Court to decide the case on the basis of the leading judgment **Todorov and Others v. Bulgaria** (nos. 50705/11 and 6 others, 13 July 2021), which concerned forfeiture under the same legislation.

The Court joined the applications because of their similar subject matter and examined them under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. In **Todorov and Others**, the Court had identified potential flaws in the 2005 Act and its application. These included: the wide scope of the Act as to predicate crimes and the periods for which defendants’ revenues and expenses were checked; the difficulties defendants faced in proving “lawful” income during such periods, especially amid inflation and economic changes; and the presumption that any asset not shown to have a “lawful” provenance was proceeds of crime. The Court held that these flaws did not automatically make every forfeiture contrary to Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, but they placed a considerable burden on defendants and could tilt the balance in favour of the State.

As a counterbalance and safeguard, the Court required national courts to establish a **causal link** between the assets being forfeited and the defendants’ criminal conduct. The Court was prepared to defer to national courts’ assessment of that link only if it was not arbitrary or manifestly unreasonable. In **Todorov and Others**, violations were found where national courts failed to justify such a causal link and ordered forfeiture relying merely on the statutory presumption and on discrepancies between the applicants’ expenses and their “lawful” income during the relevant periods.

In the present applications, the Court found that the national courts had adopted the same flawed approach. When ordering forfeiture of the applicants’ assets, they did not attempt to justify the required causal link between those assets and alleged criminal conduct. Instead, they relied on the presumption and reasoning already criticized in **Todorov and Others**. The Court saw no reason to reach a different conclusion. Accordingly, it found a **violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1**. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision. The reproduced text then refers to the application of Article 41 of the Convention, but no further details are included.

In *Nikolaev and Others v. Bulgaria* (Applications nos. 48806/11 and 11138/12), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section, sitting as a Committee) delivered judgment on 12 January 2023. The case originated in two applications against Bulgaria lodged under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants complained about the forfeiture of assets alleged to be proceeds of crime. They relied, expressly or in substance, on Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, which protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions and permits deprivation only in the public interest and subject to law.

The Court joined the applications because they raised similar issues. The Government did not provide further factual details and invited the Court to decide the case on the basis of the leading judgment *Todorov and Others v. Bulgaria* (2021), which concerned forfeiture under the same legislation: the Forfeiture of Proceeds of Crime Act 2005 (“the 2005 Act”).

In *Todorov*, the Court identified several potential flaws in the 2005 Act and its application. These included the wide scope of forfeiture regarding predicate crimes and the periods for which defendants’ revenues and expenses were checked; the difficulty for defendants to prove “lawful” income during those periods, particularly given inflation and economic changes; and the statutory presumption that any asset not shown to have had a “lawful” provenance was the proceed of crime. The Court held that these flaws did not automatically make every forfeiture under the 2005 Act contrary to Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, but they placed a considerable burden on defendants and could tilt the balance in favour of the State.

To counterbalance these risks and guarantee applicants’ rights, the Court required national courts to establish a causal link between the assets subject to forfeiture and the defendants’ criminal conduct. The Court was prepared to defer to national courts’ assessment of that link only if it was not arbitrary or manifestly unreasonable. In *Todorov*, violations were found where national courts failed to justify such a causal link and instead ordered forfeiture relying merely on the statutory presumption and on discrepancies between applicants’ expenses and their “lawful” income during the relevant periods.

The applications in *Nikolaev and Others* were similar. When ordering forfeiture of the applicants’ assets, the national courts did not attempt to justify the causal link required by the Court. Instead, they adopted the same flawed approach criticised in *Todorov*. In particular, they relied on the presumption contained in the 2005 Act and on discrepancies between the applicants’ expenses and lawful income, without demonstrating a sufficient connection between the forfeited assets and criminal conduct.

The Court therefore saw no reason to reach a conclusion different from *Todorov*. It found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 in respect of the applicants. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation were thus the domestic courts’ failure to establish a reasoned causal link between the assets and criminal conduct, combined with the burden-shifting operation of the 2005 Act, which placed the applicants at a significant disadvantage in the forfeiture proceedings. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

Bulgaria* (Applications nos. 48806/11 and 11138/12), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 12 January 2023. In *Al-Masudi v. Denmark* (Application no. 35740/21), the European Court of Human Rights examined an Article 8 complaint arising from Denmark’s expulsion of a settled migrant with a permanent re-entry ban following serious criminal convictions. The applicant, Mohamad Mustafa Hamid Al-Masudi, an Iraqi national born in 1994, entered Denmark in 1998 at age three through family reunification and received a permanent residence permit in 2002. He had a criminal record beginning in 2010. As a minor, he was convicted of theft and a weapons offence, robbery, and a controlled-substances violation. As an adult, he was convicted of violence and drug offences in 2013; aggravated violence in 2017, for which he received a six-month sentence and a suspended expulsion order with a two-year probation period; violence and drug offences in 2018, for which he received six months’ imprisonment and a caution about expulsion; and multiple fines for drug offences between 2013 and 2020.

The decisive conviction occurred in March 2020. The District Court convicted the applicant of possessing 57.1 grams of MDMA and 12.1 grams of amphetamine for distribution, and of keeping a sawn-off shotgun and spare cartridges in an unlocked cabinet in his living room under particularly aggravating circumstances. He was sentenced to two years and nine months’ imprisonment and expelled from Denmark with a lifelong re-entry ban. The District Court found the expulsion conditions under the Aliens Act met. Because the applicant had lawful residence exceeding nine years, expulsion was required unless it would “with certainty” be contrary to Denmark’s international obligations, including Article 8. Applying the *Maslov v. Austria* proportionality criteria, the court considered society’s need to expel him, the nature of his current and prior offences, his length of stay, and his ties to Denmark and Iraq. It noted he entered Denmark at three, had visited Iraq once at age ten, had no close family there, spoke broken Arabic, grew up in Denmark with parents and siblings, lacked education or permanent employment, received benefits, was unmarried and had no children, but had a Danish fiancée; the relationship began only days before he was remanded in custody. The court found expulsion not certainly contrary to Denmark’s international obligations.

On appeal, the High Court of Eastern Denmark upheld the judgment on 7 September 2020. It held that expulsion and a permanent re-entry ban were not disproportionate under Article 8, and that his engagement during detention and his fiancée’s pregnancy did not change the outcome. Their child was born in December 2020. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused in November 2021, and the applicant was deported to Iraq in July 2022.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged that the expulsion and lifelong ban violated Article 8. He argued that the domestic courts failed to properly weigh relevant circumstances: his sentence was moderate, his previous convictions had not exceeded six months, he had strong ties to Denmark including a partner and child, he had no ties to Iraq, and there were no “very compelling reasons” for a lifelong expulsion. The Government contended that the domestic courts thoroughly conducted the proportionality test and considered all relevant circumstances. It stressed that the relationship began days before detention, the child was conceived during detention, the applicant had committed serious offences, had a history of robbery and repeated violence, had previously received a suspended expulsion order and a caution, and posed a serious threat to public order. The Government also invoked subsidiarity, noting that domestic courts expressly applied Article 8 and the Court’s case-law. The Court declared the complaint admissible, finding it neither manifestly ill-founded nor inadmissible. The judgment’s headnote indicates that the Court found the domestic proportionality assessment compatible with Article 8, given the very serious reasons for expelling a settled migrant with his criminal history and prior warnings.

**Al-Masudi v. Denmark** (Application no. 35740/21), decided by the European Court of Human Rights on 5 September 2023, concerned an Article 8 challenge to the expulsion of a settled migrant with a lifelong re-entry ban.

The applicant, Mohamad Mustafa Hamid Al-Masudi, was an Iraqi national born in 1994. He entered Denmark in 1998 at age three through family reunification and received a permanent residence permit in 2002. He had lived in Denmark for most of his life and had parents and four siblings there. He reportedly visited Iraq only once, at age ten, had no close family there, spoke broken Arabic, and had no education or permanent employment. He was unmarried but had a Danish fiancée; their relationship began only a few days before he was remanded in custody in November 2019. Their child was conceived during his detention and born in December 2020.

The applicant had a criminal record beginning in 2010. As a minor, he was convicted of theft and a weapons offence, robbery, and a controlled-substances violation. As an adult, he was convicted of violence and drug offences in 2013; aggravated violence in 2017, receiving a six-month sentence and a suspended expulsion order with a two-year probation period; and violence and drug offences in 2018, receiving six months’ imprisonment and a caution about expulsion. Between October 2013 and January 2020, he was also fined in eight judgments for violations of the Controlled Substances Act.

The index offences arose from a District Court judgment of 9 March 2020. The applicant was convicted of possessing 57.1 grams of MDMA and 12.1 grams of amphetamine for distribution, contrary to Article 191 of the Penal Code, and of keeping a sawn-off shotgun and spare cartridges in an unlocked cabinet at home, contrary to Article 192a, with particularly aggravating circumstances. He was sentenced to two years and nine months’ imprisonment and expelled from Denmark with a permanent re-entry ban.

In ordering expulsion, the District Court noted that he had lawful residence exceeding nine years and applied the Aliens Act. It considered that expulsion was required unless it would “with certainty” violate Denmark’s international obligations, including Article 8 ECHR, and assessed proportionality under the Maslov criteria. It weighed his long residence from age three, weak ties to Iraq, family and social ties to Denmark, lack of education or stable employment, relationship with a Danish fiancée, and extensive criminal history, including the prior suspended expulsion and later caution. It concluded expulsion was not certainly contrary to Denmark’s international obligations.

On appeal, the High Court of Eastern Denmark upheld the judgment on 7 September 2020, finding that expulsion with a permanent re-entry ban was not disproportionate under Article 8. It stated that his engagement and his fiancée’s pregnancy during detention did not change the outcome. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 22 November 2021, and he was deported to Iraq on 18 July 2022.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant argued that the domestic courts failed to properly balance the factors, emphasizing his moderate sentence, previous sentences under six months, strong ties to Denmark through his partner and child, and absence of ties to Iraq. He contended there were no “very compelling reasons” for a lifelong ban. The Government argued that the courts had thoroughly assessed proportionality, noting the relationship began days before detention, the child was conceived during detention, and he had committed serious crimes, had a long criminal history, had previously received a suspended expulsion and a caution, and posed a serious threat to public order.

The Court declared the complaint admissible but ultimately found no violation of Article 8, accepting that there were very serious reasons for expulsion and that the domestic courts had duly assessed proportionality in light of the Court’s case-law.

In *Al-Masudi v. Denmark* (ECtHR, 5 September 2023), the applicant, an Iraqi national born in 1994, challenged his expulsion from Denmark with a lifelong re-entry ban under Article 8 ECHR. He entered Denmark in 1998 at age 3 through family reunion and had held a permanent residence permit since 2002. He had spent almost all his childhood and youth in Denmark, where his parents and siblings lived. By contrast, he had visited Iraq only once, at age 10, spoke broken Arabic, and had no close family there. He was unmarried but had a Danish fiancée and a child born in December 2020; the relationship began shortly before his detention, and the child was conceived while he was in custody. He had no education, no permanent employment, and received cash benefits.

His criminal record began in 2010. As a minor, he was convicted of theft and a weapons offence, robbery, and a drug offence. As an adult, he was convicted of violence and drugs in 2013, aggravated violence in 2017, and violence and drugs in 2018. The 2017 conviction resulted in a six-month prison sentence and a suspended expulsion order with a two-year probation period; the 2018 conviction led to another six-month sentence and a caution about expulsion. Between 2013 and January 2020, he was also fined eight times for controlled-substance violations.

The expulsion arose from a March 2020 District Court judgment. The applicant was convicted under Article 191 of the Danish Penal Code for possessing 57.1 grams of MDMA and 12.1 grams of amphetamine for distribution, and under Article 192a for keeping a sawn-off shotgun and spare cartridges in an unlocked cabinet in his living room under particularly aggravating circumstances. He was sentenced to two years and nine months’ imprisonment and expelled with a permanent lifelong re-entry ban.

The District Court applied the Aliens Act and considered whether expulsion would “with certainty” breach Denmark’s international obligations, especially Article 8. It weighed the *Maslov* factors: the nature and gravity of current and prior offences, length of stay, ties to Denmark and Iraq, family and social links, age, and criminal history. It noted his long residence and family ties in Denmark but also his extensive record, prior suspended expulsion order, later caution, lack of education or employment, and the seriousness of the new crimes. It concluded expulsion was not certainly contrary to Denmark’s obligations.

The High Court upheld the order on 7 September 2020, finding that permanent expulsion and the re-entry ban were not disproportionate under Article 8. It stated that his engagement and his fiancée’s pregnancy during detention did not change the outcome. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused on 22 November 2021, and he was deported to Iraq on 18 July 2022.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant argued that the domestic courts had failed to properly balance his moderate sentence, prior non-serious convictions, strong ties to Denmark, partner and child, and absence of ties to Iraq. He claimed there were no “very compelling reasons” for a lifelong ban. The Government argued that the courts had thoroughly assessed proportionality and that he posed a serious threat, given his serious drug and weapons offences, repeated violence, prior suspended expulsion, post-warning offending, and the timing of his relationship. The Court declared the complaint admissible but found no violation of Article 8, accepting that very serious reasons justified expelling this settled migrant and that the domestic courts had duly assessed proportionality in light of its case-law.

**J&C Properties Limited v. Malta (Application no. 16680/21)**

This case concerns an application lodged against Malta with the European Court of Human Rights by J&C Properties Limited, a company registered in Ħamrun, Malta. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights, stemming from a unilaterally imposed lease on its property.

The key facts are as follows: The applicant company owns a property at 18 St. Joseph High Street, Ħamrun. As of June 2007, this property was subject to a lease imposed under Act XXIII of 1979, which amended Chapter 158 of the Laws of Malta (the Ordinance). The tenant held title under this old, protected lease regime. At the outset, the annual rent payable to the applicant was €390. This amount was subject to periodic increases, rising to €450 in 2013 and €459 in 2016, with further increases linked to the cost-of-living index planned for every three years.

The applicant company initiated constitutional redress proceedings in Malta, arguing that the application of Article 12 of the Ordinance, which governed this lease, breached its property rights. Crucially, the applicant limited its claim to the period ending in December 2017.

Central to the case is the stark disparity between the contractual rent and the actual market rental value of the property. A court-appointed expert estimated the annual market rental value at €4,590 in 2007, €6,300 in 2012, and €9,800 in 2017, for a property with an estimated sale value of €320,000. Over the relevant period, the estimated total market rent was approximately €87,000. In contrast, the applicant’s own expert provided estimates that were half these figures. Even so, the discrepancy between the rent actually received, which was fixed at a few hundred euros annually, and any of the market valuations was substantial.

In a judgment dated 9 July 2019, the Civil Court (First Hall) in its constitutional competence found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It awarded the applicant €15,000 in compensation and ruled that the tenant could no longer rely on the impugned law to maintain title to the property. In its reasoning, the court acknowledged the significant difference between the two expert valuations and determined that the true value was likely a mean between them. This judgment was subsequently confirmed by the Constitutional Court on 6 October 2020, following an appeal by the State.

Subsequently, proceedings were held before the Rent Regulation Board, where the rent was increased in accordance with 2018 amendments to the Ordinance. Following this rent increase, the tenants vacated the property.

Despite winning the constitutional case and receiving compensation, the applicant company remained dissatisfied. It brought the present application to the European Court of Human Rights, complaining that it was still a victim of the violation of its Convention rights. The core of its complaint was that the €15,000 compensation awarded by the domestic courts was too low, given the extensive period during which its property was leased at a rent far below its market value. It argued that this inadequate compensation, coupled with the imposition of the lease itself, continued to constitute a disproportionate interference with its property rights and that it lacked an effective remedy to address this ongoing grievance.

Malta* (Application no. 16680/21), the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) examined a complaint by a Maltese-registered company concerning a unilaterally imposed lease under Act XXIII of 1979, which amended Chapter 158 of the Laws of Malta (the Ordinance). The lease affected the applicant company’s property at 18 St Joseph High Street, Ħamrun, from June 2007. At that time, the annual rent was €390. It increased to €450 in 2013 and €459 in 2016, with further increases every three years linked to the cost-of-living index. The applicant alleged that the application of Article 12 of the Ordinance breached its property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention.

The applicant brought constitutional redress proceedings, limiting its claim to the period ending December 2017. Expert evidence addressed the disparity between the controlled rent and market rental value. The court-appointed expert estimated the annual market rent at €4,590 in 2007, €6,300 in 2012, and €9,800 in 2017. The property’s sale value was estimated at €320,000. On that basis, the estimated market rent over the relevant period was approximately €87,000. The applicant company’s own expert estimated the values at roughly half those amounts.

On 9 July 2019, the Civil Court (First Hall), in its constitutional competence, found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It awarded €15,000 in compensation and held that the tenant could no longer rely on the impugned law to maintain title to the property. The court noted the significant discrepancy between the two experts’ reports and considered that the real value was likely to lie between their estimates. On appeal by the State, the Constitutional Court confirmed the first-instance judgment on 6 October 2020.

Following further proceedings before the Rent Regulation Board, the rent was increased in line with the 2018 amendments to the Ordinance. The tenants subsequently left the property.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant company complained that it remained a victim of the violation of its Convention rights because the compensation awarded was too low. Relying on Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 alone and in conjunction with Article 13 of the Convention, it argued that the domestic redress was insufficient. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore the long-standing controlled lease, the substantial gap between the rent actually received and the property’s market rental value, the domestic finding of a violation, and the allegedly inadequate €15,000 compensation award. The applicant submitted that this award failed to provide just satisfaction or an effective remedy for the breach of its property rights. The application was lodged on 26 March 2021, and the applicant was represented by Dr M. Camilleri and Dr E. Debono.

**J&C Properties Limited v. Malta** (Application no. 16680/21) concerns a unilaterally imposed lease over the applicant company’s property at 18 St Joseph High Street, Ħamrun, Malta. The applicant company, registered in Ħamrun, lodged the application with the European Court of Human Rights on 26 March 2021. The case focuses on Act XXIII of 1979, which amended Chapter 158 of the Laws of Malta (“the Ordinance”), particularly Article 12, and its effect on the applicant’s property rights.

It limited the claim to the period ending December 2017. A court-appointed expert assessed the annual market rental value of the property at EUR 4,590 in 2007, EUR 6,300 in 2012, and EUR 9,800 in 2017. The property’s sale value was estimated at EUR 320,000. The estimated market rent over the relevant period was around EUR 87,000. The applicant’s own expert valued the property at about half those figures. The domestic courts noted the significant discrepancy between the experts and considered the true value likely lay between them.

It awarded EUR 15,000 in compensation and held that the tenant could no longer rely on the impugned law to maintain title to the property. The key issue before the Court was therefore whether the domestic award of EUR 15,000, measured against the market rent evidence and the prolonged statutory control of the lease, was sufficient to provide just satisfaction or whether the applicant continued to suffer from the violation.

In *Ovcharenko and Kolos v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 27276/15 and 33692/15, judgment of 12 January 2023), the applicants were Ukrainian nationals and judges of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine, appointed by Parliament on 4 August 2006 under Parliament’s quota. They complained under Articles 6, 8 and 18 of the Convention that their dismissal from office by Parliament for alleged “breach of oath” violated their rights.

The case arose from a politically sensitive constitutional dispute. In 2004, Parliament amended the Constitution. In 2010, the Constitutional Court declared those amendments unconstitutional because they had allegedly been adopted in breach of procedure, thereby restoring the 1996 Constitution. This judgment was controversial and later criticised, including by the Venice Commission, for raising legitimacy questions. After the 2013–14 Euromaidan protests and the extraordinary change of State power in February 2014, Parliament adopted a resolution on 24 February 2014 titled “On responding to the ‘breach of oath’ by judges of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine.” Parliament dismissed the Constitutional Court judges appointed under its quota, including the applicants, for “breach of oath.” Parliament relied mainly on the judges’ participation in the 2010 judgment, claiming that the Constitutional Court had unconstitutionally amended the Constitution, usurped parliamentary powers, breached democracy and separation of powers, and changed the constitutional order. It also cited two other judgments, from 2012 and 2013, concerning social payments and elections. Parliament further asked the Prosecutor General to investigate the 2010 judgment.

The applicants challenged their dismissal in administrative courts. The first applicant initially succeeded before the Higher Administrative Court, which found that Parliament had failed to follow the procedure for dismissing Constitutional Court judges and had disregarded their functional immunity under section 28 of the Constitutional Court Act for votes cast. However, the Supreme Court quashed that judgment in December 2014. It held that the 2010 judgment had contradicted the constitutional amendment procedure, that the Constitutional Court had no power to invalidate constitutional norms, and that the first applicant’s conduct had obviously breached his oath. It found the other two judgments to be within the Court’s discretion and not a breach of oath. The second applicant’s claim was dismissed on the same reasoning, and the Supreme Court upheld that decision in April 2015.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 8 (private life) and Article 6 (fair hearing). The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were that the applicants were dismissed for participating in a debatable judicial interpretation, not for a clear, serious and flagrant breach of law. Parliament used the vague notion of “breach of oath” without clarifying the scope of Constitutional Court judges’ functional immunity or the mental element required. There had been no legislative change since *Oleksandr Volkov v. Ukraine* to make such dismissal more foreseeable. Domestic judicial review was inadequate: the Supreme Court failed to give an elaborate response to crucial issues, including whether judges could be liable for votes and how to distinguish disputable legal interpretation from arbitrariness or serious misconduct. Although the context involved massive protests and an extraordinary change of power, the Court held that this did not justify discretionary dismissal undermining legal certainty. It stressed that strict and narrow grounds, detailed reasons, and utmost caution are required when Parliament dismisses Constitutional Court judges.

**Summary of Ovcharenko and Kolos v. Ukraine**

The case of *Ovcharenko and Kolos v. Ukraine* concerns the dismissal of two judges of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine (the applicants) for "breach of oath" following a contentious judicial decision. The applicants, Vyacheslav Ovcharenko and Mykhaylo Kolos, were appointed to the Constitutional Court by Parliament in August 2006. The events leading to their dismissal are rooted in Ukraine's turbulent political and constitutional history.

A central fact is the Constitutional Court's judgment of 30 September 2010. In this judgment, the court declared unconstitutional the 2004 amendments to the Constitution, finding they had been enacted through an improper procedure. This ruling effectively reverted the Constitution to its 1996 version, significantly altering the balance of power between the President, Parliament, and the Cabinet. This decision was highly controversial and was later criticized by the Venice Commission for raising questions about the legitimacy of state institutions elected under the now-invalidated constitutional rules. Both applicants participated in adopting this judgment.

The political landscape shifted dramatically in late 2013 and early 2014, culminating in massive anti-government protests and a change of state power in February 2014. On 24 February 2014, the newly constituted Parliament adopted a resolution dismissing the applicants and other Constitutional Court judges appointed under its quota. The stated reason was "breach of oath."

Parliament's resolution justified the dismissal by citing the applicants' role in several judgments. The primary ground was their participation in the 30 September 2010 judgment, which Parliament claimed had unconstitutionally amended the Constitution, infringed fundamental principles of democracy and separation of powers, and changed the constitutional order. Parliament argued this action failed the judges' obligation to ensure the supremacy of the Constitution. The resolution also referenced two other judgments from 2012 and 2013, alleging they violated citizens' rights to elections and social security, though these were later deemed by the Supreme Court to be within the court's discretionary scope and not a basis for dismissal.

The applicants challenged their dismissal in the Higher Administrative Court (HAC). The HAC initially ruled in favour of the first applicant, finding that Parliament had failed to follow the proper dismissal procedure stipulated by the Constitutional Court's own rules and that judges had immunity for their votes. However, this decision was overturned by the Supreme Court in December 2014.

The Supreme Court upheld the dismissal, reasoning that the 30 September 2010 judgment was an "obvious non-compliance" with the judge's oath. It found that the Constitutional Court had overstepped its authority by effectively amending the Constitution, an act reserved for Parliament. The Supreme Court concluded that this action gave Parliament sufficient grounds to dismiss the applicant. It further dismissed procedural arguments, stating that the Constitutional Court's internal rules were not a valid legal basis for challenging the dismissal procedure. The second applicant's subsequent challenge was rejected based on this same legal position.

The applicants alleged violations of Articles 6 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, concerning their right to a fair hearing and private life. The key facts for the Court's assessment were the absence of a clear legal definition of "breach of oath" for Constitutional Court judges, the lack of functional immunity for their judicial decisions, and the use of discretionary parliamentary power to dismiss them for a debatable interpretation of the law, without adequate judicial review.

In *Ovcharenko and Kolos v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 27276/15 and 33692/15, judgment 12 January 2023), the European Court of Human Rights examined the dismissal of two judges of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine by Parliament on 24 February 2014 for “breach of oath.”

The applicants, Mr Ovcharenko and Mr Kolos, were appointed to the Constitutional Court by Parliament in August 2006 under Parliament’s quota. They participated in the Constitutional Court’s judgment of 30 September 2010, which declared the 2004 constitutional amendments unconstitutional because of procedural violations and restored the 1996 version of the Constitution. That judgment was politically controversial and later criticised by the Venice Commission as raising questions about the legitimacy of State institutions.

After the change of power in Ukraine in February 2014, amid massive protests and the flight of President Yanukovych, Parliament adopted a resolution “On responding to the ‘breach of oath’ by judges of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine.” Relying on Article 126 of the Constitution, Parliament dismissed the Constitutional Court judges appointed under its quota, including the applicants, for “breach of oath.” Parliament stated that the 30 September 2010 judgment had unconstitutionally amended the Constitution, usurped parliamentary powers, violated democracy and separation of powers, and altered the constitutional order. Parliament also referred to two other Constitutional Court judgments—of 25 January 2012 on social payments and 29 May 2013 on elections in Kyiv and Ternopil—but the Supreme Court later found that those judgments fell within the court’s discretion and did not amount to a breach of oath.

The applicants attempted to resign voluntarily and challenged their dismissal in administrative courts. The first applicant initially succeeded: on 18 June 2014 the Higher Administrative Court declared his dismissal unlawful, finding that Parliament had not followed the Constitutional Court’s internal procedure requiring preliminary consideration, had used a simplified procedure, and had disregarded section 28 of the Constitutional Court Act, which protected judges from liability for the results of their votes. However, on 2 December 2014 the Supreme Court quashed that judgment and dismissed the claim. It held that the 2010 judgment contradicted the constitutional amendment procedure, that the Constitutional Court could not invalidate constitutional norms, and that the applicant’s participation showed obvious non-compliance with his oath. It rejected the procedural objections, saying the Constitutional Court’s internal rules could not regulate dismissal and that Parliament’s procedure was valid. The second applicant’s challenge was dismissed by the Higher Administrative Court on 26 January 2015 and upheld by the Supreme Court on 28 April 2015, relying on the first applicant’s case.

The applicants alleged violations of Articles 6, 8 and 18 of the Convention. The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 8 (private life) and Article 6 (civil fair hearing). It emphasised that dismissing Constitutional Court judges for participating in a debatable judgment, without a clear interpretation of “breach of oath” or the scope of their functional immunity, undermined legal certainty. No legislative change since *Oleksandr Volkov v. Ukraine* had made such dismissals more foreseeable. The Court stated that utmost caution and detailed reasons are crucial when Parliament dismisses constitutional judges, and that broad discretionary powers were not justified by mass protests or an extraordinary change of State power. Judicial review was inadequate because domestic courts failed to address crucial issues. The Court also noted a European trend towards strict and narrow grounds for sanctioning constitutional judges, distinguishing a disputable interpretation or application of law from serious and flagrant breaches, arbitrariness, serious distortion of facts, or an obvious lack of legal basis. Finally, it stressed that judges’ liability requires consideration of the mental element of the alleged misconduct.

In *Gallo v. Italy* (Application no. 11061/05), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section) delivered judgment on 9 February 2023. The applicant, Mr Michele Gallo, an Italian national born in 1939 and living in Fasano, complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention that he had been unlawfully deprived of his land through indirect or “constructive” expropriation and had received no compensation.

The applicant was co-owner, together with F.L., of a plot of land in Mottola. On 25 July 1974 F.L. sued the Mottola municipality in the Taranto District Court, alleging that the municipality had occupied part of the land without permission and built a road on it. He sought compensation for the dispossession and for depreciation of the remaining land. That first action was struck out on 5 March 1980 because both parties failed to appear at two consecutive hearings. On 6 April 1984 F.L. brought the same damages action again. The District Court ordered an independent expert valuation. On 3 April 1986 the applicant joined the proceedings, claiming that he was co-owner of part of the occupied land and seeking compensation for its dispossession.

By judgment of 29 March 1989, the Taranto District Court declared the occupation unlawful and held that ownership of the land had been transferred to the municipality under the constructive-expropriation rule. The expert assessed the 1974 market value of the applicant’s share at ITL 10,946,450. The court ordered the municipality to pay F.L. ITL 143,139,473 and the applicant ITL 58,891,901 (EUR 30,415), corresponding to the 1974 market value adjusted for inflation.

The municipality appealed. On 14 March 1994 the Lecce Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. The municipality then appealed to the Court of Cassation, arguing, among other things, that the applicant’s compensation claim was time-barred. By judgment of 3 March 1997, the Court of Cassation partly upheld the appeal and remitted the case to the Bari Court of Appeal. On 12 July 2000, the Bari Court of Appeal declared the applicant’s right to compensation time-barred because he had lodged his claim more than five years after the road’s construction was completed on 20 November 1974. It relied on the Court of Cassation’s case-law that, in constructive expropriation, ownership transferred to the administration upon completion of the public works. The applicant appealed to the Court of Cassation, which dismissed his appeal on 23 September 2004.

Later, in judgment no. 735/2015 of 19 January 2015, the Court of Cassation sitting as a full court held that the constructive-expropriation rule was incompatible with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It ruled that individuals were entitled to seek restitution unless they chose to claim damages, and that the five-year limitation period for damages should run from the date the claim was lodged with the court.

Before the European Court, the applicant relied on Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, complaining that he had been unlawfully deprived of his land by constructive expropriation and had obtained no compensation for that deprivation.

ITL 143,139,473 and the applicant ITL 58,891,901 (EUR 30,415), corresponding to the 1974 market value adjusted for inflation.

By judgment of 12 July 2000, the Bari Court of Appeal declared the applicant’s right to compensation time-barred because he had lodged his claim more than five years after the road construction had been completed on 20 November 1974. It relied on Court of Cassation case-law holding that, in constructive expropriation, ownership transferred to the administration upon completion of the public works. The applicant appealed to the Court of Cassation, which dismissed his appeal on 23 September 2004.

In judgment no. 735/2015 of 19 January 2015, the Court of Cassation sitting as a full court later found the constructive-expropriation rule incompatible with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. It held that individuals were entitled to request restitution of their property unless they chose to claim damages, and that the five-year limitation period for damages should start to run from the date the claim was lodged with the court.

**Case: Gallo v. Italy (Application no. 11061/05), European Court of Human Rights, First Section, judgment of 9 February 2023.**

The applicant, Michele Gallo, an Italian national born in 1939, was co-owner of a plot of land in Mottola, Italy. His complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention concerned the deprivation of that land through indirect or “constructive” expropriation and the failure to receive compensation.

The underlying facts began in the 1970s, when the Mottola municipality occupied part of the land without permission and built a road on it. On 25 July 1974, the other co-owner, F.L., sued the municipality in the Taranto District Court for damages. He alleged that the municipality had occupied part of the land without authorisation, had built a road on it, and sought compensation both for the dispossession of the relevant land and for depreciation in the value of the remaining land. In 1980, that action was struck out because both parties had been absent from two consecutive hearings. In April 1984, F.L. brought the same action again. An independent expert valuation was later ordered. In April 1986, Gallo joined the proceedings, claiming that he was co-owner of part of the occupied land and seeking compensation for its dispossession.

By judgment of 29 March 1989, the Taranto District Court found that the occupation had been unlawful. It further held that ownership of the land had been transferred to the municipality under the constructive-expropriation rule. Relying on the expert valuation, the court found that the market value of the applicant’s share in 1974 had been 10,946,450 Italian liras (ITL). It ordered the municipality to pay F.L. ITL 143,139,473 and the applicant ITL 58,891,901, equivalent to about EUR 30,415, representing the 1974 market value adjusted for inflation.

The municipality appealed in June 1989. In March 1994, the Lecce Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. The municipality then appealed to the Court of Cassation in July 1994, arguing, among other things, that the applicant’s right to compensation had become time-barred. In March 1997, the Court of Cassation partly upheld the appeal and remitted the case to the Bari Court of Appeal.

By judgment of 12 July 2000, the Bari Court of Appeal declared the applicant’s right to compensation time-barred. It reasoned that he had lodged his claim more than five years after the road construction had been completed on 20 November 1974. Referring to the Court of Cassation’s case-law on constructive expropriation, it found that the transfer of ownership to the administration had occurred upon completion of the public works. The applicant appealed to the Court of Cassation, but in September 2004 that court dismissed his appeal.

The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 21 March 2005. He complained that he had been unlawfully deprived of his land by indirect or constructive expropriation and had not obtained any compensation for the dispossession, in violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

A significant later development was the Court of Cassation’s full-court judgment no. 735/2015 of 19 January 2015. That judgment held that the constructive-expropriation rule was incompatible with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It stated that individuals were entitled to seek restitution of their property unless they chose to claim damages, and that the five-year limitation period for damages should begin to run from the date the claim was lodged with the court, not from completion of the public works.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore: the unauthorised occupation and road construction; the deemed transfer of ownership under constructive expropriation; the initial award of compensation; the later finding that the compensation claim was time-barred; and the applicant’s resulting inability to obtain compensation for the taking of his land.
