In *Bild GmbH & Co. KG v. Germany* (ECtHR, 31 October 2023), the applicant company operated the German news website *bild.de*. The case concerned an injunction ordering it to stop publishing CCTV footage of a police arrest unless the face of one police officer, P., was blurred.

The facts arose from a police intervention at a Bremen nightclub on 23 June 2013. Police were called because D., a customer, had behaved aggressively toward staff. On 10 July 2013, *bild.de* published an article headlined “Here the police beat up D. (28),” together with CCTV footage obtained from the club owner. The video showed several police officers forcing D. to the ground. One officer appeared to hit D. with a police baton and kick him while he was already immobilised. A voice-over described the footage as “shocking” and stated that it showed how brutally Bremen police dealt with a “supposed troublemaker.” On 12 July 2013, the applicant published a second article and additional CCTV footage showing D.’s prior aggressive conduct before police arrived.

P. was one of the officers involved. He appeared in the footage helping to bring D. down; his face was clearly visible for several seconds, although the video did not indicate that P. himself used excessive force. P.’s lawyer asked the applicant to cease publishing the unblurred footage. When it refused, P. sued. He said he had been confronted with critical comments by members of the public and by his children. German courts ordered the applicant to stop publishing the CCTV footage without blurring P.’s face.

The Regional Court accepted that the footage portrayed an aspect of contemporary society and that the state’s use of force was a matter of public interest. However, it found that P.’s personality rights prevailed. P. had not sought public attention, was unknown beforehand, had not consented to the recording, and the public interest primarily concerned the police as an institution rather than P. individually. It also emphasised that the voice-over aggravated the infringement and that the first video omitted D.’s prior actions. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, reasoning that any unpixelated depiction would be unlawful: negative future coverage would require pixelation, and even positive or accurate coverage would also require it because the footage would then show only a routine police intervention. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to hear the applicant’s complaint.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained that the injunction violated its freedom of expression under Article 10. The Court found the interference prescribed by law and aimed at protecting P.’s rights, but held that it was not “necessary in a democratic society” as regards the second publication and any future publication. While the domestic courts’ balancing could be accepted for the first publication, given its selective footage and critical voice-over, the injunction was broader. It also covered future publication of unedited footage regardless of accompanying coverage. The domestic courts failed to assess how the unblurred image could contribute to public debate, particularly the public interest in police use of force. Their general reasoning risked an unacceptable ban on future publication of unedited images of police officers performing their duties, irrespective of public interest. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 10.

Bild GmbH & Co. KG v. Germany (ECtHR, 31 October 2023) concerned an injunction requiring the news website bild.de to stop publishing CCTV footage of a police arrest without blurring the face of one police officer. The applicant company published an article on 10 July 2013 headlined “Here the police beat up D. (28)” about a police intervention at a Bremen nightclub on 23 June 2013. Police had been called because customer D. behaved aggressively toward staff. With the article, Bild published CCTV footage obtained from the club owner showing several officers forcing D. to the ground; one officer struck D. with a baton and kicked him while he was already immobilised. A voice-over described “shocking footage” and claimed it showed “how brutally the Bremen police deal with a supposed troublemaker.” On 12 July 2013, Bild published a second article, “How the night of the beating unfolded,” with additional footage showing D.’s earlier aggressive actions. The story was then picked up by national newspapers.

P. was one of the officers involved. The CCTV footage showed him helping bring D. to the ground, and his face was clearly visible for several seconds. However, the footage did not indicate that P. had used excessive force. P.’s lawyer asked Bild to cease publishing the footage without blurring P.’s face. When Bild refused, P. sought an injunction and damages before the Oldenburg Regional Court, claiming he had been confronted with critical comments by the public and his children. On 14 May 2014, the Regional Court ordered Bild to stop publishing the CCTV footage without P.’s face being blurred, while dismissing the rest of the claim. It accepted that the footage portrayed an aspect of contemporary society and concerned the State’s monopoly on the use of force, an important public issue. Nevertheless, balancing P.’s personality rights under the Civil Code and Copyright Act, it found that publication violated his rights. P. had not sought publicity, was unknown before the incident, and had been filmed without consent during official duties. The public interest primarily concerned the police as an institution, not P. individually. The voice-over aggravated the infringement by portraying him as a violent thug, and the first video omitted D.’s prior actions, giving an incomplete picture.

The Court of Appeal dismissed Bild’s appeal in 2015. It held that any unpixelated depiction was unlawful; accompanying text might change the context but was not decisive. Future negative coverage suggesting criminal responsibility would require pixelation, and even positive coverage reflecting the actual circumstances would require it because the footage would then show only a routine police intervention. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to hear Bild’s complaint.

Before the ECtHR, Bild complained under Article 10 that the injunction violated its freedom of expression. The Court found the interference not “necessary in a democratic society.” Although police officers may retain privacy interests, and no general rule bars recognizable images, the domestic courts failed to properly balance the second publication and any future publication. The injunction broadly banned any future unedited publication regardless of coverage and without evaluating how the image could contribute to public debate. Such general reasoning risked an unacceptable ban on non-consensual publication of unedited images of police performing duties, irrespective of the public interest in police use of force. There was therefore a violation of Article 10.

In the case of Bild GmbH & Co. KG v. Germany (Application no. 9602/18), the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) examined an injunction by German courts that prohibited a news website from publishing CCTV footage of a police arrest without blurring the face of a police officer.

The case originated from events on 23 June 2013, when police were called to a Bremen nightclub to handle an aggressive customer, D. The applicant company, Bild GmbH & Co. KG, operates the news website bild.de. On 10 July 2013, it published an article headlined "Here the police beat up D. (28)" along with CCTV footage obtained from the club owner. The video showed several officers forcing D. to the ground, with one officer hitting him with a baton and kicking him while immobilised. A voice-over commentary described the footage as showing "how brutally the Bremen police deal with a supposed troublemaker."

A second article, published on 12 July 2013, included additional footage depicting D.'s actions before the police arrived, showing him throwing flyers and making aggressive gestures. The story gained traction in national newspapers.

P., one of the police officers involved in the arrest, was identifiable in the footage for several seconds, although the video did not indicate he used excessive force. On 18 July 2013, P.'s lawyer requested the applicant company cease publishing the unblurred footage. Upon refusal, P. lodged a claim with the Oldenburg Regional Court, seeking an injunction and damages for the violation of his personality rights.

On 14 May 2014, the Regional Court ordered the applicant company to cease publication of the unblurred CCTV footage. Applying Articles 823 and 1004 of the Civil Code and sections 22 and 23 of the Copyright Act, the court acknowledged the footage portrayed an aspect of contemporary society and that the publications concerned the state's monopoly on the use of force—a matter of public interest. However, it found that the publications violated P.'s personality rights. The court noted P. had not sought public attention, the recording was made without his consent during his professional duties, and the voice-over aggravated the infringement by depicting him as violent. It emphasised the first video omitted D.'s prior actions, suggesting deliberate editorial manipulation.

The applicant company appealed. On 27 May 2015, the Oldenburg Court of Appeal indicated it would dismiss the appeal, confirming that the footage portrayed an aspect of contemporary society but that using the unblurred image violated P.'s personality rights. The court held that any unpixelated depiction was unlawful; future coverage, whether negative or positive, would require pixelation. On 21 July 2015, the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, reasoning that unpixelated publication would violate P.'s rights regardless of accompanying coverage, as the coverage could not change the unlawful nature of the depiction.

The Federal Constitutional Court declined to accept the applicant company's constitutional complaint on 3 August 2017 without providing reasons.

The applicant company complained to the ECtHR under Article 10, arguing the injunction violated its freedom of expression. The key legal issue was whether the injunction was "necessary in a democratic society." The ECtHR found that the domestic courts' balancing of competing rights was sufficient for the first publication but not the second and any future publication. It noted the courts failed to evaluate how the image's publication could contribute to public debate and that general reasoning that any unpixelated coverage would be unlawful could lead to an unacceptable ban on future publications, irrespective of public interest in police use of force. The Court held the interference was not "necessary in a democratic society."

**Vashchenko and Tretyak v. Ukraine** (Applications nos. 42489/16 and 74213/17), judgment of 12 March 2026. The case concerned the Supreme Court of Ukraine’s extraordinary reversal of final, binding judgments in the applicants’ favour on the basis of later case-law that did not exist when those judgments became final. Both applicants alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair hearing/legal certainty) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of possessions).

**First applicant – Mr Vashchenko (no. 42489/16).** Vashchenko, a judge at the Khmelnytskyi Regional Court of Appeal, brought an administrative claim in November 2008 against that court, the Ministry of Finance, the State Treasury, and the State Judicial Administration. He sought salary arrears accumulated in 2005–06 and compensation for underpaid income, arguing that judges’ salaries had to be calculated as a percentage of the President of the Supreme Court’s salary, which had increased. On 11 June 2015, the Higher Administrative Court upheld lower decisions awarding him UAH 70,247.73 (about €6,540) in salary arrears, while dismissing the compensation claim. The decisions became final and were enforced on 2 September 2015.

On 19 January 2016, the State Judicial Administration asked the Supreme Court to review the case, citing a different application of substantive law by the Higher Administrative Court in a decision of 20 October 2015—i.e., after Vashchenko’s case had become final. On 30 March 2016, the Supreme Court granted review, set aside the lower decisions, and dismissed his claim in full. It relied on a legal position it had adopted on 4 November 2015, again after finality. There was no indication that Vashchenko repaid the awarded amount or remained liable to reimburse it.

**Second applicant – Mr Tretyak (no. 74213/17).** Tretyak worked since 31 May 2013 at a State-owned energy company in Crimea. After Russia asserted jurisdiction over Crimea, the company’s new pro-Russian management dismissed him on 19 March 2014. In April 2014, he sued the company’s Kyiv headquarters, seeking reinstatement, unpaid wages, compensation for forced absence, and non-pecuniary damages. On 28 October 2015, the Higher Specialised Civil and Criminal Court upheld lower decisions in his favour, finding the dismissal unlawful because the new management in Crimea lacked authority under Ukrainian law. He was awarded UAH 10,897.83 (about €432) in salary arrears and UAH 394,128.91 (about €14,500) in compensation. Those decisions became final and enforceable.

On 13 May 2016, the Kyiv headquarters sought Supreme Court review, relying on different substantive-law applications in later decisions, notably of 16 March 2016 and 23 March 2016. On 12 April 2017, the Supreme Court set aside the decisions on reinstatement and compensation but left the salary-arrears award unchanged. It reasoned that the dismissal had no legal consequences and Tretyak remained an employee. As to compensation, it relied on a December 2014 Chamber of Commerce certificate confirming force majeure for the company’s commercial activities in Crimea and on Article 617 of the Civil Code, exempting the employer from liability.

**Key violation findings.** The European Court of Human Rights found that both final judgments were reversed through an extraordinary review procedure after later case-law post-dated their finality by several months. Applying that subsequent case-law retroactively was unforeseeable and generated legal uncertainty. The reversals were not aimed at correcting an error of fundamental importance to the judicial system or justified by substantial and compelling circumstances. They therefore breached the principle of res judicata under Article 6 § 1. The Court further held that the enforceable judgment debts constituted “possessions”; setting aside the final judgments unlawfully interfered with them, violating Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Article 13 complaint was not separately examined.

**Case: Vashchenko and Tretyak v. Ukraine**  
Applications nos. 42489/16 and 74213/17 – Judgment of 12 March 2026

The case concerned two Ukrainian nationals whose final and binding court judgments in their favour were later reversed by the Supreme Court of Ukraine through an extraordinary review procedure based on subsequent, different case-law. Both applicants alleged that this breached the principle of legal certainty under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and deprived them of their possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

**Application no. 42489/16 – Mr Vashchenko**  
The first applicant, a judge serving at the Khmelnytskyi Regional Court of Appeal, brought an administrative claim in November 2008 against that court, the Ministry of Finance, the State Treasury and the State Judicial Administration. He sought salary arrears accumulated in 2005–06 and compensation for underpaid income, relying on special legislation providing that a judge’s salary be calculated as a percentage of the President of the Supreme Court’s salary, which had increased. On 11 June 2015, the Higher Administrative Court upheld lower decisions awarding him UAH 70,247.73 (approximately EUR 6,540) in salary arrears and dismissing the compensation claim. Those decisions became final and were enforced on 2 September 2015.

On 19 January 2016, the State Judicial Administration asked the Supreme Court to review the decisions because of a different application of substantive law by the Higher Administrative Court in an October 2015 decision in another case. On 30 March 2016, the Supreme Court allowed the review, set aside the lower decisions and dismissed the applicant’s claim in full. It reasoned that a judge’s salary amount and its payment were regulated by different laws, and that budget provisions did not allow the additional payments at the material time. It also relied on its own resolution of 4 November 2015.

**Application no. 74213/17 – Mr Tretyak**  
The second applicant worked from 31 May 2013 at a State-owned energy company in Crimea. After Russia asserted jurisdiction over Crimea, he was dismissed on 19 March 2014 by the company’s new pro-Russian management. In April 2014 he sued the company’s Kyiv headquarters, seeking reinstatement, unpaid wages, compensation for forced absence and non-pecuniary damages.

On 28 October 2015, the Higher Specialised Civil and Criminal Court upheld lower decisions in his favour. It found the dismissal unlawful because the new management in Crimea had no authority under Ukrainian law, and awarded UAH 10,897.83 (about EUR 432) in salary arrears and UAH 394,128.91 (about EUR 14,500) in compensation. These decisions became final and enforceable.

On 13 May 2016, the company’s Kyiv headquarters requested Supreme Court review, citing later decisions of March 2016. On 12 April 2017, the Supreme Court set aside the decisions on reinstatement and compensation, while leaving the salary arrears award unchanged. It held that, under special legislation on temporarily occupied territories, the dismissal had no legal consequences and the applicant remained an employee. On compensation, it relied on a force majeure certificate issued by the Ukrainian Chamber of Commerce and Industry and Article 617 of the Civil Code, exempting the employer from liability.

**Findings relevant to alleged violations**  
The European Court of Human Rights found the complaints admissible. It noted that the Supreme Court’s review procedure at the time allowed final decisions to be challenged solely because subsequent case-law pointed to a different legal solution. The final decisions in both applicants’ cases were reversed after later case-law post-dated them by four and five months. The Court found this retroactive application unforeseeable and generating legal uncertainty. There was no indication that reversal was needed to correct an error of fundamental importance or that substantial and compelling circumstances existed. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1, and, because enforceable judgment debts constituted possessions and the setting aside was not lawful under the Convention, also a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

**Case: Vashchenko and Tretyak v. Ukraine (Apps. nos. 42489/16 and 74213/17), Judgment of 12 March 2026**

The applicants, two Ukrainian nationals, complained that final and binding court decisions in their favour were reversed by the Supreme Court of Ukraine on the basis of case-law that post-dated those decisions. They alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, particularly the principle of legal certainty and res judicata, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, because they lost or risked losing monetary awards they had obtained through enforceable judgments.

**Vashchenko’s case:** The applicant, a judge in Khmelnytskyi, brought an administrative claim in November 2008 against the Khmelnytskyi Regional Court of Appeal, the Ministry of Finance, the State Treasury and the State Judicial Administration. He sought salary arrears accumulated in 2005–06 and compensation for underpaid income, relying on special legislation on judges’ salaries. On 11 June 2015, the Higher Administrative Court upheld lower court decisions granting him UAH 70,247.73 (approximately EUR 6,540) in salary arrears but dismissing the compensation claim. That decision became final and was enforced on 2 September 2015. On 19 January 2016, the State Judicial Administration asked the Supreme Court to review the case, citing a different application of substantive law in another Higher Administrative Court decision of 20 October 2015. On 30 March 2016, the Supreme Court allowed the review, set aside the lower decisions and dismissed Vashchenko’s claim in full. It relied on its later resolution of 4 November 2015, holding that judges’ salary payments depended on the State budget, which had not provided for the additional payments. There was no indication that Vashchenko repaid the awarded sum or remained liable to reimburse it.

**Tretyak’s case:** The applicant worked from 31 May 2013 at a State-owned energy company in Crimea. After Russia asserted jurisdiction over Crimea, the new pro-Russian management dismissed him on 19 March 2014. In April 2014, he sued the company’s Kyiv headquarters for reinstatement, unpaid wages, compensation for forced absence and non-pecuniary damage. On 28 October 2015, the Higher Specialised Civil and Criminal Court upheld lower decisions in his favour, finding the dismissal unlawful and awarding UAH 10,897.83 (approximately EUR 432) in salary arrears and UAH 394,128.91 (approximately EUR 14,500) in compensation. Those decisions became final and enforceable. On 13 May 2016, the company’s Kyiv headquarters requested Supreme Court review based on later decisions of 16 March 2016 and a Supreme Court resolution of 23 March 2016. On 12 April 2017, the Supreme Court set aside the decisions on reinstatement and compensation, while leaving the salary arrears unchanged. It stated that the dismissal had no legal consequences because Tretyak remained an employee, but found no grounds to hold the employer liable due to force majeure in Crimea and Article 617 of the Civil Code.

The domestic law at the material time allowed the Supreme Court to review final decisions where cassation courts had diverged in applying substantive law or where a later Supreme Court resolution pointed to a different solution. The time-limit was three months from the subsequent decision, but no later than one year after the contested decision.

The European Court of Human Rights found that this review procedure generated uncertainty because it depended on future case-law outside the parties’ control. In both cases, final decisions were reversed retroactively on the basis of later case-law adopted only four to five months after finality. The reversals were not aimed at correcting a fundamental judicial error or compelling circumstances, but were routine applications of the review mechanism. The Court therefore concluded that the reversals breached legal certainty and res judicata under Article 6 § 1, and amounted to an unlawful interference with possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

**Metalla v. Albania (Application no. 19646/20)** concerns an Albanian judge’s complaint to the European Court of Human Rights about his dismissal from judicial office through Albania’s vetting process. The communicated complaint concerned the applicant’s right to respect for private life. The key facts relate to the decisions of the Independent Qualification Commission (“IQC”) and the Special Appeal Chamber (“SAC”) under the Vetting Act (“VA”).

The applicant, Ervin Metalla, served as a judge at Durrës District Court from 2001, as its President from 2005, and at Tirana Court of Appeal from 2013. He also chaired the Union of Judges from 2011. Vetting institutions found no concerns regarding links to organised crime, professional skills, or general ethical compliance. The IQC refused his request to investigate those remaining criteria.

On 23 July 2018, the IQC dismissed him under section 61(3) VA because of irregularities concerning his brother E.M.’s assets and the applicant’s asset declarations. It found his conduct unethical, stating that judges must act with integrity in extrajudicial activities and that he had engaged in fictitious transactions.

The applicant appealed and again requested assessment of the remaining criteria, arguing that his teaching, legal manuals, and union work showed his contribution to justice. On 30 October 2019, the SAC upheld the dismissal by a 3–2 majority and added a ground under section 61(5) VA: that an overall assessment showed he had undermined public trust in the justice system.

The SAC’s key findings were as follows. The applicant lived in a rented Tirana flat while commuting to Durrës. In 2007 he signed a preliminary sale contract and commercial loan for that flat; ownership would pass after legalisation and registration, which occurred in 2013. From 2008, Council of Ministers’ Decision no. 600/2007 allowed judges a soft loan with State-covered interest above 4% if they or close relatives did not own a dwelling in their judicial district, limited to housing there. In 2011, annexes replaced the applicant with E.M. as buyer and loan debtor. The applicant admitted this was to make him eligible for the soft loan. The SAC held this created the appearance he no longer owned the flat, though he continued living there; the annex was neither notarised nor declared in his 2011 asset declaration.

The applicant also signed a compliance declaration, a Durrës flat purchase contract, and a 5,000,000 Albanian lek soft-loan agreement, with E.M. as guarantor. E.M. mortgaged a 2008 flat as collateral. Through transactions, the loan was transferred to his father N.M.’s account as “debt repayment.” The funds remained available to the applicant but were not declared as disposable liquidity in 2011. In 2012, debt-exchange agreements directed the funds toward a new Tirana flat; N.M. stated the funds belonged to the applicant. The applicant withdrew from the Durrës contract, allegedly due to delays, but the SAC found the sole purpose was to meet soft-loan conditions. He signed a preliminary contract for the new flat but did not declare it in 2012. In 2013, the applicant, E.M., and a real-estate company agreed that the new flat would go to E.M. and the 2007 flat would remain with the applicant.

The SAC concluded that the applicant hid or misrepresented his use of the 2007 flat while benefiting from the soft loan and allowed inaccuracies about his liquidity in his declarations. It found he obtained the loan in breach of legal criteria and appeared to use it for the Tirana flat, not Durrës. It considered the fictitious transactions for personal gain unethical and damaging to public trust. It also treated E.M. as an “other related person” under VA sections 3(14) and 32(4), shifting the burden to the applicant to prove E.M.’s lawful income. E.M. had replaced him as debtor/buyer, guaranteed the loan, paid 1,000,000 lek in 2011, and had prior financial dealings; evidence showed his foreign income was modest. Two SAC judges dissented, disputing the ethics findings, the legal interpretation concerning E.M., and the finding that the transactions were fictitious.

In *Metalla v. Albania* (Application no. 19646/20), the applicant, Ervin Metalla, an Albanian judge born in 1976, challenged his dismissal from judicial office under Albania’s Vetting Act. He had served at the Durrës District Court from 2001, as its President from 2005, and as a Tirana Court of Appeal judge from 2013. He also chaired the Union of Judges from 2011. The communicated complaint before the European Court of Human Rights concerned his right to respect for private life; the remainder of his application was declared inadmissible.

The vetting institutions found no concerns regarding links to organised crime, professional skills, or general ethical compliance, and the Independent Qualification Commission (IQC) refused the applicant’s request to investigate those criteria. On 23 July 2018, however, the IQC dismissed him under section 61(3) of the Vetting Act based on irregularities concerning his brother E.M.’s assets and his own asset declarations. It found his conduct unethical because he had engaged in fictitious transactions.

The applicant appealed, again requesting assessment of the remaining criteria, including his teaching, legal manuals, and union chairmanship. On 30 October 2019, the Special Appeal Chamber (SAC) upheld the dismissal by a 3–2 majority and added a ground under section 61(5): that the applicant had undermined public trust in the justice system.

The key facts concerned the applicant’s housing and loans. He lived in a rented Tirana flat while commuting to Durrës. In 2007 he signed a preliminary sale and commercial-loan contract for that flat, with ownership to transfer after legalisation and registration in 2013. From 2008, judges could receive a State-subsidised soft loan if they or close relatives did not own a dwelling in their judicial district; the loan was limited to housing there. In 2011, annexes replaced the applicant with E.M. as buyer and loan debtor. The applicant admitted this was to become eligible for the soft loan. The SAC found this created the appearance that he no longer owned the flat, although he continued living there, and the annex was neither notarised nor declared in his 2011 asset declaration.

He then signed a declaration of compliance, a contract to buy a Durrës flat, and a soft loan of 5,000,000 Albanian leks, with E.M. as guarantor. E.M. offered a 2008 flat as collateral. The funds were transferred to his father N.M. as “debt repayment” but remained available to the applicant and were not declared as liquidity. In 2012, debt-exchange agreements redirected the funds toward a new Tirana flat; the applicant withdrew from the Durrës contract, which the SAC considered a device solely to satisfy the soft-loan conditions. He did not declare the new Tirana preliminary contract in his 2012 declaration. In 2013, the new flat passed to E.M., while the 2007 flat remained with the applicant.

The SAC also found the applicant had failed to prove E.M.’s lawful income. It treated E.M. as an “other related person” because of a relationship of interest, including his role as guarantor, the transfer of ALL 1,000,000 in 2011, and the flat transactions. The burden thus shifted to the applicant to prove E.M.’s lawful income, but evidence showed E.M.’s foreign income had been very modest. Two judges dissented, disputing the ethics findings, the interpretation of domestic law concerning E.M., and the conclusion that the transactions were fictitious.

In *Metalla v. Albania* (App. no. 19646/20), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) examined an Albanian judge’s complaint concerning his right to respect for private life under Article 8 of the Convention. The applicant, Ervin Metalla, born in 1976, had served as a judge at the Durrës District Court from 2001, as its President from 2005, as a judge at the Tirana Court of Appeal from 2013, and as Chair of the Union of Judges from 2011. The case arose from his dismissal by the Independent Qualification Commission (“IQC”) and the Special Appeal Chamber (“SAC”) under the Vetting Act. Only the complaint concerning his private life was communicated to the Albanian Government; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The institutions assisting the IQC found no concerns relating to links to organised crime, professional skills, or general ethical compliance. The IQC nevertheless refused the applicant’s request to investigate those criteria. On 23 July 2018, the IQC dismissed him under section 61(3) of the Vetting Act because of irregularities concerning his brother E.M.’s assets and the applicant’s asset declarations. It found that his extrajudicial conduct had been unethical because he had engaged in fictitious transactions. The applicant appealed and again requested an assessment of the remaining criteria, arguing that this would show his contributions to the justice system, including teaching, manuals for legal professionals, and his chairmanship of the Union of Judges.

On 30 October 2019, the SAC upheld the IQC’s findings by a three-to-two majority and added an additional ground under section 61(5) of the Vetting Act: that an overall assessment showed he had undermined public trust in the justice system. The SAC relied on a series of property and loan transactions. The applicant had lived in a rented flat in Tirana while commuting to Durrës. In 2007, he signed a preliminary sale contract and a commercial-loan contract for that flat, with ownership passing in 2013 after legalisation and registration in the seller’s name. From 2008, judges could receive a soft loan if they or close relatives did not own a dwelling in their judicial district; the loan was limited to housing in that district. In 2011, annexes replaced the applicant with E.M. as buyer and loan debtor. The applicant admitted agreeing to this to become eligible for the soft loan. The annex was neither notarised nor declared in his 2011 asset declaration.

The applicant also signed a declaration of compliance, a contract to buy a flat in Durrës, and a soft-loan agreement for ALL 5,000,000, with E.M. acting as guarantor. E.M. offered a flat as collateral. The funds were transferred to the applicant’s father, N.M., as “debt repayment,” but remained available to the applicant; he did not declare them as disposable liquidity. In 2012, debt-exchange agreements redirected the funds toward a new Tirana flat. The applicant withdrew from the Durrës contract, allegedly due to construction delays, but the SAC found the Durrës contract’s sole purpose was to meet the soft-loan conditions. He signed a preliminary contract for the new Tirana flat but did not declare it in 2012. In 2013, it was agreed that the new flat would pass to E.M., while the 2007 flat would remain with the applicant.

The SAC found the applicant had hidden or misrepresented his use of the 2007 Tirana flat while benefiting from the soft loan, and had allowed inaccuracies about his liquidity. It held that he obtained the soft loan in breach of legal criteria, appeared to use it for the Tirana flat rather than Durrës, and engaged in unethical fictitious transactions for personal gain that undermined public trust.

The SAC also treated E.M. as an “another related person” under the Vetting Act, shifting the burden to the applicant to prove E.M.’s lawful income. It cited E.M.’s role as guarantor, his replacement of the applicant as debtor and buyer, a payment of ALL 1,000,000 in 2011, a vehicle sale, and the applicant’s continued use of the flat. The SAC found E.M. had assumed less favourable financial conditions for the applicant’s unilateral benefit and that his foreign income from Italy was very modest. Two judges dissented, disputing the ethics findings, the interpretation of E.M.’s relationship, and the finding that the transactions were fictitious.

**Case O.J. and J.O. v. Georgia and Russia** (Apps. nos. 42126/15 and 42127/15, ECtHR, 19 December 2023) concerned two Georgian nationals arrested on 15 March 2012 at a house in Tagiloni, Gali Region, Abkhazia, by the de facto Abkhaz Security Services. A search found two hand grenades and a hunting knife. The applicants were accused of espionage: allegedly recruiting D.K., a Russian border-guard soldier, as an informant for Georgia’s Military Intelligence Department and acting as intermediaries. On 16 April 2013, the de facto Supreme Court of Abkhazia convicted them; the first applicant was sentenced to 11 years and 6 months, the second to 13 years. They were released on 10 March 2016 after negotiations and interventions by the Georgian authorities.

The applicants alleged ill-treatment at arrest and during questioning. They claimed they were beaten while handcuffed to chairs, waterboarded, and subjected to threats. The first applicant allegedly had his teeth loosened with forceps and was threatened with rape; the second had a rope tied around his neck in a simulated strangulation. Lawyers assigned on 19 March 2012 advised them to confess to stop the beatings. They confessed to ties with Georgian military intelligence and were charged on 23 March 2012. They alleged continued ill-treatment by Abkhaz security services and Russian Federal Security Service staff. They further claimed the de facto Supreme Court relied on confessions extracted under torture, despite their retraction. An appeal was theoretically possible but not pursued as futile.

Jurisdictionally, the Court found that Abkhazia was part of Georgia but outside the Georgian Government’s effective control. Georgia nevertheless had positive obligations to use diplomatic, legal, and other available means to protect Convention rights. Russia, however, exercised effective control over Abkhazia through a strong military and political presence and the Abkhaz authorities’ dependency on it. Russia was therefore responsible for the acts of the de facto Abkhaz authorities in relation to the applicants’ detention.

The applicants complained under Article 3 (torture/inhuman or degrading treatment), Article 5 § 1(a) and (c) (unlawful arrest and detention), and Article 6 § 1 and § 3(c) (unfair trial, lack of an independent and impartial tribunal established by law, and lack of effective legal assistance). They also complained of the absence of effective remedies.

The Court declared the Article 3 complaints inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded. Although the applicants gave a detailed account, they produced no medical certificates, psychological evaluations after release, or corroborating statements from lawyers or family. The Court could not find prima facie evidence of the alleged ill-treatment.

The Article 5 complaints were admissible. Applying *Mamasakhlisi and Others v. Georgia and Russia*, the Court found no information on applicable Abkhaz law or official sources showing a judicial system compatible with the Convention. The de facto Abkhaz authorities and courts could not order “lawful” arrest or detention under Article 5 § 1(a) and (c). Violations were found.

The Article 6 complaints also succeeded. The de facto Abkhaz courts could not qualify as a “tribunal established by law.” The applicants lacked a fair hearing before an independent and impartial tribunal and had no real opportunity to organise their defence or effectively benefit from a lawyer throughout the proceedings. The situation of the legal and judicial system in Abkhazia was not attributable to Georgia. Russia was responsible due to its effective control.

In *O.J. and J.O. v. Georgia and Russia* (Applications nos. 42126/15 and 42127/15), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by two Georgian nationals about ill-treatment, unlawful detention, and an unfair trial in Abkhazia.

On 15 March 2012, a special-forces team of the de facto Abkhaz Security Services arrested both applicants at the second applicant’s house in Tagiloni, Gali Region, Abkhazia. A search found two hand grenades and a hunting knife. The authorities accused them of espionage, alleging that they had acted on instructions from Georgia’s Department of Military Intelligence (DMI) and had recruited D.K., a Russian border-guard soldier, as an informant.

The applicants alleged that during arrest and subsequent questioning they were beaten while handcuffed to chairs and subjected to waterboarding. The first applicant claimed his teeth were loosened with extraction forceps, and he was threatened with rape and having footage posted online. The second applicant said a rope was tied around his neck to simulate strangulation. On 19 March 2012, lawyers were assigned and allegedly advised them to confess to stop the beatings. They then admitted ties to the DMI. On 23 March 2012, they were charged with espionage; the second applicant was also charged with unlawful possession of ammunition and a cold weapon. They claimed ill-treatment continued twice weekly by Abkhaz security services and Russian Federal Security Service personnel. They were held first at Abkhaz security premises in Sukhumi, then in temporary detention, and later in Dranda Prison.

On 16 April 2013, the de facto Supreme Court of Abkhazia convicted them of endangering Abkhazia’s constitutional order through espionage. The first applicant received eleven years and six months’ imprisonment; the second received thirteen years. They told the court that their confessions had been extracted under torture, but the court relied on those statements. They did not appeal, considering it futile. They were released on 10 March 2016 after Georgian negotiations.

The Court found that Russia exercised effective control over Abkhazia because of its strong military and political presence and the de facto authorities’ dependency on Russia. Thus, the acts of the Abkhaz authorities fell within Russia’s jurisdiction. Georgia also had jurisdiction because Abkhazia is part of its territory, but it lacked effective control; its obligation was limited to positive diplomatic and legal measures. The Court found Georgia had satisfied those obligations and was not responsible for the violations.

Under Article 3, the applicants’ ill-treatment complaints were rejected as manifestly ill-founded because they lacked medical certificates, psychological reports, or other corroborating evidence. Under Article 5 § 1(a) and (c), the Court found their arrest and detention unlawful. Applying *Mamasakhlisi and Others*, there was no adequate information on applicable law and no basis to assume a Convention-compatible judicial system in Abkhazia. Russia was responsible; Georgia was not. Under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3, the de facto Abkhaz courts were not a “tribunal established by law,” and the applicants had no real opportunity to organise their defence or effectively use a lawyer. This violation was also attributable to Russia, not Georgia. The case therefore confirmed Russian responsibility for Abkhaz authorities’ acts while dismissing the Article 3 claims and finding no Georgian responsibility.

In *O.J. and J.O. v. Georgia and Russia* (Apps. nos. 42126/15 and 42127/15, ECtHR, 19 December 2023), two Georgian nationals complained about ill-treatment, unlawful detention, and an unfair trial in Abkhazia, a region of Georgia outside the Georgian Government’s effective control.

On 15 March 2012, de facto Abkhaz Security Services special forces arrested both applicants at the second applicant’s home in Tagiloni, Gali Region, Abkhazia. A search allegedly found two hand grenades and a hunting knife. They were charged with espionage, accused of recruiting D.K., a Russian border guard, as an informant for Georgia’s Department of Military Intelligence and acting as intermediaries. On 16 April 2013, the de facto Supreme Court of Abkhazia convicted them, sentencing the first applicant to 11 years and 6 months’ imprisonment and the second to 13 years.

The applicants alleged torture at arrest and during interrogations: beatings while handcuffed to chairs, waterboarding, threats of rape, the first applicant’s teeth being loosened with forceps, and the second having a rope tied around his neck in a simulated strangulation. Lawyers assigned on 19 March 2012 allegedly advised them to confess to stop the beatings. They confessed to ties with the Georgian intelligence service and were charged on 23 March 2012. They claimed ill-treatment continued, including questioning by de facto security services and Russian Federal Security Service staff. They were held first at security premises in Sukhumi, then in temporary detention, then Dranda Prison. They told the de facto Supreme Court that their confessions were extracted by torture, but the court relied on them. They did not appeal, believing it futile. They were released on 10 March 2016 after negotiations by the Georgian authorities.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the key jurisdictional finding was that Russia exercised effective control over Abkhazia and was responsible for the acts of the de facto Abkhaz authorities, including the applicants’ detention. Georgia had jurisdiction because Abkhazia remained its territory, but it lacked effective control; its positive obligations were satisfied, and it was not responsible for the Abkhaz authorities’ acts.

The Article 3 ill-treatment complaint was inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded. Despite detailed allegations, the applicants provided no medical certificates, psychological reports, or corroborating evidence such as statements from family or lawyers.

Under Article 5 § 1(a) and (c), the Court found the arrest and detention unlawful. Applying *Mamasakhlisi and Others v. Georgia and Russia*, there was no information on applicable laws, scarce official information about Abkhazia’s legal system, and no basis to assume a Convention-compatible judicial tradition. The de facto authorities and courts could not order “lawful” arrest or detention.

Under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c), the applicants lacked a fair hearing before an independent and impartial tribunal established by law. The de facto Abkhaz courts did not qualify as a “tribunal established by law,” and the applicants had no real opportunity to organise their defence or effectively benefit from a lawyer. This situation was not attributable to Georgia.

The Court therefore found violations by Russia under Articles 5 and 6, dismissed the Article 3 complaint, and found no responsibility on Georgia’s part for the Abkhaz judicial system.

In *Petryk v. Ukraine* (no. 11103/18, 12 March 2026), the ECtHR examined a father’s Article 2 complaint about the death of his son, P.S., during military service. P.S., 26, married with two minor children, was mobilized in March 2014 and assigned to repair vehicles. On 18 February 2015 he had brief home leave, said he would finish service in about two weeks, and showed no signs of depression. The applicant alleged he overheard P.S. being threatened by superiors V.K. and K.S., but provided no further details. On the evening of 22 February 2015, P.S. returned from the active fighting zone and called his father, saying he was very tired. He promised to call later but never did.

Witnesses said P.S. played dominoes, then left the dugout. A gunshot was heard from his lorry. He was found in the locked cabin, face bleeding, with a rifle between his legs; a soldier broke the window. P.S. had a perforating head wound, was unconscious but alive, and died before reaching hospital. The applicant questioned why he was taken to a hospital 64 km away when another was 14 km away. Some witnesses said P.S. had been upset or irritated during a mobile call shortly before; one said P.S. told him, “You will not drive the lorry after me.”

Two parallel investigations began on 23 February 2015: one into a possible firearm-handling breach, another into murder by unidentified persons. They were not coordinated. The first was discontinued in April 2015. The second was discontinued three times, but each ruling was set aside as unlawful; it remains pending.

The investigation suffered serious delays and omissions. A bone fragment and bullet shell found at the scene were lost without documented seizure. Blood and histological material from the autopsy were destroyed before the parallel investigator requested them. Hand swabs were retrieved only in 2019/2020 and showed no gunpowder. The lorry and gun were returned to the military unit shortly after the death; proper forensic examinations occurred only in 2019 and 2021. P.S.’s mobile phone was first inspected in May 2016 after being stored unsealed. Later, the operator disclosed that P.S. had sent seven SMS messages on the day of his death, but the investigator waited until February 2024 to seek restoration; by then they had been destroyed. The woman linked to the recipient number was questioned only in March 2024; she admitted speaking to P.S. but remembered nothing and denied debts. The Government argued that suicide-prevention mechanisms existed, all possible measures were taken, and deficiencies were compensated. The Court declared the complaint admissible and examined the procedural limb first. In *Petryk v. Ukraine* (Application no. 11103/18, Fifth Section, judgment of 12 March 2026), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint under Article 2 of the Convention concerning the death of the applicant’s son, P.S., during military service in Ukraine.

P.S. was mobilised in March 2014 at age 26. He was married with two minor children and worked repairing vehicles. On 18 February 2015 he had brief home leave and told his family he would finish service in about two weeks. The applicant claimed he had overheard a telephone conversation in which P.S. was threatened by his superiors, but provided no further details. On the evening of 22 February 2015, P.S. returned from the active fighting zone and last spoke to his father by telephone, saying he was very tired. He died that evening.

According to witness servicemen, P.S. played dominoes, left the dugout, and shortly afterwards a gunshot was heard from the direction of his lorry. He was found in the locked cabin with a heavily bleeding face and a rifle between his legs. He had a perforating gunshot wound to the head and died before reaching hospital. The applicant alleged that P.S. was taken to a hospital 64 km away although one was only 14 km away. Witnesses said P.S. had sounded upset or irritated during a telephone call shortly before the incident; one reported that P.S. had said, “You will not drive the lorry after me,” and seemed sad. Most noticed nothing unusual.

Two parallel criminal investigations were opened on 23 February 2015: one into a possible breach of firearm handling rules, and another into murder by unidentified persons. They were not coordinated. The first was discontinued in April 2015. The second was discontinued several times, but those decisions were set aside as unlawful, and the investigation remained pending for over nine years.

The applicant complained that the State had failed both its substantive and procedural obligations under Article 2: it had not protected P.S. while he was under exclusive State control, had not provided a plausible explanation for his death, and had not carried out an effective investigation. The Government argued that suicide-prevention mechanisms existed, all necessary measures had been taken, and the investigation was still examining suicide, firearm mishandling, and murder. It also relied on a social allowance and small non-pecuniary damages later awarded to the family.

The Court declared the application admissible and focused on the procedural limb. It found the investigation had lasted more than nine and a half years and was still pending, which strongly indicated defective proceedings absent convincing justification. No such justification was provided. The main cause was prohibitive delays and manifest lack of diligence. Key deficiencies included: lost bone fragment and bullet shell; destroyed blood and histological material; hand swabs retrieved only in 2019–2020; the lorry and gun returned to the military unit shortly after the incident and examined only in 2019 and 2021; P.S.’s mobile phone inspected first in 2016 after unsealed storage; seven SMS messages sent on the day of death discovered in 2020 but restoration requested only in 2024, after they were destroyed; a relevant woman questioned only in March 2024; and a posthumous psychiatric examination in November 2024 that treated suicide as established. Experts could not determine whether P.S. could technically have shot himself given the wound location and direction, shot distance, and body/gun position.

The Court concluded that Ukraine failed to conduct an effective investigation into P.S.’s death, violating the procedural aspect of Article 2, and found it unnecessary to examine the other aspects.

In *Petryk v. Ukraine* (no. 11103/18), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, judgment 12 March 2026) examined the applicant’s complaint under Article 2 of the Convention concerning the death of his son, P.S., during military service.

P.S., aged 26, married with two minor children, was mobilised in March 2014 and worked repairing vehicles. On 18 February 2015 he had brief home leave and reportedly showed no signs of depression. The applicant alleged he overheard a telephone conversation in which P.S. was threatened by superiors V.K. and K.S. On the evening of 22 February 2015, P.S. called his father after returning from the active fighting zone, said he was very tired, and promised to call later, but never did.

P.S. died that evening from a gunshot wound. Witness evidence, including from superiors and fellow soldiers, stated that after playing dominoes P.S. left the dugout. A gunshot was heard from the direction of his assigned lorry. He was found in the locked cabin, face bleeding, with a rifle between his legs. A soldier broke the window. P.S. had a perforating head wound, was unconscious but alive, and died before reaching hospital. The applicant noted that he was taken to a hospital 64 km away although one existed 14 km away. Some witnesses said P.S. had sounded upset or irritated during a phone call shortly before the incident; one soldier recalled P.S. saying, “You will not drive the lorry after me.”

Two parallel criminal investigations began on 23 February 2015: one into a possible breach of firearm handling rules (case no. 0111) and another into possible murder by unidentified persons (case no. 0223). They were not coordinated. Case no. 0111 was discontinued in April 2015. Case no. 0223 was discontinued three times, each decision later set aside; it remained pending more than nine years later.

The investigation suffered major deficiencies. A bone fragment and bullet shell were lost without documented seizure. Blood and histological material were destroyed before the parallel investigator could examine them. Hand swabs were retrieved only in 2019 or 2020, and no gunpowder traces were found. The lorry and gun were returned to the military unit without thorough forensic examination, with examinations only in 2019 and 2021. P.S.’s mobile phone was first inspected in 2016 after being stored unsealed; later, the operator reported seven SMS messages sent on the day of death to the same contact, but the investigator waited until 2024 to seek their restoration, by which time the operator refused due to lack of judicial authorisation and destruction after the limitation period. The woman contact was first questioned only in March 2024; she admitted speaking with P.S. but remembered no details. Forensic medical examinations could not determine whether self-shooting was technically possible given the wound’s location, direction, distance, body position, and gun position. A posthumous psychiatric examination occurred only in November 2024 and assumed suicide as established.

The applicant argued that P.S. had been murdered and that the State failed both to protect him and to conduct an effective investigation. The Government maintained that suicide-prevention mechanisms existed, all necessary measures were taken, and the ongoing investigation considered suicide, accidental discharge, and murder; certain deficiencies had been compensated.

The Court declared the application admissible and focused first on the procedural limb of Article 2. It found the investigation excessively long—over nine and a half years and still pending—without convincing justification. The main cause was authorities’ delays and lack of diligence. Essential measures, including digital evidence and posthumous psychiatric examination, occurred nine years after death. The passage of time eroded evidence and, combined with past omissions, fatally undermined the investigation. The Court concluded that Ukraine failed to carry out an effective investigation into P.S.’s death, violating the procedural limb of Article 2, and found it unnecessary to examine other aspects.

In *Hakobyan v. Armenia* (Application no. 21350/19), the European Court of Human Rights’ Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 2 April 2026. The applicant lodged the application against Armenia on 15 April 2019 under Article 34 of the Convention. He was represented by Ms D. Shakhramanyan, a lawyer practising in Yerevan. The application was communicated to the Armenian Government.

The applicant complained of an unfair trial in the criminal proceedings against him. His central allegation was that he had not been given an opportunity to put questions in court to the witness whose testimony had played a significant role in securing his conviction. He relied on Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (d) of the Convention, which guarantee the right to a fair trial and, specifically, the right of a defendant to examine or have examined witnesses against him. The key factual issue was therefore that the prosecution relied on evidence from a witness whom the applicant could not effectively challenge through questioning. The witness’s statement was admitted as evidence even though it remained untested by the defence. The full factual details, including the applicant’s identity and the amounts awarded, were set out in an appended table.

In its legal analysis, the Court referred to the general principles established in *Schatschaschwili v. Germany*, concerning cases where a prosecution witness does not attend trial and prior statements are admitted as evidence. The Court noted that those principles usually apply to absent witnesses, but can also apply where witnesses do appear before the trial court yet procedural irregularities prevent the applicant from examining them. They may also guide cases where the issue is not non-appearance but the modalities of cross-examination that limit defence rights, as in *Chernika v. Ukraine*. In the present case, the Court found that the applicant was not provided with an opportunity to put key questions to the witness in question.

The Court examined all the material, including the parties’ observations, and found no fact or argument that led it to a different conclusion on admissibility or merits. It held that the lack of opportunity to question the key witness weighed heavily in the balance when assessing the overall fairness of the criminal proceedings. It also observed that nothing in the materials suggested any effort by the national judicial authorities to use counterbalancing measures to compensate for the difficulties caused by admitting the witness’s untested statement as evidence. The absence of such measures, together with the importance of the witness’s testimony, meant the proceedings did not satisfy Article 6 requirements.

The applicant also complained under Article 6 § 1 that the domestic courts had failed to adequately address his arguments regarding the assessment of the untested witness statement. Having regard to the facts, the parties’ submissions, and its findings, the Court considered that it had dealt with the main legal questions and that there was no need to examine that remaining complaint separately, citing *Centre for Legal Resources on behalf of Valentin Câmpeanu v. Romania*.

Under Article 41, the Court considered it reasonable to award the sums indicated in the appended table, referring to *Avetisyan v. Armenia*. Overall, the Court found a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (d) because the applicant was convicted on testimony he could not challenge through questioning, and no counterbalancing measures ensured the overall fairness of the trial.

Hakobyan v. Armenia (Application no. 21350/19) is a European Court of Human Rights case decided by the Fifth Section Committee on 2 April 2026. The applicant lodged the application against Armenia on 15 April 2019 under Article 34 of the Convention, represented by Yerevan lawyer D. Shakhramanyan. The application was communicated to the Armenian Government.

The case concerned criminal proceedings in Armenia. The applicant complained that his trial was unfair because he did not have an opportunity to put questions in court to a prosecution witness whose testimony played a significant role in securing his conviction. In particular, the witness’s statement was admitted as evidence and was central to the case against him, but the defence was unable to question that witness effectively. The applicant relied on Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (d) of the Convention, which guarantees the right to a fair trial and the right to examine or have examined witnesses against the accused.

The Court applied the general principles established in Schatschaschwili v. Germany concerning cases where a prosecution witness does not attend trial and previously made statements are admitted as evidence. It observed that those principles may also apply where witnesses appear before the trial court but procedural irregularities prevent the applicant from examining them, and where the modalities of cross-examination limit defence rights, as in Chernika v. Ukraine. The central factual issue was therefore not merely the witness’s absence, but the absence of a meaningful opportunity for the applicant to put key questions to the witness whose untested statement helped secure his conviction.

After examining all material, including the parties’ observations, the Court found no fact or argument that would lead to a different conclusion on admissibility or merits. It held that the applicant’s inability to put key questions to the witness weighed heavily in the overall fairness assessment. The Court also emphasized that nothing in the materials suggested that the national judicial authorities had made any effort to use counterbalancing measures to compensate for the difficulties caused by admitting the witness’s untested statement as evidence. Such counterbalancing measures are important under the Court’s case-law when untested prosecution evidence is admitted, because they may restore overall fairness. Their absence, combined with the significance of the witness’s testimony, rendered the proceedings unfair.

The applicant also complained under Article 6 § 1 that the domestic courts had failed to adequately address his arguments concerning the assessment of the untested witness statement. The Court considered that it had already dealt with the main legal questions raised by the case and found no need to examine that remaining complaint separately, citing Centre for Legal Resources on behalf of Valentin Câmpeanu v. Romania.

Accordingly, the Court found a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (d) of the Convention. Under Article 41, having regard to the documents and its case-law, particularly Avetisyan v. Armenia, it considered it reasonable to award the sums indicated in the appended table. The key facts relevant to the violation were therefore that a conviction rested significantly on a prosecution witness’s testimony, the applicant was denied an effective opportunity to question that witness, and the domestic authorities did not apply adequate counterbalancing measures to ensure the overall fairness of the criminal trial.

In **Sobczyńska and Others v. Poland** (Applications nos. 62765/14, 62769/14 and 62772/14), the applicants were three Polish nationals—Aleksandra Sobczyńska, Adrian Klepacz and Rafał Brukiewicz—who at the relevant time worked as junior judges (*asesorzy sądowi*) in Polish district courts.

In 2006, each applied for a vacant district court judge post in Słubice, Jelenia Góra and Gliwice respectively. Under the applicable law, junior judges generally needed at least three years’ service to be eligible for appointment as judges. The applicants’ candidacies were approved by the relevant general assemblies of judges and then by the National Council of the Judiciary (“NCJ”). In 2006 and 2007, the NCJ forwarded their applications to the President of the Republic with motions that they be appointed.

In August 2007, the NCJ informed the applicants that the President did not intend to appoint them. In November 2007, they requested the President to remedy the alleged breach of law. On 3 January 2008, the President issued a decision refusing to appoint nine candidates, including the applicants, to judicial posts. The decision was published on 16 January 2008 in the *Monitor Polski*. It contained no reasons. This was reportedly the first time a President had declined to appoint candidates put forward by the NCJ.

The applicants challenged the refusal. They first lodged complaints alleging inaction by the President with the Warsaw Regional Administrative Court. In early 2008, that court declared the complaints inadmissible, holding that the President was not a public administrative authority and that the appointment of judges was not subject to administrative-court review. The Supreme Administrative Court dismissed their cassation appeals in October 2012.

The applicants also sought annulment of the President’s refusal decision before the administrative courts. In 2011, the Regional Administrative Court declared those appeals inadmissible on similar grounds, and in October 2012 the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed their cassation appeals.

Before the Constitutional Court, the first two applicants lodged a constitutional complaint in 2008, arguing that section 55(1) of the 2001 Act allowed the President to refuse appointment without reasons and without any appeal. On 19 June 2012, the Constitutional Court discontinued the proceedings, finding that the matter concerned the application of the Constitution rather than the constitutionality of a law, and that the complaint was premature. After the administrative proceedings ended, all three applicants lodged further constitutional complaints in 2013. On 12 June 2013, the Constitutional Court refused to entertain them, and on 5 March 2014 a panel dismissed their appeals.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the central alleged violation was under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The Court found Article 6 § 1 applicable because there was a genuine and serious dispute over an arguable right under domestic law to a fair procedure for examining an application for judicial office, including protection against arbitrary rejection. It held that the second condition of the *Eskelinen* test was not met. Denying applicants who met statutory eligibility requirements any judicial review of the President’s refusal was not in the interest of a State governed by the rule of law. The refusal decision contained no reasons, was subject to no review, and bore prima facie appearances of arbitrariness. The essence of the applicants’ right of access to a court was therefore impaired.

The Court also addressed Article 35 § 1, finding the applications timely: the six-month period ran from the final decision refusing to entertain their complaints, as the applicants only became aware of the ineffectiveness of domestic remedies after that decision, in a novel and unprecedented situation.

In *Shabratskyy and Shabratska v. Ukraine* (no. 19234/18), the European Court of Human Rights examined the death of the applicants’ son, D.Sh., in the Ukrainian army and the domestic investigation. The applicants alleged violations of Article 2 of the Convention, concerning both the circumstances of his death and the State’s alleged failure to conduct an effective investigation. The first applicant died in 2024; the second applicant continued the case.

D.Sh. was commander of a reconnaissance and sabotage squad in the Aidar military unit based in Lysychansk, fighting in eastern Ukraine under the Ministry of Defence. He allegedly accused his superiors, company commander I.R. and platoon commander A.Y., of unlawful activities and reported them to the State Security Service. In early March 2015 he told his parents he might be killed by or on the instruction of I.R. and A.Y. On the evening of 25 March 2015 he telephoned them, mentioned a severe headache, and said he planned a brief visit. The unit doctor heard him speaking “in raised tones” with his girlfriend and asking for sedatives. An acquaintance, V.T., said D.Sh. possessed confidential incriminating information about I.R. and A.Y., had been threatened by them, and that evening said he feared for his life and asked V.T. to take him out of Lysychansk.

On 26 March 2015 at about 10:50 a.m., D.Sh. died on military premises. Fellow soldiers K.M. and D.S. said he woke them by firing shots into the wall, told them to stand against the wall and pointed a gun at them; when K.M. asked what was happening, D.Sh. hit him with his left hand, holding a grenade. They left the room. Later, gunshots and a grenade explosion were heard. Witness accounts conflicted about the number of shots, their order relative to the explosion, and timing. D.Sh. was found dead with a perforating gunshot wound to the head and multiple grenade injuries, including a torn-off left hand.

A criminal investigation began that day. The register referred to murder but also noted possible suicide. Police inspected the scene and seized the gun, magazine, bullets, shells and grenade fragments. A May 2015 forensic report said D.Sh. died from combined gunshot and blast injuries and could not exclude self-infliction; no struggle or defence injuries were found. June 2015 experiments suggested it was technically possible for him to pull the grenade pin and shoot himself. The applicants were questioned and described his conflicts with I.R. and his report about unlawful activities. D.Sh.’s girlfriend, A.S., said he had distrusted K.M. and D.S. and had sounded distressed shortly before death; she was never questioned due to difficulties locating her. In March 2016 the investigation was discontinued for lack of evidence, concluding suicide. A court overturned that in June 2016 and ordered resumption.

Later evidence undermined the suicide conclusion. In January 2019, swabs from D.Sh.’s right hand showed no gunshot or explosion residue. Another forensic report found it impossible for him to have shot himself after the grenade exploded, because the wound was inflicted by the left hand, which had been torn off. A July 2021 experiment indicated the grenade exploded while held in his left hand, with him standing, and that a left-handed person might have shot him after the explosion. A November 2021 explosives report ruled out two seated scenarios and found the standing scenario plausible. Meanwhile, authorities repeatedly criticised the investigation as stagnant, incomplete and ineffective, noting failure to question witnesses, ignored prosecutor instructions and delayed measures requested by the applicants in 2016. By 2024, some witnesses could not be located; the investigation remained pending.

**Case Summary: Epidavr S.R.L. v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 29895/16)**

Epidavr S.R.L. is a Moldovan company, registered in Chișinău, specialising in the sale of consumer goods. The case concerns searches of its commercial premises, seizure of its possessions, and the alleged resulting restriction of its business operations. The applicant relied on Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

On 22 September 2015, Moldovan authorities initiated a criminal investigation against the company for tax evasion by a criminal group. An investigator’s internal report later stated that Epidavr might be involved in the criminal activity under investigation.

On 3 November 2015, the prosecutor issued four search orders for the applicant’s headquarters, sales points, and warehouses at four locations. The orders were submitted for authorisation by an investigating judge. Except for the location, their text was identical. They referred to an organised criminal group that allegedly created or acquired “ghost” companies to facilitate tax evasion, money laundering, cash withdrawal, and legalisation of smuggled goods. The orders stated that Epidavr might have been involved and had carried out suspicious transactions with ghost companies between 2010 and 2015. The searches were aimed at identifying and seizing broad categories of accounting records, audit reports, invoices, VAT declarations, contracts, cash-flow records, employee salary information, digital devices, stamps and seals of offshore companies, financial resources, and other documents and objects reflecting the company’s economic activity.

On 5 November 2015, the Centru District investigating judge authorised all four searches, using the same broad wording as the prosecutor’s orders. Between 7 and 9 November 2015, police searched the four locations and seized all accounting documentation and all information carriers. On 9 November 2015, the company requested the return of the accounting server, arguing that its seizure had blocked the company’s economic activity.

On 10 November 2015, Epidavr appealed against all four search warrants. It argued that it had had no procedural standing in the criminal proceedings when the searches were ordered; that there was no reasonable suspicion it had committed a crime; that the warrants contained no reasons and were extremely broad, giving investigators unfettered discretion; and that the search and seizure had made the company unable to operate.

On 19 November 2015, the Chișinău Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal concerning the first location, endorsing the prosecutor’s and investigating judge’s reasoning. It found that the prosecutor’s request was not vague or merely formal because it was based on the decision to initiate criminal proceedings and the investigator’s report.

On 24 and 30 November 2015, a differently constituted panel of the Chișinău Court of Appeal allowed the appeals concerning the second and third locations. It quashed the authorisations and rejected the prosecutor’s search requests as unfounded. The court found that the search warrants lacked reasons; the judge relied solely on the investigator’s report; ownership of the premises was not verified; there was no convincing evidence that the locations contained relevant evidence; and no showing that the information could not be obtained by other means, such as document seizure, audit reports, or tax inspections. It also criticised the overly broad and imprecise list of premises and the vague, wide-ranging objects to be seized. The court noted there was no substantiated causal link between Epidavr and the criminal proceedings and that the company had not been mentioned after the investigation was initiated. It suggested that seizure of objects or documents under Article 126 of the Code of Criminal Procedure would have been more appropriate.

On 14 December 2015, the same panel that had upheld the first search allowed the appeal concerning the fourth location, quashing the authorisation and rejecting the search request for the same reasons given on 24 and 30 November.

According to the Government, all seized documents and objects were examined and later returned to Epidavr, though no date was specified. The case file indicated no further proceedings concerning the company after the searches. The applicant complained that the search warrants were unlawful and that the seizure of its assets and the resulting restriction of its operations violated Articles 6 and 8 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In *Ukrayinskyy and Others v. Ukraine*, 42 Ukrainian nationals detained at Zhovti Vody Correctional Colony No. 26 complained under Articles 3, 8, 13, and 34 of the Convention about inadequate detention conditions, the lack of effective domestic remedies, and interference with their right of individual application to the European Court of Human Rights.

The conditions-of-detention allegations arose after monitoring visits by the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group (KHRPG) in March 2019. During the first visit, monitors met inmates, inspected accommodation units, the canteen, laundry, and bathing facilities, took photographs, and collected complaints. Eighty-four detainees, including 11 applicants, submitted handwritten complaints to the Prosecutor General, the Ministry of Justice, and the Ombudsperson. The subsequent KHRPG report described severe shortcomings: unsanitary and neglected premises, dampness, mould and fungus, poor or absent lighting, limited electricity, overcrowding, thin mattresses, infestations of bedbugs and cockroaches, inadequate access to drinking water, poor tap water, very low winter temperatures, leaking rusty pipes, flooding, toilets without doors or sufficient partitions, insufficient showers, water supplied for only short periods, no flushing water, mould in the canteen, broken taps, lack of soap and towels, poor food quality, and old rusty laundry equipment. The applicants largely repeated these allegations before the Court, adding rodents, lack of hot and potable water, insufficient toiletries and clothing, power cuts, lack of privacy, and poor food served in unsanitary conditions.

The Government disputed the severity of the conditions, claiming renovations, repairs, anti-fungal treatment, pest control, adequate heating, weekly showers, and compliant drinking water. However, it admitted that water was cut off daily for several hours and electricity was disconnected during the day because of utility arrears. Ombudsperson reports from 2017 and July 2020 corroborated recurring violations, including insufficient living space, leaks, outdated sanitary equipment, lack of ventilation and fresh air, inadequate lighting, dirty or rusty dishes, tensions with the administration, and failure to remedy most earlier problems. The prison was closed in July 2020, and applicants were transferred.

The Article 34 issue concerned events after the applications were communicated to the Government. On 11 March 2020, prison officials organized meetings with applicants about their complaints to the Court. Further interviews occurred on 28 and 31 August 2020 at Zhovti Vody and other detention facilities. During these interviews, four applicants made written statements and six made oral statements saying they had no complaints about detention conditions; 26 declined to comment. Reports were drawn up for each. Some statements allegedly claimed KHRPG representatives had given them blank forms to sign without any intention of applying to the Court. No reports were prepared for applicants nos. 37–40, while applicants nos. 41 and 42 had been released in 2019 before the interviews.

In September and October 2020, representatives visited several applicants. Applicants nos. 4, 18, 23, 26, and 37 reported coercion by prison authorities to withdraw their applications, citing insistent demands, deception, inducement, and pressure. Their handwritten statements were sent to the Court on 2 November 2020. After the Court forwarded these allegations, the authorities re-interviewed the five applicants in December 2020 and January 2021. The Government claimed two said they had signed representative-prepared statements without reading them, three refused to comment, and applicant no. 37 denied pressure. No copies of those statements were submitted.

The Court found an undue interference with Article 34 for 40 applicants through questioning about their applications and, for some, compelling oral or written statements. It found no such interference for two applicants who left prison before the relevant events. It also found a substantive violation of Article 3 due to degrading detention conditions and a violation of Article 13 for the lack of effective domestic remedies.
