**Case summary: Vanesyan and Others v. Armenia**

**Citation and procedural posture.** The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment in *Vanesyan and Others v. Armenia* on 26 February 2026. The case concerned applications nos. 35710/22 and two others, lodged against Armenia under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights on various dates listed in the appended table. The Committee comprised Judges Andreas Zünd (President), Diana Sârcu, and Mykola Gnatovskyy, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The judgment is final but subject to editorial revision.

**Factual background and alleged violations.** The applicants complained principally that the length of their pre-trial detention was excessive, relying on Article 5 § 3 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to trial within a reasonable time or to release pending trial. In one application, no. 38190/23, the applicant also raised a complaint under Article 5 § 1 (c), concerning the lawfulness of detention. The provided judgment does not reproduce the applicant-specific facts—such as names, charges, exact detention dates, or the precise duration of each applicant’s detention—because those details are set out in the appended table, which is not included in the full text supplied.

**Government objection and joinder.** The Armenian Government was given notice of the applications. It argued that the applications were inadmissible for failure to exhaust domestic remedies. The Court examined the Government’s arguments and supporting evidence but found no sufficient grounds to accept the objection. It therefore rejected the non-exhaustion plea, referring to its earlier case-law in *Arzumanyan v. Armenia*, *Vardan Martirosyan v. Armenia*, and *Avushyan v. Armenia*. Because the applications raised similar subject matter, the Court decided to examine them jointly in a single judgment.

**Court’s assessment on Article 5 § 3.** On the merits, the Court recalled the general principles concerning the right under Article 5 § 3 to trial within a reasonable time or to release pending trial, as set out in *Kudła v. Poland* and *McKay v. the United Kingdom*. It noted that in the leading case of *Muradkhanyan v. Armenia*, it had already found a violation in respect of similar issues. After examining all material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on admissibility or merits. Having regard to its case-law, the Court considered that the length of the applicants’ pre-trial detention was excessive. It therefore found a violation of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention.

**Remaining complaint.** In application no. 38190/23, the applicant also complained under Article 5 § 1 (c). The Court examined this complaint and concluded that, in light of all material and insofar as the matters complained of fell within its competence, the complaint either did not meet the admissibility criteria under Articles 34 and 35 of the Convention or did not disclose any appearance of a violation of Convention rights or Protocols. That part of the application was accordingly rejected under Article 35 § 4.

**Key takeaway.** The central alleged violation was the unreasonable duration of pre-trial detention in Armenia. The Court rejected the Government’s non-exhaustion objection, applied its established case-law on Article 5 § 3, and found that the detention had been excessively long, violating the applicants’ right to trial within a reasonable time or release pending trial. The separate Article 5 § 1 (c) complaint was rejected as inadmissible or manifestly ill-founded.

Armenia* (Applications nos. 35710/22 and two others) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights’ Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, in a judgment dated 26 February 2026. **Dzyon v. Ukraine** (Application no. 44249/17) concerns the death of the applicant’s son, a police investigator, at his workplace and the alleged failure of the authorities to conduct an effective investigation. The applicant complained under Article 2 of the Convention that State agents were responsible for his son’s death and that the investigation was ineffective. The European Court of Human Rights declared both the substantive and procedural complaints admissible.

The applicant’s son began working as an investigator at the Staromiskyi district police station in Vinnytsya on 28 February 2010. Pre-employment medical and psychological examinations revealed no abnormalities, except emotional immaturity when facing difficulties. On 19 May 2010, at about 6:13 p.m., he died in his office from a gunshot wound to the chest near the heart. He also had scratches and bruises on his head. A pistol belonging to his superior, S., was found at the scene. The prosecutor’s office opened a criminal investigation into official negligence.

Forensic examinations found a close-range gunshot entry wound to the front of the chest and an exit wound to the back, with a downward trajectory. Experts ruled out a shot from behind and said the son could have been sitting at his desk. There was no objective evidence that his body had been moved after death. The head injuries could, according to some early expert assessments, have been caused by contact with blunt objects such as the pistol bolt or surrounding objects during a fall, though no defensive injuries were recorded. Experts noted no signs of suicidal ideation or increased suggestibility.

Witness accounts were conflicting. S. and K. claimed the son locked and barricaded himself in his office, took S.’s service pistol from a safe, and shot himself. K. telephoned the applicant, saying his son had barricaded himself and that K. “did not want to go to prison.” The applicant testified that his son had conflicts with superiors K. and S., and later alleged that they had pressured him to arrest a suspect, L., in order to obtain a bribe. According to the applicant, when his son refused, he was beaten and shot by superiors and colleagues. His wife and other son supported this account. L.’s lawyer confirmed an argument about arresting her client. Colleagues described a generally friendly atmosphere and no ongoing conflict, but viewed the son as isolated.

S. was charged with negligent official duties and later convicted of negligent storage of a service weapon; his sentence was suspended. The Vinnytsya City Court rejected the applicant’s claim that his son had been murdered. In 2013, the Court of Appeal quashed that decision due to contradictions in witness statements and forensic evidence, and ordered a fresh investigation, criticising the failure to properly check the murder allegation, possible motive, and the alleged theft of S.’s pistol. A new investigation covered murder, theft and appropriation of a weapon, abuse of power, and expert misconduct. In 2020, proceedings against S. were terminated because the limitation period had expired.

In 2022, an additional forensic medical examination concluded that multiple bruises on the son’s head could not have resulted from a fall during the agonal period and that witness statements about his position when shot were questionable and contradicted the forensic evidence. In 2024, an investigation was opened into alleged torture and murder by colleagues, later joined with the existing proceedings. The investigation remains ongoing.

The Government argued that the domestic investigation had been effective and established suicide and negligence, and that the substantive complaint was incompatible with the Convention. The Court found the Article 2 complaints admissible, reiterating that an effective investigation must be adequate, prompt, independent, and involve the deceased’s family, though it is an obligation of means, not results.

**Summary**

The applicant, Mr Valentyn Ivanovych Dzyon, a Ukrainian national born in 1954, complained under Article 2 of the Convention that State agents were responsible for the death of his son, a police investigator, at his workplace, and that the investigation into the incident was ineffective.

His son was appointed as an investigator at the Staromiskyi district police station in Vinnytsya on 28 February 2010. Pre-employment medical and psychological examinations revealed no abnormalities, except emotional immaturity when facing difficulties.

On 19 May 2010, at about 6.13 p.m., the son died in his office from a gunshot to the chest near the heart. He also had multiple scratches and bruises on his head. The pistol found at the scene belonged to his superior, S.

Forensic examinations established a single entry wound to the front of the chest and an exit wound to the back, the bullet having been fired at close range from in front of the deceased on a downward trajectory. Experts ruled out a shot from behind. At the time of firing, the son could have been sitting behind a desk. There was no objective forensic evidence that the body had been moved or touched after death. The head injuries could have occurred shortly before death, possibly from contact with blunt objects such as the pistol bolt or surrounding objects during a fall in the agonal period. No other injuries suggesting assault or a struggle were recorded. The experts noted no history of suicidal ideation.

A criminal investigation into negligence in official duties was opened on 21 May 2010, and S. was charged on 27 May 2010. The applicant and his family were granted victim status. The applicant initially testified about work-related disputes between his son and his superiors K. and S. On the day of the death his son had telephoned his mother calling K. and S. “bitches”, and at about 6.10 p.m. K. telephoned the applicant saying his son had barricaded himself in his office and that K. “did not want to go to prison”. The applicant later changed his testimony, alleging that K. and S. had pressured his son to arrest a suspect, L., to obtain a bribe, and that after his refusal he had been severely beaten and shot by his superiors and colleagues. His wife, his other son and L.’s lawyer gave corroborating accounts.

S., K. and other colleagues stated that S. had left his service pistol in an office safe with the key in a drawer; the son allegedly took it and shot himself after locking himself in his office and blocking the door with a bookcase. Colleagues described a friendly atmosphere, though the son was reserved and sometimes stayed overnight.

On 7 June 2011 S. was indicted on the basis that the son had taken the pistol and shot himself. On 29 April 2013 S. was convicted and given a suspended four-year sentence; the court rejected the applicant’s murder allegation. On 12 August 2013 the Court of Appeal quashed that decision, citing contradictions in witness statements and forensic evidence and the authorities’ failure to verify the applicant’s claims or prove that his son had stolen the pistol. A fresh investigation opened in September 2013 into murder, theft of a weapon and abuse of power by police and experts.

Between 2013 and 2018 more than 20 forensic examinations were conducted. In 2019 the case was transferred to the State Bureau of Investigations. In February 2020 S. was again charged with negligent storage of a weapon and negligence; in June 2020 the proceedings against him were terminated on expiry of the five-year limitation period, upheld on appeal and by the Supreme Court.

A December 2022 forensic report concluded that the bruises on the son’s head could not have resulted from a fall during the agonal period, and that witness statements about his position when shot were questionable and contradicted the forensic evidence. In August 2024 an investigation was opened into alleged torture and murder by colleagues with extreme cruelty, later joined to the main proceedings, which remain ongoing.

The Court declared the applicant’s complaints admissible.

Ukraine* (Application no. 44249/17, judgment of 12 February 2026), the applicant, Valentyn Dzyon, complained under Article 2 of the Convention that State agents were responsible for his son’s death at his workplace and that the ensuing investigation was ineffective. The pistol found at the scene belonged to his superior, S. A criminal investigation was opened for negligence in official duties causing grave consequences.

Forensic examinations found a single entry wound to the front of the chest and an exit wound to the back. The shot was fired at close range from in front of the deceased, with a downward trajectory; experts ruled out a shot from behind. At the time, the son could have been sitting on a chair behind a desk. There was no objective forensic evidence that his body had been moved or touched after death. The head injuries could have been caused shortly before death by contact with blunt objects, such as the pistol bolt, or by surrounding objects during a fall in the agonal period. The applicant testified that his son had work-related disputes with superiors K. and S. On the day of his death, the son told his mother that K. and S. were “bitches.” K. later telephoned the applicant, saying the son had barricaded himself in his office and that K. “did not want to go to prison.” The applicant later alleged that K. and S. had pressured his son to arrest a suspect, L., to obtain a bribe, and that after his refusal, superiors and colleagues beat and shot him. His wife and other son confirmed this account in part, and L.’s lawyer corroborated a conflict between the son and K. over the arrest.

Witnesses gave a different account. S. said he had secured his service pistol in a safe and left the key in a drawer. After the son locked himself in his office and blocked the door with a bookcase, access was gained. While S. removed case files, he heard a gunshot; the son had shot himself. K. said the son was smiling, had no ongoing conflict, handled routine matters, but had difficulties coping. Another investigator saw the son slumped with the pistol in his right hand. Colleagues described a friendly atmosphere, though the son appeared isolated.

In 2011, S. was indicted on the basis that the son had taken the pistol and shot himself. In 2013, S. was convicted of negligent storage and given a suspended sentence; the court rejected the applicant’s murder allegation. The Court of Appeal quashed that decision due to contradictions and inconsistencies and ordered a fresh investigation, noting that authorities had not properly examined the lack of suicide motive or the murder claim. A new investigation opened into murder, theft, abuse of power, and expert misconduct. S. was charged again in 2020, but proceedings were terminated due to the limitation period. In 2022, an additional forensic report concluded that the head bruises could not have resulted from an agonal fall and that witness statements on the son’s position contradicted the forensic evidence. In 2024, an investigation was opened into alleged torture and murder by colleagues. The investigation remains ongoing.

The Government argued the procedural complaint was manifestly ill-founded and the substantive complaint incompatible, because the investigation established suicide and negligence. The Court declared the Article 2 complaints admissible under both the substantive and procedural limbs. It reiterated that the obligation to conduct an effective investigation is one of means, not results, and is assessed by adequacy, promptness, family involvement, and independence.

In **D.M. v. Sweden** (Application no. 32694/23, ECtHR First Section, judgment 26 March 2026), the applicant was an Afghan national of Hazara ethnicity facing deportation from Sweden to Afghanistan. He complained that removal would breach **Articles 2 and 3** of the European Convention on Human Rights and that the domestic asylum proceedings did not meet the required standards, including under **Article 13**.

The applicant applied for asylum in Sweden in October 2015. He claimed to be an unaccompanied minor born in 1999, but German records showed a different name and a 1993 birth date. He declined a medical age assessment. Swedish authorities therefore treated him as an adult and found his identity not established as probable. His Afghan nationality was accepted, and his place of origin was ultimately treated as **Mazar-e Sharif**.

In his first asylum proceedings, he relied on a land dispute, participation in a demonstration, and conversion to Christianity. The Migration Agency rejected his application in October 2017 and ordered his deportation. The Migration Court upheld that decision in March 2018, and the Migration Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal. Later requests for residence permits or re-examination failed, although he briefly received a temporary study permit. After the Taliban takeover in 2021, he lodged a fresh asylum application in June 2022.

In the second proceedings, he repeated his earlier grounds and added claims based on his **Hazara ethnicity**, his **westernisation** after years in Sweden, his alleged apostasy, continued Christian activity, social-media threats, and inability to live as a Muslim under Taliban rule. He submitted church documents and evidence of adaptation to Swedish society, including education, language accent, Western dress, and being clean-shaven.

In March 2023, the Migration Agency again rejected his asylum request. It found his identity still unestablished, maintained that he was from Mazar-e Sharif, and concluded that neither Hazaras nor “westernised” returnees generally faced a protection risk. It did not accept that his conversion was genuine or that he risked being perceived as an apostate. It also found no province with indiscriminate violence at the level required for subsidiary protection and considered return via Kabul to Mazar-e Sharif safe. The Stockholm Migration Court upheld this in May 2023, and the Migration Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal in August 2023. The ECtHR later indicated an interim measure under Rule 39 staying deportation.

Before the ECtHR, the central alleged violation was that removal to Afghanistan would expose the applicant to a real risk of ill-treatment contrary to **Article 3**. The Court accepted that the general security and human-rights situation in Afghanistan after the Taliban takeover was serious, but held that this alone did not mean every removal would breach Article 3. It also found that Hazaras, though in a dire situation, were not a group systematically exposed to ill-treatment attaining the Article 3 threshold.

However, the Court identified individual risk-enhancing factors: his **Hazara ethnicity**, his **area of origin**, his **long stay in Sweden**, his **westernisation**, and behaviour perceived as transgressing religious and moral norms in Afghanistan. Crucially, the domestic authorities had not carried out a **cumulative risk assessment**. Considering the cumulative effect of his personal circumstances against the general human-rights situation and the situation of Hazaras, the Court found a real risk of ill-treatment. Deportation would therefore violate **Article 3**.

In D.M. v. Sweden (no. 32694/23), the ECtHR considered whether Sweden’s deportation of an Afghan national to Afghanistan would breach Articles 2 and 3, and whether domestic proceedings complied with Article 13. The applicant, D.M., is an Afghan of Hazara ethnicity from Mazar-e Sharif. He applied for asylum in Sweden in October 2015, initially as an unaccompanied minor. German records showed a different name and birth date, and he refused a medical age assessment. Swedish authorities doubted his identity and treated him as an adult. After Dublin proceedings ended, Sweden processed his claim.

In the first asylum round, D.M. claimed risk from a land dispute, a demonstration, and conversion to Christianity. In October 2017 the Migration Agency rejected asylum and ordered deportation. It found his identity unproven and his credibility undermined. It accepted he was Afghan, later accepted Mazar-e Sharif as his origin, but not a genuine Christian conversion. It found no reliable risk from the land dispute or demonstration. Hazaras faced difficulties, but mere ethnicity did not establish persecution. The general security situation in Kabul, Herat and Balkh was serious but not enough to protect all civilians. The Migration Court upheld this in March 2018; the Court of Appeal refused leave.

From 2018 to 2021, D.M. sought reopening or stays, citing Afghanistan and his adaptation to Sweden. He received a temporary study permit, but extensions were refused. After the Taliban takeover in 2021, his case was reopened and later struck out because the deportation order had expired.

In June 2022, D.M. applied anew. He repeated the earlier grounds and added Taliban takeover risks, Hazara ethnicity, apostasy, and “westernisation”. He said he had practised Christianity for years, could not live as a Muslim under Taliban rules, spoke Dari with a Swedish accent, dressed Western-style, and was cleanshaven. In March 2023 the Migration Agency rejected asylum again: identity still unproven; no new grounds; conversion not genuine; no individual Hazara risk; westernisation could be adapted or concealed; no generalised indiscriminate violence; return via Kabul to Mazar-e Sharif was safe. The Migration Court dismissed the appeal in May 2023, and the Court of Appeal denied leave in August 2023. The ECtHR then stayed deportation under Rule 39.

The key issue before the ECtHR was Article 3. The Court held that Afghanistan’s grave general situation did not automatically make every removal unlawful, and Hazaras were not a group systematically exposed to Article 3 ill-treatment. However, the applicant had individual risk-enhancing factors: Hazara ethnicity, area of origin, long stay in Sweden, westernisation, and behaviour perceived as transgressing Taliban religious and moral norms. The domestic authorities failed to assess these factors cumulatively. The Court found a real risk of ill-treatment based on the cumulative effect of D.M.’s personal circumstances in light of the general human rights situation and the situation of Hazaras in Afghanistan. Removal would therefore violate Article 3.

F.B. and Others v. the Netherlands concerned seven applicants—one Azerbaijani, one Moroccan and five Dutch nationals—convicted in separate Dutch proceedings between 2012 and 2018 of very serious offences, including multiple murders, manslaughter, complicity in murder, attempted murder, participation in a criminal organisation, firearms offences and fraud. Each was sentenced to life imprisonment, and all had been in custody since dates ranging from 2006 to 2014. Their convictions became final after Supreme Court proceedings.

The applicants complained under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights that Dutch law and practice made their life sentences de jure and de facto irreducible, so that they had no real prospect of release. Some raised specific circumstances: Rasnabe, a foreign national without a residence permit, argued that his status prevented rehabilitation and reintegration; Admilson Richter cited his psychiatric or personality disorder and related care needs; Marcos Richter and Henriquez challenged the clarity, certainty and judicial review of the review procedure.

Domestically, the Supreme Court initially held in F.B.’s case in July 2016 that the existing execution of life sentences violated Article 3 because Dutch law lacked a specific review mechanism. It adjourned the case. After the Advisory Board Life-Sentence Prisoners Decree and related implementing legislation entered into force, the Supreme Court reversed its position in December 2017. It held that the new system allowed a life sentence to be reduced or pardoned in appropriate cases. Under that system, the first review generally occurs no later than 25 years after imposition, with an ex officio pardon assessment around 27–28 years after detention began, and periodic review thereafter. The Advisory Board assesses progress; criteria include whether continued execution reasonably serves a penological purpose, the prisoner’s behaviour and development, risk of reoffending, and reintegration prospects. The Minister may depart from the Advisory Board’s advice only with reasons, and negative decisions are subject to judicial review. Prisoners may request pardon at any time, and during detention they must be offered activities, work, education, behavioural interventions, and medical or psychiatric care to prepare for possible return to society.

In 2019 the Supreme Court dismissed the other applicants’ appeals, relying on the 2017 ruling. It held that life imprisonment was not per se contrary to Article 3, that the criteria were sufficiently clear, that foreign-national status and psychiatric disorder did not preclude review, and that future uncertainties did not make the sentences irreducible. It noted that if life sentences were never reduced in practice under the new system, that would be a significant factor in future cases.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the central alleged violation was that the life sentences remained irreducible. The Court examined the new mandatory ex officio review mechanism, the publicly accessible and objective criteria, reasoned decision-making, and the availability of judicial review. It found sufficient procedural guarantees. Post-2017 statistical data did not show that life sentences were not reducible in practice, that life prisoners had negligible release prospects, or that pardon was always an isolated exception. The time frame fell within the State’s margin of appreciation. Considering the applicants’ individual circumstances, the Court concluded their sentences were neither de jure nor de facto irreducible. It nevertheless observed that release circumstances could be further specified through procedural refinement and domestic practice. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 3.

In F.B. and Others v. the Netherlands (apps. nos. 28157/18 and six others, judgment 21 April 2026), seven applicants—one Azerbaijani, one Moroccan and five Dutch nationals—complained that Dutch law and practice made their life sentences de jure and de facto irreducible, contrary to Article 3 ECHR. All had been convicted of serious offences, including multiple murders, complicity in murder, attempted murder, soliciting murder and participation in a criminal organisation, and sentenced to life imprisonment between 2015 and 2018. One applicant, Rasnabe, was a foreign national without valid residence status and argued this blocked reintegration. The Richter brothers initially received determinate sentences because trial courts considered life sentences contrary to Article 3, but the Court of Appeal imposed life on appeal.

Domestically, the Dutch Supreme Court initially indicated in 2016 that executing life sentences without a review mechanism was incompatible with Article 3. After the Advisory Board Life-Sentence Prisoners Decree and related legislation entered into force, the Supreme Court in 2017 and 2019 held that Dutch law now provided a review system permitting reduction of life sentences in appropriate cases. Review took the form of a pardon procedure, with mandatory ex officio assessment after a set period (no later than 27 years after initial detention; 25 years after imposition in the applicants’ cases), plus possible applications by the prisoner at any time. Criteria included the prisoner’s behaviour and development, reoffending risk, and whether continued execution served no reasonable penological purpose. The Minister could depart from Advisory Board advice only with reasons, and decisions were subject to judicial review. The Supreme Court found life sentences not per se incompatible with Article 3, while noting that if life sentences were never reduced in practice, the issue could be revisited.

The applicants argued that the review mechanism was unclear, executive-dominated and lacked sufficient procedural guarantees; that rehabilitation activities came too late; and that their individual circumstances—including foreign-national status and psychiatric issues—made release prospects negligible.

The European Court of Human Rights found no violation of Article 3. It held that the sentences were reducible de jure under the new mandatory ex officio review mechanism. The system enabled prisoners to know what they must do to be considered for release and the conditions of review. It involved reasoned executive decision-making combined with judicial review, providing sufficient procedural guarantees. Post-2017 statistics did not show that life sentences were irreducible in practice, that prisoners had negligible release prospects, or that pardon was always exceptional. The criteria were publicly accessible, objective, sufficiently clear and reflected legitimate penological grounds recognised in the Court’s case-law. The applicants’ sentences would be reviewed no later than 25 years after imposition, a timeframe within the State’s margin of appreciation. On the individual facts, the sentences were not de jure or de facto irreducible. The Court added that release conditions could be further specified through procedural refinement, domestic case-law and practice.

F.B. and Others v. the Netherlands (Applications nos. 28157/18 and six others) concerned seven life-sentence prisoners—one Azerbaijani national, one Moroccan national and five Dutch nationals—who complained under Article 3 ECHR that Dutch law and practice rendered their life sentences de jure and de facto irreducible. The applicants had been convicted by Dutch courts for very serious offences, including multiple murders, complicity in murder, attempted murder, manslaughter, participation in a criminal organisation, firearms and fraud offences. Their convictions and life sentences became final between 2015 and 2019 after appeals. They had generally been in detention since dates between 2006 and 2014.

The alleged violation arose from the absence, at the time of sentencing and during execution, of a real possibility of review of a life sentence leading to reduction, conditional release or pardon. The applicants relied on the Court’s case-law requiring that life sentences be reducible both in law and in practice, with clear criteria and adequate procedural safeguards. Some applicants also argued that their individual circumstances—such as foreign-national status without residence, psychiatric disorder, or delayed access to reintegration activities—made release prospects negligible.

Domestically, the Dutch Supreme Court initially accepted in F.B.’s case in 2016 that the then practice of executing life sentences was incompatible with Article 3 because Dutch law lacked a specific review mechanism. It adjourned the case. Meanwhile, the Netherlands introduced the Advisory Board Life-Sentence Prisoners Decree and related implementing legislation. In its final judgment of 19 December 2017, the Supreme Court held that the new system allowed life sentences to be reduced in appropriate cases. The first review would occur no later than twenty-five years after imposition; an ex officio assessment for pardon would occur no later than twenty-seven years after the start of detention, with periodic review thereafter. Criteria included the prisoner’s behaviour and development, risk of reoffending and dangerousness, and other Article 4 § 4 criteria. The responsible Minister could depart from the Advisory Board’s advice only with reasons, and decisions were subject to civil and post-sentencing judicial review. In later 2019 judgments concerning the other applicants, the Supreme Court rejected Article 3 complaints, including claims that the criteria were unclear, that reintegration activities were too late, or that foreign-national status or psychiatric problems made review ineffective.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the key issue was whether this post-2017 review mechanism made the applicants’ life sentences reducible in conformity with Article 3. The Court examined the mandatory ex officio executive review after twenty-eight years’ detention. It found that the mechanism made life sentences reducible de jure and enabled applicants to know what they must do to be considered for release and the conditions of review. The system combined reasoned executive decision-making with the possibility of judicial review, amounting to sufficient procedural guarantees. Post-2017 statistical data did not show that life sentences were irreducible in practice, that life prisoners had negligible prospects of release, or that pardon would always be an isolated exception. The review criteria were publicly accessible, objective, sufficiently clear and reflected legitimate penological grounds. The applicants’ life sentences would all be reviewed no later than twenty-five years after imposition by the appellate criminal court. That timeframe fell within the respondent State’s margin of appreciation. Given the individual circumstances, the life sentences could not be regarded as de jure or de facto irreducible. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 3, while noting that the circumstances for seeking release could be further specified through procedural refinement, domestic case-law and practice.

In *Selami v. Greece* (Application no. 43274/16), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by Kledi Selami, an Albanian national born in 1984, concerning criminal proceedings in Greece. The applicant was charged with intentional homicide and other crimes. By judgment no. 65-78/2011, the Syros Assize Court found him guilty and sentenced him to life imprisonment. He appealed.

The key events relevant to the alleged Convention violations occurred on 22 September 2014, when the Northern Aegean Assize Court of Appeal held the appeal hearing. The applicant appeared in person. Because he did not speak Greek, but only Albanian, the presiding judge appointed an interpreter. The applicant then requested an adjournment. He stated that he had been trying to sell property in his home country to obtain the resources to hire a lawyer of his own choosing. The appellate court refused the adjournment, finding the request vague and ill-founded. Since the applicant had no representative, the court appointed Ms H.H., from the relevant list of lawyers, as his defence counsel under Article 340 § 1 of the Greek Code of Criminal Procedure. The court then suspended the hearing for one hour so that the applicant and the appointed lawyer could prepare his defence.

When the trial resumed, the applicant again requested an adjournment in order to hire a lawyer of his own choosing. The appeal court refused and proceeded with the hearing. By judgment no. 46-55/2014, it found the applicant guilty as charged and confirmed the sentence of life imprisonment.

The applicant then lodged an appeal on points of law with the Court of Cassation, represented by a lawyer of his own choosing. He complained, among other things, that the Northern Aegean Assize Court of Appeal had wrongly refused his request for an adjournment to hire a lawyer of his choosing. He further claimed that the one-hour suspension granted by the appeal court had been inadequate for preparing his defence and that the interpreter had not been made available to him and his representative during that time. By judgment no. 1339/2015 of 18 December 2015, the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal. It held that the presiding judge’s obligation was limited to appointing a lawyer for the defendant; that it was the lawyer’s and the defendant’s omission that they had not informed the court that the time granted was inadequate; and that, after the appointment of Ms H.H. from the relevant list of lawyers, no request for an adjournment in order to hire a lawyer could be raised.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(b) and (c) of the Convention that he had been deprived of legal assistance of his own choosing and had not been given adequate time and facilities to prepare his defence with the lawyer appointed by the court. The case therefore centred on whether the Greek courts’ refusal to adjourn, the immediate appointment of a defence lawyer, the one-hour preparation period, and the alleged lack of interpreter assistance during that period violated the applicant’s fair-trial rights. The Albanian Government did not intervene in the proceedings.

In Damian v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 32935/13), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) examined complaints under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The applicant, Livia Damian, a Moldovan national born in 1977, complained about domestic court decisions annulling the contract by which she had become owner of a non-residential building in Chișinău. The Court gave notice of those complaints and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

The property dispute began in 2002, when Chișinău local authorities allowed a private company L. to erect a building. Another private company M. sued the local authorities, alleging that company L.’s building blocked access to its premises, and sought transfer of similar real estate. On 5 July 2005 the Economic District Court ordered the local authorities to transfer a specific non-residential building to company M. No appeal was filed, and the judgment became final. A political party had rented the building from the local authorities since 2002. The local authorities later transferred ownership to company M., which registered it.

On 10 May 2006 company M. sold the building to E.P., whose purchase and property right were notarised and registered. On 25 November 2006 E.P. sold the building to the applicant for MDL 321,000 (about EUR 18,800). The contract was authenticated by a notary, and the applicant registered her property right on 27 November 2006. At the time of sale, the real estate register contained no limitation or condition on E.P.’s title. After buying the building, the applicant discovered that the political party occupied it. Her requests that it vacate were unsuccessful.

Meanwhile, the political party asked the local authorities to sell it the building through privatisation. On 21 December 2006 the Republican Commission of the Privatisation Agency authorised the political party to privatise the building, and it paid the State MDL 500,000 (about EUR 29,000).

On 5 March 2007 the applicant sued the political party, seeking eviction and annulment of the privatisation decision. The political party counterclaimed, seeking annulment of the contracts between company M. and E.P. and between E.P. and the applicant. It also requested reopening of the proceedings between company M. and the local authorities. On 26 August 2008 the Economic Court of Appeal annulled the final judgment of 5 July 2005 because the political party, an affected third party, had not been involved. The political party participated in those proceedings; the applicant was apparently unaware of them. E.P. had died on 2 June 2007.

After several retrials, on 19 April 2011 the first-instance court rejected the applicant’s action and granted the political party’s counterclaim. It reasoned that annulment of the 2005 judgment destroyed company M.’s basis for ownership, so company M. could not validly sell to E.P.; that contract was null and void. The court also annulled the E.P.–applicant contract as fictitious because the applicant had never taken possession of the building. On 13 March 2012 the Chișinău Court of Appeal upheld that judgment, repeating the nullity and fictitious-contract findings and noting the applicant’s lack of possession. It also observed that the political party had obtained privatisation approval in 2003 for MDL 204,000 (about EUR 12,800) and, as tenant, had priority. On 8 November 2012 the Supreme Court of Justice upheld the lower courts’ decisions.

The applicant lodged her application on 20 April 2013. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are that she acquired and registered what appeared to be clear title, paid the purchase price, and faced retrospective annulment of her ownership because a final judgment underlying her predecessor’s title was reopened and annulled without her involvement. The domestic courts also treated her contract as fictitious due to non-possession, even though the building was occupied by a tenant. These facts underpin her complaints about unfair proceedings under Article 6 § 1 and disproportionate interference with property under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In *Shkuropatskyy and Others v. Ukraine*, the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 16 April 2026. The case originated in four applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates, led by application no. 9085/24. The Ukrainian Government were given notice of the applications. Because the applications concerned similar subject matter, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment.

The applicants’ principal complaints concerned the excessive length of civil proceedings in Ukraine and the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law for that delay. They relied on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees a fair hearing within a “reasonable time,” and Article 13, which requires an effective remedy for arguable Convention violations. The specific applicants, procedural histories, and exact lengths of the domestic civil proceedings were set out in an appended table to the judgment. That table is not reproduced in the provided text, so the precise durations are not visible from the narrative. However, the essential alleged violation was that the civil proceedings had continued too long without adequate justification and that no domestic mechanism existed to provide redress.

In its legal analysis, the Court reiterated that the reasonableness of the length of proceedings must be assessed in light of the circumstances of the case and by reference to the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicants and the relevant authorities, and what was at stake for the applicants. It noted that in the leading case of *Karnaushenko v. Ukraine* (no. 23853/02, 30 November 2006), it had already found violations in respect of similar issues. Having examined all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of justifying the overall length of the proceedings at the national level. It therefore concluded that the length of the civil proceedings was excessive and failed to meet the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1. The Court further found that the applicants did not have at their disposal an effective remedy for those complaints, contrary to Article 13.

In one application—referred to in the judgment as application no. 9085/25—the applicant also raised additional complaints under Article 2 concerning an allegedly ineffective investigation of a traffic accident. The Court examined those complaints but considered that, in light of all the material and insofar as the matters fell within its competence, they either did not meet the admissibility criteria under Articles 34 and 35 of the Convention or disclosed no appearance of a violation. That part of the application was therefore rejected under Article 35 § 4.

As to just satisfaction under Article 41, the Court took into account the documents before it and its case-law, particularly *Karnaushenko*, and considered it reasonable to award the sums indicated in the appended table.

Overall, the key findings were that Ukraine violated Article 6 § 1 by the excessive length of the civil proceedings and violated Article 13 by failing to provide an effective domestic remedy. The separate Article 2 complaint concerning the traffic accident investigation was rejected as inadmissible or manifestly ill-founded. The judgment was final but remained subject to editorial revision.

In *Leocádio de Lemos v. Portugal* (Application no. 34122/23), the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) examined a complaint by Joel Leocádio de Lemos, a Portuguese national born in 1984, living in Silveira. The application was lodged on 4 September 2023. The case concerned the alleged excessive length of the review of the lawfulness of the applicant’s pre-trial detention. He relied on Article 5 §§ 3 and 4 and Article 13 of the Convention. The Court gave notice to the Portuguese Government only of the complaint concerning the length of that review and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

The underlying facts concerned criminal proceedings for drug trafficking. On 10 November 2017 the applicant was questioned by the investigating judge at the Torres Vedras Criminal Court. On the same day, the investigating judge ordered his remand in custody. On 27 November 2017 the applicant requested house arrest with electronic surveillance; that request was dismissed on 28 November 2017. On 4 December 2017 he appealed the remand decision to the Lisbon Court of Appeal. On 5 December 2017 the Torres Vedras Criminal Court declared the appeal admissible. On 5 January 2018 the public prosecutor at the Torres Vedras Criminal Court submitted observations on the appeal. On 23 January 2018 the file was sent to the Lisbon Court of Appeal. On 30 January 2018 the public prosecutor at the Lisbon Court of Appeal issued an opinion under Article 416 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On 1 February 2018 the applicant was notified and given ten days to reply under Article 417; he replied on 8 February 2018. On 28 February 2018 the Lisbon Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and upheld the investigating judge’s decision of 10 November 2017 to keep him in pre-trial detention. On 1 March 2018 the Lisbon Court of Appeal dismissed a further appeal, lodged on 11 December 2017, against the decision rejecting his request for house arrest with electronic surveillance. The applicant was released from pre-trial detention on 28 November 2018.

In 2018 the applicant brought an action against the State in the Lisbon Administrative Court, claiming EUR 3,000 for damage caused by the alleged excessive length of the review of his pre-trial detention. On 25 June 2023 the Lisbon Administrative Court dismissed the action. It observed that the 30-day time limit to decide the appeal in Article 219 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure had been complied with. It further noted that, according to a Supreme Court judgment of 16 March 2018, such an appeal neither suspended the proceedings nor barred the investigating judge from suspending the pre-trial detention or replacing it with another measure. It considered that the time taken to decide the review was therefore not incompatible with Article 5 § 4 of the Convention and that, in any event, it was necessary to ensure compliance with procedural rules, notably the adversarial principle and the requirement for a three-judge panel to decide the appeals.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained that the examination of his appeal against pre-trial detention had been excessively long and that he had lacked an effective domestic remedy in that regard. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore the dates of his detention, appeal, and the appellate court’s decision, together with the domestic compensation proceedings. **Case: A.N. and Others v. Greece** (Apps. nos. 65267/19, 13892/20, 18958/20), European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, judgment of 22 January 2026. The case concerned Afghan unaccompanied minors seeking international protection in Greece who were accommodated at the Samos Reception and Identification Centre (“RIC”) between February 2019 and May 2020. The central alleged violation was Article 3 of the Convention, on account of inhuman and degrading living conditions and the State’s failure to provide adequate reception and protection for vulnerable children.

The applicants arrived on Samos at various dates in 2019. Some were initially registered as adults and later had their age corrected; others were registered as minors from the outset. The authorities sent referrals to the Public Prosecutor for guardianship and to the National Centre for Social Solidarity (NCSS) for accommodation. Due to severe overcrowding, several applicants initially stayed in the informal settlement around the RIC, known as “the Jungle,” or in inadequate areas inside the RIC before being moved to the minors’ “safe zone.” They alleged that the RIC, designed for 648 people, housed several thousand; the Jungle lacked electricity, running water, toilets and waste disposal; sanitation was insufficient; and medical and psychosocial support was extremely limited. The safe zone was overcrowded, lacked heating, bedding and privacy, and offered little supervision or education. Effective guardianship was absent, and transfers to suitable shelters were delayed for months. Some applicants obtained interim measures under Rule 39 requiring transfer to appropriate accommodation, but implementation was delayed.

Individual circumstances included: D.F., whose application was later struck out after an age assessment found he had reached majority and had given false age information; A.N. (no. 13892/20), who was initially registered as an adult, detained after a brawl, later recognised as a minor, attempted suicide and was hospitalised before transfer; and A.M. (no. 18958/20), who was placed in a 22 sq. m dormitory with 11 other minors. Several applicants reported psychological distress, skin infections, respiratory problems and PTSD symptoms. Others were eventually transferred to mainland facilities or relocated to other EU States.

The Government acknowledged overcrowding but argued it was temporary, caused by exceptional migration pressure and COVID-19. It stated that the informal settlement lay outside the RIC perimeter, that a safe zone existed, that basic services were provided, and that Greece expanded accommodation capacity, created a Special Secretariat for Unaccompanied Minors, and implemented relocation and guardianship programmes. It also raised non-exhaustion and abuse-of-application arguments.

The Court found the applicants’ identity, arrival and registration largely undisputed. Their accounts were detailed, consistent and corroborated by official correspondence and independent reports. This constituted prima facie evidence of prolonged exposure to conditions incompatible with their age and vulnerability, shifting the burden to the Government. The Government failed to show that measures were timely and adequate or to rebut the applicants’ accounts. The non-exhaustion objection was dismissed because unaccompanied minors lacked effective guardianship and legal standing, and the suggested remedies were not timely or effective. D.F.’s part was struck out; the remaining Article 3 complaints were admissible and the alleged living conditions were accepted as established.

**A.N. and Others v. Greece** (ECtHR, Fifth Section, judgment of 22 January 2026) concerned several Afghan unaccompanied minors seeking international protection in Greece who were accommodated at the Samos Reception and Identification Centre (“Samos RIC”) between February 2019 and May 2020. The applications alleged a violation of Article 3 of the Convention due to inhuman and degrading living conditions and the authorities’ failure to provide age-appropriate accommodation, care and guardianship.

The applicants arrived on Samos as minors, although some were initially registered as adults or had their birth dates corrected later. Upon arrival or recognition as minors, referrals were sent to the public prosecutor for appointment of a guardian and to the National Centre for Social Solidarity (NCSS/EKKA) to identify suitable accommodation. In practice, the public prosecutor acted only as temporary guardian. The applicants applied for international protection, but asylum interviews were often scheduled years later.

Many applicants initially stayed in the informal “Jungle” settlement around the RIC or in the general RIC area, rather than in the minors’ safe zone. They alleged that the Samos RIC was severely overcrowded, unsanitary and unsafe. The official capacity was 648 persons, but thousands were present. The informal settlement reportedly lacked electricity, running water, toilets and waste disposal. Within the RIC, sanitation, medical and psychosocial support were inadequate. The safe zone for unaccompanied minors had insufficient capacity, and minors allegedly remained for months without effective supervision, education, heating, bedding, privacy or legal representation. They claimed exposure to violence, theft and intimidation, and some suffered psychological distress, infections, respiratory problems or post-traumatic symptoms. One applicant attempted suicide.

Several applicants obtained interim measures under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court in December 2019 and March 2020, requiring Greece to transfer them to suitable accommodation for unaccompanied minors. However, transfers were delayed until January, February or May 2020, despite the Court’s orders. Eventually the applicants were transferred to mainland shelters or relocated to other European countries, including Switzerland, the United Kingdom, Portugal, Finland, France and Germany.

The Government acknowledged that the RIC was overcrowded and that an informal settlement had developed outside the official perimeter. It stated that the safe zone existed but had limited capacity, so not all minors could be accommodated immediately. It relied on the migration crisis and COVID-19 pressures and cited efforts to expand accommodation, establish the Special Secretariat for Unaccompanied Minors, operate a guardianship programme with METAdrasi, and implement relocation schemes. It claimed basic services were provided and deficiencies were temporary.

Third-party interveners supported the applicants, describing persistent overcrowding, inadequate shelter, hygiene, health care and protection, and insufficient access to the safe zone.

The Court struck out the part of application no. 65267/19 concerning D.F., because an age assessment later found he had reached majority and the application had been pursued on false age information. For the remaining applicants, the Court dismissed the Government’s non-exhaustion objection, finding that unaccompanied minors lacked effective guardianship and could not realistically access the remedies cited. The Court found the applicants’ accounts coherent, detailed and corroborated by official records and independent reports, shifting the burden to the Government. The Government failed to provide specific persuasive evidence that its measures were timely and adequate.

The Court reiterated that unaccompanied minors are extremely vulnerable and require special protection. Reception and care must be adapted to their age, and failure to meet basic material, physical or emotional needs may amount to degrading treatment under Article 3. Migration pressure and COVID-19 could not absolve Greece of its absolute Article 3 obligations. The alleged violation therefore concerned prolonged exposure to overcrowded, unsanitary and unsafe conditions, lack of adequate supervision, medical and psychosocial care, effective guardianship, and delayed transfers despite interim measures.

**A.N. and Others v. Greece** (ECtHR, Fifth Section, 22 January 2026) concerned several Afghan unaccompanied minors who sought international protection in Greece and were accommodated at the Samos Reception and Identification Centre (“RIC”) between February 2019 and May 2020. They alleged a violation of Article 3 of the Convention due to degrading living conditions and the authorities’ failure to provide timely, age-appropriate accommodation and care.

At the material time, the Samos RIC had an official capacity of 648 but hosted several thousand people. A large informal settlement known as “the Jungle” developed nearby. The applicants claimed that most new arrivals, including unaccompanied minors, were forced to live there in tents and makeshift shacks lacking electricity, running water, toilets and waste disposal. Sanitation, food, medical and psychosocial support were severely inadequate. The “safe zone” for minors had insufficient capacity, was often overcrowded, lacked heating and bedding, and provided little supervision, education or privacy. Guardianship was formally exercised by prosecutors but, in practice, minors remained effectively unrepresented. Transfers to mainland shelters were delayed for months, even after the Court indicated interim measures under Rule 39.

Individually: D.F. arrived in February 2019, was registered as a minor, stayed in the Jungle until mid-May 2019, and was transferred only in January 2020 after Rule 39; later an age assessment found he was an adult, and his application was struck out. A.N. (no. 65267/19) arrived in June 2019, was initially in the safe zone, had his asylum interview set for 2022, obtained Rule 39 in December 2019, and was transferred in January 2020 before moving to Switzerland. S.N. arrived in February 2019, was initially registered as an adult, corrected in April 2019, stayed in the Jungle until mid-May, obtained Rule 39, and was transferred in February 2020 before going to the UK. A.A. arrived in September 2019, stayed in the Jungle, obtained Rule 39, and was transferred in January 2020. M.H. arrived in March 2019, had his date of birth corrected in November 2019, stayed in the Jungle until mid-April, obtained Rule 39, and was transferred in January 2020. A.N. (no. 13892/20) arrived in July 2019, was wrongly registered as an adult, was detained in October 2019, corrected his age in November 2019, attempted suicide in February 2020, obtained Rule 39 in March 2020, and was transferred in May 2020 before relocation to France. A.M. arrived in September 2019, was registered as a minor, was transferred to the safe area only in June 2020, where he shared a 22 sq m dormitory with eleven others, and was relocated to Finland in July 2020.

The Government acknowledged overcrowding but attributed it to migration pressure and COVID-19, claiming basic services, a safe zone, guardianship and relocation efforts, and only temporary deficiencies. It also raised non-exhaustion and abuse arguments.

The Court rejected the non-exhaustion objection, finding that unaccompanied minors could not effectively access the cited remedies without a guardian. On the merits, it found the applicants’ accounts coherent, detailed and corroborated by official records and independent reports. The Government did not contest their identity or presence, only the adequacy and timeliness of measures. The Court held that the applicants had established prima facie evidence of prolonged exposure to conditions incompatible with their age and vulnerability, shifting the burden to the Government, which failed to rebut it. The key alleged violation was therefore the failure to provide adequate reception conditions and timely transfer to appropriate accommodation, amounting to inhuman or degrading treatment under Article 3.

In *Gahraman v. Azerbaijan* (Apps. 14307/17 and 44088/18), the ECtHR Third Section reviewed an Azerbaijani national’s complaints. Applicant Elgiz Gahraman, born 1986, Baku, was member of Nida civic movement. Context: On 28 July 2016, A.A., senior ruling party official, publicly supported constitutional amendments before Sept 2016 referendum, including removing 35-year minimum age for presidential candidates. He cited Shah Ismail Khatai, 16th-century ruler who ascended at 14 and died at 36. Media speculated amendment aimed to allow President’s son into politics. Same day applicant posted on Facebook: “God willing [his] life will be as short as that of Shah Ismail.” Authorities allegedly saw this as veiled reference to President’s son.

On 12 Aug 2016 applicant was arrested. He claimed five plainclothes officers took him to Organised Crime Unit, where narcotics planted en route were “discovered” during search.

**Gahraman v. Azerbaijan (Applications nos. 14307/17 and 44088/18)**

The applicant, Elgiz Jamal oglu Gahraman, is an Azerbaijani national born in 1986 and living in Baku. At the relevant time, he was a member of the Nida civic movement. The case arises from a Facebook post and his subsequent arrest, prosecution, and alleged ill-treatment.

On 28 July 2016, A.A., a senior official of the ruling party, made a public statement supporting proposed constitutional amendments ahead of a September 2016 referendum. One proposed change would remove the minimum age requirement of 35 for presidential candidates. A.A. cited Shah Ismail Khatai, who became ruler at 14 and died at 36. Some local media speculated that the amendment was intended to allow the President’s son to enter politics. The same day, the applicant posted on Facebook: “God willing [his] life will be as short as that of Shah Ismail.” He later said the authorities interpreted this as a veiled reference to the President’s son.

On 12 August 2016, the applicant alleged that five plain-clothed officers arrested him and took him to the Organised Crime Unit, where narcotics allegedly planted en route were “discovered” during a search. The Government claimed that police officers, accompanied by attesting witnesses, approached him on the street, presented a same-day operational-search decision, and found 3.315 grams of heroin on him. A search and seizure record was drawn up at the station. Criminal proceedings were instituted that day, and he was charged under Article 234.4.3 of the Criminal Code with illegal possession of a large quantity of narcotics with intent to sell. On 13 August 2016, the Narimanov District Court ordered his detention for four months; the appellate court upheld the decision.

Although his lawyers were authorised to meet him on 15 and 16 August 2016, they were not permitted to do so until 18 August, and he did not meet lawyers of his own choosing until 21 August. On 19 August, he was transferred to the Baku pre-trial detention facility and complained to the investigator that he had been ill-treated on 12 and 15 August, leading to self-incriminating statements, which he retracted. He later claimed he had been punched in the head on 12 August and beaten with a baton about fifty times on 15 August. A forensic medical examination on 29 September produced a report dated 13 October concluding that his injuries likely occurred a year and a half earlier. On 17 October, the prosecuting authorities refused to open a criminal investigation, relying on police statements and the medical report. The applicant challenged this before the Sabail District Court, arguing he had been unlawfully detained at the OCU for six days, no cross-examination of police officers had occurred, and the refusal lacked sufficient reasons. The court upheld the refusal on 5 December, and the Baku Court of Appeal upheld that on 20 December 2016.

At trial, the applicant sought exclusion of the search report. On 16 January 2017, the Baku Court of Serious Crimes convicted him based on his self-incriminating statements, police and attesting witness statements, search records, and expert reports, sentencing him to five years and six months. The Baku Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 18 May 2017. On 29 November 2017, the Supreme Court reclassified the charge to Article 234.1 and reduced the sentence to three years.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 3, and Article 13 read with Article 3, of ill-treatment in police custody leading to self-incriminating statements and an ineffective investigation. He also alleged confinement in a metal cage during a pre-trial detention hearing. Under Article 5, he complained that his arrest and detention were unlawful and lacked reasonable suspicion. Under Articles 6 § 1 and 10, he alleged unfair proceedings, conviction on planted evidence, and prosecution intended to punish him for his Facebook post. Under Article 18, he claimed his arrest and conviction pursued purposes not prescribed by the Convention.

**Gahraman v. Azerbaijan** (Applications Nos. 14307/17 and 44088/18) concerned an Azerbaijani national, Elgiz Jamal oglu Gahraman, born in 1986, who at the relevant time was a member of the Nida civic movement. The case arose from events surrounding a 2016 constitutional referendum campaign and the applicant’s subsequent arrest, alleged ill-treatment, and criminal conviction.

On 28 July 2016, A.A., a senior official of the ruling party, publicly supported proposed constitutional amendments, including removal of the minimum age requirement of 35 for presidential candidates. He cited Shah Ismail Khatai, who allegedly ascended the throne at 14 and died at 36. Media speculated the amendment was intended to allow the President’s son to enter politics. The same day, the applicant posted on Facebook: “God willing [his] life will be as short as that of Shah Ismail.” He later stated that the authorities interpreted this as a veiled reference to the President’s son.

On 12 August 2016, the applicant was arrested by five plain-clothed officers and taken to the Organised Crime Unit (OCU). According to him, narcotics were planted en route and then “discovered” during a search. The Government claimed police officers, accompanied by attesting witnesses, approached him on the street, presented an operational-search decision, and found 3.315 grams of heroin on him; a search and seizure record was drawn up at the station. Criminal proceedings were instituted the same day, and he was charged under Article 234.4.3 of the Criminal Code with illegal possession of a large quantity of narcotics with intent to sell.

On 13 August 2016, the Narimanov District Court ordered four months’ pre-trial detention, upheld on appeal. Although his legal representatives were authorised to meet him on 15 and 16 August, they were not permitted to do so until 18 August; he first met lawyers of his own choosing on 21 August. On 19 August he was transferred to the Baku pre-trial detention facility and complained to the OCU investigator that he had been ill-treated on 12 and 15 August and had made self-incriminating statements, which he retracted. The complaint was forwarded to the prosecuting authorities on 10 September. In later interrogation with his own lawyer, he alleged he had been punched in the head on 12 August and beaten with a baton about fifty times and struck on various body parts on 15 August.

A forensic medical examination on 29 September 2016 led to a report dated 13 October 2016 concluding that his injuries were likely to have occurred a year and a half earlier. On 17 October 2016, prosecutors refused to open criminal proceedings concerning the alleged ill-treatment, citing police statements and the forensic report. The Sabail District Court upheld that refusal on 5 December 2016 without addressing the applicant’s arguments that he had been unlawfully detained at the OCU for six days, that no cross-examination of police officers had occurred, and that the refusal was insufficiently reasoned. The Baku Court of Appeal upheld that decision on 20 December 2016.

At trial, the applicant sought exclusion of the search report, relying on a 4 March 2011 Plenary decision of the Supreme Court stating that admissibility of evidence from a personal search before arrest must be assessed by courts. On 16 January 2017, the Baku Court of Serious Crimes convicted him based on his self-incriminating statements during police interrogation, police officers’ statements, attesting witnesses, search and seizure records, and expert reports. He was sentenced to five years and six months. The Baku Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 18 May 2017. On 29 November 2017, the Supreme Court reclassified the charge to Article 234.1 and reduced the sentence to three years.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged violations of Article 3 (ill-treatment in custody and ineffective investigation under Article 13), Article 5 (unlawful arrest and detention without reasonable suspicion), Articles 6 § 1 and 10 (unfair proceedings and punishment for his Facebook post), and Article 18 (ulterior purposes). He also complained of being confined in a metal cage during a pre-trial detention hearing.

In the case of *Borzenkov and Others v. Russia*, Applications nos. 5841/23 and 2 others, the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 26 March 2026. The applications were lodged against Russia under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants complained of torture or inhuman or degrading treatment and of the lack of an effective investigation into those events. Some applicants also raised other complaints under the Convention. Because the applications raised similar issues, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment.

The judgment states that the list of applicants and the relevant details are set out in an appended table. That table is not included in the provided text, so the applicant-specific facts—dates, alleged injuries, domestic proceedings, and the precise treatment complained of—are not reproduced. What is clear is that the alleged violations occurred before 16 September 2022, when the Russian Federation ceased to be a party to the Convention. The Court therefore confirmed it had jurisdiction to examine the applications, relying on *Fedotova and Others v. Russia*.

The applicants relied, expressly or in substance, on Article 3 of the Convention. The Court reiterated that Article 3 enshrines one of the most fundamental values of a democratic society and prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment in absolute terms, irrespective of the victim’s conduct. Where a person is confronted by law-enforcement officers, any physical force not made strictly necessary by that person’s own conduct diminishes human dignity and infringes Article 3. In particular, when authorities use force to quell mass unrest, such force must be indispensable and must not be excessive. The burden rests on the Government to show that force used by State agents, which resulted in the applicants’ injuries, was not excessive.

The Court also applied its established case law on the procedural obligation under Article 3. It noted that a refusal to open a fully-fledged criminal investigation into credible allegations of ill-treatment, a failure to assess the necessity and proportionality of the use of “lawful” force by State agents, and a refusal either to carry out an official inquiry or to register complaints are all indicative of a State’s failure to comply with its procedural obligations. These failures are especially serious where authorities neither investigate nor officially register complaints.

Having examined all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on the admissibility and merits of the Article 3 complaints. The excerpt does not reproduce the final operative provisions or any just satisfaction award, but the reasoning indicates that the Court found the applicants’ allegations concerning ill-treatment and/or the absence of an effective investigation to be established, engaging Russia’s responsibility under Article 3. The case of *Lukashuk v. Ukraine* (Application no. 9079/24) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), delivered in Strasbourg on 22 January 2026. It was adopted following private deliberations on 18 December 2025 and was issued by a Committee composed of Judges Andreas Zünd (President), Diana Sârcu, and Mykola Gnatovskyy, with Viktoriya Maradudina acting as Deputy Section Registrar. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The application was lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights on 13 March 2024. The Ukrainian Government was given notice of the application. However, the provided excerpt of the judgment does not reproduce the applicant’s personal details or the specific factual circumstances of the alleged ill-treatment. Instead, it states that those details are set out in an appended table. As a result, the available text only discloses the core nature of the complaint and the legal issue before the Court.

The applicant complained under Article 3 of the Convention that there had been no effective investigation into ill-treatment to which he had been subjected by private individuals. Article 3 prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. Although the prohibition is primarily directed at State agents, the European Court of Human Rights has recognised that States also have positive obligations under Article 3. These include a procedural obligation to conduct an effective investigation where an individual raises a credible allegation of serious ill-treatment, including ill-treatment inflicted by private parties, particularly where the authorities knew or ought to have known of the risk or the incident.

The key fact relevant to the alleged violation is therefore not merely that the applicant suffered ill-treatment by private individuals, but that the domestic authorities allegedly failed to investigate that ill-treatment effectively. The applicant’s complaint is procedural in focus: he does not complain only about the acts of private individuals, but about the State’s response to those acts. In Article 3 cases, an effective investigation generally must be independent, adequate, prompt, thorough, and capable of leading to the identification and punishment of those responsible. It must also allow the victim or his relatives to participate meaningfully in the proceedings to the extent necessary to safeguard their legitimate interests.

The judgment excerpt indicates that the Court examined the case under the heading “THE LAW — ALLEGED VIOLATION OF ARTICLE 3 of the Convention.” It records that the applicant relied on Article 3 and complained of the ineffective investigation into ill-treatment inflicted by private parties. The available text does not, however, include the Court’s full factual findings, its assessment of the domestic investigation, the parties’ submissions, or the final conclusion on whether a violation was found. The excerpt ends before setting out the Court’s reasoning and operative provisions.

In summary, *Lukashuk v. Ukraine* concerns Ukraine’s alleged failure to comply with its positive procedural obligation under Article 3 to effectively investigate serious ill-treatment suffered by the applicant at the hands of private individuals. The central legal question is whether the domestic authorities carried out an investigation that met Convention standards. Because the supplied judgment text omits the appended factual table and the remainder of the Court’s reasoning, the exact dates, injuries, identity of the perpetrators, and domestic proceedings are not available in the excerpt. The known facts are limited to the applicant’s Article 3 complaint, the procedural history of the application, and the Court’s identification of the alleged violation for examination.
