In *Z v. Iceland*, the applicant, a 16-year-old Icelandic girl, alleged that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into sexual harassment and that the handling of her case reflected gender-based discrimination.

In June 2019, while at a festival, the applicant became intoxicated and went into a tent. She later reported that she sent a Snapchat video at 6:20 a.m. showing she was unwell and the back of a man’s head; she alleged he was groping her, though this was not visible in the video. She said she then passed out and woke around 8:00 a.m. with her trousers pulled down and jumper lifted to her breasts. She recalled hearing a belt being loosened and alleged that O., a 23-year-old man, was touching her breasts and genitals over and under her clothing. She said she pushed him away and told him to stop before leaving the tent.

The applicant went to the Emergency Reception Unit. She declined a gynaecological examination but sought STD testing. Because she was a minor, Child Protection Services were notified. She gave a police statement and provided the video. O. was interviewed. He denied guilt but admitted something was “a little wrong” because he acted before “asking her.” He claimed he found her half-asleep, they cuddled for warmth, and he placed his hand under her jumper and touched her breast, with her bra between them. He said he stopped when she seemed uncomfortable and shook her head, and that the contact lasted about five seconds. He denied touching her genitals or removing her clothing. He said no conversation occurred and she did not touch or kiss him. He described the touching as not sexual and said he knew she was a minor.

The investigation proceeded under Article 199 of the General Penal Code on sexual harassment. Ten witnesses were questioned, but none were direct witnesses. Several confirmed the applicant’s account that she awoke to groping with her trousers down and jumper up, and described her as shocked, traumatised and crying. A later encounter with O. allegedly caused a panic attack requiring an ambulance. Snapchat messages were not preserved because they auto-deleted; recipients reported she had said a man would not let her out and sent crying photos and a man’s head on her chest. Hospital records noted prior psychological support at the Children’s House for earlier sexual violence.

In March 2020 the District Prosecutor discontinued the case, finding conviction unlikely. The prosecutor cited the applicant’s limited recollection, the fact that most witnesses were her friends, unavailable Snapchat messages, unclear video evidence, and a medical report containing no information about the alleged violations. For Article 199, intent to sexually harass had to be established. The benefit of the doubt was given to O., who admitted touching her breast but said he stopped immediately upon realising she did not consent. The State Prosecutor upheld that decision in August 2020, finding insufficient evidence and uncertainty as to O.’s intent.

The applicant argued that the authorities should have focused on the absence of consent, not O.’s denial of sexual intent. She stressed that O. admitted touching her breasts while she was asleep or half-asleep, without her prior consent. The Government maintained that the investigation was thorough and Article 199 was correctly applied, with reasonable doubt as to O.’s intent.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 8. The prosecuting authorities had failed to apply a consent-centred standard to the admitted touching and interpreted the intent requirement unduly narrowly. They focused on whether O. subjectively intended sexual harassment rather than whether he could reasonably have assumed consent when he initiated sexual contact with a sleeping or half-asleep 16-year-old without any prior indication of consent. The fact that he stopped upon perceiving discomfort was not decisive. The investigation therefore did not secure the applicant’s physical and psychological integrity. As to Article 14, the Court found insufficient prima facie evidence of structural gender bias or disproportionate effect, so no violation was established.

In **Z v. Iceland** (Application no. 3538/21, judgment 13 January 2026), the applicant was a 16-year-old girl who reported that a 23-year-old man, O., sexually assaulted her at a festival in June 2019. She had been drinking and withdrew to a tent. In the early hours, she sent a Snapchat video showing she was unwell; O.’s head appeared in the footage. She alleged that O. groped her without consent while she was intoxicated, and that she later passed out. She woke around 8:00 a.m. with her trousers pulled down and jumper lifted, and O. beside her with his belt undone. She said O. touched her breasts and genitals, over and under her clothing; she pushed him away and told him to stop before leaving the tent. She reported the incident to police on 19 June 2019 and attended an emergency reception unit for sexual abuse victims.

O. denied guilt but admitted entering the tent, finding the applicant half-asleep or sleeping, cuddling with her, and putting his hand under her jumper on her breast without asking first. He claimed the contact lasted only seconds, was not sexual, and that he stopped when she seemed uncomfortable and shook her head. He denied touching her genitals or removing her clothing and denied sexual intent, though he knew she was a minor.

Police investigated under Article 199 of Iceland’s General Penal Code, which criminalises sexual harassment, including groping breasts or genitals inside or outside clothing. Ten witnesses were interviewed, but none directly witnessed the incident. Friends described the applicant as shocked, traumatised and crying soon afterwards. Snapchat messages were not preserved; a screenshot showed friends were concerned. Video evidence was unclear. The District Prosecutor discontinued the case in March 2020, finding conviction unlikely: the applicant’s recollection was limited, witness evidence mostly corroborated only parts of her account, the Snapchat messages were unavailable, the video was inconclusive, and O.’s intent under Article 199 was not sufficiently established. The State Prosecutor upheld that decision in August 2020, finding uncertainty as to whether O. intended sexual harassment, especially because he claimed to have stopped immediately upon realising the applicant did not consent.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (private life, including physical and psychological integrity). It accepted that Icelandic law had shifted toward consent-based sexual offences, including Article 194 on rape and Article 199 on sexual harassment. However, the Court found that the prosecuting authorities applied Article 199 unduly narrowly. They focused on O.’s subjective intent and whether he stopped when he perceived discomfort, rather than whether he could have assumed the applicant consented before initiating sexual touching. O. had admitted touching a sleeping or half-asleep 16-year-old’s breast without prior communication or consent. The Court held that the authorities failed to apply a consent-centred standard to this admitted touching, so the investigation did not secure the applicant’s physical and psychological integrity. There was therefore a violation of Article 8. The Court did not decide whether O. was guilty.

As to Article 14, the applicant alleged gender-based discrimination in the handling of sexual violence cases. The Court found insufficient prima facie evidence of structural bias or disproportionate effect to shift the burden of proof to the State, noting various legislative and policy measures adopted to combat sexual violence. The judgment became final on 13 April 2026.

**Case:** *Z v. Iceland* (Application no. 3538/21), European Court of Human Rights, Second Section, judgment of 13 January 2026 (final 13 April 2026).

The applicant, an Icelandic national, was 16 years old in June 2019 when she reported that a 23-year-old man, O., had sexually assaulted her at a festival. She stated that after drinking she withdrew to a co-worker’s tent. Early on 15 June, she sent a friend a video showing she was unwell; the footage also captured the back of O.’s head. She alleged that O. was groping her without consent at that time, though this was not visible in the video. She then passed out. She said she later woke around 8:00 a.m. with her underwear on but her trousers pulled down and her jumper lifted to her breasts. O. was beside her with his jumper removed and belt undone. She alleged that he touched her breasts and genitals, over and under her clothing. She tried to push him away about three times and told him to stop; he stopped only when she managed to leave the tent.

The applicant went to an emergency reception unit for sexual-abuse victims, declined a gynaecological examination, and was tested for sexually transmitted diseases. Child Protection Services were notified because she was a minor. Police investigated primarily under Article 199 of the General Penal Code, which criminalises sexual harassment, including groping breasts or genitals inside or outside clothing. O. admitted entering the tent, finding the applicant asleep or half-asleep, cuddling with her, and placing his hand under her jumper and touching her breast. He claimed he stopped immediately when she shook her head and apologised. He denied touching her genitals, removing her clothing, or having sexual intent, saying he had merely thought the position was comfortable. He acknowledged knowing she was a minor. Witnesses confirmed the applicant’s distress after the incident and reported messages she had sent via Snapchat, but those messages were not preserved; no direct witnesses existed.

On 30 March 2020, the District Prosecutor discontinued the case, finding conviction unlikely. The prosecutor cited the applicant’s limited recollection, the lack of direct evidence, the unclear video, the unavailable Snapchat messages, and the absence of medical evidence of the alleged violations. For Article 199, intent to sexually harass had to be established. Because O. admitted touching the applicant’s breast but said he stopped as soon as he realised she did not consent, the doubt was resolved in his favour. The State Prosecutor upheld that decision on 7 August 2020, finding uncertainty as to O.’s intent specifically regarding the admitted breast touching.

The applicant complained under Articles 2, 8 and 14 of the Convention, alleging that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into sexual violence and that the handling of such cases involved gender-based discrimination. She argued that the authorities should have focused on consent, not merely O.’s denial of intent, because O. admitted touching a sleeping or half-asleep minor without prior consent. The Government submitted that Icelandic law provided an adequate framework, that the case was correctly assessed under Article 199, and that O.’s subjective intent had to be proved beyond reasonable doubt.

The Court examined the case under Article 8 and found a violation. It held that Icelandic law was in principle capable of protecting sexual autonomy, but the prosecuting authorities applied an unduly narrow, intent-centred approach. The decisive issue was not only whether O. stopped when he perceived discomfort, but whether he had initiated sexual contact without any prior indication of consent from the applicant, who was a minor. By failing to apply a consent-centred standard to the admitted touching, the investigation did not secure the applicant’s physical and psychological integrity. As to Article 14, the Court found insufficient prima facie evidence of structural gender bias or a disproportionate effect capable of shifting the burden of proof to the State.

**Remez v. Ukraine** (Application no. 25395/19) concerned the effectiveness and length of a criminal investigation into the ill-treatment of a minor, Ms Sofiya Remez, by her father during an attempted kidnapping. The applicant, a Ukrainian national born in 2014, was represented by her mother. The European Court of Human Rights examined her complaints under Articles 3, 6 and 13 of the Convention, ultimately characterising the issue as the procedural limb of Article 3.

The key facts were as follows. On 8 June 2017, when the applicant was two years and eight months old, she was walking on a suburban street in Kherson with her grandmother. Her father, the former husband of her mother, grabbed her from her grandmother’s hands and pushed her into a nearby car. Bystanders intervened and stopped the attempted kidnapping.

The same day, the applicant’s mother complained to the Korabelnyi District Police Department, which immediately ordered a forensic medical examination. A paediatrician diagnosed the applicant with abrasions and haematomas of the upper limbs and torso. On 9 June 2017, a forensic medical doctor found abrasions and haematomas on both forearms and a bruise on the left abdomen. The doctor concluded that the injuries were minor and could not have resulted from a fall from the applicant’s height.

On 9 June 2017, the police opened criminal case no. 12017230020002105 concerning the infliction of minor bodily injuries under Article 125 § 1 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. However, on 30 June 2017, the police closed the case for lack of evidence. On 10 October 2017, the Kherson City Court quashed that decision, citing insufficient reasoning and the police’s failure to take any procedural action other than ordering the medical examination.

The investigation then stalled. On 25 December 2017, the police again closed the case for lack of evidence. On 5 April 2018, the Kherson City Court quashed that decision for procedural irregularities, including the failure to send the closure decision to the applicant or submit it to the court. Between December 2017 and January 2019, the applicant’s mother repeatedly asked the police to perform procedural actions and complained to the Kherson City Court about police inactivity. The court ordered the police to examine those applications. On 16 November and 28 December 2018, the Kherson Regional Police Department acknowledged the investigation’s ineffectiveness, dismissed investigator B., and assigned investigator K., ordering acceleration of the investigation.

On 13 February 2019, the police rejected one of the mother’s applications on the ground that the applicant was not a party to the criminal proceedings. On 27 March 2019, the Kherson City Court overturned that refusal and found the refusal to perform certain procedural actions unlawful. Nonetheless, on 8 September 2021, the police again closed the criminal case for lack of evidence.

Before the Court, the Government argued non-exhaustion, claiming the applicant should have brought a civil claim for non-pecuniary damage, and noted the case file had been destroyed during Russian occupation of Kherson. The Court dismissed that objection, holding that a damages-only remedy could not provide redress for an ineffective or lengthy investigation into ill-treatment.

On the merits, the Court found that although the investigation began promptly, it soon became dormant. The mother’s attempts to speed it up were futile, and even the regional police’s acknowledgment of ineffectiveness and replacement of the investigator did not lead to acceleration. The Court therefore found a violation of the procedural aspect of Article 3 of the Convention due to the lengthy and ineffective investigation. It awarded the applicant EUR 4,500 in non-pecuniary damage and rejected the pecuniary claim.

**Summary of *Martynovskiy v. Ukraine* (Application no. 69358/13)**

The case concerns the temporary suspension of the applicant's licence to practise as an advocate in Ukraine, which he alleged violated his rights under Articles 6, 8, and 13 of the Convention.

The applicant, a Ukrainian national born in 1965, received his advocate's licence in 1993 and practised in Sevastopol, Crimea. In October 2012, members of the Sevastopol Bar elected him to represent them in the Higher Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Bar ("HQDCB"), a governing body of the Ukrainian Bar.

On 7 December 2012, the HQDCB held its first meeting, which the applicant did not attend. He claimed he had not been informed of it. The HQDCB had posted a message on its website announcing the meeting date and place. Lawyer D. subsequently complained to the HQDCB that the applicant's absence violated Article 62 of the Rules of Professional Conduct—adopted on 17 November 2012 but published only on 18 January 2013—which required advocates elected to self-government bodies to avoid actions blocking their work. D. requested suspension of the applicant's licence.

On 24 January 2013, the head of the HQDCB transferred the complaint to the Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Regional Bar of Zakarpattya ("QDC of Zakarpattya"), citing Article 63 §2 of the Rules, which required complaints against advocates elected to self-government bodies to be examined by a regional Bar outside the region of election. The applicant learned of the proceedings in February 2013 and wrote to the QDC on 5 March 2013, arguing that the website message did not mention his name, that the HQDCB had nonetheless adopted its Rules of Procedure on 7 December 2012 (proving its work was not blocked), and that the transfer was unlawful under the Law on the Bar and practice of law.

On 17 April 2013, in the applicant's absence, the Disciplinary Chamber of the QDC of Zakarpattya suspended his licence for six months for failing to attend the meeting and violating Article 62. The Chamber found, without concrete evidence, that all HQDCB members had been informed via the website. The applicant was notified on 22 April 2013. On 16 May 2013, the QDC upheld the decision. The applicant appealed to the HQDCB, complaining about lack of competence, unlawful transfer, and violation of equality of arms. The appeal had no suspensive effect.

Between 2013 and 2016, the HQDCB held hearings but failed to reach a decision. In July 2014, the Bar Council adopted changes to the HQDCB's Rules, requiring a majority vote for a draft decision to pass. In 2016, a draft decision favouring the applicant received 11 votes in favour, 6 against, and 2 abstentions out of 19 present, but was rejected under the new rules.

The applicant then appealed to the Kyiv District Administrative Court in October 2016, raising multiple complaints including retroactive application of rules, lack of notice, and unlawful transfer. The proceedings were suspended in February 2017 pending a parallel case, resumed only in May 2018, and remained largely dormant despite the applicant's enquiries. On 8 April 2021, the court upheld the Bar bodies' decisions. The Supreme Court rejected his appeals on 9 December 2021.

In *Martynovskiy v. Ukraine* (Application no. 69358/13, ECtHR, 12 February 2026), the applicant was a Ukrainian advocate, licensed in 1993 and practising in Sevastopol. In October 2012 he was elected by Sevastopol Bar members to the Higher Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Bar (“HQDCB”), a Bar self-government body. He failed to attend the HQDCB’s first meeting on 7 December 2012, claiming he had not been informed of it.

Lawyer D. complained that the applicant’s absence violated Article 62 of the Rules of Professional Conduct, which had been adopted on 17 November 2012 but published only on 18 January 2013 and required advocates elected to self-government bodies to avoid actions that might block their work. D. asked for the applicant’s licence to be suspended. The head of the HQDCB transferred the complaint to the Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Regional Bar of Zakarpattya (“QDC of Zakarpattya”), relying on a rule that complaints against advocates elected to self-government bodies be examined by a regional Bar outside the region of election.

In March 2013 the applicant objected, arguing that the website notice did not identify him, that the HQDCB had still adopted its Rules of Procedure so its work had not been blocked, that the transfer was unlawful, and that D.’s rights had not been affected. On 17 April 2013, in the applicant’s absence, the QDC of Zakarpattya suspended his advocate’s licence for six months for failing to attend the meeting and violating Article 62. It stated, without concrete evidence, that all HQDCB members had been informed through the website. The applicant was informed on 22 April 2013, and the decision was upheld on 16 May 2013. His appeal to the HQDCB did not have suspensive effect and was delayed; a 2016 draft decision in his favour was rejected after a change to the voting rules, leaving the suspension in force. Domestic court proceedings begun in October 2016 ended with the Supreme Court on 9 December 2021 upholding the Bar decisions, finding the procedure lawful but declining to re-examine the facts.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Articles 6, 8 and 13. Under Article 8, he complained that the suspension deprived him of the ability to practise as an advocate and harmed his professional reputation and private life. The Court applied the *Denisov v. Ukraine* principles and found the six-month suspension temporary and not severe enough to engage Article 8. It noted no causal link between the suspension and his later limited court authorisations, and that he continued working in the legal field for an NGO and a government legal-aid body, wrote manuals, and received remuneration. Article 13 therefore also failed because it had no independent existence.

Under Article 6, the applicant complained that his appeal against the 17 April 2013 decision lacked suspensive effect, but the Court found the measure did not produce irreversible effects requiring such a remedy. His other fairness complaints—retroactive application of the Rules, unlawful transfer, in absentia hearing, and failure to examine whether he had been informed—were rejected as the domestic courts had examined them without arbitrariness. However, the Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1 regarding the excessive length of proceedings: court proceedings lasted from October 2016 to December 2021, after about three years of Bar proceedings, and the Government failed to justify the delay, especially from 2018 to 2021. The finding of a violation was sufficient just satisfaction, and no damages were awarded.

In *Martynovskiy v. Ukraine* (Application no. 69358/13, judgment of 12 February 2026), the applicant was a Ukrainian national and advocate, licensed in 1993, practising in Sevastopol. In October 2012, the Sevastopol Bar elected him to the Higher Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Bar (“HQDCB”). The HQDCB’s first meeting was set for 7 December 2012, but the applicant did not attend. He claimed he had not been informed of it. Lawyer D. complained to the HQDCB that the applicant’s absence violated Article 62 of the Rules of Professional Conduct, adopted on 17 November 2012 and published on 18 January 2013, which required advocates elected to self-government bodies not to block their work. D. relied on a website message announcing the meeting and asked for the applicant’s licence to be suspended.

The complaint was transferred to the Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Regional Bar of Zakarpattya (“QDC of Zakarpattya”) under Article 63 §2 of the Rules, because complaints against advocates elected to a self-government body had to be examined outside the region of election. The applicant objected: the website notice did not name him; his absence had not blocked the meeting, since the HQDCB adopted its Rules of Procedure that day; D. wrongly stated he had been elected by the Chernigiv Bar; and under the Law on the Bar, the complaint should have been examined in Sevastopol. He also said it was unclear how D.’s rights had been affected.

On 17 April 2013, in the applicant’s absence, the Disciplinary Chamber of the QDC of Zakarpattya suspended his advocate’s licence for six months for failing to attend the 7 December 2012 meeting and violating Article 62. It found, without concrete evidence, that all HQDCB members had been informed via the website. The applicant learned of the decision on 22 April 2013. The QDC upheld it on 16 May 2013. His appeal to the HQDCB did not suspend enforcement. He complained that the QDC lacked competence, that the HQDCB head had no power to transfer the case, and that his equality-of-arms rights were breached because he was informed of the 17 April hearing only afterwards. Because his licence was suspended, he was also barred from attending a HQDCB meeting on 19 April 2013. The HQDCB failed to decide his appeal in 2013 or 2014.

In July 2014, the Bar Council changed the HQDCB’s Rules so that a draft decision was rejected unless a majority of all HQDCB members voted in favour. In July 2016, a rapporteur proposed allowing the applicant’s appeal, but at a meeting with 19 of 30 members present, 11 voted for, 6 against, and 2 abstained. Under the 2014 rule, the draft was rejected and the suspension remained valid. The applicant then challenged the Bar decisions in the Kyiv District Administrative Court, arguing among other things that the amended rules were unlawfully applied retroactively, that he had not been informed of the 7 December meeting, and that the transfer and hearing in absentia were unlawful. Parallel proceedings and delays meant the court resumed review only in May 2018. In April 2021, it found the Bar decisions lawful; the Supreme Court rejected his appeals in December 2021.

The applicant alleged violations of Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention. Under Article 8, he complained that the suspension deprived him of the ability to practise as an advocate and harmed his professional reputation. The Court held Article 8 inapplicable because the six-month suspension did not cross the severity threshold: there was no sufficient causal link to his later reduced authorisations, he continued legal work for an NGO and a governmental legal-aid body, and he wrote methodological materials. The Article 13 complaint therefore had no independent existence. Under Article 6, the Court rejected the complaint about lack of a suspensive-effect remedy as manifestly ill-founded, since the measure had no irreversible effects. However, it found a violation of Article 6 §1 regarding the excessive length of the proceedings from October 2016 to December 2021. The remaining Article 6 procedural complaints were manifestly ill-founded because the domestic courts had examined them without arbitrariness. The finding of a violation was sufficient just satisfaction.
001-250107:
In **K.A. v. Austria**, the applicant, a Kosovo national living in Austria, was convicted of sustained domestic violence against his wife and four children and ordered confined in a forensic therapeutic centre (formerly an institution for mentally ill offenders) under Article 21 § 2 of the Austrian Criminal Code. He complained under Article 5 §§ 1 and 4 that his confinement was not based on reliable proof that he was of unsound mind and that the lawfulness of his detention was not properly reviewed. He also complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d)–(e) that he could not effectively challenge or question the prosecution witnesses.

The key facts concerned long-running violence. From at least 2009 until May 2021, the applicant allegedly abused his wife and children verbally and physically, including with tools and kitchenware, and became more aggressive when intoxicated. A 2011 restraining order had been issued but he ignored it. On 30 May 2021, after the applicant beat his children and had allegedly struck his wife with a drill the previous evening, his daughter B. called the police. His son C. said the applicant had threatened him with a knife and that the applicant had threatened to kill the family. The applicant denied everything. Police issued a restraining order, which he refused to obey, and he was arrested and then placed in pre-trial detention.

During the criminal investigation, the children B., C. and D. were cross-examined in June 2021 by audio-video link as particularly vulnerable victims. The applicant, his defence lawyer and the prosecutor were in a separate room but could follow and ask questions. An Albanian interpreter provided summary translations. The defence asked B. some questions but asked nothing of C. or D. In September 2021, psychiatric expert Dr K. reported that the applicant had an accentuated personality structure or suspected personality disorder and alcohol abuse. She found examination practically impossible because he denied everything and was evasive. Assuming the children’s testimony was credible, she described him as a “family tyrant” with narcissistic, dominance-oriented and sadistic traits, lacking empathy, and posing a high risk of serious or fatal violence against family members who testified. She considered the criteria for confinement met.

At trial in December 2021, the children refused further testimony. The court played the audio-video recordings and read the transcripts, refusing the defence request to summon them again. The applicant was convicted of continual use of force, deprivation of liberty, bodily harm and dangerous threats, sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment, and ordered confined. Appeals failed. In October 2022 he was transferred to the Garsten forensic therapeutic centre.

After a March 2023 legal reform replaced “high degree of mental or emotional abnormality” with “severe and persistent mental disorder,” the applicant sought release. He relied on a private report saying he had adjustment disorder or suspected mild retardation and that danger was limited to his family. The court-appointed expert Dr K. maintained in September 2023 that he still suffered from a severe and persistent mental disorder and remained highly dangerous. In February 2024 the Regional Court continued his confinement, and in April 2024 the Court of Appeal upheld that decision, finding that a diagnosis need not match ICD or DSM categories and that Dr K.’s examination without an interpreter was not a procedural error.

The European Court of Human Rights found that the domestic courts had relied on objective medical expertise and had reliably established and reviewed the persistence of a true mental disorder warranting compulsory confinement. The Article 6 complaints concerned the use of the pre-trial recordings and summary interpretation.

K.A. v. Austria concerned an Austrian resident, born in 1971 in Kosovo, who was convicted of prolonged domestic violence and ordered confined in a forensic-therapeutic centre. The facts central to his complaints under Article 5 §§ 1 and 4 and Article 6 §§ 1, 3(d) and (e) arose from the criminal proceedings, the use of video-recorded witness examinations, and the psychiatric evidence supporting his preventive confinement.

The applicant lived with his wife, E., and four children. From at least 2005 until May 2021, he allegedly subjected his wife and children to repeated physical and verbal abuse, including hitting, spitting, insults, threats, and assaults with household objects, often after drinking alcohol. A 2011 restraining order had not deterred him; his violence reportedly worsened after his family sought protection.

On 29 May 2021, he struck his wife on the head with a drill and threatened his son C. with a 30-cm knife, causing C. to flee. The next day, his daughter B. called the police. Police issued a restraining order, but the applicant refused to comply and was taken to a police station and then arrested, partly because he had threatened to kill the family.

During the investigation, the children B., C. and D. were cross-examined as particularly vulnerable victims in June 2021. The examinations were audio-video recorded. The applicant, his defence lawyer, and the prosecutor were in a separate room, able to watch and ask questions by video link. An Albanian interpreter provided summary translations during breaks rather than continuous full interpretation. The applicant and his lawyer asked few or no questions. The children later refused to testify at trial because it would be too distressing; the court therefore played the recordings and read the transcripts. The defence objected and asked for the children to be summoned, but the court refused.

A psychiatric expert, Dr K., prepared a report. She found examination practically impossible because the applicant denied the offences and blamed his family. She diagnosed an accentuated personality structure or suspected personality disorder and alcohol abuse, but no mental illness excluding criminal responsibility. However, assuming the children’s accounts were credible, she described him as a “family tyrant”: narcissistic, dominance-oriented, lacking empathy, with sadistic tendencies and a high risk of seriously injuring or killing family members. The Regional Court convicted him of continual use of force, deprivation of liberty, bodily harm, and dangerous threats; sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment; and ordered confinement in an institution for mentally ill offenders under Article 21 § 2 of the Criminal Code, finding the offences were committed under a severe mental disorder not excluding responsibility.

Appeals failed. The Supreme Court found no Article 6 breach in the cross-examination because the applicant and his lawyer had been present, could question the witnesses, and had interpreter assistance. The Court of Appeal upheld the confinement based on Dr K.’s findings.

After his transfer to Garsten in October 2022 and the 2023 legal reforms, the applicant sought release, submitting a private expert report arguing that he had no ICD/DSM diagnosis and that any risk was limited to his family. The Regional Court commissioned Dr K. again; she maintained the diagnosis and high risk. The courts refused release, holding that ICD/DSM classification was not required. The European Court of Human Rights found no violation of Article 5 §§ 1 and 4, accepting that the applicant’s mental disorder and need for continued confinement were reliably established and reviewed on objective, up-to-date medical evidence.

**K.A. v. Austria** (Applications nos. 44001/22 and 22881/24) is a European Court of Human Rights case concerning the applicant’s confinement in a forensic-therapeutic centre after convictions for domestic violence. The applicant, a Kosovo national living in Austria since 2001, complained primarily under Article 5 §§ 1(e) and 4 that it had not been reliably shown that he was a person of “unsound mind” and that his continued confinement was not properly reviewed. He also complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) and (e) that he had been unable to challenge and question prosecution witnesses.

The key facts concern long-running domestic violence. The applicant was married to E. and had four children. Until May 2021 he lived with his wife and several children in Upper Austria. According to the children’s statements, family life was marked by frequent physical and verbal abuse over many years. The applicant allegedly insulted, spat at, and struck his wife and children with his hands, feet, and household objects, becoming especially aggressive when intoxicated. A 2011 restraining order did not deter him; his violence reportedly worsened after the family sought protection.

On 30 May 2021 the daughter B. called the police after the applicant beat her siblings. The children told police that the previous evening the applicant had struck their mother on the head with a drill; he had also threatened his son C. with a 30-cm knife, causing C. to flee. The applicant allegedly telephoned another daughter and threatened to kill the whole family. When police issued a restraining order, the applicant refused to leave, so officers removed and arrested him. He was taken into pre-trial detention on 31 May 2021.

In June 2021 the children B., C., and D. were cross-examined at the pre-trial stage via audio-video link as particularly vulnerable victims. The applicant, his defence lawyer, and the prosecutor were in a separate room but could watch and ask questions via video. An Albanian interpreter provided summary translations during breaks. The children gave detailed accounts of violence. The applicant mostly denied the allegations and asked few or no questions. His wife and eldest daughter refused to testify.

A psychiatric expert, Dr K., reported in September 2021. She diagnosed an accentuated personality structure or suspected personality disorder and alcohol abuse. She found examination practically impossible because the applicant was evasive and denied everything. Assuming the children were credible, she described him as a “family tyrant”: highly narcissistic, dominance-oriented, lacking empathy, and sadistic. She considered him criminally responsible but concluded that Article 21 § 2 confinement criteria were met if the children’s statements were believed.

At trial in December 2021, the children did not attend. The audio-video recordings of their cross-examinations were played and transcripts read. The defence objected and requested that the children be summoned for further questioning; the court refused. The applicant was convicted of continual use of force, deprivation of liberty, bodily harm, and dangerous threats, sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment, and ordered confined in an institution for mentally ill offenders under Article 21 § 2. Appeals upheld the conviction and confinement.

After transfer to Garsten in October 2022, the applicant sought release in 2023–24, arguing he had no mental disorder. A privately commissioned report found adjustment disorder and suspected mild mental retardation, and claimed “family tyrant” was not an ICD diagnosis. The centre opposed release. Dr K.’s second report maintained the diagnosis and high risk of serious violence against family members. In February 2024 the Regional Court continued confinement; the Court of Appeal upheld that decision in April 2024, holding that an ICD/DSM diagnosis was not required and that the amended law had not changed the scope of confinement.

The Court’s headnote records that the applicant was reliably shown, on objective medical expertise, to suffer a true mental disorder warranting compulsory confinement, and that its persistence was reliably reviewed under Article 5.
001-248598:
In *Simoncini v. San Marino* (Application no. 14396/24, judgment 19 February 2026), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) found violations of Article 6 § 1 (civil) and Article 8. The applicant, Massimiliano Simoncini, a San Marinese national born in 1963, had served as an Uditore Commissariale since 2009 and was eligible for appointment as Commissario della Legge (CoL), a first-instance judicial office. On 12 February 2019 the Judicial Council in plenary session (CGP) appointed him CoL; Parliament acknowledged the appointment and he took up service on 22 March 2019.

A dispute arose over the CGP’s composition. Two other UDs, X and Y, who were possible candidates, brought administrative proceedings no. 13/2019 on 11 April 2019, challenging the recruitment and appointment. They argued, among other things, that the CGP had been unlawfully composed because it included Judge C, an Appeal Judge still in his probationary period and not permanently confirmed. While those proceedings were pending, the legislature intervened twice. Qualified Law no. 1/2019 addressed the external Chief’s position. More importantly, Qualified Law no. 1/2020 introduced Article 3, an “authentic interpretation” with retroactive effect, requiring CGP magistrates to be confirmed on a permanent basis. The applicant alleged this was designed to reconstitute the CGP and invalidate lawful appointments, including his.

On 28 September 2020, relying on that retroactive provision, the CGP annulled ex officio both the decision to initiate the recruitment procedure and the applicant’s appointment. The applicant, who had not been a party to proceedings no. 13/2019 and whose later attempt to intervene was rejected as time-barred, brought administrative proceedings no. 37/2020 challenging the annulment. The domestic courts (first instance on 25 January 2023; appeal on 9 January 2024) rejected his claims. They held that the retrospective legislative clarification was necessary, reasonable and proportionate, that the CGP’s self-annulment was lawful, and that there was no breach of Articles 6 or 8 of the Convention. They stressed the public interest in a lawfully composed CGP and the rights of X and Y.

The ECtHR found Article 6 § 1 applicable and violated. The annulment was directly decisive for the applicant’s arguable civil right to his judicial office. Key facts included that the legislative intervention occurred during separate proceedings brought by competing candidates and before the applicant instituted his own proceedings. The Court found insufficient consideration of the irremovability of judges during their term of office. The retrospective law amounted to an unjustified, arbitrary course of action circumventing the rule of law and fair trial. It disrupted equality of arms, making the applicant’s proceedings unwinnable, and no compelling general interest justified it.

Article 8 was also applicable and violated. The annulment’s cumulative effects on the applicant’s private life—his career, professional status and reputation—were sufficiently serious. Domestic courts failed to acknowledge or properly balance that right. The lawfulness requirement was not met, and there were no relevant and sufficient reasons showing the measure was necessary in a democratic society. The length of proceedings did not exceed a reasonable time.

In *Simoncini v. San Marino* (Application no. 14396/24), the applicant was a San Marinese national and an *Uditore Commissariale*, a junior judicial officer qualified by experience to be appointed *Commissario della Legge* (CoL), a first-instance judge. On 12 February 2019, the Judicial Council in plenary session (CGP) appointed him CoL by eleven votes. The CGP’s composition was disputed because it included judge C, who had not yet been confirmed on a permanent basis. Under later legislation, such inclusion was said to be contrary to the correct interpretation of the rules governing the CGP.

Parliament acknowledged the appointment on 15 March 2019, and the applicant took up service on 22 March 2019. On 11 April 2019, two other *Uditori*, X and Y, who had been possible candidates, brought administrative proceedings (no. 13/2019) challenging the appointment. They alleged, among other things, that the CGP had been unlawfully composed because judge C was not yet confirmed on a permanent basis, that required reports were missing, and that selection criteria were unclear.

While those proceedings were pending, on 20 February 2020, following a change of government, San Marino enacted Qualified Law no. 1/2020. It contained an “authentic interpretation” provision with retroactive effect, clarifying that CGP judicial members had to be confirmed on a permanent basis. On 28 September 2020, the CGP, acting of its own motion in self-protection (*autotutela decisoria spontanea*), annulled both its earlier recruitment decision and the applicant’s appointment, relying on the retroactive interpretation. It considered that the CGP had been defectively composed when it appointed him.

The applicant had not been a party to proceedings no. 13/2019. His attempt to intervene in November 2020 failed as out of time. He then brought administrative proceedings no. 37/2020 against the annulment. The first-instance court dismissed his claims on 25 January 2023, and the Judge of Appeal for Civil Liability Actions of Magistrates dismissed his appeal on 9 January 2024. The domestic courts held that the CGP’s ex officio annulment was lawful, that the retrospective legislative intervention was necessary, reasonable and proportionate, and that there was no breach of Articles 6 or 8 of the Convention. The applicant later participated unsuccessfully in new competitions for the post.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 (fair hearing) and Article 8 (private life) about the annulment of his appointment. The Court found Article 6 applicable because the annulment was directly decisive for his arguable civil right relating to judicial office. It found a violation of Article 6: the retrospective legislative intervention occurred during proceedings brought by competing candidates, before the applicant had instituted his own challenge; insufficient regard was given to the irremovability of judges; and the intervention disrupted equality of arms, making the applicant’s proceedings unwinnable. There were no compelling general interest reasons justifying retrospective legislation. The length of proceedings, however, did not exceed a reasonable time.

Under Article 8, the Court found the annulment had sufficiently serious cumulative effects on the applicant’s private life and professional reputation. Domestic courts failed to acknowledge or balance that right, the lawfulness requirement was not met, and no relevant or sufficient reasons justified the measure as necessary in a democratic society. The Court therefore also found a violation of Article 8.

Simoncini v. San Marino (App. no. 14396/24) arose from the annulment of the applicant’s appointment as Commissario della Legge (CoL), a first-instance judicial office. Simoncini, a San Marinese national and former Uditore Commissariale, was qualified for the post. In September 2018 the Judicial Council in plenary session (CGP) began a recruitment procedure. On 12 February 2019 the CGP appointed him CoL by eleven votes; Parliament acknowledged the appointment on 15 March 2019, and he took office on 22 March 2019.

The legality of the CGP’s composition was disputed. Under Qualified Law no. 145/2003, as amended, the CGP’s judicial component had to be chosen primarily from permanently confirmed magistrates with seniority, with supplementation rules if numbers fell short. At the time of the applicant’s appointment, Appeal Judge C sat on the CGP although he was still within his three-year probationary period and not permanently confirmed. Earlier interpretations had varied; after 27 April 2018 the CGP interpreted the rules so as to exclude a CoL and include C. Concerns were also raised about the role of an external Chief.

On 11 April 2019, X and Y, rival Uditore candidates, challenged the appointment in administrative proceedings no. 13/2019, alleging defective CGP composition and procedural defects. While those proceedings were pending, on 20 February 2020 San Marino enacted Qualified Law no. 1/2020. Its Article 3 was an authentic interpretation with retroactive effect, requiring priority to magistrates confirmed on a permanent basis; other provisions removed the voting rights of an external Chief. The Government said this clarified ambiguity and addressed concerns.

On 28 September 2020, relying on that retrospective interpretation, the CGP annulled ex officio its own recruitment decision and the applicant’s appointment because the CGP had included C while he was not permanently confirmed. The applicant, who was not a party to proceedings no. 13/2019, challenged the annulment in proceedings no. 37/2020. Domestic courts dismissed his claims: the first-instance judge on 25 January 2023 and the appeal judge on 9 January 2024. They held the annulment lawful: the CGP could act in self-protection; the retroactive law was necessary, reasonable and proportionate for legal certainty and lawful judicial composition; public interest prevailed; and the applicant had no subjective right to an unlawful appointment. They found no breach of Articles 6 or 8.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Article 6 (fair hearing) and Article 8 (private life). The Court found Article 6 applicable because the annulment was directly decisive for an arguable civil right. The key violations were that the legislative intervention occurred during separate proceedings brought by competing candidates and before the applicant’s own proceedings, retrospectively changing the legal basis; insufficient consideration was given to the irremovability of judges during their term; the retroactive law was an unjustified arbitrary course circumventing the rule of law and fair trial; equality of arms was disrupted, making the applicant’s case effectively unwinnable; and no compelling general interest outweighed the dangers of retrospective legislation. Article 6 was violated (the length complaint was rejected). Under Article 8, the annulment had sufficiently serious cumulative effects on the applicant’s private life, career and professional reputation; domestic courts failed to recognise or balance that right; and the lawfulness requirement and relevant, sufficient reasons for necessity were absent. Article 8 was also violated.
001-249527:
In *Khoman v. Ukraine* (Application no. 12308/19), the applicant, a Ukrainian national born in 1954, complained under Article 2 of the Convention that Ukraine failed to carry out an effective investigation into her son’s death during military service. The application was lodged on 14 February 2019. The Court gave notice only of the complaint about the allegedly ineffective investigation; the remainder was declared inadmissible.

The applicant’s son, A.K., was called up in April 2015 under a special military mobilisation. He served in Maryinka, Donetsk region, near a combat zone. On 25 June 2015, he died on premises occupied by his military unit after sustaining head injuries in unclear circumstances. An ambulance crew pronounced him dead immediately. For unknown reasons, the body was taken to a hospital rather than a morgue. That evening, after the hospital telephoned police, a criminal investigation was opened into murder. A police officer inspected the body in the ambulance.

A post-mortem examination was performed from 26 June to 10 July 2015. The expert found death resulted from a blunt-object head injury involving subdural haemorrhage and cerebral oedema. No alcohol odour was noted at autopsy on 26 June 2015. Although blood and stomach samples were extracted for toxicological analysis, they were ultimately disposed of due to a lack of transportation or preservation facilities. No toxicology test was therefore conducted.

On 2 July 2015, an internal inquiry concluded, based on evidence from two soldiers and their superior, that A.K. had been intoxicated, tripped over a balcony doorstep, fell, hit his head, and died. Later, the applicant learned of bullying allegations in the unit. One fellow soldier claimed he had been told A.K. was hit in the head before falling. She asked the investigator to examine those matters.

From 5 July to 27 October 2017, a commission of experts examined the case file. It concluded that the fatal head injuries resulted from at least seven “traumatic impacts” with limited-surface blunt objects. Because the objects could not be identified, and given the nature of the trauma and injury localisation, a fall from standing height could not be ruled out. There was no indication the fall was accelerated or the body dragged. It was impossible to establish whether the blunt objects were fists or feet. The experts also could not determine whether A.K.’s injuries resulted from tripping over the balcony doorstep, and noted that no forensic toxicological analysis for alcohol had been performed. In September 2019, A.K.’s former superior changed his account, saying A.K. had tripped and fallen during mortar shelling.

The investigation was discontinued three times for lack of indication of a criminal offence—on 23 September 2015, 28 February 2018, and 24 December 2019. Each decision was quashed—on 11 March 2016, 12 March 2019, and 8 April 2020—as premature, ungrounded, and unlawful. In April 2020, the Donetsk garrison military prosecutor criticised the investigation as incomplete: it had followed only the “accidental death” version without verifying other witness and applicant accounts, had not carried out measures regarding all involved persons, and had not performed a single investigative measure aimed at solving the crime and establishing the truth. No factual update after 2020 was provided. The alleged violation is thus the State’s failure to conduct an effective investigation under Article 2.

In *Khoman v. Ukraine* (Application no. 12308/19), the European Court of Human Rights examined the applicant’s complaint under Article 2 that Ukraine failed to conduct an effective investigation into her son’s death during military service. The applicant, Nataliya Vasylivna Khoman, a Ukrainian national born in 1954, lodged the application on 14 February 2019. The Court communicated only the complaint concerning the allegedly ineffective investigation; the remainder was declared inadmissible.

The applicant’s son, A.K., was mobilised in April 2015 and served in Maryinka, Donetsk region, near a combat zone. On 25 June 2015 he died on military unit premises after suffering head injuries in unclear circumstances. An ambulance pronounced him dead at the scene; for unknown reasons his body was taken to a hospital rather than a morgue. A murder investigation began that evening after the hospital called police, and a police officer inspected the body in the ambulance.

A post-mortem examination, conducted from 26 June to 10 July 2015, found death due to blunt-object head injury causing subdural haemorrhage and cerebral oedema. Although no alcohol odour was noted during the autopsy, blood and stomach samples prepared for toxicological analysis were later disposed of because facilities for transport or preservation were lacking. On 2 July 2015, an internal inquiry concluded, based on evidence from two soldiers and their superior, that A.K. had been under the influence of alcohol, tripped over a balcony doorstep and fell, hitting his head.

The applicant later learned of bullying allegations in the unit. A fellow soldier claimed he had been told A.K. was hit in the head before falling. She asked the investigator to examine these matters. From 5 July to 27 October 2017, a commission of experts reviewed the file. It found the fatal head injuries resulted from at least seven traumatic impacts with limited-surface blunt objects. It could not identify those objects; could not rule out a fall from standing height; found no indication the fall was accelerated or the body dragged; and could not determine whether fists or feet caused the injuries. Given missing information and the scene inspection report, the experts could not conclude whether the injuries resulted from tripping over the balcony doorstep. They noted no forensic toxicological analysis for alcohol had been performed.

In *Khoman v. Ukraine* (Application no. 12308/19), the European Court of Human Rights examined the applicant’s complaint under Article 2 of the Convention that Ukrainian authorities failed to carry out an effective investigation into the death of her son, A.K., during military service. The applicant, a Ukrainian national, lodged the application on 14 February 2019. The Court gave notice only of the complaint concerning the allegedly ineffective investigation into A.K.’s death; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

In April 2015, A.K. was called up for military service following a special military mobilisation. He served in Maryinka, in the Donetsk region, close to a combat zone at the material time. On 25 June 2015, A.K. died on premises occupied by his military unit after suffering head injuries in unclear circumstances. A medical specialist from the ambulance that arrived after a telephone call immediately pronounced him dead. For unknown reasons, the body was transferred to a hospital rather than a morgue. Later that evening, after the hospital telephoned the police, a criminal investigation was launched on a charge of murder. A police officer inspected the body in the ambulance vehicle.

A post-mortem forensic examination was carried out from 26 June to 10 July 2015. The expert found that A.K.’s death was caused by a head injury from a blunt object, involving subdural haemorrhage and cerebral oedema. No odour of alcohol was identified during the autopsy on 26 June 2015. Although blood and stomach contents were extracted for forensic toxicological analysis, they were ultimately disposed of due to lack of facilities for transportation or preservation. Consequently, no toxicological analysis for alcohol was performed.

On 2 July 2015, an internal inquiry concluded, based on evidence from two soldiers and their superior, that A.K., while under the influence of alcohol, had tripped over a doorstep on a balcony, fallen, hit his head on the balcony floor, and died. Later, the applicant learned of allegations of bullying in the unit where A.K. had served. One fellow soldier claimed he had been told that A.K. had been hit in the head before falling. The applicant asked the investigator to examine those matters.

The commission concluded that the fatal head injuries resulted from at least seven “traumatic impacts” with limited-surface blunt objects. Because the objects could not be identified, and given the nature of the closed craniocerebral trauma and localisation of external head injuries, the experts could not rule out that A.K. sustained the injuries in a fall from a standing height. There was no indication that the fall had been accelerated or that the body had been dragged. As the blunt objects could not be identified, it was impossible to establish whether they might have been fists or feet. The experts also found it impossible to conclude whether the injuries could have resulted from A.K. tripping over the balcony doorstep, falling, and hitting his head against the balcony’s hard surface. They noted that no forensic toxicological analysis for alcohol had been performed.

In September 2019, A.K.’s former superior changed his account and submitted that A.K. had tripped and fallen during mortar shelling.

The criminal investigation into A.K.’s death was discontinued three times for lack of indication of a criminal offence: on 23 September 2015, 28 February 2018, and 24 December 2019. All those decisions were quashed—on 11 March 2016, 12 March 2019, and 8 April 2020—as premature, ungrounded, and unlawful. The Donetsk garrison military prosecutor’s decision of 8 April 2020 criticised the investigation as incomplete, stating that it had followed the “accidental death” version as the only line of inquiry without verifying other versions indicated by witnesses and the applicant, had not carried out investigative measures concerning all those involved, and had not performed a single investigative measure aimed at solving the crime and establishing the truth. In *Gatsko and Panov v. Ukraine* (Application no. 52709/13, judgment of 12 March 2026), two Ukrainian nationals and leaders of political party “D” complained under Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights that they had been sanctioned for holding peaceful demonstrations.

The key facts concerned two planned demonstrations in April 2013. On 1 April 2013 the first applicant notified the Novi Petrivtsi Village Council that on 10 April 2013 he intended to organise a demonstration in front of the President of Ukraine’s residence at 19 Ivana Franka Street, Novi Petrivtsi. The stated aim was to draw attention to the poor state of road infrastructure, with up to 500 possible participants. The Village Council then asked the Kyiv District Administrative Court to prohibit the event. On 5 April 2013 that court banned the party from holding the demonstration, relying on a local executive committee decision of 31 July 2012 governing public events and noting that the demonstration might disrupt road works repairing flood damage. Both applicants were present when the decision was pronounced and did not appeal.

On 10 April 2013, according to the applicants, they went to the President’s residence with journalists to check whether the road works were actually taking place. While leaving, police stopped them, took them to a police station and later to the Vyshgorodskyy District Court. They were accused of breaching Articles 185 and 185-1 of the Code of Administrative Offences. The same day, the first applicant was fined UAH 170 (about EUR 16) for participating in a demonstration and refusing to follow a police officer; his appeal was later rejected on 3 June 2013. The second applicant was fined for disobeying a police officer under Article 185, and the police were ordered to investigate the remaining accusations. He did not appeal that fine.

On 11 April 2013 the second applicant was found guilty of conducting the 10 April demonstration despite the 5 April ban. The court found that he had organised the demonstration and sentenced him to seven days’ administrative detention under Article 185-1 § 2 of the Code. It relied on police witness statements and statements by the head of the Village Council, who said the second applicant had informed him of the planned demonstration. The judgment also referred to a prior 27 December 2012 finding against him, although those proceedings had been closed as time-barred. His appeal was dismissed on 19 April 2013; he alleged that the appellate court refused to call witnesses or examine video footage.

On 12 April 2013 the first applicant returned to Novi Petrivtsi intending to demonstrate for the second applicant’s release. He was detained and brought before the Vyshgorodskyy District Court but was then released and went home. On 13 April 2013 the same court sentenced him to five days’ administrative detention under Article 185-1 § 2 of the Code for repeatedly breaching the procedure for holding demonstrations, referring to a 1988 Soviet Presidium decree and Article 39 of the Constitution. The court found he had organised the meeting and had notified the Village Council only one hour before it was due to start. His appeal was dismissed on 28 May 2013.

The Government’s six-month objection was rejected because the initial application had been lodged on 9 August 2013. The Court found the remaining complaint admissible. **Case: Felemez and Others v. Türkiye**  
**Applications nos. 30027/20 and 3 others**  
**European Court of Human Rights, Second Section, Committee Judgment**  
**Strasbourg, 22 January 2026**

The case concerned four applications lodged against Türkiye under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights on various dates listed in the appended table. The Turkish Government was given notice of the applications. Because the applications raised similar subject matter, the Court decided to examine them jointly in a single judgment.

The applicants’ central complaint was that the domestic court decisions in their cases lacked reasoning or contained inadequate reasoning. They relied, expressly or in substance, on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to a fair trial. The full judgment refers to an appended table for the list of applicants and the relevant details of each application, including the specific procedural failings later identified by the Court. The body of the judgment does not reproduce those individual facts; it relies on the table for the concrete circumstances of each applicant’s domestic proceedings.

The Court reiterated its established case-law that the right to a fair trial includes a duty for courts and tribunals to adequately state the reasons on which their judgments are based. This duty is linked to the proper administration of justice. The extent of the obligation varies according to the nature of the decision and must be assessed in light of the circumstances of each case. The Court explained that domestic courts are not required to provide a detailed answer to every argument raised by a complainant. However, parties to judicial proceedings are entitled to receive a specific and explicit reply to the arguments that are decisive for the outcome of those proceedings. Furthermore, in cases involving interference with rights protected under the Convention, the Court examines whether the reasons given by domestic courts are automatic or stereotypical.

The Court noted that these principles concerning the right to a reasoned decision under Article 6 § 1 have been applied in numerous Turkish cases, citing examples such as Emel Boyraz v. Turkey, Deryan v. Turkey, Cihangir Yıldız v. Turkey, Hülya Ebru Demirel v. Turkey, Murat Akın v. Turkey, Pişkin v. Turkey, Korkut and Amnesty International Türkiye v. Türkiye, and Onat and Others v. Türkiye.

Reviewing the facts of the present applications in light of those principles, the Court found that the domestic courts had failed in their duty to provide reasons for their decisions. In particular, they had not addressed pertinent and important arguments raised by the applicants. The specific procedural deficiencies were set out in the appended table. On that basis, the Court concluded that the applicants’ right to a reasoned court decision had not been secured, and it found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

As to just satisfaction under Article 41, the Court considered the documents in its possession and its case-law, referring in particular to Pronina v. Ukraine and Korkut and Amnesty International Türkiye v. Türkiye. It considered it reasonable to award the applicants the sums indicated in the appended table.

In sum, the case is a procedural fair-trial judgment: the applicants did not succeed on the underlying merits of their domestic disputes as such, but established that the domestic courts violated Article 6 § 1 by failing to provide adequate reasons and by failing to engage with decisive arguments. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

In *Levchenko v. Ukraine* (Application no. 58785/15), the applicant, a Ukrainian national born in 1961, complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention about the seizure of his car in criminal proceedings concerning third parties. The central issue was whether that seizure, and its prolonged retention, unlawfully and disproportionately interfered with his property rights.

On 4 April 2014 the applicant bought a used car. It was later established that the car had been sold to him on the basis of a forged authority form. In December 2014 a criminal investigation was launched into fraudulent property appropriation in that regard.

On 28 May 2015, while the applicant was driving the car, the Uman traffic police stopped him and withheld the vehicle because it was listed as wanted by the police. The car was taken to the local traffic police pound. On 25 June 2015 the investigator applied to the Zhytomyr Bohunskyi District Court for seizure of the car. On 30 June 2015 that court allowed the application at a hearing attended by the prosecutor, but the applicant was not notified of the hearing. The applicant later challenged the ruling on appeal once he discovered it existed.

In his appeal, the applicant relied in particular on Article 171 § 5 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which provided that if an investigator did not apply for seizure of property within one day of its temporary withholding, the property was to be immediately returned to the person from whom it had been withheld. In the applicant’s case, however, the investigator applied for seizure about one month after the car was withheld. He also argued that the seizure was disproportionate. On 5 August 2015 the Zhytomyr Regional Court of Appeal rejected the appeal as unfounded. It stated in general terms that the Bohunskyi Court had complied with the applicable legal provisions and that the legitimate owner of the car had not yet been established.

On 25 March 2016 the applicant was granted the procedural status of victim in the ongoing criminal proceedings. He applied many times for the seizure to be lifted. On 1 December 2016 the Bohunskyi Court allowed one such application in part. Although it upheld the ban on disposal or encumbrance of the car, it ordered that the car be transferred to the applicant for safekeeping. The court noted that the applicant had victim status, that the car showed no traces of involvement in an offence, and that continued storage in an open outdoor space at the police pound since 28 May 2015 meant it would deteriorate.

On 4 November 2019 the same court lifted the seizure altogether. It noted that no investigative measures had been carried out in the criminal investigation since September 2016 and that no suspicion had been announced. The judge also referred to the fact that the applicant’s bona fide ownership of the car had never been questioned. On 17 June 2020 the criminal investigation was discontinued because it was found impossible to identify any suspects.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation were therefore the seizure of the applicant’s car in proceedings against third parties, the delay in applying for seizure contrary to national procedural rules, the lack of notification of the seizure hearing, the prolonged restriction on disposal or encumbrance until November 2019, and the applicant’s unchallenged bona fide ownership and later victim status. These factors formed the basis of his complaint that the interference with his property was unlawful and disproportionate.

**Kis and Levchuk v. Ukraine (App. no. 910/18)** concerns the alleged lack of an effective investigation into an attack on two Ukrainian nationals who participated as a same-sex couple in a 2015 social experiment in Kyiv. The applicants complained under Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention that the authorities failed to investigate treatment they suffered because of their sexual orientation.

In 2015, the online magazine *Bird in Flight* organized an experiment, similar to one in Moscow, to gauge Ukrainian society’s tolerance toward same-sex couples. On 15 July 2015, the applicants walked through central Kyiv holding hands for about an hour, accompanied by bodyguards and filmed. After nothing happened, they escalated their public display of affection. With the organizers’ approval, one applicant sat on the other’s lap on a bench on Khreshchatyk Street, holding a bouquet.

A group of young people approached, asking whether they were patriots and wanted their nation to be best. The applicants replied that patriotism, for them, meant supporting equality. The group reportedly made remarks such as “The guys have [this place] mixed up with America” and “Europe! Europe!” They then pepper-sprayed and kicked the applicants. Bodyguards intervened immediately, so the physical confrontation lasted only three to five seconds. The applicants did not seek medical help or undergo a forensic medical examination.

On 22 July 2015, the experiment video was published online; some attackers’ faces were visible. News websites reported on it. On 29 July 2015, the first applicant filed a criminal complaint for himself and the second applicant, describing the attack and asking police to open a case under Article 161 § 2 of the Criminal Code—violation of equality committed with violence—and to investigate discrimination against them as homosexuals. He did not mention injuries and referred to the online video. The second applicant also complained. When questioned on 4 August 2015, he said he had not sought medical assistance; police stated he refused a forensic medical examination.

On 5 August 2015, police opened proceedings under Article 296 § 2 (group hooliganism), not Article 161. On 12 August 2015, they closed the case for lack of evidence, citing only the victims’ statements, no eyewitnesses, no usable video surveillance, and the second applicant’s refusal of an allegedly obligatory forensic examination. The lawyer was informed on 2 October and received a copy on 25 November 2015. She appealed, arguing police failed to include the magazine’s video, interview the cameraman, or classify the offence under Article 161, and wrongly treated forensic examination as obligatory. Courts and prosecutors repeatedly set aside closure decisions as premature and returned the case for investigation.

In May 2016, the lawyer sought reclassification under Article 161; police refused in June 2016 because no elements were apparent from unidentified persons. Police later collected mobile phone base-station data but reported inability to question the magazine’s editor or journalist or identify perpetrators. In September 2017, the applicants recognized a woman allegedly from the attacking group in a video from an unrelated picket and identified a group, S.; there was no apparent follow-up. By 2021–2023, police still reported difficulties identifying perpetrators; in July 2023 they questioned the editor and sought access to mobile operators’ data. The criminal proceedings remain pending.

**Case: Kis and Levchuk v. Ukraine (Application no. 910/18)**

The case concerns an alleged failure by Ukrainian authorities to conduct an effective investigation into discriminatory treatment and violence experienced by two Ukrainian nationals, Mr Zoryan Kis and Mr Tymur Levchuk, a same-sex couple. The applicants complained under Articles 8 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights; the Court gave notice of those complaints and declared the remainder inadmissible.

In 2015 an online magazine, *Bird in Flight*, organized a social experiment in Kyiv, similar to one previously held in Moscow, to gauge Ukrainian society’s tolerance toward same-sex couples. The applicants agreed to participate. On 15 July 2015, they walked around central Kyiv holding hands for about an hour. When nothing occurred, and with the organizers’ approval, one applicant sat on the other’s lap on a bench on Khreshchatyk Street, holding a bouquet. Soon afterward, a group of young people approached them and asked whether they were patriots and wanted their nation to be the best. The applicants replied that their patriotism meant favoring equality. The group allegedly remarked that they had confused the place with America and shouted “Europe! Europe!” The group then pepper-sprayed and kicked the applicants. Bodyguards intervened immediately, and the violent confrontation lasted only three to five seconds. The applicants did not seek medical assistance or undergo a forensic medical examination. The experiment was filmed, and on 22 July 2015 the video was published online, showing the faces of some attackers; news websites then reported on the incident.

On 29 July 2015 the first applicant lodged a criminal complaint on behalf of both men. He described the experiment and attack and asked police to open a case under Article 161 § 2 of the Criminal Code—violation of equality committed with violence—to investigate whether they were discriminated against as homosexuals. He mentioned no injuries and referred to the online video. The second applicant also complained. On 4 August 2015 police questioned him; he reiterated that he had not sought medical help. Police stated he was offered a forensic medical examination but refused.

On 5 August 2015 the police opened proceedings under Article 296 § 2—group hooliganism—rather than Article 161. On 12 August 2015 they closed the case for lack of evidence, citing only victim statements, no eyewitnesses, no usable video surveillance, and the second applicant’s refusal of a forensic examination, which police treated as obligatory. The applicants’ lawyer was informed belatedly, and after appeals, the closure decision was set aside as premature and returned for investigation. Similar closures and remittals followed.

The applicants’ lawyer repeatedly sought reclassification under Article 161, but police refused in June 2016. In July 2016 police collected mobile-phone base-station data. In October 2016 an investigator reported inability to question the magazine’s editor or journalist or identify perpetrators. Another closure in December 2016 was set aside in June and August 2017. In September 2017 the lawyer informed police that the applicants had recognized a woman allegedly among the attackers from a video of an unrelated picket near the Russian embassy and identified a group, “S.” No apparent follow-up occurred. In 2021 and 2022 investigators repeated that they could not question the editor/journalist or identify perpetrators. In July 2023 the editor was finally questioned and corroborated the applicants; police sought access to mobile operators’ data. The criminal proceedings remain pending.

The key alleged violation is the lack of an effective investigation into discriminatory treatment, including delayed and flawed classification, failure to pursue video and witness evidence, repeated premature closures, refusal to reclassify, and failure to follow up identification leads.

The applicants replied that their patriotism meant supporting equality. The group reportedly said, “The guys have [this place] mixed up with America” and “Europe! Europe!” They then pepper-sprayed the applicants and kicked them. Bodyguards intervened immediately, and the violent confrontation lasted only three to five seconds. Police claimed he was offered a forensic medical examination to determine injury severity but refused. In July 2023, police finally questioned the editor, who reiterated the applicants’ statements, and sought court permission to access mobile operator documents and data. According to the latest information, the criminal proceedings remain pending.
