Case Simoncini v. San Marino (Application no. 3106/24) concerns disciplinary proceedings against Mr Massimiliano Simoncini, a San Marinese national born in 1963 and a member of the San Marino judiciary. The proceedings arose from misconduct he committed in February 2023. On 13 July 2023, the Judicial Council (Consiglio Giudiziario), sitting as a court of first instance, found him disciplinary liable under section 12 of Constitutional Law no. 1/2021 and imposed the sanction of a warning (ammonimento).

On 4 September 2023, Simoncini appealed to the Constitutional Court (Collegio garante della costituzionalità delle norme) under section 16(10) of Constitutional Law no. 1/2021. By decree of 12 September 2023, the President of the Constitutional Court declared the appeal inadmissible because Simoncini was not represented by a lawyer. Legal representation was mandatory under section 9(1) of Qualified Law no. 55/2003 and section 12(1) of the Constitutional Court’s Internal Regulations.

On 15 September 2023, a lawyer appointed by Simoncini submitted a brief formally ratifying the appeal, thereby seeking to remedy the initial lack of representation. The lawyer argued that Simoncini had initially filed the appeal without a representative because it was difficult to find a lawyer during the summer holidays, and that he had been entitled to do so under certain provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which also applied to disciplinary proceedings. However, by decree of 22 September 2023, the President of the Constitutional Court again declared the appeal inadmissible. The President reiterated that representation was mandatory and held that the lawyer’s ratifying brief had been submitted after the expiry of the 30-day time-limit for appeal.

Simoncini subsequently filed a plea of nullity (querela nullitatis), seeking annulment of the two decrees, and a constitutional complaint challenging several provisions regulating the disciplinary proceedings. At the time of the European Court’s judgment, no decision appeared to have been delivered on those applications.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Simoncini lodged his application on 20 January 2024. The Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, gave notice to the San Marinese Government of the complaints raised under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention concerning the right to a tribunal established by law and the right to a reasoned decision. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The Government was represented by its Agent, Ms S. Bernardi, while Simoncini was represented by Mr A. Masiello, a lawyer practising in Borgo Maggiore.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations therefore centre on the disciplinary finding and warning imposed by the Judicial Council, and particularly on the Constitutional Court’s refusal of Simoncini’s appeal on procedural grounds—first for lack of mandatory legal representation, and then because the later ratification by counsel came after the expiry of the appeal deadline. Those procedural rulings, together with Simoncini’s challenge to the applicable disciplinary-proceedings provisions, form the factual basis for his Article 6 § 1 complaints about the right to a tribunal established by law and the right to a reasoned decision. The Court gave notice only of those Article 6 complaints; the other complaints were rejected as inadmissible. The judgment was adopted on 19 March 2026 and delivered on 9 April 2026, and is final but subject to editorial revision.

In *Stalović v. Serbia* (Application no. 35786/22), the applicants are Marko Stalović, a Serbian national of Roma origin, and Sandra Stalović, an Austrian national, who are married. They complained to the European Court of Human Rights of racially motivated police ill-treatment and the lack of an effective investigation.

On 21 April 2017 the applicants reported a car theft to Mladenovac Police Station, stating their passports had been left in the car. They were then subjected to a polygraph test and “informal” questioning at the Belgrade Police Directorate. No minutes were made of those interviews. The applicants were placed in separate rooms. The first applicant alleged that he was forced to kneel, slapped, kicked in the stomach, struck on the hands with a leather whip, suffocated with a plastic bag, threatened with shooting and electrocution, insulted with the racist phrase “Gypsy mother,” and warned that his children would be placed in care. The second applicant alleged threats of detention, accusations of being “the mask of an organised criminal group,” racist insults such as “white woman with a black man” and “Shqiptar in disguise,” and threats to take her children.

They were later returned to Mladenovac Station, where they gave formal statements. The minutes recorded the interviews as ending at 9.30 p.m. and stated that the applicants had no remarks and that the first applicant had no complaints about police treatment in Mladenovac or Belgrade. At 10.35 p.m., the first applicant was medically examined. The report documented head injuries, red spots near the left kidney region, and a pressure mark on his right knee. A further examination the next day revealed multiple head injuries and muscle pain. On 26 April 2017 he was diagnosed with PTSD attributed to the incident.

On 9 May 2017 the applicants lodged a criminal complaint against eight police officers, alleging ill-treatment because of the first applicant’s Roma origin. The prosecutor instructed the Department for the Control of Lawfulness of the Police to gather information. Five officers were questioned by 31 August 2017, while the applicants were heard on 8 December 2017. The officers denied ill-treatment but admitted informal questioning after the polygraph. Other officers present during parts of the questioning were not interviewed. The first applicant said he had not been informed what he was signing. The second applicant claimed psychological ill-treatment but said she had not given a statement at the Belgrade Police Directorate.

On 17 May 2018 the Prosecutor’s Office rejected the criminal complaint. It relied on the officers’ statements and the signed minutes showing no complaints. It also referred to CCTV footage from Mladenovac Station showing the applicants leaving without visible injuries. The first medical report was disregarded because the first applicant had no identity documents; the second was disregarded as made the day after the alleged ill-treatment; photographs were disregarded as undated. The second applicant’s psychological complaint was not addressed. The second-instance prosecutor upheld that decision on 29 August 2018.

In parallel, the applicants brought a discrimination claim against the State. On 1 June 2020 the Belgrade Court of Second Instance found that police officers had applied unjustified physical and psychological pressure amounting to degrading treatment. It awarded the first applicant EUR 4,700 and the second EUR 1,700 in non-pecuniary damages. It found their claim credible that the conduct was motivated at least partly by the first applicant’s Roma origin and the second applicant’s marriage to him, and that the State had not disproved this. That judgment became final on 17 December 2020.

On 28 October 2021 the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicants’ constitutional appeal concerning the rejection of their criminal complaint. It found the investigation adequate, thorough, and prompt, and held that discrimination could not be breached unless another constitutional right had first been violated. Before the European Court, notice was given only of the complaints concerning alleged ill-treatment by police; the remainder was declared inadmissible.

In *Stalović v. Serbia* (Application no. 35786/22), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints of racially motivated police ill-treatment and the lack of an effective investigation. They were then subjected to a polygraph test and “informal” questioning at the Belgrade Police Directorate. No minutes of those interviews were made. According to the applicants, they were placed in separate rooms. Mr Stalović alleged that he was forced to kneel, slapped, kicked in the stomach, struck on the hands with a leather whip, suffocated with a plastic bag, threatened with shooting and electrocution, racially insulted as a “Gypsy mother,” and warned that his children would be placed in care. They were returned to Mladenovac Station, where they gave formal statements. The minutes recorded that questioning ended at 9:30 p.m. and contained no remarks or complaints about police treatment. Later that night, at 10:35 p.m., Mr Stalović was examined at Mladenovac Health Centre. The medical report documented head injuries, red spots near the left kidney and a pressure mark on his right knee; the doctor reported this to the police. A further examination the next day revealed multiple head injuries and muscle pain in the neck and back. On 26 April 2017, he was diagnosed with PTSD attributed to the incident.

On 9 May 2017, the applicants filed a criminal complaint against eight police officers, alleging ill-treatment motivated by Mr Stalović’s Roma origin. The prosecutor instructed the Department for Control of Lawfulness of the Police to gather information. Five officers were questioned by 31 August 2017; the applicants were heard on 8 December 2017. The officers admitted informal questioning but denied ill-treatment. Other officers present during parts of the questioning were not interviewed. Mr Stalović said he had signed the minutes without knowing what he was signing; Ms Stalović claimed psychological ill-treatment and said she had not given a statement at the Belgrade Police Directorate.

On 17 May 2018, the first-instance prosecutor rejected the criminal complaint, accepting the officers’ statements and noting the signed minutes contained no complaints. On 1 June 2020, the Belgrade Court of Second Instance found that police had applied unjustified physical and psychological pressure amounting to degrading treatment, motivated at least partly by the first applicant’s Roma origin and the second applicant’s marriage to him. In *Begić v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Application no. 5067/23), the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section), by judgment of 3 February 2026, found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 (general prohibition of discrimination). The applicant, Zlatan Begić, born in 1975 and living in Tuzla, was a high-ranking official of the Democratic Front and a member of the House of Representatives of the Parliamentary Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He did not declare affiliation with any constitutionally defined “constituent people” (Bosniacs, Croats, and Serbs), and therefore belonged to the constitutional category of “Others.”

The Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina is annexed to the 1995 Dayton Agreement. It creates two Entities—the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republika Srpska—and the Brčko District. At State level, it establishes power-sharing arrangements, including a vital-interest veto, an Entity veto, a bicameral Parliament, a House of Peoples composed of five Bosniacs, five Croats, and five Serbs, and a tripartite Presidency. Although no ethnic requirement applies to election to the House of Representatives, Article IV § 3(b) requires each chamber to select from its members one Serb, one Bosniac, and one Croat as Chair and Deputy Chairs, with the Chair rotating among them. Consequently, a member who does not declare affiliation with a “constituent people” cannot be elected Chair or Deputy Chair. The Constitution also provides that Convention rights and freedoms have priority over all other law (Article II § 2) and secures certain international rights without discrimination (Article II § 4). The ethnic privileges were reportedly not part of the initial Agreed Basic Principles; international mediators accepted them later under pressure from some parties, while inserting provisions allowing for possible phase-out. However, the relevant provisions were not amended. The domestic Constitutional Court held in decisions nos. U 5/04 and U 13/05 that it lacked jurisdiction to review the Constitution’s conformity with the Convention and that the Convention could not have superior status to the Constitution.

On 1 December 2022, two members of the House of Representatives nominated the applicant for the position of Chair/Deputy Chair. The minutes show that his nomination was not put to a vote because it did not comply with the House’s Rules of Procedure—effectively because he did not belong to a constituent people. On 20 January 2023, he lodged an application complaining under Articles 14 and 17 of the Convention and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 about his ineligibility to stand for election to the position of Chair/Deputy Chair. The Court gave notice of those complaints to the Government and declared the remainder inadmissible.

The central alleged violation was that the applicant was ineligible to stand for election to the Chair/Deputy Chair of the House of Representatives without declaring affiliation with a constitutionally defined “constituent people.” The Court concluded that this restriction lacked objective and reasonable justification. The case therefore concerns discriminatory exclusion from a parliamentary leadership post based on ethnic/status classification, even though the applicant was eligible to be elected as an ordinary member of the House.

In the case of **Begić v. Bosnia and Herzegovina** (Application no. 5067/23), the European Court of Human Rights’ Fourth Section delivered judgment on 3 February 2026. The applicant, Zlatan Begić, born in 1975 and living in Tuzla, is a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a high-ranking official of the Democratic Front, and a member of the House of Representatives of the Parliamentary Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He does not declare affiliation with any of the constitutionally defined “constituent peoples”—Bosniacs, Croats and Serbs—and therefore belongs to the constitutional category of “Others and citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina.”

The Bosnian Constitution is an annex to the 1995 Dayton Agreement. It establishes a complex power-sharing system based on distinctions between constituent peoples and Others. At State level, this includes a House of Peoples with fixed ethnic quotas, a tripartite Presidency, an Entity veto and a vital-interest veto. Although elections to the House of Representatives do not formally require ethnic affiliation, Article IV § 3(b) of the Constitution provides that each chamber shall select from its members one Serb, one Bosniac and one Croat to serve as Chair and Deputy Chairs, with the chair rotating among them. As a result, a member who does not declare affiliation with a constituent people, such as the applicant, cannot be elected or selected to those positions.

On 1 December 2022, two members of the House of Representatives nominated the applicant for the position of Chair/Deputy Chair. According to the minutes of that meeting, his nomination was not put to a vote because it did not comply with the Rules of Procedure of the House of Representatives. The applicant alleged that this exclusion violated his rights. He complained under Articles 14 and 17 of the Convention and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 that he was ineligible to stand for election to the position of Chair/Deputy Chair because he did not declare affiliation with a constitutionally defined constituent people.

The Court gave notice to the Government of the complaints under those provisions and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. It ultimately found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 12, the general prohibition of discrimination. The key violation was that the applicant’s ineligibility to stand for election to the Chair/Deputy Chair position, unless he declared affiliation with one of the constituent peoples, had no objective and reasonable justification.

The background shows that these ethnic privileges were not included in the initial Agreed Basic Principles for the Dayton settlement. International mediators reportedly accepted them reluctantly later due to strong demands from parties to the conflict. They were aware the arrangements probably conflicted with human rights and inserted Article II § 2 of the Constitution, giving the Convention and its Protocols priority over all other law, partly to allow future phasing out. However, the provisions were never amended or declared unconstitutional. The domestic Constitutional Court, in decisions U 5/04 and U 13/05, held that it lacked jurisdiction to review the Constitution’s conformity with the Convention and that the Convention did not have priority over the Constitution. Thus, the applicant could not obtain a domestic ruling on the discriminatory character of the constitutional requirement. The Strasbourg Court therefore found that his exclusion from eligibility for the Chair/Deputy Chair posts amounted to unjustified discrimination contrary to Article 1 of Protocol No. 12.

**Case:** *Begić v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Application no. 5067/23), European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, Judgment of 3 February 2026.

The applicant, Zlatan Begić, is a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina, born in 1975 and living in Tuzla. He is a high-ranking official of the Democratic Front and a member of the House of Representatives of the Parliamentary Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Importantly, he does not declare affiliation with any of the constitutionally defined “constituent peoples” — Bosniacs, Croats, or Serbs — and therefore belongs to the constitutional category of “Others.”

The case concerns his ineligibility to stand for election to the position of Chair or Deputy Chair of the House of Representatives. Under Article IV § 3(b) of the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina — which is annexed to the 1995 Dayton Agreement — each chamber of the State Parliament must select, by majority vote, one Serb, one Bosniac, and one Croat from among its members to serve as Chair and Deputy Chairs, with the Chair rotating among them. Although no ethnic requirement applies to election to the House of Representatives itself, the Chair/Deputy Chair positions are reserved for members of the three “constituent peoples.” Persons like the applicant, who do not declare affiliation with a constituent people, are therefore excluded from those offices.

On 1 December 2022, two members of the House of Representatives nominated the applicant for the position of Chair/Deputy Chair. However, the nomination was not put to a vote because it did not comply with the Rules of Procedure of the House, which reflect the constitutional ethnic requirement. The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights on 20 January 2023, alleging violations of Articles 14 and 17 of the Convention and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12. He argued that his ineligibility for the Chair/Deputy Chair position, based solely on his refusal to declare affiliation with a “constituent people,” constituted unjustified discrimination.

The Court gave notice to the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina of the complaints under Articles 14 and 17 and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12, declaring the remainder of the application inadmissible.

A key domestic-law background is that the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina has held that it lacks jurisdiction to review the Constitution’s conformity with the European Convention, despite Article II § 2 of the Constitution providing that Convention rights have priority over all other law. The Constitutional Court considered the Convention not superior to the Constitution itself. Thus, the challenged constitutional provisions have neither been amended nor struck down.

The European Court found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 12, which contains a general prohibition of discrimination. The essential violation was that the applicant was ineligible to stand for election to the position of Chair/Deputy Chair of the House of Representatives without declaring affiliation with one of the constitutionally defined “constituent peoples.” The Court concluded that this restriction lacked any objective and reasonable justification. The ethnic power-sharing arrangements, while historically aimed at protecting constituent peoples, could not justify the blanket exclusion of “Others” from these parliamentary leadership positions. The judgment therefore reinforces that the ineligibility of persons who do not declare affiliation with a constituent people from such offices violates the prohibition of discrimination under Article 1 of Protocol No. 12.

Italy on 7 May 2026. The applications (nos. 54213/19 and 61041/19) were lodged against Italy under Article 34 of the Convention. The Government was represented by Mr L. D’Ascia. The judgment was adopted on 2 April 2026 after private deliberations.

The case concerns the effectiveness and duration of civil proceedings concerning alleged medical negligence that resulted in the deaths of the applicants’ next of kin. The applicants relied on Articles 2 and 6 of the Convention, complaining that the domestic civil proceedings were ineffective and excessively long. The Court decided to give notice to the Italian Government only of the complaint concerning Article 2 in its procedural limb. The remainder of the applications was declared inadmissible.

Application no. 54213/19: The applicants’ mother was hospitalised from 2 to 17 January 2004 and died on 18 January 2004. On 29 April 2005 the applicants brought a civil action against the hospital, seeking compensation for damage resulting from their mother’s death, which they alleged had been caused by the negligence of medical staff. The proceedings lasted a total of 14 years for three levels of jurisdiction. They ended with a judgment of the Court of Cassation delivered on 15 April 2019.

Application no. 61041/19: The applicant’s daughter, who had been affected since birth by congenital heart problems, was hospitalised from 12 to 20 December 1999. On 29 December 1999 the hospital decided not to readmit her, and she died the same day. On 18 January 2001 the applicant brought a civil action against the hospital, seeking compensation for damage sustained on account of alleged medical negligence in the treatment of his child. The proceedings ended with a judgment of the Court of Appeal on 14 May 2019, after the case had been remitted to that court by the Court of Cassation on 10 January 2017. The civil proceedings lasted a total of 16 years and 7 months for four levels of jurisdiction.

**Musina and Others v. Ukraine** (Application no. 48419/16) concerns four Ukrainian applicants—relatives of A.M.—who complained under Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights about A.M.’s death while he was under State control and about the alleged ineffectiveness of the investigation.

A.M., then 40 and medically fit, was called up for military service in April 2014 under a special mobilisation. He was due to be discharged in March 2015. An order for his discharge was dated 25 March 2015, but he remained in the military unit for several days to complete formalities.

At about 11 p.m. on 27 March 2015, a patrol found a heavily drunk soldier, V.S., lying near the gasmask distribution tent, about 20 metres from the central checkpoint. His upper and lower limbs were tied, and he had had a gag in his mouth, which he had removed to call for help. The guards freed him and let him go towards the barracks without obtaining explanations.

At about 6.10 a.m. on 28 March 2015, the patrol found A.M. dead inside the same tent. His wrists had been tied behind his back with two plastic hose clamps, his feet tied with electric cable to a tent pole, and his mouth covered with adhesive tape. A textile gag fell out when the tape was removed.

A criminal investigation was opened into murder/sudden death, but the register entry noted no indication of violent death. The military authorities claimed A.M. was no longer in service and thus outside military command jurisdiction; the investigation was allocated to the Novomoskovsk city police. Separately, the military prosecutor’s office investigated possible security/access omissions by the military unit; that inquiry was discontinued on 30 June 2015 for absence of a criminal offence.

At the scene, A.M.’s wristwatch was found outside the tent. A sniffer dog picked up a scent, went towards the checkpoint, reached the fence, and lost it. Several soldiers, including the patrol, were questioned. They claimed nothing unusual except drunk comrades and the V.S. incident. V.S. said he had been drinking with A.M. and two “unidentified” soldiers; he remembered little and alleged an unidentified soldier had gagged him. Two soldiers said they drank with A.M. and V.S. until about 2 p.m. on 27 March and knew nothing later.

A death certificate of 30 March 2015 attributed death to acute coronary insufficiency. A forensic report of 10 April 2015 concluded coronary insufficiency exacerbated by heavy alcohol intoxication. It noted minor injuries—sores and bruises on A.M.’s mouth and cheeks—before death, but no causal link to death. It also observed dried soil around and inside his nostrils and on his mouth. A later forensic examination in November 2015 again found no causal link between the tying of A.M.’s hands and feet and his death.

The investigation was marked by alleged omissions. On 16 June 2015, the criminal investigation unit reported that military unit management refused to provide information on who had been present on 27–28 March 2015. On 27 June 2015, police discontinued the investigation for absence of a criminal offence, relying on the forensic report. On 6 July 2015, the prosecutor’s office quashed that decision as premature and unlawful, and the first and second applicants were granted victim status. A November 2015 operational meeting noted that prosecution instructions had not been followed and that serious omissions had undermined the investigation.

In January 2016, cytological examination found no DNA; blood on the tape and gag could not be attributed because no blood samples had been provided, and skin cells under A.M.’s fingernails were unsuitable for analysis. The acting commander, R.K., was first questioned only on 18 June 2016. He said A.M. stayed beyond 25 March to hand over his position, denied knowing who tied A.M. or V.S., and stressed the unit was secure with strict access control, ruling out unauthorised persons.

The investigation was discontinued again on 30 November 2016, quashed on 3 March 2017, and terminated again on 30 March 2017 in nearly identical terms. The investigator had been disciplined several times for poor quality. The applicants therefore alleged that A.M. died in State-controlled military custody in suspicious circumstances and that authorities failed to protect him and to conduct an effective investigation.

**Case: Ismayilova v. Azerbaijan (Applications nos. 44031/17 and 41494/20), European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, judgment of 7 April 2026.**

The applicant, Khadija Ismayilova, is an Azerbaijani investigative journalist born in 1976, living in Baku. The case concerns a travel ban imposed on her after her conditional release from prison.

In September 2015, the Baku Court of Serious Crimes convicted her of large-scale misappropriation, illegal entrepreneurship, tax evasion, and abuse of power. She was sentenced to seven years and six months’ imprisonment and barred for three years from holding managerial and financial posts in public and local self-government bodies. Her appeal was dismissed in November 2015. In May 2016, the Supreme Court quashed several convictions, upheld only illegal entrepreneurship and tax evasion, reduced her sentence to three years and six months suspended on probation for five years, and imposed a two-year ban on managerial and financial posts. Her release was conditional on not changing her permanent residence without prior notification to the Binagadi District Enforcement Department.

In June 2016, during her first meeting with a bailiff, the applicant learned that a travel ban had been imposed for the duration of her probation. On 19 June 2016, she challenged the ban before the Binagadi District Court, seeking its removal. She stated that she had received invitations to international conferences from international organisations and NGOs and that attending such events was essential to her work as an investigative journalist. She also sought permission to accompany her mother to Türkiye for heart surgery, submitting medical documentation.

On 28 June 2016, the Binagadi District Court dismissed her application. It found that allowing her to leave Azerbaijan at will would limit the authorities’ ability to monitor her behaviour during probation and might hinder her rehabilitation, thereby frustrating execution of the sentence. It also noted that there were no guarantees she would return to Azerbaijan.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the first-instance court had failed to address her reasoning or assess her personal situation and had relied on irrelevant arguments. She contended that her conduct after the Supreme Court’s May 2016 decision—including regular self-reporting to the Enforcement Department, a clean record, and her professional and social reputation—undermined the court’s claims about lack of return guarantees and inability to monitor her.

On 15 August 2016, the Baku Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal, holding that the restriction was necessary to oversee execution of her conditional sentence during probation. On 8 December 2016, the Supreme Court upheld that decision, served on the applicant on 16 December 2016.

On 7 July 2019, the applicant asked the Binagadi District Court to revoke her suspended sentence, remove her conviction, and lift the travel ban, arguing that more than half of the probationary period had elapsed. On 9 August 2019, the District Court refused, finding insufficient evidence of rehabilitation and no bailiff opinion supporting it. Her appeal was dismissed by the Baku Court of Appeal on 20 September 2019, again for insufficient evidence of rehabilitation. On 6 February 2020, the Supreme Court upheld that decision.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 and Article 13 that the travel ban violated her right to leave the country and that she had no effective domestic remedy. She also complained under Articles 8 and 10, and under Article 18 taken together with Article 2 of Protocol No. 4, that the travel ban violated her private and family life and freedom of expression, and that her Convention rights were restricted for purposes other than those prescribed. Third-party comments were submitted by the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights and Article 19 in application no. 44031/17.

They also referred to general security considerations for short-term meetings, without linking them to the applicant’s personal situation, and to alternative means of communication. The authorities noted that section 31(21) of the Internal Prison Rules gave prison authorities discretion to allow meetings without a glass partition in certain situations, but they did not indicate that the applicant’s circumstances fell within any of the listed categories. It considered that alternative means of contact existed and that the applicant had been passive in addressing the issue. The interference was therefore not particularly severe. The court noted that the applicant had never complained about the visit arrangements and had never requested visits in a room without a glass partition. He had thus failed to use a primary remedy—an application to oblige the administrative body to adopt a decision or take measures (*kohustamiskaebus*)—which was a prerequisite for a compensation claim. The court admitted, however, that this remedy might not have been effective in preventing interference with respect to each meeting request. It also stated that it did not consider the use of the glass partition unlawful, referring, among other things, to the applicant’s general dangerousness. **Nikitin v. Estonia** (Application no. 49257/22) concerns an Estonian life prisoner’s complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights about being separated from his visitors by a glass partition during short-term prison meetings.

The applicant, Vladimir Nikitin, born in 1968 and detained in Viru Prison, had eight short-term meetings with his wife and her son between 2 June 2018 and 19 December 2019. During each meeting, he was separated from his visitors by a glass partition and could communicate only through an intercom system. He alleged that this arrangement unlawfully interfered with his right to respect for family and private life.

In November 2020, the applicant asked the Viru Prison authorities for compensation for those meetings. The prison authorities rejected the request. They stated that he had never asked for meetings to be held without a glass partition, which they described as the more appropriate remedy and as required under the State Liability Act. They also relied on general security considerations for short-term meetings, available alternative means of communication, and section 31(21) of the Internal Prison Rules, which gave prison authorities discretion to allow meetings without a partition in certain situations. However, in later submissions, the authorities said the applicant’s circumstances did not fall within any of the exceptions listed in that provision.

The applicant challenged the refusal before the Tartu Administrative Court. On 31 May 2021, that court dismissed his appeal. It found that alternative means of maintaining contact existed and that the interference with his rights was not severe enough to justify compensation. The court also considered that requiring a glass partition during short-term meetings was proportionate to prison security needs, noting that exceptions were possible under section 31(21) of the Internal Prison Rules.

On 28 February 2022, the Tartu Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment. It again emphasised alternative contact methods and the applicant’s own passivity. The court found that the interference had not been particularly severe. It noted that the applicant had never complained about the visit arrangements or requested a room without a glass partition. In its view, he had failed to use a primary remedy—an application to oblige the administrative body to adopt a decision or take measures (*kohustamiskaebus*)—which was a precondition for a compensation claim. The Court of Appeal nevertheless acknowledged that this remedy might not have effectively prevented interference for each individual meeting request. It further found that the use of the glass partition was not unlawful, referring in part to the applicant’s general dangerousness. Even assuming the measure had been unlawful, the court said monetary compensation would not have been warranted.

On 7 June 2022, the Supreme Court refused to examine the applicant’s appeal on points of law.

The applicant then lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 6 October 2022, complaining under Article 8 of the Convention about the refusal to allow him short-term meetings without a glass partition. The Court gave notice of that complaint to the Estonian Government and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The central issue before the Court is therefore whether the use of the glass partition during the eight short-term meetings, and the domestic refusal to award compensation, violated the applicant’s Article 8 rights.

**Gazin v. Ukraine (Application no. 43898/19), European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, Judgment of 5 March 2026**

The case concerned allegedly ineffective domestic proceedings in respect of medical malpractice. The applicant, Mr Andriy Yuriyovych Gazin, a Ukrainian national born in 1967 and living in Dnipro, complained that criminal proceedings into his allegations of medical negligence were lengthy and ineffective. Although he initially relied on Articles 3 and 13, the Court examined the complaint under the procedural limb of Article 8 of the Convention.

The key facts are as follows. On 3 August 2012, the applicant was admitted to Dnipro Municipal Clinic no. 4 with acute flank pain. He was diagnosed with a ureteral stone and renal colic. In the early hours of 4 August 2012, duty doctor M.P. performed urinary catheterisation. The applicant’s condition subsequently deteriorated: he developed fever, lower abdominal pain and increased urinary frequency, and was diagnosed with acute pyelonephritis. He was discharged on 17 August 2012 in satisfactory condition. In October 2012, he was readmitted with increased urinary frequency, up to once hourly, and blood in the urine. Tests revealed a urethral stricture and chronic cystitis. Despite treatment, his urinary frequency did not significantly improve.

On 6 June 2013, after the applicant complained against M.P., the police instituted criminal proceedings into medical malpractice. During the investigation, police obtained medical records, questioned the applicant and M.P., and commissioned three forensic examinations. The final forensic report, completed in December 2015, concluded that the applicant’s medium-severity injuries—urethral stricture, cystitis and chronic urinary retention—had resulted from an improperly performed catheterisation.

Within the criminal proceedings, the applicant lodged a civil claim, first against the clinic and then against M.P., seeking more than 3 million Ukrainian hryvnias (over 100,000 euros at the time) in pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages for pain and suffering. On 28 September 2016, M.P. was formally notified of suspicion of medical negligence under Article 140 § 1 of the Criminal Code. On 5 December 2016, the criminal case and the civil claim were referred to the Leninskyi District Court of Dnipro for trial.

During the trial, the court heard the applicant and four witnesses. Both the applicant and M.P. submitted new forensic evidence: M.P. relied on a report stating that his actions met medical standards and that the complications might have been unrelated to the catheterisation, while the applicant submitted a contrary report. As of October 2025, the trial remained pending at first instance, with no decision on either the criminal charges or the civil claim.

The Government argued that the applicant had not exhausted domestic remedies because he had not sought compensation from the State for ineffective proceedings, and that the application was premature since the criminal case was still pending. The applicant disagreed, noting that he had lodged a civil claim within the criminal proceedings. The Court joined these objections to the merits and declared the application admissible.

On the merits, the Court reiterated that victims of medical negligence must have access to proceedings capable of establishing the facts, holding those at fault accountable, and providing redress, and that such proceedings must operate effectively and within a reasonable time. It found that the applicant’s choice to pursue criminal proceedings with a civil claim was appropriate under Ukrainian law and was accepted by the authorities. It also rejected the Government’s argument that a separate civil remedy was available, noting that parallel civil remedies during pending criminal medical-negligence proceedings were not effective in Ukraine.

The Court found that the criminal proceedings had not operated effectively. They began in June 2013, were referred to court in December 2016, and had remained at first instance for many years without a final judgment or decision on the civil claim. Although the case was complex and some sessions were postponed at the applicant’s request, those factors could not justify proceedings lasting more than 12 years at first instance. The Court therefore found a violation of the procedural limb of Article 8 of the Convention.

In Gazin v. Ukraine (no. 43898/19, judgment 5 March 2026), the ECtHR considered the applicant’s complaint that domestic criminal proceedings concerning medical malpractice were lengthy and ineffective.

Andriy Gazin, a Ukrainian national born in 1967, was admitted on 3 August 2012 to Dnipro Municipal Clinic No. 4 with acute flank pain. Diagnosed with a ureteral stone and renal colic, he underwent urinary catheterisation by duty doctor M.P. early on 4 August 2012. In October 2012 he was readmitted with frequent urination and blood in urine. Tests revealed a urethral stricture and chronic cystitis; urinary frequency did not significantly improve.

Investigators gathered medical records, questioned the applicant and M.P., and commissioned three forensic examinations. The final forensic report in December 2015 concluded that the applicant’s injuries—urethral stricture, cystitis and chronic urinary retention, classified as medium severity—resulted from improperly performed catheterisation. The applicant lodged a civil claim within the criminal proceedings, later directed against M.P., seeking over UAH 3 million (more than €100,000) in pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages. On 28 September 2016 M.P. was notified of suspicion of medical negligence under Article 140 § 1 of the Criminal Code. On 5 December 2016 the criminal case and civil claim were referred to the Leninskyi District Court of Dnipro. Both sides later submitted conflicting forensic evidence. As of October 2025, the trial remained pending at first instance with no decision on the criminal charge or the civil claim.

The applicant complained that the proceedings were lengthy and ineffective. Originally relying on Articles 3 and 13, he later added Articles 6 and 8. The Court examined the complaint under the procedural limb of Article 8. The Government argued non-exhaustion, saying he should have sought State compensation for ineffective proceedings, and that the application was premature because the criminal case was still pending. The applicant replied that his civil claim formed part of the criminal proceedings and that separate civil proceedings were not an effective remedy. The Court joined these objections to the merits.

On the merits, the Court held that victims of medical negligence must have access to proceedings capable of establishing the facts, holding those at fault accountable, and providing redress within a reasonable time. It found the applicant’s decision to pursue a civil claim within the criminal proceedings appropriate; a parallel civil remedy would not have been effective while the criminal proceedings were pending, and the Government’s examples concerned different pre-trial situations. Although the case was complex and some delays were caused by the applicant—25 of 98 hearings were postponed at his request—the proceedings had lasted over 12 years and remained at first instance. The State must organise its judicial system to meet Convention requirements. The prolonged failure to decide M.P.’s liability and the civil claim meant the proceedings did not operate effectively in practice. The Court therefore found a violation of the procedural limb of Article 8.

In *Gazin v. Ukraine* (Application no. 43898/19), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, Committee) delivered judgment on 5 March 2026. The applicant complained under Articles 3, 13, and later Articles 6 and 8 that the criminal proceedings were lengthy and ineffective. The Court examined the case under the procedural limb of Article 8. The Government argued non-exhaustion and prematurity, claiming the applicant could have sought State compensation and that the criminal proceedings were still pending. The Court joined those objections to the merits.

The Court noted its prior case law that, in Ukraine, a parallel civil remedy was not effective while medical-negligence criminal proceedings were pending. It found that the proceedings had begun in June 2013, reached trial in December 2016, and had remained at first instance for over 12 years. In **Gazsó v. Hungary** (Application no. 48322/12), the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) delivered judgment on 16 July 2015; it became final on 16 October 2015. The applicant, Mr György Gazsó, a Hungarian national, complained that the litigation of his labour dispute had lasted unreasonably long and that Hungary provided no effective remedy for that delay. He relied on Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention.

The key facts arose from a dispute with his former employer. Earlier litigation between the applicant and the employer ran from 25 February 2002 to 18 May 2005 and ended with an order requiring the employer to re-employ him. The applicant did not accept the position offered in implementation of that order. Consequently, new litigation began on 5 January 2006. On 18 November 2008, the Budapest Labour Court dismissed the applicant’s action. On appeal, on 9 July 2010, the Budapest Regional Court reversed that decision and found for the applicant. The respondent then pursued a petition for review before the Kúria. On 29 February 2012, the Kúria reversed the appeal judgment and found for the respondent.

For the purposes of the applicant’s complaint, the relevant period therefore began on 5 January 2006 and ended on 29 February 2012. It lasted almost six years and two months and involved three levels of jurisdiction. On 13 November 2014, the application was communicated to the Government, and the Court proposed the pilot judgment procedure, indicating that the case might concern a systemic problem of delayed proceedings and inadequate remedies in Hungary. The parties submitted comments on that proposal.

As to Article 6 § 1, the applicant alleged that the length of the proceedings was incompatible with the “reasonable time” requirement. The Government contested this. The Court declared the complaint admissible. On the merits, it applied the established criteria: complexity of the case, conduct of the applicant and authorities, and what was at stake. It stressed that special diligence is required in employment disputes. The dispute was not particularly complex; it concerned the applicant’s re-employment. The authorities did not exercise the requisite due diligence to bring the case to an end. Neither the applicant nor the respondent was shown to have caused any particular delay. The Government failed to provide facts or arguments capable of justifying the duration. The Court therefore found that the length of the proceedings was excessive and violated the “reasonable time” requirement of Article 6 § 1.

As to Article 13 read in conjunction with Article 6 § 1, the applicant complained that no effective domestic remedy existed by which he could accelerate the proceedings or obtain compensation for their length. The Government contested this in general terms. The Court declared this complaint admissible. It noted that the Convention institutions had already held that no effective domestic remedy was available in Hungary in respect of protracted civil proceedings, citing *Bartha v. Hungary* and *Mr T.K. and Mrs T.K. v. Hungary*. The Government had not shown that the situation had changed, either in terms of acceleratory remedies or compensatory remedies. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 13 read in conjunction with Article 6 § 1.

The case thus concerned both excessive delay in a labour dispute and Hungary’s systemic lack of an effective remedy for such delay.

It emphasised that special diligence is required in employment disputes. The dispute was not particularly complex; it concerned the applicant’s re-employment. The Court was not satisfied that the authorities had exercised the requisite due diligence in bringing the case to an end. It also found that neither the applicant nor the respondent had caused any particular delay. Hungary and Mr T.K. and Mrs T.K. v. Hungary. The Government did not show that the situation had changed, whether in terms of acceleratory or compensatory remedies.
