**Miclea v. Romania** (Application no. 69582/12, judgment of 13 October 2015) concerned Alexandru Miclea, a Romanian national, who alleged that he was ill-treated by two police officers at the Arad police station on 8 August 2010 and that the subsequent investigation and court proceedings were ineffective, violating Articles 3 and 6 of the Convention.

According to the applicant, at around 4 a.m. on 8 August 2010, after a fight outside a bar, police took him and his friends to the police station to give statements. While waiting, Miclea saw officer D.C.I. behaving roughly with an arrestee and commented loudly that a police officer represented State authority and should not hit people. D.C.I. allegedly became angry and asked another officer, M.C., to take Miclea “to the toilets to teach him how to speak.” When Miclea resisted, the officers took him outside and then into a back office, handcuffed him to a radiator, and punched and kicked him. Another officer intervened after hearing screams. Miclea was allegedly warned not to report the beating. He was later escorted home.

That same day, Miclea went to Arad County Hospital, where he was diagnosed with maxillofacial trauma and contusions of the lower lip and thorax. A forensic certificate issued on 9 August 2010 recorded a sutured cut on the lower lip, bruising on the upper lip and left chest, excoriations on the back, grazes and bruising on the right elbow, right leg and left knee, and excoriations on both wrists. The injuries were consistent with an impact with or on a hard object on 8 August 2010 and would require nine days of medical treatment absent complications. The wrist excoriations were potentially consistent with Miclea’s claim that he had been handcuffed.

The Government denied that police officers had beaten Miclea. It claimed his injuries resulted from the street brawl. The police officers stated that they had merely asked the group to wait outside.

On 15 September 2010, Miclea lodged a criminal complaint against the two officers for abusive conduct and bodily harm. He was heard on 23 September 2010. Two witnesses who had been taken to the station with him, S.L. and S.N., were heard in February 2011; they said they had heard Miclea screaming outside the police station and later saw his injuries. The two accused officers were not heard until June 2011, and then by an internal affairs officer rather than a prosecutor. Three additional police officers testified in July 2011. In January 2012, the prosecutor declined to pursue charges, finding Miclea’s account contradicted by the accused officers and their colleagues and that the injuries could have come from the street fight. Miclea complained that a proposed witness, K.A., who allegedly saw him punched, was not heard, and that the police witnesses were not impartial. The head prosecutor dismissed his complaint in February 2012. On 18 April 2012, the Arad District Court rejected Miclea’s challenge as manifestly ill-founded, relying on discrepancies in the accounts—such as whether he was beaten inside or outside and whether he was handcuffed to a radiator or behind his back—without hearing witnesses or addressing his objections.

The European Court of Human Rights declared the application admissible and examined the complaints under Article 3. It found the investigation ineffective: there were significant delays, the accused officers were heard only nine months after the complaint, key witness K.A. was not heard, the medical evidence of wrist excoriations was not clarified, the authorities preferred police statements without adequate explanation, other complaints against the same officers were ignored, and the domestic court relied on police statements without hearing witnesses or addressing the applicant’s criticisms. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 3 in its procedural aspect. Because the evidence was conflicting and the investigation defective, the Court could not establish beyond reasonable doubt whether the alleged ill-treatment itself occurred, and it found no need to examine the complaint separately under Article 6.

**Miclea v. Romania** (Application no. 69582/12), European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, judgment of 13 October 2015.

The applicant, Alexandru Miclea, a Romanian national born in 1989, alleged that on 8 August 2010 he was ill-treated by two police officers at the Arad police station and that the subsequent investigation and court proceedings were ineffective. The Court examined his complaints under Article 3 of the Convention.

The key facts were disputed. Around 4 a.m. on 8 August 2010, the applicant and friends were involved in a street fight outside a bar. Police were called; the aggressors fled, and the applicant and others were taken to the police station to give statements. While waiting, the applicant allegedly saw officer D.C.I. behaving roughly with an arrestee and commented that police should not hit people. According to the applicant, D.C.I. became angry and asked colleague M.C. to “take him to the toilets to teach him how to speak.” The applicant resisted and was allegedly taken into a back office, handcuffed to a radiator, and punched and kicked by D.C.I. and M.C. Another officer stopped the assault after hearing screaming. One officer allegedly warned him not to report it. The applicant was later escorted home. That day he went to Arad County Hospital with maxillofacial trauma and lip and thorax contusions. A forensic certificate the next day recorded a sutured lower lip, bruising, excoriations on the back and limbs, and excoriations on both wrists, consistent with handcuffing. The injuries required nine days of medical treatment. The Government claimed the injuries came from the street brawl, not police violence.

On 15 September 2010 the applicant lodged a criminal complaint against the officers and asked that several witnesses, including K.A./K.E., be heard. The investigation was delayed. The applicant was heard on 23 September 2010. Two witnesses, S.L. and S.N., were heard in February 2011; both said they heard the applicant screaming and later saw his injuries. The accused officers were first heard only in June 2011, nine months after the complaint, by an internal-affairs officer rather than a prosecutor. Three police witnesses were heard in July 2011.

In January 2012 the prosecutor decided not to pursue charges, finding the applicant’s and his witnesses’ statements contradicted by the accused officers and their police colleagues, so it was not certain he had been assaulted. The head prosecutor upheld that decision. The applicant challenged it in court, arguing that the prosecutor ignored important evidence and that K.A. had partly witnessed the ill-treatment. On 18 April 2012 the Arad District Court dismissed the challenge as ill-founded, relying on discrepancies: S.L. said he heard screaming outside while the applicant said he was beaten inside; the applicant said he was handcuffed to a radiator while S.L. referred to hands behind his back; and the injuries could have come from the street fight. The court did not hear the applicant or any witnesses.

The ECtHR found the investigation ineffective. The authorities delayed hearing the accused officers and police witnesses, relied heavily on police accounts, failed to explain why the applicant’s witnesses were less credible, did not clarify the wrist excoriations, and ignored other complaints against the same officers. The domestic court also decided without hearing witnesses or addressing the applicant’s concerns. Because of this ineffective investigation, the Court could not establish whether the alleged ill-treatment occurred. It therefore found a violation of Article 3 in its procedural aspect concerning the failure to conduct an effective investigation.

**Miclea v. Romania** (Application no. 69582/12) concerned allegations of police ill-treatment and an ineffective investigation, examined by the European Court of Human Rights under Article 3 of the Convention.

On 8 August 2010, at around 4 a.m., the applicant, Alexandru Miclea, and his friends were involved in a fight outside a bar in Arad. Police were called, and Miclea and others were taken to the Arad police station to give statements. Miclea alleged that, while waiting, he criticized police officer D.C.I. for behaving roughly toward an arrestee. D.C.I. allegedly told officer M.C. to take Miclea “to the toilets to teach him how to speak.” When Miclea resisted, he was taken outside and then into a back office, where D.C.I. and M.C. allegedly handcuffed him to a radiator and punched and kicked him. Another officer stopped the beating after hearing screams. Miclea claimed one officer warned him not to report the incident or he would be beaten again. The Government denied police violence, asserting that Miclea’s injuries came from the street fight and that police merely escorted the group home.

Later that day, Miclea went to Arad County Hospital and was diagnosed with maxillofacial trauma and contusions to the lower lip and thorax. On 9 August 2010, a forensic certificate recorded a sutured lower-lip cut, bruising to the upper lip and chest, excoriations on the back and wrists, and grazes and bruising on the elbow, leg, and knee. It estimated nine days of medical treatment and noted the injuries could have been caused by impact with a hard object on 8 August 2010.

On 15 September 2010, Miclea lodged a criminal complaint against the two officers, accusing them of abusive conduct and bodily harm. He requested that several witnesses be heard, including K.A./K.E. The investigation was transferred between prosecutor’s offices. In February 2011, Miclea and witnesses S.L. and S.N. were heard. They said they heard screaming, later saw Miclea’s injuries, and were told he had been beaten by police. The accused officers were first heard in June 2011 by an internal-affairs officer; they denied violence. Three other police witnesses were heard in July 2011. One said Miclea had injuries from the street fight; another said Miclea did not complain while being escorted home.

On 12 January 2012, the prosecutor decided not to pursue charges, finding Miclea’s and his witnesses’ statements contradicted by the officers and their colleagues, so it could not be established with certainty that police assaulted him. Miclea’s complaint was dismissed in February 2012. On 18 April 2012, the Arad District Court rejected his challenge as manifestly ill-founded. It relied on discrepancies: S.L. said he heard screaming outside, while Miclea said he was beaten inside; S.L. said Miclea was handcuffed behind his back, while Miclea said he was handcuffed to a radiator. The court also found injuries could have come from the brawl. It did not hear witnesses or confront versions.

The European Court of Human Rights found the investigation ineffective. Authorities delayed taking key statements: the applicant was heard a week after his complaint, witnesses four months later, the accused officers nine months later, and other police witnesses ten months later. The prosecutor gave more credibility to officers without adequate explanation, dismissed the applicant’s witnesses, ignored wrist excoriations consistent with handcuffing, and overlooked similar complaints against the same officers. The domestic court decided without hearing witnesses and failed to address investigative shortcomings. Consequently, the Court found the State failed to conduct a proper investigation and could not establish beyond reasonable doubt whether the alleged ill-treatment occurred.
001-249531:
In **Novák v. the Czech Republic**, the applicant, Stanislav Novák, is the father of two daughters (born 2014 and 2018). After separating from the children’s mother in April 2021, the parents initially agreed to share custody in Brno. In September 2021, the mother filed for divorce and sought sole custody, while the applicant sought shared custody. From January 2022, the mother refused shared custody, although the applicant continued regular contact, including overnight visits on Tuesdays and alternate weekends. Counselling efforts failed.

While the custody proceedings were pending, the applicant sought interim shared custody. The Brno Municipal Court granted this on 18 May 2022, but the Brno Regional Court overturned it on 14 June 2022, finding no urgent need because the mother was caring for the children and the applicant had contact. On 14 July 2022, the Municipal Court awarded weekly shared custody, relying on a counselling report and the guardian ad litem’s opinion. The mother appealed, which suspended the decision.

On 28 August 2022, the mother unilaterally relocated with the children from Brno to Prague and enrolled them in school there, without the applicant’s consent. She proposed alternate-weekend and holiday contact. The social welfare authority declared the children “endangered.” The applicant applied for interim measures seeking custody or the children’s return and re-enrolment in their original schools. These applications were dismissed in September 2022, mainly because the courts found no urgent endangerment, noted the applicant still had contact, and relied on the earlier Regional Court decision. One application failed because a required deposit was paid late. The applicant’s appeals were dismissed on 2 December 2022. The Regional Court accepted that the mother had relocated without agreement but found no serious impairment or urgent need for an interim measure; it considered further change contrary to the children’s best interests and left residence and schooling to the merits.

The applicant sought expedition. A guardian ad litem reported that the children had settled in Prague and recommended fresh examination. In March 2023, the mother made a criminal complaint alleging inappropriate behaviour by the applicant toward one daughter and refused handovers; expert evidence later found no danger or deviance. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal against the interim refusals on 5 April 2023.

On 20 April 2023, the Regional Court overturned the shared-custody judgment and granted the mother sole custody, with the applicant having contact every second weekend and during holidays. It found both parents capable but held that the children had adapted well in Prague, the distance exceeded 200 km, shared custody would burden them with travel and two schools, and the children wished to stay with their mother. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 17 October 2023.

Afterwards, the mother repeatedly refused handovers. Enforcement proceedings followed, with fines imposed. On 6 December 2023, the District Court enforced contact rights, rejected the applicant’s sole-custody request, and authorised the relocation and school change. Later expert evidence found no danger, and contact resumed. In February 2025, the mother was convicted of obstructing enforcement of contact rights.

The alleged Article 8 violation concerned the domestic courts’ failure to strike a fair balance after the mother’s unilateral and unlawful relocation, their insufficiently reasoned dismissal of the applicant’s interim measures, and their eventual decisions that consolidated and legitimised the situation she had created, making the possibility of sole or shared custody merely theoretical.

The case concerns an application by Stanislav Novák, a Czech national, against the Czech Republic under Article 8 of the Convention. The applicant is the father of two daughters, born in 2014 and 2018. In April 2021, after separating from the children’s mother, the parents agreed to share custody. In September 2021 the mother filed for divorce and sought sole custody, while the applicant sought shared custody. From January 2022 the mother refused to continue shared custody, although the applicant maintained regular contact, including overnight visits and alternate weekends.

In May 2022 the Brno Municipal Court granted the applicant interim shared custody, but the Brno Regional Court overturned that decision in June 2022, finding no urgent need because the children were properly cared for by the mother and the applicant had contact. In July 2022 the Municipal Court awarded shared custody on the merits, relying on a counselling report and the guardian ad litem’s opinion that both parents were capable and the children had positive relationships with each. The mother appealed, and the appeal had suspensive effect.

On 28 August 2022 the mother informed the applicant by email that she had moved with the children from Brno to Prague, more than 200 km away, and enrolled them in school there. She proposed contact every other weekend and during holidays. The next day she sought court authorisation for the relocation and school change without the applicant’s consent. The social welfare authority subsequently declared the children “endangered.” On 7 September 2022 the applicant applied for interim measures: one granting him custody and fortnightly contact to the mother, and another ordering the children’s return and re-enrolment in their original schools. On 12 September 2022 the Municipal Court dismissed the first application, referring to the June 2022 Regional Court decision and finding no urgent need. It dismissed the return application because the required deposit of about EUR 400 had been paid one day late. A second return application was dismissed on 21 September 2022, the court finding no sufficient endangerment. The applicant’s appeals were dismissed on 2 December 2022. The Regional Court accepted that the mother had relocated without agreement, but found that the applicant had not shown serious impairment or endangerment and that further change was not in the children’s best interests. It left the issue of residence and schooling to the merits.

The applicant sought expedition of the merits. In March 2023 the guardian ad litem reported that the children had settled in Prague, though there had been a significant change in circumstances. The mother also lodged a criminal complaint against the applicant concerning alleged inappropriate behaviour and refused to hand over the children. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal against the interim-measure decisions in April 2023 as manifestly ill-founded.

On 20 April 2023 the Regional Court overturned the shared-custody judgment and granted the mother sole custody, with the applicant having contact every second weekend and during holidays. It found that both parents were capable, but that the children had adapted well to Prague, lived near relatives, and that the distance made shared custody impractical. It also relied on the children’s wishes to remain with their mother. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s further appeal in October 2023.

From March 2023 onward the mother repeatedly refused handovers, leading to enforcement proceedings. In December 2023 the District Court fined her for missed visits, rejected the applicant’s request for sole custody, and authorised the relocation. Further fines followed in 2024, and an expert found no danger posed by the applicant. In February 2025 the mother was convicted of obstructing contact rights and given a suspended sentence.

The ECtHR found an Article 8 violation, holding that the domestic courts failed to strike a fair balance between the parties’ interests. Their interim decisions lacked sufficient reasons, and by consolidating and eventually legitimising the situation unlawfully created by the mother, they rendered the applicant’s possibility of obtaining sole or shared custody merely theoretical.

In *Novák v. the Czech Republic*, the applicant father complained under Article 8 that Czech courts failed to protect his family life after the mother of his two daughters unilaterally relocated them and was ultimately awarded sole custody. The daughters were born in 2014 and 2018. After the parents separated in April 2021, they initially agreed to shared custody. In September 2021 the mother sought divorce and sole custody, while the father sought shared custody. From January 2022 the mother refused shared custody, although the father maintained weekly contact, including overnight visits and alternate weekends. Counselling attempts did not produce agreement.

In May 2022, pending the merits, the Brno Municipal Court granted interim shared custody. The Brno Regional Court overturned that decision in June 2022, finding no urgent need because the mother cared properly for the children and the father had regular contact. In July 2022 the Municipal Court awarded weekly shared custody based on counselling and the guardian’s report. The mother appealed, and the appeal had suspensive effect.

On 28 August 2022, while the appeal was pending, the mother informed the father that she had moved with the children from Brno to Prague and enrolled them in school there. She proposed contact every other weekend, during holidays, and by telephone/online. The next day she sought court authorisation for the relocation and school change. The father notified the social welfare authority, which declared the children “endangered.” On 7 September he applied for interim measures seeking either custody or the children’s return and re-enrolment.

On 12 September the Municipal Court dismissed both applications. It found no urgent need, citing the mother’s proper care and the father’s continuing contact. The return application failed because the required deposit was not paid on the day of filing, though it was received the next day. The father filed a new return application on 20 September; it was dismissed on 21 September for lack of sufficient endangerment. On appeal, the Regional Court dismissed his appeals on 2 December 2022. It accepted that the mother had acted without agreement but found no serious impairment or endangerment, noted the alternate-weekend contact, and held that further change was not in the children’s best interests. It said residence and schooling would be decided on the merits.

A March 2023 guardian report noted the children had settled in Prague and that circumstances had significantly changed. The mother then made a criminal complaint against the father and refused handovers. In April 2023 the Constitutional Court dismissed the father’s interim-measure appeal. On 20 April 2023 the Regional Court overturned the shared-custody judgment and granted the mother sole custody, with the father having contact every second weekend and holidays. It relied on the children’s eight-month adaptation, the 200 km distance making shared custody impractical, and the children’s wishes to stay in Prague. The Constitutional Court dismissed the father’s appeal in October 2023.

Later enforcement proceedings showed repeated withheld contact, supervised visits, fines against the mother, and an expert finding no danger from the father. The mother was convicted in February 2025 of obstructing contact rights. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 8: the domestic courts failed to strike a fair balance, gave insufficient reasons in dismissing interim measures, and ultimately consolidated and legitimised the mother’s unlawful relocation, making the father’s possibility of obtaining sole or shared custody merely theoretical.
001-155102:
In *PSMA, spol. s r.o. v. Slovakia* (Application no. 42533/11), the applicant was a Slovak private limited company. It complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that a final and binding judgment in its favour had been quashed after an extraordinary appeal on points of law lodged by the Prosecutor General, following a petition by the opposing party. The central alleged violation concerned fair hearing, access to court, equality of arms, adversarial proceedings, and legal certainty, particularly the principle that finally determined matters should not be reopened without compelling justification.

In 1995 PSMA contracted with Slovak Radio to act as exclusive agent for selling broadcasting time for advertising. The contract was amended several times and was valid until 31 December 2007. In 2004 relations deteriorated. Slovak Radio billed PSMA for an alleged shortfall between estimated and actual profit. PSMA refused to pay, and Slovak Radio terminated the contract for fundamental breach, with the notice period ending on 30 September 2005. PSMA initially challenged the termination in court but later withdrew that action. Slovak Radio then sued PSMA for the disputed profit difference; the outcome of that case was not provided.

PSMA later demanded approximately €693,000 as indemnity for termination, calculated using its average yearly commission over the preceding five years and including barter transactions. It sued Slovak Radio for that sum and late-payment interest.

On 14 May 2007 the Bratislava I District Court granted PSMA’s claim in full. Although Slovak Radio was represented by a lawyer, it submitted no written observations and did not appear at hearings. The District Court therefore examined the case under Article 101 § 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, based on available elements. It found the termination valid, held PSMA eligible for indemnity, and accepted that barter transactions should be included. On 28 November 2007 the Bratislava Regional Court upheld that judgment. The judgment became final on 9 January 2008 and enforceable on 12 January 2008.

Slovak Radio’s constitutional complaint was declared inadmissible on 3 July 2008 because it had not exhausted an appeal on points of law. On 25 April 2008 Slovak Radio petitioned the Prosecutor General to lodge an extraordinary appeal. The Prosecutor General agreed and, on 23 October 2008, challenged the judgments before the Supreme Court, arguing that the lower courts had erred regarding the validity of termination and the indemnity, and that barter transactions should not have been included. The Supreme Court suspended enforceability on 8 December 2008.

PSMA objected that the extraordinary appeal was inadmissible because an ordinary appeal on points of law had been available, that the Prosecutor General exceeded the scope of the petition, and that reopening the case violated legal certainty. On 12 August 2009 the Supreme Court allowed the extraordinary appeal, quashed both lower judgments, and remitted the case to the first-instance court for re-examination, finding that the courts had failed properly to examine the validity of the contract and the termination notice. PSMA’s subsequent constitutional complaint was rejected as manifestly ill-founded on 25 November 2010.

The European Court of Human Rights distinguished an abstract challenge to the extraordinary appeal framework, which was inadmissible, from PSMA’s concrete complaint about the quashing of the final judgment in its favour. It declared the latter complaint admissible and examined whether the Prosecutor General’s intervention and the Supreme Court’s quashing of a final judgment amounted to a violation of Article 6 § 1, especially in light of legal certainty and res judicata.

PSMA, spol. s r.o. v. Slovakia (ECtHR, Third Section, 9 June 2015) concerned a Slovak company’s complaint under Article 6 § 1 that a final judgment in its favour was quashed after an extraordinary appeal lodged by the Prosecutor General.

The applicant company, PSMA, concluded a 1995 contract with Slovak Radio to act as exclusive agent for advertising sales. The contract was amended and remained valid until 2007. In 2004 relations deteriorated after Slovak Radio billed PSMA for an alleged shortfall in profit. PSMA refused to pay, and Slovak Radio terminated the contract for fundamental breach; the notice expired on 30 September 2005. PSMA initially challenged the termination but withdrew that action. Slovak Radio separately sued PSMA for the disputed sum.

In 2006 PSMA demanded approximately EUR 693,000 as indemnity for termination, calculated using average yearly commission and including barter transactions, and sued Slovak Radio. On 14 May 2007 the Bratislava I District Court granted the claim in full. Slovak Radio had failed to submit observations or attend hearings, so the court proceeded under Article 101 § 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It found the termination valid and included barter transactions in the indemnity. The Bratislava Regional Court dismissed Slovak Radio’s appeal on 28 November 2007. The judgment became final on 9 January 2008 and enforceable on 12 January 2008.

Slovak Radio then filed a constitutional complaint, which was declared inadmissible on 3 July 2008 because it had not exhausted an appeal on points of law. It also petitioned the Prosecutor General. The Prosecutor General filed an extraordinary appeal on 23 October 2008, arguing that the lower courts had failed to examine independently the validity of the termination and had wrongly included barter transactions. The Supreme Court suspended enforceability on 8 December 2008. On 12 August 2009 it allowed the extraordinary appeal, quashed both lower judgments, and remitted the case to the District Court for fresh examination, finding that the courts had failed to examine the validity of the contract and notice. PSMA’s constitutional complaint against that decision was declared inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded on 25 November 2010.

Before the ECtHR, PSMA alleged that quashing the final and binding judgment in its favour following the Prosecutor General’s extraordinary appeal violated Article 6 § 1. It argued that this breached legal certainty, access to a court, equality of arms, and adversarial proceedings. The extraordinary appeal was, in substance, an appeal in disguise for the losing party, which had an ordinary appeal on points of law available but did not use it. PSMA also complained that the Prosecutor General’s appeal exceeded the scope of Slovak Radio’s petition, lacked statutory admissibility grounds, and that the Supreme Court ignored PSMA’s observations and denied it access to the case file.

The Government disputed admissibility, arguing prematurity and non-exhaustion, but the Court rejected the prematurity objection because the complaint concerned the quashing of a final judgment, not the eventual outcome of the reopened proceedings. The Court declared the Article 6 complaint admissible. Applying principles of legal certainty, it emphasised that final rulings should not be reopened merely for a re-hearing or because there are two views on the case; reopening is justified only for fundamental defects, not as an appeal in disguise, and must strike a fair balance. The Court found that the extraordinary appeal and the Supreme Court’s quashing of the final judgment violated Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

In *PSMA, spol. s r.o. v. Slovakia* (Application no. 42533/11, ECtHR Third Section, 9 June 2015), the applicant was a Slovak private limited company. In 1995 it concluded a contract with Slovak Radio, Slovakia’s public-service broadcaster, under which it acted as exclusive agent for the sale of advertising broadcasting time. The contract was amended several times and was valid until 31 December 2007. In 2004 relations deteriorated over the profits generated by the applicant. Slovak Radio billed the applicant for an alleged shortfall; when the applicant did not pay, Slovak Radio terminated the contract for fundamental breach. The notice period expired on 30 September 2005. The applicant later demanded approximately EUR 693,000 as contractual indemnity for termination, including amounts for barter transactions. After Slovak Radio refused to pay, the applicant sued on 1 June 2006.

On 14 May 2007 the Bratislava I District Court granted the applicant’s claim in full. Slovak Radio had failed to submit written observations and did not attend hearings, so the court proceeded under Article 101 § 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It found the termination valid—apparently because it had not been contested—and included barter transactions in the indemnity calculation. Slovak Radio appealed. On 28 November 2007 the Bratislava Regional Court upheld the judgment. It noted that Slovak Radio had acknowledged the legal basis of the indemnity and disputed mainly the barter element. It also found that the lower court had been justified in proceeding despite Slovak Radio’s absence. The judgment became final and binding on 9 January 2008 and enforceable on 12 January 2008.

Slovak Radio then filed a constitutional complaint, which was declared inadmissible on 3 July 2008 because it had not exhausted an appeal on points of law. On 25 April 2008 Slovak Radio petitioned the Prosecutor General to challenge the final judgments by an extraordinary appeal on points of law. The Prosecutor General agreed and, on 23 October 2008, lodged an extraordinary appeal with the Supreme Court. He argued that the lower courts had erred by failing to examine properly the validity of the contract and the termination notice, and that barter transactions should not have been included in the indemnity. The Supreme Court suspended enforceability on 8 December 2008. On 12 August 2009 it allowed the extraordinary appeal, quashed both lower judgments, and remitted the case to the first-instance court for fresh examination.

The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. It alleged that the quashing of a final and binding judgment in its favour, following an extraordinary appeal lodged by the Prosecutor General at the request of the losing party, breached its rights to a fair hearing, access to a court, equality of arms, adversarial proceedings and legal certainty. It argued that the extraordinary appeal was an ordinary appeal in disguise; that no statutory admissibility grounds were met; that the Prosecutor General exceeded the scope of Slovak Radio’s petition; that Slovak Radio could have used an ordinary appeal on points of law; and that the Supreme Court ignored its observations and denied it access to the case file. Its subsequent constitutional complaint against the Supreme Court’s decision was declared inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded on 25 November 2010. The central issue before the ECtHR was therefore whether the Prosecutor General’s extraordinary appeal and the Supreme Court’s resulting quashing of a final judgment were compatible with Article 6 § 1, particularly the principle of legal certainty and the fairness of the proceedings.
001-155374:
In *Kovárová v. Slovakia* (Application no. 46564/10, judgment of 23 June 2015), the applicant, Eva Kovárová, complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about access to court and a fair hearing.

On 9 May 2007, the applicant brought a civil action in the Bratislava V District Court against the community of owners of flats in her building. She sought a declaration that a meeting of flat owners held on 24 April 2007 was contrary to law and that its decisions were void. The defendant was officially registered with the local District Authority.

On 2 January 2008, a lawyer informed the District Court that the defendant had ceased to exist. A letter from the District Authority showed that the defendant had been struck from the register on 14 December 2007, because administration of the building had been transferred to a specialised agency. After learning of this, the applicant asked on 24 January 2008 to postpone an upcoming hearing, saying she needed time to analyse the situation and would make a further submission. The hearing was adjourned. Nevertheless, on 3 March 2008, the District Court discontinued the proceedings. It held that the defendant had no legal successor and that neither the individual flat owners nor the new administration agency had succeeded to its position.

The applicant appealed on 20 March 2008. She argued, first, that the administration agency was the legal successor, so the proceedings should continue against it. Alternatively, she argued that the court should have stayed the proceedings pending separate litigation challenging the 11 September 2007 decision to wind up the defendant. On 30 May 2008, the Bratislava Regional Court upheld the discontinuance. It stated that the defendant lacked capacity to be a party and that discontinuance was unavoidable, but gave no real reasons for rejecting the request to stay. On 7 May 2009, the Supreme Court declared the applicant’s appeal on points of law inadmissible. It found that the alleged errors did not fall within Article 237(f) of the Code of Civil Procedure and that staying proceedings was optional, not mandatory. It did not examine the merits.

On 17 August 2009, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint against all levels of the ordinary courts. She alleged that the discontinuance was unlawful, that her claim had never been examined on the merits, and that this breached her rights of access to court and to a fair hearing under Article 6 § 1. On 16 December 2009, the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible. It rejected as belated the part concerning the Regional Court because it was filed outside the two-month statutory time-limit. As to the Supreme Court, it held that its admissibility decision was reasoned and not arbitrary. It noted that if the other proceedings declared the winding-up void, reopening might be possible, but that a judicial declaration would not automatically restore the defendant’s legal existence.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged that the ordinary courts’ decisions were arbitrary and that the Constitutional Court had breached her access to court by rejecting as belated her complaint against the Regional Court. The Government argued that the Constitutional Court had in fact examined important parts of her arguments.

The European Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1. The applicant’s civil claim had never been examined on the merits. Her two main objections—existence of a legal successor and the failure to stay proceedings—were raised before the appellate court, the Supreme Court, and the Constitutional Court. The Regional Court dismissed them summarily. The Supreme Court did not examine the first argument and considered the second only for admissibility. The Constitutional Court excluded the Regional Court’s decision as belated, and its review of the Supreme Court was limited to the procedural admissibility question. Its comments on possible reopening were inconclusive. Therefore, an essential part of the applicant’s access-to-court arguments was excluded from constitutional review. By rejecting that part as belated, the Constitutional Court prevented her from effectively using the Article 127 remedy. The Court did not separately examine whether the ordinary courts’ discontinuance was arbitrary.

In *Kovárová v. Slovakia* (Application no. 46564/10, judgment 23 June 2015), the applicant, Eva Kovárová, a Slovak national, brought a civil action on 9 May 2007 before the Bratislava V District Court against a registered “community of owners” of flats. She sought a declaration that a meeting of flat owners held on 24 April 2007 was unlawful and that its decisions were void.

On 14 December 2007, the defendant was struck out of the relevant District Authority register and ceased to exist legally; administration of the building was transferred to a specialised agency. On 2 January 2008, a lawyer informed the District Court of this. The applicant requested an adjournment on 24 January 2008, stating that she had just learned of the defendant’s deletion and needed time to respond. On 3 March 2008, the District Court discontinued the proceedings because the defendant no longer existed and had no legal successor. It held that neither the individual flat owners nor the new administration agency had succeeded to the defendant’s position.

The applicant appealed on 20 March 2008. She argued, first, that the administration agency was the defendant’s successor and the proceedings should continue against it. Second, alternatively, the court should have stayed the proceedings pending separate proceedings challenging the decision to wind up the defendant. On 30 May 2008, the Bratislava Regional Court upheld the discontinuance, finding that the defendant had lost capacity to be a party and there was no alternative. It gave no reasons for rejecting the applicant’s alternative arguments.

On 7 July 2008, the applicant appealed on points of law under Article 237(f) of the Code of Civil Procedure, arguing that the courts had prevented her from pursuing her case. On 7 May 2009, the Supreme Court declared the appeal inadmissible. It held that the alleged shortcomings did not fall within Article 237(f), and that staying proceedings was optional, not mandatory. It did not examine the merits of her arguments.

On 17 August 2009, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint against all three levels of ordinary courts, alleging breach of her rights of access to court and fair hearing under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. On 16 December 2009, the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible. The part concerning the Regional Court’s decision was rejected as belated. As regards the Supreme Court, it found that the inadmissibility decision was not arbitrary and gave relevant reasons. It noted possible future reopening depending on the other proceedings, but observed that even invalidating the winding-up would not automatically restore the defendant’s legal existence.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that the ordinary courts’ discontinuance was arbitrary and that the Constitutional Court had breached her access to court by rejecting the part of her complaint concerning the Regional Court as belated. The Government sought to distinguish the case from *Franek v. Slovakia*, arguing that the Constitutional Court had in fact examined important parts of her arguments.

The Court rejected that distinction. The applicant’s civil claim was never examined on the merits. Her two principal arguments—that a legal successor existed and that the proceedings should have been stayed—were summarily dismissed by the Regional Court. The Supreme Court did not examine the first argument at all and treated the second only as an admissibility issue. The Constitutional Court then refused to examine the Regional Court part as belated and limited its review to the Supreme Court’s admissibility decision. The Court found that this excluded an essential part of the applicant’s arguments from constitutional review, as in *Franek*. Consequently, the Constitutional Court’s rejection of the relevant part of her complaint prevented her from effectively using the Article 127 constitutional remedy. There was therefore a violation of the applicant’s right of access to court under Article 6 § 1. Given that finding, the Court did not separately examine whether the ordinary courts’ discontinuance was arbitrary.

**Case: Kovárová v. Slovakia (Application no. 46564/10), ECtHR, Third Section, 23 June 2015**

The applicant, Ms Eva Kovárová, a Slovak national, lodged a civil action on 9 May 2007 with the Bratislava V District Court against a “community of owners” of flats in her building. She sought a declaration that a meeting of flat owners held on 24 April 2007 was unlawful and that its decisions were void. The defendant was registered with the local District Authority.

On 2 January 2008, a lawyer acting for the defendant informed the District Court that the defendant had ceased to exist on 14 December 2007 and had been struck off the register. The building’s administration had been transferred to a specialised agency. After learning of this, the applicant requested an adjournment on 24 January 2008 so she could analyse the situation; the hearing was adjourned. On 3 March 2008, the District Court discontinued the proceedings because the defendant no longer existed and had no legal successor. It held that neither the individual flat owners nor the new administration agency could be regarded as successors.

The applicant appealed on 20 March 2008. She argued first that the administration agency was the legal successor and that proceedings should continue against it. Alternatively, she argued that the court should have stayed the proceedings pending separate proceedings challenging a decision of 11 September 2007 to wind up the defendant. On 30 May 2008, the Bratislava Regional Court upheld the discontinuance, stating that the defendant lacked capacity to be a party, with no alternative to terminating the case. It provided no substantive reasons for rejecting the applicant’s arguments.

The applicant then appealed on points of law under Article 237(f) of the Code of Civil Procedure, claiming the courts had prevented her from pursuing her case. On 7 May 2009, the Supreme Court declared the appeal inadmissible, holding that the alleged shortcomings did not fall within that provision and that staying proceedings was an option, not a duty. It did not examine the merits.

On 17 August 2009, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint under Article 127 of the Constitution against all three levels of the ordinary courts. On 16 December 2009, the Constitutional Court declared it inadmissible. The part concerning the Regional Court’s decision was rejected as belated under the two-month time-limit. As to the Supreme Court, the Constitutional Court found its admissibility decision was not arbitrary. It noted that if the other proceedings declared the defendant’s winding up void, the applicant might seek reopening, though this would not automatically restore the defendant’s legal existence.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention: that the ordinary courts’ decisions were arbitrary and that the Constitutional Court had breached her right of access to court by rejecting part of her complaint as belated. The ECtHR declared the application admissible.

On the merits, the Government argued that the Constitutional Court had actually examined important parts of her arguments and that the case was distinguishable from *Franek v. Slovakia*. The applicant maintained that the Supreme Court had only reviewed admissibility, while the Constitutional Court reviewed only the Supreme Court, leaving the lower courts’ decisions and her central arguments unexamined.

The ECtHR found that the applicant’s civil claim was never examined on its merits. Her first main argument—that a legal successor existed—was summarily dismissed by the Regional Court and never examined by the Supreme Court or Constitutional Court. Her second argument—that proceedings should have been stayed—was considered only as an admissibility issue, not on its merits. By rejecting the part of her constitutional complaint concerning the Regional Court as belated, the Constitutional Court excluded an essential part of her arguments. The ECtHR therefore found a violation of the right of access to court under Article 6 § 1. It did not separately examine whether the ordinary courts’ discontinuance was arbitrary.
001-154354:
In *Santos Silva v. Portugal* (Application no. 52246/12, judgment of 30 April 2015), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by José António Oliveira Santos Silva, a Portuguese national, concerning the excessive length of civil proceedings and the absence of an effective domestic remedy.

On 19 December 2005 the applicant brought an action before the Santa Maria da Feira Court against several defendants regarding a right to use a water channel. After rectifying his application, complications arose because two defendants had died—one in 1973 and another in May 2005—and heirs were living in Brazil. In May 2006 the court stayed the proceedings pending inheritance proceedings and asked the applicant to submit death certificates. In November 2006 the applicant sought leave to continue against the heirs, filing supporting documents in January 2007. In July 2007 the court admitted the heirs as parties, and the main proceedings later resumed.

Further delay followed. On 23 April 2008 the applicant was notified that the court had failed to summon defendant A.G. On 27 January 2010 the court interrupted the proceedings for lack of action by the parties. On 26 January 2011 the applicant provided a new address for one of the heirs. The proceedings were eventually resumed. On 24 November 2011 the first-instance court dismissed the applicant’s claim as time-barred. The applicant appealed on 6 December 2011. On 4 June 2013 the Porto Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance decision and ordered a new trial. The case remained pending at first instance. The relevant period therefore began on 19 December 2005 and had not ended, lasting over nine years for two levels of jurisdiction.

The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 that the length of the proceedings violated the “reasonable time” requirement, and under Article 13 that Portuguese law provided no effective remedy for excessive length. The Government acknowledged delay but argued that the applicant’s conduct had caused it.

The Court declared the application admissible. Applying the criteria of complexity, conduct of the applicant and authorities, and what was at stake, it found the case not particularly complex. Although the applicant was responsible for some delay, the main protractedness resulted from the national authorities. In particular, the proceedings stood still for approximately three years between April 2008 and 2011, when the first-instance court remained inactive while waiting for information about a defendant’s address and interrupted the proceedings. The Court stressed that even in systems where parties drive procedure, courts must ensure expeditious trials under Article 6 § 1. It also noted that the appeal lasted about a year and a half, and the case then remained pending more than a year awaiting retrial. The Government offered no justification for delays of about three years attributable to the authorities. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1.

On Article 13, the Court recalled that an effective remedy must exist for allegedly excessive proceedings. Following its case-law, notably *Martins Castro and Alves Correia de Castro v. Portugal*, and absent contrary arguments from the Government, it found that the applicant had no effective domestic remedy in Portugal. It accordingly also found a violation of Article 13.

The European Court of Human Rights (First Section) decided *Santos Silva v. Portugal* (Application no. 52246/12) on 30 April 2015. The applicant, José António Oliveira Santos Silva, a Portuguese national born in 1957, complained under Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention that civil proceedings in Portugal had exceeded a reasonable time and that he had no effective domestic remedy for that delay.

On 19 December 2005 the applicant brought an action before the Santa Maria da Feira Court against several defendants concerning a right to use a water channel. He rectified the initial application in January 2006. In February 2006, one defendant replied and informed the court that her husband, defendant A., had died in May 2005. Another defendant stated that defendant A. J. had died in 1973 and that his heirs lived in Brazil. On 5 May 2006 the court stayed the proceedings pending inheritance proceedings concerning the deceased defendants, giving the applicant a deadline to submit death certificates. In November 2006 the applicant applied for leave to continue the proceedings against the heirs, submitting supporting documents in January 2007. On 2 July 2007 the court admitted the heirs as parties and later resumed the main proceedings.

On 23 April 2008 the applicant was notified that the court had failed to summon defendant A. G. There followed a long period of inactivity. On 27 January 2010 the court interrupted the proceedings because of lack of action by the parties. On 26 January 2011 the applicant informed the court of a new address for defendant A.’s heir, and the proceedings were later resumed. On 24 November 2011 the first-instance court dismissed the applicant’s claim as time-barred. The applicant appealed in December 2011. On 4 June 2013 the Porto Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance decision and ordered a new trial. The proceedings were still pending at first instance at the time of the Strasbourg judgment.

The ECtHR noted that the relevant period began on 19 December 2005 and had not yet ended, lasting over nine years and one month for two levels of jurisdiction. The Government acknowledged delay but argued that the applicant’s conduct had caused it. The Court found the case not particularly complex. Although the applicant could be held responsible for some delays, the overall protractedness resulted mainly from the domestic authorities. In particular, the proceedings stood still for approximately three years between April 2008 and 2011 while the court remained inactive, awaiting information about a defendant’s address, which led it to interrupt the proceedings. The Court stressed that even in systems where procedural initiative lies with the parties, courts must ensure compliance with the expeditious-trial requirement under Article 6 § 1. It also noted that the appeal had lasted almost one and a half years and that the new first-instance trial had been pending for more than a year. Finding no justification for delays attributable to national authorities, the Court concluded that the length of proceedings was excessive and violated Article 6 § 1.

As to Article 13, the applicant complained that Portuguese law provided no court before which he could complain about the excessive length of proceedings. The Court recalled that Article 13 guarantees an effective remedy for an alleged breach of the reasonable-time requirement. Relying on its case-law and the absence of contrary arguments from the Government, it found that the applicant had no effective remedy. The Court therefore found violations of both Article 6 § 1 and Article 13.

**Case:** *Santos Silva v. Portugal* (Application no. 52246/12), European Court of Human Rights, First Section, judgment of 30 April 2015.

The applicant, José António Oliveira Santos Silva, a Portuguese national born in 1957, lived in Louredo, Santa Maria da Feira. On 19 December 2005 he brought a civil action before the Santa Maria da Feira Court against several defendants concerning a right to use a water channel. He rectified the initial application in January 2006.

The proceedings were complicated early on by the deaths of certain defendants. In February 2006, one defendant stated that her husband, defendant A., had died in May 2005. Another defendant informed the court that defendant A.J. had died in 1973 and that his heirs lived in Brazil. In May 2006, the Santa Maria da Feira Court stayed the proceedings pending inheritance proceedings concerning the deceased defendants and gave the applicant time to file death certificates. In November 2006, the applicant applied for leave to proceed against the deceased defendants’ heirs, filing supporting documents in January 2007. In July 2007, the court admitted the heirs as parties and later resumed the main proceedings.

Progress remained slow. On 23 April 2008, the applicant was notified that the court had failed to summon defendant A.G. On 27 January 2010, the first-instance court interrupted the proceedings for lack of action by the parties. On 26 January 2011, the applicant supplied the new address of defendant A.’s heir. The proceedings were later resumed. On 24 November 2011, the Santa Maria da Feira Court dismissed the applicant’s claim as time-barred. The applicant appealed on 6 December 2011. On 4 June 2013, the Porto Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance decision and ordered a new trial. At the time of the Strasbourg judgment, the case was still pending at first instance.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged that the length of the proceedings violated the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. He also alleged that Portugal provided no effective remedy for excessive length, contrary to Article 13. The Government contested both claims. It acknowledged that the proceedings had been delayed and had exceeded what could reasonably be expected, but argued that the delay was caused by the applicant’s conduct and was not attributable to the domestic courts.

The Court found the application admissible. The relevant period began on 19 December 2005 and had not yet ended, lasting over nine years for two levels of jurisdiction. Applying the criteria of complexity, conduct of the applicant and authorities, and what was at stake, the Court found the case was not particularly complex. Although the applicant was responsible for some delays, the main protractedness was attributable to the authorities. In particular, the proceedings stood still for approximately three years between April 2008 and 2011 while the Santa Maria da Feira Court remained inactive awaiting information about a defendant’s address. The Court reiterated that even in systems where procedural initiative lies with the parties, courts must ensure expeditious proceedings under Article 6 § 1. It also noted the appeal lasted almost one and a half years and that more than a year had passed awaiting retrial.

The Court found no justification for delays of approximately three years attributable to national authorities. It therefore held that the length of proceedings was excessive and violated Article 6 § 1. As to Article 13, the Court recalled that an effective domestic remedy must exist for complaints of excessive length. Following its case-law, notably *Martins Castro and Alves Correia de Castro v. Portugal*, and absent contrary arguments from the Government, it found that the applicant had no effective remedy. Accordingly, it also found a violation of Article 13.

K.F. v. Cyprus (ECtHR, Fourth Section, 21 July 2015) concerned a Syrian national of Kurdish origin who entered Cyprus illegally in February 2005 and applied for asylum. His asylum claim was rejected in August 2008, and the Reviewing Authority upheld that rejection in June 2009. The authorities found credibility problems: K.F. initially gave different reasons for leaving Syria, later claiming he had fled after participating in the 2004 Qamishli Kurdish events, being detained and ill-treated, and fearing an honour-killing vendetta. He also submitted a Syrian document allegedly ordering his arrest, but the Reviewing Authority doubted its authenticity and his overall credibility.

In August 2009, deportation and detention orders were issued against him as a “prohibited immigrant.” He was detained but released in December 2009 when those orders were revoked. In May 2010 he applied to reopen his asylum file and joined a Kurdish protest in Nicosia against Cypriot asylum policies. On 11 June 2010, police cleared the encampment; 149 people were transferred, and K.F. was among those arrested and detained as an unlawful stayer. New deportation and detention orders were issued. The European Court of Human Rights applied Rule 39 on 14 June 2010, preventing his deportation to Syria. He remained in detention until 20 April 2011. His reopened asylum claim and Supreme Court recourse were rejected, and his habeas corpus application was dismissed in March 2011; his appeal was later dismissed as moot after release. In 2012, he left Cyprus for Northern Iraq.

The applicant alleged that deportation to Syria would breach Article 3 (risk of torture or inhuman/degrading treatment), that he lacked an effective remedy under Article 13, that his detention violated Article 5 §§ 1(f), 2 and 4, and that deportation would breach Article 4 of Protocol No. 4. The Government argued he was no longer a victim under Article 3 and had failed to exhaust domestic remedies.

The Court struck out the Article 3 and Article 13 complaints under Article 37 § 1(c). Because K.F. had voluntarily left Cyprus and was living in Iraq, he no longer faced deportation from Cyprus to Syria, and no special human-rights circumstances required continued examination. It therefore did not need to decide the Government’s victim-status or exhaustion objections.

On Article 5 § 4, K.F. complained that he had no effective and speedy remedy to challenge the lawfulness of his detention from 11 June 2010 to 20 April 2011. The Court found the issue concerning the Article 146 recourse proceedings identical to M.A. v. Cyprus. Following that judgment, it held that there had been a violation of Article 5 § 4 because the recourse did not satisfy the “speediness” requirement. It also declared admissible and assessed his complaint concerning delays in the habeas corpus proceedings, applying the general principle that speediness must be assessed overall. Thus, the key alleged violations concerned the risk of deportation under Articles 3 and 13—rendered moot by his departure—and the lack of speedy judicial review of his detention under Article 5 § 4.

**Summary of K.F. v. Cyprus (Application no. 41858/10)**

The applicant, K.F., a Syrian national of Kurdish origin born in 1979, entered Cyprus illegally in February 2005 and applied for asylum. His application was dismissed in August 2008, with the Asylum Service citing contradictions between his written application and interview statements that undermined his credibility. He appealed, but the Reviewing Authority dismissed his appeal in June 2009, finding he had given inconsistent reasons for leaving Syria—first claiming he came "for living," then alleging persecution by the family of a girl with whom he had eloped, who was killed in an honour killing.

In August 2009, deportation and detention orders were issued, and the applicant was arrested. These orders were revoked in December 2009, and he was released. In May 2010, he sought reopening of his asylum file, submitting a document purportedly from the Syrian Ministry of Interior instructing his arrest. The Reviewing Authority rejected this in May 2011, finding the document unauthentic and the applicant's claims incoherent and inconsistent, noting he had never previously claimed political persecution.

In June 2010, following a protest encampment by Kurdish asylum seekers in Nicosia, Cypriot authorities conducted a large-scale removal operation. The applicant was among 149 people transferred to police headquarters; 44 were arrested for unlawful stay. Deportation and detention orders were issued against him on 11 June 2010, and he was detained at Larnaca Police Station.

The applicant alleged that deportation to Syria would expose him to torture or inhuman treatment (Article 3), citing his Kurdish origin, prior detention and torture in Syria following the 2004 Qamishli events, an outstanding arrest warrant, and his involvement in demonstrations in Cyprus. He also complained of the lack of an effective remedy (Article 13), unlawful detention (Article 5 §§ 1(f), 2, 4), and that deportation would breach Article 4 of Protocol No. 4 (prohibition of collective expulsion).

The Court applied Rule 39 in June 2010, preventing deportation. The applicant escaped from detention in March 2011, was injured, returned, and was released in April 2011 after the orders were revoked. His habeas corpus application was dismissed in March 2011; his appeal was ultimately dismissed in October 2012 as without object following his release.

In 2012, the applicant voluntarily left Cyprus for Northern Iraq despite the Rule 39 measure, which was then lifted. The Court struck out the Article 3 and 13 complaints, finding he was no longer at risk of deportation from Cyprus to Syria and that no special circumstances justified continued examination.

Regarding Article 5 § 4, the Court found a violation concerning the recourse proceedings, following its judgment in M.A. v. Cyprus, as recourse under Article 146 of the Constitution did not satisfy the "speediness" requirement. The habeas corpus complaint was declared admissible, with the Court conducting an overall assessment of the proceedings' length.

The case primarily concerns the intersection of asylum procedures, immigration detention, and the effectiveness of judicial review in Cyprus, with the Court's findings largely tracking its earlier jurisprudence in M.A. v. Cyprus.
