001-158279:
In *Pentikäinen v. Finland* (ECtHR Grand Chamber, 20 October 2015), the applicant was a Finnish photographer and journalist employed by *Suomen Kuvalehti*. On 9 September 2006 he was assigned to cover the “Smash ASEM” demonstration in Helsinki, held in protest against the Asia-Europe Meeting. Police risk assessments, based on earlier violent demonstrations and the absence of clear organisers, led to an exceptional deployment of 480 officers. The police arranged a media area at Paasikivi Square, though the applicant disputed its adequacy and accessibility.

The demonstration began at 6 p.m. Violence soon broke out: bottles, stones and paint-filled jars were thrown, and officers were kicked. Police declared a riot, cordoned off the area, and repeatedly ordered the crowd to disperse. Families and media representatives were allowed to leave. The applicant remained inside the cordon, claiming his presence was necessary to report on the event and that police lines, minibuses and buses blocked visibility. Around 9 p.m., an officer told him he had one last chance to leave. The applicant said he was reporting for *Suomen Kuvalehti* and intended to follow the event to its end. Later, as he photographed near a former MP, police allegedly shouted “Get the photographer!” and apprehended him. He stated he was a journalist and had a press card; the police disputed how clearly he identified himself. His camera and memory cards were not confiscated, and he retained his photographs.

The applicant was detained from 9:26 p.m. on 9 September until 3:05 p.m. on 10 September—about seventeen and a half hours—and was interrogated the next day. He alleged that this prevented him from transmitting information online. He was charged with contumacy towards the police under Chapter 16, section 4(1), of the Finnish Penal Code for disobeying police orders. In December 2007, Helsinki District Court found him guilty but waived punishment, treating the offence as comparable to an excusable act because of conflicting expectations from the police and his profession. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal, and the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal in September 2009.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Pentikäinen alleged a violation of Article 10 (freedom of expression). He complained that the police order to leave, his detention preventing transmission of information, and the suspicion, charge and conviction created a “chilling effect” on his journalism. He argued that the interference was not prescribed by law or proportionate: the dispersal order was categorical, the violence was limited, his detention exceeded the twelve-hour limit for contumacy, he was not a rioter, there was no adequate secure media area, he identified himself as a journalist, and the situation was calm when he was apprehended. The Government maintained that police acted lawfully; the applicant knew of the dispersal orders and chose to stay; media could leave; his equipment was preserved; and no penalty was imposed.

The Grand Chamber accepted that there had been an interference with Article 10 but ultimately found no violation. It held that the measures were prescribed by law, pursued public safety and the prevention of disorder, and were proportionate, emphasising journalists’ duties and responsibilities during violent demonstrations and the fact that the applicant could have left without consequence and still reported on the event.

In *Pentikäinen v. Finland* (ECtHR Grand Chamber, 20 October 2015), the applicant, Markus Pentikäinen, was a Finnish photographer and journalist for the weekly magazine *Suomen Kuvalehti*. On 9 September 2006 he was assigned to cover the “Smash ASEM” demonstration in Helsinki against the Asia-Europe Meeting. The event attracted heavy media interest. Police risk assessments, based partly on two earlier violent Helsinki demonstrations, indicated the protest could be hostile, and posters encouraged disorder. Police deployed 480 officers and set up a media area near Paasikivi Square.

The demonstration began at 6 p.m. Soon bottles, stones, and paint-filled jars were thrown at police and bystanders; some demonstrators kicked or hit officers. At about 6:30 p.m. police declared a riot, cordoned off the area, and announced that a peaceful static demonstration was allowed but marching was not. They later repeatedly ordered the crowd to disperse; families and media were allowed to leave through checkpoints. Pentikäinen remained inside the cordon, believing his journalistic task required him to follow events to the end. Around 9 p.m. an officer personally told him he had one last chance to leave. Pentikäinen said he was reporting for *Suomen Kuvalehti* and intended to stay; the officer left him alone. Later, as police broke up remaining demonstrators, Pentikäinen heard an officer shout “Get the photographer!” and was apprehended while photographing. He told the arresting officer he was a journalist and had a press card; he was allowed to stow his camera equipment. The stated basis for apprehension was contumacy towards police.

Pentikäinen was detained from 9:26 p.m. on 9 September until 3:05 p.m. on 10 September—17.5 hours—and interrogated the following day. He alleged he could not transmit information during detention. The Government maintained his camera, memory cards, and photographs were not confiscated and he could use them freely. He was charged with contumacy towards the police under Chapter 16, section 4(1), of the Finnish Penal Code for failing to obey a police order. In December 2007 the Helsinki District Court convicted him but waived punishment under Chapter 6, section 12, treating the act as comparable to an excusable act due to conflicting expectations from police and his profession/employer. The court found police orders were lawful, clear, and applied to everyone in the crowd; Pentikäinen knew of them but ignored them. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal, and the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal.

Before the ECtHR, Pentikäinen alleged a violation of Article 10 (freedom of expression). The alleged interference consisted of the police order to leave, his inability to report during 17.5-hour detention, and the criminal suspicion, charge, and conviction, which he said created a chilling effect. He argued the measures lacked a proper legal basis, were disproportionate, and ignored his journalist status; he disputed that an adequate press area existed or was usable. The Government argued the interference was prescribed by law and pursued public safety and prevention of disorder. The Chamber found no violation (5–2), and the Grand Chamber, after referral, likewise held no violation. It accepted that the measures interfered with Article 10 but found them lawful and justified: the applicant had knowingly disobeyed clear police orders, could have left or reported from the media area, was not prevented from taking photographs, retained his material, and received no penalty. The domestic courts had struck a fair balance between freedom of expression and public order.

**Case: Pentikäinen v. Finland (ECtHR Grand Chamber, 20 October 2015)**

The applicant, Markus Pentikäinen, was a Finnish photographer and journalist employed by the weekly magazine *Suomen Kuvalehti*. On 9 September 2006, he was assigned to cover the “Smash ASEM” demonstration in Helsinki, a protest against the Asia-Europe Meeting (ASEM). The demonstration was large, and police had assessed it as potentially hostile based partly on two earlier Helsinki demonstrations that had turned violent. At the start of the event, bottles, stones and paint-filled jars were thrown at police and bystanders; some demonstrators kicked or hit officers. Around 6:30 p.m. police declared the event a riot, sealed off the Kiasma area, and repeatedly announced that a peaceful demonstration could continue on the spot but that marching was not allowed. Later, police ordered the crowd to disperse.

Pentikäinen remained inside the cordoned area to photograph the events. He claimed he stood between police and demonstrators, wore a press badge, carried professional camera equipment, and identified himself as a journalist. The Government maintained that a separate media area had been reserved at Paasikivi Square and that media representatives could pass through the police cordon. At about 9 p.m., an officer personally told Pentikäinen he had one last chance to leave. Pentikäinen allegedly replied that he was reporting for *Suomen Kuvalehti* and would follow the event to its end. He was later apprehended while taking photographs; according to him, an officer shouted “Get the photographer!”

Pentikäinen was detained from 9 September at 9:26 p.m. until 10 September at 3:05 p.m., about seventeen and a half hours, and was interrogated the following day. He alleged that his camera equipment and memory cards were confiscated. The Government said that once police learned he was a journalist, his equipment was treated as journalistic material and was not confiscated; he retained his photographs and could use them without restriction. He was charged with contumacy towards the police under Chapter 16, section 4(1), of the Finnish Penal Code for failing to obey a police order to disperse. In 2007, Helsinki District Court convicted him but imposed no penalty, finding the offence comparable to an “excusable act” because he had faced conflicting expectations as a journalist. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal, and the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal.

Pentikäinen complained under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights that there had been an unjustified interference with his freedom of expression. He argued that the police order to leave, his detention, and the criminal suspicion, charge and conviction created a “chilling effect” on his journalistic work. He contended that the measures were not prescribed by law, lacked a legitimate aim, and were disproportionate. In particular, he said the detention exceeded the twelve-hour limit applicable to his situation, that no effective secure press area was available or its use should have been optional, and that the police cordon prevented journalists from observing events. He also stressed that the situation had become calm before his apprehension and that he was clearly identifiable as a journalist.

The Government relied on police powers under the Police Act to cordon off and disperse a crowd. The Chamber found no violation of Article 10, and the Grand Chamber agreed. It held that the interference was prescribed by law and pursued legitimate aims, notably public safety and the prevention of disorder. The order to disperse was necessary in the context of a violent riot and applied to everyone present, including journalists. Journalists enjoy no immunity from general criminal law or police orders issued to maintain public order. Pentikäinen knowingly remained after clear orders to leave. Considering that no penalty was ultimately imposed, his photographs were retained, and the domestic courts balanced the competing interests, the Grand Chamber found no violation of Article 10.
001-157967:
**Lunev v. Ukraine** (no. 4725/13), judgment of 22 October 2015, concerned a Ukrainian man arrested in January 2012 on suspicion of drug trafficking and detained in the Starobilsk Pre-Trial Detention Centre (SIZO). On arrival he was diagnosed with HIV (clinical stage 3), chronic bronchitis, toxic encephalopathy and neuropathy caused by prolonged drug use, and residual tuberculosis changes. He weighed 55 kg and was 1.78 metres tall. The Government claimed he refused a CD4+ cell count in February 2012 and did not seek medical help until January 2013; the applicant denied refusing relevant HIV testing and said staff failed to take blood because his veins were collapsed. For over a year he received no HIV treatment. In September 2012 he saw a tuberculosis specialist; in November 2012, in another facility, he had bronchitis and kidney pain. On 8 January 2013 he complained of cough and fever and was diagnosed with chronic bronchitis. On 9 January he was found unconscious. The SIZO head asked a court to expedite proceedings or release him because he needed urgent specialised treatment. The court kept him in detention but ordered placement in a specialised prison or civilian hospital. He was hospitalised from 9 to 11 January with acute serous meningoencephalitis, described as being in a soporose state, then returned to the SIZO medical unit until 15 February and was also held in the Alchevsk Temporary Detention Facility. On 17 January he asked the European Court to order his hospital placement under Rule 39. His CD4 count on 26 February was 119 cells. On 12 March an infectious diseases specialist recommended antiretroviral therapy (ART). He was hospitalised in Lugansk in March–May 2013 and started ART on 16 April. In June 2013 the local court released him under house arrest, noting he needed treatment unavailable in detention.

The second alleged violation concerned ill-treatment. On 25 January 2013 he was placed in the Alchevsk Temporary Detention Facility. On 30 January an ambulance was called for liver pain; he was taken to hospital and returned. Around 5:25 p.m., he alleged, two policemen beat him—six or seven blows to the liver and four to the kidneys—and forced him to write that the SIZO had provided adequate medical treatment, that he had no complaints or pressure, and to confess. On 31 January his lawyer complained in court. An ambulance diagnosed “possible blunt abdominal trauma,” but a surgeon found a soft, pain-free abdomen and no acute surgical pathology. The applicant and his lawyer complained to prosecutors. The investigation was repeatedly terminated and reopened or quashed. A forensic expert concluded he had no injuries. A cellmate testified that Lunev was absent for 40–60 minutes, returned with a red cheek and cheekbone and a swollen liver, and said police had beaten him to make him refuse medical treatment. Another cellmate said Lunev told him police beat him to force a confession. Others gave no evidence or refused to testify. Officer So denied involvement, and CCTV was not working from 26 January to 4 February. Domestic courts quashed terminations due to an incomplete investigation, including failure to confront So and reliance on a superficial medical examination.

The Court declared the medical-assistance complaint admissible and held that the prolonged failure to provide adequate treatment for HIV and other serious diseases in detention amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment under Article 3. It also found the ill-treatment complaint admissible and criticised the ineffective investigation, which relied on superficial medical findings and was repeatedly terminated despite shortcomings, violating the procedural aspect of Article 3.

In *Lunev v. Ukraine* (no. 4725/13, judgment 22 October 2015), the applicant, a Ukrainian national, was arrested in January 2012 on suspicion of drug trafficking and placed in Starobilsk Pre-Trial Detention Centre (“SIZO”) on 30 January 2012. On arrival he was diagnosed with HIV (clinical stage 3), chronic bronchitis, toxic encephalopathy and neuropathy caused by prolonged drug use, and residual tuberculosis changes. He weighed 55 kg and was 1.78 metres tall. The Government claimed he refused a CD4+ cell count in February 2012; the applicant denied this, saying his veins had collapsed and that he never refused HIV-related treatment. Until January 2013, he allegedly received no effective treatment. Medical records showed only limited examinations: a tuberculosis specialist and X-ray in September 2012, and bronchitis/kidney pain in November 2012 at another facility.

On 8 January 2013, after complaining of cough and fever, he was diagnosed with chronic bronchitis and prescribed treatment. On 9 January 2013 he was found unconscious. The SIZO head asked the court to expedite proceedings or release him for urgent hospital treatment. On 10 January the court kept him in detention but ordered placement in a specialised prison or civilian hospital. From 9–11 January he was hospitalised with acute serose meningoencephalitis and was described as “soporose.” He returned to the SIZO until 15 February and was also held at Alchevsk Temporary Detention Facility. On 17 January he sought interim hospital placement from the European Court under Rule 39, citing need for psychiatric examination, antiretroviral therapy (“ART”), tuberculosis assessment and epilepsy care. On 26 February his CD4+ count was 119 cells (13.1%). On 12 March an infectious diseases specialist recommended ART; on 14 March he was approved for the Lugansk Temporary Detention Centre Hospital. He was hospitalised from 20–25 March with weight loss over 10% and chronic hepatitis C. Further hospital stays followed from 29 March–5 April and 12 April–12 May; ART was prescribed on 16 April. His conviction was later quashed, and on 19 June 2013 he was released under house arrest because required treatment was unavailable in detention.

The applicant also alleged ill-treatment. On 25 January 2013 he was placed in Alchevsk ITT. On 30 January, after being taken to hospital for liver pain, he returned around 4 p.m. At about 5:25 p.m., two policemen allegedly beat him, telling him to write that the SIZO had provided adequate medical treatment. One allegedly struck his liver six or seven times and the other his kidneys four times. He then wrote the requested statement. On 31 January his lawyer complained in court; an ambulance diagnosed “possible blunt abdominal trauma,” but a surgeon found his abdomen soft and pain-free. The applicant and his lawyer complained to the prosecutor. On 14 February a forensic expert found no injuries; on 25 February the prosecutor terminated proceedings for lack of evidence. That decision was quashed on 26 March. On 24 April the ambulance station confirmed the blunt abdominal trauma diagnosis. Proceedings were again terminated on 25 April and 27 June, and again quashed on 3 June and 4 November. A cellmate testified that the applicant returned with a red cheek and swollen liver and said policemen had beaten him to force him to refuse medical treatment; another officer, So., denied involvement. Surveillance was not working from 26 January to 4 February. No final outcome was reported.

The applicant complained under Article 3 of inadequate medical assistance, ill-treatment intended to discourage his application to the Court, and failure to investigate. The Court declared the complaints admissible and found that the prolonged failure to provide adequate medical assistance for his HIV and other diseases amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment. It also found an arguable ill-treatment claim requiring a thorough investigation, noting the superficial initial medical examination and repeated flawed terminations.

In *Lunev v. Ukraine* (Application no. 4725/13, judgment 22 October 2015), the applicant, a Ukrainian national born in 1977, was arrested in January 2012 on suspicion of drug trafficking and placed in the Starobilsk Pre-Trial Detention Centre (SIZO). On admission he was diagnosed with HIV (clinical stage 3), chronic bronchitis, toxic encephalopathy and neuropathy caused by prolonged drug use, and residual tuberculosis changes. He weighed 55 kg and was 1.78 metres tall. The Government claimed that in February 2012 he refused a CD4+ cell count or blood test; the applicant denied refusing, saying collapsed veins made the test difficult. He alleged that for more than a year he received no adequate treatment for HIV or other serious conditions. Although he was seen by a tuberculosis specialist and had an X-ray in September 2012, his health deteriorated. On 8 January 2013 he was diagnosed with chronic bronchitis; on 9 January he was found unconscious and hospitalised with acute serose meningoencephalitis. A court ordered that he remain in detention but be placed in a specialised prison or civilian hospital. He returned to the SIZO and was later hospitalised several times. In February 2013 his CD4 count was 119 cells (13.1%), and in April 2013 antiretroviral therapy was prescribed. On 19 June 2013 he was released under house arrest; the court noted that he required treatment unavailable in detention. The Court found that the prolonged failure to provide adequate medical assistance for his HIV and other diseases amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment, violating Article 3 of the Convention.

The applicant also alleged ill-treatment and denial of an effective investigation. On 25 January 2013 he was placed in the Alchevsk Temporary Detention Facility (ITT). On 30 January 2013, after being taken to hospital for liver pain, he claimed that at about 5:25 p.m. two policemen beat him, hitting his liver and kidneys, and forced him to write that the SIZO had provided adequate medical treatment and that he had no complaints. The next day his lawyer complained in court. An ambulance diagnosed a possible blunt abdominal trauma, but a hospital surgeon found his abdomen soft and pain-free and no acute surgical pathology. The applicant and his lawyer complained to the prosecutor. He testified that two unknown policemen had beaten him when he refused to write a no-complaints statement. A forensic expert later concluded he had no injuries. The prosecutor terminated proceedings for lack of evidence, relying on officers’ and the surgeon’s statements that no beating occurred. That decision was quashed by a court in March 2013 because cellmates had not been questioned. The investigation was terminated again in April and June 2013, and both decisions were quashed for procedural shortcomings. A cellmate testified that the applicant returned after 40–60 minutes saying policemen had beaten him to force him to refuse medical treatment, and that he had a red cheek and swollen liver. Another cellmate gave conflicting evidence; officer So. denied involvement; CCTV was not working. No final outcome was provided. The Court found the ill-treatment complaint arguable and the investigation neither thorough nor effective, violating the procedural limb of Article 3.

**Andonovski v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia** (App. no. 24312/10) concerned a Macedonian surgeon who alleged police ill-treatment on 17 September 2004 and an ineffective investigation into his allegations, contrary to Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention.

The applicant, born in 1948 and in poor cardiac health, parked in Kumanovo and received a parking ticket. He followed a police car to discuss it. The parties gave conflicting accounts. The applicant claimed he flashed his lights; the police claimed he sounded his horn, shouted, kicked the car and spat at them. The applicant alleged that when he approached, officers P.J. and M.A. insulted him. P.J., a neighbour with whom he had bad relations, opened the car door hard, striking his legs. Both officers then grabbed him by the shoulders and neck and punched him. P.J. kicked and punched him all over, kneed him in the back causing fractures to two spinal vertebrae, and M.A. kicked his lower back. He was handcuffed and taken to Kumanovo police station, where he said the beating continued until he lost consciousness. An ambulance was called about an hour later. He was hospitalised from 17 to 28 September 2004.

Medical evidence was central. Kumanovo Hospital recorded head contusion, concussion, chest and back bruises, and arm bruises. Skopje City Hospital noted a compressive fracture of two vertebrae, concussion, head trauma, and contusions. Dr Z.T. later certified serious bodily injury with permanent consequences. A Forensic Institute report concluded that multiple blunt impacts caused concussion, vertebral fracture and widespread bruising, amounting to serious bodily injury with a considerable but not permanent negative effect. The applicant’s heart condition was also noted.

The police officers’ own reports admitted some force: twisting his arms, kicking his leg, and P.J. punching his head after the applicant allegedly bit M.A. The Ministry’s internal control department concluded that the applicant had insulted and resisted the officers and bitten M.A., and that the force used—twisting arms and handcuffing—was necessary and justified.

In parallel criminal proceedings, the applicant was convicted of assaulting police officers and sentenced to five months’ imprisonment, suspended for two years. The domestic courts relied mainly on the officers’ and some witnesses’ accounts and largely disregarded the medical evidence of the applicant’s serious injuries. The conviction was upheld on appeal. Witnesses S.H. and V.V. gave mixed accounts: they did not see the alleged bite and described the applicant as shouting and resisting, but generally did not confirm serious police violence.

The applicant filed criminal complaints against P.J. and M.A. for assault, serious bodily harm, abuse of office, false testimony and degrading treatment. The prosecutor initially rejected the complaint, relying on witness statements and the internal police report. The applicant then pursued a subsidiary prosecution. An investigating judge opened an investigation for serious bodily injury, supported by the 2006 Forensic Institute report. However, the public prosecutor repeatedly refused to take over the prosecution. In 2009, the trial court stayed the proceedings after the applicant reportedly withdrew his subsidiary indictment; he objected, saying he had not understood the judge and had wanted the public prosecutor to prosecute ex officio.

These facts formed the basis of his complaints that he had been subjected to police brutality and that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into it.

Case No. 24312/10, *Andonovski v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia*, concerned alleged police ill-treatment and the alleged ineffectiveness of the subsequent investigation. The applicant, Vladimir Andonovski, born in 1948, was a surgeon at Kumanovo Hospital. On 17 September 2004, after finding a parking ticket on his car, he followed a police car to discuss the matter. The parties gave conflicting accounts. According to the applicant, after he flashed his lights, officers P.J. and M.A. insulted him. P.J. opened the passenger door hard, hitting his legs. Both officers then grabbed him, punched his back, and P.J. kicked and punched him all over his body. A knee to his back allegedly fractured two spinal vertebrae. He was handcuffed and taken to Kumanovo police station, where the beating allegedly continued until he lost consciousness. He had a history of heart problems and heart surgery. The police claimed the applicant was aggressive, shouted, kicked the car, spat at P.J., resisted arrest, and bit M.A.’s thumb. They said the force used was limited to twisting his arms, handcuffing him, and one punch by P.J.; they denied any further beating.

Medical evidence recorded serious injuries. Kumanovo Hospital noted head contusion, concussion, and bruises to the chest, back, and arms. A forensic external examination noted contusions on the head, nose, chest, back, hip, arms, and legs. Skopje City Hospital’s discharge notice recorded a compressive fracture of two lower vertebrae, concussion, head trauma, and contusions; the applicant was hospitalized from 17 to 28 September 2004. Dr Z.T. certified serious bodily injury with permanent reduction in daily activities. A 2006 Forensic Institute report concluded that the injuries resulted from multiple blunt impacts and qualified as serious bodily injury with considerable, but not permanent, negative effects.

Domestic proceedings were central to the alleged violations. The Ministry charged the applicant with assaulting police officers. In October 2005 the trial court convicted him and imposed a suspended five-month sentence. It found he insulted officers, kicked the car, spat, bit M.A., and resisted; P.J. punched him. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction in 2006.

The applicant also filed criminal complaints against P.J. and M.A. in February 2005 for assault, serious bodily harm, abuse of office, and degrading treatment. In May 2005 the Kumanovo public prosecutor rejected the complaint, relying on witness statements and an internal police report (DCPS) that found the force used—twisting arms and handcuffs—necessary and justified. The applicant then proceeded as a subsidiary prosecutor. In September 2005 an investigating judge opened an investigation into serious bodily injury. The 2006 Forensic Institute report supported that charge, but the public prosecutor repeatedly refused to take over the prosecution, despite the offence being subject to ex officio prosecution. In March 2009 the applicant allegedly withdrew the subsidiary indictment; the court stayed the proceedings. He immediately objected, claiming he had misunderstood and had wanted the public prosecutor to take over.

The applicant complained under Articles 3 and 13 that he had been ill-treated by police and that the investigation was ineffective. The key facts relevant to those alleged violations were the credible medical evidence of serious injury, the conflicting accounts of the arrest, the adequacy of the investigation, reliance on the police internal finding, and the prosecutors’ repeated refusal to pursue charges against the officers.

**Summary of *Andonovski v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia***

The case of *Andonovski v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia* (Application no. 24312/10) concerns allegations of police brutality and the subsequent failure to conduct an effective investigation. The applicant, Vladimir Andonovski, a surgeon, lodged the application with the European Court of Human Rights on 20 April 2010, complaining under Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention.

The key facts relate to an incident on 17 September 2004 in Kumanovo. After finding a parking ticket on his car, the applicant followed a police vehicle to discuss the matter. The parties present starkly conflicting accounts of what transpired next.

According to the applicant, upon approaching the police car, the officers insulted him. One officer, P.J., with whom the applicant had a pre-existing poor relationship, opened the car door hard, striking his legs. Both officers then exited the vehicle, grabbed him, and began punching and kicking him. The applicant alleged that P.J. kneed him in the back, causing fractures to two spinal vertebrae, and that M.A. also kicked him. He was then handcuffed and beaten further, including at the police station where he lost consciousness. An ambulance was eventually called, and he was hospitalized from 17 to 28 September 2004.

Medical evidence was central to the case. Reports from Kumanovo Hospital, Skopje Clinic, and Skopje City Hospital documented head contusion, concussion, bruises, and a compressive fracture of two vertebrae. A Forensic Institute report concluded that the injuries, resulting from "multiple dynamic impacts from a blunt object," constituted serious bodily injury with a considerable negative effect on vital body parts. A later medical certificate from Dr. Z.T. described the injuries as serious, with permanent consequences.

The police officers' account, which formed the basis for criminal proceedings against the applicant, claimed he was aggressive, used offensive language, kicked their car, and resisted arrest. They stated that force was limited to twisting his arms and using handcuffs, with one officer admitting to punching the applicant in the head after being bitten.

The domestic legal aftermath was complex and central to the alleged violations. The applicant was convicted of assaulting police officers and received a suspended sentence. Conversely, his own criminal complaints against P.J. and M.A. for excessive force were rejected by the public prosecutor. An internal police inquiry concluded that the force used was "necessary and justified." While an investigation was eventually opened against the officers, the public prosecutor repeatedly refused to take over the prosecution. The proceedings, pursued by the applicant as a subsidiary prosecutor, were terminated in March 2009 after the trial court recorded that he had withdrawn his indictment. The applicant immediately contested this, stating he, as a layperson, had misunderstood the judge and had intended to insist on the public prosecutor's duty to prosecute.

The applicant brought his case to the European Court, alleging that the treatment he received constituted torture and inhuman and degrading treatment in violation of Article 3, and that the state failed to provide an effective remedy and investigation into his credible allegations of ill-treatment, as required by Article 13.

A.K. v. Liechtenstein (App. no. 38191/12, ECtHR 9 July 2015) concerned a German national’s complaint that the Liechtenstein Constitutional Court was not impartial in interim injunction proceedings, contrary to Article 6 § 1 ECHR.

The applicant, A.K., had been in a long-running civil dispute with F.H. over property rights in 75% of bearer shares in two Liechtenstein companies, EMK and EMK Engineering. In 2009–2010, the Regional Court granted F.H. interim injunctions prohibiting the commercial register from recording decisions made at a 2004 extraordinary shareholders’ meeting. Those decisions had removed F.H. as a representative and elected A.K. as sole managing director. The injunction preserved F.H.’s claim in main proceedings seeking a declaration that the 2004 decisions were null and void and should not be registered. The Court of Appeal dismissed A.K.’s appeal.

A.K. then lodged a constitutional complaint. The Constitutional Court informed him that five named judges would decide it in private. A.K. filed motions for bias against all five judges and the secretary. He alleged, among other things, that judges B., V., and W. had previously decided against him in related proceedings; that the court delayed assigning the case and discriminated against German nationals; that judge B. had refused suspensory effect and had links to judges of the Supreme Court and to judge H., F.H.’s brother; that judge Bu. had worked for the government as an expert and lecturer and with judge H.; that judge S. sat on the supervisory board of a state-owned company; that judge V. had government links and was a friend of judge H.; and that judge W.’s law firm was connected to the opposing company and to a lawyer involved in separate inheritance proceedings with A.K.

The same five judges dismissed the bias motions. In practice, the four remaining judges decided the motion against each challenged judge, but all five had been challenged, and the decision as a whole was taken by the five judges. The Constitutional Court held that prior adverse decisions, five-year judicial terms, previous government work, and friendships or working relationships with judge H. did not objectively justify doubts about impartiality, especially in a small jurisdiction.

Before the ECtHR, A.K. complained only about the Constitutional Court’s alleged lack of impartiality. The Government argued that Article 6 did not apply to interim injunction proceedings and that, in any event, the court was impartial. Applying Micallef v. Malta, the Court found Article 6 applicable: the underlying dispute concerned civil property rights, and the interim injunction effectively determined, at least temporarily, the same right to manage and represent the company, being immediately enforceable and going beyond a purely protective measure.

On the merits, the Court found no subjective bias and considered the applicant’s individual grounds insufficient, by themselves, to establish objective bias. However, the procedure used to reject the bias motions raised a serious impartiality problem. Because the judges were challenged on identical grounds and participated in decisions on motions against their colleagues, they appeared, in substance, to decide on motions directed against themselves. A.K.’s grounds were specific and not abusive, and Liechtenstein law allowed substitute judges to decide such motions, so the system would not have been paralysed. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1 due to the objectively justified doubts about the Constitutional Court’s impartiality.

A.K., a German national, was involved in a long-running civil dispute with F.H. over property rights in 75% of the bearer shares in the EMK stock corporation and EMK Engineering stock corporation, Liechtenstein companies trading in building units. In December 2009, the Regional Court granted F.H. an immediately enforceable interim injunction, later confirmed on 30 July 2010, prohibiting the Real Property and Commercial Registry from registering certain changes decided at the EMK Engineering extraordinary shareholders’ meeting of 23 July 2004. Those changes included F.H.’s removal as a representative and supervisory board member and A.K.’s election as managing director with sole representative power. The Court of Appeal dismissed A.K.’s appeal on 23 September 2010. A.K. then lodged a constitutional complaint with Liechtenstein’s Constitutional Court on 22 October 2010.

On 7 November 2011, the Constitutional Court informed A.K. that judges B., Bu., S., V. and W. would deliberate on his complaint. On 18 November 2011, acting without counsel, A.K. filed motions for bias against all five judges and the responsible secretary. He alleged, among other things, that the court and several judges had previously decided against him in related proceedings; that the assignment of judges was delayed; that the court discriminated against German nationals; that judge B. had refused suspensory effect and sat on committees with other judges and with judge H., the Constitutional Court vice-president and F.H.’s brother; that judge Bu. worked for the Government as an expert and lecturer; that judge S. was a supervisory board member of a state-owned company; that judge V. had worked for the Government and university and was a friend of judge H.; and that judge W.’s law firm had connections to a lawyer involved in proceedings with A.K. and to the EMK company.

On 28 November 2011, the same five judges dismissed the bias motions. Each challenged judge did not participate in the vote on the motion against himself, but the remaining four judges—who were also challenged—decided on their colleagues’ motions. The final decision was attributed to all five challenged judges. The same composition later dismissed A.K.’s constitutional complaint except for his complaint about length of proceedings.

A.K. complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 6 that the five Constitutional Court judges had been partial, especially because of the procedure used to reject his bias motions. The Government argued that Article 6 did not apply to interim injunction proceedings and that there was no impartiality violation. The Court found Article 6 applicable because the interim injunction was immediately enforceable and effectively determined, for a limited period, the same civil right at stake in the main proceedings—the right to manage and represent the corporation. On the merits, the Court found no subjective personal bias and held that the individual grounds alone did not objectively justify doubts. However, the procedure did: the judges partly faced identical bias challenges and then participated in decisions rejecting motions against one another, giving the appearance that they were deciding motions concerning themselves. A.K.’s grounds were sufficiently specific and not abusive. Although Liechtenstein relied on its small size and lack of a higher court, the Constitutional Court Act allowed substitute judges, so the system would not have been paralysed. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1.

In **A.K. v. Liechtenstein** (Application no. 38191/12, judgment of 9 July 2015), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether the Liechtenstein Constitutional Court lacked impartiality when it rejected the applicant’s bias motions, contrary to Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

The applicant, a German national, was involved in a long-running private dispute with F.H. over property rights in bearer shares of EMK Engineering, a Liechtenstein company. In 2010, the Regional Court issued an immediately enforceable interim injunction preventing the commercial registry from registering decisions taken at a 2004 extraordinary shareholders’ meeting. Those decisions had removed F.H. and elected A.K. as managing director. The injunction preserved F.H.’s position and effectively prevented A.K. from managing and representing the company pending the main proceedings. After his appeal failed, A.K. lodged a constitutional complaint.

The Constitutional Court informed A.K. that five named judges would decide his complaint. He then challenged all five judges and the secretary for bias. His grounds included prior adverse decisions in related proceedings, delay in assigning judges, alleged discrimination against German nationals, and individual allegations: Judge B had refused suspensive effect and sat on committees with another judge; Judge Bu had worked for the Government as an expert and lecturer; Judge S sat on the supervisory board of a state-owned company; Judge V had worked for the Government and was a friend of Judge H; Judge W’s law firm had links to A.K.’s opponent and to Judge H. Several judges also had working or social ties to Judge H, the Constitutional Court’s vice-president and brother of F.H., the opposing party.

The Constitutional Court dismissed the motions. Its procedure was key: for each challenged judge, the four remaining challenged judges decided the bias motion, while the fifth did not participate; the decision as a whole was taken by the five challenged judges. It found no objective bias and stressed that in a small state like Liechtenstein, excessively strict bias standards could obstruct justice. No substitute judges were used.

The ECtHR first held Article 6 applicable. Although the proceedings concerned an interim injunction, the underlying dispute involved civil property and share rights, and the injunction effectively determined the same right for its duration by blocking registration of the disputed corporate decisions. The Court added that tribunal impartiality is indispensable even in interim proceedings.

On the merits, the Court found no proof of subjective bias and held that most individual grounds, taken alone, did not raise legitimate doubts. However, it found an objective impartiality violation in the procedure. Because all five judges had been challenged, partly on identical grounds, and because each participated in decisions on bias motions against colleagues, they gave the impression of deciding on their own cause. The four remaining judges deciding each motion were themselves challenged. The Court acknowledged concerns about paralyzing a court, especially in small jurisdictions, but noted that Liechtenstein law allowed substitute judges or substitute appointments. Thus, the procedure was unnecessary. The applicant’s doubts about the Constitutional Court’s impartiality were objectively justified, and there was a violation of Article 6 § 1.

The applicant was a Saudi Arabian and American binational living in Miami. In 2008, the US Internal Revenue Service discovered that thousands of US taxpayers held undeclared UBS accounts. To resolve the conflict between Swiss banking secrecy and US enforcement, Switzerland and the United States concluded Agreement 09 on 19 August 2009, later amended by Protocol 10 (together often called “Convention 10”). The agreement allowed Switzerland to process a US mutual assistance request covering approximately 4,450 UBS accounts.

The IRS requested information on US taxpayers who, between 2001 and 2008, had signing authority or access rights to UBS accounts in Switzerland. The Swiss Federal Tax Administration ordered UBS to provide the relevant files and decided to grant mutual assistance. The applicant appealed. Initially, the Federal Administrative Court set aside the decision because his right to be heard had been violated. After he submitted observations, the Federal Tax Administration again granted assistance on 4 November 2010. On 2 March 2011, the Federal Administrative Court dismissed his appeal. It held that Convention 10 was binding on Swiss authorities, provided a sufficient legal basis, could apply retroactively, did not require an optional referendum, and that even if Article 8 ECHR applied, the interference was justified by Switzerland’s international commitments and economic interests. He also claimed that the measure discriminated against UBS customers, since customers of other banks were not treated the same way.

G.S.B. v. Switzerland (App. no. 28601/11) concerned the disclosure of the applicant’s UBS bank data to the US Internal Revenue Service (IRS). The applicant was a Saudi Arabian and American binational living in Miami. In 2008, the IRS discovered, largely through a former UBS employee, that thousands of US taxpayers held undeclared UBS accounts or economic rights in such accounts. UBS faced criminal prosecution. On 18 February 2009, UBS signed a deferred prosecution agreement with the US Department of Justice, acknowledging wrongdoing and paying USD 780 million. The IRS then brought a “John Doe summons” action seeking the identities of 52,000 UBS customers. Switzerland feared a conflict between Swiss and US law and negotiated an extra-judicial solution.

On 19 August 2009, Switzerland and the United States concluded “Agreement 09,” intended to resolve the IRS request for mutual assistance. Under it, Switzerland would process the US request concerning UBS’s American customers according to criteria in an Appendix, covering about 4,450 open or closed accounts. Switzerland also set up a special task force. The IRS requested information on US taxpayers who, between 2001 and 2008, had authority to sign or access rights to UBS accounts held, supervised or maintained by UBS in Switzerland. The Swiss Federal Tax Authority (AFC) ordered UBS to provide the relevant files and initiated mutual assistance proceedings.

The domestic litigation was central to the alleged violations. In January 2010, the Federal Administrative Court held that Agreement 09 was a mutual agreement that had to remain within the Switzerland–US double taxation convention (CDI-US 96). Under that convention, mutual assistance was available for tax fraud or similar offences, but not for simple tax evasion. The court also found that Agreement 09 should have been approved by Parliament and subjected to an optional referendum. It therefore voided AFC decisions based on Agreement 09. To avoid US retaliation, Switzerland negotiated Protocol 10 in March 2010, extending the criteria to cases of tax evasion. The Federal Assembly approved Agreement 09 and Protocol 10 in June 2010, stating that no optional referendum was available. A pilot judgment later held that the consolidated “Convention 10” was binding, took precedence over prior treaties including the ECHR, and could apply retroactively as procedural law.

As to the applicant, UBS transmitted his file to the AFC in January 2010. In June 2010, the AFC granted mutual assistance. The Federal Administrative Court set that decision aside because the applicant’s right to a hearing had been breached. After the AFC re-decided and again granted assistance in November 2010, the applicant appealed, arguing that there was no valid legal basis, that Convention 10 applied retroactively, and that his rights to private life, presumption of innocence, equality and non-discrimination, and silence were violated. In March 2011, the Federal Administrative Court dismissed the appeal. It held that Convention 10 was binding, that it provided a sufficient legal basis despite the lack of a referendum, that retroactive application was permissible, and that any Article 8 ECHR interference was justified. The Federal Court declared his further appeal inadmissible in April 2011. His banking data were transmitted to the US tax authorities on 14 December 2012.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Articles 8 and 14. He complained that disclosure of his banking data breached his right to respect for private life and that the measure discriminated against him as a UBS customer. The Government accepted that the measure interfered with Article 8 but argued it was justified by Agreement 09, Protocol 10 and CDI-US 96, that retroactive procedural rules were permissible, and that no referendum was required. The Court found that banking information is personal data protected by Article 8 and that an interference occurred at the latest when the data were transmitted. It then examined whether the interference was in accordance with the law, pursued legitimate aims, and was necessary in a democratic society.

**Case of G.S.B. v. Switzerland** concerns an application by a Saudi Arabian/American dual national whose Swiss banking data were transferred to US tax authorities under Swiss–US mutual assistance arrangements following the UBS tax affair. The applicant alleged violations of Article 8 (right to respect for private life) and Article 14 (non-discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

In 2008, the IRS discovered that thousands of US taxpayers held undeclared UBS accounts. UBS entered a deferred prosecution agreement and paid USD 780 million; the IRS then issued a “John Doe summons” seeking data on 52,000 US customers. To avoid a conflict between Swiss and US law, Switzerland and the United States concluded “Agreement 09” on 19 August 2009. It allowed Switzerland to process the IRS request under criteria in an Appendix, covering about 4,450 accounts. On 31 August 2009 the IRS requested information on US taxpayers with authority or access rights to UBS accounts in Switzerland between 2001 and 2008. On 1 September 2009 the Swiss Federal Tax Administration (AFC) ordered UBS to provide customer files and began mutual assistance proceedings.

On 21 January 2010 the Federal Administrative Court (TAF) held that Agreement 09 remained within the Swiss–US double taxation convention, which allowed assistance only in cases of tax fraud, not mere tax evasion. It also found that Agreement 09 should have been approved by Parliament and subjected to an optional referendum, and it voided AFC decisions based on it. Fearing US retaliation, Switzerland negotiated “Protocol 10,” signed on 31 March 2010, which amended Agreement 09 and became provisionally applicable. Parliament approved Agreement 09 and Protocol 10 on 17 June 2010, stating that no optional referendum was available. On 15 July 2010 the TAF held in a pilot case that “Convention 10” was binding, that later international law took precedence over earlier ECHR/ICCPR provisions unless *jus cogens*, and that even if Article 8 applied, its conditions were met.

As to the applicant, UBS transmitted his file to the AFC on 19 January 2010. The AFC granted mutual assistance on 7 June 2010, but the TAF set that decision aside for breach of the applicant’s right to a hearing. On 4 November 2010 the AFC again granted assistance. The applicant appealed, arguing no sufficient legal basis, impermissible retroactivity, violation of private life, presumption of innocence, equality/non-discrimination, and his right to remain silent. On 2 March 2011 the TAF dismissed the appeal, holding that Convention 10 was binding and provided a sufficient legal basis, that retroactive procedural rules were permissible, and that the different treatment of UBS customers was not reviewable because Convention 10 took precedence. The Federal Court declared his further appeal inadmissible on 11 April 2011. The applicant’s banking data were transmitted to the US tax authorities on 14 December 2012. He later said US tax inspection continued and no criminal charge had been brought.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained that the transfer of his banking data breached Article 8 and discriminated against him under Article 14. The Government disputed this. The Court found an interference with his right to respect for private life at the latest when the data were transmitted in December 2012, since bank account information constitutes protected personal data. It then examined whether the interference was “in accordance with the law,” pursued a legitimate aim, and was necessary. The applicant argued that Agreement 09/Protocol 10 lacked a valid legal basis because they were not put to an optional referendum, applied retroactively to 2001–2008 conduct, and were not yet parliamentary-approved when the AFC first ordered disclosure. The Government responded that Parliament had discretion on referendums, any procedural defect was not manifest under the Vienna Convention, retroactive procedural rules were permissible, and provisional application had been ratified. The Court also addressed the Article 14 claim based on Convention 10 targeting only UBS SA customers.

In *Lambert and Others v. France* (Application no. 46043/14), the applicants were Vincent Lambert’s parents, half-brother and sister. Vincent, born in 1976, sustained severe head injuries in a road-traffic accident in September 2008. He became tetraplegic and completely dependent, and was later diagnosed as being in a chronic vegetative or minimally conscious state. From 2009 he was cared for in a Reims University Hospital unit and received artificial enteral nutrition and hydration through a gastric tube. A 2011 assessment by Liège University Hospital described him as “minimally conscious plus.” However, an expert report later ordered by the Conseil d’État in 2014 found that he was in a vegetative state, with irreversible brain damage, no functional communication, non-conscious reactions to care, and a poor clinical prognosis.

In 2013 Dr Kariger, the doctor in charge, initiated the collective procedure under the 2005 Leonetti Act on patients’ rights and end-of-life issues. He decided to withdraw Vincent’s artificial nutrition and reduce hydration, and this was implemented on 10 April 2013. The applicants obtained an urgent administrative injunction on 11 May 2013. The judge found procedural shortcomings: Vincent’s parents had not been properly informed or involved, and the decision amounted to a serious and manifestly unlawful breach of the right to life. Feeding and hydration resumed.

A second procedure began in September 2013. Dr Kariger consulted six doctors, held two family meetings, and received views from Vincent’s wife and siblings. Vincent’s wife and six siblings supported withdrawing artificial nutrition and hydration; the applicants opposed it. On 11 January 2014 Dr Kariger decided to discontinue treatment. He reasoned that Vincent’s brain damage was irreversible, that treatment was futile and disproportionate, and that it had no effect other than sustaining life artificially. He also concluded that Vincent had previously expressed a wish not to be kept alive in a highly dependent state.

The applicants again sought urgent relief. On 16 January 2014 the Administrative Court suspended the decision. It accepted that artificial nutrition and hydration constituted “treatment,” but held that Dr Kariger had wrongly assessed Vincent’s wishes, that Vincent was in a minimally conscious state, and that the treatment was not futile or disproportionate. It found a serious breach of the right to life. The Conseil d’État ordered an expert medical report and, on 24 June 2014, set aside that judgment. It held that the statutory conditions for withdrawal were met and that the French framework was compatible with the Convention.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged that withdrawal of Vincent’s artificial nutrition and hydration would breach Article 2 (right to life), Article 3 (torture or inhuman or degrading treatment), and Article 8 (physical integrity and private life). They argued that the State had a positive obligation to protect Vincent’s life, that discontinuing feeding and hydration would cause death and suffering amounting to ill-treatment, and that the domestic procedure failed to protect him. The Grand Chamber ultimately found no violation of Articles 2, 3, or 8.

**Milić and Nikezić v. Montenegro** (Apps. nos. 54999/10 and 10609/11), European Court of Human Rights, Second Section, judgment of 28 April 2015.

The applicants, Igor Milić and Dalibor Nikezić, were Montenegrin nationals detained at the Institution for the Execution of Criminal Sanctions (IECS) in Podgorica. They alleged that on 27 October 2009 they were tortured and ill-treated by prison guards and that Montenegro failed to conduct an effective official investigation. The case concerned Article 3 of the Convention.

On 27 October 2009, the first applicant was to be transferred to a disciplinary unit and his cell was to be searched. The parties gave conflicting accounts. The applicants claimed that several guards entered the cell, grabbed the first applicant, threw him onto the concrete corridor floor, handcuffed him, and beat him with batons and fists while swearing at him. They also alleged that two rows of guards beat him as he was taken away. The second applicant said he protested and was then kicked and beaten by four guards with fists and batons; eight more guards allegedly continued the beating in the corridor and later in the cell. The Government claimed that the applicants resisted the guards and that the second applicant attacked and injured a guard, triggering the intervention.

Medical and witness evidence was central. The first applicant refused examination by a prison doctor, allegedly saying he was healthy and had not been ill-treated, and later refused an external forensic examination because his bruises were fading. The second applicant was examined by an external forensic doctor on 4 November 2009. The doctor found light injuries: a 10-day-old haematoma measuring 8 x 15 cm on the back of his left thigh and haematomas on the lower eyelids. An undated report also confirmed bruises around his eyes. The prison medical documentation was described as largely illegible and inconsistent. The applicants’ mothers observed visible bruises and haematomas and lodged criminal complaints. Several detainees confirmed that the first applicant had been beaten, and three detainees confirmed that the second applicant had been beaten by several guards. One guard admitted hitting the first applicant once with a baton; another saw a cut below his eye and a leg injury.

The Ombudsman and Deputy Ombudsman visited the applicants and observed injuries. In a 29 March 2010 opinion, the Ombudsman found that the applicants’ rights had been violated, that they had offered no resistance, and that the use of force was unjustified. Disciplinary proceedings were later brought against three guards, I.M., I.B., and R.T. On 31 May 2010 they were found responsible and fined 20% of their salaries for excessive force disproportionate to any resistance. I.M. had hit both applicants once with a rubber baton, I.B. had kicked the first applicant, and R.T. had hit the second applicant with a baton. Four other guards were transferred, although force against the applicants was not proved.

Criminal proceedings were largely unsuccessful for the applicants. The State prosecutor rejected complaints against I.M. and R.T. on 12 February 2010, finding that their force was used within official powers to overcome resistance and disclosed no criminal offence. Later complaints and attempts at subsidiary prosecution were rejected, and on 18 March 2011 the Court of First Instance dismissed the applicants’ request for an investigation for lack of reasonable suspicion; the High Court upheld that decision. The Constitutional Court rejected their appeal on procedural grounds.

In civil proceedings, the applicants sought compensation under Article 3. The Supreme Court ultimately awarded them EUR 1,500 each, holding that the guards’ force could not be justified by resistance and degraded human dignity, but that it did not constitute torture or inhuman treatment. The Government admitted excessive force but argued it was justified to overcome resistance and did not amount to ill-treatment. The ECtHR declared the Article 3 complaint admissible and found the applicants remained victims, as the compensation was not sufficient redress and the domestic courts had not adequately acknowledged the violation.

In **A.V. v. Ukraine** (Application no. 65032/09, judgment of 29 January 2015), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by a Ukrainian national that he had been ill-treated by police, denied access to a lawyer at the initial investigation stage, and convicted using evidence obtained through ill-treatment.

On the evening of **29 December 2006**, the applicant was arrested on a street in Kyiv and taken to the Shevchenkivskyy District Police Department. He alleged that police officers knocked him down, handcuffed him, took him to their car, planted small bags of cocaine on him, beat him, and threatened sexual abuse, continuing until he reached the police station. At the police department, he was asked to empty his pockets in the presence of two unemployed attesting witnesses and produced bags containing cocaine.

At 10 p.m. that day, police detained him administratively under Article 263 of the Administrative Offences Code for violating drug circulation rules under Article 44. He was interviewed and wrote a confession admitting unlawful purchase of cocaine for personal use. He claimed the confession was forced and dictated by a police officer. He was then placed in a police cell. He alleged insufficient food and water, poor sanitary conditions, and being locked for one night in a dirty, stinking toilet; he felt unwell and had acute lower back pain.

On **2 January 2007**, a specialist report stated that the seized substance contained **1.18 grams of cocaine**. That day, an investigator instituted criminal proceedings under Article 309 § 2 of the Criminal Code for illegal purchase and storage of narcotic drugs in large quantities. At 5:25 p.m., the investigator ordered his arrest and detention as a criminal suspect under Articles 106 and 115 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, authorising up to 72 hours’ preliminary detention. He was questioned again and gave details of the purchase. A lawyer hired by his parents joined later; the applicant complained of poor health. The Government said a medical examination diagnosed intercostal neuralgia and considered his condition satisfactory.

On **5 January 2007**, the prosecutor refused to approve pre-trial detention, and the applicant was released on a written undertaking not to abscond. After release, an ambulance diagnosed acute pyelonephritis and lumbosacral radiculitis. He received inpatient treatment from 9 to 19 January and was later noted by a psychiatrist to show signs of post-traumatic stress disorder. On **22 January 2007**, the District Court found that the investigator’s 2 January decision to arrest and detain him as a criminal suspect had been unlawful because grounds for such arrest had existed from 29 December 2006.

On **9 February 2007**, the prosecutor refused to institute criminal proceedings against the police officers, finding no elements of an offence and relying on police explanations and custody records. The applicant’s father and the applicant later complained about violations, but the prosecutor said the issues could be raised at trial. On **15 June 2007**, a linguistic expert reported that the 29 December confession had been written by the applicant with another person dictating the text. At a hearing on **18 June 2007**, the applicant sought to admit that report and exclude his 29 December and 2 January statements as obtained in breach of his rights; the court rejected the requests. He denied the charges throughout, alleging that drugs had been planted and that he had been pressured and ill-treated. Police officers denied the allegations, and the attesting witnesses stated they had seen no visible injuries.

On **8 July 2008**, the District Court convicted him and sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment, suspended for two years’ probation. It found no indication of ill-treatment or procedural violation relating to his initial self-incriminating statements. The Kyiv Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on **7 November 2008**, and the Supreme Court dismissed his cassation appeal on **22 May 2009**. The communicated complaints concerned Article 3 ill-treatment, Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) lack of a lawyer at the initial stage, and Article 6 § 1 use of evidence allegedly obtained through ill-treatment.

In *Yegorov v. Slovakia* (Application no. 27112/11, ECtHR, 2 June 2015), the applicant, Volodymyr Yegorov, a Ukrainian national, complained under Article 5 §§ 1(c), 3, and 4 of the Convention about his arrest and pre-trial detention in Slovakia, particularly under remand orders of 16 July 2010 and 29 July 2011, and about the lack of procedural guarantees in his interlocutory appeal against the first order.

From 25 June 2002 until 19 September 2013, the applicant was continuously deprived of liberty in Slovakia, mainly in pre-trial detention on various charges, some pursued in parallel and some consecutively. The first relevant detention arose in the context of a murder charge. While the applicant was already detained on a money-laundering charge, the murder prosecution began in 2007. On 13 July 2010, after his money-laundering sentence was effectively served through detention, he was released but immediately taken into administrative detention pending expulsion at Medveďov. On 16 July 2010, police brought him before the Bratislava I District Court, which, after a private session, remanded him in pre-trial detention on the murder charge.

The applicant orally appealed and said he would give reasons after receiving the written remand order. On 19 July 2010 he submitted written reasons in Russian; they were received on 21 July 2010. That same day, the written Slovak-language remand order was served on him and the file was sent to the Bratislava Regional Court. On 26 July 2010 he sent further reasons, received on 28 July 2010. Nevertheless, on 28 July 2010 the Regional Court dismissed his appeal as unfounded, stating that no reasons had been submitted. The Constitutional Court later rejected his complaint as manifestly ill-founded, noting that his submissions had not been available to the Regional Court when it ruled, that detention appeals required speedy determination, that he had been heard at first instance, and that his lawyer had failed to act effectively. The applicant alleged that his arrest and bringing before the court were unlawful, that the remand was arbitrary, and that his appeal was not properly examined.

The second relevant detention began on 27 July 2011. Having been acquitted of the first murder charge, the applicant was released and immediately re-arrested the same day. He was charged with conceiving, setting up, and supporting a criminal and terrorist group. On 29 July 2011, the Specialised Criminal Court remanded him under Article 71 § 1(a) and (c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure to prevent flight and further offending. It cited his foreign nationality, unregistered residence, frequent foreign travel, prior conviction, and other pending charges. The Supreme Court dismissed his appeal on 8 August 2011. The Constitutional Court rejected his complaint on 18 October 2011, finding he had been informed of the reasons for arrest and that the length of detention had to be assessed from 27 July 2011 only.

On 22 February 2012, the Supreme Court ordered his release. It observed that the earlier detention on the same charge from 2002 to 2005, combined with detention after 27 July 2011, had exceeded statutory limits, and that splitting charges and consecutive remands might amount to arbitrary detention. Later Constitutional Court judgments also found Article 5 violations in similar contexts but declined to award just satisfaction.

Before the ECtHR, the Government argued loss of victim status and non-exhaustion. The Court rejected the victim-status objection because the applicant had obtained no redress. It found he had failed to exhaust domestic remedies under the State Liability Act only as regards the lawfulness, arbitrariness, and length of detention under the 16 July 2010 murder remand, since an acquittal-based compensation remedy was available. It dismissed the non-exhaustion objections concerning the Article 5 § 4 complaint about the interlocutory appeal and the 29 July 2011 detention.

**Case: Yegorov v. Slovakia (App. no. 27112/11), ECtHR Third Section, 2 June 2015**

The applicant, Volodymyr Yegorov, a Ukrainian national, was continuously deprived of liberty in Slovakia from 25 June 2002 until 19 September 2013, mainly in pre-trial detention on various charges, including attempted legalisation of criminal proceeds, two murder charges, and conceiving, setting up and supporting a criminal and terrorist group. His detentions were partly consecutive and partly parallel. He complained under Article 5 §§ 1(c), 3 and 4 of the Convention that his detention under remand orders of 16 July 2010 and 29 July 2011 was unlawful, arbitrary and excessively long, and that his interlocutory appeal against the 16 July 2010 remand order lacked required procedural guarantees.

As to the first challenged detention, on 13 July 2010 the applicant was released from detention on the legalisation charge but was immediately administratively detained pending expulsion. On 16 July 2010 police took him from the Medveďov detention centre to the Bratislava I District Court. After questioning, the court remanded him in pre-trial detention on the first murder charge. He orally appealed and said he would provide reasons after receiving the written decision. On 19 July he submitted written reasons in Russian, received by the court on 21 July, and on 26 July he sent further reasons, received on 28 July. The written remand order was served on him on 21 July in Slovak, and the file was sent to the Bratislava Regional Court the same day. On 28 July the Regional Court dismissed his appeal as unfounded, stating that no reasons had been submitted orally or in writing. The Constitutional Court later rejected his complaint as manifestly ill-founded, noting that his written reasons had not been available to the Regional Court when it decided, that remand appeals must be decided within five working days, and that he had been heard at first instance and represented by a lawyer.

As to the second challenged detention, after being acquitted and released on the first murder charge on 27 July 2011, the applicant was immediately re-arrested the same day on the 2003 charge of conceiving, setting up and supporting a criminal and terrorist group. On 29 July 2011 the Specialised Criminal Court remanded him in custody under Article 71 § 1(a) and (c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure to prevent flight and further offending. It cited his lack of stable registered residence, frequent foreign travel, other pending charges, and a prior conviction. He appealed, arguing that his arrest was unlawful because he had not been informed of the reasons, contesting the grounds for detention, complaining of over nine years’ deprivation of liberty, and alleging a pattern of arbitrary consecutive remands on different charges. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 8 August 2011. On 18 October 2011 the Constitutional Court declared his complaint inadmissible, finding that the arrest report showed he had been informed of the reasons and limiting its length review to detention since 27 July 2011. The Supreme Court later released him on 22 February 2012, finding that the statutory maximum detention period had been exceeded because the detention arose from the same matter previously removed to separate proceedings and could not be fragmented by individual charges.

Before the ECtHR, the Government argued that the applicant had lost victim status and had not exhausted domestic remedies. The Court found he retained victim status because he had received no adequate redress or just satisfaction and because earlier constitutional findings concerned different charges and periods. On exhaustion, the Court held that he should have used the State Liability Act remedy for acquittal-based compensation regarding the 16 July 2010 detention, so that part was inadmissible. However, it rejected the non-exhaustion plea concerning the Article 5 § 4 procedural complaint and the alleged arbitrariness/excessive length of the 29 July 2011 detention. The Court then proceeded to examine the merits of the alleged unlawfulness of the 29 July 2011 detention.

Yegorov v. Slovakia (Application no. 27112/11) is a European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) judgment of 2 June 2015. The applicant, Volodymyr Yegorov, a Ukrainian national, complained under Article 5 §§1(c), 3 and 4 that his remand and detention in Slovakia were unlawful or arbitrary, excessively long, and that his interlocutory appeal against a 16 July 2010 remand order lacked required procedural guarantees.

From 25 June 2002 to 19 September 2013, the applicant was continuously deprived of liberty in Slovakia on various charges, partly in parallel and partly consecutively. The relevant allegations concerned two remand orders: one of 16 July 2010 on a first murder charge, and one of 29 July 2011 on a charge of conceiving, setting up and supporting a criminal and terrorist group.

As to the first remand, prosecution for murder began in 2007 while the applicant was already detained on a money-laundering charge. On 13 July 2010 he was released when that sentence was covered by detention. He was immediately taken by police, subjected to an administrative expulsion order and detained pending expulsion in Medveďov. On 16 July 2010 police seized him there and brought him before the Bratislava I District Court. After questioning and a private session, the court remanded him pending trial on the murder charge. The applicant orally appealed and said he would give reasons upon receiving the written decision. On Monday 19 July he filed written reasons in Russian; the court received them on 21 July. That same day, the written Slovak-language remand order was served and the file was sent to the Bratislava Regional Court. On 26 July he sent further reasons, received on 28 July. On 28 July the Regional Court dismissed the appeal as unfounded, stating he had submitted no reasons orally or in writing. The Constitutional Court rejected his complaint on 7 December 2010 as manifestly ill-founded, noting that his reasons had not been available to the Regional Court and that the appeal had to be decided speedily.

As to the second remand, on 27 July 2011 the applicant was acquitted of the first murder charge and released. He was immediately re-arrested the same day and charged with the criminal/terrorist group offence. On 29 July 2011 the Specialised Criminal Court remanded him under Article 71 §1(a) and (c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, finding risks of flight and further offending. He appealed, arguing unlawful arrest because he had not been informed of the reasons, contesting the charge and grounds, complaining of over nine years’ deprivation of liberty, and alleging a pattern of arbitrary consecutive remands. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 8 August 2011. His subsequent Constitutional Court complaint was declared inadmissible on 18 October 2011. The Constitutional Court acknowledged the long total detention but treated the challenged decision as concerning only detention from 27 July 2011, which had not yet become unconstitutional.

The applicant was released on 22 February 2012. The Supreme Court noted possible arbitrariness and that statutory maximum detention periods may have been exceeded. Later Constitutional Court judgments found Article 5 violations in other detention stages, but no just satisfaction was awarded. He was finally released on 17 September 2013. Before the ECtHR, the Government argued loss of victim status and non-exhaustion. The Court rejected the victim-status objection, dismissed non-exhaustion for the Article 5 §4 appeal complaint and the 29 July 2011 detention complaints, but held that the applicant should have used the State Liability Act remedy regarding detention followed by acquittal for the 16 July 2010 remand.
