**Case Summary: Iustin Robertino Micu v. Romania**  
*(ECtHR, Third Section, Application no. 41040/11, Judgment of 13 January 2015)*

The applicant, Iustin Robertino Micu, a Romanian border guard police officer, was investigated by Romania’s National Anticorruption Department (NAD) for bribe-taking and abetting bribe-taking. The prosecution alleged that in 2007 he and colleagues had asked seven Turkish nationals to pay money to be allowed to leave Romania. In early March 2010, a prosecutor issued a warrant to appear requiring the applicant’s presence for questioning as an accused.

On 9 March 2010, two police officers executed the warrant at the applicant’s workplace at 8:40 a.m. He was shown the warrant, told he could retain a lawyer, and declined to choose his own. He was taken to the NAD office. At noon, the prosecutor informed him that a criminal investigation had been opened against him and that he would be assisted by a publicly appointed lawyer. The applicant informed the authorities that he suffered from diabetes, needed insulin treatment kept at his workplace, and asked that his wife be notified if he were placed in custody. The prosecutor arranged for the insulin kit to be brought to him. The applicant alleged that he did not receive the kit until about 6 p.m. and that he was refused food throughout the day. The authorities claimed the kit arrived within about thirty minutes and that a police officer also bought food for him. The applicant acknowledged receiving food only at about 10 p.m., after being transferred to a detention centre.

The documentary record initially stated that the applicant’s hearing as an accused lasted from noon to 9:34 p.m., but the NAD later explained this was an error; the Court accepted that the hearing ended at 12:34 p.m. At 7:08 p.m., the applicant was charged as a defendant and refused to make further statements. At 9:15 p.m., the NAD ordered his placement in police custody for twenty-four hours, citing reasonable suspicion, the seriousness of the offence, and danger to public order. On 10 March 2010, the Court of Cassation rejected the request for pre-trial detention and ordered his release, finding insufficient grounds. The applicant was later convicted in 2011 but acquitted by the Court of Cassation in 2013.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged violations of Articles 3, 5, and 13 of the Convention. Under Article 3, he complained that despite his diabetes and need for insulin, he was denied food and appropriate medical care while under police control and at the NAD, causing physical suffering. Under Article 5, he alleged unlawful deprivation of liberty from the time he was taken from his workplace until his formal placement in police custody, arguing that the warrant to appear authorised only his hearing and that he was held longer than necessary. He also complained that his total detention exceeded the twenty-four-hour limit. Under Article 13, he alleged that he had no effective domestic remedy, because his criminal complaints against prosecutors G.B. and L.P. were dismissed as non-existent or as attempts to challenge investigative acts within pending criminal proceedings.

The Court found the Article 3 complaint admissible. It noted that the applicant did not tell the police officers at his workplace about his illness. It accepted that the insulin kit was made available within about two hours and without restriction. However, the Government failed to prove that the applicant received food before 10 p.m., despite his medical condition. Medical evidence recorded elevated blood sugar and a relatively good but affected condition. The Court concluded that the treatment before his placement in police custody exceeded the inherent suffering caused by legal proceedings and questioning, amounting to a breach of Article 3.

In *Micu v. Romania*, the applicant, a Romanian border guard police officer, was investigated by the National Anticorruption Department (NAD) in 2010 for bribe-taking. On 8 March 2010, prosecutor G.B. authorised enforcement of a warrant to appear requiring Micu to be heard as an accused. On 9 March 2010, two police officers went to his workplace at 8:40 a.m., showed him the warrant, and informed him he could retain a lawyer; he declined. They took him to the NAD offices.

He remained under police control at the NAD for most of the day before being formally placed in police custody at 9:15 p.m. for 24 hours. According to prosecution records, at noon he was informed of the investigation and his rights in the presence of a publicly appointed lawyer. He told authorities he suffered from type-two diabetes requiring insulin, which was at his workplace, and asked that his wife be notified if he were detained. Prosecutors later said his hearing as an accused lasted from noon to 12:34 p.m., although the record erroneously showed 9:34 p.m. At 7:08 p.m. he was charged with bribe-taking; at 7:36 p.m. he refused to make further statements. He was placed in police custody at 9:15 p.m., handcuffed, and taken to a detention centre around 10 p.m. On 10 March, the Court of Cassation refused the NAD’s request to detain him pending trial and ordered his release, finding inconsistencies in the evidence and no grounds for detention. He was later convicted in 2011 but acquitted in 2013.

The applicant alleged violations of Articles 3, 5 and 13. Under Article 3, he claimed that despite his diabetes and need for insulin, he was held all day without food while under police/NAD control, was denied a medical examination, and had his insulin, syringe and glucose tester taken at the detention centre; he said food was offered only around 10 p.m. The Government replied that once informed at noon, an officer retrieved his treatment kit within about thirty minutes and bought him food, and that his condition was generally good. The Court found the facts disputed but accepted the signed records that his hearing ended at 12:34 p.m. It noted he received the medical kit within about two hours and had unrestricted access, but found no conclusive evidence he was given food before 10 p.m. Given his diabetes and elevated blood sugar, it considered the treatment before his formal remand exceeded the suffering inherent in legal proceedings.

Under Article 5, Micu complained that he was unlawfully deprived of liberty during the period he was under escort and at the NAD before formal police custody; he alleged the warrant to appear was unjustified and that he was held longer than the legal 24-hour limit. Under Article 13, he complained of no effective domestic remedy. He filed criminal complaints against prosecutors G.B. and L.P. alleging abuse of office, unlawful arrest, torture and improper investigation, but these were dismissed as non-existent offences or as matters to be raised within the pending criminal proceedings. His appeals and requests to remove the prosecutor were also unsuccessful.

**Case Summary: Iustin Robertino Micu v. Romania (Application no. 41040/11)**

The applicant, Iustin Robertino Micu, a Romanian border guard police officer born in 1969, brought proceedings against Romania alleging violations of Articles 3, 5, and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The case originated from criminal proceedings instituted against him and three co-accused border officers for bribe-taking and abetting bribe-taking. The authorities suspected that on 6–7 September 2007, the applicant and colleagues had demanded money from seven Turkish nationals to allow them to leave Romania.

On 8 March 2010, prosecutor G.B. of the National Anticorruption Department (N.A.D.) authorised police officers to enforce a warrant to appear (mandat de aducere) requiring the applicant's presence for questioning as an accused. The warrant stated no reasons beyond the need for his hearing.

On 9 March 2010, at 8:40 a.m., two police officers took the applicant from his workplace. He was shown the warrant, informed of his right to legal representation, and declined to retain his own lawyer. At N.A.D. offices at noon, he was informed of the criminal investigation. He notified authorities that he suffered from type-two diabetes (diagnosed 1997, insulin-dependent since 2009) and needed his insulin treatment, which had to be retrieved from his workplace.

The parties disputed the day's timeline. Records indicated the hearing lasted from noon to 9:34 p.m., but the N.A.D. later claimed this was a clerical error and the hearing actually ended at 12:34 p.m., with the prosecutor thereafter occupied with co-accused matters. At 7:36 p.m., the applicant was charged with bribe-taking; he refused to make a statement as a defendant. At 9:15 p.m., he was placed in police custody for twenty-four hours.

The applicant alleged that during his time under police control and at the N.A.D. offices—approximately thirteen hours—he was denied food despite his medical condition, was refused a medical examination, had his syringe, insulin, and blood-sugar monitor confiscated at the detention centre, and was denied family contact. He claimed his insulin kit was returned only after two hours, and he received food only at 10 p.m. after being transferred to detention.

The Government contended that once informed of his condition, authorities promptly retrieved his treatment kit within thirty minutes and that a police officer purchased food for him.

Medical evidence showed the applicant was examined by a detention-centre nurse at 10:30 p.m. on 9 March 2010; his general condition was "relatively good," though he reported elevated blood sugar at 9 p.m. A doctor confirmed his insulin regimen on 10 March 2010.

On 10 March 2010, the Court of Cassation dismissed the N.A.D.'s request to detain the applicant pending trial, ordering his release. On 17 March 2011, the Bucharest Court of Appeal convicted him, but on 11 February 2013, the Court of Cassation acquitted him. The applicant also brought criminal complaints against prosecutors G.B. and L.P., which were dismissed as addressing procedural matters rather than offences.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged that his inability to obtain food despite his medical condition constituted inhuman and degrading treatment under Article 3; that his detention under police control and at N.A.D. before formal custody was unlawful under Article 5; and that he lacked an effective domestic remedy under Article 13. The Court declared the Article 3 complaint admissible and examined the conflicting evidence regarding food provision and the applicant's physical condition.

**Summary of M.N. and Others v. San Marino (Application no. 28005/12)**

The case originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by four Italian nationals against San Marino. The applicants alleged violations of Articles 6, 8, and 13 of the Convention, claiming they were denied access to a court to challenge a decision that affected their private life and correspondence.

The factual background stems from criminal proceedings instituted in Italy in or before 2009 against individuals suspected of conspiracy, money laundering, and other financial crimes. The investigation centered on a network of companies linked to San Marino Investimenti S.A. (S.M.I.), which was suspected of facilitating money laundering for Italian clients through fiduciary operations. As part of this investigation, Italian authorities issued a letter rogatory to San Marino in May 2009, seeking assistance to obtain documentation and conduct searches in San Marino banks and trust companies.

On 27 November 2009, the San Marino first-instance tribunal (Commissario della Legge) accepted the request, ordering a broad investigation into all banks and fiduciary institutes. The purpose was to acquire banking documents, emails, and other records related to S.M.I. and any accounts traceable to it, including those of third parties. Critically, the order warned that documentation could not be used for purposes other than the specified criminal proceedings.

Subsequently, the Commissario ordered that Italian citizens who had entered fiduciary agreements with S.M.I. (1,452 individuals, including the applicants) be notified of the decision. The applicants were served with these notifications between January and June 2011. Although not charged with any crimes, their documents were seized as part of the investigation.

The applicants challenged the seizure decision before the judge of criminal appeals (Giudice delle Appellazioni Penali), arguing they were not persons charged and that the seizure violated principles of the San Marino Declaration on Citizens’ Rights. They contended there was no link between the crimes and their positions. However, the judge declared their complaints inadmissible, ruling they lacked juridical interest because they were not direct victims of the seizure. The court held that only persons involved in the investigation or subjected to coercive measures could challenge an exequatur decision, and any grievances should be raised in Italian jurisdictions.

The applicants appealed to the third-instance criminal judge, reiterating their complaints under the Convention. They argued that the seizure was irrelevant to the crimes and only aimed to identify Italians dealing with S.M.I., and that they were not allowed to present submissions. The third-instance judge confirmed the appeal decision on similar grounds, finding no juridical interest and rejecting constitutional complaints.

The applicants also filed objections with the Commissario to revoke the seizure, but these were discontinued, with the Commissario noting that third parties could be subject to such measures. A further objection to restrict the use of seized documents was rejected, as the original decision already limited their use.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are that the applicants, as third parties not charged with any crimes, had their documents seized through an exequatur decision. Their attempts to challenge the seizure in San Marino courts were consistently rejected for lack of standing, effectively denying them access to a court to contest the measure. This formed the basis of their complaint that they were denied access to court, in violation of Articles 6, 8, and 13 of the Convention.

In *M.N. and Others v. San Marino*, four Italian nationals—S.G., M.N., C.R., and I.R.—complained under Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention that they had been denied access to court to challenge a decision interfering with their private life and correspondence. The case arose from Italian criminal proceedings begun in or before 2009 against persons other than the applicants. Italian authorities suspected a network of companies traceable to San Marino Investimenti S.A. (“SMI”) of money laundering, conspiracy, fraud, embezzlement, tax evasion and unlawful financial services. The alleged scheme used fiduciary mandates to conceal the true source of funds for Italian clients.

In May 2009, the Rome prosecutor sent a letter rogatory to San Marino under the 1939 Bilateral Convention, seeking searches and documents from San Marino banks, fiduciary institutes and trust companies. On 27 November 2009, the Commissario della Legge accepted the request by an exequatur decision, finding the relevant offences also punishable under San Marino law. It ordered seizure of copies of bank documents, statements, cheques, fiduciary dispositions, emails and electronic data relating to named accounts and any accounts traceable to SMI or connected persons. Under San Marino law, acquiring copies of documents amounted to seizure. The decision also set safeguards for electronic data, sealing, custody and notification.

In April 2010, the Commissario ordered that 1,452 Italian citizens who had opened fiduciary positions with SMI be notified. The decision stated that information transmitted to Italy could not be used for purposes other than the criminal proceedings identified in the exequatur decision unless a court later decided otherwise. The applicants were notified in 2011: M.N. on 24 January, S.G. on 16 June, and C.R. and I.R. on 4 February. They were not charged with any offence.

The applicants challenged the seizure before the judge of criminal appeals under Article 30 of Law no. 104/2009. They argued that they had no link to the alleged crimes or Italian companies, that the seized documents were irrelevant, and that the seizure merely identified Italians who had dealt with SMI. They also alleged violation of the San Marino Declaration and argued that Article 30(3) was incompatible with it because domestic courts had interpreted it as denying standing to persons subjected to document seizure but not charged.

By decisions in February and June 2011, the judge of criminal appeals declared the complaints inadmissible for lack of juridical interest. The court held that an exequatur decision could be challenged only by someone involved in the requested authority’s investigation or by a third party subjected to the measure. The applicants were not interested parties in relation to the exequatur decision; they had only an eventual interest in its effects, and any alleged rights breaches should be raised before the Italian courts. The third-instance criminal judge confirmed this in July and October 2011, also rejecting constitutional objections. Parallel objections to the Commissario to revoke the exequatur or restrict use of the seized documents were unsuccessful; the Commissario discontinued the revocation objection and noted that the exequatur already limited use of the material. The applicants therefore alleged before the European Court that their exclusion from any effective domestic review violated their rights of access to court and respect for private life and correspondence.

The case *M.N. and Others v. San Marino* (Application no. 28005/12) began with an application lodged on 26 April 2012 by four Italian nationals, S.G., M.N., C.R., and I.R. They alleged that San Marino denied them access to court to challenge a decision affecting their private life and correspondence, contrary to Articles 6, 8, and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The case arose from Italian criminal proceedings against individuals other than the applicants for conspiracy, money laundering, abuse of a position of influence in financial trading, embezzlement, tax evasion, and fraud. Investigators suspected that Mr EMP organised and controlled a network of companies in San Marino, Italy, Malta, Portugal (Madeira), and Vanuatu, all traceable to San Marino Investimenti S.A. (“SMI”). SMI was allegedly used to provide illicit investment and fiduciary services and to launder money for Italian clients through a double system of fiduciary mandates.

In May 2009, the Rome prosecutor’s office sent a letter rogatory to San Marino requesting assistance, searches, and documentation from banks, fiduciary institutes, and trust companies. On 27 November 2009, the San Marino *Commissario della Legge* accepted the request (the exequatur decision) for crimes including conspiracy, money laundering, aggravated fraud, and embezzlement. It ordered an investigation of all banks, fiduciary institutes, and trust companies in San Marino and the acquisition of banking documents, statements, cheques, fiduciary dispositions, and emails relating to named accounts and any account traceable to SMI or connected persons. Copies of documents amounted to seizure. Electronic data was to be cloned and backed up, and seals could be removed only with notice to interested persons. The decision stated that the material could not be used for purposes other than the specified criminal proceedings unless the court decided otherwise after further assessment.

On 26 April 2010, the *Commissario* ordered that Italian citizens who had entered fiduciary agreements with SMI—1,452 in total—be notified. The applicants were among them. M.N. was notified on 24 January 2011, S.G. on 16 June 2011, and C.R. and I.R. on 4 February 2011.

The applicants, who were not charged with any offence, challenged the seizure of documents related to them before the judge of criminal appeals under Article 30 of Law no. 104/2009. They argued that the crimes were not punishable under San Marino law, that there was no *fumus delicti* or link between them and the alleged offences, and that Article 30(3) was incompatible with the San Marino Declaration because it did not allow persons whose documents were seized as a result of an exequatur decision to lodge a complaint. The domestic courts declared the complaints inadmissible for lack of standing. They held that an exequatur decision could only be challenged by a person involved in the investigation or a third party subjected to the measure; persons merely affected by its execution were not interested parties, and any breach should be raised in Italian jurisdictions. Appeals to the third-instance criminal judge were rejected, and constitutional complaints were dismissed on the same basis. Parallel requests to revoke or restrict use of the seized documents were discontinued or rejected because the exequatur decision already limited their use.

The applicants therefore alleged before the ECtHR that they had no effective access to court to challenge measures affecting their private life and correspondence, in violation of Articles 6, 8, and 13.

**CASE OF NIKOLIĆ v. CROATIA** (Application no. 5096/12) is a European Court of Human Rights case from the First Section. The judgment was delivered on 29 January 2015 and became final on 1 June 2015. The applicant, Nada Nikolić, a Croatian national born in 1964 and living in Vukovar, alleged that Croatia had failed, contrary to the procedural requirements of Article 2 of the Convention, to provide an adequate official response to the killing of her husband.

The events occurred during the armed conflict in Croatia. Vukovar was heavily attacked by the Yugoslav People’s Army and Serbian paramilitary forces from August to November 1991 and was occupied by late November 1991. Between 1992 and 1996 it formed part of a United Nations Protected Area, and from 1996 to 1998 it was included in the UNTAES administration. On 15 January 1998 the transfer of power to the Croatian authorities began.

On 2 October 1991, between 4 p.m. and 5 p.m., during a general alert, two unknown uniformed and armed men apprehended the applicant’s husband, Lj.N., in the basement or courtyard of a building in Kudeljarska Street in Vukovar and drove him away. On 24 November 1991 his body was found in the River Danube at Novi Sad, Serbia. An autopsy carried out on 25 November 1991 by the Institute for Forensic Medicine in Novi Sad concluded that death was caused by a gunshot wound from a handgun.

The investigation began only later. In 2004 the applicant brought a civil action against the State for damages. In that context, the State Attorney’s Office asked the Vukovar police for information, and the police learned of the death and opened an enquiry. On 24 January 2005 the police interviewed the applicant, who said her husband had been taken by two Croatian soldiers and named six people present: B.Š., K.Š., J.T., S.P., M.P. and J.M. Three of them had since died. J.T. said the abductors were two uniformed, armed and masked men. On 3 February 2005 B.Š. denied being present. On 15 February 2005 the police filed a criminal complaint against an unknown perpetrator as a war crime against the civilian population.

In May 2009 the applicant told the Vukovar County State Attorney’s Office that B.Š. had been present and that, after K.Š. died, one abductor returned to take J.M.; on that occasion B.Š. allegedly whispered: “This is the man who took Lj.N.” She also said B.Š. lived in Zagreb. In July 2009 the Zagreb police interviewed B.Š., who again denied involvement. J.M. said she had been present but had not seen the abductors. In March 2011 an investigating judge of the Zagreb County Court heard B.Š., who repeated his denial. In May 2011 a Vukovar County Court investigating judge interviewed the applicant, who repeated her statement. On 12 November 2011 the Vukovar police informed the State Attorney’s Office that no new information had been obtained.

The applicant’s civil claim was dismissed in 2008 and upheld on appeal in 2009 and 2011 on limitation grounds. Her constitutional complaint was dismissed in July 2011. Domestic law included the constitutional right to life and Code of Criminal Procedure provisions requiring authorities to collect information, identify perpetrators and open an investigation where suspicion existed. The key facts relevant to the alleged Article 2 violation were that the investigation commenced only years after the killing, initially against an unknown perpetrator, and that later information from the applicant did not lead to effective further action against any identified suspect.

**Case Summary: Milenković and Veljković v. Serbia (Applications nos. 7786/13 and 47972/13)**

**Judgment Date:** 20 October 2015

**Parties:** Ms Dobrica Milenković (first applicant) and Mr Miroslav Veljković (second applicant) v. Serbia.

**Key Facts:**

The applicants, both Serbian nationals residing in Vladičin Han, were employed by DP "PK Delišes," a socially-owned company ("the debtor"). Their complaints stem from the failure of the Serbian authorities to enforce final domestic court judgments rendered in their favour for unpaid salary arrears and social insurance contributions.

**Proceedings for the First Applicant (Ms Milenković):**
On 20 October 2003, the Vladičin Han Municipal Court ordered the debtor to pay Ms Milenković specified amounts for salary arrears and social insurance contributions. This judgment became final and enforceable by 31 October 2003. Subsequently, on 31 December 2003, upon her request, the court issued an enforcement order, also instructing the debtor to cover the enforcement costs.

**Proceedings for the Second Applicant (Mr Veljković):**
Similarly, on 18 February 2004, the same Municipal Court ordered the debtor to pay Mr Veljković specified amounts for salary arrears and social insurance contributions. This judgment became final and enforceable by 11 April 2004. On 4 May 2004, following his request, the court ordered its enforcement and awarded him enforcement costs.

**Subsequent Developments Regarding the Debtor:**
The debtor company underwent significant changes. On 18 February 2004, the Privatisation Agency ordered its restructuring. Nearly a decade later, on 30 January 2014, the Leskovac Commercial Court initiated insolvency proceedings against the debtor. The applicants properly reported their claims based on the judgments to the insolvency administration. As of the Court's judgment, these insolvency proceedings were still ongoing, and the final court judgments in the applicants' favour remained unenforced.

**Alleged Violations and Legal Arguments:**

The applicants brought their case to the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR), complaining about the respondent State's failure to enforce the final court judgments and the lack of an effective domestic remedy for this non-enforcement. They relied on Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial within a reasonable time) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property).

The Serbian Government contested the applications' admissibility, arguing that the applicants had failed to exhaust effective domestic remedies. They claimed that because the debtor was undergoing insolvency proceedings, the applicants should have lodged constitutional appeals before applying to the ECtHR, citing relevant case law.

The ECtHR rejected the Government's objection. It noted its established case law that a constitutional appeal is generally considered an effective remedy for non-enforcement against socially-owned companies undergoing insolvency for applications lodged from 22 June 2012 onwards, and for those undergoing restructuring for applications introduced from 4 October 2013 onwards. However, the first applicant lodged her application on 18 December 2012, and the second on 5 July 2013. These dates preceded both the opening of insolvency proceedings against the debtor (January 2014) and the critical cut-off date of 4 October 2013 established in the *Ferizović* decision regarding restructuring. Applying the general rule that the exhaustion of domestic remedies is assessed by reference to the date the application was lodged, the Court found the applicants were not obligated to pursue a constitutional appeal. The applications were thus declared admissible.

On the merits, the ECtHR found that the final judgments remained unenforced, mirroring issues in numerous prior cases against Serbia. It concluded that the Government had not provided convincing arguments to distinguish this case, leading to findings of violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court did not deem it necessary to examine the complaint under Article 13 separately, as it was essentially the same as the others.

In the case of *Milenković and Veljković v. Serbia* (Applications nos. 7786/13 and 47972/13), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered judgment on 20 October 2015. The case originated in two applications by Ms Dobrica Milenković and Mr Miroslav Veljković, Serbian nationals living in Vladičin Han. Both were employed by DP “PK Delišes,” a socially-owned company based in Vladičin Han (the debtor). They complained that Serbia failed to enforce final court judgments rendered in their favour and that no effective domestic remedy existed. They relied on Article 6 § 1 (fair trial within a reasonable time), Article 13 (effective remedy), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property).

The key facts concerned two sets of civil proceedings. On 20 October 2003, the Vladičin Han Municipal Court ordered the debtor to pay the first applicant specified amounts for salary arrears and social insurance contributions. That judgment became final and enforceable by 31 October 2003. On 31 December 2003, at her request, the same court ordered enforcement and awarded enforcement costs. The second applicant obtained a similar judgment on 18 February 2004, ordering the debtor to pay salary arrears and social insurance contributions. It became final and enforceable by 11 April 2004. On 4 May 2004, the court ordered enforcement and awarded enforcement costs in his favour.

Other relevant facts were that on 18 February 2004 the Privatisation Agency ordered restructuring of the debtor. On 30 January 2014, the Leskovac Commercial Court opened insolvency proceedings against the debtor. The applicants duly reported their claims, based on the judgments, to the insolvency administration. The insolvency proceedings remained ongoing. Critically, the final judgments in the applicants’ favour had still not been enforced.

The Government contested admissibility, arguing that the applicants had failed to exhaust effective remedies. It submitted that because the debtor was undergoing insolvency and/or restructuring, the applicants should have lodged constitutional appeals before applying to the Court, relying on *Marinković v. Serbia* and *Ferizović v. Serbia*. The Court rejected that objection. The applications were lodged on 18 December 2012 and 5 July 2013—before insolvency proceedings were opened and while the debtor was only in restructuring, but before 4 October 2013. Under the Court’s settled approach, exhaustion of domestic remedies is normally assessed by reference to the date the application was lodged. Therefore, the applicants had no obligation to use constitutional redress before coming to Strasbourg. The complaints were admissible.

On the merits, the Court observed that the final judgments remained unenforced. It had frequently found violations of Article 6 § 1 and/or Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 in similar cases concerning non-enforcement of judgments against socially-owned companies. The Government had not presented any fact or convincing argument distinguishing this case. Accordingly, the Court found violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Having reached that conclusion, it did not find it necessary to examine the essentially same complaint under Article 13.

Thus, the alleged violations arose from the prolonged failure of the respondent State to enforce final and enforceable judgments awarding the applicants salary arrears and social insurance contributions, despite the debtor’s later restructuring and insolvency. The Court held that this non-enforcement breached the applicants’ rights to a fair trial and peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

Case Milenković and Veljković v. Serbia (Applications nos. 7786/13 and 47972/13) is a European Court of Human Rights judgment delivered on 20 October 2015 by the Third Section. The applicants, Dobrica Milenković (born 1957) and Miroslav Veljković (born 1966), are Serbian nationals living in Vladičin Han. Both worked for DP “PK Delišes,” a socially-owned company in Vladičin Han (“the debtor”). Their complaints concerned Serbia’s failure to enforce final court judgments ordering the debtor to pay salary arrears and social insurance contributions, and the absence of an effective remedy for that non-enforcement.

The first applicant, Ms Milenković, obtained a judgment from the Vladičin Han Municipal Court on 20 October 2003 ordering the debtor to pay specified amounts for salary arrears and social insurance contributions. That judgment became final and enforceable by 31 October 2003. On 31 December 2003, at her request, the court ordered enforcement of the judgment and further ordered the debtor to pay enforcement costs.

The second applicant, Mr Veljković, obtained a similar judgment from the same court on 18 February 2004, ordering the debtor to pay specified salary arrears and social insurance contributions. That judgment became final and enforceable by 11 April 2004. On 4 May 2004, at his request, the court ordered enforcement and awarded enforcement costs.

Additional relevant facts concerned the debtor’s status. On 18 February 2004, the Privatisation Agency ordered the debtor’s restructuring. On 30 January 2014, the Leskovac Commercial Court opened insolvency proceedings against the debtor. The applicants duly reported their claims based on the judgments to the insolvency administration. The insolvency proceedings were still ongoing.

The applicants lodged their applications with the Court on 18 December 2012 and 5 July 2013. They alleged violations of Article 6 § 1, Article 13, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, complaining that the final judgments in their favour remained unenforced and that no effective domestic remedy existed. The Government objected that the applicants had failed to exhaust effective remedies, arguing that because the debtor was undergoing restructuring and/or insolvency, they should have lodged constitutional appeals. The Court rejected that objection. It recalled that a constitutional appeal is generally considered effective for non-enforcement against socially-owned companies undergoing insolvency, or which have ceased to exist, for applications lodged from 22 June 2012 (Marinković). For companies undergoing restructuring, it became effective for applications introduced from 4 October 2013 (Ferizović). Here, the applications were lodged before insolvency proceedings opened, while the debtor was undergoing restructuring, and before 4 October 2013. Since exhaustion is normally assessed by reference to the date the application was lodged, the applicants were not required to use constitutional redress. The applications were therefore admissible.

On the merits, the Court noted that the final judgments in the applicants’ favour remained unenforced. It observed that it had frequently found violations of Article 6 § 1 and/or Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 in similar cases concerning non-enforcement of final judgments against socially-owned companies. The Government failed to provide any fact or convincing argument capable of leading to a different conclusion. The Court accordingly found violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Having reached that conclusion, it did not find it necessary to examine the essentially same complaint under Article 13. The applications had been joined because of their common factual and legal background, and the Government’s objection to examination by a Committee was rejected.
001-150668:
**Rinas v. Finland** (Application no. 17039/13) concerned a Russian national, Pavel Rinas, who alleged that Finland violated the **ne bis in idem** principle under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the European Convention on Human Rights. The case arose from two parallel sets of proceedings—tax surcharge proceedings and criminal tax fraud proceedings—based on the same conduct: the applicant’s failure to declare income received from foreign companies.

In 2004–2005, Finnish tax authorities inspected the applicant’s foreign companies. On 22 December 2005, they imposed additional taxes and tax surcharges of EUR 6,727 for the 1999 tax year, finding that he had received disguised dividends. On 26 June 2006, further additional taxes and tax surcharges were imposed for the 2000, 2002, 2003 and 2004 tax years, with surcharges ranging from EUR 824 to EUR 5,000. The applicant sought rectification, but the Tax Rectification Committee rejected his applications on 4 October 2006. He appealed to the Helsinki Administrative Court, which rejected the appeals on 8 April 2011, and then to the Supreme Administrative Court, which refused leave to appeal on 13 September 2012. The tax proceedings therefore became final on that latter date.

Meanwhile, criminal proceedings had begun. On 15 April 2005, the tax authorities asked the police to investigate possible aggravated tax fraud. On 17 November 2008, the public prosecutor charged the applicant with aggravated tax fraud for the tax years 1999–2000 and 2002–2004, alleging that he had failed to declare income and thereby paid too little tax. The tax authorities also claimed EUR 48,870 in unpaid taxes. On 12 June 2009, the Vantaa District Court convicted him and imposed a suspended prison sentence of 1 year and 6 months, plus compensation. On appeal, the Helsinki Appeal Court on 21 December 2010 dismissed the charges for 1999–2000 without examining the merits, because the tax decisions for those years had already become final before the charges were brought. It upheld the conviction for 2002–2004, however, reducing the sentence to 10 months suspended and compensation to EUR 10,718. The Supreme Court upheld that result on 31 May 2012, reasoning that for 2002–2004 the tax decisions had not been final when the charges were brought, since the applicant still had a right to appeal in the tax proceedings. The criminal judgment thus became final on 31 May 2012.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained that he had been tried and punished twice for the same matter. The Court noted that tax surcharge proceedings are criminal in nature for Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 purposes, and that the tax and criminal proceedings concerned substantially the same facts for the 2002–2004 tax years. For 1999–2000, the applicant could no longer claim to be a victim because the Appeal Court had dismissed those charges on ne bis in idem grounds.

The key violation related to 2002–2004. The two sets of proceedings ran concurrently. The criminal proceedings became final on 31 May 2012, while the tax surcharge appeal remained pending before the Supreme Administrative Court until 13 September 2012. Since the tax proceedings were not discontinued after the criminal case became final, the applicant was convicted and punished twice for the same matter. The Court found no sufficiently close connection between the tax and criminal sanctions, unlike earlier driving-licence cases. Accordingly, Finland violated Article 4 of Protocol No. 7.

In *Rinas v. Finland*, the applicant, a Russian national living in Finland, complained under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention that he had been subjected to double jeopardy (*ne bis in idem*). The case arose from tax inspections of his Finnish and foreign companies. In December 2005 and June 2006, the Finnish tax authorities imposed additional taxes and tax surcharges on him for receiving disguised dividends from foreign companies for tax years 1999, 2000, 2002, 2003 and 2004. The tax surcharges ranged from EUR 824 to EUR 6,727. The applicant sought rectification, but the Tax Rectification Committee rejected his applications in October 2006. His appeals were later rejected by the Helsinki Administrative Court in April 2011, and the Supreme Administrative Court refused leave to appeal on 13 September 2012, making the tax proceedings final on that date.

In parallel, the tax authorities had asked the police in April 2005 to investigate suspected aggravated tax fraud. In November 2008, the prosecutor charged the applicant with aggravated tax fraud for tax years 1999–2000 and 2002–2004, based on the same failure to declare income from the foreign companies. The Vantaa District Court convicted him in June 2009, imposing a suspended prison sentence of 1 year and 6 months and ordering compensation. On appeal, the Helsinki Appeal Court in December 2010 dismissed the charges for 1999–2000 without examining the merits, finding that the tax surcharge decisions for those years had already become final and that *ne bis in idem* barred criminal proceedings. It upheld the conviction for 2002–2004, reducing the sentence to 10 months and the compensation amount. The Supreme Court upheld that result on 31 May 2012, reasoning that for 2002–2004 the tax decisions had not become final when charges were brought because the applicant still had a right to appeal to the administrative courts.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that the tax surcharge proceedings and the criminal proceedings concerned the same facts and therefore amounted to double jeopardy. The Government accepted that both sets of proceedings were criminal in nature and arose from the same circumstances, but argued that they were parallel and that the first set had not become final before the second was initiated. The ECtHR found that both the tax surcharge proceedings and the aggravated tax fraud proceedings were criminal for the purposes of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7, relying on *Jussila v. Finland*. It also found that, for tax years 2002–2004, the two proceedings arose from identical or substantially the same facts.

The tax proceedings became final on 13 September 2012; the criminal conviction became final on 31 May 2012. Because the tax appeal remained pending when the criminal proceedings became final and was not discontinued, the applicant was ultimately subjected to two final criminal proceedings for the same matter. The Court found no sufficiently close connection in substance and time between the Finnish tax surcharge and criminal systems. It therefore held that there had been a violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 concerning tax years 2002–2004. As for 1999–2000, the Appeal Court had already dismissed the charges on *ne bis in idem* grounds, so the applicant could no longer claim victim status for those years.

In *Rinas v. Finland* (Application no. 17039/13, judgment 27 January 2015), the applicant, a Russian national living in Finland, complained that Finnish authorities violated the *ne bis in idem* principle under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention. The case concerned parallel tax surcharge proceedings and criminal tax fraud proceedings based on the same alleged failure to declare income from foreign companies.

In December 2005, the tax authorities imposed additional taxes and tax surcharges on Rinas for the 1999 tax year, based on disguised dividends from foreign companies; the surcharge was €6,727. In June 2006, further additional taxes and surcharges were imposed for 2000 and 2002–2004, with surcharges ranging from €824 to €5,000. Rinas sought rectification, but the Tax Rectification Committee rejected his applications in October 2006. He appealed to the Helsinki Administrative Court, which rejected the appeals in April 2011. The Supreme Administrative Court refused leave to appeal on 13 September 2012, making the tax surcharge decisions final.

Meanwhile, in April 2005 the tax authorities asked police to investigate aggravated tax fraud for tax years 1998–2004. In November 2008, the prosecutor charged Rinas with aggravated tax fraud for 1999–2000 and 2002–2004, alleging he failed to declare income from foreign companies, causing too-low taxation. The tax authorities also claimed €48,870 in unpaid taxes. In June 2009, the District Court convicted Rinas, imposed a suspended 1-year-6-month prison sentence, and ordered compensation. On appeal, the Helsinki Appeal Court in December 2010 dismissed the charges for 1999–2000 without examining the merits, relying on *ne bis in idem* because those tax matters had already become final. For 2002–2004, however, it upheld the conviction, reducing the sentence to 10 months suspended and compensation to €10,718. The Supreme Court upheld that result on 31 May 2012, finding that the tax decisions for 2002–2004 had not been final when charges were brought because Rinas still had a right to appeal in the tax proceedings.

Before the European Court, Rinas alleged double jeopardy. The Court found both the tax surcharge proceedings and the criminal tax fraud proceedings criminal in nature for Convention purposes; tax surcharges were punitive and deterrent. It also found the facts were substantially the same for the relevant tax years. For 1999–2000, the applicant could no longer claim victim status because the Appeal Court had already dismissed those charges on *ne bis in idem* grounds. For 2002–2004, the criminal proceedings became final first on 31 May 2012, while the tax surcharge appeal was still pending and later became final on 13 September 2012. Because the tax proceedings were not discontinued after the criminal judgment became final, Rinas was convicted or punished twice for the same matter. The Court rejected the Government’s argument that the proceedings had a sufficiently close connection, noting they were conducted by separate authorities with no real interaction and no mutual consideration of sanctions. It therefore found a violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 concerning the tax years 2002–2004.

In *Alves v. Portugal* (Application no. 79925/12, ECtHR, 30 April 2015), the applicant, Ms Cretka Ivanic Alves, a Slovenian national born in 1953 and living in Braga, Portugal, brought a civil liability action on 22 November 2006 in the Braga Court against F., a lawyer who had acted for her in earlier proceedings. She claimed damages for professional negligence. F. was notified on 12 December 2006, submitted his reply on 25 January 2007, and requested that his professional liability insurer intervene. The insurer was allowed to intervene on 11 July 2007, filed submissions on 14 September 2007, and the applicant replied on 11 October 2007.

Between January and April 2008, the parties disputed the applicant’s legal capacity to be a party. On 28 April 2008, the first-instance judge absolved F. from the proceedings because he found the applicant lacked legal capacity. The applicant appealed. On 4 December 2008, the Guimarães Court of Appeal held that she did have legal capacity and ordered the case to be re-examined at first instance. In February 2009, the case was reallocated to the Braga Court. On 29 April 2009, the judge issued directions identifying established and outstanding matters. Between 28 May and 6 November 2009, the parties made three requests; the judge replied to each within less than one month. The hearing was set for 10 March 2010, adjourned to 15 June 2010, and a second hearing was held on 7 October 2010. On 29 October 2010, the Braga Court partially found in the applicant’s favour. Both parties appealed; the Guimarães Court of Appeal dismissed the appeals on 20 October 2011. The parties then appealed to the Supreme Court, which dismissed the appeals on 29 May 2012.

The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the length of the proceedings violated her right to a hearing within a reasonable time. The relevant period ran from 22 November 2006 to 29 May 2012, lasting five years and six months across three levels of jurisdiction. The Government contested the complaint. The Court declared the application admissible.

On the merits, the Court applied the criteria of complexity, the applicant’s conduct, the authorities’ conduct, and what was at stake. It found the subject matter was not especially complex, as it concerned a damages claim against a lawyer for professional negligence. The applicant had not caused delays. Although there were appeals and procedural requests, the Court found no substantial period of inactivity attributable to the national authorities. The domestic courts responded promptly and did not remain passive. Recalling that a delay at one stage may be acceptable if the overall duration is not excessive, the Court concluded that the authorities showed due diligence and that the total length was not incompatible with the “reasonable time” requirement. It therefore found no violation of Article 6 § 1.

**Case: Alves v. Portugal (Application no. 79925/12), European Court of Human Rights, First Section, Judgment of 30 April 2015.**

The applicant, Ms Cretka Ivanic Alves, a Slovenian national born in 1953 who lives in Braga, Portugal, lodged an application against the Portuguese Republic on 4 December 2012. She was represented by a lawyer. The Portuguese Government were represented by their Agent. The Slovenian Government did not exercise their right to intervene.

The case concerned a civil liability action. On 22 November 2006, the applicant sued “F.”, a lawyer who had previously represented her, in the Braga Court, claiming damages for professional negligence. F. was notified on 12 December 2006. On 25 January 2007, F. filed his defence and requested that his insurance company intervene, since he had transferred his professional responsibility to it. The applicant filed further submissions on 8 March 2007. On 11 July 2007, the Braga Court accepted the insurer’s intervention. The insurer filed submissions on 14 September 2007, and the applicant replied on 11 October 2007.

Between January and April 2008, the parties disputed the applicant’s legal capacity to be a party to the proceedings. On 28 April 2008, the judge issued a despacho saneador absolving F. from the proceedings because the applicant allegedly lacked legal capacity. The applicant appealed to the Guimarães Court of Appeal. By decision of 4 December 2008, the Court of Appeal held that the applicant did have legal capacity and ordered the first-instance court to re-analyse the case. In February 2009, the proceedings were reallocated to the Braga Court.

On 29 April 2009, the judge issued directions identifying established and outstanding matters. Between 28 May and 6 November 2009, the parties made three requests, all of which the judge answered within less than one month. The case was set down for hearing on 10 March 2010, later adjourned to 15 June 2010. A second hearing took place on 7 October 2010. On 29 October 2010, the Braga Court partially found in favour of the applicant. Both parties appealed to the Guimarães Court of Appeal, which dismissed the appeals on 20 October 2011. The parties then challenged that decision before the Supreme Court, which dismissed the appeals on 29 May 2012.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained that the length of the proceedings violated the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The Government contested that argument. The Court declared the application admissible, finding it not manifestly ill-founded.

On the merits, the Court noted that the relevant period began on 22 November 2006 and ended on 29 May 2012, lasting five years and six months across three levels of jurisdiction. Applying the criteria of complexity, conduct of the applicant, conduct of the authorities, and what was at stake, the Court found that the subject matter—a damages claim against a lawyer for professional negligence—was not especially complex. The applicant had not caused delays. As to the national authorities, although there were appeals and procedural requests, the Court found no substantial period of inactivity attributable to the State. The domestic courts did not remain passive and handled the parties’ requests and appeals without substantial delays. The authorities therefore showed due diligence. Accordingly, the Court concluded that the length of the proceedings was not unreasonable and found no violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

In *Alves v. Portugal* (Application no. 79925/12, judgment 30 April 2015), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint under Article 6 § 1 that civil proceedings in Portugal exceeded a reasonable time. The applicant, Ms Cretka Ivanic Alves, a Slovenian national living in Braga, Portugal, brought a liability action on 22 November 2006 in the Braga Court against F., a lawyer who had represented her in earlier proceedings, claiming damages for professional negligence.

The procedural chronology was central to the length complaint. F. was notified on 12 December 2006 and replied on 25 January 2007, requesting that his insurance company intervene. The applicant filed a further reply on 8 March 2007. On 11 July 2007 the Braga Court accepted the insurer’s intervention; the insurer was summoned on an unknown date, filed submissions on 14 September 2007, and the applicant responded on 11 October 2007. Between January and April 2008 the parties disputed the applicant’s legal capacity. On 28 April 2008 the judge absolved F. from the proceedings because the applicant allegedly lacked legal capacity. The applicant appealed to the Guimarães Court of Appeal, which on 4 December 2008 found she did have legal capacity and ordered the first-instance court to re-examine the case. In February 2009 the case was reallocated to the Braga Court. On 29 April 2009 the judge issued directions identifying established and outstanding matters. Between 28 May and 6 November 2009, the parties made three requests, each answered by the judge within less than a month. A hearing was set for 10 March 2010, adjourned to 15 June 2010, and a second hearing took place on 7 October 2010. On 29 October 2010 the Braga Court partially ruled in the applicant’s favour. Both parties appealed to the Guimarães Court of Appeal, which dismissed the appeals on 20 October 2011. Further challenges to the Supreme Court were dismissed on 29 May 2012.

The applicant lodged her application on 4 December 2012. The Portuguese Government contested the complaint, and the Slovenian Government did not exercise its right to intervene. The Court declared the application admissible, finding it not manifestly ill-founded. The relevant period ran from 22 November 2006 to 29 May 2012, lasting five years and six months across three levels of jurisdiction.

On the merits, the Court applied the standard criteria of complexity, conduct of the applicant, conduct of the authorities, and what was at stake. It considered the case not especially complex, as it concerned a damages claim against a lawyer for professional negligence. The applicant had not caused delays. Although there were several appeals and procedural requests, the Court found no substantial period of inactivity attributable to the national authorities. The domestic courts did not remain passive; they responded promptly and handled the case without substantial delays, showing due diligence. Consequently, the Court concluded that the length of the proceedings did not violate the “reasonable time” requirement of Article 6 § 1.
