001-158504:
The case concerns Qing Xu, a Chinese national born in 1964, living in Parede, Portugal. She worked as a Chinese-Portuguese translator, was married to a Portuguese national, had two young children, and had lived in Portugal for at least 20 years. In December 2010, Portuguese authorities opened criminal proceedings against her, her husband, and others for aiding illegal immigration, money laundering, and forgery.

In April 2011, before her arrest, she wrote to the Attorney General and the Immigration and Borders Service stating that she knew she was under investigation and was willing to be questioned. She even suggested specific dates. On 9 June 2011, a public prosecutor issued an arrest warrant under Articles 254 and 257(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, citing sufficient evidence and risks that she would abscond, obstruct the investigation, or continue criminal activity. She was arrested at home on 14 June 2011 between 5 and 6 a.m., and questioned by an investigating judge on 15–16 June.

She challenged the arrest and sought alternative measures. She argued there was no risk of absconding: she had no criminal record, two young children, a permanent residence in Portugal for at least 20 years, and was willing to surrender her passport. She proposed lesser measures such as prohibiting contact with co-defendants and avoiding places attended by immigrants. On 16 June 2011, the investigating judge rejected her arguments. The judge found an evident risk of absconding because she was a Chinese national and, once confronted with the seriousness of the allegations, could flee to China. The judge also found risks of obstructing the investigation, since many witnesses remained to be examined, and of continuing criminal activity. She was remanded in custody. By contrast, co-defendants B.G., J.G. (her Portuguese husband), and M.M. received non-custodial measures such as passport surrender, contact bans, and weekly police reporting.

She appealed. In July 2011, the prosecutor requested that the case be classified as particularly complex; in August the judge granted this and extended pre-trial detention to 12 months. On 14 September 2011, the Lisbon Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal. It stated that the prosecutor’s reasoning that she would not voluntarily appear “could not eventually be justified,” but the warrant was not unlawful. It accepted there was no high risk of absconding because she had volunteered and had not fled. However, it upheld detention due to a high risk to the investigation—particularly given the nature of the Chinese community in Portugal—and the risk of continuing crime, which it said family circumstances or electronic surveillance could not prevent.

From October 2011 to February 2012, she filed three release requests and two requests to expedite the inquiry. The investigating judge repeatedly rejected release, saying the grounds remained unchanged or strengthened. The Prosecutor General rejected expedition requests as ill-founded given the case’s complexity. Periodic reviews in 2012 upheld detention.

On 29 January 2013, the judge replaced detention with house arrest and electronic surveillance; she was released from pre-trial detention on 30 January 2013. On 20 February 2013, the Lisbon Criminal Court acquitted her of money laundering and forgery but convicted her of aiding illegal immigration, imposing a five-year suspended sentence with an annual EUR 1,500 payment. She was released from house arrest and appealed; proceedings were still pending as of 29 April 2015.

The applicant alleged that her pre-trial detention was arbitrary, unreasonably lengthy, and imposed because of her foreign nationality. Key legal provisions required detention to be necessary, proportionate, and a last resort; arrest without flagrante only if there were well-grounded reasons to believe the suspect would not voluntarily appear; and non-national status alone should not suffice to establish flight risk.

*Qing v. Portugal* (Application no. 69861/11) concerned Ms Qing Xu, a Chinese national born in 1964, living in Parede, Portugal. She worked as a Chinese-Portuguese translator, was married to a Portuguese national, had two young children, and had lived in Portugal for about twenty years. On 16 December 2010 Portuguese authorities began criminal proceedings against her, her husband, and others for suspected aiding of illegal immigration, money laundering, and forgery.

In April 2011, aware she was under investigation, the applicant wrote to the Attorney General and the Immigration and Borders Service, stating her willingness to be questioned and suggesting dates for that purpose. On 9 June 2011, a public prosecutor issued an arrest warrant under Articles 254 and 257(1) of the Portuguese Code of Criminal Procedure, finding sufficient evidence and risks that she would abscond, obstruct the investigation, or continue criminal activity. She was arrested at home on 14 June 2011 between 5 and 6 a.m. and questioned by an investigating judge on 15–16 June 2011.

The applicant challenged the arrest and sought non-custodial measures. She relied on having no criminal record, two young children, permanent residence, long residence in Portugal, readiness to surrender her passport, and proposed travel/contact restrictions. On 16 June 2011 the investigating judge dismissed her challenge, finding a risk of absconding because she was a Chinese national who could flee to China. The judge remanded her in pre-trial detention. Some co-defendants, including her Portuguese husband, received less restrictive measures such as passport surrender, weekly police reporting, and restrictions on contact.

She appealed. In July 2011 the prosecutor requested that the case be classified as particularly complex; in August 2011 the judge agreed and extended detention to twelve months. On 14 September 2011 the Lisbon Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal. It acknowledged there was no high risk of absconding because she had volunteered to be questioned and had not fled, but upheld detention based on risks of obstructing evidence-gathering, especially within the Chinese community, and continuing criminal activity from home.

From October 2011 to February 2012 the applicant repeatedly sought release or alternatives such as police supervision, house arrest, or electronic monitoring. The investigating judge maintained detention in October 2011, December 2011, and February 2012, finding the grounds unchanged. Requests to expedite the inquiry were rejected in November 2011 and February 2012. Periodic reviews in 2012 also maintained detention.

On 29 January 2013 the judge replaced pre-trial detention with house arrest and electronic surveillance; she was released from detention on 30 January 2013. On 20 February 2013 the Lisbon Criminal Court acquitted her of money laundering and forgery but convicted her of aiding illegal immigration, imposing a suspended five-year sentence with an annual €1,500 payment. She was released from house arrest that day. Her appeal was still pending as of April 2015.

The applicant alleged that her pre-trial detention—roughly 19.5 months in custody—was arbitrary, unreasonably lengthy, and imposed because of her Chinese nationality. Key facts for those claims include the arrest despite her earlier offer to appear, the judge’s reliance on foreign nationality as evidence of flight risk despite long residence, family ties, and voluntary cooperation, the availability and use of less restrictive measures for other co-defendants, repeated extensions and reviews, and the eventual replacement of detention with electronic monitoring before trial.

In *Qing v. Portugal* (ECtHR, First Section, 5 November 2015), the applicant, Ms Qing Xu, a Chinese national born in 1964, lived in Parede, Portugal. She was married to a Portuguese national, worked as a Chinese-Portuguese translator, had two young children, and claimed at least twenty years’ residence in Portugal. She alleged that her pre-trial detention was arbitrary, unreasonably lengthy, and imposed because of her foreign nationality.

On 16 December 2010, Portuguese authorities opened criminal proceedings against her, her husband, and others for alleged aiding of illegal immigration, money laundering, and forgery. In April 2011, before being made a defendant, the applicant wrote to the Attorney General and the Immigration and Borders Service stating that she knew she was under investigation and was willing to be questioned. She volunteered specific dates in late April and May 2011.

On 9 June 2011, a public prosecutor issued an arrest warrant under Articles 254 and 257 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The prosecutor cited sufficient evidence, risk of absconding, risk of obstructing the investigation, and risk of continuing criminal activity. The applicant was arrested at her home on 14 June 2011 between 5 and 6 a.m. and questioned by an investigating judge on 15 and 16 June 2011.

On 16 June 2011, the investigating judge rejected her challenge to the arrest and ordered her pre-trial detention. The judge found a clear risk that she would abscond because she was a Chinese national and, if confronted with the serious allegations, could flee to her home country. The judge also found risks of obstructing the investigation, particularly witness evidence, and of continuing the alleged crimes. The judge noted that the applicant and another defendant were allegedly primarily responsible for a criminal organisation in Portugal. Other defendants, including her husband, received non-custodial measures.

The applicant appealed. On 14 September 2011, the Lisbon Court of Appeal upheld the detention. It acknowledged that there was no high risk of absconding, since she had volunteered to be questioned and had not fled. However, it found a very high risk to the gathering of evidence, “especially given the nature of the Chinese community in Portugal,” and a risk that criminal activity would continue because it was allegedly run from home and conducted with third parties.

Between October 2011 and February 2012, the applicant repeatedly sought release or replacement of detention with police supervision or house arrest with electronic surveillance. She stressed her family ties, long residence, lack of criminal record, willingness to surrender her passport, and the absence of flight risk. The investigating judge rejected these requests, generally stating that the reasons for detention remained unchanged. Periodic reviews in March, May, August, and November 2012 also maintained detention. The proceedings were classified as particularly complex, and the prosecutor general refused requests to expedite the inquiry.

On 29 January 2013, the investigating judge replaced pre-trial detention with house arrest and electronic surveillance. The applicant was released from pre-trial detention on 30 January 2013. On 20 February 2013, the Lisbon Criminal Court acquitted her of money laundering and forgery but convicted her of aiding illegal immigration, imposing a five-year suspended sentence conditioned on an annual payment of EUR 1,500. She was released from house arrest that day. Her appeal was reportedly still pending as of April 2015. The key facts underlying her complaints were thus the authorities’ repeated reliance on her Chinese nationality as a flight risk, their refusal to accept her voluntary cooperation and community ties, and her detention from June 2011 to January 2013.
001-156073:
**Summary of *Temchenko v. Ukraine* (Application no. 30579/10)**

The case of *Temchenko v. Ukraine* concerns an application lodged by Mr Anatoliy Georgiyevich Temchenko, a Ukrainian national born in 1942, against Ukraine. The applicant, formerly a university rector, was arrested on 29 September 2009 on suspicion of accepting bribes and detained in pre-trial facilities. The central violations alleged relate to the inadequate medical assistance provided during his detention and the lack of effective domestic remedies, contrary to Articles 3 and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Prior to his arrest, on 23 September 2009, an endocrinologist diagnosed the applicant with type-2 diabetes and prescribed insulin injections, recommending that treatment commence on an in-patient basis. Despite this, he was detained shortly thereafter. On 2 October 2009, the Dzerzhynskyy District Court ordered his detention for three months, citing risks of absconding or hindering the investigation, without reference to concrete facts. This decision was upheld on appeal, with the Court of Appeal noting unspecified medical documents indicating he was fit for detention, though these were never disclosed.

Throughout his detention, the applicant’s health deteriorated significantly. He suffered from multiple chronic conditions, including ischemic heart disease, hypertension, and diabetes. Medical examinations in October 2009 revealed abnormally high blood pressure and other serious ailments. Although he received some treatment in municipal hospitals, the SIZO medical unit repeatedly acknowledged—in February, March, and June 2010—that it lacked the equipment and staff to provide adequate care and that his condition warranted specialist in-patient treatment, which was not arranged promptly.

The applicant made numerous requests for release, arguing his health was incompatible with detention and that he no longer posed a risk of hindering the investigation. These requests were rejected by the District Court, which cited potential witness influence and claimed he was receiving necessary medical aid, without substantiating these findings or addressing the medical evidence. Crucially, forensic medical examinations conducted on 12 November 2010, 28 January 2011, and 8 June 2011 concluded that the treatment provided during detention had been inadequate and contributed to his deterioration. The experts warned that without proper in-patient care at a specialist institution, he risked potentially fatal complications such as cardiac arrest or brain haemorrhage. They also deemed transportation unsafe without appropriate medical equipment.

Despite these findings, the authorities were slow to act. Only after the European Court applied interim measures under Rule 39 in March 2011 was the applicant transferred to a specialist hospital for examination. Following his conviction on 23 May 2011, his sentence was reduced on appeal to five years’ suspended imprisonment, and he was released on 5 October 2011.

The European Court found that the State failed to comply with its obligations under Article 3, noting the domestic experts’ conclusive findings of inadequate treatment, the SIZO’s own admissions of inability to provide proper care, the courts’ insufficiently reasoned decisions rejecting release, and the dangerous transportation conditions. It also held that the applicant had no effective remedy under Article 13. The case highlights systemic failures in safeguarding detainees’ health, particularly where serious chronic conditions require specialist care beyond prison facilities.

In **Temchenko v. Ukraine** (App. no. 30579/10, judgment 16 July 2015), the applicant, born in 1942, was a Ukrainian university rector arrested on 29 September 2009 on suspicion of bribery. Before arrest, he had type-2 diabetes, hypertension and other conditions; an endocrinologist advised that insulin treatment begin and be adjusted in hospital. He was held in Kryvyy Rig ITT and then SIZO. On 2 October 2009, a district court ordered his detention for three months, citing risks of absconding, hindering the investigation or continuing crime. This was upheld and later extended. He remained detained until 5 October 2011, when his sentence was changed to suspended imprisonment and he was released.

The alleged violations concerned a lack of adequate medical assistance in detention and the absence of an effective domestic remedy. The facts showed the authorities knew of his serious health problems. Upon arrival at SIZO, he was hospitalised with high blood pressure and diagnosed with ischemic heart disease, stage II hypertension, type-2 subcompensated diabetes, kidney and prostate issues, and other conditions. After discharge, the SIZO medical unit lacked equipment and specialist staff to provide adequate care. On 11 February, 9 March and 2 June 2010, SIZO medical staff stated that he needed in-patient examination and treatment in a specialist institution. On 2 June 2010, the head of the SIZO medical unit told the judge that adequate treatment was impossible in SIZO and asked for the preventive measure to be changed; the judge did not respond. Although he received insulin from April 2010 and occasional hospital treatment, forensic experts on 12 November 2010, 28 January and 8 June 2011 found that the treatment during detention was inadequate, that his condition had deteriorated, and that he required comprehensive in-patient treatment at a specialist endocrinology/cardiology hospital, such as the Strazhesko Institute in Kyiv. They warned of potentially fatal complications, including cardiac arrest, brain haemorrhage or aortic dissection, and said ordinary transportation was dangerous.

Domestic courts repeatedly rejected release requests from May 2010 onward. They relied on generic findings that he could influence witnesses, without concrete facts, and on unspecified medical certificates saying he was receiving treatment. They did not examine the adequacy of that treatment or address expert conclusions that SIZO could not provide appropriate care. The District Court also failed to order a fitness-for-transportation assessment until late 2010, despite knowing of his poor health since October 2009. From September 2009 to February 2011, he was transported in a regular van or police car on many occasions; only after April 2011 was he transported by ambulance with a doctor. The European Court’s Rule 39 measure in March 2011 led to his transfer to an outside hospital.

The Court rejected the Government’s non-exhaustion objection. It found that the State had failed to comply with its positive obligation under Article 3 to safeguard the applicant’s health in detention, because authorities knew of his need for specialist in-patient care but delayed and failed to provide it, while courts upheld detention without meaningful review. It also found no effective remedy under Article 13 for these complaints. The case thus concerned primarily Ukraine’s failure to provide adequate medical assistance to a seriously ill detainee and the lack of effective domestic remedies.

In *Temchenko v. Ukraine* (App no. 30579/10, judgment 16 July 2015), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Articles 3 and 13 that an elderly detainee received inadequate medical care in detention and lacked an effective remedy. The applicant, born in 1942, was a former State university rector arrested on 29 September 2009 on suspicion of bribery and held in the Kryvyy Rig ITT and later SIZO. Before arrest, he had type-2 diabetes, and an endocrinologist had prescribed insulin, advising that treatment begin and be adjusted on an in-patient basis.

In detention, doctors diagnosed ischemic heart disease, angina, stage II hypertension, chronic cholecystitis and pancreatitis, medium-severity subcompensated diabetes, kidney cyst, prostate adenoma and chronic pyelonephritis. His condition was unstable and deteriorated. The SIZO medical unit lacked equipment and staff for specialist treatment. On 11 February and 9 March 2010 it informed his lawyer that he needed in-patient examination in a specialist institution. On 2 June 2010, the head of the SIZO medical unit told the trial judge that adequate treatment could not be provided in the SIZO, that further insulin adjustment without an endocrinologist’s supervision risked undesirable results, and asked the judge to reconsider detention. The judge did not react. A similar request by the SIZO governor on 15 April 2011 also received no response. From 1 March 2011, the SIZO medical unit had no doctors. The applicant received insulin from April 2010, but bought it himself and relied on relatives for syringes; the prescribed fractional diet was not provided by the SIZO.

Three forensic medical reports (12 November 2010, 28 January 2011 and 8 June 2011) found that treatment during detention had been inadequate and had caused deterioration. They described his condition as grave, highly unstable and unpredictable, requiring comprehensive in-patient treatment in specialist endocrinology and cardiology institutions, such as the Strazhesko Cardiology Institute in Kyiv. Without such treatment, he risked potentially fatal complications, including cardiac arrest, brain haemorrhage or aortic dissection. Transport in ordinary vehicles was dangerous and potentially fatal; if necessary, he required a special cardiac ambulance accompanied by a doctor. Short hospitalisations in 2010–2011 merely stabilised acute deteriorations and did not amount to comprehensive treatment.

The domestic courts repeatedly rejected his release requests on 7 and 17 June 2010 and 28 March and 28 April 2011. They generally asserted that he might influence witnesses and was receiving medical aid, without concrete facts or examining the adequacy of treatment. They also found him fit for detention based on unspecified medical certificates. Detention was extended on similar generic grounds. Although the authorities knew of his poor health from 5 October 2009, no fitness-for-transport assessment was ordered until late 2010. He was transported in a regular van 26 times and once in a police car, without medical equipment; later, 19 times by ambulance. Only after the ECtHR’s Rule 39 decision of 16 March 2011 did the authorities place him in specialist institutions, and even then only briefly.

The Court found that Ukraine failed its obligations under Article 3 because of inadequate medical assistance and dangerous transportation. It also found no effective remedy under Article 13, as the domestic courts did not thoroughly examine his complaints.
001-153910:
**Summary of Vamvakas v. Greece (No. 2)**

The case of *Vamvakas v. Greece (No. 2)* concerns an alleged violation of the right to a fair trial under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) of the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically regarding the effectiveness of legal assistance provided to the applicant, Mr. Alexandros Vamvakas, during his appeal before the Court of Cassation.

The applicant, a Greek national born in 1953, was convicted of fraud and forgery by the Athens Criminal Court of Appeal in 2006 and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. His initial appeal in 2009 resulted in a reduced sentence of seven years. Subsequently, on 1 June 2009, the applicant lodged an appeal on points of law with the Court of Cassation, arguing that his offences should have been classified under tort law, not criminal law, and were therefore statute-barred. He prepared the appeal himself with some legal assistance, submitting it via the Grevena Prison authorities where he was detained.

On 5 November 2009, while in prison, the applicant received a summons for a hearing before the Court of Cassation scheduled for 5 February 2010. Citing financial hardship, he requested the President of the Court of Cassation to appoint an official lawyer to represent him. On 2 January 2010, the President appointed lawyer F.K. to represent him at the hearing.

However, F.K. failed to attend the hearing on 5 February 2010. The applicant, still in prison, had been assured by F.K. that he would be present. The lawyer later claimed to have telephoned the court registry to request an adjournment, but there was no evidence of a formal adjournment request submitted in the manner required by domestic law (either through a physical appearance by another lawyer or a written request from the client). Consequently, the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal as abandoned, on the grounds that the applicant had failed to appear, despite having been properly summoned. The judgment was finalised on 29 March 2010, and the applicant learned of it on 18 October 2010.

The applicant complained that he had not received effective legal assistance, as the officially appointed lawyer’s unexplained absence led to the dismissal of his appeal without a substantive review. The Greek Government argued that the applicant had not requested an adjournment or replacement of counsel and that the state could not be held responsible for every shortcoming of a legal aid lawyer. They maintained that the Court of Cassation had no reason to doubt F.K. would fulfil his duties.

The European Court of Human Rights reiterated that while states are not responsible for every failing of appointed counsel, they must intervene when a failure is manifest or sufficiently brought to authorities’ attention. The Court found that F.K.’s absence, without any valid adjournment request, constituted a “manifest defect” requiring positive measures from the Court of Cassation. The court should have adjourned the proceedings to clarify the situation and ensure the applicant’s defence rights were practically and effectively respected, rather than dismissing the appeal. Therefore, the Court concluded that Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) had been violated.

In *Vamvakas v. Greece (No. 2)*, the European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) of the Convention because the applicant did not receive effective legal assistance before the Court of Cassation. The applicant, Alexandros Vamvakas, a Greek national born in 1953, had been convicted by the Athens Criminal Court of Appeal on 16 January 2006 of fraud and forgery to the detriment of a bank and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. He appeared in person with a lawyer of his choosing. On appeal, at a hearing on 11 February 2009, he appeared with two chosen lawyers. The hearing was adjourned and later postponed to 20 May 2009 because of a lawyers’ strike. The court informed the applicant that he would not be summoned to the 20 May hearing. The applicant wrote that he would not be present but would be represented by his lawyers. Neither lawyer appeared on 20 May. The court then appointed G.M. as official counsel and adjourned to 27 May so he could familiarize himself with the case. G.M. attended and argued that the offences were petty and that mitigating circumstances applied. On 27 May 2009 the Court of Appeal reduced the sentence to seven years but rejected the tort-law classification and found Act No. 1608/1950 applicable.

On 1 June 2009 the applicant lodged an appeal on points of law, mainly complaining of the erroneous application of Act No. 1608/50 and alleging that the offences were time-barred and that Articles 6 and 7 had been violated. He prepared the appeal himself, with some legal assistance, and filed it through Grevena Prison authorities. On 5 November 2009 he received a summons for a Court of Cassation hearing on 5 February 2010. On 30 December 2009, invoking financial hardship, he asked the President of the Court of Cassation to appoint an official lawyer. On 2 January 2010 the President appointed F.K. to represent him at the 5 February 2010 hearing and/or any other hearing in the case. The applicant later said F.K. assured him he would attend. F.K. did not attend. According to the applicant, F.K. later told him he had telephoned the registry to request an adjournment. However, no valid adjournment was made: under domestic practice, a request required either a lawyer attending court on the day or a prior written request from the client to the registry. A telephone call was not sufficient.

The Court of Cassation, by judgment of 25 February 2010, dismissed the appeal as abandoned because the applicant, although summoned within time, had failed to appear. The applicant complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) that he had not received effective legal assistance from the officially assigned lawyer. The Government argued that access to court was respected and that the applicant never requested an adjournment, replacement of counsel, or informed the authorities of any problem. The ECtHR held that assigning counsel does not by itself guarantee effective assistance. States must act when a failure by counsel is manifest or brought to their attention. F.K.’s unexplained absence, only one month and three days after appointment, without any valid adjournment request, constituted a “manifest defect” requiring positive measures. The Court of Cassation should have adjourned proceedings to clarify the situation rather than dismiss the appeal as abandoned. The Court therefore held that Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) had been violated.

In *Vamvakas v. Greece (No. 2)*, the applicant, Alexandros Vamvakas, a Greek national, was convicted in 2006 by the Athens Criminal Court of Appeal of fraud and forgery against a bank and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. He appealed. At a 2009 hearing, he appeared with two lawyers of his choosing. The hearing was adjourned due to a lawyers’ strike. The court told him he would not be summoned to the next hearing. Before that hearing, he wrote that he would not attend but would be represented by his lawyers. Neither lawyer attended. The court appointed an official lawyer, G.M., and adjourned to allow him to examine the file. On 27 May 2009, the Court of Appeal reduced the sentence to seven years, acknowledging mitigating circumstances.

Vamvakas then lodged an appeal on points of law with the Court of Cassation, arguing that the offences fell under tort law, not criminal law, were time-barred, and that Articles 6 and 7 had been violated. He prepared the appeal himself, evidently with legal assistance, and filed it through Grevena Prison authorities. On 5 November 2009, while in prison
001-156069:
The case of *Metalla and Others v. Albania* concerned four applications (nos. 30264/08, 42120/08, 54403/08 and 54411/08) lodged against Albania by nine Albanian nationals between 13 June and 8 October 2008. The applications were communicated to the Government on 21 January 2010. The Fourth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 16 July 2015. The Court noted that the underlying legal issue was already the subject of well-established case-law, particularly *Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania*.

All four applications shared a similar factual pattern. Albanian commissions recognised the applicants’ inherited property rights and ordered either partial physical restoration or compensation for occupied portions. The final commission decisions, however, remained unenforced.

In application no. 30264/08 (*Metalla*), on 9 August 1995 the Shijak Commission recognised the applicants’ inherited title to 1,020 sq. m of land. Of that, 747 sq. m were restored, while the remaining 272 sq. m were occupied. The applicants were to be compensated in one of the ways provided by law. The decision remained unenforced.

In application no. 42120/08 (*Bushati*), on 8 February 1995 the Shkodër Commission recognised the applicant and other heirs’ inherited title to a two-storey building and a surrounding plot of 500 sq. m. Because the plot was occupied, they were to receive compensation; the building was to be restored to them. The applicant claimed that in 1995 and 1997 he brought legal actions against a third party for vacation and restoration of the property, but discontinued them because of pending proceedings in other cities. The third party apparently built unauthorised constructions on the plot. The commission’s decision remained unenforced.

In application no. 54403/08 (*Metalla and Others*), on 12 May 1994 the Shijak Commission recognised the applicants’ inherited title to 5,527 sq. m. Of that, 5,000 sq. m were restored; the remaining 527 sq. m were occupied and were to be compensated. The decision remained unenforced.

In application no. 54411/08 (*Metalla and Others*), on 13 August 2007 the Durrës Commission recognised the applicants’ inherited title to 65,000 sq. m. Of that, 60,000 sq. m were restored; the remaining 5,000 sq. m, consisting of arable land, roads and channels, were occupied and were to be compensated. The decision remained unenforced.

The relevant domestic law and practice were described in *Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania* and *Ramadhi v. Albania*. In 2013 and 2014 the Government approved new property valuation maps including reference prices per square metre. Council of Europe materials showed that the Committee of Ministers repeatedly examined Albania’s failure to enforce final domestic judicial and administrative decisions awarding compensation in lieu of physical restoration. Its decisions in 2014 and 2015 referred to the pilot judgment in *Manushaqe Puto*, welcomed an action plan and later a draft law, but stressed the need for a concrete and effective compensation mechanism without further delay.

The alleged violations therefore concerned the prolonged non-enforcement of final domestic decisions granting property restitution or compensation. This interfered with the applicants’ possessions and their right to effective execution of final decisions, raising complaints under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court considered the legal issue to be already covered by well-established case-law.

**Metalla and Others v. Albania** (ECtHR, 16 July 2015) concerned four applications brought by nine Albanian nationals between June and October 2008. The applicants complained, in substance, about the Albanian authorities’ failure to enforce final decisions of local property restitution commissions. These decisions recognised their inherited property rights and either ordered physical restoration of part of the property or provided that, where land or buildings were occupied, the applicants would be compensated “in one of the ways provided for by law.” The decisions remained unenforced. The Court noted that the underlying legal issue was already covered by well-established case-law, particularly **Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania**.

The key facts of each application were similar.

In application no. 30264/08 (**Metalla**), on 9 August 1995 the Shijak Commission recognised the applicants’ inherited title to 1,020 sq. m of land. Of this, 747 sq. m were restored to them, while the remaining 272 sq. m were occupied, so compensation was to be awarded under the statutory scheme. The decision was never enforced.

In application no. 42120/08 (**Bushati**), on 8 February 1995 the Shkodër Commission recognised the applicant’s and other heirs’ inherited title to a two-storey building and a surrounding plot of 500 sq. m. The building was to be restored, but because the 500 sq. m plot was occupied, compensation was due in one of the ways provided by law. The applicant stated that he had brought legal actions in 1995 and 1997 against a third party seeking vacation and restoration of the property, but discontinued them because of pending judicial proceedings in other cities. It appears that the third party later built unauthorised constructions on the plot. The Commission decision nonetheless remained unenforced.

In application no. 54403/08 (**Metalla and Others**), on 12 May 1994 the Shijak Commission recognised the applicants’ inherited title to 5,527 sq. m. It restored 5,000 sq. m, while the remaining 527 sq. m were occupied and subject to compensation. That decision also remained unenforced.

In application no. 54411/08 (**Metalla and Others**), on 13 August 2007 the Durrës Commission recognised the applicants’ inherited title to 65,000 sq. m. Of this, 60,000 sq. m were restored, but the remaining 5,000 sq. m—described as arable land, roads and channels—were occupied, so compensation was to be provided. This decision likewise remained unenforced.

The common factual core was therefore that final administrative decisions recognised the applicants’ property rights and entitlement to restitution or compensation, but the Albanian State failed to execute them for years. That non-enforcement formed the basis of the alleged violations, principally of the right to a fair trial under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and the right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The case formed part of a wider structural problem in Albania concerning the failure to enforce final property compensation decisions. The Court referred to domestic law and practice examined in **Manushaqe Puto** and **Ramadhi**, and to later government measures such as property valuation maps approved in 2013 and 2014. Council of Europe Committee of Ministers decisions in 2014 and 2015 monitored Albania’s efforts to establish an effective compensation mechanism, including an action plan and draft legislation. These materials highlighted that the applicants’ individual decisions were not isolated failures but part of a systemic delay in providing compensation for occupied property.

Case Metalla and Others v Albania (Applications nos. 30264/08, 42120/08, 54403/08 and 54411/08) is a 2015 European Court of Human Rights judgment concerning Albania’s failure to enforce final property decisions. Nine Albanian applicants filed four applications between June and October 2008. They alleged that final administrative decisions recognizing their inherited property rights and providing for restitution or compensation remained unenforced. The Court noted the issue was already covered by well-established case-law, especially Manushaqe Puto and Others v Albania.

In application no. 30264/08 (Metalla), the Shijak Commission on 9 August 1995 recognized the applicants’ inherited title to 1,020 sq m of land. It restored 747 sq m but found the remaining 272 sq m occupied; the applicants were to receive compensation in one of the forms provided by law. The decision remained unenforced.

In application no. 42120/08 (Bushati), on 8 February 1995 the Shkodër Commission recognized the applicant and other heirs’ inherited title to a two-storey building and 500 sq m of surrounding land. The building was to be restored to them. Because the 500 sq m plot was occupied, they were to be compensated under law. The applicant said he brought actions in 1995 and 1997 against a third party for vacation and restoration, but discontinued them due to other pending proceedings. A third party apparently built unauthorised structures on the plot. This decision also remained unenforced.

In application no. 54403/08 (Metalla and Others), on 12 May 1994 the Shijak Commission recognized the applicants’ inherited title to 5,527 sq m. It restored 5,000 sq m; the remaining 527 sq m was occupied, so compensation was due. The decision remained unenforced.

In application no. 54411/08 (Metalla and Others), on 13 August 2007 the Durrës Commission recognized the applicants’ inherited title to 65,000 sq m. It restored 60,000 sq m. The remaining 5,000 sq m—consisting of arable land, roads and channels—was occupied, so compensation was to be provided. That decision also remained unenforced.

The domestic law and practice were described in Manushaqe Puto and Ramadhi. The Albanian Government later approved property valuation maps in 2013 and 2014. Council of Europe materials showed that the Committee of Ministers repeatedly examined Albania’s failure to enforce final domestic judicial and administrative decisions awarding compensation in lieu of physical restoration. The Committee welcomed an action plan and later a draft law to create an effective compensation mechanism, but noted delays and a structural problem.

The key alleged violation was therefore the Albanian authorities’ continued non-enforcement of final decisions that had recognized the applicants’ property rights and ordered restitution or compensation. These facts formed the basis for complaints under the Convention, particularly the right to a fair trial (Article 6) and protection of property (Article 1 of Protocol No. 1), as the applicants had obtained final favourable decisions but received neither full restitution nor the alternative compensation. The Court disposed of the case under established case-law.
001-157538:
**Korošec v. Slovenia** (Application no. 77212/12) concerned a Slovenian national, Mr Tadej Korošec, born in 1980, who suffers from progressive spinal muscular atrophy and requires twenty-four-hour assistance with daily activities. In 2006 the Pensions and Disability Insurance Institute of Slovenia (“the Institute”) awarded him an assistance and attendance allowance set at 70% of the reference amount.

In May 2009 the applicant’s general practitioner applied for an increase in the allowance because his condition, especially his respiratory function, had worsened. The doctor stated that he needed twenty-four-hour assistance from a family member or lay care assistant, as well as permanent professional assistance. At the time, the applicant organised care by hiring students and relying heavily on family members.

The Institute’s first-instance disability commission examined the applicant and his medical documentation. It concluded that he did not need permanent professional medical assistance. On 20 July 2009 the Institute dismissed his request for an increased allowance. The applicant appealed. In September 2009 the second-instance disability commission likewise concluded that he did not need permanent professional assistance and could be cared for by care assistants without specific medical knowledge, together with family members. The Institute dismissed the appeal on 24 September 2009, relying on a 1998 ministerial decision under which a higher allowance was payable only where the beneficiary needed twenty-four-hour family assistance and further professional medical assistance.

The applicant then brought court proceedings before the Ljubljana Labour and Social Court, requesting that an independent medical expert be appointed. In September 2010 the court dismissed his claim and refused the request for an independent expert. It held that the opinions of the first- and second-instance disability commissions, together with other evidence, sufficiently established that the applicant did not need professional assistance. The applicant appealed, arguing that the court lacked medical expertise and should have appointed an independent expert. In January 2011 the Higher Labour and Social Court dismissed the appeal, finding that the commissions were composed of experts capable of assessing the applicant’s needs.

The applicant sought leave to appeal on points of law, relying on Supreme Court case-law, notably decision no. VIII Ips 3/2006, which held that the opinions of the Institute’s disability commissions could not be regarded as independent expert opinions in judicial proceedings brought against the Institute itself and should not be used as evidence in such proceedings. The Supreme Court dismissed his application in May 2011, finding no departure from established case-law. In June 2012 the Constitutional Court dismissed his constitutional complaint under section 55.b of the Constitutional Court Act.

The applicant alleged before the European Court of Human Rights that the proceedings had been unfair under Article 6 of the Convention. The key issue was that the domestic courts refused to appoint an independent medical expert and instead relied decisively on the opinions of disability commissions established by the Institute, which was the opposing party in the social-security dispute. Under domestic law, section 243 of the Civil Procedure Act required expert evidence where the court lacked the necessary expertise. The Supreme Court’s own case-law recognised the commissions’ lack of independence in proceedings against the Institute. The ECtHR ultimately found a violation of Article 6 § 1, holding that the reliance on the Institute’s commissions without a genuinely independent expert deprived the applicant of a fair hearing.

Korošec v. Slovenia concerned a disabled Slovenian man’s complaint under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights that social-security proceedings determining his assistance allowance were unfair. The applicant, born in 1980, suffered from progressive spinal muscular atrophy and required twenty-four-hour assistance. In 2006 the Pensions and Disability Insurance Institute of Slovenia awarded him an assistance and attendance allowance at 70% of the reference amount. In May 2009 his general practitioner applied for an increase because his condition had worsened, especially his respiratory function, and stated that he needed round-the-clock assistance from family members or lay care assistants, plus permanent professional assistance. The applicant arranged care through students and relied significantly on family help.

The Institute’s first-instance disability commission, composed of an internal medicine specialist and an occupational medicine specialist, examined the file and the applicant. It concluded that he did not need permanent professional medical assistance. Relying on that opinion, the Institute dismissed his request in July 2009. On appeal, the second-instance disability commission, composed of an occupational medicine specialist and a neuropsychiatrist, reviewed the file and likewise concluded that he did not require permanent professional assistance. It considered that a combination of lay care assistants and family members could care for him. The Institute dismissed the appeal, relying on the 1998 ministerial decision under which a higher allowance required twenty-four-hour family assistance and further professional medical assistance from at least one care assistant.

The applicant challenged that decision before the Ljubljana Labour and Social Court and requested an independent medical expert. In September 2010 the court heard him and dismissed his claim. It refused to appoint an independent expert, holding that the opinions of the Institute’s first- and second-instance disability commissions, along with other evidence, sufficiently established that he did not need professional assistance. The court explicitly stated that it fully accepted the commissions’ opinions. The applicant appealed, arguing that the court lacked medical expertise and could not properly assess his care needs without an independent expert. In January 2011 the Higher Labour and Social Court dismissed the appeal, finding that the first-instance court could rely on the commissions because they were made up of experts capable of assessing the need for professional assistance.

The applicant then sought leave to appeal to the Supreme Court. He argued that the lower courts’ approach contradicted established Supreme Court case-law, particularly decision no. VIII Ips 3/2006, which held that opinions of the Institute’s disability commissions could only be considered expert opinions in the Institute’s own pre-judicial proceedings. Because the Institute was the opposing party in judicial proceedings, such opinions could not serve as independent expert evidence; relying on them while refusing an independent expert violated procedural rights. In May 2011 the Supreme Court dismissed his application, finding no departure from its case-law. In June 2012 the Constitutional Court dismissed his constitutional complaint under section 55b of the Constitutional Court Act.

The alleged violation was therefore under Article 6 § 1: the applicant complained that the proceedings were unfair because the courts refused his request for an independent medical expert and instead based decisive findings on the opinions of disability commissions that formed part of, and were appointed within, the Institute—the defendant in the case. The key factual issue was whether reliance on those commission opinions, rather than a truly independent expert, undermined equality of arms and the fairness of the proceedings. The European Court of Human Rights ultimately found a violation of Article 6 § 1.

**Case Korošec v. Slovenia** (Application no. 77212/12, ECtHR, 8 October 2015) concerned a Slovenian man with progressive spinal muscular atrophy who required twenty-four-hour assistance. In 2006 the Pensions and Disability Insurance Institute awarded him an assistance and attendance allowance at 70% of the reference amount. In May 2009, after his condition worsened—particularly his respiratory function—his general practitioner applied for an increase, stating that he needed round-the-clock help from family members or lay assistants plus permanent professional assistance. The Institute’s first-instance disability commission examined him and the medical records but concluded that he did not need permanent professional medical assistance. The Institute rejected the request. On appeal, the second-instance commission also found that he could be cared for by lay assistants and family members. The Institute dismissed the appeal, relying on the 1998 rule requiring both twenty-four-hour family assistance and further professional assistance for the higher allowance.

The applicant challenged that decision before the Ljubljana Labour and Social Court and requested an independent medical expert. The court heard him and reviewed the file but dismissed his claim without appointing an expert. It accepted the first- and second-instance commissions’ opinions as sufficient to show that he did not need professional care. The applicant appealed, arguing that the court lacked medical expertise and should have appointed an independent expert. The Higher Labour and Social Court dismissed the appeal, finding that the commissions were composed of qualified experts capable of assessing his needs. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal, holding that the lower courts had not departed from established case-law. The Constitutional Court dismissed his constitutional complaint under section 55b of the Constitutional Court Act.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged under Article 6 § 1 that the proceedings had been unfair. The central issue was the domestic courts’ refusal to appoint an independent medical expert and their reliance on the opinions of the Institute’s disability commissions. Those commissions were not independent: they assisted the Institute, which was the defendant in the court proceedings, and their members were appointed by the Institute’s board. Under the Civil Procedure Act, a court must obtain an expert opinion if it lacks the expertise to establish a fact. Moreover, in a 2006 decision, the Supreme Court itself had held that the Institute’s disability commission opinions could not be treated as expert opinions in judicial proceedings against the Institute, because they were opinions of representatives of one of the parties. Despite this, the courts in Korošec’s case treated those opinions as decisive evidence on the key medical question—whether he required permanent professional assistance—and rejected his request for an independent expert.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 6 § 1. Because the medical assessment was decisive and the defendant’s own commissions supplied the expert evidence, the proceedings lacked the independence and equality of arms required for a fair trial. The domestic courts should have appointed an independent expert or otherwise ensured a neutral medical assessment. The Court awarded the applicant just satisfaction for non-pecuniary damage and costs. The case illustrates that reliance on an opposing party’s internal expert bodies, without independent expert review, can violate fair-trial guarantees when the dispute turns on specialized medical facts.

In *Myumyun v. Bulgaria* (Application no. 67258/13), the applicant, Mr Nuray Bayramali Myumyun, complained that Bulgaria failed to provide an adequate procedural response under Article 3 of the Convention to his ill-treatment by police officers intended to obtain a confession from him.

No formal criminal investigation had yet been opened. At the station, according to findings later made by the Bulgarian criminal courts, the applicant was taken to a room with three officers. After one officer left, I.K. struck the applicant’s left shoulder with a wooden bat, and after further blows the applicant fell to the ground. N.K. then kicked him and repeatedly hit him with a rubber truncheon. Another officer, T.A., entered with an electroshock prod and administered an electric shock to the applicant’s left leg. The beating continued intermittently, with further electric shocks, hitting and kicking. When the applicant’s head was low, he was kicked on the nose and began bleeding, after which the beating stopped.

The applicant sustained a haematoma on his nose and haematomas and bruises on his upper left back, left side of the torso and left shoulder. The next day, a forensic doctor confirmed numerous haematomas and bruises on his face and upper body, likely caused by hard blunt objects and cylindrical objects. At about 4 p.m., N.K. prepared a written statement on the applicant’s behalf saying he knew nothing about the burglary and presented it for signature. The applicant was released around 5 p.m.

After the applicant complained, criminal proceedings were opened against the three officers. On 1 February 2013, they were charged with causing minor bodily harm while carrying out their duties under Article 131 § 1 (2) read with Article 130 § 2 of the Criminal Code. Because that offence carried a penalty of up to one year’s imprisonment, the prosecutor informed the applicant that the officers’ criminal liability would be waived and replaced with administrative penalties under Article 78a of the Code.

The applicant asked the authorities to consider charges under Article 282 § 1 (abuse of office) and Article 287 (coercing a confession or statements). The prosecutor’s office replied that it had no competence concerning Article 282 and apparently did not reply concerning Article 287. When the applicant later asked the trial court to refer the case back for consideration of Article 287, the court refused. It said the applicant was not a party to the proceedings and that Article 287 did not apply because the ill-treatment had occurred before criminal proceedings were instituted, when the applicant was not yet an accused, witness or expert as required by that provision.

T.A. received no disciplinary penalty. In *Kristiansen v. Norway*, the applicant, Jørgen Kristiansen, was convicted in Norwegian criminal proceedings of attempted rape and other offences. The alleged attempted rape occurred in March 2008, when he and a 17-year-old woman, Ms A, left a party to buy mineral water in a borrowed car. After the car battery failed, a taxi-driving friend collected them. The applicant claimed that their sexual contact had been voluntary, but the City Court and later the High Court rejected that account. On 5 February 2009, the Borgarting High Court, sitting with a jury, convicted him and sentenced him to one year’s imprisonment and compensation to Ms A.

The alleged violation concerned Article 6 § 1 of the Convention—the right to a fair hearing by an impartial tribunal—because of the participation of a juror, “J”. During a pause after Ms A and the applicant had testified, J informed the presiding judge that she was the foster mother of a child who had been in the same school class as Ms A. She had had contact with Ms A at birthday celebrations and class outings and remembered her from years earlier as a “quiet and calm person.” She said she had no further personal knowledge and that the last contact was long past.

Defence counsel requested that J be disqualified for lack of impartiality under section 108 of the Administration of Courts Act and Article 6 § 1. Ms A’s assistant advocate supported the motion, and the prosecutor expressed understanding for it without taking a formal stance. The High Court deliberated and decided that J should not withdraw. It found the contacts sporadic and dated, and concluded that J’s statement could not influence her assessment of Ms A’s credibility or the question of guilt. J therefore took part in the jury’s deliberations and vote on guilt, and later in the sentencing and compensation deliberations with professional judges.

The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court, which rejected his appeal by three votes to two on 26 June 2009. The majority held that prior knowledge of Ms A did not itself indicate bias and that the “quiet and calm” remark was a neutral observation, not a credibility judgment. The minority disagreed. It stressed that the victim’s credibility was decisive because only Ms A and the applicant were in the car. The statement was positively loaded and, coming after the oral evidence, could easily be understood as suggesting that Ms A was someone who would not make a false rape accusation. The minority also noted that both defence counsel and the victim’s advocate had sought J’s recusal.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the central issue was whether the High Court was impartial. The Court found the prior contacts alone insufficient to disqualify J. However, it treated J’s “quiet and calm” statement as a preconceived value judgment with possible positive connotations for Ms A. Its timing, after the oral evidence, and the fact that Ms A’s credibility was decisive meant it could have influenced J or other jurors to the applicant’s disadvantage. The recusal requests by opposing legal representatives reinforced the importance of appearances. Because the High Court neither discharged J nor redirected the jury to rely solely on evidence, the cumulative effect created justifiable grounds to doubt the High Court’s impartiality. The ECtHR therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1.

**Case: Kristiansen v. Norway (Application no. 1176/10), European Court of Human Rights, 17 December 2015.**

The applicant, Jørgen Kristiansen, was convicted in Norway of attempted rape and other offences. The charge arose from an incident during the night of 9 March 2008, when he and Ms A, then aged 23 and 17 respectively, left a party to buy mineral water. They sat in a car borrowed from Ms A’s boyfriend. When the car battery failed, the applicant called a taxi-driving friend, Mr B. The prosecution alleged that before Mr B arrived, the applicant attempted to rape Ms A. The Sarpsborg City Court convicted him, and the Borgarting High Court, sitting with a jury, upheld the conviction on appeal. He was sentenced to one year’s imprisonment and ordered to pay compensation to Ms A.

The alleged violation concerned Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, specifically the right to a fair hearing by an impartial tribunal. During the High Court trial, after both Ms A and the applicant had given evidence, a juror, “J,” informed the presiding judge of previous contacts with Ms A. J was the foster mother of a child who had been in the same school class as Ms A. Ms A had attended birthday celebrations at J’s home and class outings J had attended as a parent. J said she had formed a picture of Ms A from years earlier as a “quiet and calm person.” She had no further personal knowledge of Ms A.

Defence counsel moved for J’s disqualification for lack of impartiality. Ms A’s assistant advocate supported the motion, and the public prosecutor expressed understanding for it without taking a formal stance. The High Court refused to discharge J. It found the contacts sporadic and dated, and considered J’s statement neutral, not capable of affecting her assessment of guilt. J therefore participated in the jury’s deliberations and vote on the attempted rape charge, and later in sentencing and compensation deliberations.

The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that J’s participation breached domestic impartiality rules and Article 6 § 1. By a 3–2 majority, the Supreme Court rejected the appeal. The majority held that prior acquaintance and J’s “quiet and calm” impression did not objectively undermine impartiality. The minority disagreed, stressing that the victim’s credibility was decisive, that J’s positively loaded statement came after hearing evidence, and that the timing risked appearing to endorse Ms A’s credibility. The minority also noted that both defence counsel and the victim’s advocate had sought J’s recusal.

Before the European Court, the applicant argued that J’s prior contacts and statement created an objectively justified fear of bias. The Government contended that the contacts were ordinary and distant, and the statement was neutral. The Court applied the objective impartiality test: whether there were ascertainable facts raising a legitimate doubt, and whether any such fear was objectively justified.

The Court found no problem with the mere prior contacts. However, it focused on J’s value judgment that Ms A was “quiet and calm,” made after both sides had given evidence. Even if vague, it could carry positive connotations for Ms A and affect J’s or other jurors’ assessment. This was especially important because the case turned on whether the High Court believed Ms A’s or the applicant’s version. The Court also noted that defence counsel, the victim’s advocate, and even the prosecutor expressed concerns. Despite this, the High Court neither discharged J nor redirected the jury.

Considering the cumulative effect—the content and timing of J’s statement, the failure to discharge her or give corrective instructions, and the objections from all legal representatives—the Court concluded that there were justifiable grounds to doubt the High Court’s impartiality. It accordingly found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

Kristiansen v. Norway (Application no. 1176/10) concerned a Norwegian national convicted of attempted rape and other offences. The applicant alleged that the criminal proceedings before the Borgarting High Court were unfair under Article 6 § 1 because a juror lacked impartiality.

The charge arose from the night of 9 March 2008. The applicant, then 23, and Ms A, then 17, left a party to buy mineral water in a car borrowed from Ms A’s boyfriend. When the car battery failed, the applicant called Mr B, a taxi-driving friend, to collect them. The prosecution alleged that while waiting, the applicant attempted to rape Ms A. The applicant claimed they had kissed and touched voluntarily. The Sarpsborg City Court convicted him, rejecting his account. On appeal, the High Court, sitting with a jury, convicted him of attempted rape, sentenced him to one year’s imprisonment, and ordered him to pay NOK 60,000 in compensation to Ms A. It found that the applicant forcibly tried to obtain sexual contact, held Ms A’s arms, and continued despite her resistance until Mr B’s car lights appeared. Ms A later cried at the party, though Mr B noticed nothing conspicuous when he arrived.

The alleged violation centred on juror J. During a pause after Ms A and the applicant had testified, J told the presiding judge that she had prior contacts with Ms A. J was the foster mother of a child who had been in the same school class as Ms A; Ms A had attended birthday celebrations at J’s home and class outings J had attended as a parent. J recalled Ms A from several years earlier and said she had formed a picture of her as a “quiet and calm person.” Defence counsel requested J’s disqualification under section 108 of the Administration of Courts Act and Article 6 § 1. Ms A’s assistant advocate supported the motion, and the prosecutor expressed understanding without taking a stance.

The High Court refused to discharge J, finding the contacts sporadic and many years old and not indicative of prejudice. J then sat on the jury, voted on the attempted rape questions, and participated in sentencing and compensation deliberations. The applicant appealed. The Supreme Court, by three votes to two, rejected the appeal. The majority treated the prior contacts and J’s “quiet and calm” recollection as neutral, not an assessment of credibility. The minority found the timing significant: J’s statement came after the victim and accused testified, credibility was decisive, and the phrase was positively loaded. Since all legal representatives had raised concern, the fear of partiality was objectively justified.

The European Court of Human Rights declared the application admissible. Applying the subjective and objective impartiality tests, it accepted that prior contacts alone did not disqualify J. However, the “quiet and calm” statement was more problematic. It was a value judgment reflecting a preconceived view and could have positive connotations regarding Ms A, especially because it was made after both sides gave evidence and because guilt turned on whose version was credible. The objections from defence counsel, the victim’s advocate, and the prosecutor reinforced the importance of appearances. The High Court neither discharged J nor redirected the jury. Cumulatively—the content of the statement, its timing, and the failure to discharge or redirect—there were justifiable grounds to doubt the High Court’s impartiality. General safeguards did not cure the defect. The Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1.

**Case: Prilutskiy v. Ukraine (Application no. 40429/08)**

The case concerned the death of the applicant’s son during an organised driving game in Donetsk and the subsequent investigation. The applicant, a Ukrainian national, complained under Article 2 of the Convention that the State had failed to take preventive measures to protect his son’s life and that the criminal proceedings concerning the death had been ineffective.

On the night of 30 September 2006, the applicant’s son, born in 1984, took part in “AutoQuest”, a location-based driving game. Teams travelled by car to different locations in the city, solved riddles to find the next destination, and competed to finish first. The son was a passenger in a car driven by P. During the game, P. lost control of the vehicle and collided with a pillar. P. was injured, while three passengers, including the applicant’s son, died.

On 1 October 2006, the Donetsk police opened a criminal investigation under Article 286 § 3 of the Criminal Code for a fatal traffic accident. The applicant was admitted as a victim on 3 October 2006. The investigation examined the activities of the game’s organisers, but on 23 February 2007 the police refused to institute criminal proceedings against them. Psychiatric examinations in 2007 and 2011 found that P. had been aware of and able to control his actions at the time of the accident, but had later developed a chronic mental disability, including organic brain impairment and amnestic syndrome. He therefore required compulsory psychiatric treatment.

In June 2011, the first-instance court found that P. had committed the crime by exceeding speed limits and losing control, causing the deaths. Because of his later mental disability, the court ordered compulsory outpatient psychiatric assistance rather than punishment. The applicant appealed, arguing that the medical findings were wrong and that procedural rules had been breached. In January 2012, the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal quashed the decision and remitted the case for additional investigation, noting witness statements suggesting P. might have swerved to avoid a pedestrian. After further investigation, the case was again sent to the first-instance court in October 2012, but proceedings were still pending as of March 2013.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged that the State had failed in its positive obligation to protect life. He argued that the authorities knew driving games were systemic in Donetsk and should have licensed or supervised them. The Government contended that P. alone caused the death by violating traffic rules and that Ukraine had adequate legislative and administrative road-safety measures.

The Court examined the preventive aspect under Article 2. It reiterated that States must put in place an effective legal and administrative framework for dangerous activities, including licensing, operation and supervision, but that this obligation must not impose disproportionate burdens or unduly interfere with personal autonomy. The applicant’s son was an adult who voluntarily participated in a private initiative. Participants remained bound by traffic regulations, backed by criminal sanctions. The applicant did not show that specific operational measures were required, that authorities knew the exact time and place of the game, or that the activity was so widespread or inherently different from ordinary road-traffic danger as to require special regulation. The Court therefore found no failure of the State’s positive obligation to prevent the death. The investigation’s effectiveness also formed part of the applicant’s Article 2 complaint.

In *Prilutskiy v. Ukraine* (Application no. 40429/08, judgment of 26 February 2015), the applicant, Mr Igor Prylutskyy, complained under Article 2 of the European Convention that Ukraine had failed to protect his son’s life and that the investigation into his son’s death had been ineffective. The case arose from a fatal car accident on the night of 30 September 2006 in Donetsk. The applicant’s adult son, born in 1984, took part in “AutoQuest,” a private location-based driving game. Teams travelled by car to different locations, solved riddles to identify the next destination, and competed to finish first. The son was a passenger in a car driven by P. During the game, P. lost control and collided with a pillar. P. was injured, while the applicant’s son and two other passengers died.

The authorities opened a criminal investigation under Article 286 § 3 of the Criminal Code for traffic-safety violations causing several deaths. The applicant was admitted as a victim. Investigators examined the organisers’ role but in February 2007 refused to institute criminal proceedings against them. Psychiatric examinations in 2007 and 2011 found that P. had been aware of and able to control his actions at the time of the accident, but later developed a chronic mental disability, including organic brain impairment and amnestic syndrome. He required compulsory psychiatric treatment. In June 2011 the first-instance court found that P. had committed the crime by speeding and losing control, but ordered compulsory outpatient psychiatric assistance because of his post-accident mental condition. The applicant appealed, disputing the medical findings and complaining of procedural breaches. In January 2012 the Court of Appeal quashed the decision and remitted the case for additional pre-trial investigation, noting witness evidence that P. might have swerved to avoid a pedestrian and that the facts had not been properly established. After further investigation, the case was again referred to the first-instance court in October 2012; as of March 2013, proceedings were still pending.

Before the European Court, the applicant argued that the State had failed to take preventive measures to protect his son during a known life-threatening activity and that the criminal proceedings were ineffective. He relied on Articles 2 and 13, but the Court examined the complaints solely under Article 2. On the substantive positive obligation, the Court reiterated that Article 2 may require a legislative and administrative framework to deter threats to life, especially in dangerous activities. However, AutoQuest was a private initiative without State involvement; the applicant’s son was an adult who voluntarily participated and remained bound by traffic regulations. The applicant did not show that the authorities knew of a real and immediate risk, that they knew the exact time and place of the game, that prior requests for specific measures had been made, or that the existing legal framework was insufficient. The Court therefore found no violation of the State’s positive obligation to protect life. The application was declared admissible. The Court also examined the procedural complaint concerning the effectiveness of the criminal proceedings and found a violation of Article 2 in that respect, owing to the lengthy and repeatedly remitted investigation and court proceedings, which failed to ensure a prompt and effective response to the son’s death.

**Case: Kiiveri v. Finland (Application no. 53753/12), ECtHR, 10 February 2015**

The applicant, Timo Veikko Kiiveri, a Finnish national, owned 90% of a limited liability construction and decoration company and served as its managing director and board member. In 2005, tax authorities inspected the company and concluded that it had failed to declare and pay substantial taxes, paid salaries off the books, and engaged in other fraudulent activity.

On 8 September 2008, the tax authorities imposed additional income tax and tax surcharges on both the company and the applicant personally for tax years 2002, 2003, 2005 and 2006. The applicant did not appeal those tax decisions. As a result, the tax matters became final when the appeal periods expired: for 2002 on 31 December 2008, for 2003 on 31 December 2009, for 2005 on 31 December 2011, and for 2006 on 31 December 2012. The bailiff seized the imposed sums.

In parallel, a criminal investigation began in June 2007. On 6 March 2009, the prosecutor charged the applicant with an accounting offence and two counts of aggravated tax fraud. The first count concerned the company’s tax years 2000–2006 and alleged fabricated receipts, failure to declare the company’s real income, off-the-books salaries, and underpaid company tax. The second count concerned the applicant’s personal tax years 2000–2003 and 2005–2006, alleging that he had failed to declare his own income, leading to too low personal tax. The tax authorities also presented a compensation claim.

On 9 September 2009, the District Court convicted the applicant of two counts of aggravated tax fraud and an accounting offence, sentencing him to three years’ imprisonment, ordering compensation of EUR 685,080.66 plus interest, and banning him from business activities for six years. The Court of Appeal mostly upheld the judgment, finding no ne bis in idem issue because, for some tax years, the appeal period had not expired when charges were brought. It noted that the 2002 tax matter had become final before charges, but considered that another tax appeal route existed. The Supreme Court, on 27 February 2012, dismissed the charge concerning tax year 2002 without examining the merits because tax surcharges had become final before charges were brought; it otherwise upheld the conviction and reduced the sentence to two years and ten months.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged a violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7, arguing that he had been punished twice: first through tax surcharges and later through criminal conviction based on the same facts.

The Court found both tax surcharge proceedings and criminal proceedings to be “criminal” in nature. It also found that, for the applicant’s personal tax years 2003, 2005 and 2006, the tax surcharge proceedings and aggravated tax fraud charges arose from the same facts—failure to declare personal income. However, for 2002, the Supreme Court had already remedied the issue by dismissing the charge. For 2006, the applicant could still have appealed the tax decision after the criminal case became final and thus could have prevented double jeopardy, but he failed to do so. For 2003 and 2005, the tax decisions became final while the criminal proceedings were still pending, and the criminal proceedings were not discontinued; they continued until final conviction in 2012. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 as regards tax years 2003 and 2005.
