The applicant did not appeal, and the amounts were seized.

Meanwhile, in June 2007, police began a criminal investigation. On 6 March 2009, the prosecutor charged the applicant with an accounting offence and two counts of aggravated tax fraud. One count concerned the company’s tax years 2000–2006 and the applicant’s role as managing director/board member; the other concerned his personal tax years 2000–2003 and 2005–2006. The tax authorities joined the charges and sought compensation.

On 9 September 2009, the District Court convicted the applicant on all charges, sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment, ordered compensation of about EUR 685,000, and imposed a six-year business ban. On appeal, the Court of Appeal largely upheld the conviction in September 2010. It found no ne bis in idem issue for tax years where the appeal period had not expired when charges were brought, and for 2002 it found the tax decision final but held that another tax appeal route existed. The Supreme Court, on 27 February 2012, dismissed the aggravated tax fraud charge concerning tax year 2002 without examining the merits because the tax surcharges had become final before the charges. It upheld the rest and reduced the sentence to two years and ten months.

The applicant complained under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention that he had been tried and punished twice: first by tax surcharges and later by criminal conviction for the same facts.

The European Court of Human Rights held that both the tax surcharge proceedings and the criminal proceedings were “criminal” for Convention purposes. It then examined whether the offences were the same. The accounting offence was not based on identical facts because bookkeeping duties are separate from tax assessment. Charges relating to the company were not identical to the applicant’s personal tax surcharges because different legal entities were involved. The personal tax fraud years 2000–2001 were not covered by tax surcharges. For tax year 2002, the Supreme Court’s dismissal remedied the double jeopardy issue. However, for personal tax years 2003, 2005, and 2006, the tax surcharge proceedings and criminal tax fraud proceedings arose from the same facts—failure to declare income.

On finality and duplication, the Court noted that tax decisions became final on 31 December 2009, 2011, and 2012, while the criminal case became final on 27 February 2012. For 2006, the applicant could still have sought rectification/appeal against the tax decision when the criminal case became final; failing to do so meant he had not exhausted effective remedies. But for 2003 and 2005, the tax proceedings became final while the criminal proceedings were still pending. The criminal proceedings were not discontinued after the tax decisions became final but continued to a final conviction. Under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7, parallel proceedings may be permissible, but if the first set becomes final and the second is not discontinued, a violation occurs.

The Court therefore found a violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 concerning tax years 2003 and 2005.

In *Kiiveri v. Finland*, the applicant, a Finnish national, owned 90% of shares and was managing director and board member of a construction and decoration company. A 2005 tax inspection found that the company had failed to declare and pay substantial taxes, paid salaries off the books, and engaged in other fraudulent activity. On 8 September 2008, tax authorities imposed additional income tax and tax surcharges on both the company and the applicant personally for tax years 2002, 2003, 2005 and 2006. The applicant did not appeal. The tax decisions became final on 31 December 2008 (2002), 31 December 2009 (2003), 31 December 2011 (2005), and 31 December 2012 (2006). Seized sums were collected by the bailiff.

Meanwhile, police began a criminal investigation in June 2007. On 6 March 2009, the prosecutor charged the applicant with an accounting offence and two counts of aggravated tax fraud. The first count concerned the company’s operations for tax years 2000–2006; the second concerned the applicant’s personal taxation for 2000–2003 and 2005–2006, alleging failure to declare income and fabricated receipts. The District Court convicted him on 9 September 2009 and sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment, ordered compensation of EUR 685,080.66 plus interest, and banned him from business activities for six years. The Court of Appeal largely upheld the judgment on 15 September 2010, rejecting the *ne bis in idem* argument for most years because appeal time-limits had not expired when charges were brought. The Supreme Court on 27 February 2012 dismissed the 2002 charge without examining the merits because the tax surcharges had become final before the charges, but upheld the rest and reduced the sentence to two years and ten months. An extraordinary appeal was refused in 2013.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged a violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7, arguing that he had been tried and punished twice: first by tax surcharges, then by criminal conviction based on the same facts. The Government contested this, arguing that the company charges involved a different legal entity, that the applicant was no longer a victim regarding 2002, and that Article 4 did not apply to parallel proceedings, although it conceded that proceedings should have been discontinued for 2003 and 2005 once the tax decisions became final.

The Court held that both tax surcharge proceedings and criminal proceedings were “criminal” in nature. It found that the accounting offence was separate, the company-related charges concerned a different legal entity, and the 2002 issue had been remedied by the Supreme Court. However, for the applicant’s personal tax years 2003, 2005 and 2006, the tax surcharge and tax fraud proceedings arose from the same facts. The Court noted that Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 prohibits consecutive proceedings if the first set has become final before the second is initiated; parallel proceedings are not prohibited as such, but a violation arises if the second set continues after the first becomes final. For 2006, the applicant could still have appealed the tax decision after the criminal case became final, so he failed to exhaust effective remedies. For 2003 and 2005, however, the tax decisions became final while the criminal proceedings were pending, and those criminal proceedings were not discontinued but continued until 2012. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 regarding tax years 2003 and 2005.

The applicant, Mehmet Ali Tatar, is a Turkish national born in 1950. He arrived in Switzerland in June 1988 and claimed he had been detained and tortured by Turkish authorities in 1987–88 because of his membership in a Turkish Communist Party. He and two politically active sons were recognized as refugees and granted asylum in 1994. His wife and other children later joined him. In 1990 he suffered a serious work injury and received an invalidity pension. His children and grandchildren are Swiss nationals, though he retained contacts in Turkey.

In 2001, the applicant killed his wife during a dispute, shooting her three times in the head and once in the stomach. In 2003 he was sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. Psychiatric evidence diagnosed a recurrent depressive disorder with psychotic symptoms, classified as schizophrenic disease syndrome, and he was found to have diminished responsibility. His imprisonment was postponed so he could receive treatment in a closed psychiatric facility. In 2009, the Federal Office for Migration revoked his asylum status because of the serious crime, but did not withdraw his refugee status under the 1951 Refugee Convention.

In April 2010, he was paroled on condition that he remain in psychiatric care for three years. He was later moved to an open residence with continuous psychiatric supervision, but suffered relapses requiring temporary stays in a closed psychiatric hospital. Expert reports indicated he could not live independently, required regular psychotropic medication and therapy, and would relapse into hallucinations and psychotic delusions, potentially harming himself or others, if treatment stopped. Expulsion was expected to worsen his condition, especially to Turkey, where he said he felt persecuted. He was also appointed a legal guardian.

In June 2010, the Zurich Migration Office revoked his residence permit and ordered him to leave Switzerland within three months. His appeals failed. Before the Federal Supreme Court, he argued that he had not been adequately heard, that non-refoulement still applied, that removal would endanger his life because of his deteriorating mental health, that he faced a blood feud with his wife’s relatives, and that he risked torture or inhuman treatment in Turkey. He mentioned Article 8 in a heading but did not substantively claim a violation of private or family life.

On 2 August 2012, the Federal Supreme Court dismissed his appeal. It held that he could be returned to Turkey despite his refugee recognition because he had committed a serious crime. It found it unproven that expulsion would make his mental health life-threatening, noting psychiatric facilities existed in Turkey. As to the blood-feud risk, it found he had not substantiated that Turkish authorities could not protect him and that he could relocate; his wife’s relatives had visited Switzerland and merely avoided him. As to torture for past TCP membership, his political activities were over 20 years old, Turkey’s human rights situation had changed, and family members had visited Turkey without difficulties.

The expulsion order remained in force, though no removal date was set. The applicant alleged violations of Articles 2, 3, 6 and 8 of the Convention, claiming his proposed expulsion exposed him to inhuman and degrading treatment, threatened his physical and moral integrity, and that the Federal Supreme Court proceedings were unfair. Nalbandyan v. Armenia (Apps. 9935/06 and 23339/06, judgment 31 March 2015) concerned three Armenian applicants—Bagrat, Narine, and Arevik Nalbandyan—who alleged ill-treatment in police custody in June–July 2004, ineffective investigation, lack of effective legal assistance, and first applicant’s unlawful denial of access to the Court of Cassation.

The case began after the body of a local girl, the daughter’s classmate, was found near the applicants’ home on 8 June 2004. The first applicant alleged he was taken to Vardenis Police Department and held without formal arrest, then repeatedly beaten to force a murder confession. On 24 June, a court sentenced him to 15 days’ administrative imprisonment for disobeying police; he claimed this was a fabricated charge used to legitimize his unlawful detention. The second and third applicants alleged they were frequently taken to the police and pressured to confess or incriminate one another. On 30 June, the second applicant and other residents complained to the General Prosecutor and Police Chief that the first applicant had been unlawfully detained since 8 June and that the family was being terrorized.

The most serious allegations occurred on 8–10 July. The second applicant alleged that when she refused to testify against her husband, she was beaten by Chief Vi.H., deputy N.H., officers K.N. and K.M., and Deputy Regional Prosecutor F.B. She was struck on the feet with a baton, lost consciousness, and was revived so the beating could continue. The third applicant was allegedly brought to the police station, locked in a dark, rat-infested room, and threatened with rape unless her mother confessed. The second applicant then confessed; the first also confessed to assisting. On 9 July the first and second applicants were formally arrested. They refused the investigator’s lawyer because they did not trust him and did not request another. The third applicant was allegedly held overnight in a dark cell. On 10 July the second applicant took part in a filmed crime-scene reconstruction, appearing to walk freely. The third applicant was questioned as a witness and allegedly said her mother’s confession was false and possibly drug-induced; later that day she alleged she was beaten by F.B. and others. A 16 July medical examination found concussion and bruising; the second applicant’s 14 July admission examination recorded bruised, swollen feet, while the first showed no injuries.

001-153960:
**Case: A.T. v. Luxembourg (Application no. 30460/13), ECtHR, 9 April 2015**

The applicant, A.T., a British national born in 1973, was charged in Luxembourg with rape and indecent assault of a girl under sixteen, with the aggravating circumstance that he held a position of authority over her. On 9 October 2009 the Public Prosecutor ordered an investigation. On 4 December 2009 the applicant was arrested in the United Kingdom under a European Arrest Warrant and was surrendered to Luxembourg on 17 December 2009.

The alleged violations concerned his questioning by police and by the investigating judge. On 17 December 2009, after being served with the European Arrest Warrant at Luxembourg airport, he was questioned at a police station at 3:20 p.m. in the presence of an interpreter. The police report stated that he initially refused to make any statement, invoked British legislation, and claimed his right to legal assistance. After receiving explanations about Luxembourg procedure, he agreed to take part in the questioning without a lawyer. He was informed of the victim’s statements and the suspicions against him, denied all charges, and at the end requested legal assistance for the next day’s interrogation before the investigating judge.

On the morning of 18 December 2009, the investigating judge questioned him in the presence of an interpreter. He was informed of his right to choose a defence lawyer or have one officially appointed. He availed himself of that right and was assigned Mr W. He was questioned in the presence of his lawyer and repeated his police statements. He was later released on 10 March 2010, but convicted on 31 March 2011 and sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment with a three-year partial probation period. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 7 February 2012, and the Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal on 22 November 2012.

The applicant complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) that he had not had a lawyer during police questioning and had not received effective legal assistance before the investigating judge. The Court examined only those complaints.

As to the police questioning, the Government argued that the applicant had waived his right to a lawyer: he had known the charges since his UK arrest, had received explanations, had agreed voluntarily, and had signed the translated record. The applicant argued that his alleged waiver was not voluntary or fully informed and that Luxembourg law at the material time systematically excluded legal assistance for persons in his situation. The Court found a violation. At the relevant time, Luxembourg law provided for legal assistance during certain police interrogations—such as in flagrante cases or where a person was remanded for other facts—but not for police questioning in a preliminary investigation following a European Arrest Warrant. The applicant was therefore automatically deprived of counsel. The waiver issue was moot. Moreover, his police statements were later used by the domestic courts to assess his credibility and inconsistency, and the Court of Appeal expressly referred to them. The domestic courts failed to exclude those statements or otherwise redress the lack of legal assistance. This violated Article 6 § 3(c) in conjunction with Article 6 § 1.

As to the investigating judge’s interrogation, the applicant argued that his lawyer was ineffective because he was appointed only that morning, could not consult the case file before the first interrogation, and allegedly could not communicate with him. The Court found no violation on the case-file issue: postponing access until after the first interrogation could be justified to protect investigative interests, and Article 6 does not guarantee unlimited pre-interrogation access. The lawyer’s assistance was not rendered ineffective merely by the lack of prior file access. The key violation was thus the automatic denial of counsel during the initial police interrogation and the failure of the domestic courts to remedy the consequences.

**A.T. v. Luxembourg (Application no. 30460/13)** concerned a British national convicted in Luxembourg of rape and indecent assault of a girl under sixteen, with the aggravating circumstance that he held a position of authority over her. He complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) of the Convention that he had lacked legal assistance during police questioning and had not received effective assistance before the investigating judge. The Strasbourg Court found a violation only in respect of the police questioning and the domestic courts’ failure to redress it.

The facts relevant to the alleged violations began in October 2009, when the public prosecutor ordered an investigation against the applicant. On 4 December 2009 he was arrested in the United Kingdom under a European Arrest Warrant and was surrendered to Luxembourg on 17 December 2009. On arrival, he was formally served with the warrant at 2:45 p.m. and questioned at a police station from 3:20 p.m. in the presence of an interpreter. The police report recorded that he initially refused to make any statement, invoked British legislation and claimed his right to legal assistance. After receiving explanations about procedure, he agreed to take part in the questioning. He was informed of the victim’s statements and the suspicions against him, denied all charges, and requested legal assistance for the next day’s interrogation before the investigating judge.

At the material time, Luxembourg law provided for legal assistance during certain police interrogations, but not for a person in the applicant’s situation—namely, someone questioned in a preliminary investigation following a European Arrest Warrant. Later circulars and a 2011 police memorandum extended the right to counsel, but they came after his interrogation. The Court therefore found that he had been automatically deprived of a lawyer during the police hearing, making any issue of waiver irrelevant.

On 18 December 2009 the investigating judge questioned him in the presence of an interpreter. He was informed of his right to choose or be appointed a lawyer, and Mr W. was officially appointed. The applicant then made detailed statements in the lawyer’s presence and confirmed what he had told the police. He nevertheless alleged that this assistance was ineffective because domestic law prevented communication with his lawyer before or during the first interrogation and barred access to the case file until after that interrogation. The Government disputed this, saying communication was possible and the lawyer could interrupt and ask questions; only full file access was postponed.

Domestically, the District Court convicted him on 31 March 2011 and sentenced him to seven years’ imprisonment. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 7 February 2012, noting that he had agreed to speak without a lawyer during the police interview. It also referred to inconsistencies in his statements, including differences between his police statements and later depositions. The Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal on 22 November 2012, holding that the Court of Appeal had found no violation because he had agreed to give evidence without counsel.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 6 § 3(c) in conjunction with Article 6 § 1 regarding the lack of a lawyer during the police hearing. It held that the applicant’s police statements had not been wholly irrelevant, because the domestic courts later used them to assess his credibility and consistency. The domestic courts had failed to exclude or otherwise redress the consequences of that procedural defect. However, the Court found no violation regarding the first interrogation by the investigating judge, since restrictions on case-file access before that stage were justified and the lawyer’s assistance was not rendered ineffective on that basis.

A.T. v. Luxembourg (Application no. 30460/13, ECtHR, 9 April 2015) concerned the fairness of criminal proceedings against a British national under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) of the Convention, particularly his right to legal assistance.

In October 2009, the Luxembourg Public Prosecutor ordered an investigation against the applicant for rape and indecent assault of a girl under sixteen, with the aggravating circumstance that he held a position of authority over her. On 4 December 2009, he was arrested in the United Kingdom under a European Arrest Warrant and surrendered to Luxembourg on 17 December 2009. At 2:45 p.m. he was served with the warrant at Luxembourg airport, and at 3:20 p.m. he was questioned at a police station in the presence of an interpreter. The police report stated that he initially refused to make any statement and, citing British legislation, claimed his right to legal assistance. After receiving explanations about Luxembourg procedure “in cases such as his,” he agreed to take part in questioning without a lawyer. He was informed of the victim’s statements and the suspicions against him, denied all charges, and at the end requested legal assistance for the next day’s interrogation before the investigating judge.

On the morning of 18 December 2009, the investigating judge questioned him with an interpreter. The judge informed him of his right to choose a defence lawyer or have one officially appointed. He requested a lawyer, and Mr W. was appointed. He was questioned in the presence of that lawyer and the interpreter, made detailed statements, and confirmed his earlier police statements. He was remanded in custody, released in March 2010, later convicted and sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment, and his appeals were dismissed.

Before the Court, the applicant complained that he had lacked a lawyer during police questioning on 17 December 2009 and that his lawyer’s assistance before the investigating judge on 18 December 2009 had been ineffective because the lawyer could not access the case file or communicate with him beforehand. He also complained that the domestic courts failed to redress these alleged breaches. The Government acknowledged the absence of counsel at the police stage but argued that the applicant had voluntarily waived the right after explanations and that his statements had not influenced the conviction, since he consistently denied guilt. It also contended that the lawyer was present during the judicial interrogation and that later circulars had clarified access to counsel.

The Court found a violation of Article 6 § 3(c) read with Article 6 § 1 concerning the police questioning. At the material time, Luxembourg law granted the right to counsel only in certain police interrogations—such as flagrante detention or remand for other facts—but not for police questioning in a preliminary investigation following a European arrest warrant. The applicant was therefore automatically deprived of counsel under a systemic rule, making the issue of waiver moot. Although he made no incriminating confession, his police statements were later used to assess his credibility and consistency; the Court of Appeal referred to them when noting he had changed his version of events. The domestic courts merely found he had agreed to proceed without a lawyer and failed to exclude or redress the breach. By contrast, the Court found no violation regarding the first interrogation by the investigating judge: the lack of pre-interrogation access to the case file was justified, and the lawyer’s assistance was not shown to be ineffective.

Case Berland v France (no. 42875/10) concerned Daniel Berland, a French national born in 1987, who alleged a violation of Article 7 §1 of the Convention (no punishment without law). The central complaint was that, after offences he committed in 2007, French courts applied the Law of 25 February 2008 on preventive detention and declarations of criminal insanity, resulting in compulsory psychiatric hospitalisation and long-term prohibitions that he argued amounted to retrospective penalties.

On 12 September 2007, aged 20, Berland went to the workplace of C.G., his former girlfriend, who had ended the relationship after threats and violence. He stabbed her several times, causing death, and wounded two other people. On 14 September 2007 he was charged with premeditated murder and intentional wounding, remanded in custody, and the same day the Prefect ordered his compulsory admission to the Sevrey specialised hospital centre. In **Elberte v. Latvia** (Application no. 61243/08, judgment of 13 January 2015), the applicant, Dzintra Elberte, was the widow of Egils Elberts. She complained under Articles 3 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that tissue had been removed from her deceased husband’s body without her consent or knowledge, and that he had been buried with his legs tied together.

On 19 May 2001, Mr Elberts died in a car accident. His body was taken to Sigulda Hospital mortuary and then to the State Centre for Forensic Medical Examination in Riga for autopsy. During the autopsy on 20 May 2001, a forensic expert, N.S., removed a 10 cm by 10 cm piece of dura mater from the body. According to the Government, N.S. checked Mr Elberts’ passport and found no stamp indicating an objection to tissue removal. The applicant disputed this, saying the passport was at home in Sigulda and could not have been checked; she also believed more tissue was removed than claimed.

The body was returned for the funeral on 26 May 2001. The applicant first saw her husband’s remains then and noticed that his legs had been tied together. He was buried that way. She was pregnant at the time.

The applicant did not learn that tissue had been removed until about two years later, when the security police informed her that a criminal inquiry had been opened into illegal removal of organs and tissue for a German pharmaceutical company between 1994 and 2003. The inquiry revealed that the Forensic Centre had an agreement with the company: tissue was removed from deceased persons, sent to Germany, processed into bio-implants, and returned to Latvia for transplantation. Experts could initiate removals themselves, were paid for the work, and were supposed to check passports for objection stamps. They did not contact relatives or obtain their consent, although they said relatives’ objections would have been respected if known. The legal dispute centered on whether Latvia operated under “presumed consent” or “informed consent.” Investigators concluded the Law on the protection of the body of a deceased person and use of human organs and tissue required that removal not occur against the deceased’s known wishes and, absent express wishes, only if no closest relative objected. Section 4 gave relatives a right to object, but did not clearly impose a duty on experts to inform them of that right.

Criminal proceedings were repeatedly discontinued and reopened. Superior prosecutors found in 2006 and 2007 that the experts had breached the Law and that tissue removal had been unlawful. A 14 April 2008 decision found N.S. and others had contravened section 4 and breached relatives’ rights, but discontinued the case because the five-year limitation period had expired. In June 2008, a domestic court upheld the experts’ appeal, quashed that decision, and found no legal obligation to inform relatives of their right to refuse, no proof of unlawful purpose, and no criminal offence. A final discontinuation followed on 27 June 2008. The applicant’s complaints were rejected.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore: the removal of tissue from Mr Elberts without the widow’s knowledge or consent; the disputed passport check; the failure of experts to contact relatives or establish their wishes; the tied legs and manner of burial; the unclear domestic legal framework on consent; and the lengthy, ultimately unsuccessful criminal investigation that left no one accountable due to limitation and exoneration.

**Summary of Elberte v. Latvia (Application no. 61243/08)**

The case of Elberte v. Latvia concerns the removal of tissue from the applicant’s deceased husband without her knowledge or consent, and the subsequent failure of Latvian authorities to provide an effective remedy.

The applicant, Dzintra Elberte, is the widow of Egils Elberts, who died on 19 May 2001 from injuries sustained in a car accident. His body was transported to the State Centre for Forensic Medical Examination in Riga for an autopsy. During the autopsy, forensic expert N.S. removed a 10 cm by 10 cm piece of dura mater from the body. According to the Government, N.S. verified that the deceased’s passport contained no stamp indicating an objection to tissue removal. The applicant disputed this, stating the passport was at her home at the time. She also alleged that a larger area of tissue was removed and that it was not only dura mater.

The applicant first saw her husband’s body at the funeral on 26 May 2001 and noticed that his legs had been tied together. He was buried in that condition. She remained unaware that tissue had been removed until approximately two years later, when the security police informed her that a criminal inquiry had been opened into the illegal removal of organs and tissue.

The criminal inquiry, opened on 3 March 2003, investigated the removal of organs and tissue for supply to a German pharmaceutical company between 1994 and 2003. The Forensic Centre had an agreement with the company to remove tissue from deceased persons selected according to international standards, sending it to Germany for processing into bio-implants, which were then returned to Latvia for transplantation. Experts were permitted to remove tissue on their own initiative, checking only whether passports contained stamps denoting objection. They did not contact relatives or obtain their consent. Although relatives’ objections were respected if raised, experts did not inform relatives of the removal or their right to object.

The inquiry was repeatedly discontinued and reopened. On 14 April 2008, it was discontinued due to the expiry of the five-year limitation period, with findings that experts had contravened section 4 of the Law and breached relatives’ rights. However, on 26 June 2008, the Riga City Vidzeme District Court upheld an appeal by the experts, finding that the experts had no legal obligation to inform relatives of their right to refuse tissue removal and therefore did not breach the Law. No elements of a crime were established. On 27 June 2008, a new decision discontinued the inquiry based on the court’s findings.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) regarding the removal of tissue without her consent or knowledge, and Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) concerning the distress caused and the manner in which her husband’s body was treated. The European Court of Human Rights found that the removal of tissue without the applicant’s knowledge or consent, combined with the lack of any effective mechanism for her to object or be informed, violated her rights under Article 8. The Court also found a violation of Article 3 regarding the suffering caused by the authorities’ handling of the matter and the lack of effective investigation.

The case of *Satakunnan Markkinapörssi Oy and Satamedia Oy v. Finland* (Application no. 931/13) concerns two Finnish limited liability companies that challenged Finland’s interference with their publication of personal tax data. The first applicant, Satakunnan Markkinapörssi Oy, had published the *Veropörssi* magazine since 1994, which annually disclosed the taxable income and assets of natural persons—information that is public under Finnish law. In 2002, the magazine published data on 1.2 million individuals, roughly one-third of all taxable persons in Finland, organized by geographical area. The second applicant, Satamedia Oy, operated a text-message service from 2003 that allowed users to query taxation information about named individuals, using a database compiled from the magazine’s published data. Both companies were owned by the same persons.

In response, the Data Protection Ombudsman contacted the companies and advised them to cease publishing taxation data in the manner and to the extent carried out in 2002. When the companies refused, the Ombudsman requested the Data Protection Board to forbid the processing of taxation data as done in 2002 and its transfer to the SMS service. The Ombudsman argued that the companies had no right under the Personal Data Act to establish such personal data registers and that the journalism derogation did not apply.

The Data Protection Board initially dismissed the request in January 2004, finding that the journalism exemption applied and that the SMS service fell outside the Act because the data had already been published. The Ombudsman appealed to the Helsinki Administrative Court, which rejected the appeal in September 2005, holding that the magazine had a journalistic purpose and that publishing the data served the public interest.

The Ombudsman further appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court, which in February 2007 requested a preliminary ruling from the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) on the interpretation of Directive 95/46/EC. In December 2008, the CJEU ruled that the activities constituted “processing of personal data” under the Directive. While journalism should be interpreted broadly, derogations from data protection must apply only insofar as strictly necessary to reconcile privacy with freedom of expression. Activities involving data from public documents could be classified as journalistic if their object was to disclose information, opinions, or ideas to the public, regardless of the medium or profit motive.

In September 2009, the Supreme Administrative Court quashed the earlier decisions and referred the case back to the Data Protection Board. It found that publishing the entire database collected for journalistic purposes could not be regarded as journalistic activity. The public interest did not require such extensive publication of personal data, and the derogation in the Personal Data Act had to be interpreted strictly. The SMS service was likewise not protected. Consequently, the Board in November 2009 forbade both companies from processing taxation data in the manner and extent of 2002 and from forwarding such information to the SMS service.

The SMS service was shut down after the Supreme Administrative Court’s decision was served. The magazine continued publishing taxation data in autumn 2009 with only one-fifth of its previous content, then ceased publication entirely. The companies’ subsequent appeals to the Turku Administrative Court and the Supreme Administrative Court were rejected in October 2010 and June 2012, respectively. The domestic courts held that the case concerned only the Data Protection Board’s decision and that the matter had already been determined by the Supreme Administrative Court; they found no violation of the prohibition of censorship or freedom of expression.

The applicant companies alleged before the European Court of Human Rights that their right to freedom of expression under Article 10 had been violated, that the proceedings were excessively long, and that they had been discriminated against vis-à-vis other newspapers.

The first applicant, Satakunnan Markkinapörssi Oy, had published *Veropörssi* magazine since 1994, annually printing information on natural persons’ taxable income and assets. He argued that the Personal Data Act did not permit their personal data registers and that the journalism derogation did not apply; he characterized the activity as non-journalistic processing of personal data. In 2004, the Board refused the request, finding the journalism derogation applicable. As the SMS data had already been published in the magazine, the Act did not apply to it.

The Ombudsman appealed. In 2005, the Helsinki Administrative Court rejected the appeal, holding that the journalism derogation derived from EU Directive 95/46/EC should not be interpreted too strictly, that the magazine had a journalistic purpose, that publication was in the public interest, and that the data was public. The Ombudsman appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court, which in 2007 requested a preliminary ruling from the Court of Justice of the European Union.

In December 2008, the CJEU held that the activities constituted “processing of personal data” under the Directive, including files containing solely unaltered material already published by the media. “Journalism” should be interpreted broadly and could cover profit-making activities aimed at disclosing information, opinions or ideas. However, derogations from data protection had to be limited to what was strictly necessary to reconcile privacy and freedom of expression. In September 2009, the Supreme Administrative Court quashed the earlier decisions and referred the case back, ordering the Board to prohibit processing tax data as in 2002. It found that publishing the entire collected database could not be regarded as journalistic activity and that the public interest did not require publication to that extent. The same applied to the SMS service.

In November 2009, the Data Protection Board prohibited the first company from processing tax data as in 2002 and forwarding it to SMS; the second was prohibited from collecting, saving or forwarding such data from the first company’s registers. The companies’ appeals failed before the Turku Administrative Court in 2010 and the Supreme Administrative Court in 2012, which held the matter was not about the right to publish tax information as such or preventive censorship.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant companies alleged violations of freedom of expression, excessive length of proceedings, and discrimination compared with other newspapers. The key facts concern the domestic prohibition on processing and disseminating public taxation data through the magazine and SMS service, which the companies claimed amounted to an unjustified interference with, and indirect censorship of, their expression.

Case: **Gasimli and Others v. Azerbaijan** (Applications nos. 25330/11, 25340/11, 25345/11, 25361/11 and 25645/11), European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, judgment of 17 December 2015. Five Azerbaijani nationals stood as candidates in the parliamentary elections of 7 November 2010. Four were nominated by the Popular Front–Müsavat coalition; Natig Jafarov was self-nominated. Under the Electoral Code, each candidate needed at least 450 voter signatures. They submitted signature sheets containing more than 450 signatures to their respective Constituency Electoral Commissions (ConECs).

Before deciding on registration, ConEC working groups examined the signature sheets. The applicants were not invited to these examinations. The ConECs refused registration after finding that some signatures were invalid and that the remaining valid signatures numbered fewer than 450. Invalidity grounds included falsified or repeat signatures, incorrect voter information, expired identity cards, voters registered outside the constituency, uncertified corrections, signatures allegedly obtained by deceptive means, and unspecified “other grounds.”

The applicants were also not invited to the ConEC meetings where refusals were decided. Despite legal requirements, working-group documents—expert opinions, minutes, records and results tables—and the ConEC decisions were made available only after the refusal decisions, sometimes never or only during later judicial appeal proceedings. The applicants complained to the Central Electoral Commission (CEC). They alleged that the invalidation findings were factually wrong, unsubstantiated and arbitrary; that there were no handwriting experts among working-group members; that the ConECs failed to contact voters to verify disputed signatures; and that procedural safeguards were breached. In particular, they said they were not informed of examinations under Article 59.3 of the Electoral Code, were not given minutes twenty-four hours before meetings under Article 59.13, were not allowed to correct rectifiable errors, and were not invited to meetings. They also argued that some invalidation grounds were not provided by law, including expired identity documents and vague “other grounds,” and that local officials and police had pressured voters or collectors to withdraw signatures. Some applicants submitted voters’ statements confirming their signatures, but the CEC ignored them.

The CEC re-examined the sheets through its own working group without inviting the applicants. It found different numbers of invalid signatures and often different grounds from those given by the ConECs, including signatures that “appeared” falsified. The CEC rejected the complaints without inviting applicants to its meetings, and again disclosed relevant documents late or not at all. The Baku Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeals, and the Supreme Court dismissed their cassation appeals as unsubstantiated.

The applicants alleged violations of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention—the right to stand as a candidate in free elections—as well as Article 13 and, for some, Article 14, alleging discrimination against opposition candidates. The Government argued that the 450-signature requirement had a legitimate aim and that legal safeguards existed. The Court joined the applications and refused the Government’s request to strike them out based on unilateral declarations. Following its earlier judgment in **Tahirov v. Azerbaijan**, the Court found serious concerns about the impartiality and transparency of the electoral commissions, unclear expert qualifications, failure to investigate signature authenticity, systematic disregard of statutory safeguards, ignoring relevant evidence, and inadequate judicial review. It concluded that each applicant’s right to stand as a candidate under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 had been breached because they lacked sufficient safeguards against arbitrary refusal of registration. No separate examination under Article 13 was necessary.

The case concerned their right to stand as candidates in the parliamentary elections of 7 November 2010.

The applicants were nominated either by a coalition of the Popular Front and Müsavat parties or, in Mr. Jafarov’s case, were self-nominated. To register as candidates, the Electoral Code required each to submit signatures from at least 450 voters in their constituency. All applicants submitted sheets containing more than the minimum required signatures to their respective Constituency Electoral Commissions (ConECs).

Before a registration decision could be made, the signature sheets had to be verified by special working groups established by the ConECs. A key procedural flaw alleged by the applicants was that none were invited to participate in this examination of their signatures. Subsequently, each ConEC refused the applicants' registration requests. The working groups had declared a large number of signatures invalid on various grounds, leaving fewer than the required 450 valid signatures. These grounds included falsified or repeat signatures, incorrect voter information, signatures from voters registered outside the constituency, uncertified corrections, and unspecified "other grounds."

Crucially, the applicants were not invited to the ConEC meetings where the decisions to refuse their registration were taken. Furthermore, all relevant documents, including working group expert opinions and minutes, were only made available to them *after* the refusal decisions had been made. In some instances, these documents were never provided or were only disclosed much later during judicial proceedings.

The applicants contended that the ConEC decisions violated procedural requirements of the Electoral Code, including the failure to notify them of examinations, to ensure their presence, and to provide required documents in advance. Some also reported that local officials and police had pressured voters to "withdraw" their signatures.

The CEC rejected the applicants' complaints without inviting them to meetings and again only provided documents after the fact.

The Court of Appeal dismissed their appeals, finding no grounds to quash the CEC decisions. Subsequent cassation appeals to the Supreme Court were also dismissed as unsubstantiated. The applicants alleged violations of their right to stand for election under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, citing arbitrary refusal of registration and procedural unfairness.

Azerbaijan* (ECtHR, Fifth Section, 17 December 2015), five Azerbaijani nationals challenged the refusal to register them as candidates in the 7 November 2010 parliamentary elections. They submitted signature sheets containing more than 450 signatures to their respective Constituency Electoral Commissions (“ConECs”).

Before registration, ConEC working groups examined the signature sheets. The applicants were not invited to participate in that examination. The ConECs refused registration after finding some signatures invalid and concluding that fewer than 450 valid signatures remained. Invalidity grounds included falsified or repeated signatures, incorrect voter information, expired identity cards, voters registered outside the constituency, uncertified corrections, signatures allegedly obtained by deceptive means, and unspecified “other grounds.” The applicants were also not invited to the ConEC meetings where refusal decisions were taken. Working-group documents, expert opinions, minutes and the decisions themselves were generally disclosed only after the refusal; in some cases they were never provided or were disclosed only during later court proceedings.

The applicants complained to the Central Electoral Commission (“CEC”). They argued that the invalidation findings were factually wrong, unsubstantiated and arbitrary; that no handwriting experts were involved; that voters were not contacted to verify disputed signatures; that many errors were rectifiable but they were not notified or given a chance to correct them within 24 hours; and that the procedure breached the Electoral Code because they received no advance notice of the signature examination, could not attend, and did not receive the minutes at least 24 hours before the ConEC meeting. They also alleged that some invalidation grounds were not provided by law, and that local officials or police pressured voters or signature collectors to withdraw signatures.

The CEC re-examined the sheets without inviting the applicants. Its working group found different numbers of invalid signatures and, in many cases, different invalidity grounds from those given by the ConECs. Some signatures were rejected because they “appeared” to have been falsified. The CEC rejected the complaints without inviting the applicants, again disclosing relevant documents late or not at all. The Baku Court of Appeal dismissed their appeals, and the Supreme Court dismissed cassation appeals without detailed examination. The applicants relied on Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, claiming a violation of their right to stand as candidates in free elections, and also raised Article 13 and Article 14 complaints.

The European Court of Human Rights joined the five applications. It refused the Government’s request to strike them out on the basis of unilateral declarations. On the merits, the Court accepted that the 450-signature requirement pursued the legitimate aim of reducing fringe candidates, but examined whether the procedures contained sufficient safeguards against arbitrary decisions. It found the issues essentially identical to *Tahirov v. Azerbaijan*. The Court identified serious concerns about the impartiality and transparency of the electoral commissions, unclear qualifications and appointment criteria for working-group experts, failure to take further investigative steps to verify expert opinions, systematic failure to comply with statutory safeguards, failure to consider evidence submitted by candidates, and the domestic courts’ failure to deal properly with appeals.

Consequently, the Court found that each applicant’s right to stand as a candidate had been arbitrarily breached, in violation of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1. It found no separate issue under Article 13 and, in light of that finding, did not examine the Article 14 complaint separately.

Romania** (Application no. 34456/07, judgment of 23 June 2015) concerned a Romanian applicant charged in 1996 with bribery, influence peddling, complicity in fraud, intellectual forgery, and use of forged documents. In 2000, the first-instance court acquitted him, but the Court of Appeal reversed the acquittal, convicted him, and sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment. In 2002, the Court of Cassation quashed those judgments and referred the case back to the prosecutor’s office because the investigation had been defective, superficial, largely conducted by police rather than the prosecutor, and had failed to clarify key evidence and damage. After reopening, the National Anticorruption Prosecutor’s Office discontinued the bribery and influence-peddling charges for lack of an unlawful act. The Sibiu Prosecutor’s Office then discontinued the remaining charges on the ground that, although the applicant’s criminal liability was undeniable, prosecution was time-barred.

The applicant challenged that decision and asked for the investigation to continue so that he could establish his innocence. The investigation was reopened, then again discontinued as time-barred, with the prosecutor relying on existing evidence and stating that the applicant was guilty. A court initially quashed that order because the same prosecutor had previously confirmed the indictment and because the ordered reinvestigation had not been properly carried out. In the third round, in 2005, the Sibiu Prosecutor’s Office again discontinued the case as time-barred, but expressly found the applicant guilty of complicity in fraud and forgery of privately signed documents. The applicant appealed, asking the court to quash the order, retain the case, and acquit him. The final appeal was dismissed in 2007.

Mr Andrej Furman, a Slovenian national born in 1955, lived with M.P. from 1991 to 1997. Their daughter, P., was born on 14 December 1993. After the couple separated in 1997, the applicant agreed with the Maribor Social Work Centre to pay child maintenance. On 23 February 1998, a further agreement established a provisional contact schedule from 24 February to 13 April 1998. When no permanent agreement could be reached with M.P., the applicant asked the Centre on 24 February 1998 to issue a contact order. He sought regular contact: every Tuesday afternoon, every second Thursday afternoon, every other weekend, one week during the winter holiday and one month during the summer holiday. However, from 13 April 1998, M.P. stopped allowing contact between the applicant and P.

The first hearing was set for 18 June 1998 but was adjourned at M.P.’s request because she was on holiday. On 14 June 1998, M.P. informed the Centre that she would live abroad from 1 July 1998 to 31 August 1999 for doctoral studies and asked for the proceedings to be suspended. The applicant objected. The Centre made three visits to M.P.’s Maribor address but could not find her. On 30 July 1998, it asked her employer, Maribor University, for her foreign address. Meanwhile, on 26 August 1998, the applicant sought an interim contact order.

On 4 September 1998, Maribor University replied that M.P. was studying in Graz, Austria, but that her address was unknown; it offered to serve her with a summons. A hearing scheduled for 22 October 1998 was adjourned because the university could not reach her. On 29 October 1998, the Centre issued an interim order granting the applicant contact once a month and for one week during both the winter and summer holidays. The applicant was to collect and return P. at M.P.’s permanent address in Maribor.

Another hearing on 10 December 1998 was adjourned because M.P. could not be served. On 12 January 1999, Maribor University provided the address of the Austrian university where M.P. was studying. The Centre sent the interim order and a summons for a hearing on 11 February 1999 to that address. On 24 February 1999, M.P. appealed against the interim order, arguing that she and her daughter were temporarily living in Graz and that the schedule could not be implemented. On 1 March 1999, the Centre rejected her appeal as out of time. She then appealed to the Ministry of Labour, Family and Social Affairs.

On 28 April and 18 June 1999, the Centre submitted the applicant’s requests for enforcement of the interim order to the Maribor Administrative Unit. On 24 August 1999, the requests were granted. On 16 September 1999, M.P. appealed, claiming that the decision had not been correctly served on her and objecting to the order’s contents. On 27 September 1999, the Ministry upheld her appeal, quashed the interim order and remitted the provisional contact schedule for fresh examination by the Centre. The Ministry found that service of the interim order and the summons to the 11 February 1999 hearing had not complied with administrative procedure. It noted that if a party was absent or lived abroad, she had to be invited to appoint a representative authorised to receive official mail.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that he had been unable to enjoy family life with his daughter because the Slovenian and Austrian authorities had failed to act with due diligence in regulating and enforcing contact. The application, no. 16608/09, was lodged on 23 March 2009 and communicated to the Governments on 3 July 2012. The key alleged violation was under Article 8, arising from the prolonged inability to secure contact, procedural delays, difficulties serving M.P. in Austria, and the eventual quashing of the interim contact order.

In *Blesa Rodríguez v. Spain* (Application no. 61131/12), the applicant, a Spanish professor at La Laguna University’s Faculty of Pharmacy, complained under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights that he had not been tried by an impartial tribunal. The case originated in a criminal complaint filed by La Laguna University on 27 May 2003, accusing him of forgery. The university alleged that he had submitted a falsified curriculum vitae in a public tender for pharmaceutical establishment licences.

On 6 February 2004, investigating judge no. 1 suspended the criminal investigation, finding no objective reasons to believe a crime had been committed. The university appealed. On 19 May 2006, the Santa Cruz de Tenerife Audiencia Provincial allowed the appeal, quashed the suspension, and ordered further investigation. That chamber included Judge A. as president, along with Judges S. and C. On 19 January 2008, the investigating judge confirmed the end of the investigation and the continuation of abbreviated proceedings. The applicant appealed, but on 21 June 2008 an Audiencia Provincial chamber composed of Judges S. (president), Sa., and C. declared the appeal inadmissible.

On 8 June 2010, the Audiencia Provincial ordered that the case be sent for trial and indicated that the trial bench would be composed of Judges A. (president), S., and G. However, at the preliminary hearing on 1 July 2010, the bench was instead composed of Judges A. (president), G., and Sa. as substitute judge. The defence lawyer was informed at the beginning of the hearing that the composition had changed, although the applicant claimed he was not personally given the names of the new judges. The trial hearings on 15 and 20 July 2010 proceeded before the same bench.

On 27 July 2010, that bench convicted the applicant of forgery and sentenced him to three years and six months’ imprisonment, suspension from office for the same period, and a fine of EUR 25 per day for eight months.

The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court, alleging lack of impartiality by two judges. First, he claimed that Judge A. had previously sat on the appellate bench that had heard the appeal against the suspension of the criminal investigation. Second, he claimed that Judge Sa. had participated as a substitute judge while simultaneously being an associate professor and administrative employee at La Laguna University, the complainant. He argued that this university role was incompatible with Judge Sa.’s judicial role.

On 20 May 2011, the Supreme Court rejected these complaints. Regarding Judge A., it found that the applicant had failed to challenge him despite being informed of the bench composition on 8 June 2010. Under section 223(1) of the Organic Law on the Judiciary, a challenge must be made as soon as the ground is known. The Supreme Court also held that the 2006 decision merely found the investigation incomplete and did not undermine objective impartiality. Regarding Judge Sa., the Supreme Court acknowledged that the late notification of the new bench composition was unjustified, but found that the alleged circumstances did not fall within the statutory grounds for challenge or incompatibility. The applicant had not shown that Judge Sa. had an interest in the outcome or any link between his university role and the criminal proceedings. The Supreme Court did, however, reduce the sentence to one year and six months’ imprisonment and a fine for four months because the proceedings had lasted over seven years.

The applicant then filed an *amparo* appeal before the Constitutional Court, alleging breach of his right to an independent and impartial tribunal under Article 24 of the Spanish Constitution. On 7 March 2012, the Constitutional Court declared the appeal inadmissible for non-exhaustion, finding that he had failed to raise his impartiality complaints in the earlier judicial proceedings. The order was served on 13 March 2012. The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 7 September 2012, alleging a violation of Article 6 § 1.

**Tolmachev v. Estonia** (Application no. 73748/13) concerned an Estonian national, Mr Kirill Tolmachev, who was fined EUR 80 by a police officer on 17 September 2012 in misdemeanour proceedings for a breach of public order after allegedly breaking a glass panel of a bus shelter. The applicant contested the police decision before the Viru County Court. He denied committing the act, challenged the assessment of witness statements, complained that the police had failed to present him to a witness for identification, and argued that the police decision did not specify the local public-order provisions he had allegedly breached.

The County Court summoned the applicant to a hearing on 21 March 2013 at 12:30 p.m. The summons stated that his participation was mandatory and warned that, under Article 126 § 2 of the Code of Misdemeanour Procedure, if a complainant failed to appear despite being notified of the obligation to attend, and the hearing was not adjourned, the court would refuse to examine the complaint. **Case summary: Oliari and Others v. Italy (ECtHR, 21 July 2015)**

The case concerned six Italian nationals—three same-sex couples—who complained that Italian law did not allow them to marry or enter into any other type of civil union. They alleged violations of Articles 8, 12, and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights, arguing that the lack of any legal recognition for same-sex couples discriminated against them based on sexual orientation.

**Key facts.** Mr Oliari and Mr A. were in a committed relationship. In July 2008 they asked the Trent Civil Status Office to issue marriage banns. Their request was refused because the Civil Code required spouses to be of opposite sexes. They challenged the refusal, but the Trent Tribunal rejected their claim in February 2009. The Trent Court of Appeal referred the constitutional issue to the Italian Constitutional Court. In judgment no. 138/2010, the Constitutional Court declared the challenge inadmissible. It held that Article 2 of the Italian Constitution recognised homosexual unions as social groups and that same-sex couples had a fundamental right to legal recognition, but Parliament had discretion to decide the form of that recognition. Article 29’s reference to marriage was interpreted as traditional opposite-sex marriage, and the Court found no unreasonable discrimination. The Court of Appeal then rejected the applicants’ claims in September 2010.

Mr Felicetti and Mr Zappa had been together since 2003, cohabited from 2005, registered their cohabitation in 2008, and designated each other as guardians in 2009. In February 2011 they requested marriage banns; the request was refused in April 2011. They did not pursue the domestic remedy under Article 98 of the Civil Code because the Constitutional Court’s judgment made it futile.

Mr Perelli Cippo and Mr Zaccheo had been together since 2002, cohabited, opened a joint bank account in 2006, and registered their cohabitation in 2007. They requested marriage banns in November 2009; the request was refused. The Milan Tribunal rejected their challenge in June 2010, citing the Constitutional Court. They did not appeal further because it had no prospect of success.

**Domestic context.** Italian law prohibited same-sex marriage and provided no alternative civil union or registered partnership, whether for same-sex or different-sex couples. Only private “cohabitation agreements” and symbolic municipal registers existed. The Constitutional Court and Court of Cassation acknowledged that same-sex couples deserved protection and urged Parliament to legislate, but no general legal framework was enacted.

The Government argued that the applicants had failed to exhaust domestic remedies, lacked victim status, and had not complied with Rule 47. The Court rejected these objections. It found the applicants were directly affected by the absence of any legal framework, and that at the time of application, settled Constitutional Court case-law made domestic challenges futile. The Government failed to show any effective remedy could have provided recognition.

On the merits, the ECtHR held that Italy had violated Article 8 ECHR by failing to provide a legal framework allowing same-sex couples to have their relationship recognised, such as a civil union or registered partnership. It found no separate issue under Article 14 and reiterated that Article 12 does not oblige States to permit same-sex marriage. The key facts—stable same-sex relationships, repeated refused marriage banns, adverse domestic rulings, and the complete absence of alternative legal status—established that Italian law left same-sex couples in a legal vacuum, breaching their right to respect for private and family life.

In *Rohlena v. the Czech Republic* (Application no. 59552/08, Grand Chamber, 27 January 2015), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether the applicant’s conviction for a continuous domestic-abuse offence breached Article 7 of the Convention, which prohibits retroactive criminal law. The applicant, Petr Rohlena, a Czech national born in 1966, was indicted on 29 May 2006 for repeatedly abusing his wife physically and mentally while drunk, at least between 2000 and 8 February 2006. The alleged conduct included verbal abuse, hitting her head with his hand and fist, slapping her, grabbing her by the throat, attempting to strangle her, throwing her against furniture or onto the ground, pushing her down stairs, and kicking her. He was also accused of hitting the children, gambling household money on gaming machines, and smashing crockery. His wife suffered haematomas, bruising and a fractured nose, and sought medical help on 26 June 2000, 18 July 2003 and 8 February 2006 after assaults committed on 24 June 2000, 17 July 2003 and 8 February 2006.

The prosecutor classified the conduct as the continuous criminal offence of abusing a person living under the same roof under Article 215a §§ 1 and 2(b) of the Criminal Code. Because Article 215a was introduced only on 1 June 2004, the prosecution relied on the fact that the pre-2004 conduct had been punishable under the earlier offences of violence against an individual (Article 197a) and assault occasioning bodily harm (Article 221). On 18 April 2007 the Brno Municipal Court convicted the applicant of that offence, finding it committed at least between 2000 and 8 February 2006. It imposed a suspended sentence of two and a half years, five years’ probation, supervision, and alcohol-dependency treatment. The court treated the conduct as a continuous offence and applied Article 215a, reasoning that the offence was completed by the last act in 2006 and that the earlier acts had been criminal under the previous law.

The Brno Regional Court dismissed his appeal on 6 September 2007. On 21 February 2008 the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal on points of law, relying on settled case-law that a continuous offence is assessed under the law in force when the last occurrence completes it, provided the earlier acts were punishable when committed. The Constitutional Court dismissed his constitutional appeal on 10 June 2008, finding no prohibited retroactivity.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged a violation of Article 7. He argued that the domestic courts had retroactively applied Article 215a to acts committed before 1 June 2004. He claimed that the pre-2004 acts did not satisfy all the elements of the old criminal offences but were merely regulatory; that the assaults lacked the same intent and close temporal connection required for a continuous offence; that two individual assaults were already statute-barred; and that he faced a heavier penalty than under the old law. The Government maintained that the legal basis was clear and foreseeable: Article 89 § 3 and Article 215a existed before his conduct ended, the case-law was long-standing, and the earlier acts were criminal under prior law.

The Grand Chamber held that there had been no violation of Article 7. It found it reasonably foreseeable under Czech law that a continuous offence completed after 1 June 2004 would be governed by Article 215a, and that the pre-2004 conduct was punishable under the earlier criminal provisions. The conviction therefore did not amount to retroactive criminalisation.

**Lhermitte v. Belgium** (Application no. 34238/09) concerned an Article 6 § 1 complaint by Geneviève Lhermitte, a Belgian national, that her criminal trial was unfair because neither the jury’s guilty verdict nor the Assize Court’s sentencing judgment contained adequate reasons.

On 28 February 2007 the applicant called the emergency services stating that she had killed her five children and had tried to commit suicide. Police and medical services found the applicant injured and the bodies of her five children with their throats slit. She was committed for trial for having knowingly and intentionally killed her five children with premeditation.

The case was dominated by psychiatric evidence. Initially, three court-appointed psychiatrists concluded that the applicant had been in a severe state of anxiety and depression which impaired her judgment, but that she had not suffered from a mental disorder or severe mental disturbance making her incapable of controlling her actions. Two psychologists described inner fragility, maternal omnipotence and an over-investment in her children, suggesting that by killing them she was also killing herself as a mother.

During the trial before the Assize Court of Walloon Brabant in December 2008, the applicant’s psychiatrist produced two letters she had sent shortly before the killings. The court ordered a supplementary psychiatric report. On 14 December 2008 the three psychiatrists unanimously concluded that at the time of the events the applicant had suffered from a severe mental disturbance making her incapable of controlling her actions, and that she still required long-term treatment.

At the end of the trial, the jury was asked five questions: whether the applicant was guilty of intentionally killing the five children; whether the killings were premeditated; an alternative question on the same acts; an alternative premeditation question; and whether she suffered from a mental disorder or severe mental disturbance making her incapable of controlling her actions. The jury answered “yes” to the first two questions and “no” to the fifth. It therefore convicted her of premeditated murder and rejected the conclusion that she lacked criminal responsibility.

On 19 December 2008 the Assize Court sentenced her to life imprisonment. The judgment gave reasons for sentence, referring to the particularly heinous nature of the offences, the applicant’s “cold-blooded” conduct, her family responsibilities, isolation, dependence, mental fragility and depression, but held that these did not sufficiently explain the extreme violence or constitute mitigating factors. Ancillary penalties were imposed, including loss of civic rights and public display of the conviction.

The applicant appealed on points of law, repeating her complaint that the jury’s verdict and the sentencing judgment lacked reasons. On 6 May 2009 the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal. It noted that the jury’s “yes/no” verdict form was prescribed by Article 348 of the Code of Criminal Procedure; that Article 6 did not require trial only by professional judges; and that the Assize Court’s judgment had sufficiently explained why it rejected the social-protection defence based on mental disturbance. It also held that certain ancillary penalties were mandatory and required no reasons.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1. She argued that the jury’s verdict gave no explanation, that the questions were succinct and ambiguous, and that the jury had disregarded seven expert reports and unanimous psychiatric conclusions without explanation. She further complained that the sentencing reasons were contradictory and insufficient, particularly regarding mitigating circumstances. The Government argued that the indictment and trial record provided sufficient context, that the main issue was her capacity to control her actions, and that expert reports were opinions rather than binding truths. The Court declared the complaint admissible and examined the merits. The Chamber judgment was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 29 November 2016.

The Assize Court endorsed the guilty verdict and sentenced her to life imprisonment, citing the heinous nature of the offences and finding no mitigating circumstances. Ancillary penalties included deprivation of civic rights and public display of the judgment. The Court of Cassation dismissed her appeal on 6 May 2009.

**Alleged violation:** The applicant complained that the jury's verdict and the Assize Court's judgment lacked reasons, violating her right to a fair trial. She argued that the questions put to the jury were succinct and ambiguous; that the jury disregarded seven unanimous expert reports and statements under oath without explanation; that the lack of reasoning prevented her from scrutinising the lawfulness of the verdict; that the sentencing reasons were contradictory; that the court failed to adequately explain its finding of no mitigating circumstances; that it omitted her divorce; and that it gave undue consideration to her defence strategy.

The Government contended that the indictment detailed the investigations and expert conclusions, that the main issue was her capacity to control her actions, that expert reports were informed opinions rather than scientific truths, and that the Assize Court explained why it did not accept the mental disturbance defence, enabling the applicant to understand the verdict. They argued the procedure had sufficient safeguards against arbitrariness.

The Court found the complaint admissible and examined the merits.

In *Ljajić v. Serbia* (Application no. 58385/13), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint about Serbia’s failure to enforce a final domestic judgment. The original applicants were four Serbian nationals—Fuad Ljajić and his children Alma, Ertan, and Samra Ljajić—living in Novi Pazar. The case concerned their late wife and mother, Sadija Ljajić, who had been employed by “Raška” Holding kompanija AD Novi Pazar, a company predominantly composed of socially-owned capital at the relevant time.

On 14 December 2005, the Municipal Court in Novi Pazar ordered the debtor company to pay Sadija Ljajić salary arrears, social insurance contributions, and the costs of the civil proceedings. On 10 October 2006, at her request, the same court ordered enforcement of that judgment by bank transfer and awarded her enforcement costs. Despite the judgment being final and enforceable, the debtor did not pay.

Sadija Ljajić died on 24 April 2013. On 9 September 2013, the Novi Pazar First Instance Court declared Fuad Ljajić her sole inheritor. Alma, Ertan, and Samra Ljajić later informed the Court that they no longer intended to pursue the application. The Court struck out their part of the application under Article 37 § 1(a) of the Convention, leaving Fuad Ljajić as the remaining applicant.

In the meantime, on 25 October 2013, the Commercial Court in Kraljevo opened insolvency proceedings against the debtor. On 5 January 2014, Fuad Ljajić submitted a claim in those proceedings for payment of the amount ordered by the 2005 judgment. The insolvency proceedings remained pending. By the time the European Court considered the case, the final judgment had remained unenforced for more than nine years.

Before the Court, Fuad Ljajić complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Article 6 § 1 guarantees a fair hearing within a reasonable time in the determination of civil rights and obligations, while Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. His core complaint was that the final judgment in favour of his late wife had not been enforced, thereby depriving him of the benefit of that judgment and affecting his patrimonial rights as her heir.

The Serbian Government disputed the applicant’s locus standi. The Court rejected that objection. It found that Fuad Ljajić, as the sole inheritor, was a first-order and compulsory heir. The application concerned transferable rights, and he had a definite pecuniary interest in the enforcement proceedings. The alleged violations could also have a direct effect on his patrimonial rights. The application was therefore declared admissible.

On the merits, the Court noted that the domestic judgment had remained unenforced for over nine years. It had frequently found violations of Article 6 § 1 and/or Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 in similar cases involving non-enforcement of final judgments against socially-owned companies in Serbia. The Government had not submitted any fact or argument capable of leading to a different conclusion. The Court accordingly found a violation of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The case *Ljajić v. Serbia* (Application no. 58385/13) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) on 21 July 2015. It concerned four Serbian nationals—Mr Fuad Ljajić, Ms Alma Ljajić, Mr Ertan Ljajić and Ms Samra Ljajić—who lived in Novi Pazar. The application arose from the non-enforcement of a final domestic judgment obtained by their late wife and mother, Ms Sadija Ljajić.

Sadija Ljajić died on 24 April 2013. On 9 September 2013, the Novi Pazar First Instance Court declared Mr Fuad Ljajić the sole inheritor of her estate. The other three applicants then informed the Court that they no longer intended to pursue the application; the Court struck out their part of the case under Article 37 § 1 (a) of the Convention. The Court rejected that objection. It found that Mr Fuad Ljajić had standing because he had been declared his late wife’s sole inheritor; he belonged to the first order of heirs and was a compulsory heir; the rights at issue were transferable; he had a definite pecuniary interest in the proceedings; and the alleged violations could directly affect his patrimonial rights. The application was therefore admissible.

On the merits, the Court noted the prolonged non-enforcement of the final judgment—more than nine years—and observed that it had repeatedly found violations of Article 6 and/or Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 in similar Serbian cases involving socially-owned debtors, such as *R. Kačapor and Others v. Serbia* and *Crnišanin and Others v. Serbia*. The Government failed to present any fact or argument capable of leading to a different conclusion. Accordingly, the Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning Mr Fuad Ljajić.
