**Summary of Meimanis v. Latvia (Application no. 70597/11)**

The applicant, Mr. Mairis Meimanis, a Latvian national and former head of a division in the Economic Crime Bureau in Riga, was facing criminal proceedings for an attempt to take a bribe. The case before the European Court of Human Rights concerned the interception of his telephone conversations by the Bureau for the Prevention and Combating of Corruption (KNAB) and the subsequent legal remedies available to him.

In December 2005, the KNAB opened an operational investigation concerning the applicant's co-defendant, A.S. On 28 December, a Supreme Court judge authorised the interception of A.S.'s telephone conversations, and the prosecutor's office approved an undercover operation. The following day, the Head of the KNAB authorised the interception of another co-defendant's (A.B.) conversations, which also captured conversations with the applicant. The legal basis for this action was section 7(5) of the Law on Operational Activities, which permitted immediate operational measures without prior judicial approval in urgent cases, provided that a prosecutor was informed within 24 hours and a judge's approval was obtained within 72 hours.

The applicant first learned of the operational investigation during his criminal trial in 2009. He then requested the prosecution authorities to review the lawfulness of the surveillance. A specialised prosecutor confirmed that while his conversations were not independently intercepted, they were recorded as part of the interception of A.B.'s conversations. The prosecutor concluded that the measures were lawful and that the domestic law did not provide for independent judicial supervision of such activities; instead, this was the responsibility of the Prosecutor General and specially authorised prosecutors. The applicant's subsequent complaints to higher-ranking prosecutors were rejected.

Consequently, in June 2010, the applicant lodged an individual constitutional complaint, arguing that section 7(5) of the Law on Operational Activities, which allowed for warrantless interception, was incompatible with Articles 89 and 96 of the Latvian Constitution and Articles 8 and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights. He also contested the first sentence of section 35(1) of the same Law, which governed prosecutorial oversight of operational activities, as being incompatible with fair trial guarantees under Article 92 of the Constitution.

The Constitutional Court accepted the case for review but only in part. It examined the compatibility of section 7(5) with the Constitution and Article 13 of the Convention. Before the Constitutional Court, the applicant was not permitted to see the case materials until after the decision to adjudicate was taken. The court ultimately decided to proceed via a written procedure, without a public hearing, a decision the applicant objected to. On 11 May 2011, the Constitutional Court delivered its ruling, finding that the contested provisions complied with the Constitution and the Convention. It interpreted section 7(5) as requiring judicial approval for the interception measures, even for the initial 72-hour period, and deemed this sufficient to protect against arbitrary interference. It further held that prosecutorial supervision, combined with subsequent judicial scrutiny, constituted an effective remedy.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged violations of Article 8 (right to respect for private life) due to the interception of his calls, Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) regarding the lack of judicial oversight, and Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair hearing) concerning the non-public proceedings before the Constitutional Court. The key facts relevant to these alleged violations were the warrantless interception of his conversations under an exceptional legal provision, the limited scope of review by prosecutors, and the written nature of the constitutional proceedings.

The case *Meimanis v. Latvia* (Application no. 70597/11) concerned Mr Mairis Meimanis, a Latvian national who headed a division in the Economic Crime Bureau in Riga. He was prosecuted for attempted bribery together with A.B. and A.S. During the criminal proceedings, he learned that an operational investigation had been opened concerning his co-defendant A.S., and that his own telephone conversations had been intercepted when he spoke with another suspect whose line was being monitored.

The operational measures began in late December 2005. On 27 December 2005, the Bureau for the Prevention and Combating of Corruption (KNAB) opened an operational investigation based on information from a private person. On 28 December, a Supreme Court judge authorised interception of A.S.’s telephone conversations, and a prosecutor authorised an undercover operation. On 29 December, the Head of KNAB authorised interception of A.B.’s telephone conversations under section 7(5) of the Law on Operational Activities; this interception captured conversations between A.B. and the applicant. On 30 December, KNAB informed the prosecutor’s office. The Government did not produce evidence concerning these authorisations.

When the applicant requested information in 2009, a specialised prosecutor stated that no interception of the applicant’s own telephone conversations had been carried out in the operational investigation, but that his conversations were recorded when he spoke to A.B., whose conversations were lawfully intercepted. The prosecutor also explained that domestic law did not provide for independent judicial supervision of operational activities; supervision was instead carried out by the Prosecutor General and specially authorised prosecutors under section 35(1). The applicant’s complaints to higher prosecutors and ultimately to the Prosecutor General were rejected as unfounded.

The applicant then lodged an individual constitutional complaint. He alleged that section 7(5) of the Law on Operational Activities was incompatible with Articles 89 and 96 of the Latvian Constitution and Articles 8 and 13 of the Convention, and that section 35(1) was incompatible with fair-trial guarantees under Article 92 of the Constitution and Articles 6 § 1 and 13 of the Convention. The Constitutional Court accepted only parts of the complaint. The applicant also objected to the constitutional proceedings: he could not access the case materials until after the adjudication decision, and the court decided to proceed by written procedure rather than an oral hearing. He argued that this denied him a public hearing and the right to be heard. The Constitutional Court eventually ruled that the contested provisions complied with the Constitution and the Convention. It interpreted section 7(5) as requiring notification to a prosecutor within 24 hours and judicial approval within 72 hours, and found that prosecutor supervision plus subsequent judicial scrutiny provided adequate protection.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Article 8 (interception of his telephone conversations), Article 13 (lack of effective remedies), and Article 6 § 1 (lack of a public hearing and right to be heard in the Constitutional Court proceedings). The Court noted the special role of constitutional courts and the fact that the applicant had admitted that the written procedure itself did not violate his right to be heard; he had been able to access the case materials and submit comments after the adjudication decision. The key factual dispute therefore centred on whether the legal framework for urgent interception under section 7(5), and the prosecutor-based review mechanism under section 35(1), provided sufficient safeguards and effective remedies for the interference with his private life.

In *Meimanis v. Latvia* (ECtHR, Fourth Section, 21 July 2015), the applicant, Mairis Meimanis, was a Latvian national and then head of a division in the Riga Economic Crime Bureau. He was being tried for attempted bribery together with A.B. and A.S. In December 2005, the KNAB opened an operational investigation concerning A.S. A Supreme Court judge authorised interception of A.S.’s telephone conversations, and a prosecutor authorised an undercover operation. On 29 December 2005, the Head of the KNAB authorised interception of A.B.’s telephone conversations under section 7(5) of the Law on Operational Activities, without prior judicial approval because immediate action was allegedly required. This interception captured conversations between A.B. and the applicant. KNAB informed the prosecutor’s office the next day.

The applicant only learned during his criminal appeal in October 2009 that an operational investigation had existed and that his conversations had been recorded because he spoke with a person whose telephone was intercepted. He complained to prosecutors about the lawfulness of these measures. A specialised prosecutor replied that no interception of the applicant’s own telephone had been carried out under the operational investigation, but that his conversations were recorded when he spoke to A.B. The prosecutor also stated that domestic law did not provide for independent judicial supervision of operational activities; supervision was carried out by the Prosecutor General and specially authorised prosecutors under section 35(1). The prosecutor found no illegality. Further complaints were rejected, finally by the Prosecutor General on 29 December 2009.

The applicant then lodged an individual constitutional complaint. He alleged that section 7(5) was incompatible with Articles 89 and 96 of the Latvian Constitution and Articles 8 and 13 of the Convention, and that the first and second sentences of section 35(1) were incompatible with Article 89 and Article 92 of the Constitution and Articles 6 § 1 and 13 of the Convention. The Constitutional Court accepted only limited parts: section 7(5) against Article 96 of the Constitution and Article 13 of the Convention, and the first sentence of section 35(1) against Article 92. During those proceedings, the applicant was not allowed to inspect the case file until after the decision to adjudicate had been taken on 14 December 2010. He objected to the written procedure and requested an oral hearing. On 25 January 2011, in a closed preparatory meeting, the Constitutional Court decided to proceed in writing; the applicant was later given 15 days to inspect materials and comment, which he did. On 11 May 2011, the Constitutional Court upheld the contested provisions, interpreting section 7(5) as requiring prosecutor notification and judicial approval even if operational measures ended within 72 hours. It found that prosecutor monitoring plus subsequent judicial scrutiny provided sufficient safeguards and considered the prosecutor’s office an effective remedy.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged: (1) that interception of his telephone conversations violated Article 8; (2) that there were no effective domestic remedies for that breach, contrary to Article 13; and (3) that the Constitutional Court proceedings were not public and that he was denied the right to be heard, contrary to Article 6 § 1. The key facts relevant to these alleged violations are therefore the secret interception of his conversations under section 7(5), the absence of prior judicial authorisation in the actual operation, the limited prosecutorial supervision, the applicant’s late discovery of the measures, the rejection of his complaints, and the written, non-public nature of the constitutional review.

**Kagirov v. Russia** (Application no. 36367/09) concerned the alleged abduction of Rustam Kagirov by State agents in Chechnya in May 2009 and the authorities’ alleged failure to conduct an effective investigation. The applicant, Ziyavdi Kagirov, was Rustam’s brother.

Rustam Kagirov, born in 1979, suffered from a disability after removal of a lung. He held strong religious beliefs and had studied at an “Islamic Institute” in Grozny. The applicant believed the authorities may have viewed him as a follower of Wahhabism and therefore as connected to illegal armed groups. In autumn 2004, officers from a Chechen traffic-police unit allegedly detained and tortured Rustam for two days, demanding that he confess to involvement in illegal armed groups. They allegedly suspected him because of a photograph showing two men, one thought to be an illegal armed-group leader and the other resembling Rustam.

On 17 May 2009, President Ramzan Kadyrov was expected to travel on the Kavkaz motorway, and the route between Grozny and Zakan-Yurt was heavily guarded by traffic police. At about 6 p.m., Rustam and his friend Mr Kh.Kh. were walking near the Zakan-Yurt village administration. A black VAZ Priora with registration number A 720 AT 95 was parked nearby. Three armed men in black uniforms got out. Two grabbed Rustam and forced him into the back seat; the third pointed a gun at Mr Kh.Kh. and shouted in Chechen: “Turn around or I will shoot you!” The men drove off at high speed.

The applicant saw the abduction and, with Mr Kh.Kh., pursued the car. They saw the abductors pass unimpeded through a roadblock manned by traffic police. At the roadblock, the applicant asked the officers about the car and whether documents had been checked. The officers replied that they had not checked the documents because the men were in a hurry. Although the applicant immediately told them his brother had been abducted, the police took no steps to alert other officers or stop the car. Rustam has not been seen since.

The Government did not contest the basis of the applicant’s account of the abduction but described the perpetrators as unidentified armed men in a civilian vehicle during “peacetime,” with no curfew. It also pointed to inconsistencies in the applicant’s initial complaints—whether the abduction occurred from home, from the street, or after Rustam left and failed to return—and said the alleged enhanced security measures and roadblocks were not corroborated.

The applicant complained to the authorities on 18 May 2009. A criminal case for aggravated kidnapping was opened on 19 June 2009. Investigators examined the scene without collecting evidence, requested information about the vehicle and traffic police, compiled photo fits, and questioned numerous witnesses. Some witnesses confirmed that the abductors’ car had been allowed through the roadblock, with one saying the men claimed to be police officers. Investigators also checked whether Rustam had been detained by police or had joined illegal armed groups; those leads were not substantiated. The investigation was repeatedly suspended and resumed and remained pending.

The Government argued non-exhaustion because the investigation was ongoing and civil remedies existed. The Court joined that objection to the merits, finding that a civil claim alone could not be an effective remedy for the Article 2 complaints, and that the effectiveness of the criminal investigation had to be examined on the merits.

The key issues were whether the abduction was attributable to State agents and whether the domestic investigation was effective.

In *Kagirov v. Russia* (Application no. 36367/09), the European Court of Human Rights examined an application by Mr Ziyavdi Kagirov, a Russian national from Zakan-Yurt, Chechnya. He alleged that in May 2009 his brother, Mr Rustam Kagirov, had been abducted by State agents and that the Russian authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation. The application was declared admissible on 27 August 2013.

Rustam Kagirov, born in 1979, suffered from a disability caused by the removal of a lung. According to the applicant, Rustam held strong religious beliefs and had studied at an Islamic Institute in Grozny. In autumn 2004, officers from the Chechen traffic police allegedly detained and tortured him for two days after suspecting him of links to illegal armed groups based on a photograph. This background suggested the authorities may have viewed him as a follower of Wahhabism and a possible target.

On 17 May 2009, President Ramzan Kadyrov was expected to travel on the Kavkaz motorway, so the Grozny–Zakan-Yurt route was heavily guarded by traffic police checking identity documents. At about 6 p.m., Rustam and his friend Mr Kh.Kh. were walking near the village administration on Sovetskaya Street. A black VAZ Priora, registration number A 720 AT 95, was parked nearby. Three armed men in black uniforms got out. Two grabbed Rustam and forced him into the back seat, while the third pointed a gun at Kh.Kh. and ordered him to turn around. The men drove off at high speed.

The applicant and Kh.Kh. followed. They saw the abductors pass unimpeded through a roadblock manned by traffic police on the road from Zakan-Yurt to the Kavkaz motorway. At the roadblock, police said they had not checked the Priora’s documents because the occupants were in a hurry. Although the applicant immediately told them his brother had been abducted, the police ignored him, continued checking other vehicles, and did not alert other officers or stop the car. Rustam has not been seen since.

The Government did not contest the basic circumstances of the abduction but stressed that it occurred in “peacetime,” involved unidentified armed men in a civilian vehicle, and pointed to inconsistencies in the applicant’s initial complaints about whether Rustam was taken from home or from the street. They also disputed the alleged enhanced security measures. Witness statements largely supported the applicant’s account of the abduction and the roadblock.

The applicant complained to authorities on 18 May 2009. A criminal investigation was opened on 19 June 2009 for aggravated kidnapping under Article 126 § 2 of the Criminal Code. The investigation was repeatedly suspended and resumed. Investigators examined the scene without collecting evidence, traced the Priora’s owner, made photo fits, and requested information from police and detention facilities. Traffic police claimed no roadblocks except a permanent checkpoint. Operational information suggested Rustam had joined an illegal armed group and may have been killed in a November 2009 special operation, but DNA testing excluded that possibility, and a witness did not identify him. The investigation remained pending.

The Government argued that the application should be rejected for non-exhaustion because the investigation was still ongoing. The Court dismissed the need for a civil remedy and joined the question of the criminal investigation’s effectiveness to the merits, as it was closely linked to the applicant’s Article 2 complaints. The key alleged violations were the abduction by State agents and the failure to conduct an effective investigation.

**Case summary: Kagirov v. Russia (Application no. 36367/09)**

The case concerned an application lodged against Russia by Mr Ziyavdi Kagirov, a Russian national living in Zakan-Yurt, Chechnya. He alleged that in May 2009 his brother, Mr Rustam Kagirov, had been abducted by State agents and that the authorities had failed to conduct an effective investigation. The European Court of Human Rights declared the application admissible on 27 August 2013.

Rustam Kagirov, born in 1979, suffered from a disability after the removal of one lung. According to the applicant, Rustam held strong religious beliefs and had studied at an “Islamic Institute” in Grozny. The applicant believed that his brother’s religious convictions may have led the authorities to regard him as a follower of Wahhabism and therefore as someone linked to illegal armed groups in Chechnya. In autumn 2004, officers from the Chechen traffic police allegedly detained Rustam and tortured him for two days, demanding that he confess to involvement with illegal armed groups. They allegedly suspected him because of a photograph showing two men, one thought to be a militant leader and the other resembling Rustam.

The events giving rise to the application occurred on 17 May 2009. President Ramzan Kadyrov of Chechnya was expected to travel on the Kavkaz/Rostov-Baku motorway, and the route between Grozny and Zakan-Yurt was heavily guarded by traffic police, with identity checks at intersections. At about 6 p.m., the applicant returned home and saw a black VAZ Priora vehicle, registration number A 720 AT 95, parked near the village administration. Rustam and his friend Mr Kh.Kh. were walking nearby. Three armed men in black uniforms got out of the car. Two seized Rustam and forced him into the back seat. The third pointed a gun at Mr Kh.Kh. and threatened to shoot if he turned around. The men then drove off at high speed.

The applicant and Mr Kh.Kh. pursued the vehicle. They saw the abductors pass unimpeded through a roadblock on the road leading to the Kavkaz motorway, manned by traffic police officers. At the roadblock, the police said they had not checked the abductors’ documents because the men had been in a hurry. Although the applicant immediately told them that his brother had been abducted, the officers ignored the information, continued checking other vehicles, and took no steps to alert other police units or stop the car. The applicant has had no news of Rustam since.

The Government did not contest the basis of the applicant’s account of the abduction. They noted, however, that it occurred in “peacetime” without a curfew, that the culprits were unidentified armed men in a civilian vehicle, and that the applicant’s initial complaints contained inconsistencies about whether the abduction occurred at home or in the street. They also argued that the alleged enhanced security measures and roadblocks were supported only by the applicant and Mr Kh.Kh.

The official investigation into the abduction began on 19 June 2009 under Article 126 § 2 of the Criminal Code (aggravated kidnapping), case no. 74024. The investigation examined the crime scene twice without collecting evidence, sought information about the roadblock officers and the Priora’s owner, compiled photo fits, and checked detention facilities. It also examined information that Rustam had joined illegal armed groups, but DNA comparison after a special operation excluded him. The investigation was repeatedly suspended and resumed and remained pending.

The Government argued that the application should be rejected for non-exhaustion because the criminal investigation was still ongoing and civil remedies existed. The applicant maintained that the only potentially effective remedy, a criminal investigation, had been ineffective. The Court joined the exhaustion objection to the merits, noting that civil remedies alone are generally insufficient for claims under Article 2 of the Convention.
001-152780:
**Summary of Bujković v. Montenegro (Application no. 40080/08)**

The case of *Bujković v. Montenegro* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr Vladimir Bujković, a Montenegrin national, on 31 July 2008. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, specifically that the length of civil proceedings he initiated in 2000 was incompatible with the "reasonable time" requirement.

The key facts are as follows: On 24 April 2000, the applicant instituted civil proceedings against the Municipality of Bar regarding a plot of land. The procedural history was complex and protracted. Following a remittal, the Court of First Instance in Bar ruled partly in his favour in January 2003. This judgment was partially upheld and partially quashed by the High Court in Podgorica in April 2004. In September 2004, the applicant filed both a request for reopening of the proceedings and an appeal on points of law. The domestic courts took nearly four years to rule on the request for reopening, which consequently delayed the Supreme Court’s decision on the appeal on points of law until June 2008. The case was subsequently subject to multiple remittals. After the Convention entered into force for Montenegro on 3 March 2004, the first-instance decision was quashed three separate times before a final judgment against the applicant was upheld by the High Court and Supreme Court in late 2012 and early 2013, respectively.

The Government contested the application, arguing that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies and that he was mainly responsible for the delay. They cited his filing of multiple claims, requests to join and subsequently withdraw proceedings, and his amendment of claims as primary causes for the protracted timeline. They further argued the case was complex and not of vital importance, thus requiring no urgent action.

The Court’s assessment focused on the criteria of complexity, conduct of the applicant and authorities, and what was at stake. The Court found that the Government failed to prove exceptional complexity. It rejected the Government's arguments that the applicant's conduct was the main cause of delay, noting his amendments were minor and that the courts had joined proceedings on their own motion. Crucially, the Court identified significant delays attributable to the State. It highlighted the nearly four-year period for the domestic courts to rule on the request for reopening, which directly delayed the Supreme Court's decision on the appeal on points of law. The Court also noted that the repeated remittals of the case by higher courts, occurring three times after the Convention's entry into force, disclosed a serious deficiency in the judicial system.

The proceedings fell within the Court's jurisdiction for a period of over eight years and eleven months, having already been pending for more than three years and ten months prior to ratification. In view of these factors, particularly the substantial delays caused by the domestic courts' handling of procedural matters and the repeated re-examinations, the Court concluded that the length of the proceedings failed to satisfy the reasonable time requirement, thereby violating Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The Court dismissed the Government's objections regarding the non-exhaustion of domestic remedies, finding that the remedies cited were not effective at the relevant time.

**Summary of *Bujković v. Montenegro* (Application no. 40080/08)**

The case of *Bujković v. Montenegro* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 31 July 2008 by Mr. Vladimir Bujković, a Montenegrin national. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically that the length of civil proceedings he initiated was incompatible with the "reasonable time" requirement.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation center on the prolonged civil proceedings regarding a plot of land. On 24 April 2000, the applicant filed a claim against the Municipality of Bar before the Court of First Instance in Bar. The procedural history was marked by significant delays and repeated remittals over more than a decade.

Following the initial claim, a first-instance judgment was rendered on 23 January 2003. This was partly upheld and partly quashed by the High Court in Podgorica on 27 April 2004. The applicant then filed both a request for reopening of proceedings and an appeal on points of law in September 2004. A notable delay occurred when it took the domestic courts nearly four years, until 20 October 2006, to rule on the request for reopening, which consequently delayed the Supreme Court's decision on the appeal on points of law until 13 June 2008.

After the Convention entered into force for Montenegro on 3 March 2004, the proceedings experienced further protracted delays. The case was remitted multiple times. The first-instance court declared it lacked competence in November 2009, a decision later quashed. The first-instance court ruled against the applicant on 17 February 2011, but this decision was also quashed by the High Court on 20 September 2011. It was not until 10 May 2012 that a final first-instance judgment was rendered against the applicant, which was subsequently upheld by the High Court and the Supreme Court on 19 October 2012 and 7 February 2013, respectively. The total period under the Court's consideration was from 24 April 2000 to 7 February 2013, a span of nearly 13 years.

The Montenegrin Government contested the application, arguing that the applicant had not exhausted domestic remedies, namely a request for review, an action for fair redress, and a constitutional appeal. They also claimed the case was complex and that the applicant himself contributed to the delay by amending his claim and requesting the suspension of other proceedings.

The European Court of Human Rights dismissed the Government's objections on admissibility, noting that at the time the application was lodged, the domestic remedies cited were not considered effective. On the merits, the Court assessed the case using established criteria: complexity, conduct of the applicant, and conduct of the authorities. The Court found that while the applicant had amended his claim, this did not significantly contribute to the delay, and the Government had failed to prove exceptional complexity. Crucially, the Court identified significant periods of delay attributable to the State, including the nearly four years it took to decide on the request for reopening, which directly stalled the appeal process. Furthermore, the Court highlighted that the first-instance decision was quashed three times after the Convention's entry into force, which it noted could in itself disclose a serious deficiency in the judicial system. Based on these factors, the Court concluded that the length of the proceedings failed to satisfy the "reasonable time" requirement, thereby finding a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

**Case: Bujković v. Montenegro (Application no. 40080/08), European Court of Human Rights, Second Section, Judgment of 10 March 2015.**

The applicant, Vladimir Bujković, a Montenegrin national born in 1972, complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that civil proceedings concerning a plot of land had exceeded the “reasonable time” requirement.

**Key facts.** On 24 April 2000 the applicant sued the Municipality of Bar over a plot of land. After a remittal, the Court of First Instance in Bar ruled partly in his favour on 23 January 2003. On 27 April 2004 the High Court in Podgorica upheld part of that judgment but quashed the remainder. On 16 September 2004 the applicant simultaneously filed a request for reopening of the proceedings before the Court of First Instance and an appeal on points of law before the Supreme Court concerning the upheld part. The case file was sent to the Supreme Court on 2 February 2005 and returned to the first-instance court on 20 December 2005. The reopening request was dismissed on 20 October 2006, upheld by the High Court on 9 May 2008. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on points of law on 13 June 2008.

On 9 October 2008 the first-instance court joined the remainder of the applicant’s claim with two other claims. The applicant made further submissions in October 2008 and specified his claim in May 2009. Hearings restarted anew on 18 June 2009 and 9 September 2009 because the case was assigned to new judges. On 2 November 2009 the first-instance court declared it lacked competence and rejected the claim; the High Court quashed that decision, and by March 2010 the proceedings were again pending before the first-instance court. Friendly settlement attempts in 2010 failed. On 14 February 2011 the hearing started afresh before another judge. On 17 February 2011 the first-instance court ruled against the applicant, but the High Court quashed that decision on 20 September 2011. On 10 May 2012 the first-instance court again ruled against him; this was upheld by the High Court on 19 October 2012 and the Supreme Court on 7 February 2013.

Other facts: the applicant had asked in 2003 and 2004 for another set of civil proceedings to be suspended, and in November 2006 asked for them to continue. In March 2013 he instituted further civil proceedings, still pending before the High Court.

**Admissibility and merits.** The Government argued non-exhaustion, saying the applicant had not used a request for review, an action for fair redress, or a constitutional appeal. The Court rejected this: because the application was lodged in 2008, before the relevant 2013 case-law cutoff, the request for review was not required; fair redress would have been time-barred and depended on an ineffective remedy; and a constitutional appeal was not effective for length complaints. The length complaint was therefore admissible.

On the merits, the Court examined the period from 24 April 2000 to 7 February 2013. The Convention entered into force for Montenegro on 3 March 2004, so the period within the Court’s competence exceeded eight years and eleven months, with the case already pending for more than three years and ten months beforehand. The Court found the case not exceptionally complex. The applicant’s amendments had not significantly contributed to delay, and the joinder was made by the court itself. Nearly four years to decide the reopening request delayed the appeal on points of law and was attributable to the State. After the Convention entered into force, the first-instance decision was quashed three times, requiring three remittals before final adjudication, revealing a serious deficiency. The Court thus found a violation of Article 6 § 1. Other complaints about the outcome of the Supreme Court decision and pending proceedings were rejected as manifestly ill-founded or premature.

In *Šablij v. Slovakia* (Application no. 78129/11), the applicant, a Ukrainian national, was arrested on 31 December 2007 and remanded in custody on 4 January 2008 on charges of conspiracy and murder. His pre-trial detention was extended, and he was indicted on 11 August 2009. On 22 August 2009 the Bratislava I District Court dismissed a request for release. The trial court heard the case on 27–29 October 2010, with a further hearing scheduled for 12–14 January 2011. The applicant was eventually acquitted on 27 July 2011, and the acquittal was upheld on appeal on 18 April 2013.

The alleged violations arose from his September 2010 request for release. On 16 September 2010, while still in detention and acting through his lawyer, he requested release, arguing that he was innocent and that his detention was an arbitrary means of keeping him in custody for another trial. The request was received by the District Court on 20 September 2010. The court did not act promptly. Only on 12 January 2011 did it hear him in private; he confirmed that he sought a response to the September request. The same day, the District Court dismissed the request. The applicant appealed, submitting written reasons on 17 January 2011 and offering a pledge to live lawfully if released. On 25 January 2011, the Bratislava Regional Court dismissed the appeal and rejected the pledge. It observed that there had been unjustified delay at first instance, potentially warranting action against the President of its Chamber, but held that this did not justify release. The written decision was served on 23 February 2011. The final resolution of the September 2010 release request thus took 154 days across two levels of jurisdiction.

In March 2011, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint alleging a violation of his Article 5 § 4 right to a speedy review of the lawfulness of his detention. On 21 June 2011, the Constitutional Court found a violation. It described the District Court’s handling as “particularly lengthy” and “extraordinarily and unacceptably long”; the delay could not be excused by the fact that at the October 2010 hearing the applicant had not demanded a decision. The Constitutional Court awarded reimbursement of legal costs but rejected his claim for €6,000 in non-pecuniary compensation, stating that the finding of a violation was sufficient just satisfaction. Its decision was served on 23 September 2011.

The applicant then applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 18 December 2011, complaining that the length of the release proceedings breached the “speediness” requirement of Article 5 § 4 and that he had been denied financial compensation, in substance under Article 5 § 5. The Government argued that he had lost victim status because the Constitutional Court had found a violation, and that he had failed to exhaust domestic remedies under the State Liability Act. The ECtHR rejected the non-exhaustion objection, relying on *Horváth v. Slovakia*, and joined the victim-status issue to the merits. On the merits, it found that the 154-day delay was incompatible with Article 5 § 4; the Government conceded this. It further held that the Constitutional Court’s finding, without compensation for non-pecuniary damage and with only vague reasoning, did not provide sufficient redress, especially given the extraordinary delay and the Regional Court’s own criticism. The applicant therefore remained a “victim.” The Article 5 § 5 complaint was not examined separately. The Court concluded that Slovakia had violated Article 5 § 4.

In *Šablij v. Slovakia*, the applicant was a Ukrainian national detained in Slovakia pending trial on charges of conspiracy and murder. He was arrested on 31 December 2007 and remanded in custody on 4 January 2008. The alleged violations arose from the handling of his request for release from pre-trial detention made in September 2010 and from the lack of financial compensation for the delay in deciding that request.

On 16 September 2010, while still detained, the applicant asked through his lawyer to be released. He argued that he was innocent and that his continued detention was arbitrary, essentially serving to keep him in custody for another trial. The request was sent by mail and received by the Bratislava I District Court on 20 September 2010. The court did not decide promptly. It first heard the applicant in private on 12 January 2011, when he confirmed that he was seeking a decision on his September 2010 release request. The District Court dismissed the request that same day. The applicant indicated he wished to appeal. Through his lawyer, he filed written appeal reasons on 17 January 2011 and offered a pledge that he would live lawfully if released.

On 25 January 2011, the Bratislava Regional Court dismissed the appeal and rejected his pledge. It noted that there had been unjustified delay in handling the release request at first instance, which could potentially justify calling the President of its Chamber to account, but found that this did not itself require releasing the applicant. The written decision was served on the applicant via the District Court on 23 February 2011. From receipt of the request on 20 September 2010 to service of the final decision on 23 February 2011, the proceedings lasted 154 days and were reviewed at two levels of jurisdiction.

In March 2011, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint, alleging that the length of the proceedings on his release request violated his right under Article 5 § 4 of the Convention to a speedy review of the lawfulness of his detention. On 21 June 2011, the Constitutional Court found a violation. It described the District Court’s handling of the request as “particularly lengthy” and “extraordinarily and unacceptably long,” and rejected the explanation that the applicant had failed to demand a decision during an October 2010 hearing. The Constitutional Court awarded reimbursement of legal costs but refused the applicant’s claim for €6,000 in non-pecuniary compensation. It relied on the “principle of fairness,” the particular circumstances, and the idea that monetary compensation only mitigates loss, concluding that the finding of a violation was sufficient just satisfaction. That decision was served on 23 September 2011.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 5 § 4 that the release proceedings were not “speedy” and under Article 5 § 5 that he had been denied financial compensation. The Government argued that he had lost his victim status because the Constitutional Court had found a violation, and that he had failed to exhaust domestic remedies under the State Liability Act. The European Court rejected the non-exhaustion objection. It found that the 154-day delay breached the speediness requirement of Article 5 § 4, as the Government conceded and the Constitutional Court had already found. On victim status, the Court held that a favourable domestic decision must both acknowledge the breach and afford redress. Although the Constitutional Court acknowledged the violation and awarded costs, its refusal of compensation was not adequately reasoned and was difficult to reconcile with its strong findings of delay. Financial redress was called for. The applicant therefore remained a “victim” under Article 34. Given those findings, the Court did not examine the Article 5 § 5 complaint separately.

**Šablij v. Slovakia** (App. no. 78129/11, judgment of 28 April 2015) concerned a Ukrainian national, Mr Nikolaj Šablij, whose identity was disputed in domestic proceedings. He was arrested on 31 December 2007 and remanded in custody on 4 January 2008 pending trial on charges of conspiracy and murder. His pre-trial detention was extended by the Bratislava I District Court and upheld on appeal in 2009. He was indicted on 11 August 2009, and his request for release was dismissed later that month. The District Court held hearings on 27–29 October 2010, with further hearings scheduled for January 2011. He was eventually acquitted on 27 July 2011, and the acquittal was upheld on appeal on 18 April 2013.

The alleged violations arose from his request for release made on 16 September 2010, while he was still in detention. Acting through his lawyer, he argued that he was innocent and that his detention was being used arbitrarily to keep him in custody for another trial. The request was mailed and received by the District Court on 20 September 2010. However, the court did not decide it until 12 January 2011, when it heard him in private, confirmed that he sought a decision, and dismissed the request the same day. He appealed. On 25 January 2011, the Regional Court dismissed his appeal and rejected his pledge to live lawfully if released. The Regional Court nevertheless observed that there had been unjustified delay at first instance, which could potentially lead to disciplinary action against the President of the Chamber, but that this did not itself justify release. The written decision was served on the applicant on 23 February 2011. Thus, the proceedings on his release request lasted 154 days and were examined at two levels of jurisdiction.

In March 2011, the applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court under Article 127 of the Constitution. He alleged a violation of Article 5 § 4 of the Convention, namely the right to a speedy review of the lawfulness of detention. He sought reimbursement of legal costs and EUR 6,000 in compensation. On 21 June 2011, the Constitutional Court found a violation, describing the District Court’s handling of the request as “particularly lengthy” and “extraordinarily and unacceptably long.” It awarded reimbursement of legal costs but rejected non-pecuniary compensation, stating that the finding of a violation was sufficient just satisfaction under the principle of fairness and the particular circumstances.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 5 § 4 about the lack of speediness and under Article 5 § 5 about the denial of financial compensation. The Government argued that he had lost victim status because the Constitutional Court had found a violation, and that he had failed to exhaust domestic remedies under the State Liability Act. The Court dismissed the non-exhaustion objection, relying on its case-law, especially Horváth v. Slovakia. The Government conceded that the detention review had not been speedy.

The Court found a violation of Article 5 § 4: 154 days across two levels was incompatible with the “speediness” requirement. On victim status, the Court held that a favourable domestic decision must both acknowledge the breach and afford redress. Although the Constitutional Court acknowledged the breach and awarded costs, it gave no compensation and no detailed reasoning. This was difficult to reconcile with its strong findings of extraordinary delay, and the Regional Court itself had noted first-instance delays. The Court concluded that financial redress was called for and that the applicant remained a victim. The Article 5 § 5 complaint was declared admissible but not examined separately on the merits in light of the Article 5 § 4 findings.

**Case Summary: Bouyid v. Belgium (Application no. 23380/09)**

The case of *Bouyid v. Belgium* concerns two Belgian brothers, Saïd and Mohamed Bouyid, who alleged they were slapped in the face by police officers while at the Saint-Josse-ten-Noode police station. They complained that this constituted degrading treatment in violation of Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. The events occurred against a backdrop of longstanding, tense relations between the Bouyid family and local police.

The first incident involved Saïd Bouyid on 8 December 2003. At approximately 4 p.m., he was outside his home ringing the doorbell when a plain-clothes officer, A.Z., demanded to see his identity card. Saïd refused and asked the officer to show his credentials. The officer then grabbed him by his jacket, tearing it, and took him to the nearby police station. While alone with Officer A.Z. in a room, Saïd was slapped in the face as he protested his arrest. A medical certificate issued later that day noted he was in a state of shock, with erythema (redness) on his left cheek and left ear canal.

The second incident involved Mohamed Bouyid on 23 February 2004. He was at the same police station being interviewed by Officer P.P. regarding an altercation involving his mother. During the interview, after being asked not to lean on the officer's desk, Mohamed was slapped in the face. He was then allegedly forced to sign his statement under threat of being placed in a cell. A medical certificate issued the same day recorded bruising on his left cheek.

The applicants argued these acts were part of a pattern of police harassment against their family, which they claimed began in 1999 following a dispute involving another brother and a scratched police car. They reported several prior incidents of alleged police violence and verbal abuse. Both applicants filed complaints with the Standing Committee for the oversight of police services (Committee P) immediately after the respective incidents. They later applied to intervene as civil parties in a judicial investigation.

The judicial investigation led to charges of violence and arbitrary acts against Officers A.Z. and P.P. However, in November 2005, the Crown Prosecutor called for the case to be discontinued, arguing the investigation had not established that the facts constituted a criminal offence or adduced sufficient evidence for further action. The Committals Division discontinued the proceedings in November 2007. This decision was upheld by the Indictments Division of the Brussels Court of Appeal in April 2008, which found no evidence to justify committal. The Court of Cassation dismissed a further appeal in October 2008.

Before the European Court, the key facts were the alleged slaps, which the Belgian Government disputed. The applicants relied on the medical certificates as evidence of injury. They also highlighted a background of tense family-police relations. Central to the legal question was whether an isolated slap by a police officer, not intended to extract a confession, could reach the minimum level of severity required to constitute degrading treatment under Article 3, particularly given the applicants were in police custody and thus under the control of the authorities.

Bouyid v. Belgium (Application no. 23380/09) concerned two Belgian brothers, Saïd and Mohamed Bouyid, who lived with their family next to the Saint-Josse-ten-Noode police station in Brussels. They alleged that police officers slapped them in the face while they were at the police station—on 8 December 2003 and 23 February 2004 respectively—and that this amounted to degrading treatment contrary to Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights. They also complained that the domestic investigation was ineffective, incomplete, biased and excessively long.

First applicant: On 8 December 2003, around 4 p.m., Saïd was outside his home, ringing the doorbell because he had forgotten his keys. A plain-clothes officer, A.Z., asked for his identity card. Saïd refused and asked to see the officer’s credentials. The officer allegedly grabbed him by his jacket, tearing it, and took him to the police station. While alone with A.Z. and protesting his arrest, Saïd said A.Z. slapped him in the face. A doctor’s certificate issued that evening recorded that he was “in a state of shock” and had erythema on the left cheek and left external auditory canal. The Government claimed Saïd had refused identification, caused a scene, insulted an officer, and was taken to the station only for identification; A.Z. denied slapping him and filed a criminal complaint against Saïd for resistance, abusive behaviour and threats.

Second applicant: On 23 February 2004, Mohamed was at the police station being interviewed by Officer P.P. about an altercation involving him, his mother and a third party. He alleged that P.P. slapped him in the face after telling him not to lean on the desk, then threatened to put him in a cell if he did not sign his statement. A medical certificate issued the same day recorded bruising on his left cheek; it was presented to the oversight body before 11:20 a.m. The Government described Mohamed as arrogant and provocative during the interview—slouching, laughing, changing his statement and threatening officers—but said P.P. remained calm and denied slapping him, stating only that he had grabbed his arm to make him leave.

The applicants also alleged a background of tense and hostile relations between their family and the local police since 1999, including earlier incidents involving family members and numerous complaints. After the alleged slaps, both applicants complained to the Standing Committee for police oversight (Committee P). Officers A.Z. and P.P. were charged with violence and arbitrary acts. The investigation included a report on the family-police relationship and noted the problematic nature of those relations. The Crown Prosecutor sought discontinuance; the Committals Division discontinued the case in 2007, and the Indictments Division upheld that decision in 2008, finding no evidence against the officers and referring to inconsistent statements and the context. The Court of Cassation dismissed the applicants’ appeal in October 2008.

Before the European Court, the Chamber initially found no violation of Article 3 even assuming the slaps occurred, viewing them as isolated, thoughtless reactions without serious or long-term effects. The Grand Chamber later reversed, holding that slaps to the face of persons under police control can amount to degrading treatment violating Article 3, and that the Government had failed to provide a convincing explanation for the injuries.

In *Nassr Allah v. Latvia* (ECtHR, Fourth Section, 21 July 2015), the applicant, a Syrian national, complained under Article 5 §§ 1 and 4 of the Convention about his detention as an asylum seeker in Latvia and the judicial review of that detention.

The applicant fled Syria in December 2012, entered Russia, and applied for asylum there, but left in May 2013 before his application was decided. On 4–5 May 2013 he crossed the Latvian border on foot and was stopped by the State Border Guard Service. He had no valid identity or travel documents and initially identified himself under a false name, “Adnan Haiiak.” Documents later found near the arrest location revealed his real identity and that he had an asylum application pending in Russia. He explained that he had hidden his documents to avoid being returned to Russia.

On 5 May 2013 he was detained under the Immigration Law for undetermined identity, but refused to sign the detention record. On 7 May 2013, after completing an asylum application with an Arabic-speaking interpreter, he was detained under section 9(1)(1) (undetermined identity) and section 9(1)(2) (misuse of the asylum procedure) of the Asylum Law. He was placed in the Daugavpils accommodation centre for detained foreigners and asylum seekers.

On 10 May 2013 the Daugavpils City Court ordered his detention for two months after a hearing with an interpreter. The applicant was not assisted by a lawyer. The court found that his identity was undetermined and that there were grounds to believe he was misusing the asylum procedure: he had crossed the border illegally, had not come directly from a country where he faced danger, had spent months in Russia where he had applied for asylum, and had left Russia illegally without awaiting a final decision. The applicant appealed in English; the appeal was translated and examined by the Latgale Regional Court, which dismissed it on 5 July 2013 through a written procedure.

On 8 July 2013 the City Court extended detention for a further two months. The applicant’s lawyer requested release or placement in an open centre, arguing that he had provided identity documents and had not misused the asylum procedure. The court refused, citing a risk that he might abscond or obstruct the asylum procedure, especially given his earlier departure from Russia. The Regional Court dismissed his appeal on 30 July 2013. On 6 September 2013 the City Court extended detention again for two months. The applicant did not appeal, because the asylum decision was expected within a month and previous detention appeals had taken about a month to decide.

On 3 October 2013 the asylum authority refused asylum but granted subsidiary protection and a temporary residence permit. On 4 October the Border Guard informed the applicant of the decision but stated it could not release him until the original decision arrived by post. He was released on 7 October 2013, when the decision was received and the detention grounds ceased. His detention had thus lasted about five months.

The facts relevant to Article 5 § 1 concerned whether the detention was lawful and justified, particularly the reliance on “misuse of the asylum procedure,” the applicant’s false identity, his prior Russian asylum application, and the alleged risk of absconding. The facts relevant to Article 5 § 4 concerned the speed and effectiveness of judicial review: the first two detention appeals were decided by written procedure, translation caused delays, the first detention hearing took place without a lawyer, and the applicant chose not to appeal the third extension.

CASE OF NASSR ALLAH v. LATVIA (Application no. 66166/13) concerned a Syrian national who complained under Article 5 §§1 and 4 of the European Convention on Human Rights about his detention as an asylum seeker in Latvia.

The applicant fled Syria in December 2012 and entered Russia, where he apparently applied for asylum. In May 2013 he left Russia before his claim was decided and crossed the Latvian border on foot on 4–5 May 2013. On 5 May the State Border Guard stopped him. He had no valid identity or travel document and falsely identified himself as “Adnan Haiiak.” He was detained under section 51(2)(1) of the Immigration Law. Documents later found near the arrest revealed his true identity, Aladdin Nassr Allah, and a Russian asylum application. He said he had hidden them to avoid being returned to Russia.

On 7 May 2013 he applied for asylum in Latvia and was detained under section 9(1)(1) (undetermined identity) and 9(1)(2) (misuse of the asylum procedure) of the Asylum Law. He was placed in the Daugavpils accommodation centre. A city court authorised his detention for two months on 10 May; on 8 July and 6 September it extended detention for further two-month periods. The later extensions relied on the alleged misuse of the asylum procedure. The courts cited his illegal border crossing, his failure to come directly from a country where he was endangered, his departure from Russia before its asylum decision, his initial concealment of identity, and his statement that he would seek asylum in another European country if Latvia refused him. They rejected his lawyer’s request to move him to an open centre, finding a risk that he would abscond or obstruct the asylum process.

The applicant appealed the first two detention orders. The Latgale Regional Court examined them in written procedure and dismissed them on 5 and 30 July 2013. There were translation and notification delays. He did not appeal the 6 September extension because his asylum decision was expected soon and previous appeals had taken about a month. On 3 October 2013 the asylum authority refused asylum but granted subsidiary protection and a one-year temporary residence permit. Under domestic law the decision took effect upon notification. On Friday 4 October the decision and copies were sent to the Border Guard in Daugavpils; they arrived on Monday 7 October. The applicant was informed and released at about 4 p.m. that day.

He complained to the Ombudsman about prolonged detention, but the Ombudsman found the detention lawful and the periodic reviews observed. He alleged violations of Article 5 §1, arguing that the detention, particularly after the grant of subsidiary protection (4–7 October), lacked a sufficient legal basis and was arbitrary, and Article 5 §4, arguing that the domestic judicial review of his detention was not effective because of written proceedings, delays, translation problems, and the courts’ failure to address his arguments or consider less restrictive alternatives. The ECtHR ultimately found violations of Article 5 §§1 and 4, concerning the failure to release him promptly once protection was granted and deficiencies in the judicial review of his detention.

**Nassr Allah v. Latvia** (Application no. 66166/13), European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, judgment of 21 July 2015, concerned a Syrian national, Mr Aladdin Nassr Allah, who alleged violations of Article 5 §§ 1 and 4 of the Convention arising from his detention in Latvia during asylum proceedings.

The applicant fled Syria in December 2012 and entered the Russian Federation, where he apparently applied for asylum. In early May 2013, before that application was examined, he left Russia and crossed the Latvian border on foot. On 5 May 2013 the State Border Guard Service stopped him. He was initially detained under the Immigration Law on the ground that his identity had not been determined. He refused to sign the detention record and identified himself as “Adnan Haiiak,” born in 1983. The next day, documents were found at the place of arrest revealing his real identity and showing that he had applied for asylum in Russia. The applicant explained that he had hidden the documents to avoid being returned to Russia.

On 7 May 2013 he was re-detained under section 9(1)(1) (undetermined identity) and section 9(1)(2) (misuse of the asylum procedure) of the Asylum Law and placed in the Daugavpils accommodation centre for detained foreigners and asylum seekers. On 10 May 2013, after a hearing in his presence and with an Arabic interpreter but without a lawyer, the Daugavpils City Court authorised his detention for two months. The court found grounds to suspect misuse of the asylum procedure: he had crossed the border illegally, had not arrived directly from a country where his life was in danger, had spent months in Russia where he had applied for asylum, had left Russia before a final decision, had used a false identity, and had stated he would seek asylum elsewhere if Latvia refused his claim.

His detention was extended by the Daugavpils City Court on 8 July and 6 September 2013 for further two-month periods. The courts maintained that he might abscond or obstruct the asylum procedure. His lawyer argued that identity documents had been provided and that there was no evidence of misuse, but the courts rejected those arguments, relying on his earlier conduct in Russia and his statements about leaving Latvia. Appeals to the Latgale Regional Court were dismissed on 5 July and 30 July 2013, largely on the same grounds, following a written procedure before a single judge.

There were delays in the appeal process. The applicant lodged an appeal on 10 May 2013, but translation was received only on 7 June and the regional court examined it on 5 July. A second appeal lodged on 8 July was examined on 30 July. He did not appeal the third extension because the asylum decision was due soon and previous appeals had taken about a month.

On 3 October 2013 the asylum authority refused asylum but granted subsidiary protection and a one-year temporary residence permit. The decision took effect upon notification. A letter and copies were sent on Friday 4 October to the Border Guard in Daugavpils; they were received on Monday 7 October. The applicant was informed then and released around 4 p.m., meaning he remained detained after the protection decision until formal notification.

The applicant complained to the Ombudsman on 13 August 2013, but was told his detention had been lawful and reviews had been observed. A CPT report noted concerns at the Daugavpils centre about lack of written procedural information, no legal counselling, and complaints about interpretation and untranslated detention decisions. The applicant alleged that his detention violated Article 5 § 1 because it was prolonged, based on an allegedly unsubstantiated “misuse” ground, and continued after subsidiary protection was granted. He also alleged under Article 5 § 4 that judicial review of his detention was not speedy or effective due to translation delays, written procedures, lack of legal assistance at the initial hearing, and language obstacles.

**Vrountou v. Cyprus** (ECtHR, 13 October 2015) concerned alleged sex discrimination in access to Cyprus’s refugee assistance scheme. The applicant, Maria Vrountou, a Cypriot national born in 1980, was the daughter of a displaced mother and a non-displaced father. Her mother had held a refugee card since 1974. Under the Cypriot scheme introduced in 1974, displaced persons and war victims could obtain refugee cards, giving holders access to various benefits, including housing assistance. A 1975 circular provided that children whose fathers were displaced could be registered on their father’s refugee card, but made no equivalent provision for children of displaced mothers. In 1995, the Council of Ministers expressly decided not to extend the term “displaced” to children whose mother was displaced but whose father was not, citing demographic, financial and electoral concerns.

In February 2003, after marrying and seeking housing assistance, Vrountou applied for a refugee card based on her mother’s place of displacement. In March 2003, the authorities rejected her application because her father was not displaced. She challenged the refusal before the Supreme Court, arguing that it violated the constitutional equality principle and Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights taken together with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, as well as Article 13. The first-instance court dismissed her recourse in May 2004. On appeal, a five-judge panel of the Supreme Court dismissed her case on 3 March 2006, holding that the courts could not extend the scheme by judicial interpretation; only the legislature could do so, and earlier proposals to broaden the scheme had not been approved.

At the material time, holding a refugee card was the primary condition for housing assistance. In 2003, applicants for certain housing grants were not subject to a means test; they only had to show that they had not previously received a subsidised State loan. The applicant met the other conditions, so but for the lack of a refugee card, she would have had an enforceable right under Cypriot law to housing assistance. The basic amount available ranged from CYP 8,520 to CYP 11,540.

She also complained that the refusal breached her property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Government argued that the scheme reflected 1975 socio-economic conditions, when men were typically breadwinners, and that extending it to children of displaced women would have significant budgetary and demographic consequences. It also stressed that the scheme was progressively extended and fell within the State’s wide margin of appreciation in social and economic policy.

The Court noted that the scheme had been criticised by the Ombudsman and international bodies as discriminatory. It examined whether the facts fell within the ambit of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It found that housing assistance was a benefit, that possession of a refugee card was the key entitlement condition in 2003, and that the applicant would otherwise have had an enforceable right to assistance. The Court therefore found the complaint admissible and that the facts fell within the ambit of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It then considered whether the difference in treatment was based on sex and whether it had an objective and reasonable justification. **Summary of Vrountou v. Cyprus**

The applicant, Ms. Maria Vrountou, is a Cypriot national born in 1980. The case concerns a refugee assistance scheme established by the Cypriot government in 1974 to aid persons displaced by the Turkish invasion. Under this scheme, displaced persons were issued refugee cards, which granted holders access to a range of benefits, including housing assistance.

The central issue arose from a 1975 circular issued by the Director of the Care and Rehabilitation of Displaced Persons Service. This circular stipulated that when a displaced man married a non-displaced woman, the wife and children could be registered on his refugee card. However, when a displaced woman married a non-displaced man, neither the husband nor the children could be registered as displaced persons. Consequently, the children of displaced women were denied refugee status and the associated benefits. This gender-based distinction was rooted in the socio-economic concepts of the time, which regarded men as the primary breadwinners. The government later argued that this policy was justified by budgetary constraints and the need to prioritize those most in need.

The applicant's mother has been a refugee since 1974 and holds a refugee card. In 2003, after her marriage, the applicant applied to the Civil Registry and Migration Department for a refugee card, with the aim of obtaining housing assistance. Her application was rejected on the grounds that she was not a displaced person because, while her mother was displaced, her father was not.

Ms. Vrountou challenged this decision before the Supreme Court of Cyprus. She argued that the refusal constituted discrimination on the grounds of sex, violating Article 28 of the Cypriot Constitution and Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), taken in conjunction with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The Supreme Court dismissed her recourse and subsequent appeal in March 2006. The Court held that it did not have the jurisdiction to extend the legislative arrangement to cover children of displaced mothers, as this would be a matter for the legislature. The Court noted that proposals to amend the law had been discussed but never approved by the Council of Ministers.

Following her domestic appeals, Ms. Vrountou lodged her application with the European Court of Human Rights on 25 July 2006. She alleged that the failure to grant her a refugee card, thus denying her benefits like housing assistance, amounted to discrimination on the grounds of sex, in violation of Article 14 of the Convention taken in conjunction with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The government contested these claims, arguing that the scheme was designed to assist those most in need and that the applicant did not have a right to housing assistance. They also claimed that the difference in treatment was objectively and reasonably justified given the historical socio-economic context. The Court, however, found that but for the condition of having a refugee card, the applicant would have been entitled to housing assistance, bringing the facts within the ambit of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court ultimately found that the difference in treatment based on sex was discriminatory, violating Article 14 of the Convention. The scheme was amended in 2013 to allow children of displaced women to be eligible for housing assistance.

Maria Vrountou, a Cypriot national, alleged sex discrimination in Cyprus’s refugee assistance scheme. The scheme, introduced in 1974 after the Turkish invasion, granted “refugee cards” to displaced persons. Holders became eligible for various benefits, including housing assistance. “Displaced” was defined as having one’s permanent home in areas occupied by Turkish forces, inaccessible areas, or areas evacuated for the National Guard. A 1975 circular implementing the scheme provided that a non-displaced woman married to a displaced man could be registered on her husband’s refugee card, and children whose father was displaced could be registered on the father’s card. No provision allowed children of displaced mothers to be registered through their mother. This patrilineal rule was later maintained. In 1995, the Council of Ministers extended “displaced” to certain categories but expressly refused to extend it to children whose mother was displaced but whose father was not, citing demographic, electoral and budgetary concerns. At the time of the applicant’s request, section 119 of the Census Bureau Law also treated children as displaced if their father was displaced.

The applicant’s mother was displaced from occupied Skylloura in 1974 and held a refugee card. Her father was not displaced. In September 2002, the applicant married and sought housing assistance. On 27 February 2003, she applied for a refugee card, listing her mother’s place of displacement. By letter of 6 March 2003, the authorities rejected her application because she was not a displaced person: although her mother was displaced, her father was not. She challenged the refusal before the Supreme Court, arguing breach of the constitutional equality principle and discrimination under Article 14 of the Convention taken with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The first-instance Supreme Court dismissed her recourse on 12 May 2004. On appeal, a five-judge panel dismissed on 3 March 2006. The Supreme Court accepted that the issue had been discussed, but held that it could not extend the scheme by judicial interpretation; doing so would exceed its jurisdiction and violate the separation of powers. A similar challenge in Giagkozi also failed.

The applicant principally complained that the refusal to grant her a refugee card, and thus to deny her access to benefits such as housing assistance available to cardholders, amounted to discrimination on grounds of sex. She argued that if she had held a card, she would have had a legitimate expectation of housing assistance and met the other criteria. The Government contended that the scheme aimed to assist those most in need, that 1975 socio-economic conditions justified the distinction, and that budgetary and demographic concerns justified gradual extension. The Court noted that after the application, the law was amended: by 2013, children of displaced mothers became eligible for housing assistance on the same terms as children of displaced fathers, and the Census law was amended. However, those changes did not undo the 2003 refusal. The Court examined whether the facts fell within Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, whether there was a difference in treatment, whether it was based on sex, and whether it was justified. It considered housing assistance a benefit within the Protocol, and found that but for the refugee-card requirement, the applicant would have had an enforceable right to it. The alleged violation was therefore the sex-based exclusion of children of displaced women from refugee status and associated benefits. The Court ultimately found a violation of Article 14 taken in conjunction with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

**Ferreira Alves v. Portugal** (Application no. 78165/12) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, First Section, delivered on 30 April 2015. The applicant, Jorge de Jesus Ferreira Alves, is a Portuguese national born in 1953 and a practising lawyer living in Matosinhos. He lodged an application against Portugal on 23 November 2012 under Article 34 of the Convention. The Portuguese Government were represented by Mrs M. F. da Graça Carvalho, Deputy Attorney General. The application was communicated to the Government on 4 March 2014.

The case arose from disciplinary proceedings brought against the applicant by the Porto Ethics Council of the Portuguese Bar Association. On 22 February 2008, the Ethics Council instituted disciplinary proceedings no. 100/2008 against him. The proceedings followed a complaint made by the Administrative Central Court of the North. The complaint concerned the applicant’s conduct while acting as a legal representative in four separate tort actions against the State. In those proceedings, the applicant requested that a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights be translated and that the domestic court bear the cost of the translation. That request led the Administrative Central Court to complain to the Portuguese Bar Association.

On 10 March 2008, the applicant was summoned in the disciplinary proceedings. On 13 March 2008, he submitted his response. No substantive decision followed for several years. Ultimately, on 9 November 2012, the Ethics Council dismissed the case because it was time-barred. The disciplinary proceedings had therefore lasted approximately four years and eight months, ending without any finding on the merits and without the imposition of a penalty.

The relevant domestic law included Article 125 of the Statute of the Portuguese Bar Association. It listed the disciplinary penalties available, including suspension for up to ten years and expulsion. Those possible sanctions meant the proceedings carried serious potential consequences for the applicant’s professional career.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are that the disciplinary proceedings were initiated after the applicant made a procedural request, as a lawyer, for the translation of an ECtHR judgment in domestic litigation against the State; that he had to respond to a disciplinary complaint carrying possible severe professional sanctions; and that the proceedings remained unresolved for over four years before being dismissed on limitation grounds. The length and context of the disciplinary process formed the factual basis for the applicant’s Convention complaint, particularly his complaint that the proceedings did not comply with the reasonable-time requirement under Article 6 §1 of the Convention. The case therefore concerns the effect of lengthy professional disciplinary proceedings on a lawyer who had exercised a procedural right in domestic litigation.

In *Ferreira Alves v. Portugal* (Application no. 78165/12, judgment of 30 April 2015), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint by Jorge de Jesus Ferreira Alves, a Portuguese lawyer born in 1953 and living in Matosinhos. The case concerned disciplinary proceedings brought against him by the Porto Ethics Council of the Portuguese Bar Association. Those proceedings, numbered 100/2008, began on 22 February 2008 following a complaint by the Administrative Central Court of the North. The complaint related to the applicant’s conduct as legal representative in four tort actions against the State. In those domestic cases, he had requested that the court order the translation of a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights and that the domestic court bear the translation cost. The Administrative Central Court considered this request sufficiently improper to refer it to the Bar Association’s ethics body.

On 10 March 2008, the Ethics Council summoned the applicant in the disciplinary proceedings. He submitted his defence on 13 March 2008. After that initial stage, however, the proceedings remained pending for several years. It was only on 9 November 2012 that the Ethics Council dismissed the case because it was time-barred. The applicant therefore faced potential disciplinary liability for approximately four years and eight months.

The relevant domestic law was Article 125 of the Statute of the Portuguese Bar Association, which set out disciplinary penalties including suspension for up to ten years and expulsion. This provision was significant because, under the Court’s case-law, disciplinary proceedings that may result in such severe sanctions can be considered “criminal” for the purposes of Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. As a result, the applicant was entitled to the guarantees of Article 6 §1, including the right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal.

The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 23 November 2012, shortly after the domestic disciplinary proceedings ended. The Portuguese Government was represented by Mrs M. F. da Graça Carvalho, Deputy Attorney General. On 4 March 2014, the application was communicated to the Government. The central alleged violation was that the disciplinary proceedings had been excessively long, contrary to Article 6 §1 of the Convention.

The Court found that the proceedings had lasted from 22 February 2008 to 9 November 2012, a period of about four years and nine months. It considered that the case was not factually or legally complex and that the applicant had not significantly contributed to the delay. The domestic authorities had failed to progress the proceedings with the required diligence. The fact that the Ethics Council ultimately dismissed the case as time-barred did not remedy the excessive duration; rather, it underscored the failure to decide promptly. The European Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 §1 on account of the unreasonable length of the disciplinary proceedings. It awarded the applicant just satisfaction for non-pecuniary damage.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore the initiation of disciplinary proceedings in February 2008, the applicant’s early submissions in March 2008, the prolonged inactivity until November 2012, and the severe potential penalties that made Article 6 §1 applicable. The case illustrates that professional disciplinary proceedings can engage criminal-law guarantees when the possible sanctions are severe, and that authorities must conduct such proceedings within a reasonable time.

In *Ferreira Alves v. Portugal* (Application no. 78165/12), judgment of 30 April 2015, the European Court of Human Rights (First Section, sitting as a Committee) examined an application lodged by Mr Jorge de Jesus Ferreira Alves, a Portuguese lawyer born in 1953 and living in Matosinhos.
