The complaint concerned his conduct as a legal representative in four tort actions against the State. In those domestic proceedings, the applicant had requested that a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights be translated and that the domestic court pay for the translation. That procedural request—made in his professional capacity as a lawyer—was the basis for the disciplinary complaint.

On 10 March 2008 the applicant was summoned in the disciplinary proceedings. He submitted his response on 13 March 2008. However, the proceedings were not concluded promptly. It was only on 9 November 2012—more than four years and eight months after they began—that the Ethics Council dismissed the case as time-barred. As a result, no disciplinary penalty was ultimately imposed, but the applicant had remained subject to pending disciplinary proceedings for a substantial period and had been required to defend his professional conduct.

The relevant domestic law included Article 125 of the Statute of the Portuguese Bar Association, which listed disciplinary penalties including suspension for up to ten years and expulsion. The potential severity of these sanctions is important in assessing the impact of the proceedings on the applicant and in determining whether fair-trial guarantees, especially the reasonable-time requirement, applied.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore: (i) the disciplinary action was triggered by the applicant’s request, as a lawyer, that an ECtHR judgment be translated and paid for by the domestic court in cases against the State; (ii) the Bar Association’s disciplinary proceedings were initiated and remained pending for over four years before being dismissed as time-barred; and (iii) the applicable disciplinary penalties could have seriously affected his ability to practise law. These facts formed the background to the applicant’s complaints that the disciplinary proceedings violated his Convention rights—principally the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time under Article 6 §1 and freedom of expression/professional activity under Article 10. The Court ultimately found a violation of Article 6 §1 on account of the excessive length of the disciplinary proceedings and a violation of Article 10, considering that the disciplinary proceedings arising from the request for translation of an ECtHR judgment amounted to an unjustified interference with the applicant’s freedom of expression.

In *Jovičić and Others v. Serbia* (Applications nos. 37270/11 et al., judgment 13 January 2015), eight Serbian nationals, former employees of Raketa-Putnički Saobraćaj AD, Užice, complained that Serbia failed to enforce final domestic judgments ordering the company to pay salary arrears and various social-security contributions. They relied on Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, alleging non-enforcement of final court decisions and the lack of an effective remedy. The applications were declared admissible on 15 October 2013.

The applicants had obtained final court decisions in their favour against the debtor company. On 12 July 2010, the Užice Commercial Court opened insolvency proceedings, which stayed all ongoing enforcement proceedings. Notice was posted on the court’s notice board that day and published in the Official Gazette on 4 August 2010. The applicants reported their claims to the insolvency administration. At hearings between September 2010 and June 2011, the court partially accepted their claims on 8 June 2011. On 17 April 2012, some of the debtor’s property was sold; remaining assets were advertised and a public auction was scheduled for 29 June 2012, although it was unclear whether anything sold. The insolvency proceedings remained ongoing.

A key issue was the debtor’s ownership status. The debtor was privatised on 30 December 2002. Because the buyer failed to fulfil contractual obligations, the privatisation was annulled on 17 July 2007. Thereafter the State owned 58.18% of shares. On 11 December 2008, the State sold its shares to a private company. The Government argued that Serbia could not be directly responsible for the debts of a privately owned company and that earlier State shareholding alone did not create liability.

The Court reiterated that execution of a final judgment is an integral part of a “trial” under Article 6, and that failure to enforce a judgment can also interfere with possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. For debts of State-controlled companies, the State is directly liable even after privatisation where the judgment became final while the company was State-controlled, or where the privatisation was subsequently annulled. Accordingly, for decisions that became final before 11 December 2008, Serbia was directly liable; the Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, and found it unnecessary to examine Article 13 separately.

For decisions that became final after 11 December 2008, when the debtor was privately owned, the State’s obligation was limited to assisting enforcement. The insolvency proceedings began about a year later, the applicants’ claims were recognised, some assets were sold, and an auction was scheduled. The Court found no evidence that the authorities failed to act diligently, and thus no violation of Articles 6 or 13 or Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 as to those later decisions.

Separately, the Government objected to the fifth applicant’s complaint because his enforcement order of 4 January 2007 was based on a 22 September 2006 decision rendered in favour of a third person, not him. The applicant did not comment. The Court rejected that complaint as incompatible *ratione personae*.

The European Court of Human Rights case *Jovičić and Others v. Serbia* (13 January 2015) concerned eight Serbian nationals employed by Raketa-Putnički Saobraćaj AD, a company based in Užice. The company failed to pay salary arrears and social-security contributions. The applicants obtained final domestic court decisions ordering the debtor to pay specified sums, but the debtor did not comply.

On 12 July 2010 the Užice Commercial Court opened insolvency proceedings against the debtor. This automatically stayed all ongoing enforcement proceedings. The insolvency decision was posted on the court’s notice board the same day and published in the Official Gazette on 4 August 2010. The applicants reported their claims to the insolvency administration. On 8 June 2011 the court partially accepted their claims. On 17 April 2012 some of the debtor’s property was sold; remaining assets were advertised and an auction was scheduled for 29 June 2012. It was unclear whether anything was sold at that auction, and the insolvency proceedings remained ongoing.

The debtor’s ownership history was central. It was privatised on 30 December 2002, but that privatisation was annulled on 17 July 2007 because the buyer had breached contractual obligations. Following the annulment, the State owned 58.18% of the shares. On 11 December 2008 the State sold its shares to a private company.

The applicants alleged that Serbia had failed to enforce final court decisions in their favour and had provided no effective remedy. They relied on Article 6 §1 (fair trial), Article 13 (effective remedy), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of possessions). The Government argued that the State could not be held directly liable for debts of a privately owned company, and that mere State shareholding was insufficient. It also submitted that only two relevant decisions had been rendered while the debtor was under State control.

The Court reiterated that execution of a final judgment is an integral part of Article 6 and that non-enforcement may breach Protocol No. 1. For private entities, the State must assist creditors through enforcement or insolvency procedures. For State-controlled entities, however, the State is directly liable and cannot rely on lack of funds. If the State sells its shares, it may still be liable for a judgment debt arising before the sale where the decision became final while the company was State-controlled; this also applies if the privatisation was later annulled.

Applying these principles, the Court found violations of Article 6 §1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 for decisions that became final before 11 December 2008, the date of final privatisation. For decisions final after that date, the State’s duty was limited to assisting enforcement. Because insolvency proceedings were opened, claims were recognised, assets were sold or advertised, and no evidence showed inadequate diligence, the Court found no violation of Articles 6 or 13 or Protocol No. 1. It also did not separately examine Article 13 for the pre-2008 complaints. Separately, the fifth applicant’s complaint regarding a 22 September 2006 decision was rejected as incompatible *ratione personae* because that decision had been rendered in favour of a third person, not the applicant.

**Summary of *Jovičić and Others v. Serbia* (Applications nos. 37270/11 et al.)**

**Background and Core Complaint**
The case originated from eight applications lodged against Serbia by former employees of Raketa-Putnički Saobraćaj AD, a company based in Užice. The applicants had obtained final domestic court judgments ordering the debtor company to pay them salary arrears and social security contributions. Their central complaint before the European Court of Human Rights was that the respondent State failed to enforce these final judgments, thereby violating their rights under Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial), Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the Convention, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property).

**Key Factual Circumstances**
The debtor had failed to meet its obligations to its employees, leading the applicants to pursue separate civil claims. They each secured final court decisions in their favor. The critical events unfolded as follows:

1.  **Insolvency Proceedings:** On 12 July 2010, the Užice Commercial Court opened insolvency proceedings against the debtor. This action automatically stayed all ongoing enforcement proceedings against the company. The applicants duly reported their claims, based on their court judgments, to the insolvency administration. These claims were partially accepted by the court on 8 June 2011.

2.  **Asset Liquidation:** The insolvency process moved slowly. Some of the debtor's property was sold on 17 April 2012, and other assets were advertised for a public auction scheduled for 29 June 2012. However, it remained unknown whether any assets were actually sold at that auction, and the insolvency proceedings were still ongoing at the time of the ECHR judgment.

**The Debtor's Shifting Status**
A pivotal point for the Court’s assessment was the changing ownership status of the debtor company. The debtor was originally a socially-owned company. It was privatised on 30 December 2002, but this privatisation was annulled on 17 July 2007 due to the buyer's failure to meet contractual obligations. As a result, the State came to own a 58.18% share. Finally, on 11 December 2008, the State sold its shares to a private company, marking the debtor's final transition to private ownership.

**Legal Reasoning and Violations Found**
The Court's assessment distinguished between judgments that became final before and after the debtor's final privatisation on 11 December 2008.

- **Judgments Final Before 11 December 2008:** Applying its established case-law, the Court held that the State is directly liable for the debts of companies it controls, even after privatisation, if the judgment at issue became final while the company was under State control. Therefore, Serbia was directly responsible for the non-enforcement of court decisions that had become final before this date. The Government's arguments that it was not responsible for a privately-owned company's debts were rejected for this category of judgments. Consequently, the Court found a **violation of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1**. It did not find it necessary to separately examine the complaint under Article 13.

- **Judgments Final After 11 December 2008:** For these judgments, the debtor was considered a private entity. The State's obligation was limited to providing adequate assistance to creditors, such as through bankruptcy procedures. The Court found that the State authorities had acted diligently by opening insolvency proceedings, recognising the applicants' claims, and attempting to sell assets. The State could not be held liable for the debtor's lack of funds. Thus, the Court found **no violation** for this category.

**Conclusion**
The Court ultimately found a violation of the Convention regarding the non-enforcement of judgments that became final before the debtor's final privatisation in December 2008, holding the State directly liable. Conversely, it found no violation concerning judgments that became final after that date.

**V.M. and Others v. Belgium** concerned seven Serbian nationals of Roma origin—parents V.M. and G.S.M. and their five children—who alleged that Belgium had exposed them to treatment contrary to Articles 2 and 3 ECHR through reception conditions in Belgium and their “forced” return to Serbia, and that they lacked an effective remedy under Article 13.

The family had lived mainly in Serbia and claimed discrimination and ill-treatment as Roma in employment, healthcare, and schooling. Their eldest daughter, born in 2001, was physically and mentally disabled and suffered from epilepsy. After failing to improve their situation in Kosovo, they went to France in March 2010 and applied for asylum, but their application was finally rejected on 4 June 2010. They claimed they then returned to Kosovo and Serbia in May 2010 because of precarious conditions. In March 2011, they travelled to Belgium and lodged an asylum application on 1 April 2011.

During a Dublin interview on 4 April 2011, the father said they chose Belgium to obtain better treatment for their disabled daughter and that he suffered psychological problems. The mother stated she was six months pregnant and mentioned the daughter’s health problems. The applicants claimed they explained why they refused to return to France and were not asked for evidence of having left the EU or medical documents.

On 12 April 2011, Belgium requested France to take the family back under the Dublin II Regulation, saying they had not proved they left EU territory for Serbia. France initially refused on 22 April, stating the family had disappeared since May 2010, which supported their claim that they had left the Schengen area and re-entered in March 2011 after more than three months. Belgium asked France to reconsider, and on 6 May France accepted responsibility under Article 16(1)(e).

On 17 May 2011, the Aliens Office refused leave to remain and ordered the family to leave for France, finding Belgium not responsible for the asylum claim. It noted no evidence of their stay in Kosovo after France or medical certificates, considered France rights-respecting, and declined to use the sovereignty clause. The applicants had seven days to leave and report to French border authorities. On 19 May they submitted evidence that they had left the EU for more than three months, including gynaecologist certificates, a health card, and school enrolment proof. On 25 May, execution was extended to 25 September because the mother was due to give birth.

On 16 June 2011, the applicants appealed to the Aliens Appeals Board, seeking annulment and suspension. They argued the decisions failed to provide the examination required by Article 13 read with Article 3 of their fears of return to Serbia and their health problems. They claimed the reasoning was erroneous and incomplete: it misidentified them as Kosovars rather than Serbs and omitted their return to Serbia and Roma origin. They also argued they could not be blamed for not providing documents during the Dublin interview, where no lawyer assisted them and no documents were requested. They further submitted that France was not the responsible State under Article 16(3) because they had left the EU for at least three months, and that Belgium should have used the sovereignty or humanitarian clauses given their vulnerability, the situation of Roma in Serbia, and reception conditions in France.

The hearing took place on 26 August 2011. On 23 September, a further extension was refused. On 27 September, the applicants sought interim measures from the European Court of Human Rights to suspend transfer; the Court refused on 28 September. On 29 November 2011, the Aliens Appeals Board rejected the Article 3 complaint concerning reception in France, finding no evidence of difficulties or ill-treatment, but set aside the decisions because the Aliens Office had not established the legal basis for France’s responsibility. Belgium appealed to the Conseil d’État on 23 December 2011, and the appeal was declared admissible on 12 January 2012.

The case of *V.M. and Others v. Belgium* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by seven Serbian nationals of Roma origin, including a disabled child, against Belgium. The applicants alleged that the Belgian authorities had exposed them to a situation endangering their lives and physical integrity through the reception conditions in Belgium and their "forced" return to Serbia, violating Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention. They also complained about the lack of an effective remedy.

The applicants had left Serbia due to discrimination and ill-treatment against Roma, seeking better conditions. After an unsuccessful asylum application in France, which was rejected in June 2010, they returned to Kosovo and then Serbia. In March 2011, they traveled to Belgium and applied for asylum on 1 April 2011.

During their Dublin interview on 4 April 2011, the applicants expressed fears about returning to Serbia. On 12 April 2011, Belgium requested France to take the applicants back, asserting they had not proven they left the EU for Serbia since their stay in France. **Volovod v. Ukraine** (Application no. 527/07, judgment of 21 May 2015) concerned a Ukrainian father’s complaint that authorities failed to conduct an effective criminal investigation into his son’s murder, contrary to the procedural limb of Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant, Mr Nikolay Volovod, was born in 1929. His son, V., lived in Severodonetsk, Lugansk Region. On the evening of 11 August 2002, V. was sitting in the courtyard of his apartment block when a man approached and shot him in the head. V. died in hospital about an hour later. Several eyewitnesses described the attacker as 25–30 years old, approximately 175–180 cm tall, wearing sunglasses, dark jeans, a red T-shirt and a cap. Police promptly opened a criminal investigation, examined the scene, recovered the bullet, and collected fingerprints and biological material. Forensic experts established that V. had been shot with a TT pistol.

The initial investigation moved quickly. Police questioned eyewitnesses, V.’s wife and his business partner K. K. stated that a man named Bo. had threatened V. with violence. Employees of V.’s bar said that P., a member of Bo.’s criminal gang, had been looking for V. shortly before the murder. Prosecutors knew P. had been wanted since 1999 for another killing allegedly committed with a TT pistol on Bo.’s orders. They therefore treated P. and Bo. as possible suspects and declared them wanted.

Other investigative steps included identifying and questioning people who had called V., comparing fingerprints and biological material, searching homes, and conducting identity parades. No fingerprint match linked several suspects, including P., to the scene. In October 2002 police found the TT pistol used in the killing in the possession of Sh., who said he had bought it from a minor, A. A. claimed he had found the gun and sunglasses near garages on 12 August 2002. Investigators found no evidence linking Sh., A., or the garage owners to Bo. or V. Identity parades did not identify Sh. or P. as the killer.

The investigation was repeatedly suspended and resumed between 2003 and 2010. Higher prosecutors quashed several suspension decisions and ordered additional measures, including finding and questioning further witnesses. Nevertheless, by 15 March 2010 the investigation was again suspended because the killer could not be identified. The applicant repeatedly asked about progress and received replies in 2002, 2003 and 2005. He never formally applied to be recognised as an injured party, although V.’s wife had been recognised as such.

Before the Court, the applicant complained that the investigation had been excessively long and that his son’s killer had not been identified or punished. The Government argued that authorities had taken all possible steps and had kept the applicant informed.

The Court examined the complaint under the procedural limb of Article 2. It reiterated that the obligation to investigate is an obligation of means, not result, but the investigation must be thorough, prompt and capable of establishing the facts and identifying those responsible. The Court noted that the authorities had responded promptly, conducted key initial steps, quickly found the weapon, and investigated possible suspects. Although the investigation was suspended several times, supervising authorities ordered resumptions and additional measures. The applicant did not suggest what further steps should have been taken. The Court also found that, despite not being formally recognised as an injured party, the applicant had been sufficiently informed. It therefore found no violation of Article 2.

In *Volovod v. Ukraine* (Application no. 527/07, judgment 21 May 2015), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint under the procedural limb of Article 2 of the Convention concerning Ukraine’s alleged failure to effectively investigate the murder of the applicant’s son and to identify and punish the perpetrator.

The applicant, Nikolay Volovod, was a Ukrainian national born in 1929. His son, V., lived in Severodonetsk. Eyewitnesses described the killer as a man aged 25–30, about 175–180 cm tall, wearing sunglasses, dark jeans, a red T-shirt and a cap. Experts established that V. had been shot with a TT pistol.

The early investigation pursued several leads. K.Y., who had previously stolen money from V., had an alibi and his fingerprints did not match those found at the scene. Employees of V.’s bar said that P., a member of a criminal gang led by Bo., had been looking for V. on 10 August. Further suspensions occurred in 2005, 2006, 2008 and 2009, with prosecutors sometimes ordering additional investigative steps. On 15 March 2010, the investigation was again suspended because it was impossible to identify the killer; the applicant was informed on 23 March 2010.

The Government argued that the authorities had taken all possible steps and had kept the applicant informed, even though he had not formally requested aggrieved-party status.

It found that the authorities had responded promptly, secured forensic evidence, interviewed witnesses, quickly found the weapon and pursued plausible leads, including the Bo./P. line. Although the investigation was suspended several times, supervising authorities reviewed those decisions and ordered resumptions. The applicant did not suggest specific missing measures. The Court therefore declared the application admissible but found no violation of Article 2 of the Convention.

In *Volovod v. Ukraine* (Application no. 527/07), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint under the procedural limb of Article 2 of the Convention concerning the allegedly ineffective investigation into the applicant’s son’s murder.

The applicant, a Ukrainian national, lived in Krasnyy Liman. His son, V., lived in Severodonetsk. On the evening of 11 August 2002, V. was sitting in the courtyard of his apartment block when a man approached and shot him in the head. He died about an hour later. Eyewitnesses described the assailant as 25–30 years old, about 175–180 cm tall, wearing sunglasses, dark jeans, a red T-shirt and a cap.

The police immediately opened a criminal investigation. They examined the crime scene, collected the bullet, fingerprints and biological material, and sent evidence for forensic examination. The bullet had been fired from a TT pistol. They questioned V.’s wife, who knew of no motive, and K.Y., who had previously stolen money from V.; he had an alibi and his fingerprints did not match those found at the scene. Bar employees stated that P., a member of Bo.’s criminal gang, had been looking for V. on 10 August. P. was already wanted for a 1999 killing with a TT pistol allegedly carried out on Bo.’s instructions. V.’s business partner also reported that Bo. had threatened V. The authorities therefore treated P. and Bo. as possible suspects and declared them wanted.

The investigation pursued multiple leads. Police checked telephone calls made to V., questioned acquaintances, compared fingerprints and biological materials, searched homes and conducted identity parades. In October 2002, the murder weapon was found in the possession of Sh., who said he had bought it from a minor, A. A. claimed he had found the gun and sunglasses near garages. The evidence did not link Sh., A., the garage owners, Bo. or V. Eyewitnesses failed to identify Sh., P. or other suspects. Bo and P were later questioned and denied involvement; P.’s fingerprints did not match. Other potential suspects were checked, but no evidence of involvement emerged.

Between 2003 and 2010, the investigation was repeatedly suspended and resumed. Higher prosecutors quashed several suspension decisions and ordered further investigative measures, including finding and questioning additional witnesses and checking whether another suspect, F., could have been involved. Eventually, the killer was not identified. The applicant was informed about the progress of the investigation in response to his requests, although he never formally asked to be recognised as an aggrieved party.

Before the Court, the applicant complained that the investigation had been lengthy and ineffective and that his son’s killer had not been identified and punished, in violation of the procedural obligation under Article 2. The Government submitted that the authorities had taken all possible steps.

The Court reiterated that Article 2 requires an effective, thorough and timely investigation, but not necessarily a successful result. It found that the authorities had responded promptly, collected key evidence, questioned eyewitnesses, located the weapon, investigated credible suspects and pursued reasonable leads. Although there were delays and repeated suspensions, supervising prosecutors ordered resumptions and further measures. The applicant did not point to additional important steps that should have been taken, and he had been kept informed. The Court declared the application admissible but found no violation of Article 2.

In *Maslák and Others v. Slovakia* (Application no. 11037/12, judgment 16 July 2015), three Slovak nationals complained under Article 5 §§ 4 and 5 of the Convention that their pre-trial detention reviews were not decided speedily and that they had no enforceable right to compensation. Since 2007 they had faced multiple charges, mainly violent offences linked to organised crime, and had been repeatedly arrested, remanded, released and re-arrested. The relevant facts concerned three unsuccessful release requests after their 1 April 2010 arrest on a perjury charge, and an interlocutory appeal against a remand order after their 1 April 2011 arrest on an extortion charge.

First, the first applicant requested release on 2 May 2010. The District Court received it on 11 May; he amended it on 19 May. On 21 May he challenged the judge for bias. That challenge was dismissed, and his appeal against dismissal was decided by the Regional Court on 10 June, served on 21 June. His release request was then dismissed by the District Court on 25 June and by the Regional Court on 20 July, served on 26 July. His constitutional complaint was declared inadmissible on 4 October 2011; the Constitutional Court found no undue delay.

Second, on 10 May 2010 the second and third applicants requested release. The prosecution transmitted it to the District Court on 17 May; the court received the file on 21 May but found it incomplete and requested completion, which came on 2 June. They waived an oral hearing. The District Court dismissed the request on 3 June and the Regional Court on 15 July. Service was delayed because one of their lawyers had terminated his mandate without informing the court; the decisions were served in early August 2010. Their constitutional complaint was declared inadmissible on 9 November 2011. The Constitutional Court accepted some delay was caused by the incomplete file and the lawyer’s conduct, but found no breach.

Third, on 22 December 2010 all applicants made a further release request. The District Court replied on 3 January 2011 that, absent new relevant information, a new request could not be filed until thirty days after the final determination of the previous request, which had ended on 16 December 2010. The applicants amended their request on 20 and 31 January 2011. It was dismissed on 7 February and, on appeal, on 23 February 2011, served on 2 March. Their constitutional complaint was declared inadmissible on 14 June 2011; the Constitutional Court held that the relevant period ran only from the January amendments and was acceptable.

Finally, after their 1 April 2011 arrest on an extortion charge, they were remanded on 4 April. Their interlocutory appeal was dismissed on 21 April, served on 19 May. Their constitutional complaint was declared inadmissible on 13 December 2011. They were indicted on 27 September 2011 and released on 15 November 2011.

The European Court of Human Rights found the Article 5 § 4 complaints admissible. The periods lasted 84 days, 83 days, 40/30 days, and 212 days respectively. The case was not particularly complex. Although some delay was attributable to the applicants’ lawyer, the authorities also caused delay, notably by submitting an incomplete file. The Court therefore found that on all four counts the lawfulness of detention was not decided “speedily”, violating Article 5 § 4. As their constitutional complaints had failed and Slovak law provided no compensation claim following an ECtHR finding, the applicants also had no enforceable right to compensation, violating Article 5 § 5.

In *Maslák and Others v. Slovakia*, three Slovak nationals alleged violations of Article 5 §§ 4 and 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Since 2007, they had faced multiple charges, mainly violent offences linked to organised crime, and had been repeatedly arrested, remanded, released and re-arrested. They alleged that the lawfulness of their detention was not decided “speedily” and that they had no enforceable right to compensation.

On 1 April 2010, they were arrested on a perjury charge. The first applicant requested release on 2 May 2010. The District Court received the request on 11 May, heard him on 21 May, and dismissed his bias challenge the same day. His appeal against that decision was dismissed on 10 June and served on 21 June. His release request was refused by the District Court on 25 June and by the Regional Court on 20 July, served on 26 July. The ECtHR counted this as 84 days before two levels of ordinary jurisdiction.

The second and third applicants requested release on 10 May 2010, offering a pledge. The prosecution sent the request to the District Court on 17 May; it arrived on 21 May, but the file was incomplete and completed only on 2 June. The District Court dismissed the request on 3 June; the Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 15 July. Service was delayed partly because one lawyer failed to inform the court that his mandate had ended. This period lasted 83 days. The ECtHR noted State-caused delay from the incomplete file but accepted that about one month was attributable to those applicants’ lawyer.

On 22 December 2010, all applicants filed another release request. The District Court told them on 3 January 2011 that, absent new relevant information, a new request could not be filed until 30 days after the final determination of the previous request, which had ended on 16 December 2010. Their January 2011 amendments were treated as new requests. The request was refused by the District Court on 7 February and by the Regional Court on 23 February, served on 2 March 2011. This lasted 40 days for the first applicant and 30 days for the other two.

After being released on 1 April 2011, they were immediately re-arrested and remanded on an extortion charge by order of 4 April 2011. Their interlocutory appeal was dismissed by the Regional Court on 21 April, served on 19 May. They challenged this before the Constitutional Court, which declared the complaint inadmissible on 13 December 2011. They were indicted on 27 September 2011 and released on 15 November 2011. This procedure lasted 212 days before one ordinary court and the Constitutional Court.

The Government argued delays were caused by the applicants’ bias challenge, the incomplete file, and the lawyer’s failure. The ECtHR found the detention cases were not complex. Although some delay was attributable to the second and third applicants, State-caused delays remained. It concluded that on all four occasions the lawfulness of detention was not decided speedily, violating Article 5 § 4. Because the Constitutional Court complaints failed and Slovak law provided no enforceable compensation claim based on an ECtHR finding, the Court also found a violation of Article 5 § 5.

**Summary of *Maslák and Others v. Slovakia* (Application no. 11037/12)**

The case of *Maslák and Others v. Slovakia* concerns three Slovak nationals who alleged violations of their rights under Article 5 §§ 4 and 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants, facing multiple charges related to organised crime since 2007, were repeatedly arrested, remanded, and released. The central issue involved the alleged lack of speediness in reviewing the lawfulness of their pre-trial detention and their inability to obtain compensation for this procedural failing.

The case focused on four specific detention-related proceedings:

1.  **Request for Release of 2 May 2010 (First Applicant):** The first applicant filed a release request, which reached the District Court on 11 May 2010. During a hearing on 21 May 2010, he challenged the presiding judge for bias, which was dismissed. He appealed this dismissal, and the Regional Court rejected his appeal on 10 June 2010. His request for release was not decided by the District Court until 25 June 2010, and the Regional Court dismissed his subsequent appeal on 20 July 2010, with the decision served on 26 July 2010. He complained to the Constitutional Court about the lack of speed, but his complaint was declared inadmissible in October 2011.

2.  **Request for Release of 10 May 2010 (Second and Third Applicants):** These applicants filed a release request with the prosecution service, which forwarded it to the District Court. The court received an incomplete case file and had to request a complete version, which was submitted on 2 June 2010. The District Court dismissed the request on 3 June 2010, and the Regional Court dismissed their appeal on 15 July 2010. Service of the decision was delayed due to a third lawyer failing to inform the court that his mandate had ended. Their constitutional complaint was declared inadmissible in November 2011.

3.  **Request for Release of December 2010 (All Applicants):** The applicants filed a new release request on 22 December 2010. The District Court informed them that the request could not be entertained as it was filed before the statutory 30-day period had elapsed since their previous request was finally determined and contained no new relevant information. The applicants amended their request in January 2011. The District Court dismissed it on 7 February 2011, and the Regional Court dismissed their appeal on 23 February 2011 (served on 2 March 2011). Their constitutional complaint was declared inadmissible in June 2011, with the Constitutional Court finding that the relevant period only began from the date of the amendments.

4.  **Interlocutory Appeal against Detention Order of 4 April 2011 (All Applicants):** Following their re-arrest on 1 April 2011 on an extortion charge, the applicants were remanded in detention by a District Court order of 4 April 2011. They filed an interlocutory appeal on 14 April 2011. The Regional Court dismissed it on 21 April 2011, serving the decision on 19 May 2011. Their subsequent constitutional complaint, which included the proceedings before the Constitutional Court itself, was declared inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded in December 2011.

The European Court of Human Rights found that the periods under consideration for these four sets of proceedings lasted 84, 83, 40/30, and 212 days respectively. Despite accepting that some delays were attributable to the applicants (e.g., a lawyer’s conduct), the Court identified delays attributable to the state authorities, such as the time taken to examine an appeal against a bias challenge and the submission of an incomplete case file. Consequently, the Court found a violation of Article 5 § 4 on all four counts, concluding that the lawfulness of the applicants’ detention had not been decided "speedily."

Furthermore, the Court found a violation of Article 5 § 5. It noted that the applicants' constitutional complaints regarding the speediness of their detention were unsuccessful, and Slovakian law provided no avenue for them to claim compensation based on a finding by the European Court. Therefore, they were denied an enforceable right to compensation for the established violation of their Article 5 § 4 rights.

Catalina Filip v. Romania (Application no. 15052/09) concerned a Romanian national’s complaint that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into her husband’s death during the violent events of December 1989. The application was lodged on 9 March 2009 and communicated to the Government on 11 September 2013. The European Court of Human Rights’ Third Section delivered judgment on 21 April 2015; it became final on 19 October 2015.

The background was the December 1989 military crackdown in Romania, during which many civilians were killed or injured. According to official figures cited in the case, more than 1,200 people died, over 5,000 were injured, and thousands were unlawfully detained or ill-treated in Bucharest and other towns. In Bucharest alone, a 1990 report stated that 48 people died and 150 were injured in the night of 21–22 December 1989 as a result of the armed forces’ violent crackdown, including firearms. Many victims were also killed after 22 December 1989, when the Head of State was deposed.

The applicant’s husband was shot in the head and killed at his home in Bucharest on 25 December 1989. He had been sitting in front of an apartment window when a bullet came from outside. A ballistic report of 17 April 1990 concluded that the bullet had been fired by an AKM-type semi-automatic rifle. In 1990 the Bucharest Military Prosecutor’s Office opened a criminal investigation. Between 1990 and 1994, witnesses were heard. In parallel, a separate investigation, file no. 97/P/1990, concerned the use of violence in Bucharest during late December 1989. On 23 May 2007, the file concerning the applicant’s husband was joined to file no. 97/P/1990.

On 15 January 2008, military prosecuting authorities separated the investigation concerning sixteen civilian defendants, including a former President of Romania and a former head of the Romanian Intelligence Service, from the investigation involving military personnel, and transferred jurisdiction to the prosecutor’s office at the High Court of Cassation and Justice. A letter of 5 June 2008 stated that between 2005 and 2007, 6,370 individuals had been questioned in case no. 97/P/1990; 1,100 ballistics reports had been prepared; and more than 10,000 investigative measures and 1,000 on-site inquiries had been conducted. The letter attributed delays to repeated transfers of the case between prosecutors, lack of cooperation by institutions involved in the December 1989 crackdown, the extreme complexity of the investigation, and the failure to conduct necessary measures immediately after the killings. A February 2009 press release indicated that the High Council of the Judiciary intended to ask the Judicial Inspection to identify reasons preventing a rapid investigation. The criminal investigation was still pending before the domestic authorities.

In civil proceedings, on 22 December 2004 the applicant sued the Ministry of Public Finances for 1,000,000,000 ROL in non-pecuniary damages, arguing that the State was liable for the lack of diligence in investigating the December 1989 events and for failing to identify and punish those responsible for her husband’s death. On 2 February 2006, the Bucharest District Court dismissed the claim as time-barred. On 12 March 2007, the Bucharest County Court allowed her appeal, quashed that judgment, and remitted the case. On 12 June 2008, the District Court awarded her RON 100,000 in non-pecuniary damages plus court fees, finding that the criminal investigation had not been effective or prompt under Article 2 of the Convention; it noted that for more than eighteen years the only measure taken had been to join her husband’s file to the main case. The Ministry appealed. On 3 February 2009, the Bucharest County Court partially allowed the appeal and reduced the award to RON 50,000, while upholding the court fees.

The applicant’s central alleged violation was that no effective investigation had been carried out into her husband’s death. Relevant context included the Court’s earlier findings in Association “21 December 1989” and Others v. Romania and Mocanu and Others v. Romania, and a Committee of Ministers decision inviting Romania to assess measures concerning the independence of military prosecutors and cooperation with investigators.

In *Bekerman v. Liechtenstein* (App. no. 34459/10, judgment 3 September 2015), the applicant, a German national born in 1955 and living in Berlin, complained under the Convention that civil proceedings in Liechtenstein had lasted unreasonably long and that he had exhausted effective domestic remedies for that delay. The underlying dispute concerned property rights to more than CHF 14 million that the applicant had placed in five Liechtenstein foundations, including the H. foundation, in 1999. He was the beneficiary. His mother and sisters claimed that parts of the assets belonged to his mother and to his deceased father, not to him.

The proceedings began on 30 August 2001, when the Regional Court, at the sisters’ request, prohibited the H. foundation and the applicant from disposing of assets. On 27–28 September 2001 the sisters sued the H. foundation and the applicant for about EUR 3.3 million. The applicant’s legal aid was initially refused in November 2003, but the Court of Appeal quashed that refusal in March 2004, and legal aid was granted in July 2004. The sisters then withdrew their claim against the applicant personally and pursued only the H. foundation.

On 30 December 2004, after taking evidence, the Regional Court ordered the H. foundation to pay each sister about EUR 240,000, finding that the applicant had not proved that the assets were a gift from his mother and that they had come from the deceased father’s estate. Appeals followed. In March 2005 the applicant sought to intervene as a third party and requested legal aid; he was granted legal aid in June 2005 and joined in August 2005. In September 2005 the Court of Appeal quashed the judgment and dismissed the sisters’ action as inadmissible. In May 2006 the Supreme Court reversed that decision, found the sisters had standing, and remitted the case. The applicant’s constitutional complaint was dismissed in March 2007 as inadmissible because a remittal did not terminate the proceedings by a final decision. In September 2006 the Court of Appeal had already remitted the case to the Regional Court for further fact-finding.

In November 2007 the Regional Court terminated the applicant’s appointed lawyer; he was then represented by his wife. In June 2008 the Regional Court again ordered the H. foundation to pay the sisters about EUR 240,000 each. On appeal, in March 2009 the Court of Appeal allowed the applicant’s and the foundation’s appeal and dismissed the action, finding the assets had belonged to the mother alone and had been validly gifted to the applicant in 1993. In October 2009 the Supreme Court quashed that judgment and remitted the case again, finding the donation had not been sufficiently established.

In October 2009 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint, relying on Article 6 and complaining that the proceedings had lasted unreasonably long. On 21 May 2010 the Constitutional Court dismissed it as inadmissible because the Supreme Court’s remittal was not a final decision. It added that, although it could later find a breach of the reasonable-time requirement, it could only declare the length unreasonable; it could not undo delays. It ordered the applicant to pay the sisters’ lawyer’s costs of CHF 3,087.05. Relevant domestic law included supervisory review for procedural delays and the Official Liability Act, while the Constitutional Court’s case-law allowed cost exemptions or reimbursement as compensation for unreasonable delay. The Court of Appeal later stayed the case pending the Strasbourg application; in April 2014 the proceedings were stayed perpetually after the other parties settled. The applicant’s Strasbourg complaint concerning the excessive length was communicated to the Government; the remainder was declared inadmissible.

**Bekerman v. Liechtenstein** (Application no. 34459/10) concerned a German national, Michael Bekerman, born in 1955 and living in Berlin. He applied to the European Court of Human Rights against Liechtenstein on 9 July 2010, alleging in particular that the length of civil proceedings had been excessive and that he had exhausted all effective domestic remedies. On 12 July 2013, the Court communicated only the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The underlying dispute formed part of extensive litigation before Liechtenstein courts since 2001. It concerned property rights to substantial assets—more than 14 million Swiss francs—that the applicant had placed into five Liechtenstein foundations in 1999, including the H. foundation, of which he was the beneficiary. His mother, represented by a guardian, and his sisters claimed that the applicant had not owned all the assets he contributed, because part belonged to his mother and part to their deceased husband and father.

In September 2001, the applicant’s sisters brought an action against both the H. foundation and the applicant for approximately EUR 3.3 million. The applicant’s request for legal aid was initially dismissed in November 2003 but granted in July 2004 after the Court of Appeal found the Regional Court had failed to investigate sufficiently. In July 2004, the sisters withdrew the action against the applicant personally and continued only against the H. foundation. On 30 December 2004, the Regional Court ordered the foundation to pay the sisters about EUR 240,000 each, finding that the applicant had not proved that the assets were a gift from his mother and had therefore not been authorised to transfer assets from his deceased father’s estate into the foundation.

The case then entered a prolonged appellate cycle. In February 2005, the sisters and the foundation appealed. The applicant intervened as a third party in August 2005 and was granted legal aid. On 7 September 2005, the Court of Appeal quashed the Regional Court judgment and dismissed the action as inadmissible, but on 4 May 2006 the Supreme Court quashed that decision and remitted the case, finding the plaintiffs had standing. The applicant’s constitutional complaint against that remittal was dismissed in March 2007 because the decision did not finally terminate the proceedings. In September 2006, the Court of Appeal again remitted the case to the Regional Court for further fact-finding. On 10 June 2008, the Regional Court again ordered the foundation to pay the sisters roughly EUR 240,000 each.

On 25 March 2009, the Court of Appeal reversed, finding that the assets had belonged to the applicant’s mother alone and that he had received them as a valid gift in 1993. However, on 1 October 2009, the Supreme Court quashed that judgment and remitted the case again, finding the facts insufficiently established. The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint on 19 October 2009, relying on Article 6 and alleging excessive length. On 21 May 2010, the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint as inadmissible because the Supreme Court’s remittal was not a final decision; it also noted that it could only declare a delay unreasonable, not undo it.

The Court of Appeal later stayed the proceedings pending the Strasbourg application. By April 2014, after the parties settled, it declared the proceedings terminated or permanently stayed. Overall, the key facts relevant to the alleged violation were the proceedings’ duration from September 2001 to at least 2010/2014, multiple appeals and remittals, repeated fact-finding, legal-aid delays, and the Constitutional Court’s limited ability to remedy length complaints before a final decision.

In *Bekerman v. Liechtenstein* (ECtHR, App. no. 34459/10, judgment of 3 September 2015), the applicant, Michael Bekerman, a German national born in 1955, complained that civil proceedings in Liechtenstein had exceeded a reasonable length and that he had exhausted all effective domestic remedies for that delay. The Court communicated only the length complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The case arose from disputes over assets worth more than CHF 14 million that Bekerman had transferred in 1999 into five Liechtenstein foundations, including the H. foundation, of which he was the beneficiary. His mother and two sisters, R. and K., claimed that part of those assets had not belonged to Bekerman but to his mother and to his deceased father’s estate. In August/September 2001, after the sisters obtained an interim injunction freezing over EUR 3 million held at a bank, they sued both the H. foundation and Bekerman for approximately EUR 3.3 million.

The litigation then went through repeated cycles of first-instance decisions, appeals, remittals, and renewed proceedings. In December 2004, the Regional Court ordered the H. foundation to pay each sister about EUR 240,000 and dismissed the remainder of their claim. It found that Bekerman had not proven that the assets he placed in the foundation were a gift from his mother, and that he had therefore not been authorised to transfer assets from his father’s estate into the foundation. Appeals followed. Bekerman, as beneficiary, was granted leave to intervene in 2005 and received legal aid, though he was later represented by his wife. In September 2005, the Court of Appeal dismissed the sisters’ action as inadmissible; in May 2006, the Supreme Court quashed that decision and remitted the case, finding that the sisters had standing. Bekerman’s constitutional complaint against that decision was dismissed in March 2007 as inadmissible because the remittal was not a final decision.

In September 2006, the Court of Appeal again remitted the case for further fact-finding. In June 2008, the Regional Court once more ordered payments of about EUR 240,000 to each sister. On appeal, in March 2009, the Court of Appeal reversed and dismissed the action, finding that the assets had belonged to Bekerman’s mother alone and had been validly gifted to him in 1993. In October 2009, the Supreme Court again quashed that judgment and remitted the case, holding that the Court of Appeal had insufficiently established the alleged donation. Bekerman then lodged a constitutional complaint, alleging, inter alia, that the proceedings had exceeded a reasonable time.

On 21 May 2010, the Constitutional Court dismissed his complaint as inadmissible because the Supreme Court’s remittal did not finally terminate the dispute. As to the length complaint, it stated that it could examine the issue after a final decision, but that excessive delay could not be effectively remedied; it could only declare the length unreasonable, not undo the delay. It also ordered Bekerman to pay the sisters’ lawyer’s costs of CHF 3,087.05 and declared court costs uncollectible. The underlying civil proceedings remained unresolved: after the ECtHR application, the Court of Appeal stayed proceedings, and in April 2014 the proceedings were declared terminated/stayed perpetually after the sisters and the H. foundation reached a settlement. These facts formed the basis of Bekerman’s complaint that the civil proceedings had been excessively long and that domestic remedies were inadequate.

**Summary of Vékony v. Hungary (Application no. 65681/13)**

The case of *Vékony v. Hungary* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr. László Vékony, a Hungarian national, against Hungary on 14 October 2013. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights, both alone and in conjunction with Article 14, claiming that the loss of his tobacco retail licence constituted an unjustified and discriminatory deprivation of possessions.

The facts are rooted in a significant regulatory change in Hungary. Since 1994, the applicant and his family operated a grocery business in Sopron that sold excise goods, including tobacco. Tobacco sales accounted for approximately one-third of the family enterprise's turnover. The applicant held a shop-keeping licence since 1999 and was registered as an excise goods trader in his own right since 2005.

On 11 September 2012, the Hungarian Parliament enacted Act no. CXXXIV of 2012, which fundamentally restructured tobacco retail. The Act, effective 1 July 2013, transformed tobacco retail from a market activity into a state monopoly, exercised through a state-owned company, ND Zrt. Retailers would be licensed via a concession tender. The tender required applicants to submit business plans aligned with new public health goals, such as limiting minors' access to tobacco products through separate shop entrances and obscured windows. The application deadline was 22 February 2013, with no privilege given to existing retailers.

The applicant applied for a concession on 4 February 2013 and amended his application on 20 February 2013. However, on 23 April 2013, he was informed that his application was unsuccessful. The decision provided no reasons or score. Consequently, his family business was forced to cease tobacco sales by 14 July 2013. The remaining business became unprofitable and was wound up. No compensation was available to former licence holders who lost their livelihood after failing to secure a concession. The applicant alleged considerable financial hardship in supporting his family.

The applicant argued that the loss of his business, without compensation and under allegedly discriminatory circumstances, violated his property rights. He contended that others, including those with no prior tobacco retail experience, were granted concessions, suggesting political favouritism. He pointed to successful tenderers who obtained multiple licences.

Regarding admissibility, the Government contested the application on two grounds. First, they argued the applicant was not a victim *ratione personae* because his mother held the prior excise licence. The Court rejected this, noting the licence benefited the family enterprise and the applicant himself held a shop-keeping licence for the same grocery and was registered as an excise goods trader, establishing a direct link to the harm. Second, the Government claimed the applicant failed to exhaust domestic remedies, arguing he should have filed a constitutional complaint. The applicant countered that this remedy was discretionary and exceptional, thus ineffective. The Court noted it required examination of whether this constitutional complaint, possibly combined with a civil action for damages, constituted an effective remedy. The judgment proceeds to assess the merits of these admissibility arguments and the substantive complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

Vékony v. Hungary (Application no. 65681/13) is a European Court of Human Rights case lodged on 14 October 2013 by László Vékony, a Hungarian national born in 1950. Since 1994, his family ran a grocery in Sopron, selling alcohol and tobacco under his mother’s excise licence; tobacco sales represented about one-third of the family business. Vékony held a shop-keeping licence from 1999, qualified as a trader and shop manager in 2001, and was registered in his own right as a trader of excise goods in 2005.

In September 2012, Hungary enacted Act no. CXXXIV of 2012 on tobacco retail, finalised in June 2013 and effective from 1 July 2013. The Act made tobacco retail a State monopoly exercised through ND Zrt and replaced the previous system of about 42,000 retail points with a concession tender granting approximately 6,800 licences nationwide. Existing tobacco retailers had no preferential treatment. Tenderers had to submit business plans reflecting public-health aims, especially limiting minors’ access to tobacco; sales were permitted only in shops with separate entrances, obscured windows, and a limited range of other goods. The application deadline was 22 February 2013.

Vékony applied on 4 February 2013 and amended his application on 20 February 2013 for use in the family enterprise. The Government later claimed the application was succinct and lacked an adequate business plan. On 23 April 2013, he was informed that he had not obtained a concession. The decision contained no reasons, no score on the 120-point tender sheet, and was not subject to legal remedy. The family was required to stop selling tobacco by 14 July 2013; wholesalers were obliged to repurchase stock. The remaining business became unprofitable and was wound up. No compensation was available for former tobacco retailers who lost part of their livelihood. Vékony claimed considerable difficulty supporting his family, including a minor son.

Before the Court, Vékony alleged that the loss of his tobacco retail licence amounted to an unjustified deprivation of possessions in discriminatory circumstances, violating Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 alone and in conjunction with Article 14 of the Convention. He argued that others in comparable—and even non-comparable—situations received concessions, which he attributed to political adherence, and noted that some successful tenderers obtained multiple selling points. The Hungarian Constitutional Court had dismissed similar complaints, holding that long-standing tobacco retail did not create acquired possessions or constitutionally protected legitimate expectations; no specific tobacco retail licence existed before the new law; excise and shop-keeping licences were revocable, non-transferable permits, not possessions. It found no permanent deprivation of entrepreneurial activity and considered the public-health restriction proportionate.

The Government contested admissibility. It argued that Vékony was not a victim ratione personae because his mother formally held the previous excise licence. It also argued that he should have filed a constitutional complaint, which could lead to damages. Vékony replied that Constitutional Court admission was discretionary and exceptional, and that the damages case law concerned an individual legislative act, not ordinary legislation.

The Court found a sufficiently direct link between Vékony and the harm: although his mother was the formal licence holder, the licence benefited the family enterprise, and Vékony himself held a shop-keeping licence and was registered as an excise goods trader entitling him to sell tobacco. The application was therefore not incompatible ratione personae. The Court examined the complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 alone.

In *Vékony v. Hungary* (App no 65681/13, 13 January 2015), the ECtHR examined Hungary’s tobacco retail monopoly and its effect on a family grocery. The applicant, László Vékony, a Hungarian national in Sopron, had from 1994 operated a family grocery selling excise goods, including alcohol and tobacco. Tobacco represented about one-third of turnover. He held a shop-keeping licence from 1999, qualified as a trader/shop manager in 2001, and in 2005 was registered as a trader of excise goods. Although the original excise licence was in his mother’s name, the business was familial and the applicant personally held licences permitting tobacco sales.

In 2012, Parliament enacted Act CXXXIV on the Repression of Smoking of the Youth and on Tobacco Retail. It made tobacco retail a State monopoly through ND Zrt and replaced about 42,000 retail points with a concession tender for up to five points per applicant. New rules required separate entrances, obscured windows, limited other goods, and no entry for under-18s. Existing tobacco retailers received no preference. The tender was advertised in December 2012, with a deadline of 22 February 2013. ND Zrt decided without reasons or scoring, and no legal remedy was available. About 6,800 licences were granted.

The applicant applied on 4 February 2013 and amended on 20 February. On 23 April 2013 he was told he had not obtained a concession. The decision gave no reasons or score and was not appealable. His family business had to stop tobacco sales by 14 July 2013. Wholesalers had to buy back stock, but the remaining grocery became unprofitable and closed. No compensation was available for former tobacco retailers who lost their licences.

The applicant alleged under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, alone and with Article 14, that the loss of his tobacco retail licence was an unjustified deprivation of possessions in discriminatory circumstances. He claimed others, including those without prior tobacco experience, received concessions, possibly due to political adherence, and some successful tenderers obtained multiple points. He also said he had difficulty supporting his family.

Domestically, the Constitutional Court admitted related complaints but dismissed them. It held that tobacco retail activity was not an acquired possession or legitimate expectation; the specific tobacco retail licence was created only by the new law. The excise licence was a revocable, non-transferable permit, not property. The law did not prevent the applicant from applying for a concession. The restriction on entrepreneurial activity was proportionate to public-health aims, especially reducing youth smoking, and fell within the State’s wide margin of appreciation.

Before the ECtHR, the Government argued the application was incompatible *ratione personae* because the previous licence was in the mother’s name, and that the applicant should have exhausted a constitutional complaint followed by a damages action. The Court rejected the victim-status objection: the applicant held a shop-keeping licence and was registered as an excise trader, giving a sufficiently direct link to the alleged harm. It also considered the constitutional complaint remedy discretionary and not effective, so it did not require exhaustion.

The Court examined the complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 alone and found a violation. It concluded that the loss of the applicant’s tobacco retail business without compensation imposed an excessive individual burden, despite the public-health objectives of the legislation.

In *Botezatu v. the Republic of Moldova* (Application no. 17899/08, judgment of 14 April 2015), the applicant, Radu Botezatu, a Moldovan police officer, complained that the Moldovan authorities failed to enforce a final domestic judgment ordering the Chișinău municipality to provide him and his family with social housing. On 21 July 2004, the Centru District Court issued that judgment; it was upheld on 19 October 2004 and became final on 4 November 2004. Enforcement proceedings began on 11 May 2005, but the judgment remained unexecuted for years. The applicant relied on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, alleging a breach of the right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, alleging interference with his possessions due to non-enforcement.

After the case was communicated to the Government, the applicant used the new domestic remedy created by Law No. 87, seeking enforcement and compensation. He claimed EUR 10,000 for non-pecuniary damage and MDL 129,700 (about EUR 7,886) for pecuniary damage, including MDL 123,200 for rent paid for alternative accommodation from September 2004 to December 2011, plus costs. He submitted four lease contracts, each concluded for less than three years.

On 30 November 2011, the Rîșcani District Court found violations of Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to non-enforcement lasting over seven years. It rejected the Ministry of Finance’s objections that the leases were fictitious or invalid for lack of registration, holding that contracts under three years were not subject to mandatory registration in the land register. It awarded MDL 112,000 (EUR 7,050) in non-pecuniary damages and granted the pecuniary and costs claims in full.

On 29 February 2012, the Chișinău Court of Appeal allowed the Ministry’s appeal, quashed the first-instance judgment, and found only an Article 6 violation for a delay of 78 months, from 11 May 2005 to 30 November 2011. It awarded MDL 36,000 (EUR 2,270) in non-pecuniary damages and MDL 8,965 (EUR 565) for costs, but dismissed the pecuniary damage claims as unsubstantiated. It held that the lease contracts were ineffective vis-à-vis the State under Article 876 of the Civil Code because they had not been registered in the land register. That judgment became final. On 8 August 2012, the municipality issued the applicant an occupancy voucher for a new flat; the Government informed the Court that the final judgment had been enforced that day. The applicant did not dispute this, meaning the total delay was 87 months.

Before the European Court, the Government argued that the applicant had lost victim status because the Law No. 87 remedy had acknowledged the violation and awarded compensation. The applicant disagreed, arguing that the domestic court had not expressly acknowledged the Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 violation and had failed to award pecuniary damages and full costs.

The Court joined the victim-status issue with the merits. It accepted that the domestic authorities had acknowledged a violation, but found the redress insufficient. The lease contracts did not exceed three years and were therefore not subject to mandatory land-register registration; dismissing the pecuniary claims was manifestly unreasonable. Following *Prodan v. Moldova*, the applicant must have suffered pecuniary damage from being deprived of control and use of the social housing awarded by final judgment for 87 months. The Court thus dismissed the Government’s objection, held that the applicant retained victim status, and found violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to delayed enforcement and inadequate domestic redress.

In *Botezatu v. the Republic of Moldova* (Application no. 17899/08, ECtHR, 14 April 2015), the applicant, Radu Botezatu, a Moldovan police officer, obtained a final domestic judgment on 4 November 2004 ordering the Chișinău municipality to provide him and his family with social housing. The judgment had been delivered by the Centru District Court on 21 July 2004 and upheld by the Chișinău Court of Appeal on 19 October 2004. Enforcement proceedings began on 11 May 2005, but the municipality failed to enforce the judgment for years.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights on 21 March 2008 under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, alleging that the authorities’ failure to enforce the final judgment violated his right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time and his right to peaceful enjoyment of his possessions.

After the case was communicated to the Government, the applicant used a new domestic remedy under Law no. 87, which entered into force on 1 July 2011 and allowed victims of unreasonable length of proceedings or non-enforcement of final judgments to seek acknowledgment and compensation. In August 2011, he asked the domestic courts to enforce the judgment and award damages: €10,000 for non-pecuniary damage, MDL 129,700 (about €7,886) for pecuniary damage, including MDL 123,200 in rent paid from September 2004 to December 2011 for alternative accommodation, and costs. He submitted four lease contracts, each for less than three years.

The Ministry of Finance challenged the lease contracts as fictitious, arguing that the landlady was a relative, lacked commercial registration for renting property, and had not registered the contracts with tax authorities until 2011 or in the land register. On 30 November 2011, the Rîșcani District Court found violations of Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to non-enforcement lasting over seven years. It rejected the Ministry’s arguments, holding that leases under three years did not require land-register registration and that the landlady’s tax failures did not invalidate the contracts or bind the applicant. It awarded MDL 112,000 (about €7,050) for non-pecuniary damage and allowed the pecuniary and costs claims in full.

On appeal, the Chișinău Court of Appeal reversed the judgment on 29 February 2012. It acknowledged only an Article 6 violation for a delay of 78 months, from 11 May 2005 to 30 November 2011. It awarded MDL 36,000 (about €2,270) for non-pecuniary damage and MDL 8,965 (about €565) for costs, but dismissed the pecuniary claim as unsubstantiated, finding the lease contracts ineffective against the State under Article 876 of the Civil Code. That judgment became final.

The municipality issued an occupancy voucher on 8 August 2012, and the Government stated that the final judgment had then been enforced; the applicant did not dispute this. The total delay was therefore 87 months.

Before the Court, the Government argued that the applicant had lost victim status because the domestic court had acknowledged the violation and awarded compensation. The applicant maintained that the domestic redress was insufficient, especially because no pecuniary damages were awarded and no violation of Protocol No. 1 was expressly acknowledged. The Court joined the victim-status question to the merits and declared the application admissible. It found that while the breach had been acknowledged domestically, the redress was inadequate: the applicant had been deprived of the use of the social housing for 87 months and had submitted lease contracts for alternative accommodation, which did not require land-register registration. The failure to award pecuniary compensation was manifestly unreasonable. The applicant thus retained victim status, and the Court found violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to the delayed enforcement and insufficient domestic redress.

Botezatu v. the Republic of Moldova (ECtHR, Third Section, 14 April 2015, app. no. 17899/08) concerned the non-enforcement of a final domestic judgment granting social housing. The applicant, Radu Botezatu, a Moldovan police officer, obtained a judgment on 21 July 2004 from the Centru District Court ordering the Chișinău municipality to provide him and his family with social housing. The Chișinău Court of Appeal upheld it on 19 October 2004, and it became final on 4 November 2004. Enforcement proceedings began on 11 May 2005, but the municipality did not provide housing for years.

After the case was communicated to the Government, the applicant used the domestic remedy under Law no. 87, which allows acknowledgment and compensation for unreasonable length of proceedings or non-enforcement of final judgments. He sought enforcement plus non-pecuniary damages of EUR 10,000, pecuniary damages of MDL 129,700 (about EUR 7,886), including MDL 123,200 for rent paid from September 2004 to December 2011, and costs.

The Ministry of Finance disputed the lease contracts supporting the rent claim, alleging they were fictitious because the landlady was a relative, lacked commercial registration, and the contracts were not registered with tax authorities until 2011 or in the land register.

On 30 November 2011, the Rîșcani District Court found violations of Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to non-enforcement of the final judgment for over seven years. It rejected the Ministry’s arguments, noting the leases were for less than three years and thus not subject to mandatory land-register registration. It awarded MDL 112,000 (EUR 7,050) non-pecuniary damages and granted pecuniary and costs claims in full.

On appeal, the Chișinău Court of Appeal, by final judgment of 29 February 2012, quashed that decision. It acknowledged only an Article 6 violation for non-enforcement lasting 78 months (11 May 2005 to 30 November 2011). It awarded MDL 36,000 (EUR 2,270) non-pecuniary damages and MDL 8,965 (EUR 565) costs, but dismissed pecuniary damages as unsubstantiated, holding the leases ineffective against the State under Article 876 of the Civil Code because they were not registered. The applicant later received an occupancy voucher on 8 August 2012, meaning the final judgment was enforced after an 87-month delay.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged that the authorities had failed to fully enforce the final judgment, violating Article 6 § 1 (reasonable time) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions). The Government argued he had lost victim status because Law no. 87 proceedings had acknowledged the violation and awarded compensation.

The ECtHR joined the victim-status issue to the merits. It found that although domestic courts acknowledged the Article 6 breach, the redress was inadequate. The lease contracts did not exceed three years, so under domestic law they were not subject to mandatory land-register registration. The domestic court’s refusal to award any pecuniary damages for rent/loss of use was manifestly unreasonable under the Court’s case-law. The applicant therefore remained a victim. The Court dismissed the Government’s objection and found violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to the delayed enforcement and insufficient domestic redress.
