**M.S. v. Croatia (No. 2)** concerned a Croatian woman, M.S., who complained that she had been unlawfully confined in a psychiatric hospital and ill-treated there, in violation of Article 3 and Article 5 §§ 1 (e) and 4 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

In the background, M.S. had been under the supervision of a social care centre and received financial assistance. In 2008 her family doctor noted various somatic complaints and a “peculiar interpretation” of her health issues, recommending psychological/psychiatric treatment, but stating that her consent had not been obtained. The social care centre later sought to divest her of legal capacity, although that request was withdrawn in 2013.

The key events occurred on 29 October 2012. M.S. visited her family doctor complaining of severe lower-back pain. After examination, she was sent to the emergency service. The emergency doctor found her general condition good, conscious and well oriented, but with difficulty moving; he diagnosed lumbago and referred her to a neurologist. The neurologist found her information incoherent and disproportionate to her pain and noted she had not taken her medication. He diagnosed back pain and anxiety disorder and referred her to a psychiatrist. The psychiatrist found fanciful and confusing allegations of persecution by doctors, diagnosed acute psychotic disorder, systemic delusional disorder and delusional dysmorphic disorder, and prescribed hospitalisation.

M.S. was immediately admitted to a psychiatric clinic. The admission record recorded that she refused examination by a psychiatrist, requested a somatic examination, was suspicious, tense, distanced and had ideas of persecution and control. She refused hospitalisation; consent was marked “NO”; and physical restraint—tying to a bed—was recorded. A later examination noted she had been brought on a stretcher, tied down, negative, yelling, agitated and paranoid, with a diagnosis of acute psychotic disorder.

M.S. alleged that she was tied to a bed with four belts around her wrists and ankles, forcefully injected with a strong drug, and kept restrained overnight. She claimed this caused severe back pain, especially because her left leg was restrained in a painful position, and that the room was small and had no windows. The Government disputed this account. It stated that she received usual treatment for psychotic agitation, was placed in an isolation room with video surveillance, measuring 2.50 by 2.12 metres, equipped with a bed, heating, air-conditioning and access to sanitary facilities. The belts were specially adapted to avoid injury. The Government said she was restrained from admission at 8:50 p.m. on 29 October until the next morning, then in a regular room until noon, and monitored throughout; she was not restrained again. Medical records indicated restraint from 8:50 p.m. on 29 October until around noon on 30 October 2012.

On 30 October the hospital informed the County Court of the involuntary admission, stating that M.S. refused further hospitalisation and that her mental condition prevented a sound decision. The court instituted involuntary-retention proceedings and appointed a legal-aid lawyer. On 31 October a judge visited M.S. She said she had gone to the doctor for back pain but had been placed in hospital by subterfuge, and alleged that patients would be used for “practising” by foreign doctors. She said she had never previously been treated in a psychiatric hospital. The judge provisionally extended her detention until 6 November and commissioned a psychiatric expert report.

The expert found a serious psychotic disorder and considered that release could seriously endanger her health, requiring involuntary retention for a further month. At the hearing on 6 November, which lasted ten minutes, neither M.S.’s representative nor the judge asked the expert questions. The court ordered her retention until 28 November 2012. M.S. appealed, arguing there was no reason for confinement and that she was under strong medication. Her sister also appealed, complaining that M.S. had been forcefully taken to hospital, tied to a bed all night in agony from back pain, that nobody explained the procedure, and that the legal-aid lawyer never visited her.

M.S. also wrote to the hospital director on 8 November, complaining about being tied to a bed without reason, violation of her dignity, ignored back pain, lack of explanation, and the lawyer’s failure to visit. The complaint was never forwarded to the director or any competent hospital authority. On 13 November the County Court dismissed the appeals and referred complaints about rights and treatment to the State Board and Hospital Ethical Board. No further action appears to have been taken. M.S. was discharged on 29 November 2012. These facts formed the basis of her allegations of ill-treatment and unlawful, arbitrarily prolonged psychiatric detention with ineffective judicial review.

M.S. v. Croatia (No. 2) (Application no. 75450/12) concerned a Croatian woman born in 1962 who alleged that she had been unlawfully confined in a psychiatric hospital and ill-treated there, in violation of Article 3 and Article 5 §§ 1(e) and 4 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

She had long been under the supervision of a social care centre. In June 2008 her family doctor noted multiple health complaints and suggested psychiatric treatment, but she did not consent. The social care centre sought to divest her of legal capacity, later withdrawing that request in 2013.

On 29 October 2012 she visited her family doctor for severe lower-back pain. Emergency and neurological examinations found back pain and anxiety; she was conscious and oriented but gave incoherent information and had not taken her medication. A psychiatrist then found fanciful allegations of persecution by doctors and diagnosed acute psychotic disorder, systemic delusional disorder and delusional dysmorphic disorder, prescribing hospitalisation. She refused consent but was immediately admitted to the psychiatric clinic of the R. Clinical Hospital Centre. Admission records note she refused psychiatric examination, requested a somatic examination, was suspicious, had persecutory/control ideas, refused hospitalisation, consent “NO,” and was physically restrained and tied to a bed. An evening examination described her as brought on a stretcher, tied down, negative, arguing, yelling, agitated, with paranoid ideas.

The applicant alleged that she was tied to a bed with four belts around her wrists and ankles and forcibly injected with a strong drug. She remained restrained overnight, suffered severe back pain, and her left leg was restrained painfully; the room was small and windowless. The Government said this was usual treatment for psychotic agitation. She was placed in an isolation room measuring 2.50 by 2.12 metres, under video surveillance, with a bed and sanitary access; the belts were specially adapted. According to the Government, she was restrained from 8:50 p.m. on 29 October until the next morning, then in a regular room until noon, and monitored. Medical records confirm restraint from 8:50 p.m. on 29 October until about noon on 30 October, recording screaming, restiveness, threats, back pain, poor sleep, water intake and refusal to sign consent.

On 30 October the hospital informed R. County Court of the involuntary admission. The court appointed a legal-aid lawyer. On 31 October a judge visited her; she said she had been hospitalised by subterfuge, claimed no prior psychiatric hospital treatment, and mentioned being used for practice by foreign doctors. The judge provisionally extended detention until 6 November and ordered a psychiatric expert report. The expert found a manifest psychotic disorder and serious mental illness, concluding that release would seriously endanger her health and that one month’s involuntary retention was necessary. At the 6 November hearing, lasting ten minutes, neither her representative nor the judge questioned the expert. The court ordered retention until 28 November.

She appealed on 7 November; her sister appealed on 9 November, complaining of forceful taking to hospital, being tied to a bed all night in agony from back pain, lack of explanation, and that the legal-aid lawyer never visited. A handwritten complaint to the hospital director was never forwarded. On 13 November a three-judge panel dismissed the appeals, endorsing the lower court and advising her to complain to the State Board for Protection of Individuals with Mental Disorders or the hospital Ethical Board. She was discharged on 29 November 2012. These facts underpinned her complaints that the involuntary confinement and restraint lacked adequate legal and procedural safeguards and amounted to ill-treatment.

M.S. v. Croatia (No. 2) concerned a Croatian woman, born 1962, who had received social-care assistance and had earlier legal-capacity proceedings. On 29 October 2012 she saw her family doctor for severe lower-back pain. The doctor sent her to emergency care. A neurologist found her account incoherent and disproportionate to her pain, noted she had not taken medication, and diagnosed back pain and anxiety, referring her to a psychiatrist. The psychiatrist found fanciful allegations of persecution by doctors and diagnosed acute psychotic disorder, systemic delusional disorder and delusional dysmorphic disorder, prescribing hospitalisation. She refused, but was immediately admitted to a psychiatric clinic.

The admission record noted she refused psychiatric examination, requested a somatic examination, was suspicious and paranoid, refused hospitalisation, and recorded “Consent: NO” and “physical restraint, tying to a bed.” An evening examination described her as brought on a stretcher, tied down, agitated, yelling, with paranoid ideas. She alleged she was tied to a bed with four belts around her wrists and ankles, forcibly injected with a strong drug, and left overnight, causing severe back pain; the room was small and windowless. The Government said she was in an isolation room under video surveillance, with a bed, heating, air-conditioning and sanitary facilities; the belts were adapted to avoid injury. She was restrained from 8.50 p.m. on 29 October until about noon on 30 October, monitored regularly, and not restrained again. Medical records noted screaming, restiveness, kicking, fixed hands and legs, complaints of lower-back pain, poor sleep, and that she did not sign consent.

On 30 October the hospital informed the County Court of her involuntary admission, stating she refused further hospitalisation and her mental condition prevented a sound decision. The court appointed a legal-aid lawyer and opened involuntary-retention proceedings. On 31 October a judge visited her. She said she had gone to her doctor for back pain but was hospitalised by subterfuge and believed she would be used for “practising” by foreign doctors; she had no prior psychiatric hospital treatment. The judge provisionally extended detention until 6 November and ordered a psychiatric report. The expert, on 2 November, found a psychotic disorder amounting to serious mental illness and that release could endanger her health, requiring further retention for a month. At the 6 November hearing, lasting ten minutes, neither the judge nor her representative questioned the expert. The court ordered retention until 28 November.

The applicant appealed on 7 November, claiming no reason for confinement and that she was under strong medication. Her sister appealed on 9 November: she had been forcefully taken to hospital, tied to a bed all night in agony from back pain, never had the procedure explained, and the legal-aid lawyer never visited. A handwritten complaint to the hospital director also alleged unjustified tying, violated dignity, ignored back pain, and no explanation; it was never forwarded. The appeals were dismissed on 13 November, with complaints referred to the State Board and Ethical Board. She was discharged on 29 November 2012. In *M.A. v. Austria* (Application no. 4097/13, judgment of 15 January 2015), the applicant, an Italian national, alleged that Austria violated his right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the Convention by failing to enforce Italian court orders requiring his daughter’s return to Italy.

Under Italian law, the parents had joint custody. On 31 January 2008, D.P. left the family home with the child and moved to Austria. The applicant obtained an Italian travel ban on 8 February 2008, but D.P. had already left Italy with the child.

On 23 May 2008, the Venice Youth Court lifted the travel ban, granted preliminary joint custody, allowed the child to reside with her mother in Austria, and granted the applicant access rights. The applicant then sought the child’s return under the 1980 Hague Convention. Austrian courts initially refused return, finding that returning the child to Italy would create a grave risk of psychological harm under Article 13(b) of the Hague Convention because it would separate her from her mother.

Meanwhile, the Venice Youth Court issued a judgment on 10 July 2009 ordering the child’s return to Italy. Under that order, the child would live with her mother if the mother returned to Italy; otherwise she would live with the applicant. The Venice court certified the judgment as enforceable under Article 42 of the Brussels IIa Regulation. Austrian courts eventually recognized the order’s enforceability. In *C-211/10 PPU* (1 July 2010), the CJEU confirmed Italian jurisdiction and the enforceability of the return order, holding that Austrian courts could not refuse enforcement because of changed circumstances; such issues had to be raised before the Italian courts. In *Ruban v. Ukraine* (Application no. 8927/11), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Ukraine violated Article 7 of the Convention by sentencing the applicant to life imprisonment rather than applying what he claimed was the most lenient version of the criminal law.

The applicant, Mr Vladimir Nikolayevich Ruban, a Ukrainian national born in 1972, was serving a life sentence. The charges arose from crimes committed in 1996 and 1999. Investigations concerned the 1996 murder of four persons, the 1999 murder of A., and hooliganism/grievous bodily harm involving R. Several suspects, including the applicant, were alleged to have acted as an organised group. In December 1999 the applicant was charged in absentia and placed on a wanted list; proceedings against other suspects continued, and in 2002 G., P., and F. were convicted. The applicant was apprehended in Russia in June 2007 and extradited to Ukraine. In March 2008 the investigation resumed, and he was charged with participation in an organised criminal group, strangling A., killing four persons together with G. in 1996, and inflicting grievous bodily harm on R. in a murder attempt linked to extortion. In July 2009 the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal convicted him of aggravated murder and banditry and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The Supreme Court upheld that judgment on 15 July 2010.

The Article 7 issue concerned the sentencing law. Under the 1960 Criminal Code, aggravated murder was punishable by 8 to 15 years’ imprisonment or the death penalty. On 29 December 1999 the Constitutional Court declared the death penalty unconstitutional, ruling that the relevant provisions were null and void immediately and ordering Parliament to align the Code. Parliament then adopted Law no. 1483, which replaced the death penalty with life imprisonment and entered into force on 29 March 2000. A new Criminal Code entered into force in 2001, also providing life imprisonment for aggravated murder. In 2008, a humanisation amendment confirmed retroactive effect for laws mitigating liability. In 2011, the Constitutional Court interpreted the transition, deciding that after 29 December 1999 the 1960 Code had not become a new law mitigating liability to only 15 years; rather, Law no. 1483 was the new mitigating law with retroactive effect.

The applicant argued that the domestic courts should have applied the most favourable version of the law—the period between 29 December 1999 and 29 March 2000—when the death penalty had been abolished but life imprisonment had not yet been introduced. He claimed that during this gap the maximum penalty was 15 years’ imprisonment. The Government maintained that no such separate lenient version existed and that the courts correctly applied life imprisonment.

The ECtHR declared the complaint admissible but found no violation. It accepted that Article 7 implicitly requires retroactive application of more lenient criminal laws. However, it was primarily for domestic authorities to interpret national law. The Constitutional Court’s 1999 decision removed the death penalty immediately, creating an unintentional gap. Yet there was no legislative intent to reduce aggravated murder to a maximum of 15 years. At the time of the crime the death penalty applied; Parliament replaced it with life imprisonment, which it considered proportionate. Since life imprisonment is not heavier than the death penalty, the domestic courts did not violate Article 7 by sentencing the applicant to life imprisonment.

In *Ruban v. Ukraine* (Application no. 8927/11, judgment 12 July 2016), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Ukraine violated Article 7 by sentencing the applicant to life imprisonment instead of applying an allegedly more lenient interim version of the Criminal Code. The applicant, a Ukrainian national, was accused of crimes committed in 1996, including aggravated murder of four persons, another murder, hooliganism, and grievous bodily harm during an extortion attempt. In December 1999 he was charged in absentia and placed on the wanted list. Other suspects were convicted in 2002. Ruban was arrested in Russia in June 2007, extradited to Ukraine, and in March 2008 charged with participation in an organised criminal group and the earlier offences. In July 2009 the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal convicted him of aggravated murder and banditry and imposed life imprisonment. The Supreme Court upheld that judgment in July 2010.

The Article 7 complaint concerned the sequence of Ukrainian criminal-law changes. When the crimes were committed in 1996, the 1960 Criminal Code provided for 8–15 years’ imprisonment or the death penalty for aggravated murder. On 29 December 1999, the Constitutional Court declared the death penalty unconstitutional and stated that the relevant provisions were null and void immediately. Parliament did not replace the death penalty with life imprisonment until Law no. 1483, which entered into force on 29 March 2000. The applicant argued that between these dates there was a legal gap: the death penalty had been abolished, but life imprisonment had not yet been introduced. Therefore, the most favourable wording of the law available before his final conviction allowed a maximum of fifteen years’ imprisonment. He contended that the domestic courts’ failure to apply that version violated Article 7.

The Government argued that no such separate version of the Code existed. Criminal law could only be amended by Parliament, and the death penalty provisions retained their alternative character until the March 2000 amendments. It relied on the Constitutional Court’s 2011 interpretation, which held that the replacement of the death penalty with life imprisonment was a new mitigating law with retroactive effect, but that the 1960 Code had not become a new law immediately after the 1999 decision.

The European Court reiterated that Article 7 implicitly requires retroactive application of the most lenient criminal law enacted before final conviction. It accepted that the Constitutional Court’s 1999 decision immediately voided the death penalty and created an unintentional interim gap. Nevertheless, the Court examined the legislature’s intent and the wider context. Ukraine abolished the death penalty as part of human-rights reforms, and Parliament then chose life imprisonment as the proportionate replacement. At the time of the offence, the death penalty was applicable, and life imprisonment is not a heavier penalty than death. There was no indication that the State intended to reduce the maximum penalty for aggravated murder to fifteen years during the interim period. The domestic courts therefore did not upset the applicant’s Article 7 rights by applying the version of the law in force at conviction, which provided for life imprisonment. The Court declared the complaint admissible but found no violation of Article 7.

**Summary of *Ruban v. Ukraine* (Application no. 8927/11)**

In *Ruban v. Ukraine*, the European Court of Human Rights considered an Article 7 complaint concerning the retroactive application of the most lenient criminal law. The applicant, Mr Vladimir Nikolayevich Ruban, a Ukrainian national born in 1972, was serving a life sentence. He alleged that Ukrainian courts had violated Article 7 by failing to apply the most favourable version of the Criminal Code when sentencing him.

The underlying crimes occurred in 1996. Investigations began into the murder of four persons, the murder of A., and hooliganism concerning R. These investigations were joined in November 1999, and several suspects, including the applicant, were suspected of acting as a group. In December 1999, the applicant was charged in absentia and placed on a wanted list; proceedings continued against other suspects, who were convicted in 2002. The applicant was arrested in Russia in June 2007 and extradited to Ukraine. In March 2008, he was formally charged with participation in an organised criminal group, strangling A., killing four persons together with G. in 1996, and inflicting grievous bodily harm on R. in an attempted murder connected to extortion.

In July 2009, the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal, acting as a first-instance court, found the applicant guilty of aggravated murder and banditry and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The Supreme Court of Ukraine upheld that judgment in July 2010. In an additional appeal, the applicant argued that the courts should have applied the version of the 1960 Criminal Code in force between 29 December 1999 and 29 March 2000. On 29 December 1999, the Constitutional Court had declared the death penalty unconstitutional and immediately void. Life imprisonment was only introduced as a replacement on 29 March 2000. According to the applicant, during that interim period the maximum penalty for aggravated murder was therefore fifteen years’ imprisonment, so imposing life imprisonment violated Article 7.

The Government disputed this, arguing that the Constitutional Court’s decision did not create a new, more lenient criminal law. It contended that the Criminal Code changed only when Parliament replaced the death penalty with life imprisonment, and that life imprisonment was in any event less severe than the death penalty.

The Court reiterated that Article 7 includes the principle that a more lenient criminal law enacted before final conviction must be applied retroactively. However, it noted that domestic authorities primarily interpret national law. The Court accepted that the death penalty provisions had lost force immediately and that an unintended legislative gap existed between 29 December 1999 and 29 March 2000. Nevertheless, it found no legislative intention to reduce the punishment for aggravated murder to only fifteen years. At the time of the crime, the offence was punishable by death; Parliament later chose life imprisonment as the proportionate replacement. Since life imprisonment is not a heavier penalty than the death penalty, the domestic courts’ refusal to apply the interim wording did not violate the applicant’s rights under Article 7. The Court therefore declared the complaint admissible but found **no violation of Article 7 of the Convention**.

R.B.A.B. and Others v. the Netherlands (Application no. 7211/06) concerned five Sudanese nationals—parents Mrs R.B.A.B. and Mr H.S., their daughters X and Y, and son Z—who had lived in the Netherlands since 2001. They complained under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights that the daughters faced a real risk of female genital mutilation (FGM) if expelled to Sudan.

The family’s asylum history was central. In 2001 the parents sought asylum, claiming they fled after Mr H.S. attracted attention from Sudanese authorities for opposition activities. The Deputy Minister rejected their requests in January 2002, finding their statements lacking credibility due to contradictions, inability to answer basic tribal questions, lack of topographic knowledge of their alleged home area, and ignorance about the opposition movement. Their appeals were declared inadmissible for failure to submit grounds, and an objection was dismissed. A second asylum request in April 2003 was rejected as not based on new facts or altered circumstances; they did not appeal.

In June 2005 the family filed a third asylum request, now claiming that daughters X and Y would be subjected to FGM in Sudan because of tribal and social pressure. The parents said they opposed FGM but could not protect the girls. They submitted a Sudanese Embassy document acknowledging they were Sudanese citizens but lacked documents for a laissez-passer. The Minister intended to reject the request, doubting the sincerity of the FGM fear because it had not been raised earlier. She relied on the 2004 Sudan official report and WBV 2004/36, which stated that higher-educated women in large cities could resist FGM without social stigma, while low-educated rural women had little choice. Since identity and origin remained unsubstantiated and earlier asylum statements lacked credibility, the applicants had not shown they fell outside the educated group able to reject FGM. The father’s shoplifting penalty was also noted. The applicants argued the first applicant had only primary education and offered an IQ test; the Minister said the burden was on them to prove identity and background.

The Regional Court granted provisional relief and quashed the refusal. It noted nationality was undisputed, the daughters—then 14 and 11—were uncircumcised, and Dutch policy required a risk of FGM, lack of state protection, and no internal relocation option. FGM was widespread, the law was hardly enforced, educated urban women generally did not circumcise their daughters, and internal relocation was unclear, with individual declarations decisive. The refusal based largely on unproven identity and prior credibility could not stand, especially because the present claim concerned protection of the daughters. In August 2005 the Council of State allowed the Minister’s further appeal. Under the Aliens Act, applicants bore the burden to make eligibility plausible; prior credibility findings were res judicata; and the Minister could reasonably find the policy conditions, lack of protection, and absence of internal relocation were not established. No further appeal lay.

Later, X received a residence permit in 2015 and withdrew her application. Y’s 2012 request was rejected in 2015: her parents opposed FGM and likely would not force her, she had no identity or Dilling-origin documents, and internal relocation was not addressed. Z’s request under the transitional children regulation failed because the family had evaded immigration monitoring for over three months. Country materials indicated FGM prevalence around 90%, no specific criminal prohibition or effective prosecution, parental choice tied to family and community pressure, educated urban families increasingly refusing without problems, rural and low-educated women facing pressure, no shelters, and relocation to avoid FGM practically not occurring. Sudan signed but did not ratify the Maputo Protocol.

**Summary of Manucharyan v. Armenia (Application no. 35688/11)**

The case of *Manucharyan v. Armenia* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr Spartak Manucharyan, an Armenian national, on 31 May 2011. The applicant alleged that he had been denied a fair trial under Article 6 of the Convention because his conviction was based on untested witness evidence—specifically, his inability to obtain the attendance and examination of a witness against him. This complaint was communicated to the Armenian Government on 11 July 2013, while the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The facts arise from the murder of K.S., who was shot dead at approximately 1:30 a.m. on 1 July 2009 in Alaverdi. Later that day, the applicant presented himself to the police, surrendered a gun, and confessed to the murder. He was charged with murder and illegal possession of firearms. The same day, police interviewed K.M., K.S.'s girlfriend, who had witnessed the shooting. She stated that the applicant, her neighbour, had yelled and sworn before shooting at K.S.'s car moments after she got out of it. The applicant subsequently denied the charges and refused to testify.

On 14 January 2010, the applicant's brother, V.M., was killed. At an additional questioning on 9 March 2010, the applicant retracted his confession, claiming he had confessed to cover up for V.M., who had a newborn baby and cared for their parents. He stated there was no longer any need to protect V.M. because he was dead. The applicant's alibi was that he had visited V.J., a friend of his father, at around 10:30 p.m. on the night of the murder and stayed until around 2:30 a.m. However, V.J. was interviewed on 12 March 2010 and denied the applicant had stayed that late, stating the applicant arrived around 10 p.m., stayed only about an hour and a half, and left with V.M. at around 11:30 p.m. V.J. reiterated this account during a formal confrontation with the applicant.

The prosecution relied on statements from several witnesses, including K.M., K.S.'s sister S.S., K.M.'s parents S.M. and A.M., and V.J., as well as forensic evidence showing gunshot residue on the applicant's clothes. The case was referred to the Lori Regional Court for trial, with the first hearing scheduled for 21 May 2010. K.M. was summoned but failed to appear. The Regional Court repeatedly ordered her attendance, compelling her appearance through police enforcement, but she remained absent. Certificates indicated she was absent from her residence, and on one occasion her mother stated she was abroad. The Regional Court eventually examined the case in K.M.'s absence and convicted the applicant on 4 November 2010, sentencing him to thirteen years' imprisonment. The court relied heavily on K.M.'s pre-trial statements, which were the only direct evidence incriminating the applicant.

The applicant appealed, complaining that K.M., the sole eyewitness, had not been examined in court. The Criminal Court of Appeal summoned her for a hearing on 11 January 2011, but she again failed to appear. The applicant sought to have her statements declared inadmissible, but the Court of Appeal failed to address this application. On 26 January 2011, the Court of Appeal upheld the conviction, relying on the same evidence and not addressing K.M.'s non-attendance. The applicant's appeal on points of law was declared inadmissible by the Court of Cassation on 12 April 2011 for lack of merit.

The key alleged violation is that the applicant's conviction was based decisively on the untested pre-trial statement of K.M., the sole eyewitness, whom the applicant never had an opportunity to examine or have examined in court, thus breaching his right to a fair trial under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention.

**Case summary: Manucharyan v. Armenia (Application no. 35688/11)**

The case concerns an Armenian national, Spartak Manucharyan, who complained that his criminal conviction was unfair because it relied on untested witness evidence, contrary to Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The key alleged violation was his inability to obtain the attendance and examination of a witness against him, particularly K.M.

On 1 July 2009, K.S. was shot dead at about 1:30 a.m. in Alaverdi. Later that day, the applicant presented himself to the police, surrendered a gun, and confessed to the murder. He was charged with murder and illegal possession of firearms. K.M., K.S.’s girlfriend, had been present at the scene. In her police interview, she stated that the applicant, her neighbour, after yelling and swearing, started shooting at K.S.’s car moments after she got out of it. Other witnesses also gave statements: K.S.’s sister described prior tension, and K.M.’s parents said they heard gunshots and that K.M. ran into their house crying, saying the applicant had killed K.S.

The applicant initially denied the charges and refused to testify. Later, on 9 March 2010, he retracted his confession, claiming he had confessed to protect his brother, V.M., who had been killed in January 2010. He said he had been at V.J.’s house until about 2:30 a.m. V.J., however, contradicted him, stating that the applicant had left around 11:30 p.m. with V.M. A formal confrontation between the applicant and V.J. took place.

The prosecution relied on statements from S.S., K.M., S.M., A.M., and V.J., the confrontation record, forensic evidence—including gunshot residue on the applicant’s clothes—and records of his confession and surrender of the gun. At trial before the Lori Regional Court, K.M. was repeatedly summoned but failed to appear. The police reported that she was absent from her residence and later that she was abroad. The court ordered her compelled attendance, but this remained unenforced. Eventually, the Regional Court examined the case in K.M.’s absence. On 4 November 2010, the applicant was convicted and sentenced to thirteen years’ imprisonment. The judgment relied on K.M.’s pre-trial statement, among other evidence.

The applicant appealed, arguing that K.M., the sole eyewitness whose pre-trial statement was the only direct evidence directly incriminating him, had never been examined in court. The Court of Appeal summoned K.M., but she again did not appear. According to the applicant, his request to exclude her statements was not ruled upon. On 26 January 2011, the Court of Appeal upheld the conviction without addressing her non-attendance. On 12 April 2011, the Court of Cassation declared his appeal inadmissible.

The central fair-trial issue was whether the domestic courts could rely on K.M.’s untested pre-trial statement without giving the defence an opportunity to cross-examine her. Since she was a key witness and her evidence was important to the conviction, the European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 6 § 1 in conjunction with Article 6 § 3(d), holding that the proceedings had been unfair.

Armenia*, the applicant, Spartak Manucharyan, complained under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights that he had been denied a fair trial because his murder conviction was based on untested witness evidence—specifically, the pre-trial statement of K.M., the sole eyewitness, whom he was unable to have attend and examine in court.

The case arose after K.S. was shot dead in Alaverdi at about 1:30 a.m. on 1 July 2009. Later that day, Manucharyan presented himself to the police, surrendered a gun and confessed to the murder. He was charged with murder and illegal possession of firearms. K.M., K.S.’s girlfriend, had been present at the scene and told police that Manucharyan, her neighbour, had shouted and sworn before shooting at K.S.’s car moments after she got out. Other witnesses, including K.S.’s sister and K.M.’s parents, gave statements about prior tensions and about K.M. saying immediately after the shooting that Manucharyan had killed K.S.

Manucharyan initially denied the charges and refused to testify. On 9 March 2010, after his brother V.M. was killed, he changed his account. He claimed he had confessed to cover for V.M., who had a newborn baby and cared for their parents, and that there was no longer any need to protect V.M. because he was dead. He gave an alibi that he had been at V.J.’s house until about 2:30 a.m. V.J. disputed this, stating that Manucharyan had arrived around 10 p.m. but left about an hour and a half later with V.M.; he maintained that account during a formal confrontation.

The prosecution relied on pre-trial statements from K.M., S.S., K.M.’s parents and V.J., records of investigative actions, forensic examinations, and biochemical evidence showing gunshot residue on the clothes Manucharyan wore on the day of the murder. At trial, K.M. did not appear. The Regional Court summoned her several times, issued orders to compel her attendance, and involved the police, but she could not be found. Her mother reportedly said K.M. was abroad. The Regional Court eventually tried the case in K.M.’s absence and, on 4 November 2010, convicted Manucharyan as charged, sentencing him to thirteen years’ imprisonment. In its judgment, the court expressly relied on K.M.’s pre-trial statement as evidence proving the crime. Because K.M. was the only eyewitness and her statement was the only direct evidence identifying Manucharyan as the shooter, her untested evidence was central to the conviction.

Manucharyan appealed, arguing that K.M. had never been examined in court. The Court of Appeal summoned K.M. again, but she did not appear. The applicant asked that her statements be declared inadmissible; according to him, the Court of Appeal did not address that request and, on 26 January 2011, upheld the conviction based on the same evidence, without discussing K.M.’s non-attendance. His cassation appeal complained about the lack of examination of witnesses against him at both court levels, but on 12 April 2011 the Court of Cassation declared it inadmissible for lack of merit.

The Strasbourg Court communicated only the complaint concerning the applicant’s inability to obtain the attendance and examination of a witness against him; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The key issue was therefore whether reliance on K.M.’s untested pre-trial statement, without any opportunity for the defence to question her, violated the applicant’s fair-trial rights, particularly his right to examine witnesses against him.

In *Bimuradova v. Russia* (Application no. 3769/11), the European Court of Human Rights’ First Section delivered judgment on 12 November 2015; it became final on 14 March 2016. The application was lodged on 2 December 2010 and communicated to the Russian Government on 9 September 2011.

According to the applicant, at about 3 p.m. on 27 May 2002 (also referred to as 26 May 2002), Magomed Bimuradov was abducted from a street near his house in Bas-Gordali by a group of armed masked men in a white car. He was forced into the car, which drove towards the village of Shuani in the Nozhay-Yurt district of Chechnya. The abductors allegedly belonged to the federal forces. He has been missing since. The applicant stated that two villagers, Mr E.Ts. and Ms Kh.Ts., witnessed the abduction, but she did not provide their statements to the Court, and they apparently did not testify in the official investigation. She submitted an undated joint statement by herself and two sisters, none of whom were present during the abduction. The Government did not dispute the facts as presented, but denied any involvement of State servicemen.

On 1 October 2002 the Nozhay-Yurt district prosecutor’s office opened criminal case no. 71056 under Article 105 of the Criminal Code (murder). On 14 October 2002 the applicant was granted victim status. In October and November 2002 investigators sent information requests to various law-enforcement agencies about possible detention; replies were negative. On 2 December 2002 the investigation was suspended for failure to identify suspects. In July 2003 investigators provided statements that Magomed had gone missing and had not been involved in an illegal armed group. On 31 March 2004 the military prosecutor’s office of military unit no. 20116 replied to the applicant’s sister that it was impossible to verify the theory that military servicemen were involved. Kalda v. Estonia (Application no. 17429/10) concerned Romeo Kalda, an Estonian national serving a life sentence, who complained under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights that prison authorities violated his right to receive information through the Internet.

In 2005, while at Pärnu Prison, Kalda requested access to the online State Gazette (Riigi Teataja), online Supreme Court and administrative court decisions, and the ECtHR’s HUDOC database. The Governor refused. Domestic courts initially upheld the refusal, but in 2007 the Supreme Court partly ruled for him. It found that because the online Riigi Teataja had become the primary official version, prisoners had to have reasonable access to legal acts. It also held that refusing access to administrative court rulings and ECtHR judgments unlawfully interfered with the constitutional right to obtain information for public use.

After transfer to Tartu Prison, in October 2007 Kalda asked for access to three additional websites: www.coe.ee (Council of Europe Information Office in Tallinn), www.oiguskantsler.ee (Chancellor of Justice), and www.riigikogu.ee (Estonian Parliament). He claimed he needed them to defend his rights in ongoing legal disputes with prison authorities. Tartu Prison refused, and the Ministry of Justice dismissed his complaint.

In July 2008, Tartu Administrative Court partly upheld his complaint, ordering supervised access to www.coe.ee via a specially adapted computer. It reasoned that HUDOC contained ECtHR judgments only in English and French, while Estonian translations were available on www.coe.ee. It rejected access to the other two sites. The Court of Appeal upheld that ruling. However, on 7 December 2009, the Supreme Court’s plenary session quashed the order granting access to www.coe.ee and upheld Tartu Prison’s appeal.

The Supreme Court held that section 31-1 of the Imprisonment Act prohibited prisoners from using the Internet except, under supervision, on computers adapted for access to official legislation databases and the judicial decisions database. It found the prohibition constitutional. The aims were prison security, public safety, and steering prisoners toward law-abiding behaviour. Internet access could facilitate prohibited communication or misuse and increase control costs. The court considered the denial of access to the three sites a low-intensity restriction and noted alternative means: mail, information requests, prison libraries, and access to ECtHR case law through permitted databases. Four of eighteen judges dissented, arguing that access should be granted, especially to www.coe.ee, because Estonian translations of ECtHR judgments were necessary for effective court access and not adequately available elsewhere.

Before the ECtHR, Kalda alleged that this refusal violated Article 10. The Court assessed whether the interference was lawful, pursued legitimate aims, and was proportionate. It ultimately found a violation of Article 10 regarding the refusal to grant access to www.coe.ee, largely because that site provided Estonian translations of ECtHR judgments relevant to his ability to protect his rights, and the broad security justification did not sufficiently justify denying that specific access. It found no violation concerning the Chancellor of Justice and Parliament websites, since alternative means of obtaining information and contacting those institutions existed.

In *Kalda v. Estonia* (Application no. 17429/10), the applicant, Romeo Kalda, was an Estonian prisoner serving a life sentence. He alleged that the refusal by prison authorities to allow him access to certain Internet sites violated his right under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights to receive information without interference by public authority.

The case involved two sets of refusals. First, in July 2005, while at Pärnu Prison, Kalda asked for access to the online version of *Riigi Teataja* (the State Gazette), the online decisions of the Supreme Court and administrative courts, and the HUDOC database of European Court of Human Rights judgments. The prison governor refused. Domestic courts initially dismissed his complaint, but on 31 May 2007 the Estonian Supreme Court partly ruled in his favour. It held that the refusal to allow access to the online *Riigi Teataja* was lawful because the paper version was available. However, it found that refusing access to the administrative court rulings and ECtHR judgments interfered with the constitutional right to freely obtain information disseminated for public use. Since no specific restriction applied to prisoners, their right had to receive equal protection; the refusal regarding those materials was therefore unlawful.

Second, after Kalda was transferred to Tartu Prison, he requested access on 18 October 2007 to three websites: www.coe.ee (Council of Europe Information Office in Tallinn), www.oiguskantsler.ee (Chancellor of Justice), and www.riigikogu.ee (Estonian Parliament). He stated that he was involved in legal disputes with the prison administration and needed the sites to defend his rights. Tartu Prison refused, and the Ministry of Justice dismissed his complaint. The Tartu Administrative Court on 17 July 2008 allowed supervised access to www.coe.ee, finding it analogous to judicial decision databases and noting that Estonian translations of ECtHR rulings were available there, unlike in HUDOC. It rejected access to the other two sites because section 31-1 of the Imprisonment Act did not cover them and he could request information directly. The Court of Appeal upheld that judgment.

On further appeal, the Supreme Court’s plenary session on 7 December 2009 quashed the access to www.coe.ee and dismissed Kalda’s appeal. It found that section 31-1 of the Imprisonment Act, in force from 1 June 2008, prohibited prisoners from using the Internet except on specially adapted computers for official legislation databases and judicial decisions. The three sites fell outside that exception. Although the restriction interfered with the constitutional right to obtain information, the Supreme Court held it was justified by the aims of imprisonment, especially public safety and preventing unauthorised communication. It reasoned that additional Internet access increased security risks and costs, and that no equally effective alternative existed. Prisoners could contact the Parliament and Chancellor of Justice by post or information requests, and Council of Europe materials were otherwise available. The restriction was considered “low intensity.” Four of eighteen judges dissented, arguing that access to all three sites should be allowed because it aided court access and posed no general threat.

Kalda therefore complained before the ECtHR that the prison’s refusal to grant him Internet access to these public information sites infringed his Article 10 right to receive information. The key facts concern the prison Internet ban, the domestic courts’ balancing of security and prisoners’ rights, and the availability of alternative means of obtaining information.

**Case summary: El Ghatet v. Switzerland (Application no. 56971/10)**

The case concerned a complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights about Switzerland’s refusal to grant family reunification to an Egyptian national seeking to join his father, a Swiss and Egyptian dual national settled in Switzerland.

The first applicant, Saleh El Ghatet, born in 1952, entered Switzerland in 1997 and applied for asylum. His asylum request was rejected. His son, the second applicant Mohamed Saleh El Ghatet, born in 1990, remained in Egypt in the care of his mother. In 1999 the first applicant married a Swiss national and obtained a residence permit. A daughter was born to the couple in 2000. The first applicant later obtained a permanent residence permit in 2004 and Swiss nationality in 2004.

The son first visited Switzerland in 2002 for three months on a tourist visa. In July 2003 he returned to Switzerland for family reunification with his father. However, after difficulties at school and conflict with his stepmother, he returned to Egypt in January 2005, where he was cared for by his mother and paternal grandmother. In 2006 the first applicant separated from his Swiss wife.

On 1 March 2006, when the son was 15½ years old, the first applicant applied for family reunification. He had custody of his son under Egyptian law. The cantonal migration authorities refused the request in February 2007, and an internal appeal was dismissed in June 2007. The Cantonal Court of Appeal in Foreigners’ Law then allowed the appeal in September 2007, finding that Article 8 interests outweighed public immigration interests. However, the Federal Office of Migration refused consent in March 2008. The Federal Administrative Court dismissed the applicants’ appeal in February 2010, holding that the requirements for family reunification were not met and that Article 8 did not apply because the son had reached adulthood and was not dependent on his father.

In July 2010 the Federal Supreme Court dismissed the final appeal. It found that the father-son relationship was not “paramount,” despite the father’s custody rights under Egyptian law. It emphasised that the father had not sought reunification immediately after arriving in Switzerland; that the son had lived almost all his life in Egypt and had stronger social and personal ties there; that he had returned to Egypt after his earlier stay; and that integration in Switzerland would now be more difficult. It also noted that the father had family life with his daughter in Switzerland and could not reasonably be expected to relocate to Egypt.

The applicants complained that this refusal violated their right to respect for family life under Article 8. The Government accepted that family life existed but argued that the domestic authorities had struck a fair balance, particularly because the son was 15½ when the application was lodged, had adequate care in Egypt, and had experienced integration difficulties in Switzerland.

The European Court of Human Rights declared the application admissible. On the merits, the Court found that the case did not clearly favour either the applicants’ interest in reunification or the State’s immigration-control interest. However, it held that the domestic courts, especially the Federal Supreme Court, had examined the child’s best interests only briefly and in a summary manner. They had not placed those interests sufficiently at the centre of their balancing exercise, as required by Article 8 and international child-protection standards. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 8 of the Convention.

The case of *El Ghatet v. Switzerland* concerned the refusal by Swiss authorities to grant family reunification to a son living in Egypt, alleged to violate Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to respect for family life).

The first applicant, Saleh El Ghatet, a Swiss and Egyptian national, entered Switzerland in 1997 and applied for asylum, which was rejected. In 1999 he married a Swiss national and obtained a residence permit; in 2004 he received permanent residence and Swiss nationality. His son, Mohamed Saleh El Ghatet, the second applicant, remained in Egypt with his mother. The son visited Switzerland in 2002 for three months on a tourist visa and then came in July 2003 for family reunification. However, after difficulties at school and conflict with his stepmother, he returned to Egypt in January 2005, where he was cared for by his mother and paternal grandmother. In 2006, the father separated from his Swiss wife.

On 1 March 2006, when the son was 15½ years old, the father applied for family reunification. He had custody of his son under Egyptian law. The Canton of Aargau Migration Office refused the request in February 2007. On appeal, the Cantonal Court of Appeal granted the request in September 2007, relying largely on Article 8 and finding that the applicants’ family-life interests outweighed the public interest. However, in March 2008 the Federal Office of Migration refused consent, saying the statutory requirements were not met and the cantonal decision contradicted Federal Supreme Court case law.

The Federal Administrative Court dismissed the appeal in February 2010, finding that domestic family reunification requirements were not satisfied and that Article 8 could not be relied on because the son had reached adulthood and was not dependent on his father. The Federal Supreme Court dismissed a further appeal in July 2010. It found that the father-son relationship was not “paramount” despite the custody right; the father had not applied for reunification immediately after settling in Switzerland; the son had lived almost all his life in Egypt and had stronger social and personal ties there; he had returned to Egypt after his earlier stay; and integration in Switzerland would now be harder. The court distinguished *Tuquabo-Tekle v. the Netherlands*, where the child’s mother was the only living parent, had sought reunification promptly, and the child faced serious risks such as forced marriage.

Before the European Court, the applicants argued that the refusal violated Article 8. They stressed that the son was 15½ when the application was lodged, that the father had custody, and that the son had previously lived with him in Switzerland for 1½ years. They also argued that the mother’s move to Kuwait and the grandmother’s care had not been properly assessed, and that it was unreasonable to expect the father to relocate to Egypt because he had family life with his daughter in Switzerland.

The Government accepted that family life existed but argued that the domestic authorities had struck a fair balance. It emphasised that the son’s care in Egypt was adequate, that he had integration difficulties during his earlier stay, that he was already 15½, and that the father was unemployed and lived in a one-room apartment when the request was lodged.

The Court declared the application admissible. It reiterated that family reunification cases require a fair balance between individual and public interests, and that the best interests of the child must be central to domestic reasoning. It found it would be unduly difficult for the applicants to enjoy family life anywhere but Switzerland, because the father could not reasonably relocate to Egypt given his daughter there. However, there was no presumption that reunification with the father was in the son’s best interests, since the son had lived with his mother at the time of the request. Custody was relevant but not decisive. The son had spent almost all his life in Egypt, had strong ties there, was cared for by his mother and later grandmother, and was old enough to be less dependent.

The Court concluded that no clear answer existed as to whether reunification interests outweighed immigration control if a thorough balancing had been performed. But the Swiss Federal Supreme Court and other domestic courts examined the child’s best interests only briefly and summarily, failing to place them sufficiently at the centre of the balancing exercise. Switzerland was therefore found to have violated Article 8, not necessarily because the refusal was substantively wrong, but because the domestic reasoning and balancing were inadequate.

**Case:** *El Ghatet v. Switzerland* (Application no. 56971/10), European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, judgment of 8 November 2016.

The applicants were Saleh El Ghatet, a Swiss and Egyptian national living in Switzerland (the first applicant), and his son Mohamed Saleh El Ghatet, an Egyptian national living in Egypt (the second applicant). They alleged that Switzerland’s refusal to grant family reunification violated their right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The first applicant entered Switzerland in 1997 and applied for asylum, but his application was rejected. His son remained in Egypt, cared for by his mother. In 1999 the first applicant married a Swiss national and obtained a residence permit; a daughter was born in 2000. In 2002 the son visited Switzerland for three months, and in July 2003 he came to Switzerland for family reunification. The father obtained a permanent residence permit in 2004 and Swiss nationality in August 2004. However, after difficulties at school and conflicts with his stepmother, the son returned to Egypt in January 2005, where he was cared for by his mother and paternal grandmother. In 2006 the father separated from his Swiss wife; their daughter remained in Switzerland with her mother.

On 1 March 2006 the father applied for family reunification for his son, then 15½ years old and for whom he had custody under Egyptian law. The cantonal Migration Office refused the request in February 2007. The Aargau Court of Appeal allowed an appeal in September 2007, finding that although statutory requirements were not met, the applicants’ Article 8 interests outweighed the public interest. The Federal Office of Migration then refused consent in March 2008, relying on Federal Supreme Court case-law. The Federal Administrative Court dismissed the applicants’ appeal in February 2010, holding that statutory conditions were not met and that Article 8 could not be relied on because the son had by then reached adulthood and was not dependent on his father. In July 2009 the applicants had informed authorities that the son’s mother had moved to Kuwait and that he was now cared for exclusively by his paternal grandmother.

In July 2010 the Federal Supreme Court dismissed the final appeal. It considered that the father-son relationship was not “paramount,” despite the father’s custody right. The son had lived almost all his life in Egypt, had stronger social and personal ties there, had been cared for by his mother and grandmother, and had returned to Egypt after living in Switzerland for about 18 months. Integration in Switzerland would now be more difficult. The court distinguished *Tuquabo-Tekle v. the Netherlands*, where the child’s other parent was dead, the mother sought reunification promptly, and there were serious risks in the country of origin.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants argued that the refusal breached Article 8 and that the decisive age should be the date of the reunification request. The Government accepted that family life existed but argued that the domestic authorities had struck a fair balance and acted within their margin of appreciation.

The Court found the application admissible. It emphasized that in all decisions concerning children, the child’s best interests must be paramount and must be sufficiently reflected in domestic reasoning. While the case was finely balanced, the Federal Supreme Court and other domestic courts had examined the son’s best interests only briefly and summarily. They failed to place those interests at the centre of their balancing exercise, contrary to Article 8 and relevant international and domestic standards. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 8.

**Halimi and Others v. Albania** (Application no. 33839/11) is a 2016 European Court of Human Rights judgment concerning Albania’s prolonged failure to enforce a final domestic property-compensation decision. The applicants were nine Albanian nationals represented by Tirana lawyer S. Puto. On 30 May 1995, the Vlora Commission recognised their inherited property rights over a plot of land measuring 10,000 sq. m. Because the plot was occupied, the applicants were entitled to compensation in one of the forms provided by law instead of restitution of the land. However, no compensation had been paid by the time the case reached the Strasbourg Court.

The applicants complained under Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Their central allegation was that the Albanian authorities had failed to enforce a final domestic decision awarding them compensation in lieu of restitution. Article 6 § 1 guarantees the right to a fair hearing, including enforcement of final judicial decisions; Article 13 guarantees an effective remedy for Convention violations; and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. The applicants also complained under Article 6 § 1 about the length of the proceedings, which they linked to the non-enforcement of the Commission’s decision.

The Government did not contest the admissibility of the complaints. It also did not dispute the merits, acknowledging that the application fell within well-established case-law, particularly **Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania** (2012). The Court declared the complaints admissible, finding they were not manifestly ill-founded.

On the merits, the Court relied on its earlier Albanian cases concerning non-enforcement of final compensation awards. It found that the domestic authorities’ failure over many years to enforce the final domestic decision and, notably, to pay the compensation awarded breached the applicants’ rights under Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court also concluded that there was, and continued to be, no effective domestic remedy allowing adequate and sufficient redress for the prolonged non-enforcement of final decisions awarding compensation. This constituted a violation of Article 13.

As to the separate complaint about the length of proceedings, the Court considered that the issue was absorbed by the non-enforcement complaint. It therefore found it unnecessary to examine that length complaint separately.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were thus: the applicants held a final, recognised entitlement to compensation for inherited property; the land was occupied and could not be restored; the State failed to pay compensation for many years; and no effective domestic remedy existed to address that failure. The judgment is final and follows the Court’s established case-law against Albania in similar property-compensation cases.

**Case: Halimi and Others v. Albania (Application no. 33839/11), European Court of Human Rights, First Section, 7 April 2016**

The case concerned an application lodged against Albania by nine Albanian nationals under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants complained about the Albanian authorities’ failure to enforce a final domestic decision awarding them compensation in lieu of restitution of inherited property.

The key facts were largely undisputed. On 30 May 1995, the Vlora Commission recognised the applicants’ inherited property rights over a plot of land measuring 10,000 square metres. Because the plot was occupied by others, restitution in kind was not possible. Under Albanian law, the applicants were therefore entitled to compensation in one of the ways provided by law. The decision became final, but no compensation was ever paid. By the time the case reached the European Court of Human Rights, many years had passed without enforcement of the final domestic decision.

The applicants alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, concerning the right to a fair hearing and the non-enforcement of a final judgment; Article 13, concerning the lack of an effective domestic remedy; and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, concerning protection of property. They also complained under Article 6 § 1 about the length of proceedings, which was effectively caused by the non-enforcement.

Before the Court, the Albanian Government did not contest the admissibility of these complaints and did not dispute the merits. It acknowledged that the application was covered by the Court’s well-established case-law against Albania, particularly *Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania*, which concerned similar failures to enforce final decisions awarding compensation for occupied or confiscated property. The Government put forward no arguments that would justify a departure from that case-law.

The Court declared the complaints admissible. On the merits, it relied on its previous findings in cases such as *Manushaqe Puto and Others*, *Sharra and Others*, *Metalla and Others*, and *Siliqi and Others*. It found that the domestic authorities’ failure over many years to enforce the final domestic decision and, notably, to pay the compensation awarded, breached the applicants’ rights under Article 6 § 1 and under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court also concluded that there was, and continued to be, no effective domestic remedy capable of providing adequate and sufficient redress for the prolonged non-enforcement of final domestic decisions awarding compensation. There was accordingly a violation of Article 13.

As to the separate complaint about the length of proceedings, the Court considered that this issue was absorbed by the non-enforcement complaint. It therefore found it unnecessary to examine that complaint separately.

The judgment was delivered by the First Section, sitting as a Committee, on 7 April 2016. It was final, and a rectified version was issued on 26 April 2016 under Rule 81 of the Rules of Court. In essence, the case concerned Albania’s systemic failure to compensate applicants whose property rights had been recognised but whose land was occupied, and the absence of an effective remedy for that prolonged non-enforcement.

**Case: Halimi and Others v. Albania (Application no. 33839/11)**  
**Court:** European Court of Human Rights, First Section (Committee)  
**Judgment:** 7 April 2016 (rectified 26 April 2016)

The case originated in an application lodged against the Republic of Albania under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights by nine Albanian nationals. The applicants were represented by Mr S. Puto, a lawyer practising in Tirana, while the Albanian Government was represented by Ms A. Hicka of the State Advocate’s Office. The application was communicated to the Government on 20 December 2013.

The key facts concerned property rights. On 30 May 1995, the Vlora Commission recognised the applicants’ inherited property rights over a plot of land measuring 10,000 square metres. However, because the plot was occupied, the applicants were not restored possession. Instead, under domestic law, they were entitled to compensation in one of the forms provided by law. Despite this final domestic decision recognising their entitlement, no compensation had been paid by the time the case reached the European Court of Human Rights. This prolonged failure to pay compensation formed the factual basis of the applicants’ complaints.

The applicants alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, Article 13 of the Convention, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. Article 6 § 1 guarantees the right to a fair hearing in the determination of civil rights and obligations. Article 13 guarantees an effective remedy before a national authority for alleged Convention violations. Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. The applicants’ core complaint was that the final domestic decision awarding them compensation in lieu of restitution of their property had not been enforced. They also complained under Article 6 § 1 about the length of proceedings, which they said resulted from the non-enforcement of the Commission’s decision.

The Government did not contest the admissibility of the complaints. The Court found that the complaints were not manifestly ill-founded and were not inadmissible on any other grounds, and declared them admissible. On the merits, the Government did not dispute the applicants’ complaints and acknowledged that the case was covered by well-established case-law, particularly the judgment in *Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania*.

The Court relied on its previous findings in cases against Albania, including *Manushaqe Puto and Others*, *Sharra and Others*, *Metalla and Others*, and *Siliqi and Others*. It found that the domestic authorities’ failure over many years to enforce the final domestic decision and, in particular, to pay the compensation awarded, breached the applicants’ rights under Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court further concluded that there was, and continued to be, no effective domestic remedy capable of providing adequate and sufficient redress for the prolonged non-enforcement of final domestic decisions awarding compensation. Accordingly, there was also a violation of Article 13.

As regards the separate complaint about the length of proceedings under Article 6 § 1, the Court declared it admissible but considered that the issue was absorbed by the issue of non-enforcement. It therefore found it unnecessary to examine that complaint separately. The central violations thus arose from Albania’s long-standing failure to enforce a final property compensation decision and from the absence of an effective domestic remedy for that failure.
