**Case Summary: Al-Dulimi and Montana Management Inc. v. Switzerland (Application no. 5809/08)**

The case originated in an application against Switzerland lodged on 1 February 2008 by Khalaf M. Al-Dulimi, an Iraqi national born in 1941 and living in Amman, Jordan, and Montana Management Inc., a Panamanian company of which Al-Dulimi was managing director. According to the UN Security Council, Al-Dulimi had been head of finance for Iraqi secret services under Saddam Hussein.

After Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in 1990, the Security Council imposed sanctions. Switzerland adopted the Iraq Ordinance, freezing the applicants' assets. In 2003, Resolution 1483 required states to freeze and transfer to the Development Fund for Iraq assets of former Iraqi officials and entities controlled by them. The 1518 Sanctions Committee added the applicants to its list on 26 April 2004, and Switzerland transposed this into national law in May 2004.

On 16 November 2006, the Federal Department for Economic Affairs ordered confiscation of CHF 86,276.85 belonging to the first applicant and over CHF 269 million held in the applicant company's name at two banks, to be transferred to the Development Fund for Iraq. The Department stated it was bound by the Sanctions Committee's listing and could only delete names if the Committee did so.

The applicants appealed to the Federal Court, arguing that the confiscation breached property rights and procedural safeguards under Article 14 ICCPR, Articles 6 and 13 ECHR, and the Swiss Constitution. They contended that the Swiss courts had jurisdiction to review the legality and Convention-compatibility of the Sanctions Committee's listing decision, and that no conflict existed between UN Charter obligations and Convention rights.

On 23 January 2008, the Federal Court dismissed the appeals. It confined itself to verifying that the applicants' names appeared on the Sanctions Committee's lists and that the assets belonged to them. It held that under Article 103 of the UN Charter, Switzerland's Charter obligations prevailed over conflicting obligations under the ECHR and ICCPR. The court found that procedural safeguards under Article 6 ECHR and Article 14 ICCPR were not peremptory norms of general international law (*jus cogens*), and therefore Switzerland was not authorised to scrutinise the validity of Security Council decisions or provide redress for procedural defects. It concluded that implementing Resolution 1483 left no room for examining the listing procedure or verifying its justification, even to ensure Convention procedural safeguards.

The applicants alleged before the European Court that the confiscation of their assets by Swiss authorities, pursuant to the UN Security Council resolution, had been ordered without any procedure complying with Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The core of the alleged violation was that they had no access to an independent tribunal to challenge the merits or fairness of the listing and confiscation, as the Swiss courts refused to review the Sanctions Committee's decision, and the Committee's own procedure was not judicial.

A Chamber of the Second Section found a violation of Article 6 § 1 on 26 November 2013. Following a government request, the Grand Chamber granted referral. The Grand Chamber delivered its judgment on 21 June 2016. Subsequent developments included the applicants' unsuccessful delisting application in 2009 and the Swiss authorities staying execution of the confiscation pending the Court's judgment.

Al-Dulimi and Montana Management Inc. v. Switzerland (Application no. 5809/08) is a Grand Chamber judgment of the European Court of Human Rights delivered on 21 June 2016. The applicants were Khalaf M. Al-Dulimi, an Iraqi national alleged by the UN to have been head of finance for the Iraqi secret services under Saddam Hussein, and Montana Management Inc., a Panama-incorporated company of which he was managing director. Their complaint concerned Switzerland’s confiscation of assets linked to them under United Nations Security Council sanctions and the absence of a procedure complying with Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

After Iraq invaded Kuwait, the UN imposed sanctions. Resolution 1483 (2003) required states to freeze and transfer to the Development Fund for Iraq funds and economic resources of the former Iraqi Government, Saddam Hussein, senior former Iraqi officials, and entities owned or controlled by them. A Sanctions Committee created by Resolution 1518 (2003) was responsible for listing individuals and entities concerned. In April 2004 the Committee listed both applicants. Swiss authorities then added their names to the Iraq Ordinance. In May 2004 the Federal Council adopted a Confiscation Ordinance allowing frozen Iraqi assets to be confiscated and transferred to the Development Fund for Iraq.

In November 2006 the Swiss Federal Department for Economic Affairs ordered confiscation of assets held in the applicants’ names in Swiss banks: CHF 86,276.85 belonging to the first applicant and substantial sums held by the applicant company, approximately CHF 164.7 million and CHF 104.7 million with two banks. The funds were to be transferred to the Development Fund for Iraq.

The applicants appealed to the Federal Court. They argued that the confiscation violated property rights and, importantly, fair-procedure guarantees under Article 6 ECHR, Article 13 ECHR and Article 14 ICCPR. They complained that they had never been informed of the reasons for their inclusion on the UN list, could not comment on the evidence, and could not obtain effective judicial review of either the listing or the confiscation. They contended that Swiss courts could review the measures for conformity with the Convention and the ICCPR, and that no conflict existed between those obligations and the UN Charter.

On 23 January 2008 the Federal Court dismissed the appeals. It held that it could only verify whether the applicants’ names appeared on the Sanctions Committee list and whether the assets belonged to them. Relying on Article 103 of the UN Charter, it considered that Switzerland’s Charter obligations prevailed over the ECHR and ICCPR. It found no power to review Security Council decisions except for possible breaches of jus cogens, and held that Article 6 ECHR and Article 14 ICCPR procedural safeguards were not jus cogens. It noted the UN delisting procedure introduced by Resolution 1730 (2006). The applicants later sought delisting, but their application was rejected in January 2009. Swiss authorities stayed execution of the confiscation pending the Strasbourg proceedings.

A Chamber of the Court initially found a violation of Article 6 § 1 on 26 November 2013. Following a government request, the Grand Chamber examined the case. On 21 June 2016 the Grand Chamber also found a violation of Article 6 § 1. The essential violation was that the Swiss courts had confined themselves to a purely formal review of the UN listing and asset ownership, thereby failing to provide the applicants with sufficient judicial scrutiny of the confiscation measures. The Grand Chamber held that Switzerland was not prevented by the UN resolutions from ensuring a fair procedure, and that the domestic courts should have reviewed the measures in a manner compatible with Article 6 § 1.

**Case summary: Al-Dulimi and Montana Management Inc. v. Switzerland**  
*(Application no. 5809/08, Grand Chamber, 21 June 2016)*

The case concerned UN sanctions against Iraq and Swiss measures freezing and confiscating the applicants’ assets. The first applicant, Khalaf M. Al-Dulimi, an Iraqi national, was alleged by the UN Security Council to have been head of finance for the Iraqi secret services under Saddam Hussein. The second applicant, Montana Management Inc., was a Panamanian company managed by the first applicant.

After Iraq’s invasion of Kuwait in 1990, the UN Security Council adopted resolutions imposing an embargo and asset freeze on Iraq. Switzerland adopted the Iraq Ordinance in August 1990, and the applicants alleged their Swiss assets had been frozen since then. In 2003, UN Security Council Resolution 1483 required all States to freeze funds and assets of the former Iraqi government, Saddam Hussein, senior officials and entities owned or controlled by them, and to transfer those assets to the Development Fund for Iraq. A Security Council sanctions committee created by Resolution 1518 was tasked with listing the individuals and entities concerned.

In April 2004, the 1518 Sanctions Committee added the second applicant and the first applicant to its list. The first applicant was described as a former head of finance of Iraqi secret services who controlled companies managing assets of the former regime and its senior members. Switzerland then added the applicants’ names to the annex to the Iraq Ordinance. In May 2004, the Federal Council adopted a Confiscation Ordinance.

On 16 November 2006, the Federal Department for Economic Affairs ordered the confiscation and transfer to the Development Fund for Iraq of CHF 86,276.85 belonging to the first applicant and two large bank deposits in the company’s name, amounting to CHF 164,731,213 and CHF 104,739,882.57. The Department relied on the applicants’ presence on the Sanctions Committee list, saying Switzerland was bound by UN Security Council resolutions and could not itself remove names from the list.

The applicants appealed to the Federal Court. They argued that the confiscation and the listing procedure breached procedural safeguards under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights, Article 14 of the ICCPR and the Swiss Constitution. They sought judicial review of the legality of their inclusion on the UN list and of the merits of the confiscation. On 23 January 2008, the Federal Court dismissed their appeals. It confined its review to verifying that the applicants’ names actually appeared on the Sanctions Committee list and that the assets belonged to them. It held that UN Charter obligations prevailed over conflicting ECHR and ICCPR obligations, and that Swiss courts could not scrutinise the validity of Security Council decisions or the listing procedure, except possibly for breaches of *jus cogens*. It found that Article 6 procedural rights were not *jus cogens*. The Swiss courts therefore refused to examine whether the listing was justified or procedurally fair, or whether the confiscation complied with Article 6.

The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging in particular that the confiscation of their assets pursuant to the UN Security Council resolution had been ordered without any procedure complying with Article 6. A later delisting attempt under Resolution 1730 was rejected in January 2009. The Grand Chamber ultimately found a violation of Article 6 § 1, holding that Switzerland had sufficient latitude and should have ensured court review capable of protecting the applicants against arbitrariness, rather than merely checking whether their names appeared on the UN list.

**Summary of Mikhno v. Ukraine (Application no. 32514/12)**

The case of *Mikhno v. Ukraine* concerns the tragic crash of a military aircraft during an air show in Lviv, Ukraine, and the subsequent failures of the Ukrainian authorities to adequately investigate and provide redress. The application was brought by two Ukrainian nationals: Mrs. Nina Mikhno and her granddaughter, Miss Anastasiya Mikhno.

**Key Facts:**

On 27 July 2002, the Ukrainian Air Force organized a military aviation show at the Sknyliv aerodrome in Lviv to commemorate the 60th anniversary of the 14th Air Force Corps. The event, attended by several thousand spectators, included a live aerobatics performance by military pilots. Among the attendees were the second applicant, Anastasiya Mikhno—then five years old—accompanied by her father, Sergiy Mikhno, and her mother, Tetiana Mikhno. Sergiy was the son of the first applicant, Nina Mikhno.

During the aerobatics display, an SU-27 military aircraft piloted by two colonels crashed into the static aircraft display area where numerous spectators were gathered. Both pilots successfully ejected before the aircraft exploded. The crash resulted in the deaths of 77 people and injured over 290 others. Sergiy and Tetiana Mikhno, who were at the epicenter of the accident, died at the scene from multiple fractures and severe cerebral trauma. The second applicant, Anastasiya, witnessed her parents being crushed by the aircraft while she was inside the cabin of an IL-76 airplane on static display. Although she sustained no physical injuries, she subsequently underwent psychological rehabilitation for emotional trauma.

Following the tragedy, multiple concurrent investigations were initiated by various bodies, including a Special Government Commission established by the President of Ukraine. The Commission’s investigation revealed significant organizational and safety failures. Key findings included: the pilots had only one training flight as a team, which was not a proper rehearsal; a planned on-site rehearsal was cancelled due to fuel shortages; the pilots were provided with a different aircraft than the one used in training; they flew without mandatory anti-gravitation suits; and they immediately began the performance upon arrival without familiarizing themselves with the new site. Critically, during the performance, the aircraft exited the designated aerobatics zone, but ground directors failed to warn the pilots or direct them back. The lead pilot then attempted a manoeuvre he had never practised, leading to a loss of control and the fatal crash.

The applicants alleged that the State authorities were responsible for the deaths of their relatives and failed to conduct an effective investigation into the circumstances. They further complained that the domestic courts handling their claim for damages lacked independence and impartiality, that the proceedings were inordinately lengthy, and that there were no effective remedies for the length of proceedings complaint.

**Relevance to Alleged Violations:**

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations center on the State’s failure to prevent the tragedy through adequate safety measures and its subsequent failure to provide an effective and timely investigation. The Special Commission’s findings of multiple organizational failures—including inadequate training, cancelled rehearsals, and the absence of proper safety protocols—point directly to State responsibility. Furthermore, the applicants’ complaints regarding the lack of judicial independence, the excessive length of proceedings, and the absence of effective remedies for procedural delays highlight additional violations under the Convention, particularly concerning the right to a fair trial and an effective remedy.

**Summary of Mikhno v. Ukraine**

The case of *Mikhno v. Ukraine* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by two Ukrainian nationals: Mrs. Nina Mikhno and her granddaughter, Miss Anastasiya Mikhno. The applicants alleged violations by the State regarding the deaths of their relatives, Sergiy and Tetiana Mikhno, in a catastrophic military air show accident and the subsequent failure to provide an effective investigation and fair judicial proceedings.

The key facts stem from the "Sknyliv" air show held on 27 July 2002 at an aerodrome in Lviv, organized by the Ukrainian Air Force. The event was attended by thousands, including five-year-old Anastasiya Mikhno, accompanied by her parents, Sergiy and Tetiana. During a live aerobatics performance, an SU-27 military aircraft piloted by Colonels V.T. and Y.Y. crashed into a static display area filled with spectators. The crash and subsequent explosion resulted in the deaths of 77 people and injured over 290 others. Both Sergiy and Tetiana Mikhno were in the epicentre of the accident and died at the scene from severe trauma.

Anastasiya, the second applicant, witnessed the horrific event from the cabin of a stationary IL-76 display aircraft, where she was posing for a photograph. While she escaped physical injury, she witnessed her parents being crushed and subsequently required psychological rehabilitation for the emotional trauma.

Following the disaster, multiple investigations were initiated. A special Government Commission was established to determine the causes. Its findings, detailed in the case file, highlighted a series of serious organizational and operational failures. These included:

- **Inadequate Preparation:** The pilots had only one training flight together, in a different aircraft, and a planned on-site rehearsal was cancelled due to fuel shortages.
- **Procedural Violations:** The pilots were not formally briefed on the aerobatics zone boundaries or spectator placements. They took off without mandatory anti-gravitation suits and began their performance immediately upon arrival, without familiarizing themselves with the new site.
- **Command Failures:** During the performance, the aircraft exited the designated flight zone. Ground directors failed to warn the pilots or direct them back. The pilot then decided to perform a complex, unpracticed manoeuvre not in his mission order, leading to a loss of control and the fatal crash.
- **Equipment and Personnel Issues:** The pilots used an aircraft different from their training one, and the command had refused requests for additional training flights.

The applicants' legal claims centered on these facts. They argued that the State authorities were responsible for the deaths of their relatives due to these systemic failures. Furthermore, they alleged that the subsequent official investigation into the circumstances was ineffective, failing to ensure accountability. They also complained that the domestic court proceedings for their damages claim were inordinately lengthy and lacked independence and impartiality, with no effective remedy available for the length of those proceedings.

It is these core facts surrounding the preventable nature of the tragedy, the direct loss suffered by the applicants, and the alleged subsequent failures of the justice system that form the basis of the violations brought before the European Court of Human Rights.

In *Mikhno v. Ukraine* (Application no. 32514/12), the European Court of Human Rights examined an application brought by two Ukrainian nationals, Nina Vasylivna Mikhno (born 1940) and her granddaughter Anastasiya Sergiyivna Mikhno (born 1997), the first applicant being the second’s legal guardian. They live in Lviv. The application was lodged on 30 August 2006 and communicated to the Ukrainian Government on 4 September 2012. The judgment was delivered on 1 September 2016 and became final on 30 January 2017.

The applicants alleged that Ukrainian State authorities were responsible for the deaths of their relatives, Sergiy and Tetiana Mikhno, and had failed to conduct an effective investigation into the circumstances. They further alleged that the courts dealing with their damages claim lacked independence and impartiality, that the proceedings had been excessively lengthy, and that no effective remedies existed for the length-of-proceedings complaint.

The underlying facts concerned the Sknyliv air-show disaster. On 27 July 2002 the Ukrainian Air Force organised a military aviation show at the Sknyliv aerodrome in Lviv to commemorate the sixtieth anniversary of the 14th Air Force Corps. Several thousand spectators attended, including the second applicant, then five years old, with her father Sergiy Mikhno and mother Tetiana Mikhno. During an aerobatics display, an SU-27 military aircraft piloted by Colonels V.T. and Y.Y. crashed into the static aircraft display area and exploded. Both pilots ejected successfully, but seventy-seven people died and over 290 were injured. Sergiy and Tetiana, who were at the epicentre, died at the scene from multiple fractures and severe cerebral trauma. The second applicant was inside the cabin of an IL-76 aircraft on static display, posing for a photograph and waving to her parents. She witnessed her parents being crushed by the crashing aircraft, though she suffered no physical injuries; she later underwent psychological rehabilitation.

Multiple investigations were opened, including by a Special Government Commission, the Ministry of Defence, the Lviv City Council, the Prosecutor’s Office, and a survivors’ NGO. The Special Commission’s findings were central to the applicants’ complaints. It established that the Air Force command had authorised the show, but there were serious safety and organisational failings. The pilots had conducted only one training flight as a team, in a different aircraft, and an on-site rehearsal was cancelled because of fuel shortages. The pilots were not formally informed of the aerobatics zone boundaries or the location of spectators. They flew a different aircraft with engine asynchronism, without g-suits, and began the display immediately without familiarising themselves with the site. During the performance, the aircraft left the designated aerobatics zone, the boundary of which was about 150 metres from spectators. Ground controllers did not warn or redirect the pilots. The first pilot then performed an unauthorised manoeuvre called “the trunk”, which he had never practised, made a technical error, and lost control. These facts underpinned the allegations of State responsibility for the deaths and of failure to protect life.

Before the Court, the applicants invoked, in essence, the right to life, the right to an effective investigation, the right to a fair hearing before an independent and impartial tribunal, the right to a hearing within a reasonable time, and the right to an effective remedy. The case therefore concerned whether Ukraine’s organisation of the air show and its subsequent investigative and judicial response met Convention standards.

It instructed the first-instance court to assess whether continued use of the vehicle would constitute a "use of a forged document" offence.

On 22 February 2011, the first-instance court dismissed the applicant's application and ordered the confiscation of the vehicle and its registration certificate. It found that the chassis number had been forged and that the vehicle could be used for committing an offence. For reasons of road safety, it was necessary to confiscate the vehicle. The court noted that, irrespective of the fact that there had been no proceedings against the applicant and that he was not an offender, confiscation was necessary for general safety reasons.

On 11 March 2011, the applicant appealed, arguing that the first-instance court had wrongly applied Article 100-a (2) and (3) of the Code and that he had not known that the vehicle had been used to commit a crime. On 19 May 2011, the appellate court dismissed the appeal and upheld the confiscation. It acknowledged that the applicant did not know the chassis had been forged, but held that under Article 100-a (2), objects used to commit an offence shall be confiscated notwithstanding that they are not in the ownership of the offender or that they are in the ownership of a third person, if general safety requires so. The court found that the use of the vehicle with forged identification numbers would affect road safety and general safety.

The applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention about the confiscation of his vehicle in criminal proceedings against a third person. The complaint was communicated to the Government on 2 October 2014.
001-167797:
Case Name: *Otgon v. the Republic of Moldova* (Application no. 22743/07), European Court of Human Rights, 25 October 2016.

The case concerned an Article 8 complaint about contaminated drinking water and alleged insufficient compensation for an established violation of the applicant’s private-life rights. Svetlana Otgon, a Moldovan national born in 1963, lived in Călărași. On 26 October 2005, she and her daughter drank tap water in their apartment and soon felt unwell. Her twelve-year-old daughter was hospitalized on 29 October 2005 with “serious acute dysentery.” The applicant was hospitalized on 31 October 2005 with the same diagnosis and released on 13 November 2005.

The applicant sued the local State-owned utilities provider for MDL 100,000 (about EUR 6,700), seeking compensation for harm to her health and related inconveniences, including investigations and disinfection. On 1 March 2006, the Călărași District Court ruled in her favour. It relied on sanitary, medical, and technical reports showing that near her apartment block a leaking sewage pipe was situated above the drinking-water pipe. The water pipe cracked on 26 October 2005, allowing sewage to infiltrate the drinking water. The pipes had been used since 1977 despite an expected lifespan of fifteen years. Five people who drank from the same water pipe were hospitalized with the same diagnosis around the same time. The court awarded her MDL 10,000 (about EUR 648) for physical and mental suffering.

Both parties appealed. On 26 April 2006, the Chişinău Court of Appeal rejected the applicant’s appeal and partly allowed the provider’s appeal, reducing the award to MDL 5,000 (about EUR 310), finding both the claimed and awarded sums exaggerated. On 25 October 2006, the Supreme Court of Justice upheld that reduction, stating that the lower court had considered the nature and seriousness of the mental suffering and the defendant’s degree of guilt. That judgment was final.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 8, alleging that her health had been endangered by contaminated water and that the compensation was insufficient for the violation found domestically. She also submitted evidence of continuing health problems, including acute ulcer, chronic cholecystitis, hypothyroidism, and a metabolic disorder. The Government argued that the domestic courts had in substance acknowledged the violation and awarded compensation, so she was no longer a victim. It also argued that the amount was reasonable given her relatively short hospitalization and lack of evidence of long-lasting effects.

The Court declared the application admissible. It reiterated that Article 8 protects physical and psychological integrity and may apply in environmental pollution cases where an individual is directly and seriously affected. A domestic remedy deprives an applicant of victim status only if the authorities acknowledge the breach and afford appropriate and sufficient redress. The Court found an interference with Article 8 because the applicant’s physical integrity had been affected by an unhealthy environment. Although the domestic courts did not expressly cite the Convention, their findings on the company’s responsibility and the suffering caused could be interpreted as acknowledging a breach. The remaining issue was the amount of compensation. The first-instance award of EUR 648 was halved on appeal without specific reasons. Considering her two-week hospitalization and the suffering involved, and comparing the award with the Court’s Article 8 case-law concerning Moldova, the Court found the sum considerably below the minimum generally awarded. Consequently, the applicant could still claim to be a victim of an Article 8 violation.

**Case of Otgon v. the Republic of Moldova** (Application no. 22743/07), judgment of 25 October 2016, concerned a Moldovan applicant, Ms Svetlana Otgon, who alleged that her rights under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights were violated after she and her daughter drank contaminated tap water and subsequently received inadequate compensation.

The key facts were as follows. The applicant was born in 1963 and lived in Călărași. On 26 October 2005, she and her 12-year-old daughter drank water from taps in their apartment and soon felt unwell. Her daughter was admitted to hospital on 29 October 2005 with “serious acute dysentery.” The applicant was admitted on 31 October 2005 with the same diagnosis and was discharged on 13 November 2005, one day after her daughter. The applicant sued the local utilities provider, a State-owned company, seeking 100,000 Moldovan lei (MDL), approximately EUR 6,700 at the time, for harm to her health and related inconveniences, including investigations and disinfection.

On 1 March 2006, the Călărași District Court found in her favour. Sanitary, medical and technical reports established that near the applicant’s apartment block a sewage pipe was situated above the drinking water pipe and was leaking. The water pipe had cracked on 26 October 2005, allowing sewage water to infiltrate the drinking water pipe. The pipes had been used since 1977, although their expected lifespan was fifteen years. Five people who had drunk water from the same pipe were admitted to hospital with the same diagnosis around the same time. Considering the physical and mental suffering caused to the applicant and her daughter, the first-instance court awarded her MDL 10,000 (approximately EUR 648).

Both parties appealed. On 26 April 2006, the Chişinău Court of Appeal rejected the applicant’s appeal but partly accepted the provider’s appeal, reducing the award to MDL 5,000 (approximately EUR 310). It considered both the sum claimed and the sum awarded exaggerated. On 25 October 2006, the Supreme Court of Justice upheld the reduced award, finding that the lower court had taken into account the nature and seriousness of the mental suffering and the defendant’s degree of guilt. That judgment was final.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 8 that her health had been endangered by contaminated water and that the compensation awarded domestically was insufficient for the established violation. She submitted evidence that she continued to suffer health problems after 2005, including acute ulcer, chronic cholecystitis, uncompensated hypothyroidism and a metabolic disorder, for which she had been regularly treated. The Government argued that the domestic courts had in substance acknowledged the Article 8 breach and awarded compensation, so the applicant no longer had victim status. They maintained that the award was reasonable given the relatively short inpatient treatment and lack of evidence of long-lasting effects.

The Court reiterated that Article 8 protects physical and psychological integrity and may apply in environmental pollution cases where an individual is directly and seriously affected. It found that the domestic courts had established the State-owned company’s responsibility and awarded compensation, which could be interpreted as finding a breach of Article 8. The remaining issue was whether the compensation constituted appropriate and sufficient redress. The first-instance court awarded EUR 648 in non-pecuniary damages, but the higher courts halved it without specific reasons beyond the defendant’s degree of responsibility. Although the applicant’s hospital stay was relatively short and long-term effects were not proven, she had been hospitalized for two weeks, implying physical and mental suffering. The Court found the award considerably below the minimum generally granted in Article 8 cases against Moldova. Consequently, the applicant could still claim to be a victim of an Article 8 violation due to insufficient compensation.

In *Otgon v. the Republic of Moldova* (ECtHR, 25 October 2016), the applicant, Svetlana Otgon, complained under Article 8 that she received insufficient compensation after contaminated drinking water harmed her health. The key facts concerned events in Călărași in October 2005. On 26 October, Otgon and her daughter drank tap water and soon felt unwell. Her twelve-year-old daughter was hospitalized on 29 October 2005 with serious acute dysentery; Otgon was hospitalized on 31 October with the same diagnosis and released on 13 November 2005. She sued the local State-owned utilities provider for MDL 100,000 (about EUR 6,700) for health damage and related inconvenience.

On 1 March 2006, the Călăraşi District Court found for her. Reports showed that near her apartment block a sewage pipe ran above the drinking-water pipe and was leaking. The water pipe cracked on 26 October 2005, allowing sewage to infiltrate the drinking water. The pipes had been in use since 1977 despite a fifteen-year expected lifespan. Five people who drank from the same water pipe were hospitalized with the same diagnosis around the same time. The court awarded MDL 10,000 (about EUR 648) for physical and mental suffering. On appeal, the Chişinău Court of Appeal reduced the award to MDL 5,000 (about EUR 310), finding both the claim and the original award exaggerated. On 25 October 2006, the Supreme Court upheld that reduction, referring to the nature and seriousness of the mental suffering and the defendant’s degree of guilt. The judgment became final.

In her ECtHR application lodged on 20 April 2007, Otgon alleged that, although the domestic courts had established a violation of her rights, the compensation was too low. She also claimed continuing health problems after 2005, including acute ulcer, chronic cholecystitis, uncompensated hypothyroidism, and a metabolic disorder, for which she had been regularly treated. The Government argued that the domestic courts had essentially acknowledged an Article 8 breach and awarded compensation, meaning she was no longer a victim; the amount was reasonable given her relatively short hospital stay and no proven long-lasting effects.

The European Court of Human Rights considered the case admissible. It recalled that Article 8 protects physical and psychological integrity and may apply to environmental pollution that directly and seriously affects an individual. The State has a positive duty to take reasonable measures to secure Article 8 rights. Domestic authorities can remove victim status only if they acknowledge the violation, expressly or in substance, and afford appropriate and sufficient redress. The Court found an interference with Otgon’s Article 8 rights because her physical integrity had been affected by an unhealthy environment. It accepted that the domestic courts had established the utility provider’s responsibility and awarded compensation, and their judgments could be interpreted as acknowledging an Article 8 breach.

The remaining issue was whether the compensation was sufficient. The first-instance award was about EUR 648, but the higher courts halved it without detailed reasons. Although the Government relied on the short hospitalization and lack of long-term evidence, Otgon had been hospitalized for two weeks, indicating real mental and physical suffering. The Court found the reduced award considerably below the minimum generally awarded in Article 8 cases against Moldova. Therefore, Otgon could still claim to be a victim, and the Court found a violation of Article 8 due to insufficient compensation.
001-159880:
In **Milojević and Others v. Serbia** (ECtHR, Third Section, 12 January 2016), three Serbian police officers—Ivan Milojević, Miodrag Radosavljević, and Petar Veličković—complained that their dismissal from the Ministry of Interior violated their right to private life and that the domestic judicial decisions upholding those dismissals were arbitrary. The Court communicated those complaints; the remainder of the applications was declared inadmissible.

The first and second applicants were arrested and charged on 26 April 2004 with abuse of power and instigation to abuse of power. Criminal proceedings were instituted, and the Ministry simultaneously began disciplinary proceedings and suspended them. On 7 June 2004, the Ministry dismissed both under Article 45 of the 1991 Ministry of Interior Act, relying on the fact that criminal proceedings were pending. Their appeals were rejected. The disciplinary proceedings were later stopped without a merits decision because their dismissal had made them redundant. Both were acquitted on 29 November 2004, and the acquittals became final on 29 March 2005.

After acquittal, they brought civil proceedings seeking annulment of the dismissals. The Municipal Court accepted their claims and ordered reinstatement, reasoning that Article 45 conferred broad discretionary power on the Ministry, left room for abuse, and that the applicants had been acquitted and dismissed without any disciplinary finding. The District Court upheld those decisions. However, in 2007 the Supreme Court quashed them. It held that the Ministry had lawfully exercised discretionary power under Article 45, that the acquittals and lack of disciplinary decisions were irrelevant, and that the lower courts had exceeded their authority by reviewing the necessity, proportionality, and correctness of the dismissals.

The third applicant was indicted in 1999 for unauthorized possession of weapons and ammunition. He was convicted in December 1999 and sentenced to one year’s imprisonment. In June 2000, the Ministry dismissed him under Article 45; no disciplinary proceedings were instituted. His conviction was confirmed in 2001, but after reopening, he was acquitted in September 2005, and the acquittal became final in February 2006. His civil claim for annulment initially succeeded before the Municipal Court in October 2006, but the District Court quashed that decision in February 2007, and the Supreme Court upheld it in August 2007, using reasoning similar to the first and second applicants’ cases: the dismissal was based solely on the initiation of criminal proceedings, and the later acquittal did not affect its legality.

The relevant legal framework was Article 45 of the 1991 Ministry of Interior Act, which allowed dismissal of police officers if criminal proceedings were pending or if they ceased to meet employment requirements. The Act did not expressly address the consequences of acquittal. Later, the 2005 Police Act repealed this regime and allowed only suspension pending criminal proceedings. The Constitutional Court, in decisions from 2011 and 2012, held that Article 45 gave a possibility, not an obligation, to dismiss, and that civil courts had to assess the lawfulness and proportionality of such dismissals and the purpose of the discretionary power. It found that failure to do so violated fair-trial and work rights.

The applicants alleged that dismissing them because criminal proceedings were pending—and refusing to revisit that dismissal after acquittal—breached their private life and produced arbitrary judicial decisions. The third applicant also noted that a co-defendant charged with the same offence was acquitted and remained employed, while he had received separate compensation for detention and reputational damage.

**Milojević and Others v. Serbia** concerned three Serbian nationals—Ivan Milojević, Miodrag Radosavljević, and Petar Veličković—who were employed as police officers and dismissed after criminal proceedings were brought against them. They complained to the European Court of Human Rights that their dismissals violated their right to private life and that the domestic judicial decisions upholding those dismissals were arbitrary.

The first two applicants’ cases arose from the same events. On 26 April 2004, criminal complaints were filed against them: Milojević was accused of instigating Radosavljević, his superior, to abuse power, while Radosavljević was accused of abuse of power. Both were arrested, criminal proceedings were instituted, and disciplinary proceedings were opened. They were suspended and, on 7 June 2004, dismissed from the police force under Article 45 of the 1991 Ministry of Interior Act. That provision allowed dismissal where a police officer allegedly no longer met employment requirements, including the requirement that no criminal proceedings were pending. Their appeals were rejected. The disciplinary proceedings were later discontinued without a merits decision because the dismissals had already occurred. Both applicants were acquitted in November 2004, and the acquittals became final in March 2005.

After acquittal, they brought civil proceedings challenging their dismissals. The municipal courts ordered their reinstatement, reasoning that Article 45 gave the Ministry broad discretionary power and “most certainly left the possibility of abuse.” The courts also noted that the applicants had been acquitted and that no disciplinary responsibility had been determined. The district courts upheld those decisions. However, on the Ministry’s appeals on points of law, the Supreme Court quashed the decisions in 2007. It held that the dismissals were lawful, that the Ministry had properly exercised its discretionary power under Article 45, and that the acquittals and the absence of a disciplinary decision on the merits were irrelevant. It further concluded that the lower courts had exceeded their authority by examining the necessity, proportionality, and correctness of the dismissals.

The third applicant, Veličković, was indicted in 1999 for unauthorised possession of weapons and ammunition. He was convicted in December 1999 and sentenced to one year’s imprisonment. In June 2000, he was dismissed from the police force under Article 45, without disciplinary proceedings. His conviction became final in 2001, but after reopening, he was acquitted in September 2005; the acquittal became final in February 2006. His civil challenge initially succeeded in October 2006, but the District Court reversed that decision in February 2007, and the Supreme Court upheld the reversal in August 2007, using reasoning similar to the first two cases. Notably, a co-defendant charged with the same offence was acquitted and remained employed as a police officer. Veličković also received separate compensation for unlawful detention and reputational harm.

Relevant domestic law provided that police officers could not be employed if criminal proceedings were pending against them, and Article 45 permitted dismissal on that basis. In similar cases, the Constitutional Court later held that civil courts were obliged to examine whether discretionary dismissals were proportionate and not used contrary to their purpose, especially where the officer had subsequently been acquitted.

The applicants therefore alleged that their dismissals—based on pending criminal proceedings and maintained despite acquittal—violated their right to private life. They also alleged that the Supreme Court’s refusal to review the proportionality of the dismissals rendered the judicial decisions arbitrary.

In *Milojević and Others v. Serbia* (Applications nos. 43519/07, 43524/07 and 45247/07), three Serbian nationals—all former police officers—complained that their dismissal from the Ministry of Interior violated their right to private life and that the judicial decisions upholding those dismissals were arbitrary.

The first and second applicants were dismissed on 7 June 2004 under Article 45 of the 1991 Ministry of Interior Act after criminal complaints were filed against them on 26 April 2004 for abuse of power and instigation to abuse of power. They were arrested and criminal proceedings began. The same day, disciplinary proceedings were opened and they were suspended. The dismissal decisions relied on the fact that criminal proceedings were pending; no disciplinary decision on the merits was ever issued, as those proceedings were later stopped as redundant. Both applicants were acquitted on 29 November 2004, confirmed on 29 March 2005.

After acquittal, they brought civil proceedings to annul the dismissals. The Municipal and District Courts ruled in their favour, reasoning that Article 45 gave the Ministry broad discretion and could be abused; the applicants had been acquitted, and no disciplinary responsibility had been established. However, in 2007 the Supreme Court quashed those decisions. It held that the Ministry had lawfully exercised its discretionary power under Article 45, that the acquittal and the absence of a disciplinary ruling were irrelevant, and that the lower courts had overstepped by reviewing the necessity, proportionality and correctness of the dismissal.

The third applicant was indicted in 1999 for unauthorised possession of weapons and ammunition. He was convicted and sentenced to one year’s imprisonment in December 1999. On 14 June 2000, while the criminal proceedings were still pending, the Ministry dismissed him under Article 45 with similar reasoning. No disciplinary proceedings were instituted. His conviction became final in 2001, but after reopening, he was acquitted on 2 September 2005, confirmed by the Supreme Court on 22 February 2006. He then sought annulment of his dismissal. A Municipal Court ordered his reinstatement, but the District Court quashed that decision, essentially following the Supreme Court’s reasoning in the first two cases; the Supreme Court upheld that outcome in August 2007. A co-defendant charged with the same offence was acquitted and remained employed.

Article 45 of the 1991 Ministry of Interior Act permitted dismissal of a police officer who was convicted by final decision of certain offences, and allowed discretionary dismissal where he ceased to meet employment requirements, including no pending criminal proceedings. It was repealed in 2005. Constitutional Court case-law later indicated that civil courts had to assess the legality and proportionality of such discretionary dismissals, particularly after acquittal, because Article 45 did not regulate the consequences of acquittal.

The applicants alleged that their dismissals and the domestic courts’ refusal to annul them violated their right to private life and were arbitrary. The key issue was that they were dismissed solely because criminal proceedings were pending, despite later acquittal, while the courts refused to examine proportionality or the effect of acquittal. These complaints were communicated to the Government; the remainder of the applications was declared inadmissible.
001-160619:
**Case: A.K. v. Liechtenstein (No. 2), App. No. 10722/13 (ECtHR, 18 Feb. 2016)**

The applicant, A.K., a German national born in 1970, was involved since 2004 in civil litigation with F.H. over ownership of 75% of bearer shares in two Liechtenstein companies, EMK and EMK Engineering. In June 2005, F.H. sued A.K. in the Regional Court, seeking transfer of specified bearer shares and a declaration that A.K. never owned them. The action was served on A.K.’s counsel on 18 June 2005. A.K. unsuccessfully challenged the Liechtenstein courts’ jurisdiction; the Regional Court accepted jurisdiction based on assets in Liechtenstein. His appeal was dismissed in February 2006, and his constitutional complaint on jurisdiction was dismissed in March 2007.

The Regional Court then held hearings on 31 May, 28 June, and 6 September 2007, hearing the parties, counsel, and twelve witnesses. After the final hearing, no judgment was issued for more than two years. A.K. requested a decision in April 2009. On 28 December 2009, the Regional Court upheld F.H.’s action, finding F.H.’s account more credible. It ordered A.K. to hand over the shares and declared he had never owned them. A.K.’s appeal was dismissed by the Court of Appeal on 27 May 2010, and his appeal on points of law was dismissed by the Supreme Court on 13 January 2011. The domestic civil proceedings thus lasted almost seven years.

On 18 February 2011, A.K. lodged a constitutional complaint, alleging violations of Articles 6, 13, and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. He specifically complained about the excessive length of the proceedings, stressing that the outcome affected his means of subsistence, and claimed there was no effective domestic remedy to speed up the proceedings or complain about delay.

A central issue arose on 8 May 2012, when A.K. challenged all five Constitutional Court judges called to decide his complaint. He alleged bias: President B. had delayed appointments and was a close friend of Vice President H., brother of F.H.; Judge Bu. worked for the Government and with Judge H.; Judge Sn. had published on judicial appointment; Judge S. sat on a state-owned company’s supervisory board; and Judge W. had law-firm connections to opposing parties and Judge H. On 15 May 2012, the Constitutional Court dismissed the bias complaints. The procedure was that each challenged judge did not participate in the decision on the complaint against himself, but the five challenged judges sat on the bench deciding complaints against the others, with the four remaining judges deciding each individual challenge. The court found no objectively justified doubts about impartiality.

On the same day, the Constitutional Court partly upheld A.K.’s complaint. It found a violation of the Article 6 § 1 reasonable-time requirement due solely to the two-year and three-month delay between the last Regional Court hearing and its judgment. It did not find the total duration unreasonable, noting A.K.’s own interlocutory proceedings. Because Liechtenstein law lacked express redress for such delay, the court ordered the State to bear court costs and reimburse fees as compensation. It dismissed the remainder, including property and independence complaints.

A.K. then applied to the ECtHR, alleging that the Constitutional Court judges had been partial, particularly because of the procedure used to examine his bias complaints, in breach of Article 6 § 1. He further complained about the length of the civil proceedings under Article 6 § 1 and the lack of an effective remedy for that length under Article 13.

In *A.K. v. Liechtenstein (No. 2)*, the applicant was a German national living in Switzerland. Since 2004, he had been in a civil dispute with F.H. over property rights in 75% of the bearer shares in two Liechtenstein companies, EMK and EMK Engineering. In June 2005, F.H. sued the applicant before the Regional Court, seeking transfer of shares and a declaration that the applicant had never owned them. The applicant’s objection to Liechtenstein jurisdiction was rejected, and his constitutional complaint against that decision was dismissed in 2007. The Regional Court then heard evidence, including twelve witnesses, in 2007, but did not deliver judgment until 28 December 2009. It upheld F.H.’s claim, finding that the applicant’s mother had never owned the shares and that the applicant had not acquired them in good faith. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal in May 2010, and the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal on points of law in January 2011.

In February 2011, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint, alleging, among other things, excessive length of the civil proceedings and the absence of an effective remedy. The President of the Constitutional Court granted suspensive effect. In April 2012, the applicant was informed that five judges—B., Bu., Sn., S. and W.—would decide his complaint at an in camera hearing on 15 May 2012. On 8 May 2012, he filed a detailed bias complaint against all five judges. He alleged that President B. had delayed appointments and was a close friend of Vice President H., the brother of F.H.; that Judge Bu. worked for the Government and regularly with H.; that Judge Sn. was a professor who had published on judicial terms; that Judge S. sat on the supervisory board of a state-owned company; and that Judge W. had law-firm connections with opposing parties and with EMK/EMK Engineering. He also alleged executive influence and discrimination against foreigners.

On 15 May 2012, the Constitutional Court dismissed the bias complaints. The five challenged judges formed the bench, but each did not participate in the decision on the complaint against himself; the remaining four decided. The court found that prior adverse decisions, renewable five-year terms, and ties to Vice President H. did not objectively justify doubts about impartiality. On the same day, the Constitutional Court partly upheld the applicant’s constitutional complaint, finding a violation of the reasonable-time guarantee under Article 6 § 1 because of the two years and three months between the last hearing and the judgment. It ordered the State to reimburse the applicant’s complaint and judgment fees and to pay F.H.’s lawyers’ fees as compensation. It dismissed the remainder, including complaints about property rights and judicial independence.

The applicant then complained to the ECtHR under Article 6 § 1 that the Constitutional Court judges had been partial, particularly because of the procedure used to decide his bias complaints; under Article 6 § 1 that the civil proceedings had been excessively long; and under Article 13 that no effective national remedy existed for the length. The German Government did not intervene. The ECtHR ultimately found a violation of Article 6 § 1 concerning the impartiality of the Constitutional Court, but no violation as regards the length of the proceedings or Article 13.

A.K. v. Liechtenstein (No. 2) (Application no. 10722/13) concerned a German national, A.K., who had been in litigation since 2004 with F.H. over ownership of 75% of bearer shares in two Liechtenstein companies, EMK and EMK Engineering. In June 2005 F.H. sued A.K. in the Regional Court, seeking transfer of specified shares and a declaration that A.K. had never held shares in the companies. A.K. challenged jurisdiction, but the Regional Court accepted jurisdiction based on assets in Liechtenstein, namely salary and fee claims against the companies. That jurisdictional dispute contributed significantly to delay: an appeal was dismissed in February 2006, and A.K.’s constitutional complaint against jurisdiction was only dismissed in March 2007.

After the Constitutional Court proceedings ended, the Regional Court resumed the case and took extensive evidence in 2007, hearing the parties, counsel, and twelve witnesses. The last hearing was on 6 September 2007. A.K. asked the court to deliver judgment in April 2009, but judgment was not issued until 28 December 2009. The Regional Court ruled for F.H., finding that A.K.’s mother had never validly owned the shares and that A.K. had not acquired them in good faith. A.K. appealed unsuccessfully to the Court of Appeal in May 2010 and then to the Supreme Court, which dismissed his appeal on points of law in January 2011.

In February 2011, A.K. lodged a constitutional complaint, alleging inter alia that the proceedings had been excessively long and that he lacked an effective remedy for that delay. In April 2012, he was informed that five Constitutional Court judges—B., Bu., Sn., S., and W.—would decide his complaint. On 8 May 2012, A.K. filed a detailed bias complaint against all five judges. He alleged that President B. had delayed appointing judges and was a close friend of Vice President H., who was the brother of the opposing party, F.H. Judge Bu. allegedly worked for the Government on constitutional matters and with Judge H. Judge Sn. had published views on judicial tenure. Judge S. sat on the supervisory board of a state-owned company. Judge W. was connected to a law firm that had represented the companies and had previously worked in Judge H.’s firm. A.K. also claimed prior adverse decisions, executive influence, and discrimination against foreign nationals showed bias.

On 15 May 2012, the Constitutional Court dismissed the bias complaints. It stated that each challenged judge did not participate in deciding the complaint against himself, with the remaining four judges deciding. It found prior adverse decisions insufficient, five-year judicial terms unproblematic, and no substantiated executive influence or objective doubt arising from friendship or professional ties to Vice President H. That same day, the Constitutional Court partly upheld A.K.’s length complaint. It found a violation of Article 6 §1 due to the two-year-and-three-month delay between the final hearing in September 2007 and the judgment in December 2009. It ordered the State to reimburse A.K.’s constitutional complaint fee and bear court costs, and to reimburse F.H.’s lawyers’ fees. The remaining complaints, including property rights and lower-court independence, were dismissed.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, A.K. alleged that the Constitutional Court judges had been partial, particularly because of the procedure used to examine his bias complaints, in breach of Article 6 §1. He also complained that the civil proceedings exceeded a reasonable time under Article 6 §1 and that he had no effective national remedy for excessive length under Article 13. These complaints were communicated to the Liechtenstein Government in June 2013.
001-165750:
In Svitlana Atamanyuk and Others v. Ukraine, four Ukrainian applicants (relatives of the Mykhayliv family) complained about the Ukrainian authorities’ response to the 27 July 2002 Sknyliv air-show disaster in Lviv. The Air Force organized a military aviation show to mark the 60th anniversary of the 14th Air Force Corps, attended by several thousand spectators. During an aerobatics display, an SU-27 piloted by Colonels V.T. and Y.Y. crashed into the static aircraft display and spectator area and exploded. Both pilots ejected safely, but 77 people died and nearly 300 were injured. Four members of the Mykhayliv family—the first applicant’s daughter, her husband and their two daughters—died at the scene. The third applicant, who attended the show, suffered post-traumatic stress reaction.

The applicants alleged that the State failed to protect their relatives’ lives and to investigate effectively. The Special Government Commission found serious organisational and safety failures: the pilots had only one joint training flight, not a rehearsal; an additional training flight and on-site rehearsal were cancelled; the pilots were not informed of the aerobatics zone or spectator placement; they flew a different aircraft from the one used in training and without mandatory g-suits; they began immediately without familiarising themselves with the site. During the display the aircraft left the designated aerobatics zone, whose boundary was about 150 metres from spectators. Ground directors did not warn or redirect them. The first pilot then performed an unpractised manoeuvre not in his mission order. He made a technical error, the second pilot did not intervene, and control was lost, causing the crash.

The applicants further alleged inhuman and degrading treatment in the aftermath. They claimed that military authorities immediately cleaned the site, piled bodies, washed away blood and small remains, buried fragments and tried to prevent photography, thereby concealing evidence. Senior officials allegedly fled, obstructing emergency access. The Government denied this, saying law enforcement arrived promptly and bodies were inspected and transported carefully. The first and third applicants said they waited hours in heat at the mortuary and had to search through decomposing bodies and fragments. Forensic experts examined the bodies on 5 August 2002, finding fatal cerebral trauma and other injuries, based on external examination. The applicants complained that autopsies were performed despite objections, that a gold earring and body fragments, including Mrs Mykhayliv’s head extracted from the engine, were not returned. The Government said unidentified fragments were buried in a common grave after identification efforts; a distorted female head could not have been Mrs Mykhayliv’s because experts found her head completely destroyed.

Multiple investigations were opened by a presidential Special Commission, the Ministry of Defence, Lviv City Council, Prosecutor’s Office and an NGO. The applicants alleged that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into the deaths; that the courts hearing their damages claim were not independent and impartial; that those proceedings were excessively lengthy; and that they had no effective remedy for the length complaint. These allegations formed the core of their applications to the European Court of Human Rights.

In *Svitlana Atamanyuk and Others v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 36314/06, 36285/06, 36290/06 and 36311/06), four Ukrainian applicants alleged violations by Ukraine arising from the 27 July 2002 Sknyliv air-show disaster in Lviv. Their relatives—the Mykhayliv family—were killed when an SU-27 military aircraft crashed into spectators during an aerobatics display. The applicants complained, in particular, that the State failed to protect their relatives’ lives and to conduct an effective investigation into the deaths; that they were subjected to inhuman and degrading treatment; that the courts hearing their damages claim were not independent and impartial; that the proceedings were inordinately lengthy; and that they had no effective remedy for the length complaint.

The event was organized by the Air Force to commemorate the 14th Air Force Corps. Several thousand people attended, including the third applicant and Natalya Mykhayliv, the first applicant’s daughter; her husband Andriy Mykhayliv; and their daughters Natalya and Andriana. During the performance, the SU-27 piloted by Colonels V.T. and Y.Y. crashed into the static aircraft display area and exploded. The pilots ejected successfully. Seventy-seven people died and nearly three hundred were injured. Four members of the Mykhayliv family died at the scene; the third applicant suffered post-traumatic stress.

Facts relevant to the alleged failure to protect life included findings by a Special Government Commission. It found serious organizational and safety failures: the pilots had only one joint training flight, in a different aircraft; an on-site rehearsal was cancelled due to fuel shortage; the pilots were not formally informed of aerobatics boundaries or spectator placement; they flew without mandatory anti-gravitation suits; they began the display without familiarizing themselves with the site; the aircraft left the designated zone; ground directors failed to warn or redirect them; and the first pilot performed an unauthorized, unpractised manoeuvre, causing loss of control.

As to the alleged inhuman and degrading treatment, the applicants claimed that after the crash military authorities immediately cleaned the site, piled bodies, washed away blood and remains, buried body fragments, and tried to prevent photographing and filming. They also alleged that fleeing VIPs caused a traffic jam that obstructed police and medical access. The Government denied this, saying law-enforcement authorities arrived promptly, no improper military conduct was recorded, and bodies were inspected and transported to mortuaries. The applicants further alleged that at the mortuary they waited for hours in intense heat and then had to search through decomposing bodies and fragments to identify their relatives. Forensic experts examined the bodies on 5 August 2002 and found fatal cerebral trauma and other injuries; Mrs Mykhayliv’s head had been completely destroyed and the children’s heads partly destroyed. The applicants said autopsies were performed despite objections, one girl’s gold earring was missing, and Mrs Mykhayliv’s head, recovered from the aircraft engine, was not returned. The Government said unidentified fragments were buried in a common grave after identification efforts; prosecutor’s documents rejected some requests, stating the distorted female head could not belong to Mrs Mykhayliv because her head had been completely destroyed.

Several investigations were opened, including by a Special Government Commission, the Ministry of Defence, Lviv City Council, the Prosecutor’s Office, and an NGO. The case therefore concerned whether Ukraine breached positive obligations to protect life and investigate deaths, whether post-crash handling amounted to inhuman or degrading treatment, and whether judicial and remedial guarantees were violated.

**Summary of the Case of *Svitlana Atamanyuk and Others v. Ukraine***

The case of *Svitlana Atamanyuk and Others v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 36314/06, 36285/06, 36290/06 and 36311/06) originated from a catastrophic military aviation accident at the Sknyliv airdrome in Lviv, Ukraine, on 27 July 2002. The event was a public air show organized by the Ukrainian Air Force to commemorate the 60th anniversary of the 14th Air Force Corps. Four Ukrainian nationals, all relatives of the Mykhayliv family, brought the case before the European Court of Human Rights, alleging violations of the Convention, particularly concerning the right to life, the prohibition of inhuman and degrading treatment, the right to a fair trial, and the right to an effective remedy.

**Key Facts Relevant to the Alleged Violations:**

The core of the case revolves around the crash of an SU-27 military aircraft during an aerobatics performance. The aircraft, piloted by two colonels, crashed into a static display area filled with spectators, resulting in a massive explosion. The tragedy claimed the lives of 77 people and injured nearly 300 others. Among the deceased were four members of the Mykhayliv family: Mrs. Natalya Mykhayliv, her husband Mr. Andriy Mykhayliv, and their two young daughters. The third applicant, who was present at the event, suffered a post-traumatic stress reaction.

The applicants raised several key factual allegations relevant to the alleged violations:

1.  **Failure to Protect Life:** The applicants argued that the State authorities failed to protect the lives of their relatives. The subsequent investigation revealed significant organizational and safety failures leading to the disaster. These included:
    - Inadequate preparation for the pilots, who had only one training flight as a team, in a different aircraft, and with a different fuel load than used during the fatal performance.
    - A rehearsal flight scheduled for the day before the show was canceled.
    - The pilots were not formally informed of the aerobatics zone boundaries or the placement of spectators.
    - During the performance, the aircraft exited the designated safety zone. Ground directors failed to warn the pilots or direct them back. The lead pilot then performed a manoeuvre he had never practiced, leading to a loss of control and the crash.

2.  **Inhuman and Degrading Treatment:** The applicants alleged they were subjected to inhuman and degrading treatment following the disaster. They described being forced to wait for long hours in the heat at the mortuary before being allowed to search for their relatives' remains among numerous decomposing bodies and body fragments piled on the floor. They also claimed that the bodies were autopsied despite their objections and that some body parts, including the head of Mrs. Mykhayliv, were not returned to them for burial. The applicants further alleged that military authorities initially tried to conceal evidence by cleaning the site, shovelling body parts, and preventing photography.

3.  **Failure to Conduct an Effective Investigation:** The applicants contended that the State failed to conduct an effective investigation into the deaths. While multiple investigations were initiated, including a high-level Special Government Commission, the applicants' claims for damages faced lengthy court proceedings, which they argued were not independent or impartial. The investigation established a series of systemic failures but did not, in the applicants' view, provide adequate redress or accountability.

4.  **Lack of Effective Remedy:** The applicants also complained that the court proceedings regarding their claim for damages were inordinately long and that they had no effective remedy to complain about this length.

The Ukrainian Government disputed several of the applicants' factual claims, particularly regarding the alleged mistreatment of bodies at the scene and the mortuary, stating that law enforcement acted promptly and that victims' remains were handled with care.

The case was communicated to the Government on 24 September 2012, marking a formal step in the proceedings before the European Court of Human Rights, where the applicants sought to establish that the State was responsible for the aforementioned violations.
