In **Naku v. Lithuania and Sweden** (Application no. 26126/07), the applicant, Ms Sniegė Naku, a Lithuanian national, worked at the Swedish embassy in Vilnius from 2 March 1992 until 2 January 2006. She began as a receptionist and translator and was later promoted to cultural, information and press officer. Her 2001 contract described her as an information officer handling cultural affairs, social secretarial duties, and replacements. A 2005 job description titled her “Cultural, Information and Press Officer,” with duties including coordinating cultural and information events, budgets, press matters, translations, and financial support applications. In 2004, Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry issued her an accreditation certificate describing her as part of the embassy’s administrative-technical staff and stating that she had no diplomatic immunities or privileges. Her terms of employment provided that Lithuanian law applied to tax, social security, overtime, leave and dismissal, and that dismissal required objective grounds.

The applicant was also chairperson of the embassy’s locally employed staff trade union, registered in 1999. Between 2004 and 2005, the union complained about working conditions and proposed a collective agreement. The embassy refused, stating it was not bound by the Lithuanian Labour Code because of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations.

In autumn 2005, a Swedish counsellor became her superior and conflict arose over her duties. On 8 November 2005, the embassy drafted a new job description, which she disputed. The next day, the ambassador gave her a “letter of caution” alleging difficulties in cooperation, lack of performance, and constant questioning of duties, and asked her to resign within two days or face other action. She was asked to hand over her keys and leave the premises. On 11 November 2005, she went on sick leave and was later hospitalized for a neurological condition.

On 23 November 2005, the embassy proposed dismissing her for gross misconduct, citing allegations that she called a colleague “unbalanced,” opened a security-risk window, and held a private meeting at the embassy. She replied that these were pretexts linked to her trade-union activities and that she had received no prior warning. On 30 December 2005, the embassy dismissed her effective 2 January 2006 under Article 136 §3(2) of the Lithuanian Labour Code for gross misconduct. It also claimed she had not provided further sick certificates, although she maintained that certificates were delivered.

She sued the Swedish embassy in the Vilnius Regional Court, seeking a declaration that her dismissal was unlawful, reinstatement, and damages. She argued that dismissal while on sick leave violated Lithuanian law, that the misconduct allegations were false, and that her health and reputation had suffered. Sweden claimed State immunity from Lithuanian jurisdiction.

On 5 June 2006, the Vilnius Regional Court left the merits unexamined because Sweden invoked diplomatic immunity. It accepted limited immunity but found that her position as head of culture and information projects presupposed a public-law civil-service relationship linked to Swedish sovereignty. The Court of Appeal upheld that ruling, holding that the job title alone showed her duties contributed to Sweden’s sovereign functions and that she had not proven otherwise. The Supreme Court dismissed her appeal, ruling that all administrative and technical staff at a foreign embassy contribute to the represented State’s sovereign functions and are therefore in its civil service. It held that Sweden’s demand for immunity was sufficient to bar the Lithuanian courts. It also refused to refer the case to the European Court of Justice.

The applicant alleged before the European Court of Human Rights that the Lithuanian courts’ upholding of Sweden’s immunity deprived her of access to a court, contrary to Article 6 §1 of the Convention. The key alleged violation was that the Lithuanian courts failed to properly examine the nature and scope of her duties and instead relied on her job title and Sweden’s immunity claim, despite her being a locally employed worker under a private-law labour contract governed by Lithuanian law and without diplomatic immunity. The application was lodged on 18 June 2007 and communicated to the respondent Governments on 7 December 2010.

**Case: Naku v. Lithuania and Sweden (Application no. 26126/07), European Court of Human Rights, 8 November 2016**

The applicant, Sniegė Naku, a Lithuanian national, worked at the Swedish embassy in Vilnius from 2 March 1992 until 2 January 2006. She began as a receptionist and translator and was later promoted to cultural, information and press officer. In October 2004, Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry issued her an accreditation certificate describing her as a member of the embassy’s administrative and technical staff, expressly stating that she enjoyed no diplomatic immunities or privileges. A November 2004 employment document provided that Lithuanian law governed her employment relationship, including dismissal, and that the employer needed objective grounds for dismissal. The applicant was also chairperson of the locally employed staff’s trade union, which made several complaints about working conditions between late 2004 and mid-2005. The embassy refused to sign collective agreements, asserting that the Vienna Convention meant it did not have to adhere to the Lithuanian Labour Code.

In autumn 2005, after a new cultural counsellor became her superior, tensions arose over her job description and duties. On 9 November 2005, the ambassador gave her a “Letter of caution” stating there was no future for her at the embassy due to alleged cooperation and performance difficulties, and gave her two days to resign. She went on sick leave on 11 November 2005. On 23 November 2005, the embassy imposed a disciplinary sanction of dismissal for alleged gross misconduct: calling a colleague “unbalanced,” opening an unbarred street-level window, and conducting a private meeting during working time. The applicant denied or explained these allegations and claimed they were a pretext linked to her trade-union activities. On 30 December 2005, the embassy dismissed her effective 2 January 2006, relying on Article 136 §3(2) of the Lithuanian Labour Code, which allows dismissal without notice for gross misconduct. It also claimed she had failed to submit continuous sick-leave certificates, though she said the embassy had been kept informed.

The applicant brought proceedings in the Vilnius Regional Court against the Swedish embassy, seeking reinstatement and damages. She argued that her dismissal was unlawful, including because she had been dismissed while on sick leave, and that the gross-misconduct allegations were unfounded. Sweden claimed State immunity from Lithuanian jurisdiction on 19 May 2006. The Vilnius Regional Court discontinued the case, holding that her position as “Head of Culture and Information Projects” presupposed a public-law, civil-service relationship connected to Sweden’s sovereign functions. The Court of Appeal upheld that decision, reasoning that the very title of her job showed her duties helped Sweden exercise sovereign functions, and that Sweden’s immunity request was sufficient. The Supreme Court dismissed her further appeal, stating that all persons working at a foreign diplomatic representation—including administrative, technical and service staff—were considered to be in the civil service of the represented State and contributed to its sovereign functions. It found the embassy’s immunity request sufficient and held that the applicant should have brought her claim in Sweden.

The alleged violation concerned Article 6 §1 of the Convention: the applicant claimed she had been deprived of access to a court because the Lithuanian courts upheld State immunity without examining the actual nature and scope of her duties. She emphasised that she was locally hired, had no diplomatic immunity, had an employment contract governed by Lithuanian law, and was dismissed while on sick leave and in connection with trade-union activity. The key issue was whether the Lithuanian courts’ reliance on her job title and Sweden’s immunity request, rather than a substantive examination of her employment relationship, breached her right of access to a court.

In *Naku v. Lithuania and Sweden*, the applicant, Ms Sniegė Naku, a Lithuanian national, worked at the Swedish embassy in Vilnius from 1992 until 2006. She began as a receptionist and translator and was later promoted to cultural, information and press officer, also serving as chairperson of the locally employed staff trade union. Her contract and embassy terms stated that Lithuanian law governed employment conditions, including dismissal, and that objective grounds were required. Her accreditation certificate identified her as administrative-technical staff and stated that she did not enjoy diplomatic immunities or privileges.

From 2004–2005, relations at the embassy deteriorated. Disputes arose over her job description, authority over cultural projects and financial support, and trade-union complaints about working conditions. In November 2005, after a new ambassador and a Swedish cultural counsellor took up posts, the ambassador gave Naku a letter of caution, stating there was no future for her at the embassy and asking her to resign within two days or face other action. She was allegedly asked to hand over her keys and leave. She went on sick leave on 11 November 2005 and was later diagnosed with neurological problems.

On 23 November 2005, the embassy notified her of a disciplinary sanction—dismissal for gross misconduct—citing alleged remarks about a colleague, security breaches, and improper private use of embassy time. Naku denied the accusations and argued they were retaliation for her trade-union activity. On 30 December 2005, while still on sick leave, the embassy dismissed her effective 2 January 2006 under the Lithuanian Labour Code for gross misconduct.

Naku brought civil proceedings in Lithuania against the Swedish embassy, seeking reinstatement and damages. She argued that dismissal while on sick leave and without proof of gross misconduct was unlawful under Lithuanian law. On 19 May 2006, Sweden claimed State immunity. The Vilnius Regional Court declined jurisdiction, reasoning that although an employment contract existed, her post as head of culture and information projects presupposed a public-law civil-service relationship linked to Sweden’s sovereign functions. The Court of Appeal upheld that finding, stating that the job title itself showed her duties helped Sweden exercise sovereign functions. The Supreme Court dismissed her appeal, holding that all administrative and technical staff at foreign diplomatic missions contributed to sovereign functions and were therefore in public-law civil-service relationships; once the embassy requested immunity, Lithuanian courts had no jurisdiction. It also refused to refer the case to the EU Court of Justice.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Naku alleged that the Lithuanian courts’ immunity ruling deprived her of access to a court under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. She contended that immunity was applied automatically based essentially on her job title, without examining the real nature of her duties or the employment relationship. She stressed that her work was cultural, information-related and clerical, governed by an employment contract and Lithuanian labour law, and did not involve the exercise of governmental authority. The case therefore concerned whether Lithuania violated her right of access to a court by upholding Sweden’s immunity claim in an employment dispute, and whether Sweden bore responsibility in that connection.
001-165230:
The case of Adam v. Slovakia concerned allegations of police ill-treatment and an ineffective investigation in Slovakia. The applicant, Jaroslav Adam, was a Slovak national of Romani origin who was sixteen years old at the relevant time. On 18 December 2010, a twelve-year-old boy was mugged and his mobile phone taken. Police searched the area with the boy and his father and, around 8 p.m., spotted the applicant, another minor, and a third person, all of Romani origin. The boy identified them as his assailants, and they were arrested.

The circumstances of the arrest were disputed. The Government maintained that the suspects resisted and tried to flee, so police used “self-defence mechanisms for holding and grabbing” and no injuries were sustained. The applicant denied resisting or being restrained. The three were taken to the county police station. Breathalyser tests indicated they had consumed alcohol, and the applicant was slightly intoxicated. They were held in rooms used as offices, not detention cells.

The applicant alleged that during preliminary questioning police used psychological pressure and physical violence to obtain a confession. He claimed he was slapped and punched in the head, forced to remain standing without sitting, lying down, or resting throughout his detention, and given no food or water. The Government denied ill-treatment, saying the suspects were kept separately, checked every fifteen minutes, and had access to a toilet with drinkable water.

In the early hours of 19 December 2010, the applicant was charged with robbery. A lawyer was appointed, and between noon and 1 p.m. he was interviewed by an investigator in the presence of his mother and lawyer. No ill-treatment was mentioned. Later he was placed in a provisional detention cell; documents stated he reported no violence and had received dinner. He was released at 6:05 p.m. and taken home. His mother later declined to give evidence and made no mention of ill-treatment. An appeal against the charge also did not raise ill-treatment, and the charge was withdrawn on 12 January 2011.

On 5 January 2011, the applicant and his associates filed a written criminal complaint with the Ministry of the Interior against county police officers. They alleged pressure to confess, slapping until confession, forced standing, lack of food and water, and failure to notify guardians. A medical report dated 19 December 2010 recorded an allegation of a slap to the right cheek, a sensitive and slightly swollen cheek, no haematoma, and a slight injury requiring recovery under seven days.

The complaint was examined by the Control and Inspection Section, which dismissed it on 9 March 2011. It reasoned that the applicant had not complained during his interview with his mother and lawyer, that the medical findings did not match later claims of sustained beating, that any injury could have occurred during a resisted arrest, and that the officers were only guarding him and had no reason to pressure a confession. Appeals to the prosecution authorities were dismissed in September 2011. A separate complaint about failure to notify guardians, provide food and water, and hear him promptly was rejected without explanation in June 2011.

The applicant then lodged a constitutional complaint, alleging violations of Article 3 (ill-treatment and ineffective investigation), Article 13 (no effective remedy), and Article 14 (discrimination), relying on known police violence against Roma in Slovakia. On 10 April 2012, the Constitutional Court rejected it as manifestly ill-founded, saying he had not raised ill-treatment before the investigator or in his appeal against the charge, and that the availability of those means excluded its jurisdiction.

**Adam v. Slovakia** concerns Jaroslav Adam, a Slovak national of Romani origin, born in 1994. On 18 December 2010, a twelve-year-old boy was mugged and his mobile phone taken. Police searched the area with the victim and his father; around 8 p.m., they spotted the applicant—then sixteen—along with another minor and a third person, all of whom the victim identified as his assailants. All three were of Romani origin and were arrested. The Government claimed the suspects resisted and tried to flee, so police subdued them using “self-defence mechanisms,” with no injuries. The applicant denied resisting or being restrained.

The suspects were taken to the county police station. Breathalyser tests showed they had consumed alcohol; the applicant was slightly intoxicated. They were kept in offices, not detention cells. The applicant alleged that officers subjected him to psychological pressure and physical violence to extract a confession: he was slapped and punched in the head, forced to stand without sitting, lying down, or resting, and given no food or water. The Government denied ill-treatment, saying the suspects were held separately, checked every fifteen minutes, and had access to a toilet with drinkable water.

At 11:10 p.m., responsibility for the detention passed to a district investigator. Early on 19 December, the applicant was charged with robbery, and provisional detention was ordered but not implemented due to lack of space. A legal-aid lawyer was appointed. Between noon and 1 p.m., the investigator interviewed him in the presence of his mother and lawyer; no ill-treatment was mentioned. At 1:50 p.m., he was placed in a provisional detention cell; the protocol stated he denied violence and had received dinner. He was released at 6:05 p.m. His mother later declined to give evidence without mentioning ill-treatment. On 21 December, through his lawyer, he appealed the charge without alleging ill-treatment. The charge was later withdrawn.

On 5 January 2011, the applicant and his associates filed a criminal complaint with the Ministry of the Interior against county police officers for abuse of authority. They alleged pressure to confess, that the applicant was slapped in the face and head until he confessed, that officers wore uniforms, that he had to stand throughout detention, was given no food or water, and that his guardians were not notified or present. A medical report of 19 December recorded an allegation of police beating and a slap to the right cheek, with slight swelling and sensitivity but no haematoma; the injury was classified as slight, with recovery under seven days. The applicant’s mother allegedly complained orally earlier, but the Government said no record existed.

The Control and Inspection Section investigated and dismissed the complaint on 9 March 2011. It relied on the absence of any complaint during the 19 December interview with his mother and lawyer, inconsistencies between the doctor’s findings and later beating allegations, the possibility the injury occurred during a forceful arrest he resisted, and the fact that the officers involved had only guarded him, not investigated him, so had no reason to pressure him into confessing. The applicant appealed, arguing he had not resisted, feared repercussions, and that a racial motive was not excluded under Article 3. The prosecutor’s offices upheld the dismissal, endorsing the CIS findings and concluding without explanation that no racial motive appeared. Another part of his complaint—failure to notify guardians, provide food and water, and hear him promptly—was also dismissed without explanation.

On 2 December 2011, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint under Article 127, alleging breaches of Articles 3, 13, and 14. On 10 April 2012, the Constitutional Court rejected it as manifestly ill-founded, stating he had no right to have third persons prosecuted, and that he had not raised ill-treatment before the investigator or in his appeal against the charge; the availability of those remedies excluded its jurisdiction.

The applicant applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 22 October 2012, alleging under Articles 3 and 13 that he had been mistreated in police detention, that the investigation was inadequate, and that no effective domestic remedy existed. The application was communicated to the Government on 2 April 2014.

**Case summary: Adam v. Slovakia (Application no. 68066/12)**

The case concerned Jaroslav Adam, a Slovak national of Romani origin born in 1994. On 18 December 2010, aged 16, he was arrested with two other Romani youths after a 12-year-old boy identified them as the robbers who had taken his mobile phone. The police claimed the suspects resisted arrest and had to be restrained; Adam denied resisting or being restrained. At the county police station, a breathalyser showed slight inebriation. The three were held overnight in rooms not designed as detention cells. Adam alleged that officers slapped and punched him in the head, psychologically pressured him to confess, forced him to stand throughout his detention, and denied him food, water, and rest. The Government denied ill-treatment, saying the suspects were kept separately, checked regularly, and given access to a toilet with drinkable water.

At 11:10 p.m. the prosecution was informed and responsibility passed to a district investigator. Early on 19 December Adam was charged with robbery; provisional detention was ordered but could not be implemented due to lack of space. A legal-aid lawyer was appointed. Between noon and 1 p.m. on 19 December he was interviewed by the investigator in the presence of his mother and lawyer, and allegedly made no ill-treatment complaint. At 1:50 p.m. he was placed in a detention cell; the protocol recorded no violence and that he had received dinner. He was released at 6:05 p.m. His mother later declined to give evidence and did not mention ill-treatment. His interlocutory appeal against the charge also did not allege ill-treatment. The charge was withdrawn in January 2011.

Adam claimed his mother later complained by telephone/visit but it was not registered. On 5 January 2011, he and his associates filed a criminal complaint with the Ministry of the Interior against the officers, alleging abuse of authority: pressure to confess, slapping of his face and head until confession, forced standing, no food or water, and failure to notify or involve his guardians. A medical report of 19 December noted an allegation of police beating and a slap to the right cheek, with no haematoma but slight swelling; he was diagnosed with a bruised left cheek, a slight injury with recovery under seven days.

The Control and Inspection Section investigated and dismissed the complaint on 9 March 2011. It reasoned that Adam had not complained during the 19 December interview despite having his mother and lawyer present; that the alleged sustained beating did not match the medical report; that the injury could have occurred during his forceful arrest; and that the officers had merely been guarding him, so had no reason to extract a confession. Appeals to the prosecution and General Prosecutor’s Office failed; the PPS also found no racial motive without explanation. A separate complaint about failure to notify guardians, provide food/water, and hear him immediately was answered by district police with no explanation that no error had occurred.

On 2 December 2011 Adam filed a constitutional complaint, stressing his minority, overnight detention without sitting or lying down, denial of food and water, and pressure and violence to confess. He alleged violations of Article 3, an inadequate investigation, no effective remedy, and discrimination (Articles 13 and 14), citing patterns of police violence against Roma in Slovakia. On 10 April 2012 the Constitutional Court rejected the complaint as manifestly ill-founded, holding that he had no right to third-party prosecution, that his criminal complaint had been dealt with, and that because he could have raised ill-treatment before the investigator or in his interlocutory appeal, the Constitutional Court lacked jurisdiction.

On 22 October 2012 Adam applied to the European Court of Human Rights under Articles 3 and 13, alleging mistreatment during police detention, an inadequate investigation, and no effective domestic remedy. International reports submitted in the case described concerns about police ill-treatment of Roma and impunity in Slovakia.
001-164434:
In *Özçelik v. the Netherlands* (ECtHR, Third Section, 28 June 2016, App. No. 69810/12), the applicant was convicted of shoplifting on 21 May 2010 and subjected to a two-year placement in a Persistent Offenders Institution (ISD), a preventive detention measure aimed at protecting society and addressing addiction. The Regional Court relied on reports describing him as a drug addict unlikely to cooperate voluntarily with treatment. After the measure was reviewed, the Regional Court refused to terminate it on 1 December 2010, finding a high risk of reoffending; the Arnhem Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal on 19 April 2011.

On 19 May 2011, the applicant’s case officer reported that he was progressing reasonably well in FPA De Cederborg but that release would leave him without income, housing, or daily activities, creating a high risk of reoffending. The Regional Court prolonged the measure on 9 June 2011. The applicant appealed on 15 June 2011. His appeal was not decided on the merits until 16 May 2012—more than ten months later. During the delay, counsel requested priority on 8 November 2011 and requested an Aramaic or Assyrian interpreter on 18 November 2011. At the hearing of 12 December 2011, the applicant could not understand the Assyrian interpreter. With his agreement, the case was adjourned for up to three months for written questions, for the case officer to testify as an expert, and for an Aramaic interpreter at the next hearing. After three months, counsel made further inquiries on 13 March and 2 April 2012. The hearing resumed on 10 May 2012. The case officer testified that the applicant was no longer addicted, that the risk of reoffending was maximally reduced, that treatment options had been insufficient, and that the institution could have signalled earlier that further treatment was impossible. The applicant was in a halfway house and awaiting sheltered accommodation, which became available on 11 May 2012.

On 16 May 2012, the Court of Appeal held that the appeal had not been dealt with speedily—though it mistakenly referred to Article 6 ECHR—and considered that finding alone sufficient satisfaction. It terminated the measure because its execution had not been sufficiently expeditious, the difficult progress was not solely the applicant’s fault, the risk to society was small, and accommodation prospects existed. The applicant was released ahead of the scheduled end date of 4 June 2012.

The applicant complained about the length of proceedings under Article 6 § 1, but the European Court of Human Rights recharacterised the complaint under Article 5 § 4, which requires that the lawfulness of continued detention be decided “speedily.” Both parties agreed there had been a violation, and the Court found that the appeal against continued ISD detention from June 2011 to May 2012 was not decided speedily, violating Article 5 § 4.

The applicant also complained that the Court of Appeal acknowledged the delay but gave no redress, such as compensation or immediate release. The Government argued that he was no longer a victim and had suffered no significant disadvantage because he was released early and the finding sufficed. The Court rejected this: a favourable finding must be accompanied by redress. Since the domestic court acknowledged the violation but awarded no compensation, the Court found a violation of Article 5 § 5, which guarantees an enforceable right to compensation for detention contrary to Article 5.

**Case: Özçelik v. the Netherlands (Application no. 69810/12), ECtHR, 28 June 2016**

The applicant, Mr Isteyfo Özçelik, a Netherlands national born in 1959, was convicted of shoplifting on 21 May 2010 by the Almelo Regional Court. The court imposed a two-year measure of placement in a Persistent Offenders Institution (PIO) under Article 38m of the Criminal Code. The measure aimed to protect society and prevent reoffending; it was based on evidence that the applicant was a drug addict who would not voluntarily cooperate with treatment. A review was scheduled six months after the judgment became final on 5 June 2010.

On 1 December 2010 the Regional Court reviewed the measure and declined to terminate it, finding a high risk of reoffending. The applicant’s appeal against that decision was dismissed by the Arnhem Court of Appeal on 19 April 2011. On 19 May 2011, his case officer reported that his placement was progressing reasonably well, but that release would leave him without income, housing, or daily activities, creating a high risk of reoffending. On 9 June 2011 the Regional Court again prolonged the measure. The applicant appealed on 15 June 2011.

The appeal proceedings were delayed. On 8 November 2011 counsel requested priority. Before the hearing, counsel asked that an Aramaic or Assyrian interpreter be present and named a suitable interpreter. At the hearing of 12 December 2011, the applicant could not understand the Assyrian interpreter. With his agreement, the case was adjourned for up to three months so counsel could put written questions to counsellors, and so case officer G.D. could testify as an expert with an Aramaic interpreter at the next hearing. After three months, counsel made further inquiries on 13 March and 2 April 2012. The hearing resumed on 10 May 2012. G.D. stated that the applicant was no longer addicted, the risk of reoffending was maximally reduced, and the institution could have signalled earlier that treatment possibilities were exhausted. The applicant was in a halfway house and waiting for sheltered accommodation, which became available on 11 May 2012.

On 16 May 2012 the Court of Appeal held that the appeal had not been dealt with speedily, amounting to a violation of Article 6 ECHR. It considered that finding a violation was sufficient satisfaction. It also terminated the PIO measure because execution had not been sufficiently expeditious, the difficult progress was not solely the applicant’s fault, he had accommodation prospects, and the risk to society was small.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained that the lawfulness of his continued detention had not been decided “speedily” as required by Article 5 §4. The Court recharacterised the complaint from Article 6 §1 to Article 5 §4. The Government accepted that Article 5 §4 had been violated. The ECtHR found a violation, accepting that the Court of Appeal had acknowledged the delay but noting it had referred incorrectly to Article 6.

The applicant further complained under Article 5 §5 that he had received no redress, such as immediate release or compensation, after the domestic finding of delay. The Government argued he was no longer a victim and had suffered no significant disadvantage because he was released early. The ECtHR rejected those objections. It held that a finding of a violation alone does not remove victim status unless redress is provided. Since the domestic court acknowledged the Article 5 §4 breach but offered no compensation, the applicant remained a victim. Article 5 §5 requires an enforceable right to compensation once a violation of Article 5 §§1–4 is established. The ECtHR therefore found a violation of Article 5 §5 as well.

In Özçelik v. the Netherlands, the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints arising from prolonged detention under a Dutch “Persistent Offenders Institution” measure. The applicant, a Netherlands national born in 1959, was convicted of shoplifting on 21 May 2010. The Almelo Regional Court imposed a two-year placement in a Persistent Offenders Institution, a measure aimed at protecting society and addressing addiction-related offending. The judgment became final on 5 June 2010 and was subject to periodic review.

On 1 December 2010 the Regional Court reviewed the measure and refused to terminate it, finding a high risk of reoffending. The applicant’s appeal was dismissed by the Arnhem Court of Appeal on 19 April 2011. On 19 May 2011 his personal case officer reported that he was progressing reasonably well at FPA De Cederborg but that, if released, he would have no income, housing or daily activities, making reoffending likely. On 9 June 2011 the Regional Court prolonged the measure again.

In **Žekonienė v. Lithuania**, the applicant, Janina Žekonienė, was a Lithuanian woman born in 1940. Her son, V.Ž., was arrested on 17 February 2010 on suspicion of unlawful possession of narcotic substances with intent to distribute. The same day, police searched the applicant’s apartment, where she lived with her son, and found small plastic bags. The next day, they searched her daughter V.B.’s apartment; because V.B. lived abroad, the applicant provided the keys and was present. Officers found plastic bags, digital scales, and remnants of herbal substances. While in detention, V.Ž. was found with an illegal mobile phone. Recovered text messages from his fiancée included statements such as “mother already knows what to do,” “It’s all hidden now,” and “Your mother was questioned today and almost got arrested.” Police suspected the applicant had hidden drugs from investigators.

On 3 March 2010, the applicant, then 69 years old, went to Šakiai police station to bring her detained son food and clean clothes. At 4 p.m., a senior investigator placed her under provisional arrest under Article 140 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. She was suspected of unlawful possession of narcotic substances with intent to distribute under Article 260 § 1 of the Criminal Code. The arrest decision cited the need to prevent her from fleeing, interfering with the investigation, or committing further crimes, and noted suspicion that she had hidden drugs. The record stated that her rights, including the right to a lawyer, were explained; she refused to sign. She was placed in a cell near her son, and her husband was informed.

On 4 March 2010, she was served with an official notice that she was a suspect and was questioned with a lawyer; she denied the crimes. She later felt weak and suffered a headache and chest pain, and an ambulance was called. At 3:50 p.m. that day, police released her because the necessary investigative actions had been completed and there were no grounds to believe she would interfere. In September 2010, the pre-trial investigation against her was discontinued for insufficient evidence. Her son was later convicted.

The applicant brought a civil claim for damages, arguing that her provisional arrest had been unfounded and unnecessary. She emphasised her age, health problems, retirement, lack of prior convictions, and stable residence. She claimed the real purpose of the arrest was to pressure her to testify against her son. She also alleged health deterioration, humiliation, and distress. She further complained that her detention conditions were inadequate—the cell was damp and dilapidated, smelled of toilet, and she was subjected to an attempted strip search. Domestic courts dismissed her claim, finding sufficient grounds for suspicion and noting that discontinuation of the investigation did not make the arrest unlawful. They did not address her detention-condition complaints.

The Article 5 § 1 complaint was declared admissible. The Court reiterated that detention must be lawful and non-arbitrary, and that “reasonable suspicion” requires objective facts suggesting the person may have committed an offence, though police need not have sufficient evidence to charge. It noted she had been held for nearly twenty-four hours from 3 to 4 March 2010 on suspicion of drug possession and distribution. At 4 p.m. an investigator placed her under provisional arrest under Article 140 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The arrest decision stated she was suspected of unlawful possession of narcotics with intent to distribute and that arrest was necessary to prevent flight, interference, or further crimes, because she was suspected of hiding drugs. She was 69, placed in a cell near her son, informed of her rights including access to a lawyer, but refused to sign the arrest record. Her husband was notified.

On 4 March she was formally notified she was a suspect: allegedly acquiring drugs in February 2010, keeping them in her daughter’s apartment for distribution, and distributing them. She was questioned with a lawyer, denied the allegations, and refused further questions. She felt weak, had a headache and chest pain, and received first aid after an ambulance was called. Her lawyer sought release, arguing the arrest was intended to pressure her to testify against her son. At 3:50 p.m. police released her, stating investigative actions had been completed and there were no grounds to believe she would interfere. The next day the prosecutor rejected her release request as unfounded. On 30 September 2010 the investigation against her was discontinued for insufficient evidence. Her son was later convicted.

In 2013 the applicant sued the State for damages. She argued her provisional arrest was unfounded and unnecessary: she was elderly, ailing, had difficulty walking, no prior convictions, was retired, and lived with her husband. She stressed she had voluntarily come to the police station and that the real purpose of the arrest was to force her to testify against her son. She claimed health deterioration, humiliation before her son and villagers, and also complained of detention conditions—her purse was searched, an attempted strip search, and a damp, dilapidated cell with toilet smells. Domestic courts dismissed her claim, finding sufficient suspicion based on the searches and phone messages, and stating that the later discontinuation did not make the arrest unlawful. They did not address the detention-conditions complaint.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, she alleged violations of Article 3 (degrading detention conditions) and Article 5 § 1 (unlawful and arbitrary provisional arrest). The Court rejected the Article 3 complaint for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies, as administrative courts—not civil courts—were the effective remedy. It declared the Article 5 § 1 complaint admissible. **Case: Tchankotadze v. Georgia (Application no. 15256/05)**

Zurab Tchankotadze, a Georgian national, chaired the Civil Aviation Agency of Georgia (“CAA”) from March 2002 to March 2004. In January 2003, the Constitutional Court declared unconstitutional the “annual regulation fee for transport activities” imposed on civil aviation companies, effective 1 April 2003. The judgment indicated that the CAA could instead provide services through freely negotiated contracts. After that date, the applicant signed contracts in March and August 2003 with Sakaeronavigatsia, Tbilisi International Airport and Air-BP-Georgia under which the CAA charged a monthly “fee for services rendered in relation to the regulation of activities.” The CAA received about GEL 600,000 between April and September 2003. In November 2003, he issued Order no. 1, applied retrospectively from 1 October 2003, under which the CAA collected further fees from 22 companies, amounting to about GEL 774,376 by March 2004. Prosecutors alleged that these measures disguised the old unconstitutional regulation fee and circumvented the Constitutional Court’s judgment.

In February 2004, criminal proceedings were opened against unnamed CAA and Ministry officials. On 16 March 2004, the applicant was charged with repeated abuse of power under Article 332 §§ 1 and 3(a) of the Criminal Code and arrested. Pre-trial detention was ordered on 19 March for three months and extended on 14 June until 16 September 2004; that extension was final and not appealable. After 16 September 2004, detention was not formally extended, yet the applicant remained in custody. On 1 February 2005, he complained to the trial court that his detention since 16 September 2004 was unlawful. On 16 March 2005, the court committed him for trial and maintained detention based on the “nature of the charges,” without addressing his complaint. These facts underpinned his Article 5 § 1 complaint that his pre-trial detention was unlawful.

The Article 6 § 1 fairness complaint concerned the trial. An accountancy expert concluded that the CAA’s fees were based on valid legal acts, that the companies suffered no financial damage, that the fees were passed on to consumers, and that the applicant received no personal profit beyond salary and travel allowances. Company representatives confirmed they had freely entered contracts or paid under Order no. 1 and suffered no loss. CAA officials testified that the CAA was not state-funded and that contracts were necessary to avoid collapse of civil aviation regulation. Nevertheless, on 8 August 2005, the Tbilisi City Court convicted the applicant for the contracts and Order no. 1, acquitting him on one episode. It found he breached the Constitutional Court judgment but gave little reasoning, rejected his arguments without explanation, and disregarded the expert report. He was sentenced to five years’ imprisonment and banned from public office for two years. The Court of Appeal in December 2005 acquitted him regarding 14 companies but upheld the remaining conviction and reduced the sentence to four years. The Supreme Court dismissed his appeal in September 2006. He was released in March 2008 after serving the full sentence.

Finally, for Article 18, the applicant relied on a December 2003 speech by presidential candidate Mikheil Saakashvili, who publicly threatened that the applicant should remove a deputy CAA chairperson or “go to jail.” After Saakashvili’s election, the deputy resigned, the applicant was investigated and arrested in March 2004, and the deputy later entered parliament on Saakashvili’s party list. The applicant alleged that the prosecution and detention were politically motivated. He lodged his application on 12 March 2005, complaining of breaches of Articles 5 § 1, 6 § 1 and 18.

In *Tchankotadze v. Georgia* (ECHR, App. no. 15256/05), the applicant was a Georgian national and chairperson of the Civil Aviation Agency of Georgia (“CAA”) from 2002 to 2004. On 10 January 2003, the Constitutional Court declared unconstitutional the “annual regulation fee for transport activities,” effective 1 April 2003. The CAA was a public-law entity not funded by the State and depended on such fees. After the judgment, the applicant entered contracts with several civil aviation companies in March and August 2003 for a “fee for services rendered in relation to the regulation of activities.” On 25 November 2003, he issued Order No. 1, applied retrospectively from 1 October 2003, allowing the CAA to collect regulation fees from companies.

On 13 February 2004, criminal proceedings for abuse of power were opened against unnamed officials. On 16 March 2004, the applicant was charged with repeated abuse of power under Article 332 §§ 1 and 3(a) of the Criminal Code. The prosecution alleged that he had circumvented the Constitutional Court’s judgment by disguising the old unconstitutional fee as contractual service fees and by issuing Order No. 1 with retroactive effect. He was arrested the same day.

On 19 March 2004, a district court ordered his pre-trial detention for three months; this was upheld on 25 March 2004. On 14 June 2004, the Tbilisi Regional Court extended his detention until 16 September 2004, with no appeal available. Although that period expired on 16 September 2004, the applicant remained in detention without an extension. On 1 February 2005, he asked the trial court to release him because his detention was unlawful. On 16 March 2005, the court committed him for trial and upheld the restraint measure without addressing his complaint.

During the trial, witness and expert evidence largely supported the applicant. Witnesses stated that the contracts had been freely negotiated, that the CAA had no State funding, and that the fees were its sole revenue source. An accountancy expert concluded that the CAA’s charges were based on relevant legal acts, that companies suffered no real loss, and that costs were passed to consumers. The applicant argued that the Constitutional Court judgment permitted contractual relations, that Parliament had delayed new legislation, and that domestic law allowed the fees. On 8 August 2005, the Tbilisi City Court convicted him on two episodes—the contracts and Order No. 1—and sentenced him to five years’ imprisonment, banning him from public office for two years. The Court of Appeal acquitted him regarding fourteen companies but upheld the remaining convictions and reduced the sentence to four years. The Supreme Court dismissed his cassation appeal on 14 September 2006. He was released on 14 March 2008 after serving his full sentence.

The applicant alleged violations of the Convention. First, under Article 5 § 1, he claimed his pre-trial detention was unlawful after 16 September 2004, when it expired and was not extended, and the court failed to rule on his complaint. Second, under Article 6 § 1, he alleged unfair criminal proceedings because domestic courts ignored exculpatory expert and witness evidence and gave insufficient, arbitrary reasoning for his abuse-of-power conviction. Third, under Article 18, he claimed the criminal proceedings and detention were initiated for improper ulterior motives. In support, he relied on a December 2003 speech by Mikheil Saakashvili, then a presidential candidate, who said the applicant should either remove a deputy CAA chairman or “go to jail.” Thereafter, the deputy resigned, the applicant was investigated and arrested, and the other individual was elected to parliament. The case thus concerns alleged unlawful detention, unfair trial, and politically motivated prosecution.

Georgia** (Application no. 15256/05) concerned Zurab Tchankotadze, former chairperson of Georgia’s Civil Aviation Agency (“CAA”), a public-law entity not financed by the State budget. On 10 January 2003, the Constitutional Court declared unconstitutional the “annual regulation fee for transport activities” collected by the CAA, with effect from 1 April 2003. The court indicated that the CAA could instead provide services through negotiated contracts with aviation companies. After that judgment, the applicant signed contracts with Sakaeronavigatsia, Tbilisi International Airport, and Air-BP-Georgia on 28 March and 13 August 2003, charging a “fee for services rendered in relation to the regulation of activities.” The CAA received about GEL 600,000 between April and September 2003. On 25 November 2003, the applicant issued Order no. 1, applied retrospectively from 1 October 2003, under which 22 companies paid regulation fees.

In February 2004, criminal proceedings for abuse of power were opened against unnamed officers of the Ministry of Transport, the CAA, and two State-owned aviation companies. On 16 March 2004, the applicant was charged under Article 332 §§ 1 and 3(a) of the Criminal Code with repeated abuse of power. The prosecution alleged that he had concealed the old unconstitutional regulation fee by renaming it a “fee for services” and had circumvented the Constitutional Court’s judgment, including by giving retrospective effect to Order no. 1. He was arrested the same day and pleaded not guilty.

The applicant’s pre-trial detention was ordered on 19 March 2004 for three months and extended on 14 June 2004 until 16 September 2004. No further extension was made. On 16 March 2005, the first-instance court committed him for trial and upheld the restraint measure without addressing his complaint about the expired detention. This formed the basis of his Article 5 § 1 complaint.

At trial, representatives of aviation companies testified that they had paid the fees under freely negotiated contracts or Order no. 1; some said they had not known they were exempted by the Constitutional Court. CAA officials explained that new legislation had been delayed and that without the fees the CAA, which received no State funding, would have ceased operations, affecting flight safety and certification. The Court of Appeal later acquitted him regarding 14 companies, upheld the remaining convictions, and reduced the sentence to four years. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction in September 2006. He was released in March 2008.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 5 § 1 (unlawful pre-trial detention), Article 6 § 1 (unfair proceedings), and Article 18 (improper ulterior motives). On the fairness complaint, he argued that domestic courts failed to explain how his conduct damaged State or service interests or caused loss, and ignored expert evidence. On ulterior motives, he relied on a December 2003 speech by Mikheil Saakashvili, then a presidential candidate, who threatened that the applicant should either remove a deputy or “go to jail.” After Saakashvili became president, the applicant was investigated and arrested.
