Sagvolden v. Norway concerned the compulsory sale of an apartment in a Norwegian housing cooperative and whether the national proceedings violated Article 6 § 1 because no oral hearing was held, and Article 8 because the sale was allegedly not “necessary.”

In 2004 Ms Torill Sagvolden, an elderly Norwegian woman, acquired an apartment in Housing Cooperative X. The Board was concerned because her adult son, Mr A, had caused serious problems in her previous cooperative. Before she moved in, she confirmed through her lawyer that she alone would occupy the flat and that her household would consist of one person. The Board approved her on that basis.

Later, Mr A moved into the apartment. Between 2005 and 2008 he repeatedly threatened, harassed and assaulted neighbours. He was convicted by Oslo City Court on 10 March 2006 of violent assault and frightening/disturbing behaviour, sentenced to 120 days’ imprisonment, and again on 23 June 2008, sentenced to 18 days’ imprisonment. Several neighbours obtained restraining orders against him between 2007 and 2009. The cooperative regarded his conduct as serious disturbance and nuisance, and as a substantial breach of the part-owner’s obligations.

After a Board meeting in September 2008, the cooperative decided to pursue eviction. On 14 April 2009 it ordered Sagvolden to sell her share under section 5-22 of the Housing Cooperative Act 2003. She refused. In September 2009 the cooperative warned of compulsory sale, and in October 2009 it petitioned Oslo City Court for compulsory sale.

Sagvolden objected. She argued that the Board decision did not validly authorise compulsory sale because it referred only to “Sagvolden” and “eviction”; that she had not substantially defaulted; that her son’s offences were old and conditions had improved; that, at age 80, she depended on him and moving would be disproportionate; and that alternative measures should be considered. She also requested that, under section 4-8(2), if her objections were not “clearly groundless,” the case be examined under ordinary procedure with an oral hearing.

On 26 April 2010 the City Court rejected her objections as clearly groundless and ordered compulsory sale by written procedure. It held that the owner is identified with household members, that Mr A’s conduct caused serious disturbance, and that substantial default existed. It found no prior warning was required because the section 5-23 eviction condition was met. The High Court rejected her appeal on 5 August 2010, deciding on the written case-file without an oral hearing. The Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee refused leave on 1 October 2010. The sale was later validated.

Before the European Court, Sagvolden complained under Article 6 § 1 that the national courts decided the compulsory-sale case without an oral hearing, despite serious factual and legal disputes and the high stakes for her home. Under Article 8 she complained that compulsory sale was not “necessary” and disproportionately interfered with her home and private life. The key facts relevant to those complaints were Mr A’s repeated violence and convictions, the cooperative’s reliance on them, Sagvolden’s age and dependence, the validity of the Board decision, the alleged improvement and alternative measures, and the domestic courts’ treatment of her objections as clearly groundless, which allowed written procedure rather than an oral hearing. The applicant died in 2015; her children pursued the application.

**Summary of the Case of Sagvolden v. Norway**

The case of *Sagvolden v. Norway* (Application no. 21682/11) concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Ms. Torill Sagvolden, an elderly Norwegian woman, against the Kingdom of Norway. The applicant complained about the compulsory sale of her apartment, alleging violations of Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair hearing) and Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life and the home) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The factual background centers on the applicant's son, Mr. A, and his disruptive and criminal behavior, which ultimately led to the loss of her home. In 2004, the applicant acquired an apartment in Housing Cooperative X. Before she moved in, the Board became aware of serious problems her son had caused in a previous housing cooperative. Consequently, the Board conditioned its approval on her written undertaking that her son would not move in with her. The applicant, through her lawyer, confirmed that her household would consist of only one person.

Despite this undertaking, Mr. A moved into the apartment. Over several years, he engaged in a pattern of frightening and violent behavior towards neighbors in the cooperative. He was convicted twice by the Oslo City Court, in 2006 and 2008, for violent assault and disturbing the peace. The convictions detailed episodes where he threatened, harassed, and physically assaulted neighbors, including an elderly man. He was also subject to several judicial restraining orders prohibiting contact with various neighbors.

In September 2008, the Board of Housing Cooperative X decided to initiate proceedings against the applicant, ordering her to sell her apartment under section 5-22 of the Housing Cooperative Act. The basis for this order was that she had substantially defaulted on her obligations as a part owner by allowing her son to live there and by his serious disturbance and nuisance to other residents.

The applicant refused to comply, arguing that the order lacked a proper legal basis and that the criminal matters were dated. The case proceeded through the Norwegian courts. The Oslo City Court upheld the compulsory sale order in April 2010, finding that the applicant was responsible for the conduct of her household members and that her son's behavior constituted a substantial breach of her obligations. Crucially, the City Court considered her objections to be "clearly groundless" and therefore decided the case based on written submissions, without holding an oral hearing. This procedural aspect formed the core of her complaint under Article 6 § 1.

The applicant appealed to the High Court and then the Supreme Court, arguing that her objections were not groundless and that her advanced age and dependence on her son's assistance made the measure disproportionate. Both higher courts rejected her appeals, affirming the lower court's findings and its decision to proceed without an oral hearing. The compulsory sale was subsequently carried out, and the applicant was eventually evicted from her apartment. Following her death in 2015, her other children were permitted by the European Court to pursue the application on her behalf.

The applicant alleged that the failure to hold an oral hearing before the national courts violated her right to a fair trial under Article 6 § 1. She further complained that the compulsory sale of her apartment was not "necessary in a democratic society" for the protection of the rights of others, as required by Article 8.

**Sagvolden v. Norway** (Application no. 21682/11) concerned the compulsory sale of a Norwegian woman’s cooperative apartment and her complaints under Article 6 § 1 (lack of an oral hearing) and Article 8 (compulsory sale not “necessary”) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

In 2004, the applicant, Torill Sagvolden, acquired an apartment in Housing Cooperative X. The cooperative’s board approved her acquisition after her lawyer confirmed that she alone would move in and that her son, Mr A, would not live there. This assurance was important because Mr A had previously caused serious problems in Housing Cooperative Y, where the applicant had lived with him. The board in X was aware of those problems and sought confirmation that Mr A would not move into the new apartment.

Despite that assurance, Mr A later lived in the applicant’s apartment. Between 2005 and 2008, he engaged in repeated violent assaults, threats, frightening behaviour, and serious disturbance toward neighbours in Housing Cooperative X. He was convicted by Oslo City Court on 10 March 2006 and again on 23 June 2008 for offences including violent assault and intimidating or disturbing behaviour. He received prison sentences, and several restraining orders were issued against him prohibiting contact with neighbours, the last lasting until April 2009. The domestic courts found that his conduct created serious insecurity and nuisance for other residents.

In 2008, the cooperative’s board decided to pursue eviction. In April 2009, it ordered the applicant to sell her share under the Housing Cooperative Act 2003. When she refused, the cooperative instituted proceedings for compulsory sale. The applicant objected on several grounds: the board’s decision allegedly referred to “Sagvolden” and “eviction” rather than compulsory sale; she was eighty years old and did not wish to move; she had become dependent on her son; the criminal incidents were old; the situation had improved; and alternative measures should have been considered.

On 26 April 2010, the City Court upheld the compulsory sale. It found that the applicant, as owner, was responsible for the conduct of household members, that Mr A’s behaviour amounted to serious disturbance and nuisance, and that she had substantially defaulted on her obligations as a part owner. It also found her objections “clearly groundless,” meaning the case could be decided in writing without an ordinary procedure or oral hearing. The court considered her age but found it did not outweigh the neighbours’ long-standing harassment.

The High Court rejected her appeal on 5 August 2010, deciding on the written case file. It relied on Mr A’s convictions, restraining orders, and pattern of behaviour, finding that the conditions for compulsory sale were met by April 2009. The Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee rejected her further appeal on 1 October 2010.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the national courts’ refusal to hold an oral hearing violated Article 6 § 1, and that the compulsory sale was disproportionate and not “necessary” under Article 8, especially given her advanced age and the impact on her home. The central procedural issue was whether her objections were properly treated as “clearly groundless” so as to justify a written procedure. The applicant died in November 2015; two of her children were later accepted as having standing to pursue the application, while her son Mr A was not permitted to do so because the applicant had earlier indicated that she did not wish him to represent her.
001-165758:
**Case: Wenner v. Germany (ECtHR, App. No. 62303/13, 1 September 2016)**

The applicant, Wolfgang Wenner, was a German national who had been addicted to heroin since 1973, from age 17. He also suffered from hepatitis C, was HIV-positive, and had polyneuropathy causing chronic pain in his feet, neck, and spine. From 1991 to 2008, his heroin addiction was treated with medically prescribed and supervised drug substitution therapy, mainly Polamidon. In 2008 he was arrested for drug trafficking and detained on remand in Kaisheim Prison, where his substitution treatment was interrupted against his will. In 2009 he was convicted and sentenced to imprisonment, with an order for placement in a drug detoxification facility. He later underwent abstinence-based treatment at a rehabilitation centre, but no substitution treatment was provided. In April 2010 he was returned to Kaisheim Prison, where he received painkillers but continued to suffer severe pain.

An external doctor, H., suggested that the prison medical service reconsider substitution treatment. A specialist in addiction treatment, Dr B., opined that substitution was medically required. He considered opioid addiction a serious chronic disease, stated that substitution was the best available therapy for long-standing addicts, and noted that forced abstinence caused severe physical and mental strain. Substitution could also prevent health deterioration, reduce infection risks, and support treatment of coexisting illnesses such as hepatitis C.

In June 2011 the applicant requested Diamorphin, Polamidon, or another substitute, or alternatively an examination by an external addiction specialist. The prison authorities refused in January 2012. They found substitution neither medically necessary nor suitable for rehabilitation, noting that he no longer had physical withdrawal symptoms, that his HIV and hepatitis C were stable, and that prison doctors were qualified to decide. The Augsburg Regional Court dismissed his appeal, the Munich Court of Appeal dismissed his further appeal, and the Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider his constitutional complaint in April 2013.

The applicant alleged that the refusal to grant him substitution treatment, and the refusal to have its necessity assessed by an external expert, breached Article 3 of the Convention, amounting to inhuman treatment. He argued that substitution was the only suitable treatment for his chronic pain and other conditions, that it continued treatment he had received for 17 years, and that the authorities failed to obtain independent specialist advice. The Government argued that he received adequate medical care, that substitution was not necessary, and that the choice of treatment fell within the State’s margin of appreciation.

The European Court of Human Rights accepted that States have a margin of appreciation in choosing between abstinence-oriented therapy and substitution therapy. However, it stressed the principle that prisoners should receive medical care equivalent to that available in the community, and that adequate specialist assessment is required. Given the applicant’s long-term addiction, failed abstinence attempts, 17 years of prior substitution treatment, supporting external medical opinions, and the availability of substitution in many German prisons, the Court found strong indications that substitution was requisite. It held that Germany had not provided credible and convincing evidence that his health and treatment needs were adequately assessed and that he received comprehensive and adequate medical care. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 3.

In *Wenner v. Germany* (Application no. 62303/13, ECtHR 2016), the applicant, Wolfgang Wenner, was a German national born in 1955 who had been addicted to heroin since 1973. He also suffered from hepatitis C since 1975, was HIV-positive since 1988, and was considered 100% disabled. From 1991 to 2008, his heroin addiction was treated with medically prescribed and supervised drug substitution therapy using Polamidon/methadone. In 2008 he was arrested on drug-trafficking suspicion and detained in Kaisheim Prison, where his substitution treatment was interrupted against his will. In 2009 he was convicted and sentenced to imprisonment; the court also ordered his placement in a drug detoxification facility after six months. He was transferred to a rehabilitation centre in Günzburg, where he received abstinence-based treatment without substitution. In April 2010 the detoxification placement was terminated and he was returned to Kaisheim Prison. There he suffered chronic pain from polyneuropathy and often spent most of his time in bed; prison doctors gave him painkillers.

In October 2010 an external internist, Dr H., examined the applicant at the prison authorities’ request and suggested that the prison medical service reconsider substitution treatment; he confirmed that the applicant should be examined by a drug-addiction specialist. In July 2011 an external addiction specialist, Dr B., opined that substitution treatment was medically necessary. He stated that substitution was internationally recognised as the best therapy for long-standing opioid addicts, that forced abstinence caused serious physical and mental strain and risk, and that substitution could prevent deterioration, reduce HIV/hepatitis C transmission, and make interferon treatment for hepatitis C possible. The applicant therefore requested Diamorphin, Polamidon or another substitute, or at least an external specialist examination.

The prison authorities refused in January 2012. Relying on prison doctor S., they found substitution neither medically necessary nor suitable for rehabilitation. They said the applicant had no physical withdrawal symptoms after three years, his HIV and hepatitis C were stable, and he should use prison to wean himself off opioids. They also claimed substitution could risk his life if he continued consuming illicit drugs. The Augsburg Regional Court dismissed his appeal in March 2012, endorsing those reasons and holding that an external expert was unnecessary because the prison doctors were sufficiently qualified. The Munich Court of Appeal dismissed his further appeal in August 2012, finding that he had not shown substitution was the specific treatment he needed or that the prison doctors were unqualified. In April 2013 the Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider his constitutional complaint without giving reasons.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that the refusal to grant him drug substitution therapy during imprisonment, and the refusal to have its necessity examined by an external medical expert, amounted to inhuman treatment contrary to Article 3 of the Convention. He argued that substitution was the only suitable treatment for his condition and that the authorities had failed to assess it properly. The Government denied a violation, arguing that he had received adequate medical care, that substitution was not medically necessary, and that the State enjoyed a margin of appreciation in choosing treatment.

The Court declared the application admissible and examined whether Germany had complied with its positive obligation to provide adequate medical care in detention. It stressed the principle of equivalence of care: prisoners should receive treatment comparable to that available in the community. Although States have a margin of appreciation in choosing between treatments, authorities must adequately assess a prisoner’s health and provide comprehensive care. The Court found strong indications that substitution was the requisite treatment: the applicant’s long-term addiction, failed abstinence attempts, chronic pain, 17 years of prior substitution, domestic medical guidelines recognising substitution as established therapy, its availability in German prisons outside Bavaria, external doctors’ recommendations, and the fact that substitution resumed immediately after his release. It concluded that Germany had violated Article 3 by failing to adequately assess the necessity of substitution treatment and to provide the requisite medical care.

In *Wenner v. Germany*, the applicant, Wolfgang Adam Wenner, born in 1955, had been addicted to heroin since 1973. He also suffered from hepatitis C, HIV, polyneuropathy and chronic pain, and was considered 100% disabled. From 1991 to 2008, his heroin addiction was treated with medically prescribed and supervised drug substitution therapy, mainly Polamidon. In 2008 he was arrested for drug trafficking and detained in Kaisheim Prison, where his substitution treatment was interrupted against his will. In June 2009 he was convicted and sentenced to imprisonment; he was also ordered into a drug detoxification facility. After a period in prison, he was transferred in December 2009 to a drug rehabilitation centre in Günzburg, where he received abstinence-based treatment without substitution therapy. In April 2010 the detoxification order was terminated and he was returned to Kaisheim Prison.

In prison, the applicant received painkillers for chronic pain linked to his long-term drug use and polyneuropathy, but his pain became severe. In October 2010, an external doctor, H., suggested that the prison medical service reconsider drug substitution treatment. A drug-addiction specialist, doctor B., later provided an opinion—based on written records but without examining the applicant—that substitution treatment was medically necessary. He relied on the Federal Medical Association’s Guidelines, stating that substitution was the best therapy for long-standing opioid addicts, helped prevent health deterioration, reduced infection risks, and supported treatment of hepatitis C and HIV.

In June 2011, the applicant requested Diamorphin, Polamidon or another heroin substitute, or alternatively that an external addiction specialist examine whether substitution was necessary. The prison authorities refused in January 2012. They argued that substitution was not medically necessary or suitable for rehabilitation, that after three years he had no physical withdrawal symptoms, that his HIV and hepatitis C were stable, and that he should use prison to become opioid-free. They also claimed substitution could be life-threatening if he continued to consume heroin. The Augsburg Regional Court upheld the refusal in March 2012, finding no need for an external expert because the prison doctors were sufficiently qualified. The Munich Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal in August 2012, and the Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider his constitutional complaint in April 2013.

The applicant alleged that the refusal to grant him substitution treatment, and the refusal to have its necessity examined by an external medical expert, amounted to inhuman treatment contrary to Article 3 of the Convention. He argued that substitution was the only suitable treatment for his condition, had previously alleviated his pain, and was necessary for proper treatment of his other serious illnesses. The Government denied a violation, arguing that he had received adequate medical care, that substitution was not medically necessary, and that the State had a margin of appreciation in choosing treatment methods.

The European Court of Human Rights found the application admissible. It reiterated that prisoners are entitled to medical care comparable to that available in the community and that the State must adequately assess and treat serious medical conditions. Given the applicant’s long-term addiction, his prior 17 years of substitution therapy, failed abstinence attempts, external medical opinions supporting substitution, and domestic guidelines requiring continuity of substitution in prison, the Court found strong indications that substitution could be the requisite treatment. The domestic authorities had not sufficiently scrutinised the change to abstinence-oriented therapy or obtained an independent specialist opinion despite divergent medical views. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 3.
001-166689:
In *Johansen v. Germany* (Application no. 17914/10), the applicant, a German national, was convicted by a penal order issued by the Frankfurt am Main District Court on 16 October 2008 for withholding and embezzlement of employee salaries. She was fined 100 daily rates of EUR 50. The central issue was whether she had validly received the penal order, because her later objection was rejected as out of time.

According to the record of service, a courier attempted to hand the penal order to the applicant at her home on 7 November 2008 at 2:10 p.m. When personal delivery was not possible, the courier placed the penal order in the mailbox attached to her residence, which constituted substituted service under Article 180 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

On 27 December 2008, the applicant filed an objection and applied for reinstatement of the proceedings. She claimed the penal order had never been served on 7 November. She said she first learned of it on 20 December 2008, when she found a court cashier’s bill in her mailbox demanding payment of the fine. She asserted that on 7 November she had checked her mailbox in the presence of her lawyer and found neither the penal order nor any notice of deposit.

In support, her lawyer, husband, and mother provided affirmations in lieu of an oath. They stated that the lawyer and applicant had returned to her house around 12:15 p.m. after a hearing at the Hanau District Court; her husband and mother were already there. No one rang the doorbell; the applicant’s dogs would have barked if someone had. Around 3:30 p.m., when the group left, the applicant took the mail from her mailbox and checked it. There was no official court letter, which would have been in a conspicuous yellow envelope. The lawyer also submitted that the private postal company J., responsible for delivering court mail, was unreliable and had become insolvent in December 2008.

The District Court rejected the objection as inadmissible and refused reinstatement on 9 April 2009. It relied on the record of service, which under Article 418 of the Code of Civil Procedure has probative value unless counter-evidence shows there was no possibility the certified facts were correct. A police interview of the courier revealed that she said she always rang doorbells and left a notification notice if no one answered; she confirmed her signature but said her husband filled in the date and time. She did not remember the specific delivery. The company reported no known irregularities. The court found the applicant’s account fabricated because the witnesses were close to her, she had initially omitted some of them, and it was unusual to check mail in front of family. Even if the courier failed to ring the doorbell, actual service by placing the order in the mailbox was valid.

The Regional Court dismissed her appeal on 10 June 2009, endorsing the District Court’s reasoning. It found insufficient counter-evidence: the courier and her husband had no motive to embezzle or forge, and the affirmations could not prove the penal order was absent. It said the applicant might have been inattentive and thrown it away or ignored it. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider her complaint on 22 September 2009 without reasons.

The applicant alleged a breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, arguing that the refusal to accept her late objection and reinstate the proceedings denied her a fair trial and effective access to court to challenge the criminal conviction. The key facts therefore concerned the validity of substituted service, the weight of the service record, and the domestic courts’ treatment of her counter-evidence.

**Johansen v. Germany (Application no. 17914/10)** concerned a German national, Ms Ruth Marion Johansen, who alleged that her right to a fair trial, including access to a court, was breached in criminal proceedings against her.

On 16 October 2008, the Frankfurt am Main District Court issued a penal order against the applicant, finding her guilty of withholding and embezzlement of employee salaries and imposing a fine of 100 daily rates of EUR 50. Under German criminal procedure, a penal order can impose punishment without a main hearing; the accused may file an objection within two weeks, failing which the order becomes final.

The dispute centred on service. The record of service stated that on 7 November 2008 at 2:10 p.m., a courier attempted to hand the penal order to the applicant at her residence, and, when that was impossible, placed it in her mailbox under substituted-service rules. The applicant said she never received it. She claimed she only learned of the penal order on 20 December 2008, when she found a court cashier’s bill in her mailbox. She filed an objection and sought reinstatement of the proceedings on 27 December 2008, arguing that her objection was not late because service had not occurred on 7 November.

Her account was supported by affirmations in lieu of oath from her lawyer, her husband, and her mother. They said that on 7 November the applicant’s lawyer and husband had attended a hearing at the Hanau District Court and returned to her house around 12:15 p.m. No one rang the doorbell; the applicant’s dogs would allegedly have barked if someone had. At about 3:30 p.m., the applicant checked her mailbox in their presence and found no official court letter, which would have been in a distinctive yellow envelope, and no notification of deposit. The applicant also argued that the private postal company J., responsible for delivering court mail, was unreliable and became insolvent in December 2008.

On 9 April 2009, the District Court rejected the objection as inadmissible and refused reinstatement. It relied on the record of service, which had probative value under the Code of Civil Procedure. The court interviewed the courier by police; she said she always rang doorbells and left notification if no one answered, though she had no specific memory of 7 November. The court found the applicant’s account fabricated because her witnesses were close and interested, her first submission omitted some allegedly present persons, and it was unusual to check mail in front of family. It held that any failure to ring the doorbell was cured by placing the order in the mailbox.

On 10 June 2009, the Frankfurt am Main Regional Court dismissed her appeal. It confirmed that service was effective when the penal order was placed in the mailbox. The applicant had not provided sufficient counter-evidence; the courier had no motive to embezzle mail, and the affidavits could not prove the order was absent. It suggested the applicant might have overlooked or discarded the letter.

The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider her constitutional complaint on 22 September 2009 without reasons. Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that the domestic courts’ acceptance of service and refusal to reopen the proceedings violated her right of access to court under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, because she was effectively prevented from challenging the penal order.

In *Johansen v. Germany* (Application no. 17914/10), the applicant, Ruth Marion Johansen, a German national born in 1970 and living in London, alleged that her right to a fair trial, including her right of access to a court, had been breached in criminal proceedings against her. The case concerned a penal order (*Strafbefehl*) issued by the Frankfurt am Main District Court on 16 October 2008. The court found her guilty of withholding and embezzling employee salaries and imposed a fine of 100 daily rates of EUR 50.

Under German criminal procedure, a penal order becomes final if no objection is filed within two weeks of service. According to the record of service, a courier attempted to hand the penal order to the applicant at her residence on 7 November 2008 at 2:10 p.m. When personal delivery was not possible, the courier placed the penal order in the mailbox appurtenant to her residence under Article 180 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

The applicant disputed that service. She claimed she only learned of the penal order on 20 December 2008, when she found a court cashier’s bill in her mailbox requesting payment of the fine. On 27 December 2008, she filed an objection against the penal order and applied for reinstatement of the proceedings, arguing that the objection was not time-barred because the penal order had never been served on 7 November 2008.

The applicant and several witnesses—her counsel, her husband, and her mother—submitted that they had been at her house on 7 November 2008. Counsel and her husband had attended a hearing at the Hanau District Court and returned around 12:15 p.m. They claimed no one rang the doorbell; the applicant’s dogs would have barked if someone had. At around 3:30 p.m., the applicant checked her mailbox in the presence of her counsel and husband. She found neither the penal order nor a notification that it had been deposited elsewhere. Official court letters came in bright yellow envelopes and would have stood out. Her mother and husband also paid special attention because some of their mail was sometimes delivered to that mailbox. Counsel further argued that the private postal company J., responsible for delivering official court mail, was unreliable and had registered insolvency in December 2008, shortly after the alleged delivery.

On 9 April 2009, the Frankfurt am Main District Court rejected the objection as inadmissible and dismissed the reinstatement application. It found that the record of service proved delivery on 7 November 2008 and could only be disproved by showing that the certified facts were impossible. The courier, interviewed by police, did not remember the specific delivery but stated that she always rang doorbells and left a notification if no one answered; her signature was on the record, though the date and time were filled in by her husband. The court found the applicant’s account fabricated because her witnesses were close and interested, her initial account omitted some persons, and checking mail with family members was unusual.

The Regional Court dismissed her appeal on 10 June 2009, agreeing there was insufficient counter-evidence. It noted the courier and her husband had no apparent motive to embezzle mail or forge documents, and that the affirmations could not prove the penal order was absent. It suggested the applicant may have been inattentive or the order may have been hidden and discarded. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider her constitutional complaint on 22 September 2009 without reasons.

The applicant lodged her application with the European Court of Human Rights on 29 March 2010. The central alleged violation was that the German courts, by treating the penal order as validly served and refusing to hear her objection as time-barred, denied her access to a court and a fair trial on the merits of the criminal charge.
001-163331:
**Summary of Qerimi and Canaj v. Albania (Applications nos. 12878/10 and 74858/12)**

The case of *Qerimi and Canaj v. Albania* concerns two separate applications lodged by Albanian nationals against the Republic of Albania, which were joined by the European Court of Human Rights due to their shared legal issue. The central facts of both applications revolve around the failure of Albanian authorities to enforce final domestic decisions that awarded the applicants compensation for property that could not be restituted in kind.

In the first application (no. 12878/10), the applicant, Qerimi, had their inherited property rights recognized by the Durrës Commission on Restitution and Compensation of Properties on 1 November 2002. The decision concerned a plot of land measuring 8,000 sq. m. Because this plot was occupied by third parties, the Commission ordered that the applicant and other heirs be compensated in kind with an equivalent plot of land. The final decision, however, was not enforced by the domestic authorities.

In the second application (no. 74858/12), the applicant, Canaj, had their inherited property rights recognized by the Fier Commission on 23 November 2001. The decision concerned a plot of land measuring 1,121 sq. m. Of this, 598 sq. m were physically restored to the applicant, but the remaining 523 sq. m were occupied. Consequently, the Commission awarded the applicant and other heirs monetary compensation in the amount of 251,040 Albanian Lek (ALL). As in the Qerimi case, this final decision was not enforced by the domestic authorities.

The applicants alleged that the non-enforcement of these final decisions constituted a violation of their rights. They specifically invoked Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to the peaceful enjoyment of one's possessions. The Court also raised, on its own motion, potential violations of Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair hearing) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy).

In its judgment, the Court noted that the Albanian Government did not contest the admissibility or the merits of the complaints, acknowledging that the applications were subject to well-established case-law, particularly the case of *Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania*. The Government recognized the prolonged failure to enforce the final decisions.

The Court found that the domestic authorities’ failure over many years to enforce the final decisions and pay the awarded compensation breached the applicants' rights under Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. Furthermore, it concluded that there was no effective domestic remedy available for the prolonged non-enforcement of these decisions, leading to a violation of Article 13. The judgment became final on 8 September 2016.

In *Qerimi and Canaj v. Albania* (Applications nos. 12878/10 and 74858/12), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section, Committee) delivered judgment on 8 September 2016. The case concerned two Albanian nationals who complained that final domestic decisions awarding them compensation for property that could not be restituted remained unenforced. Because both applications raised the same issue, the Court joined them under Rule 42 §1 of the Rules of Court.

The facts relevant to the alleged violations were as follows. In application no. 12878/10 (*Qerimi*), on 1 November 2002 the Durrës Commission on Restitution and Compensation of Properties recognised, among others, the applicant’s inherited property rights over a plot of land measuring 8,000 sq m. Since the plot was occupied, the applicant and other heirs were to be compensated in kind with an equivalent plot of land. In application no. 74858/12 (*Canaj*), on 23 November 2001 the Fier Commission recognised, among others, the applicant’s inherited property rights over a plot measuring 1,121 sq m. Of that area, 598 sq m were restored; the remaining 523 sq m was occupied, so the applicant and other heirs were to receive compensation of 251,040 Albanian Lek. These commission decisions were final domestic decisions entitling the applicants to compensation in lieu of restitution.

The applicants alleged a breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention because the domestic authorities failed to enforce those final decisions and pay the compensation awarded. The Court also raised of its own motion whether there had been violations of Article 6 §1 (fair hearing in determination of civil rights) and Article 13 (effective remedy). The Government did not contest admissibility and did not dispute the merits. It acknowledged that the applications were covered by well-established case-law, particularly *Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania*.

The Court declared the complaints admissible, finding they were not manifestly ill-founded. On the merits, the Court relied on earlier Albanian cases concerning prolonged non-enforcement of property compensation decisions, including *Çaush Driza*, *Manushaqe Puto*, *Sharra*, *Metalla*, and *Siliqi*. It found that the domestic authorities’ failure over many years to enforce the final decisions and, notably, to pay the compensation awarded breached the applicants’ rights under Article 6 §1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court further concluded that there was and continued to be no effective domestic remedy allowing adequate and sufficient redress for the prolonged non-enforcement, resulting in a violation of Article 13. The applicants did not submit claims for just satisfaction within the time-limit under Rule 60.

In *Qerimi and Canaj v. Albania* (Applications Nos. 12878/10 and 74858/12), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section, Committee) issued judgment on 8 September 2016. The applicants were two Albanian nationals. The case concerned the Albanian authorities’ failure to enforce final domestic decisions granting them compensation in lieu of restitution of inherited property. Because the applications raised the same issue, the Court joined them and noted that the underlying legal issue was already covered by well-established case-law, notably *Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania*. The applications were communicated to the Government on 20 December 2013. The applicants later failed to submit just satisfaction claims within the time allowed under Rule 60.

The key facts for each applicant are as follows. In application no. 12878/10, applicant Qerimi’s case arose from a decision of 1 November 2002 by the Durrës Commission on Restitution and Compensation of Properties. The Commission recognised, among others, Qerimi’s inherited property rights over a plot of land measuring 8,000 sq. m. Because the plot was occupied, the Commission determined that Qerimi and the other heirs would be compensated in kind with an equivalent plot of land. In application no. 74858/12, applicant Canaj’s case arose from a decision of 23 November 2001 by the Fier Commission. That Commission recognised, among others, Canaj’s inherited property rights over a plot of land measuring 1,121 sq. m. Of this, 598 sq. m were restored to the heirs. The remaining 523 sq. m were occupied, so the Commission ordered that Canaj and the other heirs be awarded compensation of 251,040 Albanian Lek.

Despite these final domestic decisions, the Albanian authorities failed for many years to enforce them. In particular, they did not pay the compensation awarded for the occupied property. That prolonged non-enforcement formed the basis of the alleged violations. The applicants complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the failure to enforce the final decisions deprived them of their possessions and the compensation intended to replace them. The Court also raised of its own motion complaints under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair hearing/access to court) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy).

The Government did not contest the admissibility of the complaints and did not dispute their merits. It acknowledged that the applications were covered by well-established case-law. The Court declared the complaints admissible. On the merits, relying on previous cases against Albania, including *Çaush Driza*, *Manushaqe Puto and Others*, *Sharra and Others*, *Metalla and Others*, and *Siliqi and Others*, the Court found that the domestic authorities’ failure over many years to enforce the final decisions and pay the compensation breached the applicants’ rights under Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It further found that there was, and continued to be, no effective domestic remedy capable of providing adequate and sufficient redress for the prolonged non-enforcement. Accordingly, there was also a violation of Article 13 of the Convention. No just satisfaction award was made because the applicants did not submit claims in time.

The applicant is a Swedish law firm, Lindstrand Partners Advokatbyrå AB (formerly Hagenfeldt Advokatbyrå AB). In 2006 the Tax Agency audited three Swedish companies—Ergonia Sweden AB, SNS-LAN Trading AB (“SNS”), and Mouse Trapper Nordic AB—for VAT, employers’ contributions, and income tax for June 2001–June 2005. It suspected significant tax evasion through transactions with a Swiss company controlled by the same persons, including Toivo Jurik. Because SNS had been liquidated and lacked its own premises, the Tax Agency applied on 4 March 2008 to the Stockholm County Administrative Court for coercive measures, seeking searches and seizures at two addresses: a flat registered to Draupner Universal AB (“Draupner”) and used by Jurik, and Jurik’s office at the applicant law firm. The Agency asked that SNS not be notified beforehand because of a risk that documents would be destroyed.

On 10 March 2008 the County Administrative Court granted the application, finding good reason to assume relevant documents were at those addresses and that the measures outweighed the intrusion into privacy. The search took place on 14 March 2008, conducted by Enforcement Authority officials and Tax Agency auditors. At the flat, they seized 19 files, an external hard drive, a torn document, and copied a computer hard drive and USB memory stick. During the search, the audit manager decided to audit Draupner and took interim coercive measures allowing searches at the flat and at the applicant law firm because Jurik and Roland Möller had offices there. The law firm was searched in the presence of its lawyer and Möller; cupboards, shelves, computers, and a safe were examined, but no relevant material was found.

The applicant requested exemption of material seized or copied at the flat—especially the external hard drive and USB stick—claiming attorney-client privilege because SNS and Draupner were clients and the devices had been used by its lawyer, Jurik. The County Administrative Court dismissed the request for lack of standing, since the material had been seized from Draupner and was not under the applicant’s control. The Administrative Court of Appeal upheld that decision, and the Supreme Administrative Court refused leave to appeal in January 2009. Similar appeals by SNS and Draupner also failed, partly because the measures had already been enforced or because the parties lacked standing. Draupner’s later exemption requests were largely rejected; a few private documents were exempted, but no attorney-client privilege was applied because the material had not been seized at a law firm and the Tax Agency had not ordered the law firm to provide information. The audit decision itself was not appealable. The applicant also unsuccessfully challenged a co-opted judge who was a Tax Agency civil servant on leave.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights on 3 April 2009, alleging violations of Articles 6, 8, and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The key alleged violations concerned the search of the law firm and the seizure/copying of electronic material allegedly protected by legal professional privilege, the applicant’s lack of standing to challenge the measures or obtain exemptions, the absence of effective judicial review, and interference with property. The Government argued that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies because it had not sought compensation. The Court rejected that objection, finding that at the time of application there was no clearly available general domestic compensation remedy, and declared the application admissible except for the Article 6 complaint.

The applicant, a Swedish law firm then named Hagenfeldt Advokatbyrå AB, complained about a Tax Agency search of its offices and the related seizure and copying of electronic material during a tax audit. In 2006 the Tax Agency audited three companies, including SNS-LAN Trading AB, concerning VAT, employer contributions and income tax for 2001–2005. It suspected that significant profits had been diverted through a Swiss company to evade Swedish tax. Because SNS had been liquidated and had no business premises, the Agency in March 2008 sought judicial permission under the Coercive Measures Act to search two addresses linked to Mr Toivo Jurik: a flat registered to Draupner Universal AB and the applicant law firm’s office, where Jurik had an office. The Agency asked that SNS not be notified in advance because of the risk that documents would be destroyed. On 10 March 2008 the County Administrative Court granted the application, finding a substantial risk and good reason to assume that relevant documents would be found at both addresses, and made the decision immediately enforceable.

On 14 March 2008 officials searched the flat. They found material belonging to Draupner, and the audit manager on site decided to audit Draupner and took an interim coercive-measures decision under section 15 of the Act, allowing searches and seizures at the flat and at the law firm, citing the risk of corruption and the earlier court judgment. At the flat, 19 files, an external hard drive and a torn document were seized, and a computer hard drive and USB memory stick were copied. The law firm’s offices—those of Mr Jurik and Mr Möller—were then searched in the presence of the applicant’s representatives. No relevant material was found there. The applicant later requested that the external hard drive and USB stick be exempted because they could contain information protected by attorney-client privilege, as SNS and Draupner were clients.

The applicant’s attempts to challenge the measures and obtain exemption were largely unsuccessful on standing and procedural grounds. The Administrative Court of Appeal found that the applicant could not appeal the SNS search order because the measures were directed at SNS, not the law firm; the Supreme Administrative Court refused leave to appeal. Draupner’s challenge to the interim decision was confirmed by the County Administrative Court, but later appeals were struck out or dismissed because the measures had already been enforced. The applicant’s exemption request was rejected for lack of legal standing because the seized material had come from Draupner and was not under the applicant’s disposition. Draupner’s exemption requests eventually led to some private documents being exempted, but no documents were found to be covered by legal privilege; the audits were discontinued and the documents returned. Separately, the applicant objected to a co-opted appellate judge who was a Tax Agency employee on leave, but the courts rejected the objection as unfounded.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, focusing on the search of its premises, possible access to privileged material, lack of effective judicial review and standing, and interference with property. The Government argued non-exhaustion because the applicant had not sought domestic compensation. The Court dismissed that objection, finding that the general compensation remedy was not clearly available when the application was lodged in April 2009. It declared the Article 8, 13 and Protocol No. 1 complaints admissible, but not the Article 6 complaint.

In *Svystoruk v. Ukraine*, the applicant, a Ukrainian national, complained under Article 2 of the Convention that the investigation into his daughter’s violent death was ineffective. The key facts concerned the murder of Inna Puzyr, the applicant’s daughter, who was found stabbed to death in roadside bushes on 11 August 2007. Criminal proceedings were opened the same day by the Poltava Regional Police. The applicant was initially called to testify as a witness, and for that reason his request to join the proceedings as an aggrieved party was refused. His other daughter, V.K., was admitted as an aggrieved party on 18 August 2007.

On 25 August 2007, O.T., a local resident, was arrested on suspicion of the murder. He initially pleaded guilty but later retracted his confession, denied involvement, and complained that police had ill-treated him. The proceedings against him were discontinued because no evidence corroborated his confession and it conflicted with other evidence. In September 2007, V.K. complained that the investigation was ineffective, that she could not consult the case file, and that she was poorly informed. The police replied that there were no irregularities and that aggrieved parties could not consult the file until the pre-trial investigation was complete.

In October 2007, the investigation was suspended for lack of leads. The prosecutor’s office quashed that decision and ordered further inquiry, noting that the investigation had been perfunctory. In November 2007, V.K. again complained and suggested that R.P., the victim’s husband, might be responsible. In January 2008, the police acknowledged many inadequacies, reprimanded supervisors, and replaced the investigator. On 5 March 2008, R.P. was arrested and confessed to killing the victim because she refused to divorce him. A crime-scene reconstruction followed, but R.P. later retracted his confession, claiming duress. In August 2008, proceedings against him were discontinued due to irreconcilable discrepancies, and the case was suspended.

In May 2009, after further complaints, the Deputy Minister of Interior renewed proceedings. He found that leads to at least two potential perpetrators had not been properly followed, identified some twenty-five investigative steps that could have been taken, and stated that virtually no action had been taken in 2008 and that police work had been perfunctory. Nevertheless, the investigation was again suspended in December 2009 and repeatedly renewed and suspended in 2010 and 2011 due to insufficient measures. Only on 15 April 2013, under the new Code of Criminal Procedure, was the applicant admitted as an aggrieved party and allowed to consult the file.

The applicant alleged that the investigation had been marred by unjustified delays, repeated suspensions, deterioration of evidence, failure to pursue leads comprehensively, and his inability to participate effectively. The Government denied this, arguing that the investigation had been thorough and that failure to identify the perpetrator was not itself a violation.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 2. It held that the investigation had lasted over nine years without foreseeable progress. The repeated suspensions and resumptions, based on insufficient measures, caused evidence to deteriorate and undermined public confidence. Domestic authorities themselves had acknowledged delays and police failures. The Court also stressed that next-of-kin must be able to participate actively and have prompt access to relevant material. Overall, Ukraine had failed to take all reasonable steps to secure evidence and identify those responsible for the murder.

**Case: Svystoruk v. Ukraine (Application no. 50067/13), ECtHR, 24 November 2016**

The applicant, Mr Viktor Petrovych Svystoruk, is a Ukrainian national whose daughter, Inna Puzyr, was found stabbed to death in roadside bushes on 11 August 2007. The Poltava Regional Police immediately opened a murder investigation. The applicant was initially called to testify as a witness, and for that reason his request to join the proceedings as an aggrieved party was refused. His other daughter, V.K., joined as an aggrieved party on 18 August 2007. The applicant was not admitted as an aggrieved party until 15 April 2013, after the new Code of Criminal Procedure entered into force, when he was also given access to the case file.

The investigation was marked by repeated arrests, confessions, retractions, suspensions and renewals. On 25 August 2007, O.T., a local resident, was arrested and initially confessed, but later retracted, denied involvement and alleged police ill-treatment. The proceedings against him were discontinued because no evidence corroborated the confession and it conflicted with other evidence. On 10 October 2007, the investigation was suspended for lack of leads. The District Prosecutor’s Office then quashed that decision and ordered further inquiry, noting that the investigation had been conducted perfunctorily. V.K. repeatedly complained about the investigation’s ineffectiveness, lack of meaningful participation and poor access to information. She also suspected R.P., her sister’s husband. On 23 January 2008, the police acknowledged many inadequacies, reprimanded supervisors and replaced the investigator.

On 5 March 2008, R.P. was arrested and confessed to killing the applicant’s daughter because she had refused to divorce him. A crime-scene reconstruction followed. R.P. later retracted his confession, claiming duress, and in August 2008 the proceedings against him were discontinued because of irreconcilable discrepancies. The investigation was again suspended. In May 2009, after further complaints, the Deputy Minister of Interior ordered renewal. He found that leads concerning at least two potential perpetrators had not been properly pursued, identified some twenty-five possible investigative steps, stated that virtually no action had been taken in 2008, and described the operative officers’ work as perfunctory.

Proceedings were renewed and suspended repeatedly in 2010 and 2011, each time with reference to insufficient measures. By August 2013, after studying the file, the applicant complained of prohibitive delays, inactivity and a prolonged focus on the husband hypothesis rather than prompt examination of objective evidence. He suggested further witnesses, the possible knife type and persons who might possess such a weapon. The authorities replied that no new leads had been uncovered but that his suggestions would be considered.

Before the Court, the applicant alleged a violation of Article 2 of the Convention, arguing that the State had failed to conduct an effective investigation into his daughter’s violent death. He relied on unjustified protractions, repeated suspensions, deterioration of evidence, failure to pursue leads concurrently and comprehensively, and his inability to participate effectively because of delayed aggrieved-party status and poor access to file material and information. The Government denied the allegations, claiming the investigation had been thorough and that the failure to identify the perpetrator did not itself breach the Convention.

The Court found the application admissible and concluded that Ukraine had violated Article 2. It emphasised that the investigation had lasted over nine years without foreseeable progress, was repeatedly suspended and resumed because of insufficient measures, and had been acknowledged domestically as suffering from delays and ineffective police work. The Court also stressed that next-of-kin must be able to participate actively and have prompt access to relevant evidence and decisions. Overall, the authorities had not done everything possible to ensure prompt and comprehensive collection of evidence aimed at identifying and prosecuting those responsible.
001-162424:
In *Abdi Mahamud v. Malta* (ECtHR, 3 May 2016), the applicant, a Somali national born in 1992, entered Malta irregularly by boat on 6 May 2012. She was registered, given an identification number, and served with a Return Decision and Removal Order under the Immigration Act as a prohibited immigrant without means of subsistence. She was immediately detained at Lyster Barracks Detention Centre in Ħal Far. The documents advised her of a right to appeal to the Immigration Appeals Board within three working days. On 9 May 2012 she registered an asylum application. The Office of the Refugee Commissioner rejected it on 30 June 2012, and the Refugee Appeals Board dismissed her appeal on 18 December 2012. Malta did not in practice remove persons to Somalia or Somaliland, and the applicant remained detained until 12 September 2013.

She alleged violations of Article 3 (inhuman and degrading conditions of detention) and Article 5 §§1 and 4 (arbitrary or unlawful continued detention and lack of a remedy to challenge its lawfulness). A central fact was her vulnerability. From arrival she suffered headaches, earaches, fainting, dehydration, anxiety and depression, worsened after her asylum rejection. She was initially hospitalised and made frequent hospital visits; medical certificates noted low mood, insomnia, somatic symptoms, deterioration, and suggested she be considered vulnerable. On 1 October 2012 the Jesuit Refugee Service referred her to AWAS for an Adult Vulnerability Assessment seeking release on health grounds. She was interviewed in December 2012, allegedly told verbally she would be released, but only on 10 August 2013 was she verbally informed of release; she was actually released on 12 September 2013. Government policy since 2005 stated that vulnerable irregular immigrants should be exempt from detention, but the AWAS procedure was not adequately regulated by law, gave no written reasons and had no appeal.

As to conditions, she was held in Hermes Block, in Zones C, D and A, described as basic and prison-like. Zone C held over eighty single women; at times there were insufficient beds and detainees slept on metal tables. She complained of overcrowding, lack of privacy and sanitation, no constructive activities, limited open-air access, poor communication, inadequate heating and cooling, and limited medical care and interpreters. She also alleged a lack of female staff: male soldiers entered the dormitory each morning while women slept for headcounts and removed sheets, forcing her to sleep fully dressed, including her headscarf. The CPT report noted only one female officer at Lyster and recommended round-the-clock female staffing.

The Government argued non-exhaustion, relying on constitutional redress and tort damages, with possible interim measures. The Court dismissed this objection, holding that the remedies were not effective in the circumstances because constitutional proceedings were delayed, tort actions were not preventive, and interim release for immigration detainees was not shown to be regularly available. The Article 3 complaint was declared admissible. The case therefore focuses on whether the applicant’s medical vulnerability, prolonged detention, and the conditions at Lyster Barracks amounted to inhuman or degrading treatment, and whether she had any effective means to challenge her detention.

Abdi Mahamud v. Malta (Application no. 56796/13) concerned a Somali woman, born in 1992, who arrived in Malta irregularly by boat on 6 May 2012. She was registered by immigration police, issued a Return Decision and Removal Order, and immediately detained at Lyster Barracks Detention Centre in Ħal Far under Article 14(2) of the Immigration Act. The Return Decision classified her as a prohibited immigrant because she lacked means of subsistence and was liable to become a charge on public funds. The Removal Order stated she would remain in custody until removal and that an entry ban would be issued. She applied for asylum on 9 May 2012. The Office of the Refugee Commissioner rejected her claim on 30 June 2012, and the Refugee Appeals Board rejected her appeal on 18 December 2012. Although no removal steps were taken and Malta in practice did not remove people to Somalia or Somaliland, she remained in detention until 12 September 2013.

She complained under Articles 3 and 5 §§1 and 4 that her continued detention was arbitrary and unlawful, that she lacked an effective remedy to challenge its lawfulness, and that the conditions of detention amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment.

Key facts on detention and vulnerability: She suffered from headaches, earaches, fainting, dizziness, anxiety and depression, and possible fits. From May to September 2012 she had about sixteen medical consultations, was prescribed medication, and had been hospitalised on arrival for dehydration. A March 2013 medical certificate recorded low mood, insomnia, somatic chest pain and evident deterioration, and suggested she be considered vulnerable. A May 2013 doctor’s attestation said her health posed challenges in keeping her at Ħal Far. On 1 October 2012 the Jesuit Refugee Service referred her to the Agency for the Welfare of Asylum Seekers (AWAS) for release on vulnerability grounds. AWAS interviewed her briefly in December 2012, in English and with assistance from a non-fluent detainee, and allegedly told her she would be released. In August 2013 AWAS verbally confirmed release, and she was released on 12 September 2013. The vulnerability procedure could determine continued detention but was not adequately regulated by law or public rules and gave no written reasons or appeal.

Conditions of detention: She was held in Hermes Block, described as prison-like and basic. In Zone C there were over eighty women, insufficient beds, and some slept on metal tables. Zone D was less crowded but lacked privacy and sanitation. At peak in August 2012, with 69 detainees, shelter space was about 4.3 sq m; in May, with 61 detainees, about 4.9 sq m. She complained of no constructive activities, overcrowding, lack of privacy, limited open-air access, communication difficulties, lack of information, extreme heat and cold, poor food, and limited medical care and interpreters. Notably, male soldiers entered the female dormitory each morning for headcounts while women were asleep and removed sheets; she therefore slept fully dressed, including her headscarf. She also highlighted the lack of female staff. The Government disputed these claims, saying basic needs, medical care, provisions and some female officers were provided. The Court dismissed the Government’s non-exhaustion objection regarding Article 3, finding domestic remedies ineffective, and declared the complaint admissible.

**Abdi Mahamud v. Malta (Application no. 56796/13), European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, Judgment of 3 May 2016.**

The applicant, Ms Sagal Abdi Mahamud, a Somali national born in 1992, entered Malta irregularly by boat on 6 May 2012. On arrival, immigration police registered her and issued a Return Decision and Removal Order under the Immigration Act. The Return Decision stated that she was a prohibited immigrant because she lacked means of subsistence and was liable to become a charge on public funds. The Removal Order stated that her request for voluntary departure had been rejected and that she would remain in custody until removal, with an entry ban. She was immediately detained at Lyster Barracks Detention Centre in Ħal Far under Article 14(2) of the Immigration Act. She was informed of a right to appeal to the Immigration Appeals Board within three working days.

On 9 May 2012, the applicant registered her wish to apply for asylum. The Office of the Refugee Commissioner rejected her claim on 30 June 2012, doubting, among other things, that she was from central/southern Somalia. The Refugee Appeals Board dismissed her appeal on 18 December 2012. In practice, Malta effected no removals to Somalia or Somaliland, and she remained in detention. She lodged her application with the European Court on 19 August 2013, while still detained, and was released on 12 September 2013 after the Agency for the Welfare of Asylum Seekers (AWAS) accepted her vulnerability request.

The applicant alleged that her continued detention was arbitrary and unlawful, that she lacked an effective remedy to challenge its lawfulness, and that her conditions of detention amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment. She relied on Articles 3 and 5 §§ 1 and 4 of the Convention.

Facts relevant to her Article 3 complaint concerned conditions at Hermes Block, described as prison-like and basic. She was held in Zones C, D and A. Zone C at one point held over eighty single women; there were not enough beds, and some detainees slept on metal tables. At peak capacity, around sixty-nine detainees shared the zone, giving approximately 4.3–5 square metres of shelter space each. She complained of overcrowding, lack of privacy and sanitation, lack of constructive activities, limited access to open air, inadequate heating and cooling, poor and culturally inappropriate food, and limited information and communication with the outside world. She also alleged a lack of female staff: male soldiers entered the female dormitory each morning for headcounts and removed sheets, forcing her to sleep fully dressed, including her headscarf. She complained of limited medical care and lack of interpreters.

Her vulnerability was central. She suffered headaches, earaches, fainting, anxiety and depression, and was frequently hospitalised or prescribed medication. In October 2012 she was referred to AWAS for release on vulnerability grounds. She was interviewed in December 2012, allegedly briefly and in English without proper interpretation, and was later verbally told she would be released. The procedure was said to be inadequately regulated, without written reasons or appeal, despite its decisive impact on detention.

The Government argued that she had not exhausted domestic remedies, including constitutional redress and tort damages. The Court found those remedies ineffective in the circumstances, particularly because constitutional proceedings were delayed and did not provide a timely preventive remedy while she remained detained. The case therefore proceeded to assessment of her complaints.
