In **Kleutin v. Ukraine** (no. 5911/05, judgment 23 June 2016), the applicant, a Ukrainian national born in 1979, complained under Article 3 that police beat him during his apprehension on 22 January 2004 and that the investigation was ineffective; that conditions in Odesa SIZO were inhuman and degrading; and under Article 5 that his arrest and pre-trial detention were unlawful and lacked effective judicial review.

Criminal proceedings began on 22 January 2004 after a robbery. The applicant was arrested that day under Article 115 of the Criminal Procedure Code on suspicion of robbery. He alleged that three police officers, including K., the brother of an alleged accomplice, came to his flat, armed, threatened him with firearms, beat him on the head and body, fractured two ribs, and tried to make him confess. The Government claimed he voluntarily went with police and no force was used. His sister later testified that she saw no beating but heard raised voices. A police officer questioned in 2007 said the applicant agreed voluntarily and no force was used.

The domestic investigation was delayed. On 29 March 2005 the trial court ordered the prosecutor to identify and question the apprehending officers and the applicant’s sister by 11 April 2005. This was not complied with. The sister was questioned in July 2005; the officer in June 2007. On 4 June 2007 the prosecutor refused to open criminal proceedings against the officer, finding no force. The applicant did not challenge that decision. Medical evidence was disputed: he was admitted to Odesa SIZO on 26 January 2004, where authorities said he was healthy and had no complaints; an X-ray of 25 January 2004 was mentioned, and the applicant claimed it showed rib injuries, although the city hospital said he received no inpatient treatment.

As to detention conditions, the applicant was held in Odesa SIZO from 26 January 2004 to 23 November 2007. He alleged overcrowding, poor sanitation, no outdoor exercise, and confinement for most of the day. The Government listed cells, many measuring about 6.73–7.85 sq m intended for four detainees, plus larger cells for 12, 42, and 14 detainees. It claimed adequate furnishings, ventilation, light, running water, and partitioned toilets. CPT standards recommend at least 4 sq m per prisoner.

Regarding Article 5, on 24 January 2004 the District Court remanded him in custody in his absence and without setting a maximum duration. On 18 March 2004 it extended detention by one month, again in his absence. After the investigation was completed on 8 April 2004, committal hearings on 5 May 2004 made no ruling on detention. The case was remitted for additional investigation on 18 June 2004 and 18 April 2005 without addressing detention. On 15 September 2005 the court maintained detention without reasons or time-limits. His repeated requests to change the preventive measure were not properly examined. He was convicted on 8 June 2007 and sentenced to five years; appeals failed, and he was released on 22 January 2009.

The Court examined these facts in relation to alleged violations of Article 3 (ill-treatment, ineffective investigation, and detention conditions) and Article 5 (unlawful detention and lack of effective judicial review).

**Kleutin v. Ukraine** (App. No. 5911/05; judgment 23 June 2016) concerned a Ukrainian national, Mr Denis Vasilyevich Kleutin, born in 1979 and living in Odesa. He alleged under Article 3 that police had beaten him during apprehension on 22 January 2004 and that no effective investigation followed, and that conditions in Odesa SIZO were inhuman and degrading. He also alleged under Article 5 that his arrest and pre-trial detention were unlawful and that courts failed to conduct an effective judicial review of his detention.

On 22 January 2004, criminal proceedings were instituted against the applicant and two others for a robbery committed the previous night. That same day, at 1:40 p.m., an investigator arrested him under Article 115 of the Criminal Procedure Code on suspicion of robbery under Article 186 of the Criminal Code. The applicant claimed that police officers, including K. — the brother of an alleged accomplice — came to his apartment, threatened him with firearms, beat him on the head and body, fractured two ribs, and tried to force him to confess. He said he was then forced to go to the police station. The Government denied any force and said he went voluntarily. The applicant’s sister testified that she opened the door to K. and two other men identifying themselves as police, woke the applicant, and saw him dress and leave with them; she did not witness ill-treatment but heard raised voices. The apprehending officer later stated that no force was used and that the applicant agreed to go voluntarily.

During his criminal trial, the applicant repeated his ill-treatment complaint. On 29 March 2005, the District Court ordered the prosecutor’s office to identify and question the officers and the applicant’s sister and to issue a procedural decision. This order was not complied with by 18 April 2005. On 23 November 2005, the applicant lodged a formal complaint with the prosecutor’s office. On 17 May 2007, the District Court again ordered the authorities to verify the allegations, noting the earlier non-compliance. On 4 June 2007, the prosecutor questioned the apprehending officer and refused to institute criminal proceedings, finding no physical force and voluntary compliance. The applicant did not challenge that refusal. Medical records showed he was admitted to Odesa SIZO on 26 January 2004; authorities claimed he was healthy and did not complain of injury. His file contained an X-ray from 25 January 2004, which the applicant claimed showed a rib fracture, while SIZO staff allegedly described it as a missing part of the third left rib.

As to detention, on 23 January 2004 the investigator sought pre-trial detention. On 24 January 2004, the District Court remanded the applicant in custody without setting a maximum duration and in his absence, citing the gravity of the charges, previous convictions, and risks of absconding or reoffending. On 18 March 2004, it extended detention by one month, again in his absence. After the investigation was completed on 8 April 2004, committal hearings and later remittals did not address continued detention. On 15 September 2005, the court maintained detention without reasons or time limits. The applicant repeatedly sought a non-custodial measure in 2005–2007; the court replied that such requests should be examined at a hearing. He was convicted on 8 June 2007 and sentenced to five years, appeals were dismissed, and he was released on 22 January 2009.

The applicant was held in Odesa SIZO from 26 January 2004 to 23 November 2007. He alleged overcrowding, poor sanitation, prolonged cell confinement, and no outdoor activity. The Government stated cells were adequate, with furnishings, partitioned toilets, ventilation, and running water. The Court declared the ill-treatment and ineffective-investigation complaint admissible, finding serious issues requiring examination on the merits.

In *Kleutin v. Ukraine*, the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by Denis Vasilyevich Kleutin, a Ukrainian national, concerning events beginning on 22 January 2004. On that date, criminal proceedings were instituted against him and two others for robbery. He was arrested by an investigator the same day. The applicant alleged that, before being taken to the police station, police officers—including K., the brother of an alleged accomplice—came to his Odesa apartment, threatened him with firearms, struck him on the head and body, fractured two of his ribs, and forced him to accompany them in order to make him confess. His sister was present in the apartment; she stated that she opened the door to K. and two others, woke the applicant, and heard raised voices, but did not witness any beating. The Government denied the allegations, claiming that no force was used and that the applicant voluntarily agreed to go with the officers.

Regarding the ill-treatment investigation, the District Court on 29 March 2005 ordered the prosecutor’s office to identify and question the officers involved and the applicant’s sister, and to issue a procedural decision. The prosecutor failed to comply by the deadline, and the case was remitted for additional investigation on 18 April 2005. The applicant lodged a complaint with the prosecutor’s office on 23 November 2005. On 4 June 2007, the prosecutor questioned one police officer, who repeated that no force had been used and that the applicant had complied voluntarily. The same day, the prosecutor refused to institute criminal proceedings against the officer. The applicant did not challenge that refusal. Medical records showed that on admission to Odesa SIZO on 26 January 2004, the authorities described him as healthy and noted no complaints, though his file contained an X-ray from 25 January 2004. The applicant claimed the X-ray showed a rib fracture and alleged a cover-up; the city hospital stated he received no inpatient treatment in January 2004. The Court found the ill-treatment and ineffective-investigation complaint admissible.

As to detention, on 24 January 2004 the Prymorsky District Court remanded the applicant in custody without setting a maximum duration, in his absence, relying on the gravity of the charges, his previous convictions, and risks that he might abscond, reoffend, or obstruct justice. On 18 March 2004, his detention was extended by one month. The case was sent to trial on 8 April 2004. During committal hearings, the court made no ruling on further detention. The case was remitted for additional investigation in June 2004 and April 2005, again without addressing his detention. On 15 September 2005, the court maintained his detention without reasons or time limits. The applicant repeatedly asked for a non-custodial preventive measure in 2005–2007, but the court replied that such petitions should be lodged at a hearing. He was convicted on 8 June 2007 and sentenced to five years’ imprisonment. His appeal was dismissed on 15 November 2007, the Supreme Court refused leave on 2 June 2008, and he was released on 22 January 2009. He complained that his arrest and detention were unlawful and lacked effective judicial review.

Finally, the applicant was held in Odesa SIZO from 26 January 2004 to 23 November 2007. He alleged overcrowding, poor sanitation, no outdoor activity, and confinement in cells for most of the day. The Government claimed the cells were adequate, with furnishings, partitioned toilets, ventilation, natural light, running water, and drainage. The listed cells were mostly 6.73–7.85 sq m for four detainees, with some larger cells. The CPT recommended at least 4 sq m per prisoner. The key alleged violations concerned Article 3 ill-treatment, ineffective investigation, and inhuman conditions of detention, as well as Article 5 unlawful detention and lack of judicial review.
001-160800: In *Meier v. Switzerland* (Application no. 10109/14, judgment 9 February 2016), the applicant, Beat Meier, a Swiss national born in 1946, was serving a custodial sentence in Switzerland. In 2003 he was sentenced to four years and four months’ imprisonment for multiple sexual acts with minors and multiple acts of sexual coercion. In 2010 the Court of Appeal suspended execution of the sentence and replaced it with preventive detention

**Meier v. Switzerland** (Application no. 10109/14, judgment of 9 February 2016) concerned a Swiss national, Beat Meier, born in 1946 and detained in Regensdorf/Pöschwies Prison. In 2003, the Zurich Court of Appeal sentenced him to four years and four months’ imprisonment for multiple sexual acts with minors and multiple acts of sexual coercion. In 2010, execution of the sentence was suspended and replaced by preventive detention aimed at preventing reoffending.

After reaching retirement age, Meier requested exemption from the requirement to work in prison on 6 December 2011. The Judicial Enforcements Office refused on 19 March 2012. When he refused to work, Pöschwies Prison placed him under a stricter regime on 29 May 2012, confining him to his cell and confiscating his television and computer for fourteen days. Although that disciplinary decision was later revoked, the refusal of his work exemption remained. His appeals to the Directorate of Justice and Internal Affairs, the Administrative Court of Zurich, and the Federal Court were dismissed. In July 2013, the Federal Court held that compulsory prison work was not in itself a human rights breach, including under Article 4 ECHR. It found that work served resocialisation, daily structure, prison order, and prevention of mental and physical deterioration; that pension-age rules did not apply to prisoners; and that voluntary activity would not achieve the same aims. However, work for older prisoners had to be tailored to their abilities and should not be excessive.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Meier alleged that being required to work after retirement age violated Article 4 (prohibition of forced or compulsory labour) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination). The Government disputed admissibility on exhaustion grounds, but the Court found that the substance of the Article 4 complaint had been raised domestically and declared it admissible.

On the merits, the Government argued that Meier’s work was appropriate. He had a medical certificate assessing his work capacity at 50% and worked only about three hours per working day, or 18 hours and 20 minutes per week. He was housed in the “dependent and retired prisoners” wing and performed supervised tasks such as colouring mandalas, cleaning his cell, and making sculptures from driftwood. He was paid, and prisoners unfit for work were exempted. The Government maintained that prison work is not comparable to free-market employment and fell within Article 4 § 3(a)’s exception for work required in the ordinary course of detention.

The Court accepted that Meier’s work was exacted under threat of penalty and was not voluntary. However, examining the aim, nature, extent, and manner of the work, it found that it fell within Article 4 § 3(a). Suitable light work could reduce the harmful effects of detention and structure daily life. Meier’s tasks were age-appropriate, part-time, and performed in a specialised wing. A comparative survey showed that 16 of 28 Council of Europe states did not require prisoners to work beyond retirement age, while 12 did not explicitly address the issue. Nevertheless, the Court concluded that the applicant’s specific work was within the ordinary course of detention and did not constitute forced or compulsory labour. It found no violation of Article 4 § 2 and no separate violation of Article 14. The case was significant as the first ECHR examination of compulsory prison work after retirement age.

Meier v. Switzerland (Application no. 10109/14), ECtHR Third Section, 9 February 2016, concerned whether a Swiss prisoner could be required to work after reaching retirement age. The applicant, Beat Meier, born in 1946, was sentenced in 2003 to four years and four months’ imprisonment for multiple sexual acts with minors and multiple acts of sexual coercion. In 2010, execution of that sentence was suspended and replaced by preventive detention intended to prevent reoffending. He was detained in Pöschwies Prison.

In December 2011, after reaching retirement age, Meier requested exemption from the statutory requirement for prisoners to work. The Judicial Enforcements Office of the Canton of Zurich refused in March 2012. In May 2012, after he refused to work, prison authorities placed him under a stricter regime, confined him to his cell, and confiscated his television and computer for fourteen days. That disciplinary decision was later revoked, but the refusal decision stood. His appeals failed before the Directorate of Justice and Internal Affairs in June 2012, the Administrative Court of Zurich in January 2013, and the Federal Court in July 2013.

The Federal Court held that compulsory prison work was not inherently contrary to human rights. It served resocialisation, structured daily life, maintained order, and reduced the harmful effects of detention. For prisoners over 65, work had to be tailored to their abilities and not impose an excessive burden. The Federal Court also held that pension and employment rules did not apply to prisoners and that voluntary occupation would not fulfil the same aims.

Before the ECtHR, Meier alleged that the requirement to work after retirement age violated Article 4 (prohibition of forced or compulsory labour) and Article 14 (non-discrimination) of the Convention. He argued that the law exempted prisoners only for physical or mental incapacity, not for age; that requiring work under threat of disciplinary penalties breached human dignity; and that European Prison Rules, especially Rule 105.2, permitted required work only for sentenced prisoners who had not reached normal retirement age
001-167490:
The applicant, a Swiss hairdresser born in 1954, had compulsory accident insurance. In 1995 she was hit by a motorcycle and suffered head and neck injuries. She was initially certified totally unfit for work. A long dispute followed between her and her accident insurer over whether her continuing health problems were causally linked to the accident and whether she remained incapacitated. Multiple medical reports conflicted: some found a causal link and total incapacity, while others found no causal link or only 10–20% incapacity. In 2002 she was granted a full disability pension by the social security authority, and in 2005 the Social Insurance Court found a causal link and remitted the case to the insurer for a benefits decision.

The insurer then invited her to undergo a functional-capacity evaluation, which she refused. The insurer sent a formal notice under Article 43(3) of the Social Security Act warning her about the consequences of refusing to cooperate, but it did not mention the possibility of covert surveillance. In October 2006, the insurer commissioned private investigators who secretly monitored her on four dates over twenty-three days, for several hours each time. They followed her over long distances and produced a detailed report and video footage. The applicant apparently became aware of the surveillance on the final day. The insurer initially refused her representative access to the report, but later sent her the report and footage and stated that a fresh neurological assessment was necessary. She again refused examination and asked for a decision on her benefits.

In March 2007 the insurer refused benefits based on the surveillance images and her refusal to undergo a neurological examination. Later, using the images, an expert assessed her incapacity at 10%. In April 2008 the insurer refused to destroy the images and granted benefits based on 10% disability. The applicant appealed, seeking compensation, a higher pension, and removal of the surveillance material from her file. She argued that the surveillance was reprehensible, inappropriate, and an attack on her personality.

In 2009 the Social Insurance Court held that the surveillance lacked a legal basis, so the monitoring record was inadmissible; the expert opinion relying on it also had no probative value. It further held that she was entitled to refuse further examinations. The insurer appealed. In 2010 the Federal Court reversed, relying on earlier case law that secret surveillance of insured persons by accident insurers was lawful under Articles 28 and 43 of the Social Security Act, at least where limited to public activities. It found the surveillance file to be valid evidence. It concluded that images of her walking her dog, driving long distances, shopping, carrying groceries, and lifting her arms above her head without obvious restriction contradicted the medical reports. It held that a neurological reassessment was necessary and admissible because she had refused to cooperate. The Federal Court therefore quashed the Social Insurance Court’s decision except as to interest on arrears.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the secret surveillance ordered by her compulsory accident insurer violated her right to respect for private life under Article 8, and that the use of the surveillance material and related proceedings breached her right to a fair trial under Article 6. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were that a public-function insurer had secretly monitored her daily activities without a clear prior warning or specific legal basis, then used the footage as evidence to reduce or deny her social-insurance benefits.

In *Vukota-Bojić v. Switzerland*, the applicant, a Swiss hairdresser, was injured in 1995 when hit by a motorcycle. She was covered by compulsory accident insurance. Medical assessments over the following years conflicted: some found total incapacity for work, while others found she was fit to work or only partially incapacitated. Her insurer terminated daily allowances from April 1997, sparking a long dispute. In 2000 the Social Insurance Court remitted the case for clarification. In 2002 the social security authority granted her a full disability pension. In 2005 the Social Insurance Court recognised a causal link between the accident and her health problems and referred the matter back to the insurer.

The insurer then invited her to undergo a functional-capacity assessment, which she refused. It issued a formal notice under Article 43(3) of the Social Security Act warning of consequences for non-cooperation, but did not mention possible covert monitoring. Nevertheless, in October 2006 the insurer commissioned private investigators to monitor her on four days over 23 days, for several hours each time. The investigators followed her over long distances and produced a detailed surveillance report and footage. She apparently became aware of the surveillance on the last day. The insurer initially refused her representative access to the report, then sent it to her in December 2006, together with the footage, and required a fresh neurological assessment. She refused.

In March 2007 the insurer denied benefits based on the surveillance images and her refusal to undergo further examination. A neurologist, Dr H., relying on earlier medical assessments and the surveillance images, found only 10% incapacity and minimal restriction on her normal life. The insurer granted daily allowances and a pension at 10%, but refused to destroy the images.

The applicant appealed, seeking higher benefits, compensation, and removal of the surveillance material. She argued the surveillance was reprehensible, inappropriate, and an attack on her personality. In 2009 the Social Insurance Court ruled in her favour: it found no legal basis for the surveillance, declared the monitoring record inadmissible, and held that the expert opinion based on the illegal surveillance had no probative value. It also held she could refuse further examinations.

On appeal, the Federal Court reversed in 2010. It held that, under its case-law, Articles 43 and 28(2) of the Social Security Act provided a legal basis for insurer-ordered surveillance by private investigators. The surveillance was therefore lawful and the surveillance file was valid evidence. The Federal Court found that the images—showing her walking her dog, driving long distances, shopping, carrying groceries, and opening the car boot with arms above her head—contradicted the medical reports of total incapacity. It held that a fresh neurological examination was necessary and admissible because she had refused a functional assessment. It denied probative value to the earlier medical reports and upheld the reassessment.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that the secret surveillance of her daily activities violated Article 8 (right to respect for private life) and that the domestic proceedings, especially the admission and use of the surveillance evidence and the expert report based on it, violated Article 6 (fair trial). The central issues were whether the insurer, acting as a public authority in the compulsory accident-insurance system, had a sufficient legal basis and safeguards for covert surveillance, and whether reliance on covertly obtained evidence rendered the proceedings unfair. The ECtHR ultimately found a violation of Article 8, but no violation of Article 6 § 1.

The case concerned Ms Savjeta Vukota-Bojić, a Swiss national and hairdresser who had compulsory accident insurance. In August 1995 she was hit by a motorcycle and suffered head and neck injuries. She initially received insurance benefits, but her insurer later ended daily allowances from April 1997, disputing whether the accident had caused lasting incapacity. Over the following years, numerous medical reports conflicted: some found a causal link and total incapacity for work, while others questioned causation or assessed only limited incapacity. In 2000 the Social Insurance Court of Zurich remitted the case for clarification, and in 2002 the applicant was granted a full disability pension by the social security authority. In December 2005 the Social Insurance Court accepted a causal link between the accident and her health problems and referred the matter back to the accident insurer to decide on benefits.

After that decision, the insurer invited the applicant to undergo a functional-capacity evaluation, which she refused. The insurer then sent her a formal notice under Article 43(3) of the Social Security Act, warning of the consequences of failing to cooperate, but it did not mention that covert surveillance might be used. In October 2006, the insurer commissioned private investigators to monitor her secretly. They observed her on four dates over 23 days, for several hours each time, and followed her over long distances. A detailed surveillance report and video footage were produced. The applicant became aware of the surveillance on the last day.

The insurer initially refused her representative access to the surveillance report, then later disclosed it and required a fresh neurological assessment. The applicant refused further examinations. In March 2007 the insurer refused benefits, relying on the surveillance images and her refusal to undergo a neurological examination. A neurologist later assessed her incapacity at 10%, relying partly on the surveillance images, and in 2008 the insurer granted benefits at that level and refused to destroy the surveillance file.

On appeal, the Social Insurance Court in 2009 found that the surveillance lacked a legal basis, so the monitoring record was inadmissible and the expert opinion based on it had no probative value. It also held that the applicant was entitled to refuse further examinations. The insurer appealed. In March 2010, the Federal Court reversed that decision. It held, under its earlier case-law, that covert surveillance of an insured person by private investigators was lawful and that the surveillance file was valid evidence. The images showed the applicant walking her dog, driving long distances, shopping, carrying groceries and opening a car boot with her arms above her head without apparent restrictions, which contradicted the medical reports. The Federal Court quashed the lower court’s decision except as to interest on arrears.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that the secret surveillance violated her right to respect for private life under Article 8 and that the proceedings, including the use of the surveillance evidence, breached her right to a fair trial under Article 6. The key facts for the alleged violations were therefore that a compulsory accident insurer, exercising public functions, secretly monitored her daily activities without a sufficiently clear legal basis or procedural safeguards, and then used the resulting surveillance material in benefit proceedings. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 8, holding that Swiss law did not provide adequate safeguards against abuse in such covert surveillance, but found no violation of Article 6 § 1.
001-159882:
The case *M.R.A. and Others v. the Netherlands* (ECtHR, 2016) concerned five Afghan nationals—a married couple and their three children—who alleged that their removal from the Netherlands to Afghanistan would breach Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention, and that they lacked an effective remedy under Article 13.

The first applicant, born in 1959, entered the Netherlands in April 1999 with his wife and two eldest children and applied for asylum. He claimed he had joined the PDPA in 1978, performed guard duties, and then served for six months as a guard at Pol-e-Charki prison, where political prisoners were held. In 1982 he transferred to KhAD/WAD, the Afghan security service, as a construction engineer until 1992. He built offices and ammunition depots, claimed the rank of major or lieutenant-colonel, was decorated, and had some involvement with party propaganda and political affairs. He denied knowing of serious human rights abuses, aside from one incident he later retracted. After the communist regime fell, he fled to Mazar-e-Sharif and worked as an engineer. In 1998 Taliban fighters raided his home, found his PDPA card and medals, and detained him for about seven months. He was questioned about his KhAD/WAD past and released after a bribe on condition that he leave Afghanistan; he had been believed executed. He fled abroad.

The Dutch authorities rejected his asylum claim under Article 1F of the 1951 Refugee Convention. They found serious reasons to consider that he had knowingly and personally participated in KhAD/WAD human rights violations, relying on his voluntary guard service, transfer to KhAD, rank, decorations, political affairs role, and knowledge of systemic torture. He claimed that removal would expose him to Taliban or mujahideen reprisals because of his communist and KhAD/WAD background, and that a relative had been killed. The authorities found no individual real risk: no one was specifically looking for him, his past detention occurred under different political conditions, and while former communists might face some risk, not all did.

The second applicant, born in 1966, had studied education, taught from 1989 to 1991, and joined the PDPA women’s organisation. She was beaten once for wearing a short burka during the Taliban period while her husband was detained. Her asylum claim was rejected because authorities found no real personal risk; the single burka incident was insufficient, and the Taliban were unlikely to remain interested in her. She was later excluded from categorical protection.

The third applicant, born in 1991, arrived as a child. As an adult, his asylum claim was rejected because he had two criminal convictions for public violence and posed a public-order danger. He argued that as a westernised young man he faced Article 3 risk in Afghanistan. His later asylum and family-life residence applications were also rejected. His Article 8 claim was based on family life with his parents and siblings in the Netherlands, but the authorities issued a return decision. A provisional measure suspended that decision pending objection proceedings.

In 2011, the second, fourth, and fifth applicants were granted temporary asylum residence permits under a new policy for westernised Afghan school-aged girls; the fifth applicant had been born in the Netherlands. The first applicant’s fresh asylum request was again rejected under Article 1F, and an entry-ban intention was issued. The alleged violations therefore centred on the first applicant’s Article 3 risk upon removal despite Article 1F exclusion, the second applicant’s claimed risk as a former PDPA member and spouse, the third applicant’s Article 3 and Article 8 family-life claims, and the alleged lack of an effective Article 13 remedy against removal.

The case of *M.R.A. and Others v. the Netherlands* concerns five Afghan nationals—a married couple and their three children—who entered the Netherlands in 1999 and sought asylum. They alleged that their removal to Afghanistan would violate Articles 3 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and that they lacked an effective remedy under Article 13.

The first applicant, born in 1959, had been a member of the communist People’s Democratic Party of Afghanistan (PDPA). He guarded PDPA headquarters, then performed military service at Pol-e-Charki prison, block 3, guarding political prisoners for six months. He later worked for the KhAD/WAD, the Afghan security service, from 1982 to 1992 as a construction engineer. He built offices and ammunition depots, reached the rank of major or lieutenant-colonel, received decorations, and was involved in party propaganda. After the communist regime fell, he fled to Mazar-e-Sharif. In August 1998, Taliban fighters raided his home, found his PDPA identity card, medals, and a bayonet, and arrested him. He was detained for about seven months, questioned about his KhAD/WAD past, allegedly ill-treated and forced to labour, and released after a bribe on condition that he leave Afghanistan immediately. He was reportedly believed to have been executed. A relative was later killed.

The Dutch authorities rejected the first applicant’s asylum claim under Article 1F of the 1951 Refugee Convention, finding serious reasons to consider that he had knowingly participated in or facilitated KhAD/WAD human rights violations. They relied on country reports describing the KhAD/WAD’s cruel methods, the notoriety of Pol-e-Charki prison, his rank, loyalty, decorations, and access to KhAD/WAD buildings. The courts upheld this exclusion. After one remittal, the Minister again rejected asylum. On Article 3, the Minister found no real risk: no one was specifically looking for him; his past Taliban detention occurred in a different political context; the general risk to former communists did not mean every former KhAD/WAD member was at risk; and his relative’s killing was not reliable or individually relevant.

The second applicant, his wife, had been a teacher and a member of the PDPA women’s organisation. She said she was beaten once for wearing a burka judged too short and that her husband was mistreated in detention. Her asylum claim was rejected because the threats had been directed at the men, the burka incident was isolated, and the Taliban had no continuing interest in her. She and the fourth and fifth applicants later received temporary asylum residence permits under a 2011 policy for westernised Afghan schoolgirls.

The third applicant, an adult son with criminal convictions in the Netherlands, was refused asylum as a danger to public order. His application for residence based on Article 8 family life was rejected, although a provisional measure suspended that decision pending an objection. The first applicant faced an intended exclusion order or entry ban, but no final decision was issued.

The applicants’ alleged violations therefore centre on the first applicant’s KhAD/WAD past and Article 1F exclusion, his Taliban-era detention, the claimed risk of ill-treatment in Afghanistan, the family’s mixed residence status, and the third applicant’s criminal record and family ties.

In *M.R.A. and Others v. the Netherlands* (Application no. 46856/07, ECtHR, 12 January 2016), five Afghan nationals—a married couple and their three children—complained that their removal from the Netherlands to Afghanistan would violate Articles 3 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and that they lacked an effective remedy under Article 13. The first four applicants entered the Netherlands in April 1999 and applied for asylum; the fifth child was born there in 2007.

The first applicant, M.R.A., was a former Afghan communist and KhAD/WAD officer. He joined the PDPA in 1978, guarded party headquarters, and, after university, avoided front-line military service by reporting to a security battalion in 1982. He then served for six months as a guard at Pol-e-Charki prison, where political prisoners were held. He claimed he had no contact with prisoners and witnessed only one ill-treatment incident, later saying it involved detainees. From 1982 to 1992 he worked as a construction engineer for KhAD/WAD, building offices and ammunition depots. He reached the rank of major or lieutenant-colonel, was decorated, and was involved in party propaganda. After the communist regime fell, he fled to Mazar-e-Sharif and worked for the municipality. In August 1998, Taliban fighters raided his home, found his PDPA card, medals, and a bayonet, and arrested him and his brother. He was detained for about seven months, interrogated, and disclosed his KhAD/WAD past. He was released through a bribe on condition that he leave Afghanistan immediately; he had been due to be executed. A relative was later reportedly killed in Kabul.

The second applicant, his wife, was a former teacher and PDPA women’s organisation member who had once been beaten by the Taliban for wearing a short burka.

Dutch asylum authorities rejected the first applicant’s claim under Article 1F of the 1951 Refugee Convention. They found serious reasons to consider that he had knowingly participated in or facilitated KhAD/WAD human rights violations. They relied on country reports describing systemic torture and repression by KhAD/WAD, and on his service at Pol-e-Charki, his construction work for the intelligence service, his rank, decorations, and political work. The second applicant and children were initially denied asylum, though in 2011 the second, fourth, and fifth applicants were granted temporary asylum residence under a new policy for westernised Afghan school-aged girls. The third applicant, an adult, was denied asylum because of criminal convictions in the Netherlands; his application for residence based on family life was also rejected, although a provisional measure suspended that decision.

The applicants alleged that removal to Afghanistan would expose them to a real risk of treatment contrary to Article 3, due to the first applicant’s PDPA/KhAD/WAD past, prior Taliban detention, the general security situation, and the third applicant’s westernised profile. They also invoked Article 8, particularly the third applicant’s family ties to his mother and siblings in the Netherlands. Finally, they complained under Article 13 that domestic remedies were ineffective because the courts failed to properly examine the Article 3 risk and because removal could proceed without adequate suspensive review.
001-163356:
Geotech Kancev GmbH v. Germany (ECtHR, 2 June 2016, no. 23646/09) concerned German building-sector social welfare contributions. The applicant, a company specialising in drilling for soil samples and geological examinations, was not a member of any employers’ association. Under collective agreements in the German building industry, a Social Welfare Fund (“SOKA-BAU”, comprising ZVK and ULAK) provided holiday pay, pension allowances and vocational training. The relevant collective agreement (VTV) was declared generally binding, so all building employers, including non-members, had to contribute 19.8% of gross wages to the Fund. The VTV covered drilling. After the applicant objected to registration, the Wiesbaden Labour Court ordered it to pay EUR 63,625.58 in arrears for September 2002–March 2004 and to produce wage slips. Appeals to the Hesse Labour Court of Appeal, Federal Labour Court and Federal Constitutional Court failed. The domestic courts held that the VTV bound the applicant; that the Fund did not require membership in an association; that any pressure to join an employers’ association to influence the Fund was insufficient; and that contributions were largely reimbursed if properly declared, serving the public interest given high employee fluctuation and competition concerns.

The applicant complained to the ECtHR under Article 11 that compulsory contributions violated the negative aspect of freedom of association, effectively forcing association, and under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the payments violated peaceful enjoyment of possessions, allegedly driving it into bankruptcy and disadvantaging it against competitors. The Article 11 and Protocol No. 1 complaints were declared admissible.

On Article 11, the Court accepted that compulsory financial contributions can interfere with the negative right not to join an association. However, the applicant could not join SOKA-BAU, and was not obliged to join any employers’ association. The payments were not membership dues; they financed sector-wide social benefits and were offset by reimbursement entitlements. Members of employers’ associations received no fee reductions or better treatment, and non-members received the same information and annual reports. The de facto incentive to join an association to gain influence over the Fund was too remote to strike at the substance of Article 11. The positive aspect was also unaffected: the applicant remained free to form, promote or join an association.

On Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, compulsory social-insurance contributions amounted to an interference. But it was lawful under the generally binding VTV and the Collective Agreements Act; domestic courts found drilling fell within its scope. It pursued the legitimate aim of ensuring social protection for all building-industry employees. Given the wide margin of appreciation in social and economic policy, the Court found a fair balance: all employers were included on solidarity grounds; contributions were used only for benefits and reimbursements; the applicant could offset its entitlements and suffered no financial or other disadvantage compared with members; and the Fund was state-supervised and transparent. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 11 or Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In *Geotech Kancev GmbH v. Germany* (ECtHR, Fifth Section, 2 June 2016), the applicant was a German limited company specialising in drilling soil samples for geological and construction-related assessments. In the German building industry, employers’ associations and the trade union IG Bauen-Agrar-Umwelt concluded the VTV, a collective agreement governing the Social Welfare Fund known as SOKA-BAU, comprising the ZVK and ULAK. The Federal Ministry for Labour and Social Affairs declared the VTV generally binding, meaning all building-industry employers—including those not belonging to an employers’ association—had to contribute 19.8% of gross wages. SOKA-BAU administered holiday pay, supplementary pension, and vocational training schemes on a sector-wide solidarity basis.

The applicant was not a member of any employers’ association. In 2004 and 2005 SOKA-BAU informed it of its contribution duties and opened an account; the applicant objected. In 2007 the Wiesbaden Labour Court ordered the applicant to pay EUR 63,625.58 in arrears for September 2002–March 2004 and to submit wage slips. It found the applicant’s drilling work fell within the VTV and that the generally binding agreement covered non-members. The Hesse Labour Court of Appeal rejected the applicant’s appeal, and the Federal Labour Court and Federal Constitutional Court declined further review.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged violations of Article 11 (freedom of association) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of possessions). Under Article 11, it argued that the compulsory contribution violated the negative aspect of freedom of association: although it did not join the Fund or an employers’ association, it had to finance a body jointly set up by associations it did not belong to, without control over how its interests were protected. This allegedly pressured it to join an employers’ association to gain influence. It also complained of insufficient transparency and claimed the payments left it without funds to found its own association. Under Protocol No. 1, it claimed the contribution deprived it of possessions, contributed to its bankruptcy, and that its activities did not fall within the VTV or public interest.

The Government disputed that there was any interference. It noted the applicant was not and could not become a member of SOKA-BAU and was not obliged to join an employers’ association. Contributions were offset by reimbursements for employee benefits. The scheme pursued social protection, and non-members received the same information and treatment as members.

The Court declared the complaints admissible but found no violation. On Article 11, it accepted that compulsory financial contributions can interfere with negative freedom of association if akin to membership. Here, however, the contributions were not membership dues; they financed solidarity-based social welfare benefits for all building workers and were offset by reimbursements. Non-members were not treated less favourably regarding transparency, and members lacked direct control over the Fund. Any incentive to join an employers’ association to influence SOKA-BAU was too remote to strike at the substance of Article 11. There was no interference with the positive right to form or join associations.

On Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, the Court found an interference with possessions, but it was lawful, pursued the legitimate general-interest aim of social protection, and was proportionate. Germany had a wide margin of appreciation in social and economic policy, and a fair balance was struck. Thus, there was no violation of either provision.

Case Geotech Kancev GmbH v. Germany concerned a German drilling company that challenged compulsory contributions to the building industry’s Social Welfare Fund (“SOKA-BAU”) as violating Article 11 (freedom of association) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (property). The applicant specialised in soil sampling and drilling for geological examination, including for building-site suitability and wells. In the German building industry, employers’ associations and the trade union concluded the VTV, a collective agreement governing SOKA-BAU, which comprised the ZVK and ULAK. The Federal Ministry for Labour and Social Affairs declared the VTV generally binding, meaning all building-industry employers—even those not belonging to a signatory employers’ association—had to contribute 19.8% of gross wages. The applicant was not a member of any such employers’ association. In 2004–05 SOKA-BAU informed it of the contribution duty and opened an account for benefits. The applicant objected in April 2005.

In domestic proceedings, the Wiesbaden Labour Court in 2007 ordered the applicant to pay EUR 63,625.58 in welfare-fund arrears for September 2002 to March 2004 and to submit wage slips, finding that its drilling activity fell within the VTV’s scope. The Hesse Labour Court of Appeal rejected the applicant’s appeal. It held that the generally binding effect did not require it to join an employers’ association or the Fund; any pressure to join was insufficient to breach the negative aspect of freedom of association; most contributions would be reimbursed if properly declared; and the scheme addressed high employee fluctuation and prevented competition distortion. The Federal Labour Court and Federal Constitutional Court refused further review.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that being obliged to contribute like a member, without controlling the Fund, pressured it to join an employers’ association, violating the negative aspect of Article 11. It also complained about lack of transparency and claimed the contributions deprived it of funds to found its own association. It further alleged that the EUR 63,625.58 obligation drove it into bankruptcy, made it less competitive, and was not in the public interest, violating Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Government argued that there was no compulsion to join any association, the Fund had no employer members, contributions were offset by reimbursements, and the scheme pursued legitimate social policy. The third party ZVK provided details on SOKA-BAU’s financing, benefits, and reporting.

The ECtHR found no violation of Article 11. It was legally impossible for the applicant to join SOKA-BAU, and it was not obliged to join an employers’ association. The financial contribution was not a membership contribution: it funded solidarity-based social benefits, was offset by entitlements, and was accompanied by state supervision and transparent reporting. Any de facto incentive to join an employers’ association to influence the Fund was too remote to interfere with Article 11. The Court also found no violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Although the contribution interfered with possessions, it was lawful, pursued the legitimate general-interest aim of ensuring social protection for building workers, and struck a fair balance. The State enjoyed a wide margin of appreciation in social and economic policy. The case therefore establishes that generally binding collective agreements imposing social-fund contributions on non-member employers did not, on these facts, breach the Convention.

Colloredo Mannsfeld v. the Czech Republic concerned restitution claims for movable property located in Opočno Castle. The applicant’s predecessor had the property confiscated in 1942 by the German Secret State Police as an enemy of the German Reich. After the Second World War, it was confiscated again in 1945 by the Czechoslovak State under the Beneš decrees because he was considered to be of German nationality. That expropriation was quashed on appeal in January 1947 after it was established that he was Czechoslovak and loyal to the State. What happened to the property afterwards remained disputed.

In 1992 the applicant’s father and a cousin claimed restitution of movable property from Opočno Castle. The applicant continued the proceedings as his father’s heir. Because many items were involved, the case was decided in three sets of proceedings. The first, concerning 68 paintings, ended in the applicant’s favour and is not part of the applications.

The second proceedings (application no. 15275/11) began with a 2006 District Court judgment ordering the National Heritage Institute to return property. The District Court found that the applicant’s predecessor owned the property on the critical date of 25 February 1948 and that restitution conditions were met. In 2007 the Regional Court reversed that decision, holding that the property had been taken from the predecessor before 25 February 1948, so restitution law did not apply. It relied on a 1947 letter from the castle’s national administrator and a 1947 Ministry of Agriculture decision declaring Opočno Castle State cultural property. The 1947 decision had not been raised with the parties at the hearing; they had no chance to comment on it, and the court said it knew of it through its official functions. The Supreme Court and Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeals, despite his complaint that he had not seen the 1947 decision.

The third proceedings (application no. 76058/12) concerned the remaining items. The District Court dismissed the claim, relying on the second proceedings. The Regional Court upheld that decision, using a 1957 ministry letter referring to the 1947 decision. Although the applicant repeatedly asked for the 1947 decision, it was not produced. The Supreme Court and Constitutional Court again dismissed his appeals.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 because the domestic courts based their decisions on evidence he could not see or comment on, especially the 1947 decision. He also alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, arguing that he had a legitimate expectation of restitution and that the courts arbitrarily found the property had passed to the State before the critical date. He further complained of insufficient reasoning and misinterpretation of domestic law.

The Court joined the applications. It found a violation of Article 6 § 1. The right to a fair hearing includes the adversarial principle: parties must be able to know and comment on all evidence capable of influencing the court’s decision, including material raised by the court itself. The 1947 decision was central to rejecting the restitution claim in both sets of proceedings, yet it was never properly disclosed or discussed. In the third proceedings it was not even produced despite requests. The applicant should have been given notice and an opportunity to comment on its existence, contents and authenticity.

As to Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, the Court declared the complaint incompatible ratione materiae. Article 1 does not guarantee a right to acquire property or impose a general restitution obligation. The applicant could only claim “possessions” if he had a sufficiently established restitution claim or legitimate expectation. The domestic courts found the property had passed to the State before 25 February 1948, so the statutory conditions were not met. Their conclusion was not arbitrary or manifestly unreasonable. The Article 6 defect did not establish a direct impact on the property outcome. The remaining complaints were dismissed as manifestly ill-founded.

In *Colloredo Mannsfeld v. the Czech Republic* (ECtHR, First Section, 15 December 2016), the applicant, Jerome Colloredo Mannsfeld, a Czech national, brought two applications concerning restitution of movable property located in Opočno Castle. The castle itself belonged to another person; the applicant was not its heir. The movables had been confiscated from his predecessor in 1942 by the German Secret State Police as enemy property. After World War II, in 1945, the Czechoslovak State confiscated them again under the Beneš decrees because the predecessor was considered German. That expropriation was quashed in January 1947 after it was established that he was Czechoslovak and loyal. What happened to the property afterwards was disputed.

In 1992, the applicant’s father and cousin sought restitution of the movable property. The applicant later joined as heir after his father’s death. Because of the large number of items, the case was decided in three sets of proceedings. The first, involving 68 paintings, was not at issue. In the second proceedings (application no. 15275/11), the District Court on 27 October 2006 ordered the National Heritage Institute to return certain movables, finding that the applicant’s predecessor owned them on the critical date of 25 February 1948 and that restitution conditions were met. On 18 October 2007, the Regional Court reversed and dismissed the claim, holding that the property had passed to the State before 25 February 1948, so restitution legislation did not apply.

The key fair-trial complaint concerned the Regional Court’s reliance on two documents: a letter of 24 June 1947 from the national administrator of Opočno Castle and, especially, a Ministry of Agriculture decision of 30 April 1947 declaring the castle State cultural property (“the 1947 decision”). At the hearing on 8 October 2007, the court did not raise this evidence or allow the parties to comment on it; it merely heard their comments on the first-instance judgment. The Regional Court nevertheless based its decision on the 1947 decision, noting it knew the document through its functions. The Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal, referring to the 1947 decision but not addressing his complaint that he had never seen or commented on it. The Constitutional Court dismissed the constitutional appeal, stating that facts known to the court through its functions did not need to be proved.

In the third proceedings (application no. 76058/12), the District Court dismissed the remaining restitution claim by referring to the earlier judgments. The Regional Court upheld that decision on 27 January 2011, relying on a 1957 ministry letter referring to the 1947 decision. Despite the applicant’s requests, the 1947 decision was not produced. The Supreme Court and Constitutional Court later dismissed his appeals.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (fair hearing/adversarial proceedings) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (property). The Court joined the applications. On Article 6, it found a violation: parties must have the opportunity to know and comment on all evidence capable of influencing the court’s decision. Because the 1947 decision was central to determining when the property passed to the State relative to the critical date, and the applicant had no chance to comment on its existence, content, or authenticity, the fair-hearing guarantee was breached. On Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, the Court found the complaint incompatible *ratione materiae*: the applicant had no established “possession” or enforceable restitution claim, and the domestic courts’ conclusion was not arbitrary or manifestly unreasonable. Other complaints were rejected as manifestly ill-founded.

This case concerned the applicant’s restitution claim for movable property formerly located in Opočno Castle. The applicant’s predecessor had the property confiscated in 1942 by the German Secret State Police, and again in 1945 by the Czechoslovak State under the Beneš decrees because he was considered German. In 1947, that expropriation was quashed after authorities found him Czechoslovak and loyal. In 1992, the applicant’s father and cousin sought restitution; the applicant later entered as heir. Because many items were involved, the case was decided in three separate proceedings. Only the second and third were before the European Court of Human Rights.

In the second proceedings (application no. 15275/11), the District Court in 2006 ordered the National Heritage Institute to return certain movables, finding the applicant’s predecessor owned them on the critical date of 25 February 1948 and that restitution conditions were met. In 2007 the Regional Court reversed and dismissed the claim, holding the property had passed to the State before 25 February 1948, so restitution law did not apply. It relied on a 24 June 1947 letter and a Ministry of Agriculture decision of 30 April 1947 declaring Opočno Castle State cultural property (“the 1947 decision”). That decision had not been raised at the hearing or shown to the parties. The Regional Court said it knew the document through its functions. The Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal without addressing his complaint that he had not seen the decision; the Constitutional Court dismissed his constitutional appeal.

In the third proceedings (application no. 76058/12), the District Court in 2009 dismissed the remaining restitution claim by relying on the earlier judgments. In 2011 the Regional Court upheld that outcome, referring to a 1957 Ministry letter mentioning the 1947 decision. Despite the applicant’s requests, the 1947 decision was not produced. The Supreme Court and Constitutional Court later dismissed his appeals.

The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 because the courts relied on the 1947 decision without giving him an opportunity to comment on it. He also alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, claiming the refusal of restitution breached his property rights.

The European Court of Human Rights joined the applications. On Article 6 § 1, it found a violation. The right to a fair hearing includes adversarial proceedings: parties must be able to know and comment on all evidence capable of influencing the court’s decision, including material relied on by the court of its own motion. The 1947 decision was central to determining whether the property passed to the State before or after the critical date. The Regional Court relied on it, and the Supreme Court and Constitutional Court treated it as relevant. In the third proceedings it was not in the file and was not produced despite requests. No documentary evidence was read at the hearing, and the applicant could not comment on the decision’s existence, contents or authenticity.

On Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, the Court rejected the complaint as incompatible ratione materiae. Restitution legislation can create a new property right if statutory conditions are met, but the domestic courts found the property had passed to the State before 25 February 1948. The Court’s review was limited to arbitrariness or manifest unreasonableness and found none. The Article 6 procedural breach did not show a direct impact on the outcome. The applicant therefore had no sufficiently established enforceable claim amounting to a “possession.” Other complaints were dismissed as manifestly ill-founded.

The case *Cunha Martins da Silva Couto v. Portugal* (Applications nos. 69053/13, 69374/13, 69377/13, 71135/13 and 8088/14) concerned a Portuguese national, José Luís Cunha Martins da Silva Couto, born in 1961 and living in Porto. He lodged five applications against Portugal, complaining that five sets of civil proceedings had exceeded the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and that there was no effective domestic remedy for that delay, contrary to Article 13.

The domestic civil proceedings were instituted by or against the applicant’s company, not by the applicant personally. They began between 1 January and 5 July 2003. The applicant was the company’s main shareholder. After the company was liquidated in 2008, he replaced it as a party in the domestic proceedings. However, he only became a party from February 2009 in applications nos. 69053/13, 69374/13, 69377/13 and 71135/13, and from October 2010 in application no. 8088/14. Between 20 February 2009 and 13 October 2010, he lodged requests with the European Court seeking to replace the company as a party.

Before the Court, the Portuguese Government contested admissibility. It argued that the applicant lacked victim status for the entire duration of the proceedings because he had not been a party from 2003 until 2009/2010. The Court agreed in part. It reiterated that a person cannot complain of a violation of his or her rights in proceedings to which he or she was not a party, even if he or she was a shareholder and/or director of a company that was a party. Consequently, although the domestic proceedings began in 2003, the applicant could be considered a victim of the alleged excessive length only from February 2009 for four applications and from October 2010 for the fifth.

The Government also argued that the applications should be rejected for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies. The Court noted that, prior to 27 May 2014, Portuguese practice did not provide an effective legal remedy allowing a claimant to obtain compensation for length-of-proceedings violations. The five applications were lodged with the Court between 28 October and 30 December 2013, before that date. The Court therefore declared the applications admissible, finding they were not manifestly ill-founded or inadmissible on any other grounds.

On the merits, the Court assessed the length of the proceedings in light of the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicant and the authorities, and what was at stake. Having examined the material, it found no reason to depart from its case-law, notably *Martins Castro and Alves Correia de Castro v. Portugal*. It concluded that the length of the proceedings was excessive and failed to meet the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1. It further found a violation of Article 13 because the applicant had no effective domestic remedy by which to complain about the excessive length of the proceedings. The judgment was delivered on 26 April 2016 by the Fourth Section sitting as a Committee.

Cunha Martins da Silva Couto v. Portugal (European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, 26 April 2016) concerned five joined applications (nos. 69053/13, 69374/13, 69377/13, 71135/13 and 8088/14) brought by Mr José Luís Cunha Martins da Silva Couto, a Portuguese national born in 1961 and living in Porto. He alleged that five sets of civil proceedings had exceeded the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and that he had no effective remedy in that respect, contrary to Article 13.

The relevant domestic proceedings had been initiated between 1 January and 5 July 2003. Crucially, however, they were brought by or against the applicant’s company, not by the applicant personally. The applicant was the company’s main shareholder. Following the company’s liquidation in 2008, he replaced it as a party in the domestic proceedings. For four of the sets of proceedings (applications nos. 69053/13, 69374/13, 69377/13 and 71135/13), he became a party from February 2009; for the fifth (application no. 8088/14), he became a party from October 2010. Between 20 February 2009 and 13 October 2010 he lodged requests seeking to replace the company as a party.

Before the Court, the Government disputed the applicant’s victim status for the entire duration of the proceedings. They submitted that he could not complain about delays occurring before he became a party. The Court agreed. It reiterated that a person cannot complain of a violation of his or her rights in proceedings to which he or she was not a party, even if he or she was a shareholder and/or director of a company that was a party. Consequently, although the proceedings had started in 2003, the applicant could be regarded as a victim only from February 2009 for the first four applications and from October 2010 for the fifth.

On admissibility, the Government also argued that the applicant had not exhausted domestic remedies. The Court rejected this. It noted that, prior to 27 May 2014, Portuguese law and practice did not provide an effective remedy enabling a claimant to obtain compensation for excessively lengthy proceedings. The applications had been lodged with the Court between 28 October and 30 December 2013. The complaints were therefore neither manifestly ill-founded nor inadmissible on other grounds, and the Court declared them admissible.

On the merits, the Court assessed the length of proceedings by reference to the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicant and the authorities, and what was at stake. Having examined all the material, it found no fact or argument capable of leading to a different conclusion. Relying on its case-law, especially Martins Castro and Alves Correia de Castro v. Portugal, the Court held that the length of the proceedings had been excessive and had failed to satisfy the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1.

As to Article 13, the Court recalled that this provision guarantees an effective remedy before a national authority for an alleged breach of the Article 6 § 1 reasonable-time requirement. Since no such remedy existed in Portugal before 27 May 2014, the applicant had no effective domestic remedy for his length-of-proceedings complaints. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 13 as well.
001-169521:
**Summary of Vaščenkovs v. Latvia (Application no. 30795/12)**

The case of *Vaščenkovs v. Latvia* concerns an application lodged against the Republic of Latvia with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicant, Mr Maksims Vaščenkovs, a Latvian national born in 1986, complained under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention that domestic courts failed to provide sufficient reasons for the suspicion that he had committed robbery when extending his pre-trial detention. The applicant died on 3 November 2015, and his grandmother, Ms N. Zīmele, expressed her wish to pursue the proceedings on his behalf. The complaint was communicated to the Government on 10 July 2014 under Article 5 §§ 3 and 4, while the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The relevant facts centre on the applicant's detention. In July and August 2011, police opened four criminal investigations into three theft incidents and one robbery incident, which were joined on 29 August 2011. On 12 August 2011, the applicant was arrested on suspicion of robbery. He was held in custody on this basis until 14 August 2011, when he was placed under arrest on suspicion of theft. On 15 August 2011, police applied to the Ludza District Court for the applicant's pre-trial detention in relation to the theft investigation.

On 16 August 2011, an investigating judge granted the application. Regarding the suspicion of theft, the judge reasoned that there were reasons to suspect the applicant had committed theft under section 175(3) of the Criminal Law, and that these suspicions were confirmed by evidence gathered in the criminal case. The applicant appealed on 18 August 2011. On 2 September 2011, the Latgale Regional Court dismissed the appeal, stating that the suspicion was confirmed by information in the file. No further appeal lay against this decision.

On 19 September 2011, the public prosecutor charged the applicant with robbery, theft, involving a minor in theft, and petty theft. On 28 September 2011, the prosecutor transferred the case to the Ludza District Court for adjudication. On 17 October 2011, the investigating judge decided to keep the applicant in detention, reasoning that the accusations under sections 175(3) (theft), 176(2) (robbery), 180(2) (petty theft), and 172 (involving a minor in theft) were confirmed by evidence in the case file. Again, no appeal lay against this decision.

The applicant's detention was subsequently extended on 28 December 2011 and 23 April 2012. The judge stated that the detention was based on the suspicion of theft under section 175(3), noted that in other criminal proceedings the applicant had been declared a suspect for petty theft and robbery, and that there had been no change in the reasons from the 16 August 2011 detention order, which had been re-examined in subsequent decisions.

On 3 February, 19 June, and 6 August 2012, the applicant complained to the Ludza District Court that it had failed to assess his detention in relation to the alleged robbery. On 6 August and 2 November 2012, and on 25 January 2013, the judge decided to continue the applicant's detention, using largely the same wording as previous decisions. Additionally, the judge noted that the twenty-four-month period allowed by section 277(7) of the Criminal Procedure Law for detention had been observed because the applicant had also been accused of an especially serious offence—robbery—under section 176(2) of the Criminal Law. These decisions were not subject to appeal.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are that, despite the applicant being charged with robbery, the domestic courts' detention orders primarily referenced the suspicion of theft and relied on generic references to "evidence gathered in the criminal case" or "information contained in the file" without providing specific reasons for the robbery suspicion. The courts failed to substantively assess the detention in relation to the robbery charge, instead maintaining detention based on earlier reasons and the seriousness of the offence for the purpose of the statutory time limit.

In *Vaščenkovs v. Latvia*, the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint under Article 5 §§ 3 and 4 that Latvian courts extended the applicant’s pre-trial detention without sufficient reasons for the suspicion that he had committed robbery. The applicant, Maksims Vaščenkovs, a Latvian national born in 1986, lodged the application on 16 May 2012. He died on 3 November 2015, and his grandmother, Ms N. Zīmele, informed the Court of her wish to pursue the proceedings.

The relevant facts began in July–August 2011, when police opened four investigations into three thefts and one robbery; these were joined on 29 August 2011. On 12 August 2011 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of robbery and held on that basis until 14 August, when he was placed under arrest on suspicion of theft. On 15 August the police applied to the Ludza District Court for his pre-trial detention in connection with the theft investigation. On 16 August an investigating judge granted the application. As to the theft suspicion, the judge stated that there were reasons to suspect the applicant had committed theft under section 175(3) of the Criminal Law and that this was confirmed by evidence. The applicant appealed, but on 2 September 2011 the Latgale Regional Court dismissed the appeal, stating that the suspicion of theft was confirmed by information in the file. No further appeal lay.

On 19 September 2011 the prosecutor charged the applicant with robbery, theft, involving a minor in theft, and petty theft. After he familiarised himself with the case, the prosecutor transferred it to the Ludza District Court on 28 September 2011, setting out the case and evidence. On 17 October 2011 an investigating judge decided to keep the applicant in detention, reasoning that the accusation of theft, robbery, petty theft and involving a minor was confirmed by evidence. No appeal lay against that decision.

The applicant’s detention was extended on 28 December 2011 and 23 April 2012. The judge stated that detention was based on suspicion of theft and noted that in other criminal proceedings the applicant was a suspect for petty theft and robbery. The judge said there had been no change in the reasons given in the 16 August 2011 detention order. On 3 February, 19 June and 6 August 2012 the applicant complained to the Ludza District Court that it had failed to assess his detention in relation to the alleged robbery. On 6 August and 2 November 2012 and 25 January 2013, the judge continued detention using largely the same wording. The judge added that the 24-month detention limit under section 277(7) of the Criminal Procedure Law had been observed because the applicant was also accused of an especially serious offence—robbery under section 176(2). Those decisions were not subject to appeal.

Domestic law set a 12-month maximum for serious offences and a 24-month maximum for especially serious offences. The alleged violation was therefore that, although the initial detention application concerned theft, the courts later relied on the robbery charge to justify continuing detention, including its length, without giving specific or sufficient reasons for the suspicion that the applicant had committed robbery. The repeated references to evidence and earlier orders, together with the lack of appeal, formed the factual core of the Article 5 §§ 3 and 4 complaints.
