Latvia* (Application no. 30795/12, judgment of 15 December 2016), the applicant, Mr Maksims Vaščenkovs, complained under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention that, when extending his pre-trial detention, the Latvian domestic courts had failed to provide sufficient reasons for the suspicion that he had committed robbery. The complaint was communicated to the Government under Article 5 §§ 3 and 4, while the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The facts relevant to the alleged violation began in July and August 2011, when the police opened four criminal investigations into three incidents of theft and one incident of robbery. On 29 August 2011 these investigations were joined. On 12 August 2011 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of robbery. He was held on that basis until 14 August 2011, when he was placed under arrest on suspicion of theft. On 15 August 2011 the police applied to the Ludza District Court for the applicant’s pre-trial detention in relation to the theft investigation. On 16 August 2011 an investigating judge granted that application. As regards the suspicion of theft, the judge stated that there were reasons to suspect the applicant had committed theft under section 175(3) of the Criminal Law and that those suspicions were confirmed by evidence gathered in the criminal case. The applicant appealed. On 2 September 2011 the Latgale Regional Court dismissed the appeal, stating that the suspicion of theft was confirmed by information in the file. No further appeal lay against that decision.

On 19 September 2011 the prosecutor charged the applicant with robbery, theft, involving a minor in theft, and petty theft. On 26 September 2011 he familiarised himself with the case material. On 28 September 2011 the prosecutor transferred the case to the Ludza District Court for adjudication, setting out the case against him and the evidence on which the prosecution intended to rely. On 17 October 2011 the investigating judge decided to keep the applicant in detention. The judge reasoned that the accusation of crimes under sections 175(3) (theft), 176(2) (robbery), 180(2) (petty theft) and 172 (involving a minor in theft) was confirmed by the evidence gathered in the criminal case. No appeal lay against that decision.

On 28 December 2011 and 23 April 2012 the applicant’s detention was extended. The judge stated that his detention was based on the suspicion that he had committed theft, and noted that in other criminal proceedings he had been declared a suspect in relation to petty theft and robbery. The judge added that there had been no change in the reasons given in the detention order of 16 August 2011, which had been re-examined in subsequent decisions.

On 3 February, 19 June and 6 August 2012, the applicant complained to the Ludza District Court that it had failed to assess his detention in relation to the alleged robbery. On 6 August and 2 November 2012, and on 25 January 2013, the judge again decided to continue his detention, using largely the same wording as before. She also noted that the twenty-four-month period allowed by section 277(7) of the Criminal Procedure Law had been observed because the applicant had also been accused of an especially serious offence, robbery, under section 176(2) of the Criminal Law. Those decisions were not subject to appeal.

Under domestic law, a person charged with a serious offence could not be held in detention for more than twelve months, while a person charged with an especially serious offence could be held for up to twenty-four months. The applicant died on 3 November 2015, and his grandmother informed the Court of her wish to pursue the proceedings.

The key alleged violation was therefore that, although the applicant’s detention had initially been ordered in relation to theft, its continued length and justification became linked to the robbery charge, yet the courts allegedly failed to give sufficient reasons for the suspicion that he had committed robbery. They relied on generic references to evidence in the file or repeated earlier reasons, without specifically assessing the reasonable suspicion underlying the robbery accusation.
001-161369:
In *Morari v. the Republic of Moldova* (Application no. 65311/09, judgment 8 March 2016), the applicant, Oleg Morari, complained under Article 6 § 1 that he had been entrapped by police into committing a criminal offence and that the domestic courts refused to hear the undercover agents who had incited him.

In January 2008, the Bălți police placed a newspaper advertisement reading “Need help with obtaining passport (Romanian-Bulgarian)” with a telephone number. The applicant, interested in obtaining a Romanian passport to work in the EU, called the number. He met a person called E., who claimed also to be seeking a Romanian passport. They agreed to share information. Later, the applicant’s friend D. recommended Z., who could allegedly obtain a Romanian passport for EUR 1,500. The applicant did not have the money.

About three weeks later, E. called the applicant and asked whether he had found a way to obtain a passport. The applicant told E. about Z. and proposed that E. contact Z. directly. E. refused and instead proposed that the applicant act as intermediary with an acquaintance, T., who also wanted a Romanian passport. The applicant was to tell T. the price was EUR 2,300, with the EUR 800 difference split between the applicant and E. The applicant accepted.

Z. provided a list of documents for T.’s Romanian identity card. The applicant claimed he believed the card would not be forged and that Z. would merely represent T. before Romanian authorities. Z. later said he had told the applicant the card would be false. On 3 April 2008, the applicant met T., received documents and EUR 750, and passed them to Z. The identity card was produced in the United Kingdom. On 16 April 2008, the applicant gave the card to T. in exchange for the remaining money and was arrested. He was charged with manufacturing and trading in forged official documents. Z. pleaded guilty and received a suspended sentence.

During the criminal proceedings, the applicant argued that he had been entrapped and asked the courts to hear E. and T. The courts refused, relying on the rule that undercover officers could be heard only if they consented. On 17 December 2008, the first-instance court convicted the applicant and fined him about EUR 200; it did not address his entrapment claim. The Court of Appeal dismissed the entrapment argument solely because the applicant had first called the newspaper number, and the Supreme Court upheld the conviction.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 6 § 1. The domestic courts also failed to examine his entrapment plea properly and refused to hear E. and T., despite the applicant having seen them and despite the possibility of using false names. **Morari v. the Republic of Moldova** (Application no. 65311/09), judgment of 8 March 2016, concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights, namely the right to a fair hearing. He met a person called E., who introduced himself as someone also seeking a Romanian passport. Later, a friend recommended Z., who could allegedly obtain a Romanian passport for €1,500. When E. later called the applicant to ask about his progress, the applicant told him about Z. E. refused to contact Z. directly and instead proposed that the applicant act as an intermediary for another person, T., who also wanted a Romanian passport. **Case: Morari v. the Republic of Moldova**  
**Application no. 65311/09 — ECtHR, Second Section, judgment of 8 March 2016 (final 8 June 2016).**

The applicant, Oleg Morari, a Moldovan national, alleged that he had been incited by police to commit a criminal offence, in violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair trial). The case concerned an undercover police operation organised in January 2008 by the Bălți police, aimed at catching a group producing and circulating forged documents. As part of the operation, police placed an advertisement in a local newspaper stating: “Need help with obtaining passport (Romanian-Bulgarian),” followed by a telephone number.

The applicant, then interested in obtaining a Romanian passport to seek work in Romania or the EU, called the number and met a person called E., who introduced himself as also seeking a Romanian passport. Later, a friend recommended Z., who could allegedly help obtain a Romanian passport for €1,500. After about three weeks, E. called the applicant and asked whether he had made progress. The applicant told E. about Z. and proposed that E. contact Z. directly. E. refused and instead proposed that the applicant act as an intermediary for E.’s acquaintance T., telling T. the price was €2,300. The €800 difference was to be split between the applicant and E. The applicant agreed.

In April 2008, the applicant met T., collected documents and a €750 advance, and passed them to Z. A false Romanian identity card was later produced in the United Kingdom and reached the applicant. On 16 April 2008, the applicant gave the identity card to T. in exchange for the remaining money and was immediately arrested. He was charged with producing and selling forged official documents. Z. pleaded guilty and received a suspended sentence. On 17 December 2008, the Bălți District Court convicted the applicant and fined him approximately €200.

The key alleged violation arose from the applicant’s claim that he had been entrapped by E. and T. He asked the domestic courts to hear them as witnesses. The first-instance court refused and did not address his entrapment plea. On appeal, he repeated the complaint. The Bălți Court of Appeal initially agreed to hear E. and T. but later refused. On 4 March 2009, it dismissed his appeal, rejecting entrapment solely because the applicant had been the first to call the newspaper number. It also said hearing E. and T. was unnecessary because their statements had not been used against him and, under domestic law, undercover officers could be heard only with their consent. The Supreme Court of Justice dismissed his appeal on points of law on 8 July 2009.

Before the ECtHR, the Government argued that the applicant had initiated the contact and that the undercover officers had played a passive role. The Court disagreed. It found that although the applicant first called the advertisement, E. later contacted him, insisted that he act as an intermediary, and promised him financial gain. There was no indication that the applicant would have committed the offence without this intervention, nor that the authorities had prior evidence of his involvement in forged-document offences. The Court therefore concluded that he had been subjected to police incitement.

The Court also found serious procedural failings: the domestic courts failed to carefully examine the entrapment plea and refused to hear E. and T., despite the applicant having seen them in person. The ECtHR held that this breached Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

Topallaj v. Albania (no. 32913/03, judgment 21 April 2016) concerned property and lengthy civil proceedings in Albania. The applicant, Marketin Topallaj, born in 1951 and later a U.S. citizen, claimed rights over a petrol station, fuel tanks and installations on land inherited by several landowners. In 1995–96, Albanian courts recognized the landowners’ inherited rights over 24 hectares and the related installations. In early 1996, the applicant concluded agreements with one landowner acting for the heirs to finance privatization of the fuel tanks and installations. In May 1996, he signed a notarized sales contract to purchase almost all of them for USD 100,000, and the mortgage office registered title in his name.

Meanwhile, after the Commission on Property Restitution and Compensation refused restitution, the Tirana District Court in April 1996 allocated 56,500 sq m to the landowners and ordered restoration of the installations; that judgment became final. Between 1996 and 1998, State institutions unsuccessfully challenged the landowners’ rights. In 2000, the Ministry of Economy and State-owned oil companies obtained supervisory review, and the Supreme Court Joint Benches reopened the case. The rehearings, marked by repeated remittals among the District Court, Court of Appeal and Supreme Court, ended on 20 September 2009 in the landowners’ favour.

Separately, the landowners sued the applicant in 2002 and again in 2005 to annul the 1996 agreements and sales contract. In 2006, the District Court declared them absolutely null and void as fictitious, finding that the property was then State-administered, no rights had been transferred to the landowners, no joint company was formed, and the loans were not executed. It also ordered erasure of the applicant’s property registration. The Court of Appeal upheld that decision in 2007, with a dissent; the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal as inadmissible in 2010; and the Constitutional Court rejected his appeal in 2010.

The applicant complained to the European Court under Article 6 § 1 (fair trial and length), Article 13 (effective remedy), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). He alleged that the proceedings concerning the landowners’ property rights were excessively long, that he had no effective domestic remedy for that delay, and that the annulment of his contracts and erasure of his registration violated his property rights.

The Government argued that the applicant, as only a third party, was not a victim and had not exhausted domestic remedies. The Court held that Article 6 § 1 applied because the reopened proceedings directly affected the property rights he claimed, and it accepted him as a victim. It rejected the exhaustion objection, finding no effective remedy in Albania for excessive length. On the merits, the relevant proceedings lasted 9 years, 4 months and 8 days, from 12 May 2000 to 20 September 2009. Although complex, the delay was caused mainly by repeated remittals due to lower-court errors and systemic deficiencies, not by the applicant. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1. It also found the Article 13 complaint admissible and, consistent with earlier Albanian cases, held that there was no effective remedy for the length violation.

The Court rejected both objections, relying on earlier case law such as *Petrović v. Serbia*, and declared the applications admissible.

On the merits, the Court noted that it had frequently found violations of Article 6 and/or Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 in similar cases concerning non-enforcement of final judgments against State or socially-owned companies undergoing restructuring. The Government had not offered any convincing argument to distinguish the applicant’s case. The key facts relevant to the violation were therefore that final enforceable decisions in the applicant’s favour remained unenforced for a prolonged period because domestic authorities stayed enforcement due to the debtors’ restructuring, and the applicant had no effective means of obtaining enforcement. The Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In *Jovanović v. Serbia* (Applications nos. 21497/13 and 21907/13), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered judgment on 19 July 2016. The applicant, Radoslav Jovanović, a Serbian national born in 1943 and living in Niš, complained that Serbian authorities failed to enforce final judgments obtained in his favour against two socially/State-owned companies. The complaints were examined under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, concerning the right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, concerning protection of property. The two applications were joined because of their similar factual and legal background.

The first set of enforcement proceedings arose from an action brought on 28 April 2010 before the Smederevo Court of First Instance against FŽV Želvoz a.d. Smederevo. On 15 December 2010, the court ordered direct enforcement of an outstanding invoice based on a credible document. However, on 15 June 2011, the Privatisation Agency ordered the debtor’s restructuring as part of privatisation. On 25 October 2011, enforcement proceedings were stayed because the debtor was undergoing restructuring. The applicant appealed on 3 November 2011, but his appeal was rejected on 10 February 2012. On 21 March 2013, he urged the court to continue enforcement. On 7 June 2013, the court informed him that the debtor was still restructuring and that proceedings could not continue. It appears he did not appeal that response.

The second set concerned an enforcement action brought on 11 January 2010 before the Niš Commercial Court against Vagonka a.d. Niš. On 29 January 2010, the court ordered direct enforcement of an outstanding invoice. Earlier, on 4 November 2009, the Privatisation Agency had ordered the debtor’s restructuring. On 4 February 2010, enforcement was stayed because of that restructuring. The applicant did not appeal, and this decision became final on 17 February 2010. On 20 March 2013, he urged continuation. On 22 March 2013, the court replied that the debtor was still restructuring, so enforcement could not continue.

Before the ECtHR, the Government challenged admissibility. It argued that the applications were lodged out of time because the enforcement proceedings had been terminated by final decisions on 10 February 2012 and 17 February 2010, while the applications were lodged on 13 March 2013, outside the six-month limit. The Government also alleged non-exhaustion, claiming the applicant should have appealed the stay decisions. The Court rejected both objections, relying on its prior case law, particularly *Petrović v. Serbia*, and declared the applications admissible.

On the merits, the Court emphasized that it had repeatedly found violations of Article 6 and/or Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 in similar cases concerning Serbia’s failure to enforce final domestic judgments, especially where debtors were socially/State-owned companies undergoing restructuring. It cited *R. Kačapor and Others*, *Crnišanin and Others*, and *Adamović*. The Court found that the Government had not presented any fact or convincing argument to distinguish the present case. It therefore concluded that there had been a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The key factual basis for the violation was that the applicant held final enforcement orders but was unable to obtain their execution because the domestic courts stayed proceedings indefinitely due to the debtors’ restructuring, leaving him without effective enforcement or peaceful enjoyment of his possessions.

The applicant alleged that the respondent State failed to enforce two final judgments rendered in his favour, thereby violating his rights under Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applications were joined by the Court due to their similar factual and legal background.

The relevant facts pertain to two separate sets of enforcement proceedings initiated by the applicant against two different socially/State-owned companies.

**First Set of Enforcement Proceedings:**
On 28 April 2010, the applicant filed an enforcement action before the Smederevo Court of First Instance against the company "FŽV Želvoz a.d. Smederevo" to collect an outstanding invoice. On 15 December 2010, the court ordered direct enforcement. However, on 15 June 2011, the Privatisation Agency ordered the debtor's restructuring as part of a privatisation process. Consequently, on 25 October 2011, the enforcement proceedings were stayed. The applicant's appeal against this stay was rejected on 10 February 2012. On 21 March 2013, the applicant urged the court to continue the proceedings, but on 7 June 2013, the court informed him that the debtor was still undergoing restructuring and that enforcement could not proceed. The applicant did not appeal this decision.

**Second Set of Enforcement Proceedings:**
On 11 January 2010, the applicant initiated an enforcement action before the Niš Commercial Court against the company "Vagonka a.d. Niš." The court ordered direct enforcement on 29 January 2010. However, the Privatisation Agency had already ordered the debtor's restructuring on 4 November 2009. As a result, the enforcement proceedings were stayed on 4 February 2010. The applicant did not appeal this decision, which became final on 17 February 2010. On 20 March 2013, he urged the court to continue the proceedings, but on 22 March 2013, the court informed him that the debtor was still restructuring, preventing continuation.

The applicant complained to the European Court about the respondent State's failure to enforce the final judgments. The Government raised objections regarding admissibility, arguing that the applications were lodged out of time (six-month rule) and that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies by not appealing the stay decisions. The Court rejected these objections, citing its established case-law in similar cases against Serbia (e.g., *Petrović v. Serbia*).

On the merits, the Court noted that it had frequently found violations of Article 6 and/or Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 in cases raising similar issues concerning non-enforcement of final judgments against socially/State-owned companies undergoing restructuring. The Court found that the Government had not provided any convincing argument to depart from this established case-law. It therefore concluded that there had been a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In *Pugžlys v. Poland* (Application no. 446/10, judgment 14 June 2016), the applicant, Juozas Pugžlys, a Lithuanian national born in 1966, was arrested in the Netherlands in April 2003 and extradited to Poland in October 2003. He was suspected of leading an international organised criminal group and of six counts of kidnapping for ransom. He was detained on remand. In 2010 the Lublin Regional Court convicted him and sentenced him to 12 years’ imprisonment; the conviction was upheld on appeal, and his cassation appeal was dismissed in 2012.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 3 arising from the “dangerous detainee” regime imposed on him for about nine years and from being kept in a metal cage, handcuffed or shackled, during court hearings. He also complained under Articles 6 and 13 about unfair proceedings and lack of an effective remedy, under Article 6 § 3 about interpreter and defence rights, and under Article 8 about restrictions on contact with his family.

The key facts concerning the “dangerous detainee” regime were that on 21 October 2003 the penitentiary commission classified him under Article 212a of the Code of Execution of Criminal Sentences. The request relied on the serious charges, his alleged leadership of an armed international gang, violent offences, boxing and combat skills, and his claimed danger to society. The regime was reviewed every three months and repeatedly maintained until 25 July 2012—over eight years and nine months. It involved high-security confinement and segregation, constant CCTV monitoring of his cell including sanitary facilities, joined shackles whenever he left the cell, and daily or multiple daily full strip searches requiring him to strip naked and perform deep knee bends for anal inspection. Family contact was restricted, although he could make telephone calls from 2007 and received regular supervised visits. Extension decisions repeated the same grounds—serious charges, violent character, personal situation, combat skills, low moral character and lack of rehabilitation—without addressing changes in his circumstances. Domestic courts upheld the decisions. The European Court found the prolonged, routine application of the full regime unjustified and in violation of Article 3.

As to the courtroom cage, the Government admitted that during some hearings before the Lublin Regional Court the applicant was held in a metal cage while handcuffed. Hearings ran from January 2007 to January 2010, with at least 65 public hearings; the applicant claimed around 104. He alleged he was caged and shackled throughout, causing bruises and preventing note-taking. No reasoned court decision justified the cage, and his requests for removal were dismissed. The Court found this amounted to degrading treatment under Article 3.

On fair trial and interpreter issues, the applicant’s court-appointed lawyer spoke only Polish while the applicant spoke Lithuanian. Interpreters attended hearings and file examinations; appellate courts found interpreters also assisted during recess meetings with counsel and that translations of important documents were provided. The Court rejected the Article 6 § 3 complaint as manifestly ill-founded. The Article 6/13 complaint about the dangerous-detainee review procedure was linked to the Article 3 finding, so no separate finding was made. The applicant also alleged Article 8 violations over restricted family visits and delayed telephone access.

**Pugžlys v. Poland** (Application no. 446/10, ECtHR, 14 June 2016) concerned a Lithuanian national, Juozas Pugžlys, arrested in the Netherlands in April 2003 and extradited to Poland. He was charged with leading an international organised criminal group and six counts of kidnapping for ransom. In January 2010 the Lublin Regional Court convicted him and sentenced him to twelve years’ imprisonment; the conviction was upheld on appeal in December 2010, and his cassation appeal was dismissed in April 2012.

The main alleged violations arose from three sets of facts. First, from 21 October 2003 until 25 July 2012—almost nine years—the applicant was classified as a “dangerous detainee” and subjected to a high-security regime. The initial decision relied on the serious nature of the charges, his alleged leadership of an armed criminal group, his combat training, and his perceived dangerousness. The regime was reviewed every three months but repeatedly extended on broadly the same grounds. It involved placement in a high-security or solitary wing, constant CCTV monitoring including sanitary facilities, joined shackles whenever he left his cell, daily or repeated full strip searches whenever he entered or left the cell, and significant restrictions on family contact. He was allowed telephone calls only from October 2007, generally two ten-minute calls per week, and visits were limited and often conducted behind a grille or glass partition. Although some appeals against the regime were lodged, domestic courts upheld the decisions.

Second, during hearings before the Lublin Regional Court between 2007 and 2010, the applicant was held in a metal cage and handcuffed or shackled. He claimed this occurred at all 104 hearings, amounting to about 400 hours; the Government admitted it occurred at some hearings. The domestic court gave no reasoned decision for keeping him in the cage, and his requests to remove the cage and restraints were refused. He alleged that this was humiliating and hindered his ability to participate in his trial.

Third, he complained about his defence rights. A court-appointed lawyer spoke only Polish. The applicant alleged that he could not communicate properly with counsel, that an interpreter was not present during lawyer meetings, and that unsupervised meetings were refused. The Government maintained that a Lithuanian interpreter attended hearings, file examinations, and meetings with counsel during trial recesses, and that relevant documents were translated. The Court of Appeal and Supreme Court found no breach of his defence rights.

He also complained that restrictions on family visits and telephone contact violated Article 8.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 3 in respect of both the prolonged “dangerous detainee” regime and the use of the metal cage and restraints during hearings. It held that the initial classification was legitimate, but continuing the full regime for almost nine years was not necessary; the daily strip searches and shackling caused distress beyond ordinary detention, and the reviews were formalistic. The cage amounted to degrading treatment, especially without reasoned justification. The Article 6 § 3 complaints concerning interpreters and defence rights were rejected as manifestly ill-founded, and the Court found no separate issue under Articles 6 and 13. It found no violation of Article 8.

**Case: Mihhailov v. Estonia (App. No. 64418/10), ECtHR, 30 August 2016**

The applicant, Aleksandr Mihhailov, a stateless person living in Narva, Estonia, alleged that police used unwarranted violence against him during his arrest and later detention at a police station on 29–30 April 2009, contrary to Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment). The case concerned both the alleged ill-treatment and the effectiveness of the domestic investigation.

**Key facts.** On 29 April 2009, police received a call about two men, one possibly carrying a knife and the other visibly drunk. Officers found the applicant and M.Z. at a playground. The applicant was intoxicated. According to the applicant, he did not behave aggressively. He alleged that Officer S.B. punched him on the jaw, causing him to fall and briefly lose consciousness; that an officer knelt on his neck; and that after being handcuffed he was punched and kicked all over his body and head, losing consciousness until he reached the police station.

The Government’s account, based on the domestic investigation, was different. It claimed the applicant was aggressive, swore, waved his arms, refused orders, and resisted. Officers allegedly used only necessary force to restrain and handcuff him. While being placed in the police van, he allegedly hit his left temple against the van door, and noises were heard from the back of the van during transport.

At the police station, the applicant alleged further violence. He claimed Officer S.B., wearing black leather gloves, systematically punched and kicked him, kneed him near his left ear, and once put his head under a running tap. He alleged he lost consciousness and later had blood on his face. The police claimed the applicant remained aggressive, shouted, refused orders, and fell off a chair twice. They denied beating him, saying force was used only to make him sit or lie down.

Medical evidence showed haematomas on the left side of the skull, a swollen right wrist, a fracture of the right hand/wrist, and concussion. A later examination also found a haematoma around the left eye. A forensic expert concluded the injuries were caused by blunt force shortly before the medical examinations, but the exact cause could not be established due to insufficient documentation.

Several witnesses supported the applicant. Detainees A.P. and R.L. heard or saw police beating him at the station. M.Z. stated he saw police beat the applicant and said he gave a statement against the applicant out of fear after hearing the beating. The applicant identified S.B. from photographs. However, the domestic investigation discontinued criminal proceedings in January 2010, finding no evidence of abuse and that the force used had been lawful.

In separate misdemeanour proceedings, the Viru County Court acquitted the applicant in November 2010. It found the evidence had been unlawfully obtained and that M.Z. had been unduly influenced by hearing the applicant being beaten.

**Court’s findings.** The European Court of Human Rights focused on whether the Government had provided a plausible explanation for injuries sustained while the applicant was in police custody. The Government attributed them to resistance, falls, hitting the van, or self-infliction. The Court found these explanations insufficient, especially for the fractured wrist and head injuries. It therefore found a violation of Article 3 in its substantive aspect. It also found that the domestic investigation was ineffective, having failed to clarify contradictions, properly assess witness evidence, conduct necessary confrontations or a forensic examination, and having been discontinued prematurely. The Court accordingly found a violation of Article 3 in its procedural aspect.

Case Mihhailov v. Estonia (Application no. 64418/10) concerns a stateless applicant, Aleksandr Mihhailov, who alleged police violence during his arrest and subsequent detention in Narva, Estonia, on 29 April 2009, raising issues under Article 3 of the Convention. Police had responded to a call about two men, one possibly carrying a knife, the other drunk and unsteady. Officers S.B. and E.V. found Mihhailov and M.Z. at a playground around 6 p.m. Mihhailov was intoxicated.

The accounts diverge sharply. Mihhailov claimed he was not aggressive, spoke to officers about a knife, and was then punched in the jaw by S.B., fell face-first into a pavement hole, was kneed on the neck, handcuffed, and punched and kicked. He allegedly lost consciousness and awoke at the police station. There, while handcuffed, S.B. allegedly kneed him near the left ear, threw him off a chair, punched and kicked him with leather gloves, and put his head under a running tap. E.V. allegedly also participated when present. Mihhailov later needed an ambulance. The Government maintained that Mihhailov was aggressive, used obscene language, waved his arms, ignored orders, resisted handcuffing, and kicked a police car. Officers forced him to the ground and restrained him. While being placed in the van, he hit his left temple on the door. At the station he remained aggressive, ran toward other cells, had to be restrained, and fell off a chair twice; police denied beating him.

Medical evidence was significant. At 1:42 a.m. on 30 April, an ambulance recorded pain in the left head and right wrist, nausea, vomiting, hearing loss in the left ear, haematomas on the left cranium and a swollen right wrist; he was diagnosed with an intracranial injury and fracture of the right hand/wrist. Hospital records later noted concussion and haematomas/oedema around the left ear and eye. On 1 May, further examination found left-ear haematoma, left-eye oedema, neck and upper-limb bruises, and concussion.

Mihhailov complained of ill-treatment on 30 April; a criminal investigation opened on 5 May. Witnesses from the police station’s sobering-up cells, A.P. and R.L., said they saw or heard officers beating a handcuffed man. M.Z. said Mihhailov was beaten at the station and slapped during arrest. Children who saw the arrest said officers restrained but did not punch or kick Mihhailov, and that he hit his head on the van. Police officers denied excessive force. A forensic expert concluded the injuries were caused by blunt force, likely shortly before 29 April, but could not determine the exact cause; the left-eye haematoma could have arisen on 29, 30 April, or 1 May.

In January 2010 the investigation was discontinued: force was found lawful, justified and non-excessive. The applicant’s appeal was rejected as out of time. Separately, he was acquitted in November 2010 of misdemeanour breach of the peace; the County Court found evidence unlawfully obtained, cited M.Z.’s account that he was influenced by hearing the applicant beaten, and noted procedural violations concerning the delay before sobering-up and the timing of his statement and report. The ECtHR communicated the police-violence complaint, and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

In **B.A.C. v. Greece** (App. no. 11981/15), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section) delivered judgment on 13 October 2016. The applicant was a Turkish national, born in 1977, living in Athens. He complained principally that Greece’s Ministry of Public Order failed for twelve years to decide his asylum request, violating Article 8 alone and with Article 13, and also raising Articles 3, 13, and 14.

The key facts concerned his political persecution in Turkey and his prolonged legal limbo in Greece. While studying in Turkey from 1994 to 1999, he became a pro-communist and pro-Kurdish activist and opened a literary café frequented by like-minded people. In 2000 Turkish police arrested him, and he was prosecuted for infringing the constitutional order under Article 146 of the Turkish Criminal Code. He was held in isolation cells in Kandra Prison, where he went on hunger strike for 171 days and developed Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, a potentially fatal and irreversible condition. He was released due to the threat to his life.

In 2002 he fled to Greece and applied for asylum on 15 January 2002. On 18 February 2002, the General Secretary of the Ministry of Public Order rejected the application at first instance with summary reasons. He appealed on 21 March 2002. On 29 January 2003, the Advisory Board on Asylum issued a favourable opinion after receiving documents showing he had suffered torture in Turkey because of his political opinions, including a Greek medical report and an Amnesty International document. Under Presidential Decree No. 61/1999, the Minister for Public Order should have decided within twenty-four hours whether to grant international protection. Instead, no decision was taken for over twelve years; the Minister neither ratified nor rejected the Board’s favourable opinion.

During this period, the applicant lived in Athens and renewed his asylum-seeker’s card every six months. That card did not amount to a residence permit and gave only “tolerated status,” preventing expulsion while the asylum application remained pending. It did not permit him to work, undertake vocational training, marry, obtain a driving licence, hold a bank account, or apply for family reunion. His wife joined him from Turkey in 2003, but her presence became lawful only in 2008 when she obtained a short-term work permit. They had a son in 2010; in 2011 his wife and child returned to Istanbul due to health problems, and the couple divorced in 2012.

Meanwhile, in 2005, Turkish Interpol issued an extradition request based on accusations similar to those already assessed in his asylum case. In March 2013 the applicant was arrested in Patras. The Patras Court of Appeal indictment division unanimously rejected extradition, finding a risk of ill-treatment on account of his political opinions and noting that the alleged offences were described only vaguely. The Court of Cassation upheld that decision in April 2013. The applicant repeatedly sought a final decision, writing to the Ombudsman in 2012 and the Minister in 2013, 2014, and 2015; correspondence confirmed the asylum request still remained pending.

The Court found that the Convention does not grant a right to enter or reside in a particular State or to a specific residence permit. However, Article 8 imposes positive obligations: the State must establish an effective and accessible procedure to protect private life and must examine asylum requests promptly so that insecurity and uncertainty remain as short-lived as possible. The Government argued the failure to grant refugee status had no real effect on the applicant’s private or family life and that he had worked and renewed his card. The Court rejected this, finding the twelve-year delay unjustified and unexplained, especially given the Advisory Board’s favourable opinion and the rejection of extradition. It held that Greece violated Article 8 and Article 13 read in conjunction with Article 8.

**Case: B.A.C. v. Greece (Application no. 11981/15)**

The applicant, B.A.C., is a Turkish national born in 1977. While studying in Turkey, he became a pro-communist and pro-Kurdish political activist and opened a literary café frequented by people with similar views. In 2000, Turkish police arrested him and prosecuted him for infringing the constitutional order. He was held in isolation cells and went on hunger strike for 171 days, developing Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, a potentially fatal condition. He was released because of the threat to his life.

In 2002, the applicant fled to Greece and applied for asylum on 15 January 2002. On 18 February 2002, the General Secretary of the Ministry of Public Order rejected the application at first instance with summary reasons. The applicant appealed on 21 March 2002. On 29 January 2003, the Advisory Board on Asylum heard him and issued a favourable opinion, relying on documents including a medical report from the Greek Medical Centre for the Rehabilitation of Torture Victims and an Amnesty International document. Under Presidential Decree No. 61/1999, the Minister for Public Order should then have decided within twenty-four hours whether to grant international protection. However, no decision was taken for more than twelve years and the application remained pending.

Between 2003 and 2015, the applicant lived in Athens and renewed his asylum-seeker’s card every six months. That card did not constitute a residence permit. It merely allowed him to remain in Greece with “tolerated status” and not be expelled while his application was examined. It did not permit him to work, undertake vocational training, marry, obtain a driving licence, hold a bank account, or apply for family reunion. He worked in construction without a work permit. Their son was born in 2010, but in 2011 his wife returned to Istanbul with the child due to health problems, and the couple divorced in 2012.

The Patras Court of Appeal’s indictment division unanimously rejected extradition, finding a risk of ill-treatment because of his political opinions and noting that the alleged offences were described vaguely. The Court of Cassation upheld that decision on 26 April 2013. Meanwhile, the applicant repeatedly sought a final decision, writing to the Ombudsman in 2012 and to the Minister for Public Order in 2013, 2014 and 2015. Official correspondence confirmed that his asylum application was still pending.

The applicant complained primarily under Article 8 of the Convention, alone and with Article 13, and also under Articles 3 and 13 and Article 14. The central alleged violation was the Greek authorities’ twelve-year failure to decide his asylum request despite the Advisory Board’s favourable opinion and the rejection of Turkey’s extradition request. He argued that this created prolonged insecurity and uncertainty affecting his private and family life, work, and social relations. The Government contended that his asylum-seeker status had not affected his private life and that he had enjoyed the rights ordinarily granted to asylum-seekers.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 8, holding that Greece failed in its positive obligation to establish an effective and accessible procedure to examine the applicant’s asylum request within a reasonable time, so that his insecurity would be as short-lived as possible. The Court also found a violation of Article 13 read in conjunction with Article 8 because he lacked an effective remedy for that situation.

In *Armani Da Silva v. the United Kingdom* (ECtHR Grand Chamber, 30 March 2016), the applicant, Patricia Armani Da Silva, was the cousin of Jean Charles de Menezes, a Brazilian national shot dead by Metropolitan Police Service officers at Stockwell Underground Station on 22 July 2005. She complained that the decision not to prosecute any individual officers after the fatal shooting breached the procedural aspect of Article 2 of the Convention, which requires an effective investigation capable of establishing the facts, determining whether the force used was justified, and identifying and, if appropriate, punishing those responsible.

The shooting occurred amid the 7 July 2005 London suicide bombings and the failed 21 July bombings. Intelligence identified Hussain Osman as a suspect living at 21 Scotia Road. The police launched Operation THESEUS 2. The strategy was to keep the address under covert surveillance, follow anyone leaving, and stop and arrest them safely once SO19 specialist firearms officers were in position. A Crown Prosecution Service review later found that if this strategy had been followed—particularly if SO19 had been deployed on time—events would not have unfolded as they did.

On 22 July 2005, Jean Charles de Menezes left 17 Scotia Road. SO19 had not yet reached the scene, so he was followed rather than stopped. Surveillance officers’ descriptions varied; some on the ground did not identify him as Osman, while control room personnel believed a positive identification had been made. He boarded a bus, later reboarded it, and then entered Stockwell Underground Station. The Designated Senior Officer ordered that he be stopped. SFOs intercepted him on a train, pinned him down, and two officers shot him multiple times, believing he was a suicide bomber. He was entirely innocent.

After the shooting, the Independent Police Complaints Commission conducted a major investigation. Its Stockwell One Report examined command, briefings, deployment, surveillance and the shooting. It found that a combination of circumstances and failings had led to the killing of an innocent man. It criticised the late deployment of SO19 and briefings that heightened fears of suicide bombers without cautioning officers that not everyone leaving Scotia Road was a bomber or that lethal force was a last resort. The IPCC identified possible criminal offences, including murder, gross negligence manslaughter, misconduct in public office and perverting the course of justice.

The CPS decided that no individual officer should be prosecuted. It concluded there was insufficient evidence to disprove that the two SFOs honestly and genuinely believed they were acting in self-defence. Other alleged failings, including command errors, did not meet the criminal threshold for gross negligence manslaughter or misconduct. There was also insufficient evidence regarding an allegedly altered surveillance log or missing CCTV. The CPS instead prosecuted the Office of the Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis under health and safety legislation.

The applicant argued that this absence of individual prosecutions meant the Article 2 procedural obligation had not been met. The Grand Chamber found no violation. It held that the procedural duty requires an effective investigation, not a prosecution in every case. The IPCC investigation had been independent, thorough and capable of leading to prosecution; the CPS applied the correct tests and gave reasoned decisions. The decision not to prosecute individuals was not arbitrary, so the United Kingdom had not breached the procedural aspect of Article 2.

**Case: Armani Da Silva v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 5878/08, Grand Chamber, 30 March 2016)**

The case concerned the fatal shooting of Jean Charles de Menezes by London police on 22 July 2005 and whether the United Kingdom breached the procedural aspect of Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights by not prosecuting any individual officers. The applicant, Patricia Armani Da Silva, was Mr de Menezes’ cousin.

Following the 7 July 2005 London suicide bombings and the failed 21 July attacks, the Metropolitan Police launched Operation THESEUS 2. Intelligence identified Hussain Osman as a suspect living at 21 Scotia Road. Commander McDowall’s strategy was covert surveillance at Scotia Road, followed by safe arrest once SO19 firearms officers were in place. However, SO19 was not deployed in time. Briefings to firearms officers allegedly heightened fears that they would confront suicide bombers and suggested they might need to shoot; they lacked clear warnings that lethal force was a last resort and only for positively identified suspects.

On 22 July, Mr de Menezes, who lived at 17 Scotia Road, left his flat. He was followed by surveillance officers as no firearms team was available to stop him. He took a bus, reboarded it, and entered Stockwell Underground station. Surveillance descriptions varied between “possible likeness” and “not identical,” but control room personnel apparently believed he was Osman. Commander Cressida Dick, the Designated Senior Officer, ordered that he be stopped. Firearms officers intercepted him on a train; eyewitness accounts conflicted, but he was restrained and then shot multiple times by two Special Firearms Officers, Charlie 2 and Charlie 12, who said they believed he was a suicide bomber and acted in self-defence.

After the shooting, the scene was initially retained by the Anti-Terrorist Branch, and the matter was not immediately referred to the Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC). The Department of Professional Standards gathered evidence. The two shooters made statements about 36 hours later, after learning Mr de Menezes was unconnected to the bombings. A surveillance log was allegedly altered, and CCTV recordings had gaps. The IPCC’s Stockwell One Report identified serious operational failings: inadequate briefings, failure to deploy SO19, command confusion, and delayed IPCC involvement. It referred possible criminal liability of the shooters, Commander Dick, Trojan 84, and others.

The Crown Prosecution Service considered murder, gross negligence manslaughter, misconduct in public office, forgery, and perverting the course of justice. It decided not to prosecute any individual because there was insufficient evidence for a realistic prospect of conviction—especially since the shooters may have genuinely believed they faced a lethal threat—and because planning failures were not sufficiently criminal. It instead prosecuted the Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis as employer under health and safety law. The IPCC later decided no disciplinary action against frontline officers.

The applicant complained that the decision not to prosecute anyone breached Article 2’s procedural duty to conduct an effective investigation capable of establishing the facts, determining whether force was justified, and punishing those responsible. The Grand Chamber examined the investigation and prosecutorial system as a whole. It ultimately found no violation, holding that the United Kingdom had provided an effective investigation and that the CPS’s decision not to prosecute individuals, based on the evidential test, did not breach Article 2. Key facts were the mistaken identity, flawed command and briefing, fatal shooting, extensive but delayed investigations, and reasoned non-prosecution.

**Case: Armani Da Silva v. the United Kingdom (ECtHR Grand Chamber, 30 March 2016)**

The applicant, Patricia Armani Da Silva, was the cousin of Jean Charles de Menezes, a Brazilian national mistakenly shot dead by London police on 22 July 2005. She complained that the United Kingdom breached the procedural aspect of Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights because no individual police officer was prosecuted after the fatal shooting. Article 2 required an effective investigation capable of establishing the facts, determining whether the force used was justified, and identifying and, if appropriate, punishing those responsible.

The shooting occurred amid intense pressure following the 7 July 2005 London suicide bombings and the failed 21 July bombings. Police launched Operation THESEUS 2 after intelligence linked suspect Hussain Osman to an address at Scotia Road. Commander McDowall devised a strategy of surveillance, following persons leaving the premises, and stopping them safely once armed firearms officers from SO19 were in place. However, SO19 was deployed late, so the plan was not properly implemented. Commander Cressida Dick was the Designated Senior Officer in charge. Before deployment, briefings allegedly heightened firearms officers’ fears that they might confront a suicide bomber, without adequately clarifying that lethal force under the “KRATOS” policy was a last resort.

On the morning of 22 July, Mr de Menezes left his flat, was followed by surveillance officers, but was not stopped because SO19 was not in position. He boarded a bus; surveillance identification was uncertain, though the control room apparently believed he had been positively identified as the suspect. At Stockwell Underground Station, the DSO ordered officers to stop him. Firearms officers intercepted him on a train, pinned him down, and two officers, Charlie 2 and Charlie 12, shot him multiple times. It soon became clear that he was entirely innocent.

After the shooting, the scene was initially retained by the Anti-Terrorist Branch rather than immediately handed to the Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC). The IPCC later conducted a detailed investigation, producing the Stockwell One Report. It identified serious failings in the briefings, the delayed deployment of SO19, command and control, and post-incident management, but found no evidence of a cover-up. It also noted evidential problems: officers made statements the next day after learning Mr de Menezes was innocent; some accounts were contradicted by CCTV; a surveillance log had been altered; and CCTV recordings had gaps. The IPCC considered possible criminal or disciplinary action against several officers, but no disciplinary action was ultimately pursued against the frontline or surveillance officers.

The Crown Prosecution Service considered murder, gross negligence manslaughter, misconduct in public office, forgery, and perverting the course of justice. It concluded that there was insufficient evidence for a realistic prospect of conviction against any individual officer. In particular, the firearms officers claimed they genuinely believed they were acting in self-defence against a suicide bomber, and the CPS could not disprove that belief beyond reasonable doubt. Other errors were not considered criminal enough for gross negligence manslaughter. The CPS instead prosecuted the Office of the Commissioner of the Police of the Metropolis as an employer under health and safety legislation, not any individual.

The applicant argued that the absence of any individual prosecution meant the investigation and prosecutorial system failed Article 2’s procedural requirements. The Grand Chamber examined the investigation and the CPS decision-making. It found no violation of Article 2: the investigation was independent and thorough, and the decision not to prosecute individuals was not arbitrary. Although no individual officer was prosecuted, the system as a whole was held to have complied with the procedural obligation.

**Case Šilović v. Serbia (Application no. 32883/08)** is a European Court of Human Rights judgment delivered by the Third Section Committee on 8 November 2016. The Court was composed of Judges Pere Pastor Vilanova, Branko Lubarda, and Georgios A. Serghides, with Fatoş Aracı as Deputy Section Registrar. It deliberated on 11 October 2016 and adopted the judgment on 8 November 2016. The case concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees a hearing within a reasonable time in the determination of civil rights and obligations.

The applicant, Mr Goran Šilović, a Serbian national born in 1952 and living in Belgrade, filed a claim on 10 June 2002 with the former Supreme Military Court in Belgrade. He sought payment of certain benefits. After the Supreme Court of Serbia took over the jurisdiction of the former Supreme Military Court, that court rejected the applicant’s claim on 10 August 2007. The applicant was served with the judgment on 2 October 2007. He lodged his application with the European Court on 19 March 2008. The application was communicated to the Serbian Government on 18 December 2014. The Government objected to the examination of the case by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

The applicant complained only that the length of the domestic proceedings was incompatible with the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1. The Government contested this, arguing that the specific circumstances—particularly the transfer of a large number of cases from the former Supreme Military Court to the Supreme Court—meant the length of proceedings could not be considered excessive.

In assessing the complaint, the Court first defined the relevant period. Although the domestic claim began in 2002, the Convention entered into force in respect of Serbia on 3 March 2004. Therefore, the period to be considered began on 3 March 2004 and ended on 2 October 2007, when the applicant received the Supreme Court’s judgment. This amounted to three years and seven months in one level of jurisdiction.

The Court declared the application admissible, finding that it was neither manifestly ill-founded nor inadmissible on any other grounds. On the merits, it reiterated that the reasonableness of proceedings must be assessed in light of the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicant and the relevant authorities, and what was at stake for the applicant. It noted its frequent findings of Article 6 § 1 violations in similar cases, including *Frydlender v. France*, and its prior case-law in *Nemet v. Serbia*.

Having examined all the material, the Court found no fact or argument capable of leading to a different conclusion. In particular, the transfer of cases and administrative burden relied on by the Government did not justify the delay. It held that the length of the proceedings in the applicant’s case was excessive and failed to meet the “reasonable time” requirement. Accordingly, there was a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The key facts relevant to the violation were therefore the long delay in resolving the applicant’s civil claim for benefits, the fact that the relevant period lasted three years and seven months before one level of jurisdiction, and the Government’s failure to provide a sufficient justification for that delay.

It began on 3 March 2004, when the Convention entered into force in respect of Serbia, and ended on 2 October 2007, when the applicant was served with the Supreme Court’s judgment. The period to be considered therefore lasted three years and seven months in one level of jurisdiction. Although the applicant had originally filed his claim in 2002, the Court could only examine the period falling after Serbia’s acceptance of the Convention’s temporal jurisdiction.

On admissibility, the Court found that the application was neither manifestly ill-founded within the meaning of Article 35 § 3 nor inadmissible on any other grounds. It therefore declared the application admissible.

On the merits, the Court reiterated that the reasonableness of the length of proceedings must be assessed in light of the circumstances of the case and by reference to criteria including the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicant and the relevant authorities, and what was at stake for the applicant. The Court noted that it had frequently found violations of Article 6 § 1 in cases raising similar issues, referring in particular to *Frydlender v. France*. Having examined all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion. Applying its case-law, especially *Nemet v. Serbia*, the Court considered that the length of the proceedings in the instant case was excessive and failed to meet the “reasonable time” requirement. **Case:** *Šilović v. Serbia* (Application no. 32883/08)  
**Court:** European Court of Human Rights, Third Section  
**Date:** 8 November 2016

The applicant, Mr Goran Šilović, a Serbian national born in 1952 and living in Belgrade, complained under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights that the length of civil proceedings before the Serbian courts had been incompatible with the “reasonable time” requirement. The case concerned his claim for payment of certain benefits.

On 10 June 2002, the applicant filed a claim with the former Supreme Military Court in Belgrade. On 10 August 2007, the Supreme Court of Serbia, which had taken over the jurisdiction of the former Supreme Military Court, rejected the applicant’s claim. The applicant received that judgment on 2 October 2007. He lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 19 March 2008.

The Government contested the complaint. It argued that, given the specific circumstances—namely the transfer of a large number of cases from the former Supreme Military Court to the Supreme Court—the length of the proceedings could not be considered excessive. The Government also objected to the examination of the application by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

For the purposes of the length-of-proceedings complaint, the Court calculated the relevant period as beginning on 3 March 2004, when the Convention entered into force in respect of Serbia, and ending on 2 October 2007, when the applicant was served with the Supreme Court’s judgment. The proceedings had therefore lasted three years and seven months before one level of jurisdiction. The earlier period before 3 March 2004 was not taken into account because the Convention was not yet in force for Serbia at that time.

The Court declared the application admissible, finding that it was neither manifestly ill-founded within the meaning of Article 35 § 3 nor inadmissible on any other grounds.

On the merits, the Court reiterated the standard criteria for assessing the reasonableness of proceedings: the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicant and the relevant authorities, and what was at stake for the applicant. It referred to its established case-law, particularly *Frydlender v. France*, and to a similar Serbian case, *Nemet v. Serbia*. The Court examined the material submitted and found no fact or argument capable of leading to a different conclusion.

The key factors relevant to the alleged violation were that the applicant’s case concerned a claim for payment of benefits, the proceedings remained pending for over three years and seven months after the Convention entered into force, and the delay occurred even though the case was examined only at one level of jurisdiction. The Government’s explanation about the transfer of a large number of cases from the former Supreme Military Court to the Supreme Court was not sufficient to justify the overall length of the proceedings. The Court therefore concluded that the length of the proceedings was excessive and failed to satisfy the “reasonable time” requirement.

Accordingly, the Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The judgment was final but subject to editorial revision.

In *Paposhvili v. Belgium* (Application no. 41738/10, Grand Chamber, 13 December 2016), the applicant was a Georgian national born in 1958 who arrived in Belgium in 1998 with his wife and child. He had a substantial criminal record, including convictions for theft, robbery and involvement in a criminal organisation; in 2005 he was sentenced to three years’ imprisonment. His asylum application was rejected, and subsequent requests for regularisation on exceptional grounds also failed. In 2007 the Minister of the Interior issued a deportation order and a ten-year re-entry ban based on his criminal record.

The alleged violations arose mainly from his serious medical condition. In 2006 he was diagnosed with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL). By 2007 he required chemotherapy, and his condition later progressed to Binet stage C and then lymphocytic lymphoma. He also suffered from tuberculosis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, hepatitis C and the effects of a stroke. Belgian doctors reported that without continuous specialised treatment, in particular Ibrutinib and a donor stem-cell transplant, his life expectancy would be roughly three months, and that such treatment would allegedly be unavailable in Georgia. He claimed that removal would expose him to a real risk of death and inhuman or degrading treatment, contrary to Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention, and would separate him from his wife and children, who had been granted indefinite leave to remain in Belgium, contrary to Article 8.

He lodged requests for regularisation on medical grounds under section 9ter of the Aliens Act. These were rejected without examination of his medical evidence because he was excluded from that provision as a person suspected of serious crimes. The Aliens Appeals Board upheld that approach, holding that the exclusion clause made any medical examination superfluous. It also reasoned that any Article 3 risk should be assessed only at the time of enforcement of a removal measure and that, since the impugned decisions were not accompanied by removal measures, the alleged risk was hypothetical. In 2010, after his third exceptional regularisation request was refused, an order to leave the country and a detention order were issued. A Georgian travel document was obtained, and his removal appeared imminent.

The applicant applied to the European Court of Human Rights and requested interim measures. On 28 July 2010 the Court indicated under Rule 39 that Belgium should not remove him pending the domestic proceedings. He remained in Belgium and died there in 2016; his family pursued the case. A Chamber of the Court in 2014 found no violation of Articles 2 and 3 and no violation of Article 8. The Grand Chamber, however, clarified the Article 3 threshold: it is not limited to imminent death but may cover a real risk of serious, rapid and irreversible decline in health causing intense suffering or a significant reduction in life expectancy due to the absence of appropriate treatment or lack of access to it. It found that the Belgian authorities had failed to adequately assess the applicant’s individual medical risk before removal, in violation of Article 3, and did not examine Articles 2 and 8 separately. The case is a leading authority on the removal of seriously ill migrants.

In *Paposhvili v. Belgium*, the applicant was a Georgian national born in 1958. He arrived in Belgium in November 1998 with his wife and child and remained after his asylum claim failed. He had a significant criminal record, including convictions for theft, robbery with violence and involvement in a criminal organisation. In 2007 Belgium issued a ministerial deportation order barring him from re-entry for ten years. His wife and children later obtained indefinite leave to remain in Belgium.

The key facts concerned his health. In 2006 he was diagnosed with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, which later progressed to an advanced stage. He also suffered from pulmonary tuberculosis, COPD, hepatitis C and a stroke. In Belgium he received chemotherapy and, from 2014, Ibrutinib. Medical reports stated that he depended on continuous treatment; if Ibrutinib were stopped, his average life expectancy would be about three months. A donor stem-cell transplant was considered the only prospect of a cure and was available only in Belgium. His doctors indicated that he would not have access to equivalent specialised treatment in Georgia. Belgian medical advisers, by contrast, concluded that his illnesses were serious but currently controlled and not directly life-threatening, so the Article 3 threshold was not met.

He alleged that removal to Georgia would violate Articles 2, 3 and 8 of the Convention. Under Articles 2 and 3, he claimed that removal would expose him to death or inhuman and degrading treatment because his life would be significantly shortened and he would suffer without adequate medical care. Under Article 8, he alleged permanent separation from his wife and children.

His asylum and regularisation requests were rejected. His medical regularisation requests under section 9ter of the Aliens Act were refused without substantive examination because he was excluded as having committed serious crimes. The Aliens Appeals Board considered any medical risk hypothetical absent an actual removal measure, or said it should be assessed when removal was enforced. Deportation and leave orders were issued, and in July 2010 a Georgian travel document was prepared. The European Court of Human Rights indicated an interim measure under Rule 39 staying removal pending domestic proceedings. Domestic courts nevertheless rejected his appeals; the Conseil d’État held that the medical assessment could be carried out at the time of removal. The applicant died in June 2016, and his family pursued the case.

The Grand Chamber found a violation of Article 3. It held that removal of a seriously ill alien would breach Article 3 only in very exceptional cases, but that such a case could arise where substantial grounds showed a real risk of serious, rapid and irreversible deterioration in health leading to intense suffering or a significant reduction in life expectancy because appropriate treatment was unavailable or inaccessible in the receiving country. Belgium had failed to properly assess that risk before removal. The Court found no violation of Article 8.

Paposhvili v. Belgium (Application no. 41738/10) is a Grand Chamber judgment of 13 December 2016. The applicant, Georgie Paposhvili, was a Georgian national born in 1958. He arrived in Belgium in November 1998 with his wife and a child, and later had two more children in Belgium. He had a significant criminal record: convictions for theft, robbery with violence, and involvement in a criminal organisation; in 2005 he was sentenced to three years’ imprisonment. His asylum application was rejected, and his subsequent requests for regularisation on exceptional and medical grounds were refused. In 2007 the Minister of the Interior issued a deportation order and a ten-year re-entry ban. In July 2010 further orders to leave the country and detention were served.

The alleged violations arose from his proposed removal to Georgia. The applicant suffered from chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, diagnosed in 2006 while in prison. It progressed to Binet stage C and later to lymphocytic lymphoma. He also had active tuberculosis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, hepatitis C with liver fibrosis, and had suffered a stroke causing permanent paralysis of his left arm. He underwent several courses of chemotherapy. From December 2014 he received Ibrutinib, which produced partial remission and was considered necessary to prepare for a donor stem cell transplant—his only prospect of cure. Medical reports stated that if Ibrutinib were discontinued, his average life expectancy would be about three months; Ibrutinib and the transplant were not available in Georgia.

Belgian medical advisers, however, concluded that his condition was under control, not terminal or directly life-threatening, and did not reach the Article 3 threshold as interpreted in N. v. the United Kingdom. His requests under section 9ter of the Aliens Act for regularisation on medical grounds were rejected because he was excluded from that provision due to his serious crimes. The Aliens Appeals Board declined to examine the medical evidence, holding that exclusion alone was sufficient and that any Article 3 risk should be assessed when removal was enforced.

The applicant alleged that removal to Georgia would violate Articles 2 and 3 because he would be deprived of life-sustaining treatment and face death or inhuman and degrading treatment. Under Article 8, he argued that removal would permanently separate him from his wife and children, who had been granted indefinite leave to remain in Belgium in July 2010. On 23 July 2010 he applied to the European Court of Human Rights and requested interim measures. On 28 July 2010 the Court indicated to Belgium under Rule 39 that it was desirable not to remove him pending the proceedings before the Aliens Appeals Board.

A Chamber in 2014 found no violation of Articles 2 and 3 and no violation of Article 8. The case was referred to the Grand Chamber. The applicant died on 7 June 2016, and his wife and children continued the proceedings. The Grand Chamber clarified that Article 3 may be engaged where removal would lead to a serious, rapid and irreversible decline in health causing intense suffering or a significant reduction in life expectancy, even without imminent death, and imposed procedural obligations on States to assess such risks. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore his severe treatment-dependent illness, the absence of comparable treatment in Georgia, the domestic refusal to assess that risk, and his family ties in Belgium.

In *Goryayeva v. Ukraine* (no. 58656/10, 6 October 2016), the European Court of Human Rights examined the death of the applicant’s son in police detention and the effectiveness of Ukraine’s investigation. The applicant, a Ukrainian national, complained under Article 2 that her son A.G. had been murdered in a temporary detention centre (ITT) or that authorities were responsible for failing to protect his life, and that the investigation was ineffective.

A.G., born in 1966, suffered from tuberculosis, HIV/AIDS, drug addiction, and an infected phlegmon on his right shin. On 4 May 2007 he was arrested on suspicion of drug-related crimes and placed in the Mykolayiv police ITT. On 7 May a district court ordered his pre-trial detention. During detention, ambulance doctors treated him; on 19 May he was transferred to a hospital surgical ward for the phlegmon and later returned to the ITT after doctors considered detention appropriate.

On 23 May 2007, around 9:30 p.m., an ITT officer heard moaning from A.G.’s cell. A.G. was alone, breathing heavily, saying he felt bad and needed air. Officers removed him to an entrance area for fresh air and administered first aid. An ambulance arrived at 9:43 p.m. and confirmed death. The post-mortem attributed death to ischaemic heart disease aggravated by acute heart failure. Linear strangulation bruises on his neck indicated interrupted asphyxiation about ten minutes before death, which could have aggravated his chronic illnesses.

Between 2007 and 2012, local prosecutors conducted only pre-investigation inquiries; more than fifteen decisions refusing criminal proceedings were quashed as unfounded and remitted for further inquiry. In December 2012 criminal proceedings were opened. In March 2013 an investigator terminated them, finding no crime by ITT officers; a court quashed this as unfounded. In October 2013 the investigator again terminated the case, finding no evidence ITT staff caused death and admitting key evidence could not be examined: bed linen and a rope made from bed linen had been destroyed after post-mortem; reconstruction was impossible; and the 24 May 2007 site inspection produced no video, sketches, or photographs. The investigator concluded A.G. had attempted suicide by asphyxiation using the bed-linen rope, that his serious illnesses would have deteriorated regardless, and that ITT officers could not have foreseen the fatal outcome. He also found A.G. had been medically supervised, adequately fed, and had not required hospitalisation during his ITT detention.

On the substantive Article 2 complaint, the Court rejected allegations of murder or failure to protect life. Because death occurred in custody, authorities had to provide a convincing explanation. The domestic explanation was based on reliable, coherent medical and other evidence; A.G. was alone; and no evidence supported murder by others. There was also no known real and immediate suicide risk: no psychiatric diagnosis or expressed suicidal intent, and officers responded promptly, gave first aid, and called an ambulance. That part was manifestly ill-founded.

However, the procedural complaint succeeded. The Court held that the State must conduct an effective official investigation into deaths in custody, taking all reasonable steps to secure evidence and acting promptly. From 2007 to 2012, authorities used only pre-investigation inquiries, lacking adequate procedural safeguards. The repeated terminations and quashings—over fifteen—revealed serious deficiencies. When a full investigation finally began in December 2012, evidence had already been destroyed or initial steps mishandled. The final termination came more than six years and five months after the incident. The Court therefore found a violation of the procedural obligation under Article 2.
