In *Goryayeva v. Ukraine* (App. no. 58656/10, 6 October 2016), the applicant, a Ukrainian national, complained under Article 2 of the Convention about her son A.G.’s death in a temporary detention centre (“ITT”) in Mykolayiv and the alleged failure to investigate it effectively.

A.G., born in 1966, suffered from tuberculosis, AIDS, drug addiction, and an infected phlegmon on his right shin. He was arrested on suspicion of drug-related crimes on 4 May 2007 and placed in the ITT. On 7 May 2007, a district court ordered his pre-trial detention. While in detention, ambulance doctors treated him, and he was transferred to a local hospital for treatment of his phlegmon. After doctors considered him fit for detention, he was returned to the ITT.

At about 9:30 p.m. on 23 May 2007, an ITT officer heard moaning from A.G.’s cell. A.G. was alone, breathing heavily, and saying he felt bad and needed air. Officers removed him to the entrance area, gave first aid, and called an ambulance. It arrived at 9:43 p.m. and confirmed he was dead. The post-mortem report stated that A.G. died from ischaemic heart disease aggravated by acute heart failure. Linear strangulation bruises on his neck indicated interrupted asphyxiation about ten minutes before death, which could have aggravated his chronic illnesses.

Domestically, between 2007 and 2012, investigators refused more than fifteen times to initiate criminal proceedings. Those decisions were repeatedly quashed as unsubstantiated by supervising prosecutors and courts, which ordered further pre-investigation inquiries. In December 2012, criminal proceedings were finally opened under the 2012 Code of Criminal Procedure. In March 2013, an investigator terminated the proceedings, finding no crime by ITT officers. A court quashed that decision as unfounded. In October 2013, the investigator again terminated the case, finding no evidence that ITT staff had caused A.G.’s death. He noted that key evidence could not be examined: bed linen and a rope made from it had been destroyed after the post-mortem; no reconstruction was possible; and a 24 May 2007 site inspection produced no video, sketches, or photographs.

Based on available evidence, the investigator concluded that A.G. had attempted suicide by asphyxiating himself with a rope made from bed linen. The latest medical findings indicated death from interrupted mechanical asphyxiation, with neck injuries suggesting heart failure from the attempted strangulation. He found no acute condition requiring hospital admission during detention, noted that A.G. had been medically supervised, and considered that his serious illnesses would have worsened regardless. He concluded ITT officers could not have foreseen the fatal outcome.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged that her son had been murdered in detention, that the authorities were responsible for his death, and that the investigation was ineffective. The Court accepted the domestic authorities’ explanation. It found A.G. had been alone, the medical evidence supported suicide-related asphyxiation and heart failure, and there was no evidence of murder. It dismissed the substantive complaints as manifestly ill-founded. It also found no operational failure: there was no psychiatric diagnosis or expressed suicidal intent, and officers responded promptly by giving first aid and calling an ambulance.

However, the procedural complaint was admissible. The Court found the investigation ineffective: for over five years, authorities used only pre-investigation inquiries, repeatedly terminating and remitting the case. A full investigation began only in December 2012, by which time crucial evidence had been destroyed and initial steps had not been properly taken. The last termination came more than six years and five months after the death. The Court concluded that the domestic inquiries and investigations did not comply with Article 2’s procedural requirements.

**Case Salikhova and Magomedova v. Russia** (Application no. 63689/13), European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, judgment of 26 January 2016, final on 6 June 2016. The applicants were Ruzmay Salikhova and Rapiyat Magomedova, Russian nationals living in Makhachkala, Dagestan, respectively the mother and wife of Mr Sakhrab Abakargadzhiyev. They alleged that State agents abducted their relative on 20 May 2013, that he subsequently disappeared, and that the authorities failed to investigate effectively.

According to the applicants, for about eighteen months before the abduction, Sakhrab had been suspected of illegal activities and followed by Dagestani law-enforcement agencies, particularly the Centre against Extremism (CPE). On 20 May 2013 at about 6:45 p.m., while driving his white GAZ Volga-3110 car in Makhachkala, he was stopped and abducted by eight armed, masked men in civilian clothing. The men used two civilian vehicles, including a silver VAZ and a black VAZ-21099. A relative, Mr Ub.Ub., called Sakhrab during the abduction and heard him screaming, then informed the applicants. The first applicant and Mr Ub.Ub. went along Sakhrab’s route and found his car with police vehicles and officers from the Sovetskiy district police station. Police said he had been abducted minutes earlier, told them to wait at home, and took the car to the police station.

About twenty days after the abduction, CPE officers searched the applicants’ house. Around 20 June 2013, the applicants obtained video footage of the abduction from a local resident and recognised one abductor by his voice as CPE officer “Shakir”; they informed the authorities. On 1 July 2013, a burnt male corpse was found near Gurbuki. On 23 December 2013, authorities identified it as Sakhrab based on a 99.93% DNA match. The applicants disputed that identification, stating the corpse had gold teeth while Sakhrab had none. The Government did not dispute the facts but denied State involvement.

The official investigation began after the applicants complained immediately and gave statements. A criminal case was opened on 14 June 2013. Investigators examined the crime scene and Sakhrab’s car, but collected fingerprints that were later found unfit for identification. A witness, Mr Ma.Ma., described masked men beating and abducting Sakhrab and provided video footage, which investigators seized. Investigators questioned relatives and obtained text messages stating Sakhrab had become a “shahid” and that a neighbour had set him up. In September 2013, the first applicant reported a caller claiming to be an FSB officer holding Sakhrab and demanding ransom; RUB 50,000 was paid but no release occurred, and call logs traced the caller to Volgograd. The applicant requested voice analysis of an abductor linked to CPE officer Shakir. Shakir N. denied involvement but admitted participating in the search of the applicants’ home and alleged Sakhrab supported terrorist groups. A November 2013 internal inquiry could not verify the complaints due to discrepancies and stated that resolution required a criminal case. Voice analysis found the recording unfit for identification. The investigation was suspended on 30 December 2013, resumed in January 2014, and joined with the case concerning the corpse. Proceedings remained pending.

The Court joined the Government’s preliminary objection that the investigation was unfinished to the merits, because its effectiveness was closely linked to the applicants’ complaints. The key alleged violations concerned an unlawful abduction and disappearance by State agents and the failure to conduct an effective investigation, raising issues under Articles 2, 3, 5 and 13 of the Convention.

**Case: Salikhova and Magomedova v. Russia (Application no. 63689/13)**  
**Court:** European Court of Human Rights, Third Section  
**Judgment:** 26 January 2016 (final 6 June 2016)

The applicants, Ms Ruzmay Salikhova and Ms Rapiyat Magomedova, are Russian nationals living in Makhachkala, Dagestan. They are the mother and wife of Mr Sakhrab Abakargadzhiyev, born in 1990. They alleged that he was abducted by State agents in Dagestan, subsequently disappeared, and that the Russian authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation.

The applicants claimed that for about eighteen months before the incident, Mr Abakargadzhiyev had been suspected of illegal activities and followed by Dagestani law-enforcement agencies, particularly the Centre against Extremism of the Dagestan Ministry of the Interior (“CPE”). On 20 May 2013, at about 6 p.m., he drove in a white GAZ Volga-3110 car to visit relatives. At about 6.45 p.m., his car was stopped and he was abducted by eight armed, masked men in civilian clothing. The men used two civilian vehicles, a silver VAZ-21014 and a black VAZ-21099. A relative, Mr Ub.Ub., called Mr Abakargadzhiyev during the abduction and heard him screaming. He and the first applicant went to the scene and found the victim’s car with police officers from the Sovetskiy district police station. The police said they had arrived shortly after the abduction, told the applicants to wait for a telephone call, and took the car to the police station.

About twenty days later, CPE officers searched the applicants’ house. Around 20 June 2013, the applicants obtained video footage of the abduction from a local resident. They recognised one abductor’s voice as that of a CPE officer named “Shakir” and informed the authorities. On 1 July 2013, a burnt male corpse was found near Gurbuki village. In December 2013, the authorities identified it as Mr Abakargadzhiyev based on a 99.93% DNA match. The applicants disputed the identification, claiming the corpse shown in a photograph had five gold teeth, whereas their relative had none.

An official investigation began after the applicants complained on 20 and 24 May 2013. A criminal case was opened on 14 June 2013. Investigators examined the crime scene and the car, but fingerprints were unusable. Witnesses were questioned, including a neighbour who filmed the abduction. The video was seized and examined. A voice analysis was ordered but proved inconclusive. Phone logs were obtained for the victim, a ransom caller, and officer Shakir. The first applicant reported that on 5 September 2013 a man claiming to be an FSB officer said he was holding her son and demanded 250,000 roubles; 50,000 roubles were deposited, after which the caller disappeared. Other messages claimed the victim had become a “shahid” and had been set up by a neighbour working for police. Officer Shakir denied involvement. An internal inquiry noted conflicting statements but could not verify the allegations. The investigation was suspended on 30 December 2013, resumed on 28 January 2014, and joined with a related case after the body was identified. Proceedings remained pending.

The Government did not dispute the applicants’ account but denied State involvement. The applicants alleged violations concerning the right to life, liberty and security, inhuman treatment, and the lack of an effective remedy. The Court joined the Government’s preliminary objection on the effectiveness of the investigation to the merits.

**Summary of *Salikhova and Magomedova v. Russia* (Application no. 63689/13)**

The case originated from an application lodged against Russia by two Russian nationals, Ms Ruzmay Salikhova and Ms Rapiyat Magomedova, the mother and wife of Mr Sakhrab Abakargadzhiyev. They alleged that their relative had been abducted by State agents in Dagestan, Russia, on 20 May 2013, and subsequently disappeared, and that the authorities had failed to conduct an effective investigation.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are as follows. On the evening of 20 May 2013, Mr Abakargadzhiyev was driving in Makhachkala when his car was stopped by a group of eight armed men in civilian clothing and masks, driving two civilian vehicles. The men forcibly pulled him from his car, beat him, and abducted him. A relative who was on the phone with him at the time heard him screaming. Shortly after, the applicants arrived at the scene and found police officers from the Sovetskiy district police station (ROVD) next to the abandoned car. The police, who took the vehicle to their station, told them to wait for a call. The applicants claimed that for about eighteen months prior to the abduction, the victim had been suspected of illegal activities and followed by Dagestani law enforcement agencies, specifically the Centre against Extremism (CPE).

Approximately twenty days after the abduction, police officers from the CPE searched the applicants’ house. About a month after the events, the applicants obtained video footage of the abduction from a local resident. They recognised one of the abductors by his voice as a CPE officer named "Shakir" and informed the authorities. The investigation, opened on 14 June 2013, questioned several witnesses, including the applicant’s relatives, who provided accounts consistent with the applicants’ version of events. However, the investigation was marked by delays and apparent failures, such as the initial examination of the crime scene on 3 June yielding no evidence. A crucial piece of evidence, the abduction video, was seized on 21 June and examined, but a subsequent expert analysis of the voices on the footage concluded they were "not fit for identification."

On 1 July 2013, a burnt male corpse was found in a vehicle in a different district. On 23 December 2013, the authorities identified the body as that of Mr Abakargadzhiyev based on a 99.93% DNA match. However, the applicants disputed this, stating that the photograph they were shown depicted a corpse with five gold teeth, whereas their relative had none.

During the investigation, the first applicant received threatening text messages about her son's death and, on 5 September 2013, received a call from a man claiming to be an FSB officer holding her son, demanding a ransom. The ransom was paid, but the caller disappeared. The investigation was suspended on 30 December 2013, then resumed, but remained pending. The Government denied any State involvement in the abduction.

The applicants brought their case to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging violations of Articles 2 (right to life), 3 (prohibition of torture), 5 (right to liberty), and 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the Convention, based on the abduction by State agents and the subsequent ineffective investigation.

In *Kulyk v. Ukraine* (no. 30760/06, 23 June 2016), applicant Anatoliy Kulyk alleged police ill-treatment, an ineffective investigation, and interference with his right of individual application to the European Court.

On 30 December 2002, Kulyk saw youths on nearby factory premises. He entered an abandoned factory building through a wall opening and then left. Soon after, police officer L. came to his home, allegedly armed, swore at him, grabbed him, struck his head with a gun handle, and kicked him. L. took him to a police station, accusing him of stealing aluminium sheets. There, Kulyk claimed L. kicked him in the kidneys; then L. and officer P. beat him on the head and body for 15–20 minutes, later joined by officer G., to make him confess. He was placed in a cell. A person in a white coat gave him Analgin and Dimedrol. On 31 December, he was taken to court and fined for disobeying police; he allegedly tried to show his injuries, but the judge refused. Back at the station, he signed a statement that no force had been used. A decision not to prosecute him for theft noted he had no intent to steal.

Kulyk later suffered headaches, nausea and fever. On 2 January 2003 he was examined and hospitalised from 3 January to 11 February 2003. Medical records noted bruises, scratches, a large left-thigh bruise, and diagnoses including multitrauma, closed brain injury, brain contusion, two broken ribs, post-traumatic pneumonia, and kidney injury. A 12 May 2003 forensic report found medium-severity injuries caused by a blunt hard object, possibly on 30 December.

After his complaint in February 2003, authorities repeatedly refused to institute criminal proceedings; those decisions were quashed and reopened. Police and factory employees said Kulyk fled, fell several times—through a conveyor opening, from a 2.5-metre fence, and at his home—and hid in a coal bunker. His mother-in-law said L. aimed a blow and later kicked him. A judge who saw him on 31 December said he had no visible head or hand injuries and did not complain. Forensic experts said the injuries could have resulted from beatings or multiple falls; a 2008 expert considered falls most probable. Officers P. and L. were charged with abuse of power in April 2005, but proceedings were repeatedly terminated for lack of evidence and finally closed in October 2008, partly because six years had passed.

The Court found the injuries serious enough to engage Article 3. However, because it was not clear Kulyk was in good health when taken into custody, he delayed hospitalisation, and witness and forensic evidence supported possible falls, the Court could not conclude beyond reasonable doubt that police caused the injuries. The investigation was nevertheless marked by repeated closures and reopenings, delays, and failures to obtain medical records, question relevant witnesses, or clarify how the injuries occurred. Separately, in 2010, in criminal proceedings concerning alleged pornographic material on an Internet page linked to Kulyk’s representative, police searched premises where the representative worked for a human rights organisation and seized three computers. One allegedly contained confidential correspondence with the Court in this case. The prosecutor refused to institute criminal proceedings over the search; appeals failed, though the representative was later acquitted in 2013. The Court ultimately found violations concerning the ineffective investigation and the interference with the right of individual application.

**Kulyk v. Ukraine (Application no. 30760/06)**

The case originated from an application lodged against Ukraine on 17 July 2006 by Mr. Anatoliy Kulyk, who alleged ill-treatment by police, a failure to effectively investigate his complaints, and interference with his right of individual application to the Court.

The key facts concern events on 30-31 December 2002. According to the applicant, while at his home in Shargorod, he noticed intruders at a nearby factory and entered the premises out of curiosity. Finding no one, he returned home. Shortly after, police officer L. arrived, accused him of theft, struck him on the head with a gun handle, and kicked him. The applicant was then taken to the police station. He claimed that he was subsequently beaten by officers L., P., and G. for 15-20 minutes, resulting in a severe headache, nausea, and injuries. He was held overnight and, the next morning, taken to court, where he was fined for disobeying a police order. He alleged that the judge refused to see his injuries. He further stated that he was brought back to the station and forced to sign a statement that he had not been ill-treated. He was released on 31 December 2002.

The Government presented a different account, aligning with the findings of the national investigation. They contended that the applicant was discovered by police officer L. and factory employees while stealing aluminium sheets. While fleeing, the applicant fell multiple times: while climbing through a conveyor belt opening, while climbing over a 2.5-metre fence, and again while jumping over the fence of his own house. The Government argued that the applicant's injuries—including a concussion, broken ribs, and a kidney injury—were sustained during these falls, not from a beating.

The applicant was hospitalised from 3 January to 11 February 2003. Medical records documented numerous bruises and a large haematoma on his left thigh. Forensic examinations concluded that his injuries were of "medium severity" and could have been caused either by being beaten with a blunt object or by multiple falls from a height.

The domestic investigation, initiated in February 2003, was protracted and marked by numerous procedural failures. Between 2003 and 2008, prosecutors repeatedly terminated criminal proceedings against the police officers for lack of evidence, only for these decisions to be quashed by higher prosecutors or courts due to incomplete investigations. Authorities failed to promptly question key witnesses, secure the applicant’s medical records, or conduct crucial reconstructions of the events. The investigation finally concluded on 19 October 2008, finding no evidence of a crime and determining that the applicant's injuries were most likely the result of his multiple falls while fleeing from the police officer.

Separately, on 22 September 2010, a search was conducted at premises linked to the applicant's legal representative, during which a computer containing confidential correspondence with the European Court was seized. This formed the basis of his complaint regarding interference with his right of individual application.

Before the Court, the applicant alleged violations of Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention regarding the ill-treatment and the ineffective investigation. The Government argued that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies by not appealing the final termination decision. The Court, however, joined this objection to the merits of the case.

Sousa Goucha v. Portugal (Application no. 70434/12) is a European Court of Human Rights case decided by the Fourth Section on 22 March 2016 and final on 22 June 2016. The applicant, Manuel Luís Sousa Goucha, a Portuguese national born in 1954, is one of Portugal’s best-known television hosts. He publicly declared his homosexuality in 2008.

The facts concerned a live talk show, “Five Minutes to Midnight” (“5 Para a Meia-Noite”), broadcast on RTP2 between midnight and 1 a.m. on 28 December 2009. The programme was hosted by F.C. and featured two media guests. During a quiz, F.C. asked what was described as the most important question: “Who is the best Portuguese female TV host?” The options included three female television hosts and the applicant. The applicant was the “correct” answer. In the exchange, guest J.M. hesitated, said the choice was difficult and that the other three were “gorgeous,” and initially selected C.V. F.C. called that answer “extremely dishonest” and contrary to what J.M. believed, then revealed the correct answer: “Manuel Luís Goucha!” J.M. responded that he knew it and said, “She was the one telling me not to say it, that it could be bad.” The joke thus placed the applicant in the category of “female” hosts, using feminine references.

In 2010 the applicant filed a criminal complaint for defamation and insult (injúria) with Lisbon authorities against the State-owned television company RTP, the production company, presenter F.C., and programming/content directors. He claimed they had damaged his reputation and dignity by including his name among possible answers to the “best female TV host” question. On 2 March 2011 a prosecutor discontinued proceedings, finding no intent to offend the applicant.

The applicant then sought to intervene as an assistant to the prosecutor and filed a private prosecution. The defendants requested a judicial investigation. On 24 June 2011 the investigating judge dismissed the case against the individual defendants, finding insufficient evidence of defamation or insult. The judge reasoned that the subjective element was absent: the defendants did not intend to attack the applicant’s honour, nor foresee doing so. The judge added that the applicant was a public figure who must be used to comedians capturing his characteristics for humour, and stated that it was public knowledge that his characteristics reflected behaviour attributed to the female gender, such as his manner of expression, colourful feminine clothes, and having always lived in a world of women. The judge noted the applicant had recently made his homosexuality public, but found the defendants never intended to criticise his sexual orientation. Proceedings against the two companies were discontinued under Article 11 of the Criminal Code, which excludes legal persons from liability for defamation and insult.

The applicant appealed to the Lisbon Court of Appeal, arguing specifically that his name had been included because of his sexual orientation. On 17 April 2012 the appeal was dismissed. The Court of Appeal upheld the finding of insufficient evidence of defamation. It said that offensiveness is not simply what the complainant considers offensive, but what the majority of reasonable people would regard as an offence to respect. It characterised the programme as a comedy show and the remark as a typical joke in a playful, irreverent style. Even if in bad taste, it did not reach the legal threshold for protecting honour and consideration. It repeated the reasoning about the applicant’s public profile, feminine characteristics, and lack of intent to criticise sexual orientation.

The applicant lodged his ECtHR application on 23 October 2012. He alleged in particular that the unfavourable outcome of his defamation case before the Portuguese courts amounted to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, relying on Article 14 of the Convention. The application was communicated to the Government on 1 October 2014. Both parties filed observations, and third-party comments were received from Alliance Defending Freedom.

In *Sousa Goucha v. Portugal*, the applicant, Manuel Luís Sousa Goucha, is a well-known Portuguese television presenter who publicly disclosed his homosexuality in 2008. The case arose from a live comedy/talk show, *Five Minutes to Midnight*, broadcast on RTP2 between midnight and 1 a.m. on 28 December 2009. During the show, host F.C. asked a guest, J.M., a quiz question: “Who is the best Portuguese female TV host?” The options included three female presenters and the applicant, a man. J.M. initially selected C.V., but the “correct” answer revealed by F.C. was Manuel Luís Goucha. The exchange was presented in a humorous, joking manner.

The applicant lodged a criminal complaint for defamation and insult (*injúria*) against the State-owned broadcaster RTP, the production company, presenter F.C., and programming directors. He claimed that including his name among possible answers to a question about the best female TV host damaged his reputation and dignity. On 2 March 2011, the Lisbon Criminal Department for Investigation and Prosecution discontinued proceedings, finding no intent to offend. The applicant then sought to intervene as an *assistente* and brought a private prosecution.

On 24 June 2011, the investigating judge refused to indict the individual defendants, finding insufficient evidence of defamation or insult and no subjective intent to attack his honour. The judge reasoned that the applicant was a public figure who should expect comedians to use his characteristics, noting public knowledge that his behaviour, manner of expression, colourful feminine clothes, and history of working in a “world of women” were attributed to the female gender. The judge also observed that the applicant had recently made his homosexuality public and that the defendants never intended to criticise his sexual orientation. Proceedings against the corporate defendants were discontinued because Portuguese law excludes legal persons from liability for defamation and insult.

The applicant appealed, arguing that his name had been included in the quiz because of his sexual orientation. On 17 April 2012, the Lisbon Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It upheld the finding that there was insufficient evidence of defamation, applying a standard of what a majority of reasonable people would consider offensive. The Court of Appeal emphasised the context of a comedy show, describing the question as a joke typical of such programmes. It accepted that the applicant, as a public figure, must be used to comedians capturing his characteristics for humour, and repeated the references to his feminine-attributed behaviour and public homosexuality. It concluded that the expression, though possibly in bad taste, was used in a playful and irreverent context and did not reach the legal threshold for protecting honour.

The applicant applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 23 October 2012. He alleged that the unfavourable outcome of his defamation case before the Portuguese courts amounted to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, relying on Article 14 of the Convention. The key facts relevant to that alleged violation are therefore the television quiz referring to him as a possible “female” host, the domestic courts’ rejection of his defamation and insult claims, and the reasoning that treated the incident as comedy while referring to his homosexuality and gender-stereotyped characteristics.

In *Petschulies v. Germany* (ECtHR, 2 June 2016), the applicant, a German national born in 1952, complained that his preventive detention in a supervised residential facility attached to a psychiatric hospital had been extended beyond the former statutory maximum of ten years, in breach of Article 5 §1 of the Convention, and also raised an Article 7 §1 complaint.

In 1984 the Hildesheim Regional Court convicted the applicant of seven counts of dangerous assault, four counts of assault, coercion and attempted coercion committed between 1982 and 1984. He was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment and ordered into preventive detention under Article 66 §2 of the Criminal Code. The offences were violent: he attacked mostly male victims, including schoolchildren, acquaintances, random people and homeless persons, by punching or kicking them, setting an Alsatian dog on them, and using a knife. Psychiatric and psychological experts found that he had full criminal responsibility for most offences, with diminished responsibility possible only for two offences due to alcohol intoxication. They found no pathological mental disorder, but a personality marked by lack of empathy, dominance and a propensity to serious violent offences.

After serving his prison term, he was placed in preventive detention in 1990. By 2000 he had spent ten years in preventive detention—the former statutory maximum. Following the 1998 abolition of that maximum, the courts continued his detention. In 2005 he was transferred to a psychiatric hospital because his rehabilitation could be better promoted there. From 2011 he lived provisionally in Friedland Castle, a supervised residential facility.

On 19 July 2011 the Göttingen Regional Court again ordered continued preventive detention in a psychiatric hospital under Article 67d §3. It relied on expert S., who diagnosed a dissocial personality disorder with marked psychopathic elements and alcohol abuse under ICD-10, confirmed by treating doctors. The court found a high risk that, if released, the applicant would commit extremely serious violent offences, especially when drunk, and that detention remained proportionate despite exceeding twenty years. His appeal was dismissed, and the Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider his constitutional complaint without reasons.

The legal context was the Federal Constitutional Court’s leading judgment of 4 May 2011. It held that retrospective extension of preventive detention beyond ten years was unconstitutional but allowed a transitional period until 31 May 2013 if the detainee was highly likely to commit the most serious violent or sexual offences and suffered a mental disorder under the Therapy Detention Act, interpreted consistently with Article 5 §1(e) “unsound mind”. That Act covered dissocial personality disorders and did not require diminished criminal responsibility.

The applicant alleged that his detention beyond ten years breached Article 5 §1: he was not of unsound mind, his dissocial personality disorder was not a true mental disorder, he had no alcohol addiction, and there was no legal basis. The Government argued the detention was justified under Article 5 §1(e) as detention of a person of unsound mind.

The Court found that the detention amounted to a deprivation of liberty but no violation of Article 5 §1. Although dissocial personality disorder alone may be doubtful, here it was exacerbated by alcohol abuse and manifested in gratuitously brutal offences against random victims. A prior assault while drunk in detention showed continuing risk. The 2005 psychiatric hospital order indicated a need for therapeutic treatment. The disorder warranted compulsory confinement, and the facility affiliated to a psychiatric hospital was appropriate. Detention was lawful under the transitional provision and not arbitrary. The Article 7 complaint was inadmissible for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies.

Case *Petschulies v. Germany* (no. 6281/13, 2 June 2016) concerned the preventive detention of a German national, Mr Dirk Petschulies, beyond the former ten-year statutory maximum. He alleged that his continued detention in a supervised residential facility affiliated to a psychiatric hospital breached Article 5 § 1 of the Convention and that the retrospective extension of his detention breached Article 7 § 1.

In 1984 the Hildesheim Regional Court convicted the applicant of multiple violent offences—dangerous assault, assault, coercion and attempted coercion—committed between 1982 and 1984. The attacks were unprovoked and brutal: he punched and kicked victims, set a dog on them, and attacked homeless people with a knife. He was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment and preventive detention under Article 66 § 2 of the Criminal Code. Experts found no pathological mental disorder and full criminal responsibility for most offences, although diminished responsibility due to alcohol intoxication could not be excluded for two offences.

After serving his prison sentence, he was placed in preventive detention in 1990. Under the law applicable at the time of conviction, initial preventive detention could not exceed ten years. In 1998 the law was amended to abolish that maximum. In 2000, after ten years, the Lüneburg Regional Court ordered continued detention. In 2001 he was convicted of assaulting his daughter while drunk. In 2005 he was transferred to a psychiatric hospital. From 2011 he resided provisionally in Friedland Castle, a supervised residential facility linked to Moringen Hospital.

In 2011 the Göttingen Regional Court ordered continued preventive detention in a psychiatric hospital under Article 67d § 3, applying the Federal Constitutional Court’s transitional criteria of 4 May 2011. Relying on expert evidence, it found that the applicant suffered from a dissocial personality disorder with marked psychopathic elements and alcohol abuse, creating a high risk of serious violent offences if released. It considered detention proportionate and rehabilitation better promoted in a psychiatric setting. His appeal and constitutional complaint failed.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant argued under Article 5 § 1 that he was not of unsound mind, had no true mental disorder or alcoholism, and that his detention beyond the former ten-year maximum lacked a legal basis. The Government argued that his detention was justified under Article 5 § 1(e) as detention of a person of unsound mind.

The Court held that the supervised placement amounted to deprivation of liberty, so Article 5 § 1 applied. On the merits, applying *Winterwerp v. the Netherlands*, it found that the applicant had been reliably shown to be of unsound mind. His dissocial personality disorder, aggravated by alcohol abuse, was sufficiently serious and manifested in brutal, random attacks. It warranted compulsory confinement because of the high risk of life-threatening violence, and continued detention depended on persistence of the disorder. The facility affiliated to a psychiatric hospital was appropriate, and the detention had a legal basis in transitional German law and was not arbitrary despite lasting over twenty years. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 5 § 1. The Article 7 § 1 complaint was rejected as inadmissible because the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies, not having raised it before the Federal Constitutional Court.

**CASE OF PETSCHULIES v. GERMANY** (Application no. 6281/13, ECtHR 2 June 2016) concerned Dirk Petschulies, a German national born in 1952. He complained that his preventive detention in a supervised residential facility affiliated to a psychiatric hospital, extended retrospectively beyond the former statutory maximum of ten years, violated Article 5 §1 and Article 7 §1 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

His criminal history included multiple convictions. In 1977 he was convicted of offences committed while drunk and ordered into a psychiatric hospital, but that judgment was quashed in 1981; a court found he had no pathological mental disorder, although he had an abnormal personality. In 1984 the Hildesheim Regional Court convicted him of seven counts of dangerous assault, four counts of assault, coercion and two counts of attempted coercion committed between 1982 and 1984. He attacked mostly male victims, including schoolchildren, acquaintances, strangers and homeless people. He punched and kicked victims, set an Alsatian dog on them, and used a knife. He was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment and ordered preventive detention under Article 66 §2 of the Criminal Code. Psychiatric experts found full criminal responsibility for most offences, no pathological mental disorder, but a propensity to serious violence, lack of empathy and a dominating self-image.

After serving his prison sentence, preventive detention began in 1990. By 2000 he had spent ten years in preventive detention, but the Lüneburg Regional Court ordered it to continue. In 2001 he was convicted of assaulting his daughter while drunk. In 2005 the Göttingen Regional Court ordered further preventive detention in a psychiatric hospital under Article 63, rather than a detoxification facility, because his rehabilitation could be better promoted there. In March 2011 he was authorised to reside provisionally in Friedland Castle, a supervised residential facility. He received staff visits, had limited shopping and escorted outings, and attended work therapy but no specific treatment.

In July 2011 the Göttingen Regional Court again ordered continued preventive detention in a psychiatric hospital under Article 67d §3, applying the stricter transitional criteria set out by the Federal Constitutional Court on 4 May 2011. It found he suffered from dissocial personality disorder with marked psychopathic elements (ICD-10), exacerbated by alcohol abuse, and posed a high risk of committing life-threatening violent offences if released. The expert’s report was based on case files because the applicant refused examination. The Braunschweig Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal. CASE OF GUK v. UKRAINE concerns Ukrainian national Viktor Guk. In 2001, he was convicted of murder, attempted murder, and illegal possession of firearms and sentenced to life imprisonment; the conviction was upheld in 2002. In 2009, the Supreme Court reduced his sentence to fifteen years. He was held in Cherkasy SIZO, Kyiv SIZO, Sokalska Prison from October 2004 to November 2007, and later Zamkova Prison. In May 2012 he suffered an ischemic stroke and was released in October 2012.

His main ECtHR complaints arose under Articles 3, 8, 13, and 34. Under Article 3, he alleged that on 15 October 2004, upon arrival at Sokalska Prison, guards beat him, causing an eye injury, bruises, and scratches. He said he complained to the prison governor and medical officer, but his injuries were not recorded and he received no treatment; he was later diagnosed with traumatic left-eye mydriasis. He alleged that prison authorities blocked his complaints, and that in August 2006 a prosecutor refused to open a criminal investigation, finding no evidence; the courts upheld that refusal. He also alleged inadequate medical assistance for hypertension and heart problems, and humiliating detention conditions: 12 sq m cells shared with three inmates, less than 3 sq m each, 23-hour confinement, damp and unventilated cells, insufficient heating, sometimes sharing with TB inmates, poor food and water, handcuffing, guard dogs, a felt-lined bag over his head, hands raised while handcuffed, no work, and blocked letters to prosecutors. The Court found the beating, inadequate medical care, and other abuse allegations unsupported or manifestly ill-founded. However, it declared admissible his complaint about material conditions in Sokalska Prison, finding severe overcrowding and no reason to depart from case law indicating a violation of Article 3.

Under Article 8, he alleged restrictions on family visits and telephone calls: visits generally once every six months for up to four hours, limited numbers of visitors, travel difficulties because his family lived about 700 km away, shortened visits, visits through glass and cages with a guard and dog, monitored telephone conversations, no intimate contact with his wife, no telephone calls until November 2005, and thereafter only once every three months. The Government disputed many details and said some complaints had not been raised domestically. Under Article 13, he alleged no effective domestic remedy for his Article 3 complaints. Under Article 34, he alleged interference with his right of individual application: a Court letter was allegedly opened and read by Zamkova Prison administration in January 2012; he was placed in solitary confinement from 28 January to 15 May 2012, had documents and his pen taken, had no family contact for two months, and was disciplined after receiving Court letters. The Government denied opening letters or persecuting him, saying discipline was for prison breaches. Earlier, he also complained that authorities obstructed access to his criminal case file and refused copies needed to substantiate a previous Court application, and that courts refused to consider his complaints.

In summary, the key factual focus is the applicant’s alleged ill-treatment and poor detention conditions in Sokalska Prison, restricted family contact, lack of effective remedies, and alleged retaliation or interference with his ECtHR correspondence, alongside prior difficulties accessing case-file documents for an earlier application.

In *Guk v. Ukraine* (ECtHR, Fifth Section, App. No. 16995/05, Judgment of 8 December 2016), the applicant was a Ukrainian national convicted in August 2001 of murder, attempted murder and illegal possession of firearms and sentenced to life imprisonment; the Supreme Court upheld the conviction in 2002. In 2009 his sentence was reduced to fifteen years because life imprisonment had not been lawfully imposed. He was held in Cherkasy SIZO No. 30 until September 2004, then Kyiv SIZO No. 13, then Sokalska Prison from October 2004 to November 2007, and later Zamkova Prison. He was released in October 2012 after suffering a stroke.

The alleged violations concerned treatment and detention conditions. Under Article 3, he claimed that on 15 October 2004, upon arrival at Sokalska Prison, several guards beat him, causing an eye injury, bruises and scratches. He alleged that he complained to prison officers but received no medical assistance, and that prison authorities refused or delayed sending his complaints to prosecutors. In June 2006 he handed a complaint to a visiting prosecutor, but in August 2006 the prosecutor refused to open a criminal investigation, finding no evidence of beating. Domestic courts upheld that decision, relying on prison staff and prisoner statements; the applicant alleged he was not heard in person and witnesses were not questioned.

He also complained under Article 3 of inadequate medical assistance for hypertension and heart problems, and of degrading conditions in Sokalska Prison. He stated he was held in a 12-square-metre cell with three other inmates, with sanitary facilities and furniture, confined for 23 hours a day, in damp, unventilated and poorly heated cells. For several weeks he was allegedly held with inmates suffering from open tuberculosis. He described being handcuffed whenever outside his cell, sometimes with hands raised behind his back, a felt-lined bag over his head, and escorted by officers with a guard dog. He also alleged poor food and water, lack of work, and inability to buy medicine. The Government disputed these claims and said he had not exhausted domestic remedies or raised material conditions domestically.

Under Article 8, he complained of restrictions on family visits and telephone calls. He had a wife, two minor children, mother and other relatives. As a life prisoner, visits were limited to once every six months, up to four hours; Sokalska Prison was about 700 km from his family. Visits allegedly took place in a cage behind a glass partition, by telephone, monitored by guards, with no intimate contact. He claimed he could not make telephone calls until November 2005, after which calls were limited. The Government disputed several details and said he had not raised them domestically. He also complained under Article 13 of no effective domestic remedy for Article 3 complaints, and under Article 34 that authorities interfered with his right of application, including by opening Court letters, placing him in solitary confinement in 2012, taking his documents and pen, and restricting family contact. The Government denied interference.

The Court rejected as manifestly ill-founded the alleged 15 October 2004 beating, inadequate medical assistance, and other unsupported abuses. It admitted the Article 3 complaint about material conditions in Sokalska Prison, finding the Government’s non-exhaustion objection unfounded and the complaint timely. On the merits, it reiterated that serious overcrowding may violate Article 3, noted the applicant had less than 3 sq m of personal space for over three years while confined most of the day, and indicated no reason to depart from its case-law finding a violation.

**Case: Guk v. Ukraine (Application no. 16995/05)**

The applicant, Viktor Mykhaylovych Guk, a Ukrainian national born in 1966, was convicted in 2001 of murder, attempted murder, and illegal possession of firearms and sentenced to life imprisonment; the Supreme Court upheld the conviction in 2002. In 2009 his sentence was reduced to fifteen years because life imprisonment had been imposed unlawfully. He was detained in several facilities: Cherkasy SIZO No. 30, Kyiv SIZO No. 13, Sokalska Correctional Colony No. 47 from October 2004 to November 2007, and later Zamkova Correctional Colony No. 58. He was released in October 2012 after suffering an ischemic stroke.

The applicant’s complaints before the European Court of Human Rights concerned several alleged violations. Initially, he complained that the authorities obstructed his access to his criminal case file and refused to provide copies of documents needed to substantiate a previous application to the Court, and that he lacked access to a court in that regard. Subsequently, his main complaints were under Article 3 (ill-treatment by prison guards, conditions of detention, and inadequate medical assistance), Article 8 (restrictions on family visits and telephone calls), Article 13 (lack of an effective domestic remedy for his Article 3 complaints), and Article 34 (hindrance of his right of application).

The key Article 3 facts were as follows. The applicant alleged that on 15 October 2004, upon arrival at Sokalska Prison, he was beaten by several guards, suffering an eye injury, bruises, and scratches. He claimed he received no medical assistance and that his complaints to the authorities were blocked. In June 2006 he handed a complaint to a supervising prosecutor, but in August 2006 the prosecutor refused to open a criminal investigation, finding no evidence of beating. His challenges before the courts were unsuccessful, and the Supreme Court later refused to consider his cassation appeal because he had not supplied certified copies of lower court decisions.

Regarding conditions of detention in Sokalska Prison, the applicant alleged that he was held for over three years in a twelve-square-metre cell with three other inmates. Because the cell contained sanitary facilities, bunks, a table, and benches, each prisoner had less than three square metres of living space and was confined for most of the day. He described the cells as damp, unventilated, and insufficiently heated, and claimed he was sometimes held with inmates suffering from open tuberculosis. He also alleged that whenever he left the cell he was handcuffed, escorted by officers with a guard dog, and sometimes had a felt-lined bag placed over his head; that he was forced to walk with handcuffed arms raised above his head; and that food and water were inadequate. He further alleged that prison authorities refused or delayed sending about twenty complaints to prosecutors.

As to medical assistance, the applicant claimed he suffered from hypertension and had four heart attacks in 2005, but received inadequate treatment and was not allowed to keep needed medication. A prosecutor found the medical assistance adequate, relying on his medical file. The applicant’s attempts to challenge this in court were initially refused on jurisdiction grounds; the case was later remitted but then returned because he failed to submit a formal claim.

Under Article 8, the applicant alleged severe restrictions on family contact. As a life prisoner, he was generally allowed visits only once every six months for up to four hours, with limits on the number of visitors. His family lived about 700 km away. Visits allegedly took place in a cage behind a glass partition, with a guard and dog present, and conversations were monitored by telephone. He claimed no telephone calls were allowed until November 2005, after which calls were limited to once every three months. He was also refused intimate contact with his wife.

Finally, the applicant alleged that in 2012, while in Zamkova Prison, a Court letter was opened by the administration and he was persecuted for communicating with the Court, including being placed in solitary confinement from 28 January to 15 May 2012, having documents and a pen taken, and being denied family contact. The Government denied these allegations.

The Court declared the beating, inadequate medical assistance, and several other Article 3 complaints inadmissible as unsubstantiated. However, it admitted the complaint about material conditions in Sokalska Prison and found a violation of Article 3 due to severe overcrowding and related hardships.

Cano Moya v. Spain (Application no. 3142/11) concerned a Spanish prisoner, Vicente Manuel Cano Moya, who complained that prison disciplinary sanctions violated his right to be presumed innocent and his freedom of expression, and that domestic authorities obstructed his right of individual petition to the European Court of Human Rights.

At the time, the applicant was on remand in Foncalent Prison, Alicante. On 20 October 2009, the Alicante Prison disciplinary board found him guilty of three disciplinary offences under the General Prison Rules: threatening prison officers (very serious, Rule 108(b)); disobeying officers’ orders (serious, Rule 109(b)); and damaging prison property (serious, Rule 109(e)). The punishments were four weekends in isolation for the threats, twenty days without group recreational activities for disobedience, and twenty days without group recreational activities for property damage.

The applicant appealed to the post-sentencing judge No. 2 of the Comunidad Valenciana. On 17 November 2009, that judge partly allowed the appeal and revoked the sanction imposed for disobedience. Because the applicant had been transferred to Villena Prison, attempts to serve him personally failed; he was eventually served on 28 January 2010 and signed an acknowledgment. A further reforma appeal was rejected by the same judge on 18 February 2010, and that decision was also served on him.

The applicant then lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court, invoking Articles 20 (freedom of expression) and 24 (presumption of innocence) of the Spanish Constitution. On 22 March 2010, the Constitutional Court requested his case file; the post-sentencing judge sent it on 12 April 2010. On 30 September 2010, the Constitutional Court declared the amparo appeal inadmissible as devoid of special constitutional significance. The decision was served on 7 October 2010.

On 22 December 2010, the applicant requested a copy of his case file from the post-sentencing judge in order to submit it to the European Court of Human Rights, relying on sections 234 and 454 of the Judicature Act. On 4 January 2011, he notified the Court of his intention to apply; the Registry invited him to submit an application form by 11 March 2011. On 26 January 2011, the judge refused his request, saying the case was still pending before the Constitutional Court.

The applicant sent his application form on 2 February 2011, raising complaints under Article 6 § 2 and Article 10 § 1 of the Convention. He enclosed the Constitutional Court’s decision but not the lower post-sentencing decisions, although he referred to them. **Summary of *Kiril Zlatkov Nikolov v. France* (Applications nos. 70474/11 and 68038/12)**

**Key Facts Relevant to Alleged Violations:**

The applicant, Mr. Kiril Zlatkov Nikolov, a Bulgarian national born in 1971, was the subject of two applications against France lodged with the European Court of Human Rights. The case originated from an investigation into an international prostitution ring. In August and September 2009, French authorities intercepted telephone conversations pursuant to judicial orders. Two specific conversations recorded on 4 September 2009 implicated the applicant, referred to as "Kiril," in the prostitution ring.

On 28 July 2010, a French investigating judge issued an arrest warrant for the applicant for offences including living on the earnings of prostitution with aggravating circumstances committed as part of an organised gang, human trafficking, and criminal conspiracy. After his arrest in Germany, the applicant was handed over to French authorities on 16 December 2010. On 20 December 2010, he was formally placed under investigation by an investigating judge in Lyons and subsequently remanded in custody by the liberties and detention judge.

A critical fact underlying the alleged violation concerns the recording of the applicant's interviews during the judicial investigation. Under the seventh paragraph of Article 116-1 of the French Code of Criminal Procedure, as applicable at the time, video recording of interviews with persons under formal investigation was mandatory for serious offences, except where the investigation concerned organised crime, offences undermining fundamental national interests, or terrorism. Because the applicant was charged with organised crime offences under Article 706-73, his interviews by the investigating judge were not video recorded, although this safeguard was automatically applied to persons charged with other serious offences.

The applicant applied to have various procedural steps declared void, including the order for his detention and the interviews conducted without recording. He submitted requests for preliminary rulings on constitutionality regarding the relevant provisions. On 6 April 2012, the Constitutional Council declared the seventh paragraphs of Articles 64-1 and 116-1 unconstitutional, holding that the exception to compulsory video recording infringed the principle of equality. However, this abrogation applied only prospectively to persons questioned from the date of the decision. The Court of Cassation subsequently dismissed the applicant's appeal on 10 May 2012, finding no infringement of his Convention rights.

The applicant was convicted on 28 October 2011 by the Lyons Criminal Court and sentenced to four years' imprisonment. On appeal, the Lyons Court of Appeal increased his sentence to six years on 20 July 2012. His further appeal was rejected on 12 June 2013.

**Alleged Violation:**

The applicant complained under Article 14 of the Convention taken in conjunction with Article 6 § 1, alleging discrimination. He argued that, having been prosecuted for a serious organised crime offence, he was denied the safeguard of video-recorded interviews afforded to persons charged with other serious offences. The Court declared this complaint inadmissible, finding that the lack of recording had no significant impact on his rights and that the matter had been resolved at the domestic level through the Constitutional Council's decision.

The applicant, Kiril Zlatkov Nikolov, a Bulgarian national born in 1971, was prosecuted in France in connection with an international prostitution ring. In 2009, French authorities intercepted telephone conversations under Article 706-95 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Two calls recorded on 4 September 2009, involving a phone belonging to a certain I.K., incriminated the applicant: one between a woman identified as R.G. and a man called “Kiril,” later identified as the applicant, and another in which Kiril was referred to as involved in the prostitution network. A judicial investigation opened on 2 October 2009 for living on the earnings of prostitution as part of an organised gang, human trafficking as part of an organised gang, and criminal conspiracy.

On 28 July 2010, an investigating judge in Lyons issued an arrest warrant, later converted into a European arrest warrant. The applicant was arrested in Germany and handed over to French authorities on 16 December 2010 at 11:45 a.m. He was brought before the Strasbourg public prosecutor and placed in administrative detention. He first appeared before the investigating judge on 20 December 2010 at 10:56 a.m., was placed under formal investigation, and later that day was remanded in custody by the Lyons liberties and detention judge. Because the alleged offences fell under Article 706-73 (organised crime), his interviews and confrontations were not video-recorded, pursuant to the seventh paragraph of Article 116-1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

The applicant challenged the procedure. On 17 June 2011, he applied to have various steps declared void, including the detention order, interviews, confrontations, and telephone interceptions. He also submitted priority preliminary rulings on constitutionality (QPCs), arguing that the absence of mandatory video recording for organised-crime cases breached equality. On 6 September 2011, the Investigation Division dismissed most claims but referred the QPCs to the Court of Cassation. On 6 April 2012, the Constitutional Council declared the relevant seventh paragraphs unconstitutional because they infringed equality, but the abrogation applied only prospectively. On 10 May 2012, the Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal, finding no Convention violation: he had been assisted by counsel, could review transcripts, and the lack of recording did not breach his fair-trial rights.

The applicant was convicted on 28 October 2011 by the Lyons Criminal Court, though the human-trafficking charge was dismissed. He received four years’ imprisonment and a €10,000 fine. In July 2012, the Lyons Court of Appeal upheld guilt and imposed six years’ imprisonment with a minimum two-thirds term, a fine, and a five-year exclusion order from certain departments. His appeal on points of law was rejected in June 2013, and he was released in June 2015.

The Court found the Article 14/6 complaint inadmissible: the lack of video recording had no significant impact on his rights or personal situation, and the matter had been resolved domestically by the Constitutional Council’s decision

**Case Summary: Kiril Zlatkov Nikolov v. France**

The case concerned two applications brought by Kiril Zlatkov Nikolov, a Bulgarian national, against France. The applicant was implicated in a French investigation into an international prostitution ring. In 2009, authorities intercepted telephone conversations, including two recorded on 4 September 2009 on a mobile telephone belonging to a certain I.K. These conversations appeared to incriminate the applicant, referred to as “Kiril,” in the prostitution ring.

A judicial investigation was opened in October 2009 for living on the earnings of prostitution with aggravating circumstances, human trafficking as part of an organised gang, and criminal conspiracy. An arrest warrant was issued in July 2010 and converted into a European arrest warrant. The applicant was arrested in Germany and handed over to French authorities on 16 December 2010 at 11:45 a.m. He was brought before the Strasbourg public prosecutor and placed in administrative detention. He first appeared before the investigating judge on 20 December 2010 at 10:56 a.m., when he was placed under formal investigation. At about 5 p.m. that same day, the Lyons liberties and detention judge remanded him in custody.

The key alleged violations before the European Court of Human Rights concerned Article 5 § 3, Article 14 read with Article 6 § 1, and Article 13 of the Convention. Under Article 5 § 3, the issue was whether the applicant was brought promptly before a judge after his transfer to France, given the period between 16 and 20 December 2010. Under Article 13, he complained of the lack of an effective remedy for his complaints.

Most centrally, under Article 14 in conjunction with Article 6 § 1, the applicant alleged discrimination in the enjoyment of his fair-trial rights. Because he was charged with offences linked to organised crime under Article 706-73 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, his interviews and confrontations before the investigating judge were not video recorded, pursuant to the former seventh paragraph of Article 116-1. That exception meant that the automatic video-recording safeguard applicable to many other serious offences did not apply to him. He argued that this difference in treatment, based on the nature of the offence, discriminated against him in the exercise of his right to a fair trial, especially given the seriousness of the penalties.

The applicant sought annulment of various procedural steps, including his detention order, interviews, confrontations, and telephone interceptions. He also raised preliminary rulings on constitutionality regarding the absence of video recording. On 6 April 2012, the Constitutional Council declared the seventh paragraphs of Articles 64-1 and 116-1 unconstitutional, finding that the exception to compulsory video recording for organised-crime cases infringed the principle of equality. However, the abrogation applied only prospectively. On 10 May 2012, the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s appeal, holding that the lack of video recording did not violate his Convention rights because he had legal assistance, could review the transcripts, request corrections, and challenge his statements.

Criminal proceedings continued: in October 2011 the Lyons Criminal Court convicted him and sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment and a fine; in July 2012 the Court of Appeal increased the sentence to six years, with a minimum two-thirds term, a fine, and an exclusion order. The Court of Cassation rejected his final appeal in June 2013. He was released in June 2015 after serving his sentence.

Before the ECtHR, the Article 14/Article 6 § 1 complaint was declared inadmissible. The Court found no significant disadvantage because the lack of recording had no significant impact on his rights or personal situation. It also noted that the relevant provision had been abrogated and the complaint had been considered domestically, so no merits examination was required. The remaining communicated complaints under Article 5 § 3 and Article 13 formed the other focus of the case.
001-161738:
In *Seton v. the United Kingdom* (Application no. 55287/10, 31 March 2016), the European Court of Human Rights considered whether the admission of hearsay evidence at a murder trial violated Article 6 § 1 and Article 6 § 3(d) of the Convention, particularly the applicant’s right to examine witnesses against him.

The applicant, John Seton, was convicted by a jury at the Central Criminal Court of murdering Jon Bartlett, who was shot dead on 31 March 2006. Witnesses described the gunman as wearing a baseball cap and driving a silver Vauxhall Vectra, which was later found burned. Seton fled to the Netherlands and was extradited. At trial, the central issue was whether Seton or a man named Pearman was the killer. Seton claimed that Pearman, a serving prisoner with convictions for drugs, firearms, and murder, had been involved in a drug deal with Bartlett and had driven the Vectra. The prosecution investigated this defence but found no link between Pearman and Bartlett or Seton. Pearman, a category A prisoner, refused to make a statement or give evidence. When questioned by police, he answered “no comment”; in recorded prison telephone calls to his son and wife, he denied any involvement and said he had never heard of Seton.

The prosecution sought to adduce the recordings of those calls under section 114(1)(d) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003, which permits hearsay in the interests of justice. The defence objected, arguing that admitting the calls without calling Pearman would breach Seton’s right to cross-examine. The trial judge admitted the evidence after considering the statutory factors: the calls had strong probative value because Pearman appeared genuinely outraged at being implicated; Pearman was unwilling to testify and compelling him would likely be futile; the evidence was important and reliable because recorded; and any prejudice could be addressed by directions. The judge told the jury that the calls were self-serving, that Pearman knew prison calls were recorded, and that the jury had not seen or heard him under cross-examination. The jury asked to rehear the recordings during deliberations and convicted Seton by a majority.

Seton appealed, arguing that the judge should have tried to compel Pearman to attend. The Court of Appeal granted leave but dismissed the appeal. It held that the judge’s finding that Pearman would not give evidence was not challenged; calling him would have been fruitless, especially given his privilege against self-incrimination. The judge had properly applied section 114(2), and the admission was not unreasonable.

Before the European Court, Seton complained that the hearsay evidence deprived him of a fair trial under Article 6 § 1 and § 3(d). Applying the principles in *Al-Khawaja and Tahery*, the Court examined whether there was a good reason for the witness’s absence, whether the evidence was sole or decisive, and whether counterbalancing measures existed. It found a good reason: Pearman refused to testify. The recordings were important but not sole or decisive; other evidence implicated Seton, including eyewitness descriptions, the hired white van, mobile phone cell-site evidence, a £24,000 drug debt to the victim, CCTV, and evidence that Pearman did not match the gunman’s description. The trial judge gave careful warnings about the limitations of the hearsay, the defence could attack its reliability, and the jury could assess its weight. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 6 § 1 or § 3(d).

In *Seton v. the United Kingdom* (no. 55287/10, 31 March 2016), the applicant, John Seton, was convicted by a jury at the Central Criminal Court of murdering Jon Bartlett, who was shot dead on 31 March 2006. Witnesses described a gunman in a baseball cap driving a silver Vauxhall Vectra, which was later found burned. Seton fled to the Netherlands and was extradited. At trial, the central disputed issue was whether Seton or Mr Pearman, a man then serving life for murder and with serious drug and firearms convictions, was the killer. Seton’s defence alleged that Pearman had murdered Bartlett during a drug transaction.

Pearman refused to make a statement or give evidence. The prosecution therefore sought to adduce recordings of Pearman’s prison telephone calls to his son and wife, in which he denied any involvement in the murder, relying on section 114(1)(d) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003, which permits hearsay in the interests of justice. The defence objected, arguing the calls were self-serving and made by a man who knew prison calls were recorded. The trial judge admitted the recordings after considering the section 114(2) factors. He found they had strong probative value, were important and reliable, that Pearman would not testify, and that prejudice could be addressed by directions. He told the jury that Pearman had not been seen or cross-examined, that the statements were self-serving, and that Pearman knew they were recorded. During deliberations, the jury asked to hear the tapes again; they were replayed. Seton was convicted by a majority and sentenced to life imprisonment with a minimum term of thirty years.

Other evidence included Seton’s involvement with Bartlett in large-scale drug dealing; a debt list showing Seton owed Bartlett £24,000; phone contact on the day of the murder; evidence about the purchase of the Vectra and a hired white van with distinctive orange writing seen near the shooting; cell-site evidence placing Seton nearby; eyewitness descriptions of a baseball-capped gunman; CCTV from a petrol station; and police evidence finding no connection between Pearman and Bartlett or Seton and that Pearman did not match witness descriptions. Pearman’s bad character and previous convictions were also before the jury.

Seton appealed, arguing that the hearsay recordings should not have been admitted without calling Pearman. The Court of Appeal granted leave but dismissed the appeal. It held that the trial judge had correctly applied section 114(2), that compelling Pearman to attend would have been fruitless because he would not give sensible evidence, and that the decision to admit the tapes was not legally erroneous or irrational.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Seton complained under Article 6 § 1 and Article 6 § 3(d) that the admission of Pearman’s untested hearsay statements denied him a fair trial and the right to examine witnesses. The key fairness issue was whether the counterbalancing safeguards—the judge’s careful directions, the defence’s ability to attack the reliability and motive of the statements, the bad-character evidence, and the other prosecution evidence—sufficiently offset the inability to cross-examine Pearman. The ECtHR ultimately found no violation of Article 6.

**Seton v. the United Kingdom** concerned the fairness of a murder trial in which the prosecution relied on hearsay evidence from an absent witness. The applicant, John Edward Seton, was convicted of murdering Jon Bartlett, who was shot dead on 31 March 2006. Witnesses described the gunman as wearing a baseball cap and driving away in a silver Vauxhall Vectra; the car was later found burned. Seton fled to the Netherlands and was extradited to the United Kingdom.

At trial, the central issue was whether Seton or Mr Pearman was the murderer. In his defence statement, Seton alleged that Pearman—a Category A prisoner with previous convictions for drug offences, firearms offences and murder—had killed Bartlett. Seton claimed he had been involved in a drug deal with Pearman and Bartlett; he said he bought the Vectra for Pearman, who drove it, and met Pearman shortly before the killing.

To rebut this defence, the prosecution sought to introduce recordings of Pearman’s prison telephone calls to his son and wife. In those calls, Pearman denied any involvement in Bartlett’s murder and said he did not know Seton. Pearman refused to make a statement to police or give evidence at trial. The prosecution applied to admit the recordings as hearsay under section 114(1)(d) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003. The trial judge admitted them, having considered the statutory factors in section 114(2). He found the recordings had strong probative value, were important and reliable, and that Pearman would not testify. He also noted that the defence could argue the statements were self-serving because Pearman, as a category A prisoner, knew his calls were recorded. The judge gave the jury careful directions about the limitations of the hearsay evidence, including that Pearman had not been seen, heard or cross-examined.

The prosecution also relied on substantial other evidence: Seton owed Bartlett £24,000; there was phone contact between them on the day of the murder; Seton had arranged to buy the Vectra; a white van linked to the co-accused was seen near the scene; cell-site evidence placed Seton near the murder and later near the burned car; CCTV showed him at a petrol station; and eyewitness descriptions matched Seton. Police found no connection between Pearman and either Bartlett or Seton, and Pearman did not match the eyewitness description of the gunman. Seton was convicted by a majority and sentenced to life imprisonment with a minimum term of thirty years.

On appeal, Seton argued that admitting the recordings without calling Pearman breached his fair-trial rights. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that the trial judge had properly applied the statutory test and that compelling Pearman to attend would have been fruitless.

Seton then applied to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention—essentially, that he could not cross-examine Pearman and that the hearsay evidence made his trial unfair. The Court examined whether the recordings were the sole or decisive evidence and whether sufficient counterbalancing factors existed. It found no violation: the recordings were not the sole or decisive evidence, the judge had given appropriate directions, the defence could challenge Pearman’s credibility and motives, and Pearman’s absence was due to his own refusal to testify. The trial as a whole was therefore fair.
