In *Gyuleva v. Bulgaria* (Application no. 38840/08, ECtHR, 9 June 2016), the applicant, Valentina Gyuleva, alleged violations of Article 6 § 1, Article 13, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Her central complaint was that she was never personally notified of civil unjust enrichment proceedings brought against her, could not defend herself, and later could not obtain reopening of the case, forcing her to pay a substantial sum.

The background concerned a flat occupied by the applicant and her family. After restitution proceedings between 1992 and 2000, the pre-nationalisation owners were recognised as owners and sold the flat to Mr and Mrs P in February 2002. Mr and Mrs P brought *rei vindicatio* proceedings; the applicant vacated the flat on 10 January 2003 and registered her address in the village of Hrabrino on 4 February 2003.

On 4 May 2005, Mr and Mrs P brought a further action against the applicant for unjust enrichment, seeking compensation for her occupation of the flat between 1 February 2002 and 10 January 2003. On 16 May 2005, the Plovdiv District Court issued a summons and sent it to the mayor of Hrabrino for service. On 16 June 2005, the mayor returned it, stating that “no such person has been registered” in the village. On 8 July 2005, following a request by the claimants, the police certified that the applicant’s last declared address was in Hrabrino. Without further attempts to locate her, the District Court concluded on 26 August 2005 that her address was unknown and published a notification in the State Gazette under Article 50 § 1 of the 1952 Code of Civil Procedure.

The court then appointed an *ex officio* lawyer to represent the applicant. The applicant alleged that this lawyer was ineffective: she did not contact her, did not appeal, made no evidentiary requests, and did not contest the claim, including a possible limitation objection. On 6 April 2006, the District Court ordered the applicant to pay BGN 3,573 plus interest. On appeal by the claimants, the Plovdiv Regional Court on 10 July 2006 increased the award by BGN 1,006.21; that judgment became final. The applicant only learned of the proceedings on 22 February 2008, when a bailiff notified her. She ultimately paid BGN 8,767.07 (approximately EUR 4,473).

Several facts were relevant to the diligence issue. The applicant was a juror at the Plovdiv District Court from 2005 to 2009 and received court notifications at her brother’s address in Plovdiv. In 2007 and 2008 she received other summonses there, and in February 2008 the bailiff’s notice was sent there. She was also a well-known piano teacher at the Plovdiv music academy, so her workplace could have been known.

Bulgarian law allowed reopening where a party had been deprived of participation or an *ex officio* lawyer had been appointed despite a known address, but requests had to be made within three months of learning of the judgment and no later than one year after it became final. When the applicant learned of the judgment in February 2008, more than one year had passed since July 2006. A May 2008 amendment removed the one-year limit, but by then the three-month period had also expired. The Government also argued non-exhaustion, suggesting a tort action against the mayor, but the Court rejected this because the District Court, not the mayor, was responsible for summoning and service, and courts were not liable for defective service.

The ECtHR found that the authorities had not acted with sufficient diligence: they did not try the applicant’s workplace or known brother’s address, did not resolve the contradiction about her registered address, and used publication in the State Gazette prematurely. The *ex officio* representation was ineffective, and the applicant had not waived her rights because she was unaware of the proceedings. No effective avenue existed for a fresh adversarial hearing. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1 and also of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

**Case: Gyuleva v. Bulgaria (Application no. 38840/08), judgment of 9 June 2016**

The applicant, Valentina Atanasova Gyuleva, a Bulgarian national born in 1947 and living in Plovdiv, complained under Article 6 § 1 ECHR that she was never notified of civil proceedings brought against her and could not defend herself. She also complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that she was forced to pay a substantial sum as a result of those proceedings.

The case arose from a long-running property dispute. Between 1992 and 2000, restitution proceedings concerning a flat she occupied ended with the pre-nationalisation owners being recognised as the true owners. That earlier litigation had already led to a finding by the European Court of Human Rights of violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 6 § 1 due to length. In February 2002, those owners sold the flat to Mr and Mrs P. Mr and Mrs P. then brought *rei vindicatio* proceedings against the applicant; the first-instance claim was allowed in October 2002. The applicant vacated the flat on 10 January 2003 and moved to Hrabrino, registering her address there on 4 February 2003.

On 4 May 2005, Mr and Mrs P. brought a further action against the applicant for unjust enrichment, seeking compensation for her occupation of the flat between 1 February 2002 and 10 January 2003. On 16 May 2005, the Plovdiv District Court issued a summons and sent it to the mayor of Hrabrino for service. On 16 June 2005, the mayor returned the summons, stating that no such person was registered in the village. On 8 July 2005, the police issued a certificate confirming that the applicant’s last declared address was in Hrabrino.

Despite this information, the District Court made no further attempts to locate the applicant. On 26 August 2005, it concluded that her address was unknown and published a notification of the proceedings in the State Gazette under Article 50 § 1 of the 1952 Code of Civil Procedure. An ex officio lawyer was appointed to represent her. The applicant alleged that this lawyer never contacted her, failed to appeal, made no evidentiary requests, and did not contest the claim meaningfully, including by raising a possible time-bar objection.

On 6 April 2006, the Plovdiv District Court allowed the unjust enrichment claim and ordered the applicant to pay BGN 3,573 plus interest. On appeal, the Plovdiv Regional Court, in a final judgment of 10 July 2006, ordered an additional BGN 1,006.21. The applicant only learned of these proceedings on 22 February 2008, when a bailiff notified her to pay. She ultimately paid BGN 8,767.07, approximately EUR 4,473.

Several facts were relevant to the alleged violations. In 2004, the applicant had been appointed as a juror at the Plovdiv District Court for 2005–2009. She received court notifications at her brother’s address in Plovdiv, where she also received other summonses from Mr and Mrs P. in 2007 and 2008, as well as the 2008 bailiff notice. She was a well-known piano teacher at the Academy of Music, Dance and Fine Arts in Plovdiv. Thus, the authorities could have attempted service at her workplace or at her brother’s address. Domestic law permitted service at a place of work, and publication in the State Gazette was meant to be a last resort after checking the address.

The Government argued that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies by not suing the mayor under the State liability act. The Court rejected that objection, finding the District Court responsible for summoning and that the mayor did not bear direct liability. On the merits, the Court found no waiver because the applicant was unaware of the proceedings. Although domestic law allowed re-opening where a party had been deprived of participation, time limits barred her: she learned of the final judgment more than a year after it became final, and the three-month period from awareness had also expired. No effective fresh adversarial hearing was available. The Court therefore found violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

Gyuleva v. Bulgaria (no. 38840/08) concerned Valentina Gyuleva’s complaint that she was never notified of civil proceedings against her and could not defend herself, violating Article 6 §1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1; she also invoked Article 13.

Between 1992 and 2000, restitution proceedings determined that pre-nationalisation owners owned the flat the applicant occupied. The ECtHR later found violations of Article 1 Protocol No. 1 and Article 6 §1 due to length. In February 2002 those owners sold the flat to Mr and Mrs P., who brought rei vindicatio proceedings. The claim succeeded at first instance in October 2002. The applicant vacated in January 2003, moved to Hrabrino, and registered her address there in February 2003.

In May 2005 Mr and Mrs P. brought an unjust enrichment claim for her occupation between February 2002 and January 2003. On 16 May 2005 the Plovdiv District Court sent a summons through the Hrabrino mayor. On 16 June 2005 the mayor returned it, saying no such person was registered. A police certificate of 8 July 2005 confirmed her last declared address was Hrabrino. Without further attempts, on 26 August 2005 the court treated her address as unknown and published notice in the State Gazette. An ex officio lawyer was appointed and served with all later documents. The applicant alleged that lawyer did not contact her, appeal, request evidence, or raise a time-bar objection.

In April 2006 the District Court ordered her to pay BGN 3,573 plus interest. On appeal, in July 2006 the Regional Court added BGN 1,006.21, final. She learned of the proceedings on 22 February 2008 through a bailiff and paid BGN 8,767.07 (about EUR 4,473).

Key facts for the violation were that the authorities could have served her at her brother’s Plovdiv address, used since 2004 for court notices, or at her workplace; she was a well-known piano teacher at the Plovdiv Academy. Domestic law allowed service at work and required diligence before State Gazette publication. The Court found the District Court failed to act diligently: it did not try those addresses or resolve the contradiction between the mayor’s statement and police information. The ex officio representation was ineffective and the Government did not contest that. The applicant did not waive her rights because she was unaware of the proceedings.

The Government argued non-exhaustion, saying she should have sued the mayor under the State and Municipalities Responsibility for Damage Act. The Court rejected this because the District Court was responsible for summoning, the mayor was involved only in one stage, and the remedy was not shown to be effective.

As to reopening, domestic law allowed it where a party was deprived of participation or an ex officio lawyer was improperly appointed. But the applicant could not use it: she learned of the final judgment more than one year after it became final. Reopening had to be sought within three months of awareness but no later than one year after finality. A May 2008 amendment removed the one-year limit, but her three-month period had expired. Divergent Supreme Court case-law did not provide a clear avenue. The Court therefore found no effective means for a fresh adversarial hearing and concluded that Article 6 §1 had been violated. It also examined her Article 1 Protocol No. 1 complaint about the resulting payment.
001-162864:
**Case Summary: Fürst-Pfeifer v. Austria (Applications nos. 33677/10 and 52340/10)**

**Key Facts Relevant to the Alleged Violation**

The applicant, Ms. Gabriele Fürst-Pfeifer, is an Austrian psychiatrist and a court-certified psychological expert. Since 2000, she has been regularly appointed by courts to provide expert opinions in highly sensitive cases, particularly those involving child custody, contact rights, and child abuse.

The alleged violation stems from an article published on 23 December 2008 by two different media companies, appearing both online (meinbezirk.at) and in a free regional print weekly (Bezirksblatt). The article, headlined "The quality of experts in the spotlight" and sub-headed "Disclosed: Court Expert for custody proceedings a case for therapy," revealed highly personal and sensitive medical information about the applicant.

The article disclosed that a psychological expert report from 1993, commissioned during civil proceedings, had found the applicant suffered from mood swings, panic attacks, suicidal thoughts, hallucinations, and paranoid ideas. It suggested these impairments were hereditary. The article juxtaposed these past medical findings with her current role as a court expert, implying a link between her historical mental state and her present professional competence. It also noted that she had examined over 3,000 couples in custody disputes over the last 12 years.

The publication prompted professional repercussions for the applicant, including questions from colleagues and patients, and the initiation of proceedings at the Wiener Neustadt Regional Court to review her fitness to continue as a court-appointed expert.

**Domestic Proceedings and Outcome**

The applicant brought separate legal actions against the two publishers under Section 7 of the Austrian Media Act, seeking compensation for the violation of her "strictly personal sphere of life." She argued that the article unlawfully published details of her private life and damaged her reputation.

Initially, she won both cases before the respective Regional Courts, which found that the article created a misleading link between her past medical history and current professional abilities, thereby compromising her publicly. However, both decisions were overturned on appeal by the Vienna Court of Appeal (for the online publication) and the Innsbruck Court of Appeal (for the print publication).

The appellate courts dismissed her actions, finding no violation. Their reasoning was crucial to the final outcome. They held that while the information was part of her private life, the article's content was essentially true and had a direct connection to her public role. They reasoned that as a court-certified expert influencing judicial decisions in the sensitive area of child custody, her psychological fitness was a matter of legitimate public interest. The courts found the article to be balanced, noting it also mentioned that her integrity had not been questioned for over a decade and included comments from relevant public officials. They concluded that the public interest in the proper administration of justice justified the publication of the true information.

**ECtHR Ruling**

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) under Article 8 (right to respect for private life), arguing that the Austrian courts had failed to protect her reputation.

The ECtHR, while noting the information concerned her private life, agreed with the domestic appellate courts. It found that the Austrian courts had struck a fair balance between the applicant's right to privacy (Article 8) and the publisher's right to freedom of expression (Article 10). The Court emphasized the significant public interest in the mental fitness of an expert who plays a decisive role in child custody proceedings, a matter that affects families and vulnerable individuals. It concluded that the publication of true and relevant information, even if from the distant past, did not violate the State's positive obligation to protect the applicant's private life. Therefore, no violation of Article 8 was found.

**Case Summary: Fürst-Pfeifer v. Austria (Applications nos. 33677/10 and 52340/10)**

The case of *Fürst-Pfeifer v. Austria* concerns an application brought by Ms. Gabriele Fürst-Pfeifer, an Austrian national and psychiatrist, against the Republic of Austria. The applicant alleged that the Austrian courts failed to protect her reputation against defamatory allegations published in a newspaper article, thereby violating her right to respect for private life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant, born in 1964, has been a court-certified psychological expert since 2000. Her work primarily involves providing expert opinions in sensitive custody and contact-rights disputes, as well as cases involving child abuse. She is frequently appointed by courts to examine children and adolescents.

The events central to the case occurred on 23 December 2008, when an article was published both online (on "meinbezirk.at") and in a free regional weekly print publication (*Bezirksblatt*). The article, headlined "Disclosed: Court Expert for custody proceedings a case for therapy," made serious allegations about the applicant's mental health. It stated that she suffered from mood swings, panic attacks, suicidal thoughts, hallucinations, and paranoid ideas. The article based these claims on a psychological expert report from 1993, commissioned during civil proceedings related to a breach of promise of marriage. It further noted that the report's author concluded her impairments were hereditary and mentioned that her integrity had been unquestioned for a decade until the report's disclosure. The article also included comments from a Green Party member, a Youth Advocate, and the Vice-President of the Wiener Neustadt Regional Court. It concluded by stating the applicant had withdrawn from her cases.

The publication had immediate negative consequences for the applicant. She faced questioning from colleagues and patients, and proceedings were initiated at the Wiener Neustadt Regional Court to assess her fitness to continue as a court-appointed expert, including an examination of her mental status.

The applicant initiated separate legal actions against the two publishing companies, seeking damages under section 8a of the Austrian Media Act, claiming the article violated her intimate personal sphere. While she won in the first-instance courts, which found the article to be incomplete, manipulative, and not directly linked to her public role, both judgments were overturned on appeal.

The Vienna Court of Appeal and the Innsbruck Court of Appeal dismissed her actions. They acknowledged that the article touched upon her private life and was capable of compromising her. However, they found that the published information was true, as it was based on an undisputed 1993 expert report. Crucially, the appellate courts determined that the article was sufficiently balanced and directly related to the applicant's public status. They reasoned that as a frequently appointed expert in the highly sensitive area of custody proceedings, her psychological integrity was of paramount public interest and had to be beyond doubt to maintain trust in the justice system. Consequently, they concluded that the public interest in the subject matter justified the article's critical questioning of her abilities, and the publishers had not violated her rights. The applicant then brought her case to the European Court of Human Rights.

**Case summary: Fürst-Pfeifer v. Austria (ECtHR, 17 May 2016)**

The applicant, Ms Gabriele Fürst-Pfeifer, is an Austrian psychiatrist and, since 2000, a court-certified psychological expert in custody, contact-rights, public-care and child-abuse proceedings. On 23 December 2008, an article was published online on “meinbezirk.at” and in the free weekly print publication *Bezirksblatt*. The headline stated that the “quality of experts” was in the spotlight and that a court expert for custody proceedings was herself “a case for therapy.” The article claimed that the applicant suffered from mood swings, panic attacks, suicidal thoughts, hallucinations and paranoid ideas, yet worked as a court-appointed expert and had examined over 3,000 married couples in custody disputes over twelve years.

The article relied on a 1993 psychological expert report by Dr M., prepared in civil proceedings concerning an alleged breach of promise of marriage. It stated that the report found the applicant’s impairments to be hereditary and that she had later joined the court expert community at the Wiener Neustadt Regional Court, with her integrity unquestioned for a decade. It also quoted a Green Party member who had filed a criminal complaint against her, the Youth Advocate of the Lower Austria Regional Government, and the Vice-President of the Wiener Neustadt Regional Court responsible for the expert list. It noted that the applicant had stopped answering her phone and had withdrawn from her cases.

As a result, the applicant faced questions from colleagues and patients, and proceedings were initiated to determine whether she remained fit to act as a court-appointed expert, including an examination of her mental status.

The applicant sued both publishers under section 8a of the Media Act, seeking damages and publication of the judgment. She alleged that the article violated her intimate personal sphere and damaged her reputation. The St Pölten and Innsbruck Regional Courts each awarded her €5,000. They found that the average reader would link the 1993 report to her current work, question her professional quality, and that the article intruded into her private life. They considered the article incomplete and manipulative, and found no direct link to public life because custody proceedings are generally not public.

The Vienna and Innsbruck Courts of Appeal reversed and dismissed her claims. They accepted that the article concerned her private sphere and could compromise her, but found the published facts true and undisputed. The article was balanced, quoted different sides, and noted that her integrity had not been questioned for over a decade. It was directly linked to her public role: she was on the court expert list, regularly appointed, worked with the state judiciary, and influenced judges in sensitive custody cases. Her psychological fitness was therefore relevant, and reasoned doubts warranted investigation. The press could report on this as a public watchdog.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 8, arguing that Austria had failed to protect her reputation and private life. The Government contended that the domestic courts had struck a fair balance with Article 10, given the public interest in the functioning of justice and the fitness of court experts.

The ECtHR joined the applications and rejected the non-exhaustion objection. On the merits, it reiterated that reputation is protected by Article 8 but must be balanced against freedom of expression under Article 10. The health information was private, but it came from a court-appointed expert report in public civil proceedings, was not obtained unlawfully, and its truth was undisputed. The article was balanced, not abusive, and formed part of an ongoing public debate. A serious debate about the mental fitness of a psychological expert in child custody matters was of general interest, because such experts play an important and sometimes decisive role and public trust in the judiciary must be maintained. The national courts had a wide margin of appreciation, and the ECtHR found no strong reasons to substitute its view. It therefore held that there had been no violation of Article 8.

The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered judgment on 15 March 2016 in *Menéndez García and Álvarez González v. Spain*, concerning two Spanish nationals convicted in lengthy criminal proceedings.

In 2000 the applicants acted as intermediaries or purchase agents in the sale of three cars to a company. On 20 November 2000, a Gijón investigating judge opened criminal proceedings against them and eight other suspects for fraud and forgery of documents. On 16 and 18 April 2001, respectively, the applicants were detained, charged with document forgery, informed of their rights as detainees, and interrogated by the Guardia Civil in the presence of counsel. The investigation lasted until 8 November 2004, when the judge ordered the opening of oral proceedings and sent the file to the Asturias Audiencia Provincial. Hearings were held on 6 May 2009. On 5 June 2009, the Audiencia Provincial convicted the first applicant and sentenced him to three years and six months’ imprisonment, and the second applicant to five years’ imprisonment for fraud and document forgery. The Audiencia refused their request to reduce the sentence for undue delay under Article 21 of the Criminal Code. It acknowledged the proceedings had been unusually long but attributed this to complexity, including evidence-gathering in different jurisdictions, many parties, difficulties notifying defendants, and the applicants’ lawyers’ lack of celerity. On cassation, the Supreme Court on 27 May 2010 partially allowed the appeal, reducing both sentences to three years and eight months for fraud, but rejected the undue-delay claims, finding the lower court’s justification sound and detailed. The Constitutional Court later declared the applicants’ amparo appeals inadmissible on 20 May and 12 September 2011 for lack of constitutional relevance.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants complained that the length of the investigatory and first-instance proceedings violated the “reasonable time” requirement of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. Their applications (nos. 73818/11 and 19420/12), lodged on 18 November 2011 and 22 March 2012, were joined. The length complaints were communicated to the Government; the remainder were declared inadmissible.

The Court determined that the relevant period began on 16 and 18 April 2001, when each applicant was officially notified of criminal allegations, and ended on 5 June 2009, when the first-instance judgment was issued. The proceedings therefore lasted over eight years and one month at one level. The Government argued complexity and the applicants’ conduct, including many defendants, voluminous evidence, lawyers’ lack of diligence, and the first applicant’s failure to notify a change of address. The Court accepted that the case had some complexity—fraud and forgery involving three plaintiffs and ten defendants—but found no exceptional difficulty. It held that the lawyers’ allegedly late submissions did not cause particular delay justifying the overall length. It found no justification for the four-year investigation from 20 November 2000 to 8 November 2004, and considered the period from 8 November 2004 to 5 June 2009 particularly long. The Government advanced no fact or argument warranting a different conclusion. The Court accordingly held that the length of the proceedings was excessive, failed the “reasonable time” requirement, and violated Article 6 § 1.

In *Menéndez García and Álvarez González v. Spain* (ECtHR, 15 March 2016, Applications nos. 73818/11 and 19420/12), two Spanish nationals complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the criminal proceedings against them had exceeded a reasonable time. The first applicant, Gerardo Menéndez García, and the second, Sigifredo Álvarez González, were involved in 2000 as intermediaries or purchase agents in the sale of three cars to a company.

On 20 November 2000, a Gijón investigating judge opened criminal proceedings against the applicants and eight other suspects for fraud and forgery of documents. On 16 and 18 April 2001 respectively, the applicants were detained, charged with document forgery, informed of their rights, and interrogated by the Guardia Civil in the presence of their lawyer. These dates later marked the start of the relevant period for assessing the length complaint.

On 8 November 2004, the investigating judge ordered the opening of oral proceedings and sent the case file to the Asturias Audiencia Provincial. The hearings took place only on 6 May 2009. On 5 June 2009, the Audiencia Provincial convicted the first applicant and sentenced him to three years and six months’ imprisonment, and the second applicant to five years’ imprisonment, for fraud and document forgery. The applicants requested a sentence reduction for undue delay under Article 21 of the Criminal Code. The court refused, acknowledging that the proceedings had been “unusually” long but attributing the delay to the case’s complexity, including difficulties gathering evidence in different jurisdictions, the number of parties, problems notifying some defendants, and alleged slowness by the applicants’ lawyers.

The applicants appealed in cassation. On 27 May 2010, the Supreme Court partly allowed the appeal, sentencing both applicants to three years and eight months’ imprisonment for fraud, but rejected the undue-delay claim. It found that although the proceedings might appear excessively long, the Audiencia Provincial had provided a sound and detailed justification. The applicants then filed amparo appeals with the Constitutional Court, complaining, among other things, about the length of proceedings. By decisions of 20 May 2011 and 12 September 2011, the Constitutional Court declared both appeals inadmissible for lack of constitutional relevance.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, only the complaints concerning the length of proceedings were communicated to the Government; the rest were declared inadmissible. The Court joined the two applications and declared the remaining length complaint admissible.

The Court determined that the relevant period began on 16 and 18 April 2001, when the applicants were officially notified of the criminal allegations, and ended on 5 June 2009, when the first-instance judgment was issued. The proceedings therefore lasted over eight years and one month at one level of jurisdiction.

On the merits, the Court applied the criteria of complexity, the applicants’ conduct, and the authorities’ conduct. It accepted that the case had some complexity because it concerned fraud and document forgery, a car purchase, three plaintiffs, and ten defendants. However, it found no exceptional difficulty. It also held that the alleged delays by the applicants’ lawyers did not cause particular delay justifying the overall length. The Court found no justification for the four-year investigation stage from 20 November 2000 to 8 November 2004. It further considered the period from 8 November 2004, when oral proceedings were opened, to 5 June 2009 particularly long. Consequently, the Court found that the proceedings were excessive in length and violated Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

001-164454:
**Krahulec v. Slovakia (Application no. 19294/07), European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, judgment 5 July 2016**

The applicant, Štefan Krahulec, a Slovak national born in 1945 and living in Zvolen, complained that Slovakia’s rent-control scheme violated his right to peaceful enjoyment of his possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. He lodged the application on 30 April 2007; it was declared partly admissible on 7 June 2011.

The property at issue was a house in Piešťany built by the applicant’s grandfather in 1929. It contained four flats: two of 108 sq. m and two of 123 sq. m. Ownership passed to the applicant from his mother on 21 December 1998. At the time of the application, all four flats were occupied by tenants whose right to use them had originated in municipal decisions between 1953 and 1986. After 1 January 1992, those rights were transformed into tenancies with regulated rent for an indefinite period. Under the rent-control legislation, the applicant was required to accept the tenants and could charge no more than the maximum rent fixed by the State. He could not unilaterally terminate the leases.

The regulated rents were very low. In 1999, the maximum monthly rent for the flats was equivalent to approximately EUR 13 to EUR 33. After several increases, by 2004 the applicant could charge EUR 115 per month for each smaller flat and EUR 124 for each larger flat. He claimed that he in fact received less than even those maximum amounts and became involved in disputes with tenants and the local municipality. The parties disputed market rent levels. The applicant relied on National Association of Real Estate Agencies data claiming market rents of EUR 600–800 per month between 2004 and 2007 for similar flats. The Government submitted an expert valuation stating that in 2010 market rent would have been EUR 265.50 and EUR 325 respectively.

Rent control ended for the first flat in May 2007, for the second and third flats in August 2007, and for the fourth flat in April 2008. The Court therefore examined the interference from 21 December 1998, when the applicant acquired title, until those dates. It noted that the rent control lasted about eight years for the first flat, almost nine years for the second and third flats, and over nine years for the fourth flat. The Court also limited the scope of the case to the difference between the rent the applicant was entitled to charge under the rent-control scheme and the rent he could likely have obtained on the open market, because he provided no information about the rent he had actually claimed.

The applicant argued that the scheme was a disproportionate interference, amounted in practice to de facto deprivation, forced him to house others at his own expense, and prevented him from terminating leases or receiving adequate compensation. He also alleged that the legislation was incoherent and unforeseeable and that the regulated rent did not cover maintenance costs. The Government admitted that the scheme limited the use of his property but contended it was lawful, clear, foreseeable, and pursued a legitimate social-housing aim. They distinguished the case from *Bittó and Others v. Slovakia*, where regulated rent had been only 20–26% of market rent, arguing that here it reached 44–50%. They also said the applicant failed to substantiate his maintenance expenses.

The Court found that the case followed the same pattern as *Bittó and Others*. The rent-control scheme was an interference with property, constituted State control of use under the second paragraph of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, was lawful, and pursued a legitimate social-policy aim in the general interest. However, as in *Bittó*, the authorities had failed to strike a fair balance between the general interest and the applicant’s property rights. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

**Krahulec v. Slovakia** (Application no. 19294/07), European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, judgment of 5 July 2016, concerned a Slovak landlord’s complaint that the State’s rent-control scheme violated his right to peaceful enjoyment of his possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention.

The applicant, born in 1945, acquired ownership of a four-flat house in Piešťany from his mother on 21 December 1998. The house had been built by his grandfather in 1929. At the time of the application, all four flats were occupied by tenants under regulated rents. The tenants’ or their predecessors’ right to use the flats had been established by municipal decisions between 1953 and 1986, and after 1 January 1992 those rights became indefinite tenancies with regulated rent. Under the rent-control scheme, the applicant had to accept the tenants and could charge no more than the maximum rent fixed by the State. He could not unilaterally terminate the leases.

The rents were very low. In 1999, the maximum monthly rent for the flats was approximately EUR 13 to EUR 33. After increases, by 2004 the applicant could charge EUR 115 per month for the two smaller flats (108 sq. m each) and EUR 124 for the two larger flats (123 sq. m each). The applicant claimed he in fact received less than the maximum and litigated with tenants and the local municipality. The parties disputed market rent: the applicant relied on National Association of Real Estate Agencies data claiming EUR 600–800 per month for similar flats between 2004 and 2007; the Government’s expert valued market rent in 2010 at EUR 265.50 and EUR 325. Rent control ended for the first flat in May 2007, for the second and third flats in August 2007, and for the fourth flat in April 2008. The application was lodged on 30 April 2007.

The applicant alleged that the rent-control scheme interfered with his property rights. He argued that the restrictions and their duration amounted to de facto deprivation; that he was forced to satisfy others’ housing needs at his own expense; that he could not terminate the leases or receive adequate compensation; that the legislation was incoherent and unforeseeable; and that the scheme lacked a legitimate aim and imposed a disproportionate burden. He also claimed the controlled rent did not even cover maintenance costs.

The Government admitted the scheme limited his use of property but argued it was lawful, accessible, clear, foreseeable, and pursued a legitimate social-housing aim. It disputed the market-rent figures and contended that controlled rent reached 44–50% of market rent, unlike 20–26% in *Bittó and Others v. Slovakia*. It also said the applicant failed to substantiate maintenance expenses.

The Court limited the scope to the period from 21 December 1998 until rent control ceased for each flat. Because the applicant provided no information about the rent he was entitled to under the scheme, it considered only the difference between controlled rent and likely open-market rent. Applying *Bittó*, the Court found the rent-control scheme was an interference with property, a State control measure under the second paragraph of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, and lawful and aimed at a legitimate social-policy objective. However, as in *Bittó*, the authorities failed to strike a fair balance between the general interest and the applicant’s property rights. The Government’s attempt to distinguish the case based on a smaller rent differential did not alter that conclusion. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

CASE OF KRAHULEC v. SLOVAKIA (Application no. 19294/07), judgment of 5 July 2016, concerned a Slovak homeowner’s complaint that Slovakia’s rent-control scheme violated his right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The applicant, Štefan Krahulec, owned a house in Piešťany containing four flats. Ownership passed to him from his mother on 21 December 1998. The flats were occupied by tenants whose right to use them originated in municipal decisions between 1953 and 1986. After 1 January 1992, those rights became tenancies with regulated rent for an indefinite period. Under the scheme, the applicant had to accept the tenants and could charge no more than the maximum rent fixed by the State; he could not unilaterally terminate the leases.

The rent limits were low. In 1999, the maximum monthly rent for the flats was equivalent to about EUR 13–33. After several increases, by 2004 the applicant could charge EUR 115 monthly for each smaller flat (108 sq m) and EUR 124 for each larger flat (123 sq m). He claimed he actually received less than the permitted maximum and litigated with tenants and the municipality. The parties disputed market rent. The applicant, relying on NAREA data, said comparable flats could fetch EUR 600–800 monthly between 2004 and 2007. The Government’s expert valued market rent in 2010 at EUR 265.50 and EUR 325 monthly. The Government argued that the regulated rent reached 44–50% of market rent, whereas in Bittó and Others v. Slovakia it had been only 20–26%, so the burden here was less severe.

Rent control on the applicant’s flats ended in May 2007 (first flat), August 2007 (second and third flats), and April 2008 (fourth flat). The alleged interference therefore lasted from December 1998 until those dates—roughly eight to more than nine years per flat.

The applicant alleged that the rent-control scheme restricted his property rights, amounted to de facto deprivation, forced him to satisfy others’ housing needs at his own expense, and gave him no possibility of terminating the leases or receiving adequate compensation. He also argued that the scheme lacked a sufficiently clear statutory basis, did not pursue a legitimate aim, and imposed a disproportionate burden; the controlled rent allegedly did not cover maintenance costs. The Government admitted the scheme limited his use of property but maintained it was lawful, accessible, foreseeable, and pursued a legitimate social-housing aim. It disputed the market-rent figures and said the applicant had not substantiated his maintenance expenses.

The Court defined the application’s scope as the period from 21 December 1998 until rent control ceased, and limited it to the difference between the rent the applicant was entitled to under the scheme and the likely open-market rent, because he provided no information about actual rent claims. Following Bittó and Others, the Court accepted that the rent-control scheme was an interference through State control of property use, was lawful, and pursued a legitimate social-policy aim in the general interest. However, as in Bittó, the authorities failed to strike a fair balance between community interests and the owner’s property rights. The Government’s attempt to distinguish the case by the higher rent-to-market ratio and alleged lack of substantiation did not prevent that conclusion. The Court accordingly found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In *Tuchin and Tuchina v. Ukraine* (Application no. 40458/08, judgment 26 May 2016), the applicants were Ukrainian nationals and parents of a daughter who died after a traffic accident. They complained that Ukraine failed to conduct an effective investigation into her death. Although they relied on Article 6, the European Court of Human Rights recharacterised the complaint as concerning only the procedural limb of Article 2—the State’s duty to investigate deaths effectively.

The key facts were as follows. On 30 April 2002, the applicants’ daughter was struck by a car driven by P. while crossing the street. She died in hospital. Between April 2002 and October 2010, the prosecution authorities issued at least ten decisions refusing to institute or discontinuing criminal proceedings against P., mainly for lack of *corpus delicti*. All these decisions were quashed by supervising authorities as unsubstantiated, and further investigations were ordered. On 9 July 2009, the first applicant lodged a civil claim against P. within the criminal proceedings, and on 15 July 2009 he was granted the status of an aggrieved party. On 26 October 2010, the Odessa Suvorivskyy District Court discontinued the criminal proceedings against P. as time-barred. That decision was upheld by the Odessa Regional Court of Appeal on 21 December 2010 and by the Higher Specialised Court for Civil and Criminal Matters on 20 November 2012.

On 20 November 2012, the Higher Specialised Court issued a separate ruling identifying serious shortcomings. It stated that the pre-trial investigation had been perfunctory and lengthy; that since 2002 there had been hardly any investigative measures; that the numerous refusals to institute criminal proceedings were unfounded and had been quashed; that guidelines for remedying investigative defects had been ignored; and that the overall investigation, lasting over ten years, was unjustified. It concluded that the investigation had not complied with domestic legislation or the Convention and instructed the relevant authorities to prevent similar violations.

Before the ECtHR, the Government argued that the applicants had failed to exhaust domestic remedies because they had not brought a civil claim against the investigating authorities for damages, especially after the Higher Specialised Court had acknowledged the investigation’s flaws and length. The Court dismissed this objection, noting that the Government had shown only a theoretical possibility of such a remedy, without any case-law indicating it was available in practice.

On the merits, the applicants alleged that the investigation was ineffective due to excessive delays and lack of diligence. The Government claimed numerous investigative steps had been taken. The Court observed that the criminal proceedings lasted more than ten years and eventually became time-barred. The domestic authorities themselves acknowledged serious deficiencies and unjustified duration. By the time the Higher Specialised Court issued its ruling, it was already impossible to establish the facts surrounding the daughter’s death or to impose criminal liability on the driver if guilt had been established. Referring to previous case-law under Article 2, the Court held that proceedings concerning a fatal accident and redress for relatives must not be unreasonably delayed. The Government failed to provide any fact or argument distinguishing the case. The Court therefore found a violation of the procedural limb of Article 2: Ukraine had not conducted an effective and prompt investigation into the death of the applicants’ daughter.

On the same date, the Higher Specialised Court issued a separate ruling noting serious shortcomings: the pre-trial investigation had been perfunctory and lengthy; since 2002 there had been hardly any investigative measures; the repeated refusals to institute proceedings were unfounded and had been quashed; and the overall investigation lasting over ten years was unjustified and non-compliant with domestic legislation and the Convention. On the merits, the applicants alleged excessive delays and a lack of diligence. The Government claimed numerous investigative measures had been taken. The Court observed that the criminal proceedings lasted more than ten years and eventually became time-barred. The domestic authorities themselves acknowledged serious deficiencies and unjustified duration. By the time the Higher Specialised Court made its ruling, however, it was already impossible to establish the facts surrounding the daughter’s death or to impose criminal liability on the driver if guilt had been established. Relying on prior Ukrainian cases concerning unreasonably delayed fatal accident proceedings, the Court found that the Government had not offered any fact or argument to reach a different conclusion. In *Bărbulescu v. Romania* (Application no. 61496/08), the applicant, a Romanian national born in 1979, worked from 1 August 2004 to 6 August 2007 for a private company as a sales engineer. At his employer’s request, he created a Yahoo Messenger account to respond to clients’ enquiries. On 13 July 2007, the employer informed him that his Yahoo Messenger communications had been monitored from 5 to 13 July 2007 and that the records showed he had used the Internet for personal purposes, contrary to internal regulations. The applicant replied in writing that he had used Yahoo Messenger only for professional purposes. The employer then presented a 45-page transcript of his communications. It contained all messages exchanged with his fiancée and brother during the monitoring period and concerned personal matters. It also included five short messages exchanged with his fiancée on 12 July 2007 through a personal Yahoo Messenger account; those messages did not disclose intimate information.

On 1 August 2007, the employer terminated the applicant’s employment contract for breach of internal regulations, which strictly prohibited using company computers, photocopiers, telephones, telex and fax machines for personal purposes.

The applicant challenged the dismissal before the Bucharest County Court, arguing that the decision was null and void because the employer had violated his right to correspondence protected by the Romanian Constitution and Criminal Code. On 7 December 2007, the County Court dismissed his complaint. It found that the employer had complied with Labour Code dismissal procedures and that the applicant had been informed of the rules prohibiting personal use. Monitoring his Yahoo Messenger communications during working hours, even if illegal, could not affect the validity of the disciplinary proceedings. Since the applicant claimed he had used Yahoo Messenger only to advise clients, checking the content was the only way to verify that defence. The employer had the right to monitor use of company computers and to check how professional tasks were performed. The court noted that employees had been warned that their activity was under surveillance, including by notice no. 2316 of 3 July 2007, which the applicant had signed, and that another colleague had been dismissed for personal Internet use. The Internet at work was a professional tool, and the employer could monitor personal use to prevent damage to IT systems, illicit activities, or disclosure of commercial secrets.

The applicant appealed, claiming that e-mails were protected by Article 8 of the Convention as “private life” and “correspondence”. He also complained that the County Court had refused to hear witnesses to show the employer suffered no harm. On 17 June 2008, the Bucharest Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and upheld the County Court judgment. Relying on EU Directive 95/46/EC, it found the employer’s conduct reasonable and the monitoring of communications the only method of establishing whether there had been a disciplinary breach. The employer had the right and obligation to ensure the company’s functioning and could check how employees completed their tasks. Since the applicant denied personal use after being warned, the employer was entitled to monitor and transcribe his Yahoo Messenger communications. The Court of Appeal concluded that the violation of his correspondence was the only way to achieve a legitimate aim and that a proper balance had been struck between protecting his private life and the employer’s right to supervise its business.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that the employer’s decision to terminate his contract had been based on a breach of his right to respect for private life and correspondence and that the Romanian courts had failed to protect that right.

The relevant legal framework included Romanian constitutional and criminal-law protections for correspondence, Labour Code provisions allowing employer monitoring while requiring confidentiality of personal data, and EU data-protection standards requiring monitoring to be transparent, necessary, fair and proportionate.

In *Nait-Liman v. Switzerland* (Application no. 51357/07), the applicant, Abdennacer Naït-Liman, was born in Tunisia in 1962, later acquired Swiss nationality, and lived in Versoix, Geneva. He alleged that on 22 April 1992 Italian police arrested him and took him to the Tunisian Consulate in Genoa, after which Tunisian agents transferred him to Tunis. From 24 April to 1 June 1992, he claimed he was arbitrarily detained and tortured at the Tunisian Ministry of the Interior on the orders of A.K., then Minister of the Interior. He described being held in the “roast chicken” position, deprived of sleep and basic physiological needs, beaten on the soles of his feet with a baseball bat, and struck with telephone cords. He submitted that he suffered medically attested physical and psychological injuries, with a plausible causal link to the alleged abuse. He fled Tunisia in 1993, sought asylum in Switzerland, and was granted political asylum in 1995.

In 2001, while A.K. was receiving treatment in a Swiss hospital, the applicant lodged a criminal complaint in Geneva for severe bodily injury, illegal confinement, insults, endangering health, coercion, and abuse of authority, and sought to join as a civil party. The proceedings were discontinued because A.K. had left Switzerland and could not be arrested. In 2003, the applicant allegedly consulted a Tunisian lawyer, who advised that a civil action in Tunisia was impossible or would never succeed. On 8 July 2004, he brought a civil claim before the Geneva Court of First Instance against Tunisia and A.K., seeking CHF 200,000 plus interest for non-pecuniary damage caused by the alleged torture.

On 15 September 2005, the Court of First Instance declared the claim inadmissible for lack of territorial jurisdiction. It found that the Swiss courts had no jurisdiction under the Federal Law on Private International Law (LDIP), because the defendants were not domiciled or habitually resident in Switzerland and no unlawful act or detrimental result occurred there. It also rejected jurisdiction under the “forum of necessity” in section 3 LDIP, finding no sufficient connection with Switzerland: the alleged acts occurred in Tunisia in 1992 by Tunisian State agents, and the applicant’s later asylum and residence in Switzerland did not suffice. The Cantonal Court rejected his appeal on 15 September 2006, noting his difficulty in suing in Tunisia but holding that the defendants enjoyed immunity because the alleged torture was an act *iure imperii*, relying on *Al-Adsani v. the United Kingdom*.

On 22 May 2007, the Federal Court dismissed the applicant’s further appeal. It held that section 3 LDIP required cumulative conditions: no Swiss forum otherwise, impossibility or unreasonableness of proceedings abroad, and a sufficient connection with Switzerland. The first condition was met; the second was problematic but left undecided; the third was absent. All specific features of the case pointed to Tunisia, except the applicant’s residence in Italy at the time, and his later move to Switzerland was a subsequent fact not forming part of the case. The Federal Court therefore found that the Swiss courts lacked jurisdiction, without examining immunity.

The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 ECHR that the Swiss civil courts’ refusal to examine his compensation claim for non-pecuniary damage caused by alleged torture violated his right of access to a court. The key alleged violation concerned the denial of jurisdiction based on lack of sufficient connection to Switzerland and the forum of necessity, rather than the merits of the torture claim. The Redress Trust and the World Organisation Against Torture intervened. The case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 15 March 2018.

In February 2001, while A.K. was in a Swiss hospital, the applicant lodged a criminal complaint in Geneva for severe bodily injury, illegal confinement, insults, endangering health, coercion and abuse of authority, and sought to join as a civil party. The proceedings were discontinued on 19 February 2001 because A.K. had left Switzerland and could not be arrested. The applicant later said a Tunisian lawyer advised him in 2003 that a civil action in Tunisia was impossible or had never been successful.

On 8 July 2004, the applicant sued Tunisia and A.K. before the Geneva Court of First Instance, seeking CHF 200,000 plus interest for non-pecuniary damage caused by the alleged torture. The defendants did not appear. On 15 September 2005, the court declared the claim inadmissible for lack of territorial jurisdiction. It held that the Swiss courts had no jurisdiction under the Federal Private International Law Act because the defendants were not domiciled or habitually resident in Switzerland and no unlawful act or harmful result occurred there. It also found no “forum of necessity” because there was no sufficient connection with Switzerland; asylum and later residence alone were insufficient.

On appeal, the Geneva Court of Justice rejected the appeal on 15 September 2006. It accepted that the applicant could not bring proceedings in Tunisia, but held that the defendants enjoyed immunity from jurisdiction because the alleged torture was performed in the exercise of sovereign authority (iure imperii). Citing Al-Adsani v. the United Kingdom, it found no violation of the applicant’s right of access to a court.

The applicant appealed to the Federal Court, arguing that the Swiss courts had jurisdiction and that torture could not attract immunity. The Federal Court dismissed the appeal on 22 May 2007. It held that the forum of necessity required, cumulatively: no ordinary Swiss forum; impossibility or unreasonableness of proceedings abroad; and a sufficient connection with Switzerland. The first condition was met, and the second was problematic but not decisive. The third failed because all relevant features of the case were linked to Tunisia, except the applicant’s residence in Italy at the time. His later move to Switzerland could not create a sufficient connection. The Federal Court therefore dismissed the appeal without examining immunity.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that the Swiss courts’ refusal to examine his compensation claim denied him access to a court under Article 6 § 1. The Redress Trust and the World Organisation Against Torture intervened. The Chamber judgment was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 15 March 2018.
