In *Soares v. Portugal* (Application no. 79972/12), the applicant, António Alberto Mota Soares, was a Portuguese chief corporal in the National Republican Guard (GNR) stationed at the Góis territorial post. On 7 November 2009, he sent an email to the General Inspectorate of Internal Administration entitled “Suspected misuse of money.” He alleged that Commander M.C. of the Arganil GNR post had misused public funds. According to the email, in December 2008 the Coimbra GNR Territorial Group had distributed money to territorial posts for a Christmas dinner. At Arganil, allegedly only Commander M.C. and Corporal M. attended the dinner, and the full amount allocated to the post’s military was paid to the restaurant manager in exchange for a receipt. Soares stated that it seemed the Commander had since taken his family to that restaurant, with the cost deducted from the unspent dinner money. He said he had learned of the matter through rumours among military personnel at Arganil, who had not reported it for fear of reprisals, and requested secrecy because he was also a GNR member.

The Inspectorate forwarded the email to the GNR General Command and the Lousã public prosecutor’s office. The prosecutor investigated but discontinued proceedings on 28 February 2010, finding no evidence of the alleged offence. The Inspectorate discontinued its own inquiry on 21 June 2010. The GNR opened an internal inquiry on 4 December 2009; after hearing Commander M.C. on 23 December 2009, it was converted into disciplinary proceedings against the Commander on 9 February 2010. Those proceedings were discontinued on 30 July 2010 for insufficient evidence.

On 22 April 2010, Commander M.C. filed a criminal defamation complaint against Soares. On 7 July 2011, the public prosecutor charged Soares with aggravated defamation, alleging that the email had intentionally attacked the Commander’s honesty, honour and professional reputation. The Commander also claimed EUR 5,000 in damages. On 17 January 2012, the Lousã Criminal Court convicted Soares of aggravated defamation and sentenced him to 80 day-fines totalling EUR 720, plus EUR 1,000 in damages. The court found the rumour unproved, concluded that Soares intended to undermine the Commander’s honour, knew the allegation was untrue, and could easily have clarified its authenticity with the restaurant owner. It held that whistle-blowing could not justify unsubstantiated suspicions. The Coimbra Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 19 September 2012.

Separately, on 3 August 2011, the GNR General Command instituted disciplinary proceedings against Soares. On 20 February 2013, the inquiry report concluded that he had breached his duty of loyalty by failing to inform his hierarchical superiors through the proper chain of command. It noted that all investigations into his allegations had been discontinued and that he had been criminally convicted. On 27 March 2013, Soares received a disciplinary sanction of six days’ suspension, suspended for twelve months. He apparently did not appeal that sanction.

Relevant domestic law included Criminal Code Article 180, which criminalises defamation, including accusations framed as suspicion, and Article 184, which aggravates the offence where the victim is an agent of authority. GNR rules required members to refrain from statements affecting the Guard’s cohesion or reputation or breaching hierarchical discipline, and imposed a duty of loyalty requiring faults to be communicated through hierarchical channels.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Soares complained under Article 10 that his criminal conviction for reporting an alleged misuse of public money violated his right to freedom of expression. The key issue was whether the conviction and related sanctions constituted a justified interference with his right to impart information of public interest, particularly in a military context.

In *Soares v. Portugal*, the applicant, António Alberto Mota Soares, was a Portuguese national and a chief corporal in the National Republican Guard (GNR) serving at the Góis territorial post. He complained under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights that his criminal conviction for defamation, following his report of an alleged misuse of public money, violated his right to freedom of expression.

On 7 November 2009, the applicant sent an email to the General Inspectorate of Internal Administration entitled “Suspected misuse of money.” He reported alleged misconduct by Commander M.C. of the Arganil GNR territorial post. According to information he said he had heard from colleagues at Arganil, in December 2008 the Coimbra GNR Territorial Group had distributed money to territorial posts for a Christmas dinner. At Arganil, only Commander M.C. and Corporal M. attended the dinner, and the money allocated to the post’s military personnel was paid to the restaurant manager in exchange for a receipt. The applicant further alleged that Commander M.C. had since been going to that restaurant with his family, with the cost of meals deducted from the unspent dinner funds. He asked the Inspectorate to investigate and requested secrecy because he feared reprisals within the military.

The Inspectorate forwarded the email to the GNR General Command and the Lousã public prosecutor’s office. The prosecutor opened an investigation but discontinued it on 28 February 2010, finding no evidence of the alleged offence. The Inspectorate also discontinued its inquiry in June 2010. The GNR began an internal inquiry, which led to disciplinary proceedings against Commander M.C.; those proceedings were discontinued in July 2010 for insufficient evidence.

Commander M.C. then lodged a criminal complaint against the applicant for defamation. In July 2011, the public prosecutor charged the applicant with aggravated defamation. Commander M.C. also claimed EUR 5,000 in damages. On 17 January 2012, the Lousã Criminal Court convicted the applicant of aggravated defamation, sentencing him to eighty day-fines totalling EUR 720 and ordering him to pay EUR 1,000 in damages. The court found that the rumour had not been proved, that the applicant intended to attack Commander M.C.’s honour and reputation, and that he knew the allegation was untrue. It reasoned that although whistle-blowing may be a duty in certain circumstances, it cannot be used to cast suspicion without factual support. The court noted that the applicant could have checked the allegation with the restaurant owner. The Coimbra Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 19 September 2012.

Separately, the GNR instituted disciplinary proceedings against the applicant in August 2011. In February 2013, the official responsible concluded that the applicant had breached his duty of loyalty by not informing his hierarchical superiors through the proper chain of command. The report noted that the investigations had been discontinued and that the applicant had been criminally convicted. On 27 March 2013, the GNR imposed a six-day suspension, suspended for twelve months. The applicant apparently did not appeal that disciplinary sanction.

Under Portuguese law, Article 180 of the Criminal Code criminalised defamation, including accusations made in the form of suspicion or judgments harming honour or reputation. Article 180 § 4 excluded good faith where the person had not verified the information. Article 184 aggravated the offence when the victim was an agent of authority. GNR rules also required servicemen to refrain from statements affecting the Guard’s cohesion or reputation and to comply with hierarchical and disciplinary principles.

The key Article 10 issue was therefore whether the criminal conviction—and related disciplinary consequences—for reporting suspected misuse of public funds by a superior to an oversight body disproportionately interfered with the applicant’s freedom of expression, particularly in a military context where whistle-blowing and hierarchical duties intersect.

In *Soares v. Portugal* (Application no. 79972/12, ECtHR Fourth Section, judgment 21 June 2016), the applicant was a Portuguese chief corporal in the National Republican Guard (GNR), stationed at Góis. On 7 November 2009 he emailed the General Inspectorate of Internal Administration under the subject “Suspected misuse of money.” He reported an alleged misuse of public funds by Commander M.C. of the Arganil territorial post. He said he had learned through rumours and conversations with colleagues that in December 2008 the Coimbra GNR Territorial Group had distributed money to territorial posts for a Christmas dinner; at Arganil, only Commander M.C. and Corporal M. attended; the amount allocated was paid to the restaurant manager in exchange for a receipt; and the Commander allegedly later took his family to that restaurant, with the cost deducted from unspent dinner money. The applicant asked the Inspectorate to investigate and requested secrecy, fearing reprisals as a serviceman.

The Inspectorate forwarded the email to the GNR General Command and the Lousã public prosecutor’s office. The prosecutor opened an investigation and discontinued it on 28 February 2010, finding no evidence of the reported offence. The Inspectorate’s own inquiry ended on 21 June 2010. The GNR also began an internal inquiry on 4 December 2009. Commander M.C. was heard on 23 December 2009 and learned of the email. On 9 February 2010 the inquiry became disciplinary proceedings against the Commander, but these were discontinued on 30 July 2010 for insufficient evidence, also noting the prosecutor’s decision.

On 22 April 2010 Commander M.C. filed a criminal complaint for defamation. On 7 July 2011 the public prosecutor charged the applicant with aggravated defamation, alleging that the email attacked the Commander’s honesty, honour and professional reputation. The Commander also claimed EUR 5,000 in damages. On 17 January 2012 the Lousã Criminal Court convicted the applicant of aggravated defamation, sentencing him to 80 day-fines totalling EUR 720 and ordering EUR 1,000 damages. The court found the rumour unproved, concluded the applicant intended to undermine the Commander’s honour, knew the allegation was untrue, and could have checked its authenticity with the restaurant owner. The Coimbra Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 19 September 2012.

Separately, on 3 August 2011 the GNR instituted disciplinary proceedings against the applicant. A final report of 20 February 2013 found that he had breached his duty of loyalty by not informing his hierarchical superiors through the proper channels. On 27 March 2013 the General Command imposed a six-day suspension, suspended for twelve months. The applicant apparently did not appeal that disciplinary sanction to the Minister of Home Affairs.

Portuguese law made defamation criminal, including accusations even in the form of suspicion, and aggravated it when the victim was an authority. Article 180(4) excluded good faith where the discloser failed to verify information. Military rules also required GNR servicemen to refrain from statements damaging the Guard’s cohesion or reputation and to follow hierarchical channels. Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained under Article 10 that his criminal conviction for reporting an alleged misuse of public money violated his right to freedom of expression. The key factual issues were whether his email amounted to protected whistle-blowing in the public interest, whether he acted in good faith and fulfilled any verification duty, and whether the criminal conviction, damages award and disciplinary sanction were proportionate given his military status and duties.
001-164917:
E.S. v. Romania and Bulgaria (Application no. 60281/11) concerns the alleged disruption of family life under Article 8 of the Convention after the applicant’s daughter was taken from Romania to Bulgaria and retained there by her paternal grandparents. The applicant, a Romanian national, gave birth in Spain in 2004 to a daughter. The father, R.E.N., was Bulgarian. After the couple separated in 2008, the child lived for periods in Spain, Bulgaria and Romania. From June 2008 she stayed in Romania with her maternal grandmother while the applicant worked in Spain. In November 2008 the paternal grandparents visited Romania, took the child out with the maternal aunt’s consent, expelled the aunt from the car, and drove the child to Bulgaria without the applicant’s knowledge or consent. The child remained in Bulgaria with the paternal grandparents.

The applicant alleged that Romania and Bulgaria failed to respond adequately to the abduction and retention, disrupting her family life. In Romania, she began custody proceedings in July 2008. The District Court awarded her custody on 30 January 2009, but the father later appealed out of time, arguing that he had lived in Bulgaria and had not been properly summoned. In December 2009 the County Court quashed the decision and remitted the case because the father had not been legally summoned. After further proceedings, the District Court again granted custody to the applicant on 11 November 2010. On appeal, the County Court reversed in October 2011 and granted custody to the father, finding that the child had lived in Bulgaria for four years, did not speak Romanian, and was integrated there. On 9 January 2012 the Piteşti Court of Appeal quashed that decision and restored custody to the applicant. Her request for interim measures in Romania was refused because the child had already lived in Bulgaria for over three years and removal was considered contrary to her interests.

In Bulgaria, the applicant sought recognition and enforcement of the Romanian custody judgments. In May 2009 the Pazardzhik Regional Court recognised the January 2009 judgment, upheld on appeal in April 2010. Enforcement began in August 2010. Attempts to serve the father failed, and a handover was scheduled for 9 February 2011 with police and social services. The child was not found; the father was fined and another handover was set. A social services report warned that abruptly removing the child from her settled environment would harm her and that she needed assistance to re-establish a relationship with her mother. The Supreme Court of Cassation then suspended enforcement and, in January 2012, quashed the recognition because the father had not been properly summoned. A second recognition of the later Romanian judgment was granted in May 2012, upheld in April 2013, and became final in May 2014. However, in July 2014 the Pazardzhik District Court suspended enforcement at the father’s request because he had started change-of-custody proceedings and because the child was settled in Bulgaria, spoke only Bulgarian, and had a close relationship with her paternal grandparents.

The applicant also tried international mechanisms. The Hague Convention had not entered into force between Romania and Bulgaria at the relevant time, so Bulgaria refused her return request. A request under Brussels II bis was also refused by Bulgaria. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation therefore concern the child’s abduction and retention, the conflicting and delayed custody decisions, the repeated difficulties in obtaining recognition and enforcement in Bulgaria, and the Bulgarian authorities’ eventual suspension of enforcement based on the child’s integration and pending custody proceedings.

The case E.S. v. Romania and Bulgaria concerns the applicant’s complaint that both States disrupted her family life by failing to respond effectively to the abduction and retention of her daughter by the child’s paternal grandparents in Bulgaria.

The applicant, a Romanian national, gave birth to a daughter in Spain in 2004. The father was a Bulgarian national. After the couple separated in 2008, the child lived at different times in Spain, Bulgaria and Romania. In June 2008, with the father’s consent, the applicant returned to Romania with the child for a short stay, then left her with the maternal grandmother while working in Spain.

On 4 November 2008, the paternal grandparents visited the child in Romania. With the maternal grandmother’s consent, they took the child out for ice cream with an aunt. They then stopped the car, expelled the aunt, and took the child to Bulgaria without the applicant’s knowledge or consent. The child has lived in Bulgaria with the paternal grandparents ever since.

In July 2008, the applicant had already sought full custody from the Romanian courts. In January 2009, the Râmnicu Vâlcea District Court awarded her custody. However, the father successfully applied in September 2009 to appeal out of time, arguing that he had not been properly summoned. In December 2009, the County Court quashed the custody decision and remitted the case. In November 2010, the District Court again awarded custody to the applicant, noting the father’s criminal past and the manner in which the child had been taken to Bulgaria. On appeal, in October 2011, the County Court awarded custody to the father, finding that the child was integrated in Bulgaria and did not speak Romanian. The applicant appealed, and on 9 January 2012 the Piteşti Court of Appeal restored the applicant’s custody in a final judgment.

Meanwhile, in Bulgaria, the applicant sought recognition and enforcement of the Romanian custody decisions. The first Romanian judgment granting her custody was recognised in Bulgaria in May 2009, but enforcement attempts in 2010–2011 failed. A handover scheduled for February 2011 did not take place because the child could not be located at the paternal grandparents’ address. The father was fined, and social services warned that abruptly removing the child would harm her development. In June 2011, the Bulgarian Supreme Court of Cassation suspended enforcement following the father’s request to reopen recognition proceedings. In January 2012, it quashed the earlier recognition because the father had not been properly summoned.

After the final Romanian judgment of January 2012 granting custody to the applicant, the Pazardzhik Regional Court recognised that judgment in May 2012. This was upheld by the Sofia Court of Appeal in April 2013 and became final before the Bulgarian Supreme Court of Cassation in May 2014. New enforcement proceedings were brought, but in July 2014 the Pazardzhik District Court suspended enforcement because the father had started Bulgarian proceedings to change custody and because the child had settled well in Bulgaria, spoke only Bulgarian, and was closely attached to her paternal grandparents.

The applicant also attempted international remedies. In July 2011, she sought the child’s return under the Hague Convention, but Bulgaria refused, stating that the Convention had not yet entered into force between Romania and Bulgaria. A request under the Brussels II bis Regulation was also refused by Bulgaria. The Romanian Ministry of Justice advised her to use other avenues, including the Luxembourg Convention or direct application to Bulgarian courts.

The applicant alleged that Romania and Bulgaria failed to protect her family life and to secure the return or enforcement of custody, allowing the child to remain unlawfully with the paternal grandparents. The key facts therefore concern the abduction in Romania, the prolonged custody proceedings, the Bulgarian recognition and enforcement delays and suspensions, and the refusal or unavailability of international return mechanisms.

E.S. v. Romania and Bulgaria concerned an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by a Romanian mother who alleged that Romania and Bulgaria failed to respond adequately to the kidnapping of her daughter and the child’s subsequent retention in Bulgaria, disrupting her family life.

The applicant’s daughter was born in Spain in 2004. The father, R.E.N., was a Bulgarian national. The couple separated in 2008. After living in Spain and Bulgaria, the child returned to Romania with the applicant in mid-2008 and stayed with her maternal grandmother while the applicant went to Spain to work. On 4 November 2008, the paternal grandparents visited the child in Romania. With the maternal grandmother’s consent, they took the child out, ostensibly for ice cream, accompanied by an aunt. They then stopped the car, expelled the aunt, and drove the child to Bulgaria without the applicant’s knowledge or consent. The child remained with the paternal grandparents in Bulgaria thereafter.

The applicant began Romanian custody proceedings in July 2008. In January 2009, the Râmnicu Vâlcea District Court awarded her custody. The father later appealed out of time, arguing he had been in Bulgaria and had not been properly summoned. In December 2009, the Vâlcea County Court quashed the custody decision and remitted the case. In November 2010, the District Court again awarded custody to the applicant, noting the father’s criminal past and the manner of the child’s removal. However, on appeal, the County Court in October 2011 granted custody to the father, relying on the child’s integration in Bulgaria, her preference to stay there, and the fact that she spoke no Romanian. In January 2012, the Piteşti Court of Appeal quashed that decision and upheld the applicant’s custody, making the Romanian judgment final.

In parallel, the applicant sought recognition and enforcement of the Romanian custody judgment in Bulgaria. A Bulgarian court recognised the January 2009 judgment in 2009, upheld on appeal in 2010, and enforcement proceedings began. A handover scheduled for February 2011 failed when the child could not be located; the father was fined. Social services warned that abruptly removing the child from her environment would harm her. In June 2011, the Bulgarian Supreme Court of Cassation suspended enforcement after the father sought reopening of the recognition proceedings, on the ground that he had not been properly summoned. In January 2012, that court quashed the earlier recognition and remitted the case. In May 2012, the Pazardzhik Regional Court recognised the later Romanian judgment of November 2010, upheld on appeal and final in May 2014. New enforcement proceedings were nevertheless suspended in July 2014 because the father had started proceedings to change custody and the child was settled in Bulgaria, spoke only Bulgarian, and had a close relationship with her paternal grandparents.

Attempts to use international mechanisms also failed or were delayed. The Hague Convention had not entered into force between Romania and Bulgaria until June 2013, and Bulgaria refused the applicant’s 2011 request on that basis. A request under the Brussels II bis Regulation was also refused in early 2012, with Bulgaria arguing that the Hague Convention did not apply and that the Regulation did not operate outside its scope. The applicant’s central complaint was that the respondent States’ delays, conflicting decisions, and failure to enforce custody effectively prevented her from restoring family life with her daughter.

In *Jurišić v. Croatia (No. 2)* (Application no. 8000/21, judgment of 7 July 2022), the European Court of Human Rights examined the applicant’s complaint under Article 8 that Croatia had failed to ensure his right to family life through contact with his son, I.R. (born 2006). In an earlier judgment (*Jurišić v. Croatia*, 16 January 2020), the Court had already found a violation of Article 8 because judicial decisions granting the applicant contact rights had not been enforced. Execution of that judgment was still pending before the Committee of Ministers. In January 2021, the applicant filed a new application, arguing that subsequent domestic decisions and his continued inability to have contact with his son constituted a fresh violation.

The relevant facts concerned the period after the earlier judgment. Under a final 2010 contact order, the applicant was to see I.R. every other weekend and during part of school holidays. In May 2019, the child’s psychiatrist, Dr J.G., who had treated I.R. for four years, warned that further expert evaluation or hearing the child in court would harm him. He proposed gradual meetings in his office. The applicant refused, saying he distrusted J.G. and believed he was manipulating the child. In January 2020, the Slavonski Brod Municipal Court terminated enforcement of the 2010 order for a second time. Relying on a psychologist’s report, it found that gradual contact was more appropriate and that coercive enforcement of the outdated 2010 order would traumatise the child. Since the parties refused any agreement and the enforcement court could not amend the final order, enforcement was discontinued. The County Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal in June 2020, and the Constitutional Court declared his complaint inadmissible in October 2020.

Meanwhile, in fresh contact proceedings initiated by the mother in 2019, the child’s guardian ad litem reported that I.R. was willing to give his father one final chance at Dr J.G.’s office. The applicant again refused. The Social Welfare Centre proposed weekly supervised contact in a neutral location without the mother. In November 2020, the Municipal Court issued a new contact order providing for supervised weekly contact, later moving to every other weekend and school holidays if trust developed. The court found that both parents had obstructed contact: the mother had isolated the child, ignored the Centre and delayed proceedings; the applicant denied the child’s medical problems, questioned experts, refused to cooperate with Dr J.G., insisted on his own conditions, and involved police. The court stressed that institutions had taken necessary steps, but the parents themselves were violating the child’s rights. The County Court upheld this decision in May 2021.

Enforcement attempts under the new order also failed. In January 2021, the child refused contact at home. In June and July 2021, scheduled meetings collapsed when the parents argued; I.R., then fourteen, said he did not want contact and alleged past abuse. The applicant told the child his mother would go to prison, focused on the Centre’s staff and his own rights, and did not attend one September 2021 session. The mother was convicted twice of obstructing contact for earlier periods, and further criminal proceedings were pending.

The Government argued that the application concerned only execution of the prior judgment, within the Committee of Ministers’ competence. The applicant claimed that the termination of the old enforcement and the new contact order created new violations. The Court confined its examination to the new period and new domestic decisions. It found no Article 8 violation: the authorities had taken numerous steps consistent with the child’s best interests, and continued non-enforcement was mainly due to the parents’ conduct, particularly the applicant’s refusal to cooperate with gradual contact, rather than any lack of State diligence.

In *Jurišić v. Croatia (No. 2)*, App. No. 8000/21, the European Court of Human Rights (First Section, 7 July 2022) examined the applicant father’s complaint under Article 8 that the Croatian authorities had continued to fail to secure his contact with his son, I.R. (born 2006), despite judicial decisions. A previous judgment, *Jurišić v. Croatia* (no. 29419/17, 16 January 2020), had already found an Article 8 violation for non-enforcement of contact rights; execution of that judgment remained pending before the Committee of Ministers. The applicant’s 2021 application alleged a fresh breach based on later domestic decisions and his continued inability to have contact with I.R.

Under a final 2010 contact order, the applicant was to see I.R. every other weekend and during part of school holidays. Enforcement repeatedly failed. In May 2019, the child’s treating psychiatrist, Dr J.G., advised against further expert evaluation or hearing the child in court and proposed gradual meetings at his office to build trust. The applicant refused, claiming Dr J.G. was biased and was manipulating the child. In January 2020, the Slavonski Brod Municipal Court terminated enforcement for a second time. Relying on a 2018 psychologist report and other expert evidence, it found the 2010 order outdated and impossible to enforce; coercion would further traumatise the child, while gradual contact was preferable. The Zagreb County Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal in June 2020, and the Constitutional Court declared his complaint inadmissible in October 2020.

In parallel, fresh contact proceedings were brought by the mother, M.R., in 2019. The child’s guardian ad litem reported that I.R. was willing to give his father “one final chance” to meet at Dr J.G.’s office; the applicant did not accept. The Social Welfare Centre proposed supervised weekly meetings in a neutral location without the mother. On 2 November 2020, the Municipal Court issued a new contact order: supervised weekly contact in a neutral place, later progressing to every other weekend and school holidays once contact became continuous and trust was established. The court found both parents responsible. The mother had obstructed contact, ignored professional assistance and isolated the child. The father denied the child’s medical problems, questioned experts and doctors, insisted on contact on his own terms, involved the police, and refused to cooperate with Dr J.G. The court stressed that the institutions had taken steps to protect I.R.; contact was failing because of the parents’ conduct, not institutional inaction. This decision became final on 10 May 2021.

Attempts under the new order in January, June, July and August 2021 also failed. The child refused contact, left or protested; the parents argued; the applicant told I.R. that his mother would go to prison. In September 2021, the applicant did not attend. Meanwhile, the mother was convicted twice, in July 2020 and September 2021, of obstructing contact and received suspended sentences; further criminal complaints were pending.

The Government argued the application merely concerned execution of the 2020 judgment and fell within the Committee of Ministers’ competence. The applicant contended that new decisions and the termination of the earlier enforcement order created a fresh violation. The Court confined its review to the new period and new domestic decisions. It found that the continued lack of contact was not due to any lack of diligence by the authorities, who had taken numerous steps in line with the child’s best interests; enforcement mainly failed because of the parents’ conduct. It therefore found no violation of Article 8.

**Case: Jurišić v. Croatia (No. 2), Application no. 8000/21, ECtHR, 7 July 2022**

The applicant, Stjepan Jurišić, a Croatian national, complained under Article 8 of the Convention that he remained unable to have regular contact with his son, I.R., born in 2006, despite judicial decisions granting him contact rights. In an earlier case, *Jurišić v. Croatia* (2020), the Court had already found an Article 8 violation because the authorities failed to enforce contact decisions. That execution process remained pending before the Committee of Ministers. In January 2021, the applicant lodged a fresh application, alleging that subsequent domestic decisions and his continued inability to see his son amounted to a new breach of Article 8.

The key facts concerned two enforcement proceedings and fresh contact proceedings. A final 2010 contact order allowed the applicant contact every other weekend and part of school holidays. In 2019, during enforcement proceedings, the child’s treating psychiatrist, Dr J.G., recommended gradual meetings at his office to build trust. The applicant refused, claiming the doctor was biased and manipulating the child. In January 2020, the Slavonski Brod Municipal Court terminated enforcement of the 2010 order, relying on a 2018 psychologist report which found that gradual contact was appropriate and that coercive enforcement of the outdated order would traumatise the child. The appeal was dismissed in June 2020, and a constitutional complaint was declared inadmissible in October 2020.

In parallel fresh contact proceedings, initiated by the mother in 2019, the child’s guardian ad litem reported that I.R. was willing to give his father “one final chance” at Dr J.G.’s office, but the applicant refused. The Social Welfare Centre proposed weekly supervised contact in a neutral location without the mother present. In November 2020, the court issued a new contact order providing supervised weekly contact, with possible progression to alternate weekends and holidays if trust developed. The court found that both parents had contributed to the failure: the mother obstructed contact, ignored professional help, and delayed proceedings; the applicant denied the child’s medical issues, questioned experts, insisted on his own conditions, involved police, and refused to cooperate with the child’s treating doctor. The court stressed that contact was the child’s right and that both parents were harming his interests. The Zagreb County Court upheld this decision in May 2021.

Subsequent enforcement attempts failed. In January 2021, visits to the child’s home were unsuccessful. In June and July 2021, scheduled meetings broke down when the parents argued; the child left, saying he was fourteen and did not want to be forced. On one occasion the applicant told the child that his mother would end up in prison, while the report noted he stood with crossed arms and focused on the Centre staff rather than engaging with his son. In July and August 2021, the child refused contact or to speak with his father. In September 2021, the applicant did not attend. Meanwhile, the mother was convicted twice of obstructing contact for earlier periods and received suspended sentences; further criminal complaints were pending.

The Government argued that the application concerned only execution of the earlier judgment, within the Committee of Ministers’ competence. The applicant contended that new decisions—the termination of the earlier enforcement order and the new contact order—created fresh violations.

The Court confined its examination to the new period and new domestic decisions. It found that the authorities had taken numerous steps to facilitate contact in line with the child’s best interests. The continued lack of contact was not due to a lack of diligence by the authorities but mainly to the parents’ conduct, particularly the applicant’s refusal to cooperate with gradual arrangements and the mother’s obstruction. Accordingly, the Court found no fresh violation of Article 8.

The case of **Naddur v. the Republic of Moldova** (Application no. 22939/19) concerns criminal proceedings in Moldova in which the applicant’s first-instance acquittal was reversed on appeal and replaced with a conviction, without the appellate court rehearing the witnesses or the victim. The applicant, Mr Issam Naddur, is a Ukrainian national born in 1966 and living in Kiev. He was represented before the European Court of Human Rights by Mr I. Cernolev, a lawyer practising in Chișinău. The application was lodged under Article 34 of the Convention on 12 April 2019. The Moldovan Government was represented by its Agent, Mr O. Rotari. The Ukrainian Government decided not to intervene in the proceedings under Article 36 § 1 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 1 (b) of the Rules of Court.

The case was heard by the Second Section of the Court, sitting as a Committee composed of Judges Jovan Ilievski, Lorraine Schembri Orland and Diana Sârcu, with Dorothee von Arnim as Deputy Section Registrar. The Committee deliberated in private on 22 November 2022 and delivered its judgment on 13 December 2022.

Factually, the applicant was charged with fraud. The prosecution alleged that he had been part of a group of persons who had defrauded a foreign businessperson of a large amount of money. The case therefore depended substantially on the evidence of the victim, the applicant and numerous witnesses, as well as other material in the case file. At first instance, the court heard the victim, the applicant and numerous witnesses, and examined all the available evidence. After that full evidentiary examination, the first-instance court acquitted the applicant.

The Chișinău Court of Appeal then reversed that acquittal and found the applicant guilty as charged. The emergency placement was confirmed by the County Social Welfare Board and upheld by the courts, becoming final in October 2015. After a retrial in October 2017, the District Court on 16 November 2017 found serious deficiencies in the parents’ care. Relying on expert evidence, it found reduced caring skills, difficulty understanding X’s needs, and that X had elevated care needs and adverse reactions after contact. It treated the placement as permanent “for growing up” and set contact at three one-hour supervised sessions per year. The foster home’s address was kept undisclosed. Appeals were refused in 2018.

The Court declared the grandmother’s complaint inadmissible for non-exhaustion because she had not been a party to domestic proceedings. It declared admissible the Article 8 complaint brought by the parents and child. The applicants argued that authorities failed to investigate possible placement with relatives in Slovakia and that the evidence did not justify removal or severe contact restrictions. The Government maintained that the emergency placement and contact limitations were necessary due to serious care deficiencies and failed assistance measures, and that the placement was not intended to be permanent. Third-party interveners, including Slovakia and the Czech Republic, focused on the need to balance the child’s interests with family reunification.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 8. While the initial care concerns and foster placement were supported by relevant reasons, the severe limitations on parental contact were incompatible with the aim of family reunification. The domestic court treated the placement as permanent and for the child’s entire upbringing, yet failed to examine whether any alternative arrangement could avoid permanent foster care, including placement with relatives abroad or other reunification possibilities. The contact restrictions—three supervised hours per year—were therefore not adequately justified. (mother, Norwegian national), their child X, born in January 2015, and J.L., the paternal grandmother living in Slovakia. They complained under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention about Norwegian child-welfare measures. The Court declared the grandmother’s complaint inadmissible for non-exhaustion, found no conflict of interest preventing the parents from acting for X, and found a violation of Article 8 regarding severe contact restrictions and the failure to examine alternatives to permanent foster care.

The key facts began shortly after X’s birth. On 26 March 2015, X was taken into emergency foster care. The hospital had alerted child-welfare services because the parents left with X despite being told she needed treatment and was not ready for discharge. Child-welfare services had offered extensive guidance on feeding, nursing, sleep, routines and safety. Concerns included leaving X alone on a nursing table or sofa, switching off an alarm, the father shooing X when she cried, and a lack of interaction and social stimuli. X showed irregular development. The emergency placement was confirmed by the County Social Welfare Board on 31 March 2015, upheld by the District Court on 25 June 2015, and became final on 30 October 2015 when the High Court refused leave to appeal.

Initial parental contact was one hour every fourteen days, supervised. A care-order application followed on 7 May 2015. Contact was reduced in November 2015 to one hour every six weeks, upheld in February 2016. On 7 March 2016, the Board rejected the care-order application. The child-welfare services then increased contact to every three weeks. After procedural problems, including a finding of judicial bias, the case was retried before a different District Court, which gave judgment on 16 November 2017.

The District Court found that returning X to her parents would involve serious care deficiencies. It relied on a court-appointed expert who assessed both parents as having reduced caring skills. The mother had difficulty understanding X’s needs; the father was intense and invasive; and neither had benefited sufficiently from extensive guidance. X had elevated care needs and developmental delay. Contact sessions were stressful and produced adverse reactions in X. The court viewed the placement as permanent, “for growing up,” and set contact at three times per year for one hour, supervised, effective immediately. It also allowed non-disclosure of the foster home address because of pressure from the parents and X’s need for stability. The High Court refused leave to appeal on 20 March 2018, and the Supreme Court’s Appeals Committee dismissed the further appeal on 12 June 2018.

The applicants alleged that the authorities failed to investigate relatives in Slovakia, including the grandmother, who had medical education, and failed to consider whether X could live with relatives there. They argued there was no evidence they posed a risk and that the contact restrictions were unjustified. The Government argued that the emergency placement was necessary after assistance measures failed, and that contact restrictions were justified by the long-term placement, the parents’ inability to care for X, the need to protect her from stress, and the foster family’s safety.

The Court found the Article 8 complaint admissible for the first three applicants. It held that the severe limitations on parental contact—three one-hour sessions per year—were at variance with the aim of family reunification. The authorities treated foster care as permanent without examining whether another arrangement, such as placement with relatives in Slovakia, could avoid permanent foster care. This failure, together with the severe contact restrictions, violated Article 8.

**Case: Chakvetadze v. Georgia (Application no. 55949/10), ECtHR Fifth Section, judgment 22 September 2022.**

The applicant, Zurab Chakvetadze, a Georgian national, complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the authorities’ delay in enforcing a final judgment in his favour.

On 25 December 2008 police stopped and searched him, seizing a Subutex tablet and a bullet. A search of his apartment found heroin, another bullet, and USD 230,050 in cash. The cash was seized as evidence and deposited with the National Bank of Georgia. He was charged with unlawful acquisition and possession of narcotic substances and ammunition.

On 23 September 2009 the Tbilisi City Court acquitted him on the heroin charge but convicted him regarding the Subutex tablet and bullet. He received one year’s imprisonment and a fine of GEL 352,000 (about USD 212,385). The trial court found the seized cash was not linked to the criminal proceedings and ordered its return to the applicant, unless he chose to use it to pay the fine. On 4 December 2009 the Tbilisi Court of Appeal maintained only the criminal fine and ordered his immediate release. The Supreme Court rejected his appeal on 12 March 2010.

On 14 April 2010 the Court of Appeal issued two enforcement writs: one for the criminal fine and one for return of the seized cash by the police. The applicant was told the police had been instructed to return the money. On 25 April 2010 the National Bureau of Enforcement asked him to pay the fine voluntarily, plus a 7% enforcement fee of GEL 24,640 (about USD 14,867). On 30 April he gave a power of attorney to J.Kh. to receive the cash, transfer USD 220,000 to alleged owners, and use USD 10,050 toward the fine. That request was apparently unanswered. On 3 May the enforcement bureau sought a list of his assets; on 7 May the applicant replied that he had not received the cash, repeated his claims about shared ownership, and said enforcement could proceed against his own USD 10,050 share. During May 2010 he repeatedly asked the police and prosecutor to enforce the return of the cash, but received no response.

On 30 November 2011 the police requested the National Bank to release the cash, and it was returned to the police the same day. The applicant was asked to come to the police station. After he signed the return report, a bailiff appeared and seized the entire amount to enforce the criminal fine and related enforcement fee. The applicant claimed the cash was never physically returned to him before seizure. The excess GEL 4,714 (about USD 2,800) was later returned on 4 February 2012. The alleged owners did not complain.

On 31 December 2011 the applicant challenged the enforcement proceedings. He argued that enforcement of the final judgment in his favour had been delayed for almost two years; that the 30 November 2011 return was a sham because the cash was seized immediately after he signed the report and before he could take it; that the delay had prevented him from paying the fine voluntarily; and that the 7% enforcement fee was unlawful and unfair. On 27 April 2012 the Tbilisi City Court rejected his claim, relying on section 38 of the Enforcement Proceedings Act. The Court of Appeal upheld that decision on 4 July 2012, and the Supreme Court rejected his appeal on 11 February 2013.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to the unjustifiably lengthy delay in enforcing the judgment. The Government argued that he had failed to exhaust domestic remedies and, regarding the property complaint, had not shown victim status due to the alleged shared ownership of the cash.

**Case Name:** *Drelon v. France* (Applications nos. 3153/16 and 27758/18), European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, judgment of 8 September 2022.

The applicant, Laurent Drelon, a French national born in 1970, complained under Articles 8 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights about the collection and retention of personal data reflecting his presumed sexual orientation and about the rejection of his offers to donate blood. The respondent was France.

The key facts concerned Mr Drelon’s attempts to donate blood through the Établissement français du sang (“EFS”), a State-run blood donation body. On 16 November 2004, during a pre-donation medical interview at an EFS site in Île-de-France, he was asked whether he had ever had sexual intercourse with another man. He refused to answer. As a result, his offer to donate blood was rejected. During the interview, EFS entered personal data about him into a computer database, including his identification and contact details and a contraindication code “FR08,” which at the time was used for men who had had sexual intercourse with another man.

On 9 August 2006, the applicant tried again to give blood. He was told that he was listed under code “FR08” and was deferred. When he requested a copy of his personal data, a section on applicable disqualifications showed that the contraindication had been registered on 16 November 2004 and was valid until 2278. On 26 May 2016, he attempted to donate again and presented negative biological tests for HIV-1, HIV-2 and HCV. He was nevertheless rejected, and the doctor noted that his previous offers had been rejected because of his presumed homosexual behaviour.

The applicant lodged a criminal complaint in 2007 for discrimination, alleging the refusals in 2004 and 2006 and the registration of his presumed homosexuality. The investigation initially found no discrimination, but the Paris Court of Appeal in 2009 directed an investigation into whether the recording or retention of sensitive personal data without express consent amounted to an offence under Article 226-19 of the Criminal Code. The EFS confirmed that its Île-de-France branch operated a database containing contraindications, including code “FR08,” that the processing had been disclosed to the CNIL, and that the applicant’s data had been transferred in 2007 to a new database where a specific code was still used for the same contraindication. The criminal proceedings were ultimately discontinued. In 2015, the Court of Cassation held that no criminal offence had been committed because the processing fell within a statutory exception for preventive medicine and health services performed by health professionals, so express consent was not required.

Separately, the applicant challenged ministerial orders defining contraindications to blood donation. The 2009 order provided for a permanent contraindication for men who had had sexual intercourse with another man. The 2016 order replaced this with a twelve-month deferral for such men. In 2017, the Conseil d’État dismissed his claim, finding that the measure was based on sexual behaviour rather than sexual orientation, was justified by blood safety concerns, and did not itself require the collection or retention of personal data.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 8. It held that the collection and retention of data on the applicant’s sexual behaviour was based on speculation, because he had refused to provide information during the pre-donation interview, and that the retention of the data until 2278 was excessive. Although blood safety provided relevant and sufficient reasons, the measure exceeded the State’s margin of appreciation.

In 2006, when he tried again, he was told he was listed under FR08 and was deferred. A copy of his data showed the contraindication had been registered on 16 November 2004 and was valid until 2278. In 2016, despite presenting negative HIV and hepatitis C tests, he was again rejected; the doctor noted that his previous offers had been refused because of his presumed homosexual behaviour.

The applicant complained that the EFS had collected and retained personal data reflecting his presumed sexual orientation and had refused his blood donations. He alleged violations of Article 8 (right to respect for private life) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

In 2007 he lodged a criminal complaint for discrimination and applied to join the proceedings as a civil party. The investigation initially found no criminal discrimination, but the Paris Court of Appeal considered whether the facts might constitute the offence of recording sensitive personal data without express consent under Article 226-19 of the Criminal Code. The criminal proceedings were eventually discontinued. In 2015, the Court of Cassation held that the data processing fell within a statutory exception for preventive medicine and health services under the 1978 Data Processing Act, and that no violation of Articles 8 or 14 arose because the measure was legitimate, necessary to protect health, and sufficiently precise.

The applicant also challenged the ministerial orders defining blood-donation contraindications. The 2009 order provided a permanent contraindication for any man who had had sexual intercourse with another man. The 2016 order replaced this with a twelve-month deferral for whole-blood donations and a four-month deferral for certain plasma donations, based on sexual behaviour. In 2017 the Conseil d’État dismissed his challenge, finding that the measure pursued blood safety, was based on epidemiological evidence concerning HIV prevalence and the “window period”, and did not discriminate because it referred to sexual behaviour rather than sexual orientation. It also found that the order did not itself require collection or retention of personal data on rejected donors.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the central alleged violations concerned the collection and retention by a public body of data revealing the applicant’s presumed sexual orientation, without express consent and for an excessive period until 2278, and the deferral from blood donation based on the contraindication for men who had had sexual intercourse with another man. The Government relied on blood safety. The Court accepted that blood safety could constitute relevant and sufficient reasons for the deferral itself, but found that the collection of data on the applicant’s sexual behaviour was based on mere speculation resulting from his refusal to provide information during the pre-donation interview, and that the retention period was excessive. France therefore exceeded its margin of appreciation, resulting in a violation of Article 8 concerning the collection and retention of the applicant’s personal data.

France** (Applications nos. 3153/16 and 27758/18, ECtHR, 8 September 2022) concerned a French man, born in 1970, who attempted to donate blood and complained about the collection and retention of data reflecting his presumed sexual orientation and about being refused as a donor. He relied on Articles 8 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

In November 2004, during a pre-donation medical interview at a blood donation site run by the Établissement français du sang (EFS), a State-run body, the applicant was asked whether he had ever had sexual intercourse with another man. He refused to answer. His offer to donate was consequently rejected. The EFS entered personal data about him into its computer database, including a contraindication code “FR08”, which was then used for men who had had sexual intercourse with another man. In May 2016, he tried once more, presenting negative HIV-1, HIV-2 and HCV tests, but was again rejected; the doctor noted that his earlier offers had been rejected because of his presumed homosexual behaviour.

The applicant lodged a criminal complaint in 2007 alleging discrimination and unlawful recording of sensitive personal data. French courts found that the facts did not constitute discrimination. The Paris Court of Appeal initially identified a possible offence under Article 226-19 of the Criminal Code, which criminalised recording personal data on health or sexual orientation without express consent, but the proceedings were later discontinued. In 2013, the Investigation Division held that the collection of the data was lawful because the processing had been disclosed to the CNIL and was covered by health regulations. In 2015, the Court of Cassation found that the processing fell within an exception in the Law of 6 January 1978 for preventive medicine and health services, performed by health professionals bound by secrecy. It held that the measure was legitimate, necessary to protect health, sufficiently precise, and struck a not unbalanced reconciliation between privacy and public health.

Separately, the applicant challenged ministerial orders defining contraindications to blood donation. The 2009 order permanently deferred men who had had sex with men. After that order was repealed, the Conseil d’État found his challenge moot. He then challenged the Order of 5 April 2016, which replaced the permanent deferral with a twelve-month deferral for men who had had sexual intercourse with another man for whole-blood donations, and a four-month deferral for apheresis plasma donations in certain circumstances. In December 2017, the Conseil d’État dismissed the claim, relying on public-health data about HIV prevalence among men who have sex with men, the “window period” for detection, transfusion risk, and the lack of data on shorter deferral periods. It held that the Minister acted on grounds of sexual behaviour, not sexual orientation, and that the order itself did not require collection or retention of data on rejected donors.

Before the ECtHR, the key facts were that the EFS recorded a contraindication based not on actual disclosed sexual behaviour but on the applicant’s refusal to answer, effectively presuming his sexual orientation. The data were then retained until 2278. Although blood safety provided relevant and sufficient reasons for donor selection, the Court found that collecting data on sexual behaviour based on speculation, and retaining it excessively by a public body, exceeded the State’s margin of appreciation, violating Article 8.

In *Gherardi Martiri v. San Marino* (App. no. 35511/20, judgment 15 December 2022), the applicant, an Italian national, alleged that she had been defrauded by Banca Commerciale San Marinese S.p.A., some of its employees, and third persons. She complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that San Marino failed its positive obligation to protect her property rights, and under Article 6 § 1 that the related civil proceedings were excessively long.

The fraud arose from a 2005 real-estate sale. The buyer required the applicant to open an account with the bank. She deposited €200,000 in May 2005, and the remaining €1.3 million was paid in July 2005. On 22 July 2005, while at the bank to guarantee a friend’s €100,000 loan, she signed documents opening a joint current account and securities deposit. In 2009 she discovered that a €100,000 credit had been used and that an account she believed held about €800,000 had a zero balance. Bank records showed that from 2005 M.R. had made high-risk investments under an alleged power of attorney. The applicant denied giving such a mandate: it was undated, did not refer to an account, lacked bank signatures or stamp, and bore a contested signature. On 22 July 2005, while she was at the bank, M.R. allegedly made three high-risk investments totaling €1.1 million. Other assets were transferred to unknown persons, including €73,001.42 without authorization. Amicable settlement attempts failed.

She reported the matter to San Marino’s banking supervisory authority in 2011 and filed a criminal complaint in March 2012 for fraud against the bank and several individuals. In 2014 the Investigating Judge discontinued proceedings, finding that high-risk investments had caused losses of about €700,000 but that fraud was time-barred; M.R.’s conduct was negligent and the bank indirectly involved, though wilful intent and profit were not fully proven. On appeal, the Judge of Appeals reopened the investigation in November 2014, finding it incomplete and that deception and malicious intent might be established. In 2017 the Investigating Judge again discontinued: M.R. had acted without a regular mandate, which was not recorded in the bank’s system; bank officials were aware of and did not object to the transactions. However, no more serious offence emerged, and fraud remained time-barred.

In parallel, in April 2015 the applicant brought civil proceedings against M.R., bank officials, the bank, and its successor, A.B. S.p.a., seeking damages for unauthorized use and misappropriation. The defendants relied on the alleged mandate. In 2018 the judge declared the claim inadmissible against A.B. S.p.a. because it had been placed in compulsory administrative winding-up, and found the action could not continue against the others because liability was pleaded jointly and severally. The applicant was refused inclusion in the statement of liabilities and filed an objection in 2018. In 2019 the objection court found it lacked competence because the file had been assigned to the wrong judge, but ordered reopening before the competent judge. The proceedings were still pending in 2022. A further attempt in 2021 was held inadmissible while the winding-up remained on the register.

The European Court of Human Rights found that San Marino had provided adequate criminal and civil remedies for the protection of the applicant’s property rights, so there was no violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. However, it found a violation of Article 6 § 1 (civil) due to the excessive length of the ongoing civil proceedings.

Maria Cristina Gherardi Martiri, an Italian national, alleged that San Marino violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) and Article 6 § 1 (reasonable time) because she was defrauded by Banca Commerciale San Marinese S.p.A., its officials and third persons, and because her civil proceedings were excessively long.

In 2005 the applicant sold a property in Rimini for about EUR 1.5 million. The buyer required that the transaction go through an account at Banca Commerciale San Marinese. In May 2005 an account was opened with EUR 200,000; in July 2005 the remaining EUR 1.3 million was paid. On 22 July 2005, when she went to the bank to guarantee a friend’s EUR 100,000 loan, the bank required her to open a joint account and a securities deposit. She signed documents after brief explanations. She later discovered that a EUR 100,000 credit had been granted without her knowledge and that the account she believed held about EUR 800,000 had a zero balance.

Investigations showed that M.R., a third person connected to the buyer, had made high-risk investments totalling EUR 1.1 million using an alleged power of attorney. The applicant denied giving such a mandate; it was undated, did not refer to the account, was not stamped or signed by bank staff, and her signature was disputed. M.R. also transferred securities to unknown persons and to the applicant’s trusted person, and EUR 73,001.42 was moved without authorisation. The loss was approximately EUR 700,000, though EUR 40,300 was later repaid.

In 2011 the applicant reported the matter to San Marino’s banking supervisory authority. The authority said disputes fell to the judicial authorities and requested information from the bank. The bank was placed under extraordinary administration in 2011 and later transferred its branch to Asset Banca S.p.a. In 2012 criminal proceedings for fraud were opened. In 2014 the Investigating Judge discontinued the case, finding that M.R. had made unauthorised high-risk investments and the bank had been negligent, but that wilful intent and profit were not fully proven and the fraud was time-barred. On appeal, the investigation was reopened in 2014 because it was incomplete. In 2017 the Investigating Judge again discontinued the case, confirming that M.R. had acted without a regular mandate and that the bank had not objected to obvious irregularities, but no more serious offence emerged and the fraud remained time-barred.

Meanwhile, in April 2015 the applicant sued M.R., bank officials, the bank and Asset Banca in civil proceedings, seeking joint and several liability for the unauthorised use and misappropriation of her funds. The defendants relied on the alleged mandate. In 2017 Asset Banca was placed in compulsory administrative winding-up. In 2018 the civil court declared the action inadmissible against Asset Banca because winding-up rules barred proceedings concerning its assets and required all related matters to be heard by one judge; because the applicant had pleaded joint liability, the case against the other defendants could not continue. Her attempt to be included as a creditor in the liquidation was refused. Related objection proceedings were later transferred to the competent judge and, as of 2022, remained pending. These facts underpinned her complaints that San Marino failed its positive obligation to protect her property and that the civil proceedings were excessively long

**Gherardi Martiri v. San Marino** (Application no. 35511/20) concerned an Italian national who alleged that she had been the victim of organised fraud by Banca Commerciale San Marinese (“the bank”), its employees and third persons, and that San Marino had failed to protect her property rights and had delayed her civil proceedings.

In 2005 the applicant sold a property in Rimini. The buyer required that the transaction be handled through an account with the bank. She opened a current account and paid in EUR 200,000 as an advance; the remaining EUR 1,300,000 was later paid in July 2005. On the same occasion, she also opened a joint account and securities deposit account as security for a friend’s EUR 100,000 loan. In 2009 the bank asked her to review that credit. She then discovered that the account she believed held around EUR 800,000 had a zero balance and that EUR 80,000 of the credit had been used.

Investigations showed that, from 2005, a third person, M.R., had carried out high-risk investments and transfers using an alleged power of attorney. The applicant denied knowingly granting such a mandate; it was undated, did not refer to a bank account, and was not signed or stamped by the bank. She alleged that M.R., with the involvement or tolerance of bank officials, made investments totalling about EUR 1,100,000, causing her to lose approximately EUR 700,000. She also alleged unauthorised transfers from her accounts.

In 2011 the applicant reported the matter to San Marino’s banking supervisory authority, which stated that disputes between banks and customers fell to the judicial authorities. The bank was placed under extraordinary administration in 2011 and later transferred its branch and legal relationships to Asset Banca S.p.a.

In March 2012 the applicant lodged a criminal complaint for fraud against the bank, C.G., M.R. and P.D. In September 2014 the Investigating Judge discontinued the proceedings. He found that the investments had been made without the applicant’s consent and that M.R.’s conduct, and indirectly the bank’s, had been negligent, but the evidence did not fully establish M.R.’s profit or wilful intent; the fraud charge was also time-barred. On appeal, the investigation was reopened in November 2014 because it had been incomplete. In March 2017 the Investigating Judge again discontinued the case. Further investigation confirmed that M.R. had acted without a regular mandate and that the bank had not objected to obvious irregularities, but no more serious offence emerged and the fraud was time-barred.

In parallel, in April 2015 the applicant brought civil proceedings against M.R., bank officials, the bank and Asset Banca, seeking reimbursement and damages for unauthorised use and misappropriation of her funds. Asset Banca was placed in administrative compulsory winding-up in June 2017. The civil judge declared the action inadmissible because winding-up rules required all asset-related matters to be dealt with by a single judge, and the applicant had pleaded joint and several liability. Her attempt to be included as a creditor in the statement of liabilities was rejected. Her objection proceedings were affected by a competence issue, then reopened before the competent judge, and remained pending as of 2022. Although the winding-up was later declared illegal, Asset Banca remained inoperative.

The applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that San Marino had breached its positive obligations to protect her possessions by failing to provide adequate criminal and civil remedies for the fraud. She also complained under Article 6 § 1 that the civil proceedings were excessively long. The Court ultimately found that adequate criminal and civil remedies existed for the Article 1 Protocol No. 1 complaint, but that the length of the civil proceedings violated Article 6 § 1.

In *Alleh and Others v. Norway* (Application no. 569/20, 23 June 2022), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Norway’s expulsion of the first applicant, a Djiboutian national, and its two-year re-entry ban violated Article 8 of the Convention as regards her family life with her Norwegian husband and their four Norwegian children.

The first applicant arrived in Norway in 2001 and applied for asylum under the false pretext of being Somali, giving a fabricated personal history. Her asylum application was rejected in 2002 and her appeal dismissed in 2003. She remained in Norway unlawfully. In 2002 she met the second applicant, a Norwegian citizen; they married in April 2004 while she had no lawful residence. Shortly afterwards, she applied for residence based on the marriage, repeating her false identity and country of origin. She received temporary residence permits in 2005 and 2006. In 2007 she applied for and obtained Norwegian citizenship by again claiming to be Somali and signing that her information was correct and complete. The couple had four children, born in 2005, 2009 (twins), and 2013.

In 2014, following a police inquiry into persons who had claimed to be Somali, suspicions arose that the first applicant was Djiboutian. When questioned, she maintained her false account, but in December 2014 she finally gave her correct identity and origin. In June 2015 the Directorate of Immigration withdrew her Norwegian citizenship. In November 2015 she was expelled from Norway with a two-year re-entry ban. Her administrative appeal was dismissed in March 2016. The Immigration Appeals Board found that the husband could adequately care for the children in Norway if the mother left, that the family could potentially move to Djibouti, and that the seriousness of her repeated immigration-law breaches, general deterrence, and respect for the law outweighed the children’s best interests. It also noted that contact could continue and that the ban was limited and potentially revisable.

Before the domestic courts, the Oslo City Court upheld the expulsion. It found her violations intentional, serious, and repeated over approximately 13 years, involving false identities, false documents, and false asylum claims. It considered her ties to Djibouti, the possibility of family relocation or visits, the husband’s ability to care for the children, and the children’s sadness, but found no disproportionate burden. The Borgarting High Court later declared the expulsion invalid as disproportionate vis-à-vis the children. It emphasized that the mother was the primary carer, the children were more attached to her, the twins were somewhat vulnerable, the youngest was closely attached, and the father worked long hours and might struggle as sole carer. The Supreme Court reversed in December 2019. It held that where family life was established while residence was precarious and based on false information, expulsion generally breaches Article 8 only in exceptional circumstances. It found no insurmountable obstacles to family life in Djibouti, no unusually great burden on the children, and that the two-year ban was limited and could be revised or relaxed. The ECtHR agreed, finding no Article 8 violation. The domestic courts had duly assessed proportionality, no exceptional circumstances existed, and Norway’s margin of appreciation had not been exceeded.

**Case: Alleleh and Others v. Norway (ECtHR, 23 June 2022)**

The applicants were Ms Neima Aden Alleleh, a Djiboutian national; Mr Rolf Erik Kristensen, a Norwegian national; and their four children, who are Norwegian citizens. They complained under Article 8 of the Convention that the first applicant’s expulsion from Norway with a two-year re-entry ban unlawfully interfered with their family life.

The key facts concerned the first applicant’s long-running immigration fraud. She arrived in Norway in September 2001 and applied for asylum, falsely claiming to be Somali and giving a detailed but untrue personal history. Her asylum application was rejected in 2002 and her appeal dismissed in 2003. She remained in Norway unlawfully. In 2004 she married the second applicant, a Norwegian citizen, while she had no lawful residence. Shortly afterwards she applied for residence based on the marriage, repeating her false Somali identity and false information. She was granted temporary residence in 2005, renewed in 2006, and was granted Norwegian citizenship in 2007, all on the basis of false information. The couple had four children, born in 2005, 2009 (twins), and 2013.

In 2014 the police suspected she was actually Djiboutian. She maintained her false account until December 2014, when she finally disclosed her correct identity and country of origin. In June 2015 her Norwegian citizenship was withdrawn. In November 2015 she was expelled from Norway with a two-year re-entry ban. The Immigration Appeals Board dismissed her appeal in March 2016. It found that the second applicant could adequately care for the children in Norway if she left; alternatively, the family could move to Djibouti, where they had a family network. It considered the burden on the children not exceptional and held that the seriousness of her immigration breaches and general deterrence outweighed family interests.

The Oslo City Court upheld the expulsion. The Borgarting High Court reversed, finding the expulsion disproportionate for the children because the first applicant was their primary carer, the children were strongly attached to her, two twins were somewhat vulnerable, and the second applicant worked long hours and might struggle as sole carer. The Supreme Court reversed again. It stressed that the first applicant had repeatedly and intentionally provided false information over about 13 years; her residence and citizenship were based on fraud; and family life was established on a precarious basis. It found no insurmountable obstacles to family life in Djibouti, no extraordinary circumstances, and noted the two-year ban was limited and could be revised.

Before the ECtHR, the central Article 8 issues were whether expulsion would rupture family life disproportionately and whether the children’s best interests outweighed immigration control. The Court noted the serious breaches, the precarious residence, the family’s ties to Norway, the possibility of relocating to Djibouti, and the father’s ability to care for the children. It found no insurmountable obstacles and no exceptional circumstances. Domestic courts had duly assessed proportionality in light of the Court’s case-law, and the margin of appreciation was not transgressed. There was therefore no violation of Article 8.

In *Alleh and Others v. Norway* (App. no. 569/20, ECtHR 23 June 2022), the applicants were a Djiboutian national, Ms Neima Aden Alleleh; her Norwegian husband, Mr Rolf Erik Kristensen; and their four Norwegian-citizen children. They complained under Article 8 of the Convention that the first applicant’s expulsion from Norway with a two-year re-entry ban violated their right to respect for family life.

The first applicant arrived in Norway in 2001 and applied for asylum, falsely claiming to be Somali and giving a detailed but untrue personal history. Her asylum application was refused in 2002 and her appeal dismissed in 2003. She remained in Norway unlawfully. In 2003 she sought revision of the refusal, again giving false information and presenting false identity papers. Meanwhile, she met the second applicant in 2002 and married him in April 2004, while she had no lawful residence. Shortly afterward she applied for residence based on the marriage, repeating her false Somali identity and history. She was granted temporary residence in 2005, renewed in 2006, and in 2007 was granted Norwegian citizenship based on her false claim to be Somali.

The couple had four children: born in 2005, twins in 2009, and a fourth child in 2013. The first applicant was the primary daily caregiver, while the second applicant worked long hours.

In 2014, following a general police inquiry into persons who had claimed to be Somali, suspicion arose that the first applicant was Djiboutian. When questioned, she maintained her false story. In late 2014 she finally revealed her correct identity and country of origin. In June 2015 the immigration authorities withdrew her Norwegian citizenship. In November 2015 she was expelled from Norway with a two-year re-entry ban, based on serious and repeated breaches of immigration law—providing materially incorrect and misleading information, using false identity documents, and obtaining residence and citizenship on false premises.

The Immigration Appeals Board upheld the expulsion. It found the breaches serious, general deterrence important, and considered the children’s best interests. It noted that the second applicant could care for the children in Norway and that the family could move to Djibouti, where the first applicant had family and knew the language and culture. The Oslo City Court agreed. The Borgarting High Court reversed, finding the expulsion disproportionate for the children because they were more strongly attached to their mother, she was their primary caregiver, two twins were somewhat vulnerable, the youngest was very attached to her, and the father’s long working hours created a risk of unusually heavy burden. The Supreme Court restored the expulsion decision. It emphasised the gravity of the first applicant’s repeated fraud over about 13 years, the precarious basis of her residence, the absence of insurmountable obstacles to family life in Djibouti, the children’s generally positive development, and the limited, revisable two-year ban. It found no exceptional circumstances or unusually great burden on the children.

Before the European Court, the key Article 8 issues were whether the expulsion and re-entry ban struck a fair balance between immigration control and family life. The Court noted that family life was created when the first applicant’s residence was precarious due to her false information; that there were no insurmountable obstacles to the family moving to Djibouti; that the father could adequately care for the children in Norway; and that the two-year ban could be revised if circumstances worsened and brief visits might be possible. The Court found the domestic courts had properly assessed proportionality and that Norway had not exceeded its margin of appreciation. It held there was no violation of Article 8.
