The European Court of Human Rights case *Theo National Construct S.R.L. v. the Republic of Moldova* (2022) concerned a Romanian road-construction company’s complaint that it was the victim of a “raider attack”—illegal seizure of its assets with the assistance of compliant courts and officials—and was deprived of its possessions contrary to Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention.

In 2007 the applicant agreed with a Moldovan businessman and political party leader, Mr Ș., to enter Moldova’s road-construction market. Under an April 2007 agreement, it was to become a 50% partner in company Q. by contributing 23 pieces of road-construction equipment worth over €1 million. On 3 May 2007 the State Registration Chamber registered the amended charter, making the applicant a 50% partner and increasing company Q.’s capital to about €1 million. The equipment was imported and re-examined on 8 May 2007. In October 2007 company Q. signed a state road renovation contract worth about €24.5 million. To finance the works, company Q. took bank loans exceeding €1.5 million, pledging the equipment; the applicant’s chief executive also pledged his Chișinău house.

Relations deteriorated in 2010 after company Q.’s CEO, without consulting the applicant, gave interest-free loans of about €255,000 to company S., controlled by Mr Ș. The applicant had the CEO replaced, and company Q. sought recovery of the loans. Company S. then challenged the valuation report underlying the applicant’s contribution to company Q. It asked the Moldovan Chamber of Commerce (MCC) to revoke its 2007 valuation, claiming the equipment had not been physically inspected. The MCC refused, noting that document-based valuation was permitted and that the equipment had in fact been inspected on arrival in May 2007. In May 2010 company S. nevertheless began administrative proceedings before the Chișinău Court of Appeal seeking annulment of the valuation, initially without naming the applicant as a defendant.

The proceedings were marked by serious procedural irregularities. The applicant was joined late. It alleged that minutes of a 22 December 2010 hearing were fabricated, that a purported supplement seeking its exclusion had not been in the case file when inspected, and that hearing dates and summons were altered. Although the applicant understood the next hearing would be on 2 March 2011, the file indicated 2 February 2011; handwritten dates appeared corrected from “02.03.11” to “02.02.11.” The applicant did not attend the 2 February hearing. On that date, the Court of Appeal annulled the MCC valuations and the State Registration Chamber’s 2007 registration decision, reinstated the parties as before 3 May 2007, and thereby excluded the applicant from company Q.’s partners. It ordered immediate enforcement without explaining the urgency.

On 4 February 2011 a State Registration Chamber officer—later shown to be the wife of the deputy president of Mr Ș.’s party—implemented the exclusion, reducing company Q.’s capital to about €14,000. The applicant’s separate challenge failed. On appeal to the Supreme Court of Justice, it raised time-bar, jurisdiction, and case-file tampering objections; the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal without addressing them.

Afterward, company Q.’s management changed, the equipment was used or taken by the bank, the pledged house was lost, and company Q. entered bankruptcy. The ECtHR found that the applicant’s exclusion caused loss of its 50% shareholding and participation in the multi-million contract. The domestic decisions were contrary to domestic law, arbitrary and manifestly unreasonable; the courts failed to address the applicant’s serious allegations of tampering and its time-bar objection. The State thus failed to provide a proper forum for the applicant to assert and enforce its rights, violating Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The applicant, Theo National Construct S.R.L., is a Romanian road-construction company. In 2007 it agreed with a Moldovan businessman and political party leader, Mr Ș., to enter Moldova. Under an April 2007 agreement, it was to acquire a 50% stake in company Q. by contributing 23 pieces of road construction equipment worth over EUR 1,031,965. The contribution and amended charter were registered on 3 May 2007, raising Q.’s statutory capital from about EUR 14,000 to about EUR 1 million. The equipment was imported and its value confirmed by the Moldovan Chamber of Commerce (MCC). In October 2007, Q. signed a road renovation contract with the State Road Administration worth about EUR 24.5 million. Q. took bank loans exceeding EUR 1.5 million, pledging the equipment; the applicant’s CEO also pledged his Chișinău house.

In 2010 relations deteriorated after Q.’s CEO, without consulting the applicant, gave interest-free loans to company S., controlled by Mr Ș. Company S. then asked the MCC to revoke its 2007 valuation, arguing the equipment had not been physically inspected; the MCC refused, noting the equipment was later physically examined and the report was advisory. In May 2010, S. brought administrative proceedings before the Chișinău Court of Appeal seeking annulment of the valuation. The applicant was not initially a party and was joined only in December 2010. It alleged serious procedural abuses: although the 22 December 2010 hearing was postponed because S.’s lawyer attended a funeral, the file contained minutes showing that hearing took place; the minutes bore a 2011 case number. The applicant’s representative attended only the 20 January 2011 hearing. He claimed no written supplement seeking its exclusion was then in the file. The next hearing was allegedly set for 2 March 2011, but summons and confirmation forms showed handwritten corrections from “02.03.11” to “02.02.11.” On 2 February 2011, in the applicant’s absence, the Court of Appeal annulled the MCC valuations and the State Registration Chamber’s registration decision, reinstated the parties to their pre-3 May 2007 position, and thereby excluded the applicant from Q.’s partners. It ordered immediate enforcement. The exclusion was executed by a registration officer who was the wife of a deputy president of Mr Ș.’s party. Q.’s statutory capital fell to about EUR 14,377. The applicant lost its 50% shareholding and participation in the multi-million road contract; attempts to recover its equipment failed because of pledges, and the bank later acquired the equipment and the CEO’s house.

The Supreme Court of Justice dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 20 May 2011 without addressing its arguments that the case file had been tampered with, that it had no effective opportunity to object, or that S.’s action was time-barred. The ECtHR found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It held that the domestic courts’ decisions were contrary to domestic law, arbitrary and manifestly unreasonable, that the State failed to address the applicant’s serious allegations of file tampering and the time-bar objection, and that Moldova failed to provide a proper forum allowing the applicant company to assert and enforce its rights effectively. The case was characterized as a “raider attack” depriving the applicant of its possessions.

**Theo National Construct S.R.L. v. the Republic of Moldova** (ECtHR, 11 October 2022) concerned an alleged “raider attack” violating Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions). The applicant, a Romanian road-construction company, claimed it was illegally deprived of its 50% shareholding in a Moldovan company, “Q,” and of participation in a multi-million-euro state road contract.

In 2007 the applicant agreed with Moldovan businessman and political party leader Mr Ș. to enter the Moldovan road-construction market. Under an April 2007 agreement, the applicant was to contribute 23 pieces of road equipment worth over €1 million to company Q and receive 50% of its statutory capital. The changes were registered on 3 May 2007, raising Q’s capital from about €14,000 to approximately €1 million. In October 2007, Q signed a state road renovation contract worth about €24.5 million. The equipment was later pledged for bank loans, and the applicant’s CEO pledged his Chișinău house as security.

In early 2010, relations deteriorated after Q’s CEO made interest-free loans to company S, controlled by Mr Ș., without consulting the applicant and allegedly in breach of Q’s charter. Company S then asked the Moldovan Chamber of Commerce (MCC) to revoke its 2007 valuation of the applicant’s equipment. The MCC refused, noting that valuation by documents and photographs was permitted and that it had physically inspected the equipment upon import in May 2007.

In May 2010, company S. brought administrative proceedings before the Chișinău Court of Appeal seeking annulment of the valuation report, without initially naming the applicant as a defendant. The applicant was joined late. Serious procedural irregularities followed. Although a hearing was postponed because the plaintiff’s representative had to attend a funeral, the case file later contained minutes of a hearing on that same date bearing a case number that could not yet exist. A supplement seeking the applicant’s exclusion allegedly appeared later. Summons and confirmation forms showed handwritten corrections changing the next hearing date from 2 March to 2 February 2011. The applicant attended only the 20 January 2011 hearing and understood the next hearing would be 2 March. The court nevertheless held a hearing on 2 February 2011, the applicant was absent, and the court completed the merits.

On 2 February 2011, the Court of Appeal ruled for company S. It annulled the MCC valuation reports and the State Registration Chamber’s decision of 3 May 2007, reinstated the parties to their pre-3 May position, and thereby excluded the applicant from Q’s partners, eliminating its 50% shareholding. It ordered immediate enforcement. On 4 February 2011, the State Registration Chamber implemented the exclusion; the officer involved was the wife of the deputy president of Mr Ș.’s party. Q’s statutory capital fell to about €14,000. The applicant’s challenge to this registration was dismissed.

The Supreme Court of Justice dismissed the applicant’s appeal on points of law on 20 May 2011 without addressing its arguments that the proceedings were procedurally defective, that the case file had been tampered with, or that company S.’s action was time-barred. Later, Q’s new management withdrew recovery actions; the equipment remained in use and was eventually transferred to the bank; the CEO’s house was taken; and Q entered bankruptcy in 2014.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It held that the domestic courts’ decisions were contrary to domestic law, arbitrary and manifestly unreasonable. They failed to address serious allegations of case-file tampering and the time-bar objection. The State also failed to provide a proper forum enabling the applicant to assert and enforce its rights effectively.

**Case: Hrnčić v. Croatia (Application no. 53563/16), European Court of Human Rights, First Section, judgment of 29 September 2022.**

The applicant lodged an application against Croatia under Article 34 of the Convention on 1 September 2016. He was represented by Ms L. Horvat, a lawyer practising in Zagreb. The Croatian Government was given notice of the application. The applicant complained under Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, about the inadequate conditions of his detention. The complaints concerned several periods of detention, including a period in Varaždin Prison between 27 January and 17 March 2008. The details of the remaining periods were set out in an appended table. The central allegation was that the applicant had been held in poor conditions, particularly owing to serious lack of personal space and overcrowding.

As to the Varaždin Prison period of 27 January to 17 March 2008, the Court examined the Government’s objection that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies. The applicant had taken the relevant preliminary step to bring a civil action for compensation for inadequate detention conditions on 8 January 2013. The Court found that this civil action had been brought outside the three-year statutory limitation period. It therefore accepted the Government’s objection that the applicant had not properly exhausted domestic remedies in respect of that period. That part of the application was declared inadmissible under Article 35 §§ 1 and 4 of the Convention.

As to the remainder of the application, the Court assessed the merits of the Article 3 complaint. It noted that the applicant had been kept in detention in poor conditions. The Government argued that the applicant had spent only between seven and nine hours in his cell during the night, while the rest of the time he had either worked or had been able to move freely within his ward. It also stated that he had been allowed two hours per day outdoors. The Government relied on *Dolenec v. Croatia*, where the Court had found no violation of Article 3 in similar circumstances.

The Court, however, applied the principles established in the Grand Chamber judgment in *Muršić v. Croatia*. Under *Muršić*, a strong presumption of a violation of Article 3 arises where the personal space available to a detainee falls below 3 square metres of floor surface. That presumption can only be rebutted if certain factors are cumulatively met, including that reductions in the required minimum personal space of 3 square metres are short, occasional and minor. The Court found that, in the applicant’s case, the periods in which he had less than 3 square metres of personal space were neither short nor occasional. The lack of space therefore weighed heavily and disclosed degrading treatment.

The Court also referred to its earlier findings in *Muršić* and *Ulemek v. Croatia*, where it had found violations in respect of similar issues. Having examined all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on the admissibility and merits of the remaining complaints. It therefore held that the applicant’s conditions of detention were inadequate and that there had been a violation of Article 3 of the Convention in respect of the remaining periods complained of. The part concerning Varaždin Prison in 2008 was rejected as inadmissible. The judgment became final, subject to editorial revision, and the Court proceeded to consider the application of Article 41 concerning just satisfaction, though the supplied text does not set out the details of that assessment.

**Summary: Hrnčić v. Croatia (Application no. 53563/16)**

The case of *Hrnčić v. Croatia* concerned an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 1 September 2016 under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, represented by lawyer L. Horvat, complained primarily that the conditions of his detention in Croatia violated Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

The applicant alleged inadequate conditions of detention. His complaint covered several periods, including detention in Varaždin Prison between 27 January and 17 March 2008. The Croatian Government was given notice of the application and contested the claims.

A procedural issue arose concerning the Varaždin Prison period. The Court noted that the applicant had taken the relevant preliminary step to bring a civil action for compensation for inadequate detention conditions on 8 January 2013. However, because he brought that civil action outside the applicable three-year statutory limitation period, the Government’s objection that he had failed to properly exhaust domestic remedies was accepted. Consequently, that part of the application was declared inadmissible under Article 35 §§ 1 and 4 of the Convention.

As to the remaining periods complained of, the Court examined the applicant’s detention conditions on the merits. It noted that the applicant had been kept in detention in poor conditions, with details set out in an appended table. The Court relied on its established case-law concerning inadequate detention conditions, particularly the Grand Chamber judgment in *Muršić v. Croatia* and the later case of *Ulemek v. Croatia*, where similar issues had already resulted in findings of Article 3 violations.

The Government argued that the applicant had spent only between seven and nine hours in his cell during the night, while during the rest of the time he had either worked or been able to move freely within his ward. He had also been allowed two hours per day outdoors. The Government relied on *Dolenec v. Croatia*, where the Court had previously found no violation of Article 3 in allegedly similar circumstances.

The Court, however, reiterated the principle established in *Muršić* that a strong presumption of a violation of Article 3 arises where the personal space available to a detainee falls below 3 square metres of floor surface. That presumption can only be rebutted if certain factors are cumulatively met, including that reductions in the required minimum personal space of 3 square metres are short, occasional, and minor. In the applicant’s case, the periods in which he had less than 3 square metres of personal space were neither short nor occasional.

The Court therefore found that the applicant’s conditions of detention in the relevant remaining periods were inadequate and amounted to degrading treatment contrary to Article 3. It concluded that there had been a violation of Article 3 of the Convention. The judgment was delivered by a Committee of the First Section on 29 September 2022 and became final, though it remained subject to possible editorial revision.

In essence, the key facts relevant to the violation were the applicant’s prolonged detention in overcrowded prison conditions, particularly with less than 3 square metres of personal space for non-short and non-occasional periods, which triggered the *Muršić* presumption of an Article 3 violation. The Varaždin Prison complaint was rejected as time-barred for failure to exhaust domestic remedies within the statutory limitation period.

In the case of *Hrnčić v. Croatia* (Application no. 53563/16), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section, sitting as a Committee) delivered a judgment on 29 September 2022. The applicant lodged his application under Article 34 of the Convention on 1 September 2016 and was represented by Ms L. Horvat, a lawyer practising in Zagreb. The Croatian Government were given notice. The applicant complained exclusively of inadequate conditions of detention, relying on Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

The facts relevant to the alleged violation concerned the applicant’s detention in Croatian prisons. He complained inter alia about conditions in Varaždin Prison between 27 January and 17 March 2008. However, he took the relevant preliminary step to bring a civil action for compensation for inadequate detention conditions only on 8 January 2013. Since Croatian law set a three-year statutory limitation period, the Government objected that he had failed to properly exhaust domestic remedies. The Court accepted that objection, finding that the civil action had been brought outside the limitation period. That part of the application was therefore inadmissible under Article 35 §§ 1 and 4 of the Convention.

As to the remainder of the application, the applicant alleged that he had been kept in poor detention conditions. The detailed periods and conditions were set out in an appended table. The central issue was whether those conditions amounted to inhuman or degrading treatment. The Government argued that the applicant spent only between seven and nine hours in his cell during the night, while the rest of the time he either worked or could move freely within his ward. He was also allowed two hours outdoors per day. The Government relied on *Dolenec v. Croatia*, where the Court had found no violation of Article 3 in similar circumstances.

The Court rejected that argument, referring to the Grand Chamber judgment in *Muršić v. Croatia* and to *Ulemek v. Croatia*. It reiterated that a serious lack of space in a prison cell weighs heavily in assessing whether detention conditions are degrading under Article 3. In particular, where a detainee’s personal space falls below 3 square metres of floor surface, a strong presumption of a violation arises. That presumption can be rebutted only if certain cumulative factors are met, including that the reductions in the required minimum personal space are short, occasional and minor. The Court noted that in the applicant’s case the periods in which he had less than 3 square metres were neither short nor occasional.

Consequently, the Court found that the Government’s explanations about working, free movement within the ward and daily outdoor exercise did not rebut the presumption. Having examined all the material, it found no fact or argument capable of leading to a different conclusion. It therefore held that the applicant’s conditions of detention in the remaining periods complained of were inadequate and constituted a violation of Article 3 of the Convention. The application was inadmissible in respect of the Varaždin Prison period from 27 January to 17 March 2008, but a violation of Article 3 was established for the remaining periods. The judgment then addressed just satisfaction under Article 41.

In *Vool and Toomik v. Estonia*, two Estonian nationals complained under Article 14 read with Article 8 that, while held on remand, they were barred from receiving long-term family visits even though convicted prisoners were generally allowed such visits. The key issue was whether the statutory ban on long-term visits for remand prisoners under section 94(5) of the Imprisonment Act, and its application after prosecutor-imposed restrictions had been lifted, discriminated against them in their family life.

The first applicant, Tarko Vool, was remanded in April 2014 on suspicion of extortion and membership in a criminal organisation. The prosecutor initially ordered complete isolation and restricted visits, correspondence and telephone use. In September 2014, some short-term visits, correspondence and calls with his partner, mother and brother were allowed. By 5 November 2014, all additional restrictions on contact and communication were lifted. Nevertheless, from February 2015 onward, Tallinn Prison repeatedly refused his requests for long-term visits with his cohabiting partner, relying on section 94(5). He received 51 short-term visits, 351 calls, letters and parcels. In March 2016 the Tallinn Administrative Court dismissed his complaint; in June 2016 the Court of Appeal found the provision unconstitutional in his case and referred the issue to the Supreme Court. In November 2016 the Supreme Court upheld the ban as proportionate, citing risks that unsupervised visits could facilitate witness manipulation or destruction of evidence, especially given the criminal organisation context. Vool was convicted in September 2016, and after the judgment became effective in November 2016 he became entitled to long-term visits as a convicted prisoner.

The second applicant, Janek Toomik, was remanded in December 2011 on suspicion of large-scale drug handling. The prosecutor prohibited short and long-term visits, correspondence and telephone use with his next of kin. In August 2012 the Court of Appeal allowed correspondence, telephone use and short-term visits; in December 2013 it lifted all communication restrictions. He was convicted in May 2013, final in June 2014. In April 2014 he applied for a long-term visit with his cohabiting partner; Tartu Prison refused under section 94(5). He had already received 46 short-term family visits, calls and letters. The administrative court awarded compensation, but the Court of Appeal and, in October 2017, the Supreme Court upheld the refusal as proportionate. The Supreme Court reasoned that although restrictions had been lifted, a risk of influencing proceedings had not ceased because the case could be remitted and evidence re-examined. It did not separately address discrimination. A dissent argued that once all additional restrictions were lifted, the blanket ban on long-term visits was disproportionate.

Both applicants argued that remand prisoners were treated less favourably than convicted prisoners regarding long-term visits, without objective justification, and that the domestic courts never properly assessed the impact on family life separately from detention grounds. In 2019 the Supreme Court en banc later declared section 94(5) unconstitutional, but refused to reopen the applicants’ cases. The ECtHR found a violation of Article 14 read with Article 8, holding that Estonia failed to reasonably justify prohibiting long-term visits for remand prisoners even after other restrictions had been lifted and despite such visits being generally authorised for convicted prisoners.

In *Vool and Toomik v. Estonia* (Apps. nos. 7613/18 and 12222/18, ECtHR, 29 March 2022), two remand prisoners alleged that Estonia discriminated against them under Article 14 read with Article 8 ECHR by refusing them long-term family visits solely because they were detained on remand, whereas convicted prisoners could generally receive such visits.

The first applicant, Tarko Vool, was remanded in April 2014 on suspicion of extortion and membership in a criminal organisation. The prosecutor initially imposed complete isolation and banned visits, correspondence and telephone use. In September 2014, restrictions were partly lifted to allow short visits and contact with his cohabiting partner, mother and brother; in November 2014 all additional restrictions were lifted completely. Nevertheless, from February 2015 Vool repeatedly asked Tallinn Prison for long-term visits with his cohabiting partner. The prison refused under section 94(5) of the Imprisonment Act, which excluded remand prisoners from long-term visits available to convicted prisoners. Administrative courts dismissed his complaint, and in November 2016 the Supreme Court found the ban proportionate. It reasoned that unsupervised long-term visits could allow a criminal organisation to manipulate witnesses or evidence, that Vool’s background and the organisation’s support for families created risk, and that the distinction between remand and convicted prisoners was justified because convicted prisoners could no longer undermine ongoing proceedings. Vool was convicted in September 2016 and became eligible for long-term visits in November 2016. In 2019 the Supreme Court en banc later declared section 94(5) unconstitutional *ex nunc*, but Vool’s reopening request was refused in January 2020.

The second applicant, Janek Toomik, was remanded in December 2011 on suspicion of handling large quantities of narcotic drugs. The prosecutor initially prohibited all visits, correspondence and telephone contact with his next of kin. In August 2012, the Court of Appeal allowed correspondence, telephone use and short visits with his cohabiting partner, mother and children. In December 2013, it lifted all communication restrictions. He was convicted in May 2013, and his conviction became final in June 2014. In April 2014, while still a remand prisoner, he applied for a long-term visit with his cohabiting partner. Tartu Prison refused under the same section 94(5). The Administrative Court awarded him €500 compensation, but the appeal courts reversed. In October 2017, the Supreme Court found the ban proportionate. It held that even after additional restrictions were lifted, the risk of influencing proceedings had not ceased because the case could be remitted or evidence reheard; preventing further offences also justified restrictions. A dissenting judge argued that once all additional restrictions were lifted in December 2013, the blanket ban on long-term visits was disproportionate. Toomik’s reopening request was refused in June 2020.

The relevant framework was that section 25 of the Imprisonment Act allowed convicted prisoners unsupervised long-term visits of 24–72 hours, at least every six months, while section 94(5) expressly excluded remand prisoners. Article 1431 of the Code of Criminal Procedure allowed prosecutors or courts to impose additional restrictions on visits and communication for investigative purposes. The ECtHR found a violation of Article 14 read with Article 8, because the domestic courts failed to reasonably justify prohibiting the applicants from receiving long-term visits while in remand detention, particularly after other additional restrictions had been lifted and despite such visits being generally authorised for convicted prisoners.

**Case:** *Vool and Toomik v. Estonia* (ECtHR, 29 March 2022)

**Issue:** The applicants, both held in detention on remand, complained that they were prohibited from receiving long-term family visits, although convicted prisoners were generally allowed such visits. They alleged discrimination in the enjoyment of their right to family life under Article 14 read with Article 8 of the Convention.

**First applicant (Vool):** He was remanded in custody in April 2014 on suspicion of extortion and membership of a criminal organisation. The prosecutor initially imposed extensive additional restrictions, including complete isolation and bans on visits, correspondence and telephone use. These restrictions were partly lifted in September 2014 and completely lifted in November 2014. Between September 2014 and November 2016, he was allowed 51 short-term visits, including 32 with his cohabiting partner, as well as telephone calls, letters and parcels. However, from February 2015 he repeatedly sought long-term visits with his partner. The prison refused under section 94(5) of the Imprisonment Act, which categorically excluded remand prisoners from long-term visits available to convicted prisoners. Domestic courts, including the Supreme Court in November 2016, upheld the refusal as proportionate, citing risks that unsupervised visits could facilitate witness manipulation or destruction of evidence, especially given his alleged links to a criminal organisation. He was convicted in September 2016, and his conviction became final in November 2016, after which he became eligible for long-term visits.

**Second applicant (Toomik):** He was remanded in December 2011 on charges of large-scale drug handling. The prosecutor initially banned short- and long-term visits, correspondence and telephone use. In August 2012 the Court of Appeal allowed limited contact with family, and in December 2013 it lifted all communication restrictions. He was convicted in May 2013, and the conviction became final in June 2014. In April 2014, while still a remand prisoner, he applied for a long-term visit with his cohabiting partner. The prison refused under section 94(5). Domestic courts upheld the refusal. In October 2017, the Supreme Court found the ban proportionate, noting the seriousness of the charges, his criminal record, the risk of influencing proceedings, and that his remand status ended less than a month after the refusal.

**Legal framework:** Section 25 of the Imprisonment Act allowed long-term visits for convicted prisoners, but section 94(5) stated they “shall not be applied to remand prisoners.” The Code of Criminal Procedure allowed prosecutors to impose individual additional restrictions on visits and communication. The domestic courts assessed the need for continued detention but, according to the applicants, did not separately assess the impact of the blanket ban on long-term visits on their family life.

**Later development:** In 2019, the Estonian Supreme Court en banc declared section 94(5) unconstitutional *ex nunc*, finding it disproportionately interfered with some remand prisoners’ family life because the public interest in detention would in practice always outweigh family-life restrictions. The applicants’ attempts to reopen their cases were refused.

**Outcome:** The ECtHR found a violation of Article 14 read with Article 8. The key fact was that the authorities continued to prohibit long-term visits even after all other additional restrictions had been lifted, without reasonably justifying why remand prisoners should be treated less favourably than convicted prisoners in those circumstances.

In *Vlasenko v. Ukraine* (no. 17863/13, judgment 3 February 2022), the European Court of Human Rights examined two key complaints: the prosecution authorities’ access to the applicant’s banking documents under Article 8 and a ban on his travelling abroad under Article 2 of Protocol No. 4.

The applicant, Sergiy Volodymyrovych Vlasenko, was a Ukrainian Member of Parliament. At the relevant time, MPs enjoyed immunity from measures restricting their rights and freedoms without Parliament’s prior consent. After losing a civil dispute with his former spouse, he was ordered by a final judgment of 31 October 2012 to pay her 125,000 Ukrainian hryvnias. On 23 November 2012, the Pecherskyy Court, without informing the applicant, banned him from travelling abroad at a bailiff’s request to ensure enforcement of the judgment and prevent evasion. On 14 December 2012, relying on that ruling, the State Border Service prevented him from boarding a flight from Kyiv to Strasbourg despite his claim of parliamentary immunity. On 18 December 2012 criminal proceedings were opened against him for deliberate non-compliance with the judgment. On 26 December 2012 he paid the debt and enforcement fees in full.

Despite this payment, on 24 January 2013 he was again stopped from travelling to Strasbourg as a member of Ukraine’s parliamentary delegation to the PACE, and on 13 March 2013 he was prevented from flying to Brussels, even after showing proof of payment. The criminal proceedings were discontinued on 5 March 2013; enforcement was declared complete on 5 April 2013; and the travel ban was lifted on 9 April 2013.

As to Article 8, on 16 and 23 January 2013 an investigating judge granted the investigator temporary access, for thirty and fourteen days, to virtually all of the applicant’s banking documents in two banks for the entire period his accounts had existed. The investigator’s applications and the judge’s rulings did not mention that the applicant had already paid the debt. The judge examined the applications without summoning the applicant, citing a real risk that the information might be modified or destroyed. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, temporary access to bank secrecy required a judge’s ruling; ex parte examination was permitted only where sufficient grounds showed a risk of alteration or destruction, and access required proof that the documents had evidential value and that other evidence could not be used. The applicant’s attempt on 21 January 2013 to challenge the first ruling was apparently disregarded.

The Court found that banking documents constitute personal data and that the measure interfered with private life. The Government submitted no observations. The Court found the interference arbitrary: it was ordered in a criminal investigation into non-compliance after the applicant had voluntarily and fully complied with the judgment, yet that fact was omitted from the investigator’s requests and the judicial rulings. No explanation was given as to why the banking documents had evidential value or why virtually all records for the entire account period were needed. The ex parte procedure was also inexplicable. The interference was therefore unjustified and lacked sufficient safeguards against arbitrariness, violating Article 8.

Regarding the travel ban, the Court noted that it lasted from 23 November 2012 to 9 April 2013, although the debt was paid on 26 December 2012. After that date, with no relevant Government observations, the ban was entirely arbitrary. Even for the earlier period, the authorities never explained how the ban could help recover the debt in the applicant’s circumstances or assessed whether he would evade payment. The ban thus breached Article 2 of Protocol No. 4.

**Vlasenko v. Ukraine** (Application no. 17863/13, ECtHR Fifth Section, 3 February 2022) concerned a Ukrainian Member of Parliament (MP), Mr Sergiy Volodymyrovych Vlasenko, who at the material time enjoyed parliamentary immunity under domestic law against measures restricting an MP’s rights and freedoms without prior parliamentary consent.

The case arose from a civil dispute with the applicant’s former spouse, Ms O. By a judgment of the Kyiv District Pecherskyy Court of 21 February 2012, which became final on 31 October 2012, the applicant was ordered to pay her 125,000 Ukrainian hryvnias. On 23 November 2012, the Pecherskyy Court, without informing the applicant, banned him from travelling abroad at a bailiff’s request to ensure enforcement of the judgment and prevent him from evading it by leaving Ukraine. On 14 December 2012, relying on that ruling, the State Border Service prevented him from boarding a flight from Kyiv to Strasbourg, even though he invoked his MP immunity. On 18 December 2012, criminal proceedings were instituted against him on suspicion of deliberate non-compliance with the judgment. On 26 December 2012, the applicant paid the debt plus enforcement fees in full.

Despite that payment, the travel ban remained in force. On 24 January 2013, the State Border Service again refused to let him leave Ukraine for Strasbourg as part of the Ukrainian parliamentary delegation to PACE, even though he provided proof of payment. On 13 March 2013, he was similarly prevented from flying to Brussels. The criminal proceedings were discontinued on 5 March 2013 for absence of constituent elements of a crime. On 5 April 2013, enforcement was completed, and on 9 April 2013 the Pecherskyy Court lifted the travel ban.

Separately, on 16 and 23 January 2013, an investigating judge of the Pecherskyy Court granted the investigator’s applications for temporary access to virtually all of the applicant’s banking documents in two banks for the entire period of the accounts’ existence. The access was granted for thirty and fourteen days respectively. The judge examined the applications without summoning the applicant, relying on an alleged “real risk of modification or destruction” of the information. The applicant’s application of 21 January 2013 for review of the first ruling, lodged after he had fully paid the debt, apparently remained disregarded. The Government did not submit observations within the time-limit.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 8 of the Convention regarding access to banking documents. It held that information retrieved from banking documents amounts to personal data and that the prosecutorial measure interfered with the applicant’s right to respect for private life. The interference was arbitrary: the investigation continued after the applicant had voluntarily and fully complied with the judgment, and neither the investigator’s applications nor the judge’s rulings explained what evidence of “deliberate non-compliance” was expected from virtually all banking documents for the entire period of the accounts. The ex parte examination was also inexplicable, and the applicant lacked sufficient guarantees against arbitrariness.

The Court also found a violation of Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 concerning the travel ban. The ban was arbitrary after 26 December 2012, when the debt had been paid in full, yet it continued. For the earlier period, the authorities never explained how the travel ban could help recover the debt or whether the applicant’s conduct gave reason to believe he would evade payment.

**Case: Vlasenko v. Ukraine (Application no. 17863/13, judgment 3 February 2022)**

The applicant, Sergiy Volodymyrovych Vlasenko, was a Ukrainian Member of Parliament who, under domestic law, enjoyed immunity from measures restricting an MP’s rights and freedoms without Parliament’s prior consent. The case concerned two alleged violations: the prosecution authorities’ access to his banking documents under Article 8 of the Convention, and a ban on his travelling abroad under Article 2 of Protocol No. 4.

The underlying facts began with a civil dispute between the applicant and his former spouse, Ms O. By a judgment of the Kyiv District Pecherskyy Court of 21 February 2012, which became final on 31 October 2012, the applicant was ordered to pay her UAH 125,000. On 23 November 2012, at a bailiff’s request, the Pecherskyy Court banned the applicant from travelling abroad without informing him. The stated aim was to ensure enforcement of the judgment and prevent him from evading it by leaving Ukraine.

On 14 December 2012, relying on that ban, the State Border Service refused to allow the applicant to board a flight from Kyiv to Strasbourg, even though he invoked his parliamentary immunity. On 18 December 2012, criminal proceedings were instituted against him on suspicion of deliberate non-compliance with the judgment. However, on 26 December 2012, the applicant transferred the full debt plus enforcement fees to the Bailiffs Service’s account.

On 16 and 23 January 2013, an investigating judge of the Pecherskyy Court granted the investigator temporary access, for thirty and fourteen days respectively, to virtually all of the applicant’s banking documents in two banks, covering the entire period during which his accounts existed. The judge examined the applications without summoning the applicant, citing a real risk that the information might be modified or destroyed. On 21 January 2013, after having fully paid the debt, the applicant sought review of the first access ruling; his request was apparently disregarded.

On 24 January 2013, the applicant was again refused permission to leave Ukraine for Strasbourg, where he was to attend a PACE meeting as part of the Ukrainian parliamentary delegation, despite producing proof of payment. On 28 February 2013, the Bailiffs Service transferred the money to Ms O.’s account. On 5 March 2013, the criminal proceedings against the applicant were discontinued for lack of constituent elements of a crime. On 13 March 2013, the State Border Service again prevented him from boarding a flight, this time to Brussels. On 5 April 2013, the Bailiffs Service declared enforcement complete, and on 9 April 2013, the Pecherskyy Court lifted the travel ban.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 8. It held that banking documents constitute personal data, so their retrieval interfered with private life. The interference was arbitrary: the temporary access was ordered in a criminal investigation into non-compliance even though the applicant had already voluntarily and fully complied. That crucial fact was omitted from the investigator’s applications and the judge’s rulings. The authorities never explained what evidence relating to “deliberate non-compliance” they expected to find in virtually all banking documents for the entire account history, nor why the ex parte procedure was justified. The Government submitted no observations.

The Court also found a violation of Article 2 of Protocol No. 4. After 26 December 2012, when the applicant fully paid the debt, the travel ban was entirely arbitrary. For the earlier period, the authorities never explained how a travel ban could help recover the debt in the applicant’s circumstances, nor did they assess whether he was likely to evade payment if allowed to leave.

Ilyin and Others v. Ukraine (Application no. 74852/14) concerned nine Ukrainian nationals and followers of the Unification Church (“UC”), founded by Reverend Sun Myung Moon. They created a UC religious community and sought registration as a legal entity with the Kyiv City State Administration. Their complaint under Articles 9 and 11 of the Convention alleged that the refusal to register the community violated their freedom of religion or belief and freedom of association.

In 2001, the founders applied to register the community under the name “Holy Spirit Association for the Unification of World Christianity Religious Community in the Kyiv Obolonsky District.” The submitted constitution stated that the community’s faith was based on Christian theology, the Bible, and Rev. Moon’s work Divine Principle. The Administration requested a report from the State Committee for Religious Affairs. That report described the UC as a widespread “non-traditional synthetic religion,” founded by Rev. Moon, which reinterpreted the Bible through Taoism and aimed to unify not only Christianity but all world religions. It highlighted UC doctrines concerning “blood purity,” “true families,” sexual harmony blessed by Rev. Moon, and the creation of God’s Kingdom on Earth through unpaid labour and donations. The Committee noted that some international experts denied Moon’s teachings were Christian and criticised their anti-Semitic nature. It warned that UC doctrine could complicate inter-confessional relations in Ukraine and recommended an in-depth study before registration.

The Administration delayed its decision, stating it needed to examine the community’s social activities and worship practices. In 2007, it replied to Mr Ilyin that it had received complaints about destructive influence at UC seminars and that the community had refused to allow an official to observe those seminars, hindering examination of its legality. The complaints included: a mother’s account that her son changed after a 21-day UC seminar and became overly involved; a former participant’s claim that he was forced to study UC doctrines for fourteen hours a day in isolation, with telephone calls and unrelated reading prohibited, sometimes sleeping on the floor and becoming ill; and a father’s statement that his son joined a UC-linked “youth centre,” was forced to attend seminars, abandoned his studies, and began begging for the UC.

In June 2007, the community reapplied for registration. In August 2007, the Committee for Nationalities and Religion reported again, describing the UC as a new religious trend combining Eastern religions with Christian elements, but not a branch of Christianity. It emphasised Rev. Moon’s blessing for marriage, collective marriage ceremonies, strict regulation and subordination, and missionary “leadership seminars.” It also referred to international press reports of UC business monopolies and information that UC representatives in Ukraine had considered establishing commercial entities, buying shares in leading companies, and investing in charitable projects to create a UC lobby within NGOs and small political parties.

Registration was ultimately refused. The European Court of Human Rights examined the refusal under Article 9 read in light of Article 11. The judgment indicates that the refusal was found justified because the community’s name was liable to mislead believers and the general public, particularly by presenting the UC as Christian despite the authorities’ view that it was a non-traditional, syncretic, and controversial movement. The key facts supporting the State’s position were the misleading name, expert reports characterising the UC as non-Christian and potentially disruptive to inter-confessional relations, complaints about coercive or harmful practices, and the community’s reapplication. The Court therefore concluded that the refusal did not amount to a violation of the applicants’ Convention rights.

**Ilyin and Others v. Ukraine (Application no. 74852/14)**  
**European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, judgment of 17 November 2022 (final 3 April 2023)**

The applicants were nine Ukrainian nationals and followers of the Unification Church (“UC”), founded by the Reverend Sun Myung Moon. They formed a religious community and sought registration as a legal entity with the Kyiv City State Administration. The proposed name was the “‘Holy Spirit Association for the Unification of World Christianity’ Religious Community in the Kyiv Obolonsky District.” Their submitted constitution stated that the community followed Christian theology, the Bible, and Rev. Moon’s work *Divine Principle*.

The first registration application was lodged in 2001. The Administration requested an expert report from the State Committee for Religious Affairs. That report described the UC as a non-traditional, synthetic religion that reinterpreted the Bible through Taoism and aimed to unify all world religions. It noted controversial features, including teachings on “blood purity,” marriages blessed only by Rev. Moon, and the creation of a global infrastructure involving business, media, education, and law. The Committee stated that some experts denied that Moon’s teachings were Christian and criticized their allegedly anti-Semitic character. It warned that the UC’s doctrine and practices could complicate inter-confessional relations in Ukraine and recommended further study of the community’s activities.

Registration was delayed. The Administration later said it had received complaints about the community’s destructive influence and that it had been prevented from examining its seminars because the community refused to allow an official to observe them. The case file included complaints from a mother, a former participant, and a father. They alleged isolation during seminars, long hours of forced doctrinal study, restrictions on communication and reading, poor conditions, family estrangement, abandonment of studies, and street begging for the UC.

In June 2007 the community reapplied. A new report by the Committee for Nationalities and Religion repeated much of the earlier assessment. It described the UC as a new religious trend combining Eastern religions with elements of Christianity, but not a Christian denomination. It emphasized Rev. Moon’s blessing for marriages, collective marriage ceremonies, strict regulation of relationships, subordination to leadership, and missionary “leadership seminars.” It also referred to international press reports of UC business monopolies and information that UC representatives in Ukraine had considered establishing commercial entities, buying shares in leading companies, and investing in charity projects to create a UC lobby among NGOs and small political parties.

The Ukrainian authorities ultimately refused registration. The refusal was based on the view that the proposed name was liable to mislead believers and the general public, because the UC was not a Christian denomination and its doctrines and practices differed from Christianity. Domestic courts upheld that refusal.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants complained under Article 9 and Article 11 of the Convention that the refusal to register their religious community violated their right to manifest religion or belief in community with others. The Court examined the case under Article 9 read in light of Article 11. It accepted that the refusal amounted to an interference with the applicants’ rights, but found it justified: it was prescribed by law, pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the rights of others and public order, and was proportionate. The domestic authorities had relevant and sufficient reasons for considering the name misleading. The State enjoyed a margin of appreciation in regulating the legal status of religious communities. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 9 read in light of Article 11.

In *Ilyin and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 74852/14), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) examined a complaint by nine Ukrainian nationals who were followers of the Unification Church (“UC”), founded by Rev. Sun Myung Moon. They formed a religious community in Kyiv and sought registration as a legal entity. When registration was refused, they complained under Articles 9 and 11 of the Convention that their freedom of religion and association had been violated. In its judgment of 17 November 2022, the Court found the refusal justified because the proposed name was liable to mislead believers and the general public.

In 2001, the applicants applied to the Kyiv City State Administration to register the “‘Holy Spirit Association for the Unification of World Christianity’ Religious Community in the Kyiv Obolonsky District.” Their constitution stated that the community followed Christian theology, the Bible, and Rev. Moon’s *Divine Principle*. The Administration requested a report from the State Committee for Religious Affairs. The November 2001 report described the UC as a widespread “non-traditional synthetic religion” that reinterpreted the Bible through Taoism and sought to unify Christianity and all world religions. It highlighted doctrines of “blood purity,” “true families,” and sexual harmony blessed only by Rev. Moon. It also described plans to build God’s Kingdom on Earth through an infrastructure uniting business, media, science, education, and law, funded by followers’ unpaid labour and donations. The report noted that some experts denied Moon’s teachings were Christian, criticised their anti-Semitic nature, and warned that the UC’s controversial reception could complicate inter-confessional relations. The Committee advised an in-depth study of the community’s social and worship activities. The Administration told the founders in December 2001 and again in August 2002 that it would continue examining those activities.

In 2007, the Administration replied to Mr Ilyin’s complaint, saying it had received complaints about destructive influence on seminar participants and that the community had prevented officials from observing its seminars. The file contained three complaints: a mother said her son attended a 21-day UC seminar, had limited family contact, and returned overly involved; a former participant alleged forced 14-hour daily study, isolation from families, restrictions on phone calls and reading, sleeping on the floor, and illness; a father said his son joined a UC-linked youth centre, was forced to attend seminars, abandoned his studies, and begged for the UC.

In June 2007 the community reapplied. An August 2007 report repeated that the UC was a new religious trend combining Eastern religions with Christianity, not a Christian denomination. It emphasised Moon’s blessing for marriages, collective marriage ceremonies, strict regulation, subordination, and missionary leadership seminars. It also referred to international press reports of UC business monopolies in banking, hotels, and energy drinks, and said UC representatives in Ukraine had considered commercial entities, shares, and charitable projects to create a lobby within NGOs and small political parties.

The Court considered that the authorities’ refusal to register the community did not breach Article 9 read in light of Article 11. Although registration affected the applicants’ ability to manifest their religion collectively, the refusal pursued a legitimate aim and was justified, particularly because the proposed name was liable to mislead believers and the general public as to the community’s Christian character and identity.
001-216349:
**Summary of Mickovski v. North Macedonia (Applications nos. 39107/18 and 39726/18)**

**Key Facts:**
The applicant, Mr. Vlado Mickovski, is a bailiff who established his practice in Kichevo, North Macedonia, in 2006 after registering with the Chamber of Bailiffs. On 3 February 2011, the Gostivar Court of First Instance opened a criminal investigation against him for alleged negligence in performing his duties, specifically concerning the double enforcement of a pecuniary claim.

On 11 April 2011, pursuant to section 60(2) of the Enforcement Act, the Chamber of Bailiffs ordered the compulsory suspension of his bailiff practice. This provision mandated suspension whenever a criminal investigation was initiated against a bailiff regarding their official duties. During the suspension, a deputy bailiff was appointed to handle necessary activities, with income from those services credited to the applicant's practice, minus certain fees.

The suspension lasted until 21 November 2011 (approximately seven months), when it was lifted after the investigation was terminated for lack of evidence. Following this, the applicant sought compensation from the State and the Chamber under the Obligations Act for pecuniary damage (actual losses of approximately €10,418 and loss of income of approximately €23,845) and non-pecuniary damage (€15,450 for reputational harm).

The Kichevo Court of First Instance initially granted €10,418 for actual losses, relying on expert reports and evidence of ongoing office expenses during the suspension. However, the Gostivar Court of Appeal overturned this decision, dismissing all claims. The appellate court held that state liability required a wrongful conviction or imprisonment under the Criminal Proceedings Act, which did not apply since the applicant was neither convicted nor imprisoned. The Supreme Court upheld this judgment.

**Alleged Violation:**
The applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights that the seven-month suspension of his bailiff practice constituted an unjustified interference with his business interests and possessions, and that domestic courts failed to compensate him for resulting losses.

**Court's Analysis:**
The European Court of Human Rights addressed several preliminary issues. First, it found State responsibility engaged because the Chamber, though a professional body, exercised regulatory and disciplinary powers conferred by law, and because domestic courts refused compensation.

Regarding the applicant's standing, the Court held that Mr. Mickovski (as a physical person) and his registered practice (as a legal person) were so closely identified—given the sole proprietorship nature of bailiff practices—that distinguishing between them would be artificial.

The Court rejected the Government's objections on non-exhaustion and timeliness, finding the compensation proceedings were appropriate remedies and that the six-month period ran from the final Supreme Court decision, not the earlier Constitutional Court decision on abstract review.

On the merits, the Court found the bailiff practice constituted a "possession" under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The applicant had a vested economic interest in running his practice and had established "goodwill" over five years—advantages from reputation and client connections relevant to clients' choices. The suspension therefore interfered with his right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

However, the Court ultimately concluded there was no violation, finding the applicant failed to demonstrate that the temporary suspension imposed an individual and excessive burden upon him.

In Mickovski v. North Macedonia (Applications nos. 39107/18 and 39726/18), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. The applicant, Vlado Mickovski, was a Macedonian citizen and registered bailiff in Kichevo. He had operated his bailiff practice as a sole practitioner since 2006.

On 3 February 2011, the Gostivar Court of First Instance opened a criminal investigation against him for alleged negligence in performing his bailiff duties, specifically concerning the alleged double enforcement of a pecuniary claim. On 11 April 2011, the Chamber of Bailiffs ordered the suspension of his practice as a compulsory measure under section 60(2) of the Enforcement Act. At the time, that provision required suspension of a bailiff’s practice once a criminal investigation was opened in relation to his or her official duties. The Minister of Justice appointed a deputy bailiff, M.D., to carry out necessary activities during the suspension. Income from the deputy’s services was credited to the applicant’s practice, except for certain fees charged by the deputy.

The suspension lasted from 11 April to 21 November 2011, about seven months. On 21 November 2011, after the criminal investigation was terminated for lack of evidence, the Chamber lifted the suspension. The applicant then sued the State and the Chamber under the Obligations Act, seeking compensation for actual damage and loss of income—approximately EUR 10,418 in costs and EUR 23,845 for lost income—and non-pecuniary damage for reputational harm of EUR 15,450.

On 2 March 2016, the Kichevo Court of First Instance awarded him EUR 10,418 for actual loss but dismissed the non-pecuniary claim. On 10 November 2016, the Gostivar Court of Appeal reversed that judgment and dismissed all claims, holding that the State could not be liable absent a wrongful conviction or imprisonment under sections 549 and 553 of the Criminal Proceedings Act. The Supreme Court upheld that decision on 17 May 2018.

Before the European Court, the applicant argued that the seven-month suspension of his bailiff practice was an unjustified interference with his business interests and possessions, and that he had received no compensation. The Government objected that the State was not responsible for a dispute with the Chamber, that the suspension affected only the legal person/practice and not Mr Mickovski personally, that the applications were late, and that he had no “possessions” within the meaning of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The Court found the complaints admissible. It held that State responsibility was engaged because the Chamber exercised statutory regulatory and disciplinary powers, including compulsory suspension under the Enforcement Act, and because the domestic courts later refused compensation. It also found that Mr Mickovski and his sole-proprietor bailiff practice were so closely identified that distinguishing between them would be artificial. The Court accepted that the practice, its clientele and goodwill had economic value and fell within the scope of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, especially because the suspension temporarily prohibited the usual conduct of his business.

However, on the merits, the Court concluded that the applicant had failed to demonstrate that the temporary suspension imposed an individual and excessive burden on him. The judgment therefore found no violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The case is relevant because it addresses compulsory suspension of a bailiff’s practice pending criminal investigation, the State’s responsibility for professional-body measures, and the threshold for showing a disproportionate economic burden under property rights.

**Mickovski v. North Macedonia** (Applications nos. 39107/18 and 39726/18, ECtHR Fifth Section, 24 March 2022) concerned the temporary suspension of a bailiff’s practice after a criminal investigation and the applicant’s inability to obtain full compensation for resulting losses.

The applicant, Vlado Mickovski, was a bailiff registered with the Chamber of Bailiffs in 2006 and ran a bailiff practice in Kichevo. On 3 February 2011, the Gostivar Court of First Instance opened a criminal investigation against him for negligence in the performance of his duties, alleging double enforcement of a pecuniary claim. On 11 April 2011, the Chamber of Bailiffs ordered the suspension of his practice as a compulsory measure under section 60(2) of the Enforcement Act. The Minister of Justice appointed a deputy bailiff to carry out necessary work during the suspension. Income from the deputy’s services was credited to the applicant’s practice, except for certain fees charged by the deputy. On 21 November 2011, after the investigation was terminated for lack of evidence, the Chamber lifted the suspension. The suspension therefore lasted about seven months.

The applicant later sued the State and the Chamber under the Obligations Act, seeking compensation for actual damage, loss of income, and non-pecuniary damage. He claimed approximately EUR 10,418 in actual costs, EUR 23,845 for lost income, and EUR 15,450 for reputational harm. In March 2016, the Kichevo Court of First Instance granted EUR 10,418 for actual loss against the State, relying on expert evidence, employment-suspension decisions, bank statements, utility bills, and a services agreement. It dismissed the non-pecuniary claim because he had not been convicted or fined. In November 2016, the Gostivar Court of Appeal overturned that judgment and dismissed all claims, holding that the State could not be liable absent wrongful conviction or imprisonment under sections 549 and 553 of the Criminal Proceedings Act. The Supreme Court upheld that decision in May 2018.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the seven-month suspension unjustifiably interfered with his business interests and that he was not compensated for the resulting loss.

The Government argued that the Chamber was not a State body, that the suspension affected only the bailiff practice as a legal person, that the application was late, that no “possessions” were involved, and that loss of income fell outside Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court rejected these objections. It found that State responsibility was engaged because the Chamber was established by the Enforcement Act and exercised statutory regulatory and disciplinary powers, and because domestic courts refused compensation. It also found that the physical applicant and his sole-proprietor practice were closely identified. The compensation proceedings were an effective remedy, so the six-month time-limit ran from their conclusion. Finally, the Court held that Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 applied: the applicant had a vested economic interest and goodwill from five years of practice.

On the merits, the Court examined whether the temporary suspension imposed an individual and excessive burden. It noted that the measure was temporary, prescribed by law, and that a deputy bailiff continued the practice and generated income for the applicant. Although the applicant suffered some loss, he failed to demonstrate that the suspension resulted in an individual and excessive burden or a disproportionate interference. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

**Case Summary: Perspektyvnyy v. Ukraine (Applications nos. 9225/20 and 6773/21)**

The case of *Perspektyvnyy v. Ukraine* concerned two applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant was represented by Mr S.M. Rybiy, a lawyer practising in Dnipro. The Ukrainian Government were given notice of the applications. The Fifth Section of the European Court of Human Rights, sitting as a Committee composed of Judges Stéphanie Mourou-Vikström (President), Ivana Jelić, and Kateřina Šimáčková, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar, deliberated in private on 25 August 2022 and delivered its judgment on 6 October 2022. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The applicant complained principally of the inadequate conditions of his detention and the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law, invoking Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention. Article 3 prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. Article 13 guarantees an effective remedy before a national authority for violations of Convention rights. The applicant also raised other complaints under the Convention. The Court joined the two applications because they concerned similar subject matter.

The factual basis for the complaints is set out in the appended table to the judgment, which is not reproduced in the provided text. According to the judgment, the applicant was kept in detention in poor conditions. While the specific details—such as dates, detention facilities, cell measurements, number of occupants, and sanitary or other shortcomings—are not included in the excerpt, the Court relied on those details to assess the conditions.

In its legal analysis, the Court referred to established case-law on inadequate detention conditions, particularly *Muršić v. Croatia* and *Ananyev and Others v. Russia*. It reiterated that a serious lack of space in a prison cell weighs heavily as a factor in determining whether detention conditions are “degrading” under Article 3. Such a lack of space may disclose a violation both alone and when combined with other shortcomings. The Court also cited its leading judgments in *Melnik v. Ukraine* and *Sukachov v. Ukraine*, where it had already found violations for similar issues.

Having examined all material, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on admissibility or merits. It therefore concluded that the applicant’s conditions of detention were inadequate, in violation of Article 3. The Court further found that the applicant did not have at his disposal an effective remedy in respect of these complaints, in violation of Article 13. The other complaints raised by the applicant also concerned issues covered by well-established case-law; they were not manifestly ill-founded within the meaning of Article 35 § 3 (a) of the Convention, nor inadmissible on any other ground.

In sum, the case is a typical Ukrainian detention-conditions case. The Court found violations of Articles 3 and 13, following its consistent approach that overcrowding and poor detention conditions, coupled with the absence of an effective domestic remedy, breach the Convention.
