**P.H. v. Slovakia** (ECtHR, First Section, 8 September 2022, App. No. 37574/19) concerned a 16-year-old Roma girl arrested in January 2017 on suspicion of petty theft and taken to a police station. She alleged that during transport, two officers insulted her because of her Roma origin and each slapped her once. The Government denied any abuse. At the station, after she admitted further thefts, the prosecutor instructed that she not be detained and be released after paperwork. Officer A completed records alone with her. When she asked to use the toilet, he escorted her to a second-floor bathroom area at the end of a corridor containing an openable window. He showed her the toilet, stood less than a metre away, then turned his back to wait. He next saw her falling from the open window. She fell about 7.7 metres onto snow-covered ground, suffering life-threatening injuries: unconsciousness, coma, endocranial injury, rib and other fractures, pneumothorax, and lung contusions. She was hospitalised until 24 February 2017 and later diagnosed with organic mental disorder, cognitive impairment, and retrograde amnesia. She said she remembered the alleged insults and slaps in the police car but not the fall.

The applicant complained under Articles 2, 3, 6, and 13 of the Convention—and later Article 14—that she had been ill-treated in the police car and at the station; that the State failed to protect her life and health while she was in custody and failed to provide a plausible explanation for her fall; and that the investigation was ineffective and discriminatory. The domestic authorities split the two incidents. The Inspection Service found no criminal ill-treatment in the police car, relying largely on the officers’ accounts and doubting the applicant’s credibility because of her amnesia. As to the police-station incident, the investigator found that Officer A had breached the internal 2011 Decree on escorting persons by failing to continuously watch her and prevent her escape. However, the matter was treated only as a disciplinary offence, resulting in a 5% salary reduction for Officer A. The applicant was not informed and had only witness, not victim, status. The prosecutor’s office and Constitutional Court dismissed her complaints; the Constitutional Court found no standalone right to criminal prosecution and declared her complaint manifestly ill-founded. The Ombudsperson found no human-rights violation.

The Government argued non-exhaustion, including failure to appeal investigation decisions, file a separate constitutional complaint regarding the station incident, or bring civil claims. The applicant replied that her injuries were life-threatening, civil remedies were inadequate, and she could not challenge the station outcome because she was never recognised as a victim.

The ECtHR examined the interrelated incidents under Articles 2 and 3. The key facts triggering the alleged violations were that the applicant was a vulnerable minor in police custody, later shown to have mental/intellectual disabilities, and Officer A was responsible for supervising her under domestic escort rules. He failed to watch her continuously, lost sight of her at an open second-floor window, and she fell. The Court found the State responsible for her injuries under Article 2 and held that the investigation was ineffective, including for failing to address the possible link between the alleged abuse and her fall, for not involving her adequately, and for not examining possible discriminatory motives.

In *P.H. v. Slovakia*, the applicant was a 16-year-old Slovak Roma girl with intellectual disabilities. On 17 January 2017, police arrested her for petty theft at a shopping mall. She alleged that, while being transported to the county police station, two officers racially insulted her, told her she would be put in a cage, and each slapped her once. The Government denied any physical or verbal abuse. At the station, she confessed to further thefts. A supervising prosecutor instructed that she should not be detained but released after paperwork. She was searched, after which Officer A remained alone with her and continued filling in records. When she asked to use the toilet, Officer A escorted her to a second-floor bathroom area at the end of a corridor with a window. According to Officer A, he pointed out the toilet, stood less than a metre away, then turned his back to wait. He saw a shadow, turned, and saw her falling from the open window. The window sill was 90 cm above the floor, and the bottom edge was about 770 cm above the ground. She suffered severe, life-threatening injuries: coma, endocranial injury, rib and skeletal fractures, pneumothorax, and lung contusions. She remained hospitalised until 24 February 2017 and later suffered retrograde amnesia and an organic mental disorder.

The applicant had no memory of the fall but recalled being slapped and insulted in the police car. Her brother stated that he saw her crying at the police station, heard her shouting to be released, heard a female voice threatening and racially insulting her, and then saw officers running and shouting that she had jumped out of the window.

The investigation was split. Criminal proceedings concerning the fall were opened, quashed, then reopened regarding the officers’ alleged failure to guard the applicant under an internal 2011 Decree on escorting persons. The investigator found that Officer A had a duty to continuously watch her and failed to do so: he turned his back, lost sight of her, and did not verify whether the window was locked or arrange same-sex supervision. The prosecution service found no grounds for criminal prosecution but considered the negligence disciplinary. Officer A received a one-off 5% salary reduction, and the applicant was not informed. A separate investigation into the alleged ill-treatment in the police car ended in July 2017 with no finding of wrongdoing; authorities doubted her account, partly because of her amnesia, and noted Officer A’s experience in Roma-related issues. Her later requests for review were dismissed, the Constitutional Court declared her complaint inadmissible, and the Ombudsperson found no violation.

The applicant alleged violations of Articles 2, 3, 6, and 13 of the Convention. She claimed the State failed to protect her life and health while in custody, failed to provide a plausible explanation for her fall, conducted an ineffective investigation, ignored possible racial motives, and failed to provide procedural accommodations for a minor with disabilities. The European Court of Human Rights examined the complaints under Articles 2 and 3 together. It found the State responsible for her injuries under Article 2 because Officer A failed to continuously watch her as required by domestic escort rules. It also found the investigation ineffective, violating Article 2’s procedural limb.

**P.H. v. Slovakia** (ECtHR, 8 September 2022) concerned a 16-year-old Slovak Roma girl arrested on 17 January 2017 for petty theft at a shopping mall. She was transported to a county police station by Officers A and B. The applicant alleged that during the police-car journey the officers insulted her because of her Romani origin, told her she would be “put in a cage,” and each slapped her once. The Government denied any physical or verbal abuse, relying on police records stating that no coercive measures were used because she was a cooperative minor.

At the police station, after the supervising prosecutor instructed that she should not be detained but released after paperwork, the applicant was searched. Officer A then filled in records alone with her. When she asked to use the toilet, he accompanied her to the second-floor ladies’ bathroom at the end of a corridor. The corridor ended in a window. Officer A showed her the toilet area, stood less than a metre away, and then turned his back to wait. He saw a shadow, turned, and saw the applicant falling through the open window. She fell about 7.7 metres onto snowy grass, sustaining a coma, rib and skeletal fractures, and pneumothorax. She later said she had no memory of the events surrounding the fall, but believed ill-treatment may have continued at the station. Her brother later stated that he had heard her shouting to be released and heard threats, insults, and racial slurs.

The investigation was split. As to the station fall, criminal proceedings were opened against unknown officers for failing to guard the applicant under an internal 2011 Decree, which required continuous watching and readiness to prevent escape. The investigator found Officer A negligent: he turned his back, did not check whether the window was locked, and did not arrange same-sex supervision. The prosecution service found no grounds for criminal prosecution, treating the matter as disciplinary only. Officer A received a 5% salary reduction. The applicant was not informed and had no victim status.

As to the alleged car ill-treatment, separate proceedings ended with no suspicion of wrongdoing. The authorities found her allegations improbable, citing her cooperation, the officers’ positions in the car, and her amnesia. Her repeated review requests failed. The Constitutional Court declared her complaint manifestly ill-founded, and the Ombudsperson found no violation.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, she complained under Articles 2, 3, 6 and 13 that she had been ill-treated in the police car and at the station, that the State failed to protect her life and health during detention, that no plausible explanation was provided, and that the investigation was ineffective, arbitrary, and failed to examine possible racial motives. The Court examined the complaints under Articles 2 and 3, assessing the car and station incidents together. It found violations of Article 2, both substantive and procedural: the State was responsible for the applicant’s injuries because Officer A failed to continuously watch her as required by domestic escort rules, and the resulting investigation was ineffective. The case therefore concerned positive obligations to protect a detained minor’s life and to carry out an effective investigation into her fall from a police station window, alongside unresolved allegations of ill-treatment and discriminatory motive.

**Case Summary: Communauté genevoise d’action syndicale (CGAS) v. Switzerland**

The case concerned Switzerland’s COVID-19 restrictions and their impact on the right to freedom of peaceful assembly under Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Communauté genevoise d’action syndicale (CGAS), is a Geneva-based association established in 1962 to defend workers’ interests and trade-union and democratic freedoms. Before the pandemic, it organised and participated in numerous public gatherings, demonstrations and marches each year.

In early 2020, Switzerland introduced emergency measures to combat COVID-19. On 28 February 2020, the Federal Council declared a “special situation” under the Epidemics Act and banned events of more than 1,000 people. On 13 March 2020, Ordinance 2 on COVID-19 prohibited gatherings of more than 100 people but allowed cantonal exemptions for events linked to political or training rights. On 16 March 2020, the Federal Council declared an “extraordinary situation” and amended the ordinance, effective 17 March 2020, to ban all public and private gatherings, including associative and political activities. The exemption for political rights was removed. From 20 March 2020, gatherings of more than five people in public places were also banned.

Criminal sanctions were attached. Intentionally organising or conducting a prohibited gathering under Article 6 could lead to up to three years’ imprisonment or a fine. Breaching the public-gathering ban could attract a fixed fine of 100 Swiss francs. The general ban lasted approximately two and a half months, until relaxations began in late May and June 2020.

CGAS alleged that it was prevented from organising and participating in public meetings. In particular, it had planned a gathering for 1 May 2020 but withdrew its authorisation request after police indicated that no gatherings would be permitted under the ordinance. CGAS argued that it had been forced to cancel the event and, more generally, to alter its activities under threat of criminal penalties. It complained that the Federal Council’s ordinances were general measures that could not be directly challenged before domestic courts, so it had not applied to the Swiss courts.

The Government disputed CGAS’s victim status, arguing that it had not applied for an exemption or received a formal refusal. It claimed that CGAS could have requested authorisation under Article 7 of the ordinance and, if refused, appealed to the cantonal courts and then the Federal Supreme Court, which could review the ordinance’s compatibility with higher law in a preliminary ruling. The Government also noted that CGAS had withdrawn its request.

The Court found that CGAS could claim victim status. It had been obliged to change its behaviour and refrain from organising public meetings to avoid criminal penalties, creating a sufficient link between the association and the alleged harm. On exhaustion of domestic remedies, the Court noted that the possibility of exemption for political rights existed only briefly, until 16 March 2020, and the Government provided no example of an exemption being granted in Geneva during the relevant period. After 17 March 2020, all gatherings were banned and the political exception was removed. Federal Council ordinances could not be challenged directly in abstract review, and the Federal Supreme Court could not review Federal Council acts. Although implementing decisions could be appealed, the general ban itself was not subject to effective judicial review of proportionality. The Court also emphasised that Switzerland had not used Article 15 to derogate from its Convention obligations.

The case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 27 November 2023. The key alleged violation was that the blanket ban on public gatherings, backed by criminal sanctions and lacking rigorous judicial review, disproportionately interfered with CGAS’s rights under Article 11.

**Case Summary: Communauté genevoise d’action syndicale (CGAS) v. Switzerland**

The case concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 26 May 2020 by CGAS, a Swiss trade-union association based in Geneva and established in 1962. Its statutory aim is to defend workers’ interests, particularly trade-union and democratic freedoms, and it regularly organised dozens of public gatherings each year. Relying on Article 11 of the Convention (freedom of peaceful assembly), CGAS alleged that Switzerland’s COVID-19 measures deprived it of the right to organise and participate in public meetings.

The pandemic context is central. The first Swiss COVID-19 case was detected on 25 February 2020. On 28 February, the Federal Council declared a “special situation” under the Epidemics Act and banned events exceeding 1,000 persons. On 13 March, Ordinance 2 COVID-19 banned gatherings of more than 100 persons, allowing cantonal exemptions for political or training rights. On 16 March, the Federal Council declared an “extraordinary situation” and, effective 17 March, prohibited all public and private gatherings, removing the political-rights exemption. Article 10d imposed criminal sanctions—up to three years’ imprisonment or a fine—for intentionally organising prohibited gatherings. On 20 March, gatherings of more than five persons in public places were banned. Measures were extended until 26 April, then gradually relaxed from 11 May; political gatherings were authorised again from 6 June, and the prohibition was lifted on 20 June 2020.

CGAS claimed it was forced to cancel a May Day gathering planned for 1 May 2020 and withdrew its authorisation request after Geneva police announced no gatherings would be authorised. It argued it was deprived of any possibility to organise or participate in public meetings, and that no appeal lay against the Federal Council’s ordinances before domestic courts.

The Government contested admissibility. It argued CGAS was not a victim because it had withdrawn its request and never received a formal refusal, and that exemptions under Article 7 remained possible. It also contended that CGAS failed to exhaust domestic remedies: a refusal of authorisation could have been appealed to the Geneva Court of Justice and then the Federal Supreme Court, which could review the ordinance’s compatibility with higher-ranking law, including the Convention.

The Court rejected both objections. On victim status, it found that CGAS had regularly organised demonstrations, was prevented from doing so under threat of criminal sanctions, and was obliged to alter its behaviour to avoid penalties; there was a sufficient link between the association and the alleged harm. On exhaustion, the Court noted that the political-rights exemption existed only from 13 to 16 March 2020, and the Government provided no example of an exemption granted in Geneva during the relevant period. Moreover, the Federal Supreme Court judgment relied on by the Government (finding judicial review available) was delivered only in March 2021, about a year after the events. The Chamber found a violation of Article 11, emphasising the drastic general ban, criminal sanctions, and lack of rigorous judicial review of proportionality. The case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 27 November 2023.

**Case: Communauté genevoise d’action syndicale (CGAS) v. Switzerland (App. no. 21881/20)**

The applicant, CGAS, is a Geneva-based association established in 1962 to defend workers’ interests and trade-union and democratic freedoms. It regularly organised and participated in public gatherings in Geneva. Its complaint arose from Switzerland’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic.

The first Swiss COVID-19 case was detected on 25 February 2020. On 28 February, the Federal Council declared a “special situation” and banned events of more than 1,000 people. On 13 March, it adopted Ordinance 2, banning public or private gatherings of more than 100 people, while allowing limited cantonal exemptions, including for political or training rights. On 16 March, the Federal Council declared an “extraordinary situation” under the Epidemics Act. From 17 March, all public and private gatherings, including associative activities, were forbidden, and the earlier political-rights exemption was removed. From 20 March, gatherings of more than five people in public places were also banned. Breaches could lead to up to three years’ imprisonment or a fine, and public-place violations could attract fixed fines of 100 Swiss francs. Restrictions began easing from 11 May, and political gatherings were again authorised from 6 June 2020.

CGAS relied on Article 11 of the Convention, alleging that the general ban deprived it of the right to organise and participate in peaceful public assemblies. It claimed it had planned a May Day gathering but withdrew its authorisation request after the Geneva police indicated that no gatherings would be authorised under the ordinance. More broadly, it argued that the Federal Council’s ordinances applied generally, that no direct appeal lay against them, and that it had therefore been unable, for about two and a half months, to organise or participate in public meetings on pain of criminal sanctions.

The Government disputed victim status and non-exhaustion. It argued that CGAS had withdrawn its own request and had never applied for an exemption or received a refusal. It said the applicant could have sought an exemption under Article 7, appealed any refusal to the Canton of Geneva courts and then to the Federal Supreme Court, which could review the ordinance’s compatibility with higher law, including the Convention. Criminal convictions could also be appealed. CGAS countered that after 17 March no political exemption existed in practice; that no individual decision could adequately remedy a blanket ban; and that Swiss courts could not directly review Federal Council ordinances.

The Court found CGAS could claim victim status. Before the pandemic it regularly organised demonstrations; the ban obliged it to alter its conduct and cancel a planned gathering under threat of prosecution. There was a sufficient link between the association and the alleged harm. On exhaustion, the Court stressed that remedies must be effective in practice. The political exemption existed only from 13 to 16 March, and the Government provided no example of a Geneva exemption being granted during the relevant period. Because the measure was general, backed by criminal sanctions, and the Federal Supreme Court did not examine the merits during the lockdown, the applicant lacked effective judicial review of proportionality.

The case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 27 November 2023. The Grand Chamber found a violation of Article 11. The general ban was a drastic measure affecting CGAS’s activities for a considerable period and required strong justification and particularly rigorous judicial review. Switzerland had not used Article 15 to derogate from its Convention obligations. The absence of judicial review of the proportionality of the ban, combined with criminal sanctions, rendered the interference unjustified under Article 11.

In *De Legé v. the Netherlands* (ECtHR, 4 October 2022), the applicant, a Dutch national living in Spain, complained under Article 6 § 1 that documents he was forced to disclose were used to recalculate punitive tax fines, violating the privilege against self-incrimination.

The case began when Dutch tax authorities received information from Belgian authorities, derived from stolen bank data found in a criminal investigation, identifying Dutch residents with accounts at X Bank in Luxembourg. The applicant was identified as an account holder. Luxembourg banking secrecy at the time prevented lawful transmission of account information without the account holder’s cooperation.

In March 2007, a tax inspector wrote to the applicant about an investigation into foreign bank accounts. He asked him to complete declaration and statement forms concerning accounts held abroad and to provide copies of all bank statements for 1995–2000. The inspector relied on section 47 of the General State Taxes Act, which obliges taxpayers to provide information and documents relevant to taxation. The applicant refused, invoking the privilege against self-incrimination. He argued that the request was effectively a criminal charge because it would lead to tax fines, that the information could not be obtained without his cooperation, and that it was uncertain whether the documents existed.

The tax inspector then issued estimated additional income-tax and capital-tax assessments, together with 100% tax fines. The State brought civil interim proceedings to compel disclosure. In November 2008, the provisional-measures judge ordered the applicant to declare whether he had held foreign bank accounts after 31 December 1995 and to provide bank statements and portfolio summaries for 1996–2000. Non-compliance was punishable by penalty payments of EUR 5,000 per day, up to EUR 50,000. The applicant complied in December 2008, submitting the forms and bank documents. The tax inspector used the material to recalculate the assessments and reduced the fines accordingly.

The applicant challenged the use of the documents in the tax proceedings. The domestic courts rejected his complaint, relying on the distinction between will-dependent and will-independent material. They held that bank statements and portfolio summaries existed independently of the applicant’s will and could be used for tax fines, even if obtained under threat of penalty payments. The Supreme Court dismissed his further appeal, finding that the authorities could assume the documents existed, the order had specified them, and the completed declarations had no independent significance.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged a breach of Article 6 § 1. The Court examined the scope of the privilege against self-incrimination in the financial-law context. It accepted that both prerequisites for the privilege were met: coercion through penalty payments and an actual interference with the right. However, it found that the bank documents had an existence independent of the applicant’s will. The authorities already had information identifying him as the account holder; the judicial order specifically indicated which documents were to be supplied; and the documents were pre-existing bank records. The privilege did not therefore extend to their use for recalculating the tax fines. The penalty payments imposed for non-compliance did not amount to treatment contrary to Article 3. The Court consequently found no violation of Article 6 § 1.

**Case Name:** *De Legé v. the Netherlands* (Application no. 58342/15), ECtHR Fourth Section, 4 October 2022 (final 30 January 2023).

The applicant, Mr Levinus Adrianus de Legé, was a Dutch national resident in Spain. The Dutch Tax and Customs Administration obtained information from Belgian authorities concerning Luxembourg bank accounts held at X Bank. The information had been stolen from the bank and included account balances for 1994, 1995 and 1996. The authorities identified the applicant as an account holder. Luxembourg banking secrecy at the time prevented lawful transmission of account information to foreign tax authorities without the account holder’s cooperation.

In March 2007 the tax inspector requested the applicant to declare any foreign bank accounts held after 31 December 1994 and to provide bank statements for 1995–2000 under section 47 of the General State Taxes Act. The applicant invoked the privilege against self-incrimination, arguing that the information could lead to tax fines and that he could not be compelled to provide it. He refused to comply. The tax inspector then issued estimated additional income and capital tax assessments for 1995 and 1996, together with fines initially set at 100% of the assessments.

Because the applicant still did not provide the documents, the State brought interim civil proceedings. In November 2008 the provisional-measures judge ordered the applicant to declare whether he held foreign bank accounts after 31 December 1995 and to provide the requested bank statements and documents for 1996–2000 within fourteen days, on pain of penalty payments of EUR 5,000 per day, up to EUR 50,000. The applicant complied in December 2008, submitting forms declaring a joint account at X Bank and providing bank statements and portfolio summaries.

The tax inspector used those bank documents to recalculate the actual figures, reducing the additional assessments and tax fines. The applicant objected and appealed, arguing that the use of documents he had been coerced to provide, under threat of penalty payments, for the purpose of calculating tax fines violated Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, particularly the privilege against self-incrimination. The domestic courts rejected this. Relying on Supreme Court case-law, they distinguished “will-dependent” material, such as statements, from “will-independent” material, such as pre-existing bank documents. They found the bank statements were will-independent and could be used for the tax fines. The Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s further appeal in 2015.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 (criminal head) that the use of the compelled bank documents for recalculating tax fines breached his fair-trial rights. The Court reiterated that the privilege against self-incrimination is not absolute and does not extend to material obtained through compulsory powers but which has an existence independent of the accused’s will, such as documents. It considered that the authorities had already been aware of pre-existing documents showing the foreign account, that the judicial order specifically indicated the documents to be supplied, and that the applicant was not compelled to make incriminating statements used against him. The bank statements and portfolio summaries were pre-existing records whose existence did not depend on his will. The penalty payments imposed for non-compliance did not amount to treatment contrary to Article 3.

Accordingly, the Court found that the use of the bank documents for the recalculation of the tax fine did not fall within the scope of the privilege against self-incrimination and did not violate Article 6 § 1. There was no violation of the Convention.

In *De Legé v. the Netherlands* (Application no. 58342/15, ECtHR Fourth Section, judgment 4 October 2022, final 30 January 2023), the applicant was a Dutch national living in Spain. Dutch tax authorities in 2005 received information from Belgium concerning bank accounts held with X Bank in Luxembourg. The data had been stolen from the bank and included account balances. The Dutch Tax and Customs Administration identified the applicant as an account holder. At the time, Luxembourg banking secrecy prevented lawful transmission of such account information to foreign tax authorities except with the account holder’s cooperation.

In March 2007, the tax inspector wrote to the applicant, stating that he appeared to hold or have held foreign bank accounts and requiring him under section 47 of the General State Taxes Act to declare past or present foreign accounts and provide bank statements for 1995–2000. The applicant, through counsel, invoked the privilege against self-incrimination. He argued that such requests would lead to additional tax assessments and punitive tax fines, meaning Article 6 of the Convention applied under its criminal head, and that the authorities could not obtain the information without his cooperation. He refused to comply.

The tax inspector then issued additional income tax and capital tax assessments, together with tax fines initially set at 100% of the additional assessments. The State subsequently brought civil interim proceedings to compel disclosure. On 27 November 2008, the provisional-measures judge ordered the applicant to state whether he had held foreign accounts after 31 December 1995, to complete forms, and to provide bank statements and portfolio summaries for the relevant period. The order was made on pain of penalty payments of EUR 5,000 per day or part of a day, up to EUR 50,000. The applicant did not appeal and complied on 9 December 2008, submitting the forms and bank documents.

The tax inspector used the bank statements and portfolio summaries to recalculate the tax assessments and fines, ultimately reducing the fines. The applicant objected and appealed, arguing that the use of documents obtained under coercion for the purpose of tax fines violated his Article 6 § 1 right not to incriminate himself. The domestic courts rejected that argument. They classified bank statements and portfolio summaries as “will-independent” material under *Saunders v. the United Kingdom*, holding that Article 6 did not preclude their use. The Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s further appeal, although the Advocate-General had advised that exclusion of the evidence was required.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the alleged violation was Article 6 § 1, specifically the privilege against self-incrimination. The key issue was whether bank documents obtained by a judicial disclosure order, enforced by penalty payments, could be used to recalculate a tax fine. The Court considered that the privilege requires both coercion and an actual interference with the right. Coercion existed because of the penalty payments. However, the documents were pre-existing bank statements and portfolio summaries whose existence did not depend on the applicant’s will. The authorities already knew of the account and had identified the applicant as holder; the judicial order specifically indicated the documents to be supplied. The Court therefore held that the use of those documents for recalculating the tax fine did not fall within the scope of the privilege against self-incrimination. It also found that the penalty payments did not amount to treatment contrary to Article 3. Accordingly, there was no violation of Article 6 § 1.

In *Cosovan v. the Republic of Moldova*, the applicant, Serghei Cosovan, a Moldovan businessman and local councillor, was arrested on 26 September 2017 on suspicion of abuse of office and fraud. On 29 September 2017, the Chișinău court ordered his pre-trial detention for 30 days, relying on reasonable suspicion, the serious nature of the alleged offence (up to 15 years’ imprisonment), and risks that he might abscond, reoffend, or obstruct the investigation. His detention was repeatedly extended on essentially the same grounds. The applicant argued that he had known of the investigation since 2014, had always appeared when summoned, and had not absconded or interfered; alternatives such as seizing his passport or house arrest were available.

The most significant facts concerned his health. Cosovan suffered from hepatitis C, decompensated cirrhosis, and hypersplenism, and his illness was in a terminal phase. Medical councils confirmed the diagnosis and recommended specialist hepatologist care, albumin and plasma transfusions, and evaluation for a liver transplant. However, the care provided in detention was allegedly inadequate. Prison hospital no. 16 lacked a hepatologist and intensive-care facilities, was not accredited as a medical institution, and had no contract with a liver-transplant centre. Recommended treatments were delayed or not fully followed, his treatment was supervised by a family doctor rather than a specialist, and transfers to public hospitals were intermittent or refused. He complained about missing medication records and lack of proper specialist oversight. The Ombudsman and medical experts found that his condition was worsening and that his illness fell within the list allowing seriously ill convicted persons to be exempted from serving their sentence. The national anti-discrimination body found that denying seriously ill pre-trial detainees the possibility of release, while granting it to convicted prisoners, constituted discrimination.

On 24 April 2018, a judge replaced detention with house arrest, finding no sufficient risk and noting that continued detention of a person in a terminal stage could amount to torture. Yet, upon leaving prison, the applicant was immediately re-arrested in a new prosecution opened on 1 March 2018 concerning similar alleged victims. A new pre-trial detention order was issued on 27 April 2018 without mentioning the existing house arrest, and the house-arrest decision was later annulled. He was convicted of fraud in July 2018 and sentenced to seven years, but appeals and retrials followed. He was eventually released on health grounds in November 2019 and died in March 2021; his wife continued the proceedings.

The applicant also complained under Article 2 that the failure to provide adequate medical care and transfer him to a suitable public hospital endangered his life. Under Article 3, the key issue was whether the authorities fulfilled their positive obligation to provide adequate medical treatment and whether continued detention was compatible with his terminal condition. Under Article 5 § 3, he alleged that the domestic courts gave insufficient reasons for his prolonged pre-trial detention and that the investigation had been artificially divided into separate cases to obtain procedural advantages or circumvent mandatory legal provisions.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 3 (substantive) and Article 5 § 3. It held that inadequate medical treatment and continued detention despite a terminal illness amounted to degrading treatment, and that there was no justification for distinguishing between convicted and pre-trial detainees where detention caused suffering incompatible with the person’s medical condition. It also found that the domestic courts failed to provide sufficient reasons for extending pre-trial detention and that the artificial division of the criminal investigation was incompatible with Article 5.

In *Cosovan v. the Republic of Moldova*, the applicant, Serghei Cosovan, was a Moldovan businessman and local councillor representing an opposition party. On 26 September 2017 he was arrested at a prosecutor’s office on suspicion of abuse of office and fraud. He allegedly accepted money from several persons while falsely promising them ownership of metal kiosks. On 29 September 2017 the Chișinău Court ordered his pre-trial detention for 30 days. That detention was repeatedly extended, with courts relying on largely identical reasons: the alleged offence was serious and punishable by up to 15 years’ imprisonment; there was a reasonable suspicion; and he allegedly posed risks of absconding, reoffending, obstructing the investigation, or disturbing public order.

The case’s central Article 3 issue concerned the applicant’s medical condition. Before arrest he suffered from hepatitis C and cirrhosis. After detention, doctors diagnosed decompensated cirrhosis, severe hypersplenism, and other complications. Medical councils confirmed the diagnosis and recommended specialist hepatological care, albumin and plasma transfusions, and assessment for a liver transplant. However, prison hospital no. 16 lacked a hepatologist and intensive-care facilities, was not accredited as a medical institution, and had no contract with a liver-transplant institution. There were delays in specialist examinations and transfers to public hospitals. The Ombudsman and the Council for the Prevention of Torture raised concerns about inadequate care and the applicant’s worsening condition. Medical evidence later showed his illness was terminal, progressive, and associated with limited life expectancy.

On 24 April 2018 an investigating judge replaced detention with house arrest. The judge found no sufficient evidence of absconding or witness interference, noted the terminal nature of the illness, and considered continued detention incompatible with his medical condition. The judge also criticised the fact that release on health grounds was available only to convicted persons, not pre-trial detainees. Immediately after leaving prison, however, the applicant was re-arrested in a new prosecution opened on 1 March 2018 concerning a similar group of alleged victims. A new 30-day pre-trial detention order was issued on 27 April 2018 and extended monthly; the earlier house-arrest decision was annulled in May 2018.

The applicant was convicted of fraud in July 2018 and sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment, but the case was later quashed and sent for retrial. His requests for release on health grounds under Article 95(2) of the Criminal Code and Ministry of Justice Order No. 331 were rejected while his conviction was not final. An expert confirmed that his disease was on the list permitting exemption from sentence, that his health was deteriorating, and that he had limited life expectancy. In October 2018 the CPEDAE found discrimination: seriously ill pre-trial detainees could not benefit from the same release mechanism as convicted prisoners. He was eventually released on health grounds in November 2019 and died in March 2021.

The Court examined alleged violations of Article 3 and Article 5 § 3. Under Article 3, the key facts were the authorities’ knowledge of a serious, terminal illness; inadequate prison medical facilities; failure to ensure timely specialist care and transfers; and continued detention despite suffering incompatible with his condition. Under Article 5 § 3, the key facts were the courts’ repeated, insufficiently reasoned extensions of pre-trial detention and the immediate re-arrest and new prosecution after house arrest, which suggested an artificial division of the criminal investigation to obtain procedural advantages or circumvent mandatory release provisions.

In *Foutas Aristidou v. Cyprus*, the applicant, Christakis Foutas Aristidou, a Cypriot national born in 1955 and living in Limassol, complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about the length of criminal proceedings and the delay by the authorities in bringing the case against him after the investigation had concluded.

The underlying criminal case concerned an allegation of indecent assault. On 26 January 2010, following a complaint, the applicant visited the place where the alleged offence took place with the police. He was questioned, charged by the police, and pleaded not guilty. On 8 April 2010, the police forwarded the investigation file to the Police Prosecution Service. The file was returned to the police with instructions from the Attorney General to prosecute on 22 March 2011. An indictment was then prepared, and on 6 July 2011 the case was listed with the District Court of Limassol (case no. 9886/11). The applicant appeared in court for the first time on 26 September 2011, when he again pleaded not guilty.

The case was postponed several times, mainly because the court did not have time to hear it. The hearing eventually commenced on 18 September 2013. On 25 June 2014, the District Court of Limassol found the applicant guilty of indecent assault. On 9 July 2014, taking into account the applicant’s personal circumstances, as well as the delay in filing the indictment with the court and the delay in the proceedings, the court sentenced him to three months’ imprisonment. On 3 October 2014, the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal (no. 180/14).

The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 4 March 2015. The Court gave notice to the Cypriot Government of the complaint concerning the length of the criminal proceedings under Article 6 § 1 and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The Government was represented by the Attorney General of the Republic of Cyprus.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore the chronology and conduct of the domestic proceedings. The applicant was charged in January 2010. The investigation file was sent for prosecution in April 2010, but the case was not listed until July 2011—about fifteen months later—and his first court appearance was in September 2011. After that, the case was repeatedly adjourned because of court scheduling difficulties, and the hearing did not begin until September 2013, nearly two years after the first appearance. The trial court convicted him in June 2014 and sentenced him in July 2014; the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal in October 2014. Thus, the applicant’s Article 6 § 1 complaint focused on the overall duration of the criminal process and, specifically, on the delay between the conclusion of the police investigation and the bringing of proceedings before the court. The domestic courts’ own acknowledgment of delay—reflected in the sentencing decision—was also relevant to his complaint. The ECtHR delivered its judgment on 7 June 2022.

The Cypriot Government was represented by the Attorney General, C. Clerides. The applicant lodged the application on 4 March 2015. The Court decided to give notice of only one complaint—the length of criminal proceedings under Article 6 §1 of the Convention—and declared the remainder inadmissible.

He was questioned, charged by the police, and pleaded not guilty. On 8 April 2010, the police sent the investigation file to the Police Prosecution Service. The file was then returned to the police with instructions for prosecution by the Attorney General on 22 March 2011. This meant that, after the investigative file was forwarded, approximately eleven months elapsed before the prosecution decision/instructions were provided.

An indictment was prepared, and on 6 July 2011 the case was listed before the District Court of Limassol (case no. 9886/11). The applicant made his first court appearance on 26 September 2011 and again pleaded not guilty. The proceedings were then postponed several times. According to the case summary, these postponements occurred mainly because the court did not have time to hear the case. The hearing did not begin until 18 September 2013—almost two years after the first appearance and more than three and a half years after the initial police charge. On 25 June 2014, the District Court of Limassol found the applicant guilty of indecent assault. On 9 July 2014, when sentencing him to three months’ imprisonment, the court considered his personal circumstances as well as the delay in filing the indictment with the court and the delay in the proceedings. On 3 October 2014, the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal (no. 180/14).

The applicant’s complaint under Article 6 §1 concerned the length of the criminal proceedings before the District Court of Limassol and the delay by the authorities in bringing proceedings against him after the investigation had concluded. The key periods relevant to that alleged violation were therefore: (1) the delay between the police forwarding the investigation file in April 2010 and the Attorney General’s prosecution instructions in March 2011; (2) the period from the indictment being prepared/listed in July 2011 to the applicant’s first appearance in September 2011; (3) the repeated postponements before the hearing finally commenced in September 2013, attributed mainly to lack of court time; and (4) the further period until conviction in June 2014 and sentencing in July 2014, with the appeal dismissed in October 2014. The domestic sentencing court expressly acknowledged both the delay in filing the indictment and the delay in the proceedings, treating them as mitigating factors. The European Court of Human Rights gave notice of the Article 6 §1 length complaint to the Cypriot Government and declared the rest of the application inadmissible.

001-219293:
In Gerasyutin and Others v. Ukraine (Applications nos. 23698/20 and 3 others), the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 29 September 2022. The case concerned applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants and the relevant details of each application were set out in an appended table. The Ukrainian Government was given notice of the applications. Because the applications raised similar subject matter, the Court decided to examine them jointly in a single judgment.

The central factual complaint was that criminal proceedings involving the applicants had lasted excessively long. The applicants alleged that the duration of those proceedings was incompatible with the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. They also alleged that Ukrainian domestic law did not provide them with any effective remedy by which to complain about the excessive length, contrary to Article 13 of the Convention. Article 6 § 1 guarantees that in determining any criminal charge, everyone is entitled to a hearing within a reasonable time by a tribunal. Article 13 guarantees an effective remedy before a national authority for anyone whose Convention rights have been violated, even where the violation was committed by persons acting in an official capacity.

The Court reiterated its established case-law on assessing the reasonableness of the length of proceedings. It stated that this assessment depends on the particular circumstances of the case and on several criteria: the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicants, the conduct of the relevant authorities, and what was at stake for the applicants in the dispute. Those criteria derive from prior Court judgments, including Pélissier and Sassi v. France and Frydlender v. France. The Court also noted that it had already found a violation in a similar case, Nechay v. Ukraine, concerning comparable issues of excessive length of criminal proceedings and the absence of an effective remedy in Ukraine.

After examining all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of justifying the overall length of the proceedings at the national level. It therefore concluded that the length of the criminal proceedings in the applicants’ cases was excessive and failed to satisfy the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1. The Court further found that the applicants did not have an effective domestic remedy for their complaints about the length of proceedings. Consequently, there was also a violation of Article 13 of the Convention.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore that the applicants were involved in criminal proceedings in Ukraine; those proceedings were not completed within a reasonable time; the delay was not justified by complexity, applicant conduct, or other circumstances; and domestic law provided no effective remedy to address the excessive length. The Court upheld the applicants’ complaints and found violations of both Article 6 § 1 and Article 13. The judgment was final but remained subject to possible editorial revision.

In *Gerasyutin and Others v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 23698/20 and 3 others), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 29 September 2022. The Committee was composed of Stéphanie Mourou-Vikström, President, Ivana Jelić, and Kateřina Šimáčková, judges, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The case originated in four applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants complained of two related matters: first, that the criminal proceedings against them had lasted excessively long, contrary to the “reasonable time” requirement in Article 6 § 1; and second, that Ukrainian law did not provide any effective remedy by which they could complain about that delay, contrary to Article 13. The Ukrainian Government was given notice of the applications.

The Court joined the applications because they concerned similar subject matter. The judgment notes that the list of applicants and the relevant details of each application are set out in an appended table. That table would ordinarily contain the specific dates of the domestic criminal proceedings, the length of those proceedings, the applicants’ identities, and the dates on which they lodged their applications with the Strasbourg Court. The body of the judgment does not reproduce those individual details, but the central factual allegation is clear: each applicant was subject to criminal proceedings in Ukraine whose overall duration was alleged to be incompatible with the Convention.

The Court reiterated the standard test for assessing the length of proceedings under Article 6 § 1. Reasonableness must be assessed in light of the particular circumstances of the case and by reference to four criteria: the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicants, the conduct of the relevant authorities, and what was at stake for the applicants. The Court also relied on its earlier leading case, *Nechay v. Ukraine* (no. 15360/10, 1 July 2021), in which it had already found a violation of the Convention in relation to similar complaints of excessive length of criminal proceedings in Ukraine.

After examining all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of justifying the overall length of the proceedings at the national level. It therefore concluded that the length of the proceedings was excessive and failed to satisfy the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1. The Court further found that the applicants did not have at their disposal an effective remedy in respect of those complaints, as required by Article 13. Consequently, the Court found violations of both Article 6 § 1 and Article 13.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are thus not the underlying criminal charges or the merits of the domestic cases, but the duration of the criminal proceedings and the absence of a domestic mechanism to challenge that duration. The Government failed to show that the delays were justified by complexity, the applicants’ conduct, or any other relevant factor. The case therefore forms part of the Court’s established jurisprudence concerning excessive length of criminal proceedings in Ukraine and the lack of effective domestic remedies for such delays.

**Case Summary: Gerasyutin and Others v. Ukraine**  
*Applications nos. 23698/20 and 3 others – ECtHR Fifth Section, 29 September 2022*

The case of *Gerasyutin and Others v. Ukraine* concerned four applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants complained primarily about the excessive length of criminal proceedings brought against them and about the absence of any effective remedy in Ukrainian domestic law for that delay. They relied on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to a hearing within a reasonable time in the determination of a criminal charge, and Article 13, which guarantees an effective remedy before a national authority for Convention violations.

In **Suslov v. Ukraine** (Application no. 46298/19), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee) delivered judgment on **6 October 2022** (rectified on 8 December 2022). The applicant, represented by Kharkiv lawyer A.A. Kristenko, lodged his application against Ukraine on **10 August 2019** under Article 34 of the Convention.

The applicant was detained in Ukraine and suffered from serious medical conditions, including **Hepatitis C and mercury poisoning**. These conditions affected his everyday functioning and caused considerable anxiety about whether the medical care provided in detention was adequate. His principal complaint was under **Article 3** of the Convention: that he did not receive adequate medical treatment while in detention.

A key fact in the case is that on **14 November 2019**, the Court applied an interim measure under **Rule 39** of the Rules of Court. It directed the Ukrainian Government to:
- immediately transfer the applicant to a specialist civil hospital to complete medical examinations concerning his Hepatitis C, in accordance with his doctor’s recommendations;
- conduct medical examinations regarding mercury poisoning in compliance with the doctor’s recommendations; and
- provide him with necessary medical treatment for both Hepatitis C and mercury poisoning based on those examinations.

The case was also given priority under Rule 41. The Russian Government did not intervene. The Armenian Government intervened under Article 36 § 1 and Rule 44 and submitted written comments, arguing that there had been a violation of Article 3. The Ukrainian Government denied any violation.

On the Article 3 complaint, the Court reiterated that authorities must ensure diagnosis and care are prompt and accurate. Where required by the nature of the condition, supervision must be regular and systematic and involve a comprehensive therapeutic strategy aimed at successfully treating the detainee’s health problems or preventing their aggravation. Prison medical treatment must be appropriate and comparable to the quality of treatment the State has committed to providing for the general population, though not necessarily equal to the best available outside prison.

After examining the material, the Court identified shortcomings in the applicant’s medical treatment, as listed in the appended table. It found similar violations in cases such as **Nevmerzhitsky v. Ukraine**, **Melnik v. Ukraine**, and **Logvinenko v. Ukraine**. The Court concluded that the applicant did not receive comprehensive and adequate medical care while in detention, in violation of **Article 3**.

The applicant also complained under **Articles 6 and 13** about the excessive length of civil proceedings and the lack of an effective domestic remedy. He further argued under **Article 34** that the Ukrainian Government’s failure to comply with the Rule 39 interim measure violated his right of individual application. The Ukrainian Government denied violations; the Armenian Government considered there were violations; the applicant maintained his complaints. The Court found the complaints about excessive civil proceedings and absence of domestic remedies not manifestly ill-founded under Article 35 § 3 (a) and not inadmissible on other grounds.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore: the applicant’s serious medical conditions in detention; the specific medical needs recognized by the Court’s interim measure; the alleged failure to transfer him to a civil specialist hospital, conduct required Hepatitis C and mercury poisoning examinations, and provide necessary treatment; the identified shortcomings in prison medical care; and the alleged non-compliance with the interim measure. The case concerns Ukraine’s obligations to provide adequate medical care to detainees and to comply with Court interim measures, as well as procedural guarantees in domestic civil proceedings.

In *Elmazova and Others v. North Macedonia* (ECtHR, 13 December 2022), 87 Roma children and their parents complained that Roma pupils were segregated in two State-run primary schools in Bitola and Shtip. They relied principally on Article 14 of the Convention read with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1, alleging discriminatory denial of equal access to education through Roma-only schooling or Roma-only classes, without objective and reasonable justification.

**Bitola (Application no. 11811/20):** The applicants lived in Bair, a residential district in Bitola. Two State primary schools, G.S. and T.A., were about 600 metres apart and belonged to the same catchment area. Under domestic law, children had a guaranteed place at their catchment school, but parents could request transfer to another public school with the admitting school’s consent. In the 2018/19 academic year, G.S. had 584 pupils, 488 of whom were Roma (83.5%); T.A. had 589 pupils, 560 of whom were ethnic Macedonians (95.1%), with only 15 Roma pupils (2.54%). Of 145 first-grade children in the relevant catchment area (42 ethnic Macedonians and 103 Roma), G.S. enrolled 5 ethnic Macedonian and 63 Roma pupils, while T.A. enrolled 6 Roma pupils. G.S. was widely known as a “Romani or Gypsy school.” The applicants alleged that Roma from Bair were effectively enrolled in G.S., while ethnic Macedonians attended T.A., and that Roma pupils were unable to transfer to T.A. although Macedonian pupils could. The Constitutional Court accepted that the district’s children attended two ethnically divided schools but rejected the complaint, finding the statistics insufficient to prove segregation and noting that no applicant had shown a concrete transfer request or refusal. A dissenting opinion found sufficient evidence of different treatment.

**Shtip (Application no. 13550/20):** The child applicants attended G.D. primary school, where Roma pupils were placed in Roma-only classes. In 2017/18 and 2018/19, the first grade had three classes: two mixed and one Roma-only. Roma pupils made up 64% and 67% of first-grade pupils respectively. Many non-Roma pupils from the catchment area enrolled in other schools. G.D.’s efforts to attract non-Roma pupils and redistribute Roma pupils failed, partly because parents of pupils in mixed classes objected. The Constitutional Court rejected the complaint, holding that Roma-only class composition alone did not prove discrimination, that there was no evidence of inferior education in those classes, and that the complaint was premature because a civil discrimination remedy under the Discrimination Act was available.

**Context:** Ombudsman reports since 2011 had warned of Roma segregation in Bitola and Shtip. A 2015 report noted that 73 of 86 first-grade pupils in G.S. were Roma and that three Roma-only classes existed. Later figures showed persistent segregation: in 2020/21, 80 of 93 first-graders in G.S. were Roma; in 2021/22, all 77 were Roma. In G.D., by 2021/22, 63 of 78 first-graders were Roma, with two Roma-only classes. The Commission for Prevention and Protection against Discrimination found indirect discrimination and systemic segregation in education and recommended stricter enforcement of catchment rules.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 14 read with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1. It held that the Roma pupils’ segregation in G.S. and in Roma-only classes at G.D. was not objectively and reasonably justified. The State had failed to take desegregation measures to correct factual inequality and prevent the perpetuation of discrimination caused by Roma over-representation in G.S. and separate classes in G.D. Under Article 46, North Macedonia was required to take individual measures to end the segregation in both schools.

**Case: Elmazova and Others v. North Macedonia (ECtHR, 13 December 2022)**

The applicants were 87 Roma children and their parents from Bitola and Shtip, North Macedonia. They alleged that Roma pupils were segregated in two state-run primary schools—G.S. in Bitola and G.D. in Shtip—in violation of Article 14 of the Convention read together with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education without discrimination). The applicants complained of a Roma-only school in Bitola and Roma-only classes in Shtip.

**Bitola (G.S. school).** The applicants lived in Bair, a district of Bitola. G.S. and another school, T.A., were in the same catchment area and only 600 metres apart. Under domestic law, children were entitled to attend their catchment-area school, but parents could request a transfer to another public school with the admitting school’s consent. Roma children from Bair allegedly attended G.S., while ethnic Macedonian pupils attended T.A. The applicants claimed that T.A. permitted transfers of Macedonian pupils from G.S. but refused Roma transfers. In 2018/19, the Constitutional Court found that G.S. was 83.5% Roma (488 of 584 pupils), while T.A. was 95.1% Macedonian (560 of 589 pupils; only 15 Roma pupils, or 2.54%). Of first-grade pupils in the relevant catchment area, five Macedonian pupils and 63 Roma pupils enrolled in G.S., while six Roma pupils enrolled in T.A. Ethnic Macedonian pupils were placed together in a single class at each grade, except the final two years. Between 2016 and 2019, 58 transfer requests to T.A. were submitted, only three by Roma pupils; T.A. stated that all requests were granted. The Constitutional Court rejected the complaint, finding the statistics insufficient to prove segregation and noting no concrete evidence that any applicant had requested or been refused a transfer. Later, in 2020/21, 80 of 93 first-grade pupils at G.S. were Roma; in 2021/22, all 77 first-grade pupils were Roma. The Commission for Prevention and Protection against Discrimination found indirect discrimination and systemic ethnic segregation.

**Shtip (G.D. school).** In the 2017/18 and 2018/19 academic years, G.D. had three first-grade classes: two mixed and one Roma-only, each with 18 pupils. Fewer ethnic Macedonian pupils enrolled at G.D.; in 2017/18, 51 Macedonian pupils from G.D.’s catchment area enrolled in four out-of-catchment schools. G.D. tried home visits, flyers, meetings, redistribution of pupils, and sought stricter catchment enforcement and free transport, but without success. Roma pupils made up 64% of first graders in 2017/18 and 67% in 2018/19. The alleged Roma-only class in 2017/18 contained one non-Roma pupil. Mixed classes were larger, with 31, 32, 25, and 27 pupils. The Constitutional Court rejected the complaint, finding no evidence that Roma-only classes received inferior education and holding the complaint premature because civil remedies under the Discrimination Act had not been exhausted. Later, in 2020/21, 57 of 87 first graders were Roma; in 2021/22, 63 of 78 were Roma, with two of four classes Roma-only. The Commission again found indirect discrimination and “conscious separation” of Roma and non-Roma children.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 14 taken in conjunction with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1. It held that the Roma pupils were segregated in both schools and that the State had failed to take desegregation measures to correct their factual inequality and avoid perpetuating discrimination. The segregation was not objectively and reasonably justified by a legitimate aim. Under Article 46, North Macedonia was required to take individual measures to end the segregation in G.S. and G.D.

**Case: Elmazova and Others v. North Macedonia**  
**Court:** European Court of Human Rights, Second Section  
**Judgment:** 13 December 2022; final 13 March 2023  
**Applications:** nos. 11811/20 and 13550/20

The applicants were eighty-seven Roma children and their parents from Bitola and Shtip, North Macedonia, represented by the European Roma Rights Centre and a local lawyer. They alleged that Roma pupils were segregated in two State-run primary schools, contrary to Article 14 of the Convention read together with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1. The case concerned both a school attended predominantly by Roma children and Roma-only classes within another school.

In the first application, concerning primary school G.S. in Bitola, the applicants lived in Bair, a residential district with a large Roma population. Under a 2009 municipal decision, G.S. and another school, T.A., belonged to the same catchment area and were about 600 metres apart. Schools were obliged to admit children from their catchment area, but parents could request transfer to another school with the admitting school’s consent. In the 2018/19 academic year, 83.5% of pupils in G.S. were Roma (488 of 584), while 95.1% of pupils in T.A. were ethnic Macedonian (560 of 589). Of 145 first-grade pupils eligible in the relevant catchment area—42 ethnic Macedonians and 103 Roma—only five ethnic Macedonian pupils and 63 Roma pupils enrolled in G.S., while six Roma pupils enrolled in T.A. G.S. was widely known as the “Romani or Gypsy school.” The applicants alleged inferior education there, including fewer courses, less-skilled teachers and inadequate resources. The Constitutional Court rejected their complaint, finding that statistics alone did not prove segregation and that there was no concrete evidence Roma pupils had been refused transfer to T.A. or treated differently.

The second application concerned primary school G.D. in Shtip. In the 2017/18 and 2018/19 academic years, the first grade had three classes: two mixed and one Roma-only. Roma pupils made up 64% and 67% of first-grade pupils respectively. Many non-Roma pupils from the catchment area enrolled in schools outside it. G.D. took steps to attract non-Roma pupils and to redistribute Roma pupils, but these efforts largely failed; parents of pupils in mixed classes opposed redistribution. The Constitutional Court rejected the complaint, holding that the ethnic composition of classes did not automatically prove discrimination and that there was no evidence Roma-only classes received inferior education. It also considered the complaint premature because a civil discrimination claim was available.

Later, the Commission for Prevention and Protection against Discrimination found indirect discrimination and systemic ethnic segregation stemming from the Primary Education Act, recommending stricter application of catchment-area rules.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 14 taken together with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1. It held that the segregation of Roma pupils in both G.S. and G.D. was not objectively and reasonably justified by a legitimate aim. The State had failed to take desegregation measures to correct the applicants’ factual inequality and to prevent the perpetuation of discrimination caused by Roma over-representation. The Court required North Macedonia to take individual measures to end the segregation of Roma pupils in the two schools.

Case Lukošin v. Lithuania (Application no. 25059/20) is a European Court of Human Rights case decided by the Second Section, sitting as a Committee, with judgment delivered in Strasbourg on 18 January 2022. The applicant, Andrej Lukošin, a Lithuanian national born in 1973, was detained at Pravieniškės Correctional Facility. He lodged his application on 9 June 2020, complaining under Article 3 of the Convention about inadequate conditions of detention and about the domestic courts’ failure to award him compensation. The Court gave notice to the Lithuanian Government only of the complaint concerning conditions of detention and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

The case concerns two distinct periods of the applicant’s detention at Pravieniškės Correctional Facility.

The first period ran from 18 June to 18 August 2018. During that time, the applicant was held in dormitory-type rooms. He complained to the domestic administrative courts that he had been kept in overcrowded conditions. The administrative courts found that for 47 days he had only 2.97 square metres of personal space. That level of personal space was below the relevant domestic regulations. The domestic courts therefore accepted that the applicant’s detention conditions had breached national standards concerning personal space.

The second period ran from 5 September to 3 October 2018. During that period, the applicant was held in disciplinary cells. He complained that the cells were dilapidated and not properly lit. The administrative courts upheld those complaints. They found that the relevant domestic regulations had been breached during the entire 29-day period. The domestic courts thus acknowledged that the material conditions in the disciplinary cells fell short of domestic requirements.

In both sets of domestic proceedings, the courts found violations of domestic regulations but did not award the applicant any monetary compensation. Instead, they considered that the mere acknowledgment of a violation constituted sufficient just satisfaction for any non-pecuniary damage the applicant had sustained. The applicant then brought the matter to the European Court of Human Rights.

Before the Court, the applicant complained under Article 3 of the Convention that he had been detained in inadequate conditions and that he had not been awarded any compensation. The core alleged violations were therefore twofold: first, that the overcrowding during the first period and the dilapidated, poorly lit disciplinary cells during the second period amounted to inhuman or degrading treatment contrary to Article 3; and second, that the domestic authorities’ response—finding violations but awarding no compensation—failed to provide adequate redress for those alleged Article 3 breaches.

The Government submitted observations in the case. The Court deliberated in private on 14 December 2021 and adopted the judgment on that date. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision. The excerpt provided sets out the subject matter and procedural background, centering on the applicant’s Article 3 complaint about conditions of detention and the lack of compensation. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are the two detention periods, the domestic findings that the applicant had insufficient personal space for 47 days and was held in inadequate disciplinary cells for 29 days, and the domestic courts’ decision that acknowledging those violations was sufficient without any monetary award.

In *Lukošin v. Lithuania* (Application no. 25059/20), the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) examined a Lithuanian national’s complaint about inadequate conditions of detention. The applicant, Andrej Lukošin, born in 1973 and detained at Pravieniškės Correctional Facility, lodged his application on 9 June 2020 under Article 34 of the Convention. He alleged a violation of Article 3, complaining that he had been held in inadequate conditions and that he had received no compensation for that treatment. The Court gave notice of the complaint concerning conditions of detention to the Lithuanian Government and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The Government was represented by Ms K. Bubnytė-Širmenė.

The alleged violations concerned two distinct periods of detention. The first period ran from 18 June to 18 August 2018. During that time, the applicant was held in overcrowded dormitory-type rooms. He complained to the Lithuanian administrative courts. Those courts found that for 47 days he had only 2.97 square metres of personal space. That amount was below the relevant domestic regulations, so the domestic authorities themselves acknowledged that the detention conditions had breached the applicable standards. This finding of significant overcrowding over a sustained period was the central factual basis for the applicant’s Article 3 complaint regarding the first period.

The second period of detention ran from 5 September to 3 October 2018. During that time, the applicant was held in disciplinary cells. He complained that the cells were dilapidated and not properly lit. The administrative courts upheld those complaints and found that the relevant domestic regulations had been breached throughout the entire period, a total of 29 days. The physical deterioration of the disciplinary cells and their inadequate lighting therefore formed the factual core of the alleged Article 3 violation for the second period.

In both sets of domestic proceedings, the administrative courts accepted that violations had occurred. However, they considered that the mere acknowledgment of a violation constituted sufficient just satisfaction for any non-pecuniary damage the applicant had suffered. Consequently, they did not award him any monetary compensation. The applicant then brought his complaint to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 3, arguing that he had been detained in inadequate conditions and had not been awarded compensation for those conditions.

The case therefore focused on two key issues: whether the established conditions of detention—overcrowding with 2.97 square metres of personal space for 47 days, and dilapidated, poorly lit disciplinary cells for 29 days—amounted to treatment contrary to Article 3; and whether the domestic courts’ refusal to award compensation after acknowledging the breaches provided adequate redress. The essential facts are the two identified detention periods, the domestic courts’ findings that domestic standards were breached during those periods, and the absence of any monetary award despite those acknowledged violations. These facts grounded the applicant’s allegation that Lithuania failed both to ensure humane detention conditions and to provide adequate remedial compensation.

**Bjarki H. Diego v. Iceland** (ECtHR, Third Section, 15 March 2022, App. no. 30965/17) concerned fair-trial complaints arising from Iceland’s 2008 banking collapse. The applicant, an Icelandic lawyer, was director of the loan division and a member of the group credit committee at Kaupþing Bank until its collapse on 9 October 2008. After the crisis, Iceland’s Special Prosecutor investigated alleged market manipulation and related financial offences. In March 2010, telephone-tapping warrants were granted in connection with four Kaupþing-related investigations—Al Thani, Holt, CLN, and Desulo. The prosecutor’s requests stated there was suspicion that Diego had taken part in decisions concerning allegedly criminal conduct, and tapping reports referred to him as a “suspect.”

On 19 April 2010, Diego was questioned in the Al Thani investigation but was not prosecuted in that case. On 14 May 2010, he was questioned as a witness in the Holt investigation. He was reminded of his duty to testify truthfully and of his right not to incriminate himself, but he was not accompanied by a lawyer and does not appear to have been informed of any right to legal assistance. On 12 November 2011, he was questioned again, this time formally as a suspect and with defence counsel present.

In March 2013, Diego was indicted with several others on seven counts of fraud through abuse of position. Three counts concerned allegedly improper loans to Holt Investment Group Ltd.; four concerned allegedly improper loans to Desulo Trading Ltd. He was accused of participating in decisions to grant loans contrary to the bank’s rules and without properly protecting the bank’s interests. In June 2015, the Reykjavik District Court convicted him on six counts and sentenced him to two and a half years’ imprisonment. On appeal, the Supreme Court of Iceland in October 2016 convicted him on all seven counts and upheld the sentence. Before the Supreme Court, Diego argued that the case should be dismissed because he had been questioned as a witness in May 2010 while he was actually considered a suspect.

Two main Article 6 issues arose. First, Diego complained that he had not received a fair hearing before an impartial tribunal because Justice V.M.M., a Supreme Court judge on his panel, had owned shares in Kaupþing and Landsbanki before their collapse. This information emerged publicly in December 2016. Justice V.M.M. had owned 36 Kaupþing shares—nominal value ISK 360, real value about EUR 140—and substantial Landsbanki shares worth approximately EUR 62,860 before Landsbanki collapsed. Diego argued these holdings and losses created objectively justified doubts about impartiality, especially because the 2008 bank collapses were widely seen as a collective event. The Government argued the Kaupþing holding was minimal and predated his appointment, and that other bank losses were unrelated to Diego’s case. The Court declared the complaint admissible but ultimately found the holdings and losses insufficient to raise doubts as to Justice V.M.M.’s objective impartiality.

Second, Diego complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(a) and (c) that he had been questioned as a witness on 14 May 2010 when he was already considered a suspect, without being informed of the charges or provided legal assistance. The Court found that a “criminal charge” already existed at that time. Because that interview related to the investigation ultimately resulting in his indictment and conviction, the failure to inform him of the charges and provide legal assistance irretrievably prejudiced the overall fairness of the criminal proceedings. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6, while rejecting the impartiality complaint.

**Case: Bjarki H. Diego v. Iceland (Application no. 30965/17), ECtHR, 15 March 2022**

On 15 March 2013, the applicant was indicted on seven counts of fraud through abuse of position. His Kaupþing holding was small: 36 shares with nominal value of ISK 360, real value about EUR 140 at the time. His Landsbanki shares had a purchase price of ISK 14,753,256 and were valued at ISK 8,518,692, about EUR 62,860, before being lost in the collapse.
