On impartiality, it found that Justice V.M.M.’s losses in the Kaupþing and Landsbanki collapses were not sufficient to raise objective doubts about his impartiality; there was no violation of Article 6 § 1 on that ground. However, on the fair-hearing complaint, the Court found that by 14 May 2010 there was already a “criminal charge” because the applicant was considered a suspect. The failure to inform him of the charges and to provide legal assistance during that witness interview—an interview connected to the investigation that ultimately led to his indictment and conviction—irretrievably prejudiced the overall fairness of the criminal proceedings. **Case: FU QUAN, s.r.o. v. the Czech Republic**

The applicant was a Czech limited liability company. In April 2005 its only two associates, one of whom was also its managing director, were accused of tax evasion and remanded in custody. On 27 April 2005 the Prague Municipal Prosecutor’s Office ordered the seizure of the applicant company’s property, including clothing merchandise and a leased vehicle, under Article 347 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The order banned disposal of the seized property unless necessary to prevent imminent damage. The merchandise was seized between 2 May and 27 June 2005 in the managing director’s presence and entrusted to the Office for Government Representation in Property Matters. Its expert value was CZK 62,424,027 (about EUR 2.39 million). Complaints by the associates were dismissed; the courts cited their links to China and a risk that property would be transferred abroad.

The associates were indicted in April 2006. After convictions were repeatedly quashed, the Prague High Court acquitted them on 27 February 2009. It found it had not been proved that they committed tax evasion in relation to the seized merchandise and transferred money. Some electronic devices and the leased car had already been returned in 2005. Despite the acquittal, the seized merchandise was not returned. After delays involving the prosecutor, court and OGRPM, on 22 July 2010 the Prague Municipal Court ordered its return under Article 80 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. That decision became final on 17 August 2010, and the goods were handed back between 14 and 23 September 2010—after about five years of storage and roughly a year and a half after acquittal.

The applicant claimed that the clothing had deteriorated and become unsaleable because of long storage and changing fashion. It said it sold part of the merchandise only for a fraction of its original value. In January 2011 it sought CZK 63,294,609 in compensation from the Ministry of Justice under the State Liability Act for damage caused by the five-year storage, plus other losses. The Ministry dismissed the claim in May 2011, stating that it was not responsible for the passage of time and that the alleged depreciation was unsubstantiated and speculative.

The compensation courts also dismissed the claim. The District Court held in December 2011 that the company lacked locus standi because it was not a party to the criminal proceedings against its managing director and associate, and there was no causal link. The Municipal Court upheld that in May 2012, adding that the company could not claim under provisions concerning detention or acquittal, and that an acquittal did not make the seizure, storage or return unlawful or irregular official conduct. The Supreme Court dismissed its appeal in November 2012, and the Constitutional Court dismissed its complaint in September 2013 as manifestly ill-founded.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Article 6 § 1, Article 13, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It complained that its operations were paralysed, that it was wrongfully deprived of and damaged by the seized property, and that domestic law’s formalistic locus standi rule denied it access to compensation. The Government argued non-exhaustion, saying the company had never challenged the seizure before the Constitutional Court and could have sought cancellation or limitation of the seizure or refiled its compensation claim with a clearer cause. The Court found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning the unlawful retention of the applicant’s merchandise, particularly after the acquittal.

**FU QUAN, s.r.o. v. the Czech Republic** concerns a Czech limited liability company whose property was seized during criminal proceedings against its two associates, one of whom was also its managing director. In April 2005 the two men were accused of tax evasion and remanded in custody. On 27 April 2005 the Prague Municipal Prosecutor’s Office ordered the seizure of the applicant company’s property, including clothing merchandise and a leased vehicle, under Article 347 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The merchandise was seized between May and June 2005 and entrusted to the Office for Government Representation in Property Matters (OGRPM). Its expert value was CZK 62,424,027 (about EUR 2.39 million). Complaints against the seizure were rejected in June 2005, partly because the accused had connections to China and were considered a flight risk. Some personal items were returned in November 2005, and the leased car was returned to the leasing company.

The associates were indicted in April 2006. After convictions were repeatedly quashed, the Prague High Court acquitted them on 27 February 2009; that judgment became final the same day. Despite the acquittal, the applicant company’s merchandise was not promptly returned. The authorities delayed: the presiding judge asked the prosecutor’s office to decide on the seized evidence, the OGRPM enquired when the goods would be released, and an attempt to notify the company’s agent failed. In September 2009 the company’s agent stated that all the seized goods belonged to FU QUAN. Only on 22 July 2010 did the Municipal Court order the merchandise’s return under Article 80 of the Code of Criminal Procedure; the decision became final on 17 August 2010. The goods were inspected on 6 September and handed back between 14 and 23 September 2010—about eighteen months after the final acquittal and more than five years after seizure. The applicant claimed the clothing was returned in deplorable condition and largely unsaleable because of long storage and changing fashion.

The applicant sought compensation from the Ministry of Justice in January 2011, claiming CZK 63,294,609 (about EUR 2.43 million). It mainly claimed the difference between the original value of the seized merchandise and the amount obtained from selling part of it, plus compensation for stolen office equipment, enforcement action over unpaid telephone bills, and penalties under the vehicle leasing contract. The Ministry dismissed the claim in May 2011, stating that the State was not liable for the passage of time and that the alleged depreciation was speculative.

The company then brought compensation proceedings. In December 2011 the Prague 2 District Court dismissed the action, holding that the company lacked locus standi because it had not been a party to the criminal proceedings against its managing director and associate, and that there was no causal link between those proceedings and the alleged damage. The Municipal Court upheld that judgment in May 2012, reasoning that claims concerning custody or indictment belonged to the prosecuted individuals. The Supreme Court dismissed the company’s appeal in November 2012, relying on the same party requirement. The Constitutional Court dismissed its complaint in September 2013 as manifestly ill-founded.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, Article 6 § 1, and Article 13. It complained that the seizure and prolonged retention of its merchandise, and the domestic courts’ refusal to examine its compensation claim on formalistic standing grounds, unlawfully controlled or deprived it of property and denied it access to court and an effective remedy. The key finding was a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning the unlawful retention of the applicant company’s merchandise for almost a year and a half after the acquittal.

The associates were indicted in April 2006. After repeated convictions and reversals, the Prague High Court finally acquitted them on 27 February 2009. It found that the alleged tax-evasion events had not been proved in a manner attributing specific criminal acts to the accused, including in relation to the seized merchandise and transferred money. Despite the acquittal, the merchandise was not returned promptly. Correspondence in 2009 concerned identification and return of the goods, but the Municipal Court only decided on 22 July 2010 to return the merchandise under Article 80 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Ministry dismissed the claim in May 2011, describing the depreciation claim as speculative and stating that the State was not responsible for the mere passing of time.

The company then sued before the Prague 2 District Court. In December 2011 the court dismissed the action, finding that the company lacked locus standi because it had not been a party to the criminal proceedings against its managing director and associate, and that there was no causal link between those proceedings and the alleged damage. It complained that its operations had been paralysed for about five years and that it had been wrongfully deprived of its property through the authorities’ conduct, without effective access to compensation. The key violation found concerned Article 1 of Protocol No. 1: the unlawful retention and control of use of the merchandise, especially the prolonged failure to return it after acquittal, which exposed it to depreciation and prevented its use.

E.M. and Others v. Norway concerned a Czech mother and her two sons, B (born 2005) and C (born 2008), who lived in Norway. In May 2011 the children were placed in emergency foster care amid concerns of sexual abuse and violence by their father, A. Contact with the mother was initially permitted but stopped in August 2011 after further disclosures and a police investigation. In February 2012 the County Social Welfare Board took the children into public care, finding serious neglect and physical abuse and concluding they would likely face serious neglect if returned to the mother. The Board allowed supervised contact four times a year.

On appeal, the District Court in July 2012 upheld the care order but withdrew the mother’s contact rights. It found it probable that A had sexually abused the children and that the mother had been aware of the abuse, sometimes observed it, and failed to stop it. It also noted physical punishment and the children’s fear and association of the mother with violence and abuse. In March 2013 the High Court restored limited supervised contact twice a year. It did not find sufficient grounds to conclude that the mother had sexually abused the children or knowingly failed to intervene, but found she had failed to shield them from A’s abuse, had slapped them, caused them significant fear, and was jointly responsible for their neglect. The Supreme Court refused further appeal in May 2013, and an earlier ECtHR application was declared inadmissible in August 2014.

In December 2014 the mother applied to lift the care order. The child welfare services sought continuation of care, removal of her parental responsibilities for both children, refusal of contact with B, and authorisation for C’s adoption. In September 2015 the Board refused to lift the care orders, withdrew the mother’s parental responsibilities for both children, refused contact with B, and authorised C’s adoption. On appeal, the District Court in June 2016 upheld these decisions except adoption, which it refused. It found the mother’s caring abilities had improved, but B had PTSD caused by complex and continued neglect and needed a stable, secure care situation; his caregivers could not be those who caused his trauma. B did not want to return and showed severe physical anxiety at the prospect of contact, including shaking, perspiration and pain; in March 2015 staff considered forced contact an immediate health risk. C had weak attachment to his mother and strong attachment to his foster family, and showed adverse reactions after visits, including anxiety and defecating. The mother had also exposed the children to extensive media publicity, posting sensitive information and photos online, including about sexual abuse and B’s health, harming B’s privacy and wellbeing. The court found she could not meet the children’s needs and that removing her parental responsibilities was necessary to protect their privacy. The High Court refused leave to appeal in November 2016, and the Supreme Court dismissed her appeal in January 2017.

Before the ECtHR, the mother complained under Article 8 about the continued foster care, withdrawal of parental responsibilities and refusal of contact. The Court found the measures justified, based on relevant and sufficient reasons and the children’s best interests, with extensive proceedings and adequate safeguards. Under Article 34, it also held that the mother lacked standing to act on her sons’ behalf because of conflicting interests arising from the serious neglect and her failure to protect them.

E.M. and Others v. Norway concerned a Czech national mother, E.M., and her two sons, B (born 2005) and C (born 2008), who lived in Norway. In May 2011 the children were placed in emergency foster care after concerns about sexual abuse and violence. In February 2012 the County Social Welfare Board took them into public care and placed them in foster homes. It found serious neglect and physical abuse, and that returning them to their mother would likely place them in serious neglect. Contact was initially limited and then withdrawn.

In July 2012 the District Court upheld the care order but withdrew the mother’s contact rights. It found it probable that the father, A, had sexually abused the children, that the mother had been aware of the abuse and failed to stop it, and that the children associated her with violence and abuse. In March 2013 the High Court restored supervised contact twice a year. It found insufficient grounds to conclude that the mother had sexually abused the children or known of A’s abuse, but found that she had failed to shield them from A’s abusive behaviour, had slapped them, caused them significant fear, and was jointly responsible for their neglect. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal in May 2013. An earlier application to the European Court concerning that period was declared inadmissible in 2014.

In December 2014 the mother applied to have the care order lifted. The child welfare services sought continuation of care, removal of her parental responsibilities for both children, refusal of contact with B, and authorisation for C’s adoption. In September 2015 the Board decided not to lift the care orders, withdrew the mother’s parental responsibilities, refused contact with B, and authorised C’s adoption. It relied heavily on the mother’s repeated exposure of the children in the media, including photographs and information about sexual abuse, which had seriously affected B.

On appeal, the District Court gave judgment in June 2016 after hearing extensive evidence. It accepted that the mother’s caring abilities had improved, but found that B suffered from PTSD caused by complex and continued neglect and needed stability. B clearly did not want to return to his mother and showed severe physical anxiety at the prospect of contact, such that forced contact could risk his health. C was strongly attached to his foster family, weakly attached to his mother, did not want to return, and had serious adverse reactions after contact visits, including agitation, anxiety, sleep problems, and defecating. The District Court continued the care orders, removed the mother’s parental responsibilities for both children due to privacy risks and her misuse of parental access, refused contact with B, and refused contact with C based on his reactions. It declined to authorise C’s adoption because of his ties to his brother. The High Court refused leave to appeal, and the Supreme Court dismissed the further appeal in January 2017.

Before the European Court, the mother complained under Article 8 about the refusal to lift the care order, the removal of her parental responsibilities, and the refusal of contact. The Court also examined Article 34 standing. It found that the mother lacked standing to act on behalf of her children because her interests conflicted with theirs, given the serious joint parental neglect and the care order based on her failure to protect them. On Article 8, the Court found the measures justified: the proceedings were extensive and had adequate safeguards; the domestic decisions were based on relevant and sufficient reasons and the children’s best interests; the measures were neither irreversible nor permanent; and considerable attention had been given to the mother-child relationship. There was therefore no violation of Article 8.

**Case summary: E.M. and Others v. Norway (Application no. 53471/17)**

The case concerned a Czech mother, E.M., and her two sons, B and C, born in Norway in 2005 and 2008. The children were placed in emergency care in May 2011 because of concerns about sexual abuse and violence within the family. The parents separated, and in February 2012 the County Social Welfare Board took B and C into public care and placed them in foster homes. The Board found serious neglect and physical abuse, and considered it highly likely that returning the children to E.M. would expose them to serious neglect. Contact was initially limited and supervised; a District Court later withdrew it because the children associated E.M. with violence and sexual abuse and showed fear and stress. In March 2013 the High Court reinstated limited supervised contact twice a year. It found that E.M. had failed to shield the children from the father’s abuse, had slapped them, and was jointly responsible for the neglect they suffered, although it did not conclusively find that she had sexually abused them or known of the father’s abuse. The Supreme Court refused further appeal. An earlier application to the European Court concerning those facts was declared inadmissible in 2014.

In December 2014 E.M. applied to have the care order lifted. The child welfare services sought its continuation, removal of E.M.’s parental responsibilities, refusal of contact, and authorisation of C’s adoption. After hearings with witness evidence, a children’s representative and expert psychological assessments, the Board in September 2015 maintained the care orders, withdrew E.M.’s parental responsibilities for both children, refused contact with B, and authorised C’s adoption.

On appeal, the District Court in June 2016 made a fresh assessment. It accepted that E.M.’s caring abilities had improved, but found that B suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder caused by complex and continued neglect. He needed stability and could not be cared for by those who had caused his trauma. Contact with E.M. triggered severe physical anxiety, shaking and pain, and he did not want to return to her. C was strongly attached to his foster family, did not want contact with E.M., and showed serious adverse reactions before and after visits. The court also found that E.M. had exposed the children extensively in the media and posted sensitive material online, including sexual-abuse allegations and B’s health information. This harmed their privacy and made her continued parental access to information contrary to their best interests. The District Court continued foster care, removed E.M.’s parental responsibilities, refused contact for both children, but declined to authorise C’s adoption because of his ties to B and his biological family. The High Court refused leave to appeal in November 2016, and the Supreme Court dismissed the further appeal in January 2017.

Before the European Court, E.M. alleged violations of Article 8 of the Convention, complaining about the continued foster care, the removal of her parental responsibilities and the refusal of contact rights. The Court found that the measures interfered with family life but were justified. The domestic decisions were based on relevant and sufficient reasons, principally the children’s best interests, their trauma, their strong resistance to contact, their stable foster placements, E.M.’s lack of understanding of their needs, and her harmful media exposure. The proceedings had been extensive and accompanied by adequate safeguards, including expert evidence, children’s representation and consideration of the children’s views. The measures were neither irreversible nor permanent and could be reviewed. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 8. It also held that E.M. lacked standing under Article 34 to act on her children’s behalf because their interests conflicted with hers, given the findings of serious joint parental neglect and her failure to protect them.

**Case Summary: Dahman Bendhiman v. Spain (Application no. 48512/20)**

The applicant, Mr. Zouhair Dahman Bendhiman, a Spanish national, lodged an application against Spain under Article 34 of the Convention, alleging a violation of his right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1, and discrimination under Article 14. The case concerned his eviction from a public housing flat for non-payment of rent and the subsequent refusal of his appeal.

In March 2011, the applicant signed a subsidised seven-year tenancy agreement with the Madrid Housing Authority (IVIMA) for a flat in Navalcarnero. He received a 90% rent reduction, paying approximately €49.10 per month. In October 2013, IVIMA sold the block of flats, including the applicant’s home, to a private company (A.G.), which transferred it to a subsidiary, E.C. E.C. refused to honour the rent reduction, demanding the full contractual rent of €393.21 per month plus communal expenses and property tax. Consequently, between November 2013 and October 2017, the applicant failed to pay the full rent demanded.

In November 2017, E.C. initiated summary civil proceedings (verbal proceedings) for eviction and recovery of unpaid rent, claiming €14,420.72. The applicant opposed the claim, arguing that E.C. lacked standing because a parallel administrative court had declared the sale of the public housing blocks null and void. However, this administrative judgment was not yet final. The first-instance civil court rejected his arguments and, on 10 July 2019, ordered him to vacate the dwelling and pay the claimed amount. The court found that the lease existed and the rents were unpaid.

The applicant appealed, but on 7 October 2019, his appeal was declared inadmissible. The court relied on section 449 of the Civil Procedure Act, which requires a tenant to pay or secure the overdue rent as a precondition for lodging an appeal in eviction proceedings. The applicant argued that his legal aid status should exempt him from this requirement, but his subsequent appeal against this decision was dismissed on 9 January 2020. The Audiencia Provincial confirmed that the requirement in section 449 was an essential prerequisite for an appeal and did not analyse the merits of his case.

Meanwhile, the administrative proceedings finalised in 2020, confirming the sale of the public housing was null and void due to procedural irregularities. However, the civil proceedings for his eviction had already concluded, and the effects of the administrative judgment on individual tenancy contracts, like the applicant's, remained subject to further civil court determination.

The applicant complained to the European Court that the requirement to pay the debt before appealing denied him access to a second-instance court, given his poor economic situation, which was a form of discrimination.

The Court examined the case primarily under Article 6 § 1. It found that the applicant's complaint concerning the first-instance proceedings was inadmissible for failure to exhaust domestic remedies or for being out of time. However, it declared the complaint regarding the appeal proceedings admissible.

On the merits, the Court assessed whether the restriction on access to the appeal court impaired the very essence of his right. It noted that the requirement under section 449 aimed to prevent tenants from using the appeal process to delay paying rent and to protect the landlord's interests. The Court observed that the applicant had acknowledged owing a substantial amount of rent and that the first-instance court had found E.C. to be his legitimate landlord at the time. Importantly, the Court highlighted that the applicant was not barred from bringing separate ordinary civil proceedings to address complex issues, such as the validity of the sale's effect on his tenancy. The Court concluded that the requirement did not constitute a disproportionate restriction and that a fair balance had been struck, falling within Spain's margin of appreciation. Therefore, there was no violation of Article 6 § 1. The Court also found no separate issue under Article 14.

**Dahman Bendhiman v. Spain** (Application no. 48512/20, ECtHR Third Section, 15 November 2022) concerned a Spanish tenant’s complaint that he was denied access to an appeal court in eviction proceedings because he could not pay overdue rent as a precondition for appealing, despite receiving legal aid. He also alleged discrimination based on social origin.

The applicant lived with his wife and two children in public housing allocated by Madrid’s housing authority, IVIMA, under a subsidised tenancy from 2011. He received rent reductions of 75% and later 90%, reducing his monthly rent to about EUR 49.10. In 2013, IVIMA sold the block containing his flat to a private company, later transferred to E.C. E.C. refused to honour the 90% reduction, demanded full rent plus communal expenses and property tax, and adjusted rent by inflation. Between November 2013 and October 2017, the applicant paid only the old reduced amount for some months, disputing E.C.’s status as landlord.

In November 2017, E.C. brought summary verbal proceedings seeking EUR 14,420.72 in unpaid rent, expenses and taxes, plus eviction. The applicant opposed, arguing that E.C. lacked standing because an administrative court had declared the sale of the public housing blocks null and void; that the amount claimed was wrong; and that summary eviction proceedings were inadequate for such complex issues. The first-instance court initially stayed proceedings pending the administrative case, but the Madrid Audiencia Provincial reversed that stay and resumed the eviction case. In July 2019, the first-instance court ordered the applicant to vacate the flat and pay EUR 14,420.72, finding he had not proven payment.

The applicant appealed, but in October 2019 the appeal was declared inadmissible under section 449 of the Civil Procedure Act because he had not paid or secured the debt ordered in the first-instance judgment, a mandatory precondition for appealing in eviction cases. His legal aid did not exempt him from that obligation. A further recurso de queja was dismissed in January 2020, and the appellate court did not examine the merits. His constitutional amparo appeal was declared inadmissible in July 2020 for lack of “special constitutional importance.”

In parallel, the administrative courts had declared the sale of the public housing blocks null and void in 2018, upheld in 2019 and final in 2020. The applicant was not a party to those proceedings, and the effects on individual tenancies remained to be determined by civil courts. His eviction was repeatedly postponed.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged violations of Article 6 §1 (right of access to court) and Article 14 (discrimination). The Court held that the complaint about the first-instance court failing to answer all submissions was inadmissible, either for non-exhaustion or for being out of time. The complaint about lack of access to the appeal court was admissible. On the merits, the Court found that the requirement to pay or secure overdue rent before appealing did not impair the very essence of the right of access to a court. It pursued legitimate aims—preventing delaying tactics and protecting landlords—and the applicant could still bring other ordinary civil proceedings concerning tenancy and ownership issues. A fair balance was struck, and the limitation fell within Spain’s margin of appreciation. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 6 §1.

In *Dahman Bendhiman v. Spain* (no. 48512/20), the European Court of Human Rights examined a tenant’s complaint that he was denied access to an appeal court because he could not pay the rent debt ordered in first-instance summary eviction proceedings. The applicant, a Spanish national, lived with his wife and two children in public housing in Navalcarnero, Madrid. In 2011 IVIMA granted him a subsidised seven-year tenancy. Rent was initially EUR 393.21 per month, later reduced by 75% and then 90% to EUR 49.10 because of severe financial hardship. The family was unemployed and dependent on social welfare.

In 2013 IVIMA sold blocks of public housing to private company A.G., later transferred to E.C. E.C. considered itself not bound by the 90% reduction, demanded full rent plus communal expenses and property tax, and applied indexation. Between November 2013 and October 2017, the applicant paid only the old reduced rent in some months. In November 2017 E.C. brought summary civil verbal proceedings seeking EUR 14,420.72 in unpaid rent, expenses and taxes, and eviction.

The applicant opposed the claim. He argued that E.C. lacked standing because an administrative court had declared the sale of the public housing blocks null and void (21 May 2018, upheld in 2019 and final in 2020). He also contested the amount and applicable law, though he admitted owing some rent to the legitimate owner. The first-instance civil court initially stayed the case pending the administrative proceedings, but the Audiencia Provincial overturned the stay. It held that the administrative decision was not clearly binding in the civil summary case and that the applicant had not been a party to the administrative proceedings. On 10 July 2019, the first-instance court ordered him to vacate the flat and pay EUR 14,420.72.

The applicant appealed. On 7 October 2019, the first-instance court declared the appeal inadmissible because he had not paid or secured the debt as required by section 449 of the Civil Procedure Act as a precondition for appealing eviction and rent judgments. He had been granted legal aid, but Spanish law exempted legal-aid beneficiaries from court fees and appeal deposits, not from the substantive rent debt. His *recurso de queja* was dismissed on 9 January 2020. The Audiencia Provincial held that the requirement applied despite his legal aid and did not examine the merits. His Constitutional Court *amparo* was declared inadmissible on 8 July 2020 for lack of special constitutional importance. Social services repeatedly confirmed the family’s vulnerability and recommended suspending eviction; the eviction was adjourned.

Before the ECtHR, he alleged under Article 6 § 1 and Article 14 that he had been denied access to an appeal court because poverty prevented him from paying the rent debt, amounting to discrimination based on social origin. He also complained that the first-instance court had not answered all his submissions. The Court declared the first-instance complaint inadmissible (exhaustion/time-bar) and examined the access-to-appeal complaint. It found no violation of Article 6 § 1: the section 449 requirement did not impair the very essence of access to court, since he could bring additional ordinary civil proceedings concerning tenancy issues, and a fair balance was struck between the landlord’s interests and the tenant’s rights. The limitation fell within Spain’s margin of appreciation.

In *Pejřilová v. the Czech Republic*, the applicant complained under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that Czech authorities refused to allow her to use her late husband’s cryopreserved sperm for assisted reproduction, thereby violating her right to respect for private life.

The applicant and her husband married in 2012. Because they could not conceive naturally and the husband had a serious disease, they sought medically assisted reproduction. On 26 June 2014, the husband’s sperm was cryopreserved. The consent form stated that further written consent would be required before each thawing and that, unless clearly determined otherwise, storage would be discontinued upon the donor’s death. On 15 December 2014, both spouses signed informed consent forms for IVF/ICSI, agreeing to notify the centre of any relationship change that could terminate treatment.

The husband’s health deteriorated, and he died on 16 June 2015, before the applicant had begun hormone treatment or had her ova collected. On 7 September 2015, the applicant asked the Centre to fertilise her eggs with her late husband’s frozen sperm. The Centre refused, saying the procedure would be unlawful, and suggested court proceedings. The applicant sued to compel the treatment, relying on her husband’s wishes and the earlier consent forms.

The domestic courts refused. Under the Specific Health Services Act, artificial fertilisation required a written application by an infertile couple, consent less than six months old, and repeated consent before each attempt. Because the husband had died, the applicant was no longer part of a couple; the consent had expired on 15 June 2015; and there was no valid current consent. The Regional Court added that the law aimed to give a child at least an initial chance to grow up with both parents, and that the husband’s later wishes could not be presumed or replaced by a court decision. The Supreme Court found a possible interference with private life, but not family life. It noted no European consensus and a wide margin of appreciation. It accepted legitimate aims: protecting the child’s best interests, the man’s free will, and the unborn child’s right to know his or her parents. It also noted the consent form’s clause on destruction of sperm after death made the husband’s post-mortem wishes unclear, and that the applicant could still conceive naturally or with another partner. The Constitutional Court dismissed her appeal, holding that assisted-reproduction rules reflected moral, cultural, religious and ethical values and were primarily for the legislature. A dissenting judge argued that the law should only prevent a birth against a man’s will and that courts should have investigated the husband’s actual wishes.

Before the ECtHR, the Government did not dispute an Article 8 private-life interference, based on sections 6(1) and 8(2) of the Act. It argued the cumulative conditions were unmet: no existing infertile couple after death, and no consent less than six months old or repeated. It justified the interference as protecting the unborn child’s chance of a complete family, the man’s autonomy, and morals, with a wide margin because of no European consensus. The applicant argued the law was unforeseeable and formalistic, that her husband had repeatedly consented and never withdrew, and that their shared wish was to have a biological child.

The ECtHR held Article 8 applicable because private life includes decisions to have a child and to use medically assisted procreation. The application was admissible. On the merits, the Court found the refusal pursued legitimate aims and, given the lack of European consensus, the State’s wide margin of appreciation was not overstepped. There was therefore no violation of Article 8.

Pejřilová v. the Czech Republic (ECtHR, Fifth Section, 8 December 2022, application no. 14889/19) concerned a widow’s request to use her deceased husband’s cryopreserved sperm for assisted reproduction. The applicant and her husband married in 2012. Because they could not conceive naturally and the husband had a serious illness, in June 2014 his sperm was cryopreserved. The consent form stated that further written consent would be required before each thawing/use, and that storage would be discontinued on the donor’s death unless clearly determined otherwise. On 15 December 2014 the couple signed informed consent for IVF/ICSI using the frozen sperm and agreed to notify the centre of any relationship change that could terminate treatment.

The husband’s health deteriorated and he died on 16 June 2015 before further steps were taken. The applicant had not started hormone treatment or had eggs collected. On 7 September 2015 she asked the centre to fertilise her eggs with his frozen sperm. The centre refused, saying Czech law prohibited it, and suggested court proceedings. She sued to compel the procedure, arguing it reflected her and her late husband’s wish to have a biological child.

Domestic courts rejected her claim. Under the Specific Health Services Act, artificial fertilisation required a written application and written consent from an infertile couple, with consent less than six months old and repeated before each attempt. After the husband died, the couple no longer existed as an “infertile couple” under the Act; the consent had expired and could not be replaced by a court. The courts also found the husband’s later wishes could not be presumed, especially because the consent form provided for destruction of sperm upon death. The Supreme Court accepted that Article 8 private life was engaged but held the interference justified: the law protected the man’s autonomy and the unborn child’s right to know both parents, and reflected moral and ethical choices. It noted no European consensus and a wide margin of appreciation. The Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged a violation of Article 8, arguing the refusal breached her private life and her decision to have a child with her late husband. She claimed Czech law was not foreseeable, lacked an explicit post-mortem ban, and that the couple’s initial consent should suffice. The Government accepted an interference with private life but argued it was lawful and necessary to protect the free will of the deceased and the child’s interests, and that no European consensus existed.

The ECtHR examined the case under Article 8 as respect for private life and declared it admissible. It found no violation. The Court emphasised the absence of European consensus on post-mortem assisted reproduction, the sensitive moral and ethical issues, and the State’s wide margin of appreciation. The Czech requirement of a living couple and recent, repeated consent was intended to protect the man who consented and the unborn child. The domestic courts had balanced the competing interests and had not overstepped the margin. Therefore, the dismissal of the widow’s request did not breach Article 8.

**Case: Pejřilová v. the Czech Republic** (ECtHR, App. no. 14889/19, 8 December 2022)

The applicant, Hana Pejřilová, complained under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that Czech authorities had refused her request to use her late husband’s cryopreserved sperm in assisted reproduction. She married in 2012. Because the couple could not conceive naturally and her husband suffered from a serious disease, they sought medically assisted reproduction. On 26 June 2014, the husband’s sperm was cryopreserved. The consent form stated that further written consent would be required before each thawing and that storage would be discontinued on the donor’s death unless clearly determined otherwise. On 15 December 2014, the applicant and her husband signed informed consents for IVF/ICSI and for the thawing and use of his sperm. The husband’s health then deteriorated, and he died on 16 June 2015 before the applicant had begun necessary hormone treatment or had her ova collected.

On 7 September 2015, the applicant asked the reproduction centre to fertilise her eggs with her late husband’s sperm. The centre refused, saying the procedure would be unlawful, and suggested court proceedings. The domestic courts dismissed her action. Under the Specific Health Services Act, artificial fertilisation could be performed only for an “infertile couple” on the basis of a written application by the woman and the man intending to undergo treatment together, with the application and repeated written consent being less than six months old. By the time of the husband’s death, the couple no longer existed as a couple, and the consent had expired on 15 June 2015. The courts found there was no valid informed consent from the husband and that his earlier consent could not automatically be treated as a binding wish for post-mortem fatherhood. They also noted that the consent form provided for destruction of the sperm on death, making his post-mortem wishes uncertain.

The Supreme Court accepted that the refusal could interfere with the applicant’s private life but found legitimate aims: protecting the free will and autonomy of a man who had consented to assisted reproduction, protecting the unborn child’s interest in knowing his or her parents and being born into a complete family, and protecting morals. It noted there was no European consensus: some Council of Europe States allowed post-mortem assisted reproduction, while others prohibited it. It also observed that the applicant had not been deprived of all ways to become a mother, as she could conceive naturally or with another partner. The Constitutional Court dismissed her appeal, holding that rules on medically assisted reproduction reflected moral, cultural, religious and ethical choices for the legislature.

The applicant argued that the State should respect her choice and her late husband’s wish to have a child; that Czech law was not sufficiently foreseeable; that there was no explicit ban on post-mortem use; and that her husband had never withdrawn consent. The Government maintained that the interference was based on accessible law, pursued legitimate aims, and fell within a wide margin of appreciation given the sensitive moral issues and lack of European consensus.

The ECtHR examined the case under Article 8’s protection of private life, which includes decisions to have a child and to use medically assisted procreation. It declared the application admissible but found no violation. The key facts—the request was made after the husband’s death; the applicant was no longer part of a couple under the Act; the consent had lapsed; and there was no clear post-mortem consent—supported the conclusion that the Czech authorities had not overstepped their wide margin of appreciation.

The case of *Bartus and Others v. Hungary* concerns five applications (no. 10214/21 and four others) lodged against Hungary under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants complained principally that the length of civil proceedings in Hungary had been incompatible with the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. In applications nos. 10214/21 and 35908/21, the applicants also raised complaints under Article 13, alleging that they had no effective domestic remedy for the excessive length of those civil proceedings. The European Court of Human Rights (First Section), sitting as a Committee, joined the applications because they concerned a similar subject matter and delivered judgment on 31 March 2022.

The specific factual details—the identities of the applicants, the dates the applications were lodged, the domestic proceedings at issue, and their exact durations—were set out in the appended table to the judgment. That table is not included in the supplied extract. What the Court’s text makes clear, however, is that each application arose from civil proceedings before the Hungarian authorities whose overall length the applicants considered excessive. The Hungarian Government was given notice of the applications and had the opportunity to respond. After examining the material, the Court found no fact or argument capable of justifying the overall length of the proceedings at the national level.

In its legal assessment, the Court reiterated that the reasonableness of the length of proceedings must be assessed in light of the circumstances of the case and by reference to the criteria established in *Frydlender v. France*: the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicants and the relevant authorities, and what was at stake for the applicants in the dispute. The Court also referred to its leading judgment in *Gazsó v. Hungary* (no. 48322/12, 16 July 2015), in which it had already found violations in respect of similar issues concerning excessive length of civil proceedings and the absence of an effective domestic remedy.

Applying that case-law, the Court examined all the material submitted and concluded that the length of the civil proceedings in the applicants’ cases was excessive and failed to meet the “reasonable time” requirement. It therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

As to the additional complaints raised in applications nos. 10214/21 and 35908/21, the Court considered that they raised issues under Article 13 of the Convention in light of well-established case-law. It declared those complaints admissible, finding that they were not manifestly ill-founded or inadmissible on any other ground. Having examined the material, the Court concluded that those complaints also disclosed violations of the Convention, relying on its findings in *Gazsó*, cited above, § 21. In essence, the applicants in those two applications had not had an effective domestic remedy for their complaints about the length of civil proceedings.

The Court accordingly found violations of Article 6 § 1 in all applications and violations of Article 13 in the two applications where that complaint was raised. Under Article 6 § 1, “In the determination of his civil rights and obligations ... everyone is entitled to a ... hearing within a reasonable time by [a] ... tribunal ...”. These complaints were not manifestly ill-founded within the meaning of Article 35 § 3 (a) and were not inadmissible on any other ground. They were therefore declared admissible. On the merits, the Court concluded that they also disclosed violations of the Convention in light of its findings in *Gazsó*, § 21. Ferhatović v. Slovenia (ECtHR, First Section, 7 July 2022) concerned the seizure of copper wire from the applicant and its later handover to an alleged injured company. The applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that this amounted to an unjustified interference with his property.

In February 2009, police investigated burglaries at Company E in Ljubljana, where copper cable had been stolen on 5–6 February. On 7 February, officers saw the applicant and others unloading copper-like wire from a van into the applicant’s garage. The next day, under a search order, police searched the applicant’s home and seized eight large canvas bags containing mostly copper wire. A certificate of seizure was handed to the applicant. Police later considered that three of the bags matched the dimensions of cable stolen from Company E.

On 24 April 2009, without a court order, police gave those three bags to Company E. The remaining five bags were returned to the applicant on 11 May 2009. In April 2010, police filed a criminal complaint accusing the applicant of concealment under the Criminal Code, alleging he had accepted and hidden copper wire knowing it came from crime. Charges were lodged in December 2011 but withdrawn in November 2012, and criminal proceedings were discontinued in December 2012. In January 2013, the applicant asked the Ljubljana District Court for the three bags to be returned to him. He was informed they had already been handed to Company E in April 2009.

The applicant then sued the State for compensation of EUR 13,750. He claimed he collected and sold waste metals and had stored the wire for over two years to sell in bulk. At hearings, he said his family collected scrap metal from various sites, sometimes by payment, services, or for free, though he could not remember the exact acquisition. Company E’s representative said the three bags were later sold and the money given to Company E’s director. Asked whether the wire came from Company E’s stolen cables, he said this could not be determined because the wire had been cleaned and cut and was not examined when collected. A police officer testified that the wire certainly came from “the kind of cables” stolen, but such cables were available everywhere; police believed it belonged to Company E due to the chain of events. The bags were not weighed, and no court order authorised the handover.

Domestic courts dismissed the applicant’s compensation claim. The local court found that ownership had not been proved and that, although the conditions for returning the items to Company E under the Criminal Procedure Act may not have been met, the police had acted with due diligence and reasonable belief, so their conduct was not unlawful. The Higher Court affirmed that, without proof of ownership, the applicant could not show damage. The Supreme Court and Constitutional Court refused further review.

Before the ECtHR, the Government argued that the applicant had not proved ownership or victim status and had failed to exhaust remedies. The Court declared the application admissible. It found Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 applicable because the wire was seized from the applicant and, absent confiscation, should have been returned to him. His explanation of acquisition, though vague, was not baseless, especially since the wire’s origin from Company E was not reliably established. The Court also rejected the exhaustion objection.

On the merits, the ECtHR found a violation. The key problem was that the police returned seized items to the alleged injured party without a legal procedure adequately safeguarding the interests of the person from whom they were seized against arbitrariness. The domestic courts failed to rectify this, upsetting the fair balance between competing interests.

**Case: Ferhatović v. Slovenia (Application no. 64725/19), ECtHR, 7 July 2022**

The applicant, Sebastjan Ferhatović, complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention that the seizure of his copper wire and its handover to Company E., the alleged victim of theft, violated his right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

In February 2009, police investigating burglaries at Company E.’s premises noticed suspicious activity near the applicant’s address.
