A seizure certificate was issued in his name. Police later considered that wire in three of the bags matched the dimensions of cables stolen from Company E.

On 24 April 2009, without a court order, police handed those three bags to Company E. The remaining five bags were returned to the applicant in May 2009. In 2010, police filed a criminal complaint accusing the applicant of concealment under the Criminal Code, alleging he accepted and hid copper wire knowing it came from crime. Charges were lodged in December 2011, but the State Prosecutor’s Office withdrew them in November 2012, and criminal proceedings were discontinued in December 2012. No confiscation decision was made.

After the proceedings ended, the applicant asked the Ljubljana District Court to return the three bags, stating each weighed around 800 kg. He was told they had already been given to Company E. He then sued the State for compensation of EUR 13,750. In the civil proceedings, the applicant explained he collected and sold waste metals, had accumulated the wire over two years, and planned to sell it in bulk. Company E.’s representative admitted the wire had later been sold and that it could not be determined whether it had been stripped from the stolen cables. A police officer said the wire certainly originated from the same kind of cables stolen, but such cables were available practically everywhere; he confirmed the bags had been handed to Company E. without any court order.

The domestic courts dismissed the applicant’s compensation claim. They found he had not proved ownership of the wire. They also held that even if the police had wrongly applied section 110(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act—which permits return of seized items to an injured party before trial only if they “without doubt” belong to that party—the officers had acted with reasonable care and diligence, so their conduct was not unlawful. Appeals to the Higher Court, Supreme Court, and Constitutional Court failed.

Before the ECtHR, the Government argued the applicant was not the owner or a victim and had not exhausted domestic remedies. The Court rejected those objections. It found Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 applicable because the wire had indisputably been seized from the applicant, no proceedings had proved it was stolen or illegally obtained, and absent confiscation it should have been returned to him. The Court also found domestic remedies exhausted, as the applicant had challenged the lawfulness of the police handover.

On the merits, the ECtHR found a violation. The central problem was the lack of a legal procedure safeguarding the interests of persons affected against arbitrariness when seized items were returned to an alleged injured party. The domestic courts themselves acknowledged that the conditions for returning the wire to Company E. may not have been met, yet they failed to rectify the situation. The handover, combined with the later denial of compensation, upset the fair balance between competing interests.
001-220866:
The case *Marcinkevičius v. Lithuania* concerned a defamation order requiring a Lithuanian businessman to retract a statement made in a media interview. The applicant, Mindaugas Marcinkevičius, was a founder and shareholder of Vilniaus Prekyba, a major retail group. He was in conflict with N.N., another founder and major shareholder. In 2015 the applicant complained to law-enforcement authorities that Vilniaus Prekyba had avoided taxes through financial deals and that N.N. had been unjustly enriched. A pre-trial investigation was opened but discontinued in August 2016; that decision was upheld in November 2016. The applicant sought reopening in November 2016, and in December 2016 the prosecutor rejected that request, forwarding new material to tax authorities. A tax inquiry into N.N. began in March 2017 and was still pending when the case reached Strasbourg.

On 1 December 2016 the applicant answered written questions from Delfi for an article on his conflict with N.N. The article was published on 2 January 2017. It reported that, according to the applicant, companies in Vilniaus Prekyba had allegedly been used to transfer shareholders’ money to N.N.’s personal accounts, avoid Lithuanian taxes, and appropriate other shareholders’ funds. He also said that company T. had allegedly laundered over EUR 20 million and hidden at least EUR 3 million in taxes, and that it was “obvious” that the shareholders and the Lithuanian State had suffered huge damage.

N.N. sued, claiming three statements were false and defamatory and seeking public retraction. The Vilnius District Court on 22 December 2017 found the first two statements and the first sentence of the third statement to be value judgments with sufficient factual basis and not insulting. However, it found the second sentence of the third statement—“It is obvious that not only we [the shareholders] but also the Lithuanian State have sustained huge damage”—to be a verifiable statement of fact. Because no damage had been proved, it held it false and insulting and ordered retraction. The Regional Court initially quashed that order, but after a Supreme Court remittal for procedural fairness, the Regional Court on 25 February 2020 upheld the District Court. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal. Delfi published the retraction in March 2020.

The applicant complained under Article 10 of the Convention that the retraction order violated his freedom of expression, arguing the statement was a value judgment. The European Court of Human Rights agreed. It held that the domestic courts’ classification of the sentence as a statement of fact was not based on an acceptable assessment of the relevant facts. Read in context, the sentence followed the applicant’s statement “In my opinion,” answered a journalist’s question about possible goals of the alleged scheme, and was followed by his statement that he had raised the issue with the company and prosecutor. An average reader would understand the damage allegation as a subjective opinion, not an established fact. The words “obvious” and “huge damage” were exaggerated and evaluative. The Court therefore found the interference not “necessary in a democratic society” and violated Article 10.

In *Marcinkevičius v. Lithuania* (Application no. 24919/20), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether a Lithuanian court order requiring a businessman to publicly retract a statement made in a media interview violated Article 10 of the Convention (freedom of expression).

The applicant, Mindaugas Marcinkevičius, was a founder and shareholder of Vilniaus Prekyba, one of the largest retail companies in the Baltic region. He and another founder/major shareholder, referred to as N.N.—described as one of Lithuania’s richest people—were public figures. In 2015 the applicant complained to law-enforcement authorities that Vilniaus Prekyba had used financial deals to avoid taxes and unjustly enrich N.N. A pre-trial investigation was opened in August 2015 but discontinued in August 2016, a decision upheld in November 2016. The applicant’s later requests to reopen the investigation were dismissed. In January 2017 he complained to the tax authorities, and in March 2017 a tax inquiry into N.N. began; it was still pending at the time of the ECtHR proceedings.

On 1 December 2016 the applicant replied in writing to questions from the news website *Delfi*. On 2 January 2017 *Delfi* published an article about his conflict with N.N. It quoted the applicant alleging that companies belonging to Vilniaus Prekyba were used to transfer shareholders’ money to N.N.’s personal accounts, avoid Lithuanian taxes, and appropriate other shareholders’ funds. He also said that one company, T., had allegedly laundered over €20 million and hidden at least €3 million in taxes. The article further quoted him: “In my opinion, the main goal was to appropriate the profit … without paying taxes in Lithuania. It is obvious that not only we [the shareholders] but also the Lithuanian State have sustained huge damage.”

N.N. brought civil defamation proceedings, seeking retraction of three statements. The domestic courts found that the first two statements and the first sentence of the third statement were value judgments with sufficient factual basis and were not insulting. However, they singled out the second sentence of the third statement—“It is obvious that … the Lithuanian State have sustained huge damage”—and held it to be a false statement of fact insulting to N.N.’s honour and dignity. The Vilnius District Court ordered the applicant to publicly retract it. That decision was initially reversed on appeal, but after a Supreme Court remittal for procedural fairness, the Vilnius Regional Court upheld the retraction order on 25 February 2020. A retraction was published on 4 March 2020. The Supreme Court later refused to accept the applicant’s further appeals.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained that the sentence was a value judgment and that the retraction order breached Article 10. The Court agreed. It held that the domestic courts’ finding of a “statement of fact” was not based on an acceptable assessment of the relevant facts. The impugned statement should have been characterised as a value judgment, especially when read in context: it followed the words “In my opinion,” responded to a journalist’s question about possible goals, concerned a matter of public interest, and related to ongoing investigations and a pending tax inquiry. The retraction order was therefore not “necessary in a democratic society,” and there was a violation of Article 10.

**Marcinkevičius v. Lithuania** (App. no. 24919/20) concerned an alleged violation of Article 10 (freedom of expression). The applicant, Mindaugas Marcinkevičius, was a founder and shareholder of Vilniaus Prekyba, one of the largest retail groups in the Baltic region, and was regarded as a public figure and influential businessman. He was in a prolonged conflict with N.N., another founder and major shareholder, described as the richest person in Lithuania.

In 2015 the applicant complained to law-enforcement authorities that Vilniaus Prekyba had used financial deals to avoid taxes and unjustly enrich N.N. An investigation was opened but discontinued in August 2016 for lack of evidence of unlawful conduct; that decision was upheld in November 2016. The applicant sought reopening in November 2016, but the prosecutor refused in December 2016, and a judge upheld the discontinuation in January 2017, later confirmed in February 2017. A tax inquiry into N.N. began in March 2017 and was still pending at the relevant time.

On 1 December 2016 the applicant answered written questions from a journalist of the website Delfi. On 2 January 2017 Delfi published an article about his conflict with N.N., quoting the applicant. The impugned statements suggested that companies belonging to Vilniaus Prekyba were used to transfer shareholders’ money to N.N.’s personal accounts, avoid Lithuanian taxes and appropriate other shareholders’ funds; that one company, T., had allegedly laundered more than €20 million and hidden at least €3 million in taxes; and that “In my opinion, the main goal was to appropriate the profit … without paying taxes in Lithuania. It is obvious that not only we [the shareholders] but also the Lithuanian State have sustained huge damage.”

N.N. brought civil proceedings, claiming the statements were false and defamatory and seeking public retraction of three statements. The domestic courts found that the first two statements and the first sentence of the third statement were value judgments, had a sufficient factual basis, and were not insulting. However, the second sentence of the third statement—“It is obvious that not only we … but also the Lithuanian State have sustained huge damage”—was held to be an independent statement of fact. The courts found it unproven and insulting to N.N.’s honour and dignity and ordered the applicant to retract it. The regional court initially reversed that finding, treating the sentence as subjective opinion in context, but the Supreme Court remitted the case due to a procedural breach. On remand, the regional court upheld the district court’s decision, and a retraction was published on 4 March 2020. The applicant’s further appeals were refused by the Supreme Court in 2020.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant argued that the retraction order violated Article 10 because the statement was a value judgment, not a verifiable fact. He submitted that the domestic courts had wrongly isolated one sentence from the article’s context, ignoring that it followed “In my opinion” and formed part of his explanation of suspicions he had referred to the authorities.

The Court (Second Section, 15 November 2022; final 15 February 2023) found a violation of Article 10. It held that the domestic courts’ finding that the impugned sentence was a statement of fact was not based on an acceptable assessment of the relevant facts. The statement should have been characterised as a value judgment. Consequently, the order to retract it was not “necessary in a democratic society.”
001-217039:
In *Lings v. Denmark* (Application no. 15136/20), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Denmark violated Article 10 of the Convention by convicting a retired physician for assisted suicide based partly on advice he gave about suicide methods. The applicant, Svend Lings, was a Danish physician and advocate for euthanasia. He founded an association called “Physicians in Favour of Euthanasia” and prepared an online guide titled “Medicines suited for suicide,” listing about 300 common pharmaceuticals, doses, combinations, and methods to ensure death, including using a plastic bag and rubber band. Publishing such a general guide was lawful in Denmark.

In February 2017, after a radio interview in which Lings stated that he had helped a terminally ill patient die by administering Fenemal, the Patient Safety Authority reported him to the police and withdrew his licence to practise. He was charged under section 240 of the Danish Penal Code with two counts of assisted suicide and one count of attempted assisted suicide. The Supreme Court ultimately upheld convictions on all three counts and imposed a suspended 60-day prison sentence.

The factual counts were central to the alleged Article 10 violation. First, in March 2017, Lings arranged for a co-defendant to prescribe Fenemal to A, knowing A intended to use it to commit suicide. The attempt failed. Second, in spring 2017, he was convicted of procuring medication for B, a man paralysed after a stroke who wished to die, knowing B intended to use it for suicide; B later died. Third, between July and August 2018, Lings exchanged emails with C, an 85-year-old woman with infirmities who had obtained pills herself and wanted to die. Lings confirmed her medication was suitable, referred her to the general guide, helped her find it, and advised that combining medication with a plastic bag and rubber band would make death “100% certain.” C was later found dead with a plastic bag over her head.

Lings complained that his conviction breached Article 10, arguing he had merely provided general advice about suicide. He maintained the information was already available in the lawful online guide and that his communications did not amount to assisting a specific suicide. The Supreme Court majority rejected that argument as to C, finding his particularised advice assisted her in a specific and significant way and was not exempt merely because it drew on a lawful general guide. Two dissenting judges would have acquitted him on that count, finding the information merely repeated the lawful guide and did not encourage or advocate suicide.

The European Court of Human Rights declared the application admissible but ultimately found no violation of Article 10. The Court emphasised that the case concerned assistance directed at specific individuals, not the mere publication or dissemination of general suicide information. The conviction and suspended sentence were prescribed by law and pursued legitimate aims, including preventing crime and protecting health, morals, and the rights of others. Given the lack of European consensus on assisted suicide and the sensitive moral and ethical issues involved, Denmark enjoyed a wide margin of appreciation. The interference with Lings’s expression was therefore justified and proportionate, and his Article 10 rights were not overstepped.

In *Lings v. Denmark* (Application no. 15136/20), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Denmark breached Article 10 by convicting Svend Lings, a retired Danish physician and euthanasia advocate, of assisted suicide and attempted assisted suicide. The judgment was delivered on 12 April 2022 and became final on 12 July 2022.

Lings founded “Physicians in Favour of Euthanasia” and prepared an online guide, “Medicines suited for suicide,” listing about 300 pharmaceuticals, doses, combinations, caveats, and methods intended to ensure death, including combining drugs with a plastic bag and rubber band. Publishing such a general guide was lawful in Denmark. In a February 2017 radio interview, Lings said he had helped a terminally ill patient die using Fenemal. The Patient Safety Authority reported him to the police and withdrew his medical licence.

Lings was charged under Article 240 of the Danish Penal Code with two counts of assisted suicide and one count of attempted assisted suicide. Count 1 concerned A, who had neurological diseases and wanted to die. Because Lings could no longer prescribe medication, he arranged for a co-defendant to prescribe Fenemal for A, knowing A intended to use it for suicide. The attempt failed, and A later improved. Count 2 concerned B, who was largely paralysed after a stroke and wanted to die. Lings visited B and advised him how to commit suicide based on the guide, then discussed procuring pills with another person. B’s former wife stated that Lings indicated he could contact someone who could obtain the medication; she later received and gave it to B. B took the medication, became unresponsive, and died days later. Lings denied personally supplying B’s medication.

Count 3 concerned C, an 85-year-old woman with multiple infirmities who was not seriously ill but wished to end her life. She had already procured pills and emailed Lings. Over at least nine emails, Lings confirmed her medications were “excellent,” referred her to the general guide, helped her find it, and advised combining the medication with a plastic bag over her head, adding that a rubber band around the neck would make death “100% certain.” C was later found dead with a plastic bag over her head.

The Danish Supreme Court upheld Lings’s conviction on 23 September 2019 and sentenced him to 60 days’ suspended imprisonment. The majority found counts 1 and 2 were punishable assistance and that, on count 3, Lings’s specific emails assisted C in a specific and significant way. It rejected the argument that the advice was exempt because it derived from a lawful general guide; the tailored advice intensified her resolve. Two judges dissented on count 3, finding the information was already publicly available, that Lings did not encourage or advocate suicide, and that convicting him would breach Article 10.

Before the ECtHR, Lings argued that his conviction violated Article 10 because he had merely provided general advice about suicide. The Court declared the application admissible. Considering the absence of European consensus on assisted suicide and the wide margin of appreciation, the Court found that the conviction and suspended sentence were justified and proportionate, and that Denmark had not overstepped its margin under Article 10. Thus, no violation was found.

In *Lings v. Denmark* (Application no. 15136/20), the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) examined whether Denmark breached Article 10 by convicting a retired physician for assisted suicide. The judgment was delivered on 12 April 2022 and became final on 12 July 2022.

The applicant, Svend Lings, a Danish national born in 1941, worked as a physician until 2010. Around 2015 he founded “Physicians in Favour of Euthanasia.” He prepared an online guide, “Medicines suited for suicide,” listing about 300 common pharmaceuticals, doses, combinations, and caveats. Publishing such a general guide was lawful in Denmark. Lings argued that his later conviction essentially punished his expression and advice.

In February 2017, in a radio interview, Lings said he had assisted a patient with a terminal pulmonary condition in dying by administering Fenemal. The Patient Safety Authority reported him to the police and withdrew his doctor’s licence. He was charged under section 240 of the Danish Penal Code with two counts of assisted suicide and one count of attempted assisted suicide. Section 240 criminalises assisting someone in deliberately ending their life, punishable by fine or up to three years’ imprisonment; attempts are also punishable. General encouragement or suicide “recipes” not aimed at specific persons were not criminalised.

The convictions concerned three specific individuals. First, Lings was convicted of attempted assisted suicide in March 2017 for arranging, through a co-defendant, to prescribe Fenemal to A, knowing A intended to use it to commit suicide. The attempt failed, and A later improved. Second, he was convicted of assisted suicide in spring 2017 after B, largely paralysed by a stroke, wanted to die. Lings advised him on suicide methods and was found to have procured or dispensed Fenemal knowing it was intended for suicide. B died in May 2017. Third, he was convicted of assisted suicide between July and August 2018 concerning C, an 85-year-old woman with many infirmities who wanted to die and had already obtained pills. In at least nine emails, Lings confirmed her medication was excellent, recommended the general guide, suggested combining the medication with a plastic bag, and wrote that with a rubber band around the neck she would be “100% certain.” C was found dead with a plastic bag over her head.

The District Court convicted Lings on some counts; the High Court convicted him on all three and imposed 60 days’ imprisonment, suspended. On 23 September 2019, the Supreme Court upheld the conviction. The majority found that his advice to C was specific and significant assistance, not exempt because it drew on a lawful general guide; it was suited to intensifying her intent. Two judges dissented on that count, considering the advice general and protected by Article 10. The sentence was suspended, with aggravating factors including systematic conduct and an act after provisional charging, and mitigating factors including his age.

Before the ECtHR, Lings complained that his conviction breached Article 10. The Court declared the application admissible but found no violation. The conviction was prescribed by law and pursued legitimate aims, notably protecting health, morals, and the rights of others. Given the lack of European consensus on assisted suicide and the wide margin of appreciation, Denmark had not overstepped. The Court distinguished lawful publication of a general guide from targeted advice and practical assistance to specific individuals. The conviction and suspended sentence were therefore justified and proportionate.
001-219984:
In *Muhammad v. Spain* (ECtHR, 18 October 2022), the applicant, a Pakistani national with long-term residence in Spain, alleged that a police identity check was racially motivated. On 29 May 2013, while walking in Barcelona with his Pakistani friend K.A. in an area known for pickpocketing and thievery, two National Police officers stopped them and asked for identification. The applicant claimed he asked whether the check was because of his skin colour and that one officer allegedly replied, “Yes, because you are black, and that’s all. I am not going to stop a German citizen.” He said he protested, was softly slapped, placed in the police car, arrested, threatened concerning renewal of his residence permit, and called a “monkey.” He also claimed K.A. was asked for ID and complied.

The police contested this version. According to their report, they approached the applicant because he laughed at them and used disrespectful slang. When asked to show ID, he allegedly refused, saying, “Why? Because I’m black? No way!” After being warned that refusal could lead to an administrative fine or criminal offence, he continued to refuse. He was then taken to a police station, where he produced his NIE and was released. The police issued an administrative notice for refusing to identify himself, showing a lack of respect towards authority, and an insolent attitude. No record was made concerning K.A.; the police said he was not asked to identify himself because he made no comments.

The applicant pursued criminal and administrative proceedings. A criminal complaint concerning unlawful detention, insults, threats, and related matters was discontinued, and appeals were dismissed; he did not bring that aspect before the ECtHR. In April 2014, he filed an administrative State liability claim alleging that the identity check was discriminatory and caused humiliation. He relied on his friend’s notarised statement, the criminal file, statistical expert reports, and reports from human rights bodies and NGOs indicating widespread racial profiling by Spanish police. He requested that the officers be heard and that video footage be obtained. The administrative authorities rejected the claim on 6 November 2014 for lack of evidence, relying on police reports denying racial motive. The Central Administrative Court dismissed his appeal in September 2015, finding the evidence contradictory, the applicant’s version unsupported, and no causal link established. It refused further witness and expert evidence because the statements and affidavit were already in the file. The Constitutional Court declared his *amparo* appeal inadmissible in November 2016.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained under Article 14 read with Article 8 that the identity check was racially discriminatory and that domestic authorities failed to investigate effectively. The Court held that identity checks can fall within the ambit of private life under Article 8, and Article 14 is applicable where there is an arguable claim that a person was targeted on account of specific physical or ethnic characteristics. It found such a claim arguable because the applicant alleged he was stopped solely because of his dark skin and the officer allegedly made a racial remark.

On the merits, the Court recognised a positive obligation to investigate possible racist motives, but stated that this obligation is not absolute: authorities must use best endeavours, collect evidence, explore practical means of discovering the truth, and give reasoned, impartial decisions. The Court concluded that the Spanish administrative courts had duly examined the applicant’s allegations and found them unsubstantiated; their decisions were sufficiently reasoned, and Spanish law provided an adequate framework to seek a remedy against discrimination. There was therefore no violation of Article 14 read in conjunction with Article 8.

**Muhammad v. Spain** (Application no. 34085/17), judgment of 18 October 2022, concerned an alleged racially motivated police identity check and the adequacy of Spain’s investigation into the applicant’s discrimination complaint.

The applicant, Mr Zeshan Muhammad, a Pakistani national with long-term residence in Spain, was stopped by two National Police officers on a Barcelona street on 29 May 2013. According to the applicant, he was walking with his friend K.A., also Pakistani, when officers asked for identity documents. The applicant allegedly asked whether he was being stopped because of his skin colour. He claimed an officer replied, “Yes, because you are black, and that’s all. I am not going to stop a German citizen.” When he protested, the officer allegedly slapped him, called him a “monkey,” arrested him, and threatened negative consequences for his residence permit. He was taken to a police station and later released.

The police gave a different account. They stated that they approached the applicant because he laughed at them and used disrespectful slang. When asked to identify himself, he allegedly refused and said, “Why? Because I’m black? No way!” After being warned that refusal could lead to an administrative fine or criminal offence, he was taken to the police station, where he showed his NIE and was released. He received an administrative notice for refusing to identify himself, showing lack of respect toward authority, and insolence. The police said K.A. was not asked for ID because he made no comments. No video footage was found.

The applicant first pursued criminal proceedings against the officers for alleged unlawful detention, insult, and bodily harm. Those proceedings were discontinued for lack of evidence. Separately, he brought an administrative State-liability claim alleging that the identity check was discriminatory racial profiling. He relied on his own account, a notarised witness statement from K.A., statistical expert reports, and reports from international and national human rights bodies indicating widespread police racial profiling in Spain. He requested that the officers be examined and video footage obtained. The administrative authorities dismissed the claim, finding contradictory versions and no evidence supporting discriminatory treatment. The Central Administrative Court upheld that decision, refusing additional witness and expert evidence, and found no causal link between the alleged harm and State action. The Constitutional Court declared his amparo appeal inadmissible.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 14 read with Article 8 that the identity check was racially discriminatory and that domestic authorities failed to investigate his racial-profiling allegation effectively.

The Court accepted that an identity check can interfere with private life under Article 8 where the person has an arguable claim of being targeted on physical or ethnic characteristics. It found the applicant’s complaint admissible. On the merits, the Court held that where racial discrimination is alleged, States have a special duty to investigate possible racist motives, but this obligation is not absolute; it requires best endeavours, not guaranteed results. Authorities must collect and secure evidence, explore practical means of discovering the truth, and give reasoned, impartial decisions. Reviewing the domestic proceedings, the Court considered that the Spanish administrative courts had duly examined the applicant’s allegations and evidence and had provided sufficient reasons for finding the discrimination claim unsubstantiated. The legal framework also offered adequate remedies against discrimination. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 14 taken together with Article 8 of the Convention.

In *Muhammad v. Spain*, the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) examined an allegation of racial profiling by police during an identity check. The applicant, Mr Zeshan Muhammad, a Pakistani national who had lived in Spain since 2005 and held a long-term residence permit, complained under Article 14 taken with Article 8 that he had been stopped solely because of his dark skin colour and that Spanish authorities failed to investigate his racial-profiling claim effectively.

On 29 May 2013, in Barcelona, two National Police officers stopped the applicant and his friend K.A., both Pakistani nationals of the same ethnicity, while they were walking in an area known for pickpocketing. The applicant alleged that when he asked why they were being checked, an officer replied: “Yes, because you are black, and that’s all. I am not going to stop a German citizen.” He claimed he protested, was softly slapped, arrested, called a “monkey,” and threatened concerning his residence permit. He was taken to a police station, identified, and released.

The police gave a different account. They said they approached the applicant because he laughed at them and used disrespectful slang. When asked for identification, he allegedly refused, saying: “Why? Because I’m black? No way!” He was then taken to the station for identification and later received an administrative notice for refusing to identify himself, showing a lack of respect toward authority, and behaving insolently. The officers said K.A. was not checked because he made no comments.

The applicant pursued criminal proceedings regarding unlawful detention, insults, bodily harm, humiliation, intimidation, and forgery, but not the discriminatory identity check itself. Those proceedings were discontinued for lack of evidence. He also brought an administrative State-liability claim alleging discriminatory racial profiling. He submitted a notarised witness statement from K.A., statistical expert reports, and reports by international, regional, and national human rights bodies documenting widespread police racial profiling in Spain. He requested that the officers, his friend, and an expert be heard and that video footage be obtained. The administrative authorities dismissed the claim, finding no evidence of discrimination, contradictory versions of events, and no causal link. Judicial review and an *amparo* appeal failed.

Before the ECtHR, the Court examined the complaint under Article 14 read with Article 8. It held that an identity check can fall within the scope of private life where there is an arguable claim that the person was targeted because of specific physical or ethnic characteristics. The Court found such a claim existed, so Article 8 was engaged and Article 14 applicable. It recognised that States have a positive obligation to investigate possible racist motives behind police conduct, especially where racial discrimination is alleged. However, that investigative obligation is not absolute; it requires best endeavours, not guaranteed proof. Authorities must collect relevant evidence, explore practical means of discovering the truth, and give reasoned, impartial decisions.

On the facts, the Court found that the Spanish administrative courts had duly examined the applicant’s racial-profiling allegation and found it unsubstantiated. Their decisions were sufficiently reasoned, and Spanish law provided an adequate framework for seeking remedies against discrimination. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 14 read in conjunction with Article 8.

**Fischer v. the Czech Republic** (App. no. 24314/13, ECtHR, 24 February 2022) concerned a German national and minority shareholder in the Czech joint-stock company Cestovní kancelář FISCHER. In 2003 the applicant, Mr Václav Fischer, entered into a consortium agreement with K & K Capital Group, controlled by K.K. After transferring 75% of the company’s shares to K & K, he retained 25%. On 3 March 2004, a general meeting controlled by K & K resolved to increase the company’s share capital from CZK 1,000,000 to CZK 11,000,000. The resolution excluded existing shareholders’ pre-emptive subscription rights and offered the new shares to another K & K-controlled entity. The applicant objected and voted against the resolution. As a result, his shareholding was diluted from 25% to 2.3%.

The applicant challenged the capital-increase resolution before the Prague Municipal Court on 9 March 2004. He alleged that the exclusion of pre-emptive rights was unlawful, breached the consortium agreement, and served only to allow K.K. to seize control of the company. Before that challenge was decided, the company approved a merger with three other companies on 17 December 2004. The merger was registered in the Commercial Register on 18 March 2005 and further reduced the applicant’s shareholding from 2.3% to 0.07%. He separately challenged the merger resolution, arguing that it had not been approved by the required 90% majority because he still held 25% at the relevant time.

In the capital-increase proceedings, the Municipal Court dismissed the application in April 2005, finding the resolution lawful; it also noted that even if unlawful, the resolution could not be set aside because the merger had already been registered. The High Court upheld that decision. In 2008 the Supreme Court quashed the decision and held that Article 204a § 5 of the Commercial Code had not been complied with. On remittal, however, the High Court in 2009 found that although the resolution breached the consortium agreement, was contrary to good morals, and circumvented the law, it could not be set aside under Article 131 § 3(b) of the Commercial Code because third parties had acquired bona fide rights through the merger. The Supreme Court endorsed that reasoning in 2010 and observed that the applicant could seek damages and just satisfaction under Article 131 § 4. The Constitutional Court dismissed his constitutional appeal in 2012, finding that his access to court was secured and that the compensation route remained available. The merger challenge was ultimately dismissed because the applicant no longer held 25% and because the merger had been registered.

The relevant legal framework barred courts from setting aside general meeting resolutions where annulment would substantially interfere with third-party rights or where a merger had been registered. However, Article 131 § 4 allowed persons harmed by an unlawful resolution to claim damages and just satisfaction even if the resolution was not set aside. Domestic practice, confirmed by the Constitutional Court and Supreme Court, provided that the lawfulness of the resolution could be examined as a preliminary question in such compensation proceedings. Following the earlier *Kohlhofer and Minarik* judgment, the Czech authorities amended the law in 2012 to improve minority shareholders’ access to court after registrations of transformations.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 that the domestic courts had refused to protect his rights, and that this violated his property rights. The key issue was whether the statutory bars on annulment deprived him of genuine access to court. The Court found that, despite the refusal to set aside the resolutions for legal-certainty reasons, the applicant could pursue compensation or just satisfaction proceedings in which the unlawfulness of the resolution could be determined as a preliminary issue. That alternative route, together with the evolution of domestic practice, sufficiently protected his right of access to court. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 6 § 1; the property complaint did not give rise to a separate violation.

**Case: Fischer v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 24314/13), ECtHR, 24 February 2022**

The applicant, Václav Fischer, a German national, was the sole shareholder of Cestovní kancelář FISCHER, a Czech joint-stock company. In 2003 he entered into a consortium agreement with K & K Capital Group, controlled by K.K., which provided that if the company’s share capital were increased, both parties would have the right to participate proportionally. Fischer then transferred 75% of the company’s shares to K & K Capital Group.

On 3 March 2004, at a general meeting, the company adopted a resolution—by K & K’s vote—to increase its share capital from CZK 1,000,000 to CZK 11,000,000. Shareholders’ pre-emptive subscription rights were excluded so that newly issued shares could be offered to Kapitálová společnost K & K, another entity controlled by K.K., ostensibly to reinforce the company’s internal finances due to negative equity. Fischer objected and voted against the resolution. The increase diluted his shareholding from 25% to 2.3%.

On 9 March 2004 Fischer applied to the Prague Municipal Court to set aside the resolution. He argued that it breached the Commercial Code, particularly Article 204a § 5, and violated the consortium agreement. In his view, excluding pre-emptive rights was unlawful because there was no serious reason on the company’s side; the real purpose was to allow K.K. to seize control.

Before the Municipal Court ruled, the company approved a merger with three other companies on 17 December 2004. The merger was registered in the Commercial Register on 18 March 2005, and Fischer’s stake fell further to 0.07%. On 13 April 2005 the Municipal Court dismissed Fischer’s application, finding the resolution lawful and, alternatively, incapable of being set aside under Article 131 § 3(c) of the Commercial Code because the merger had already been recorded. The High Court upheld that decision, but the Supreme Court quashed it in 2008, finding Article 204a § 5 had not been complied with.

On remittal, the High Court again upheld the dismissal in 2009. It accepted that the resolution breached the consortium agreement, was contrary to good morals, and circumvented the law, but refused to set it aside under Article 131 § 3(b) because the merger had created bona fide third-party rights. The Supreme Court dismissed a further appeal in 2010, observing that Fischer could claim damages and just satisfaction under Article 131 § 4. The Constitutional Court dismissed his constitutional appeal in 2012, holding that his access to court had been secured and that compensation proceedings remained available.

Separately, Fischer sought to set aside the merger resolution, arguing that he still held 25% and that the resolution lacked the required 90% majority. The courts dismissed this in 2012–2013 because the earlier capital-increase application had failed, so he no longer held 25%; moreover, even if unlawful, the merger’s registration and third-party rights barred annulment under Article 131 § 3(b) and (c).

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Fischer complained under Article 6 § 1 that the domestic courts refused to protect his rights against the general meeting resolution, and under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that this violated his property rights. The central access-to-court issue was whether the statutory bars to annulment left him without any genuine examination of the resolution’s lawfulness. The Court noted that domestic practice, especially Constitutional Court and Supreme Court decisions, allowed lawfulness to be examined as a preliminary question in compensation or just-satisfaction proceedings under Article 131 § 4. Reforms also abolished Article 131 § 3(c) and permitted challenges after registration. The ECtHR found no violation of Article 6, as Fischer could pursue compensation proceedings involving a genuine merits determination, and the property complaint disclosed no separate issue.

In *Fischer v. the Czech Republic* (App. no. 24314/13, ECtHR 24 February 2022), the applicant, Václav Fischer, a German national, originally owned 100% of Cestovní kancelář FISCHER, a.s., a Czech joint-stock company. In 2003 he entered a consortium agreement with K & K Capital Group, controlled by K.K., and transferred 75% of the shares to it, retaining 25%. The agreement allegedly entitled both parties to participate proportionally in any future capital increase.

On 3 March 2004, the company’s general meeting, controlled by K & K, resolved to increase share capital from CZK 1,000,000 to CZK 11,000,000. It excluded existing shareholders’ pre-emptive subscription rights so newly issued shares could be offered to Kapitálová společnost K & K a.s., another K.K.-controlled entity, ostensibly to strengthen the company’s negative equity. Fischer objected and voted against. The increase diluted his holding from 25% to 2.3%.

On 9 March 2004 Fischer applied to the Prague Municipal Court to set aside the capital-increase resolution. He alleged it violated Article 204a §5 of the Commercial Code and the consortium agreement because pre-emptive rights could be excluded only for serious company reasons, while the real aim was K.K.’s takeover. Before judgment, a merger with three companies was approved on 17 December 2004 and registered on 18 March 2005, further diluting Fischer’s stake to 0.07%.

The Municipal Court dismissed his application on 13 April 2005, finding the resolution lawful and, in any event, not subject to set-aside under Article 131 §3(c) because the merger had been registered. The High Court upheld. On 24 June 2008 the Supreme Court quashed, finding Article 204a §5 had been breached. On remittal, the High Court again refused set-aside on 12 February 2009: although the resolution breached the consortium agreement, was contrary to good morals, and circumvented the law, Article 131 §3(b) barred set-aside because the merger had created bona fide third-party rights. The Supreme Court upheld on 16 June 2010, noting Fischer could seek damages and just satisfaction under Article 131 §4. On 8 October 2012 the Constitutional Court dismissed his appeal, holding that access to court was safeguarded and compensation remained available.

Fischer also challenged the 17 December 2004 merger resolution, arguing he still held 25% and the resolution lacked the required 90% majority. The Municipal Court dismissed this on 17 January 2012, relying on the earlier refusal to set aside the capital increase and finding he no longer held 25%; the High Court upheld on 17 May 2013.

Before the ECtHR, Fischer complained under Article 6 §1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the domestic courts’ refusal to set aside the resolutions denied him access to court and violated his property rights. The central issue was whether dismissal of the set-aside applications for legal certainty—merger registration and third-party rights—left him without genuine judicial examination. The Court found Czech practice permitted courts to examine the lawfulness of such resolutions as a preliminary question in compensation/just-satisfaction proceedings under Article 131 §4, a possibility developed since its earlier case-law. It therefore found no violation of Article 6 §1 and no violation of property rights.

The European Court of Human Rights (First Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 31 March 2022 in *D.S. and Others v. Hungary* (applications nos. 41602/17 and nine others). The applicants were individuals who had been held in pre-trial detention in Hungary and who complained about the length of that detention. Their applications were lodged under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights on various dates set out in the appended table. The Hungarian Government was given notice of the applications. Because the applications raised similar subject matter, the Court decided to join them and examine them in a single judgment.

The principal alleged violation was that the applicants’ pre-trial detention had been unreasonably long, contrary to Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. That provision guarantees that everyone arrested or detained under Article 5 § 1(c) is entitled to trial within a reasonable time or to release pending trial. Release may be conditioned by guarantees to appear for trial. The judgment states that the list of applicants and the relevant details of the applications are set out in the appended table, so the individual dates and specific lengths of each applicant’s detention are not reproduced in the main body of the judgment. The central factual issue, however, was that the applicants had remained in pre-trial detention for periods the Court considered excessive. Some applicants also raised additional complaints under other Convention provisions.

In examining the Article 5 § 3 complaints, the Court recalled the general principles established in its case-law, particularly *Kudła v. Poland* and *McKay v. the United Kingdom*. It also noted its earlier leading cases of *Gál v. Hungary* and *Lakatos v. Hungary*, in which it had already found violations concerning similar issues of excessive pre-trial detention in Hungary. After considering all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument that would lead it to a different conclusion. It therefore held that the length of the applicants’ pre-trial detention had been excessive, in violation of Article 5 § 3.

Some applicants also complained under Article 5 § 4 of the Convention. That provision concerns the right of a detained person to take proceedings by which the lawfulness of the detention is decided speedily by a court, and to be released if the detention is unlawful. The Court found these complaints admissible: they were not manifestly ill-founded within the meaning of Article 35 § 3(a) and were not inadmissible on any other ground. On the merits, the Court concluded that these complaints also disclosed violations of the Convention in light of its well-established case-law, particularly *Bandur v. Hungary*. That authority concerned deficiencies in domestic detention-review procedures and the failure to provide adequate judicial review of the lawfulness of detention under Article 5 § 4.

Overall, the key facts relevant to the alleged violations were that the applicants had been held in pre-trial detention in Hungary for excessively long periods and, for some applicants, that the domestic procedures for reviewing the lawfulness of that detention were deficient. The Court did not depart from its prior case-law. It found a violation of Article 5 § 3 on account of the excessive length of pre-trial detention and violations of Article 5 § 4 for those applicants who raised review-related complaints. The judgment was final, though it remained subject to possible editorial revision.

**Case: A and B v. Georgia (ECtHR, 10 February 2022)**

The case concerned allegations that Georgia failed to protect a woman from domestic violence and failed to investigate law-enforcement failures, contrary to Article 2 and Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants, A and B, were the mother and son of C, who was killed by D—C’s former partner, a police officer, and B’s father.

In 2011, when C was 17, D kidnapped her for marriage. She lived with him from December 2011 to June 2012 and became pregnant, but left because of physical and psychological abuse. From December 2011 onward, D regularly threatened and abused C and her family, invoking his police status and connections. In July 2012, C called the police complaining that D had threatened to kill her mother; she received no response.

On 31 August 2013, D beat C during an argument over child support. Three patrol officers, who were D’s acquaintances or colleagues, interviewed C in D’s presence. One officer said wife-beating was commonplace. D mocked and shouted at C, but the officers did not intervene. Their report described only a “minor family altercation” and omitted the violence. C initially refused to sign it, but D forced her to do so with death threats overheard by the officers. One officer warned C not to contact police again without a valid reason. D left in the police car with the officers. C filed a criminal complaint with prosecutors, also alleging police negligence and stating she could not trust the police because her abuser was an officer. Prosecutors interviewed D and one officer, accepted D’s written undertaking never to abuse C again, and opened no criminal investigation.

On 5 July 2014, C complained to the General Inspectorate that D had assaulted her twice in public. Witnesses confirmed that between 2011 and 2014 D used his official position to abuse her: he flaunted his service pistol, threatened false charges against her relatives, and said he was not afraid of law enforcement because he was part of it. On 20 July 2014, D was promoted to senior police lieutenant. On 25 July 2014, shortly after C’s interview with the Inspectorate, D stalked her, argued with her in a public park, pulled out his service pistol, and shot her five times at close range. She died instantly.

D was convicted of premeditated murder of a family member and sentenced to 11 years. The conviction did not address gender-based discrimination. The applicants complained that police and prosecutors had failed to protect C and to investigate their own omissions. A criminal investigation into police negligence was opened, but the officers claimed they had not viewed the incident as violent, while other witnesses described serious violence. No charges were brought. A civil court awarded damages, finding a causal link between the authorities’ inactivity and C’s killing and criticising their failure to respond to discrimination and protect her life.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants alleged substantive and procedural violations of Article 2, read with Article 14. They argued that the authorities failed to take preventive measures, inadequately recorded domestic-violence evidence, responded discriminatorily, and failed to investigate the implicated officers. The Government argued the applicants had lost victim status because of D’s conviction and the civil compensation; the Court joined that objection to the merits. The key issue was whether Georgia’s passive and accommodating response to gender-based violence contributed to C’s death and whether an effective investigation existed.

The case arose from the killing of C by her partner D, a police officer, on 25 July 2014. The applicants—C’s mother (A) and son (B)—complained that Georgia failed to protect C from domestic violence and to investigate effectively the law-enforcement response, alleging violations of Articles 2 and 14 of the Convention.

In 2011, when C was seventeen, D kidnapped her for marriage. She began living with him under constant threat. Their unregistered cohabitation lasted until June 2012, when C, pregnant and exhausted by physical and psychological abuse, returned to her parents. From December 2011, D regularly abused C and her family verbally and physically, threatened to kill them, and invoked his police status and connections. The family reported only the most violent incidents.

In July 2012, C called police after D threatened to kill her mother, but received no response. On 31 August 2013, D beat C at her parents’ home over child support. Three patrol officers—D’s acquaintances and colleagues—interviewed C in D’s presence. They downplayed wife-beating, did not stop D from mocking and threatening her, and recorded the incident as a “minor family altercation.” D forced C to sign the inaccurate report by threatening to kill her, which officers overheard. One officer warned C not to contact police again without good reason.

That same day, C filed a criminal complaint with the prosecutor against D and the officers. She described ongoing harassment, death threats, violence, and fear of abduction of her child, and said she could not trust police because D was an officer. After interviews in which D denied abuse, D gave a written undertaking not to abuse C or her family. Prosecutors accepted this and did not open a criminal investigation.

On 5 July 2014, C complained to the General Inspectorate that D had assaulted her twice in public. Witnesses confirmed D used his official position: he flaunted his service pistol, threatened false charges against C’s family, and said he was not afraid of law enforcement because he was part of it. Authorities knew this. On 20 July 2014, D was promoted to senior lieutenant.

On 25 July 2014, after an interview with the General Inspectorate, C reiterated D’s systematic abuse but asked that he not be treated too harshly because he was her child’s father. Shortly afterward, D stalked her, argued with her in a public park, drew his service pistol, and shot her five times at close range. She died instantly. D was convicted of premeditated murder of a family member and sentenced to eleven years; the conviction did not address gender-based discrimination.

The applicants’ subsequent complaints against police and prosecutors led to a criminal investigation into officers’ alleged negligence, but no charges or victim status. A civil action resulted in an award of GEL 20,000; the Tbilisi City Court found a causal link between authorities’ inactivity and C’s death, citing failure to respond to discrimination allegations, failure to issue a restraining order or restrict D’s service pistol, and prosecutorial failure to investigate adequately. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under the substantive and procedural limbs of Article 2, read with Article 14, and found that passive, accommodating attitudes of law enforcement contributed to gender-based violence culminating in C’s murder and to an inadequate investigation.

In *A and B v. Georgia* (Application no. 73975/16, judgment of 10 February 2022), the applicants—A, C’s mother, and B, C’s young son—complained that Georgia failed to protect C from domestic violence and failed to effectively investigate the law-enforcement response to her abuse. C was killed by her partner, D, a police officer and B’s father. The Court examined the case under Article 2 (substantive and procedural) read together with Article 14 of the Convention, concerning the right to life and discrimination.

The key facts began in 2011, when C, then 17, was kidnapped for marriage by D, a 22-year-old police officer. Under threat, she cohabited with him from December 2011 to June 2012. After suffering physical and psychological harassment, she returned to her parents’ home while pregnant. From December 2011 onward, D regularly abused C and her family, threatened to kill them, invoked his police status and connections, and intimidated them with his service pistol. Although the family reported some violent incidents, they feared the police.

In July 2012, C called police to report that D had threatened to kill her mother, but received no response. On 31 August 2013, D beat C at her parents’ home during a dispute over child support. Police were called, but the three patrol officers who responded were D’s acquaintances and colleagues. They interviewed C in D’s presence, did not stop him from mocking and shouting at her, and one officer said wife-beating was commonplace. Despite visible injuries, the officers described the incident as a “minor family altercation,” omitted the violence, and did not interview D as the alleged abuser. D forced C to sign the report by threatening to kill her, which the officers overheard. They warned C not to contact police again without a valid reason and left with D in the same car.

C then filed a criminal complaint with the prosecutor against D and the officers, describing ongoing harassment, death threats, and abduction threats concerning her child. She said she distrusted police because her abuser was a police officer. The prosecutor interviewed C, D, and one officer; D denied abuse. On 9 September 2013, D gave a written undertaking never to abuse C or her family. The prosecution accepted this and declined to open a criminal investigation.

On 5 July 2014, C complained to the General Inspectorate that D had assaulted her twice in public. Evidence showed D had used his official position to abuse C between 2011 and 2014: he flaunted his service pistol at least seven times, threatened false charges against C’s father and brother, and said he was not afraid of law enforcement because he was part of it. Authorities knew this. On 20 July 2014, D was promoted to senior police lieutenant. On 25 July 2014, after C gave an Inspectorate interview in which she reiterated systematic abuse but asked that D not be treated too harshly because he was her child’s father, D stalked her, argued with her publicly, pulled out his service pistol, and shot her five times in the chest and stomach. She died instantly.

D was convicted of premeditated murder of a family member and sentenced to 11 years; his insanity claim was rejected. The conviction did not address gender-based discrimination. The applicants argued that the passive, accommodating response of police and prosecutors to domestic violence contributed to C’s death. A civil court partly awarded compensation, finding a causal link between the authorities’ inactivity and C’s killing and noting failures to respond to discrimination, interview witnesses, issue a restraining order, restrict D’s firearm, and investigate adequately. The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 2, both substantively and procedurally, read with Article 14, due to the State’s failure to prevent gender-based violence and to investigate the law-enforcement response.

**Case: Vegotex International S.A. v. Belgium (Application no. 49812/09), Grand Chamber, 3 November 2022**

Vegotex International S.A., a Belgian public limited company based in Antwerp, was assessed for corporation tax for the 1993 tax year. The tax authorities disallowed deductions relating to certain expenses connected to a stock-exchange transaction and investment costs. On 11 December 1995, the tax office assessed tax of BEF 12,054,089 and imposed a 50% penalty of BEF 6,027,045. The applicant objected and later challenged the assessment and penalty before the Antwerp Court of First Instance.

A key dispute arose over whether the State’s tax claim had become time-barred. On 24 October 2000, while the tax debt was still disputed, the tax authorities served a “demand for payment interrupting the limitation period.” The document stated that it was not aimed at enforcing payment, since the debt was disputed, but only at interrupting the five-year limitation period. The applicant argued that, under Court of Cassation case-law from 2002, such a demand could not validly interrupt the limitation period where no amount was “indisputably due.” The Antwerp Court of Appeal in 2007 found that the demand did not interrupt the limitation period under Article 2244 of the Civil Code, but held that the period had been suspended under Article 2251 while the tax dispute was pending, so recovery was not time-barred.

The Belgian legislature then intervened. Section 49 of the Miscellaneous Provisions Act of 9 July 2004 provided that a demand for payment interrupted the limitation period even where the disputed tax debt was not certain and of a fixed amount. The Constitutional Court upheld the provision, finding it justified by compelling general-interest grounds and exceptional circumstances. On 13 March 2009, the Court of Cassation applied section 49 retrospectively, substituted its own grounds for those of the Court of Appeal, held that the claim was not time-barred, and dismissed the applicant’s appeal as inadmissible for lack of interest.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Vegotex complained under Article 6 § 1 that: (1) the legislature had intervened during pending judicial proceedings and retroactively reinstated a time-barred tax debt; (2) the Court of Cassation’s substitution of grounds breached its right of access to a court, the adversarial principle, and equality of arms; and (3) the proceedings had exceeded a reasonable time. The Government did not dispute that the criminal limb of Article 6 was applicable because of the tax penalty. The Grand Chamber agreed, applying the Engel criteria: the penalty was deterrent and punitive and severe. However, it held that Article 6 guarantees do not apply with full stringency in tax matters, which fall outside the hard core of criminal law.

On the retrospective legislation, the Grand Chamber found that the legislature’s intervention pursued a compelling general interest in restoring legal certainty and protecting the Treasury’s rights, and that the retrospective effect was foreseeable in the circumstances. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 6 § 1 concerning the legislative intervention. It also found that the Court of Cassation’s substitution of grounds did not breach the applicant’s right of access to court, the adversarial principle, or equality of arms. However, the Grand Chamber found a violation of Article 6 § 1 on account of the excessive length of the proceedings.

In essence, the case concerned a disputed tax debt that became time-barred under new case-law but was retroactively revived by legislation while proceedings were pending. The Court accepted that the legislative response did not violate fair-hearing rights, but the prolonged duration of the proceedings did.

In *Vegotex International S.A. v. Belgium*, the applicant was a Belgian public limited company based in Antwerp. In October 1995 the tax authorities notified it of an intended rectification of its 1993 corporate tax return, disallowing deductions for certain expenses relating to a stock exchange transaction and for investment costs. On 11 December 1995 the tax office assessed corporation tax of BEF 12,054,089 (about EUR 298,813), plus a 50% penalty of BEF 6,027,045 (about EUR 149,406) for a “first offence of attempting to evade payment of tax.” The company objected in February 1996; the objection was rejected in September 2000.

On 24 October 2000 the authorities served a “demand for payment interrupting the limitation period.” It stated explicitly that it was not aimed at enforcing payment, because the tax debt was disputed, but served only to interrupt the five-year limitation period. The applicant brought court proceedings in December 2000. It later argued that the State’s recovery claim was time-barred. It relied on Court of Cassation case-law from 2002 holding that service of a demand for payment in respect of a disputed tax debt did not interrupt the limitation period where no amount was “indisputably due.” On that basis, the debt allegedly became time-barred on 15 February 2001.

While the dispute was still pending, the Belgian legislature enacted the Miscellaneous Provisions Act of 9 July 2004, in force on 25 July 2004. Section 49 provided that a demand for payment had to be interpreted as an act interrupting the limitation period under Article 2244 of the Civil Code even where the disputed tax debt was not certain and of a fixed amount. The Constitutional Court later upheld the retrospective effect, finding exceptional circumstances and compelling general interest in protecting the Treasury’s rights in pending tax disputes.

In February 2007 the Antwerp Court of Appeal held that the demand did not interrupt limitation under Article 2244, but that limitation had been suspended under Article 2251 while the tax debt was contested, so recovery was not time-barred. Both sides appealed to the Court of Cassation. The advocate-general proposed substituting new grounds based on section 49. The applicant received the submissions and filed a memorandum objecting that such substitution would breach Article 6 because it had no real opportunity to challenge the new ground. In March 2009 the Court of Cassation applied section 49 retrospectively, held that the demand validly interrupted limitation, found the lower decision had a proper legal basis, and dismissed the applicant’s appeal as inadmissible for lack of interest.

The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 about: (1) legislative intervention during pending proceedings and the retrospective reinstatement of an allegedly time-barred tax debt; (2) the Court of Cassation’s substitution of grounds, allegedly breaching access to court, the adversarial principle and equality of arms; and (3) excessive length of proceedings. The Government accepted the criminal limb applied because of the tax penalty; the Chamber found the criminal limb applicable under the *Engel* criteria, given the penalty’s deterrent/punitive purpose and severity, while the civil limb did not apply. The Grand Chamber held that Article 6 does not apply with full stringency in tax matters outside the hard core of criminal law, and that retrospective legislation restoring legal certainty during a pending dispute could be justified by compelling general interest and was foreseeable. It found no violation regarding the legislative intervention or substitution of grounds, but found a violation for excessive length.

Vegotex International S.A., a Belgian public limited company based in Antwerp, was assessed for the 1993 tax year. In 1995 the tax authorities disallowed deductions relating to a stock-exchange transaction and investment costs. They assessed corporation tax of BEF 12,054,089 and imposed a 50% penalty of BEF 6,027,045, citing a first offence of attempted tax evasion. Vegotex objected in November 1995; the objection was rejected in September 2000.

On 24 October 2000, the tax authorities served a “demand for payment interrupting the limitation period.” The document stated that it was not aimed at enforcing payment because the debt was disputed, but only at interrupting the five-year limitation period. In December 2000 Vegotex brought proceedings before the Antwerp Court of First Instance to set aside the tax penalty.

In 2004 the Court of First Instance reduced the penalty to 10% only in respect of investment costs, but upheld the 50% penalty concerning the stock-exchange expenses. Vegotex appealed. It argued that the State’s claim was time-barred, relying on Court of Cassation case-law from 2002 holding that service of a demand for payment in respect of a disputed tax debt did not interrupt the limitation period.

While the proceedings were pending, the Belgian legislature intervened. After the 2002 case-law, it enacted the Miscellaneous Provisions Act of 22 December 2003 and then section 49 of the Miscellaneous Provisions Act of 9 July 2004. Section 49 provided retrospectively that a demand for payment interrupted the limitation period under Article 2244 of the Civil Code even where the disputed tax debt was not certain and of a fixed amount. The Constitutional Court later upheld this measure as justified by exceptional circumstances and compelling general interest, aimed at protecting the Treasury’s rights in pending tax disputes and counteracting the retrospective effect of the Court of Cassation’s case-law.

In February 2007 the Antwerp Court of Appeal held that the demand had not interrupted the limitation period, but that the period had been suspended under Article 2251 of the Civil Code while the tax debt was contested. It therefore found that recovery was not time-barred.

Vegotex appealed on points of law. The State also appealed. The advocate-general at the Court of Cassation proposed substituting new grounds based on section 49: even if the Court of Appeal’s reasoning on suspension was wrong, the demand of 24 October 2000 validly interrupted the limitation period. Vegotex received the advocate-general’s submissions on 5 March 2009 and filed a memorandum on 9 March, arguing that substitution of grounds would breach Article 6 because it would have no opportunity to challenge the new basis, and that the section 49/Convention issue had not been debated before the lower courts.

On 13 March 2009 the Court of Cassation held that section 49 was not interpretative but had to be applied retrospectively according to the legislature’s intention. The demand therefore interrupted the limitation period, and the tax claim was not time-barred. It dismissed Vegotex’s appeal as inadmissible for lack of interest and the State’s appeal as inadmissible because the outcome favoured the State.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Vegotex complained under Article 6 § 1 that: (1) the legislature’s retrospective intervention during pending proceedings reinstated a time-barred tax debt, undermining a fair hearing and legal certainty; (2) the Court of Cassation’s substitution of grounds breached its right of access to court, the adversarial principle and equality of arms; and (3) the proceedings were excessively long. The Grand Chamber examined these complaints in light of the criminal limb of Article 6, given the punitive and deterrent nature of the 50% tax penalty. It ultimately found no violation concerning the retrospective legislation or the substitution of grounds, but found a violation of Article 6 § 1 owing to the excessive length of the proceedings.
