**P.C. v. Ireland** (Application no. 26922/19, ECtHR Fifth Section, 1 September 2022) concerned an Irish national, P.C., born in 1940, who had paid Pay Related Social Insurance contributions and qualified for the State Pension (Contributory) at age 66 in 2006, receiving about €230 weekly. In March 2011 he was convicted of sixty counts of sexual assault and fourteen counts of rape and sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment, with the final three years suspended. Under section 249(1)(b) of the Social Welfare Consolidation Act 2005, persons undergoing imprisonment or detention in legal custody were disqualified from receiving benefits under Part 2 of the Act, including the State Pension (Contributory). His pension payments therefore ceased when he was imprisoned. He served his sentence in what the High Court described as a well-run, modern prison, with an anticipated release date in March 2020.

In 2013 P.C. brought domestic proceedings against the State. He sought a declaration that the impugned provision was unconstitutional and incompatible with the Convention, damages, and an injunction requiring payment of his pension. He alleged that the stoppage of his pension breached his constitutional rights and Articles 3, 5, 6, 8, 13 and 14 of the Convention, as well as Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. He claimed the loss left him practically destitute: his only income was a prison gratuity initially worth €18.90 per week, later reduced to €11.90 because age-related ailments and a wrist injury prevented him from working in prison. Had he been able to work, he could have earned about €3.50 extra weekly. He said he could not buy extra food, clothing or small electronic appliances, referred to a €50 hardship payment in 2013, and estimated his total loss at over €100,000.

Evidence before the High Court showed that about thirty to forty prisoners had their State Pension (Contributory) payments stopped each year; the pension was non-means-tested and paid regardless of other income; maintaining a prisoner cost about €65,000 per year; five to ten prisoners in P.C.’s age group worked in prison for €4.50 weekly; and prisoners could receive additional funds, including private pensions, lodged by family into a prison account.

The High Court dismissed the case in 2016. It held that the State Pension (Contributory) was not a property right under either the Constitution or Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, because the benefit system was partly tax-funded and required flexibility; States enjoyed a wide margin of appreciation in social and economic policy. It rejected the discrimination claim: prisoners with private pensions were not in a comparable position; the disqualification applied to all social welfare benefits; and withholding the pension while the State met essential prison needs was rational and proportionate. It also rejected the other Convention complaints.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, P.C. alleged violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 alone and with Article 14, and Article 13. The Court held that the withheld old-age pension payment, due to statutory disqualification while incarcerated, was not a “possession” under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Under Article 14 read with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, the payments fell within the ambit of property, but there was no discrimination: there was no evidence of greater impact on older prisoners as a group; differing impact based on income level or source was not related to personal status; and convicted prisoners were not relevantly similar to persons detained for mental illness or remand prisoners. The Article 13 complaint was manifestly ill-founded, as the Supreme Court’s approach and the damages awarded fell within the authorities’ margin of appreciation. The application therefore did not establish a Convention violation.

In *P.C. v. Ireland* (ECtHR, 1 September 2022), the applicant was an Irish national born in 1940. He had paid Pay Related Social Insurance contributions and, from age 66 in February 2006, received the State Pension (Contributory) (“SPC”) of about €230 per week. In March 2011 he was convicted of sixty counts of sexual assault and fourteen counts of rape and sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment, with the final three years suspended. Under section 249(1)(b) of the Social Welfare Consolidation Act 2005, persons undergoing imprisonment or detention in legal custody were disqualified from receiving benefits under Part 2 of the Act, including the SPC. His pension therefore stopped when he was imprisoned.

The applicant alleged that the statutory disqualification violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (“A1P1”), alone and together with Article 14, and that the failure of the Supreme Court to determine his Convention complaints denied him an effective remedy under Article 13. He claimed the loss of his pension left him practically destitute. His only income was a prison gratuity, initially €18.90 per week and later €11.90 per week after he could not work due to age-related ailments and a wrist injury. He said he could not buy extra food, personal clothing or small electronic appliances for his cell, and estimated his loss at over €100,000. Evidence before the High Court showed that 30–40 prisoners had their SPC stopped each year; the SPC was non-means-tested; the annual cost of maintaining a prisoner was about €65,000; 5–10 prisoners in the applicant’s age group worked in prison earning €4.50 per week; and family members could lodge private funds into a prisoner’s account.

In 2013 the applicant brought High Court proceedings seeking a declaration of unconstitutionality, damages, an injunction, and a declaration of incompatibility under the European Convention on Human Rights Act 2003. He relied on Articles 3, 5, 6, 8, 13 and 14 of the Convention and A1P1. The High Court dismissed the case in 2016. It held that the SPC was not a property right despite its contributory nature, that the welfare system required flexibility, and that the State enjoyed a wide margin of appreciation. The discrimination claim failed because private pension recipients were not comparable, the disqualification applied to all social welfare benefits and all SPC recipients, and withholding the benefit was rational and proportionate while the State met the prisoner’s basic needs. The Convention arguments were also rejected.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the key issues were whether the withheld pension was a “possession,” whether the prisoner’s disqualification discriminated contrary to Article 14, and whether Article 13 required a remedy. The Court held that A1P1 did not apply *ratione materiae*: a withheld old-age pension payment, due to statutory disqualification while incarcerated, was not a “possession.” On Article 14 read with A1P1, even assuming the payments fell within the ambit of A1P1, there was no discrimination. There was no evidence that older-age prisoners as a group were more affected; the differing impact depended on a person’s income level and source, not personal status; and convicted prisoners were not in a relevantly similar position to persons detained for mental illness or remand prisoners. The Article 13 complaint was manifestly ill-founded, because the Supreme Court’s decision to uphold the constitutional complaint without fully considering the Convention complaints fell within the authorities’ margin of appreciation, and no issue arose from the damages awarded.
001-219946:
**Dolenc v. Slovenia (Application no. 20256/20), European Court of Human Rights, First Section, 20 October 2022**

The applicant, Mr Vincenc Vinko Dolenc, a Slovenian neurosurgeon, performed surgery in May 1992 on E.M., an Israeli citizen, at Ljubljana University Hospital. After surgery and/or postoperative care, E.M. was left severely disabled. In 1995, E.M. sued the applicant for medical negligence in Israel; the lawsuit was served on the applicant during a visit there. The case proceeded before the Tel Aviv District Court. The applicant participated through an Israeli lawyer, submitted a defence, expert medical opinion, statements of eleven witnesses from Ljubljana University Hospital, his own written statement, and an opinion from a Slovenian legal expert on applicable Slovenian law. He did not appear personally.

A central issue was the examination of witnesses. The applicant argued that his witnesses refused to travel to Israel and that he feared being served with another lawsuit. He requested that he and his witnesses be examined in Slovenia, preferably under the Hague Evidence Convention. The Israeli court initially ordered video-link examination. Slovenian authorities stated that no bilateral agreement existed, that the Hague Evidence Convention could be used, but that Slovenian law did not provide for direct video-link examination from abroad. The applicant refused video-link examination and repeated his request for examination in Slovenia. Israeli courts upheld the video-link arrangement and later excluded his main written statement because he refused to cooperate. The Israeli court then ordered his witnesses to be examined in Slovenia under the Hague Evidence Convention. However, requests between Israeli and Slovenian authorities encountered difficulties, including questions about translation, costs, cross-examination, and foreign lawyers. Delays followed and the procedure was eventually terminated.

In 2004, the applicant cancelled his Israeli lawyer’s power of attorney. The Israeli court ordered that documents continue to be served through the former lawyer’s office; the applicant disputed receiving notice of subsequent decisions. Later in 2004, the Israeli court cancelled the Slovenian witness-examination procedure due to prolonged delays and decided to take evidence in Israel, giving the applicant further opportunities to participate. No one appeared for him. The court excluded his witnesses’ statements and the Slovenian legal expert’s opinion because the witnesses had not been directly examined, attributing this to the applicant’s conduct.

In June 2005, the Israeli district court found the applicant fully liable for E.M.’s damage. Because the Slovenian law expert’s opinion had been excluded, the court applied Israeli law, treating Slovenian law as unproven. It found that the applicant was responsible for the surgery and postoperative care and that there was negligence, including failure to perform an immediate CT scan and inadequate postoperative monitoring.

E.M. subsequently sought recognition of the Israeli judgments in Slovenia. The Slovenian courts recognised the judgments. The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the recognition violated his right to a fair hearing. He argued that the Slovenian courts had failed to duly satisfy themselves that the Israeli proceedings were fair, particularly given that his witnesses were not examined, his evidence and submissions were excluded, and documents were served on his former representative.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 6 § 1. It held that the Slovenian courts recognised the Israeli judgments without sufficiently scrutinising the fairness of the Israeli trial. In particular, they attached insufficient weight to the consequences of the non-examination of witnesses and the exclusion of the applicant’s statements on his right to present evidence.

In *Dolenc v. Slovenia*, the applicant was a Slovenian neurosurgeon who in 1992 performed surgery on an Israeli citizen, E.M., in Ljubljana. E.M. was left severely disabled. In 1995 E.M. sued the applicant for medical negligence in the Tel Aviv District Court; the applicant was served while visiting Israel. The applicant defended through Israeli counsel, submitting a defence, a medical expert opinion, statements of eleven Ljubljana hospital witnesses, his own written statement, and an expert opinion on Slovenian law. He argued that Slovenian law applied, that liability lay with the hospital, and that the claim was time-barred. Israeli courts nonetheless held that Israel was the proper forum.

The trial began in 1999. The plaintiff’s witnesses and expert testified. The applicant did not appear personally but sought to have himself and his witnesses examined in Slovenia or by video link. The Israeli court initially allowed video-link examination. The Slovenian Ministry of Justice said there was no bilateral civil legal assistance agreement with Israel, but the Hague Evidence Convention could apply; however, Slovenian law did not provide for direct video examination of witnesses from abroad. The applicant then declined video-link participation and repeatedly requested examination before a Slovenian court under the Hague Convention. Israeli courts rejected this, finding video examination practicable and adequately balancing the parties’ interests.

The Israeli court warned that the applicant’s main statement would be excluded if he maintained his refusal. In June 2003 it excluded his main statement and ordered his witnesses to be examined in Slovenia under the Hague Evidence Convention. A request was sent in September 2003. The Ljubljana District Court raised issues concerning translation, interpretation, costs, the impossibility of cross-examination under Slovenian law, and participation of foreign lawyers. Delays followed. In 2004 the applicant cancelled his Israeli lawyer’s representation, and the Israeli court ordered documents to be served through the former lawyer’s office; the applicant disputed being informed. In September 2004, after fifteen months without progress, the Israeli court cancelled the Slovenian examination and decided to take evidence in Israel. The applicant did not appear and disputed receiving later deadlines. In his absence, the Israeli court excluded his witnesses’ statements and the Slovenian-law expert opinion because they had not been directly examined, attributing this to his conduct.

In June 2005 the Israeli district court found the applicant fully liable. Because the Slovenian-law expert opinion had been excluded, foreign law was not proven, so Israeli law was applied. The court found a direct contractual relationship with the applicant, deficient postoperative care, causation, and significant damage.

E.M. then sought recognition of the Israeli judgments in Slovenia. The Slovenian courts recognized them. The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 that recognition violated his right to a fair hearing because he had been unable to present key evidence in Israel. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation: the Slovenian courts had recognized the Israeli judgments without duly satisfying themselves that the Israeli trial was fair. They gave insufficient weight to the consequences of the non-examination of the applicant’s witnesses and the exclusion of their statements, which deprived him of the opportunity to present evidence central to liability and the applicable law. The key violation concerned Slovenia’s failure to scrutinize the fairness defects of the foreign proceedings.

In *Dolenc v. Slovenia* (Application no. 20256/20, judgment 20 October 2022), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Slovenian courts violated Article 6 § 1 of the Convention by recognising Israeli civil judgments against the applicant, a Slovenian neurosurgeon, without adequately assessing the fairness of the Israeli proceedings.

The underlying facts began in May 1992, when the applicant performed surgery on E.M., an Israeli citizen, at Ljubljana University Hospital in Slovenia. E.M. was left severely disabled after the surgery and/or postoperative care. In 1995, E.M. sued the applicant for medical negligence in the Tel Aviv District Court. The Israeli Supreme Court ultimately held that Israel was the proper forum, despite the surgery having occurred in Slovenia.

The applicant participated through an Israeli lawyer but never appeared personally. He submitted a defence, a medical expert opinion, statements of eleven witnesses—mostly doctors and nurses from Ljubljana University Hospital—his own written statement, and an opinion from a Slovenian legal expert on the applicability of Slovenian law. The central fairness problem concerned the Israeli court’s treatment of this evidence.

The applicant and his witnesses were not examined in Israel. He requested that they be examined by video link or, alternatively, by a Slovenian court under the Hague Evidence Convention. The Israeli court initially ordered video-link examination, but the Slovenian Ministry of Justice indicated that Slovenian law did not provide for direct video-link examination from a foreign country and that assistance would have to follow the Hague Evidence Convention. The applicant declined to participate by video link and repeatedly asked that he and his witnesses be examined in Slovenia under the Hague Convention. Israeli courts rejected those requests, finding video link feasible and balancing the parties’ interests.

In 2003, after warning the applicant, the Israeli district court excluded his main written statement from the case file. It then ordered his witnesses to be examined in Slovenia under the Hague Evidence Convention. An Israeli request was sent to Slovenian authorities in September 2003, but the Ljubljana District Court raised practical and legal issues, including translation, costs, cross-examination, and participation of foreign lawyers. Delays followed, and the procedure was eventually treated as terminated. In 2004, the Israeli court cancelled the Slovenian examination, noting that fifteen months had passed without progress and nine years since the lawsuit began. It decided to take evidence in Israel instead.

The applicant later cancelled his lawyer’s representation. He disputed that he was properly informed of subsequent Israeli decisions, since documents were served on his former representative’s office. He did not appear at later hearings. The Israeli district court excluded his witnesses’ statements and the Slovenian-law expert opinion because the witnesses had not been directly examined, attributing this to the applicant’s conduct. In 2005, it found him fully liable. Because the Slovenian-law expert opinion was excluded, the court applied Israeli law rather than Slovenian law, and found the applicant personally liable for deficient postoperative care.

The applicant complained that Slovenian courts later recognised these Israeli judgments without ensuring that the Israeli trial had been fair. The ECtHR found a violation of Article 6 § 1. It held that the Slovenian recognition courts had not duly satisfied themselves of the fairness of the Israeli proceedings. In particular, they attached insufficient weight to the consequences of the non-examination of the applicant’s witnesses and the exclusion of their statements and his own evidence, which severely impaired his right to present evidence in the proceedings that formed the basis for the damages judgment recognised against him.

In *Razgon and Others v. Russia* (Applications nos. 5386/20 and 5 others), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 10 November 2022. The case concerned six applications lodged against Russia under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates. The Russian Government were given notice of the applications. Because the applications raised similar issues, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are that the applicants had been involved in Russian administrative-offence proceedings. They complained that the tribunal lacked impartiality because the prosecuting party was absent from those proceedings. They relied, expressly or in substance, on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal in the determination of any criminal charge. Although the proceedings were classified under national law as administrative offences, the Court treated them as falling within the criminal limb of Article 6 for Convention purposes.

The Court assessed this complaint in light of its leading judgment in *Karelin v. Russia* (no. 926/08, 20 September 2016). In *Karelin*, the Court examined Russian rules of administrative procedure and held that statutory requirements allowing national judicial authorities to consider an administrative-offence case within the criminal limb of Article 6 in the absence of a prosecuting authority were incompatible with the principle of objective impartiality. The absence of a prosecuting party meant that the judge could not be regarded as objectively impartial, because the tribunal was not structurally balanced and the judge effectively assumed or appeared to assume both prosecutorial and adjudicative functions. In the present case, the Court examined all the material and found no fact or argument capable of leading to a different conclusion. It therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1.

The applicants also raised other complaints under the Convention. The Court found these complaints admissible and concluded that they disclosed violations under well-established case-law. Specifically, it found violations concerning disproportionate measures taken by the authorities against organisers and participants of public assemblies, as established in *Frumkin v. Russia*, and unlawful administrative arrest, as established in *Tsvetkova and Others v. Russia*. These elements indicate that the administrative-offence proceedings were connected to public assemblies and related arrests.

Having already found a lack of impartiality of the tribunal under Article 6, the Court did not consider it necessary to examine separately the remaining Article 6 complaints about the administrative-offence proceedings raised in applications nos. 5386/20, 6001/20, 6789/20, 8737/20 and 12772/20.

Overall, the judgment found that Russia violated Article 6 § 1 of the Convention because administrative-offence proceedings were conducted without a prosecuting party, undermining the tribunal’s objective impartiality. The Court also found violations regarding disproportionate measures against assembly participants and unlawful administrative arrests. The appended table, not reproduced in the extract, contains the individual applicants’ details and the specific facts of each application. The judgment was final but subject to editorial revision.

In *Hovhannisyan and Nazaryan v. Armenia* (ECtHR, 8 November 2022), the applicants were the mother and sister of A. Nazaryan, a 31-year-old Armenian armed forces lieutenant who died on 27 July 2010 at military base no. 12 from a gunshot wound to the mouth. The official account was suicide, using his assigned assault rifle. The case concerned Armenia’s obligations under Article 2 of the Convention, both substantive (protecting life) and procedural (conducting an effective investigation).

The key facts concerned sustained harassment and ill-treatment before A. Nazaryan’s death. On 19 July 2010, after an argument about using Captain H.M.’s water bottle for diesel fuel, H.M. struck A. Nazaryan. Later, H.M. and Lieutenant V.H. jointly beat him, causing a nosebleed and humiliating him in front of other servicemen. H.M. repeatedly insulted and demeaned him, excluded him, and threatened a “court of honour.” Conscripts A.H., M.M., and H.K. also mocked, debased, and used violence against him, exploiting his vulnerable psychological state. The Minister of Defence’s internal order later found that H.M. had abused his authority and created an unhealthy moral environment; the conscripts had ill-treated A. Nazaryan; and the situation had been concealed from command, leading to an unbearable psychological condition and fatal outcome.

On 26 July 2010, H.M. allegedly ordered officers to remove the firing pin from A. Nazaryan’s rifle because he was at risk of self-harm, but this was not done. The next morning A. Nazaryan was found dead. H.M. removed A. Nazaryan’s notebook from his pocket before handing it to Major M.N., fearing his fingerprints might remain. Inside was a note said to be in A. Nazaryan’s handwriting stating he was tired of everything. Forensic medical examination confirmed a fatal shot to the mouth but also found recent and older abrasions and bruises, plus alcohol intoxication. A posthumous psychological examination concluded that the suicide was linked to humiliation, debasement, and ill-treatment by H.M., V.H., and conscripts.

Domestic criminal proceedings charged H.M., V.H., A.H., M.M., and H.K. In May 2013 they were convicted; H.M. received ten years’ imprisonment. However, the applicants alleged the investigation was ineffective. Key procedural problems included scene-record date errors, contradictory ballistic/cartridge evidence, unexplained blood traces, and refusal to give the first applicant access to handwriting documents before the investigation ended so she could challenge the suicide note. The Constitutional Court upheld that restriction. Many servicemen were placed in disciplinary isolation after the death; some later retracted or alleged coerced pre-trial statements. The second applicant’s requests to exclude tainted statements and order additional forensic measures were dismissed. The Court of Appeal conducted only a cassation-style review without fully re-examining the evidence, and the Court of Cassation declared further appeals inadmissible.

The ECtHR found violations of Article 2. Substantively, Armenia failed to take appropriate and effective measures to protect A. Nazaryan’s life despite known harassment, ill-treatment, and self-harm risk, and lacked a regulatory framework safeguarding military personnel, particularly regarding suicide prevention. Procedurally, the domestic authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into the circumstances of death and failed to secure the applicants’ involvement to a sufficient degree.

**Case: Hovhannisyan and Nazaryan v. Armenia**  
*(Applications nos. 2169/12 and 29887/14, European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, judgment of 8 November 2022)*

The applicants were the mother and sister of A. Nazaryan, a 31-year-old officer in the Armenian armed forces who died on 27 July 2010 at military base no. 12 from a gunshot wound to the mouth, allegedly by suicide. The case concerned Armenia’s obligations under Article 2 of the Convention to protect life and to conduct an effective investigation.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations concern a pattern of harassment and ill-treatment before A. Nazaryan’s death. He was assigned to the base under Captain H.M. According to domestic findings, H.M. verbally abused and physically assaulted A. Nazaryan, including an incident on 19 July 2010 when H.M. punched him and, together with Lieutenant V.H., beat him in front of other servicemen, causing a nosebleed and humiliation. H.M. also repeatedly demeaned him and said he did not merit being an officer. Three conscripts—A.H., M.M. and H.K.—subsequently mocked, debased and used violence against A. Nazaryan, taking advantage of his vulnerable condition. On 26 July 2010, H.M. allegedly ordered that the firing pin be removed from A. Nazaryan’s rifle so that he would not harm himself, but this was not done. A note found in A. Nazaryan’s notebook stated that he felt obliged to act because he was tired of everything and could not find his place in life. A posthumous forensic psychological and psychiatric report concluded that his suicide was linked to humiliation, debasement and ill-treatment by H.M., V.H. and conscripts.

After the death, criminal proceedings were opened for incitement to suicide. Investigators carried out scene examinations, an autopsy, ballistic and fingerprint tests, and psychological assessments. The forensic evidence indicated that the shot was fired into the mouth and that self-infliction was possible, though other injuries were found on the body and their origin was not fully clarified. Several witnesses described ill-treatment, but some later retracted or claimed their pre-trial statements were obtained under duress, including during disciplinary isolation. The applicants complained that the investigation was ineffective, that evidence was mishandled, and that they were not sufficiently involved. The first applicant was refused access to handwriting samples before the investigation’s completion, and the Constitutional Court upheld the relevant procedural restrictions.

Domestically, in 2013, H.M., V.H., A.H., M.M. and H.K. were convicted in connection with the abuse and humiliation that led to A. Nazaryan’s suicide, receiving prison sentences of three to ten years. Appeals were largely upheld, but the applicants argued that the appellate review was superficial and that requests for further evidence were wrongly dismissed.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 2 both substantively and procedurally. Substantively, Armenia failed to take appropriate and effective measures to protect A. Nazaryan’s life despite known harassment, ill-treatment and suicide risk. The Court also found a lack of a regulatory framework to safeguard the lives of military personnel, particularly regarding suicide prevention. Procedurally, the domestic authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into the circumstances of the death and did not sufficiently involve the applicants in the proceedings.

In *Hovhannisyan and Nazaryan v. Armenia* (Applications nos. 2169/12 and 29887/14, judgment of 8 November 2022), the European Court of Human Rights examined the death of A. Nazaryan, a 31-year-old Armenian military officer, and the investigation that followed. The applicants were his mother and sister. The case concerned alleged violations of Article 2 of the Convention, both substantive and procedural.

A. Nazaryan was recruited into the Armenian armed forces in 2009 and served as a lieutenant at military unit no. 21127. On 27 July 2010 he was found dead at military base no. 12 with a gunshot wound to his mouth, using his assigned assault rifle. Initial reports described the death as suicide, and criminal proceedings were opened for incitement to suicide.

The key facts relevant to the alleged substantive violation concerned persistent harassment and ill-treatment before his death. In July 2010, Captain H.M., his superior, repeatedly humiliated and assaulted A. Nazaryan. On 19 July 2010, after a dispute over a water bottle used for diesel fuel, H.M. struck him; later, together with Lieutenant V.H., he beat him in front of others, causing a nosebleed and facial swelling. H.M. demeaned him, threatened a “court of honour,” and said he did not merit being an officer. Conscripts A.H., M.M., and H.K. also bullied, mocked, and used violence against him. Witnesses described A. Nazaryan as being subjected to humiliation and ill-treatment. H.M. later admitted he suspected A. Nazaryan might harm himself. On 26 July 2010 he allegedly ordered that the firing pin be removed from A. Nazaryan’s rifle to prevent self-harm, but this was not done. After the death, H.M. removed A. Nazaryan’s notebook from his pocket and gave it to Major M.N., concealing it; the notebook later revealed a note suggesting suicidal thoughts.

The investigation was criticised for failing to clarify key circumstances. The scene-examination record was misdated; blood-like traces were not conclusively linked; injuries on the body were not fully explained; there were discrepancies about cartridges and photographs; and clothing was not tested for another person’s blood. Numerous servicemen were placed in disciplinary isolation after the death, and some later alleged that their pre-trial statements were obtained under duress. Many retracted their statements at trial. The applicants were denied pre-trial access to the case file, and the Constitutional Court upheld the relevant restrictions.

At trial, Captain H.M., Lieutenant V.H., and conscripts A.H., M.M., and H.K. were convicted; the domestic courts found that A. Nazaryan’s suicide resulted from their abuse and humiliation. However, appellate review was limited, and the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicants’ appeal on points of law.

The European Court of Human Rights found violations of Article 2. Substantively, Armenia failed to take appropriate and effective measures to protect A. Nazaryan’s life against the known backdrop of harassment and ill-treatment, and lacked a regulatory framework to safeguard military personnel from suicide. Procedurally, the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into the circumstances of his death and did not sufficiently involve the applicants in the proceedings.

In *Khuren-ool and Others v. Russia* (Applications nos. 77300/17 and 5 others), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 13 October 2022. The applications were lodged against Russia under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates. The Russian Government was given notice. Because the applications raised similar complaints, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment.

The applicants were detainees held in pre-trial or post-conviction detention facilities in Russia. Their principal complaint concerned permanent video surveillance of detainees in their cells. They relied, expressly or in substance, on Article 8 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to respect for private life. They alleged that continuous video monitoring while confined to their cells amounted to an unlawful interference with their privacy.

The Court noted that it had already examined Russia’s legal framework on permanent video surveillance in *Gorlov and Others v. Russia* (2019). In that case, the Court held that placing a detainee under permanent video surveillance was a serious interference with the right to respect for private life. It further found that Russian national law was not sufficiently clear, precise, or detailed to protect detainees against arbitrary interference. The law also did not require any balancing exercise between the detainee’s privacy and legitimate security interests, and it did not allow an individual to obtain judicial review of the proportionality of permanent video surveillance. In the present case, the Court examined all submissions and found no fact or argument capable of leading to a different conclusion. It therefore held that the applicants’ placement under permanent video surveillance while confined to their cells in pre-trial and post-conviction detention facilities was not “in accordance with law,” contrary to Article 8 of the Convention.

The applicants also raised other complaints. These included complaints about conditions of detention during transport and the related review of pre-trial detention, the lack of an effective remedy regarding conditions during transport, conditions of post-conviction detention, placement of a defendant in a metal cage during court hearings, and the lack of an effective remedy for permanent video surveillance. The Court found these complaints admissible and concluded that they disclosed violations of the Convention in the light of well-established case-law, including *Idalov v. Russia*, *Tomov and Others v. Russia*, *Sergey Babushkin v. Russia*, *Svinarenko and Slyadnev v. Russia*, and *Gorlov and Others*. Since it had already found violations, the Court did not need to deal separately with the applicants’ Article 13 complaints concerning the alleged lack of effective remedies for post-conviction detention conditions and metal cage placement during court hearings.

In applications nos. 33010/18, 41663/18 and 23017/21, the applicants raised additional complaints. The Court rejected those parts as either inadmissible under Articles 34 and 35 or as disclosing no appearance of a violation. The central finding remained that Russia violated Article 8 by subjecting the applicants to permanent video surveillance in detention.

In *Khuren-ool and Others v. Russia* (Applications nos. 77300/17 and 5 others), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 13 October 2022. Because the applications concerned similar subject matter, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment. The Court noted that it had already established in *Gorlov and Others v. Russia* (2019) that Russia’s national legal framework governing the placement of detainees under permanent video surveillance in penal institutions fell short of Article 8 standards. In *Gorlov*, the Court held that permanent video surveillance of detainees was a serious interference with the right to respect for private life. It further found that Russian law was not sufficiently clear, precise or detailed to protect detainees against arbitrary interference, and that it did not require any balancing exercise or allow an individual to obtain judicial review of the proportionality of permanent video surveillance. In the present case, the Court found no fact or argument capable of leading to a different conclusion. It therefore held that placing the applicants under permanent video surveillance while confined to their cells in pre-trial and post-conviction detention facilities was not “in accordance with law” under Article 8. This was the principal alleged violation.

The applicants also submitted other complaints based on well-established case-law. These included complaints about conditions of detention during transport and the related review of pre-trial detention, relying on *Idalov v. Russia*; the lack of an effective remedy regarding complaints about conditions of detention during transport, relying on *Tomov and Others v. Russia*; conditions of post-conviction detention, relying on *Sergey Babushkin v. Russia*; placement of a defendant in a metal cage during court hearings, relying on *Svinarenko and Slyadnev v. Russia*; and the lack of an effective remedy for complaints about permanent video surveillance, relying on *Gorlov and Others*. The Court declared those complaints admissible and found violations in light of its established case-law.

In view of those findings, the Court considered that there was no need to deal separately with the applicants’ Article 13 complaints concerning the alleged lack of an effective remedy for their complaints about conditions of post-conviction detention and placement in a metal cage during court hearings. The Court also examined remaining complaints raised in applications nos. 33010/18, 41663/18 and 23017/21. It concluded that those complaints either did not meet the admissibility criteria under Articles 34 and 35 of the Convention or did not disclose any appearance of a violation. Accordingly, that part of the applications was rejected under Article 35 § 4.

It therefore held that the placement of the applicants under permanent video surveillance while confined to their cells in pre-trial and post-conviction detention facilities was not “in accordance with law” under Article 8 § 2. It found violations concerning: conditions of detention during transport and the related review of pre-trial detention, contrary to *Idalov v. Russia*; conditions of post-conviction detention, contrary to *Sergey Babushkin v. Russia*; placement of a defendant in a metal cage during court hearings, contrary to *Svinarenko and Slyadnev v. Russia*; and the lack of an effective remedy for the complaint about permanent video surveillance, contrary to *Gorlov and Others*. These complaints were declared admissible and violations were found. 001-216686:
**Case: Gloveli v. Georgia (App. no. 18952/18), European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, judgment of 7 April 2022 (final 7 July 2022).**

The applicant, Marina Gloveli, a Georgian national, was a practising lawyer with over twenty years’ experience and had previously served as a judge on the Tbilisi Court of Appeal between 1999 and 2005. She participated in judicial competitions six times, most recently in October 2017, when the High Council of Justice (HCJ) announced a competition for a vacant appellate court judgeship.

The applicant applied and, because she met the statutory eligibility requirements, was admitted to the competition. The HCJ reviewed her documents, conducted a background check, interviewed her on 29 December 2017, and assessed her using competency and integrity score sheets. On 20 January 2018, she was notified that her application had been rejected because she had not achieved the minimum competency score. She later obtained the individual score sheets.

On 2 February 2018, the applicant appealed to the Supreme Court’s Qualifications Chamber, seeking invalidation of the HCJ decision. She alleged that the decision was arbitrary and discriminatory. In support, she submitted a recording of a televised statement by N.J., a non-judicial member of the HCJ, who claimed that several HCJ members had “protégé” candidates during the competition and arbitrarily lowered the scores of other candidates. The applicant argued that the very low scores she received from several HCJ members indicated such bias.

On 6 February 2018, the Qualifications Chamber declared her appeal inadmissible for lack of jurisdiction. It reasoned that, because she had failed to achieve the minimum competency score, her candidacy had never been put to a vote before the HCJ. Therefore, the precondition under section 35(12) of the Courts Act was not met, and the HCJ had not issued a formal decision refusing her appointment that could be challenged. The Chamber’s decision was final and not amenable to appeal. As a result, the applicant had no judicial review of the decision excluding her from the competition.

This followed earlier reforms. After a constitutional complaint by the applicant and others, amendments to the Courts Act entered into force in March 2017, allowing HCJ decisions refusing judicial appointments to be appealed to the Qualifications Chamber. In April 2017, the Constitutional Court rejected the complaint, finding that the new remedy had resolved the access-to-court issue. It recognised that judicial appointments involved a fair-procedure right and that decisions on public office should be subject to judicial review. However, the Qualifications Chamber’s practice limited appeals to formal refusal decisions made after a candidate reached the voting stage, thereby excluding candidates eliminated for insufficient competency scores.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that she had been denied access to a court to challenge the refusal to appoint her to a judicial post. The Government argued that Article 6 was inapplicable: there was no domestic “right” to judicial appointment, the matter was not “civil,” there was no genuine and serious dispute, and only formal final refusals were appealable. The applicant maintained that domestic law and the Constitutional Court recognised her civil right to equal access to public service and to a fair procedure, and that the HCJ’s decision had determined her right to participate equally in the competition.

The Court found Article 6 § 1 applicable. There was a genuine and serious dispute over a domestic-law right to a fair procedure in the examination of an application for a judicial post. The second condition of the *Eskelinen* test was not met. Excluding an applicant who met statutory eligibility requirements from a judicial competition without any judicial review was not in the interest of a State governed by the rule of law. The Court emphasised the link between the integrity of judicial appointment processes and judicial independence, and the importance of procedural fairness in the selection, appointment and career of judges. The very essence of the right of access to court had been impaired. There was therefore a violation of Article 6 § 1.

In *Gloveli v. Georgia* (Application no. 18952/18, ECtHR, 7 April 2022), the applicant, Marina Gloveli, was a Georgian lawyer and former judge of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal. She had applied unsuccessfully for judicial positions six times. After earlier unsuccessful applications, she and others lodged a constitutional complaint arguing that domestic law provided no court to review disputes over judicial appointments. In March 2017, amendments to the Courts Act created a Qualifications Chamber of the Supreme Court to hear appeals against decisions of the High Council of Justice (HCJ) refusing judicial appointments. In April 2017, the Constitutional Court rejected the complaint, finding that the new remedy resolved the access-to-court issue.

In October 2017, the HCJ announced a new judicial competition for an appellate court vacancy. Gloveli applied and was admitted to the competition. The HCJ conducted a background check, interviewed her, and its members completed score sheets assessing competency and integrity. On 20 January 2018, she was notified that her application had been rejected because she did not meet the minimum competency score. She later obtained copies of the score sheets.

On 2 February 2018, Gloveli appealed to the Supreme Court’s Qualifications Chamber under section 354(3)(b) of the Courts Act. She alleged that the HCJ’s decision was arbitrary and discriminatory. In support, she submitted a recording of a televised statement by N.J., a non-judicial member of the HCJ, who claimed that during the competition several HCJ members had “protégé” candidates and arbitrarily lowered the scores of other candidates. Gloveli argued that the very low scores assigned to her by several HCJ members showed bias.

On 6 February 2018, the Qualifications Chamber declared her appeal inadmissible for lack of jurisdiction. It reasoned that because she had not achieved the minimum competency score, her candidacy had not been put to a vote before the HCJ. Therefore, no formal decision refusing her appointment under section 35(12) of the Courts Act had been issued, and the Chamber could not review it. The Chamber also stated that it did not have “full jurisdiction” to review the facts and that its decision was final and not appealable.

Under the relevant domestic framework, the HCJ is responsible for judicial recruitment. Section 35(12) provides that voting occurs only for candidates who meet integrity criteria and obtain at least 70% of the highest possible competency score. Section 354 permits appeals against HCJ decisions refusing appointment where bias, discrimination, or abuse of power is alleged. However, the Supreme Court interpreted this remedy narrowly, excluding candidates eliminated at the competency-scoring stage even if they satisfied statutory eligibility requirements.

Before the ECtHR, Gloveli complained under Article 6 § 1 that her inability to obtain judicial review of the refusal violated her right of access to a court. The Government argued Article 6 was inapplicable: there was no domestic right to judicial appointment, the matter was not civil, there was no genuine and serious dispute, and the outcome was not decisive. Gloveli relied on the Constitutional Court’s recognition that judicial posts are public service positions and that fair procedure and access to court apply. The ECtHR found Article 6 applicable and held that excluding an eligible candidate from a judicial competition without judicial review impaired the very essence of access to court, particularly given the link between fair judicial appointment procedures and judicial independence.

**Case Summary: Gloveli v. Georgia (Application no. 18952/18)**

**Parties:** Ms. Marina Gloveli (applicant), a Georgian national and practising lawyer, against the Government of Georgia.

**Core Issue:** The applicant alleged a violation of her right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. This stemmed from her inability to obtain judicial review of a decision by the High Council of Justice (HCJ) that effectively rejected her application for a judicial post.

**Key Facts:**
The applicant, a lawyer with over twenty years' experience and a former judge, applied for a vacant appellate court judge position in a competition announced by the HCJ on 18 October 2017. She was admitted to the competition, interviewed, and assessed by HCJ members based on competency and integrity criteria.

On 20 January 2018, the HCJ notified her that her application had been rejected because she did not meet the minimum competency score. Under Georgian law, this preliminary assessment determined whether a candidate's application would proceed to a formal vote by the HCJ.

The applicant appealed this decision to the Qualifications Chamber of the Supreme Court. She alleged that the decision was arbitrary and discriminatory, citing a televised statement from an HCJ member claiming that some members had "protégé" candidates and had arbitrarily lowered scores of others. She argued that her very low scores were indicative of such bias.

On 6 February 2018, the Qualifications Chamber declared her appeal inadmissible for lack of jurisdiction. It reasoned that because the applicant failed to achieve the minimum competency score, her candidacy was never put to a vote before the HCJ. Consequently, the HCJ had not issued a formal "decision refusing appointment" that could be challenged under section 354 of the Courts Act. The Chamber's decision was final.

**Relevant Domestic Law:**
The Courts Act was amended in March 2017 to allow unsuccessful judicial candidates to appeal HCJ decisions refusing appointment to the Qualifications Chamber. However, this remedy was limited to formal refusal decisions following a vote. The Constitutional Court had previously noted that this amendment created a judicial remedy for arbitrary refusals. The applicant argued that the law, as applied, denied her access to court for a dispute over her right to a fair procedure in the judicial competition, which the Constitutional Court had recognised as a constitutional right.

**Alleged Violation:**
The applicant complained that this lack of judicial review violated her right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1. The key question before the European Court was whether the dispute over her rejection concerned a "civil right" and whether the exclusion of judicial review for candidates eliminated at the preliminary scoring stage—despite meeting statutory eligibility requirements—was compatible with the rule of law and the principle of judicial independence.

Case *Tetik and Others v. Turkey* (Applications nos. 25885/19 and 37 others) is a 15 March 2022 judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Second Section, sitting as a Committee. The case concerns the non-enforcement of final domestic court decisions in favor of the applicants despite findings by Turkey’s Compensation Commission that the non-enforcement breached the applicants’ right to a fair trial.

The applicants were creditors of Yüksekova Municipality under labour agreements. In 2008, 2009 and 2010, they obtained compensation awards from the Yüksekova Civil Court of First Instance in three sets of civil proceedings. The municipality failed to pay these awards, except for compensation awarded in the first set of proceedings brought by applicants in application no. 26026/19. Thus, the core factual complaint is that final and binding judicial decisions remained unexecuted for years.

In 2011, 2012 and 2013, the applicants applied to the ECtHR complaining about the non-enforcement of the domestic judgments. In 2013, the ECtHR declared those applications inadmissible for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies because the applicants had not used the Compensation Commission established under Law no. 6384, which was intended to provide redress for complaints including non-enforcement of domestic decisions.

In 2014, the Compensation Commission awarded the applicants non-pecuniary damage for excessive length of proceedings. It also transmitted its decision to the Municipality and requested that the judicial decisions be executed. However, this did not result in full payment of the underlying compensation awards. In the same year, the applicants applied to the Constitutional Court, complaining that the Municipality had still failed to enforce the relevant judicial decisions despite the Compensation Commission’s decision.

In July 2018, while those Constitutional Court applications were pending, Turkish law was amended. The amendment empowered the Compensation Commission under Law no. 6384 to deal with applications pending before the Constitutional Court concerning, among other things, non-enforcement complaints. Later that year, the Constitutional Court found the applicants’ applications inadmissible for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies, again pointing to the Compensation Commission. On unspecified dates, some minor parts of the receivables were paid to some applicants, but the main awards remained largely unsatisfied.

The ECtHR case therefore focuses on whether Turkey violated the applicants’ Convention rights—particularly the right to a fair trial under Article 6, as found by the Compensation Commission—by failing to enforce final domestic judgments. It also raises the issue of whether the domestic remedies available, especially the Compensation Commission and the Constitutional Court, were effective and whether the continued non-enforcement, after a domestic finding of breach, amounted to a violation. The key facts are the original labour-related awards, the Municipality’s non-payment, the first ECtHR inadmissibility for non-exhaustion, the Compensation Commission’s finding and request for execution, the applicants’ Constitutional Court applications, the 2018 legislative change, the Constitutional Court’s subsequent inadmissibility decision, and only partial, minor payments.

In *Tetik and Others v. Turkey* (Applications nos. 25885/19 and 37 others), the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) delivered judgment on 15 March 2022. The case concerned complaints that final domestic court decisions awarding compensation to the applicants remained unenforced, even after Turkey’s Compensation Commission had found a breach of the applicants’ right to a fair trial.

Between 2008 and 2010, in three sets of civil proceedings before the Yüksekova Civil Court of First Instance, the applicants obtained judgments against Yüksekova Municipality (“the Municipality”) for receivables arising from labour agreements. The compensation amounts awarded by the court were not paid, except for the compensation awarded in the first set of proceedings brought by the applicants in application no. 26026/19. The unpaid judgments therefore became the basis of the applicants’ enforcement complaints.

The applicants first applied to the European Court of Human Rights in 2011, 2012 and 2013, complaining of the non-enforcement of the domestic judicial decisions in their favour. In 2013, the Court declared those applications inadmissible for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies, because the applicants had not used the Compensation Commission established under Law no. 6384, a domestic remedy designed to provide redress for complaints including non-enforcement of domestic decisions.

The applicants then applied to the Compensation Commission. In 2014, the Commission awarded them non-pecuniary damage for the excessive length of the proceedings. It also transmitted its decision to the Municipality and requested that the judicial decisions in question be executed. Despite this, the underlying compensation awards were not enforced. Only some minor parts of the receivables were paid to some applicants on unspecified dates. Thus, the Commission’s finding of a fair-trial breach did not result in the actual payment of the sums awarded by the civil courts.

In 2014, while the enforcement problem continued, the applicants also applied to the Constitutional Court. They complained that the Municipality had failed to enforce the relevant judicial decisions despite the Compensation Commission’s decision. In July 2018, while those applications were still pending, a provision was added to Law no. 6384 empowering the Compensation Commission to deal with applications pending before the Constitutional Court concerning, inter alia, non-enforcement complaints. In the same year, the Constitutional Court found the applicants’ applications inadmissible for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies, namely the Compensation Commission. The applicants were therefore directed back to the Compensation Commission after having already pursued that remedy and after years of unresolved enforcement.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the existence of final and binding domestic judgments in the applicants’ favour; the Municipality’s failure to pay most of the awarded sums; the Compensation Commission’s recognition of a fair-trial breach but its inability to secure actual enforcement; the continued non-payment except for minor sums; and the Constitutional Court’s subsequent inadmissibility decision based on non-exhaustion of the Compensation Commission remedy. The case raised issues concerning the non-enforcement of domestic judicial decisions and the effectiveness of domestic remedies intended to address that non-enforcement. In particular, the alleged violations concerned the applicants’ right to a fair trial under Article 6 §1 of the Convention, in so far as execution of final judgments is part of that right, and their right to protection of property under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, because they were deprived of the practical benefit of the compensation awarded by domestic courts. The Government’s objection to examination by a Committee was rejected.

In *Tetik and Others v. Turkey* (Applications nos. 25885/19 and 37 others), the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section, sitting as a Committee) delivered judgment on 15 March 2022. The case concerns the non-enforcement of final domestic court decisions despite findings by Turkey’s Compensation Commission that the applicants’ right to a fair trial had been breached. The applicants were individuals who held receivables arising from labour agreements with Yüksekova Municipality.

Between 2008 and 2010, the Yüksekova Civil Court of First Instance awarded compensation to the applicants in three sets of civil proceedings. These awards concerned unpaid receivables owed by the Municipality. However, the compensation amounts were not paid, except for the compensation awarded in the first set of proceedings brought by the applicants in application no. 26026/19. This failure to execute the judgments formed the basis of the applicants’ complaints.

In 2011, 2012 and 2013, the applicants applied to the European Court of Human Rights, complaining of the non-enforcement of the domestic judicial decisions in their favour. In 2013, the Court declared those applications inadmissible for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies. It held that the applicants should first have used the Compensation Commission established under Law no. 6384, which provided redress for complaints concerning, among other matters, non-enforcement of domestic decisions.

In 2014, the Compensation Commission awarded the applicants non-pecuniary damage for the excessive length of proceedings. It also transmitted its decision to the Municipality, requesting that the judicial decisions in question be executed. Despite this, the Municipality apparently did not comply. In the same year, the applicants applied to the Constitutional Court, complaining about the Municipality’s failure to enforce the relevant judicial decisions notwithstanding the Compensation Commission’s decision.

While those applications were pending before the Constitutional Court, a provision was added to Law no. 6384 in July 2018. It empowered the Compensation Commission to deal with applications pending before the Constitutional Court concerning, inter alia, non-enforcement complaints. Later in 2018, the Constitutional Court found the applicants’ applications inadmissible for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies, namely the Compensation Commission. This meant the applicants were again directed to the same domestic body whose earlier decision had not led to enforcement of the judgments.

The facts also indicate that, on unspecified dates, some minor parts of the receivables were paid to some of the applicants. However, the core judicial awards remained largely unpaid.

The case therefore concerns the repeated failure of the authorities, particularly Yüksekova Municipality, to enforce final domestic court decisions in the applicants’ favour. The alleged violations relate to the applicants’ right to a fair trial, including the binding nature of judicial decisions and access to court, and to the protection of their property, because they were deprived of compensation they had been awarded. The procedural history also raises issues about the effectiveness of the Compensation Commission and the Constitutional Court’s treatment of non-enforcement complaints, since the applicants were repeatedly required to exhaust a remedy that had not resulted in execution of the judgments. The European Court of Human Rights had to examine whether these circumstances breached Turkey’s obligations under the Convention.
001-219309:
In *Nadtochiy v. Ukraine* (Application no. 32899/13, judgment of 20 September 2022), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning deprivation of property.

The applicant, Ms Zinayida Sergiyivna Nadtochiy, a Ukrainian national born in 1928 and living in Sumy, was granted a plot of land free of charge by Sumy Town Council on 4 June 2008. The land was allocated for construction of a house as part of the privatization process. She planned to start construction within two years but did not do so; instead, she mainly used the land for gardening.

In August 2011 the Deputy Prosecutor of the Sumy Region brought civil proceedings seeking to have her title to the land declared void (“the first set of proceedings”). The prosecutor argued that the designated use of the land contradicted the town’s general zoning plan and violated the town’s right to construct apartment buildings there. On 9 February 2012 the Sumy Regional Court of Appeal finally rejected the action. It reasoned that the prosecutor had not challenged the Council’s decision of 4 June 2008 and that using the land for gardening was not a reason to deprive her of it.

In February 2012 the prosecutor brought a second action, this time against both the Council and the applicant. It relied on similar grounds but added that the Council’s 2008 decision had not been based on a detailed zoning plan and specific construction limits. On 25 July 2012 the Kovpakivskyy District Court of Sumy allowed the action, and on 18 January 2013 the Higher Specialised Court of Civil and Criminal Matters upheld that judgment. The Council’s decision and the applicant’s title were declared void, and the land was returned to the municipality. The courts found that the Council had failed to develop a detailed zoning plan and construction limits, thereby failing to serve community interests.

Before the Strasbourg Court, the applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that she had been deprived of her land without a legitimate purpose, since no apartment building had been erected; that the second proceedings violated legal certainty by re-examining matters already finally determined in the first proceedings; and that she received no compensation even though the authorities were at fault. The applicant died in 2016, and Mrs N. Bratushka, as an heir, was permitted to continue the application.

The Court dismissed the Government’s abuse-of-application objection and declared the application admissible. On the merits, it accepted that the two sets of proceedings were similar but not identical: the second raised additional questions about the process leading to the Council’s decision, so it did not amount to a mere re-examination. The Court assumed the interference had a legal basis and pursued a legitimate aim—ensuring effective use of municipal land. However, it found the interference disproportionate. The applicant had acquired the land in good faith and should not bear all negative consequences of the Council’s mistake without compensation or appropriate reparation. The fact that she received the land free of charge did not preclude a violation, and the Government did not show that another comparable plot was available. The domestic courts had already held that her failure to build and her use of the land for gardening was not a lawful ground for deprivation. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

**Nadtochiy v. Ukraine** (Application no. 32899/13), European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, judgment of 20 September 2022, concerned the allegedly unlawful and disproportionate deprivation of property under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention.

The applicant, Ms Zinayida Sergiyivna Nadtochiy, a Ukrainian national born in 1928 and living in Sumy, died in 2016. Mrs N. Bratushka, the wife of the applicant’s nephew and a designated heir under the applicant’s 2016 will, was permitted to continue the pecuniary claim.

In June 2008, the Sumy Town Council granted the applicant a plot of land free of charge for house construction as part of a privatisation process. She did not begin construction within two years and mainly used the land for gardening. In August 2011, the Deputy Prosecutor of the Sumy Region brought civil proceedings seeking to have her title declared void. He argued that the land’s designated use contradicted the town’s zoning plan and violated the town’s right to construct apartment buildings on the land. The first set of proceedings was rejected in a final decision by the Sumy Regional Court of Appeal on 9 February 2012. The court found that the prosecutor had not challenged the Council’s 2008 decision and that the applicant’s use of the land for gardening was not a reason to deprive her of it.

In February 2012, the prosecutor brought a second action, this time against the Council and the applicant. It relied on similar grounds but also alleged that the Council’s 2008 decision had not been based on a detailed zoning plan or specific construction limits. On 25 July 2012, the Kovpakivskyy District Court of Sumy allowed the action; this was upheld by the Higher Specialised Court of Civil and Criminal Matters on 18 January 2013. The Council’s decision and the applicant’s title were declared void, and the land was returned to the municipality. The domestic courts found that the Council had failed to develop a detailed zoning plan and construction limits, thereby failing to serve the community’s interests.

The applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that she had been deprived of her land without a legitimate purpose, since no apartment building had been erected; that the second proceedings breached legal certainty by re-examining matters already decided in the first; and that she received no compensation despite the authorities’ fault.

The Government objected that the applicant had abused the right of application by not informing the Court of 2011 criminal proceedings against her nephew, a 2008 Council member, concerning alleged fraudulent allocation of land to her. The Court dismissed this objection, noting that the initial submissions contained information about the criminal proceedings, the proceedings were still ongoing, and the applicant’s complaints concerned civil decisions based on reasons unrelated to the criminal case. The application was declared admissible.

The Court assumed the interference had a basis in domestic law and pursued a legitimate public-interest aim: ensuring effective use of municipal land. However, it found the interference disproportionate. The applicant had acquired the land in good faith and did not know that the Council had failed to protect community interests. She should not have to bear all negative consequences of the Council’s mistake without compensation or other appropriate reparation. The fact that she received the land free of charge did not rule out a violation, and the Government did not show that a comparable plot was actually available to her. The Court also noted that domestic courts had found she could not be deprived of title merely for failing to build or for using the land for gardening. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In *Nadtochiy v. Ukraine* (Application no. 32899/13, judgment 20 September 2022), the applicant, Ms Zinayida Sergiyivna Nadtochiy, was a Ukrainian national living in Sumy. In June 2008, the Sumy Town Council granted her a municipal plot of land free of charge for the construction of a house as part of the privatisation process. She intended to begin construction within two years but did not, instead using the land mainly for gardening.

In August 2011, the Deputy Prosecutor of the Sumy Region brought civil proceedings seeking to have her title to the land declared void. He argued that the land’s designated use conflicted with the town’s general zoning plan and violated the town’s right to construct apartment buildings on the plot. In the first set of proceedings, the Sumy Regional Court of Appeal rejected the prosecutor’s action on 9 February 2012. It held that the prosecutor had not challenged the Council’s 2008 decision itself and that the applicant’s use of the land for gardening was not a valid reason to deprive her of it.

In February 2012, the prosecutor brought a second action, this time against both the Council and the applicant. The grounds were similar but broader: he argued that the Council’s 2008 decision had not been based on a detailed zoning plan or specific construction limits. On 25 July 2012, the Kovpakivskyy District Court of Sumy allowed the action, declaring the Council’s decision and the applicant’s title void and returning the land to the municipality. The Higher Specialised Court of Civil and Criminal Matters upheld that outcome on 18 January 2013. The domestic courts found that the Council had failed to develop the required detailed zoning plan and construction limits, thereby failing to serve the community’s interests.

The applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention that she had been unlawfully and disproportionately deprived of her property. She alleged that the deprivation had no legitimate purpose because no apartment building had been built; that the second proceedings violated legal certainty by re-examining matters already finally determined in the first proceedings; and that she had received no compensation even though the authorities’ mistake had caused her loss.

The applicant died in December 2016. Mrs N. Bratushka, the wife of the applicant’s nephew, was allowed to continue the application because she was named as an heir in the applicant’s will and the case concerned pecuniary issues. The Government objected that the applicant had abused the right of application by failing to disclose criminal proceedings brought in 2011 against her nephew, a former Council member, concerning alleged fraudulent allocation of land to her. The Court dismissed that objection because the initial materials already mentioned the criminal proceedings, the charges remained undetermined, and the applicant’s complaints concerned civil judgments based on reasons unrelated to the criminal case.

On the merits, the Court accepted that the interference had a basis in domestic law and pursued a legitimate public-interest aim—ensuring the effective use of municipal land. However, it found the deprivation disproportionate. The applicant had acquired the land in good faith and did not know that the Council had failed to protect community interests. She should not have had to bear all negative consequences for the Council’s mistake without any compensation or other appropriate reparation. The fact that she had received the land free of charge did not rule out a violation, and the Government did not show that a comparable plot was actually available to her. The domestic courts themselves had found that her gardening use was not a valid ground for deprivation. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.
