**Marina Aucanada Group S.L. v. Spain** (Application no. 7567/19) concerned an alleged breach of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights because the applicant company was not personally served with a summons in Spanish administrative judicial proceedings that led to annulment of a public tender in which it had participated.

The applicant, a Spanish limited liability company registered in Madrid on 15 April 2015, submitted a tender on 5 May 2015 in a call for tenders published by the Port Authority of the Balearic Islands on 4 February 2015. The tender concerned management of moorings in the old Port of Alcúdia. Before the applicant submitted its bid, however, the Alcúdia City Council had already challenged the tender decision before the High Court of the Balearic Islands on 7 April 2015, seeking annulment on the ground that it infringed a 2004 agreement between the City Council and the Port Authority.

On 20 April 2015, the High Court admitted the City Council’s claim and ordered that the administrative file be sent to it and that notice be given to “any interested party” so they could participate. On 7 May 2015, the Port Authority published a public notice (*edicto*) in the Official Gazette of the Balearic Islands, informing interested parties of the proceedings and inviting them to take part. No direct summons was served on the applicant or the other tenderers. The applicant’s tender was accepted for consideration on 18 May 2015 and, on 18 May 2016, the Port Authority selected it as the most advantageous.

The applicant later learned of the annulment proceedings through press reports, including articles in 2015 and 2016 that mentioned the judicial challenge and named the applicant as a tenderer. On 31 March 2017, the High Court annulled the call for tenders. The applicant then sought leave to intervene on 20 April 2017, claiming it had only learned of the proceedings through the press. It also appealed in cassation, arguing that Spanish law required direct service on interested parties. On 17 April 2018, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, holding that publication of the notice in the Official Gazette complied with section 49 of the Administrative Jurisdiction Act and that the applicant could still appear despite acquiring its interest after the proceedings began. A subsequent nullity plea was rejected by the High Court on 14 June 2018, and the Constitutional Court declared the applicant’s *amparo* appeal inadmissible on 18 December 2018 for lack of constitutional relevance.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained that it had not been directly summoned in proceedings affecting its rights. The Government argued that the applicant was not a victim and had suffered no significant disadvantage, since it knew of the proceedings and its participation would not have changed the outcome. The Court ultimately found no violation of Article 6 § 1, emphasizing that publication of the public notice in the Official Gazette constituted sufficient notice in the circumstances and that the applicant had failed to act with the necessary diligence to keep informed of the procedural developments.

**Marina Aucanada Group S.L. v. Spain** concerned a Spanish company’s complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights that it was not personally summoned to participate in judicial administrative proceedings that affected its rights, despite having submitted a successful tender in a public concession procedure.

In February 2015, the Port Authority of the Balearic Islands published a call for tenders for the management of moorings in the old Port of Alcúdia. The Alcúdia City Council considered that the tender infringed a 2004 agreement with the Port Authority and, on 7 April 2015, brought judicial administrative proceedings before the High Court of the Balearic Islands seeking annulment of the tender decision.

On 20 April 2015, the High Court admitted the City Council’s claim. It requested the administrative file from the Port Authority and ordered that notice be given to “any interested party” within five days so that they could participate within nine days. On 7 May 2015, the Port Authority published a public notice, or *edicto*, in the Official Gazette of the Balearic Islands, citing the relevant administrative procedure laws. It did not directly serve summonses on the three tenderers.

Meanwhile, the applicant company submitted its tender on 5 May 2015. On 18 May 2015, its tender and three others were accepted for consideration. A press article dated 8 June 2015 mentioned the City Council’s judicial challenge and listed the applicant as one of the tenderers. On 18 May 2016, while the annulment proceedings were still pending, the Port Authority selected the applicant’s tender as the most advantageous. Press articles in May and June 2016 noted that the applicant had been successful even though the tender was still subject to judicial review. In separate proceedings brought by another tenderer, the applicant obtained access to the file in November 2016, including the file concerning the City Council’s challenge.

On 31 March 2017, the High Court annulled the call for tenders, finding that it violated prior undertakings between the Port Authority and the City Council. On 20 April 2017, the applicant sought leave to intervene and appeal, stating that it had only learned of the proceedings through the press. It then lodged a cassation appeal, arguing that Spanish law required interested parties to be directly summoned. On 17 April 2018, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, holding that publication of the notice in the Official Gazette satisfied the legal requirements and that an interested party acquiring a legitimate interest later could still appear. A subsequent nullity plea was rejected by the High Court on 14 June 2018, and the applicant’s *amparo* appeal was declared inadmissible by the Constitutional Court on 18 December 2018.

The central alleged violation was that the failure to personally summon the applicant deprived it of access to court and a fair hearing under Article 6 § 1. The applicant argued that the authorities and courts knew, or could readily identify, the interested tenderers, especially once its tender had been accepted and later selected.

In its judgment of 8 November 2022, the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) found that publication of the public notice in the Official Gazette constituted sufficient notice in the circumstances. It held that the applicant had failed to act with the necessary diligence to keep itself informed of procedural developments. Accordingly, there was no violation of Article 6 § 1.

Case: **Marina Aucanada Group S.L. v. Spain** (ECtHR, Third Section, 8 November 2022). The applicant, a Spanish company, complained under Article 6 §1 that it was not personally summoned to judicial administrative proceedings concerning annulment of a public tender in which it had bid. The central issue was whether publication of a public notice in an Official Gazette provided sufficient notice.

In February 2015, the Port Authority of the Balearic Islands announced a call for tenders for managing moorings at the old Port of Alcúdia. The Alcúdia City Council opposed the tender, claiming it breached a 2004 agreement affecting buildings over which it held occupation rights. On 7 April 2015, the City Council brought judicial administrative proceedings before the High Court of the Balearic Islands seeking annulment of the 22 January 2015 tender decision. On 20 April 2015, the High Court admitted the case, ordered the Port Authority to send the administrative file, and directed that interested parties be notified so they could participate.

The applicant submitted a tender on 5 May 2015. On 18 May 2015, its tender and three others were accepted for consideration. Meanwhile, on 7 May 2015, following High Court instructions and relying on Spanish law, the Port Authority published a public notice (*edicto*) in the Official Gazette of the Balearic Islands informing interested parties of the proceedings and inviting them to appear. No tenderer was personally served. Press articles in 2015 and 2016 reported the tender, the judicial challenge, and later the applicant’s successful bid. On 18 May 2016, the Port Authority selected the applicant’s tender as most advantageous. When a competing tenderer challenged that selection in separate proceedings, the applicant obtained access to the file on 29 November 2016, which included the annulment proceedings file. On 31 March 2017, the High Court annulled the tender call. The applicant learned through the press and sought leave to intervene on 20 April 2017; its cassation appeal was dismissed by the Supreme Court on 17 April 2018. The Supreme Court held that publication in the Official Gazette complied with section 49 of the Judicial Review Act and that a party acquiring a legitimate interest later could still appear. A plea of nullity was rejected, and the Constitutional Court declared the *amparo* appeal inadmissible on 18 December 2018.

Under Spanish law, section 49 required notice to identifiable interested parties, but publication in the Official Gazette was permitted when personal service could not be effected. Section 59 of Law 30/1992 allowed edictal notification when interested parties were unknown or service unsuccessful. The applicant argued that authorities knew or could identify the tenderers and should have directly summoned it. The Government argued it was not a victim and suffered no significant disadvantage because it knew or should have known of the proceedings and failed to act. The European Court of Human Rights examined whether the public notice sufficed and whether the applicant acted diligently. It found that publication constituted sufficient notice in the circumstances and that the applicant had failed to keep itself informed. Accordingly, there was no violation of Article 6 §1.

**M.T. and Others v. Sweden** (ECtHR, First Section, 20 October 2022) concerned three Syrian nationals: M.T. (the mother), A.A.K. (her son living in Sweden), and M.A.K. (her younger son living in Syria). A.A.K. arrived in Sweden in March 2016 as an unaccompanied minor, aged 15, and applied for asylum. In November 2016, he was granted a temporary residence permit as a person eligible for subsidiary protection, initially for 13 months and later extended for two years.

In February 2017, M.T. and M.A.K. applied at the Swedish embassy in Khartoum for residence permits based on family reunification with A.A.K. The Migration Agency refused their applications in August 2017. It relied on Sweden’s Temporary Act (in force from 20 July 2016 to 19 July 2019), which suspended family reunification for persons with subsidiary protection who had applied for a residence permit after 24 November 2015. Because A.A.K. had applied after that date and had subsidiary protection status, his mother and younger brother could not obtain residence permits through him. Their appeals were rejected by the Migration Court in October 2017 and by the Migration Court of Appeal in November 2017. A.A.K. turned 18 in August 2018, meaning that in principle he could no longer seek family reunification with parents or siblings.

The applicants complained under Article 8 that the refusal violated their right to respect for family life. They also complained under Article 14 read with Article 8 that they were discriminated against because persons with refugee status could still access family reunification, while persons with subsidiary protection could not. They argued that the authorities failed to carry out an individualised balancing of interests, particularly the best interests of the child, and that although the suspension was formally temporary, it became indefinite in their case because A.A.K. reached adulthood before the Temporary Act was relaxed.

The Government justified the Temporary Act as a response to Sweden’s 2015 asylum crisis. Sweden received approximately 163,000 asylum seekers that year—around 12.5% of all asylum seekers in the EU. The Act aimed to reduce immigration and align Swedish rules with minimum EU standards. It included a safety-valve provision allowing an individual assessment where refusal would conflict with Sweden’s international obligations, including the European Convention on Human Rights.

The European Court of Human Rights found no violation of Article 8. Unlike *M.A. v. Denmark*, Sweden did not impose a fixed three-year waiting period. The suspension was temporary and gradually reduced. The applicants were de facto affected only from February 2017 until A.A.K. turned 18 in August 2018—less than 18 months. A.A.K. had limited ties to Sweden and showed no particular vulnerability or dependence on his mother; the mother and younger brother had no ties to Sweden beyond him. The Court held that Sweden had struck a fair balance between family life and immigration control.

On Article 14, the Court found no discrimination. Refugees and subsidiary protection beneficiaries were not necessarily in analogous situations, and the difference reflected the generally longer-lasting protection needs of refugees. In the absence of European or international consensus, and given the State’s wide margin of appreciation, the temporary distinction was objectively and reasonably justified and proportionate. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 8 or Article 14.

In *M.T. and Others v. Sweden* (Application no. 22105/18, ECtHR First Section, judgment 20 October 2022), three Syrian nationals challenged Sweden’s refusal to grant family reunification. The first applicant is the mother, living in Syria. The second applicant is her son, who arrived in Sweden as an unaccompanied minor in March 2016 and applied for asylum. In November 2016 he was granted a temporary residence permit—initially thirteen months, later extended by two years—as a person eligible for subsidiary protection because of the security situation in Syria. He was not recognised as a refugee. The third applicant is the mother’s younger son, also living in Syria.

In February 2017 the mother and younger son applied at the Swedish Embassy in Khartoum for residence permits based on family ties with the second applicant. In August 2017 the Migration Agency refused their applications. It relied on Sweden’s Temporary Act, in force from July 2016 to July 2019, which suspended family reunification for beneficiaries of subsidiary protection whose sponsor had applied for a residence permit after 24 November 2015. The Act contained a safety clause allowing a permit where refusal would breach Sweden’s international obligations, but the agency found no breach. Appeals were rejected by the Migration Court in October 2017 and leave to appeal was refused by the Migration Court of Appeal in November 2017. Because the second applicant turned eighteen in August 2018, he would generally no longer qualify for family reunification as a child, making the refusal effectively final.

The applicants alleged a violation of Article 8 of the Convention, arguing that the refusal breached their family life and that the authorities had failed to carry out a proper balancing of interests, particularly the child’s best interests. They also argued that the temporary suspension had an indefinite effect because the second applicant reached adulthood before reunification could be reconsidered. In addition, they complained under Article 14 read with Article 8 that they were discriminated against because refugees could apply for family reunification while persons with subsidiary protection could not.

The Government justified the Temporary Act by reference to the 2015 migration crisis. Sweden received approximately 163,000 asylum-seekers that year—12.5% of all asylum-seekers in the EU. The law aimed to reduce asylum numbers and align Swedish rules with EU minimum standards. The Court noted that the Swedish measure was temporary, gradually reduced over time, and included an individual-assessment safety valve. In the applicants’ case, they were de facto covered by the suspension only from February 2017 until August 2018—less than one and a half years—because of the second applicant’s age. The second applicant had limited ties to Sweden and showed no vulnerability or dependence on the first applicant. There was no disruption of essential cohabitation.

Applying *M.A. v. Denmark*, the Court found that Sweden had struck a fair balance under Article 8 between the applicants’ family-life interests and the State’s interest in controlling immigration and protecting economic well-being. On Article 14, the difference in treatment between refugees and beneficiaries of subsidiary protection was reasonably and objectively justified, given different protection grounds, the lack of European consensus, and the State’s wide margin of appreciation. The Court declared the complaints admissible but found no violation of Article 8 or Article 14 read in conjunction with Article 8.

**M.T. and Others v. Sweden** (App. no. 22105/18, judgment 20 Oct. 2022) concerned three Syrian nationals: a mother (M.T.) and her two sons, A.A.K. and M.A.K. A.A.K. arrived in Sweden on 5 March 2016, aged 15, and applied for asylum. On 4 November 2016, Sweden granted him a temporary residence permit as a person eligible for **subsidiary protection**, not refugee status, based on the security situation in Syria. His permit was later extended for two years.

While A.A.K. remained in Sweden, his mother and younger brother M.A.K. remained in Syria. On 17 February 2017, they applied at the Swedish embassy in Khartoum for residence permits based on family reunification with A.A.K. M.A.K., then 13, also cited an eye injury requiring medical care, study plans, and a wish to join his brothers in Sweden. The family was dispersed: the father had lived in Saudi Arabia since 2012; another brother lived in Turkey; a sister lived in Germany; and two adult twin brothers lived in Sweden.

On 24 August 2017, the Swedish Migration Agency refused the applications. It relied on the **Temporary Act** (in force 20 July 2016 to 19 July 2019), which temporarily restricted family reunification. Under section 7, family reunification was suspended for beneficiaries of subsidiary protection whose sponsor had applied after 24 November 2015. Since A.A.K. had applied in March 2016 and held subsidiary protection, his mother and brother could not obtain permits through him. The Migration Court upheld the refusal on 16 October 2017, and the Migration Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal on 22 November 2017.

A key fact was that A.A.K. turned 18 on 8 August 2018. Under Swedish rules, adult children are generally no longer eligible for family reunification with parents or siblings. Thus, although the Temporary Act’s family-reunification restriction was formally temporary and ended on 19 July 2019, the refusal effectively became final for these applicants. They were **de facto** covered by the suspension only from 17 February 2017 until 8 August 2018—less than one and a half years.

The applicants alleged a violation of **Article 8** (right to family life), arguing that Sweden failed to strike a fair balance and did not sufficiently assess their individual circumstances, especially the child’s best interests. They also alleged **Article 14 read with Article 8**, claiming discriminatory treatment because persons granted subsidiary protection were treated less favourably than refugees: refugees could still access limited family reunification, while subsidiary-protection beneficiaries faced suspension. The Government justified the Temporary Act by the 2015 migration crisis: Sweden received about 163,000 asylum seekers that year, 12.5% of all EU asylum seekers, creating severe pressure on reception and integration systems. The Act aimed to align Swedish law with minimum EU/international standards and contained a safety-valve provision (section 13) requiring individual assessment where refusal would breach international obligations.

The European Court of Human Rights found no violation of Article 8 and no violation of Article 14 in conjunction with Article 8. It accepted that the temporary suspension pursued a legitimate aim and that the difference between refugees and subsidiary-protection beneficiaries was reasonably and objectively justified, particularly given the absence of European consensus and the gradual reduction of the suspension. The applicants’ individual circumstances—limited dependence on A.A.K. and scattered family ties—also supported the fair balance struck.

In *Radmilli v. Malta* (Application no. 28711/19), the European Court of Human Rights examined an application lodged on 17 May 2019 by Alessandra Radmilli, a Maltese national born in 1948 and living in Sliema. The case concerned a long-standing statutory lease over her property and the adequacy of domestic redress for an alleged breach of property rights.

The property had originally been leased to a third party under temporary emphyteusis by the applicant’s ancestors. Although that contract expired in 1980, the tenant remained in occupation because Act XXIII of 1979 amended Chapter 158 of Malta’s laws. Under that regime, the tenant retained the property under a lease at approximately €420 per year, with only slight increases over time. As a result, the applicant, as owner, could not recover possession or obtain a market-level rent.

In domestic constitutional proceedings, on 15 February 2018 the Civil Court (First Hall) found a violation of the applicant’s property rights. It observed that the original legitimate aim of the rent legislation had diminished, particularly after 1995 when most of the property market was liberalised. Given the growing discrepancy between the controlled rent and market value, especially from 2008, the court awarded €30,000 in pecuniary damages and €1,000 in non-pecuniary damages. It also declared that the tenant could no longer rely on the impugned law to maintain title to the property. The applicant was not ordered to pay costs.

Both the State and the tenant appealed. On 14 December 2018 the Constitutional Court confirmed the finding of a violation but reduced the pecuniary award to €25,000. It reasoned that it should not depart from the limits of compensation usually awarded in similar cases. The applicant was ordered to pay one quarter of the costs of the appeal.

A further complication arose from Act No. XXVII of 2018, which entered into force on 1 August 2018. Article 12B provided that, even where a judgment had been given in the owner’s favour, the owner could not lawfully request the eviction of the occupier without first availing himself of the new procedure established by that law. This provision was relevant to the effectiveness of the domestic judgment and to the applicant’s ability to recover her property.

At some point before 8 May 2020, the applicant regained possession of the vacant property. Nevertheless, she had brought the case to Strasbourg, complaining about interference with her property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation were the expiry of the emphyteutic contract in 1980, the statutory continuation of the tenant’s lease at a very low rent, the domestic courts’ recognition that the rent regime had become disproportionate, the compensation eventually awarded, and the 2018 legislative measure that restricted eviction despite a favourable judgment.

The Court was therefore called upon to assess whether the prolonged restriction on the applicant’s property rights, and the redress provided by the Maltese authorities, struck a fair balance between the tenant’s interests and the applicant’s right to the peaceful enjoyment of her possessions.

**Summary of Radmilli v. Malta (Application no. 28711/19)**

The case of *Radmilli v. Malta* concerns an application lodged against the Republic of Malta with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicant, Ms Alessandra Radmilli, a Maltese national born in 1948, alleged a violation of her property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention.

The facts of the case center on a property owned by the applicant’s family in Malta. The property had been leased to a third party under a temporary emphyteusis contract, a type of long-term lease. This contract expired in 1980. However, due to Act XXIII of 1979, which amended Chapter 158 of the Laws of Malta, the tenant was legally permitted to retain the property under a new lease agreement. The rent was set at approximately 420 euros per year, with only slight increases over the subsequent decades. This legal framework effectively forced the applicant to continue the lease on terms highly unfavorable to her, as the rent was significantly below the property's market value.

In response to this situation, the applicant initiated proceedings before the Civil Court (First Hall) in its constitutional competence. On 15 February 2018, the court found a violation of her property rights. It noted that the legitimate aim of the law had diminished, particularly after 1995 when the majority of the property market was liberalised. The court highlighted the stark discrepancy between the low rent received by the applicant and the property's actual market value, especially from 2008 onwards. Consequently, it awarded the applicant €30,000 in pecuniary damages and €1,000 in non-pecuniary damages. Crucially, the court also declared that the tenant could no longer rely on the impugned law to maintain title to the property, and no costs were to be paid by the applicant.

Both the State and the tenant appealed this decision. On 14 December 2018, the Constitutional Court confirmed the finding of a violation but reduced the pecuniary award to €25,000. The court justified this reduction by stating it should not depart from the limits of compensation typically awarded in similar cases. Furthermore, the applicant was ordered to pay one-quarter of the costs of the appeal proceedings.

A significant development occurred with the introduction of Act No. XXVII of 2018, which came into force on 1 August 2018. Article 12B of this new law stipulated that even with a judgment in the owner's favor, it was not lawful for the owner to request the eviction of the occupier without first utilizing a new procedure outlined in that law. This new legislation effectively delayed the applicant's ability to enforce the judgment she had won. The applicant eventually regained possession of the vacant property on an unspecified date before 8 May 2020.

The applicant brought her case to the European Court of Human Rights on 17 May 2019, complaining about the violation of her property rights. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation include the prolonged and ongoing interference with her property rights due to the 1979 law, the inadequate level of rent she was forced to accept, and the actions of the domestic courts. While the domestic courts acknowledged the violation, the reduced compensation and the imposition of appeal costs, coupled with the subsequent Act No. XXVII of 2018 which further delayed her ability to reclaim her property, form the core of her grievance before the European Court.
001-219194:
**Case summary: Anatoliy Yeremenko v. Ukraine (App. no. 22287/08)**

The applicant, Anatoliy Yeremenko, was a Ukrainian journalist working for the national weekly newspaper *Dzerkalo Tyzhnya* (circulation about 57,000). On 12 March 2005 the newspaper published his article “Black triad: nothing else matters in the case,” which was placed online on 18 March 2005. The article alleged systemic judicial corruption in the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal. It discussed case no. 27/37, in which a judgment was allegedly based on a forged copy of a guarantee letter; delays by the Higher Commercial Court; the liquidation of the State enterprise Intertrans before a hearing; payments to a law firm; the “distribution” of cases to the “right judge”; and an alleged “organised group” and “black triad” ensuring required results. The article relied partly on information from Ch., a company director who had sent a letter to a parliamentary anti-corruption subcommittee alleging an organised group in those courts. The applicant claimed he also reviewed case files. The article did not name individual judges but referred to the courts and to case no. 8/55.

Six judges from those courts sought preventive measures and later brought defamation proceedings. On 8 April 2005 the Voroshylovsky District Court ordered the newspaper’s editorial board to remove the article from its website pending examination of the defamation case. The decision contained little reasoning and was upheld on 26 August 2005; the Kyiv Court of Appeal, acting as cassation court, rejected the applicant’s appeal on 15 January 2008. The article was removed from the website by 18 August 2005.

On the merits, the Petrovskyy Local Court on 20 October 2005 partly allowed the judges’ claim. It found that statements in the final paragraphs were false and defamatory, not value judgments. The court reasoned that they accused the judges and courts of organised crime and corruption, that the claimants were identifiable from the courts and cases mentioned, that no criminal verdict established such accusations, and that the applicant had failed to verify the information. The court ordered a retraction and required the applicant to pay each claimant UAH 333 in non-pecuniary damages plus legal and court fees—about EUR 331 in non-pecuniary damages and EUR 430 in fees initially. Ch. was ordered to pay more. The Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal upheld the judgment on 27 January 2006, and the Kyiv Court of Appeal finally rejected the applicant’s cassation appeal on 5 November 2007 without substantive reasoning.

The applicant complained under Article 10 of the Convention. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation. It held that the domestic courts had failed to conduct a proper balancing exercise between freedom of expression and the judges’ reputation, had not given relevant and sufficient reasons, and had failed to apply Article 10 standards or an acceptable assessment of the facts, particularly regarding public interest in alleged judicial corruption. However, the interim injunction, limited to removing the article from the website pending the defamation case, did not by itself hamper the applicant’s ability to disseminate information or undermine the essence of public debate.

In *Anatoliy Yeremenko v. Ukraine* (Application no. 22287/08), the applicant was a Ukrainian journalist working for the weekly newspaper *Dzerkalo Tyzhnya*. On 12 March 2005, the newspaper published his article “Black triad: nothing else matters in the case,” which was also posted on its website on 18 March 2005. The article alleged systemic corruption and manipulation in the Donetsk commercial courts. It discussed case no. 27/37, claiming that a judgment had been based on a forged copy of a document even though the original existed in a criminal case file. It described a purported scheme in which an interested plaintiff hired a law firm, paid a substantial fee, and the case was then assigned to the “right judge” and decided in the client’s favour; appeals allegedly met a “black triad” and the principle “nothing else matters in the case.” The article also relied on statements by businessman Ch., who claimed an organised group operated in the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal, referring to case no. 8/55. The article did not name the claimant judges.

After publication, six judges applied for preventive measures and securing of evidence. On 7 April 2005, they alleged that the article contained untrue negative statements defaming their honour, dignity and professional reputation. They asked the court to order removal of the article from the newspaper’s website. On 8 April 2005, the Voroshylovsky District Court granted that request, citing Article 152 § 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure but giving little reasoning. The Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal upheld the decision on 26 August 2005, stating that because Internet information is widely accessible and difficult to control, removal from the website was the only protective measure pending examination of the defamation case. The Kyiv Court of Appeal later rejected the applicant’s cassation appeal on 15 January 2008. The article was removed from the website by 18 August 2005.

They identified as defamatory statements concerning the alleged organised group, the detailed scheme, “pressure of the system,” the law firm, the case being “distributed” to the right judge, decisions always favouring the client, the “black triad,” and the phrase “all tarred with the same brush.” The applicant argued that the article concerned matters of public interest, that he had relied on Ch.’s letter to a parliamentary sub-committee and case files, that he had checked the information, and that no judge was named.

On 20 October 2005, the Petrovskyy Local Court partly allowed the claim. It found the eighth and ninth paragraphs defamatory and untrue, holding that the organised-group allegations amounted to criminal accusations requiring a court verdict and that the Press Act source-protection did not apply because Ch. was not a State official. It ordered a retraction and required the applicant to pay UAH 333 per claimant in non-pecuniary damages plus legal and court fees (about EUR 331 and EUR 430.51 in total). Ch. was ordered to pay more. The Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal upheld the merits on 27 January 2006, reducing some fees. On 5 November 2007, the Kyiv Court of Appeal rejected the applicant’s cassation appeal without substantive reasoning.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 10. The key violation was that the domestic courts failed to conduct an adequate balancing exercise between freedom of expression and protection of reputation. They imposed civil liability without relevant and sufficient reasons, failed to apply Article 10 standards, and did not properly assess the public-interest context or distinguish facts from value judgments. However, the interim injunction, limited to removing the article from the website pending the defamation case, did not by itself hamper the applicant’s ability to disseminate information or undermine the essence of public debate.

In *Anatoliy Yeremenko v. Ukraine* (no. 22287/08), the European Court of Human Rights examined a Ukrainian journalist’s complaint under Article 10 of the Convention. The applicant worked for the newspaper *Dzerkalo Tyzhnya*. On 12 March 2005, the newspaper published his article “Black triad: nothing else matters in the case”; it appeared on the newspaper’s website on 18 March 2005.

The article alleged serious judicial corruption in the Donetsk commercial courts. It discussed case no. 27/37, claiming that a judgment had been based on a forged copy of a guarantee letter even after the original was found in a criminal case file. It described an alleged “system for obtaining a required result”: a law firm was paid a substantial fee but then took no active role; courts passed the case up to the Higher Commercial Court; that court delayed examination for months; the case was remitted because of a missing ruling; and the plaintiff company was later liquidated, allegedly hiding wrongdoing. The article also cited a letter by Ch. to a parliamentary subcommittee alleging an organised group in the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal, naming alleged members and describing a scheme. It referred to a “right judge,” a “black triad,” and said those involved were “all tarred with the same brush.” No judge was named, but the courts and case no. 8/55 were identified.

Six judges from those courts applied for preventive measures and later brought defamation claims. They alleged that statements about an organised group, “pressure of the system,” allocation to the “right judge,” the “black triad,” and similar claims were untrue and damaged their honour, dignity and professional reputation. On 8 April 2005, the District Court ordered the newspaper to remove the article from its website pending the defamation case. That decision was upheld on 26 August 2005, and the cassation appeal was rejected on 15 January 2008. The article was removed from the website by around August 2005.

In the defamation proceedings, the judges sued the applicant, Ch. and the newspaper. On 20 October 2005, the local court partly allowed their claim. It found that paragraphs 8 and 9 of the article contained factual assertions, not value judgments, and that those assertions were defamatory and untrue. The court rejected the applicant’s defence that the information came from Ch.’s letter and was protected under the Press Act, because Ch. was not a State official. It applied the presumption of innocence, reasoning that allegations of an organised criminal group could only be proved by a criminal verdict, which did not exist. The applicant was ordered to pay modest non-pecuniary damages and costs, and the newspaper was ordered to publish a retraction. Appeals were upheld on 27 January 2006, and the cassation court rejected the applicant’s appeal on 5 November 2007 without substantive reasoning.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 10. The key issue was that the article concerned a matter of public interest: alleged corruption and lack of independence in the judiciary. The domestic courts failed to conduct a proper balancing exercise between freedom of expression and protection of reputation. They did not give relevant and sufficient reasons, did not apply Convention-compatible standards, did not properly distinguish facts from value judgments, and did not consider the applicant’s good faith, due diligence, or the fact that judges as public officials must tolerate wider criticism. The interim injunction ordering removal from the website, however, was limited and did not by itself hamper dissemination or undermine the essence of public debate. The violation arose from the civil defamation liability and the lack of adequate balancing.

In *TB Inžinjering d.o.o. v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Application no. 8181/21), the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 25 May 2022. The applicant was a company represented by Mr M. Alić, a lawyer practising in Tešanj. It lodged its application against Bosnia and Herzegovina on 10 December 2020 under Article 34 of the Convention. The Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina were given notice of the application.

The applicant’s central complaint concerned the non-enforcement of a domestic decision issued in its favour against the municipality of Maglaj. The specific details of the applicant company and the relevant facts were set out in an appended table. According to the judgment, the domestic decision ordered specific action to be taken. The applicant alleged that the authorities had failed to enforce that final decision fully and in due time. It relied, expressly or in substance, on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees a fair hearing in the determination of civil rights and obligations, and on Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, which protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

The Court reiterated its established case-law that the execution of a judgment given by any court must be regarded as an integral part of a “hearing” for the purposes of Article 6. It referred to *Hornsby v. Greece*, where it had held that the right to a court would be illusory if a final, binding judicial decision remained unenforced. The Court further noted that the domestic decision in the present case ordered specific action to be taken. Consequently, that decision constituted “possessions” within the meaning of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The failure to enforce it therefore engaged both the fair-hearing guarantee under Article 6 § 1 and the property-protection guarantee under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In examining the merits, the Court found that the issues raised were similar to those already decided in the leading cases of *Spahić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* and *Kunić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina*, both dated 14 November 2017. In those cases, the Court had already found violations concerning the non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of final domestic decisions against public authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. After reviewing all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on admissibility or merits.

The decisive factual assessment was that the authorities did not deploy all necessary efforts to enforce fully and in due time the decision in the applicant company’s favour. This failure was attributed to the respondent State. The Court therefore concluded that there had been a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision. The case thus focused not on the underlying dispute with the municipality of Maglaj, but on the State’s failure to secure timely and complete enforcement of a final domestic decision that required specific action and had created a possession for the applicant company.

**Case: TB INŽINJERING D.O.O. v. Bosnia and Herzegovina (Application no. 8181/21)**

The European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered its judgment on 25 May 2022 in the case of *TB INŽINJERING d.o.o. v. Bosnia and Herzegovina*. The applicant was a company, represented by Mr M. Alić, a lawyer practising in Tešanj. The application was lodged against Bosnia and Herzegovina under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms on 10 December 2020. The Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina was given notice of the application.

The central factual basis of the application was the non-enforcement of a domestic decision issued in the applicant company’s favour against the municipality of Maglaj. The judgment does not set out all the underlying facts in the main text, noting instead that the applicant company’s details and information relevant to the application were set out in an appended table. However, the essential complaint was clear: despite obtaining a final domestic decision against the municipality, the applicant company did not receive the benefit of that decision because it was not enforced.

The applicant relied, expressly or in substance, on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to a fair hearing in the determination of civil rights and obligations, and on Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, which protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. The alleged violation therefore concerned both the procedural guarantee of access to an effective judicial process and the property right to enjoy the fruits of a final court decision.

The Court reiterated its settled case-law that the execution of a judgment given by any court must be regarded as an integral part of a “hearing” for the purposes of Article 6. It referred to *Hornsby v. Greece* (1997), where it held that the right to a court would be illusory if a final, binding judicial decision remained inoperative to the detriment of one party. The Court also found that the domestic decision in question ordered specific action to be taken and therefore constituted “possessions” within the meaning of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The Court noted that the same issues had already been examined in leading cases against Bosnia and Herzegovina, namely *Spahić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (2017) and *Kunić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (2017). In those cases, the Court had already found violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 in respect of the non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of final domestic judgments. Having examined all the material submitted in the present application, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on admissibility or merits.

The decisive finding relevant to the alleged violations was that the authorities did not deploy all necessary efforts to enforce fully and in due time the domestic decision in the applicant company’s favour. Consequently, the Court found that there had been a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The case illustrates the Court’s consistent approach that final domestic judgments must be enforced within a reasonable time and that a failure to do so may breach both fair hearing guarantees and property rights.

The case **TB Inžinjering d.o.o. v. Bosnia and Herzegovina** (Application no. 8181/21) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, sitting as a Committee, in a judgment delivered on 25 May 2022. The application was lodged under Article 34 of the Convention on 10 December 2020. The applicant company was represented by Mr M. Alić, a lawyer practising in Tešanj. The Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina were given notice of the application.

The applicant company complained of the non-enforcement of a domestic decision issued in its favour against the municipality of Maglaj. The judgment states that the applicant company’s details and information relevant to the application are set out in an appended table. The essential factual complaint was that a final domestic decision in the applicant’s favour remained unenforced. The applicant relied, expressly or in substance, on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

Article 6 § 1 guarantees that, in the determination of civil rights and obligations, everyone is entitled to a fair hearing by a tribunal. Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions and prohibits deprivation of possessions except in the public interest and subject to legal conditions.

In its legal assessment, the Court reiterated that the execution of a judgment given by any court must be regarded as an integral part of a “hearing” for the purposes of Article 6. It referred to its established case-law on non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of final domestic judgments, including **Hornsby v. Greece**. The Court further noted that the domestic decision in the present case ordered specific action to be taken. It therefore considered that the decision constituted “possessions” within the meaning of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The Court observed that in the leading cases of **Spahić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina** and **Kunić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina**, it had already found violations in respect of issues similar to those in the present case. These cases concerned the failure of authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina to enforce final domestic decisions, particularly against public authorities such as municipalities.

Having examined all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on the admissibility and merits of the complaints. Having regard to its case-law, the Court considered that the authorities did not deploy all necessary efforts to enforce fully and in due time the decision in the applicant’s favour.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore: (1) there was a final domestic decision in the applicant company’s favour against the municipality of Maglaj; (2) that decision required specific action; (3) it was not fully and promptly enforced; (4) the authorities failed to take all necessary steps to ensure timely execution; and (5) the failure to enforce the final decision interfered with the applicant’s right to a fair hearing under Article 6 § 1 and its right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The Court consequently found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The case is representative of the Court’s broader jurisprudence concerning systemic non-enforcement of final domestic judgments against public authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

**Case of Goulandris and Vardinogianni v. Greece** (Application no. 1735/13), ECtHR, 16 June 2022, concerned the right not to be tried or punished twice under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. The applicants, Georgios Goulandris and Christianna Vardinogianni, are Greek nationals and spouses. In 2003 they purchased a coastal plot at Korakia near Kranidi, Argolida. On 5 October 2004, an urban-planning inspection found two stone walls built without the required building permit: one 119.5 metres long and 1.9 metres high, and another 99.4 metres long and 1.8 metres high. The first applicant was named as owner.

The inspection report declared the walls unlawful and imposed two administrative fines: a construction fine of EUR 18,102 and an annual preservation fine of EUR 1,802 for each year the walls remained. The report was received by an employee of the applicants on 4 November 2004. No complaint was lodged, and the fines became final. In 2005, the municipality requested recovery of a reduced construction fine of EUR 7,241 from the first applicant; he paid EUR 7,414.78 including fees. In 2011, the tax office was asked to recover preservation fines of EUR 5,379.80 from each co-owner; the first applicant paid EUR 10,759.60 in total.

In parallel, the inspection report was sent to the prosecutor in January 2005. A bill of indictment followed in July 2006. On 17 September 2008, the Nafplio Criminal Court of First Instance convicted both applicants of jointly and intentionally constructing the walls without a permit; the permit authorised only a 0.6-metre fence. They received a seven-month prison sentence, later upheld on appeal and suspended for three years. Before the domestic courts, the applicants argued that the administrative fines were criminal in nature and final, so the subsequent criminal prosecution violated Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. The Court of Appeal dismissed this, holding that the administrative fines were not criminal sanctions but compliance measures aimed at legalisation or demolition. The Court of Cassation agreed in September 2012, finding that administrative sanctions did not amount to criminal punishment for *ne bis in idem* purposes.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. It considered that the administrative fines were criminal in nature because of their potential severity, the absence of an upper limit and their punitive element. The duplication of proceedings—the administrative construction fine and the criminal proceedings for constructing the stone walls without a permit—was not sufficiently linked in substance and time to form a coherent and proportionate whole. The Court further noted that the criminal proceedings were sufficiently separate from the annual preservation fine for continuing the infringement. However, the cumulative administrative and criminal response for the construction itself breached the right not to be tried or punished twice. The case illustrates the need for a sufficiently close connection between parallel administrative and criminal sanctions to satisfy *ne bis in idem*.

In *Goulandris and Vardinogianni v. Greece* (Application no. 1735/13, judgment of 16 June 2022), the applicants were a married couple, Greek nationals living in London, who owned coastal land in Korakia near Kranidi. In October 2004, an urban-planning inspection found two stone walls on their property—one approximately 119.5 metres long and 1.9 metres high, and another 99.4 metres long and 1.8 metres high—constructed without the required building permit. A later permit authorised only a 0.6-metre-high fence. The inspection report declared the constructions unlawful and imposed a one-off construction fine of EUR 18,102 and an annual preservation fine of EUR 1,802 for each year the walls remained. The report was received by an employee of the applicants in November 2004, and no complaint was lodged.

In March 2005, the tax office was asked to recover EUR 7,241 from the first applicant; he paid EUR 7,414.78, including fees. In November 2011, further notices sought preservation fines of EUR 5,379.80 from each applicant as 50% co-owners. The first applicant paid the total of EUR 10,759.60. Meanwhile, the inspection report had been sent to the public prosecutor in January 2005, and a bill of indictment against both applicants was issued in July 2006. In September 2008, the Nafplio Criminal Court of First Instance convicted them of jointly and intentionally constructing the walls without a permit. They were sentenced to seven months’ imprisonment, converted into a pecuniary penalty of EUR 10 per day.

On appeal, the applicants argued that the administrative fines and criminal conviction amounted to double punishment for the same offence, contrary to the *ne bis in idem* principle under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention and domestic res judicata rules. In December 2011, the Nafplio Court of Appeal rejected that plea. It held that the administrative fines were not criminal sanctions but compelling administrative measures aimed at ensuring compliance, legalisation, or demolition, and that they did not have res judicata effect for criminal courts. It upheld the conviction, finding that the applicants were aware of the unlawfulness and that the walls harmed the coastal natural landscape. The sentence was suspended for three years. In September 2012, the Court of Cassation dismissed their appeal on points of law, reasoning that administrative sanctions were not criminal punishment for Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 purposes and that cumulative administrative fines and criminal sanctions did not breach *ne bis in idem*.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants complained that they had been tried and punished twice for the same offence. The Court examined whether the administrative fines were criminal in nature and whether the administrative and criminal proceedings were sufficiently linked to form a coherent and proportionate whole. It found that the administrative fines were criminal in nature, given their potential severity, lack of an upper limit, and punitive element. It further found that the criminal proceedings were sufficiently separate from the annual preservation fine for continuing the infringement, and that the two sets of proceedings were not sufficiently linked in substance and time to form a coherent and proportionate whole. Accordingly, Greece violated Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention. The judgment became final on 16 September 2022.

In *Goulandris and Vardinogianni v. Greece* (Application no. 1735/13), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Greece breached the applicants’ right not to be tried or punished twice under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention.

The applicants, Greek nationals and a married couple living in London, purchased a coastal plot in Korakia near Kranidi, Argolida, on 17 September 2003. On 5 October 2004, an urban-planning inspection found that two stone walls had been built on the property without the required building permit. The first wall was 119.5 metres long and 1.9 metres high; the second was 99.4 metres long and 1.8 metres high. A later building permit apparently authorised only a 0.6-metre-high fence. The inspection report declared the constructions unlawful and imposed a construction fine of EUR 18,102 and an annual preservation fine of EUR 1,802 for each year the walls remained. The report was received by an employee of the applicants on 4 November 2004, and no administrative complaint was lodged.

In 2005, the first applicant paid a reduced construction fine of EUR 7,241 plus EUR 173.78 in fees, totalling EUR 7,414.78. In 2011, the municipality sought payment of the preservation fines from both applicants as co-owners; the first applicant paid EUR 10,759.60 on 29 November 2011.

Separately, the inspection report was sent to the public prosecutor in January 2005. In 2006, the applicants were indicted. In September 2008, the Nafplio Criminal Court of First Instance convicted them of jointly and intentionally constructing the walls without a valid permit. They received seven-month prison sentences, converted into a pecuniary penalty of EUR 10 per day. On appeal in 2011, the applicants argued that the administrative fines were criminal in nature and that their payment barred later criminal prosecution under the *ne bis in idem* principle. The Court of Appeal rejected this, holding that the administrative fines were coercive administrative measures, not criminal sanctions, and did not have the effect of res judicata for criminal courts. The Court of Cassation upheld that reasoning in 2012, concluding that administrative sanctions were not criminal punishment under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants complained that they had been punished twice for the same conduct: first through urban-planning administrative fines, then through a criminal conviction and sentence for constructing the same walls. The key issue was whether the administrative fines were “criminal” for Convention purposes and whether the two sets of proceedings formed a coherent and proportionate whole.

The Court found that the administrative fines were criminal in nature, given their potential severity, the absence of an upper limit, and their punitive element. It then assessed whether the administrative and criminal proceedings were sufficiently linked in substance and time. It concluded that they were not sufficiently linked to form a coherent and proportionate whole. The duplication of the construction fine and the criminal proceedings therefore violated Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. The later regularisation of the constructions in 2013–2017 did not remove the prior double punishment. The judgment became final on 16 September 2022.

The case of *Boguta and Tereshchenko v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 13094/19 and 37726/19) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered on 13 January 2022. The applications were lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights on various dates. The Ukrainian Government were given notice of the applications. Because the two applications raised similar subject matter, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment.

The core factual background is that each applicant’s relative had died, and the applicants complained that the domestic authorities had conducted an ineffective investigation into those deaths. The full details of the applicants and the relevant facts are set out in the appended table to the judgment, which is not reproduced in the excerpt. The central alleged violation therefore concerned the State’s failure to comply with the procedural obligation under Article 2 § 1 of the Convention, which provides that “Everyone’s right to life shall be protected by law.”

The applicants relied on Articles 2, 6 § 1, and 13 of the Convention. The Court, acting as master of the characterisation to be given in law to the facts, considered that the complaints should be examined under Article 2 rather than under Articles 6 § 1 and 13. Under the Court’s established case-law, Article 2 imposes on the State not only a negative obligation to refrain from unlawful killing, but also a positive procedural obligation to conduct an effective official investigation when an individual dies in circumstances potentially engaging State responsibility. Such an investigation must be prompt, thorough, independent, impartial, and capable of identifying and punishing those responsible and providing redress to the victim’s relatives.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are that criminal proceedings were initiated into the deaths of the applicants’ relatives, but the investigations allegedly failed to meet the requirements of Article 2. The applicants complained that the authorities did not conduct an effective investigation, which prevented them from establishing the truth about the deaths and from obtaining accountability. Although the excerpt does not set out every factual particular, the alleged shortcomings typically include delays, repeated suspensions or reopenings of proceedings, failure to take necessary investigative steps, failure to question witnesses or obtain expert evidence, and an overall lack of diligence.

The Government were given notice of the applications and had the opportunity to respond. The Court deliberated in private on 9 December 2021 and adopted the judgment on 13 January 2022. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

In its legal analysis, the Court examined whether the domestic investigation satisfied the procedural guarantees of Article 2 § 1. The Court found that the investigation into the deaths of the applicants’ relatives had been ineffective, amounting to a violation of Article 2 of the Convention. The Court accordingly upheld the applicants’ core complaint concerning the procedural limb of the right to life. The case illustrates the European Court’s continued scrutiny of Ukraine’s compliance with its positive obligation to investigate deaths effectively and to safeguard the procedural rights of victims’ relatives.

The case of *Boguta and Tereshchenko v. Ukraine* concerns two applications (nos. 13094/19 and 37726/19) lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee composed of Judges Hüseynov, Chanturia, and Bårdsen, deliberated on 9 December 2021 and adopted a final judgment on 13 January 2022. The applications were lodged on various dates and were joined by the Court because they raised similar subject matter.

The central factual allegation, as stated in the main body of the judgment, is that the applicants—Boguta and Tereshchenko—complained of ineffective investigations into the deaths of their relatives. In other words, the alleged violation is primarily procedural: the Ukrainian authorities are said to have failed to conduct an effective official investigation into deaths involving their relatives. Under Article 2 of the Convention, the right to life requires not only that the State refrain from intentionally depriving individuals of life, but also that it conduct an adequate, independent, prompt, and effective investigation where individuals die in circumstances potentially engaging State responsibility.

The applicants originally relied on Articles 2, 6 § 1, and 13 of the Convention. Article 2 protects the right to life; Article 6 § 1 guarantees a fair hearing; and Article 13 guarantees an effective remedy for alleged Convention violations. However, the Court, acting as “master of the characterisation to be given in law to the facts,” considered that the complaints should be examined under Article 2 of the Convention. It cited *Igor Shevchenko v. Ukraine* (no. 22737/04, § 38, 12 January 2012) for that approach. The Court therefore treated the applicants’ allegations about the inadequacy of the domestic investigations as engaging the procedural obligation under Article 2, rather than as separate complaints under Articles 6 or 13. Article 2 § 1, as quoted in the judgment, provides: “Everyone’s right to life shall be protected by law.”

That appended table is not included in the text supplied. As a result, the available excerpt does not permit a detailed factual narrative. It establishes only that the applicants’ relatives died, that the applicants alleged the official investigations into those deaths were ineffective, and that the Court accepted this as a proper Article 2 complaint.

Procedurally, the Ukrainian Government were given notice of the applications. Because the applications were similar, the Court joined them in a single judgment. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision. The excerpt ends before the Court’s full reasoning and final conclusion on the merits. Therefore, while the key alleged violation is clear—ineffective investigation into deaths under Article 2 § 1—the precise factual particulars and the ultimate finding (violation or no violation) cannot be summarized from the provided text alone. **Boguta and Tereshchenko v. Ukraine** (Applications nos. 13094/19 and 37726/19) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered on 13 January 2022. The applicants lodged their applications against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention on the dates indicated in the appended table. The Ukrainian Government was given notice of the applications. The Committee consisted of Judges Lətif Hüseynov (President), Lado Chanturia, and Arnfinn Bårdsen, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The Court deliberated in private on 9 December 2021.

The core complaint concerned the alleged ineffectiveness of domestic investigations into the deaths of the applicants’ relatives. The applicants relied on Articles 2, 6 § 1, and 13 of the Convention. The specific facts—such as the identities of the deceased, the dates and circumstances of death, the family relationships, and the exact course of the domestic proceedings—are set out in an appended table to the judgment. That table is not reproduced in the excerpt provided. Therefore, the summary below is limited to the information available in the text.

Because the two applications raised similar subject matter, the Court decided to examine them jointly in a single judgment. The Court, acting as the master of the characterisation to be given in law to the facts, considered that the complaints fell to be examined under Article 2 of the Convention, rather than separately under Articles 6 § 1 and 13. Article 2 § 1 provides that “Everyone’s right to life shall be protected by law.” This provision imposes on States not only a substantive obligation to refrain from intentionally depriving life, but also a procedural obligation to conduct an effective official investigation when individuals have died in circumstances potentially engaging State responsibility.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore: (1) the applicants’ relatives died; (2) those deaths triggered the procedural obligation under Article 2 to carry out an effective investigation; (3) the Ukrainian authorities allegedly failed to conduct such an investigation; (4) the applicants, as next-of-kin, complained about that failure; and (5) although they invoked fair-trial and effective-remedy guarantees, the Court channeled the case into Article 2. An effective investigation under Article 2 must be independent, adequate, prompt, and transparent. In *Atristain Gorosabel v. Spain* (Application no. 15508/15, judgment 18 January 2022), the applicant, a Spanish national, was investigated for alleged membership of the terrorist group ETA. After an earlier case against him was discontinued, new inquiries began. On 29 September 2010 the Guardia Civil arrested him. On 30 September an investigating judge authorised his detention incommunicado, citing the need to prevent frustration of the investigation, primarily the location of explosives. While incommunicado, he was assigned a State-funded legal-aid lawyer. He was informed of his rights, including the right to silence and not to incriminate himself, but under Spanish law he could neither choose a lawyer of his own nor meet privately with the assigned legal-aid lawyer before police questioning.

During police custody he gave two statements in the presence of the legal-aid representative. In the first, on 1 October 2010, he admitted cooperating with ETA, described attempted kidnapping, verifying a businessman for assassination, and providing information about police officers so an attack could be planned. He also indicated a storage room containing explosives. A search there uncovered a large quantity of explosives, detonators, ammunition, USB manuals, and other material. On 3 October, despite the legal-aid representative’s opposition, he gave a second statement, disclosing a hidden firearm, cartridges, USB keys, false licence plates, and other items, which police then found. While incommunicado he was examined daily by a forensic doctor; he reported no mistreatment but alleged threats that his girlfriend would be arrested if he did not cooperate. On 4 October he appeared before the investigating judge, stated that his police statements had been made during five days of incommunicado detention and were self-incriminatory, and the incommunicado measure was lifted; he then appointed a lawyer of his own choosing.

In 2013 the Audiencia Nacional convicted him of membership of a terrorist group and possession of explosives, sentencing him to 17 years’ imprisonment. The conviction relied on computer material, explosives found at locations he indicated, statements of co-defendants, witness evidence, and his silence at trial. The courts rejected mistreatment and found his statements voluntary. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction, and a Constitutional Court *amparo* appeal was declared inadmissible.

The alleged violation concerned Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (c) of the Convention: that while held incommunicado he was denied access to a lawyer of his own choosing and could not communicate with the legal-aid lawyer before or during police questioning, and that his self-incriminatory statements supplied evidence used to convict him. He argued that the legal-aid lawyer had no access to the case file and no private meeting with him, making the defence ineffective. The Government maintained that legal assistance was provided, rights were explained, and incommunicado detention was judicially authorised and necessary because of terrorism and explosives risks and possible ETA-linked lawyers. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation: the use at trial of the initial confession, obtained while he was held incommunicado and denied—without individualised reasons—access to a lawyer of his own choice and to a legal-aid lawyer, undermined the overall fairness of the criminal proceedings.

Although he was assigned a State-funded legal-aid lawyer, the incommunicado regime prevented him from choosing his own lawyer and from meeting the assigned lawyer privately before police questioning. He was informed of his rights, including the right to remain silent and not to incriminate himself.

In Davtyan v. Armenia (Applications nos. 54261/13 and 18361/16; judgment of 1 March 2022), the European Court of Human Rights considered complaints by Samvel Davtyan, an Armenian national born in 1968. The case concerned alleged ill-treatment in police custody, the alleged failure to carry out an effective investigation, and the fairness of his criminal trial because the courts relied on a confession allegedly obtained under duress. The complaints arose under Articles 3 and 6 of the Convention.

On 23 September 2011 at 8:30 a.m., the applicant was taken to the Principal Department for the Fight Against Organised Crime (PDFAOC) of the Armenian Police. He alleged that police officers immediately subjected him to several hours of ill-treatment, hitting him on various parts of his body. At 11:30 a.m., an investigator of the Principal Department for Investigations (PDI) questioned him and placed him under arrest. The alleged ill-treatment reportedly continued. The applicant claimed he was stripped, handcuffed by his hands and feet to a chair, beaten with rubber batons, subjected to electric shocks, and kicked on the soles of his feet, back, ribs, and other areas, while officers demanded that he confess to a crime.

At 11:30 p.m. that day, the applicant was admitted to a police temporary holding facility. Medical records documented injuries including a wound and swelling on the left temple, reddish traces on his back, wounds on both shins, swelling of the right hand, swelling of both feet, and a wound on the right wrist. A notification of these injuries was sent to the PDI. On 24 September 2011, the PDI investigator questioned the applicant, who confessed to the crime. On 1 October 2011, the investigator examined the holding facility’s medical register. On 3 October 2011, the applicant refused to testify about his injuries. On 4 October 2011, a forensic medical expert, ordered by the investigator, confirmed part of the injuries and found they had been inflicted by a blunt hard object.

In October 2011, the applicant appointed a lawyer, who contested the forensic examination results and alleged ill-treatment. On 6 April 2012, the PDI investigator took statements from two PDFAOC officers who had arrested the applicant. Both gave identical one-paragraph statements denying ill-treatment and claiming the applicant resisted arrest, that force was used, and that he fell during the incident, which may have caused his injuries. The investigator asked no questions.

In June and July 2012, the applicant complained in detail to the General Prosecutor and requested an investigation by the Special Investigative Service (SIS). The July complaint was forwarded to the SIS, which questioned the applicant on 15 August 2012. He maintained his complaint but refused to answer questions about his injuries. On 23 August 2012, the SIS refused to institute criminal proceedings, relying on the two officers’ statements and the applicant’s refusal to testify. It concluded that his injuries resulted from the lawful use of force by arresting officers seeking to prevent his flight. The applicant’s appeals against that decision were dismissed by the courts.

Separately, the applicant was convicted and sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment. In reaching that verdict, the courts relied, among other evidence, on his confession of 24 September 2011 and rejected his requests to exclude it. The applicant therefore alleged that he had been ill-treated in custody, that no effective investigation followed, and that his trial was unfair because the conviction rested on a confession allegedly obtained under duress.

**Lysak v. Ukraine** (Application no. 52299/14) is a European Court of Human Rights case decided by the Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, with judgment delivered on 20 October 2022. The applicant, Ms Svitlana Vasylivna Lysak, a Ukrainian national born in 1949 and living in Cherkasy, was a private entrepreneur. She owned and operated three kiosks—temporary structures used for selling goods—situated on municipal land in three locations in Cherkasy. The case concerns her complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention that her equipment and goods had been unlawfully dismantled by municipal authorities and that she had been unable to obtain compensation.

The dispute began when the municipal authorities took the position that the applicant’s rights to use the land had expired. The applicant challenged that assessment before the Cherkasy Regional Commercial Court. That court issued preliminary injunctions on 14 August 2008 and 19 May 2009 prohibiting the municipal authorities from dismantling her equipment. On 31 March 2010, in a final decision, the commercial court declared the authorities’ assessment unlawful and ruled that the applicant continued to have the right to rent the land in question.

Despite those injunctions, on 28 April 2009 the city’s executive committee ordered the municipal working group dealing with unlawful structures to proceed with removal of the applicant’s equipment. Mr K., the director of a municipal company and a member of the working group, was directed to provide equipment for the dismantling operation and to arrange storage of the dismantled equipment. On 28 May 2009, the municipal working group dismantled the applicant’s equipment and its contents—including kiosks, cash registers, and stock of goods for sale—and put them in storage. The applicant alleged that the equipment was damaged during dismantling and became unusable, and that the stock of goods was lost.

On 21 September 2010, the Cherkasy Sosnivsky District Court, in a final decision, declared the executive committee’s decision of 28 April 2009 unlawful. It specifically noted that the decision had been taken in disregard of the commercial court’s injunctions.

The applicant then lodged a criminal complaint accusing city officials of abuse of public office and other crimes. Mr K. was eventually charged with criminal dereliction of duty. Within those criminal proceedings, the applicant lodged a civil claim for damages against Mr K. and the State Treasury. On 4 October 2013, Mr K. was found guilty but released from serving his sentence. The civil claim was dismissed, with the court stating that it could be resubmitted in separate civil proceedings. The conviction was later quashed and the case was remitted for further investigation, most recently on 16 February 2016. No further developments in those proceedings were reported.

The applicant also sued the city council and the city executive committee in the administrative courts, seeking a declaration that their actions in removing her equipment had been unlawful and claiming damages. On 22 January 2014, the High Administrative Court upheld the lower courts’ decisions rejecting her claim. Those courts reasoned in particular that it would be appropriate for the applicant to seek compensation within the framework of the criminal proceedings against Mr K.

Before the European Court, the Government argued that the application was inadmissible for failure to exhaust domestic remedies. It submitted that the applicant could have lodged a separate civil claim against Mr K., brought a damages claim against the City Council after its demolition decision had been declared unlawful, or requested review of the High Administrative Court’s decision of 22 January 2014 in light of “newly discovered circumstances” following the quashing of Mr K.’s conviction. The Court gave notice only of the complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and declared the remainder inadmissible. The central issue was whether the applicant’s possessions had been unlawfully interfered with and whether she had effective access to compensation for the dismantling and loss.
