In *Lysak v. Ukraine* (Application no. 52299/14, judgment of 20 October 2022), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention concerning the unlawful dismantling of the applicant’s property and her inability to obtain compensation. The applicant, Ms Svitlana Vasylivna Lysak, a Ukrainian national born in 1949 and living in Cherkasy, was a private entrepreneur who owned and operated three kiosks—temporary structures used for selling goods—on municipal land in three locations in Cherkasy.

The dispute arose when the municipal authorities took the position that the applicant’s rights to use the land had expired. The applicant challenged that assessment before the Cherkasy Regional Commercial Court. That court issued preliminary injunctions on 14 August 2008 and 19 May 2009 prohibiting the municipal authorities from dismantling her equipment. On 31 March 2010, in a final decision, the commercial court declared the authorities’ assessment unlawful and ruled that the applicant continued to have the right to rent the land.

Despite those injunctions, on 28 April 2009 the city executive committee ordered its municipal working group dealing with unlawful structures to remove the applicant’s equipment. Mr K., the director of a municipal company and a member of the working group, was directed to provide equipment for the dismantling operation and to arrange storage for the dismantled property. On 28 May 2009, the working group dismantled the applicant’s kiosks, cash registers, and stock of goods for sale and placed them in storage. The applicant alleged that the equipment was damaged during dismantling and became unusable, and that her stock of goods was lost. The removal therefore occurred while court injunctions were in force and before the commercial court confirmed her land-use rights.

On 21 September 2010, the Cherkasy Sosnivsky District Court declared the executive committee’s decision of 28 April 2009 unlawful. It specifically noted that the decision had been taken in disregard of the commercial court’s injunctions. The applicant also lodged a criminal complaint accusing city officials of abuse of public office and other crimes. Mr K. was eventually charged with criminal dereliction of duty in that connection. Within those criminal proceedings, the applicant brought a civil claim for damages against Mr K. and the State Treasury.

On 4 October 2013, Mr K. was found guilty but released from serving his sentence. The civil claim was dismissed, with the court stating that it could be resubmitted in separate civil proceedings. The conviction was later quashed and the case was remitted for further investigation, most recently on 16 February 2016. No further developments in those proceedings were reported.

The applicant also sued the city council and the city executive committee in the administrative courts, seeking a declaration that their actions in removing her equipment were unlawful and claiming damages. On 22 January 2014, the High Administrative Court upheld the lower courts’ rejection of that claim. The administrative courts reasoned that it would be appropriate for the applicant to seek compensation within the criminal proceedings against Mr K.

Before the Strasbourg Court, the applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that her equipment, situated on municipal land, had been unlawfully dismantled and that she had been unable to obtain compensation. The Government contested admissibility, arguing that she had failed to exhaust domestic remedies. They submitted that she could have lodged a separate civil claim against Mr K., brought a damages claim against the City Council after its demolition decision was declared unlawful, or requested review of the High Administrative Court’s decision of 22 January 2014 based on newly discovered circumstances following the quashing of Mr K.’s conviction. The application was lodged on 15 July 2014; the Court gave notice of the Article 1 Protocol No. 1 complaint and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.
001-220885:
Case: A and Others v. Iceland (ECtHR, Third Section, 15 November 2022). The applicants were two parents, A and B, and their two children, X and Y. They complained under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that the deprivation of the parents’ custody of X and Y violated the family’s right to respect for private and family life.

The case began in October 2015, when X’s school notified the municipal child protection committee that X had described domestic violence and drawn a picture indicating that her father had touched her and her brother on their “private parts.” X allegedly said that her father’s penis had entered her vagina. Y was also said to have been harassed. The father was arrested and detained for four days; he consistently denied the allegations. At the Children’s House, X initially gave inconsistent accounts but later described sexual touching. Y initially denied any abuse, but after being placed in foster care in September 2016, he disclosed that his father had rubbed his penis, applied cream, and inserted a finger into his rectum, saying his mother must not be told.

Child protection authorities found the family home disordered and the children badly cared for. The mother was being treated for depression and anxiety. X was placed in temporary foster care in February 2016 and Y in September 2016. Reports indicated that the mother allowed contact between the children and the father despite restrictions, pressured X, and did not protect the children. A psychologist concluded that the mother lacked sufficient capacity to have custody.

In criminal proceedings, the father was charged with sexual offences against X and Y but was acquitted in November 2017 because guilt was not proven beyond reasonable doubt. The acquittal became final. In parallel child protection proceedings, the committee sought to deprive both parents of custody. A court-appointed psychologist found that the parents lacked custody capacity, that the children’s accounts were consistent and credible, that both children feared their father, that the mother sided with the father and could not provide safety, and that the children were deeply attached to their foster parents and wished to remain together in foster care. The District Court granted deprivation of custody; the Court of Appeal overturned that decision, finding that less intrusive measures had not been sufficiently attempted after the acquittal; the Supreme Court reinstated the deprivation in March 2020. It held that the father’s acquittal was not determinative in childcare proceedings, that the children’s best interests were paramount, and that their severe fear and the parents’ inability to care for or protect them justified the measure. Custody passed to the committee, and the children remained in permanent foster care, with limited contact for the mother and no contact for the father.

Before the ECtHR, the parents alleged that the interference was excessive, based on the acquitted abuse allegations, and unsupported by sufficient attempts at less restrictive measures. The Government acknowledged interference but argued it was lawful, pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the children, and was necessary and proportionate.

The ECtHR found no violation of Article 8. The decision fell within the State’s margin of appreciation and was based not on the sexual abuse charges of which the father was acquitted, but on the parents’ inability to care properly for the children and the children’s own wishes. The Court emphasised the children’s best interests, extensive professional evidence, prior less restrictive measures, procedural safeguards, and the reviewable nature of the custody arrangement.

In *A and Others v. Iceland*, the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Iceland violated Article 8 by depriving two parents of custody of their children following child protection concerns and the father’s criminal acquittal. The first and second applicants, A and B, were married parents of X (born 2008) and Y (born 2011). In October 2015, X’s school notified the child protection committee that X had disclosed domestic violence and drawn a picture indicating that her father had touched her and her brother on their private parts; she reportedly said a penis had entered her vagina. Police arrested A, who was detained for four days. At Children’s House interviews, X initially gave evasive or inconsistent accounts but later described A touching her private parts with his penis and finger and applying cream. Y initially denied abuse; after being placed in foster care in September 2016, he described A rubbing his penis, applying cream, and inserting a finger into his rectum, saying Y’s mother must not be told. Authorities also found the home disorderly and the children poorly cared for.

The children were temporarily placed outside the home. X entered foster care in February 2016, and Y in September 2016. A psychologist concluded in November 2016 that B lacked sufficient ability to care for them, citing neglect, emotional and interpersonal problems, allowing A contact, pressuring X, and a considerable risk if the children returned to her. A was indicted in March 2017 for sexual offences against X and Y but was acquitted in November 2017 because guilt was not established beyond reasonable doubt; the children’s statements were not entirely consistent and were largely uncorroborated. The prosecution did not appeal.

The child protection committee nevertheless sought deprivation of custody. A court-appointed assessor in May 2018 found both parents unfit: the children were afraid of A, had bonded with their foster parents, did not wish to live with their mother, and B could not protect them. The District Court allowed deprivation, but the Court of Appeal overturned that decision, finding the committee had failed to reconsider after the acquittal and had not shown that less intrusive measures were impossible. In March 2020, the Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeal and deprived both parents of custody. It held that the criminal acquittal was not determinative in childcare proceedings, which apply a different standard and prioritize the children’s best interests. The children had a severe fear of A, and B could not provide the safety and support they needed; the siblings should remain together.

Before the ECtHR, A and B complained under Article 8 that the loss of custody and limited contact violated their and their children’s family life. They argued that the authorities improperly relied on the acquitted sexual abuse allegations, failed to attempt less restrictive measures, and allowed overly limited contact. The Government maintained that the interference was lawful and necessary, based on extensive evidence, with less invasive measures tried and procedural safeguards provided. The ECtHR found no violation. It held that the domestic decisions fell within Iceland’s margin of appreciation and were not based on the sexual abuse charges alone, but on the children’s fear, parental incapacity, and best interests, supported by professional assessments. Less restrictive measures had been attempted, the proceedings had adequate safeguards, the custody measure remained reviewable, and contact between the mother and children was maintained.

In *A and Others v. Iceland* (2022), four applicants—parents A and B and their children X and Y—complained under Article 8 ECHR that Iceland violated their private and family life by removing the children and depriving the parents of custody.

The case began in October 2015, when X’s school reported that she had described domestic violence and drawn a picture suggesting her father had touched her and her brother’s “private parts”; she referred to a penis entering her vagina. Police arrested and detained the father, who consistently denied the allegations. In Barnahús interviews, X initially gave no clear account and was distressed, but later described her father touching her genitals with his penis and finger and applying cream, and expressed fear for Y. Y initially denied touching, but after his September 2016 foster placement, his foster mother reported urinary and bowel problems and a “secret” that his father had applied cream to his genitals. In a later interview, Y said his father rubbed his penis, applied cream, and inserted a finger into his rectum, saying his mother must not be told. Home visits found severe disorder and poor care. The mother, treated for depression and anxiety, initially agreed to temporary placement. X was placed in foster care in February 2016; Y in September 2016 after concerns about extensive contact with his father. A psychologist found the mother lacked sufficient custody ability, citing neglect, possible violence, emotional problems, allowing the father in the home, pressuring X, and failing to protect the children.

In March 2017 the father was indicted for sexual offences against both children. In November 2017 he was acquitted: the district court found guilt not proven beyond reasonable doubt, noting his credible denial, inconsistencies in X’s statements, no corroborating medical or other evidence, and Y’s inconsistent, uncorroborated testimony. The prosecution did not appeal.

Meanwhile, in July 2017 the child protection committee decided the parents could not have custody and sought court deprivation. A court-appointed psychologist in May 2018 found the parents’ custody ability lacking, signs of neglect, the mother uncooperative and untruthful about the father’s contact, the children’s disclosures credible, and the children deeply bonded to foster parents, afraid of their father, and unwilling to live with their parents. The mother could not create safety because she sided with the father. Reports showed improvement in foster care. The district court allowed deprivation in June 2019; the Court of Appeal overturned in November 2019, faulting the failure to reconsider after acquittal and lack of proof that less intrusive measures could not work. In March 2020 the Supreme Court reversed, depriving both parents of custody. It held the father’s acquittal was not determinative in childcare proceedings; the children’s best interests governed. Both children had severe fear of the father; the mother’s limited capacities and the children’s mistrust meant she also could not have custody; siblings should not be separated. The children remained in permanent foster care, with limited maternal contact and no paternal contact.

The parents alleged the custody loss and restricted contact violated Article 8. The Government acknowledged interference but argued it was lawful under the Child Protection Act, pursued the children’s health and rights, and was necessary, with less intrusive measures tried and procedural safeguards. The ECtHR found no violation: the decision fell within Iceland’s margin of appreciation, was not based on the acquitted sexual-abuse charges, gave paramount importance to the children’s best interests, relied on extensive professional evidence and the children’s wishes, and was reviewable with the mother’s contact maintained.
001-220537:
The case concerns N.V., a Maltese national, and C.C., a British national, who were partners. N.V. had a son, E., in 2006 with her former husband, J. After separating in 2008, N.V. had custody of E. and J. had access. In 2009 N.V. moved to Malta with E. and began living with C.C. They later had a child together in November 2016.

In 2012 J. brought Family Court proceedings concerning access, including disputes over C.C.’s presence during visits. In July 2015 a violent incident occurred between J. and C.C. J. alleged that C.C. had threatened to kill E, had psychological problems, and that E. feared N.V.; C.C. claimed he was the victim and had been injured. J. sought custody and E.’s forced removal from N.V. On 1 October 2015, after a Children’s Advocate report was sealed and not made accessible to the parties, the Family Court ordered N.V. not to expose E. to C.C., with immediate effect. It also admonished N.V. over J.’s access rights and appointed a psychologist and social-work monitoring. N.V.’s requests to vary the order, to have C.C. heard, and to have C.C. evaluated were dismissed on 28 October 2015 without a hearing and without specific reasons. A November 2015 psychologist’s report found that E. was fond of C.C., missed him, and that there was nothing dangerous in their relationship; it recommended continued contact. The Family Court nonetheless did not revoke its order. As a result, N.V., who lived with E. and was pregnant by C.C., could not live with C.C. or receive his daily support whenever E. was present.

In June 2016 the applicants brought constitutional redress proceedings. They alleged a violation of Article 8 because the order prevented them from living, travelling, or being together in E.’s presence, despite their stable relationship and expected child. They also alleged Article 6 violations: C.C. was affected by an order without ever being a party, being heard, or being investigated; the Children’s Advocate report was sealed; N.V. was denied oral hearings; there was no effective remedy because challenges went back to the same judge; and decrees lacked reasoning. In November 2016 the constitutional court declined an interim measure but invited a concession; after their child’s birth, the couple resumed living as a family.

In 2019 the first-instance constitutional court found violations of Articles 8 and 6. It held the order unjustified and not in E.’s best interests; apart from the violent incident, no basis existed, and the objective facts showed C.C. was injured, not J. It found Article 6 breaches due to the failure to hear C.C., the sealed report, lack of oral hearings, and unreasoned decisions. In 2020 the Constitutional Court varied the judgment: it annulled the Article 8 finding, holding that once the decree was annulled and the status quo ante restored, no separate finding was needed; it dismissed C.C.’s Article 6 complaint because he was not a party and had not requested a hearing, but confirmed Article 6 violations concerning N.V.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 8. The key problems were that the domestic order disproportionately prevented a stable couple from living together while purportedly protecting E.; the domestic decision-making was flawed; there was no proper balancing of the interests involved; C.C. was never heard; the sealed report was inaccessible; reasons were lacking; and the authorities failed to facilitate reunification as soon as reasonably feasible once the order was no longer necessary.

In *N.V. and C.C. v. Malta* (ECtHR, App. no. 4952/21, 10 Nov. 2022), the applicants were N.V., a Maltese woman, and C.C., her British partner. N.V. had a son, E., born in 2006 from her marriage to J. After separating in 2008, N.V. obtained E.’s care and custody and later moved with him to Malta, where she began living with C.C. They later had a child together in 2016. J. brought Family Court proceedings in 2012 concerning access, and relations between the parents became hostile.

In July 2015, J. alleged that C.C. had been violent and had threatened to kill E.; N.V. claimed C.C. was actually the victim. J. sought custody and a psychological assessment. A Children’s Advocate was appointed, but her report was submitted to the court without being disclosed to the parties. On 1 October 2015, the Family Court ordered N.V. not to expose E. to C.C., with immediate effect. C.C. had never been a party to the proceedings and was not heard. The order also admonished N.V. for hindering J.’s access and appointed a psychologist and social workers. N.V. asked to vary the order and for C.C. to be heard and evaluated. On 28 October 2015, without a hearing, the court dismissed all requests without specific reasons. A November 2015 psychologist’s report found that E. was fond of C.C., missed him, and that their relationship was not dangerous; it saw both households as potentially beneficial. Nevertheless, the order remained, preventing N.V., then pregnant with C.C.’s child, from living with him while E. was present and preventing C.C. from assisting her daily. The couple only resumed living as a family after constitutional proceedings and the birth.

In June 2016, the applicants brought constitutional redress. They alleged violations of Article 8 (family life) and Article 6. Under Article 8, they complained that the decree de facto prevented them from living, travelling, or being together in E.’s presence, severely affecting their stable relationship and unborn child. Under Article 6, they complained that C.C. was bound by an order though never a party, never heard, and refused a hearing; that the Children’s Advocate report was sealed and inaccessible; that N.V. had no oral hearings; that the decrees were unreasoned; and that there was no effective remedy because challenges returned to the same judge/court.

The first-instance constitutional court found breaches of Articles 8 and 6 and annulled the 2015 decree. It treated the applicants and E. as a de facto family and found the interference unjustified and not in E.’s best interests; the only violent incident showed C.C. was injured, not J. On appeal, the Constitutional Court annulled the Article 8 finding because the decree had already been annulled, and dismissed C.C.’s Article 6 claim since he was not a party and had not applied to be heard. It confirmed Article 6 violations concerning N.V.

The ECtHR focused on Malta’s positive obligations under Article 8. It found the domestic decision-making process flawed: the Family Court made a drastic order without properly hearing the affected partner or balancing the child’s interests against the couple’s family life; it relied on inaccessible material and unreasoned decisions; and it failed to revoke or facilitate reunification once the order was no longer necessary. The order was disproportionate and violated Article 8, with procedural failings central to that violation. The key facts were therefore the lasting prohibition on C.C.’s presence around E., C.C.’s lack of party status or hearing, the sealed report

In *N.V. and C.C. v. Malta*, the applicants were N.V., a Maltese mother of a son, E. (born 2006), and C.C., her British partner. N.V. had separated from E.’s father, J., in 2008. Under their separation agreement, N.V. had care and custody of E., while J. had access rights. In 2009 N.V. moved to Malta with E. and began living with C.C.; they later had a child together in November 2016. From 2012, J. brought family proceedings concerning access, and relations between the parents became hostile. In July 2015, after an alleged violent incident between C.C. and J., J. accused C.C. of threatening to kill E and of having psychological problems, and sought custody of E.

On 1 October 2015, the Family Court ordered N.V. not to expose E. to C.C., with immediate effect. The order appeared to rely on a sealed Children’s Advocate report that was not accessible to the parties. N.V. asked for the order to be varied and for C.C. to be heard or assessed, but on 28 October 2015 the Family Court dismissed her requests without a hearing and without specific reasons. A court-appointed psychologist later reported, after fourteen meetings, that E. was fond of C.C., missed him, and that there was nothing untoward or dangerous in their relationship. She recommended continued contact and possible family therapy. Despite this, the decree was not revoked. As a result, N.V. and C.C., who lived together, could not live together or be together when E. was present; C.C. could not assist N.V. during her pregnancy.

The applicants brought constitutional redress proceedings in June 2016. They alleged breaches of Article 8, because the order interfered with their de facto family life by preventing them from living together, travelling together, or being together if E. was present. They also alleged Article 6 breaches: C.C. was affected by an order despite never being a party, without a hearing or investigation, despite asking to be heard; the Children’s Advocate report was sealed and inaccessible; N.V. was denied oral hearings; the decrees lacked reasoning; and there was no effective remedy because challenges returned to the same judge. In November 2016, the constitutional court invited a cautious concession, and after the baby’s birth the couple resumed living as a family.

In 2019, the first-instance constitutional court found violations of Articles 8 and 6, holding that the applicants and E. were a de facto family and that the order was not justified in E.’s best interests. It noted that the only objective fact in the violent incident was that C.C. was injured, not J. It found Article 6 violations due to the lack of a hearing for C.C., the sealed report, and the unreasoned, practically unappealable decisions. On appeal in 2020, the Constitutional Court set aside the Article 8 finding because the decree had been annulled and the parties restored to the status quo ante; it dismissed C.C.’s Article 6 complaint because he was not a party, while confirming other Article 6 violations for N.V.

Ultimately, the European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 8 positive obligations. The domestic decision-making was flawed, had failed to balance the interests at stake, and had not facilitated the couple’s reunification when the order was no longer necessary.
001-216348:
In *A.M. v. Norway* (ECtHR, Fifth Section, 24 March 2022), the applicant, a Norwegian national, complained under Articles 8 and 14 about Norway’s refusal to recognise her as the legal mother of X, a child born through gestational surrogacy in the United States.

The applicant and her then partner, E.B., began a relationship in 2002 and tried to have a child after unsuccessful IVF and egg-donation attempts. In 2010 they contacted a US surrogacy agency. Their relationship deteriorated, and E.B. moved out in September 2012; by early 2013 it was over. Nevertheless, they continued the surrogacy process. In 2013, an embryo created using E.B.’s sperm and a donor egg was transferred to a surrogate mother in the US. The applicant had no genetic or biological link to the child. A Texas court declared her the legal mother under Texas law, and she was listed as mother on X’s US birth certificate. X was born in March 2014; E.B. was the biological father.

After the family entered Norway, the authorities accepted E.B.’s paternity but refused to register the applicant as X’s mother. Under the Children Act, the woman who gives birth is the legal mother; the surrogate was therefore X’s legal mother under Norwegian law. Recognition of the applicant as a parent could only occur through adoption, but E.B. did not consent, and the temporary Surrogacy Act’s deadline had expired. The applicant’s application for recognition of maternity or adoption was rejected in 2015. She also sought contact with X. E.B. cut off contact in August 2015, and X thereafter lived with E.B. Norwegian courts, including the Oslo City Court and Borgarting High Court, dismissed her claims, finding no violation of domestic law, the Convention, or the UNCRC. The ECtHR examined her complaints under Article 8 and Article 14 in conjunction with Article 8.

The central alleged violation was Norway’s lack of legal recognition of the applicant as the intended mother of a child born through gestational surrogacy abroad, despite the US court order and birth certificate. The applicant argued that this interfered with her private life and discriminated against her compared with biological or adoptive parents, or those covered by the temporary Surrogacy Act. The Government maintained that Norwegian law, which bans surrogacy and egg donation and bases maternity on giving birth, pursued legitimate aims and fell within its margin of appreciation.

The ECtHR found Article 8 private life applicable. However, it held that the Norwegian authorities had conducted a meticulous balancing exercise between all conflicting interests, including the child’s best interests, the father’s rights, the legal mother’s status, and the general interests protected by Norway’s ban on surrogacy. The applicant had no biological ties, the relationship with E.B. had ended before implantation, and there was no shared plan to raise the child together. The child had lived with E.B. since August 2015. Norway had not overstepped its margin of appreciation. The Court also found no issue of discrimination under Article 14. There was therefore no violation of the Convention.

A.M. v. Norway (ECtHR, 24 March 2022) concerned a Norwegian woman, A.M., who sought legal recognition as the mother of X, a child born in the United States in 2014 through gestational surrogacy. X was conceived using E.B.’s sperm and an anonymous donor’s egg, implanted in an American surrogate, K.J. A.M. had no genetic or biological link to X. A.M. and E.B. had been a couple but separated before the embryo transfer; by early 2013 their relationship had ended, although they continued the surrogacy process. A Texas court declared A.M. X’s legal mother under Texan law, and her name appeared on the US birth certificate.

After X entered Norway, Norwegian authorities refused to register A.M. as his mother. Under section 2 of the Children Act, the woman who gives birth is the legal mother. A.M. could become a legal parent only through adoption, but the Adoption Act required consent from the person with parental responsibility—E.B., the biological father—and he did not consent. The temporary Surrogacy Act did not apply because the application deadline had passed and its conditions included a shared wish by the father and applicant to raise the child together, which was doubtful after the couple’s separation. A.M.’s applications for recognition of maternity or adoption were dismissed in 2015. She also sought contact rights; interim applications were rejected. X initially alternated daily between A.M. and E.B., but in August 2015 E.B. cut off contact, and X remained with E.B.

Domestic proceedings (Oslo City Court 2016; Borgarting High Court 2017) rejected A.M.’s claims to be recognized as mother and for contact. The courts found the US parentage ruling not enforceable, Norwegian law clear, adoption unavailable without E.B.’s consent, and no legal basis for contact. They considered X’s best interests, noting his settled life with E.B., the high conflict between adults, and risks of role confusion and loyalty conflict.

Before the ECtHR, A.M. complained under Article 8 (right to private and family life) and Article 14 (non-discrimination) that Norway’s refusal to recognize her as X’s mother and to grant contact violated her rights and discriminated against her as an intended/social parent in an international surrogacy arrangement. The Court held Article 8 private life applicable but found no violation. Norway had not overstepped its margin of appreciation. The domestic authorities had carried out a meticulous balancing of all conflicting interests, including A.M.’s private life, X’s best interests, E.B.’s rights, and the general public interests protected by Norway’s ban on surrogacy. The lack of biological ties, the father’s opposition to adoption, and the child’s situation justified refusing legal recognition. There was no separate Article 14 violation: the difference in treatment was objectively and reasonably justified and did not amount to discrimination. The case confirms that States may refuse legal parenthood to intended mothers in foreign gestational surrogacy cases, provided the individual circumstances are carefully balanced.

**Case: A.M. v. Norway (Application no. 30254/18), European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, Judgment of 24 March 2022 (final 24 June 2022).**

The applicant, A.M., a Norwegian national, lived with E.B. from 2002. After unsuccessful natural conception, IVF and egg-donation attempts, they pursued gestational surrogacy in the United States. Their relationship deteriorated, and E.B. moved out in September 2012; by early 2013 it had definitively ended. Nonetheless, they continued cooperating in the surrogacy process. In July 2013, an embryo created with E.B.’s sperm and an anonymous donor’s egg was transferred to a US surrogate. The child, X, was born in March 2014 in the United States. A Texas court declared A.M. the legal mother under Texas law, and she was listed as mother on X’s US birth certificate.

Under Norwegian law, however, maternity is based on the woman who gives birth. The surrogate was therefore regarded as X’s legal mother. E.B. acknowledged paternity, and Norwegian authorities registered him as X’s father with sole parental responsibility. The Tax Directorate refused to register A.M. as X’s mother, stating that recognition could only occur through valid adoption. The temporary Surrogacy Act did not apply because the application deadline had passed and the facts did not show that A.M. and E.B. had a shared wish to raise the child together. Adoption required consent from the person with parental responsibility; E.B. did not consent. A.M. applied for recognition of maternity or adoption, but the administrative authorities rejected her application. She also sought contact rights. Domestic courts, including the Oslo City Court and Borgarting High Court, upheld the refusal.

The facts showed significant conflict. After X’s birth, A.M. and E.B. initially shared care in a daily alternating arrangement, but child welfare services expressed concern about the arrangement’s stress on X. In August 2015, E.B. cut off contact between A.M. and X, and X lived with E.B. thereafter.

A.M. complained before the European Court of Human Rights under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination). She alleged that Norway’s refusal to legally recognise her as X’s mother—despite the US court ruling and her role as intended mother—violated her private life and discriminated against her. She had no biological or genetic link to X; the child was born through gestational surrogacy abroad.

The Court found Article 8 applicable in respect of A.M.’s private life. It emphasised that the case required a meticulous balancing of all conflicting interests: A.M.’s interest in legal recognition, X’s best interests, E.B.’s rights as biological and legal father, the surrogate’s legal position, and the general interests protected by Norway’s ban on surrogacy. The Court held that Norway’s margin of appreciation was not overstepped. The domestic authorities had adequately considered the child’s best interests and the complex legal and ethical issues raised by international surrogacy. It found no violation of Article 8. It further found no issue of discrimination under Article 14, as the difference in treatment was justified and did not amount to discriminatory treatment. The judgment therefore upheld Norway’s refusal to recognise the intended mother as legal parent.
001-216454:
In *Starkevič v. Lithuania* (ECtHR, 29 March 2022), the applicant, Edvin Starkevič, was a Lithuanian police officer. In October 2015, V.M., a suspect arrested for burglary, informed the police internal affairs division that the applicant had asked him to steal goods. V.M. had met the applicant and others in public on 25 October and 11 November 2015. The internal affairs division opened a pre-trial investigation into suspected abuse of office. Because the applicant was a police officer familiar with surveillance methods, a prosecutor sought court authorisation to intercept his electronic communications and to use a criminal conduct simulation model. On 16 November 2015, the Vilnius City District Court authorised secret surveillance, interception of communications, and the use of V.M. to simulate criminal acts—namely, agreeing up to twice to the applicant’s demands for stolen goods in exchange for payment, with recordings. The authorisation was based on Article 159 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

The applicant met V.M. on 7 January 2016 at a police station and again on 8 January 2016 in public, when V.M. delivered a bottle of whiskey. The applicant was arrested in flagrante delicto and given a notice of suspicion for abuse of office. He denied the accusations but refused to testify. On 29 January 2016, the police issued a disciplinary misconduct notice, alleging that he had demanded that V.M. unlawfully acquire goods, damaging the police’s prestige and possibly discrediting an officer’s name. The applicant was invited to explain but instead asked the police to rely on his pre-trial testimony, in which he had refused to testify. The disciplinary proceedings were suspended pending the criminal case.

On 9 September 2016, the prosecutor discontinued the criminal investigation, finding no *corpus delicti* because no significant criminal damage had been caused. However, the prosecutor concluded that the applicant’s actions contained elements of a disciplinary violation and forwarded the decision to the police. The applicant did not appeal. On 26 October 2016, a disciplinary report found that his actions were contrary to law, had features of a crime, breached police ethics, and discredited an officer’s name. On 27 October 2016, he was dismissed under the Statute of Internal Service. Administrative courts upheld the dismissal, noting that sufficient evidence existed even without the simulation model, including V.M.’s testimony, CCTV footage, and telephone data. The Supreme Administrative Court of Lithuania (1 September 2017) held that the misconduct notice was sufficiently informative and that the prosecutor’s discontinuation decision was valid proof in the administrative case.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained that the interception of his electronic communications and the criminal conduct simulation model, and the later use of that material in disciplinary proceedings leading to dismissal, violated Article 8 (private life) and Article 6 § 1 (fair hearing). He also initially raised the presumption of innocence. He argued that evidence obtained through criminal intelligence measures should not have grounded disciplinary liability.

The ECtHR found no violation. It held that the relevant domestic law was accessible and foreseeable, and that judicial authorisation and procedural safeguards existed. The interference with private life was proportionate and necessary in a democratic society, given the need to investigate possible official misconduct and ensure accountability. The fair hearing was not impaired: the applicant had notice of the allegations, access to the file, the right to explanations and counsel, and judicial review. His refusal to testify or explain and his failure to appeal the prosecutor’s decision were relevant. The use of the obtained information did not render the disciplinary proceedings unfair. Accordingly, there was no violation of Article 6 § 1 or Article 8.

In *Starkevič v. Lithuania* (ECtHR, 29 March 2022), the applicant, a Lithuanian police officer, was dismissed after disciplinary proceedings based on material obtained during a discontinued criminal investigation. He complained that the use of intercepted electronic communications and a criminal conduct-simulation model in the criminal investigation, and the later use of that information in disciplinary proceedings, violated his right to a fair hearing under Article 6 § 1 and his right to respect for private life under Article 8 of the Convention.

In October 2015, a burglary suspect, V.M., told the police internal affairs division that the applicant had asked him to steal goods. They met on 25 October and 11 November 2015. On 12 November 2015, internal affairs opened a pre-trial investigation into suspected abuse of office. A prosecutor sought, and on 16 November 2015 the Vilnius City District Court authorised, interception of the applicant’s electronic communications, secret surveillance, and a criminal conduct-simulation model. V.M. was allowed, no more than twice between 16 November 2015 and 13 January 2016, to agree to the applicant’s demands for stolen goods in exchange for payment, with the actions recorded. The court noted that the applicant was a police officer and that investigating his potential criminal conduct would otherwise be particularly difficult.

On 8 January 2016, the applicant met V.M., who delivered a bottle of whiskey; the applicant was arrested in flagrante delicto. He was notified that he was suspected of abuse of office under Article 228 § 2 of the Criminal Code, alleged to have occurred between 25 October 2015 and 8 January 2016 in complicity with his wife and another person. He denied the accusations and refused to testify. On 29 January 2016, internal affairs began a disciplinary investigation, alleging that he had demanded that V.M. unlawfully acquire goods for him, thereby damaging the police’s prestige and possibly discrediting an officer’s name. The disciplinary proceedings were later suspended pending the criminal investigation.

On 9 September 2016, the prosecutor discontinued the pre-trial investigation, finding no *corpus delicti*: there was no significant pecuniary or non-pecuniary damage to the State or police. However, the prosecutor considered that the applicant’s actions contained elements of a disciplinary violation and forwarded the decision to the police under Article 214 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The prosecutor relied on material from the criminal conduct-simulation model, V.M.’s and other witnesses’ testimony, CCTV recordings, telephone data, and the whiskey bottle. The applicant did not appeal that decision.

The internal affairs division then obtained access to the discontinued file. On 26 October 2016, a disciplinary report found that the applicant’s actions had been contrary to law, had features of a crime, breached police law and ethics, and discredited an officer’s name with direct intent. Under Article 62 § 1 (7) of the Statute of Internal Service, dismissal was mandatory. On 27 October 2016, the applicant was dismissed.

The applicant challenged his dismissal in administrative courts, arguing that the disciplinary and criminal grounds differed, that he had not had a proper opportunity to explain or submit evidence, that the evidence lacked a concrete basis, and that evidence from the simulation model and interception should not have been used in disciplinary proceedings, especially as disproportionate. The courts dismissed his claims. They found that the misconduct notice was sufficiently informative, that he had legal representation and an opportunity to respond but chose not to, that other evidence corroborated V.M.’s account, and that the prosecutor’s decision was valid proof in the administrative case. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld the dismissal on 1 September 2017, finding sufficient evidence even without the simulation material.

The ECtHR found no violation of Article 6 § 1 or Article 8. The domestic law was accessible and foreseeable; the interference was proportionate and necessary in a democratic society, given the constitutional duty to investigate official misconduct. The applicant had procedural safeguards, including judicial authorisation, notice, access to the file, legal representation, and an opportunity to respond.

Case Starkevič v. Lithuania (Application no. 7512/18, 29 March 2022) concerned a Lithuanian police officer, Mr Edvin Starkevič, who was dismissed after a criminal investigation into suspected abuse of office. In October 2015 police arrested V.M. for burglary. On 12 November 2015 V.M. told the police internal affairs division that the applicant had asked him to steal goods. The authorities opened a pre-trial investigation into abuse of office under Article 228 § 2 of the Criminal Code.

A prosecutor sought, and the Vilnius City District Court authorised, interception of the applicant’s electronic communications, secret surveillance, and use of a criminal conduct simulation model. V.M. was permitted, up to twice between 16 November 2015 and 13 January 2016, to agree to the applicant’s demands for stolen goods in exchange for payment. The prosecutor reasoned that because the applicant was a police officer, he knew criminal intelligence methods and avoided detection, making investigation otherwise difficult.

On 7 January 2016 the applicant met V.M. at a police station. On 8 January 2016 he met V.M. in a public place, where V.M. delivered a bottle of whiskey previously requested. The applicant was arrested in flagrante delicto. He received a notice of suspicion, said he understood its essence, denied the accusations, and refused to testify.

On 9 September 2016 the prosecutor discontinued the criminal investigation, finding no corpus delicti because no significant damage had been caused to the State or police. However, the prosecutor concluded that the applicant’s actions had features of a disciplinary violation and forwarded the file to the police. The evidence included the simulation material, V.M.’s testimony, other witnesses, CCTV recordings, telephone data, and the whiskey bottle.

In disciplinary proceedings, a misconduct notice informed the applicant of the alleged violation, including the period, the actions concerning V.M., and the possible discrediting of an officer’s name. He was asked to explain but refused, instead asking the police to rely on his pre-trial testimony, where he had also refused to testify. The disciplinary report found his actions contrary to law and incompatible with police duties. On 27 October 2016 he was dismissed for discrediting an officer’s name under Article 62 § 1 (7) of the Statute of Internal Service.

The applicant sought reinstatement, arguing that disciplinary proceedings should not rely on evidence from the criminal simulation and interception, and that his defence rights were breached. The Vilnius Regional Administrative Court dismissed his claim on 10 May 2017. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld that decision on 1 September 2017, finding the misconduct notice sufficiently informative and the applicant’s refusal to explain a matter of his own defence strategy. It also held that, even excluding the simulation evidence, other evidence sufficiently supported dismissal.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 and Article 8 that the use of intercepted communications and the criminal conduct simulation during the criminal investigation, and their use in disciplinary proceedings leading to dismissal, violated his right to a fair hearing and private life. The Court found that domestic law was accessible and foreseeable, that the applicant had procedural safeguards—notice of allegations, opportunity to respond, legal representation, and judicial review—and that the interference was proportionate and necessary in a democratic society. It found no violation of Article 6 § 1 or Article 8.

In *Arnar Helgi Lárusson v. Iceland* (App. no. 23077/19, 31 May 2022), the applicant was an Icelandic national born in 1976 who became permanently paralysed from the chest down after a 2002 accident and uses a wheelchair. He lived in Reykjanesbær. In 2015, he and an association of people with spinal injuries sued the municipality and its holding company, alleging that two municipal buildings were inaccessible to wheelchair users.

The first building, Duushús, was Reykjanesbær’s main arts and cultural centre. It was a three-storey building made of adjoining houses built in 1877 and 1954–70, extensively renovated between 2006 and 2014. The second, 88 Húsið, was a two-storey former engine house built in 1963 and used since 2004 as a municipal youth centre. The applicant sought declaratory relief requiring specific improvements. For Duushús, he requested a wheelchair lift between floors, ramps between ground-floor galleries no steeper than 1:20, and modification of the main entrance threshold. For 88 Húsið, he requested a wheelchair lift between floors, ramps no steeper than 1:20 from the car park and between rooms, and a disabled parking space within 25 metres of the entrance. He also claimed ISK 1,000,000 (about EUR 7,300) in non-pecuniary damages.

A court-appointed assessor found that Duushús had no lift between floors, a ground-floor ramp with an incline of about 1:7 and width of 96–161 cm, and a 51 mm threshold at the main entrance. 88 Húsið had no lift between floors, no lift or ramp between its halls, a ramp of about 1:9 from the car park to the entrance, and no designated disabled parking. The applicant argued that these conditions breached building regulations and hindered his and other wheelchair users’ private life on an equal basis, contrary to the Icelandic Constitution, the European Convention on Human Rights, and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD).

The domestic courts rejected the claims. The District Court (24 November 2016) found that access needed improvement but that the buildings did not violate applicable building regulations because they predated those rules. It held that the municipality had a legal duty to work towards improving access and had an initiative, but that courts should respect municipal discretion and separation of powers. The Supreme Court (25 October 2018) upheld that conclusion. It noted that the CRPD had been ratified but not incorporated, so it could not be directly relied on, though domestic law should be interpreted harmoniously with international obligations. The municipality had complied with its duty to devise an accessibility strategy and had taken steps. Responsibility for disability matters had transferred to municipalities in 2010, and municipalities had autonomy and a wide margin of appreciation in prioritising funds. The Supreme Court did not address the Convention or the equality/non-discrimination arguments.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Articles 8 and 14 about lack of access to public cultural and social buildings. The Court considered the issue within the ambit of Article 8 and examined whether Iceland had fulfilled positive obligations to make reasonable accommodations without a disproportionate or undue burden. It found no discrimination: although lack of access to the two buildings hindered the applicant’s participation in cultural activities and social events, the State had taken considerable measures to gradually achieve universal accessibility. The case illustrates the distinction between gradual accessibility duties and individual reasonable accommodation, and the margin of appreciation in local prioritisation.

In *Arnar Helgi Lárusson v. Iceland* (Application no. 23077/19, judgment 31 May 2022, final 10 October 2022), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Iceland breached Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention by failing to ensure wheelchair access to two municipal public buildings.

The applicant, an Icelandic national born in 1976, was permanently paralysed from the chest down after a 2002 accident and uses a wheelchair. He lives in Reykjanesbær. In 2015, together with an association of people with spinal injuries, he sued the municipality and its holding company, F., seeking declaratory orders requiring accessibility improvements to two buildings and ISK 1,000,000 in non-pecuniary damages.

The first building, Duushús, was a three-storey main arts and cultural centre, renovated between 2006 and 2014. The second, 88 Húsið, was a two-storey former engine house used since 2004 as a municipal youth centre. A court-appointed assessor found serious access barriers. In Duushús, there was no lift between floors, a ground-floor ramp with an incline of about 1:7 and width of 96–161 cm, and a 51 mm threshold at the main entrance. In 88 Húsið, there was no lift between floors, no lift or ramp between halls, a car park-to-entrance ramp of about 1:9, and no designated disabled parking near the entrance. The applicant argued that these conditions breached building regulations and hindered his private life on an equal basis with others, contrary to the Icelandic Constitution, the Convention, and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD).

The District Court ruled for the defendants in 2016. It accepted that access needed improvement but found no violation of applicable building regulations because the buildings predated them. It nevertheless held that the municipality had a legal duty to work towards improving wheelchair access and noted that it had an improvement initiative. The court found municipalities had a margin of appreciation in prioritising such projects, and separation-of-powers principles limited judicial intervention. The Supreme Court upheld that judgment in 2018. It noted that the CRPD had been ratified but not incorporated into domestic law, so it could not be directly relied on, although domestic law should be interpreted harmoniously with international obligations. It found the municipality had complied with its legal duty to devise and act on an accessibility strategy. Municipalities enjoyed autonomy and a wide margin in allocating funds. The Supreme Court did not directly address the Convention or the equality/non-discrimination arguments.

Before the European Court, the remaining complaint concerned Articles 8 and 14. The key issue was whether the State had made “necessary and appropriate modification and adjustments” not amounting to a “disproportionate or undue burden” so as to accommodate the applicant, and whether the lack of access discriminated against him. The Court accepted that lack of access to two clearly identified public buildings that played an important role in local cultural and social life, hindering the applicant’s participation in cultural activities and social events, fell within the ambit of Article 8. However, it found no violation of Article 14 read with Article 8. The decisive factor was that the municipality had taken other considerable measures to gradually achieve universal accessibility; the failure to adapt these two buildings did not exceed the margin of appreciation or impose a disproportionate burden. The case therefore recognised accessibility and reasonable accommodation duties but found no discrimination on the facts.

In *Arnar Helgi Lárusson v. Iceland* (ECtHR, Third Section, 31 May 2022), the applicant, born in 1976, is permanently paralysed from the chest down after a 2002 accident and uses a wheelchair. He lives in Reykjanesbær. In 2015, together with an association of people with spinal injuries, he sued the municipality Reykjanesbær and its holding company, F., challenging wheelchair access to two municipal buildings: Duushús and 88 Húsið. He sought a declaratory judgment requiring specific accessibility improvements and ISK 1,000,000 (about EUR 7,300) in non-pecuniary damages. He alleged that the lack of access hindered his private life on an equal basis with others, violating the Icelandic Constitution, the ECHR and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD).

Duushús is Reykjanesbær’s main arts and cultural centre. It comprises adjoining buildings from 1877 and 1954–70 and was extensively renovated between 2006 and 2014. A court-appointed assessor found no lift between floors; a ground-floor ramp with an incline of about 1:7 and width of 96–161 cm; and a 51 mm threshold at the main entrance. The applicant requested a wheelchair lift, ramps no steeper than 1:20 and threshold changes. 88 Húsið is a two-storey former engine house from 1963, used as a municipal youth centre since 2004. The assessor found no lift between floors, no lift or ramp between halls, a car-park ramp of about 1:9, and no designated disabled parking near the entrance. The applicant requested a lift, compliant ramps and disabled parking within 25 metres.

The Reykjanes District Court, on 24 November 2016, found that access needed improvement but that the buildings did not violate building regulations because they predated them. It accepted that the municipality had a legal duty to work towards improving access and had an ongoing initiative, but held that municipalities had a margin of appreciation in prioritising such projects and that separation-of-powers principles prevented courts from ordering specific measures. The Supreme Court upheld that judgment on 25 October 2018. It noted that the CRPD had been ratified but not incorporated into domestic law, so it could not be relied on directly, though domestic law should be interpreted harmoniously with international obligations. The municipality had complied with its duty to devise and implement an accessibility strategy and had taken steps to improve certain public buildings. Responsibility for disability matters had transferred to municipalities in 2010, and municipalities had constitutional autonomy and a wide margin in allocating funds. The Supreme Court did not address the ECHR or the applicant’s equality and non-discrimination arguments.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained under Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention that the lack of access to the two buildings discriminated against him as a wheelchair user and breached positive obligations. The Court considered the complaint within Article 8’s ambit because the buildings played an important role in local cultural and social life and the lack of access hindered his participation in cultural activities and social events. However, it found no violation of Article 14 read with Article 8. Although the State had to make necessary and appropriate modifications and adjustments not amounting to a disproportionate or undue burden, it had taken considerable measures to gradually achieve universal accessibility. On the facts, the lack of access to two clearly identified older public buildings did not amount to discriminatory treatment, given the broader accessibility efforts and the margin of appreciation. The judgment became final on 10 October 2022.
001-219944:
In **Fabbri and Others v. San Marino** (Applications nos. 6319/21 and 3 others; ECtHR, Second Section, 18 October 2022), four applicants complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that, as injured parties in criminal proceedings, they could not have their civil claims determined because the prosecutions against third parties were discontinued after becoming time-barred due to the judicial authorities’ total inactivity. Under San Marino law, victims could join criminal proceedings as civil parties and seek damages; a conviction judgment could determine civil liability. The applicants alleged that the authorities’ failure to investigate deprived them of that access to court.

**Mr Foschi** complained in August 2014 to Italian police against MKT, a Bulgarian national, alleging fraud and misappropriation of EUR 354,370. Italian investigators found insufficient evidence, considered the dispute essentially civil/commercial, and noted that most transfers occurred from San Marino to other States. In June 2015 the file was transferred to San Marino, where a criminal investigation file was opened in July 2015. The assigned investigating judge took no steps. In May 2019 the Acting Chief Justice invited submissions on the non-observance of investigation time-limits. In February 2020 a new investigating judge was assigned. In March 2020 that judge found the offence time-barred because no investigative act had occurred since the file was opened. The Prosecutor agreed, and the charge was discontinued.

**Mr Fabbri and Ms Marro** lodged a complaint in San Marino in April 2016 against N., a national of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for personal injury. They expressed their intention to join eventual proceedings as civil parties, asked to be informed if proceedings were discontinued, appointed lawyers and elected domicile. A criminal investigation file was opened, but the investigating judge took no steps. In May 2019 the Acting Chief Justice raised the investigation time-limits. In November 2020 a newly assigned investigating judge declared the charge time-barred. He noted that no investigative measures had been undertaken at all and that N. had not even been notified of the investigation; without evidence, no criminal proceedings could ensue. The Prosecutor agreed to discontinuation.

**Mr Forcellini**, a minor at the relevant time, was involved in separate proceedings. In 2015 a teacher, C., brought defamation proceedings against his parents. In March 2018 the parents were convicted, and the file was sent to investigate possible offences by third persons. A criminal investigation was opened against V. and D. for private violence and persecution against the fourth applicant. A request was made for him to join as a civil party. The assigned investigating judge took no steps. In November 2020 a newly assigned investigating judge archived the case under Article 135 of the Code of Criminal Procedure because the charge had become time-barred; no investigative acts had been carried out and no evidence had been collected. The Prosecutor agreed.

The domestic framework allowed victims to pursue civil claims within criminal proceedings and to join as civil parties. Criminal Code Article 54 set short limitation periods. Law no. 93/2008 required the investigating judge to ensure quick completion of investigations and respect peremptory time-limits. Once those expired, the file was transferred and the Chief Justice could order discontinuation. Although a time-barred crime did not automatically extinguish a separate civil action, the applicants’ opportunity to have their civil claims decided in the criminal proceedings was lost solely because the prosecutions were archived following the authorities’ inactivity. The Court therefore examined whether this breached the applicants’ right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1 (civil) and found a violation.

Fabbri and Others v. San Marino (ECtHR, Second Section, 18 October 2022) concerned four applications brought by Mr Foschi, Mr Fabbri, Ms Marro and Mr Forcellini, the latter a minor represented by his mother. All were injured parties or complainants in separate criminal proceedings in San Marino. They complained under Article 6 § 1 that they could not have their civil claims determined as entitled by law because criminal proceedings against third parties were discontinued after becoming time-barred due to the judicial authorities’ total inactivity.

In application no. 345/21, Mr Foschi lodged a complaint with Italian police in August 2014 against MKT, a Bulgarian national, for fraud and misappropriation of EUR 354,370. The file was transferred to San Marino in June 2015 and a criminal investigation was opened in July 2015. However, the investigating judge took no steps. In May 2019 the Acting Chief Justice raised the non-observance of investigation time-limits. A new investigating judge was assigned in February 2020 and found that the offence had become time-barred because no investigative act had occurred after the file was opened. The Prosecutor agreed to discontinuation, and in March 2020 the judge declared the charge discontinued due to time-bar, without prejudice to any future civil claims.

In applications nos. 6319/21 and 6321/21, Mr Fabbri and Ms Marro lodged a complaint in April 2016 against N., a national of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for personal injury. They stated their intention to join the eventual proceedings as civil parties, appointed lawyers, elected domicile and asked to be informed if proceedings were discontinued. Investigation no. 210/RNR/2016 was opened, but the investigating judge took no steps. In May 2019 the Acting Chief Justice again raised time-limit issues. In November 2020 a newly assigned investigating judge discontinued the charge as time-barred. He noted that no investigative measures had been undertaken and that N. had never even been notified of the investigation. Even assuming the charge was not time-barred, no criminal proceedings could ensue without evidence. The Prosecutor agreed.

In application no. 9227/21, defamation proceedings were initiated in 2015 by a teacher, C., against Mr Forcellini’s parents. In March 2018 the trial judge found the parents guilty and referred the file to the investigating judge to consider whether third persons should be investigated. An investigation was opened in March 2018 against V. and D. for private violence and persecution against the fourth applicant, a minor. A request to join as a civil party was submitted. The investigating judge took no steps. In November 2020 a new investigating judge archived the case under Article 135 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, finding the charge time-barred. He noted that no investigative acts had been undertaken and no evidence had been collected to substantiate an indictment. The Prosecutor agreed.

Under San Marino law, an injured party could pursue a civil claim within criminal proceedings. The applicants alleged that the authorities’ complete inactivity caused the criminal charges to become time-barred, thereby preventing the criminal court from determining their civil claims. The ECtHR examined the case as an access-to-court issue under Article 6 § 1 in its civil aspect. It found that the applicants, as injured parties, were unable to have their civil claims determined because the prosecution had become time-barred as a result of the judicial authorities’ inactivity. The Chamber therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1.

Fabbri and Others v. San Marino concerned four applicants—Mario Foschi, Stellino Fabbri, Andrea Forcellini, and Angelina Marro—who were injured parties in criminal proceedings in San Marino. They complained under Article 6 § 1 that the judicial authorities’ total inactivity caused prosecutions to become time-barred, thereby preventing their civil claims from being determined within the criminal proceedings, as domestic law allegedly allowed.

Mr Foschi complained to Italian police in August 2014 against MKT, a Bulgarian national, alleging fraud and misappropriation of EUR 354,370. Italian investigators found insufficient evidence, considered the dispute largely civil, and transferred the file to San Marino in June 2015. San Marino opened criminal investigation no. 420/2015 on 8 July 2015. The assigned investigating judge took no steps. In May 2019 the Acting Chief Justice raised the failure to observe investigation time-limits. In February 2020 a new investigating judge was assigned. On 4 March 2020 he noted that the offence had become time-barred because no investigative act had been carried out after the file was opened. The Prosecutor agreed to discontinuation without prejudice to future civil claims, and on 10 March 2020 the judge discontinued the charge as time-barred.

Mr Fabbri and Ms Marro lodged a complaint in April 2016 against N., a national of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for personal injury. They stated their intention to join the criminal proceedings as civil parties and asked to be informed if the case were discontinued. They appointed lawyers and elected domicile. Criminal investigation no. 210/RNR/2016 was opened. Again, the assigned investigating judge took no steps. In May 2019 the Acting Chief Justice invited submissions on the non-observance of investigation time-limits. On 16 November 2020 a newly assigned judge declared the charge time-barred. He noted that no investigative measures had been undertaken, that N. had not even been notified of the investigation, and that absent evidence no criminal proceedings could ensue under Article 135 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Prosecutor agreed on 20 November 2020.

Mr Forcellini’s situation arose from defamation proceedings brought in 2015 by a teacher against his parents concerning a complaint letter about her conduct toward their son, including an alleged failure to protect him from bullying. In March 2018 the trial judge convicted the parents and sent the file to an investigating judge to consider whether third persons should be investigated. On 28 March 2018, criminal investigation no. 178/RNR/2018 was opened against V. and D. for private violence and persecution against Mr Forcellini, then a minor. A request was submitted for him to join as a civil party. The assigned investigating judge took no steps. On 25 November 2020 a new investigating judge archived the case under Article 135, noting that the charge was time-barred and that no investigative acts had been carried out, so no elements supported an indictment. The Prosecutor agreed on 27 November 2020.

A common pattern emerges: in each case, after the applicants lodged complaints and investigations were opened, the responsible investigating judges remained inactive. The investigation time-limits expired. Newly assigned judges then discontinued or archived the prosecutions solely because they had become time-barred, without gathering evidence or determining the applicants’ civil claims. Under San Marino law, victims could pursue damages within criminal proceedings by constituting themselves as civil parties, but this depended on the proceedings reaching the appropriate stage. Because the prosecutions were time-barred through judicial inactivity, the applicants could not have their civil claims determined in those proceedings. The Chamber found a violation of Article 6 § 1 concerning access to court.

The European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR), Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 24 February 2022 in *Pukhyr and Others v. Ukraine*, applications nos. 10791/20 and six others. The applications were lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms on various dates. The Ukrainian Government was given notice of the applications. Because the applications raised similar subject matter, the Court found it appropriate to join them and examine them in a single judgment.

The applicants’ principal complaints concerned the inadequate conditions of their detention and the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law in that connection. They relied on Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, and Article 13, which guarantees an effective remedy before a national authority for violations of Convention rights. The applicants also raised other complaints under the Convention, which the Court considered in light of its well-established case-law. The specific facts of each applicant’s detention—including the facilities, periods, cell conditions, and other relevant circumstances—were set out in an appended table to the judgment. That table is not reproduced in the full text provided, so the individual details are not available here; however, the Court treated those appended details as the factual basis for its assessment.

In its legal analysis, the Court noted that the applicants had been kept in detention in poor conditions. It referred to the principles established in its case-law on inadequate detention conditions, particularly *Muršić v. Croatia*, and reiterated that a serious lack of space in a prison cell weighs heavily as a factor in determining whether detention conditions are “degrading” for the purposes of Article 3. Such a lack of space may disclose a violation either alone or taken together with other shortcomings. The Court also cited *Ananyev and Others v. Russia*. It observed that in leading cases such as *Melnik v. Ukraine* and *Sukachov v. Ukraine*, it had already found violations in respect of similar issues.

Having examined all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on the admissibility and merits of the complaints. It therefore considered that the applicants’ conditions of detention, as described in the appended table, were inadequate. The Court further found that the applicants did not have at their disposal an effective remedy in respect of those complaints. The other complaints raised by the applicants also disclosed issues under the Convention, given the Court’s relevant well-established case-law. Those complaints were not manifestly ill-founded within the meaning of Article 35 § 3(a) of the Convention, nor were they inadmissible on any other ground.

The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision. In essence, *Pukhyr and Others v. Ukraine* concerns Ukraine’s failure to ensure adequate conditions of detention and to provide an effective domestic remedy for such complaints. The Court’s findings align with its prior case-law identifying systemic problems in Ukrainian detention facilities, particularly regarding overcrowding and poor conditions, and the absence of effective redress at the national level. The case therefore illustrates violations of Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention in the context of detention conditions in Ukraine.

In *Pukhyr and Others v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 10791/20 and six others), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee) delivered judgment on 24 February 2022. The case concerned seven applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights on various dates. The Ukrainian Government was given notice of the applications. Because the applications raised similar subject matter, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment.

The applicants’ principal complaints concerned the alleged inadequate conditions of their detention and the lack of any effective domestic remedy in that connection. They relied on Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, and Article 13, which guarantees an effective remedy before a national authority for violations of Convention rights. The applicants also raised other complaints under the Convention.

The specific facts relevant to the alleged violations—such as the dates and duration of detention, the detention facilities, cell sizes, number of detainees, sanitary and other conditions—were set out in the appended table to the judgment, which is not reproduced in the provided text. However, the Court noted that the applicants were kept in detention in poor conditions. It referred to its established case-law on inadequate detention conditions, particularly *Muršić v. Croatia*, and reiterated that a serious lack of space in a prison cell weighs heavily in assessing whether detention conditions are “degrading” under Article 3. Such a lack of space may disclose a violation either alone or in combination with other shortcomings. The Court also cited *Ananyev and Others v. Russia* on the same principles.

The Court further observed that in the leading cases of *Melnik v. Ukraine* and *Sukachov v. Ukraine*, it had already found violations in respect of issues similar to those in the present case. Having examined all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on admissibility or merits. It therefore considered that the applicants’ conditions of detention, as described in the appended table, were inadequate. It further found that the applicants did not have an effective remedy at their disposal in respect of these complaints.

As to the other complaints raised by the applicants, the Court noted that they also raised issues under the Convention in light of well-established case-law. Those complaints were not manifestly ill-founded within the meaning of Article 35 § 3 (a) and were not inadmissible on any other ground.

The Court’s reasoning indicates findings that the applicants’ detention conditions violated Article 3 and that there was a violation of Article 13 because no effective remedy existed. The excerpt provided does not include the final operative provisions, such as just satisfaction awards, but the Court’s legal analysis clearly supports violations of Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention.

In *Pukhyr and Others v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 10791/20 and six others), the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 24 February 2022. The case concerned multiple applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates. The Ukrainian Government were given notice of the applications. The applicants’ identities and the specific details of their detention were set out in an appended table.

The applicants complained principally of the inadequate conditions of their detention and of the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law. They relied on Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, and Article 13, which guarantees an effective remedy before a national authority for Convention violations. They also raised other complaints under the Convention. Because the applications concerned similar subject matter, the Court decided to examine them jointly in a single judgment.

On the main complaints, the Court noted that the applicants had been kept in detention in poor conditions. Although the specific facts were listed in the appended table, the Court applied its established case-law on inadequate detention conditions, particularly the principles in *Muršić v. Croatia*. It reiterated that a serious lack of space in a prison cell weighs heavily as a factor in establishing whether detention conditions are “degrading” under Article 3. Such a lack of space may disclose a violation either alone or when taken together with other shortcomings. The Court also referred to *Ananyev and Others v. Russia* regarding prison overcrowding and conditions.

The Court observed that in the leading cases of *Melnik v. Ukraine* and *Sukachov v. Ukraine*, it had already found violations concerning similar issues of inadequate detention conditions and the absence of effective domestic remedies. Having examined all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion in the present applications. It therefore considered that the applicants’ conditions of detention, as described in the appended table, were inadequate and amounted to a violation of Article 3.

The Court further found that the applicants did not have at their disposal any effective remedy in domestic law in respect of those complaints. Consequently, there was also a violation of Article 13. As to the other complaints raised by the applicants, the Court noted that they too raised issues under the Convention in light of well-established case-law. Those complaints were not manifestly ill-founded within the meaning of Article 35 § 3 (a) of the Convention and were not inadmissible on any other ground. The Court therefore examined them together with the main complaints and found the applications admissible.

In sum, the case concerned systemic problems in Ukrainian detention facilities, namely overcrowding and poor conditions, coupled with the lack of an effective domestic remedy. The Court concluded that Ukraine had violated Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention in respect of the applicants.
