In *Grabovskiy v. Ukraine* (Application no. 4442/07, ECtHR, 29 November 2018), the applicant was a Ukrainian national convicted of aggravated robbery and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. The charges arose from an attack on a shop clerk, G., in Kharkiv on 22 July 2005. G. suffered multiple cuts, including a chest wound causing pneumothorax. The prosecution alleged that the applicant attacked G. and stole cash from the shop. The applicant maintained that G. owed him money; when he went to collect it, she attacked him with scissors, and he defended himself, taking money only after the alarm sounded. He never retracted this account.

The key alleged violations concerned Article 3 (detention conditions) and Article 6 (fair trial/legal assistance). On 22 July 2005, the applicant was arrested and interviewed by police. He alleged that his request for a lawyer was ignored. He was not formally made a suspect until 23 July, when his rights—including the right to legal aid—were explained and he waived counsel. A forensic examination on 25 July found injuries consistent with his account. At trial in October 2005, he again waived legal assistance and represented himself, later claiming police guards forced the waiver. He was convicted on 18 October 2005, based on his admissions, the victim’s testimony, seized money and clothing, testimony denying any debt, and a witness who saw someone resembling him near the shop.

On appeal, the applicant repeatedly requested a lawyer—in November 2005 and January 2006. In February 2006, the Vice-President of the Court of Appeal asked the regional Bar association to assign counsel, but no follow-up occurred. In July 2006, the Court of Appeal upheld the conviction. The applicant then asked the trial court to appoint a lawyer for a cassation appeal; in August 2006, the court refused, saying no legal aid grounds existed after appellate affirmance. He filed a handwritten cassation appeal in December 2006, raising procedural complaints, including lack of counsel. In February 2007, a Supreme Court judge refused leave, treating the appeal as concerning only facts and evidence.

As to detention, after arrest the applicant was held in a police station, hospital, and temporary detention facility before being transferred in August 2005 to the Kharkiv pre-trial detention centre (SIZO). He alleged severe overcrowding—a cell with 24 sleeping places holding over 50 inmates. Government records showed some cells with as little as 1.34 or 2.09 square metres per detainee, and the Government failed to specify actual occupancy or rebut the overcrowding allegations. He also complained of bugs and poor food.

The Court found a violation of Article 3 due to serious overcrowding at the Kharkiv SIZO. It found the strong presumption of a violation was not rebutted by the Government.

Under Article 6, the Court accepted the waivers of counsel after 23 July 2005 and at trial. However, there was no valid waiver at the appeal stage: the applicant repeatedly requested a lawyer, and the Court of Appeal’s request to the Bar showed it considered him entitled to free legal aid and unable to represent himself. The failure to verify whether counsel was actually assigned made the right illusory. The Supreme Court also failed to examine his procedural complaints. Additionally, the police interviewed him on 22 July before formally advising him of his right to counsel, even though sufficient grounds to suspect him existed. Considering this early limitation together with the lack of counsel on appeal, the Court found a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c).

**Grabovskiy v. Ukraine (Application no. 4442/07)**

The applicant, Mr Nikolay Aleksandrovich Grabovskiy, a Ukrainian national born in 1969, complained mainly about lack of legal assistance in criminal proceedings, degrading detention conditions, and difficulties obtaining documents for his Strasbourg application.

**Criminal proceedings and right to legal assistance**

On 22 July 2005 a sales clerk, G., was attacked in a Kharkiv shop. She suffered multiple cuts, including a penetrating chest wound causing pneumothorax, and was hospitalised. The prosecution alleged that the applicant attacked G., whom he knew, and stole cash belonging to her employer.

The applicant claimed G. owed him money. He said he went to collect the debt, but G. attacked him with scissors; while defending himself he hit her, seized the scissors, stabbed her, took money and fled when the alarm sounded.

He was arrested late on 22 July 2005. According to him, police questioned him and ignored his request for a lawyer. A police statement dated 22 July set out his version. On 23 July, arrest and rights records were drawn up; he was informed of his rights, including legal aid, and allegedly waived them. He was questioned as a suspect. A forensic examination on 25 July noted a jaw haematoma and hand cuts consistent with his account; he said police had not ill-treated him.

During trial, on 17 October 2005, he chose to defend himself and waived legal assistance. He later alleged police guards forced him to do so. The trial court refused his requests to call certain witnesses because he did not identify names or addresses. On 18 October 2005 he was convicted of aggravated robbery and sentenced to eight years, based on his trial admissions, the victim’s testimony, seized money/clothing, testimony from his girlfriend and others, and a pre-trial witness statement.

He appealed and requested a lawyer. On 6 January 2006 he repeated the request. In February 2006 the Court of Appeal vice-president asked the regional Bar association to assign a lawyer, but there was no follow-up. On 20 July 2006 the Court of Appeal upheld the conviction. He later asked for a lawyer for cassation; in August 2006 the trial court refused, saying he could hire one. His December 2006 handwritten cassation appeal complained, among other things, that he had no lawyer before the first police interview, was forced to waive counsel at trial, and was denied a lawyer on appeal. In February 2007 the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal, treating his grounds as matters of fact and evidence assessment.

**Detention conditions**

After arrest, he was held in a police station, hospital and temporary detention facility. On 17 August 2005 he was transferred to Kharkiv SIZO. He alleged severe overcrowding—a cell with 24 sleeping places holding more than 50 inmates—plus bugs and poor food. Government information showed very low personal space in some periods and did not specify actual occupancy; it did not rebut his overcrowding allegations. He had inactive tuberculosis and later minor health issues, but the main complaint was overcrowding.

**Documents for the Court**

In 2008 a lawyer examined his case file. The applicant said authorities refused to provide copies of certain documents, including witness statements, victim statement, civil claim documents, hearing transcript, his 2005 statements, and search records. He had only poor-quality copies. The Registry later requested missing documents; he supplied some but said others were not provided.

The Court found violations concerning degrading detention conditions due to overcrowding and lack of effective legal assistance, particularly at the appeal stage and during the initial police interview.

Grabovskiy v. Ukraine concerned criminal proceedings and detention following a July 2005 attack in Kharkiv. On 22 July 2005 a shop clerk, G., was attacked and seriously injured, and cash belonging to her employer was taken. The applicant claimed G. owed him money, that she attacked him with scissors, and that he defended himself before taking the money and fleeing. Police arrested him late that day. He alleged that his request for a lawyer was ignored. On 22 July he gave a police statement repeating his account. On 23 July an arrest report, rights notification, waiver of legal assistance, and suspect questioning record were prepared. He was formally treated as a suspect and waived counsel, later maintaining that his initial account was true. A forensic examination on 25 July noted a jaw hematoma and cuts on his hand consistent with his account; he said police had not ill-treated him.

At trial on 17 October 2005, the applicant again waived legal assistance, later alleging that police guards in the courtroom forced him to do so. On 18 October 2005 the Kharkiv Kyivsky District Court convicted him of aggravated robbery and sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment. The court relied on, among other things, his trial admissions, the victim’s testimony, seized money and clothing, and witness statements. It rejected his requests to call additional witnesses because he failed to identify them clearly.

The applicant appealed in November 2005 and asked the Court of Appeal to appoint a lawyer. He repeated the request in January 2006. In February 2006 the Vice-President of the Court of Appeal asked the regional Bar association to assign counsel, but no follow-up occurred. In July 2006 the Court of Appeal upheld his conviction while he was still unrepresented. He then asked the trial court to appoint a lawyer for cassation proceedings; in August 2006 that request was refused on the ground that he could hire a lawyer himself. In December 2006 he lodged a handwritten cassation appeal, raising evidentiary complaints and procedural issues, including the lack of counsel before his first police interview, the alleged forced waiver at trial, and the failure to appoint counsel on appeal. In February 2007 the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal, treating his arguments as matters of fact and evidence only.

These facts underpinned his Article 6 complaints: that he lacked legal assistance before the first police interview; that his waiver at trial was not genuinely voluntary; and that, despite repeated requests, he was not provided with counsel at the appeal or cassation stages, even though the Court of Appeal took steps suggesting it believed he needed a lawyer. The Court noted the eight-year sentence and the broad powers of the appellate court.

As to Article 3, after arrest the applicant was held in police, hospital, and temporary detention facilities before being transferred on 17 August 2005 to the Kharkiv pre-trial detention centre (SIZO). He alleged severe overcrowding—for example, a cell with twenty-four sleeping places holding over fifty inmates—along with bugs and poor food. Government records indicated extremely limited personal space, such as 1.34 or 2.09 square metres per inmate, and sometimes no information. The Government did not specify actual occupancy or rebut his overcrowding claims. The Court found a strong presumption of degrading treatment due to serious overcrowding and did not separately examine the other material conditions.

Finally, the applicant complained that domestic authorities refused to provide copies of documents needed for his application to the European Court, including witness M.’s statement, the victim’s statement, civil claim materials, a hearing transcript, his 22–23 July 2005 statements, and search/seizure records. He said he had only poor-quality copies. These facts formed part of his complaints about obstacles to exercising his Convention rights.

In *Otegi Mondragon and Others v. Spain*, five Spanish nationals complained under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights that they had not received a fair hearing before an impartial tribunal. The alleged violation arose from the composition of the Fourth Section of the *Audiencia Nacional* in the so-called “Bateragune” case, particularly because the presiding judge had previously been found to have shown bias against the first applicant, Arnaldo Otegi Mondragón.

In 2010, Otegi was convicted by the Fourth Section of *enaltecimiento del terrorismo* (encouragement of terrorism). During that trial, after Otegi refused to answer whether he condemned ETA violence, the presiding judge said she already knew he would not answer. On appeal, the Supreme Court found that this exchange revealed a preconceived idea about Otegi’s guilt and objectively justified doubts about the judge’s impartiality. It voided the judgment and ordered a retrial before a different panel. Otegi was acquitted in July 2011.

Meanwhile, in 2009, criminal proceedings had been brought against all five applicants in the Bateragune case. They were accused of creating a political party controlled by ETA and of membership or leadership in a terrorist organisation. The case was assigned to the same Fourth Section of the *Audiencia Nacional*, composed of the same judges who had sat in Otegi’s earlier trial, although the previously biased presiding judge was not the rapporteur.

Otegi challenged the entire panel. He argued that the prior finding of bias created an objective situation that contaminated the panel’s impartiality and gave rise to legitimate subjective mistrust. On 26 April 2011, a special chamber of the *Audiencia Nacional* rejected the challenge. It reasoned that the new case concerned different offences—membership in a terrorist organisation rather than encouragement of terrorism—and that the earlier question and reaction did not show prejudice.

In September 2011, the *Audiencia Nacional* convicted all applicants. Otegi and the third applicant received ten years’ imprisonment; the other three received eight years. All were disqualified from standing for election for the same period. On appeal, the Supreme Court in May 2012 reduced the sentences but rejected the impartiality complaint. By a 3–2 majority, it held that bias shown in previous, different proceedings did not automatically contaminate the judges in the new trial and that there was no further evidence of partiality. Two dissenting judges disagreed: one found a violation of the right to an impartial tribunal; the other found insufficient evidence for conviction.

The applicants then lodged *amparo* appeals. In July 2014, the Constitutional Court, by 7–5, rejected the main appeals. It found that doubts about the presiding judge were neither objectively nor subjectively justified because the earlier proceedings had a different subject matter. Five dissenting judges considered that the presiding judge’s prior conduct showed a preconceived idea about Otegi’s guilt, making her impartiality in the later proceedings questionable. A separate *amparo* by the third applicant was also rejected.

The applicants applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 14 January 2015. On 3 November 2015, the Court communicated the Article 6 § 1 impartiality complaint, declared the remainder inadmissible, and joined the applications. The Court ultimately found a violation of Article 6 § 1, holding that the domestic courts had failed to dispel objectively justified doubts about the impartiality of the Fourth Section. The prior finding of bias against Otegi, combined with the same judge’s participation in the Bateragune trial, meant the applicants’ right to an impartial tribunal had been breached.

In *Vasilevska and Bartoševič v. Lithuania* (ECtHR, 18 December 2018), two Lithuanian applicants alleged that their property rights were annulled because of mistakes by public authorities and that they had not been fully compensated, contrary to Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention.

Their grandfather, P.S., applied in 1991 to have nationalised property restored. In 1994 the authorities recognised his right, and in September 2004 the Vilnius County Administration restored 8.17 hectares of land in Kryžiokai and Naujaneriai, near Vilnius. In May and June 2005, P.S. sold 0.50 hectares to S.M. and 1.27 hectares to Ž.J. He died in July 2005, and the applicants inherited his estate.

The prosecutor later brought three claims, arguing that parts of the restored land were covered by forest of national importance, which under domestic law could only be owned by the State. The courts annulled P.S.’s and the applicants’ property rights to 2.50 hectares, 0.15 hectares sold to S.M., and 0.87 hectares sold to Ž.J., a total of 3.52 hectares. The sale agreements concerning the 0.15 and 0.87 hectares were partly annulled. As P.S.’s heirs, the applicants were ordered to repay S.M. LTL 49,500 (about EUR 14,340) and Ž.J. LTL 188,730 (about EUR 54,660). In 2013 they paid Ž.J., plus bailiff’s expenses; it was unclear whether they repaid S.M.

The applicants complained that the annulments resulted from official errors and that restitution or compensation was delayed. In 2012 the National Land Service confirmed that, after the annulments, P.S. retained a right to restoration of 3.52 hectares. It asked the applicants to choose a restitution form. The applicants claimed pecuniary damage of LTL 627,630 (about EUR 181,770), sought priority allocation of a plot in Vilnius, and refused other forms of restitution except possibly land in Kryžiokai.

In December 2012 the applicants chose four plots totalling 0.8035 hectares at a candidates’ meeting, but those plots were not allocated. In August 2014 they were listed for two plots totalling 0.203 hectares, which they said contained third-party buildings. In April 2015 they asked to suspend planning of those plots while proceedings continued. In May 2016 they chose three plots totalling 0.23 hectares. In July 2018 they refused a 0.1239-hectare plot in joint ownership. In October 2018 the authorities agreed to restore only 0.23 hectares; rights to the remaining 3.29 hectares were still unrestored.

The Government argued that the applicants had failed to cooperate and caused delays. The Court rejected that. It held that annulling the restoration to protect national forests was lawful and pursued a legitimate aim, so the annulment itself did not violate Protocol No. 1. However, correcting official errors required prompt and adequate restitution or compensation. The Court found significant periods of inactivity attributable solely to the authorities, especially December 2012–August 2014 and May 2016–July 2018, and noted that the applicants’ request for priority treatment was never addressed. Because rights to 3.29 hectares remained unrestored more than seven years after the final annulment decisions, Lithuania violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court found no separate issues under Articles 6 and 13, and rejected the Article 14 complaint as manifestly ill-founded.

The case concerns two Lithuanian applicants, Lilija Vasilevska and Tadeuš Bartoševič, whose grandfather, P.S., had land nationalized by the Soviet regime. In 1991 P.S. applied for restoration of his property rights; in 1994 the authorities recognized his right. In September 2004 the Vilnius County Administration restored 8.17 hectares of land to him in Kryžiokai and Naujaneriai, in the Vilnius city municipality. In 2005 P.S. sold 0.50 hectares to S.M. and 1.27 hectares to Ž.J. He died in July 2005, and the applicants inherited his estate.

In 2008 the prosecutor brought three claims seeking annulment of P.S.’s property rights to 2.50 hectares, 0.15 hectares, and 0.87 hectares—3.52 hectares in total—on the ground that the land was covered by forest of national importance, which, being in a city, could only be owned by the State. The domestic courts allowed the claims. They annulled P.S.’s and the applicants’ property rights to those parcels. As regards the land already sold, the courts also annulled the sale agreements and ordered the applicants, as P.S.’s heirs, to repay S.M. LTL 49,500 (about EUR 14,340) and Ž.J. LTL 188,730 (about EUR 54,660). By 2013 the applicants had paid Ž.J. plus bailiff’s expenses; it is unclear whether they paid S.M. The annulments became final in 2010 and 2011.

After the annulments, the National Land Service (NLS) confirmed that P.S. retained the right to have property rights to 3.52 hectares restored. The applicants claimed pecuniary damage of about EUR 181,770 and sought priority restitution, preferably a plot in Vilnius, while refusing other forms. In December 2012 they were included in the list for 3.52 hectares and chose four plots totaling 0.8035 hectares, but those plots were not ultimately given to them. In August 2014 they were entitled to two plots totaling 0.203 hectares, but said those contained third-party buildings and installations. In April 2015 they asked the NLS to suspend planning those two plots while court proceedings were ongoing. In May 2016 they chose three plots totaling 0.23 hectares. In July 2018 they refused a 0.1239-hectare joint-ownership plot. In October 2018 the NLS restored rights by granting 0.23 hectares, leaving 3.29 hectares unrestored.

The applicants alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, arguing that their property rights were annulled because of authorities’ mistakes and that they had not been promptly or fully compensated through restitution or money. The European Court of Human Rights found the annulment itself lawful and in the public interest—protecting forests of national importance—so correcting the authorities’ mistake was permissible. However, the authorities had to promptly and adequately restore or compensate. The Government blamed delays on the applicants, but the Court rejected that argument: the applicants participated in the process, chose plots, and refused some for arguably justified reasons. The 2015 suspension request concerned only specific plots and did not suspend the whole process. The Court identified significant periods of inactivity attributable to the authorities, especially December 2012–August 2014 and May 2016–July 2018. The applicants’ priority request was never addressed. More than seven years after the final annulments, 3.29 hectares remained unrestored. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to the authorities’ failure to act with sufficient promptness. It found no separate issues under Articles 6 and 13, and rejected the Article 14 complaint as manifestly ill-founded.

**Case Summary: Vasilevska and Bartoševič v. Lithuania**

The case of *Vasilevska and Bartoševič v. Lithuania* (Applications nos. 38206/11 and 18054/12) concerns two Lithuanian nationals, Ms. Lilija Vasilevska and Mr. Tadeuš Bartoševič, who alleged a violation of their right to the peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights. The core of their complaint was that their inherited property rights were annulled due to mistakes by state authorities, and that the subsequent restitution process was unreasonably delayed, leaving them without adequate compensation for over seven years.

The facts originate from 1991, when the applicants’ grandfather, P.S., applied to have his property rights restored after nationalization by the Soviet regime. In 2004, the Vilnius County Administration (VCA) restored his rights by granting him 8.17 hectares of land. Subsequently, P.S. sold two plots from this land: 0.50 hectares to S.M. and 1.27 hectares to Ž.J. After P.S. died in 2005, the applicants inherited his estate.

Between 2008 and 2009, the prosecutor of the Vilnius Region initiated three separate legal actions to annul P.S.’s property rights to portions of the restored land. The prosecutor argued that specific areas—2.50 hectares, 0.15 hectares, and 0.87 hectares—were covered by forest of national importance, which by law could only be owned by the State. The domestic courts ruled in favor of the prosecutor in all three cases. These final decisions, upheld by the Supreme Court in 2010 and 2011, annulled the property rights of P.S. and, consequently, the applicants. Importantly, the annulments also invalidated the sale agreements with S.M. and Ž.J., and the courts ordered the applicants, as P.S.’s heirs, to repay the buyers the amounts they had paid: approximately EUR 14,340 to S.M. and EUR 54,660 to Ž.J. The applicants paid the latter amount in 2013.

Following these annulments, the applicants were entitled to have their property rights restored for the total 3.52 hectares of land that had been taken away. However, the restitution process, managed by the National Land Service (NLS), was fraught with prolonged delays. Although the authorities contacted the applicants in 2012 and invited them to choose new plots, their efforts were ineffective. In December 2012, the applicants chose four plots totaling 0.8035 hectares, but these were never allocated. They were next offered plots in 2014, which they refused because the land contained buildings belonging to third parties. Further offers were not made until 2016, and the plots chosen then were only formally granted in October 2018. By the date of the Court’s judgment, the applicants’ rights to the remaining 3.29 hectares had still not been restored.

The European Court of Human Rights found that while the initial annulment of property rights was a lawful and legitimate action to correct the authorities’ mistakes, the state had a positive obligation to compensate the applicants promptly and adequately. The Court identified significant periods of inactivity by the authorities—particularly from December 2012 to August 2014 and from May 2016 to July 2018—that were solely responsible for the protracted restitution. The Government’s argument that the applicants caused the delays was rejected, as they had participated in the process and refused plots for valid reasons. Consequently, the Court held that the Lithuanian authorities failed to act with sufficient promptness, violating the applicants’ rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court found no separate issues under Articles 6 and 13 and rejected the complaint under Article 14 as manifestly ill-founded.

**Summary of Danilczuk v. Cyprus (Application no. 21318/12)**

The case of *Danilczuk v. Cyprus* originated from an application lodged against the Republic of Cyprus by Mr. Robert Tadeusz Danilczuk, a Polish national, on 8 April 2012. The applicant alleged that the conditions of his detention at Nicosia Central Prisons violated Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. The European Court of Human Rights communicated this complaint to the Cypriot Government on 18 November 2013, while declaring the remainder of the application inadmissible.

The key facts concern the applicant's detention from 14 September 2010 to 18 May 2012. He was initially held on remand in Block 5 until his conviction on 11 January 2011 for offences including burglary, theft, and unlawful residence. He was subsequently sentenced to concurrent prison terms and transferred to Block 2B, where he remained until 5 October 2011, before being moved to the renovated Block 2A until his release.

The applicant's central allegations focused on severe overcrowding and inadequate sanitary facilities. He claimed that personal space in the cells ranged from only 0.5 to 1.7 square metres. He described the cells as cold and poorly lit, with no in-cell toilets. Critically, he alleged that when cells were locked, particularly at night, he sometimes had to wait two to three hours to use a toilet, forcing him to urinate into a bottle and defecate into a waste bag.

The Government provided a different account, detailing the specific blocks and occupancy rates. In Block 5, the applicant likely had 3.10 square metres of personal space. In Block 2B, conditions varied; depending on whether he was in a double cell, a larger cell, or a dormitory, his personal space could have ranged from 1.8 to 4.99 square metres. In the renovated Block 2A, he would have had 4.9 square metres. The Government maintained that the prison had central heating and that detainees could move freely outside their cells from 6 a.m. until at least 5 p.m. Regarding the toilet issue, they stated that following a 2008 report by the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT), the practice of switching off cell bells at night was discontinued, and an order was issued to ensure detainees had access to toilets when necessary.

The case facts were further contextualized by several official reports. The CPT's 2012 report (based on a 2008 visit) found severe overcrowding, with an occupancy rate over 152%, and noted that most inmates lacked night-time toilet access, forcing them to use makeshift receptacles—a practice the CPT deemed degrading. A 2011 report by the Cypriot Ombudsman echoed these findings, confirming complaints that detainees were obliged to relieve themselves in bottles and waste bags due to deactivated cell bells. While a later CPT report from 2014 welcomed renovations to Block 2, it noted that serious overcrowding persisted in other parts of the prison and that difficulties in accessing toilets at night continued to be reported.

The applicant was released on 18 May 2012 following a presidential decree suspending his sentence. The case before the Court centered on whether these conditions, particularly the lack of timely access to sanitary facilities and the resulting need to use bottles and bags, amounted to degrading treatment in violation of Article 3.

Bradshaw and Others v. Malta concerned 24 Maltese nationals and a Maltese company who jointly owned a four-storey, 864-square-metre property at 274 Republic Street, Valletta, known as the King’s Own Band Club (“KOBC”). The property is on a prime site in Malta’s capital. In 1946, the applicants’ ancestors voluntarily leased it to KOBC for GBP 500 per year, then about EUR 1,164.69. From 1955, Maltese law specifically regulated leases to band clubs. Under the Civil Code and the Re-letting of Urban Property (Regulation) Ordinance, the applicants were obliged to renew the lease annually, could not terminate it, and could not increase the rent. Part of the property was used as a band club; another part operated as a restaurant and bar, allegedly generating substantial income for the caterer. The applicants claimed the 2014 market rental value was EUR 269,100 annually; the Government estimated EUR 93,000.

In 2009, the Civil Code was amended to allow rent increases and to set a cut-off date—2028—for existing protected commercial leases. These amendments did not affect band-club leases. The applicants alleged this was discriminatory: commercial landlords could eventually regain possession or charge higher rent, while they remained bound to yearly renewal and controlled rent. In 2014, new regulations for club leases raised rent by 10% annually until 2016, then 5% until 2023, and thereafter by inflation; they also required an additional 5% of income from economic activities. Even so, the rent paid was only EUR 2,876.26 in 2015 and EUR 3,017.20 in 2016—far below market value and below the EUR 17,000 the club received from subletting part of the ground floor.

In domestic constitutional proceedings, the First Hall found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and awarded EUR 300,000 in damages. In 2015, the Constitutional Court reversed, holding that the lease had been entered into voluntarily, that pacta sunt servanda applied, and that the 2009 amendments did not affect the applicants. A retrial request was rejected in 2016.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the rent-control regime was an ongoing, disproportionate interference with their property rights. They complained under Article 14 that they were discriminated against compared with commercial landlords, because commercial leases had been liberalised in 2009 while band-club leases were not. The Government argued that any interference was lawful, pursued the legitimate aim of protecting Malta’s cultural identity, and that the 2014 regulations had restored a fair balance. It also contended that the applicants’ ancestors had knowingly accepted the lease conditions.

The Court found that there was an interference with the applicants’ right to use their property. It accepted that the regime was lawful and pursued a legitimate aim—supporting the cultural and social role of band clubs. However, it held that the fair balance was not struck: the rent was extremely low, the lease was indefinitely renewable, the applicants could not set or effectively increase rent, there were no adequate procedural safeguards, and part of the premises was used commercially. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It examined the Article 14 complaint in conjunction with that provision but found no violation of Article 14.

In *Bradshaw and Others v. Malta* (Application no. 37121/15), 24 Maltese nationals and a Maltese company jointly owned a four-storey, 864-square-metre property at 274 Republic Street, Valletta, known as the King’s Own Band Club (“KOBC”). In 1946 their ancestors voluntarily leased the property to KOBC for GBP 500 annually (about EUR 1,164.69). Under Maltese rent-control legislation, particularly the 1955 amendments specifically covering band clubs, the owners were required to renew the lease annually, could not terminate it, and could not increase the rent. Part of the building was used as a band club, while another part operated as a restaurant/bar generating significant income. By 2014 the applicants claimed the market rental value was EUR 269,100 annually, later EUR 350,000; the Government valued it at EUR 93,000. The KOBC sublet part of the ground floor for EUR 17,000 annually.

In 2009, amendments to the Civil Code liberalised many commercial leases by allowing rent increases and setting a 2028 cut-off date, but they excluded band-club leases. In 2014, new Regulations increased band-club rents by 10% yearly until 2016, then 5% yearly until 2023, followed by inflation-based increases, plus 5% of the club’s income from economic activity. The resulting rents were only EUR 2,876.26 in 2015 and EUR 3,017.20 in 2016—still far below market value.

The applicants brought constitutional proceedings in 2011, alleging an ongoing violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention because they were deprived of adequate compensation and control over their property, and Article 14 discrimination because commercial landlords had been freed from automatic renewal while band-club landlords had not. The Civil Court (First Hall) found a violation of Protocol No. 1 and awarded EUR 300,000 damages. In 2015 the Constitutional Court reversed, holding there was no violation because the original lease had been entered into voluntarily and *pacta sunt servanda* applied; the 2009 amendments did not affect the applicants’ position. A retrial request was rejected in 2016.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants maintained both complaints. The Court rejected the Government’s objection that the applicants lacked victim status, finding that although their ancestors had knowingly accepted the lease, they could not have foreseen decades of inflation and property-price increases. The rent-control scheme and mandatory renewal constituted an interference with the applicants’ property rights, amounting to control of use under the second paragraph of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court accepted that the measure pursued a legitimate aim—supporting the cultural and social role of band clubs—and was lawful. However, it found no fair balance. The rent was extremely low for a prime multi-storey property, the lease could continue indefinitely, and there were no effective procedural safeguards. The 2014 reforms still left the applicants receiving only a tiny fraction of market rent, while the club profited from commercial activities. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

As to Article 14, the applicants alleged discrimination compared with commercial leases liberalised in 2009. The Court considered Article 14 applicable and admissible, but ultimately found no violation, as the difference in treatment could be justified by the special cultural and social role of band clubs and the State’s gradual, piecemeal approach to rent reform.

The case of *Bradshaw and Others v. Malta* (Application no. 37121/15) concerns twenty-four Maltese nationals and a Maltese company who jointly own a four-storey property at 274 Republic Street, Valletta, known as the "King's Own Band Club" (KOBC). The building measures 864 square metres and occupies a prime site in Malta's capital city.

The property originally belonged to the applicants' ancestors, who in 1946 voluntarily leased it to the KOBC for GBP 500 annually (approximately EUR 1,164.69). In 1955, Maltese legislation specifically regulating the lease of property to band clubs was introduced. Under Maltese law, the applicants were obliged to renew the lease annually and were prohibited from increasing the rent or terminating the agreement. Part of the property operated as a band club, while another part functioned as a restaurant and bar generating substantial income—approximately EUR 150,000 or more annually for the caterer. The KOBC sub-let part of the ground floor for EUR 17,000 annually.

The applicants alleged that their property's market rental value in 2014 was EUR 269,100 annually, while the Government estimated it at EUR 93,000. Despite these valuations, the applicants received only EUR 1,164.69 annually—roughly EUR 97 per month for a multi-storey property in a prime location.

In 2009, amendments to the Civil Code allowed rent increases and established cut-off dates (2028) for existing protected commercial leases. However, these amendments did not apply to properties leased as band clubs. The applicants argued this constituted discrimination, as commercial landlords were freed from perpetual renewal obligations while they remained bound indefinitely. In 2014, new Regulations increased club rents by 10% annually until 2016, then 5% until 2023, after which rents would follow inflation. Tenants also paid an additional 5% of income from commercial activities. As a result, the applicants received EUR 2,876.26 in 2015 and EUR 3,017.20 in 2016—still merely around 3% of the Government's own estimated market rental value.

In 2011, the applicants filed constitutional redress proceedings. The Civil Court (First Hall) found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 in 2013, awarding EUR 300,000 in damages, but found no discrimination. On appeal, the Constitutional Court overturned the violation finding in 2015, holding that because the 1946 lease was entered into voluntarily, the applicants could not allege a rights violation, invoking *pacta sunt servanda*. A retrial application was rejected in 2016.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged ongoing interference with their property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, and discrimination under Article 14 read in conjunction with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. They emphasized that the lease would never terminate, that they could never enjoy their property as owners, and that the 2014 Regulations failed to remedy the disproportionality. The Court found the complaint admissible, rejecting the Government's objections on *ratione temporis* and victim status, and ultimately held that the Maltese State failed to strike a fair balance between general community interests and the applicants' property rights.

In **Falzon v. Malta** (Application no. 45791/13), the applicant was Michael Falzon, a Maltese former member of parliament and government minister who later wrote weekly opinion columns. The case concerned his complaint under **Article 10** of the European Convention on Human Rights that Maltese courts had fined him for defamation, thereby violating his freedom of expression.

The dispute arose from a public speech in May 2007 by Dr Michael Falzon (“M.F.”), deputy leader of the Malta Labour Party. M.F. stated that he had received an anonymous email and threatening letters and had complained to the Commissioner of Police (“CoP”). He described contacting the CoP, asking for an investigation, and authorising the police to proceed against whoever was responsible. A journalist, K.S.N., then published an article about the email and an alleged admirer being questioned by police.

On 13 May 2007, the applicant published an opinion piece in *Maltatoday* entitled **“Policing one’s enemies.”** The article opened by referencing the Stasi and questioned how political parties viewed the police. It criticised M.F. for persuading the CoP to investigate what the applicant described as a trivial anonymous email. It suggested the CoP had offered to act discriminatorily depending on who the culprit turned out to be. It further stated that police had traced the email’s sender, impounded his computer, and required him to sign daily at police headquarters even though he was not accused of a crime. The applicant asked whether M.F. had “successfully used the Police Force to control the freedom of an innocent, law-abiding private citizen whom he suspected could be a political enemy.” He also questioned whether the police were interfering in Labour’s internal politics and whether M.F. carried more influence with the CoP than the Deputy Prime Minister. He called for an inquiry by the Minister of the Interior.

M.F. sued the applicant and the newspaper editor for libel under the Press Act. The applicant defended the article as fair comment, value judgment, and substantially true based on M.F.’s own public statements. He argued that M.F., as a public figure, was subject to wider limits of acceptable criticism. The CoP testified that he had not been persuaded or influenced by M.F.; M.F. had requested a normal appointment, shown him a threatening letter, and later provided the email. The CoP passed the matter to the Criminal Investigation Department and said it received no priority.

The Court of Magistrates found the applicant guilty of defamation and ordered him to pay €2,500 in damages; the editor was also liable for €1,000. It accepted that politicians faced wider criticism but found the article damaged M.F.’s reputation. It rejected the defences because it was not proved that M.F. had manipulated the CoP, used the police for personal aims, or acted as a “deus ex machina” pulling strings.

The Court of Appeal upheld the judgment. It held that the applicant’s assumptions were not fair comment and exceeded just criticism. M.F. had a right to report the matter to police, and the attack was not supported by factual evidence. Freedom of expression had to respect objective veracity and restraint.

The applicant then brought constitutional redress proceedings, alleging a breach of Article 10. The Civil Court dismissed the claim, finding that the article implied abuse, even if the word “uses” did not exactly mean “manipulate.” The Constitutional Court also dismissed the appeal. It accepted that the interference was prescribed by law but found no Article 10 violation. Politicians had wider criticism limits, but still retained reputation rights. The court found that the article contained factual assertions disguised as questions, such as “Has not M.F. ...”, and that allegations of illegitimate or abusive influence had not been proved. The fine was not considered particularly severe. The applicant’s Article 10 complaint was communicated to the Maltese Government; other complaints were declared inadmissible.

In May 2007 Dr Michael Falzon (M.F.), deputy leader of the Malta Labour Party, publicly stated he had received an anonymous email and threatening letters and had reported the matter to the Commissioner of Police (CoP). Referencing a film about the Stasi, he questioned the use of police in politics. He called for an inquiry.

The applicant defended the article as fair comment and value judgment based on M.F.’s public statements, arguing politicians accept wider criticism. The CoP testified M.F. had not influenced him: M.F. made a normal appointment, showed a threatening letter, requested investigation, and the email was passed to police/CID. The Court of Magistrates found defamation, ordering the applicant to pay EUR 2,500. It held it was not proved that M.F. manipulated the CoP, used police for personal aims, or was a deus ex machina pulling police strings. The Court of Appeal upheld the judgment: the applicant’s assumptions were not fair comment; an ordinary reader would see them as factual allegations that M.F. illegitimately influenced police, not objectively reasonable, balanced or corroborated. M.F. had a right to report the matter.

He argued his column was legitimate criticism of a public figure and that the ordinary courts had invented allegations such as “manipulation”, “pressure” and “deus ex machina”. The Civil Court dismissed the claim, finding the article implied abuse by M.F., the Stasi reference regrettable, and a fair balance struck. The Constitutional Court dismissed his appeal. It found the defamation award was an interference prescribed by law and justified: politicians had wider criticism limits but still retained reputation rights. Value judgments could not conceal untrue factual assertions; questions such as “Has not M.F. …” could be factual allegations. Since the claim that M.F. illegitimately or abusively influenced the CoP was unproven and the fine was not severe, there was no Article 10 violation. The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 8 July 2013, complaining that the domestic defamation judgments and fine breached his freedom of expression.

**Summary of Delecolle v. France (Application no. 37646/13)**

The case of *Delecolle v. France* concerns an application lodged against the French Republic under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alleging a violation of Article 12 (the right to marry). The applicant, Mr. Roger Delecolle, a French national born in 1937, was placed under an "enhanced protective supervision" order (*curatelle renforcée*) by a French guardianship judge on 23 June 2009. This five-year measure was imposed due to medical evidence of slight cognitive impairment, psychological fragility, and concerns about his ability to manage his substantial personal assets, estimated at around 6,000,000 euros.

Under French Civil Code Article 460(1), a person under such a supervision order can only marry with the authorisation of their supervisor, or failing that, the guardianship judge. In late 2009, Mr. Delecolle sought his supervisor's permission to marry his partner, M.S., a friend since 1996 who had become his partner in 2008. The supervisor refused, citing a lack of background knowledge about the applicant. This refusal initiated a series of legal proceedings.

The guardianship judge, after ordering a social inquiry and a psychiatric examination, dismissed the applicant's request on 24 June 2010. The judge reasoned that while the applicant was attached to M.S., the marriage was not in his interest. Key factors included the applicant's intellectual disorders, which, while not negating his capacity to consent, rendered him incapable of understanding the financial and legal consequences of marriage. The judge also noted a serious family conflict between the applicant's daughter and M.S., both of whom accused each other of being primarily interested in his fortune. A social inquiry report highlighted this financial stake and suggested the applicant viewed marriage as a way to secure companionship and avoid ending his life alone.

The Paris Court of Appeal upheld this decision on 6 September 2011, emphasising the applicant's failing perception of financial realities, his past unreasonable spending (e.g., 250,000 euros on apartment renovations), and a will drafted in M.S.'s favour shortly after his wife's death. The Court of Cassation later dismissed his final appeal on 5 December 2012. The applicant also unsuccessfully challenged the constitutionality of Article 460(1) before the Constitutional Council, which declared the provision constitutional, noting it did not prohibit marriage but merely regulated it to protect vulnerable individuals.

The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 5 June 2013, alleging that the refusal to authorise his marriage violated his right to marry under Article 12. He argued that the requirement for authorisation was a disproportionate restriction on a fundamental freedom. The Government countered that the measure was necessary to protect the applicant's interests and ensure his consent was informed.

The Court, after considering the case, held that there was no violation of Article 12. It found that the restrictions on the applicant's right to marry, based on his lack of full legal capacity, fell within the State's margin of appreciation. The Court noted that the domestic decisions were fully reasoned, based on extensive medical and social evidence, and were subject to judicial review with adversarial proceedings. Consequently, the restrictions were not deemed arbitrary or disproportionate.

**Case: Delecolle v. France (ECtHR, 25 October 2018)** concerned an alleged violation of Article 12 of the European Convention on Human Rights—the right to marry. The applicant, Roger Delecolle, a French national born in 1937, was placed in June 2009, at age 72, under enhanced protective supervision (*curatelle renforcée*) for five years. The measure was initially sought by his adoptive daughter. Medical reports noted slight cognitive impairment, psychological fragility, and vulnerability, though not dementia. The guardianship judge considered protection necessary, particularly because of the applicant’s substantial personal assets and difficulty managing his affairs.

The applicant wished to marry M.S., a friend he had known since 1996 and his partner since 2008. Under Article 460(1) of the French Civil Code, a person under supervision may marry only with the authorisation of the supervisor or, failing that, of the guardianship judge. In December 2009 the supervisor refused authorisation, saying she had known the applicant for only a few months and lacked sufficient background to approve the marriage.

The guardianship judge then ordered a social inquiry and a psychiatric assessment. The psychiatrist concluded in January 2010 that the applicant suffered from intellectual disorders. Although he could consent to marriage, he was considered incapable of understanding its consequences for his property and finances. A social report by the UDAF highlighted a major family conflict with a financial stake. The applicant’s daughter and M.S. accused each other of being mainly interested in his fortune, and it was unclear whether the applicant was being influenced. The report noted that the applicant saw marriage as a way to ensure companionship and assistance in daily life.

On 24 June 2010 the guardianship judge refused to authorise the marriage. The judge accepted the applicant’s attachment to M.S. but found this insufficient. The judge noted former alcoholism, possible continued drinking, uncertainty over the financial implications, and the serious conflict between the applicant’s daughter and M.S. The judge concluded that the planned marriage was not in the applicant’s interests. The Paris Court of Appeal upheld that decision on 6 September 2011. It found that the applicant’s serious disorders had severely affected his judgment, that he suffered from anosognosia, and that he could not plan a joint life or understand the financial and legal implications of marriage. It also cited concerns about his management of assets, including expensive work on the family apartment and a draft will favouring M.S. The Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal in December 2012, after the Constitutional Council upheld Article 460(1), holding that it did not prohibit marriage but subjected it to authorisation and judicial review.

The applicant complained that the authorisation requirement violated Article 12. The Government argued that it protected vulnerable adults and ensured valid consent. The applicant died in February 2016, and M.S. was permitted to continue the proceedings. The ECtHR found no violation. It held that Article 12 permits capacity-based restrictions and that states have a margin of appreciation. The applicant was not absolutely barred from marriage; the restriction was based on his legal protection order. The domestic decisions were reasoned and subject to adversarial judicial review, and the applicant had been heard and had used available remedies. The Court concluded that the restriction was neither arbitrary nor disproportionate.

Delecolle v. France (ECtHR, 25 October 2018) concerned the Article 12 right to marry of a man placed under enhanced protective supervision. Roger Delecolle, born in 1937, was placed in 2009 at age 72 under enhanced *curatelle renforcée* for five years on his adopted daughter’s request. Medical opinions noted slight cognitive impairment, psychological fragility, and vulnerability, including inability to manage property and financial affairs. His challenge to the protective measure failed in December 2009, though the court allowed some autonomy, such as holding a bank account and withdrawal card.

In 2009 Delecolle sought his supervisor’s authorisation to marry M.S., a friend since 1996 and partner since 2008. They emphasised the religious importance of marriage. On 17 December 2009 the supervisor refused, saying she had known Delecolle for only a few months. The guardianship judge then ordered a social inquiry by the UDAF and a medical opinion. A January 2010 psychiatrist found intellectual disorders; while Delecolle could consent to marriage, he could not understand its property and financial consequences. The June 2010 UDAF report described a major family conflict with financial stakes: Delecolle’s daughter and M.S. accused each other of pursuing his fortune. Delecolle appeared to see marriage as securing assistance and companionship and avoiding loneliness.

On 24 June 2010 the guardianship judge refused authorisation. Although Delecolle’s attachment to M.S. was undisputed, the judge found it insufficient. She noted alcohol history and possible drinking, concerns about a possible break-up and loneliness, and unclear financial implications amid family conflict. The Paris Court of Appeal upheld this on 6 September 2011. It found serious disorders had affected Delecolle’s judgment and that anosognosia prevented him from planning joint life and understanding the financial/legal implications of marriage. It cited unreasonable management since cohabitation: €250,000 apartment works after his wife’s death, questionable storage of furniture, a draft will favouring M.S., assets around €6 million, and deteriorated relations with his daughter. It concluded he could not give informed consent. The Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal on 5 December 2012, after the Constitutional Council (QPC no. 2012-260) held Article 460(1) of the Civil Code constitutional: it did not prohibit marriage but subjected it to supervisor or judge authorisation, with adversarial judicial review and appeal.

Delecolle alleged a violation of Article 12, complaining that his marriage was subject to his supervisor’s or the guardianship judge’s authorisation. He died on 4 February 2016. His partner M.S. sought to continue the case. The Government asked the Court to strike it out, arguing she was not an heir or relative. The ECtHR allowed continuation: M.S. had a legitimate interest, their long cohabitation constituted family life under Article 8, and the issue—restrictions on marriage for protected adults—transcended the applicant.

On the merits, the ECtHR found no violation of Article 12. The right to marry is fundamental, but national laws may impose formal and substantive conditions, including capacity, provided the essence of the right is not impaired. Unlike Article 8, Article 12 does not require “necessity” or “pressing social need”; the Court asks whether the interference was arbitrary or disproportionate. Persons under supervision are not deprived of marriage; prior authorisation reflected restricted legal capacity. The supervision order followed medical reports and was appealable. The refusal was reasoned, based on medical and social evidence, and made in adversarial proceedings. The Constitutional Council found Article 460(1) preserved marriage and was proportionate given marriage’s personal and pecuniary effects. The authorities had a margin of appreciation to protect a vulnerable adult. Thus the restrictions were not arbitrary or disproportionate. The PACS comparison was extraneous and also required supervisor assistance. No Article 12 violation was found.
001-181859:
**Case: Aganikyan v. Armenia (Application no. 21791/12), Judgment of 5 April 2018**

The applicant, Hrayr Aganikyan, an American national born in 1953 and living in Yerevan, complained under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights that the length of criminal proceedings against him exceeded the “reasonable time” requirement. On 16 November 2016, that complaint was communicated to the Armenian Government, while the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The criminal proceedings began on 30 December 2004, when an investigator instituted proceedings against the applicant for usury under Article 213 of the Criminal Code. In January 2005, the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court ordered a search of his apartment. On 20 June 2005, he was formally charged with professional usury causing dire financial consequences; he was ordered not to leave his residence, and in June 2005 his property was confiscated for security. In August 2005, the prosecutor refused to approve the indictment and returned the case for further investigation. In October 2005, separate fraud proceedings were opened and merged with the usury case. Handwriting examinations were ordered in December 2005, with results received in January 2006.

In March 2006, the charges were expanded to include large-scale fraud, extortion, usury, and forgery of evidence. The District Court refused to detain the applicant, but on appeal the Court of Appeal ordered his detention for two months. Further search and bank-secrecy warrants were granted in March and April 2006. The indictment was approved in July 2006, and the case reached the District Court on 24 July 2006. Trial was set for 18 August 2006.

The trial phase was marked by extensive delay. Between August 2006 and October 2007, twelve hearings were adjourned because victims or witnesses failed to appear; ten were adjourned due to prosecutor applications or the court’s own motion; nine were adjourned after granting the applicant’s applications; and on three occasions absent witnesses or victims were ordered to be brought by force. In July 2007, the applicant was released on bail. In October 2007, the presiding judge’s powers were suspended; a new judge took over in November 2007, and the trial began anew.

From November 2007 to December 2010, forty hearings were adjourned because the applicant or his lawyer was absent or because they lodged applications; thirty-five were adjourned due to absent victims or witnesses or their applications; and thirty-two were adjourned because the prosecutor’s applications were granted or the court adjourned on its own motion. On five occasions, the court ordered absent witnesses or victims to be brought by force. The charges were further amended in August 2009 and October 2010.

On 31 January 2011, the District Court convicted the applicant on five counts of fraud, extortion, usury, and forgery of evidence. He was sentenced to nine years’ imprisonment, confiscation of half his property, and a fine of 400,000 Armenian drams. On 3 October 2011, the Criminal Court of Appeal upheld the judgment. On 21 November 2011, the Court of Cassation declared his appeal on points of law inadmissible.

The relevant period thus lasted from 30 December 2004 to 21 November 2011—almost six years and eleven months across three levels of jurisdiction. The pre-trial investigation and appeal phases were relatively short, but the District Court phase lasted about four and a half years. The Government argued that the case was complex, involving eight victims, thirty-four witnesses, multiple forensic examinations, extensive evidence, and 136 hearings. The applicant blamed delays on repeated non-appearance of victims and witnesses, prosecutor absences, the restart of the trial, and repeated amendments of charges.

The Court found that although there were no especially long periods of inactivity by the authorities, the case was adjourned 136 times, the trial restarted after one year and three months, and charges were amended during trial. The District Court could have controlled adjournments and secured attendance. Complexity alone did not justify the entire length. The Court therefore held that the proceedings were excessively long, violating Article 6 § 1.

In *Aganikyan v. Armenia* (Application no. 21791/12, judgment of 5 April 2018), the European Court of Human Rights considered a complaint by Mr Hrayr Aganikyan, an American national born in 1953 and living in Yerevan, that the length of criminal proceedings against him violated the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant was represented by A. Ghazaryan; the Armenian Government by G. Kostanyan. Only the length-of-proceedings complaint was communicated to the Government; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The criminal proceedings began on 30 December 2004, when an investigator opened a case against the applicant for usury under Article 213 § 1 of the Armenian Criminal Code. On 10 January 2005, the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan ordered a search of his apartment. On 20 June 2005, he was formally charged under Article 213 § 2 with professional usury causing dire financial consequences for victims, and was ordered not to leave his residence. His property was confiscated for security on 23 June 2005. On 10 August 2005, the indictment was sent to the prosecutor, but on 15 August 2005 the prosecutor refused to approve it and returned the case for further investigation.

On 15 October 2005, a separate fraud case under Article 178 § 2 was opened and merged with the usury case. Handwriting examinations were ordered in December 2005, with results in January 2006. On 7 March 2006, the charges were substantially amended to include fraud in large and particularly large amounts, extortion, usury, and forgery of evidence. That same day, the investigator sought the applicant’s detention; the District Court refused, but on 28 March 2006 the Court of Appeal reversed that decision and ordered two months’ detention. Search and bank-secrecy warrants were granted in March and April 2006. The prosecutor approved the indictment on 14 July 2006, and the District Court received the case on 24 July 2006. Trial was set for 18 August 2006.

The trial phase proved lengthy. Between 25 August 2006 and 11 October 2007, twelve hearings were adjourned because victims or witnesses were absent; ten were adjourned due to prosecutor applications or the court’s own motion; and nine due to applications by the applicant. On 9 July 2007, the applicant was released on bail. On 15 October 2007, the presiding judge’s powers were suspended; a new judge took over on 1 November 2007 and the examination of the case began anew. Between 21 November 2007 and 23 December 2010, forty hearings were adjourned because of the applicant or his lawyer, thirty-five because of absent victims or witnesses, and thirty-two because of prosecutor applications or the court’s own motion. Charges were further amended in 2009 and 2010.

On 31 January 2011, the District Court convicted the applicant on five counts—fraud, extortion, usury, and forgery of evidence—sentencing him to nine years’ imprisonment, confiscating half his property, and imposing a fine. The Criminal Court of Appeal upheld the judgment on 3 October 2011, and the Court of Cassation declared his appeal inadmissible on 21 November 2011.

The total proceedings lasted almost six years and eleven months across three levels. The Government argued the case was complex, involving eight victims, thirty-four witnesses, forensic examinations, and extensive evidence. The applicant argued that many adjournments were caused by the State’s failure to secure witnesses and by charge amendments, and that the trial restarted after the judge changed. The Court found that although the pre-trial and appeal phases were relatively quick, the District Court phase lasted about four and a half years, with 136 adjournments, a restart, and repeated charge amendments. It held that the length was excessive and violated Article 6 § 1.
