**Summary**

*Cuenca Zarzoso v. Spain* (Application no. 23383/12) concerned a Spanish national, Mr Miguel Cuenca Zarzoso, born in 1930 and living in the San José district of Valencia since 1962. He alleged that Spain had breached his right to respect for his home under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights because of excessive night-time noise caused by licensed bars, pubs, and discotheques near his home.

Since 1974, Valencia City Council had allowed licensed entertainment premises to operate in the area. In 1983 the Council resolved not to permit any further such premises, but the resolution was never implemented and new licences continued to be granted. A 1993 university study commissioned by the Council found that night-time weekend noise levels in San José were notably higher than the legal norm. In 1994 the applicant became president of the local neighbourhood association and lodged complaints and requests to withdraw licences. The Council responded that some premises were inactive, others were not especially noisy, and many licences had expired.

In 1996 the Council adopted a municipal ordinance on noise and vibrations. In December 1996, published in January 1997, the area where the applicant lived was designated an “acoustically saturated zone.” In July 2000, at the applicant’s request, the pub in his building’s basement was required to install a noise limiter. Nevertheless, noise levels did not decrease, and the applicant installed double glazing and air conditioning to cope with having his windows closed.

In 1999 the applicant brought a State liability claim before the City Council, relying on constitutional rights to life, physical integrity, privacy, and inviolability of the home. After no response and then a denial by the Council, he complained to the Valencia High Court. The evidence included municipal reports from 1998 and 2000 stating that night noise had exceeded 65 decibels before the saturated-zone declaration and that limits were still exceeded after corrective measures. An expert report measured street noise up to 70 decibels and estimated bedroom noise at 50–60 dBA, compared with a recommended night-time maximum of 30 dBA. Medical evidence linked his anxiety to the noise, and a court-appointed expert found that nocturnal noise necessarily altered his sleep and produced an anxious depressive syndrome. The City Council disputed that noise inside the applicant’s specific flat was proven to exceed limits, noting variations by height and aspect and its enforcement efforts.

In June 2003 the High Court dismissed the claim, finding no causal link because there was no evidence that noise in the applicant’s particular flat exceeded limits. It noted that he had replaced his windows before requesting an interior measurement under the ordinance and that his fourth-floor flat would likely be less noisy. The applicant filed an *amparo* appeal, initially dismissed in October 2004. After the ECtHR’s judgment in *Moreno Gómez v. Spain*, the public prosecutor appealed and the Constitutional Court admitted the case in January 2005. In September 2011 the Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the cases were not identical, that the applicant had not proved excessive noise inside his flat, that the Council had adopted specific measures, and that his health problems were not shown to be directly caused by noise. Three judges dissented, arguing that under *Moreno Gómez* the decisive factor was proof of excessive street noise in an acoustically saturated area, not measurements inside the individual home, and that the expert report confirmed health effects.

The alleged violation therefore centred on whether Spain failed to protect the applicant’s home and private life from severe, prolonged noise pollution, and whether the domestic courts imposed an excessive evidentiary burden by requiring proof of noise levels inside his specific dwelling.

**Summary of *Cuenca Zarzoso v. Spain* (Application no. 23383/12)**

The case of *Cuenca Zarzoso v. Spain* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr. Miguel Cuenca Zarzoso, a Spanish national born in 1930, who has resided in the San José district of Valencia since 1962. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to respect for private life and the home, due to prolonged exposure to excessive noise pollution caused by licensed entertainment venues in his neighbourhood.

Since 1974, Valencia City Council permitted numerous bars, pubs, and discotheques to operate near the applicant’s home. Despite a 1983 resolution to stop granting new licences in the area, the resolution was never enforced, and additional licences were issued. A 1993 study by the Polytechnic University of Valencia, commissioned by the City Council, confirmed that night-time noise levels in San José significantly exceeded legal limits. In 1997, the area was officially designated an “acoustically saturated zone” under a municipal ordinance adopted in 1996.

The applicant, as president of the local neighbourhood association from 1994, campaigned extensively to address the noise issues. He requested the withdrawal of business licences and sought compensation for expenses incurred, including installing double glazing and air conditioning to mitigate the noise and heat from keeping windows closed. Despite some measures, such as requiring a pub in his building to install a noise limiter in 2000, noise levels remained excessive.

The applicant submitted multiple reports to domestic courts, including municipal environmental reports from 1998 and 2000 confirming that night-time noise limits were still exceeded, an expert report estimating indoor noise levels at 50–60 decibels (well above the recommended 30 decibels), and a medical report linking his anxiety and depressive syndrome to the noise. A court-appointed medical expert also confirmed that nocturnal noise disrupted his sleep and caused psychiatric issues.

In 2001, the applicant filed a complaint with the Valencia High Court of Justice, seeking State liability. The High Court dismissed his claim in 2003, finding no causal link between noise pollution and damage, as the applicant had not proven that noise levels inside his specific flat exceeded legal limits. The court noted that his fourth-floor flat would experience less noise and criticised him for replacing windows without requesting an official noise measurement.

The applicant then lodged an *amparo* appeal before the Constitutional Court, initially dismissed in 2004. Following the European Court’s judgment in *Moreno Gómez v. Spain* (2004), which addressed similar noise pollution issues, the public prosecutor successfully sought reconsideration. However, in 2011, the Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal, distinguishing the case from *Moreno Gómez* on the grounds that the applicant had not proven excessive noise inside his home, the City Council had taken specific measures, and his health issues were not directly linked to noise. Three judges dissented, arguing that the Court’s case-law required only proof of excessive street noise, not indoor measurements, and that prolonged exposure to unbearable noise violated constitutional rights.

The applicant’s central complaint before the European Court was that Spain failed to protect his right to respect for his home under Article 8, given the authorities’ failure to effectively address the severe and persistent noise pollution despite its known and documented impact on his health and quality of life.

Miguel Cuenca Zarzoso, a Spanish national born in 1930, has lived in the San José district of Valencia since 1962. He lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 13 April 2012, alleging that Spain had breached his right to respect for his home under Article 8 of the Convention because of prolonged, severe noise pollution from licensed premises near his home.

Since 1974, Valencia City Council had authorised bars, pubs and discotheques in his neighbourhood. After residents complained, the Council resolved in 1983 not to permit further licensed premises in the area, but that resolution was never implemented and new licences continued to be granted. A 1993 study by the Polytechnic University of Valencia found that weekend night-time noise in San José was notably above legal limits. In 1994 the applicant became president of the neighbourhood association and lodged claims and requests to withdraw business licences. The Council replied that some premises were inactive, others were not especially noisy, and many licences had expired.

In 1996 the Council adopted a municipal Ordinance on noise and vibrations. In 2000, at the applicant’s request, a pub in the basement of his building was required to install a noise limiter. In 1996–1997 the area was designated an “acoustically saturated zone” under a Council resolution published in 1997. Despite this, noise pollution did not decrease. The applicant replaced his windows with double glazing and installed air conditioning because he had to keep windows closed in summer.

In 1999 he brought a preliminary State liability claim before the City Council, relying on constitutional rights to life and physical integrity and to privacy and inviolability of the home. He sought compensation for expenses and pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. After the Council denied the claim, he complained to the Valencia High Court in 2001.

The evidence included municipal reports from 1998 and 2000 stating that night-time noise had exceeded 65 decibels and that permitted limits were still being exceeded after the saturated-zone declaration and corrective measures. An expert report estimated street and in-home noise at around 70 decibels, with a front bedroom at about 50 decibels, sometimes 60 decibels, compared with a recommended night-time maximum of 30 dBA. However, the expert acknowledged this was a general estimate and had not measured inside the dwellings. A medical report said the applicant suffered anxiety due to excessive noise, and a court-appointed expert found that nocturnal noise altered his sleep and produced an “anxious depressive syndrome,” though the intensity could not be fully ascertained without sleep studies.

The City Council argued that the applicant had not proved that noise in his particular flat exceeded limits, that noise perception varies by height and aspect, and that it had enforced noise legislation. In 2003 the High Court dismissed his complaint, finding no causal link because there was no evidence his flat exceeded noise limits; he had replaced windows without prior measurement; and his fourth-floor flat would likely be less affected.

The applicant then filed an amparo appeal before the Constitutional Court under several constitutional provisions, including Articles 15 and 18 § 2. It was initially dismissed in 2004, but after the ECtHR’s Moreno Gómez v. Spain judgment (2004), the public prosecutor appealed and the Constitutional Court admitted the amparo in 2005. In 2011 the plenary dismissed it, holding that the cases were not identical, that the applicant had not proved excessive noise inside his flat, that the Council had adopted measures, and that his health problems were not directly proven to result from noise. Three judges dissented, arguing that under Moreno Gómez, proof of excessive street noise in an acoustically saturated area was sufficient, and that prolonged avoidable and unbearable noise violated the right to privacy and home. The applicant’s Article 8 complaint therefore centred on the State’s alleged failure to protect his home from persistent night-time noise.
001-183542:
**T.K. v. Lithuania (Application no. 14000/12)** concerned a Lithuanian national, granted anonymity, who alleged that: (1) the police’s taking of his spectacles after arrest amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment; and (2) his criminal trial was unfair, particularly because he could not examine certain witnesses. The European Court of Human Rights communicated those complaints to the Government; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The applicant lived with V.K. and two boys, Ra.K. and Ro.K. In October 2011 he was convicted of causing physical pain to the boys and attempting to influence a witness; he was released after time served. In July 2011 V.K. complained that the applicant had shown pornographic films to the children and sexually abused them in 2009. On 22 August 2011 the boys were questioned by a pre-trial investigation judge and a psychologist. They described sexual abuse. Ro.K., then seven, said his mother had told him to testify and that if he and his brother stayed silent, their father would be released and their mother imprisoned. V.K. was present at the police station but not in the questioning room. Later forensic psychological and psychiatric examinations concluded that the boys could remember the events and had no tendency to fantasise, but noted the two-year delay and influence from both parents; the experts recommended no further questioning because of stress.

The applicant was arrested on 23 November 2011. In 2012 he was charged with sexual assault of a young child and possession of child pornography. The trial court convicted him and sentenced him to eleven years’ imprisonment. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction in December 2013, and the Supreme Court refused to examine his further appeals in 2014.

As to the fair-trial complaint, the applicant repeatedly asked the prosecutor and courts to confront or cross-examine V.K., arguing that she had coached the children and had motives to fabricate the accusations. The prosecutor refused a confrontation during the pre-trial investigation, and the courts upheld that refusal. At trial, V.K. could not be located; police reported that she was hiding from authorities and had no registered residence. The Court of Appeal initially agreed to summon her, and the prosecutor supported that step, but summonses failed and she never appeared. The appellate court proceeded without her, noting that the trial court had not relied on V.K.’s testimony when convicting the applicant. The applicant also requested examination of experts, teachers, neighbours and doctors, and inclusion of material from an earlier criminal case allegedly showing V.K. had lied or coached the children; those requests were refused as irrelevant or unnecessary. His conviction rested mainly on the boys’ statements to the pre-trial judge and experts, plus testimony from Z.S. and V.F. He alleged a breach of Article 6 § 3 (d) of the Convention.

As to the spectacles complaint, during the applicant’s arrest on 23 November 2011 a body search resulted in his spectacles, telephone and comb being taken. While in pre-trial detention he complained that the spectacles were not returned. In April 2012 the prosecutor ordered the investigator to resolve the matter, and the spectacles were returned on 20 April 2012. The applicant later brought civil proceedings, claiming difficulties in reading, writing and communicating, and worsened eyesight. The first-instance court awarded him EUR 1,000 in non-pecuniary damages, finding the taking unlawful and degrading. The appellate court acknowledged there had been no legal basis for taking the spectacles, but reduced the remedy to an acknowledgment: there was no proof they were prescribed, no medical evidence of worsened eyesight, he had managed to write without them, and he could have requested their return earlier. The Supreme Court refused his appeal. He alleged that the deprivation amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment.

T.K. v. Lithuania (Application no. 14000/12) concerns a Lithuanian national, T.K., who alleged two main Convention violations: inhuman and degrading treatment after police confiscated his spectacles following arrest, and an unfair criminal trial because he could not examine key witnesses. The application was lodged on 29 February 2012, and in July 2015 the Court communicated the complaints concerning degrading treatment and trial fairness, including the right to examine witnesses; the remainder was declared inadmissible.

As to the first complaint, T.K. was arrested on 23 November 2011. During a body search, police took his telephone, comb and spectacles. He was placed in pre-trial detention in Kaunas. T.K. complained that without his spectacles he had difficulty reading and writing, communicating, and that his eyesight deteriorated. He wrote to the Seimas Committee on Legal Affairs in November 2011, and the prosecutor later said an investigator would resolve the issue. On 20 March 2012 T.K. again requested their return; on 6 April 2012 the prosecutor ordered an inquiry, and the spectacles were returned on 20 April 2012. He then sued for damages. In February 2015 the Vilnius City District Court awarded him EUR 1,000, finding the confiscation unlawful and capable of degrading his human dignity. On appeal, the Vilnius Regional Court accepted that there had been no legal basis for taking the spectacles, but noted there was no proof they had been medically prescribed, no medical evidence that his eyesight worsened, that detainees had access to medical care, and that T.K. had managed to write while without them. It also found he had not requested their return until March 2012 and held that the acknowledgement of unlawful conduct was sufficient compensation. The Supreme Court refused to examine his further appeal in May 2016.

The second complaint arose from criminal proceedings in which T.K. was convicted of sexual assault of his two young sons, Ra.K. and Ro.K., and possession of child pornography. The boys’ mother, V.K., complained in July 2011 that T.K. had shown the children pornographic films and sexually abused them in 2009. On 22 August 2011 the boys were questioned by a psychologist in a special room. V.K. was present at the police premises but did not take part in the questioning itself. The boys described sexual abuse. One son, Ro.K., said his mother had told him not to perjure himself and that if he and his brother stayed silent, their father would be released and their mother imprisoned. Later forensic psychological and psychiatric experts found the boys could remember events and did not tend to fantasise, but noted the two-year lapse and both parents’ influence: the mother’s direct and indirect influence, and the children’s fear of the applicant. The experts recommended no further questioning to avoid stress.

T.K. repeatedly asked for confrontations with V.K. and the children, a new forensic examination, a polygraph test, a psychiatric examination of V.K., and inclusion of material from an earlier criminal case. Prosecutors refused, and courts upheld those refusals. At trial, V.K. could not be located despite summonses and police efforts; she was on maternity leave and had no registered address. The Court of Appeal initially agreed to summon her but ultimately proceeded without her, finding all efforts exhausted and noting the trial court had not relied on her testimony. T.K. was convicted largely on the boys’ prior statements, expert reports, and testimony from Z.S. and V.F. His appeals complaining that he could not cross-examine V.K. and other witnesses, and that evidence was wrongly excluded, were rejected; the Supreme Court refused his points-of-law appeals. These facts underpin his fair-trial complaint.

**T.K. v. Lithuania** (Application no. 14000/12, judgment of 12 June 2018) concerned a Lithuanian national serving a prison sentence. The case raised complaints under the Convention about (1) inhuman and degrading treatment after police took his spectacles following arrest, and (2) unfair criminal proceedings, particularly his inability to examine key witnesses.

The criminal proceedings arose after V.K., the applicant’s partner and mother of two boys, complained in July 2011 that the applicant had shown the children pornography and sexually abused them in 2009. The children, who had been placed in care, were questioned in August 2011 by a judge and a psychologist. They described sexual abuse. One boy stated that his mother had told him not to give false testimony, and that if he and his brother remained silent, their father would be released and their mother imprisoned. Later forensic psychologists found the boys could remember the events and did not tend to fantasise, but noted the two-year delay and both parents’ influence. They recommended no further questioning because it would be too stressful.

The applicant was arrested in November 2011 and charged with sexual assault of a young child and possession of child pornography. During the pre-trial investigation and trial, he repeatedly sought to challenge the evidence. He requested confrontations with V.K., the children and other witnesses; a polygraph test; fresh psychological examinations of the children; a psychiatric examination of V.K.; and admission of material from an earlier criminal case allegedly showing that V.K. had coached the children and had a prior perjury conviction. Prosecutors refused most requests, citing the children’s vulnerability, lack of contradictions, and irrelevance.

At trial, V.K. could not be located despite summons. The Court of Appeal initially agreed to summon and examine her, and the prosecutor supported this, but she remained missing. The appellate court continued without her, finding that all possible measures had been taken. The applicant’s conviction was based mainly on the children’s statements to the pre-trial judge and forensic experts, as well as testimony from Z.S. and V.F. He was convicted and sentenced to eleven years’ imprisonment. His appeals were rejected. His main fair-trial complaint was that he could not cross-examine V.K., a key accuser and alleged influencer of the children, and that courts refused to admit evidence or witnesses supporting his defence.

Separately, during the applicant’s arrest on 23 November 2011, police confiscated his spectacles in a body search. They were not returned until 20 April 2012, despite his requests. He alleged this amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment: without glasses he had difficulty reading, writing and communicating, and his eyesight worsened. In domestic civil proceedings, a district court initially awarded him EUR 1,000 in non-pecuniary damages, finding the deprivation unlawful and degrading. The appellate court later held that merely acknowledging the illegality was sufficient compensation, because it was not proven that the spectacles were medically prescribed, he could have sought medical assistance, he had managed to write, and he had delayed requesting their return.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the communicated issues were whether the taking of the applicant’s spectacles violated Article 3 and whether the criminal proceedings, especially the inability to examine V.K. and other witnesses, violated Article 6 fair-trial guarantees, including the right to examine witnesses.

**M.T. v. Estonia (Application no. 75378/13)** concerned the continued coercive psychiatric detention of O.T. and the procedural safeguards surrounding review of that detention.

The applicant, M.T., a stateless person living in Tallinn, was the mother and court-appointed guardian of her son O.T., born in 1984. In May 2010, the Harju County Court found that O.T. had restricted active legal capacity. Relying on a forensic psychiatric opinion of March 2010, it concluded that he suffered from permanent paranoid schizophrenia and could not understand or control his actions. M.T. was appointed his guardian.

In October 2010, O.T. committed acts of a sexual nature against a ten-year-old girl and threatened to kill her. In the resulting criminal proceedings, a forensic psychiatric expert confirmed the earlier diagnosis and found that O.T. posed a danger to society and needed coercive psychiatric treatment. In May 2011, the Harju County Court terminated the criminal proceedings and ordered coercive psychiatric treatment, which began in June 2011.

In December 2012, M.T. applied to the Tartu County Court to discontinue O.T.’s coercive treatment or replace inpatient treatment with outpatient treatment. She relied on a June 2012 opinion by a medical committee composed of O.T.’s attending doctor and Dr E.K., acting head of the hospital’s coercive treatment department. That opinion stated that contact with O.T. was deficient, his answers were sparse, he denied the offence and did not consider himself mentally ill, and he remained dangerous. M.T. argued that the opinion was not impartial and requested an independent expert assessment.

In February 2013, the Tartu County Court dismissed her application. It relied on a December 2012 opinion by another medical committee, composed of O.T.’s attending doctor and Dr S.K., head of the coercive treatment department. That opinion stated that O.T.’s condition was unchanged, that he had deficient contact, sparse and incoherent answers, inappropriate laughter, and faked psychotic experiences, and that continued treatment was necessary. The court found no need for an additional expert opinion, since Article 403 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure allowed reliance on the medical committee’s opinion.

M.T. appealed. In March 2013, the Tartu Court of Appeal quashed the decision because the first-instance court had not held oral proceedings. At the rehearing in May 2013, O.T. received State-funded legal aid and a lawyer. The court heard Dr S.K., who said O.T. had not recovered, did not adhere to treatment, accused his mother of poisoning him, and could not be treated as an outpatient. O.T. said he understood nothing and did not wish to make statements. The County Court again dismissed the application.

M.T. appealed, arguing that O.T.’s dangerousness had not been established, that no independent expert assessment had been carried out, and that the hospital committee opinions were superficial and repetitive. She also invoked Article 5 § 4 of the Convention, arguing that O.T. himself should have been able to initiate review proceedings at reasonable intervals. She pointed to Article 402-1 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and its explanatory annex, under which persons subjected to coercive psychiatric treatment had no such right.

In July 2013, the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It held that independent expert examination was mandatory only when coercive treatment was initially ordered, not when discontinuation or replacement was sought. The danger posed by O.T. had already been established in 2011. In September 2013, the Supreme Court refused M.T.’s request for legal aid for a further appeal, stating that she had no personal rights to protect in the proceedings and that O.T.’s legal aid lawyer could appeal instead.

The ECtHR application alleged that the review proceedings concerning O.T.’s continued confinement did not meet Article 5 procedural requirements, particularly regarding the use of expert medical evidence and O.T.’s inability to initiate such review himself.

M.T. v. Estonia (Application no. 75378/13, ECtHR, 23 October 2018) concerned M.T., a stateless woman in Tallinn, acting on behalf of her son O.T. In 2010 the Harju County Court found O.T. (born 1984) had restricted active legal capacity due to permanent paranoid schizophrenia and appointed M.T. as his guardian. In October 2010 O.T. committed sexual acts against a ten-year-old girl and threatened to kill her. Criminal proceedings were terminated in May 2011, and based on forensic psychiatric evidence that he posed a danger to society, the court ordered coercive inpatient psychiatric treatment, which began in June 2011.

In December 2012 M.T. applied to the Tartu County Court to discontinue O.T.’s coercive treatment or replace inpatient treatment with outpatient treatment. She relied on a June 2012 medical committee opinion by O.T.’s attending doctor and the acting head of the coercive treatment department, Dr E.K. That opinion stated that contact with O.T. was deficient, he denied the offence, did not consider himself mentally ill, and needed continued treatment because he was dangerous. M.T. argued that the opinion was not impartial and requested a new independent expert assessment.

In February 2013 the County Court dismissed her request. It relied on a December 2012 medical committee opinion by O.T.’s attending doctor and the head of the coercive treatment department, Dr S.K. That opinion said O.T.’s mental condition was unchanged: he had deficient contact, sparse answers, incoherent statements, inappropriate laughter, occasional anger, and had faked psychotic experiences. The committee concluded continued psychiatric treatment was needed. The court found no additional expert opinion necessary because Article 403 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure allowed reliance on the medical committee’s opinion.

The Court of Appeal quashed that decision because the first-instance court had not held oral proceedings. On rehearing in May 2013, O.T. had a State-funded lawyer. The court heard Dr S.K., who said O.T. had not recovered, did not understand what was happening, did not adhere to treatment, accused his mother of poisoning him, and could not be treated as an outpatient. O.T. stated he did not understand anything and did not wish to make statements. The County Court again dismissed the request, finding no reason to doubt the committee or Dr S.K.

M.T. appealed. In July 2013 the Court of Appeal dismissed, holding that an independent expert examination was mandatory only when coercive treatment was initially ordered, not in later review proceedings. The danger and preconditions had been established in 2011, and another expert report would be irrelevant because O.T.’s condition and treatment adherence had not improved and doctors excluded outpatient treatment. M.T. then sought legal aid before the Supreme Court, but in September 2013 the Supreme Court refused, saying she had no personal rights at issue and O.T.’s legal aid lawyer could have appealed.

The applicant complained to the ECtHR that the review of O.T.’s continued confinement did not meet the procedural requirements of Article 5 of the Convention. The key alleged violations were: (1) reliance on expert medical evidence from hospital committees and treating doctors, without an independent expert despite impartiality concerns; and (2) O.T.’s inability to initiate review proceedings himself. Domestic law allowed requests by close persons, guardians, health-care providers, or counsel, but not expressly by the patient, though courts could order expert assessment if necessary. The CPT had recommended that forensic patients be able to request judicial review at reasonable intervals and that such reviews include objective medical expertise. O.T.’s treatment was ultimately terminated in September 2016.

**Summary of M.T. v. Estonia (Application no. 75378/13)**

The case of *M.T. v. Estonia* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by a stateless person, M.T., on behalf of her son, O.T. The applicant alleged that the review proceedings regarding her son's continued confinement in a psychiatric institution violated Article 5 of the Convention, specifically concerning the use of expert medical evidence and her son's inability to initiate such proceedings himself.

The key facts are as follows: O.T., born in 1984, was diagnosed with permanent paranoid schizophrenia. In May 2010, the Harju County Court determined he had restricted active legal capacity and appointed his mother, M.T., as his guardian. In October 2010, O.T. committed sexual acts against a ten-year-old girl and threatened to kill her. A forensic psychiatric expert confirmed his diagnosis, stating he posed a danger to society and required coercive psychiatric treatment. In May 2011, the criminal proceedings were terminated, and the court ordered O.T. to undergo coercive psychiatric treatment, which commenced in June 2011.

In December 2012, the applicant requested the Tartu County Court to discontinue O.T.'s coercive treatment or replace inpatient treatment with outpatient care. She challenged the impartiality of an opinion from the hospital's medical committee, which included O.T.'s attending doctor, and sought an independent expert assessment. The County Court dismissed her application in February 2013, relying on another medical committee opinion from December 2012, which concluded O.T. still required continued psychiatric treatment. The court held that no additional expert opinion was necessary under Article 403 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, as the medical committee's opinion sufficed as evidence.

Following an appeal, the Tartu Court of Appeal quashed the decision in March 2013 due to a procedural error (lack of oral proceedings) and remitted the case. In April 2013, State-funded legal aid was granted to O.T., and a lawyer was appointed. At the re-hearing in May 2013, the court heard Dr. S.K., head of the coercive treatment department, who stated O.T. had not recovered and outpatient treatment was not feasible. The County Court again dismissed the request, finding no reason to doubt the medical committee's conclusions. The Court of Appeal upheld this decision in July 2013, noting that an independent expert examination was mandatory only for initially ordering coercive treatment, not for reviewing its continuation.

The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court, reiterating her complaints and requesting legal aid. In September 2013, the Supreme Court refused her request, stating she did not have rights in the proceedings that could be protected via legal aid and that O.T.'s appointed lawyer could have lodged an appeal. The applicant complained that the review proceedings failed to meet Article 5 procedural requirements, particularly regarding expert evidence and her son's inability to initiate reviews himself.

The case also refers to relevant domestic law, including the Penal Code and Code of Criminal Procedure, which outline the conditions for coercive psychiatric treatment and the procedures for its alteration or termination. Notably, Article 402-1 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure did not list the patient as someone entitled to request a change in treatment, as they were presumed mentally incapacitated. However, subsequent case law (including a 2017 Supreme Court judgment) clarified that a patient's personal request should be treated as an application for legal aid.

International law considerations include reports from the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT), which recommended that forensic patients should be able to request judicial reviews at reasonable intervals and that regular judicial reviews should be automatic. The CPT noted that Estonian law did not explicitly allow forensic patients to request judicial review, though in practice such requests were examined.

The Government later informed the Court that O.T.'s psychiatric treatment was terminated in September 2016.

**Gafà v. Malta** (App. no. 54335/14) concerned Kenneth Gafà, a Maltese national arrested on 11 December 2010 on suspicion of murdering his former partner. On 13 December 2010 he was charged with wilful homicide and remanded in custody. From arraignment until August 2012, he filed ten bail requests, all rejected. After he had been held for the maximum statutory period, he became entitled to bail under Article 575(6)(a)(iii) of the Criminal Code, namely after twenty months for a crime punishable by nine years’ imprisonment or more.

On 22 August 2012 the Court of Magistrates granted bail subject to stringent conditions: he had to appear at all hearings; not go abroad or abscond; not contact prosecution witnesses; not commit voluntary crimes; report daily at the District Police Station between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m.; observe a curfew from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m.; notify address changes; deposit EUR 15,000 in the court registry; and provide a personal guarantee of EUR 25,000. Breach of any condition would forfeit EUR 40,000 to the State.

The Attorney General appealed, arguing the conditions were too lenient, and sought a higher deposit and a ban on the applicant entering locality R, where the victim and her family lived. The applicant objected and requested a reduction, saying he had been detained over twenty months, was unemployed, and could not pay. On 7 September 2012 the Criminal Court rejected the Attorney General’s request to increase the deposit but added the condition that the applicant could not be in the vicinity of locality R. It rejected the applicant’s reduction request.

The applicant made further requests to reduce the deposit in October and December 2012 and January/February 2013. He argued that he remained in detention solely because he could not afford the deposit, despite being legally entitled to bail, and noted that the main witnesses had already been heard. The Attorney General opposed, citing the seriousness of the crime, risk of absconding or tampering, and the victim’s family’s fear. The courts repeatedly refused to reduce the amount, finding it balanced the seriousness of the offence and the need to secure compliance.

On 22 July 2013 the applicant asked the court to accept his mother and relatives as surety instead of the deposit, offering inherited property valued at EUR 95,000. On 2 August 2013 the court accepted his mother as surety by hypothec over the property. On 6 August 2013, after he signed the personal guarantee and his mother effected the hypothec, he was released after thirty-two months of pre-trial detention.

In constitutional redress, his first complaint about detention exceeding fifteen months was rejected in 2012. His second complaint, filed in February 2013, alleged that the “exorbitant” deposit made bail illusory. The First Hall rejected it on 3 July 2013, finding he had not sufficiently documented his finances or shown an objective inability to find a surety. The Constitutional Court rejected his appeal on 31 January 2014, holding that the onus was on him to prove the deposit was excessive; he had only later proposed his mother as surety although the property was available earlier; and EUR 15,000 was justified given the crime’s seriousness, especially since a surety was permitted.

Later, on 7 April 2014, he was found to have breached bail conditions and bail was revoked. On 26 January 2015 an indictment issued, and on 20 July 2015 he pleaded guilty and was sentenced to thirty-five years’ imprisonment.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged a breach of Article 5 § 3, claiming that the excessive bail conditions—particularly the EUR 15,000 deposit—prevented him from effectively enjoying bail and prolonged his detention. The complaint concerning detention following the grant of bail was communicated to the Government; the remainder was declared inadmissible.

In *Gafà v. Malta* (Application no. 54335/14, judgment 22 May 2018), the applicant, Kenneth Gafà, alleged a violation of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention because the bail conditions imposed after he became entitled to release were so excessive—particularly the €15,000 cash deposit—that he remained in detention despite being granted bail.

On 11 December 2010, Gafà was arrested on suspicion of murdering his former partner. On 13 December 2010, he was charged with wilful homicide and remanded in custody. Between arraignment and August 2012, he made ten unsuccessful bail requests. Under Article 575(6)(a)(iii) of the Maltese Criminal Code, after twenty months’ detention for an offence punishable by nine years or more, he became entitled to bail.

On 22 August 2012, the Court of Magistrates granted bail subject to stringent conditions: he had to appear at all hearings; not leave Malta or abscond; not contact prosecution witnesses; not commit voluntary crimes; report daily to a District Police Station between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m.; observe a curfew from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m.; notify address changes within twelve hours; deposit €15,000 in the court registry; and sign a personal guarantee of €25,000. Any breach would forfeit €40,000 to the State. Because Gafà could not pay the €15,000 deposit, he remained in custody.

The Attorney General appealed, arguing the conditions were too lenient and seeking a higher deposit and a ban on entering locality R, where the victim’s family lived. On 7 September 2012, the Criminal Court rejected the higher deposit but added the locality ban and rejected Gafà’s request to reduce the deposit. Gafà repeatedly applied to reduce it in October and December 2012 and January/February 2013. He argued he had been detained over twenty months, was unemployed, had received only unemployment benefits in 2009–2010, and could not afford the sum. He submitted tax assessment forms. The courts refused, citing the seriousness of the charge, potential punishment, risk of tampering, and his duty to provide full checkable information on his finances and to prove objective inability to pay or find a surety.

In July 2013, Gafà proposed that his mother and relatives stand as surety using inherited property valued at €95,000. On 2 August 2013, the court accepted his mother as surety through a hypothec over the property. On 6 August 2013, after signing the €25,000 personal guarantee and the hypothec, he was released after thirty-two months’ pre-trial detention.

In constitutional redress, Gafà complained that the “exorbitant” deposit made bail ineffective. The Civil Court rejected the claim on 3 July 2013; the Constitutional Court upheld that decision on 31 January 2014. They held that while bail amounts must be proportionate to the accused’s financial circumstances, the burden lay on the applicant to provide sufficient evidence of his means and inability to find a surety. They found he could have proposed his mother’s property earlier and that the €15,000 deposit was justified by the offence’s gravity and the availability of a surety.

The ECtHR communicated the Article 5 § 3 complaint concerning detention following the grant of bail; the remainder was inadmissible. Later, Gafà breached bail, his bail was revoked in April 2014, and in July 2015 he pleaded guilty and was sentenced to thirty-five years’ imprisonment. The key issue for Strasbourg was whether the bail conditions, especially the cash deposit, were so excessive as to amount to continued detention incompatible with Article 5 § 3.

Kenneth Gafà, a Maltese national, was arrested on 11 December 2010 on suspicion of murdering his former partner. On 13 December 2010 he was charged with wilful homicide before the Court of Magistrates and remanded in custody. Between his arraignment and August 2012, he filed ten bail requests, all of which were rejected. An earlier constitutional complaint alleging that his pre-trial detention exceeded a reasonable time under Article 5 § 3 was rejected in 2012.

After the maximum statutory detention period under Article 575(6)(a)(iii) of the Criminal Code expired, Gafà became entitled to bail. On 22 August 2012 the Court of Magistrates granted bail subject to strict conditions: he had to appear at all hearings; not go abroad or abscond; not contact prosecution witnesses; not commit a voluntary crime; report daily to a District Police Station between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m.; observe a curfew from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m.; notify address changes; deposit €15,000 in the court registry; and provide a personal guarantee of €25,000. Any breach would forfeit €40,000 to the State.

The Attorney General appealed, seeking a higher deposit and a ban on the applicant entering locality R, where the victim’s family lived. On 7 September 2012 the Criminal Court refused to increase the deposit but added the locality R restriction and rejected Gafà’s request to reduce the deposit.

Because Gafà could not pay the €15,000 deposit, he remained in detention despite having been granted bail. From October 2012 to February 2013 he repeatedly asked the court to reduce the deposit. Meanwhile, on 6 February 2013, Gafà filed a second constitutional redress application, alleging a violation of Article 5 § 3 because the “exorbitant” deposit prevented him from effectively enjoying bail. The Civil Court (First Hall) rejected the claim on 3 July 2013, holding that an accused must provide sufficient, checkable information about his means, assets and possible sureties, and show objective inability to pay or find a surety. In *Bakchizhov v. Ukraine* (Application no. 24874/08), the applicant, a Ukrainian national, was convicted in January 2007 of inflicting bodily injuries and sentenced to five years’ imprisonment. His conviction was upheld on appeal and by the Supreme Court. From 13 April 2007 to 17 June 2011 he served his sentence in Boryspil Correctional Colony, before being released on probation. He lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 7 May 2008. The Court later communicated complaints concerning alleged ill-treatment in prison, poor conditions of detention, lack of adequate medical assistance and an effective remedy, forced labour, monitoring of correspondence, and hindrance of his right of individual application.

The applicant alleged that his cells were dirty, poorly ventilated and insufficiently heated in winter. He claimed prisoners with HIV and tuberculosis were held together with healthy inmates, and that food and water were unsatisfactory. He also alleged overcrowding in four cells: approximately 70 sq m holding 50 prisoners; 100–120 sq m holding 85; 120–130 sq m holding 110; and 45 sq m holding 35. Guards allegedly subjected prisoners to arbitrary solitary confinement, verbal and physical abuse and threats. Daytime searches while prisoners were absent left cells messy, and some personal belongings and case documents allegedly went missing; some searches occurred at night, causing fear and stress. He further alleged that medical assistance was inadequate: he did not receive a thorough examination or long-term treatment plan, only occasional symptomatic treatment. Under threat of disciplinary punishment, he was allegedly forced to work overtime, often 12–14 hours per day, seven days a week, without adequate remuneration. Prison authorities allegedly screened all correspondence, including letters to and from the Court, selectively failed to send letters, or delayed sending or delivery. For example, his 23 February 2009 letter to the Court was not sent by the prison, although the Court received it in time, and the Court’s 21 January 2011 letter reached him a month late. He sent some letters through friends and submitted copies bearing a prison stamp. His complaints to domestic authorities, including the prosecutor’s office, were allegedly ignored or not dispatched.

The Government disputed these claims. It said tuberculosis patients were detained separately, food and water were checked, heating was maintained at 18–20°C, and sanitary conditions were adequate. It submitted prison governor’s information notes, bedding records and disinfection records. It maintained that medical care was adequate: the applicant was healthy on arrival in April 2007 and later received treatment for chronic bronchitis, lumbar radiculoneuritis, dermatitis and possible hypertension. The Government could provide no information about alleged force or searches because relevant records had been destroyed, and said the ill-treatment complaint was general and unsupported. It denied forced labour, stating that work was normally required and paid, and that when he refused job offers he did unpaid maintenance work for no more than two hours per day. It denied that all letters were opened, relying on a prison certificate stating that he had sent only one letter to the Court, on 3 December 2008, and received no reply. It also said he made no domestic complaints about material conditions, ill-treatment or medical assistance.

Separately, the applicant complained about lack of access to his criminal case file. He was provided with various documents and judgments, but in 2008 the Brovary Town Court informed him that the file did not contain cassation appeals or Supreme Court judgments and refused a copy of the entire file. After the Court requested the Supreme Court judgment, he obtained it in April 2009. He accessed records relating to his detention in 2009 and, after release in 2011, full access to his criminal case file.

In the excerpt, the Court found the Article 3 ill-treatment complaint unclear and unsubstantiated; the stress from searches did not reach the required severity threshold, and the remaining allegations were general or unsupported.

He complained of ill-treatment by guards, including arbitrary solitary confinement in disciplinary cells, verbal and physical abuse, and threats. As to correspondence, he claimed prison authorities screened all letters, including those to and from the Court, and selectively failed to send, delayed, or withheld them. He said one letter to the Court of 23 February 2009 was not sent by the prison administration, although the Court received it in time, and a Court letter of 21 January 2011 reached him a month late. It submitted prison records, bedding information, and disinfection records. On medical care, it said the applicant was healthy on arrival in April 2007, did not request assistance until March 2009, and thereafter received treatment for bronchitis, lumbar radiculoneuritis, dermatitis, and possible hypertension. In *Bakchizhov v. Ukraine* (Application no. 24874/08), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by Aleksandr Viktorovich Bakchizhov, a Ukrainian national born in 1969. He was convicted in January 2007 of inflicting bodily injuries and sentenced to five years’ imprisonment; his conviction was upheld on appeal in March and October 2007. From 13 April 2007 to 17 June 2011 he served his sentence in Boryspil Correctional Colony, after which he was released on probation. He lodged his application on 7 May 2008 and was granted legal aid.

The applicant alleged violations arising mainly from his detention. He complained that prison conditions were inhuman: dirty cells, poor ventilation, insufficient winter heating, overcrowding, unsatisfactory and hazardous food and water, and mixing of HIV/TB-positive prisoners with healthy inmates. He claimed he had been held in four cells with severe overcrowding, including a 70-sq-m cell housing 50 prisoners and a 120–130-sq-m cell housing 110 prisoners. The Government denied these allegations, stating that TB patients were separated, food and water were checked, heating was adequate at 18–20°C, and sanitation was appropriate. It relied on prison governor notes, detention-card extracts and disinfection records.

The applicant also alleged ill-treatment by guards, including arbitrary solitary confinement in disciplinary cells, verbal and physical abuse, threats, and frequent cell searches—sometimes at night—that left belongings and case documents missing and caused fear and stress. The Government said records had been destroyed due to expiry of retention periods, and that the complaint was general and unsupported by evidence. Ukraine** (App. No. 13124/08), decided on 22 November 2018, concerned a Ukrainian national, Vasyl Ivanovych Bosyy, who was prosecuted in 2005–2006 for various crimes and ultimately convicted of aggravated robbery, receiving a seven-year prison sentence in a final decision of 19 September 2006. He complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Articles 3, 8, 13, and 34 of the Convention about prison conditions, alleged ill-treatment by guards, monitoring of his correspondence, lack of an effective domestic remedy, and hindrance of his right of individual application.

The applicant’s detention had three main stages. From 27 May 2005 to 3 October 2006 he was held in a pre-trial detention centre in Kropyvnytskyi. He was then transferred to correctional colony no. 6 in Kropyvnytskyi, where he remained until 20 March 2008. On 23 May 2008 he was moved to correctional colony no. 78 in Raikivtsi, Khmelnytsk Region, and stayed there until his release on 25 May 2012.

Under Article 3, Bosyy alleged that detention conditions were inhuman and degrading. In the first colony, he claimed he was held in a dormitory measuring 6 by 8 metres with twelve double bunk beds. The Government disputed this, saying the dormitory measured 41.68 sq. m and contained ten single beds. The applicant also alleged that electricity was regularly switched off or that voltage was reduced from 220 to 110 V, leaving the cell dimly lit and unsuitable for reading or sewing. He complained of inadequate food and poor sanitary conditions, including cockroaches and sometimes mice and rats, in both colonies. He further alleged that he had been beaten, humiliated, tortured, and placed in a disciplinary cell; specifically, he said he was beaten on arrival at the first colony on 4 October 2006 and that guards tried to place him in a psychiatric clinic in March 2007. He also alleged repeated ill-treatment by prison guards. The Government denied these claims and submitted prison logs, reports, and inmate statements indicating adequate food, clothing, and sanitation.

Under Article 8, the applicant alleged that prison authorities intercepted, reviewed, blocked, and delayed his correspondence, especially letters to the Court and the Parliamentary Commissioner for Human Rights. He also claimed persecution and threats for applying to the Court. Domestic law generally allowed automatic monitoring of prisoner correspondence, subject to exemptions. A law of 1 December 2005 exempted correspondence to the Court and other international institutions; a 2010 law added lawyers and incoming mail from exempt organisations; and a 2014 law added courts. Prison registers showed that between 17 June 2008 and 1 December 2011 the applicant sent and received over sixty letters to non-exempt public entities, including courts, judges, Parliament members, and the Presidential Administration, which were subject to monitoring. A November 2011 cover letter summarising one of his letters showed that monitoring occurred.

Under Article 34, Bosyy alleged that authorities denied him access to his criminal case file, preventing him from obtaining documents for his application; interfered with his communication with the Court; and intimidated him because of the application. The Government denied this, submitting evidence that he examined his case file on 23 December 2011 and 11 January 2012 and received copies on 25 January 2012.

The Court rejected the Article 3 complaints concerning the pre-trial detention centre as out of time and the remaining Article 3 and Article 13 complaints as manifestly ill-founded. It found a violation of Article 8 only in respect of monitoring of correspondence with entities not exempt from monitoring under domestic law, because that interference was not “in accordance with the law.” The other complaints, including those under Article 34, were rejected as inadmissible or manifestly ill-founded.

**Bosyy v. Ukraine** (Application no. 13124/08, judgment 22 November 2018) concerned a Ukrainian national, Vasyl Ivanovych Bosyy, convicted of aggravated robbery in 2006 and sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment. He was detained in a pre-trial detention centre in Kropyvnytskyi from 27 May 2005 to 3 October 2006, then in correctional colony no. 6 until 20 March 2008, and later in colony no. 78 in Raikivtsi until his release on 25 May 2012. He complained mainly under Articles 3, 8, 13 and 34 of the Convention about prison conditions, ill-treatment by guards, monitoring of his correspondence, lack of an effective remedy, and hindrance of his right of individual application to the Court.

Under Article 3, Bosyy alleged overcrowding, poor food, inadequate sanitation, insufficient lighting, and beatings and humiliation by prison guards. He claimed the dormitory in the first colony measured 6 by 8 metres and held twelve double bunk beds; the Government said it measured 41.68 sq. m and contained ten single beds. He also alleged that electricity was regularly cut off or reduced to dim lighting, that food was inadequate, and that there were cockroaches, mice and rats. He alleged beatings on arrival at the colony in October 2006 and an attempt to place him in a psychiatric clinic in March 2007. The Government denied these claims and submitted records showing adequate food, sanitation and conditions. The Court declared the pre-trial detention complaints inadmissible as time-barred, and the alleged pre-trial ill-treatment inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded. For the colonies, it found that personal space below 4 sq. m was not established, and the remaining allegations were insufficiently substantiated. The ill-treatment allegations lacked prima facie evidence, medical proof, or consistent pursuit domestically; indeed, Bosyy withdrew some domestic complaints, and his later revocation of his lawyer’s authority further undermined his credibility. Article 13 therefore also failed because there was no arguable Article 3 claim.

The key violation found concerned Article 8. Domestic law allowed automatic monitoring and censorship of prisoners’ correspondence, except for certain exempt addressees. Before December 2005, only correspondence with the Parliamentary Commissioner for Human Rights and prosecutors was exempt. From December 2005, letters to the Court and other international institutions were exempt. From February 2010, incoming correspondence from exempt bodies and correspondence with lawyers was added; courts were added in 2014. Prison registers showed that Bosyy sent and received many letters to and from non-exempt public entities, including courts, members of Parliament and the Presidential Administration. A prison cover letter summarising one of his letters confirmed that monitoring occurred. Following *Belyaev and Digtyar v. Ukraine* and *Vintman v. Ukraine*, the Court held that the monitoring regime for non-exempt correspondence was not “in accordance with the law”: it was automatic, had no time limits, required no reasoned decision, allowed no prisoner participation, and provided no effective remedy. There was thus a violation of Article 8 regarding monitoring of non-exempt correspondence. Allegations that exempt correspondence was monitored were not corroborated.

Finally, Bosyy complained under Article 34 that authorities failed to provide documents for his application, interfered with his communication with the Court, and intimidated him. The Court examined this complaint but did not find that Ukraine had hindered the effective exercise of his right of individual application.

**Case: Kin v. Ukraine (Application no. 46990/07), ECHR Fourth Section, 18 December 2018**

The applicant, Vira Maksymivna Kin, a Ukrainian national born in 1956, was the principal of a private school in Dubno, Rivne Region. Criminal proceedings were initiated against her on 30 March 2000 for failure to comply with a court decision ordering the reinstatement of a teacher.

The alleged violations arose on 29 May 2000. According to the applicant, at about 9:00 a.m. Dubno police officers broke down the front door of her house. Inside, an investigator from the Dubno inter-district prosecutor’s office ordered her to go to his office for questioning. When she refused, the investigator asked police officers to ensure her compulsory appearance. The police allegedly beat her, twisted her arms behind her back, and forced her out of the house barefoot. They placed her in a police car and took her to the investigator’s office. She was released at about 1:00 p.m. The next day, a doctor noted injuries on her shoulders. A later medical expert found five bruises to her shoulders and an injury to her left shoulder ligaments, caused by blunt objects, and stated they could have been sustained in the circumstances she described.

On 2 June 2000, the applicant complained to the Rivne regional prosecutor’s office. On 30 June 2000, after a pre-investigation inquiry, the prosecutor’s office refused to initiate criminal proceedings against the police officers for lack of constituent elements of a criminal offence. On 20 March 2001, following her complaint, the Prosecutor General’s Office reversed that decision as unsubstantiated and ordered an additional inquiry. The applicant was not informed of the outcome. In 2016, the Government Agent’s Office was told that the file had been destroyed after the statutory retention period. Thus, the material did not show any effective investigation into her ill-treatment allegations.

Separately, the criminal case against the applicant was discontinued on 9 April 2001 for insignificance, but that decision was quashed in August 2001. The investigation was completed and referred to court. Trial judgments in 2004 and 2006 were quashed. On 30 January 2007, the Dubno Town Court convicted her, imposed a fine, but released her from punishment because the statute of limitation had expired. The Rivne Regional Court of Appeal upheld that judgment on 17 April 2007. On 13 November 2007, the Supreme Court refused to examine her appeal on points of law because she had not complied with procedural rules. This formed the basis of her Article 6 § 1 complaint about the length of proceedings.

On 29 May 2003, the applicant lodged a civil claim seeking damages for violation of the inviolability of her home, unlawful arrest, and ill-treatment. On 9 July 2007, the Dubno Town Court found that she had been ill-treated and unlawfully taken from her home to the investigator’s office. It found violations of her right to inviolability of home, liberty, and respect for human dignity, and awarded her UAH 500 (approximately EUR 73) in non-pecuniary damages. The Lviv Administrative Court of Appeal upheld this on 26 May 2008. Her subsequent appeal on points of law contesting the amount was returned on 13 July 2009 without examination on the merits due to procedural non-compliance.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained under Article 3 (ill-treatment and humiliation), Article 5 § 1 (unlawful deprivation of liberty from 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m.), Article 8 (respect for home), and Article 6 § 1 (length of criminal proceedings). The Government argued that she had lost victim status because domestic courts had acknowledged the violations and awarded compensation, and that she had failed to exhaust domestic remedies regarding the sufficiency of damages. The applicant maintained that no effective investigation had been conducted and that the compensation was inadequate. The Court accepted that the domestic courts had acknowledged the violations in substance, but found that redress remained in issue. In cases of willful ill-treatment, an Article 3 breach cannot be remedied only by compensation; the State must also effectively prosecute and punish those responsible. The inquiries were ineffective, the applicant was not informed of their outcome, and the file was destroyed. While a civil award had been made, she failed to properly raise its insufficiency before the Higher Administrative Court, without undue restriction on access.

An investigator from the Dubno inter-district prosecutor’s office ordered her to come for questioning. When she refused, the investigator asked police officers to compel her appearance. The police allegedly beat her, twisted her arms behind her back, forced her out of the house barefoot, placed her in a police car, and took her to the investigator’s office. She was released at about 1:00 p.m. The next day, a doctor noted injuries to her shoulders. A later medical expert found five bruises to her shoulders and injured left shoulder ligaments, caused by blunt objects, and stated that the injuries could have been sustained in the circumstances she described.

On 2 June 2000, the applicant complained to the Rivne regional prosecutor’s office. On 30 June 2000, after a pre-investigation inquiry, the prosecutor refused to initiate criminal proceedings against the police officers for lack of constituent elements of a criminal offence. On 20 March 2001, the Prosecutor General’s Office reversed that decision as unsubstantiated and ordered an additional inquiry. The applicant was not informed of the outcome. In 2016, it was learned that the file concerning those inquiries had been destroyed after the statutory retention period. No full criminal investigation appears to have been opened, and the applicant alleged that there had been no effective investigation into her ill-treatment.

Separately, the criminal case against the applicant continued. On 9 April 2001, the investigation was discontinued because of the insignificance of the offence, but that decision was quashed. The applicant also brought a civil claim on 29 May 2003, seeking damages for violation of the inviolability of her home, unlawful arrest, and ill-treatment on 29 May 2000. On 9 July 2007, the Dubno Town Court found that she had been ill-treated and unlawfully taken from her home to the investigator’s office. It found violations of her right to inviolability of home, liberty, and respect for human dignity, and awarded her UAH 500 (approximately EUR 73) in non-pecuniary damages. The Lviv Administrative Court of Appeal upheld that judgment on 26 May 2008. On 13 July 2009, the Higher Administrative Court returned her cassation appeal without examining it on the merits because she had not complied with procedural requirements.

The Government argued that she had lost victim status because the domestic courts had acknowledged the violations and awarded compensation, and that she had not exhausted domestic remedies regarding the sufficiency of damages. The applicant argued that the compensation was inadequate and that no effective investigation had been conducted. The Court therefore examined whether Ukraine had acknowledged the violations and provided appropriate redress, particularly whether the absence of an effective criminal investigation could be remedied by civil compensation alone.
001-186424:
**Case: Martinović v. Bosnia and Herzegovina (Application no. 41749/12), ECtHR, 25 September 2018**

The applicant, Ms Božana Martinović, a Bosnian national born in 1955 and living in Italy, complained about the delayed enforcement of two final domestic decisions in her favour. She alleged violations of Article 6 of the Convention (right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of possessions).

**First set of proceedings.** On 4 December 2006, the Cantonal Prosecutor of Hercegovina-Neretva Canton granted the applicant reimbursement of costs she had incurred as a witness, in the amount of 519 convertible marks (BAM). Enforcement of this decision proved protracted. On 29 February 2008, the Mostar Municipal Court rejected her enforcement request, deeming the decision unenforceable. The Mostar Cantonal Court quashed that decision in September 2008, and a writ of execution was issued in November 2008. Further objections and remittals followed. On 18 February 2011, the Municipal Court partly accepted an objection concerning interest, and the Cantonal Court upheld that decision on 2 December 2011. The Supreme Court of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina dismissed the applicant’s revision request as inadmissible on 19 September 2013. On 23 December 2013, the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina found a violation of the applicant’s right to a trial within a reasonable time due to non-enforcement of the 18 February 2011 decision. It ordered the Canton to take measures to enforce it within a reasonable time, but awarded no non-pecuniary damages. On 21 October 2014, the Constitutional Court confirmed the decision remained unenforced. It was finally enforced on 18 December 2014, when the applicant was paid in cash.

**Second set of proceedings.** By a judgment of 3 April 2009, final on 16 December 2009, the Municipal Court ordered a certain P.M. to pay the applicant BAM 1,959 in civil proceedings costs. The applicant requested enforcement on 31 October 2010 and later sought acceleration in 2011 and 2012. A writ of execution was issued on 5 December 2012. P.M. objected, and the Municipal Court dismissed the objection on 13 June 2013; P.M. appealed. On 17 September 2013, the Constitutional Court found a violation of the applicant’s right to a trial within a reasonable time due to the duration of the enforcement proceedings before the Municipal Court. It ordered the Cantonal Court to rule urgently on P.M.’s appeal, but again awarded no non-pecuniary damages. The Cantonal Court dismissed the appeal on 16 October 2013. A further writ of execution was issued on 11 June 2015, and the judgment was finally enforced on 4 August 2016, with payment made to the applicant’s bank account in Bosnia and Herzegovina, although she was living in Italy.

**Relevant issues before the ECtHR.** The Government objected that the application abused the right of petition because the applicant failed to inform the Court that the second decision had been enforced by August 2016, and that she had lost victim status because the decisions were fully enforced. The Court rejected both objections. It found no abuse: the application was lodged in 2012 before enforcement, the payment was made to an account in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the applicant was self-represented. It also held that although domestic authorities had acknowledged the delays, they had awarded no compensation, so the applicant remained a victim. The application was declared admissible.

On the merits, applying principles from *Hornsby v. Greece* and *Jeličić v. Bosnia and Herzegovina*, the Court found that the prolonged non-enforcement of final domestic decisions violated Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Government had not provided facts or arguments capable of leading to a different conclusion.

The final judgment was enforced on 4 August 2016, when the money was paid into the applicant’s bank account in Bosnia and Herzegovina; she was living in Italy.

The application was lodged on 12 June 2012. The Government argued abuse of the right of application because the applicant allegedly failed to inform the Court that the second decision had been fully enforced by August 2016. The Court rejected this, noting the application was filed while enforcement was still pending, the payment was made in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the applicant was self-represented. It held that the right to a court includes execution of final judgments and that the prolonged non-enforcement of the two final decisions violated Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. On 10 November 2009 the 11th Chamber held a hearing, with both the applicant and his lawyer present, and ordered that detention continue. On 10 December 2009 his lawyer objected. On 21 December 2009 the 12th Chamber dismissed the objection without a hearing, relying on the public prosecutor’s written opinion, which had not been communicated to the applicant or his representative. On 28 August 2012 the Assize Court again convicted him and imposed 15 years. On 8 July 2013 the Court of Cassation upheld the conviction, ending the detention.

The Government argued non-exhaustion, saying he could claim compensation under Article 141 §1(d) of the Code on Criminal Procedure. The Court noted that the detention ended when the Court of Cassation upheld his conviction on 8 July 2013. It held that he was entitled—and required—to use that compensation remedy. Although exhaustion is normally assessed at the date the application was lodged (25 June 2010), the Court applied an exception because the remedy had become applicable only after the criminal proceedings became final. It therefore rejected this complaint for non-exhaustion under Article 35 §§1 and 4.

Second, under Article 5 §4, he complained that he could not appear before the court when his detention was reviewed. He said he had not appeared between 5 October 2004 and 28 April 2005, and could not appear when the objection was examined on 21 December 2009. The Court rejected the first period as out of time because the application was lodged on 25 June 2010. As to the 21 December 2009 objection, the Court noted that he and his lawyer had attended the 10 November 2009 hearing, only 41 days earlier, at which the detention decision was made. It found no further oral hearing before the appeal court was required for Article 5 §4 and no equality-of-arms problem. This part was manifestly ill-founded.

The case of *Galea and Others v. Malta* (Application no. 68980/13) concerned six Maltese nationals who alleged violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants held the *utile dominium* of a portion of land in Zabbar, Malta, by way of sub-emphyteusis expiring in 2047; the State held the *directum dominium*. Their ancestors had acquired the property through inheritance, and it included a shop rented to third parties as a snack bar.

In 1965, a Governor’s declaration under the Land Acquisition (Public Purposes) Ordinance declared 80 sq. m. of the property, including the approximately 50 sq. m. shop, as needed for a public purpose. The Government took possession, demolished the shop, and planned to build a civic centre and service roads. In 1972, however, the plan changed: the road was repositioned, and a new, larger shop was built at Government expense mostly on the applicants’ land. That shop was leased to the same third party for use as a snack bar. The part of the land taken but not used was returned to the applicants only in 1988. Extra-judicial requests for return of the property used as the snack bar failed. In 2010, the Commissioner of Land extended the third party’s lease until 2020 at a rent of about EUR 2,100 per year. Also in 2010, following Act I of 2006, a President’s declaration offered EUR 13,000 for the 1965 taking, based on a 2005 architect’s valuation.

The applicants brought constitutional redress proceedings in 2010. They complained that their land had not been taken in the public interest and that they had been deprived of their possession without compensation and without access to a court to claim compensation. The first-instance Constitutional Court upheld their claims in 2012. It found that the taking was not in the public interest because the property had been leased to third parties for commercial purposes, and that the applicants had received no compensation for 45 years. It also found that the 2010 offer was inadequate, based on an old valuation and far below the property’s value, and that the applicants had lacked procedural safeguards or access to court. It annulled the declarations, ordered return of the property, and awarded EUR 40,000 in compensation.

On appeal, the Constitutional Court in 2013 partly reversed. It held that the original 1965 taking had been in the public interest and that the later commercial use of the snack bar did not remove that public-interest character. Nevertheless, it found a violation of the applicants’ property rights because they had been deprived of their property for many years without compensation: the unused portion was returned only after 23 years, and the used portion remained uncompensated. The Constitutional Court awarded EUR 10,000 in non-pecuniary damages, stated that any pecuniary claim could be pursued under Article 12(3) of the Ordinance with 5% interest, and annulled the return order.

The applicants refused to collect the award, and in January 2014 the Commissioner deposited it in court. In September 2015, the Government asked the applicants to submit evidence of title. Before the European Court, the applicants alleged that they had been deprived of their possessions without compensation and had no possibility of accessing a court to raise their compensation claims.

In 1965, a Governor’s declaration under the Land Acquisition (Public Purposes) Ordinance declared 80 sq. m. of the property, including the approximately 50 sq. m. shop, needed for a public purpose. The Government took possession of the entire area and demolished the shop to build a local civic centre and service roads. In 1972, however, the plan changed: the road was repositioned, and a new, larger shop was built mostly on the applicants’ land at Government expense. That shop was leased to the same third party for use as a snack bar, serving the square, civic centre, government offices, and bus terminus. The unused portion of the taken land was returned only in 1988.

The applicants unsuccessfully made extra-judicial requests for the return of the property used as a snack bar. Meanwhile, in 2010, the Commissioner of Land extended the third party’s lease until 2020 at a rent of about €2,100 per year. Also in 2010, following Article 9 of the Ordinance and Act I of 2006, a President’s declaration offered €13,000 for the 1965 taking, based on a 2005 architect’s valuation.

In March 2010, the applicants brought constitutional redress proceedings. They alleged a breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, because their land had not been taken in the public interest, and of Article 6, because they lacked access to a court to challenge the taking and claim compensation. They sought annulment of the declaration, return of the property, and adequate redress.

The Civil Court (First Hall) upheld their claims in 2012. It found that the taking was not in the public interest because the property had been leased to third parties for commercial purposes, serving private rather than public interests. It also noted that the applicants had received no compensation for 45 years and that the 2010 offer was based on an outdated 2005 valuation. It found a lack of procedural safeguards and no access to court to claim compensation. The court annulled the Governor’s declaration and the 2010 President’s declaration, ordered return of the property, and awarded €40,000 in compensation.

On appeal, the Constitutional Court in 2013 allowed the appeal in part. It held that the original taking had been in the public interest, and that leasing the shop did not eliminate that public interest. Nevertheless, it found a violation of the applicants’ property rights because they had been deprived of their property for years without compensation: the unused part was returned only after 23 years, and no compensation had been paid for the remaining used part. In 2015, the Government asked the applicants to submit evidence of title regarding the 2010 President’s declaration. The relevant domestic law allowed challenges to public purpose only within 21 days after 2009 amendments, fixed certain values as at 1 January 2005, and provided for compensation offers and Land Arbitration Board determinations.
