**Case: Kešelj and Others v. Montenegro (Application no. 33264/11, judgment of 13 February 2018)**

The case concerned ten nationals of Bosnia and Herzegovina who complained that Montenegro had failed to enforce a final court settlement concluded in their favour. The applicants had reached a court-approved settlement on 28 February 1996 before the Cetinje Municipal Court with the debtor, JSP “Tara” Cetinje. Under that settlement, the debtor undertook to pay the applicants specified amounts in respect of pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. The settlement became final on the same date. The debtor subsequently paid only part of the sums owed.

On 26 May 1997, the Podgorica Commercial Court opened insolvency proceedings against the debtor. On 19 August 1997, the applicants submitted their claims based on the settlement. In the course of the insolvency proceedings, the Podgorica Commercial Court acknowledged those claims. On 23 December 2009, the Commercial Court terminated the insolvency proceedings against the debtor but continued the proceedings against the debtor’s estate. That decision was upheld by the Appellate Court on 9 April 2010. The proceedings against the estate remained pending. On 14 October 2010, the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicants’ constitutional appeal on procedural grounds. The court settlement therefore remained partly unenforced.

A key fact for the alleged violations was the debtor’s legal status. At the time the settlement was concluded and became final, the debtor was a company predominantly comprised of State-controlled capital. The Government neither contested this nor provided any evidence to the contrary. This was relevant to the Court’s assessment of the State’s responsibility for the non-enforcement of the final settlement.

The applicants complained about the national authorities’ failure to enforce the final court settlement. Although they did not expressly rely on particular Convention provisions, the Court, as master of the characterisation of the facts, examined the complaints under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees a fair hearing within a reasonable time in the determination of civil rights and obligations, and under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, which protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

The Government argued that the complaints should be rejected for failure to comply with the six-month time-limit. They submitted that time had begun to run when the commercial court’s decision terminating the insolvency proceedings against the debtor became final, since a constitutional appeal had not been an effective domestic remedy at the relevant time. The Court rejected that objection. It distinguished the earlier Sokolov and Others v. Serbia case, where insolvency proceedings had ended and the debtor had been liquidated with no remaining estate. In the present case, proceedings in respect of the debtor’s estate were still continuing, so the six-month time-limit could not have started to run. The complaints were therefore declared admissible.

On the merits, the Court noted that the applicants had obtained only part of the amounts specified in the final settlement of 28 February 1996, while the remainder was still unenforced. It recalled that it had frequently found violations of Article 6 § 1 and/or Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 in similar cases, particularly those concerning companies undergoing restructuring, privatisation and/or other forms of transition from a planned to a market economy. After examining all the material, the Court considered that the Government had not put forward any fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion. It accordingly found violations of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The judgment also addressed a separate issue concerning Mr Drago Kandić, whose complaint had earlier been rejected for abuse of the right of individual petition. His lawyer later submitted a notarised document confirming that Mr Kandić had been alive when the application was lodged. The Court declined to take that matter up in the context of this application.

In *Annen v. Germany (No. 2)* (Application no. 3682/10, ECtHR, 20 September 2018), the Court examined whether a German civil injunction violated the applicant’s freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention.

The applicant, Klaus Günter Annen, was a German anti-abortion campaigner who operated the website *babycaust.de*. At the relevant time, the site compared abortion to the Holocaust, displaying images of graves under the caption “then: Holocaust” and linking to a page titled “Abortion – the new Holocaust?”. A page called “Prayer requests for Germany” led users to an alphabetical list of doctors who performed abortions, including names and practice addresses, and asked readers to pray for them. The site stated: “Perverted doctors murder unborn children at the request of the mothers.” It also urged prayers for doctors who “personally undertake the AGGRAVATED MURDER of abortion killing” and said counselling centres “are enabling and facilitating the unpunished aggravated murder of children in their mother’s womb.”

One listed doctor, Dr Q., first sought an injunction to remove his name and address. The Mannheim Regional Court refused in 2006. On appeal, Dr Q. changed his request, seeking an order that Annen desist from labelling abortions such as his “aggravated murder.” In 2007 the Karlsruhe Court of Appeal granted the injunction. It found the website could be understood as a personalised accusation that Dr Q. had committed the criminal offence of aggravated murder. Although the term could be read as a moral judgment, the overall presentation—the emphasis on “aggravated murder,” the Holocaust comparison, and the failure to clarify that abortions under Article 218a of the Criminal Code were exempt from criminal liability—did not exclude a factual reading. The Federal Court of Justice refused legal aid, and the Federal Constitutional Court declined to admit Annen’s constitutional complaint.

Before the ECtHR, Annen alleged that the injunction violated Article 10. The Court found the interference had a legal basis and pursued the legitimate aim of protecting Dr Q.’s reputation and rights under Article 8. The key issue was whether it was necessary in a democratic society. The Court accepted the domestic courts’ classification: the statements could be understood as factual accusations that Dr Q. had perpetrated aggravated murder, or at least as value judgments lacking sufficient factual basis. Annen did not argue that Dr Q.’s abortions were aggravated murder in the legal sense. Under German law, abortions performed in accordance with Article 218a were unlawful but not punishable, whereas aggravated murder under Article 211 carried life imprisonment. There was therefore no factual foundation for the allegation.

The Court distinguished *Annen v. Germany (No. 1)*, where the applicant’s leaflet clearly explained that abortions were unlawful but not criminally liable. Here, the website mentioned “unpunished” only once and did not sufficiently clarify the legal position. The accusations were very serious and could incite hatred or aggression. However, the remedy was limited: Annen was not criminally convicted or ordered to pay damages, but only required to desist from labelling abortions such as Dr Q.’s “aggravated murder.” The ECtHR concluded that the injunction was proportionate and the domestic reasons were relevant and sufficient. There was no violation of Article 10.

The applicant, Klaus Annen, operated an anti-abortion website, babycaust.de. The site compared abortion to the Holocaust, displayed text such as “then: Holocaust” and “Abortion – the new Holocaust?”, and included a page calling for prayers for doctors who performed abortions. It listed doctors by name and practice address. It also stated that “perverted doctors murder unborn children at the request of the mothers” and asked readers to pray for doctors “who personally undertake the AGGRAVATED MURDER of abortion killing.” Another passage said counselling centres enabled an “unpunished aggravated murder of children in their mother’s womb.”

Dr Q., one of the listed doctors, initially sought removal of his name and address. In 2006 the Mannheim Regional Court rejected that application, finding that it was a fact Dr Q. performed abortions and that the website’s content was protected by freedom of expression and lacked a comparable “pillory effect.” On appeal, Dr Q. changed his request, seeking an injunction to stop Annen from labelling abortions, such as those performed by Dr Q., as “aggravated murder.” In 2007 the Karlsruhe Court of Appeal granted the injunction. It found the website could be understood as accusing Dr Q. of committing the criminal offence of aggravated murder, especially because the term was emphasized and abortion was compared to the Holocaust. The applicant had failed to make sufficiently clear that abortions performed under section 218a of the Criminal Code were unlawful but exempt from criminal liability. The Federal Court of Justice refused legal aid, and the Federal Constitutional Court declined to admit Annen’s constitutional complaint.

Before the ECHR, Annen argued that the injunction violated Article 10. He claimed his website contributed to a public debate and did not personally attack Dr Q.; his aim was to criticise the German legal situation on abortion. The Government argued that the domestic courts had carefully balanced Annen’s expression against Dr Q.’s personality rights and had found a serious personal attack.

The ECHR found that the injunction interfered with Article 10 but had a legal basis and pursued the legitimate aim of protecting Dr Q.’s reputation and rights. The key issue was whether the interference was necessary in a democratic society. The Court accepted that the statements concerned a public-interest debate. However, it held that the national courts were entitled to classify the statements as capable of being understood as factual accusations that Dr Q. had committed aggravated murder. The applicant had not clearly explained the section 218a exemption; his single reference to abortions being “unpunished” could easily go unnoticed. There was no factual foundation for alleging that Dr Q. had committed legal aggravated murder, and even value judgments require sufficient factual basis. The accusations were extremely serious—aggravated murder carries life imprisonment—and could incite hatred or aggression. Since Annen was not criminally convicted or ordered to pay damages, but only subjected to a civil desist order, the injunction was not disproportionate. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 10, distinguishing the case from *Annen v. Germany (No. 1)*, where the applicant had clearly stated abortions were not criminally punishable.

**Summary of *Annen v. Germany (No. 2)* (Application no. 3682/10)**

The case of *Annen v. Germany (No. 2)* concerns an application brought by Mr. Klaus Günter Annen, a German national and anti-abortion campaigner, against the Federal Republic of Germany. The applicant alleged that a domestic court injunction ordering him to cease labelling abortions as "aggravated murder" on his website violated his right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant operated an anti-abortion website named "babycaust.de." The website's content compared abortion to the Holocaust, displaying images of graves with the text "then: Holocaust" and featuring a page titled "Abortion – the new Holocaust?". More critically, the site included a location-based list of doctors who performed abortions, accompanied by requests for prayers for them. On a page linked to this list, the text stated, "Perverted doctors murder unborn children at the request of the mothers." Another section urged visitors to pray for doctors "who personally undertake the AGGRAVATED MURDER of abortion killing," with the term highlighted in the original. It also claimed that counselling centres were "enabling and facilitating the unpunished aggravated murder of children in their mother’s womb."

A doctor identified on the list, Dr. Q., initially sought a civil injunction to have his name and address removed from the website. The Mannheim Regional Court initially rejected this application, finding that publishing the doctor's name did not have a comparable "pillory effect" to other cases involving personalised leaflets. However, during the appeal, Dr. Q. modified his claim to seek an order preventing the applicant from labelling abortions, such as those he performed, as "aggravated murder."

The Karlsruhe Court of Appeal granted this injunction. It reasoned that the website's overall presentation could be understood as a personalised accusation that Dr. Q. had perpetrated the criminal offence of aggravated murder. The court noted that while "aggravated murder" could be a moral judgment, the applicant had failed to clarify that abortions performed by doctors like Dr. Q., following counselling and within the legal timeframe, were exempt from criminal liability under section 218a of the German Criminal Code. The court found that the applicant's emphasis on the term and the Holocaust comparison contributed to this interpretation. The applicant's subsequent appeals to the Federal Court of Justice and the Federal Constitutional Court were unsuccessful.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant argued that the injunction unjustifiably interfered with his freedom of expression and his contribution to a public debate. He contended that his intention was to criticise the German legal situation, not to personally attack Dr. Q. The German Government maintained that the domestic courts had carefully balanced the applicant's freedom of expression against Dr. Q.'s personality rights under Article 8, concluding that the serious personal attack justified the restriction.

The European Court of Human Rights found that the injunction constituted an interference with the applicant's Article 10 rights, which was prescribed by law and pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the reputation and rights of Dr. Q. The central question was whether this interference was "necessary in a democratic society." The Court observed that the Court of Appeal had undertaken a detailed balancing exercise, classifying the applicant's statements as potentially factual accusations of criminal conduct. The Court agreed that the statements could be understood as an accusation that Dr. Q. had committed aggravated murder, a very serious charge carrying a life sentence. Crucially, the applicant had not provided a sufficient factual basis for this allegation and had not clearly explained the legal exemption from criminal liability for abortions under German law. Consequently, the Court held that the injunction was not disproportionate and that the domestic courts' reasons were relevant and sufficient.

In *Edina Tóth v. Hungary* (Application no. 51323/14), the European Court of Human Rights considered a Hungarian mother’s complaint that the Hungarian State failed to help her reunite with her abducted son, thereby disrupting her family life. She relied on Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention.

The applicant married H.B., a Hungarian citizen, in the United States in 2000. Their son was born in the US in 2003 and had dual citizenship. The family returned to Hungary in 2004. On 26 December 2004, after a quarrel, H.B. took the child and left for an unknown destination. He telephoned a few times over the next two weeks, but after January 2005 all contact ceased. The applicant has had no contact with her son since then.

The applicant filed for divorce. In November 2005, the Szentendre District Court issued an interim measure placing the child with the applicant; this became final in January 2006. In February 2007, the District Court pronounced the divorce, granted the applicant sole custody, terminated H.B.’s parental rights, ordered child maintenance and gave H.B. no visiting rights. The judgment became final in April 2007. H.B. did not participate in the proceedings and was represented by a guardian ad litem; the judgment appears to have been served on the guardian but not on H.B.

The applicant repeatedly sought State assistance. In November 2005 she lodged a criminal complaint alleging child abduction. Police carried out identity checks on H.B. in December 2005 and March 2006 in Sopron, where he declared an address. The applicant complained that the authorities failed to interrogate him despite these opportunities. A warrant was issued in May 2006, but the investigation was suspended later that month because H.B.’s residence had become unknown. In May 2007, police again checked H.B.; he gave an incomplete London address, claiming the child was with his grandmother, and was released. The investigation was resumed and then terminated in August 2007 for lack of offence, on the basis that unlawful change of a minor’s residence requires intent and H.B. was allegedly unaware of the custody judgment. A 2008 complaint about failure to pay child maintenance was terminated for the same reason. A 2008 complaint of endangering a minor was terminated in 2009 for lack of evidence. In 2013, after a school-book notice revealed the child was registered in Sopron, the applicant’s father lodged another complaint; the investigation was suspended in October 2013 because H.B.’s address again became unknown and a warrant was issued.

Enforcement efforts were also ineffective. In February 2006 the applicant requested enforcement of the interim custody measure. In March 2006 the bailiff visited H.B.’s registered address but found neither H.B. nor the child there; it appeared they might be in the US. No further measures were apparently taken. In 2012 the applicant was told that the bailiff was not responsible because H.B. and the child were abroad and diplomatic steps were required.

Internationally, the applicant contacted the Ministry of Justice in 2007. In 2009, international and European warrants were issued against H.B. in separate fraud proceedings. H.B. was later detained in Canada, expelled, escaped, and reportedly booked a flight to Vienna under a false name; Austrian cooperation produced no result. In 2012, Hungary made a Hague Convention request to the US, which was transferred to Canada; both were unsuccessful. In 2013 Canada was asked to establish the child’s residence but could not. On 8 May 2014 H.B. was apprehended in Budapest and the child was finally located. Because the applicant was then living abroad, the child was temporarily placed with her father in Csobánka.

The alleged violation thus concerns the State’s repeated failure to enforce custody and reunite the applicant with her son: delayed and suspended investigations, missed opportunities to interrogate or detain H.B., ineffective bailiff action, and unsuccessful international cooperation, leaving the applicant without contact from January 2005 until 2014.

Enforcement of the interim custody measure began in February 2006. In *Leonov v. Russia* (no. 77180/11), the applicant, a Russian national living in Moscow, alleged that the Russian courts’ refusal to make a residence order in his favour for his son, and an interim measure barring him from contact with the child during the proceedings, violated his Article 8 right to respect for family life and amounted to discrimination on grounds of sex and inequality between spouses.

The applicant and his wife, Ch., had a son, A., in August 2007. The family lived in the applicant’s flat, where A. was registered, received paediatric care and attended nursery. In November 2009 Ch. left the applicant, took A. to her parents’ home, and A. remained with her. In March 2010 the applicant applied for a residence order. Ch. counterclaimed for residence with her and sought an interim measure, alleging that the applicant might abduct A. to Belarus and had already tried to take him from nursery. On 26 April 2010 the district court granted the interim measure, forbidding the applicant from contacting A. or collecting him from nursery without Ch.’s prior permission. The applicant learned of this on 30 April 2010, when nursery staff refused him access.

Both parents’ flats were inspected and found suitable for a young child. In June 2010 a childcare authority reported that, because A. was very young, he should live with his mother until the age of five or six. A psychological examination was ordered. The applicant appealed against the interim measure, arguing that it was unjustified, harmed A.’s best interests, interrupted his attachment to the paternal family, risked estranging him from his father, and prejudged the case. In February 2011 the Moscow City Court quashed the interim measure as unrelated to the subject matter, disproportionate and prejudicial; a renewed request was rejected in April 2011.

In September 2010 Ch. was convicted of assaulting the applicant after he hugged A. at a beach; she was fined. In November 2010 experts found A. equally attached to both parents, both equally capable of raising him, and the parental conflict harmful. In December 2010 another childcare authority recommended that A. live with his mother due to his young age and established routine. At a December 2010 hearing the applicant objected to the judge, claiming she had said she would rule against him because the Timiryazevskiy District Court always awarded residence to mothers; the objection was dismissed.

In April 2011 the district court granted Ch.’s residence application and dismissed the applicant’s. It found serious parental conflict, accepted that both parents were capable and A. equally attached, noted that Ch.’s criminal conviction was not yet final, and concluded that A., then under four, should remain with his mother because of his established way of life and the likely negative impact of separation. It held that the applicant’s better finances or concerns about Ch.’s polluted neighbourhood and relatives’ smoking were not decisive, and that his request was premature; he could reapply when A. was older. The Moscow City Court upheld this in June 2011. In December 2011 a contact schedule was ordered for the applicant and paternal relatives.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Article 8 and sex discrimination. The Court dismissed the interim-measure complaint as out of time, because the measure had been quashed in February 2011 and finally discontinued in April 2011, while the application was lodged in December 2011. The residence-order complaint was declared admissible. The Government accepted interference with family life but argued it was lawful, pursued A.’s best interests and was necessary. The Court reiterated that custody decisions require relevant and sufficient reasons, an in-depth examination of the family situation, and a fair decision-making process, with the child’s best interests paramount.

In *Leonov v. Russia*, the applicant, Sergey Leonov, a Russian national, complained under Article 8 of the Convention that the refusal to grant him a residence order for his son and the interim contact ban imposed during custody proceedings violated his right to respect for family life. He also alleged breach of spousal equality and discrimination on grounds of sex.

The applicant married Ch., and their son A. was born in August 2007. The family lived in the applicant’s flat, where A. was registered and received paediatric care, and attended a local nursery. In November 2009 Ch. left the applicant, moved to her parents’ home, and took A. with her. A. lived with his mother thereafter.

In March 2010 the applicant sought a residence order in his favour. On 26 April 2010 Ch. counterclaimed for residence and requested an interim measure, claiming a risk that the applicant might abduct A. to Belarus and that he had tried to take the boy from nursery. The same day, the Timiryazevskiy District Court granted the interim measure, prohibiting the applicant from contacting A. or collecting him from nursery without Ch.’s permission. The court reasoned that A. lived with his mother and that the measure was proportionate to preserve the forthcoming judgment. The applicant learned of the order on 30 April 2010 when nursery staff refused him access.

Childcare authorities inspected both homes and found them suitable. In June 2010, one childcare authority recommended that A. reside with his mother because of his young age. A psychological expert report in November 2010 found A. equally attached to both parents and both parents equally capable, but noted that the ongoing parental conflict could harm A. Meanwhile, Ch. was convicted in September 2010 of assault and battery for attacking the applicant in June 2010 when he hugged A. at a beach; that conviction became final in February 2012. The interim contact ban was quashed on appeal in February 2011 as disproportionate and as prejudging the case; a renewed request was rejected in April 2011.

On 12 April 2011 the District Court granted Ch.’s residence application and dismissed the applicant’s. It found a serious parental conflict, but noted each parent was capable and A. was equally attached to both. It nevertheless held that A., not yet four, had an established life with his mother and that changing residence would be traumatic. The mother’s criminal charges were not decisive, and the father’s better housing and finances were also not decisive. Childcare authorities favoured the mother. The court said the applicant could reapply when A. was older. The Moscow City Court upheld this on appeal in June 2011. In December 2011 a contact order granted the applicant and paternal relatives scheduled contact.

The applicant alleged that the residence refusal and interim contact ban violated Article 8, spousal equality, and discriminated against him as a father. He argued, among other things, that the judge had suggested local practice always favoured mothers, that the mother’s misconduct and obstruction were ignored, and that proceedings were lengthy. The Government accepted that the residence order interfered with family life but claimed it was lawful, legitimate, and necessary.

The European Court of Human Rights held that Article 8 applied to the interim contact order, but that complaint was lodged out of time: the interim measure was quashed in February 2011 and finally terminated in April 2011, while the application was filed in December 2011. The residence-order complaint was declared admissible.

**Summary of *Leonov v. Russia* (Application no. 77180/11)**

**Case Background and Facts**

The applicant, Sergey Aleksandrovich Leonov, is a Russian national born in 1983. He married Ch. in 2007, and their son, A., was born on 21 August 2007. The family lived in the applicant's flat in Moscow, where A. was registered and attended a neighbourhood nursery school. In November 2009, Ch. left the applicant, taking A. to live at her parents' residence.

On 9 March 2010, the applicant applied for a residence order for A. to live with him. On 26 April 2010, Ch. filed a counterclaim seeking residence and an interim measure. The Timiryazevskiy District Court granted the interim measure, prohibiting the applicant from contacting A. or collecting him from nursery without Ch.'s permission. The court reasoned this was proportional to ensure the forthcoming judgment's execution, noting A. was living with his mother. The applicant learned of this on 30 April 2010 when nursery staff refused him access.

Childcare authorities examined both parents' flats and found them suitable. On 22 June 2010, the Lyublino authority recommended A. reside with his mother due to his young age and the importance of maternal care until age five or six. An expert psychological examination ordered on 29 June 2010 reported in November 2010 that A. was equally attached to both parents, both were equally capable, and parental conflict could harm him psychologically.

During hearings, the applicant argued he had better living conditions, flexible working hours, and that Ch. was aggressive and had been criminally convicted of assaulting him in front of A. on 20 June 2010. Ch. countered that the applicant would lack time for childcare.

**Key Legal Proceedings**

On 18 January 2011, the residence proceedings were stayed pending criminal proceedings against Ch. On 8 February 2011, the Moscow City Court quashed the interim measure as disproportionate and disconnected from the case's subject matter. On 12 April 2011, the Timiryazevskiy District Court granted Ch. residence, dismissing the applicant's claim. The court acknowledged parental conflict, found both parents capable, but emphasised A.'s young age (under four), established residence with his mother, and that changing this would harm him. It noted the applicant could reapply when A. reached a "more conscious age." The Moscow City Court upheld this on 30 June 2011.

On 6 December 2011, a court established Ch. was hindering contact and set a specific contact schedule for the applicant and his family. Ch.'s assault conviction became final on 2 February 2012.

**Alleged Violations**

The applicant complained under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that the residence order in favour of the mother and the interim measure prohibiting contact violated his right to respect for family life, breached spousal equality, and discriminated on grounds of sex. He argued the courts ignored relevant factors and based the decision solely on the belief that small children should be raised by mothers. The domestic courts' decisions, particularly the interim measure and residence order, formed the basis of his allegations regarding violations of his family rights and discriminatory treatment.

In *Gestur Jónsson and Ragnar Halldór Hall v. Iceland* (Applications nos. 68273/14 and 68271/14), the applicants were Icelandic attorneys appointed as defence counsel for two defendants, Y and Z, in a criminal case involving fraud and market manipulation. During 2012–2013, repeated disputes arose over prosecution evidence, disclosure, deadlines, and trial scheduling. The applicants and other defence counsel sought postponements and access to evidence; the District Court and Supreme Court rejected several requests.

On 8 April 2013, the applicants wrote to the District Court judge stating that they could not, for reasons of conscience, continue as defence counsel. They alleged procedural violations, including late evidence, lack of access to important documents, telephone tapping, and unfair procedure. They asked to be relieved of their duties under the Attorneys’ Act. The judge refused. The applicants replied that they would not attend the trial set for 11 April 2013.

On 11 April, the clients attended with new defence counsel; the applicants were absent and not summoned. The judge relieved them of their duties, appointed replacement counsel, postponed the trial, and the prosecution requested contempt fines. A new trial was held in November 2013 before a different judge. On 12 December 2013, the clients were convicted, and in the same judgment the applicants were each fined ISK 1,000,000 under Section 223(1)(a) and (d) of the Criminal Procedures Act for offending the court and causing unnecessary delay by not attending the trial. The judgment was delivered in the applicants’ absence. They had not been notified that the court was considering fines and had no separate hearing before the District Court on that issue.

The applicants appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing violations of Article 6 of the Convention and Article 70 of the Icelandic Constitution. They claimed they were penalised without notice or an opportunity to defend themselves; that they had valid reasons to resign; that the fines were imposed after they were no longer defence counsel; that their conduct did not occur “during proceedings”; and that the fines were excessive, lacked a statutory maximum, and violated legality and *lex certa* principles. They also relied on Article 7 and Article 2 of Protocol No. 7.

Before the Supreme Court, there was an oral hearing. The applicants were represented by counsel but did not give statements or call witnesses. On 28 May 2014, the Supreme Court majority upheld the fines. It found the applicants’ conduct unlawful and contrary to their clients’ interests. Although the fines were substantial and thus amounted to criminal punishment, the majority held that the lack of a special District Court hearing was cured by the appeal, because the applicants could defend themselves before the Supreme Court. It cited *Weber v. Switzerland* and *T v. Austria*. The minority agreed the conduct was unlawful and the fines criminal, but would have annulled the fines: the District Court should have held an immediate hearing, notified them of the charges, and allowed them to object. Instead, fines were imposed months later without notice, and no legal provision permitted remittal.

The applicants therefore alleged before the European Court of Human Rights that the domestic judgments violated Articles 6 and 7 and Article 2 of Protocol No. 7, principally because a criminal fine was imposed on defence counsel without prior notice or an adequate opportunity to be heard. The Chamber judgment of 30 October 2018 was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 22 December 2020.

**Summary of the Case**

The case of *Gestur Jónsson and Ragnar Halldór Hall v. Iceland* concerns two Icelandic attorneys who were fined for contempt of court after refusing to continue representing their clients in a complex fraud and market manipulation trial. The applicants alleged violations of their rights under Articles 6 and 7 of the European Convention on Human Rights and Article 2 of Protocol No. 7.

The first applicant, Gestur Jónsson, and the second applicant, Ragnar Halldór Hall, were appointed as defence counsel for two co-defendants (Y and Z) in criminal proceedings initiated in February 2012. The case involved multiple accused individuals and extensive evidence. From March to December 2012, numerous preliminary hearings took place, during which the defence repeatedly raised concerns about the prosecution's late submission of evidence. The Supreme Court issued three procedural rulings during this period.

On 19 December 2012, the District Court scheduled the trial for 11–23 April 2013. The applicants objected, noting that the prosecution had not yet submitted requested evidence or a witness list. Despite further evidence being submitted in January and March 2013, the court rejected defence requests for postponement to allow adequate preparation time. The Supreme Court upheld this decision on 4 April 2013.

On 8 April 2013, both applicants wrote to the District Court judge stating they could not, for reasons of conscience, continue as defence counsel. They cited multiple violations: lack of notice regarding Supreme Court filing deadlines, failure by the prosecution to share pleadings, inadequate access to documents, and unlawful tapping of lawyer-client communications. They argued that their clients' rights had been grossly violated and requested revocation of their appointment under Section 21(6) of the Attorneys' Act. Their clients approved this decision.

The judge rejected their requests the same day. The applicants responded that they would not attend the trial. On 11 April 2013, the applicants did not appear; the court relieved them of their duties, appointed new defence counsel, and postponed the trial. The prosecution requested fines for contempt under Section 223 of the Criminal Procedures Act.

A new trial was held in November 2013 before a different judge. On 12 December 2013, the District Court convicted the defendants and fined each applicant ISK 1,000,000 (approximately €6,200) under Section 223(1)(a) and (d) of the Criminal Procedures Act for offending the court and causing unnecessary delay. The judgment was delivered in the applicants' absence.

The applicants appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing they had been penalised without opportunity to defend themselves, in violation of Article 6. They contended that the legal conditions for fines were not met and that they had valid reasons to resign. They also argued that, as they were no longer defence counsel when the judgment was delivered, they should have been fined immediately as "others" under Section 224.

On 28 May 2014, the Supreme Court (3–2 majority) upheld the fines. It held that the applicants should have been summoned to a special hearing when the court considered imposing fines, but found that their right to defend themselves was adequately protected through the appeal process, which included an oral hearing. The minority disagreed, concluding that the District Court proceedings were flawed and the fines should be annulled.

The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging that the proceedings leading to their fines violated their right to a fair trial.

The prosecution requested that the applicants be fined for contempt of court under Section 223 of the Criminal Procedures Act.

On 12 December 2013, the District Court convicted Y and Z and also fined each applicant ISK 1,000,000 under Section 223(1)(a) and (d) of the Criminal Procedures Act for offending the court and causing unnecessary delay by not attending trial, thereby harming their clients’ and other defendants’ interests. The judgment concerning the fines was delivered in the applicants’ absence.

The applicants appealed to the Supreme Court against the fines. They argued that they had been penalised without being informed that fines were being considered and without any opportunity to defend themselves before the District Court, violating Article 6 §§ 1–3 of the Convention and Article 70 of the Icelandic Constitution. They also argued that the legal conditions for fining them were not met: they were no longer defence counsel when the judgment was delivered; Section 224 required an immediate ruling if they were treated as “others”; their conduct did not occur “during proceedings”; their clients had approved their decision; and the fines were excessive and lacked a clear statutory maximum, raising legality and *lex certa* concerns.

The Supreme Court held an oral hearing, but no witnesses were heard and the applicants did not give statements. The majority upheld the fines, reasoning that although the applicants should have been summoned to a special hearing, their right to defend themselves was sufficiently protected by the oral appeal hearing. The minority would have annulled the fines because the District Court had imposed them without notice or a prior hearing.

The applicants alleged violations of Articles 6 and 7 of the Convention and Article 2 of Protocol No. 7, centring on the fairness of the proceedings that led to criminal fines imposed on them as defence counsel.

**Case: R.I. and Others v. Romania (App. no. 57077/16), ECtHR, 4 December 2018**

The applicants were a Romanian mother, R.I., and her two minor children, M.I. (born 2006) and I.I. (born 2009). The mother brought the application on her own behalf and on behalf of the children. The Court granted anonymity. The case concerned alleged failures by Romanian authorities to enforce court decisions concerning the children’s residence, effectively allowing the father to sever the mother’s relationship with her children. The central alleged violation was under Article 8 of the Convention, concerning the right to respect for family life.

The mother and father, R., separated in 2010. Initially, the children remained with the mother by agreement, and the father was to have unrestricted access. In November 2013, after the children and their maternal grandmother were involved in a traffic accident, the father took the children from the mother’s home without her consent. From then until May 2014, the mother saw them only occasionally and always in the father’s presence. After June 2014, all contact stopped.

In November 2013, the mother began custody proceedings and sought an interim injunction. On 5 May 2014, the Bucharest County Court issued a final interim decision ordering that the children reside with the mother and that the father pay monthly child support. Enforcement efforts began in June 2014. On 6 June, the mother went to the children’s school to collect them, but the father appeared, became abusive, and police had to intervene; she could not take the children home.

Subsequent bailiff enforcement meetings failed. On 17 July 2014, the father and children did not attend. On 14 August 2014, the father brought the children, but they refused absolutely to return to their mother, alleging that she had shouted at them and occasionally beaten them. The bailiff could not enforce the order. The child protection authority initially found no signs of abuse, though it noted the children suffered anxiety due to parental conflict. Later, a psychological report of 17 November 2015 found no indication of physical abuse by the mother, but indications of psychological abuse in the form of parental alienation by the father. It recommended counselling and removing the children from the parental conflict.

On 24 September 2014, the Bucharest District Court granted the mother physical custody. Enforcement of the return of the children also stalled. The father contested enforcement, moved with the children to Năvodari, and sought stays. In March 2017, a first-instance court granted the father custody, relying on the children’s long stay with him and their refusal to live with their mother. However, on 24 April 2018, the Bucharest County Court allowed the mother’s appeal, quashed that decision, and dismissed the father’s custody request. It found that the mother was not at fault for the non-enforcement and that Romania had a positive obligation to urgently return the children to avoid parental alienation. Nevertheless, on 16 July 2018, the children again refused to move in with their mother.

The mother also filed a criminal complaint against the father for disobeying the court order. Prosecutors investigated but declined to extend the investigation to ill-treatment, finding no evidence.

The key issue was whether the Romanian authorities failed, over more than four years, to enforce final custody and interim decisions, thereby allowing the father’s conduct and the children’s alienation to destroy the mother-child family relationship. The case raised the State’s positive obligations under Article 8 to protect family life and enforce custody/access orders promptly and effectively, balancing the children’s best interests against the father’s obstruction.

**Summary of R.I. and Others v. Romania (Application no. 57077/16)**

The case concerns a Romanian mother and her two minor children. The first applicant, R.I., was in a relationship with R., with whom she had two children, M.I. (born 2006) and I.I. (born 2009). After the relationship ended in 2010, the parents agreed the children would live with their mother, with R. having unrestricted access.

On 28 October 2013, the children were involved in a traffic accident while with their maternal grandmother. In November 2013, R. took the children from the first applicant's home without her consent. From that time until May 2014, she saw them only occasionally. Contact became even scarcer after 5 May 2014 and ceased entirely after 6 June 2014.

On 25 November 2013, the first applicant initiated custody proceedings and sought an interim injunction to have the children reside with her during the proceedings. On 20 December 2013, she alerted the Bucharest child protection authority, fearing the children showed signs of emotional abuse from their father. Reports in January and February 2014 found the children well cared for and no signs of abuse, though experts noted significant anxiety and distress due to parental conflict.

On 5 May 2014, the Bucharest County Court issued a final interim decision ordering the children to reside with their mother. On 6 June 2014, when the mother attempted to collect the children from school, R. became abusive, police intervened, and she was unable to take them home.

Enforcement efforts proved futile. R. failed to comply with a bailiff's order in June 2014, and neither he nor the children attended a scheduled meeting on 17 July 2014. At a second meeting on 14 August 2014, the children absolutely refused to return to their mother, alleging she had shouted at and occasionally beaten them. Psychological counselling was ordered, and a November 2015 expert report found no indication of physical abuse by the mother but identified psychological abuse through parental alienation by the father, noting symptoms of parent alienation syndrome.

On 24 September 2014, the Bucharest District Court granted the mother physical custody. R. appealed but withdrew his appeal in January 2016. Enforcement of the return of the children was repeatedly obstructed, with R. contesting proceedings and seeking stays. Further attempts in 2016 and 2017 to enforce the return failed as the children continued to refuse.

Meanwhile, the first applicant lodged a criminal complaint against R. for disobeying the court order. In June 2016, the prosecutor refused to extend the investigation to cover ill-treatment allegations, finding no evidence.

On 20 March 2017, the Bucharest District Court granted R. physical custody, citing the children's long residence with him and their refusal to live with their mother. On appeal, the Bucharest County Court quashed this decision on 24 April 2018, finding the Romanian State had failed in its positive obligation to urgently enforce the return of the children to their mother, thereby enabling parental alienation. The court noted the mother was not at fault for non-enforcement and that state inaction had effectively penalized her.

The applicants alleged a violation of Article 8 of the Convention, complaining that Romanian authorities failed to enforce the final court decision ordering the children's return, thereby breaching their right to respect for family life.

**R.I. and Others v. Romania** (Application no. 57077/16, judgment of 4 December 2018) concerned a Romanian mother, R.I., and her two children, M.I. and I.I. The mother had been in a relationship with R.; after separation in 2010, the children initially remained with her, and R. was to have unrestricted access.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations began in November 2013, when R. took the children from R.I.’s home without her consent. Contact thereafter became sporadic and eventually stopped by June 2014. R.I. started custody proceedings and sought an interim injunction. On 5 May 2014 the Bucharest County Court issued a final interim decision ordering that the children reside with their mother and that R. pay monthly child support pending the custody case.

The central problem was the repeated failure to enforce that decision. On 6 June 2014 R.I. went to the children’s school to collect them, but R. appeared, became abusive, and police had to intervene; she was unable to take the children home. Bailiff enforcement attempts also failed. R. did not appear at a scheduled meeting in July 2014. At a second meeting on 14 August 2014, he brought the children, but they refused absolutely to return to their mother, alleging that she had shouted at and occasionally beaten them. Subsequent child-protection and psychological reports found no confirmation of physical abuse by the mother, but noted significant anxiety caused by parental conflict. A later expert report of 17 November 2015 found indications of psychological abuse in the form of parental alienation exercised by the father, and recommended counselling.

On 24 September 2014 the Bucharest District Court granted the mother physical custody. R. appealed but later withdrew. Enforcement remained ineffective. R. moved with the children to Năvodari, contested enforcement, and obtained a stay in September 2017; his appeal was dismissed only in May 2018. New enforcement attempts in 2016 failed because R. and the children did not appear. In July 2018 the children again refused to move to their mother. A criminal complaint against R. for disobeying the custody order was investigated, but no ill-treatment charges were brought.

In 2017 R. sought custody. On 20 March 2017 the first-instance court transferred custody to him, relying on the children’s three-year status quo with their father and their refusal to live with their mother. On 24 April 2018 the Bucharest County Court reversed that decision. It held that R.I. was not at fault for the non-enforcement of the 5 May 2014 decision and that the Romanian State had a positive obligation to take urgent legal measures to return the children to their mother in order to protect her right to family life and prevent parental alienation. The court found that non-enforcement had allowed R. to influence the children against their mother and that, if they remained with him, family ties would become permanent and any visitation would be illusory.

The applicants alleged before the European Court of Human Rights that the Romanian authorities failed to enforce final custody and return decisions, thereby breaching the mother’s and children’s right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the Convention. The facts emphasise prolonged enforcement delays, ineffective bailiff, police and child-protection action, and the domestic court’s own finding that State inaction caused the alienation.

**Case Summary: Bondarenko and Others v. Ukraine**  
*Applications nos. 27052/09 and 11 others – ECtHR Fifth Section, Judgment of 28 June 2018*

The case originated in twelve applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants were individuals who had been arrested and held in pre-trial detention in Ukraine in connection with criminal proceedings. The exact personal details, charges, detention dates, and domestic decisions were set out in an appended table, which the provided excerpt does not reproduce. The central complaint, common to all applications, was that the applicants’ pre-trial detention had been unreasonably long. They relied on Article 5 § 3 of the Convention, which guarantees that anyone arrested or detained on suspicion of having committed an offence is entitled to trial within a reasonable time or to release pending trial. Release may be conditioned by guarantees to appear for trial.

Some applicants also raised additional complaints under other Convention provisions. According to the judgment, these complaints were based on the Court’s well-established case-law and were not considered manifestly ill-founded. Their details are found in the appended table. The applications were communicated to the Ukrainian Government, and because they raised similar subject matter, the Court decided to join them and examine them in a single judgment.

In assessing the Article 5 § 3 complaints, the Court reiterated the general principles established in its case-law, particularly *Kudła v. Poland* and *McKay v. the United Kingdom*. It noted that the leading Ukrainian cases of *Kharchenko v. Ukraine* and *Ignatov v. Ukraine* had already found violations of Article 5 § 3 in respect of similar issues. The Court examined the materials submitted by the parties and found no fact or argument that would justify a different conclusion. It therefore held that the length of the applicants’ pre-trial detention was excessive.

The Court’s finding was based on the absence of relevant and sufficient reasons for continuing detention. Under Article 5 § 3, authorities must justify detention with specific facts and cannot rely solely on the gravity of the charges or abstract risks. They must also consider whether less restrictive measures could suffice and conduct meaningful periodic review. In the applicants’ cases, the domestic authorities failed to meet those requirements, leading to detention that exceeded the reasonable-time standard.

Consequently, the Court found a violation of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. It also considered the additional complaints raised by some applicants under well-established case-law and found them admissible. The excerpt provided does not include the final sections on just satisfaction, costs, or the precise amounts awarded, but the judgment was adopted on 28 June 2018 and became final, subject to editorial revision.

In essence, *Bondarenko and Others v. Ukraine* is a typical Article 5 § 3 case concerning systemic problems of lengthy pre-trial detention in Ukraine. The key facts relevant to the violation are that the applicants remained in detention pending trial for excessive periods, while the domestic authorities failed to provide adequate justification or review, contrary to the Convention’s requirement of trial within a reasonable time or release pending trial.

001-187474:
**S.S. v. Slovenia** concerns a Slovenian mother, S.S., diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia, whose parental rights over her fourth child, E., were withdrawn, leading to E.’s adoption by her foster parents. S.S. alleged violations of Articles 6, 8, 13 and 14 of the Convention, complaining that the withdrawal of her parental rights, E.’s adoption, the denial of contact, and the State’s treatment of her mental illness infringed her rights and lacked effective remedies.

S.S. had four children. Her first child was placed in foster care in Slovenia in 2005; her second was placed in foster care in France and later adopted; her third lived with his father in France from December 2010. E. was born on 31 December 2010. Social services quickly noted concerns about S.S.’s ability to care for E., her refusal of psychiatric examination and medication, and her unstable lifestyle. In late January 2011, S.S. travelled to France and left E. with her mother, who was unwilling to care for the child. On 1 February 2011, the Cerknica Social Work Centre removed E., placed her in a crisis centre, and then with foster parents. A final removal and care order followed in March 2011. E. remained with the foster parents.

In March 2011, the Centre applied to divest both parents of parental rights. S.S. received legal aid and was represented. A first-instance decision in November 2012 withdrew her rights, but the Higher Court quashed it in April 2013, requiring clarification whether her conduct resulted from mental illness or voluntary action. On remittal, psychiatrists found S.S. suffered from schizophrenia that was treatable but incurable, with poor prognosis, impaired insight, reduced empathy, and permanent inability to care for E. Another expert found no emotional bond between S.S. and E. and considered contact forced and burdensome for the child. In April 2014, the Ljubljana District Court again withdrew her parental rights under section 116 of the Family Act, prioritising E.’s best interests and permanent stability. The Higher Court dismissed her appeal in October 2014, and the Constitutional Court dismissed her complaint in December 2015 by five votes to three. The majority held that the withdrawal was not based on mental illness as such but on her permanent incapacity to care for E. and the absence of any prospect of reunification. Dissenting judges criticised the severity of the interference, E.’s right to know her parents, and the authorities’ failure to sufficiently support bonding.

Contact between S.S. and E. occurred sporadically from 2011 to 2014, usually supervised. Reports described S.S. as largely passive and distant; E did not initiate contact. The Centre advised S.S. to seek court regulation of contact if dissatisfied. After the Constitutional Court decision, contact stopped. In May 2016, the foster parents adopted E.; S.S. was not a party to the adoption proceedings. When S.S. then sought contact, the Koper District Court dismissed her application in August 2016, relying on an expert opinion that contact would be harmful or traumatic for E. and that no family-type attachment existed. The Higher Court dismissed her appeal in April 2017, and the Supreme Court rejected leave to appeal in August 2017. Her request for legal aid for a constitutional complaint was refused as having no prospects, and she did not lodge a constitutional complaint. Before the European Court, she alleged violations of Articles 6, 8, 13 and 14, focusing on the withdrawal of parental rights, adoption, denial of contact, discrimination linked to mental illness, and lack of effective remedies.

S.S., a Slovenian national born in 1979, is the biological mother of four children. She has been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia and has had several psychiatric hospitalisations. Her first child was placed in foster care in Slovenia, her second was placed in foster care and later adopted in France, and her third lived with his father in France. The application concerns her fourth child, E., born on 31 December 2010.

After E.’s birth, the Cerknica Social Work Centre and other services provided support but observed that S.S. could not adequately care for the newborn. On 30 January 2011 S.S. travelled to France, leaving E. with her mother, who was unwilling to care for the child. On 1 February 2011 the Centre removed E. and placed her in a crisis centre; she was later placed with foster parents and eventually adopted by them. S.S. did not challenge the removal or care order.

In March 2011 the Centre sought to divest S.S. and the alleged father of parental rights, alleging neglect and abandonment. The first-instance decision in 2012 was quashed on appeal because the court had not clarified whether S.S.’s conduct resulted from mental illness or voluntary choice. In the renewed proceedings, expert psychiatrists and psychologists concluded that she suffered from chronic schizophrenia-spectrum disorder, lacked insight into her illness, could not care for E., had diminished empathy, and that there was no realistic prospect of reunification. The Ljubljana District Court withdrew her parental rights in April 2014 under section 116 of the Family Act. The Koper Higher Court dismissed her appeal in October 2014, holding that E.’s best interests required permanent substitute care and that foster care was only temporary. The Constitutional Court dismissed her complaint in December 2015 (5–3), finding that the measure was not based on mental illness as such but on her permanent incapacity to care for E. and the absence of any prospect of reunification; E.’s interests prevailed. S.S. v. Slovenia concerns a Slovenian mother, S.S., diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia, whose parental rights over her fourth child, E., were withdrawn, leading to E.’s adoption by her foster parents. The applicant alleged violations of Articles 6, 8, 13 and 14 of the Convention, arguing that her parental rights were wrongly removed, that E. was put up for adoption, that she was discriminated against because of her mental illness, and that she lacked fair proceedings and effective remedies.

S.S. had four children. Her older children were not in her care: one son lived in foster care in Slovenia, another child was adopted in France, and a third lived with his father in France. E. was born on 31 December 2010. Social and medical staff immediately considered that S.S. was unable to care for the newborn and needed supervision. The local social work centre provided home help, nursing and psychiatric support. In late January 2011, S.S. travelled to France and left E. with her mother; when the grandmother refused to care for E., the social work centre issued an interim removal order on 1 February 2011 and placed E. in a crisis centre. E. was later placed with foster parents and, on 23 March 2011, a final removal and care order was issued. S.S. did not challenge that removal order.

Mental-health evidence was central. S.S. had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia and had several hospitalisations. Experts found she had capacity to participate in proceedings, but described her illness as chronic and incurable, with unstable remission and likely deterioration. They found she lacked insight into her illness, had reduced empathy, did not understand E.’s emotional needs, and could not provide stable care. One expert described contact with S.S. as burdensome and forced upon E.

Contact between S.S. and E. began in June 2011. Over subsequent years there were limited sessions, usually supervised. Reports described S.S. as largely passive and distant; E did not initiate contact and showed no strong bond. The social work centre said contact could be arranged on request and advised S.S. to seek court regulation if dissatisfied. She did not do so until May 2016.

In March 2011 the social work centre applied to divest both parents of parental rights. After an initial decision in 2012 was quashed on appeal, new expert evidence was obtained. In April 2014 the Ljubljana District Court again withdrew S.S.’s parental rights, finding permanent inability to care for E. and no prospect of family reunification. The Higher Court upheld that decision in October 2014. In December 2015 the Constitutional Court dismissed S.S.’s complaint by five votes to three, holding that the decision was based not on her diagnosis as such but on her permanent incapacity to care for E. and E.’s best interests in stable substitute care. E. was adopted by her foster parents in May 2016; S.S. was not a party.

S.S. then sought contact. In August 2016 the District Court dismissed her request, relying on an expert who found that contact would be emotionally harmful and possibly traumatic for E. because S.S. could not form an adequate relationship with her and viewed the adoptive parents negatively. The Higher Court affirmed in April 2017, and the Supreme Court rejected her further appeal in August 2017. She did not lodge a constitutional complaint in the contact proceedings.

**Case summary: O’Sullivan McCarthy Mussel Development Ltd v. Ireland (ECtHR, App. No. 44460/16)**

The applicant, O’Sullivan McCarthy Mussel Development Ltd, is an Irish company that has cultivated mussels in Castlemaine Harbour, County Kerry, since the late 1970s. Its business involves annually fishing immature “mussel seed” in the harbour and re-laying it for cultivation. The activity requires an aquaculture licence, a sea-fishing boat licence, entry of the boat in the Register of Fishing Boats, and an annual mussel-seed fishing authorisation from the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine. Castlemaine Harbour was designated a Special Protection Area (SPA) in 1994 under the Birds Directive and a Special Area of Conservation (SAC) in 2000 under the Habitats Directive, making it part of the Natura 2000 network. In 1993, a public notice had stated that designation was not envisaged to change traditional usage.

Following EU infringement proceedings, the Court of Justice of the European Union held in December 2007 in *Commission v. Ireland* that Ireland had failed to ensure aquaculture programmes likely to affect SPAs were subject to appropriate prior environmental assessment under the Habitats Directive. To comply, the Minister considered commercial activity could not continue until assessments were completed. On 6 June 2008, a statutory instrument prohibited mussel-seed fishing in 24 locations, including Castlemaine Harbour, from 9 June to 1 July 2008. The applicant, which had just purchased a new boat for €1 million, was informed that day and protested. The Department replied that baseline data had to be gathered for the required assessment, that Castlemaine was prioritised, and that interim resumption would be sought from the European Commission.

In August 2008, the applicant received an authorisation beginning 23 August, but the prohibition remained in force. On 3 October 2008, after the Commission accepted an interim assessment, the Minister removed Castlemaine Harbour from the prohibition. Fishing resumed on 5 October 2008. By then, natural predators had decimated the mussel seed. Because mussels need two years to mature, the financial consequences were felt in 2010, when the applicant had no mussels for sale. It estimated lost profits of €289,599. It claimed no viable alternative seed source existed and that, had it known of the restriction, it would not have bought the new boat.

In 2009, the harbour was opened and the applicant obtained the usual seed. In August 2009, a new fisheries Natura permit was required for fishing in SACs/SPAs. In 2010, the applicant could not fish during the first authorised period because it lacked that permit; when it later fished, seed had again been depleted by predators. It estimated a further loss of €119,941. The Government said it had begun compliance work immediately after the CJEU judgment, coordinated with BIM, the Marine Institute and NPWS, negotiated with the Commission, and completed the Castlemaine appropriate assessment in April 2011, which found no anticipated environmental disturbance from mussel fishing.

In February 2009, the applicant and another company sued the State in the High Court for breach of legitimate expectation, operational negligence and breach of the constitutional right to earn a livelihood. In May 2013, the High Court found for the applicant, awarding €275,000 for 2008 and 2010 losses. The State appealed. In February 2016, the Supreme Court overturned the findings: there was no legitimate expectation, and the majority rejected operational negligence and any duty of care. A minority would have upheld negligence for 2008 only.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 8 due to economic loss attributed to the authorities without compensation, violation of Article 13 concerning an effective remedy, and, under Article 6, excessive duration of domestic proceedings.

It held that the 1993 notice—stating that restrictions on traditional activities were “not envisaged”—did not create a clear commitment, especially as EU law later imposed mandatory environmental assessment. The Minister had no discretion under EU law to permit the activity without appropriate assessment, and no actionable duty of care was owed to the applicant. The Minister’s duty was to comply with EU environmental law.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 8 due to uncompensated economic loss for which it blamed the State. It also alleged no effective remedy under Article 13 and excessive duration under Article 6, the domestic proceedings having lasted from February 2009 to February 2016. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were that the restrictions were temporary, imposed by lawful statutory instruments, aimed at ensuring compliance with EU environmental obligations, and lifted once an interim assessment allowed fishing to resume. The applicant could still harvest previously laid mussels, and the authorities engaged with the European Commission to reopen the harbour as soon as legally possible. The domestic courts ultimately rejected State liability. The ECtHR found the interference with property rights justified and proportionate, with no violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, no separate issue under Article 8, no violation of Article 13, and no violation of Article 6 concerning length.

**Boldijar and Others v. Romania** (European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, 29 March 2018) concerned 16 applications lodged against Romania under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants were detained in various Romanian prisons and complained about the inadequate conditions of their detention, relying on Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. Because the applications raised similar issues, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations concerned the physical conditions in which the applicants were held. The judgment states that the specific details of each applicant’s detention were set out in an appended table, but it identifies common problems: overcrowding or limited personal space, insect-infested cells, poor-quality bedding and bed linen, poor food, and a lack of adequate furniture. The applicants alleged that these conditions were sufficiently serious to amount to degrading treatment under Article 3.

The Romanian Government contested the admissibility of one application, no. 51850/15, by raising a preliminary objection based on the six-month time limit. The Government argued that, from 18 November 2014 to 25 May 2015, the applicant had 5.04 sq m of personal space, which it said interrupted the continuity of his allegedly inadequate detention. On that basis, it argued that his complaint about detention in Giurgiu Prison from 13 October 2014 to 25 May 2015 had been lodged out of time, and that the Court should examine only the period from 25 May 2015 onwards concerning Giurgiu and Jilava Prisons.

The Court rejected that objection. It held that even if an applicant had more than 4 sq m of personal space, other aspects of the physical conditions of detention remained relevant to the Article 3 assessment. In this applicant’s case, those aspects included an infestation of the cell with insects, poor-quality bedding and bed linen, poor food, and a lack of adequate furniture. The Court was not convinced by the Government’s arguments that these conditions were adequate. It found that, overall, the conditions of detention in Giurgiu Prison remained inadequate. The Government’s preliminary objection was therefore dismissed.

On admissibility, the Court found that the applications were not manifestly ill-founded within the meaning of Article 35 § 3 (a) and were not inadmissible on any other grounds. They were accordingly declared admissible.

On the merits, the Court reiterated its case-law, in particular **Muršić v. Croatia**, that a serious lack of space in a prison cell weighs heavily in determining whether detention conditions are “degrading” under Article 3, and may disclose a violation either alone or in combination with other shortcomings. It also noted that in the pilot case **Rezmiveș and Others v. Romania**, it had already found a violation in respect of similar issues concerning Romanian prison conditions. After examining all the material, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion. It therefore held that the applicants’ conditions of detention were inadequate and that there had been a violation of Article 3 of the Convention.

The judgment then proceeded to the application of Article 41 concerning just satisfaction; the excerpt provided does not specify the amounts, if any, awarded.
