Jishkariani v. Georgia (ECtHR, 20 Sept 2018) concerned whether Georgia violated Article 8 by failing to protect the applicant’s reputation from defamatory statements by the Minister of Justice. The applicant was a psychiatrist, founder/director of NGO Empathy, which provided psychosocial rehabilitation in Tbilisi Prison No. 1 under a Ministry of Justice agreement. She was also a member of the Public Monitoring Commission and the Inmates’ Mental Health Research and Monitoring Commission.

In September 2005, inmate L.Ts. was transferred to the prison hospital after the applicant assessed him; he later assaulted hospital staff. Another inmate died around the same time, and media alleged corruption and mismanagement in prison medical services. The Minister ordered an internal investigation on 13 September. On 16 September, before it concluded, he spoke live on Rustavi 2 and named the applicant. He accused her of exceeding her powers, writing medical conclusions bypassing the commission, giving illegal notes that led to transfers of allegedly healthy inmates, and involvement in illegal arrangements. He called her “shameless” and suggested she would be investigated. On 20 September, a newspaper interview repeated the allegations, implying she had signed documents to transfer healthy inmates to the prison hospital in exchange for money, was an accomplice in corruption, and had committed a crime. The applicant sued for defamation, seeking retraction and non-pecuniary damages. She argued her conclusions were based on verifiable medical documents and that no criminal proceedings had been brought against her.

The domestic courts dismissed her claim. Treating her as a public figure under the Freedom of Expression and Speech Act, they required her to prove that the statements contained substantially false facts, that she suffered damage, and that the Minister knew they were false or acted with apparent and gross negligence. The Tbilisi City Court accepted that the accusations “may have contained erroneous facts” and that she had not been a suspect, but found she failed to prove damage and culpable knowledge. It held that the Minister had taken verification steps by ordering an internal investigation before speaking. The Court of Appeal upheld this reasoning; the Supreme Court declared her appeal inadmissible.

Later, the Inspectorate’s report indicated that the inmate had mental health problems and a head trauma, and that the Medical Department director had bypassed the commission. The criminal investigation was discontinued for absence of a crime.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained under Article 8. The Court found the accusations serious, as they publicly implied criminal corruption and harmed her professional and civil-society reputation. There was a public debate about prison medical management, and she was a public figure, so wider criticism was acceptable. However, even value judgments require a sufficient factual basis. The Minister had not waited for the investigation’s outcome and had no verified information against her. The domestic courts failed to address the core factual allegation and placed the burden on her to prove gross negligence. Merely commissioning an inquiry without awaiting its result did not demonstrate due diligence. The Court found that the domestic courts failed to strike a fair balance between Articles 8 and 10, violating Article 8.

**Case: Jishkariani v. Georgia (App. no. 18925/09), ECtHR, 20 September 2018**

The applicant, Mariam Jishkariani, was a Georgian psychiatrist and founder/director of the NGO “Empathy,” which rehabilitated torture victims. In 2003 her NGO contracted with the Ministry of Justice to create a psychosocial rehabilitation office in Tbilisi Prison No. 1. She later became a member of the Public Monitoring Commission for prisons and of the Inmates’ Mental Health Research and Monitoring Commission.

In September 2005, an inmate, L.Ts., assaulted prison hospital staff. He had been transferred to the prison hospital after the applicant had recorded a medical opinion that he needed psychiatric supervision. Around the same time, another inmate died amid reports of corruption and mismanagement in prison medical services. These events attracted wide media coverage.

On 16 September 2005, the then Minister of Justice, Mr K.K., speaking live on Rustavi 2 TV, accused the applicant of grossly exceeding her powers by writing medical conclusions about inmates, bypassing the relevant commission. He suggested that her “scribbles” had caused allegedly healthy inmates to be transferred to the prison hospital without legal grounds, called her a “shameless person,” and implied she had found a corrupt “business” for herself. He said she would become an object of investigation along with the Medical Department director. On 20 September 2005, the newspaper *Rezonansi* published an interview in which the Minister accused the applicant of involvement in corrupt arrangements: issuing false psychiatric reports so healthy inmates could be transferred to the prison hospital in exchange for money, calling her an accomplice. These statements strongly suggested criminal conduct.

The applicant sued the Minister for civil defamation, seeking retraction and non-pecuniary damages. She argued that her medical conclusions were based on verifiable records and that no criminal proceedings had been brought against her. The domestic courts dismissed her claim. They treated her as a “public figure” under the Freedom of Expression and Speech Act, meaning the burden was on her to prove that the statements were substantially false, that she suffered damage, and that the Minister knew they were false or acted with gross negligence. Although the courts accepted that the accusations “may have contained erroneous facts” and that she had never been criminally investigated, they found she had not proved damage or the required fault. They held that the Minister had taken verification measures by ordering an internal inspection three days before his TV statement, even though he did not await its outcome. The Court of Appeal upheld the judgment, finding the statements acceptable criticism in a public debate; the Supreme Court declared her appeal inadmissible.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 8 that Georgia had failed to protect her reputation against the Minister’s defamatory statements. The Court found the accusations serious and capable of harming her professional and civil-society reputation. It accepted that there was a public debate about prison medical management and that the applicant was a public figure, so criticism could be wider. However, the Minister’s statements amounted to serious factual accusations of criminal corruption, not mere value judgments. They lacked sufficient factual basis: the later internal investigation confirmed the inmate had health issues, and the criminal investigation was discontinued for absence of a crime. The Minister had not waited for verification. The domestic courts thus failed to strike a fair balance between the applicant’s Article 8 right to reputation and the Minister’s Article 10 freedom of expression, resulting in a violation of Article 8.

**Jishkariani v. Georgia (Application no. 18925/09)** concerned a Georgian psychiatrist, Ms Mariam Jishkariani, who complained that domestic courts failed to protect her reputation under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights against defamatory statements made by the then Minister of Justice.

The applicant was a psychiatrist and founder/director of “Empathy”, an NGO providing rehabilitation for torture victims. In 2003, her NGO contracted with the Ministry of Justice to create a psychosocial rehabilitation office in Tbilisi Prison No. 1. She later became a member of the Public Monitoring Commission for prisons and of the Inmates’ Mental Health Research and Monitoring Commission.

The dispute arose after an incident on 10 September 2005, when an inmate, L.Ts., physically assaulted the director and head doctor of the prison hospital. L.Ts. had been transferred to the hospital based on the applicant’s medical opinion. The incident and separate allegations of corruption and mismanagement in the prison medical system attracted widespread media attention.

On 16 September 2005, the Minister of Justice, Mr K.K., stated live on Rustavi 2 TV that the applicant had grossly exceeded her powers, written medical conclusions bypassing the relevant commission, and been involved in illegal arrangements. He suggested that her “scribbles” had caused healthy inmates to be placed in the prison hospital without legal grounds, called her a “shameless person”, and said she would become an object of investigation. In a 20 September 2005 newspaper interview, the Minister further alleged that the applicant had been involved in corrupt schemes, issuing false psychiatric reports in exchange for money, and that she and the Medical Department director were “accomplices.”

A criminal investigation was opened concerning the 10 September incident, and the applicant was questioned as a witness. The Minister also commissioned an internal investigation on 13 September 2005, but did not wait for its outcome before making the public accusations. The General Inspectorate’s report of 13 October 2005 mainly criticised the Medical Department director and noted that the inmate had a history of mental illness and head trauma. The criminal investigation was discontinued in December 2007 for absence of a crime.

The applicant brought civil defamation proceedings, seeking retraction and non-pecuniary damages. Domestic courts applied the Freedom of Expression and Speech Act, treating her as a public figure. They required her to prove that the statements were false, that she suffered damage, and that the Minister knew they were false or acted with gross negligence. The Tbilisi City Court found that the accusations “may have contained erroneous facts” and that she had never been criminally investigated, but still dismissed her claim. It held that the Minister had taken verification measures by ordering an internal investigation and that his statements were acceptable criticism in a matter of public interest. The Court of Appeal upheld this, and the Supreme Court declared her appeal inadmissible.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged that the domestic courts’ refusal to protect her reputation violated Article 8. The Court found the complaint admissible and held that the Minister’s accusations were serious, implied criminal conduct, and damaged her reputation as a medical professional and civil-society activist. Although the statements contributed to a debate of general interest and the applicant was a public figure, the Court held that the domestic courts had failed to require a sufficient factual basis for the serious allegations. The Minister did not wait for the internal investigation and had no verified information. Therefore, the domestic courts failed to strike a fair balance between the applicant’s right to reputation under Article 8 and the Minister’s freedom of expression under Article 10.

*Sandu and Others v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* (ECtHR, 17 July 2018) concerned eight applications brought by 1,646 Moldovan natural persons and three companies. The applicants lived in Moldovan-controlled villages on the left bank of the Dniester—Doroțcaia, Pîrîta, Molovata Nouă, Pohrebea and Cocieri—in the Dubăsari region. Their farmland lay across a road controlled by the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Transdniestrian Republic” (“MRT”). The applicants had obtained land titles under Moldova’s “Pamântul” privatisation programme. In 1999, the MRT local administration reportedly did not object to the creation of peasant farms under that reform. Until 1998, the applicants used or rented the land without interference. From 1998, MRT checkpoints charged taxes and fees on agricultural movement.

In August 2004, the MRT authorities declared that the land owned or rented by the applicants was MRT property. They could continue working it only if they paid rent to the MRT authorities. The applicants refused because they were already lawful owners or renters. As a result, the MRT blocked all access to the land, causing harvest losses; some agricultural machinery was seized. No cultivation occurred for two years, damaging the land. The MRT refused requests for passage, treating the land as its own. Moldovan authorities replied that they could not compel the MRT to allow access. The applicants complained to Moldovan prosecutors, the Russian embassy and the OSCE.

The applicant companies had rented land from villagers. They submitted mayoral certificates, tax and audit reports, and MRT customs decisions showing fines and seizure of tractors, wheat, barley and apples for alleged undeclared transport across the MRT “border”. Moldova later provided compensation measures and, in 2006, negotiated a temporary MRT registration system allowing owners to cultivate the land and be exempt from MRT payments.

The alleged violation was Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention: denial of access to land and conditioning its use on payments to the MRT, with no effective remedies. Russia denied jurisdiction. Moldova accepted territorial jurisdiction but described limited influence. The Court held both States had jurisdiction: Moldova as territorial State with positive obligations, and Russia because the MRT’s dependency on Russian military, economic and political support showed effective control and decisive influence. It rejected Russia’s non-exhaustion objection.

On the merits, the Court found the applicants had “possessions”: natural persons owned land; companies had protected interests under rental contracts for commercial farming. The MRT’s declaration of ownership, demand for rental contracts, and blocking of access after refusal amounted to interference with peaceful enjoyment of possessions, though not formal expropriation. The Court ultimately found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 by the Russian Federation. Moldova was not held responsible, having taken reasonable available diplomatic, economic and other measures. The case is significant for affirming Russian jurisdiction over Transdniestrian acts and protecting landowners’ and lessees’ property rights against separatist interference.

**Case Summary: Sandu and Others v. Moldova and Russia (App. Nos. 21034/05 et al.)**

This case originated in eight applications lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by 1,646 Moldovan natural persons and three companies against both the Republic of Moldova and the Russian Federation. The applicants were residents of several villages—Doroțcaia, Pîrîta, Molovata Nouă, Pohrebea, and Cocieri—situated on the left bank of the Dniester River in the Dubăsari region. These villages are under Moldovan control, but parts of the applicants’ agricultural land lie across a road controlled by the authorities of the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Transdniestrian Republic” (MRT).

The applicants had obtained titles to their land through Moldova’s “Pamântul” (Land) privatisation programme. Some titles were later transferred via gift or inheritance. The applicant companies, Posedo-Agro S.R.L., Agro-Tiras S.R.L., and Agro-S.A.V.V.A. S.R.L., rented land from village owners during the relevant period. The applicants’ primary income derived from working this land.

Between 1992 and 1998, they used the land without interference. However, in 1998, MRT authorities established checkpoints along the road, imposing taxes and fees. In August 2004, the MRT authorities declared the land to be MRT property and demanded that the applicants sign rental contracts with them. The applicants refused, as they were already lawful owners or renters. Consequently, all access to their land was blocked, harvests were lost, and some agricultural machinery was seized.

The applicants complained to MRT authorities, who refused passage. Moldovan authorities replied they could not compel the MRT to allow access. Complaints to the Russian embassy and the OSCE were also unsuccessful. Events complained of occurred primarily in 2004–2006.

Before the Court, the applicants alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention (protection of property), claiming denial of access to their land and lack of effective remedies. The Moldovan Government acknowledged jurisdiction but argued it had taken reasonable measures. The Russian Government denied jurisdiction, arguing the applicants did not fall within its responsibility and that domestic remedies in Russia were not exhausted.

The Court first addressed jurisdiction. It reaffirmed its prior case-law (Ilaşcu, Catan, Mozer), finding that Moldova, as the territorial State, had jurisdiction but its responsibility was limited to positive obligations. Regarding Russia, the Court found that the MRT’s high dependency on Russian military, economic, and political support meant Russia exercised effective control over the Transdniestrian authorities. Thus, the applicants fell within Russia’s jurisdiction under Article 1 of the Convention. The Russian Government’s objections *ratione personae* and *ratione loci* were dismissed. The objection on non-exhaustion of Russian domestic remedies was also rejected, as Russia denied involvement and failed to specify available remedies.

On admissibility, the Court addressed the standing of Posedo-Agro S.R.L., which had been liquidated but had transferred its rights to Serghei Popa FP before liquidation. The Court accepted this substitution. It also struck out applications from three applicants who withdrew and 172 others lacking sufficient information or deceased without heirs. The remaining applications were declared admissible.

On the merits, the Court examined whether there had been an interference with the applicants’ “possessions” under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It found that the natural persons had established ownership through documents, and the companies had shown they rented land for commercial purposes, thus holding “possessions.” The Court considered that by blocking access to the land after the applicants refused to sign rental contracts with the MRT, the authorities interfered with their property rights. This interference did not amount to formal deprivation but fell under the general principle of peaceful enjoyment of possessions. The case was thus centered on the alleged violation of property rights through denial of access and the lack of effective remedies, with the Court ultimately holding both respondent States responsible under the Convention.

Sandu and Others v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia concerned eight applications brought by 1,646 Moldovan individuals and three companies. The applicants lived in villages on the left bank of the Dniester in the Dubăsari region—Doroțcaia, Pîrîta, Molovata Nouă, Pohrebea and Cocieri—which were under Moldovan control. Their land was situated near these villages, across a road linking the northern and southern parts of the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Transdniestrian Republic” (“MRT”). Although the road cut through Moldovan-controlled zones, it was controlled by MRT authorities.

The applicants obtained titles from Moldova under the “Pamântul” land privatisation programme; some land was later transferred by gift or inheritance. Three applicant companies rented land from villagers. Farming was their main source of income. Until 1998 they used or rented the land without interference. In 1998 the MRT set up checkpoints to monitor agricultural products across the road, and applicants had to pay MRT taxes and fees.

In August 2004 the MRT authorities declared that the land owned or rented by the applicants was MRT property. They allowed continued use only if applicants paid rent to the local MRT authorities. The applicants refused because they were already lawful owners or renters. As a result, all access to their land was blocked and the harvest was lost. Some agricultural machines were seized. No work was done for two years, making it difficult to restore the land’s capacity. Complaints to the MRT for passage were refused. Moldovan authorities said they could not compel the MRT to allow passage; complaints to the Russian embassy and OSCE also failed.

Company-specific facts were important. Agro-S.A.V.V.A. S.R.L. rented 104 hectares and could not cultivate 105 hectares. Agro-Tiras S.R.L. rented 450 hectares across the road; MRT customs seized a tractor and 5.8 tonnes of wheat for alleged undeclared importation. Posedo-Agro S.R.L. rented land from hundreds of villagers; MRT customs seized 16 tonnes of barley and 6.1 tonnes of apples, imposed fines equal to market value, and threatened confiscation of trucks and tractors. These measures showed MRT enforcement at the road.

Moldova later passed compensation laws and, in 2006, negotiated a temporary MRT registration mechanism allowing landowners to cultivate the land and be exempt from MRT payments.

The applicants alleged that being denied access to their land breached Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention (protection of property), and that they had no effective remedies. The Court joined the cases. It found Moldova had territorial jurisdiction but limited positive obligations, while Russia had jurisdiction because the MRT depended on Russian military, economic and political support and Russia exercised effective control or decisive influence. The Court rejected Russia’s non-exhaustion and standing objections; Posedo-Agro was replaced by Serghei Popa FP, some applications were struck out, and heirs continued others.

On the property complaint, the Court found the individual applicants had “possessions” as landowners, and the companies had protectable interests as renters cultivating land commercially. The MRT’s declaration of ownership and demand for rental contracts, followed by blocking access when refused, constituted interference with the peaceful enjoyment of possessions—not formal deprivation or mere control of use. The key alleged violation was therefore the effective prevention of owners and renters from accessing and farming their land in 2004–2006 through MRT measures.

Aviso Zeta AG v. Austria (ECtHR, 21 June 2018, no. 5734/14) concerned a Vienna-based bank that purchased and held IF shares for third parties. After IF shares lost substantial value from 2007, clients F.M. and H.H. sued Aviso for annulment of their share purchases, alleging inadequate advice by A., an investment adviser and distribution partner. In 2012 the Vienna Commercial Court held Aviso liable because of its close professional ties to A. The Vienna Court of Appeal reversed, finding A.’s inadequate advice could not be attributed to Aviso. In June 2013 the Supreme Court (Second Section, five judges) restored the Commercial Court’s judgment, holding Aviso liable due to its significant interest in selling IF shares and the inadequate information provided.

The alleged violation arose from the participation of Judge N. in that Supreme Court panel. Judge N. had personally purchased IF shares following advice from A.; their value later fell. In 2009 he offered his shares or possible claims to a litigation funder to bring actions against IF or others involved, potentially including Aviso. He had withdrawn from at least two comparable IF-share cases, which the Supreme Court accepted. In another comparable case, on 13 November 2013, the Supreme Court declared Judge N. biased because his impartiality could appear doubtful. The applicant learned the panel’s composition only when the Supreme Court judgment was served, so it could not challenge Judge N. beforehand. It filed an action for nullity, arguing bias. The Supreme Court excluded Judge N. from the nullity proceedings but rejected the nullity action, holding that only statutory exclusion, not mere bias, could ground nullity, and no particularly grave reason existed. It noted Judge N. no longer intended to sue after the funder terminated the contract.

The Government argued non-exhaustion: Aviso could have asked the Supreme Court registry for the file number, discovered the section/panel, and challenged Judge N. before judgment; failure to do so amounted to waiver. The ECtHR rejected this. Aviso had no actual knowledge of the panel; domestic law required a challenge once actually aware, not when it ought to have known. Requiring a registry inquiry was not provided by law or reasonable. Judges had a duty to self-report possible bias, and Judge N. had withdrawn in comparable cases. The application was therefore admissible.

On the merits under Article 6 § 1, the Court applied subjective and objective impartiality tests. There was no proof of personal prejudice. Under the objective test, the key issue was whether legitimate doubt about impartiality was objectively justified. Judge N. had considered suing Aviso, had assigned possible claims to a funder, had previously withdrawn from comparable cases, and had recently been found biased in another comparable case. His later change of mind after the funder terminated the contract was insufficient to dispel doubts, especially since the Supreme Court itself had dismissed that same argument shortly before. His role as an ordinary panel member, not presiding judge, was not decisive because closed deliberations made his influence impossible to assess. The Court concluded that the Supreme Court’s composition did not guarantee impartiality, violating Article 6 § 1.

**Summary of *Aviso Zeta AG v. Austria* (Application no. 5734/14)**

The case concerns a violation of the right to an impartial tribunal under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights, arising from civil proceedings before the Austrian Supreme Court.

The applicant, Aviso Zeta AG, was a bank that purchased and held shares, predominantly in the "IF" company, for third parties. The bank and IF were closely related through shared management and staff. The "A. company," an investment advisor, served as a key distribution partner for the bank. Following a significant drop in the value of IF shares starting in 2007, numerous legal actions were brought against the bank.

In 2009, two clients, F.M. and H.H., sued the bank to annul their share purchases, claiming they had received inadequate risk advice from the A. company. On 17 June 2013, a five-judge panel of the Supreme Court ruled in favour of the clients, holding the bank liable for the inadequate advice.

The central issue arose after this judgment was served. The applicant discovered that one of the five judges on the panel, Judge N., had a potential conflict of interest. Judge N. had personally purchased IF shares on the advice of the A. company and had suffered financial losses. He had even offered his shares to a litigation funder to potentially bring a claim against parties including the applicant bank. Crucially, Judge N. had previously withdrawn from at least two comparable cases involving IF shares, and the Supreme Court had accepted his bias in those instances.

The applicant filed an action for nullity, arguing Judge N.'s participation breached the impartiality requirement. However, the Supreme Court rejected this action on 27 November 2013. It held that under domestic law, a final judgment could only be contested on the ground that a judge was excluded by law, and that mere bias was not a sufficient reason. It found no "particularly grave" reason to make an exception, as Judge N. no longer intended to sue.

The applicant also faced a procedural hurdle. Because the Supreme Court's panel composition was not publicly known before judgment, the applicant could not challenge Judge N. beforehand. The Government argued that the applicant failed to exhaust domestic remedies by not enquiring about the panel's composition and challenging the judge pre-emptively.

The European Court of Human Rights found that the applicant could not be reproached for this failure, as the suggested procedure was not required by law and was not reasonable. The Court noted that Judge N. himself had a legal duty to report potential bias.

On the merits, the Court focused on the objective test of impartiality. It found that Judge N.’s prior intention to sue the applicant, combined with his repeated withdrawals from similar cases, would raise legitimate doubts about his impartiality in the eyes of an external observer. The Court was particularly critical of the Supreme Court's contradiction: just two weeks before rejecting the applicant's nullity action, it had accepted Judge N.'s bias in another comparable case. The Court concluded that the composition of the Supreme Court panel failed to guarantee objective impartiality, violating Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

Aviso Zeta AG v. Austria (ECtHR, 21 June 2018) concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention because the Supreme Court was not impartial. The applicant was a Vienna bank, later in liquidation, which purchased and held shares, mainly in the IF company, for third parties. The bank and IF were closely related, sharing management and staff, and the A. company was an important distribution partner. After IF shares lost substantial value from 2007, clients F.M. and H.H., who had been advised through the A. company, sued the bank in 2009 to annul their share purchases. IF joined on the bank’s side.

In April 2012 the Vienna Commercial Court found for the clients, holding that they had not been adequately informed of the risks and that the bank was accountable for the inadequate advice given by A. company due to their close professional ties. The Court of Appeal reversed, finding the advice could not be attributed to the bank. On 17 June 2013, the Supreme Court (Second Section), sitting as a five-judge panel, granted the clients’ appeal and restored the Commercial Court judgment, finding the bank liable because of its significant interest in selling IF shares and its responsibility for inadequate information.

The key issue was that Judge N., one of the five Supreme Court judges, had himself purchased IF shares on advice from the A. company and suffered losses. In 2009 he had offered his shares or possible claims to a litigation funder to bring actions against IF and potentially the applicant bank. He had withdrawn of his own motion from at least two comparable cases concerning IF shares, and the Supreme Court had accepted his withdrawal on bias grounds. In the present case, however, he did not withdraw because after the litigation funder terminated the contract, he decided not to pursue claims and no longer considered withdrawal necessary.

The applicant only learned of the panel composition when the Supreme Court judgment was served, so it could not challenge Judge N. earlier. It filed an action for nullity, claiming bias. The Supreme Court’s Seventh Section excluded Judge N. from the nullity proceedings, but the Second Section rejected the nullity action. It held that bias was not a ground for nullity under section 529 of the Code of Civil Procedure; only legal exclusion from office qualified, and no particularly grave reason comparable to exclusion was shown.

The Government argued non-exhaustion, saying the applicant should have asked the registry for the file number, discovered the panel, and challenged Judge N. before judgment. The ECtHR rejected this, finding the applicant had no prior knowledge and that requiring such an inquiry was neither provided by law nor reasonable. Judge N. had a duty to self-report and had withdrawn in comparable cases.

On the merits, the Court found no proof of subjective personal bias. However, under the objective test, Judge N.’s previous intention to sue the applicant and his withdrawals in similar cases created objectively justified doubts about his impartiality. His later change of mind did not dispel those doubts, especially since the Supreme Court had declared him biased in another comparable case only two weeks earlier. His non-presiding role was not decisive, and closed deliberations made any influence impossible to ascertain. The Supreme Court’s composition therefore failed to guarantee impartiality, violating Article 6 § 1.

The applications were communicated to the Russian Government. The applicants complained principally about inadequate conditions of detention in Russia. Some applicants also complained under Article 13 of the Convention that they had no effective domestic remedy for those conditions.

The full text states that the list of applicants and the specific details of their applications were set out in the appended table. The Court treated the applicants as having been kept in detention in poor conditions.

The main alleged violation concerned Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. The Court referred to its established case law on inadequate detention conditions, particularly *Kudła v. Poland* and *Ananyev and Others v. Russia*. It reiterated that extreme lack of space in a prison cell, or overcrowding, weighs heavily in assessing whether detention conditions are “degrading” under Article 3. Overcrowding may disclose a violation either alone or together with other shortcomings. The Court also noted its earlier leading case, *Sergey Babushkin v. Russia*, where it had already found a violation in respect of similar issues.

After examining all the material, the Court found no fact or argument that could persuade it to reach a different conclusion on admissibility or merits. **Case Summary: Prokhorenko and Others v. Russia (Application no. 12204/15 and 2 others)**

The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered judgment on 29 March 2018 in *Prokhorenko and Others v. Russia*, concerning three applications lodged against Russia under Article 34 of the Convention. The applications were joined because they raised similar subject matter.

The central complaint was that the applicants were detained in inadequate conditions, in violation of Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. The applicants alleged that the conditions of their detention were poor. Although the specific facts—such as dates, detention facilities, and cell measurements—were set out in an appended table rather than in the main judgment, the Court accepted that the applicants had been kept in detention in poor conditions.

In application no. 12204/15, the applicant also raised additional complaints under the Convention. These included allegations concerning the poor conditions of transport of detainees and the lack of an effective domestic remedy to complain about inadequate detention conditions. The applicant also raised another Article 3 complaint, which the Court later rejected.

The Court recalled its established case-law on inadequate detention conditions, particularly *Muršić v. Croatia* and *Ananyev and Others v. Russia*. It reiterated that a serious lack of space in a prison cell weighs heavily in determining whether detention conditions are “degrading” under Article 3. Such a lack of space may amount to a violation either alone or combined with other shortcomings, such as poor sanitation, lack of privacy, inadequate bedding, or restricted access to fresh air or exercise.

The Russian Government was given notice of the applications, but the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to depart from its previous case-law. It therefore concluded that the applicants’ conditions of detention were inadequate and that there had been a violation of Article 3.

Second, it found a violation concerning the poor conditions of transport of detainees, consistent with *Idalov v. Russia*. These complaints were declared admissible and disclosed violations of the Convention.

The remaining complaint under Article 3 in application no. 12204/15 was rejected. The Court held that it either did not meet the admissibility criteria under Articles 34 and 35 of the Convention or did not disclose any appearance of a violation of Convention rights.

The judgment was final but subject to editorial revision. The Court’s findings on just satisfaction under Article 41 were also addressed in the judgment, though the excerpt provided does not include the full reasoning or award.

One applicant also faced poor transport conditions and had no effective domestic remedy for complaining about detention conditions. **Patalakh v. Germany** (Application no. 22692/15) is an 8 March 2018 judgment of the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section). The applicant, Ivan Patalakh, a Russian national, complained under Article 5 §§ 1 and 4 that the German courts failed, or significantly delayed, reviewing the lawfulness of his remand detention, resulting in its automatic and arbitrary continuation.

On 30 October 2013 the Frankfurt am Main District Court issued an arrest warrant against the applicant. He was strongly suspected of aiding aggravated fraudulent conversion, corruption, corruption in commercial practice, and aggravated tax evasion through bribes and fictitious invoices in international business dealings. The warrant was based on risk of absconding, given the possible heavy sentence, his wife’s status as a co-accused, and his lack of legal residence or significant ties to Germany; risk of collusion was also cited. He was arrested the same day and placed in remand detention. Additional charges were added in September 2014. On 19 December 2014 the prosecution brought charges; a 280-page indictment was translated and served on 26 January 2015. The main proceedings opened on 6 May 2015, trial began on 8 June 2015, and on 14 July 2016 he was convicted and sentenced to four years and six months’ imprisonment. Appeals remained pending. The arrest warrant was set aside on 26 October 2016.

The detention-review chronology was central. From 15 January 2014 the applicant unsuccessfully challenged his detention. On 28 July 2014 the Frankfurt Court of Appeal ordered continued detention and set the next review for no later than 28 October 2014, transferring competence for interim reviews. A constitutional complaint was rejected in October 2014. On 24 October 2014 the prosecution submitted the file to the Court of Appeal seeking extension. On 7 November 2014 the applicant sought release and a decision on earlier objections; this was dismissed on 10 November. After judges were disclosed, he lodged bias complaints on 25 November and 15 December 2014. The second bias complaint was rejected on 22 January 2015. The Court of Appeal then initially contacted the wrong court on 26 January and only asked the correct Darmstadt Regional Court on 3 February 2015. The applicant submitted further materials on 10 March, requested prompt decisions on 27 March and 10 April, and filed another constitutional complaint on 21 April, rejected on 27 April. The Court of Appeal’s decision of 15 April 2015, served on 15 May 2015, continued detention, finding continued risk of absconding, no undue delay in the criminal proceedings, and proportionality. It did not address the duration of the review proceedings.

Under domestic law, remand detention exceeding six months required Court of Appeal review, with further periodic reviews every three months. No fixed time-limit for decision existed, and time was suspended when the file was submitted before expiry.

The Court examined the complaint under Article 5 § 4, finding a violation. The relevant period ran from 24 October 2014, when review proceedings began, to service on 15 May 2015—six and a half months, prima facie incompatible with “speediness.” The delay until 22 January 2015 was explained mainly by the applicant’s bias complaints. But from 22 January to 15 May 2015, particular expedition was required. Despite case complexity and changed circumstances after indictment, the Court of Appeal contacted the wrong court, decided almost three months after rejecting the bias complaint, and served the decision a month later. Almost four months passed after 22 January and nearly seven months after review began. The Court also noted the periodic review was terminated nine and a half months after the previous decision, not a reasonable interval. It therefore found a violation of Article 5 § 4 and did not separately examine Article 5 § 1.

**Patalakh v. Germany** (Application no. 22692/15), European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, judgment of 8 March 2018.

The applicant, Mr Ivan Patalakh, a Russian national born in 1961 and living in Frankfurt am Main, was arrested on 30 October 2013 under a Frankfurt am Main District Court arrest warrant. He was suspected of aiding aggravated fraudulent conversion, corruption, corruption in commercial practice, and aggravated tax evasion through a complex system of bribes and fictitious invoices. The warrant rested on a strong suspicion and a risk that he would abscond, given the likely heavy sentence, his Russian nationality, his marriage to a co-accused, and his lack of legal residence or significant ties to Germany. A risk of collusion was also found. He was placed in detention on remand. The warrant was later extended to additional charges, and on 19 December 2014 the prosecution brought criminal proceedings against him. On 14 July 2016 he was convicted and sentenced to four years and six months’ imprisonment, but that conviction was not final. The arrest warrant was set aside on 26 October 2016.

The alleged violation concerned the review of his remand detention. Under German law, detention on remand may exceed six months only if justified, and the Court of Appeal must conduct reviews no later than every three months. On 28 July 2014 the Frankfurt am Main Court of Appeal ordered continuation of detention and set the next periodic review for no later than 28 October 2014. On 24 October 2014 the prosecution submitted the case file to the Court of Appeal, requesting an extension. The applicant requested that the detention order be set aside on 7 November 2014 and asked for a decision on earlier objections. On 10 November 2014 the Court of Appeal dismissed those objections.

The applicant then lodged two complaints of bias against judges, on 25 November and 15 December 2014. The first was rejected on 30 December 2014; the second on 22 January 2015. After that, on 26 January 2015, the Court of Appeal mistakenly enquired with the Frankfurt Regional Court rather than the Darmstadt Regional Court, where the case was pending, and only contacted Darmstadt on 3 February 2015. The applicant submitted further material on 10 March 2015 and twice asked for a prompt decision, on 27 March and 10 April 2015. He also lodged a constitutional complaint on 21 April 2015, which was rejected on 27 April 2015. The Court of Appeal decided on 15 April 2015 to continue detention; its ten-page decision was served on 15 May 2015. It did not address the delay.

The applicant complained under Article 5 §§ 1 and 4 that the domestic court failed, or significantly delayed, review of the lawfulness of his detention, causing automatic and arbitrary continuation contrary to his right to liberty and security.

The Court examined the case first under Article 5 § 4, which requires a speedy judicial decision on detention lawfulness. The relevant period ran from initiation of review proceedings on 24 October 2014 until service of the decision on 15 May 2015—six and a half months. The Court accepted that the delay until 22 January 2015 was largely explained by procedural guarantees and the applicant’s bias complaints. However, after 22 January 2015, particular expedition was required. Although the criminal case was complex and the procedural situation had changed, the Court of Appeal did not act with the necessary diligence: it contacted the wrong court, waited until 3 February to contact the correct court, decided only on 15 April, and served the decision on 15 May—nearly four months after rejecting the second bias complaint and almost seven months after review proceedings began. The interval between the previous detention decision (28 July 2014) and the service of the next decision (15 May 2015) was nine and a half months, contrary to the requirement of reasonable periodic review. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 5 § 4 and did not examine separately the complaint under Article 5 § 1.

**Case: Patalakh v. Germany (Application no. 22692/15), ECtHR, 8 March 2018**

The applicant, Mr Ivan Patalakh, a Russian national born in 1961 and living in Frankfurt am Main, was arrested on 30 October 2013 under a warrant issued by the Frankfurt am Main District Court. The warrant rested on a strong suspicion that he had aided several serious economic crimes, including aggravated fraudulent conversion, corruption, corruption in commercial practice and aggravated tax evasion, committed through an elaborate system of bribes and fictitious invoices linked to international business undertakings. The court found risks of absconding and collusion, noting the possible heavy sentence, his lack of legal residence or significant ties to Germany, and his marriage to a co-accused.

He remained in remand detention. On 19 December 2014, the prosecution brought criminal proceedings against him. The Regional Court opened the main proceedings on 6 May 2015, trial began on 8 June 2015, and on 14 July 2016 he was convicted and sentenced to four years and six months’ imprisonment. Appeals were pending. The original arrest warrant was set aside on 26 October 2016.

The alleged violation concerned the review of his remand detention. Under German law, once remand detention exceeds six months, the Court of Appeal must review its lawfulness, with further periodic reviews no later than every three months under Articles 121–122 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On 28 July 2014, the Frankfurt am Main Court of Appeal ordered the continuation of detention and set the next review for no later than 28 October 2014. On 24 October 2014, the prosecution submitted the file to the Court of Appeal requesting an extension. On 7 November 2014, the applicant requested that the detention order be set aside.

Subsequently, the applicant lodged two complaints of bias against the judges concerned, on 25 November and 15 December 2014. The Court of Appeal rejected the first on 30 December 2014 and the second on 22 January 2015. After that, on 26 January 2015, the Court of Appeal mistakenly asked the wrong court about the state of the criminal proceedings, only contacting the correct Darmstadt Regional Court on 3 February 2015. On 10 March 2015, the applicant’s lawyer submitted comprehensive submissions. The applicant twice asked the Court of Appeal to decide without delay, on 27 March and 10 April 2015. The Court of Appeal decided on 15 April 2015 to continue detention; its decision was served on 15 May 2015. It found the absconding risk still existed and detention proportionate, but gave no reasons for the duration of the review proceedings.

The applicant complained under Article 5 §§ 1 and 4 of the Convention that the competent domestic court failed, or significantly delayed, to review the lawfulness of his remand detention, resulting in automatic and arbitrary continuation of detention. The Government contested this, arguing that the delay was caused primarily by the applicant’s bias complaints, the complexity of the case, and the changed procedural situation after the indictment.

The Court examined the complaint under Article 5 § 4 first. The relevant period ran from 24 October 2014, when review proceedings were instituted, until service of the decision on 15 May 2015—about six and a half months. The Court accepted that the delay until 22 January 2015 was explained by procedural guarantees and the applicant’s bias complaints. However, from 22 January to 15 May 2015, the Court of Appeal failed to act with the “special diligence” required. It initially contacted the wrong court, decided almost three months after rejecting the second bias complaint, and served the decision a month later. The interval between the previous detention decision (28 July 2014) and the next (15 May 2015) was nine and a half months, exceeding the domestic three-month periodic review requirement and not a reasonable interval. The Court found a violation of Article 5 § 4 and did not separately examine Article 5 § 1.

In *Sergey Smirnov v. Ukraine* (Application no. 36853/09, ECtHR, 18 December 2018), the applicant was a Ukrainian national arrested on 3 April 2008 after shooting a person and causing serious injury. He remained in detention during criminal proceedings, mainly at the Kharkiv pre-trial detention centre. On 14 April 2009 the Kharkiv Court of Appeal sentenced him to ten years and six months’ imprisonment and confiscation of property; the Supreme Court upheld that judgment on 29 December 2009. He served his sentence in several correctional colonies, including the Slovyanoserbsk Correctional Colony in the Luhansk Region from 11 May 2010 to 7 April 2011. He was transferred to a semi-open institution in May 2015 and released in December 2015.

The Court communicated the applicant’s complaints concerning: (1) conditions of detention at the Slovyanoserbsk Colony; (2) inadequate medical assistance in detention; (3) interception and monitoring of his correspondence; and (4) the lack of an effective domestic remedy. Other parts of the application were declared inadmissible.

As to detention conditions, the applicant was placed in a single-occupancy cell on 13 May 2010 at his own request because he feared violence from other inmates. Decisions isolating him from the general prison population were taken in July and August 2010, and prison reports from October 2010 to February 2011 stated that he refused to move to a dormitory for the same reason. He described the isolation cell as measuring 4.5 sq. m in total, including toilet and washbasin, with only about 1 sq. m of living space. He later alleged that average dormitory space was 2.8 sq. m per inmate, citing a CPT report on overcrowding. However, the Court did not consider a later complaint of unjustified solitary confinement because his original submissions stressed that the placement was at his own request.

Regarding correspondence, the applicant alleged that prison authorities systematically monitored all his mail. He stated that letters from the Court, received on 22 July and 9 September 2009, and a letter from the parliamentary secretariat on 18 December 2010, had been opened by the administration. Prison registers showed that between July 2009 and December 2010 he sent at least forty-seven letters to public bodies subject to monitoring, including courts, the High Council of Justice, the Department for the Execution of Sentences, and Parliament. Those entries included brief content summaries or labels such as “application” or “complaint.” By contrast, letters to the Court and his lawyer, which were exempt from monitoring, were marked as “sealed letter.” Domestic law exempted correspondence with the Parliamentary Commissioner, the ECtHR, international institutions, prosecutors, and later lawyers.

On medical care, the applicant alleged that he developed chronic gastroduodentitis after being poisoned in November 2009. His medical records were missing from his arrest until 26 January 2010. He was later diagnosed with chronic gastroduodentitis, acute pancreatitis, chronic hepatitis, and other digestive problems. He alleged that prescribed medication and diet were not provided and that authorities failed to determine the type of hepatitis. He also suffered from lumbar osteochondrosis since 1998. During detention, medical recommendations, including transfer to specialist facilities, neurology examination, painkillers, anti-inflammatory medication, and back support, were allegedly not implemented. In 2015 he underwent spinal surgery and was recognised as a Category 2 disabled person.

In its Article 3 assessment, the Court emphasised that the State must provide adequate medical care and that the Government bore the burden of proving this. The Government failed to rebut the applicant’s allegations; the missing records aggravated the situation. The authorities apparently never determined his hepatitis type, and there was no indication he had digestive disease before detention. His spinal condition deteriorated to disability, and the Government did not show this was due to natural progression rather than inadequate care. The Court therefore found that the Government failed to prove the applicant received adequate medical care.

He was later transferred to a semi-open institution and released in December 2015.

The Court communicated four main complaints on 9 November 2016: the conditions of detention at Slovyanoserbsk, inadequate medical assistance in detention, interception and monitoring of his correspondence, and the lack of an effective domestic remedy. Other parts of the application were declared inadmissible.

As to conditions, the applicant was placed in a single-occupancy cell on 13 May 2010 at his own request because he feared attacks by other inmates. Decisions isolating him from the general prison population were taken in July and August 2010. Prison reports from October 2010 to February 2011 stated that he repeatedly refused to move to a dormitory, again citing fear of violence. He alleged that the isolation cell measured 4.5 sq. m in total, including toilet and washbasin, leaving about 1 sq. m of living space. He also alleged that average dormitory space was 2.8 sq. m per inmate, relying on a CPT report concerning overcrowding. The Court declined to examine a late solitary-confinement complaint because the applicant had not originally raised it and had stressed that isolation was at his own request.

On correspondence, the applicant alleged systematic monitoring. On 22 July and 9 September 2009, prison staff handed him two letters from the Court, and on 18 December 2010 a letter from the parliamentary secretariat, all of which had been opened. These were sometimes summarised or marked as applications, petitions, or complaints. Letters to the Court and his lawyer were recorded as “sealed letter.” Domestic rules permitted automatic monitoring unless correspondence was exempt, including letters to the Court, prosecutors, and later lawyers.

On medical care, the applicant alleged inadequate treatment. From November 2009 he suffered from chronic gastroduodentitis; his medical records before January 2010 were missing. He was diagnosed and treated at times, but claimed prescribed medication and recommendations were not implemented. In October 2011 a civilian hospital diagnosed acute pancreatitis, congestive duodenopathy, gastric stasis, oesophagitis, and chronic hepatitis, yet authorities never determined the hepatitis type. In *Sergey Smirnov v. Ukraine* (Application no. 36853/09, judgment 18 December 2018), the European Court of Human Rights’ Fourth Section examined complaints by a Ukrainian national arrested on 3 April 2008 after shooting and seriously injuring a person. He was sentenced in 2009 to ten years and six months’ imprisonment and confiscation of property, upheld by the Supreme Court. He was held mainly in Kharkiv SIZO and later in various correctional colonies, including the Slovyanoserbsk Correctional Colony in the Luhansk Region from 11 May 2010 to 7 April 2011. He was transferred to semi-open detention in May 2015 and released in December 2015.

The communicated complaints concerned conditions of detention at Slovyanoserbsk, inadequate medical assistance, alleged interception and monitoring of correspondence in detention, and the lack of an effective domestic remedy. The Court later declined to examine a new complaint about solitary confinement because it was not raised in the original submissions; the applicant had initially said his placement in a single-occupancy cell was at his own request due to fear of attacks by other inmates. He described the isolation cell as measuring 4.5 sq. m including toilet and washbasin, with about 1 sq. m of living space. He later alleged that average dormitory space was 2.8 sq. m per inmate, citing CPT findings on overcrowding.

As to correspondence, the applicant alleged systematic monitoring by prison authorities. He stated that in July and September 2009 prison staff handed him opened letters from the Court, and in December 2010 an opened letter from a parliamentary secretariat. Prison registers showed that at least forty-seven letters to public authorities were monitored, summarized or marked as applications, petitions or complaints. However, letters to the Court and his lawyer were marked as “sealed letter.” Under domestic law, most prisoner correspondence was subject to automatic monitoring, while correspondence with the Parliamentary Commissioner, the Court, international institutions, prosecutors, and later lawyers was exempt.

The medical-care facts were central. The applicant alleged that poisoning in November 2009 caused chronic gastroduodenitis. His health records before January 2010 were missing. In January 2010, Kharkiv SIZO diagnosed chronic gastroduodenitis and prescribed medication, which he said he did not receive. In February 2011, a colony doctor confirmed an exacerbation and recommended transfer to Luhansk SIZO hospital; no transfer followed. In October 2011, a civilian hospital diagnosed acute pancreatitis, duodenopathy, gastric stasis, esophagitis and chronic hepatitis, prescribing medication and diet. He refused transfer to a prison hospital, citing mistrust. Later, he was diagnosed with chronic pancreatitis and biliary dyskinesia; he alleged prescribed medication and diet were not provided. Despite the hepatitis diagnosis, authorities apparently did not determine its type.

Regarding his back, the applicant had suffered osteochondrosis since 1998. In 2012 he received colony treatment and an MRI; a surgeon recommended specialist neurological examination, allegedly not implemented. In 2013, a traumatologist prescribed painkillers, anti-inflammatory drugs and a back-support device, also allegedly not implemented. In September 2015 he underwent spinal surgery in a civilian institution, and in November 2015 was recognised as a Category 2 disabled person due to his back condition.

The Court assessed the medical-care complaint under Article 3. It held that detention authorities must provide requisite medical care, keep comprehensive records, ensure prompt and accurate diagnosis, regular supervision, a comprehensive therapeutic strategy, and conditions actually to follow prescribed treatment. The Government had to provide credible evidence of adequate care but failed to rebut the applicant’s allegations. The missing records aggravated the situation. The Court was particularly struck that no steps were taken to determine the type of hepatitis. There was no proof of prior digestive disease, and the serious spinal deterioration leading to disability was not shown to be natural. The Government therefore failed to discharge its burden of proving adequate medical care for his digestive/hepatitis and back conditions.

In *Vujović v. Montenegro* (Application no. 75139/10, 15 May 2018), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by Igor Vujović, a Montenegrin and Norwegian national born in 1973 and living in Oslo, concerning criminal proceedings arising from a traffic accident in which a child died.

On 26 April 2000, criminal proceedings were brought against the applicant and another person. On 25 February 2003, the Court of First Instance in Podgorica convicted the applicant of endangering public traffic and sentenced him to one year and six months’ imprisonment. In 2006, the High Court in Podgorica quashed that judgment and remitted the case. On 18 April 2007, the Court of First Instance again convicted the applicant and his co-accused, reducing the sentence to one year and four months. On 13 November 2009, the High Court reduced the co-accused’s sentence but upheld the applicant’s conviction. The applicant’s appeal was rejected on 14 June 2010. His further appeal on points of law to the Supreme Court was rejected on 26 October 2010. He then lodged an action for fair redress with the Supreme Court on 11 December 2010, complaining about the length of the proceedings; it was rejected on 31 December 2010. His ultimate appeal was rejected by the Constitutional Court on 19 April 2013.

The main alleged violation was under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention: that the criminal proceedings exceeded a reasonable time. The Government objected that the complaint was out of time, arguing that the applicant should have applied within six months of the second-instance judgment because an appeal against that judgment was not an effective remedy. The Court rejected this, noting that the Supreme Court had ruled on the merits of the applicant’s appeal on points of law, which is in principle an effective domestic remedy. The Government also argued non-exhaustion because the applicant had not used a request for review. The Court rejected this too, since at the relevant time no effective remedies existed for length complaints in Montenegro: the request for review became effective on 4 September 2013, an action for fair redress on 18 October 2016, and a constitutional appeal on 20 March 2015. The length complaint was therefore admissible.

On the merits, the proceedings ran from 26 April 2000 to 26 October 2010, but the Court could only assess the period from 3 March 2004, when the Convention entered into force for Montenegro, to 26 October 2010—almost six years and eight months across three instances. The Court applied the usual criteria: complexity, conduct of the applicant and authorities, and what was at stake. It found that the applicant had unjustifiably failed to appear at hearings on 13 September 2006 and 30 November 2006, causing nearly seven months of delay. The applicant did not identify any period of inactivity by the domestic courts. The remaining length of approximately six years at three levels of jurisdiction was not excessive or unreasonably long. Accordingly, there was no violation of Article 6 § 1.

The applicant also complained under Article 6 §§ 2 and 3 that his presumption of innocence was breached because he was not allowed to examine witnesses on his behalf. The Court found that he provided no supporting evidence and that it was unclear how the refusal to hear witnesses could breach the presumption of innocence. Those complaints were therefore manifestly ill-founded and rejected under Article 35 § 3. Overall, the Court found no violation of the reasonable-time requirement and dismissed the remaining complaints.

In *Healy v Ireland* (App. no. 27291/16), the applicant, Mary Healy, an Irish national born in 1946, had been treated for a pituitary brain tumour since 1982. In 1995 she became a patient of Dr B, a consultant endocrinologist. An August 2000 MRI showed no significant change since 1995, though the tumour remained large. After tests, Dr B told her by telephone in September 2000 that the tumour was “very unsatisfactory.” Because she believed the 1982 surgery had removed almost the entire tumour, she understood this to mean rapid growth and grave danger. Dr B prescribed a newly available drug, injected monthly by her GP from September 2000. She developed severe gastrointestinal side effects; the dose was halved. In January 2001 she was hospitalised with vomiting, diarrhoea, exhaustion, headaches, cramps and spasms, and severe hypothyroidism later found to be an unknown side effect of the drug. She received further injections in February and March 2001 and began seeing another endocrinologist.

In May 2004 the applicant commenced High Court civil proceedings against Dr B and the hospital. She alleged negligence in prescribing and monitoring the drug, and claimed her consent was vitiated by insufficient or misleading information about her condition and treatment. The statement of claim was served in October 2004. Dr B defended in February 2005 and sought particulars, supplied in June 2005. The hospital defended in June 2005 and also sought particulars. According to the Government, eleven interim motions were brought between February 2005 and September 2008. In October 2009 the case was included in a “positive callover” and a hearing was set for April 2010. The hearing ran from 13 April to 7 May 2010; judgment was given on 20 May 2010.

The High Court dismissed all claims. It preferred the defence experts and found that Dr B had complied with the drug’s therapeutic indications, adequately monitored the applicant, and fulfilled his duty to explain the treatment. It accepted that the applicant misunderstood the exact state of her tumour, but held this was not caused by Dr B, who had given accurate and appropriate information. It found she gave valid informed consent. Only the gastrointestinal side effects required warning; other potential side effects had not materialised.

The applicant appealed on 1 July 2010. The appeal remained pending before the Supreme Court until transferred to the Court of Appeal on 29 October 2014. It was heard on 30 July 2015 and dismissed on 17 November 2015. The Court of Appeal found no basis to disturb the findings on treatment or consent. It held that Dr B reasonably considered the condition serious and requiring treatment, that surgery was impossible, and that medication was the only alternative; he explained the benefits and unpleasant side effects. A “do nothing” option was “somewhat unreal.” The Supreme Court refused leave on 8 March 2016.

The applicant lodged her ECtHR application on 12 May 2016. The facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the duration of the civil proceedings—from May 2004 to the final refusal of leave in March 2016, nearly twelve years—and the absence of an effective domestic remedy for that delay. The domestic law note refers to *Nash v DPP* (24 October 2016), recognising at least in principle a possible damages claim for breach of the constitutional right to a timely trial, but that judgment post-dated the applicant’s domestic proceedings and application. The ECtHR case concerned complaints under Article 6 §1 (length of proceedings) and Article 13 (lack of an effective remedy).
