The High Court heard the case over twelve days from 13 April to 7 May 2010. Judgment on 20 May 2010 dismissed all claims. The judge preferred the defence experts, found Dr B complied with the drug’s therapeutic indications and monitored adequately, and held that Healy had given valid informed consent. He accepted she misunderstood the tumour’s state but found Dr B had provided accurate, appropriate information and sufficient warnings; other potential side-effects had not materialised.

Healy appealed on 1 July 2010. The appeal remained pending before the Supreme Court until transferred to the newly established Court of Appeal on 29 October 2014. It was heard on 30 July 2015. On 17 November 2015 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, upholding the trial judge on treatment and consent and rejecting the argument that a “do nothing” option should have been presented. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 8 March 2016.

The ECtHR application was lodged on 12 May 2016. Overall, the civil proceedings lasted from May 2004 to March 2016, approximately eleven years and ten months. Relevant domestic law includes Nash v. D.P.P. (24 October 2016), in which the Supreme Court recognised, at least in principle, a potential claim for damages for breach of the constitutional right to a timely trial, and under the European Convention on Human Rights Act 2003. This is relevant to the alleged lack of an effective domestic remedy for the delay.

**Healy v. Ireland** (Application no. 27291/16) concerned an Irish national, Mary Healy, born in 1946, who had been treated since 1982 for a pituitary brain tumour. The case before the European Court of Human Rights centred on the alleged excessive length of civil proceedings she brought in Ireland, and relatedly on whether Irish law provided an effective remedy for that delay.

Healy received treatment from Dr B, a consultant endocrinologist. In 2000, after an MRI scan and a telephone discussion with Dr B, she came to believe her tumour was growing rapidly and gravely endangering her health. She was prescribed a newly available drug, administered monthly from September 2000. She suffered severe gastrointestinal side effects, her dosage was halved, and in early 2001 she was hospitalised with vomiting, diarrhoea, exhaustion, headaches, cramps and muscular spasms. Tests also showed severe hypothyroidism, later established as a previously unknown side-effect of the drug. She had further discussions with Dr B and received two more injections in February and March 2001. From February 2001 she was treated by another endocrinologist.

In May 2004, Healy commenced civil proceedings in the High Court against Dr B and the hospital. She alleged negligence in prescribing and monitoring the drug, and argued that her consent to treatment was invalid because she had been given insufficient or misleading information about her condition and the proposed medication.

The procedural timeline is central to the alleged violations. Her statement of claim was served in October 2004. Dr B entered his defence in February 2005 and sought further particulars, which the applicant provided in June 2005. The hospital entered its defence in June 2005 and also sought particulars. According to the Government, between February 2005 and September 2008, eleven interim motions were brought and decided. In October 2009, the case was listed for a “positive callover” to assign a hearing date, and a hearing was set for April 2010. In January 2010, the applicant replied to the second defendant’s outstanding request for particulars from June 2005.

The High Court hearing ran from 13 April to 7 May 2010 over twelve days. Judgment was delivered on 20 May 2010, dismissing the claim. The judge preferred the defence experts, found Dr B had complied with the drug’s therapeutic indications, monitored the applicant adequately, and gave sufficient warning of gastrointestinal side effects. He also concluded that the applicant had given valid, informed consent, and that Dr B was not responsible for her misunderstanding of her tumour’s exact state.

Healy appealed on 1 July 2010. The appeal remained pending before the Supreme Court until it was transferred to the newly established Court of Appeal on 29 October 2014. The Court of Appeal heard the appeal on 30 July 2015 and dismissed it on 17 November 2015, upholding the High Court’s findings on treatment and consent. The applicant sought leave to appeal, but the Supreme Court refused on 8 March 2016.

The applicant lodged her ECtHR application on 12 May 2016. The case was communicated to the Irish Government on 29 September 2016. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the duration of the domestic civil proceedings—from May 2004 to March 2016, approximately eleven years and ten months—and the delays at various stages, particularly the period before the High Court hearing, the long pendency of the appeal, and its transfer to the Court of Appeal. The domestic law context included the Supreme Court’s later judgment in **Nash v. D.P.P.** (24 October 2016), which recognised, at least in principle, a possible damages claim for breach of the constitutional right to a timely trial and under the European Convention on Human Rights Act 2003, subject to the availability of other remedies.
001-181393:
In *R.Š. v. Latvia* (Application no. 44154/14, ECtHR, 8 March 2018), the applicant was a Latvian pilot/trainee who was seriously injured in a private aircraft accident. He complained under Articles 2 and 8 that he could not obtain compensation for his injuries from those involved and that Latvia should be responsible for shortcomings in the legal regulation of private flight safety. The Court considered the complaint under Article 2.

In 2008 the applicant used KD.C., a company solely owned and managed by D.K., which provided private flights and private pilot training. It was not a commercial operator and lacked air operator certification. On 16 August 2008 KD.C. organised a private flight from Riga to Tukums in a Piper PA-31. The applicant and six others were passengers; the applicant sat next to pilot G.V. and handled radio communication. The pilot lost control and crashed, killing G.V. and seriously injuring all passengers. The applicant suffered life-threatening injuries, permanent loss of vision in his right eye, and other permanent health damage.

The TAIIB accident report found the primary cause was human error: G.V. lacked the skills and experience to operate the multi-engine Piper PA-31 under instrument flight rules. He had begun but not completed differences training and had no authorisation. Contributing factors included poor weather and unsafe supervision by the Civil Aviation Agency. KD.C. had failed to follow up the pilot’s training, did not check his documents, and unjustifiably handed him the aircraft and verbally authorised the flight. The report recommended procedures for aircraft handovers to prevent unqualified pilots from flying.

Criminal proceedings followed. D.K. was charged with negligent performance of professional duties and violation of air traffic safety/operation rules. The first-instance court convicted him, imposing a suspended sentence and ordering compensation to the applicant. The appellate court acquitted him, and the Supreme Court Senate upheld the acquittal. It found no actus reus: D.K. was not the required special subject or transport employee; the indictment did not identify specific violated regulations; and at the material time Latvian law had no procedure for handing over an aircraft or designating who must verify a pilot’s qualifications. Owner responsibility under the Chicago Convention came later, and the Law on Aviation was amended only in 2013 to prohibit handing an aircraft to an unqualified person.

The applicant also sued KD.C., D.K. and the insurer. KD.C. became bankrupt and was later excluded from the register. The civil courts dismissed the claim. They found no unlawful act or causal link by D.K.; the flight was the pilot’s arbitrary act; D.K. was neither owner nor pilot nor the pilot’s employer; and the insurer was not liable because the pilot was unqualified. The Supreme Court Senate dismissed his final appeal in 2016.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant argued that he could not obtain compensation from the responsible third parties and that, if domestic law did not require owners to check pilots’ qualifications, the State was responsible for a regulatory gap in private flight safety. The Government maintained that existing law sufficiently protected flight safety and that the pilot’s misconduct caused the accident.

The Court held Article 2 applicable because the accident threatened the applicant’s life and physical integrity. It rejected the Government’s abuse and non-exhaustion objections, finding the complaint admissible.

In *R.Š. v. Latvia* (no. 44154/14, judgment 8 March 2018), the applicant was a Latvian pilot licence holder and aviation trainee who was seriously injured in a private aircraft accident. On 16 August 2008, a company, KD.C., organised a private flight from Riga to Tukums using a Piper PA-31 aircraft. The applicant travelled as a passenger in the front seat next to pilot G.V. The aircraft crashed after the pilot lost control in cloudy weather. The pilot died, and the applicant suffered life-threatening injuries, permanently lost vision in his right eye, and sustained other permanent health damage. He later worked as an aviation specialist but with limitations, including being unable to operate aircraft independently.

The investigation by the Transport Accident and Incident Investigation Bureau found that the primary cause was “human error”: G.V. lacked sufficient skills and experience to operate a multi-engine Piper PA-31 under instrument flight rules and had not obtained Civil Aviation Agency authorisation for that aircraft type. He had begun but not completed differences training. Contributing factors included poor weather and “unsafe supervision” by the Civil Aviation Agency. KD.C. had failed to follow up the pilot’s training, failed to check his documents, and had unjustifiably handed him the aircraft and verbally authorised the flight.

Criminal proceedings were brought against D.K., KD.C.’s sole owner and board member. He was initially convicted of negligence in professional duties and violation of air traffic safety/operation regulations, and ordered to pay the applicant compensation. On appeal he was acquitted; the Supreme Court upheld the acquittal. It found no proof of the required criminal act, held that D.K. was not a transport employee or “special subject” under the relevant provisions, and noted that at the material time no law required an aircraft owner to verify a pilot’s qualifications or to establish a handover procedure. Only later did Latvian law prohibit handing over an aircraft to an unqualified, uninsured pilot.

The applicant also sued KD.C., D.K. and the insurer in civil proceedings. These claims were dismissed. KD.C. became bankrupt and was later dissolved. D.K. was found not liable because the pilot had acted arbitrarily and outside the planned instructor-supervised flight, because D.K. was not the aircraft owner under the Law on Aviation, and because the Chicago Convention did not impose owner liability before 18 November 2010. The insurer refused cover because the pilot lacked the right to operate the aircraft.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that he had been unable to obtain compensation for the accident and that the State should bear responsibility for shortcomings in the legal regulation of safety in private flights. The Court examined the complaint under Article 2 (right to life), finding it applicable because the accident posed a serious threat to his life and physical integrity. The Government objected on grounds of abuse of application and non-exhaustion, but the Court rejected those objections and declared the Article 2 complaint admissible. The key alleged violation was therefore Latvia’s alleged failure to maintain an adequate regulatory framework for private/general aviation safety—particularly regarding an owner’s duty to verify pilot qualifications—and the applicant’s consequent inability to obtain compensation.

In **R.Š. v. Latvia** (ECtHR, 8 March 2018), the applicant, a Latvian pilot and aviation trainee, was a passenger on a private flight on 16 August 2008 from Riga to Tukums. The flight was organised by KD.C., a company providing private flights and pilot training, using a Piper PA-31 aircraft. The applicant sat in the front seat next to pilot G.V. The aircraft crashed after G.V. lost control. The pilot died, while the applicant suffered life-threatening injuries, permanently lost vision in his right eye, sustained permanent health damage, and later faced restrictions on operating aircraft independently.

The Transport Accident and Incident Investigation Bureau found the primary cause was “human error”: G.V. lacked sufficient skill and experience to operate the multi-engine Piper PA-31 under instrument flight rules and had not obtained authorisation from the Civil Aviation Agency for that aircraft type. He had begun, but not completed, differences training. Contributing factors included poor weather and “unsafe supervision” by the Civil Aviation Agency. KD.C. had not followed up on the pilot’s training, failed to check his documents, and unjustifiably handed over the aircraft and verbally authorised the flight. The investigation also found that, at the material time, Latvian law had no procedure for handing over an aircraft for general aviation flights and did not require an owner to verify a pilot’s qualifications. The Civil Aviation Agency later said the owner was responsible for airworthiness, not safe operation, which was the pilot’s responsibility. Only in 2013 was the Law on Aviation amended to prohibit handing an aircraft to an unqualified or uninsured person.

Criminal proceedings were brought against D.K., KD.C.’s sole owner and board member. The first-instance court convicted him of negligence and air-traffic safety violations and ordered him to pay the applicant compensation. However, the appellate court acquitted him, and the Supreme Court upheld the acquittal. It held that the prosecution had not established the required actus reus, that the relevant duties applied to the pilot or a transport employee rather than D.K., and that no legal regulation required an owner to check pilot qualifications. It also noted that Chicago Convention Annex 6, Part II, imposing owner responsibility, entered into force only in 2010.

The applicant also sued KD.C., D.K., and the insurer in civil proceedings. KD.C. became bankrupt and was later excluded from the Companies Register. The civil courts dismissed the claim: the primary cause was pilot error; D.K. was not the aircraft’s owner and had not acted unlawfully or with sufficient causal link; the pilot’s independent flight was arbitrary; and the insurer was not liable because the accident involved an unqualified pilot. Thus the applicant obtained no compensation.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained under Articles 2 and 8 that he could not obtain compensation and that the State should bear responsibility for shortcomings in the legal regulation of private-flight safety. The Government argued that domestic law provided sufficient safeguards and that the pilot’s misconduct was the main cause. The Court found Article 2 applicable because the accident threatened the applicant’s life and physical integrity, declared the complaint admissible, and rejected the Government’s abuse-of-application and non-exhaustion objections.

In *Ciocodeică v. Romania*, Maria Ciocodeică complained under Article 6 § 1, Article 13, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that Romania failed to assist her in enforcing a final judgment against a private company and that she lacked an effective domestic remedy.

In 2004 she sued her employer, C.G.H.T., seeking annulment of her dismissal and salary entitlements. On 29 September 2004 the Timișoara Court of Appeal gave final judgment in her favour, ordering the company to revoke its dismissal decision and pay all salary entitlements from 17 October 2003 until judgment, updated and indexed, plus costs. The judgment was validated in November 2004. In January 2005 the applicant instructed bailiff office M.S.R. & S.A.I. to enforce it. The bailiff served a payment notice on 26 January. On 11 February, after visiting the company and finding no legal representative, the bailiff gave it five days to comply voluntarily. The company refused and filed a complaint to annul enforcement. On 24 February 2005 the Timișoara District Court suspended enforcement pending final judgment, subject to a deposit of about EUR 90. The applicant tried to lift the suspension urgently, but on 18 May 2005 the court dismissed her request for lack of imminent damage. On 2 June 2005 the District Court allowed the company’s complaint and annulled enforcement because the bailiff had not served the company with a copy of the enforceable judgment. Her appeal was dismissed on 6 October 2005. A bank-account restriction was also annulled on 21 April 2005 because it had been issued after suspension.

The bailiff issued another payment notice on 29 June 2005, posted with the judgment at the company’s entrance on 4 July. On 2 November 2005 the applicant asked whether the company had complied; the bailiff replied no on 4 November. This was the last exchange. On 28 May 2007 the bailiff declared the enforcement time-barred under Article 389 RCCP due to creditor passivity; it is unclear whether the applicant was notified.

She also tried other remedies. In May 2005 she sought immediate enforcement under Article 5803 RCCP; in August 2005 the District Court imposed a daily coercive fine of ROL 500,000. In December 2005 the County Court reversed this, holding that the fine did not apply because the debt could be enforced by bailiff. She complained to the Minister of Justice in July 2005, but the Court of Appeal noted the relevant judgment was final. In 2005 she filed criminal complaints against company representatives. In 2006 an investigation began against M.D., the administrator. In February 2008 the prosecutor discontinued proceedings and fined him RON 1,000 (about EUR 250), finding no offence. Appeals were dismissed, finally on 28 January 2009.

In 2014 the company’s shareholders decided to liquidate it; this was published in August 2014. An accounting report stated that the only creditors were the shareholders. In October 2014 the company was struck off the register, and no appeal was lodged. The Government argued that the applicant failed to act diligently, allowed enforcement to become time-barred, and did not challenge the dissolution/strike-off; available remedies existed. The applicant argued that the bailiff lacked diligence, should have sought bank information and issued a restriction, and that non-enforcement revealed deficiencies and lenient sanctions. The Court declared the complaints admissible.

**Summary of *Ciocodeică v. Romania* (Application no. 27413/09)**

The case of *Ciocodeică v. Romania* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Ms. Maria Ciocodeică, a Romanian national, on 30 April 2009. The applicant alleged that the Romanian State failed to effectively assist her in enforcing a final domestic judgment and that she lacked an effective remedy to obtain this enforcement, violating Articles 6 § 1 and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The key facts are as follows: In 2004, the applicant successfully sued her former employer, a private company (C.G.H.T.), for wrongful dismissal. The Timișoara Court of Appeal issued a final judgment on 29 September 2004, ordering the company to revoke her dismissal and pay her all outstanding salary entitlements and legal costs, updated and index-linked.

Despite this final judgment, the company refused to pay. The applicant initiated enforcement proceedings through a bailiff on 21 January 2005. However, the process was immediately obstructed. The company lodged a complaint against the enforcement, leading the Timișoara District Court to suspend the proceedings on 24 February 2005. The applicant's subsequent request to lift the suspension was dismissed in May 2005. The company's challenge to the enforcement was ultimately successful in June 2005, with the court finding procedural errors in the bailiff's service of documents; this decision was upheld in October 2005.

In parallel, the bailiff's efforts were unsuccessful. An attempt to seize the company's bank accounts was annulled in April 2005 because it occurred during the court-ordered suspension. A new notice of payment was issued in June 2005 at the company's main entrance, but the company still did not comply. The applicant made her last inquiry to the bailiff in November 2005. After a period of inactivity, on 28 May 2007, the bailiff officially declared the enforcement procedure time-barred, citing the applicant's passivity as the creditor under Article 389 of the Romanian Code of Civil Procedure.

The applicant also pursued other legal avenues. A complaint to speed up enforcement, which initially resulted in a coercive fine against the company, was ultimately rejected on appeal in December 2005. A criminal complaint filed against the company's administrator for refusing to execute a judgment was discontinued in 2008, with the prosecutor imposing only an administrative fine. The company itself was liquidated and struck off the commercial register in 2014.

Before the European Court, the applicant argued that the State had failed in its positive obligation to provide an effective enforcement mechanism. She claimed the bailiff was not diligent and that the procedure was plagued by deficiencies, including insufficient pressure on non-compliant debtors.

The Romanian Government contended that the applicant had failed to properly pursue the enforcement and other available domestic remedies, such as challenging the bailiff's actions or the company's dissolution.

The Court found the case admissible. Its assessment centered on whether the State had fulfilled its positive obligation to assist the applicant in enforcing a judgment against a private party. While the judgment was final, the domestic enforcement process proved entirely ineffective, allowing the debtor company to evade its obligations through procedural challenges and eventual liquidation. The applicant was therefore unable to obtain what was rightfully hers, despite the favorable final judgment. The Court held that this failure to assist effectively constituted a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

**Starenkiy and Rudoy v. Ukraine** (Applications nos. 44807/10 and 15752/14) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, delivered on 11 January 2018. The case concerned two applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants complained principally about the inadequate conditions of their detention and the absence of any effective domestic remedy in that respect, relying on Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention. Article 3 prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, while Article 13 guarantees an effective remedy before a national authority for violations of Convention rights.

The Court joined the two applications because they raised similar subject matter. The applicants were kept in detention in poor conditions. The judgment states that the specific details of their detention—such as dates, cell space, number of occupants, and other conditions—are set out in an appended table. That table is referenced in the text but not reproduced in the excerpt provided, so the exact applicant-specific facts are not available in the supplied material. Nevertheless, the Court treated the core factual allegation as being that the applicants’ detention conditions were inadequate and that they had no effective domestic remedy to challenge those conditions.

In its legal assessment, the Court recalled its established case-law on inadequate detention conditions, particularly **Muršić v. Croatia** and **Ananyev and Others v. Russia**. It reiterated that a serious lack of space in a prison cell weighs heavily in determining whether detention conditions are “degrading” under Article 3 and may amount to a violation either alone or in combination with other shortcomings. The Court also noted that in the leading case of **Melnik v. Ukraine**, it had already found a violation in respect of similar issues. Having examined all the material, the Court found no fact or argument capable of leading to a different conclusion. It therefore considered that the applicants’ conditions of detention were inadequate and that they did not have an effective remedy in domestic law for those complaints. Accordingly, the facts disclosed violations of Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention.

The judgment also records that in application no. 15752/14, the applicant raised another complaint under the Convention, which was in accordance with the Court’s well-established case-law. The Court found that this additional complaint was not manifestly ill-founded within the meaning of Article 35 § 3 (a) and was not inadmissible on any other ground. However, the excerpt does not specify the exact nature of that additional complaint.

Overall, the key facts relevant to the alleged violations are that the two applicants were detained in conditions that the Court found to be poor and inadequate, primarily engaging Article 3, and that Ukrainian law did not provide them with an effective remedy to address those conditions, engaging Article 13. The Court relied on its prior case-law, especially concerning lack of space in detention, and concluded that there had been violations. The case is therefore an example of the Court’s repetitive examination of inadequate detention conditions in Ukraine and the systemic absence of effective domestic remedies for such complaints.

001-186770:
Dainelienė v. Lithuania (ECtHR, 16 October 2018) concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, specifically the applicant’s right to a fair hearing before an impartial tribunal. The applicant, Dalia Regina Dainelienė, a Lithuanian national, was suspected in April 2009 and charged in May 2009 with organising the embezzlement of high-value property. She denied guilt. In July 2011 the Vilnius Regional Court found that the charges were misclassified because the property was not of high value, reclassified the offence as less serious, held that prosecution was time-barred, and discontinued the proceedings. The prosecutor appealed, and in October 2011 the Court of Appeal quashed that decision and remitted the case.

On 10 June 2013 the Vilnius Regional Court convicted the applicant, imposed a fine of LTL 12,000 (approximately EUR 3,475), and ordered her to pay LTL 2,800 (approximately EUR 810) in damages. The Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal on 18 October 2013.

On 7 January 2014 the applicant lodged an appeal on points of law with the Supreme Court. On 17 February 2014, a three-judge selection panel refused to examine the appeal because it did not comply with formal requirements of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The chair of that panel was Judge V.G., whose son, M.G., had been the prosecutor in the applicant’s case before both the first-instance and appellate courts. The Supreme Court’s Criminal Division had sixteen judges.

The applicant complained that the presence of Judge V.G. on the selection panel violated her right to an impartial tribunal. Under domestic law, a judge had to withdraw if he or she was a close relative of a prosecutor in the case, and parties could generally seek a judge’s removal. However, there was no rule requiring parties to be informed of the composition of the initial three-judge selection panel or allowing them to request removal at that stage; such rights arose only after an appeal on points of law had been accepted for examination.

The Government argued that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies. It said she should have corrected and resubmitted her appeal or sought renewal of the time-limit. It also claimed that panel compositions were published monthly online, that the inclusion of Judge V.G. was an accidental clerical oversight, that all three judges voted against the appeal, and that there was no proof of bias. The applicant countered that she could not know the panel’s composition when filing, that panels changed monthly, and that removal was unavailable before the admission decision.

The Court rejected the non-exhaustion objection. The suggested remedy was to the same Supreme Court, not a higher court, and applicants are generally not required to repeatedly apply to a body that has already rejected them. The applicant also could not have sought Judge V.G.’s removal before the written decision because she was unaware of the panel’s composition.

On the merits, the Court found no evidence of subjective bias, but examined objective impartiality. The key facts were that Judge V.G. and prosecutor M.G. were father and son; M.G. had brought the charges and played a major role; and Judge V.G. presided over the panel that dismissed the cassation appeal. There was no system preventing a judge from receiving a case involving his son, and the judge did not verify or disclose the conflict. The law did not require the prosecutor’s name in the cassation appeal. The Court held that this close family link compromised the Supreme Court’s impartiality and gave rise to legitimate doubt. Although the judge’s actual influence could not be measured, he presided over the panel, and a substitute among sixteen judges was available. The defect was not remedied, and the Supreme Court was the last resort. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1.

**Case: Dainelienė v. Lithuania (Application no. 23532/14), European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, 16 October 2018.**

The applicant, Dalia Regina Dainelienė, a Lithuanian national, was prosecuted for organising the embezzlement of property of high value. In April 2009 she was notified that she was a suspect, and in May 2009 she was charged. She denied guilt. In July 2011 the Vilnius Regional Court held that the charges had been misclassified because the allegedly embezzled property was not of high value. It reclassified the charges as a less serious offence, found the prosecution time-barred, and discontinued the proceedings. The prosecutor appealed. In October 2011 the Court of Appeal quashed that decision and remitted the case. In June 2013 the Vilnius Regional Court convicted the applicant, fined her LTL 12,000 (approximately EUR 3,475), and ordered her to pay LTL 2,800 (approximately EUR 810) in damages. In October 2013 the Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal and upheld the conviction.

In January 2014 the applicant lodged an appeal on points of law with the Supreme Court. On 17 February 2014 a three-judge selection panel refused to examine it, finding that it did not comply with the formal and cassation-ground requirements of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The chair of that selection panel, Judge V.G., was the father of M.G., the prosecutor who had acted in the applicant’s case before the first-instance and appellate courts.

The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that her case before the Supreme Court had not been examined by an impartial tribunal, because a judge on the selection panel was the father of the prosecutor in her case. The Government argued that she had failed to exhaust domestic remedies: she should have corrected and resubmitted her cassation appeal, sought renewal of the time-limit, or checked the published composition of the selection panel and sought Judge V.G.’s removal. The Government described his inclusion as an accidental clerical oversight in a small country and noted that all three judges had voted against accepting the appeal. The applicant argued that resubmission was not an effective remedy, that domestic law did not allow removal at the selection stage, and that she could not have known the panel’s composition when she filed her appeal.

The Court declared the complaint admissible and rejected the non-exhaustion objection. It found that the suggested remedy was an application to the same Supreme Court after it had already rejected her appeal, and no examples showed that resubmission was effective. The applicant could not have sought removal because the procedure was written and she was unaware of the panel’s composition; the Supreme Court should have provided clear instructions on where and when to find that information.

On the merits, the Court applied the subjective and objective impartiality tests. There was no evidence of personal bias by Judge V.G. However, under the objective test, the applicant’s doubts were objectively justified. Judge V.G.’s son had been the prosecutor in her case and had played a major role, including bringing the charges. Judge V.G. presided over the selection panel deciding whether to admit her cassation appeal. Although domestic law required judges related to prosecutors to withdraw, no system prevented him from receiving the case, and he did not disclose the link. The cassation appeal did not name the prosecutor. The Criminal Division had sixteen judges, so a substitute was available. Because the Supreme Court was the final instance, the defect was not remedied. The Court concluded that the selection panel’s composition failed to guarantee impartiality and violated Article 6 § 1.

In *Dainelienė v. Lithuania* (ECtHR, 16 October 2018), the applicant, a Lithuanian national, was suspected in 2009 of organising embezzlement of property of high value and was charged. She denied guilt. In 2011 the Vilnius Regional Court found that the charges had been misclassified, reclassified them as a less serious offence, held the prosecution time-barred, and discontinued the proceedings. On the prosecutor’s appeal, the Court of Appeal quashed that decision and remitted the case. In 2013 the Regional Court convicted the applicant and imposed a fine of LTL 12,000 (about EUR 3,475) and damages of LTL 2,800 (about EUR 810). The Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal in October 2013.

In January 2014 the applicant lodged an appeal on points of law with the Supreme Court. On 17 February 2014, a three-judge selection panel refused to examine it, finding that it did not comply with Articles 368 § 2 and 369 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The chair of that panel, Judge V.G., was the father of M.G., the prosecutor who had acted in the applicant’s case before the first-instance and appellate courts. The Supreme Court’s Criminal Division had sixteen judges.

The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 that the Supreme Court was not impartial because of Judge V.G.’s participation. Domestic law allowed a judge to be removed if he or she was a close relative of a prosecutor in the same proceedings, and parties could seek removal. However, the CCP contained no provisions requiring parties to be informed of the composition of the initial cassation selection panel or allowing them to seek removal at that stage. Parties were informed of the chamber’s composition and their removal rights only after an appeal on points of law had been accepted for examination. The selection panel’s decision was final and not open to appeal.

The Government argued that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies: she should have corrected and resubmitted her cassation appeal or sought renewal of the time-limit, and she could have found the panel composition online, as it was published monthly, and sought Judge V.G.’s removal. The applicant argued that these remedies were ineffective. She could not have known the panel’s composition when lodging her appeal, the panel changed monthly, and removal was not available at the selection stage.

The Court rejected the non-exhaustion objection. It held that the applicant could not reasonably be expected to keep applying to the same court after it had already rejected her appeal, especially absent examples showing that resubmission was effective. She also could not have sought Judge V.G.’s removal before the decision because the procedure was written, she was unaware of the panel’s composition, and the Supreme Court should have provided clear instructions about that information.

On the merits, the Court applied subjective and objective impartiality tests. It found no evidence of actual bias. Under the objective test, however, the applicant’s doubts were objectively justified. Judge V.G. and prosecutor M.G. were father and son; M.G. had brought the charges and played a major role in the case. There was no system preventing the judge from receiving a case involving his son, and no evidence that Judge V.G. checked or disclosed the conflict. The cassation appeal did not require naming the prosecutor, making the conflict harder to detect. Judge V.G. presided over the panel that dismissed the appeal. Given the Supreme Court’s sixteen Criminal Division judges, replacing him would have been practicable. The defect was not remedied because the Supreme Court was the final instance. The Court concluded that the selection panel’s composition failed to guarantee impartiality, violating Article 6 § 1.

Vella v. Malta (Application no. 73182/12) concerned Josephine Mary Vella, a Maltese national born in 1932, who owned 14 Kirkop Square, Kirkop, a two-storey tenement of about 175 sq.m. She inherited it with her brothers and became sole owner by partition in 1998. The property had been requisitioned in 1955 and allocated to the San Leonard Band Club. The owners never recognised the club as tenant or accepted rent from it; a 1958 judgment held this was permissible because the tenement had not been leased as a dwelling. Rent was paid to the owners by the housing authority at 30 Maltese lira annually—about EUR 70, or less than EUR 6 monthly. The applicant later claimed the 2007 rental value was about EUR 1,747 monthly; the Government disputed this, relying on a valuation of another property, 3 Kirkop Square, at about EUR 1,021 monthly.

The applicant alleged the band club made extensive structural alterations without consent or permits, destroying the historic layout and devaluing the property. The Government argued she had not pursued domestic remedies and that the alterations increased value. She also alleged the club breached the tenancy by manufacturing fireworks and running unauthorised commercial activities, such as a bar and wedding venue; the Government said these were unproved. From 2008 the club began depositing rent in court.

An adjacent property owned by the applicant and her brothers had also been requisitioned and assigned to the band club. In 1993 the Court of Appeal declared that requisition null and void as not in the public interest, and damages for structural alterations were later awarded.

In 2007 the applicant brought constitutional redress concerning the 1955 property. She alleged breaches of Article 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to the requisition and continued occupation, seeking compensation and release. In October 2011 the Civil Court (First Hall) in its constitutional jurisdiction upheld her claims. It found the requisition served a private entity, was not in the public interest, and was disproportionate; the derisory rent imposed an excessive burden, violating Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It also found Article 14 violated because only her property had been requisitioned for the band club. It awarded EUR 60,000 compensation, three quarters payable by the Director of Social Housing and one quarter by the band club, and ordered the club to vacate within three months.

On appeal, the Constitutional Court in May 2012 partly upheld the judgment. It confirmed a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 only because the requisition was disproportionate, but held it was in the public interest for social and cultural purposes. It found no Article 14 violation. It revoked the eviction order, holding that compensation sufficed to redress the unfair balance and the lease’s validity was not at issue. It confirmed the EUR 60,000 award and sharing. It reasoned that disproportionality had not persisted since 1955 but only after the 1980s; the applicant had received rent and only instituted proceedings in 2007, so reduced compensation was legitimate. Since the property was taken in the public interest, compensation need not reflect market values. It retained the award because the property was not vacated, and held that damages for depreciation from structural works fell outside the constitutional complaint. The applicant was ordered to pay costs of the cross-appeal and half the judicial costs.

**Summary of Vella v. Malta (Application no. 73182/12)**

The case of *Vella v. Malta* concerns an application lodged by Ms. Josephine Mary Vella, a Maltese national, against the Republic of Malta under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant alleged violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the Convention.

The applicant owned a two-storey tenement at 14 Kirkop Square, Kirkop, which she inherited through a deed of partition in 1998, becoming its sole owner. The property had been requisitioned in 1955 by a requisition order and allocated to the San Leonard Band Club. The owners never recognised the tenant or accepted rent from the club directly; instead, rent was paid by the competent authority (Director of Social Housing/Housing Authority) at an annual rate of approximately EUR 70, or less than EUR 6 per month. The applicant submitted an architect’s valuation from 2007 estimating the property’s rental value at MTL 750 (approximately EUR 1,747) per month, though the Government challenged this estimate.

Over the years, the band club carried out extensive structural alterations without the owners’ consent or necessary permits, allegedly devaluing the property’s historical and architectural significance. The applicant also claimed the band club breached the tenancy agreement by manufacturing fireworks and conducting commercial activities such as running a bar and renting the premises for weddings without authorisation.

In 2007, the applicant instituted constitutional redress proceedings, alleging that the requisition order and continued occupation violated her property rights and constituted discrimination. By a judgment of 11 October 2011, the Civil Court (First Hall) in its constitutional jurisdiction upheld her claims. It found that the requisition had not been in the public interest, as the property was enjoyed by a private entity, and that the derisory rent imposed a disproportionate burden on the applicant, violating Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It also found a violation of Article 14, as only her property had been requisitioned for the band club’s use. The court awarded EUR 60,000 in compensation and ordered the band club to vacate the premises within three months.

The band club, the Attorney General, and the Director of Social Accommodation appealed, while the applicant cross-appealed, arguing the compensation was too low. By a judgment of 25 May 2012, the Constitutional Court upheld the finding of a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 only insofar as the requisition was disproportionate, but reversed the finding that it was not in the public interest. It held that the requisition served a social and cultural purpose for the general public. It further found no violation of Article 14. The Constitutional Court revoked the eviction order, reasoning that the unfair balance could be redressed through compensation without evicting the tenant.

Regarding redress, the Constitutional Court confirmed the EUR 60,000 compensation but noted that the disproportionality had only arisen after the 1980s, and that the applicant had received rent and delayed instituting proceedings until 2007. It held that compensation need not reflect market values since the taking was in the public interest. The court also determined that claims for damages due to structural depreciation fell outside the scope of constitutional complaints, and ordered the applicant to pay certain judicial costs.

The applicant subsequently brought her case before the European Court of Human Rights, complaining about the continued violation of her property rights due to the disproportionate rent and the Constitutional Court’s refusal to order eviction or award adequate compensation, as well as the alleged discriminatory treatment.

In *Vella v. Malta* (Application no. 73182/12), the applicant, Josephine Mary Vella, a Maltese national born in 1932, owned 14 Kirkop Square, Kirkop, a two-storey tenement inherited with her brothers and assigned solely to her by a 1998 deed of partition. In 1955 the property was requisitioned and allocated to the San Leonard Band Club. The owners never recognised the club as tenant or accepted rent from it; a 1958 civil judgment held they were entitled to do so because the tenement had not been leased as a dwelling and greater risks were involved. Rent was instead paid to the owners by the competent housing authority. The annual rent was only 30 Maltese Lira (about EUR 70, or less than EUR 6 per month). The applicant’s 2007 architect valued the rental at MTL 750 (about EUR 1,747) per month. The Government disputed this, relying on a valuation for another property, 3 Kirkop Square, at EUR 1,021 per month.

The band club allegedly carried out extensive structural alterations without the owners’ consent or permits. According to the applicant, these altered the traditional layout and historic character of the property, devaluing it. The Government argued that the applicant had not pursued ordinary remedies to substantiate loss and that the alterations had increased the property’s value and left it in good repair. The applicant also alleged that the band club breached the tenancy by manufacturing fireworks, running a bar, and letting the premises as a wedding venue without authorisation; the Government said these allegations were unsubstantiated. From 2008, following constitutional proceedings, the band club began depositing the annual rent in court.

In a related case concerning an adjacent property, 18 St. John’s Alley, Kirkop, requisitioned in 1986 and also assigned to the band club, the Court of Appeal in 1993 declared the requisition null and void as not being in the public interest and ordered possession within six months. Later damages of EUR 72,000 were awarded in 2009 for missing objects, structural changes, and loss of use, upheld in 2012.

In 2007 the applicant instituted constitutional redress proceedings concerning the 1955 requisition. She alleged violations of Article 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, asking for compensation, release of the property, and measures to prevent continuing violation. The defendants denied any violations.

In 2011 the Civil Court (First Hall) in its constitutional jurisdiction upheld her claims. It found the requisition had not been in the public interest because the property was enjoyed by a private entity, and that the measure was disproportionate due to the derisory rent, causing an excessive burden. It found violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 14, the latter because only her property had been requisitioned for the band club. It awarded EUR 60,000 compensation, payable three quarters by the Director of Social Housing and one quarter by the band club, and ordered the band club to vacate within three months.

On appeal, the Constitutional Court in 2012 upheld only the finding of a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, in so far as the requisition was disproportionate. It found the requisition had served a social and cultural purpose and was in the public interest, and that there was no Article 14 violation. It revoked the eviction order, holding that correcting the unfair balance sufficed. It confirmed the EUR 60,000 award but reasoned that disproportionality began only after the 1980s, that the applicant had received rent and delayed proceedings until 2007, and that public-interest takings did not require market-value compensation. Damages for structural depreciation were held outside the constitutional complaint. The applicant was ordered to pay costs. The Strasbourg application concerned whether these facts disclosed violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 14.

In *Abdilla v. Malta* (ECtHR, 17 July 2018), the applicant, Jean Pierre Abdilla, a Maltese national born in 1975, was serving a sixteen-year prison sentence for drug-related offences at Corradino Correctional Facility. From December 2009 he was held mainly in Division 2, except for two brief periods in the high-security Division 6 in 2011. After 4 December 2011 he was placed in cell no. 45 until 26 December 2014, and then in cell no. 70. He complained under Article 3 that his conditions of detention amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment, and under Article 13 that he had no effective domestic remedy.

The applicant described Division 2 as an old, poorly maintained area lacking light and air. Windows were triple-barred; skylights remained closed even in summer, causing excessive heat; and the environment was squalid and smelly. Cell no. 45 was near the prison bakery, exposing him to fumes and heat, and was nearly underground, humid, cold in winter, and poorly ventilated. Cell no. 70 was very small, poorly ventilated, and claustrophobic, with little access to running water. Food was allegedly poor, non-nutritious, and too small in portion; in September 2015, prisoners were hospitalized after food poisoning, and mice were reportedly found dead in the kitchen. Toilets lacked automated flushing, so inmates had to use buckets; water was limited and not potable, forcing purchases of bottled water. Showers often lacked hot water, were dirty and insufficient, and one had a broken tray. Telephone calls were expensive, and the prison allowance was too low. The emergency buzzer allegedly did not work; once, while ill, he waited thirty minutes for staff. Petitions and other inmates’ constitutional cases led to no change.

The Government contested these claims. It said cells measured 9 sq m and were above ground; natural light and air reached Division 2; running water was available through tanks; bakery ovens faced away from the division; there was no humidity in cell no. 45; blankets were provided; food portions were adequate; only one food-poisoning incident occurred and did not affect the applicant; pest control was in place; gratuity and work pay were sufficient; showers had been refurbished; water was potable; telephone cards were provided; and the buzzer system was upgraded.

The Court declared the Article 3 complaint admissible only for the period after 4 December 2011. The earlier period was inadmissible under the six-month rule because the brief stays in Division 6 meant there was no continuing situation. On the merits, relying on *Story and Others v. Malta* and *Yanez Pinon and Others v. Malta*, the Court found no Article 3 violation. The 9 sq m single-occupancy cells exceeded CPT minimum standards, and detainees could spend more than ten hours daily outside their cells. Many additional allegations were unsubstantiated or minor: no details about the smell; the buzzer problem occurred once without consequence; the bakery fumes could have justified a transfer request, but none was shown; and the allowance was sufficient since basic needs were met. Overall, the conditions did not exceed the unavoidable suffering inherent in detention.

However, the Court found a violation of Article 13. Because the Article 3 complaint was arguable, Article 13 applied. The domestic remedies relied on by the Government—complaints to the Board of Prisoners, judicial review, civil tort action, and constitutional redress—were not effective, especially because constitutional proceedings were too slow. No new timely preventive or compensatory remedy had been introduced. The applicant therefore lacked an effective domestic remedy for his detention-condition complaints.

In *Abdilla v. Malta* (Application no. 36199/15), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by Jean Pierre Abdilla, a Maltese national, about prison conditions at Corradino Correctional Facility and the absence of an effective domestic remedy.

Abdilla was serving a 16-year sentence for drug-related offences, confirmed on appeal in 2013. From December 2009 he was held mainly in Division 2, except for two brief periods in the high-security Division 6 in 2011. After 4 December 2011, he remained in Division 2, first in cell no. 45 until 26 December 2014, then in cell no. 70.

He alleged violations of Article 3 due to allegedly inhuman and degrading conditions. Division 2 was said to be about 200 years old, requiring major maintenance, and lacking light and air. Windows were triple-barred, skylights stayed closed even in summer, and the environment was squalid with a bad smell. Cell no. 45 was described as nearly underground, humid, cold, poorly ventilated, and affected by fumes and heat from a nearby bakery; he could barely see outside. Cell no. 70 was small, poorly ventilated, and caused claustrophobia. He claimed running water was often unavailable. Food was poor, non-nutritious, and portions were small; in September 2015 prisoners were hospitalised after food poisoning, and mice were allegedly found dead in the kitchen. Toilets lacked automated flushing, so inmates used buckets. Water was limited and not potable, forcing inmates to buy bottled water. Showers were insufficient, sometimes only one for Division 2, with dirty water, often no hot water, and a cracked tray. Telephone calls were expensive and the prison allowance was low. He also complained of illness, a broken emergency buzzer, and a 30-minute delay before staff responded. Petitions and other inmates’ constitutional cases allegedly produced no change.

He complained under Article 3 and Article 13 that he lacked an effective remedy. The Government argued he had not exhausted domestic remedies because he did not request a cell transfer or bring constitutional redress proceedings. The Court rejected this: constitutional redress was too slow, and transfer would not help because most cells in Divisions 2 and 3 were similarly poor. However, complaints about the period before 4 December 2011 were time-barred because his brief stay in Division 6 broke the “continuing situation.” The period after 4 December 2011 was admissible.

On the merits, the Court relied on prior Maltese prison cases (*Story*, *Yanez Pinon*, *Peñaranda Soto*). It found that the main conditions—cell size, light, ventilation, heat/cold, hygiene, showers, toilet flushing, water, food, and pest control—did not reach Article 3 severity. Cells were above ground and 9 sq m, exceeding CPT guidance, and inmates could spend over ten hours daily outside. Additional claims were unsubstantiated or minor: the bad smell lacked detail; the buzzer delay was isolated; bakery fumes might have justified a transfer, but no request was shown; the allowance was adequate as basic needs were met. Overall, the conditions did not cause suffering beyond unavoidable detention hardship. The Court therefore found no violation of Article 3. However, because the Article 3 complaint was arguable and Malta’s remedies remained too slow and ineffective, it found a violation of Article 13.

In *Abdilla v. Malta* (Application no. 36199/15, ECtHR, 17 July 2018), the applicant, Jean Pierre Abdilla, a Maltese national born in 1975, was serving a sixteen-year prison sentence and a €40,000 fine for drug-related offences, confirmed on appeal in 2013. From December 2009 he was detained mainly in Division 2 of Corradino Correctional Facility. He alleged that his conditions of detention violated Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and that he lacked an effective remedy under Article 13.

The alleged conditions were central. Division 2 was described as about 200 years old and in need of major maintenance, lacking light and air. Windows were triple-barred, and skylights were kept closed even in summer, causing excessive heat. The environment was alleged to be squalid and smelly. In cell no. 45, where he stayed until 26 December 2014, he claimed to suffer fumes and heat from a nearby bakery; the cell was nearly underground, humid and cold in winter, and poorly ventilated. In cell no. 70, to which he moved thereafter, the cell was very small, poorly ventilated and made him claustrophobic. He alleged little or no running water, no automated toilet-flushing system—inmates had to flush with buckets—and non-potable water; bottled water was costly. Showers were inadequate: often no hot water, dirty water, only one or two working showers, and a broken tray. Food was poor, non-nutritious and portions small; in September 2015 food poisoning led to prisoners being hospitalised, and mice were allegedly found dead in the kitchen. Telephone calls were expensive, the prison allowance was too low, and the emergency buzzer did not work; once, when ill in bed, he waited thirty minutes for staff after trying to use it. Petitions and other inmates’ constitutional cases brought no change.

The Government disputed these claims, stating cells measured 9 sq m, were above ground, had natural light and air, running water, adequate meals and showers, and that the food-poisoning incident did not affect the applicant. It argued he had failed to request a cell transfer or use constitutional redress.

The Court declared admissible only the complaint concerning detention after 4 December 2011; earlier periods were time-barred because brief placements in Division 6 broke continuity. It rejected the Government’s non-exhaustion objections, finding constitutional redress too slow and a transfer request unlikely to improve conditions because most cells were similar.

On the merits, the Court found no Article 3 violation. Relying on prior cases such as *Story and Others* and *Yanez Pinon*, it held that the overall conditions—single-occupancy 9 sq m cells, freedom to move for over ten hours daily, and the matters raised—did not exceed the unavoidable suffering inherent in detention. Additional complaints about smell, food portions, allowance and the buzzer were unsubstantiated or minor. The bakery fumes could have been alleviated by transfer, but there was no evidence he requested one.

However, the Court found a violation of Article 13. The Article 3 complaint was arguable, yet domestic remedies were not effective in practice, particularly due to delays, and no new timely remedy had been introduced. The applicant therefore lacked an effective remedy for his detention conditions.
