**Summary of *Ruiz Pena and Perez Oberght v. Malta* (ECtHR, 17 July 2018)**

The case concerned two applicants detained at Corradino Correctional Facility in Paola, Malta, who alleged that their conditions of detention violated Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment).

The first applicant, Mr Ruiz Pena, a Venezuelan national, had been detained since September 2009 and was serving a ten-year sentence. Since January 2013 he had been held in Division 3, cell no. 148. The second applicant, Mr Perez Oberght, a Dominican national, had been detained since November 2009 and was serving a nine-year sentence. Since January 2012 he had been held in Division 3, cell no. 155.

The applicants complained about several conditions. They alleged inadequate ventilation, including blocked or clogged air vents, and cell windows positioned too high, requiring them to climb onto sinks or beds to open or close them. They claimed extreme temperatures—very hot in summer and cold in winter—without heaters, and said fans merely circulated hot air. They also complained about having only one blanket, with additional blankets received from NGOs. They alleged the tap water was rusty, filthy and undrinkable, forcing them to buy bottled water despite limited prison earnings. Toilets had to be flushed manually using buckets due to low water pressure, which they described as deplorable, especially in summer. Dust fell from the ceilings of the old building, which the second applicant claimed aggravated his asthma. He also alleged humidity, poor natural and artificial light, and an unsafe spiral staircase in emergencies.

The Government disputed these claims. It stated that both applicants occupied individual cells; windows measured 50cm x 80cm and were 210cm high; vents were on opposite sides; tools were available to open windows; artificial lighting supplemented natural light; and water had been certified as potable, though bottled water was available for purchase. Fans were allowed, heaters were prohibited for security reasons except for medical need, and blankets could be requested. Cells were unlocked from 7:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. and from 2:00 p.m. to 8:30 p.m., giving inmates over ten hours daily access to the exercise yard and other facilities. Showers, cleaning materials, paint and maintenance assistance were available. After the complaints were communicated, authorities offered transfers, but the applicants refused.

The Court joined the applications. It rejected the Government’s request to strike them out and its non-exhaustion objection, finding that constitutional redress was not an effective remedy and that the transfer offer did not show the applicants’ situation would have improved, since many cells in Divisions 2 and 3 were of similar poor quality and had been criticised by the CPT.

On the merits, the Court referred to its earlier judgments in *Story and Others v. Malta* and *Yanez Pinon and Others v. Malta*. It expressed concern about the lack of heating, humidity, blocked vents, high windows, manual toilet flushing and dust. However, it found insufficient evidence of specific extreme temperatures, no proof that blankets were refused, no evidence that the second applicant’s asthma worsened, and no indication that tools or painting assistance were requested and denied. Given that cells were open for more than ten hours daily and inmates had access to various facilities, the Court concluded that the overall conditions did not reach the threshold of inhuman or degrading treatment. There was therefore no violation of Article 3.

**Ruiz Pena and Perez Oberght v. Malta** (ECtHR, Fourth Section, 17 July 2018) concerned two foreign nationals detained at Corradino Correctional Facility, Malta, who alleged that their conditions of detention violated Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits inhuman or degrading treatment.

Mr Ruiz Pena, a Venezuelan national, had been detained since September 2009 and was serving a ten-year sentence. Since January 2013 he occupied Division 3, cell 148. Mr Perez Oberght, a Dominican national, had been detained since November 2009 and was serving a nine-year sentence. Since January 2012 he occupied Division 3, cell 155.

Ruiz Pena alleged that his cell had only one high window and a clogged air vent, causing poor ventilation. He claimed extreme temperatures—35–40°C in summer and severe cold in winter—without a heater. He received only one blanket, with others coming from NGOs, and his two fans merely circulated hot air. The toilet had to be flushed manually with a bucket due to low water pressure. The 150-year-old building released dust, and the tap water was rusty and filthy, forcing him to buy drinking water despite earning only €0.60 per day.

Perez Oberght alleged that his window was over two metres high, difficult and dangerous to open, and that metal bars restricted natural light. One ventilation opening was blocked. He claimed the water was undrinkable, ceiling dust aggravated his asthma, humidity and lack of heating caused frequent flu, and poor lighting made reading difficult. He also said the spiral staircase was unsafe for emergency evacuation.

After the applications were communicated, the authorities asked whether the applicants wished to transfer cells. Both declined. Ruiz Pena feared losing his individual cell and being moved to a dormitory, harming his privacy. Perez Oberght argued that transfer would not remedy his suffering, that conditions were similar elsewhere, and that language barriers impeded verbal complaints. The Government argued that they had refused available transfers and failed to exhaust domestic remedies. It described the cells as individual, with functional vents, tools to open high windows, adequate artificial light, certified potable water, bottled water available for purchase, fans in summer, blankets, hot showers, cleaning materials, and paint. Heaters were prohibited for security reasons except for medical need. Cells were open from 7:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. and 2:00 to 8:30 p.m., giving over ten hours daily access to exercise and facilities. The Government admitted Division 3 lacked automated flushing and was old, but said maintenance and cleaning were provided.

The Court joined the applications, rejected the Government’s request to strike them out, and dismissed its non-exhaustion objection. It declared the complaints admissible. On the merits, it reiterated concerns from prior Maltese prison cases about lack of heating, humidity, poor ventilation, manual toilet flushing, and dust. It noted that lack of heating could itself raise Article 3 issues in extreme temperatures, especially for vulnerable detainees. However, the applicants did not provide sufficiently detailed evidence about specific cold periods, requests for blankets or window-opening tools, or asthma complications. The Court also weighed the significant out-of-cell time and access to recreational facilities. While concerned about several matters, it was not convinced that the overall conditions subjected the applicants to distress or hardship exceeding the unavoidable suffering inherent in detention. It therefore found no violation of Article 3.

**Ruiz Pena and Perez Oberght v. Malta** (ECtHR, Fourth Section, 17 July 2018) concerned two foreign nationals detained at Corradino Correctional Facility, Malta, who alleged that their conditions of detention violated Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits inhuman or degrading treatment.

The first applicant, Mr Ruiz Pena, a Venezuelan national, had been detained since September 2009 and was serving a ten-year sentence. Since January 2013 he was held in Division 3, cell 148. He complained that his cell had only one high window and one clogged air vent, causing poor ventilation and extreme temperatures—very hot in summer (35–40°C) and cold in winter. He lacked a heater, had only one blanket, and said his two fans merely circulated hot air. His toilet had to be flushed manually with buckets because of low water pressure. He also alleged that dust fell from the old ceiling, that tap water was rusty and undrinkable, and that he had to buy bottled water despite very low prison earnings.

The second applicant, Mr Perez Oberght, a Dominican national, had been detained since November 2009 and was serving a nine-year sentence. Since January 2012 he was held in Division 3, cell 155. He alleged that his cell window was over two metres high and dangerous to open, while metal bars restricted natural light. One ventilation opening was blocked, causing poor ventilation. He claimed the water was undrinkable, dust from the ceiling aggravated his asthma, and humidity plus lack of heating caused frequent flu. He also complained of poor lighting and an unsafe spiral staircase for emergencies.

The Maltese Government disputed the allegations. It submitted that both applicants occupied individual cells. Windows measured 50cm x 80cm and were 210cm high, with tools available to open them. Vents were placed on opposite sides, and artificial lighting supplemented natural light. Cold water was provided for security reasons, but hot water was available elsewhere. The Government claimed tap water was certified potable, bottled water was available, fans were allowed, heaters were permitted only for medical needs, extra blankets could be requested, and showers, cleaning materials, pest control, and cell painting assistance were available. Cells were unlocked from 7:30 to 12:30 and 14:00 to 20:30, allowing access to the exercise yard and other facilities. Manual toilet flushing with buckets remained necessary, but water and cleaning materials were said to be available. After the applications were communicated, authorities offered transfers, but the applicants refused.

The Court joined the applications and rejected the Government’s request to strike them out. It also dismissed the non-exhaustion objection, relying on its earlier finding in *Story and Others v. Malta* that constitutional redress was not an effective remedy. The Government’s transfer offer did not defeat admissibility because it was not shown that the proposed cells would materially improve conditions; most cells in Divisions 2 and 3 were of similar quality.

On the merits, the Court repeated concerns about lack of heating, humidity, non-functional vents, dangerous high windows, manual toilet flushing, and hygiene. However, the applicants had not provided sufficiently detailed evidence on winter temperatures, and the second applicant’s asthma was not shown to have worsened. Painting and emergency alternatives existed, and prisoners had substantial out-of-cell time daily. Considering the cumulative effect, the Court was not convinced that the overall conditions exceeded the unavoidable level of suffering inherent in detention. It therefore found **no violation of Article 3**.
001-181202:
**Mockutė v. Lithuania** concerned Neringa Mockutė, a Lithuanian lawyer who was involuntarily admitted to Vilnius Psychiatric Hospital on 7 May 2003. She had prior psychiatric treatment in 1992, 1994, 1996, and 2002. In February 2003 she began meditating at the Ojas Meditation Centre, the Lithuanian branch of the Osho movement. On 7 May 2003 she suffered an emotional breakdown at the Ministry of Economy: she became agitated, left work, undressed at home, and screamed from her balcony. Her family called an ambulance, and she was taken by force to Vilnius Psychiatric Hospital. She refused to consent to admission or treatment; her cousin signed the consent form. She was physically restrained and forcibly given neuroleptics. She remained in hospital for 52 days, until 26 June 2003, diagnosed with a transitory psychotic disorder. During her stay, medical records noted that doctors questioned her about the Ojas Centre, sought to form a “critical attitude” toward her non-traditional religious beliefs, and continued psycho-correction directed at her meditation. The applicant alleged that psychiatrists pressured her to renounce meditation, mocked it, said it harmed her mental health, told her to follow Catholicism, and delayed her release when she refused to accept their views.

As to Article 8, on 17 June 2003, while she was still hospitalized, the LNK television programme *Srovės* aired. It featured her mother and sister, identified by their real first names, who claimed the Ojas Centre had a destructive influence. Doctor D.Š., a head of division and psychiatrist at Vilnius Psychiatric Hospital, was interviewed on hospital premises. She disclosed that a young woman (called “Violeta”) had acute psychosis, was being treated at Vilnius Psychiatric Hospital, had studied in the United States for a master’s degree, and had held an important State job. The programme implied Osho followers took part in sex orgies and linked the applicant’s psychosis to meditation. Although her full name was not used, the applicant alleged that these details, together with her mother’s and sister’s participation, made her identifiable. She also alleged that information about her health was disclosed to her mother without consent. She responded with an open letter in August 2003, confirming the broadcast was about her.

As to Article 9, the applicant complained that the psychiatric hospital prevented her from practising her religion by attempting to cure her of meditation and alter her religious convictions. In 2006 she sued the hospital for non-pecuniary damage. The first-instance court found unlawful forced hospitalization, a privacy breach, and a religious-freedom breach, awarding her damages. The Court of Appeal upheld the unlawful-detention finding but reversed the privacy and religion findings, holding that she was not sufficiently identifiable from the broadcast, that disclosure to her mother was not a breach, and that attempts to make her critical of her beliefs did not restrict religious rites. The Supreme Court refused to admit her appeal. She applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 14 December 2009, alleging violations of Article 8 (private life and confidentiality) and Article 9 (freedom of religion).

In *Mockutė v. Lithuania*, the applicant, Neringa Mockutė, a Lithuanian lawyer, complained that a psychiatric hospital disclosed private information about her to journalists and her mother, breaching Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and that psychiatrists interfered with her religion by pressuring her to abandon meditation at the Ojas Meditation Centre, an Osho movement, breaching Article 9.

The applicant had a history of psychiatric treatment between 1992 and 2002. In February 2003 she began meditating at the Ojas Meditation Centre, which she described as spiritual and emotional healing. On 7 May 2003, after stress at work, she behaved erratically: she left work agitated, returned home, undressed, and screamed on her balcony. Her mother sought help; her sister and cousin called an ambulance, and she was taken forcibly to Vilnius Psychiatric Hospital. She refused to consent to admission, but her cousin signed the consent form. She was restrained and given neuroleptics. She remained in the hospital until 26 June 2003, a total of fifty-two days.

Although doctors recorded by 8 May that she was oriented, clear-headed and responsive, no court order was obtained for her continued involuntary detention beyond the 48-hour limit under Lithuanian law. Domestic courts later found that her initial admission on 7 May may have been justified, but that her continued detention and treatment after 8 May were unlawful. During hospitalization, medical records showed that doctors discussed her attendance at the Ojas Centre, tried to make her adopt a critical attitude towards non-traditional religious beliefs and meditation, and noted that she insisted it was a personal matter. These facts underpin her Article 9 complaint that psychiatrists interfered with her freedom of religion.

On 17 June 2003, while she was still hospitalized, the LNK television programme *Srovės* aired an episode about the Ojas Meditation Centre. It suggested the centre involved secretive or sexual practices and linked the applicant’s psychosis to meditation. The programme featured her mother and sister, identified by their real first names, and Dr D.Š., a psychiatrist and head of division at Vilnius Psychiatric Hospital. Dr D.Š. disclosed that a young woman patient had acute psychosis, was being treated at Vilnius Psychiatric Hospital, had studied in the United States for a master’s degree, and was of high morals. Although the applicant was called “Violeta” and not directly named, the broadcast gave details—age, education abroad, state employment, and current psychiatric treatment—that allegedly made her identifiable. This formed the core of her Article 8 privacy complaint. She also alleged that the hospital disclosed information to her mother.

In August 2003 the applicant published an open letter responding to the broadcast. She said it was one-sided, denied that meditation caused her breakdown, and described psychiatric pressure: interrogations about the Ojas Centre, demands that she promise not to meditate, claims that meditation was harmful and incompatible with Catholic tradition, and threats that refusing treatment could affect her diagnosis and future employment. She noted earlier hospitalizations unrelated to meditation.

In 2006 she sued the hospital for non-pecuniary damage. In 2008 the first-instance court found the forced hospitalization and treatment after 8 May unlawful, a breach of privacy by Dr D.Š., and a breach of religious freedom, awarding about EUR 31,850. In 2009 the Court of Appeal upheld the unlawful detention finding but dismissed the privacy claim because the disclosure did not sufficiently identify her, and dismissed the religion claim because there was no evidence she was forbidden from performing rites. It reduced the award to about EUR 5,800. The Supreme Court refused further appeal. The European Court of Human Rights later examined whether these facts violated Articles 8 and 9.

**Mockutė v. Lithuania** (Application no. 66490/09) concerned Neringa Mockutė, a Lithuanian lawyer with a history of psychiatric treatment between 1992 and 2002. In February 2003 she began attending the Ojas Meditation Centre, linked to the Osho movement. On 7 May 2003, while working at the Ministry of Economy, she became agitated, left work abruptly, returned home, undressed, and screamed on her balcony. Her family called an ambulance, and she was taken by force to Vilnius Psychiatric Hospital. She refused to consent to admission; her cousin signed the consent form instead. She was physically restrained and forcibly given neuroleptics, including haloperidol. She remained in the hospital until 26 June 2003—52 days—under increasingly relaxed but still restricted regimes. Her diagnosis was a transitory psychotic disorder.

Her medical records noted her attendance at the Ojas Meditation Centre, described her as “uncritical” towards it, and recorded that psycho-correction was aimed at forming a critical attitude towards non-traditional religious beliefs and meditation. The applicant later alleged that psychiatrists interrogated her about the Centre, pressured her to stop meditating, mocked meditation, invoked Catholic tradition, and treated her refusal to accept their views as a sign of mental illness. She claimed they threatened that refusing treatment could lead to a diagnosis affecting future employment and that her release was postponed because of her religious/spiritual views.

On 17 June 2003, while she was still hospitalised, the LNK television programme *Srovės* was broadcast. It used the first name “Violeta” but stated that the woman had obtained a master’s degree in the United States, had an important State job, and was being treated in a psychiatric hospital for acute psychosis after involvement with the Ojas Centre. Dr D.Š., a head of division and psychiatrist at Vilnius Psychiatric Hospital, was interviewed on hospital premises. She commented on the young woman’s morals, her studies in America, and her alleged membership in a sect; the domestic first-instance court found that Dr D.Š. had disclosed the applicant’s diagnosis of acute psychosis, her hospital treatment, and her US studies without consent. The applicant’s mother and sister appeared in the programme, identified by their real first names, and blamed the Ojas Centre for her condition. The applicant herself was not shown.

On 14 August 2003, the applicant published an open letter under her real name, describing her involuntary admission, the pressure to renounce meditation, and her continuing commitment to meditation.

In 2006 she sued the hospital for non-pecuniary damage, alleging unlawful detention, privacy breach, violation of religious freedom, violation of bodily inviolability, inadequate care, and failure to inform her properly. In 2008 the Vilnius Regional Court found forced hospitalisation after 8 May unlawful, a privacy breach due to Dr D.Š.’s disclosures

**Summary of *Salakhbekov and Abukayev v. Russia* (Applications nos. 28368/09 and 28636/09)**

**Case Background and Parties**
The case originated from two applications lodged against the Russian Federation with the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants were two Russian nationals who had participated in the clean-up operation at the Chernobyl nuclear disaster site. They were entitled to specific social benefits under Russian law. The applicant in application no. 28636/09 was represented by a lawyer, while the Russian Government was represented by its official representative to the ECtHR.

**Key Facts and Domestic Proceedings**
The central facts pertain to the applicants' pursuit of social benefits and the subsequent legal battle. In 2008, both applicants applied for a recalculation of the social benefits they were receiving. Their claims were successful in domestic courts, which issued judgments in their favour.

However, the relevant defendant authority (likely a social security or pension body) did not accept these final judgments. The authority requested an extension of the statutory time limit for lodging an appeal (cassation appeal). The domestic courts granted this extension, thereby allowing the defendant to appeal out of time. As a result of this appeal, the final judgments that had been issued in the applicants' favour were subsequently quashed. The summary of these specific developments in each applicant's case was provided in an Appendix to the Court's judgment.

**Alleged Violations and the Court's Assessment**
The applicants brought their case to the ECtHR, complaining that the unlawful extension of the time limit for appeal and the subsequent quashing of final judgments in their favour violated their rights under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair trial, specifically the right to a court) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention (protection of property).

The applicants argued that granting the defendant authority an extension to appeal, after the judgments had become final, upset the legal certainty of their court victories and deprived them of the enforceable benefits they had been awarded. The Government contested these claims.

In its judgment, the ECtHR noted that the factual circumstances and the legal issues raised in this case were substantively similar to those it had previously examined in the case of *Magomedov and Others v. Russia*. Following the precedent set in *Magomedov*, the Court found that the domestic courts' decisions to restore the time limit for appeal to the defendant and to subsequently quash the final judgments in the applicants' favour constituted a violation of their right to a court under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

Having reached this conclusion, the Court found it unnecessary to examine the admissibility or merits of the separate complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning the deprivation of possessions. The judgment was delivered by a Committee of the Third Section on 29 May 2018, finding a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

In *Salakhbekov and Abukayev v. Russia* (Applications nos. 28368/09 and 28636/09), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered judgment on 29 May 2018. The applicants were two Russian nationals who had taken part in the clean-up operation at the Chernobyl nuclear disaster site. In 2008 they applied for a recalculation of the social benefits to which they claimed entitlement as Chernobyl clean-up workers. The domestic courts granted their claims, giving judgments in their favour.

The alleged violations arose after those judgments were challenged by the defendant authority. The ordinary time limit for lodging an appeal had expired, so the authority requested an extension or restoration of the appeal time limit. The domestic courts granted that request. As a result, the defendant authority was able to appeal out of time, and the appellate courts subsequently quashed the final judgments that had been given in the applicants’ favour. The applicants therefore lost the benefit of the domestic decisions that had already been issued in their favour.

Before the European Court, the applicants complained that the extension of the time limit for appeal, granted at the defendant authority’s request, had unlawfully allowed the final judgments in their favour to be reopened and quashed. They relied on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, arguing that this infringed their right to a court and to a fair hearing in the determination of their civil rights. They also relied on Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, complaining that they had been deprived of possessions represented by the social benefits awarded by the final domestic judgments. In substance, their complaint was that the final and binding nature of the judgments in their favour had been undermined by the unjustified extension of the appeal period, enabling a state authority to escape the consequences of final judicial decisions.

Procedurally, on 24 April 2017 the Court communicated to the Government the complaints concerning the extension of the time limits for lodging appeals and the subsequent quashing of the final judgments in the applicants’ favour. The remainder of application no. 28368/09 was declared inadmissible. The Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection. The Court joined the two applications because of their similar subject matter.

On the merits, the Court noted that the factual setting and legal issues were substantively similar to those previously examined in *Magomedov and Others v. Russia* (nos. 33636/09 and 9 others, 28 March 2017), which concerned the restoration of time limits for appeal and the quashing of final judgments. After examining the material, the Court found no fact or argument capable of leading to a different conclusion. It therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention: the unlawful extension of the appeal time limit following the defendant authority’s request had resulted in the final judgments in the applicants’ favour being quashed, thereby violating their right to a court. Having reached that conclusion, the Court considered that there was no need to examine separately either the admissibility or the merits of the complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section, sitting as a Committee) delivered judgment on 29 May 2018 in *Salakhbekov and Abukayev v. Russia* (applications nos. 28368/09 and 28636/09). The applicants were two Russian nationals. Application no. 28636/09 was represented by lawyer Z.S. Salimov. The Russian Government was represented first by G. Matyushkin and later by M. Galperin. On 24 April 2017, the Court communicated the complaints concerning the extension of appeal time limits and the subsequent quashing of final judgments in the applicants’ favour; the remainder of application no. 28368/09 was declared inadmissible. The Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection. The Court joined the applications because they raised similar issues.

The key facts concerned the applicants’ social benefits. In 2008, the applicants—persons who had taken part in the clean-up operation at the Chernobyl nuclear disaster site—applied for recalculation of the social benefits to which they were entitled. Domestic courts granted their claims, resulting in final judgments in their favour. However, the defendant authority later requested an extension of the time limit for lodging an appeal. The domestic courts granted that extension, and the final judgments in the applicants’ favour were consequently quashed. The applicants alleged that the unlawful extension of the appeal time limit, followed by the quashing of those final judgments, violated their right to a court under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. They also relied on Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, arguing that the quashing deprived them of the peaceful enjoyment of their possessions, namely the social benefits confirmed by the final judgments.

Article 6 § 1 guarantees a fair and public hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law. Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 protects every person’s right to the peaceful enjoyment of their possessions and prohibits deprivation of possessions except in the public interest and subject to legal conditions. The Government contested the applicants’ position.

The Court noted that the factual setting and legal issues raised by the applicants were substantively similar to those previously examined in *Magomedov and Others v. Russia* (nos. 33636/09 and 9 others, §§ 6–13 and 35–43, 28 March 2017). That case concerned the restoration of time limits for appeal and the resulting quashing of final judgments. Having examined all the material, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on admissibility or merits. It therefore followed *Magomedov and Others*, where comparable circumstances had led to findings of violations. The Court concluded that the extension of the appeal time limit and the quashing of the final judgments in the applicants’ favour breached their right to a court under Article 6 § 1. In light of that conclusion, the Court considered it unnecessary to examine separately either the admissibility or the merits of the complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision. The case reinforces the principle that final judgments should not be undone through unjustified extensions of appeal time limits, as doing so can violate the right to a fair hearing and legal certainty under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.
001-183373:
**CASE OF NOVOTNÝ v. THE CZECH REPUBLIC**  
*(Application no. 16314/13, judgment of 7 June 2018)*

The applicant, František Novotný, was born in 1942. In 1965 he had a sexual relationship with a woman who gave birth to a daughter, Z., on 2 March 1966. The applicant denied paternity. After Z.’s birth, but before paternity proceedings began, the mother married another man. In 1970 the Jihlava District Court declared the applicant to be Z.’s father and ordered him to pay maintenance. The court relied on witness evidence, documents, and a “bio-hereditary” blood test. It found that the applicant had had intercourse with the mother between 300 and 180 days before Z.’s birth, creating a presumption of paternity under Article 54 of the Family Code. Another man had also had intercourse with the mother during the relevant period, but blood-test evidence excluded him as the father. The applicant appealed and requested another expert opinion, but the Brno Regional Court refused because the facts were sufficiently established. The Regional Court upheld the District Court’s judgment on 2 June 1970, and it became final on 10 June 1970.

In 2011 the applicant asked the Prosecutor General to challenge his paternity in court. By letter of 21 June 2011 he was told that the requirements of Article 62 of the Family Code were not met: Z., then an adult, did not wish to challenge paternity, it was not in her interests, and the applicant had not produced expert evidence credibly disproving paternity.

On 29 February 2012 the applicant and Z. underwent a DNA examination. The report of 19 April 2012 unequivocally confirmed that the applicant was not Z.’s biological father. On 9 May 2012 the applicant again asked the Prosecutor General to challenge paternity. On 12 September 2012 the Prosecutor General replied that the applicant’s paternity had been determined by a judicial declaration under Article 54 of the Family Code, not by a statutory presumption under Articles 51 § 1 or 52. The Prosecutor General therefore could not initiate proceedings under Articles 62 and 62a. Once paternity had been established by a final judicial declaration, Czech law provided no possibility to challenge it.

The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, arguing that the DNA evidence proved he was not Z.’s father and that Articles 61 § 1 and 62 § 1 of the Family Code were unconstitutional. On 13 December 2012 the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint. It noted that his paternity had been established by a final judicial decision and that the Prosecutor General’s competence applied only if all legal requirements were fulfilled, which was not the case.

The applicant alleged violations of Articles 6, 8 and 14 of the Convention. The central alleged violation concerned Article 8, the right to respect for private and family life: after the 2012 DNA test proved he was not the biological father, he had no effective possibility to challenge the final paternity declaration. The Government argued that the application was time-barred because it was lodged more than six months after the DNA report. The European Court of Human Rights rejected that objection. It found the application was lodged on 19 February 2013, within six months of both the Prosecutor General’s letter of 12 September 2012 and the Constitutional Court’s decision of 13 December 2012. The Court declared the Article 8 complaint admissible.

On the merits, the Court reiterated that paternity disputes concern private life and personal identity, including a putative father’s right to deny paternity where scientific evidence shows he is not the biological father. It examined whether the Czech authorities had struck a fair balance between legal certainty, the stability of family relationships, and the child’s interests, on one hand, and the applicant’s interest in reviewing paternity in light of DNA evidence, on the other. Because no legal mechanism allowed the applicant to challenge the final judicial declaration under Article 54, and because the Prosecutor General could not act, the Court found a violation of Article 8.

**Case Summary: Novotný v. the Czech Republic (App. no. 16314/13, 7 June 2018)**

The case concerned František Novotný, a Czech man born in 1942, who was declared the father of Z., born on 2 March 1966, after a sexual relationship with Z.’s mother in 1965. Novotný denied paternity. The mother later married another man, and Z.’s guardian brought paternity proceedings. In 1970 the Jihlava District Court found Novotný to be Z.’s father and ordered him to pay maintenance. The court relied on witness and documentary evidence, a “bio-hereditary” blood test, and the fact that Novotný had had intercourse with the mother between 300 and 180 days before Z.’s birth, creating a presumption under Article 54 of the Family Code. Another man who had also had intercourse at the relevant time was excluded by blood test. The Brno Regional Court upheld the judgment on 2 June 1970, and it became final on 10 June 1970.

In 2011 Novotný asked the Prosecutor General to challenge his paternity. The Prosecutor General refused, stating that the requirements of Article 62 of the Family Code were not met, that Z. was by then an adult and did not wish to challenge paternity, and that Novotný had produced no expert evidence disproving paternity. In February 2012 Novotný and Z. underwent DNA testing. The report of 19 April 2012 unequivocally confirmed that Novotný was not Z.’s biological father. On 9 May 2012 he renewed his request to the Prosecutor General. On 12 September 2012 the Prosecutor General replied that paternity had been established by a judicial declaration under Article 54, not by statutory presumption under Articles 51 or 52, so the Prosecutor General had no competence under Articles 62 and 62a to challenge it. Once the 1970 judgment became final, Czech law provided no possibility to challenge it.

Novotný filed a constitutional complaint, relying on Article 6 § 1 and arguing that he had proved he was not the father and that Articles 61 and 62 of the Family Code were unconstitutional. On 13 December 2012 the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint, noting that paternity had been established by a final judicial decision and that the Prosecutor General could act only if all legal requirements were fulfilled.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Novotný alleged violations of Articles 6, 8 and 14 of the Convention. The Court focused on Article 8, the right to respect for private and family life. The Government argued that the application was time-barred because it was lodged more than six months after the DNA report. The Court rejected that objection, finding the application was lodged within six months of both the Prosecutor General’s letter of 12 September 2012 and the Constitutional Court’s decision of 13 December 2012. It declared the Article 8 complaint admissible.

On the merits, the Government relied on res judicata, legal certainty, and protection of family relationships, arguing that the 1970 proceedings had been thorough and non-arbitrary. The Court reiterated that paternity disputes engage private life and personal identity, and that Article 8 may require the State to provide adequate procedures for resolving paternity with certainty. Although legal certainty and the child’s interests are legitimate aims, inflexible rules or the absence of any possibility to challenge a judicial paternity declaration in light of new biological evidence can violate Article 8. Because the Prosecutor General could not challenge an Article 54 judicial declaration, Novotný had no effective mechanism to contest paternity despite conclusive DNA evidence. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 8 and did not examine Articles 6 and 14 separately.

**Summary**

*Novotný v. the Czech Republic* (ECtHR, First Section, 7 June 2018, app. no. 16314/13) concerned a man’s inability to challenge a final paternity declaration after DNA testing proved he was not the biological father. The applicant, František Novotný, born in 1942, had a sexual relationship in 1965 with a woman who gave birth to a daughter, Z., on 2 March 1966. He denied paternity. Z.’s guardian brought paternity proceedings on her behalf. Before those proceedings began, the mother married another man.

In 1970 the Jihlava District Court declared the applicant Z.’s father and ordered him to pay maintenance. It relied on witness evidence, documents, a “bio-hereditary” blood test, and a finding that the applicant had had intercourse with the mother between 300 and 180 days before Z.’s birth. Under Article 54 of the Family Code, this raised a presumption of paternity unless serious grounds excluded it. Another man had also had intercourse with the mother at the relevant time, but the blood test excluded him. The applicant appealed and requested another expert opinion. The Brno Regional Court refused because the facts were sufficiently proved, and upheld the judgment on 2 June 1970; it became final on 10 June 1970.

In 2011 the applicant asked the Prosecutor General to challenge paternity. On 21 June 2011 he was told that the requirements of Article 62 of the Family Code were not met: Z., then an adult, did not wish to challenge paternity, it was not in her interests, and the applicant had not produced expert evidence credibly disproving paternity. On 29 February 2012 the applicant and Z. underwent DNA testing. The report of 19 April 2012 unequivocally confirmed that the applicant was not Z.’s father. On 9 May 2012 he made a new request to the Prosecutor General. On 12 September 2012 the Prosecutor General replied that paternity had been determined by the District Court under Article 54 and that the prosecution service could not initiate proceedings under Articles 62 and 62a. Its competence only covered statutory presumptions under Articles 51 § 1 and 52. Once paternity had been established by a final judicial declaration under Article 54, Czech law provided no possibility to challenge it.

The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint under Article 6 § 1, arguing that he had proved he was not the biological father and asking the Constitutional Court to order the Prosecutor General to bring proceedings. He also challenged the constitutionality of Articles 61 § 1 and 62 § 1 of the Family Code. On 13 December 2012 the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint, noting that paternity had been established by a final judicial decision and that the Prosecutor General’s competence applied only if all legal requirements were fulfilled, which was not the case.

The applicant alleged violations of Articles 6, 8 and 14 of the Convention. The Government argued that the application was out of time, calculating the six-month period from the DNA report. The Court rejected that objection: the application was lodged on 19 February 2013, within six months of the Prosecutor General’s letter of 12 September 2012 and the Constitutional Court’s decision of 13 December 2012. The Article 8 complaint was declared admissible.

On the merits, the Court treated the case as concerning private life under Article 8. Although the original proceedings were lawful and pursued legitimate aims—legal certainty, security of family relationships, and child protection—the key issue was fair balance. The Court’s case-law recognises a putative father’s right to challenge paternity in light of scientific evidence and criticises inflexible time-limits or the absence of any mechanism to revisit a paternity declaration after new biological evidence. Here, the applicant’s paternity had been based on a presumption, and the 2012 DNA test excluded him, yet domestic law offered no procedure for review. The Court ultimately found a violation of Article 8.
001-183586:
**Case: Ashayev and Others v. Ukraine (Applications nos. 24329/08 and 6 others)**  
**Court:** European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section (Committee)  
**Judgment date:** 14 June 2018  
**Final:** Yes, subject to editorial revision  

The case originated in seven applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights on various dates. The applicants’ details and the specific facts of each underlying domestic case were set out in an appended table, which is not reproduced in the supplied text. The applications were communicated to the Ukrainian Government. Because the applications raised the same core complaint, the Court decided to join them and examine them in a single judgment.

The applicants complained about the excessive length of civil proceedings before the Ukrainian courts. They also complained that Ukrainian law did not provide them with any effective domestic remedy for that length complaint. In Convention terms, they relied on Article 6 § 1, which guarantees the right to a hearing within a reasonable time in the determination of civil rights and obligations, and Article 13, which guarantees an effective remedy before a national authority for violations of Convention rights.

The Court reiterated the standard test for assessing the reasonableness of the length of proceedings. Under its case-law, particularly *Frydlender v. France*, the reasonableness of proceedings must be assessed in light of the circumstances of the case and by reference to four criteria: the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicants, the conduct of the relevant authorities, and what was at stake for the applicants in the dispute.

The Court noted that it had already found violations of the Convention in similar cases against Ukraine, especially the leading case of *Krasnoshapka v. Ukraine* (no. 23786/02, 30 November 2006). In that earlier case, the Court had addressed comparable complaints about unreasonably long civil proceedings and the absence of an effective domestic remedy. The Court examined the material submitted in the present applications and found no fact or argument that would justify departing from that established case-law.

Accordingly, the Court concluded that the length of the civil proceedings in the applicants’ cases was excessive and failed to satisfy the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. It further found that the applicants did not have at their disposal any effective remedy at the national level in respect of those length complaints, contrary to Article 13 of the Convention.

The judgment therefore involved findings of violations of both Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention. The Court’s reasoning was brief because the issues were well settled and the case was suitable for determination by a Committee. The judgment then turned to the application of Article 41 of the Convention, which concerns just satisfaction, but the supplied text does not include the Court’s specific conclusions on damages or costs. Overall, the key facts relevant to the alleged violations were that the applicants were parties to civil proceedings in Ukraine that lasted an excessive period, and that Ukrainian domestic law provided no effective remedy to challenge or obtain redress for that delay.

In Ashayev and Others v. Ukraine (Applications nos. 24329/08 and six others), the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 14 June 2018. The Committee consisted of Yonko Grozev (President), Gabriele Kucsko-Stadlmayer, and Lətif Hüseynov, judges, with Liv Tigerstedt as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. It deliberated in private on 24 May 2018. The applications were lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates. Because they raised similar subject matter, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment. The applications had been communicated to the Ukrainian Government.

The applicants complained of two related violations. First, they alleged that civil proceedings in Ukraine involving them had lasted excessively long, contrary to Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees a hearing within a reasonable time by a tribunal in the determination of civil rights and obligations. Second, they alleged that they had no effective remedy in domestic law for that delay, contrary to Article 13 of the Convention, which requires an effective remedy before a national authority for Convention violations.

The full facts of each application—including the applicants’ names, the relevant dates, the course of the domestic civil proceedings, and the duration of those proceedings—were set out in the appended table. That table is not reproduced in the excerpt. For purposes of the alleged violations, the key facts are that each applicant was party to civil proceedings before Ukrainian courts or authorities; those proceedings allegedly continued for an unreasonable length of time; and the applicants allegedly lacked any effective domestic mechanism to complain about the excessive length or to obtain redress. **Nicholas v. Cyprus** (Application no. 63246/10) concerned a complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights that the applicant’s civil appeal had been heard by a Supreme Court bench lacking objective impartiality.

The applicant, Charalambos Nicholas, a Cypriot and British national, had been dismissed from Cyprus Airways Ltd as a trainee pilot. In 1998 he brought a civil action for wrongful dismissal and defamation against the company. The District Court dismissed his action in 2006. He appealed to the Supreme Court. A three-judge bench heard the appeal on 11 March 2007 and unanimously dismissed it on 21 April 2010. The defendant company was represented by a law firm. At the appeal hearing, the firm’s managing partner, P.G.P., appeared for the company and addressed the court. Other lawyers from the same firm had previously appeared for the company.

After the Supreme Court judgment, the applicant discovered that Judge A.K., one of the judges on the appeal bench, had a significant connection with P.G.P. Judge A.K.’s son was married to P.G.P.’s daughter. Both the judge’s son and his daughter-in-law worked at P.G.P.’s law firm, where P.G.P. was managing partner. The applicant said he had not sought the judge’s recusal because neither he nor his lawyer knew of the relationship during the proceedings.

The Government argued that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies. It said he could have objected to Judge A.K.’s participation had he known, and after discovering the facts he could have sought reopening of the appeal. The Court rejected that objection. It found no concrete indication that the applicant or his lawyer knew of the connection while the appeal was pending. It also held that reopening was an extraordinary, discretionary remedy without clear time limits and was not shown to be effective for an impartiality complaint.

On the merits, the applicant did not allege subjective bias; he relied on the objective test. The key issue was whether there were ascertainable facts creating an objectively justified fear of lack of impartiality. The Court focused on two facts: first, the in-law relationship between Judge A.K. and P.G.P. through their children’s marriage; second, the employment connection—Judge A.K.’s son and daughter-in-law worked for P.G.P.’s law firm, which represented the opposing party, and P.G.P. himself appeared at the appeal hearing.

The Court found that the in-law relationship alone was sufficient to objectively justify the applicant’s fears. It noted that domestic judicial practice at the time did not require recusal for “in-laws,” though a judge could withdraw for personal reasons, and the code was later amended to include such relationships. As for the employment link, the Court said it did not automatically disqualify a judge, but it could raise impartiality concerns depending on factors such as the relative’s involvement in the case, position in the firm, firm size, and financial interest.

Because no disclosure was made, the applicant learned of the connection only after judgment. The Court found an appearance of partiality and concluded that domestic law and practice did not provide sufficient procedural safeguards. It therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1.

**Case: Nicholas v. Cyprus (Application no. 63246/10), ECtHR Third Section, judgment of 9 January 2018.**

The applicant, Charalambos Nicholas, a Cypriot and British national, was dismissed from Cyprus Airways Ltd as a trainee pilot. In 1998 he brought a civil action before the District Court of Nicosia for wrongful dismissal and defamation. The defendant company was represented by a law firm. At the hearing on 11 March 2007, P.G.P., the managing partner of the law firm representing the defendant company, appeared before the Supreme Court and addressed the bench. Until then, other lawyers from the same firm had appeared for the defendant. On 21 April 2010 the Supreme Court unanimously dismissed the appeal.

After the Supreme Court judgment, the applicant discovered that Judge A.K., one of the judges sitting on the appeal bench, had a family connection with P.G.P.: Judge A.K.’s son and P.G.P.’s daughter were married, and both worked at P.G.P.’s law firm. The applicant’s lawyer at the domestic appeal stage had not requested the judge’s exemption because he did not know of the relationship; the applicant himself learned of it only after the appeal proceedings ended.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, alleging a lack of objective impartiality on the part of Judge A.K. because of his relationship with the defendant company’s lawyer. The Government contested the complaint and argued that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies. It submitted that, under the Cypriot judicial practice applicable at the time, judges were not required to recuse themselves where the relationship was merely between “in-laws.” The applicant could have raised an objection if aware of the connection, or could have sought reopening of the appeal under the Supreme Court’s inherent jurisdiction.

The Court rejected the non-exhaustion objection. It found no concrete evidence that the applicant or his lawyer knew of the connection during the appeal. It also held that an application for reopening was an extraordinary remedy, discretionary, without precise time-limits, and not shown to be effective for complaints of judicial non-impartiality. The complaint was therefore admissible.

On the merits, the Court applied the objective test of impartiality: whether ascertainable facts raised legitimate doubts about the judge’s impartiality. The applicant did not allege subjective bias. The Court identified two grounds: the in-law relationship between Judge A.K. and P.G.P., and the employment of Judge A.K.’s son and daughter-in-law at P.G.P.’s law firm. The Court held that the in-law tie alone objectively justified the applicant’s fears. It noted that domestic law allowed a judge to withdraw for personal reasons, and the judicial code was later amended to include in-law relationships as grounds for recusal. As for the employment connection, the Court stated that it did not automatically disqualify a judge, but could create an appearance of bias depending on factors such as the relative’s involvement in the case, position in the firm, firm size, and financial interest.

Because no disclosure occurred and the applicant discovered the connection only after judgment, an appearance of partiality arose. Domestic law and practice did not provide sufficient procedural safeguards. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

In *Nicholas v. Cyprus* (Application no. 63246/10, judgment 9 January 2018), the applicant, Charalambos Nicholas, a Cypriot and British national, complained under Article 6 § 1 ECHR that the Supreme Court bench hearing his civil appeal lacked objective impartiality.

After his dismissal from Cyprus Airways Ltd as a trainee pilot, Nicholas brought a civil action in 1998 for wrongful dismissal and defamation. The District Court dismissed the action in 2006. He appealed to the Supreme Court (appeal no. 43/07). A three-judge bench heard the appeal on 11 March 2007. At that hearing, P.G.P., the managing partner of the law firm representing the defendant company, appeared and addressed the court; previously, other lawyers from the same firm had appeared. On 21 April 2010, the Supreme Court unanimously dismissed the appeal.

After the judgment, the applicant discovered that Judge A.K., one of the appeal judges, had a son married to P.G.P.’s daughter. Both the son and daughter-in-law worked at P.G.P.’s law firm, where P.G.P. was managing partner. The applicant said his domestic lawyer had not sought Judge A.K.’s exemption because he lacked sufficient knowledge at the time; the applicant himself only learned these facts after the appeal ended.

The Government argued that the applicant had failed to exhaust domestic remedies. At the relevant time, Cypriot judicial practice required recusal where a judge and an appearing lawyer were close relatives—defined to include parents, spouses, children, children’s spouses, siblings, etc.—but not in-laws. Judge A.K. was therefore not obliged to recuse, though he could do so at his discretion. Parties could raise an objection, and the Supreme Court could decide. The Government also argued that the applicant could seek reopening under the Supreme Court’s inherent jurisdiction. The Court rejected this objection: there was no concrete evidence that the applicant or his lawyer knew of the connection while the appeal was pending. Reopening was an extraordinary, discretionary remedy with no time-limit and was not shown to be effective for an alleged lack of impartiality. The non-exhaustion objection was dismissed.

On the merits, the Court examined only objective impartiality, as the applicant did not allege subjective bias. The key facts were: (1) Judge A.K.’s son was married to P.G.P.’s daughter, creating an in-law tie between the judge and opposing counsel; and (2) the judge’s son and daughter-in-law both worked at P.G.P.’s law firm, and P.G.P. was its managing partner and appeared at the hearing. The Court found that the family tie alone sufficed to objectively justify the applicant’s fears, especially since Cypriot rules were later amended to include father-in-law/son-in-law relationships as grounds for withdrawal. As to the employment link, the Court said ties with a firm employee do not automatically disqualify a judge, but such affiliation can create misgivings depending on factors such as involvement in the case, the relative’s position, firm size, and financial interest. No disclosure occurred at the outset; the applicant learned of the connection only after judgment and could not know whether the relatives were involved or had a financial interest.

The Court emphasized that justice must not only be done but be seen to be done. In small jurisdictions, strict standards should not paralyze courts, but where a situation creates an appearance of bias, it should be disclosed and assessed. Because there was no disclosure and domestic law and practice lacked sufficient procedural safeguards, the applicant’s doubts were objectively justified. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1 concerning Judge A.K.’s lack of impartiality.

**Case Summary: Pázsi and Others v. Hungary (Application no. 72595/13 and 8 others)**

**Court:** European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section)
**Date:** 15 November 2018

**Key Facts:**
The case originated from nine separate applications lodged against Hungary with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were individuals who had been subject to criminal proceedings in Hungary.

The central and principal complaint raised by all applicants was that the length of the criminal proceedings against them was incompatible with the "reasonable time" requirement guaranteed under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. This article ensures the right to a fair and public hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal.

Additionally, in one specific application (no. 39649/15), the applicant raised a further complaint under Article 13 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to an effective remedy for violations of Convention rights.

Given the similar subject matter of all the applications, the Court found it appropriate to examine them jointly in a single judgment.

**Legal Assessment and Alleged Violations:**

The Court reiterated its established case-law for assessing the reasonableness of the length of proceedings. This assessment is based on three key criteria: the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicants and the relevant authorities, and what was at stake for the applicants in the dispute. The Court referenced its previous judgments, including *Pélissier and Sassi v. France* and *Frydlender v. France*, which set out these principles.

Crucially, the Court noted that it had already found a violation of Article 6 § 1 in a similar, leading case against Hungary, *Barta and Drajkó v. Hungary* (no. 35729/12, 17 December 2013). This established clear precedent for the issues raised in the present applications.

After examining all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument that would lead it to a different conclusion from its previous case-law. It held that the length of the criminal proceedings in the instant case was excessive and failed to meet the "reasonable time" requirement. Therefore, the Court concluded that there had been a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention in all applications.

Regarding the additional complaint under Article 13 in application no. 39649/15, the Court found that this complaint also raised issues under the Convention, in light of its well-established case-law. It determined that this complaint was not manifestly ill-founded and was not inadmissible on any other grounds. Consequently, the Court declared this Article 13 complaint admissible.

In its judgment, the Court likely awarded just satisfaction to the applicants for the excessive length of proceedings, as is standard in such cases. The case serves as another example of the Court's consistent finding that lengthy criminal proceedings in Hungary violate the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

**Summary of *Tlapak and Others v. Germany* (Applications nos. 11308/16 and 11344/16)**

The case of *Tlapak and Others v. Germany* concerns two applications brought by four parents against Germany under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants were members of the Twelve Tribes Church, residing in two communities in Wörnitz and Klosterzimmern, Germany. They challenged decisions by German courts to partially withdraw their parental authority and separate them from their children.

The factual background is critical to the alleged violations. In 2012, media reports emerged regarding the Twelve Tribes Church's endorsement of corporal punishment, specifically caning, as a method of discipline. Subsequently, in August 2013, a television reporter provided video footage to local authorities and a family court. This hidden-camera footage documented ten separate instances of children aged three to twelve being caned by community members, often non-parents.

Based on this footage and testimony from former members, the Ansbach Family Court issued an interim order on 3 September 2013, withdrawing the applicants' rights to decide their children's residence, health, and education. The court found a reasonable likelihood that the children would be subjected to caning and "restraining," a practice involving holding a child's limbs and pressing their head down. On 5 September 2013, the youth office took the community's children into care, aided by police who searched the premises and found a wooden rod. Although medical examinations revealed no physical signs of abuse, the children were placed in foster families. The applicants' son (application no. 11308/16) and two daughters (application no. 11344/16) were separated from their parents; their youngest son was initially placed with his breastfeeding mother.

The main proceedings followed. A court-appointed expert concluded that the applicants held a loving attitude but considered corporal punishment with objects an appropriate and necessary parenting method. The expert opined that there was a likelihood bordering on certainty that they would apply such punishment, causing significant developmental and psychological harm. Less intrusive measures were deemed insufficient because the applicants' religious convictions made them unwilling to abandon these methods or cooperate with authorities.

On 22 October 2014 (Tlapak) and 21 October 2014 (Pingen), the Family Court upheld the withdrawal of parental rights, citing a high, concrete probability of systematic corporal punishment. The courts emphasized that such punishment violated the children's human dignity and right to physical integrity under the German Basic Law and the Civil Code. The Nuremberg Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants' appeals on 26 May 2015 and 10 June 2015, respectively, confirming the reasoning. It found that the applicants' religious beliefs prevented them from credibly distancing themselves from corporal punishment, and that they might leave Germany to avoid supervision. The Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit their constitutional complaints.

The applicants complained under Article 8 (right to respect for family life), Article 6 (right to a fair trial), Article 9 (freedom of religion), and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education), alleging disproportionate interference, insufficient factual foundation, and religious discrimination. The case was communicated to the German Government regarding Article 8.

Tlapak and Others v. Germany concerned two applications (nos. 11308/16 and 11344/16) brought by four German parents who were members of the Twelve Tribes Church and lived in a community in Wörnitz, Germany. In 2012, press reports and statements by former members alleged that the community endorsed corporal punishment, especially caning. In August 2013, a television reporter provided the youth office and the Nördlingen Family Court with hidden-camera footage showing ten instances of caning children aged three to twelve; in most cases, the person administering punishment was not the child’s parent.

On 3 September 2013, the Ansbach Family Court issued an interim order covering all children in the community, including the applicants’ children. It withdrew the parents’ rights to decide where the children should live, and to make decisions about their health, schooling and professional training, transferring those rights to the youth office. The court relied on the video footage and testimony from the reporter and six former community members. It found a reasonable likelihood that the children would be subjected to caning and so-called “restraining.” On 5 September 2013, the youth office took the children into care with police support; the premises were searched and a wooden rod was found. Medical examinations revealed no physical signs of abuse or beating.

The children were placed in foster care. The Tlapaks’ son J. was placed with a foster family, with daily visits by his mother because he was still breastfeeding. The Pingens’ daughters A. and B. were placed with their aunt’s family, while their son G., still breastfeeding, was placed with his mother in a foster family. Later, G. was returned to the parents after an appeal.

In the main proceedings, court-appointed experts found that the parents considered corporal punishment with objects an appropriate and necessary parenting method, based on religious convictions. The experts concluded there was a high probability that the children would be systematically caned and suffer psychological harm, and that less intrusive measures would not suffice because the parents were unwilling to abandon the practice or cooperate. The parents submitted a privately commissioned expert opinion criticizing the court expert’s methodology and retrospectively withdrew consent to examination; the courts nevertheless relied on the original expert report.

The Family Court in 2014 withdrew rights concerning residence, health and schooling for the Tlapak son and the Pingen children. The Nuremberg Court of Appeal largely upheld those decisions in 2015, emphasizing the likelihood of systematic caning, the irrelevance of lasting physical injury, the parents’ lack of credible change, and the insufficiency of milder measures. The Federal Constitutional Court refused the parents’ constitutional complaints in 2015.

The applicants principally alleged a violation of Article 8 ECHR, arguing that the domestic courts disproportionately withdrew parts of their parental authority, that the decisions lacked sufficient factual foundation, and that the main family proceedings were excessively long and unfair. They also invoked Article 6 regarding the same procedural complaints. Under Article 9 and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1, they alleged that they were prevented from raising their children according to their religious beliefs and that those beliefs were the reason for the partial withdrawal of parental authority. The applications were communicated to the German Government only in respect of Article 8.

**Summary of *Tlapak and Others v. Germany***

The case of *Tlapak and Others v. Germany* (Applications nos. 11308/16 and 11344/16) concerns two families who are members of the Twelve Tribes Church, a religious community in Germany that practices corporal punishment, specifically caning with a rod, as a form of child discipline. The applicants—parents in both cases—complained under Articles 8, 6, and 9 of the European Convention on Human Rights that German courts disproportionately withdrew parts of their parental authority, prevented them from raising their children according to their religious beliefs, and conducted unfair proceedings.

The background to the case began in 2012 when media reports emerged about the Twelve Tribes Church's endorsement of corporal punishment. In August 2013, a television reporter provided hidden-camera footage to authorities showing ten instances of children aged three to twelve being caned in the Klosterzimmern community. The footage indicated that the person administering punishment was often not the child's parent. Based on this evidence and testimony from former members, the Ansbach Family Court issued an interlocutory order on 3 September 2013 withdrawing the parents' rights to decide where their children would live, as well as decisions regarding health, schooling, and professional training. These rights were transferred to the youth office. On 5 September 2013, authorities took the children into care with police support.

The applicants' children were subsequently examined, but no physical signs of abuse were found. The children were placed in foster families, with accommodations made for breastfeeding infants.

In the main proceedings, court-appointed experts evaluated the families. The experts found that although the parents had a loving attitude toward their children, they considered corporal punishment with objects an appropriate and necessary parenting method based on religious convictions. The experts concluded there was a likelihood bordering on certainty that the parents would continue using corporal punishment, which would significantly jeopardize the children's development and cause psychological problems. The parents were deemed unwilling to abandon these methods or cooperate with authorities.

The Family Court, in decisions issued in October 2014, withdrew the parents' rights to decide where their children should live and to make decisions regarding health and schooling, transferring these rights to the youth office. The court found that the risk to the children could not be averted through less drastic measures because the parents had consistently advocated their parenting style and refused to accept that their methods violated German law prohibiting violence in upbringing. The court noted that corporal punishment's physical effects are short-lived, making detection through unannounced visits difficult, while psychological consequences are harder to discern.

The Court of Appeal upheld these decisions in 2015, emphasizing that systematic caning constituted child abuse and that the parents' religious beliefs made them neither willing nor able to avert the danger. The Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit the applicants' constitutional complaints.

**Summary:**

The case of *Ciobotaru and Others v. Romania* originated from four applications lodged against Romania with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applications were submitted on various dates and were communicated to the Romanian Government.

The central factual basis of the case concerns the conditions of the applicants' detention. The applicants alleged that they were held in inadequate conditions, specifically complaining of poor conditions within Romanian detention facilities. The specific details of each applicant's detention were provided in an appended table to the judgment, which the Court referenced as the factual foundation for its assessment. The Court found that the applicants were indeed kept in detention in poor conditions.

The applicants relied on Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. The Court assessed these complaints in light of its established case-law principles regarding inadequate conditions of detention, particularly referencing the case of *Muršić v. Croatia*. A key principle reiterated by the Court is that a "serious lack of space in a prison cell" is a significant factor that can establish "degrading" treatment under Article 3. Such a lack of space may constitute a violation on its own or when combined with other shortcomings, such as poor material conditions or inadequate access to facilities.

The Court noted that the issues raised were similar to those already examined in the leading case of *Rezmiveș and Others v. Romania*, where a violation of Article 3 had been found. In the present case, the Court examined all submitted material, including the Government's objection regarding the six-month rule in one specific application (no. 41700/15). Regarding this objection, the Court found no reason to depart from its established case-law concerning continuous situations of detention conditions.

Upon review, the Court concluded that it found no fact or argument that would lead to a different conclusion from its prior case-law. Consequently, it determined that the applicants' conditions of detention amounted to inadequate treatment in violation of Article 3 of the Convention. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 3 in respect of all applicants.

The judgment became final on 14 June 2018.

Because they raised the same type of complaint, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment.

The applicants’ common complaint concerned the allegedly inadequate conditions of their detention in Romania. They relied on Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. The full judgment does not reproduce each applicant’s individual facts; the list of applicants and the relevant details of each application are set out in an appended table. What is clear from the main text is that each applicant was held in detention in poor conditions and that the complaints related to the material circumstances of detention, rather than the lawfulness or length of detention as such. The Court treated the case as one involving inadequate detention conditions, especially a serious lack of space in prison cells.

In its legal analysis, the Court referred to established case-law on inadequate conditions of detention, particularly *Muršić v. Croatia* and *Ananyev and Others v. Russia*. It reiterated that a serious lack of space in a prison cell is a weighty factor when deciding whether detention conditions are “degrading” for Article 3 purposes. Such a lack of space may amount to a violation either by itself or when combined with other shortcomings, such as poor sanitation, lack of privacy, inadequate ventilation or limited access to outdoor exercise. The Court also noted that in *Rezmiveș and Others v. Romania*, a leading case, it had already found a violation of Article 3 in respect of similar issues concerning Romanian detention conditions.

The Romanian Government raised an objection regarding the application of the six-month rule in one of the cases, no. 41700/15, arguing that the applicant’s complaint concerned a continuous situation. The Court examined that objection together with all submitted material. It found no fact or argument that would lead it to a different conclusion on admissibility or merits from its earlier case-law. In particular, it considered that the applicants’ conditions of detention were inadequate.

Consequently, the facts disclosed a violation of Article 3 of the Convention. The key violation was therefore the State’s failure to ensure detention conditions compatible with human dignity and the prohibition on degrading treatment. The Court did not examine separate complaints under other Convention articles; its focus remained on the inadequate material conditions of detention, especially overcrowding or serious lack of personal space. The case forms part of the Court’s broader jurisprudence addressing systemic prison conditions in Romania and follows the approach established in *Rezmiveș and Others v. Romania*.
