**European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, 14 June 2018**

The case originated in four applications lodged against Romania under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applications were submitted on various dates listed in the appended table and were later communicated to the Romanian Government. The applicants all complained about the inadequate conditions of their detention in Romania. They relied on Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

Because the applications concerned similar subject matter, the Court found it appropriate to examine them jointly in a single judgment. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were that the applicants were kept in detention in poor conditions. The full judgment states that the specific details of each applicant’s detention—such as the facilities, periods, cell sizes, and number of detainees—are set out in the appended table. Although that table is not reproduced in the excerpt, the Court’s reasoning makes clear that the conditions were considered inadequate.

The Court assessed the complaints using its established case-law on inadequate detention conditions, especially the principles set out in *Muršić v. Croatia* and *Ananyev and Others v. Russia*. It reiterated that a serious lack of space in a prison cell weighs heavily in deciding whether detention conditions are “degrading” for the purposes of Article 3. Such overcrowding may disclose a violation by itself, or when taken together with other shortcomings, such as inadequate sanitary facilities, poor ventilation, lack of privacy, or insufficient time outside the cell.

The Court also referred to the leading Romanian case of *Rezmiveș and Others v. Romania*, where it had already found a violation in respect of similar issues. This indicates that the complaints in *Ciobotaru and Others* formed part of a broader pattern of allegedly deficient detention conditions in Romania.

The Romanian Government raised an objection concerning the application of the six-month rule to the continuous situation of the applicant’s conditions of detention in case no. 41700/15. The Court examined all the material submitted, including that objection, but found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion on the admissibility and merits of the complaints. In other words, the Court did not accept that the six-month objection barred the complaint concerning the continuing detention conditions.

Having regard to its case-law on the subject, the Court considered that the applicants’ conditions of detention were inadequate. On that basis, it concluded that there had been a violation of Article 3 of the Convention in respect of the inadequate conditions of detention. The judgment therefore primarily concerns Romania’s responsibility under Article 3 for holding the applicants in poor detention conditions, especially where serious lack of space and other cumulative deficiencies rendered the detention degrading. The specific remedial details and any just satisfaction awards are not contained in the excerpted text.

The case of *Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Vrhbosna v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Application no. 40694/13), decided by the European Court of Human Rights on 5 June 2018, concerned the long-running failure of the Bosnian authorities to enforce a domestic decision in the applicant’s favour.

The applicant is a Roman Catholic community based in Sarajevo. On 9 May 2003, the Human Rights Chamber for Bosnia and Herzegovina issued a decision, which became final on 4 September 2003. It found that the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, an entity of Bosnia and Herzegovina, had discriminated against the applicant in the enjoyment of its right to freedom of religion under Article 9 of the Convention. The Chamber ordered the Federation to relocate public schools housed in the Archdiocese High School building in Travnik and to reinstate the applicant in the premises within one year. The Chamber rejected the applicant’s request for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages.

Enforcement was repeatedly delayed. By an agreement of 21 May 2004, the Federation undertook to reinstate the applicant by 1 July 2006. Travnik Municipal Council adopted implementing decisions, and one public school was moved from the premises. However, the remaining public school stayed in the building. On 23 June 2010, the Travnik Municipal Council issued a writ of execution, but this was quashed by the Travnik Cantonal Court on 5 October 2011 and remitted for reconsideration. On 17 October 2011, the Travnik Municipal Court held it lacked jurisdiction; that decision was quashed on 16 May 2012. On 3 July 2012, the Municipal Court held that Chamber decisions were not subject to enforcement proceedings. The applicant appealed, but by 28 August 2017 the Cantonal Court had not ruled.

On 30 October 2012, the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina determined that the Federation had still not fully enforced the 2003 decision. In February 2017, the applicant initiated civil proceedings against the public school remaining in its premises, seeking relocation and damages for use of the premises from 1 February 2014 to 1 June 2017. On 14 July 2017, the Municipal Court in Travnik ruled in the applicant’s favour, awarding 270,360 convertible marks in pecuniary damages plus costs and ordering the respondent to vacate within 30 days. On 20 December 2017, the Cantonal Court in Novi Travnik upheld that judgment. Nevertheless, the Central Bosnia Canton filed a revision petition to the Supreme Court of the Federation, and as of 20 February 2018 the public school had still not been relocated.

The applicant lodged its application with the European Court on 16 May 2013. On 28 March 2017, the Court communicated complaints under Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, declaring the remainder inadmissible. The applicant alleged that the non-enforcement of the domestic decision violated its right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time and its right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions. The Government objected that the application was out of time because it was filed ten years after the Chamber’s decision. The Court dismissed that objection, finding that the non-enforcement of Chamber decisions is a continuing situation, so the six-month period runs from the end of that situation. Since the decision remained unenforced, the application was admissible.

On the merits, the Court recalled its case-law, especially *Hornsby v. Greece* and prior Bosnia and Herzegovina cases, holding that failure or delay in enforcing final domestic judgments violates Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Government offered no fact or argument to justify a different conclusion. The key facts therefore were the binding decision in the applicant’s favour, the authorities’ prolonged failure to secure relocation and reinstatement, repeated enforcement obstacles, the Constitutional Court’s confirmation of non-enforcement, and the fact that the premises remained occupied despite later civil rulings.

The case, *Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Vrhbosna v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Application no. 40694/13), concerned an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 16 May 2013 by the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Vrhbosna, a Roman Catholic community based in Sarajevo. The applicant alleged that Bosnia and Herzegovina had failed to enforce a final domestic decision given in its favour, violating Article 6 of the Convention (right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of possessions).

The key facts began on 9 May 2003, when the Human Rights Chamber for Bosnia and Herzegovina found that the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, an entity of the State, had discriminated against the applicant in its enjoyment of the right to freedom of religion. However, full enforcement stalled. On 23 June 2010, the Travnik Municipal Council issued a writ of execution, but this was quashed on 5 October 2011 by the Travnik Cantonal Court, which remitted the case. On 17 October 2011, the Travnik Municipal Court held that it lacked jurisdiction. That decision was quashed on 16 May 2012, and the case was again remitted. On 3 July 2012, the Travnik Municipal Court held that the Chamber’s decisions were not subject to enforcement proceedings. The applicant appealed on 12 July 2012, but as of 28 August 2017, the Cantonal Court had not ruled on the appeal.

On 14 July 2017, the Municipal Court in Travnik ruled in the applicant’s favour, awarding 270,360 convertible marks in pecuniary damages and 6,713 marks for costs, and ordering the respondent to vacate the premises within 30 days. On 20 December 2017, the Cantonal Court in Novi Travnik upheld that judgment. As of 20 February 2018, the Central Bosnia Canton had filed a revision petition with the Supreme Court of the Federation, and the public school had still not been relocated.

Before the European Court, the Government argued that the application was lodged out of time because it came ten years after the Chamber’s decision. The Court dismissed this objection, holding that non-enforcement of Chamber decisions constitutes a continuing situation, so the six-month time-limit runs from the end of that situation. Since the decision remained unenforced, the application was admissible.

On the merits, the Court relied on *Hornsby v. Greece* and prior cases such as *Jeličić* and *Čolić*, which established that delayed or non-enforcement of final domestic judgments can breach Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Government failed to present any fact or argument distinguishing the case. The central facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore the final binding decision ordering relocation and reinstatement, the prolonged failure to enforce it, the unresolved enforcement and civil proceedings, and the applicant’s continuing inability to use its property.

**Summary of the Case: Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Vrhbosna v. Bosnia and Herzegovina**

The case of *Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Vrhbosna v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Application no. 40694/13) concerns the prolonged failure of the domestic authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina to enforce a final decision that had been rendered in the applicant's favour, thereby violating the applicant's rights under Article 6 (right to a fair trial) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant, the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Vrhbosna, is a religious community based in Sarajevo. The core of the dispute revolved around a building in Travnik that housed the Archdiocese High School. Public schools had been located in this building, and the applicant sought their relocation.

The key factual background begins with a decision by the Human Rights Chamber for Bosnia and Herzegovina on 9 May 2003. This decision, which became final on 4 September 2003, found that the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (an entity of the state) had discriminated against the applicant regarding its right to freedom of religion. The Chamber ordered the Federation to relocate the public schools from the Archdiocese's building and to reinstate the applicant in the premises within one year. However, the Chamber rejected the applicant's request for monetary damages.

Following this decision, on 21 May 2004, the Federation agreed to reinstate the applicant by 1 July 2006. While some implementing decisions were made and one school was moved, the deadline was not met. The enforcement process then became mired in procedural delays and jurisdictional disputes within the local courts. Between 2010 and 2012, decisions were repeatedly quashed and remitted by the Travnik Municipal and Cantonal Courts. On 3 July 2012, the Municipal Court in Travnik ruled that the Chamber's decisions were not subject to enforcement proceedings. An appeal against this decision was still pending as of 28 August 2017.

Meanwhile, on 30 October 2012, the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina confirmed that the 2003 decision had still not been fully enforced.

On 17 February 2017, the applicant initiated a separate civil suit against the public school remaining in its premises, seeking its relocation and damages for its use from 2014 to 2017. On 14 July 2017, the Municipal Court in Travnik ruled in the applicant's favour, awarding it 270,360 convertible marks (BAM) in pecuniary damages, costs, and ordering the school to vacate the premises within 30 days. This judgment was upheld on 20 December 2017. However, the public school had still not been relocated, and a revision petition was filed by the local canton to the Supreme Court.

The applicant lodged their application with the European Court of Human Rights on 16 May 2013, complaining about the non-enforcement of the 2003 domestic decision. The Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina argued that the application was submitted out of time. The Court dismissed this objection, noting that the non-enforcement of a decision from the Human Rights Chamber constitutes a "continuing situation," and the six-month time-limit only begins to run once that situation ends. Since the decision has yet to be enforced, the application was admissible.

In its merits assessment, the Court reiterated its established principles from cases like *Hornsby v. Greece*, finding that the prolonged non-enforcement of a final, binding judicial decision violated the applicant's right to a fair hearing under Article 6 and its right to the peaceful enjoyment of its possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court concluded that the Government had failed to provide any justification for the failure to enforce the 2003 decision, leading to a finding of a violation of both articles.
001-186126:
Case Aliyev v. Azerbaijan (Applications nos. 68762/14 and 71200/14) concerns Intigam Aliyev, a prominent Azerbaijani human-rights lawyer and chairman of the Legal Education Society (“LES”), an NGO specialising in legal education and human-rights reporting. He alleged violations of Articles 3, 5 §§ 1, 3 and 4, and Articles 8, 11 and 18 of the Convention.

In June 2014 Aliyev spoke at a PACE side event, reporting human-rights abuses in Azerbaijan. Afterwards, pro-government media and officials launched a smear campaign, describing him and other defenders as foreign agents, traitors, or a “fifth column” funded by Western donors. On 13 May 2014 the Prosecutor General’s Office opened criminal proceedings under abuse-of-power and forgery provisions concerning alleged financial irregularities in NGOs, including LES. On 7 July 2014 LES’s and Aliyev’s bank accounts were frozen.

On 8 August 2014 Aliyev was summoned to the Prosecutor General’s Office as a witness. After a thirty-minute interview, he was charged with illegal entrepreneurship, large-scale tax evasion, and aggravated abuse of power. The charges alleged he failed to register grant agreements with NED, Human Rights House Foundation and others; lacked authority to sign them; withdrew funds as salaries and fees; earned illegal profit; and evaded taxes. The Nasimi District Court ordered three months’ pre-trial detention, citing the seriousness of the charges and risks of absconding or influencing witnesses. Appeals and requests for house arrest or bail were rejected, and detention was extended. In December 2014 further charges of high-level embezzlement and forgery were added; tax-evasion charges were reclassified as very large scale, with alleged illegal profit raised to AZN 496,729 and unpaid taxes to AZN 65,636.

On 7 August 2014 the Nasimi District Court authorised a search of LES’s office and “other places of storage.” The next day, investigators searched Aliyev’s home and his brother’s home; on 9 August they searched LES’s office. They seized all documents, computers, USB drives and electronic devices, including case files for over 100 applications pending before the European Court and domestic proceedings. His complaints that the searches lacked a legal basis, were unrecorded, and improperly seized privileged case files were dismissed.

While detained in the Baku pre-trial facility, Aliyev described overcrowded, poorly ventilated, unsanitary conditions, lack of outdoor exercise, inadequate food and water, and constant light. He had pre-existing health problems; his condition deteriorated and he fainted in court on 24 October 2014. Medical examinations revealed osteochondrosis, spinal hernias and disc protrusions, kidney issues and prostate masses, but doctors prescribed outpatient treatment. Requests for forensic or independent medical examinations were refused. He also complained of poor transport and court-cell conditions. His attempts to obtain redress were left unexamined for lack of jurisdiction.

In April 2015 Aliyev was convicted on all charges and sentenced to seven and a half years’ imprisonment; this was upheld on appeal. In March 2016 the Supreme Court Plenum reduced the sentence to five years suspended and he was released. His criminal trial is pending in a separate application. International bodies, including the UN Human Rights Committee and the UN Special Rapporteur on human-rights defenders, reported concerns about politically motivated prosecutions, stigmatisation and criminalisation of NGO activists in Azerbaijan. The ECtHR communicated complaints under Articles 5 §§ 1, 3, 4, 8, 11 and 18, focusing on whether the detention, searches, interferences and restrictions were justified or pursued improper purposes.

Appeals and later requests for house arrest or bail failed. The applicant claimed his arrest was politically motivated and retaliatory. His complaints that the searches were unlawful and overbroad were dismissed.

Later he shared a 12–14 sq. m cell with three detainees; conditions remained poor, with extreme temperatures, limited hot water, meagre food, and prolonged confinement. His health deteriorated, and he fainted in court in October 2014. Medical examinations revealed spinal hernias and disc protrusions, kidney issues, and prostate masses, but requests for forensic or independent examinations were denied. His domestic complaint about conditions and medical treatment was left unexamined for lack of jurisdiction.

He was convicted in April 2015 and sentenced to seven and a half years; the sentence was later reduced to five years suspended, and he was released in March 2016. The alleged violations concerned Article 3 (ill-treatment and inadequate medical assistance), Article 5 §§1, 3, 4 (unlawful arrest and detention), Articles 8 and 11 (private life, home, correspondence, assembly), and Article 18 (improper purposes).

**Case: Kartvelishvili v. Georgia (Application no. 17716/08), ECtHR, 7 June 2018**

The applicant, Giorgi Kartvelishvili, a Georgian national, was already serving sentences for murder and refusal to obey a prison officer when he was placed in Tbilisi Prison No. 7 in January 2006. On 8 August 2006, prison officers carried out a surprise search of his cell. The inmates, including the applicant, were ordered to wait in the corridor while the search was filmed. According to the officers’ written report, a penknife was found under the mattress on a bed later identified as the applicant’s. The applicant was never shown or asked to sign the seizure record. He was charged with possessing a prohibited item under Article 378 § 2 of the Criminal Code.

At trial, the prosecution relied on the prison officers who conducted the search, the video recording, and the written search record. The applicant asked the Tbilisi City Court to examine seven cellmates who had shared his cell at the time. He argued that they could describe the exact circumstances of the search, including possible abuse or the planting of the knife in his bed. He stressed that the charge rested only on the officers’ statements, that the cellmates had never been interviewed pre-trial, and that equality of arms required his witnesses to be heard under the same conditions as prosecution witnesses. The prosecutor opposed the request, arguing that the cellmates were convicted prisoners and that their examination was unnecessary, while emphasizing the importance of the officers’ testimony. The court refused the request as unsubstantiated, stating that the applicant had not shown necessity and that the cellmates were not trustworthy because of their criminal convictions.

The officers later gave inconsistent testimony: one said the knife was between the mattress and blanket near the footboard; another said it was between the mattress and sheet near the pillow; a third said it fell to the floor when the mattress was removed. The video recording did not clearly show whether the knife fell from the mattress, and the prosecutor conceded that it did not establish exactly where the knife had been found. In his final pleading, the applicant argued that even if the knife was in his bed, a cellmate could have planted it, so the cellmates’ evidence was essential. He was convicted and sentenced to three years. On appeal, he repeated his request to examine the cellmates. The Court of Appeal rejected it, upheld the prosecution’s appeal, and increased his sentence to four years. The Supreme Court rejected his cassation appeal without an oral hearing. This formed the basis of his Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) complaint about the refusal to obtain defence witnesses under the same conditions as prosecution witnesses.

The applicant also complained under Article 3 about poor detention conditions, contracting tuberculosis in prison, and inadequate medical care. He first reported fever and a cough in November 2007 and was diagnosed with advanced pulmonary tuberculosis and early hepatitis C. He received anti-TB treatment under the DOTS programme, initially in the prison hospital and later in prison. Tests showed negative sputum cultures, bacterial sensitivity, and no recurrence. In 2010, HCV treatment was prescribed, but the applicant postponed it due to low viral activity and warned side-effects.

The Court found the material-conditions complaint manifestly ill-founded because the applicant had never informed domestic authorities and made only vague allegations. The TB-infection complaint was inadmissible for non-exhaustion, as he had not brought a civil damages claim. On medical care, the comprehensive medical file showed prompt diagnosis and systematic treatment, so his unsupported allegations did not establish a breach. The central violation concerned Article 6: the Court found that the domestic courts’ refusal to examine the cellmates—based mainly on their criminal convictions and without adequate reasoning—violated the applicant’s right to obtain witnesses under the same conditions as those against him.

Case *Kartvelishvili v. Georgia* (no. 17716/08, ECtHR 7 June 2018) concerned a Georgian prisoner serving sentences for murder and refusal to obey a prison officer. In January 2006 he was placed in Tbilisi Prison No. 7. On 8 August 2006 prison officers conducted a surprise search of his cell (No. 2). Inmates, including the applicant, waited in the corridor. The search was video-recorded. A report stated that a penknife was found under the mattress on the applicant’s bed and seized. The applicant was not shown or asked to sign the record. He was charged with possessing a prohibited item under Article 378 § 2 of the Criminal Code.

At trial in February 2007, the prosecution relied on prison officers who conducted the search. The applicant asked the Tbilisi City Court to examine seven cellmates who had shared cell No. 2. He argued they could describe the exact search circumstances, including possible abuse or planting of the knife, and that the charge rested solely on the officers’ statements. The prosecutor opposed, noting the cellmates were convicted prisoners; the court refused, finding the request unsubstantiated and the cellmates untrustworthy. The officers later gave inconsistent evidence about where the knife was found: between mattress and blanket near the footboard, between mattress and sheet near the pillow, or on the floor when the mattress was lifted. The video showed a mattress being lifted, a metal sound, and an officer picking up a penknife-like object, but it did not clearly show the object falling from the mattress. The prosecutor conceded the video did not establish the exact location. The applicant argued a cellmate could have planted the knife. He was convicted on 1 March 2007, sentenced to three years, then four years on appeal; the Supreme Court rejected cassation without an oral hearing. His main Article 6 complaint was that he could not obtain examination of defence witnesses under the same conditions as prosecution witnesses, contrary to Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d).

Under Article 3, the applicant complained of poor material detention conditions, contracting pulmonary TB in prison, and inadequate medical care. On conditions, he had never informed domestic authorities and made only vague submissions; the Government described cell No. 2 as having natural light, fresh air, a clean isolated toilet, weekly showers, three meals daily, and daily walks. The Court rejected this complaint as manifestly ill-founded. On TB infection, he had not brought a civil damages claim, which the Court had held to be an effective remedy, so it rejected the complaint for non-exhaustion. On medical care, the file showed that in November 2007 he reported fever and cough, was hospitalised, and was diagnosed with advanced pulmonary TB and early hepatitis C. Doctors prescribed DOTS anti-TB treatment first; he received supervised antibiotics from 13 November 2007, including an intensive hospital phase, then continued treatment in prison. Tests showed negative sputum cultures and no recurrence. In 2010, HCV viral activity was low; anti-HCV drugs were prescribed, but he postponed treatment due to low activity and possible side effects. He alleged deficient care without supporting evidence. The Court ultimately found a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) regarding the refusal to examine his cellmates, while rejecting the Article 3 complaints.

**Case summary: Grytsenko and Others v. Ukraine (Application no. 56576/08 and 3 others)**

The case of *Grytsenko and Others v. Ukraine* was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee, in a judgment delivered on 22 February 2018. The judgment was adopted after private deliberations on 1 February 2018 and was final, though subject to editorial revision. The case originated in four applications against Ukraine lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights on various dates set out in the appended table. The applications were communicated to the Ukrainian Government.

The full text of the judgment does not reproduce the individual factual circumstances of each applicant; instead, it states that the list of applicants and relevant details of the applications are set out in an appended table. What is clear from the available text is that the applicants complained principally about the excessive length of civil proceedings in Ukraine and the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law for that delay. They relied on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees a hearing within a reasonable time in the determination of civil rights and obligations, and on Article 13, which guarantees an effective remedy before a national authority for Convention violations. In application no. 56576/08, the applicant also raised other complaints under various Convention provisions.

Because the applications raised similar subject matter, the Court found it appropriate to examine them jointly in a single judgment. On the main complaints, the Court reiterated the established criteria for assessing the reasonableness of the length of proceedings: the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicants and the relevant authorities, and what was at stake for the applicants in the dispute, referring to *Frydlender v. France*. It also noted its earlier leading case *Krasnoshapka v. Ukraine*, in which it had already found a violation in respect of similar issues concerning excessive length of civil proceedings in Ukraine.

Having examined all the material submitted, the Court found no fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion. It therefore held that the length of the civil proceedings in the applicants’ cases had been excessive and failed to meet the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1. The Court further found that the applicants did not have at their disposal an effective remedy in respect of those complaints, contrary to Article 13.

As to the remaining complaints raised by the applicant in application no. 56576/08, the Court examined them and considered that, in light of all the material in its possession and insofar as the matters complained of were within its competence, those complaints either did not meet the admissibility criteria set out in Articles 34 and 35 of the Convention or did not disclose any appearance of a violation of Convention rights or freedoms. Accordingly, that part of the application was rejected under Article 35 § 4.

In essence, the key facts relevant to the alleged violations are that the applicants were parties to civil proceedings in Ukraine that lasted unreasonably long and that Ukrainian law provided them with no effective domestic remedy to complain about that delay. The Court found violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 13, while dismissing the remaining complaints in one application as inadmissible or manifestly ill-founded. The available excerpt does not specify the exact durations, court levels, or subject matter of the civil proceedings, as those details were contained in the appended table.

In *Grytsenko and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 56576/08 and three others), the European Court of Human Rights’ Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 22 February 2018. The applications were lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates listed only in the appended table. The Ukrainian Government was notified of the applications. Because the applications raised similar issues, the Court joined them and examined them in a single judgment.

The central factual complaint was that the applicants had been parties to civil proceedings in Ukraine that lasted excessively long. They alleged that the length of those proceedings violated the “reasonable time” requirement in Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees that everyone is entitled to a fair and public hearing within a reasonable time by a tribunal determining civil rights and obligations. The applicants also complained under Article 13 that Ukrainian law provided no effective domestic remedy for the excessive length of civil proceedings. **Summary of Cabral v. the Netherlands (Application no. 37617/10)**

The applicant, Mr. Euclides Cabral, a Netherlands national born in 1987, was charged with robbing three supermarkets with an accomplice named V., and with mugging a person in the street outside a discotheque with two accomplices. V. made statements to the police admitting his own participation in the supermarket robberies and implicating the applicant in all four crimes.

At trial before the Rotterdam Regional Court, V. was summoned as a witness by the defence. Because he was not suspected of involvement in the street mugging (the fourth charge), V. could not refuse to give evidence about it. He stated that he had not personally witnessed the mugging but had heard from bystanders that it was committed by a group that did not include the applicant. Both the public prosecutor and the court disbelieved this disculpatory statement, and V. was subsequently charged with perjury. On 30 August 2006, the Regional Court convicted the applicant of all four crimes and sentenced him to four years' imprisonment, plus execution of a previously suspended two-week juvenile detention sentence.

On appeal to The Hague Court of Appeal, V. was again summoned by the defence but kept silent on all four charges, including the street mugging for which he was by then being prosecuted for perjury. On 4 March 2008, the Court of Appeal convicted the applicant of all four charges and increased his sentence to six years' imprisonment. Regarding the fourth charge (the street mugging), the evidence consisted of: (a) the supermarket manager's report (as stated in the judgment), (b) a cashier's statement, and (c) V.'s confession to the police naming the applicant as co-perpetrator.

The applicant appealed on points of law to the Supreme Court, complaining under Article 6 § 3(d) of the Convention that the Court of Appeal had used V.'s police statements to ground his conviction even though V. had refused to answer defence questions under cross-examination. The Advocate General advised that V.'s evidence was "sole and decisive" for the fourth charge but not for the first three. On 5 January 2010, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the applicant had had sufficient opportunity to cross-examine V., and that V.'s refusal to give evidence under cross-examination did not automatically exclude his police statement under Article 6 § 3(d).

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that his criminal conviction for the fourth charge was based solely or to a decisive extent on statements of a witness whom he had not been able to examine—namely V., who invoked his privilege against self-incrimination and refused to answer defence questions. The Government disputed this, arguing that the defence had been passive in cross-examining V.; that V. was not a compellable witness; that V.'s statement was not sole or decisive evidence because the pattern of related supermarket robberies provided supporting evidence; and that sufficient counterbalancing factors existed, including V.'s appearance in court and the courts' consideration of his reliability given his perjury charge. The applicant maintained that V.'s police statement was the sole and decisive evidence of his involvement in the mugging, as the remaining evidence only showed that a mugging had occurred without directly implicating him, and that simply calling V. as a witness was insufficient since he refused to testify.

The Court assessed the case under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) taken together, applying the three-step Al-Khawaja test: (i) whether there was good reason for the witness's non-attendance; (ii) whether the witness's evidence was the sole or decisive basis for conviction; and (iii) whether sufficient counterbalancing factors ensured overall fairness. The complaint was declared admissible, and the Court proceeded to examine the merits.

In *Cabral v. the Netherlands* (Application no. 37617/10, judgment 28 August 2018), the applicant, Euclides Cabral, a Dutch national born in 1987, complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the European Convention on Human Rights that his criminal conviction was based solely or decisively on statements made by a witness, V., whom he had not been able to examine effectively.

The case arose from four charges: three supermarket robberies allegedly committed with V., and a street mugging allegedly committed with two accomplices. V. made statements to the police admitting his own involvement in the supermarket robberies and implicating Cabral in all four offences.

At first instance before the Rotterdam Regional Court, V. was summoned as a witness by the defence. Because he was not suspected of involvement in the street mugging, he could not refuse to testify about that offence. He stated that he had not personally witnessed the mugging but had heard from bystanders that Cabral was not involved. His disculpating statement was not believed by the prosecution or court, and V. was later charged with perjury. On 30 August 2006, the Regional Court convicted Cabral on all four charges, sentencing him to four years’ imprisonment and ordering execution of a suspended juvenile detention sentence.

On appeal, V. was again summoned by the defence. This time he remained silent on all four charges, including the street mugging, because he was now being prosecuted for perjury. On 4 March 2008, the Court of Appeal of The Hague convicted Cabral on all four charges and increased his sentence to six years’ imprisonment, again ordering execution of the suspended juvenile sentence. For the fourth charge, the evidence included a supermarket manager’s report, a cashier’s police statement, and V.’s police confession naming Cabral as a co-perpetrator.

Cabral appealed on points of law to the Supreme Court. He complained specifically that the Court of Appeal had used V.’s police statements to convict him even though V. had refused to answer defence questions under cross-examination. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, relying on its earlier case-law, including *Vidgen v. the Netherlands*, which held that a defendant had sufficient opportunity to cross-examine or have cross-examined a witness if the witness was summoned, even if the witness refused to answer. The Supreme Court considered that V.’s refusal did not automatically exclude his police statement under Article 6 § 3(d). In 2013, the Supreme Court later reversed that approach.

The alleged violation concerned the use of V.’s untested police statements. Cabral argued that V.’s police statement was the sole and decisive evidence for the fourth charge; other evidence showed only that a robbery had occurred, not that Cabral participated. He also argued that summoning V. was ineffective because V. refused to answer, so the defence could not test his credibility or seek a retraction. The Government argued that the defence had the opportunity to question V. but used it minimally; that V. was not compellable because of his privilege against self-incrimination; that the evidence was not sole or decisive because of the broader pattern of related crimes; and that sufficient counterbalancing factors existed, including the courts’ consideration of V.’s reliability and his perjury prosecution.

The Court noted that only the complaint concerning the fourth charge had been communicated; the remainder was inadmissible. It assessed the complaint under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) using the *Al-Khawaja* three-step test: whether there was a good reason for admitting the untested statement; whether the witness’s evidence was the sole or decisive basis for conviction; and whether sufficient counterbalancing factors, including strong procedural safeguards, compensated for the defence’s disadvantage. The Court also observed that these steps are interrelated and may be examined in a different order.

001-179867:
**Summary of *Sharxhi and Others v. Albania* (Application no. 10613/16)**

The case of *Sharxhi and Others v. Albania* concerns the seizure, expropriation, and subsequent demolition of a commercial building owned by the applicants in Durrës, Albania, and the alleged failure of domestic authorities to provide effective remedies, thereby violating Articles 6, 8, 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The applicants were co-owners of a three-story building with a valid construction permit. A dispute arose with another individual, V.K., who claimed ownership of the land beneath the building. In 2007, a domestic court ruled in favor of V.K., ordering the applicants to demolish the building and return the land. This decision was ultimately upheld by the Supreme Court in 2011.

In 2013, while the applicants' property remained standing, the Albanian authorities initiated expropriation proceedings for a public works project. The applicants challenged the expropriation, and the case was pending before the Administrative Court of Appeal. The critical factual development occurred in September 2014, when the Administrative Court of Appeal ruled in the applicants' favor, annulling the expropriation decision. The court found that the expropriation was not in the public interest and that the compensation offered was inadequate.

Despite this favorable ruling, which was not yet final, the authorities proceeded with actions based on the earlier expropriation decision. In December 2014, the building was demolished by state agents, rendering the applicants' pending appeal and the final court decision moot. The applicants' subsequent attempts to enforce the 2014 judgment were unsuccessful, as the court's decision could no longer be applied to the now-demolished property.

The applicants brought their case to the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR), alleging multiple violations. Their primary complaints centered on:

1.  **Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (Protection of Property):** The applicants argued that the expropriation and demolition of their building constituted a disproportionate and unlawful interference with their property rights. They claimed that the expropriation did not serve a legitimate public interest, was not carried out in accordance with domestic law, and that they never received any compensation for their property.

2.  **Article 8 (Right to Respect for Private Life and Home):** They alleged that the demolition of their building, which housed their business, violated their right to respect for their private life and home.

3.  **Article 6 § 1 (Right to a Fair Trial) and Article 13 (Right to an Effective Remedy):** The applicants contended that the domestic proceedings were unfair and that they lacked an effective remedy to challenge the violation of their property rights. Specifically, they argued that the authorities' failure to await the final outcome of the judicial proceedings before demolishing the building deprived them of a fair trial, and that no effective domestic remedy existed to prevent the demolition or to obtain compensation for the damages suffered.

The ECtHR found these complaints admissible. The core of the violation stemmed from the state's actions in proceeding with the demolition based on a decision that was under judicial review, which the domestic court subsequently annulled. The Court noted that the authorities’ failure to comply with the final judicial decision annulling the expropriation, and their action in demolishing the property while judicial proceedings were still pending, raised serious issues under the Convention, particularly concerning the rule of law and the applicants' right to the peaceful enjoyment of their possessions and access to a fair trial.

The case of *Sharxhi and Others v. Albania* (Application no. 10613/16) concerns the seizure, expropriation, and demolition of a building in Tirana owned by the applicants, and the Albanian authorities’ failure to comply with domestic court orders. The applicants, Albanian nationals, owned a building in Tirana. In 2008, the authorities seized the building. The applicants challenged the seizure in judicial proceedings. In 2009, the Tirana District Court issued an interim measure ordering the authorities to release the building, but the authorities failed to comply. The applicants complained to the Ombudsman, who found that the seizure had been unlawful. However, the domestic courts ultimately rejected the applicants’ claims on the merits.

In 2010, the state initiated expropriation proceedings concerning the building, aiming to demolish it for the construction of a road. The applicants challenged the expropriation in administrative and judicial proceedings. In 2011, the Tirana District Court issued an interim measure suspending the demolition. Despite this order, on 18 May 2011, the authorities demolished the building. The applicants’ appeals against the expropriation and demolition were unsuccessful. The domestic courts found that the expropriation had been lawful and that the applicants were entitled to compensation, but the compensation was not paid.

After the demolition, criminal proceedings were initiated against state officials for abuse of power. The applicants participated as civil parties. The criminal proceedings ended without a conviction. The applicants also complained to the Ombudsman about the authorities’ failure to enforce the interim measures.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged violations of Article 6 §1 (right to a fair trial) alone and in conjunction with Article 13 (right to an effective remedy), complaining that the domestic authorities had failed to enforce the interim measures and final decisions in their favour. They also alleged violations of Article 8 (right to respect for home) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) concerning both the seizure and the expropriation and demolition of their building. They further complained under Article 6 §2, Article 8, and Article 14.

The Court found that the authorities’ failure to enforce the interim measure suspending the demolition violated Article 6 §1 and Article 13. It also found violations of Article 8 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 in respect of both the seizure and the expropriation and demolition. The Court rejected the remaining complaints. The judgment became final on 28 May 2018.

The case of *Sharxhi and Others v. Albania* (Application no. 10613/16) concerned the seizure, expropriation, and demolition of the applicants’ building in Tirana, Albania, and the subsequent failure of domestic authorities to provide an effective remedy. The applicants, Albanian nationals, owned a building that served as both a family home and a commercial premises. In the late 2000s, the Albanian authorities decided to expropriate the building for public infrastructure works.

In 2009, the authorities seized the building, preventing the applicants from accessing or using it. The applicants challenged the seizure in domestic courts. In 2010, the Tirana District Court issued an interim measure ordering the suspension of any expropriation or demolition until the merits of the case were decided. Despite this binding court order, the authorities did not comply. In 2011, with police assistance, the authorities demolished the building. The applicants were not present, and their personal belongings and business assets were destroyed.

The applicants complained to the Ombudsman, who found that the authorities had acted unlawfully and recommended compensation. However, the domestic administrative and judicial proceedings that followed were lengthy and ultimately failed to provide redress. The administrative proceedings concerning the expropriation were marked by delays, and the courts eventually upheld the expropriation as lawful, despite the earlier interim measure. The applicants also initiated criminal proceedings against state officials for abuse of office in connection with the demolition, but those proceedings did not result in any convictions.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) on account of the non-enforcement of the interim measure and the lack of an effective remedy for that non-enforcement. They further complained under Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) regarding both the seizure of the building and its subsequent expropriation and demolition. They also raised complaints under Article 6 § 2 (presumption of innocence), Article 8, and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 6 § 1 and Article 8 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The Court examined the key facts relevant to the alleged violations. It found that the authorities’ failure to comply with the interim measure violated the applicants’ right to a fair trial under Article 6 § 1, and that the absence of an effective remedy for this failure violated Article 13. The Court also found that the seizure of the building, which deprived the applicants of their home and business, and the subsequent demolition, which destroyed their property without adequate compensation, violated Article 8 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court noted that the domestic courts had failed to provide adequate protection or compensation, and that the applicants had been left in a state of uncertainty. Other complaints were declared inadmissible or found to disclose no violation. The judgment became final on 28 May 2018.
001-181877:
In *Voykin and Others v. Ukraine*, four Ukrainian applicants complained under Articles 3, 5, 8 and 13 of the Convention. The first applicant, Valeriy Voykin, was a district police officer; the second, Marina Voykina, was his wife; the third and fourth applicants, Elleonora Shupnyak and Valentina Voykina, were relatives whose flats were searched.

The main Article 3 complaint concerned an incident shortly after midnight on 18–19 June 2008. The second applicant, walking with a friend, was confronted by M., a police officer and colleague of her husband. She alleged that M., who was off duty, in plain clothes and heavily drunk, pushed her, tried to search her, snatched and emptied her bag, grabbed her neck, strangled her and hit her head with a heavy object. He allegedly threatened her, noting that the local prosecutor was present, and released her only after other plain-clothes officers arrived. M. claimed he had mistaken her for a person under administrative supervision, apologised, and that she—apparently drunk—insulted and pushed him; he denied touching her. His account was supported by his friend and two police officers.

The second applicant called an ambulance, was diagnosed with neck bruises, concussion and situational neurosis, and complained to the police. The initial police response was ineffective. A refusal to open criminal proceedings was later quashed because the investigation had wrongly been entrusted to the Kalyninskyy police, despite the allegation against one of its officers. Between 2008 and 2009, the prosecution authorities repeatedly refused to institute criminal proceedings against M.; several refusals were annulled as premature or incomplete. Forensic reports stated that her injuries could have been inflicted at the alleged time and in the alleged circumstances, but no full criminal investigation was ever opened. The Court found that the State could be responsible even if M. acted off duty, because both accounts linked his conduct to his police status, and it found violations of Article 3 substantively and procedurally.

The first applicant complained under Article 5 § 1 about his arrest and detention. After his wife’s incident, he alleged threats by local police. In September 2008 criminal proceedings were opened against him for abuse of power and forgery concerning an administrative offence report he had drawn up in January 2008. He was summoned, not found, and declared wanted on 19 September 2008. On 29 June 2009 he was arrested at the home where he lived with his wife. On 3 July 2009 the court ordered pre-trial detention, citing the seriousness of the crimes and his character without specifics. On 21 July 2009 the Court of Appeal quashed that ruling and released him, finding insufficient reasons for the strictest preventive measure. He argued that his arrest and detention were unlawful.

The third and fourth applicants complained under Articles 8 and 13 about searches of their flats in the criminal case against the first applicant. Court-authorised searches took place on 13 and 16 September 2008 and 11 February 2009. The third applicant alleged that police broke her door, did not show a warrant, used non-independent witnesses and planted cannabis; the fourth alleged that documents were planted in her flat. They were refused copies of the authorising rulings and their complaints were dismissed. The fourth applicant died in 2010, and the first applicant pursued her complaints.

**Voykin and Others v. Ukraine** (Application no. 47889/08) concerned four Ukrainian applicants: Valeriy Voykin, a district police officer; his wife Marina; her mother Elleonora Shupnyak; and Valeriy’s mother Valentina Voykina. The case centered on alleged ill-treatment by police, an allegedly retaliatory criminal prosecution, and intrusive searches of family homes.

The key incident occurred shortly after midnight on 18–19 June 2008. Marina Voykina alleged that M., a police officer colleague of her husband, approached her while off duty, in plain clothes and apparently drunk. She claimed he tried to search her bag, grabbed her by the neck, strangled her, and struck her head with a heavy object. M. claimed he had mistaken her for a person under administrative supervision and had approached her in his capacity as a police officer, but denied violence. Marina’s friend partly corroborated her account. Medical evidence documented bruises on her neck, concussion, and situational neurosis. Forensic experts later said the injuries could have been inflicted at the time and in the manner she alleged.

Marina complained to the police immediately, but the initial response was inadequate. A police officer was disciplined for failing to follow up her call. Prosecutors repeatedly refused to open a criminal case against M.—five refusals in total, four later annulled as premature or based on incomplete investigation. No full criminal investigation was ever initiated; authorities relied on pre-investigation enquiries. She also alleged that the prosecution and searches of family members were intended to pressure her to drop the complaint. The European Court of Human Rights found this sufficient to establish a violation of Article 3, both substantively and because the domestic investigation was ineffective. It rejected Ukraine’s argument that M. acted purely privately, since both accounts linked his conduct to his police role.

The first applicant, Valeriy Voykin, faced criminal proceedings after his wife’s complaint. In September 2008, cases were opened against him for abuse of power and forgery relating to an allegedly inaccurate administrative-offence report; later charges included bribe-taking. He was summoned, did not appear, and was declared wanted on 19 September 2008. On 29 June 2009 he was arrested at the home he shared with his wife. A court ordered his pre-trial detention on 3 July 2009, citing the seriousness of the charges and his character, without detailed reasons. On 21 July 2009 the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal quashed that detention order as insufficiently reasoned and released him under an undertaking not to leave town. He complained under Article 5 § 1 that his arrest and detention had been unlawful, and alleged that the prosecution was retaliation for his wife’s complaint against a police officer.

The third and fourth applicants complained about police searches of their flats. In September 2008, police searched the flat of Marina’s mother, Elleonora, and later the flat of Valeriy’s mother, Valentina. Court warrants were issued, but the applicants alleged that police acted aggressively, failed to show warrants, broke the entrance door with an electric saw, seized documents and a mobile phone, and in Elleonora’s case allegedly planted cannabis. Valentina alleged documents were planted in her flat. They also claimed they were denied copies of the court rulings authorizing the searches and that their complaints to prosecutors were ineffective. These facts formed the basis of complaints under Articles 8 and 13 concerning home searches and lack of effective remedies.

In sum, the case concerned alleged police violence against the second applicant, an ineffective investigation, the first applicant’s arrest and detention, and searches of relatives’ homes, with the Court finding at least a violation of Article 3.

In *Voykin and Others v. Ukraine*, four applicants—Valeriy Voykin, a police officer; his wife Marina; his mother-in-law Elleonora Shupnyak; and his mother Valentina Voykina—complained about events in Ukraine. Valentina died after applying, and Valeriy pursued her complaints.

**Article 3 complaint (second applicant):** On the night of 18–19 June 2008, Marina had an altercation with M., an off-duty police officer and colleague of her husband. Marina alleged that M., drunk and in plain clothes, tried to search her, grabbed her bag, strangled her, hit her head, and threatened her, referring to the local prosecutor’s presence. Her friend partly supported her account but later said M. only held her. M. claimed he mistook Marina for a person under administrative supervision, approached her in his official capacity, apologised after realising his mistake, and denied violence. His friend and two officers supported him. Marina called an ambulance and was diagnosed with neck bruises, situational neurosis, and later concussion. Forensic reports found injuries from blunt objects consistent with her account and timing. The police initially failed to follow up her call. Prosecutors repeatedly refused to open criminal proceedings against M.; four refusals were annulled as premature. No full investigation was opened, only pre-investigation enquiries. The Court rejected the Government’s claim that M. acted purely privately and found violations of Article 3 substantively and because the investigation was ineffective.

**Article 5 complaint (first applicant):** Valeriy had knee surgery in May 2008. On 10 September 2008, criminal proceedings were opened against him for abuse of power and forgery concerning an inaccurate administrative-offence report. A summons was sent, but police could not find him. On 13 September a court ordered his arrest to bring him before court, and on 19 September he was declared wanted. He claimed local police threatened him after his wife’s complaint, requested the prosecutor’s withdrawal, and said he feared going to hospital. On 29 June 2009 he was arrested at the home where he lived with his wife. The investigator cited the wanted list, obstruction, and serious offences. On 30 June the court extended his arrest; on 3 July it ordered pre-trial detention, citing the seriousness of the charges and his character without detail. On 21 July the Court of Appeal quashed that detention ruling and released him under an undertaking not to leave town, finding no adequate reasons for the strictest measure. He alleged unlawful arrest and detention under Article 5 § 1.

**Article 8/13 complaints (third and fourth applicants):** They complained about searches of their flats during the first applicant’s criminal case. Court-authorised searches targeted the first applicant’s registered residence, the fourth applicant’s flat, and the second applicant’s registered residence, the third applicant’s flat. On 12 September 2008 police went to the third applicant’s flat; she refused entry and alleged violent knocking, threats, and a three-hour presence by 9–10 officers without a warrant. The Government said three officers left after she refused. On 13 September police searched her flat, allegedly breaking the door, not showing a warrant, and seizing documents, a phone, and a cannabis package she said was planted. On 16 September they searched the fourth applicant’s flat and seized documents allegedly planted. A further search on 11 February 2009 found nothing. The third and fourth applicants complained repeatedly and sought copies of the court rulings, but were denied. Prosecutors refused criminal cases. They alleged unlawful searches under Article 8 and lack of effective remedy under Article 13.

**Case summary: Yakushev v. Ukraine (Application no. 15978/09)**

The applicant, Igor Viktorovych Yakushev, a Ukrainian national born in 1971, complained that Ukrainian courts arbitrarily refused to allow him to challenge his paternity of a child, K., thereby violating his right to respect for private life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

K. was born on 17 November 1993 to a woman identified as M. The applicant had had a relationship with M. at the relevant time. On 2 December 1993, he accepted paternity of K. by submitting the required declaration to the authorities. At that time, the applicant was married to another woman. He and M. later married in 2000 and divorced in 2006.

In July 2006, the applicant brought proceedings in the Malyn District Court seeking to challenge his paternity. He claimed that although he had accepted paternity because he believed he was K.’s father, he began to doubt this in 2005. On 24 March 2008, the District Court allowed his claim, relying on a genetic expert opinion which excluded him as K.’s biological father. The court found that there was no evidence that the applicant had known he was not the father when he accepted paternity.

M. appealed. She argued that she and the applicant had lived together from January 1993, that she had never doubted his paternity, and that the genetic test was unreliable. On 29 May 2008, the Zhytomyr Regional Court of Appeal reversed the first-instance decision. It held that under Article 56 § 2 of the Marriage and Family Code of Ukraine, a man who accepted paternity by his own declaration could not later challenge it if he had been aware at the time that he was not the child’s father. The Court of Appeal concluded that the applicant had known he was not K.’s father because, before the birth, he and M. had not been married and had not lived together—noting that he had lived in another town between February and April 1993—and because he had been married to another woman.

The applicant appealed on a point of law, arguing that there was no evidence he had known he was not the biological father, and that the Court of Appeal had exceeded its powers in making that finding. On 9 September 2008, the Supreme Court of Ukraine rejected his appeal as unfounded.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Articles 6 and 8 that he had been unable to challenge his paternity because the domestic courts had arbitrarily rejected his claim. The Court examined the complaint solely under Article 8. It found Article 8 applicable and admissible, since paternity proceedings concern an important aspect of personal identity and private life.

On the merits, the Court observed that the issue was not whether restrictions on challenging paternity can be justified, but whether the domestic courts reached the crucial factual conclusion—that the applicant knew he was not the father when he accepted paternity—through a fair, non-arbitrary procedure. The Court emphasized that both the applicant and M. admitted having had relations at the material time. Neither party claimed the applicant knew he was not the father when he accepted paternity. The applicant said he had no doubts until 2005, while M. said she never doubted his paternity and instead challenged the reliability of the genetic test.

The Court found that the Court of Appeal had disregarded these submissions, decided the appeal on grounds never raised by the parties, and made a new factual finding based on assumptions unsupported by evidence. It also overturned the first-instance court’s factual conclusions without new evidence or explanation. The Supreme Court failed to address these issues. Consequently, the decision-making process was not fair and free from arbitrariness, and Ukraine violated the applicant’s right to respect for private life under Article 8.

In **Yakushev v. Ukraine** (Application no. 15978/09, judgment of 4 December 2018), the European Court of Human Rights examined the applicant’s complaint that Ukrainian courts arbitrarily refused to allow him to challenge his paternity, contrary to Article 8 of the Convention.

The facts concerned a child, K., born to M. in November 1993. The applicant had had sexual relations with M. at the relevant time and, on 2 December 1993, accepted paternity by submitting a declaration. At that time, however, he was married to another woman; he and M. were not married, and the Court of Appeal later noted that they had not lived together and that the applicant had lived in another town between February and April 1993. The applicant and M. married in 2000 and divorced in 2006. In July 2006, the applicant challenged K.’s paternity, claiming that he had believed he was the father when he accepted paternity but had begun to doubt this in 2005. A genetic expert opinion excluded him as K.’s biological father. On 24 March 2008, the Malyn District Court allowed his claim, finding no evidence that he had known he was not the father when he accepted paternity.

M. appealed, stating that she and the applicant had lived together from January 1993, that she had never doubted his paternity, and that the genetic opinion was unreliable. On 29 May 2008, the Zhytomyr Regional Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance decision. It held that under Article 56 § 2 of the Marriage and Family Code, the applicant had no right to challenge paternity because, at the time of his declaration, he had been aware that he was not K.’s father. The Court of Appeal inferred this from the facts that the parties had not been married before K.’s birth, had not lived together, the applicant had lived elsewhere for part of 1993, and had been married to another woman. The applicant’s appeal on a point of law was rejected by the Supreme Court on 9 September 2008.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained under Articles 6 and 8. The Court examined the case under Article 8 alone and declared it admissible, because paternity proceedings concern private life and personal identity. On the merits, the Court accepted that a legal restriction on challenging paternity may be justified where a man knew he was not the father. However, the domestic courts still had to reach that factual conclusion through a fair, non-arbitrary procedure and to balance the competing interests, including those of the putative father and the child.

The ECtHR found that the Court of Appeal failed to conduct such a balancing exercise. Both parties admitted they had had relations at the material time, and neither claimed the applicant knew he was not the father when he accepted paternity. The applicant stated he had no doubts until 2005, while M. said she had never doubted his paternity and challenged only the reliability of the genetic test. Nevertheless, the Court of Appeal disregarded these submissions, decided on grounds never advanced by the parties, and made a crucial new factual finding based on unsupported assumptions. It overturned the first-instance court’s factual conclusions without new evidence or explanation, and the Supreme Court did not address these issues. The Court therefore held that the domestic decision-making process was not fair and free from arbitrariness, violating the applicant’s right to respect for private life under Article 8.

**Case: Yakushev v. Ukraine (Application no. 15978/09), European Court of Human Rights, 4 December 2018**

The applicant, Mr Igor Viktorovych Yakushev, a Ukrainian national born in 1971, complained that Ukrainian courts arbitrarily prevented him from challenging his paternity of a child, K., in violation of Article 8 of the Convention (right to respect for private and family life).

The key facts are as follows. On 17 November 1993, M. gave birth to a daughter, K. The applicant had had sexual relations with M. around the relevant time, and on 2 December 1993 he formally accepted paternity by submitting the required declaration. At that time, however, the applicant was married to another woman and did not live with M.; the domestic appellate court later noted that between February and April 1993 he lived in another town. The applicant and M. married in 2000 and divorced in 2006.

In July 2006, the applicant brought proceedings in the Malyn District Court against M., seeking to challenge his paternity of K. He claimed that although he had had relations with M. and had believed he was K.’s father when he accepted paternity, he began to have doubts in 2005. On 24 March 2008, the District Court ruled in his favour, relying on a genetic expert opinion excluding him as K.’s biological father. The court found that he was entitled to challenge paternity because there was no evidence that he had known, when accepting paternity, that he was not the father.

M. appealed. She stated that she and the applicant had lived together from January 1993 without being married and that she had never doubted his paternity. She also challenged the reliability of the genetic test. On 29 May 2008, the Zhytomyr Regional Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance decision. It held that, under Article 56 § 2 of the Family and Marriage Code, the applicant had no right to challenge paternity because at the time he accepted paternity he had known he was not K.’s biological father. The Court of Appeal based this conclusion on the facts that the applicant and M. had not been married before K.’s birth, had not lived together, the applicant had lived in another town for part of 1993, and he had been married to another woman. The applicant appealed on a point of law, arguing that there was no evidence he had known he was not the father. On 9 September 2008, the Supreme Court of Ukraine rejected his appeal as unfounded.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained under Articles 6 and 8. The Court examined the case under Article 8 alone. It confirmed that paternity proceedings concern a man’s private life and declared the complaint admissible.

On the merits, the Court found that the domestic courts had failed to ensure respect for the applicant’s private life. The central issue was not whether domestic law could restrict a paternity challenge where the man knew he was not the father, but whether the Court of Appeal reached that crucial factual finding through a fair, non-arbitrary process. The Court emphasised that both the applicant and M. admitted they had had relations at the material time, and neither claimed the applicant knew he was not the father when he accepted paternity. The applicant said he had no doubts until 2005, while M. said she never doubted his paternity and only challenged the genetic test. Yet the Court of Appeal disregarded these submissions and decided the case on grounds never advanced by the parties. Its new factual finding was based on assumptions, not specific evidence, and it overturned the first-instance court’s factual conclusions without new evidence or adequate explanation. The Supreme Court did not address these issues.

The ECtHR concluded that the procedural failings made the decision-making process unfair and arbitrary, amounting to a violation of Article 8.

**Yalanskyy and Galunka v. Ukraine** (Applications nos. 15131/17 and 36543/17) is a European Court of Human Rights judgment delivered on 3 May 2018 by a Committee of the Fifth Section. The case concerned two applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention.

The applicants complained principally that the length of criminal proceedings brought against them was incompatible with the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. They also alleged that they had no effective remedy in domestic law for that complaint, contrary to Article 13. In application no. 36543/17, the applicant additionally raised a complaint under Article 2 of Protocol No. 4, which protects liberty of movement.

The judgment’s factual section is brief and states that the list of applicants and relevant details are set out in an appended table, which is not reproduced in the body of the text. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore that the applicants were involved in criminal proceedings in Ukraine which remained pending for an excessive period. The applicants alleged that the duration of those proceedings exceeded what could be considered reasonable and that the domestic authorities were responsible for the delay. They also maintained that Ukrainian law did not provide them with an effective remedy capable of expediting the proceedings or providing adequate compensation for the excessive length. For the applicant in application no. 36543/17, the criminal proceedings also involved a restriction on freedom of movement, which he challenged under Article 2 of Protocol No. 4.

The Court joined the two applications because they raised similar subject matter. On the main complaint, it reiterated the established criteria for assessing the reasonableness of length of proceedings: the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicants and the authorities, and what was at stake for the applicants. The Court referred to its leading case *Merit v. Ukraine*, where it had already found violations in respect of similar delays in Ukrainian criminal proceedings. Having examined the material, the Court found no fact or argument that would justify a different conclusion. It held that the length of the criminal proceedings was excessive and failed to meet the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1. It further found that the applicants did not have an effective remedy at the national level for those complaints, in violation of Article 13.

As to the additional complaint under Article 2 of Protocol No. 4, the Court considered that it raised issues covered by well-established case-law. It was not manifestly ill-founded within the meaning of Article 35 § 3 (a) and was not inadmissible on any other ground. Applying its settled jurisprudence, the Court found a violation of that provision as well.
