The case *Khani Kabbara v. Cyprus* (Application no. 24459/12) concerns a Canadian national, Hani Abdul Khani Kabbara, who complained under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights that Cypriot police ill-treated him during his detention at Limassol central police station and that the authorities failed to carry out an effective investigation into his complaint.

On 27 February 2011, police received information from a card-processing company about illegal ATM withdrawals using a fake credit card in Limassol. Special Constable G.S., in uniform and on motorcycle patrol, approached the applicant at the ATM, touched his shoulder, identified himself as police, and asked for identification. According to the police, the applicant attacked G.S., fled, fell on the pavement, struggled, and was arrested by G.S. and another officer for assaulting a police officer and resisting lawful arrest. A fake credit card was later retrieved from the ATM.

The applicant gave a very different account. He alleged that he was suddenly attacked from behind by someone he did not recognize, thought he was being robbed, and was illegally arrested without a warrant. He claimed that he was handcuffed behind his back for about six hours at the police station and tortured to force him to confess to credit-card theft. He alleged repeated beatings with a wooden stick/baseball bat and a metal chair, punches and kicks to his head, face and body, a broken tooth, death threats, refusal of his asthma medicine, and refusal of hospital treatment until his lawyer intervened. He further alleged ill-treatment at the ATM, in the police car, and at the station during questioning while handcuffed, including being beaten after speaking to his lawyer.

At the police station, body searches were conducted and an interview took place with an interpreter. A prisoner record noted abrasions on the applicant’s left forehead and left shoulder blade. His lawyer visited him and complained of ill-treatment; the applicant was then taken to Limassol General Hospital. Medical examinations found a cephalohaematoma in the right temporal region, abrasions and oedema on the nose, bruising of the lower lip, a broken upper incisor, chest bruising, wrist abrasions, knee abrasions and pain, and neck/lumbar sensitivity. CT scans and X-rays showed no fractures. A later private examination found a chest bruise, restricted spinal movement, and a broken tooth. Officer G.S. was also examined and diagnosed with a lumbar strain after the alleged assault.

Police officers denied ill-treatment. Their accounts varied: some mentioned only redness and messy clothes; others saw facial wounds or minor abrasions. A police administrative investigation found no ill-treatment proven and closed the case. A subsequent investigation by the Independent Authority for the Investigation of Allegations and Complaints against the Police (IAIACAP) found no concrete evidence warranting criminal or disciplinary charges, although its president rejected claims that the applicant had no external injuries. The Attorney General concluded that force had been necessary and proportionate to prevent the applicant from fleeing and closed the file.

The applicant was later charged with theft, assault occasioning actual bodily harm, and resisting lawful arrest. He was convicted in 2012 and his appeal was dismissed in 2013. He was deported. After a tip that Inspector I.S. had admitted the applicant was ill-treated at the police station, a second IAIACAP investigation began in 2013, naming nine officers as suspects and gathering further evidence. The core Article 3 issues were whether the applicant suffered treatment reaching the Convention threshold and whether Cyprus conducted an effective, independent, and prompt investigation capable of identifying and punishing those responsible.

Khani Kabbara v. Cyprus concerns a Canadian national who complained under Article 3 that Cypriot police ill-treated him during detention at Limassol central police station and that the authorities failed to carry out an effective investigation. The events occurred on 27 February 2011, after police received information about illegal ATM withdrawals using a fake credit card in Limassol.

According to the applicant, while standing near an ATM, he was attacked from behind by a police officer, arrested without a warrant, and detained for six hours with his hands cuffed behind his back. He alleged that officers tortured him to force a confession to theft by forged credit card. He claimed repeated beatings with a wooden stick and a metal chair, punches and kicks to his head, face, and body, a broken tooth, and death threats. He also said officers refused his asthma medicine and delayed hospital treatment until his lawyer intervened. Around 3:30 p.m. he was taken to Limassol General Hospital; he alleged police told the doctor he had fallen and withheld painkillers until the Canadian Consul visited.

The Government’s account, based on investigation files, differed. Special Constable G.S., in uniform, approached the applicant, said “police,” and asked for identification. The applicant allegedly attacked him and fled, then fell and hit his head during a struggle. He was arrested for assaulting an officer and resisting lawful arrest. Officers denied ill-treatment and said his injuries occurred during arrest. After handcuffing, he was taken to the police station, searched, interviewed, and allowed to call his lawyer at 11:45 a.m. At 1:35 p.m., a detention officer recorded abrasions on his forehead and left shoulder blade. At 3:05 p.m., his lawyer complained he had been beaten and requested hospital transfer; he was taken to hospital at about 3:50 p.m.

Medical evidence partly corroborated injuries. The hospital pathologist found a cephalohaematoma, abrasions, nasal oedema, a bruised lower lip, a broken upper incisor, a chest bruise, wrist and knee abrasions, and neck and spine pain. CT and X-rays showed no fractures. A private doctor later found a chest bruise, restricted movement in the back and neck, and the broken tooth. G.S. was also examined and diagnosed with lumbar strain.

Investigations followed. A police administrative investigation concluded none of the ill-treatment allegations were proven. The Independent Authority for Investigation of Allegations and Complaints against the Police then investigated. Its investigator found the applicant’s account inconsistent and unconvincing, though he noted the injuries suggested some force. The IAIACAP president rejected claims that the applicant had no external injuries, but still found no proof of disproportionate force or criminal or disciplinary offences. The Attorney General closed the file in February 2012, finding that some force had been necessary to prevent escape.

The applicant was charged and convicted of theft, assaulting G.S., and resisting arrest. The courts found his testimony unreliable and his ill-treatment claims unsubstantiated. In 2013, after identifying gaps and omissions, and receiving information that Inspector I.S. had allegedly admitted the applicant was ill-treated at the police station, the Attorney General ordered a second IAIACAP investigation. These facts formed the basis for the applicant’s Article 3 complaints of substantive ill-treatment and ineffective investigation.
001-186048:
**Case: Big Brother Watch and Others v. the United Kingdom**  
(Applications nos. 58170/13, 62322/14 and 24960/15)

The case arose from Edward Snowden’s 2013 disclosures about mass surveillance. The applicants—including NGOs, journalists, and digital-rights organisations—challenged three UK surveillance regimes as violating Articles 8, 10, 6 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

**1. Section 8(4) RIPA bulk interception regime.**  
GCHQ intercepted “external communications” under warrants issued by the Secretary of State under section 8(4) of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000. Because “external” meant that at least one party was outside the British Isles, the regime could capture vast quantities of communications involving people in the UK. Warrants were broad, did not necessarily name individual targets, and allowed GCHQ to search intercepted material using selectors and algorithms. The applicants alleged that the regime lacked sufficient safeguards against arbitrary or indiscriminate surveillance, especially regarding selection, retention, searching, and sharing of intercepted communications. They also claimed the absence of independent judicial authorization and notification violated Article 8, and that it risked chilling journalistic activity under Article 10.

**2. Intelligence sharing with the United States.**  
The applicants relied on evidence that GCHQ received material from the US National Security Agency through programmes known as PRISM and Upstream, and that UK agencies could request NSA interception. They alleged that this allowed UK authorities to circumvent domestic RIPA safeguards by obtaining from the US communications that they could not lawfully intercept themselves. They argued that the receipt, use, and sharing of foreign intercept material lacked a clear legal framework and adequate safeguards, breaching Article 8.

**3. Chapter II RIPA communications data regime.**  
The applicants also challenged the acquisition of communications data—metadata such as time, duration, and parties to communications—under Chapter II of RIPA. Public authorities, including police and intelligence agencies, could require communications service providers to disclose such data. Authorizations were given internally rather than by a court, and there was no requirement to notify those affected. The applicants alleged that this broad access to communications data, without prior judicial review, violated Article 8 and created risks for journalistic sources under Article 10.

The Investigatory Powers Tribunal heard the domestic claims, partly in closed proceedings. It examined the PRISM issue, the section 8(4) regime, and the Chapter II regime. In its 2014–2015 judgments, the IPT largely upheld the legality of the UK schemes, though it made some findings on the PRISM issue and section 8(4) warrants.

Before the Strasbourg Court, the First Section judgment of 13 September 2018 found violations of Article 8 in respect of the section 8(4) bulk interception regime and the Chapter II communications data regime, due to inadequate safeguards. It found no violation concerning intelligence sharing, and no violation of Articles 10, 6 or 14. The case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 25 May 2021. The Grand Chamber confirmed Article 8 violations regarding bulk interception and communications data, found no Article 8 violation concerning intelligence sharing, and found Article 10 violations concerning protection of confidential journalistic material. It found no violation of Articles 6 or 14.

In essence, the key facts concerned UK bulk interception of external communications, receipt of US intelligence, and broad access to communications metadata, all alleged to lack sufficient legal safeguards against arbitrary surveillance.

Big Brother Watch and Others v. the United Kingdom (Applications nos. 58170/13, 62322/14 and 24960/15) concerned UK secret surveillance schemes. The applicants—NGOs, journalists, and human rights organisations—challenged three regimes: (1) GCHQ’s bulk interception under section 8(4) of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 (RIPA); (2) intelligence sharing with the US National Security Agency (NSA) through PRISM and Upstream; and (3) acquisition of communications data under Chapter II RIPA. They alleged violations of Articles 8 (privacy), 10 (expression), 6 (fair trial), and 14 (discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Under section 8(4) RIPA, the Secretary of State could issue warrants authorising GCHQ to intercept “external” communications—those sent or received outside the UK—and related communications data. The regime allowed GCHQ to use selectors (e.g., email addresses, phone numbers) and search terms to filter and examine intercepted material. There was no requirement for independent judicial authorisation, and the applicants argued there were inadequate safeguards against abuse, especially regarding unrelated communications, metadata, and confidential journalistic material.

The intelligence sharing regime involved GCHQ receiving material collected by the NSA under PRISM (from internet companies) and Upstream (from fibre-optic cables). The applicants claimed the UK was circumventing domestic safeguards by requesting the NSA to collect communications on its behalf, without sufficient oversight.

The Chapter II regime permitted public authorities to acquire communications data—metadata such as call records, location, and web logs—from communication service providers. The applicants alleged that access was too broad, not independently authorised, and subject to insufficient safeguards.

Domestic proceedings were brought before the Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT). The IPT made several rulings on the PRISM issue and the section 8(4) regime, but the applicants ultimately brought the case to the European Court of Human Rights. The First Section judgment of 13 September 2018 was referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 25 May 2021.

The Grand Chamber found violations of Article 8 in respect of the section 8(4) bulk interception regime. It held that the regime lacked adequate “end-to-end” safeguards, particularly regarding the selection of related communications data, the use of selectors, and the handling of journalistic communications. It also found a violation of Article 10 because the regime did not provide sufficient protection for journalistic sources and confidential journalistic material.

Regarding the Chapter II regime, the Grand Chamber found a violation of Article 8 because the acquisition of communications data was not subject to independent authorisation. However, it found no violation of Article 8 in respect of the intelligence sharing regime with the NSA, concluding that the UK’s arrangements did not exceed the margin of appreciation. It also found no violation of Article 6 concerning the IPT’s procedures, and no violation of Article 14.

In summary, the key facts relevant to the alleged violations centred on the UK’s bulk interception of external communications, its receipt of NSA-collected intelligence, and its acquisition of communications data. The Grand Chamber held that the bulk interception and communications data regimes violated Articles 8 and 10, while the intelligence sharing and procedural complaints did not.

**Big Brother Watch and Others v. the United Kingdom** concerned three joined applications (nos. 58170/13, 62322/14 and 24960/15) brought by UK civil liberties organisations, journalists, media groups, and NGOs. They challenged secret surveillance regimes operated by the UK, especially GCHQ, alleging violations of Articles 8 and 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and also raising issues under Articles 6 and 14.

The factual background arose from revelations about widespread electronic surveillance. The applicants challenged three main regimes.

First, the **section 8(4) RIPA regime**. Under this, the Secretary of State could issue warrants allowing GCHQ to intercept “external communications”—communications with at least one end outside the UK. These warrants were broad and untargeted, not limited to specific individuals or premises, and could permit bulk interception of huge volumes of communications, including related communications data. The applicants alleged the regime lacked clear legal rules, independent prior authorisation, and adequate safeguards for selecting, searching, retaining, and disclosing intercepted material. They also claimed it failed to protect confidential journalistic material, thereby interfering with privacy and free expression.

Second, the **intelligence-sharing regime** with the United States’ NSA. The applicants relied on disclosures about **PRISM** and **Upstream**. PRISM involved the NSA obtaining communications from US internet service providers, while Upstream involved intercepting data as it travelled across networks. GCHQ allegedly received and accessed material from both programmes, including communications of UK persons. The applicants argued that this sharing allowed UK authorities to circumvent domestic interception safeguards, lacked sufficient legal basis and oversight, and violated Article 8. They further complained that the British-US Communication Intelligence Agreement did not provide adequate protection for private communications.

Third, the **Chapter II RIPA regime** for acquiring communications data—metadata such as call records, email headers, and internet usage. Public authorities could obtain such data without independent judicial authorisation and for a broad range of purposes, not limited to serious crime. The applicants alleged this interfered with private life and could reveal journalistic sources, thereby threatening Article 10 rights.

The applicants pursued domestic remedies before the Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT). The IPT examined issues including the lawfulness of PRISM-related intelligence sharing, the section 8(4) warrant regime, and Chapter II communications data acquisition. In *Hülya Ebru Demirel v. Turkey* (Application no. 30733/08, judgment of 19 June 2018), the applicant, a Turkish woman, complained that the refusal to appoint her as a security officer and her subsequent dismissal were discriminatory on grounds of sex, and that the administrative proceedings were unfair. She relied on Articles 6 and 14 of the Convention. The Court communicated the complaints under Article 14 in conjunction with Article 8 and under Article 6; the remainder was declared inadmissible.

The key facts concerned access to employment. In 1999 the applicant passed a civil-service examination and was informed by the State Personnel Department that she had been appointed to the post of security officer at the Kilis branch of TEDAŞ, a State-run electricity company. TEDAŞ then refused to appoint her because she did not meet the requirements of “being a man” and “having completed military service.”

The applicant brought administrative proceedings. In May 2001 the Gaziantep Administrative Court stayed execution of TEDAŞ’s refusal, finding that being male was not a requirement for the post. TEDAŞ thereafter offered her a contract subject to a six-month probationary period, and she began working. In October 2001 the Administrative Court annulled the refusal, holding that the military-service requirement applied only to male candidates and that there was no restriction on women serving as security officers in TEDAŞ. It found that rejecting her solely because of her sex was unlawful.

TEDAŞ appealed. In April 2002 the Twelfth Division of the Supreme Administrative Court stayed execution of that judgment, and TEDAŞ terminated the applicant’s employment in May 2002. In December 2002 the Supreme Administrative Court quashed the lower court’s judgment, reasoning that because the post required completion of military service, it was reserved for male candidates only, and that the refusal to appoint the applicant had therefore been lawful. On remand, in October 2003, the Gaziantep Administrative Court dismissed her case, following the Supreme Administrative Court’s reasoning.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the interpretation reserving the post for men violated equality and the State’s positive obligation to ensure non-discrimination, citing the Turkish Constitution, CEDAW and the ICESCR. In November 2007 the Twelfth Division upheld the dismissal without addressing her discrimination arguments. In December 2007, however, the Supreme Administrative Court’s General Assembly of Administrative Proceedings Divisions decided a similar case, *R.B.*, involving a female candidate rejected by TEDAŞ for the same reasons. It held that the military-service requirement applied only to male candidates and that refusing to appoint R.B. was unlawful. The applicant sought rectification of the November 2007 decision, relying on *R.B.* and CEDAW Article 11. The judge rapporteur recommended rectification, but in June 2009 the Twelfth Division dismissed the application, saying the grounds did not fall within the exhaustive statutory list and that its earlier decision was lawful.

Before the European Court, the Government argued that Article 14 in conjunction with Article 8 was inapplicable because the case concerned access to a particular profession. The Court rejected that objection, following *Emel Boyraz v. Turkey*. On the merits, the Government claimed the male-only requirement was objectively justified because the post involved firearms and night work. The applicant maintained that sex was the sole reason for her exclusion. The Court found the case identical to *Emel Boyraz*: the administrative authorities and the Supreme Administrative Court treated the security-officer post as reserved for men and excluded the applicant as a woman, giving no reason other than sex. This amounted to a discriminatory difference in treatment contrary to Article 14 taken in conjunction with Article 8.

The applicant maintained that sex was the sole reason for her exclusion and that many Turkish women worked in dangerous roles, such as police officers, army pilots, and prison guards.

In December 2002 the Supreme Administrative Court quashed the lower court’s judgment. It reasoned that because the post required completion of military service, the post was reserved for male candidates, so the refusal to appoint the applicant had been lawful. In October 2003 the Gaziantep Administrative Court dismissed her case following that reasoning. Her appeal was dismissed in November 2007.

The General Assembly held that although the military-service requirement applied only to male candidates, it was unlawful to refuse to appoint R.B. as a security officer. The applicant relied on this decision in seeking rectification of the judgment against her. She also complained that the administrative proceedings were unfair. She relied on Articles 6 and 14 of the Convention. The Court communicated the complaints under Article 14 in conjunction with Article 8 and under Article 6; the remainder was declared inadmissible.

The Government argued that Article 14 was not applicable because the case concerned access to a particular profession, and that any difference in treatment was objectively justified: the security-officer post was reserved for men who had completed military service, and the duties involved firearms and night work. The applicant maintained that the sole reason for her rejection was her sex and that women in Turkey worked successfully in dangerous occupations such as policing and prison guarding.

The Court rejected the Government’s admissibility objection, relying on *Emel Boyraz v. Turkey*. On the merits, it found the present case identical to *Emel Boyraz*: the administrative authorities and the Supreme Administrative Court treated the security-officer post as reserved for men and excluded the applicant because she was a woman. **Summary of the Case of Rrapo v. Albania (Application no. 58555/10)**

The case of *Rrapo v. Albania* concerns the extradition of Mr. Almir Rrapo, a dual Albanian and American national, from Albania to the United States and the alleged violations of the European Convention on Human Rights that arose from this process.

**Key Facts:**

Mr. Rrapo was arrested in Tirana on 2 July 2010 at the request of the United States Embassy, based on a US arrest warrant for serious criminal charges, including membership in an organized racketeering enterprise, drug distribution, kidnapping, and murder. On 30 August 2010, the US Embassy formally requested his extradition. The charges included one count—the murder of E.S. in aid of racketeering—that carried a potential penalty of death or life imprisonment under US federal law.

The Albanian District Court and Court of Appeal both approved the extradition request in September and November 2010, respectively. Notably, these lower courts rejected Mr. Rrapo's arguments regarding the risk of the death penalty, ruling that US assurances against capital punishment were not legally required.

A critical development occurred on 12 October 2010, when the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR), acting under Rule 39 of its Rules of Court, issued an interim measure indicating to the Albanian Government that the applicant should not be extradited until further notice. This measure was prolonged on 2 November 2010. The Albanian authorities were formally reminded of this binding measure on multiple occasions, including on 3 November and 18 November 2010.

Despite these clear instructions, the Albanian Minister of Justice proceeded with the extradition. On 24 November 2010, Mr. Rrapo was extradited to the United States. The Albanian government later justified its actions by citing diplomatic assurances received from the US on 8 November 2010, which stated that the death penalty would not be sought or imposed. They also argued that the applicant's detention was set to expire on 1 December 2010, and his release would pose a significant flight risk.

Following the extradition, on 26 November 2010, the Albanian Supreme Court quashed the lower courts' decisions. It found that the extradition had been improperly granted because the lower courts had failed to obtain assurances against the death penalty and had not properly evaluated the evidence of guilt.

**Alleged Violations:**

Mr. Rrapo brought his case to the ECtHR, alleging two main violations:

1.  **Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention (Right to Life and Prohibition of Torture):** The applicant claimed that his extradition to the US exposed him to a real risk of being subjected to the death penalty, thereby violating his fundamental rights.
2.  **Article 34 of the Convention (Individual Applications):** He further alleged that the Albanian authorities' failure to comply with the Court's binding interim measure (the Rule 39 indication) constituted a separate and serious breach of the Convention.

The case centered on whether the assurances provided by the US were sufficient to mitigate the risk of the death penalty and whether Albania's decision to extradite the applicant in direct defiance of the ECtHR's order violated its obligations under the Convention.

**Summary of the Case of Rrapo v. Albania**

The case of *Rrapo v. Albania* (Application no. 58555/10) concerns the extradition of Mr. Almir Rrapo, an Albanian and American national, from Albania to the United States, and the alleged violations of Articles 2, 3, and 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The key facts are as follows: On 2 July 2010, the applicant was arrested in Tirana by Albanian police at the request of the US Embassy, based on a US arrest warrant and a request for provisional arrest for the purpose of extradition. He was subsequently detained, with his detention repeatedly extended by Albanian courts.

On 30 August 2010, the US Embassy formally requested his extradition to face charges in the United States. These charges included nine counts related to an organised racketeering enterprise, involving conspiracy to distribute drugs, kidnapping, and firearms offences. Crucially, one charge was for the murder of an individual in aid of racketeering. The diplomatic note stated that this specific charge carried a potential penalty of either death or life imprisonment.

The domestic extradition proceedings followed. On 30 September 2010, the Tirana District Court granted the extradition request. The applicant appealed. During the appeal process, on 12 October 2010, the European Court of Human Rights (the Court) indicated an interim measure to the Albanian Government under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, stating that the applicant should not be extradited until the Court had sufficient time to review the case. This measure was later prolonged.

On 1 November 2010, the Tirana Court of Appeal upheld the extradition decision, ruling that there was no legal obligation to seek assurances from the US against the death penalty. The next day, the Minister of Justice ordered the extradition to be carried out by 16 November 2010.

Following a request from the Albanian Minister of Justice, the US Embassy provided a diplomatic note on 8 November 2010, assuring the Albanian government that "the death penalty will not be sought or imposed against Almir Rrapo." On 15 November 2010, the ECtHR President confirmed that the Rule 39 interim measure remained in force, despite the assurances.

Despite this binding interim measure, the Albanian authorities proceeded with the extradition. On 24 November 2010, Mr. Rrapo was extradited to the United States, without prior notice to his lawyer or the Court.

The applicant alleged that his extradition violated Articles 2 (Right to Life) and 3 (Prohibition of Torture) of the Convention, as he faced a real risk of the death penalty. He also alleged a violation of Article 34 (Right of Individual Petition), as his extradition was in direct breach of the Court's binding interim measure.

The Albanian Government justified its actions by citing the US assurances against the death penalty and the imminent expiry of the applicant's detention period under domestic law on 1 December 2010. They argued that his release would pose a significant flight risk.

Subsequent to his extradition, Mr. Rrapo pleaded guilty in a US court and was sentenced to 80 months' imprisonment, with the death penalty not being sought. The Albanian Supreme Court later quashed the extradition decisions, finding that the lower courts had failed to secure sufficient assurances against capital punishment before authorising the extradition.

The case before the ECtHR centred on determining whether Albania had violated its obligations under the Convention by extraditing the applicant in these circumstances.

**Case summary: Rrapo v. Albania (Application no. 58555/10)**

The case concerned the extradition of Almir Rrapo, an Albanian and American national, from Albania to the United States and Albania’s compliance with a European Court of Human Rights interim measure. Rrapo alleged that his extradition exposed him to a real risk of the death penalty, contrary to Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 13. He also alleged that Albania violated Article 34 by failing to comply with the Court’s Rule 39 indication not to extradite him.

On 2 July 2010, while applying to renew his US passport at the US Embassy in Tirana, Rrapo was arrested by Albanian police at the Embassy’s request. The US sought his provisional arrest for extradition. Albanian courts authorised and repeatedly extended his detention, relying on a US arrest warrant and Interpol notice.

On 30 August 2010, the US Embassy formally requested Rrapo’s extradition. The diplomatic note listed nine federal charges, including participation in an organised racketeering enterprise involving murder, kidnapping, drug distribution, robbery and firearms offences; conspiracy to distribute large quantities of marijuana and controlled substances; conspiracy to commit robbery; firearms offences; kidnapping in aid of racketeering; and the murder of E.S. in aid of racketeering. Several charges carried maximum life sentences, while the murder charge carried either death or life imprisonment.

On 30 September 2010, the Tirana District Court granted extradition. It rejected Rrapo’s objection that the US had not provided assurances against the death penalty, holding that no such assurances were legally required. On 1 November 2010, the Court of Appeal upheld extradition, again finding no legal obligation to seek death-penalty assurances. The Minister of Justice then ordered extradition by 16 November and asked the US whether Rrapo would face capital punishment.

On 8 November 2010, the US Embassy sent diplomatic note no. 91, assuring Albania that the US Department of Justice had directed the US Attorney not to seek the death penalty and that it would neither be sought nor imposed if Rrapo were extradited. Rrapo appealed to the Supreme Court and requested suspension of extradition, citing the Court’s Rule 39 measure.

Meanwhile, on 12 October 2010, the European Court indicated under Rule 39 that Rrapo should not be extradited until ten days after notification of the Court of Appeal’s decision. On 2 November 2010, this was extended until fifteen days after notification of the Supreme Court’s decision. Albania was informed and warned that non-compliance could breach Article 34. On 15 November 2010, the Court maintained the interim measure despite the US assurances.

Nevertheless, Albania extradited Rrapo on 24 November 2010. On 26 November 2010, the Supreme Court quashed the lower decisions, finding that they had failed to obtain death-penalty assurances and had not properly assessed evidence. The case was remitted, but Rrapo had already been extradited. Later US diplomatic notes reaffirmed that the assurances were binding on the US Department of Justice. In the US, Rrapo pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 80 months’ imprisonment.

The European Court found no violation of Articles 2 or 3 or Article 1 of Protocol No. 13 because the US assurances were specific, clear, unequivocal and binding, and there was no evidence that the death penalty would be sought or imposed. However, Albania violated Article 34 by extraditing Rrapo in disregard of the Rule 39 interim measure.

In *Macharik v. the Czech Republic* (ECtHR, 13 February 2025), the applicant, Michaela Macharik, was convicted of tax evasion mainly on the basis of the content of her email communications with another convict. Those emails were obtained by police under a judicial order issued on 14 November 2011 by the Prague 3 District Court pursuant to Article 88a of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The order, sought by a prosecutor at police request in a tax-evasion investigation concerning M.P., the P. company, and around 40 other companies, required a communications service provider to disclose all data on past telecommunications traffic through the P. company mailbox, including registration data, IP addresses, and the contents of all messages. The order stated that the Constitutional Court’s judgment repealing section 97(3) of the Electronic Communications Act was not an obstacle because the necessary guarantees were met and the investigation concerned a serious offence punishable by five to ten years’ imprisonment.

On 30 November 2011, the service provider supplied the registration data and the mailbox contents, including messages written by the applicant that had been forwarded to M.P. by another suspect. The provider noted that, in line with the Constitutional Court’s judgment, it did not store operational and location data, which could therefore not be provided. After inspecting the applicant’s messages, police opened an investigation into her. She was charged in August 2012 with tax evasion for entering fictitious advertising leases into accounting records and filing a tax return based on those invoices. She was indicted in June 2013 and convicted in March 2015 as an accomplice to tax evasion, receiving a suspended two-year sentence and a fine. The emails were said to show that the lease agreements and invoices had been backdated.

The applicant argued before domestic courts that the content of her emails could not be considered “communications data” under Article 88a and that service providers were not authorised to store message content, so the provider should have refused to hand it over. The first-instance court found that the order should have been based on Article 88, which concerned the content of communications, but treated this as a formal shortcoming because the conditions for Article 88 were met. The appellate court held that Article 88a was correct for past communications, since Article 88 concerned future interception. The Supreme Court acknowledged that email content could not be obtained under Article 88 and that Article 88a covered only communications data, but found that Article 88a imposed stricter conditions than Article 158d and that practice had been inconsistent at the time, so the evidence was not inadmissible. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal on similar grounds.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained under Article 8 that her email communications had been obtained without a proper legal basis. She stressed that Article 88a allowed only communications data, not content, and that after the repeal of section 97(3), providers were not allowed to store content. The Government accepted that there had been an interference but argued it was lawful, foreseeable, and proportionate.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 8. The interference was not “in accordance with the law”: the judicial order sought content despite domestic law not allowing service providers to store it; domestic courts failed to adequately address the applicant’s specific complaints about the provider’s duty of confidentiality; and the interpretation and application of domestic law lacked clarity, consistency, and foreseeability. Under Article 6 § 1, however, there was no violation: admission of the unlawfully obtained but accurate and reliable evidence, although decisive for conviction, did not irretrievably prejudice the overall fairness of the trial. The police had not acted in bad faith or intentionally breached formal rules, and the applicant was able to oppose the evidence before four levels of jurisdiction.

In *Macharik v. the Czech Republic* (Application no. 51409/19, ECtHR Fifth Section, judgment 13 February 2025, final 13 May 2025), the applicant, Michaela Macharik, complained about her criminal conviction, which was based mainly on email communications obtained by the police. On 14 November 2011, the Prague 3 District Court issued an order under Article 88a of the Code of Criminal Procedure directing a communications service provider to give the police all data on past telecommunications traffic through the mailbox of the P. company, including registration data, IP addresses, and the contents of all messages. The order was issued at the prosecutor’s request, following a police proposal, in an investigation into suspected tax evasion by M.P., the authorised representative of the P. company, and representatives of about 40 other companies. The order stated that the Constitutional Court’s judgment no. Pl. ÚS 24/10, which repealed section 97(3) of the Electronic Communications Act, did not prevent the order because the necessary guarantees were met.

The provider supplied registration data and the mailbox contents, including messages written by the applicant that had been forwarded to M.P. by another suspect. The provider noted that, under the Constitutional Court’s judgment, it did not store operational and location data. After inspecting the messages, the police opened an investigation into the applicant. She was charged on 16 August 2012 with tax evasion for entering fictitious advertising lease invoices into accounting records. She unsuccessfully sought to exclude her emails, arguing that their content could not be considered communications data under Article 88a, that providers were not authorised to store message content, and that the provider should have refused to forward it. She was indicted on 24 June 2013 and convicted on 18 March 2015 by the Prague Municipal Court, receiving a two-year suspended sentence and a 50,000 CZK fine. The emails showed the lease agreements and invoices had been backdated.

Domestic courts acknowledged legal-basis problems but upheld the evidence. The first-instance court said the order should have been based on Article 88, not Article 88a, but treated this as a formal shortcoming because Article 88’s conditions were met. The appellate court held that Article 88 concerned future interception, while Article 88a concerned past traffic data, so Article 88a was correct for past email communications. The Supreme Court held that Article 88 could not obtain past content and Article 88a covered only communications data; under Constitutional Court decision III. ÚS 3812/12, data stored on tracked computers fell under Article 158d. Although Article 158d required prior judicial authorisation for correspondence privacy, it lacked reasoning and proportionality guarantees; Article 88a was stricter. Given inconsistent practice, the evidence was not inadmissible. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal, noting that when the order was issued practice was inconsistent and both Articles 88a and 158d had been used for email content; Article 88a gave stricter protection.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant argued under Article 8 that the interference was unlawful: Article 88a allowed only communications data, not content; Article 158d concerned a different situation and lacked adequate guarantees; and after section 97(3) was repealed, no provision allowed ordering a provider to disclose content. The Government maintained the interference was lawful, foreseeable, and proportionate.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 8. The interference was not “in accordance with the law”: domestic law did not permit communications service providers to store message content, yet the judicial order was issued anyway. The domestic courts failed to adequately address the applicant’s specific complaints about the provider’s duty of confidentiality, and the interpretation and application of domestic law lacked clarity and consistency and was not foreseeable. Under Article 6, however, the overall fairness of the trial was not irretrievably prejudiced by admitting the impugned evidence, even though it was decisive for the conviction. There was no indication the police acted in bad faith or intentionally breached formal rules; the evidence was accurate and reliable, albeit unlawfully obtained, and the applicant could effectively oppose its use before four levels of jurisdiction. Defence rights were duly respected.

On 14 November 2011, a judge of the Prague 3 District Court issued an order under Article 88a of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It required a communications service provider to disclose all past telecommunications traffic data relating to P. company’s mailbox, including registration data, IP addresses, and the contents of all messages. The order stated that the Constitutional Court’s judgment no. Pl. ÚS 24/10, repealing section 97(3) of the Electronic Communications Act, was not an obstacle because the requisite guarantees were met. The provider supplied registration data and the mailbox contents, including messages written by the applicant that another suspect had forwarded to M.P. The provider noted that, in line with the Constitutional Court’s judgment, it did not store operational and location data.

After inspecting the applicant’s messages, the police opened an investigation into her activities. In August 2012 she was charged with tax evasion for entering fictitious advertising lease invoices into accounting records and filing a tax return based on them. She was indicted in June 2013. In March 2015 the Prague Municipal Court convicted her as an accomplice, imposing a suspended two-year sentence and a fine. According to the court, the emails showed that the leasing agreements and invoices had been backdated.

The applicant argued that the content of her emails could not be considered communications data under Article 88a and that communications service providers were not authorised to store message content, so the provider should have refused to transfer it. The domestic courts rejected these arguments on varying grounds. The first-instance court said the order should have been based on Article 88, but treated this as a formal shortcoming. The High Court held that Article 88a correctly covered past communications. The Supreme Court stated that email content could not be obtained under Article 88, which concerned future interception, or Article 88a, which concerned traffic data; however, given inconsistent practice at the time and because Article 88a imposed stricter safeguards than Article 158d, the evidence was not inadmissible. The Constitutional Court dismissed her appeal on similar reasoning.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Article 8 (private life and correspondence) and Article 6 § 1 (fair trial). On Article 8, the Court found an interference with her correspondence. The judicial order allowed the transfer of all message content from a third party’s mailbox even though domestic law did not permit communications service providers to store the content of such communications. The domestic courts failed to adequately address her specific complaints regarding the provider’s duty of confidentiality. The interpretation and application of domestic law lacked clarity and consistency and was not foreseeable. The interference was therefore not “in accordance with the law,” violating Article 8.

On Article 6, although the impugned evidence was decisive for her conviction, the overall fairness of the trial was not irretrievably prejudiced. There was no indication that the police acted in bad faith or intentionally breached formal rules. The evidence was accurate and reliable, albeit unlawfully obtained. The applicant was able to oppose its use before four levels of jurisdiction, and her defence rights were respected. There was no violation of Article 6.

In *Mortier v. Belgium*, the European Court of Human Rights examined the euthanasia of the applicant’s mother, G.T., and the subsequent official reviews. G.T. had suffered from chronic depression since adolescence and had been treated for about forty years. In 2011 she sought euthanasia. Her general practitioner declined to act as main doctor and referred her to Professor D., who became her main doctor under Belgium’s 2002 Euthanasia Act. Several psychiatrists were consulted. Dr V initially considered the request premature; Dr T later found G.T. rational and suffering intolerably from an incurable condition; Dr V.D. also approved. G.T. lodged a formal handwritten request on 14 February 2012. She did not want direct contact with her children. On 31 January 2012 she emailed her son and daughter about her request. The daughter replied respecting her wishes; the applicant did not reply. Doctors repeatedly encouraged her to inform her children, but she refused telephone contact and insisted her wishes be respected. Professor D. performed euthanasia on 19 April 2012. The applicant was informed by the hospital the next day.

Afterwards, the Federal Euthanasia Monitoring and Assessment Board received the registration document on 20 June 2012 and reviewed it on 26 June 2012. Professor D., who had performed the euthanasia, was co-chair of the Board and participated in the review, which concluded that the Act’s conditions had been met. The Board relied on the anonymous part of the registration document. The applicant’s requests for the document were refused on confidentiality grounds. His complaint to the Medical Association was confidential. A criminal complaint in April 2014 was discontinued in May 2017 for insufficient evidence. His first ECtHR application was declared inadmissible for non-exhaustion. In 2019 the criminal investigation was reopened. A medical expert report in 2020 found that G.T. had intolerable mental suffering, had requested euthanasia freely and consistently, and that the statutory waiting period and consultations had been respected. It noted, however, that the applicant learned of the death in a very unfortunate way and that the file did not contain the euthanasia declaration or the Board’s assessment. In December 2020 the Pre-Trial Division closed the investigation, finding no grounds for prosecution.

The applicant complained under Articles 2, 8 and 13. Under Article 2, he alleged the Belgian euthanasia framework did not adequately protect life, especially for mental suffering where death was not imminent, and that the procedural review was inadequate. Under Article 8, he alleged violation of private and family life because doctors did not involve him in the procedure. The Court found the substantive legislative framework capable in principle of protecting the right to life, with additional safeguards for mental suffering, and within Belgium’s margin of appreciation. However, it found procedural shortcomings: the Board was not sufficiently independent because the doctor who performed the euthanasia could take part in reviewing its lawfulness; review solely on the anonymous part and the doctor’s discretion over silence were insufficient; and the criminal investigation was excessively long. It found no Article 8 violation, holding that the law struck a fair balance between confidentiality, patient autonomy and family interests.

In *Mortier v. Belgium* (ECtHR, 4 October 2022), the applicant, Tom Mortier, complained about the euthanasia of his mother, G.T., without him or his sister being informed beforehand. G.T. had suffered from chronic depression and a serious personality and mood disorder for about forty years, receiving psychiatric treatment since she was nineteen. In 2011–2012 she sought euthanasia because of intolerable mental suffering. After her general practitioner declined to act as main doctor, she was referred to Professor D., who became her main doctor under Belgium’s 2002 Euthanasia Act. Several psychiatrists were consulted. One initially considered the request premature, but later consultants concluded that G.T. was legally capable, that her suffering was constant and intolerable, and that her condition was incurable with no prospect of improvement. G.T. was socially isolated, estranged from her son, and did not wish to contact her children. Doctors repeatedly encouraged her to inform them. On 31 January 2012 she emailed her son and daughter about her euthanasia request; her daughter replied that she respected her wishes, but the applicant did not reply. G.T. submitted a formal written request on 14 February 2012, and euthanasia was performed by Professor D. on 19 April 2012 in a public hospital. The applicant learned of his mother’s death the next day.

After the euthanasia, Professor D. submitted the required registration document to the Federal Euthanasia Monitoring and Assessment Board. Professor D. was also co-chair of that Board. The Board reviewed the anonymous second part of the registration document and concluded that the euthanasia complied with the Euthanasia Act. The applicant’s requests for a copy of the document were refused on confidentiality grounds. His complaint to the Medical Association did not yield information, and his criminal complaint, lodged in April 2014, was initially discontinued in May 2017 for insufficient evidence. After the applicant brought his case to the European Court of Human Rights in November 2017, the criminal investigation was reopened in 2019. An expert report in 2020 found that G.T. had suffered intolerably, acted freely, and that the statutory waiting period had been respected; it noted that the applicant had learned of the death in an unfortunate way and that the file did not contain the Board’s assessment. In December 2020 the Pre-Trial Division closed the investigation with no grounds for prosecution, and no appeal was lodged.

The applicant alleged violations of Articles 2, 8, and 13 of the Convention. Under Article 2, he argued that Belgium had failed to protect his mother’s life and that the post-euthanasia review was inadequate. The Court found that the substantive legislative framework, including additional safeguards for euthanasia based on mental suffering where death is not expected in the short term, was in principle capable of protecting the right to life, and that Belgium enjoyed a wide margin of appreciation. However, it found a procedural violation of Article 2. The Board lacked independence because the doctor who had performed the euthanasia, Professor D., was its co-chair and could participate in reviewing the lawfulness of his own act; his discretion to remain silent was insufficient. The Court also held that review based solely on the anonymous part of the registration document did not satisfy Article 2, and that the criminal investigation was excessively long. Under Article 8, the doctors’ failure to involve the applicant in the procedure, absent his mother’s wish to do so, was consistent with confidentiality and medical secrecy and struck a fair balance between the interests at stake.

In *Mortier v. Belgium* (App. no. 78017/17, Third Section, 4 October 2022), the applicant, Tom Mortier, complained about the euthanasia of his mother, G.T., who had suffered from chronic depression and a personality/mood disorder for about forty years. She had been treated by several psychiatrists. In 2011–2012 she sought euthanasia under Belgium’s Euthanasia Act. Professor D. became her main doctor. Consulting psychiatrists included Dr V., Dr T. and Dr V.D. Dr V. initially considered her request premature and suggested further treatment. G.T. later said she did not want contact with her children, claiming her son was aggressive and she feared him. On 31 January 2012 she emailed her children about her euthanasia request; the applicant did not reply, while her daughter replied respecting her wishes. On 14 February 2012 G.T. lodged a formal written request. After further consultations, her doctors concluded that her mental suffering was intolerable and incurable. Professor D. performed euthanasia on 19 April 2012 in a public hospital. The applicant learned of his mother’s death the next day from the hospital; he had not been informed or involved beforehand.

The applicant invoked Articles 2, 8 and 13 ECHR. The key Article 2 issues concerned both substantive and procedural positive obligations. Substantively, he argued that Belgian law did not sufficiently protect his mother’s life, especially because euthanasia was allowed for mental suffering where death was not otherwise expected in the short term. The Court found the legislative framework capable in principle of ensuring the right to life, including additional safeguards for non-terminal mental suffering, and allowed a margin of appreciation. Procedurally, he complained about the post-death review. The Federal Euthanasia Monitoring and Assessment Board examined Professor D.’s registration document and found the euthanasia compliant. However, Professor D., who carried out the euthanasia, was co-chair of the Board. The Board also reviewed only the anonymous part of the registration document to preserve confidentiality. The Court found that allowing the doctor who performed the act to participate in reviewing its lawfulness, and reviewing only the anonymous part, did not satisfy Article 2’s procedural requirements. It also found the criminal investigation excessively long.

Under Article 8, the applicant complained that the doctors failed to involve him in the procedure leading to his mother’s death, depriving him of a chance to say goodbye and causing pathological mourning. The Court noted that G.T. had been encouraged to contact her children but had refused; she had only agreed to send an email, and the applicant did not reply. The law required respect for patient confidentiality and medical secrecy unless the patient wished otherwise. The Court found that the legislation struck a fair balance between the applicant’s private and family life interests and his mother’s autonomy, confidentiality and medical secrecy.

The applicant also requested the euthanasia registration document from the Board, but was refused on confidentiality grounds; he complained to the Medical Association and lodged a criminal complaint. The first investigation was discontinued in 2017, then reopened in 2019. An expert report found the substantive conditions complied with, and in 2020 the Pre-Trial Division closed the investigation. The Court’s main findings thus concerned the substantive and procedural protection of life under Article 2 and the family-life/confidentiality balance under Article 8.
